question: What does Christ's saying 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30) teach about the Father and the Son: are they one person, or distinct persons who are one?
synthesis: Athanasius, Hippolytus, Novatian, Ambrose, Hilary and Augustine all read the text as excluding the identification of Father and Son (against Sabellius or Noetus) while affirming their oneness. Hippolytus, Novatian and Augustine argue this from the plural 'we are' (Augustine tying it to relation). But they differ on the kind of oneness. Athanasius, Hilary and Augustine ground it in one essence or nature, through eternal generation and mutual indwelling. Ambrose speaks of a unity of power with equality. Hippolytus explains it as a oneness of power and disposition, like the unity Christ asks for his disciples in John 17. Owen focuses on deity instead, arguing that the Jews' accusation of blasphemy shows Jesus was plainly claiming to be God.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: Father and Son are two in that the Father is Father and the Son is Son, not the same Person as Sabellius said. They are one because the Son is from the Father's Essence by nature, His own Word. The Word is never separated from the Father, and the Father was never Wordless, which is also why Christ says 'I in the Father and the Father in Me.'
sources.quote: and they are one, because He is Son of the Essence of the Father by nature, existing as His own Word. This the Lord said, viz. ‘I and the Father are One;’ for neither is the Word separated from the Father, nor was or is the Father ever Wordless
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean by 'I and the Father are One' (John 10:30)?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Preface
sources.answer: Yes. The Jews who heard him understood the words well as a plain assertion that he was God, which is why they took up stones and charged him with blasphemy, because "being a man, makest thyself God." Jesus did not correct that understanding, and the Jews themselves still hold that he declared himself God and was slain for it.
sources.quote: They understood well enough the meaning of those words, “I and my Father are one,” — namely, that they were a plain assertion of his being God. This caused their rage.
sources.raw_question: Does Jesus' statement "I and my Father are one" (John 10:30) assert his deity?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Christ did not say 'I and the Father am one' but 'are one.' The plural verb refers to two persons and one power. The unity meant is like the unity Christ asks for his disciples in John 17, a oneness of power and disposition, not one body or person.
sources.quote: For the word are is not said of one person, but it refers to two persons, and one power.
sources.raw_question: Does 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30) prove that the Father and the Son are a single person?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus C. Introductory to the Fourth Discourse against the Arians.
sources.answer: They are one by the eternal divine generation: the Son is distinct from the Father yet one with him. This excludes Sabellius's identification of Father and Son. It also excludes Marcellus's explanation of the divine γέννησις, which is paradoxical.
sources.quote: In what sense Christ and the Father are, and are not, one. The divine γέννησις.
sources.raw_question: In what sense are Christ and the Father 'one' according to John 10:30?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: It shows both equality and unity. 'I and the Father' reveals equality, which excludes confusion and distinguishes the Persons. 'Are One' asserts unity, which excludes separation. The Son thus shows His equality with the Father in a unity of power, since He acquires persons to Himself and gives life as the Father does.
sources.quote: Equality excludes confusion; Unity excludes separation. Equality distinguishes between the Father and the Son; Unity does not separate the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: What does 'I and the Father are One' (John 10:30) show about how the Son relates to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: It teaches that they share one common nature and true divinity while remaining Begetter and Begotten. The Son has all things in perfect communion with the absolute Existence from whom he is. So they must be believed to be one, just as they are also two in being Begetter and Begotten.
sources.quote: Believe that They are One, even as They are also Begetter and Begotten. Why deny the common nature? Why impugn the true Divinity?
sources.raw_question: What does 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30) teach about the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Skilfully Replies to a Passage Which the Heretics Employed in Defence of Their Own Opinion.
sources.answer: No. By saying "I" and then "the Father," Christ distinguishes his own person as Son from the Father, and he says "we are," not "I am," showing two persons. Had he meant he was the Father, he would have said "I the Father."
sources.quote: Finally, He adds, and says, “We are,” not “I am,” so as to show, by the fact of His saying “I and the Father are,” that they are two persons.
sources.raw_question: Does Jesus' saying "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30) show that the Son is the same person as the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: It means a distinct Son who is one with the Father. Christ explains 'One' by saying 'I am the Son of God' and 'the Father is in Me and I in the Father.' The union therefore lies not in His being the Father but in mutual indwelling. Christ thus refutes Sabellius by saying He is the Son and not the Father, and Arius by saying 'are One.'
sources.quote: For thus He overthrows both Sabellius, in saying, ‘I am’ not, “the Father,” but, ‘the Son of God;’ and Arius, in saying, ‘are One.’
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'I and the Father are One' (John 10:30-38) mean that He is the Father, or that He is a distinct Son one with the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: "One" refers to the essence, because Father and Son are the same God. "We are" is plural because of relation, since one is Father and the other is Son. So the text expresses both unity of essence and distinction of relative persons.
sources.quote: “one,” according to essence, because they are the same God; “we are,” according to relation, because the one is Father, the other is Son.
sources.raw_question: What do the words "one" and "we are" signify in John 10:30, "I and my Father are one"?

question: Does Christ's statement in Mark 13:32 that not even the Son knows the day and hour of judgment prove that the Son is ignorant of it, and so not equal to the Father in Godhead?
synthesis: All the authors answer no, but their grounds differ. Athanasius, Ambrose, Bickersteth and Waterland (in 5269 and 8702) refer the ignorance to Christ's human nature. Ambrose adds that the Spirit is not excepted, so the Son cannot be less than the Spirit, and Bickersteth adds that Christ was not commissioned to reveal the day. Hilary and Augustine instead treat the 'ignorance' as a deliberate withholding of disclosure, which Hilary calls the divine plan of silence and Augustine explains by the idiom of making others not know. Hilary also argues that the Author of all times cannot be ignorant of them, while Waterland (in 1128) and Hilary (in 4306) say the Father is given only a preference or prerogative as source or Unbegotten, not greater knowledge.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: No. On Waterland's reading of Irenaeus, the Father is not said to be superior in knowledge but only to be declared as having the preference. Father and Son are equally knowing. Christ gave the Father the preference for three reasons: to teach that the Father is the fountain even of the Son, because in his state of condescension it became him to refer all to the Father, and to give us an example of humility.
sources.quote: So that the question, with Irenzeus, is not why the Father is superior in knowledge ; but why, since Father and Son are equally knowing, our Saviour makes such a declaration as gave the preference to the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that only the Father knows the day of judgment imply that the Son is less knowing than the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Christ did not number the Spirit among those who do not know, so the Spirit is excepted from ignorance, and the Son cannot be less than the Spirit. If the saying applied to the Son's divinity, the Spirit would be greater than the Son, which is absurd even by Arian standards. The ignorance must therefore be referred to his human nature, in which he could be numbered with created beings.
sources.quote: acknowledge to what you ought to refer it that He said that the Son knew not. For as man He could [in His human nature] be numbered with creatures Who were created.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that no one, not even the angels, knows the day and hour prove that the Son of God is ignorant of the day of judgment?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The Son's professed ignorance belongs to the economy of hidden knowledge, not to a nature capable of ignorance. He says He does not know so that others may not know, and He says the Father alone knows to show that He Himself also knows, since the Father's knowing is declared precisely in revealing it to the Son.
sources.quote: The fact that the Father alone knows, is no proof that the Son is ignorant: He says that He does not know, that others may not know: that the Father alone knows, to shew that He Himself also knows.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that the Father alone knows the day of judgment prove that the Son is ignorant of it?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Father and Son abide in unity of nature, and in the Son are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; His professed ignorance belongs to a divine plan of silence, not to weakness. That the Father alone knows does not imply that the Son does not know.
sources.quote: The Son is ignorant, then, of nothing which the Father knows, nor does it follow because the Father alone knows, that the Son does not know.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that only the Father knows the day and hour mean that the Son is truly ignorant of it?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: No. He said He knew not according to the flesh, because ignorance is proper to man; as Word, Wisdom, Judge and Bridegroom who is to come, He knows when He comes. Just as on becoming man He hungers, thirsts and suffers with men, so with men as man He knows not, though divinely, being in the Father, there is nothing He knows not.
sources.quote: For as, on becoming man, He hungers and thirsts and suffers with men, so with men as man He knows not; though divinely, being in the Father Word and Wisdom, He knows, and there is nothing which He knows not.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that 'not even the Son' knows the day and hour (Mark 13:32) mean that the Son as Word is ignorant of the day of judgment?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Jesus speaks there in his human nature, as Luke 2:52 shows he increased in wisdom as man; the point was not made known to his manhood by the Spirit, and as Prophet and ambassador he was not commissioned to reveal it. Other texts show he shares the Father's counsels, knows the Father as the Father knows him, and knows all things, so he is himself omniscient.
sources.quote: Jesus is speaking in his human nature. This point was not made known to him as man, by the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement in Mark 13:32 that the Son does not know the day and hour disprove his divine omniscience?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: No. The Word through whom all things, including times and seasons, were made cannot be ignorant of His own work. Christ spoke this as man, by reason of the flesh, whose property it is to be ignorant. So the ignorance belongs to His human nature, not to the Word's Godhead.
sources.quote: Through the Word all things have been made, times and seasons and night and day and the whole creation; and is the Framer of all said to be ignorant of His work?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement in Mark 13:32 that 'not the Son' knows the day and hour prove that the Son is ignorant and therefore not true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Even if He had not known it, this would be no ground for attacking His Godhead. The Father's reserving of the day marks only His prerogative as Unbegotten, not a defect in the Son's nature, which holds by birth the full divine nature. In fact the Son kept silence according to the Divine Plan, not from ignorance.
sources.quote: when He said that He knew not the day, He kept silence not from ignorance, but in accordance with the Divine Plan
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's saying that He does not know the day and hour of judgment prove He is inferior in Godhead to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. To believe him really ignorant would contradict the Apostle, who says all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him. Some knowledge must stay hidden, and declaring it would reveal it. So he professes ignorance in order to keep it hidden. The ignorance comes from this purpose, not from his omniscient nature.
sources.quote: If we believe Him to have been really ignorant, we contradict the Apostle, who says, In Whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's saying that he does not know the day or the hour of judgment prove that he is truly ignorant, and so inferior to the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. The text shows that the Father and the Son are two distinct Persons, which refutes the Sabellians. The Son, having both a divine and a human nature, could speak of himself in either capacity. He was ignorant only in his human capacity. The Father was not ignorant in any respect, because he never took human nature, and with it human ignorance, into personal union with himself.
sources.quote: one ignorant in such a capacity, the other not ignorant in any capacity at all, as having never taken human nature, and therewith human ignorance, mto a personal union with himself.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that the Son does not know the day of judgment, though the Father does, show that the Son is inferior to the Father in his divine nature?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Jesus speaks there in his human nature, as one who grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52); the point was not revealed to his manhood, and as Prophet he was not commissioned to reveal it. Parallel texts show his divine knowledge: the Father shows him all things, he knows the Father as the Father knows him, and Peter confesses "Thou knowest all things."
sources.quote: so in Mark 13:32, Jesus is speaking in his human nature. This point was not made known to him as man, by the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does Mark 13:32, where the Son does not know the day or hour, prove that the Son is not omniscient God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. It is not credible that he who is the Author of all things, present and future, should not know all things. Everything exists through him and in him, and he knows even men's future thoughts. Scripture says that Jesus knew from the beginning who would not believe and who would betray him. So what is through him and within him cannot lie beyond his knowledge.
sources.quote: Is it credible, that He, Who stands to all things as the Author of their present and future, should not know all things?
sources.raw_question: Does the saying that the Son does not know the day and the hour (Mark 13:32) prove that the Son lacks the perfection of the divine nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. The Son is said not to know in the sense that he makes others not know, that is, he did not know it so as to reveal it to his disciples at that time. Scripture uses the human idiom by which something hidden is called unknown, as a hidden ditch is called blind. So the text expresses a withholding of disclosure, not a defect of knowledge in the Son.
sources.quote: For He is ignorant of this, as making others ignorant; that is, in that He did not so know as at that time to show His disciples
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that the Son does not know the day and hour of judgment (Mark 13:32) prove the Son is ignorant and therefore not equal to the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: No. These texts are plainly meant only of Christ's human nature. They are parallel to Luke 2:52, that he increased in wisdom, which cannot be literally understood of the Logos with any tolerable consistency, even on the Arian hypothesis.
sources.quote: Matt. xxiv. 36. as well as Mark xiii. 32. is plainly meant only of the human nature; and is to the same effect with Luke 1]. 52, ‘“ That he ‘‘ increased in wisdom,”
sources.raw_question: Do the texts saying that the Son does not know the day or hour of judgment (Matthew 24:36; Mark 13:32) prove that the Son as the divine Word is ignorant?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Common sense forbids it: Christ is the Author through whom and in whom all things, including the times, exist, and no one is ignorant of what is through and in himself. Since the day is His own day, the day of His coming, fixed by His mystery and in His power, He cannot fail to know it.
sources.quote: No one is ignorant of that which is through himself and within himself: shall Christ come, and does He not know the day of His coming?
sources.raw_question: Does Mark 13:32 ('of that day and hour knoweth no one... neither the Son') prove that the Son of God was truly ignorant of the day of judgment?

question: To whom does God speak in Genesis 1:26, 'Let us make man in our image', and does the plural point to a plurality of Persons within the one God?
synthesis: All the authors read the plural as pointing to divine Persons rather than to angels, a solitary God, or many gods. Irenaeus says the Father addresses the Word, or the Son and Spirit as his Word and Wisdom, and Waterland follows Irenaeus in extending 'us' and 'our image' to all three Persons. Warfield argues from verse 27 against an angelic reading, and Hilary argues that a solitary being could not say 'us'. Augustine insists the plural refers only to the relative Persons, so man is made in the image of the one Trinity, not of gods; Bickersteth adds the plural name Elohim but gives the argument no great prominence.

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Verse 27 says that God created man in His own image. This does not encourage reading the previous verse as announcing that man would be made in the image of the angels. The Trinitarian interpretation therefore remains the most natural one.
sources.quote: for surely verse 27: “And God created man in his own image,” does not encourage us to take the preceding verse as announcing that man was to be created in the image of the angels
sources.raw_question: Does the plural 'Let us make man in our image' in Genesis 1:26 refer to God consulting with the angels?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XV.—Proofs of the resurrection from Isaiah and Ezekiel; the same God who created us will also raise us up.
sources.answer: Yes. The same Word who formed Adam at the beginning is the one the Father addressed in "Let Us make man." In the last times this same Word revealed himself to men and formed eyes for the man born blind.
sources.quote: But He, the very same who formed Adam at the beginning, with whom also the Father spake, [saying], “Let Us make man after Our image and likeness,”
sources.raw_question: Is the Word the one to whom the Father spoke in Genesis 1:26, "Let Us make man after Our image"?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus understood Genesis 1:26 as the Father speaking to the Son and Spirit, his 'hands'. Both 'Let us make' and 'after our image' therefore cover all three Persons. The image of any one of them is the image of all, which implies their unity of nature.
sources.quote: 2. From *his understanding Gen. i. 26. of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, Let us make; and also, after our image; so that the image of any one is the image of all.
sources.raw_question: Do the plural words 'Let us make man in our image' in Genesis 1:26 refer to the Father, Son and Holy Ghost, so that man bears the image of all three?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The plural words "Us" and "Our" cannot be used by a solitary being, because an isolated being cannot be his own partner. A solitary God would have said "I" and "Mine." The words therefore show a Partner, which demolishes the theory of God's isolation.
sources.quote: For an isolated being cannot be partner to himself; and again, the words, Let Us make, are inconsistent with solitude, while Our cannot be used except to a companion.
sources.raw_question: In Genesis 1:26, "Let Us make man after Our image," was God speaking to Himself alone?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes, though the author gives this argument no great prominence. He believes the language was intended to awaken the conviction that a mysterious plurality subsists in Jehovah's essential unity. Israel was set apart to protest against polytheism and had a rich language, including the singular form Eloah. Yet the ordinary name of the one God is plural and is sometimes joined with plural verbs. No necessity of language explains this.
sources.quote: I believed this language was intended to foster when kindled, and to awaken when dormant, the persuasion that there subsisted a mysterious plurality in the essential unity of Jehovah.
sources.raw_question: Does the plural form of the Hebrew divine name Elohim, and God's use of plural language such as "Let us make man in our image," point to a plurality within the one God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: God speaks to the Son and the Spirit, his Word and Wisdom, who were always present with him. By them and in them he made all things.
sources.quote: For with Him were always present the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, by whom and in whom, freely and spontaneously, He made all things, to whom also He speaks, saying, “Let Us make man after Our image and likeness;”
sources.raw_question: To whom does God speak when he says "Let Us make man after Our image and likeness" in Genesis 1:26?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: No. The plural must be understood only of the relative persons. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit made man after the image of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that man is the image of God, and God is the Trinity. It does not mean that gods made man after the image of gods.
sources.quote: For it was not that gods might make, or make after the image and likeness of gods; but that the Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit might make after the image of the Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Does the plural in Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man after our image," imply a plurality of gods?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Why This Opinion is to Be Rejected.
sources.answer: It shows that man was made in the image of the Trinity, not of one person alone. The plural "our" would not be rightly used if man were made in the image of the Father only, or the Son only, or the Spirit only.
sources.quote: the word “our” would not be rightly used if man were made in the image of one person, whether of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit; but because he was made in the image of the Trinity
sources.raw_question: What does the plural "our" in Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man in our image," show about whose image man was made in?

question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me a beginning of His ways for His works,' prove that the Son (the Wisdom of God) is a creature in His essence?
synthesis: All five authors agree the verse does not make the Son a creature, and most refer 'created' to the Incarnation. Athanasius stresses proverbial speech, 'for the works' (not 'a work'), and the following 'He begat me'; he also reads it as the created impress of Wisdom in the works. Gregory of Nyssa argues that Proverbs' dark sayings cannot be read literally and that the Hebrew reads 'possessed', referring it to Christ's human nature or to the beginning of virtue in men. Hilary separates creation 'for' the ways from eternal birth and says the text shows Christ existed before Mary; Ambrose refers it to the predestined assumed body, and Augustine to the form of a servant as against the form of God.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. Scripture nowhere calls the Lord a 'creature'; it only says 'He created' in a proverb, which is figurative speech. The phrase refers to the human nature which became His, to which creation properly belongs. The Father prepared a body for Him and so 'created' Him for men's salvation.
sources.quote: let ‘He created’ be understood, not of His being a creature, but of that human nature which became His, for to this belongs creation.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me a beginning of His ways,' prove that the Son is a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. The surrounding verses in Proverbs cannot be taken at face value without absurdity, so the phrase "The Lord created me," written in close connection with them, must not be received without examination either. Its pious meaning has to be sought beyond the immediate sense of the words, as the following context concludes.
sources.quote: it is consequently probable that the phrase we are discussing, being written in close connection with them, is not received by prudent men absolutely and without examination.
sources.raw_question: Should the text of Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created me," be read in its literal, surface sense as proof that the Son (Wisdom) is a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. If 'for the works' meant his essence, he would be later than the works, which already existed for his sake. That contradicts his being before all things and the One through whom all things were made. 'He created me' refers to his putting on created flesh, spoken in the manner of proverbs.
sources.quote: For the Word of God is not creature but Creator; and says in the manner of proverbs, ‘He created me’ when He put on created flesh.
sources.raw_question: Does 'The Lord created me a beginning of His ways for His works' (Proverbs 8:22) show that the Word is a creature in his essence?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Being created for the beginning of God's ways and works is entirely different from birth from everlasting. Where birth is meant, Scripture speaks of birth alone; where creation is mentioned, the cause of that creation is named first. There is a Wisdom born before all things, and a different wisdom created in time for particular purposes. The word 'creation' must therefore be rejected from our confession of the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: creation for these purposes and birth from everlasting are two entirely different things. Where birth is meant, there birth, and nothing but birth, is spoken of; where creation is mentioned, the cause of that creation is first named.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created Me for a beginning of His ways for His works,' prove that Christ is a creature rather than the eternally begotten Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > These doctrines of our Faith witnessed to and confirmed by Scripture passages.
sources.answer: No. Such proverbial expressions are metaphors with a deeper meaning than the obvious one, so they give reverent inquirers no reason to suspect that the Lord was created. They must be read in light of the evangelist's plain teaching that all things were made by Him.
sources.quote: It is therefore clear that these are metaphors, which contain a deeper meaning than the obvious one: so that there is no reason from them that any suspicion that our Lord was created should be entertained by reverent inquirers
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22 ("The Lord created me"), with its metaphorical language, give grounds for thinking the Son is a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. The Word of God is not creature but Creator; He says 'He created me' in the manner of proverbs, referring to when He put on created flesh. Solomon elsewhere calls Him God's Offspring and Wisdom, not a creature.
sources.quote: For the Word of God is not creature but Creator; and says in the manner of proverbs, ‘He created me’ when He put on created flesh.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me a beginning of His ways for His works,' prove that the Son (Wisdom) is a creature in His divine essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. First, the opponents give no reason why the text must refer to the Lord at all. Second, other translators render the Hebrew 'possessed' or 'constituted.' Third, even on that reading, proverbial discourse hides its meaning and must not be taken literally, as the surrounding metaphors show.
sources.quote: They do not give reasons why we must refer that text to our Lord at all: neither will they be able to show that the idea of the word in the Hebrew leads to this and no other meaning
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me,' prove that the Son is a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. Scripture does not say 'He created Me a work' or 'with the works' or 'before the works', but 'for the works', meaning the Father made Him into flesh, that He might become man. As one who enters a house is other than the house, He who is created for the works is by nature other than the works, an Offspring, not a work.
sources.quote: For as he who comes into a house, is not part of the house, but is other than the house, so He who is created for the works, must be by nature other than the works.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22 ('He created Me ... for the works') teach that the Word is a creature or work?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. The words do not proceed from the divine and immortal nature but from the created human nature joined to it in the Incarnation. The eternal Son, who needs no creation in order to be, was 'created' as man to become the new way and the beginning of ways for God's works, that is, for men who had lost the first way through disobedience.
sources.quote: Accordingly the words “created me” do not proceed from the Divine and immortal nature, but from that which was commingled with it in the Incarnation from our created nature.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase "The Lord created me" in Proverbs 8:22 refer to the divine nature of the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. It refers to his bodily presence, not his essence. He is called a beginning because of the resurrection, and that resurrection happened when he bore our flesh and gave himself to death. Death belonged to the body, and so likewise does the word 'created'.
sources.quote: it is evident that His words, ‘He created me a beginning of ways,’ is indicative not of His essence, but of His bodily presence. For to the body death was proper
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'The Lord created me' in Proverbs 8:22 describe the essence of the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. Wisdom, in whom all things were framed, is the Creator and cannot number itself among the creatures. When Wisdom speaks of itself, 'He created' must mean nothing contrary to 'He begat.' The text refers to the incarnation, not to Wisdom's essence.
sources.quote: if it be the Wisdom of God, in whom all things originate have been framed, that speaks concerning Itself, what ought we to understand but that ‘He created’ means nothing contrary to ‘He begat?’
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me,' prove that the Son or Wisdom of God is a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: No. The text refers to the created wisdom imprinted in the works, which is the impress or image of the true Wisdom. The true Wisdom, the only-begotten Son, speaks of this impress as if of Himself. The wisdom in the world is created, while the true Wisdom is creative and the Framer of all things.
sources.quote: let no one, overlooking the wisdom created in the world and in the works, think that ‘He created’ is said of the Substance of the Very Wisdom, lest, diluting the wine with water, he be judged a defrauder of the truth.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22 ('The Lord created me a beginning of His ways for His works') teach that the Son, the Wisdom of God, is a creature in His essence?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Wisdom says it was created for the beginning of God's ways and works to show that it subsisted before Mary, not to call its birth a creation. Wisdom also declares itself established before the ages, and this establishing is prior to the creation. So the infinite birth is not made subject to time.
sources.quote: yet has not employed this word ‘created’ in order to signify that its birth was a creation, since it was created for the beginning of God’s ways and for His works.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created Me for the beginning of His ways," prove that Christ, as Wisdom, is a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: No. Gregory notes that the Hebrew and more ancient copies read "possessed" rather than "created," and in the allegorical language of Proverbs "possession" denotes the slave-form the Son took for our sakes. Even if the Church reading "created" is kept, it admits an orthodox interpretation: it refers to the incarnate Christ, who was truly created in the last days when the Word, being God from the beginning, became flesh and man.
sources.quote: Thus we say that this expression, as well as the other, admits of an orthodox interpretation. For He Who for our sakes became like as we are, was in the last days truly created,—He Who in the beginning being Word and God afterwards became Flesh and Man.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created Me as the beginning of His ways," prove that the Son of God is a creature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Hilary treats this as the chief wave of the heretical storm, which breaks harmlessly against the faith. Christ is no creature nor something made, since He is Himself Lord of all things made; He is God, the true generation of God the Father.
sources.quote: For we recognise the Lord Christ as no creature, for indeed He is none such; nor as something that has been made, since He is Himself the Lord of all things that are made
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created Me as the beginning of His ways,' prove that the Only-begotten Son is a creature rather than begotten?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VI. To those who object that according to the words of Amos the Spirit is created, the answer is made that the word is there understood of the wind, which is often created, which cannot be said of the Holy Spirit, since He is eternal, and cannot be dissolved in death, or by an heretical absorption into the Father. But if they pertinaciously contend that this passage was written of the Holy Spirit, St. Ambrose points out that recourse must be had to a spiritual Interpretation, for Christ by His coming established the thunder, that is, the force of the divine utterances, and by Spirit is signified the human soul as also the flesh assumed by Christ. And since this was created by each Person of the Trinity, it is thence argued that the Spirit, Who has before been affirmed to be the Creator of all things, was the Author of the Incarnation of the Lord.
sources.answer: No. Wisdom speaks of the mystery of the assumed Body. The past tense "created" is used for something foretold because the Lord's coming was predestined, and it shows that the Body of Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary once only, not repeatedly.
sources.quote: Wisdom herself, speaking after the mystery of the assumed Body, says: “The Lord created Me.”
sources.raw_question: Does "The Lord created me" (Proverbs 8:22) refer to the eternal nature of Wisdom (the Son)?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. Just as men are not sons by nature but become sons by adoption and grace, the Word is not a creature by nature but is said to be created because, in grace toward us, He became man. The word 'created' refers to His taking flesh for the sake of the works.
sources.quote: if we become sons by adoption and grace, then has the Word also, when in grace towards us He became man, said, ‘The Lord created me.’
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me,' show that the Word is a creature by nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: No. The Word says 'created' not of His essence but because He put on our flesh and came for our salvation; since He came not for Himself but for us, He is 'created' not for Himself but for us, and so is not Himself a creature but uses such language as man.
sources.quote: but if not for Himself, but for us, by consequence not for Himself but for us is He created. But if not for Himself is He created, but for us, then He is not Himself a creature, but, as having put on our flesh, He uses such language.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement in Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me for the works,' show that the Word is a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. Scripture does not say 'He created me a work' or 'with the works' or 'before the works', but with exact discrimination 'for the works', meaning the Father made him into flesh to be man. Just as one who enters a house is not part of the house, he who is created for the works must be by nature other than the works, an Offspring rather than a work.
sources.quote: For as he who comes into a house, is not part of the house, but is other than the house, so He who is created for the works, must be by nature other than the works.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'created me for the works' in Proverbs 8:22 imply that the Word is himself a work or creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: No. The Word did not call Himself a creature by nature but spoke in a proverb whose sense is latent. Since the Only-begotten Wisdom is Creator and Framer of all things, He cannot be created; the verse refers to the created impress of Wisdom in the works, which the true Wisdom speaks of as if of Himself.
sources.quote: The Word has not called Himself a creature by nature, but has said in proverbs, ‘The Lord created me;’ and He plainly indicates a sense not spoken ‘plainly’ but latent
sources.raw_question: Does Wisdom's saying 'The Lord created me a beginning of His ways' in Proverbs 8:22 prove that the Son, the Wisdom of God, is a creature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. The word 'created' there does not signify that Wisdom's birth was a creation; it was created 'for the beginning of God's ways and for His works,' referring to the mystery of the incarnation and economy. The text was meant to silence the Jew by showing Christ subsisted before Mary, not to make Christ a creature.
sources.quote: yet has not employed this word ‘created’ in order to signify that its birth was a creation, since it was created for the beginning of God’s ways and for His works.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created Me for the beginning of His ways,' prove that Christ (Wisdom) is a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. The verse should not be taken at its obvious surface meaning as the Only-begotten acknowledging that He was created. Proverbs is by its own title a book of 'proverbs,' meaning dark sayings whose true sense is hidden and reached only by a 'turn' of the words. So no passage cited from it can be used as a plain proof text, especially an obscure one like this. Rightly understood, the verse does no injury to the doctrine of the faith and gives heresy no support.
sources.quote: they allege this passage as though the Only-begotten God Himself, under the name of Wisdom, acknowledges that He was created by the Maker of all things. I imagine, however, that the godly sense of this utterance is clear to moderately attentive and painstaking persons
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me in the beginning of His ways,' spoken by Wisdom, prove that the Son, whom Paul calls Wisdom, is a created being?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: It refers to the beginning of the ways of virtue in men, not to the Son's pre-temporal existence. The following verse, 'blessed is he that keepeth my ways,' shows that 'ways' means the approaches to virtue, whose beginning is the possession of Wisdom. So the text gives no ground for counting the Only-begotten among created things.
sources.quote: meaning of course by “ways” the approaches to virtue, the beginning of which is the possession of Wisdom.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22 ('The Lord created me') refer to the eternal generation of the Son, or to the formation of Wisdom/virtue in the ways of human beings?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: It refers to his manhood, not his essence. Because the text says he was created 'for the works,' it signifies the Economy undertaken for the works, which comes second to being. It does not describe the Word's coming into existence.
sources.quote: For the passage in the Proverbs, as I have said before, signifies, not the Essence, but the manhood of the Word; for if He says that He was created ‘for the works,’ He shews His intention of signifying, not His Essence, but the Economy
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me a beginning of His ways for His works,' refer to the essence of the Word or to his manhood?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. The text adds 'But before all the hills He begat me.' This would be superfluous if offspring and creature were the same. The conjunction 'But' guards the term 'created' and shows that 'begat' is prior to 'created.' 'Created' is said with a purpose, namely the Incarnation.
sources.quote: If then the Word were by nature and in His Essence a creature, and there were no difference between offspring and creature, He would not have added, ‘He begat me,’ but had been satisfied with ‘He created,’
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me a beginning of His ways,' prove that the Word is by essence a creature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. This is said of Christ according to the form of a servant, whereas 'Before all the hills He begat me' is said according to the form of God. As the first-begotten of the dead and Head of the Church, he made a way to eternal life, and so he was 'created in the beginning of the ways' of God in his work. According to the form of God he is the Beginning in which God created heaven and earth.
sources.quote: therefore He was “created in the beginning of the ways” of God in His work. For, according to the form of God, He is the beginning
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me in the beginning of His ways', show that the Son is a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: It refers to his bodily generation, not his essence. The Word received the works to perfect not at creation (they did not yet exist) nor before the incarnation (which would make his coming superfluous), but when he became man, healing our wounds and granting resurrection. Hence 'He created' is said of him when he became flesh.
sources.quote: Not of His essence then is ‘He created’ indicative, as has many times been said, but of His bodily generation.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me... for His works,' refer to the Word's divine essence or to his becoming man?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. Gregory argues that no part of this passage of Proverbs can be taken at face value without examination, since its other statements (Wisdom being created, set up, and begotten, the throne on the winds, etc.) cannot be squared with the obvious sense. Therefore the text must be searched with care for what can be piously understood, not taken according to the sense that first presents itself.
sources.quote: so not to interpret the text, “The Lord created me,” according to that sense which immediately presents itself to us from the phrase, but to seek with all attention and care what is to be piously understood from the utterance
sources.raw_question: Should Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created me," be read in its immediate literal sense as proof that Wisdom (the Son) is a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: No. The Arian reading is their own comment, not Solomon's meaning. Read as a whole, the passage in Proverbs shows that the Son is not a creature in nature and essence. He is the proper Offspring of the Father, true Wisdom and Word, by whom all things were made.
sources.quote: the passage in the Proverbs, as well as all that is above said, proves that the Son is not a creature in nature and essence, but the proper Offspring of the Father, true Wisdom and Word
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22, 'The Lord created me a beginning of His ways,' prove that the Son is a creature by nature?

question: Is Christ the Son of God by nature, or only by adoption and name in the same way that believers and saints are called sons of God?
synthesis: All five authors agree that Christ is Son by nature and believers only by adoption, but they argue it differently. Hilary relies most on Scripture: the Father's own words, Peter's blessed confession, 'thy Son' and 'own Son', and the claim that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father; he also argues that a title of adoption would divorce the name from the nature. Gregory of Nyssa argues that the one who makes others sons needs no adoption himself and does not change as men do; Augustine contrasts Christ, Son of God by nature and son of man by mercy, with believers, sons of men by nature and sons of God by grace; Athanasius and Bickersteth stress that believers' sonship comes only by participation in the Son's Spirit or in Christ, and Bickersteth adds that believers share 'a' divine nature, not 'the' divine nature.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Believers receive the name of sons through regeneration and faith, and they cry 'Abba, Father' by adoption. That cry does not change their essential nature. It is one thing for God to be addressed as Father, and another for Him to be by nature the Father of His Son.
sources.quote: Abba, Father, is the cry which we raise, not the expression of our essential nature. For that essential nature of ours is untouched by that tribute of the voice. It is one thing for God to be addressed as Father; another thing for Him to be the Father of His Son.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's sonship the same kind of sonship as that of believers who are called sons of God through the Spirit of adoption?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Hilary calls this view, which makes the Son a creature named Son by grace, most godless. The scriptural phrases 'from Him', 'from the womb', and 'I went forth from the Father' show a true birth from the Father's own Godhead. The Son is therefore Son by nature, not created out of nothing by an act of will.
sources.quote: He uses language which assists our understanding to assure us that His Only-begotten Son was ineffably born of His own true Godhead.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ called Son of God only by adoption and favour, in the same sense in which holy men are told 'Ye are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High', rather than by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: He is Son by nature, not merely in name. If He were only one of a multitude of sons, the confession that Jesus is the Son of God would have no eminence, since all feeble created beings are sons in that sense. Christ's words 'He that hateth Me hateth My Father also' assert a relation to the Father shared by none.
sources.quote: In what does the eminence of a faith, which has confessed that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, consist, if He, as one of a multitude of sons, have the name only, and not the nature, of the Son?
sources.raw_question: Is Christ the Son of God only in name, as one of the many sons of God like the saints, or is He Son by nature?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Christ is Son of God in a sense peculiar to himself: only-begotten, his own Son, the Son of his love. The difference between that essential Sonship and believers' adopted sonship is infinite, since adoption is theirs only in Christ. Believers become partakers of "a" divine nature, not "the" divine nature.
sources.quote: we see how infinite the difference betwixt that essential Sonship, and our privileges, as adopted sons, which are only ours in Christ
sources.raw_question: Does believers' being called sons of God and joint heirs with Christ make their sonship the same as Christ's sonship?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Christ is the Son of God in a sense peculiar to himself, the only-begotten, the Father's own Son, whereas believers' sonship is an adopted privilege that is theirs only in Christ. Romans 8 shows the infinite difference between his essential Sonship and our adoption, and we become partakers of 'a' (not 'the') divine nature only through him.
sources.quote: From a cursory glance into the eighth of Romans, we see how infinite the difference betwixt that essential Sonship, and our privileges, as adopted sons, which are only ours in Christ
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's Sonship of God the same kind of sonship as believers' adoption as sons of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: By nature, not by adoption. Every work and word of Christ transcends the power of those who bear the title of sons, and the name of God is given Him by absolute ownership rather than by admission to joint use of a title. He does not hold the name Son as a title shared with a widespread company of friends.
sources.quote: The name of God is given Him in the right of absolute ownership, not because He has been admitted to joint use with others of the title.
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus Christ Son of God by nature or merely by adoption, sharing the title of 'son' with other godly people?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: By nature. If Christ were Son only by adoption, Peter's confession "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God" would have stated something true of every regenerate believer and would have deserved no special blessing. Since the Father's revelation was praised as beyond flesh and blood, it must have revealed the Divine nature of the Son, not a mere title shared with others.
sources.quote: If He be Son by adoption, wherein lay the blessedness of Peter’s confession, which offered a tribute to the Son to which, in that case, He had no more title than any member of the company of saints?
sources.raw_question: Is Christ the Son of God by nature, or only by name and adoption like the saints?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Christ is not called Son through God's condescension or because he earned the title by holiness, as martyrs and confessors receive it by favor. The Sonship marked by the Father's words 'This', 'My', and 'Hear Him' is different in kind. It is the true, real, and genuine Sonship.
sources.quote: It is not through condescending kindness on the part of God the Father that Christ bears the name of Son; not by holiness that He has earned the title, as many have won it by enduring hardness in confession of the faith.
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics claiming His name is a gift by adoption
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's Sonship the same in kind as the adoptive sonship granted to holy people or confessors?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Believers are named and adopted as sons of God by His goodness, but Christ is the one true Son, the true and perfect birth. Our religion is to confess Him as Son not adopted but born, not chosen but begotten.
sources.quote: this only, and this alone, is our religion, to confess Him as the Son not adopted but born, not chosen but begotten
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's sonship the same as believers' adoptive sonship to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Thereafter he expounds the appellation of “Son,” and of “product of generation,” and very many varieties of “sons,” of God, of men, of rams, of perdition, of light, and of day.
sources.answer: No. A man becomes a son of God through spiritual generation by being joined to Christ. He who makes men sons of God does not need another Son to give Him adoption. Men change, putting off the old man and putting on the new, but the Son is always the same and has nothing to receive or give up. So He bears the name 'Son' by nature.
sources.quote: He Who by Himself makes the man to be a son of God does not need another Son to bestow on Him the adoption of a son, but has the name also of that which He is by nature.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ a son of God by adoption, in the same way that believers become sons of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > We Say that Future Blessedness is Truly Eternal, Not Through Human Reasonings, But by the Help of Faith. The Immortality of Blessedness Becomes Credible from the Incarnation of the Son of God.
sources.answer: No. Christ is by nature the Son of God and became Son of man through mercy. Believers are by nature sons of men and are made sons of God by grace, being born not of blood or the will of the flesh but of God.
sources.quote: For if He who is by nature the Son of God was made the Son of man through mercy for the sake of the sons of men
sources.raw_question: Is Christ Son of God in the same way that believers become sons of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
