sources.answer: No. Believers were once sons of wrath and have been made sons through the Spirit of adoption, receiving the title by favour, not by right of birth. They were made and purchased, not begotten, whereas Christ alone is Son by true birth from the Father.
sources.quote: Moreover, we have not been born, but made; not begotten, but purchased. For God purchased a people for Himself, and by this act begot them.
sources.raw_question: Are believers sons of God in the same sense that Christ is the Son of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. He is the true Son of God, as shown by His claim that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father, which no adopted son could say.
sources.quote: It is no mere adoption, for He is the true Son of God and cries, He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father also
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God a son merely by adoption?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The Arian claim that Christ uses the names God and Son by a kind of adoption has been silenced. The Son has no origin outside God and was not created from nothing. He is a true Son by a true birth from God.
sources.quote: The assertion that He bears the name of Son by virtue of adoption has been put to silence, and He stands forth as a true Son by a true birth.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ called Son of God and God only by adoption rather than by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The notion of Christ's adoption is a device of the Evil One meant to remove from believers the assurance of the Son's divine nature. Scripture's witness, including Paul's calling Him God's 'own' Son, teaches true divine Sonship, not adoption.
sources.quote: His first object is to pluck from our hearts the confident assurance of the Divine nature of the Son; next, he would fill our minds with the notion of Christ's adoption
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's sonship to God a sonship by adoption?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. To grant Him the name of Son while calling Him a creature adorned with that title is to divorce the name from the nature. The heretics would rob Him of the name too if they could, but since they cannot, they deny He is the true Son. Christ claimed true Sonship, which is why the Jews condemned Him for making Himself the Son of God; denying it shares their verdict.
sources.quote: you allow Him the name as a title of adoption, and feign that He is a creature adorned, like others, with the right to call Himself a Son.
sources.raw_question: Can Christ be called 'Son of God' as a title of adoption while being in nature a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. There is one Son by nature, true and only-begotten; we become sons by adoption and the grace of Him who calls, through partaking of His Spirit. We are called gods not as the True God or His Word but as it pleased God to give that grace. The Son is by nature and essence true God, as John testifies.
sources.quote: although there be one Son by nature, True and Only-begotten, we too become sons, not as He in nature and truth, but according to the grace of Him that calleth
sources.raw_question: Are believers sons and gods in the same sense as the Son of God is Son and God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. By saying 'thy Son,' Christ asserted that he is God's Son in nature, not in name only. Many are sons of God by adoption, but he is God's true and own Son by origin, born and not created. The centurion's confession that he was truly the Son of God confirms this.
sources.quote: For He is God’s true and own Son, by origin and not by adoption, not by name only but in truth, born and not created.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ the Son of God in the same sense as believers who are called sons of God?

question: Does calling the Father 'the only true God' in John 17:3 exclude the Son from being true God?
synthesis: All agree the text does not exclude the Son, but their grounds differ. Athanasius says 'only true' excludes false gods, not Him who is the Truth, and that Christ ranks Himself with the Father by adding 'and Jesus Christ'; Novatian, Hilary and Bickersteth likewise stress that Christ is joined with the Father in the knowledge that is eternal life. Hilary also argues that the Son shares the one true nature by birth, so the Father's sole true deity is the very ground of the Son's. Bickersteth adds 1 John 5:20, where the Son is called the true God. Waterland follows Novatian and antiquity: he says the Son is tacitly included as partaker of the same nature, or the Father is 'only true God' primarily, not exclusively, and he turns the text against the Arians, who must admit two true Gods.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. These texts prove only that the Father is sometimes called the only true God, not that he is so called in opposition to the Son. The phrase may be set against idols only, as all antiquity held. Or it may mean that the Father is primarily, not exclusively, the only true God, as the first Person and the Root and Fountain of the other two. Novatian applied the title to both Father and Son, since both are joined in the same sentence and eternal life depends on knowing each.
sources.quote: It may be meant in opposition to idols only, as all antiquity has thought; or it may signify, that the Father is 4primarily, not exclusively, the only true God, as the first Person of the blessed Trinity, the Root. and Fountain of the other two.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father 'the only true God' in John 17:3 and similar texts exclude the Son from being the only true God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eighthly, John xvii. 3. and the Like. Our Lord's divinity cannot interfere with His Father's prerogatives, as the One God, which were so earnestly upheld by the Son. 'One' is used in contrast to false gods and idols, not to the Son, through whom the Father spoke. Our Lord adds His Name to the Father's, as included in Him. The Father the First, not as if the Son were not First too, but as Origin.
sources.answer: No. The phrase is said not to deny Him who said 'I am the Truth,' but to exclude those who by nature are not true, i.e. false gods. Christ immediately adds 'and Jesus Christ whom Thou didst send,' ranking Himself with the Father, which a creature could not do, since there is no fellowship between the True and the not true.
sources.quote: If then the Father be called the only true God, this is said not to the denial of Him who said, ‘I am the Truth,’ but of those on the other hand who by nature are not true, as the Father and His Word are.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father 'the only true God' (John 17:3) deny that the Son is true God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: The Son is tacitly included in the phrase 'only true God' because he is intimately united to the Father as partaker of the same divine nature. What would be strange is the Arian position, which must either let a creature count as God or admit two Gods in the face of the text. The Catholic confession of one God fits the text better than its opponents' views.
sources.quote: We can give a reason why the Son was tacitly included, being so intimately united to the Father, as partaker of the same divine nature
sources.raw_question: How can the Son be God if Scripture calls the Father the only true God, without excluding the Son from the one Godhead?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. In John 17:3 Jesus Christ is joined with the Father in the knowledge that is eternal life. In 1 John 5:20 the very same title, 'the true God' (ho alēthinos Theos), is applied to the Son: 'This is the true God and eternal life.' Christ is also the image of the invisible God and the express image of His Person. So the title belongs to the Son as well as the Father.
sources.quote: His Son, Jesus Christ. This (person) is the true God (ουτός εστιν ο αληθινος Θεος) and eternal life. – 1 John 5:20.
sources.raw_question: Does John 17:3, which calls the Father 'the only true God,' exclude Jesus Christ from being the true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The heretics read 'only true God' as solitariness excluding the Son, but by these very words Christ proclaims himself true God in the nature of the only true God. What is excluded is a true God of a foreign nature, not the Son who shares the one nature by birth.
sources.quote: But by these very words He proclaims Himself plainly to be true God in the nature of the only true God.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ calling the Father 'the only true God' in John 17:3 exclude the Son from being true God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. The text cannot hurt those who acknowledge only one God, of which the Son is a partaker. It sits far worse with the Arians, who admit two true Gods by calling the Son true God with true divine power and dominion. The Son is tacitly included because he is intimately united to the Father in the same divine nature.
sources.quote: If you can reconcile two true Gods with the doctrine of that text ; sure, we need not despair, nor have any thing to fear from that text, who agree
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father 'the only true God' exclude the Son from being true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. In the words "Thee, the only true God" the Son pays due honour to his Father. By adding "and Jesus Christ Whom Thou hast sent" he joins himself to the true Godhead, since eternal life rests on knowing both. The terms Sender and Sent imply no difference in Godhead. They guide us to confess the two as Begetter and Begotten.
sources.quote: these terms of Sender and of Sent are not intended, under any semblance of distinction or discrimination, to convey a difference between the true Godhead of Father and of Son
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father "the only true God" in John 17:3 exclude Jesus Christ from true Godhead?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Immediately after 'Thee the only true God' Christ adds 'and Him Whom Thou didst send, even Jesus Christ,' so belief in Christ is joined to belief in the only true God as the condition of eternal life. Just as the Father's being the one God does not stop Christ from being the one Lord, the Father's one true Godhead leaves Christ none the less true God.
sources.quote: The fact that God the Father is one, leaves Christ none the less the one Lord: and similarly the Father’s one true Godhead makes Christ none the less true God
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's calling the Father 'the only true God' in John 17:3 exclude Christ himself from being true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: The Father's being the only true God is the very ground of the Son's true deity. The Church confesses Christ true God because it confesses the Father the only true God, since the Son was born God from the living God by a natural birth. By the truth of that nature he cannot be separated from the only true God.
sources.quote: It confesses Christ true God, because it confesses the Father the only true God. Thus the fact that God the Father is the only true God constitutes Christ also true God.
sources.raw_question: How does the Father's being the only true God bear on the Son's being true God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again from the Gospel He Proves Christ to Be God.
sources.answer: Yes. By linking himself to the Father in the rule of saving faith, Christ wished to be understood as God also. Had he been only man, he would have said 'the man Jesus Christ' and placed himself among men. He is silent about his humanity because no one doubts it. He joins himself to God in order to establish the formula of his divinity for believers.
sources.quote: nor did Christ deliver Himself to us as man only, but associated Himself with God, as He wished to be understood by this conjunction to be God also, as He is
sources.raw_question: Does John 17:3, which joins 'the only true God' with 'Jesus Christ whom Thou hast sent', imply that Jesus Christ is God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. The heretics take the text in isolation. The same Christ also says 'all things that are Mine are Thine, and Thine are Mine.' The apparent variance is explained by distinguishing his gradual revelation from the full expression of his nature and power.
sources.quote: a difference so wide as that between Father, all things that are Mine are Thine, and Thine are Mine, and That they may know Thee, the only true God
sources.raw_question: Does John 17:3, 'that they should know Thee the only true God,' mean that the Father alone is true God and the Son is neither true nor God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Following Novatian, the title of the only true God applies to both Father and Son, since they are joined in the same sentence and eternal life is made to depend on knowing the one as much as the other. The exclusive term 'only' does not carry the force against the Son that the Arian reading supposes.
sources.quote: both, since they are joined together in the same sentence, and eternal life is made to depend upon the knowing of one, as much as of the other.
sources.raised_by_detail: Dr. Clarke's defender (Dr. Whitby/the Modester Pleader)
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father 'the only true God' in John 17:3 exclude the Son from being true God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eighthly, John xvii. 3. and the Like. Our Lord's divinity cannot interfere with His Father's prerogatives, as the One God, which were so earnestly upheld by the Son. 'One' is used in contrast to false gods and idols, not to the Son, through whom the Father spoke. Our Lord adds His Name to the Father's, as included in Him. The Father the First, not as if the Son were not First too, but as Origin.
sources.answer: No. It excludes those who are not true by nature, not Him who said 'I am the Truth.' Christ at once added 'and Jesus Christ whom Thou didst send,' ranking Himself with the Father, which a creature could not do. This shows He is of the Father's nature, true Offspring of the true Father, as John also says, 'This is the True God.'
sources.quote: by adding Himself to the Father, He has shewn that He is of the Father's nature; and He has given us to know that of the True Father He is True Offspring.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father 'the only true God' in John 17:3 exclude Jesus Christ from true deity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Eternal life consists in confessing both the only true God and Jesus Christ. Christ cannot be separated from the true God in our faith when he is not separable from him in our salvation. Christ omits all his usual titles here and names only 'Jesus Christ', so that name carries the full sense of 'God'.
sources.quote: how, pray, can Christ be separated from the true God for our faith, when He is not separable for our salvation?
sources.raw_question: Does John 17:3, 'that they should know Thee, the only true God, and Him Whom Thou didst send, Jesus Christ', separate Christ from the true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Christ immediately joins himself to the Father as an object of the faith that gives eternal life. The Father's being the one God does not stop Christ from being the one Lord. In the same way, the Father's one true Godhead leaves Christ none the less true God.
sources.quote: The fact that God the Father is one, leaves Christ none the less the one Lord: and similarly the Father’s one true Godhead makes Christ none the less true God
sources.raw_question: If the Father is called 'the only true God', does that leave no room for Christ to be true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Eternal life consists in knowing the Father together with Jesus Christ, so there is no eternal life in confessing the Father without the Son. Moreover, the only true God glorifies Christ in Himself. So Christ is not outside or estranged from the only true God but is contained in His glory.
sources.quote: For if the Father glorifies Him in Himself, and the Father is the only true God, Christ is not outside the only true God, since the Father, Who is the only true God, glorifies in Himself Christ, Who is raised into the glory of God.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father "the only true God" in John 17:3 exclude Christ from being true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. By these very words Christ proclaims Himself to be true God in the nature of the only true God. Read in continuity with the preceding discourse, where He says that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father and that He is in the Father and the Father in Him, the passage shows that the Son shares the one true divine nature rather than standing outside it.
sources.quote: But by these very words He proclaims Himself plainly to be true God in the nature of the only true God.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer to the Father as "the only true God" (John 17:3) exclude the Son from being true God?

question: In what sense is the Father greater than the Son in John 14:28 ('The Father is greater than I'), and does this prove that the Son is inferior to the Father by nature?
synthesis: All agree the text does not make the Son inferior in nature, but they ground the Father's being greater differently. Augustine, Bickersteth and Owen refer it to the Son's servant form, human nature or mediatorial state, which Owen calls an economical inferiority. Athanasius instead refers it to the Son's being generated from the Father, arguing that 'greater' rather than 'better' shows the Son is proper to the Father's essence; Hilary combines both grounds (the Father as Giver and Begetter, and the Son's self-emptying in the Incarnation) and adds that such sayings must be read in light of their occasion and of texts like 'I and the Father are One.'

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: The Father is greater as Giver and Begetter. He makes another to be all that he himself is, imparts to the Son by birth the image of his unbegotten nature, and restores him from the servant's form to the form of God. This greatness lies in the prerogative of giving, not in any inferiority of the Son's nature.
sources.quote: for manifestly He is greater, Who makes another to be all that He Himself is, Who imparts to the Son by the mystery of the birth the image of His own unbegotten nature, Who begets Him from Himself into His own form
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Father greater than the Son, according to John 14:28 'The Father is greater than I'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > By What Rule in the Scriptures It is Understood that the Son is Now Equal and Now Less.
sources.answer: No. The saying refers to the form of a servant, in which the Son is less than the Father. In the form of God, the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal to the Father, since neither of them is a creature.
sources.quote: but according to the form of a servant He is less than the Father, because He Himself has said, “My Father is greater than I;”
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "My Father is greater than I" prove that the Son is by nature inferior to the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: The Father is greater in rank only with respect to Christ as man, mediator, and the Father's apostle and servant, a position the Son took voluntarily when he stooped from his throne. John 5:18-29 proves his equality of nature, shown in cooperation with the Father, self-existence, infinite knowledge and universal trust.
sources.quote: Inferiority of rank as man, as mediator, as the apostle and servant of his Father, – having for us spontaneously stooped from the throne of his glory, – is asserted in the first quotation: equality of nature
sources.raw_question: How can the Father be greater than the Son (John 14:28) if the Son is equal with God (John 5:18)?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. The same Speaker also says 'I and the Father are One.' Hilary explains such contrasts by attending to the questions Christ was answering, the times he spoke, and the partial knowledge he chose to impart. He does not force the circumstances to fit a literal reading of isolated words.
sources.quote: that for instance between The Father is greater than I, and I and the Father are One
sources.raw_question: Does 'The Father is greater than I' prove that the Son lacks the dignity and nature of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Christ spoke of the Father as greater in respect of his present condition in the form of a servant, carrying on the work of mediation. Because it might be supposed that in that humbled state he could not hold his sheep, he committed them also to the Father's hand, from which none can take them. The inferiority is economical, tied to his mediatorial state, not a denial of his own power to keep them.
sources.quote: because he was then in the form of a servant, and it might be supposed that he might not be able to hold them, he tells them true, as to his present condition of carrying on the work of mediation, his “Father was greater than he;”
sources.raw_question: How can Christ say in John 14:28 that the Father is greater than he, given that he is equal with the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. The Son, having freely emptied himself of his glory (not his Godhead) and taken the form of a servant, spoke as the man Christ Jesus looking forward to his return from afflicted humanity to the Father's glory. Such language is exactly what one would expect from the incarnate Son in his state of humiliation, and does not deny his essential equality as God.
sources.quote: how otherwise could He describe his return from that present estate of afflicted humanity, than in such or such like words – “If ye loved me ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father, for my Father is greater than I.”
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement "my Father is greater than I" (John 14:28) prove that the Son is by nature inferior to the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. Christ says 'greater,' not 'better,' lest we think Him foreign to the Father's nature. The Father is 'greater' not in magnitude or time but because the Son is generated from the Father Himself, and the very use of 'greater' shows the Son is proper to the Father's essence.
sources.quote: but ‘greater,’ not indeed in greatness, nor in time, but because of His generation from the Father Himself, nay, in saying ‘greater’ He again shows that He is proper to His essence.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'My Father is greater than I' (John 14:28) imply that the Son is foreign to the Father's nature or inferior in being?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Those who argue so neglect the mystery of the divine birth and of God's emptying Himself and taking flesh. The Son's asking for glory, fearing death and dying belong to that self-emptying, not to an inferior divine nature.
sources.quote: Neglecting the mystery of the Divine birth, and the mystery of God’s emptying Himself and taking flesh, they will argue the inferiority of His nature from His assertion that the Father is the greater.
sources.raw_question: Does "The Father is greater than I" prove that the Son is inferior in nature to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The Father is greater because he is Father, and because he glorifies the manhood the Son assumed. But the Son, because he is Son, is not less. His nature by birth does not allow him to be less, and he receives back his own glory in the Father. To read the saying as making the Son inferior turns the mystery of the Incarnation into a blasphemy.
sources.quote: The Father therefore is greater, because He is Father: but the Son, because He is Son, is not less. By the birth of the Son the Father is constituted greater: the nature that is His by birth, does not suffer the Son to be less.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'The Father is greater than I' (John 14:28) mean that the Son is less than the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Less Than the Father, and Than Himself.
sources.answer: No. Such texts are said of Christ according to the flesh, that is, in the form of a servant he took for our salvation, and they are wrongly transferred to his eternal substance. In the form of God he remains equal to the Father, so Scripture can truly say both that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Father is greater.
sources.quote: have endeavored to transfer those things which are said of Jesus Christ according to the flesh, to that substance of His which was eternal before the incarnation, and is eternal
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement "My Father is greater than I" prove that the Son is by nature inferior to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The saying is spoken by the incarnate Son, who emptied himself of the form of God and took the form of a servant, while the Father remained in his incorrupt eternity without taking flesh. The Church does not confess two Unbegotten or two Fathers, so the Father's being greater refers to the Incarnation and to his being the Begetter, not to an inequality of nature.
sources.quote: can you be ignorant that the Incarnation for your salvation was an emptying of the form of God, and that the Father, unaffected by this assumption of human conditions, abode in the blessed eternity of His own incorrupt nature without taking our flesh?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement "The Father is greater than I" (John 14:28) disprove the Son's equality and unity of nature with the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Whether One or the Three Persons Together are Called the Only God.
sources.answer: No. The words are spoken by the Word already made flesh. The Father is greater than him only according to his humiliation, that is, his human nature. In his divinity the Son has one being with the Father.
sources.quote: especially since it is the Word already made flesh that speaks; and according to this His humiliation also, the Father is greater than He, as He says, “for my Father is greater than I;”
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'my Father is greater than I' (John 14:28) deny the Son's equality with the Father?

question: Does calling the Son 'the first-born of all creation' (Colossians 1:15) mean that he is himself a creature, the first among created things?
synthesis: All agree the title does not make the Son a creature, but they ground this differently. Athanasius argues from the wording ('of the whole creation', not 'of the other creatures') and from his being Only-begotten, and takes 'first-born' to refer to his condescension by which creatures are adopted into sonship. Gregory of Nyssa refers the title wholly to the saving economy, the Son being first-born of the new creation in Christ. Bickersteth and Warfield instead read 'first-born' as priority to all creation (Bickersteth adding lordship and contrasting πρωτότοκος with πρωτόκτιστος), while Hilary, like Bickersteth and Athanasius, stresses that all things were created in and through him, so he is their origin, not one of their products.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eighthly, John xvii. 3. and the Like. Our Lord's divinity cannot interfere with His Father's prerogatives, as the One God, which were so earnestly upheld by the Son. 'One' is used in contrast to false gods and idols, not to the Son, through whom the Father spoke. Our Lord adds His Name to the Father's, as included in Him. The Father the First, not as if the Son were not First too, but as Origin.
sources.answer: No. 'First-born' is said to show that all things are framed and adopted into sonship through the Son, not to rank Him with creatures. As the Father is First, so the Son is also First, as Image of the First and because the First is in Him, and as Offspring of the Father.
sources.quote: when the Son is called First-born, this is done not for the sake of ranking Him with the creation, but to prove the framing and adoption of all things through the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'First-born' rank Him with creation as the first of creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says 'First-born of the whole creation,' not 'First-born above the rest of the creatures,' which shows he is other than the whole creation. Just as Reuben is called first-born of Jacob's children and not of 'all the children of Jacob,' the phrasing marks distinction, not membership. If the Word were a creature, Scripture would have said he was first-born of other creatures.
sources.quote: if He is simply ‘First-born of the whole creation,’ then He is other than the whole creation; for he says not, ‘He is First-born above the rest of the creatures,’ lest He be reckoned to be as one of the creatures
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'First-born of all creation' (Colossians 1:15) imply that he is himself one of the creatures?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Had Paul meant that Christ was created he would have written 'first created' (πρωτόκτιστος), not 'firstborn' (πρωτότοκος), as Chrysostom observes. 'Firstborn' imports lordship and dignity, or priority to all creation, meaning 'begotten before the worlds.' The next verse says all things were created by him. If he were a creature he would have made himself, which is absurd.
sources.quote: it absolutely resists the interpretation that Christ is himself a creation of God, for then it would have been πρωτόκτιστος, first created, as Chrysostom observes (see Scott), not πρωτότοκος, firstborn.
sources.raw_question: Does calling Christ 'the firstborn of all creation' (Col. 1:15) mean that he is a created being?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The phrase may convey no hint of coming into being. It may merely assert Christ's priority of existence over all creation.
sources.quote: such a phrase as “the first-begotten of all creation” (Col. i. 15) may convey no intimation of coming into being, but merely assert priority of existence
sources.raw_question: Does Colossians 1:15, calling Christ "the firstborn of all creation," imply that he came into being?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. He cannot be merely the first of the creatures, since He is the 'Only-begotten.' 'First-born' refers to the Word's condescension to creation, by which He became the Brother of many. Paul gives the reason, 'for in Him all things were created,' which shows He is other than the creatures and is their Creator.
sources.quote: But if all the creatures were created in Him, He is other than the creatures, and is not a creature, but the Creator of the creatures.
sources.raw_question: Does calling Christ 'First-born of all creation' place Him among the creatures as merely the first in time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then again admirably discusses the term πρωτότοκος as it is four times employed by the Apostle.
sources.answer: No. The Apostle does not use 'first-born' of the Son's eternal nature. It is a name the Son 'once received for our sakes' when He entered the world and became first-born of the dead, of His brethren, and of all creation, in order to restore humanity. All four uses of the title point to this saving economy, not to a shared created essence.
sources.quote: does not, when He comes again into the world as He that judges the world in righteousness, as the prophecy saith, cast off the name of the first-begotten, which He once received for our sakes
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'first-born of all creation' (Colossians 1:15) imply that the Son is of the same essence as creation, and therefore not of one essence with God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He further very appositely expounds the meaning of the term “Only-Begotten,“ and of the term “First born,“ four times used by the Apostle.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that the title "first-born" must carry one and the same meaning in all four Pauline uses, and in the other uses it plainly refers to Christ's leading the way in the new creation of humanity. So "first-born of all creation" refers to His being first-born of the new creation of men in Christ through regeneration, not to His being the first product of the original creation.
sources.quote: Accordingly whatever view we entertain concerning this title in the other combinations, the same we shall in consistency apply to the phrase “first-born of all creation.” For since the title is one and the same it must needs be that the meaning conveyed is also one.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's calling Christ the "first-born of all creation" mean the Son is the first creature, differing from other creatures only by priority in time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then again admirably discusses the term πρωτότοκος as it is four times employed by the Apostle.
sources.answer: No. The 'creation' of which he is first-born is the new creation in Christ, made necessary after the first creation was spoiled by disobedience. The Word who once formed man from dust took flesh from the Virgin and was himself 'created' in the economy. So he became the first-fruits and first-born of those regenerated and raised.
sources.quote: Of this new creation therefore in Christ, which He Himself began, He was called the first-born, being the first-fruits of all, both of those begotten into life, and of those quickened by resurrection of the dead
sources.raw_question: Does Christ being 'the first-born of all creation' mean the Son was the first thing created before the rest of creation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. He is called first-born because all things were created in him and through him. He is before all things, all things consist for him, and the creation of all things in himself may be referred to no one else. He therefore holds in himself the origin of the universe rather than being one of its products.
sources.quote: He is accordingly the first-born of every creature because in Him all things were created. And lest any one should dare to refer to any other than Him the creation of all things in Himself
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'the first-born of every creature' (Colossians 1:15) mean that he is himself a creature?

question: Is the Son eternal, or was there a time when the Son was not and the Father existed without him?
synthesis: Irenaeus, Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Athanasius and Novatian all agree that the Son is eternal and never was not, but they argue on different grounds. Irenaeus points to the Son having always revealed the Father. Hilary argues that a Father once without the Son would be either imperfect or superfluous, and that what is born before times eternal is always born. Gregory reasons that the Father would otherwise once have lacked his Power, Wisdom and Life, and that the Father's bosom was never void of the Son. Athanasius appeals to Scripture's use of 'ever' for the Word and to the eternal radiance of an eternal Light. Novatian argues that the Son is always in the Father because the Father was always Father, adding that 'always' marks him as born, not unborn.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: The Son eternally co-exists with the Father, from of old and from the beginning. For this reason he has always revealed the Father, not only to men but to angels, archangels, powers and all to whom he wills that God be revealed.
sources.quote: But the Son, eternally co-existing with the Father, from of old, yea, from the beginning, always reveals the Father to Angels, Archangels, Powers, Virtues
sources.raw_question: Has the Son existed eternally with the Father, or did he come into being later?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: The Son is eternal. Hilary confesses the Father as 'Father of the Eternal and Only-begotten God' and the Lord Jesus Christ as 'born of Thee from everlasting.' The Father alone is without birth. The Son's birth, however, is everlasting and not a temporal beginning.
sources.quote: of Thee, O God Eternal, Father of the Eternal and Only-begotten God, Who alone art without birth, and of the One Lord Jesus Christ, born of Thee from everlasting
sources.raw_question: Is the Son eternal, or did his birth from the Father have a beginning in time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. He who is in the bosom of the Father does not allow us to conceive that bosom as ever void of Him. He is not one of the things that come into it from without, but is conceived as always in the eternity of the Father's Godhead, not waiting to arise by creation.
sources.quote: But surely He Who is in the bosom of the Father does not permit us to conceive the bosom of the Father as ever void of Himself.
sources.raw_question: Was there ever a time when the Father's bosom was without the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: He is eternal. Since Scripture reserves temporal terms for creatures but uses 'ever' of the Word, the Son did not come from nothing and is not numbered among originated things. He is the Father's eternal Image and Word, never having not been, as the eternal radiance of an eternal Light.
sources.quote: the Son did not come out of nothing, nor is in the number of originated things at all, but is the Father’s Image and Word eternal, never having not been, but being ever, as the eternal Radiance of a Light which is eternal
sources.raw_question: Is the Son eternal, or did he come into being out of nothing as one of the originated things?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. To say the Father once existed without the Son would charge Him either with imperfection, as being unable to generate before, or with superfluousness after the generation. Eternal generation therefore means that the Father is the eternal Father of the Only-begotten, who was born of Him before times eternal.
sources.quote: For we must never assert that Thou didst once exist without Thy Son, lest we should be reproaching Thee either with imperfection, as then unable to generate, or with superfluousness after the generation.
sources.raw_question: Was there ever a time when God the Father existed without the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: The Son ever was and is and never was not. Because the Father is everlasting, his Word and Wisdom must also be everlasting. The Arian claim that God became a Father afterwards is rejected.
sources.quote: And He ever was and is and never was not. For the Father being everlasting, His Word and His Wisdom must be everlasting.
sources.raw_question: Was there a time when the Son was not, or is the Son eternal?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. What is born before time is always born, since what exists before time eternal always exists. And what has always been born cannot at any time have been non-existent, because non-existence at a given time contradicts eternity of existence.
sources.quote: For what is born before time is always born; since that which exists before time eternal, always exists. But what has always been born, cannot at any time have had no existence; since non-existence at a given time is directly contrary to eternity of existence.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being born before times eternal mean that He has always been born and always existed?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: He has always been in the Father. Being begotten of the Father, he is before all time, and no time can be assigned to one who is before all time; he is always in the Father unless the Father were not always Father. Yet 'always' is said to show him born, not unborn.
sources.quote: But He who is before all time must be said to have been always in the Father; for no time can be assigned to Him who is before all time.
sources.raw_question: Has the Son always existed in the Father, or was there a time when he was not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: The Son is contemplated in the Father from all eternity. Since Scripture calls the Son the Power, Wisdom, Truth, Light and Life of God, to say the Father once existed without the Son would mean the Father was once without these excellences. That is impious and absurd, because the Divine nature always possesses what is excellent.
sources.quote: if the Son, as the Scripture saith, is the Power of God, and Wisdom, and Truth, and Light, and Sanctification, and Peace, and Life, and the like, then before the Son existed, according to the view of the heretics, these things also had no existence at all.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son exist eternally with the Father, or was there a time when the Father existed without the Son?

question: If the Son is called an 'Angel' or 'Messenger' in Scripture, does that mean he is a created angel and not truly God?
synthesis: All agree that the title 'Angel' does not exclude Christ's deity, but they ground this differently. Augustine, Novatian (in some passages), Gregory of Nyssa and Waterland say 'angel' names an office or work of conveying the Father's will, not a nature; Gregory adds the analogy of a word as messenger of the mind, and Augustine extends the title to the Spirit as well. Novatian also argues that the same Scripture calls him Lord and God, and that since lesser angels are called gods, Christ must be all the more. Hilary says the title marks the Son's distinction as one sent from God, while the added titles Lord and God secure his deity, and Waterland explicitly follows Novatian in calling it inconsistent to grant 'angel' and deny 'God'.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Appearance in the Bush.
sources.answer: Yes. 'Angel' in Greek means messenger, and the term describes a work, not a nature. Christ is called 'the Angel of Great Counsel' by the prophet. The Spirit's work of showing things to come fits the name too, though both the Son and the Spirit are God and Lord of the angels.
sources.quote: we read most evidently of the Lord Jesus Christ in the prophet, that He is called “the Angel of Great Counsel,” while both the Holy Spirit and the Son of God is God and Lord of the angels
sources.raw_question: Can the Son or the Holy Spirit be called an 'angel' without implying they are created angels?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God Also Appeared to Jacob as an Angel; Namely, the Son of God.
sources.answer: No. The same Scripture that calls Christ an Angel also calls him God and invokes him as God in blessing. So whoever is willing to call Christ an Angel should not hesitate to call him God as well.
sources.quote: Let no one, therefore, who does not shrink from speaking of Christ as an Angel, thus shrink from pronouncing Him God also
sources.raw_question: If Christ is called an Angel in Scripture, does that rule out calling him God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God Also Appeared to Jacob as an Angel; Namely, the Son of God.
sources.answer: No. Angels subjected to Christ are themselves called gods. It is unfitting to deny to the greater what is granted to the lesser, so Christ, to whom all angels are subject, must much more rightly be called God.
sources.quote: For if an angel who is subjected to Christ is exalted as God, much more, and more consistently, shall Christ, to whom all angels are subjected, be said to be God.
sources.raw_question: Even if Christ were properly an angel, would that prevent him from being called God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: He is called angel, meaning messenger, because of his office, not his nature. He became the 'angel of great counsel' and declares the bosom of the Father, as John teaches. Scripture shows him to be not only man, and not only angel, but also God.
sources.quote: to Him also is applied the name of angel, since He became the “angel of great counsel.” And He is the angel, in that He declares the bosom of the Father, as John sets forth.
sources.raw_question: In what sense can the Son of God be called an 'angel' without ceasing to be God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: The title 'Angel of God' clearly marks the distinction between the Persons, since he is sent from God. The titles Lord and God are added so that he receives the honour due to him. This also keeps us from supposing that he who is God is only an angel. The title protects against the error that God is solitary while still affirming the Son's deity.
sources.quote: To discriminate clearly between the Persons, He is called the Angel of God; He Who is God from God is also the Angel of God, but, that He may have the honour which is His due, He is entitled also Lord and God.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son called 'Angel of God' in the Old Testament if he is truly God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: The title is given on account of His operation of conveying the Father's will, not because of an inferior nature. Just as our word is the messenger of the movements of the mind, so the true Word who was in the beginning is styled Angel when He announces His Father's will.
sources.quote: the true Word that was in the beginning, when He announces the will of His own Father, is styled “Angel” (or “Messenger”), a title given to Him on account of the operation of conveying the message
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son called "Angel" or "Messenger" if He is truly God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > It is Proved from the Scriptures that Christ Was Called an Angel. But Yet It is Shown from Other Parts of Holy Scripture that He is God Also.
sources.answer: No. Even if a heretic insists Christ was properly an angel, it follows that he is God, since angels subjected to Christ are themselves called gods. If an inferior angel can be called god without blasphemy, much more Christ, who is greater and better than all angels, must be called God. What is conceded to the lesser cannot be denied to the greater.
sources.quote: For if an angel who is subjected to Christ is exalted as God, much more, and more consistently, shall Christ, to whom all angels are subjected, be said to be God. For it is not suitable to nature, that what is conceded to the lesser should be denied to the greater.
sources.raw_question: If Christ is called an angel in the Old Testament appearances, does that mean he is merely an angel and not God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Yes, the same Person can be both, and it is not consistent to grant one title and deny the other. Christ is God because he is the Son of God, and he is an angel because he is sent to reveal his Father's will. Novatian says heretics who admit Christ is an angel but refuse to call him God go against Scripture.
sources.quote: but it may comport with the Person of Christ to be God, as “ the Son of God, and to be an angel too, as sent to reveal his “ Father’s will
sources.raw_question: Can the same Person be both an angel and God, and is it consistent to call Christ an angel while denying that he is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: Yes. The heretics who grant that Christ was an angel but refuse to call Him God set themselves against Scripture. In the Old Testament the one who came to visit the human race is called both Lord and God. Since Christ is in so many ways proved to be God, there is no reason to hesitate to call Him God.
sources.quote: while they say that they believe Christ to have been also an angel, they are unwilling to declare Him to have been also God, when they read in the Old Testament that He often came to visit the human race
sources.raw_question: If Christ is acknowledged to have appeared as an angel in the Old Testament, must he also be acknowledged as God?

question: If the Father is God and the Son is God, are they two Gods or one God?
synthesis: All agree that Father and Son are one God, not two, but they give different grounds. Hilary rests the unity on one indivisible nature, shared through the Son's birth, which the single name 'God' signifies; Gregory of Nyssa argues that only a difference of essence or operation could multiply Gods. Basil uses the analogy of a king and his image, adding that the Son is by nature what an image is by imitation; Augustine argues from Paul's 'one spirit' with the Lord to the far closer inseparable union of Father and Son; Waterland appeals mainly to the testimony of the Ante-Nicene writers.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The one name 'God' is the name of one indivisible nature, and it is inherent in each. So Father and Son are One both in nature and in name. The Son's birth from the divine nature preserves this unity rather than producing a second God.
sources.quote: The one name does not embrace two Gods; for the one name God is the name of one indivisible nature. For since the Father is God and the Son is God, and that name which is peculiar to the Divine nature is inherent in Each, therefore the Two are One.
sources.raw_question: If both the Father and the Son are called God, are there two Gods?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. Hilary holds that true God the Father and true God the Son must be confessed as one true God. This unity rests on their sharing one nature, not on merging the Persons into one, so the distinction of Father and Son is kept.
sources.quote: true God the Father and true God the Son, must be confessed as One true God, by unity of nature and not by confusion of Persons
sources.raw_question: Can the Father and the Son both be called true God without there being two Gods?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Same Argument Continued.
sources.answer: No. The name God belongs to each, yet both together are not two Gods but one God. If even a human spirit cleaving to the Lord becomes 'one spirit' with Him though their substances differ, much more are Father and Son one where the union is absolutely inseparable and eternal.
sources.quote: whether we say God of God in such way that this name belongs to each, yet not so that both together are two Gods, but one God
sources.raw_question: If the Father is God and the Son is God, are they two Gods?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: Because no difference either of nature or of operation is seen in the Godhead. Only a diversity of essence would extend the number to a plurality of Gods. The divine nature is single and unchanging and rejects all diversity in essence, so it does not admit the signification of multitude. God is therefore one, though each Person is proclaimed God.
sources.quote: The Father is God: the Son is God: and yet by the same proclamation God is One, because no difference either of nature or of operation is contemplated in the Godhead.
sources.raw_question: If the Father is God and the Son is God, why are they not two Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: Yes. The Ante-Nicene writers repeatedly called the Father and the Son one God. Waterland has cited them more than once, and Dr. Fiddes gives some of the testimonies at length.
sources.quote: That Father and Son (or any two Persons) ought not to be called one God. I have referred to the Ante-Nicene writers, who so called them, more than once.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father and the Son be properly called one God?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: Because they are one by community of nature, as we speak of a king and the king's image, not two kings. The majesty and glory are not divided, and the sovereignty over us is one. The difference is that what the image is by imitation, the Son is by nature, and the union consists in the communion of the Godhead.
sources.quote: How, then, if one and one, are there not two Gods? Because we speak of a king, and of the king’s image, and not of two kings. The majesty is not cloven in two, nor the glory divided.
sources.raw_question: If the Father and the Son are 'one and one' as Persons, why are they not two Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland repeatedly points to Ante-Nicene writers who expressly called Father and Son one God, and further testimonies are collected in Dr. Fiddes. Denying this therefore runs against antiquity.
sources.quote: That Father and Son (or any two Persons) ought not to be called one God. I have referred to the Ante-Nicene writers, who so called them, more than once.
sources.raw_question: May the Father and the Son, two distinct Persons, properly be called one God?

question: Whom did Isaiah see in his vision of the Lord of hosts enthroned (Isaiah 6): was it the Son of God, as John 12:41 indicates, and does the vision also refer to the Father and the Holy Spirit?
synthesis: All agree that John 12:41 refers Isaiah's vision to the Son, but they differ in scope. Bickersteth (in two places) and Owen use it simply to identify Christ as the Lord of hosts. Waterland reads it as showing Father and Son as one holy Lord of hosts, so it marks both the distinction of Persons and the unity of Godhead. Gregory of Nyssa and Ambrose add Paul's attribution of the passage to the Holy Spirit and conclude the vision belongs to all three Persons. Gregory makes this a general rule for every theophany, while Ambrose grounds it in the one majesty and rule of the Trinity.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: Yes. As may be inferred from John 12:41, the 'Lord of hosts' Isaiah saw includes the Son. Isaiah thus makes Father and Son both one holy Lord of hosts. This signifies at once the distinction of Persons and the unity of Godhead.
sources.quote: the Prophet Isaiah, as may be inferred from 4 St. John, makes them both to be one holy, holy, Lord of hosts, therein signifying both the distinction of Persons and unity of Godhead
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah's vision of the thrice-holy Lord of hosts refer to both the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: All three. Tradition referred the vision to the Father, John refers it to the Son ("when he saw His glory"), and Paul attributes the same passage to the Holy Spirit ("Well spoke the Holy Ghost by Esaias"). This shows that every divine vision, theophany, and word spoken in the Person of God is to be understood of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: every specially divine vision, every theophany, every word uttered in the Person of God, is to be understood to refer to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Who appeared in Isaiah's vision of the Lord on the throne high and lifted up: the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah says he saw the King, Jehovah of hosts. John says Isaiah said these things when he saw Christ's glory and spoke of him. The message John cites shows it is the same occasion. So Jesus is the Jehovah of hosts before whom the seraphim veiled their faces.
sources.quote: The message recorded determines the occasion to be the same. Therefore, Jesus Christ, of whom the inspired apostle is speaking, is Jehovah of hosts, before whom the seraphim veiled their faces in lowliest adoration.
sources.raw_question: Does John 12:41 show that the Jehovah of hosts whom Isaiah saw in his temple vision was Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah saw 'the King, the Lord of hosts,' and John expressly says Isaiah said these things when he saw Christ's glory and spoke of him. Thus Christ is the Lord of hosts.
sources.quote: These things said Esaias, when he saw his (Christ’s) glory, and spake of him. (John 12:41.)
sources.raw_question: Does John 12:41 show that the Lord of hosts whom Isaiah saw was Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXII. In proof of the Unity in Trinity the passage of Isaiah which has been cited is considered, and it is shown that there is no difference as to its sense amongst those who expound it of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Spirit. If He Who was crucified was Lord of glory, so, too, is the Holy Spirit equal in all things to the Father and the Son, and the Arians will never be able to diminish His glory.
sources.answer: All three interpretations are correct, which shows the oneness of majesty and rule in the Trinity. Many say it was the Father, Paul and Luke say the Spirit spoke, and John refers it to the Son's glory. Since the majesty and rule of Father, Son and Spirit are one, these readings do not conflict.
sources.quote: It is now possible to recognize the oneness of the majesty and rule in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For many say that it was God the Father Who was seen at that time by Isaiah.
sources.raw_question: Whom did Isaiah see in his vision of the Lord on the throne (Isaiah 6): the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen says Isaiah's vision of the thrice-holy Lord of hosts is applied to the Son in John 12:41, where John says Isaiah saw Christ's glory. So the Son is the Lord of hosts of the Old Testament.
sources.quote: And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.” Applied unto the Son, John xii. 41.
sources.raw_question: Was the 'Lord of hosts' whom Isaiah saw enthroned in his temple vision the Son of God?

question: Does 2 Corinthians 3:17, "Now the Lord is that Spirit," call the Holy Spirit Lord (and so God), rather than referring to the Son?
synthesis: All five answers agree that the verse calls the Holy Spirit Lord, but they argue from different parts of the text. Bickersteth links 'the Lord' to Jehovah in verse 16 and concludes the Spirit is the Most High God. Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine both rest on the follow-up phrase 'the Spirit of the Lord': Gregory says it keeps the reader from confusing the Spirit with the Son, while Augustine says it rules out reading the verse of the Son as incorporeal spirit. Ambrose and Basil instead argue from conversion to the Lord and transformation 'from glory to glory,' which they take as the Spirit's work.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. In verse 16 "the Lord" refers to Jehovah, into whose presence Moses entered, and so designates the Most High. The apostle continues without break, "the Lord is the Spirit," a plain affirmation that the Holy Ghost is one with the Father and the Son, very and eternal God.
sources.quote: we have in this plain, unambiguous affirmation a crowning and convincing argument that the Holy Ghost is one with the Father and the Son, – very and Eternal God.
sources.raw_question: Does 2 Corinthians 3:17, "Now the Lord is that Spirit," affirm that the Holy Spirit is the Most High God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: It refers to the Holy Spirit. Paul calls the Spirit "Lord" to show the supremacy of His nature by the honour implied in lordship. He then adds "the Spirit of the Lord" so that the reader will not confuse the Spirit with the Only-begotten, who is also called "Lord."
sources.quote: that the supremacy of His Nature may be shown by the honour implied in lordship, while at the same time he may avoid confusing in his argument the individuality of His Person
sources.raw_question: In 2 Corinthians 3:17, does "the Lord" who "is the Spirit" refer to the Holy Spirit or to the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: It calls the Holy Spirit Lord. Paul adds "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty," which rules out reading it of the Son called spirit because of his incorporeal substance. No one has ever doubted that the Spirit of the Lord is the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: lest any one should think the Son to be signified, and to be called the Spirit on account of His incorporeal substance, has gone on to say, “And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty;”
sources.raw_question: Does "Now the Lord is that Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:17) call the Holy Spirit Lord, or does it refer to the Son as an incorporeal spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIV. Besides the evidence adduced above, other passages can be brought to prove the sovereignty of the Three Persons. Two are quoted from the Epistles to the Thessalonians, and by collating other testimonies of the Scriptures it is shown that in them dominion is claimed for the Spirit as for the other Persons. Then, by quotation of another still more express passage in the second Epistle to the Corinthians, it is inferred both that the Spirit is Lord, and that where the Lord is, there is the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. The course of the passage shows that it speaks of the Holy Spirit. The Lord to whom we are converted is the Spirit, who forms us anew 'from glory to glory, as from the Lord the Spirit.' He who forms anew must receive those who are converted, so the Spirit is the Lord to whom conversion is made.
sources.quote: since it is the Lord to Whom we are converted, but the Lord is that Spirit by Whom we are formed anew, who are converted to the Lord, assuredly the Holy Ghost is pointed out
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture explicitly call the Holy Spirit 'Lord' in 2 Corinthians 3:17, 'Now the Lord is the Spirit'?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Proof from Scripture that the Spirit is called Lord.
sources.answer: Yes, it distinctly calls the Spirit Lord.
