The veil is the obscurity of the letter of the Law; turning to the Lord is passing from the letter to spiritual contemplation, which is turning to the Spirit, like Moses unveiling before God. He who fixes his gaze on the Spirit is transfigured by the Spirit's glory, 'from glory to glory.'
sources.quote: He, then, who in the reading of the Law takes away the letter and turns to the Lord,—and the Lord is now called the Spirit,—becomes moreover like Moses, who had his face glorified by the manifestation of God.
sources.raw_question: Does 2 Corinthians 3:17, 'Now the Lord is that Spirit,' distinctly call the Holy Spirit Lord, and what does turning to the Lord mean there?

question: Does Romans 9:5, which calls Christ 'over all, God blessed for ever,' teach that Christ, descended from Israel according to the flesh, is truly God?
synthesis: All five authors read Romans 9:5 as calling Christ God, but they stress different points. Hippolytus stresses that Christ remains God after becoming man, and Hilary that he is true God over creation rather than an exalted creature. Irenaeus and Owen stress that the one descended from David according to the flesh is the same one who is God over all, while Bickersteth defends the reading on grammatical grounds as the fair construction of the Greek.

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: Yes. Hippolytus says the verse declares the mystery rightly: he who is over all is God, has been born, and having been made man is yet God for ever. Christ himself confirms this when he says all things are delivered to him by the Father.
sources.quote: He who is over all, God blessed, has been born; and having been made man, He is (yet) God for ever.
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 9:5, which calls Christ 'over all, God blessed for ever,' teach that Christ is God, and that he remains God after becoming man?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. Paul calls Christ 'God over all'. This is not a creature reckoned as God but the God of created things, who is also Spirit inseparable from the Father.
sources.quote: Now that He Who is God over all is also Spirit inseparable from the Father, learn also from that very utterance of the Apostle
sources.raw_question: Is Christ called God in the true sense in Romans 9:5, rather than as an exalted creature?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The commonly received construction, that Christ is "over all, God blessed forever," is the fair and just grammatical reading, as every Greek scholar must admit.
sources.quote: “Every Greek scholar must admit, that the fair and just construction of the sentence is that which is generally received.”
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 9:5 call Christ "God blessed forever"?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture plainly says that the same Christ came from the fathers and from David as concerning the flesh, and in himself is over all, God blessed for ever. Owen says no reason can be given for refusing to believe this firmly.
sources.quote: the same Christ, as concerning the flesh, came of the fathers, of David, and, in himself, is over all, God blessed for ever.
sources.raw_question: Do Romans 1:3-4 and 9:5 teach that the same Christ is both descended from David according to the flesh and God over all?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus cites Paul saying that Christ came from the fathers according to the flesh and is God over all, blessed for ever. He uses this to show that the one born of David's line is the divine Son, not a mere man.
sources.quote: from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever.
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 9:5 teach that Christ, who came from Israel according to the flesh, is God?

question: Does the Son's being begotten (born) of the Father imply that He had a beginning, so that there was a time when He was not?
synthesis: All four authors answer no, but on different grounds. Hilary argues that birth differs from beginning and that a birth from an eternal Source is itself eternal. Athanasius (who also cites Hilary) answers the Arian argument 'He is a son, therefore He had a beginning' by saying the Son's generation is from the unoriginate Father and so is eternal. Gregory of Nyssa argues that the Son's life admits no 'sometime', using the image of brightness shining concurrently with glory and the point that being and not-being are contradictories. Waterland argues more defensively that opponents have not proved that all generation implies a beginning, and that inferring a beginning from the word 'production' is an equivocation.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. To be born and to be unborn differ only in that the one has origin from another and the other from none; being born does not entail ever having been non-existent. Where the Source of being is eternal, the birth from that Source is also eternal, so the Son is co-eternal with the Father while having Him as Source.
sources.quote: For while we declare in so many words that He was born, nevertheless we do not assert that He was ever not born
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being born of the Father imply that there was a time when the Son was not?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. The Father is eternal and the Son is eternal, and the Son has an absolute, not a limited, pre-existence. His eternity is consistent with sonship and his sonship with eternity, for his birth is a birth from everlasting. While birth implies a Father, Divinity is inseparable from eternity. The contrary paradox draws its apparent force from a purblind pagan philosophy.
sources.quote: that His eternity is consistent with sonship, and His sonship with eternity; that there was in Him no unique exemption from birth but a birth from everlasting, for, while birth implies a Father, Divinity is inseparable from eternity
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being born (begotten) imply that there was a time when he did not exist and that he was made out of nothing?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Birth differs from beginning: what begins either comes from nothing or develops from one state into another, ceasing to be what it was. The Son did not begin out of nothing to be God, nor had a prior existence of another kind; he was born as God, so his Godhead had neither beginning nor development.
sources.quote: the Son of God did not begin, out of nothing, to be God, but was born as God; nor had He an existence of another kind before the Divine.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being born of God mean that he began to exist?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. His existence did not begin out of nothing but went forth from the Eternal. The going forth is rightly called a birth, but it would be false to call it a beginning, since God's proceeding from God is entirely different from a new substance coming into existence.
sources.quote: His existence did not take its beginning out of nothing, but went forth from the Eternal; and this going forth is rightly entitled a birth, though it would be false to call it a beginning.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being born from God imply that he had a beginning or came into existence from nothing?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. The opponent has not proved, and cannot prove, that all generation implies a beginning. Unless the absurdity of eternal generation is demonstrated, the Church may sincerely and properly call the Son's generation eternal in the strict sense. The Father is the Son's principle without beginning in time, as Cyril teaches.
sources.quote: you have not proved that all generation implies beginning ; and what is more, cannot. You endeavour to make the notion of it absurd ; but, unless you can demonstrate the absurdity of it, how will you charge us with equivocation
sources.raw_question: Does all generation necessarily imply a beginning, so that the Son, being begotten, must have had a beginning?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. If the word 'production' is used at all, it is always explained in a good sense. The eternal generation is never imagined to be a temporal production, so arguing from 'production' to a beginning of the Son equivocates on the word.
sources.quote: which if we use at all, we always take care to explain to a good sense; and never once imagine, that the eternal generation is a temporal production
sources.raw_question: Is eternal generation of the Son a kind of production, i.e. a temporal bringing-into-being of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: No. The Son, being with the Father before the ages in a way that admits no 'sometime,' exists by generation yet never begins to exist. His life is neither in time nor in place, and nothing can be thought of as before Him except the Father, in whom He is.
sources.quote: He exists by generation indeed, but nevertheless He never begins to exist. His life is neither in time, nor in place.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's existing by generation from the Father mean that there was a time when the Son began to exist?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. The objector has not proved that all generation implies a beginning, and cannot prove it. Unless the absurdity of eternal generation is demonstrated, the orthodox can sincerely call it eternal without equivocation. They never imagine that eternal generation is a temporal production.
sources.quote: you have not proved that all generation implies beginning ; and what is more, cannot.
sources.raw_question: Does the generation of the Son necessarily imply that he had a beginning, so that 'eternal generation' is a contradiction?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius treats the Lord's generation like a human pedigree, as with Ishmael, who did not exist before his birth. But the Son is the brightness of the Father's glory, and brightness shines forth concurrently with glory, so 'before' and 'after' have no place; there was no time when He was not.
sources.quote: But with Him Who is “the brightness of glory,” “before” and “after” have no place: for before the brightness, of course neither was there any glory
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being begotten mean that a generation preceded His existence, so that He began at a definite point in time?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: No. Hilary, cited by the author, answers that the Only-begotten God never was not a Son, nor was anything before he was Son. Where the Father is author, there is birth, and since the author is eternal, the birth is eternal too. So the Son's birth does not mark a beginning of his existence.
sources.quote: Ubi pater auctor est, ibi et nativitas est; et vero ubi auctor æternus est, ibi et nativitatis æternitas est
sources.raised_by_detail: objectors cited by Hilary, de Trin. xii.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being born of the Father imply that he began to exist and therefore did not exist before his birth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The Son's beginning is from eternity. This is not because He has no source, but because He is the Son of the Father, Who is unbegotten from everlasting. He is born from eternity, receiving His birth from the eternal Father. Birth and eternity are therefore not in conflict.
sources.quote: She confesses the Father eternal and without beginning; she confesses also that the Son’s beginning is from eternity. Not that He has no beginning, but that He is Son of the Father Who has none
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being born require that He began to exist in time, so that eternity is incompatible with being begotten?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: No. This was the main Arian argument: 'He is a son, therefore He had a beginning,' and so 'once He was not' and 'He is from nothing.' The Catholic answer is that the Son could not be 'before His generation' because His generation is eternal, being from the Father. Creatures have a beginning in being made, but the Word has His being in no other origin than the unoriginate Father, and so exists unoriginately in Him as His offspring, not His creature.
sources.quote: He could not be before His generation because His generation is eternal, as being from the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being begotten by the Father imply that he had a beginning of existence and therefore once was not?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. His nature forbids saying that he ever began to be, because his birth lies beyond the beginnings of time. Faith confesses him existing before all ages and born in timeless eternity. It believes in his birth while knowing that this birth never had a beginning.
sources.quote: His nature forbids us to say that He ever began to be, for His birth lies beyond the beginnings of time.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being begotten imply that he had a beginning in time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Though the Son exists by generation, it does not follow that he once was not. Being and not-being are immediate contradictories, and it is impious to cut short the Divine being by non-existence at any time, whether before or after; he who denies the Son will ever cease to be must equally deny he once was not.
sources.quote: Yet we shall not, because we say that He exists by generation, therefore admit that He “once was not.”
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's existing by generation from the Father imply that he 'once was not'?

question: When the Son emptied himself and took the form of a servant in the incarnation, did he lose, change or diminish his divine nature?
synthesis: All four authors answer no. Hilary of Poitiers says the Son emptied himself without losing himself and that his power stayed active even in the emptying, though his answers differ on wording: some say the form of God was laid aside while the divine nature remained, and others say he remained in the form of God. Augustine grounds the answer in the Son assuming our changeableness while remaining unchangeably equal to the Father, and Gregory of Nyssa says the servile condition is absorbed into lordship rather than God becoming a servant. Owen alone distinguishes the person, who was abased, from the essential glory of the Deity, which was only eclipsed in its manifestation.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: No. Nothing could be taken from the essential glory of the Deity. What happened was that the glory was eclipsed in its manifestation, because the person appeared in the form of a servant. So the person was abased but the divine nature was not. This is why Christ prays to be glorified with the glory he had before the world was, meaning the manifestation of that glory.
sources.quote: And so, though the divine nature was not abased, the person was.
sources.raw_question: In the Son's self-emptying, was the divine nature itself diminished or abased?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Christ is one Person of two natures united for his mediatorship, and he is the full reality of each. He does not stop being God by becoming man, nor fail to be man because he remains God for ever. God alone could become something he was not before without ceasing to be what he always was.
sources.quote: while abiding in each, He is wanting in neither; He does not cease to be God because He becomes man, nor fail to be man because He remains for ever God.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God cease to be God, or lack anything of either nature, when he became man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. He emptied Himself not by changing His own divinity but by assuming our changeableness in taking the form of a servant. He did this to give fallen man, who cannot see God, an example he could perceive and follow, since man should follow only God to blessedness.
sources.quote: “He emptied Himself;” not by changing His own divinity, but by assuming our changeableness: and “taking upon Him the form of a servant”
sources.raw_question: Did the Son's self-emptying in the incarnation involve a change in his divinity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: No. God, though he submits to take the form of a servant, does not himself become a servant. Instead he takes away the slavish subordination and absorbs it into lordship and royalty, so that what was human and lowly becomes both Lord and Christ. Likewise, the Life in death remains secure in itself.
sources.quote: does not Himself become a servant, but takes away the slavish subordination and absorbs it into lordship and royalty, making that which was human and lowly to become both Lord and Christ
sources.raw_question: When God the Son took the form of a servant, did he himself become a servant in his divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The emptying did not abolish his nature: he emptied himself but did not lose himself, and he took a new form while remaining what he was. Only one who exists can take something, so the same Person who was in the form of God took the form of a servant. The assumption of another nature did not put an end to his eternal divinity.
sources.quote: The emptying of the form does not then imply the abolition of the nature: He emptied Himself, but did not lose His self: He took a new form, but remained what He was.
sources.raw_question: When Christ emptied himself and took the form of a servant, did he cease to be God or lose his divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The weakness of the assumed humanity did not weaken the divine nature. Rather, divine power was imparted to the humanity without the Godhead being lost. The aim was not that God be lowered to man but that man be raised to God, as the name Emmanuel, 'God with us', signifies.
sources.quote: For when God was born to be man the purpose was not that the Godhead should be lost, but that, the Godhead remaining, man should be born to be God.
sources.raw_question: Did the Incarnation, in which the Son emptied Himself of the form of God, weaken or diminish His divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Christ took a new nature not by loss of virtue or nature but by change of fashion; He abided in the virtue of His nature. What was affected was only the unity of the assumed humanity with the divine nature, which had to be restored by the Father's glorifying.
sources.quote: Christ, born man, took to Himself a new nature, not by loss of virtue or nature but by change of fashion. He emptied Himself of the form of God and took the form of a servant, when He was born.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son, in emptying Himself and taking the form of a servant at the Incarnation, lose His divine nature or power?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. When the Son of God was born Son of Man, he emptied himself of the form of God without losing his own self and power. God the Word formed the perfect man while remaining in the form of God, and by virtue of his origin he never ceased to be God.
sources.quote: For when He emptied Himself of the form of God and received the form of a servant when the Son of God was born also Son of Man, without losing His own self and power, God the Word formed the perfect living Man.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God lose his divine form or power when he became man and took the form of a servant?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. We confess Him as one and the same Person, not by loss of the Godhead but by the assumption of manhood. He remained in the form of God just as truly as He received the form of a slave.
sources.quote: we confess Him as one and the same Person, not by loss of the Godhead, but by assumption of the manhood
sources.raw_question: Did the Son lose His Godhead by taking the form of a servant?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Christ remained in the form of God when he took the form of a servant. He was not changed but emptied himself, hiding within himself and remaining master of himself. His unbounded might contracted itself only so that the assumed humanity could bear it and render obedience. Since he was self-contained even in emptying, his authority suffered no diminution.
sources.quote: But since He was self-contained even when He emptied Himself, His authority suffered no diminution, for in the humiliation of the emptying He exercised within Himself the power of that authority which was emptied.
sources.raw_question: When Christ emptied himself and took the form of a servant, did he cease to be in the form of God or lose any of his divine power and authority?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Less Than the Father, and Than Himself.
sources.answer: No. He took the form of a servant in such a way that he did not lose the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father. He remains the same only-begotten Son in both forms.
sources.quote: For He did not so take the form of a servant as that He should lose the form of God, in which He was equal to the Father.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son lose the form of God, and so his equality with the Father, when he emptied himself and took the form of a servant?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The form of God was laid aside, but the divine nature still abode in him. It took on the humility of earthly birth and exercised its own power within that humble condition. So he was at once God, as his miracles proved, and man, being found in human fashion.
sources.quote: The divine nature had not ceased to be, but still abiding in Him, it had taken upon itself the humility of earthly birth, and was exercising its proper power in the fashion of the humility it assumed.
sources.raw_question: When the Son emptied himself and took the form of a servant, did his divine nature cease to exist?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Hilary holds that he emptied himself within himself and was not effaced. Had he been effaced, he would have become something different in kind. His power remains even in the act of self-emptying, and putting off the form of God is itself a mighty act of divine power, not a loss of divine nature.
sources.quote: the transition into the form of a servant does not mean the loss of the nature of God, since to have put off the form of God is nothing less than a mighty act of divine power.
sources.raw_question: When Christ emptied himself of the form of God to take the form of a servant, did he lose the divine nature or cease to be what he was?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > There Was No Other More Suitable Way of Freeing Man from the Misery of Mortality Than The Incarnation of the Word. The Merits Which are Called Ours are the Gifts of God.
sources.answer: No. The Son, unchangeably good, remained what he was in himself and received from us and for us what he was not. He took human nature into fellowship with his own without any loss of his own nature.
sources.quote: the Son of God, unchangeably good, remaining what He was in Himself, and receiving from us and for us what He was not, apart from any loss of His own nature
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God lose or change his divine nature by becoming man?

question: Does Christ's prayer that believers 'may be one as We are' (John 17:11, 21-23) mean that believers become one with God in the same way the Son is one with the Father, so that the Son's unity with the Father is no more than the moral unity believers can have?
synthesis: Athanasius, Hilary, Bickersteth and Augustine all answer no, but on different grounds. Athanasius argues that 'as' signifies a pattern for imitation rather than identity, and that 'in Us' rather than 'in Thee' marks the distance between the Son and believers. For him the Son is in the Father by nature, while believers are joined through the Spirit and by grace in concord of spirit. Hilary argues instead that the prayer's wording speaks of mutual indwelling rather than agreement of will. Augustine and Bickersteth hold that Father and Son are one in substance (Bickersteth adds power and operation) as well as in will, Augustine noting that Christ did not say 'I and they are one' and Bickersteth reading John 17 as the saints' union in contrast with the essential oneness of John 10:30.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. The word 'as' signifies not identity or equality but a parallel viewed in a certain respect. Just as Christ's comparison with Jonah does not make Jonah equal to the Saviour, so believers becoming one 'as' the Son in the Father are not thereby as the Son or equal to Him; they are united in mind and agreement of spirit, while He is in the Father by nature.
sources.quote: if we too become one, as the Son in the Father, we shall not be as the Son, nor equal to Him; for He and we are but parallel.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer 'As Thou, Father, art in Me, and I in Thee, that they may be one' (John 17:21) imply that believers become one with God in the same way and degree that the Son is one with the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. The Arians take what is given to men by grace and make it equal to the Godhead of the Giver. Hearing that men are called sons, they think themselves equal to the true Son by nature, and they make the same mistake with this text. Scripture's 'as' is a pattern for imitation, not a claim of identical nature. Men can no more become what the Son is in the Father than they can become beasts when told not to be like the horse.
sources.quote: For what is given to man by grace, this they would make equal to the Godhead of the Giver. Thus hearing that men are called sons, they thought themselves equal to the True Son by nature such
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer that believers 'may be one, as We are' (John 17:11, 21-23) show that the Son is one with the Father only in the way believers can become one in God, and therefore not proper to the Father's Essence?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. The words of the prayer speak of mutual indwelling, not of agreement of will. Had Christ, who is the Word and the Truth, meant a unity of will, he would not have lacked suitable words to pray, 'as We are one in will, so may they be one in will.' The unity of believers is patterned on the Father being in the Son and the Son in the Father.
sources.quote: For there would have been no lack of suitable words for our Lord, if it were will that made them one, to have prayed in this fashion,—Father, as We are one in will, so may they also be one in will
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer in John 17:21 that believers 'may be one as Thou Father art in Me and I in Thee' show that the unity of Father and Son is merely a unity of will and love?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. John 10:30 teaches that the Son and the Father are one in essence, power, operation and will, which is why the flock is equally safe in either's hand. John 17:22 speaks of the intimate union of the saints with each other and with the Lord. Even the privileges asked for there flow equally from the Father and the Son as the one fountain of eternal life.
sources.quote: equally safe, for He and his Father are one in essence, power, operation, and will
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer that believers 'may be one even as we are one' show that the oneness of the Father and the Son in John 10:30 is merely a moral union like that of the saints?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. The prayer does not signify that we are to have identity with the Son. It is a request to the Father that the Spirit be given through the Son to believers. Through the Spirit we are found to be in God and joined in Him, whereas the Son is in the Father by nature.
sources.quote: does not signify that we were to have identity with Him; for this was shewn from the instance of Jonah; but it is a request to the Father, as John has written, that the Spirit should be vouchsafed through Him to those who believe
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer in John 17:21, 'that they too may be one in Us, as Thou Father art in Me,' mean that believers will have the same identity or oneness with the Father that the Son has?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In What Manner Christ Wills that All Shall Be One in Himself.
sources.answer: No. Christ did not say 'I and they are one thing.' He spoke so as to show his own Godhead consubstantial with the Father, as in 'I and my Father are one.' The Father and Son are one both in equality of substance and in will. Believers are made one by sharing the same nature and the same union of love, and they are one in Christ rather than in themselves.
sources.quote: as the Father and Son are one, not only in equality of substance, but also in will, so those also may be one, between whom and God the Son is mediator, not only in that they are of the same nature, but also through the same union of love
sources.raw_question: When Christ prays in John 17 that believers 'may be one, even as we are one,' does this mean the Father and Son are one only in the way believers are one, by agreement?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. The Son is one with the Father by nature and essence, being God's Word and Wisdom and true God, whereas we are fashioned from the earth. The 'as' sets the Son's natural unity before us as a pattern, so that by imitation we become one with each other in concord and oneness of spirit, like the believers in Acts. The Arian reading that Father and Son are one only as believers are one therefore fails.
sources.quote: therefore not that we might become such as He, did He say ‘that they may be one as We are;’ but that as He, being the Word, is in His own Father, so that we too, taking an examplar and looking at Him, might become one towards each other
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer in John 17 that believers 'may be one as We are' imply that believers become one with each other in the same way the Son is one with the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. Had that been meant, it would say 'one in Thee'; 'in Us' marks the distance and difference. The Son alone is in the Father alone as only Word and Wisdom, while we are in the Son and through Him in the Father, and 'in Us' means 'learn of Us', as Paul uses it.
sources.quote: by saying ‘in Us’ He has pointed out the distance and difference; that He indeed is alone in the Father alone, as Only Word and Wisdom; but we in the Son, and through Him in the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'that they may be one in Us' (John 17:21) mean believers are in the Father in the same way the Son is?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. Christ did not say 'that they may be one in Thee' as the Son is in the Father, but 'in Us,' which marks the distance and difference. The Son alone is in the Father alone as His only Word and Wisdom, whereas we are in the Son and through Him in the Father. 'In Us' signifies an example and pattern from which believers learn unity, as Paul used himself and Apollos as a figure for the Corinthians.
sources.quote: by saying ‘in Us’ He has pointed out the distance and difference; that He indeed is alone in the Father alone, as Only Word and Wisdom; but we in the Son, and through Him in the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer that believers 'may be one in Us' (John 17:21) mean believers become one with God in the same way the Son is in the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. Whoever uses 'as' signifies not identity or equality but an image and pattern of the matter in question, viewed in a certain respect. The Son has true identity of nature with the Father, while believers are given only to imitate it. Similarly Jonah's three days in the whale parallel Christ's three days in the earth without Jonah being as the Saviour.
sources.quote: whoso uses the particle ‘as’ implies, not identity, nor equality, but a pattern of the matter in question, viewed in a certain respect
sources.raw_question: Does the comparative word 'as' in 'that they may be one as We are one' (John 17:22) imply that believers' unity is identical or equal to the unity of Father and Son?

question: When the Word became flesh, was the Word changed into flesh or did He cease to be God?
synthesis: Augustine, Hilary, John Owen and Athanasius all deny any change in the Word, but they ground this differently. Augustine uses the analogy of the inner word assuming sound without becoming it, and adds that Christ has a rational soul. Hilary stresses that 'dwelt' implies an abiding Word who cannot vacate His Source's nature. Owen calls such a change impossible. Athanasius uses the image of Aaron robed in priestly garments and says the incarnation promoted men, not the Word, who remained omniscient.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Likeness of the Divine Word, Such as It Is, is to Be Sought, Not in Our Own Outer and Sensible Word, But in the Inner and Mental One. There is the Greatest Possible Unlikeness Between Our Word and Knowledge and the Divine Word and Knowledge.
sources.answer: No. Just as our inner word becomes an articulate sound by assuming the sound in order to be manifested to the senses, without being changed into it, so the Word of God became flesh by assuming flesh, not by consuming itself so as to be changed into it.
sources.quote: For both that word of ours became an articulate sound, and that other Word became flesh, by assuming it, not by consuming itself so as to be changed into it.
sources.raw_question: When the Word of God became flesh, was the Word changed into flesh?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Concerning the Word of the Mind, in Which We See the Word of God, as in a Glass and an Enigma.
sources.answer: No. Our inner word becomes an articulate sound by assuming that sound, yet it is not changed into it. In the same way the Word of God became flesh by assuming flesh in which He might be manifested to men's senses, not by being consumed or changed into it.
sources.quote: And as our word becomes an articulate sound, yet is not changed into one; so the Word of God became flesh, but far be it from us to say He was changed into flesh.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God become flesh by being changed into flesh, on the analogy of the inner word becoming sound?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. By assuming flesh He became all that we are without losing what He was before. 'Dwelt' implies one who abides, so He was still truly the Word and truly God as well as man, God in the reality of our body.
sources.quote: By assuming flesh, however, He acquired our nature in our totality, and became all that we are, but did not lose that which He was before.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word cease to be God or lose His divine nature when He became flesh?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The Word made flesh truly was the flesh he was made, yet by virtue of his origin he could not vacate the nature of his Source and always remained the Word. When he dwelt among us, the flesh was not the Word itself; it was the flesh of the Word dwelling in the flesh.
sources.quote: As the Word made flesh could not vacate the nature of His Source, so by virtue of the origin of His nature He could not but remain the Word
sources.raw_question: When the Word became flesh, did he cease to be the Word or give up his divine nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: No. When he became man he did not alter, for 'the Word of God abideth for ever.' Assuming the mortal was no advancement to the Immortal, and putting on the temporal was no promotion to the Everlasting. It was done so that mortal men might be made immortal. It is men, not the Word, who were promoted.
sources.quote: What advancement then was it to the Immortal to have assumed the mortal? or what promotion is it to the Everlasting to have put on the temporal?
sources.raw_question: Was the Word changed or improved by becoming man?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: No. Such a change is utterly impossible, and the text does not say it. The Word stayed the Word and took our flesh or nature as his own. Continuing to be God, he also became man, which he was not before.
sources.quote: Himself continuing God, as he was, became man also, which before he was not.
sources.raw_question: Does 'the Word was made flesh' in John 1:14 mean that the divine Word was converted into flesh and ceased to be God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: No. He did not cease to be God when he became man, nor did he as God shrink from what is human. Being God, he took flesh and deifies it; in the same flesh in which he asked questions he raised the dead, showing that he who quickens the dead much more discerns all secrets.
sources.quote: For He did not, when He became man, cease to be God; nor, whereas He is God does He shrink from what is man’s; perish the thought; but rather, being God, He has taken to Him the flesh, and being in the flesh deifies the flesh.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word cease to be God, or lose divine attributes such as omniscience, when he became man?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. Aaron stayed the same man when he put on the high-priestly garments and was only robed. In the same way the Word remained the same as before and was clothed with a body. Saying He 'became' or 'was made' means He was made High Priest by putting on an originate body, not that the Word as Word was made.
sources.quote: He did not become other than Himself on taking the flesh, but, being the same as before, He was robed in it
sources.raw_question: Did the Word become something other than Himself when He took flesh?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Of the Sensible Showing of the Holy Spirit, and of the Coeternity of the Trinity. What Has Been Said, and What Remains to Be Said.
sources.answer: The Word was made flesh, that is, made man, but was not turned or changed into what was made. In Christ there are the Word of God, the flesh of man, and also a rational human soul. The whole is called God on account of God and man on account of man.
sources.quote: the Word of God itself was made flesh, that is, was made man, yet not turned and changed into that which was made; but so made, that there should be there not only the Word of God and the flesh of man, but also the rational soul of man
sources.raw_question: Was the Word of God changed into flesh in the incarnation, and what does the incarnate Christ consist of?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. To think the incarnation is an alteration of the Word is a degraded, Gentile notion. Hearing 'the Word became flesh,' one should not think the Word ceased to be, which is absurd, but understand the union as one simple divine mystery in which the mortal is swallowed up by Him who is Life itself.
sources.quote: For as when a man heard ‘The Word became flesh,’ he would not think that the Word ceased to be, which is absurd, as has been said before
sources.raw_question: Does the Word's becoming flesh mean that the Word was altered or ceased to be what he was?

question: Does 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1) show that the Word is eternal and without a beginning of existence, unlike creatures made 'in the beginning'?
synthesis: Owen, Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa and Athanasius all deny that the Word had a beginning, but on different grounds. Owen argues that existence before all creation can only be existence in God's eternal nature, and he cites Proverbs 8 and John 17. Hilary and Athanasius contrast John's timeless 'was' or 'beginning' with the datable beginning of creatures in Genesis 1:1. Gregory identifies the Beginning with the Father and argues that what is in the Beginning cannot be severed from it or come after it.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. If it does not formally express eternity, it at least expresses existence before the whole creation, which comes to the same thing. Nothing can exist before all creatures except in the eternal nature of God, unless one supposes a creature before any creation. Scripture also explains the phrase as 'from everlasting' (Prov. 8:23) and as glory the Son had with the Father before the world was (John 17:5).
sources.quote: for nothing can pre-exist unto all creatures, but in the nature of God, which is eternal; unless we shall suppose a creature before the creation of any.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that the Word 'was in the beginning' (John 1:1) imply the eternity of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The 'beginning' of Genesis fixes the moment of creation and can be dated, but John's 'was' has no limit of time and no commencement. Whatever date one fixes for the beginning, the Word already was; the uncreated Word is beyond the beginning.
sources.quote: For his was has no limit of time and no commencement; the uncreated Word was in the beginning.
sources.raw_question: Does 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1) mean the Word had a beginning in time, like the creation in Genesis 1:1?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He then discusses the “willing” of the Father concerning the generation of the Son, and shows that the object of that good will is from eternity, which is the Son, existing in the Father, and being closely related to the process of willing, as the ray to the flame, or the act of seeing to the eye.
sources.answer: It teaches that the Son is not after the beginning but in it. The Father is the Beginning of all, and the Son is declared to be in this Beginning, being by nature what the Beginning is, since both are God. John conjoins the Word with the Beginning so that the hearer never conceives the Beginning alone, but the Word enters the mind together with It.
sources.quote: Now the beginning of all is the Father; but in this beginning the Son also is declared to be, being in His Nature that very thing which the Beginning is.
sources.raw_question: What does John 1:1, 'In the beginning was the Word', teach about the Son's eternity in relation to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: No. Whatever is true of the Beginning must be true of Him who is in the Beginning, since what is in the beginning cannot be severed from it. If the Word in the beginning had a beginning, the Beginning itself would need another beginning. However far back thought reaches, the Word is found there, so no 'was not' can precede His 'was'.
sources.quote: is not aware that if He Who is in the beginning has a beginning, then the Beginning itself must needs have another beginning.
sources.raw_question: Does the Word who was 'in the beginning' (John 1:1) himself have a beginning of existence, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. The 'beginning' in the Gospel signifies the Father, and the Son is confessed together with Him. Since the Son is in the Father, as the Lord says, He cannot begin His being in Him from any particular point.
sources.quote: it is the Father Who is there signified, and the confession of the Son together with Him is there pointed to, nor can it be that He Who is in the Father, as the Lord says, can begin His being in Him from any particular point
sources.raw_question: Does the 'beginning' in which the Word was (John 1:1) imply that the Son's existence started from some point?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. John does not say "Of the Beginning was begotten the Word," lest any interval of time be imagined between them. He applies "was" both to the Beginning and to the Word, so that the Word does not linger after the Beginning. Nothing could more strongly show community of essence, real relationship, and coeternity.
sources.quote: he does not say, “Of the Beginning was begotten the Word,” that he may not separate the Word from the Beginning by any conception of extension in time
sources.raw_question: Does "In the beginning was the Word" show that the Word is coeternal with the Beginning (the Father) rather than coming after him in time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: No. If he who is in the beginning had a beginning, then the Beginning itself would need another beginning. What is in the beginning cannot be severed from it, and no "was not" can precede the "was." The Word therefore never begins or ceases to exist in the one beginning, where it is indivisibly united to the Father.
sources.quote: He declares Him Who was in the beginning Himself to have a beginning: and is not aware that if He Who is in the beginning has a beginning, then the Beginning itself must needs have another beginning.
sources.raw_question: Does the Word, who "was in the beginning" (John 1:1), himself have a beginning, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. For creatures, 'In the beginning He made' means 'from the beginning He made', i.e. He began to make them, so they have a beginning of existence connected with an interval, as Genesis 2:3 ('which God began to make') and Matthew 19:4 show. But the Word has no other beginning than the Father, who is without beginning, so He exists without beginning in the Father.
sources.quote: the Word has His being, in no other beginning than the Father, whom they allow to be without beginning, so that He too exists without beginning in the Father, being His Offspring, not His creature.
sources.raw_question: Does 'In the beginning' mean the same thing in 'In the beginning God created' (Genesis 1:1) as in 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1)?

question: Why did the Son of God become man?
synthesis: All agree the Incarnation was for human salvation, but they stress different grounds. Irenaeus centers on exchange and adoption: the Word became what we are so that we might become sons of God, be united to incorruptibility, grow accustomed to God, and learn the Father by seeing and hearing him as a man. Novatian argues that a mediator must belong to both sides and so join God to man; Athanasius roots the Incarnation in man's prior need, naming the Father's will, giving light, and destroying the devil's works; Hilary emphasizes that he became man so people might believe, being a witness to divine things through the weakness of the flesh.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And This is So Manifest, that Some Heretics Have Thought Him to Be God the Father, Others that He Was Only God Without the Flesh.
sources.answer: A mediator had to belong to both sides. So the Word had to be made flesh, uniting the pledges of both natures in himself and joining God to man and man to God. Thus the Son of God became Son of man by assuming flesh, and the Son of man became Son of God by receiving the Word. This mystery was ordained before the worlds for human salvation.
sources.quote: if He came to man, that He might be Mediator of God and men, it behoved Him to be with man, and the Word to be made flesh, that in His own self He might link together the agreement of earthly things with heavenly things
sources.raw_question: Why was it necessary for the Son of God to become man in order to be Mediator between God and men?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XX.—God showed himself, by the fall of man, as patient, benign, merciful, mighty to save. Man is therefore most ungrateful, if, unmindful of his own lot, and of the benefits held out to him, he do not acknowledge divine grace.
sources.answer: So that he might accustom man to receive God and God to dwell in man, according to the Father's good pleasure. Made in the likeness of sinful flesh, he condemned sin and called man into his own likeness. He grants man adoption and the power to receive the Father and see God.
sources.quote: the Word of God who dwelt in man, and became the Son of man, that He might accustom man to receive God, and God to dwell in man, according to the good pleasure of the Father
sources.raw_question: Why did the Word of God become the Son of man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Preface.
sources.answer: Out of his transcendent love, so that by becoming what we are he might bring us to be what he himself is. He is the only true and steadfast Teacher, and in becoming man he lifts humanity up to share in what he is. The following chapter adds that only the Father's own Word could reveal the things of the Father, and we could learn them only by seeing and hearing him as a man.
sources.quote: the only true and stedfast Teacher, the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, become man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: He became the Son of man so that through Him we might receive adoption as sons. In the incarnation humanity sustains, receives and embraces the Son of God.
sources.quote: the Son of God being made the Son of man, that through Him we may receive the adoption,—humanity sustaining, and receiving, and embracing the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Why did the Son of God become the Son of man?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: Man's need came before the Incarnation, and without it He would not have put on flesh. Christ names this need himself: to do the Father's will by losing none and raising them up at the last day, to be a light so believers do not abide in darkness, and to bear witness to the truth. John adds that the Son was manifested to destroy the works of the devil. In the following section the author adds that He took a mortal body so as to die for us and raise man up.
sources.quote: For the need of man preceded His becoming man, apart from which He had not put on flesh.
sources.raw_question: What was the reason for the Son's becoming man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XIX.—Jesus Christ was not a mere man, begotten from Joseph in the ordinary course of nature, but was very God, begotten of the Father most high, and very man, born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: So that man, taken into the Word and receiving adoption, might become a son of God. We could not attain incorruptibility and immortality unless united to them, and we could not be united to them unless incorruptibility and immortality first became what we are, so that the mortal might be swallowed up by immortality.
sources.quote: For it was for this end that the Word of God was made man, and He who was the Son of God became the Son of man, that man, having been taken into the Word, and receiving the adoption, might become the son of God.
sources.raw_question: Why was it necessary for the Son of God to become the Son of man?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: He was made man so that people might believe on him. Sprung from our own race, he could be a witness to divine things and preach to weak, carnal humans about God the Father through the weakness of the flesh. In this he fulfilled the Father's will.
sources.quote: The Son of God, therefore, having the charge of mankind, was first made man, that men might believe on Him; that He might be to us a witness, sprung from ourselves, of things Divine
sources.raw_question: Why did the Son of God become man?

question: Does 1 Corinthians 8:6, calling the Father 'one God' and the Son 'one Lord', exclude the Son from being God?
synthesis: All answer no. Waterland, Bickersteth and Hilary rest mainly on a parity argument: if 'one God' denied Godhead to the Son, then 'one Lord' would deny Lordship to the Father. Waterland adds that the context sets both Father and Son against idols and nominal gods. Bickersteth adds that 'by whom are all things' marks the Son as efficient Cause, and he reads the verse against Deut. 6:4. Warfield argues differently: in asserting that there is only one God, Paul takes Christ up into that unique Godhead, which shows a distinction of Persons within one Being.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. The Father is emphatically called one God without any intent to exclude the Son from being God. Likewise the Son is emphatically called one Lord without excluding the Father from being Lord. The surrounding verses concern idols and nominal gods and lords. Father and Son are equally distinguished from these, which suggests the texts declaring God's unity do not exclude the Son.
sources.quote: the Father is there emphatically styled one God; but without design to exclude the Son from being God also: as the Son is emphatically styled one Lord; but without design to exclude the Father from being Lord alsos.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 8:6, calling the Father 'one God' and the Son 'one Lord', exclude the Son from being God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. The Son is there called the 'one Lord' by whom are all things, the very phrase Paul uses of the Eternal Father as immediate and efficient Cause. The Deity of Christ can no more be denied because the Father is called the 'One God' than the Father's dominion can be denied because the Son is called the 'One Lord.' Read against Deut. 6:4, the verse is strong proof of the Messiah's divine supremacy.
sources.quote: the Deity of Christ can no more be denied because the Father is here called the “One God,” than the dominion of the Father can be denied because the Son is called the “One Lord.”
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 8:6, calling the Father the 'one God,' exclude the deity of Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. The Father is emphatically styled one God without design to exclude the Son from being God, just as the Son is emphatically styled one Lord without design to exclude the Father from being Lord. The context concerns idols and nominal gods and lords, from which Father and Son are equally distinguished, suggesting that texts declaring God's unity do not exclude the Son, by whom are all things.
sources.quote: the Father is there emphatically styled one God; but without design to exclude the Son from being God also: as the Son is emphatically styled one Lord; but without design to exclude the Father from being Lord also
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 8:6, calling the Father 'one God' and the Son 'one Lord', exclude the Son from being God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. In the very act of asserting that there is no God but one, Paul takes Christ up into this unique Godhead. The 'one God, the Father' and 'one Lord, Jesus Christ' are embraced together in the one God who alone is, showing a distinction of Persons within the unity of His Being.
sources.quote: Obviously, this “one God, the Father,” and “one Lord, Jesus Christ,” are embraced together in the one God who alone is.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 8:6, which speaks of 'one God, the Father' and 'one Lord, Jesus Christ,' exclude Christ from the one Godhead?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. If calling the Father the one God denied Godhead to Christ, then by the same reasoning calling Christ the one Lord would deny Lordship to the Father. Since the heretic will not deny that the Father is Lord, he cannot use 'one God' to deny that Christ is God. Greatness and power make the one who is Lord to be God, and the one who is God to be Lord.
sources.quote: Hence if thou deniest that the one Lord Christ is also God, thou must needs deny that the one God the Father is also Lord.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's confession of 'one God the Father' in 1 Corinthians 8:6 exclude Christ from being God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The oneness of God and the oneness of the Lord are not exclusive unities but a mystery. If 'one God' excluded Christ from Godhead, then by the same logic 'one Lord Christ' would exclude the Father from Lordship, which is absurd. So the one Lord Christ does not take Lordship from the Father, nor does the one God the Father deny Godhead to Christ.
sources.quote: If, because God is one, Christ is not also by nature divine, then we cannot allow that the one God is Lord, because there is one Lord Christ
sources.raw_question: Does the confession that there is 'one God' the Father exclude Christ from being God by nature?

question: Does Philippians 2:6, which says the Son 'thought it not robbery to be equal with God,' teach that the Son is equal with the Father in substance or nature?
synthesis: Augustine and Hilary both read the verse as teaching that the Son is truly equal with God. Augustine argues that the apostle uses the very word 'equal', that 'God' here means the Father, and that the Son is therefore equal in all things and of one substance; he also presses a dilemma on the Arians about what is said of God according to substance. Hilary grounds the equality in the Son being the form of God who images all that God possesses, and holds that he emptied himself of that equality only by obedience. Novatian reads the verse differently: Christ, mindful that he was God from the Father, did not grasp at equality or compare himself with the Father. Waterland answers that this 'never compared himself' reading does not deny equality of nature, because the Son declined comparison only with respect to origin, being second in order but not inferior in nature.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Argument of the Arians is Refuted, Which is Drawn from the Words Begotten and Unbegotten.
sources.answer: Yes, on the Arians' own premise. If the Son is not equal according to substance, the Arians must admit that something can be said of God not according to substance, and then begotten and unbegotten need not be substantial either. If they refuse that admission and hold that everything is said of God according to substance, then the Son is equal to the Father in substance.
sources.quote: And if they do not admit this, on the ground that they will have all things to be spoken of God according to substance, then the Son is equal to the Father according to substance.
sources.raw_question: Does Philippians 2:6, which says the Son "thought it not robbery to be equal with God," show that the Son is equal to the Father in substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
