sources.answer: Yes. The apostle uses the very word, saying that the Son, "being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God." Here "God" refers specifically to the Father, as it does in "the head of Christ is God."
sources.quote: the apostle has not refrained from using the very word itself, but has said most expressly, “Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God;” using here the name of God specially of the Father
sources.raw_question: Does Philippians 2:6 expressly teach that the Son is equal with God the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Same Argument Continued.
sources.answer: Yes. Since inequality in anything signifying the divine substance would make the Son unequal in every respect, and the apostle says He is equal with God, the Son must be equal with the Father in all things and of one and the same substance.
sources.quote: But the apostle has said that He is equal. Therefore the Son is equal with the Father in all things, and is of one and the same substance.
sources.raw_question: Does Philippians 2:6 prove that the Son is equal with the Father in all things and of the same substance?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is in Christ, He Once More Asserts by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: Novatian reads it to mean that Christ did not grasp at equality with the Father. Mindful that he was God from God the Father and had his being as the Father's gift, he never compared himself with the Father or set himself alongside him. He considered such a claim to equal himself with the Father would be robbery, and so he yielded obedience to the Father before the incarnation, after it, and after the resurrection.
sources.quote: He never either compared or associated Himself with God the Father, mindful that He was from His Father, and that He possessed that very thing that He is, because the Father had given it Him.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that Christ 'thought it not robbery to be equal with God' (Philippians 2:6)?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. The Son declined comparison only with respect to origin. He remembered that he was from the Father, that is, begotten and not unbegotten. He is second in order of the Persons, not inferior in nature. Hilary and Phoebadius, who cannot be suspected of Arianism, use similar language.
sources.quote: He never pretended to an equality with the Father, in respect of his origina/, knowing himself to be second only in order, not the first Person of the ever blessed Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Does the reading of Philippians 2:6 that the Son 'never compared himself with God the Father' deny that the Son is equal to the Father in nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. The one whom God sealed can be nothing other than the form of God, and he must image forth all that God possesses. Paul teaches that He is God abiding in the form of God and equal with God. He emptied Himself of that equality only through obedience, in order to take the form of a servant.
sources.quote: For He, Whom God had sealed, could be naught else than the form of God, and that which has been sealed in the form of God must needs present at the same time imaged forth within itself all that God possesses.
sources.raw_question: Does Philippians 2:6-7 teach that the Son, being in the form of God, is truly equal with God?

question: When Scripture ascribes bodily members to God, such as hands, fingers, eyes and feet, does it mean that God has a body, and how should such language be understood?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa, Hilary of Poitiers, Novatian and Ambrose of Milan all deny that such language implies a bodily God. Gregory says it must be read in a way worthy of God, as Scripture accommodating itself to human capacity. Hilary and Novatian take each member to signify a real incorporeal power or activity: the hand stands for creative work and the eyes for knowledge of all things. Ambrose gives a distinctive reading: such expressions point to the oneness of the Godhead and the inseparability of the Son and Spirit from the Father, with the Son called the Father's Right Hand.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They must not be taken in their plain literal sense, which would present an anthropomorphous deity. Rather one should deduce from them ideas worthy of God and not degrade His pure nature by carnal imaginations, since the difference between our notions and His majesty is as great as the difference between His nature and ours.
sources.quote: deduces from such words ideas worthy of God, and does not degrade the idea of His pure nature by carnal and sensuous imaginations
sources.raw_question: How should bodily expressions in Scripture about God, such as His fingers, hand, arm, eyes, and feet, be understood?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He further shows the operations of God to be expressed by human illustrations; for what hands and feet and the other parts of the body with which men work are, that, in the case of God, the will alone is, in place of these. And so also arises the divergence of generation; wherefore He is called Only-begotten, because He has no community with other generation such as is observed in creation, but in that He is called the “brightness of glory,” and the “savour of ointment,” He shows the close conjunction and co-eternity of His Nature with the Father.
sources.answer: Scripture uses familiar human terms to convey truths that transcend language, accommodating itself to our capacity. None of these bodily terms belongs to the Divine Nature in its primary sense; rather each leads us analogically to a more exalted conception. For example, "fingers," "hand," and "arm" signify God's effective and operative power, not a limb of bones and flesh.
sources.quote: none of which things is apprehended to belong in its primary sense to the Divine Nature,—but turning its teaching to what we can easily perceive, it describes by terms well worn in human use, facts that are beyond every name
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture speak of God in bodily terms such as hands, eyes, fingers and feet, and how should such language be understood?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is no less the author of spiritual creation or regeneration than the Father and the Son. The excellence of that creation, and wherein it consists. How we are to understand holy Scripture, when it attributes a body or members to God.
sources.answer: No. In the Godhead there are neither members nor parts; such expressions signify the oneness of the Godhead, so that we believe the Son and the Holy Spirit cannot be separated from the Father. Thus the Son is called the Right Hand of the Father, since the fulness of the Godhead dwells in the substance of the Trinity.
sources.quote: since in the Godhead are neither members nor parts, but are expressions of the oneness of the Godhead, that we may believe that it is impossible for either the Son or the Holy Spirit to be separated from God the Father
sources.raised_by_detail: those who suppose God is fashioned after a bodily manner
sources.raw_question: When Scripture speaks of God's hand, finger, or other members, does it mean that God has a body?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Someone who takes "God said" as articulate speech must, by the same reasoning, take "God saw" and "He heard" as bodily perception, and so ends with an anthropomorphic deity. These expressions are to be read in a way worthy of God's pure nature: verbal utterances indicate His will, not articulate sounds.
sources.quote: taking them, I say, in their plain literal acceptation, he will present to us an anthropomorphous deity, after the similitude of what is seen among ourselves.
sources.raw_question: Should scriptural expressions that ascribe bodily senses and organs to God, such as seeing, hearing, smelling, hands or eyes, be taken literally?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: As denoting real non-corporeal powers in God, not physical members. 'Hands' signifies His creative activity, 'eyes' His knowledge of all things, and 'heart' His desire or will. God uses the names of bodily members so that through corporeal functions we may understand incorporeal powers.
sources.quote: He does not will or see or act through bodily faculties, but uses the names of these members in order that through the services performed by corporeal forces we may understand the power of forces which are not corporeal.
sources.raw_question: How should bodily terms applied to God in Scripture, such as hands, eyes and heart, be understood?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And That, Although Scripture Often Changes the Divine Appearance into a Human Form, Yet the Measure of the Divine Majesty is Not Included Within These Lineaments of Our Bodily Nature.
sources.answer: No. Scripture describes divine agencies by means of members, not God's actual appearance or bodily lineaments. The law is spiritual, and God's majesty is unbounded and cannot be enclosed in the outlines of a human body. Each member signifies an activity: eyes that He sees all, ear that He hears all, hand that He is author of every creature, feet that He fills all things.
sources.quote: Thus the divine agencies are there exhibited by means of members; it is not the appearance of God nor the bodily lineaments that are described.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's ascription of bodily members (eyes, hand, finger, mouth, feet) to God mean that God has a bodily form?

question: Does the phrase 'in the form of God' in Philippians 2:6 signify that Christ truly has the divine essence, rather than a mere appearance or the status of a man or angel?
synthesis: All four authors agree that 'the form of God' signifies Christ's true deity, but they argue for it on different grounds. Gregory of Nyssa, Owen and Waterland all reason from the contrast with 'the form of a servant': since that phrase means true human nature, 'the form of God' must mean true divine nature. Owen adds that only God is equal to God, and Waterland stresses that this reading fits the context and agrees with antiquity. Novatian argues differently: Scripture says man was made in God's 'image', and never speaks of the 'form of God' in men or angels, so the one described must be the Son, who holds divine power over every creature.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds to show that there is no “variance” in the essence of the Father and the Son: wherein he expounds many forms of variation and harmony, and explains the “form,” the “seal,” and the “express image.”
sources.answer: It signifies essence. Just as "taking the form of a servant" means that Christ was formed in the essence of a servant, not merely in its form apart from the essence, so being "in the form of God" means having the divine essence. Hence the Son is formed by no impression different from the Father.
sources.quote: For as, “being made in the form of a servant,” He was formed in the essence of a servant, not taking upon Him the form merely, apart from the essence, but the essence is involved in the sense of “form,”
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase "in the form of God" in Philippians 2:6 signify the divine essence, or only an outward appearance?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. In that form Christ was equal to God, that is, to his Father, and nothing but God is equal to God, since only the infinite is equal to the infinite. Also, the form of God is set against the form of a servant, which means true human nature. So the form of God must mean true divine nature.
sources.quote: That the “form of God” is here the essence of the Deity, sundry things inevitably evince
sources.raw_question: Does the 'form of God' in Philippians 2:6 mean the divine essence itself?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Yes. 'Being in the form of God' means being truly God, which best answers the antithesis 'the form of a servant', meaning truly man. Therefore Christ might justly have appeared and been honoured as God, but at his incarnation chose, as a pattern of humility, to veil his glory and take human nature. Waterland says this reading fits the scope and context and agrees with Catholic antiquity both before and after Nicaea.
sources.quote: “ Who being in the form of God,” that is, “ truly God, (which “ best answers to the antithesis following, the form of a servant “‘ signifying as much as ¢ru/y man,)
sources.raw_question: Does Philippians 2:6, 'who being in the form of God', teach that Christ was truly God before his incarnation?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is in Christ, He Once More Asserts by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. If Christ were only a man, Scripture would have said he was in the 'image' of God, since man was made after the image or likeness of God, not after the form of God. Being in the form of God means that Christ, being above all things and having divine power over every creature, is God after the example of the Father.
sources.quote: If Christ had been only man, He would have been spoken of as in “the image” of God, not “in the form” of God. For we know that man was made after the image or likeness, not after the form, of God.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that Christ was 'in the form of God' (Philippians 2:6) show that Christ is more than a mere man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is in Christ, He Once More Asserts by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. Scripture nowhere speaks of the form of God in angels. The one in the form of God is the chief and royal one above all: the Son and Word of God, who imitates all his Father's works and works as the Father works.
sources.quote: But neither do we read of the form of God in angels, except because this one is chief and royal above all—the Son of God, the Word of God, the imitator of all His Father’s works
sources.raw_question: Could the one described as 'in the form of God' in Philippians 2:6 be merely an angel?

question: How should Scripture texts that seem to subordinate the Son to the Father be reconciled with texts that call him equal to the Father?
synthesis: Augustine gives a single rule, drawn from Philippians 2:6-7: texts of equality refer to the form of God and texts of inferiority to the form of a servant. Bickersteth and Warfield likewise refer subordination texts to Christ's humanity or incarnate condition, with Bickersteth setting parallel assertions of his supremacy as God beside them and Warfield using this to cast doubt on inferring an eternal subordination. Waterland differs: he refers some texts to Christ as Man or Mediator, but explains those about his higher capacity by the Father's priority of order as first of the Three.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > By What Rule in the Scriptures It is Understood that the Son is Now Equal and Now Less.
sources.answer: Distinguish what is said according to the form of God and what is said according to the form of a servant. In the form of God the Son is equal to the Father; in the form of a servant he took on, he is less than the Father. Once this rule is applied, the seemingly contrary sayings of Scripture cause no difficulty.
sources.quote: we are to distinguish in them what relates to the form of God, in which He is equal to the Father, and what to the form of a servant which He took, in which He is less than the Father
sources.raw_question: By what rule should Scripture texts that call the Son equal to the Father and texts that call him less than the Father be reconciled?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Some refer to Christ as Man or as Mediator, and those that concern him in a higher capacity are explained by the priority of order that the ancients reserved to the Father as first of the blessed Three. This serves as a general key for such texts.
sources.quote: some are meant of Christ as Man, or as Mediator: and those which certainly respect him in a higher capacity, may be accounted for on this principle, that we reserve, with the ancients, a priority of order to the Father, the first of the blessed Three.
sources.raw_question: How should texts that seem to subordinate the Son to the Father be explained consistently with the Son's divinity?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. By taking a creaturely nature into union with Himself, the Son enters into new relations with the Father of a definitely subordinate character. Passages that speak of His subordination may therefore reflect this incarnate condition and humiliation rather than eternal relations. This casts doubt on inferring an eternal subordination from them.
sources.quote: the Son, by the assumption of a creaturely nature into union with Himself, enters into new relations with the Father of a definitely subordinate character.
sources.raw_question: Does the incarnation complicate how we interpret New Testament statements about the Son's subordination to the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: By comparing spiritual things with spiritual: whenever an assertion of his subordination as man appears, a parallel assertion of his supremacy as God can be placed beside it. Often the immediate context supplies the corrective; otherwise the whole of Scripture does. Old Testament examples include Gen 3:15, Ps 2, Ps 110, Isa 9:6, Isa 11, Isa 53 and Zech 12–13, where Christ's humanity and Godhead stand side by side.
sources.quote: wherever we find any assertion of his subordination as man, if we can place by its side a parallel assertion of his supremacy as God, faith demands nothing more
sources.raw_question: How should Scripture passages asserting the Son's subordination to the Father be interpreted?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Less Than the Father, and Than Himself.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul gives it in Philippians 2:6-7. There the Son is described as being in the form of God and equal with God, yet emptying himself and taking the form of a servant. Texts of equality refer to the form of God, and texts of inferiority refer to the form of a servant, so there is no contradiction or confusion. The Son is equal to the Father in nature but less in 'fashion.'
sources.quote: The Son of God, then, is equal to God the Father in nature, but less in “fashion.”
sources.raw_question: Is there a scriptural rule for interpreting texts that call the Son equal to the Father and texts that call the Father greater?

question: Is God simple and uncompounded, or is he made up of distinct parts, faculties or elements?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa, Irenaeus, Hilary and Novatian all affirm that God is simple and without parts, but they ground and develop the point differently. Gregory rules out any definition of God's being that would make him multiform or a combination of opposites. Irenaeus and Hilary stress that God's attributes or faculties (mind, will, light, life, power) are each identical with his whole being, and Hilary ties this to God's immutability ('I change not'). Novatian argues that diversity of members belongs to things that are born and dissolve, so the immortal God must be one and simple.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: Yes. The Church teaches no doctrine that makes the One who is single and incomposite multiform, patchwork, or a combination of opposites. Any definition of God's being that implies composition must therefore be rejected.
sources.quote: there is not, neither shall there be, in the Church of God a teaching such as that, which can make One who is single and incomposite not only multiform and patchwork, but also the combination of opposites.
sources.raw_question: Is God simple and incomposite, so that his being cannot be made up of multiple or opposing elements?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: God is simple and uncompounded, without diverse members, and wholly like and equal to Himself. He is wholly understanding, spirit, thought, intelligence, reason, hearing, seeing and light, and the whole source of good. He is not a set of separate faculties.
sources.quote: He is a simple, uncompounded Being, without diverse members, and altogether like, and equal to himself, since He is wholly understanding, and wholly spirit, and wholly thought
sources.raw_question: Is God a simple, uncompounded being, or is He made up of parts and faculties?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. God is not built up of various and lifeless portions. All that is within Him is one: what is Spirit is also Light, Power and Life, and these attributes unite entirely in His whole being. Since He says "I am, and I change not," He can undergo neither change in detail nor transformation in kind.
sources.quote: All that is within Him is One; what is Spirit is Light and Power and Life, and what is Life is Light and Power and Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Is God composed of distinct parts, so that His attributes such as Life, Power, Light and Spirit belong to different portions of Him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XII.—The doctrines of the followers of Ptolemy and Colorbasus.
sources.answer: God is simple. He is all thought, all will, all mind, all light, all eye, all ear. In him thinking and willing coincide, so he does not need distinct powers interacting within him in order to act.
sources.quote: since He is all thought, [all will, all mind, all light,] all eye, all ear, the one entire fountain of all good things
sources.raw_question: Is God composed of distinct parts or faculties, or is he simple, wholly mind and wholly will?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And That, Although Scripture Often Changes the Divine Appearance into a Human Form, Yet the Measure of the Divine Majesty is Not Included Within These Lineaments of Our Bodily Nature.
sources.answer: Yes. God is all equal and the same throughout, having no diversity in Himself. Diversity of members belongs to things that arise by birth and go to dissolution; what is immortal is one and simple, and because it is one it cannot be dissolved and is freed from the laws of death.
sources.quote: And what is immortal, whatever it is, that very thing is one and simple, and for ever. And thus because it is one it cannot be dissolved
sources.raw_question: Is God simple, without diversity of parts?

question: Who was the 'Angel of the Lord' who appeared to Moses in the burning bush and called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: God himself, or a created angel speaking in God's person?
synthesis: The authors differ. Augustine leaves the identity uncertain: it may be the Saviour, or an angel bearing the person of his Lord, in which case it is unclear whether he represented the Father, the Son, the Spirit or the whole Trinity; he stresses that an angel can speak in God's person as a prophet does. Athanasius says Moses saw an angel in whom God spoke, and that God always speaks through the Word. Hilary holds that the one seen is the one who speaks and is truly the Lord and God of Abraham, while Waterland, following the early Fathers, identifies him as God the Son, since a mere angel could not bear the divine titles and the Father does not act ministerially.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Appearance in the Bush.
sources.answer: It is not certain which Person it was. Since a created angel cannot be the God of Abraham, it may reasonably be understood as the Saviour Himself, who is 'over all, God blessed for ever.' But it might also be one of the angels bearing the person of his Lord, in which case it is not apparent whether he represented the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, or the whole Trinity.
sources.quote: Was an angel, then, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? Therefore He may be rightly understood to be the Saviour Himself
sources.raw_question: Who is the 'Angel of the Lord' who appeared to Moses in the burning bush and called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > In How Many Ways the Creature is to Be Taken by Way of Sign. The Eucharist.
sources.answer: No, not necessarily. An angel can speak in the person of God, bearing God's person as a messenger, just as a prophet speaks in God's person without any prefix like "Thus saith the Lord." Scripture itself says just before that "the angel of the Lord appeared to him," showing the speaker is an angel representing God.
sources.quote: An angel speaks in the person of God to man, saying, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob;” the Scripture having said just before, “The angel of the Lord appeared to him.”
sources.raw_question: When an angel in the Old Testament says "I am the God of Abraham," does this mean the speaker is God himself appearing in his own substance?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. What Moses saw was an angel, but God spoke in the angel, just as He spoke to Moses in the pillar of cloud. Whatever God speaks, He speaks through the Word and not through another.
sources.quote: yet was not the Angel the God of Abraham, but in the Angel God spoke. And what was seen was an Angel; but God spoke in him
sources.raw_question: At the burning bush, was the angel who appeared to Moses himself the God of Abraham?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. The one who appeared in the bush is the one who speaks from the bush; the place of vision and voice is one, so the speaker is none other than the one seen. He who is the Angel of God to the eye is the Lord to the ear, and that Lord identifies himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
sources.quote: He who appeared in the bush speaks from the bush; the place of the vision and of the voice is one; He Who speaks is none other than He Who was seen.
sources.raw_question: Was the Angel of the Lord who appeared to Moses in the burning bush truly God, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: It was God the Son. The early Fathers argued that he could not be a mere angel, since titles like God, Lord, Jehovah and Almighty could never belong to a mere angel. He could not be the Father either, because his office was ministerial. So he must be the Son, who is really God and could rightly take those titles, and who as second in the Trinity could suitably act ministerially among men.
sources.quote: Well then, who could he be but God the Son? who being really God, might, in his own right, truly and justly assume those high titles
sources.raw_question: Who was the divine Person who appeared in the Old Testament theophanies, being called both an angel and God, as at the burning bush?

question: Did the Son exist before his incarnation, and even before the world and time itself?
synthesis: Hilary, Hippolytus, Athanasius and Owen all affirm that the Son pre-existed, but they argue on different grounds. Hilary and Owen gather scriptural testimonies: Hilary cites Paul, Wisdom and the Psalms to place the Son before time itself, and Owen cites John 8:58, 3:13, 17:5 and Proverbs 8. Athanasius reasons that the Framer of the world must exist before what he frames, while Hippolytus stresses that the Word was a distinct person in heaven before taking flesh, as shown by his offering that flesh to the Father.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says the Son existed before times eternal. Wisdom testifies that it was founded before the ages and was present when the heavens were prepared. David says His name is before the sun and for generations of generations before the moon. Since time is reckoned from the sun and moon, Christ is before time itself.
sources.quote: In your judgment the times were established by the sun and the moon; but David shews that Christ remains before the sun, saying, His is name is before the sun.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that the Son existed before all time and ages?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: Yes. The Word was in heaven before any flesh existed there, and from the beginning He was called the Word of God. By the Holy Spirit and the Virgin, He later took flesh and was shown to be the perfect Son of God. He then offered that flesh to the Father, which shows that He is distinct from the Father to whom He offered Himself.
sources.quote: It is evident, therefore, that He offered Himself to the Father. And before this there was no flesh in heaven.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son pre-exist the incarnation as a distinct person, the Word of God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: The Son existed before the world. Framing the world is common to the Word and the Son, and the Framer must of necessity be before the things brought into being; the Evangelist's 'He was in the world' also signifies the Son's existence prior to His birth according to the flesh.
sources.quote: so that from this the Son is shewn to be before the world; for of necessity the Framer is before the things brought into being.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son exist before the creation of the world, or only from the Incarnation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen cites John 8:58 ('Before Abraham was, I am'), John 3:13 (the one who came down from heaven), and John 17:5, where Christ speaks of the glory he had with the Father before the world was. He also cites Proverbs 8:22-31, on Wisdom set up from everlasting. These texts show a real pre-existence of the Son in another nature before he took flesh.
sources.quote: And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that the Son existed before his incarnation, and even before the world?

question: What does John 15:26, where the Son promises to send the Spirit of truth from the Father, teach about the relations among the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?
synthesis: All four read the verse as showing the Spirit's relation to both Father and Son, but each draws a different lesson from it. Augustine holds that the Spirit is of both Father and Son, yet notes that Christ never says the Father sends the Spirit 'from me', so the Father is the principium of the whole deity. Hilary uses the verse mainly to show the Son's unity of nature with the Father: as Sender of the Spirit, the Son exercises the Father's own power. Ambrose stresses that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and witnesses to the Son with the Son's own knowledge, showing the unity of divine power, while Warfield stresses the Spirit's personal distinctness from the Son, his eternal home with the Father, and his being sent here by the Son.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: It shows the Spirit to be both of the Father and of the Son. John 14:26 likewise says the Father sends him 'in my name'. Yet Christ never said the Father sends the Spirit 'from me'. This shows that the Father is the beginning (principium) of the whole deity.
sources.quote: Yet He did not say, Whom the Father will send from me, as He said, “Whom I will send unto you from the Father,”—showing, namely, that the Father is the beginning (principium) of the whole divinity
sources.raw_question: How does John 15:26, 'Whom I will send unto you from the Father', show the relation of the Spirit to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It shows the Son's unity of nature with the Father. One who sends shows his power in what he sends. The Son sends from the Father the Spirit who proceeds from the Father, so He is revealed as the Sender, not a mere recipient. He thus exercises the Father's own power over the Spirit.
sources.quote: He will send from the Father that Spirit of truth which proceedeth from the Father; He therefore cannot be the Recipient, since He is revealed as the Sender.
sources.raw_question: What does John 15:26, where the Son sends the Spirit of truth from the Father, show about the Son's relation to the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter I. St. Ambrose commences his argument by complimenting the Emperor, both for his faith and for the restitution of the Basilica to the Church; then having urged that his opponents, if they affirm that the Holy Spirit is not a servant, cannot deny Him to be above all, adds that the same Spirit, when He said, “All things serve Thee,” showed plainly that He was distinct from creatures; which point he also establishes by other evidence.
sources.answer: It teaches that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and bears witness of the Son. As a faithful and true witness, the Spirit has the same knowledge as the Son, who shares the Father's secrets. This shows clearly the unity of the Divine Power and supports Paul's teaching that the Spirit searches the deep things of God.
sources.quote: So the Holy Spirit both proceeds from the Father, and bears witness of the Son.
sources.raw_question: What does John 15:26 teach about the Holy Spirit's relation to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: It teaches that the Spirit is personally distinct from the Son. Yet like the Son, the Spirit has His eternal home in fellowship with the Father and comes forth from Him for His saving work. In this instance He is sent not by the Father but by the Son.
sources.quote: it is intimated that the Spirit is personally distinct from the Son, and yet, like Him, has His eternal home (in fellowship) with the Father, from whom He, like the Son, comes forth for His saving work
sources.raw_question: What does John 15:26 teach about the relation of the Holy Spirit to the Father and the Son?

question: Is the Holy Spirit who spoke in the Old Testament prophets the same Spirit who was given to the New Testament apostles?
synthesis: Ambrose, Irenaeus, Novatian and Hilary all affirm that it is one and the same Spirit, but each grounds the claim differently. Ambrose argues from parallel with the one Father and one Son acting in both Testaments, and turns this against those who divide the God of the Old Testament from the God of the New. Irenaeus stresses the single Spirit's continuous witness to Christ's advent from prophecy to fulfilment, while Hilary simply lists the Spirit's work from the patriarchs through John to the apostles. Novatian alone adds a distinction: the difference lies only in the manner of the Spirit's presence, occasional and sparing in the prophets but abiding and full in the apostles.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IV. The Holy Spirit is one and the same Who spake in the prophets and apostles, Who is the Spirit of God and of Christ; Whom, further, Scripture designates the Paraclete, and the Spirit of life and truth.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as the one Father spoke both to the fathers by the prophets and to us by His Son, and the one Son was seen by Abraham and worshipped by Jacob, so the one Holy Spirit energized in the prophets, was breathed upon the apostles, and was joined to the Father and Son in baptism. This also refutes heretics who split the God of the Old Testament from the God of the New.
sources.quote: so, too, the Holy Spirit is one, who energized in the prophets, was breathed upon the apostles, and was joined to the Father and the Son in the sacrament of baptism.
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who distinguished the God of the Old Testament from the God of the New
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit who spoke in the Old Testament prophets the same Spirit who was given to the New Testament apostles?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. One and the same Spirit of God proclaimed by the prophets what the Lord's advent would be, gave the elders a just interpretation of it, and announced through the apostles that the fulness of times had arrived. He also dwells in those who believe on Him who was born Emmanuel of the Virgin.
sources.quote: For the one and the same Spirit of God, who proclaimed by the prophets what and of what sort the advent of the Lord should be, did by these elders give a just interpretation of what had been truly prophesied
sources.raw_question: Is it the same Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets and who spoke through the apostles about Christ's advent?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Next Teaches Us that the Authority of the Faith Enjoins, After the Father and the Son, to Believe Also on the Holy Spirit, Whose Operations He Enumerates from Scripture.
sources.answer: He is one and the same Spirit. He is not new in the Gospel: it was he who accused the people through the prophets and who gave the apostles their appeal to the Gentiles. The difference lies only in the manner of his presence. In the prophets he was present occasionally and given sparingly; in the apostles he abides always and is poured out fully. Paul's "having the same Spirit" confirms this.
sources.quote: He is therefore one and the same Spirit who was in the prophets and apostles, except that in the former He was occasional, in the latter always.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit who worked in the Old Testament prophets the same Spirit given to the apostles, or a new Spirit introduced in the Gospel?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Yes. The Holy Ghost is everywhere One: He enlightened the patriarchs, prophets and the company of the Law, inspired John in his mother's womb, and was given in due time to the Apostles and believers.
sources.quote: For the Holy Ghost is everywhere One, enlightening all patriarchs and prophets and the whole company of the Law, inspiring John even in his mother’s womb, given in due time to the Apostles and other believers
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit who inspired the patriarchs and prophets the same Spirit given to the Apostles?

question: Can God be circumscribed or confined to a place, such as heaven, a temple or a mountain?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa, Novatian, Irenaeus and Hilary all deny that God can be confined to a place, but they argue differently. Gregory argues from what divinity is: nothing circumscribed is divine, and the Godhead pervades all things. Novatian and Irenaeus work from the text 'heaven is my throne': Novatian reasons that one whom the world cannot contain is still less contained by a temple, while Irenaeus warns against reading the throne bodily and insists that God contains all things rather than being contained. Hilary grounds the denial in God being Spirit, immeasurable and fully present everywhere, containing all things while being self-contained.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He discusses the incomprehensibility of the Divine essence, and the saying to the woman of Samaria, “Ye worship ye know not what.“
sources.answer: No. Nothing that is conceived as circumscribed is divine. It belongs to the Godhead to be in all places, to pervade all things, and to be limited by nothing.
sources.quote: nothing is Divine that is conceived as being circumscribed, but it belongs to the Godhead to be in all places, and to pervade all things, and not to be limited by anything
sources.raw_question: Can God be circumscribed or confined to a place?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God is the Founder of All Things, Their Lord and Parent, is Proved from the Holy Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. When God says heaven is His throne and earth His footstool, He shows that He whom the world does not contain is much less contained in a temple. He says this not out of boastfulness but to give us knowledge and religious wisdom.
sources.quote: that He may show that He whom the world does not contain is much less contained in a temple
sources.raw_question: Can God be contained in a place such as a temple?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter III.—Answer to the cavils of the Gnostics. We are not to suppose that the true God can be changed, or come to an end because the heavens, which are His throne and the earth, His footstool, shall pass away.
sources.answer: No. God is not contained within bounds but contains all things. To read 'heaven is my throne' as if God sat bodily like a man is to be ignorant of what God is.
sources.quote: they imagine that He sits after the fashion of a man, and is contained within bounds, but does not contain.
sources.raw_question: Is God contained or circumscribed by place, such as heaven being his throne?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Because God is Spirit, invisible, incomprehensible and immeasurable. Spirit cannot be cabined or confined but is omnipresent in space and time and present in its fulness under all conditions; God contains all things and is self-contained.
sources.quote: For Spirit cannot be cabined or confined; it is omnipresent in space and time, and under all conditions present in its fulness.
sources.raw_question: Why can God not be confined to a particular place such as a mountain or temple?

question: Does confessing both the Father and the Son as God mean confessing two Gods?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers, Athanasius and Novatian all deny that it yields two Gods, but on different grounds. Hilary rests on the perfect birth that gives the Son the Father's one nature (with mutual indwelling and real personal distinction), and he repeatedly rejects both two Gods and a solitary God. Athanasius holds that the Son's Godhead is the Father's own Godhead and adds that treating two Persons as two Gods would force Sabellianism. Novatian argues instead from origin: the Son is not a second unbegotten beginning but has all he is from the Father, so he points back to the one God.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Hilary avoids both extremes. God is One not by any confusion of the Two, and there is no plurality of Gods. Yet the distinction between Father and Son is real, not merely nominal.
sources.quote: We teach that it is by no confusion of the Two that God is One; we do not rend Him in pieces by preaching a plurality of Gods, nor yet do we profess a distinction only in name.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing both the Father and the Son as God require either two gods or a Sabellian merging of the Persons?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: No. The Son's Godhead was not procured from without or foreign to the Father's; it is the Father's own Godhead. Though the Son is other as Offspring, He is the same as God, one with the Father in propriety of nature and identity of the one Godhead, so there is one God and none other.
sources.quote: Wherefore neither is the Son another God, for He was not procured from without, else were there many, if a godhead be procured foreign from the Father's
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the Son as God introduce a second God alongside the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. The Son is of the Father's substance, inseparable from Him in nature though distinct in Person. God is One because God is from the nature of God, and the Prophets never class the Only-begotten apart as a second God. So the unity of nature stands alongside the Son's personal existence.
sources.quote: the Only-begotten, Who is of the substance of the Father, shall be known as indivisible and inseparable in nature, not in Person. We shall set forth God as One, because God is from the nature of God.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the Son as true God introduce a second God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Neither. The faith of the Church confesses that God is not solitary and that there are not two Gods. The real birth of God from God means God cannot be solitary, since there is a begetting Father and a begotten Son. Because that birth is perfect, the two cannot have different natures, so they are not two Gods.
sources.quote: so that the faith of the Church should neither confess that God is single nor that there are two Gods. For neither would the birth of God allow God to be solitary, nor would a perfect birth allow different natures to be ascribed to two Gods.
sources.raw_question: Does the true birth of the Son from the Father force the Church to confess either a single, solitary God or two Gods?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Father and Son are in each other through the perfect birth of the living nature, so they cannot be added together and counted as two Gods. They are one God. Yet they cannot be confused, because they are not one Person.
sources.quote: Thus you cannot add together God the Father and God the Son, and count Them as two Gods, for They Two are One God. You cannot confuse Them together, for They Two are not One Person.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing both the Father and the Son as God mean confessing two Gods?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: No. The Son cannot make two Gods because he does not constitute a second beginning: he received the source of his nativity before all time from the Father, who alone has no beginning. Since the Son is from the unbegotten Father, he points back to the Father as the one source, and so even though he is God born, he shows the Father to be the one God.
sources.quote: And thus He could not make two Gods, because He did not make two beginnings, seeing that from Him who has no beginning He received the source of His nativity before all time.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the Son as God, alongside God the Father, result in two Gods?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Unless Father and Son are two in name only, or as parts and so each imperfect, or two gods, they are coessential, one in Godhead, and the Son from the Father.
sources.answer: No. If acknowledging Father and Son meant holding two Gods, then confessing one God would require denying the Son and becoming Sabellian, which is unacceptable. Rather, when we call Father and Son two, we still confess one God. They are one in the Godhead, and the Father's Word is indissoluble, indivisible and inseparable from him.
sources.quote: as when we say that Father and Son are two, we still confess one God, so when we say that there is one God, let us consider Father and Son two, while they are one in the Godhead
sources.raised_by_detail: those who mock 'You hold two Gods'
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the Father and the Son as two amount to believing in two Gods?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. God from God does not multiply God by two, because the One in begetting the One conferred nothing that was not His own, and the begotten One received only what belongs to one nature. One Divine nature and one Divine name belong to both, so the term 'One God' signifies the Two.
sources.quote: God from God, or God in God, does not mean that there are two Gods, for God abides, One from One, eternally with the one Divine nature and the one Divine name
sources.raw_question: Does confessing that the Son is God from God mean that there are two Gods?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary's soul did not disperse its faith among a plurality of deities because it heard that the Son is God of God, that is, God from the one God. The Son's deity is derived from the Father, not set up as a separate godhead.
sources.quote: It did not disperse its faith among a plurality of deities, for it heard that He is God of God
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the Son as 'God of God' introduce a plurality of gods?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: No. The Son is God proceeding from God, a second person, but he does not take from the Father the characteristic of being the one God. If he were unborn, without beginning, invisible or a Father like the Father, there would be two unborn beings and two Gods; but because whatever he is he has from the Father by birth, he takes his beginning from the one God and cannot cause two Gods.
sources.quote: He could not make a disagreement in the divinity by the number of two Gods, since He gathered His beginning by being born of Him who is one God.
sources.raw_question: Does the confession that Christ is God mean there are two Gods?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Neither. Paul's language avoids both errors. The one in the form of God does not end as another God, nor does He lose His Godhead, since He cannot be severed from the form in which He exists. Being in the Father's glory, He possesses divinity naturally from the Father, so He cannot be proclaimed another god. Yet He is a real Son who exists, not a mere aspect of a solitary God.
sources.quote: neither does the Apostle’s faith, by calling Him a God of a different order, fall away to the confession of two Gods, nor by making God the Son inseparable from the Father does it leave an opening for the unholy doctrine of a single and solitary God.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the Son as God in the form and glory of the Father lead either to two Gods or to a single solitary God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Because the Son is God of God, faith is not spread across a plurality of deities. Because He is full of grace and truth, no difference of nature is attributed to Him. Nor is there anything contrary to reason in God of God, since He was revealed as having been God with God in the beginning.
sources.quote: It did not disperse its faith among a plurality of deities, for it heard that He is God of God; nor did it fall into the error of attributing a difference of nature to this God of God, for it learnt that He is full of grace and truth.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the Son as 'God of God' introduce a plurality of gods or a difference of nature between the Father and the Son?

question: Can human reason comprehend the divine nature or essence, or must we rely on what God reveals of Himself?
synthesis: Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa and Bickersteth all deny that human reason can comprehend God's nature, but they ground this differently. Gregory argues from the infinity of the divine essence and the gap between uncreated and created: no faculty, not even an angel's, and no word can grasp it, and God's silence about His essence shows the knowledge is beyond us; what is revealed suffices for salvation. Hilary and Bickersteth stress humble dependence on God's self-revelation, Hilary warning against rash conjecture and Bickersteth arguing from the mystery of even created light that on the Trinity we must ask what Scripture says.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. No earthly mind can define God or penetrate the depth of His wisdom; His judgments and ways are incomprehensible to creatures. We must echo the Apostle's exclamation to curb our feeble intellect, lest we try by rash conjecture to snatch from God more than He has revealed.
sources.quote: No earthly mind can define God, no understanding can penetrate with its perception to sound the depth of His wisdom.
sources.raw_question: Can human reason comprehend or define the depth of the divine nature and God's wisdom?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Human reason cannot attain it by itself; we must believe God's word about Himself. Our created bodily faculties and the reason given for ordinary life cannot ascertain or pronounce upon the nature and work of God. We must accept humbly the insight He gives and think of Him in the aspect in which He presents Himself to us.
sources.quote: We must believe God’s word concerning Himself, and humbly accept such insight as He vouchsafes to give.
sources.raw_question: Can human reason by its own powers attain knowledge of the nature of God, or must we rely on God's self-revelation in Scripture?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory proceeds to discuss the relative force of the unnameable name of the Holy Trinity and the mutual relation of the Persons, and moreover the unknowable character of the essence, and the condescension on His part towards us, His generation of the Virgin, and His second coming, the resurrection from the dead and future retribution.
sources.answer: No. The divine essence is ineffable and incomprehensible. If human nature could be taught God's essence, God, who wills all men to come to knowledge of the truth, would not have withheld it. His silence about the essence in the delivery of the faith shows such knowledge is beyond our power. What is revealed in the profession of faith suffices for salvation.
sources.quote: if it were possible for human nature to be taught the essence of God, He “Who will have all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” would not have suppressed the knowledge upon this matter.
sources.raw_question: Can the divine essence be known or comprehended by human beings?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Our knowledge cannot reach what lies beyond knowledge, and words lack the power to express fully our thoughts about what is divine. No faculty in human nature, and not even the understanding of angels, is adequate to comprehend the infinite divine essence.
sources.quote: There is no faculty in human nature adequate to the full comprehension of the divine essence.
sources.raw_question: Can the divine essence be fully grasped by human knowledge or expressed in human words?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. There is no faculty in human nature adequate to the full comprehension of the divine essence. Even angels, whose pure intelligence far exceeds ours, are probably not much nearer comprehending Him Who really is, because an insurmountable interval separates uncreated from created nature.
sources.quote: There is no faculty in human nature adequate to the full comprehension of the divine essence.
sources.raw_question: Can any human faculty fully comprehend the divine essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The divine nature transcends all intelligence, being as far above human calculation as the stars are above the touch of our fingers, or more. It is safer and more reverent to believe God's majesty greater than we can understand than to circumscribe His glory by our conceptions.
sources.quote: For it is both safer and more reverent to believe the majesty of God to be greater than we can understand, than, after circumscribing His glory by our misconceptions, to suppose there is nothing beyond our conception of it.
sources.raw_question: Can human reason comprehend or know the divine essence of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He discusses the incomprehensibility of the Divine essence, and the saying to the woman of Samaria, “Ye worship ye know not what.“
sources.answer: No. The divine nature is infinite, and what is unlimited cannot be comprehended. Interpreting something through words and names implies some comprehension of it, so the divine essence cannot be expressed in speech. We therefore honour in silence what transcends speech and thought, and we are not to blame for ignorance of what no one should presume to define.
sources.quote: it is not possible that that which is by nature infinite should be comprehended in any conception expressed by words
sources.raw_question: Can the divine essence be comprehended or defined by any concept expressed in words?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Reason supplies only a dim and imperfect comprehension of God's nature, yet the knowledge drawn from the names piety allows us to apply to Him suffices for our limited capacity. God transcends reason and sense; human thought can only touch His sublime nature and catch a faint glimpse of it.
sources.quote: reason supplies us with but a dim and imperfect comprehension of the Divine nature; nevertheless, the knowledge that we gather from the terms which piety allows us to apply to it is sufficient for our limited capacity.
sources.raw_question: Can human reason attain a full comprehension of the divine nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: No. Thought ascending past the ages finds the divine nature like an immense ocean with no sign of a beginning; what it seeks always moves on before it. Time and its contents are the limit of human thought, and since the divine has no form, place, size or reckoning of time, the mind must fall back to creation as its congenial sphere.
sources.quote: Every discursive effort of thought to go back beyond the ages will ascend only so far as to see that that which it seeks can never be passed through
sources.raw_question: Can human reason, tracing back beyond the ages, reach a beginning or comprehend the divine nature?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: We know Him only as He reveals Himself. Science is soon out of its depth in understanding even created light, which remains a great deep of mystery; how much more must we be humbled before the Creator who dwells in light no man can approach. Hence on the Trinity the question must always be, what saith the Scripture?
sources.quote: Is light a mystery? How much rather He who dwelleth in the light that no man can approach unto! We know him only as He reveals himself.
sources.raw_question: Can human reason comprehend the nature of God, or do we know Him only as He reveals Himself?

question: Does Christ's statement that 'the Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He seeth the Father do' (John 5:19) imply that the Son is weaker than or inferior in nature to the Father?
synthesis: Hilary, Augustine and Waterland all deny that the text implies inferiority, but they argue differently. Hilary reads it against the Sabbath controversy as a statement about authority and true birth rather than strength, and stresses that the Son does 'whatever' the Father does and receives equal honour. Augustine holds that it speaks of the Son in the form of God rather than the form of a servant, and that it shows the Son as being of the Father: his inability to act otherwise is strength, and Father and Son work indivisibly, though the Son's power is given by the Father. Waterland argues that, being one in nature with the Father, the Son can do nothing contrary to him, and that the Arian reading makes the rest of the verse incoherent.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The words were spoken to affirm that His equality with God rested on a true birth from the Father, not to deny His power. They show a nature whose power of action derives not from successive gifts of strength for particular deeds but from knowledge, because the power and nature of God dwell consciously in Him; His liberty of action coincides with His knowledge of the Father's nature, which is inseparably His by birth.
sources.quote: a nature which derives its power of action not from successive gifts of strength to do particular deeds, but from knowledge
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that 'the Son can do nothing of Himself but what He seeth the Father do' (John 5:19) imply that the Son is weaker than or inferior in nature to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Some Things Concerning the Holy Spirit are to Be Understood According to the One Rule Only.
sources.answer: No. Christ said this not according to the form of a servant but according to the form of God, and the words set him forth not as less than the Father but as being of the Father.
sources.quote: these words do not set Him forth as less than, but as of the Father
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's saying "The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He seeth the Father do" show that the Son is less than the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The saying answers the Jews' charge of Sabbath-breaking, and "can do nothing" refers to authority, not strength. Seeing does not confer the power to act, so the Son is not weak. Rather, His authority rests on His awareness that the Father's nature abides and works in Him. Since the Father works even on the Sabbath, the Son who works with Him is cleared of blame.
sources.quote: For the words, can do nothing, refer not to strength but to authority; He can do nothing of Himself, except what He has seen. Now, to have seen does not confer the power to do, and therefore He is not weak
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement "The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He hath seen the Father doing" (John 5:19) imply that the Son is weaker than the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. The obvious meaning is that, being related to God as a Son to a Father and perfectly one with him in nature, the Son can do nothing contrary or foreign to the Father, since both always unite in operation. Hence whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. The Arian reading makes the verse incoherent, since 'for what things soever he doth, these also doth the Son likewise' would not follow from a limitation of powers; instead of retracting the claim to equality, Christ extends it.
sources.quote: He, as a Son, being perfectly one with his Father, could do nothing ἐναντίον τῷ Πατρὶ, against his Father, nothing ἀλλότριον, nothing ξένον, (as Chrysostom expresseth it,) both having the same nature; and harmoniously uniting always in operation and energy.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that 'the Son can do nothing of himself' (John 5:19) imply that the Son is inferior in nature and acts only by delegated commission?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. It shows his birth: having no power of initiation, he cannot be unbegotten and must have been born. His ability to see the Father's works shows he has the understanding proper to a possessor of divinity. He also does whatever the Father does, which proves his true divine nature.
sources.quote: He cannot be unbegotten, because He can do nothing of Himself; He has no power of initiation, and therefore He must have been born. But the fact that He can see the Father’s works proves that He has the comprehension which belongs to the conscious Possessor of Divinity.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement 'The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He seeth the Father do' imply that the Son is inferior in nature or ignorant?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Word of God is in All Things Equal to the Father, from Whom It is.
sources.answer: No. The Son's inability to do otherwise than the Father is not infirmity but strength. It is the strength by which truth cannot be false, and it flows from the Son's unchangeable being from the Father.
sources.quote: Through power He cannot do this; nor is it infirmity, but strength, by which truth cannot be false.
sources.raw_question: Does 'the Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He seeth the Father do' (John 5:19) imply weakness or inferiority in the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The same passage affirms that whatever the Father does, the Son does in like manner, and 'whatever' includes all things without exception, so there is nothing the Father does that the Son cannot do. Moreover the same honour is demanded for the Son as for the Father. Where there is the same power of operation and equal honour, no inferiority can exist.
sources.quote: But if what things soever includes all things without exception; in what is He found weak, when there is nothing that the Father doeth, which He cannot also do?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that the Son can do nothing of Himself but what He sees the Father doing prove that the Son is weaker than or inferior to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The saying was a reply to the Jews' double charge that Christ broke the Sabbath and made Himself equal with God. Its form must not be detached from its substance. The Father works in the Son, so the Son's work is the working of the Father's nature in Him. The text therefore shows unity of nature and power, not powerlessness.
sources.quote: But Christ was answering in the same sentence the double charge of the Jews, who accused Him of violating the Sabbath, and of making Himself equal with God by calling God His Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the saying "The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He hath seen the Father doing" (John 5:19) confess a weakness in the Son that is incompatible with His being true God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > There is a Double Rule for Understanding the Scriptural Modes of Speech Concerning the Son of God. These Modes of Speech are of a Threefold Kind.
sources.answer: No. If it referred to the servant form, the Father would have had to walk on water or heal the blind with clay before the Son did. No one, even a madman, would think that. The text means that the working of Father and Son is indivisible, yet the Son's power to work is given him by the Father, of whom he is.
sources.quote: it will follow that the Father must have walked on the water, or opened the eyes with clay and spittle of some other one born blind, and have done the other things which the Son appearing in the flesh did among men, before the Son did them
sources.raised_by_detail: some unlearned Catholics and those who infer the Son is less
sources.raw_question: Does 'The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He seeth the Father do' (John 5:19) refer to the Son as less in his human form?

question: Does the worship given to the Son show that he is truly God and not a creature?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa, Daniel Waterland and Athanasius all hold that because worship belongs to God alone, the Son's being worshipped shows he is not a creature, and that worshipping a created Son would be idolatry. Their grounds differ. Gregory points to Paul's adoration of Christ as 'God over all', poses a dilemma from the division of created and uncreated, and likens worship of a Son who 'once was not' to the worship of new gods or Dagon. Waterland rests on the fundamental rule of Law and Gospel, following Origen. Athanasius cites Peter and the angels refusing worship while the Son accepted it, and grounds this worship in his being the proper offspring of the Father's Essence.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul adored Christ, yet he classed those who worship the creature besides the Creator as idolaters. Had the Son been created, Paul would either not have worshipped him or would have condemned himself. He worshipped Christ because he knew him to be 'God over all', as Romans says.
sources.quote: But he knew that He Whom he adored was God over all, for so he terms the Son in his Epistle to the Romans.
sources.raw_question: Does the worship of Christ show that the Son is not a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: Yes. The fundamental rule of both Law and Gospel is that God alone may be worshipped. If the Son is very God, Jehovah and Creator, he may and ought to be worshipped by that rule. If he were only a creature, worshipping him would break that rule. So if the Son is to be worshipped, he is not a creature; if he is a creature, he is not to be worshipped.
sources.quote: In a-word; if the Son of God is to be worshipped, he is not a creature: if a creature, he is not to be worshipped.
sources.raw_question: Does the worship of the Son of God show that he is not a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
