sources.answer: Yes. What now is but formerly was not is new and not eternal. Moses calls the worship of new gods the service of demons. So those who say the Son "once was not" yet worship Him are worshipping a new and strange god. They must be reckoned among idolaters, and their position is a departure from Christianity.
sources.quote: If then everything that is new in worship is a service of demons, and is alien from the true Godhead, and if what is now, but was not always, is new and not eternal
sources.raw_question: Is worshipping a Son who once did not exist a form of idolatry?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: Yes. He would not have been worshipped or spoken of in this way if He were merely a creature. Because He is the proper offspring of the Essence of the God who is worshipped, and His Son by nature, He is worshipped and believed to be God, Lord of armies, and Almighty, just as the Father is.
sources.quote: But He had not been thus worshipped, nor been thus spoken of, were He a creature merely. But now since He is not a creature, but the proper offspring of the Essence of that God who is worshipped, and His Son by nature, therefore He is worshipped
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Christ is worshipped and called God, Lord of hosts and Almighty show that the Son is not a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > The fifth book promises to speak of the words contained in the saying of the Apostle Peter, but delays their exposition. He discourses first of the creation, to the effect that, while nothing therein is deserving of worship, yet men, led astray by their ill-informed and feeble intelligence, and marvelling at its beauty, deified the several parts of the universe. And herein he excellently expounds the passage of Isaiah, “I am God, the first.”
sources.answer: No. All existence is divided into the created and the uncreated, so a created Son would force a dilemma. Either Christians must refuse to worship God the Word, against the Gospel, or they must give the created and the Uncreated the same honour. Since the Gospels compel the worship of the Word, he cannot be a creature.
sources.quote: we should be absolutely compelled either to set at naught the proclamation of the Gospel, and to refuse to worship that God the Word Who was in the beginning, on the ground that we must not address worship to the creation
sources.raw_question: If the Son of God were a creature, could Christians consistently worship him?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. Following Origen, the author holds that if the Son were a creature, not Creator, or not truly God, he should not be worshipped at all. Worship belongs only to the one God as opposed to every created thing.
sources.quote: That God the Son, if a creature, or not Creator, or not truly God, should not be worshipped at all.
sources.raw_question: Should the Son be worshipped if he were a creature or not truly God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: Yes. Worship belongs to God alone; creature does not worship creature, as shown when Peter refused Cornelius's worship, the angel refused John's, and the angel refused Manoah's sacrifice. Yet angels and Gentiles worship the Son, and He accepted His disciples' worship and Thomas's confession 'My Lord and my God', so He is true God.
sources.quote: For if He was worshipped as excelling them in glory, each of things subservient ought to worship what excels itself. But this is not the case; for creature does not worship creature, but servant Lord, and creature God.
sources.raw_question: Does the worship given to the Son prove that he is God and not a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Christians are taught by the law to worship nothing that is not very God. So by the very act of worshipping the Son they confess that the Only-begotten is God in truth, not a God falsely so called.
sources.quote: taught by the law to worship nothing that is not very God, and by that very act of worship confess that the Only-begotten is God in truth
sources.raw_question: Does the worship Christians give to the Son show that the Son is truly God and not God in name only?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then clearly and skilfully criticises the doctrine of the impossibility of comparison with the things made after the Son, and exposes the idolatry contrived by Eunomius, and concealed by the terminology of “Son” and “Only-begotten,” to deceive his readers.
sources.answer: Yes. Whoever applies the name of Son to a creature and worships him is to be ranked among idolaters, since he draws near as though to God but finds a creature set forth for worship. Just as giving the name of God to Dagon, Bel and the Dragon did not make them God, calling a creature "Son" or "God" does not make its worship the worship of God.
sources.quote: if any one applies the name of Son to the creation, he is to be ranked among idolaters. For they too gave the name of God to Dagon and Bel and the Dragon, but they did not on that account worship God.
sources.raw_question: Is worshipping the Son as a creature of God a form of idolatry?

question: Does Christ's saying 'Why callest thou Me good? None is good save one, that is, God' deny that the Son is good or truly God, or imply that the Father's substance is of greater goodness than the Son's?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa, Hilary and Augustine all deny that the saying excludes the Son, but they argue differently. Gregory and Augustine say Christ answered the questioner according to the human or servant form the man saw. Gregory adds that confessing the Lord as God already asserts His goodness. Hilary stresses the circumstances of the saying, holding that Christ rebuked the unbelief of a man who addressed Him as a mere teacher, and reads it alongside His other self-revealing words. Augustine adds that 'one God' means the whole Trinity, and he accepts any interpretation that does not make the Father's substance better than the Son's.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He also ingeniously shows from the passage of the Gospel which speaks of “Good Master,” from the parable of the Vineyard, from Isaiah and from Paul, that there is not a dualism in the Godhead of good and evil, as Eunomius' ally Marcion supposes, and declares that the Son does not refuse the title of “good” or “Existent,” or acknowledge His alienation from the Father, but that to Him also belongs authority over all things that come into being.
sources.answer: No. The rich young man addressed Christ only as a man, flattering the servant-form he saw, so Christ answered as He was addressed, through His humanity. The word "Me" points to the human nature He bore, which since the fall is barred from the title "good," while by ascribing goodness to the Godhead He declared Himself good, since the Gospel proclaims Him God.
sources.quote: suggesting in His answer by the word “Me” that human nature which encompassed Him, while by attributing goodness to the Godhead He expressly declared Himself to be good, seeing that He is proclaimed to be God by the Gospel
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "There is none good but one, that is, God" show that the Son is excluded from the title of "good" and thus not of the Father's nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary holds that the heretics distort Christ's words by ignoring the circumstances in which they were spoken. Read against sayings such as 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father,' it is the same Speaker revealing his nature gradually, and his true Godhead is in no way impaired.
sources.quote: or between None is good save One, even God, and He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father also
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'Why callest thou Me good? None is good save One, even God' exclude him from the goodness and true divinity of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He also ingeniously shows from the passage of the Gospel which speaks of “Good Master,” from the parable of the Vineyard, from Isaiah and from Paul, that there is not a dualism in the Godhead of good and evil, as Eunomius' ally Marcion supposes, and declares that the Son does not refuse the title of “good” or “Existent,” or acknowledge His alienation from the Father, but that to Him also belongs authority over all things that come into being.
sources.answer: No. Gregory accepts the statement but denies it excludes the Son: whoever confesses the Lord is God thereby asserts goodness of Him, since goodness is a property of God. The saying therefore confirms rather than denies the Son's goodness once His Godhead is established.
sources.quote: I do not, however, for this cause deny the Godhead of the Son. But he who confesses that the Lord is God, by that very confession assuredly also asserts of Him goodness.
sources.raw_question: Does the text 'There is none good but one, that is God' exclude the Son from being good or from being God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Christ did not resent being called good, since he testified to his own goodness when he called himself meek and lowly. What he rebuked was the unbelief of the questioner, who addressed him merely as a teacher of the law. His added words, 'None is good save one, God', show that he accepts the name 'good' when it is given to him as God.
sources.quote: He Who witnesses to His own goodness would not repudiate the name of Good. Plainly, then, He was not angry because He was called good
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'Why callest thou Me good? None is good save one, God' show that the Son is not God by nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whatever is Spoken of God According to Substance, is Spoken of Each Person Severally, and Together of the Trinity Itself. One Essence in God, and Three, in Greek, Hypostases, in Latin, Persons.
sources.answer: No. Jesus did not say that none is good except the Father alone, but "except one, that is, God." The name of God signifies the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, since the Trinity is one God. Jesus spoke this way so that the man calling him "Good Master" would not take him to be a man only.
sources.quote: does not therefore say, There is none good, save the Father alone; but, “None is good, save one, that is, God.”
sources.raw_question: Does Jesus' saying "None is good, save one, that is, God" deny that the Son is good or that the Son is God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: No. The man who asked did not understand with whom he was speaking and thought Christ to be only the Son of man. Christ's reply refers to the form of the servant he could see, not to the form of God in which he is equal with the Father. Understood according to that divine form, the Son is good, since the one God who alone is good is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: If you understand me after this latter form, then I am good; but if according to that former only, then why askest thou me about good?
sources.raw_question: When Christ says "Why askest thou me about good? there is none good but One, that is, God," does he deny that he himself, the Son, is good or is God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: No. Any interpretation of the text is acceptable only if it does not imply that the Father's substance is of greater goodness than the Son's. As the Word by whom all things were made, the Son shares the Father's substance and goodness. The one God who alone is good is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together.
sources.quote: provided only that the substance of the Father be not therefore believed to be of greater goodness than that of the Son, according to which He is the Word by whom all things were made
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's words "there is none good but One, that is, God" imply that the Father's substance is of greater goodness than the Son's?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: No. Augustine allows any explanation of the saying that is consistent with sound doctrine. The one condition is that the Father's substance is not thereby believed to be of greater goodness than the Son's. In that substance the Son is the Word by whom all things were made, and so he is equal in goodness.
sources.quote: provided only that the substance of the Father be not therefore believed to be of greater goodness than that of the Son, according to which He is the Word by whom all things were made
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that 'there is none good but One, that is, God' imply that the Father's substance is of greater goodness than the Son's?

question: In what sense is the Son subject to the Father in 1 Corinthians 15:28, and does this subjection make him inferior to the Father in divinity?
synthesis: Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary all deny that the subjection implies an inferior divine nature, but they explain it differently. Augustine refers it to the form of a servant or the Son's priesthood: as God he is equal to the Father, and only in his assumed nature is he subject. Gregory makes it the subjection of those in whom the Son dwells, so that the adoration given to the Son by his united body redounds to the Father. Hilary ties it to the temporal Dispensation and the glorifying and promotion of Christ's assumed body. He argues that it cannot be a new obedience, since Christ always does the Father's will, and that it is even a sign of his true divinity.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to God, Even the Father. The Kingdom Having Been Delivered to God, Even the Father, Christ Will Not Then Make Intercession for Us.
sources.answer: No. The Son is subject only in so far as he is a Priest who has taken the form of a servant. In so far as he is God, he together with the Father puts us under himself. As Priest, he together with us is put under the Father.
sources.quote: so that, in so far as He is God, He with Him will have put us under Himself; in so far as He is a Priest, He with us will be put under Him.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being subject to the Father (1 Cor 15:28) make him inferior to the Father in his divinity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: The Son's subjection is the subjection of those in whom He dwells. When all people are united by faith into one body of the Lord who is in all, the adoration that all things pay to the Son redounds to the Father's glory. Paul therefore says the Son, who is in all, is subject to the Father by virtue of the subjection of those in whom He is. It does not mean the Son is inferior in nature.
sources.quote: the mighty wisdom of Paul affirms that the Son, Who is in all, is subject to the Father by virtue of the subjection of those in whom He is
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Son said to be subject to the Father in 1 Corinthians 15:28?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: The Son's subjection is part of the same mystery by which we are subjected to the glory of His body. First all things are subjected to Christ. Then Christ, who reigns in the glory of His body, is in turn subjected to the Father, who subjects all things to Himself. The subjection concerns the order of His bodily reign and the glorifying of His body. It is not a lessening of His divine nature.
sources.quote: As we are subjected to the glory of the rule of His body, so He also, reigning in the glory of His body, is by the same Mystery in turn subjected to Him, Who subjects all things to Himself.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Son subjected to the Father according to 1 Corinthians 15:28, that God may be all in all?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The subjection is not a debasement of his divinity but the promotion of his assumed nature. The Father's divine nature imposes itself on the assumed body, so that he who is God and Man becomes wholly God. He is subjected not that he may cease to be, but that God may be all in all.
sources.quote: this subjection is not the debasement of His divinity, but the promotion of His assumed nature, for He Who is God and Man is now altogether God.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's subjection to the Father, 'that God may be all in all' (1 Corinthians 15:28), imply that the Son is inferior in divinity or will cease to exist?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary argues from these very words of the Apostle that subjection is no evidence of want of power in Christ. Rather, it is actually a sign of His true Divinity as God the Son.
sources.quote: it proves from these very words of the Apostle not only that subjection is no evidence of want of power in Christ but that it actually is a sign of His true Divinity as God the Son
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's final subjection to the Father in 1 Corinthians 15:27-28 prove that the Son lacks divine power and is inferior in nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: No. The Son is subject according to the created nature he assumed, in which the Son of God was made Son of man, when the whole creation is made subject to God. Delivering up the kingdom means bringing the just to the vision of God, including the sight of the Son's own divine form. In that form he is equal to the Father.
sources.quote: Because, according to this creature, “The Son also Himself shall be subject unto Him, that put all things under Him, that God may be all in all.”
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that the Son will deliver up the kingdom to the Father and be subject to him (1 Corinthians 15:24-28) imply that the Son is inferior to the Father in divinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: No. The subjection is said of Christ according to the form of a servant, the human nature he took, not according to the form of God in which he is equal to the Father. Whatever interpretation one gives of that future subjection, the human nature plainly still existed when Christ said "My Father is greater than I," so the Father is greater than the form of a servant, while the Son in the form of God is equal.
sources.quote: whence there is no question that it was said in this sense, that the Father is greater than the form of a servant, to whom in the form of God the Son is equal.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 15:28, which says the Son will be subject to the Father, prove that the Son is inferior to the Father in his divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The word 'then' denotes the temporal Dispensation, not a natural subordination. If subjection meant a new obedience, Christ would now be an unsubjected rebel, which contradicts his own words that he always does the Father's will. His allegiance is eternal; the subjection is an event in time that simply demonstrates the Mystery.
sources.quote: this subjection is no sign of a fresh obedience, but the Dispensation of the Mystery, for the allegiance is eternal, the subjection an event within time.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's future subjection to the Father (1 Corinthians 15:28) imply that he is of a different, inferior nature, as servant to lord?

question: Did God need intermediaries, instruments or matter in order to create the world, or did he create by himself through his Word?
synthesis: All three authors deny that God needed any intermediary or instrument to create, but on different grounds. Irenaeus says God created by himself through his own Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit as his 'hands', with angels having no share in the work. Athanasius argues that God's will alone suffices, so a created mediator in creation is superfluous. Gregory of Nyssa likewise makes God's almighty will itself the matter, instrument and all else creation required.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: No. God's almighty will was itself everything needed for creation—matter, instrument, place, time, quality—since his power kept pace with his will and turned it into act. Moses ascribes each created thing simply to the word that bade it be, without mention of matter or instruments.
sources.quote: so that for Him the impulse of His almighty will was everything and instead of everything, matter, instrument, place, time, essence, quality, everything that is conceived in creation.
sources.raw_question: Did God need matter or instruments in order to create the world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: God made all things by himself, that is, through his Word and his Wisdom. He needed no other agent: heaven, earth, the seas and all in them are his own work, done by his Word and Wisdom.
sources.quote: He the Creator, who made those things by Himself, that is, through His Word and His Wisdom— heaven and earth, and the seas, and all things that are in them
sources.raw_question: Did God create the world by means of intermediaries outside himself, or by himself through his Word and Wisdom?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter II.—The world was not formed by angels, or by any other being, contrary to the will of the most high God, but was made by the Father through the Word.
sources.answer: No. It belongs to God's pre-eminence not to need other instruments for creating; His own Word is both suitable and sufficient for forming all things. Moses records that God created heaven and earth, and neither gods nor angels had any share in the work.
sources.quote: For this is a peculiarity of the pre-eminence of God, not to stand in need of other instruments for the creation of those things which are summoned into existence. His own Word is both suitable and sufficient for the formation of all things
sources.raw_question: Did God need intermediary instruments, such as angels or lesser powers, to create the world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIX.—Earthly things may be the type of heavenly, but the latter cannot be the types of others still superior and unknown; nor can we, without absolute madness, maintain that God is known to us only as the type of a still unknown and superior being.
sources.answer: He created through the Son and Spirit, not angels. God did not need other beings as if He lacked His own hands; the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, were always present with Him, and by and in them He freely made all things, addressing them in "Let Us make man."
sources.quote: For with Him were always present the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, by whom and in whom, freely and spontaneously, He made all things, to whom also He speaks, saying, “Let Us make man after Our image and likeness;”
sources.raw_question: Did God the Father need angels or intermediate powers to create man, or did He create through the Word and Wisdom (the Son and the Spirit)?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: No. God's will alone suffices to constitute whatever He pleases, as Scripture says 'He hath done whatsoever pleased Him' and 'Who hath resisted His will?' So a created mediator in creation is superfluous, and the analogies of Moses and the heavenly lights fail.
sources.quote: why, when He would create us, does He seek for a mediator at all, as if His will did not suffice to constitute whatever seemed good to Him?
sources.raw_question: Does God need a created intermediary in order to create the world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VII.—Recapitulation of the foregoing argument, showing that Abraham, through the revelation of the Word, knew the Father, and the coming of the Son of God. For this cause, he rejoiced to see the day of Christ, when the promises made to him should be fulfilled. The fruit of this rejoicing has flowed to posterity, viz., to those who are partakers in the faith of Abraham, but not to the Jews who reject the Word of God.
sources.answer: No. The Father needed neither angels nor any instrumentality to frame created things. His own offspring and similitude minister to Him in every respect: the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Word and Wisdom. All the angels serve these two and are subject to them.
sources.quote: For His offspring and His similitude do minister to Him in every respect; that is, the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Word and Wisdom; whom all the angels serve, and to whom they are subject.
sources.raw_question: Did God the Father need angels or any other intermediary instrument to create the world and form man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: God needed no intermediaries, because he possessed his own hands. The Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, were always present with him. By them and in them he freely made all things, and to them he speaks when he says, "Let Us make man."
sources.quote: For God did not stand in need of these [beings], in order to the accomplishing of what He had Himself determined with Himself beforehand should be done, as if He did not possess His own hands.
sources.raw_question: Did God need intermediary beings to create the world, or did he create through the Son and the Spirit as his own 'hands'?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter II.—The world was not formed by angels, or by any other being, contrary to the will of the most high God, but was made by the Father through the Word.
sources.answer: God needs nothing. He created all things himself through his own Word, without angels or any lesser power to help. Using many instruments is typical of needy humans. It is God's pre-eminence that his own Word is both suitable and sufficient to form all things, as John 1:3 says.
sources.quote: those who know that God stands in need of nothing, and that He created and made all things by His Word, while He neither required angels to assist Him in the production of those things which are made
sources.raw_question: Did God need intermediary beings or instruments to create, or did he create through his Word?

question: Does Philippians 2:9, 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted Him', mean that the divine Word was promoted, rewarded for virtue, or given something he did not have by nature?
synthesis: Athanasius, Waterland and Augustine all deny that the Word himself was promoted and refer the exaltation to Christ's humanity or 'form of a servant'. Athanasius adds that the exaltation is 'for us' and that a Son rewarded for virtue would be Son only by grace, not by nature. Waterland, following Hippolytus, reads it as a return to the glory Christ always had, while Augustine simply places the exaltation in the form of a servant.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > When the Word and Son hungered, wept, and was wearied, He acted as our Mediator, taking on Him what was ours, that He might impart to us what was His.
sources.answer: It means that we are exalted in him. Just as he humbled himself for our sake, he is also said to be exalted for our sake. So 'He gave to him' means 'to us for his sake', and 'He highly exalted him' means 'us in him'. It is therefore no absurdity that the eternal Word is said to be exalted.
sources.quote: So ‘He gave to Him,’ that is, ‘to us for His sake;’ ‘and He highly exalted Him,’ that is, ‘us in Him.’
sources.raw_question: How should the statement in Philippians 2:9 that God 'highly exalted' Christ be understood, given that the Word is already God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. If the Son received his dignity as a reward of virtue and promotion, he would be called Son and God only by grace and not be very Son. A true offspring is from another by nature, like the radiance from the sun, whereas sons by grace hold an acquired gift that can be lost, as Israel's rebellion shows. Since the Son is truly Son by nature, the 'wherefore' cannot mean moral probation of the Word.
sources.quote: If He was exalted and received grace, on a ‘wherefore,’ and on a ‘wherefore’ He was anointed, He received a reward of His purpose; but having acted from purpose, He is altogether of an alterable nature.
sources.raw_question: Do the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted Him' (Phil. 2:9) and 'Wherefore God hath anointed Thee' (Ps. 45:7) prove that the Son received exaltation as a reward for his moral choice and is therefore of an alterable nature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: No. Following Hippolytus, the exaltation is spoken of only in respect of his humanity. In reality nothing was given him that he did not naturally have from the beginning; it was rather his return to the glory he had essentially and unalterably, as shown by his prayer 'Father, glorify me with the glory which I had,' since he was always invested with divine glory, coexisting with the Father before all ages.
sources.quote: He is said to be exalted, as having “ wanted it before ; but in respect only of his humanity
sources.raw_question: Does Philippians 2:9, where God 'highly exalted' Christ and gave him a name above every name, imply that the Son received something he did not have by nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: In the form of a servant, as the Son of man. The Son, equal to the Father in the form of God, emptied himself by taking the form of a servant. In that form he acts, suffers, is raised and exalted.
sources.quote: For this is said of the Son of man, in respect to whom the Son of God was raised from the dead
sources.raw_question: In what form or nature does Christ receive exaltation and "a name which is above every name" according to Philippians 2?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. The exaltation and the giving are said of the Word as man, because of the body which was truly His own. It was His body that was raised from the dead and taken into heaven, and since the Word was not external to it, He is said, as man, to be exalted. The Word Himself always possessed such exaltation according to the Father's Godhead and perfection.
sources.quote: the Body being His, and the Word not being external to it, it is natural that when the Body was exalted, He, as man, should, because of the body, be spoken of as exalted.
sources.raw_question: Does Philippians 2:9's statement that God 'highly exalted' the Son and 'gave' Him a name imply a defect or change in the essence of the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. Paul did not imply any prize of virtue or promotion from advance, but stated the cause why exaltation was bestowed upon us. Because the one existing in the form of God humbled himself and became a servant on our behalf, we are redeemed, raised, and exalted; the words 'highly exalted' and 'given' are spoken because of us and in our behalf.
sources.quote: For in saying this he did not imply any prize of virtue, nor promotion from advance, but the cause why the exaltation was bestowed upon us.
sources.raw_question: Does the word 'wherefore' in Philippians 2:9 ('Wherefore God hath highly exalted Him') show that the Son received exaltation as a reward for virtue or moral advancement?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. The passage says that, existing in the form of God, he took the form of a servant and humbled himself. That is a descent, not a promotion. Since God is highest of all, his Word must be highest too, and so cannot be exalted further. The exaltation refers to his manhood, not to the essence of the Word, which was always equal to God.
sources.quote: He was not from a lower state promoted: but rather, existing as God, He took the form of a servant, and in taking it, was not promoted but humbled Himself.
sources.raw_question: Does Philippians 2:9-10, 'Wherefore God also highly exalted Him', show that the Son was promoted from a lower state as a reward for his virtue?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. The exaltation is of the manhood, not of the Word's essence, since the Word was ever 'equal to God' and the Most High before any exaltation. 'Humbled' and 'exalted' are both said because of His taking flesh, and are not said of Him before the Word became flesh.
sources.quote: the term in question, ‘highly exalted,’ does not signify that the essence of the Word was exalted, for He was ever and is ‘equal to God,’ but the exaltation is of the manhood.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement in Philippians 2:9 that God 'highly exalted' Christ mean that the essence of the divine Word was raised to a higher status than it had before?

question: When the Father is called the 'one' or 'only' God, does this exclude the Son and the Holy Spirit from being that one God?
synthesis: Waterland, Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine all answer no, but on different grounds. Waterland appeals to the Ante-Nicene writers, to Tertullian's point that such texts exclude another God and idols rather than the Son, to the Church's Liturgy, and to the Father's priority of order as Fountain. Gregory rests on Christ's words 'I and My Father are one', while Augustine stresses that the Persons are inseparable, so that calling the Son the only God likewise does not exclude the Father or the Spirit.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Though 'the one God' primarily denotes the Father, it does not do so exclusively but comprehends the Son too. The Ante-Nicene writers testify to this whenever they speak of Father and Son together as the one God in the singular.
sources.quote: though the one God primarily denotes the Father, yet not exclusively, but comprehends the Son too.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'the one God' denote the Father in a way that excludes the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Following Tertullian, Waterland holds that such declarations exclude another God, not the Son, since the Son is not 'another' from the Father. They are directed chiefly against idol-makers and worshippers, so that the divine unity expels the multitude of false gods while including the Son, who is undivided and inseparable from the Father and implied in him though not named.
sources.quote: that the divine unity may “ exclude the multitude of false gods, while it includes the Son; «‘ who, inasmuch as he is undivided and inseparable from the “ Father, is to be understood as implied in the Father
sources.raw_question: Do Scripture's declarations that there is one God and none besides him exclude the Son from being that one God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. The Father is called the one God in the personal sense, distinct from but not exclusive of the Son and Spirit, and each of them is likewise God and the one God. The Father is peculiarly styled the one God to signify his priority of order as Father and Fountain of all, not to exclude the other Persons.
sources.quote: There is a further reason, why the Father is peculiarly and eminently styled the one God: not to exclude the other Persons; but to signify his priority of order, as Father, and as Fountain of all.
sources.raw_question: When Trinitarians say the Father alone is the one God, does this exclude the Son and Holy Spirit from being the one God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next skilfully confutes the partial, empty and blasphemous statement of Eunomius on the subject of the absolutely existent.
sources.answer: It includes the Son with the Father. The Lord himself said, "I and My Father are one," so the term "one" in its significance comprehends the Son together with the Father.
sources.quote: the word “one” does not indicate the Father alone, but comprehends in its significance the Son with the Father, inasmuch as the Lord said, “I and My Father are one.”
sources.raw_question: Does the word "one" in confessing the one God refer to the Father alone, or does it include the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. Waterland says the Church's Liturgy teaches one God the Father in a sense that includes the Son and the Holy Ghost. It does not teach one God who excludes both of them, which is Dr. Clarke's doctrine. Clarke finds his view in the Liturgy only by drawing an inference the text does not support.
sources.quote: He sees, in our Liturgy, the doctrine of one God the Father, inclusive of Son and Holy Ghost; but does not see one God exclusive of both; which is his doctrine.
sources.raw_question: When the Father is called the 'one God', does this exclude the Son and the Holy Spirit from being that one God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: No. When the Father is called the only God, the Son and Holy Spirit are not to be separated from Him, for together with Him the Son is the only God. Likewise when the Son is called the only God, it is to be taken without separating the Father or the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: And when he is told that the Father only is God, let him not separate from Him the Son or the Holy Spirit; for together with Him He is the only God
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says the Father alone is the only God, does this exclude the Son and the Holy Spirit from being that only God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Waterland holds that such exclusive titles do not shut out the Son, and he says he has shown that reading them that way runs directly against the judgment of the ancients.
sources.quote: That the titles of one, only, Se. are exclusive of the Son. This also I have shewn, in these papers, to be directly contrary to the judgment of the ancients.
sources.raw_question: Do the scriptural titles 'one' and 'only' God exclude the Son from being God?

question: Do the texts calling God invisible and the one 'who only hath immortality' (1 Timothy 1:17; 6:16) refer to the Father alone, excluding the Son and the Holy Spirit from these attributes?
synthesis: Augustine and Gregory of Nyssa agree that these texts do not exclude the Son, but on different grounds. Augustine says they speak of the one divine substance, so the whole Trinity is the invisible, immortal God, and he traces the opposite view to the error that the Son is visible and changeable in himself. Gregory instead reads 'immortality' as the Son himself, who is the Life. Bickersteth differs from Augustine: he grants that Scripture never calls Christ invisible, but denies this weakens Christ's deity, explaining it by Christ's role as mediator between Creator and creatures.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Entire Trinity Invisible.
sources.answer: No. These texts are said of the one only God, and the whole Trinity is understood in that one God. Those who apply them to the Father alone misuse Scripture to prop up their error that the Son is visible in himself.
sources.quote: take that, which is said of the one only God, in whom the Trinity itself is understood, to be said only of the Father, and neither of the Son nor of the Holy Spirit
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold the Son visible in himself
sources.raw_question: Do the texts calling God 'the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God' and the one 'who only hath immortality... whom no man hath seen' refer only to the Father, excluding the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Vision of Daniel.
sources.answer: No. These texts concern the one divine substance by which Father, Son and Holy Spirit are the one God. That substance cannot be shown by any bodily likeness, whether to a sleeper or to one awake. This is true not of the Father only but also of the Son and the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: His own very substance, whereby He Himself is that which He is, cannot be shown by any bodily likeness to one who sleeps, or by any bodily appearance to one who is awake; but this not of the Father only, but also of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who say the Father alone is invisible
sources.raw_question: Do texts calling God invisible, such as 'whom no man hath seen, nor can see', apply to the Father alone and not to the Son and Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > How the Back Parts of God Were Seen. The Faith of the Resurrection of Christ. The Catholic Church Only is the Place from Whence the Back Parts of God are Seen. The Back Parts of God Were Seen by the Israelites. It is a Rash Opinion to Think that God the Father Only Was Never Seen by the Fathers.
sources.answer: They refer to the whole Trinity. Sound faith understands these texts of the highest, unchangeable divine substance. By that one substance the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are the one and only God. The opposite opinion arose from people who could not understand these texts in light of the unity of the Trinity.
sources.quote: Which texts are understood by a sound faith in that substance itself, the highest, and in the highest degree divine and unchangeable, whereby both the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit is the one and only God.
sources.raw_question: Do texts calling God 'invisible' and one 'whom no man hath seen, nor can see' refer to the Father alone, as distinct from the visible Son, or to the whole Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Against Those Who Believed the Father Only to Be Immortal and Invisible. The Truth to Be Sought by Peaceful Study.
sources.answer: They refer to the one only God, in whom the Trinity is understood, not to the Father alone. The substance of the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, remains ever invisible and unchangeable, and so possesses true immortality. Restricting these texts to the Father rests on the false premise that the Son and Spirit are in themselves visible and changeable.
sources.quote: the substance of the one and only God, that is, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, remains ever not only invisible, but also unchangeable, and that hence it possesses true and real immortality
sources.raised_by_detail: those who believed the Father only to be immortal and invisible
sources.raw_question: Do the texts "the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God" and "who only hath immortality" refer to the Father alone, or to the one God who is the Trinity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next skilfully confutes the partial, empty and blasphemous statement of Eunomius on the subject of the absolutely existent.
sources.answer: No. The 'immortality' meant there is the Son himself. Life is immortality, and the Lord said, 'I am the Life.' Likewise the unapproachable light is the Only-begotten, the true Light, in whom the Father is.
sources.quote: But we, even when we are told that God “only hath immortality,” understand by “immortality” the Son. For life is immortality, and the Lord is that life, Who said, “I am the Life.”
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Timothy 6:16, which says God 'only hath immortality' and dwells in unapproachable light, exclude the Son from immortality and divinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. It refers to the one only God, the Trinity. The Son is Himself eternal life and so is not mortal through any changeableness. The passage names neither Father, Son nor Spirit specifically but 'the blessed and only Potentate', the one true God. Creatures share in eternal life, but the life they share is distinct from themselves.
sources.quote: In which words neither is the Father specially named, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit; but the blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings, and Lord of lords; that is, the One and only and true God, the Trinity itself.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's description of God as the one 'who only hath immortality' (1 Timothy 6:16) refer to the Father alone, excluding the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: No, it does not weaken it. Invisibility is the only attribute of the Father not ascribed to Christ. Christ has already been shown to be incomprehensible in his divine nature. The reason for the difference is his role as the medium of communication between the Creator and the creatures.
sources.quote: the reason of this is manifest from the character He sustains as the medium of communication betwixt the Creator and the creatures of his hand
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture call the Father "invisible" but never apply that attribute to Christ, and does this weaken the case for Christ's deity?

question: Was God always Father, or did He become Father at some point, as would follow if the Son had a beginning?
synthesis: Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary all deny that God became Father at some point and affirm eternal Fatherhood, but they argue on different grounds. Athanasius argues that God would otherwise have been without His Word, cites Scripture, and holds that adventitious Fatherhood would make God alterable and leave Him at times without the good. Gregory argues from divine immutability and eternity, holding that God never fails to be what He now is, and he charges Eunomius with self-contradiction. Hilary argues from the correlative names Father and Son: any time denied to the Son is time in which the Father was not Father.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections to the Foregoing Proof. Whether, in the generation of the Son, God made One that was already, or One that was not.
sources.answer: No. To say so implies that God was once without His Reason (Word). This is intolerable, and it is already refuted by many proofs. Scripture affirms the Son's eternal being: John says 'the Word was,' Paul calls Him 'the brightness of His glory' and 'God over all, blessed for ever.'
sources.quote: one would fain not hear them disputing at all, that God was not always Father, but became so afterwards (which is necessary for their fantasy, that His Word once was not)
sources.raw_question: Was God at some point not Father, becoming Father only later when the Son came to be?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: No. Fatherhood is not adventitious to God, for that would make Him alterable. And if being Father is good, but He had not always been Father, then good would not always have been in Him.
sources.quote: nor is the character of Father adventitious to God, lest He seem alterable; for if it is good that He be Father, but has not ever been Father, then good has not ever been in Him.
sources.raw_question: Could God have become Father at some point rather than being Father eternally?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: God was always Father. The Deity is unchangeable, so it never failed to be anything it now is. If God were not always what He now is, He would have changed either from worse to better or from better to worse, and both claims are impious. Since He is now named Father by the Word, He always was Father, and so the Son always existed.
sources.quote: Since then He is named Father by the very Word, He assuredly always was Father, and is and will be even as He was.
sources.raw_question: Was God always Father, or did He become Father at some point, as would follow if the Son had a beginning?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that as God is indestructible and eternal, so also He is Father. Eunomius' claim that God became Father only when He purposed to beget contradicts his own thesis that all divine names coincide in meaning.
sources.quote: for as God is indestructible and eternal, so also He is Father
sources.raw_question: Did God become Father at some later time, so that the name Father is later than His other names?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. The names Father and Son imply each other with no intermediate position: if the Father was always Father, there was always a Son. Whatever time is denied to the Son is that much time the Father was not Father. So a non-eternal Son means the Father was not Father for the whole infinity in which He is God, which is impious.
sources.quote: For either He was not always a Father, unless there was always also a Son; or if He was always a Father, there was always also a Son
sources.raw_question: Could God have always been God but not always Father, so that the Son is not eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then shows, from the instance of Adam and Abel, and other examples, the absence of alienation of essence in the case of the “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: He is Father from eternity. What has its being without beginning does not derive any of its attributes from a beginning; God did not become but is a Father, for in God what was, both is and will be. If He once was not Father, then He neither is nor will be Father.
sources.quote: Well, God is a Father. It follows that He is what He is from eternity: for He did not become, but is a Father: for in God that which was, both is and will be.
sources.raw_question: Did God become Father at some point, or is he Father from eternity?

question: Is the Holy Spirit included among the "all things" said to be made through the Son (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16)?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose and Hilary all deny that the Spirit is among the things made through the Son, but on different grounds. Gregory and Ambrose (in one place) point to Paul's list of created things, which never names the Spirit, and Gregory adds that Scripture gives the Spirit independent authority. Ambrose elsewhere argues that the Spirit knows the Father as no creature can, that Scripture never says the Spirit was made, and that Psalm 33 credits the Spirit with the heavens' strength; he also holds that 'before all' refers to creatures and does not put the Son before the Father. Hilary appeals to Paul calling Him simply God's Spirit, never a creature, and counsels saying nothing beyond that.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: No. The phrase "all things" covers only the things that were made, which Paul lists as things visible and invisible, thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, including Cherubim and Seraphim. Paul never names the Holy Spirit in this list, because the Spirit is above the nature of things that have come into being. So the text implies neither the Spirit's subordination nor that the Spirit came into being.
sources.quote: But of the Holy Spirit, as being above the nature of things that have come into being, Paul said not a word in his enumeration of existing things, not indicating to us by his words either His subordination or His coming into being
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:3's statement that "all things were made by" the Son prove that the Holy Spirit is one of the things made through the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: No. The things made, as Paul lists them, are things visible and invisible, thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, and Paul never names the Spirit among them. Scripture instead ascribes independent authority to the Spirit, who works all in all as He wills and breathes where He wills.
sources.quote: But of the Holy Spirit, as being above the nature of things that have come into being, Paul said not a word in his enumeration of existing things
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit included among the "all things" made through the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: No. Paul defines "all things" as created things in heaven and earth, both visible and invisible, such as thrones, dominions, principalities and powers. "Before all" therefore refers to creatures and does not place the Son before the Father. Likewise the Spirit is not included, since Psalm 33 says the heavens' strength comes from the Spirit of his mouth.
sources.quote: Does he, then, include the Holy Spirit here amongst creatures? Or when he says that the Son of God is before all things, is he to be supposed to have said that He is before the Father? Certainly not
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement in Colossians that all things were created by the Son, and that he is before all things, include the Holy Spirit among created things or place the Son before the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit knows the Father, which no creature can do save the Son, so when the totality of created things is spoken of, the Holy Spirit is not included in it.
sources.quote: And the Spirit is not to be numbered with all things which were made by the Son, since He knew the Father, Whom (as it is written) who can know save the Son?
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit to be counted among the 'all things' made through the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. John and Paul declare that everything was created in and through Christ. With respect to the Holy Spirit, however, Paul thought it sufficient to call Him God's Spirit, not a creature. Following their example, one should say nothing beyond comprehension and simply declare that He is God's Spirit.
sources.quote: And, while he declared that everything was created in Christ and through Christ, he thought, with respect to the Holy Spirit, that the description was sufficient, when he called Him Thy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Do the Scriptures saying that all things were made through the Son (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16) include the Holy Spirit among the things created?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter II. The words, “All things were made by Him,” are not a proof that the Holy Spirit is included amongst all things, since He was not made. For otherwise it could be proved by other passages that the Son, and even the Father Himself, must be numbered amongst all things, which would be similar irreverence.
sources.answer: No. The argument would only work if the opponents first proved that the Holy Spirit was made, since Scripture says that all things which were made were made by the Son. But Scripture nowhere teaches that the Spirit was made or created, so He cannot be counted among the "all things" made through the Word.
sources.quote: For Scripture says that all things which were made were made by the Son; but since we are not taught that the Holy Spirit was made, He certainly cannot be proved to be amongst all things Who was neither made as all things are, nor created.
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:3, "All things were made by Him," prove that the Holy Spirit is one of the created "all things" made through the Son?

question: How can the Word be God and yet be 'with God' (John 1:1-2); does this teach a personal distinction between the Son and the Father?
synthesis: Owen, Hilary and Waterland agree that 'with God' marks the Word as a Person distinct from the Father while still being God. Owen argues from the absence of any creature for the Word to be with, and he adds that the Word is one with God. Hilary stresses that the text says 'with' rather than 'in', so the Word is not a mere internal thought of God. Waterland rebuts the objection that orthodoxy makes God be with himself: being 'with God' means being with the Father, and 'God of God' supposes two Persons.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: It means the Word was with the Father as a distinct person. Since no creature existed then, he could be nowhere but with God, that is, the Father. Proverbs 8, where Wisdom is possessed by the Lord and is 'by him as one brought up with him' before his works, describes the same thing.
sources.quote: There being no creature then existing, he could be nowhere but with God; that is, the Father
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that the Word was 'with God' in the beginning (John 1:1)?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. The Word was with God, that is, with the Father, in such a way that he himself was also God. Verse 2 is added to show that the Word, while being God in the beginning, was distinct in something from God the Father, who afterward sent him into the world. Since no creature then existed, the Word could be nowhere but with God.
sources.quote: to show that he was so God in the beginning, as that he was one distinct, in something, from God the Father, by whom afterward he was sent into the world, he adds, verse 2, “The same was in the beginning with God.”
sources.raw_question: How can the Word be God and yet be 'with God'? Does John 1:1-2 teach a personal distinction between the Son and the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. No orthodox writer says or thinks that St. John meant God was with himself. The objection misrepresents the orthodox sense, which distinguishes the Persons while holding the Word to be God, and evades the real issue of reconciling an inferior creature-God with Isaiah's exclusion of other gods.
sources.quote: you tell us, God could not be with himself, as if any of us said, or thought, that was St. John’s meaning.
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:1, 'the Word was with God', imply that orthodox teaching makes God be with himself?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: It shows the Word is distinct from the Father, not merely an internal thought within him. The text says that which was in the beginning was with, not in, Another, so the Word has his own identity alongside God.
sources.quote: The assertion is that Which was in the beginning was with, not in, Another.
sources.raw_question: What does the phrase 'the Word was with God' (rather than 'in God') in John 1:1 show about the Word's relation to the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. Being 'with God' means being with the Father (cf. 1 John 1:2), who is eminently styled God as first in order. 'God and God' or 'God of God' supposes two Persons, so there is no question of the Son being with himself; and unless he were always inseparably with the Father he could not be God properly.
sources.quote: God and God, or God of God, supposes two Persons ; and therefore there is no foundation for the objection of the Son's being with himself.
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:1, saying the Word was God and was with God, require that the Word be God in a different, subordinate sense, since otherwise God would be with himself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. The text says directly that the Word was with God, so he is distinct from him, and that he was God, so he is one with him. He existed in the beginning, before creation, and made all things. We know God only by his name, his properties and his works. All three are here ascribed to the Son, so either he is God or we do not know who or what God is.
sources.quote: all the ways whereby we may know God are, his name, his properties, and his works; but they are all here ascribed by the Holy Ghost to the Son, to the Word: and he therefore is God, or we know neither who nor what God is.
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:1-3 prove that the Word is both distinct from God and one with God, and that he is truly God?

question: Who was the angel who appeared to Hagar and was called Lord and God: a mere created angel, God the Father, or God the Son?
synthesis: Novatian, Hilary and Waterland agree that the angel was God the Son, truly God and called angel because he was sent. Novatian argues by elimination: the Father cannot be called an angel, angels are never called God, and only God could promise to make a great nation. Hilary stresses the promise of countless seed as beyond an angel's power, together with Hagar's confession of him as God, and identifies him with the Angel of great counsel whose name fits his nature. Waterland explicitly follows Novatian, and adds that the title God belongs to Christ in his own Person as consubstantial Son, not merely as representing the Father.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Yes. Following Novatian, the passage cannot fit the Father, who would not be called an angel, nor a mere angel, who would not be called God, but it fits Christ, who is God as the Son of God and an angel as sent by the Father. So the title God belongs to Christ in his own Person, as consubstantial Son, not merely by representing the Father.
sources.quote: it was to the Person of Christ, not to the Person of God the Father, that the title of God and Lord, in this or the like instances, belonged ; and that therefore they are given to him in his own Person, in his own right, as God’s Son
sources.raw_question: Does the angel who appeared to Hagar and is called Lord and God show that Christ is God in his own right?

sources.author: Novatian
