sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: He was God as well as angel. The text first says God heard the lad and then says the angel called Hagar from heaven. The angel promises, 'I will make of him a great nation,' which is a power belonging to God and not to an angel. Scripture then confirms his deity by saying God opened her eyes and God was with the lad.
sources.quote: Why does this angel, if angel only, claim to himself this right of saying, I will make of him a great nation, since assuredly this kind of power belongs to God, and cannot belong to an angel?
sources.raw_question: Was the angel who spoke to Hagar in the desert merely a created angel, or God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: No. The name 'angel' cannot fittingly be applied to the Father, who is God only. It fits Christ, who is declared to be both God and angel. Otherwise we would have to make an angel God, or count God the Father Almighty among the angels.
sources.quote: if we will not consent to apprehend that it was Christ who then spoke to Hagar, we must either make an angel God, or we must reckon God the Father Almighty among the angels.
sources.raw_question: Could the one who appeared to Hagar as both angel and God have been the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: He is God the Son. He promises to multiply Hagar's seed beyond number, and the power of multiplying nations lies outside the ministry of an angel. Scripture then calls him Lord, and Hagar addresses him as God. The one called the Angel of God is therefore also Lord and God. He is the Son, whom the prophet calls the Angel of great counsel.
sources.quote: The power of multiplying nations lies outside the ministry of an angel. Yet what says the Scripture of Him Who is called the Angel of God, yet speaks words which belong to God alone?
sources.raw_question: Is the 'Angel of the Lord' who spoke to Hagar a mere created angel, or is he God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: He is truly God in name and nature. Hagar's confession reveals Him as Lord and God, and the narrative moves from calling Him the Angel to revealing that God Himself spoke. He is called Angel because of His ministry of declaring the great counsel, but the name corresponds to the nature rather than the nature being falsified to fit the name.
sources.quote: Thus He Who, while He executes the ministry of declaring the great counsel is God’s Angel, is Himself in name and nature God. The name corresponds to the nature; the nature is not falsified to make it conform to the name.
sources.raw_question: Is the Angel of God who spoke to Hagar truly God by nature, or merely an angel called God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: It was God the Son. It cannot be the Father, for the Father may not be called an angel, since that would make Him subordinate to another whose messenger He was. Nor can it be a mere angel, for the name God is nowhere given to angels, and only God could promise the blessing of seed. So it fits Christ alone: He is God because He is Son of God, and an angel because He announces the Father's will.
sources.quote: it is suited to the person of Christ that He should be both God because He is the Son of God, and should be an angel because He is the Announcer of the Father’s mind
sources.raw_question: Who was the angel who appeared to Hagar and was called Lord and God?

question: What does Christ's cry on the cross, 'My God, my God, why hast Thou forsaken me?', signify? Does it mean that the Son was truly forsaken by the Father or shown to be weak?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary agree that the cry does not mean the Son was actually abandoned or that his divinity was weakened, but they ground this differently. Athanasius says the words were spoken as from a man while the impassible Word remained in the Father, and that the signs at the crucifixion showed the Father was still in him. Hilary argues that the cross led to his glorification at the right hand of power, that the cry assured us of his true death and humanity, and that it cannot mean the Word departed from a separate man, since Jesus and Christ are one. Augustine differs in approach: he reads the cry as a mystery about our inner man, signifying the death of our old, ungodly self in repentance, rather than addressing the Son's own divinity.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The One Death and Resurrection of The Body of Christ Harmonizes with Our Double Death and Resurrection of Body and Soul, to the Effect of Salvation. In What Way the Single Death of Christ is Bestowed Upon Our Double Death.
sources.answer: It was uttered as a mystery concerning our inner man, signifying the death of our soul. The crucifixion of our old man means the pains of repentance and a wholesome agony of self-control. By this inner death the death of ungodliness is destroyed, and it is in this death that God has left us.
sources.quote: For it was in a mystery as regards our inner man, so as to signify the death of our soul, that those words were uttered, not only in the Psalm, but also on the cross
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's cry 'My God, my God, why hast Thou forsaken me?' signify, given that Christ was sinless?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Christ foretold that the Son of Man would be seen sitting at the right hand of power and coming with the clouds of heaven. It is through the cross that He sits at God's right hand, so the cross was not a dishonour that degraded Him.
sources.quote: it is because of the cross that we can now see the Son of Man sitting on the right hand of power, that He Who was born man of the womb of the Virgin has returned in His Majesty with the clouds of heaven
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's cry 'My God, My God, why hast Thou forsaken Me?' show that the Father's help left Him in weakness and disgrace on the cross?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Twelfthly, Matthew xxvi. 39; John xii. 27, &c. Arian inferences are against the Regula Fidei, as before. He wept and the like, as man. Other texts prove Him God. God could not fear. He feared because His flesh feared.
sources.answer: No. The Son is ever in the Father, both before and when He uttered the cry; the words were said as from a man, the Word being impassible. The Father showed He was even then in Him through the trembling earth, rent veil, darkened sun and rising dead, so that onlookers confessed He was truly the Son of God.
sources.quote: Whence neither can the Lord be forsaken by the Father, who is ever in the Father, both before He spoke, and when He uttered this cry.
sources.raw_question: Does the cry 'Why hast Thou forsaken Me?' mean that the Son was actually forsaken by the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. To read it as a bitter complaint of desertion is a violent and irreligious interpretation, repugnant to the whole tenor of the Lord's words. He hastened to the death that was to glorify him and lead to his sitting at the right hand of power. With such expectations he could not fear death or complain of being betrayed to it, since it was the entrance to eternal blessedness.
sources.quote: He hastened to the death, which was to glorify Him, and after which He was to sit on the right hand of power; with all those blessed expectations could He fear death
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's cry on the cross, 'My God, My God, why hast Thou forsaken Me?', prove that he was deserted by God and given over to weakness?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Christ spoke such words to assure us that he truly died and had assumed true humanity, not as a confession of his own weakness. Ever secure of his divinity and indifferent to death, he made his death clear for the sake of our faith, scattering our doubts.
sources.quote: that we might be sure that He did die, was not this, in His care for our faith, rather a scattering of our doubts, than a confession of His weakness?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's cry on the cross, "My God, My God, why hast Thou forsaken Me," show weakness or lack of divinity in the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Hilary rejects both readings as deadly errors: that the cry shows weakness in God the Word, or that it is the lament of a man whom an extraneous divine power had left. Since Jesus and Christ are one and not divided, the cry cannot mean the Word departed from a separate human subject.
sources.quote: Thus in every way arises a deadly danger of error in belief, whether it be thought that the cry of complaint denotes a weakness of nature in God the Word
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's cry "My God, My God, why hast Thou forsaken Me?" show that the divine Word withdrew from a mere man, or that God the Word suffered weakness of nature?

question: Does Christ know and search the hearts of all people, and does this knowledge show that he is truly God?
synthesis: All three authors affirm that Christ searches and knows the hearts of all people, citing texts such as 'he knew what was in man' and Revelation's 'he which searcheth the reins and hearts.' Bickersteth argues that Scripture reserves this knowledge to God alone, so Christ claims a divine prerogative; he also adds Christ's role as Judge of all. Hilary argues that this knowledge shows the divine nature in Christ rather than a mere messenger. Owen stresses the completeness and penetration of Christ's sight, through hypocrisy to every contrite sigh, and its pastoral bearing, noting that the comfort lies in our being enabled to make our hearts known to him.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ knows what is in man and needs no one to testify of him. He searches the hearts and tries the reins of all, whether they will or not. Owen adds, however, that comfort lies not in Christ's knowing our hearts but in our being enabled to make our hearts known to him.
sources.quote: Christ knows the minds of all. He knows what is in man, and needs not that any man testify of him, John ii. 25. He searcheth the hearts and trieth the reins of all, Rev. ii. 23.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ know the hearts of all people, and does this attribute show his divine knowledge?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says God "only" knows the hearts of all the children of men. Christ declares that all the churches shall know he is the one who searches the reins and hearts. He therefore claims an attribute Scripture reserves to God alone.
sources.quote: Thou, even Thou only, knowest the hearts of all the children of men. – 1 Kings 8:39.
sources.raw_question: Since only God knows the hearts of all people, does Christ's claim to search hearts prove his Deity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ's eyes are 'as a flame of fire', so the churches may know that he searches reins and hearts. Even during his earthly life he 'knew all men' and 'knew what was in man'. Nothing is hidden from him. He sees through the coverings of hypocrites and notices every sigh of a contrite soul.
sources.quote: He hath discerning eyes, nothing is hid from him; all things are open and naked before him with whom we have to do.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ, as the one who 'searcheth the reins and hearts', possess complete knowledge of the inner state of every person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. The disciples recognized the nature of God in Him through the divine powers He exercised. Knowing all things and reading the thoughts of the heart belong to the Son, not to a mere messenger. They therefore confessed that He came from God, because the power of the divine nature was in Him.
sources.quote: for to know all things, and to read the thoughts of the heart belongs to the Son, not to the mere messenger of God. They confessed, therefore, that He was come from God, because the power of the divine nature was in Him.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's knowledge of all things and of men's hearts show that he has the divine nature, rather than being a mere messenger of God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. In Revelation the Son of God declares that he is the one who searches reins and hearts, and John says Christ knew what was in man. Scripture also says all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, who will sit on his throne and separate the nations. These are divine prerogatives of the Father.
sources.quote: all the churches shall know that I am He who searcheth the reins and hearts”; and He, writes St. John, knew all men, and needed not that any should testify of man
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture present Christ as the Searcher of hearts and the Judge of all men?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Like doves' eyes, Christ's eyes see quickly, clearly and thoroughly, to the bottom of what they look upon. Revelation calls him the one who searches the reins and hearts. While he was in this world, he knew all men and knew what was in man. Nothing is hidden from him: he sees through the pretences of hypocrites and notices every sigh of a contrite soul.
sources.quote: It is said of him, whilst he was in this world, that “Jesus knew all men, and needed not that any should testify of man; for he knew what was in man,” John ii. 24, 25.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ, in his incarnate life, possess a discerning knowledge that searches the hearts of men?

question: Does Genesis 19:24, 'the Lord rained fire and brimstone from the Lord out of heaven,' show two distinct divine Persons, the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Novatian, Hilary of Poitiers and Irenaeus all answer yes and identify the Lord who rains fire as the Son, but on different grounds. Novatian argues from visibility: the Lord seen and touched as Abraham's guest cannot be the invisible Father, so he must be the Son. Hilary stresses that both are called Lord with no difference of nature, and like Irenaeus explains the verse by the Son receiving judgment or power to judge from the Father; Irenaeus also identifies this Son as the one who had been talking with Abraham.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord who rained fire on Sodom did so 'from the Lord,' so two are called Lord. The Lord on earth is the God who was seen and touched as Abraham's guest, while the Father remains invisible. That Lord is the Son, the Word of God who was later made flesh, that is, Christ.
sources.quote: Therefore the Lord overturned Sodom, that is, God overturned Sodom; but in the overturning of Sodom, the Lord rained fire from the Lord. And this Lord was the God seen by Abraham; and this God was the guest of Abraham, certainly seen because He was also touched.
sources.raw_question: Does Genesis 19:24, where 'the Lord rained fire and brimstone from the Lord out of heaven,' show that the one who visited Abraham was a divine Person distinct from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture calls both 'Lord', making no distinction of nature by difference of name, yet distinguishes the two Persons. Since the Father has given all judgment to the Son, the Lord who judged Sodom received this judgment from the Lord, the Father.
sources.quote: It is The Lord from the Lord; Scripture makes no distinction, by difference of name, between Their natures, but discriminates between Themselves.
sources.raw_question: Does Genesis 19:24, 'The Lord rained brimstone and fire from the Lord,' show a distinction of Persons who share the same divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. Beyond doubt the Law says the Lord rained from the Lord in order to reveal to us the Father and the Son, two Persons each called Lord.
sources.quote: when the Lord rained from the Lord, beyond a doubt the Law tells us that the Lord rained from the Lord in order to reveal to us the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that 'the Lord rained from the Lord' in Genesis 19:24 reveal a distinction of Father and Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. The phrase 'Lord from the Lord' can mean nothing else than that the Persons are distinguished, the true Lord raining from the true Lord. Both are Lord, and the one who rains from the Lord is the Son.
sources.quote: Have you any alternative to this Lord, and Lord? Or any other meaning for the terms, except that in Lord, and Lord, their Persons are distinguished?
sources.raw_question: Does the statement in Genesis that 'the Lord rained from the Lord' on Sodom and Gomorrah show two distinct divine Persons?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: Yes. It shows that the Son, who had also been talking with Abraham, received power from the Father to judge the Sodomites for their wickedness.
sources.quote: For it here points out that the Son, who had also been talking with Abraham, had received power to judge the Sodomites for their wickedness.
sources.raw_question: Does Genesis 19:24, where the Lord rains fire "from the Lord out of heaven," refer to two distinct Persons?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord who rained fire on Sodom from the Lord out of heaven was the God seen by and entertained by Abraham. That God was touched and seen, and so was not the invisible Father but the Son, the Word made flesh. The text thus distinguishes two who are both Lord.
sources.quote: And this Lord was the God seen by Abraham; and this God was the guest of Abraham, certainly seen because He was also touched.
sources.raw_question: Does Genesis 19:24, "the Lord rained from the Lord," show that the one who visited Abraham was a divine Person distinct from the Father?

question: Can human thought or speech adequately comprehend or express the nature of God?
synthesis: Hilary, Novatian and Augustine all answer no: God exceeds thought, and speech falls short even of thought. Their grounds differ. Novatian argues that anything the mind could contain would be smaller than the mind, so God is known in silence. Hilary says God is known through devotion and that our weakness forces us to use analogies from visible things as clues to invisible realities. Augustine cites Paul's seeing 'through a glass, in an enigma' and looks to the final vision, when our many words will cease and God alone will be all in all.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. God's nature transcends even the conceptions of thought, and thought itself often outruns words. God can be known only by devotion, and reverence contemplates Him as lacking nothing.
sources.quote: What presumption to suppose that words can adequately describe His nature, when thought is often too deep for words, and His nature transcends even the conceptions of thought!
sources.raw_question: Can human words or thought adequately describe or comprehend the nature of God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > God is Above All Things, Himself Containing All Things, Immense, Eternal, Transcending the Mind of Man; Inexplicable in Discourse, Loftier Than All Sublimity.
sources.answer: No. God is greater than mind and discourse; if He could be conceived or declared, He would be smaller than the mind or speech that contains Him. Whatever can be thought or said of Him is less than He; we can be conscious of Him in silence but not unfold Him as He is.
sources.quote: For He is greater than mind itself; nor can it be conceived how great He is, seeing that, if He could be conceived, He would be smaller than the human mind wherein He could be conceived.
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind comprehend God or human speech adequately express Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. God is ineffable and spiritual, so He cannot be confined by definitions or likened to bodily things. Yet the weakness of our intellect forces us to use ordinary natures and ordinary speech to express what we grasp. Such analogies are not meant to make God resemble bodies; they use visible things as a clue to invisible realities.
sources.quote: We are well aware that neither the speech of men nor the analogy of human nature can give us a full insight into the things of God. The ineffable cannot submit to the bounds and limits of definition
sources.raw_question: Can human speech and analogies drawn from human nature give a full understanding of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What the Author Entreats from God, What from the Reader. In God Nothing is to Be Thought Corporeal or Changeable.
sources.answer: No. Even our thought about God the Trinity falls far short of Him and does not comprehend Him as He is, and speech falls short even of thought. Even someone as great as the Apostle Paul sees God only "through a glass and in an enigma."
sources.quote: even our very thought, when we think of God the Trinity, falls (as we feel) very far short of Him of whom we think, nor comprehends Him as He is
sources.raw_question: Can human thought or speech comprehend God the Trinity as He actually is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Conclusion of the Book with a Prayer, and an Apology for Multitude of Words.
sources.answer: No. Our words fall short of God, as the wise man says: "We speak much, and yet come short; and in sum of words, He is all." When we come to God, these many inadequate words will cease and God as One will remain all in all. We ourselves, made one in Him, will then say one thing without end in praising Him.
sources.quote: When, therefore, we shall have come to Thee, these very many things that we speak, and yet come short, will cease; and Thou, as One, wilt remain “all in all.”
sources.raw_question: Can human speech adequately comprehend the Triune God, and what will replace our many words in the final vision of God?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being sent by the Father and the Son imply that he is inferior to them?
synthesis: Augustine, Ambrose and Bickersteth all deny that being sent makes the Spirit inferior, but on different grounds. Augustine says the sending refers to the visible creature or signifies procession, and notes the Spirit took no servant form by which he could be called less. Ambrose argues that the Son and the Spirit send each other, as the Father does, so sending shows a shared power. Bickersteth appeals to a human analogy (a senate sending its own member) and to the Spirit's sanctifying office, which only God can carry out.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Of the Sensible Showing of the Holy Spirit, and of the Coeternity of the Trinity. What Has Been Said, and What Remains to Be Said.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit's mission is recorded either because of the visible creature through which he was shown, or to signify his procession from the Father and the Son. It does not signify inequality or difference of substance.
sources.quote: not on account of inequality, or imparity, or unlikeness of substance
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being sent by both the Father and the Son make the Spirit inferior to them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son.
sources.answer: No. The same account applies to the Spirit's sending as to the Son's. Being sent does not imply inferiority in the divine nature, so the Spirit is not less because both the Father and the Son sent him.
sources.quote: and that the same account is to be given of the sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being sent by the Father and the Son make him less than they are?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Scripture nowhere says the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit. The creature in which the Spirit appeared was not taken into personal union as the Son took human nature. So there is no form of a servant in the Spirit by which he could be called less.
sources.quote: It is, then, for this reason nowhere written, that the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit is less than God the Father, because the creature in which the Holy Spirit was to appear was not taken in the same way as the Son of man was taken
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being sent imply that he is less than the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Even among men being sent is not always a sign of subordination, as when a senate sends one of its own members on a weighty mission. The Spirit's mission concerns the office he undertakes in the economy of grace, sanctifying the elect, a work none less than God can effect.
sources.quote: If any object that He is said to be sent by the Father and the Son, and that this mission implies inferiority, we answer that even among men the being sent is by no means always a mark of subordination.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being sent by the Father and the Son imply that he is inferior to them?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter I. Not only were the prophets and apostles sent by the Spirit, but also the Son of God. This is proved from Isaiah and the evangelists, and it is explained why St. Luke wrote that the same Spirit descended like a dove upon Christ and abode upon Him. Next, after establishing this mission of Christ, the writer infers that the Son is sent by the Father and the Spirit, as the Spirit is by the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit also sent the Son, and the Father sends the Spirit just as the Son does. Since the Son and the Spirit send each other, as the Father sends, sending implies no inferiority of subjection but a community of power.
sources.quote: If, then, the Son and the Spirit send each other, as the Father sends, there is no inferiority of subjection, but a community of power.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's sending of the Holy Spirit show that the Spirit is inferior to the Son?

question: Should the Son be honoured equally with the Father?
synthesis: Hilary, Owen and Gregory of Nyssa all affirm equal honour, but on different grounds. Hilary bases it on the Son's equal power and working, since He does whatever the Father does. Gregory points to Scripture applying the same names of glory to both, to creation's worship of the Son, and to the claim that denying the Son's glory insults Him rather than adding honour to the Father. Owen dwells less on the ground than on how the honour is given: by believing in and obeying the Son.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. The Son does in like manner whatever the Father does, so His power and working are not distinct from the Father's. Christ demands that all honour the Son as they honour the Father. When both are equal in honour and work with the same power, no inferiority or weakness can be found.
sources.quote: Discover, if you can, the inferiority, when Both are equal in honour; make out the weakness, when Both work with the same power.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son equal to the Father in power and in the honour due to Him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. It is God's will that all men honour the Son even as they honour the Father. This is done by believing in him and obeying him, so that the Son is glorified in believers, as he himself says in John 17.
sources.quote: It is the will of God that as all men honour the Father, so should they honour the Son, John v. 23. And how is this done? By believing in him, John xiv. 1; obeying of him.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son to be honoured equally with the Father, and how is that honour given?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > Then, distinguishing between essence and generation, he declares the empty and frivolous language of Eunomius to be like a rattle. He proceeds to show that the language used by the great Basil on the subject of the generation of the Only-begotten has been grievously slandered by Eunomius, and so ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Basil rightly honours the Son even as he honours the Father, associating Him in the Father's majesty. Eunomius, by contrast, severs Him from the Father's good nature. The Son is worshipped by all creation in heaven, on earth and under the earth, which befits only the Lord and not a creature.
sources.quote: Basil is slandered as dishonouring the Son, who honours Him even as he honours the Father
sources.raw_question: Should the Son be honoured equally with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The blasphemy of these heretics is worse than the Jewish unbelief.
sources.answer: No. Gregory compares this to the Jews, who thought they honoured the Almighty by excluding the Son from equal reverence. On his view, taking away the Son's glory does not add honour to the Father. It is an insult heaped upon the Only-begotten, and the Son rightly shares equal reverence with the Father.
sources.quote: The Jews thought to honour the Almighty by excluding the Son from equal reverence: these men, by annihilating the glory of the Son, think to bestow more honour on the Father.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father given greater honour when the Son is denied equal glory and reverence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Orthodox confession teaches that all men should honour the Son even as they honour the Father. Scripture applies the same names of glory to both alike, and these signify that the Son is equal in greatness and dignity to the Father.
sources.quote: an orthodox confession teaches us to believe in the Only-begotten God so that all men should honour the Son even as they honour the Father
sources.raw_question: Should the Son be honoured equally with the Father?

question: In John 1:1, is the Word called God in the same proper sense as the Father, or only in an improper or subordinate sense, by office, dignity or later exaltation?
synthesis: Waterland, Owen and Hilary all hold that the Word is God in the full and proper sense. Waterland argues from the unlikelihood that John shifts the word's sense within one verse, and from the point that a merely figurative title is not proper Godhead. Owen argues that deity by office or later exaltation is impossible for one who was God 'in the beginning' before creation. Hilary argues that the name is given without any qualification, unlike Moses' title 'a god to Pharaoh', and that a name describes a nature.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. Before Dr. Clarke's distinction of supreme and subordinate senses can be used, the word must first be divided into proper and improper senses. Anyone called God merely by resemblance, such as for dominion alone, is called so figuratively and is not properly God. The Arian appeal to texts calling men gods therefore does not show that the Son is God in a lower but proper sense.
sources.quote: The first and most general distinction of the senses of the word God, should be into proper and improper; after which it will be soon enough to come to your famed distinction of supreme and subordinate.
sources.raw_question: Can the word "God" reasonably be taken in different senses when applied to the Father and to the Son in the same verse, as in John 1:1?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. The Word was God in the full sense that nature and Scripture give to the name, as Thomas confessed him 'Our Lord and our God' and Paul called him 'over all, God blessed for ever.' A deity by office or exaltation cannot be claimed for the Word before the creation of the world, yet John says he was God 'in the beginning.'
sources.quote: not a god by office, one exalted to that dignity (which cannot well be pretended before the creation of the world), but as Thomas confessed him, “Our Lord and our God,”
sources.raw_question: Does 'the Word was God' in John 1:1 mean that the Word was only a god by office or exalted dignity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: In the same proper sense. The word God is used of the Father in the strict sense in the very same verse, and it is unreasonable to think St. John would immediately use the same word in a very different sense. Moreover, the Word is said to be God in the beginning, before creation, and the work of creation is attributed to him.
sources.quote: If therefore the word Θεὸς, God, be once used by St. John in the strict and proper sense, how can we imagine, that immediately after, in the very same verse, he should use the same word in a sense very different from. that of the former?
sources.raw_question: In John 1:1, is the Word called God in the same proper sense as the Father, or only in an improper, relative sense?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. The words plainly affirm that the Word was God in the beginning, and so he is still, since one who is once God cannot cease to be God. Talk of Christ being 'made God' offends sober Christians. It is also incoherent, since properly making someone God is impossible, and the text speaks of what he was in the beginning, not of something done after his resurrection.
sources.quote: the Word was in the beginning, and was God; and therefore is so still, unless he who is once God can cease so to be.
sources.raw_question: Does 'the Word was God' in John 1:1 mean that Christ was later exalted and made God in rule, authority and power, rather than being God by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. The name God is given to the Word plainly and without any qualifying addition that might raise doubt, and a name describes a nature. With no reason to contradict the statement, there is no loophole for supposing He received the name as a favour or assumed it, unlike Moses, who was made 'a god to Pharaoh,' a qualified title.
sources.quote: Here is no loophole for any such conjecture as that He has received this name as a favour or taken it upon Himself, so possessing a titular Godhead which is not His by nature.
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:1, 'the Word was God', show that the Son is God by nature rather than by a merely titular or bestowed Godhead?

question: If the Son knew the day and hour of judgment, why did Christ say that only the Father knows it, and was the statement true?
synthesis: Athanasius says Christ spoke truly as man, according to the flesh, and did so for our profit, to stop the disciples' further questions without grieving or harming them. Irenaeus says the saying teaches that the Father is above all things and that we should leave lofty questions to God. Waterland says it teaches us to refer everything to the Father as the original, since the Son has his knowledge by communication from the Father; he does not appeal to the human nature as Athanasius does.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: For our profit. He made known the signs before the end so we would not be startled, but declined to say 'I know' of the day itself, speaking after the flesh which was ignorant, lest the disciples ask further and He either grieve them by silence or harm them and us by telling. Whatever He does, He does for our sakes, and He was not untrue since He spoke humanly.
sources.quote: And concerning the day and the hour He was not willing to say according to His divine nature, ‘I know,’ but after the flesh, ‘I know not,’ for the sake of the flesh which was ignorant
sources.raw_question: Why would Christ say 'not even the Son knows' the day if as Word He knew it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: So that we might learn through Him that the Father is above all things, as He also says 'the Father is greater than I.' The Lord thereby teaches us, while in this world, to leave perfect knowledge and lofty questions to God, and not, by probing the Father's sublime nature, fall into asking whether there is another God above God.
sources.quote: he will find at present no more suitable, or becoming, or safe reason than this (since, indeed, the Lord is the only true Master), that we may learn through Him that the Father is above all things.
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ say that only the Father, and not the Son, knows the day and hour of judgment, given that the Father has fellowship with the Son in all things?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: Christ's saying is true in the sense that it teaches us to refer everything to the Father as the original of all things. The Son yields the Father the preference in knowledge not because he knows less, but because what he knows he has by communication from the Father. He therefore refers to the Father such secrets as were not proper to reveal nor fit for men to inquire into.
sources.quote: His answer is, that we are thereby taught to refer every thing to the Father, as the original of all things. To him knowledge ought to be principally, and in the first place, ascribed
sources.raw_question: If the Father communicates all things, including knowledge of the day of judgment, to the Son, how can Christ truly say that only the Father knows that day and hour?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: He said it for our profit, speaking according to the flesh, which was ignorant, not according to His divine nature. By saying 'I know not' as man He stopped the disciples' further questions. Otherwise He would have had either to grieve them by silence or to harm them and us by revealing the time. Whatever He does, He does for our sakes, since for us the Word became flesh.
sources.quote: concerning the day and the hour He was not willing to say according to His divine nature, ‘I know,’ but after the flesh, ‘I know not,’ for the sake of the flesh which was ignorant
sources.raw_question: If the Son knew the day and hour of the end, why did Christ say in Mark 13:32 that not even the Son knows it?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: No. He said it humanly, as man, and in His flesh He was ignorant, so the statement was true of Him as man. At the same time, as the Word, He knew the day. By speaking this way He also ended the disciples' inquiries.
sources.quote: neither was He untrue in thus saying (for He said humanly, as man, ‘I know not’), nor did He suffer the disciples to force Him to speak
sources.raw_question: Was Christ speaking untruly when he said 'No, not the Son knoweth' while in fact knowing the day?

question: What does the saying "The Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son" mean, and why is judgment committed to the Son?
synthesis: All three authors deny that the text lowers the Son, but they ground this differently. Gregory of Nyssa reads it as showing the Son's supreme authority rather than subjection. Waterland says the Father holds judgment by prerogative while the Son exercises it, so that all should honour the Son as they honour the Father, which manifests his equality. Augustine instead explains it by the form that will appear: the Father still judges, but only the Son will be seen in the judgment, in the form of the Son of man.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: It shows His supreme authority. Both the Churchman and the heretic affirm the same words, but they read them differently. The heretic takes the committing of judgment to signify subservience and subjection. The orthodox rightly understand it as the Son's possession of supreme authority.
sources.quote: By the same words the Churchman understands supreme authority, the other maintains subservience and subjection.
sources.raw_question: Does the saying "the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son" show the Son's subservience and subjection to the Father, or His supreme authority?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: The Father has judgment primarily by right of his prerogative as Father, while the Son has it in exercise and execution, so as to manifest the Son's equality. This belongs to the pattern whereby whatever the Father does, quickening, having life in himself, the Son does likewise, so that all should honour the Son as they honour the Father.
sources.quote: if the Father was primarily Judge of the world, in right of his prerogative as Father, the Son should have it in the exercise and execution, to manifest the equality.
sources.raw_question: If the Father is primarily Judge of the world, why is judgment committed to the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: Because the Son will appear as Judge in the form of the Son of man, which is not the Father's form, so that he may be visible to both the good and the bad. The Father still judges, but no one will see the Father in the judgment. Christ himself confirms this when he says authority to judge was given him "because He is the Son of man."
sources.quote: because He will appear as Judge in the form of the Son of man, which is not the form of the Father, but of the Son; nor yet that form of the Son in which He is equal to the Father, but that in which He is less than the Father
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ say that the Father judges no man but has committed all judgment to the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: No. The Father judges together with the Son, since the Son says "There is One that seeketh and judgeth." The text means that no one will see the Father in the judgment, but all will see the Son, because the form of the Son of man, not the form of God, will appear.
sources.quote: as if it were said, No one will see the Father in the judgment of the quick and the dead, but all will see the Son
sources.raw_question: Does the statement "The Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son" mean that the Father does not judge at all?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: The Father did it so that all men would honour the Son as they honour the Father. The Father's honour was already secure, but men were apt to belittle the Son, both from a love of disputing and because he became man. Making the Son Judge of all, before whose tribunal everyone must appear, shows his excellence and reminds men that it is both their duty and their interest to give him the full honour his Person deserves.
sources.quote: for the more effectually securing a point of this high concernment, it pleased the Father to leave the final judgment of the great day in the hands of his Son
sources.raw_question: Why did the Father commit all judgment to the Son rather than keep it himself?

question: Does the oneness of the Father and the Son (as in "I and the Father are one") mean, as the Sabellians hold, that they are one Person?
synthesis: Ambrose, Augustine and Novatian all deny that the oneness makes Father and Son one Person. Ambrose and Augustine point to the plural 'we are' and to 'I and the Father' as showing two distinct Persons who share one substance. Novatian likewise stresses 'I and the Father' and 'we are,' but he reads the neuter 'one' as signifying concord and association rather than one substance.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: No. According to the Godhead the Son is one with the Father by natural substance, "not according to the Sabellian falsehood." Their unity of substance makes them inseparable in operation while they remain distinct Persons.
sources.quote: the Son according to the Godhead is One with the Father, One by natural substance, not according to the Sabellian falsehood
sources.raw_question: Does the oneness of the Father and Son in substance amount to the Sabellian view that they are one Person?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: Yes. By saying "I and the Father" Christ indicates that He is one and the Father another, so the two are distinct. And by saying "We are One" rather than "I am one," He signifies one substance, not one person, so the unity He asserts is not a unity of person.
sources.quote: Therefore, when He says, “I and the Father,” He rejects the Sabellian, for He says that He is one, the Father another;
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "I and the Father are One" refute the Sabellian view that the Father and the Son are one and the same person?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whatever is Spoken of God According to Substance, is Spoken of Each Person Severally, and Together of the Trinity Itself. One Essence in God, and Three, in Greek, Hypostases, in Latin, Persons.
sources.answer: No. Christ said "are one," not "is one," as the Sabellians would have it. The plural verb shows that the Father and the Son are distinct, while "one" shows their unity.
sources.quote: And so it is said plurally, “I and my Father are one.” For He has not said, “is one,” as the Sabellians say; but, “are one.”
sources.raw_question: Does the saying "I and my Father are one" support the Sabellian view that the Father and the Son are one person?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, Against the Sabellians He Proves that the Father is One, the Son Another.
sources.answer: No. By saying "I and the Father" Christ distinguishes his own person from the Father. He uses "one" in the neuter, which signifies concord and association, not one person. He also says "we are," not "I am," which shows that they are two persons.
sources.quote: And since He said “one” thing, let the heretics understand that He did not say “one” person. For one placed in the neuter, intimates the social concord, not the personal unity.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "I and the Father are one" prove that the Son and the Father are one person?

question: What does Christ mean by 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father' (John 14:9), and in what way is the Father seen in the Son?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa, Basil and Hilary agree that the Father is not seen in Christ's flesh or in any bodily form. Gregory says one must look through the flesh to the unchangeable Godhead, the same in both. Basil says what is seen is the goodness of the will, which is the same in Father and Son. Hilary speaks of a vision of the understanding: Christ's works reveal the power of his nature and so its unity with the Father's.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: Philip was looking only at what had changed, the flesh. Christ bids him look through it to the unchangeable Godhead, the Son who is in the Father. Whoever sees that sees the Father Himself, because the very same character of Godhead is beheld in both.
sources.quote: will have seen that Father Himself in Whom I am, because the very same character of Godhead is beheld in both
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean when He tells Philip, 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father'?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: It does not mean an image or form is seen, since the divine nature admits of no composition. What is seen is the goodness of the will. That will goes together with the essence and is like and equal in Father and Son, or rather the same.
sources.quote: but the goodness of the will, which, being concurrent with the essence, is beheld as like and equal, or rather the same, in the Father as in the Son.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean by "He that hath seen me hath seen the Father"?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Christ spoke of a mental vision, the eye of the understanding, not perception by the eye of flesh. The body born of the Virgin could not show the image and likeness of the incorporeal God. Rather, those who recognised Christ as Son from the powers of his divine nature recognised God in him, and knowing the Son brings knowledge of the Father.
sources.quote: It was not the carnal body, which He had received by birth from the Virgin, that could manifest to them the image and likeness of God. The human aspect which He wore could be no aid towards the mental vision of the incorporeal God.
sources.raw_question: When Christ says "He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father also" (John 14:9), does he mean that the Father was seen with bodily eyes in Jesus' human body?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It means the Father and Son are of equal nature, so to behold the Son is to behold the Father. It does not mean the Father is seen in Christ's body. Christ therefore pointed to his works: they show the power of his nature, and through that power one recognises his unity with the Father's nature and that there is no distinction of nature between them.
sources.quote: And, lest they should misunderstand Him, as though when they beheld His body, they beheld the Father in Him, He had added, Believe Me, that I am in the Father and the Father in Me: or else believe Me for the very works’ sake
sources.raw_question: What does "He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father" (John 14:9) mean, and how is the Father seen in the Son?

question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Son as well as from the Father?
synthesis: Augustine answers yes outright. He argues from Scripture calling the Spirit the Spirit of both and from Christ breathing on the disciples, a sign that the Spirit proceeds also from the Son. Gregory of Nyssa places the Spirit's source of being in the Father alone and says the Spirit shines forth through the Son. Ambrose says the Spirit proceeds from the Father and is also the Spirit of the Son, without explicitly calling the Son a source of procession.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is rightly called the Spirit of both the Father and the Son. When Christ breathed on the disciples and said 'Receive ye the Holy Ghost', the breath was not the Spirit's substance. It was a fitting sign that the Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father.
sources.quote: a declaration by a fitting sign, that the Holy Spirit proceeds not only from the Father, but also from the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Son as well as from the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > A passing repetition of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: Yes, in the sense that the Spirit shines forth by means of the Son yet traces the source of its being to the Primal Light, the Father. So the Spirit's origin is in the Father, while its shining forth is through the Son.
sources.quote: while shining forth by means of It yet tracing the source of its being to the Primal Light
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father through the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture calls Him the Spirit of both, the Spirit of the Son and the Spirit of the Father. The Son says He will send the Spirit from the Father, and the Father will send Him in the Son's name. When the risen Christ breathed on the disciples and said 'Receive the Holy Ghost', He showed that the Spirit proceeds also from Himself.
sources.quote: He breathed upon them, and said, Receive the Holy Ghost,”[^1051] so as to show that He proceeded also from Himself.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Son as well as from the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: Yes. Ambrose states that whoever speaks of the Spirit names the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, and also the Son, because the Spirit is the Spirit of the Son as well.
sources.quote: if you speak of the Spirit, you name also God the Father, from Whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Son, inasmuch as He is also the Spirit of the Son
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father, and is He also the Spirit of the Son?

question: Does the baptismal formula show that the Son is truly divine and not a creature?
synthesis: Athanasius, Bickersteth and Gregory of Nyssa all deny that the formula allows the Son to be a creature, but they argue differently. Athanasius says the formula names Father and Son, not Creator and creature, and that a creature-Son could not join us to God. Bickersteth says God would never let a creature's name be joined with his own in so solemn a rite. Gregory says the formula nowhere calls the Son a creature and accuses Eunomius of altering the divine words.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > Eunomius again speaks of the Son as Lord and God, and Maker of all creation intelligible and sensible, having received from the Father the power and the commission for creation, being entrusted with the task of creation as if He were an artizan commissioned by some one hiring Him, and receiving His power of creation as a thing adventitious, ab extra, as a result of the power allotted to Him in accordance with such and such combinations and positions of the stars, as destiny decrees their lot in life to men at their nativity. Thus, passing by most of what Eunomius had written, he confutes his blasphemy that the Maker of all things came into being in like manner with the earth and with angels, and that the subsistence of the Only-begotten differs not at all from the genesis of all things, and reproaches Him with reverencing neither the Divine mystery nor the custom of the Church, nor following in his attempt to discover godliness any teacher of pious doctrine, but Manichæus, Colluthus, Arius, Aetius, and those like to them, supposing that Christianity in general is folly, and that the customs of the Church and the venerable sacraments are a jest, wherein he differs in nothing from the pagans, who borrowed from our doctrine the idea of a great God supreme over all. So, too, this new idolater preaches in the same fashion, and in particular that baptism is “into an artificer and creator,” not fearing the curse of those who cause addition or diminution to the Holy Scriptures. And he closes his book with showing him to be Antichrist.
sources.answer: No. Christ commanded baptism into the Name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and nowhere in those words does he call the Son a creature, the Father the Son's artificer, or the Son God's servant. Eunomius's formula adds to and takes from the Divine utterance and so falls under the curse on those who alter Scripture.
sources.quote: Where did He call the Son a creature? Where did the Word teach that the Father is creator and artificer of the Only-begotten? Where in the words cited is it taught that the Son is a servant of God?
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 teach that Christians are baptized into a creator and artificer of the Son, with the Father as the Son's God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. God foresaw that this would be the standard formula of Christian baptism. It is inconceivable that he would let the name of a creature with a derived being be joined with his own name in so solemn a rite. When the formula is read as the Unitarians read it, it turns into a confusion between God and man and between a person and an abstraction.
sources.quote: would suffer that in this most solemn rite, the name of a creature with a derived being, should coalesce into his own name, which alone is Jehovah, the increate Father?
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula 'into the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost' imply the deity of the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ bade us be baptized not into the name of Unoriginate and originate, nor of Creator and creature, but into the Name of Father, Son and Holy Ghost. Through this initiation we, who are among God's works, are made sons. Using the name of the Father, we also acknowledge the Word in the Father himself.
sources.quote: not into the name of Unoriginate and originate, nor into the name of Creator and creature, but into the Name of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula into the name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit show that the Son is not a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. A creature would not be ranked with the Creator in our consecration. If baptism joins us to the Godhead, a creature is unnecessary. If it joins us to a creature-Son, naming him is superfluous, since God who made him a son could make us sons directly. Moreover, all rational creatures share one nature and all need grace from God, so a creature could give creatures no help.
sources.quote: if the Son be a creature, the nature of rational creatures being one, no help will come to creatures from a creature, since all need grace from God.
sources.raw_question: Would naming the Son in the baptismal formula make sense if the Son were a creature?

question: Does Scripture teach that the Holy Spirit is God?
synthesis: Augustine, Warfield and Owen all answer yes, but on different grounds. Augustine and Warfield both argue from the Spirit's indwelling making believers God's temple: Augustine reasons from Paul's 'temple of the Holy Ghost… glorify God in your body', and Warfield from the Spirit being related to God as a man's spirit is to the man. Owen instead argues from the works Scripture ascribes to the Spirit, such as creation, which require divine attributes like omnipotence and omniscience.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Appearance in the Bush.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says the body is the temple of the Holy Ghost and then concludes, 'Therefore glorify God in your body.' The one whose temple the body is, is thereby called God.
sources.quote: and the Holy Spirit, since the same apostle says, “Therefore glorify God in your body;” when he had said above, “Know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture show that the Holy Spirit is God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says believers are the temple of God and immediately adds that the Spirit of God dwells in them, and God dwells in His own temple. Elsewhere he calls our body the temple of the Holy Spirit and concludes 'glorify God in your body', so the Spirit does not dwell there as a servant but as God.
sources.quote: For the Spirit of God does not dwell in the temple of God as a servant
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that the Holy Spirit is God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit of God is related to God as the spirit of man is to man, so the Spirit's indwelling is God dwelling in us. By that indwelling believers are constituted temples of God.
sources.quote: The Spirit of God is to him related to God as the spirit of man is to man (I Cor. ii. 11), and therefore if the Spirit of God dwells in us, that is God dwelling in us
sources.raw_question: Does Paul teach that the Holy Spirit is God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture makes the Spirit the author of creation and of all sorts of divine operations. These works require immensity, omnipotence, omniscience and the other divine excellencies, so the one who performs them must be God.
sources.quote: It declares, also, that he is the author and worker of all sorts of divine operations, requiring immensity, omnipotence, omniscience, and all other divine excellencies, unto their working and effecting.
sources.raw_question: Do the works Scripture ascribes to the Holy Spirit, such as creation, prove that he is God?
