question: Do the prepositions in 1 Corinthians 8:6 ('of whom' said of the Father, 'through whom' said of the Son) imply a difference of nature or substance between the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Ambrose, Basil and Hilary all deny that the prepositions imply a difference of nature. Ambrose and Basil argue alike: Paul uses the particles to distinguish the Persons (hypostases) without confusion, and the phrases are not opposed, since Romans 11:36 applies them all to one subject. Hilary argues differently: the addition of 'through Christ' would be needless unless being 'from God' and 'through Christ' were the same, so both phrases signify an Author of one nature exercising the same power in the same work.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IX. A passage of St. Paul abused by heretics, to prove a distinction between the Divine Persons, is explained, and it is proved that the whole passage can be rightly said of each Person, though it refers specially to the Son. It is then proved that each member of the passage is applicable to each Person, and as to say, of Him are all things is applicable to the Father, so may all things are through Him and in Him also be said of Him.
sources.answer: No. The Apostle did not use these particles to show that the substance of the Father and the Son could be severed, but to teach a distinction of Persons without confusion. The particles are not opposed to one another but allied and agreed, so that they often all apply to one Person, as in Romans 11:36.
sources.quote: For the Apostle did not so say, All things are of God, and all things are through the Son, as to signify that the substance of the Father and the Son could be severed, but that he might teach that by a distinction without confusion the Father is one, the Son another.
sources.raw_question: Do the prepositions in 1 Corinthians 8:6 ('of whom' said of the Father, 'through whom' said of the Son) imply a difference of substance between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That v: not found “of whom” in the case of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Paul was not laying down a rule but carefully distinguishing the hypostases, so as to show the notions of Father and Son as unconfounded. He did not intend to introduce a diversity of nature. The phrases are not set against each other, as Paul himself applies both to one and the same subject.
sources.quote: Yes; but these are the words of a writer not laying down a rule, but carefully distinguishing the hypostases.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 8:6 ("one God the Father of whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ through whom are all things") establish a rule that "of whom" belongs to the Father alone and "through whom" to the Son, implying a difference of nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Hilary argues that if it sufficed to say creation is from God, there would be no need to add that things are through Christ unless being through Christ and from God is one and the same thing. 'From Whom' and 'through Whom' signify an Author of the same nature engaged in the same work, since by each the same power is exercised.
sources.quote: from Whom are all things and through Whom are all things must signify an Author of the same nature engaged in the same work
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's distinction that all things are 'from' God the Father and 'through' the Son (1 Cor 8:6) imply a difference of nature or power between Father and Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That there is no distinction in the scriptural use of these syllables.
sources.answer: No. Paul is not laying down a rule but carefully distinguishing the hypostases, showing that Father and Son are not confounded. The phrases are not opposed to each other. Paul applies both to one and the same subject in Romans 11:36: 'of him and through him and to him are all things.'
sources.quote: The object of the apostle in thus writing was not to introduce the diversity of nature, but to exhibit the notion of Father and of Son as unconfounded.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 8:6, which speaks of the Father 'of whom' and the Lord Jesus Christ 'through whom' are all things, teach a difference of nature between Father and Son?

question: In what sense are the Father and the Son each in the other (John 14:10), given that one being cannot both contain and be contained by another?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Athanasius ground the mutual indwelling in the one identical Godhead possessed fully by both. Hilary adds the Son's works as evidence and the Father as the Son's sole Origin, and denies any bodily containment. Gregory of Nyssa instead explains it through the image analogy, with the Son in the Father as an image's beauty is in its model and the Father in the Son as the original is in its image, with no interval of time between them. Athanasius likewise stresses that seeing the Son is seeing the Father, because the Son's Godhead and Form are the Father's own.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: It does not mean one body enclosed in or poured into another. It means equal power and the full Godhead exist in both. The Son's works demonstrate this. The Father is not diminished by the Son's existence, and the Son is not a mutilated fragment of the Father.
sources.quote: the meaning of Father in Son and Son in Father is that there is the perfect fulness of the Godhead in Both.
sources.raw_question: How should 'the Father in Me, and I in the Father' (John 14:10) be understood, given that one body cannot be contained in another?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: Each is in the other in a different sense: the Son is in the Father as the beauty of an image is found in the form from which it was outlined, and the Father is in the Son as the original beauty is found in its image. Unlike hand-made images, no interval of time separates model and image here.
sources.quote: the Son being in the Father as the beauty of the image is to be found in the form from which it has been outlined; and the Father in the Son, as that original beauty is to be found in the image of itself.
sources.raw_question: In what sense are the Father and the Son each in the other, according to John 14:10?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: They are in each other because their Godhead is one and the same. The Son's Godhead and Form are the Father's own, so whoever sees the Son sees the Father. The propriety of the Father's Godhead, present in the Son, shows the Son to be in the Father and inseparable from Him.
sources.quote: the Godhead and the Form of the Son is none other’s than the Father’s, this is what He says, ‘I in the Father.’
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father (John 14:10)?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: Mutual indwelling holds because each Person possesses the same fulness of Godhead. The Father is in the Son because the Son is from Him, and the Son is in the Father because the Father is His sole Origin. Since all is perfect in the unbegotten Father and all is perfect in the only-begotten Son, what is in the one is in the other.
sources.quote: The Father is in the Son, for the Son is from Him; the Son is in the Father, because the Father is His sole Origin; the Only-begotten is in the Unbegotten, because He is the Only-begotten from the Unbegotten.
sources.raw_question: How can the Father and the Son each be in the other (John 14:10) when it seems impossible for one being both to contain and be contained by another?

question: Does the Son have full and perfect knowledge equal to the Father's, and how is His knowledge related to the Father's?
synthesis: All three authors affirm that the Son's knowledge is perfect and lacks nothing. Athanasius argues from Matt. 11:27 that knowing the Father is the greatest knowledge, so the Son knows all things. Augustine adds that the Son has His knowing from the Father as He has His being, since in God to know and to be are one: the Father knows by begetting and the Son by being born. Hilary stresses the exclusive, mutual and complete knowledge between Father and Son, and concludes that the Son is the only faithful witness who reveals the Father.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes. Knowledge of both Father and Son is revealed through the Son, so the revelation to Peter came through Him. The Son knows all things, knowing His own Father, than which no knowledge can be greater or more perfect.
sources.quote: The Son then knew, as knowing all things, and knowing His own Father, than which knowledge nothing can be greater or more perfect.
sources.raw_question: Since the Son alone knows the Father and reveals Him (Matt. 11:27), does it follow that the Son knows all things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Word of God is in All Things Equal to the Father, from Whom It is.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son knows all that the Father knows, but He has His knowing from the Father, just as He has His being from the Father. In God, to know and to be are one. So as the Father does not have His being from the Son, neither does He have His knowing from the Son.
sources.quote: He knows all that the Father knows; but to Him to know, as to be, is from the Father, for to know and to be is there one
sources.raw_question: Does the Son know everything the Father knows, and from whom does the Son have His knowledge?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Word of God is in All Things Equal to the Father, from Whom It is.
sources.answer: The Father knows all things in Himself as Himself, and in the Son as His own Word, which is spoken concerning all things in Him. The Son knows all things in Himself as born of what the Father knows, and in the Father as their source. They know mutually, but the Father does so by begetting and the Son by being born.
sources.quote: The Father then, and the Son know mutually; but the one by begetting, the other by being born.
sources.raw_question: How do the Father and the Son each know all things, and how does their mutual knowledge differ?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Only the Son knows the Father, and only the Father knows the Son, so each has perfect and complete knowledge of the Other. Our thoughts of the Father must therefore agree with those of the Son, the only faithful Witness who reveals Him.
sources.quote: Each has perfect and complete knowledge of the Other. Therefore, since no one knoweth the Father save the Son, let our thoughts of the Father be at one with the thoughts of the Son
sources.raw_question: Who has true knowledge of the Father, and what does this imply about the Son?

question: In what sense is Christ called 'the first-born from the dead'?
synthesis: All three authors read the title as referring to Christ's work in the flesh and the resurrection he opens to humanity, not to his being the first to die. Irenaeus frames it as an Adam–Christ parallel: Adam began those who die and Christ begins those who live, regenerating the ancient fathers into God's life. Athanasius stresses that Christ is first-born not because he died first but because he abolished death and first rose as man by raising his own body, and Gregory of Nyssa likewise says he first loosed the pains of death and so implanted the power of rising in human nature, explicitly assigning the title to the incarnate economy rather than his eternal existence.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXII.—Christ assumed actual flesh, conceived and born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: Adam became the beginning of those who die, and Christ became the beginning of those who live. Born as the First-begotten of the dead, Christ took the ancient fathers into himself and regenerated them into the life of God. Irenaeus sees this reversal in the Lord's saying that the first shall be last and the last first. He also sees it in the prophecy that 'instead of fathers, children have been born unto thee.'
sources.quote: For the Lord, having been born “the First-begotten of the dead,” and receiving into His bosom the ancient fathers, has regenerated them into the life of God, He having been made Himself the beginning of those that live
sources.raw_question: In what sense is Christ, as 'the First-begotten of the dead', the beginning of a new humanity parallel to Adam?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: He is not first-born from the dead because He died before us, since we died first. He is called so because He underwent death for us, abolished it, and was the first to rise as man by raising His own body. Because He rose, we also rise from Him and on account of Him in due course.
sources.quote: not that He died before us, for we had died first; but because having undergone death for us and abolished it, He was the first to rise, as man, for our sakes raising His own Body.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is Christ called 'First-born from the dead,' given that others died before Him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He further very appositely expounds the meaning of the term “Only-Begotten,“ and of the term “First born,“ four times used by the Apostle.
sources.answer: He is first-born from the dead because He first, by His own act, loosed the pains of death. He thereby implanted in human nature the power of rising again. His new birth from the dead became a way for us also, so He is the first-fruits of them that slept.
sources.quote: He becomes the “first-fruits of them that slept” and the “first-born from the dead,” in that He first by His own act loosed the pains of death
sources.raw_question: In what sense is Christ "the first-born from the dead"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then again admirably discusses the term πρωτότοκος as it is four times employed by the Apostle.
sources.answer: These titles refer to Christ's incarnate economy, not his eternal existence. He is first-born from the dead because he first loosed the pains of death, opening the way of resurrection for all. He is first-born among many brethren because he was first born by the new birth of regeneration in water, with the Spirit as Dove attending, making those who share that birth his brethren.
sources.quote: He is the first-born from the dead, Who first by Himself loosed the pains of death, that He might also make that birth of the resurrection a way for all men
sources.raw_question: In what sense is Christ called 'the first-born from the dead' and 'the first-born among many brethren'?

question: Does the name Emmanuel, 'God with us' (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23), show that the one born of the Virgin is God and not a mere man?
synthesis: Owen, Irenaeus and Novatian all affirm that the name Emmanuel shows Christ to be God, but they argue it differently. Owen holds that it describes the condition of his person, God in our nature, rather than a name he actually bore, since his name was Jesus. Irenaeus reads it through Matthew as showing he is not a mere man, and links it to the God 'known in Judea' whom David speaks of. Novatian grounds it in Christ's promise to be with us to the end of the world, so that he is God with us and indeed in us.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: It signifies the condition of his person: God in our nature. His actual name was Jesus, as Matthew shows, and the prophecy that he should be Emmanuel was fulfilled in that the child born was God with us. A child born to be God with us can only mean God in that child taking our nature upon him.
sources.quote: Now, a child born to be “God with us,” is God in that child taking our nature upon him; and no otherwise can the words be understood.
sources.raw_question: Does the name Emmanuel in Isaiah 7:14 signify that Christ is God in our nature, or merely a title he would bear?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: Yes. Matthew calls him Emmanuel, "God with us," so that we should not think of him as a mere man. The Word was made flesh not by the will of man but by the will of God. So the Son of God himself was born of a virgin, and he is the Christ the prophets foretold.
sources.quote: and that He is Emmanuel, lest perchance we might consider Him as a mere man: for “not by the will of the flesh nor by the will of man, but by the will of God was the Word made flesh;”
sources.raw_question: Does the name Emmanuel in Matthew's account show that the one born of the Virgin is more than a mere man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IX.—One and the same God, the Creator of heaven and earth, is He whom the prophets foretold, and who was declared by the Gospel. Proof of this, at the outset, from St. Matthew’s Gospel.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus takes the virgin's son from David's line, whom Matthew calls Emmanuel ('God with us'), as the one David speaks of. This is the God who is 'known in Judea' and whose dwelling is in Zion. So the one God proclaimed by the prophets and the Gospel has his Son, who is himself God with us in the flesh.
sources.quote: His Son, who was of the fruit of David’s body, that is, of the virgin of [the house of] David, and Emmanuel
sources.raw_question: Does the name Emmanuel, 'God with us', show that the Son born of the Virgin is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That Christ is God, is Proved by the Authority of the Old Testament Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ says, 'Lo, I am with you, even to the consummation of the world', so he is the one who is with us. Because he is with us he was called Emmanuel, God with us, and so he is God. Indeed he is not only with us but in us.
sources.quote: But because He is with us He was called Emmanuel, that is, God with us. God, therefore, because He is with us, was called God with us.
sources.raw_question: Does the name Emmanuel, 'God with us', in Isaiah's prophecy apply to Christ and prove his divinity?

question: Does the fact that one can lie to or sin against the Holy Spirit, as Ananias and Sapphira did, prove that the Holy Spirit is God?
synthesis: All agree that it does, but their grounds differ. Basil and Ambrose argue from the wording of Peter's rebuke: the one lied to is the Holy Spirit, and Peter then says 'not unto men but unto God.' Ambrose adds that either way, whether through shared Godhead or Scripture's plain naming, the Spirit's Godhead follows. Owen argues more generally that whoever can be formally and ultimately sinned against is owed faith, obedience and worship, which can be owed only to God and never to a mere quality or power.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Sin is a failure in faith, obedience or worship. Whoever can be sinned against formally and ultimately must be owed faith, obedience and worship. One cannot lie to 'the efficacy of God' or be bound to obey a quality, so the Spirit must be God himself.
sources.quote: Against whom a man may sin formally and ultimately, him he is bound to obey, worship, and believe in. And this can be no quality, but God himself.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that people can sin against the Holy Spirit prove that he is God and not a quality?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter speaks of tempting the Spirit of the Lord and then says they have lied not to men but to God. This shows that sinning against the Holy Spirit is the same as sinning against God.
sources.quote: show that sins against the Holy Spirit and against God are the same
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's rebuke of Ananias and Sapphira show that the Holy Spirit is God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IX. That the Holy Spirit is provoked is proved by the words of St. Peter, in which it is shown that the Spirit of God is one and the same as the Spirit of the Lord, both by other passages and by reference to the sentence of the same Apostle on Ananias and Sapphira, whence it is argued that the union of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, as well as His own Godhead, is proved.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter says Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit and then says "Thou hast not lied unto men but unto God." So either the Spirit shares the one Godhead, or, if one denies that oneness, Scripture still plainly calls the Spirit God. Either way, the Spirit's Godhead follows.
sources.quote: you must necessarily either understand the oneness of the Godhead in the Holy Spirit, since when the Holy Spirit is tempted a lie is told to God; or, if you endeavour to exclude the oneness of the Godhead, you yourself according to the words of Scripture certainly believe Him to be God.
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's rebuke of Ananias for lying to the Holy Spirit prove that the Holy Spirit is God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen argues that sin and obedience have the same ground: whoever can be sinned against formally and ultimately is one to whom faith, obedience and worship are owed. Such obligations can be owed only to God himself, not to a quality, since no one can be formally obliged to obey a quality or lie to 'the efficacy of God in his operations.' Therefore faith, obedience and worship are due to the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: Against whom a man may sin formally and ultimately, him he is bound to obey, worship, and believe in. And this can be no quality, but God himself.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that a person can sin against the Holy Spirit (as Ananias did in lying to him) show that the Holy Spirit is God and a person rather than a quality or power?

question: What does God's name "I Am that I Am" reveal about His nature or being?
synthesis: Hilary holds that the name reveals absolute existence and through it God's eternity, since absolute being cannot belong to what begins or ends. Augustine stresses instead that being is said of God in a unique, proper sense, since creatures such as bodies and souls are also said in some sense to be. Novatian reads the name as signifying immutability: God always remains the same, because change would destroy the force of "I Am." All three tie the name to a divine attribute but differ in which one they emphasize (eternity, unique being, unchangeability).

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Because nothing the mind can grasp is more characteristic of God than absolute existence. Existence in the absolute sense cannot be said of what will end or what has begun, and what is divine can neither be originated nor destroyed. Since God's eternity is inseparable from Him, revealing simply that He is serves as the assurance of His absolute eternity.
sources.quote: For no property of God which the mind can grasp is more characteristic of Him than existence, since existence, in the absolute sense, cannot be predicated of that which shall come to an end, or of that which has had a beginning
sources.raw_question: Why is existence ("I Am that I Am") the most fitting name or property by which God reveals Himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > This Work is Written Against Those Who Sophistically Assail the Faith of the Trinity, Through Misuse of Reason. They Who Dispute Concerning God Err from a Threefold Cause. Holy Scripture, Removing What is False, Leads Us on by Degrees to Things Divine. What True Immortality is. We are Nourished by Faith, that We May Be Enabled to Apprehend Things Divine.
sources.answer: It teaches that being is said properly of God in a special sense not found in any creature. Bodies and souls are said in some sense to be, so Scripture would not speak this way unless it meant a unique sense of being proper to God.
sources.quote: For since both body and soul also are said in some sense to be, Holy Scripture certainly would not so express itself unless it meant to be understood in some special sense of the term.
sources.raw_question: What does God's name "I am that I am" teach about God's being, given that bodies and souls are also said to be?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, He is Good, Always the Same, Immutable, One and Only, Infinite; And His Own Name Can Never Be Declared, and He is Incorruptible and Immortal.
sources.answer: It signifies that God always keeps the same quality of himself. Anything that changes ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not. Change would therefore remove the force of the name "I Am."
sources.quote: And thus He says, “I am that I am.” For what He is has this name, because it always maintains the same quality of Himself. For change takes away the force of that name “That I Am;”
sources.raw_question: What does God's name "I am that I am" signify about his nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: It reveals existence, and through existence His absolute eternity. Existence in the absolute sense cannot be predicated of what has a beginning or will come to an end. Whatever is divine can neither be originated nor destroyed. It was therefore fitting for God to reveal that He is, as the assurance of His eternity.
sources.quote: For no property of God which the mind can grasp is more characteristic of Him than existence, since existence, in the absolute sense, cannot be predicated of that which shall come to an end, or of that which has had a beginning
sources.raw_question: What property of God does the divine name 'I Am that I Am' reveal as most characteristic of Him?

question: Is God really subject to passions such as anger, pity or hatred, as Scripture's language seems to suggest?
synthesis: Novatian, Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine all deny that God is subject to passions, but they argue differently. Novatian says Scripture speaks anthropopathically, and that passions corrupt only impressible matter, which God, being incorruptible, lacks. Gregory stresses that Scripture uses human idioms for our benefit: to restrain sinners by fear, keep the fallen from despair and encourage the upright. Augustine locates the change in the creature rather than in God, as light is painful to weak eyes and pleasant to healthy ones.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Preface.
sources.answer: No. According to the summary of Novatian's treatise, neither passions nor members can be attributed to God. Where Scripture ascribes such things to God, it speaks anthropopathically, that is, in human terms adapted to our understanding. This fits with the divine attributes Novatian defends from reason and Scripture, such as spirituality, immutability and immortality.
sources.quote: adds that neither passions nor members can be attributed to God, and that these things are only asserted of God in Scripture anthropopathically
sources.raw_question: Can passions or bodily members properly be attributed to God, given that Scripture speaks of God as having them?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > If We Regard the Anger, and Indignation, and Hatred of God Described in the Sacred Pages, We Must Remember that They are Not to Be Understood as Bearing the Character of Human Vices.
sources.answer: No. Such passions are rightly said to be in men but not in God, because man can be corrupted by them while God cannot be corrupted. These affections exert force only where there is a material capable of being impressed, not in a substance that cannot be impressed.
sources.quote: For man may be corrupted by these things, because he can be corrupted; God may not be corrupted by them, because He cannot be corrupted.
sources.raw_question: Do the descriptions of God's wrath, indignation and hatred in Scripture mean that God is subject to passions in the same way humans are?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Anyone who has thought about the truth of things sees it would be irreverent to imagine God subject to such passions. Scripture attributes them to Him by using our own idioms, to help our weakness. Fear of punishment restrains sinners, the sight of His mercy keeps the fallen from despair, and the upright are encouraged by knowing they please Him.
sources.quote: For that it is irreverent to imagine that God is subject to any passion such as we see in respect to pleasure, or pity, or anger, no one will deny who has thought at all about the truth of things.
sources.raw_question: Is God really subject to passions such as anger, pity or pleasure, as Scripture's language seems to suggest?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said of God in Time, is Said Relatively, Not Accidentally.
sources.answer: No. It is the people who are changed, not God. Light is troublesome to weak eyes and pleasant to strong ones because of a change in the eyes, not in the light. In the same way, God's wrath or gentleness reflects the creature's condition.
sources.quote: when He is said to be wroth with the unrighteous, and gentle with the good, they are changed, not He: just as the light is troublesome to weak eyes, pleasant to those that are strong; namely, by their change, not its own.
sources.raw_question: Does God change when Scripture says He is angry with the unrighteous and gentle with the good?

question: Does Christ's saying 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father' (John 14:9) mean that the Son is the Father, one and the same Person?
synthesis: Hilary, Hippolytus and Novatian all deny that the text identifies the Son with the Father, but on different grounds. Hilary argues from the word 'also' and explains the seeing by unity of nature. Hippolytus says the Son is the image through which the Father is known and points to the surrounding chapter on the Son's being sent. Novatian appeals to what Philip had been taught, that Christ was the Son, and reads the text as faith in the Son leading on to the Father.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The word 'also' shows that the Father is named in addition to the Son, so this is no case of identity. The Father is seen in the Son because they are one God and alike in nature, not because they are one Person. The saying thus teaches that God is not solitary and yet has no differences within the Divine nature.
sources.quote: This is no case of identity; the use of the conjunction also shews that the Father is named in addition to the Son. These words, The Father also, are incompatible with the notion of an isolated and single Person.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father also' mean that the Father and the Son are one and the same Person?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. The text actually works against the Noetians. Christ means that whoever has seen him may know the Father through him, because the Son is the image like the original, through which the Father is readily known. The rest of the chapter shows that the Son was sent from the Father and goes to the Father.
sources.quote: By which He means, If thou hast seen me, thou mayest know the Father through me. For through the image, which is like (the original), the Father is made readily known.
sources.raw_question: Does 'He that hath seen me hath seen the Father' (John 14:9) mean that Christ is himself the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Proves Also that the Words Spoken to Philip Make Nothing for the Sabellians.
sources.answer: No. Philip had never heard or learned from Christ that Christ was the Father, but often that He was the Son. The saying means that whoever draws near to the Son with full faith will through the Son attain to the Father and see Him. It is not that the Son Himself is the Father being seen.
sources.quote: He said not as wishing to be understood Himself to be the Father, but implying that he who thoroughly, and fully, and with all faith and all religiousness, drew near to the Son of God, by all means shall attain, through the Son Himself, in whom he thus believes, to the Father, and shall see Him.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying to Philip, "He who hath seen me hath seen the Father also," show that the Son is the Father, as the Sabellians claim?

question: Can the Son, through whom all things were made, be himself a creature?
synthesis: Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary all deny that the Son can be a creature, because he is the Creator through whom all things were made. Athanasius argues from absurdity: the Son would be First-born of himself and would both create all things and consist among them. Gregory calls the claim a blind, unsupported assertion and frames the real issue as whether the Son and Spirit belong to created or uncreated existence. Hilary appeals both to human reason, since creation comes into being through the Creator, and to Scripture's naming of the one through whom all things were made as Creator.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. If he were a creature he would be First-born of himself, before and after himself, which is absurd. And he cannot both create the whole creation and be one of the things that consist in him. So he is the Creator, not a creature.
sources.quote: if He is a creature, and the whole creation through Him came to be, and in Him consists, how can He both create the creation and be one of the things which consist in Him?
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be a creature if all creation came to be through him and consists in him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no reason for distinguishing a plurality of beings in the Trinity. He offers no demonstration that it is so.
sources.answer: No. It is a blind and unsupported statement to call the Creator and Maker of all things a creature made. The conclusion built on it, that the Son is alien in nature and unlike the Father in being, is just as groundless. The real question at issue is whether the Son and Spirit belong to created or uncreated existence, and the Church denies that they are created.
sources.quote: it is a truly blind and unsupported statement to say that the Creator and Maker of all things is a creature made
sources.raw_question: Can the Son, as Creator and Maker of all things, be a creature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Hilary argues that human reason itself repudiates the claim that the Creator is a creature, since creation comes into existence by means of the Creator. Scripture applies the title Creator to the one through whom all things were made, so he cannot be placed among the works of his hands.
sources.quote: In the first place our human intelligence repudiates this statement that the Creator is a creature; since creation comes to exist by means of the Creator.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son, through whom all things were made, be a creature in the same category of nature as the things he created?

question: Is the Son a created thing, given that all things were made through him?
synthesis: All three authors deny that the Son is created, but on different grounds. Gregory of Nyssa argues from John's testimony that a created Word would have to have made himself, which is absurd. Athanasius argues that the one through whom all things are is excluded from that 'all' just as God the Father is, because the Son is proper to the Father's essence. Waterland argues historically, holding that Clarke's party in effect makes the Son a creature, contrary to the doctrine of the ancients.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: No. John testifies that all things were made by him. If the Word were one of the things that came into being, he would have to have been made by himself. That absurdly makes the Lord of creation his own work.
sources.quote: If then all things that came into being were made by Him, and the Word is one of the things that came into being, who is so dull as not to draw from these premises the absurd conclusion
sources.raw_question: If all things were made through the Son, can the Son himself be a created thing?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says all things were made through Wisdom, the Word, Christ, so he through whom all things are is not one of that 'all'. Whoever counts the Son among the all would by the same logic count God, from whom are all things, among them. If we rightly exclude God, we must also exclude the Only-Begotten, who is proper to the Father's essence. So it is sin to say of him 'He was not.'
sources.quote: And if all things are through Him, He Himself is not to be reckoned with that ‘all.’ For he who dares to call Him, through whom are things, one of that ‘all,’ surely will have like speculations concerning God, from whom are all.
sources.raw_question: If all things were made through the Son, can the Son himself be counted among the created 'all things'?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Clarke's party does not say so in words, but in reality and in other terms they make the Son a creature. Waterland holds that this position is flatly contrary to the doctrine of the ancients.
sources.quote: This neither you nor the Doctor admit iz terms ; but in reality, and in other words, you both do; as hath been shewn. This position is flatly contrary to the doctrine of the ancients.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son himself made or created?

question: Is the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 the foundational and authoritative confession of the Christian faith in the Trinity?
synthesis: Owen, Hilary and Gregory of Nyssa all affirm it, with different emphases. Owen stresses that baptism initiates the church into an express profession of the Trinity, making it the church's doctrinal foundation. Hilary stresses that it contains the whole mystery of salvation, confessing the Father as Creator, the Only-begotten Son and the Spirit as Gift. Gregory stresses that, as the Lord's own rule of faith, it may not be altered, added to or subtracted from.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Preface
sources.answer: Yes. By Christ's special institution, the church is initiated through baptism into an express profession of the Trinity. This confession comprises the whole truth contended for. Because it is placed at the very entrance into all obedience to Christ, it is the doctrinal foundation of the church.
sources.quote: which confession comprises the whole of the truth contended for, and by the indispensable placing of it at the first entrance into all obedience unto him, is made the doctrinal foundation of the church
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost" make the doctrine of the Trinity foundational for the church?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > The second book declares the Incarnation of God the Word, and the faith delivered by the Lord to His disciples, and asserts that the heretics who endeavour to overthrow this faith and devise other additional names are of their father the devil.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord Himself set forth the faith to His disciples in Matthew 28:19, and through this word of the mystery our nature is renewed to incorruption. Nothing may be subtracted, altered or added. Whoever perverts these divine words by quibbling 'is of his father the devil', since whatever departs from exact accord with the truth is false. The following section applies this to the Eunomian practice of calling the Father 'Maker' of the Son and the Spirit a 'creature of a creature'. Such renamings are rejected as a denial of the Godhead revealed in these titles.
sources.quote: In the Faith then which was delivered by God to the Apostles we admit neither subtraction, nor alteration, nor addition, knowing assuredly that he who presumes to pervert the Divine utterance by dishonest quibbling, the same “is of his father the devil,”
sources.raw_question: Is the baptismal formula 'in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost' the authoritative rule of faith about God, so that it may not be altered or supplemented with other names?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Yes. Hilary holds that the command to baptize in the Name of the Father, Son and Holy Ghost contains everything in the mystery of salvation and an insight into the Divine nature. It is a confession of the Creator, the Only-begotten and the Gift: the One Father from Whom are all things, the One Son through Whom are all things, and the One Spirit, God's Gift, Who pervades all things.
sources.quote: He bade them baptize in the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, that is with confession of the Creator and of the Only-begotten, and of the Gift.
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 contain a sufficient confession of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit and their distinct roles?

question: In John 1:14, 'The Word was made flesh,' does 'flesh' mean only a body without a human soul, or the whole human nature?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine and Athanasius agree that 'flesh' here means the whole man or human nature, and all argue from Scripture's custom of naming humanity by 'flesh'. Gregory adds the converse case of 'souls' standing for whole persons. Augustine and Gregory explicitly deny a soulless flesh, while Athanasius simply glosses 'flesh' as 'man'.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: No. Scripture customarily signifies the whole by a part. "Unto Thee shall all flesh come" does not mean bodies without souls, and Jacob's going down to Egypt with seventy-five "souls" includes their bodies. So "flesh" in John 1:14 means the whole human nature.
sources.quote: let them learn that it is customary for Holy Scripture to imply the whole by the part. For He that said, “Unto Thee shall all flesh come,” does not mean that the flesh will be presented before the Judge apart from the souls
sources.raw_question: Does "The Word was made flesh" (John 1:14) mean that the Word took flesh without a human soul, since the soul is not mentioned?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: 'Flesh' means man, or human nature. It is Scripture's custom to call mankind 'flesh,' as Joel does ('I will pour out My Spirit upon all flesh') and as Daniel does in saying God has sovereignty over all flesh.
sources.quote: it being the custom of Scripture to call man by the name of ‘flesh,’ as it says by Joel the Prophet, ‘I will pour out My Spirit upon all flesh;’
sources.raw_question: What does 'flesh' mean in John 1:14, 'the Word became flesh'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Creature is Not So Taken by the Holy Spirit as Flesh is by the Word.
sources.answer: No. In this text "flesh" stands for the whole man, as when Scripture says "all flesh shall see the salvation of God." There it plainly means every man, not flesh lacking soul and mind.
sources.quote: For it does not mean flesh without soul and without mind; but “all flesh,” is the same as if it were said, every man.
sources.raw_question: Does 'The Word was made flesh' mean the Word took only a body, without a human soul and mind?

question: Why did the Word of God become flesh?
synthesis: Augustine, Irenaeus and Athanasius give complementary purposes. For Augustine it was to cleanse and heal sin-darkened minds so they could partake of the Word. Irenaeus says it was so the Word might have preeminence on earth and below, and humanity might attain immortality through the Father's light on His flesh. Athanasius says it was to make man capable of Godhead and sons of God by receiving the Spirit of the true Son.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > How We are Rendered Apt for the Perception of Truth Through the Incarnate Word.
sources.answer: Because human minds were darkened by vicious desires and unbelief and made unfit by the uncleanness of sin to partake of the Word, who is the life that is the light of men. Our enlightening is a partaking of the Word, but we first had to be cleansed. Therefore the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us to care for and heal those darkened minds.
sources.quote: For our enlightening is the partaking of the Word, namely, of that life which is the light of men. But for this partaking we were utterly unfit, and fell short of it, on account of the uncleanness of sins. Therefore we were to be cleansed.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Word of God, through whom all things were made, need to become flesh in order to enlighten human minds?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: The Word became flesh so that, as he had sovereignty in the heavens, he might also have it on earth as a righteous man without sin, and preeminence under the earth as the first-begotten of the dead. Through this, the Father's light would rest on his flesh and come to us, and humanity, clothed with that light, would attain immortality.
sources.quote: that the paternal light might meet with and rest upon the flesh of our Lord, and come to us from His resplendent flesh, and that thus man might attain to immortality, having been invested with the paternal light.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Word of God become flesh?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Creatures can become sons only by receiving the Spirit of the natural and true Son. The Word therefore became flesh so that He might make man capable of Godhead. God is our Father not by nature but on account of the Word dwelling in us.
sources.quote: they could not become sons, being by nature creatures, otherwise than by receiving the Spirit of the natural and true Son. Wherefore, that this might be, ‘The Word became flesh,’ that He might make man capable of Godhead.
sources.raw_question: How can creatures become sons of God, and why did the Word become flesh?

question: Can the doctrine of the Trinity be discovered or judged by natural reason, or must it be known by divine revelation?
synthesis: All three authors deny that natural reason readily reaches the Trinity, but on different grounds and with different strength. Augustine says only that it is difficult: every attribute reason ascribes to God applies both to the whole Trinity and to each Person, so the attributes do not show the distinction of Persons. Owen and Warfield deny it outright and say the doctrine is known only by revelation. Owen appeals to Scripture: the Spirit alone knows the things of God, and the Son and Father must reveal one another. Warfield appeals to history: no ethnic thought or religion has ever arrived at a Trinitarian conception of God.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What Universal Nature Teaches Us Concerning God.
sources.answer: Yes. Every attribute reason ascribes to God can be predicated both of the whole Trinity and of each Person. The attributes therefore do not by themselves show where or how the Trinity manifests itself.
sources.quote: If, then, these things, and all others of the kind, can be predicated both of the Trinity itself, and of each several one in that Trinity, where or how shall the Trinity manifest itself?
sources.raw_question: Is it difficult to discover the Trinity of Persons by natural reason from God's attributes?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: It must be known by revelation. The things of God are known only by the Spirit of God. No one knows the Father unless the Son reveals him, and no one knows Christ to be the Son of the living God unless the Father reveals it. These mysteries are therefore grasped through faith, prayer and God's revelation, not through the carnal reasoning of men.
sources.quote: It is by faith and prayer, and through the revelation of God, that we may come to the acknowledgment of these things, and not by the carnal reasonings of men of corrupt minds.
sources.raw_question: Can natural human reason judge the mystery of the Trinity, or must it be known by divine revelation?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The Trinity is purely a revealed doctrine, a truth never discovered and indiscoverable by natural reason. Man by searching cannot find out the deepest things of God, and accordingly no ethnic thought or religion has attained a Trinitarian conception of God.
sources.quote: the doctrine of the Trinity is purely a revealed doctrine. That is to say, it embodies a truth which has never been discovered, and is indiscoverable, by natural reason.
sources.raw_question: Can the doctrine of the Trinity be discovered by natural reason apart from revelation?

question: Can the Father be known except through the Son?
synthesis: Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa and Irenaeus all answer no: the Father is known only through the Son. Their grounds differ. Hilary holds that God can be apprehended and worshipped only through God, and draws from this that the Son is true God. Gregory says the invisible Archetype is known exactly only in its image, the Son. Irenaeus says the invisible, infinite Father is declared only by the Word's own manifestation, adding that only the Father knows the Word.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. God can be apprehended only through God, and God accepts worship only through God. We could not know that the Father is to be reverenced or is God unless the Son, who is Himself God, had taught us. This dependence implies that the Son is true God.
sources.quote: God cannot be apprehended except through God; even as also God accepts no worship from us except through God.
sources.raw_question: Can God the Father be known or rightly worshipped except through God the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > A passing repetition of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. An exact knowledge of the invisible Archetypal Good is possible only as it appears in its image, the Son. So the God over all is found through the Lord, who is the Cause of all things.
sources.quote: nor, indeed, is it possible to gain an exact knowledge of the Archetypal Good, except as it appears in the (visible) image of that invisible
sources.raw_question: Can the Father be known except through the Son as his image?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VI.—Explanation of the words of Christ, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” etc.; which words the heretics misinterpret. Proof that, by the Father revealing the Son, and by the Son being revealed, the Father was never unknown.
sources.answer: No. No one can know the Father except through the Word revealing him, for the Father is invisible and infinite as regards us and cannot be declared by anyone else. The Son reveals the Father through his own manifestation, since the manifestation of the Son is the knowledge of the Father; likewise only the Father knows his own Word.
sources.quote: For the manifestation of the Son is the knowledge of the Father; for all things are manifested through the Word.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father be known except through the Son, the Word?

question: What does Hebrews 1:3, in calling the Son the 'express image' of the Father's person (or substance), imply about the Son's relation to the Father?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa reads the phrase as showing that the Father's majesty is fully expressed in the Son's power, using the analogy of the sun's disc imaging its whole body. Hilary of Poitiers agrees that it implies no difference of nature, since a perfect resemblance excludes difference, but adds that it marks the Son's distinct existence. Waterland, following Eusebius against the Sabellians, stresses the other side: an image cannot be the same as what it images, so Father and Son are really distinct Persons, though the substance is not divided.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
sources.answer: It means the Father's majesty is fully expressed in the greatness of the Son's power. The Apostle uses a sensible image for those who cannot rise to pure contemplation: the sun's whole body is imaged by its disc. In the same way, the Father may be believed to be as great as the Son is known to be.
sources.quote: so, he says, the majesty of the Father is expressly imaged in the greatness of the power of the Son, that the one may be believed to be as great as the other is known to be
sources.raw_question: What does Hebrews 1:3 mean in calling the Son "the express image of His Person"?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. The phrase distinguishes Christ from the one he comes from only to establish their distinct existence, not a difference of nature. An image implies its original, and nothing can be like God unless it has its source in him. A perfect resemblance rules out any element of difference.
sources.quote: discriminate between Christ and Him from Whom He is, but only to establish Their distinct existence, not to teach a difference of nature
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son the 'Image of His substance' (Hebrews 1:3) imply that he differs in nature from the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Yes. As Eusebius argued against the Sabellians, the image and that of which it is the image cannot be the same thing. So the Father is not the Son, and they are really distinct. This is in no way repugnant to the Trinitarian position, which asserts a real distinction of Persons without dividing the substance.
sources.quote: from whence he rightly infers, or plainly means to do, that the Father is not the Son, but that they are really distinct. What is there in this at all repugnant to what the Querist maintains ?
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1:3, calling the Son the 'express image' of the Father's person, show that the Father and the Son are really distinct?

question: Is the Word of God a created being who had a beginning, or did He exist eternally before all created things?
synthesis: Augustine, Athanasius and Irenaeus agree that the Word was not made and had no beginning, but their grounds differ. Augustine argues from John 1 that all things could not have been made by the Word unless He was before all things and not made. Athanasius contrasts creatures, whose being is measured by their becoming, with the Word as their eternal Framer, while Irenaeus contrasts man, who receives a beginning and learns from the Word, with the Word who always co-existed with God as eternal teacher.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > We are Made Perfect by Acknowledgement of Our Own Weakness. The Incarnate Word Dispels Our Darkness.
sources.answer: The Word was not made. In the beginning the Word was with God and was God, and all things were made by Him; and all things could not have been made by Him unless He Himself had been before all things and not made.
sources.quote: Since, “in the beginning,” the Word was not made, but “the Word was with God, and the Word was God, and all things were made by Him;” neither had all things been made by Him, unless He had Himself been before all things and not made.
sources.raw_question: Was the Word of God made, or did He exist before all created things?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. Creatures began to be made, and their being is measured by their becoming, but the Word, not being of things that come to be, did not begin to be or to come to be but was ever. He is rather the Framer of things that have a beginning.
sources.quote: Therefore the creatures began to be made; but the Word of God, not having beginning of being, certainly did not begin to be, nor begin to come to be, but was ever.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God have a beginning of existence?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXV.—God is not to be sought after by means of letters, syllables, and numbers; necessity of humility in such investigations.
sources.answer: No. Man is not uncreated and did not always co-exist with God, but the Word did always co-exist with God. Man receives the beginning of his creation and gradually learns from the Word the dispensations of God, whereas the Word is the eternal teacher who is with God.
sources.quote: For thou, O man, art not an uncreated being, nor didst thou always co-exist with God, as did His own Word
sources.raw_question: Is the Word of God a created being who began to exist, like man?

question: Is the divine nature of the Son capable of suffering and death, or was it affected by Christ's death?
synthesis: Novatian, Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine all deny that Christ's divinity suffered or died, assigning the suffering and death to the human nature the Son assumed. Novatian stresses that what died was the man, not God, and that the Word was not drawn down into mortality. Gregory grounds his answer in the incorruptibility and impassibility of the divine nature, adding that the suffering was the body's while the saving work was God's. Augustine frames the point as nothing in the divinity being diminished or changed, while still holding that it was the eternal Son of God who underwent death in his humanity.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And that It Does Not Follow Thence, that Because Christ Died It Must Also Be Received that God Died; For Scripture Sets Forth that Not Only Was Christ God, But Man Also.
sources.answer: No. The divinity is impassible, though the human weakness assumed by the Word is liable to suffering. In Christ it was not that which is God that died but that which is man, and the Word was not drawn down into mortality.
sources.quote: it was not that in Christ that died which is God, but that in Him died which is man?
sources.raw_question: Is the divinity of Christ capable of suffering and death?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > The sixth book shows that He Who came for man's salvation was not a mere man, as Eunomius, falsely slandering him, affirmed that the great Basil had said, but the Only-begotten Son of God, putting on human flesh, and becoming a mediator between God and man, on Whom we believe, as subject to suffering in the flesh, but impassible in His Godhead; and demonstrates the calumny of Eunomius.
sources.answer: No. Gregory says we may not admit that the incorruptible and divine nature can suffer or die. As God, the Son is impassible and incorruptible. Whatever suffering the Gospel ascribes to him, he underwent through his human nature, which could suffer. In the Passion the suffering belonged to the body, while the saving work was God's.
sources.quote: We, then, neither attribute our own salvation to a man, nor admit that the incorruptible and Divine Nature is capable of suffering and mortality
sources.raw_question: Is the divine nature of the Son capable of suffering and death?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Remains of Death and the Evil Things of the World Turn to Good for the Elect. How Fitly the Death of Christ Was Chosen, that We Might Be Justified in His Blood. What the Anger of God is.
sources.answer: No. In Christ's death nothing was diminished or changed from His divinity. The death was undergone in the humanity He took upon Him, by the eternal Son of God who was also the Son of man.
sources.quote: wherein neither was anything diminished or changed from His divinity
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God's suffering death change or diminish his divine nature?

question: Is Christ to be worshipped with divine worship, and what does Scripture show about this?
synthesis: All three affirm that Christ is rightly given divine worship, but on different grounds. Owen grounds it doctrinally in Christ's being God, adding what he has done for us as man. Ambrose points to New Testament worship of Christ by Mary, the apostles and the angels, while Bickersteth appeals to Old Testament saints who prayed to and worshipped the Son as the Angel of Jehovah, and argues that this worship proves his deity.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Christ, God and man, is to be believed in, worshipped with religious and divine worship, trusted and obeyed because he is God, and also on account of what he has done for us as man. Scripture asserts this as a common principle of Christian profession.
sources.quote: That this Christ, God and man, is, because he is God, and on the account of what he has done for us as man, to be believed in, worshipped with worship religious and divine
sources.raw_question: Is Christ to be worshipped with divine worship, and on what ground?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: Yes. Mary worshipped Christ after the Resurrection, the apostles worshipped Him when He rose in the glory of His flesh, and the angels are commanded to worship Him. So the acts of the pious and the course of Scripture refute any denial of His worship.
sources.quote: For Mary worshipped Christ, and therefore is appointed to be the messenger of the Resurrection to the apostles
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture show that Christ is to be worshipped?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Old Testament saints prayed to and worshipped the Son appearing as the Angel of Jehovah: Abraham interceded with him, Jacob wrestled in prayer with him and sought his blessing, Moses and Joshua worshipped him. Such direct prayer and worship paid to Christ establishes that he is Jehovah God.
sources.quote: Scripture sanctions prayer to Christ, and commands the highest adoration and worship to be paid to him.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture sanction prayer and worship directed to Christ, and does this prove his deity?

question: Does Psalm 45 ('Thy throne, O God... God, thy God, hath anointed thee') call the Son God?
synthesis: Owen, Irenaeus and Hilary all answer yes. Owen rests on Hebrews 1:8 applying the psalm directly to the Son. Irenaeus notes that both the Anointer and the Anointed are called God, and Hilary adds that 'Thee' and 'Thy' distinguish the Persons without implying any difference of nature.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen points out that the psalm's words "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever" are applied directly to the Son in Hebrews 1:8. Scripture therefore addresses the Son as God whose throne is eternal.
sources.quote: Applied unto Christ, Heb. i. 8, “But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever.”
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 45:6, as applied in Hebrews 1:8, call the Son God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit designates both by the name of God: the Son, who is anointed, and the Father, who anoints.
sources.quote: For the Spirit designates both [of them] by the name, of God—both Him who is anointed as Son, and Him who does anoint, that is, the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 45, "Thy throne, O God... God, thy God, hath anointed thee," call both the Father and the Son God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. The words "Thee" and "Thy" mark a distinction of Persons, Anointer and Anointed, but nothing in them suggests a difference of nature. "Thy" points to the Author and "Thee" to His offspring, so the Son is God from God. The single title "God" given to both assures us that in character and majesty They are One.
sources.quote: No; the distinction of Persons is indicated by Thee and Thy, but nothing suggests a difference of nature. Thy points to the Author, Thee to Him Who is the Author’s offspring.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 45's "God, Thy God, hath anointed Thee" show that the Son is God, distinct from the Father yet not different in nature?

question: In what sense did the invisible Word of God become visible in the Incarnation?
synthesis: All three authors affirm that the invisible Word became visible in the flesh, but they stress different things. Athanasius and Augustine qualify the claim: for Athanasius the Word was seen not in his Godhead but in its working through the body he made his own, and for Augustine there was no change of substance, since he took the form of a servant while remaining invisible with the Father who sent him. Irenaeus instead stresses the reality of the event: the Word, invisible by nature, was made palpable and visible and himself descended to death on the cross.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
