sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: He was seen not in his invisible Godhead but in the operation of the Godhead through the human body and the whole Man. Before the incarnation he was invisible even to the heavenly powers, but he became visible because he is one with the visible Man whom he renewed by appropriating it to himself.
sources.quote: seen, I say, not in His invisible Godhead but in the operation of the Godhead through the human body and whole Man, which He has renewed by its appropriation to Himself
sources.raw_question: In what sense was the invisible Word of God seen in the incarnation?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. He took the form of a servant while the unchangeable form of God remained. If his substance had been changed into a creature, he would be only sent and not also, with the Father, sending. Because he remained invisible with the Father, the invisible Father with the invisible Son sent the Son so as to be visible.
sources.quote: But since He so took the form of a servant, as that the unchangeable form of God remained, it is clear that that which became apparent in the Son was done by the Father and the Son not being apparent
sources.raw_question: Did the Son's becoming visible in the Incarnation involve a change of the invisible Word's substance into a visible creature?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXIV.—The conversion of the Gentiles was more difficult than that of the Jews; the labours of those apostles, therefore who engaged in the former task, were greater than those who undertook the latter.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus says the Gentiles had to be taught that God's Word, invisible by nature, was made palpable and visible among men and descended to death, even the death of the cross. Believers in Him will then become incorruptible and receive the kingdom of heaven. The one who died is therefore the divine Word himself, made visible in the flesh.
sources.quote: His Word, invisible by nature, was made palpable and visible among men, and did descend “to death, even the death of the cross;”
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God, invisible by nature, become visible and undergo death in the incarnation?

question: Are the divine and human natures in Christ united in one person, or do they make two persons?
synthesis: Owen, Novatian and Augustine agree that Christ is one person in whom two natures or substances are united. Owen argues from Scripture: texts such as the Word made flesh and God's blood shed for the church require one person. Novatian stresses that the two substances are woven together in one Lord while their distinction remains. Augustine adds that the one person is in a sense made of three (God, soul and flesh), and draws from this the high dignity of human nature.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: The scriptural statements require one person. The Word could not be made flesh, take on him the seed of Abraham, be a child born as the mighty God, or shed God's blood for the church unless the two natures expressed were united in one person. Otherwise, being two natures, they would also be two persons.
sources.quote: nor could God shed his blood for his church, but that the two natures so directly expressed must be united in one person; for otherwise, as they are two natures still, they would be two persons also.
sources.raw_question: How does Scripture show that the divine and human natures in Christ are united in one person rather than being two persons?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That These Have Therefore Erred, by Thinking that There Was No Difference Between the Son of God and the Son of Man; Because They Have Ill Understood the Scripture.
sources.answer: He is one Lord in whom both substances are joined. Christ Jesus is connected on both sides, woven and grown together, and associated in the agreement of both substances by a mutual alliance. He is thus both man and God, as Scripture declares, while the distinction between the natures remains.
sources.quote: Christ Jesus the Lord, connected on both sides, so to speak, is on both sides woven in and grown together, and associated in the same agreement of both substances
sources.raw_question: Is Christ one subject in whom divine and human substances are united, or two separate beings?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Other Advantages of the Incarnation.
sources.answer: One person is made of two substances, God and man, and thereby in a sense of three: God, soul, and flesh. The union does not yield a plurality of persons but a single person. This shows what a high place human nature has among God's creatures, since it could be joined to God in such a unity.
sources.quote: since human nature could so be joined to God, that one person could be made of two substances, and thereby indeed of three—God, soul, and flesh
sources.raw_question: In the incarnation of Christ, how many substances are united in the one person, and does this make two persons?

question: What does 1 Corinthians 12:4-6, on diversities of gifts, ministrations and workings, teach about the Spirit, the Lord and God?
synthesis: Hilary reads the passage as a fourfold statement and stresses the same Spirit, Lord and God behind the diverse gifts, with their bestowal a manifestation of the Spirit. Owen and Warfield emphasize the distinct attribution to three persons. Owen says gifts come from the Spirit, administrations from the Lord Jesus and operations from the Father, and are received distinctly. Warfield argues that the somewhat artificial threefold division strengthens rather than weakens the passage as evidence of Paul's Trinitarian sense of a threefold causality.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It makes a fourfold statement. In the diversity of gifts it is the same Spirit, in the diversity of ministrations the same Lord, and in the diversity of workings the same God. The fourth point is that the bestowal of what is profitable is a manifestation of the Spirit. Paul then enumerates the gifts, such as wisdom, knowledge, faith and healing, which Hilary treats as the very gifts through which the Spirit is manifested.
sources.quote: in the diversity of gifts it is the same Spirit, in the diversity of ministrations it is the very same Lord, in the diversity of workings it is the same God, and in the bestowal of that which is profitable there is a manifestation of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: What does 1 Corinthians 12:4-7, on diversities of gifts, ministrations and workings, teach about the Spirit, the Lord and God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The very artificiality of assigning the church's endowments as graces to the Spirit, services to the Lord, and energizings to God reveals the Trinitarian conception all the more strikingly. Paul writes this way not because gifts, ministrations and workings are greatly different things. He writes so because God, the Lord, and the Spirit constantly suggest to his mind a threefold causality behind every manifestation of grace.
sources.quote: But thus there is only the more strikingly revealed the underlying Trinitarian conception as dominating the structure of the clauses
sources.raw_question: Does the seemingly artificial threefold division of spiritual gifts in 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 (gifts, ministrations, workings) undermine its value as evidence for the Trinity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. The apostle ascribes gifts and graces distinctly to the persons as the fountain of their communication. Gifts come from the same Spirit, administrations from the same Lord, Jesus, and operations from the same God, the Father. As the gifts are bestowed distinctly, so they are received distinctly.
sources.quote: ascribes them distinctly, in respect of the fountain of their communication, unto the distinct persons
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 attribute spiritual gifts distinctly to the Spirit, the Lord Jesus, and the Father?

question: Does the Son act of himself and by his own will, or in carrying out the will of the Father?
synthesis: All three deny that the Son acts independently of the Father, but on different grounds. Irenaeus speaks of creation: the Son creates as the Father's hand, so there is no creator other than the one God working through his Word. Hilary appeals to unity of nature, under which the Son truly acts in his own Person yet not of himself, because the Father acts jointly in him. Novatian stresses obedience: the Son does nothing by his own will and, as minister of the Father's will, points to the one God the Father.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XV.—Proofs of the resurrection from Isaiah and Ezekiel; the same God who created us will also raise us up.
sources.answer: The Son creates in carrying out the Father's will. The Lord who formed the blind man's eyes is the one who made the whole man, acting as the Father's hand. There is therefore no other creator and no other Father besides the one God who works through his Word.
sources.quote: For the Lord who formed the visual powers is He who made the whole man, carrying out the will of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son create in his own right, or in carrying out the will of the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Because the unity of Their nature means each One's action implies the joint action of Both. The Son acts not of Himself, since the Father abides in Him and teaches Him. Yet He truly acts Himself, as befits His birth as Son, and so does what is pleasing. Thus the Son acts but not of Himself, while the Father, though not acting separately, is still active, and the unity of nature is kept in Their action.
sources.quote: the unity of Their nature is such, that the several action of Each implies the conjoint action of Both, and Their joint activity a several activity of Each.
sources.raw_question: How can the Son act in His own Person and yet not act of Himself, with the Father acting through Him?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: No. The Son does nothing by his own will or determination and does not come from himself, but obeys all his Father's commands. His birth shows him to be Son, and his obedience even to death shows him the minister of the will of the Father from whom he is. By this obedience he points to the one God the Father.
sources.quote: Moreover, the Son does nothing of His own will, nor does anything of His own determination; nor does He come from Himself, but obeys all His Father’s commands and precepts
sources.raw_question: Does the Son act by his own will independently of the Father?

question: Is Moses, who was made 'a god to Pharaoh,' called God in the same proper sense in which the Son is called God?
synthesis: Irenaeus, Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary agree that Moses' title does not make him God in the proper sense. Their grounds differ. Irenaeus appeals to Scripture's usage: Moses is never properly called Lord or God, only God's faithful servant. Gregory argues that Moses stayed equal in nature with other men and was raised only in authority, so giving the Son the name in that sense would leave him a mere creature. Hilary reads the qualifiers in the texts: 'to Pharaoh' and 'I have said' mark a limited or bestowed title, not a divine nature, and being appointed a god differs from being God.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: No. Moses was indeed given as a god before Pharaoh, but he is not properly termed Lord. Nor do the prophets call him God. The Spirit speaks of him only as the faithful minister and servant of God, which he was.
sources.quote: he is not properly termed Lord, nor is called God by the prophets, but is spoken of by the Spirit as “Moses, the faithful minister and servant of God,”
sources.raw_question: Since Moses was made 'a god to Pharaoh,' is Moses properly called God or Lord in Scripture?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. Moses' being called a god did not lift him beyond humanity; he was equal in nature with his fellows and raised above them only in authority. Granting the Son the name of God in that equivocal sense leaves him merely one of the angels. Such a title only salves over the error rather than confessing true Godhead.
sources.quote: his being called a god did not hinder him from being man. So too in this case Eunomius, while making out the Son to be one of the angels, salves over such an error by the appellation of Godhead
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'God' in the way Moses was called 'a god to Pharaoh' preserve his true deity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Because those titles are qualified or bestowed, while the Son's is not. 'To Pharaoh' limits Moses' title to how he appeared through God's wonders; he did not receive the divine nature. 'I have said' marks a description by favour, not a definition of nature. To be appointed a god is different from being God.
sources.quote: It is one thing to be appointed a god; it is another thing to be God. He was made a god to Pharaoh; he had not that nature and that name wherein God consists.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son called 'god' in a different sense from Moses, who was made 'a god to Pharaoh,' or those addressed 'Ye are gods'?

question: Does the prologue of John's Gospel (John 1:1-18) teach that the Word, Jesus Christ, is God and the Creator of all things?
synthesis: All three authors answer yes. Irenaeus and Bickersteth both rest their case on the text's statements that the Word was with God and was God, that all things were made by Him, and that He became flesh. Irenaeus draws from this that there is one God the Father and one Word through whom all things were made. Bickersteth identifies the Word with Christ by citing John's other use of the title 'the Word of God'. Owen instead stresses why the prologue was written: as an inspired declaration of Christ's eternal Deity meant to refute Cerinthus, which settles the controversy.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Preface
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that John prefixed to his Gospel a plain declaration of the eternal Deity of Christ, and that all authors agree he did so to stop the errors of Cerinthus, who opposed the doctrine of Christ's person and therein of the Trinity. This determination came by infallible inspiration and so settles the controversy for anyone who owns Christ and the Scriptures.
sources.quote: To put a stop unto his abominations, all authors agree that John, writing his Gospel, prefixed unto it that plain declaration of the eternal Deity of Christ which it is prefaced withal.
sources.raw_question: Does the prologue of John's Gospel teach the eternal Deity of Christ, and why was it written?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. John states that the Word was with God and was God, that all things were made by him, and that this Word became flesh. Since the same apostle elsewhere says Christ's name is called the Word of God, it follows that Christ is the Word, Christ is the Creator, Christ is God.
sources.quote: Christ then, is the Word, Christ is the Creator, Christ is God.
sources.raw_question: Does the prologue of John's Gospel (John 1:1-18) teach that the Word, Jesus Christ, is God and the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVIII.—God the Father and His Word have formed all created things (which They use) by Their own power and wisdom, not out of defect or ignorance. The Son of God, who received all power from the Father, would otherwise never have taken flesh upon Him.
sources.answer: Yes. John testifies that the Word was with God and was God, and that all things were made by Him. This plainly shows that there is one God the Father over all and one Word of God through whom all things were made. The same Word was made flesh, the Only-begotten of the Father.
sources.quote: there is one God, the Father over all, and one Word of God, who is through all, by whom all things have been made
sources.raw_question: Does John's Prologue teach that the Word is God and that all things were made through Him?

question: What does Christ mean by saying to the Father 'All mine are thine, and thine are mine' (John 17:10), and does it show the Son's unity with the Father?
synthesis: Basil reads the verse as concerning creation: sovereignty over creatures is conferred on the Son, while the creating Cause comes to Him from the Father, so His creative authority is His own yet derived. Waterland, interpreting Basil, denies that this means a lower, merely delegated power, holding that creative power passes from Father to Son together with the essence, so the Father's creatures are equally the Son's. Hilary does not focus on creation but takes the words as Christ's witness to His eternal abiding in and with the Father as God, grounding the Son's adoration together with the Father.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: 'All mine are thine' expresses that sovereignty over created things was conferred on the Son, and 'thine are mine' that the creating Cause came to Him from the Father. Thus the Son's creative authority is His own yet derived from the Father as source.
sources.quote: “All mine are thine,” as though the sovereignty over created things were conferred on Him, and “Thine are mine,” as though the creating Cause came thence to Him.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean by saying to the Father 'All mine are thine, and thine are mine'?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is the convincing Witness to the faith professed in baptism in the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. His words show Him abiding in the Father, from the Father, and with the Father, for ever God. Hence the Son is to be adored together with the Father.
sources.quote: Father, all Mine are Thine, and Thine are Mine[^1357], even my Lord Jesus Christ, abiding in Thee, and from Thee, and with Thee, for ever God
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'all Mine are Thine, and Thine are Mine' witness to the Son's eternal unity with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No, not in the sense of a lower, merely delegated power. Basil means that the origin of the creatures is referred up to the Father, while the power of creating descends from the Father to the Son together with his essence. Basil thus distinguishes the Son from the creatures and holds that the Father's creatures are the Son's creatures as well.
sources.quote: inasmuch as the power of creating descends “from him to the Son:” that is, with his essence, as Basil explains it a little after.
sources.raw_question: When Christ says 'all mine are thine, and thine are mine', does Basil take this to mean that the Son received a derived creative power, as distinct from the Father's?

question: In what sense is Christ the one Mediator between God and men?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa, Hilary and Augustine all hold that Christ mediates because one and the same Person is both God and man. Gregory argues from the name "Son": it applies to both natures, so by sharing in each he joins in himself what nature had divided. Hilary stresses that, as the One born from God, he is a unique Mediator, active both in the giving of the Law and in taking our body. Augustine adds that his humility heals human pride, the chief obstacle to cleaving to God.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He thus shows the oneness of the Eternal Son with the Father the identity of essence and the community of nature (wherein is a natural inquiry into the production of wine), and that the terms “Son” and “product” in the naming of the Only-Begotten include a like idea of relationship.
sources.answer: The name "Son" applies equally to both his natures, the divine and the human. One and the same Person is Son of God and became Son of Man in the Incarnation. By his communion with each, he links together in himself what were divided by nature.
sources.quote: the same Person is Son of God, and was made, in the Incarnation, Son of Man, that, by His communion with each, He might link together by Himself what were divided by nature
sources.raw_question: How does the name "Son" show Christ to be the mediator between God and man?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: He is Mediator as being both God and Man. He mediated both in the giving of the Law and in taking our body. Being One born from God into God, He is the unique Mediator to whom none other can be likened.
sources.quote: For there is one Mediator between God and Men, Who is both God and Man; Mediator both in giving of the Law and in taking of our body.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is Christ the one Mediator between God and men?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Other Advantages of the Incarnation.
sources.answer: He is a fitting Mediator because he is both God and man. As God he assists men by his divinity, and as man he agrees with men by his weakness. His great humility also confutes and heals human pride, which is the chief hindrance to cleaving to God.
sources.quote: such a Mediator, who both as God assists men by His divinity, and as man agrees with men by His weakness
sources.raw_question: How can Christ be a fitting Mediator between God and men?

question: What does the apostolic benediction of 2 Corinthians 13:14 teach about the Father, Son and Holy Spirit?
synthesis: All three read the benediction as naming the three Persons together, but they draw different points from it. Ambrose uses it to show the Spirit shares one nature and equal dignity with the Father and the Son. Warfield sees it as the natural expression of Paul's habitually trinal thinking, with redemptive blessings assigned to each Person. Owen likewise stresses that grace, love and communion are distributed to Christ, the Father and the Spirit, but he uses this to show that each Person communicates a distinct blessing to the saints.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XII. From the fact that St. Paul has shown that the light of the Godhead which the three apostles worshipped in Christ is in the Trinity, it is made clear that the Spirit also is to be worshipped. It is shown from the words themselves that the Spirit is intended by the apostles. The Godhead of the same Spirit is proved from the fact that He has a temple wherein He dwells not as a priest, but as God: and is worshipped with the Father and the Son; whence is understood the oneness of nature in Them.
sources.answer: Yes. Ambrose cites the Apostle joining the communion of the Holy Spirit with the grace of Christ and the love of God as evidence that the Spirit abides with the Father and the Son in one nature.
sources.quote: Whence, too, the Apostle joined the Communion of the Holy Spirit with the grace of Jesus Christ and the love of God
sources.raw_question: Does the apostolic blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14 associate the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son as equal in divine dignity?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: It shows that Paul habitually thinks of the divine source of redemptive blessings in a trinal fashion. He attaches the three highest redemptive blessings distributively to the three Persons. He could have written "the grace and love and communion of God," but instead he names the Lord Jesus Christ, God, and the Holy Spirit. This is not formal teaching but the natural expression of a Trinitarian consciousness.
sources.quote: He therefore does not say, as he might just as well have said, “The grace and love and communion of God be with you all,” but “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, be with you all.”
sources.raw_question: What does the benediction of 2 Corinthians 13:14 show about Paul's conception of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. In that benediction the communication of spiritual blessings from the several Persons to the saints is exactly distinguished: grace is ascribed to the Lord Jesus Christ, love to God the Father, and communion to the Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: wherein the communication of spiritual blessings from the several persons unto the saints is so exactly distinguished; it is grace that is ascribed to our Lord Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Does the apostolic benediction in 2 Corinthians 13:14 distinguish distinct communications of blessing from each Person of the Trinity?

question: Does Christ's power to lay down his life and take it up again (John 10:18) show that he is God?
synthesis: Athanasius, Hilary and Augustine agree that this power shows something beyond a mere man, but their grounds differ. Athanasius contrasts it with human death, which comes by necessity and against the will, and assigns it to Christ as God while ascribing his troubling to the flesh. Hilary sees Christ declaring himself God and claiming the Resurrection as his own work, yet still referring everything to the Father's command. Augustine grounds the power in the Word's uniting the flesh to himself as one, which made Christ's death voluntary and under his own authority.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Twelfthly, Matthew xxvi. 39; John xii. 27, &c. Arian inferences are against the Regula Fidei, as before. He wept and the like, as man. Other texts prove Him God. God could not fear. He feared because His flesh feared.
sources.answer: Yes. Being troubled was proper to the flesh, but having power to lay down and take up His life at will is no property of men, who die by necessity of nature and against their will. The Lord, immortal yet having mortal flesh, had power as God to separate from the body and take it again.
sources.quote: For man dies, not by his own power, but by necessity of nature and against his will; but the Lord, being Himself immortal, but having a mortal flesh, had power, as God, to become separate from the body and to take it again
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's power to lay down His life and take it again show that He is God and not a mere man?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. By the power to take up his soul again and to raise the temple of his body, Christ declares himself God and claims the Resurrection as his own work. He still refers all to the authority of his Father's command, which keeps the glory directed to the Father.
sources.quote: By the power to take His soul again and to raise the Temple up, He declares Himself God, and the Resurrection His own work: yet He refers all to the authority of His Father’s command.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's power to lay down his life and take it up again prove his divinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: Because the Word of God so united him with the flesh as to make him one. That is why he could say, "I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again." His death was therefore voluntary and under his own authority.
sources.quote: For because He is so commingled [with the flesh] by the Word of God as to be one, He says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again.
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ have the power to lay down his life and take it up again?

question: What does the bowing of every knee at the name of Jesus (Philippians 2:9-11) show about who Christ is: could he be a mere man?
synthesis: All three read the universal bowing as excluding a merely creaturely Christ. Bickersteth and Novatian both argue that worship given to a mere man could not be to the glory of God the Father, so Christ must be God. Novatian adds that creatures existing before man would not be subjected to a man. Gregory of Nyssa frames the point as Christ's sovereignty: the bowing shows that creation recognizes him as the ruler of all, who rules it for its salvation.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. If Jesus were only a man, the passage would describe the universal exaltation of a creature, with every being from archangel to saint adoring a creature's name and a creature's supremacy overshadowing heaven, earth and hell. That could not be to the glory of God the Father. The name above every name therefore belongs properly to Christ as 'God, our Saviour.'
sources.quote: if Jesus were man only, it would prefigure the universal exaltation of a creature.
sources.raw_question: Could the universal bowing of every knee to the name of Jesus in Philippians 2:9-11 be consistent with Jesus being a mere man?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: It shows that Christ is the ruler of all creation. Every knee in heaven, on earth and under the earth would not bow to him unless creation recognized in Christ the one who rules it for its own salvation.
sources.quote: For assuredly every knee would not thus bow, did it not recognize in Christ Him Who rules it for its own salvation.
sources.raw_question: What does the fact that every knee bows at the name of Christ show about his sovereignty?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is in Christ, He Once More Asserts by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. If Christ were not God, every knee would not bend in his name. Nor would every creature, visible and invisible, be subjected to a man, since those creatures existed before man. This worship is said to further the glory of God the Father, which shows that Christ Jesus is Lord and God.
sources.quote: For neither, if Christ were not God, would every knee bend itself in His name, “of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth;”
sources.raw_question: Does the universal bowing of every knee in heaven, on earth and under the earth at Jesus' name prove his divinity?

question: Was Christ's death on the cross voluntary, or was he overpowered or compelled to die?
synthesis: Hippolytus, Augustine and Gregory of Nyssa all hold that Christ's death was voluntary: he laid down his life of himself. Hippolytus and Gregory both appeal to Christ's words about having power to lay down his life and take it again; Hippolytus stresses that as Life itself he could not be mastered by death, and Gregory that he himself separated soul from body in commending his spirit to the Father. Augustine argues instead that the death was not owed, since no sin preceded it, so Christ died because he willed it and rendered that death for us.

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. He laid down his life of himself. Being himself Life, he was not overmastered by death. This is why he could say, "I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again."
sources.quote: because He was not overmastered by death, as being Himself Life, He said this: “I lay it down of myself.”
sources.raw_question: Was Christ overpowered by death when he died on the cross?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: It was voluntary. Christ was not stripped of the flesh by obligation of any authority but stripped Himself; He who was able not to die, if He would not, died because He would. His death was not due, since no sin preceded it, and He rendered it for us.
sources.quote: For He was not stripped of the flesh by obligation of any authority, but He stripped Himself. For doubtless He who was able not to die, if He would not, did die because He would
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's death on the cross voluntary, or was he compelled to die by some authority or necessity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: He brought it about voluntarily. He himself separated his soul from his body, commending his spirit into the Father's hands, since he had power to lay down his life and to take it again.
sources.quote: at His death (which He brought about at His will, Who separated His soul from His Body, Who said to His own Father “Into Thy hands I commend My Spirit,”
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's death something that happened to him against his will, or did he bring it about voluntarily?

question: Is God the author or cause of evil?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa, Irenaeus and Novatian all deny that God is the author of evil, but on different grounds. Gregory argues against Manes that God cannot even be conceived as the fashioner of evil, nor can there be a second First Principle of evil. Irenaeus says that when God lets the wicked act, He only exposes their hearts and tests the righteous, while the evildoer is judged for his own deeds. Novatian locates evil in man's freely willed departure from God and argues that the Perfect One, who judges evil, cannot be its architect.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Proof that the Anomœan teaching tends to Manichæism.
sources.answer: Neither. Gregory says Manes rightly wished to keep evil away from God but erred by positing a separate principle of evil, not seeing that it is impossible even to conceive of God as the fashioner of evil, or of any other First Principle besides Him.
sources.quote: it is impossible even to conceive of God as the fashioner of evil, or on the other hand, of any other First Principle besides Him
sources.raw_question: Can God be the author of evil, or can there be a second First Principle besides God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVIII.—Concerning sacrifices and oblations, and those who truly offer them.
sources.answer: No. God reveals what is hidden in the heart but works no evil. By exposing the inner wish of the wicked, He shows Himself blameless. He gives up the righteous to suffering so that, having been tested, they may at last be accepted. The evildoer is judged and rejected for the actions he himself performed.
sources.quote: that God who reveals what is hidden [in the heart], but who worketh not evil
sources.raw_question: When God allows the wicked, such as Cain or Pilate, to have power over the righteous, is God the author of the evil done?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, He is Good, Always the Same, Immutable, One and Only, Infinite; And His Own Name Can Never Be Declared, and He is Incorruptible and Immortal.
sources.answer: No. Every evil is a departure from God, and he who is called the Perfect, and who avenges and judges every evil work, cannot be the architect of evil. Evil arises in man only through his own willed departure from the good God, not out of necessity. This shows where evil came from, so that God should not seem envious.
sources.quote: evil does not occur to man from any other cause than by his departure from the good God. Moreover, this very thing is specified in man, not because it was necessary, but because he himself so willed it.
sources.raw_question: Is God the author or cause of evil?

question: Does Peter's statement in Acts 2:36 that God 'made' Jesus Lord and Christ mean that the Son's pre-temporal essence was created, or does it refer to the humanity he assumed?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Athanasius agree that 'made' does not refer to the Word's essence and that the Son was eternally Lord. Gregory grounds this mainly in the context: the demonstrative 'this Jesus whom ye crucified', the human name, and the Cross. On that basis he reads 'made' as the transformation of the crucified humanity from lowly to lofty. He adds two further arguments: a parity argument from 'made Him to be sin', and the point that Lordship and Christhood name dignity, not nature. Athanasius also appeals to 'whom ye crucified' and notes that Peter says 'made Lord', not 'made Word'. His distinctive emphasis is that 'made' means the Father's manifesting the Word's Lordship by grace toward us through the incarnation and Cross, said to Jews who took Christ for a mere man.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: No. The context of the passage — the Cross, the human name "Jesus," and the demonstrative "this Jesus whom ye crucified" — shows that Peter speaks of the crucified humanity. What "made" indicates is not the Lord's eternal existence but the change of the lowly into the lofty, effected after the Passion by the right hand of God.
sources.quote: It is not therefore the pre-temporal existence of the Lord which the Apostle indicates by the word “made,” but that change of the lowly to the lofty which was effected “by the right hand of God.”
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's statement in Acts that God "made" Jesus Lord and Christ refer to the pre-temporal existence of the Son, implying the Son is a made thing?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that the whole context points to the Humanity: the Cross, the human name "Jesus," and the phrase "exalted by the right hand of God." God, being the Highest, does not need to be exalted, so it was the lowly human nature that was raised to be Lord and Christ after the Passion. The word "made" refers to this change of the lowly to the lofty, not to the Lord's existence before time.
sources.quote: It is not therefore the pre-temporal existence of the Lord which the Apostle indicates by the word “made,” but that change of the lowly to the lofty which was effected “by the right hand of God.”
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's statement that God "made" Jesus Lord and Christ mean that the Son is a created being in his pre-temporal existence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: No. The Word was Lord by nature eternally; 'made' refers to the Father's manifesting His Lordship in the incarnate Word named Jesus, as if to say 'He made Him to rule and to reign' among men. Peter's words were addressed to Jews who thought the Christ a mere man, to show that the crucified Jesus is Lord and God.
sources.quote: Therefore the Word Himself became flesh, and the Father called His Name Jesus, and so ‘made’ Him Lord and Christ, as much as to say, ‘He made Him to rule and to reign;’
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's statement in Acts 2:36 that God 'made' Jesus both Lord and Christ mean that the Son was created or first became Lord at that point?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: No. The word "made" in these texts refers to the dispensation of the Incarnation, not to the Son's eternal essence. Gregory argues by parity: Paul says God "made Him to be sin for us," and if Eunomius consistently referred "made" to the essence he would have to find sin in the Son's essence, which is manifestly absurd. Since Eunomius must refer "made to be sin" to the dispensation of the last times, the same reasoning requires the other uses of "made" to be read the same way.
sources.quote: But if he shrinks from this by reason of its manifest absurdity, and argues that, by saying, “He made Him to be sin,” the Apostle indicates the dispensation of the last times, let him persuade himself by the same train of reasoning that the word “made” refers to that dispensation in the other passages also.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's use of the word "made" of Christ (Acts 2:36, Hebrews 3:1-2) prove that the Son in his pre-temporal essence is a thing made?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: No. Just as He was made Priest and Apostle for the dispensation, He is said to be made Lord and Christ by the change and transformation of the Human to the Divine; "making" here means "making anew." To apply these words to His pretemporal existence is to wrest words about the dispensation.
sources.quote: so here He is said to have been made Lord and Christ,—the latter for the dispensation on our behalf, the former by the change and transformation of the Human to the Divine (for by “making” the Apostle means “making anew”)
sources.raw_question: When Peter says God "made" Jesus Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36), does "made" refer to the creation of the Son's essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No. Even on Eunomius' own reading, Peter speaks of one who already was God in the beginning becoming Lord and Christ, as David, already a man, was anointed king. Lordship names authority, not being, and 'Christ' indicates kingdom, and the idea of kingdom is distinct from that of nature. So 'made' concerns dignity, not the formation of essence.
sources.quote: For Lordship is not a name of His being but of His being in authority, and the appellation of Christ indicates His kingdom, while the idea of His kingdom is one, and that of His Nature another.
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's statement that God 'made' Jesus Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36) prove that the essence of the Son was created?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No. Peter speaks of 'this Jesus whom ye crucified,' that is, of the man seen in the flesh after the dispensation, not of the Word who existed before the ages. The Jews, the Cross, Pilate and the birth under Augustus all came long after the Word who was God in the beginning, so the 'making' refers to the humanity, not to the divine essence.
sources.quote: so that it is clear from this that Peter is speaking, not of what was before the ages, but of what was after the dispensation.
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's statement in Acts 2:36 that 'God made Him Lord and Christ' prove that the essence of the Only-begotten Son is created?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > He then explains the phrase of S. Peter, “Him God made Lord and Christ.” And herein he sets forth the opposing statement of Eunomius, which he made on account of such phrase against S. Basil, and his lurking revilings and insults.
sources.answer: It refers to the human nature, not to the Word's divine essence. Eunomius argued that Peter must be speaking of the Word who was in the beginning, so the Son was 'made' Lord and Christ in his very essence. Gregory, defending Basil, replies that the subjection and 'making' belong to the Human Nature. They do not belong to what the Only-begotten has from the Father. He also points to the good gifts the Godhead bestowed on the humanity it was joined with.
sources.quote: a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father.
sources.raw_question: When Peter says in Acts 2:36 that God 'made' Jesus 'Lord and Christ', does this refer to the pre-existent essence of God the Word, so that the Word himself was made or promoted, or does it refer to the human nature the Word assumed?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: No. Scripture nowhere says 'God made Himself a Son' or 'the Word is a work'; Peter says God made Him Lord, not made Him Word. The context, 'this Jesus whom ye crucified,' shows that 'made' refers to His manhood, since what was crucified was the body, not the Essence of the Word.
sources.quote: which makes it plain to any one, even, if so be, to them, provided they attend to the context, that not the Essence of the Word, but He according to His manhood is said to have been made.
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's statement in Acts 2:36 that God 'made' Jesus Lord and Christ prove that the Son (the Word) is a created work?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: No. Peter knew Christ to be the Son of the Living God, and by 'made' he meant not the Word's essence but His Kingdom and Lordship formed according to grace and relative to us. The Son was made Lord among us because of His manhood, while He ever was Lord and Sovereign of all as Son.
sources.quote: Peter say this without meaning that the Essence of the Word was a work; for he knew Him to be God’s Son, confessing, ‘Thou art the Christ, the Son of the Living God;’
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's statement in Acts 2:36 that God 'made' Jesus both Lord and Christ imply that the Son is a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: No. The Word was from the beginning uncreatedly Lord, Christ, Word and God from the Father. Peter refers to the Incarnation: the crucified human nature was made, by the overwhelming power of the indwelling Word, to be Christ and Lord. 'Making' names the transmutation of mortal to immortal, servant to Lord, man to Christ.
sources.quote: which calls by the name of “making” the transmutation of the Mortal to the Immortal, of the Servant to the Lord, of Sin to Righteousness, of the Curse to the Blessing, of the Man to Christ
sources.raw_question: When Peter says God 'made' Jesus both Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36), does this mean the eternal Word was made or created?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > He then explains the phrase of S. Peter, “Him God made Lord and Christ.” And herein he sets forth the opposing statement of Eunomius, which he made on account of such phrase against S. Basil, and his lurking revilings and insults.
sources.answer: No. The word 'made' is not to be referred to the Divine Nature of the Only-begotten. It belongs to the 'form of a servant' which came into being through the Incarnation, when he appeared in the flesh. Following Basil, Gregory holds that Peter speaks not of the essence of God the Word who was in the beginning with God, but of him who emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and was crucified through weakness.
sources.quote: it is not pious to refer the word “made” to the Divine Nature of the Only-begotten, but that it is to be referred to that “form of a servant,” which came into being by the Incarnation
sources.raw_question: In Acts 2:36, 'God made him Lord and Christ', does the word 'made' refer to the divine nature and pretemporal generation of the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > He then explains the phrase of S. Peter, “Him God made Lord and Christ.” And herein he sets forth the opposing statement of Eunomius, which he made on account of such phrase against S. Basil, and his lurking revilings and insults.
sources.answer: It shows that Peter is speaking of Christ's humanity, not of the mode of his divine existence. The demonstrative word points to what in him was human and was seen by all, namely the one who was crucified. So the Apostle is using the terms that belong to the Incarnation rather than describing the eternal being of the Word.
sources.quote: he is not setting forth to us the mode of the Divine existence, but is introducing the terms which belong to the Incarnation
sources.raw_question: What does the demonstrative phrase 'this Jesus whom ye crucified' in Acts 2:36 show about whom Peter says God made Lord and Christ?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: To the humanity seen after the Incarnation. Everything in the text agrees on this: the demonstrative "this", the human name Jesus, the charge of blood-guilt against the hearers, and the mention of the Cross. All of these point to Him who was visible to the senses. Gregory adds that the word order ("Whom ye crucified, Him God made") shows Peter is speaking of what followed the dispensation, not of what was before the ages.
sources.quote: When everything, then, is found to concur—the demonstrative word denoting Him Who is spoken of by the Name of His Humanity, the charge against those who were stained with blood-guiltiness, the suffering of the Cross—our thought necessarily turns to that which was apparent to the senses.
sources.raw_question: In Acts 2:36, "God made this Jesus whom ye crucified both Lord and Christ," does Peter refer to the Son's pre-temporal existence or to the humanity seen after the Incarnation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No. "Made" attaches to "Lord" and "Christ", not to "this". So the text says that He, already being whatever He was, was made Lord and Christ. Eunomius himself compares this to David being anointed king without being made a man. Lordship names authority and "Christ" names kingship, not His being or nature.
sources.quote: For Lordship is not a name of His being but of His being in authority, and the appellation of Christ indicates His kingdom, while the idea of His kingdom is one, and that of His Nature another.
sources.raw_question: Even if Acts 2:36 referred to the pre-existent Word, would 'God made Him Lord and Christ' prove that the Son's essence was made?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: No. Peter speaks not of the Son's essence being made but of His Lordship over us, which 'became' when He became man and by the Cross redeemed all and became Lord and King of all. The Word was already everlasting Lord and King before the incarnation, as Scripture attests.
sources.quote: it is very plain again that Peter said not that the Essence of the Son was made, but spoke of His Lordship over us, which ‘became’ when He became man, and, redeeming all by the Cross, became Lord of all and King.
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's statement in Acts 2:36 that God 'made' Jesus Lord and Christ mean that the Son's essence was created or that he began to be Lord only at the incarnation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: It refers to the crucified humanity, not the eternal Word. Peter's demonstrative 'this Jesus whom ye crucified' points to the one his hearers had crucified, and it was the flesh, not the Godhead, that was crucified. So being 'made' Lord and Christ is said of the human nature, which implies no creation of the Word's essence.
sources.quote: That the demonstrative word declares that that person was made Christ, Who had been crucified by the hearers;—for he says, “ye crucified,”
sources.raw_question: In Acts 2:36, when Peter says God made Jesus 'Lord and Christ,' does this refer to the eternal Word who was in the beginning with God, or to the crucified humanity?

question: Does Paul's statement in 1 Corinthians 15:50 that 'flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God' mean that the substance of human flesh is excluded from salvation and resurrection?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Novatian agree that the text does not condemn the substance of the flesh, which God made and which will be raised. Irenaeus reads 'flesh and blood' as flesh without the Spirit, or as carnal works. He argues this from Paul's own list of the works of the flesh, from Paul's use of 'flesh and blood' for Christ, from the need to keep Paul consistent with 'this corruptible must put on incorruption', and from the image of the grafted olive. Novatian instead says the text rebukes the guilt of the rebellious flesh, which is restored to innocence in baptism and death and raised to salvation.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter IX.—Showing how that passage of the apostle which the heretics pervert, should be understood; viz., “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.”
sources.answer: No. The phrase 'flesh and blood' refers to people who lack the Spirit of God. Such people are spiritually dead, as Christ's saying 'Let the dead bury their dead' shows. Flesh that is possessed by the Spirit of the Father is made alive and conformed to the Word of God. So the text excludes only flesh 'in itself', flesh without the Spirit, not the body as such.
sources.quote: Those then, as many as they be, who have not that which saves and forms [us] into life [eternal], shall be, and shall be called, [mere] flesh and blood; for these are they who have not the Spirit of God in themselves.
sources.raised_by_detail: the heretics (Gnostics) who deny the salvation of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement in 1 Corinthians 15:50 that 'flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God' show that the human body, God's handiwork, is not saved?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIV.—Unless the flesh were to be saved, the Word would not have taken upon Him flesh of the same substance as ours: from this it would follow that neither should we have been reconciled by Him.
sources.answer: No. The apostle elsewhere uses "flesh and blood" of Christ Himself, both to establish His human nature and to confirm the salvation of our flesh. Since flesh and blood procure life for us, the saying does not refer to them literally. It refers to the carnal deeds that pervert man to sin and deprive him of life.
sources.quote: inasmuch as the apostle has not pronounced against the very substance of flesh and blood, that it cannot inherit the kingdom of God, the same apostle has everywhere adopted the term “flesh and blood” with regard to the Lord Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God" condemn the very substance of flesh and blood?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIII.—In the dead who were raised by Christ we possess the highest proof of the resurrection; and our hearts are shown to be capable of life eternal, because they can now receive the Spirit of God.
sources.answer: No. The phrase refers to fleshly works, not to the flesh strictly so called. Reading it of the flesh itself makes the apostle contradict himself, since in the same Epistle he says that this corruptible must put on incorruption and this mortal must put on immortality. Death will be truly vanquished only when the flesh it holds down rises from under its dominion.
sources.quote: For thus they will allege that this passage refers to the flesh strictly so called, and not to fleshly works, as I have pointed out, so representing the apostle as contradicting himself.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that 'flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God' exclude the physical flesh from salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIII.—In the dead who were raised by Christ we possess the highest proof of the resurrection; and our hearts are shown to be capable of life eternal, because they can now receive the Spirit of God.
sources.answer: No. Paul plainly teaches elsewhere that this corruptible must put on incorruption, and that Jesus' life will be manifested in our mortal flesh. Reading the saying as a denial would make Paul contradict himself, or force a twisting of all these clear passages. The apostle does not condemn the very substance of flesh and blood. He even uses "flesh and blood" of Christ himself, to affirm Christ's humanity and the salvation of our flesh.
sources.quote: these men must either allege that the apostle expresses opinions contradicting himself, with respect to that statement, “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God;” or, on the other hand, they will be forced to make perverse and crooked interpretations of all the passages
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's saying "Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God" deny the resurrection of the flesh?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XI.—Treats upon the actions of carnal and of spiritual persons; also, that the spiritual cleansing is not to be referred to the substance of our bodies, but to the manner of our former life.
sources.answer: No. Paul himself explains the phrase by listing the 'works of the flesh' (adulteries, fornications, idolatries, heresies and the like). Those who do these things walk after the flesh and cannot live unto God. So 'flesh and blood' refers to a carnal manner of life without the Spirit, not to the body's substance.
sources.quote: Thus does he point out to his hearers in a more explicit manner what it is [he means when he declares], “Flesh and blood shall not inherit the kingdom of God.”
sources.raised_by_detail: unbelievers who pervert the apostle's meaning (Gnostics)
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that 'flesh and blood shall not inherit the kingdom of God' mean that the bodily substance of human beings is excluded from salvation?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That Jesus Christ is the Son of God and Truly Man, as Opposed to the Fancies of Heretics, Who Deny that He Took Upon Him True Flesh.
sources.answer: No. The text does not condemn the substance of the flesh, which God's hands built so that it should not perish. It rebukes only the guilt of the flesh, which rebelled against divine law. In baptism and in death the flesh is restored to innocency and raised to salvation.
sources.quote: it is not the substance of the flesh that is condemned, which was built up by the divine hands that it should not perish, but only the guilt of the flesh is rightly rebuked
sources.raw_question: Does 'flesh and blood do not inherit the kingdom of God' (1 Corinthians 15:50) condemn the substance of the flesh and deny its resurrection?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter X.—By a comparison drawn from the wild olive-tree, whose quality but not whose nature is changed by grafting, he proves more important things; he points out also that man without the Spirit is not capable of bringing forth fruit, or of inheriting the kingdom of God.
sources.answer: No. Paul is not repudiating the substance of flesh but showing that the Spirit must be infused into it. Just as a grafted wild olive keeps the substance of its wood while changing the quality of its fruit, a man grafted in by faith keeps his flesh but becomes a spiritual man; only mere flesh and blood, without the Spirit, cannot inherit the kingdom.
sources.quote: not repudiating [by these words] the substance of flesh, but showing that into it the Spirit must be infused.
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics denying the salvation of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that 'flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God' (1 Cor 15:50) mean that the substance of human flesh is excluded from salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIV.—Unless the flesh were to be saved, the Word would not have taken upon Him flesh of the same substance as ours: from this it would follow that neither should we have been reconciled by Him.
sources.answer: No. Since Scripture says we are saved and given life through the flesh and blood of the Lord, flesh and blood in themselves cannot be what is excluded. Paul's words refer to carnal deeds that pervert man to sin and deprive him of life. This is confirmed by Romans 6, where the same bodily members that once served sin are to become instruments of righteousness and bear fruit unto life.
sources.quote: it has not been declared of flesh and blood, in the literal meaning (proprie) of the terms, that they cannot inherit the kingdom of God; but [these words apply] to those carnal deeds already mentioned
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who deny the salvation of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that 'flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God' mean that the literal human body is excluded from salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter IX.—Showing how that passage of the apostle which the heretics pervert, should be understood; viz., “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.”
sources.answer: No. Strictly speaking, the flesh does not inherit but is inherited: the living Spirit of God takes possession of the flesh and carries it into the kingdom. Paul's words mean that those who live as mere flesh and blood, without the indwelling Word and the Spirit of the Father, cannot inherit the kingdom.
sources.quote: the flesh cannot by itself possess the kingdom of God by inheritance; but it can be taken for an inheritance into the kingdom of God. For a living person inherits the goods of the deceased; and it is one thing to inherit, another to be inherited.
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostic heretics who pervert the passage
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God" mean that the flesh is excluded from salvation?

question: Can the Son be both 'Only-begotten' and 'First-born' without contradiction, and to what does each title refer?
synthesis: Athanasius and Gregory of Nyssa agree that the titles cannot apply in the same respect: 'First-born' implies brethren while 'Only-begotten' excludes them. Both refer 'Only-begotten' to the Son's eternal generation from the Father. Gregory refers 'First-born' to the Incarnation and dispensation, the Word made flesh as first-fruits among many brethren. Athanasius ties it more broadly to the Son's condescension to creation, stamping His image on it as Prototype and root of creation, and he adds that Scripture uses 'Only-begotten' absolutely but always gives creation as the reason for 'First-born'.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He further very appositely expounds the meaning of the term “Only-Begotten,“ and of the term “First born,“ four times used by the Apostle.
sources.answer: No. "First-born" necessarily implies brethren, while "Only-begotten" necessarily excludes the notion of brethren. So whoever refers "first-born" to the Son's eternal existence cannot preserve the proper sense of "Only-begotten." The two titles must therefore refer to different things.
sources.quote: Let the discerning reader consider whether these things agree with one another, when the term “first-born” necessarily implies brethren, and the term “Only-begotten” as necessarily excludes the notion of brethren.
sources.raw_question: Can the title "First-born" be applied to the Son's pre-temporal existence without contradicting the title "Only-begotten"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He further very appositely expounds the meaning of the term “Only-Begotten,“ and of the term “First born,“ four times used by the Apostle.
sources.answer: "Only-begotten" refers to the Son's pre-temporal existence as the Word who was in the beginning. "First-born" refers to his manifestation in the flesh, when the Word was made flesh and became the first-fruits among many brethren. Keeping the two meanings distinct preserves each name's natural significance without confusion.
sources.quote: so that in “Only-begotten” we regard the pre-temporal, and by “the first-born of creation” the manifestation of the pre-temporal in the flesh.
sources.raw_question: To what do the titles "Only-begotten" and "First-born of creation" respectively refer in Christ?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: No. 'First-born' implies brethren, while 'only-begotten' implies there are no other brethren. If the Son were numbered among brethren, he would not be only-begotten. So Eunomius's sense of 'first-born' cannot stand alongside 'only-begotten'.
sources.quote: For “first-born” implies brethren, and “only-begotten” implies that there are no other brethren. Thus the “first-born” is not “only-begotten,”
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be both 'only-begotten' and 'first-born' in the same sense?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: Following Cyril, 'Only-begotten' belongs to the Son by nature, because He alone is from the Father, God from God and Light from Light. 'First-born' is said of Him for our sakes and with reference to creation. It makes Him a kind of immortal root into which the whole creation might be grafted and from which it might grow from the Everlasting. All things were made by Him and are held together in Him.
sources.quote: He is Only-begotten according to nature, as being alone from the Father, God from God, Light kindled from Light; and He is First-born for our sakes
sources.raw_question: How does the Son's title 'Only-begotten' differ from His title 'First-born'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Only in different respects. 'Only-begotten' is used where there are no brethren, while 'First-born' is used because of brethren, so the two terms cannot apply in the same respect. He is Only-begotten because of His generation from the Father. He is First-born because of His condescension to creation and His making the many His brethren.
sources.quote: For the same cannot be both Only-begotten and First-born, except in different relations;—that is, Only-begotten, because of His generation from the Father, as has been said; and First-born, because of His condescension to the creation
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be both 'Only-begotten' and 'First-born' without contradiction?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: 'Only-begotten' takes precedence, because there is no other Word or Wisdom and He alone is true Son of the Father. Scripture says 'Only-begotten' absolutely, with no reason attached, as in 'the Only-begotten Son which is in the bosom of the Father.' 'First-born,' by contrast, always has creation given as its reason.
