Scripture never says 'the first-born of God' or 'the creature of God,' but uses 'Only-begotten,' 'Son,' 'Word' and 'Wisdom' as proper to the Father.
sources.quote: not in connection with any reason, but absolutely it is said of Him, ‘The Only-begotten Son which is in the bosom of the Father;’ but the word ‘First-born’ has again the creation as a reason in connection with it
sources.raw_question: Which title better expresses the Word's own relation to the Father, 'Only-begotten' or 'First-born'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: He is first-born because, by condescending at the creation, he stamped his image and Sonship on creation. He thus became the Archetypal Son and the Prototype of all creation. 'First-born' therefore means the Only-begotten holding first place in creation, the origin of creation, the one Begotten among things made.
sources.quote: He, as it were, stamped His image, His Sonship, upon creation, and became the first-born in the sense of being the Archetypal Son.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Son called 'first-born' if he is the Only-begotten from eternity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then again admirably discusses the term πρωτότοκος as it is four times employed by the Apostle.
sources.answer: No. One who is truly only-begotten has no brethren, so 'first-born' cannot describe his eternal being. Like the pairs God and man, form of God and form of a servant, he is Only-begotten by his supreme nature. He becomes first-born of creation in his dispensation of love toward humanity.
sources.quote: For he who is truly only-begotten has no brethren, for how could any one be only-begotten if numbered among brethren?
sources.raw_question: Can the title 'first-born' apply to the Son in respect of his pre-temporal existence, given that he is called 'Only-begotten'?

question: What does it mean that Christ will 'deliver up the kingdom to God, even the Father' (1 Corinthians 15:24), and does this mean the Son loses or resigns his kingdom?
synthesis: Augustine and Hilary agree that the delivering up is not the Son giving up his rule. They read it as Christ presenting the redeemed, who are themselves the kingdom, to the vision of God. Augustine frames this as the Mediator bringing believers from faith to face-to-face contemplation of the Father, a contemplation that includes the Son himself. He grounds the Son's not being excluded in his being one God with the Father, and he explains that 'until' does not imply the reign ends. Hilary argues from Paul's wording 'the Kingdom' rather than 'his Kingdom': what is handed over are those conformed to the glory of Christ's body.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to God, Even the Father. The Kingdom Having Been Delivered to God, Even the Father, Christ Will Not Then Make Intercession for Us.
sources.answer: It means that Christ will bring believers to the contemplation of God, the end of all good actions, where they find everlasting rest and joy. Mary sitting at the Lord's feet prefigured this, as the 'best part' that shall not be taken away. In that contemplation God will be all in all, because nothing but God himself will be needed for us to be enlightened by and to enjoy.
sources.quote: In that contemplation, therefore, God will be all in all; because nothing else but Himself will be required, but it will be sufficient to be enlightened by and to enjoy Him alone.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that Christ will deliver up the kingdom to God the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The Son delivers the Kingdom not by resigning his power but by handing over to the Father those who, conformed to the glory of his body, have been made the Kingdom. Paul does not say 'his Kingdom' but 'the Kingdom', meaning the redeemed, whom Christ as King presents to the Father so that they may see God.
sources.quote: He shall deliver the Kingdom to God the Father, not in the sense that He resigns His power by the delivering, but that we, being conformed to the glory of His body, shall form the Kingdom of God.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's delivering up the Kingdom to God the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24) mean that the Son resigns or loses his power?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > All are Sometimes Understood in One Person.
sources.answer: No. Just as 'I will manifest myself' includes the Father, so delivering the kingdom to the Father does not exclude the Son. When He brings believers to the contemplation of God the Father, He brings them also to the contemplation of Himself.
sources.quote: when He shall bring believers to the contemplation of God, even the Father, doubtless He will bring them to the contemplation of Himself, who has said, “And I will manifest myself to him.”
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that Christ will deliver up the kingdom to God the Father mean the Son takes the kingdom away from Himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to God, Even the Father. The Kingdom Having Been Delivered to God, Even the Father, Christ Will Not Then Make Intercession for Us.
sources.answer: It means Christ will bring believers, who are his kingdom, from faith to the direct contemplation of God. His faithful ones, redeemed by his blood, are called his kingdom. When he has brought them to sight, he makes them abide in himself where he is equal to the Father. So it describes the completion of his work as Mediator. It does not describe a surrender of his divine rule.
sources.quote: For His faithful ones, whom He has redeemed with His blood, are called His kingdom, for whom He now intercedes; but then, making them to abide in Himself there, where He is equal to the Father, He will no longer pray the Father for them.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that Christ will "deliver up the kingdom to God, even the Father" (1 Corinthians 15:24), and does it imply the Son ceases to reign or is inferior in deity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: No. When he delivers the kingdom to God the Father, the Son is not excluded, because he is one God together with the Father. The word "until" in "He must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet" does not imply his reign ends. It is used as in Psalm 112:8, where the man will not be afraid "until" he sees his desire on his enemies, and he is not afraid afterward either.
sources.quote: He Himself is not excluded; because He is one God together with the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's handing over the kingdom to God the Father mean the kingdom will be taken away from Christ himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: It means that Christ the Mediator will bring the just, over whom he now reigns as they live by faith, to the contemplation of God the Father. It does not mean that the Son ceases to reign or loses the kingdom. The 'delivering up' is the passage of believers from faith to sight, when the Father is manifested to them.
sources.quote: that is, when He shall have brought the just, over whom now, living by faith, the Mediator between God and man, the man Christ Jesus, reigns, to the contemplation of God, even the Father.
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean in 1 Corinthians 15:24 when he says Christ 'shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: No. Christ is not excluded from the God to whom the kingdom is delivered, because he is one God together with the Father. The delivering up does not mean a transfer away from himself.
sources.quote: For when it is said, “He shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father,” He Himself is not excluded; because He is one God together with the Father.
sources.raw_question: When Christ delivers up the kingdom to God the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24), does he thereby lose the kingdom himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: It means that Christ the Mediator, who now reigns over the just as they live by faith, will bring them to the face-to-face contemplation of God the Father. The Father will then be revealed by the Son, as Matthew 11:27 says that no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son reveals him.
sources.quote: the words, “When He shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father,” are as much as to say, When He shall have brought believers to the contemplation of God, even the Father.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that Christ will deliver up the kingdom to God the Father, given that the Father already has the kingdom now?

question: Does the confession 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord' (Deuteronomy 6:4) refer to the Father alone, so as to deny the Godhead of the Son?
synthesis: Augustine and Hilary both deny that the text excludes the Son, but their arguments differ. Augustine reads the 'one Lord our God' as the Trinity itself, the Son and Spirit included. Hilary grants that the one God from whom are all things is meant, but argues that Moses, the same witness, also teaches 'God and God': the Son, through whom creation was made. He adds that the Father's distinctive property is unbegottenness, not sole possession of Godhead.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: No. The text ought not to be understood as if the Son or the Holy Spirit were excepted. The one Lord our God is the Trinity, which can also be called our Father by grace of regeneration.
sources.quote: ought certainly not to be understood as if the Son were excepted, or the Holy Spirit were excepted; which one Lord our God we rightly call also our Father, as regenerating us by His grace.
sources.raw_question: Does 'the Lord our God is one Lord' in Deuteronomy 6:4 refer to the Father alone, excluding the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The unity of God is not doubted by any believer, but it offers no ground for denying the Son's Godhead. Moses' command was given to a people prone to idols, and is true because God from Whom are all things is One; yet the same Moses also confesses that He through Whom are all things is God.
sources.quote: Yet this fact of the Unity of God offers no chance for denying the Divinity of His Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the confession that God is One (Deuteronomy 6:4) rule out the divinity of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Moses, who proclaimed the unity of God, is himself the authority for confessing the Godhead of the Son, and the Gospels confirm both. So the revelation to Israel of one God gives no sanction to denying the Son's Divinity.
sources.quote: proving that the revelation to Israel of the unity of God gives no sanction to the refusal of Divinity to the Son of God; since he who is our authority for asserting that there is One God is our authority also for confessing the Godhead of His Son
sources.raw_question: Does the confession that God is One (Deuteronomy 6:4) imply that the Son of God is not God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. Hilary treats the attempt to praise the Godhead of the Father only, so as to deprive the Son of divinity, as a fraudulent confusion of issues and texts. To make the Father the solitary possessor of divine attributes would strip the Son of everything divine, which is impious. The Father's peculiar property is unbegottenness, not exclusive possession of Godhead.
sources.quote: Who can fail to observe that these statements are full of fraud and fallacy? Cleverly as issues have been confused and texts combined, malice and folly is the character indelibly imprinted upon this laborious effort of cunning and clumsiness.
sources.raw_question: Does the declaration 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is One' prove that only the Father is God and deny the Godhead of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. Moses, who spoke this text, also proclaimed the Son as God at the very foundation of the world, in the God through whom creation was made. The texts "All things were made through Him" and "one Jesus Christ through Whom are all things" confirm that "God made" refers to the Son.
sources.quote: you will cease to regard that text, Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is One, as a refusal of Divinity to the Son of God, since at the very foundation of the world He Who spoke it proclaimed that His Son also is God.
sources.raw_question: Does "Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is One" deny the Godhead of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. Hilary grants that it is true there is one God from whom are all things. But this truth gives no excuse for denying the Son's Godhead. Throughout his writings Moses clearly shows the existence of "God and God," that is, God co-ordinate with God.
sources.quote: this truth is no excuse for denying the Godhead of the Son, since Moses throughout the course of his writings clearly indicates the existence of God and God
sources.raw_question: Does the teaching of Moses that there is one God require denying the Godhead of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. It is true that there is One God from Whom are all things. But this is no excuse for denying the Son's Godhead, because Moses throughout his writings clearly indicates the existence of God and God.
sources.quote: this truth is no excuse for denying the Godhead of the Son, since Moses throughout the course of his writings clearly indicates the existence of God and God.
sources.raw_question: Does the truth that there is one God from Whom are all things justify denying the Godhead of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. Hilary argues that whenever Moses confesses that God is One he never fails also to teach the Son's divinity. The heretics' use of the unity text against the Son is therefore a blasphemy that defies the clear warning of their own witness.
sources.quote: The heretics imagine that they can use his assertion of the Unity of God in disproof of the Divinity of God the Son; a blasphemy in defiance of the clear warning of their own witness
sources.raw_question: Does Moses' confession that God is One ("Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is One") disprove the divinity of God the Son?

question: Is the Son of God of the same divine nature as the Father, or of a different and lesser nature, given that he is born of the Father?
synthesis: Jonathan Edwards and Hilary of Poitiers agree that the Son is the very same divine nature as the Father, not a lesser or alien being, but they argue from different grounds. Edwards grounds the Son's full deity in his being God's perfect, substantial idea of Himself. Hilary argues that a true birth can only transmit the begetter's own nature, so being born of God rules out an inferior or creaturely nature, and he also appeals to Scripture calling the Son full of grace and truth. Hilary adds that the birth implies a secondary position as to origin but no inequality of nature or separation from the Father.

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: The Son is the very same divine nature. The Person begotten by God's perfect idea of Himself is another infinite, eternal, almighty and most holy Person, yet the same God. He is the eternal, necessary, perfect, substantial and personal idea which God has of Himself.
sources.quote: Hereby there is another person begotten, there is another Infinite Eternal Almighty and most holy and the same God, the very same Divine nature.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God the same divine nature as the Father, or a different and lesser being?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Universal reason rejects that a being can become different in nature by birth from the being that begets it; even hybrid animals only receive qualities already present in their parents. Since begetting is a function of the true nature of the one who transmits life, the birth of the Only-begotten from God cannot produce an inferior nature.
sources.quote: is it not a form of madness to assert that the birth of God the Only-begotten was the birth from God of a nature inferior to Himself? For the giving of birth is a function of the true nature of the transmitter of life
sources.raw_question: Can the Son of God, by being born from God, have a nature different from or inferior to the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: He shares the same Divinity. Hilary undertakes to show from the Evangelists and Apostles that the Son is not of an alien nature from the Father. The Son possesses the same Godhead, and he has a distinct existence because he was truly born.
sources.quote: true God, the Son of God, is not of a different, an alien nature from that of the Father, but possesses the same Divinity while having a distinct existence through a true birth
sources.raised_by_detail: the Arian confession sent to Alexander
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God of a different nature from the Father, or does he share the same Divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Birth cannot confer on the offspring any nature other than that of the parent it is born from. Therefore the Son, being truly born of God, has the same divine nature as the Father. This refutes the Arian claim that He is a creature who merely excels other creatures.
sources.quote: For birth cannot confer any nature upon the offspring other than that of the parent from whom that offspring is born.
sources.raw_question: Can a true birth from God give the Son a nature different from the Father's, such as that of an excellent creature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. His birth is not after anything but before all things, so it only testifies that the Father is the Source of His being. It does not predicate any incongruity between the offspring and the Source. It implies a secondary position as to origin, yet the Son cannot be separated from the Father.
sources.quote: birth, moreover, not after anything, but before all things, so that birth only bears witness to a Source of being, and does not predicate any incongruity between the offspring and the Source of being.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from the Father imply any inequality or incongruity of nature between the Son and the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. In relation to God there are only two modes of being, birth and eternity. The Son's birth is before all things, not after anything. It only bears witness to a Source of being and implies no incongruity between the offspring and the Source. Because it is from God, it implies a secondary position with respect to the Source, yet the Son cannot be separated from that Source.
sources.quote: birth, moreover, not after anything, but before all things, so that birth only bears witness to a Source of being, and does not predicate any incongruity between the offspring and the Source of being.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from God imply any inequality of nature between the Son and the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary refused to attribute a difference of nature to the God who is of God, because Scripture says He is full of grace and truth. The Only-begotten from the Father possesses the Father's divine nature fully.
sources.quote: nor did it fall into the error of attributing a difference of nature to this God of God, for it learnt that He is full of grace and truth
sources.raw_question: Is the Son, as God of God, different in nature from the Father?

question: Does Christ's saying "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30) assert a unity of divine nature or essence between the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Hilary and Augustine agree that the text asserts one nature or essence, but they argue differently. Hilary relies on the Jews' reaction, who took up stones because He made Himself God, on Christ's appeal to His Sonship and birth, and on the Apostle's interpretation, and he rejects readings that reduce it to a concord of wills. Augustine argues that 'one' said without qualification signifies the same essence, and that the Persons are one by essence, not by relation, since by relation one is Father and the other Son.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. Hilary holds that these words reveal the saving mystery of one and the same nature in the Father and the Son. The Jews understood them as a claim to Godhead: they took up stones at these words and accused Him of making Himself God. To deny that the words assert one nature in Both is to repeat the Jews' unbelief.
sources.quote: you deny that His words, I and the Father are One, contain the assertion of one and the same nature in Both.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement 'I and the Father are One' assert that the Father and the Son share one and the same divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It means unity of nature, not a solitary single Being. Hilary argues that the Apostle himself interprets the saying this way. The Father and Son are distinct, yet one Spirit and one nature.
sources.quote: Now the Apostle asserts that those words in the Gospel, I and the Father are one, imply unity of nature and not a solitary single Being
sources.raw_question: Does "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30) mean a single solitary Person or a unity of nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. The Jews understood the words as a claim to be God, and Christ's answer defends exactly that claim by appealing to His Sonship and to His doing the Father's works. So the words were spoken with regard to the nature He has by birth. He thereby professes Himself Son of God first in name, then in nature, and lastly by birth.
sources.quote: There remains, I conceive, no possibility of doubt but that the words, I and the Father are One, were spoken with regard to the nature which is His by birth.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement 'I and the Father are One' (John 10:30) refer to a unity of nature that the Son has by birth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. The words are so precise that only lethargy or sophistry could obscure them; they reveal the Son's Godhead and his unity of nature with the Father. Those who have the Gospels as their only source of knowledge about God should draw faith, not just knowledge, from this statement.
sources.quote: What lethargy can blunt so utterly the edge of our understanding as to render so precise a statement for one moment obscure to us?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30) teach that the Son has the divine nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > What is Said of the Father and Son Together, and What Not.
sources.answer: A unity of essence. "We are one" means that what the Father is, the Son is also. They are one according to essence, not according to relation, since in relation one is Father and the other Son.
sources.quote: For “we are one” means, what He is, that am I also; according to essence, not according to relation.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "I and my Father are one" (John 10:30) express a unity of essence or of relation?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > That the Unity of the Essence of the Father and the Son is to Be Gathered from the Words, ‘We are One.’ The Son is Equal to the Father Both in Wisdom and in All Other Things.
sources.answer: Yes. When things are simply called 'one' without adding in what respect they are one, the same essence and nature is signified, not differing or disagreeing. Since Christ says 'we are one' without qualification, the Father and the Son are one according to unity of substance, so that there is one God, one great, one wise.
sources.quote: When, therefore, anything is so called one, that it is not added in what it is one, and yet more things than one are called one, then the same essence and nature is signified, not differing nor disagreeing.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement 'I and my Father are one' signify a unity of essence between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Hilary holds that the heretics pervert the text by reducing it to a concord of wills, when it teaches unity of essence. He refutes them even from the very passages they cite as examples of mere moral unity, showing that those unities themselves rest on a shared nature rather than on agreement alone.
sources.quote: For the words of Christ, I and the Father are one, they endeavour to refer to a mere concord of unanimity, so that there may be in them a unity of will not of nature
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "I and the Father are one" mean only a unity of will or agreement between the Father and the Son, rather than a unity of nature?

question: Should objections from reason against the Trinity outweigh the testimony of Scripture and lead to rejecting the doctrine?
synthesis: Owen and Waterland agree that rational objections cannot override revelation. Owen distinguishes the true reason of things, which revelation never contradicts, from the weak reason of particular men, and dismisses the objections as trifling sophisms. Waterland adds the argument from tradition: the Church long ago weighed these old heretical objections and found them too slight. He also holds that our ignorance of God's nature makes such objections mere presumptions resting on the false principle that human understanding measures all truth.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Owen calls such objections a few poor, trifling sophisms, whose terms are scarcely understood by most who repeat them. They cannot be set against the many testimonies of the Holy Ghost. Those who know Scripture and submit to God's word in conscience could never have their faith shaken by them.
sources.quote: Shall a few poor trifling sophisms, whose terms are scarcely understood by the most that amongst us make use of them, according as they have found them framed by others, be thought meet to be set up in opposition unto these multiplied testimonies of the Holy Ghost
sources.raw_question: Should philosophical or logical objections against the Trinity outweigh the plain testimonies of Scripture to the deity of Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Nothing contrary to reason in the absolute sense, the true reason of things, is to be admitted. But reason as it exists in particular men is weak, maimed and imperfect, and is no measure of the nature of all things. Even the least intimation of a truth by divine revelation should be embraced, even if it seems contrary to such human reasoning.
sources.quote: So that though we will not admit of any thing that is contrary to reason, yet the least intimation of a truth by divine revelation will make me embrace it, although it should be contrary to the reason of all the Socinians in the world.
sources.raw_question: Should the doctrine of the Trinity be rejected because it is said to be contrary to reason?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. These objections are old and were raised long ago by heathens and by heretics such as Praxeas, Noetus, Sabellius and Arius. The Catholic Church knew them and weighed them carefully. It judged them far too slight to stand against the combined force of Scripture and tradition.
sources.quote: The Catholics were sensible of them: but having well considered them, they found them of much too slight moment, to bear up against the united force of Scripture and tradition.
sources.raw_question: Should the alleged contradictions in the doctrine of the Trinity outweigh the evidence of Scripture and tradition for it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Reason in the abstract, the true reason of things, is never contradicted by revealed truth, but reason as it exists in particular men is weak, maimed and imperfect and cannot be the measure of all things. Therefore even the least intimation of a truth by divine revelation should be embraced, though it seem contrary to the reason of all the Socinians, and men's apparent reasonings carry no weight against the express and multiplied testimonies of Scripture.
sources.quote: the least intimation of a truth by divine revelation will make me embrace it, although it should be contrary to the reason of all the Socinians in the world
sources.raw_question: Should the doctrine of the Trinity be rejected because it seems contrary to human reason, as the Socinians claim?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Such metaphysics are only presumptions about the nature of a thing of which we know little. Scripture and antiquity are the best guides in these searches. Where Catholics went further in explanation, they did so chiefly to answer those who would not rest content with the general truth Scripture lays down.
sources.quote: to play their metaphysics (that is, their presumptions about the nature of a thing whereof they know little) against Scripture and antiquity, the best guides in those searches
sources.raw_question: Should reasonings about the nature of God be allowed to override the testimony of Scripture concerning the Trinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. We cannot judge what may or may not be in the mode of God's existence as we judge ordinary matters within our capacity. Many things about God's incomprehensible nature may be true though we cannot conceive how, and apparent inconsistencies may arise only from our ignorance. Such objections finally rest on the false principle that human understanding is the measure of all truth, which cannot outweigh a doctrine supported by Scripture and antiquity.
sources.quote: many things, especially those relating to the incomprehensible nature of God, may be true, though we cannot conceive how; and it may be only our ignorance, which occasions some appearing inconsistencies
sources.raw_question: Can objections from natural reason against the doctrine of the Trinity justify rejecting it?

question: Does Psalm 45:7, 'Wherefore God hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows', mean that the Son became God or King, or was promoted, as a reward for virtue?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary agree that the anointing did not make the Son God or King and was not a promotion of the Word. Athanasius argues that he was already eternally God and King and was anointed with the Spirit as man for our sakes; on his reading 'wherefore' gives the reason he came down, not a reward. Hilary argues that a reward presupposes an already existing subject, so it cannot be the origin of his Godhead, and that the anointing sanctified the manhood he assumed, though Hilary allows that it came in time as a reward.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: No. He was God before and held the Kingdom eternally as God's Image. Israel's kings, such as David, Hezekiah and Josiah, became kings only when anointed. The Saviour was already God, ruling in the Father's Kingdom and Himself the giver of the Holy Spirit. He is said to be anointed as man, for our sake, so that He might provide us with exaltation, resurrection and the indwelling of the Spirit.
sources.quote: not that He may become God, for He was so even before; nor that He may become King, for He had the Kingdom eternally, existing as God’s Image
sources.raw_question: Does the statement in Psalm 45 that God 'anointed' the Son mean that the Son became God or King through the anointing, as a reward?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. A reward presupposes someone already existing who can earn it, so the anointing cannot be the origin of His Godhead. Making it so would mean He advanced gradually to divinity and was conditioned, though He is the final cause of all conditions and is before all things. He was born God, God by origin, one in kind with the Father because begotten of Him, and not deified for any cause.
sources.quote: The Lord Jesus Christ was not deified because of anything, or by means of anything, but was born God: God by origin, not promoted to divinity for any cause after His birth, but as the Son; and one in kind with God because begotten of Him.
sources.raw_question: Does the anointing of Christ 'above His fellows' as a reward for loving righteousness (Psalm 45:7) mean that the Son was promoted to divinity rather than born God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: No. The argument would have some faint plausibility only if he had not been God and later became God, or had not been King and was later raised to the Kingdom. But he is God, and his throne is everlasting. God cannot advance, and nothing was lacking to the one sitting on his Father's throne. The 'oil of gladness' is the Spirit, given to him when he came in the flesh.
sources.quote: But if He is God and the throne of His kingdom is everlasting, in what way could God advance? or what was there wanting to Him who was sitting on His Father’s throne?
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 45:7 ('anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows') teach that Christ became God or King as a reward for virtue?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: No. 'Wherefore' gives the reason he came down to us and was anointed for our sakes, not a reward. The sense is: since you are God and King, you were anointed, because none but you could unite man to the Holy Ghost. He is the Image of the Father, and the Spirit is his.
sources.quote: the word ‘wherefore’ does not imply reward of virtue or conduct in the Word, but the reason why He came down to us, and of the Spirit’s anointing which took place in Him for our sakes.
sources.raw_question: In Psalm 45:7, does the word 'wherefore' ('Wherefore God hath anointed thee') imply that the Word was anointed as a reward for his virtue?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The anointing did not exalt the incorruptible Begotten, who abides in the nature of God. It sanctified the manhood He assumed, so that the regeneration of flesh might be accomplished. The Word, being Himself the Spirit and power of God, had no need to be anointed with them. The anointing came in time, as a reward, so it cannot be the cause of His divine birth.
sources.quote: That anointing did not exalt the blessed and incorruptible Begotten Who abides in the nature of God, but it established the mystery of His body, and sanctified the manhood which He assumed.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 45:7, 'Thy God, O God, hath anointed Thee', mean that the divine Son was exalted or promoted by the anointing?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: No. 'Wherefore' does not signify a reward of virtue or conduct in the Word but the reason why He came down to us and why the Spirit's anointing took place in Him for our sakes. The Psalm does not say He was anointed in order to become God, King, Son or Word, for He was these before and for ever; rather, because He is God and King, He was anointed.
sources.quote: the word ‘wherefore’ does not imply reward of virtue or conduct in the Word, but the reason why He came down to us, and of the Spirit’s anointing which took place in Him for our sakes
sources.raw_question: Does the word 'wherefore' in Psalm 45:7 ('Wherefore God, even Thy God, hath anointed Thee') imply that the Word was anointed as a reward for virtue?

question: Do God's holiness and justice as supreme Judge necessarily require that sin be punished, so that God could not pardon sin without satisfaction?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It was necessary, because God's holiness and righteousness require that sin be punished. Owen holds that those who ground satisfaction merely in God's free decree leave no indispensable foundation for Christ's death. God's not sparing his only Son, and admitting no atonement except in his blood, shows that punishing sin is necessary to him.
sources.quote: God, in that he spared not his only Son, but made his soul an offering for sin, and would admit of no atonement but in his blood, hath abundantly manifested that it is of necessity to him (his holiness and righteousness requiring it) to render indignation, wrath, tribulation, and anguish unto sin.
sources.raw_question: Was the satisfaction made by Christ's death absolutely necessary for the forgiveness of sinners, or did it rest only on a free determination of God's will?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No, it does not make him weaker. God cannot do many things men can do, not from imperfection but because of his perfection: he cannot lie, deny himself, or change. To pardon sin without satisfaction, for one who is absolutely holy, righteous, true and faithful, the supreme Governor and author of the law with its threatened punishment, would be to deny himself.
sources.quote: God cannot do many things that men can do, — not that he is more imperfect than they, but he cannot do them on the account of his perfection. He cannot lie, he cannot deny himself, he cannot change
sources.raw_question: If God can freely pardon sin, why does he not pardon it without any satisfaction, and does his inability to do so make him weaker than a man who can forgive without satisfaction?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Opponents grant that it would not become the holy God to pardon impenitent sinners. By the same reasoning we should believe God's own frequent declarations that he would not remit sin without fulfilling his law and satisfying his justice.
sources.quote: let not these persons be offended if we believe him when he so frequently declares it, that it was so to remit sin, without the fulfilling of his law and satisfaction of his justice.
sources.raw_question: If it is contrary to God's holiness to pardon sinners without faith and repentance, does it follow that it is also contrary to his holiness to remit sin without satisfaction of his justice?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Because God is righteous and holy as supreme Judge, it is necessary that he do right in punishing sin. Without this the order of creation could not be preserved. Sin is the creature withdrawing itself from its dependence on and obedience to the Creator, and unless it is brought back into order by punishment, confusion would come upon the whole creation.
sources.quote: For sin being the creature’s deduction of itself from the order of its dependence upon, and obedience unto, the Creator and supreme Lord of all, without a reduction of it by punishment, confusion would be brought into the whole creation.
sources.raw_question: Is it necessary that God, as righteous Judge, punish sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that God's justice and holiness as judge of all the world require that sin be punished. He grounds this in texts declaring that God will by no means clear the guilty, cannot look upon iniquity, and that it is a righteous thing for him to take vengeance, since otherwise he could not judge the world.
sources.quote: That the justice and holiness of God, as he is the supreme governor and judge of all the world, require that sin be punished
sources.raw_question: Do God's justice and holiness, as supreme governor and judge of the world, require that sin be punished?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: To the Reader
sources.answer: Yes, God's holiness and justice indispensably require that sin be punished. For sin to go absolutely unpunished would be repugnant to the holy properties of God's nature. Owen holds that Scripture fully confirms this principle and that the best defenders of Christ's satisfaction against the Socinians have kept to it. He sides with those who blamed schoolmen such as Aquinas, Durandus and Biel for allowing that God could pardon without satisfaction, since that concession opens the way to the Socinian error and leaves the truth indefensible.
sources.quote: the essential holiness of God with his justice or righteousness, as the supreme governor of all, did indispensably require that sin should not absolutely go unpunished; and that it should do so, stands in a repugnancy to those holy properties of his nature
sources.raw_question: Do God's essential holiness and justice, as supreme governor of all, indispensably require that sin not go unpunished, or could God pardon sin without any satisfaction?

question: Does the word 'God' (Theos, Theotes) properly signify the divine substance or nature, or something else such as dominion or one of God's operations?
synthesis: Waterland denies that 'God' is a merely relative term of dominion. He argues from Scripture that dominion is a secondary notion following from the divine perfections, so whoever is called God for dominion alone is so called only figuratively. He argues from Catholic antiquity that the Fathers took Theos and Theotes to signify the divine substance, which is why they grounded the unity of the Godhead in unity of substance. Gregory of Nyssa differs sharply on the substance point: deriving Theos from 'to see', he holds that the word names one of God's operations, His all-seeing oversight, and does not grasp His substance at all.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. Dominion is only a part of the idea of God in Scripture, and a small part at that. Whoever is called God merely on account of dominion is called so by figure and resemblance, not properly. A man who lives free and independent may be called a king in some respect, yet he is not properly a king.
sources.quote: I maintain that dominion is not the full import of the word God in Seripture ; that it is but a part of the idea, and a small part too; and that, if any person be called God, merely on account
sources.raw_question: Is the proper Scripture meaning of the word "God" a relative term of dominion, so that anyone having dominion is truly and properly God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It names an operation. Gregory derives Theos from theasthai, 'to see', because faith teaches that the Deity is everywhere and sees all things. The Psalms' cries 'Attend', 'Look' and 'God knoweth the secrets of the heart' show this meaning. The word therefore teaches one sectional operation of God and does not grasp His substance.
sources.quote: We are taught, then, by this word one sectional operation of the Divine Being, though we do not grasp in thought by means of it His substance itself
sources.raw_question: Does the word 'God' (Theos) name the divine substance, or one of God's operations?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: Substance. The Fathers believed God to be a word denoting substance, not dominion only, and one Divinity (Theotes) meant one divine substance. Hence they necessarily resolved the unity of Godhead into unity of substance rather than of rule.
sources.quote: they believed God to be a word denoting substance, not dominion only; and one Divinity, Θεότης, was with them the same thing as one Divine substance.
sources.raw_question: Does the word 'God' (Theos, Theotes, Divinitas) in the early Fathers denote dominion or substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. Dominion is only a secondary notion that follows from the primary divine perfections: infinite wisdom, invincible power, all-sufficiency and the like. Even then, only supreme dominion fits the Scripture notion of God. Scripture shows this when it rebukes the prince of Tyre and the Lycaonians. It tells them they are not God because their nature is weak and mortal, not because their dominion is small.
sources.quote: These are the ground and foundation of dominion ; which is but a secondary notion, a consequence of the former: and it must be dominion supreme, and none else, which will suit with the Seripture notion of God.
sources.raw_question: Is dominion the essential content of the Scripture notion of God, so that a being with dominion is properly God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Treating 'God' as a merely relative word for dominion is directly contrary to all Catholic antiquity, with very few exceptions. The ancients took the word to signify the divine substance.
sources.quote: That God is a relative word, θεὸς and θεότης signifying not substance, but dominion and authority. This is directly * contrary to all Catholic antiquity, a very few instances excepted.
sources.raw_question: Does the word 'God' (theos, theotes) signify dominion and authority rather than substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. With very few exceptions, all Catholic antiquity used θεότης for the divine nature, just as ἀνθρωπότης was used for human nature. Strictly, τὸ θεῖον and θεότης differ roughly as concrete and abstract, but θεότης still refers to nature and substance, as Θεός generally does, and not to dominion.
sources.quote: but still θεότης refers to nature and substance, (as Θεὸς also generally does,) not dominion
sources.raw_question: Does the word 'God' (θεός, θεότης) signify a relation of dominion and authority rather than substance or nature?

question: How can Christ say in John 3:13 that the Son of man came down from heaven and 'is in heaven' while speaking on earth, and does this show his divine immensity and pre-existence?
synthesis: Owen and Hilary agree that 'is in heaven' refers to Christ's divine nature, which stayed in heaven and is present everywhere while he was on earth in the flesh. Owen argues from God's own claim to fill heaven and earth (Jer. 23:24) to prove divine immensity and pre-existence, and rejects the Socinian reading of mere heavenly meditation. Hilary grounds it in the Word never ceasing to be the Word when made flesh. In one passage he also stresses that the manner is a mystery beyond reason that we can affirm but not explain.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Being in heaven, that is with God, while on earth shows the immensity of his nature, matching God's claim to fill heaven and earth (Jer. 23:24). It also shows his distinction as a person. His coming down from heaven before he was incarnate shows his pre-existence. The Socinian claim that he was there only by heavenly meditation, or was taken up to heaven in his human nature, is an evasion.
sources.quote: whereby he declares the immensity of his nature, and the distinction of his person; and his coming down from heaven before he was incarnate on the earth, declaring his pre-existence
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that the Son of man 'is in heaven' while speaking on earth (John 3:13) show his divine immensity and his pre-existence?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Christ affirms that he was in heaven, with God, at the same time he was on earth, which matches God's own description of his immensity in filling heaven and earth. His coming down from heaven before his incarnation declares his pre-existence. Both together show what John means by saying the Word was 'in the beginning with God.'
sources.quote: whereby he declares the immensity of his nature, and the distinction of his person; and his coming down from heaven before he was incarnate on the earth, declaring his pre-existence
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement in John 3:13 that the Son of man came down from heaven and 'is in heaven' while speaking on earth prove his divine immensity and pre-existence?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. The words 'which is in heaven' answer to God's own description of his immensity: 'Do not I fill heaven and earth?' They therefore express Christ's real divine presence everywhere, not a mental elevation that any man might share.
sources.quote: “The Son of man which is in heaven,” answerable to the description of God’s immensity, “Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the Lord,” Jer. xxiii. 24
sources.raw_question: Can Christ's being 'in heaven' while on earth (John 3:13) be understood as being there merely by heavenly meditation, as any man might be?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: These texts show that the person of Christ came down from heaven by taking on human nature, and went back up to heaven in that nature. As to his divine nature, he was still in heaven while he was on earth in the flesh he had assumed.
sources.quote: to have been in heaven as to his divine nature, when he was on the earth in the flesh that he had assumed
sources.raw_question: How can Christ be said to have come down from heaven and to be in heaven while he was on earth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: 'Descended from heaven' refers to his body's origin from the Spirit, 'Son of Man' to the flesh born of the Virgin, and 'Who is in heaven' to his infinite eternal nature, which could not be confined to the body. Because the Word made flesh never ceased to be the Word, as Word he remained in heaven and present everywhere as Lord of all while as flesh he was Son of Man.
sources.quote: So He descended from heaven and is the Son of Man, yet is in heaven: for the Word made flesh did not cease to be the Word. As the Word, He is in heaven, as flesh He is the Son of Man.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ say in John 3:13 that the Son of Man descended from heaven and yet is in heaven?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: It is a true mystery beyond reason, not a contradiction to be dissolved by the laws of bodies. Because the Word became flesh, God became Man, so that the Man is in heaven and the God is from heaven; He descends and yet does not descend. We can perceive that it is so, and know Christ thus, but cannot explain the manner, and seeking to comprehend further loses Him altogether.
sources.quote: The Word becomes flesh, that is, God becomes Man: the Man is in heaven: the God is from heaven. He ascends Who descended: but He descends and yet does not descend.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ, the Son of Man, be said both to descend from heaven and to remain in heaven at the same time?

question: Does Christ's sorrow in Gethsemane and his prayer that the cup pass from him show that he feared his own suffering and sought to escape it?
synthesis: Both authors deny that the prayer shows the divine Son shrinking from his Passion, but on different grounds. Hilary of Poitiers holds that Christ did not fear death at all: he desired to drink the cup, and his sorrow and prayer were for his disciples' preservation, with 'pass away' meaning the cup's ending through its completion. Athanasius instead grants real fear but assigns it to Christ's flesh, while the willing to suffer belonged to him as God, both being said by the one Person.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Christ Himself said 'the cup which My Father hath given Me, shall I not drink it?' and was hastening to fulfil the Divine Plan. It is inconsistent to say He shrank from the suffering He desired, and the opponents themselves allow that He suffered willingly.
sources.quote: Could fear induce Him to pray for the removal from Him of that which, in His zeal for the Divine Plan, He was hastening to fulfil? To say He shrank from the suffering He desired is not consistent.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer 'remove this cup from Me' show that He prayed to escape suffering out of fear?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. His prayer was not for Himself but for His Apostles, whom He commended to the Father to preserve during His Passion. He bade them pray lest they be tempted, could have summoned legions of angels, and did not fear death; His fear and prayer were on our account, as John's prayer 'Holy Father, keep them in Thy Name' shows.
sources.quote: That prayer was not for Himself but for His Apostles; nor was He sorrowful for Himself, since He bids them pray that they be not tempted; nor is the angel sent to Him
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's sorrow and prayer in Gethsemane for Himself, out of fear of His own death?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. 'To pass away' means not merely to leave a place but to cease to exist, as in 'Heaven and earth shall pass away' and 'the old things are passed away.' The cup could only pass away by being drunk, so He prays for the ending of the Passion's offence through its completion, and for the disciples' preservation.
sources.quote: Again, He does not pray that the cup may pass over Himself, but that it may pass away from Himself, though before it could pass away He must have drunk it.
sources.raw_question: When Christ prays that the cup may pass from Him, does He ask to be spared from suffering?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Twelfthly, Matthew xxvi. 39; John xii. 27, &c. Arian inferences are against the Regula Fidei, as before. He wept and the like, as man. Other texts prove Him God. God could not fear. He feared because His flesh feared.
sources.answer: No. The terror belonged to the flesh, while the willing was His own as God, for He came for that very purpose. Both were said by the same Person, showing He was God willing in Himself, yet as man having a flesh that feared; and He rebuked Peter for wishing to avert His suffering.
sources.quote: For He willed what He deprecated, for therefore had He come; but His was the willing (for for it He came), but the terror belonged to the flesh.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer that the cup might pass show that the Godhead of the Word was in terror?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Christ was sorrowful and prayed not for himself but for his disciples, whom he exhorted to watch and pray lest they enter into temptation. Though they promised in faithful spirit not to be offended, through weakness of the flesh they would be offended, and he prayed that the cup he would drink might not abide with them.
sources.quote: It is not, therefore, for Himself that He is sorrowful and prays: it is for those whom He exhorts to watchfulness and prayer, lest the cup of suffering should be their lot
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's sorrow in Gethsemane ('My soul is sorrowful even unto death') sorrow for himself and his own impending suffering?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Read together with the prayer in John 17 and the prayer against Satan in Luke, the Gethsemane prayer shows that Christ's sorrow was for his disciples, not for himself. He asked the Father to preserve the disciples during his coming passion. His later command to 'sleep on' shows he was confident the prayer had been answered.
sources.quote: It is not from Himself that the Lord prays the suffering may be taken away. He beseeches the Father to preserve the disciples during His coming passion.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's prayer in Gethsemane that the cup pass from him a prayer to be spared his own suffering?

question: Does the Father's begetting of the Son divide or diminish the Father's essence, so that the Son cannot truly be of the Father's essence?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary of Poitiers agree that the begetting involves no division or diminution of the Father's essence. Gregory argues from the analogy of human generation, where the nature stays whole in both begetter and begotten, and turns this against Eunomius's objection. Hilary instead appeals to God's incorporeal, unchangeable nature and to the image of light that pours itself forth without loss.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: No. Just as a man begets a man without his nature being divided or diminished, the Father begets the Son without division of essence. The Father begat "another self," not passing out of Himself and yet appearing in His fulness in the Son, so the Son is truly of the Father without any mutilation of the Father's nature.
sources.quote: then the Father begat another self, not passing out of Himself, and at the same time appearing in His fulness in Him
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's begetting of the Son divide or diminish the Father's essence, so that the Son cannot truly be of the Father's essence?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The birth was a gift of the existing Life that did not lessen the store from which it was taken. It is like light that pours itself forth without losing anything. The unchangeable God begat God, so the Son has the same nature and source as the Father.
sources.quote: his birth was the gift of the existing Life, a gift which did not lessen the store from which it was taken; and that They Two are One
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's begetting of the Son diminish or impoverish the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: No. Generation does not divide a nature even among creatures: a man who begets a man keeps his nature entire, and it exists whole both in the one who begets and in the one begotten. So much more the incorruptible God begets his Son without any division or diminution of his essence. Eunomius's worry that true begetting would divide the Father's essence is therefore groundless.
sources.quote: a man in begetting a man from himself does not divide his nature, but it remains in its fulness alike in him who begets and in him who is begotten, not split off and transferred from the one to the other
sources.raw_question: Would the Father's truly begetting the Son out of his own essence require dividing or diminishing the divine essence?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. The incorporeal and unchangeable God begets, according to his own nature, God incorporeal and unchangeable. This perfect birth involves no diminution of the Begetter's substance.
sources.quote: this perfect birth of incorporeal and unchangeable God from incorporeal and unchangeable God involves, as we see in the light of the revelation of God from God, no diminution of the Begetter’s substance.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's begetting of the Son diminish or change the Father's substance?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: No. Even among human beings, who are born one of another, there is no division of essence: the definition of the essence remains entire in both begetter and begotten. The begetter suffers no diminution and the begotten gains no augmentation, so Eunomius's claim that the Son does not share the Father's essence is meaningless.
sources.quote: The definition expressive of essence remains in its entirety in each, in him that begets and in him who is begotten, without admitting diminution in him who begets, or augmentation in him who is begotten.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being begotten of the Father imply a division or diminution of the divine essence between Father and Son?

question: Does the difference between the Father being unbegotten and the Son being begotten prove that they are of different substances?
synthesis: Augustine and Gregory of Nyssa both answer no, but on different grounds. Augustine argues that not everything said of God is said according to substance. 'Begotten' is said relatively, and 'unbegotten' merely denies a relation (it means 'not a son'), so neither names a substance; he also turns the Arian premise against itself. Gregory instead argues that begotten and unbegotten are contemplated in the subject but lie apart from the essence, which in its definition is beyond them, so the one essence is in both Persons without variation.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Argument of the Arians is Refuted, Which is Drawn from the Words Begotten and Unbegotten.
sources.answer: No. The Arian argument assumes that everything said of God is said according to substance, but this premise defeats itself. If everything is said according to substance, then "I and the Father are one" is said according to substance, and the Father and Son have one substance. If that saying is not about substance, then some things are said of God not according to substance, and so begotten and unbegotten need not be taken as terms of substance either.
sources.quote: If whatever is spoken of God is spoken according to substance, then that which is said, “I and the Father are one,” is spoken according to substance. Therefore there is one substance of the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Father is unbegotten and the Son is begotten prove that the Father and the Son are different substances?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > He then shows the eternity of the Son's generation, and the inseparable identity of His essence with Him that begat Him, and likens the folly of Eunomius to children playing with sand.
sources.answer: No. Being unbegotten and being begotten are contemplated in the subject but are not the essence itself, which in its proper definition is something beyond these. Since the difference of begotten and unbegotten lies apart from the essence and does not affect it, the essence must be acknowledged to be in both Persons without variation.
sources.quote: since no difference is found in the subject, because the difference of “begotten” and “unbegotten” is apart from the essence, and does not affect it, it necessarily follows that the essence must be allowed to be in both Persons without variation
sources.raw_question: Are 'unbegotten' and 'begotten' identical with the divine essence, so that the Father and Son differ in essence?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: No. Not everything predicated of God is predicated according to substance. Goodness and greatness are said of God in respect to himself, but some things are said relatively, in respect to something other than himself. 'Father' is said in relation to the Son, so begetting and being begotten mark relations, not diverse substances.
sources.quote: not everything that is predicated of God is predicated according to substance, as He is called good and great according to substance
sources.raised_by_detail: those who think everything predicated of God is predicated according to substance
sources.raw_question: Does the difference between begotten and unbegotten prove that the Father and the Son are of different substances?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Addition of a Negative Does Not Change the Predicament.
sources.answer: No. 'Unbegotten' means simply 'not begotten,' which is equivalent to 'not a son,' and this denies a relation rather than asserting a substance. Since 'begotten' is said relatively (in reference to a begetter), 'unbegotten' is also said relatively, declaring only that he is not of a begetter. Therefore, though begotten and unbegotten are diverse, they do not denote different substances.
sources.quote: But that which is asserted relatively does not denote substance, and accordingly, although begotten and unbegotten are diverse, they do not denote a different substance
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics arguing from their own conceptions (Eunomian-type argument)
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father 'unbegotten' predicate something of His substance, so that the unbegotten Father must differ in substance from the begotten Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Reply is Made to the Cavils of the Heretics in Respect to the Same Words Begotten and Unbegotten.
sources.answer: No. 'Unbegotten' does not say what the Father is but what he is not. When a relative term is denied, it is not denied according to substance, because the relative term itself was never affirmed according to substance. So the difference between unbegotten and begotten does not make a difference of substance.
sources.quote: But when the Father is said to be unbegotten, it is not said what He is, but what He is not; and when a relative term is denied, it is not denied according to substance, since the relative itself is not affirmed according to substance.
sources.raw_question: Since 'unbegotten' is said of the Father in respect to himself and 'begotten' of the Son, and whatever is said of a thing in respect to itself is said according to substance, does it follow that the Father and the Son differ in substance?

question: Is the Son co-eternal with the Father, eternal in the same way the Father is?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Athanasius agree that the Son is eternal just as the Father is, but they argue differently.
