Gregory gives several arguments: bounding the Son's life by a beginning and end would reduce it to non-existence; Scripture forbids a 'new' God; the Son is in all that the Father is, including His eternity; and He is 'Eternal from Eternal' as Light from Light. Athanasius argues that because the Father always is, so is His Word, citing Proverbs 8:30 and John 14:10, and he refers creaturely language about the Son to the Incarnation.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. The only alternative to sound doctrine is to bound the Son's life by both a beginning and an end, which reduces his limitless life to non-existence. Since that is impious, we must contemplate Him Who is of the Father as united with the Father's eternity.
sources.quote: either they must revert to sound doctrine under the compulsion of the foregoing arguments, and contemplate Him Who is of the Father in union with the Father’s eternity, or if they do not like this, they must limit the eternity of the Son in both ways
sources.raw_question: Is the Son co-eternal with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture forbids any "new" God, so whatever is truly God is not new; since the Only-begotten is God, he is not new and therefore is eternal. Nor is he "alien" from true Deity, being of the Father, in his bosom, and having the Father in himself.
sources.quote: If, then, He is God, He is not “new,” and if He is not new, He is assuredly eternal.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being God imply that he is eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is in the Father not in one respect only but in all that the Father is conceived to be. Being in the Father's incorruptibility, goodness and might, He is incorruptible, good and powerful. In the same way, being in the Father's eternity, He is eternal. Moreover, if God now is, He always was.
sources.quote: being in the Father, He is not in Him in one respect only, but He is in Him altogether, in respect of all that the Father is conceived to be.
sources.raw_question: Since the Son is in the Father, is He eternal because the Father is eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: Yes. As the Son is Light from Light, Life from Life, Good from Good, so he is Eternal from Eternal. His life is not marked by any intervals of time, but flows back before the ages and onward beyond them, so he 'hath neither beginning of days, nor end of life.'
sources.quote: For as He is Light from Light, Life from Life, Good from Good, and Wise, Just, Strong, and all else in the same way, so most certainly is He Eternal from Eternal.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son eternal in the same way the Father is eternal?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: Yes. Since the Father always is, so is His Word, who always being says 'I was daily His delight, rejoicing always before Him' and 'I am in the Father and the Father in Me.' The creaturely language belongs only to His becoming man for our need.
sources.quote: And as, since the Father is always, so is His Word, and always being, always says ‘I was daily His delight, rejoicing always before Him,’
sources.raw_question: Is the Word eternal in the same way the Father is?

question: Did the Word of God truly become flesh and suffer, or did He only appear to be human?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Hippolytus agree that the Word truly became man, not in mere appearance. Irenaeus argues from redemption: real blood is needed for redemption, God's works are true, and death must be vanquished. He also rejects the view that the Christ descended on a separate Jesus. Hippolytus adds that the incarnation was not a conversion, since the Word kept His heavenly nature while taking flesh from Adam's line through the Virgin.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter X.—Unity of the faith of the Church throughout the whole world.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus lists among the articles of the one faith that the Word of God became flesh and suffered, and that the advent of the Son of God took place in the last times. The skilled teacher may gratefully explain on what account this happened, but not deny it.
sources.quote: gratefully describe on what account the Word of God became flesh and suffered; and relate why the advent of the Son of God took place in these last times
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God truly become flesh and suffer?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter II.—When Christ visited us in His grace, He did not come to what did not belong to Him: also, by shedding His true blood for us, and exhibiting to us His true flesh in the Eucharist, He conferred upon our flesh the capacity of salvation.
sources.answer: He truly became man. Christ could not have redeemed us by his own blood unless he really became man, for blood comes only from veins, flesh and the substance of man, such as the Word of God was actually made. Paul's statement that we have redemption through his blood presupposes this real flesh.
sources.quote: For blood can only come from veins and flesh, and whatsoever else makes up the substance of man, such as the Word of God was actually made. By His own blood he redeemed us
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God truly become man with real flesh and blood, or only in appearance?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: He truly became man. What he appeared to be, he also was. If he only seemed to be flesh, his work would not be true, yet Scripture says God's works are true. Those who say he appeared only putatively remain under the old condemnation, because on their view death has not been vanquished.
sources.quote: But if, not having been made flesh, He did appear as if flesh, His work was not a true one. But what He did appear, that He also was
sources.raised_by_detail: Docetists (those who assert He appeared putatively)
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God truly become flesh, or did he only appear to be human, as the Docetists claimed?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. He became man in truth, not in mere appearance and not by conversion. He kept the heavenly nature he had from the Father as the Word. He also took the earthly nature, flesh from Adam's line, through the Virgin. So he was manifested as God in a body and as a perfect man.
sources.quote: For it was not in mere appearance or by conversion, but in truth, that He became man.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word become man only in appearance, or by being converted into flesh, rather than truly?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: The Word truly became flesh. The heretics variously claim that the Christ descended like a dove upon Jesus, that Jesus passed through Mary like water through a tube, or that the Word appeared only as a transfigured man. On every one of these systems, the Word remains fleshless and impassible. John refutes all of them as false witnesses by declaring that "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
sources.quote: Therefore the Lord’s disciple, pointing them all out as false witnesses, says, "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God (the Christ) truly become flesh, or did an impassible heavenly Christ merely descend upon a human Jesus and leave before the suffering?

question: Should the doctrine of the Trinity be rejected because it, or the manner of it, cannot be understood or comprehended?
synthesis: Waterland and Augustine agree that it should not be rejected. Waterland argues that demanding full comprehension is bargaining too strictly with God, and that other incomprehensible truths such as omnipresence are believed in general without knowing their manner. Augustine urges believing what Scripture teaches and seeking understanding through prayer, comparing the denier to a man born blind who denies the sun.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. Waterland names this assumption as an error shared by Sabellians and Arians: that if the modus, or manner, of a thing is unintelligible, the thing itself cannot be believed. He rejects the assumption, holding that our most refined thoughts are infinitely unworthy of this subject and that imagination has no place in it.
sources.quote: both seem to suppose, or take for granted, that if the modus, or manner, be unintelligible, the thing itself is incredible.
sources.raw_question: If the manner of the Trinity cannot be understood, does that make the doctrine itself incredible?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What It is that Suffices Here to Solve the Question Why the Spirit is Not Said to Be Begotten, and Why the Father Alone is Unbegotten. What They Ought to Do Who Do Not Understand These Things.
sources.answer: No. Those unable to grasp it should believe what Scripture teaches rather than demand a clear reason the weak human mind cannot comprehend. They should then seek understanding through prayer, inquiry and good living. Denying the Trinity because one cannot discern it is like a man born blind denying that there is a sun.
sources.quote: But if they think they ought to deny that these things are, because they, with their blind minds, cannot discern them, they, too, who are blind from their birth, ought to deny that there is a sun.
sources.raw_question: Should one deny the doctrine of the Trinity because one cannot understand it or see it clearly by reason?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Refusing to admit what one can understand unless one is allowed to understand more is too familiar a posture for a creature towards his Creator. It amounts to bargaining with Almighty God more strictly than becomes us. We are required to believe only as far as we apprehend.
sources.quote: he will not admit so far as he may understand, unless he may have the privilege to understand something more: which, whether it be not too familiar from a creature towards his Creator
sources.raw_question: Is it reasonable to refuse assent to the doctrine of the Trinity because one cannot fully and adequately comprehend it?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Opponents have at least a general, confused, or inadequate idea of the mystery, so they cannot claim to have no idea of it at all. Refusing assent merely because one cannot fully comprehend it is to bargain too strictly with God. If someone claims to see real contradictions, he should show them. Otherwise the only fair question is whether the doctrine is scriptural.
sources.quote: If he means that he has no idea at all of the mystery, not so much as a general, confuse, or inadequate apprehension. of it ; that must be a mistake ; as may appear from what hath been before observed.
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity unintelligible, so that it cannot be assented to?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: No. Other incomprehensible matters, such as God's omnipresence, raise equal or greater difficulties under any hypothesis once reasoned on minutely. If one is content to rest in generals about omnipresence without the modus, the Trinity deserves the same treatment.
sources.quote: if they choose to rest in generals, without any hypothesis at all, and without descending to the modus and minutie of it: this is the very thing which we desire and contend for, in regard to the blessed Trinity
sources.raw_question: Should the doctrine of the Trinity be rejected because its manner (modus) cannot be explained in detail?

question: Does Paul's phrase 'His own Son' in Romans 8:32 show that Christ is God's Son by nature rather than by adoption or creation?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Gregory of Nyssa agree that the word 'own' marks a true, natural Sonship that sets Christ apart from sons by adoption or by creation. Hilary grounds this in the Greek wording (idios rather than Paul's usual heautou, which he says the Latin translators missed) and in the logic of Paul's comparison about the greatness of God's love. Gregory instead contrasts the Son with other sons who were begotten, exalted or adopted and brought into being at God's command, and he ties the point to the Church's confession that the true Father is Father of His own Son.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. The word 'own' (Greek idios) emphatically marks a genuine, natural Sonship. Paul uses it in a comparison meant to show the greatness of God's love. That comparison only works if God gave His true Son for strangers, not an adopted son for those He meant to adopt or a creature for creatures.
sources.quote: Can Son, by any remaining possibility, be a title received through adoption, when He is expressly called God’s own Son?
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's phrase that God 'spared not His own Son' (Romans 8:32) rule out the view that Christ is Son only by adoption?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. Elsewhere Paul writes 'ton heautou huion', but here he writes 'tou idiou huiou', which is more exactly rendered 'His own'. Hilary says the Latin manuscripts that read only 'His Son' reflect the translators' failure to grasp the point. The deliberate change expressly signals Christ's true divine nature, setting the Only-begotten apart from the many sons by adoption.
sources.quote: in this passage uses the words ὅς γε τοῦ ἰδίου υἱοῦ οὐκ ἐφείσατο, that is, Who spared not His own Son, expressly and emphatically indicating His true Divine nature.
sources.raw_question: Is there a significant difference between Paul's usual phrase 'His Son' and the phrase 'His own Son' in Romans 8:32?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: The word "own" marks the Son's distinct nature. It sets the true Son apart from other sons, who are begotten, exalted, or adopted. Those other sons were brought into being at God's command, so "own" shows that the Son is not a creature.
sources.quote: he contrasts the true Son with the other sons, begotten, or exalted, or adopted[^765] (those, I mean, who were brought into being at His command), marking the specialty of nature by the addition of “own.”
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean by calling Christ God's "own Son" in Romans 8:32?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: Yes. The Church believes the true Father is truly Father of his own Son, not of a Son alien from him. By adding "own," the Apostle distinguishes Christ from those who are made sons by grace through adoption and not by nature.
sources.quote: distinguishing Him, by the addition of “own,” from those who are counted worthy of the adoption of sons by grace and not by nature
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's phrase "His own Son" in Romans 8:32 show that Christ is the Father's Son by nature rather than by adoption?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: It marks the specialty of the Son's nature. By adding "own," Paul contrasts the true Son with the other sons, whether begotten, exalted or adopted, who were brought into being at God's command.
sources.quote: he contrasts the true Son with the other sons, begotten, or exalted, or adopted
sources.raw_question: What does the word "own" in "He spared not His own Son" (Romans 8:32) signify about the Son?

question: Does Christ's saying 'I ascend unto My Father and your Father, and My God and your God' (John 20:17) show that the Son is a creature sharing our servile nature and is not truly God?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Gregory of Nyssa agree that the text does not make the Son a creature, and both explain it as spoken from His assumed humanity. Gregory reads it as summing up Christ's mediating work as Man: through the first-fruits of human nature He assumed, He brings mankind back to the Father as their God. Hilary's answers combine several lines: Christ speaks as a servant to servants, He ascends as our Representative to receive glory as Man, and being 'God the Begotten' He belongs to the divine nature, unlike those who are sons by adoption.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Christ spoke these words as a man in the form of a servant, speaking as a servant to servants; so the Father is His Father as ours and His God as all men's only in His human aspect. The words cannot be transferred to the divine nature, which had nothing of the servant in it.
sources.quote: Jesus Christ was speaking as a man in the form of a servant to men and servants; what difficulty is there then in the idea, that in His human aspect the Father is His Father as ours, in His servant’s nature God is His God as all men’s?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'I ascend to My Father and your Father, and My God and your God' prove that the Son shares our creaturely and servile nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary teaches that the Father being both Christ's Father and God and ours is an infinite advantage to us and no degradation to Him. It is the Son, born as Man and having suffered the afflictions of our flesh, who ascends to our God and Father. He does so to receive His glory as Man, our Representative.
sources.quote: that the fact that His Father and God is also our Father and God is an infinite advantage to us and no degradation to Him, since He Who has been born as Man and suffered all the afflictions of our flesh has gone up on high to our God and Father
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'I ascend unto My Father and your Father, to My God and your God' show that the Son is a creature, sharing our relation to God and excluded from true divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. To know Christ as God we must know Him as God the Begotten, and to be born God is to belong to the nature of God. The name 'Begotten' signifies the manner of His origin but does not make Him different in kind from the Begetter. So the Father's being 'His God' does not reduce the Son to the created, servile nature of those who share a Father with Him by adoption.
sources.quote: But to be born God is to belong to the nature of God, for the name Begotten signifies indeed the manner of His origin, but does not make Him different in kind from the Begetter.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'I ascend unto My Father and your Father, and My God and your God' prove that the Son shares a creaturely nature with us and is not truly God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He further very appositely expounds the meaning of the term “Only-Begotten,“ and of the term “First born,“ four times used by the Apostle.
sources.answer: No. Christ speaks here not in His divine character but in the humanity He shares with us, as mediator who assumed the first-fruits of human nature. The words sum up His dispensation as Man. Through the humanity He assumed, He presents all mankind to the true God and Father from whom they had revolted, making Him their Father and God.
sources.quote: sends to His brethren the announcement of Himself not in His divine character, but in that which He shares with us
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "I go to My Father and your Father, and to My God and your God" show that the Son is by nature a creature subject to God like other men?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Hilary denies it. He presents this, together with the subjection text of 1 Corinthians 15, as the heretics' strongest objection. He proposes to refute it by drawing out the true meaning from the words themselves, since the Lord spoke plainly for our instruction. His aim is to show that these texts do not overthrow the truth of the divine birth.
sources.quote: Let us adopt once more our usual method of drawing out from the words themselves their true signification, that so we may discover the truth precisely where they think to overthrow it.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'I ascend unto My Father and your Father, and My God and your God' show that He shares a creaturely origin with us and is not God by nature?

question: Does Hebrews 1, in calling the Son 'better' than the angels, show that the Son is of the same nature as the angels or of a different and higher nature?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Athanasius agree that Hebrews 1 sets the Son apart from the angels in nature. Gregory argues from the passage's contrasts: the angels worship and minister, while the Son is addressed as God with an eternal throne. Athanasius also points to the contrasts of Son and servants and of Framer and things framed, but he adds a linguistic argument: 'better', unlike 'greater' or 'more', marks a difference in kind rather than a comparison within one kind.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He convicts Eunomius of having used of the Only-begotten terms applicable to the existence of the earth, and thus shows that his intention is to prove the Son to be a being mutable and created.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says the Son alone is called Son because he is not of the angels' nature but of a more excellent one. The angels are commanded to worship him and are called ministers, while the Son is addressed as God with an eternal throne. His Godhead is as far above the angels as a master is above his slaves.
sources.quote: Why is it that he says that He alone has been called Son? Because He is not of the nature of angels, but of that which is more excellent.
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1 show that the Son is of a different and higher nature than the angels?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. If the Son were among the angels, He would not differ from them in nature, and they would sit at the right hand or He would stand ministering with them. Scripture instead sets Him apart from them, as Son excels servants and as Framer excels things framed.
sources.quote: If the Son be in the number of the Angels, then let the word ‘become’ apply to Him as to them, and let Him not differ at all from them in nature
sources.raw_question: Does the comparison 'better than the angels' imply that the Son shares the same nature as the angels?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. Comparison properly belongs to things of one kind, and for such things Scripture says 'rather' or 'more,' not 'better.' 'Better' is used to mark difference between things unlike in kind, as wisdom and jewels. Had the Apostle said 'greater' or 'has precedence,' there might be a plea, but by saying 'better' and contrasting Son with servants he shows the Son is other than the angels in nature.
sources.quote: but, as it is, in saying that He is ‘better,’ and differs as far as Son from servants, the Apostle shews that He is other than the Angels in nature.
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1:4's statement that the Son is 'better' than the angels imply that the Son is of the same kind or nature as the angels?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. The Apostle deliberately uses 'better' rather than 'greater' or 'more honourable' to contrast, not compare, marking the difference of the Son's nature from things originated. Scripture uses 'better' of things different in kind, as wisdom is better than rubies and a day in God's courts better than a thousand. Comparison belongs to things one in kind; 'better' marks things differing in nature, so the Son differs from the Angels as Son from servants.
sources.quote: In like manner there is nought akin between the Son and the Angels; so that the word ‘better’ is not used to compare but to contrast, because of the difference of His nature from them.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'better' than the Angels imply that the Son is of the same kind as the Angels?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. Holding that Angels are one in kind with Christ repeats the errors of Valentinus and Carpocrates. Comparison belongs only to things one in kind, and God is beyond comparison, as the Psalm says none among the gods is like the Lord; the Apostle, by saying 'better' and distinguishing Son from servants, shows the Son is other than the Angels in nature.
sources.quote: in saying that He is ‘better,’ and differs as far as Son from servants, the Apostle shews that He is other than the Angels in nature.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of the same nature as the Angels, so that He can be compared with them?

question: When God begins in time to stand in a relation to creatures, as when He creates them or becomes 'our refuge' or 'Lord', does God Himself undergo any change?
synthesis: Augustine and Athanasius agree that God does not change: the change lies on the side of creatures, not in God. Augustine grounds this in the claim that such names are said of God relatively, and that God, as the only unchangeable essence, has no accidents. Athanasius makes the point to argue that creation offers no precedent for God changing into a Father.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said of God in Time, is Said Relatively, Not Accidentally.
sources.answer: No. God is called our refuge relatively, because He is referred to us when we flee to Him. The change takes place in us, who become better by fleeing to Him. In Him there is no change.
sources.quote: In us therefore some change does take place; for we were worse before we fled to Him, and we become better by fleeing to Him: but in Him there is no change.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says God was 'made our refuge', does anything change in God's nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: No. Such relative predicates arise in time on the side of the creature. Nothing happens to God that would change him, and he remains altogether unchangeable in his own nature or essence.
sources.quote: then nothing happens to Him so as to work a change in Him, but He Himself continues altogether unchangeable in His own nature or essence
sources.raw_question: When God is given a relative name in time, such as becoming 'our refuge' or 'Lord' of creatures, does God undergo change?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance.
sources.answer: No. Even when a relative predicate is said of God as beginning in time, as in 'Lord, thou hast become our refuge,' nothing happens to God that changes Him. He remains absolutely unchangeable in His own nature or essence.
sources.quote: yet nothing happens to God so as to work a change in Him, but He Himself remains absolutely unchangeable in His own nature or essence
sources.raw_question: When something is said of God relatively as happening in time, such as His becoming our refuge, does this imply a change in God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What the Author Entreats from God, What from the Reader. In God Nothing is to Be Thought Corporeal or Changeable.
sources.answer: No. God makes changeable things without any change in Himself and without passion. He is the only unchangeable essence, since in Him there can be no accident by which change is produced.
sources.quote: making things that are changeable, without change of Himself, and without passion
sources.raw_question: Does God undergo change or passion when He creates changeable things?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No. When God makes creatures, the change lies in the things that come to be afterwards, not in God. So creation offers no precedent for God changing into a Father.
sources.quote: if they argue that in the instance of creation He became afterwards a Maker, let them know that the change is in the things which afterwards came to be, and not in God.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who separate Word and Son
sources.raw_question: Does God's becoming Maker of the creation at a certain time imply a change in God?

question: Does Psalm 2:7, 'Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee,' refer to a temporal beginning of the Son's sonship or to his eternal generation, and what does 'this day' signify?
synthesis: All three readings deny that the text gives the Son's sonship a temporal beginning, but they read 'this day' differently. Waterland, following Methodius, stresses that the text says 'Thou art', not 'Thou becamest', so the sonship has no limit of time, and he takes 'this day' as a temporal manifestation to the world of the already-existing Son. Hilary instead refers the words, spoken at Christ's baptism, to the sanctification and anointing of his assumed manhood rather than to his eternal birth. The reading Waterland attributes to Origen takes 'today' as God's eternity, so the verse describes the Son's beginningless generation itself.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. Following Methodius, Waterland notes that Scripture says 'Thou art', not 'Thou becamest', my Son. This expresses the sonship without any limit of time: the Son did not acquire a new filiation and will have no end, but is always the same. The words 'This day have I begotten thee' refer to a manifestation of the Son, not to a new sonship.
sources.quote: For he said, Thou art, not, Thou be“ camest my Son; signifying that he did not acquire any new “ filiation, nor should ever have an end of his existence, but that “he is always the same.”
sources.raw_question: Does the wording of Psalm 2:7, 'Thou art my Son', imply that the Son's sonship is eternal rather than acquired at some point in time?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Following Methodius, the 'day' refers not to a temporal generation but to a temporal manifestation: the Son already existing before the ages in the heavens was made known to the world, to which he had previously been unknown.
sources.quote: explaining it, not of any temporal generation, (for he allows no such thing,) but of a temporal manifestation.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 2:7, 'This day have I begotten thee,' refer to a temporal generation of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The voice at the Jordan testifies to the sanctification of His flesh, and in it we must recognise His anointing with the power of the Spirit. It concerns His assumed manhood, not His eternal birth as God.
sources.quote: Thus is testified the sanctification of His flesh, and in this testimony we must recognise His anointing with the power of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does 'Thou art My Son, this day have I begotten Thee', spoken at Christ's baptism, refer to the Son's eternal divine generation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Following Methodius, the sonship is stated without limit of time: the text says 'Thou art,' not 'Thou becamest' my Son. This shows that he did not acquire a new filiation and is always the same. The 'this day have I begotten thee' refers to a later manifestation, not to the beginning of his sonship.
sources.quote: εἶ γὰρ υἱὸς, αὐτῷ ἔφη, καὶ οὐ, γέγονας
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 2:7, 'Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee,' imply that the Son acquired his sonship at some point in time?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: He took the 'today' to be God's eternity, so the Son's generation has no beginning. With God it is always today, without evening or morning, and the 'today' in which the Son is begotten is coextended with the Father's unbegotten and eternal life. Origen also called it presumption to ascribe any beginning to the Son, who is always with the Father.
sources.quote: the time coextended, if I may so speak, “ with his unbegotten and eternal life is the to-day in which the “Son is begotten; there being no beginning found of his “‘ generation, any more than of the to-day.
sources.raw_question: How did Origen interpret 'this day have I begotten thee' in Psalm 2 with respect to the Son's generation?

question: Does Christ's saying 'I came forth from the Father (God), and am come into the world' (John 16:28) refer to his eternal birth from the Father, or to his being sent into the world?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers consistently distinguishes 'went forth from God' (the Son's birth, his entry into substantial existence) from his coming or being sent into the world (his mission for salvation). He points to the order of the phrases and to the Apostles' confession, made only after this saying, as evidence that it revealed his true Divinity. Augustine reads it differently: he takes 'I came forth from the Father' to mean the Son's appearing not in the form in which he is equal to the Father but as less than the Father, in the servant form he took on. Augustine therefore refers the phrase to the incarnation rather than to the eternal birth.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Christ first records His going forth from God and then His coming from the Father, which forbids identifying them. They may be paraphrased as 'Birth' and 'Presence.' The first is His entry by birth into substantial existence. The second is His coming into the world to accomplish our salvation.
sources.quote: It is one thing to have gone forth from God, and entered by birth upon a substantial existence; another to have come from the Father into this world to accomplish the mysteries of our salvation.
sources.raw_question: Are the Son's going forth from God and His coming from the Father into the world the same event?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The Apostles had often heard that He was sent and came from the Father into the world, and this caused no surprise; but 'I went forth from God' was a new truth revealing His birth from God. Their response, 'By this we believe that Thou wentest forth from God,' answers only that statement, showing it disclosed His true Divinity and the birth that accounts for His omnipotence.
sources.quote: They knew that He had been sent from God, but they knew not that He had gone forth from God. Now at last, taught by this utterance to understand the ineffable and perfect birth of the Son
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement 'I went forth from God' mean the same thing as his being sent from the Father into the world?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: They understood it as a birth of the divine nature. They had often heard him say he was sent, which awakened no surprise, but only on hearing that he had gone forth from God did they confess, "Now speakest Thou plainly... we believe that Thou wentest forth from God." This statement opened their eyes to his true Divinity.
sources.quote: By this the holy Apostles did not understand that He had gone forth, in the sense of having been sent, from God. For they had often heard Him confess, in His earlier discourses, that He was sent
sources.raw_question: Did the Apostles understand Christ's words "I went forth from God" (John 16:28) as meaning merely that he was sent, or as a birth of the divine nature from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It refers to His birth. Christ answered not that He was sent from God but that He came out from God, and these words signify His birth from the incorporeal God. Because He adds that He came from the Father, this "coming out," joined to the Father's name, is simply and solely the birth.
sources.quote: answered not that He was sent from, but that He was come out from, God, signifying by the words “come out from” the great fact of His birth from the incorporeal God.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that he "came out from" God or the Father refer to his eternal birth, or only to his being sent?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to God, Even the Father. The Kingdom Having Been Delivered to God, Even the Father, Christ Will Not Then Make Intercession for Us.
sources.answer: Each phrase refers to the two forms of the Son. "I came forth from the Father" means he appeared not in the form in which he is equal to the Father, but as less than the Father, in the creature he took on. "I am come into the world" means he showed the servant form to sinners. "I leave the world" means he withdraws that form from their sight. "I go to the Father" means he teaches the faithful to understand him in the being in which he is equal to the Father.
sources.quote: What is meant by “I came forth from the Father,” unless this, that I have not appeared in that form in which I am equal to the Father, but otherwise, that is, as less than the Father, in the creature which I have taken upon me?
sources.raw_question: What do Christ's words "I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world; again, I leave the world, and go to the Father" mean in relation to his equality with the Father?

question: Are God's attributes, such as greatness, goodness, wisdom, justice and truth, really distinct from one another and from God's being, or are they identical in God?
synthesis: Augustine and Owen agree that God's attributes are not really distinct in Him but are one and the same. Augustine grounds this in God's absolute simplicity: unlike the changeable soul, for God to be is the same as to be great, wise or just, so that greatness is truth and naming one attribute names all. Owen adds that the attributes are distinguished only by different respects as God exerts them through acts of His will, so that their effects differ but they can never truly be contrary to one another.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > It is Shown by Reason that in God Three are Not Anything Greater Than One Person.
sources.answer: Yes. In the substance of truth, which alone truly is, nothing is greater except by being more truly. Hence where magnitude itself is truth, whatever has more of magnitude must have more of truth, and to be great is the same as to be true. Therefore what is equally true must be equally great.
sources.quote: since in regard to the essence of truth, to be true is the same as to be, and to be is the same as to be great; therefore to be great is the same as to be true.
sources.raw_question: In God, is greatness the same thing as truth or being?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > God is a Trinity, But Not Triple (Triplex).
sources.answer: They are identical. God is called great, good, wise, blessed and true in many ways, but His greatness is the same as His wisdom, since He is great not by bulk but by power, and His goodness and truth are the same as these. In God it is not one thing to be blessed and another to be great, wise, true, good, or to be Himself.
sources.quote: in Him it is not one thing to be blessed, and another to be great, or wise, or true, or good, or in a word to be Himself.
sources.raw_question: Are God's attributes such as greatness, goodness, wisdom, and truth distinct things in God, or are they identical with one another and with God's being?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Same Argument Continued.
sources.answer: Yes. In the human mind to be is not the same as to be strong, prudent or just, since a mind can exist without these virtues. But God's substance is incomparably more simple, so in God to be is the same as to be strong, just or wise; His is a 'simple multiplicity, or multifold simplicity.'
sources.quote: But in God to be is the same as to be strong, or to be just, or to be wise, or whatever is said of that simple multiplicity, or multifold simplicity, whereby to signify His substance.
sources.raw_question: Is God's being identical with his attributes such as wisdom, justice and strength?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. God's attributes are essentially the same in him. They are distinguished only under different habitudes or respects, according to how they are exerted by acts of his will. Their effects are diverse, but because they are one in God they cannot truly be contrary to one another.
sources.quote: as they are all essentially the same in him, and considered only under a different habitude or respect, as they are exerted by acts of his will
sources.raw_question: Are God's attributes, such as mercy and justice, really distinct from one another in God's nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: They are one and the same. Although they go under several names, greatness is power, goodness is wisdom, and wisdom is power, so naming one is naming all. For God it is not one thing to be great and another to be God, nor one thing to be and another to be great. Unlike the changeable soul, which can be wise at one time and unwise at another, God is absolutely and perfectly simple.
sources.quote: so that that is greatness which is power, that is goodness which is wisdom, and that again is wisdom which is power, as we have already argued; then let us remember, that when I mention any one of these, I am to be taken as if I mentioned all
sources.raw_question: In God, are greatness, power, wisdom, goodness and being itself distinct things, or are they one and the same?

question: Who are 'the seven Spirits' before the throne in the Book of Revelation, and do they denote the personal Holy Spirit rather than angels or abstract powers?
synthesis: Owen and Bickersteth agree that the seven Spirits are the Holy Spirit, with the number seven expressing his perfection. Owen rests this mainly on the Spirit being named with the Father and Christ as a source of grace and peace. Bickersteth adds further arguments: the threefold 'from... and from... and from' shows the three are distinct; praying to abstractions or to angels would be inconceivable or forbidden; and the repeated identification of the seven Spirits with the eyes of the Lamb points to the personal Spirit.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit of God. He is named there with the Father and with Christ as a source of grace and peace. The number seven presents him as the perfect fountain of every perfect gift and dispensation.
sources.quote: The seven Spirits before the throne, are the Holy Spirit of God, considered as the perfect fountain of every perfect gift and dispensation.
sources.raw_question: Who is meant by "the seven Spirits before the throne" in Revelation 1:4?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. They are distinguished from God because they stand before the throne, yet mysteriously united with him as the eyes of Jehovah and of the Lamb. Since in oriental style the number seven expresses perfection, and Christ applied "The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me" to himself, the expression represents the Holy Ghost in his infinite perfection, wisdom of operation and munificence of gifts.
sources.quote: we may fairly conclude this expression represents to us “this heavenly Agent, the Holy Ghost, in his own original and infinite perfection, in the consummate wisdom of his operations, and in the gracious munificence of his gifts.”
sources.raw_question: Do the "seven spirits of God" in the Book of Revelation refer to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Had they been mentioned only once, like the seven horns, an abstract reading might suffice, but their repeated and varied introduction forbids it. Their conjunction with the horns parallels texts where Jesus acts in the power of the personal Spirit, as in Luke 4:14 and Acts 10:38.
sources.quote: but the repeated and varied way in which they are introduced prevents our resting in this abstract interpretation
sources.raw_question: Are the 'seven eyes' and 'Seven Spirits of God' of the Lamb in Revelation 5:6 merely an abstract symbol of perfect knowledge rather than the personal Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: They are the Holy Spirit, set forth emblematically in his manifold perfection, and he is distinct from both the Father and Christ. Grace and peace are invoked separately from each of the three, 'from... and from... and from', so a distinction is intended among them. The seven spirits are 'before the throne', so they cannot be identified with the Father or the Lamb. The passages calling them the eyes of Jehovah and of the Lamb show their union with God. The 'seven' expresses the multiplicity of perfections comprised in one Spirit of Jehovah, as in Isaiah 11:2.
sources.quote: Here we learn, from (3) and (5) the distinction to be observed between God and the seven spirits – for they are said to be before the throne. Therefore you could not identify them with the Father or the Lamb.
sources.raw_question: Who are 'the seven spirits which are before the throne' in Revelation 1:4, and are they distinct from the Father and Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. It is inconceivable that St. John would pray to seven abstractions, in parity with the Father and the Son, for grace and peace, so they denote a willing intelligence. They cannot be angels either, because the worship of angels is expressly forbidden.
sources.quote: for to imagine that St. John prays to seven abstractions in parity with the Father and the Son for grace and peace is inconceivable. That they cannot be angels is manifest, for the worshipping of angels is expressly forbidden.
sources.raw_question: Could the 'seven spirits' of Revelation 1:4 be angels or mere abstract powers rather than the Holy Spirit?

question: Are there two gods differing in nature, a good God and the Creator, as Marcion held?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Irenaeus both reject Marcion's dualism, but on different grounds. Irenaeus argues against it directly and from several angles: one God gave both the law and the gospel, each fitted to its time; goodness and justice cannot be split without destroying deity on both sides; two gods would bound one another and lead to gods without number; and a god who draws men from their Maker is neither just nor fully good. Gregory simply treats Marcion's doctrine as depraved and uses it as a foil, charging that Eunomius goes further by separating the Son from the Father's goodness, which the Son as God fully shares.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He also ingeniously shows from the passage of the Gospel which speaks of “Good Master,” from the parable of the Vineyard, from Isaiah and from Paul, that there is not a dualism in the Godhead of good and evil, as Eunomius' ally Marcion supposes, and declares that the Son does not refuse the title of “good” or “Existent,” or acknowledge His alienation from the Father, but that to Him also belongs authority over all things that come into being.
sources.answer: No. Gregory treats Marcion's dualism of gods differing in nature as a depraved doctrine. He charges that Eunomius goes beyond it by separating the Only-begotten from the nature of good, whereas Marcion at least ascribed goodness to the God of the Gospel. The Son, as God, shares the Father's goodness and is not alien from Him.
sources.quote: You however actually separate the Only-begotten God from the nature of good, that you may surpass even Marcion in the depravity of your doctrines.
sources.raw_question: Is there a dualism in the Godhead, with one god different in nature from another, as Marcion held?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. Both the Mosaic law and the grace of the new covenant were bestowed by one and the same God for the benefit of the human race, each fitted to its time. Those who set them against each other failed to investigate the causes of the difference between the covenants, and Marcion's doctrine of two gods, one good and one evil, blasphemes the Creator.
sources.quote: both the Mosaic law and the grace of the new covenant, as both fitted for the times [at which they were given], were bestowed by one and the same God for the benefit of the human race.
sources.raw_question: Does the difference between the Mosaic law and the Gospel prove that they come from two different gods, as Marcion held?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXV.—This world is ruled by the providence of one God, who is both endowed with infinite justice to punish the wicked, and with infinite goodness to bless the pious, and impart to them salvation.
sources.answer: No. Such a division destroys deity on both sides: a judge who is not good is no God, since one from whom goodness is absent is no God at all, and a good being without judicial power is likewise deprived of deity. A judge without goodness is neither just nor wise, and goodness without judgment is imperfect.
sources.quote: Marcion, therefore, himself, by dividing God into two, maintaining one to be good and the other judicial, does in fact, on both sides, put an end to deity.
sources.raw_question: Can God be divided into two deities, one merely good who saves and another merely just who judges, as Marcion held?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter I.—There is but one God: the impossibility of its being otherwise.
sources.answer: No. Marcion's two gods would be circumscribed by the immense interval that separates them. The same reasoning would then require a multitude of gods bounded by one another on every side, ending in uncertainty and in gods without number. In the end none of them could truly be God or Omnipotent, because each would lack what the others possess.
sources.quote: For his two gods will also be contained and circumscribed by an immense interval which separates them from one another.
sources.raw_question: Is Marcion's doctrine of two gods coherent?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: No. A god who draws men away from the one who made them is not truly good. He would be unjust toward the Creator by robbing him of his possessions. His goodness would also be defective, since it does not save all. So Marcion's supposedly good god undermines itself, and there is one God, the Maker.
sources.quote: Or how can he be good who draws away men that do not belong to him from him who made them, and calls them into his own kingdom? And why is his goodness, which does not save all [thus], defective?
sources.raw_question: Can there be two gods, the Creator and a higher good God, separated from each other by an infinite distance, as Marcion taught?

question: Was the one who wrestled with Jacob at Peniel only a man, or also God (the Son, Christ, both God and man)?
synthesis: Novatian and Hilary of Poitiers agree that the one who wrestled with Jacob was God as well as man. Novatian argues from the new name Israel, 'the one who sees God,' and from Jacob naming the place the Vision of God. He reads the episode as a type of Christ, fulfilled in the Gospel struggle and foreshadowing the incarnation. Hilary meets the objection from the wrestler's weakness: Jacob overpowered Him in the flesh, yet by faith saw true God, not God by adoption, and sought His blessing. For Hilary the weakness prefigures Christ's passion and the blessing signifies His Godhead.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God Also Appeared to Jacob as an Angel; Namely, the Son of God.
sources.answer: He was God as well as man. The renaming of Jacob as Israel, 'the man who sees God,' and the explanation 'thou hast prevailed with God' show that Jacob saw God in the one he wrestled with as a man. Jacob himself confirmed this by naming the place the Vision of God, saying he had seen God face to face.
sources.quote: if Israel is the man who sees God, the Lord was beautifully showing that it was not only a man who was then wrestling with Jacob, but God also.
sources.raw_question: Was the one who wrestled with Jacob at Peniel only a man, or also God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God Also Appeared to Jacob as an Angel; Namely, the Son of God.
sources.answer: Yes. The wrestling was a type fulfilled in the Gospel struggle between Christ and the people of Jacob. Since the type itself shows the one wrestled with to be both man and God, Christ, in whom it was fulfilled, must be acknowledged as God as well as man.
sources.quote: Who will hesitate to acknowledge that Christ, in whom this type of a wrestling was fulfilled, was not man only, but God also, since even that very type of a wrestling seems to have proved Him man and God?
sources.raw_question: Does Jacob's wrestling with the man at Peniel show that Christ is both God and man?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Jacob held the Man powerless in bodily strength, yet by faith saw in Him true God, not God by adoption, and sought His blessing. The weakness of the flesh was a type of Christ's passion, while the blessing was a sign of His Godhead; His humanity is no bar to His being God, and being God He must be true God.
sources.quote: Though He is Man, His humanity is no bar to His being God, His Godhead no bar to His being true God; for, being God, He must indeed be true
sources.raw_question: Does the weakness of the Man who wrestled with Jacob, and whom Jacob overpowered, show that this figure (the Son) was not true God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God Also Appeared to Jacob as an Angel; Namely, the Son of God.
sources.answer: He was not a mere man. Scripture shows Christ there as both man and God, foreshadowing the incarnation He would later take in the truth of His substance. Jacob's new name Israel means "the one who sees God." Jacob also named the place the Vision of God, saying he had seen God face to face. So the one he held as a man was also God.
sources.quote: Certainly Jacob saw God, with whom he wrestled, although he was holding the man in his own struggle.
sources.raw_question: Was the man who wrestled with Jacob at Peniel a mere man, or a figure of Christ who is both God and man?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. It was certainly God who wrestled in human guise. Jacob prevailed against God, and Israel saw God.
sources.quote: It was certainly God Who wrestled, for Jacob prevailed against God, and Israel saw God.
sources.raw_question: Was the one who wrestled with Jacob God?

question: How does the Son's being the image of God differ from human beings' being the image of God?
synthesis: Augustine and Athanasius agree that the Son alone is the image by nature, equal to the Father, while humans bear the image in a lesser, derived way. Their grounds differ. Augustine contrasts being born with being created, and the Son as unimitating pattern with humans who imitate; he holds that man may truly be called 'the image and glory of God' while also being 'after the image' because his likeness is unequal. Athanasius says humans are made only 'after' the Image and receive the title as a grace from the Word dwelling in them.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: The Son is the image equal to the Father, born of the Father and of the very same substance, while we are made in the image by the Father through the Son. He is the light that enlightens and so is a pattern without a pattern, whereas we are enlightened and imitate Him. He imitates no one going before Him with respect to the Father, from whom He is never separable.
sources.quote: not indeed that which is equal to Him, since we are made so by the Father through the Son, and not born of the Father, as that is.
sources.raw_question: How does the Son's being the image of God differ from human beings' being the image of God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Humans are made 'after' the Image, not as the Image itself. They bear the title image and glory of God not on their own account but because the true Image and Glory of God, the Word made flesh, dwells in them. Their designation is therefore a grace derived from the Son, who alone is the Image by nature.
sources.quote: yet not on our own account still, but for that Image and true Glory of God inhabiting us, which is His Word, who was for us afterwards made flesh, have we this grace of our designation
sources.raw_question: In what sense are human beings called the image and glory of God, and how does this differ from the Son's being the Image of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: No. The apostle calls man "the image and glory of God," not merely "after the image." Man is said to be "after the image" because his likeness is unequal: he was created rather than born of God. He therefore approaches God by a certain likeness, whereas the Son is the image equal to the Father.
sources.quote: But the apostle refutes them, saying, “For a man indeed ought not to cover his head, forasmuch as he is the image and glory of God.” He did not say after the image, but the image.
sources.raised_by_detail: some who distinguish the Son as image and man as after the image
sources.raw_question: Is only the Son properly the image of God, while man is merely "after the image"?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: The Son is the image equal to the Father, being born of Him. Man is not equal, because he is created rather than born. Man therefore approaches God not by parity but by a sort of likeness.
sources.quote: because that image of God was not made altogether equal to Him, as being not born of Him, but created by Him
sources.raw_question: How does the Son's being the image of God differ from man's being the image of God?

question: Are the Father and the Son merely two names for one and the same Person or being, as Sabellius taught?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary both reject the Sabellian view, but they argue differently. Athanasius argues from the concept of sonship: one being cannot both beget and not beget. He also reads John 10:30 grammatically: 'I and the Father' names two, where Sabellius would require 'I am the Father'. Hilary instead appeals to a series of Gospel sayings, such as 'My beloved Son', 'The Father is greater than I' and 'I go to the Father', which show a real distinction of Persons within a unity.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: No. Then the same being would be both begetting and not begetting: begetting because it produces from itself, and not begetting because what is produced is nothing other than itself. Father and Son would be so called only notionally, which is unseemly. Sabellians are refuted from the very notion of a Son.
