sources.quote: But if He be from Him, yet not another, He will be both begetting and not begetting; begetting because He produces from Himself, and not begetting, because it is nothing other than Himself.
sources.raw_question: Can Father and Son be merely two names for one and the same being, as Sabellius taught?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Marcellian illustration from 1 Cor. xii. 4, refuted.
sources.answer: No. Athanasius rejects as raving the claim that the Father is Son and the Son Father, one in subsistence and two in name. If that were so, the Son's words 'I and the Father' would be untrue, since he would really be the Father himself. The Father and the Son are truly distinct: the one begets and the other is begotten.
sources.quote: Sabellius also raves in saying that the Father is Son, and again, the Son Father, in subsistence One, in name Two
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and the Son one subsistence with two names, as Sabellius taught?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Unless Father and Son are two in name only, or as parts and so each imperfect, or two gods, they are coessential, one in Godhead, and the Son from the Father.
sources.answer: No. That is the expedient of Sabellius, which abolishes the Father when there is a Son and the Son when there is a Father. Had Christ meant this, he would have said 'I am the Father' or 'I and the Father am'. Instead 'I' signifies the Son and 'and the Father' signifies him who begat him.
sources.quote: For if not, He would have said, ‘I am the Father,’ or ‘I and the Father am;’ but, in fact, in the ‘I’ He signifies the Son, and in the ‘And the Father,’ Him who begat Him
sources.raw_question: Does 'I and the Father are one' mean that Father and Son are merely two names for a single person, as Sabellius taught?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The Gospels repeatedly show the Father and Son as distinct: the Father speaks of 'My beloved Son,' the Son says 'The Father is greater than I,' 'I go to the Father,' 'Father, I thank Thee,' and 'Glorify Me, Father.' These words imply a real distinction of Persons within a unity, not one Person under two names.
sources.quote: Let Sabellius, if he dare, confound Father and Son as two names with one meaning, making of them not Unity but One Person. He shall have a prompt answer from the Gospels
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and the Son merely two names for one Person, as Sabellius taught?

question: Does calling the Son the "Word" of God mean that He is merely the Father's spoken voice or utterance rather than a subsisting being?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary of Poitiers agree that the Word is no mere voice or transient utterance but a real, subsisting being who is God. Their grounds differ somewhat. Gregory appeals to John's statements that the Word was in the beginning, with God, and was God, which show that the Word subsists in the first and blessed Nature itself. Hilary stresses the clause 'the Word was God' and the Son's true birth as God from God, which shows His unity of nature with the Father.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He further shows the operations of God to be expressed by human illustrations; for what hands and feet and the other parts of the body with which men work are, that, in the case of God, the will alone is, in place of these. And so also arises the divergence of generation; wherefore He is called Only-begotten, because He has no community with other generation such as is observed in creation, but in that He is called the “brightness of glory,” and the “savour of ointment,” He shows the close conjunction and co-eternity of His Nature with the Father.
sources.answer: No. John takes special care that hearers do not fall into the common understanding of "word" as a voice. By proclaiming that the Word "was in the beginning" and "was with God" and was God, he teaches us to regard the Word as subsisting in essence, not in a foreign or separated essence, but in the first and blessed Nature itself.
sources.quote: the hearer may not by any means by inattention or feebleness of thought fall into the common understanding of “Word,” so that the Son should be supposed to be the voice of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son the "Word" of the Father mean that the Son is merely the Father's spoken voice or utterance?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. John adds 'And the Word was God,' which overthrows the objection that the Word is the sound of a voice or utterance of a thought. The Word is a reality, a Being, and God, not a transient sound that exists only while heard.
sources.quote: The Word is a reality, not a sound, a Being, not a speech, God, not a nonentity.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'the Word' in John 1:1 mean he is merely a spoken sound or uttered thought that exists only briefly?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: No. John guarded against this lower notion of 'word' by stating that the Word essentially subsisted in the first and blessed nature itself. John says the Word was in the beginning, with God, and was God, Light, and Life. So whatever the Beginning is, the Word is also.
sources.quote: That the reader might not through inattention and unworthy conceptions sink to the common notion of “word,” so as to deem the Son to be merely a voice of the Father
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son the 'Word' of God mean he is merely an utterance or voice of the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The Son is not a sound uttered but God from God, subsisting through a true birth, indistinguishable from the Father in nature and therefore inseparable. The name Word teaches His unity of nature with the Father, while the Unbegotten Father is never without His Word.
sources.quote: Not that the nature of the Son is that of a sound which is uttered. He is God from God, subsisting through a true birth; God’s own Son, born from the Father, indistinguishable from Him in nature, and therefore inseparable.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son the 'Word' of God mean He is merely an uttered sound or an attribute of the Father rather than a subsisting Person?

question: Is God wise by receiving or partaking of a wisdom distinct from himself, or is his wisdom identical with his essence?
synthesis: Augustine and Athanasius agree that God does not receive wisdom by participation as humans do. They differ in grounds: Augustine appeals to divine simplicity, holding that God's wisdom (and knowledge, life and power) is his very essence, so that for God to be wise is simply to be. Athanasius instead argues that God partakes of nothing and is the Father of his own Wisdom, which he identifies as an Offspring proper to the Father rather than a passion or part.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How There is a Trinity in the Very Simplicity of God. Whether and How the Trinity that is God is Manifested from the Trinities Which Have Been Shown to Be in Men.
sources.answer: No. God does not receive wisdom from anyone as we receive it from him; he is himself his own wisdom. His wisdom is not one thing and his essence another, since for him to be wise is to be.
sources.quote: For God does not receive wisdom from any one as we receive it from Him, but He is Himself His own wisdom; because His wisdom is not one thing, and His essence another, seeing that to Him to be wise is to be.
sources.raw_question: Does God possess wisdom as something received or distinct from his essence?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Still Further of the Difference Between the Knowledge and Word of Our Mind, and the Knowledge and Word of God.
sources.answer: No. In the simplicity of the divine nature, God's knowledge is his wisdom and his wisdom is his essence; for God to be wise is simply to be. Human knowledge differs, since for us to be is not the same as to know, so our knowledge can be lost and recovered.
sources.quote: the knowledge of God is itself also His wisdom, and His wisdom is itself His essence or substance. Because in the marvellous simplicity of that nature, it is not one thing to be wise and another to be, but to be wise is to be
sources.raw_question: Is God's knowledge or wisdom something distinct from his essence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: No. Men are capable of wisdom and receive it by participation, but God partakes in nothing. He is Himself the Father of His own Wisdom, and those who partake of it are called wise. This Wisdom is neither a passion nor a part, but an Offspring proper to the Father.
sources.quote: God partakes in nothing, but is Himself the Father of His own Wisdom, of which whoso partake are given the name of wise.
sources.raw_question: Is God wise by partaking of a wisdom distinct from Himself, as men are?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Difficult It is to Demonstrate the Trinity by Natural Reason.
sources.answer: God is himself wisdom. He did not receive wisdom in order to be wise. This same wisdom is also his life, power and beauty, for nothing is more powerful or beautiful than wisdom, which 'reaches from end to end mightily.'
sources.quote: For He did not receive wisdom whereby to be wise, but He is Himself wisdom. And this is life, and again is power or might, and yet again beauty
sources.raw_question: Is God wise by possessing a wisdom he has received, or is God himself wisdom?

question: Does giving glory to God "in" the Holy Spirit rather than "with" the Holy Spirit imply that the Spirit is lower in dignity than the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Basil and Ambrose both deny that "in" implies inferiority, but on different grounds. Basil argues that every sense of "in" (form in matter, power in what is capable of it, art in the artist, and so on) magnifies the Spirit, and that Scripture often uses "in" where it means "with". Ambrose argues that both "in" and "with" are conjunctive particles that imply no division, and that Scripture uses "in" of Christ without lessening Him.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That Scripture uses the words “in” or “by,” ἐν, cf. note on p. 3, in place of “with.” Wherein also it is proved that the word “and” has the same force as “with.”
sources.answer: No. The opponents cling to "in" because they think it lowers the Spirit. Basil argues that every sense the word "in" bears actually helps our conception of the Spirit's dignity. The Spirit is in the soul as form is in matter, as a power is in what is capable of it, and as an art is in the one who has it. So the word "in" turns out to be a deserter to the side of the Spirit's glory.
sources.quote: I shall be astonished if they do not, when they have heard what we have to urge, reject the in as itself a traitor to their cause, and a deserter to the side of the glory of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does giving glory to God "in the Holy Spirit" rather than "with" or "and to" the Holy Spirit imply that the Spirit is lower than the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That Scripture uses the words “in” or “by,” ἐν, cf. note on p. 3, in place of “with.” Wherein also it is proved that the word “and” has the same force as “with.”
sources.answer: No. Basil denies that "in" implies lower dignity than "with". Rightly understood it points to the highest meaning, because Scripture often uses "in" where it means "with", as in "I will go into thy house in burnt offerings". Glory given "in" the Spirit is therefore not a lesser glory.
sources.quote: I should, for my own part, deny that the word in [or by] implies lower dignity than the word “with;” I should maintain on the contrary that, rightly understood, it leads us up to the highest possible meaning.
sources.raw_question: Does the absence in Scripture of the phrase glory "with the Spirit", and the preference for glory "in the Spirit", show that the Holy Spirit is of lower dignity than the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VIII. St. Ambrose examines and refutes the heretical argument that because God is said to be glorified in the Spirit, and not with the Spirit, the Holy Spirit is therefore inferior to the Father. He shows that the particle in can be also used of the Son and even of the Father, and that on the other hand with may be said of creatures without any infringement on the prerogatives of the Godhead; and that in reality these prepositions simply imply the connection of the Three Divine Persons.
sources.answer: No. Both 'in' and 'with' are conjunctive particles, and conjunction implies no division or lessening. Scripture uses 'in' even of Christ, as when the Father says men will pray 'in Thee', without derogation to Christ, so no derogation to the Spirit follows from saying Christ's glory is in Him.
sources.quote: No division, then, is implied in those particles, for each is a particle of conjunction.
sources.raw_question: Does saying that God is glorified 'in the Holy Spirit' rather than 'with the Holy Spirit' show that the Spirit is inferior to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Every sense in which "in" is used actually helps our conception of the Spirit and, far from lowering Him, glorifies Him. The Spirit is "in" creatures as form in matter, power in what is capable, art in the artist, reason in the soul, whole in parts and even as place; these describe His perfecting and indwelling work in the saints, not inferiority of nature.
sources.quote: For of the senses in which “in” is used, we find that all help our conceptions of the Spirit. Form is said to be in Matter; Power to be in what is capable of it; Habit to be in him who is affected by it; and so on.
sources.raised_by_detail: Pneumatomachi who insisted on 'in the Holy Ghost' rather than 'with'
sources.raw_question: Does the use of the preposition "in" when speaking of the Holy Spirit (e.g., glory to God "in" the Spirit) imply that the Spirit is lower in rank than the Father and Son?

question: Does the title 'Son of God' show that Christ truly shares the Father's divine nature, and not merely the name?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Gregory of Nyssa agree that the title 'Son' signifies a real sharing of the divine nature, but they argue differently. Hilary grounds it in the reality of the birth and charges that a sonship by name without the nature would forfeit even the name. Gregory argues by parallel with 'Son of Man': just as that title shows Christ's real kinship with humanity, 'Son of God' shows his kinship in essence with the Father, so the one word 'Son' claims both natures for him.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Yes. His name accurately describes him, and the title of Son is evidence of a real birth. In his birth he kept the divine nature, and with it the divine power. That power shows itself in his deliberate self-revelation, so he is very God of very God.
sources.quote: the title of Son is an evidence of birth, that in His birth He retained His Divine Nature, and with His nature His power, and that that power manifested itself in conscious and deliberate self-revelation.
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'Son of God' prove that Christ is truly God by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Hilary charges that the Arian creed speaks much of the Son's having the name of Son but nothing of his having the nature. Without the nature, sonship is not truly attributed to him. A Son by name only would in the end have no right even to the name.
sources.quote: They say much about His having the name of Son, but nothing about His having the nature. That is kept out of sight, that He may seem to have no right even to the name.
sources.raw_question: Is it enough to give Christ the title 'Son of God' without affirming that he has the Father's nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He thus shows the oneness of the Eternal Son with the Father the identity of essence and the community of nature (wherein is a natural inquiry into the production of wine), and that the terms “Son” and “product” in the naming of the Only-Begotten include a like idea of relationship.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is called Son of Man because his flesh is kin to the one of whom he was born. Likewise he is Son of God because his essence is connected with that from which he has his existence. Since he shared the whole of human nature, being tempted in all points as we are, he must equally have every property of the transcendent divine essence. The one word "Son" claims both natures for him.
sources.quote: For as He is called the Son of Man by reason of the kindred of His flesh to her of whom He was born, so also He is conceived, surely, as the Son of God, by reason of the connection of His essence
sources.raw_question: Does the title "Son of Man" show that the title "Son of God" implies Christ shares the divine essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He thus shows the oneness of the Eternal Son with the Father the identity of essence and the community of nature (wherein is a natural inquiry into the production of wine), and that the terms “Son” and “product” in the naming of the Only-Begotten include a like idea of relationship.
sources.answer: Just as the name 'Son of Man' teaches Christ's real kinship with true humanity, so 'Son', and even 'product', teaches his kinship in essence with the Father who produced him. The name 'Son' claims for him both natures alike: the human in the man, and the divine in the God.
sources.quote: As, therefore, when we hear from Scripture that the Only-begotten God is Son of man, we learn by the kindred expressed in the name His kinship with true man
sources.raw_question: How does the title 'Son of Man' illuminate what the title 'Son of God' implies about Christ's nature?

question: Since the Father is eternal, can the Son ever have been non-existent, or must an eternal Father have an eternal Son?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Gregory of Nyssa agree that an eternal Father must have an eternal Son, and both rest this on the correlation of Father and Son. Hilary argues that generation consists in the Son's birth with no interval, so any lack of eternity in the Son would equally be lacking in the Father's fatherhood; elsewhere he also appeals to reason, experience and revelation. Gregory argues from the name 'Father', which implies the Son, and from the Son being in the Father, so that the Son could be non-existent only if the Father once was not.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. Fatherhood and sonship are correlatives: generation by the Father consists in the birth of the Son, and there can be no interval between them. Hence whatever measure of eternity is lacking to the Son would equally be lacking to the Father as Source, so denying the Son's eternity denies the Father's eternal fatherhood.
sources.quote: Therefore if any measure of eternity is wanting to Him Who has been born of the eternal Father, clearly the very same measure is wanting to the Author of His being
sources.raw_question: If the Son were not eternal, would that diminish the eternity of the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: No. The Son cannot be thought of apart from the Father, since the very name 'Father' implies the Son and conveys both Persons equally. Only if the Father once was not could the Son's eternity be cancelled; since the Father always is, the Son always is.
sources.quote: if the Father is always, how can the Son ever be non-existent, when He cannot be thought of at all by Himself apart from the Father, but is always implied silently in the name Father.
sources.raw_question: If the Father is eternal, can the Son ever have been non-existent?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Neither reason nor experience allows us to speak of any but an eternal Son proceeding from an eternal Father. God has revealed to us the fact of the Son's birth, and the knowledge of the eternity of that birth sustains piety.
sources.quote: since neither reason nor experience allow us to speak of any but an eternal Son as proceeding from a Father Who is eternal.
sources.raw_question: Can an eternal Father have a Son who is not eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: No. The Son cannot be thought of apart from the Father, because the name 'Father' itself implies the Son. If the Father always is, the Son always is, since the Son is in the Father. He was before all times and is in no place apart from the Father, so there is no category in which his non-existence could be found.
sources.quote: but if the Father is always, how can the Son ever be non-existent, when He cannot be thought of at all by Himself apart from the Father, but is always implied silently in the name Father.
sources.raw_question: Since the Father is eternal, can the Son ever have been non-existent?

question: Does the Son share the Father's own glory in full, or does he have a different or merely received glory?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Gregory of Nyssa agree that the Son has the Father's own glory, not a different or lesser one, but they argue differently. Hilary reasons from the Son giving believers the glory he received, which unites them to the Father's glory. Gregory argues that the 'Brightness of glory' cannot lack glory in itself, cites Scripture that all the Father has is the Son's, and holds that the Son possesses the Father's glory whole and undivided, turning Eunomius's phrase 'no divider of His glory' against him.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. The glory the Son gives is the very glory he received from the Father. Through that glory all believers are brought into the unity of the Father's glory. A Son whose glory unites believers to the Father's glory cannot himself have a different glory.
sources.quote: I ask how can the Son be of a different glory from the Father’s, since the glory of the Son brings all that believe into the unity of the Father’s glory
sources.raw_question: Can the Son possess a glory different from the Father's?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: No. To say the Brightness of the Father's glory has glory only by receiving it is to say that the Brightness of glory is in itself devoid of glory. That would make it needy of glory, which is absurd.
sources.quote: one who says concerning the Brightness of the Father’s glory, that He has the glory by having received it, says in effect that the Brightness of the glory is in Itself devoid of glory
sources.raw_question: Does the Son possess glory only as something received from the Father rather than sharing the Father's glory?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: No. To say the Brightness of the Father's glory has glory only by receiving it makes him devoid of glory in himself. Scripture says the Son will be seen in the glory of the Father and that all things the Father has are his. Glory is surely included among those "all things." As heir of all things, the Son shares in the Father's glory.
sources.quote: one who says concerning the Brightness of the Father’s glory, that He has the glory by having received it, says in effect that the Brightness of the glory is in Itself devoid of glory
sources.raw_question: Does the Son merely receive glory from the Father without sharing the Father's glory?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: The Son does not divide the glory. He has the Father's glory in its entirety, just as the Father has all the Son's glory. Christ says to the Father, "All Mine are Thine and Thine are Mine." Eunomius's phrase "no divider of His glory" is therefore true in a sense he does not understand.
sources.quote: the Son does not divide the glory with the Father, but has the glory of the Father in its entirety, even as the Father has all the glory of the Son
sources.raw_question: Does the Son divide the Father's glory with Him, or does He possess the Father's glory whole?

question: Can God the Father be truly known apart from the Son, whether through creation or otherwise?
synthesis: Owen and Athanasius both answer no, citing Christ's words that the Father is known only through the Son. Their grounds differ. Owen argues that God is known only by the love and pardoning mercy revealed in Christ, and that without the Son one knows an idol; he appeals to John 1:18 and the Son as the true Light. Athanasius argues that because creation was made through the Word, rightly contemplating creation means contemplating the Son, and through him the Father.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Whoever does not know God by the properties revealed only in Christ, his love and pardoning mercy, does not know him at all but knows an idol. He that has not the Son has not the Father, and God is known as Father only as he is love and full of pardoning mercy in Christ. The Son gives us understanding to know him that is true.
sources.quote: He that hath not the Son, the same hath not the Father, 1 John ii. 23; and not to have God as a Father, is not to have him at all
sources.raw_question: Can one truly know God the Father without knowing the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: No. Creation came to be through the Son, so contemplating it rightly means contemplating the Word who framed it, and through Him one begins to apprehend the Father. Christ himself says no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom he reveals Him, and he told Philip not 'behold the creation' but 'he that hath seen Me hath seen the Father.'
sources.quote: he who contemplates the creation rightly, is contemplating also the Word who framed it, and through Him begins to apprehend the Father
sources.raw_question: Can creation make God the Father known apart from the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Owen points to John 1:18: no one has seen God at any time, but the only begotten Son, who is in the Father's bosom, has revealed him. God is known on no other basis than the Son's revelation. The Son is the true Light who has light in himself, and no one has any light except from him.
sources.quote: He is not seen at another time, John i. 18, nor known upon any other account, but only the revelation of the Son. He hath manifested him from his own bosom
sources.raw_question: Can God be truly known apart from the revelation given by the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: No. Creation came to be through the Son, and in him all things consist. Whoever rightly contemplates creation therefore contemplates the Word who framed it, and through him begins to apprehend the Father. Christ himself says that no one knows the Father except through the Son, and 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father.'
sources.quote: it must follow that he who contemplates the creation rightly, is contemplating also the Word who framed it, and through Him begins to apprehend the Father
sources.raw_question: Can creation make God known apart from the Son?

question: What does the Holy Spirit's descent as a dove at Christ's baptism signify about the Spirit's relation to the Father and the Son?
synthesis: The two authors read the event differently. Edwards takes the dove as Scripture's emblem of love and says the Spirit coming from the Father onto the beloved Son shows that the Spirit is the Father's infinite love for the Son, the same meaning as the voice from heaven. Ambrose instead sees the event as displaying the Spirit's unity with the Father and the Son in operation, honour and the gift of baptism, with the Spirit bearing witness to Christ.

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: It signified the Father's infinite love for the Son. The visible sign of the Spirit descending as a dove meant the same thing as the audible voice heard at the same moment, "This is My beloved Son in whom I am well pleased." The dove is the emblem of love, so the Spirit coming from the Father to the Son shows that the Spirit is the Father's love to the Son.
sources.quote: The same was signified by what was exhibited to the eye in the appearance there was of the Holy Ghost descending from the Father to the Son in the shape of a dove, as was signified by what was exhibited to the eye in the voice
sources.raw_question: What did the Holy Spirit's descent as a dove from the Father onto Christ at His baptism signify?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: It signifies that the Spirit is the infinite love of the Father toward the Son. Scripture, especially the Song of Solomon, uses the dove as an emblem of love or a lover. The Spirit descended from the Father on Christ, the true beloved, in that form. The voice from heaven at the same moment, 'This is my beloved Son', signified the same thing.
sources.quote: It was under this similitude that the Holy Ghost descended from the Father on Christ at His baptism, signifying the infinite love of the Father to the Son, Who is the true David, or beloved
sources.raw_question: What does the dove at Christ's baptism signify about the Holy Spirit's relation to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIV. Besides the evidence adduced above, other passages can be brought to prove the sovereignty of the Three Persons. Two are quoted from the Epistles to the Thessalonians, and by collating other testimonies of the Scriptures it is shown that in them dominion is claimed for the Spirit as for the other Persons. Then, by quotation of another still more express passage in the second Epistle to the Corinthians, it is inferred both that the Spirit is Lord, and that where the Lord is, there is the Spirit.
sources.answer: It shows that the Spirit's working is one with that of the Father and the Son. The Father himself pointed out the Spirit descending and abiding on Christ, and the Spirit thereby bore witness to Christ, perfected the sacrament of baptism, and displayed the unity of divine operation.
sources.quote: that He might both bear witness to His wisdom, and perfect the sacrament of the spiritual laver, and show that His working is one with that of the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: What does the descent of the Spirit as a dove at Christ's baptism show about the Spirit's relation to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter I. Not only were the prophets and apostles sent by the Spirit, but also the Son of God. This is proved from Isaiah and the evangelists, and it is explained why St. Luke wrote that the same Spirit descended like a dove upon Christ and abode upon Him. Next, after establishing this mission of Christ, the writer infers that the Son is sent by the Father and the Spirit, as the Spirit is by the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: It shows that the Spirit shares one honour in authority, one operation in the mystery, and one gift in baptism with the Father and the Son. It would be absurd to think the Spirit, in whom the Lord himself was baptized, too weak for a servant to be baptized in him.
sources.quote: that He had a share of the one honour in authority, the one operation in the mystery, the one gift in the bath, together with the Father and the Son
sources.raw_question: What does the Spirit's manifestation at Christ's baptism show about the Spirit's relation to the Father and the Son?

question: Why does Scripture describe the Son's generation from the Father through several different images, such as sonship, radiance, savour and word from mind?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Athanasius agree that the images accommodate human incapacity to grasp the Son's divine generation, but their emphases differ. Gregory argues that no single image is adequate, so the Holy Spirit lovingly supplies many, each taken only in the respect fitting God; together they show the Son is eternally and inseparably from and with the Father. Athanasius stresses that, because God is incomprehensible, such illustrations give dim but sufficient knowledge of the Son's Godhead, and further disputing about it is madness.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He further shows the operations of God to be expressed by human illustrations; for what hands and feet and the other parts of the body with which men work are, that, in the case of God, the will alone is, in place of these. And so also arises the divergence of generation; wherefore He is called Only-begotten, because He has no community with other generation such as is observed in creation, but in that He is called the “brightness of glory,” and the “savour of ointment,” He shows the close conjunction and co-eternity of His Nature with the Father.
sources.answer: Because no single species of generation suffices to give us an adequate idea of the unspeakable existence of the Only-begotten. Sonship conveys community of nature, so Scripture adds generation by efflux to express further aspects of the Son's divine nature, taking from each only what may reverently be admitted of God.
sources.quote: since this particular species of generation did not suffice to produce in us an adequate idea of the unspeakable existence of the Only-begotten, it employs also another species of generation, that which is the result of efflux
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture use several different images of generation (sonship, brightness, savour, breath) for the Only-begotten rather than one?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He further shows the operations of God to be expressed by human illustrations; for what hands and feet and the other parts of the body with which men work are, that, in the case of God, the will alone is, in place of these. And so also arises the divergence of generation; wherefore He is called Only-begotten, because He has no community with other generation such as is observed in creation, but in that He is called the “brightness of glory,” and the “savour of ointment,” He shows the close conjunction and co-eternity of His Nature with the Father.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit, out of loving-kindness, gives us conceptions of the Only-begotten from many sources. Each familiar mode of generation from a cause is applied only in the way that fits divine conceptions. Taken together, these images teach that the Son is both from the Father and with Him, eternally and inseparably. They therefore remove any force from heresy's claims.
sources.quote: the grace of the Holy Spirit has ordered that our conceptions concerning the Only-begotten Son should arise in us from many sources, it has added also the remaining species of things contemplated in generation,—that, I mean, which is the result of mind and word.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture use several different images of generation (brightness, savour, word from mind) for the Son's begetting?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: No single kind of generation is enough to give us an adequate notion of the Son's ineffable mode of subsistence. Out of loving-kindness, the Holy Spirit arranged for divine conceptions about the Only-begotten to reach us from many quarters. Each image is taken only in the respect in which it fits God.
sources.quote: the grace of the Holy Spirit so ordered that the divine conceptions concerning the Only-begotten should reach us from many quarters, and so be implanted in us
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture use several different kinds of generation (sonship, effulgence, word from mind) to describe the Only-begotten?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Because human nature cannot comprehend God, Scripture offers such illustrations so that we can form ideas of him from them, however poorly and dimly. Creation gives sufficient knowledge of God's being and providence. In the same way, these images are sufficient regarding the Son's Godhead, and it is mad to dispute further about it.
sources.quote: such illustrations and such images has Scripture proposed, that, considering the inability of human nature to comprehend God, we might be able to form ideas even from these however poorly and dimly, and as far as is attainable
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture use images like light and radiance or mind and reason to describe the Son's relation to the Father?

question: Is the Holy Spirit to be worshipped and believed in as God?
synthesis: Owen and Ambrose agree that the Holy Spirit is to be worshipped, but they argue differently. Owen extends Christ's call for faith in himself alongside the Father to the Spirit, and appeals to the distinct operations of the Persons. Ambrose argues that we serve the Spirit and only God may be served and adored, that Scripture never places the Spirit among those who worship, and that the Spirit's work in the adored Incarnation shows he too is to be adored.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ called for faith in himself as well as in the Father ("Believe in God, believe also in me"), and this extends equally to the Holy Spirit. The Spirit, now carrying out his delegated work, requires the same. Scripture also mentions the distinct operations of the Persons.
sources.quote: I say that we are distinctly to worship the Holy Ghost. As it is in the case of faith in respect of the Father and the Son, John xiv. 1, “Believe in God, believe also in me,” — this extends itself no less to the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: Should the Holy Spirit be distinctly worshipped and believed in?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVIII. As he purposes to establish the Godhead of the Holy Spirit by the points already discussed, St. Ambrose touches again on some of them; for instance, that He does not commit but forgives sin; that He is not a creature but the Creator; and lastly, that He does not offer but receives worship.
sources.answer: He is to be worshipped. Scripture never says the Spirit worships, though it bids the angels worship the Son. The Spirit is not among the servants; with the Father and the Son He receives the service of the just ("We serve the Spirit of God"). Since only the Lord God is to be served and worshipped, the Spirit we serve we also adore.
sources.quote: For how can He worship Who is not amongst servants and ministers, but, together with the Father and the Son, has the service of the just under Him, for it is written: “We serve the Spirit of God.”
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit to be worshipped, or does He Himself worship?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: Yes. The mystery of the Incarnation is to be adored, and Scripture attributes the Incarnation to the Holy Spirit coming upon Mary. Therefore since He who according to the flesh was born of the Spirit is adored, the Spirit also is without doubt to be adored.
sources.quote: without doubt the Holy Spirit also is to be adored, since He Who according to the flesh was born of the Holy Spirit is adored
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Incarnation is the work of the Holy Spirit show that the Holy Spirit is to be worshipped?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVIII. As he purposes to establish the Godhead of the Holy Spirit by the points already discussed, St. Ambrose touches again on some of them; for instance, that He does not commit but forgives sin; that He is not a creature but the Creator; and lastly, that He does not offer but receives worship.
sources.answer: Yes. The Apostle teaches that we serve the Spirit of God, and the law commands that we serve and worship the Lord God alone. Whom we serve we also adore. Therefore the Spirit, whom we serve, is to be worshipped as God.
sources.quote: He is, therefore, to be worshipped by us, Whom the Apostle taught that we must serve, and Whom we serve we also adore
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit to be worshipped as God?

question: Are Jesus, born of Mary, and the Christ, the eternal Son of God, one and the same, or two distinct beings or persons?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Ambrose agree that the one born of Mary and the eternal Son of God are one and the same. Irenaeus argues against the Gnostic separation of Jesus from a Christ who descended on him, appealing to the apostolic witness of Matthew, Paul (Romans and Galatians) and Peter on Jesus's anointing with the Spirit. Ambrose states it as a two-birth formula: the same one born of the Father before the world was born in the world as man by taking flesh.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: They are one and the same. Irenaeus argues that the apostles, and Matthew in particular, recognised one and the same Jesus Christ, born as man of the Virgin. The Gnostic division of Jesus who was born from a Christ who descended from above contradicts the apostolic witness, and those teaching it are agents of Satan overturning the faith.
sources.quote: that we should not imagine that Jesus was one, and Christ another, but should know them to be one and the same.
sources.raw_question: Are Jesus (born of Mary) and Christ (the divine Saviour) two distinct beings, with Christ descending upon the man Jesus as a receptacle, or are they one and the same?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXII. In proof of the Unity in Trinity the passage of Isaiah which has been cited is considered, and it is shown that there is no difference as to its sense amongst those who expound it of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Spirit. If He Who was crucified was Lord of glory, so, too, is the Holy Spirit equal in all things to the Father and the Son, and the Arians will never be able to diminish His glory.
sources.answer: No. Christ is not one of two but one. The same one was born as Son of God from the Father before the world and was born in the world as man by taking flesh.
sources.quote: For Christ is not one of two, but is one, and was born as Son of God of the Father before the world; and in the world born as man by taking flesh.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ two persons, the eternal Son and the man born of Mary?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: They are one and the same. Paul's words to the Romans and Galatians show one God who promised His Son through the prophets, and one Jesus Christ who was of David's seed by birth from Mary and was also declared Son of God with power. The Son of God himself was made the Son of man.
sources.quote: plainly indicating one God, who did by the prophets make promise of the Son, and one Jesus Christ our Lord, who was of the seed of David according to His birth from Mary
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics (Valentinians, Cerinthians) who distinguish Jesus from Christ
sources.raw_question: Are Jesus, born of Mary, and the Christ, the Son of God, one and the same Person, or is the Christ a separate being who descended upon a merely human Jesus?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: They are one and the same. Peter testified that Jesus himself is the Son of God, who, having been anointed with the Holy Spirit, is called Jesus Christ. He is the same being who was born of Mary.
sources.quote: he witnessed that Jesus was Himself the Son of God, who also, having been anointed with the Holy Spirit, is called Jesus Christ. And He is the same being that was born of Mary
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus, the Christ anointed with the Holy Spirit, the same being as the Son of God who was born of Mary, or are they distinct beings?

question: Does Christ's saying that he came not to do his own will but the will of the Father who sent him (John 6:38) show that the Son's will is opposed, subordinate or unfree relative to the Father's?
synthesis: Hilary and Bickersteth both deny that the saying makes the Son's will inferior or opposed, and both cite 'Father, I will' (John 17:24) as evidence. Hilary grounds his answer in the one nature of Father and Son: the saying distinguishes the Persons, but the Son's will is the same in nature as the Father's and is freely to do it. Bickersteth instead distinguishes the two natures: as man Christ's will was subjected to the Father's, while as God it was free, self-existent and in perfect harmony with the Father's.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The saying serves to prove His birth by distinguishing His Person from the Father's, but His will is the same in nature as the Father's. This is shown when He says, 'Father, those whom Thou hast given Me, I will, that where I am they also may be with Me': the Father wills that we be with Christ, and the Son wills the same.
sources.quote: His will is, therefore, the same in nature as the Father’s will, though to make plain the fact of the birth it is distinguished from the Father’s.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that He came not to do His own will but the will of the Father who sent Him show that the Son's will differs from or is subordinate to the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The Son does not cast out those given him or do his own will instead of the Father's in order to reveal Sender and Sent as one indistinguishable nature. It is not that he does not will what he does; rather he shows that all he wills, says and does is the will and work of the Father because they share one nature.
sources.quote: not that He does not will what He does, or is not Himself heard when He teaches; but in order that He may reveal Him Who sent Him, and Himself the Sent, under the aspect of one indistinguishable nature
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that he came not to do his own will but the will of the Father who sent him show that the Son lacks free will and is subject to necessity through weakness of nature?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. As man his will was subjected to the Father's; but as God his will was always in perfect harmony with the Father's while being self-existent, free and efficacious. This is shown by Christ's sovereign "Father, I will" (John 17:24) and his "I will" in healing the leper (Matt 8:3).
sources.quote: His will, therefore, as man, was subjected to that of his Father: as God, was ever in perfect harmony with his Father’s will, but was self-existent, free, efficacious.
sources.raw_question: Does John 6:38 ("not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me") show that the Son's will is merely subordinate to the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. The Son was not unwilling; he spoke this way to manifest his obedience as flowing from the Father's will. His own will is precisely to do the Father's will, so there is no opposition between them.
sources.quote: It was not that He Himself was unwilling, but that He might manifest His obedience as the result of His Father’s will, for His own will is to do His Father’s.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that he came not to do his own will but the will of the Father who sent him imply that the Son's will was opposed to or unwilling toward the Father's will?

question: Does Christ's saying 'To sit on my right hand and on my left is not mine to give' (Matthew 20:23) show that the Son lacks authority to bestow glory?
synthesis: Both authors say no, but on different grounds. Augustine reads the saying as spoken according to the form of a servant, while in the form of God the Son is equal to the Father and prepares and gives glory with him. Bickersteth argues from the Greek, holding that the English adds words not in the original and that the idiom means 'save to those for whom it is prepared'. He then cites Revelation 3:21 to show that Christ disposes heavenly dignities as he wills.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. The English translation adds words that are not in the original. The Greek idiom means 'save to those for whom it is prepared', as in the parallel at Matthew 19:11. The promise in Revelation 3:21, 'To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne', proves that Christ does as he wills with his own in heavenly dignities.
sources.quote: The promise to the church of Laodicea sufficiently proves that in respect of heavenly dignities, Jesus Christ does as He wills with his own.
sources.raw_question: Does Matthew 20:23, 'to sit on my right hand ... is not mine to give', show that Christ lacks authority to bestow heavenly dignities?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. 'It is not mine to give' is spoken according to the form of a servant and means it is not in human power to give. He gives it through that by which he is God equal to the Father. Since all things the Father has are his, this belongs to him too, and he prepared these things with the Father.
sources.quote: we are so to understand “It is not mine to give,” as if it were said, This is not in the power of man to give; that so He may be understood to give it through that wherein He is God equal to the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement 'It is not mine to give' deny that the Son has power to give glory, unlike the sending texts which do not deny the other Person's role?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. It must be read the same way as "believeth not on me" and "I will not judge." In such sayings Christ turns attention to the Father according to the form of a servant, without separating himself from the Father. According to the form of God he is equal to the Father.
sources.quote: so also, when He says, “It is not mine to give, but [it shall be given to them] for whom it is prepared by my Father,” it is I think plain in what relation both are to be taken.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "It is not mine to give, but it shall be given to them for whom it is prepared by my Father" show that the Son lacks the Father's authority?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. According to the form of God, Christ is the Lord of glory who justifies and therefore also glorifies his saints. The saying was spoken according to the form of a servant. What the Father prepares, the Son also prepares, because he and the Father are one and the Trinity works indivisibly.
sources.quote: If, therefore, He has also glorified those whom He has justified, He who justifies, Himself also glorifies; who is, as I have said, the Lord of glory.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'To sit on my right hand and on my left is not mine to give' show that the Son lacks the Father's power to bestow glory?

question: Do Christ's weeping, suffering and death imply weakness or inferiority in his divine nature?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Bickersteth both deny that Christ's lowliness, suffering or death imply any weakness or inferiority in his divine nature, but on different grounds. Hilary distinguishes the two natures in the one Person, assigning death and tears to the assumed humanity and life to the divine power, and says Christ wept and died for us rather than for himself. Bickersteth instead treats the humiliation as a voluntary act: Christ became poor for our sakes and laid down his life of his own accord, so it shows God's condescension and should kindle gratitude rather than offence.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Paul attributes Christ's death to human infirmity, that is, to the body he assumed, and his life to divine power. Christ is one Person of two natures. His death belongs to the nature he shared with us, and his life belongs to God, whose nature it is to live.
sources.quote: For though He was crucified through weakness, yet He liveth through the power of God, attributing His death to human infirmity, but His life to divine power
sources.raw_question: Did Christ's death through weakness and his life through the power of God imply that the divine nature in Christ suffered infirmity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Far from being a reason to take offence, the lowliness of his incarnation and the degradation of his death should kindle greater gratitude. Though he was rich, for our sakes he became poor. He laid down his life of his own accord and took it again. His humiliation therefore shows the condescension of God rather than any inferiority of nature.
sources.quote: so far from taking offence at the inferiority of the position which He assumed, the very lowliness of his incarnation and the very degradation of the death He died, will kindle in us a brighter and a more burning gratitude
sources.raw_question: Does the lowliness of Christ's incarnation and death detract from his divine glory?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The body weeps only at the command of a sorrowing soul. 'Far less' can God have wept, since he was about to be glorified in Lazarus and to give life. Tears and grief do not belong to the one about to restore the dead and receive glory as God; yet the same Christ who wept was also the Giver of life.
sources.quote: Far less can God have wept, for He was to be glorified in Lazarus.
sources.raw_question: Can Christ's weeping and grieving be ascribed to God the Word in his divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Christ wept not for Himself but for us, to prove the reality of the manhood He had assumed. He died not for Himself but for our life, so that human life might be renewed by the death of the deathless God.
sources.quote: Christ died not for Himself, but for our life, to renew human life by the death of the deathless God
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's weeping and dying show weakness in His divine nature?

question: In John 16:14-15, when Christ says 'All things that the Father hath are mine' and that the Spirit 'shall take of mine,' is he speaking of the divine nature and essential attributes shared by Father and Son, or of something else such as gifts or grace?
synthesis: The authors differ. Owen denies that Christ speaks of the essence and essential properties: the 'things' are the grace and fruits of Christ's mediation, purchased by his death and provided in the Father's love, which the Spirit receives and bestows on believers. Hilary holds that the words refer to the divine nature itself, the Father's power, eternity, providence and authority, which the Son has as his own and not as outward possessions, so that they declare his unity of nature with the Father.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No. Christ speaks not of the divine essence and essential properties but of the grace communicated to believers by the Father and Son. These are 'his things' as the fruit of his purchase and mediation, namely what the Father in eternal love provided to be dispensed in the blood of the Son, all the fruits of election. The Spirit receives these to dispose and declare them for believers' good.
sources.quote: It is not of the essence and essential properties of the Father and Son that our Saviour speaks; but of the grace which is communicated to us by them. This Christ calls, “My things,” being the fruit of his purchase and mediation
sources.raw_question: In John 16:14-15, when Christ says the Spirit 'shall take of mine' and 'all things that the Father hath are mine,' is he speaking of the essence and essential properties of the Father and Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It refers to the divine nature. There is no mention of coming into possession; possessing external things differs from being self-existent and describable by one's own properties. The Son's 'all things' are those of which He Himself subsists, declaring His unity of nature with the Father as only-begotten.
sources.quote: When He says, therefore, that all things which the Father has, are His, He alludes to the divine nature, and not to a joint ownership of gifts bestowed.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'All things whatsoever the Father hath are Mine' refer to a joint ownership of gifts or to the divine nature itself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: It refers to what belongs properly and peculiarly to Christ as mediator. This is the fruit of his life and death unto holiness. Christ furnishes the Spirit with this, and the Spirit bestows it on the saints. This shows how Christ sends the Spirit.
sources.quote: He shall take of mine (of that which is properly and peculiarly so, — mine, as mediator, — the fruit of my life and death unto holiness), and give it unto you.
sources.raw_question: In John 16:14-15, what is meant by Christ's saying that the Spirit 'shall take of mine' and give it to believers?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: He is not speaking of created things or material processes. He means the glory of the perfect Divinity: the Father's power, eternity, providence and authority. These are not extraneous possessions but the ways God himself is expressed to our understanding. So the Son has all that the Father has, and the Spirit receives from the Son. These gifts give the Son the same attributes as the Father.
sources.quote: All that the Father hath are His, delivered and received: but these gifts do not degrade His divinity, since they give Him the same attributes as the Father.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean by saying 'All things whatsoever the Father hath are Mine' (John 16:15)?

question: Was it the Son, the Word of God, who appeared and spoke to the patriarchs and Moses in the Old Testament theophanies?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Hilary agree that the Son was the one who appeared and spoke in the Old Testament theophanies. Irenaeus grounds this in Christ's saying that Moses wrote of him and in the unity of the one Word who gave both covenants and so spans the law and the Gospel. Hilary stresses the mode of these appearances: the Son took created forms (angel, man, fire) so that he could be seen and heard, teaching men to know God for their salvation.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter X.—The Old Testament Scriptures, and those written by Moses in particular, do everywhere make mention of the Son of God, and foretell His advent and passion. From this fact it follows that they were inspired by one and the same God.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ said Moses wrote of him, because the Son of God is implanted throughout Moses' writings. It was the Son who spoke with Abraham, gave Noah the dimensions of the ark, sought Adam, judged Sodom, directed Jacob, and spoke with Moses from the bush.
sources.quote: because the Son of God is implanted everywhere throughout his writings: at one time, indeed, speaking with Abraham, when about to eat with him; at another time with Noah, giving to him the dimensions [of the ark]
sources.raw_question: Was the Son of God the one who appeared and spoke in the Old Testament theophanies recorded by Moses?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. The Son assumed the guise of created beings, angel, man, fire, so that He could be heard, seen and touched, as when Adam heard Him walking or Jacob wrestled Him. This was the 'creation for the ways of God' from the beginning of the ages, designed to teach men to know God and to profit their salvation.
sources.quote: to all the rest to whom He presented Himself in the form of various created beings, for the ways of God and for the works of God, that is to say, to teach us to know God, and to profit our eternal state.
sources.raw_question: Were the Old Testament theophanies (to Adam, Hagar, Abraham, Jacob, Moses) appearances of the Son in a created form?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VII.—Recapitulation of the foregoing argument, showing that Abraham, through the revelation of the Word, knew the Father, and the coming of the Son of God. For this cause, he rejoiced to see the day of Christ, when the promises made to him should be fulfilled. The fruit of this rejoicing has flowed to posterity, viz., to those who are partakers in the faith of Abraham, but not to the Jews who reject the Word of God.
sources.answer: Yes. The God who spoke in human shape to Abraham, and who told Moses that He had seen His people's affliction and come down to deliver them, was the Son, the Word of God. The Son arranged these things beforehand from the beginning. Those who reject the Word are therefore ignorant of the God who spoke to the patriarchs.
sources.quote: they being ignorant of that God who spake in human shape to Abraham, and again to Moses, saying, “I have surely seen the affliction of My people in Egypt, and I have come down to deliver them.”
sources.raw_question: Was it the Son, the Word, who spoke and appeared to Abraham and Moses in the Old Testament theophanies?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IX.—There is but one author, and one end to both covenants.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus identifies the householder who produced both covenants as the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who spoke with both Abraham and Moses. The same Lord who gave the law now gives the Gospel, so the Son's activity spans both dispensations.
sources.quote: the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who spake with both Abraham and Moses, and who has restored us anew to liberty, and has multiplied that grace which is from Himself.
sources.raw_question: Was the Word of God (Christ) the one who spoke with Abraham and Moses in the Old Testament?

question: Who appeared to Abraham at Mamre, and what does that appearance reveal about God?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers holds that the one 'Man' Abraham worshipped was truly the Lord God. He argues that the Man who made the promise is the Lord who fulfilled it, and sees the scene as a foreshadowing of the Incarnation. Augustine instead reads the three men, none greater than the others and addressed in the singular as one Lord, as a created sign of the one substance and equality of the Trinity. He explicitly denies that the appearance shows the Son alone.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture calls the speaker a Man, yet says the Lord visited Sarah and God did as He had said, at the time of which God had spoken; so the Man who promised is the Lord God who fulfilled the promise. Abraham worshipped Him as Lord, beholding in mystery the coming Incarnation.
sources.quote: The Man made the promise in the power of God; by the same power God fulfilled the promise. Thus God reveals Himself both in word and deed.
sources.raw_question: Was the 'man' who appeared to Abraham at Mamre and promised Sarah a son truly God and Lord, rather than a mere man or angel?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: The narrative opens with "The Lord appeared to him" and then explains how: by three men. Abraham invites them in the plural but speaks to them in the singular as to the Lord God, who as one promises a son and reveals Sodom's destruction. The appearance therefore points to one Lord shown through three, and it does not identify the Son alone as the one who appeared.
sources.quote: whom Abraham invites to his hospitality in the plural number, and afterwards speaks to them in the singular number as one; and as one He promises him a son by Sara
sources.raw_question: What does it signify that at Mamre Abraham saw three men but addressed them in the singular as one Lord?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Abraham, though he saw three, worshipped One and acknowledged Him as Lord. Nothing in outward appearance distinguished them, but by the eye of faith he recognized his Lord. This One then promises Sarah's son and later fulfils it as the Lord, so the Man seen is the Lord God, a mysterious foreshadowing of the Incarnation.
sources.quote: Abraham, though he sees three, worships One, and acknowledges Him as Lord. Three were standing before him, Scripture says, but he knew well Which it was that he must worship and confess.
sources.raw_question: When Abraham saw three men at Mamre, whom did he worship, and what does this show about the One who appeared?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Of the Same Appearance.
sources.answer: It visibly intimates, through a created form, the equality of the Trinity and one substance in three persons. Three men appeared, none of them said to be greater than the others in form, age, or power, and yet Scripture says 'the Lord appeared' and Abraham addresses them as one Lord.
sources.quote: why should we not here understand, as visibly intimated by the visible creature, the equality of the Trinity, and one and the same substance in three persons?
sources.raw_question: What does the appearance of three men to Abraham at Mamre signify about the Trinity?

question: Can a sinner become righteous or acceptable before God by his own righteousness or by keeping the law, apart from Christ?
synthesis: Owen and Augustine agree that no one can be made fit for God by their own righteousness, but on different grounds. Owen argues from the law's weakness through the flesh, Scripture concluding all under sin, and the error of trying to establish one's own righteousness instead of submitting to God's. Augustine says those who think they can be cleansed apart from the Mediator are stained above all by pride, which only the cross of the Lord overcomes.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. The Jews caught hold of the law, and it could not relieve them. Setting up their own righteousness kept them from submitting to the righteousness of God. The law is weak through the flesh, and Paul counts all his own righteousness as loss. Nothing a person has done, can do, or ever will do can justify him before God.
sources.quote: The law put them upon setting up a righteousness of their own. This kept them doing, and in hope; but kept them from submitting to the righteousness of God.
sources.raw_question: Can a person's own righteousness, or the works of the law, make him acceptable to God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
