sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > They are Proud Who Think They are Able, by Their Own Righteousness, to Be Cleansed So as to See God.
sources.answer: No. Those who think so are stained above all by their very pride, the sin to which the divine law is most opposed and over which the devil gains the greatest mastery. That proud spirit is overcome only by the cross of the Lord, prefigured by Moses holding out his hands against Amalek.
sources.quote: There are, however, some who think themselves capable of being cleansed by their own righteousness, so as to contemplate God, and to dwell in God; whom their very pride itself stains above all others.
sources.raw_question: Can human beings be cleansed by their own righteousness so as to contemplate God and dwell in him, apart from the Mediator?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. The law has fair pleas: it came from God, it contains all the obedience he requires, and it carries the promise of life. Yet Israel, which earnestly pursued the law of righteousness, did not attain it. Their failure came not merely from lack of effort but from the nature of the thing itself. Since Scripture concludes all under sin, and the law speaks only death to sinners, it cannot give life, and God himself declared this way insufficient.
sources.quote: It was not solely for want of endeavour in themselves that they were disappointed, for they earnestly followed after the law of righteousness; but from the nature of the thing itself, — it would not bear it.
sources.raw_question: Can a sinner obtain a righteousness that will stand before God by keeping the law?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Owen argues this seeking of righteousness "as it were by the works of the law" springs from ignorance of God's righteousness and the exact conformity he requires. Those who go about to establish their own righteousness do not submit to God's righteousness; such a mixture may pacify conscience for a time, but fails when the Spirit convinces of righteousness.
sources.quote: Had they known the righteousness of God, and what exact conformity to his will he requireth, they had never undertaken such a fruitless business as to have compassed it “as it were by the works of the law.”
sources.raw_question: Can sinners attain righteousness before God by combining their own works of atonement or new obedience with a hope of God's general mercy?

question: How should Christ's statement 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30) be understood?
synthesis: Both authors ground the oneness in the Son's birth from the Father. Hilary of Poitiers explains it as a unity of nature through which the Father speaks, works and abides in the Son, a unity in the one Spirit. He insists it is neither the oneness of a single solitary person nor a division into two. Novatian uses the text mainly to argue that Christ is God: no mere man could say it, and Christ can be called one with the Father because, as Son born from the Father, he is also God.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It should be understood through what Christ himself explained: the Father speaks in His words, works through His works, judges through His judgment, is seen in Him and abides in Him. Through the truth of the birth and the unity of nature, whatever the Son did and said, the Father did and said in the Son.
sources.quote: through the truth of the birth and the unity of the nature, it is declared that whatever the Son did and said, the Father said and did in the Son?
sources.raw_question: How should Christ's statement 'I and the Father are one' be understood?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It is not the oneness of a single solitary being. It is unity in the one Spirit. One cannot collapse them into a union of person that makes God single, and one cannot divide the Spirit so as to keep the Two from being One.
sources.quote: signifies that Both are One not after the manner of the soleness of a single being, but in the unity of the Spirit
sources.raw_question: What kind of oneness does Christ mean when he says 'I and the Father are one'?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: He could not say it if he were merely a man. He can be called one with the Father because he is the Son, born of the Father and proceeding from him. It is by this birth from the Father that he is also God.
sources.quote: For how can it be that “I and the Father are one,” if He is not both God and the Son?
sources.raw_question: How can Christ say "I and the Father are one" if he is not God?

question: Can the Son be called a creature and still be truly God, or is he truly God from God?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary of Poitiers agree that a created Son cannot truly be God, but argue differently. Gregory builds a dilemma: calling a creature 'God' is an empty title, so his opponents are either Jews in disguise who deny the Son's Godhead or idolaters who worship a created God. Hilary rests the Son's true Godhead on a real birth of the divine nature from the divine nature, and says that without it the Son becomes either an alien god of another kind from the Father or no God at all.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: No. Calling a creature alien from the Father's essence 'God' is an empty title, like calling Bel or Dagon God. Those who hold the Son created must either admit he is not God at all, which makes them Jews in disguise, or confess a created God, which makes them idolaters.
sources.quote: Let those, therefore, who affirm that He is created, acknowledge that He is not God at all, that they may be seen to be nothing but Jews in disguise, or, if they confess one who is created to be God, let them not deny that they are idolaters.
sources.raw_question: Can someone consistently call the Son a creature and still call him God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Hilary argues that calling the Son 'a creature' is the same blasphemy as the Jews' charge that He was a mere man making Himself God. If the Son does not subsist by a true birth from God, He becomes a strange, alien god of another kind from the Father, or else not God at all. True Godhead in the Son rests on His being God begotten of God by a true birth.
sources.quote: you make Him God of another kind from the Father, or else not God at all, as not subsisting by a birth from God.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be called a creature, or God of a different kind from the Father, without denying that He is truly God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: He is truly God going forth from God. He is not a creature picked out to bear the name of God; his going forth is a real birth of the divine nature from the divine nature.
sources.quote: It is God going forth from God, not a creature picked out to bear the name of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son a creature given the name of God, or truly God from God?

question: Do texts saying that God alone stretched out the heavens, or calling God 'One', 'Only' and 'First' with none beside Him, exclude the Son from being God?
synthesis: Athanasius and Waterland agree that the Son is not excluded. Waterland explicitly follows Athanasius: since the heavens were made through the Word yet God says 'I alone', the Word is included in the 'alone', as radiance is implied in light. Athanasius adds that these texts deny only that any other is like the Father and His Word, since all other things came from nothing.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eighthly, John xvii. 3. and the Like. Our Lord's divinity cannot interfere with His Father's prerogatives, as the One God, which were so earnestly upheld by the Son. 'One' is used in contrast to false gods and idols, not to the Son, through whom the Father spoke. Our Lord adds His Name to the Father's, as included in Him. The Father the First, not as if the Son were not First too, but as Origin.
sources.answer: No. Since the heavens were made through the Word, yet God says 'I only,' the Word is evidently included in the 'Only.' Likewise in 'One God,' 'I Only,' and 'I the First,' the coexisting Word is understood, as the radiance is in the light. This applies to the Word alone, since all other things came from nothing and differ in nature.
sources.quote: if it be said, ‘One God,’ and ‘I Only,’ and ‘I the First,’ in that One and Only and First is understood the Word coexisting, as in the Light the Radiance.
sources.raw_question: Do texts saying God alone stretched out the heavens, or that He is 'One' and 'Only,' exclude the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Following Athanasius, when God says 'I alone stretch forth the heavens,' the Word, in whom all things were made, is also signified in him who is alone. Since the heavens were made by the Word and yet God says 'I alone,' the Son is understood to be with the alone God, as effulgence is implied in light.
sources.quote: it is very “ manifest to every man, that in him, who is said to be alone, “the Word of that alone is also signified, in whom all things “ were made, and without whom nothing was made.
sources.raw_question: Do texts saying God alone stretched out the heavens exclude the Son, by whom all things were made?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: No. These texts are not said to deny the Son, who is in that One, Only and First God as His only Word, Wisdom and Radiance. The Son too is First, as the fulness of the Godhead. The texts deny only that there is any other like the Father and His Word.
sources.quote: this is not said to the denial of the Son, perish the thought; for He is in that One, and First and Only, as being of that One and Only and First the Only Word and Wisdom and Radiance.
sources.raw_question: Do texts calling God 'One', 'Only' and 'First', or saying 'beside Me there is no God', exclude the Son from being God?

question: Can the Son be said either to have existed before His birth from the Father or not to have existed before it?
synthesis: Hilary and Athanasius, who here cites Hilary, agree that neither alternative applies. Being born when one already exists would not be true birth but a change, while non-existence before birth would imply time. The Son's eternal birth therefore rules out both options.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Because the Son's birth is before times eternal, it transcends the conditions of human thought, which operate within time. Existence before birth contradicts the very idea of birth, while previous non-existence implies time; so neither alternative applies, and we can only confess that He was born and always existed.
sources.quote: He debars thought from determining concerning Him, whether He was or was not before He was born; since existence before birth is incompatible with the idea of birth, and previous non-existence involves the idea of time.
sources.raw_question: Can we meaningfully ask whether the Son existed before He was born of the Father, or did not exist before His birth?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: No. Hilary holds that to be born when one already was is not really to be born, but to change oneself by being born. Being eternally born before eternal times is not the same as existing before birth. Since being always born means simply being born, the question of whether the Son was or was not before his birth does not apply to him.
sources.quote: Non est itaque id ipsum, natum ante tempora æterna semper esse, et esse antequam nasci.
sources.raised_by_detail: Bishop Bull's proposition 'He was before His generation'
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be said to have existed before his generation, as if he already was and was then born?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Hilary calls the Son only 'born', and for Him eternal existence and birth mean the same thing. The birth of one already existing would not be true birth but a self-wrought change; eternal birth means He is prior to any conception of time, not that He existed prior to His birth. Since existence before birth is incompatible with birth, and non-existence before birth implies time, neither can be thought of Him.
sources.quote: For the birth of One already existing is not really birth, but a self-wrought change through birth, and the eternal existence of One Who is born means that in His birth He is prior to any conception of time
sources.raw_question: If it is inconceivable that the Son did not exist before He was born, does it follow that the Son already existed before He was born?

question: If God is one and Christ is God, does it follow that Christ is God the Father himself?
synthesis: Novatian and Owen agree that Christ's being the one true God does not make him the Father. Novatian argues from Scripture: it holds both the oneness of God and Christ's deity, offers parallels (Christ is called Lord though there is 'one Lord'), and everywhere presents the Son as a second person born of, sent by and obedient to the Father. Owen argues instead that 'true God' refers to the divine nature, not to paternity, and is affirmed equally of each person, so it cannot identify one person with another.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > In Fine, Notwithstanding the Said Heretics Have Gathered the Origin of Their Error from Consideration of What is Written: Although We Call Christ God, and the Father God, Still Scripture Does Not Set Forth Two Gods, Any More Than Two Lords or Two Teachers.
sources.answer: No. Scripture calls Christ God and also says God is one, and both must be held without rejecting either. The modalists' inference does not hold: Christ is called Lord though there is 'one Lord', and Paul is called master though Christ is the 'one Master', and neither case contradicts the oneness Scripture asserts. So Christ's being God does not make him identical with the Father.
sources.quote: But if they do not think that it can by any means interfere with the truth that there is one Lord, that Christ also is Lord, nor with the truth that one is our Master, that Paul also is our master
sources.raised_by_detail: those who say Jesus Christ is God the Father
sources.raw_question: If God is one and Christ is God, does it follow that Christ is God the Father himself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. When the Father is called the true God, the reference is not to his paternity or his relation to the Son but to his divine nature, essence and being. The same is affirmed of the Son and the Spirit. So each person being God does not make one person the other. To argue that it does is simply to refuse what God has revealed without giving any reason.
sources.quote: because, in saying the Father is the true God, we respect not his paternity, or his paternal relation to his Son, but his nature, essence, and being.
sources.raw_question: If the Father is the only true God and Christ is also the only true God, does it follow that Christ is the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, Against the Sabellians He Proves that the Father is One, the Son Another.
sources.answer: No. Those who infer this are misled by the sound of a name and do not know Christ; Scripture everywhere presents the Son as a second person after the Father, born of the Father, sent by Him and obedient to Him. The texts are so numerous that the objection is easily answered.
sources.quote: For thus say they, If it is asserted that God is one, and Christ is God, then say they, If the Father and Christ be one God, Christ will be called the Father. Wherein they are proved to be in error, not knowing Christ, but following the sound of a name
sources.raw_question: If God is one and Christ is God, does it follow that Christ is God the Father?

question: Should the Holy Spirit be glorified together with the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Basil and Ambrose agree that the Spirit is to be glorified together with the Father and the Son (or with Christ), but on different grounds. Basil appeals to the Lord's own ranking of the Spirit with Himself and the Father in the baptismal formula, the warning against blasphemy of the Spirit, and the Spirit's constant association with the Godhead in confession, miracles and grace. Ambrose argues from our own co-glorification with Christ through the Spirit: since the Spirit joins even what was severed, He cannot be separated from His eternal conjunction with Christ.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: Because the Lord himself honoured the Spirit by associating Him with Himself and the Father in the baptismal formula. Our initiation into the knowledge of God takes place through this baptism. Above all, the Lord's threat against blasphemy of the Spirit rules out any thought of indignity or unworthy conception regarding Him.
sources.quote: I was in the first place led to the glory of the Spirit by the honour conferred by the Lord in associating Him with Himself and with His Father at baptism
sources.raw_question: Why should the Holy Spirit be glorified together with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Proof of the absurdity of the refusal to glorify the Spirit, from the comparison of things glorified in creation.
sources.answer: Yes, with the Father and the Son. It is unreasonable to abandon the place the Lord appointed for the Spirit and invent another. The Spirit is everywhere associated with the Godhead: in the confession of faith, in baptism, in miracles, in the indwelling of the saints, and in the graces given. No gift reaches creation without Him, so He cannot be torn from the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: What reason is there for robbing of His share of glory Him Who is everywhere associated with the Godhead; in the confession of the Faith, in the baptism of redemption, in the working of miracles, in the indwelling of the saints, in the graces bestowed on obedience?
sources.raw_question: Granting that the Holy Spirit is to be glorified, should He be glorified together with the Father and the Son rather than separately?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VIII. St. Ambrose examines and refutes the heretical argument that because God is said to be glorified in the Spirit, and not with the Spirit, the Holy Spirit is therefore inferior to the Father. He shows that the particle in can be also used of the Son and even of the Father, and that on the other hand with may be said of creatures without any infringement on the prerogatives of the Godhead; and that in reality these prepositions simply imply the connection of the Three Divine Persons.
sources.answer: Yes. If we ourselves are made joint-heirs with Christ and glorified together with Him through the Spirit, it is absurd to deny that the Spirit Himself is glorified together with Christ. The Spirit who conjoins even what was severed cannot be dissevered from His eternal conjunction with Christ.
sources.quote: If we then shall be glorified together with Christ through the Spirit, how do we refuse to admit that the Spirit Himself is glorified together with Christ?
sources.raw_question: Is it fitting to say that the Holy Spirit is glorified together with Christ?

question: Does the baptismal formula in Matthew 28:19 show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God sharing one Name?
synthesis: Ambrose and Owen both answer yes, but on different grounds. Ambrose argues from the singular 'Name' rather than 'Names'. Owen argues that being baptized into someone's name binds us to worship him as our God, so if the three were not one in nature baptism would bind us to several gods.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XII. The peace and grace of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one, so also is Their charity one, which showed itself chiefly in the redemption of man. Their communion with man is also one.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ said "in the Name," not "in the Names." So the Father, Son and Spirit do not have separate names, because God is one and there are not two or three Gods.
sources.quote: He said, “in the Name,” not “in the Names.” So, then, the Name of the Father is not one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another, for God is one
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula in Matthew 28:19 show that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit share one divine Name?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIII. St. Ambrose shows from the Scriptures that the Name of the Three Divine Persons is one, and first the unity of the Name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as each is called Paraclete and Truth.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ commanded baptism "in the Name" of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, not "in the Names." Since God is one, there are not several divine Names, for there are not two or three Gods. The singular Name thus testifies to the one Godhead of the Three.
sources.quote: He said, “in the Name,” not “in the Names.” So, then, the Name of the Father is not one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another, for God is one
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula in Matthew 28:19 show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit share one Name?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Being baptized into someone's name sacramentally binds us to religious obedience to him and to owning him as the God whose we are and whom we serve. If the Father, Son, and Spirit were not one in nature, baptism would bind us to the worship of more gods than one, which is blasphemous.
sources.quote: For if those into whose name we are baptized be not one in nature, we are by our baptism engaged into the service and worship of more gods than one.
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit prove that the three are one God?

question: Are the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ one and the same Holy Spirit?
synthesis: Hilary and Ambrose agree that it is one and the same Spirit. Hilary grounds this in the one Divinity shared by Father and Son through the birth, and in the one Spirit distributing gifts to the one body of Christ. Ambrose argues exegetically: Paul (Romans 8, 1 Corinthians 12:3) and Peter use 'Spirit of God,' 'Spirit of Christ,' 'Spirit of the Lord' and 'Holy Spirit' interchangeably for the one indwelling Spirit.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. It is the one Spirit of one Divinity, one in both God and Lord through the mystery of the birth. Paul shows that the diverse gifts come from one Lord Jesus Christ, who is the body of all. The one Spirit distributes these gifts for the perfecting of one body.
sources.quote: But if this one Spirit of one Divinity, one in both God and Lord through the mystery of the birth, does not please thee, then point out to me what Spirit both works and distributes these diverse gifts to us
sources.raw_question: Is the Spirit one and the same in God the Father and in the Lord Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IV. The Holy Spirit is one and the same Who spake in the prophets and apostles, Who is the Spirit of God and of Christ; Whom, further, Scripture designates the Paraclete, and the Spirit of life and truth.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul uses "Spirit of God" and "Holy Spirit" interchangeably in 1 Corinthians 12:3, and in Romans 8 he moves between the Spirit of God, the Spirit of Christ, and the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus as one indwelling Spirit. Therefore the Spirit of God is the same as the Spirit of Christ.
sources.quote: The same is, then, the Spirit of God, Who is the Spirit of Christ.
sources.raw_question: Are the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ one and the same Spirit as the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IX. That the Holy Spirit is provoked is proved by the words of St. Peter, in which it is shown that the Spirit of God is one and the same as the Spirit of the Lord, both by other passages and by reference to the sentence of the same Apostle on Ananias and Sapphira, whence it is argued that the union of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, as well as His own Godhead, is proved.
sources.answer: Yes. There is one Holy Spirit. Paul first speaks of the Spirit of God dwelling in us and immediately calls the same Spirit the Spirit of Christ. Peter likewise first names the Holy Spirit and then calls Him the Spirit of the Lord.
sources.quote: He first mentioned the Spirit of God and immediately adds that the Same is the Spirit of Christ.
sources.raw_question: Are the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Lord, and the Spirit of Christ one and the same Holy Spirit?

question: Is the preposition "in" used in Scripture of the Father and the Son as well as the Spirit, so that it cannot mark the Spirit as lower in nature?
synthesis: Ambrose and Basil agree that Scripture applies "in" to the Father, for example "the church in God the Father", and so it cannot denote inferiority. Ambrose adds Christ's "I in the Father". Basil also stresses that "in" is not reserved to the Spirit and, rightly understood, raises the mind to the highest thoughts about Him.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VIII. St. Ambrose examines and refutes the heretical argument that because God is said to be glorified in the Spirit, and not with the Spirit, the Holy Spirit is therefore inferior to the Father. He shows that the particle in can be also used of the Son and even of the Father, and that on the other hand with may be said of creatures without any infringement on the prerogatives of the Godhead; and that in reality these prepositions simply imply the connection of the Three Divine Persons.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture speaks of praising 'in the Lord,' doing mighty deeds 'in God,' the Church 'in God the Father,' and Christ says 'I in the Father.' Since 'in' is applied even to the Father, it cannot mark inferiority when used of the Spirit.
sources.quote: But let them learn that it is also said of God the Father: “In the Lord I will praise the word;”
sources.raw_question: Is the preposition 'in' used of God the Father in Scripture, so that it cannot denote inferiority?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That v: not found “of whom” in the case of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says "through (in) God we shall do valiantly," "in God who created all things," "to the church in God our Father," and similar, while its use of the Son and Spirit is notorious. The same preposition is thus applied to all three.
sources.quote: In the same manner it may also be said of the word “in,” that Scripture admits its use in the case of God the Father.
sources.raw_question: Is the preposition "in" used of God the Father in Scripture, so that it cannot mark the Spirit as lower in nature?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Of the origin of the word “with,” and what force it has. Also concerning the unwritten laws of the church.
sources.answer: No. Basil holds that "in" is not reserved for the Holy Spirit but is used of the Father and the Son as well. Properly understood, it takes nothing from the Spirit's dignity. Instead it lifts everyone except the wholly perverse to the highest thoughts about Him.
sources.quote: the word “in” has not been specially allotted to the Holy Spirit, but is common to the Father and the Son
sources.raw_question: Is the preposition "in" uniquely appropriate to the Holy Spirit, so that saying "in the Holy Spirit" expresses everything that should be thought about Him?

question: In what sense is the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father?
synthesis: Hilary grounds the mutual indwelling in unity of nature: the Son is born as living nature from living nature, so the same substance is in both and 'God is in God', not one body enclosing another. Hippolytus instead says the Son is in and one with the Father in power and disposition, on the model of believers' unity of mind rather than oneness of substance, and calls the Son the Father's one mind. The two therefore differ on whether the indwelling rests on shared nature or on unity of power and will.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: It happens through the birth of living nature from living nature, so that the substance remains the same. It is not two different but harmonious kinds of being joined together. Nor is it a larger substance containing a smaller one, since material things that enclose others cannot also be enclosed by them. Thus God is in God.
sources.quote: for the properties of matter make it impossible that things which enclose others should also be enclosed by them. It is by the birth of living nature from living nature.
sources.raw_question: How can the Father be in the Son and the Son in the Father at the same time?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: The Son is in the Father in power and disposition. Hippolytus argues from Christ's prayer that believers be one: they are one not as one body in substance but in the power and disposition of unity of mind. In the same way the Son is one with the Father, for the Son is the one mind of the Father.
sources.quote: the Son, who was sent and was not known of those who are in the world, confessed that He was in the Father in power and disposition. For the Son is the one mind of the Father.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Son in the Father and one with him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: By unity of nature, not by the Father entering the Son bodily. The nature begotten by the Father is of the same kind as his own, so it possesses by nature the nature which begot it. Hence they are equal in honour as Begetter and Begotten.
sources.quote: Nor do we teach that the Father is in the Son, as if He entered into Him bodily; but that the nature which was begotten by the Father of the same kind as His own, possessed by nature the nature which begot it
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father?

question: Does the Son's generation from the Father involve any temporal interval between the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Hilary and Gregory of Nyssa agree that there is no interval between Father and Son. Hilary argues from the correlation of generating and being born: neither occurs without the other, so both are eternal. Gregory instead appeals to images such as efflux and effulgence, which show the Son as both from the Father and with Him, and he holds that being caused does not entail being later.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Neither reason nor intelligence allows an interval, since the generation consists in the birth and the birth in the generation; neither occurs unless both occur. Thus the Son, who owes existence to both, is eternal because both are eternal.
sources.quote: For neither reason nor intelligence allows of any interval between the birth of God the Son and the generation by God the Father; since the generation consists in the birth, and the birth in the generation.
sources.raw_question: Is there any temporal interval between the Father's generating and the Son's being born?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He further shows the operations of God to be expressed by human illustrations; for what hands and feet and the other parts of the body with which men work are, that, in the case of God, the will alone is, in place of these. And so also arises the divergence of generation; wherefore He is called Only-begotten, because He has no community with other generation such as is observed in creation, but in that He is called the “brightness of glory,” and the “savour of ointment,” He shows the close conjunction and co-eternity of His Nature with the Father.
sources.answer: No. The efflux images show that the Son is conceived to be of the Father and also with Him, so that no interval exists between the Father and the Son who is of Him. Being caused does not entail being later.
sources.quote: points by the force of this mode of expression to the truth that He is conceived as being both from Him and with Him
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being 'from' the Father imply a temporal interval between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: No. The images of effulgence and the others show an existence at once derived from the Father and subsisting with Him. The Son is conceived of along with the Father, with no interval between them.
sources.quote: shows that we must understand by the significance of this expression, an existence at once derived from and subsisting with the Father
sources.raw_question: Does the generation of the Son from the Father involve any interval of time between them?

question: Should the Holy Spirit be ranked with the Father and the Son, or is the Spirit subordinate and inferior to them in nature and dignity?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Basil of Caesarea agree that the Spirit is of equal rank with the Father and the Son, not inferior to them. Their grounds differ: Gregory examines the scriptural senses of 'subjection', which apply to the brute creation placed under man or to conquered nations, and argues that neither can apply to the Spirit, so to say otherwise is open blasphemy. Basil appeals to Christ's baptismal command, in which the Lord himself joined the Spirit with the Father and himself, so that refusing this ranking openly resists God's commandment.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in making the being of the Father alone proper and supreme, implying by his omission of the Son and the Spirit that theirs is improperly spoken of, and is inferior.
sources.answer: No. Gregory calls this an open blasphemy. In Scripture, 'subjection' is used for the brute creation placed under man, or for nations conquered in war. Neither sense can apply to the Spirit, who is of equal, not inferior, rank with the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: It is shewn that the Holy Spirit is of an equal, not inferior, rank to the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit subject to the Father and the Son, and not to be ranked with them?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Definitive conceptions about the Spirit which conform to the teaching of the Scriptures.
sources.answer: The Spirit should be ranked with them. Christ himself commanded baptism in the name "of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost," joining the Spirit with the Father and himself. To refuse this ranking is to oppose God's commandment openly, and "we ought to obey God rather than men."
sources.quote: For if our Lord, when enjoining the baptism of salvation, charged His disciples to baptize all nations in the name “of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost,” not disdaining fellowship with Him
sources.raw_question: Should the Holy Spirit be ranked with the Father and the Son, or is the Spirit inferior in nature and dignity?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who say that it is not right to rank the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord himself, in commanding baptism in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, ranked the Spirit with the Father and himself and did not disdain fellowship with him. Those who refuse this ranking therefore openly resist God's commandment, and we must obey God rather than men.
sources.quote: if our Lord, when enjoining the baptism of salvation, charged His disciples to baptize all nations in the name “of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost,” not disdaining fellowship with Him
sources.raw_question: Is it right to rank the Holy Spirit together with the Father and the Son, given the claim that the Spirit differs in nature and is inferior in dignity?

question: If the Son is created rather than truly begotten of God's essence, can God properly be called Father and Creator, and can Christ truly be called God?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary agree that denying the Son's true generation undoes basic confessions about God, but they stress different consequences. Hilary argues that without a real birth God is only Creator, not Father, and Christ is not God by nature. Athanasius argues that without a proper Son God would be a mere Framer with a barren essence. He adds that, since all things are made through the Word and Wisdom, denying the Son also undermines God's very ability to create; generation by nature must come before creation by will.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. All things come to be through the Word and in Wisdom, and without Him nothing can be; so if God has no proper Word or Wisdom from His essence, He lacks that in and through which He makes all things. Denying the Son thus undermines God's creative activity itself.
sources.quote: But if there be not a Son, how then say you that God is a Creator? since all things that come to be are through the Word and in Wisdom, and without This nothing can be
sources.raw_question: If the Son is not truly Son but a work, can God properly be called Creator at all?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. On the heretics' view the Father is Creator rather than Begetter, and the Son is created rather than begotten. Then Christ is not very God, because He is not God by birth. Nor can God be confessed as Father, since there is no generation to make Him Father. Confessing one God the Father therefore depends on confessing a truly begotten Son.
sources.quote: Christ is therefore not very God, because He is not God by birth, and faith cannot recognise a Father in God, because there is no generation to constitute Him Father.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is created rather than begotten, can God truly be called Father and Christ truly be called God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. If there is no Son, God would be only a Framer and not a Father, and his essence would be barren, like a light that does not shine or a dry fountain. Yet all things come to be through the Word and in Wisdom. It is absurd to grant God a creative power by will while denying him a generation by nature, which comes first. If he makes external things by willing them, much more is he first Father of an Offspring from his own essence.
sources.quote: But if He frames things that are external to Him and before were not, by willing them to be, and becomes their Maker, much more will He first be Father of an Offspring from His proper Essence.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is not truly begotten of God's essence, can God properly be called Father and Creator?

question: Do the names 'Father' and 'Creator' (or 'Maker') apply to God in the same sense, so that the Son is related to the Father as creatures are related to their Maker?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Athanasius both deny that 'Father' and 'Creator' mean the same thing, and both use the distinction to defend the Son's divinity, but they argue differently. Gregory uses a reductio against Eunomius: if both names named only an operation they could be swapped, making God 'Father of a stone' and 'Creator of the Son', which would strip the Only-begotten of divinity. Athanasius argues from correlation: a maker can exist before his works, but no one is a father without a son, so the name Father at once implies the Son's existence.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, that is the monstrous consequence of Eunomius' view, which shows the view is false. If Father and Creator have the same meaning because both arise from an operation, the names become interchangeable, so one could say God is Creator of the Son and Father of a stone. Since it is absurd to deem a stone Divine, it would follow that no Divinity is recognized in the Only-begotten either. Hence 'Father' must carry a meaning of essential relation, not mere operation.
sources.quote: it is quite allowable to interchange the names, and to turn one into the other and say that God is Creator of the Son, and Father of a stone, seeing that the term Father is to be devoid of any meaning of essential relation
sources.raw_question: If the names 'Father' and 'Creator' are both applied to God merely because of an operation, does it follow that the Son is a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. If they meant the same thing, the names could be interchanged, so that God would be Creator of the Son and Father of a stone. Then 'Father' would lose any meaning of essential relation. Since it is absurd to deem a stone divine, the Only-begotten would be denied divinity too, which is a monstrous conclusion.
sources.quote: it is quite allowable to interchange the names, and to turn one into the other and say that God is Creator of the Son, and Father of a stone, seeing that the term Father is to be devoid of any meaning of essential relation
sources.raw_question: Are the names 'Father' and 'Creator' applied to God in the same sense, both signifying merely an operation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. A maker exists before his works, so calling God Maker does not necessarily imply that creatures exist. But one cannot be a father without a son. So naming God Father at once signifies the Son's existence, and the Son is implied together with the Father.
sources.quote: For, a son not being, one cannot say father; whereas when we call God a Maker, we do not of necessity intimate the things which have come to be; for a maker is before his works
sources.raw_question: Does calling God 'Father' imply the existence of the Son in a way that calling Him 'Maker' does not imply creatures?

question: Does Scripture attribute the creation of all things to the Son (the Word), and does this show that he is God?
synthesis: Bickersteth and Owen agree that Scripture ascribes the creation of all things to the Son and that this marks him as divine. Bickersteth argues from texts saying Jehovah alone created 'by Myself' and preserves all, so the Son who created and upholds all things must be Jehovah. Owen argues from John 1:3 together with the principle that 'He that built all things is God,' which places the Word outside the created order as Creator.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Jehovah alone made all things, stretching out the heavens "by Myself," and he preserves all. Yet all things were made by the Word and created by and for Christ, and by him all things consist. Since Jehovah created alone, the Son who created all things must be Jehovah.
sources.quote: By Him were all things created, that are in heaven and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: All things were created by him and for him. – Col. 1:16.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture attribute the creation and preservation of all things to Christ as it does to God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen cites John 1:3, which says all things were made by the Word and nothing was made without him. This places the Son outside the order of created things as the Creator himself.
sources.quote: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture attribute the creation of all things to the Word (the Son)?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Creating all things is a divine work, and Scripture declares that 'He that built all things is God.' John's statement that nothing was made without the Word therefore demonstrates his divine nature.
sources.quote: He was God, and he made all things: “He that built all things is God,” Heb. iii. 4.
sources.raw_question: Does the Word's creation of all things prove that the Word is God?

question: Is the Son true God, or could he be called God in some lesser sense without being true God?
synthesis: Hilary and Augustine agree that the Son is true God, not God in a lesser sense, but on different grounds. Hilary argues from the nature of things: whatever truly has a nature, like fire or water, is truly that thing, so if the Son is God at all he must be true God. Augustine grounds it in the Son's being of one substance with the Father and in 1 John's explicit naming of Jesus Christ as 'the true God, and eternal life.'

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Just as fire that is fire must be true fire, a thing that has a nature is truly that thing and loses its truth only by ceasing to exist. If the Son is God he is true God; if not true God, he is not God in any sense.
sources.quote: If the Son of God is God, then He is true God; if He is not true God, then in no possible sense is He God at all.
sources.raw_question: Is it coherent to say the Son is God but not true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Just as something that is fire must be true fire, and water while it remains water is true water, a thing can only lose its nature by ceasing to exist. Hence if the Son is God he is true God; if he is not true God he is not God at all. If the name that indicates the nature belongs to him by right, he cannot lack that nature in its truest sense.
sources.quote: If the Son of God is God, then He is true God; if He is not true God, then in no possible sense is He God at all.
sources.raw_question: Is there any coherent sense in which the Son could be called God but not true God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Being of one substance with the Father, He is not only God but very God. John affirms this expressly in his epistle, calling the Son Jesus Christ 'the true God, and eternal life.'
sources.quote: And so He is not only God, but also very God. And the same John most expressly affirms this in his epistle
sources.raw_question: Is the Son 'very God' (true God) and not merely God in a lesser sense?

question: Does the Son's receiving power from the Father, being sent by him, or acting at his command prove that the Son is inferior in nature or power to the Father?
synthesis: Hilary and Waterland agree that it does not, but they argue on different grounds. Hilary takes the Son's receiving to mean nothing other than his birth, which makes him perfectly what God is. He also holds that being able to carry out whatever the Father commands is a mark of absolute, equal power. Waterland argues that delegation can pass between beings of the same nature. In the Son's case, he says, the charge and the honour involved are too great for any inferior nature, so they point to the contrary.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The Son's receiving signifies nothing other than his Birth, by which he received all that he has. That gift does not degrade him, because it makes him perfectly and entirely what God is. To be the Author of the Birth is the Father's mystery. To be made the perfect image of his Author by a real birth is no degradation to the Son.
sources.quote: But if the receiving of power signifies neither more nor less than the Birth, by which He received all that He has, that gift does not degrade the Begotten, because it makes Him perfectly and entirely what God is.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's receiving power from the Father prove that he is inferior in nature to the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. Delegation does not imply inferiority of nature, since one man can be delegated by another man of the same nature. Rather it implies the contrary when the charge is one no inferior nature could sustain, or the honour attached to it is too great for an inferior nature to receive, as in the Son's case.
sources.quote: Acting by a delegated power does by no means infer any inferiority of nature, but rather the quite contrary; especially, if the charge be such, as no inferior nature could be able to sustain
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being sent and acting by a delegated power prove that he is inferior in nature to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Being able to do whatever is commanded is a mark of absolute power, not of inferiority. The Son can execute as Agent whatever the Father as Speaker can express. Creative power that matches the unlimited commanding word has the true nature of God, so the Son is omnipotent and equal with true God in power.
sources.quote: Absolute power is this, that its possessor can execute as Agent whatever His words as Speaker can express.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's doing what the Father commands show that his power is inferior to the Father's?

question: Does the Son possess only a portion of the Father's Godhead, or is He whole God?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary of Poitiers agree that the Son is whole God, possessing the fulness of the Father's Godhead rather than a part. Athanasius grounds this in the Son being 'in the form of God' and so equal to God, with the Father's fulness being the Son's very Being. Hilary argues from 'all that the Father has is Mine' and the fulness of the Godhead dwelling in Christ, adding that the Father bestowed His whole Divinity in the Son's birth.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: The Son is whole God. The Form of the Godhead in Him is not partial; the fulness of the Father's Godhead is the very Being of the Son. Hence, being in the form of God, He is equal to God.
sources.quote: Nor is this Form of the Godhead partial merely, but the fulness of the Father’s Godhead is the Being of the Son, and the Son is whole God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son only partially God, possessing some portion of the Father's Godhead, or is He whole God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The Son says all that the Father has is His, and the Apostle says the whole fulness of the Godhead dwells in Him; since a portion cannot possess the whole, the Son is the perfect Son of the perfect Father.
sources.quote: Nor is there a portion of the Father resident in the Son, for the Son bears witness, All things that the Father hath are Mine
sources.raw_question: Does the Son possess only a portion of the Father's divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: He received the whole. The Father bestowed His whole Divinity on that Birth, so the Son is wholly Son of Him who is wholly Father. He is not a son partially or in some respects only, for the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Him.
sources.quote: not a son partially, for the fulness of the Godhead is in the Son; not a Son in some respects, but in all
sources.raw_question: Did the Son receive the whole divinity of the Father in His birth, or only part of it?

question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity a genuine mystery, or can it be explained so that it ceases to be mysterious?
synthesis: Owen and Edwards agree that the Trinity remains a genuine mystery. Owen argues from Scripture's repeated calling of these truths mysteries, and charges those who deny it with turning the gospel into allegory. Edwards disclaims that his own account removes the mystery, admitting it lessens some difficulties while raising new ones.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: To the Reader
sources.answer: It is a genuine mystery. Scripture frequently and emphatically calls these truths mysteries, and they suit the glorious being and wisdom of God. Those who deny the mystery in the things themselves are forced to give an enigmatical sense to the words of Scripture, so they turn almost the whole gospel into an allegory.
sources.quote: whilst they deny the mysteries of the things themselves — which are such as every way become the glorious being and wisdom of God, — they are forced to assign such an enigmatical sense unto the words, expressions, and propositions
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity a genuine mystery, or can it be stripped of anything peculiarly mysterious as its opponents claim?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Edwards disclaims fully explaining how these things are and admits many objections he cannot solve. The Trinity remains the highest and deepest of divine mysteries, though Scripture with reason may lead us to say somewhat more about it than is usual.
sources.quote: I am far from pretending to explaining the Trinity so as to render it no longer a mystery. I think it to be the highest and deepest of all Divine mysteries still
sources.raw_question: Does this account of the Trinity explain it so that it ceases to be a mystery?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Neither. Edwards does not offer it as an explanation that removes the mystery. Some difficulties are lessened while new ones appear. He offers it only as a fuller showing of what Scripture reveals. Being told more about something infinitely above us naturally increases the number of visible mysteries, just as the New Testament revealed more of the Trinity than the Old yet multiplied its visible mysteries.
sources.quote: No wonder that the more things we are told concerning that which is so infinitely above our reach, the number of visible mysteries increases.
sources.raw_question: Does Edwards's account of the Trinity explain away the mystery, or is it undermined because it raises new difficulties?

question: Is the Holy Spirit a creature or the Creator?
synthesis: Ambrose and Hilary agree that the Spirit is not a creature, but they argue differently. Ambrose argues from the Spirit's creative work: making man (Job), renewing the earth and bringing about the virgin birth. Hilary appeals to apostolic authority placing the Spirit in the regenerating Trinity, and to the Spirit's searching the deep things of God, which only what belongs to God can do.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVIII. As he purposes to establish the Godhead of the Holy Spirit by the points already discussed, St. Ambrose touches again on some of them; for instance, that He does not commit but forgives sin; that He is not a creature but the Creator; and lastly, that He does not offer but receives worship.
sources.answer: He is the Creator. Job says "The Spirit of God hath made me," the face of the earth is renewed by the Spirit, and even the Lord's virgin birth was the Spirit's work. Since the Creator is not a creature, the Spirit produces all things together with the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: Therefore the Spirit is not a creature, but the Creator, and He Who is Creator is certainly not a creature.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a creature or the Creator?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. It is only mere human reasoning that ranks the Divine Spirit among creatures. On the authority of Apostles and Evangelists, the Spirit belongs to the Trinity that regenerates us. We receive the Spirit as the pledge of immortality and the source of fellowship with the sinless nature of God.
sources.quote: Men will no longer dare, on the strength of mere human reasoning, to rank among creatures that Divine Spirit, Whom we receive as the pledge of immortality and source of fellowship with the sinless nature of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a creature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. The Spirit searches and knows the deep things of God and intercedes with Him. Nothing except what belongs to God can penetrate into God, and no foreign power can measure the depth of His majesty. To call the Spirit a creature would dishonour the power of His nature, which subsists eternally, derived from the Father through the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: Nothing, except what belongs to Thee, penetrates into Thee; nor can the agency of a power foreign and strange to Thee measure the depth of Thy boundless majesty.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a creature?

question: Should our inability to understand how the Son is begotten of the Father lead us to doubt or deny that he is truly begotten?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Athanasius agree that perplexity about the manner of generation is no ground for doubting it. Hilary argues by analogy: Christ's miracles show facts we see but cannot comprehend, and we cannot even explain our own begetting, so the mode of divine birth is a secret we should accept in ignorance. Athanasius instead stresses the moral and spiritual danger: it is better to stay silent and believe than to form unworthy doctrines out of perplexity, and Scripture offers the human word as an illustration.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. Hilary argues that Christ's miracles (water made wine, the feeding of the five thousand) show facts we see but cannot comprehend, so God's action is not limited by our power of understanding His methods. To deny an event because we cannot discover how it was done is to make the limits of our understanding the limits of reality.
sources.quote: If we assume that an event did not happen, because we cannot discover how it was done, we make the limits of our understanding into the limits of reality.
sources.raw_question: Should our inability to understand how the Son is born of the Father lead us to doubt or deny that he is truly begotten of the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. It is better in perplexity to be silent and believe than to disbelieve; the perplexed who keeps quiet may obtain mercy, but one who forms unworthy doctrines from his perplexity incurs judgment without mercy. Scripture itself offers relief by allowing human word to serve as an illustration.
sources.quote: For it is better in perplexity to be silent and believe, than to disbelieve on account of the perplexity
sources.raw_question: Should perplexity about how the Son is begotten lead one to doubt or reformulate the doctrine of the Son's generation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The manner of the birth is a secret known only to Father and Son, unrevealed even to angels and apostles, yet the relation itself is certain. Since we cannot even explain how we ourselves were begotten or how we pass life and senses to our children, we should patiently accept ignorance of the mode of divine generation.
sources.quote: I ask you rather to acquiesce patiently in your ignorance of the mode of Divine generation, seeing that you know not how His creatures come into existence.
sources.raw_question: Should our inability to explain the manner of the Son's generation lead us to doubt that the Father truly begets the Son?

question: Did the Father beget the Son by a prior act of his will, so that the Father preceded the Son and the Son was begotten 'afterwards'?
synthesis: Waterland and Gregory of Nyssa both deny that the Father was prior to the Son, but on different grounds. Waterland argues that the Arian dilemma confuses approbation with free choice: the Father begat the Son willingly, not by a prior act of choice. Gregory argues that God's unchanging nature, whose power coincides with its will, rules out a delayed begetting, and that 'before' and 'after' are temporal terms with no meaning for the Son, who is before the ages.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 31: Whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration, on the side of Arianism, ought to move a wise and good man, against so great appearances of truth o
sources.answer: No. The Arian dilemma (the Father begat the Son either against his will or with his will, so a precedent act of will made the Father prior) confounds mere approbation with an act of free choice. The Father begat the Son with the approbation of his will (volens), not by a prior act of choice. To insist that the Son is God by an act of the Father's will simply begs the question.
sources.quote: The Father bégat his Son, either nolens or volens ; against his will or with his will: it could not be against his will, that is absurd ; therefore it must be with his wll ; therefore that act of the will was precedent to the Son’s existence
sources.raw_question: Did the Father beget the Son by an act of his will, so that the will preceded the Son's existence and the Father was prior to the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He then ingeniously shows that the generation of the Son is not according to the phrase of Eunomius, “The Father begat Him at that time when He chose, and not before:” but that the Son, being the fulness of all that is good and excellent, is always contemplated in the Father; using for this demonstration the support of Eunomius' own arguments.
sources.answer: No. Such an answer would suit a spider, a bee, or a human artist, whose wills change and whose power does not always match their will. But God's nature is unchanging, has no adventitious good, and its power coincides with its will. Merely decreeing a proposition is not proof, and unless a reason is given why the Son was begotten 'afterwards,' the claim has no force with sensible men.
sources.quote: It is one thing, most sapient sir, to lay down as an ordinance some proposition that you happen to approve, and another to make converts by reasoning on the points of controversy.
sources.raw_question: Is it a sufficient answer to say that God begat the Son when He willed and that no one should ask why He did not do so before?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He then ingeniously shows that the generation of the Son is not according to the phrase of Eunomius, “The Father begat Him at that time when He chose, and not before:” but that the Son, being the fulness of all that is good and excellent, is always contemplated in the Father; using for this demonstration the support of Eunomius' own arguments.
sources.answer: No. 'Before' and 'after' are temporal terms and lose all meaning where there is no time. The Lord is before times and ages, the Maker of the ages, so temporal priority or posteriority cannot be applied to His generation.
sources.quote: Since then the Lord is antecedent to times, the words “before” and “after” have no place as applied to Him.
sources.raw_question: Can one meaningfully ask why the Father did not beget the Son 'before', or say that the Son was begotten 'afterwards'?

question: Are 'Word' and 'Son' names of one and the same divine Person distinct from the Father, or of distinct beings?
synthesis: Athanasius and Irenaeus agree that Word and Son (and, for Irenaeus, Christ) are one and the same. Their grounds differ. Athanasius argues that whatever is from the Father is a son and the Word is from the Father, and he reads John's 'with God' and 'was God' as identifying the Son with the Word. Irenaeus argues against Gnostic schemes that split the Creator's Son from the Christ from above, or Monogenes from Logos, by appealing to John's identification of the Word in the beginning with the one who made all things and became flesh.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: They are the same. If he is not Son, he is not Word either, and if not Word, not Son, because whatever is from the father is a son, and the Word is from the Father. Yet the Father is not the Word, nor the Word the Father. One begets and the other is begotten.
sources.quote: For if not Son, neither is He Word; and if not Word, neither is He Son. For that which is from the father is a son;
sources.raw_question: Are 'Word' and 'Son' two distinct beings, or the same one who is distinct from the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: They are one and the same. Irenaeus rejects the claim that the Creator's Son is one being and the Christ from above another, and also the claim that Monogenes was the beginning while Logos was a son of Monogenes. John identifies the Word who was in the beginning with God, and who was God, as the one through whom all things were made and who became flesh.
sources.quote: that the Son of the Creator was, forsooth, one, but the Christ from above another, who also continued impassible, descending upon Jesus, the Son of the Creator, and flew back again into His Pleroma; and that Monogenes was the beginning, but Logos was the true son of Monogenes
sources.raw_question: Are the Son, the Word, and the Christ distinct beings (for example, the Word as the son of a separate "Monogenes"), or one and the same Son of God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: Yes. Since the Son is the Life that was with the Father, and the Word was with God, the Son must be the Word ever with the Father; and correspondingly 'God' with whom the Word was is the Father. The Son is also called 'True God,' as the Word 'was God.'
sources.quote: the Son must be the Word, which is ever with the Father. And as the ‘Son’ is ‘Word,’ so ‘God’ must be ‘the Father.’
sources.raw_question: Are 'Son' and 'Word' in John's writings names of the same divine Person?

question: Does the Father's giving the Son 'to have life in Himself' (John 5:26) make the Son's life inferior to, or different from, the Father's?
synthesis: Hilary and Augustine agree that the giving reveals the Son's birth from the Father and implies no inferiority. Hilary grounds this in God's simplicity: there is no difference between possessor and possessed, and the life given is the Father's very life, so the Son is Living from Living. Augustine stresses that the Son's life is unchangeable like the Father's, so the text shows only that the Son is from the Father, not that he is unequal.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: The Son draws his life from the Father who truly has life, Living from Living, yet he has life in himself even as the Father does. Thus the Son's life is received but not diminished; there is no diversity, since the Father's life is in the Son.
sources.quote: The Son draws His life from that Father Who truly has life; the Only begotten from the Unbegotten, Offspring from Parent, Living from Living.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's having life in himself something he receives from the Father, and does this make his life inferior?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. God is not composite, with a difference between possessor and possessed; all that He is is life, one infinite nature. Since the life was given exactly as it was possessed, the giving reveals the Son's birth but involves no difference of kind; to have what the Father has is to have the Father's very self.
sources.quote: although the fact that it was given manifestly reveals the birth of the Recipient, it yet does not involve a difference of kind since the life given was such as was possessed
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's giving the Son to have life in Himself imply that the Son's life differs in kind from the Father's?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > There is a Double Rule for Understanding the Scriptural Modes of Speech Concerning the Son of God. These Modes of Speech are of a Threefold Kind.
sources.answer: No. The Son's life is unchangeable like the Father's. The text only shows that he is from the Father, so it declares his birth, not his inequality.
sources.quote: these texts are so expressed, because the life of the Son is unchangeable as that of the Father is, and yet He is of the Father
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's giving the Son 'to have life in Himself' (John 5:26) mean the Son's life is lesser or changeable?

question: Does the Holy Spirit act by his own free and sovereign will, rather than under another's power?
synthesis: Owen and Ambrose agree that the Spirit acts by his own will, and both appeal to the text that he distributes to each as he wills. Owen makes the point about the Spirit's work of comfort, which depends on his will, power and goodness, so believers may pray to him and wait on him. Ambrose argues more broadly that the Spirit is subject to no foreign power or law, and that this places him above all things rather than among creatures as a servant.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
