sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit comforts powerfully, voluntarily and freely, and his own power, will and goodness are engaged in the work. Scripture says the Spirit works effectually and distributes to every one as he will, so the work depends on the Spirit's sovereign will.
sources.quote: the manner of the Spirit’s working this thing is always to be borne in mind, and the interest of his power, will, and goodness in his working. He doth this, — 1st. Powerfully, or effectually; 2dly. Voluntarily; 3dly. Freely.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit act by his own will and power in comforting believers, as a personal agent, rather than as a mere force?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. No account can be given of the joy he works except that the Spirit works it when and how he wills. He secretly infuses it into the soul, overcoming fears and sorrows. Owen treats the Spirit as a free, willing agent to whom believers may pray and on whom they may wait.
sources.quote: Of this joy there is no account to be given, but that the Spirit worketh it when and how he will.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit act freely and sovereignly in giving comfort, as a personal agent?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Preface.
sources.answer: He acts by his own free will. The Holy Spirit is not subject to any foreign power or law. He is the Arbiter of his own freedom and distributes all things by the decision of his own will. Scripture says he divides to each severally as he wills. This shows that he is above all things rather than a servant among creatures.
sources.quote: For the Holy Spirit is not subject to any foreign power or law, but is the Arbiter of His own freedom, dividing all things according to the decision of His own will
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit subject to another's power, or does he act by his own free will?

question: What does the name 'Son' signify about the second Person of the Trinity and his relation to the Father?
synthesis: Both authors read 'Son' as marking sameness of nature with the Father. Gregory of Nyssa says it signifies being of the Father's substance and a natural relationship, which Eunomius obscures by replacing the inspired names with impersonal terms like 'First Being'. Warfield argues from the Semitic sense of sonship as likeness that the name asserts equality rather than subordination, and that any implication of derivation is at most very distant.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It signifies that he is of the substance of the Father. 'Son' does not denote simplicity of substance, and simplicity does not include the notion of Son. Each term keeps its own proper meaning.
sources.quote: the term Son we hold to indicate that He is of the substance of the Father, and the term simple we hold to mean what the word bears upon its face
sources.raw_question: What does the name 'Son' signify about the second Person of the Trinity?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. In the Semitic consciousness underlying Scripture, sonship connotes likeness: whatever the father is, the son is also. The emphatic application of "Son" therefore asserts equality with the Father rather than subordination, and any implication of derivation is at most very distant.
sources.quote: What underlies the conception of sonship in Scriptural speech is just “likeness”; whatever the father is that the son is also. The emphatic application of the term “Son” to one of the Trinitarian Persons, accordingly, asserts rather His equality with the Father than His subordination to the Father
sources.raw_question: Does the biblical designation "Son" applied to the second Person of the Trinity imply his subordination to and derivation of being from the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Résumé of his dogmatic teaching. Objections to it in detail.
sources.answer: They convey the proper and natural relationship between the two. Anyone who hears the words father and son at once recognizes a natural relationship between them, carried by the names themselves. Eunomius drops the inspired names precisely to keep this relationship from being understood of the Father and the Only-begotten, and so to injure the truth.
sources.quote: every one, when the words father and son are spoken, at once recognizes the proper and natural relationship to one another which they imply. This relationship is conveyed at once by the appellations themselves.
sources.raw_question: What do the names 'Father' and 'Son' convey about the relation between the first and second Persons of the Trinity that impersonal terms like 'First Being' and 'second Being' do not?

question: Does the Only-begotten's being called and related to God as 'Son of God' mean that he is a creature or work of God?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Waterland both deny it. Gregory argues from ordinary language: we call what a man makes his work and what he begets his son, so 'Son' signifies one of the same nature, not a creature. Waterland argues from the relation itself: a creature's relation to its Creator could not be called ineffable, and the Son may be worshipped only because he is one in nature with the Father.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He thus shows the oneness of the Eternal Son with the Father the identity of essence and the community of nature (wherein is a natural inquiry into the production of wine), and that the terms “Son” and “product” in the naming of the Only-Begotten include a like idea of relationship.
sources.answer: No. We call what a man makes his work and what he begets his son, so that names carry their proper meanings. No one calls a bench the son of the workman. So when Scripture calls the Only-begotten Son of God, we understand not a creature but what the word "Son" really signifies: one of the same nature.
sources.quote: when we are taught that the Only-begotten is Son of God, we do not by this appellation understand a creature of God, but what the word “Son” in its signification really displays
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Only-begotten "Son of God" mean he is a creature or work of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He thus shows the oneness of the Eternal Son with the Father the identity of essence and the community of nature (wherein is a natural inquiry into the production of wine), and that the terms “Son” and “product” in the naming of the Only-Begotten include a like idea of relationship.
sources.answer: No. Ordinary usage distinguishes a man's work (a bench, a house) from his son, so that each name carries its proper meaning. Likewise, when Scripture calls the Only-begotten Son of God, we understand what 'Son' really signifies, not a creature.
sources.quote: when we are taught that the Only-begotten is Son of God, we do not by this appellation understand a creature of God, but what the word “Son” in its signification really displays.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Only-begotten 'Son of God' mean he is a creature or work of God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. The ineffable relation is not that of a creature to its Creator, which could not truly be called ineffable, but of a Son to a Father of the same nature. The Son can be worshipped only because he is one with the Father, to whom worship is appropriated in opposition to creatures, not in opposition to one coessential with him.
sources.quote: But this enefable relation is not that of a creature to his Creator; but of a Son to a Father, of the same nature with him. This may be styled meffable: the other cannot, in any true or just sense.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is honoured on account of his ineffable relation to God as the only begotten Son, does this relation imply he is a creature?

question: Is the Father of Jesus Christ the same God who made the world and sent the Old Testament prophets, as against the Marcionites?
synthesis: Owen and Irenaeus agree that the Father of Jesus Christ is the same God who spoke in the Old Testament, but their arguments differ. Irenaeus argues from prophecy: the prophets foretold the Lord's conduct, sufferings and new covenant in detail, which prophets of another God ignorant of the Father could not have done, and positing two gods multiplies deities blasphemously. Owen identifies the Father with the God who created the world, gave the law and spoke by the prophets, and traces the Marcionite error to the mistaken principle that the Son existed only in time rather than as the eternal Son.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen calls the Marcionite inference foolish: the Father of Jesus Christ is the God who created the world, gave the law, and spoke by the prophets. He traces the Marcionite error to the mistaken principle that the Son existed only in time and was not the eternal Son of God.
sources.quote: this brutish apprehension of theirs arose from no other principle but this, that the Son had only a temporal existence, and was not the eternal Son of God
sources.raw_question: Is the Father of Jesus Christ the same God who made the world and was revealed in the Old Testament, as against the Marcionites?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIV.—Proof against the Marcionites, that the prophets referred in all their predictions to our Christ.
sources.answer: No. The prophecies were fulfilled in our Lord and in no one else, so the prophets spoke of Him and were sent by the same God who is His Father. To posit a different God for the prophets and another Father for the Lord is blasphemy that fabricates a multitude of gods.
sources.quote: in opposition to those who maintain that the prophets [were inspired] by a different God, and that our Lord [came] from another Father
sources.raw_question: Were the Old Testament prophets inspired by a different God from the Father of Jesus Christ, as the Marcionites claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIV.—Proof against the Marcionites, that the prophets referred in all their predictions to our Christ.
sources.answer: No. If one reads the Gospel and the prophets carefully, one finds the whole conduct, doctrine and sufferings of the Lord predicted by the prophets. Prophets inspired by another God, ignorant of the ineffable Father and his dispensations, could not have foretold the King's advent, the liberty he gives, and the new covenant. So the prophets and the Gospel come from the one same God.
sources.quote: read with earnest care the prophets, and you will find that the whole conduct, and all the doctrine, and all the sufferings of our Lord, were predicted through them
sources.raw_question: Were the Old Testament prophets sent by a different God from the Father announced in the Gospel, as Marcion claimed?

question: Did Christ have a real human body and truly become man, or was he a man only in appearance, as the Docetists claim?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Novatian agree that Christ was truly flesh and not a phantasm. Both appeal to the blood flowing from his side and to his real death. Novatian also cites 'the Word was made flesh' and argues that if he were a phantasm nothing he did would be real. Irenaeus adds his title Son of man, his real birth, burial and resurrection, and his passing through the real conditions of human life, including the age proper to a Master.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXII.—The thirty Æons are not typified by the fact that Christ was baptized in His thirtieth year: He did not suffer in the twelfth month after His baptism, but was more than fifty years old when He died.
sources.answer: No. Christ truly was what he appeared to be. He took on real human conditions, including the age proper to a Master, and did not evade any condition of humanity. This answers the Docetists, who say he was man only in appearance.
sources.quote: For He did not seem one thing while He was another, as those affirm who describe Him as being man only in appearance; but what He was, that He also appeared to be.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ a man only in appearance, seeming to be one thing while really being another?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That Jesus Christ is the Son of God and Truly Man, as Opposed to the Fancies of Heretics, Who Deny that He Took Upon Him True Flesh.
sources.answer: He had a real body of our substance. If Christ were a phantasm, nothing he did could have been real. Scripture says the Word was made flesh, and His death proves it, since blood flowed from His hands, feet and side as He died according to the laws of our dissolution.
sources.quote: for of those things which he did, he could have done nothing real, if he himself was a phantasm, and not reality.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ have a real human body, or only the appearance of one (a phantasm), as docetic heretics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: He was truly flesh and truly born. He called himself the Son of man, which implies a real human birth. He was really crucified, and blood and water flowed from his pierced side. A real body was buried and rose from the dead, and none of this could happen to a mere appearance.
sources.quote: how, again, supposing that He was not flesh, but was a man merely in appearance, could He have been crucified, and could blood and water have issued from His pierced side?
sources.raw_question: Was Christ truly flesh and truly born as a man, or was he a man only in appearance?

question: Does God's declaration in Isaiah 42:8, 'I will not give my glory to another,' exclude the Son (and Spirit) from sharing the Father's glory and worship?
synthesis: Both Waterland and Gregory of Nyssa answer no, but on different grounds. Waterland argues that the text withholds God's glory only from creatures and other gods, which the Son and Spirit are not, and that the Father himself gave them his glory through the baptismal command and the order to honour the Son as the Father. Gregory reads the 'other' from the next clause as God's adversary worshipped through graven images, says applying it to the Son puts him in the place of God's enemy, and adds that the Only-begotten himself spoke these words through the prophet.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 30: Whether, supposing the case doubtful, it be not a wise man’s part to take the safer side; rather to think too highly, than too meanly of our blessed Saviour ; r
sources.answer: No. That declaration forbids giving God's glory to creatures or other gods. The Son and Spirit are neither, and the Father himself gave them his glory by commanding baptism in their names equally with his own and ordering all to honour the Son as they honour the Father.
sources.quote: they had given it to none but his own Son, and his Holy Spirit, whom they believed not to be creatures, nor other Gods; and whom himself had given his glory to, by commanding all men to be baptized in their names, equally with his own
sources.raw_question: Does giving divine glory to the Son and Spirit violate God's declaration 'I will not give my glory to another'?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 30: Whether, supposing the case doubtful, it be not a wise man’s part to take the safer side; rather to think too highly, than too meanly of our blessed Saviour ; r
sources.answer: No. God's glory is withheld from creatures, but the Son and Holy Spirit are not creatures nor other Gods. God himself gave them his glory by commanding baptism in their names equally with his own, and by ordering that all honour the Son as they honour the Father.
sources.quote: they had given it to none but his own Son, and his Holy Spirit, whom they believed not to be creatures, nor other Gods; and whom himself had given his glory to, by commanding all men to be baptized in their names
sources.raw_question: Does worshipping and glorifying the Son and the Holy Spirit violate God's declaration in Isaiah that he will not give his glory to another?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: No. The 'other' is God's adversary, worshipped through idols, as the next clause shows: 'neither My praise to graven images.' Applying it to the Son puts Him in the place of God's enemy. Moreover, the Only-begotten Himself spoke these words through the prophet, as Eunomius admits.
sources.quote: it is the Only-begotten Himself Who spoke these words by the prophet, as Eunomius himself subsequently confesses when he says, “this is He Who spake by the prophets.”
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah's 'My glory will I not give to another' exclude the Son from sharing the Father's glory?

question: Is the Son's generation from the Father a creation or new production, or a true birth in which He shares the Father's own nature?
synthesis: Waterland and Hilary of Poitiers agree that the Son's generation is not a creation or new production. Waterland argues historically: the Fathers who held the Son consubstantial with the Father would have contradicted themselves had they treated his generation as a creation, since they believed he existed as the substantial Word from eternity. Hilary argues from the concepts themselves: birth makes the natural Son of a natural Father, not a God of new or foreign nature, whereas creation is making, and its products are works, not sons, as a picture is not the painter's son.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Their writings clearly hold the Son's consubstantiality with the Father. They would have been the most inconsistent men in the world had they treated his generation as a creation rather than believing he existed as the living, substantial Word from all eternity.
sources.quote: they must have been the most inconsistent men in the world, had they thought that the procession, or generation, of the Son was a creation, or new production, of him
sources.raw_question: Could the Fathers who held the Son consubstantial with the Father consistently have regarded his generation as a creation or new production?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. His birth did not make Him God of a new and foreign nature. By generation He was made the natural Son of a natural Father. That is why, when He is glorified in His manhood, He shines again with the glory of His own nature, the nature He shares with the Father.
sources.quote: For His birth did not make Him God of a new and foreign nature, but by generation He was made natural Son of a natural Father.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son's generation make Him God of a new or foreign nature distinct from the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Creation is making, not birth; heaven, earth and the world are works, not sons. As a picture is not the painter's son nor a house the architect's, created things are works of making, while He alone who is born of the Father is the Son.
sources.quote: Is the picture a son of the painter, or the sword a son of the smith or the house a son of the architect? These are the works of their making: but He alone is the Son of the Father Who is born of the Father.
sources.raw_question: What distinguishes the Son's generation from the creation of the world through Him?

question: Should the Holy Spirit be ranked among created things, or with God?
synthesis: Basil and Hilary agree that the Holy Spirit is not a creature, but they argue on different grounds. Basil argues from the Spirit's works: He liberates enslaved creation and so cannot belong to it, and since God is recognized in prophets through the Spirit's gifts, the Spirit's presence is God's presence. Hilary appeals to the Spirit as the divine pledge of immortality and fellowship with God, to apostolic authority against human reasoning, and to the baptismal formula, which confesses the Spirit alongside the Father and the Son.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Proof of the absurdity of the refusal to glorify the Spirit, from the comparison of things glorified in creation.
sources.answer: No. All creation is in bondage, but the Spirit makes free, as Scripture says that where the Spirit of the Lord is there is liberty. What liberates creation cannot itself belong to enslaved creation.
sources.quote: Where then are we to take Him and rank Him? With the creature? Yet all the creature is in bondage, but the Spirit maketh free. “And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.”
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be ranked among created things?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says the unbeliever, convicted by prophecy, confesses that God is in the prophets. Yet the prophesying works through the distribution of the Spirit's gifts. So the Spirit's presence is God's presence, and the opponents must rank Him with God rather than thrust Him down among creatures.
sources.quote: If then God is known to be in the prophets by the prophesying that is acting according to the distribution of the gifts of the Spirit, let our adversaries consider what kind of place they will attribute to the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that God is recognized in prophets through the Spirit's gift of prophecy show that the Holy Spirit should be ranked with God rather than with creatures?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. The Spirit is the divine Spirit whom we receive as the pledge of immortality and the source of fellowship with God's sinless nature. Ranking him among creatures rests on mere human reasoning against apostolic authority. In the baptismal formula, the Spirit is confessed alongside the Father and the Son as the One Gift.
sources.quote: the Spirit, God’s Gift to us, Who pervades all things, is also One. Thus all are ranged according to powers possessed and benefits conferred
sources.raw_question: Should the Holy Spirit be ranked among creatures?

question: To whom does 'His eternal power and Godhead' in Romans 1:20 refer: the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit?
synthesis: Athanasius and Ambrose agree that 'eternal power' refers to the Son. Athanasius grounds this in the creation context: the Framer's Power seen in creation is the Word through whom all things were made. He adds Paul's calling Christ 'the Power of God', and argues that 'His power' is not 'He', though the power is proper to Him. Ambrose differs over 'Godhead', which he refers to the Holy Spirit rather than the Son, arguing that the Spirit, being divine, is God's eternal Godhead.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: Yes, it signifies the Son. Paul speaks of the creation and naturally refers to the Framer's Power seen in it, which is the Word by whom all things were made. Since creation came to be through the Son and in Him all things consist, whoever rightly contemplates creation contemplates the Word who framed it.
sources.quote: For after making mention of the creation, he naturally speaks of the Framer’s Power as seen in it, which Power, I say, is the Word of God, by whom all things have been made.
sources.raw_question: Does 'His eternal Power and Godhead' in Romans 1:20 refer to the Son rather than to the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter III. The same Unity may also be recognized from the fact that the Spirit is called Finger, and the Son Right Hand; for the understanding of divine things is assisted by the usage of human language. The tables of the law were written by this Finger, and they were afterwards broken, and the reason. Lastly, Christ wrote with the same Finger; yet we must not admit any inferiority in the Spirit from this bodily comparison.
sources.answer: Yes, in Ambrose's reading. 'Eternal power' is said of the Son, who is the eternal Power of the Father. 'Godhead' is said of the Spirit, who because he is divine should be believed to be God's eternal Godhead. So the Finger of God, the Spirit, is both eternal and divine, since nothing belonging to God is other than eternal and divine.
sources.quote: in the same manner as the Son is called the eternal Power of the Father, so, also, the Spirit, because He is divine, should be believed to be His eternal Godhead.
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 1:20, speaking of God's 'eternal power and Godhead', refer to the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: It refers to the Son. Paul elsewhere calls Christ 'the Power of God and the Wisdom of God'. He also says 'His power', not 'God himself is the power', and 'His' is not 'He', though it is proper to Him rather than alien. The context confirms this: the Framer's Power seen in creation is the Word through whom all things were made.
sources.quote: for he says not, ‘God Himself is the power,’ but ‘His is the power.’ Very plain is it to all that ‘His’ is not ‘He;’ yet not something alien but rather proper to Him.
sources.raw_question: Does 'His eternal power' in Romans 1:20 refer to the Father himself or to the Son?

question: In John 5:18, was the statement that Jesus 'made himself equal with God' merely a false accusation by the Jews, or a true account of what he claimed?
synthesis: Waterland and Bickersteth agree that the charge was a true account of Jesus' claim, but argue it on different grounds. Waterland argues that John states it as his own account of why the Jews sought to kill Jesus, and that it would be true even as the Jews' charge, since the other parts of the charge were true. Bickersteth argues that Jesus did not protest the Jews' reading, as a mere man would have done, but went on to set forth his essential supremacy as God.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: It was true. Jesus really had worked on the sabbath and really called God his Father in a peculiar sense, so the rest of the charge should be true as well. His saying 'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' implies either equal right with the Father or such intimate union that he acts in concert with him, confirmed by v.19. Had it been a malicious false charge, the Evangelist would likely have indicated so, as he does elsewhere; even Socinus admitted the Apostle and the Jews agreed on it.
sources.quote: It is not to be denied that he had really wrought on the sabbath, and had really called God his Father, and in a sense peculiar ; and why should not the rest of the charge be as true as the other?
sources.raw_question: Was the charge that Jesus made himself equal with God (John 5:18) merely a false accusation by the Jews, or a true account of what he claimed?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Instead of protesting against their construction, which a mere man would have done with indignation and abhorrence, he went on to set forth the original and essential supremacy of his person as God, while acknowledging the subordination of his mission as man.
sources.quote: instead of protesting against their construction of his words, which, if only a man, He would have done with indignation and abhorrence, He proceeded, while acknowledging the subordination of his mission as man, to set forth the original and essential supremacy of his person as God.
sources.raw_question: When the Jews accused Jesus of making himself equal with God in John 5, did Jesus reject that interpretation of his words?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: It is the Evangelist's own account. John is giving the reasons the Jews sought to kill Jesus, not just repeating their words, as Hilary and others held. Even Socinus admitted that the Apostle, as well as the Jews, understood Christ to have declared himself equal to God. If it were only the Jews' charge, it would still be true: he really worked on the sabbath and really called God his Father in a peculiar sense. His words 'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' and 'what things soever he doth, these also doth the Son likewise' confirm the equality, and the Evangelist would have flagged a false charge, as he does elsewhere.
sources.quote: It does not appear that the Evangelist barely repeated what the Jews had said: but he gives the reasons why the Jews sought to kill him; namely, because he had broke the sabbath, and because he “made himself ‘equal with God.”
sources.raw_question: In John 5:18, is the statement that Jesus 'made himself equal with God' merely a false charge by the Jews, or the Evangelist's own account?

question: What does Paul's salutation 'Grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' imply about Christ's relation to the Father?
synthesis: Bickersteth and Warfield agree that the salutation presents the Father and Christ jointly as the source of divine blessing. Bickersteth grounds this in eternal life being found equally in both and in prayers addressed to both without regard to order, which he takes as proof of coequal deity. Warfield instead stresses that varying the names, whether Christ is omitted in Colossians or the Spirit is added in 2 Cor 13:14, changes only the fullness of expression, since all are regarded as the common source of grace.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: It implies the Son's coequal deity. Spiritual blessing is derived mutually from the Father and the Son because eternal life is found equally in both. The apostle also prays to the Father and to the Lord Jesus Christ together, without regard to the order of their names, as equally able to grant what is asked.
sources.quote: Why this mutual derivation of spiritual blessing from the Father and the Son? Surely, because equally in the Father and in the Son have we eternal life.
sources.raw_question: What does the apostolic salutation "Grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" imply about the Son's relation to the Father?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: It presents the Father and Christ as the joint source of Divine blessings. The omission of Christ's name in Colossians or the addition of the Spirit in 2 Cor 13:14 changes only the fullness of expression, not the essence of the matter, since all are regarded as the common source of grace.
sources.quote: It is obviously no departure from this habit in the essence of the matter, but only in relative fullness of expression, when in the opening words of the Epistle to the Colossians the clause “and the Lord Jesus Christ” is omitted
sources.raw_question: What does Paul's habitual greeting of 'grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' imply about Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Because we have eternal life equally in the Father and in the Son. The blessing is drawn from both together. Prayers also ask the Father and Christ for blessings without regard to which is named first, which treats them as equal in power to grant the request.
sources.quote: Why this mutual derivation of spiritual blessing from the Father and the Son? Surely, because equally in the Father and in the Son have we eternal life.
sources.raw_question: Why do the apostolic benedictions ask for grace and peace from both God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, and what does this show about Christ?

question: Is the Word who became incarnate the same Word through whom God created the world?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Hippolytus agree that the incarnate Word is the very Word who created the world, but they argue differently. Irenaeus argues from the Word's invisible governance of creation and His role in forming Adam. On this ground he holds that the Word's coming in the flesh joins the beginning to the end and sums up all things in Himself. Hippolytus argues exegetically: he links the prophetic statement that the heavens were made by the Word of the Lord with John's statement that the world was made by Him and He came to His own.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVIII.—God the Father and His Word have formed all created things (which They use) by Their own power and wisdom, not out of defect or ignorance. The Son of God, who received all power from the Father, would otherwise never have taken flesh upon Him.
sources.answer: Yes. The Creator of the world is truly the Word of God, our Lord, who was made man in the last times. He invisibly contains and governs all created things. Therefore He came visibly to His own, was made flesh, and hung on the tree in order to sum up all things in Himself.
sources.quote: For the Creator of the world is truly the Word of God: and this is our Lord, who in the last times was made man, existing in this world, and who in an invisible manner contains all things created
sources.raw_question: Is the Word of God, who became incarnate, truly the Creator of the world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIV.—Proof against the Marcionites, that the prophets referred in all their predictions to our Christ.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord made the 'plough' and 'pruning-hook', namely the first sowing of man in the creation of Adam and the gathering in of the harvest at the last times by the Word. He joined the beginning to the end and is Lord of both; the Word, firmly united to flesh as wood joined to iron, has reclaimed the earth.
sources.quote: since He joined the beginning to the end, and is the Lord of both, He has finally displayed the plough, in that the wood has been joined on to the iron
sources.raw_question: Is the Word who became incarnate in Christ the same Lord who acted at the creation of Adam?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: Yes. John sums up the prophets and shows that the Word by whom all things were made is the one who was made manifest. The prophet says the heavens were made by the Word of the Lord. John says the world was made by Him and He came to His own. Therefore the creating Word is the Word made manifest, through whom we know the Father.
sources.quote: If, then, said he, the world was made by Him, according to the word of the prophet, “By the Word of the Lord were the heavens made,” then this is the Word that was also made manifest.
sources.raw_question: Is the Word who became incarnate the same Word through whom God created the world?

question: How can the impassible Word of God be said to suffer?
synthesis: Hippolytus and Irenaeus agree that the impassible Word became subject to suffering through the flesh or humanity he assumed in the incarnation, while remaining the same Word. Hippolytus grounds this in scriptural images and prophecy (the blood-sprinkled vesture of the Apocalypse, Micah). Irenaeus offers two lines of support: one treats it within his theme of the Word summing up all things in himself, so that he becomes visible and passible; the other simply affirms that the prophets consistently foretold the impassible one's suffering and descent into death.

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: The Word suffered through the flesh he assumed. The vesture sprinkled with blood in the Apocalypse symbolizes the flesh, through which the impassible Word came under suffering. The prophets also testify to this suffering in the flesh, as Micah does when he says they stripped off his glory.
sources.quote: the vesture sprinkled with blood denoted in symbol the flesh, through which the impassible Word of God came under suffering
sources.raw_question: How can the impassible Word of God be said to suffer?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: By taking man into himself in the incarnation. The Word, who is truly man as well as God, became visible, comprehensible and capable of suffering while remaining the same Word. In this way he sums up all things in himself, so that he holds supremacy in visible and bodily things as he does in invisible ones.
sources.quote: the invisible becoming visible, the incomprehensible being made comprehensible, the impassible becoming capable of suffering, and the Word being made man, thus summing up all things in Himself
sources.raw_question: How can the impassible and invisible Word of God become capable of suffering?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Yes. Speaking prophetically, they proclaimed that the one who was impassible would be subject to suffering. They also declared that he who was then in heaven would descend into the dust of death, which points forward to his incarnation as a man.
sources.quote: proclaiming also the impassible as subject to suffering, and declaring that He who was then in heaven had descended into the dust of death
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent for the prophets to call the impassible Son of God subject to suffering?

question: Is God's vindictive justice, by which he punishes sin, an essential property of his nature, or only a free act of his will that he could exercise or forbear?
synthesis: All three answers come from John Owen and agree that punitive justice is an essential property of God's nature. In Of Communion with God he argues from the necessity of Christ's blood for atonement and holds that a will to punish where one could justly forbear would be ill-will rather than justice. In A Brief Declaration he argues from God's role as necessary Governor and Judge and from the law's sanction, treating anger and wrath as effects of that justice.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It is a property of his nature. God would admit of no atonement except the blood of his own Son, which shows that his holiness and righteousness necessarily require him to punish sin. Making punishment a free act that God might forbear makes justice not a property of his nature. A will to punish where one could justly do otherwise is ill-will rather than justice.
sources.quote: To look upon it as that which God may exercise or forbear, makes his justice not a property of his nature, but a free act of his will
sources.raised_by_detail: those who ground the necessity of satisfaction in a free act of God's will
sources.raw_question: Is God's vindictive justice an essential property of his nature, or only a free act of his will that he could have exercised or not?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It is a property of his nature. To regard it as something God may exercise or forbear makes justice a free act of will rather than a property of his nature. And a will to punish where one could do otherwise without injustice would be ill-will rather than justice.
sources.quote: To look upon it as that which God may exercise or forbear, makes his justice not a property of his nature, but a free act of his will; and a will to punish where one may do otherwise without injustice, is rather ill-will than justice.
sources.raw_question: Is God's vindictive justice a necessary property of his nature, or merely a free act of his will that he could exercise or forbear?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: It is an essential property of his nature. God, as the necessary Governor and Judge of the world, must naturally be righteous and render to each according to his works. The sanction of the law came from his essential justice, not from anger, since no lawgiver makes laws in wrath. Anger and wrath in God name the effects of justice and are not merely free acts of his will.
sources.quote: Anger and wrath in God express the effects of justice, and so are not merely free acts of his will. This, therefore, is a tottering cause, that is built on the denial of God’s essential righteousness.
sources.raw_question: Is the justice by which God punishes sin an essential property of his nature, or only a free act of his will expressed as anger and wrath?

question: When God says to Abraham 'Now I know that thou fearest God,' does this mean God gained new knowledge He did not have before?
synthesis: Hilary and Augustine agree that God learned nothing new, but they explain the text differently. Hilary says the 'now' marks God's declaring His knowledge on a fitting occasion, citing Abraham's faith already counted for righteousness, and applies the same reading to the Father 'knowing' the day. Augustine treats it as a figure of speech naming the cause by its effect: God is said to know because the trial made Abraham himself know the firmness of his faith.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Scripture says Abraham believed God and it was counted for righteousness long before, so God knew his faith already. The 'now' marks the occasion of declaring knowledge and of Abraham receiving testimony, not of God beginning to know; God's knowledge depends on the occasion, not on any change in Him.
sources.quote: this now I know marks the time when Abraham received this testimony, not when God began to know.
sources.raw_question: Does God's word to Abraham 'now I know that thou fearest God' mean God only then learned of Abraham's faith?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. God's knowledge is not the discovery of what He did not know but its declaration. God does not learn by sudden perception; He declares His knowledge when the occasion comes. So the Father 'knowing' the day means He does not conceal it from the Son.
sources.quote: God’s knowledge is not the discovery of what He did not know, but its declaration.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says God came to know something (e.g. Abraham's love), does God's knowledge involve discovering what He did not know before?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: No. This is a figure of speech in which the cause is named by its effect, as cold is called sluggish because it makes men sluggish. God is said to know because he made Abraham himself know the firmness of his own faith through the trial. Likewise, "The Lord saw" means the Lord caused himself to be seen.
sources.quote: after that mode of speech in which the effect is signified by the efficient,—as cold is said to be sluggish, because it makes men sluggish
sources.raw_question: When God says to Abraham "Now I know that thou fearest God," does this mean God gained new knowledge?

question: Is the power of creating out of nothing proper to God alone and incommunicable to any creature?
synthesis: Waterland and Athanasius agree that no creature can create out of nothing. Waterland rests the claim on presumptive proofs: Scripture never ascribes creation to any creature, reason judges that nothing comes into being by a power less than the Author of all being, and the ante-Nicene writers agreed. Athanasius argues that creatures only arrange existing material and are not efficient causes. He adds that if one creature could create, all could and the Word would be needless, so the Word, through whom all things were made, is not a creature.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: Yes, by strong presumptive proofs. Scripture everywhere treats creation as a divine act and never says even a grain of sand was created by an angel, archangel or any creature; reason suggests nothing can come into being by any power less than that of the Author and Fountain of all being; and the sober part of mankind and the Ante-Nicene Catholic writers agreed.
sources.quote: creation every where in Scripture looked on as a divine act; not so much as a grain of sand, or a particle of matter, said to be created by an angel, or archangel, or any creature whatever
sources.raw_question: Is the power of creating out of nothing incommunicable to any creature, so that only God can create?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture everywhere treats creation as a divine act and never ascribes the creating of even a particle of matter to an angel or any creature; reason suggests nothing can come into being by power less than that of the Author of all being; and this was the doctrine of the ante-Nicene and later Catholic writers.
sources.quote: creation every where in Scripture looked on as a divine act; not so much as a grain of sand, or a particle of matter, said to be created by an angel, or archangel, or any creature whatever
sources.raw_question: Is creation out of nothing an act proper to God alone and incommunicable to any creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: No. None of the things brought to be is an efficient cause. Angels, the sun and men cannot make what is not into what is; man only arranges existing material, and it is God who fashions man and makes wood grow. If one creature could create, every creature could, and then the Word would be needless. Since all things were made through the Word, he is not among the creatures.
sources.quote: For none of things which are brought to be is an efficient cause, but all things were made through the Word: who would not have wrought all things, were He Himself in the number of the creatures.
sources.raw_question: Can a creature brought from nothing have the power to create other things out of nothing?

question: Does Psalm 110:3, 'From the womb before the morning star I begat Thee,' speak of the Son's true generation from the Father rather than his human birth from Mary?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary agree that the verse teaches a real begetting of the Son from God. Their emphases differ. Athanasius argues against reading it as the birth from Mary: many are born before the morning star rises, and the star itself signifies Christ's flesh. He also holds that 'womb', like 'heart', is said of God in human fashion and is not meant bodily. Hilary makes a similar point about 'womb', comparing it to Scripture's talk of God's hands and eyes, but uses it to show that the Father truly begot the Son from Himself, and therefore that the Son is no creature.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. Many others are born before the rising of the star, so it would be no special prerogative; and the text says 'before the morning star', not 'before its rising', so if taken bodily Christ's body would predate Adam, since the stars preceded Adam. Since Revelation calls the Offspring of David the 'Bright and Morning Star', the morning star means Christ's flesh. The verse therefore means 'I have begotten Thee from Myself before Thy appearance in the flesh.'
sources.quote: it is plain that the flesh of the Saviour is called ‘the Morning Star,’ which the Offspring from God preceded; so that the sense of the Psalm is this, ‘I have begotten Thee from Myself before Thy appearance in the flesh;’
sources.raised_by_detail: Marcellians/those who deny the Son pre-existed the Incarnation
sources.raw_question: Does 'before the morning star' in Psalm 110:3 refer to Christ's human birth from Mary rather than to an eternal begetting?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. If 'womb' must be rejected as human, so must 'heart,' which Scripture also ascribes to God; as we do not take God's heart corporeally, neither should we take his womb so, since Scripture speaks in human fashion of what is above man. Moreover, 'before the morning star' cannot mark a remarkable birth from Mary, since many are born before the star rises.
sources.quote: as when the heart of God is spoken of, we do not conceive of it as human, so if Scripture says ‘from the womb,’ we must not take it in a corporeal sense.
sources.raised_by_detail: ill-instructed men resisting the doctrine of a Son
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 110:3, 'From the womb before the morning star I begat Thee,' refer to Christ's birth from Mary rather than his eternal generation from God, since 'womb' is a human term?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: It asserts the reality of the Son's birth: that the Father truly begot the Son from Himself. Just as Scripture speaks of God's hands, eyes and heart to show that He really acts, sees and wills without bodily members, so 'womb' shows He really begot from Himself, without using a womb. Hilary asks what such a revelation would mean if the Only-begotten were a creature.
sources.quote: so from the word ‘womb’ it is clear that He really begot from Himself Him Whom He begat; not that he made use of a womb, but that He purposed to express reality.
sources.raw_question: What does the word 'womb' in Psalm 110:3 teach about the Son's origin from the Father?

question: In 1 John 4:8, 'God is love,' which divine Person is meant: does the text refer to the divine essence in general, to the Father, or to another Person?
synthesis: John Owen and Augustine both read the text as pointing to a particular Person, but they name different ones. Owen says 'God' here is the Father, because verse 9 distinguishes him from the Son he sends. Augustine says the 'love' that is 'of God' is God from God and so must be the Son or the Spirit, and he identifies it as the Holy Spirit because John links our abiding in God to the gift of the Spirit.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: It refers personally to the Father. This is evident from verse 9, where he is distinguished from his only begotten Son whom he sends into the world.
sources.quote: That the name of God is here taken personally, and for the person of the Father, not essentially, is evident from verse 9, where he is distinguished from his only begotten Son whom he sends into the world.
sources.raw_question: Does 'God' in 1 John 4:8 ('God is love') refer to the divine essence or personally to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Holy Spirit is Called Love, and Whether He Alone is So Called. That the Holy Spirit is in the Scriptures Properly Called by the Name of Love.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit. John calls the love that is 'of God' God, so it is God of God, and must be either the Son or the Spirit, since only the Father is God without being of God. John then explains our abiding in God by His having given us of His Spirit. Since that abiding is the work of love, the Spirit is the God who is love.
sources.quote: Therefore the Holy Spirit, of whom He hath given us, makes us to abide in God, and Him in us; and this it is that love does. Therefore He is the God that is love.
sources.raw_question: In 1 John 4, which divine Person is meant by 'love' when John says that love is of God and that God is love?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: It refers personally to the Father. Verse 9 distinguishes this God from his only begotten Son whom he sends into the world, so the one called love is the Father. The text means the Father is not only of a loving nature but eminently dispenses himself to us in free love.
sources.quote: That the name of God is here taken personally, and for the person of the Father, not essentially, is evident from verse 9, where he is distinguished from his only begotten Son whom he sends into the world.
sources.raw_question: In 1 John 4:8, "God is love," does the name "God" refer to the divine essence in general or personally to the Father?

question: Does the Son's sitting at the right hand of the Father imply any inequality of rank between Father and Son?
synthesis: Basil and Athanasius agree that the session at the right hand implies no inferiority, but they argue differently. Basil reads 'right hand' as non-physical language for equality of honour and shared throne, with sitting signifying the stability of the divine nature. Athanasius argues that whatever is right and precious in the Father the Son also has, and that the Son likewise sees the Father on the right, showing their mutual indwelling.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: No. The right hand signifies equality of honour, and the Son shares the Father's honour and throne. Sitting and standing signify the fixed and unchangeable stability of the divine nature, as in Baruch's words, "thou sittest for ever." Many witnesses attest this session, including Christ, Stephen, Paul, the Father himself and the Holy Spirit in Scripture. To degrade the Son from equality to a lower state is therefore indefensible.
sources.quote: Standing and sitting, I apprehend, indicate the fixity and entire stability of the nature
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's sitting at the right hand of the Father mean he holds a lower rank than the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: No. 'Right hand' is not to be understood physically, nor does it indicate a lower place, but equality of relation; Scripture uses dignified language of the seat of honour to set forth the magnificence of the Son's dignity.
sources.quote: The expression “right hand” does not, as they contend, indicate the lower place, but equality of relation
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's sitting at the 'right hand' of the Father signify inferiority of rank?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. Whatever is right and precious in the Father the Son also has, as He says 'All things that the Father hath are Mine.' The Son likewise sees the Father on the right, which shows that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son.
sources.quote: Sitting then on the right, yet He does not place His Father on the left; but whatever is right and precious in the Father, that also the Son has, and says, ‘All things that the Father hath are Mine.’
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's sitting at the Father's right hand imply that the Father is placed on the left, that is, in some inferior position?

question: Does being baptized with both water and the Holy Spirit imply that water shares the same nature, office or honour as the Spirit?
synthesis: Ambrose and Basil both answer no. Ambrose argues that because water and Spirit have different offices (water represents the death and burial of sin, the Spirit gives the pledge of life), their natures also differ, and the Spirit is far superior. Basil makes the same contrast between water as a figure of death and the Spirit as quickening power. He also gives further grounds: the Gospel contrast between John's water-baptism and Christ's baptism with the Spirit, and martyrs saved without water through their own blood.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VI. Although we are baptized with water and the Spirit, the latter is much superior to the former, and is not therefore to be separated from the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. Their offices differ: in the water is the representation of death and burial of the body of sin, while in the Spirit is the pledge of life by which we are renewed and born again in God. Since the offices differ, so do the natures, and the Spirit is far superior to the water.
sources.quote: For in the water is the representation of death, in the Spirit is the pledge of life, that the body of sin may die through the water, which encloses the body as it were in a kind of tomb
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Christians are baptized with both water and the Holy Spirit imply that water and the Spirit have the same office and nature?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Reply to the suggested objection that we are baptized “into water.” Also concerning baptism.
sources.answer: No. The grace that comes from the Spirit differs from baptism by water. John baptized with water unto repentance, but Christ baptizes with the Holy Ghost. Martyrs have been saved without the outward sign of water, baptized in their own blood. So those who use water to lower the Spirit confuse things that are distinct and compare what admits of no comparison.
sources.quote: Thus I write not to disparage the baptism by water, but to overthrow the arguments of those who exalt themselves against the Spirit; who confound things that are distinct from one another, and compare those which admit of no comparison.
sources.raised_by_detail: Pneumatomachi (those who exalt themselves against the Spirit)
sources.raw_question: Is the baptismal water comparable in dignity to the Holy Spirit, such that being baptized "into water" puts water on a level with the Spirit in baptism?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Reply to the suggested objection that we are baptized “into water.” Also concerning baptism.
sources.answer: No. In baptism water and Spirit play different roles: the water, receiving the body as in a tomb, merely figures death, while the Spirit pours in the quickening power that renews the soul. Any grace in the water is not from the nature of the water but from the presence of the Spirit, so the water is a type and instrument, not a source of divine life deserving divine honour.
sources.quote: It follows that if there is any grace in the water, it is not of the nature of the water, but of the presence of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: If being baptized into the Holy Spirit proves the Spirit's divine honour, does being baptized into water likewise imply that water should share the honour of the Father and the Son?

question: When Abraham addressed one of the three visitors at Mamre as Lord, was that one God (the Son) and the other two merely angels?
synthesis: The authors disagree. Hilary of Poitiers says Abraham honored only one of the three as God. He points to Lot addressing the two who went to Sodom with the plural 'my lords' as proof that they were mere angels. Augustine rejects this reading on the ground that Lot addresses the two in the singular as 'lord', so a singular address does not mark one superior visitor or the Son among subordinate angels.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Only One. Abraham worships and addresses one of the three as Lord and Judge, while Lot addresses the two who departed with the plural 'my lords', showing they were mere angels. Scripture never uses a plural for the One God and Lord, nor pays Divine honours to the two angels.
sources.quote: Here the plural lords shews that this was nothing more than a vision of angels; in the other case the faithful patriarch pays the honour due to One only.
sources.raw_question: When Abraham bowed before the three men at Mamre, was he honoring all three as God, or only One?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Appearance to Lot is Examined.
sources.answer: No. Scripture anticipates and contradicts this reading: after the Lord departed from Abraham, two angels came to Sodom, and Lot likewise addresses the two of them as one 'lord.' If the one recognized as Lord had already gone away and sent the two, Lot's singular address to both would make no sense; so the singular address signals the one Lord God of one substance rather than one superior among inferiors.
sources.quote: What is meant by his saying to them, “Oh! not so, my lord,” if He who was the Lord had already departed, and had sent the angels? Why is it said, “Oh! not so, my lord,” and not, “Oh! not so, my lords?”
sources.raw_question: Does Abraham's addressing one of the three visitors at Mamre as 'Lord' show that one of them was the Son of God (greater) and the other two merely his angels?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Of the Same Appearance.
sources.answer: No. Scripture anticipates and contradicts this reading: shortly afterwards two angels come to Lot, and Lot also addresses one of them as Lord. So addressing one as Lord does not mark that one as greater or as the Son with the others as subordinate angels.
sources.quote: Holy Scripture has not forgotten to anticipate, by a contradiction, such future cogitations and opinions, when a little while after it says that two angels came to Lot
sources.raw_question: Because Abraham spoke to one of the three visitors as Lord, was that one the Son of God and the other two merely his angels?

question: What does Christ mean in John 14:7 by saying that the disciples 'from henceforth know' and 'have seen' the Father?
synthesis: The two authors read the verse differently. Novatian takes the seeing of the invisible Father as still future: Scripture often speaks of future things as already done, so Christ describes the promised vision as though it had happened. Hilary instead separates sight from knowledge: the disciples had already seen the Father's nature dwelling in the Son under the flesh, and from that revelation onward they would know it.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Proves Also that the Words Spoken to Philip Make Nothing for the Sabellians.
sources.answer: Scripture often speaks of certain future things as already done. Isaiah said "unto us a child is born" before Christ was born, and the Psalms describe the passion before it happened. So Christ speaks of the future vision of the Father, which His followers will surely gain as a reward, as though it were already accomplished.
sources.quote: For the divine Scripture, foreseeing, speaks of things which it knows shall be as being already done, and speaks of things as perfected which it regards as future, but which shall come to pass without any doubt.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ say the disciples "henceforth have known and have seen" the Father, when the Father is invisible and the vision is still future?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Christ distinguishes the time of sight from the time of knowledge. The disciples had already gazed on the Father's nature dwelling in the Son under the flesh. From the time of this revelation onward, they would possess the knowledge of that nature.
sources.quote: Christ says that the Father has been seen already and shall now be known; and this, although sight, is knowledge.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean by saying that the disciples have already seen the Father and will henceforth know him (John 14:7)?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: He separates the time of sight from the time of knowledge. The Apostles had already seen the Father's nature in the Son. From the moment of this revelation onward, they would recognise and know that nature.
sources.quote: He makes a distinction between the time of sight, and the time of knowledge. He says that from henceforth they shall know Him Whom they had already seen
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ in John 14:7 distinguish between the Apostles having seen the Father and their coming to know him 'from henceforth'?

question: In what sense is the Holy Spirit given to believers called the 'earnest' of their inheritance: a pledge held as security, or a first portion of the inheritance itself?
synthesis: Owen and Irenaeus agree that the earnest is a present portion of the promised inheritance itself rather than something separate from it. Owen argues from the distinction between a pledge, which is held as security for something else, and an earnest, which is part of the thing promised, and identifies the full inheritance as the fulness of the Spirit in the enjoyment of God. Irenaeus does not draw that contrast; he stresses that the portion of the Spirit given now gradually accustoms us to bear God, prepares us for incorruption, and leads toward the full grace that will make man after God's image and likeness.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: He is an earnest, not a pledge. A pledge is a separate thing left in someone's custody as security for something else. An earnest is part of the very thing promised, given beforehand to assure the whole. The context adds that the Spirit is of the same kind as the full inheritance, which is the fulness of the Spirit in the enjoyment of God.
sources.quote: An earnest is part of the price of any thing, or part of any grant, given beforehand to assure the person to whom it is given that at the appointed season he shall receive the whole that is promised him.
sources.raw_question: Is the Spirit given as an 'earnest' of our inheritance in the sense of a pledge (a pawn), or as a first part of the inheritance itself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VIII.—The gifts of the Holy Spirit which we receive prepare us for incorruption, render us spiritual, and separate us from carnal men. These two classes are signified by the clean and unclean animals in the legal dispensation.
sources.answer: The earnest is a portion of the Spirit given now, a part of the honour God has promised. It tends toward perfection and prepares us for incorruption, gradually accustoming us to receive and bear God. Even now it makes us spiritual and leads us to cry "Abba, Father." The full grace of the Spirit will later make man after the image and likeness of God.
sources.quote: But we do now receive a certain portion of His Spirit, tending towards perfection, and preparing us for incorruption, being little by little accustomed to receive and bear God; which also the apostle terms “an earnest,”
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Holy Spirit now given to believers called an "earnest" of their inheritance?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: The Spirit is an earnest because he is an actual part of the inheritance itself, of the same kind as the whole, given to confirm God's promise of eternal life. A pledge is something different from what is owed, held as security; an earnest is a first portion of the promised whole. The full inheritance is the fulness of the Spirit in the enjoyment of God, so the Spirit given now, fitting us in some measure to enjoy God, is the first part and assurance of the whole.
sources.quote: God gives us the promise of eternal life. To confirm this to us, he giveth us his Spirit; which is, as the first part of the promise, to secure us of the whole.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Holy Spirit called the 'earnest' of the believer's inheritance, as distinct from a mere pledge?

question: In Christ's work of redemption, to whom is the ransom price of his blood paid: to the devil or to God?
synthesis: Augustine and Owen both deny that the devil gains anything by the ransom, but on different grounds and with different emphases. Augustine says Christ's blood was given 'as it were' as a price, and that by accepting it the devil was not enriched but bound, so that believers are loosed from his bonds. Owen states plainly that the price is paid to God, because God as judge and lawgiver holds sinners captive under the sentence of the law, and their debts and offences are owed to him.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Of the Same Subject.
sources.answer: No. The blood of Christ was given, as it were, as a price for us. But by accepting it the devil was not enriched; he was bound. This was so that believers might be loosed from his bonds, and so that he could not drag those whom Christ had redeemed into the second and eternal death.
sources.quote: In this redemption, the blood of Christ was given, as it were, as a price for us, by accepting which the devil was not enriched, but bound
sources.raw_question: If Christ's blood was given as a price for our redemption, was it paid to the devil in a way that enriched him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Redemption is deliverance from bondage, and from the miseries that come with it, through a price paid by the redeemer to the one by whose authority the captive is held. Sinners are prisoners and captives. It is God himself, as judge and lawgiver, who holds them under the sentence of the law. The price of Christ's death is therefore paid into the hand of God.
sources.quote: redemption is the deliverance of any one from bondage or captivity, and the miseries attending that condition, by the intervention or interposition of a price or ransom, paid by the redeemer to him by whose authority the captive was detained
