sources.raw_question: What is redemption by Christ, and to whom is the ransom of his death paid?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: To God. It is God himself who, as judge and lawgiver, holds sinners captive under the sentence of the law, since our debts are owed to him and our offences are against him. So the price of Christ's death is paid into God's hand, and by it we are delivered from his curse and wrath.
sources.quote: And all this is by the payment of the price mentioned into the hand of God, by whose supreme authority we are detained captives, under the sentence of the law.
sources.raw_question: In Christ's work of redemption, to whom is the ransom price paid: to Satan or to God?

question: Did Christ take real human flesh from the Virgin Mary, or did he take nothing from her or some other kind of body?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Novatian agree that Christ took real human flesh from Mary. Irenaeus argues that otherwise Christ would be only an apparent man, not truly the Son of man, and the analogy with Adam formed from earth would collapse. Novatian rejects an ethereal or starry body on soteriological grounds: unless we recognise our own bodily substance in him, we see no salvation for ourselves, and he cites Christ's birth and death as refuting such fables.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: He took real flesh from her. If he received no human substance, he would not truly have been made man or Son of man. He would have appeared man only putatively, and his sufferings would have accomplished nothing great. The analogy with Adam, who was formed from earth, would also be destroyed.
sources.quote: For if He did not receive the substance of flesh from a human being, He neither was made man nor the Son of man; and if He was not made what we were, He did no great thing in what He suffered and endured.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who allege that He took nothing from the Virgin
sources.raw_question: Did the Word take real flesh from the Virgin Mary, or did he take nothing from her?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That Jesus Christ is the Son of God and Truly Man, as Opposed to the Fancies of Heretics, Who Deny that He Took Upon Him True Flesh.
sources.answer: He took our flesh, not an ethereal, starry or other fabulous body. If we do not recognise the substance of our body in Him, we can see no salvation of ours in Him. His nativity and His death refute these fables.
sources.quote: Nor can we perceive any salvation of ours in him, if in him we do not even recognise the substance of our body
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who held Christ received nothing from Mary or had starry flesh
sources.raw_question: Did Christ receive his flesh from Mary, or did he take an ethereal or starry flesh?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXII.—Christ assumed actual flesh, conceived and born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: He took real flesh from Mary. Those who deny this destroy the analogy between Christ and Adam, who was formed by God's hand from the earth, and they reduce Christ to a merely apparent man. If he did not receive the substance of flesh from a human being, he was neither made man nor the Son of man.
sources.quote: For if He did not receive the substance of flesh from a human being, He neither was made man nor the Son of man; and if He was not made what we were, He did no great thing in what He suffered and endured.
sources.raised_by_detail: Docetists/Gnostics who say he took nothing from the Virgin
sources.raw_question: Did Christ take real flesh from the Virgin Mary, or did he take nothing from her as some heretics claim?

question: Why was it fitting that the devil be conquered through a man rather than by God's power alone?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Augustine agree that the devil had to be conquered through man himself, since man was the one he had conquered. Irenaeus grounds this in Christ keeping the commandment Adam broke, binding Satan with the same chains he used on man. Augustine grounds it in the Creator's justice and goodness: the victor had to come from the very race the devil held captive through its origin in one man.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: Satan had bound man through transgression, so it was necessary that he be bound, when conquered, through man himself and with the same chains. The Son of man kept the commandment that Adam broke, exposing Satan as an apostate from the law. In this way man is set free and returns to his Lord, while Satan is left with the bonds of sin. Thus he who had unjustly led men captive is justly led captive.
sources.quote: it was necessary that through man himself he should, when conquered, be bound with the same chains with which he had bound man, in order that man, being set free, might return to his Lord
sources.raw_question: Why was it fitting that Satan be conquered through a man rather than by God's power alone?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: Because the devil gained power over man by enticing him to transgress his Maker's law. It was therefore necessary that he be conquered through man himself and bound with the same chains. The Son of man observed the precept Adam broke, and so undid the infringement that occurred in Adam and set man free to return to his Lord.
sources.quote: there was done away with that infringement of God’s commandment which had occurred in Adam, by means of the precept of the law, which the Son of man observed, who did not transgress the commandment of God
sources.raw_question: Why was it fitting that Satan be defeated by Christ as man keeping God's commandment, rather than by some other means?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Other Advantages of the Incarnation.
sources.answer: It belonged to the justice and goodness of the Creator that the devil be conquered by the same rational creature he rejoiced to have conquered. That victor had to come from the very race he held captive through the corruption of its origin in one man. Augustine adds in the following chapter that God could have taken manhood from some other source, but judged it better to take it from the conquered race itself, born of a virgin.
sources.quote: It belonged also to the justice and goodness of the Creator, that the devil should be conquered by the same rational creature which he rejoiced to have conquered, and by one that came from that same race
sources.raw_question: Why was it just that the devil be conquered by a man descended from Adam's race rather than by divine power alone?

question: How can Scripture say that the 'Lord of glory' was crucified, when the suffering belonged to Christ's human nature and the divine nature did not suffer?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine agree that the crucified one is rightly called the Lord of glory. Gregory grounds this in the contact and mingling of the natures, through which the attributes and divine names pass from the Divine to the Human. Augustine grounds it in the identity of the person: the Son of man in the form of a servant is the very same as the Son of God, so God was crucified according to the weakness of the flesh, not the power of the divinity.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: Because of the contact and union of the natures, the proper attributes of each belong to both. The Lord receives the stripes of the servant, and the servant is glorified with the honour of the Lord. This is why the Cross is called the Cross of the Lord of glory and why every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord.
sources.quote: by reason of contact and the union of Natures the proper attributes of each belong to both, as the Lord receives the stripes of the servant, while the servant is glorified with the honour of the Lord
sources.raw_question: If the natures stay distinct, how can Scripture speak of the 'Lord of glory' being crucified and confess that Jesus is Lord?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Because the one who is Son of man by the form of a servant is the very same as the Son of God in the form of God, Paul can say the princes of this world 'crucified the Lord of glory.' The assumption of humanity was such as to make God man and man God. God is rightly said to have been crucified, not according to the power of the divinity but according to the weakness of the flesh.
sources.quote: even God is rightly said to have been crucified, not after the power of the divinity, but after the weakness of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Can it truly be said that God, or the Lord of glory, was crucified, given that crucifixion was suffered in Christ's human nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: Because the divine names pass to the Man through the union of the natures. The majesty implied in these names is transmitted from the Divine to the Human by the mingling of the divine nature with the lowly nature. So he who was shown on the Cross is rightly called the Lord of glory.
sources.quote: the majesty implied in these names is transmitted from the Divine to the Human by the commixture of Its Nature with that Nature which is lowly
sources.raw_question: Why can the crucified Christ be called "the Lord of glory" if the divine nature did not suffer?

question: Does Hebrews 3's citation of Psalm 95 (with Isaiah 63:10 and Acts 7:51) show that the God whom Israel provoked in the wilderness, and whom we are called to worship, is the Holy Spirit?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Bickersteth both answer yes. Both rest on the fact that Hebrews introduces the Psalm's words with 'as the Holy Ghost saith,' so what the prophecy says of God is said of the Spirit. Gregory uses this to show the Spirit's divinity. Bickersteth adds Isaiah 63:10 and Stephen's words in Acts 7:51, and draws two further points: the Spirit is the object of worship, and this does not exclude the Father and the Son, since the Spirit is essentially one with them.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. David says Israel provoked God in the wilderness, and the apostle introduces the same words with "as the Holy Ghost saith." In this way he refers to the Person of the Holy Ghost all that the prophecy refers to God, which ascribes divinity to the Spirit.
sources.quote: the apostle refers to the Holy Spirit the despite done by the Israelites to God
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews' use of Psalm 95 show that the God whom Israel provoked in the wilderness was the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes, eminently. The God whom the Psalmist calls us to worship is the one Israel provoked in the wilderness. Hebrews puts the Psalm's words in the mouth of the Holy Ghost, and Isaiah and Stephen say the fathers vexed and resisted the Holy Spirit. Yet this does not exclude the Father and the Son, since the Spirit is essentially one with them, so every command to worship God includes the Spirit.
sources.quote: We may fairly conclude that the One whom the Psalmist calls upon us to worship is the same One whom he says, the Israelites provoked. This One the parallel passages assure us was eminently the Eternal Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Do Psalm 95, Hebrews 3, Isaiah 63:10 and Acts 7:51 show that the God whom Israel is called to worship, and whom Israel provoked in the wilderness, is the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The One the Psalmist calls us to worship is the same One whom the Israelites provoked in the wilderness, and the parallel passages identify that One as eminently the Holy Spirit. Hence the Spirit is the object of worship, being the Person of the Trinity most prominently tempted and grieved, and therefore most prominently to be supplicated.
sources.quote: The Spirit was the One of the sacred Trinity most prominently tempted and grieved by the Israelites, and therefore the One most prominently to be supplicated.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 95, read alongside Hebrews 3, Isaiah 63:10 and Acts 7:51, show that the Holy Spirit is the God whom we are called to worship?

question: What does Christ mean by 'For their sakes I sanctify myself' (John 17:19), and does it imply that He Himself needed to be made holy?
synthesis: Athanasius reads the verse christologically: the Word is not sanctified by another but is the Sanctifier. He sanctifies His own assumed manhood in the Spirit so that all may be sanctified in Him, and He did not need to become holy. Owen instead reads 'sanctify' as sacrificial consecration: Christ dedicates Himself as an offering to be slain for believers. Owen does not address whether the Word was already holy; his emphasis falls on the atoning death rather than on the Word's sanctifying of His humanity.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: It shows that He is the Sanctifier. He is not sanctified by another but sanctifies Himself, and one who sanctifies himself is Lord of sanctification. As the Father's Word, He gives the Spirit to Himself when He becomes man, and He sanctifies His own manhood in the Spirit, so that all may be sanctified in Him, who is the Truth.
sources.quote: He has shown that He is not the sanctified, but the Sanctifier; for He is not sanctified by other, but Himself sanctifies Himself, that we may be sanctified in the truth.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'for their sakes I sanctify Myself' (John 17:19) show that He is the one sanctified or the Sanctifier?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: It means that Christ dedicates himself as an offering, a sacrifice to be killed and slain, for believers. All his former humiliation aimed at this end: he was born and lived so that he might die for them.
sources.quote: “For their sakes I sanctify myself;” — “I dedicate myself as an offering, as a sacrifice, to be killed and slain.” This was his aim in all the former, that he might die; he was born, and lived, that he might die.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's prayer "For their sakes I sanctify myself" in John 17:19 mean?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. He who sanctifies all sanctifies himself for our sakes, not that the Word may become holy, but that in himself he may sanctify all of us. The phrase 'highly exalted' must be read the same way.
sources.quote: not that the Word may become holy, but that He Himself may in Himself sanctify all of us, in like manner we must take the present phrase, ‘He highly exalted Him,’
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that he sanctifies himself (John 17:19) imply that the Word was not already holy?

question: Did God create human beings with genuine free will rather than compelling their obedience, and why?
synthesis: Novatian and Irenaeus agree that God made man free and does not force obedience, and both tie this to man being made in God's image or likeness. Novatian adds that bondage would be unfitting for God's image and that freedom makes deserved reward or punishment possible. Irenaeus argues from God's own freedom, from the fact that scriptural exhortations and prohibitions would be pointless without human choice, and from Christ's lament over Jerusalem, stressing that God counsels rather than coerces.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Novatian, with the View of Treating of the Trinity, Sets Forth from the Rule of Faith that We Should First of All Believe in God the Father and Lord Omnipotent, the Absolute Founder of All Things. The Works of Creation are Beautifully Described. Man's Free-Will is Asserted; God's Mercy in Inflicting Penalty on Man is Shown; The Condition After Death of the Souls of the Righteous and Unrighteous is Determined.
sources.answer: Because man is made in the image of God, and it would be unfitting for God's image to be in bondage. Freedom also lets man receive deserved rewards or punishment for his own choices. God therefore made man alone free among all the creatures he serves.
sources.quote: For, on the one hand, it had behoved him to be free, lest the image of God should, unfittingly be in bondage
sources.raw_question: Why did God create man with free will?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVII.—Men are possessed of free will, and endowed with the faculty of making a choice. It is not true, therefore, that some are by nature good, and others bad.
sources.answer: God does not compel. Man has had free will from the beginning, because God Himself has free will and man was made in His likeness. That is why God counsels rather than forces: the apostle and the Lord would have had no reason to urge some actions and forbid others unless doing or not doing them were in our power. Disobedience is possible but not expedient, since it forfeits the good.
sources.quote: But because man is possessed of free will from the beginning, and God is possessed of free will, in whose likeness man was created, advice is always given to him to keep fast the good
sources.raw_question: Does God compel human beings to obey Him, or did He create them with genuine free will?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVII.—Men are possessed of free will, and endowed with the faculty of making a choice. It is not true, therefore, that some are by nature good, and others bad.
sources.answer: God does not compel anyone. From the beginning he made man a free agent with power over himself, so that he might obey God's commands willingly. There is no coercion with God, only a constant good will that offers good counsel to all. Christ's lament over Jerusalem, 'How often would I have gathered thy children together, and thou wouldest not', shows this ancient law of human liberty.
sources.quote: For there is no coercion with God, but a good will [towards us] is present with Him continually. And therefore does He give good counsel to all.
sources.raw_question: Does God compel human beings to obey him, or does he leave them free to obey or disobey?

question: Do Christ's questions in the Gospels (such as asking where Lazarus was laid) prove that the Son was ignorant and therefore not true God?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary agree that Christ's questions do not prove ignorance. Athanasius argues that one who knows can still ask, as John shows when Christ tested Philip about the loaves, and that He asked humanly while knowing divinely; he adds that raising Lazarus's soul is greater than knowing where the body lay. Hilary argues that it would be unreasonable for one who knew of Lazarus's death from afar and reads thoughts not to know these things, so His ignorance was ignorance in words only, adopted by economy to express His true humanity.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: No. He asked humanly, though He knew divinely; He who was going to raise Lazarus knew whence to recall his soul, which is greater than knowing where the body lay. Likewise, since the Father's revelation to Peter came through the Son, the Son knew Peter's answer before asking.
sources.quote: it was a greater thing to know where the soul was, than to know where the body lay; but He asked humanly, that He might raise divinely.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's asking where Lazarus was laid, or asking the disciples who men say He is, prove that the Son lacked knowledge?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. It would be against reason that he who knew from afar of Lazarus's death and reads men's thoughts should not know the tomb, the woman's faith, or the Apostles' dispute. His ignorance was ignorance only in words. By economy he asks as if ignorant in order to express his true humanity.
sources.quote: It is against reason that He should know from afar the death and burial of Lazarus, but not the place of his sepulchre: that He should read the thoughts of the mind, and not recognise the faith of the woman
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's questions in the Gospels (who touched his garment, why the Apostles quarrelled, where Lazarus was buried) prove that he was ignorant?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: No. One who asks does not necessarily ask from ignorance; one who knows can still ask about what he knows. John states explicitly that Christ asked about the loaves to test Philip, since he himself knew what he would do, and the same applies to his other questions.
sources.quote: for one who asks, does not for certain ask from ignorance; but it is possible for one who knows, still to ask concerning what He knows.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's asking questions in the Gospels (e.g., where Lazarus was laid, how many loaves the disciples had) prove that the Son is ignorant and therefore not true God?

question: Does the Father's voice from heaven ('This is My beloved Son'), especially at the Transfiguration, confirm that Christ is truly the Son of God and truly God?
synthesis: Both authors answer yes. Hilary stresses that the words 'This' and 'My' attest true Sonship, and that 'Hear Him' makes the Father's witness from heaven confirm the Son's own witness on earth. Gregory of Nyssa says the voice, heard at both the Jordan and the Transfiguration, taught hearers to see the event as more than a figure and to believe the beloved Son truly God, and that it was articulated in the air for their salvation.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. The voice repeats 'This is My Son' and reveals Him as the Father's own true Son. It adds 'Hear Him,' so the Father's witness from heaven confirms the Son's own witness on earth. This was needed because believing in Christ's true Sonship is the way to eternal life.
sources.quote: He is revealed as His Father’s own true Son. And over and above the witness of This and My to His true Sonship, the words are uttered, Hear Him.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's voice at the Transfiguration, 'This is My beloved Son; hear Him,' confirm Christ's true Sonship?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. The heavenly voice taught men to regard the event as more than a figure and to believe the beloved Son of God to be truly God. It was articulated in the air for the salvation of the hearers.
sources.quote: there came a voice from heaven, teaching men not only to regard the phenomenon as something more than a figure, but also to believe the beloved Son of God to be truly God
sources.raw_question: Does the voice from heaven at the Jordan and the Transfiguration teach that the beloved Son is truly God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: It confirms the Son's own testimony about Himself. The words "This" and "My" attest His true Sonship, and "Hear Him" commands us to trust completely what the Son says about Himself. So the Father's witness from heaven confirms the witness the Son bore on earth.
sources.quote: It is the witness of the Father from heaven, in confirmation of the witness borne by the Son on earth; for we are bidden to hear Him.
sources.raw_question: What does the Father's voice at the Transfiguration, "This is My beloved Son; hear Him," add to the testimony about Christ's Sonship?

question: In theology about God, does the precise wording of terms (down to syllables and prepositions) matter, or is the soundness of the thought behind them what counts?
synthesis: The two authors lean in different directions. Gregory of Nyssa holds that the thought matters more than the words. Words only interpret thought and may fall short of the unspeakable divine nature, and God values the soul's right attitude above propriety of phrases, so the minutiae of names are left to grammarians. Basil defends the close investigation of syllables and prepositions: becoming like God requires knowledge, which comes through teaching and speech, so despising small elements of language blocks the way to perfect wisdom.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Defence of S. Basil's statement, attacked by Eunomius, that the terms 'Father' and 'The Ungenerate' can have the same meaning.
sources.answer: Yes. Words interpret thought; thought is not gathered from words, for the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart. God values the right attitude of the soul toward truth above propriety of phrases, as shown by his rebuke of those who honour him with their lips while their heart is far from him, and by his hearing groanings that cannot be uttered.
sources.quote: We make the words interpret the thought; we do not by a reverse process gather the thought from the words.
sources.raw_question: In matters of faith about God, is correctness of the thought more important than the particular words used?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: The thought. Because the divine world is unspeakable and words may fall short even when the conception is right, we turn from the mere sound of phrases and examine whether the thought within them is sound. The minutiae of names are left to grammarians; it is no small gain to have the right conception even if the word is inadequate.
sources.quote: turning from the mere sound of phrases, uttered well or ill according to the mental faculty of the speaker, we search for the thought, and that alone, which is found within the phrases, to see whether that itself be sound
sources.raw_question: In theological disputes about God, should one judge the precise wording of terms or the thought they express?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Prefatory remarks on the need of exact investigation of the most minute portions of theology.
sources.answer: Yes, it is worthwhile. Basil argues that our goal is to be made like God, which requires knowledge; knowledge comes through teaching, teaching begins with speech, and syllables and words are parts of speech. Therefore investigating syllables is not shooting wide of the mark, and despising small elements prevents one from reaching the perfection of wisdom.
sources.quote: It follows then that to investigate syllables is not to shoot wide of the mark, nor, because the questions raised are what might seem to some insignificant, are they on that account to be held unworthy of heed.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who laugh at the subtlety about syllables
sources.raw_question: Is it worthwhile in theology to investigate minute terms such as individual syllables and prepositions used of God, or are such questions too insignificant to matter?

question: What is the difference between the death (and life) of the soul or spirit and the death (and life) of the body?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine agree that death means something different for the soul than for the body, and both define the soul's death in relation to God. Gregory frames it as a difference in the meaning of the terms: bodily life is the activity of the senses and its death their extinction, while for intellectual natures life is nearness to the Divine and death is falling away from it. Augustine instead defines the soul's death as God leaving it, through sin and ungodliness, and the body's death as the soul leaving it; he adds that the soul's death is the graver of the two.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. For the flesh, life is the energy and motion of the bodily senses and death is their extinction; for intellectual natures, true life is approximation to the Divine and death is decadence or departure from it. Hence the devil, the original evil, is called both death and the inventor of death, and is said to have the power of death.
sources.quote: But in the case of the intellectual nature, approximation to the Divine is the true life, and decadence therefrom is named “death”: for which reason the original evil, the devil, is called both “death,” and the inventor of death
sources.raw_question: Are the terms "life" and "death" used in a single sense when applied to bodies and to intellectual beings such as angels and souls?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: The death of the spirit is when God leaves the spirit. The death of the body is when the spirit leaves the body. Since the spirit ranks above the body, the death of the spirit is the graver of the two.
sources.quote: the death of the spirit means that God has left it, but the death of the body that the spirit has left it
sources.raw_question: What is the difference between the death of the spirit and the death of the body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The One Death and Resurrection of The Body of Christ Harmonizes with Our Double Death and Resurrection of Body and Soul, to the Effect of Salvation. In What Way the Single Death of Christ is Bestowed Upon Our Double Death.
sources.answer: The soul is dead through sin, and the body through the punishment of sin, and so also through sin. The death of the soul is ungodliness, because God has left it. The death of the body is corruptibility, which ends in the soul leaving the body. So the soul becomes foolish when God departs, and the body lifeless when the soul departs.
sources.quote: Now the death of the soul is ungodliness, and the death of the body is corruptibility, through which comes also a departure of the soul from the body. For as the soul dies when God leaves it, so the body dies when the soul leaves it
sources.raw_question: In what sense are human beings dead both in soul and in body, and what is the difference between these two deaths?

question: Where in the human soul is the image of the Trinity found, and what does it consist of?
synthesis: Augustine and Edwards both place the image of the Trinity in the mind, but they answer from different angles. Augustine says it is properly found in the mind renewed in the knowledge of God and given wisdom, by which man partakes of God. Edwards instead names its parts: the mind, its understanding or idea, and its will or affection, corresponding to the Father, the Son as God's idea, and the Spirit as God's love.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: It is found in the mind as renewed in the knowledge of God and given wisdom. This wisdom is God's gift by which man partakes of God himself and contemplates eternal things. The mind, renewed after the image of Him who created it, is where a trinity is found in the image of God.
sources.quote: a trinity is discovered in the image of God, which is man in respect to his mind, which mind is “renewed in the knowledge” of God, “after the image of Him that created” man
sources.raw_question: Where in man is the image of the Trinity properly found?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: The soul shows the Trinity in the mind, its understanding or idea, and the spirit of the mind. The spirit of the mind is the will, disposition or affection. These correspond to the Father, the Son as God's idea, and the Holy Spirit as God's love.
sources.quote: The one is in the spiritual creation, the soul of man. There is the mind, and the understanding or idea, and the spirit of the mind as it is called in Scripture, i.e., the disposition, the will or affection.
sources.raw_question: What image of the Trinity is found in the human soul?

question: Do the Father and the Son share the same nature and equality even though the Father is unbegotten and the Son is begotten?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Gregory of Nyssa agree that the difference between unbegotten and begotten does not make the Son different in nature from the Father. Hilary argues that a perfect birth imparts the whole fulness of the Father's nature, so the Son is equal in nature though not unbegotten. Gregory argues by analogy: Adam (not generated) and Abel (generated) are equally 'man', so a difference in mode of origin leaves the one simple life shared by Father and Son unchanged.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes, in nature, though not as unbegotten. The Son is God of the same nature as the Father. He is not co-equal with the Unbegotten in the sense of being unbegotten Himself, but as Only-begotten He is not unequal because of being begotten. A perfect birth imparts the whole fulness of the Father's nature.
sources.quote: God the Son is God of the same nature with God the Father, not co-equal with the Unbegotten, for He was not Himself Unbegotten, but, as the Only-begotten, not unequal because begotten
sources.raw_question: Is the Son equal to the Father even though He is begotten and the Father is unbegotten?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. As Adam and Abel are equally called 'man', being rational, mortal and capable of knowledge, though one was not generated and the other was, so difference in the mode of origin does not alter the name or idea of the nature. The single simple life found in both Father and Son is one and admits no variation.
sources.quote: If, that is, the thing that is detected both in the Father and the Son, I mean the singleness of life, is one, the very idea of singleness excluding, as we have said, any variation
sources.raw_question: Do the Father and the Son share the same nature even though one is unbegotten and the other begotten?

question: Did the Son (the Word) exist and share glory with the Father before the creation of the world?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Owen both answer yes, and both appeal to Christ's prayer in John 17 for the glory he had with the Father before the world was. Irenaeus stresses that the Word remained in the Father before Adam and all creation, glorifying Him and being glorified by Him. Owen adds that the Son then shared joint counsel with the Father in carrying out the Father's love.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIV.—If God demands obedience from man, if He formed man, called him and placed him under laws, it was merely for man’s welfare; not that God stood in need of man, but that He graciously conferred upon man His favours in every possible manner.
sources.answer: Yes. Before Adam, and before all creation, the Word remained in the Father, glorified Him, and was glorified by Him. Christ declares this when He prays, "Father, glorify Thou Me with the glory which I had with Thee before the world was."
sources.quote: For not alone antecedently to Adam, but also before all creation, the Word glorified His Father, remaining in Him; and was Himself glorified by the Father
sources.raw_question: Did the Son (the Word) exist and share glory with the Father before the creation of the world?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. In John 17 the Son prays to be glorified with the glory he had before the world was. At that time he had joint counsel with the Father in carrying out the Father's love.
sources.quote: and that with the glory which he had before the world was, when his joint counsel was in the carrying on the Father’s love.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son have glory with the Father and share in the divine counsel before the creation of the world?

question: Does John 10:30 ("I and my Father are one") prove, as the Sabellians claimed, that the Father and the Son are one Person?
synthesis: Waterland and Augustine both deny it, pointing to the plural verb "are" as showing two distinct Persons, while "one" expresses their unity. Waterland adds two further grounds: the neuter "one" (unum, not unus), and the parallel with Paul and Apollos being "one" without being one person, which he presents as the Fathers' consensus against the Sabellians.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. The Fathers, both Ante-Nicene and Post-Nicene, observed against the Sabellians that the text does not prove identity of person, any more than Paul and Apollos, of whom it is said that he who plants and he who waters are one, are one person, which is absurd. The plural "we are" and the neuter "one" (unum, not unus) indicate two Persons. So whatever else the text proves, it does not prove a unity of person.
sources.quote: that that text did by no means prove an ?tdentity of person, unless Paul and Apollos were one person, which is absurd. Whatever the text might otherwise prove, it certainly did not prove, what the Sabellians pretended, an wnity of person.
sources.raw_question: Does John 10:30 ("I and my Father are one") prove that the Father and the Son are one Person, as the Sabellians claimed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Three Persons Not Properly So Called [in a Human Sense].
sources.answer: No. Christ speaks in the plural, saying 'are one,' not 'is one' as the Sabellians would have it. The plural verb shows a real distinction between Father and Son, while 'one' shows their unity.
sources.quote: And so it is said plurally, “I and my Father are one.” For He has not said, “is one,” as the Sabellians say; but, “are one.”
sources.raw_question: Does John 10:30, 'I and my Father are one,' support the Sabellian view that Father and Son are a single person?

question: What does Christ's saying "I and My Father are one" (John 10:30) teach about the relation of the Son to the Father?
synthesis: Both Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary of Poitiers read the text as teaching the unity of Father and Son without merging them into one Person. Gregory stresses the Son's identical nature together with His dependence on the Father as cause, so that the Persons' properties stay distinct while the substance remains undivided. Hilary instead treats it as the one God declaring Himself Father and Son, each speaking in the other. He draws from this unity related texts on seeing the Father in the Son and the fulness of the Godhead dwelling in Him.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Proof that the Anomœan teaching tends to Manichæism.
sources.answer: It teaches both that the Son depends on the Father as His cause and that the Son's nature is absolutely identical with the Father's. We should therefore not melt the Persons into one Person. We keep the properties of the Persons distinct while not dividing the oneness of their substance. In this way we avoid positing two diverse principles in the category of Cause.
sources.quote: we are taught in that utterance the dependence of our Lord on a cause, and yet the absolute identity of the Son’s and the Father’s nature; we do not let our idea about them be melted down into One Person
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's saying "I and My Father are one" teach about the relation of the Son to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: It is the voice of the One God proclaiming Himself to be Father and Son, the Father speaking in the Son and the Son in the Father. From this unity follow the texts that whoever sees the Son sees the Father, that the Father gave all He has and life in Himself to the Son, that only they know each other, and that the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Him bodily.
sources.quote: It is the voice of the One God proclaiming Himself to be Father and Son; Father speaking in the Son and Son in the Father.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's statement 'I and the Father are One' teach about the relation of Father and Son?

question: Does 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father' prove that the Son shares the same nature or essence as the Father?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Athanasius both answer yes, but argue differently. Gregory argues that an alien nature could not contain or display the Father. Athanasius argues from the Son's works, which show that the Son is in the Father, and from his essence being proper to the Father and like him in all points.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son were not of the same nature as the Father, He could not have had the Father in Himself or shown the Father in Himself. A foreign and alien nature cannot bear the stamp of a nature different from itself.
sources.quote: For if He were not of the same nature as the Father, how could He either have had in Himself that which was different?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "he that hath seen Me hath seen the Father" prove that the Son is of the same nature as the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is known from the works He does to be in the Father and the Father in Him, and to be seen is to see the Father, because the Son's essence is proper to the Father and He is like Him in all points.
sources.quote: ‘He that hath seen Him hath seen the Father,’ because the Son’s Essence is proper to the Father, and He in all points like Him
sources.raw_question: Does the saying 'He that hath seen me hath seen the Father' imply the Son shares the Father's essence?

question: Does confessing the Holy Spirit as God, along with the Father and the Son, amount to belief in three Gods?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Ambrose both reject the charge of tritheism, but argue differently. Gregory reasons that, since the Father and Son are one and not two, adding the Spirit cannot produce three Gods. Ambrose turns the objection back on the objectors: if 'God' named a person rather than a nature, confessing the Son would already imply two Gods; Catholics avoid this because 'God' names one nature.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: No. According to the Lord, the Father and the Son are one, not two, and the Holy Spirit is also one, so one added to one cannot make three Gods. Only someone who already holds a pair of Gods could reach a triad by adding the Spirit. Those who worship one God, expressed by the Name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost, are not tritheists.
sources.quote: For if the Father and the Son are not divided into duality, (for they are, according to the Lord’s words, One, and not Two) and if the Holy Ghost is also one, how can one added to one be divided into the number of three Gods?
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit as divine amount to belief in three Gods?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIII. To those who object that Catholics, when they ascribe Godhead to the Holy Spirit, introduce three Gods, it is answered, that by the same argument they themselves bring in two Gods, unless they deny Godhead to the Son; after which the orthodox doctrine is set forth.
sources.answer: Yes, by the objectors' own reasoning. If 'God' names one person rather than one nature, then whoever confesses the Son's Godhead must either admit two Gods or deny that the Son is God. Since the objectors cannot deny the Son's Godhead, their argument turns back on them. Catholics avoid the problem because 'God' names one nature.
sources.quote: For it is necessary according to your opinion, if you think that God is the name of one person, not of one nature, that you either say that there are two Gods, or deny that the Son is God.
sources.raw_question: If confessing the Spirit as God implied three Gods, would confessing the Son as God imply two Gods?

question: Is the Holy Spirit distinct from the Father and the Son, or identical with either of them?
synthesis: Bickersteth and Ambrose agree that the Holy Spirit is distinct from and not to be confounded with the Father or the Son. Their grounds differ. Bickersteth argues from the Spirit's descent at Christ's baptism and at Pentecost, from the baptismal formula, and from the apostolic benediction. Ambrose, answering the objection that the Father and Son are also called Spirit, argues from the fact that Christ died in the flesh while the Spirit, having taken no flesh, could not die.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. No one could say that the Father or the Son descended on Christ at his baptism or on the apostles at Pentecost. Nor could anyone say that we are baptized into the name of the Father, the Son, and someone who is also the Father or the Son, or that grace is sought from the Father and from one who under another name is also the Father. So the Holy Ghost cannot be confounded with either the Father or the Son.
sources.quote: The Holy Ghost therefore, cannot be identified or confounded either with the eternal Father, or with his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit identical with the Father or with the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IX. The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ, and the oil of gladness; and why Christ Himself is not the ointment, since He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It is not strange that the Spirit should be called Ointment, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. And there is no confusion between them, since Christ alone suffered death, Whose saving cross is then spoken of.
sources.answer: No. The Holy Spirit is not commingled with the Father and the Son but is distinct from both. This is shown by the fact that Christ died according to the flesh, whereas the Holy Spirit, having taken no flesh, did not and could not die.
sources.quote: but the Holy Spirit is not commingled with the Father and the Son, but is distinct from the Father and from the Son. For the Holy Spirit did not die
sources.raw_question: If the Father and the Son are both called Spirit, does this confuse the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son?

question: Since the Holy Spirit, like the Son, is called 'Lord', is the Spirit the same Person as the Son or a distinct Person?
synthesis: Ambrose and Gregory of Nyssa agree that the Spirit is a distinct Person from the Son, but they argue differently. Ambrose holds that the Son and Spirit are one Substance but not one Person, so sharing the title 'Lord' does not merge them. Gregory argues that calling the Spirit both 'Lord' and 'Spirit of the Lord' itself marks Him as a separate individual beside the Only-begotten, and he compares Paul's phrase 'the Spirit of Christ.'

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter I. The Spirit is the Lord and Power; and in this is not inferior to the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. The Holy Spirit and the Son are not one Person but one Substance. Hence the same title 'Lord' may be given to the Spirit without confusing Him with the Son.
sources.quote: for the Holy Spirit and the Son are not one Person [unus] but one Substance [unum].
sources.raw_question: If both the Son and the Holy Spirit are called 'Lord', are the Son and the Spirit one Person?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: Yes. Whoever calls Him both "Lord" and "Spirit of the Lord" teaches us to conceive of Him as a separate individual besides the Only-begotten. In the same way Paul elsewhere speaks of "the Spirit of Christ."
sources.quote: For he who calls Him both “Lord” and “Spirit of the Lord,” teaches us to conceive of Him as a separate individual besides the Only-begotten
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Holy Spirit both "Lord" and "Spirit of the Lord" show that the Spirit is a distinct Person from the Son?

question: Is the Holy Spirit Life, a source of spiritual life, in the same sense as the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Bickersteth and Ambrose both answer yes from Scripture. Bickersteth gathers texts naming the Father as the fountain of life, the Son as the one who quickens, and the Spirit as life who gives new birth, and concludes there is one life-giving God. Ambrose argues by parallel wording: the Bible calls the Word the 'Word of Life' and the Spirit the 'Spirit of Life', so the Spirit is Life just as the Word is.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture calls the Father the fountain of life, says that in the Word was life and that the Son quickens whom he will, and declares that the Spirit is life and that believers are born of the Spirit. So we depend on one life-giving God.
sources.quote: We depend on one life-giving God. Love the Lord thy God, ... cleave unto him, ... for He is thy life. Deut. 30:20.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit, like the Father and the Son, a source of spiritual life?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XV. The Holy Spirit is Life equally with the Father and the Son, in truth whether the Father be mentioned, with Whom is the Fount of Life, or the Son, that Fount can be none other than the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. John speaks of the "Word of Life" and of "the Life" that was with the Father, showing both God and his Word to be Life. Since Scripture likewise speaks of the "Spirit of Life," the Spirit of Life is Life just as the Word of Life is Life.
sources.quote: And as it is said the Word of Life, so, too, the Spirit of Life. Therefore, as the Word of Life is Life, so, too, the Spirit of Life is Life.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit Life in the same sense that the Father and the Son are Life?

question: Why does Scripture say both that the Father sends the Spirit and that the Son sends the Spirit from the Father?
synthesis: Augustine and Owen agree that the Spirit is sent by both the Father and the Son, and both call him the gift of each, but they ground this differently. Augustine reads the Johannine sayings as distinguishing the Spirit from the Father and the Son while showing him sent by each. Owen explains the twofold language by the order of the covenant of grace: the Spirit is the gift of the Father's love and the purchase of the Son's blood.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Because the covenant of grace is ordered from the love of the Father through what the Son procured. The Spirit is the gift of the Father's love and the purchase of the Son's blood. Hence Scripture speaks variously of the Father sending him and of the Son sending him from the Father.
sources.quote: thence is that variety of expression, of the Father’s sending him, and the Son’s sending him from the Father, he being the gift of the Father’s love, and purchase of the blood of the Son.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture say both that the Father sends the Spirit and that the Son sends the Spirit from the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Conclusion of the Book with a Prayer, and an Apology for Multitude of Words.
sources.answer: Yes. The Only-begotten speaks of the Spirit "whom the Father will send in my name" and also of the one "whom I will send to you from the Father." These sayings both distinguish the Spirit from the Father and the Son and show the Spirit as sent by each. The Spirit is also called the gift of the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: nor wouldest Thou, O Only-begotten, say of the Holy Spirit, “Whom the Father will send in my name;” and, “Whom I will send to you from the Father.”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that the Holy Spirit is sent by both the Father and the Son?

question: Does the Holy Spirit distribute spiritual gifts by His own will and authority, or merely as an instrument?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Basil agree that the Spirit distributes gifts by His own will, and both rest this on the apostle's words that the one Spirit divides to each severally as He wills. Gregory uses this against Eunomius to argue that the teachings the Spirit helps the faithful understand are appointed by the Spirit Himself. Basil adds that the Spirit dispenses gifts according to each recipient's worth.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Every good gift is a portion of the gifts of the Spirit. Scripture says that one and the self-same Spirit works all these gifts, dividing to each person severally as He wills. So the things Eunomius says the Spirit helps the faithful understand are appointed by the Spirit Himself.
sources.quote: “all these worketh that one and the self-same Spirit, dividing to every man severally as He will,” we therefore do not reject the statement of Eunomius
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit distribute the spiritual gifts and appoint good teachings by His own authority?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: By His own will. The apostle says the one Spirit divides to every man severally as He will. So the Spirit is present of His own will, dispensing gifts according to each recipient's worth.
sources.quote: all the while the Holy Spirit is present too of His own will, dispensing distribution of the gifts according to each recipient’s worth.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit distribute spiritual gifts by His own will, or merely as an instrument?

question: Can the Son be both derived from the Father and eternal, or does being from the Father imply that the Son came later or is not truly eternal?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary of Poitiers agree that the Son is both from the Father and eternal, but they argue differently. Gregory uses the analogy of the sun, which is never without its ray, to show that being from the Father implies no posteriority. Hilary argues that to be always from Him who always is constitutes eternity, since only what is eternal can spring from the Eternal, and a non-eternal Offspring would make the Father himself not eternal.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He then discusses the “willing” of the Father concerning the generation of the Son, and shows that the object of that good will is from eternity, which is the Son, existing in the Father, and being closely related to the process of willing, as the ray to the flame, or the act of seeing to the eye.
sources.answer: Yes, the Son is both of the Father and eternal. Though the two phrases may seem at first sight to disagree, the Father is never without the Son, as the sun is never without its ray. The Son's being of the Father therefore implies no posteriority in existence.
sources.quote: no one can well be longer in doubt how the Only-begotten at once is believed to be “of the Father,” and is eternally, even if the one phrase does not at first sight seem to agree with the other
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be both "of the Father" (derived from him) and eternal, or does derivation from the Father imply that the Son came later?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. To be always from Him Who always is constitutes eternity, even though this eternity comes from the Eternal and not from the Son himself. Nothing but what is eternal can spring from the Eternal. If the Offspring were not eternal, then neither would the Father, the source of generation, be eternal.
sources.quote: to be always from Him, Who always is, is eternity; but this eternity is derived not from Himself, but from the Eternal. And from the Eternal nothing can spring but what is eternal
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be eternal if his eternity is derived from the Father rather than from himself?

question: Does offering doxology 'in the Spirit' rather than 'with the Spirit' imply that the Holy Spirit is inferior in rank to the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Ambrose and Basil both deny that 'in the Spirit' implies inferiority, but they argue differently. Ambrose says a single syllable cannot measure the Godhead, and that the baptismal formula shows 'in' signifies a shared honour and working. Basil says the phrase confesses our own weakness, since our ability to glorify God comes from the Spirit, rather than stating the Spirit's rank.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VIII. St. Ambrose examines and refutes the heretical argument that because God is said to be glorified in the Spirit, and not with the Spirit, the Holy Spirit is therefore inferior to the Father. He shows that the particle in can be also used of the Son and even of the Father, and that on the other hand with may be said of creatures without any infringement on the prerogatives of the Godhead; and that in reality these prepositions simply imply the connection of the Three Divine Persons.
sources.answer: No. The greatness of the Godhead cannot be estimated from a single syllable. Christ in the baptismal command uses the same expression for the Spirit as for the Father and Himself, so 'in the Spirit' signifies not an office or subjection but a sharing of honour and working within the inseparable association of the Three.
sources.quote: The expression is the same for the Spirit as for the Father and for Himself. From which is inferred not any office of the Holy Spirit, but rather a sharing of honour or of working when we say “in the Spirit.”
sources.raised_by_detail: Macedonians/Pneumatomachi (those who deny the Spirit's deity)
sources.raw_question: Does the doxology formula giving glory to God 'in the Spirit' rather than 'with the Spirit' show that the Holy Spirit is inferior to the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. The phrase "in the Spirit" is not an acknowledgment of the Spirit's rank but a confession of our own weakness. We are not sufficient to glorify God of ourselves, and our sufficiency is in the Holy Spirit, who enables us to offer the sacrifice of praise.
sources.quote: the doxology which we offer “in the Spirit” is not an acknowledgment of His rank; it is rather a confession of our own weakness, while we shew that we are not sufficient to glorify Him of ourselves
sources.raw_question: Does offering doxology "in the Spirit" imply that the Holy Spirit is of lower rank than the Father and the Son?

question: How does the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 express both the unity and the distinction of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?
synthesis: Warfield and Gregory of Nyssa agree that the single 'Name' declares unity while the naming of three expresses distinction. Warfield grounds the distinction in the repeated article before each name. Gregory grounds it in the naming of three distinct subsistences, with the one Name declaring unity of essence.

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. The formula uses a single 'name' rather than 'names' or a repeated 'in the name of', which rules out three separate Beings and asserts their unity. Yet each is introduced with a repeated article, which rules out treating them as three designations of one person and emphasizes the distinct personality of each.
sources.quote: With stately impressiveness it asserts the unity of the three by combining them all within the bounds of the single Name; and then throws up into emphasis the distinctness of each by introducing them in turn with the repeated article
sources.raw_question: Does the phrasing of the baptismal formula in Matthew 28:19 ('into the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit') teach both the unity and the distinctness of the three Persons?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: It expresses union and distinction at once. Naming three distinct subsistences makes the distinction of Persons clear and free from confusion. The single 'Name' standing at the head of the formula declares their unity of essence.
sources.quote: the differentiation of the subsistences makes the distinction of Persons clear and free from confusion, while the one Name standing in the forefront of the declaration of the Faith clearly expounds to us the unity of essence of the Persons
sources.raw_question: How does the baptismal formula 'in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost' express both the unity and the distinction of the Persons?

question: Does the baptismal formula affirm that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are distinct persons rather than mere names or aspects of one person?
synthesis: Warfield and Bickersteth agree that the formula affirms a real distinction. Warfield reasons that the Son is Jesus himself, a distinct person, so those named alongside him are equally distinct. Bickersteth simply holds the distinction undeniable and pairs the formula with the apostolic benediction.

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. The Son in the formula is Jesus Himself, with all the implications of distinct personality. He is placed alongside the Father and the Holy Ghost yet distinguished from them, which implies their equally distinct personality.
sources.quote: that further carries with it the equally distinct personality of “the Father” and “the Holy Ghost,” with whom “the Son” is here associated, and from whom alike “the Son” is here distinguished.
sources.raw_question: In the baptismal formula, are the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit distinct persons rather than mere names or aspects of one person?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The baptismal formula names 'the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost'. The benediction joins 'the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit'. In both texts it is impossible to deny the necessary distinction they affirm.
sources.quote: it is impossible to deny the necessary distinction here affirmed.
sources.raw_question: Do the baptismal formula and the apostolic benediction affirm a distinction between the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the baptismal formula show that the Holy Spirit is divine and not a creature, sharing the divine Name with the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Ambrose agree. Gregory argues that Christ ranked the Spirit with the Father and himself in conferring life-giving power, which places the Spirit in uncreated existence. Ambrose argues from the one Name of the divine nature, which the Spirit shares.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIX. Having proved above that the Spirit abides and speaks in the prophets, St. Ambrose infers that He knows all things which are of God, and therefore is One with the Father and the Son. This same point he establishes again from the fact that He possesses all that God possesses, namely, Godhead, knowledge of the heart, truth, a Name above every name, and power to raise the dead, as is proved from Ezekiel, and in this He is equal to the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Baptism is commanded in the one Name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Spirit therefore has the Name above every name, and He has it through the oneness of the Name of the divine nature.
sources.quote: What, therefore, the Father and the Son have, the Holy Spirit also has through the oneness of the Name of His nature.
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula show that the Holy Spirit shares the Name above every name with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > These doctrines of our Faith witnessed to and confirmed by Scripture passages.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ, when giving the disciples the secret of knowing God, ordered that the life of the regenerate be imparted in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. In doing so he ranked the Spirit with the Father and himself in conferring the life-giving power. This precluded confusing the Spirit with creation and places him in uncreated existence.
sources.quote: thereby ranking the Spirit with the Father and Himself, precluded Him from being confused with the creation
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal command to baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost show that the Holy Spirit is not a creature?

question: Does the baptismal formula require that the Holy Spirit be worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Ambrose and Basil agree. Ambrose argues that since Christ joined the Spirit with the Father and Son in baptism, it is unreasonable to refuse to join them in devotion. Basil argues from a necessary sequence: we believe as we are baptized and give glory as we believe.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
