sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ did not disdain to join the Spirit with the Father and the Son in the sacrament of baptism. It is therefore unreasonable to object to joining the Spirit with them in our devotion.
sources.quote: Why, then, do some take it ill that He Whom the Lord disdained not in the sacrament of baptism, should be joined in our devotion with the Father and the Son?
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 justify worshipping the Holy Spirit together with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Of the origin of the word “with,” and what force it has. Also concerning the unwritten laws of the church.
sources.answer: Yes. We must believe as we are baptized and give glory as we believe, so the confession of faith is the parent of the doxology. Since the Spirit is numbered with the Father and Son at baptism, he must be joined with them in confession and in glory. Breaking this necessary and unbroken sequence would mean ruin everywhere.
sources.quote: They must now instruct us either not to baptize as we have received, or not to believe as we were baptized, or not to ascribe glory as we have believed.
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula require that the Holy Spirit be glorified together with the Father and the Son?

question: Does John 1:3's statement that "all things were made by" the Word admit any exceptions, or does it include absolutely everything created?
synthesis: Owen and Irenaeus agree that 'all things' is absolutely universal. Irenaeus argues that the text states no exception, so the Father made everything through the Word, visible or invisible, temporal or eternal, against claims that some beings were made by other powers. Owen grounds the universality in the clause 'without him nothing was made that was made', and adds that the Word's making all things proves His eternal Deity.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. The Word existed before all things, such that he made them all, and this is a firm declaration of his eternal Deity. The added clause 'without him nothing was made that was made' gives the 'all' an absolute universality, so it cannot be limited to any particular sort of things.
sources.quote: He was so in the beginning, before all things, as that he made them all.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that 'all things were made by' the Word (John 1:3) prove his eternal Deity, and does the 'all things' include absolutely everything created?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XXII.—Deviations of heretics from the truth.
sources.answer: No. The text states no exception or deduction, so the Father made all things through the Word, whether visible or invisible, sensible or intelligible, temporal or eternal.
sources.quote: There is no exception or deduction stated; but the Father made all things by Him, whether visible or invisible, objects of sense or of intelligence, temporal, on account of a certain character given them, or eternal
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:3 ('All things were made by Him') admit any exceptions, such as invisible or eternal beings made by other powers?

question: Is the unity of the Father and the Son a unity of nature, or merely an agreement or harmony of will such as believers can share?
synthesis: Hilary and Athanasius agree that the unity is one of nature, not of mere agreement. Hilary grounds it in the Son's birth, by which he possesses the Godhead truly and wholly, and he dismisses talk of mere harmony of will or of Christ as a creature. Athanasius stresses the Word's real identity of nature with the Father, which believers can only imitate through agreement of mind, since creatures differ from God in nature.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: By nature through birth. The Godhead abides in Christ not through condescension nor through will but by birth, truly and wholly, so talk of mere 'agreement', 'harmony of will', or of Christ as 'a creature' is empty human teaching.
sources.quote: inasmuch as God is in Him, abiding neither through condescension nor through will but by birth, true and wholly in bodily fulness according as He is
sources.raw_question: Is the unity of Father and Son merely an agreement or harmony of will, or does the Son possess the Godhead by nature through birth?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: It is a unity of nature. The Word has the real and true identity of nature with the Father, whereas believers become one only in mind and agreement of spirit by imitating that natural unity. Creatures are far from God not in place but in nature, so they can only distantly resemble the Son's being in the Father.
sources.quote: The Word then has the real and true identity of nature with the Father; but to us it is given to imitate it, as has been said
sources.raw_question: Is the unity of the Father and the Son a unity of nature or merely of agreement such as believers can share?

question: Does Christ's saying 'I ascend to My Father and your Father, and to My God and your God' (John 20:17) show that the Son is inferior in divine nature to the Father?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Gregory of Nyssa agree that the words refer to Christ's assumed human nature, not His Godhead. Hilary stresses that Christ spoke as a man in the form of a servant to fellow servants, so the words belong to the Word made flesh and cannot be transferred to His divine nature. Gregory adds a polemical point: the Eunomians err in taking 'God and Father' in the same sense for the Lord and for the disciples, which would reduce the Only-begotten to the level of Peter, Andrew and John.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Christ spoke these words as a man in the form of a servant to men and servants, so in His human aspect the Father is His Father as ours and His God as all men's. The words cannot be transferred to His divine nature, which had nothing of the servant in it; the message belongs not to the Only-begotten God the Word but to the Word made flesh.
sources.quote: Jesus Christ was speaking as a man in the form of a servant to men and servants; what difficulty is there then in the idea, that in His human aspect the Father is His Father as ours, in His servant’s nature God is His God as all men’s?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'I ascend to My Father and your Father, and My God and your God' (John 20:17) show that the Son is inferior in divine nature to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > This twelfth book gives a notable interpretation of the words of the Lord to Mary, “Touch Me not, for I am not yet ascended to My Father.”
sources.answer: No. The words were spoken by Him who humbled Himself to the level of human littleness, and so they refer to His assumed human nature, not to His Godhead. The Eunomians wrongly treat 'God and Father' as said of the Lord and of the disciples in exactly the same sense, and so reduce the Only-begotten, who was in the beginning and is in the Father, to the level of Peter, Andrew and John.
sources.quote: Now that the words addressed to Mary are not applicable to the Godhead of the Only-begotten, one may learn from the intention with which they were uttered. For He Who humbled Himself to a level with human littleness, He it is Who spake the words.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying to Mary, "I ascend unto My Father and your Father, and to My God and your God" (John 20:17), prove that the Son is of a lower nature than the Father, as far from the Father as humanity is from the Son?

question: Did the Holy Spirit exist eternally with the Father (and the Son) before creation?
synthesis: Basil of Caesarea and Irenaeus of Lyons both answer yes, but on different grounds. Basil argues conceptually: the Spirit pre-existed and co-existed with the Father and the Son before the ages, beyond anything one can conceive. Irenaeus identifies the Spirit with Wisdom and proves this from Scripture (Solomon's statements that God founded the earth by Wisdom, and that Wisdom was with him when he prepared the heavens), and also affirms the Son's eternal presence with the Father.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit existed, pre-existed and co-existed with the Father and the Son before the ages. Whatever one may conceive beyond the ages, the Spirit is found still further beyond it.
sources.quote: He existed; He pre-existed; He co-existed with the Father and the Son before the ages. It follows that, even if you can conceive of anything beyond the ages, you will find the Spirit yet further above and beyond.
sources.raw_question: Did the Holy Spirit exist eternally with the Father and the Son before creation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Yes. The Word, the Son, was always with the Father, and Wisdom, which is the Spirit, was present with him before all creation. Solomon shows this when he says that God founded the earth by Wisdom, and when Wisdom says, "When He prepared the heaven, I was with Him."
sources.quote: I have also largely demonstrated, that the Word, namely the Son, was always with the Father; and that Wisdom also, which is the Spirit, was present with Him, anterior to all creation
sources.raw_question: Did the Son and the Spirit exist eternally with the Father before creation?

question: Are the Father and the Son distinct persons, or is the Son merely another name or mode of the Father?
synthesis: Bickersteth and Novatian agree that the Son is a person distinct from the Father, but argue differently. Bickersteth appeals to Gospel evidence: the Father's voice speaking of the Son, Jesus praying to the Father and counting two witnesses, and above all his doing the will of the one who sent him rather than his own. Novatian argues from the Son's procession, as God from God who came forth from the Father and was with him as the Word.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: They are distinct persons, neither to be identified nor confounded. The Father's voice at the baptism and transfiguration speaks of the Son, Jesus prays to the Father, and he counts himself and the Father as two witnesses. Most decisively, since the will is the essence of personality, Christ's coming to do not his own will but the will of him that sent him proves distinct personality.
sources.quote: which is incontrovertible evidence – for the will is the essence of personality – “I came down from heaven not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me.”
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and the Son distinct persons, or is the Son merely another name or mode of the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: Yes. God proceeding from God, he is a person second to the Father as being the Son. He who was in the Father, because of the Father, came forth from the Father and was then with the Father, the divine substance named the Word, by whom all things were made.
sources.quote: Assuredly God proceeding from God, causing a person second to the Father as being the Son, but not taking from the Father that characteristic that He is one God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son a second person distinct from the Father?

question: In what sense are the Father and the Son two, and in what sense are they one?
synthesis: Athanasius and Warfield both affirm that the Son is distinct from the Father and yet one with him. Athanasius specifies the grounds: they are two as Father and Son, and one as one Godhead through the Son's coessentiality, which is how he reads John 10:30. Warfield presents the same twofold relation as Jesus' own teaching, without spelling out its metaphysical basis, and adds that the Spirit represents the Son as the Son represents the Father.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Unless Father and Son are two in name only, or as parts and so each imperfect, or two gods, they are coessential, one in Godhead, and the Son from the Father.
sources.answer: They are two because there is a Father and a Son, the Word. They are one because there is one God, one Godhead. Their unity rests on the Son's coessentiality with the Father and on the Word's being from the Father himself. The 'one' in John 10:30 signifies the one Godhead and the Son's coessentiality.
sources.quote: so that there are two, because there is Father, and Son, namely the Word; and one because one God.
sources.raw_question: In what sense are the Father and the Son two, and in what sense are they one?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. In his teaching Jesus speaks of God his Father as one from whom he is in some true sense distinct, and with whom he is in some equally true sense one. He also presents the Spirit as representing him just as he represents the Father.
sources.quote: He has much to say of God His Father, from whom as His Son He is in some true sense distinct, and with whom He is in some equally true sense one.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son both distinct from the Father and one with him?

question: How do the Father, Son and Holy Spirit each share in the work of creation, and what distinct role does each have?
synthesis: Waterland and Basil agree that all three Persons act together in creation and that the Father holds a distinctive originating role. Basil assigns a distinct causal role to each Person: the Father is the original cause, the Son the creative cause, and the Spirit the perfecting cause, and he uses this to show the Spirit's fellowship in the work. Waterland instead stresses that the whole Trinity creates jointly, with the Son and Spirit as the Father's 'hands' and originating authority belonging most properly to the Father, and he warns against pressing such distinctions too rigorously.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: The whole Trinity creates together. Whatever the Father does, he does through the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are therefore called the Father's hands. The originating or designing authority (αὐθεντία) was thought most properly to belong to the Father as the first Person. Such distinctions should be understood in a way fitting to God, not pressed too rigorously.
sources.quote: whatever the Father is supposed to have done, was by his Son and Holy Spirit ; therefore frequently styled manus Patris: but the avdevtia, the designing part, was thought most properly to be reserved to the Father, as the first Person.
sources.raw_question: How do the Father, Son and Holy Spirit each share in the work of creation?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: The Father is the original cause, the Son the creative cause, and the Spirit the perfecting cause. Thus created spirits subsist by the will of the Father, are brought into being by the operation of the Son, and are perfected by the presence of the Spirit. This shows the Spirit's fellowship with the Father and Son in creation.
sources.quote: bethink thee first, I pray thee, of the original cause of all things that are made, the Father; of the creative cause, the Son; of the perfecting cause, the Spirit
sources.raw_question: What distinct roles do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have in the act of creation?

question: Is the Holy Spirit good by nature, as the Father and the Son are, rather than sharing in goodness as creatures do?
synthesis: Basil and Ambrose agree that the Spirit is good by nature. Basil argues from the contrast with creatures: they share in goodness only by choosing the good, while the Spirit is good in the same way as the Father and the Son. Ambrose argues from the Spirit's origin and intimacy with God: as the Spirit of God's mouth who searches God's depths, where evil cannot enter, He cannot fail to be good, since God is good.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Proof of the absurdity of the refusal to glorify the Spirit, from the comparison of things glorified in creation.
sources.answer: He is good by nature. He is good in the same way as the Father and the Son are good, whereas a creature only shares in goodness by choosing the good. This difference separates Him from the creature.
sources.quote: He is good by nature, in the same way as the Father is good, and the Son is good; the creature on the other hand shares in goodness by choosing the good.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit good by nature as the Father and the Son are, or does He share in goodness the way creatures do?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is the Spirit of God's mouth and searches the deep things of God, and evil cannot enter into the deep things of God. Since God is good, the Spirit who is of him cannot fail to be good.
sources.quote: And so if God be good, how shall He Who is the Spirit of His mouth not be good, Who searcheth even the deep things of God? Can the infection of evil enter into the deep things of God?
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit good in his own nature, given that God the Father is good?

question: Does Scripture teach that the Son is God?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine agree that Scripture calls the Son God, but they rely on different texts. Gregory starts from the Old Testament (Psalm 44/45's anointed God and Isaiah's 'thou art God'), argues that only the Only-begotten has God in Himself and is Himself God, and adds Emmanuel, Thomas's confession and John's prologue as confirmation. Augustine rests on Paul's description of Christ as 'over all, God blessed for ever,' which he says compels even heretics to admit it.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He also ingeniously shows from the passage of the Gospel which speaks of “Good Master,” from the parable of the Vineyard, from Isaiah and from Paul, that there is not a dualism in the Godhead of good and evil, as Eunomius' ally Marcion supposes, and declares that the Son does not refuse the title of “good” or “Existent,” or acknowledge His alienation from the Father, but that to Him also belongs authority over all things that come into being.
sources.answer: Yes. Psalm 44 (45) calls the Christ God, anointed by God. Isaiah says "God is in thee... for thou art God." Gregory argues that the only one who has God in Himself and is Himself God is the Only-begotten. Emmanuel, Thomas's confession and John's prologue confirm the same.
sources.quote: For what other God there is Who has God in Himself, and is Himself God, except the Only-begotten, let them say who hearken not to the prophecy
sources.raw_question: Does the Old Testament teach that the Son is God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Appearance in the Bush.
sources.answer: Yes. The apostle calls Christ, who came of the fathers according to the flesh, the one 'who is over all, God blessed for ever,' so even heretics are compelled to acknowledge it whether they will or not.
sources.quote: but also the Son, which, whether they will or not, they are compelled to acknowledge, since the apostle says, “Who is over all, God blessed for ever;”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture show that the Son is God?

question: How does the divine Word, the Son, differ from a human word?
synthesis: Augustine and Gregory of Nyssa agree that the divine Word is vastly unlike any human word, but they ground the difference differently. Augustine contrasts it with the mind's inner word: the divine Word is born from the Father's own essence, which is knowledge and wisdom, and so is equal to the Father in all things. Gregory contrasts it with spoken words, which are created, have no reality of their own and vanish with the voice, whereas the Word is God Himself, eternal, creator and sustainer of all things.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Still Further of the Difference Between the Knowledge and Word of Our Mind, and the Knowledge and Word of God.
sources.answer: Since human knowledge is unlike God's, our word born of knowledge is unlike God's Word. The divine Word is born from the essence of the Father, that is, from the Father who is knowledge and wisdom. So the Word is equal to the Father in all things, possessing everything in the knowledge from which it is born.
sources.quote: as our knowledge is unlike that knowledge of God, so is our word also, which is born from our knowledge, unlike that Word of God which is born from the essence of the Father.
sources.raw_question: How does the divine Word, the Son, differ from the inner word of the human mind?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Human words were not in the beginning but were created with our nature, have no reality of their own, and vanish with the sound of the voice. The Word of God, by contrast, is God Himself, the Word that was in the beginning and abides for ever, through whom all things were made, ruling over all and upholding all things in being. So our word compared with Him who is the Word indeed is as nothing.
sources.quote: But the word of God is God Himself, the Word that was in the beginning and that abideth for ever, through Whom all things were and are, Who ruleth over all
sources.raw_question: How does the Word of God (the Son) differ from human words?

question: How can the Son be truly God without there being two Gods?
synthesis: Athanasius and Waterland agree that the Son is God without there being two Gods. Athanasius grounds this in the Son being proper to and inseparable from the one God's essence, and cites Christ's words that he and the Father are one. Waterland grounds it in an ineffable union of substance, will, power, presence and operation, called perichoresis, a term he says was introduced to answer the two-Gods objection.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: The Son is proper to the one God and inseparable from him in the peculiarity of his essence. So God is one, and faith in the Father and the Son is one faith. This is what Christ teaches when he says that whoever has seen him has seen the Father, and that he and the Father are one.
sources.quote: though the Word be God, the Lord our God is one Lord; for the Son is proper to that One, and inseparable according to the propriety and peculiarity of His Essence
sources.raw_question: How can the Son be God while there remains only one God and one Lord?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: Father and Son are one God by a most intimate and ineffable union of substance, will, power, presence and operation. This union is called perichoresis. The term was introduced to answer opponents who pressed the objection of two Gods.
sources.quote: Father and Son, by a most intimate and ineffable union of swdstance, will, power, presence, operation, ὅσο. (which we call zepuχώρησις,) may be one God
sources.raw_question: How can the Son be strictly God without there being two Gods?

question: Does Scripture teach that the Son is immutable and eternal in his nature?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Bickersteth both answer yes and both cite Psalm 102 as applied to the Son in Hebrews ("Thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail"). Gregory adds that the Son laid the foundations of the earth, which sets his unchanging nature apart from the creation he made. Bickersteth adds Hebrews 13:8, that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He convicts Eunomius of having used of the Only-begotten terms applicable to the existence of the earth, and thus shows that his intention is to prove the Son to be a being mutable and created.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul applies Psalm 102 to the Son: he laid the foundation of the earth and the heavens are the work of his hands. The Psalm also says "Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail." These words describe the immutability and eternity of the Son's nature, which sets him apart from the creation he made.
sources.quote: “But Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail[^620],” whereby he describes the immutability and eternity of His nature.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that the Son is immutable and eternal in his nature?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Hebrews applies to the Son the words, "Thou, Lord, art the same, and thy years shall not fail."
sources.quote: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever,” and, Unto the Son He saith, … “Thou, Lord, … art the same, and thy years shall not fail.”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ascribe immutability to the Son?

question: Do the names 'Father' and 'Son' express real, eternal relations between the divine Persons, or are they only titles of something secondary, such as creation, adoption, or the relations arising from the incarnation?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Warfield agree that the names express real, eternal relations, but they argue against different alternatives on different grounds. Hilary says God's own names truly indicate realities, so reading them as creation or adoption replaces true generation with falsehood. Warfield grants that many uses could be read as merely economical, but holds that some texts resist this. He adds that the names do not imply superiority or subordination in modes of subsistence.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: They express real relations. God gives his own things names that truly indicate the realities, so no arbitrary meaning should be forced on them. Replacing true generation with a theory of creation or adoption replaces the truth.
sources.quote: The things of God are provided with names which give a true indication of the realities; why force an arbitrary meaning upon their obvious sense?
sources.raw_question: Do the divine names 'Father' and 'Son' express real relations, or may they be read as mere titles of creation or adoption?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Warfield grants that many uses of the terms could be taken of merely economical relations. But some instances resist this treatment, so "Father" and "Son" must apply to the eternal and necessary relations of the Persons. Even so, these names do not imply superiority and subordination in modes of subsistence.
sources.quote: This question must certainly be answered in the negative. Although, no doubt, in many of the instances in which the terms “Father” and “Son” occur, it would be possible to take them of merely economical relations, there ever remain some which are intractable to this treatment
sources.raw_question: Are the names "Father" and "Son" only expressions of the relations that arose through the incarnation, with no bearing on the eternal relations between the divine Persons?

question: Does the Son possess all that belongs to the Father, including attributes such as lordship, almighty power and goodness?
synthesis: Athanasius and Gregory of Nyssa both answer yes, and both ground it in Christ's own words that all the Father has is His. Athanasius argues that having the Father's things is proper to the Son, so He is Lord and Almighty as the Father is. Gregory focuses on goodness and argues by dilemma: either the Son lacks something and the Truth lies, which is impious, or goodness is among the 'all things' He possesses.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ Himself said that all things the Father has are His. It is proper to the Son to have the things of the Father, so He is in authority and Almighty as the Father is.
sources.quote: is Lord of armies, and in authority, and Almighty, as the Father is; for He has said Himself, ‘All things that the Father hath, are Mine.’
sources.raw_question: Does the Son possess all that belongs to the Father, including being Lord and Almighty?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He also ingeniously shows from the passage of the Gospel which speaks of “Good Master,” from the parable of the Vineyard, from Isaiah and from Paul, that there is not a dualism in the Godhead of good and evil, as Eunomius' ally Marcion supposes, and declares that the Son does not refuse the title of “good” or “Existent,” or acknowledge His alienation from the Father, but that to Him also belongs authority over all things that come into being.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son said to the Father, 'All Mine are Thine, and Thine are Mine'; since goodness is among the Father's attributes, either the Son lacks something and the Truth lies, which is impious, or He possesses goodness among 'all things'. Hence the Son is good.
sources.quote: For He Who has the Father in Himself, and contains all things that belong to the Father, manifestly has His goodness with “all things.” Therefore the Son is Good.
sources.raw_question: If the Son possesses all that belongs to the Father, does He also possess the Father's goodness?

question: Is the Father greater than the Son, and if so, in what sense, and does this diminish the Son's equality and glory?
synthesis: Hilary grants that the Father is greater in a real sense, as Unbegotten to Begotten, Sender to Sent, and willing to obeying, on Christ's own words. He denies that this obscures the Son's glory, citing the mutual glorifying of John 17. Augustine instead denies outright that the Father is greater. His argument is that the Son is the Father's greatness, and in God being and being great are the same, so the two are equal.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: The Father is greater as Unbegotten to Begotten, as Sender to Sent, and as the one who wills to the one who obeys, as Christ himself says. But the Father's majesty must not be allowed to obscure the Son's glory. The mutual glorifying in John 17 rules that out.
sources.quote: Who, indeed, would deny that the Father is the greater; the Unbegotten greater than the Begotten, the Father than the Son, the Sender than the Sent, He that wills than He that obeys?
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Father greater than the Son, and does this greatness diminish the Son's glory?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > That the Unity of the Essence of the Father and the Son is to Be Gathered from the Words, ‘We are One.’ The Son is Equal to the Father Both in Wisdom and in All Other Things.
sources.answer: No. If the Father were greater, he would be greater by greatness. But the Son is his greatness, so the Son is not greater than the one who begot him. Nor is the Father greater than the greatness by which he is great. In God it is not one thing to be and another to be great, so they are equal.
sources.quote: but whereas the Son is His greatness, neither assuredly is the Son greater than He who begat Him, nor is the Father greater than that greatness, whereby He is great; therefore they are equal.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father be greater than the Son if the Son is the Father's greatness?

question: What kind of unity does the mutual indwelling of Father and Son (the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father) express, and does it confuse or mingle the two Persons?
synthesis: Hilary and Basil agree that the mutual indwelling expresses a unity of one shared nature while the Persons stay distinct. Hilary stresses the negative point that this indivisible nature is not confused or intermingled, so Father and Son remain Father and Son. Basil grounds the unity in likeness of nature: such as the Son is, such is the Father. He concludes that the Persons are 'one and one' by distinction and one by community of nature.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. The one faith confesses the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father through an indivisible nature that is not confused but inseparable, not intermingled but identical, not merely conjoined but coexisting. The Persons remain Father and Son while sharing one complete and perfect nature.
sources.quote: to confess the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father through the unity of an indivisible nature, not confused but inseparable, not intermingled but identical, not conjoined but coexisting
sources.raw_question: Is the unity of Father and Son a confusion or mingling of the two Persons?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: It shows their unity of nature. Such as the Son is, such is the Father, and such as the Father is, such is the Son, and herein is the unity. Thus by distinction of Persons they are one and one, and by community of nature they are one.
sources.quote: For the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son; since such as is the latter, such is the former, and such as is the former, such is the latter; and herein is the Unity.
sources.raw_question: What does the mutual indwelling of Father and Son (the Son in the Father and the Father in the Son) show about their unity?

question: Does the Son, having become man and been glorified, himself send the Holy Spirit?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Augustine both affirm that the Son sends the Spirit. Irenaeus ties the sending to the Word's being made man and reads it through the figure of the flying eagle, the fourth living creature, as the Spirit hovering over the Church. Augustine ties it to Christ's glorification in the resurrection, his own promise to send the Spirit, and the fulfilled prophecy that he ascended on high and gave gifts to men.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: Yes. After being made man for us, the Word sent the gift of the celestial Spirit over all the earth, protecting us with his wings. This is signified by the fourth living creature, the flying eagle, which points to the Spirit hovering over the Church.
sources.quote: Afterwards, being made man for us, He sent the gift of the celestial Spirit over all the earth, protecting us with His wings.
sources.raw_question: Does the incarnate Son of God send the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > There Was No Other More Suitable Way of Freeing Man from the Misery of Mortality Than The Incarnation of the Word. The Merits Which are Called Ours are the Gifts of God.
sources.answer: Yes. When Jesus was glorified by the resurrection, he promised that he himself would send the Spirit, and he did send him. This fulfilled the prophecy that he ascended on high and gave gifts to men.
sources.quote: And He was then given, when Jesus was glorified by the resurrection. For then He promised that He Himself would send Him, and He sent Him
sources.raw_question: Does the glorified Son himself send the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the name 'Son' applied to Christ imply that he shares the Father's nature as true God, rather than that he had a beginning?
synthesis: Athanasius and Gregory of Nyssa agree that 'Son' signifies sharing the Father's nature, so that Christ is true God. Athanasius frames this against the Arian claim that sonship implies a beginning, and holds that Christ's deity turns on what sonship means. Gregory argues that everything naturally belonging to the name must be accepted, so that a genuine Son of Very God is Very God, and he rejects substituting 'creature' or 'product' for 'Son'.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: It implies connaturality. The Arians argued that 'Son' implied a beginning and so that Christ was not true God. The Catholics held that sonship means being of the same nature as the Father, so that the Son is true God as one with God. The question of Christ's deity was therefore settled by the question of what his sonship means.
sources.quote: The Arians maintained that the very word ‘Son’ implied a ‘beginning,’ or that our Lord was not Very God; the Catholics said that it implied ‘connaturality,’ or that He was Very God as one with God.
sources.raw_question: Does the name 'Son' applied to Christ imply that he had a beginning, or does it imply that he shares the Father's nature as true God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: Yes. We must accept with the name of Son everything that naturally belongs to that name. He is the well-beloved Son, not a bastard or a counterfeit, and so He Who is of Very God is Very God. To substitute 'creature' or 'product' for 'Son' is to turn the Son into a creature answering to a creator.
sources.quote: accepting with the name of Son all that naturally belongs to that name, we should say that He Who is of Very God is Very God
sources.raw_question: Does the name 'Son' imply that Christ shares the Father's nature and is Very God of Very God?

question: Did the Son not exist before he was begotten, so that God begot him at some point when he had not yet existed?
synthesis: Both deny that the Son 'was not' before his generation and affirm his eternity, but on different grounds. The Athanasius entry (citing Basil against Eunomius) argues that the dilemma wrongly transfers to the Only-begotten what holds for animals, which first do not exist and are then generated, and appeals to the Fathers and John's prologue. Gregory of Nyssa argues that 'when' and 'was not' are temporal terms, so they lose their sense once Eunomius admits that nothing, not even time, existed before the Son; saying the Son both was and was not then contradicts Eunomius's own admission.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: No. Basil replies that Eunomius wrongly carries over to the Only-begotten what is true of animals, which first do not exist and are then generated. Following the other Fathers, Basil answers that the Lord is from everlasting. John's prologue joins the Son's generation to the Father's eternity.
sources.quote: because animals first are not, and then are generated, and he who is born to-day, yesterday did not exist, transfers this conception to the subsistence of the Only-begotten
sources.raw_question: Must God have begotten the Son either when the Son already existed or when he did not, so that the Son did not exist before his generation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He further shows that the pretemporal generation of the Son is not the subject of influences drawn from ordinary and carnal generation, but is without beginning and without end, and not according to the fabrications constructed by Eunomius, in ignorance of His power, from the statements of Plato concerning the soul and from the sabbath rest of the Hebrews.
sources.answer: No. The words 'then' and 'when' properly signify time, and 'was not' implies 'once was not,' which rests on time. Since Eunomius admits that nothing, not even time, was before the Son, the temporal signification disappears and must be replaced by eternity; so to say the Son both was and was not contradicts his own admission.
sources.quote: it would be foolish and idle to say that nothing was before the Son, and yet to maintain that the Son did not always exist.
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to hold that nothing existed before the Son of God and yet that the Son 'was not' before his generation and was begotten 'when' the Father willed?

question: What does it mean that the Holy Spirit glorifies the Son (John 16:14), and what does this show about the Spirit's relation to the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Both authors read the Spirit's glorifying of the Son as evidence of the unity of the divine Persons, but on different grounds. Augustine argues from the text's logic: the Spirit receives what is the Son's, and all the Father has is the Son's, so all that the Father has belongs to the Spirit too. Ambrose instead explains the glorifying as the Spirit revealing the Son as the Image of God, and points to the Spirit's work in the prophets and apostles to show that divine power and grace are not divided among the Persons.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Glorification of the Son by the Father Does Not Prove Inequality.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit glorifies the Son because He receives of what is the Son's, and all that the Father has is the Son's; so when the Spirit glorifies the Son, the Father glorifies the Son. Hence all that the Father has belongs not only to the Son but also to the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: Whence it may be perceived that all things that the Father hath are not only of the Son, but also of the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit is able to glorify the Son, whom the Father glorifies.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's glorifying the Son show that the Spirit shares in all that the Father has?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: The Spirit glorifies the Son by revealing him. The Spirit taught us that the Son is the Image of the invisible God, the brightness of his glory and the impress of his substance. The same Spirit spoke in the patriarchs and prophets and perfected the apostles. This shows that the divine power and grace are not separated among the Persons.
sources.quote: To glorify, because the Holy Spirit taught us that the Son is the Image of the invisible God,[^1205] and the brightness of His glory, and the impress of His substance.
sources.raw_question: In what sense does the Holy Spirit glorify the Son?

question: In what respect is the Son equal to the Father, and is there any respect in which he differs from him?
synthesis: Augustine and Waterland agree that the Son is fully equal to the Father in nature and that the only difference lies in his relation to the Father. Augustine reaches this by a logical distinction: what is said of the Son in respect to himself is said according to substance, which is the same as the Father's, while what is said relative to the Father (that he is Son) cannot be equal. Waterland, following Whitby's reading of Novatian, says the Son is equal in every respect except that he is God of God, so his derivation from the Father implies no inequality of nature or divinity.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Reply is Made to the Cavils of the Heretics in Respect to the Same Words Begotten and Unbegotten.
sources.answer: In respect to himself, and therefore according to substance. He cannot be equal in what is said relative to the Father, because relative to the Father he is Son, and the Father is not Son. What is said of a thing in respect to itself is said according to substance. So the Son is equal to the Father in substance, and the substance of both is the same.
sources.quote: it remains that He is equal according to that which is said in relation to Himself. But whatever is said in relation to self is said according to substance: it remains therefore that He is equal according to substance; therefore the substance of both is the same.
sources.raw_question: In what respect is the Son equal to the Father: in what is said of him relative to the Father, or in what is said of him in respect to himself?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: The Son is equal to the Father in every respect except that he is God of God. Waterland endorses Dr. Whitby's earlier judgment of Novatian's passage on this point. The only distinction is the Son's derivation from the Father, not any inequality of nature or divinity.
sources.quote: declare that “ Christ is God, equal to the Father in every respect, excepting “ only that he is God of God.”
sources.raw_question: Is the Son equal to the Father in every respect, or is there some respect in which he differs?

question: If God the Father was always Father, must the Son always have existed?
synthesis: Waterland and Hilary agree that the Father's eternal fatherhood requires the Son's eternal existence. Waterland grounds this in Novatian's argument that otherwise the Father would not always have been Father, and stresses that 'always' must mean strict eternity. Hilary argues from the correlativity of fatherhood and sonship, so that co-eternal fatherhood entails co-eternal sonship.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. Following Novatian, the Son must always have existed in the Father, or else the Father would not always have been Father, which is absurd. This argument only makes sense if 'always' is taken strictly as eternity.
sources.quote: the Son must have always existed in the Father, or else (which he takes to be absurd) the Father would not have been always Father
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's being always Father require that the Son always existed?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. Fatherhood and sonship are correlative properties. If God was not always Father of the Son, the Son did not always exist. But if fatherhood is co-eternal with the Father, then sonship must be co-eternal with the Son.
sources.quote: But if the property of fatherhood be co-eternal with the Father, then necessarily also the property of sonship must be co-eternal with the Son.
sources.raw_question: If God the Father was always Father, must the Son always have existed?

question: What did Christ mean when he told Philip that whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9), if he is not himself the Father?
synthesis: Both authors deny that the saying identifies the Son with the Father, but they explain it on different grounds. Novatian reads it through the Son as the Father's image: seeing the image is as if one saw the Father, and contemplating that likeness trains believers toward seeing the Father hereafter. Augustine distinguishes two ways Christ is seen: he was seen in the flesh he took in being sent, but not as the Word, in which he is equal to the Father.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Proves Also that the Words Spoken to Philip Make Nothing for the Sabellians.
sources.answer: He meant that the Son is the image of God the Father, so that seeing the Father's image in the Son is as if one saw the Father. Believers are trained by contemplating this likeness and grow toward the perfect contemplation of God the Father Almighty. In this way they see now, in some measure, the Father whom they will see hereafter.
sources.quote: every man ought henceforth to consider, in seeing the image of God the Father through the Son, that it was as if he saw the Father
sources.raw_question: What did Christ mean when he told Philip that whoever has seen him has seen the Father, if he is not himself the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In What Manner the Son Was Sent and Proclaimed Beforehand. How in the Sending of His Birth in the Flesh He Was Made Less Without Detriment to His Equality with the Father.
sources.answer: Christ was both seen and not seen. He was seen in the flesh he was made in being sent. He was not seen as the Word by whom all things were made, in which he is equal to the Father.
sources.quote: unless because He was both seen and yet not seen? He was seen, as He had been made in being sent; He was not seen, as by Him all things were made.
sources.raw_question: If the Son was seen by Philip and even by those who crucified him, how can he say that whoever has seen him has seen the Father?

question: Does Hebrews 1:3, calling the Son the brightness of God's glory and the express image of his person, show that the Son is eternal and divine?
synthesis: Waterland and Gregory of Nyssa both answer yes, arguing that brightness cannot be separated from its source, so the Son is coeternal with and inseparable from the Father. Waterland leans on the patristic tradition (Origen, Dionysius, Alexander) and on 'express image' as an established anti-Arian proof, adding that the image of the invisible is itself invisible. Gregory argues from the grammar: the participle 'being' rather than 'becoming' marks eternity, while the brightness deriving from the glory shows the Son is not ungenerate.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Yes. Following Origen, Dionysius and Alexander of Alexandria, since God is eternal light and the Son is its shining forth, the two could never be separated and so must be coeternal; and as image of the invisible he is himself invisible. The words 'express image of his person' were constantly urged by the Catholic Fathers against the Arians, so the use of this text for Christ's divinity is neither strange nor new.
sources.quote: since God is light, and Christ the ἀπαύγασμα, or shining forth of that light, quoting this text, that they could never have been separate one from the other, but must have been coeternal.
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1:3, calling the Son the brightness of God's glory and express image of his person, support the Son's eternity and divinity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: Yes. The brightness comes from the glory and not the reverse, so the Son is not Ungenerate; and the word 'being' (not 'becoming') testifies to His continuity, eternity and superiority to all marks of time, so He never began to be. As brightness cannot be separated from glory, the Son cannot be separated from the Father.
sources.quote: For the word “being” is a witness that interprets to us the Son’s continuity and eternity and superiority to all marks of time.
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1:3's description of the Son as 'being the brightness of His glory' show that the Son is eternal yet not ungenerate?

question: Does John 1:14, 'The Word was made flesh,' show that Christ is both God and man?
synthesis: Augustine and Novatian agree that the text confesses both natures in Christ. Augustine emphasizes their union in one Person by grace. Novatian argues that the Word's being God and becoming flesh requires confessing both substances in Christ's one nativity.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What in the Incarnate Word Belongs to Knowledge, What to Wisdom.
sources.answer: The Word is the true Son of God, the flesh is the true Son of man, and both are joined into one Person of God and man by an ineffable copiousness of grace. This union of man with God in unity of person is the highest grace among temporal things.
sources.quote: I understand by the Word the true Son of God, I acknowledge in the flesh the true Son of man, and both together joined into one Person of God and man, by an ineffable copiousness of grace.
sources.raw_question: How should John 1:14, 'The Word was made flesh,' be understood with respect to the divinity and humanity of Christ?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Truth is Proved from the Sacred Writings of the New Covenant.
sources.answer: Yes. Because the Word was made flesh, Christ is man; and because he is the Word of God, who was in the beginning with God and was God, he is God. The Gospel joins both substantial natures into the one nativity of Christ, so both must be confessed without hesitation.
sources.quote: because He is the Word of God, who can shrink from declaring without hesitation that He is God, especially when he considers the evangelical Scripture, that it has associated both of these substantial natures into one concord of the nativity of Christ?
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:14, 'The Word was made flesh,' show that Christ is both man and God?

question: Does Genesis 1:27, 'God made man after the image of God', prove that the Son is true God?
synthesis: The authors differ. Hilary says yes: the Son, through whom all things are made, makes man after the Father's image, and man also bears the Son's image, which proves the Son true God. Augustine rejects reading the verse as the Father making man in the Son's image to prove the Son's deity, because that would make the Son unlike the Father and the text says 'our image'; he holds the Son's deity is proved by other, clearer texts.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. Since all things are made through the Son, the God who makes man is the Son, and He makes man after the image of God the Father. Because the words "Our image" were spoken to the Son, man is made also after the Son's image. His sharing in the divine image proves Him true God, and His creative action shows Him to be God the Son.
sources.quote: For His joint possession of the Divine image proves Him true God, while His creative action displays Him as God the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does Genesis 1:27, "God made man; after the image of God made He him," prove that the Son is true God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Why This Opinion is to Be Rejected.
sources.answer: No. If man were made in the Son's image and not the Father's, the Son would be unlike the Father. But the Son is like the Father by equality of essence, so what is made like the Son is also like the Father. Also, the text says "our image," not "Thy image." Other clear texts already prove that the Son is true God.
sources.quote: if the Father made man after the image of the Son, so that he is not the image of the Father, but of the Son, then the Son is unlike the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does "God made man in the image of God" (Genesis 1:27) mean that the Father made man in the image of the Son, so as to prove the Son's deity?

question: Why does Genesis 1:27 say 'God created man in the image of God' rather than 'in his own image', after the plural 'Let us make', and what does this show?
synthesis: The authors draw different lessons from the wording. Hilary argues that it shows God acting and God as pattern, which points to two Persons ('God and God') rather than an isolated God. Augustine argues that the singular 'image of God' following the plural guards against belief in three Gods, showing that the Trinity is one God.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: The wording shows God acting and God as the pattern, which points to two Persons rather than a solitary God. The verse makes a triple reference: to the Maker, to the thing made, and to the image. If an isolated God were meant, it would have said "after His own image." Foreshadowing the Gospel, the text speaks not of two Gods but of God and God, with man made through God in the image of God.
sources.quote: If Genesis were speaking of an isolated God, it would certainly have been And made him after His own image. But since the book was foreshowing the Mystery of the Gospel, it spoke not of two Gods, but of God and God
sources.raw_question: Why does Genesis 1:27 say "God made man after the image of God" rather than "after His own image," and what does this show about the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Why This Opinion is to Be Rejected.
sources.answer: It guards against thinking there are three Gods. The Trinity is one God, so the singular "image of God" shows that the one Trinity is the one God in whose image man was made.
sources.quote: lest we should think that three Gods were to be believed in the Trinity, whereas the same Trinity is one God, it is said, “So God created man in the image of God,”
sources.raw_question: Why does Genesis 1:27 say "God created man in the image of God" in the singular after the plural "Let us make"?

question: Does Scripture teach whether the Son is uncreated, or does it leave the question open?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Waterland agree that Scripture nowhere calls the Son a creature. Their grounds differ: Gregory appeals to the silence of every inspired writer and to the traditional faith in Father, Son and Spirit. Waterland adds that what Scripture teaches by necessary consequence it truly says, so its teaching that the Logos created all things means it says the Son is uncreated.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: No. No evangelist, apostle, prophet, lawgiver, patriarch or other inspired writer ever made such a statement. The tradition of faith delivered by the Truth teaches belief in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It does not teach belief in a creature.
sources.quote: In the tradition of the faith delivered by the Truth we are taught to believe in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. If it were right to believe that the Son was created, how was it that the Truth in delivering to us this mystery bade us believe in the Son, and not in the creature?
sources.raw_question: Does any Scripture teach that the Son is 'not uncreate'?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 12: Whether the Creator of all things was not himself uncreated ; and therefore could not be ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, made out of nothing ?
sources.answer: No. What Scripture teaches by unavoidable consequence it truly says; since Scripture teaches that the Logos created all things, and the Creator must be uncreated, Scripture says the Son is uncreated. Moreover Scripture never says he is created, and it everywhere keeps the distinction between Creator and creature without confounding them.
sources.quote: Wherefore, if Scripture, by unavoidable consequence, does say, that he is uncreaied ; I hope Scripture does say it. The Scriptures, every where, carefully keep up the distinction between Creator and creature; and never confound both in one.
sources.raw_question: Since Scripture never explicitly says the Son is uncreated, is the Son's uncreatedness left undetermined by Scripture?

question: Can God's existence as Creator be known from the created universe, apart from Scripture?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Augustine agree that it can. Irenaeus argues that a made work points to its maker, so even the heathen without the prophets knew of the one Creator. Augustine adds that the Creator has given humans mind and natural reason, by which the universe's testimony alongside Scripture can be perceived.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter IX.—There is but one Creator of the world, God the Father: this the constant belief of the Church.
sources.answer: Yes. The heathen learned of the one Maker from creation itself, because a made work points to its maker. The world manifests the one who ordered it, and so even without the prophets people can know there is a Creator.
sources.quote: For even creation reveals Him who formed it, and the very work made suggests Him who made it, and the world manifests Him who ordered it.
sources.raw_question: Can God's existence as Creator be known from creation itself, apart from revelation?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What Universal Nature Teaches Us Concerning God.
sources.answer: Yes. Not only the authority of the divine books declares that God is, but the whole nature of the universe, to which we belong, proclaims that it has a most excellent Creator. This Creator has given us mind and natural reason by which we can perceive this.
sources.quote: the whole nature of the universe itself which surrounds us, and to which we also belong, proclaims that it has a most excellent Creator, who has given to us a mind and natural reason
sources.raw_question: Can the existence of God be known from the created universe as well as from Scripture?

question: How is Christ "the beginning of His ways" in Proverbs 8:22 to be understood?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary of Poitiers both read the verse through Christ's saying "I am the Way." Gregory stresses that Christ refashions believers from sin back to his image and is their foundation. Hilary stresses that Christ is the Way who guides and teaches travellers and leads men to the Father.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: Christ, who said "I am the Way," becomes the beginning of the ways of salvation to those who put him on. He makes them the work of his own hands and remodels them from the evil mould of sin back to his own image. He is also their foundation, as Paul says that no other foundation can be laid.
sources.quote: For thus it is that He, Who said “I am the Way,” becomes to us who have put Him on the beginning of the ways of salvation, that He may make us the work of His own hands
sources.raw_question: How is Christ "the beginning of His ways" in Proverbs 8:22 to be understood?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. Christ, who is Wisdom, calls Himself the Way and says no one comes to the Father except through Him. A way guides travellers and teaches unknown things, so He is 'created for the beginning of the ways' because He is the Way leading men to the Father.
sources.quote: Therefore He is created for the beginning of the ways, for the works of God; because He is the Way and leads men to the Father.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ the 'beginning of the ways' of God referred to in Proverbs 8:22?

question: Does John 1:1-3 show that the Word is of the same substance or essence as the Father?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine both answer yes, but by different routes. Gregory argues that John places the Word in the very essence from which it has its being, sharing all that the Beginning is. Augustine argues that because all things were made by the Word, he himself was not made, and so he is no creature but of the Father's substance.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He further shows the operations of God to be expressed by human illustrations; for what hands and feet and the other parts of the body with which men work are, that, in the case of God, the will alone is, in place of these. And so also arises the divergence of generation; wherefore He is called Only-begotten, because He has no community with other generation such as is observed in creation, but in that He is called the “brightness of glory,” and the “savour of ointment,” He shows the close conjunction and co-eternity of His Nature with the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. When John says the Word "was in the beginning," "was with God," and was God, he places the Word in the very essence from which It has Its being, not in an alien or severed essence. The Word is also all else that the "Beginning" is. In this way John's teaching on the Godhead affirms the eternity of the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: to regard the Word as in essence, and not in any essence foreign to or dissevered from that essence whence It has Its being, but in that first and blessed Nature
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:1 teach that the Word shares the same essence as the Father and is eternal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. John says the Word was God and that all things were made by Him; since all things that were made were made by Him, He Himself was not made. Not being made, He is not a creature, and whatever is not a creature is of the same substance with the Father.
sources.quote: From which it appears clearly, that He Himself was not made, by whom all things were made. And if He was not made, then He is not a creature; but if He is not a creature, then He is of the same substance with the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:1-3 show that the Word (the Son) is God and of the same substance as the Father?

question: Does Wisdom's description of the Son as 'the brightness of the everlasting light' show that the Son is co-eternal with the Father?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine both answer yes: the text shows the Son is co-eternal with the Father. Gregory argues that the brightness and its cause are joined in one idea with no priority between them. Augustine argues that brightness is itself light and so co-eternal with its source. He adds that it must be equal, since if it were less it would be darkness, and it cannot be greater than the source it issues from.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He who asserts that the Father is 'prior' to the Son with any thought of an interval must perforce allow that even the Father is not without beginning.
sources.answer: Yes. Wisdom teaches us to see the brightness of the everlasting light in, and together with, the everlastingness of that primal light. The brightness and its cause are joined in one idea with no priority between them, so the Son is eternal with the Father.
sources.quote: we have been taught by Wisdom to contemplate the brightness of the everlasting light in, and together with, the very everlastingness of that primal light, joining in one idea the brightness and its cause, and admitting no priority.
sources.raw_question: Does Wisdom's description of the Son as the brightness of the everlasting light show that the Son is co-eternal with the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: It shows that the Son is equal to and co-eternal with the Father. The brightness of light is light itself, and so is co-eternal with the light it comes from. Were it less, it would be that light's darkness rather than its brightness. Were it greater, it could not issue from it, since nothing surpasses its source; therefore it is equal.
sources.quote: For if it were less, then it would be its darkness, not its brightness; but if it were greater, then it could not issue from it, for it could not surpass that from which it is educed.
sources.raw_question: What does the description of Wisdom as 'the brightness of the everlasting light' show about the Son's equality with and co-eternity with the Father?

question: Does Athenagoras's description of the Son as the Father's 'first offspring, not as made' imply that the Son is not eternal or came into being at the creation of the world?
synthesis: Both Waterland and the Athanasius-attributed source answer no. Both rest on Athenagoras's point that God, as eternal Mind, always had his Word in himself. Waterland argues philologically: γενόμενον means 'made', and Whitby's rendering 'not as eternally generated' misreads it as γεννώμενον and adds 'eternally'. The Athanasius-attributed source instead explains the Son's 'going forth' at creation as his acting as the Agent, Form and Rule of the works, not as a new generation, so that 'first offspring' means prototypal offspring.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
