sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. In Athenagoras the word γενόμενον has the fixed sense 'made' or 'created'. Whitby's rendering 'not as eternally generated' reads γεννώμενον and adds 'eternally' from imagination. Athenagoras plainly meant to affirm the Son's immutable, eternal, necessary existence, since God, being eternal Mind, always had his Word in himself.
sources.quote: And that he intended to signify the Son’s tmmutable, eternal, necessary existence, in this passage, is so manifest, that a man must be of a peculiar complexion that can so much as question it
sources.raw_question: When Athenagoras calls the Son the Father's 'first offspring, not as made' (οὐχ ὡς γενόμενον), does he mean 'not as eternally generated', implying the Son is not eternal?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: No. Athenagoras expressly says the Son is first offspring 'not as come to be,' because God, being eternal Mind, always had the Word in Himself. His 'going forth' at creation was as the idea and energy of the works. He went forth as the Agent who creates and as the Form and Rule by which things are created, not through any new generation. So 'first offspring' means the prototypal offspring, the archetype of creation, not a Son who began to exist.
sources.quote: not as come to be, γενόμενον (for God being Eternal Mind had from the beginning in Himself the Word, as having Reason eternally, λογικὸς ὢν)
sources.raised_by_detail: Newman, answering Bishop Bull's reading of Athenagoras
sources.raw_question: Does Athenagoras's description of the Son as the 'first offspring' (πρῶτον γέννημα) of the Father mean that the Son came into being, or was first generated, at the creation of the world?

question: If there was a time when the Son did not exist, would God then have been without his Wisdom, Power and Word?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Waterland agree: since the Son is God's Wisdom, Power (and Word or Truth), a time without the Son would mean God once lacked these, which is absurd or blasphemous. Gregory makes the argument directly, while Waterland presents it as the argument of Dionysius of Rome and draws the explicit conclusion that there was never a time when the Son was not.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: Yes. The Only-begotten Son is and is called God's Wisdom, Power, Truth and his other glories. So whoever says God was once without the Son must say that God once lacked all these, which is blasphemous.
sources.quote: as long as He did not have this Son they must assert (may God forgive me for saying it!) that He had no Wisdom, nor Power, nor Truth, nor any of the other glories which from various points of view the Only-begotten Son is and is called.
sources.raw_question: Would a time when God had not yet begotten the Son imply that God was then without Wisdom, Power and Truth?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes, and that is absurd, so the Son never came into being. Dionysius of Rome argued that if the Son is God's Word, Wisdom and Power, then his having a beginning would mean God was once without these, which is most absurd. Therefore there was never a time when the Son was not.
sources.quote: ἦν ἄρα καιρὸς, ὅτε χωρὶς τούτων ἦν ὁ Θεός" ἀτοπώτατον δὲ τοῦτο.
sources.raw_question: If the Son came into being, would there have been a time when God was without his Word, Wisdom and Power?

question: Does Christ's saying 'I and the Father are One' (John 10:30) refute the Arian claim that the Son is unlike or unequal to the Father in essence?
synthesis: Athanasius and Ambrose agree that 'are One' refutes the Arian position. Athanasius argues that nothing is one with the Father except what is from Him, namely the Son, and adds that the same text also overthrows Sabellius by distinguishing Father and Son. Ambrose reads 'are One' as asserting unity of substance and equality, which excludes separating the Son from the Godhead, and stresses that the very text the heretics used against the Son establishes His dignity.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: Yes. By saying 'are One,' Christ overthrows Arius, since nothing is one with the Father except what is from Him, namely the Son. The same text overthrows Sabellius by distinguishing Son and Father.
sources.quote: For thus He overthrows both Sabellius, in saying, ‘I am’ not, “the Father,” but, ‘the Son of God;’ and Arius, in saying, ‘are One.’
sources.raw_question: Does 'I and the Father are One' refute the Arian view that the Son is unlike the Father in essence?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: Yes. The words "are One" assert unity of substance with the Father, which excludes separating the Son from the Godhead. Thus the same text that heretics used against the Son's dignity establishes His equality and unity with the Father.
sources.quote: With the former words He rejects those, for He said: “I and the Father;” with the latter words He rejects the Arians, for He says: “are One.”
sources.raw_question: Does "I and the Father are One" refute the Arian claim that the Son is unequal to or of a different nature from the Father?

question: Does Paul's statement that 'no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God' (1 Corinthians 2:11) exclude the Son from knowing the things of God, and do similar exclusive statements about one divine Person exclude the others?
synthesis: Ambrose and Augustine agree that the text does not exclude the Son. Their grounds differ. Ambrose says such exclusive statements are set only against creatures, and applies the same rule in reverse to 'no one knows the Father except the Son', concluding that the Persons share one nature and knowledge and that the Spirit is no creature. Augustine argues from absurdity: the reading would make the Spirit teach the Son as a greater teaches a lesser. He grounds the point in the inseparability of the Persons.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: No to both. Such exclusive statements are not set against the other divine Persons, only against creatures. The Son is not excluded by the saying about the Spirit, any more than the Spirit is excluded by the saying about the Son. This shows that Father, Son, and Spirit are of one nature and one knowledge, and that the Spirit is not counted among created things.
sources.quote: Is, then, the Son of God excluded? Certainly not, since neither is the Spirit excluded, when it is said: “And none knoweth the Father, save the Son.”
sources.raw_question: Does 'no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God' exclude the Son from knowing God, or does 'no one knows the Father except the Son' exclude the Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: No. Reading it so would lead to the absurd conclusion that the Spirit teaches the Son the things of God as a greater teaches a lesser. The exclusive wording no more shuts out the Son than other texts naming one Person shut out the others, since the Persons are inseparable.
sources.quote: In that case the apostle has excluded the Son from knowing those things which are of God, where he says, “Even so the things of God knoweth no one, but the Spirit of God:”
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that 'the things of God knoweth no one, but the Spirit of God' exclude the Son from knowing the things of God?

question: Is the Holy Spirit holy in the same way creatures are holy, by receiving sanctification, so that sharing the name 'holy' implies a shared nature?
synthesis: Basil and Ambrose agree that the Spirit's holiness differs in kind from creatures': creatures receive holiness, while the Spirit gives it. Basil grounds this in holiness being the fulfilment of the Spirit's nature, citing Scripture's description of Him as sanctifier rather than sanctified. Ambrose argues that the common word does not imply a common nature, since what sanctifies and what is corruptible cannot share one substance.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: No. Creatures receive holiness from outside themselves, but for the Spirit holiness is the fulfilment of His nature. That is why Scripture describes Him as sanctifying rather than as being sanctified.
sources.quote: for to the creature holiness was brought in from without, but to the Spirit holiness is the fulfilment of nature, and it is for this reason that He is described not as being sanctified, but as sanctifying.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit holy in the same way creatures are holy, by being sanctified?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: No. Though the word is used in common, the natures differ: the creature receives holiness, while God gives it. Sanctification and corruption cannot share one nature, so the Spirit's grace and the creature cannot be of one substance.
sources.quote: Now sanctification and corruption cannot share the same nature, and therefore the grace of the Holy Spirit and the creature cannot be of one substance.
sources.raw_question: Since both creatures and the Holy Spirit are called "holy," do they share the same nature?

question: How is the image of God in human beings, defaced or lost by sin, restored?
synthesis: Augustine and Owen agree that the image damaged by sin is restored, but they stress different things. Augustine says the mind cannot re-form itself: it must be formed again by the One who first formed it, as it is turned to the Lord. Owen says the image is restored through holiness alone, by which believers put on the new man created after God in righteousness.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How the Image of God is Formed Anew in Man.
sources.answer: No. The image must be formed again by Him by whom it was first formed. The mind could deform itself by turning to worldly lusts, but it cannot form itself again; renewal comes when it is turned to the Lord.
sources.quote: that that image may begin to be formed again by Him by whom it had been formed at first. For that image cannot form itself again, as it could deform itself.
sources.raw_question: Can the image of God in the human mind, once defaced by sin, restore itself by its own power?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Man was created in God's image, lost it by sin, and is restored to conformity with God by holiness alone. Through it believers put on the new man created after God in righteousness and holiness, as God commands them to be holy as he is holy.
sources.quote: To this honour, of conformity to God, of bearing his image, are we exalted again by holiness alone.
sources.raw_question: Is the image of God, lost by sin, restored in human beings through holiness?

question: Can Christ be both a creature and rightly worshipped, or does the worship due to Him show that He is not a creature?
synthesis: Hilary and Waterland agree that worshipping Christ and calling Him a creature cannot go together. Hilary argues from the curse on those who serve the creature rather than the Creator, so whoever worships a created Christ condemns himself and speaks by a spirit other than God's. Waterland reasons from the Fathers' principle that worship belongs to God alone: if the Son is worshipped he must be uncreated, very God, Creator and one with the Father, and if he were a creature he could not be worshipped.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Those who serve the creature more than the Creator are under a curse. So whoever affirms Christ to be a creature while worshipping Him condemns himself. Such a person speaks in a spirit other than the Spirit of God.
sources.quote: For since they are under a curse who have served the creature more than the Creator—in affirming Christ to be a creature, learn what thou art, since thou knowest full well that the worship of the creature is accursed.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to call Christ a creature and still worship Him?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: Yes. Since worship belongs to God alone, the Creator in opposition to all creatures, the Son could be worshipped on the Fathers' principles only if he is uncreated and very God, Creator and Preserver of all things, and one with the Father. Hence if he is a creature he is not to be worshipped, and if he is to be worshipped he is not a creature.
sources.quote: The conclusion from all is; if our blessed Lord is a creature, Ὁ he is not to be worshipped; if he is to be worshipped, he is not a creature.
sources.raw_question: If Christ is rightly worshipped, does it follow that he cannot be a creature?

question: To whom does Romans 11:36, 'For of Him, and through Him, and to Him are all things,' refer?
synthesis: Ambrose and Basil agree that the verse refers specially to the Son. Both ground this in the Isaiah passage Paul draws on, about the Maker who measured the waters and weighed the mountains. Ambrose adds that the verse can also rightly be said of the Father and the Spirit. Basil instead stresses that the Son is the cause 'of whom' all things exist, according to the Father's will.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IX. A passage of St. Paul abused by heretics, to prove a distinction between the Divine Persons, is explained, and it is proved that the whole passage can be rightly said of each Person, though it refers specially to the Son. It is then proved that each member of the passage is applicable to each Person, and as to say, of Him are all things is applicable to the Father, so may all things are through Him and in Him also be said of Him.
sources.answer: It is said specially of the Son. Paul takes it from Isaiah's prophecy about the Artificer of all who measured the waters and weighed the mountains. Yet it can also rightly be said of the Father and of the Spirit, which shows that all three particles fit one Person.
sources.quote: But if you really consider whence the passage is taken you will have no doubt that it is said of the Son.
sources.raw_question: To whom does Romans 11:36, 'For of Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things,' refer?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That v: not found “of whom” in the case of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul has just quoted Isaiah's "Who hath known the mind of the Lord?", and the preceding verses of Isaiah describe the one who measured the waters and weighed the mountains, that is, God the Word, the Maker of all creation. So the Son is the one of whom all things have the cause of their being, according to the Father's will. Through him all things continue and are constituted, and to him all things turn.
sources.quote: That the prophet is speaking about God the Word, the Maker of all creation, may be learnt from what immediately precedes
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 11:36 ("of him and through him and to him are all things") refer to the Son, so that "of whom" can be applied to the Son?

question: Does Romans 11:36 show that the divine Persons share one nature and are one God?
synthesis: Hilary and Augustine both answer yes, but on different grounds. Hilary argues that Paul ascribes both the Father's 'from Him' and Christ's 'through Him' to the one God, which can only be the work of one nature. Augustine, extending the verse to all three Persons, points to the singular 'to whom be glory' and to the opening reference to the wisdom 'of God'.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. Paul there ascribes to the one God both the 'from Him' proper to the Father and the 'through Him' proper to Christ, as the glory of one God. He thereby uses to indicate one nature what can only be the work of one nature.
sources.quote: He employs to indicate the one nature, that which cannot but be the work of one nature.
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 11:36, 'of Him and through Him and in Him are all things', show that Father and Son share one nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. If the three clauses are assigned severally to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the passage still continues in the singular, "to whom be glory," and opens with the wisdom and knowledge "of God," not of any one Person. Hence the three are one God.
sources.quote: it is manifest that the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one God, inasmuch as the words continue in the singular number, “To whom be glory for ever.”
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 11:36 ("of Him, and through Him, and in Him, are all things: to whom be glory") show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God?

question: Does the Son share the Father's omnipotence, being almighty equally with the Father?
synthesis: Hilary and Bickersteth agree that the Son is omnipotent equally with the Father, and both cite the Son's doing likewise whatever the Father does. Hilary rests his case on that saying alone, inferring from the Father's boundless power. Bickersteth adds that creation, upholding and governing all things require omnipotence and are ascribed to the Son, and that Revelation shows the Son calling himself "the Almighty."

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord does not deprive Himself of omnipotence, for He says that whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. Since the Father's power is boundless, the Son who does the same works shares that limitless power.
sources.quote: The Lord does not deprive even Himself of the quality of omnipotence, for He says, What things soever the Father doeth, these the Son also doeth in like manner
sources.raw_question: Does the Son share the Father's omnipotence?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. Creation, the upholding of all things, and universal government all demand omnipotence, and Scripture ascribes each to the Son. He also works coextensively with the Father, doing likewise whatever the Father does. Comparing the passages of Revelation shows that the Son of man declares of himself, "I am the Almighty."
sources.quote: Coextensive operation with God the Father in a boundless empire demands omnipotence, and Jesus Christ, when explaining his words, My Father worketh hitherto and I work, declares, “What things soever He (the Father) doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise.”
sources.raw_question: Is the Son almighty, possessing omnipotence equal to the Father's?

question: Can the Father be conceived as prior in time to the Son, and what would follow if he were?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Waterland both deny any temporal priority of the Father over the Son. Gregory argues that the divine existences are pre-temporal, so no temporal distinctions apply to the Son. He adds that even granting priority for argument's sake, earlier existence would confer no superiority in being. Waterland instead stresses the consequences of the concession: a single moment of priority implies an infinite priority and makes the Son a creature, which is why the Arians accepted it and the Catholics rejected it.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in making the being of the Father alone proper and supreme, implying by his omission of the Son and the Spirit that theirs is improperly spoken of, and is inferior.
sources.answer: No. No temporal distinctions can be conceived in the personality of the Son, and the divine existences are pre-temporal, with every measure of distance beneath the divine nature. Even granting priority in time for argument's sake, earlier existence gives no superiority in being.
sources.quote: as there is really no difference whatever in the prerogative of time, how could any one possibly entertain such an idea about these existencies which are pre-temporal?
sources.raw_question: Could the Father's being be supreme over the Son's by reason of priority in time?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. One moment of temporal priority necessarily implies an infinite priority, because an eternity stretches back before that moment. The Arians saw this consequence and accepted it. The Catholics rejected it, because it makes the Son of God a creature.
sources.quote: But the misfortune was, that one moment’s priority of time must infer an infinite priority.
sources.raw_question: Would allowing the Father even a single moment of priority over the Son, in which to will the Son's existence, be a harmless concession?

question: Why is the Father called simply "God" while the Son is called "God of God," and does this mean only the Father is truly God?
synthesis: Both authors explain the Father's unqualified title by His being the source: Edwards calls Him the fountain of the Godhead, and Augustine says the Father is God from no one while the Son is God from the Father. Their grounds differ in emphasis. Augustine argues from the logic of the father–son relation, since every son is from his father and no father is from his son. Edwards adds that the Father upholds the dignity of the Deity in the economy, and he explicitly denies that only the Father is properly God.

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: The Father is called God without addition because He is the fountain of the Godhead, from whom the Son and Spirit proceed, and because in the economy He sustains the dignity of the Deity and upholds the rights of the Godhead. This does not mean He alone is properly God; He is God by essence like the others, but also as it were by His economical office.
sources.quote: Hereby we see how the Father is the fountain of the Godhead, and why when He is spoken of in Scripture He is so often, without any addition or distinction, called God, which has led some to think that He only was truly and properly God.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Father so often called simply "God" in Scripture, and does this mean only the Father is truly God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > There is a Double Rule for Understanding the Scriptural Modes of Speech Concerning the Son of God. These Modes of Speech are of a Threefold Kind.
sources.answer: The Son has another of whom he is and to whom he is Son, but the Father is not from his Son. He is only Father to him. Every son is what he is from his father, while no father is what he is from his son. So the Son is God from God, and the Father is God from no one.
sources.quote: For we call the Son God of God; but the Father, God only; not of God. Whence it is plain that the Son has another of whom He is, and to whom He is Son
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son called 'God of God' while the Father is called simply God and not 'of God'?

question: Does Scripture present the Holy Spirit as a person, an intelligent and voluntary agent, rather than an impersonal force or influence?
synthesis: Owen and Bickersteth agree that Scripture presents the Spirit as a personal, intelligent and voluntary agent. Owen adds that the evidence is so plain that even those who denied the Spirit's deity admitted his personhood, wrongly making him a created spirit instead. Bickersteth lists the attributes and actions Scripture ascribes to the Spirit, such as mind, will, teaching, interceding and being grieved, and argues that reading them as personification fails both one by one and taken together.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture everywhere ascribes to the Spirit things that undeniably show him to be an intelligent, voluntary agent. The evidence is so plain that even those who denied his deity had to admit he is a person, an intelligent subsistence. They then wrongly made him a chief created spirit rather than God.
sources.quote: such things were everywhere ascribed unto him in the Scripture as uncontrollably evidence him to be an intelligent, voluntary agent. This they found so plain and evident, that they could not deny but that he was a person
sources.raised_by_detail: Macedonians / those who denied the Deity of the Holy Ghost
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture present the Holy Spirit as a person, an intelligent and voluntary agent, rather than an impersonal force?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: He is a personal agent. Scripture ascribes to him a mind, an independent will, knowledge of God's depths, commanding, forbidding, teaching, interceding, being grieved, testifying and inviting. If these qualities and actions do not prove personality, none could. A few might be read as personification, but most resist that reading singly, and taken together such a reading would confuse all the laws of language.
sources.quote: Unitarians axe wont to speak of the Spirit, as an effusion or emanation separate from God, or an influence or power exercised by God. Can you speak of the mind of an effusion?
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a personal, intelligent agent rather than an impersonal influence, power, or emanation from God?

question: Is the Holy Spirit a ministering spirit who serves the Son as the angels do, rather than sharing the nature of the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Ambrose and Basil both deny that the Holy Spirit is a ministering spirit like the angels. Ambrose argues from Scripture's wording: Hebrews commands the angels to worship the Son and calls them ministering spirits, but never says this of the Spirit, who is the Son's witness rather than his minister. Basil argues from the Lord's handed-down rule that ranks the Spirit with the Father, and he calls the reduction of the Spirit to a minister blasphemy against that rule.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: No. Scripture commands all the angels of God to worship the Son, but never says "Let the Holy Spirit worship." When Hebrews calls "all" of them ministering spirits, it does not include the Holy Spirit. Angels and the other Powers are appointed to serve the Son of God, while the Spirit is the Son's witness, not his minister.
sources.quote: When he says All, does he include the Holy Spirit? Certainly not, because Angels and the other Powers are destined to serve in ministering and obedience to the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit among the ministering spirits who worship and serve the Son, as the angels do?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who say that it is not right to rank the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. The Lord handed down, as a necessary and saving doctrine, that the Spirit is to be ranked with the Father. To split the Spirit off and reduce him to a ministering spirit sets one's own blasphemy above the law the Lord laid down.
sources.quote: The Lord has delivered to us as a necessary and saving doctrine that the Holy Spirit is to be ranked with the Father. Our opponents think differently, and see fit to divide and rend asunder, and relegate Him to the nature of a ministering spirit.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a ministering spirit, like the angels, rather than sharing the nature of the Father and the Son?

question: When Scripture says the Father 'gave' something to the Son, does this mean the Son lacked something and received it as a favour?
synthesis: Ambrose and Augustine agree that the Father's giving is his begetting of the Son, so it implies no prior lack. Ambrose stresses that the gift belongs to the divine nature and comes from natural love rather than bounty or adoption. Augustine argues that, unlike a creature, the Son is what he has, so giving him something to have is the same as begetting him to be.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: No. The Father gave by begetting, not by adoption. What He gave belonged to the prerogative of the Divine Nature itself, not something the Son lacked and received by bounty. The gift is the gift of natural love, not a grudging grant, and so the Son has all things equally with the Father.
sources.quote: The Father gave by begetting, not by adoption; He gave as it were that which was contained in the very prerogative of the Divine Nature, not what was lacking as it were by favour of His bounty.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's giving to the Son imply that the Son lacked something and received it as a favour?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. 'The Father gave to me' means the Father begat him. Giving him something to have is the same as begetting him to be. Unlike a creature, the Son is not one thing and has another; he is what he has.
sources.quote: not that He gave anything to Him, already existing and not possessing it; but that the very meaning of, To have given that He might have, is, To have begotten that He might be.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says the Father 'gave' something to the Son, does this mean the Son already existed and then received something he lacked?

question: Does the Father lose or give up what He gives to the Son?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary agree that the Father loses nothing by giving all things to the Son and still possesses everything. Athanasius grounds this in the Son's Godhead being the Father's own, so the Father exercises providence over all things in the Son. Hilary simply warns against two errors: thinking the Father did not truly give because He still has, or thinking He lost because He gave.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: No. Having given all things to the Son, the Father still has all things in the Son. The Son's Godhead is the Father's Godhead, so the Father exercises His providence over all things in the Son.
sources.quote: For the Father, having given all things to the Son, in the Son still hath all things; and the Son having, still the Father hath them; for the Son’s Godhead is the Father’s Godhead
sources.raw_question: Does the Father lose or give up what He gives to the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The Father gives all to the Son yet still possesses all; we must not think He did not truly give because He still has, nor that He lost because He gave.
sources.quote: Yet we must not imagine that the Father did not give, because He still possesses, or that He has lost, because He gave to the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father lose anything when He gives all He has to the Son in generating Him?

question: Is the Holy Spirit a created being, even the chief of created spirits, or is He uncreated God above all created things?
synthesis: Owen and Ambrose agree that the Spirit is not a creature but stands above all created things, though they argue differently. Owen argues from Scripture's portrayal of the Spirit as an eternally existing divine substance, the author of divine operations and the object of divine worship. Ambrose reasons that because the Spirit was not made, He is above all things, and that because He is above all things, He cannot be counted among things made.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter II. The words, “All things were made by Him,” are not a proof that the Holy Spirit is included amongst all things, since He was not made. For otherwise it could be proved by other passages that the Son, and even the Father Himself, must be numbered amongst all things, which would be similar irreverence.
sources.answer: Yes. The same text shows two things. Because the Spirit was not made, He is above all things. And because He is above all things, He is seen not to have been made and is not to be numbered among the things that were made.
sources.quote: firstly, that He is proved to be above all things, because He was not made; and secondly, that because He is above all things, He is seen not to have been made, and is not to be numbered amongst those things which were made.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Holy Spirit was not made show that He is above all created things?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Scripture reveals the Holy Spirit to be an eternally existing divine substance and the author of divine operations. He is also the object of divine worship, and so is 'over all, God blessed for ever,' not any created spirit.
sources.quote: the Holy Spirit is an eternally existing divine substance, the author of divine operations, and the object of divine and religious worship; that is, “Over all, God blessed for ever,”
sources.raised_by_detail: those who denied the Deity of the Holy Ghost (Macedonians)
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a created spirit, chief above all others, rather than God?

question: How can Christ both receive the Holy Spirit and give the Holy Spirit?
synthesis: Athanasius and Augustine agree that Christ gives the Spirit as God and receives it as man. Athanasius adds that he receives glory too, and that such receiving is said for our sake, so that we might receive and be exalted in him. Augustine grounds the point in the text saying he received the promise of the Spirit from the Father and shed it forth. He also contrasts this with believers, who can receive the gift but cannot shed it on others.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: He gives as God's Word and receives as man, while remaining unalterable. He has always had all things as Word. Words like 'took,' 'gave' and 'highly exalted' are said of him because of us, so that we might receive and be exalted in him. In the same way he asks the Father for glory so that he might give it to us.
sources.quote: remaining unalterable, and at once gives and receives, giving as God’s Word, receiving as man.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ both give and receive the Holy Spirit and glory?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: He receives the Spirit as man and gives or sheds forth the Spirit as God. Both natures are shown in the statement that He received of the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit and shed forth the Holy Spirit. We can receive the gift in our small measure but cannot shed it on others.
sources.quote: He received of the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, and shed forth the Holy Spirit:[^1065] seeing that He received as man, and shed forth as God.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ both receive the Holy Spirit and give the Holy Spirit?

question: What are the essential elements that make up the doctrine of the Trinity as revealed in Scripture?
synthesis: Owen and Warfield agree that the doctrine's core is that God is one and that this one God is Father, Son and Spirit, who are distinct. They ground the distinction differently. Owen locates it in the mutual relations of Fatherhood, Sonship and procession, and stresses that this is all faith directly needs for worship and obedience. Warfield states three propositions: one God, each Person God, each a distinct person. He grounds them in the New Testament's I-Thou-He presentation.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: That God is one; that this one God is Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; that the Father is Father of the Son, the Son Son of the Father, and the Spirit the Spirit of the Father and the Son; and that by these mutual relations they are distinct. Owen holds this is the whole of faith's direct concern, since it gives faith its proper object and directs worship and obedience.
sources.quote: the sum of this revelation in this matter is, that God is one; — that this one God is Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; — that the Father is the Father of the Son; and the Son, the Son of the Father
sources.raw_question: What is the essential substance of the doctrine of the Trinity as directly revealed in Scripture for faith?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: There are three: there is but one God; the Father, Son and Spirit are each God; and the Father, Son and Spirit are each a distinct person. The New Testament presents this composite fact, with the three standing over against each other as I, Thou, and He. The church's formulations have always aimed to do justice both to God's unity and to the true deity and distinct personality of Son and Spirit. Stating these three things enunciates the doctrine in its completeness.
sources.quote: that there is but one God, that the Father and the Son and the Spirit is each God, that the Father and the Son and the Spirit is each a distinct person – we have enunciated the doctrine of the Trinity in its completeness
sources.raw_question: What are the essential elements that together make up the complete doctrine of the Trinity?

question: How can John the Baptist say that Christ, who came after him, was before him, and does this show the Son's existence prior to his human birth?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Novatian agree that John the Baptist's testimony points to the Son's pre-existence. Irenaeus identifies the one who was 'prior' to John as the Son of God from whose fulness all have received. Novatian argues more pointedly that a mere man born after John could not have preceded him, so the statement shows Christ is God.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus cites John's testimony that the one coming after him 'was made before me, because He was prior to me,' identifying this pre-existent one as the Son of God from whose fulness all have received.
sources.quote: After me cometh a man who was made before me; because He was prior to me: and of His fulness have all we received.
sources.raw_question: Does John the Baptist's statement that the one coming after him was before him show that the Son existed prior to his human birth?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > The Author Prosecutes the Same Argument.
sources.answer: Only because Christ is God. As a mere man born after John, he could not have preceded John. John's testimony that Christ was prior to him therefore points to his divine pre-existence.
sources.quote: when, if Christ were only man, being born after John, He could not be before John, unless because He preceded him, in that He is God?
sources.raw_question: How can John the Baptist say that Christ, who was born after him, was before him?

question: Do the works and honour ascribed to the Son in John 5 (doing whatever the Father does, quickening the dead, judging all, receiving the same honour as the Father) prove his equality with the Father?
synthesis: Bickersteth and Waterland agree that John 5 establishes the Son's equality with the Father. Bickersteth argues from each divine work in turn: the Son is almighty, the source of life, raises the dead, is omniscient and is adored. Waterland stresses the claim to be the proper Son, which the Jews and the Apostle read as making himself equal with God, together with the command to honour the Son even as the Father. He adds that denying this blurs the line between creature and Creator.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son does whatever the Father does, gives life to whom he will, raises the dead and judges the universe, and all must honour him as they honour the Father, then he is equally almighty, equally the fountain of life, equally God who alone raises the dead, equally omniscient, and equally the object of adoration.
sources.quote: then is He equally Almighty: equally the communicative fountain of life: equally God who alone can raise the dead: equally the Omniscient who alone can judge an assembled world: and equally the center of universal homage and adoration.
sources.raw_question: Do the works and honour ascribed to the Son in John 5 (doing all the Father does, quickening the dead, judging all, receiving equal honour) prove his equality with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: Yes. Declaring himself the proper Son of God, which both the Jews and the Apostle understood as making himself equal with God, claiming the same right, power and authority, and saying all judgment is committed to him so that all may honour the Son even as the Father, is assuming equal honour. To deny this is to lose the distinction between what belongs to a creature and what belongs to the Creator alone.
sources.quote: if this be not assuming an equality of honour and regard with that other; we must for ever despair to understand the meaning of words, or to be able to distinguish between what is proper to a creature, and what to the Creator only.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's claim in John 5 to be the proper Son of the Father, doing whatever the Father does, amount to claiming equality of honour with the Father?

question: Does 2 Corinthians 3:17 identify the Lord and the Spirit so as to erase any distinction, and does distinguishing them undermine the Spirit's unity with the Lord?
synthesis: Both authors hold that Lord and Spirit are distinguished in the verse, but they stress different things. Hilary insists the distinction is real: the Spirit belongs to the Lord as property to proprietor, and 'the Lord is Spirit' expresses God's infinity. Ambrose argues that even granting a distinction, the Spirit is wherever the Lord is, so the unity stands and the Spirit is still confessed as Lord.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIV. Besides the evidence adduced above, other passages can be brought to prove the sovereignty of the Three Persons. Two are quoted from the Epistles to the Thessalonians, and by collating other testimonies of the Scriptures it is shown that in them dominion is claimed for the Spirit as for the other Persons. Then, by quotation of another still more express passage in the second Epistle to the Corinthians, it is inferred both that the Spirit is Lord, and that where the Lord is, there is the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Even if one distinguishes the terms, one cannot deny that where the Lord is, there the Spirit is. Whoever is converted to the Lord is therefore converted to the Spirit. Cavilling at the letter cannot injure the unity, and if one separates them, one thereby confesses the Spirit himself as Lord of power.
sources.quote: For although you may distinguish between Lord and Spirit, you cannot deny that where the Lord is, there too is the Spirit, and he who has been converted to the Lord will have been converted to the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: If someone distinguishes 'Lord' from 'Spirit' in 2 Corinthians 3:17, does that undermine the Spirit's unity with the Lord?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. Paul distinguishes between the Spirit and Him whose Spirit He is, as proprietor and property. "The Lord is Spirit" reveals God's infinity, while "the Spirit of the Lord" indicates the One who belongs to God, so the two are different in sense.
sources.quote: he has distinguished between the Spirit, Who exists, and Him Whose Spirit He is Proprietor and Property, He and His are different in sense.
sources.raw_question: Does 2 Corinthians 3:17, "the Lord is Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty," identify the Holy Spirit with the Lord so as to erase their distinction?

question: Does the Arian claim that the Son 'was not before His generation' prove that the Son had a beginning and is not eternal or of one nature with the Father?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary both deny that the formula proves the Son had a beginning. Athanasius argues that the Son's generation from the Father is itself eternal, so He exists unoriginately in the Father as offspring, not creature. Hilary treats the phrase as an evasive cover for denying the shared nature, and replies that the Son draws His existence by birth from the Father's eternal, abiding nature.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Hilary sees the phrase as a cover: it is meant to support the denial of the Son's shared nature, while offering an escape if challenged. Nobody claims that the unborn, eternal Father was born. What faith confesses is that the Father existed eternally and that the Son draws his existence through birth from that abiding nature. The Son's birth is therefore not the birth of the pre-existing God but the birth of God from the pre-existent God.
sources.quote: If, then, the Son is born from God, you must confess that His is a birth of that abiding nature; not a birth of the pre-existing God, but a birth of God from God the pre-existent.
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian claim that the Son 'did not exist before He was born' show that the Son is not of one nature with the eternal Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: No. The Son could not be before His generation because His generation is itself eternal, being from the Father. Creatures begin to come to be and their being is measured by their becoming, but the Word has His being in no other origin than the unoriginate Father, so He exists unoriginately in the Father as His offspring, not His creature.
sources.quote: the Word of God, not having beginning (ἀρχὴν) of being, surely did not begin to be, nor begin to come to be, but was always.
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian formula that the Son 'was not before His generation' prove that the Son had a beginning and is not eternal?

question: Why is denying the Holy Spirit equivalent to denying the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Ambrose and Basil agree that denying the Spirit is as grave as denying the Father and the Son, but on different grounds. Ambrose argues from the Spirit's identity: the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are one Spirit, so denying him denies the Father and the Son, a sacrilege beyond pardon. Basil argues from baptism: believers confess Father, Son and Spirit as one covenant, so denying the Spirit breaks that covenant and makes one a transgressor just as denying God or Christ does.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: The Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are one and the same Spirit. So whoever denies the Spirit also denies the Father and the Son. This is why such a denial is the fulness of sacrilege, with no possibility of pardon.
sources.quote: for he who has denied the Spirit has denied also the Father and the Son, since the same is the Spirit of God Who is the Spirit of Christ.
sources.raw_question: Why does denying the Holy Spirit amount to denying the Father and the Son as well?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That they who deny the Spirit are transgressors.
sources.answer: Yes. At baptism believers confessed faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost as one covenant of salvation; to deny the Spirit is therefore to break that covenant with God, just as denying God or Christ is. Hence the one who denies the Spirit merits the same title of transgressor.
sources.quote: And to him who denies the Spirit, what title do you wish me to apply? Must it not be the same, inasmuch as he has broken his covenant with God?
sources.raw_question: Is denying the deity of the Holy Spirit a transgression of the same kind as denying God the Father or denying Christ?

question: Does the statement that the Spirit 'searcheth the deep things of God' (1 Cor. 2:10) imply that the Spirit learns, step by step, what He did not previously know?
synthesis: Ambrose and Bickersteth both deny that 'searching' implies acquiring knowledge, but they argue differently. Ambrose reasons from the apostle's comparison with a man's spirit, which knows his own things already, and concludes that the Spirit knows by nature, not by an accident. Bickersteth argues from scriptural usage, citing 'I, the Lord, search the heart,' and takes the text as proof of the Spirit's omniscience, shared with the Son, in comprehending God.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. The apostle first says God revealed these things to us through the Spirit, and then compares the Spirit to a man's spirit, which knows the things of a man before searching. The Spirit knows by nature, not by searching, and divine knowledge is not an accident in Him but His natural knowledge.
sources.quote: not that He knows by searching, but knows by nature; not that the knowledge of divine things is an accident in Him, but is His natural knowledge.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that the Spirit 'searcheth the deep things of God' imply that the Spirit learns what He did not previously know?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. In Scripture 'search' does not necessarily mean the successive gaining of knowledge that belongs to a finite being. Jehovah himself says, 'I, the Lord, search the heart.' So the text teaches the Spirit's omniscience: with the Son alone he comprehends the incomprehensible God.
sources.quote: The word search, as used in Scripture, does not necessarily imply that successive acquisition of knowledge which belongs to a finite being, for Jehovah says, “I, the Lord, search the heart.”
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit's 'searching' the deep things of God (1 Cor. 2:10) imply that he acquires knowledge step by step like a finite being?

question: Do Christ's own sayings in Scripture teach that the Son's glory is equal to the Father's, with no difference of glory or essence between them?
synthesis: Basil and Gregory of Nyssa agree that Christ's sayings, such as "He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father" and that all should honour the Son as they honour the Father, teach equal glory. Basil adds John's witness to the glory of the only begotten in the Father's bosom. Gregory argues from the Lord's truthfulness, which Eunomius concedes, and cites "I am in the Father, and the Father in Me" to show that each is wholly in the other, so there is no difference in glory or essence.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ himself sets forth the equal dignity of his glory with the Father when he says that whoever has seen him has seen the Father, that he comes in the glory of his Father, and that all should honour the Son even as they honour the Father. John adds that his glory is that of the only begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father. These passages proclaim the majesty of the Only Begotten, not his humiliation.
sources.quote: We ask them to listen to the Lord Himself, distinctly setting forth the equal dignity of His glory with the Father, in His words, “He that hath seen me hath seen the Father;”
sources.raw_question: Do the Lord's own sayings in Scripture teach that the Son's glory is equal to the Father's?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next skilfully confutes the partial, empty and blasphemous statement of Eunomius on the subject of the absolutely existent.
sources.answer: No. If the Lord cannot lie, as Eunomius himself admits, then his words must be believed: "I am in the Father, and the Father in Me," that the Son should be honoured as the Father is, and "He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father." These teach that each is wholly in the other, the Father not exceeding the Son and the Son not falling short of the Father. They give no hint of any variation of glory or essence between them.
sources.quote: plainly, the One in His entirety, in the Other in His entirety, the Father not superabounding in the Son, the Son not being deficient in the Father
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's sayings imply any difference of glory or essence between the Father and the Son?

question: In Christ, are the Son of God and the Son of Man distinct, and if so, are they two separate subjects or one?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers stresses unity: there are not two Sons, and Christ is one who is fully God and fully man, like body and soul forming one person. Novatian stresses a real distinction between Son of God and Son of Man, though joined in association. He argues against those who would collapse Christ into a mere man, holding that only by keeping the distinction can Christ be shown to be both God and man. Their emphases differ, but neither treats Christ as a merely human subject.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. There is not one Son of Man and another Son of God, nor one in the form of God and another in the form of a servant. As a man is one being of body and soul, so Jesus Christ by his own power is one who is God and Man, possessing whole and perfect manhood and whole and perfect Godhead.
sources.quote: There is not one Son of Man and another Son of God; nor one in the form of God, and another born perfect man in the form of a servant
sources.raw_question: Are the Son of God and the Son of Man two distinct subjects in Christ?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That These Have Therefore Erred, by Thinking that There Was No Difference Between the Son of God and the Son of Man; Because They Have Ill Understood the Scripture.
sources.answer: There is a real distinction, though joined in association. The heretics who deny any distinction end up making Christ a mere man and exclude texts like "the Word was made flesh" and "Emmanuel, God with us." If the distinction is made, Christ is easily shown to be both man and God.
sources.quote: they think that there is no distinction between the Son of God and the Son of man; because if a distinction were made, Jesus Christ would easily be proved to be both man and God.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold Christ to be man only (adoptionists)
sources.raw_question: Is there a distinction between Christ as Son of God and Christ as Son of man, or are they simply the same human subject?

question: Why was it necessary for the Redeemer to be both God and man?
synthesis: Augustine and Owen agree that the Redeemer had to be man in order to suffer and die, but they give different reasons why he had to be God. For Augustine, his divinity shows that his suffering was righteousness freely preferred over power rather than a lack of power. For Owen, divinity was needed so that his suffering could be of infinite worth and satisfy for an infinite offense.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Unobligated Death of Christ Has Freed Those Who Were Liable to Death.
sources.answer: Because both natures were needed for him to conquer by righteousness rather than by power. Unless he had been man, he could not have been slain. Unless he had been God, men would have thought he could not do what he willed, rather than that he chose not to do what he could. So his suffering shows righteousness freely preferred to power, not a lack of power.
sources.quote: For unless He had been man, He could not have been slain; unless He had been God, men would not have believed that He would not do what He could, but that He could not do what He would
sources.raw_question: Why was it necessary for the Redeemer to be both man and God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Had he not been man, he could not have suffered. Had he not been God, his suffering could not have availed or satisfied. The suffering of a mere man bears no proportion to an offense that is in some respect infinite.
sources.quote: Had he not been man, he could not have suffered; — had he not been God, his suffering could not have availed either himself or us, — he had not satisfied; the suffering of a mere man could not bear any proportion to that which in any respect was infinite.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Redeemer need to be both God and man in order to satisfy for sin?

question: Can a person rightly believe in the Father and the Son while denying or rejecting the Holy Spirit?
synthesis: Ambrose and Basil both answer no, and both use the chain that whoever does not believe in the Spirit does not believe in the Son, and so not in the Father. Their grounds differ. Ambrose argues from the one shared power and dignity of the Three, so faith cannot be divided where there is no division. Basil argues that faith in the Father and Son cannot even be held without the Spirit's presence, since none can confess Jesus as Lord except by the Holy Spirit.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter II. The words, “All things were made by Him,” are not a proof that the Holy Spirit is included amongst all things, since He was not made. For otherwise it could be proved by other passages that the Son, and even the Father Himself, must be numbered amongst all things, which would be similar irreverence.
sources.answer: No. It is equal irreverence to detract from the dignity of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit. Whoever does not believe in the Son does not believe in the Father, and whoever does not believe in the Spirit does not believe in the Son. The Three share one power, so a divided faith cannot be maintained where there is no division.
sources.quote: For he believes not in the Father who does not believe in the Son, nor does he believe in the Son of God who does not believe in the Spirit, nor can faith stand without the rule of truth.
sources.raw_question: Can one rightly believe in the Father and the Son while denying the dignity of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That they who deny the Spirit are transgressors.
sources.answer: No. Faith in the Father and Son is useless without the Spirit, because one cannot even hold it without the Spirit's presence. Whoever does not believe the Spirit does not believe in the Son, and whoever does not believe in the Son does not believe in the Father, since none can confess Jesus as Lord except by the Holy Ghost, and only the Son declares the Father.
sources.quote: For he who does not believe the Spirit does not believe in the Son, and he who has not believed in the Son does not believe in the Father.
sources.raw_question: Can a person hold genuine faith in the Father and the Son while rejecting the Holy Spirit?

question: Can the manner of the Son's generation from the Father be known or described by human beings?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Irenaeus of Lyons agree that the manner of the Son's birth cannot be known, and both say it is known only to the Father and the Son. Hilary answers in a tone of personal, content faith: he does not ask for it to be revealed and simply believes the Father begot the Son perfectly. Irenaeus answers polemically: even angels do not grasp it, and heretics who describe 'productions' attempt to describe the indescribable.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. That birth is a mystery known only to the Father and the Only-begotten. Hilary does not ask that it be revealed to him. He is content to believe that the omnipotent Father begot the Son perfectly.
sources.quote: I look not that Thou shouldst reveal to me the mystery of that ineffable birth which is secret between Thyself and Thy Only-begotten.
sources.raw_question: Can the manner of the Son's ineffable birth from the Father be known by human beings?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: No. The Son's generation is altogether indescribable; no man understands it, nor do heretics or even angels and archangels, but only the Father who begat and the Son who was begotten. Hence those who try to set forth generations and productions undertake to describe the indescribable.
sources.quote: no man understands that production, or generation, or calling, or revelation, or by whatever name one may describe His generation, which is in fact altogether indescribable.
sources.raw_question: Can the manner in which the Son is generated or produced by the Father be known or described by human beings?

question: Is the work of the Son the same as the work of the Father, and why?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Athanasius agree that the Son's work is the Father's work. Hilary grounds this in the Son's birth, by which he possesses the whole nature of God and abides in his source. Athanasius argues that the Father works everything through the Son, citing 'What I see the Father do, that do I also.' He applies this to baptism, where the one baptized is consecrated in the Spirit, and illustrates the unity with the image of light and its indivisible radiance.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: By his birth the Son possesses everything that is God's. His birth has not excluded him from the nature that is his source and in which he abides. So what the Son does is the Father's work.
sources.quote: the Son’s work is the Father’s work because His birth has not excluded Him from that nature which is His source and wherein He abides, and because He has in Himself that nature to which He owes it that He exists eternally.
sources.raw_question: Why is the work of the Son the same as the work of the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Yes. Whatever the Father works, he works through the Son, as the Lord says, 'What I see the Father do, that do I also.' So whom the Father baptizes, the Son baptizes, and the one baptized is consecrated in the Holy Spirit. The light and its radiance are one and indivisible.
sources.quote: whom the Father baptizes, him the Son baptizes; and whom the Son baptizes, he is consecrated in the Holy Ghost
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's work in baptism and creation the same as the Father's work?

question: Why did God become man, suffer and die?
synthesis: Augustine stresses the Incarnation and death as an example of humility and a display of God's love, a remedy for pride and the mystery loosing the bond of sin. Hilary emphasizes taking humanity into himself to justify us and to triumph over the powers of evil, uniting our weakness to his strength. They agree it was for our salvation but differ in focus: Augustine on humility and love as healing pride, Hilary on union with our nature and victory over the devil.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Trinity May Be Loved Though Unknown.
sources.answer: He did so as an example of humility and to show God's love towards us. The humility by which God was born of a woman and led to death through insults is the chief remedy for our swelling pride. It is also the profound mystery by which the bond of sin is loosed.
sources.quote: the humility by which God was born of a woman, and was led to death through contumelies so great by mortal men, is the chiefest remedy by which the swelling of our pride may be cured
