sources.raw_question: Why did God become man and suffer death at the hands of men?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: To take us into himself, to justify us, and to avenge us on the powers of evil. Because God assumed our weakness, the devil's malice could not confirm the law of sin in us; because the immortal God submitted to death, no power can rise against him. Our manhood abides eternally in him, our weakness is united to his strength, and the spiritual powers are subdued in the triumph of our flesh.
sources.quote: Thus God was born to take us into Himself, suffered to justify us, and died to avenge us; for our manhood abides for ever in Him, the weakness of our infirmity is united with His strength
sources.raw_question: Why did the Only-begotten God become man, suffer and die?

question: Are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit distinct Persons, or, as Sabellius taught, one and the same subject under three names?
synthesis: Ambrose and Gregory of Nyssa both reject Sabellius and hold that the three are distinct as Persons while sharing one being. Ambrose takes up the language of the three being 'the same' and explains it as sameness of power and substance, not of Person, steering between Sabellian confusion and Arian division. Gregory affirms the distinction, but in answering Eunomius warns that it must be stated as a distinction of 'persons', not of 'beings'.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: No. They are 'the same' not because the same Person is Father, Son and Spirit. They are the same because they are the same Power and the same substance. The Godhead admits neither the confusion of Sabellius nor the division of Arius, nor any earthly or bodily change.
sources.quote: Not the same, so that Himself is Father, Himself Son, Himself Spirit [one and the selfsame Person]; but because both the Father and the Son are the same Power.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Spirit, Lord, and God 'the same' mean that Father, Son, and Spirit are one and the selfsame Person, as Sabellius taught?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His acknowledgment that the Divine Being is 'single' is only verbal.
sources.answer: Yes, provided the distinction is of Persons, not of being. If Eunomius were only proving that the Persons must not be confounded and the three names fitted onto one Subject, his saying would be faithful and acceptable to all the Faithful; the error lies in calling them 'beings' rather than 'persons'.
sources.quote: If, then, he were only proving that it is not right to confound the Persons, and to fit all the three names on to one Subject, his ‘saying’ would be, to use the Apostle’s words, ‘faithful, and worthy of all acceptation.’
sources.raw_question: Is it correct to say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct from one another, as against Sabellius who applied three names to one subject?

question: Whom does Wisdom in Proverbs 3 and Proverbs 8 refer to?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Owen differ: Irenaeus identifies Wisdom with the Holy Spirit, present with God before creation and distinct from the Word, the Son, while Owen identifies Wisdom with Jesus Christ as the eternal Wisdom of the Father. Owen grounds his reading in the description of Wisdom in Proverbs 8 and takes the praise of Wisdom in Proverbs 3 as praise of Christ; Irenaeus rests his on Wisdom being present with God when he prepared the heavens and founded the earth.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Wisdom refers to the Holy Spirit, who was present with God before all creation and through whom God founded the earth and adorned all things. Irenaeus reads the speaker of Proverbs 8, who was with God when he prepared the heavens, as the Spirit, distinct from the Word, the Son.
sources.quote: Wisdom also, which is the Spirit, was present with Him, anterior to all creation, He declares by Solomon: “God by Wisdom founded the earth, and by understanding hath He established the heaven.
sources.raw_question: Whom does Wisdom in Proverbs 3 and Proverbs 8 refer to?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that the Holy Ghost is speaking of Jesus Christ, the Wisdom of God and the eternal Wisdom of the Father. He takes this as evident from the description of Wisdom given in Proverbs 8. So the praise of Wisdom as more precious than silver, gold and rubies is praise of Christ and his ways.
sources.quote: It is of Jesus Christ, the Wisdom of God, the eternal Wisdom of the Father, that the Holy Ghost speaks; as is evident from the description which is given hereof, chap. viii.
sources.raw_question: Is the 'Wisdom' praised in Proverbs 3 and described in Proverbs 8 a reference to Jesus Christ as the eternal Wisdom of the Father?

question: In 2 Thessalonians 3:5, 'the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and into the patience of Christ,' is 'the Lord' who directs the Holy Spirit?
synthesis: Ambrose and Basil both read 'the Lord' here as the Holy Spirit, because love is assigned to God and patience to Christ, so the director must be a third Person. Basil argues that otherwise the text would have said 'into His own love' or 'His own patience.' Ambrose adds that Paul repeats this pattern deliberately, and that elsewhere Scripture gives the work of leading and directing to the Spirit.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIV. Besides the evidence adduced above, other passages can be brought to prove the sovereignty of the Three Persons. Two are quoted from the Epistles to the Thessalonians, and by collating other testimonies of the Scriptures it is shown that in them dominion is claimed for the Spirit as for the other Persons. Then, by quotation of another still more express passage in the second Epistle to the Corinthians, it is inferred both that the Spirit is Lord, and that where the Lord is, there is the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Since love is attributed to God and patience to Christ, the Lord who directs must be a third, namely the Spirit, and the repetition of this pattern shows Paul designedly called the Spirit Lord. Scripture elsewhere ascribes leading and directing to the Spirit, as when Christ says the Spirit of truth will lead into all truth and David says, 'Thy good Spirit shall lead me.' Otherwise one would have to invent some fourth person.
sources.quote: If love be of God and patience of Christ, it ought to be shown Who is the Lord Who directs, if we deny that the direction is of the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: In 2 Thessalonians 3:5, 'the Lord direct your hearts in the love of God and in the patience of Christ,' is the Lord who directs the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Proof from Scripture that the Spirit is called Lord.
sources.answer: Yes. Since the Lord directs hearts into the love of God and the patient waiting for Christ, the Lord meant cannot be the Father or the Son; otherwise the text would have said 'into His own love' or 'into His own patience.' Hence the Lord here is a third Person, the Holy Spirit, who is thus honoured with the title of Lord.
sources.quote: For if the argument had been about God the Father, it would certainly have said, ‘the Lord direct you into His own love,’ or if about the Son, it would have added ‘into His own patience.’
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture call the Holy Spirit 'Lord' in 2 Thessalonians 3:5, where 'the Lord' directs hearts into the love of God and the patience of Christ?

question: Can God the Creator be known from the greatness and beauty of created things?
synthesis: Augustine and Hilary agree that the Maker is known proportionately from the greatness and beauty of creatures, reasoning that the author of beautiful and mighty things must be still more beautiful and mighty. Augustine applies this to rebuke those who worshipped fire, wind or stars as gods. Hilary instead stresses that the Creator's beauty exceeds all thought and comprehension, yet still presses itself on our perception.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > God, Although Incomprehensible, is Ever to Be Sought. The Traces of the Trinity are Not Vainly Sought in the Creature.
sources.answer: Yes, proportionately. By the greatness and beauty of creatures the Maker is seen. Those who took fire, wind or stars for gods are rebuked, because they should have reasoned that the Author of beauty is better still, and the Maker of mighty things mightier still.
sources.quote: For by the greatness and beauty of the creatures proportionably the Maker of them is seen.
sources.raw_question: Can God the Creator be known from the beauty and power of created things?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Yes. The Creator is discerned by comparison with His works: whoever makes great things is supreme in greatness, and whoever makes beautiful things is supreme in beauty. Since the ordered universe is beautiful and its works go beyond our thoughts, its Maker must go beyond all thought and be confessed most beautiful. This beauty exceeds our comprehension, yet it still presses itself on our perception.
sources.quote: The Creator of great things is supreme in greatness, of beautiful things in beauty. Since the work transcends our thoughts, all thought must be transcended by the Maker.
sources.raw_question: Can the greatness and beauty of God be known from the greatness and beauty of the created world?

question: In what sense was Christ 'crucified through weakness' and yet lives 'through the power of God' (2 Corinthians 13:4)?
synthesis: Hilary and Augustine agree that the weakness in which Christ was crucified belongs to the human condition he took on: Hilary calls it the form of a servant, Augustine mortal flesh. Hilary stresses that the one who suffered and the one who lives by divine power are a single subject in whom servant-form and God-form coexist. Augustine instead stresses that the crucifixion happened through weakness rather than immortal power, adding the apostle's point that God's weakness is stronger than men.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: His weakness comes from the form of a servant he took, while his divine nature remains because of the form of God. In this one person there was both weakness to suffer and divine power to give life. Therefore the one who suffered and the one who lives is a single subject, not two.
sources.quote: His weakness arises from the form of a servant, His nature remains because of the form of God.
sources.raw_question: How can the same Christ be 'crucified through weakness' and yet 'live through the power of God'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Unobligated Death of Christ Has Freed Those Who Were Liable to Death.
sources.answer: He was crucified through weakness, not through immortal power. This was the weakness he took upon himself in mortal flesh. Yet, as the apostle says, the weakness of God is stronger than men.
sources.quote: For Christ was crucified, not through immortal power, but through the weakness which He took upon Him in mortal flesh; of which weakness nevertheless the apostle says, “that the weakness of God is stronger than men.”
sources.raw_question: Was Christ crucified through his divine power or through weakness, and what does this imply?

question: In the Incarnation, did God the Word assume a rational human soul as well as human flesh?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Hippolytus agree that the Word assumed a human soul along with the body. Gregory argues from Scripture (Christ laying down his soul, Peter on David's psalm) and from Christ's human affections such as hunger, fear and tears, which neither the Godhead nor flesh alone could undergo. Hippolytus grounds it soteriologically: the Word became all that man is except sin, so that he might save fallen man.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: Yes. The Word took with the flesh the whole of human nature, soul and body. Christ himself says he lays down his soul and takes it again, and Peter, expounding David, says his soul was not left in hell nor did his flesh see corruption. Hunger, fear, tears and trouble of spirit could only be in him if he had a soul, since the Godhead admits no such affections and flesh alone is not affected without the soul.
sources.quote: So, then, the Word, when He became flesh, took with the flesh the whole of human nature; and hence it was possible that hunger and thirst, fear and dread, desire and sleep, tears and trouble of spirit, and all such things, were in Him.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ assume a human soul as well as a human body in the Incarnation?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: He assumed a rational soul as well as flesh. The Word came down into the Virgin Mary, took flesh from her, and also took a human rational soul. He thus became all that man is, except sin, so that he might save fallen man and give immortality to believers.
sources.quote: taking the flesh from her, and assuming also a human, by which I mean a rational soul, and becoming thus all that man is with the exception of sin, He might save fallen man
sources.raw_question: In the Incarnation, did God the Word assume only human flesh, or also a rational human soul?

question: Why does the Son say 'The Son can do nothing of Himself' (John 5:19) if He performs all the divine works, and does this imply inferiority?
synthesis: Ambrose and Basil agree that the saying implies no lack of power or inferiority in the Son, but they ground it differently. Ambrose reads it, and the parallel saying that the Spirit hears what He speaks, as expressing inseparable unity of operation with the Father. Basil reads it as pointing to the Father as source, so that the Son is not imagined to be without origin and through the Son we come to know the Father.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: Because the operation of each is inseparable from the Father's. The Son can do nothing of Himself since His work cannot be separated from the Father's. Likewise the Spirit's operation is not separated, so what He speaks He is said to hear from the Father. This shows a unity of operation, not dependence or inferiority.
sources.quote: And for this reason the Son says that He can do nothing of Himself, because His operation cannot be separated from that of the Father. In like manner the operation of the Holy Spirit is not separated.
sources.raw_question: Why does the Son say He can do nothing of Himself, and why is the Spirit said to hear what He speaks from the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: These sayings keep us from imagining from the greatness of His works that the Son is without origin, and they guide us to the knowledge of the Father as source. They refer our wonder at creation back to the Father so that through the Son we may know the Father, without implying any lack of power in the Son.
sources.quote: lest we should ever be drawn away by the greatness of the works wrought to imagine that the Lord is without beginning,
sources.raw_question: Why does the Son say things like 'I live through the Father' and 'The Son can do nothing of himself' if He performs all divine works?

question: Is God's Fatherhood of the Son to be understood on the pattern of human fatherhood?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary both deny that God's Fatherhood follows the human pattern, but on different grounds. Athanasius reverses the direction of derivation: God alone is properly and truly Father, and human fathers are named from Him. Hilary stresses that, unlike men, the Father does not receive paternity from any outside source, being unbegotten and eternal, so that 'Father' names His very nature.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections to the Foregoing Proof. Whether, in the generation of the Son, God made One that was already, or One that was not.
sources.answer: No. God does not take man as His pattern. God is properly and alone truly Father of His Son. Human fathers are called fathers derivatively, from Him, since every fatherhood in heaven and earth is named from Him.
sources.quote: For God does not make man His pattern; but rather we men, for that God is properly, and alone truly, Father of His Son, are also called fathers of our own children
sources.raw_question: Is human fatherhood the pattern by which God's Fatherhood of the Son should be understood?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The Father is a Father unconditioned. He does not receive the power of paternity from an external source as men do, but is unbegotten and inherently eternal, so 'Father' names His very nature.
sources.quote: He is a Father unconditioned. He does not, as men do, receive the power of paternity from an external source. He is unbegotten, everlasting, inherently eternal.
sources.raw_question: Is God's fatherhood like human fatherhood, received from some outside source?

question: Does the union with the Godhead change or diminish the properties of Christ's human nature?
synthesis: The two authors differ. Gregory of Nyssa holds that the human nature, joined with the infinite good, does not keep its own measures and properties but is transformed into the stronger, becoming immortal, incorruptible and God, like an inferior component in a physical mixture. Owen holds that each nature stays entire with its own properties: the human nature remains finite and, before glorification, subject to infirmity, and the divine nature remains immense and omnipotent.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: Through its combination with the infinite good, the lowly human nature no longer stays within its own measures and properties but is transformed into what is more potent. It became Immortal, Light, Incorruptible, Lord, Christ, and God instead of man. The author compares this to physical mixtures, in which a far inferior component changes completely into the stronger one.
sources.quote: by virtue of its combination with the infinite and boundless element of good, remained no longer in its own measures and properties, but was by the Right Hand of God raised up together with Itself, and became Lord instead of servant
sources.raw_question: How is the human nature of Christ affected by its union with the Godhead?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: No. Each nature remains entire and keeps its own natural properties. Christ is no less perfect God for being made man, and no less a true and perfect man of soul and body. His divine nature remains immense, omniscient and omnipotent. His human nature remains finite and, before glorification, subject to the infirmities of life and death.
sources.quote: For he is no less perfect God for being made man; nor no less a true, perfect man, consisting of soul and body, with all their essential parts, by that nature’s being taken into subsistence with the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: Does the union of the divine and human natures in Christ diminish or confuse the properties of either nature?

question: Does the threefold reference to Spirit, Lord and God in 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 divide the divine working among separate beings or imply a division within the Trinity?
synthesis: Hilary and Ambrose both deny any division and affirm unity, but on different grounds. Hilary argues that the Lord in ministrations and God in workings are one and the same Spirit, one in God and Lord through the mystery of the birth. Ambrose instead calls the diversities differences of office, not severances of the Trinity, since what the Spirit works the Father also works.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It shows a unity. The Lord in ministrations and God in workings are one and the same Spirit who works and distributes as He wills. This one Spirit of one Divinity is one in both God and Lord through the mystery of the birth. The one Spirit therefore both works and distributes all the gifts.
sources.quote: grasp the idea if thou canst that the Lord in the distribution of ministrations, and God in the distribution of workings, are this one and the same Spirit Who both works and distributes as He will
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's threefold reference to Spirit, Lord and God in 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 divide the divine working among separate beings, or show a unity of divinity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: No. The text says each gift comes from 'the same Spirit,' 'the same Lord,' 'the same God Who worketh all in all.' These are diversities of offices, not severances of the Trinity. The things the Spirit works, the Father also works, so there is no diversity of operation between them.
sources.quote: There are diversities of offices, not severances of the Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Do the 'diversities of gifts, ministrations, and operations' attributed to the Spirit, the Lord, and God in 1 Corinthians 12 imply a division within the Trinity?

question: Does 1 Corinthians 12 prove the deity of the Holy Spirit by attributing to Him the working of the spiritual gifts?
synthesis: Augustine and Owen agree that it does. Owen argues textually: what the Spirit does in verse 11 is what God does in verse 6. Augustine adds that only God can work such things as wisdom, healing and prophecy, and concludes that the Spirit is one God with the Father and the Son.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > How the Word Beginning (Principium) is Spoken Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. Only God can work such great things as wisdom, healing, miracles and prophecy. Paul attributes them to the one Spirit, dividing to each as He wills, and also says it is the same God who works all in all. Therefore the Spirit is God, and with the Father and the Son He is one God.
sources.quote: certainly as God—for who can work such great things but God?—but “it is the same God which worketh all in all.”
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's working of the spiritual gifts in 1 Corinthians 12 show that the Spirit is God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Verse 6 says it is the same God who works all in all, and verse 11 says, in other words, that the one and selfsame Spirit works all these things. What the Spirit is said to do in verse 11 is what God himself is said to do in verse 6, which makes his Deity evident.
sources.quote: What he is here said to do as the Spirit bestowed on us and given unto us, there is he said as God himself to do
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 12 prove the deity of the Holy Spirit by attributing to him what is attributed to God?

question: How can the Son be ignorant of the day of judgment (Mark 13:32) if he is a divine Person equal with the Father?
synthesis: Both deny that the text shows ignorance in the Son's divine nature, but on different grounds. Waterland grants a real ignorance and assigns it to the Son's human nature, reading the verse as distinguishing two Persons, one of whom alone assumed humanity. Hilary denies that it is ignorance at all, treating the Son's not-knowing as an economic mystery of purposeful concealment that keeps believers vigilant.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: Yes. The one Person who speaks has both a divine and a human nature and may speak of himself in different capacities. Mark 13:32 presents Father and Son as two Persons: the Son ignorant only in his human capacity, the Father ignorant in no capacity, since he never took human nature and its ignorance into personal union with himself.
sources.quote: one ignorant in such a capacity, the other not ignorant in any capacity at all, as having never taken human nature, and therewith human ignorance, mto a personal union with himself.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be ignorant of the day of judgment while still being a divine Person distinct from but equal with the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. It is not ignorance but a mystery belonging to the economy: in his actions and words the Son both does not know and knows at once. His not-knowing serves a purpose of concealment, keeping believers vigilant, rather than revealing a nature capable of ignorance.
sources.quote: Manifestly, therefore, the ignorance of God is not ignorance but a mystery: in the economy of His actions and words and manifestations, He does not know and at the same time He knows, or knows and at the same time does not know.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's professed ignorance of the day of judgment real ignorance in his divine nature?

question: Does the Holy Spirit know future events?
synthesis: Ambrose and Bickersteth both affirm the Spirit's knowledge of future things and both cite Christ's promise that the Spirit will show or declare things to come. Ambrose argues from 'all truth' that the Spirit's knowledge is complete, including the day and hour, and one with that of the Father and Son. Bickersteth instead piles up scriptural instances of the Spirit's foreknowledge, such as the revelation to Simeon and John being 'in the Spirit.'

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ says the Spirit of Truth will lead the disciples into all truth and declare things to come; he who leads into all truth passes by nothing, neither the day nor the hour, neither past nor future. So the Spirit's knowledge is complete and one with that of the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: He Who says all passes by nothing, neither the day nor the hour, neither things past nor things to come.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit know all things, including future events such as the day of judgment?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. He revealed to Simeon that he would not die before seeing the Lord's Christ. Christ promised that the Spirit 'will show you things to come.' John was 'in the Spirit' when he was shown the course of providence.
sources.quote: He is prescient and unveils futurity.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit have foreknowledge of future events?

question: Does Paul's calling Christ 'Lord' designate His deity, or does it mean He is only Lord and not truly God?
synthesis: Warfield and Hilary agree that Paul's use of 'Lord' for Christ does not deny His deity, but they argue differently. Warfield holds that 'Lord' is itself Paul's Divine Name for Christ. Hilary does not argue from the title; he answers the objection by pointing to Romans 9:5, where Paul calls Christ 'God over all.'

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. 'Lord' is one of Paul's favorite designations of Christ and has become practically a proper name for him, indeed his Divine Name for Christ. Because Paul calls Christ 'Lord' when he thinks of him as Divine, it is naturally his Trinitarian name for Christ.
sources.quote: "Lord" is one of Paul's favorite designations of Christ, and indeed has become with him practically a proper name for Christ, and in point of fact, his Divine Name for Christ.
sources.raw_question: Is 'Lord' in Paul's usage a designation of Christ's deity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Paul himself calls Christ 'God over all' in Romans 9:5. The one so named is not a creature reckoned as God but the God of created things, who is God over all.
sources.quote: It is no creature here who is reckoned as God; nay, it is the God of things created Who is God over all.
sources.raw_question: Since Paul calls Christ 'Lord', does that mean Christ is only Lord and not truly God?

question: Is Christ expressly called 'God' in the New Testament?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and John Owen both answer yes and both cite Romans 9:5 ('over all, God blessed for ever'). They draw on different further texts: Gregory relies on Paul alone (Titus's 'great God and our Saviour' and 1 Timothy's 'God was manifest in the flesh'), while Owen adds John 1:1, Thomas's confession in John 20:28 and Acts 20:28. Owen also presents the Son as an object of faith.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He also ingeniously shows from the passage of the Gospel which speaks of “Good Master,” from the parable of the Vineyard, from Isaiah and from Paul, that there is not a dualism in the Godhead of good and evil, as Eunomius' ally Marcion supposes, and declares that the Son does not refuse the title of “good” or “Existent,” or acknowledge His alienation from the Father, but that to Him also belongs authority over all things that come into being.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul calls Christ not only God but "great God" and "God over all." He says Christ is "over all, God blessed for ever" (Romans), speaks of "the great God and our Saviour" Jesus Christ (Titus), and writes "God was manifest in the flesh" (Timothy). So it is shown on every side that the Only-begotten God is God.
sources.quote: who gives the Lord the appellation not only of “God,” but of “great God” and “God over all,”
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament, especially Paul, call Christ God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen cites several texts. John 1:1 says 'the Word was God', and Thomas confesses 'My Lord and my God' in John 20:28. Acts 20:28 speaks of God purchasing the church with his own blood, and Romans 9:5 calls Christ 'over all, God blessed for ever'. Together they show the Son is proposed in Scripture as God and as an object of faith.
sources.quote: Of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen.”
sources.raw_question: Is Christ expressly called 'God' in the New Testament?

question: Is the title 'God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob' confined to one divine Person (whether the Father alone or the Son alone) to the exclusion of the others?
synthesis: Augustine and Waterland both deny that the title belongs to one Person exclusively, though they face opposite restrictions: Augustine rejects confining it to the Son, Waterland rejects confining it to the Father. Their grounds also differ. Augustine argues theologically that each Person is God and the three are one God, so the title belongs to the whole Trinity. Waterland appeals historically to the Ante-Nicene writers, who did not limit the title to the Father.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Appearance in the Bush.
sources.answer: No. We cannot say the Son is the God of the fathers and the Father is not, nor deny it of the Holy Spirit or of the Trinity, which is the one God. Each Person is God and the three are one God, and only one who is God can be the God of the fathers.
sources.quote: For we cannot say that the Son of God is the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, and that the Father is not
sources.raw_question: Is the Son alone the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to the exclusion of the Father and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Waterland says he has shown that this position is contrary to the views of the Ante-Nicene writers, who did not confine that title to the Father.
sources.quote: That God the Father only was God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. ‘This position I have shewn to be contrary to the sentiments of the Ante-Nicene writers.
sources.raw_question: Was God the Father alone the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to the exclusion of the Son?

question: Does the Father's declaration 'This is My beloved Son' prove that Christ is the Father's true and proper Son rather than a creature or an adopted son?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary agree that the declaration establishes Christ's true Sonship, but argue differently. Athanasius rests on the duty to believe God's own testimony, so calling the one named a creature rather than a Son is madness. Hilary argues from the wording itself: the pronouns 'This' and 'My' mark personal ownership, and Scripture never says 'This is My Son' of the adopted sons it calls begotten, so the phrase marks Christ's unique, natural Sonship.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: Yes. Athanasius argues that anyone who has put faith in God must believe God's own testimony. When the Father says 'This is My beloved Son,' it would be madness to refuse him credit by claiming that the one named is not a Son but a creature. Scripture therefore gives the Arians no pretext; their doctrine is alien to the divine oracles.
sources.quote: who is there, who to the God in whom he has put faith, refuses to give credit, when He says, ‘This is My beloved Son,’ on the pretence that He is not a Son, but a creature?
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's declaration 'This is My beloved Son' rule out the claim that Christ is not truly a Son but a creature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. The pronouns 'This' and 'My' give an indubitable sense of ownership and identify the person, whereas titles can be attached at will. Scripture says of others 'I have begotten sons' but never 'This is My Son.' So the phrase marks Christ's peculiar, natural Sonship.
sources.quote: Titles may be appended to names at will; pronouns are a sure indication of the persons to whom they refer. And here we have, in This and My, the clearest of indications.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's declaration at Christ's baptism, 'This is My beloved Son,' prove that Christ is the Father's true and proper Son rather than one adopted son among many?

question: Did the Word exist before all time, or was there any interval before he existed?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary agree that the Word existed before all time, with no interval prior to him. Both argue from the Word's role as maker: Athanasius holds that he is Maker of the ages, within which every interval is measured, so to say 'there was once when he was not' is madness. Hilary holds that time itself is his creature, so his 'was' is unconditional and his existence immeasurable.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: No. The Word is King and Maker of all the ages, and every interval is measured within the ages, so no interval exists prior to Him. It is therefore madness to say 'there was once when the Everlasting was not' or that the Son is from nothing.
sources.quote: For if every interval in the ages is measured, and of all the ages the Word is King and Maker, therefore, whereas no interval at all exists prior to Him
sources.raw_question: Was there any interval of time before the Word existed?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: He existed without limit before all time. His 'was' is unconditional and unlimited. And since all things were made through him, time itself is his creature, so the Author of all things must have an immeasurable existence.
sources.quote: All things are from Him, without exception; time then itself is His creature.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word exist before the beginning, or only from the beginning of time?

question: Is the Holy Spirit eternal and divine?
synthesis: Novatian and Ambrose both affirm that the Spirit is eternal and divine, but on different grounds. Novatian argues from the Spirit's work: only one who is divine and eternal could produce immortality in us and prepare our bodies for resurrection. Ambrose argues from the title 'Finger of God': whatever belongs to God is eternal and divine, so the Spirit is too.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Next Teaches Us that the Authority of the Faith Enjoins, After the Father and the Son, to Believe Also on the Holy Spirit, Whose Operations He Enumerates from Scripture.
sources.answer: Yes. Novatian speaks of the "divine eternity of the Holy Spirit," to which our bodies are joined in the resurrection. The Spirit works in us for eternity and accustoms our bodies to share in heavenly power. Only one who is divine and eternal could produce immortality in us in this way.
sources.quote: accustoming them to be associated in Himself with heavenly power, and to be allied with the divine eternity of the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit himself eternal and divine?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter III. The same Unity may also be recognized from the fact that the Spirit is called Finger, and the Son Right Hand; for the understanding of divine things is assisted by the usage of human language. The tables of the law were written by this Finger, and they were afterwards broken, and the reason. Lastly, Christ wrote with the same Finger; yet we must not admit any inferiority in the Spirit from this bodily comparison.
sources.answer: Yes. Whatever belongs to God is eternal and divine. The Spirit, called God's Finger, is therefore eternal and divine, just as the Son, because he ever lives, is eternal life.
sources.quote: This Finger, then, of God is both eternal and divine. For what is there belonging to God which is not eternal and divine?
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit, as the Finger of God, eternal and divine?

question: Does the Father's saying "Let Us make" in Genesis 1:26 show that the Son is a true co-Creator equal with the Father, rather than a subordinate or powerless instrument?
synthesis: Ambrose and Hilary both read "Let Us make" as showing the Son to be a true co-Maker with the Father, but they draw different consequences from it. Ambrose argues that, as joint Maker of all things, the Son is to be worshipped with the Father, since the Trinity is what is worshipped. Hilary argues from the words as the expression of the Speaker's thought: they point to one in no discord with Himself, not alien or powerless, but with power to do what is spoken.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: Yes. By saying "Let Us make," the Father showed the Son to be joint Maker of all things and hence to be worshipped with Himself. Thus the Father is worshipped with the Son and the Spirit, because it is the Trinity that is worshipped.
sources.quote: the Father, by saying, “Let Us make,” showed that the Son was to be worshipped with Himself as the Maker of all things.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's saying "Let Us make" in Genesis show that the Son is to be worshipped with the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. The words express the Speaker's thought, and in saying "Let Us make" He indicates one in no discord with Himself, not alien or powerless, but endowed with power to do what is spoken of. The words themselves require this sense.
sources.quote: In saying Let Us make, He clearly indicates One in no discord with Himself, no alien or powerless Being, but One endowed with power to do the thing of which He speaks.
sources.raw_question: Does "Let Us make" in Genesis 1:26 imply that the Son is a powerless or subordinate instrument distinct in will from the Father?

question: In John 8:42 ('I proceeded forth and came from God'), does 'proceeded forth from God' refer to the Son's divine origin from God, distinct from his coming or being sent?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Novatian agree that 'proceeded forth from God' signifies the Son's divine origin from God. Hilary argues from the verse itself: because 'went forth' and 'am come' stand side by side, they must differ, so the first is the Son's incorporeal birth and the second his mission. Novatian argues by contrast with man, who was made by God and did not proceed from him, and links the verse to 'My heart hath uttered forth a good Word' to conclude that God proceeded from God.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The two are mentioned side by side and so must differ: 'went forth' refers to His incorporeal birth from God, while 'am come' and 'He sent Me' refer to His mission. Christ gives His birth, His origin from the Father, as the reason the Jews should love Him.
sources.quote: His going forth is obviously different from His coming, for the two are mentioned side by side in this passage, I went forth from God and am come.
sources.raw_question: In John 8:42, do 'I went forth from God' and 'I am come' mean the same thing?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: Yes. Man was made by God and did not proceed from him, but the Word proceeded from God, as in 'My heart hath uttered forth a good Word.' This Word made all things and is God, so God proceeded from God.
sources.quote: Therefore God proceeded from God, in that the Word which proceeded is God, who proceeded forth from God.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement 'I proceeded forth and came from God' (John 8:42) show that he is God proceeding from God?

question: What does Christ's statement 'God is Spirit' (John 4:24) teach about the Holy Spirit?
synthesis: Ambrose reads the text as 'The Spirit is God', a direct testimony to the Holy Spirit's Godhead, and points to the Arians' erasure of the passage as proof it concerns the Spirit. Hilary instead reads the words in light of their occasion: Christ was correcting the Samaritan woman's belief that God is confined to a place, so they teach God's infinity and omnipresence. For Hilary they do not abolish the Spirit's own Name or His being the Gift. The two differ on what the text refers to, but neither takes it to diminish the Spirit.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter X. The Divinity of the Holy Spirit is supported by a passage of St. John. This passage was, indeed, erased by heretics, but it is a vain attempt, since their faithlessness could thereby more easily be convicted. The order of the context is considered in order that this passage may be shown to refer to the Spirit. He is born of the Spirit who is born again of the same Spirit, of Whom Christ Himself is believed to have been born and born again. Again, the Godhead of the Spirit is inferred from two testimonies of St. John; and lastly, it is explained how the Spirit, the water, and the blood are called witnesses.
sources.answer: Yes. Ambrose reads Christ's words as 'The Spirit is God,' testifying to the Godhead of the Holy Spirit. The Arians' very act of erasing the passage from their copies shows they understood it to concern the Spirit. Had it referred only to the Father, they would have had no reason to remove it.
sources.quote: Why was the passage removed, “For God is a Spirit,” if it did not pertain to the Spirit?
sources.raw_question: Does the text 'God is a Spirit' (John 4:24) refer to the Holy Spirit and thus teach the Godhead of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The words "God is Spirit" must be read in light of their cause and purpose: Christ was correcting the Samaritan woman's belief that God was confined to a mountain or temple, teaching His infinity and omnipresence. They do not abolish the fact that the Holy Spirit has a Name of His own and is the Gift given to us.
sources.quote: The words, God is Spirit, do not alter the fact that the Holy Spirit has a Name of His own, and that He is the Gift to us.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement in John 4:24 that "God is Spirit" mean that the Holy Spirit is not a distinct Person with His own Name and gift?

question: What does it mean to worship the Father 'in spirit and in truth' (John 4:23-24), and does worship 'in the Spirit' imply that the Holy Spirit is subordinate or not God?
synthesis: Both Ambrose and Basil deny that worship 'in the Spirit' subordinates the Spirit, but they explain the phrase differently. Ambrose takes 'Spirit' to mean the grace of the Spirit, as opposed to wickedness of heart. Basil reads 'Truth' as the Son, the Image of the Father, and worship 'in the Spirit' as the mind working in the Spirit's light, which reveals the Lord's Godhead.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: No. 'Spirit' here is often put for the grace of the Spirit, as when Paul says the Spirit intercedes with groanings, meaning the Spirit's grace. God is worshipped not in wickedness of heart but in the grace of the Spirit, so the phrase implies no subjection of the Spirit.
sources.quote: Spirit is often put for the grace of the Spirit, as the Apostle also said: “For the Spirit Himself intercedeth for us with groanings which cannot be uttered;” that is, the grace of the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Does the statement in John 4:24 that God is to be worshipped 'in Spirit' imply that the Holy Spirit is not God or is subject to the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: Christ corrected the Samaritan woman's belief that worship is tied to a place. By "Truth" he plainly meant himself, the Image of the Father. Worship in the Son is worship offered in the Image of the Father. Likewise, worship "in the Spirit" means our intelligence operating in the Spirit's light, which shows forth the Godhead of the Lord.
sources.quote: worship ought to be offered “in Spirit and in Truth,” plainly meaning by the Truth, Himself.
sources.raw_question: What does Jesus mean in John 4:23-24 by worshipping the Father "in spirit and in truth"?

question: In Philippians 2:7, does Christ's taking 'the form of a servant' and being 'made in the likeness of men' mean that he took a true human nature in the incarnation?
synthesis: Hilary and Owen agree that the 'form of a servant' signifies Christ's real humanity taken in the incarnation. Hilary adds that the qualifying phrases 'likeness' and 'fashion' of a man keep that real birth from implying sin or the defects of our fallen nature. Owen instead reads 'likeness of men' as the text's own explanation of the servant form, supports this with Romans 8:3, and ties that human form to Christ's death.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: The form of a servant signifies the reality of his human birth. The added phrases, likeness of a man and fashion as a man, keep that birth from implying the defects of our weak nature. The appearance and reality of his body prove his humanity, yet he knew no sin, because he was conceived in the likeness of our nature, not in possession of our faults.
sources.quote: the form of a servant implies the reality of His birth, and found in fashion as a man, the likeness of our nature.
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean in Philippians 2:7 by saying Christ took the form of a servant and was made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. The text itself explains 'taking the form of a servant' by 'being made in the likeness of men', an expression used for the incarnation. Romans 8:3 uses the same language for his taking true flesh in the likeness of sinful flesh. It is the human fashion in which he poured out his blood and died.
sources.quote: Μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν, (he “took the form of a servant”), is expounded in the next words, ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος, — an expression used to set out his incarnation, Rom. viii. 3.
sources.raw_question: Does the 'form of a servant' in Philippians 2:7 refer to Christ's true human nature taken in the incarnation?

question: Does 'the Almighty' (ὁ παντοκράτωρ) in Revelation 1:8 refer to Christ the Son, and is it right to call him the Almighty?
synthesis: Hippolytus and Waterland agree that Revelation 1:8 rightly names the Son 'the Almighty.' Hippolytus grounds this in Christ's own testimony that all things were delivered to him by the Father, so that he rules all things as appointed Almighty by the Father. Waterland argues historically: the Ante-Nicene writers, Hippolytus among them, generally read the text of the Son, even in the Sabellian controversy.

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: Yes. Hippolytus holds that John rightly names Christ the Almighty, because Christ testifies that all things are delivered to him by the Father. Christ rules all things and has been appointed Almighty by the Father.
sources.quote: Christ rules all things, and has been appointed Almighty by the Father
sources.raw_question: Is it right to call Christ 'the Almighty,' as in Revelation 1:8?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: It refers to the Son. The Ante-Nicene writers in general, Catholics and heretics alike, understood the text of God the Son. Even in the Sabellian controversy, where the text was used against them, the Catholics accepted that it spoke of the Son and allowed that the Son is ὁ παντοκράτωρ as well as the Father. Tertullian, Hippolytus and probably Origen agree on this, and Clarke cites no ancient writer who read it otherwise.
sources.quote: the Catholics admitted that it was to be understood of God the Son; and readily allowed, in consequence of that text, that the Son was ὁ παντοκράτωρ, the
sources.raw_question: Does Revelation 1:8, which speaks of 'the Almighty' (ὁ παντοκράτωρ), refer only to the Father, or also to the Son?

question: Does Psalm 102:25-27 ('They shall perish, but Thou remainest... Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail') separate the unchanging, eternal God from changeable creatures, and so show that the Son is not a creature?
synthesis: Both authors read the psalm as contrasting the unchanging, everlasting One with created things that are brought into being and change. Athanasius applies it directly to the Son: Scripture sets the Son apart from all originate things, showing He is not originate and changes all else while remaining unchanged. Gregory of Nyssa states the principle more generally: God alone abides always the same, so whatever is not from eternity is alien from the true Godhead. His answer as given does not name the Son explicitly.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. How the Word has free will, yet without being alterable. He is unalterable because the Image of the Father, proved from texts.
sources.answer: Yes. Under the names of heaven and earth Scripture signifies that all originate things are changeable, yet it excepts the Son from them, showing He is not originate. It teaches that He changes all else while remaining unchanged Himself.
sources.quote: signifying under the name of heaven and earth, that the nature of all things originate and created is alterable and changeable, yet excepting the Son from these, shews us thereby that He is no wise a thing originate
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 102:25-27 ('They shall perish, but Thou remainest... Thou art the same') show that the Son is not a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
sources.answer: Yes. David proclaims that all creation was brought into being by God, while God alone exists always in the same manner and abides for ever. Whatever is not from eternity is therefore alien from the true Godhead.
sources.quote: all the creation was brought into being by God, while He alone exists always in the same manner, and abides for ever
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 102:27 ("Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail") show that God alone exists unchangingly while creatures are brought into being?

question: Does Christ's command 'Believe in God, believe also in Me' (John 14:1) show that the Son shares the divine nature and is to be believed in as the Father is?
synthesis: Hilary and Augustine agree that the verse shows the Son's divinity. Hilary argues from the inseparability of the two beliefs: faith in Christ is joined to faith in God and is required for perfect life, so the two natures cannot be separated either. Augustine reads the verse as commanding the same faith toward the Son as toward the Father, on the ground that they are one God.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. By uniting faith in Himself with faith in God, Christ is identified with God in honour, and so cannot be separated from His nature. If perfect life is given only to those who believe in Christ as well as God, then the two beliefs cannot be separated and neither can the two natures, which implies He is God.
sources.quote: these words, uniting faith in Him with faith in God, unite His nature to God’s.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's command 'Believe in God, believe also in Me' imply that the Son shares the divine nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: Yes. It means that in the same way as you believe in God, so also believe in me. The reason is that the Son and the Father are one God, so the same faith is owed to both.
sources.quote: in the same way as you believe in God, so also believe in me; because I and the Father are One God.
sources.raw_question: Does "Ye believe in God, believe also in me" show that the Son is to be believed in exactly as God the Father is?

question: Is a baptism that invokes only the name of the Holy Spirit a valid and complete baptism?
synthesis: Basil and Ambrose reach opposite conclusions. Basil denies that such a baptism is complete: scriptural phrases about baptism in the Spirit do not justify departing from the handed-down triple formula, and adding to or subtracting from that tradition means falling away from eternal life. Ambrose affirms it, citing 'ye shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit' and 'baptized into one Spirit', and arguing that because the mystery is one, the working of the Three cannot be separated.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the baptism in the name of the Father alone is sufficient.
sources.answer: No. Such texts do not justify calling a baptism perfect when only the Spirit's name is invoked. The tradition handed down by the life-giving grace must stay inviolate. To add anything to it or take anything from it is plainly to fall away from eternal life.
sources.quote: But no one on this account would be justified in calling that baptism a perfect baptism wherein only the name of the Spirit was invoked. For the tradition that has been given us by the quickening grace must remain for ever inviolate.
sources.raw_question: Since Scripture sometimes speaks of being baptized into or with the Holy Spirit alone, is a baptism that invokes only the Spirit's name a complete baptism?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture supports this alongside reason: the Lord said 'ye shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit,' and the Apostle says we were all baptized into one Spirit. The work is one because the mystery is one, so the working of the Three cannot be separated.
sources.quote: Scripture indicates that we can also be rightly baptized in the Spirit, when the Lord says: “But ye shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit.”
sources.raw_question: Can Christians rightly be baptized in the name of the Holy Spirit alone?

question: Was Christ raised from the dead by the Father, or did he raise himself by his own divine power?
synthesis: Hippolytus and Hilary both hold that God's raising of Christ does not exclude Christ's own agency. Hippolytus simply affirms both sides: the Father raised him, though he is himself the Resurrection and the Life. Hilary appeals to Colossians 2 to show that Christ works in himself what God works in him, so that the one who died and the one who raised the flesh are one Christ.

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: Both are affirmed. On the third day he was raised again by the Father, even though he is himself the Resurrection and the Life. The one who raises the dead was laid in the tomb as man and raised by the Father.
sources.quote: on the third day He is raised again by the Father, though Himself the Resurrection and the Life
sources.raw_question: Was Christ raised from the dead by the Father, or did he raise himself as the Resurrection and the Life?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The same Christ who died, stripping off his flesh, is the one who by divine power raised that flesh again. Colossians 2 shows Christ working in himself the very things God works in him. So God's raising of Christ does not exclude Christ's own divine agency; he who died and he who raised to life are one Christ.
sources.quote: it was the working of God which raised the dead Christ, and it was none other who raised Christ from the dead but Christ Himself, Who worked before His death, and put off His flesh to die.
sources.raw_question: If Scripture says God raised Christ from the dead, does that mean Christ was a mere man who did not raise himself?

question: Does the Son differ from the angels and heavenly powers only in degree of power, or in kind?
synthesis: Hilary and Waterland agree that the Son is not merely a higher-ranking power than the angels. Hilary argues that he is the one Only-begotten through whom all the heavenly Powers were made, so he differs in kind. Waterland argues that the degree-only reading equivocates on the word 'powers' and contradicts the Scripture texts that ascribe creation to the Son, noting that even Clarke excludes the Son only from absolute supremacy and independency.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: He differs in kind, not merely in degree. There are many mighty Powers in heaven, but only one Only-begotten Son. All of those Powers were made through him.
sources.quote: there is but one Only-begotten Son, and the difference between Him and them is not one of mere degree of might, but that they all were made through Him.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son only greater in degree of power than the angels and heavenly powers, or does he differ from them in kind?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. Such a reading is equivocation on an ambiguous word and limits the Son's powers not only without but against Scripture. The texts give the Son creative powers, and even Dr. Clarke concedes the Son is excluded from nothing but absolute supremacy and independency, which implies the texts themselves offer no ground for such a limitation.
sources.quote: I must blame him first for equivocating and playing with an ambiguous word; and next for restraining and limiting the powers of the Son of God; not only without, but against Scripture
sources.raw_question: If 'divine powers' ascribed to the Son mean only powers given by God in a higher degree than to angels, does that do justice to the Scripture texts ascribing creation to the Son?

question: To whom does Isaiah 45:14-15 ('God is in Thee, and there is no God beside Thee') refer, and what does it show about the Son's relation to the Father?
synthesis: Hilary and Hippolytus agree that the passage is spoken by the Father about one He has raised up, namely Christ. Their aims differ. Hilary uses it to prove the Son's Godhead, matching each clause to Paul's statements about Christ. Hippolytus uses it against Noetus to show two persons rather than one, reading 'God is in thee' as the Father being in the incarnate Son through the economy.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. God the Father speaks of a righteous King he has raised up, to whom men of stature come and make supplication, saying God is in Him and He is God. Hilary shows Paul echoes each clause: 'God was in Christ,' 'one Jesus Christ our Lord, through Whom are all things,' and 'Christ, Who is God over all.'
sources.quote: Let us see whether this ‘prisoner of Jesus Christ’ conforms in his teaching to the prophecies uttered by God concerning God His Son. God had said, They shall make supplication, for God is in Thee.
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah 45:14-15 ('God is in Thee, and there is no God beside Thee; for Thou art God') refer to the Son and prove his Godhead?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Read in its whole context, the passage begins with the Father speaking of one whom He has raised up, so the words are addressed to another, namely Christ. "God is in thee" refers to the mystery of the economy: when the Word became incarnate, the Father was in the Son and the Son in the Father. The text therefore shows two persons, not one.
sources.quote: “In thee, therefore,” says he, “God is.” But in whom is God except in Christ Jesus, the Father’s Word, and the mystery of the economy?
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah 45:14 ("God is in thee; and there is no God beside thee... the God of Israel, the Saviour") prove that the Father and the Son are one and the same person, as Noetus claimed?

question: Did Jesus, in calling Himself the Son of God, claim to be equal with God?
synthesis: Hilary and Warfield both answer yes, and both note that the Jews understood His claim this way. Their grounds differ. Hilary rests the equality on what Jesus says He does in reply to the charge: He does all the Father does, receives all judgment, and is to be honoured as the Father, which makes Him equal in honour, power and nature. Warfield rests it on the meaning of sonship itself: in Semitic usage a son is whatever his father is, so the title 'Son of God' alone claims equality with God, or simply deity.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. Answering the Jews' charge that He made Himself equal to God by calling Himself God's Son, He declared that He does all that the Father does, has received all judgment, and must be honoured as the Father. In this way He made Himself equal to the Father in honour, power and nature.
sources.quote: And in all these things having before declared Himself Son, He had made Himself equal to the Father in honour, power and nature.
sources.raw_question: Did Jesus, by claiming to do all the Father does, to receive all judgment, and to be honoured as the Father, make Himself equal to God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. In Semitic speech sonship rests on the natural implication that whatever the father is, the son is also. So in calling himself God's Son Jesus meant to make himself equal with God, or simply God, as the Jews rightly understood.
sources.quote: in accordance with the underlying significance of the idea of sonship in Semitic speech (founded on the natural implication that whatever the father is that the son is also
sources.raw_question: Did Jesus' calling himself the Son of God amount to a claim to be equal with God, indeed to be God?

question: Can the divine Persons, including Christ the Word, be seen with bodily eyes, and if not, how are they seen?
synthesis: Augustine and Ambrose agree that God is not seen with the eyes of the body, but they argue differently. Augustine grounds this in the invisibility of the divine substance common to Father, Word and Spirit. Ambrose speaks of Christ specifically and says he is seen by the grace of the Spirit, citing Paul and the prophets.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > In What Manner Moses Saw God.
sources.answer: No. No one sees God the Father with the eyes of the body. The same holds for the Word who was in the beginning with God and was God, and for the Spirit of wisdom. The divine substance, common to all three, is invisible.
sources.quote: Yet who sees God the Father with the eyes of the body? And that Word, which was in the beginning, the Word which was with God, the Word which was God, by which all things were made,—who sees Him with the eyes of the body?
sources.raw_question: Can the Father, the Word, or the Holy Spirit be seen with bodily eyes?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXII. In proof of the Unity in Trinity the passage of Isaiah which has been cited is considered, and it is shown that there is no difference as to its sense amongst those who expound it of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Spirit. If He Who was crucified was Lord of glory, so, too, is the Holy Spirit equal in all things to the Father and the Son, and the Arians will never be able to diminish His glory.
sources.answer: Christ is seen not by the eye of flesh but by the grace of the Spirit. Paul, after losing his eyesight, saw Christ only in the Spirit, and the prophets likewise received the Spirit and so saw Christ.
sources.quote: so Christ is seen not by the eye of flesh, but by the grace of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: How is Christ seen: by bodily sight or by the Holy Spirit?

question: Were all things, including angels and heavenly powers, created in their very being through the Word of God?
