synthesis: Irenaeus and Owen agree that the Word created all things, angels and heavenly powers included. Irenaeus argues from John's prologue and David's "He commanded, and they were created," which he reads as implying a Word who was commanded. Owen argues from Paul's naming of thrones, dominions, principalities and powers as created by the Son, and rejects the Socinian claim that the Son gave angels only their order and rank, not their being.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VIII.—Answer to an objection, arising from the words of Christ (Matt. vi. 24). God alone is to be really called God and Lord, for He is without beginning and end.
sources.answer: Yes. John teaches that the Word who was with the Father made all things and nothing was made without him. David's "He commanded, and they were created" implies one who was commanded, namely the Word by whom the heavens were established. Thus angels, archangels, thrones and dominions were all created by God through his Word.
sources.quote: Whom, therefore, did He command? The Word, no doubt, “by whom,” he says, “the heavens were established, and all their power by the breath of His mouth.”
sources.raw_question: Was the Word of God the one through whom God created all things, including angels and heavenly powers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Paul expressly names the most noble parts of creation, thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, as created by the Son, so none are excepted. The Socinian claim that he merely gave angels their order and rank, not their being, is directly contrary to the words "by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth."
sources.quote: The Socinians say, indeed, that he made angels to be thrones and principalities; that is, he gave them their order, but not their being: which is expressly contrary to the words of the text
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that all things were made by the Word (John 1:3, 10) include the angels and heavenly powers in their very being?

question: How should an interpreter read correctly what Scripture says about Christ, including statements that seem to conflict?
synthesis: Both authors give rules for reading Scripture's statements about Christ, but their rules differ. Athanasius requires the interpreter to establish the time, the person and the point of each passage, warning that missing any of these leads to heresy. Augustine instead tells the reader to refer every statement to the one person, discerning whether it is said according to the form of God or the form of a servant.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: The interpreter must establish the time the passage speaks of, the person it concerns, and the point being made. Missing any of these leads straight into heresy. Hymenaeus mistook the time of the resurrection, and the Jews mistook the person of Isaiah 7:14 and Isaiah 53:7. The Ethiopian eunuch, by contrast, rightly asked of whom the prophet spoke.
sources.quote: it is right and necessary, as in all divine Scripture, so here, faithfully to expound the time of which the Apostle wrote, and the person, and the point; lest the reader, from ignorance missing either these or any similar particular, may be wide of the true sense.
sources.raw_question: What must an interpreter attend to in order to read correctly what Scripture says about Christ?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: They are to be referred to the one person according to the different natures. What is said of Christ is said on account of either the form of God or the form of a servant. The thoughtful, diligent and pious reader discerns, with the Lord's help, which is said according to which. So the same one glorifies his own as God and yet was crucified as man.
sources.quote: Yet what is said on account of what, and what according to what, the thoughtful, diligent, and pious reader discerns for himself, the Lord being his helper.
sources.raw_question: How should a reader interpret the different and seemingly conflicting things Scripture says about Christ, some fitting his divinity and some his humanity?

question: Did the Son have the right to be worshipped before his incarnation and resurrection, or did he receive it only afterwards?
synthesis: Waterland and Athanasius agree that the Son's right to worship did not begin with his incarnation or exaltation, but they argue differently. Waterland distinguishes a right from its exercise: a right may exist before it can take effect through clear revelation, as with the Father's own right. Athanasius argues from the fact that the Son was already worshipped, by the patriarchs, the psalmists who invoked his Name, and the angels, so he did not receive what he already had.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: No. A right can exist before it is exercised, because it cannot take effect until it is clearly revealed. The Father likewise had full right to the worship of men and angels from the first, but that right could not take place until he made himself known.
sources.quote: He might have had the very same right and claim all along, that ever he had after; only it could not take effect, and be acknowledged, till it came to be clearly revealed.
sources.raw_question: If the Son was in fact worshipped distinctly only after his resurrection, does it follow that he had no right to worship before?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. He is the Giver of grace and was always worshipped by his Name. Before the incarnation the psalmists invoked his Name, the Patriarchs worshipped him, and Scripture commands all the angels of God to worship him. He did not receive what he already had.
sources.quote: how did He receive that Name for worship, who is always worshipped by His Name? Nay, certainly before He became man, the sacred writers invoke Him
sources.raw_question: Could the Son have received the right to be worshipped and the Name above every name only after his incarnation?

question: Why was it necessary for the eternal Son, the Word of God, to become incarnate in order to save fallen humanity?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Augustine agree that fallen humans could not save themselves and that the Son had to become incarnate, but they give different grounds. Irenaeus argues that man, conquered through disobedience, could neither reform himself nor attain salvation, so the Word became incarnate and died to recover in Christ the image and likeness lost in Adam. Augustine argues from congruity between remedy and disease: creatures bound to temporal things could only be cleansed and joined to the eternal through temporal events, so the co-eternal Truth took a beginning from earth.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: Because fallen man, once conquered and destroyed through disobedience and under the power of sin, could neither reform himself nor attain salvation. The Son, being the Word of God, descended from the Father, became incarnate, and stooped even to death, accomplishing both, so that what was lost in Adam, the image and likeness of God, might be recovered in Christ Jesus.
sources.quote: the Son effected both these things, being the Word of God, descending from the Father, becoming incarnate, stooping low, even to death, and consummating the arranged plan of our salvation
sources.raw_question: Why was it necessary for the Son, the Word of God, to become incarnate in order to save humanity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Son of God Became Incarnate in Order that We Being Cleansed by Faith May Be Raised to the Unchangeable Truth.
sources.answer: Because we could only be cleansed and joined to things eternal through things temporal, to which we were already bound. As healing must have some congruity with the disease, so the remedy for creatures held fast by temporal things had to come through temporal events. Hence the Truth, co-eternal with the Father, took a beginning from earth, so that our faith in things done in time might cleanse us and lead us to eternal truth.
sources.quote: But cleansed we could not be, so as to be tempered together with things eternal, except it were through things temporal, wherewith we were already tempered together and held fast.
sources.raw_question: Why was it necessary for the eternal Son of God to become incarnate in time in order to cleanse fallen humans?

question: What does Isaiah 43:10 ('before Me there is no other God, nor shall be after Me') imply about the Son: does it exclude Him from being God, or show that He is not posterior to the Father?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary of Poitiers agree that the verse does not exclude the Son's divinity, but they argue differently. Gregory reasons that since the Son is God and nothing after the Father is God, the verse positively proves the Son is in the Father, not after Him. Hilary reads the verse as denying any God before or after the Father without denying a God already born from Him, and notes that the Son, as the chosen Servant, shares in the witness and the name of God.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > The fifth book promises to speak of the words contained in the saying of the Apostle Peter, but delays their exposition. He discourses first of the creation, to the effect that, while nothing therein is deserving of worship, yet men, led astray by their ill-informed and feeble intelligence, and marvelling at its beauty, deified the several parts of the universe. And herein he excellently expounds the passage of Isaiah, “I am God, the first.”
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is God, and whatever is after the Father is not God. The verse therefore testifies that the Son is in the Father and not after the Father.
sources.quote: if the Son is God, and whatever is “after” the Father is not God, it is clear that the saying bears witness to the truth that the Son is in the Father, and not after the Father
sources.raw_question: If the Father is the speaker in Isaiah's 'no God shall be after Me', does the verse prove that the Son is not posterior to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The passage affirms that no God precedes the Father, since all things are from Him, and that none shall come after Him. It does not deny that God has already been born from Him. The chosen Servant, the Son, joins in bearing this witness, and so shares both the witness and the name of God. The text reveals the infinity of the Father's eternal, unchanging majesty rather than excluding the Son.
sources.quote: We have Their witness also that there shall be no God after Him; but They do not deny that God has been born from Him in the past.
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah 43:10 ("before Me there is no other God, nor shall be after Me") prove that the Son is not God?

question: Since Scripture calls Moses 'a god to Pharaoh' and calls others 'gods', is the title 'God' given to Christ, the Word, merely an honorary title like theirs rather than a statement of his divine nature?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Novatian both answer no, but on different grounds. Hilary argues from the wording: the title given to Moses and to others is qualified ('to Pharaoh', 'I have said'), marking it as conferred by favour, whereas John 1:1 gives the name to the Word without qualification, and 'was' signals an eternal, inherent nature. Novatian argues from scope and an a fortiori comparison: Moses held the name by measure, for a time and over one man, while Christ holds it over every creature, beyond measure and for all time, so if Moses with limited power bears the name, much more does Christ.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. In the cases of Moses and those called 'gods', the title is qualified by additions ('to Pharaoh', 'I have said') which show it was conferred by favour as a description depending on the speaker's will. In John 1:1 the name is given plainly without qualification, and 'was' indicates an eternal reality and inherent character of the Word's nature, not an accidental title.
sources.quote: In those previous instances, where Moses was called god and others were styled gods, there was the mere addition of a name by way of title. Here a solid essential truth is stated; The Word was God.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Scripture calls Moses 'a god to Pharaoh' and others 'gods' show that the title 'God' given to the Word in John 1:1 may be merely honorary rather than a statement of nature?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > It is Proved from the Scriptures that Christ Was Called an Angel. But Yet It is Shown from Other Parts of Holy Scripture that He is God Also.
sources.answer: No. Moses received the name with reserve, by measure, for a time, and in relation to one man, but Christ is ordained Lord and God over every creature, above all measure and for all time. The Father gives not the Spirit to the Son by measure, so Christ received the power of the divine name above all things. If Moses with limited power attains the name, much more does Christ, who has power over Moses himself.
sources.quote: And in the former case indeed this name is given with reserve, in the latter lavishly; in the former by measure, in the latter above all kind of measure
sources.raw_question: If Moses was called a god to Pharaoh, does the title 'God' given to Christ mean no more than the limited title given to Moses?

question: Does Paul's addressing prayer jointly to God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ show that the Son is God and receives divine worship?
synthesis: Owen and Bickersteth both answer yes. Owen argues that Paul both conjoins and distinguishes the Father and the Son in his supplications, and that divine worship given to anyone not God by nature would be idolatry, so each person is shown to be God and distinct. Bickersteth instead stresses that Paul names the two in either order without regard to rank, which shows equality. He links this direct prayer to Christ with Christians being known as those who 'call upon the name' of Jesus, the Septuagint's ordinary phrase for invoking God.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul expressly conjoins and expressly distinguishes the Father and the Son in directing his supplications. Since such divine worship may not be given without idolatry to any who is not God by nature, worship directed to each person shows each is God and distinct.
sources.quote: expressly conjoin, and yet as expressly distinguish, the Father and the Son in directing his supplications
sources.raw_question: Does addressing prayer jointly to the Father and to Jesus Christ imply that the Son shares in divine worship as a distinct person?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul directs supplication to the Father and to the Lord Jesus together, and he places them in either order without regard to rank. This is express and direct prayer to Christ. It fits the fact that Christians were known as those who 'call upon the name of Jesus Christ,' and that phrase is the Septuagint's ordinary term for invoking God.
sources.quote: Here is express and direct supplication, so that we need not marvel this was one distinctive name of Christian believers
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's prayer addressed jointly to God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ imply their equal deity?

question: When Scripture ascribes an action or worship to only one divine Person, does that exclude the other Persons from it?
synthesis: Bickersteth and Augustine agree that it does not. Augustine grounds this in the one substance working indivisibly, so that what is said of each Person is said of all, and he cites the Son and the Father both sending the Spirit. Bickersteth, speaking of texts about the Spirit, says such texts refer eminently to the Spirit but must be read in light of his essential unity with the Father and Son, so that every command to worship God includes worship of the Spirit.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Such texts refer eminently to the Spirit, but they do not warrant excluding thoughts of the Father and the Son. While establishing the personal Godhead of the Spirit, we must remember his essential unity with them. So for those who believe this, every simple command to worship God includes the worship of the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: While establishing the personal Godhead of the Spirit, we must not forget his essential unity with the Father and the Son. To those who believe this, every simple command “worship God” embraces the worship of the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: When Scripture ascribes an action or worship to the Holy Spirit, does that exclude the Father and the Son from it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. In the Trinity, what is said of each Person is also said of all, because the one and same substance works indivisibly. Christ says he will send the Spirit, and elsewhere that the Father will send him; neither statement denies the other. In the same way, glory 'prepared by my Father' is also prepared by the Son.
sources.quote: in this Trinity, what is said of each is also said of all, on account of the indivisible working of the one and same substance.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture attributes an action such as preparing glory or sending the Spirit to only the Father or only the Son, does it exclude the other Person?

question: Does confessing one numerical divine essence in Father, Son and Holy Spirit mean that they are one Person, so that the Father is himself the Son and the Spirit?
synthesis: Augustine and Waterland both answer no. Augustine argues from the relative names proper to each Person, such as Word for the Son and Gift for the Spirit: the three are one equal essence, yet the Father is not the Son or the Spirit. Waterland argues polemically that treating 'essence' and 'person' as the same is Whitby's chief fallacy, and that numerical unity of essence is not the Sabellian single Person, citing Bull's rejection of that sense.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: No. The three are one essence with none greater, better, or differing from another. Yet the Father is not the Son or the Spirit, nor does He bear the relative names proper to each, such as Word, said only of the Son, or Gift, said only of the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: Yet not that the Father Himself is both Son and Holy Spirit, or whatever else each is singly called in relation to either of the others; as Word, which is not said except of the Son
sources.raw_question: Does confessing one divine essence mean the Father is himself the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Treating 'essence' and 'person' as the same thing is the chief fallacy of Dr. Whitby's book. It wrongly charges the orthodox, and even Athanasius and Bishop Bull, with Sabellianism. Bull rejected that sense as strongly as anyone could, so numerical unity of essence is not one Person.
sources.quote: His principal and most general fallacy, is his making essence and person to signify the same. One individual or numerical essence, he everywhere interprets to a Sabellian sense ; understanding by it one indwvidual Hypostasis, or real Person.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing one individual or numerical divine essence in Father, Son and Spirit mean confessing one individual hypostasis or person, in the Sabellian sense?

question: Is the Son (the Word or Wisdom of God) changeable in his own divine nature?
synthesis: Augustine and Athanasius agree that the Son is unchangeable, but they argue differently. Augustine compares the Son with the human soul: Wisdom, which made the soul, shares its invisibility but not its changeability, as Scripture attests. He also adds that the Son is invisible in himself. Athanasius argues from the Son's being proper to the Father's unalterable essence and from his equality and oneness with the Father.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Entire Trinity Invisible.
sources.answer: No. The Word is both invisible and unchangeable. Even the human soul, a spiritual substance made through the Word, is invisible, although it is changeable. The Wisdom that made the soul is therefore invisible like the soul and, unlike the soul, also unchangeable, as Scripture says: 'Remaining in herself she maketh all things new.' To think the Son visible in himself comes from an over-carnal mind.
sources.quote: whereas this Wisdom is not only invisible, as the soul also is, but likewise unchangeable, which the soul is not.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who with an over carnal mind think the Word changeable and visible
sources.raw_question: Is the Word or Wisdom of God, the only Son, changeable and visible in his own divine nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. How the Word has free will, yet without being alterable. He is unalterable because the Image of the Father, proved from texts.
sources.answer: No. The Son is proper to the Father's essence, and since the Father's essence is unalterable, the Offspring proper to it must also be unalterable. One who is equal to God and one with the Father must be perfect and unchangeable.
sources.quote: must not He be unalterable, who is one with the Father, and His Son proper to His essence? and the Father’s essence being unalterable, unalterable must be also the proper Offspring from it.
sources.raw_question: Is the Word (Son of God) alterable, having a changeable nature and being good only by free choice?

question: Would pardon by a general willingness or bare act of God's will, apart from satisfaction of his justice, honour God's mercy and grace?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Pardoning mercy is God's free, gracious acceptance of a sinner upon satisfaction made to his justice in Christ's blood. To ascribe to God a general velleity or passion of mercy is a great dishonour to him. No discovery of mercy is consistent with God's glory except as it relates to the satisfaction of justice, as Romans 3:25 shows.
sources.quote: Pardoning mercy is God’s free, gracious acceptance of a sinner upon satisfaction made to his justice in the blood of Jesus
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hope in a general mercy
sources.raw_question: Is God's pardoning mercy a general willingness to accept sinners apart from satisfaction of his justice?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Such pardon makes no provision for God's holiness, truth and righteousness, which sin directly injures, and so despoils God of these. It also debases pardon itself, since having nothing behind it but a bare act of will, it loses its proper worth, derogating from grace and mercy as much as from righteousness.
sources.quote: that pardon itself, which they pretend so to magnify, having nothing to influence it but a mere arbitrary act of God’s will, is utterly debased from its own proper worth and excellency
sources.raw_question: Does pardon by a mere arbitrary act of God's will, without satisfaction, magnify God's grace?

question: Is God present everywhere without limit, both enclosing the universe and dwelling within it?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Novatian agree that God is present everywhere and that there is no place where He is not, and both cite the Psalmist: heaven, hell and the sea. Hilary grounds this in God's infinity, stressing that God both surrounds the world from outside and pervades it from inside. Novatian grounds it in God's unbounded magnitude, adding that since God cannot go beyond Himself, He needs no feet.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Yes. God is infinite, so He is present in all things, and all things are included in Him. He surrounds the world from outside and pervades it from inside, confined to no part of it. The Psalmist confirms this: whether one goes up to heaven, down to hell or to the ends of the sea, God is there. There is no space where God is not.
sources.quote: There is no space where God is not; space does not exist apart from Him. He is in heaven, in hell, beyond the seas; dwelling in all things and enveloping all.
sources.raw_question: Is God present everywhere, both enclosing the universe and dwelling within it?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And That, Although Scripture Often Changes the Divine Appearance into a Human Form, Yet the Measure of the Divine Majesty is Not Included Within These Lineaments of Our Bodily Nature.
sources.answer: Yes. God's magnitude is unbounded and there is no place where God is not. Scripture testifies that whether one ascends to heaven, descends to hell, or crosses the sea, God is there; and since there is nowhere God can go beyond Himself, He needs no feet.
sources.quote: when the feet it is unfolded that He fills all things, and that there is not any place where God is not.
sources.raw_question: Is God present everywhere without limit?

question: Did Christ, by the Father's appointment, really bear the punishment due to our sins and die in the place of sinners?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. By the will and appointment of the Father, Jesus Christ really underwent the punishment due to those sins. He answered God's justice for them as certainly as the sinner would by being cast into hell. Christ's own words describe this as an agreement made with the Father, so that God is glorified and the soul delivered.
sources.quote: Jesus Christ, by the will and appointment of the Father, hath really undergone the punishment that was due to those sins that lie now under his eye and consideration
sources.raw_question: Did Christ, by the Father's will and appointment, really bear the punishment due to believers' sins?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Christ bore our sins, or the punishment due to them, in his own body on the tree, because the Lord laid on him the iniquity of us all. He died for sin, to expiate it, and for sinners, in their stead. God did not spare him but delivered him up for us all.
sources.quote: That he died for sin, and sinners, to expiate the one, and in the stead of the other
sources.raw_question: Did Christ bear our sins, that is, the punishment due to them, and die in the place of sinners?

question: What did Christ's death, as a sacrifice for sin, accomplish with respect to God and sinners?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: It glorified God's righteousness, fulfilled and satisfied the law, reconciled God, made atonement and peace, and made an end of sin. God set Christ forth as a propitiation in order to declare his righteousness in the remission of sins. Because Christ was punished so that we might go free, he became the captain of salvation to all who obey him.
sources.quote: he being punished that we might go free, himself became a captain of salvation unto all that do obey him
sources.raw_question: What did Christ's death accomplish with respect to God and to sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Atonement and reconciliation with God. Sin had broken friendship between God and us and brought his wrath upon us. Christ's bloody sin-offering, which fulfils the typical sacrifices of the law, removes that enmity, so that we are reconciled to God by the death of his Son.
sources.quote: And this is the tendency of the death of Christ, as a sacrifice, atonement, and reconciliation with God.
sources.raw_question: What does the death of Christ, considered as a sacrifice for sin, accomplish between God and sinners?

question: Since the apostles and created things are also called 'light', is the Son light only in that lesser sense, differing in kind from the Father's light?
synthesis: Augustine and Gregory of Nyssa both deny that the Son is light only in the way the apostles are. Augustine contrasts the apostles, who are light by being illuminated, with the Son as the uncreated light and supreme wisdom who enlightens every man. Gregory argues against Eunomius that only the name 'light' is shared with the sun and the disciples, a case of mere homonymy that cannot be carried over to the relation between the Father and the Only-begotten Light.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. The apostles are light by being illuminated. The Son is the uncreated, spiritual light that enlightens every man, the supreme wisdom who is God.
sources.quote: yet not in such way spiritual, that it was wrought by illumination, as it was said to the apostles, “Ye are the light of the world,” but “the light which lighteth every man,” that very supreme wisdom itself who is God
sources.raw_question: Is the Son light in the same way that the apostles are called 'the light of the world'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then referring to the blasphemy of Eunomius, which had been refuted by the great Basil, where he banished the Only-begotten God to the realm of darkness, and the apology or explanation which Eunomius puts forth for his blasphemy, he shows that his present blasphemy is rendered by his apology worse than his previous one; and herein he very ably discourses of the “true” and the “unapproachable” Light.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius is playing on an equivocal term. With the sun and the disciples only the name 'light' is shared: the sun gives sight to the eyes, while the apostles' word illumines souls with truth. That case of mere homonymy cannot be carried over to the Father and the Only-begotten Light.
sources.quote: But who does not know that in these only the name is common, and the thing meant in each case is quite different?
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the apostles and created light are also called 'light' show that the light of the Father and the light of the Son differ in kind?

question: Does the Son, as the Wisdom of God, need to be taught or guided by the Father in order to act?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Basil agree that the Son, being Wisdom itself, needs no teacher. Gregory argues that ascribing obedience in words and deeds to the Son would imply a pupil who is not yet perfect, which is absurd for Wisdom. Basil argues that if the Son were taught piecemeal he would be taught forever and never reach perfection, since the Father's wisdom is infinite.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: Yes, and so the ascription is false. Only someone who has not yet perfected right action and speech obeys another in deeds and words, keeping his eye on a guide who trains him. To suppose that Wisdom itself needs a master to guide its imitation is an absurd fancy proper to Eunomius alone.
sources.quote: he alone is obedient to another in acts and words, who has not yet perfectly achieved in himself the condition of accurate working or unexceptionable speech, but keeping his eye ever on his teacher and guide
sources.raw_question: Does ascribing obedience in words and deeds to the Son imply that the Son, the Wisdom of God, needs a teacher?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. The Son is eternally perfect, wise without a teacher, and the one in whom all treasures of wisdom are hid. If he had to be taught piecemeal, it would follow that he is taught forever and never reaches perfection, because the Father's wisdom is infinite. So whoever denies that the Son has all things from the beginning must deny that he will ever be perfect.
sources.quote: you will find the Son being eternally taught, nor yet ever able to reach the end of perfection, inasmuch as the wisdom of the Father is infinite, and the end of the infinite is beyond apprehension.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son, as the Wisdom of God, need gradual instruction from the Father in order to carry out his works?

question: What does Colossians 2:9 mean in saying that the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Christ 'bodily'?
synthesis: Hilary and Bickersteth answer differently. Hilary reads 'bodily' as describing the Father speaking, being seen and working in the Son, God in God, whole of whole, through a perfect birth. Bickersteth ties 'bodily' to the incarnation: the essential Deity, which dwelt in the Word before he took flesh, is now manifested corporeally in Christ's glorified body.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It means the Father speaks in the Son who speaks, is seen in the Son who is seen, and works in the Son who works, God in God, whole of whole, one of one. The two are one without the One who is God differing from the Other, since a perfect birth engendered perfect God.
sources.quote: understand what it is to speak in one that speaks, to be seen in one who is seen, to work in one who works, to be God in God, whole of whole, one of one
sources.raw_question: What does it mean for the fulness of the Godhead to dwell 'bodily' in Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: It means the very Deity, the essential being of God, dwells in Christ, now manifested corporeally in his glorified body. Before the incarnation the Godhead dwelt in him as the Word without flesh, but not bodily as now that he is the incarnate Word.
sources.quote: “The Godhead, i.e. Deity, the essential being of God – bodily, i.e. manifested corporeally in his present glorified body.
sources.raw_question: What does Colossians 2:9 mean in saying that the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Christ bodily?

question: Do the passages on the 'seven Spirits' in Revelation show that the Holy Spirit is prayed to and receives divine worship?
synthesis: Owen and Bickersteth both answer yes. Owen argues from John's prayer for grace and peace from the seven Spirits, which he takes as an instance of prayer to the Spirit. Bickersteth argues from the heavenly worship scene: because the seven Spirits are the eyes of the Lamb and closely united with him, the Spirit shares in the homage given to the Father and the Lamb.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. John prays for grace and peace from the seven Spirits before the throne, meaning the Holy Ghost, whose operations are perfect and complete. This shows prayer to the Spirit is part of his worship, which Scripture expressly mentions often.
sources.quote: John prays for grace and peace from the seven Spirits that are before the throne, or the Holy Ghost, whose operations are perfect and complete.
sources.raw_question: Does the prayer for grace and peace from "the seven Spirits before the throne" in Revelation 1:4 refer to the Holy Spirit and show that he is prayed to?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The Seven Spirits appear in the opening benediction between the Father and the Son as a source of grace and peace, and in Rev. 5:6 they are identified with the seven eyes of the Lamb, implying closest union with him. Therefore when the Lamb, together with the Father on the throne, receives the universal homage of heaven, the sevenfold Spirit must have received it with him. The vision is symbolic but symbolizes the truth that the Father, Son and Holy Ghost receive the highest adoration on the eternal throne.
sources.quote: This implies their closest union with the Lamb; therefore, when He, together with the eternal Father, received that wondrous universal homage, the sevenfold Spirit of God must have received it with him.
sources.raw_question: Does the vision of heavenly worship in Revelation 4-5 show that the Holy Spirit (the 'Seven Spirits of God') receives divine worship together with the Father and the Lamb?

question: How does the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity differ from Sabellianism, and is it guilty of Sabellianism?
synthesis: Both Waterland and Gregory of Nyssa deny that orthodoxy is Sabellian, but they argue differently. Waterland states the difference directly: orthodoxy holds three real, subsisting Persons in one essence, while Sabellius made them mere names of one Hypostasis. Gregory turns the charge back on his opponent, arguing that Eunomius is the one akin to Sabellius, since both deny the Son and Spirit a share in the Deity and neither contemplates the Godhead in a Trinity of Persons.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: It differs in admitting three real, subsisting Persons. The Sabellians made Father, Son, and Spirit different names of one and the same Hypostasis, so the distinction was only nominal. Orthodoxy holds one essence with a real distinction of Persons.
sources.quote: I answer, in admitting three real subsisting persons.
sources.raw_question: How does the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity differ from Sabellianism?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > He then wonderfully displays the Eternal Life, which is Christ, to those who confess Him not, and applies to them the mournful lamentation of Jeremiah over Jehoiakim, as being closely allied to Montanus and Sabellius.
sources.answer: Eunomius's doctrine is the one akin to Sabellius, not the orthodox one. Both Sabellius and Eunomius, like the Jew, deny the Only-begotten and the Spirit a share in the Deity of the one they call the Great and First God. What Sabellius calls the God of three names, Eunomius calls the Unbegotten, and neither contemplates the Godhead in a Trinity of Persons.
sources.quote: For Whom Sabellius calls God of the three names, Him does Eunomius term unbegotten: but neither contemplates the Godhead in the Trinity of Persons.
sources.raw_question: Is the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity guilty of Sabellianism, or is Eunomius's doctrine actually closer to Sabellius?

question: In the blessing of 2 Corinthians 13:14, how are "the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ," "the love of God" and "the communion of the Holy Ghost" related: are they three different benefits?
synthesis: Edwards and Owen agree that the Spirit is the means by which believers enjoy the grace of Christ and the love of the Father. They differ on whether the three are distinct. Edwards holds that the apostle wishes one and the same benefit, the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit is that love and grace. Owen holds that, besides being the means of fellowship with the Father and the Son, the Spirit is also the object of a peculiar fellowship of his own.

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The apostle wishes one and the same benefit, namely the Holy Spirit. By partaking of the Spirit we possess and enjoy the love and grace of the Father and the Son, because the Spirit is that love and grace.
sources.quote: They are not different benefits but the same that the Apostle here wisheth, viz., the Holy Ghost: in partaking of the Holy Ghost, we possess and enjoy the love and grace of the Father and the Son, for the Holy Ghost is that love and grace
sources.raw_question: In the blessing of 2 Corinthians 13:14, are "the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ," "the love of God" and "the communion of the Holy Ghost" three different benefits?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: It is by the Spirit alone that we have fellowship with Christ in grace and with the Father in love. Yet believers also have a peculiar fellowship with the Spirit himself.
sources.quote: it is by the Spirit alone that we have fellowship with Christ in grace, and with the Father in love, although we have also peculiar fellowship with him
sources.raw_question: Why is the fellowship of the Holy Spirit mentioned alongside the grace of Christ and the love of the Father in 2 Corinthians 13:14?

question: How can Christ be both David's son and David's Lord (Psalm 110:1; Matthew 22:41-45)?
synthesis: Novatian and Hilary of Poitiers agree that Christ is David's (and Abraham's) son according to his human birth and David's Lord according to his divinity. Novatian frames this as two natures that must both be believed. Hilary grounds Christ's lordship specifically in his being the Son begotten of the Lord before the morning star.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And Indeed that Christ Was Not Only Man, But God Also; That Even as He Was the Son of Man, So Also He Was the Son of God.
sources.answer: These statements refer to his two natures. As man he is of Abraham and the Son of David, made under the law, and born after the world. As God he is before Abraham, David's Lord, Lord of the Sabbath, judge of the living and the dead, and before the world. Both kinds of statement must be believed together.
sources.quote: For in the manner that as man He is of Abraham, so also as God He is before Abraham himself. And in the same manner as He is as man the “Son of David,” so as God He is proclaimed David’s Lord.
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture call Christ both the son of Abraham and David and also prior to Abraham and David's Lord?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It teaches that Christ is David's son only in respect of his flesh and birth from Mary, but in respect of his Spirit he is David's Lord. David calls him Lord as the Son begotten of the Lord before the morning star. So the prophet's testimony proves Christ is Lord because he is the Son of God.
sources.quote: in respect of His Spirit, He is David’s Lord rather than his son; that the words, Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord, do not sever Christ from the mystery of the One Lord
sources.raw_question: What does Jesus' question about how David can call the Christ both his son and his Lord (Psalm 110:1) teach about Christ?

question: Does counting the divine Persons, or naming them in a numerical order, imply a difference in their nature or rank?
synthesis: Basil and Gregory of Nyssa agree that number does not change the nature of what is counted, since it only indicates quantity. Basil argues by analogy with measure and weight, concluding that 'numbering under' cannot make the Spirit inferior. Gregory says number follows the intention of the one counting, citing 'Paul and Silvanus and Timotheus' as equally human though named in order, and adds that joining the names shows the three acting together toward one end.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who say that the Holy Ghost is not to be numbered with, but numbered under, the Father and the Son. Wherein moreover there is a summary notice of the faith concerning right sub-numeration.
sources.answer: No. Things that are numbered remain what they naturally were. Number is only a sign we have invented to indicate a plurality of subjects, just as measure and weight are conveniences for knowing quantity. We do not 'weigh under' gold relative to tin or 'measure under' things measured. So neither can 'numbering under' establish that the Spirit is inferior.
sources.quote: Is it not the fact that things when numbered remain what they naturally and originally were, while number is adopted among us as a sign indicative of the plurality of subjects?
sources.raw_question: Does counting things, such as the divine Persons, change their nature or rank?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Examination of the meaning of 'subjection:' in that he says that the nature of the Holy Spirit is subject to that of the Father and the Son. It is shewn that the Holy Spirit is of an equal, not inferior, rank to the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. Mere numerical rank does not create a different nature; what is counted remains the same in nature whether counted or not. Number marks only quantity and follows the intention of the one counting, as 'Paul and Silvanus and Timotheus' are all equally human though named in order; the conjunction of names rather shows the harmonious action of the three toward one end.
sources.quote: Mere numerical rank does not create a different nature: that which we would count in a number remains the same in nature whether we count it or not.
sources.raw_question: Does numerical order or sequence among the divine Persons indicate a difference in their nature?

question: Does saying that things are made 'in' the Holy Spirit reduce the Spirit to a mere condition like place or time, distinct in kind from the Father and Son?
synthesis: Basil and Ambrose both deny that 'in' the Spirit reduces Him to place or time. Basil's ground is critical: he traces the usage to a pagan scheme in which 'in which' names only a necessary condition contributing nothing to what is produced, and says applying it to the Spirit slights Him. Ambrose's ground is positive: he argues that all things are in the Spirit in such a way that they are also through and from Him, since we are formed, strengthened and given eternal life by Him.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > The systematic discussion of syllables is derived from heathen philosophy.
sources.answer: No. In the pagan scheme 'in which' marks time and place, which contribute nothing to what is produced and are only necessary conditions. Transferring this to the Spirit reduces Him to such a mere condition. Basil holds that this sets at naught the Divine Spirit.
sources.quote: And though place and time contribute nothing to what is being produced, yet without these the production of anything is impossible, for efficient agents must have both place and time.
sources.raw_question: Does saying that things are 'in' the Holy Spirit mean the Spirit contributes nothing more to creation than place or time do?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IX. A passage of St. Paul abused by heretics, to prove a distinction between the Divine Persons, is explained, and it is proved that the whole passage can be rightly said of each Person, though it refers specially to the Son. It is then proved that each member of the passage is applicable to each Person, and as to say, of Him are all things is applicable to the Father, so may all things are through Him and in Him also be said of Him.
sources.answer: No. Opponents treat 'in Him' as indicating place or time to separate the Spirit's nature, but all things are in the Spirit in such a way that they are also through and from the Spirit. We are formed, strengthened and established by the Spirit and receive eternal life from Him.
sources.quote: all things are in the Spirit, so that we may teach that all things are through the Spirit, and all things from the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does saying all things are made 'in' the Holy Spirit make the Spirit a mere place or time, of a different kind from the Father and Son?

question: Does Christ's resurrection prove that he is God and not a mere man?
synthesis: Athanasius and Hilary both answer yes. Athanasius argues that the one who gives life to others could not be held by death, as any mere man would be, so the signs show that the one in the body was God, the Lord of death. Hilary argues that only a divine nature could rise by its own might, and points to Thomas's confession of Christ as God as resting on this evidence.

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: Yes. It befitted the Christ, who gives life to others, not himself to be held by death, which could not happen if he were a mere man, since all men are subject to death. The signs that took place show that He who was in a body was God, the Life and Lord of death.
sources.quote: For it became the Christ, when giving life to others, Himself not to be detained by death; but this could not have happened, had He, as you suppose, been a mere man. But in truth He is the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's resurrection and giving of life prove that he is God and not a mere man?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. Only a divine nature could rise from death to life by its own might. Thomas therefore confessed Christ as God on certain evidence, and those who believe on the assurance of the Resurrection are called blessed.
sources.quote: No nature but that of God could have risen by its own might from death to life; and it is this fact, that Christ is God, which was confessed by Thomas with the confidence of an assured faith.
sources.raw_question: Does the Resurrection prove the divinity of Christ?

question: How does the scriptural case for Christ's deity hold together: is each individual testimony sufficient on its own, or does the proof rest on the cumulative weight of many texts, so that losing any one text does not overturn it?
synthesis: Bickersteth and Owen agree that the case does not hang on any single text, but they argue it differently. Bickersteth stresses cumulative, mutually corroborating lines of evidence, so the reader may set aside any text he thinks inapplicable without weakening the whole. Owen claims that every cited text is by itself a sufficient ground for faith, and that further testimonies only add strength.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. The evidence is cumulative, not a chain whose strength is that of its weakest link. It rests on hundreds of texts and several distinct, independent lines of argument (attributes, salvation, Old Testament appearances, worship, conjunction with the Father, fulfilled prophecies, divine names). These lines corroborate one another, so the reader may dismiss any text he thinks inapplicable without weakening the conclusion.
sources.quote: It is not a long elaborate catena, the strength of which is the strength of its weakest link. If the reader thinks any text is inapplicable, let him dismiss it. This proof rests on hundreds of texts.
sources.raw_question: Does the scriptural case for the deity of Jesus Christ depend on a single chain of texts, so that if one text proves inapplicable the whole argument fails?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Each one is sufficient. Owen declares himself ready to maintain against all the Socinians that every one of the cited texts gives a sufficient ground for faith in the Deity of Christ. The many other testimonies that could be added only strengthen what each already proves.
sources.quote: there is not any one of them which does not give a sufficient ground for faith to rest on in this matter concerning the Deity of Christ, and that against all the Socinians in the world
sources.raw_question: Is any single scriptural testimony to Christ's deity enough on its own to ground faith, or is only the combined case sufficient?

question: What does Christ's statement 'All things are delivered unto me of my Father' (Matthew 11:27) signify about the Father and the Son?
synthesis: Both authors read the verse as the Father committing everything to the Son, but they draw different conclusions from it. Owen takes it soteriologically: the Father has given Christ the fulness of grace and the power to give life, and this grounds his invitation to the weary to come for rest. Irenaeus takes it against the heretics: the Father who delivers all things is the Creator handing over his own possessions, and because nothing was held back the Son is Judge of all and alone could open the Father's book.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: It signifies that the Father has committed to Christ the fulness of grace and the power and right to give life. Christ makes this delivery the ground of his invitation, 'Come unto me... and I will give you rest.' He can offer refreshment because he has received all from the Father.
sources.quote: Hence this delivering of all things unto him by his Father, he lays as the bottom of his inviting sinners unto him for refreshment
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's statement 'All things are delivered unto me of my Father' (Matthew 11:27) signify in relation to his invitation to the weary?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: It shows that the Father who delivered all things to the Son is the Creator of all things. He delivered not the things of another but his own. Since nothing was held back from the Son, the Son is Judge of the living and the dead, and alone was able to open the book of the Father.
sources.quote: manifestly by Him who made all things; for He did not deliver to Him the things of another, but His own. But in all things [it is implied that] nothing has been kept back [from Him], and for this reason the same person is the Judge of the living and the dead
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's saying "All things are delivered to Me by My Father" show about the Father and the Son?

question: Does Scripture ascribe personal properties such as mind, will and understanding to the Holy Spirit?
synthesis: Owen and Bickersteth both answer yes and argue from the Spirit's actions to his personhood. Owen cites specific texts showing will (1 Cor 12:11) and understanding (1 Cor 2:10) and argues that personal actions imply a personal agent. Bickersteth first defines personality as having mind, affection and will, then lists a broader range of attributes (love, foreknowledge, power) and works such as creating, regenerating, commanding and appointing ministers.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. He has a will, since 'he divideth to every man severally as he will.' He has understanding, since he 'searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God.' All the actions ascribed to him imply personal properties in the one who acts.
sources.quote: He has personal properties assigned unto him; as a will, 1 Cor. xii. 11, “He divideth to every man severally as he will;” and understanding, 1 Cor. ii. 10
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ascribe personal properties such as will and understanding to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Personality is shown by whatever has mind, affection and will and can act, speak and direct. Scripture ascribes to the Spirit a mind, infinite comprehension, foreknowledge, power, love and a self-determining will. He also creates, strives with men, convinces of sin, regenerates, commands and forbids, and appoints ministers, so he must possess personality.
sources.quote: that sentient, loving, determining agent, speaker, and ruler, must possess personality, or personality cannot exist.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ascribe to the Holy Spirit the properties that constitute personhood, such as mind, love, and will?

question: How does the incarnate Son restore humanity's relation to God the Father and make human beings acceptable to Him?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Gregory of Nyssa agree that the incarnate Son reconciles humanity to the Father by sharing human nature, but they stress different mechanisms. Irenaeus speaks of mutual assimilation: the Son becomes like man, so that man, resembling the Son, becomes precious to the Father. Gregory instead stresses the Son's sinless bearing of sin and the curse, slaying the enmity in Himself, and joining the new man to the Father as first-fruits that hallow all who share His nature.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVI.—Since our bodies return to the earth, it follows that they have their substance from it; also, by the advent of the Word, the image of God in us appeared in a clearer light.
sources.answer: By assimilating Himself to man and man to Himself. Through man's resemblance to the Son, man becomes precious to the Father. The visible Word assimilates man to the invisible Father.
sources.quote: assimilating Himself to man, and man to Himself, so that by means of his resemblance to the Son, man might become precious to the Father
sources.raw_question: How does the incarnate Son make human beings acceptable to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > This twelfth book gives a notable interpretation of the words of the Lord to Mary, “Touch Me not, for I am not yet ascended to My Father.”
sources.answer: Fallen humanity could not return to God by itself, so the Son, who knew no sin, was made sin for us, took our curse, slew the enmity in Himself, and became what we were. Having joined in purity the new man, in whom the fulness of the Godhead dwelt bodily, to the Father, He draws all who share His nature into the same grace, as first-fruits hallow the lump.
sources.quote: having become what we were, He through Himself again united humanity to God.
sources.raw_question: How does the incarnate Son restore humanity's relation to God as Father?

question: What does 'God is love' (1 John 4:8) mean?
synthesis: Both authors deny that the phrase means something thin, but they stress different things. Augustine argues from Scripture's usage that it predicates God's very being, as 'God is a Spirit' does, and is not a gift-expression like 'Thou art my patience.' John Owen says it means more than that God has a loving nature: God actively dispenses eternal love toward us and will fulfil purposes of love he has held from of old.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It means more than that God has a loving and tender nature. It means God will exercise himself in a dispensation of eternal love toward us. He has purposes of love for us from of old and will fulfil them all in due season.
sources.quote: not only of a loving and tender nature, but one that will exercise himself in a dispensation of his love, eternal love, towards us, — one that hath purposes of love for us from of old
sources.raw_question: What does 'God is love' (1 John 4:8) mean?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Holy Spirit is Called Love, and Whether He Alone is So Called. That the Holy Spirit is in the Scriptures Properly Called by the Name of Love.
sources.answer: No. Scripture's own usage refutes this reading. Gift-expressions take the form 'Thou art my patience', 'my hope', 'my mercy', but Scripture never says 'Thou art my love.' It says 'God is love' in the same way it says 'God is a Spirit,' which predicates God's very being.
sources.quote: And it is not said, O Lord my love, or, Thou art my love, or, God my love; but it is said thus, “God is love,” as it is said, “God is a Spirit.”
sources.raw_question: Does 'God is love' in 1 John mean only that love is a gift God gives us, as in 'Thou art my patience'?

question: Does the name Jehovah signify necessary, independent and eternal existence, so that it cannot belong to any created being and whoever bears it is the eternal God?
synthesis: Waterland and Bickersteth agree that Jehovah signifies necessary and independent existence and so marks whoever bears it as the eternal God. Waterland argues the point polemically: the Arian reading of the name as 'a person of honour and integrity' would remove this proof of Godhead even for the Father. Bickersteth argues from Scripture, which never applies the incommunicable name to a creature, and from reason, adding that the name covers past, present and future eternity and marks God as the source of all life.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds that if Jehovah signifies necessary existence and independence, it is an irrefragable proof of eternal Godhead. He uses this against the Arian, whose reduction of the name to 'a person of honour and integrity' removes this proof even for the Father.
sources.quote: It is true, he has called himself Jehovah ; which if it signified necessary existence and independence, it would be an irrefragable proof of his being the eernal God.
sources.raw_question: Does the name Jehovah signify necessary existence and independence, and so prove that whoever bears it is the eternal God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Jehovah is God's peculiar and incommunicable name and is never applied to any creature in Scripture. Reason forbids it as well, because the name imports necessary, independent and eternal existence. It covers past, present and future eternity, which is why the apostle renders it "He that is, that was, and that is to come." It marks God as the source and continual maintenance of all life. Since Christ is later shown to bear this name, the point bears directly on his deity.
sources.quote: It neither is applied to any created being throughout the Scriptures, nor can be applied in reason, for it imports the necessary, independent, and eternal existence of the Most High.
sources.raw_question: Can the name Jehovah be given to any created being, and what does the name signify?

question: Is Jesus Christ truly God, possessing the divine nature?
synthesis: Owen and Novatian both affirm that Christ is truly God, but on different grounds. Owen appeals to scriptural titles and testimony: Christ is 'Jehovah our Righteousness,' 'thy God,' the fellow of the Lord of hosts, and 'God blessed for evermore.' Novatian argues from a divine attribute: being present in every place belongs to God's nature, not man's, and Christ is present wherever he is invoked.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that Christ is excellent above all in his Deity: he is "Jehovah our Righteousness" (Jer. 23:6), the one Zion is told to behold as "thy God" (Isa. 40:9), and the one whose glory John saw as that of the only-begotten Son of God. He is called the fellow of the Lord of hosts and is "God blessed for evermore."
sources.quote: He is exceeding excellent and desirable in his Deity, and the glory thereof. He is “Jehovah our Righteousness,” Jer. xxiii. 6.
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus Christ truly God, possessing the divine nature and its glory?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > The Author Prosecutes the Same Argument.
sources.answer: Yes. Being present in every place belongs to the nature of God, not of man. Christ is present wherever he is invoked, so he is God.
sources.quote: If Christ is only man, how is He present wherever He is called upon; when it is not the nature of man, but of God, that it can be present in every place?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's presence wherever he is called upon show that he has the divine nature?

question: Do New Testament applications of Old Testament texts about Jehovah to Christ show that Christ is Jehovah?
synthesis: Bickersteth and Waterland agree that the New Testament's application of Jehovah texts to Christ proves he is Jehovah. Bickersteth rests the argument on God's refusal to give his glory to another, together with the Spirit inspiring both the text and its interpretation. Waterland instead lists specific Old Testament texts paired with their New Testament applications and insists these are not mere accommodations.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: It is the most irrefragable proof that Christ is the eternal Jehovah. God jealously refuses to give his glory to another and condemns giving the creature the worship due to the Creator. When Scripture, with the Holy Ghost interpreting his own words, transfers Jehovah's glory to Christ, Christ must be the Eternal, uncreated Jehovah of hosts. An inspired interpretation of an inspired text gives double certainty.
sources.quote: the above comparison of Scripture with Scripture, wherein the Holy Ghost interprets, explains, and applies his own language, presents the most irrefragable proof that Jesus Christ is the Eternal, Increate, Alone, Jehovah of hosts, the Highest, the Lord our God.
sources.raw_question: Given that God says he will not give his glory to another, what follows from the New Testament applying Old Testament texts about Jehovah to Christ?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: Yes. Texts addressed to or spoken by Jehovah (Ps. 102:25, Zech. 11:13, Zech. 12:10, Isa. 40:3, Hos. 1:7) are applied to Christ (Heb. 1:10, Matt. 27:9, John 19:37, Matt. 3:3, Luke 2:11). These are not mere accommodations, so Christ is called Jehovah. He is likewise the 'Lord God of the prophets' by comparing Rev. 22:6 with 22:16.
sources.quote: I refer to this author, to obviate the pretence, that these texts might be understood only by way of accommodation.
sources.raw_question: Do New Testament applications of Old Testament Jehovah texts to Christ show that Christ is Jehovah?

question: Does the demons' confession of Jesus as Son of God testify to His true divine Sonship?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Hilary both answer yes. Irenaeus argues that testimony drawn even from adversaries, such as the demons and the devil, cannot be gainsaid. Hilary stresses that the confession was wrung from the demons against their will, that their forced obedience shows divine power, and that they never call Christ a creature or adopted son.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VI.—Explanation of the words of Christ, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” etc.; which words the heretics misinterpret. Proof that, by the Father revealing the Son, and by the Son being revealed, the Father was never unknown.
sources.answer: Yes. The demons cried "We know Thee who Thou art, the Holy One of God," and the devil said "If Thou art the Son of God."
