Irenaeus argues that evidence drawing testimony even from adversaries is true and cannot be gainsaid. The Son and the Father are thus attested even by enemies who do not believe.
sources.quote: For that evidence is true, and cannot be gainsaid, which elicits even from its adversaries striking[^3864] testimonies in its behalf
sources.raw_question: Does the testimony of demons and the devil confirm that Christ is the Son of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. The demons' confession was wrung from them by truth against their will, and their forced obedience when expelled witnesses to the power of the Divine nature within Him. Nowhere in their cries do they call Christ a creature or speak of God adopting Him; they display Him as Son of God both in power and in name.
sources.quote: Truth wrung this confession from them against their will; their reluctant obedience is a witness to the force of the Divine nature within Him.
sources.raw_question: Does the demons' confession of Jesus as 'Son of God most High' testify to His true divine Sonship rather than to a created or adoptive status?

question: Is the grace and life-giving power of baptism derived from the water or from the Holy Spirit?
synthesis: Ambrose and Basil agree that the grace of baptism comes from the Spirit, not from the water. Ambrose says any grace in the water comes from the Spirit's presence, and the Spirit seals us as the earnest of our inheritance. Basil says the water only fulfils the image of death, while the Spirit gives the earnest of life and the regenerating power.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VI. Although we are baptized with water and the Spirit, the latter is much superior to the former, and is not therefore to be separated from the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: From the Holy Spirit. If there is any grace in the water, it is not from the nature of water but from the Spirit's presence; we live and are sealed in the Spirit, who is the earnest of our inheritance.
sources.quote: If, then, there be any grace in the water, it is not from the nature of water, but from the presence of the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Is baptismal grace derived from the nature of the water or from the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Reply to the suggested objection that we are baptized “into water.” Also concerning baptism.
sources.answer: The Spirit gives life. The water only fulfils the image of death, whereas the Spirit gives the earnest of life and works our new life in us. Thus the life-giving, regenerating power in baptism belongs to the Spirit, not to the element.
sources.quote: the water fulfils the image of death, and the Spirit gives us the earnest of life.
sources.raw_question: What does the Holy Spirit contribute in baptism that the water does not?

question: Does God perceive through separate faculties, such as distinct senses or a sense distinct from understanding, as humans and animals do?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine both deny that God's perception is divided into separate faculties. Gregory argues that God is not split into apprehensive faculties each with its own object, but is at once sight, hearing and knowledge, and that lower animal perceptions may not be ascribed to Him. Augustine grounds the denial in God being a spirit without a body, so that His single nature perceives as it understands and His sense and understanding are one and the same.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. God is not divided into apprehensive faculties the way creatures are, where each sense perceives only its own object. All in all, He is at once sight, hearing and knowledge. It is not permitted to ascribe the lower, animal perceptions to His refined nature.
sources.quote: But with God it is otherwise. All in all, He is at once sight, and hearing, and knowledge; and there we stop, for it is not permitted us to ascribe the more animal perceptions to that refined nature.
sources.raw_question: Does God perceive through separate sense faculties such as sight and hearing, as humans do?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Difficult It is to Demonstrate the Trinity by Natural Reason.
sources.answer: No. God is a spirit and does not consist of soul and body, so he does not perceive through a body. His single nature perceives as it understands and understands as it perceives, so his sense and understanding are one and the same.
sources.quote: And hence that single nature perceives as it understands, and understands as it perceives, and its sense and understanding are one and the same.
sources.raw_question: Are God's sense-perception and understanding two different faculties, as they are in animals and humans?

question: Does Christ's forgiving of sins prove that he is God?
synthesis: Novatian and Irenaeus agree that since only God forgives sins and Christ does so, he is God. Novatian adds his knowledge of the heart's secrets and his coming down from heaven as further proofs. Irenaeus instead frames it in terms of the Word made Son of man, who receives the power of remission from the Father and is both man and God, suffering as man and forgiving as God.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Truth is Proved from the Sacred Writings of the New Covenant.
sources.answer: Yes. Knowing the secrets of the heart and remitting sins belong to God alone. Since Christ does both, he must be God. His coming down from heaven, which no mere man can do, points the same way.
sources.quote: whereas it is the property of none but God to know the secrets of the heart, Christ beholds the secrets of the heart; and if, whereas it belongs to none but God to remit sins, the same Christ remits sins
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's knowing the secrets of the heart and forgiving sins prove that he is God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVII.—There is but one Lord and one God, the Father and Creator of all things, who has loved us in Christ, given us commandments, and remitted our sins; whose Son and Word Christ proved Himself to be, when He forgave our sins.
sources.answer: Yes. No one can forgive sins but God alone, yet the Lord remitted sins and healed men. So he was himself the Word of God made the Son of man, receiving the power of remission from the Father. He was both man and God, so that as man he suffered for us and as God he might have compassion and forgive our debts.
sources.quote: For if no one can forgive sins but God alone, while the Lord remitted them and healed men, it is plain that He was Himself the Word of God made the Son of man, receiving from the Father the power of remission of sins
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's forgiving of sins prove that he is God, the Word made Son of man?

question: How does John 17:23, 'I in them, and Thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one,' show that believers are united to God through Christ as Mediator?
synthesis: Augustine and Athanasius agree that the verse presents Christ as the one through whom believers are united to God. Augustine reads it as showing Christ standing between God and men as the Mediator who reconciles us. Athanasius grounds it in the incarnation: the Word dwells in us by putting on our body, so we become one body with one Lord dwelling in us. He adds that this unity is mediated and not equal to the Son's natural unity with the Father.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Same Argument Continued.
sources.answer: Yes. By placing Himself in believers and the Father in Himself, Christ shows that He stands between God and men. He is the one through whom we are reconciled to God and brought into unity with Him.
sources.quote: He goes on thus to intimate the truth itself, that He is the Mediator, through whom we are reconciled to God, by saying, “I in them, and Thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one.”
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'I in them, and Thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one' teach that Christ is the Mediator reconciling us to God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Believers are united through the Word's incarnation. The Word is in us because He put on our body, and the Father is in Him because He is the Father's Word. By partaking of the same body we become one body and one spirit with one Lord dwelling in us. Our unity with God is mediated through the incarnate Son, not equal to the Son's natural unity with the Father.
sources.quote: For we all, partaking of the Same, become one body, having the one Lord in ourselves.
sources.raw_question: How does 'I in them and Thou in Me, that they may be made perfect in one' (John 17:23) explain the way believers are united to God?

question: In John 5:43, who is the 'other' who will come in his own name and be received, in contrast to Christ who came in his Father's name?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Hilary both identify the 'other' as the Antichrist. Irenaeus says he is called 'other' because he is alienated from the Lord, and that he will be received by those who rejected Christ. Hilary instead stresses that he will falsely claim the Father's name and will trade glory with men while they neglect the glory of the only God.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXV.—The fraud, pride, and tyrannical kingdom of Antichrist, as described by Daniel and Paul.
sources.answer: The "other" is the Antichrist. Christ calls him "the other" because he is alienated from the Lord. He comes in his own name rather than the Father's, and he will be received by those who rejected Christ.
sources.quote: calling Antichrist “the other,” because he is alienated from the Lord.
sources.raw_question: In John 5:43, who is the "other" who will come in his own name and be received, in contrast to Christ who came in his Father's name?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: The Antichrist. He will falsely claim to come in the Father's name, and men will give him glory and receive glory from him in return, while neglecting the glory of the only God.
sources.quote: By this, doubtless, is signified the Antichrist, glorying in his false use of the Father’s name.
sources.raw_question: Who is the 'other' who will come in his own name and be received, according to John 5:43?

question: When Scripture names a subject in the third person where 'his own' would be expected, does that phrasing force us to understand a different person?
synthesis: Augustine and Athanasius agree that this scriptural idiom does not imply a second subject, but they use it on different texts and for different ends. Augustine cites the Psalms and Romans 1:3-4 to show that 'in the image of God' in Genesis means the one Trinity, not another person. Athanasius cites Moses speaking of 'Moses' to show that Peter's 'the Word sent through Jesus Christ' does not make the Word and Christ two, since they are one by the union in the incarnation.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Why This Opinion is to Be Rejected.
sources.answer: No. Scripture often speaks this way of one and the same subject. Examples are the Psalms ("Salvation belongeth unto the Lord; Thy blessing...") and Romans 1:3-4, where "Son of God... of Jesus Christ" refers to the same person. So "in the image of God" means the one Trinity, who is one God, and not another person.
sources.quote: we are not compelled to understand any other person in the Trinity, but the one and selfsame Trinity itself, who is one God, and after whose image man is made.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's habit of naming a subject in the third person where "his own" would be expected force us to understand a different person, as in "God created man in the image of God"?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: Yes. Moses speaks of 'as the Lord commanded Moses' though he is the one Moses, and in Numbers Moses speaks to his own father-in-law; Scripture uses simple, inartificial phrases. So Peter's words do not mean the Word is one and Christ another, but that they are one by the union in the incarnation.
sources.quote: it is not necessary to understand that the Word is one and Christ another, but that they were one and the same by reason of the uniting which took place in His divine and loving condescension and becoming man.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's habit of speaking of a person as if of another (e.g. Moses speaking of 'Moses') show that phrasing like 'the Word sent through Jesus Christ' need not imply two subjects?

question: Is the Son truly omniscient, or can He be ignorant of anything, for instance by having only a limited knowledge of things relating to creation and its government?
synthesis: Waterland and Hilary agree that the Son is not ignorant of anything, but they argue differently. Waterland attacks the notion of a merely 'relative omniscience' as incoherent: such knowledge would be no omniscience at all, and the distinction has no ground in Scripture or antiquity. Hilary argues from creation: since all things have their origin and present and future state from Christ, they cannot lie beyond His knowledge, and His nature cannot be ignorant even of what does not come about through Him.

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: No. A 'relative omniscience' that knows infinitely less than true omniscience is really no omniscience at all; by that standard an angel or a man would be omniscient because he knows all he knows. It would be more honest to say plainly the Son is not omniscient, and there is no ground in Scripture or antiquity for the distinction between absolute and relative omniscience.
sources.quote: Were it not better to say plainly, that he is not omniscient, than to speak of a relative omniscience, which is really no omniscience ; unless an angel be omniscient, or a man omniscient, because he knows all things which he knows?
sources.raw_question: Can the Son coherently be said to possess a merely 'relative omniscience' communicated from the Father, knowing only things relating to creation and government, while being ignorant of other things?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. What derives its origin and the efficient cause of its present and future state from Christ alone cannot lie beyond the knowledge of the nature through which it is effected and in which it is contained. His nature, which cannot be nescient, even apprehends what is not through Him, so much more what is.
sources.quote: If all things are through and in Christ, and in such a way through Christ that they are also in Him, must not that, which is both in Him and through Him, be also in His knowledge
sources.raw_question: Can the Son, through whom and in whom all things are created, be ignorant of anything that comes to pass through Him?

question: Is God self-sufficient, so that He does not need His creatures (even as objects of His love) or depend on anything outside Himself?
synthesis: Hilary and Owen both deny that God needs His creatures, but on different grounds. Hilary argues from God as Source, Maker and Container of all, who received His being from no one and so owes no recompense. Owen argues from the Father's all-sufficiency and His eternal delight in the Son, which makes His love for the saints wholly free.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. As Source, Maker and Container of all, beyond all, He does not need what is within Him, the Creator His creatures, the Possessor His possessions. No prior giver can claim recompense from Him, since He received His being from no one.
sources.quote: The Source and Maker of all, Who contains all, Who is beyond all, does not need that which is within Him, the Creator His creatures, the Possessor His possessions.
sources.raw_question: Does God need His creatures or depend on anything outside Himself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. The Father is all-sufficient and fully satisfied in his own perfections. From eternity he had his Son, his eternal Wisdom, to delight in, and that could have satisfied his whole delight. His love for the saints is therefore wholly free, and in it he seeks their good as well as his own satisfaction.
sources.quote: He had his Son, also, his eternal Wisdom, to rejoice and delight himself in from all eternity, Prov. viii. 30. This might take up and satiate the whole delight of the Father; but he will love his saints also.
sources.raw_question: Did God need to love creatures in order to have an object for his love, given that he is all-sufficient?

question: When Christ speaks of the Son of man being in heaven or ascending to where he was before, was it his flesh or humanity that pre-existed in heaven and came down?
synthesis: Hippolytus and Novatian agree that it was not the flesh or the man but the Word of God who was in heaven and came down. Hippolytus adds that the Word was called 'Son of man' beforehand because of what he would become, citing Daniel's vision. Novatian stresses that as man Christ ascended to where he had not been before, so that it was God who came down from heaven.

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Before the incarnation there was no flesh in heaven. The one in heaven was the Word unincarnate, who was Word, Spirit and Power. He was sent to show that He was on earth and also in heaven. He was called "Son of man" from the beginning on account of what He was to become, as Daniel's vision shows.
sources.quote: Who, then, was in heaven but the Word unincarnate, who was despatched to show that He was upon earth and was also in heaven? For He was Word, He was Spirit, He was Power.
sources.raw_question: Does John 3:13 ("the Son of man which is in heaven") mean that Christ's flesh existed in heaven before the incarnation?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > The Author Prosecutes the Same Argument.
sources.answer: It was the Word of God, not the man. As man Christ was not in heaven before and ascended to where he had not been. It was the Word of God, by whom all things were made, who was there and descended. So God came down from heaven.
sources.quote: It was not therefore man that thus came thence from heaven, but the Word of God; that is, God descended thence.
sources.raw_question: When Christ speaks of the Son of man ascending to where he was before, what was it that pre-existed in heaven and came down?

question: Is the God who raises the dead the same God who creates man and gives him life, or a different power?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Augustine agree that the God who raises the dead is the same God who creates and gives life, but their grounds differ. Irenaeus, arguing against a God above the Creator, appeals to Isaiah and Ezekiel, where the Creator himself promises resurrection and immortality. Augustine argues that the one who restores souls to the dead is the one who gives life in the womb, so resurrection is the same life-giving work shown in an unusual way.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XV.—Proofs of the resurrection from Isaiah and Ezekiel; the same God who created us will also raise us up.
sources.answer: The same God. In Isaiah and Ezekiel the Creator is shown vivifying dead bodies, promising resurrection from the tombs and conferring immortality. He is therefore the only God who does these things and is himself the good Father, giving life to those who do not have it from themselves.
sources.quote: He is shown to be the only God who accomplishes these things, and as Himself the good Father, benevolently conferring life upon those who have not life from themselves.
sources.raw_question: Is the God who raises the dead and gives them immortality the same God who created man, or a different God above the Creator?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > Diversity Alone Makes a Miracle.
sources.answer: Yes. The one who restored their own souls to the dead when they rose is the same one who gives life to the flesh in the mother's womb, so that mortals come into being. Resurrection is no work of a different power. It is the same divine life-giving operation shown in an unusual way.
sources.quote: And who is it that restored to the corpses their proper souls when the dead rose again, unless He who gives life to the flesh in the mother’s womb
sources.raw_question: Is the God who raises the dead the same agent who gives life in ordinary birth?

question: What does the Seraphim's threefold 'Holy, Holy, Holy' in Isaiah 6:3 teach about the Trinity?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Ambrose of Milan agree that the Seraphim's threefold 'Holy' proclaims the Trinity. Gregory reads it as the Seraphim's awe at the beauty in each Person. Ambrose argues from the form of the cry itself: the word is said three times, not once, against a single Person, and not twice, which would leave out the Spirit. Because the same singular word is repeated rather than pluralized, the cry also shows the oneness of the Godhead.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > These doctrines of our Faith witnessed to and confirmed by Scripture passages.
sources.answer: Yes. Through the Seraphim the mystery of the Trinity was clearly proclaimed. Their threefold cry of 'Holy' expressed their awe at the beauty in each Person of the Trinity.
sources.quote: Isaiah’s Seraphim, by whom the mystery of the Trinity was luminously proclaimed, when they uttered that marvellous cry “Holy,” being awestruck with the beauty in each Person of the Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Does the Seraphim's threefold 'Holy' in Isaiah 6:3 bear witness to the Trinity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: It teaches both the distinction of three Persons and the oneness of the Godhead. The Seraphim say 'Holy' three times rather than once, so that we do not think there is only one Person. They do not say it twice, which would exclude the Spirit. They repeat the same singular word rather than saying 'holies', so that we do not imagine a plurality of Godhead.
sources.quote: they repeat thrice and say the same word, that even in a hymn you may understand the distinction of Persons in the Trinity, and the oneness of the Godhead
sources.raw_question: What does the threefold 'Holy, Holy, Holy' of the Seraphim teach about the Trinity?

question: Why did Christ say the disciples should rejoice that He goes to the Father, because the Father is greater than He (John 14:28)?
synthesis: Both read the saying as consistent with the Son's Godhead, but they give different grounds. Augustine says the disciples, seeing Christ in the form of a servant, took Him to be less than the Father, and His departure would free them from that limited view. Hilary says the joy lies in His going to receive back from the greater Giver the glory He had with the Father before, a glory that proves His Godhead.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > All are Sometimes Understood in One Person.
sources.answer: Because while they saw Him in the form of a servant they held Him to be less than the Father on account of what they saw. Being taken up with the creaturely 'fashion' He had assumed, they could not perceive His equality with the Father; His departure would free them from that limited view.
sources.quote: being taken up with the creature and the “fashion” which I have taken upon me, you do not perceive the equality which I have with the Father
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ say it was good for the disciples that He go to the Father because the Father is greater than He?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Because he goes to receive back his glory from the Father. This is not a new or strange honour but the glory he had with the Father before. Love rejoices that Jesus will be confessed in the glory of God the Father, and that glory, received from the greater Giver, is the proof of his Godhead.
sources.quote: to receive back His glory from the Father: with Him, and in Him, to be glorified not with a brand-new honour, but with the old, not with some strange honour but with that which He had with Him before.
sources.raw_question: Why should the disciples rejoice that Christ goes to the Father because the Father is greater?

question: In Proverbs 8:15, where Wisdom says 'By me kings reign,' does this mean that the divine Word or Wisdom installs earthly rulers?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Gregory of Nyssa differ. Irenaeus takes the speaker to be the Word of God speaking through Solomon, so the verse shows that earthly rule comes from God rather than the devil. Gregory denies that earthly kings are meant, since Wisdom would then share the blame of bad rulers. He reads the 'kings' as the poor in spirit who inherit heaven, and the 'princes' as those who rule their passions through reason.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. If it meant this, Wisdom would be a king-maker and would share the blame of every king who rules badly. The kings meant are the poor in spirit, who inherit the endless kingdom of heaven. The princes meant are those who rule over their passions and are not enslaved to sin. Their monarchy is the rule of reason over the rebellious flesh.
sources.quote: For if by her kings are advanced to their rule, and if from her monarchy derives its strength, it follows of necessity that Wisdom is displayed to us as a king-maker, and transfers to herself the blame of those who bear evil rule in their kingdoms.
sources.raw_question: Does Wisdom's statement 'By me kings reign' in Proverbs 8 mean that Wisdom installs earthly rulers?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXIV.—Of the constant falsehood of the devil, and of the powers and governments of the world, which we ought to obey, inasmuch as they are appointed of God, not of the devil.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus reads the speaker of Proverbs 8:15-16 as the Word of God, speaking through Solomon. So the Word is the one by whom kings reign and princes rule, which shows that earthly rule comes from God and not from the devil.
sources.quote: And the Word also says by Solomon, “By me kings do reign, and princes administer justice.
sources.raw_question: Is it the divine Word who speaks through Solomon in Proverbs 8 when it says 'By me kings do reign'?

question: How can Scripture say the Lord spoke with Moses 'face to face, as a man speaks to his friend' (Exodus 33), when God then refuses to show Moses His face?
synthesis: Both authors agree that Moses did not see the divine substance, but they resolve the tension differently. Augustine says Moses saw God through a created, bodily appearance, and that 'face to face' describes the friendly manner of the speech rather than a vision of God's substance. Irenaeus identifies the speaker as the Word and reads the refusal as showing that man cannot see God, while also promising a future sight of Him in the Incarnation, fulfilled when the Lord spoke with Moses face to face at the Transfiguration.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > In What Manner Moses Saw God.
sources.answer: Moses saw God corporeally, through a created appearance, and was seeking the true, spiritual sight of God's substance. The speech in words was shaped so as to resemble a friend speaking to a friend. So 'face to face' describes the friendly manner of the communication, not a vision of the divine substance.
sources.quote: Assuredly he knew that he saw corporeally, and he sought the true sight of God spiritually. And that mode of speech accordingly which was wrought in words, was so modified, as if it were of a friend speaking to a friend.
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture say the Lord spoke to Moses 'face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend' when Moses afterwards asks God to show Himself plainly?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: It was the Word who spoke with Moses as a man speaks to a friend. The refusal to show his face signifies two things. First, it is impossible for man to see God. Second, through God's wisdom man will see him in the last times "in the depth of a rock," that is, in his coming as a man. This promise was fulfilled at the Transfiguration, where the Lord spoke with Moses face to face.
sources.quote: that it is impossible for man to see God; and that, through the wisdom of God, man shall see Him in the last times, in the depth of a rock, that is, in His coming as a man
sources.raw_question: Who spoke with Moses face to face in the Old Testament, and what does God's refusal to show Moses his face signify?

question: In Christ's sacrifice, who is the offerer and what is offered, and how can Christ be both priest and sacrifice?
synthesis: Augustine and Owen agree that Christ is both the one who offers and what is offered. Augustine frames this within the four elements of every sacrifice: Christ stays one with the God to whom he offers and makes those for whom he offers one in himself. Owen instead separates the whole person, God and man, as the offerer from his human nature, soul and body, as the thing offered, and grounds this in Heb. 9:14.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Christ the Most Perfect Victim for Cleansing Our Faults. In Every Sacrifice Four Things are to Be Considered.
sources.answer: Christ remains one with God, to whom he offers the sacrifice. He makes those for whom he offers one in himself. He is at once both the offerer and the offering. So the single Mediator reconciles us to God while not being separated from the God to whom the sacrifice is made.
sources.quote: might remain one with Him to whom He offered, might make those one in Himself for whom He offered, Himself might be in one both the offerer and the offering.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ as Mediator unite in himself the four elements of every sacrifice: to whom, by whom, what, and for whom it is offered?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: The offerer is the person of Christ, God and man, and the matter offered is his human nature, soul and body. In Heb. 9:14 'he' denotes the sacrificer, the whole person, and 'himself' the sacrifice, his human nature. Hence God is said to purchase the church with his own blood, and his soul and body are each called an offering.
sources.quote: “He,” that is, the sacrificer, denotes the person of Christ, God and man; and “himself,” as the sacrifice, denotes his human nature whence God is said to “purchase his church with his own blood,”
sources.raw_question: In Christ's sacrifice, who is the offerer and what is the thing offered?

question: What does Baruch 3:35-37 ('This is our God, and there shall be none other likened unto Him... Afterward He was seen upon earth') teach about the Father and the incarnate Son?
synthesis: Hilary and Hippolytus read the passage differently. Hilary takes 'This is our God' to refer to Christ, the one later seen on earth, and concludes that the Only-begotten is true God, one in nature with the Father. Hippolytus, answering the claim that the text proves only one divine person, applies 'This is our God' to the Father. He identifies the Son with 'Jacob His servant' and 'Israel His beloved', the one who received all knowledge from the Father and appeared on earth, so on his reading the passage distinguishes the Son from the Father.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. The God of whom the prophet speaks is the one who afterward was seen on earth and dwelt among men, that is, Christ. So the prophet teaches that the Only-begotten is of a nature one with the Father's, and that no other is likened to Him so as to be God.
sources.quote: Jeremiah also, a prophet equally inspired, has taught that God the Only-begotten is of a nature one with that of God the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does Baruch/Jeremiah's text 'This is our God, and there shall be none other likened unto Him... Afterward He was seen upon earth' teach that the incarnate Son is true God of one nature with the Father?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. The saying is rightly applied to the Father, to whom no one is to be compared. The "Jacob His servant" and "Israel His beloved" to whom the Father gave all knowledge is the Son, the beloved Son of the Father's voice. Having received all knowledge from the Father, He showed Himself on earth and conversed with men, so the passage distinguishes the Son from the Father.
sources.quote: For who is Jacob His servant, Israel His beloved, but He of whom He crieth, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear ye Him?”
sources.raw_question: Does Baruch 3:35-37 ("This is our God; there shall none other be accounted of in comparison of Him") prove that only one divine person exists?

question: Can God progress, grow, or acquire new perfections over time?
synthesis: Hilary of Poitiers and Gregory of Nyssa both answer no. Hilary argues from perfect fulness: a nature capable of progress would always have ground left ahead, while fulness that is already perfect cannot be added to. Gregory argues from the absence of any good outside God for God to share in, together with divine immutability, and he applies this to deny that the Son or the Spirit could be added to the Deity over time.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. A nature capable of progress could never reach the point where nothing is wanting to it, because it would always leave further ground ahead. But God abides in perfect fulness and for ever is. Perfect fulness cannot receive any accession of further fulness.
sources.quote: But to Him, Who abides in perfect fulness, Who for ever is, there is no fulness left by which He can be made more full, for perfect fulness cannot receive an accession of further fulness.
sources.raw_question: Can God progress or increase in perfection over time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. The Deity by nature does not admit of augmentation. There is no good outside It in which It could participate to gain anything. It is immutable, neither casting away what It has nor acquiring what It lacks.
sources.quote: the Deity by Its very nature does not admit of augmentation. For It does not perceive any other good outside of Itself, by participation in which It could acquire any accession, but is always immutable
sources.raw_question: Can the Deity grow or acquire new perfections, so that the Son or the Spirit could be added to God over time?

question: Can there be a plurality of gods, whether sharing power or ranked as greater and lesser, if God is omnipotent?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Hilary agree that omnipotence excludes a plurality of gods, but they argue differently. Irenaeus reasons that many gods, each confined to his own domain, would each lack much, which would abolish the title Omnipotent. Hilary reasons that omnipotence admits no degrees and eternity no priority or succession, so a hierarchy of greater and lesser gods is impossible and both attributes belong to One alone.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter I.—There is but one God: the impossibility of its being otherwise.
sources.answer: No. If there were many gods, each confined to his own territory, every one of them would lack much, holding only a small portion compared with the rest. The title of the Omnipotent would therefore be abolished, and such an opinion necessarily ends in impiety.
sources.quote: For there will be [much] wanting to every one of them, possessing [as he will do] only a very small part when compared with all the rest. The name of the Omnipotent will thus be brought to an end
sources.raw_question: Is a plurality of limited gods compatible with God being called Omnipotent?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Omnipotence and eternity belong to One only. Omnipotence admits no degrees of strength or weakness, and eternity admits no priority or succession. So a hierarchy of greater and lesser gods is impossible, and in God we worship absolute eternity and absolute power.
sources.quote: Hence omnipotence and eternity are the possession of One only, for omnipotence is incapable of degrees of strength or weakness, and eternity of priority or succession.
sources.raised_by_detail: pagan philosophers and teachers who held gods greater and less
sources.raw_question: Can there be several gods distinguished as greater and lesser, or must omnipotence and eternity belong to one God alone?

question: Does Stephen's dying prayer, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,' show that Christ is to be invoked and worshipped as God?
synthesis: Owen and Bickersteth both answer yes. Owen reads Stephen's prayer, including his plea for forgiveness of his killers, as resting on Christ's power to forgive sins, and links it to the wider apostolic practice of calling on Christ's name (1 Cor. 1:2), since such invocation comprises the whole worship of God. Bickersteth argues from Old Testament parallels: David and Solomon commit the spirit to God, so Stephen's addressing this prayer directly to Christ, rather than to the Father, shows he worshipped Christ as very and eternal God.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Stephen fixed his faith and hope on Jesus, praying "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" and asking him to forgive his killers, because he knew the Son of man had power to forgive sins. Paul describes the saints in every place as those who call on the name of Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 1:2). Invocation of this kind generally comprises the whole worship of God.
sources.quote: for he knew that the Son of man had power to forgive sins also. And this worship of the Lord Jesus, the apostle makes the discriminating character of the saints
sources.raw_question: Do Stephen's dying prayer and the early Christian practice of calling on Christ's name show that Christ was invoked as God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. In the Old Testament, David committed his spirit into God's hands, and Solomon said the spirit returns to God. Stephen, full of the Holy Ghost, addressed this same prayer directly to Christ, not to the Father alone and not to the Father through Christ. In doing so he worshipped Christ with his last breath as very and eternal God.
sources.quote: prompted the dying martyr to pray not to God the Father alone, nor to the Father through Christ, but to pray to Christ, worshipping him with his latest breath as very and eternal God
sources.raw_question: Does Stephen's dying prayer, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,' show that Christ is to be worshipped as God?

question: Can created beings come to share in immortality, which belongs properly to God, and from whom do they receive it?
synthesis: Augustine and Irenaeus agree that creatures receive immortality only from God and as a participation in him. Augustine stresses that the Son became partaker of our mortality to persuade us that immortality comes from God alone. Irenaeus grounds it in God's gratuitous gift of continued existence, received through subjection to God and the vision of God, while God alone remains uncreated.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > We Say that Future Blessedness is Truly Eternal, Not Through Human Reasonings, But by the Help of Faith. The Immortality of Blessedness Becomes Credible from the Incarnation of the Son of God.
sources.answer: From God alone. The blessed are made partakers of immortality only in God and from God. To persuade us of this, the Son of God became partaker of our mortality.
sources.quote: in whom alone and from whom alone the blessed can be made partakers of that immortality; of which that we might be convinced, the Son of God was made partaker of our mortality?
sources.raw_question: From whom can the blessed receive immortality?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVIII.—Why man was not made perfect from the beginning.
sources.answer: Yes, but only as a gift. Created things are not uncreated, yet by continuing in being through God's gratuitous bestowal of eternal existence, they receive a faculty of the Uncreated. Subjection to God is continuance in immortality, and seeing God produces immortality. Even so, God alone remains uncreated and the primary cause of all.
sources.quote: by their continuing in being throughout a long course of ages, they shall receive a faculty of the Uncreated, through the gratuitous bestowal of eternal existence upon them by God.
sources.raw_question: Can a created being come to share in immortality, which belongs properly to the uncreated God?

question: Why did the perfect Son of God humble himself to a lowly human condition, including infancy and growth, rather than coming in his divine glory?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Athanasius agree that the Son's humbling was for our benefit, not his own, and that it was ordered toward our receiving divine life. Irenaeus grounds it in human incapacity: we could not have endured his immortal glory, so he came as milk to nourish us until we could receive the Spirit. Athanasius identifies the humbling with his taking our flesh, so that through kinship with that flesh we might increase, be deified and be freed from sin.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVIII.—Why man was not made perfect from the beginning.
sources.answer: He came as we were capable of beholding Him, not as He might have come. Had He come in immortal glory we could not have endured it. So the perfect bread of the Father offered Himself as milk, passing through infancy for man's benefit and not His own, so that we, nourished by His flesh, might become able to receive the Spirit.
sources.quote: He might easily have come to us in His immortal glory, but in that case we could never have endured the greatness of the glory; and therefore it was that He, who was the perfect bread of the Father, offered Himself to us as milk
sources.raw_question: Why did the Son of God come in humble human form, including passing through infancy, rather than in his immortal glory?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: He humbled himself for us, so that through his humbling we might increase. His humbling is nothing else than taking our flesh, and our increase is renouncing sensible things and coming to the Word, being deified and freed from sin through kinship with the Word's flesh.
sources.quote: the Son of God, since He could not advance, being perfect in the Father, humbled Himself for us, that in His humbling we on the other hand might be able to increase.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Son of God, being perfect, humble himself to a condition where advance could be ascribed to him?

question: How should Proverbs 9:1-5 be interpreted: is the personified Wisdom who builds her house Christ, and what is the house she builds?
synthesis: Owen and Gregory of Nyssa both take the Wisdom of Proverbs 9 to be Christ, but they read the house differently. For Owen the house is the church and the feast is the riches of the gospel, offered for fellowship with Christ. For Gregory the house points darkly to the Lord's flesh, which Wisdom built for itself from the Virgin's body.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen identifies her as the Lord Christ, the eternal Wisdom of the Father, who of God is made wisdom to us. His church is the house he builds on a perfect number of pillars. The slain beasts and mingled wine are the spiritual riches of the gospel, which he freely offers to those he invites. To eat and drink at his table is therefore to have fellowship with him.
sources.quote: The Lord Christ, the eternal Wisdom of the Father, and who of God is made unto us wisdom, erects a spiritual house, wherein he makes provision for the entertainment of those guests whom he so freely invites.
sources.raw_question: Is the personified Wisdom of Proverbs 9:1-5, who builds her house and invites guests to her table, the Lord Christ?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: It refers darkly to the preparation of the Lord's flesh. The true Wisdom did not dwell in another's building but built for Itself a dwelling-place from the body of the Virgin.
sources.quote: for the trite Wisdom did not dwell in another’s building, but built for Itself that dwelling-place from the body of the Virgin
sources.raw_question: What does "Wisdom has builded herself a house" in Proverbs 9:1 refer to?

question: What did Christ mean by "temple" when he said, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19)?
synthesis: Both take the temple to be Christ's own body rather than the Jerusalem temple. Augustine grounds this in the Gospel's own comment ("He spake this of the temple of His body") and the Jonah parallel. Gregory of Nyssa specifies the temple as the union of soul and body, reads its destruction as death's separation of soul from body, and extends the image to believers as temples of God.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: The "temple" is the combination of his soul and body. Its "destruction" signifies the soul's separation from the body in death. Likewise we, through soul and body, become a temple of God who dwells in us.
sources.quote: even so the Lord terms their combination a “temple,” of which the “destruction” signifies the dissolution of the soul from the body.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean by "temple" in "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Number Six is Also Commended in the Building Up of the Body of Christ and of the Temple at Jerusalem.
sources.answer: He was speaking of the temple of his body. Augustine appeals to the Gospel's own clear and solid testimony, "He spake this of the temple of His body," and to the parallel saying that, as Jonas was three days in the whale, the Son of man would be three days in the heart of the earth. His body, destroyed by death, he raised again on the third day.
sources.quote: which being destroyed by the suffering of death, He raised again on the third day. For “He spake this of the temple of His body,” as is declared by the most clear and solid testimony of the Gospel
sources.raw_question: When Jesus said he would raise up the destroyed temple in three days, was he speaking of the temple at Jerusalem or of his own body?

question: Did Christ break the law or do wrong by healing and working on the Sabbath?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Hilary agree that Christ did no wrong, but on different grounds. Irenaeus argues from the law itself: it permitted healing and priestly work on the Sabbath and forbade only servile work, so Christ fulfilled the law rather than voiding it. Hilary grounds his answer in Christ's divine birth: the Father works with the Son in all he does, so the Lord of the Sabbath acted with the Father's sanction.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VIII.—Vain attempts of Marcion and his followers, who exclude Abraham from the salvation bestowed by Christ, who liberated not only Abraham, but the seed of Abraham, by fulfilling and not destroying the law when He healed on the Sabbath-day.
sources.answer: No. The law did not forbid healing on the Sabbath: it permitted circumcision and priestly service on that day, and even the care of animals. It forbade only servile, money-seeking work. Christ fulfilled the law rather than making it void, by acting as high priest, propitiating God for men, healing, and suffering death to free man from condemnation. This shows that the law and Christ come from the same God.
sources.quote: For He did not make void, but fulfilled the law, by performing the offices of the high priest, propitiating God for men, and cleansing the lepers, healing the sick, and Himself suffering death
sources.raw_question: Did Christ break or abolish the Mosaic law when he healed on the Sabbath?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. By virtue of his divine birth, the Father works with him in everything he does. So the Lord of the Sabbath acted with the Father's sanction.
sources.quote: the Father is working with Him in all that He does, will save us from supposing that the Lord of the Sabbath was doing wrong in working on the Sabbath
sources.raw_question: Was Christ doing wrong by working on the Sabbath?

question: Does Habakkuk 3:3, 'God shall come from the south', refer to the Son born in Bethlehem, showing that he is God?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Novatian agree that the verse refers to the Son born at Bethlehem, which lies to the south, and that it calls him God. Irenaeus also reads 'his feet shall advance in the plains' as showing that the Son is man. Novatian argues instead against applying the verse to the Father: the Father would then come from a place and be confined to it, which is the Sabellian error.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XX.—God showed himself, by the fall of man, as patient, benign, merciful, mighty to save. Man is therefore most ungrateful, if, unmindful of his own lot, and of the benefits held out to him, he do not acknowledge divine grace.
sources.answer: Yes. Habakkuk says 'God shall come from the south,' indicating clearly that the one coming, the Son of God born at Bethlehem towards the south of Judah's inheritance, is God. The words 'His feet shall advance in the plains' show that he is also man.
sources.quote: Thus he indicates in clear terms that He is God, and that His advent was [to take place] in Bethlehem, and from Mount Effrem which is towards the south of the inheritance, and that [He is] man.
sources.raw_question: Does Habakkuk 3:3-5 teach that the Son born in Bethlehem is both God and man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That Christ is God, is Proved by the Authority of the Old Testament Scriptures.
sources.answer: It refers to the Son. If it meant the Father, the Father would come from a place, be shut out of other places and be confined within a dwelling, which is the error of Sabellius. Christ, who Scripture also calls God, was born in Bethlehem, which lies toward the south. So he is rightly the God foretold to come from the south.
sources.quote: But if in Bethlehem, the region of which local division looks towards the southern portion of heaven, Christ is born, who by the Scriptures is also said to be God, this God is rightly described as coming from the south
sources.raw_question: Does Habakkuk 3:3, 'God shall come from the south', refer to God the Father or to the Son?

question: Was the brightness of Christ at the Transfiguration a display of his divine glory?
synthesis: Ambrose and Owen agree that Christ shone on the mount with the light or lustre of the Godhead itself. They differ in what they draw from it. Ambrose stresses that the apostles fell down and worshipped, and that this glory belongs to the Trinity and so is to be worshipped. Owen describes the surpassing heavenly brightness of face and raiment and links it to the white garment of the Ancient of days in Daniel.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XII. From the fact that St. Paul has shown that the light of the Godhead which the three apostles worshipped in Christ is in the Trinity, it is made clear that the Spirit also is to be worshipped. It is shown from the words themselves that the Spirit is intended by the apostles. The Godhead of the same Spirit is proved from the fact that He has a temple wherein He dwells not as a priest, but as God: and is worshipped with the Father and the Son; whence is understood the oneness of nature in Them.
sources.answer: Yes. When Christ shone with the light of His Godhead on the mount, the apostles fell on their faces, unable to bear the divine splendour, and in falling they worshipped. This glory of the Godhead, Paul shows, belongs to the Trinity, so it is to be worshipped.
sources.quote: Do not you think that they even, as they fell, worshipped, when they could not with their bodily eyes endure the brightness of the divine splendour
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles at the Transfiguration worship the divine glory in Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. At the transfiguration Christ had on him a mighty lustre of the Deity. His face shone as the sun and his raiment became white as light, which was a divine, heavenly, surpassing glory. It matches the white garment ascribed to the Ancient of days in Daniel.
sources.quote: It was a divine, heavenly, surpassing glory that was upon him
sources.raw_question: Does the brightness of Christ at the transfiguration display his divine glory?

question: What does the dew on Gideon's fleece, first on the fleece alone and then on all the ground, signify about the Holy Spirit?
synthesis: Irenaeus and Ambrose agree that the sign is a type of the Spirit first given to Israel alone and then withdrawn from them and spread over all nations. Irenaeus identifies the dew directly with the Spirit of God, who descended on the Lord and would be diffused to the whole earth. Ambrose speaks of the faith and grace of the Spirit and ties the withdrawal to the Jews' refusal of the fountain of living water.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVII.—The apostles teach that it was neither Christ nor the Saviour, but the Holy Spirit, who did descend upon Jesus. The reason for this descent.
sources.answer: It is a type showing that the Spirit, once given to Israel alone, would be withdrawn from them and spread throughout all the earth. At first the dew, which is the Spirit of God, lay only on the fleece, a figure of the people. Gideon then asked for the fleece to be dry while the dew covered the ground. So the Spirit who descended on the Lord would be diffused to all nations.
sources.quote: but that the dew, which is the Spirit of God, who descended upon the Lord, should be diffused throughout all the earth
sources.raw_question: What does Gideon's sign of the fleece signify about the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Preface.
sources.answer: It signifies the faith and grace of the Divine Spirit. This was first given to the Jews and then, after they refused the fountain of living water, withdrawn from them and poured out on the Gentiles. Now the whole world is moistened with the dew of faith, while the Jews have lost their prophets.
sources.quote: the dew of moistening faith dried up in the breasts of the Jews, and that divine Fountain turned away its course to the hearts of the Gentiles.
sources.raw_question: What does the dew on Gideon's fleece, first on the fleece alone and then on all the ground, signify?

question: Does Zechariah 12:10 ('they shall look upon me whom they have pierced'), applied by John to the crucified Christ, show that Christ is himself Jehovah?
synthesis: Bickersteth and Waterland agree that the text identifies Christ as Jehovah. Bickersteth argues from the passage itself: the pierced one is Jehovah the Creator speaking of himself, and John's inspired reading applies this to Christ crucified. Waterland answers a rival reading that Jehovah was only 'pierced in effigy' in his Son, dismissing it as a fanciful evasion, and holds instead that Christ, as the express image of the Father, is truly Jehovah just as the Father is.

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. In Zechariah the one who is pierced is Jehovah speaking of himself, the one who stretches forth the heavens and forms the spirit of man. John's inspired interpretation says this predicts Christ crucified. Therefore Christ is the creating Jehovah.
sources.quote: The prophet declares the One who is pierced is Jehovah speaking of himself, but according to St. John’s inspired interpretation, Christ crucified is here predicted.
sources.raw_question: Does Zechariah 12:10 ("they shall look upon me whom they have pierced"), as applied by John to the crucified Christ, prove that Christ is Jehovah the Creator?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. That is a fanciful turn to elude plain Scripture. Rather, since Christ is the express image of the Father, he may justly be called Jehovah, which he is as truly as the Father.
sources.quote: Say rather, that since Christ is the effigies, the express image of the Father, he might justly be called Jehovah, which indeed he is, as well as the Father.
sources.raw_question: Are the sufferings of Christ called the sufferings of Jehovah in Zechariah 12:10 only because Jehovah was 'pierced in effigy' in his Son, the image of his Person?

question: Does Psalm 33:6 ('By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth') refer to the Son and the Holy Spirit as agents in creation?
synthesis: Basil and Ambrose agree that the verse refers to the Holy Spirit at work in creation. Basil argues that 'word' and 'breath' are not mere sound and vapour but the divine Persons, so the verse shows three at work: the Lord who commands, the Word who creates and the Spirit who confirms. Ambrose focuses on the Spirit, assigning all the strength of the heavens to Him, and adds that the Spirit who moved over the waters could not have been inactive in the making of the world.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: They refer to divine Persons. The Word is not a mere impression on the air but the one who was with God in the beginning and was God. The Spirit of his mouth is not a vapour but the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father. So the verse shows three at work in creation: the Lord who commands, the Word who creates, and the Spirit who confirms.
sources.quote: The Word then is not a mere significant impression on the air, borne by the organs of speech; nor is the Spirit of His mouth a vapour, emitted by the organs of respiration; but the Word is He who “was with God in the beginning” and “was God,”
sources.raw_question: Do the 'word' and 'breath' of the Lord in Psalm 33:6 refer merely to spoken sound and exhaled breath, or to the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, as well as the Father and the Son, is pointed out in holy Scripture as Creator, and the same truth was shadowed forth even by heathen writers, but it was shown most plainly in the Mystery of the Incarnation, after touching upon which, the writer maintains his argument from the fact that worship which is due to the Creator alone is paid to the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. The verse says the heavens were established by the Word of the Lord and all their strength by the Spirit of His mouth, so all the strength of the heavens is to be referred to the Spirit. And He who moved over the waters before the earth was made could not have been inactive while it was being made.
sources.quote: Observe what he says, that all the strength of the heavens is to be referred to the Spirit. For how should He Who was moving before the earth was made, be resting when it was being made?
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 33:6 ascribe the establishment and strength of the heavens to the Holy Spirit?

question: What is the 'rock' on which Christ builds his Church in Matthew 16:18, and what does it imply about Christ's person?
synthesis: The two authors differ on what the rock is. Hilary identifies it as Peter's revealed confession that Christ is the Son of God by nature, so denying his divinity abandons the Church's foundation. Owen identifies the rock as Christ himself, grounding this in Scripture's calling God the rock for his eternal power and immutability. For Owen the confession of 'the Christ, the Son of the living God' is the faith by which the church relates to that rock.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: The rock is Peter's confession that Christ is the Son of God by nature. This faith, given by the Father's revelation, is the foundation of the Church, the reason the gates of hell cannot prevail, and the faith that holds the keys of the kingdom. To confess Christ a creature made from nothing is therefore to abandon the Church's foundation and to cut oneself off from Christ.
sources.quote: This faith it is which is the foundation of the Church; through this faith the gates of hell cannot prevail against her. This is the faith which has the keys of the kingdom of heaven.
sources.raw_question: What is the rock on which the Church is built in Matthew 16:18?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Preface
sources.answer: Christ himself is the rock on which the church is built. Scripture calls God the rock of his people because of his eternal power and immutability, and Christ is called the spiritual rock that supplied Israel in the wilderness. The church's relation to this rock consists in faith in the confession that he is 'the Christ, the Son of the living God.'
sources.quote: He is himself the rock upon which his church is built, — as God is called the rock of his people, on the account of his eternal power and immutability
sources.raw_question: In Matthew 16:18, is the 'rock' on which Christ builds his church Christ himself, and what does that imply about his person?

question: In what sense does Acts 20:28 call the blood by which the church was redeemed God's own blood, given that God is a spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: Yes, but only in a qualified sense. Christ's blood was the blood of him who was God, though not his blood as God, since God is a spirit. Calling it God's own blood plainly shows that his person as God and man is one.
sources.quote: the blood of Jesus Christ, being the blood of him that was God, though not the blood of him as God; for God is a spirit. And this undeniably testifies to the unity of his person as God and man.
sources.raw_question: Can God be said to have blood of his own, as in Acts 20:28, given that God is a spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Because of the personal union, the blood shed by the Son of man is rightly called God's own blood. Likewise 1 John 3:16 speaks of God's love in laying down his life for us. The suffering person is the divine Son in the flesh.
sources.quote: “God redeemed his church with his own blood,” Acts xx. 28; and therein was the “love of God seen, that he gave his life for us,” 1 John iii. 16.
sources.raw_question: Does Acts 20:28, which says God redeemed the church with his own blood, show that the one who suffered was God?

question: Is God himself reconciled to sinners through Christ, laying aside wrath or enmity on his part, and what does that reconciliation involve?
synthesis: Both Owen and Augustine hold that reconciliation through Christ ends God's wrath toward sinners. Owen describes a two-sided reconciliation: Christ's blood atones and turns away wrath, so God lays down enmity on his part and then slays the enmity on ours. Augustine instead locates the enmity in sin's opposition to righteousness, defines God's reconciliation as the end of his just wrath when sins are forgiven, and stresses that God loved sinners even while they were enemies.

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. By his blood Christ made atonement with God and turned away the wrath due to us, so God, being reconciled himself, lays down the enmity on his part. God then proceeds, in Christ, to slay the enmity on our part, so that we also are reconciled and accept the peace that is offered.
sources.quote: being reconciled himself, verse 18, he lays down the enmity on his part, and proceeds to what remains, — to slay the enmity on our part, that we also may be reconciled.
sources.raw_question: Does reconciliation through Christ involve God laying aside enmity on his part, as well as sinners laying aside theirs?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Remains of Death and the Evil Things of the World Turn to Good for the Elect. How Fitly the Death of Christ Was Chosen, that We Might Be Justified in His Blood. What the Anger of God is.
sources.answer: Reconciliation means that God's wrath, which is just retribution, comes to an end. Men were enemies of God only as sins are enemies to righteousness, and when sins are forgiven the enmity ceases. Yet God loved them even while they were enemies, since He spared not His own Son but delivered Him up for them.
sources.quote: And yet certainly He loved them even while still enemies, since “He spared not His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all,” when we were still enemies.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean for God to be reconciled to sinners, and does reconciliation imply that God did not love them beforehand?

question: How was God's warning that Adam would die on the day he ate the forbidden fruit fulfilled, given that Adam lived many years afterward?
synthesis: Gregory of Nyssa and Irenaeus agree that the warning came true, but they argue it differently. Gregory holds that Adam died in soul that very day, because sin alienated him from God, who is the true life, and bodily death followed later. Irenaeus says Adam became death's debtor at the moment of disobedience, and he adds two further readings: Adam died on the same weekday of creation (the sixth), and he died within a 'day of the Lord' of a thousand years.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: Adam died in soul that very day. Sin is alienation from God, who is the true and only life, so the sentence of death was ratified at once through Adam's alienation from that life. His bodily death followed much later.
sources.quote: For by the fact of his alienation from the true life, the sentence of death was ratified against him that self-same day: and after this, at a much later time, there followed also the bodily death of Adam.
sources.raw_question: How was God's warning true that Adam would die on the day he ate the forbidden fruit, when Adam lived many hundreds of years afterward?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXIII.—The devil is well practised in falsehood, by which Adam having been led astray, sinned on the sixth day of the creation, in which day also he has been renewed by Christ.
sources.answer: Yes. In every sense, God is shown to be true and the serpent a liar. Adam and Eve became forfeit to death and death's debtors the moment they disobeyed, since disobedience to God entails death. Moreover, they died on the same day of creation on which they ate, namely the sixth. Even if one reckons a day of the Lord as a thousand years, Adam died within the thousand years.
sources.quote: it follows that, in regard to all these significations, God is indeed true. For they died who tasted of the tree; and the serpent is proved a liar and a murderer
sources.raw_question: Was God's warning to Adam that he would die 'in the day' he ate of the forbidden tree actually fulfilled, given that Adam went on living for many years afterward?

question: How does the crossing of the Red Sea, with the cloud, prefigure baptism, and what does it show about the Holy Spirit's role?
synthesis: Basil and Ambrose agree that the sea and cloud are a type of baptism and that the Holy Spirit is signified in it. Their emphases differ. Basil reads the cloud as a shadow of the Spirit's gift, which cools the passions, and the sea as ending the devil's tyranny. Ambrose reasons from Paul's 'baptized in the cloud and in the sea': since the whole truth of baptism lies in the Spirit, the Spirit must have been at work in its figure as well.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Objection that some were baptized unto Moses and believed in him, and an answer to it; with remarks upon types.
sources.answer: The sea typifies baptism. As the sea destroyed Pharaoh, baptism ends the tyranny of the devil and our enmity toward God, and we come up from the water as if alive from the dead. The cloud is a shadow of the gift of the Spirit, who cools the flame of our passions by mortifying our members.
sources.quote: And the cloud is a shadow of the gift of the Spirit, who cools the flame of our passions by the “mortification” of our “members.”
sources.raw_question: Of what was the crossing of the Red Sea and the cloud a type, and what does the cloud signify about the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IV.
