To those who contend that the Spirit because He is called the Finger is less than the Father, St. Ambrose replies that this would also tend to the lessening of the Son, Who is called the Right Hand. That these names are to be referred only to the Unity, for which reason Moses proclaimed that the whole Trinity worked in the passage of the Red Sea. And, indeed, it is no wonder that the operation of the Spirit found place there, where there was a figure of baptism, since the Scripture teaches that the Three Persons equally sanctify and are operative in that sacrament.
sources.answer: Yes. The Apostle says the fathers were baptized in Moses in the cloud and in the sea, so the event was a type of the sacrament. The whole truth of baptism is in the Spirit, so its type could not exist without the Spirit's operation. We feel His operation and grace in the font itself, and so we should not doubt it was present in the figure.
sources.quote: For how without the operation of the Holy Spirit could there be the type of a sacrament, the whole truth of which is in the Spirit?
sources.raw_question: Was the Holy Spirit at work in the Red Sea crossing, given that it prefigured baptism?

question: Does Hosea 1:7, where the Father says he will save his people 'by the Lord their God', show that the Father calls the Son God?
synthesis: Novatian and Hilary agree that in Hosea 1:7 the Father himself names the Son God. Novatian argues from salvation: God saves only through Christ, so the God by whom the Father saves must be Christ, and denying his divinity forfeits that salvation. Hilary grounds the title differently, holding that the Son is 'their God' because the Father has given us to him as an inheritance (Psalm 2), thereby bestowing on him the title of his own unoriginate majesty.

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That Christ is God, is Proved by the Authority of the Old Testament Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. God the Father says he saves by God, yet God saves only through Christ, so the one by whom the Father saves is Christ, who is thus called God by the Father himself. Since the Father saves no one except by God, whoever refuses to confess Christ as God loses the salvation that is found only in Christ God.
sources.quote: If God says that He saves by God, still God does not save except by Christ. Why, then, should man hesitate to call Christ God, when he observes that He is declared to be God by the Father according to the Scriptures?
sources.raw_question: Does Hosea 1:7, where the Father says he will save his people 'by the Lord their God', show that Christ is God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. Here the Father unambiguously calls the Son "their God": the Son is God to us because the Father has given us to Him as an inheritance, as Psalm 2 says. The Father thus bestows on the Son the title of His own unoriginate majesty.
sources.quote: Here God the Father gives the name of God, without any ambiguity, to the Son, in Whom also He chose us before countless ages.
sources.raw_question: Does God the Father give the name of God to the Son in Hosea 1:7 ("I will save them in the Lord their God")?

question: In 1 Thessalonians 3:12-13, who is the 'Lord' asked to establish believers' hearts unblamable in holiness before God the Father at the coming of the Lord Jesus?
synthesis: Ambrose and Basil agree that this 'Lord' is the Holy Spirit, and both reason that he is distinguished from the Father and from Christ named in the same passage. Ambrose adds that holiness is a grace proper to the Spirit. Basil instead draws a parallel with 2 Thessalonians 3:5 and challenges those who rank the Spirit among ministering spirits to say who else this Lord could be.

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIV. Besides the evidence adduced above, other passages can be brought to prove the sovereignty of the Three Persons. Two are quoted from the Epistles to the Thessalonians, and by collating other testimonies of the Scriptures it is shown that in them dominion is claimed for the Spirit as for the other Persons. Then, by quotation of another still more express passage in the second Epistle to the Corinthians, it is inferred both that the Spirit is Lord, and that where the Lord is, there is the Spirit.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit. Since the Apostle has already named the Father and the Son in the same sentence, the one joined with them as 'the Lord' who establishes hearts in holiness must be the Spirit. Holiness is a grace proper to the Spirit, as the same epistle-writer speaks of 'holiness of the Spirit.'
sources.quote: He has named the Father and has named the Son; Whom, then, has he joined with the Father and the Son except the Spirit? Who is the Lord Who establishes our hearts in holiness. For holiness is a grace of the Spirit
sources.raw_question: In 1 Thessalonians 3:12-13, who is the 'Lord' who makes believers abound in love and establishes their hearts in holiness before God the Father at the coming of the Lord Jesus?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Proof from Scripture that the Spirit is called Lord.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit. Because the Lord entreated is distinguished both from 'God even our Father' and from 'our Lord Jesus Christ' at whose coming the hearts are established, the passage parallels 2 Thessalonians 3:5 in calling the Spirit Lord. Those who rank the Spirit among ministering spirits cannot explain who else this Lord is.
sources.quote: Now what Lord does he entreat to stablish the hearts of the faithful at Thessalonica, unblamable in holiness before God even our Father, at the coming of our Lord? Let those answer who place the Holy Ghost among the ministering spirits
sources.raw_question: In 1 Thessalonians 3:12-13, who is the Lord asked to establish hearts unblamable before God the Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ?

question: Is the Creator of heaven and earth the only true God and the same as the Father of Jesus Christ, or is there another God or Father above the Creator, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIV.—Recapitulation of the various arguments adduced against Gnostic impiety under all its aspects. The heretics, tossed about by every blast of doctrine, are opposed by the uniform teaching of the Church, which remains so always, and is consistent with itself.
sources.answer: No. The Maker and Framer who formed this world is the one above whom there is no other God, the only true God. Those who imagine another god beyond Him, or another Pleroma, blaspheme the Creator and are refuted by their own arguments. Their supposed higher god is a non-existent being they have dreamed up.
sources.quote: who bring in impious doctrines regarding our Maker and Framer, who also formed this world, and above whom there is no other God
sources.raw_question: Is there another God above the Creator of the world, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: Yes. God and the Father are truly one and the same. He was announced by the prophets and handed down by the true Gospel, and Christians worship Him as Maker of heaven and earth and all things in them. There is no separate Creator distinct from the Father.
sources.quote: Thus God and the Father are truly one and the same; He who was announced by the prophets, and handed down by the true Gospel; whom we Christians worship and love with the whole heart, as the Maker of heaven and earth
sources.raw_question: Is the Father of Jesus Christ the same being as the Maker of heaven and earth?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter X.—Perverse interpretations of Scripture by the heretics: God created all things out of nothing, and not from pre-existent matter.
sources.answer: No. The one who is truly God receives testimony from all, while the supposed higher god has never been proclaimed by anyone. The heretics invent him by forcing ambiguous parables onto him. Those passages are ambiguous only with respect to the dispensations of the true God, not because they point to another god.
sources.quote: ambiguous, however, not as if referring to another god, but as regards the dispensations of [the true] God), they have constructed another god, weaving, as I said before, ropes of sand
sources.raw_question: Is there another god above the Creator of the world, to whom ambiguous passages and parables of Scripture refer?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIX.—Absurdities of the heretics as to their own origin: their opinions respecting the Demiurge shown to be equally untenable and ridiculous.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus holds that the Demiurge, the Fashioner and Former of the universe, is in fact the only true God. To posit another god above the Creator is something no one with intelligence and even a small share of truth can tolerate, and to call the Creator the fruit of a defect is impiety against Him.
sources.quote: They are therefore not only chargeable with impiety against the Creator, declaring Him the fruit of a defect
sources.raw_question: Is there another god above the Creator of the world, as the Valentinians claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter II.—The world was not formed by angels, or by any other being, contrary to the will of the most high God, but was made by the Father through the Word.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul declares that the Creator God is the Father: 'There is one God, the Father, who is above all, and through all things, and in us all.' So there is only one God, who is both Creator and Father of Christ. This is confirmed by the prophets, the Lord and the apostles.
sources.quote: Now, that this God is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Paul the apostle also has declared, [saying,] “There is one God, the Father, who is above all, and through all things, and in us all.”
sources.raw_question: Is the God who created the world the same as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXV.—This world is ruled by the providence of one God, who is both endowed with infinite justice to punish the wicked, and with infinite goodness to bless the pious, and impart to them salvation.
sources.answer: The Creator is the only true God and the Father of Christ. Irenaeus holds that the Framer and Maker of the universe is the only true God and Lord of all, and that this same Creator is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. To posit a higher, unknown Father (Bythus) above him is to blaspheme the Creator. Irenaeus says he will confirm this from the Lord's own words in the next book.
sources.quote: to cease from blaspheming their Creator, who is both God alone, and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator and Maker of this world the only true God and the same as the Father of Jesus Christ, or is there a higher God beyond the Creator, as the Valentinian Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter III.—A refutation of the heretics, from the fact that, in the various Churches, a perpetual succession of bishops was kept up.
sources.answer: The Creator is the Father of Jesus Christ; there is no other god beyond the Maker of all things. The apostolic tradition, as shown in Clement's letter to the Corinthians, proclaimed one omnipotent God who made heaven and earth, created man, called Abraham, spoke with Moses and sent the prophets, and this God was preached by the Churches as the Father of our Lord. Since that letter predates the heretics, their doctrine of another god is a later novelty.
sources.quote: From this document, whosoever chooses to do so, may learn that He, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, was preached by the Churches
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of heaven and earth the same God as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, or is there another god beyond the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: No. John's Gospel was written precisely to establish the rule of truth that there is one Almighty God who made all things, visible and invisible, by His Word. The same Word through whom God created also brought salvation to humanity, so creation and redemption belong to one God.
sources.quote: that there is one Almighty God, who made all things by His Word, both visible and invisible; showing at the same time, that by the Word, through whom God made the creation, He also bestowed salvation on the men included in the creation
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of this world a different God from the Father of Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIX.—Absurdities of the heretics as to their own origin: their opinions respecting the Demiurge shown to be equally untenable and ridiculous.
sources.answer: The Creator is the only true God. Irenaeus concludes that the Valentinian system, which demotes the Fashioner and Former of the universe beneath a higher deity, has been shown to be wicked, deceitful and easily overthrown. Exposing its key parts is enough to reveal that it is clay painted to look like gold.
sources.quote: wicked opinions respecting the Demiurge, that is, the Fashioner and Former of this universe, and who is in fact the only true God
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of this world (whom the Valentinians call the Demiurge) the only true God, or is there a higher god above him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VI.—Explanation of the words of Christ, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” etc.; which words the heretics misinterpret. Proof that, by the Father revealing the Son, and by the Son being revealed, the Father was never unknown.
sources.answer: There is one God. Through all things there is one God the Father, one Word, one Son, one Spirit, and one salvation to all who believe. The same Word reveals both the Creator and the Father who begat the Son.
sources.quote: there is one God, the Father, and one Word, and one Son, and one Spirit, and one salvation to all who believe in Him.
sources.raw_question: Is the creator of the world and the Father revealed by Christ one God, or are there different gods?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVIII.—Concerning sacrifices and oblations, and those who truly offer them.
sources.answer: No. If the Father were different from the Creator, then the Church's offering to Him of the fruits of this creation would present Him as covetous of another's property and desirous of what is not His own. Those who say the world arose from apostasy, ignorance and passion likewise insult their Father by offering Him such fruits. Only the Church, which confesses one Creator-Father, offers a pure oblation to Him from His own creation.
sources.quote: For some, by maintaining that the Father is different from the Creator, do, when they offer to Him what belongs to this creation of ours, set Him forth as being covetous of another’s property, and desirous of what is not His own.
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who distinguish the Father from the Creator
sources.raw_question: Is the Father of Jesus Christ a different being from the Creator of the world, as some Gnostic heretics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IV.—The truth is to be found nowhere else but in the Catholic Church, the sole depository of apostolical doctrine. Heresies are of recent formation, and cannot trace their origin up to the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. The apostolic faith confesses one God, the Creator of heaven and earth and all things in them, who acts by means of Christ Jesus, the Son of God. This Son became incarnate, uniting man to God, and will judge those who despise his Father. The Creator is therefore not a lesser being distinct from Christ's Father.
sources.quote: believing in one God, the Creator of heaven and earth, and all things therein, by means of Christ Jesus, the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Is the one God, Creator of heaven and earth, the same God who is the Father of Jesus Christ, and does he create through the Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VI.—Explanation of the words of Christ, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” etc.; which words the heretics misinterpret. Proof that, by the Father revealing the Son, and by the Son being revealed, the Father was never unknown.
sources.answer: Yes. The only-begotten Son came from the one God who made the world and formed us, and the Lord's own words show the Father to be Maker of heaven and earth. Christ set forth the Father as he really is so that we receive no other Father than the one revealed by the Son, not the false father invented by Marcion, Valentinus and others.
sources.quote: But this [Father] is the Maker of heaven and earth, as is shown from His words; and not he, the false father, who has been invented by Marcion, or by Valentinus
sources.raw_question: Is the Father whom the Son reveals the same God who is Maker of heaven and earth?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter X.—Unity of the faith of the Church throughout the whole world.
sources.answer: They are the same. The Church's apostolic rule confesses one God, the Father Almighty, as Maker of heaven, earth and all things. No teacher may conceive of some other God besides the Framer, Maker and Preserver of the universe, as if he were not sufficient.
sources.quote: conceive of some other God besides Him who is the Framer, Maker, and Preserver of this universe, (as if He were not sufficient[^2791] for them), or of another Christ, or another Only-begotten
sources.raw_question: Is the one God, the Father Almighty, the same being as the Maker of heaven and earth, or is the Creator a different God from the supreme Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: No. The first principles of the Gospel are that there is one God, the Maker of the universe, who was announced by the prophets and gave the law through Moses. This God is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Gospel ignores any other God or Father besides Him. There is none beyond Him.
sources.quote: that there is one God, the Maker of this universe; He who was also announced by the prophets, and who by Moses set forth the dispensation of the law,—[principles] which proclaim the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and ignore any other God or Father except Him.
sources.raw_question: Is there any God or Father beyond or above the Creator who is the Father of Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXV.—God is not to be sought after by means of letters, syllables, and numbers; necessity of humility in such investigations.
sources.answer: No. The Creator cannot be surpassed or contained within limits. Even if one measured and passed through all creation, one could not conceive of anyone above the Father Himself. To seek a God above the Creator is folly, ending in madness and the conceit of thinking oneself greater than one's Maker.
sources.quote: nor do thou seek after any one above the Creator, for thou wilt not discover such. For thy Former cannot be contained within limits
sources.raw_question: Is there any God or power above the Creator and Father, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: Yes. Both the Lord and the apostles announce the Father as the one only God who gave the law, sent the prophets and made all things. Hence the parable speaks of 'His armies,' because every man is his workmanship and property, as the earth is the Lord's and he gives existence to all, sending sun and rain on just and unjust.
sources.quote: Both the Lord, then, and the apostles announce as the one only God the Father, Him who gave the law, who sent the prophets, who made all things
sources.raw_question: Is the Father of Jesus Christ the same God who gave the law, sent the prophets, and created all things?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: There is one God who established and completed all things out of nothing; he contains all things and is contained by none. Malachi asks, "Have we not all one Father?" and the apostle says there is one God, the Father, above all and in us all.
sources.quote: First of all believe that there is one God, who has established all things, and completed them, and having caused that from what had no being, all things should come into existence:” He who contains all things, and is Himself contained by no one.
sources.raw_question: Is the God who created all things the same one God and Father whom Scripture proclaims, or a different being?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Preface.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus holds that the God who founded and adorned the universe, the Creator of heaven and earth and all things in them, is the true God, and there is nothing more excellent to be revealed beyond Him. The Gnostics draw people away from this God by pretending to possess superior knowledge. Irenaeus calls their opinions about the Demiurge blasphemous and impious, and says they falsify the oracles of God.
sources.quote: drawing them away, under a pretence of [superior] knowledge, from Him who founded and adorned the universe; as if, forsooth, they had something more excellent and sublime to reveal, than that God who created the heaven and the earth
sources.raw_question: Is there a higher, more sublime God above the Creator (Demiurge) who made heaven and earth, as the Valentinian Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: The Creator and the Father are one and the same. Irenaeus holds that the clearly proclaimed faith is that this Being alone is truly God and Father, who formed the world, fashioned man, and brings creation to maturity. The same Creator made both the womb and the sun, and the same Lord raised the stalk and prepared the barn.
sources.quote: this Being alone is truly God and Father, who both formed this world, fashioned man, and bestowed the faculty of increase on His own creation
sources.raw_question: Is the one true God and Father the same Being who created the world and fashioned man, or is the Creator a different being from the supreme Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIX.—A comparison is instituted between the disobedient and sinning Eve and the Virgin Mary, her patroness. Various and discordant heresies are mentioned.
sources.answer: No. Some heretics posit another Father besides the Creator, or say the world was made by angels or came from defect and ignorance. Irenaeus says they do this because they are ignorant of God's arrangements and blind to the truth. The Church throughout the world receives one and the same God the Father, who is the Creator.
sources.quote: since all receive one and the same God the Father, and believe in the same dispensation regarding the incarnation of the Son of God, and are cognizant of the same gift of the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Is there another Father above or besides the Creator of the world, as the Gnostic heretics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXV.—A refutation of those who allege that the prophets uttered some predictions under the inspiration of the highest, others from the Demiurge. Disagreements of the Valentinians among themselves with regard to these same predictions.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus confesses one God, the Creator of the universe, who sent the prophets, led Israel out of Egypt, and in the last times manifested His own Son. In the parable of the vineyard the Lord shows that the one who sent the prophets as servants is the same who sent his only son. So the prophets did not speak from another god or another essence, but from one and the same Father.
sources.quote: knowing but one God, the Creator of this universe, who sent the prophets, who led forth the people from the land of Egypt, who in these last times manifested His own Son
sources.raw_question: Is the God who created the world and sent the prophets the same God who is the Father of Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter II.—The world was not formed by angels, or by any other being, contrary to the will of the most high God, but was made by the Father through the Word.
sources.answer: Yes. Moses says God created the heaven and the earth, with neither gods nor angels taking part. Paul declares that this God is the one God and Father, who is above all. So the Creator is the Father of Christ, and he made the world through his Word.
sources.quote: Now, that this God is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Paul the apostle also has declared, [saying,] “There is one God, the Father, who is above all, and through all things, and in us all.”
sources.raw_question: Is the God who created the world the same as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: No. Christ took bread and the mixed cup from the very creation we belong to and declared them his body and blood. That would be unjust if creation belonged to another father. He also forgave the sins for which we are answerable to our Maker, which shows he is the Son of the Creator God.
sources.quote: how could the Lord, with any justice, if He belonged to another father, have acknowledged the bread to be His body, while He took it from that creation to which we belong, and affirmed the mixed cup to be His blood?
sources.raw_question: Could Christ be the Son of some Father other than the Creator of this world?

question: Does the term 'ungenerate' (ungeneracy) name the very essence of God, as Eunomius claims, or is it a conception applied to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Basil's exposition shows that 'ungenerate' has a meaning far removed from essence. It only signifies that God, as First Cause, depends on nothing else. In the same way, being the son of somebody is not a man's essence.
sources.quote: Now in the case of men, the being son of somebody is not the essence; no more, in the case of the Deity Who rules the world, is it possible to say that the being ungenerate is the essence.
sources.raw_question: Does the term 'ungenerate' signify the essence of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Following Basil, Gregory holds that such terms have no existence in nature. They are attached as mental conceptions to the things they signify. To confine the infinite Divine essence within the single term "ungeneracy" is a fallacy, and the Eunomians use it to pave the way for blaspheming the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: pointed out, in regard to the terms, that they have no existence in nature, but are attached as conceptions to the things signified
sources.raw_question: Does the term "ungenerate" (ungeneracy) name the very essence of God, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. "Ungenerate" is a privative term that tells us only that birth does not belong to God, not what God positively is. Like harmless, painless, or sleepless, it removes something not inherent in God rather than declaring what is present, so it cannot serve as a definition of the divine essence.
sources.quote: this vehement adversary of the truth opposes these teachings, and hopes with the sounding word “ungeneracy” to supply a clear definition of the essence of God.
sources.raw_question: Does the term "ungenerate" (ungeneracy) define the essence of God, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: They indicate God's eternity, not his being. 'Ungenerate' means that no source or cause lies beyond him, and 'Endless' means that his kingdom will never come to a standstill. Psalm 102 shows both: 'Thou art' indicates subsistence from no cause, and 'thy years shall not fail' indicates unending life.
sources.quote: The orthodox theory allows these words, I mean “Ungenerate,” “Endless,” to be indicative of God’s eternity, but not of His being; so that “Ungenerate” means that no source or cause lies beyond Him
sources.raw_question: Do the terms 'Ungenerate' and 'Endless' signify God's essence or something else?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius claims that the divine nature simply is ungeneracy and that every other divine attribute depends on it, which would strip the Son of all divine attributes. Gregory rejects this: the ineffable Being cannot be captured by any word, and no human faculty can fully grasp the divine essence. To claim that one term contains the whole of Godhead is therefore presumption, not knowledge.
sources.quote: they maintain that the divine nature is simply ungeneracy per se, and declaring this to be sovereign and supreme, they make this word comprehend the whole greatness of Godhead
sources.raw_question: Is 'ungeneracy' the very essence of God, so that whatever is not ungenerate lacks Godhead and all the other divine attributes?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It is applied by mental conception. Eunomius argued that the term is not used by conception, by deprivation or by division, and so must name God's essence. Basil, whom Gregory defends as 'our master', agreed that God has no parts and that 'ungenerate' is not a partial predicate. But he rejected the claim that the term is not applied by way of mental conception, and he gave proofs for this.
sources.quote: but the statement that this term ought not to be applied to Him by way of mental conception he impugns, and gives his proofs
sources.raw_question: Is 'ungenerate' applied to God by mental conception (epinoia), or does it name God's essence directly, as Eunomius argued?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It is predicated of God only as a notion or conception, not as a name of His essence. Gregory follows Basil, who refuted Eunomius' contrary opinion with proofs drawn from common sense and from Scripture. Gregory adds that Eunomius could neither accept nor overturn these proofs, and that his second treatise only goes round in circles on this point.
sources.quote: affirms that “ungenerate” cannot be predicated of God except as a mere notion or conception, whereof he has adduced proofs supported by common sense and the evidence of Scripture
sources.raw_question: Does the term "ungenerate" name the very essence of God, or is it predicated of God only as a human notion or conception?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. 'Ungenerate' belongs with the privative names like imperishable and unending, which only signify the absence of conditions abhorrent to God's nature. What the Deity is not these names point out, but what He is essentially remains undivulged.
sources.quote: What the Deity is not, the signification of these names does point out; but what that further thing, which is not these things, is essentially, remains undivulged.
sources.raw_question: Does the term 'ungenerate' (unbegotten) reveal the very essence of God, as Eunomius claimed?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It is a conception, not the substance. If the term is retained alongside "conception," the truth prevails once "ungeneracy" is moved from the substance to a conception of the Deity; and if it is suppressed, no opposed name remains to detract from the Only-begotten Son's majesty.
sources.quote: when we have altered the word “ungeneracy” from the substance, into a conception, of the Deity.
sources.raw_question: Is "ungeneracy" the essence of God, or a conception applied to the Deity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The Eunomians idolize their own imagination by treating 'ungeneracy' as God or the essence of God. In fact it is only something discernible in a certain relation within the Divine nature. Like the other names applied to God, it indicates something about Him, not His essence.
sources.quote: they deify the idea expressed by this “ungeneracy” of theirs, as not being only in a certain relation discernible in the Divine nature, but as being itself God, or the essence of God.
sources.raw_question: Is 'ungeneracy' (being unbegotten) the very essence of God, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. It is true that the Father's essence is ungenerate, since no orthodox believer holds that the Father is begotten. But ungeneracy is not identical with the divine essence. If being, indestructibility and ungeneracy all meant the same thing, then lacking ungeneracy would mean lacking being and Godhead altogether. Eunomius' position therefore leads to absurdity.
sources.quote: But if, while the form of his expression indicates only this, he maintains that the ungeneracy itself is the essence, I say that we ought not to leave such a position unexamined
sources.raw_question: Is ungeneracy the very essence of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: No. They indicate God's eternity, not his being. 'Ungenerate' means that no source or cause lies beyond him. The order of cause among the Persons introduces no temporal interval and no discord in the Trinity.
sources.quote: Extensions in time find no admittance in the Eternal Life; so that, when we have removed the thought of cause, the Holy Trinity in no single way exhibits discord with itself
sources.raw_question: Do the terms 'Ungenerate' and 'Endless' signify God's essence or being?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It is a concept we form, not God's essence. Gregory holds that from seeing that the universe depends on God, we infer that there is no cause of His existence. Ungeneracy is therefore one of the many ideas by which the mind gropes toward God, whose essence remains beyond our grasp, rather than a definition of His substance.
sources.quote: from our belief that this Universe depends on Him, we get an indication that there is no cause whatever of His existence
sources.raw_question: Is ungeneracy (being without cause or origin) the very essence of God, or a concept we form about God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds it is madness to make "not generated" the definition of God's substance, since ungeneracy signifies only the absence of generation. It indicates what is not in the Father, and the indication of something absent cannot be His substance.
sources.quote: Ungeneracy indicates that which is not in the Father; so how shall we allow the indication of that which is absent to be His substance?
sources.raw_question: Does the term "Ungenerate" (Ungeneracy) express the very substance or essence of God the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The term ungeneracy is declarative of God's ungenerate subsistence, pointing to the fact that God subsists without prior cause, but it does not name or constitute the Divine nature itself. God is ungenerate, but ungeneracy is not God; the word is far removed from the Divine essence.
sources.quote: For we maintain that this term is declarative of God’s ungenerate subsistence, but not that ungeneracy is God.
sources.raw_question: Does the term 'ungenerate' (ungeneracy) denote the very essence of God, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius cannot show that "ungeneracy", which he excepts from the products of conception, is any more indissoluble and fixed when uttered than any other word, since it too does not abide in the air. Nor does he explain in what signification "ungenerate" would declare the essence. So his attempt to make ungeneracy the essence of God, rather than a term applied by conception, fails.
sources.quote: nor will he be able to show that ungeneracy itself, which he excepts from the products of conception, is indissoluble and fixed when it has been uttered
sources.raw_question: Is "ungenerate" (ungeneracy) predicated of God in a way that is exempt from human conception, so that it alone names God's essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. "Ungenerate" is one of several equivalent terms, such as without origin, eternal, First Cause, and alone without cause, all of like force in meaning. Orthodoxy lies in the mind's conception, not in sounds and syllables, so it is folly to contend for one word. Privative terms tell us what God is not, not what His essence is.
sources.quote: it is mere folly to contend for this or that vocal intonation, as if orthodoxy were a thing of sounds and syllables rather than of the mind.
sources.raw_question: Does the term "ungenerate" (ungeneracy) uniquely define the essence of God, as Eunomius holds?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It is something said about His essence, not the essence itself. The ungenerate essence is, in its inherent idea, wholly different from what 'not having been generated' expresses. The Eunomians invert this and call ungeneracy His essence, so that the verbal opposition will imply that the Son has a different nature.
sources.quote: do not say that the essence of the Father is ungenerate, but, conversely, they declare ungeneracy to be His essence, in order that by this distinction in regard to generation they may establish, by the verbal opposition, a diversity of natures
sources.raw_question: Is ungeneracy the very essence of God the Father, or is it something said about His essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Basil (whom Gregory quotes approvingly) argues that just as being the son of somebody is not the essence of a man, so being the son of no one, i.e. ungenerate, is not the essence of God. Ungenerate merely signifies that God has no cause, a negative relation, not what God's substance is.
sources.quote: Now in the case of men, the being son of somebody is not the essence; no more, in the case of the Deity Who rules the world, is it possible to say that the being ungenerate is the essence.
sources.raw_question: Is 'ungenerate' (agennetos) the essence of God, as Eunomius claims?

question: Are two or three Persons of the Trinity together greater than any one Person alone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Of the Attributes Assigned by Hilary to Each Person. The Trinity is Represented in Things that are Made.
sources.answer: No. In bodies, one thing alone is not as much as three together. In the highest Trinity, however, one Person is as much as all three together, and two are no more than one. Each Person is in each and all are in each, so all are one and infinite.
sources.quote: but in that highest Trinity one is as much as the three together, nor are two anything more than one.
sources.raw_question: Are the three Persons of the Trinity together greater than one Person alone, as three bodies are more than one?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Preface.—The Conclusion of What Has Been Said Above. The Rule to Be Observed in the More Difficult Questions of the Faith.
sources.answer: No. The equality in the Trinity is such that the Father is not greater than the Son in divinity. Nor are the Father and Son together greater than the Holy Spirit, nor is any one Person less than the Trinity itself. In the following chapter Augustine argues that in the substance of truth only what is more true is greater, and two Persons together are not more truly than one.
sources.quote: neither are the Father and Son together greater than the Holy Spirit; nor is each individual person, whichever it be of the three, less than the Trinity itself
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and Son together greater than the Holy Spirit, or is any single divine Person less than the whole Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > No Addition Can Be Made to the Nature of God.
sources.answer: Yes. Each Person alone is as great as the Father, Son and Holy Spirit together, because divine perfection cannot increase. When the equal Son or the equal Spirit is joined to the equal Father, God does not become greater than each severally, since each is perfect and the three together are perfect.
sources.quote: In God Himself, therefore when the equal Son, or the Holy Spirit equal to the Father and the Son, is joined to the equal Father, God does not become greater than each of them severally; because that perfectness cannot increase.
sources.raw_question: Is any one Person of the Trinity (Father, Son, or Holy Spirit) alone as great as all three Persons together?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity.
sources.answer: No. Not only is the Father not greater than the Son, but no two Persons together are greater than one, and the three together are not greater than each singly. Greatness is said of God according to essence, not relatively, and in God to be is the same as to be great. So each Person is as great as the whole Trinity, and there is one great God, not three greats.
sources.quote: not only the Father is not greater than the Son, but neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each severally.
sources.raw_question: Are any two Persons of the Trinity together (for example the Father and the Son) greater than the Holy Spirit alone, or are all three together greater than each Person singly?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > It is Shown by Reason that in God Three are Not Anything Greater Than One Person.
sources.answer: No. In God, magnitude is not something other than truth: to be true is the same as to be, and to be is the same as to be great. Since the Father and Son together are not more truly than the Father or Son singly, they are not greater; likewise any two together, or the whole Trinity, are not greater than any one Person.
sources.quote: But the Father and the Son together are not more truly than the Father singly, or the Son singly. Both together, therefore, are not anything greater than each of them singly.
sources.raw_question: Are two or three Persons of the Trinity together anything greater than one Person alone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > God is a Trinity, But Not Triple (Triplex).
sources.answer: Yes. When the equal Son or the equal Spirit is joined to the equal Father, God does not become greater than each of them severally, because that perfectness cannot increase. In spiritual things, which are not great by bulk, to be greater is to be better, and each Person is already perfect.
sources.quote: In God Himself, therefore when the equal Son, or the Holy Spirit equal to the Father and the Son, is joined to the equal Father, God does not become greater than each of them severally; because that perfectness cannot increase.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit alone as great as the whole Trinity together?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: No. God is a Trinity, not something triple. The Father and Son are not a double over against a single Spirit, because in the Trinity three are not anything more than one.
sources.quote: God was not triple, but a Trinity; and that the Father and the Son are not, as it were, a double as opposed to the single Holy Spirit: for therein three are not anything more than one
sources.raw_question: Is God triple, and are the Father and the Son together something greater than the Holy Spirit alone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: No. Reason also shows that the Father is not greater than the Son in the substance of truth. Nor are any two together greater than one, nor all three together greater than each one severally.
sources.quote: nor that any two at all in the same Trinity are anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each severally
sources.raw_question: Are all three Persons of the Trinity together greater than any one of them alone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: No. Among men or golden statues, three amount to more than one. But in God the three together are not a greater essence than the Father alone or the Son alone; the three together are equal to each singly. The natural man fails to grasp this because he thinks only in terms of bodily bulk and space.
sources.quote: for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together is not a greater essence than the Father alone or the Son alone; but these three substances or persons, if they must be so called, together are equal to each singly
sources.raw_question: Are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together a greater essence than any one of them alone?

question: Are the names of things, including names applied to God, invented and imposed by God himself, or devised by human reason?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. God gave men reason and voice, so attributing the invention of vocal sounds to those naturally endowed with speech involves no impiety toward the Giver. Inventing significant words is no great thing: Scripture calls the same being "man" and Job calls him "mortal," while profane writers use other names, yet no one thinks these namers equal to God.
sources.quote: Whereas, to attribute the invention of vocal sound to those who are naturally endowed with the faculty of speech, this involves no impiety towards Him Who gave them their voice.
sources.raw_question: Is it impious to hold that human beings, rather than God, invent the words used to signify things, including names applied to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They are human devising. As God gave our nature practical powers but we build houses and ploughs ourselves, so He gave us the power of speech, but the invention of particular terms is ours. This is shown by the many base and unseemly terms no sensible man would ascribe to God, and by Levitical words like ephah and hin, which it would be absurd and beneath God's majesty to think He coined.
sources.quote: so also our power of speech is the work of Him Who made our nature what it is, but the invention of each several term required to denote objects in hand is of our own devising
sources.raw_question: Are the names of things invented by God, or are they human devising?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius claims that we must either deny creation to God or concede that he imposed the names. Scripture teaches the opposite of both alternatives for the animals: God made them, but Adam named them. So creating and naming are distinct acts, and naming belongs to the rational faculty God gave humanity.
sources.quote: that neither did Adam make the animals, nor did God name them, but the creation was the work of God, and the naming of the…
sources.raw_question: Does creating things mean God must also be the one who imposes their names?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: God is the Maker of things, not of empty words. All things that exist substantially are from God, but names are provided for our guidance, and it is no offence against Providence to say they were imposed by human usage. The nature of things is not of human invention, only their names.
sources.quote: Wherefore all things that exist substantially are from God; but, for our guidance, all things that exist are provided with names to indicate them.
sources.raw_question: Does God create the names of things, or only the things themselves, with names being supplied by human beings?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Names are the work of human reason. God creates the substantial things, while the distinguishing names by which speech describes them are invented by man's reasoning faculty, though that faculty itself is God's work. As God gives animals motion without directing each step, so he gave human nature speech and it names things by itself.
sources.quote: by the Divine will the thing is produced, not the name, so that the substantial thing is the work of the Creator, but the distinguishing names of things, by which speech furnishes us with a clear and accurate description of them, are the work and the invention of man’s reasoning faculty
sources.raw_question: Did God himself invent and impose the names of things, or are names the work of human reason?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Humans invented them. Scripture records no divine teaching of words, either before or after the division of languages. God willed that men should speak different languages and left human nature free to form sounds to express its meaning. This is shown by the fact that things look the same to everyone while their names differ from people to people.
sources.quote: God, willing that men should speak different languages, gave human nature full liberty to formulate arbitrary sounds, so as to render their meaning more intelligible
sources.raw_question: Did God give human beings the names of things, or did humans invent the words they use for things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Gregory rejects Eunomius's attempt to show that God speaks after the manner of men and assigns names to things. He sides with Basil's view that names are given by the rational nature we have received from God. Naming is therefore a human activity of reason, which God made possible but does not carry out word by word.
sources.quote: Now his whole treatise is an ambitious attempt to show that God speaks after the manner of men, and that the Creator of all things gives them suitable names, indicative of the things themselves.
sources.raw_question: Does God himself give names to created things in human fashion, or are names given by the rational nature God has given to humans?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius offers a dilemma: either deny God the creation of things, or grant him the giving of names. Scripture teaches the opposite of both alternatives. Moses records that God made the animals, yet it was Adam, not God, who named them. So creating a thing and naming it are distinct acts, belonging to God and to man respectively.
sources.quote: neither did Adam make the animals, nor did God name them, but the creation was the work of God, and the naming of the things created was the work of man, as Moses has recorded.
sources.raw_question: If God is admitted to be the creator of things, must he also be held to be the one who imposed their names?

question: Does the phrase "God said" in the Genesis creation account mean that God literally spoke with a voice and articulate words in a human language?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. If "God said" were taken in a sensuous literal sense, then by parity "God saw," "heard," and "smelled" would require bodily organs, yielding an anthropomorphic deity. One who forms ideas worthy of God will regard such verbal utterances as indications of the Divine will, not as articulate sounds.
sources.quote: he will regard the verbal utterances as indications of the Divine will, but on the other he will not conceive of them as articulate sounds
sources.raw_question: Does the scriptural phrase "God said" in the creation account imply that God uses articulate speech, so that human language was His creation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Moses lived long after Babel and wrote in his own native tongue, which some hold was given to the Hebrews only after the Exodus. He used human language because there was no other way to express his meaning. To suppose that God spoke Hebrew before creation, when there was no one to hear and benefit, is both blasphemous and absurd.
sources.quote: Neither, then, did God speak in the Hebrew language, nor did He express Himself according to any form in use among the Gentiles.
sources.raw_question: When Moses records God speaking in Genesis, does that mean God actually spoke in Hebrew or some other human language?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The words "He said" do not imply voice and words on God's part; Moses uses this familiar human way of signifying will to show that God's power is concurrent with His will. Since men ordinarily signify their will by speech, Scripture represents the divine will by an image easy to grasp, sensible apprehension aiding intellectual knowledge.
sources.quote: We assert that the words “He said” do not imply voice and words on the part of God; but the writer, in showing the power of God to be concurrent with His will, renders the idea more easy of apprehension.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase "God said" in the Genesis creation account mean that God spoke with a voice and words?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. To read it so reduces God to a human standard, as if He directed His works through speech. Just as the heavens declare God's glory without a voice, God's fiat means only His will, and the names of created things signify only their actually coming into being. From the record we learn that God made all things by His will, and that the Divine will became nature without any effort.
sources.quote: let His fiat mean His will only, and let the names of those created things denote the mere reality of their coming into being
sources.raw_question: When Genesis says "God said" and names created things, does this mean God created by speaking articulate words?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Speech and hearing are correlative, so literal speech requires a hearer; if God spoke to Himself He would be issuing commands to Himself as His own minister, which is absurd, and no one needs words to form his own choice and volition. Literal vocal speech would also imply bodily organs, form, and composition, which cannot belong to God.
sources.quote: If, then, he means literally that “God said,” let him tell us also to what hearing His words were addressed. Does he mean that He said them to Himself? If so, the commands which He issues, He issues to Himself.
sources.raw_question: Does Moses' phrase "God said" in the creation account ("Let there be light") mean that God literally uttered vocal words?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Scripture itself, in Psalm 19, speaks of the heavens declaring and day uttering speech while there is neither speech nor language nor audible voice. This is no contradiction but shows that such 'speech' is a revelation of God's power to those able to perceive it, without articulate voice; Moses' language is to be understood likewise as a bodily illustration.
sources.quote: the word shouted forth by the day, is no articulate voice nor language of the lips, but is a revelation of the power of God to those who are capable of hearing it, even though no voice be heard?
sources.raw_question: Does Moses' statement that 'God said' in Genesis prove that God speaks with articulate words and sounds?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Speech and hearing are naturally correlated, so literal speech would need a hearer. Before creation there was no one to hear. And God would not need words to address Himself, since even a man's own mental act suffices for choice and will.
sources.quote: who has any need of words and speech for himself, even though a man? For every one’s own mental action suffices him to produce choice and volition.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase "God said" in Genesis 1 mean that God literally spoke words aloud?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The impulse of the divine mind is frequently called a voice in Scripture, as when God asked Moses "Wherefore criest thou unto Me?" though Moses had uttered nothing aloud. So Moses described God's will after human fashion, signified by its effects rather than expressed in actual words.
sources.quote: the thought which the Prophet had lifted up to God is called a cry, though uttered in silence in the hidden thought of his heart.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says "God said" at creation, does it mean God spoke audible words or instituted words?

question: Does the opposition between 'generate' (the Son) and 'ungenerate' (the Father) prove that the Son differs from the Father in essence or nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: No. Eunomius transfers the verbal contrariety between 'Generated' and 'Ungenerate' to the Persons themselves and argues from a difference of words to a difference of Beings, which is a quibble. Properly, 'Generated' is used only because the Son was generated and 'Ungenerate' because the Father exists without having been generated; the terms do not sunder the Son's being from the Father's nature.
sources.quote: he transfers the contrariety between the actual expressions ‘Generated’ and ‘Ungenerate’ to the Persons themselves to whom these words apply; and thereby, by this difference between the words he argues by a quibble for a difference between the Beings
sources.raw_question: Does the difference between the terms 'Generated' and 'Ungenerate' prove a difference of being or nature between the Son and the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory calls this a sophistical inference. Eunomius sets aside all the shared attributes that show the Son's equal honour and dignity with the Father and looks only at the one opposition of terms. Gregory treats this as a disguised way of denying that the Only-begotten is very God.
sources.quote: There is no need, they urge, of looking at the collective attributes by which the Son’s equality in honour and dignity with the Father is signified, but from the opposition between generate and ungenerate we must argue a distinctive difference of nature
sources.raw_question: Does the contrast between 'generate' (the Son) and 'ungenerate' (the Father) prove that the Son differs in nature or essence from the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > He says that all things that are in creation have been named by man, if, as is the case, they are called differently by every nation, as also the appellation of “Ungenerate” is conferred by us: but that the proper appellation of the Divine essence itself which expresses the Divine Nature, either does not exist at all, or is unknown to us.
sources.answer: No. Names are human-imposed signs of concepts and do not signify essences. Eunomius would first have to produce names that signify essences before he could divide the subject by the difference of names. Since the divine nature is incomprehensible and unnameable, any argument that claims to grasp and divide it by the meaning of names is futile.
sources.quote: Let him then leave his accustomed language of fable, and show us the names which signify the essences, and then proceed further to divide the subject by the divergence of their names.
sources.raw_question: Can a difference in names such as "Ungenerate" and "Generate" prove a difference of essence between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then shows, from the instance of Adam and Abel, and other examples, the absence of alienation of essence in the case of the “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. Whoever says an essence is generated already distinguishes the generation from the essence. The Gospel saying about a man being born shows the same thing: the birth is not the man, but the man exists by the birth. So the clash between the names 'generate' and 'ungenerate' cannot be carried over to the essences themselves.
sources.quote: it will no longer be possible for them, if they apply the opposition of “generate” and “ungenerate” to the essence of the Father and the Son, to apply at the same time to the things themselves the mutual conflict between these names
sources.raw_question: Does the opposition between 'generate' and 'ungenerate' prove that the Father and the Son differ in essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He thus shows the oneness of the Eternal Son with the Father the identity of essence and the community of nature (wherein is a natural inquiry into the production of wine), and that the terms “Son” and “product” in the naming of the Only-Begotten include a like idea of relationship.
sources.answer: No. The term "essence" means one thing and "generation" another, so a difference in manner of origin does not produce a difference of essence. Just as Abel, though generated, was the same in essence as the ungenerated Adam, so the Only-begotten by his generation introduces no change in the essence of the Ungenerate; he is "Light of Light, very God of very God," being all that the Father is save being the Father.
sources.quote: the Only-begotten God did not, by His own generation, produce in Himself any change in the essence of Him Who is ungenerate
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being generated (as opposed to the Father's being ungenerate) imply that the Son has a different essence from the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. Eunomius uses the contradictory pair 'generate/ungenerate' as if it marked a difference of nature like mortal and immortal, rational and irrational, in order to subordinate the Son as the irrational is subject to the rational. Gregory exposes this as a device to smuggle in a difference of essence that the names Father and Son themselves exclude.
sources.quote: just so he wants to make out that the nature of the ungenerate is one, and that of the generate another, in order to show that as the irrational nature has been created in subjection to the rational
sources.raw_question: Does the opposition between 'ungenerate' and 'generate' imply that the Father and the Son have different natures, as with 'mortal' and 'immortal'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. 'He was generated' and 'He was not generated' are like 'he is seated' and 'he is not seated.' They are formal contradictories about a mode, not definitions of essence. A man's sitting or not sitting is not his essence, so a verbal opposition about generation cannot establish a diversity of natures.
sources.quote: they pretend that this formal contradiction in expression indicates an essential difference, ascribing generation to the Son and non-generation to the Father as their essential attributes
sources.raw_question: Does the contradiction between the terms 'ungenerate' (said of the Father) and 'generate' (said of the Son) prove that the Father and the Son differ in essence?

question: Does the Son's being sent by the Father imply that the Son is less than the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Of the Sensible Showing of the Holy Spirit, and of the Coeternity of the Trinity. What Has Been Said, and What Remains to Be Said.
sources.answer: No. Scripture speaks of the Son's sending either on account of the visible creature through which he appeared, or to commend to our minds the procession (emanation) within the Godhead, not on account of any inequality, imparity, or unlikeness of substance.
sources.quote: the Son is not therefore less because He is sent by the Father, nor the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being sent by the Father imply that the Son is less than the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: No. Just as the begetter and the begotten are one, so the sender and the sent are one, because the Father and the Son are one. Sending no more implies inferiority than begetting does; both merely express that the Son is from the Father.
sources.quote: But in like manner as He who begat and He who was begotten, so both He who sent and He who was sent, are one, since the Father and the Son are one.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being sent by the Father make the Son less than or unequal to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son.
sources.answer: No. The Son is made less by being sent only with respect to the form of a servant he took. According to the form of God he is not less than the Father, because he was also sent by himself.
sources.quote: the Son of God, although made less by being sent, on account of the form of a servant which He took, is not therefore less than the Father according to the form of God, because He was sent by Himself
sources.raw_question: Does the Son of God's being sent by the Father make him less than the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: No. The Son is sent not because the Father is greater and the Son less, but because the one is Father and the other Son, the one begetter and the other begotten. Sending expresses only that the Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son, and implies no inequality of power or substance.
sources.quote: Not because the one is greater, the other less; but because the one is Father, the other Son; the one begetter, the other begotten; the one, He from whom He is who is sent; the other, He who is from Him who sends.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being sent by the Father imply that the Son is less than the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > Preface.
sources.answer: No. Augustine recalls that the previous book set out to show that the Son is not less than the Father because of being sent. Likewise the Holy Spirit is not less than the Father and the Son because the Gospel says He is sent by both. Being sent, he argues, does not imply inferiority of nature.
sources.quote: we desired to show that the Son was not therefore less than the Father, because the Father sent and the Son was sent; nor the Holy Spirit therefore less than both, because we read in the Gospel that He was sent both by the one and by the other
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Father sends the Son and the Son is sent show that the Son is less than the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In What Manner the Son Was Sent and Proclaimed Beforehand. How in the Sending of His Birth in the Flesh He Was Made Less Without Detriment to His Equality with the Father.
sources.answer: Only in respect of what he was made, not in his divinity. He is less in so far as he was made, and made in so far as he was sent. Yet because all things were made by him before he was made and sent, he is confessed equal to the sender.
sources.quote: If, therefore, the greater sends the less, we too, acknowledge Him to have been made less; and in so far less, in so far as made; and in so far made, in so far as sent.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being sent by the Father make him less than the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In What Manner the Son Was Sent and Proclaimed Beforehand. How in the Sending of His Birth in the Flesh He Was Made Less Without Detriment to His Equality with the Father.
sources.answer: It reflects only their relation. The Son is sent not because one is greater and the other less, but because one is Father and the other Son: one is the begetter and the other begotten. The Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son. So he remains equal, consubstantial and co-eternal with the sender.
sources.quote: Not because the one is greater, the other less; but because the one is Father, the other Son; the one begetter, the other begotten
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being sent by the Father imply any inequality between them, or does it reflect only their relation as Father and Son?

question: Can a transient trinity in the mind, such as faith held in memory, contemplated and loved in this life, be the image of God in man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Trinity Which is the Image of God is Now to Be Sought in the Noblest Part of the Mind.
