sources.answer: No, not the true image. Although faith begins wholly within the mind, it began to be in a mind that already existed without it, so it is somewhat adventitious. Faith will also pass away when sight succeeds it. The trinity it forms therefore changes with time and is not the abiding image.
sources.quote: because it began to be in the mind, which was a mind also before these things began to be in it, it seems to be somewhat adventitious, and will be reckoned among things past, when sight shall have succeeded, and itself shall have ceased to be.
sources.raw_question: Can the trinity formed by faith in the mind be the true image of God, given that faith arises within the mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Image of God is to Be Sought in the Immortality of the Rational Soul. How a Trinity is Demonstrated in the Mind.
sources.answer: No. A trinity that once did not exist, or that will later cease to exist, cannot be the image of God. The image must be sought in what is permanent in the rational soul, the image of the Creator "immortally implanted in its immortality."
sources.quote: Therefore neither is that trinity an image of God, which is not now, nor is that other an image of God, which then will not be; but we must find in the soul of man, i.e., the rational or intellectual soul, that image of the Creator
sources.raw_question: Can a transient trinity in the mind, such as the faith held, remembered and loved in this present life, be the image of God in man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > There is a Kind of Trinity in the Holding, Contemplating, and Loving of Faith Temporal, But One that Does Not Yet Attain to Being Properly an Image of God.
sources.answer: No. Faith is a temporal thing that will cease when we pass from walking by faith to seeing face to face. A trinity built on the holding, contemplating, and loving of this faith would then be past and done with. If it were the image of God, that image would belong among transient things rather than things that always exist. The image of God ought to be found in things eternal.
sources.quote: in the holding, contemplating, and loving this temporal faith, we have not yet reached such a trinity as is to be called an image of God; lest that should seem to be constituted in things temporal which ought to be so in things eternal
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity formed by the mind's remembering, contemplating, and loving its own temporal faith properly an image of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > A Difficulty Removed, Which Lies in the Way of What Has Just Been Said.
sources.answer: No. Since the soul is immortal and its best feature is being made after the image of its Creator, that image must endure as long as the soul does. Faith will pass into sight, so the trinity of holding, contemplating, and loving faith is transient; the image of God must be sought in what will always exist in the soul, namely its rational or intellectual nature.
sources.quote: We must find then what may be fittingly called the image of God, not in the holding, contemplating, and loving that faith which will not exist always, but in that which will exist always.
sources.raw_question: Can the image of God in the human soul be located in a transient mental trinity, such as the remembering, contemplating, and loving of present faith?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God.
sources.answer: No. Augustine holds that the image of God, which man is in respect of his mind, is not properly placed in transitory things. This holds even for the memory, understanding and love of faith as it exists in time. It is placed instead in things that are permanent, so that the mind images God when it is turned toward what is eternal.
sources.quote: the image of God, which man is in respect to his mind, is not placed properly in transitory things, as in memory, understanding, and love, whether of faith itself as existing in time
sources.raw_question: Is the image of God in the human mind properly located in the trinity of memory, understanding and love directed at temporal things, such as faith as it exists in time?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What Has Been Treated of in This Book. How We Have Reached by Steps to a Certain Trinity, Which is Found in Practical Knowledge and True Faith.
sources.answer: No. The ideas of faith held in memory, looked at by recollection and pleasing the will form a trinity of their own sort. But the image of God is not yet in that trinity. As the next book shows, the image lies not in transitory things such as faith existing in time, but in what is permanent, when the mind is renewed in the knowledge of God and contemplates what is eternal.
sources.quote: But the image of God, of which by His help we shall afterwards speak, is not yet in that trinity; a thing which will then be more apparent, when it shall have been shown where it is
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity formed in the mind by faith held in memory, recalled and loved the image of God in man?

question: Does the title 'Father' applied to God signify both that He has begotten the Son and that He Himself has no prior cause, that is, is Ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: Yes. The word Father means both the having begotten a Son and that the Begetter is not to be thought of as coming from any cause. Looking to the effect, the word reveals the Person of the Son; looking for a prior cause, the same word shows the absence of any beginning in the Begetter.
sources.quote: If you look at the effect, the Person of the Son is revealed in the word Father; if you look for a previous Cause, the absence of any beginning in the Begetter is shown by that word.
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'Father' signify both God's having begotten the Son and the Father's being without any cause (ungenerate)?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. Only if the two ideas were contradictories would affirming one require denying the other, but nothing prevents the same Existence from being both Father and Ungenerate. So the title Father can imply the absence of beginning and still mark the relation to a Son.
sources.quote: If, indeed, the one idea was totally destructive of the other, it would certainly follow, from the very nature of contradictories, that the affirming of the one would involve the denial of the other.
sources.raw_question: If the title 'Father' implies that God is ungenerate (has no cause), does it follow that 'Father' cannot also signify the begetting of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Defence of S. Basil's statement, attacked by Eunomius, that the terms 'Father' and 'The Ungenerate' can have the same meaning.
sources.answer: Yes. Basil, defended by Gregory, holds that One who essentially and alone is Father comes from none else, and what comes from none else is equivalent to the Ungenerate. So the idea of the Father's ungeneracy can be retained under the name Father without needing the non-scriptural word.
sources.quote: for One who essentially and alone is Father comes from none else; and that which comes from none else is equivalent to the Ungenerate.
sources.raw_question: Can the title 'Father' convey the same meaning as 'Ungenerate' when applied to God the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Defence of S. Basil's statement, attacked by Eunomius, that the terms 'Father' and 'The Ungenerate' can have the same meaning.
sources.answer: Yes. When we hear 'Father' we think of the Author of all beings; if he had some further cause above himself, the title Father would properly belong to that higher cause instead. Since he is the Cause from which all comes, nothing can be thought of beyond his existence, which is just to believe that his existence was not generated.
sources.quote: for if He had some further cause transcending Himself, He would not have been called thus of proper right Father; for that title would have had to be transferred higher, to this pre-supposed Cause.
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'Father' applied to God by itself imply that God the Father is ungenerate (has no cause)?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory holds that the designation Father carries both its proper meaning, having begotten a Son, and the meaning that there is no preconceivable cause of the Father. So the term Father conveys the sense of Ungenerate, though not every part of that sense is relative to the Son.
sources.quote: the designation of the Almighty as Father has both the special meaning of that word, i.e., the having begotten a son, and also that of there being no preconceivable cause of the Very Father
sources.raw_question: Does the name 'Father' applied to God include the meaning of being Ungenerate, that is, having no prior cause?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as names like 'God' and 'good' can be used both absolutely and relatively without losing their meaning, 'Father' can at once signify having begotten the Son and not being from any more transcendent Cause. The 'First Father' means Him presupposed before all existence, with nothing prior to Him, so the title implies both the begetting and the absence of origin.
sources.quote: there is nothing to prevent us, when we point out the Father and Him who comes from Him, the Firstborn before all creation, from signifying by that title of Father at one and the same time the having begotten that Son, and also the not being from any more transcendent Cause
sources.raw_question: Can the name 'Father' applied to God signify both that He has begotten the Son and that He Himself has no prior cause (is Ungenerate)?

question: Does confessing that God is One mean that God is solitary, a single isolated Person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. To confess God as One in the sense that He is alone or solitary would deny the Godhead of the Son. The true faith holds that God is One without being solitary, so the confession of unity must not be taken as isolation.
sources.quote: we cannot, as true believers, assert that God is One, if we mean by it that He is alone; for faith in a lonely God denies the Godhead of the Son.
sources.raw_question: Can Christians affirm that God is One if that means God is solitary or alone?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. The Church confesses the unity, not the solitude, of God, recognising the Father in the Son. To insist that God is One in order to teach His isolation is to be a stranger to the knowledge of God, because it denies that God is in God.
sources.quote: If in these Two you shall recognise the Unity, instead of the solitude, of God, you will share the Church’s faith, which confesses the Father in the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the oneness of God mean that God is solitary, a single isolated person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. To confess God as One is to deny that He is single. The name Father implies a Son, and the Son is the complement of the Father. Being Two by birth and generation, Father and Son are one God but not one Person.
sources.quote: When we confess that God is One we deny that He is single; for the Son is the complement of the Father, and to the Father the Son’s existence is due.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing that God is One mean that God is single or solitary?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Holding that God is solitary is blasphemy, because it would destroy the birth of the Only-begotten God. That is why Paul confessed both the Father and Christ, and why he taught one God without making God a single person.
sources.quote: not to misguide us into the blasphemy that God is solitary, which would destroy the birth of the Only-begotten God, he has confessed both Father and Christ
sources.raw_question: Is God solitary, a single person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The birth of the Son destroys the supposition of a lonely God. Father and Son are two Persons, each dwelling in the other by the power of their nature and the mystery of birth given and received. One and One can never be in solitude.
sources.quote: the birth destroys the supposition of a lonely God
sources.raw_question: Does confessing that God is One mean that God is a single, solitary Person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. God is One but not alone; the faith confesses neither an isolated God nor two Gods. Each Divine Person is in the Unity, yet no single Person is by himself the One God.
sources.quote: For we confess neither an isolated God, nor yet two Gods. Thus, neither denying that God is One nor maintaining that He is alone, we hold the straight road of truth. Each Divine Person is in the Unity, yet no Person is the One God.
sources.raw_question: Is God one in the sense of being a solitary, single Person?

question: What do the scriptural images of the Son as 'brightness of glory', 'savour of ointment' and 'breath of God' teach about the Son's relation to the Father, and do they show that He is co-eternal with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: Brightness exists concurrently with the glory from which it shines, and the two cannot be severed. The glory cannot be seen by itself before its brightness. To say the Father existed before the Son would make the Father's glory dark and dim. So the Son, as brightness of the Father's glory, has no beginning after the Father.
sources.quote: for before the brightness, of course neither was there any glory, for concurrently with the existence of the glory there assuredly beams forth its brightness; and it is impossible in the nature of things that one should be severed from the other
sources.raw_question: How does the image of the Son as the 'brightness of glory' show that the Son is coeternal with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He further shows the operations of God to be expressed by human illustrations; for what hands and feet and the other parts of the body with which men work are, that, in the case of God, the will alone is, in place of these. And so also arises the divergence of generation; wherefore He is called Only-begotten, because He has no community with other generation such as is observed in creation, but in that He is called the “brightness of glory,” and the “savour of ointment,” He shows the close conjunction and co-eternity of His Nature with the Father.
sources.answer: They teach that the Son is both from the Father and with the Father, co-eternal, with no intermediate interval between them. Purified of material sense (no dispersion of breath, transfer of scent, or emission of rays), these efflux images retain only that the radiance exists together with its source while proceeding from it.
sources.quote: this only, as we have said, is manifested by this particular mode of generation, that He is conceived to be of Him and also with Him, no intermediate interval existing between the Father and that Son Who is of Him.
sources.raw_question: What do the scriptural titles 'brightness of glory', 'savour of ointment' and 'breath of God' teach about the Son's relation to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
sources.answer: A ray is from the sun, since there would be no ray without the sun. Yet the sun is never conceived as existing without its ray. So the image conveys both the Son's derivation from the Father and the continuity and eternity of his existence with the Father. Just as the whole disc radiates, the Father's whole glory shines through the Son, the true Light.
sources.quote: yet the sun is never conceived as existing by itself without the ray of brightness that is shed from it, so the Apostle delivering to us the continuity and eternity of that existence which the Only-begotten has of the Father
sources.raw_question: How does calling the Son "the brightness of His glory" show that the Son is both from the Father and co-eternal with him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, thus passing over what relates to the essence of the Son as having been already discussed, he treats of the sense involved in “generation,” saying that there are diverse generations, those effected by matter and art, and of buildings,--and that by succession of animals,--and those by efflux, as by the sun and its beam. The lamp and its radiance, scents and ointments and the quality diffused by them,--and the word produced by the mind; and cleverly discusses generation from rotten wood; and from the condensation of fire, and countless other causes.
sources.answer: They point to the close conjunction and co-eternity of the Son's Nature with the Father. In generation by efflux, the source remains undiminished and has what flows from it concurrently with itself, as the sun has its beam. Scripture uses such familiar human modes of generation analogically, to raise the mind to what transcends language. The Son is called Only-begotten because His generation has no community with the generation observed in creation.
sources.quote: for these, while they remain in themselves without diminution, have at the same time, each concurrently with itself, that natural property which they emit: as the sun its beam, the lamp its brightness
sources.raw_question: What do the scriptural images of the Son as 'brightness of glory' and 'savour of ointment' teach about His relation to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Glory cannot be thought of as dark and lustreless, and ointment cannot exist without its sweet scent. So if the brightness "was not," the glory also was not. To deny that the Son always existed is therefore to deny the Father's eternal existence.
sources.quote: so that if the “brightness” “was not,” the “glory” also surely “was not,” and the “savour” being non-existent, there is also proved the non-existence of the “ointment.”
sources.raw_question: Do the scriptural images of the Son as "brightness of glory" and "savour of ointment" show that the Son is co-eternal with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: Because the image of sonship alone was not sufficient to convey the ineffable mode of the Only-begotten's subsistence. So Scripture adds the mode of generation by efflux, taken without any material sense. It teaches that the Son is from the Father and exists with Him, with no interval between them, as radiance is with its source.
sources.quote: by such a mode of generation is indicated this alone, that the Son is of the Father and is conceived of along with Him, no interval intervening between the Father and Him Who is of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture also describe the Son as 'brightness of glory', 'savour of ointment', and 'breath of God'?

question: Can one consistently deny that the Son is consubstantial with the Father without being committed to the Arian conclusion that he is a creature made from nothing (and so mutable and dependent)?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 14: Whether Dr. Clarke, who every where denies the consubstantiality oy the Son, as absurd and contradictory, does not, of consequence, affirm the Son to be a creat
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds that the Son is either consubstantial with the Father or a creature, with no middle ground. Denying the Son's consubstantiality, excluding him from the one Godhead, and counting him among created works therefore amounts to saying he is from nothing. This is the very essence of Arianism, whatever softer wording is used.
sources.quote: He has, by necessary consequence, asserted the Son to be ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, which is the very essence and characteristic of Arianism.
sources.raw_question: Does denying that the Son is consubstantial with the Father amount, by necessary consequence, to asserting that the Son is a creature made from nothing (ex ouk onton)?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 14: Whether Dr. Clarke, who every where denies the consubstantiality oy the Son, as absurd and contradictory, does not, of consequence, affirm the Son to be a creat
sources.answer: No. Waterland argues that the two are only different ways of saying the same thing, as he claims to have proved earlier. He thinks it absurd that someone could be blamed for stating a doctrine directly yet be blameless for affirming it indirectly. The fault cannot lie merely in sounds or syllables.
sources.quote: Or was Arius more culpable for saying, the Son was a creature, and from nothing, than another who says, he is not consubstantial with the Father, nor one God with him, or the like
sources.raw_question: Is saying the Son is 'not consubstantial with the Father, nor one God with him' really different from Arius's claim that the Son is a creature made from nothing?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 14: Whether Dr. Clarke, who every where denies the consubstantiality oy the Son, as absurd and contradictory, does not, of consequence, affirm the Son to be a creat
sources.answer: No. Waterland lists three possible grounds for condemning Arius: the claim is false, it is doubtful, or it is not stated in Scripture. If the claim is false, one cannot deny consubstantiality and coeternity. If it is doubtful, one must stay neutral rather than take a side. The third ground would equally condemn many of Clarke's own propositions. So whoever condemns Arius while denying consubstantiality condemns himself.
sources.quote: If the Doctor believed it false, he could not, consistently, disown the consubstantiality and coeternity; if he thought it dubious, he must have observed a neutrality
sources.raw_question: Can someone consistently condemn Arius's claim that the Son is from nothing while also rejecting the Son's consubstantiality and coeternity with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. The Son must be of the Father's divine substance, of some eternally pre-existing extraneous substance, or from nothing. Whoever denies the first two must hold the third. So censuring Arius for saying the Son came from nothing while denying his consubstantiality is inconsistent.
sources.quote: whether the Son be of the same divine substance with the Father; or of some extraneous substance which eternally preexisted; or from nothing ? The first you deny directly, as well as Arius; and the second also, by plain necessary consequence
sources.raw_question: Can one consistently deny that the Son is consubstantial with the Father while also denying that he was made from nothing?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 13: Whether there can be any middle between being made out of nothing, and out of something ; that is, between being out of nothing, and out of the Father's substan
sources.answer: Yes. The Arian scheme implies, though tacitly, that the Maker, Redeemer and Judge of the world is a mutable creature with a precarious existence and limited powers. On that view the Father could create another being equal or superior to him. Against this, Waterland asserts from Scripture and antiquity that the Son is infinitely removed from the condition of a creature and is truly and essentially God.
sources.quote: it is in the Father’s power, according to his own good pleasure, to create another equal, or even superior to him.
sources.raw_question: Does denying the Son's consubstantiality with the Father imply that the Son is a mutable, dependent creature whom God could surpass by creating another?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. All the Arian positions except the last (that the Son was made a little before the world) hang together as necessary consequences of one another. Those who stopped partway may have been more pious and modest, but they were less consistent. Holding a principle while disowning its plain consequences cannot be sustained.
sources.quote: indeed all of them, except the last, hang together; and are but the necessary consequences of each other.
sources.raw_question: Can someone consistently deny that the Son is consubstantial with the Father while rejecting the further Arian conclusions that he is a creature, made in time, mutable, and of limited knowledge?

question: Do names such as 'ungenerate' and 'imperishable' define God's essence, or are they human conceptions or negative attributes that only express what God is not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They are conceptions that express thoughts about God; they do not make God what he is. The life without beginning is 'styled' ungenerate, not 'made' such, and its endlessness is 'marked' as imperishable. Each term signifies one thought, that God is from no cause or that he does not pass into non-existence. The subject itself remains above every name and thought.
sources.quote: Thus, while the subject remains what it is, above everything, whether name or thought, the not being from any cause, and the not changing into the non-existent, are signified by means of the Conception implied in the aforesaid words.
sources.raw_question: Do names such as 'ungenerate' and 'imperishable' constitute or define God's essence, or are they human conceptions that express particular thoughts about the divine life?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They are negative attributes, not definitions of God's essence. Imperishability denies that the divine Life ceases in dissolution, and ungeneracy denies that it had a commencement in generation. Basil and Gregory use these words to mark the absence of limit on either side of the eternal Life, not to state what God's essence is.
sources.quote: Now it is a negative attribute of God, that neither does the Life cease in dissolution, nor did It have a commencement in generation; and this we express by these two words, imperishability and ungeneracy.
sources.raw_question: Do the terms 'imperishable' and 'ungenerate' (unbegotten) name God's essence, or are they negative attributes?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Such names only tell us what God is not, removing from Him conditions abhorrent to His nature such as beginning, end, body or destruction. What that further thing which is none of these is in its essence remains undivulged. Hence 'ungenerate' cannot serve as a definition of the divine substance.
sources.quote: What the Deity is not, the signification of these names does point out; but what that further thing, which is not these things, is essentially, remains undivulged.
sources.raw_question: Do privative names of God such as 'ungenerate', 'unending' and 'imperishable' reveal what God's essence is?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. If being imperishable only accrues to the essence, then not being generated likewise only accrues to it. So ungeneracy would be ejected from being the mark of the divine essence, undermining Eunomius' claim that ungeneracy defines God's being.
sources.quote: For if the being imperishable only accrues to the essence, the not being generated will also most certainly only accrue to it; and so the idea of ungeneracy will be ejected from being the mark of the essence.
sources.raw_question: If imperishability is only an attribute that accrues to God's essence rather than being the essence, can ungeneracy still be the defining mark of God's essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Both are names we reach by human conception (epinoia), applying different ideas to the one divine life. 'Ungenerate' or 'unbeginning' expresses that God never came from any cause. 'Imperishable' or 'unending' expresses that He is bounded by no limit and destroyed by no death. So these names put into words our intuitions about a life that is single and continuous with itself, without beginning or end.
sources.quote: we express the never having come from any cause by the term unbeginning or ungenerate; and we express the not being circumscribed by any limit, and not being destroyed by any death, by the term imperishable, or unending
sources.raw_question: What do the divine names 'ungenerate' and 'imperishable' mean, and how do we come to apply them to God?

question: Why do the Greeks speak of one essence and three hypostases (substances) while the Latins speak of one essence and three persons, and do the two formulas mean the same thing?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: Yes. What Latins mean by 'persons' is what Greeks mean by 'substances.' The Greeks say three substances and one essence in the same sense that Latins say three persons and one essence or substance.
sources.quote: they say three substances, one essence, in the same way as we say three persons, one essence or substance
sources.raw_question: Is the Greek formula 'one essence, three substances (hypostases)' equivalent to the Latin 'one essence, three persons'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: These are not adequate descriptions but ways of saying something about what cannot be uttered fully. The Greeks said three substances and the Latins three persons because in Latin essence usually means the same as substance. Either way of speaking is sufficient only if it is understood in a mystery. Its purpose is to give some answer when one is asked what the three are whom the faith confesses to be three.
sources.quote: And provided that what is said is understood only in a mystery, such a way of speaking was sufficient, in order that there might be something to say when it was asked what the three are
sources.raw_question: Why do the Greeks speak of one essence and three hypostases (substances) while the Latins speak of one essence and three persons, and are these terms meant to describe the Trinity adequately?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whatever is Spoken of God According to Substance, is Spoken of Each Person Severally, and Together of the Trinity Itself. One Essence in God, and Three, in Greek, Hypostases, in Latin, Persons.
sources.answer: No. In Latin usage essence and substance mean the same thing, so one cannot say one essence and three substances. Latin writers say instead one essence or substance and three persons, as the best available way to express what is understood without words.
sources.quote: we do not dare to say one essence, three substances, but one essence or substance and three persons
sources.raw_question: Should Latin theologians follow the Greek formula "one ousia, three hypostases" by saying "one essence, three substances"?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Three Persons Not Properly So Called [in a Human Sense].
sources.answer: Because in Latin usage 'essence' and 'substance' mean the same thing, so saying 'one essence, three substances' would sound contradictory. Latin writers of authority therefore said 'one essence or substance and three persons,' finding no more suitable way to put into words what they understood without words.
sources.quote: we do not dare to say one essence, three substances, but one essence or substance and three persons: as many writers in Latin, who treat of these things, and are of authority, have said
sources.raw_question: Why do Latin theologians say 'one essence, three persons' rather than following the Greek formula 'one essence, three substances (hypostases)'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases.
sources.answer: Both ways of speaking arise from the necessities of human speech. When we truly confess that there are three, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, we are asked 'three what?' Each term gives us an answer to that question. Neither term is a full or exact comprehension of the divine reality.
sources.quote: both modes of expression are shown to arise from the necessities of speech, that we might have an answer to give when asked, what three, while truly confessing that there are three
sources.raw_question: Why do the Latins speak of one essence and three persons in God, while the Greeks speak of one essence and three substances or hypostases?

question: Does Hebrews 3:2, which says the Son 'was faithful to Him that made Him,' prove that the Son is a creature or work?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. Once it is confessed that He is Son by nature, the word used raises no difficulty, because terms do not disparage a nature; the nature draws the terms to itself. 'He made' said of a true Offspring means 'He begat'. Alternatively, the words may be referred to His becoming man.
sources.quote: For terms do not disparage His Nature; rather that Nature draws to Itself those terms and changes them. For terms are not prior to essences, but essences are first, and terms second.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'faithful to Him that made Him' in Hebrews 3:2 prove that the Son is a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. 'Made' refers to the body the Word took like ours, by which He is called our brother. And even if referred to the Word Himself, it is used in the sense of 'begat.' So the Son is in essence the Father's offspring, while in the Economy He was made man for our sake.
sources.quote: the Apostle’s expression, ‘He made,’ does not prove that the Word is made, but that body, which He took like ours; and in consequence He is called our brother, as having become man
sources.raw_question: Does the word 'made' in Hebrews 3:2 ('faithful to Him that made Him') prove that the Word is a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. The text speaks of the Word's human economy, not His essence. Christ was 'made' Apostle and High Priest when He took part in flesh and blood and was made like His brethren, as the preceding verses of Hebrews 2 show. So the Word is Son by nature, Only-begotten, and not a work.
sources.quote: Wherefore Paul was writing concerning the Word's human Economy, when he said, 'Who was faithful to Him that made Him,' and not concerning His Essence.
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 3:2, which says Christ 'was faithful to Him that made Him,' prove that the Word of God is a creature or work?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. Scripture commonly uses 'made,' 'became,' and 'gotten' of genuine natural offspring, as with Hezekiah's children, Cain, Ephraim and Manasseh, and Job's sons. Since the Lord is shown to be the Father's natural Son, Word and Wisdom, 'He made' does not mean He is a work. The phrase therefore condemns the Arian heresy rather than supporting it.
sources.quote: For it has been shewn that the expression ‘He made’ is applied in divine Scripture even to children genuine and natural; whence, the Lord being proved to be the Father’s Son naturally and genuinely, and Word, and Wisdom, though ‘He made’ be used concerning Him, or ‘He became,’ this is not said of Him as if a work
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 3:2, which says the Son was 'faithful to Him that made Him,' prove that the Son is a creature or work?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. Texts such as Hebrews 3:2, Acts 2:36 and Proverbs 8:22 speak of the Word after he became man by the Father's good pleasure. They speak humanly of him as Son of man. Yet they have a religious meaning that declares the Word's divinity, because he who 'was God' in the beginning is the one who later 'became flesh.'
sources.quote: For all these texts have the same force and meaning, a religious one, declarative of the divinity of the Word, even those of them which speak humanly concerning Him, as having become the Son of man.
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 3:2, which says Jesus 'was faithful to Him that made Him,' prove that the Son of God is a work and a creature?

question: Is the Holy Spirit divided or diminished when He is given to many believers?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: No. What is shed forth is neither separated nor divided; the Spirit's fulness is an indivisible unity, shared in by each according to the capacity of his nature. He is not parcelled into corporeal parts, and since He abides unchanged He is eternal, unlike the changeable creature.
sources.quote: for the fulness of the grace of the Spirit is indivisible, but is shared in by us according to the capacity of our own nature.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit divided or diminished when He is given in measure to many people?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IV. The Holy Spirit is one and the same Who spake in the prophets and apostles, Who is the Spirit of God and of Christ; Whom, further, Scripture designates the Paraclete, and the Spirit of life and truth.
sources.answer: No. All, both apostles and prophets, have drunk of one Spirit. He cannot be divided, but is poured into souls and flows into the senses to quench the thirst of this world.
sources.quote: Him, as it were, Who cannot be divided, but is poured into souls, and flows into the senses
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit divided when He is given to many believers?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: No. The human mind cannot grasp His fulness, and He is not divided into portions of Himself. Rather, He pours into the soul the gift of spiritual grace, in which God is worshipped.
sources.quote: for neither does the mind of man grasp His fulness, nor is He divided into any portions of Himself; but He pours into [the soul] the gift of spiritual grace
sources.raw_question: Is the fulness of the Holy Spirit divided among believers when He gives spiritual gifts?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: No. Being indivisible, the Spirit loses nothing when he gives to all. In the same way, the Son loses nothing when the Father receives the kingdom, and the Father suffers no loss in giving what is his to the Son. He who breathes where he wills is everywhere free from loss.
sources.quote: Who, when He divides, is not Himself divided by cutting off Himself, for being indivisible He loses nothing when He gives to all
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit divided or diminished when he distributes his gifts to many?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: No. What is shed abroad of the Spirit is neither severed, nor contained in bodily parts, nor divided. He is given to each heart without any division or loss. It is not credible that the Spirit could be parcelled out.
sources.quote: That, then, which is shed abroad of the Spirit is neither severed, nor comprehended in any corporeal parts, nor divided.
sources.raw_question: When the Holy Spirit is poured out on many people, is He divided into parts?

question: Is the Creator of the world a merely 'animal' (psychic) being, inferior to the Gnostics who call themselves 'spiritual', as the Valentinians claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: No. Whether the Saviour made things through the Demiurge or the Creator made all things by his own power, the Creator is the former of the Gnostics themselves, who are among created things. A maker cannot be inferior to what he has made, so he is superior to them, not inferior.
sources.quote: he is proved in that case not to be inferior but superior to them, since he is found to have been the former even of themselves; for they, too, have a place among created things.
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of the world an inferior, merely 'animal' being, as the Valentinian Gnostics claim, while they themselves are 'spiritual'?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: No. The Creator made spiritual things, and the one who makes spiritual beings cannot himself be of an animal nature. Paradise is his, and he gives gifts to the worthy as he wills. He is truly the Spirit of God, not an animal Demiurge, or he could never have created spiritual things.
sources.quote: and He is truly the Spirit of God, and not an animal Demiurge, otherwise He should never have created spiritual things
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of the world a merely 'animal' (psychic) being inferior to spiritual beings, as the Valentinian Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: No. The Creator is the one who made his angels spirits, is clothed with light as with a garment, and holds the circle of the earth in his hand. He is the Creator and Lord of all spiritual substance. To call him animal is impious madness, a lifting up of opinions against God.
sources.quote: in whose sight its inhabitants are counted as grasshoppers, and who is the Creator and Lord of all spiritual substance, is of an animal nature,—they do beyond doubt and verily betray their own madness
sources.raw_question: Is the God who created the world merely of an 'animal' (psychic) nature, inferior to beings who are 'spiritual', as the Valentinian Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: Superiority must be proved by deeds, not by words. The Creator made the heavens, earth, stars, seasons, rivers and living creatures. He also made invisible beings such as angels, archangels, thrones and dominions. The Gnostics can point to no comparable work, and they are themselves his workmanship and creatures, so their claim to be above him fails.
sources.quote: Let them, then, prove themselves by their deeds superior to the Creator; for the superior person ought to be proved not by what is said, but by what has a real existence.
sources.raw_question: How can it be determined whether the Gnostics who call themselves 'spiritual' are superior to the Creator of the world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: No. The superior is shown by works, and all works have been accomplished by the Creator, whereas they can point to nothing produced by themselves. Like an idle tool claimed superior to the one the craftsman always uses, their claim is madness.
sources.quote: for the better man is shown by his works, and all works have been accomplished by the Creator; but they, having nothing worthy of reason to point to as having been produced by themselves, are labouring under the greatest and most incurable madness.
sources.raw_question: Can Gnostics who claim to be 'spiritual' rightly be considered superior to the Creator (Demiurge), whom they call merely 'animal' in nature?

question: Can anyone love something entirely unknown to him, as the studious or inquisitive person seems to do when he desires to know what he does not yet know?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > No One at All Loves Things Unknown.
sources.answer: No. Nothing at all can be loved which is not known. The studious person either knows the thing generically and loves an imagined form drawn from things already known, or sees something in the eternal reason and loves it there, or loves something known to which the unknown belongs, or loves knowing itself; in none of these cases is the unknown as such the object of love.
sources.quote: But how different the case really is, and that nothing at all can be loved which is not known, I think I must have persuaded every one who carefully looks upon truth.
sources.raw_question: Can anyone love something that is entirely unknown to him, as the studious person seems to do when he desires to know what he does not yet know?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Love of the Studious Mind, that Is, of One Desirous to Know, is Not the Love of a Thing Which It Does Not Know.
sources.answer: Because he already has at least a slight impression of what that learning is or what it achieves. Love of study is kindled by the praise of others or by marvelling at its results, but no one would labor at rhetoric unless he already knew it was the science of speaking. Likewise, one who sees writing done desires to learn it for the sake of a result he already knows.
sources.quote: although nevertheless we could not burn with any zeal at all for the study of it, unless we had already in our mind at least a slight impression of the knowledge of each kind of learning.
sources.raw_question: How can a person love a branch of learning that he does not yet know?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Love of the Studious Mind, that Is, of One Desirous to Know, is Not the Love of a Thing Which It Does Not Know.
sources.answer: No. The love of a studious mind is not love of what it does not know but of what it knows, on account of which it wishes to know the unknown. In the case of an unknown word, the mind already knows and loves the beauty of knowledge by which men's thoughts are mutually made known through significant words, and this known and loved fitness drives the search for the unknown word.
sources.quote: the love of a studious mind, that is, of one that wishes to know what it does not know, is not the love of that thing which it does not know, but of that which it knows; on account of which it wishes to know what it does not know.
sources.raw_question: When a studious person eagerly seeks to learn something unknown, such as the meaning of an unfamiliar word, does he love the unknown thing itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Love of the Studious Mind, that Is, of One Desirous to Know, is Not the Love of a Thing Which It Does Not Know.
sources.answer: No. Such a person is different from an ordinary student but likewise does not love unknown things. He is better said to hate things unknown, since he wishes there were none by wishing to know everything. What he loves is not the unknown things but the knowing of them.
sources.quote: he is more fitly said to hate things he knows not, of which he wishes that there should be none, in wishing to know everything.
sources.raw_question: Does a merely inquisitive person, who desires to know unknown things simply for the sake of knowing, thereby love things he does not know?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Love of the Studious Mind, that Is, of One Desirous to Know, is Not the Love of a Thing Which It Does Not Know.
sources.answer: No. Nothing can be loved unless it is known. The learner seems to love something unknown, but what he really loves is a known excellence: in the light of truth he sees how good and useful learning and the knowledge of signs are, and he loves that known 'species' and strives to make it perfect in himself.
sources.quote: The soul, then, discerns this fitting and serviceable species, and knows it, and loves it; and he who seeks the meaning of any words of which he is ignorant, studies to render that species perfect in himself as much as he can
sources.raw_question: Can a person who eagerly seeks to learn something he does not yet know be said to love a thing that is wholly unknown to him?

question: Is the God who gave the Mosaic law the same as the Father whom Christ revealed, or is there another, higher Father above the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXII.—The true Lord and the one God is declared by the law, and manifested by Christ His Son in the Gospel; whom alone we should adore, and from Him we must look for all good things, not from Satan.
sources.answer: The God of the law is the same as the Father of Christ. Christ pointed out as Father the very one whom the law proclaimed as God, and He defeated Satan by quoting that law, calling it His Father's voice. Therefore we must not seek another Father besides or above the Creator.
sources.quote: for Him whom the law proclaimed as God, the same did Christ point out as the Father, whom also it behoves the disciples of Christ alone to serve.
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics positing a higher Father above the Demiurge
sources.raw_question: Is the God proclaimed in the Mosaic law the same as the Father whom Christ revealed, or is there another higher Father above the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XII.—It clearly appears that there was but one author of both the old and the new law, from the fact that Christ condemned traditions and customs repugnant to the former, while He confirmed its most important precepts, and taught that He was Himself the end of the Mosaic law.
sources.answer: No. Christ brought no greater commandment from heaven. He renewed the law's first and greatest commandment, to love God with all the heart. Had he descended from another, 'perfect' Father, he would have tried by every means to bring a greater commandment from that Father rather than use the one given by the God of the law.
sources.quote: But if He had descended from another Father, He never would have made use of the first and greatest commandment of the law; but He would undoubtedly have endeavoured by all means to bring down a greater one than this from the perfect Father
sources.raw_question: Did Christ come from a different Father than the God who gave the Mosaic law?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XII.—It clearly appears that there was but one author of both the old and the new law, from the fact that Christ condemned traditions and customs repugnant to the former, while He confirmed its most important precepts, and taught that He was Himself the end of the Mosaic law.
sources.answer: No. Christ did not preach another God the Father besides the one proclaimed by the law from the beginning. Nor did he preach another Son, or the Gnostic Mother and Pleroma of Æons. He taught his followers to obey the commandments God gave from the beginning and to follow him. So the Father of Christ is the one God of the law.
sources.quote: And He did not preach to His followers another God the Father, besides Him who was proclaimed by the law from the beginning; nor another Son; nor the Mother, the enthymesis of the Æon
sources.raw_question: Did Christ proclaim a God the Father different from the God proclaimed in the Mosaic law, as the Gnostics claimed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IV.—Answer to another objection, showing that the destruction of Jerusalem, which was the city of the great King, diminished nothing from the supreme majesty and power of God, for that this destruction was put in execution by the most wise counsel of the same God.
sources.answer: No. The law began in time with Moses, so it had to end in time with John. Christ came to fulfil it, and God does all things by measure and in order. Its temporary character is part of the one God's ordered plan, which leads into the new covenant.
sources.quote: Since, then, the law originated with Moses, it terminated with John as a necessary consequence. Christ had come to fulfil it: wherefore “the law and the prophets were” with them “until John.”
sources.raw_question: Does the ending of the Mosaic law with John the Baptist imply that the law came from a different God from the Father of Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IX.—There is but one author, and one end to both covenants.
sources.answer: Yes. When rebuking the Pharisees for voiding the law by their tradition, Christ called the commandment "Honour thy father and mother" the word and law of God, thus plainly confessing the lawgiver to be Father and God. The true God (Christ) called no one else God besides His own Father.
sources.quote: For the true God did confess the commandment of the law as the word of God, and called no one else God besides His own Father.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ acknowledge the God who gave the Mosaic law as his own Father and the true God?

question: Did Christ's body feel the pain of His sufferings, such as the nails and wounds of the cross, in the way ordinary human bodies do?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. At the very moment of His arrest His touch created an ear out of a wound, preventing another's pain. The hand that could do this cannot belong to a body subject to weakness, so though He was flesh He did not feel the pain of fleshly wounds.
sources.quote: He shewed, when He restored the wounded flesh of the ear, that, though He was flesh, He did not feel the pain of fleshly wounds.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ feel the pain of the nails and wounds in His flesh?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Suffering laid hold of his body but did not inflict on it the nature of pain. Though he had the form of our body, by virtue of his origin he was not in the body of our weakness. His body was truly a body, because it was born of the Virgin, but it was above our weakness, because it was conceived of the Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: That body was truly and indeed body, because it was born of the Virgin: but it was above the weakness of our body, because it had its beginning in a spiritual conception.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ's body share the natural infirmity and pain of ordinary human bodies?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The three youths in the furnace felt no pain or fear through faith, and the martyrs sang as they died. If mere men could be rendered insensible to suffering, it is unthinkable that the Lord of glory, whose word and touch healed and created, felt the pain from which faith in him rescued the martyrs. Hilary holds that Christ bore our sufferings in the power of his own nature, which could not feel pain.
sources.quote: Impious heretic, you will have it that Christ suffered pain from the piercing of the nails, that He felt the bitterness of the wound, when they were driven through His hands: why, pray, did not the children fear the flames?
sources.raised_by_detail: the impious heretic who holds that Christ suffered pain
sources.raw_question: Did Christ feel pain when the nails pierced his hands on the cross?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. He truly suffered blows, crucifixion and death, but without the pain. A dart passes through water, flame or air without wounding them, and in the same way the suffering exercised its full violence on His body without its natural effect. His flesh, conceived of the Holy Ghost, had a unique nature: it walked on water, passed through walls, was transfigured, and healed by its touch. So it cannot be judged on the analogy of our bodies.
sources.quote: He had a body to suffer, and He suffered: but He had not a nature which could feel pain. For His body possessed a unique nature of its own
sources.raw_question: Did Christ feel pain in His sufferings in the way ordinary human beings do?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Hilary answers by asking what kind of body the Man Jesus had. He explains in the following context that our bodies feel pain only because they live by admixture with a weak soul that pervades them. When the soul is absent or asleep, as in a withered or drugged limb, there is no pain. He thereby prepares to show that Christ's body was not subject to pain in the same way ours is.
sources.quote: It is, therefore, because the body lives by admixture with a weak soul, that it is subject to the weakness of pain.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ's body feel the pain of the cross in the way ordinary human bodies feel pain?

question: How is wisdom (cognizance of eternal, divine things) properly distinguished from knowledge (cognizance of temporal, human things), and which is to be preferred?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What in the Incarnate Word Belongs to Knowledge, What to Wisdom.
sources.answer: Yes, properly speaking. In looser usage both can be called wisdom and both knowledge, but Paul could not have written 'to one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge' unless the two were properly called by distinct names.
sources.quote: Yet the apostle could not in any way have written, “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge,” except also these several things had been properly called by the several names
sources.raw_question: Is the distinction between wisdom (of divine things) and knowledge (of human things) a real one, given that both words are often used interchangeably?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > In Opposition to the Reminiscence of Plato and Pythagoras. Pythagoras the Samian. Of the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge, and of Seeking the Trinity in the Knowledge of Temporal Things.
sources.answer: Wisdom is the intellectual cognizance of eternal things, while knowledge is the rational cognizance of temporal things. The apostle teaches that the two are different gifts of the same Spirit, and no one doubts that the cognizance of eternal things is to be preferred to that of temporal things.
sources.quote: the intellectual cognizance of eternal things is one thing, the rational cognizance of temporal things another; and no one doubts but that the former is to be preferred to the latter
sources.raw_question: What is the difference between wisdom and knowledge, and which is to be preferred?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > What is the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge. The Worship of God is the Love of Him. How the Intellectual Cognizance of Eternal Things Comes to Pass Through Wisdom.
sources.answer: Wisdom belongs to the contemplation of eternal things, knowledge to action in the right use of temporal things. Augustine finds this in Job's saying that piety is wisdom and departing from evil is knowledge. Piety means the worship of God, the most excellent eternal thing. Departing from evil concerns temporal things, because it is in time that we are in evil.
sources.quote: In thus distinguishing, it must be understood that wisdom belongs to contemplation, knowledge to action.
sources.raw_question: What is the difference between wisdom and knowledge in Augustine's account?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > What is the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge. The Worship of God is the Love of Him. How the Intellectual Cognizance of Eternal Things Comes to Pass Through Wisdom.
sources.answer: Knowledge deals with temporal things, such as avoiding evil, acting virtuously, and gathering examples and proofs for practical use. Wisdom deals with eternal things, which neither have been nor will be but simply are. Augustine therefore keeps the two kinds of discourse apart according to their objects: the temporal and the eternal.
sources.quote: I hold it to be a discourse belonging to knowledge, and to be distinguished from a discourse belonging to wisdom, to which those things belong, which neither have been, nor shall be, but are
sources.raw_question: What distinguishes a discourse belonging to wisdom from one belonging to knowledge?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > What the Wisdom is of Which We are Here to Treat. Whence the Name of Philosopher Arose. What Has Been Already Said Concerning the Distinction of Knowledge and Wisdom.
sources.answer: Following the apostle's distinction between "the word of wisdom" and "the word of knowledge," the philosophers' definition of wisdom is to be divided. Knowledge of things divine is called wisdom, and knowledge of things human is called knowledge. Knowledge in this sense covers only the things by which saving faith is begotten, nourished, defended and strengthened.
sources.quote: this definition is to be divided, so that the knowledge of things divine shall be called wisdom, and that of things human appropriate to itself the name of knowledge
sources.raw_question: How should wisdom be distinguished from knowledge?

question: Does the mind always remember, understand, and love itself, even when it is not actively thinking of itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine holds that the mind can never be in such a state as not to remember, understand, and love itself, even though it does not always think of itself. The difficulty was that when it does think of itself, it does not in the same act distinguish itself from bodily things. For this reason he put off the argument about the Trinity, of which the mind is an image, and first looked for trinities in sensible things.
sources.quote: the mind could never be in such a case as not to remember, understand, and love itself, although it did not always think of itself
sources.raw_question: Does the mind always remember, understand, and love itself, even when it is not actively thinking of itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How a Kind of Trinity Exists in the Mind Thinking of Itself. What is the Part of Thought in This Trinity.
sources.answer: It always remembers, understands, and loves itself. It would be absurd to say a musician does not understand or love music merely because he is not thinking of it at the moment. He remembers, understands, and loves it even while thinking of geometry. So all three belong to the mind continually, not just memory.
sources.quote: This person whom you perceive disputing about geometry is also a perfect musician, for he both remembers music, and understands, and loves it
sources.raw_question: Does the mind always remember, understand, and love itself, or does it only remember itself and come to understand and love itself once it begins to think of itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Mind Loves God in Rightly Loving Itself; And If It Love Not God, It Must Be Said to Hate Itself.
