Even a Weak and Erring Mind is Always Strong in Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself. Let It Be Turned to God, that It May Be Blessed by Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Him.
sources.answer: No. The mind is so constituted that at no time does it fail to remember, understand, and love itself. Even amid the evils of weakness and delusion it cannot lose this natural memory, understanding and love of itself, which is why even fallen man still 'walketh in an image.'
sources.quote: The human mind, then, is so constituted, that at no time does it not remember, and understand, and love itself.
sources.raw_question: Does the human mind ever cease to remember, understand, and love itself, even when it is weak and erring?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Thing is Made Plain by an Example. In What Way the Matter is Handled in Order to Help the Reader.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as a skilled musician who is now thinking about geometry still remembers, understands, and loves music, so the mind has a knowledge of itself stored in its recesses. When this knowledge is thought of, it comes forth into the mind's view. The mind then finds that it remembered, understood, and loved itself even while it was thinking of something else.
sources.quote: for then the mind itself finds that it both remembers, and understands, and loves itself, even although it was not thinking of itself, when it was thinking of something else
sources.raw_question: Does the mind always remember, understand, and love itself even when it is not actively thinking of itself?

question: Is the trinity found in bodily sight (the object seen, the form impressed on the eye, and the will joining them) a true image of the divine Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: No. Bodily sight does show a trinity of the outer man: the visible object, the form it impresses on the eye of the beholder, and the purpose of the will that combines the two. But these three are plainly not equal to one another, nor of one substance. So this trinity falls short of the coequal and consubstantial divine Trinity.
sources.quote: But these three things, as was patent, were not mutually equal and of one substance.
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity found in bodily sight (the object seen, the form impressed on the eye, and the will joining them) a fitting image of the divine Trinity, whose Persons are equal and of one substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight.
sources.answer: Yes. In bodily vision there is a kind of trinity: the bodily object seen, the form it impresses on the sight of the seer, and the purpose of the will that combines the two. Yet this is only a trace, since these three are neither mutually equal nor of one substance, and the outer man is not the image of God in the same way the inner man is.
sources.quote: in the bodily object that is seen, and in the form that is impressed by it upon the sight of the seer, and in the purpose of the will that combines the two; although these three are neither mutually equal, nor of one substance
sources.raw_question: Can any image or trace of the Trinity be found in the outer man, that is, in bodily sense perception such as sight?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > The Trinity of the Outer Man, or of External Vision, is Not an Image of God. The Likeness of God is Desired Even in Sins. In External Vision the Form of the Corporeal Thing is as It Were the Parent, Vision the Offspring; But the Will that Unites These Suggests the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. This trinity is produced in the mind through the bodily sense from the corporeal creature, which is lower than the mind. Only that is properly called God's image than which God alone is higher, with no nature interposed between it and God.
sources.quote: And therefore that trinity is not an image of God since it is produced in the mind itself through the bodily sense, from the lowest, that is, the corporeal creature, than which the mind is higher.
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity found in external bodily vision (object, sight, will) an image of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Number, Weight, Measure.
sources.answer: No. The trinity found in the outer, carnal man is only a trace. The image of God according to the Trinity must be sought by passing inward to the inner man. Augustine hopes to find it there with God's help, since God has ordered all things in measure, number, and weight.
sources.quote: time admonishes us to seek for this same trinity in the inner man, and to strive to pass inwards from that animal and carnal and (as he is called) outward man
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity found in the outer man the place to seek the true image of God according to the Trinity?

question: Is the trinity of memory, understanding and love in the human mind an exact or adequate likeness of the divine Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Against Eunomius, Saying that the Son of God is the Son, Not of His Nature, But of His Will. Epilogue to What Has Been Said Already.
sources.answer: No. The image was made by the Trinity but has been changed for the worse by the person's own fault. It must not be thought like the Trinity in all points. Within whatever likeness it bears, one must also discern a great unlikeness.
sources.quote: he must not so compare this image thus wrought by that Trinity, and by his own fault changed for the worse, to that same Trinity as to think it in all points like to it
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity of memory, understanding and will in the human mind like the divine Trinity in every respect?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Great the Unlikeness is Between the Image of the Trinity Which We Have Found in Ourselves, and the Trinity Itself.
sources.answer: No, there is a great unlikeness. In man, it is the single person who remembers, understands, and loves by these three faculties; he has them but is not them. In God, by contrast, there is one God and yet three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in the simplicity of the highest nature.
sources.quote: These things, then, can be said by a single person, which has these three, but is not these three. But in the simplicity of that Highest Nature, which is God, although there is one God, there are three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Is the mental image of the Trinity in man (memory, understanding, and love) a faithful likeness of the divine Trinity, given that in man these three belong to one person?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What It is that Suffices Here to Solve the Question Why the Spirit is Not Said to Be Begotten, and Why the Father Alone is Unbegotten. What They Ought to Do Who Do Not Understand These Things.
sources.answer: No, the likeness is imperfect. The three things in a man's mind are not three persons; all three belong to one man, who is a single person. The image is therefore only an aid to understanding the highest Trinity, which is God.
sources.quote: which are not so three as to be three persons, but all three belong to a man who is one person
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity in the human mind an exact likeness of the divine Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Question Why the Holy Spirit is Not Begotten, and How He Proceeds from the Father and the Son, Will Only Be Understood When We are in Bliss.
sources.answer: No. The human mind is a real image of the Trinity, and Augustine used it, especially in the ninth book, to illustrate the relation of the Three Persons. But it is temporal and changeable. Its three elements all belong to one person, so they cannot fit the Three Persons as human understanding would require.
sources.quote: But three things belonging to one person cannot suit those Three Persons, as man’s purpose demands; and this we have demonstrated in this fifteenth book.
sources.raw_question: Can the triad found within one human mind adequately represent the relations of the three divine Persons of the Trinity?

question: Can any human name or concept comprehend or adequately signify the divine nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Measured against the universe, human capacity is next to nothing, so it cannot encompass the unspeakable Power under one appellation. Reason gives only a dim and imperfect grasp of the Divine nature. Still, the knowledge gathered from the terms piety allows us to apply to God is enough for our limited capacity.
sources.quote: they open their mouths wide against the unspeakable Power, and encompass by one appellation the infinite nature, confining the Divine essence within the narrow limits of the term ungeneracy
sources.raw_question: Can any single name or human concept comprehend the infinite divine nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: No. God is beyond every term, idea, or device of apprehension, beyond human, angelic, and all supramundane intelligence, and unutterable. The only name that represents his proper nature is that he is 'above every name.'
sources.quote: incapable of being grasped by any term, or any idea, or any other device of our apprehension, remaining beyond the reach not only of the human but of the angelic and of all supramundane intelligence
sources.raw_question: Can the divine nature be grasped or defined by any human term or concept?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
sources.answer: No. When Manoah asked the angel's name, he was told, "Why askest thou this? It also is wonderful." This teaches that the only name signifying the Divine Nature is the wonder that arises unspeakably in our hearts concerning It. The one thing we know of God is that He is.
sources.quote: so that by this we learn that there is one name significant of the Divine Nature—the wonder, namely, that arises unspeakably in our hearts concerning It
sources.raw_question: Can the divine nature be comprehended by any name?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. We assign names only to what we know, and the divine nature is above our knowledge, so no distinctive term can capture it. Therefore we are compelled to use many differing names to express our surmises about the Deity, none of which marks it adequately.
sources.quote: those things which are above our knowledge it is not possible to seize by any distinctive terms (for how can one put a mark upon a thing we know nothing about?)
sources.raw_question: Can human names or terms adequately signify the divine nature itself?

question: Does the term 'ungenerate' (and correspondingly 'generated') name the essence of the Father (and of the Son), or does it only mark the distinction between them?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > After much discourse concerning the actually existent, and ungenerate and good, and upon the consubstantiality of the heavenly powers, showing the uncharted character of their essence, yet the difference of their ranks, he ends the book.
sources.answer: No. When we say "this one was generated" or "was not generated," we form two thoughts. The subject is pointed out by "is," and something contemplated in the subject is expressed by the predicate. To think of that which is differs from thinking of what is contemplated in it, so these words name an attribute and not the essence itself.
sources.quote: But what He is, in His own Nature, Who exists apart from generation, and what He is, Who is believed to have been generated, we do not learn from the signification of “having been generated,” and “not having been generated.”
sources.raw_question: Do the terms "ungenerate" and "generated" express the essence of the Father and of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It marks a distinction of conceptions, not the essence. The Father is called ungenerate because he was not generated, just as the Son is called generated because he was generated. So the term distinguishes the generated from the ungenerate rather than defining the divine nature.
sources.quote: the term ungenerate is no part of the essence, but is indicative of a difference of conceptions, distinguishing that which is generated from that which is ungenerate.
sources.raw_question: Does the term 'ungenerate' name the Father's essence, or does it mark a distinction between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory argues that if 'ungenerate' names the essence, no term remains to express the Father's being without origin. The distinction between generated and ungenerate would then disappear, and the Eunomian argument would collapse into Sabellianism, identifying the Father with the Son.
sources.quote: their whole argument falls and collapses into Sabellianism. For by this reasoning we must hold the Father to be identical with the Son, the distinction between generated and ungenerate having been got rid of from their teaching
sources.raw_question: If 'ungenerate' is taken to signify the Father's essence, is anything left to express the distinction between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The definitions of difference and of essence are not the same, so a term denoting difference does not denote essence. 'Ungenerate' clearly expresses the difference by verbal opposition, meaning that the Father has not been generated while the Son has. But the Eunomians cannot say in what sense it would also manifest essence.
sources.quote: Accordingly if the term denotes difference, essence will in no way be denoted by the appellation. For the definitions of difference and essence are by no means the same.
sources.raw_question: Can the single term 'ungenerate' signify both the distinction of the Father from the Son and the divine essence itself?

question: If God is called imperishable because his life has no end and ungenerate because it has no beginning, does it follow that God is perishable in one respect and generated in another?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The divine life is not divided into two halves, each bearing only one name. Gregory compares it to calling man both rational and capable of knowledge: having one attribute does not exclude the other. Likewise the eternity of the divine life does not lose imperishability by being unbeginning, nor beginninglessness by being imperishable.
sources.quote: no more is the eternity of the Divine Life deprived of imperishability, if it be unbeginning, or of beginninglessness, if we recognize its imperishability.
sources.raw_question: If God is called imperishable only because his life has no end, and ungenerate only because it has no beginning, does it follow that God is perishable in the respect in which he is not imperishable and generated in the respect in which he is not ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. This objection attacks a position Basil never held. The objection treats 'without beginning' and 'without end' as two separate segments of essence. Basil instead applies the two names to the one infinite eternal Life, which transcends every limit of the ages both before and after. So nothing follows about God being partly perishable or partly generated.
sources.quote: this absence of limit or circumscription on either hand in the Eternal Life we mark in the one case with the name of imperishability, and in the other case with the name of ungeneracy.
sources.raw_question: If God is called imperishable because his life is unending and ungenerate because it is unbeginning, does it follow that God is perishable in one respect and generated in another?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Basil's terms do not divide God's life into two halves, each with its own name. The divine life is single and continuous with itself, without beginning and without end. 'Ungenerate' names it as seen looking back over the past ages, and 'imperishable' names the same life as seen looking forward to the ages to come. Eunomius gets his conclusion only by wrongly assuming that imperishability cannot belong to the whole life of God.
sources.quote: Who ever divided that Life into two parts, and then put particular names to each half of the Life, so that to the division which the one name fitted the other could not be said to apply?
sources.raw_question: If God is called 'imperishable' with reference to the endlessness of His life and 'ungenerate' with reference to its beginninglessness, does it follow that God is perishable in some respect and generated in another, so that contradictory elements are mixed in the divine substance?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Distinct names for God signify distinct thoughts about the one Divine Life, but each is true of the whole subject, so the absence of one meaning from a term does not imply the opposite attribute. Eunomius' reasoning, if valid, would equally make God 'immaterial and wrathful,' 'immutable and corporeal,' 'just and untrue,' which is plainly absurd and blasphemous.
sources.quote: By the same argument as that whereby he establishes this union of the perishable and the unbeginning, he can make sport of any proper and worthily conceived name for the Deity.
sources.raw_question: If 'ungenerate' and 'imperishable' are names applied to God according to distinct conceptions (unbeginning and unending), does it follow, as Eunomius argues, that God is ungenerate yet perishable in one respect and imperishable yet generated in another?

question: Does the Son's birth from the Father change, diminish, or divide the divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The Divine birth brings neither loss nor difference into the Godhead. The Father mixed nothing foreign into the Son's nature but gave him all that is his own, and lost nothing in giving it. That which is born of God is God, so the Son is nothing other than God.
sources.quote: The Divine birth imports neither diminution nor difference into the Godhead
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from the Father lessen or change the Divine nature in the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. He who is by nature God of God must possess the nature of his origin. The indistinguishable unity of a living nature cannot be divided by the birth of a living nature.
sources.quote: He, Who is by nature God of God, must possess the nature of His origin, which God possesses, and the indistinguishable unity of a living nature cannot be divided by the birth of a living nature
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth divide the unity of the divine nature between Father and Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The divine nature does not deteriorate or cease to be the same in passing through birth. Nor does this sameness undermine faith in a real birth, because no alien element entered the Son's nature in that birth.
sources.quote: For the Divine nature does not deteriorate or cease to be the same in passing through birth: nor yet is this sameness a bar to our faith in the birth
sources.raw_question: Does the divine nature change or diminish when it is communicated to the Son through birth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Birth works no change in the Divine nature. In both Father and Son that nature remains true to its kind, so the Son is God from God, eternally abiding, and owes His Godhead to none other than God.
sources.quote: But birth works no change in the Divine nature; both in Father and in Son that nature is true to its kind.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from the Father bring any change into the Divine nature?

question: Does being begotten make the Son different in nature from God the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The name 'Begotten' signifies the manner of His origin, not a difference in kind. The birth of God can come only from God and have only one nature; if it were not from God it would not be a birth, and if not a birth Christ would not be God. So the Son, though owing His being to the Father, is not dispossessed of the Father's nature.
sources.quote: the name Begotten signifies indeed the manner of His origin, but does not make Him different in kind from the Begetter
sources.raw_question: Does being begotten make the Son different in nature from God the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Because the Son is born of the Father, who is true God, the Son is himself true God. He may not be severed from the Father on any plea of difference of nature. Nor may he be made one of a plurality of Gods. He is God in no unreal sense.
sources.quote: We must not fail to confess Him as true God, seeing that He is born of Thee, true God, His Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being begotten make him a lesser or merely nominal God, of a different nature from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The fact of birth does not make the Son God with a different nature. The generation that produced his substance did not change its nature in kind. By his natural birth he keeps in himself the Father's nature and its natural power.
sources.quote: The fact of birth does not make Him God with a different nature, nor did the generation, which produced His substance, change its nature in kind.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being begotten make him God of a different nature from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. The one born from God cannot exist as anything other than God, since his origin is from God alone. His substance consists in all that is summed up in the Begetter's substance. Nothing novel is in him, because his life is from the Living, and nothing is absent, because the Living begot him to share his own life.
sources.quote: The nature with which God is born is necessarily the same as that of His Source. He cannot come into existence as other than God, since His origin is from none other than God.
sources.raw_question: Is the nature of the begotten Son necessarily the same as the nature of the Father who begets him?

question: Does the Son's birth from the Father give Him the same nature as the Father, or a different or alien one?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. There is birth, not separation; a true Son, not an adoption; God, not a creature. The nature was not altered by birth so as to become alien from the property of its source, so Father and Son are one in an indivisible nature, inseparable yet not confused.
sources.quote: For there is birth not separation, there is a Son not an adoption; and He is God, not a creature. Neither is He a God of a different kind, but the Father and Son are one
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from the Father make His nature different from or alien to the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. By his birth the Son partakes congenitally of the nature of his Author, so that from the One there comes an indivisible Unity, since One is from One. Thus Father and Son are one in nature though not one Person.
sources.quote: none can doubt that the Son by His birth partakes congenitally of the nature of His Author, in such wise that from the One there comes into being an indivisible Unity, because One is from One.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being born of the Father give him the same nature as the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. When the Living is begotten by the Living, nothing new comes into existence, because life was not drawn out of the non-existent. Because of the unity of nature and the perfect birth, the Son lives always in the Father and has the life of the Living in Himself. Christ shows this when He says He lives through the living Father and that the Father has given the Son to have life in Himself.
sources.quote: Nothing new comes into existence when the Living is begotten by the Living; for life was not sought out from the non-existent to receive birth
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from the Father bring a new nature into existence, or one distinct from the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The mystery of the divine nature forbids separating the birth of the living Son from His living Father. The Son undergoes no change of kind through His birth, and the truth of the Father's nature abides in Him.
sources.quote: By the mystery of the divine nature we are forbidden to separate the birth of the living Son from His living Father. The Son of God suffers no such change of kind, that the truth of His Father’s nature does not abide in Him.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from the Father involve a change of kind, so that the Father's nature does not truly abide in the Son?

question: Does the Son's being sent by the Father, or the Spirit's being sent by the Father and the Son, make the one sent less than the sender?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: No. Being sent does not make one less than the sender. The Trinity is equal in all things, equally unchangeable, invisible and everywhere present in its nature, and works indivisibly, so the sending implies no inferiority.
sources.quote: He who is sent is not therefore less than He who sends because the one sent, the other was sent; since the Trinity, which is in all things equal, being also equally in its own nature unchangeable, and invisible, and everywhere present, works indivisibly
sources.raw_question: Is the Son or the Holy Spirit less than the Father because the Father sends them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Augustine argues that the sending must be understood in a way that implies no inferiority, since the Son and the Spirit were sent to where they already were. Sending is not a change of place commanded by a superior, but the visible manifestation of one already present everywhere.
sources.quote: men betake themselves to saying, that he who sends is greater than he who is sent: therefore the Father is greater than the Son, because the Son continually speaks of Himself as being sent by the Father
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Son is sent by the Father, and the Holy Spirit by the Father and the Son, prove that the one sent is less than the one who sends?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. The one who is sent is not less than the one who sends merely because one sends and the other is sent. The Trinity is equal in all things, and sending does not introduce inequality of nature between the Persons.
sources.quote: demonstrates that He who is sent is not therefore less than He who sends, because the one has sent, the other has been sent
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Father sends the Son (and the Holy Spirit is sent) imply that the one who is sent is inferior to the one who sends?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Of the Sensible Showing of the Holy Spirit, and of the Coeternity of the Trinity. What Has Been Said, and What Remains to Be Said.
sources.answer: No. Scripture speaks of sending either because of the visible creature through which a Person appears, or to point to the procession within the Godhead. It does not imply any inequality or difference of substance. If the Father had chosen to appear visibly, it would be absurd to say He was sent by the Son He begot or by the Spirit who proceeds from Him.
sources.quote: the Son is not therefore less because He is sent by the Father, nor the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being sent by the Father, or the Spirit's being sent by the Father and the Son, make the one sent less than the sender?

question: Is the Son of God a creature, or is he truly born of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Those who deny his birth and say he was created fail to see in his deeds the works of very God. His deeds show true Godhead, and Scripture shows he was born, not made.
sources.quote: Our present adversaries deny that He was born, assert that He was created, and fail to see in His deeds the works of very God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God a creature rather than one truly born of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. No prophet, evangelist, or apostle says that Jesus Christ was created from God rather than born from him. To assert creation instead of birth denies that the Son derives his being from God by a birth that conveys the Father's nature. A creature would instead have come into being out of nothing.
sources.quote: No sentence of prophet, or evangelist, or apostle has said that Jesus Christ was created from God, rather than born from Him: yet you deny the birth, and assert the creation
sources.raw_question: Is the Son created from God rather than born from him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Those who call him a creature degrade his true birth to the level of a creation in order to cut him off from the divine unity. The centre of saving faith is belief in Christ as the Son of God, not as a creature but as God the Creator, born of God. He is God the Word who was with God in the beginning.
sources.quote: not merely in Christ, but in Christ as the Son of God; in Him, not as a creature, but as God the Creator, born of God
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God created rather than truly born of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Hilary calls it a foolish lie to make the Lord of Glory, King of the Universe and Only-begotten God a creature and not God's Son. Christ is Wisdom, so those who deny or hate Him stand outside wisdom and do not know God.
sources.quote: they do who will have it that the Lord of Glory, and King of the Universe, and Only-begotten God is a creature of God and not His Son
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God a creature of God rather than His true Son?

question: If the Father is prior to the Son by an interval of time, does it follow that the Father himself must have a beginning?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He who asserts that the Father is 'prior' to the Son with any thought of an interval must perforce allow that even the Father is not without beginning.
sources.answer: Yes. Every interval must be bounded by two ends; one end is the Son's generation, and the other can only be some beginning of the Father's life from which the interval starts. So whoever makes the Son later than the Father by an extension of life must grant a fixed beginning to the Father's existence. That undermines the Eunomians' own doctrine of the Father's Ungeneracy, since what has a beginning of being is not inoriginate.
sources.quote: when he makes the Son later than the Father by a certain intervening extension of life, he must grant a fixed beginning to the Father’s existence also, regulated by this same interval of his devising
sources.raw_question: If the Father is prior to the Son by an interval of time, does it follow that the Father himself must have a beginning?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son's everlastingness is included along with the idea of his birth in the Father's ungeneracy. So any interval imagined between the two would fix a starting point for the Father's own life as Father. That would be a monstrous supposition.
sources.quote: the everlastingness of the Son is included, along with the idea of His birth, in the Father’s ungeneracy; and that, if any interval were to be imagined dividing the two, that same interval would fix a beginning for the life of the Almighty;—a monstrous supposition.
sources.raw_question: If an interval of time separated the Father from the Son, would that imply the Father himself had a beginning?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His elaborate account of degrees and differences in 'works' and 'energies' within the Trinity is absurd.
sources.answer: Yes. Any mark that fixes a beginning for the Son's generation must also define the Father's beginning. Such an interval would have to be either infinite or limited. It cannot be infinite, because an infinite has no bounds and would leave no Father limiting it above and no Son limiting it below, which destroys the very idea of Father and Son. A limited interval, by contrast, places the Father himself within bounded time.
sources.quote: He who asserts that the Father is ‘prior’ to the Son with any thought of an interval must perforce allow that even the Father is not without beginning.
sources.raw_question: If the Father is prior to the Son by some interval, does it follow that the Father himself has a beginning?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He who asserts that the Father is 'prior' to the Son with any thought of an interval must perforce allow that even the Father is not without beginning.
sources.answer: Yes. Any interval of time placed between the Father and the Son must be bounded at both ends; one end is the Son's generation, and the other must be some definite point where the Father's life begins. Just as saying man was made five days after the heavens implies the heavens did not exist before that span, positing a definite interval of the Father's life before the Son fixes a starting-point for the Father. Thus the Eunomian 'Ungenerate' would be shown to have once not existed.
sources.quote: For any recognizing mark that is presupposed for the generation of the Son must certainly define as well the Father’s beginning.
sources.raw_question: If the Father is said to be prior in time to the Son by some interval, does it follow that the Father himself had a beginning in time?

question: Is God the Father wise only by the Wisdom He begets (the Son), or is the Father Himself wisdom, so that the Son is wisdom from wisdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: The Son is Wisdom of the Father in the way He is Light of the Father. Just as there is light from light and yet both are one light, there is wisdom from wisdom and yet both are one wisdom. Because in God to be is to be wise, they are therefore also one essence.
sources.quote: in the same manner as light from light, and yet both one light, so we are to understand wisdom of wisdom, and yet both one wisdom; and therefore also one essence
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Son called the Wisdom of the Father if the Father is Himself wisdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God from the Trinities We Have Spoken of.
sources.answer: No. If the Son understood for the Father, the Son would make the Father wise. Since in God to be is to be wise, the Father would then have His essence from the Son, which is a most absurd falsehood. Rather, the Father is wise by the wisdom which He Himself is, and the Son is wisdom begotten of wisdom.
sources.quote: But if to God to be is to be wise, and essence is to Him the same as wisdom, then it is not the Son that has His essence from the Father, which is the truth, but rather the Father from the Son, which is a most absurd falsehood.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father wise only by the wisdom He begets, namely the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: The Father who begat the Son is not only the Father of his own power and wisdom but is himself power and wisdom, and so is the Holy Spirit. Yet they are not three powers or three wisdoms but one power and one wisdom, as they are one God and one essence.
sources.quote: that God who begat the Son is not only Father of His own power and wisdom, but is Himself also power and wisdom; so, too, the Holy Spirit; and yet that they are not three powers or three wisdoms, but one power and one wisdom
sources.raw_question: Is God the Father only the father of his wisdom, or is he himself wisdom, so that wisdom begat wisdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases.
sources.answer: The Father is himself power and wisdom, not only the Father of power and wisdom. Although he begat the Son, who is called his power and wisdom, the Father is not wise only by the wisdom he begat. Wisdom and power are said of him absolutely, according to his essence. The same holds for the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: God the Father, who begat the Son, His power and wisdom, is not only the Father of power and wisdom, but also Himself power and wisdom; and similarly the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Is God the Father merely the Father of power and wisdom (the Son, called 'the power of God and the wisdom of God'), or is the Father himself power and wisdom?

question: Does the name 'Father' by itself imply the existence of the Son, so that the Father cannot exist or be named without the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: Yes. The First Father has no cause beyond Himself, and the subsistence of the Son is invariably implied in the title of Father. So acknowledging that 'Father' includes being ungenerate does not cut the Father off from His relation to the Son. Gregory openly holds both that 'Father' means the same as Ungenerate and that it brings with it the notion of the Only-begotten as a bound relative.
sources.quote: But if the First Father has no cause transcending His own state, and the subsistence of the Son is invariably implied in the title of Father, why do they try to scare us
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'Father', applied to the First Father, always imply the existence of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. "Father" is a relative term that signifies a relation to the Son and would have no meaning on its own. So in learning the name "Father" we are taught faith in the Son by the same title.
sources.quote: For the term “Father” would have no meaning apart by itself, if “Son” were not connoted by the utterance of the word “Father.”
sources.raw_question: Does the name "Father" by itself imply the existence of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: Yes. The term 'Father' by its very signification implies the Son, so the eternity of the Son cannot be detached from the eternal Father. Those who believe in the Father as the Lord commanded receive the Son in thought along with Him, with no empty interval between them; 'ungenerate', by contrast, has no relation to the Son, which is why Eunomius prefers it.
sources.quote: it is impossible to detach the eternity of the Son from the eternal Father, seeing that the term “Father” by its very signification implies the Son
sources.raw_question: Does the name 'Father' imply the eternal co-existence of the Son with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next skilfully confutes the partial, empty and blasphemous statement of Eunomius on the subject of the absolutely existent.
sources.answer: No. Without the Son the Father has neither existence nor name, just as the Powerful cannot be without Power or the Wise without Wisdom. Christ is the Power and Wisdom of God, so anyone who imagines the One God apart from these sees either nothing or what is evil, since removing the good attributes amounts to positing evil.
sources.quote: For without the Son the Father has neither existence nor name, any more than the Powerful without Power, or the Wise without Wisdom.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father exist or be named without the Son?

question: Is the doxology giving glory to the Holy Spirit 'with' (or 'and') the Father and the Son a recent innovation, or does it have ancient sanction in the Church?
synthesis: All four answers are Basil's, each denying that the doxology is an innovation. They rest on different witnesses: immemorial custom and the usage of whole nations, named Fathers such as Irenaeus, Clement and the two Dionysii, Gregory Thaumaturgus and Eastern usage, and quoted passages from Origen and Julius Africanus that readers can check.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: No. Basil argues he is no innovator, since whole nations, cities, immemorial custom, and the church's pillars used the phrase. It has been in use in the churches from the first preaching of the Gospel and has been accepted as bearing a sense in accordance with holiness and true religion.
sources.quote: from the day when the Gospel was first preached up to our own time, it is shewn to have been admitted to all full rights within the churches, and, what is of greatest moment, to have been accepted as bearing a sense in accordance with holiness and true religion
sources.raw_question: Is the doxology giving glory to the Holy Spirit 'with' or 'and' the Father and Son a theological innovation?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: No. It goes back to ancient and exact Fathers. Basil names Irenaeus, Clement of Rome, Dionysius of Rome, Dionysius of Alexandria, and Eusebius as witnesses. Dionysius of Alexandria explicitly says he received this form and rule from the presbyters before him.
sources.quote: To God the Father and the Son our Lord Jesus Christ, with the Holy Ghost, glory and might for ever and ever; amen.
sources.raw_question: Is the doxology giving glory to the Father and Son "with the Holy Spirit" a recent innovation?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: It is not an innovation. Basil appeals to Gregory Thaumaturgus, a wonder-working bishop whose churches added nothing to what he handed down, and who instituted this very form of the doxology. Firmilian and Meletius held the same, and in the East the phrase is the mark that distinguishes the orthodox. The idiom of Mesopotamia and Cappadocia, and the usage of the whole West, show that whole nations and immemorial custom stand behind it, so the charge of novelty fails.
sources.quote: Now one of the institutions of Gregory is the very form of the doxology to which objection is now made, preserved by the Church on the authority of his tradition
sources.raised_by_detail: Pneumatomachi (opponents of the Spirit's deity) accusing Basil of innovation
sources.raw_question: Is the doxology that glorifies the Holy Spirit together 'with' (or 'and') the Father and the Son a recent innovation, or does it have ancient sanction in the Church?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: It is not an innovation. Basil shows that earlier writers used it: Origen in his expositions of the Psalms and Julius Africanus in his Epitome of the Times both ascribe glory 'with the Holy Ghost.' He chooses passages quoted at length so that they cannot have been tampered with and can be checked against the actual works.
sources.quote: to whom be glory and majesty with the Holy Ghost, for ever.
sources.raw_question: Is the doxology giving glory to God 'with the Holy Spirit' a recent innovation, or is it attested in earlier Christian writers?

question: Is eternal life found in the Father alone, or is it found equally in the Son (and the Holy Spirit), so that one need not look beyond the Son to find it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > He then wonderfully displays the Eternal Life, which is Christ, to those who confess Him not, and applies to them the mournful lamentation of Jeremiah over Jehoiakim, as being closely allied to Montanus and Sabellius.
sources.answer: Eternal life resides in the Son. Gregory argues that unless eternal life is in the Son, faith is idle, preaching vain, baptism superfluous, and the labours of martyrs and Apostles useless, since they preached Christ precisely as the one through whom believers share eternal life. Eunomius's claim that the mind must pass beyond the Son to find eternal life in the Father alone amounts to a denial of the Lord.
sources.quote: For he wishes to show that the Son is something different from eternal life, while, unless eternal life is found in the Son, our faith will be proved to be idle, and our preaching to be vain, baptism a superfluity
sources.raw_question: Is eternal life found in the Son, or only in the essence of the Father beyond the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > He then wonderfully displays the Eternal Life, which is Christ, to those who confess Him not, and applies to them the mournful lamentation of Jeremiah over Jehoiakim, as being closely allied to Montanus and Sabellius.
sources.answer: Yes. The Gospel teaches us to behold eternal life alike in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. Eunomius, by seeking eternal life only in one considered apart from the Only-begotten, cuts himself off from the faith.
sources.quote: never having learned, poor wretch, that the Gospel enjoins us to behold eternal life alike in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost
sources.raw_question: Is eternal life to be seen equally in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > He then wonderfully displays the Eternal Life, which is Christ, to those who confess Him not, and applies to them the mournful lamentation of Jeremiah over Jehoiakim, as being closely allied to Montanus and Sabellius.
sources.answer: Eternal life is to be beheld alike in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Scripture says that to know the Father is life eternal, that whoever believes on the Son has eternal life, and that the Spirit's grace becomes a well springing up unto eternal life. Hence seeking eternal life in the Father apart from the Son, as Eunomius does, is a denial of the faith.
sources.quote: the Gospel enjoins us to behold eternal life alike in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost, inasmuch as the Word has thus spoken concerning the Father, that to know Him is life eternal
sources.raw_question: Is eternal life found in the Father alone, or equally in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > He then wonderfully displays the Eternal Life, which is Christ, to those who confess Him not, and applies to them the mournful lamentation of Jeremiah over Jehoiakim, as being closely allied to Montanus and Sabellius.
sources.answer: Whoever finds the true Son finds in Him the whole of the eternal life he longs for. This is because the Son is Himself life and has life in Himself. To pass the Son by as a hindrance and seek life elsewhere is to seek it where one thinks the true Life is not.
sources.quote: has found in Him in its entirety what he longed for, because He is life and hath life in Himself
sources.raw_question: Does one who finds the Son find eternal life in its entirety, or must one look beyond the Son to the Father for it?

question: Does the Son's generation from the Father's essence involve passion, parts, or division in God, as human generation does?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: No. Men beget passibly because they have a transitive nature that waits for periods through weakness, but God is not composed of parts. Being impassible and simple, He is impassibly and indivisibly Father of the Son. Scripture calls Him Son to show He is the true offspring of the Father's essence, and also Word, Wisdom, and Radiance to show that the generation is impassible and eternal.
sources.quote: But with God this cannot be; for He is not composed of parts, but being impassible and simple, He is impassibly and indivisibly Father of the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does divine generation involve passion, parts, or division in God as human generation does?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: No. God is not like man; men beget passibly because of their transitive and weak nature, but God is not composed of parts. Being impassible and simple, He is impassibly and indivisibly Father of the Son.
sources.quote: for He is not composed of parts, but being impassible and simple, He is impassibly and indivisibly Father of the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the divine generation of the Son from the Father involve passion, division, or the Son being a part of God, as human generation does?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Objection, that the Son's eternity makes Him coordinate with the Father, introduces the subject of His Divine Sonship, as a second proof of His eternity. The word Son is introduced in a secondary, but is to be understood in real sense. Since all things partake of the Father in partaking of the Son, He is the whole participation of the Father, that is, He is the Son by nature; for to be wholly participated is to beget.
sources.answer: No. To infer division is to have material thoughts about what is immaterial and to measure the Father's offspring by human nature. Denying that the Son is from the Father's essence on this ground amounts to calling him Son in name only; and since being participated is the same as begetting, what is begotten is neither affection nor division of God's essence.
sources.quote: And is it not a grievous error, to have material thoughts about what is immaterial, and because of the weakness of their proper nature to deny what is natural and proper to the Father?
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being the proper offspring of the Father's essence imply parts and divisions in God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. Even among originate and irrational things, offspring are found (radiance from light, reason from mind) that are not parts of the essences they come from, involve no passion, and do not impair their source. It is therefore madness to ascribe parts, passions and divisions to the immaterial and true God, who is beyond passion and change.
sources.quote: are they not mad again in seeking and conjecturing parts and passions in the instance of the immaterial and true God, and ascribing divisions to Him who is beyond passion and change
sources.raw_question: Does the generation of the Son from God imply division, parts or passion in the divine essence?

question: Does anything in the divine nature require the Son and the Holy Spirit to be less than the Father in goodness, power or being, as Eunomius claims with his graded 'energies'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He did wrong, when mentioning the Doctrines of Salvation, in adopting terms of his own choosing instead of the traditional terms Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. The Son and Spirit lack nothing of perfect goodness and power. Good can be limited only by its opposite, and the divine nature is unalterable and incapable of degeneracy, as even the opponents allow. Therefore their goodness is unlimited, that is, infinite. Excess and defect cannot be supposed in the infinite.
sources.quote: the personality of the Only-begotten and of the Holy Ghost has nothing lacking in the way of perfect goodness, perfect power, and of every quality like that.
sources.raw_question: Does the supremacy of being that Eunomius ascribes to the Father imply that the Son and Spirit are less good or less powerful than the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in assuming, to account for the existence of the Only-Begotten, an 'energy' that produced Christ's Person.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius has not explained this supposed necessity. Those who accept the Gospel in its plain simplicity have always held that no necessity stands above the Godhead to bend the Only-begotten, like a slave, to inferiority.
sources.quote: Hitherto there has prevailed with those who accept the Gospel in its plain simplicity the belief that there is no necessity above the Godhead to bend the Only-begotten, like a slave, to inferiority.
sources.raw_question: Is there any necessity in the Divine nature requiring the Son and the Spirit to be lesser than the Father, as Eunomius' graded 'energies' imply?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in assuming, to account for the existence of the Only-Begotten, an 'energy' that produced Christ's Person.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius has never explained what this supposed necessity is, and the plain faith of the Gospel holds that there is no necessity above the Godhead that could bend the Only-begotten, like a slave, into inferiority. To posit such a compelling necessity is to set something above God and to dogmatize an inferiority that has no ground.
sources.quote: Hitherto there has prevailed with those who accept the Gospel in its plain simplicity the belief that there is no necessity above the Godhead to bend the Only-begotten, like a slave, to inferiority.
sources.raw_question: Does any necessity in the divine nature require that the Son be less than the Father and the Holy Spirit less than the Son, as Eunomius claims when he says the energies accompanying these Beings are relatively greater and less?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. Such a difference cannot rest on material measurement, because the Persons are not material. It cannot rest on pure being, since bare being admits no difference once attributes are abstracted. It cannot rest on moral excellence either, since that would make their nature changeable and capable of opposites, which is gross profanity.
sources.quote: it has been shown by competent thinkers that it is impossible to conceive of any difference whatever, if one abstracts being from attributes and properties, and looks at it according to its bare definition
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius right that the Son and the Spirit must necessarily be relatively greater and less than the Father?

question: Does calling God 'Father' and the Only-begotten 'Son' imply that the divine generation involves passion or other bodily conditions, so that the Son must be denied to be truly begotten?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He further shows the operations of God to be expressed by human illustrations; for what hands and feet and the other parts of the body with which men work are, that, in the case of God, the will alone is, in place of these. And so also arises the divergence of generation; wherefore He is called Only-begotten, because He has no community with other generation such as is observed in creation, but in that He is called the “brightness of glory,” and the “savour of ointment,” He shows the close conjunction and co-eternity of His Nature with the Father.
sources.answer: No. Scripture uses the human name 'Son' because our poverty cannot grasp truths above speech, but it leaves out passions, dispositions, time, place and especially matter. When all these are excluded, nature alone remains, so the name 'Son' declares the close and true character of His manifestation from the Father, i.e. his sharing the Father's nature.
sources.quote: Now every such conception of matter and interval being excluded from the sense of the word “Son,” nature alone remains, and hereby in the word “Son” is declared concerning the Only-begotten the close and true character of His manifestation from the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Only-begotten 'Son' imply passion, time, place, or matter in his generation from the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: No. The mystery of theology is one thing and the physiology of unstable bodies another, and the two are widely separated. One must not draw an account of the nature of things above from those below, nor build systems for the incorporeal out of bodily passions. The names Father and Son teach that the Son is from the Father, not that he is from passion.
sources.quote: Surely truth answers you on his behalf, that the mystery of theology is one thing, and the physiology of unstable bodies is another. Wide is the interval by which they are fenced off one from the other.
sources.raw_question: Does calling God "Father" and the Son "Only-begotten" imply passion in the divine generation, since all bodily generation involves passion?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: No. John names the Son of God while purging his proclamation of every idea of passion, using "Beginning," "was," and "Word" before he speaks of Father and Only-begotten. None of these terms implies passion, yet they express community of essence and real relationship. So true relationship to the Father and freedom from passion coincide in God.
sources.quote: Not thus speaks the sublime John, not thus that voice of thunder which proclaims the mystery of the Theology, who both names Him Son of God and purges his proclamation from every idea of passion.
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that the Son is truly begotten of the Father require admitting that the divine generation involves passion?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds again to discuss the impassibility of the Lord's generation; and the folly of Eunomius, who says that the generated essence involves the appellation of Son, and again, forgetting this, denies the relation of the Son to the Father: and herein he speaks of Circe and of the mandrake poison.
sources.answer: No. Not all generation is naturally connected with passion: material generation is subject to passion, but immaterial generation is pure from it. Eunomius wrongly transfers to the incorruptible generation of the Son what properly belongs to the flesh, and so excludes the Son from affinity with the Father.
sources.quote: Therefore not all generation is naturally connected with passion, but the material generation is subject to passion, the immaterial pure from passion.
sources.raw_question: Does attributing generation to God the Father necessarily involve passion, so that the Son must be denied to be truly begotten in order to protect divine impassibility?

question: If the Son is begotten by the Father's nature rather than by His will, does it follow that the Son exists by necessity or against the Father's good pleasure?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. Just as the Father did not begin to be good 'from will' yet is not good without His will and pleasure, so the Son, though not 'from will,' is not without the Father's pleasure or against His purpose. As the Father's own Subsistence is by His pleasure, so the Son, proper to His Essence, is the object of the Father's pleasure and love.
sources.quote: so also that the Son should be, though it came not ‘from will,’ yet it is not without His pleasure or against His purpose.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is begotten by nature rather than by will, does it follow that the Son exists against or without the Father's pleasure?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. The Arian dilemma overlooks that what is according to nature transcends and precedes counsel, just as what is beside purpose is contrary to will. Generation by nature is neither forced nor against God's pleasure; it is above the category of deliberation. Applying the human contrarieties of 'necessity' and 'beside purpose' to God is illegitimate.
sources.quote: For as what is beside purpose is contrary to will, so what is according to nature transcends and precedes counselling
sources.raw_question: If the Son is not begotten by the Father's will, does it follow that God had a Son by necessity and against His good pleasure?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. God did not begin to be good by will, yet he is not good apart from his will and pleasure. In the same way the Son's existence does not come from will, but it is not against the Father's pleasure or purpose. The Father loves the Son, and one good pleasure passes between Father and Son.
sources.quote: so also that the Son should be, though it came not ‘from will,’ yet it is not without His pleasure or against His purpose.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is from the Father by nature and not by will, is he then without the Father's pleasure or against his will?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. What is contrary to will is not the only alternative to will; what is according to nature transcends and precedes counselling. A man builds a house by counsel but begets a son by nature, and the son is proper offspring of his essence rather than external to him, so as the Son transcends creatures, so natural generation transcends will.
sources.quote: For as what is beside purpose is contrary to will, so what is according to nature transcends and precedes counselling
sources.raw_question: If the Son is not begotten by the Father's will, does it follow that God had a Son by necessity and against His good pleasure?

question: Was the world created by the one God himself through his Word, or by angels or some other power separate from and ignorant of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter X.—Perverse interpretations of Scripture by the heretics: God created all things out of nothing, and not from pre-existent matter.
sources.answer: By God through His Word. The God above all formed every work of creation by His Word, in His own territory and as He pleased, like a wise architect and a most powerful monarch. Those who credit angels or an ignorant power have abandoned the truth for falsehood.
sources.quote: They do not believe that He, who is God above all, formed by His Word, in His own territory, as He Himself pleased, the various and diversified [works of creation which exist]
sources.raw_question: Was the world formed by God Himself through His Word, or by angels or some power separate from and ignorant of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXII.—That one God was the author of both Testaments, is confirmed by the authority of a presbyter who had been taught by the apostles.
sources.answer: No. There is no other God besides Him who made and fashioned us, and the claim that the world was made by angels or another power has no foundation. Whoever grants that creation was formed by any other than the one God falls necessarily into inconsistency and contradictions for which he can give no probable or true explanation.
sources.quote: the discourse of those men has no foundation who affirm that this world of ours was made either by angels, or by any other power whatsoever, or by another God
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who attribute creation to angels or another God
sources.raw_question: Was the world made by angels, some other power, or another God rather than by the one God who is Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XI.—The heretics, from their disbelief of the truth, have fallen into an abyss of error: reasons for investigating their systems.
sources.answer: The one God over all formed the world himself through his Word, in his own territory and as he pleased. He is the former of all things, like a wise architect and a most powerful monarch. Those who ascribe creation to angels or a power ignorant of God have abandoned the truth and fallen into falsehood, like Aesop's dog that dropped the bread for its shadow.
sources.quote: They do not believe that He, who is God above all, formed by His Word, in His own territory, as He Himself pleased, the various and diversified [works of creation which exist]
sources.raw_question: Did the one God over all create the world himself through his Word, or was the world formed by angels or some power separate from and ignorant of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
