sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXV.—Refutation of Basilides, and of the opinion that the prophets uttered their predictions under the inspiration of different gods.
sources.answer: No. All things visible and invisible were made by God alone, the Father, and not by angels or any other power. The apostles, the Lord's teaching, the prophets and the law all agree in praising one and the same God and Father of all. Irenaeus holds he has sufficiently proved that there is but one God, the Maker of all things.
sources.quote: all things that have been made [were created] neither by angels, nor by any other power, but by God alone, the Father
sources.raw_question: Was the world created by angels or by subordinate powers rather than by God the Father himself?

question: What does Proverbs 8:23, 'Before the world He founded me', mean, and does it show that the Son had a beginning or was created before the world?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: No. These phrases accord with 'founded' and 'created' and likewise refer to the Economy according to the flesh. They signify that God's purpose and the grace of our salvation were prepared beforehand in the Word before the world existed, not that the Word himself came into being then.
sources.quote: Nor let the words ‘before the world’ and ‘before He made the earth’ and ‘before the mountains were settled’ disturb any one; for they very well accord with ‘founded’ and ‘created;’ for here again allusion is made to the Economy according to the flesh.
sources.raw_question: Do the phrases 'before the world' and 'before He made the earth' in Proverbs 8:23-25 show that the Son is a creature who was created before the world?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: No. The verse refers to the Word's incarnate presence, not His Godhead. Since the Lord founded the earth by Wisdom, the one who founds cannot himself be founded as to his divinity; rather, Wisdom is founded for us, to become the beginning and foundation of our new creation and renewal.
sources.quote: while by Wisdom the Father frames and founds the earth to be firm and steadfast, Wisdom Itself is founded for us, that It may become beginning and foundation of our new creation and renewal
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:23, 'He founded me before the world,' refer to the Godhead of the Word, implying the Word had a beginning?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: 'Before the world' signifies God's prior counsel and purpose. Foreseeing humanity's fall, God prepared the economy of salvation in His Word before the foundation of the world. So the grace that appeared in the Incarnation was prepared beforehand, and the phrase fits the economy according to the flesh.
sources.quote: yet this grace had been prepared even before we came into being, nay, before the foundation of the world, and the reason why is kindly and wonderful. It beseemed not that God should counsel concerning us afterwards, lest He should appear ignorant of our fate.
sources.raw_question: How can Proverbs 8 say the Word was founded 'before the world' if His founding refers to the Incarnation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: It refers to Wisdom's impress in the works. Because that impress is in them, the works remain settled and lasting. It does not describe the Son's essence being founded or created.
sources.quote: And He says, ‘Before the world He founded me,’ since in Its impress the works remain settled and eternal.
sources.raw_question: What does 'Before the world He founded me' in Proverbs 8:23 mean when applied to Wisdom?

question: In what respect is man made in the image of God: according to his body or according to his mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God from the Trinities We Have Spoken of.
sources.answer: Man is the image of God not according to everything that pertains to his nature but according to his mind alone. Each individual man is one person and is an image of the Trinity in his mind, not in his body.
sources.quote: each individual man, who is called the image of God, not according to all things that pertain to his nature, but according to his mind alone, is one person, and is an image of the Trinity in his mind.
sources.raw_question: In what respect is man the image of God, and does this image extend to his whole nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > How Man is the Image of God. Whether the Woman is Not Also the Image of God. How the Saying of the Apostle, that the Man is the Image of God, But the Woman is the Glory of the Man, is to Be Understood Figuratively and Mystically.
sources.answer: According to his rational mind, not his body. Both reason and the apostle's authority show this, since it is a debased thought to hold God circumscribed by bodily members. Paul speaks of being renewed in the spirit of the mind to the knowledge of God after the image of Him that created him, so the image lies in the rational mind, where knowledge of God can exist.
sources.quote: man was not made in the image of God according to the shape of his body, but according to his rational mind. For the thought is a debased and empty one, which holds God to be circumscribed and limited by the lineaments of bodily members.
sources.raw_question: Is man made in the image of God according to the shape of his body or according to his mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > How Man is the Image of God. Whether the Woman is Not Also the Image of God. How the Saying of the Apostle, that the Man is the Image of God, But the Woman is the Glory of the Man, is to Be Understood Figuratively and Mystically.
sources.answer: No. Both reason and the apostle teach that man was made in God's image according to his rational mind, not his bodily shape, since it is debased to think God limited by bodily members. Paul speaks of being renewed in the spirit of the mind to the knowledge of God after the image of Him who created him.
sources.quote: man was not made in the image of God according to the shape of his body, but according to his rational mind.
sources.raw_question: Is the image of God in man found in the shape of the human body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > God is Above the Mind.
sources.answer: It consists in the mind, that is, the rational or intellectual soul. This is what makes man excel the other animals. Some Latin writers use the word "mind" to distinguish this excellence, which beasts lack, from the soul, which beasts also have.
sources.quote: we have now advanced so far as to His image, which is man, in that wherein he excels the other animals, i.e. in reason or intelligence
sources.raw_question: In what part of human nature does the image of God in man chiefly consist?

question: Should the Holy Spirit be subnumerated (counted beneath the Father and the Son as lower in rank) rather than connumerated with them?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who say that the Holy Ghost is not to be numbered with, but numbered under, the Father and the Son. Wherein moreover there is a summary notice of the faith concerning right sub-numeration.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit is named together with the Lord in exactly the same way that the Son is named with the Father. Since the three names form one co-ordinate series, connumeration for some and sub-numeration for the Spirit has no basis. Those who demand it are, like the heathen, assuming that things inferior in rank or substance must be subnumerated.
sources.quote: When then the names are ranked in one and the same co-ordinate series, what room is there for speaking on the one hand of connumeration, and on the other of sub-numeration?
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be numbered under (subnumerated to) the Father and the Son rather than numbered with them?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: No. Ranking the Persons as first, second and third in sub-numeration brings heathen polytheism into Christian theology. It can only end in confessing a first, a second and a third God. The order prescribed by the Lord in the baptismal formula is sufficient, and it does not dissolve the communion of nature.
sources.quote: No other result can be achieved by the fell device of sub-numeration than the confession of a first, a second, and a third God. For us is sufficient the order prescribed by the Lord.
sources.raw_question: Should the Holy Spirit be 'subnumerated' (counted as first, second, third in rank) beneath the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who say that the Holy Ghost is not to be numbered with, but numbered under, the Father and the Son. Wherein moreover there is a summary notice of the faith concerning right sub-numeration.
sources.answer: No. Counting does not confer or remove value: number cannot exalt what is cheap or destroy the dignity of what is valuable. Lead counted with gold or a brass obol counted with a gold stater is simply 'one and one,' each mentioned in the same way. Counting things separately treats them alike, and joining them unites them, so number gives no ground for ranking the Spirit lower.
sources.quote: And do you attribute so much importance to number as that it can either exalt the value of what is cheap, or destroy the dignity of what is valuable?
sources.raw_question: Is it valid to hold that connumeration belongs to things of equal dignity and sub-numeration to things of inferior dignity, so that the Holy Spirit should be numbered under rather than with the Father and Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: No. Number is only a symbol devised to indicate quantity and changes nothing in the things counted. To use counting to lower the Paraclete turns arithmetic against the faith. The divine nature is above number, so either the ineffable is honoured by silence or holy things are counted in a way consistent with true religion.
sources.quote: Count, if you must; but you must not by counting do damage to the faith. Either let the ineffable be honoured by silence; or let holy things be counted consistently with true religion.
sources.raised_by_detail: Pneumatomachi (those alleging the Spirit is subnumerated)
sources.raw_question: Should the Holy Spirit be 'subnumerated', that is, counted beneath the Father and the Son as lower in rank?

question: Does the language of 'becoming' or being 'made' in Hebrews 1:4 show that the Son is originate or created?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. Paul distinguishes the Son from things originate: He is Son and not an angel, He frames heaven and earth while they are made by Him, and He sits with the Father while they stand ministering. 'Become' therefore refers not to the essence of the Word but to His ministry and the Economy. Just as the Word 'became flesh,' so, having become man, He became better in His ministry than the ministry that came by angels.
sources.quote: who does not see that he has not used the word ‘become’ of the essence of the Word, but of the ministration come through Him? For as, being the ‘Word,’ He ‘became flesh,’ so when become man, He became by so much better in His ministry
sources.raw_question: Does the word 'become' in Hebrews 1:4 ('being made so much better than the angels') show that the Son is originate or created?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. The word 'made' is used of the angels as things originate, but to the Son the Apostle speaks not of making or becoming but of eternity, kingship, and the Framer's office: 'Thy throne, O God, is for ever' and 'Thou, Lord, hast laid the foundation of the earth.' This shows the Framer is God and other than the things framed out of nothing.
sources.quote: the word ‘made’ belongs to things originate, and he calls them things made; but to the Son he speaks not of making, nor of becoming, but of eternity and kingship, and a Framer’s office
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1 apply the language of 'making' to the Son as it does to the angels?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. The word is not used absolutely but is qualified by 'better', and the whole passage calls Him 'Son', showing He is other than things originate. Of a genuine Son, 'become' simply means that He is better. Scripture uses 'came to be' even of sons generated, as of Job's sons and Isaac, so the word does not imply creation; the Son is the proper offspring of the Father's essence.
sources.quote: Therefore since the Son is other than things originate, alone the proper offspring of the Father’s essence, this plea of the Arians about the word ‘become’ is worth nothing.
sources.raw_question: Does the word 'become' in Hebrews 1:4 show that the Son is a creature or originated being?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. The phrase must be read in the same sense as 'become' when it is said of God. It refers to the Word's ministry and Economy when he became man, not to any original becoming of his essence. When the Word became flesh, he became salvation, life and propitiation for us, and his economy on our behalf became far better than the angels'. The phrase therefore signifies the beneficence that came to us through his becoming Man.
sources.quote: do not signify that the essence of the Word is originate (perish the thought!), but the beneficence which towards us came to be through His becoming Man
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1:4, which says the Son was 'made' or 'become' better than the angels, show that the Word is originate or created?

question: Is there any middle position between the Son's being essentially God, of the Father's substance, and his being a creature made out of nothing?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 13: Whether there can be any middle between being made out of nothing, and out of something ; that is, between being out of nothing, and out of the Father's substan
sources.answer: No. Waterland reduces the whole dispute to one point: whether the Creator and Redeemer is a creature or not. He holds that Dr. Clarke's scheme, which avoids saying the Son is a creature, still implies it tacitly and by consequence. On that scheme the Son would be mutable, dependent, finite, and owe his existence to the Father's good pleasure. The refusal to name him a creature therefore only disguises the position and does not create a real third option.
sources.quote: Let every reader be apprised, that the only question between us is, whether his Creator and Redeemer be a creature, or no: and then the cause will be brought to a short issue; and it will soon be seen where the truth lies.
sources.raw_question: Is there any middle position between the Son's being essentially God, out of the Father's substance, and his being a creature made out of nothing?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. Arius rightly saw that there neither is nor can be any medium between God and creature. A Son made out of some pre-created substance would still ultimately come from nothing. Nothing outside God can be coeternal with him, so the Son is either God or a creature.
sources.quote: Arius had so much philosophy, or rather common sense, as to think, and so much frankness and ingenuity, as to confess, that there neither is nor can be any medium between God and creature.
sources.raw_question: Is there any middle ground between God and creature for the Son's nature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 13: Whether there can be any middle between being made out of nothing, and out of something ; that is, between being out of nothing, and out of the Father's substan
sources.answer: No. Waterland holds the disjunction to be as clear as a geometrical axiom: either the Son is of the same undivided substance with the Father, or he is a creature. Whoever denies the former must by consequence admit the latter, and no medium is consistent with Scripture or the reason of things.
sources.quote: Let it be said then plainly, and without disguise, that the Son of God is either consubstantial with God the Father, or else a creature. There is no medium, neither can there be any, consistent with Scripture and with the truth and reason of things.
sources.raw_question: Is there any middle option between the Son of God being consubstantial (of the same undivided substance) with the Father and his being a creature made out of nothing?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 13: Whether there can be any middle between being made out of nothing, and out of something ; that is, between being out of nothing, and out of the Father's substan
sources.answer: No. Waterland holds that no medium between being essentially God and being a creature can be found or can exist. His opponents must therefore either confess the Son to be essentially God or declare plainly that he is a creature. Their refusal to say so is evasion, not a real third option.
sources.quote: You was to find a medium between being essentially God, and being a creature: or else to declare in plain terms, that the Son is a creature. A medium you find not, nor indeed can there be any
sources.raw_question: Is there any middle state between being essentially God and being a creature, such that the Son could be neither?

question: Since Scripture commands that the Lord God alone be worshipped, does the divine worship given to and accepted by Jesus Christ prove that he is God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture commands that the Lord God alone be worshipped and served. Christ received divine worship and accepted it, and this is decisive proof that he is God.
sources.quote: we carefully ponder the Divine worship offered to him, and accepted by him, this is decisive, when we remember, “Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.”
sources.raw_question: Does the worship offered to Jesus Christ and accepted by him prove his deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ himself says, 'Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and Him only shalt thou serve.' Scripture shows the highest worship and service, on earth and in heaven, being given to the Son. It follows that the Son is the Lord our God.
sources.quote: But we have seen that the highest worship and service on earth, and in heaven, is rendered to the Son. Therefore, He is the Lord our God.
sources.raw_question: Since Scripture commands worship of the Lord God alone, does the worship given to Christ prove that he is God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ himself, summing up Scripture, said that the Lord God alone is to be worshipped and served. Yet the highest worship and service on earth and in heaven is rendered to the Son. Therefore the Son is the Lord our God.
sources.quote: But we have seen that the highest worship and service on earth, and in heaven, is rendered to the Son. Therefore, He is the Lord our God.
sources.raw_question: Does the worship given to Jesus Christ prove that he is the Lord God, given Christ's own teaching that God alone is to be worshipped?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Direct and divine worship is rendered to and received by Christ in earth and heaven, while Scripture commands that the Lord God alone be worshipped. This compels us to acknowledge that he is the Lord our God.
sources.quote: the direct and Divine worship rendered to and received by Christ, in earth and heaven, compels us to acknowledge He is the Lord our God
sources.raw_question: Does the divine worship given to and accepted by Christ prove that he is God?

question: Does the Son's being described as 'in the bosom of the Father' and 'in the beginning' mean that the Son does not exist in the strict or absolute sense?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory calls this an idle and irrational tenet. Eunomius argues that because the Son is in the Father, in the beginning, and in the bosom of the Existent, he therefore does not strictly exist. Gregory rejects this as unheard-of vain babbling about the Lord by Whom are all things.
sources.quote: Now for the first time we have heard this piece of vain babbling,—that the Lord, by Whom are all things, does not in a strict sense exist.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being in the bosom of the Father and in the beginning mean that he does not exist in a strict sense?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. John states absolutely and without relation to anything else that 'the Word was God,' which cuts off this subterfuge. Moreover, if existing in something meant not existing strictly, then the Father too would not exist absolutely, since the Gospel says the Father abides in the Son just as the Son abides in the Father.
sources.quote: For if they make out that to exist in something is an indication of not existing in the strict sense, then certainly they allow that not even the Father exists absolutely
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being described as 'in the bosom of the Father' or 'with God' imply that the Son does not exist in the strict or absolute sense?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. If being in something else excluded strict existence, then everything contained in another would not exist, which is absurd: Eunomius's own heart and brain are within him and yet certainly exist. The additions 'in the beginning' and 'in the bosom of the Father' express relation, not a diminution of real being.
sources.quote: For if the Only-begotten God does not, strictly speaking, exist, for this reason, that He is in the bosom of the Father, then everything that is in something else is thereby excluded from existence.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being 'in the bosom of the Father' and 'in the beginning' mean that the Son does not exist in the strict or proper sense?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. John says simply and without qualification that 'the Word was God,' was Life and was Light, not merely that he was in the beginning or in the Father's bosom. This absolute declaration, detached from all relation, cuts off the Eunomian subterfuge and shows the Son exists in the strict sense.
sources.quote: saying simply and without qualification “The Word was God,” and was Life, and was Light, not merely speaking of Him as being in the beginning, and with God, and in the bosom of the Father
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ever attest the Son's existence absolutely, apart from relation to the Father, so that he exists in the strict sense?

question: Is the Holy Spirit a distinct object of the believer's faith, love, prayer, worship, and communion?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen says our fellowship with the Spirit consists largely in the consolation we receive from him. This teaches us to value his love and to know whom to pray to and whom to wait on in distress. The Spirit is therefore to be addressed in prayer, not only prayed for.
sources.quote: This gives us a valuation of his love; teacheth whither to make applications in our distress, — whom to pray for, to pray to, — whom to wait upon, in perplexities.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a proper object of prayer and of distinct communion?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Because Scripture clearly and frequently ascribes the works of consolation to the immediate efficiency of the Holy Ghost, faith closes with him in that revealed truth and peculiarly worships, serves, prays to, and praises him. The person of the Spirit, revealing himself in these operations, is the peculiar object of worship, though worship directed to him as God is also directed to the other persons.
sources.quote: The person of the Holy Ghost, revealing itself in these operations and effects, is the peculiar object of our worship.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a distinct object of faith, worship, and prayer, so that believers may believe in him, praise him, and pray to him particularly?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Yes. When faith sees the Spirit's gracious will and infinite condescension as the source of all he works in us, the soul deals with him in a distinct way. Its desires, affections, and thankfulness are directed to him in particular.
sources.quote: our souls are peculiarly conversant with him, and their desires, affections, and thankfulness, terminated on him
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit himself a proper object of the believer's affection, thanksgiving, and communion?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture speaks distinctly of the love of the Spirit (Rom. 15:30). Paul directs supplication to the Spirit in the benediction of 2 Corinthians 13:14, and such benedictions are originally prayers. Baptism is also administered in the Spirit's name (Matt. 28:19), which entitles him to all instituted worship. Unbelief, in turn, is described as resisting the Spirit.
sources.quote: He is likewise entitled unto all instituted worship, from the appointment of the administration of baptism in his name, Matt. xxviii. 19.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a distinct object of the believer's love, prayer, and worship?

question: In Augustine's analogy of a trinity in the outer man, can the will that unites the object and the vision (in sight or in recollection) be called either parent or offspring?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Species is Produced by Species in Succession.
sources.answer: No. In every case the will appears only as the combiner of parent and offspring, joining the begetting form to the form begotten from it. So, wherever the will itself proceeds from, it can be called neither parent nor offspring. This marks the third member of the analogy as distinct from the generating and the generated.
sources.quote: Yet in all cases the will does not appear unless as the combiner as it were of parent and offspring; and so, proceed from whence it may, it can be called neither parent nor offspring.
sources.raw_question: In Augustine's psychological analogy of the Trinity, can the will that unites the perceived object and the vision be called either parent or offspring?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > There is Another Trinity in the Memory of Him Who Thinks Over Again What He Has Seen.
sources.answer: No, it is neither. The will to remember cannot arise unless something of the thing is already retained in memory, so it proceeds from what is retained and what is copied through recollection. Yet the will that unites both also requires something else close at hand to the one who remembers, so it is not simply generated from them; it is a third that joins both and with them completes one thing.
sources.quote: the will of remembering proceeds, indeed, from those things which are retained in the memory, with the addition also of those which, by the act of discerning, are copied thence through recollection
sources.raw_question: In the trinity of recollection, is the will that unites memory and the mind's vision itself the parent or offspring of either of them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > The Trinity of the Outer Man, or of External Vision, is Not an Image of God. The Likeness of God is Desired Even in Sins. In External Vision the Form of the Corporeal Thing is as It Were the Parent, Vision the Offspring; But the Will that Unites These Suggests the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. It is not the quasi-offspring of vision, since the will existed before the vision and applied the sense to the object. Nor is it the quasi-parent, since the vision is formed from the bodily thing seen, not from the will.
sources.quote: we can neither call the will the quasi-offspring of vision, since it existed before vision; nor the quasi-parent, since that vision was not formed and expressed from the will, but from the bodily thing that was seen.
sources.raw_question: In the analogy of vision, can the uniting will be called either the offspring or the parent of the vision?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Number, Weight, Measure.
sources.answer: No. The will is the uniter of the visible thing and the vision, which stand to each other as parent and offspring. This holds both in sense perception and in conception. The will itself cannot be called either parent or offspring, and so it serves as an analogy for a third that proceeds without being begotten.
sources.quote: the will is the uniter of the visible thing and of the vision; as it were, of parent and of offspring; whether in [sensuous] perception or in conception, and that it cannot be called either parent or offspring
sources.raw_question: In Augustine's trinity of the outer man (visible thing, vision, and will), can the will that unites the visible thing and the vision be called either parent or offspring?

question: Is the obedience of Christ's life, and not only his death, imputed to believers as their righteousness before God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Yes. Complete acceptance requires not only the non-imputation of sin but a reckoning of righteousness, and this is found in the obedience of Christ's life, which was for us and is imputed to us. By his obedience we are made righteous.
sources.quote: The obedience of the life of Christ was for us, is imputed to us, and is our righteousness before God; — by his obedience are we “made righteous,” Rom. v. 19.
sources.raw_question: Is the obedience of Christ's life imputed to believers as their righteousness before God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: No. Owen rejects this view because it puts our faith and new obedience in the place of Christ's righteousness. Christ's death removes guilt, and we also need a complete righteousness. Christ's obedience is imputed to us by God's free grace for that purpose.
sources.quote: this obedience of Christ, through the free grace of God, is imputed unto us for that end and purpose.
sources.raw_question: Is only Christ's passive righteousness imputed to believers, with faith and new obedience serving as the condition of justification?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Besides being absolved from guilt by Christ's death, believers need a positive righteousness so that they may be counted perfectly righteous. They have this by the life of Christ, whose obedience to the law is imputed to them. Together, discharge from guilt and imputed righteousness give believers friendship and peace with God.
sources.quote: Imputation of righteousness, that we may be accounted perfectly righteous before God; and this we have by the life of Christ. His righteousness in yielding obedience to the law is imputed to us.
sources.raw_question: Is the obedience of Christ's life, and not only his death, imputed to believers as their righteousness before God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as death is the wage of sin and we are freed only by Christ's death, so life requires that all the law demands be done ('Do this, and live'). The commandments must be kept either by us or by our surety, and Romans 5:19 says by the obedience of one many are made righteous.
sources.quote: They must, then, be kept by us, or our surety.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's perfect active obedience to the law reckoned (imputed) to believers for righteousness?

question: Is human flesh capable of receiving the life, power and incorruption that God gives, and therefore of resurrection?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter IV.—Those persons are deceived who feign another God the Father besides the Creator of the world; for he must have been feeble and useless, or else malignant and full of envy, if he be either unable or unwilling to extend external life to our bodies.
sources.answer: Yes. Bodies plainly live for as long as God pleases that they should live, so they cannot be said to be incapable of life. The long lives of the patriarchs, and Enoch and Elijah taken up bodily, show that nothing prevents the body from sharing in God's life.
sources.quote: Now every one must perceive that bodies are capable of receiving life. For they live to the extent that God pleases that they should live
sources.raw_question: Is the human body capable of receiving life from God, and therefore of resurrection?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIII.—In the dead who were raised by Christ we possess the highest proof of the resurrection; and our hearts are shown to be capable of life eternal, because they can now receive the Spirit of God.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says believers are an epistle written with the Spirit of the living God on the fleshly tables of the heart. Fleshly hearts already share in the Spirit in this present life. So it is not surprising that in the resurrection they will receive the life the Spirit grants.
sources.quote: If, therefore, in the present time, fleshly hearts are made partakers of the Spirit, what is there astonishing if, in the resurrection, they receive that life which is granted by the Spirit?
sources.raw_question: Can human flesh receive the Spirit of God and the life the Spirit gives?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter III.—The power and glory of God shine forth in the weakness of human flesh, as He will render our body a participator of the resurrection and of immortality, although He has formed it from the dust of the earth; He will also bestow upon it the enjoyment of immortality, just as He grants it this short life in common with the soul.
sources.answer: Yes. The flesh is shown to be capable of life by the fact that it is alive now, and God plainly has power to give life since he gives it to us at present. If the inferior temporal life can quicken our mortal members, eternal life, being far more powerful, can surely vivify flesh already accustomed to sustain life. Nothing therefore prevents the flesh from participating in incorruption.
sources.quote: But if the present temporal life, which is of such an inferior nature to eternal life, can nevertheless effect so much as to quicken our mortal members, why should not eternal life, being much more powerful than this, vivify the flesh
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who deny the salvation of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Is human flesh capable of receiving the eternal life and incorruption that God grants?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter III.—The power and glory of God shine forth in the weakness of human flesh, as He will render our body a participator of the resurrection and of immortality, although He has formed it from the dust of the earth; He will also bestow upon it the enjoyment of immortality, just as He grants it this short life in common with the soul.
sources.answer: Yes. The flesh at the beginning received the skilful workmanship of God, which formed its eyes, ears, hands, sinews, veins and organs through His great wisdom. Whatever partakes of God's skill and wisdom also partakes of His power. Therefore the flesh is fit to receive the life-giving power of God.
sources.quote: But those things which partake of the skill and wisdom of God, do also partake of His power.
sources.raw_question: Is human flesh capable of receiving the power of God?

question: How can Christ say "I will not judge him; but the word that I have spoken shall judge him" when the Son of man is to judge the living and the dead?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. The word that judges is the Father's word and commandment, which is everlasting life. The Son himself is the Word of the Father and is the true God and eternal life. So the judging word is the Son himself. The following section resolves the apparent contradiction: he will not judge by human power as Son of man, but will judge by the power of the Word as Son of God.
sources.quote: then the Father assuredly judges, whose word it is which the Son hath spoken; and the same Son Himself is the very Word of the Father.
sources.raw_question: When Christ says 'I will not judge him' but 'the word that I have spoken shall judge him', does this mean the Son will not judge?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: Both are true in different respects. The Son of man will judge because he will appear in the form of the Son of man and all nations will be gathered before him; yet he will not judge by human power but by that whereby he is the Son of God, and in that sense he says "I will not judge him" and "there is One that seeketh and judgeth."
sources.quote: Therefore both ways of speaking may be used; the Son of man will judge, and, the Son of man will not judge
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture say both that the Son of man will judge and that the Son of man will not judge?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: He will not judge by human power as Son of man, but he will judge by the power of the Word as Son of God. The Word of the Father that judges is the Son himself, so the saying is not a contradiction. It distinguishes two forms in which he acts. By pointing to the Godhead he raises human hearts upward.
sources.quote: I will not judge by human power, because I am the Son of man; but I will judge by the power of the Word, because I am the Son of God?
sources.raw_question: How can Christ say "I will not judge him; but the Word which I have spoken shall judge him" when he is himself to judge the living and the dead?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: Both sayings are true in different respects. The Son of man will judge, because the judging form that appears will be the form of the Son of man. The Son of man will not judge, because the judging is done by divine power and not human power. The Father does not judge, because in the judgment the form of God, which the Father shares, will not appear; only the Son's assumed human form will be seen.
sources.quote: For in respect to this, that in the judgment, not the form of God, but the form of the Son of man will appear, the Father Himself will not judge
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture say both that the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son, and that the Son of man will not judge?

question: Can the generation of the Word from the Father be explained by analogy with a human word produced by a human mind?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. God is all Nous and all Logos, with nothing earlier or later in Him, altogether equal, similar and homogeneous, so there is no ground for an ordered production. Those who transfer the generation of a human uttered word to the eternal Word assign Him a beginning and course of production; but then the Word of God, who is God Himself, would differ in nothing from the word of men.
sources.quote: And in what respect will the Word of God—yea, rather God Himself, since He is the Word—differ from the word of men, if He follows the same order and process of generation?
sources.raw_question: Can the generation of the Word (Logos) from God's intelligence (Nous) be understood on the analogy of a human word produced by a human mind, with a beginning and sequence?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: No. That sequence fits man, who is a compound being and whose word is uttered in successive efforts by a fleshly tongue. God is all mind, all reason, all active spirit and all light, and always exists one and the same. Such feelings and divisions of operation therefore cannot fittingly be ascribed to Him.
sources.quote: But since God is all mind, all reason, all active spirit, all light, and always exists one and the same, as it is both beneficial for us to think of God, and as we learn regarding Him from the Scriptures, such feelings and divisions [of operation] cannot fittingly be ascribed to Him.
sources.raw_question: Can the generation of God's Thought (Ennoia) and Word (Logos) be modeled on the human mind's succession of thought, intention and spoken word?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: No. The prophet asks, "Who shall describe His generation?", so the Word's generation is indescribable. Those who set it out transfer the production of human words through a tongue to the Word of God, showing they understand neither human nor divine things. As the following section adds, only the Father who begat and the Son who was begotten know it.
sources.quote: As for the prophet, he declares respecting Him, “Who shall describe His generation?” But ye pretend to set forth His generation from the Father, and ye transfer the production of the word of men which takes place by means of a tongue to the Word of God
sources.raw_question: Can the generation of the Word from the Father be described or explained, for example by analogy with human speech?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: No. That a word is uttered at the bidding of thought is something all men understand, so the emanationists reveal no mystery but simply transfer a human process to the only-begotten Word of God. In doing so they contradict themselves, calling Him unspeakable while describing His birth as if they had witnessed it, and assimilate Him to the human word.
sources.quote: have simply transferred what all understand to the only-begotten Word of God; and while they style Him unspeakable and unnameable, they nevertheless set forth the production and formation of His first generation
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to explain the Word's generation from the Father by analogy with the human word uttered from thought and mind (the Gnostic theory of emissions)?

question: Do the Old and New Covenants come from one and the same God, or from different Gods?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIII.—Christ did not abrogate the natural precepts of the law, but rather fulfilled and extended them. He removed the yoke and bondage of the old law, so that mankind, being now set free, might serve God with that trustful piety which becometh sons.
sources.answer: Yes. Precepts such as assenting to God, following His Word, loving God above all and one's neighbour as oneself, and abstaining from evil are common to both covenants. They began among the Jews and reached growth and completion among Christians, and this shared content reveals one and the same God behind both.
sources.quote: and to abstain from every evil deed, and all other things of a like nature which are common to both [covenants], do reveal one and the same God.
sources.raw_question: Do the natural moral precepts common to the Old and New Covenants show that both covenants come from one and the same God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXI.—Abraham’s faith was identical with ours; this faith was prefigured by the words and actions of the old patriarchs.
sources.answer: Yes. As Jacob begot sons from two sisters, Christ raised up sons from the two laws of one and the same Father. To all of them he gives the same gift of the life-giving Spirit, whether they are free or slaves according to the flesh.
sources.quote: there was every necessity that Jacob should beget sons from the two sisters, even as Christ did from the two laws of one and the same Father
sources.raw_question: Do the Old and New Covenants come from one and the same Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IX.—There is but one author, and one end to both covenants.
sources.answer: No. There is one salvation and one God, though the precepts forming man and the steps leading him to God are many. Just as an earthly king may grant his subjects greater advantages at times, God, being ever the same, may confer greater grace progressively through successive covenants without becoming another God.
sources.quote: For there is one salvation and one God; but the precepts which form the man are numerous, and the steps which lead man to God are not a few.
sources.raw_question: Does the existence of an old and a new covenant imply that they come from two different Gods?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IX.—There is but one author, and one end to both covenants.
sources.answer: From one and the same God. Christ's parable of the householder who brings forth things new and old from his treasure teaches that the same householder produces both; the new and old are the two covenants. The one householder is the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who spoke with Abraham and Moses and has now restored us to liberty.
sources.quote: But one and the same householder produced both covenants, the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who spake with both Abraham and Moses, and who has restored us anew to liberty
sources.raw_question: Do the Old and New Covenants come from different gods, or from one and the same God?

question: Can the Trinity be understood as a single Monad (the Father) that dilated or expanded into a Triad of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, whether so that the Word and Spirit might come to be, for the Incarnation, or for creation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Such a doctrine precludes all real distinctions of personality in the Divine Nature. Illustration of the Scripture doctrine from 2 Cor. vi. 11, &c.
sources.answer: No. If the Monad that was the Father itself dilated into a Triad, then Father, Son and Spirit would be the very same thing, as Sabellius held, since what is dilated remains identical with itself and differs only in time. A Triad when dilated is no longer a Monad, and a Monad is not yet a Triad, so the Father would not yet have been Son and Spirit, and afterwards would no longer be only Father. Such a view abolishes real personal distinctions.
sources.quote: if the Monad itself was dilated into a Triad, and that, Father and Son and Holy Ghost, then Father and Son and Spirit prove the same, as Sabellius held
sources.raw_question: Can the Trinity be understood as a single Monad (the Father) that dilated or expanded into a Triad of Father, Son and Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Such a doctrine precludes all real distinctions of personality in the Divine Nature. Illustration of the Scripture doctrine from 2 Cor. vi. 11, &c.
sources.answer: No. The Word and Spirit were not afterwards but always, otherwise God would be without a Word, as the Arians hold. If they were ever, the Godhead was never first a Monad and later dilated; if it dilated later, then the Word exists only afterwards, which is false.
sources.quote: for Word and Spirit were not afterwards, but ever, or God would be wordless, as the Arians hold
sources.raw_question: Could the Monad have dilated into a Triad so that the Word and Spirit might come to be with God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Such a doctrine precludes all real distinctions of personality in the Divine Nature. Illustration of the Scripture doctrine from 2 Cor. vi. 11, &c.
sources.answer: No. Then there would have been no Triad before the Incarnation, and it would seem that the Father Himself became flesh, since it is the Monad that was dilated in the man. The result would be only a Monad, flesh, and Spirit, a Triad in name only.
sources.quote: But if for the Incarnation it was dilated, and then became a Triad, then before the Incarnation there was not yet a Triad. And it will seem even that the Father became flesh
sources.raw_question: Could the Monad have dilated into a Triad for the sake of the Incarnation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Such a doctrine precludes all real distinctions of personality in the Divine Nature. Illustration of the Scripture doctrine from 2 Cor. vi. 11, &c.
sources.answer: No. The Monad could have made all things while remaining a Monad, since it was not lacking in power before any dilatation. Moreover, if dilatation were for the sake of creation and the Godhead returns to a Monad at the consummation, creation itself would then come to nothing.
sources.quote: for it were possible for it, remaining a Monad, to make all; for the Monad did not need dilatation, nor was wanting in power before being dilated
sources.raw_question: Could God have needed to dilate from a Monad into a Triad in order to create the world?

question: How does Christ's single death and resurrection answer to and heal humanity's double death of soul and body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The One Death and Resurrection of The Body of Christ Harmonizes with Our Double Death and Resurrection of Body and Soul, to the Effect of Salvation. In What Way the Single Death of Christ is Bestowed Upon Our Double Death.
sources.answer: Christ, being sinless, died and rose only in the flesh, yet that one death and resurrection answers to both our deaths. In it was wrought a mystery for the inner man (death to sin through repentance and inner renewal) and a type for the outer man (bodily death and future bodily resurrection). Thus his one death brought salvation to our double death and his one resurrection wrought two resurrections for us.
sources.quote: The one death therefore of our Saviour brought salvation to our double death, and His one resurrection wrought for us two resurrections
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's single death and resurrection remedy humanity's double death of soul and body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son.
sources.answer: Christ's one, single death abolished our double death. Augustine discusses how the Saviour's single harmonizes with our double to bring about salvation.
sources.quote: That our double death was abolished by His death, being one and single.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's single death relate to humanity's double death?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > How We are Rendered Apt for the Perception of Truth Through the Incarnate Word.
sources.answer: Christ's single death, freely chosen out of compassion, abolishes the sinner's death, which comes from the necessity of condemnation. His single death and resurrection answers in harmony to our double death of soul and body. The soul dies through sin and ungodliness, and the body through corruptibility as punishment for sin, so both need medicine and resurrection.
sources.quote: For the death of the sinner springing from the necessity of comdemnation is deservedly abolished by the death of the Righteous One springing from the free choice of His compassion, while His single [death and resurrection] answers to our double
sources.raw_question: How does the single death and resurrection of Christ correspond to and heal humanity's double death?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The One Death and Resurrection of The Body of Christ Harmonizes with Our Double Death and Resurrection of Body and Soul, to the Effect of Salvation. In What Way the Single Death of Christ is Bestowed Upon Our Double Death.
sources.answer: Christ was not a sinner, so He was not dead in soul. He died and rose only in His mortal flesh. Yet in that single death He answered to both of our deaths. It was a mystery for our inner man, signifying the death of the soul and its renewal through repentance. It was also a type for our outer man, prefiguring the resurrection of the body.
sources.quote: but being clothed in mortal flesh, and in that alone dying, in that alone rising again, in that alone did He answer to both for us; since in it was wrought a mystery as regards the inner man, and a type as regards the outer.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ's single death and resurrection answer to our double death of soul and body?

question: Is forgiveness of sins still free if God requires satisfaction for sin from Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Pardon is everywhere tied to Christ's blood, yet it is wholly free on God's part (in his purpose, in sending his Son, laying our punishment on him, and offering pardon in the gospel) and on the sinner's part, since it is given without satisfaction, merit, or penal suffering by the sinner. Only such things required of the sinner could impeach its freedom; God providing himself a lamb does not.
sources.quote: Whether, then, we respect the pardoner or the pardoned, pardon is every way free, — namely, on the part of God who forgives, and on the part of sinners that are forgiven.
sources.raw_question: Is forgiveness of sins still free if it rests on Christ's satisfaction by his death and blood?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. The opponents grant that God requiring faith, repentance and obedience of the sinner does not destroy the freedom of pardon. Then receiving satisfaction from another, with nothing required of the sinner, can have even less appearance of impeaching it, so they give away their cause.
sources.quote: how shall the receiving of satisfaction by another, nothing at all being required of the sinner, have the least appearance of any such thing?
sources.raw_question: If prescribing conditions does not impeach the freedom of pardon, can satisfaction by Christ impeach it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. The Socinians themselves admit that God pardons freely even though he requires faith, repentance and obedience from the sinner as conditions. If conditions laid on the sinner himself do not destroy the freedom of pardon, then receiving satisfaction from another, with nothing required of the sinner for it, can far less appear to do so.
sources.quote: how shall the receiving of satisfaction by another, nothing at all being required of the sinner, have the least appearance of any such thing?
sources.raw_question: Does God's requiring satisfaction from Christ for sin contradict the freedom of God's pardon of sinners?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: No. Satisfaction is so far from being inconsistent with free remission that it is necessary to make way for it when a righteous law has been transgressed and God's public government disturbed. God himself sets atonement before pardon in the law (Lev. 4:31). He also appointed a sacrifice for Job's friends so that he might freely pardon them. Paul likewise asks Philemon to forgive Onesimus while offering to make good the wrong himself.
sources.quote: This satisfaction is impleaded as inconsistent with free remission of sins, — how causelessly we have seen. It is so far from it, that it is necessary to make way for it, in case of a righteous law transgressed
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's satisfaction for sin inconsistent with God's free remission or forgiveness of sins?

question: Does the scriptural statement that Christ 'died for us' mean that he died in our stead, undergoing the death due to us, rather than merely for our benefit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: They mean that Christ died in our room, place, or stead, undergoing the death or punishment we should have undergone. Those who deny this sense in effect deny that he properly died for us at all, whatever benefits they grant from his death.
sources.quote: The meaning and importance, we say, of these expressions is, that Christ died in our room, place, or stead, undergoing the death or punishment which we should have undergone
sources.raw_question: What do the scriptural phrases that Christ died 'for us' and 'for our sins' properly mean?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Yes. Owen argues that in both Scripture and common usage, dying 'for' another means dying instead of him: undergoing the death he should have undergone, so that he goes free. He cites Caiaphas' counsel that one man should die for the people and Peter's offer to lay down his life for Christ. He also cites David's wish to die 'in the stead' of Absalom, where the Hebrew תחת signifies substitution, and classical examples of persons who gave their lives for others.
sources.quote: this expression of “dying for another” has no other sense or meaning, but only dying instead of another, undergoing the death that he should undergo, that he might go free.
sources.raw_question: In Scripture, does the expression that Christ 'died for' us mean that he died in our stead, as a substitute?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Yes. The constant use of the expression in Scripture, the nature of the thing, its use in all kinds of writers, and the examples of devoted persons among the nations (the Decii, Menoeceus, the Massilian and Egyptian expiations) show that 'dying for another' means substitution. To deny that Christ died in our stead is in effect to deny that he died for us at all.
sources.quote: to deny that he died and suffered in our stead, undergoing the death whereunto we were obnoxious, and the punishment due to our sins, is
sources.raw_question: Does the scriptural statement that Christ 'died for us and for our sins' mean that he died in our stead, undergoing the death and punishment due to us?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: No. The apostles and martyrs died for our good, since our benefit was one end of their sufferings in God's appointment, yet they cannot be said to have died for us or our sins. If Christ died only for our good, even more effectually, this would not change the kind of his dying, and he could not properly be said to die for us.
sources.quote: They all died for our good; our advantage and benefit was one end of their sufferings, in the will and appointment of God: and yet it cannot be said that they died for us, or our sins.
sources.raw_question: Is it enough to say that Christ died merely for our good or benefit in order to make true the claim that he died for us and our sins?

question: Does Scripture's ascription of exalted language to believers (sons of God, gods, oneness with God, partaking of the divine nature, the fullness of God) undermine the argument that similar language about Christ proves his Deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Most of Christ's names and attributes are never predicated of his people at all but are his incommunicable prerogatives, so the proof stands even without the disputed passages. Where similar language is used, the believer's privilege is derived from Christ and limited by creaturely capacity, while Christ's glory is underived and eternal, or else given to him in his subordinate character as Mediator. And no trust is ever placed in any saint on the basis of such privileges.
sources.quote: the privilege of the believer is derived from Christ, or from the Father through Christ, (the context compelling this) and is limited by the finite capacity of the creature; while the supereminent glory of Christ is either underived, eternal, increate
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Scripture describes believers' privileges in terms similar to Christ's glories (e.g., being called gods, being filled with the fullness of God) neutralize the proof of Christ's deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. However glorious these derived privileges are, none of them sets up a claim for trust or worship. Gathered onto the head of any saint or of the Church, they offer no reason to confide in that saint absolutely or to love him supremely.
