Supreme trust therefore belongs to Christ alone as essentially God.
sources.quote: is any claim set up on their behalf for trust or worship?
sources.raw_question: Do the privileges Scripture grants to believers (sonship, oneness with God, divine titles) give them any claim to trust or worship like Christ's?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Though the saints receive derived glories, Scripture never on that account claims for them trust or worship. Crown even Peter, Paul, John or the whole Church with all these privileges, and there is still no warrant to confide in or love them supremely. This is unlike Christ, who is the object of supreme trust and honour. The parallel therefore does not reduce Christ to the level of exalted creatures.
sources.quote: is there in all these lustrous glories any temptation held out to confide in absolutely, or supremely to love that saint or that church?
sources.raw_question: Do the lofty privileges Scripture ascribes to believers (being called sons of God, gods, one with the Father and Christ, filled with the fullness of God) undermine the argument that similar language about Christ proves his Deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. These privileges are the fruit of the incarnation: the Infinite One stooped to the extremity of woe in order to raise his creatures to the highest life a created being can enjoy. Believers' glories are therefore derived from him and conferred by him. His own glories are essential to him. The exaltation of creatures is a mystery only less marvellous than the Creator's humiliation, and it does not erase the difference between them and the eternal Son.
sources.quote: He, the Infinite One, stooped to the extremity of woe that He might elevate us to the highest life which a created being can enjoy – the life of God.
sources.raw_question: If Scripture applies to believers exalted language also used of Christ, such as being one as the Father and Son are one, partaking of the divine nature, sharing his throne, and doing greater works, does this weaken the argument for Christ's unique Deity?

question: Is the Christ who suffered and was crucified the same as the Son of God, or was the sufferer a different being from an impassible Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: The crucified Jesus is himself the Christ and the Son of God. Peter preached that the Son of God was made man and suffered, and that God fulfilled what the prophets foretold about the suffering of His Christ in Jesus, whom He then raised from the dead.
sources.quote: preached to the people that Christ was Jesus the crucified One, whom the same God that had sent the prophets, being God Himself, raised up, and gave in Him salvation to men
sources.raw_question: Is the Christ who suffered and was crucified the same as the Son of God, or was the sufferer a different being from an impassible Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter II.—Proofs from the plain testimony of Moses, and of the other prophets, whose words are the words of Christ, that there is but one God, the founder of the world, whom Our Lord preached, and whom He called His Father.
sources.answer: No. The Son of God whom Moses and the prophets preached is the same one who rose from the dead and gives us life, the first-begotten from the dead. Those who separate an impassible Christ from a suffering Jesus fail to know the first-begotten from the dead.
sources.quote: they do not know the first-begotten from the dead; understanding Christ as a distinct being, who continued as if He were impassible, and Jesus, who suffered, as being altogether separate [from Him].
sources.raw_question: Is Christ an impassible being distinct from the man Jesus who suffered?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVII.—The apostles teach that it was neither Christ nor the Saviour, but the Holy Spirit, who did descend upon Jesus. The reason for this descent.
sources.answer: No. The Gnostics claim to hold Jesus and Christ united, but they separate them again by saying one suffered while the other remained impassible. Irenaeus rejects this. The one Son of God became a man liable to suffering, so there are not two subjects, one passible and one impassible.
sources.quote: for they show that one did indeed undergo sufferings, but that the other remained impassible
sources.raw_question: Did one Christ suffer while another, impassible Christ remained untouched by suffering?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IX.—There is but one author, and one end to both covenants.
sources.answer: Yes. We are not to look for another Christ and Son of God besides Him who was born of the Virgin Mary and suffered, in whom we trust and whom we love. Isaiah calls Him 'our Lord God, in whom we have trusted', and Peter speaks of loving Him though not now seeing Him.
sources.quote: neither shall we look for another Christ and Son of God, but Him who [was born] of the Virgin Mary, who also suffered, in whom too we trust, and whom we love
sources.raw_question: Is the Christ who was born of the Virgin Mary and suffered the same as the Son of God who will be seen in glory?

question: Does the ultimate trust Scripture directs toward Christ, which could not rightly be given to any creature such as an archangel or a holy man, show that Christ is God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: No. If one substitutes the name of Michael, Moses, or Stephen for Jesus in such passages, the result is an intolerable discord and indeed blasphemy. This is because it would repose in a creature an exhaustive confidence due only to the infinite Creator and offer to a man the supreme gratitude that belongs to God our Saviour. Hence the confidence Scripture directs to Christ implies his Deity.
sources.quote: For you feel this would be reposing in the creature an exhaustive confidence due only to the Infinite Creator, and offering to man a supreme gratitude which is the prerogative of God our Saviour.
sources.raw_question: Could the trust and gratitude that the New Testament (e.g. Ephesians 1) directs toward Jesus Christ be rightly given to an exalted creature such as an archangel, Moses, or a martyr?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture parallels trust in the Lord with trust in the Son, rejoicing in God with rejoicing in Christ, and ascribes eternal glory, the giving of life, and being 'all in all' to both. One who is the object of such ultimate confidence, homage and delight must be God, and there are not two Gods.
sources.quote: New, One who is the object of such ultimate confidence, homage, and delight, must needs be God. But there are not two Gods. Therefore the Son is one with God, and is God.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that believers are to place ultimate trust, hope and joy in Christ, as in the Father, show that Christ is God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: No. If you substitute the name of Michael, Moses or Stephen for Christ's in such passages, the result is an intolerable discord and indeed blasphemy. That would place in a creature an exhaustive confidence due only to the infinite Creator. The trust Scripture asks us to place in Christ therefore implies his deity.
sources.quote: For you feel this would be reposing in the creature an exhaustive confidence due only to the Infinite Creator, and offering to man a supreme gratitude which is the prerogative of God our Saviour.
sources.raw_question: Could the trust Scripture directs toward Christ rightly be given to any creature, such as an archangel or a holy man?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture detaches ultimate confidence from every creature and claims it exclusively for the Creator, jealously guarding his incommunicable glory. Yet it requires us to repose ultimate confidence in Christ, a trust he claimed, his followers conceded, and his apostles commanded; hence Christ must be the one God.
sources.quote: how confessedly Scripture requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: setting him before us as possessed of all those incommunicable attributes of Godhead; as our Creator, Preserver, and final Judge
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's command to place ultimate trust in Christ show that he is God, given that Scripture forbids ultimate trust in any creature?

question: Are the evil angels working through Pharaoh's magicians properly called creators of the frogs and serpents they produced?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > God Alone Creates Those Things Which are Changed by Magic Art.
sources.answer: No. If neither Jacob nor the souls of the mothers can be called creators of the colours of the lambs, much less can the bad angels be called creators of the frogs and serpents. Creatures only apply outward operations to the nature God has made. God alone creates from within, by the unchangeable wisdom that holds the causes of all things.
sources.quote: much less can it be said that the creators of the frogs and serpents were the bad angels, through whom the magicians of Pharaoh then made them
sources.raw_question: Were the bad angels working through Pharaoh's magicians the creators of the frogs and serpents?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Original Cause of All Things is from God.
sources.answer: No. Only God creates from the innermost and highest point of causation; creatures merely apply operations from without to seeds already hidden in the elements. Just as a man who knows from what substances worms arise does not call himself their creator, the evil angels discern hidden seeds and apply them, causing things to be produced but not creating them.
sources.quote: so through certain and known opportune combinations applying these seeds by secret movements, cause them to be created, but do not create them?
sources.raw_question: Can angels or men who bring forth living things (such as Pharaoh's magicians producing frogs and serpents) properly be called creators of those things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > God Alone Creates Those Things Which are Changed by Magic Art.
sources.answer: No. The magicians and the angels behind them did not create the frogs and serpents; God alone creates. Angels, by subtle perception, may know hidden seeds placed in the elements and scatter them through fit temperings, furnishing occasions for production, but this is no more creation than parents creating men or farmers creating corn.
sources.quote: Nor, in truth, are those evil angels to be called creators, because by their means the magicians, withstanding the servant of God, made frogs and serpents; for it was not they who created them.
sources.raw_question: Are the evil angels who empowered Pharaoh's magicians to produce frogs and serpents properly called creators of those creatures?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > Great Miracles Wrought by Magic Arts.
sources.answer: No. Visible matter obeys God, not the wicked angels, and only as far as He permits. The angels create nothing. They only draw forth hidden seeds that the Creator placed in the corporeal elements of the world.
sources.quote: Nor, in truth, are those evil angels to be called creators, because by their means the magicians, withstanding the servant of God, made frogs and serpents; for it was not they who created them.
sources.raw_question: Are evil angels, through whom magicians produce frogs and serpents, the creators of those creatures?

question: Did the apostles hand down a secret teaching about God, reserved for a select few, apart from their public teaching?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XIV.—If Paul had known any mysteries unrevealed to the other apostles, Luke, his constant companion and fellow-traveller, could not have been ignorant of them; neither could the truth have possibly lain hid from him, through whom alone we learn many and most important particulars of the Gospel history.
sources.answer: No. At Miletus Paul told the Ephesian elders that he had not shunned to declare to them all the counsel of God, and he warned that false teachers would arise afterwards. The apostles therefore delivered to everyone, without respect of persons, what they had learned from the Lord. Luke in turn passed on what he received from those who were eye-witnesses and ministers of the Word from the beginning.
sources.quote: Thus did the apostles simply, and without respect of persons, deliver to all what they had themselves learned from the Lord.
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles, and Paul in particular, keep part of God's revelation back as a secret teaching for a select few?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter II.—The heretics follow neither Scripture nor tradition.
sources.answer: No. If the apostles had known hidden mysteries reserved for 'the perfect', they would above all have handed them to the bishops to whom they entrusted the Churches and whom they wished to be perfect. Yet the bishops in apostolic succession neither taught nor knew anything like what the Gnostic heretics claim. So the public apostolic tradition, which agrees with Scripture, holds the truth, and the heretics' supposed secret wisdom is their own invention.
sources.quote: For if the apostles had known hidden mysteries, which they were in the habit of imparting to “the perfect” apart and privily from the rest, they would have delivered them especially to those to whom they were also committing the Churches themselves.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that 'we speak wisdom among those that are perfect' (1 Corinthians 2:6) show that the apostles passed on a secret oral teaching about God, separate from Scripture, to a select few?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter III.—A refutation of the heretics, from the fact that, in the various Churches, a perpetual succession of bishops was kept up.
sources.answer: No. If the apostles had possessed hidden mysteries to impart privately, they would above all have delivered them to the bishops to whom they entrusted the Churches, whom they wished to be perfect and blameless. Yet the bishops in succession from the apostles neither taught nor knew anything like what the heretics rave about.
sources.quote: For if the apostles had known hidden mysteries, which they were in the habit of imparting to “the perfect” apart and privily from the rest, they would have delivered them especially to those to whom they were also committing the Churches themselves.
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles hand down secret mysteries to an elite of 'the perfect' apart from the public teaching of the Church, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XV.—Refutation of the Ebionites, who disparaged the authority of St. Paul, from the writings of St. Luke, which must be received as a whole. Exposure of the hypocrisy, deceit, and pride of the Gnostics. The apostles and their disciples knew and preached one God, the Creator of the world.
sources.answer: No. The apostles' doctrine is open and steadfast and holds nothing in reserve. They did not teach one thing privately and another publicly. Error must be disguised to seem plausible, while truth needs no disguise and is entrusted even to children. The Valentinian claim to an unspeakable private mystery of the Pleroma is therefore a deceit.
sources.quote: the doctrine of the apostles is open and stedfast, holding nothing in reserve; nor did they teach one set of doctrines in private, and another in public.
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles teach a secret doctrine about God in private that differed from what they taught in public?

question: Is the mind's not thinking of itself the same as its not knowing itself; does it still know itself when not thinking of itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether the Mind of Infants Knows Itself.
sources.answer: No. Augustine distinguishes self-knowledge from self-thought: the mind always knows itself, but it does not always actively think of itself. He says he showed this already in the tenth book, and it underlies his account of the mind's image of the Trinity.
sources.quote: And that it is one thing not to know oneself, another not to think of oneself, we have shown already in the same book.
sources.raw_question: Is not knowing oneself the same thing as not thinking of oneself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How a Kind of Trinity Exists in the Mind Thinking of Itself. What is the Part of Thought in This Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. When the mind is not thinking of itself, it is not in its own sight, yet it knows itself as a remembrance of itself. It is like a learned man whose many branches of knowledge are stored in memory even though only the one he is thinking of is in view.
sources.quote: it knows itself as though it were to itself a remembrance of itself
sources.raw_question: Does the mind still know itself when it is not actively thinking of itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Why the Soul is Enjoined to Know Itself. Whence Come the Errors of the Mind Concerning Its Own Substance.
sources.answer: No. A person learned in grammar is not ignorant of grammar just because he is thinking about medicine at the moment. In the same way, the mind may fail to think of itself while still knowing itself.
sources.quote: for we do not say of the man that is skilled in much learning, that he is ignorant of grammar, when he is only not thinking of it, because he is thinking at the time of the art of medicine
sources.raw_question: Is the mind's not knowing itself the same as its not thinking of itself?

question: In the mental image of the Trinity, how is love related to the mind and to the inner word it conceives?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > We Conceive and Beget the Word Within, from the Things We Have Beheld in the Eternal Truth. The Word, Whether of the Creature or of the Creator, is Conceived by Love.
sources.answer: The word is conceived by love, whether of the creature (changeable nature) or of the Creator (unchangeable truth). Love then acts as a mean that joins the word and the mind it is conceived from. It binds itself to them as a third, without confusion, in an incorporeal embrace. This mirrors the Spirit as the bond of Father and Son.
sources.quote: And this word is conceived by love, either of the creature or of the Creator, that is, either of changeable nature or of unchangeable truth.
sources.raw_question: By what is the mind's inner word conceived, and how does love relate to the mind and its word in the image of the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > Whether Only Knowledge that is Loved is the Word of the Mind.
sources.answer: They mutually indwell one another and the mind. The mind's word is joined to it by love. Since the mind loves its knowledge and knows its love, the word is in the love and the love is in the word, and both are in the one who loves and speaks.
sources.quote: And since it loves knowledge and knows love, both the word is in love and love is in the word, and both are in him who loves and speaks.
sources.raw_question: When the mind knows and loves itself, how are its word and its love related to each other and to the mind, as an image of the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > In What Desire and Love Differ.
sources.answer: Love is a mean or bond joining the mind and the word conceived from it. It binds itself to them as a third, without any confusion, in an incorporeal embrace. So mind, word and love form a trinity of distinct yet united terms that images the divine Trinity.
sources.quote: Therefore love, as it were a mean, conjoins our word and the mind from which it is conceived, and without any confusion binds itself as a third with them, in an incorporeal embrace.
sources.raw_question: In the mental image of the Trinity, how is love related to the mind and the inner word it conceives?

question: Is the image of the Trinity in man to be found in a family of three human persons (father, mother and child)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Why This Opinion is to Be Rejected.
sources.answer: No. If the image of the Trinity consisted in father, mother and son, then Adam would not have been made in God's image before Eve was made and before they had a son, since there was not yet a trinity. But Scripture says man was made in God's image at his creation, so the image cannot lie in the human family triad.
sources.quote: then the man was not made after the image of God before a wife was made for him, and before they procreated a son; because there was not yet a trinity.
sources.raw_question: Is the image of the Trinity in man to be found in three human beings, namely father, mother and son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > How Man is the Image of God. Whether the Woman is Not Also the Image of God. How the Saying of the Apostle, that the Man is the Image of God, But the Woman is the Glory of the Man, is to Be Understood Figuratively and Mystically.
sources.answer: No. Man is not to be understood as made in the image of the Trinity in such a way that the image is located in three human beings. The apostle calls the man by himself the image of God, which would make no sense if the woman (or a son) were needed to complete the image; and if one human person could be the image as each divine Person is God, the woman too would be so called.
sources.quote: We ought not therefore so to understand that man is made in the image of the supreme Trinity, that is, in the image of God, as that the same image should be understood to be in three human beings
sources.raw_question: Is the image of the Trinity in man to be found in three human persons (man, woman, and child), analogous to the three Persons of the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Opinion Which Devises an Image of the Trinity in the Marriage of Male and Female, and in Their Offspring.
sources.answer: No. Augustine judges the opinion improbable, indeed absurd and false, and easy to refute. Its only sound point is that not everything that comes from a person is a son. He rejects it not out of disgust at its carnal associations but because divine Scripture plainly shows it to be false: man was made in the image of the whole Trinity, which is one God.
sources.quote: All the rest of this opinion is in truth so absurd, nay indeed so false, that it is most easy to refute it.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who find an image of the Trinity in marriage and offspring
sources.raw_question: Is the image of the Trinity in human nature to be found in the family, with the man representing the Father, the child the Son, and the woman (who proceeds from the man without being his daughter) the Holy Spirit?

question: What does the term 'ungenerate' signify when applied to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It signifies only that the divine life does not exist from any cause, that is, it has no beginning. It expresses one thought associated with the divine life. It does not express the whole essence of God, which remains beyond every name.
sources.quote: One thought associated with that life is, that it does not exist from any cause; this is indicated by the term “ungenerate.”
sources.raw_question: What does the term 'ungenerate' signify when applied to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: It signifies only that the Father was never generated, i.e. it denies of him derivation from a cause. It works like the other negative divine names such as invisible, passionless, and immaterial, which signify only what in no way belongs to God. Read this way, the word leaves no ground for the Eunomian doctrine of the Son's Unlikeness.
sources.quote: to think of the God over all as Ungenerate, just as He is invisible, and passionless, and immaterial; and if he was agreed that in every one of these terms there was signified only that which in no way belongs to God
sources.raw_question: What does the term 'Ungenerate' signify when applied to God the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It means being without a cause. Luke's genealogy ascends to Adam, 'the son of God,' and stops, showing that God is the son of no one; to be the son of no one is to be without a cause, and to be without a cause is to be ungenerate.
sources.quote: Is it not obvious to every one’s intelligence that God is the son of no one? But to be the son of no one is to be without a cause, plainly; and to be without a cause is to be ungenerate.
sources.raw_question: What does the term 'ungenerate' mean when applied to God?

question: Does the natural meaning of the title 'Son' (and 'Only-begotten God') teach that the Son is truly generated from the Father and shares the Father's nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: Yes. Using the title 'God' and the term 'Son' introduces no difference of nature, so whoever hears them is led to the loftier conception of the Son. One who is truly Son of God and himself God cannot be conceived as differing from the Father's nature. Eunomius therefore has to add qualifying phrases such as 'not uncreate' to stop readers drawing this natural conclusion.
sources.quote: For how could He Who is truly the Son of God and Himself God be conceived as something else differing from the nature of the Father?
sources.raw_question: Do the titles 'Son of God' and 'Only-begotten God' imply that the Son has the same nature as the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Then he ends the book with an exposition of the Divine and Human names of the Only-Begotten, and a discussion of the terms “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: Yes. The ordinary and natural sense of "Son" teaches that he is of the same essence as the one who begat him. There is no nobler conception of the title than the one that presents the reality of his relationship to the Father who begat him.
sources.quote: if one were to reject the ordinary and natural sense of the word “Son,” by which we learn that He is of the same essence as Him that begat Him, he will of course transfer the name to some more divine interpretation
sources.raw_question: Does the natural meaning of the title "Son" teach that the Only-begotten is of the same essence as the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > This third book shows a third fall of Eunomius, as refuting himself, and sometimes saying that the Son is to be called Only-begotten in virtue of natural generation, and that Holy Scripture proves this from the first; at other times, that by reason of His being created He should not be called a Son, but a “product,” or “creature.”
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory notes that even Eunomius concedes the name "Son" would not properly apply to the Only-begotten unless "natural order" confirmed it. If the order of nature is removed from the designation, the name loses its proper and natural meaning and becomes empty. The inspired Scriptures, the "knowledge from above," confirm this natural sense, and so support the orthodox view of the Son's sonship.
sources.quote: If, then, one were to withdraw the order of nature from the consideration of the designation of “Son,” his use of this name, being deprived of its proper and natural significance, will be meaningless.
sources.raw_question: Does the title "Son" applied to the Only-begotten God carry its proper meaning only if it reflects a real, natural generation from the Father?

question: Does the Son's subordination to the Father imply that he is inferior in nature, and so a creature, or is it a subordination of order only?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 20: Whether the Doctor need have cited 300 teats, *wide of the purpose, to prove what nobody denies, namely, a subordination, in some sense, of the Son to the Fathe
sources.answer: No. A subordination may exist, and be understood, between two Persons without any inferiority of nature. Subordination of order must be distinguished from subordination of nature. The opponents have not proved that all subordination implies the kind of inferiority they contend for; they only repeat the word 'subordinate'.
sources.quote: there would be no occasion now for distinguishing between subordination of order and of nature, were it not manifest how much the Catholic faith may be endangered by the endeavours of some, to slip one upon us for the other
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's subordination to the Father imply that the Son is inferior in nature, and so a creature rather than strictly and essentially God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 20: Whether the Doctor need have cited 300 teats, *wide of the purpose, to prove what nobody denies, namely, a subordination, in some sense, of the Son to the Fathe
sources.answer: It is a subordination of order, not of nature. Waterland grants that the Son is in some sense subordinate to the Father, but he denies that subordination as such implies inferiority of nature. The Arian side cannot settle the matter by repeating the word 'subordinate'. It must prove rationally that all subordination implies the inferiority it contends for. The distinction between order and nature has to be insisted on because the Catholic faith is endangered when one is slipped in for the other.
sources.quote: there would be no occasion now for distinguishing between subordination of order and of nature, were it not manifest how much the Catholic faith may be endangered by the endeavours of some, to slip one upon us for the other.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's subordination to the Father imply an inferiority of nature, or can it be a subordination of order only?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. If 'real subordination' means the subordination of a creature to God, or of a Person of inferior nature to one of superior nature, it cannot be proved from Scripture or any other way. If it means anything else, such as subordination of order, it is not pertinent to the dispute.
sources.quote: If you mean, by real subordination, the subordination of a creature to God; or of one Person inferior in nature to another of a higher, superior, or more perfect nature ; it is not
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's real subordination to the Father, in the sense of inferiority of nature, demonstrable from Scripture or reason?

question: Does the Spirit's receiving from the Son what He declares ('He shall take of Mine') imply that the Spirit is inferior or in need?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: No. The Son received all things from the Father by unity of nature, and the Spirit received from the Son by the same unity of nature. So what the Spirit says is the Son's, and what the Son has given is the Father's. Receiving here expresses shared nature, not subordination.
sources.quote: And those things which He Himself received by Unity of nature, the Spirit by the same Unity of nature received also from Him
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit's receiving from the Son what He declares imply that the Spirit is inferior?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. The receiving happens through unity of substance. What the Father has belongs to the Son, and what the Son has the Spirit has received. This shows a unity of nature, not a transfer to a lesser being.
sources.quote: He received them, however, through Unity of Substance, as the Son received from the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit's 'receiving' from the Son, as the Son receives from the Father, imply that the Spirit is dependent or inferior?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: No. The text refers to the Spirit's office of distributing, not to a lack of Divine Power: the Spirit sanctifies those whom the Son redeemed. From the very words the heretics use for their sophistry, the unity of the Godhead is perceived, not the need of a gift.
sources.quote: from those very words, I say, from which they construct their sophistry, the Unity of the Godhead is perceived, not the need of a gift.
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit's receiving from the Son ('He shall take of Mine') imply that the Spirit is inferior or in need?

question: Is the Holy Spirit God, of the same substance as the Father and the Son, and equal to them rather than subordinate?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > What the Doctrine of the Catholic Faith is Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit is co-equal. He is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, neither of them. Yet He belongs to the unity of the Trinity in equality with them.
sources.quote: the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, Himself also co-equal with the Father and the Son, and pertaining to the unity of the Trinity
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit co-equal with the Father and the Son, or subordinate to them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Against Eunomius, Saying that the Son of God is the Son, Not of His Nature, But of His Will. Epilogue to What Has Been Said Already.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine says the Scriptures, as shown in his earlier books, establish that the Holy Spirit is God. The Spirit is not of another substance and is not less than the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: the Holy Spirit is God, and not of another substance, nor less than the Father and the Son,—as we have shown to be true in the former books, according to the same Scriptures
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit God, of the same substance as the Father and the Son, and not less than they?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Holy Spirit Also is Equal to the Father and the Son in All Things.
sources.answer: Yes. Whether the Spirit is called the unity, holiness, or love of the Father and Son, He is that through which the two are joined, and He is this not by participation or by a superior's gift but by their own essence. Hence He consists in the same unity of substance and the same equality.
sources.quote: Wherefore also the Holy Spirit consists in the same unity of substance, and in the same equality.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit of the same substance as, and equal to, the Father and the Son?

question: If the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each God (and each good, great and omnipotent), are there three Gods or one God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Preface.—The Conclusion of What Has Been Said Above. The Rule to Be Observed in the More Difficult Questions of the Faith.
sources.answer: No. There are neither three Gods, nor three goods, nor three omnipotents, but one God, good and omnipotent, the Trinity itself. These terms are spoken according to essence, not relatively, and the essence is one.
sources.quote: yet neither three Gods, nor three goods, nor three omnipotents, but one God, good, omnipotent, the Trinity itself
sources.raw_question: If the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, are there three Gods (or three omnipotents, three goods)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > What the Doctrine of the Catholic Faith is Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: One God, not three Gods. The Catholic expounders of Scripture teach that Father, Son and Holy Spirit intimate a divine unity of one and the same substance in an indivisible equality. Therefore, though each is God, they are not three Gods but one God.
sources.quote: the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit intimate a divine unity of one and the same substance in an indivisible equality; and therefore that they are not three Gods, but one God
sources.raw_question: Are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit three Gods or one God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whatever is Spoken of God According to Substance, is Spoken of Each Person Severally, and Together of the Trinity Itself. One Essence in God, and Three, in Greek, Hypostases, in Latin, Persons.
sources.answer: No. There is one God, one great, one good and one omnipotent. Substantial predicates are said of each Person singly and of the Trinity together, always in the singular, because the three share one substance.
sources.quote: Whatever, therefore, is spoken of God in respect to Himself, is both spoken singly of each person, that is, of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and together of the Trinity itself, not plurally but in the singular.
sources.raw_question: If the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each God, great, good and omnipotent, are there three Gods, three greats, three goods or three omnipotents?

question: Do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit share one knowledge, and does this show that they share one nature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father, the Son, and the Spirit speak and reveal the same things. The Father gives the Spirit of revelation, the Son reveals the Father, and the Spirit reveals what God has prepared. This identity of revelation shows a unity of knowledge and therefore of nature.
sources.quote: There is, then, a Unity of knowledge, since, as the Father, Who gives the Spirit of revelation, reveals, so also the Son reveals
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit share one knowledge and one nature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Since Scripture says none knows the Father save the Son, and also says none knows the things of God save the Spirit of God, neither excludes the other; the Spirit therefore shares the same knowledge, and Father, Son and Spirit are of one nature and one knowledge.
sources.quote: Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one nature and of one knowledge.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's knowing the Father, whom only the Son is said to know, show that the Spirit shares one nature with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IX. That the Holy Spirit is provoked is proved by the words of St. Peter, in which it is shown that the Spirit of God is one and the same as the Spirit of the Lord, both by other passages and by reference to the sentence of the same Apostle on Ananias and Sapphira, whence it is argued that the union of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, as well as His own Godhead, is proved.
sources.answer: Yes. In the story of Ananias, falsehood is detected alike by the Holy Spirit and by God the Father. This shows that the same truth and knowledge belong to both.
sources.quote: we certainly observe the unity of truth and knowledge in God the Father and the Holy Spirit, for falsehood is discovered alike by the Holy Spirit and by God the Father
sources.raw_question: Do the Father and the Holy Spirit share one and the same truth and knowledge?

question: If Christ is 'the power of God and the wisdom of God' (1 Cor 1:24), does it follow that the Father is wise and powerful only through the Son he begets, rather than by his own wisdom and power?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How There is a Trinity in the Very Simplicity of God. Whether and How the Trinity that is God is Manifested from the Trinities Which Have Been Shown to Be in Men.
sources.answer: No. As argued in the seventh book, the text must be understood so that the Son does not seem to make the Father wise. The Son is wisdom of wisdom, just as he is light of light and God of God.
sources.quote: so that the Son may not seem to make the Father wise; and our explanation came to this, that the Son is wisdom of wisdom, in the same way as He is light of light, God of God.
sources.raw_question: Does calling Christ 'the wisdom of God' imply that the Son makes the Father wise?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: No. Augustine treats this as something no one would dare to say. The Father is truly powerful and wise, and this must be held even while confessing that Christ is the power and wisdom of God.
sources.quote: or that the Father is not powerful with His own power, or wise with His own wisdom: and who shall dare to say this?
sources.raw_question: If Christ is the wisdom and power of God, does it follow that God the Father is not wise with His own wisdom or powerful with His own power?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Son, According to the Apostle, is the Power and Wisdom of the Father. Hence the Reasoning of the Catholics Against the Earlier Arians. A Difficulty is Raised, Whether the Father is Not Wisdom Himself, But Only the Father of Wisdom.
sources.answer: Augustine raises this as a real difficulty and defers a full answer, but he does not grant that it overturns the equality of Father, Son and Spirit. He shows that the inference raises its own problems. If the Father were wise only by the Wisdom he begot, he would also have to be great, good, eternal and omnipotent only by what he begot. That conclusion is implausible.
sources.quote: Somethink themselves hindered from admitting the equality of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because it is written, “Christ, the power of God, and the wisdom of God;” in that, on this ground, there does not appear to be equality
sources.raised_by_detail: some who think themselves hindered from admitting equality
sources.raw_question: Does calling Christ 'the power of God and the wisdom of God' show that the Son is not equal to the Father, since the Father would then be only the begetter of power and wisdom rather than power and wisdom himself?

question: If the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each wisdom, are there three wisdoms in God or one?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How There is a Trinity in the Very Simplicity of God. Whether and How the Trinity that is God is Manifested from the Trinities Which Have Been Shown to Be in Men.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit is also wisdom. Together with the Father and the Son, the three are altogether one wisdom, just as they are one God and one essence.
sources.quote: Nor could we find the Holy Spirit to be in any other way than that He Himself also is wisdom, and altogether one wisdom, as one God, one essence.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit also wisdom, and is the wisdom of the Father, Son, and Spirit one wisdom or three?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. Together they are not three wisdoms but one wisdom, just as they are one light and not three lights.
sources.quote: the Father is wisdom, the Son is wisdom, and the Holy Spirit is wisdom, and together not three wisdoms, but one wisdom
sources.raw_question: If the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are each wisdom, are there three wisdoms?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases.
sources.answer: No. There is one power and one wisdom, just as there is one God and one essence. Power and wisdom are said of each Person according to the one essence, not relatively. So they are not multiplied by the number of Persons.
sources.quote: yet that there are not three powers or three wisdoms, but one power and one wisdom, as there is one God and one essence
sources.raw_question: If the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each power and wisdom, are there three powers and three wisdoms in God?

question: Why does Scripture chiefly call the Son the Wisdom of God, if the Father and the Holy Spirit are also wisdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: Because wisdom is to be commended to us and imitated, and by imitating it we are fashioned rightly. The Son is the Wisdom begotten of the Father by whom all things are made, and He was made wisdom for us in becoming man. The Father is no less wisdom, but Scripture presents the Son as the wisdom we are to follow.
sources.quote: namely, because wisdom ought to be commended and imitated by us, by the imitation of which we are fashioned [rightly]?
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture almost always speak of wisdom as begotten or made by God, and thus chiefly of the Son, if the Father is also wisdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: Because the Son, as the Image equal to the Father, is given to us as an example to follow so that we may be refashioned after the image of God. We follow the Son by living wisely, so Scripture speaks of wisdom chiefly in reference to Him. This does not deny that the Father also is wisdom, just as He is light and God.
sources.quote: Scripture, when it speaks of wisdom, speaks of the Son, whom we follow by living wisely; although the Father also is wisdom, as He is both light and God.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture, when it speaks of wisdom, chiefly refer to the Son, if the Father and the Holy Spirit are also wisdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Holy Spirit is Called Love, and Whether He Alone is So Called. That the Holy Spirit is in the Scriptures Properly Called by the Name of Love.
sources.answer: Yes. The apostle expressly calls Christ the wisdom of God. Yet universally both the Father and the Holy Spirit are also wisdom, so the special name does not deny the attribute to the others.
sources.quote: As, then, we call the only Word of God specially by the name of Wisdom, although universally both the Holy Spirit and the Father Himself is wisdom; so the Holy Spirit is specially called by the name of Love
sources.raw_question: Is the Son specially called the Wisdom of God even though the Father and the Holy Spirit are also wisdom?

question: Does the Holy Spirit call, send and appoint ministers of the Church with the same authority as the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter X. Being about to prove that the will, the calling, and the commandment of the Trinity is one, St. Ambrose shows that the Spirit called the Church exactly as the Father and the Son did, and proves this by the selection of SS. Paul and Barnabas, and especially by the mission of St. Peter to Cornelius. And by the way he points out how in the Apostle's vision the calling of the Gentiles was shadowed forth, who having been before like wild beasts, now by the operation of the Spirit lay aside that wildness. Then having quoted other passages in support of this view, he shows that in the case of Jeremiah cast into a pit by Jews, and rescued by Abdemelech, is a type of the slighting of the Holy Spirit by the Jews, and of His being honoured by the Gentiles.
sources.answer: Yes. In Acts the Spirit says, "Separate Me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them," and they are said to be sent forth by the Holy Spirit. So Paul received his apostleship by the will of the Holy Spirit as well as of Christ. This shows the Spirit acts with the same divine authority as the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: So Paul received the apostleship by the will not only of Christ, but also of the Holy Spirit, and hastened to gather together the Gentiles.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit call and send ministers of the Church by His own authority, as the Father and the Son do?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XIII. Prophecy was not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Spirit; the authority and operation of the latter on the apostles is signified to be the same as Theirs; and so we are to understand that there is unity in the three points of authority, rule, and bounty; yet need no disadvantage be feared from that participation, since such does not arise in human friendship. Lastly, it is established that this is the inheritance of the apostolic faith from the fact that the apostles are described as having obeyed the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Jesus spoke to Paul, and the Spirit forbade Paul and Silas to go into Bithynia. The Father spoke through the prophets, and Agabus says "Thus saith the Holy Spirit." Wisdom sent out the apostles, and the Spirit says "Separate Me Barnabas and Saul." Those whom the Spirit sent differed in nothing from the other apostles, as though the Father sent one way and the Spirit another.
sources.quote: And how should He not be a master Who speaks what He wills, and commands what He wills, as the Father commands and the Son commands?
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit speak and command with the same authority as the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XIII. Prophecy was not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Spirit; the authority and operation of the latter on the apostles is signified to be the same as Theirs; and so we are to understand that there is unity in the three points of authority, rule, and bounty; yet need no disadvantage be feared from that participation, since such does not arise in human friendship. Lastly, it is established that this is the inheritance of the apostolic faith from the fact that the apostles are described as having obeyed the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul tells the Ephesian elders that the Holy Spirit made them overseers to rule the Church of God, and in Acts the Spirit commands, "Separate Me Barnabas and Saul," and the apostles obey. Thus the Spirit entrusts the same office and appoints the same persons as the Father and the Son, showing His commanding authority.
sources.quote: the Holy Spirit entrusts the same office as the Father and the Son, and appoints the same persons
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit appoint ministers of the Church with the same authority as the Father and the Son?

question: In what sense is the Holy Spirit said to be 'sent'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: For the Holy Spirit, being the gift of God means proceeding from the Father. Being sent means being known to proceed from the Father. His mission thus manifests his eternal procession.
sources.quote: And as to be the gift of God in respect to the Holy Spirit, means to proceed from the Father; so to be sent, is to be known to proceed from the Father.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean for the Holy Spirit to be 'sent'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: He is said to be sent because a created outward appearance was wrought in time in which he was visibly shown. Examples are the dove at Christ's baptism and the wind and tongues of fire at Pentecost. His very substance did not appear, for it is invisible and unchangeable like the Father's and the Son's. The visible signs were meant to turn human hearts from his coming in time to his hidden, ever-present eternity.
sources.quote: not that His very substance appeared, in which He himself also is invisible and unchangeable, like the Father and the Son
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Holy Spirit said to be sent, and does this mean his substance became visible?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > A Doubt Raised About Divine Appearances.
sources.answer: The Spirit is said to be sent because of corporeal forms that came into existence in time to signify and manifest him to human senses. Examples are the dove and the tongues of fire. His sending is therefore a temporal, visible manifestation through created forms that come and go, not a taking of a creature into personal union as in the Son's incarnation.
sources.quote: The Holy Spirit, then, is also said to be sent, on account of these corporeal forms which came into existence in time, in order to signify and manifest Him, as He must needs be manifested, to human senses
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Holy Spirit said to be 'sent' when he has never become incarnate?

question: If the Son is eternal, must creation also be eternal, or can creation have a beginning while the Son does not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius's objection itself proves the orthodox charge against him, because it treats the Lord of creation as no different from the general body of creation and applies to the Only-begotten what is seen in creatures. The creation has the ages for its beginning, but no beginning can be conceived for the Maker of the ages. What is asserted of the Only-begotten has no kinship with creation, so the argument does not carry over.
sources.quote: For there is no other point we blame so much as this, that you think there is no difference between the Lord of creation and the general body of creation, and what you now allege is a maintaining of the very things which we find fault with.
sources.raw_question: If the Son's eternity follows from God's eternal goodness, must creation, since creating is also good and natural to God, likewise be eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: Creation can have a beginning while the Son does not. Creation is in its own nature something other than its Creator and does not touch the pure pre-temporal world. Scripture teaches that created things are not from everlasting and will not remain for ever. To say they came from things not seen brings no dishonour on their Maker.
sources.quote: there is nothing to prevent the creation, being, as it is, in its own nature something other than its Creator and in no point trenching on that pure pre-temporal world, from having, in our belief, a beginning of its own
sources.raw_question: If the Son is eternal, must the creation also be eternal, or can creation have a beginning while the Son does not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: Neither follows. This dilemma wrongly ties the Son to creation. The Son's generation does not fall within time, any more than creation existed before time. So the Son is eternal with the Father while creation has its own beginning, being different in nature from its Creator.
sources.quote: as if it were necessary to suppose either that the Son was from everlasting along with the creation, or that He too, equally with it, was later? For the generation of the Son does not fall within time
sources.raw_question: If the Son is eternal, must creation also be eternal, or else must the Son be later like creation?

question: Does the statement that all things were made through the Son (John 1:3) prove that the Son is not himself a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > These doctrines of our Faith witnessed to and confirmed by Scripture passages.
sources.answer: Yes. If all things were made by Him and consist in Him, their Maker must have a nature different from theirs, producing them and not himself. Since the creation came by Him but He did not come by himself, He is plainly outside the creation, and the evangelist would not have spoken so if he had thought the Lord one of the things made.
sources.quote: How could all things be made by Him and in Him consist, unless their Maker possessed a nature different from theirs, and so produced, not Himself, but them? If the creation was by Him, but He was not by Himself, plainly He is something outside the creation.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that all things were made by the Son prove that the Son is not himself a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: Yes. If all things were made by him and consist in him, their Maker must have a nature different from theirs. He produced them, not himself. If creation came through him but he did not come through himself, he is plainly outside creation.
sources.quote: How could all things be made by Him and in Him consist, unless their Maker possessed a nature different from theirs, and so produced, not Himself, but them?
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that all things were made through the Word show that the Son is not a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > This third book shows a third fall of Eunomius, as refuting himself, and sometimes saying that the Son is to be called Only-begotten in virtue of natural generation, and that Holy Scripture proves this from the first; at other times, that by reason of His being created He should not be called a Son, but a “product,” or “creature.”
sources.answer: Yes. If all things that were made came to be through Him and nothing in creation was made without Him, then He who made the whole creation must be something other than the creation. John's prologue is thus an incontestable proof that the Son is Lord of creation and not counted among created things.
sources.quote: a fact which is an incontestable and positive proof of His being Lord of the creation, not reckoned in the list of created things.
sources.raw_question: Does John's statement that nothing was made without the Word prove that the Son is not a creature?

question: Should the Holy Spirit be glorified, and on what grounds is He glorified?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Proof of the absurdity of the refusal to glorify the Spirit, from the comparison of things glorified in creation.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture ascribes glory to man, to Israel, to the Psalmist, to sun, moon and stars, and even to the ministration of condemnation; it would be absurd for the Spirit alone to be unglorified. Moreover the Apostle says the ministration of the Spirit is glorious, so the Spirit Himself cannot be unworthy of glory.
sources.quote: While then so many things are glorified, do you wish the Spirit alone of all things to be unglorified? Yet the Apostle says “the ministration of the Spirit is glorious.” How then can He Himself be unworthy of glory?
sources.raw_question: Should the Holy Spirit be glorified at all, given that Scripture ascribes glory to many created things?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > The glorifying of the enumeration of His attributes.
sources.answer: Yes. Since He is divine in nature, infinite in greatness, powerful in operation and good in the blessings He confers, He is to be highly exalted and given glory. To refuse this would amount to forbidding even the mention of the good things that come to us from Him.
sources.quote: Shall we not then highly exalt Him who is in His nature divine, in His greatness infinite, in His operations powerful, in the blessings He confers, good? Shall we not give Him glory?
sources.raw_question: Should the Holy Spirit be glorified?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as the Son is glorified by the Father, the Spirit is glorified through His communion with the Father and the Son. He is also glorified by the testimony of the Only-begotten, who declares that blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven.
sources.quote: so is the Spirit glorified through His communion with both Father and Son, and through the testimony of the Only-begotten
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit himself glorified, and if so, how?

question: Did the Word become Son only at the incarnation, having been merely Word before?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
