sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No. If becoming man made him Son, then the incarnation would be the cause of his sonship and the same absurdities follow as with making the man the Son. Moreover, knowing the Father, being in the Father's bosom, being one with the Father, and revealing the Father are all said of the Son. So on this view none of these would have been true before the incarnation. The Word is always Son, not lately come to be or named Son.
sources.quote: Next, if He is first Word and then Son, it will appear that He knew the Father afterwards, not before; for not as being Word does He know Him, but as Son.
sources.raised_by_detail: Marcellians (those holding the Word became Son at incarnation)
sources.raw_question: Did the Word become Son only when he became man at the incarnation, having been merely Word before?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No. Becoming man would then be the cause of his sonship, and the same absurdities return. He would also only have come to know the Father, be in the Father's bosom, and be one with the Father after the incarnation, since Scripture says these things of the Son. Before that no one could have known the Father, because the Father is known only through the Son. Yet God was revealed to Moses and the fathers, so a Son must have existed to reveal him.
sources.quote: if He is first Word and then Son, it will appear that He knew the Father afterwards, not before; for not as being Word does He know Him, but as Son.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who say the Word became Son on his incarnation
sources.raw_question: Did the Word become Son only at the incarnation, just as he became flesh only then?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No. To say that God was first God and only afterwards Father is an Arian thought. It would also make God change, and change belongs to bodies, not to God.
sources.quote: But if afterwards there is Father, and first God, this is an Arian thought. Next, it is absurd that God should change; for that belongs to bodies
sources.raised_by_detail: those who say the Word became Son when He became man
sources.raw_question: Did the Word become Son only at the incarnation, so that God first was God and only afterwards became Father?

question: Does the scriptural phrase 'through whom' applied to the Son show that the Son is a subordinate instrument of the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > The systematic discussion of syllables is derived from heathen philosophy.
sources.answer: No. Among pagan writers the phrase 'through which' was reserved for lifeless instruments or the meanest manual service. Applying it in that sense to the Lord of all treats the Creator of the universe like a hammer or a saw. That is shameful and degrades the Word's dignity.
sources.quote: they do not shrink from transferring to the Lord of all, and Christians feel no shame in applying to the Creator of the universe language belonging to a hammer or a saw.
sources.raw_question: Does the scriptural phrase 'through whom' applied to the Son show that the Son is a mere instrument or subordinate agent of the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That v: not found “of whom” in the case of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. If Romans 11:36 is referred to the Father, then "through whom" is applied to the Father as well. If the phrase always implied ministry, the Father would have to be subordinate to some superior, which is absurd. So it conveys nothing derogatory and cannot be confined to the Son as a mark of inferiority.
sources.quote: If it always and everywhere implies ministry, let them tell us to what superior the God of glory and Father of the Christ is subordinate.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase "through whom" necessarily imply inferiority or ministerial subordination when it is applied to the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That v: not found “of whom” in the case of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.answer: It is used of the Father as well as of the Son and Spirit. Scripture says God is faithful "by whom" we were called, Paul is an apostle "by the will of God," we are heirs "through God," and Christ was raised "by the glory of the Father"; it is also used of the Spirit, as God reveals "by the Spirit." Hence "through whom" cannot signify an inferior nature.
sources.quote: It must now be pointed out that the phrase “through whom” is admitted by Scripture in the case of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost alike.
sources.raw_question: Is the phrase "through whom" used in Scripture only of the Son and Spirit as subordinate instruments, or also of God the Father?

question: Do the names Father and Son imply a difference of nature between the Father and the Son, or do they indicate one shared nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. The mystery handed down teaches that 'Father' means the Father of the Son, and 'Son' means the Son of the Father. The natural sense of these names excludes the idea of their being alien in essence. This is why Eunomius shifts to the terms 'ungenerate' and 'generate', hoping to read a difference of nature into them.
sources.quote: the natural sense of the names Father and Son excludes the idea of their being alien in essence
sources.raw_question: Do the names Father and Son imply a difference of nature or essence between them?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. The term Father points to no difference of nature from the Son, and the natural sense of Father and Son excludes the idea that they are alien in essence. This is why Eunomius must turn to the terms generate and ungenerate to support his impiety.
sources.quote: the natural sense of the names Father and Son excludes the idea of their being alien in essence
sources.raw_question: Do the names Father and Son imply a difference of nature between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: Yes. Having heard of Father and Son from the Truth, we learn the oneness of their nature in these two. The natural relation expressed by the names points to a common nature, and Christ's own words confirm it.
sources.quote: Having heard of Father and Son from the Truth, we are taught in those two subjects the oneness of their nature; their natural relation to each other expressed by those names indicates that nature
sources.raw_question: Do the names 'Father' and 'Son' indicate that the two share one nature?

question: Can temporal priority and posteriority, as found in the order of creation, be applied between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His elaborate account of degrees and differences in 'works' and 'energies' within the Trinity is absurd.
sources.answer: No. Priority belongs only to creation, where works followed in the sequence of days. The divine nature transcends all time. To make the Father prior to the Son's subsistence would make the Son later than the ages and things that were made by him.
sources.quote: he who declares the Father to be ‘prior’ to the subsistence of the Son declares nothing short of this, viz., that the Son is later than the things made by the Son
sources.raw_question: Can 'priority' and 'posteriority' be applied to the Father and the Son as they are applied to the order of creation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His elaborate account of degrees and differences in 'works' and 'energies' within the Trinity is absurd.
sources.answer: No. Priority in time applies only to creation, where the sequence of works was displayed in the order of the days and intervals can be measured. The divine nature transcends all idea of time and surpasses thought, so speaking of a 'prior' and 'later' within it is a novelty of Eunomius's new philosophy.
sources.quote: But in the divine nature, which transcends all idea of time and surpasses all reach of thought, to talk of a “prior” and a “later” in the honours of time is a privilege only of this new-fangled philosophy.
sources.raw_question: Can 'priority' and 'posteriority' in time be applied within the divine nature, as between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: No. In the pre-temporal world there are no intervals, so we cannot ascribe to it the temporal precedence we see among created things. With the Father, who is always Father, the Son is inseparably joined as coming from Him yet side by side with Him.
sources.quote: For there, with the Father, unoriginate, ungenerate, always Father, the idea of the Son as coming from Him yet side by side with Him is inseparably joined
sources.raw_question: Is there a temporal interval or priority between the Father and the Son in the divine life?

question: Does calling the Father "Light unapproachable" and the Son "true Light" imply a difference of nature between them, or that the Son's light is inferior to the Father's?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then referring to the blasphemy of Eunomius, which had been refuted by the great Basil, where he banished the Only-begotten God to the realm of darkness, and the apology or explanation which Eunomius puts forth for his blasphemy, he shows that his present blasphemy is rendered by his apology worse than his previous one; and herein he very ably discourses of the “true” and the “unapproachable” Light.
sources.answer: No. Both terms signify the same thing: absolute removal from the contrary, since the true is unapproachable by the false and the unapproachable is found in unsullied truth. One could even interchange the two attributes without error. Hence the one Light is not divergent from the other, and Eunomius's distinction rests on an equivocal use of the term "Light."
sources.quote: Accordingly the unapproachable is identical with the true, because that which is signified by each expression is equally inaccessible to evil.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father "Light unapproachable" and the Son "true Light" signify a difference of nature between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: No. The Eunomians argue the Father is greater because he alone is called 'true God'. By that same logic, the Son, called 'true Light', would be greater than the Father. They cannot make 'true' mean enhancement in one case and diminution in the other.
sources.quote: For if they say that the Father is greater than the Son because He is true God, by the same showing the Son would be acknowledged to be greater than the Father, because the former is called “true Light,”
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'true Light' and the Father 'Light unapproachable' show that the Son's light is inferior to the Father's?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then referring to the blasphemy of Eunomius, which had been refuted by the great Basil, where he banished the Only-begotten God to the realm of darkness, and the apology or explanation which Eunomius puts forth for his blasphemy, he shows that his present blasphemy is rendered by his apology worse than his previous one; and herein he very ably discourses of the “true” and the “unapproachable” Light.
sources.answer: No. The two terms mean the same thing, since each is equally removed from its contrary. The 'true' admits no mixture of falsehood, and the 'unapproachable' cannot be approached by evil. The Son's light is true and not evil, so the Father's light is not unapproachable by it. The two attributes could even be interchanged without error.
sources.quote: For the “true” and the “unapproachable” are each of them removed in an equally absolute degree from their contraries.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son the 'true' Light and the Father 'Light unapproachable' imply a difference of nature between them?

question: In glorifying the Son, is it proper to say "with whom" as well as "through whom," and what does each phrase express?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that it is not proper for “with whom” to be said of the Son, and that the proper phrase is “through whom.”
sources.answer: No. The Church recognizes both phrases and neither excludes the other. When we contemplate the majesty of the Only Begotten's nature and dignity, we testify that the glory is with the Father. When we think of the good gifts he bestows and of our access to God's household, we confess that this grace comes to us through him.
sources.quote: the Church recognizes both uses, and deprecates neither as subversive of the other. For whenever we are contemplating the majesty of the nature of the Only Begotten, and the excellence of His dignity, we bear witness that the glory is with the Father
sources.raw_question: Is it improper to glorify the Son with the phrase "with whom" (glory to the Father with the Son), so that only "through whom" should be used of him?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that it is not proper for “with whom” to be said of the Son, and that the proper phrase is “through whom.”
sources.answer: "With whom" belongs properly to the ascription of glory, because it expresses the Son's equal dignity with the Father. "Through whom" is especially suited to thanksgiving, because it expresses the benefits that come to us through the Son's mediation.
sources.quote: It follows that the one phrase “with whom” is the proper one to be used in the ascription of glory, while the other, “through whom,” is specially appropriate in giving of thanks.
sources.raw_question: What is the proper use of "with whom" and of "through whom" in speaking of the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: Both phrases are legitimate, and neither undermines the other. When we contemplate the majesty of the Only Begotten's nature and dignity, we say the glory is with the Father, so "with whom" is the proper phrase for ascribing glory. When we think of the good gifts he gives us and our access to God's household, "through whom" is fitting for giving thanks.
sources.quote: It follows that the one phrase “with whom” is the proper one to be used in the ascription of glory, while the other, “through whom,” is specially appropriate in giving of thanks.
sources.raw_question: When glorifying the Son, should one say the glory is "with" the Son or "through" the Son?

question: Can the Son be called 'eternal' in a limited or merely 'negative' sense, meaning only that we cannot fix or conceive a time when he came into being, even though he was produced at some point of duration?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. That would be an abuse of words, as unreasonable as calling an angel eternal merely because the time of its creation is unspecified. A 'limited eternity' is in reality an eternity and no eternity. Words should keep their proper sense. Otherwise even 'God,' 'truly God,' and 'God by nature' lose their force, as happened with the Arians.
sources.quote: Unless you suppose that there is an unlimited and a limited eternity, which is, in reality, an eternity. and no eternity.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be called 'eternal' in a limited sense, meaning only that the time of his coming into being is not determined?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. Such 'negative eternity' is no eternity at all. On that reasoning angels and archangels could also be called eternal, since we do not know when they were made. Every creature is produced at some point of duration by God's eternal power and will. If the Son was made at all, we can and must conceive ages before he came into being.
sources.quote: What is this negative eternity, but no eternity? And why are not angels or archangels called eternal, since we know not precisely when they were made
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be called eternal in a 'negative' sense, meaning we cannot conceive a time when he was not, even though God produced him by his will at some point of duration?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. Such a 'negative eternity' is really no eternity at all. On that reasoning angels and archangels could be called eternal, since we do not know when they were made. Every creature is produced at some point of duration by God's eternal power and will, and that does not make any creature eternal.
sources.quote: What is this negative eternity, but no eternity? And why are not angels or archangels called eternal, since we know not precisely when they were made, nor in what time they began to exist
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be called eternal in a 'negative' sense, meaning only that God could produce beings at any point of his duration so that we cannot conceive a time when they were not?

question: Do the Scripture texts declaring that there is one God exclude the Son from being the one Supreme God together with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus says Scripture declares the one only God, excluding all others, to have made all things by his Word; the others are excluded but not the Word. He also says God made all things by himself, meaning his Word and Wisdom, the Son and Spirit, so the declarations of unity cannot exclude what is so near God as to be justly called himself.
sources.quote: Others are excluded, but not his Word, that is, has Son, by whom he made all things, as Jrenzeus constantly understands it.
sources.raw_question: Do the Scripture texts asserting the unity of God exclude the Son from being the one Supreme God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 1: Whether all other beings, besides the one Supreme God, be not excluded by the texts of Isaiah, (to which many more might be added ;) and consequently, whether C
sources.answer: No. Waterland holds that this interpretation misunderstands the texts, since it cannot be reconciled with other texts that call Christ God, and it leads to absurdities the opponent himself will not admit, such as excluding Christ from being God at all. Thus the argument either proves too much or proves nothing.
sources.quote:
the interpreta- _

tion you give of them is not reconcilable with other texts; and ‘because it leads to such absurdities, as are too shocking even for yourself to admit. In short, either you prove too much, or you prove nothing.
sources.raw_question: Do the Old Testament texts declaring one God prove that the Father alone is the Supreme God and that Christ is excluded from being the Supreme God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Waterland concludes that plain Scripture texts show Christ is not excluded from being the one Supreme God in conjunction with the Father, and he has answered the opponent's objections. He adds that this is confirmed by the unanimous consent of all antiquity before the Council of Nicaea, which is the very authority his opponent appealed to.
sources.quote: having shewn from plain scripture texts, that Christ is not excluded from being the one Supreme God in conjunction with the Father; and taken off your exceptions
sources.raw_question: Is Christ excluded from being the one Supreme God together with the Father when Scripture speaks of the one God?

question: Is it legitimate, as Basil advised, to avoid the word 'Ungenerate' for God while still affirming that God the Father is ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. Basil only advised suppressing the bare word 'Ungenerate' because it had been evilly interpreted by heretics and is not found in Scripture; its meaning he affirmed fully suits our thoughts about God. The term 'Father' is an adequate substitute that leads the mind to the same idea, so the truth is guarded intact.
sources.quote: he advised us to avoid all danger by suppressing the mere word Ungenerate, that is, the expression in so many syllables, as one which had been evilly interpreted, and besides was not to be found in Scripture
sources.raw_question: Did Basil, in advising that the word 'Ungenerate' be avoided, deny that God is truly ungenerate or suppress a natural truth about God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Defence of S. Basil's statement, attacked by Eunomius, that the terms 'Father' and 'The Ungenerate' can have the same meaning.
sources.answer: Yes. Basil did not deny that the Deity is ungenerate; he accepted the idea but advised suppressing the word because heretics used it to teach the inequality of the Persons. Christ himself teaches that even precious things should be cut off if they lead to sin, so a word that serves blasphemy may be set aside while its reverent meaning is kept through other names.
sources.quote: bids us cherish the idea of an ungenerate Deity by means of other names,—therein he does not deserve their abuse.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to suppress the word 'Ungenerate' for God while still believing that God the Father is ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Defence of S. Basil's statement, attacked by Eunomius, that the terms 'Father' and 'The Ungenerate' can have the same meaning.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ and Paul teach that even good things should be set aside when they lead others into sin, as Paul would give up meat for the weak brother's sake. Because heretics used 'Ungenerate' to teach the inequality of the Persons, Basil rightly counselled keeping the truth of the ungenerate Deity in our souls while not clinging to the word, since 'Father' conveys the same meaning.
sources.quote: while we cherish in our souls a devout consciousness of this ungenerate Deity, we should not show any particular love for the actual word, which was the occasion of sin to the reprobate
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to avoid using the term 'Ungenerate' for God, as Basil advised, while still affirming that God is ungenerate?

question: Is the Holy Trinity, including the Son and the Holy Spirit, created or uncreated?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: The Trinity belongs to the uncreated. Gregory divides existence into the sensible and the intelligible, and the intelligible into created and uncreate; the Holy Trinity is defined as belonging to the uncreate, while everything else that exists or can be thought of belongs to the created.
sources.quote: in this we detect again a further distinction into the Created and the Uncreate: to the latter of which we have defined the Holy Trinity to belong, to the former all that can exist or can be thought of after that.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Trinity belong to the created or the uncreated order of existence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: Uncreated. Among intelligible beings there is a division into created and uncreate, and the whole Trinity belongs to the uncreate. The Lord himself attests that he came forth from the Father by an ineffable birth, calling God his Father, not his creator, and himself Son, not a work of God.
sources.quote: we will add that our Lord was not created, but came forth from the Father, as the Word with His own lips attests in the Gospel, in a manner of birth or of proceeding ineffable and mysterious
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Trinity, including the Son, created or uncreated?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: Yes. All creation, sensible and supramundane, derives its existence from Father, Son and Holy Spirit, as Psalm 33:6 shows by naming the Word and the Breath (Spirit) of God as creators. Since maker and made differ in nature, what effects the production of created things cannot itself be created.
sources.quote: neither is that uncreated which is made, nor is that created which effects the production of the things that are made
sources.raw_question: Are the Son and the Holy Spirit uncreated, given that creation is ascribed to them?

question: Does calling the Holy Spirit the 'Finger of God' imply that the Spirit is inferior to the Father or only a small part of God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter V. The writer sums up the argument he had commenced, and confirms the statement that unity is signified by the terms finger and right hand, from the fact that the works of God are the same as are the works of hands; and that those of hands are the same as those of fingers; and lastly, that the term hand applies equally to the Son and the Spirit, and that of finger applies to the Spirit and the Son.
sources.answer: No. The term signifies unity of power, not inequality. Scripture ascribes the same works to God, to God's hands, and to God's fingers, such as the heavens. So the image marks no difference of work by bodily member but a oneness of power.
sources.quote: But let them learn, as I have often said, that not inequality but unity of power is signified by this testimony; inasmuch as things which are the works of God are also the works of hands, and we read that the same are the works of fingers.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Holy Spirit the "finger of God" imply that the Spirit is lesser in power than the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter III. The same Unity may also be recognized from the fact that the Spirit is called Finger, and the Son Right Hand; for the understanding of divine things is assisted by the usage of human language. The tables of the law were written by this Finger, and they were afterwards broken, and the reason. Lastly, Christ wrote with the same Finger; yet we must not admit any inferiority in the Spirit from this bodily comparison.
sources.answer: No. The bodily comparison must not lead us to think the Spirit inferior in ministry or a small part of God. Spiritual things are to be compared with spiritual, not with carnal; whoever does so is a natural man to whom the things of the Spirit are foolishness. In the following chapter Ambrose adds that the same reasoning would equally make the Son, called the Right Hand, only a small portion of God.
sources.quote: lest, again, because God wrote the Law by His Spirit, we should believe any inferiority, as it were, concerning the ministry of the Spirit, or from the consideration of our own body should think the Spirit to be a small part of God
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Holy Spirit the 'Finger of God' imply that the Spirit is inferior to the Father or only a small part of God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IV. To those who contend that the Spirit because He is called the Finger is less than the Father, St. Ambrose replies that this would also tend to the lessening of the Son, Who is called the Right Hand. That these names are to be referred only to the Unity, for which reason Moses proclaimed that the whole Trinity worked in the passage of the Red Sea. And, indeed, it is no wonder that the operation of the Spirit found place there, where there was a figure of baptism, since the Scripture teaches that the Three Persons equally sanctify and are operative in that sacrament.
sources.answer: No. If the title 'Finger' made the Spirit a small portion of God, then by the same reasoning the Son, called the 'Right Hand' of God, would also be only a small portion. Whoever thinks wrongly of the Spirit cannot think rightly of the Son. Such bodily names are to be referred to the unity of the Godhead, not to inequality.
sources.quote: For if some think that the Spirit is a certain small portion of God, because He is called the Finger of God, the same persons must certainly maintain that a small portion only is in the Son of God, because He is called the Right Hand of God.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who argue from bodily figures
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being called the 'Finger of God' imply that He is a small portion of God and less than the Father?

question: Is the God of the Old Testament, confessed by the law and the prophets, the same God as the Father of Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: Yes. Mark opens his Gospel by quoting the prophets and so points at once to the one they confessed as God and Lord, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. This Father had promised to send His messenger, John the Baptist, before the face of His Son. The Gospel therefore continues the prophets' God and does not announce a new one.
sources.quote: point out Him at once, whom they confessed as God and Lord; Him, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who had also made promise to Him, that He would send His messenger before His face
sources.raw_question: Is the God whom the Old Testament prophets confessed as God and Lord the same as the Father of Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: Yes. The one Creator who formed man, sent the flood and saved Noah is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He is the one the law proclaims, the prophets preach, Christ reveals, the apostles make known and the Church believes in. He is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
sources.quote: He it is whom the law proclaims, whom the prophets preach, whom Christ reveals, whom the apostles make known to us, and in whom the Church believes. He is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Is the God of the Old Testament (the God of Abraham, the law and the prophets) the same as the Father revealed by Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter V.—The author returns to his former argument, and shows that there was but one God announced by the law and prophets, whom Christ confesses as His Father, and who, through His word, one living God with Him, made Himself known to men in both covenants.
sources.answer: Yes. God is one and the same, the Creator who made temporal things and bestows eternal ones, announced by the law and prophets and confessed by Christ as His Father. Isaiah's declarations that there is no God before or after Him show He is God over all, and those who imagine another Father err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God.
sources.quote: who was announced by the law and the prophets, whom Christ confessed as His Father. Now He is the Creator, and He it is who is God over all
sources.raw_question: Is the God announced by the Old Testament law and prophets the same God whom Christ confessed as His Father?

question: Did God create the world out of nothing, or from pre-existent matter?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter X.—Perverse interpretations of Scripture by the heretics: God created all things out of nothing, and not from pre-existent matter.
sources.answer: God created out of nothing. By His own will and power He called into being the very substance of creation when it previously had no existence. This is what sets God above men: men can only make things out of matter already existing, whereas with God things impossible to men are possible.
sources.quote: While men, indeed, cannot make anything out of nothing, but only out of matter already existing, yet God is in this point pre-eminently superior to men, that He Himself called into being the substance of His creation, when previously it had no existence.
sources.raw_question: Did God create the world out of nothing, or from pre-existent matter?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIV.—Valentinus and his followers derived the principles of their system from the heathen; the names only are changed.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus presents this Valentinian opinion as borrowed from Anaxagoras, Empedocles and Plato. He mocks the claim that it came by inspiration from their 'Mother', counting it among pagan errors rather than the truth about God's creative power.
sources.quote: they hold the Creator formed the world out of previously existing matter, both Anaxagoras, Empedocles, and Plato expressed before them
sources.raw_question: Did God the Creator form the world out of previously existing matter?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XXII.—Deviations of heretics from the truth.
sources.answer: Out of nothing. The rule of truth holds that the one God Almighty, by his Word, fashioned and formed all existing things out of that which had no existence.
sources.quote: there is one God Almighty, who made all things by His Word, and fashioned and formed, out of that which had no existence, all things which exist
sources.raw_question: Did God create the world out of pre-existing matter or out of nothing?

question: Does Athanasius's language about the Father (as Framer of every substance, or as above all created or derivative being) imply that the Son is one of the Father's works (δημιουργήματα) or a derivative being beneath the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 12: Whether the Creator of all things was not himself uncreated ; and therefore could not be ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, made out of nothing ?
sources.answer: No. The change of wording may be only rhetorical variation, so no contrast between κτίσις and ὑπόστασις need be intended. If a contrast were pressed, it would equally make the Father less widely Lord than Framer, which is absurd. In the same treatise Athanasius makes the Son the maker of all invisible powers and the framer of the universe, and a few lines later he expressly sets the Son apart from all originated things and all creation.
sources.quote: the learned Doctor may almost as reasonably bring the Father in, among the δημιουργήματα of the Son, as vice versa.
sources.raw_question: Does Athanasius's description of the Father as 'Lord of creation and Framer of every substance' (πάσης ὑποστάσεως δημιουργόν) imply that the Son is one of the Father's works (δημιούργημα) or a derivative being?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. Athanasius's Greek means 'far above all created being', not 'derivative being'. Clarke's translation slips the Son in among inferior beings, which is contrary to Athanasius's sense in that very page. The supposed concession exists only in the translation.
sources.quote: instead of far above all created being, (which the Greek words signify, and which is the certain meaning of the author,) he chooses to say, “far above all derivative being ;”
sources.raw_question: Does Athanasius describe the Father as above all 'derivative' being, so that the Son counts as a derivative being below the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 12: Whether the Creator of all things was not himself uncreated ; and therefore could not be ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, made out of nothing ?
sources.answer: No. Waterland argues that Athanasius expressly denies that the Father can be called δημιουργός with respect to the Son. Far from making the Son a δημιούργημα, Athanasius makes him the maker of all the invisible powers and the δημιουργός of the universe. Within a few lines of the passage Dr. Clarke cites, Athanasius also explicitly sets the Son apart from all generated things and from the whole creation. So Clarke's rendering of Athanasius as placing the Son among 'all derivative being' misrepresents him.
sources.quote: where he expressly pleads that the Father cannot be said to be δημιουργὸς, in respect of the Son.
sources.raw_question: According to Athanasius, can the Father be called the maker (δημιουργός) of the Son, so that the Son ranks among the derivative beings or works (δημιουργήματα) of the Father?

question: Can God's nature and actions be judged or comprehended by the standards of human reason, philosophy and natural law?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. God's action must not be examined by human faculties, nor the Creator judged by his creatures. We must accept a modest sense of our own weakness, so that God's power may teach us truths that philosophy cannot reach. We should set no bounds to God's majesty, nor tie the Lord of nature to nature's laws, since the one true faith about God is the one of which he is both Author and Witness.
sources.quote: And therefore the action of God must not be canvassed by human faculties; the Creator must not be judged by those who are the work of His hands.
sources.raw_question: Should God's actions be judged by the standards of human reasoning and natural law?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. The Creator must not be judged by the work of His hands, and God's action must not be canvassed by human faculties. Only when we recognize the helplessness of our reason are we initiated by Divine Wisdom into the wisdom of God, so that God's power teaches truths earthly philosophy cannot reach.
sources.quote: the action of God must not be canvassed by human faculties; the Creator must not be judged by those who are the work of His hands.
sources.raw_question: Can God's actions and nature be judged or comprehended by human reason and philosophy?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Although we are partakers of the divine nature, we must not measure it by our own limitations. We must judge God's assertions about himself by his own self-revelation. Since God has full knowledge of himself and can be known only through his own utterances, he is the fitting witness concerning himself.
sources.quote: let us assume that God has full knowledge of Himself, and bow with humble reverence to His words. For He Whom we can only know through His own utterances is the fitting witness concerning Himself.
sources.raw_question: Should human reason and human nature be the measure for judging what is true of God's nature?

question: Does Paul's phrase 'the gift of Christ' in Ephesians 4:7-8 refer to the Holy Spirit, even though the quoted Psalm says 'gifts' in the plural?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul adds the Psalm about the ascended Lord giving gifts to show that by 'the gift of Christ' he meant the Holy Spirit. Everyone knows that after his ascension Christ gave the Spirit, who filled the believers so that they spoke in tongues. The plural 'gifts' is no objection, because Paul is simply keeping the wording of the Psalm.
sources.quote: And let no one object that he says gifts, not gift: for he quoted the text from the Psalm.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's phrase 'the gift of Christ' in Ephesians 4 refer to the Holy Spirit, even though the quoted Psalm says 'gifts' in the plural?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul shows that by the gift of Christ he meant the Holy Spirit by immediately adding the Psalm text about Christ ascending and giving gifts to men. Everyone knows that the Lord, after his resurrection and ascension, gave the Holy Spirit, with whom believers were filled and spoke in the tongues of all nations.
sources.quote: that he might show that by the gift of Christ he meant the Holy Spirit, he has gone on to add, “Wherefore He saith, He hath ascended up on high, He hath led captivity captive, and hath given gifts to men.”
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's phrase "the gift of Christ" in Ephesians 4:7-8 refer to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: No. Paul says "gifts" because he is quoting the Psalm, which also has the plural. The plural is fitting because the many gifts proper to each member are divided among all Christ's members by the one Gift, the Holy Spirit. Not everyone has every gift, but all have the Gift himself, who distributes to each as he wills.
sources.quote: many gifts, which are proper to each, are divided in common to all the members of Christ, by the Gift, which is the Holy Spirit. For each severally has not all, but some have these and some have those
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's use of the plural "gifts" rather than "gift" in Ephesians 4:8 count against identifying the gift of Christ with the one Holy Spirit?

question: Did Christ reveal a Father other than and higher than the Creator of the world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XV.—Proofs of the resurrection from Isaiah and Ezekiel; the same God who created us will also raise us up.
sources.answer: No. The Lord plainly made known himself and the Father to his disciples so that they would not look for another God besides the one who formed man and gave him the breath of life. Nor should anyone feign another Father above the Creator.
sources.quote: the Lord most plainly manifest Himself and the Father to His disciples, lest, forsooth, they might seek after another God besides Him who formed man, and who gave him the breath of life
sources.raw_question: Did Christ reveal a Father other than and higher than the Creator of man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XIX.—Passages of Scripture by which they attempt to prove that the Supreme Father was unknown before the coming of Christ.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus calls it impious to claim that the Lord announced another Father than the Maker of this universe, or to treat the Creator as the fruit of a defect. Prophetic texts about Israel not knowing God concern the true God, the Creator. Reading them as ignorance of a hidden Bythus is a garbling of Scripture.
sources.quote: Their object in this is to show that our Lord announced another Father than the Maker of this universe, whom, as we said before, they impiously declare to have been the fruit of a defect.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ reveal a Father other than the Creator of the universe, one unknown to everyone before his coming?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXV.—A refutation of those who allege that the prophets uttered some predictions under the inspiration of the highest, others from the Demiurge. Disagreements of the Valentinians among themselves with regard to these same predictions.
sources.answer: No. The Lord would never have spoken at one time from above and at another from degeneracy below, teaching both knowledge and ignorance. Nor would he glorify as Father now the Founder of the world and now another God above him. His own saying that new wine is not put into old bottles refutes such mixing.
sources.quote: nor would He have ever glorified as Father at one time the Founder of the world, and at another Him who is above this one
sources.raw_question: Did Christ acknowledge as Father sometimes the Creator of the world and sometimes a higher God above him?

question: Does the Arian scheme succeed in avoiding Tritheism or polytheism, or does it itself imply a plurality of Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. In trying to escape what they took to be Catholic Tritheism, the Arians fell into another kind of Tritheism. They worship a divine Son and Spirit as real Persons while denying them the one true Godhead, which leaves several gods. Their scheme thus fails in its principal design of avoiding polytheism.
sources.quote: were very unhappy in this particular, that, endeavouring to avoid one kind of Tritheism, they fell into another.
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian scheme succeed in avoiding Tritheism or polytheism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: It depends on how the word God is taken. If God is taken in the strict sense, the charge is ridiculous, since Arians do not make the Son God in that sense. If God is taken in the loose popular sense, or in the Arians' own sense in which the Son is called God, the plurality cannot be denied.
sources.quote: if we understand the word God in the strict sense, it is ridiculous to charge the Arian scheme with plurality of Gods. But, if it be understood in the loose popular sense, or in your own sense of it, it is equally ridiculous to deny it.
sources.raw_question: Is the Arian scheme guilty of a plurality of Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. The Arian scheme, in trying to avoid one kind of Tritheism, falls into another, and so fails in its principal design. It also has great difficulties with Scripture, being too high for some texts and too low for others, which Catholics (and even Sabellians) handle better. Catholicism alone is the scriptural and ancient scheme, liable to the fewest difficulties.
sources.quote: The Arian scheme, besides its failing in its principal design of avoiding Polytheism, has many real and great difficulties; being as well too high for some texts, as too /ow for others
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian scheme succeed in avoiding polytheism, and is it more consistent with Scripture than the Catholic doctrine of the Trinity?

question: In what does the sending (mission) of the Son of God consist?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: For the Son to be sent means for him to be known to be from the Father. As to be born means to be from the Father, so to be sent means that this origin from the Father becomes known.
sources.quote: For as to be born, in respect to the Son, means to be from the Father; so to be sent, in respect to the Son, means to be known to be from the Father.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean for the Son of God to be 'sent'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: The Son's sending consists in his being made of a woman, that is, his birth of Mary. Paul says that God sent forth his Son, made of a woman. Insofar as he is born of God, the Son was already in the world. Insofar as he was born of Mary, he was sent and came into the world.
sources.quote: Therefore, in that He was born of God, He was in the world; but in that He was born of Mary, He was sent and came into the world.
sources.raw_question: In what does the sending of the Son by the Father consist?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In What Manner the Son Was Sent and Proclaimed Beforehand. How in the Sending of His Birth in the Flesh He Was Made Less Without Detriment to His Equality with the Father.
sources.answer: The Son's being sent is his being made, that is, born of a woman in the fullness of time. Augustine reads Galatians 4:4, "God sent forth His Son, made of a woman," as identifying the mission with the becoming-made, so that he is sent in that he is made.
sources.quote: to such a degree lowly, that He was “made;” in this way therefore sent, in that He was made.
sources.raw_question: In what does the Son of God's being sent (his mission) consist?

question: Why does Scripture not set out the doctrine of the Trinity in a brief, explicit creedal statement, such as one given by Christ himself, rather than through narrative, poetry, prophecy, and scattered references?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Because God's method in Scripture parallels his method in nature, where seemingly superfluous forests, mountains, and seas actually nourish the fruitful fields. Scripture's manifold forms of history, law, poetry, and argument likewise serve its purpose. Yet amid all this variety, the rule of faith in the one God, Father, Son, and Spirit, is marked out with precision plain enough for anyone to read.
sources.quote: the simple rule of our faith in the One living and true God – Father Son and Spirit, the source of creation, redemption, and sanctification, – is marked out with a precision that he who runs may read.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture not present the doctrine of the Trinity in the form of definitions, articles, and creeds rather than through narrative, poetry, prophecy, and argument?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. God gives no account of his matters, and it is not certain that such an article would have settled every doubt. Doubts about its text could have arisen, and minds unconvinced by plain texts like the opening of John's Gospel would likely remain unconvinced. Saving faith is the gift of God.
sources.quote: But even if the text were as impregnable as the opening of St. John’s Gospel, I doubt whether it would have convinced such minds as remain unconvinced of the Godhead of Christ
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture have to contain a short formal statement of the Trinity, given by Christ himself, for the doctrine to be credible?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: God gives no account of his matters, and such an article would likely have done more harm than good. It would have fostered a careless, contented apathy, superseding diligent study of the rest of Scripture and producing a petrified orthodoxy without influence on the heart. God instead left Scripture to prove doctrine through scattered and incidental references, whose comparison exercises the mind and improves the heart, and left the Church the office of teaching and framing creeds.
sources.quote: Their orthodoxy would have been as it were petrified; like the bodies of those animals we read of incrusted in the ice of the polar regions – firm fixed, indeed, and preserved unchangeable; but cold, motionless, lifeless.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture not contain a brief, explicit creedal article stating the doctrine of the Trinity, such as one enunciated by Christ himself?

question: Does Hebrews 1:4's statement that the Son became 'so much better than the angels' refer to the Son's divine nature or to His incarnate ministry and the Economy?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. The surrounding passage fixes the time as 'these last days,' when God spoke through His Son and purged sins. That is the time of the Incarnation. The Arians therefore wrongly apply to Christ's divinity what belongs to His manhood.
sources.quote: For had they known the person, and the subject, and the season of the Apostle’s words, they would not have expounded of Christ’s divinity what belongs to His manhood
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1:4, which says the Son was 'made so much better than the Angels,' describe the Son's divine nature as something brought into being?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: The Apostle refers to the Word's coming in the flesh and the Economy, not to comparing His essence with creatures. He shows that as the Son excelled in nature those sent before Him, so the grace through Him surpasses the ministry of angels, just as servants only demand fruits while the Son and Master forgives debts and transfers the vineyard.
sources.quote: regarding the Word’s visitation in the flesh, and the Economy which He then sustained, he wished to show that He was not like those who had gone before Him
sources.raw_question: Why does Hebrews say the Son became 'so much better than the angels' if His essence cannot be compared with theirs?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: It refers to His manhood and ministry, not His divinity. The context of the passage speaks of the last days when God spoke by His Son and when purging of sins took place, that is, after He became man. The Apostle contrasts the old ministry of prophets and angels with the new ministry of the Son, showing that as a son excels a servant, so the Son's ministry excels that of servants.
sources.quote: It appears then that the Apostle’s words make mention of that time, when God spoke unto us by His Son, and when a purging of sins took place.
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1:4, which says the Son became 'so much better than the Angels', refer to the Son's divine nature or to His incarnate ministry?

question: Is it legitimate for human beings to name God with words devised by their own thought, even though such names cannot express His nature and originate later than God Himself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Since no word suitable to express the divine nature exists, we rightly address God by many names, each adding some fresh touch to our notion and giving glimmerings of what we seek. Men may frame such names according to reverent conceptions, and there is no absurdity in this word-building, contrary to Eunomius' objection.
sources.quote: For whereas no suitable word has been found to express the Divine nature, we address God by many names, each by some distinctive touch adding something fresh to our notions respecting Him
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate for human beings to apply many different names to God, devised by their own thought, even though none expresses His nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. God's essence precedes His works, and we know His works by our senses and express them in words; so words are naturally of later origin than the things they represent and reflect them. There is no reason to fear calling things by words of later origin than themselves.
sources.quote: But if His essence is prior to His works, and we understand His works by our senses, and express them in words as we are best able, why should we be afraid of calling things by words of later origin than themselves?
sources.raw_question: Is it improper to apply to God names that originate later than God Himself, such as names formed by human thought?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The dilemma is a manifest absurdity. God has no need of words uttered by voice and tongue, and names are not a necessity for the Deity. Each human may therefore name God as he becomes able to conceive Him without sinning against Him. To insist that God needs names is itself profane, since a perfect being lacks nothing necessary and possesses nothing unnecessary.
sources.quote: it has been already explained that the Supreme Being has no need Himself of words as delivered by a voice and a tongue; and it would be superfluous to repeat what would only encumber the argument.
sources.raw_question: If names for God come from human reasoning ('conception'), must we conclude either that conception exists before those who conceive, or that the names befitting God are later than man and so dishonour God?

question: Do the names applied to God signify His essence, or His operations toward us?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They signify His operations, not His essence. The nature of Him who alone is remains unspeakable, and God receives His appellations from what are believed to be His operations in our life; e.g. the name "God" comes from His overseeing and surveying all things. Since words are formed to express operations known through His works, they are later in origin than the realities they name.
sources.quote: He is named, by those who call upon Him, not what He is essentially (for the nature of Him Who alone is is unspeakable), but He receives His appellations from what are believed to be His operations in regard to our life.
sources.raw_question: Do the names of God signify His essence or His operations toward us?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Like marks of recognition used to identify an unknown man, such as birth, wealth, or age, which do not constitute the man, the scriptural names of God set forth particular things about Him. They teach His power, His incorruptibility, that He is without cause or limit, or His supremacy. His nature, being above every name, Scripture neither names nor investigates.
sources.quote: For by these expressions we are taught either His power, or that He admits not of deterioration, or that He is without cause and without limit, or that He is supreme above all things, or, in short, something, be it what it may, respecting Him.
sources.raw_question: Do the names Scripture applies to God express His nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. God's nature is unspeakable; He is named by those who call on Him not according to what He essentially is, but from what are believed to be His operations in regard to our life. For example, He is called 'God' from His overseeing and surveying all things.
sources.quote: He is named, by those who call upon Him, not what He is essentially (for the nature of Him Who alone is is unspeakable), but He receives His appellations from what are believed to be His operations in regard to our life.
sources.raw_question: Do the names we apply to God express His essence or nature?

question: Why was it necessary for the Mediator of salvation to be both truly God and truly man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: Because each half of the work required it. Unless a man had overcome humanity's enemy, the enemy would not have been justly vanquished. Unless God had freely given salvation, we could not possess it securely. And unless man were joined to God, he could not share in incorruptibility. The Mediator, related to both, brings both to friendship, presenting man to God and revealing God to man.
sources.quote: For unless man had overcome the enemy of man, the enemy would not have been legitimately vanquished. And again: unless it had been God who had freely given salvation, we could never have possessed it securely.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Mediator of salvation need to be both truly God and truly man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: Because unless man had overcome the enemy of man, the enemy would not have been legitimately vanquished. Unless God had freely given salvation, we could not possess it securely. And unless man were joined to God, he could not partake of incorruptibility. The Mediator, related to both, brings God and man into friendship.
sources.quote: For unless man had overcome the enemy of man, the enemy would not have been legitimately vanquished. And again: unless it had been God who had freely given salvation, we could never have possessed it securely.
sources.raw_question: Why was it necessary that the Mediator be both truly God and truly man for salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVII.—There is but one Lord and one God, the Father and Creator of all things, who has loved us in Christ, given us commandments, and remitted our sins; whose Son and Word Christ proved Himself to be, when He forgave our sins.
sources.answer: He had to be both so that he could both suffer and forgive. As man he suffered for us, and as God he has compassion on us and forgives the debts we owed to God our Creator. As Mediator he propitiates the Father and cancels our disobedience by his own obedience.
sources.quote: since He was man, and since He was God, in order that since as man He suffered for us, so as God He might have compassion on us, and forgive us our debts
sources.raw_question: Why was it necessary for the Mediator who forgives sins to be both God and man?

question: If the Father is invisible, how is He made known to human beings through the Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Through His Word, the Son. Of His own will and for the benefit of those who saw Him, the Word showed the Father's brightness and explained His purposes. This fulfils the saying that the only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared Him.
sources.quote: But His Word, as He Himself willed it, and for the benefit of those who beheld, did show the Father’s brightness, and explained His purposes
sources.raw_question: If the Father is invisible, how is He made known to human beings?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VI.—Explanation of the words of Christ, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” etc.; which words the heretics misinterpret. Proof that, by the Father revealing the Son, and by the Son being revealed, the Father was never unknown.
sources.answer: The Father is seen in the Son. Irenaeus says the Father is the invisible of the Son, and the Son is the visible of the Father. Through the Word made visible and palpable, the Father was shown forth to all, though not all believed.
sources.quote: but all saw the Father in the Son: for the Father is the invisible of the Son, but the Son the visible of the Father.
sources.raw_question: How is the Father made known through the Son, and how are the Father's invisibility and the Son's visibility related?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: He is made known through the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father and declares Him. No one has seen God, but the Son reveals the invisible Father to all, and those to whom the Son reveals Him know Him. In turn, the Father gives knowledge of His Son through the Son, as Nathanael and Peter were taught to recognize Christ as the Son of God.
sources.quote: For He, the Son who is in His bosom, declares to all the Father who is invisible. Wherefore they know Him to whom the Son reveals Him; and again, the Father, by means of the Son, gives knowledge of His Son to those who love Him.
sources.raw_question: How is the invisible Father made known to human beings?

question: Does the Son's suffering in the Incarnation, while the Father is impassible, show that the Son's nature is passible and therefore different from and inferior to the Father's?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius treats the incarnation as if the Son slid into flesh by a compulsion of his nature, as a stone falls by nature. In fact the incarnation was a deliberate work of mercy and loving-kindness. It was not a sign of a passible nature, so it cannot be used to argue the Son's essence differs from the Father's.
sources.quote: by His enemies His work of mercy is reckoned a means of disparaging and maligning the Nature of the Son of God, as though not of deliberate purpose, but by a compulsion of His Nature he had slipped down to life in the flesh
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's becoming incarnate and suffering show that his nature is passible and therefore different from and inferior to the Father's?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: No. The aim of the Incarnation was not that the Son should be subject to suffering but that He should be manifested as a lover of men. Since the Father is also a lover of men, the Son is in the same case as the Father when one regards the aim. A healer is called a benefactor, not feeble, for touching the sick, so the dispensation is no sign of an inferior nature.
sources.quote: if the aim of the dispensation of the Incarnation was not that the Son should be subject to suffering, but that He should be manifested as a lover of men, while the Father also is undoubtedly a lover of men, it follows that if one will but regard the aim, the Son is in the same case with the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's undergoing suffering in the Incarnation, while the Father is impassible, prove that the Son's essence is different from and inferior to the Father's?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: No. Strictly, only what tends to sin is truly 'passion.' The composition and dissolution of our bodily nature is the natural course and work of nature, not passion. Christ, though tempted in all points as we are, was without sin and never shared in true passion, which is a diseased condition of the will. So His sufferings imply no defect in His divine nature.
sources.quote: That nothing is truly “passion” which does not tend to sin, nor would one strictly call by the name of “passion” the necessary routine of nature
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's suffering in the flesh, while the Father is impassible, show that the Son's essence differs from the Father's?

question: Does "the Lord is the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:17) prove, as Eunomius argued, that "Spirit" means "essence" and so "Lord" names the essence of the Only-begotten?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
