sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: No. If "Spirit" meant "essence," then Paul's next words, "where the Spirit of the Lord is," would have to mean "the essence of the essence," which is absurd. The verse in context contrasts the life-giving Spirit with the killing letter, so Eunomius's reading cannot be squared with the text.
sources.quote: If then “the Lord is the Spirit,” and “Spirit” means “essence,” what are we to understand by “the essence of the essence”?
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement "the Lord is the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:17) prove that the word "Lord" signifies the essence of the Only-begotten, with "Spirit" standing for "essence"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: No. In none of Paul's uses does "spirit" signify essence. If it did, "the spirit of man which is in him" would make man two essences, "the letter killeth, but the Spirit giveth life" would oppose essence to letter, and "live in the Spirit" would become the empty advice to live by means of oneself. So Eunomius's syllogism (spirit is essence, the Lord is Spirit, therefore Lord is essence) rests on a false premise.
sources.quote: if “man” is used of the essence, and “spirit” likewise, it will follow from the phrase that the man is maintained to be of two essences.
sources.raw_question: Does the word "Spirit" in Paul's letters ever mean "essence," so that "the Lord is the Spirit" proves that "Lord" names the essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: It could not. If "the Lord is the Spirit" and Spirit means essence, then "the Spirit of the Lord" would mean "the essence of the essence," another essence belonging to an essence. That absurdity shows that Eunomius's reading of the verse is untenable.
sources.quote: If then “the Lord is the Spirit,” and “Spirit” means “essence,” what are we to understand by “the essence of the essence”?
sources.raw_question: If "Spirit" meant "essence" in 2 Corinthians 3:17, how could Paul's following phrase "the Spirit of the Lord" make sense?

question: Is the worship given to the Son an inferior or lesser worship than the supreme worship given to the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. Religious worship, whether greater or smaller, longer or shorter, has the same import and acknowledges the person addressed to be divine, just as any sacrifice, whether a lamb or two pigeons, acknowledged the divinity and supremacy of the one to whom it was offered. So 'equality or inequality of worship' has no real meaning that would make the Son an inferior object of worship.
sources.quote: worship, religious worship, greater or smaller, longer or shorter, has the same import and significancy; and speaks the Person addressed to, to be divine
sources.raw_question: Can there be degrees of religious worship, such that the Son receives a lesser worship than the Father without being equally God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. The Father is God and object of worship primarily and eminently as Father and Fountain, so worship of the Son as Son redounds to the Father. Yet it is proper divine worship, acknowledging the same divine perfections communicated from Father to Son. Hence there is still one worship and one object of worship, just as there is one God, because of the intimate union of the Persons.
sources.quote: the distinct worship of the Son, considered as a Son, redounds to the Father, as the Head and Fountain of all.
sources.raw_question: If the Father is primarily the object of worship, is worship of the Son an inferior or separate worship?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. The worship of the Son is proper divine worship, an acknowledgment of the same divine excellencies and essential perfections communicated from Father to Son. Because of the intimate and ineffable union of the two Persons there is still but one worship and one object of worship, as there is one God and one Creator.
sources.quote: That the worship of the Son, considered as a Son, is not an inferior worship, nor any other than proper divine worship ; being an acknowledgment of the same divine excellencies, and essential perfections ‘communicated from Father to Son
sources.raw_question: Is the worship given to the Son, considered as Son, an inferior worship distinct from the supreme worship given to the Father?

question: Is the God who sent the Old Testament prophets the same God and Father who sent Jesus Christ, or a different god?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: By the same Father. Christ's parable of the marriage feast shows one King who prepared the marriage for His Son from the beginning, first called the men of the former dispensation by His servants (the prophets), and then called the nations. Jeremiah confirms that this same God sent His servants the prophets. So the Lord who calls us by the apostles is the one who called those of old by the prophets.
sources.quote: The Lord, therefore, who has called us everywhere by the apostles, is He who called those of old by the prophets, as appears by the words of the Lord
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics/Marcionites who distinguish the God of the prophets from the Father of Christ
sources.raw_question: Were the Old Testament prophets sent by the same God and Father who sent Jesus Christ, or by a different god?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. The apostles did not change God. The same God who sent the prophets raised Jesus up and gave salvation to men in Him, and so fulfilled what He had spoken through the prophets.
sources.quote: Thus the apostles did not change God, but preached to the people that Christ was Jesus the crucified One, whom the same God that had sent the prophets
sources.raw_question: Is the God who raised Jesus and gives salvation through him the same God who sent the Old Testament prophets?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXVI.—John and Daniel have predicted the dissolution and desolation of the Roman Empire, which shall precede the end of the world and the eternal kingdom of Christ. The Gnostics are refuted, those tools of Satan, who invent another Father different from the Creator.
sources.answer: The same God sent both the prophets and the Son. Christ fulfilled what the Creator had predicted through all the prophets. He did so serving His Father's will and completing the Father's dispensations for the human race. So those who reject the Creator, Marcionites and Valentinians alike, are refuted.
sources.quote: For those things which have been predicted by the Creator alike through all the prophets has Christ fulfilled in the end, ministering to His Father’s will, and completing His dispensations with regard to the human race.
sources.raw_question: Is the God who sent the Old Testament prophets the same Father from whom Christ came, or did the prophecies originate from diverse lesser powers?

question: Is the Holy Spirit due an equal share with the Father and the Son in the work and glory of redemption, given that the Spirit is often said merely to apply the redemption Christ purchased?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: No, not on the older view; but on Edwards's view it is equal. If the Spirit only hands to us what was purchased, that is a little thing compared with the Father giving his Son and the Son paying an infinite price. But if the Spirit is himself the love of God and the very good purchased, there is equality. The thing bought is equal in worth to the price paid, and the glory of the one who gives it arises from its worth.
sources.quote: To be the love of God to the world is as much as for the Father and the Son to do so much from love to the world, and to be the thing purchased was as much as to be the price. The price and the thing bought with that price are equal.
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit merely applies the blessings of redemption purchased by Christ, is the Spirit's share in the work and glory of redemption equal to that of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. The Father is glorified for loving the world so as to give his Son, and the Son for loving it so as to give himself, but the Holy Ghost is that very love of the Father and Son to the world. So however much the first two Persons are glorified by showing the greatness of their love, just so much is that love itself, the Holy Ghost, glorified.
sources.quote: But there is equal glory due to the Holy Ghost for He is that love of the Father and the Son to the world.
sources.raw_question: Is equal glory for the work of redemption due to the Holy Spirit as to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Merely handing on an already purchased blessing, as subordinate to the other two Persons, is a small thing compared with paying an infinite price. But if the Spirit is God's love itself and the thing purchased, there is equality. The price and the thing bought with it are of equal worth.
sources.quote: To be the love of God to the world is as much as for the Father and the Son to do so much from love to the world, and to be the thing purchased was as much as to be the price.
sources.raw_question: Does the traditional view, that the Spirit merely applies redemption, give the Holy Spirit an equal share in the glory of redemption?

question: If the term 'Godhead' signifies an operation shared by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, should they be called three Gods, as several people sharing one occupation are called many orators or farmers?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. Godhead is one of the good names, and the unity of the action prevents counting it as plural. Scripture calls God the one Saviour of all, even though salvation comes from the Trinity, with the Son working salvation through the grace of the Spirit. Scripture never speaks of three Saviours, and in the same way the Persons are not three Gods.
sources.quote: it would not be proper to divide the name into a plurality, since the unity existing in the action prevents plural enumeration
sources.raw_question: If 'Godhead' names an operation shared by the Father, Son, and Spirit, should they be called three Gods?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. Gregory grants that men who share one pursuit are counted in the plural, but only because each works separately, by himself, at his own task, without sharing in the others' individual actions. In the Divine nature the Father does nothing by Himself in which the Son does not work conjointly, and the same holds for the Spirit. So the operation is one and undivided, and the Deity is rightly spoken of in the singular as one God and one Godhead.
sources.quote: But in the case of the Divine nature we do not similarly learn that the Father does anything by Himself in which the Son does not work conjointly
sources.raw_question: If the term "Godhead" signifies an operation rather than the divine nature, does it follow that Father, Son and Holy Spirit, sharing the same operation, should be called "three Gods," just as several people sharing one occupation are called many orators or farmers?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. Men in the same pursuit are counted as many because each works separately on his own task. But the Father does nothing apart from the Son, nor the Son apart from the Spirit. Every divine operation is one action of the Three, so the name taken from that operation is not multiplied by the number of the Persons.
sources.quote: so neither can we call those who exercise this Divine and superintending power and operation towards ourselves and all creation, conjointly and inseparably, by their mutual action, three Gods.
sources.raw_question: If the term "Godhead" signifies an operation rather than a nature, should Father, Son, and Holy Spirit be called "three Gods" in the way several people sharing a profession are called three orators or philosophers?

question: Does asserting that the Father and the Son share the same substance (homoousion) imply that both are uncaused First Causes, or that one being generates itself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: No. The one who holds a real generation of the Son makes the Son's distinguishing mark consist in subsisting by generation from the Father, so he cannot possibly regard the Son as ungenerate or as a second First Cause. It is rather the one who denies a real generation and says the Son merely exists who is more open to the suspicion of making him a First Cause.
sources.quote: the second, making the representative sign of the Person of the Only-begotten to consist in subsisting generatively from the Father, cannot by any possibility be drawn into the error of supposing the Son to be Ungenerate
sources.raw_question: Does believing that the Son shares the Father's substance (homoousion) and is truly generated from him commit one to two First Causes?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: No. No one in the Church ever held that one is begotten by oneself, being one's own father and son; the idea is absurd. Just as in human nature a community of substance does not mean that the things compared are causeless or self-produced, so with the divine nature. Adam and Abel share one definition of being despite their different origins, and neither is the other's father or son in a self-generating sense. Likewise, the names Father and Son teach a oneness of nature, not self-generation.
sources.quote: who, when he hears of a community of substance, dreams either that all things that are compared together on the ground of substance are without a cause or beginning, or that something comes into existence out of itself, at once producing and being produced by itself?
sources.raw_question: Does the homoousion imply a single causeless being that divides itself into Father and Son and so generates itself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: No. Community of substance between two beings does not make both uncaused or make one its own father and son. Adam and Abel came into being in different ways, one moulded by God and the other by generation, yet they have the same definition of being because each is a man. Difference of origin, order or manner of coming into existence does not alter nature, so there is no reason to admit such an absurdity about the divine nature.
sources.quote: If, then, the idea of humanity in Adam and Abel does not vary with the difference of their origin, neither the order nor the manner of their coming into existence making any difference in their nature, which is the same in both
sources.raw_question: Does asserting that the Father and the Son share the same substance (homoousion) imply that both are without cause or beginning, or that one being generates itself?

question: Is the Wisdom of God that coexists unoriginately with the Father and frames the world identical with the Son, rather than simply God himself?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. What coexists does not coexist with itself but with another, just as the Lord was together with his disciples and not with himself. To make wisdom a constituent or complement of God's essence would make God compound. Since this coexisting, world-framing Wisdom is distinct from the Father, it is the Son.
sources.quote: for what coexists does not coexist with itself, but with some one else, as the Evangelists say of the Lord, that He was together with His disciples; for He was not together with Himself, but with His disciples
sources.raw_question: Can the unoriginate Wisdom that coexists with God simply be God himself rather than the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Yes. Neither Scripture nor the fathers know any wisdom besides the Son. Whatever Wisdom is confessed as coexisting with the Father, proper to him, and Framer of the world must therefore be the Son. Scripture says that in Wisdom God made all things. Even Asterius later confesses that the Word and Wisdom is one.
sources.quote: this must be the Son who even according to them is eternally coexistent with the Father. For He is Framer of all, as it is written, ‘In Wisdom hast Thou made them all.’
sources.raw_question: Since the Fathers confess a Wisdom coexisting unoriginately with God and framing the world, must that Wisdom be the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture knows no other Wisdom besides the Son, and the fathers speak of none other; since even the Arians confess a Wisdom coexisting with the Father unoriginately, proper to Him and Framer of the world, this must be the Son, through whom all things were made.
sources.quote: this must be the Son who even according to them is eternally coexistent with the Father. For He is Framer of all, as it is written, ‘In Wisdom hast Thou made them all.’
sources.raw_question: Is the Wisdom of God that coexists unoriginately with the Father and frames the world identical with the Son?

question: Can it be said of the Only-begotten Son of God that there was a time when He was not, or that He was not before He was born?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. No time precedes the Only-begotten. Saying that He once was not would place a 'some time' before Him. Time would then not begin after Him; instead He would begin after time. Because no time is antecedent to Him, the claim that He was not before He was born is excluded.
sources.quote: But for God Only-begotten, Who is preceded by no antecedent time, the possibility is excluded that at some time He was not, since that “some time” thus becomes prior to Him
sources.raw_question: Can it be said of the Only-begotten Son of God that there was a time when He was not?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Unlike Israel, which was a nation before it became a son, the Only-begotten was never at any time not a Son, was nothing before being Son, and is nothing but Son. Because He is always Son, it is impossible to think there was a time when He was not.
sources.quote: But God Only-begotten was neither at any time not a Son, nor was He anything before He was a Son, nor is He Himself anything except a Son.
sources.raw_question: Was there a time when the Only-begotten Son was not the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. The Apostle teaches that the Only-begotten was born before times eternal, and whatever transcends all time is eternal. The phrase 'before He was born' presupposes antecedent time, which is the measure of created things, so applying it to the Son is an impious imposition of carnal human reasoning on a birth that is prior to all time and thought.
sources.quote: we are certainly exalting by impious self-will a notion of human reason, if we maintain in a carnal sense that before He was born He was not, since He is born eternal, beyond human perception or carnal intelligence.
sources.raw_question: Can it be truly said of the Only-begotten Son that 'He was not before He was born'?

question: In the Old Testament appearances of God (such as to Abraham at Mamre or to Moses), did God, specifically the Son, become visible in His own divine substance, or did He appear through a created form?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > God Uses All Creatures as He Will, and Makes Visible Things for the Manifestation of Himself.
sources.answer: No. God works sensible and visible things in heaven, earth, sea and air in order to signify and manifest Himself, as He judges fitting, without His very substance appearing. That substance is altogether unchangeable and more inwardly exalted than all created spirits. Just as Paul could signify Christ by tongue, letter and sacrament without these being Christ, so God uses creatures as signs of Himself.
sources.quote: God works the sensible and visible things which He wills, in order to signify and manifest Himself in them, as He Himself knows it to be fitting, without any appearing of His very substance itself
sources.raw_question: When God appeared to the Old Testament saints in visible forms, did His own divine substance become visible?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > In What Manner Moses Saw God.
sources.answer: No. Moses asked to see God plainly, that is, to see His substance, and this was not granted to him even though he desired it. Therefore the forms that appeared to him were a creature serving God, not the very being that is God made visible to mortal eyes.
sources.quote: who will dare to say, that by the like forms which had appeared visibly to him also, not the creature serving God, but that itself which is God, appeared to the eyes of a mortal man?
sources.raised_by_detail: those who believe the Son is visible by Himself
sources.raw_question: Was the Son of God visible by His own substance in the Old Testament appearances, rather than through a creature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Of the Same Appearance.
sources.answer: No, Augustine argues against this view. Those who claim it reason that only the Father is invisible, but if the Son had appeared as a man whose feet were washed and who ate earthly food, he would have been 'found in fashion as a man' before he emptied himself and took the form of a servant, which Scripture places at his birth from the Virgin. While still in the form of God and equal with God, he cannot have appeared in his own substance as a man.
sources.quote: For, pray, had He already “emptied Himself, taking upon Him the form of a servant, and made in the likeness of men, and found in fashion as a man?” when we know when it was that He did this through His birth of the Virgin.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who say the Son was visible in His own substance before the incarnation
sources.raw_question: Was the Son of God visible in his own divine substance before his incarnation, so that Old Testament appearances such as the one to Abraham at Mamre were the Son appearing in his own nature?

question: If each divine Person is an individual intelligent agent or being, does the doctrine of three Persons in one God amount to three Beings or three Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. Each divine Person is an individual intelligent agent. But because the Persons subsist in one undivided substance, together they are in that respect one undivided intelligent agent. So the orthodox stand clear of Tritheism.
sources.quote: each divine Person is an individual intelligent agent: but as subsisting in one undivided substance, they are all together, in that respect, but one undivided intelligent agentk; and thus my friends stand clear of Tritheism.
sources.raw_question: If each divine Person is an intelligent agent, does the doctrine of three Persons in one God amount to Tritheism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. All that can be proved is that separate persons are so many intelligent beings. Persons who are united and have no separate existence may still be one Being, one Substance, one God. The word 'being' has two senses, and even the opponents only call something a being when it is a separate being.
sources.quote: All that the Doctor hath proved, or can prove, is only this; that separate persons are so many %ntelligent beings; which we readily admit: but united persons, or persons having no separate existence, may be one Being, one Substance, one God, notwithstanding.
sources.raw_question: Are 'intelligent being' and 'person' the same, so that three divine Persons must be three Beings or Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. Each divine Person is an individual intelligent agent. But because the three subsist in one undivided substance, they are together, in that respect, one undivided intelligent agent, and so stand clear of tritheism.
sources.quote: each divine Person is an individual intelligent agent: but as subsisting in one undivided substance, they are all together, in that respect, but one undivided intelligent agentk; and thus my friends stand clear of Tritheism.
sources.raw_question: If each divine Person is an individual intelligent agent, does the Trinitarian doctrine amount to tritheism?

question: Does the statement that God is worshipped "in Spirit and in truth" exclude the Holy Spirit from being worshipped?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: No. The phrase may refer to the grace of the Spirit or the true faith of conscience; but if taken personally, it must be taken of Christ (the Truth) and of the Spirit. Just as worshipping God in Christ does not detract from Christ but implies He is co-worshipped, so worshipping God in the Spirit implies the Spirit is co-worshipped through unity of power.
sources.quote: It makes, then, nothing against our argument that God is worshipped in Spirit, for the Spirit also is worshipped.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that God must be worshipped "in Spirit and in truth" exclude the Holy Spirit from being worshipped?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: Yes, the argument would tell equally against the Son, which shows it is invalid. Christ is the Truth, and God is worshipped in truth just as in Spirit. So either both are subject and the Son is not worshipped, which is impious, or, as is true, there is a like grace of unity and the Spirit is worshipped.
sources.quote: There is therefore either a like subjection, which God forbid that you should believe, and the Son is not worshipped; or, which is true, there is a like grace of Unity, and the Spirit is worshipped.
sources.raw_question: If worshipping the Father 'in Spirit' proved that the Holy Spirit is not to be worshipped, would worshipping the Father 'in truth' prove that the Son, who is the Truth, is not to be worshipped?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as it detracts nothing from Christ that God is worshipped in Christ, since Christ too is worshipped, so it detracts nothing from the Spirit. Paul says 'We serve the Spirit of God,' and serving implies worship, since God alone is to be worshipped and served.
sources.quote: it certainly also detracts nothing from the Spirit that God is worshipped in the Spirit, for the Spirit also is worshipped, as the Apostle has said: “We serve the Spirit of God,” for he who serves worships also
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit to be worshipped, given that God is worshipped in the Spirit?

question: If believers are accepted before God through Christ's imputed righteousness, is their own holiness and obedience still necessary?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Holiness is indispensably necessary. It is the way God has appointed to eternal life, a testimony of adoption, and the expression of our thankfulness. Yet it must not be exalted into the place of Christ's obedience and righteousness. Its necessity stands on its own grounds without its being made the cause, matter, or condition of justification.
sources.quote: He that upon these accounts doth not think universal holiness and obedience to be of indispensable necessity, unless also it be exalted into the room of the obedience and righteousness of Christ, let him be filthy still.
sources.raw_question: Is personal holiness and obedience necessary for the Christian even though it is not the ground of justification before God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes, it is indispensably necessary, though it is not raised into the place of Christ's righteousness. Believers are received into friendship with a holy God who hates uncleanness, so those admitted into his presence must be holy. The new creature within them must be nourished by the fruits of holiness. Holiness is also the appointed way to eternal life, a pledge of adoption, and the expression of thankfulness.
sources.quote: They are accepted and received into friendship with a holy God, — a God of purer eyes than to behold iniquity, — who hates every unclean thing. And is it not necessary that they should be holy who are admitted into his presence
sources.raw_question: If believers are accepted before God through Christ's righteousness, is their personal holiness and obedience still necessary?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Christ's imputed obedience and the believer's own obedience do not occupy the same place or serve the same use. Christ's righteousness is that on account of which believers are accepted and counted righteous before God. Their own obedience is not the righteousness by which they are justified. It is still pleasing to God that they abound in it.
sources.quote: But our own obedience is not the righteousness whereupon we are accepted and justified before God; although it be acceptable to God that we should abound therein.
sources.raw_question: If Christ's righteousness and obedience to the law are imputed to believers, why do believers need to obey God themselves?

question: If 'made Lord and Christ' in Acts 2:36 refers to the visible man Jesus, does it follow, as Eunomius argues, that this man 'emptied himself' anew and underwent a second becoming man?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No. The syllogism is a sophism that confuses the subjects: the emptying belongs to the Word who took the form of a servant, while the exaltation belongs to the flesh He assumed. Even if granted, it would not show that the King of creation is created; rather, the descent from lofty to lowly supports that the Uncreated came to be in the created.
sources.quote: The fact that the Apostle’s discourse refers to Him Who was “crucified through weakness” is forsooth powerfully disproved when we learn that if we believe this to be so, the man who was “seen” again becomes another
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that the man who was seen was made Christ and Lord entail, as Eunomius argues, that the man 'emptied himself' anew to undergo a second becoming of man?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No. The objection actually helps the orthodox. The change spoken of is from a lofty state to a lowly one, and only the uncreated Divine Nature transcends creation. So the argument leads to the conclusion that the Uncreated came to be in the created out of love for man. It does not show that the Son is created.
sources.quote: he will, perhaps, when he thoroughly surveys his own argument, come over to the ranks of truth, and agree that the Uncreated came to be in the created, in His love for man.
sources.raw_question: If 'made Lord and Christ' in Acts 2:36 refers to the visible man Jesus, does it follow absurdly that the Lord emptied himself anew and underwent a second birth?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius's syllogism falsely supposes that the visible man emptied himself again, as though the Cross came before the incarnation. In fact the order is: God is manifested in the flesh first, and the Cross comes afterward. The self-emptying belongs to the Word becoming flesh, not to the already-assumed humanity.
sources.quote: who says this, that the man who was seen emptied himself again to take the form of a servant? or who maintains that the suffering of the Cross took place before the manifestation in the flesh?
sources.raw_question: Does saying that the man who was 'seen' was made Lord and Christ imply that this man 'emptied himself' to take the form of a servant and become another man?

question: Did the pre-Nicene Fathers hold the Son's consubstantiality with the Father only in a figurative or oratorical sense, rather than a proper one?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: No. The ancients took the word God to signify substance and applied it to the Son in the same sense. They admitted only one strictly divine substance, abhorred inferior deities, and reserved worship for the one true God while still worshipping the Son. They also held the Son to be eternal, uncreated, omnipotent and Creator; any one of these almost alone proves a proper consubstantiality.
sources.quote: their appropriating worship to the one true God, and worshipping the Son notwithstanding; their unanimous belief of the Son’s being eternal, uncreated, omnipotent, and of his being Creator, Preserver, and Sustainer of the universe
sources.raw_question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers hold only a figurative or oratorical consubstantiality of the Son with the Father, rather than a proper one?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: No. Consubstantiality was a constant, settled doctrine across the Fathers in general, and it is implausible that all would speak rhetorically on so weighty a matter of faith without one sober writer stating the plain truth. It also appears in dry controversial debates with heretics, where precise and proper speech was required.
sources.quote: Strange, that they should all rhetoricate in a matter of faith, of so great weight and importance; and that we should not meet with so much as one grave sober writer, to strip the matter of all flourish and varnish, and to tell us the naked truth.
sources.raw_question: Did the Fathers speak of the Son's consubstantiality with the Father only in an oratorical or figurative sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: No. The doctrine of consubstantiality was a settled, constant teaching running through all the Fathers, and it appears not only in popular harangues but in dry controversial debates with heretics, where accuracy was required. It is incredible that all would rhetoricate on so weighty a matter of faith without one sober writer stating the naked truth otherwise.
sources.quote: the notion does not occur only _in popular harangues, but in dry debates ; chiefly in controversy with heretics, where it concerned the Catholics to speak accurately and properly, and to deliver their sentiments very distinctly.
sources.raw_question: Did the pre-Nicene Fathers mean the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father only in an oratorical or figurative sense?

question: Does Christ's saying 'My soul is sorrowful even unto death' (and similar expressions of anguish in His Passion) prove that He was weak, feared suffering and death, and so lacked true divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. When Judas went out Christ said 'Now is the Son of Man glorified,' so suffering was to be His glorification. It would be irrational for Him to be made sorrowful by fear of what was to glorify Him.
sources.quote: If suffering was to glorify Him, how could the fear of it have made Him sorrowful?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that His soul was sorrowful unto death prove that He was weak and feared suffering?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary argues the heretics cling to the letter and ignore the purpose of Christ's words, which must be set beside His contrasting sayings of confidence spoken in the same circumstances. When each saying is referred to its proper class, some to His Deity and some to His earthly ministry, it is clear that He had a confidence which never wavered and a will which never faltered.
sources.quote: the heretics display their impiety by ignoring the assertions of Deity and the Divine nature of Christ, which account for the one class of His words, while they concentrate their attention upon the deeds and words which refer only to His ministry on earth
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's expressions of anguish in His Passion (e.g. 'My soul is sorrowful even unto death', 'Why hast Thou forsaken Me?') prove that He lacked true divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. To be sorrowful 'unto death' means that death is the end of the sorrow, not its cause. His sadness was therefore removed by his death rather than caused by it, and its real cause must be sought elsewhere.
sources.quote: But a sadness even to death implies that death is the finish, not the cause, of the sadness.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'My soul is sorrowful even unto death' prove that he was conscious of natural infirmity and feared death?

question: Does the unity of God require, or mean, that the Godhead is a single Person (one hypostasis)?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. The divine nature is best known from Revelation, which shows that God is not a single Hypostasis but that the Father always has his coessential and coeternal Son and Spirit in him and with him. As Hippolytus said, we can have no right conception of the one God except by believing in a real Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: it is from thence we discover that God is not μονοπρόσωπος, a single Hypostasis, but that the Father has his coessential and coeternal Son and Holy Spirit always in him and with him.
sources.raw_question: Does the unity of God require that God be a single Person (one Hypostasis)?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. The Church does not make the Godhead monoprosopos, one single hypostasis, which would be all one with Sabellian singularity. The unity is a unity of substance shared by distinct Persons.
sources.quote: They do not make the Godhead μονοπρόσωπος, one single hypostasis ; which, in the main, is all one with the Sabellian singularity.
sources.raw_question: Is the catholic unity of the Godhead a single hypostasis or one-person Godhead?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. The orthodox writers did not ground the unity of God on a numerical individuality of one single hypostasis. Waterland notes that making the Godhead μονοπρόσωπος, one single hypostasis, is in effect the same as the Sabellian singularity, which the orthodox reject.
sources.quote: They do not make the Godhead μονοπρόσωπος, one single hypostasis ; which, in the main, is all one with the Sabellian singularity.
sources.raw_question: Does the Catholic doctrine that the Father and the Son are one God make the Godhead a single hypostasis or person?

question: In what does the renewal of the image of God in the human mind consist, and by whose power is it renewed and brought to happiness?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Mind Loves God in Rightly Loving Itself; And If It Love Not God, It Must Be Said to Hate Itself. Even a Weak and Erring Mind is Always Strong in Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself. Let It Be Turned to God, that It May Be Blessed by Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Him.
sources.answer: By the mind's loving God and so remembering and understanding Him. By partaking of God the image not only exists but is renewed, restored from its defacement, and made blessed. Having abandoned God, on whom alone it depended for strength and light, it became weak and dark. It fell to things beneath itself and needs God's mercy to return.
sources.quote: by partaking of whom that image not only exists, but is also renewed so as to be no longer old, and restored so as to be no longer defaced, and beatified so as to be no longer unhappy.
sources.raw_question: How is the image of God in the human mind renewed and brought to happiness?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How the Image of God in the Mind is Renewed Until the Likeness of God is Perfected in It in Blessedness.
sources.answer: It consists in progress in the knowledge of God, righteousness and true holiness, by which a person transfers his love from temporal, visible and carnal things to eternal, intelligible and spiritual things. This progress happens only in proportion as God helps, for Christ said, 'Without me ye can do nothing.'
sources.quote: transfers his love from things temporal to things eternal, from things visible to things intelligible, from things carnal to things spiritual
sources.raw_question: In what does the renewal of the image of God in the mind consist, and by whose power does it progress?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How the Image of God is Formed Anew in Man.
sources.answer: It consists in recovering righteousness and true holiness, which Paul elsewhere calls being renewed in the knowledge of God. The image lost righteousness and holiness by sin, which defaced and tarnished it, and it regains them when it is formed again.
sources.quote: But it lost righteousness and true holiness by sinning, through which that image became defaced and tarnished; and this it recovers when it is formed again and renewed.
sources.raw_question: In what does the renewal of God's image in the mind consist, according to Paul?

question: Can anything be said of God, or exist in God, according to accident?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Argument of the Arians is Refuted, Which is Drawn from the Words Begotten and Unbegotten.
sources.answer: No. An accident implies something that can be lost or changed in the thing it belongs to. Nothing in God is changeable or can be lost, so nothing in God is accidental.
sources.quote: Therefore there is nothing accidental in God, because there is nothing changeable or that may be lost.
sources.raw_question: Can anything be said of God according to accident?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Nothing is Spoken of God According to Accident, But According to Substance or According to Relation.
sources.answer: No. Nothing is accidental to God because nothing in Him is changeable or can be lost or diminished. In creatures, whatever is not said according to substance is said according to accident, but this alternative does not hold for God.
sources.quote: But in God nothing is said to be according to accident, because in Him nothing is changeable; and yet everything that is said, is not said, according to substance.
sources.raw_question: Can anything be said of God according to accident?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Accidental Always Implies Some Change in the Thing.
sources.answer: No. An accident is something that can be lost or altered through some change in the thing it belongs to, whether it is a separable or an inseparable accident. God has nothing changeable and nothing that can be lost, so nothing in God is accidental.
sources.quote: Therefore there is nothing accidental in God, because there is nothing changeable or that may be lost.
sources.raw_question: Can anything be accidental in God?

question: Does the Son's suffering on the Cross show that his divine nature is passible or created, and therefore unlike the impassible nature of the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: No. Gregory replies that the Eunomian argument, which says the Son could suffer because his created nature was akin to created human nature, abases the God made known on the Cross. Far from being a sign of inferiority, the Cross is for Paul the object of glory and the power of God. So whoever speaks basely of the Cross is the one truly ashamed of it, not the one who upholds its exalted meaning.
sources.quote: Who then is fairly charged with being ashamed of the Cross? he who speaks basely of it, or he who contends for its more exalted aspect?
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Son suffered on the Cross in the flesh prove that his nature is created and alien to the Father's impassible nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He then again charges Eunomius with having learnt his term ἀγεννησία from the hieroglyphic writings, and from the Egyptian mythology and idolatry, and with bringing in Anubis, Osiris, and Isis to the creed of Christians, and shows that, considered as admitting His sufferings of necessity and not voluntarily, the Only-begotten is entitled to no gratitude from men: and that fire has none for its warmth, nor water for its fluidity, as they do not refer their results to self-determining power, but to necessity of nature.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius's view that the begotten Son has an essence mixed of contraries, partly divine and partly subject to passion, has no support in Scripture. Gregory says it resembles the Egyptian notion of a mixed 'daemon' nature, set against an impassible 'ungenerate God'. The Son undertook the Passion by the strength of his almighty Godhead, as an act of loving-kindness, not because his nature dragged him down to it.
sources.quote: he does not think that it was by His almighty Godhead that the Son proved strong for such a form of loving-kindness, but that it was by being of a nature subject to passion that He stooped to the suffering of the Cross
sources.raw_question: Did the Son suffer the Cross because his nature is passible, unlike the impassible unbegotten Father, so that the Son is not equal to the Father as Light to Light?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: No. Gregory charges Eunomius with insulting the Son by holding that he could not have suffered unless his nature were capable of suffering. The Passion was an act of the impassible God condescending to our weakness by power, not the outworking of a passible divine nature.
sources.quote: by maintaining that He is of passible nature, on the ground that He could not have come to experience His sufferings had He not had a nature capable of such sufferings?
sources.raw_question: Must the Son have a passible nature in order to have suffered on the Cross?

question: Is Christ only a man (or only an angel), or is he both God and man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And Indeed that Christ Was Not Only Man, But God Also; That Even as He Was the Son of Man, So Also He Was the Son of God.
sources.answer: No. Whoever excludes one portion of the truth will never hold the perfect truth. Scripture announces Christ as God just as much as it announces him as man. Since both are read of in Christ, both must be believed, so that the faith may be true by being complete.
sources.quote: We must not then lean to one side and evade the other side, because any one who should exclude one portion of the truth will never hold the perfect truth.
sources.raw_question: Is it enough for the faith to hold only that Christ is man, or only that he is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God Also Appeared to Jacob as an Angel; Namely, the Son of God.
sources.answer: No. Whoever says Christ is only man or only angel is in terrible danger. Such a person withholds from Christ the power of the divine name, which Scripture continually gives Him by calling Him both Angel and God.
sources.quote: he is in terrible risk who says that Christ is either man or angel alone, withholding from Him the power of the divine name
sources.raw_question: Is it safe to hold that Christ is only a man or only an angel?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > It Is, Moreover, Proved by Moses in the Beginning of the Holy Scriptures.
sources.answer: He is both God and man. He was received later as man according to the flesh, but he was the Word of God, and God, before the foundation of the world. Those who hold him to be only a man contradict and corrupt the authority of both the Old and New Testaments, which support each other on this point.
sources.quote: Whence they who presume Christ the Son of God and man to be only man, and not God also, do so in opposition to both Old and New Testaments
sources.raised_by_detail: those who presume Christ to be only man
sources.raw_question: Is Christ only a man, or is he both God and man?

question: How and when is the image of God in the human mind brought to perfection?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How the Image of God in the Mind is Renewed Until the Likeness of God is Perfected in It in Blessedness.
sources.answer: When the sight of God is perfected, that is, when we see God face to face rather than through a glass in an enigma. Those who persevere in faith in the Mediator are led to God and perfected by Him, and in the end receive an incorruptible body for glory. Meanwhile, beholding the Lord's glory as in a glass, we are changed into the same image from glory to glory.
sources.quote: For the likeness of God will then be perfected in this image, when the sight of God shall be perfected.
sources.raw_question: When will the likeness of God in the human image of God be made perfect?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > John is Rather to Be Understood of Our Perfect Likeness with the Trinity in Life Eternal. Wisdom is Perfected in Happiness.
sources.answer: It is perfected by the sight of God itself. That sight will be face to face after the judgment, when the righteous enter eternal life, which consists in knowing the one true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent. Meanwhile the image is renewed inwardly from day to day in the knowledge of God, seeing as through a glass in an enigma.
sources.quote: But the image which is renewed in the spirit of the mind in the knowledge of God, not outwardly, but inwardly, from day to day, shall be perfected by that sight itself; which then after the judgment shall be face to face
sources.raw_question: How is the image of God in the human mind brought to perfection, and when?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God.
sources.answer: It is perfected when the mind is renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of Him who created man. The mind then attains a wisdom in which what is contemplated is eternal. True wisdom thus consists in the mind's relation to God, the eternal object, rather than to temporal things.
sources.quote: this wisdom is then perfected, when the mind is renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of Him who created man after His own Image, and thus attains to wisdom, wherein that which is contemplated is eternal
sources.raw_question: When is the image of God in the human mind brought to perfection as true wisdom?

question: If God surpasses generated beings to the same degree as He surpasses destructible beings, as Eunomius claims, does it follow that the generated Son is on a level with perishable things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, on Eunomius's premises, and this exposes those premises as blasphemous. By the axiom that things equally distanced by something else are level with one another, equating the generated with the destructible would place the begotten Lord among perishable things. Eunomius in effect treats generation as the same thing as destruction and death.
sources.quote: If, then, the destructible and the generated are surpassed in the same degree by the Deity, and if our Lord is generated, it will be for Eunomius to draw the blasphemous conclusion resulting from these data.
sources.raw_question: If God surpasses generated beings in the same degree as He surpasses destructible beings, does it follow that the generated Son is on a level with perishable things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It would follow, blasphemously, that the Son stands on a level with destructible and mortal beings. Things that are surpassed by something else to the same degree are level with one another. Eunomius treats generation as equivalent to destruction and death, just as he treats 'ungenerate' as equivalent to 'indestructible.' His premises therefore force him to rank the generated Lord with perishable things, which shows that the premises themselves are false.
sources.quote: If, then, the destructible and the generated are surpassed in the same degree by the Deity, and if our Lord is generated, it will be for Eunomius to draw the blasphemous conclusion resulting from these data.
sources.raw_question: If God surpasses both generated beings and destructible beings in exactly the same degree, as Eunomius claims, what follows for the Son, who is generated?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory charges Eunomius with wrongly equating generation with destruction and death, in the same way that he wrongly equates the ungenerate with the indestructible. If the two are treated as identical, the generated Lord would be classed with perishable things, and that conclusion is blasphemous. The equation must therefore be rejected.
sources.quote: For it is clear that he regards generation as the same thing as destruction and death, just as in his previous discussions he declares the ungenerate to be the same thing as the indestructible.
sources.raw_question: Is being generated the same as being subject to destruction and death, so that the Son's being begotten would make him perishable?

question: In a doctrine above human comprehension such as the Trinity, is private reasoning or interpretation of Scripture a safer guide than the consensus of the primitive and later Church?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: No. Waterland holds that the safest course, especially for those unable to examine the controversy thoroughly, is to follow the faith held for fourteen to sixteen centuries by the Church's most eminent teachers. Doing so is what a modest believer can best answer for to God and conscience, even if it were somehow mistaken. Those who depart from the received Catholic faith do so at their own peril.
sources.quote: As for those who choose to go out of the common road, and to run counter to all that has hitherto been called and reputed Catholic, or orthodox ; let them look to it, and be it at their own peril.
sources.raw_question: In a doctrine above human comprehension such as the Trinity, is private reasoning a safer rule than the consensus of the primitive and later Church?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: No. Waterland grants that the argument from the Church's consent is not a demonstration, but holds that it carries real weight. Religion is not to be 'coined and recoined every month'. The Nicene faith was settled deliberately and was upheld after strict examination, in full knowledge of the objections, by the wisest and most pious men in every age for fourteen to sixteen centuries. So the modest and safest course, especially for those who cannot examine the controversy thoroughly, is to distrust one's own judgment and hold to that faith rather than to private interpretations of the disputed Scriptures.
sources.quote: I do not pretend that there is demonstration in this kind of reasoning, in favour of any cause. But it will have its weight with cool and considering men
sources.raw_question: In a doctrine above human comprehension such as the Trinity, is private reasoning a safer guide than the general judgment of the primitive and later Church?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Preface
sources.answer: Yes. However forcible one's reasonings from Scripture seem, one should not be confident of them unless the general verdict of the primitive Church also supports them. It is more likely that an individual errs in interpreting Scripture than that the universal Church erred from the beginning. Bull showed this by offering to retract any proposition found repugnant to Catholic and primitive doctrine.
sources.quote: believing it easier for himself to err in interpreting Scripture, than for the universal Church to have erred from the beginning.
sources.raw_question: Should a private interpretation of Scripture on doctrine be checked against the general verdict of the primitive Church?

question: Could the Word (Logos) produced by the perfect divine Mind of the Father be imperfect and ignorant of the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: No. Since the Father is Nous and perfect in all things, He was able to produce His Logos together with the knowledge of the Father. Moreover, if the heretics grant that Christ, produced later, was perfect, much more must the Word, who is prior, have been produced perfect and not blind. Ascribing ignorance to the Word of God is absurd.
sources.quote: how could the Nous of the Father, or rather the very Father Himself, since He is Nous and perfect in all things, have produced his own Logos as an imperfect and blind Æon, when He was able also to produce along with him the knowledge of the Father?
sources.raw_question: Could a perfect divine Mind (the Father) produce His own Word (Logos) as imperfect and ignorant of the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: No. Human children may sometimes not know their parents, but this is altogether impossible for the Logos of the Father. The Logos exists in the Father, and in knowing himself he knows the One in whom he exists. Likewise, powers that are always present with him cannot be ignorant of their source, any more than rays can be of the sun.
sources.quote: For if, existing in the Father, he knows Him in whom he exists—that is, is not ignorant of himself—then those productions which issue from him being his powers (faculties), and always present with him, will not be ignorant of him who emitted them
sources.raw_question: Could the Word (Logos) of the Father be ignorant of the Father who generated him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: No. The Father is Mind and perfect in all things. He was able to produce his Logos together with knowledge of himself, so he could not have brought forth an imperfect, blind offspring. To say the Word was produced ignorant falsely ascribes blindness to the Word of God. It would also make the Father's greatness the cause of ignorance and so the author of evils.
sources.quote: how could the Nous of the Father, or rather the very Father Himself, since He is Nous and perfect in all things, have produced his own Logos as an imperfect and blind Æon, when He was able also to produce along with him the knowledge of the Father?
sources.raw_question: Could the perfect Mind of the Father produce his own Word as imperfect and blind, ignorant of the Father?

question: Does Amos 4:13 ("He that establishes the thunder and creates the spirit") teach that the Holy Spirit is a creature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VI. To those who object that according to the words of Amos the Spirit is created, the answer is made that the word is there understood of the wind, which is often created, which cannot be said of the Holy Spirit, since He is eternal, and cannot be dissolved in death, or by an heretical absorption into the Father. But if they pertinaciously contend that this passage was written of the Holy Spirit, St. Ambrose points out that recourse must be had to a spiritual Interpretation, for Christ by His coming established the thunder, that is, the force of the divine utterances, and by Spirit is signified the human soul as also the flesh assumed by Christ. And since this was created by each Person of the Trinity, it is thence argued that the Spirit, Who has before been affirmed to be the Creator of all things, was the Author of the Incarnation of the Lord.
sources.answer: No. The order and context of the passage show the prophet is speaking of the creation of this world: thunders, wind, light and mist, as in an ordinary storm. If he had meant the Holy Spirit he would not have placed thunders first, since not even heretics dare say thunder is older than the Holy Spirit; and "spirit" is often used of blasts of wind.
sources.quote: For if he had wished to speak of the Holy Spirit, he would certainly not have put the thunders in the first place. For thunder is not more ancient than the Holy Spirit; though they be ungodly, they still dare not say that.
sources.raw_question: Does Amos 4:13 ("I create the spirit/wind") prove that the Holy Spirit is a creature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VI. To those who object that according to the words of Amos the Spirit is created, the answer is made that the word is there understood of the wind, which is often created, which cannot be said of the Holy Spirit, since He is eternal, and cannot be dissolved in death, or by an heretical absorption into the Father. But if they pertinaciously contend that this passage was written of the Holy Spirit, St. Ambrose points out that recourse must be had to a spiritual Interpretation, for Christ by His coming established the thunder, that is, the force of the divine utterances, and by Spirit is signified the human soul as also the flesh assumed by Christ. And since this was created by each Person of the Trinity, it is thence argued that the Spirit, Who has before been affirmed to be the Creator of all things, was the Author of the Incarnation of the Lord.
sources.answer: No. If it must be read spiritually, the passage refers to the Incarnation: the thunders are the Lord's words sounding through all the earth, and "spirit" means the rational human soul Christ assumed. Scripture often uses "spirit" for the human soul, as in "Who creates the spirit of man within him" and Christ's "Into Thy hands I commend My Spirit."
sources.quote: we understand the word “spirit” in this place of the soul, which He took endowed with reason and perfect;
sources.raised_by_detail: those who argue from Amos that the Spirit is created
sources.raw_question: Does Amos 4:13 ("He that establishes the thunder and creates the spirit, declaring unto men His Christ") teach that the Holy Spirit is a creature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VI.
