To those who object that according to the words of Amos the Spirit is created, the answer is made that the word is there understood of the wind, which is often created, which cannot be said of the Holy Spirit, since He is eternal, and cannot be dissolved in death, or by an heretical absorption into the Father. But if they pertinaciously contend that this passage was written of the Holy Spirit, St. Ambrose points out that recourse must be had to a spiritual Interpretation, for Christ by His coming established the thunder, that is, the force of the divine utterances, and by Spirit is signified the human soul as also the flesh assumed by Christ. And since this was created by each Person of the Trinity, it is thence argued that the Spirit, Who has before been affirmed to be the Creator of all things, was the Author of the Incarnation of the Lord.
sources.answer: Because if Scripture had really meant the Holy Spirit was created, it would have said so elsewhere. It repeatedly says so of the Son according to the flesh, who was made and created. Since Scripture says nothing similar of the Spirit, the Amos text should be read either of human life and breath or of the mystery of the Lord's Body.
sources.quote: if here it had been stated that the Holy Spirit was created, undoubtedly Scripture would elsewhere have declared the same, as we often read of the Son of God, Who according to the flesh was both made and created.
sources.raw_question: Why does the absence of other scriptural statements that the Holy Spirit was created count against reading Amos 4:13 as calling the Spirit a creature?

question: How do memory, understanding and love in the human mind resemble the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Augustin Dwells Still Further on the Disparity Between the Trinity Which is in Man, and the Trinity Which is God. The Trinity is Now Seen Through a Glass by the Help of Faith, that It May Hereafter Be More Clearly Seen in the Promised Sight Face to Face.
sources.answer: Each bears a very unequal likeness. Intellectual memory resembles the Father. The understanding formed from it, an inner word of the heart belonging to no language, resembles the Son. Love proceeds from knowledge and joins memory and understanding, as though common to parent and offspring while being neither. It thus resembles the Holy Spirit, who is of both Father and Son.
sources.quote: love in the case of man proceeding from knowledge, and combining memory and understanding, as though common to parent and offspring, whereby it is understood to be neither parent nor offspring, has in that image, some, however exceedingly unequal, likeness of the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: In what way do memory, understanding and love in the human mind resemble the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Of the Likeness of the Father and of the Son Alleged to Be in Our Memory and Understanding. Of the Likeness of the Holy Spirit in Our Will or Love.
sources.answer: They intimate the Father as begetter and the Son as Word, though only in an enigma and by conjecture. Memory holds everything we know even when not thinking of it, as the Father has all things in His substance, and understanding is the thought formed from memory, an inner word begotten, as the Father speaks by His co-eternal Word all that He has.
sources.quote: to intimate God the Father and God the Son: i.e. God the begetter, who has in some way spoken by His own co-eternal Word all things that He has in His substance
sources.raw_question: How do the human mind's memory and understanding serve as an image of God the Father and God the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How There is a Trinity in the Very Simplicity of God. Whether and How the Trinity that is God is Manifested from the Trinities Which Have Been Shown to Be in Men.
sources.answer: The Father is as it were the one speaking and the Son is His Word. The Holy Spirit is the love common to both, proceeding from them. The understanding beholds these in God in a way analogous to the trinities found in ourselves.
sources.quote: we behold both Him as it were speaking, and His Word, i.e. the Father and the Son; and then, proceeding thence, the love common to both, namely, the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: In the analogy of the mind, how do the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit correspond to the speaker, the Word and the love?

question: Does the Father communicate his love to believers, and do believers return love to the Father, only through Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father communicates no fruit of his love except through Christ, and believers make no return of love except through him. Christ is the treasury in which the Father places all the riches of his grace, and the priest into whose hands believers put all their offerings to the Father. The following context adds that love is first poured out on Christ and from him drops upon the saints.
sources.quote: The Father communicates no issue of his love unto us but through Christ; and we make no return of love unto him but through Christ.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father communicate his love to believers, and do believers return love to the Father, only through Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Only through Christ. Though the Father's love has its rise in his mere grace and will, the design of its accomplishment is only in Christ: all its fruits are first given to him and dispensed to us from him. As the anointing oil was poured on Aaron's head and ran down to his garments, so love is first poured on Christ and from him drops on the saints (Eph. 1:3-4; Titus 3:6; Col. 1:18-19; John 1:16).
sources.quote: Though the love of the Father’s purpose and good pleasure have its rise and foundation in his mere grace and will, yet the design of its accomplishment is only in Christ.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father communicate his love and its blessings to believers directly, or only through Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Through the Son. Our love is fixed on the Father but conveyed to him through the Son of his love, who bears the iniquity of our offerings and adds incense to our prayers. He is the only way for our graces as well as our persons to go to God.
sources.quote: Our love is fixed on the Father; but it is conveyed to him through the Son of his love. He is the only way for our graces as well as our persons to go unto God
sources.raw_question: Do believers return love and worship to the Father directly or through the Son?

question: Is the doctrine of Christ's satisfaction inconsistent with God being gracious and merciful in forgiving sinners?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Scripture affirms both, so the worst consequence is that Scripture is true. Indeed this displays the exceeding greatness of grace: when sin could not be forgiven without satisfaction and the sinner could make none, God provided a sacrifice of atonement himself.
sources.quote: when sin could not be forgiven without satisfaction, and the sinner himself could no way make any such satisfaction, he provided himself a sacrifice of atonement, that the sinner might be discharged and pardoned.
sources.raw_question: Is it contradictory to hold that God is gracious to forgive and yet cannot forgive sin without full satisfaction?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Owen grants that nothing truly contrary to God's grace or free forgiveness may be admitted. But God is just as essentially holy, righteous, true, and faithful as he is good and merciful. His infinite wisdom arranges things so that mercy is exercised without prejudice to justice. God's grace is in fact chiefly displayed in purposing relief for sinners and in sending his Son to be a propitiation, so justice and mercy meet in harmony at the cross.
sources.quote: it belongs to his infinite wisdom, that the effects of them, though divers, and produced by divers ways and means, may no way be contrary one to the other, but that mercy be exercised without the prejudice of justice or holiness
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine of Christ's satisfaction inconsistent with God's love, grace, and mercy and with the free forgiveness of sins?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. The objection confuses God's essential properties (grace, mercy) with free acts of his will (pardoning), and 'lawful' cannot sensibly apply to natural properties of God. The doctrine only declares how God pardons: since he is also holy, righteous and true, it was fitting that he exercise mercy without impeaching his holiness and righteousness.
sources.quote: It is supposed that for God to be gracious and merciful, or to pardon sinners, are the same; which is to confound the essential properties of his nature with the free acts of his will.
sources.raw_question: Does the doctrine of satisfaction make it impossible for God to be gracious and merciful or to pardon sinners?

question: Is sin properly a monetary debt to God, with Christ's satisfaction understood as paying it off?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: No. Although the debt image has been used for illustration and has some scriptural countenance, God is properly considered as the infinitely holy and righteous author of the law and supreme governor of mankind. Man is considered as a transgressor liable to the punishment the law threatens, according to God's justice and holiness.
sources.quote: in this matter of satisfaction, God is not considered as a creditor, and sin as a debt; and the law as an obligation to the payment of that debt, and the Lord Christ as paying it
sources.raw_question: In Christ's satisfaction for sin, is God properly to be understood as a creditor and sin as a pecuniary debt that Christ pays off?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Sin is properly a transgression and only improperly a debt; if it were properly a debt it could be paid in kind with sin itself. It is called a debt only because it binds the sinner over to punishment, which is the satisfaction due.
sources.quote: Sin is not properly a debt, for then it might be paid in kind, by sin itself; but is called so only because it binds over the sinner to punishment
sources.raw_question: Is sin properly a debt to God that could simply be remitted like a monetary debt?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Satisfaction means doing or suffering as much as is enough to answer the charge of one justly angry, who has right and power to punish faults. In this matter, 'debt' must be taken as liability to punishment for crimes, not as a debt of money. The pecuniary analogy has no proper place here.
sources.quote: The true meaning of, “to satisfy, or make satisfaction,” is “tantum facere aut pati, quantum satis sit justè irato ad vindictam.”
sources.raw_question: What does it mean for Christ to make satisfaction for sin, and should it be understood as the payment of a money debt?

question: Can religious worship or divine honour be divided into sovereign worship due to God and an inferior or relative worship that may lawfully be given to lesser beings?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 4: Whether, supposing the Scripture-notion of God to be no more than that of the Author and Governor of the universe, or whatever it be, the admitting of another t
sources.answer: No. God has already claimed all divine honour for himself as the only God and sole Author and Governor of the universe. Every other being is therefore excluded from receiving divine honour. For God to command such honour for another would mean God contradicting himself.
sources.quote: then all others are precluded from receiving any
sources.raw_question: Can divine honour be rightly given to an inferior being on the grounds that it redounds ultimately to the glory of the supreme God who commanded it?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. In Rom. 1 Paul blames the heathen for giving any worship at all, sovereign or inferior, to the creature. They could hardly have thought there was more than one supreme God. The angel in Revelation likewise refused even outward adoration and said simply "Worship God," not "worship God with sovereign worship."
sources.quote: He does not blaine them for giving sovereign or absolute worship to the creatures, (they could hardly be so silly as to imagine there could be more than one supreme God,) but for giving any worship at all, sovereign or inferior, absolute or relative, to any thing but the Creator.
sources.raw_question: Is an inferior, relative or non-sovereign kind of religious worship permitted to creatures alongside the sovereign worship given to God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. God himself has fixed the meaning of religious worship: by divine institution it signifies the divinity and sovereignty of its object. All religious worship is therefore what opponents call absolute and sovereign, and 'inferior' or 'relative' worship is a contradiction in sense, like an inferior or relative God.
sources.quote: All religious worship is hereby determined to be what you call absolute and sovereign. Inferior or relative worship appears now to be contradiction in sense, as it is novel in sound ; like an inferior or relative God.
sources.raw_question: Can religious worship be divided into sovereign (supreme) worship due to God and inferior or relative worship that may lawfully be given to creatures?

question: Did the Old Testament prophets actually see God in their visions, and if not, what did they see, given that God is invisible?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: No. What they saw were similitudes of the splendour of the Lord and prophecies of things to come, not God himself. This shows that the Father is invisible, as the Lord said, "No man hath seen God at any time."
sources.quote: If, then, neither Moses, nor Elias, nor Ezekiel, who had all many celestial visions, did see God; but if what they did see were similitudes of the splendour of the Lord, and prophecies of things to come; it is manifest that the Father is indeed invisible
sources.raw_question: Did the Old Testament prophets such as Moses, Elijah and Ezekiel actually see God the Father in their visions?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: No. The prophets did not openly behold the actual face of God but saw the dispensations and mysteries through which man would afterwards see God. Ezekiel himself, after describing his vision of the throne and the likeness of a man, added that this was only the appearance of the likeness of the glory of God, lest anyone think he had seen God himself.
sources.quote: The prophets, therefore, did not openly behold the actual face of God, but [they saw] the dispensations and the mysteries through which man should afterwards see God.
sources.raw_question: Did the Old Testament prophets actually see the face of God in their visions?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: They saw God through prophetic visions given by the Spirit, not by openly beholding his actual face. What they saw were the dispensations and mysteries through which man would later see God. In this way they also saw the Son of God beforehand as a man living among men. Isaiah's words "I have seen with mine eyes the King" point to man's future beholding of God.
sources.quote: After this invisible manner, therefore, did they see God, as also Esaias says, “I have seen with mine eyes the King, the Lord of hosts,”
sources.raw_question: In what sense did the Old Testament prophets see God, given that God is invisible?

question: Can anything exist beyond or outside the supreme God, so that he would be bounded or contained by it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VIII.—Created things are not a shadow of the Pleroma.
sources.answer: No. Nothing can exist beyond the primary Father, whether a Pleroma, a void or a shadow. Otherwise God would be limited, circumscribed and contained by what lies beyond him. It is irrational and impious to imagine a place where the Father of all ceases and has an end.
sources.quote: It is, moreover, irrational and impious to conceive of a place in which He who is, according to them, Propator, and Proarche, and Father of all, and of this Pleroma, ceases and has an end.
sources.raw_question: Can anything exist beyond or outside the God who is over all, so that he is bounded or contained by it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter IV.—The absurdity of the supposed vacuum and defect of the heretics is demonstrated.
sources.answer: No. The Father of all contains all things, and nothing whatever is outside him. If anything existed outside him, he would be bounded and circumscribed by something greater than himself, which cannot be true of the supreme God.
sources.quote: for it is an absolute necessity that, [if there be anything outside of it,] it should be bounded and circumscribed by something greater than itself
sources.raw_question: Can anything exist outside the supreme God who contains all things?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter I.—There is but one God: the impossibility of its being otherwise.
sources.answer: No. If anything exists beyond God, He would have beginning, middle, and end, and would be enclosed by what lies outside Him. That which contains is greater than what is contained. What is greater is stronger and more truly Lord, so the container rather than the contained would be God.
sources.quote: who must of necessity be greater, inasmuch as that which contains is greater than that which is contained. But then that which is greater is also stronger, and in a greater degree Lord
sources.raw_question: Would a being who is bounded by something outside himself still be the supreme God?

question: Does saying in Acts 2:36 that the one who suffered was exalted and 'made Lord and Christ' imply that there are two Christs or two persons, one who suffered and another who was honoured?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says that two things were wrought in regard to one person: the Passion was inflicted by the Jews, and the honour was given by God. It is not that one person suffered while another was exalted.
sources.quote: in regard to one person two things were wrought,—by the Jews, the Passion, and by God, honour; not as though one person had suffered and another had been honoured by exaltation
sources.raw_question: Does saying that the Passion and the exaltation in Acts 2 were wrought upon Christ imply that there are two persons, one who suffered and another who was honoured?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius himself confesses that the Word who was in the beginning was made flesh, yet no one charges him with preaching two Words, since the Word who appeared in the flesh is identical with the Word who was with God. Likewise, saying the exalted humanity was made Lord and Christ by union with Him who is truly Lord and Christ does not divide the one Christ into two.
sources.quote: If, then, in view of such a confession, he does not reproach himself with the duality of Words, why are we falsely charged with dividing the object of our faith into “two Christs”?
sources.raw_question: Does saying that the one who was highly exalted after his Passion was 'made Lord and Christ' imply that there are two Christs?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: No. Gregory points out that the Apostle says the One who suffered was highly exalted after His Passion, though God the Word was Highest from the beginning. By Eunomius's logic one would have to either deny the exaltation of Him who suffered or be charged with teaching 'two Highests'; since the exaltation must be confessed, being 'made Lord and Christ' refers to the exaltation of the humanity without dividing Christ into two.
sources.quote: seeing that God the Word, Who was in the beginning, was Highest, and was also highly exalted after His Passion when He rose from the dead, as the Apostle says.
sources.raw_question: If God the Word was Highest from the beginning, does saying He was highly exalted after His Passion imply two 'Highests', and should the exaltation therefore be denied?

question: Whose Godhead is the fulness that dwells bodily in Christ according to Colossians 2:9, and does this mean the Father is confined in the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It is the Father's Godhead. Hilary argues that if it were not the Father's, the 'preacher of one God' would be introducing another God; and the Apostle himself identifies it by speaking of 'His everlasting power and divinity', so it is the Father's Godhead that dwells in Christ wholly, not partially.
sources.quote: So it is His Godhead that dwells in Christ in bodily fashion, not partially but wholly, not parcelwise but in fulness; and so dwelling that the Two are one
sources.raw_question: Whose Godhead is it whose fulness dwells bodily in Christ according to Colossians 2:9?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. If the Father abode in the Son in bodily fashion as a person, he would not exist in himself. Rather, the indwelling Godhead shows the true nature of God from God present in the Son by birth, so that the Son is wholly God, differing from the Father only in that in Christ the Godhead dwells in bodily form.
sources.quote: If you hold that the Father abides in the Son in bodily fashion, the Father, while dwelling in the Son, will not exist in Himself.
sources.raw_question: Does the fulness of the Father's Godhead dwelling bodily in Christ mean the Father himself is enclosed in the Son so that he no longer exists in himself?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It is the Father's Godhead, but the Father is not confined in the Son in such a way that He ceases to exist in Himself. The Godhead abiding in Christ bodily shows the true nature of God from God. It is present by birth, not by condescension or will, with no difference within the Godhead. This rules out reducing their unity to mere agreement, harmony of will, or creaturehood.
sources.quote: God is in Him, abiding neither through condescension nor through will but by birth, true and wholly in bodily fulness according as He is
sources.raw_question: Whose Godhead is the fulness that dwells bodily in Christ according to Colossians 2:9, and does this mean the Father is confined in the Son?

question: Can a person be truly blessed without being immortal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What Has Been Treated of in This Book. How We Have Reached by Steps to a Certain Trinity, Which is Found in Practical Knowledge and True Faith.
sources.answer: No. No one can be what all men will, namely blessed, except by being immortal. Even those who despair of immortality would will it if they thought it possible. Because they do not believe they can be immortal, they fail to live in a way that leads to it.
sources.quote: But many despair of being immortal, although no otherwise can any one be that which all will, that is, blessed.
sources.raw_question: Can a person be truly blessed without being immortal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Faith is Necessary, that Man May at Some Time Be Blessed, Which He Will Only Attain in the Future Life. The Blessedness of Proud Philosophers Ridiculous and Pitiable.
sources.answer: No. The life in which one has whatever one wills is not possible in this mortal state and will come only when immortality comes. If immortality could not be given to man at all, the search for blessedness would be in vain, since blessedness cannot exist without it.
sources.quote: And if this could not be given at all to man, blessedness too would be sought in vain, since it cannot be without immortality.
sources.raw_question: Can true blessedness exist without immortality?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Blessedness Cannot Exist Without Immortality.
sources.answer: No. The blessed man lives as he wills and wills nothing wrongly. Since all men will to be blessed, and no one can be blessed without being alive, everyone who is or wishes to be blessed must will to be immortal. A blessed life lost through death, whether willingly or unwillingly, is no true blessedness. So no life can be truly blessed unless it is eternal.
sources.quote: Therefore, whoever are either truly blessed or desire to be so, will to be immortal. But he does not live blessedly who has not that which he wills. Therefore it follows that in no way can life be truly blessed unless it be eternal.
sources.raw_question: Can a human life be truly blessed (happy) if it is not eternal?

question: When Christ in the Old Testament theophanies says 'I am the God of Bethel', does he speak only as the Father's representative, or as God in his own Person?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. The Fathers argued from these texts that Christ himself is truly Lord and God. That argument would be trifling if they had read the texts as Christ declaring that the Person he represents is God. So the basis of their whole argument assumes the opposite of Dr. Clarke's view.
sources.quote: The conclusion which Justin Martyr draws from the whole, and which he triumphantly urges against Trypho, is this; that Christ is really Lord and God
sources.raw_question: When the Old Testament theophanies have the one appearing say "I am the God of Bethel," did the early Fathers take Christ to be speaking merely as representative of the Father, so that only the Father is meant by "God"?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. The Fathers applied such texts to Christ considered in his own Person, not only as representing the Father. Clement says Christ said 'I am the Lord thy God' in his own Person; Tertullian and Irenaeus say likewise, Irenaeus concluding that Christ with the Father is the God of the living who spoke to Moses.
sources.quote: I will shew that the good Fathers applied these texts to Christ considered in his own Person, and not in the Father’s only.
sources.raw_question: When Christ in the Old Testament says 'I am the God of Bethel', does he speak only in the Person of the Father as his representative, rather than in his own Person?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Someone acting in another's name or authority need not take on that other's style or speak in the first person as him. A viceroy or ambassador represents the king but does not say 'I am the king.' So the Son's use of divine titles in his own voice shows he was God in his own Person. No sound conclusion against this can be drawn from Theophilus and Tertullian.
sources.quote: a viceroy, or an ambassador, speaks in the king’s name, and by his authority, and represents his person: but does not personate the king, in the strictest sense ; does not pretend to say, I am the king.
sources.raw_question: If the Son spoke as God in the first person ('I am the God of Bethel'), does that prove he was merely a representative acting in the Father's name?

question: Can religious worship be made sovereign (supreme) or inferior according to the worshipper's inward intention and esteem for its object?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. The signification of worship and sacrifice was fixed beforehand by God, not by the worshipper's private esteem or intention. The early martyrs died rather than sacrifice to idols they despised, which would have been pointless if a low inward esteem made such acts no real worship. They rightly judged that sacrificing to heathen deities declared them by implication to be eternal, supreme and divine.
sources.quote: They knew that the signification of worship and sacrifice depended not on their arbitrary esteem, or secret intention; but had been before fixed and determined by God.
sources.raw_question: Can the quality of religious worship (whether it is sovereign or inferior) be determined by the inward intention and secret esteem of the worshipper?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: It would justify worshipping anything, however mean. On that principle one could pray to angels, worship departed saints, or bow before a crucifix, provided one intended only proportionate respect. Such consequences show the distinction departs from the basic rule of revealed religion that God alone is to be worshipped with religious worship.
sources.quote: upon the other hypothesis, there is nothing so mean or low, but what a man might pay religious worship to. For instance; pray to angels, but consider them as angels, with proportionate respect, and there will be no harm in it.
sources.raw_question: What follows if one accepts the distinction between sovereign and inferior worship measured by the worshipper's intention?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. Scripture says nothing of absolute and relative, or supreme and inferior, prayer, and gives no rules for raising or lowering our intentions according to the object's dignity. The whole tenor of Scripture runs against the idea. Under the Law, all sacrifice was reserved to God, not merely some 'sovereign' kind of sacrifice.
sources.quote: Prayer we often read of; but there is not a syllable about absolute and relative, supreme and inferior prayer. We are commanded to pray fervently and incessantly; but never sovereignly or absolutely
sources.raw_question: Does religious worship become supreme or inferior depending on the worshipper's intention and esteem for the object?

question: Does the prologue of John's Gospel (John 1:1-14) set forth the Valentinian Ogdoad of Aeons and their paired conjunctions (such as Logos and Zoe, Anthropos and Ecclesia), as Ptolemaeus claimed, rather than speaking of the one Lord Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter VIII.—How the Valentinians pervert the Scriptures to support their own pious opinions.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus holds that this is an abuse of Scripture to support their own system. Had John intended to describe the Ogdoad, he would have kept the order of its production. He would have put the supposedly most venerable primary Tetrad first and then added the second, rather than mentioning the primary Tetrad last as if he had forgotten it.
sources.quote: if it had been John’s intention to set forth that Ogdoad above, he would surely have preserved the order of its production, and would doubtless have placed the primary Tetrad first as being, according to them, most venerable
sources.raw_question: Does the prologue of John's Gospel (John 1:1-14) set forth the Valentinian first Ogdoad of Aeons (Father, Charis, Monogenes, Aletheia, Logos, Zoe, Anthropos, Ecclesia), as Ptolemaeus claimed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter VIII.—How the Valentinians pervert the Scriptures to support their own pious opinions.
sources.answer: No. If John had meant to point to such conjunctions, he would not have left out the name Ecclesia. He would also have been consistent, either naming only the male Aeons throughout or naming the spouse of Anthropos as well, instead of leaving it to be guessed. The interpretation is therefore plainly fallacious.
sources.quote: if he had meant to indicate their conjunctions, he certainly would not have omitted the name of Ecclesia
sources.raw_question: Do the words of John's prologue (such as "the life was the light of men") indicate Valentinian conjunctions or pairs of Aeons such as Logos and Zoe, or Anthropos and Ecclesia?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter IX.—Refutation of the impious interpretations of these heretics.
sources.answer: No. If John had meant to set forth the Ogdoad he would have kept its order of production, named the primary Tetrad first, and not omitted Ecclesia or the spouse of Anthropos. His actual sequence and omissions show the exposition is a fallacy imposed on the text, not John's meaning.
sources.quote: if it had been John’s intention to set forth that Ogdoad above, he would surely have preserved the order of its production, and would doubtless have placed the primary Tetrad first
sources.raw_question: Does the prologue of John's Gospel (Logos, Life, Light, Only-begotten, Grace, Truth) describe a Gnostic Ogdoad of emanated Æons rather than one Lord Jesus Christ?

question: Was Christ Lord over all only after his resurrection, as Matthew 28:18 ('all power is given unto me') and Ephesians 1:22 might seem to imply?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: No. Christ was Lord over all before his resurrection and even before his incarnation, as Scripture shows he created all things in heaven and earth and upholds them; even the ancient Arians acknowledged this.
sources.quote: That he was “ Lord of all” before his resurrection, is very plain from the Scriptures, which carry in them irrefragable proofs of it.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's being called 'Lord of all' mean only the power given him after his resurrection?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: No. The power given after the resurrection was given in respect of Christ's human nature, which had been in a state of humiliation and was then first exalted and assumed into such power. The Word himself was Lord from the beginning, so to suppose he first began to be Lord when that honour was conferred on the man Christ Jesus is contrary to Scripture and catholic antiquity.
sources.quote: how easy it is to account for our Lord’s having all power given him, after his resurrection ; given him in respect of his human nature, which was never so high exalted, nor assumed into such power and privilege, till that time
sources.raw_question: If all power was given to Christ after his resurrection (Matthew 28:18), does that mean the Word only then first became Lord over all?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: No. Scripture plainly shows Christ was Lord of all long before his resurrection and even before his incarnation, since all things were created by him and for him and consist by him. One who is Creator and Preserver of all things from the beginning cannot fail to be Lord over all until after his resurrection.
sources.quote: Can you imagine that the Son could be Creator and Preserver of all things from the beginning, and yet not be Lord over all till after his resurrection?
sources.raised_by_detail: Dr. Clarke's defender (author of the Queries' reply)
sources.raw_question: Was Christ Lord over all things only after his resurrection, as Matthew 28:18 and Ephesians 1:22 seem to imply when they say all power was given to him?

question: Does the New Testament's joining of Christ's name with the Father's in the most solemn divine offices imply that Christ shares the Godhead and is equal with the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. To read it that way would confound all distinction between God and man. The union of the two names in offices of the highest solemnity therefore leads irresistibly to the conclusion that the Godhead of the Father and the Son is one, their glory equal and their majesty coeternal.
sources.quote: to accept this as the conjunction of the Creator with his creature would confound all distinction betwixt God and man, we are again led irresistibly to the conclusion, that the Godhead of the Father, and of the Son is one
sources.raw_question: Could the joining of Jesus Christ's name with the Father's in the most solemn divine offices be read as a conjunction of the Creator with a creature?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture sometimes names a servant alongside God when he acts plainly as God's subordinate, and even that is rare. But joining the infinite God with one who acts alongside him in evident equality of rank cannot be explained on the Unitarian hypothesis. Doing so with a mere creature would blur the infinite distinction between God and man.
sources.quote: but the conjunction of the infinite God, with one coordinately engaged in manifest equality of rank, is utterly inexplicable on the Unitarian hypothesis.
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament's practice of naming Jesus Christ alongside God the Father in divine offices imply that Christ is equal with God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ's name is united with the Father's in offices of the highest solemnity. If this were a joining of the Creator with a creature, it would blend and confuse the infinite distinction between God and man. So the conjunction shows the Son shares the Godhead.
sources.quote: the name of Jesus Christ is united with that of our heavenly. Father in offices where the coalition of the Creator with his creature would blend and confuse the infinite distinction betwixt God and man
sources.raw_question: Does the joining of Christ's name with the Father's in divine offices imply Christ's deity?

question: Do the punishments God inflicted in the Old Testament show that the God of the Old Testament is a different God from the Father revealed by Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVII—The sins of the men of old time, which incurred the displeasure of God, were, by His providence, committed to writing, that we might derive instruction thereby, and not be filled with pride. We must not, therefore, infer that there was another God than He whom Christ preached; we should rather fear, lest the one and the same God who inflicted punishment on the ancients, should bring down heavier upon us.
sources.answer: No. These sins and their punishment were written down for our instruction. First, they teach us that our God and the God of the ancients is one, and that sins displease Him even when committed by famous men. Second, they warn us to keep from wickedness. God is no respecter of persons and justly punishes whatever displeases Him, so the same God who punished the ancients may punish us even more severely.
sources.quote: that we might know, in the first place, that our God and theirs is one, and that sins do not please Him although committed by men of renown
sources.raw_question: Do the Old Testament accounts of God punishing men like David and Solomon show that the God of the Old Testament is a different God from the one Christ preached?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVIII.—Those persons prove themselves senseless who exaggerate the mercy of Christ, but are silent as to the judgment, and look only at the more abundant grace of the New Testament; but, forgetful of the greater degree of perfection which it demands from us, they endeavour to show that there is another God beyond Him who created the world.
sources.answer: No. The same righteousness of God is displayed in both Testaments when God takes vengeance: in the Old typically, temporarily and more moderately, in the New really, eternally and more rigidly. Those who contrast Old Testament punishments with Christ's mercy while ignoring Christ's own threats of judgment are senseless, since Christ himself declares eternal fire for the unbelieving.
sources.quote: in both Testaments there is the same righteousness of God [displayed] when God takes vengeance, in the one case indeed typically, temporarily, and more moderately; but in the other, really, enduringly, and more rigidly
sources.raised_by_detail: Marcionites/those who bring in another Father
sources.raw_question: Do the punishments inflicted by God in the Old Testament prove that the God of the Old Testament is a different God from the Father revealed by Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVII—The sins of the men of old time, which incurred the displeasure of God, were, by His providence, committed to writing, that we might derive instruction thereby, and not be filled with pride. We must not, therefore, infer that there was another God than He whom Christ preached; we should rather fear, lest the one and the same God who inflicted punishment on the ancients, should bring down heavier upon us.
sources.answer: No. The apostle shows beyond doubt that one and the same God judged the ancients and judges people now, and that those punishments were written down for our instruction. Those who posit a degenerate world-maker distinct from Christ's Father fail to see that just as God was displeased with sinners then, so now "many are called, but few are chosen," and the unrighteous are still excluded from the kingdom and sent into eternal fire.
sources.quote: the apostle shows that there is one and the same God, who did both enter into judgment with these former things, and who does inquire into those of the present time, and points out why these things have been committed to writing
sources.raw_question: Does God's punishment of sinners in the Old Testament prove that the God of the Old Testament is a different, inferior God from the Father whom Christ revealed?

question: Does Paul's statement that the man is the image and glory of God while the woman is the glory of the man (1 Cor 11:7) mean that women are excluded from the image of God, contrary to Genesis, which says God created male and female in His image?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > How Man is the Image of God. Whether the Woman is Not Also the Image of God. How the Saying of the Apostle, that the Man is the Image of God, But the Woman is the Glory of the Man, is to Be Understood Figuratively and Mystically.
sources.answer: No. Women are fellow-heirs of grace and are renewed in the spirit of their mind after the image of God, where there is no sex. Paul says there is neither male nor female in Christ. The woman's head-covering figuratively represents the part of reason turned to governing temporal things, while the image of God remains in the part of the mind that contemplates the eternal reasons, which women have as well as men.
sources.quote: so that the image of God may remain on that side of the mind of man on which it cleaves to the beholding or the consulting of the eternal reasons of things; and this, it is clear, not men only, but also women have.
sources.raw_question: Are women excluded from being the image of God, given that Paul calls the man the image and glory of God and the woman the glory of the man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > How Man is the Image of God. Whether the Woman is Not Also the Image of God. How the Saying of the Apostle, that the Man is the Image of God, But the Woman is the Glory of the Man, is to Be Understood Figuratively and Mystically.
sources.answer: No. Genesis teaches that human nature, complete in both sexes, was made in God's image and does not exclude the woman. Paul's saying is figurative: the woman together with her husband is the image of God as one substance, but considered separately in her role as help-meet she signifies something that is not the image, while the man alone is fully the image.
sources.quote: For this text says that human nature itself, which is complete [only] in both sexes, was made in the image of God; and it does not separate the woman from the image of God which it signifies.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that the man is the image of God but the woman the glory of the man contradict Genesis, which says God created male and female in His image?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > There is a Kind of Hidden Wedlock in the Inner Man. Unlawful Pleasures of the Thoughts.
sources.answer: Paul means to signify something to be sought within each individual human being, namely the distinction between contemplation and action within one mind. He expresses this through the different sexes of two human beings. The mind's unity is kept in both functions, and the historical truth about the first man and woman is not denied.
sources.quote: the apostle may be understood to have intended to signify something to be sought in one individual man, by assigning the image of God to the man only, and not also to the woman
sources.raw_question: Why does the apostle Paul assign the image of God to the man only and not to the woman?

question: Is the created world the work of the good and supreme God, or the product of ignorance, defect, an erring Aeon or angels?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter III.—The Bythus and Pleroma of the Valentinians, as well as the God of Marcion, shown to be absurd; the world was actually created by the same Being who had conceived the idea of it, and was not the fruit of defect or ignorance.
sources.answer: No. The world exists exactly as the Father conceived it in counsel with himself, so it must be worthy of the Father. To call what the Father of all pre-conceived the product of defect and ignorance is great blasphemy. It would make the Father generate emanations of defect in his own mind.
sources.quote: Since, then, it is just such as the Father had [ideally] formed in counsel with Himself, it must be worthy of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Can the created world, being compound, mutable and transient, be the fruit of defect or ignorance rather than a work worthy of the supreme God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVIII.—God the Father and His Word have formed all created things (which They use) by Their own power and wisdom, not out of defect or ignorance. The Son of God, who received all power from the Father, would otherwise never have taken flesh upon Him.
sources.answer: No. The fruit of ignorance and defect could not sustain Him who contains the knowledge of all things and is perfect. Since the Son is in the Father and the Father in Him, a work of angels could not bear both the Father and the Son at once. So the creation that bore Him on the cross must be His own, subsisting by God's power and wisdom.
sources.quote: how could this workmanship of the angels have borne to be burdened at once with the Father and the Son?
sources.raw_question: Could a creation produced by ignorance and defect, or made by angels, have borne the crucified Word of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXV.—This world is ruled by the providence of one God, who is both endowed with infinite justice to punish the wicked, and with infinite goodness to bless the pious, and impart to them salvation.
sources.answer: By God's goodness. Even Plato acknowledged that the Maker of the universe is good and that no envy arises in the good, establishing God's goodness as the beginning and cause of creation, not ignorance, an erring Aeon, a defect, a weeping Mother, or another God or Father.
sources.quote: thus establishing the goodness of God, as the beginning and the cause of the creation of the world, but not ignorance, nor an erring Æon, nor the consequence of a defect
sources.raw_question: Was the creation of the world caused by God's goodness or by ignorance, defect, or an erring Aeon?

question: When Genesis says God 'called the light Day,' does it mean that light and day are the same thing, or that God himself invented and uttered the word as a name?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Neither. Light and day differ in definition: light is the opposite of darkness, while day is the extent of the interval of light. Likewise darkness is the negation of light and night is the extent of darkness. The text teaches that God made the things, not empty words.
sources.quote: light is what we understand by the opposite of darkness, and day is the extent of the measure of the interval of light.
sources.raw_question: When Genesis says God 'called the light day,' does it mean that light and day are the same thing, or that God uttered a word?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. God is the Maker of things that really subsist, not of words that exist only as sounds. The names follow the nature of the things and are supplied by human speech. 'God called the light day' means that God made the day, a measure of time, out of the alternation of light and darkness. The name then followed because the nature of the thing took on that vocal notation.
sources.quote: the measure of time also was created and the name followed, not created by God in a sound of words, but because the very nature of the thing assumed this vocal notation
sources.raw_question: Does Genesis' statement that God 'called' the light Day and the darkness Night mean that God himself invented and uttered the words used as names for created things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Light is the opposite of darkness. Day is a measure of time: the regular alternation of light and darkness caused by the earth blocking the light as the heavens revolve. So when God is said to have called the light day, it means God made the day from light as something different.
sources.quote: Since, then, it is written that God called the light day, it must be understood that God made the day from light, being something different, by the force of the term.
sources.raw_question: Are 'light' and 'day' two names for the same thing in the Genesis creation account?

question: Can anything exist beyond or outside the supreme God, such as the Gnostic Pleroma or other realms, so that God would be bounded or limited by it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXI.—Recapitulation and application of the foregoing arguments.
sources.answer: No. If anything existed beyond the Father, he would be enclosed and limited by it, and so would not be the Father of all. The theory would also require many Fathers, many Pleromas and many worlds, each confined to its own domain with no fellowship between them. The name God belongs only to the Almighty, who contains all things.
sources.quote: showing how the Father of all is shut up and circumscribed by that which is beyond Him (if, indeed, there be anything beyond Him), and how there is an absolute necessity [on their theory] to conceive of many Fathers, and many Pleromas
sources.raw_question: Can anything exist beyond or outside the Father of all, such as the Gnostic Pleroma or other realms?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIX.—Earthly things may be the type of heavenly, but the latter cannot be the types of others still superior and unknown; nor can we, without absolute madness, maintain that God is known to us only as the type of a still unknown and superior being.
sources.answer: No. On the Gnostic scheme the Father is defective regarding the world outside the Pleroma and the Demiurge regarding the world within it, so neither is perfect and comprehends all things. The true God's greatness is not defective but contains all things, is above every name, and is present with each of us.
sources.quote: they represent neither of them as being perfect and comprehending all things. For the former will be defective in regard to the whole world formed outside of the Pleroma, and the latter in respect of that [ideal] world which was formed within the Pleroma
sources.raw_question: Can a God who is limited in extent, like the Gnostic Father bounded by the Pleroma or the Demiurge excluded from it, be the God of all?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter I.—There is but one God: the impossibility of its being otherwise.
sources.answer: No. If something is outside the Pleroma, the Pleroma is either contained by it or separated from it by some third existence. Any such third existence would bound both and be greater than both. This produces an endless regress of containers, so thought would never rest in one God and would drift away from the true God.
sources.quote: so that their thoughts would never rest in one God, but, in consequence of seeking after more than exists, would wander away to that which has no existence, and depart from the true God.
sources.raw_question: Can something exist outside the Gnostic Pleroma, or separated from the first God by an infinite distance, without contradiction?

question: Will the wicked see Christ in the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, at the last judgment?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: No. The sight of the form of God is granted only to the pure in heart, who shall see God. The wicked will see Christ only in the form of the Son of man, to their damnation.
sources.quote: for the sight of the form of God will not be shown except to the pure in heart, for they shall see God; that is, to the godly only, to whose love He promises this very thing, that He will show Himself to them
sources.raw_question: Will the wicked see Christ in the form of God at the judgment?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: No. At the judgment all, the ungodly included, will see Christ in the form of the Son of man, the form he took on. For the wicked this sight will be penal and evil. The vision of God's unchangeable and invisible substance, "face to face," is promised to the pure in heart alone.
sources.quote: This is the form of the Son of man, the form which has been taken, the form that will appear in judgment, not only to the righteous, but also to the ungodly; and the sight of this form will not be for good to those who are wicked.
sources.raw_question: Will the wicked see Christ at the judgment in the same way the righteous will see God in eternal life?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: No. The ungodly will see the Judge only in the form of the Son of man, though in glory and not in the lowliness in which he was judged. Only the pure in heart shall see God. The face-to-face vision of the form of God is the highest reward promised to the just. If the Son appeared to the ungodly in his equality with the Father, his promise to manifest himself to those who love him would mean nothing special.
sources.quote: But the ungodly without doubt will not see that form of God in which He is equal to the Father. For they are not pure in heart; and “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.”
sources.raw_question: Will the wicked at the last judgment see the Son in the form of God in which he is equal to the Father?

question: Does God know things successively or temporally, as humans do, so that His knowledge passes from one object to another or gains something new as events happen in time?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Word of God is in All Things Equal to the Father, from Whom It is.
sources.answer: No. Each divine Person sees all things in their knowledge, wisdom and essence simultaneously. God does not know by parts or by turning attention from one object to another. There is nothing He does not always see.
sources.quote: sees all things simultaneously, whereof there is not one that He does not always see
sources.raw_question: Does God know things successively, one part after another, as humans do?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God from the Trinities We Have Spoken of.
sources.answer: No. God's wisdom holds past, future and present all as present, and he does not think things one after another but embraces all that he knows simultaneously in one eternal, unchangeable and ineffable vision. Human knowing, by contrast, depends on sense, memory and unstable conjecture of the future from the past.
sources.quote: nor yet are things thought severally, so that thought passes from one to another, but all things simultaneously are at hand in one glance
sources.raw_question: Does God know things past and future successively, the way human thought passes from one object to another?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > How Man is the Image of God. Whether the Woman is Not Also the Image of God. How the Saying of the Apostle, that the Man is the Image of God, But the Woman is the Glory of the Man, is to Be Understood Figuratively and Mystically.
sources.answer: No. God does not see after the manner of time, and nothing new takes place in His knowledge when things are done transitorily in time, unlike the way temporal things affect the senses of animals, men, or even angels.
sources.quote: For God sees not after the way of time, neither does anything new take place in His vision and knowledge, when anything is done in time and transitorily
sources.raw_question: Does anything new occur in God's vision and knowledge when things happen in time?

question: Does the scriptural statement that God is love help us discern the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > That He Who Loves His Brother, Loves God; Because He Loves Love Itself, Which is of God, and is God.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine replies to the objector that whoever sees love does see the Trinity, though he must be helped to recognize it. Love is always love of something, so it involves one who loves, the love itself, and what is loved. This is a trace of the Trinity.
sources.quote: but when I see love, I do not see in it the Trinity. Nay, but thou dost see the Trinity if thou seest love.
sources.raw_question: If God is love, does one who sees love thereby see the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: Love involves three: one who loves, that which is loved, and love itself. Through this, those with understanding begin, however feebly, to discern the Trinity.
sources.quote: by means, too, of love, which in the Holy Scriptures is called God, by which, first of all, those who have understanding begin also, however feebly, to discern the Trinity, to wit, one that loves, and that which is loved, and love
sources.raw_question: How can love, which Scripture calls God, help us begin to discern the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How There is a Trinity in the Very Simplicity of God. Whether and How the Trinity that is God is Manifested from the Trinities Which Have Been Shown to Be in Men.
sources.answer: Yes, in some degree. When love, which Scripture calls God, is considered, a trinity begins to appear: one that loves, that which is loved, and love. The full sight of this was beyond the mind's weakness, so Augustine turned to the more familiar image in the human mind.
sources.quote: a trinity began to dawn upon us a little, i.e. one that loves, and that which is loved, and love.
sources.raw_question: Does the scriptural statement that God is love point toward a trinity in God?

question: Does the divine name Jehovah signify God's faithfulness in fulfilling his promises (as argued from Exodus 6:2-3), rather than his necessary, immutable Being?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. That reading is strained and remote, and it ignores Exod. 3:14-15, which best explains the name. The name had been revealed long before Exod. 6 (Gen. 4:1; 15:2, 7). Its primary meaning, as the opponent admits, is Being: God is Being itself, necessarily existing, independent and immutable.
sources.quote: the most obvious reason of the name is, that God is Being itself, necessarily existing, independent, immutable, always the same
sources.raw_question: Does the name Jehovah mean God's faithfulness in performing his promises, as argued from Exodus 6:2-3, rather than his necessary being?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. The primary signification of Jehovah is Being: God is Being itself, necessarily existing, independent and immutable, as Mal. 3:6 shows. Giving being to other things is only a secondary notion, and giving being to promises (fulfilling them) is a still more remote, metaphorical sense that is strained and far-fetched.
sources.quote: the most obvious reason of the name is, that God is Being itself, necessarily existing, independent, immutable, always the same ; according to that of Mal. iii. 6, “I am the Lord, (Jehovah,) I change “not.”
sources.raw_question: Does the divine name Jehovah properly signify God's faithfulness in fulfilling promises rather than his necessary, immutable Being?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. If Jehovah imports the eternal and immutable God, the same yesterday, today and for ever, that consideration is itself the strongest ground of confidence that he will never fail of his word. Moreover many passages where God declares 'I am Jehovah' have no reference to promises at all, and would lose their pertinency on the opponent's reading.
sources.quote: might not the consideration thereof be very proper to raise in men’s’ minds the greatest confidence and assurance imaginable, that he should never fail of his word ?
sources.raw_question: Does God's reminding Israel of the name Jehovah when about to fulfil his promise to Abraham show that the name means 'one faithful to his word'?

question: Does Psalm 147:4, which says God 'calls the stars all by their names,' prove that God himself invented and imposed the names of the stars and other created things, as Eunomius claimed?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. If God had given the star names in human use, he would be the author of the names of Greek idol gods and would sanction the myths attached to them, which is unworthy of God. The phrase means rather that God knows each star exactly and individually. It is like the way a man knows by name someone familiar to him, so God's knowledge reaches the minutest particulars.
sources.quote: His accurate knowledge extends to the minutest of them, and that He knows each particular respecting them, just as a man knows one who is familiar to him by name.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that God 'calls the stars all by their names' mean that God himself spoke and invented the names of the stars, as Eunomius claimed?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The verse has nothing to do with the question of names. It teaches that nothing is unknown to God, expressed through the human image of numbering and naming. It does not mean God knows things by counting units or that He gives verbal names.
sources.quote: in order that we may be taught by Holy Scripture that nothing is unknown to God, it tells us that the multitude of the stars is numbered by Him
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 147:4, "He telleth the number of the stars; He calleth them all by their names," prove that God imposed names on things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The verse teaches that God has exact knowledge of each individual star, just as a man shows accurate knowledge of a familiar person by calling him by name. To make God the author of the star names would make Him the sanctioner of the idolatrous and mythological names the Greeks gave them, which is monstrous.
sources.quote: David supports our opinion, in teaching us by this utterance, not that God gives the stars their names, but that He has an exact knowledge of them, after the fashion of men
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 147:4, which says God 'calleth them all by their names,' prove that God is the inventor of the names of created things such as the stars?

question: What does Hebrews 1:6, "When again He bringeth the first-born into the world, let all the angels of God worship Him," refer to?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He further very appositely expounds the meaning of the term “Only-Begotten,“ and of the term “First born,“ four times used by the Apostle.
sources.answer: It refers to the Lord's manifestation at the last day, his second coming in judgment. The word "again" signals this. Just as every knee bows at the name of Jesus, a human name taken for our sakes, so the First-born, a title also given for our sakes, is worshipped by all the supramundane creation when he comes again to judge the world.
sources.quote: the addition of “again” asserts that manifestation of the Lord of all which shall take place at the last day.
sources.raw_question: What does Hebrews 1:6, "When again He bringeth the first-born into the world," refer to?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then again admirably discusses the term πρωτότοκος as it is four times employed by the Apostle.
sources.answer: It refers to Christ's second coming as Judge at the end of the ages. The word 'again' shows that this is a repetition of something that has already happened once. At that coming He appears no longer in the form of a servant but enthroned in glory, and He is worshipped by all the angels.
sources.quote: He signifies, therefore, by the phrase, the dread appearing of the Judge at the end of the ages, when He is seen no more in the form of a servant, but seated in glory upon the throne of His kingdom
sources.raw_question: What does Hebrews 1:6, 'When again He bringeth the first-begotten into the world,' refer to?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He further very appositely expounds the meaning of the term “Only-Begotten,“ and of the term “First born,“ four times used by the Apostle.
sources.answer: The word "again" shows that it refers to the Lord's manifestation at the last day.
