The First-born, so named for our sakes, will then be worshipped by all the supramundane creation when He comes again to judge the world. Gregory compares this to every knee bowing at the human name of Jesus, though the Son is above every name.
sources.quote: the addition of “again” asserts that manifestation of the Lord of all which shall take place at the last day.
sources.raw_question: What does the unqualified title "first-born" mean in "When again He bringeth the first-born into the world, let all the angels of God worship Him"?

question: Can the Academic skeptics' arguments, including those from dreaming or madness, cast doubt on the mind's certain knowledge that it is alive?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Academic Philosophy.
sources.answer: Yes. Even setting aside what comes through the bodily senses, a person knows with certainty that he is alive. This is the most inward knowledge and is not seen by the eye of the flesh, so sensory illusions cannot undermine it. Since whoever is deceived must still be alive, the one who says 'I know I am alive' can neither be deceived nor lie.
sources.quote: In regard to this, indeed, we are absolutely without any fear lest perchance we are being deceived by some resemblance of the truth; since it is certain, that he who is deceived, yet lives.
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind know anything with complete certainty, against the Academic skeptics' claim that man can know nothing?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Academic Philosophy.
sources.answer: No. The person does not claim 'I know I am awake' or 'I know I am not mad', but 'I know I am alive'. Sleeping, dreaming and being mad all belong to a living man, so whether he is asleep or mad he is still alive. Such deceptions therefore cannot touch this knowledge.
sources.quote: But he who is certain of the knowledge of his own life, does not therein say, I know I am awake, but, I know I am alive; therefore, whether he be asleep or awake, he is alive.
sources.raw_question: Do the skeptical objections from dreaming or madness undermine a person's certainty that he is alive?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Academic Philosophy.
sources.answer: No. There are two kinds of knowable things: those the mind perceives through the bodily senses and those it perceives by itself. The skeptics argued much against the senses, but they could never throw doubt on the certain perceptions the mind has of itself, such as 'I know that I am alive.'
sources.quote: these philosophers have babbled much against the bodily senses, but have never been able to throw doubt upon those most certain perceptions of things true, which the mind knows by itself, such as is that which I have mentioned, I know that I am alive
sources.raw_question: Can the Academic skeptics' arguments cast doubt on what the mind knows by itself, such as the knowledge that one is alive?

question: Did Christ conquer the devil by righteousness or by power, and why?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Man Was to Be Rescued from the Power of the Devil, Not by Power, But by Righteousness.
sources.answer: Because the devil had become a lover of power and a forsaker and assailant of righteousness. God, who could easily have overpowered any creature, willed that the devil be conquered by righteousness. In this way men, imitating Christ, would also learn to conquer the devil by righteousness and not by power.
sources.quote: it pleased God, that in order to the rescuing of man from the grasp of the devil, the devil should be conquered, not by power, but by righteousness; and that so also men, imitating Christ, should seek to conquer the devil by righteousness, not by power.
sources.raw_question: Why did God choose to overcome the devil by righteousness rather than by His omnipotent power?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith.
sources.answer: By righteousness. Augustine holds that it was needful for the devil to be conquered by Christ not through power but through righteousness. He also holds that no one is set free from the devil's dominion except through Christ, by the forgiveness of sins.
sources.quote: It is shown also at length that it was needful that the devil should be conquered by Christ, not by power, but by righteousness.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ overcome the devil by power or by righteousness?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Unobligated Death of Christ Has Freed Those Who Were Liable to Death.
sources.answer: First by righteousness, then by power. By righteousness, because he had no sin and was slain most unjustly. By power, because he rose and lived again, never to die. Yet our justification and release through forgiveness of sins depend on his conquering by righteousness, not by power.
sources.quote: And therefore He conquered the devil first by righteousness, and afterwards by power: namely, by righteousness, because He had no sin, and was slain by him most unjustly; but by power, because having been dead He lived again
sources.raw_question: Did Christ conquer the devil by righteousness or by power?

question: Does Asterius's teaching that God's Wisdom and Power coexists with God unoriginately imply that there is more than one Unoriginate, contradicting the Arian claim that only the Father is unoriginate?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: Yes. Asterius, though an Arian who insists the Unoriginate is one, says God's proper wisdom and power is coexistent with Him and without beginning. Since what is coexistent coexists not with itself but with another, he thereby admits another Unoriginate alongside God, contradicting the Arian question 'Is the Unoriginate one or two?'
sources.quote: by speaking still of a wisdom coexistent with Him, he declares that the Unoriginate is not simply one, but that there is another Unoriginate with Him. For what is coexistent, coexists not with itself, but with another.
sources.raw_question: Does Asterius's teaching that God's wisdom and power coexist with God unoriginately imply that there is more than one Unoriginate?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: Yes. Asterius held that God's proper power and wisdom are without beginning and co-exist with Him unoriginately. Whatever co-exists does so with another, not with itself. So by his own words there is another Unoriginate with God, and the Arians who rely on him cannot insist the Unoriginate is simply one.
sources.quote: For what is coexistent, coexists not with itself, but with another.
sources.raw_question: Does Asterius's teaching that God's wisdom co-exists with Him unoriginately imply more than one unoriginate?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Yes. Asterius confesses one Word and one essence of Wisdom that cannot be shared out to many creatures, and the Arians say Wisdom coexists with the Father unoriginately. They thus contradict their own claim that the Father alone is unoriginate and their attack on the Church for saying the Word always exists.
sources.quote: And they battle with us for saying that the Word of God is ever, yet forget their own doctrines, and say themselves that Wisdom coexists with God unoriginately.
sources.raw_question: Does Asterius's admission that the Word and Wisdom of God is one and coexists unoriginately with God undermine the Arian denial that the Word is eternal?

question: Can the Son's office as Redeemer and Judge be fulfilled without his being eternal and having infinite powers?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 10: Whether if they (the attributes belonging to the Son) be not individually the same, they can be any thing more than faint resemblances of them, differing from t
sources.answer: No one can know this. The claim that the Son's office does not require infinite powers is only guessing in the dark, since for anything the opponent knows it may require them.
sources.quote: to which I shall only say, that it may, for any thing you know; so that this is only guessing in the dark.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's office and character be fulfilled without infinite powers?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: No, that cannot be known. Asserting it presumes a full idea of the whole work of redemption, which no man, and perhaps no angel, has. It is surer to argue for the affirmative from what we know, the greatness of redemption and the honours that follow it, than for the negative from what we do not know. Bishop Bull and others have held that the office does presuppose his eternity.
sources.quote: it is much surer arguing for the affirmative, from what we know; than for the negative, from what we know not. It is possible our proof may not be sufficient: but it is, d priori, impossible that yours should.
sources.raw_question: Is it true that the Son's office and character as Redeemer and Judge does not presuppose his eternity or infinite power?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: No, it is more perfect. By parity of reasoning one could say the Father's office of sustaining and governing the world, beginning at creation, gains nothing from his eternal past existence, which is absurd. The argument assumes the office could be discharged by a finite creature, which is the very point in question; and since a person of eternal, unlimited perfections is more capable than any creature, the office is infinitely more perfect for the eternal past duration of its holder.
sources.quote: the office must be thought as much more perfect, for the eternal past duration of his being, as God’s perfections excel those of his creatures ; and that is infinitely.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's office as Redeemer and Judge no more perfect for his having an eternal past duration of being?

question: Does a person who is not yet righteous know what righteousness is through bodily perception or from within his own mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: He knows it within himself. Righteousness belongs to the mind, not the body, so it cannot be known from outside through any bodily thing. Whoever answers truly what it is to be righteous finds the answer by seeking within himself.
sources.quote: If we know from without ourselves, we know it by some bodily thing. But this is not a thing of the body. Therefore we know in ourselves what it is to be righteous.
sources.raw_question: Does a person who is not yet righteous know what righteousness is through bodily perception or from within his own mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: No. No bodily thing is righteous in the way it is white or square. Righteousness belongs only to the mind and is a kind of beauty of the mind, which, like the mind, cannot be seen with the eyes. Even bodily signs of righteousness could not be recognized as such by someone wholly ignorant of what righteousness is.
sources.quote: For righteousness is in some sort the beauty of the mind, by which men are beautiful; very many too who are misshapen and deformed in body. And as the mind is not seen with the eyes, so neither is its beauty.
sources.raw_question: Is righteousness something perceived by the bodily senses, like color or shape?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: He finds it within himself. Righteousness is not a bodily thing, so it cannot be learned from outside through the body. Whoever answers truly about what righteousness is has found the answer within himself.
sources.quote: If we know from without ourselves, we know it by some bodily thing. But this is not a thing of the body. Therefore we know in ourselves what it is to be righteous.
sources.raw_question: Where does a person who is not yet righteous get the knowledge of what righteousness is?

question: Does Isaiah 65:16 read "they shall bless the true God" rather than "they shall bless Thee, the true God," and does the absence of "Thee" show that the Speaker himself is the true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. With "Thee" the words could be read as addressed to someone other than the speaker. Without the pronoun, "the true God" can refer only to the Speaker. The surrounding context shows that Speaker to be Christ, so the heretics' interpolation of "Thee" is a dishonest distortion.
sources.quote: Had the words been Thee, the true God, then they might have been interpreted as spoken to another. The true God can refer to none but the Speaker.
sources.raw_question: Does the reading "they shall bless the true God," rather than "they shall bless Thee, the true God," in Isaiah 65:16 show that the Speaker himself is the true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. The text reads 'They shall bless the true God'; the heretics fraudulently inserted 'Thee'. With 'Thee' the second-person pronoun would imply that another is being addressed. Without it, the true God who is blessed is the Speaker himself.
sources.quote: If Thee be retained, the pronoun of the second person implies that Another is being addressed; if Thee be omitted, True God, the object of the sentence, is the Speaker.
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah 65:16 read 'They shall bless Thee, the true God', so that it addresses the Father alone as true God, as against the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. Had the text said 'Thee, the true God,' it could have been taken as addressed to someone other than the Speaker. As written, 'the true God' can refer to none but the Speaker. The preceding verses show that this Speaker is the one who stretched out his hands to an unbelieving people.
sources.quote: Had the words been Thee, the true God, then they might have been interpreted as spoken to another. The true God can refer to none but the Speaker.
sources.raw_question: Does the absence of the second-person pronoun ('Thee, the true God') in Isaiah 65:16 show that the 'true God' named there is the Speaker himself?

question: Can knowledge of God's nature, power and dispensations be derived from numerological speculation on letters, syllables and numbers, as the Marcosian and Valentinian Gnostics attempted?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XVI.—Absurd interpretations of the Marcosians.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus treats the Marcosian reckoning of the Monad, Dyad, Decad, Duodecad and Triacontad, and the reading of the lost sheep and drachma as a defection of an Æon, as inflated wise folly. Such speculation frigidly and perversely tears apart the greatness of God's truly unspeakable power and his dispensations by reducing them to Alpha and Beta and to arithmetic. Those who follow such fables separate from the Church and condemn themselves.
sources.quote: who so frigidly and perversely pull to pieces the greatness of the truly unspeakable power, and the dispensations of God in themselves so striking, by means of Alpha and Beta, and through the aid of numbers
sources.raw_question: Can the nature of God and his saving dispensations be uncovered by numerological speculation on letters and numbers, as the Marcosians do with the Æons and the parables of the lost sheep and the lost coin?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XVI.—Absurd interpretations of the Marcosians.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus says such numerology frigidly and perversely pulls to pieces the truly unspeakable greatness of God's power and his striking dispensations. The more these teachers think they excel in wisdom, the greater fools they show themselves to be. Their notion that they can conceive of something beyond God is a deceit implanted by wicked spirits.
sources.quote: so frigidly and perversely pull to pieces the greatness of the truly unspeakable power, and the dispensations of God in themselves so striking, by means of Alpha and Beta, and through the aid of numbers
sources.raw_question: Can the power and dispensations of God be understood or explained through letter and number speculation, as the Marcosian Gnostics attempted?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXV.—God is not to be sought after by means of letters, syllables, and numbers; necessity of humility in such investigations.
sources.answer: No. Inquiry into God by numbers, syllables and letters is uncertain because such systems are varied and can be bent in any direction, even against the truth. Rather, numbers and created things should be adapted to the true doctrine already received, for system does not spring from numbers but numbers from a system, just as God does not derive His being from things made but things made from God.
sources.quote: For system does not spring out of numbers, but numbers from a system; nor does God derive His being from things made, but things made from God. For all things originate from one and the same God.
sources.raw_question: Can knowledge about God be properly derived from numerology, syllables, and letters, as the Valentinian Gnostics attempted?

question: Is Adam, the first man, saved by Christ, or is he excluded from salvation as Tatian taught?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIII.—Arguments in opposition to Tatian, showing that it was consonant to divine justice and mercy that the first Adam should first partake in that salvation offered to all by Christ.
sources.answer: Yes. Those who deny Adam's salvation speak falsely, because Adam is the sheep that had perished and has now been found by the Lord. If that lost sheep had not been found, the whole human race would still be held in perdition. To deny his salvation gains nothing; it only makes one a heretic and a patron of the serpent and of death.
sources.quote: they do not believe that the sheep which had perished has been found. For if it has not been found, the whole human race is still held in a state of perdition.
sources.raw_question: Was Adam, the first man who sinned, himself saved by Christ, contrary to Tatian's claim that he was excluded from salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIII.—Arguments in opposition to Tatian, showing that it was consonant to divine justice and mercy that the first Adam should first partake in that salvation offered to all by Christ.
sources.answer: Adam is saved. Death is destroyed only if the man over whom death first gained dominion is set free, because his salvation is death's destruction. Paul's words 'Death is swallowed up in victory' could not justly be said if Adam remained under death. When the Lord gives life to man, that is, to Adam, death is destroyed at the same time.
sources.quote: This could not be said with justice, if that man, over whom death did first obtain dominion, were not set free. For his salvation is death’s destruction.
sources.raw_question: Is Adam, the first man, saved by Christ, or is he excluded from salvation as Tatian taught?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIII.—Arguments in opposition to Tatian, showing that it was consonant to divine justice and mercy that the first Adam should first partake in that salvation offered to all by Christ.
sources.answer: Yes. Since man is saved, it is fitting that the original man be saved; it would be absurd that the one first and most deeply injured by the enemy should not be rescued by Him who conquered the enemy, while his children begotten in captivity were. Otherwise the enemy would not appear conquered, since the old spoils would remain with him.
sources.quote: For it is too absurd to maintain, that he who was so deeply injured by the enemy, and was the first to suffer captivity, was not rescued by Him who conquered the enemy, but that his children were
sources.raw_question: Was it fitting or necessary that Adam himself, the first-formed man, be saved by Christ, rather than only his descendants?

question: Does God need the sacrifices, offerings and good works that people give Him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVIII.—Concerning sacrifices and oblations, and those who truly offer them.
sources.answer: No. God needs nothing, but He accepts our good works so that He may repay us with His own good things. We offer to Him in order to give thanks and so that we are not unfruitful. Scripture shows that kindness to the poor is a loan to the Lord, and Christ rewards what is done for the least.
sources.quote: For God, who stands in need of nothing, takes our good works to Himself for this purpose, that He may grant us a recompense of His own good things
sources.raw_question: Does God need the offerings and good works that people give Him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVIII.—Concerning sacrifices and oblations, and those who truly offer them.
sources.answer: No. God does not need any sacrifice from us. The one who offers is himself glorified in what he offers if the gift is accepted, because the gift shows honour and affection toward the King. Man is thereby counted grateful and receives the honour that flows from God.
sources.quote: not that He stands in need of a sacrifice from us, but that he who offers is himself glorified in what he does offer, if his gift be accepted.
sources.raw_question: Does God need the sacrifices and offerings that people make to Him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVII.—Proof that God did not appoint the Levitical dispensation for His own sake, or as requiring such service; for He does, in fact, need nothing from men.
sources.answer: No. God did not seek sacrifices and holocausts for their own sake but faith, obedience and righteousness, for the sake of the people's salvation. The prophets Jeremiah, Isaiah, Zechariah, Hosea and David show that what God delights in is loving-kindness, justice, mercy and hearing his voice. The sacrificial precepts were received as secondary, not of primary importance.
sources.quote: From all these it is evident that God did not seek sacrifices and holocausts from them, but faith, and obedience, and righteousness, because of their salvation.
sources.raw_question: Did God command the Israelites to offer sacrifices and burnt-offerings because he needed them or valued them for their own sake?

question: Is the human mind a body, such as air, fire, blood or the brain, or a function or tempering of the body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Every Mind Knows Certainly Three Things Concerning Itself—That It Understands, that It Is, and that It Lives.
sources.answer: No. Nothing is rightly said to be known unless its substance is known. When the mind knows itself with certainty, it knows its own substance. Yet the mind is not at all certain whether it is air, fire, some body, or some function of body. Since it is certain of what it is and uncertain of these, it is none of them.
sources.quote: But it is certain about itself, as those things which are said above prove convincingly; although it is not at all certain whether itself is air, or fire, or some body, or some function of body. Therefore it is not any of these.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold the mind to be air, fire, brain, blood, atoms, or the combination or tempering of the body
sources.raw_question: Is the mind a body, such as air, fire or the brain, or a combination or tempering of the body in which understanding inheres as a quality in a subject?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Every Mind Knows Certainly Three Things Concerning Itself—That It Understands, that It Is, and that It Lives.
sources.answer: No. Whenever the mind knows itself it knows its own substance, since nothing is rightly said to be known while its substance is unknown. The mind is certain about itself, yet it is not at all certain whether it is air, fire, some body, or some function of body. Therefore it is none of these, and it is only that which it is certain that it is.
sources.quote: But it is certain about itself, as those things which are said above prove convincingly; although it is not at all certain whether itself is air, or fire, or some body, or some function of body. Therefore it is not any of these.
sources.raised_by_detail: philosophers who hold the mind to be corporeal or a tempering of the body
sources.raw_question: Is the human mind a body, such as air or fire, or a function or tempering together of the body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Opinions of Philosophers Respecting the Substance of the Soul. The Error of Those Who are of Opinion that the Soul is Corporeal, Does Not Arise from Defective Knowledge of the Soul, But from Their Adding There to Something Foreign to It. What is Meant by Finding.
sources.answer: No. The mind is a substance but not corporeal, since it does not occupy a smaller extension of place with a smaller part of itself and a greater with a greater. Those who think it bodily do not lack knowledge of the mind but add to it bodily qualities without which they cannot conceive any nature at all.
sources.quote: any one who sees that the nature of the mind is at once substance, and yet not corporeal,—that is, that it does not occupy a less extension of place with a less part of itself, and a greater with a greater
sources.raised_by_detail: philosophers who held the soul to be blood, brain, heart, atoms, air or fire
sources.raw_question: Is the human mind (soul) a corporeal thing, such as blood, brain, heart, atoms, air or fire?

question: Should the Old Testament prophecies of a restored Jerusalem and a renewed earth, where people build houses and plant vineyards, be read literally of the earthly kingdom of the righteous rather than allegorically as heavenly blessings?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXV.—He contends that these testimonies already alleged cannot be understood allegorically of celestial blessings, but that they shall have their fulfilment after the coming of Antichrist, and the resurrection, in the terrestrial Jerusalem. To the former prophecies he subjoins others drawn from Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the Apocalypse of John.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus holds that these prophecies cannot be understood of super-celestial matters, since Scripture says God will show his glory to the whole earth under heaven. In the times of the kingdom the earth is restored by Christ and Jerusalem is rebuilt after the pattern of the Jerusalem above. Nothing in these promises can be allegorized; all are steadfast, true and substantial, made by God for the enjoyment of the righteous.
sources.quote: Now all these things being such as they are, cannot be understood in reference to super-celestial matters; “for God,” it is said, “will show to the whole earth that is under heaven thy glory.”
sources.raw_question: Can the prophecies of a restored Jerusalem and a renewed earth be interpreted allegorically as referring only to super-celestial or heavenly blessings?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXV.—He contends that these testimonies already alleged cannot be understood allegorically of celestial blessings, but that they shall have their fulfilment after the coming of Antichrist, and the resurrection, in the terrestrial Jerusalem. To the former prophecies he subjoins others drawn from Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the Apocalypse of John.
sources.answer: No. Those who allegorize such prophecies will not be consistent with themselves and are refuted by the very wording of the texts. These words were spoken about the resurrection of the just, which follows the coming of Antichrist and the destruction of the nations under his rule. The righteous will then reign on this earth, and God will show Jerusalem's glory 'to the whole earth under heaven,' so the prophecies cannot refer to super-celestial matters.
sources.quote: For all these and other words were unquestionably spoken in reference to the resurrection of the just, which takes place after the coming of Antichrist, and the destruction of all nations under his rule
sources.raw_question: Can the Old Testament prophecies of a restored Jerusalem, where people build houses, plant vineyards and multiply on the earth, be interpreted allegorically as heavenly blessings?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXIV.—He fortifies his opinions with regard to the temporal and earthly kingdom of the saints after their resurrection, by the various testimonies of Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, and Daniel; also by the parable of the servants watching, to whom the Lord promised that He would minister.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus holds that these promises describe the literal reign of the righteous on a renewed earth after the resurrection of the just, which follows the coming of Antichrist. Attempts to allegorize such prophecies end up inconsistent and are refuted by the wording of the texts themselves. In that kingdom the righteous are strengthened by the sight of the Lord and through him learn to share in the glory of God the Father.
sources.quote: For all these and other words were unquestionably spoken in reference to the resurrection of the just, which takes place after the coming of Antichrist, and the destruction of all nations under his rule
sources.raw_question: Should Isaiah's prophecies of a rebuilt Jerusalem, where the people build houses and plant vineyards and enjoy their fruit, be read literally as referring to the earthly kingdom of the righteous after the resurrection?

question: When Scripture says heaven and earth will pass away, does this mean the substance of creation will be annihilated, or only its present form?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXV.—He contends that these testimonies already alleged cannot be understood allegorically of celestial blessings, but that they shall have their fulfilment after the coming of Antichrist, and the resurrection, in the terrestrial Jerusalem. To the former prophecies he subjoins others drawn from Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the Apocalypse of John.
sources.answer: No. Only the 'fashion' of this world passes away, meaning the conditions in which transgression occurred and man grew old. The substance and essence of creation remain, because the One who established it is faithful and true. A new heaven and new earth follow, in which renewed man dwells incorruptibly with God.
sources.quote: For neither is the substance nor the essence of the creation annihilated (for faithful and true is He who has established it), but “the fashion of the world passeth away;”
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says heaven and earth will pass away, does this mean the substance of creation will be annihilated?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXVI.—Men shall be actually raised: the world shall not be annihilated; but there shall be various mansions for the saints, according to the rank allotted to each individual. All things shall be subject to God the Father, and so shall He be all in all.
sources.answer: Only its present fashion passes away; the substance and essence of creation is not annihilated. God who established it is faithful and true, and what passes is the temporary form in which transgression occurred, after which there will be a new heaven and new earth in which renewed man converses with God forever.
sources.quote: For neither is the substance nor the essence of the creation annihilated (for faithful and true is He who has established it), but “the fashion of the world passeth away;”
sources.raw_question: Will the substance of the created world be annihilated at the end, or only its present form?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter III.—Answer to the cavils of the Gnostics. We are not to suppose that the true God can be changed, or come to an end because the heavens, which are His throne and the earth, His footstool, shall pass away.
sources.answer: It means that the fashion or figure of this world passes away, not that all being is annihilated. Paul says 'the figure of this world passeth away', and the Psalm says God will change the heavens like a vesture. When that happens, God remains, together with his servants, whose seed is established forever.
sources.quote: pointing out plainly what things they are that pass away, and who it is that doth endure for ever—God, together with His servants.
sources.raw_question: What does Scripture mean by the passing away of heaven and earth?

question: Is the will of God the first and highest cause of ordinary and rare natural phenomena, such as weather, the motions of stars, births of animals, eclipses and earthquakes, rather than chance or bodily causes alone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Original Cause of All Things is from God.
sources.answer: No. Of all such things, whether usual or rare, the first and chief cause is only the will of God. The Psalm, after listing fire, hail, snow and stormy wind, immediately adds "fulfilling His word" so that no one would think they come about by chance, from bodily causes alone, or from spiritual causes existing apart from God's will.
sources.quote: of which indeed the first and chief cause is only the will of God
sources.raw_question: Are ordinary natural phenomena such as weather, the motions of stars and births of animals caused by chance or by corporeal causes apart from God's will?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Will of God is the Higher Cause of All Corporeal Change. This is Shown by an Example.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine holds that none of these things takes place without the will of God, though most people do not perceive it because of their regularity or because they are explained by nearer causes. Philosophers assign them to other causes, which may be true but only proximate, while failing to see the cause higher than all others, the will of God.
sources.quote: true causes perhaps, but proximate ones, while they are not able to see at all the cause that is higher than all others, that is, the will of God
sources.raw_question: Is the will of God the highest cause even of regular natural changes and rare natural phenomena such as eclipses and earthquakes?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > Why Miracles are Not Usual Works.
sources.answer: Yes. The divine power governs the whole spiritual and corporeal creation, so God sends the seasonal rains, draws the sap up the vine to make wine, clothes trees with leaves, and gives life to every living thing at birth. The same God who works these things ordinarily also worked the corresponding miracles: Elijah's rain, water into wine, Aaron's blossoming rod, and the rod turned into a serpent.
sources.quote: Who draws up the sap through the root of the vine to the bunch of grapes, and makes the wine, except God; who, while man plants and waters, Himself giveth the increase?
sources.raw_question: Are ordinary natural processes, such as rain, the growth of grapes, and the life of animals, the work of God in the same way that miracles are?

question: Does the phrase 'the acceptable year of the Lord' mean that Christ preached for only one year after his baptism and suffered in the twelfth month?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXII.—The thirty Æons are not typified by the fact that Christ was baptized in His thirtieth year: He did not suffer in the twelfth month after His baptism, but was more than fifty years old when He died.
sources.answer: No. Christ was beginning to be about thirty when he was baptized, and he taught into a more advanced age, past forty. Irenaeus holds that limiting him to one year destroys his whole work and robs him of the age in which he most excelled as a teacher. This is confirmed by the Gospel and by the elders in Asia who received the account from John and the other apostles.
sources.quote: they are forgetful to their own disadvantage, destroying His whole work, and robbing Him of that age which is both more necessary and more honourable than any other; that more advanced age, I mean, during which also as a teacher He excelled all others.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord' mean that Christ's public ministry lasted only one year, so that he suffered in the twelfth month after his baptism?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXII.—The thirty Æons are not typified by the fact that Christ was baptized in His thirtieth year: He did not suffer in the twelfth month after His baptism, but was more than fifty years old when He died.
sources.answer: No. The Gospel of John records that after his baptism the Lord went up to Jerusalem for the passover on at least three separate occasions: after the wedding at Cana, when he healed the paralytic, and finally before his passion. Three passovers cannot fall within one year, so the Valentinians must give up either their interpretation or the Gospel.
sources.quote: Now, that these three occasions of the passover are not included within one year, every person whatever must acknowledge.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ preach for only one year after his baptism, as the Valentinians claimed from the phrase 'the acceptable year of the Lord'?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXII.—The thirty Æons are not typified by the fact that Christ was baptized in His thirtieth year: He did not suffer in the twelfth month after His baptism, but was more than fifty years old when He died.
sources.answer: No. The prophet speaks in figures, so 'year' does not mean twelve months, nor does 'day' mean twelve hours. The acceptable year is the whole present time, from Christ's advent to the consummation, in which people are called and made acceptable to God. The 'day of retribution', the judgment, follows it. If the Lord had preached for only one year, the prophecy would be false, because that year has passed and the judgment has not yet come.
sources.quote: so also the year there mentioned does not denote one which consists of twelve months, but the whole time of faith during which men hear and believe the preaching of the Gospel, and those become acceptable to God who unite themselves to Him.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'the acceptable year of the Lord' in Isaiah's prophecy mean that Christ preached for only one year after his baptism and suffered in the twelfth month?

question: When the apostles preached to the Gentiles, did they proclaim the Creator of the world, the God of the law and prophets, as the true God and Father of Jesus Christ, rather than some other God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter V.—Christ and His apostles, without any fraud, deception, or hypocrisy, preached that one God, the Father, was the founder of all things. They did not accommodate their doctrine to the prepossessions of their hearers.
sources.answer: Yes. The apostles told the Gentiles to abandon idols and worship the true God who created, nourishes and preserves the human race. They also told them to look for his Son Jesus Christ, who redeemed us with his blood and will come in his Father's power to judge. The Creator and the Father of Christ are therefore one and the same God.
sources.quote: worship the true God, who had created and made all the human family, and, by means of His creation, did nourish, increase, strengthen, and preserve them in being; and that they might look for His Son Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles preach to the Gentiles that the Creator of mankind is the true God and the Father of Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. On the Areopagus no Jews were present, so Paul could preach God with full freedom. Even there he proclaimed God as Maker of the world and all things in it. This God made one race of men, gives life and breath to all, and will judge the world by the man Jesus, whom he raised from the dead. The same appears at Lystra, where Paul preached the living God who made heaven, earth and sea. So the apostles' God is the Creator and no higher, different deity.
sources.quote: Now in this passage he does not only declare to them God as the Creator of the world, no Jews being present, but that He did also make one race of men to dwell upon all the earth
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who distinguish the Creator from the Father of Christ
sources.raw_question: When the apostle Paul preached freely to Gentiles, did he proclaim a God other than the Creator of the world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. In speaking to Cornelius, Peter retained the God already known through the law and prophets and added only the knowledge of the Son, whom men did not know. Had Peter known of another god, he would have said so freely to the awe-struck Gentiles. Instead he testified that Jesus is that God's Son and the Judge of the living and the dead.
sources.quote: The apostles, therefore, did preach the Son of God, of whom men were ignorant; and His advent, to those who had been already instructed as to God; but they did not bring in another god.
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles preach a new God, distinct from the God of the Jews, when they preached Jesus Christ to the Gentiles?

question: What does Paul mean in 1 Corinthians 13:12 by saying that in this life we see God "through a glass, in an enigma"?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Of the Term ‘Enigma,’ And of Tropical Modes of Speech.
sources.answer: By "glass" he means an image, and by "enigma" an obscure likeness that is difficult to see through. The two phrases form one sentence and must be given a single meaning. In this life we know God only through likenesses adapted to our understanding, and these are obscure, not clear sight.
sources.quote: as by the word glass he meant to signify an image, so by that of enigma any likeness you will, but yet one obscure, and difficult to see through.
sources.raw_question: What does the apostle Paul mean by saying we now see God "through a glass, in an enigma"?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Augustin Dwells Still Further on the Disparity Between the Trinity Which is in Man, and the Trinity Which is God. The Trinity is Now Seen Through a Glass by the Help of Faith, that It May Hereafter Be More Clearly Seen in the Promised Sight Face to Face.
sources.answer: It means using the mind's trinity as an image and referring what one sees in it to God, whose image it is. Through it one knows God by conjecture until the sight face to face. Merely beholding the structure of one's own mind is not enough, for the apostle says we see 'through a glass,' not that we see a glass. In the promised vision we will see the incorporeal, indivisible, unchangeable Trinity more clearly than we now see its image in ourselves.
sources.quote: For the apostle does not say, We see now a glass, but, We see now through a glass.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean in 1 Corinthians 13:12 to see God 'through a glass, in an enigma' in this life?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Apostle Says that God is Now Seen by Us Through a Glass.
sources.answer: The "glass" is a mirror, in which nothing is discerned but an image. The image in which we now see God is the image of God which we ourselves are; by examining this image, as in a mirror, we can see in some way Him by whom we are made. This is why Augustine has sought the Trinity through its image in the human mind.
sources.quote: in a glass nothing is discerned but an image. We have endeavored, then, so to do; in order that we might see in some way or other by this image which we are, Him by whom we are made, as by a glass.
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean by seeing God now "through a glass" (1 Corinthians 13:12), and how does it relate to the human mind as the image of God?

question: What does it mean that believers are sealed by the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13; 4:30): is the sealing chiefly an assurance to believers or a marking of them as God's own possession?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Owen ultimately holds that the first sense, sealing as the impression of the Spirit's image giving assurance, is chiefly intended, without excluding the second sense of appropriating and preserving believers for God. He questions the view that the Spirit seals the promise itself, since the text says we are sealed, not the grant. Still, the stamp and character of the Spirit on our souls gives us a fresh sense of God's love and a comfortable persuasion of our acceptance with him.
sources.quote: I answer, The first, not excluding the other. We are sealed to the day of redemption, when, from the stamp, image, and character of the Spirit upon our souls, we have a fresh sense of the love of God given to us
sources.raw_question: In Scripture's language of believers being sealed by the Holy Spirit, is the sealing primarily a confirmation of God's promise to us or a marking of believers as God's own possession?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Taken from the nature of a seal, sealing is stamping the seal's image on the thing sealed. So the Spirit seals believers by really communicating the image of God to them in righteousness and true holiness. This stamp is an evidence to the soul that it is accepted with God. In the same sense Christ is said to be sealed by God (John 6:27), through the impression of God's power, wisdom and majesty upon him in his office.
sources.quote: The Spirit in believers, really communicating the image of God, in righteousness and true holiness, unto the soul, sealeth us.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that believers are sealed by the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13; 4:30)?

question: When the mind knows itself, is the knowledge (word or image) it begets equal to the mind itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > That the Image or Begotten Word of the Mind that Knows Itself is Equal to the Mind Itself.
sources.answer: Yes. When the mind knows and approves itself, its knowledge is its word, altogether on a par with it, equal, and the same. This is because the knowledge is neither of a lower essence, as with bodies, nor of a higher one, as with God. Since knowledge bears a likeness to what it knows, here the likeness is perfect and equal. So it is both image and word, and what is begotten is equal to the begetter.
sources.quote: when the mind knows and approves itself, this same knowledge is in such way its word, as that it is altogether on a par and equal with it, and the same; because it is neither the knowledge of a lower essence, as of the body, nor of a higher, as of God.
sources.raw_question: When the mind knows itself, is its knowledge (its word or image) equal to the mind itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > Why Love is Not the Offspring of the Mind, as Knowledge is So. The Solution of the Question. The Mind with the Knowledge of Itself and the Love of Itself is the Image of the Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. Knowledge is generally begotten from both the knower and the thing known, but in self-knowledge the mind alone is the parent, being both knower and known. It does not know itself as less than it is, and what it knows is its own essence, not someone else's. So it begets a knowledge equal to itself.
sources.quote: In knowing itself, then, it begets a knowledge of itself equal to itself; since it does not know itself as less than itself is
sources.raw_question: When the mind knows itself, is the knowledge it begets equal to the mind itself?

question: If the mind already knows itself and is always present to itself, why is it commanded to know itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Why the Soul is Enjoined to Know Itself. Whence Come the Errors of the Mind Concerning Its Own Substance.
sources.answer: So that it may consider itself and live according to its own nature, that is, be ordered under God, by whom it ought to be ruled, and above the things it ought to rule. The command is needed because the mind, through vicious desire, acts as though it had forgotten itself.
sources.quote: I suppose, in order that, it may consider itself, and live according to its own nature; that is, seek to be regulated according to its own nature, viz., under Him to whom it ought to be subject, and above those things to which it is to be preferred
sources.raw_question: Why is the human mind commanded to know itself, if it is always present to itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > How the Mind Knows Itself, Not in Part, But as a Whole.
sources.answer: So that it may consider itself and live according to its own nature, ordered under God who rules it and above the things it ought to rule. Through vicious desire it acts as if forgetting itself, turning from God to appropriate goods to itself, and so slips downward. The command recalls it to its proper place.
sources.quote: I suppose, in order that, it may consider itself, and live according to its own nature; that is, seek to be regulated according to its own nature, viz., under Him to whom it ought to be subject
sources.raw_question: If the mind already knows itself, why is it commanded to know itself?

question: Is the human mind, in remembering, understanding, and loving itself, a trinity that images God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Trinity Which is the Image of God is Now to Be Sought in the Noblest Part of the Mind.
sources.answer: Yes. When the mind remembers, understands, and loves itself, we discern a trinity. It is not God, but it is at last an image of God. This is why the mind must first be considered in itself, before it becomes partaker of God.
sources.quote: Well, then, the mind remembers, understands, loves itself; if we discern this, we discern a trinity, not yet indeed God, but now at last an image of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the mind's remembering, understanding, and loving itself a trinity that images God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Mind is an Image of the Trinity in Its Own Memory, and Understanding, and Will.
sources.answer: Yes, though an inadequate one. Augustine calls the highest essence that of which the human mind is an inadequate image, yet still an image. The mind always remembers, understands, and loves itself, and these three are one life, one mind, one essence, which mirrors the divine Trinity.
sources.quote: to that chiefest and highest essence, of which the human mind is an inadequate image, yet an image?
sources.raw_question: Is the human mind, in its memory, understanding, and will, an image of the divine Trinity?

question: Is the mind the image of God because it remembers, understands, and loves itself, or because it can remember, understand, and love God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether Memory is Also of Things Present.
sources.answer: No, not merely that. The mind is the image of God because it can also remember, understand, and love Him by whom it was made; in doing so it becomes wise by participating in the supreme Light. If it only remembers, understands, and loves itself without turning to God, it is foolish.
sources.quote: This trinity, then, of the mind is not therefore the image of God, because the mind remembers itself, and understands and loves itself; but because it can also remember, understand, and love Him by whom it was made.
sources.raw_question: Is the mind's trinity of remembering, understanding, and loving itself what makes it the image of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Trinity in the Mind is the Image of God, in that It Remembers, Understands, and Loves God, Which to Do is Wisdom.
sources.answer: Because it can remember, understand, and love God. Augustine holds that the mind's self-directed trinity is not by itself what makes it God's image; it is the image in that it is capable of remembering, understanding, and loving Him by whom it was made. In doing so it becomes wise; if it only knows and loves itself, it is foolish.
sources.quote: This trinity, then, of the mind is not therefore the image of God, because the mind remembers itself, and understands and loves itself; but because it can also remember, understand, and love Him by whom it was made.
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity of memory, understanding, and love in the human mind the image of God because the mind remembers, understands, and loves itself, or because it can remember, understand, and love God?

question: Is the trinity found in the mind's knowledge (scientia) of temporal things, the lower practical reason, the image of God in man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: No. Augustine distinguishes knowledge from wisdom and treats knowledge as the lower of the two. A trinity proper to knowledge does reach the inner man. Yet it is not yet to be called or thought of as the image of God.
sources.quote: although we have got now in this to something pertaining to the inner man, yet it is not yet to be either called or thought an image of God
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity found in knowledge (scientia) of temporal things the image of God in man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Thing is Made Plain by an Example. In What Way the Matter is Handled in Order to Help the Reader.
sources.answer: No. A trinity exists even in the lower power by which a person reasons about temporal things and acts in this life. But it cannot yet be called an image of God. The image must be sought in the higher power by which the mind contemplates eternal things, the noblest part of the mind, by which it knows God.
sources.quote: while manifesting that a trinity exists also in it, but not yet one that can be called an image of God
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity found in the lower, practical reason that deals with temporal things an image of God?

question: When the mind ardently seeks to know itself while still unknown to itself, does it love something unknown?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > No One at All Loves Things Unknown.
sources.answer: No. Augustine notes that his earlier examples concern seeking to know things other than oneself, so the mind's seeking of itself needs separate consideration. In the following chapter he argues that when the mind loves itself it is not unknown to itself. It is not known generically through other minds, as though by report, since nothing is more present to it than itself.
sources.quote: But since the examples which we have given belong to those who desire to know something which they themselves are not, we must take thought lest perchance some new notion appear, when the mind desires to know itself.
sources.raw_question: When the mind seeks ardently to know itself while still unknown to itself, does it love something unknown?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > That When the Mind Loves Itself, It is Not Unknown to Itself.
sources.answer: No. In the very act of seeking itself, the mind knows itself as seeking and as not knowing itself. So it cannot be altogether ignorant of itself, and it is shown to be more known to itself than unknown. This preserves the principle that nothing can be loved which is not known.
sources.quote: And therefore, in the very fact that it seeks itself, it is clearly convicted of being more known to itself than unknown. For it knows itself as seeking and as not knowing itself, in that it seeks to know itself.
sources.raw_question: When the mind ardently seeks to know itself, is it wholly unknown to itself, so that it would be loving something it does not know?

question: How do memory, understanding, and will (love) form a trinity in the human mind that images the divine Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How a Kind of Trinity Exists in the Mind Thinking of Itself. What is the Part of Thought in This Trinity.
sources.answer: Memory holds the object, which acts as a begetter. When the mind beholds itself in thought, it begets its own understanding and knowledge of itself. Love, or will, joins the begetter and the begotten as a third. So a trinity of the mind is signified by memory, intelligence, and will, an image of the divine Trinity of Begetter, Begotten, and the Love uniting them.
sources.quote: And these two, the begetter and the begotten, are coupled together by love, as by a third, which is nothing else than will, seeking or holding fast the enjoyment of something.
sources.raw_question: How is a trinity of memory, understanding, and will found in the mind, and how does it reflect begetting and love?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether Memory is Also of Things Present.
sources.answer: Memory makes the mind present to itself, understanding grasps it through its own thought, and love (will) joins the two together. When the mind turns to itself in thought, a word is formed and a trinity arises, in which the image of God is sought.
sources.quote: which makes the mind at hand to itself, so that it can be understood by its own thought, and then both be joined together by love of itself.
sources.raw_question: How do memory, understanding, and love of itself form a trinity in the human mind?

question: Can the mind love itself without also knowing itself, so that self-knowledge is a necessary third alongside the mind and its self-love in the image of the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Image of the Trinity in the Mind of Man Who Knows Himself and Loves Himself. The Mind Knows Itself Through Itself.
sources.answer: No, the mind cannot love itself unless it also knows itself. Nothing can be loved that is not known, so self-love presupposes self-knowledge. This is why, beyond the mind and its love, a third element, the mind's knowledge of itself, is required for the trinity in the mind.
sources.quote: For the mind cannot love itself, except also it know itself; for how can it love what it does not know?
sources.raw_question: Can the mind love itself without also knowing itself, so that self-knowledge is a necessary third alongside the mind and its self-love in the image of the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three Things Which are Found in Love Must Be Considered.
sources.answer: No. The mind cannot love what it does not know, so self-love presupposes self-knowledge. This supplies the missing third alongside mind and love. Nor does the mind know itself only by analogy with other minds, for it could not know other minds unless it knew itself.
sources.quote: For the mind cannot love itself, except also it know itself; for how can it love what it does not know?
sources.raw_question: Can the mind love itself without knowing itself, which would make knowledge the third member of the mental trinity?

question: What does it mean for the Son to be the image of God (Colossians 1:15-20)?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It means that all things are created in Him and through Him, so that the Father whose image He is creates in Him. Because what is created in Him is also created through Him, the nature of the Father is present in the Son who is the image.
sources.quote: And since all things which are created in Him are also created through Him, recognize that in Him Who is the image there is present the nature of Him, Whose image He is.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean for the Son to be the image of God, according to Colossians 1:15-20?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It means that all things are created in him and through him. Since the Father, whose image he is, also creates all things in him, the nature of the Father is present in the Son who is his image. Likewise the Father, abiding in him through a like nature, reconciles all things to himself in Christ.
sources.quote: Do you now perceive what it is to be the image of God? It means that all things are created in Him through Him.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean for the Son to be the image of God?

question: Can the human mind comprehend the essence of God, given that it cannot comprehend even the essence of its own soul or body?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. One who is ignorant of himself cannot take knowledge of what is above himself; ignorance of our own nature should teach us not to be astonished at the incomprehensibility of mysteries outside us. This undercuts the Eunomian claim to grasp the divine essence in a single term.
sources.quote: But how can he who is ignorant of himself take knowledge of anything that is above himself? And if a man is familiarized with such ignorance of himself, is he not plainly taught by the very fact not to be astonished at any of the mysteries that are without?
sources.raw_question: Can human beings, who cannot comprehend their own soul or body, comprehend the essence of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. We do not know the essence of our own soul: whether it is material, how it unites with the body, how its contrary passions form one thing. Nor do we know what remains of a body once its qualities are removed. If a man is ignorant of himself, he cannot claim knowledge of what is above him, and he should not be astonished at mysteries beyond him.
sources.quote: we pass our lives in ignorance of much, being ignorant first of all of ourselves, as men, and then of all things besides. For who is there who has arrived at a comprehension of his own soul?
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind comprehend the essence of God, given that it cannot comprehend even the essence of the human soul or of bodies?

question: If the title 'Father' carries the meaning of 'Ungenerate', does it follow that the two are interchangeable, so that God may be called 'the Ungenerate of the Son' in place of 'the Father of the Son'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. The title 'Father' carries two distinct ideas: one relating God to His Son, the other expressing that He depends on no prior cause. Just as 'Emperor' signifies both ruling over subjects and having no superior, yet one cannot therefore speak of the 'Unruled of subjects', so one may not transfer the meaning 'Ungenerate' onto the paternal relation and absurdly say 'the Ungenerate is Ungenerate of the Son.'
sources.quote: so the title Father supplies us with two ideas about the Deity, one relating to His Son, the other to His being dependent on no preconceivable cause.
sources.raw_question: If the title 'Father' can signify that God is Ungenerate, does it follow that 'Father' and 'Ungenerate' are interchangeable, so that one may say the Father is 'Ungenerate of the Son'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. Not all predicates said of one subject refer to the same correlative object. As Adam is both Abel's father and God's first-formed creature without being the 'first-formed of Abel', so the Father's title includes both having begotten a Son and having no prior cause, yet only the former relates to the Son. So we need not say 'Ungenerate of the Son', nor drop Ungeneracy from our thoughts about God.
sources.quote: all the things which are predicated of some one do not necessarily, in their meaning, have respect to one single object; as is plain from the aforesaid instance of Abel and Adam.
sources.raw_question: If the title 'Father' carries the same meaning as 'Ungenerate', does it follow that God may be called 'the Ungenerate of the Son' in place of 'the Father of the Son'?

question: Can Eunomius consistently hold both that ungeneracy 'follows' the Deity and that ungeneracy is God's very essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His unsuccessful attempt to be consistent with his own statements after Basil has confuted him.
sources.answer: No. Following Basil, Gregory argues that whatever 'follows' a thing must be among its externals. A thing's actual being is not external to it but expresses its very existence. So if ungeneracy follows God, it cannot also be His essence; claiming both would give one subject two beings, God Himself and a second being called Ungeneracy accompanying Him.
sources.quote: a thing which “follows” must be amongst the externals, whereas the actual Being is not one of these, but indicates the very existence of anything, so far as it does exist.
sources.raw_question: If Eunomius says that the attribute of being ungenerate 'follows' the Deity, can ungeneracy still be the very essence or being of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The thing that follows is not the same as the thing that it follows.
sources.answer: No. If Ungeneracy follows God and yet also constitutes His being, two beings are attributed to one subject. God would be as He always was, with a second being, Ungeneracy, accompanying Him and distinct from Him. Eunomius's added explanation does not remove the contradiction.
sources.quote: If Ungeneracy follows God, and yet also constitutes His being, two beings will be attributed to one and the same subject in this view
sources.raw_question: Can Eunomius consistently say both that Ungeneracy 'follows' the Deity as an attribute and that Ungeneracy is God's very being?

question: Does the simplicity of the divine essence imply that the Father's essence is identical with 'ungeneracy'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The terms 'simple' and 'ungenerate' have distinct meanings: 'simple' means uncompounded, 'ungenerate' means without origin, and they are not convertible. The essence is simple but is not 'simplicity', and likewise it is ungenerate but not 'ungeneracy'. So simplicity does not force us to define the Father's essence as ungeneracy.
sources.quote: But as the essence is simple and not simplicity, so also the essence is ungenerate and not ungeneracy.
