sources.raw_question: If the divine essence is simple, does it follow that the Father's essence is identical with 'ungeneracy'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The Eunomian argument runs: God is simple and incomposite, so whatever is predicated of him must be his nature, and therefore ungeneracy is his essence. Gregory replies that the inference fails. Simplicity means God is indivisible and without composition, while ungeneracy means he was not generated. Both are true of the one God, but neither term defines his nature.
sources.quote: There is therefore no necessity that, because the Godhead is by its nature simple, that nature should be termed ungeneracy; but in that He is indivisible and without composition, He is spoken of as simple, while in that He was not generated, He is spoken of as ungenerate.
sources.raw_question: Does the divine simplicity of God the Father imply that his title 'Ungenerate' names his very essence, so that his nature is identical with ungeneracy?

question: If God is called Father because he begot the Son, does it follow that God became Father in time and was something else, or not ungenerate, before begetting the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. The orthodox never said the Almighty became Father in process of time after being something else; Eunomius attacks a doctrine no one holds. To suppose God existed in some prior state before Fatherhood leads to absurdities, as though God passed through stages of growth, and all God's attributes, Fatherhood included, are held together simultaneously in his everlastingness.
sources.quote: He attacks, as if there was no mistake about it, something which our Teacher never said, neither do we now assert, viz., that the Almighty became in process of time a Father, having been something else before.
sources.raw_question: If God is called Father because he begot the Son, does it follow that God became Father in time and was something else, or not ungenerate, before begetting the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. The objection falsely assumes that the Almighty became a Father in process of time, having been something else before, which neither Basil nor Gregory ever taught. The word Father both reveals the Son as effect and shows the absence of any beginning in the Begetter, and the Father is eternal, so there was never a 'before' the begetting.
sources.quote: He attacks, as if there was no mistake about it, something which our Teacher never said, neither do we now assert, viz., that the Almighty became in process of time a Father, having been something else before.
sources.raw_question: If God is called Father because He begot the Son and 'Father' implies being Ungenerate, does it follow that God was not Ungenerate before He begat the Son?

question: Can the human mind comprehend the divine essence, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > The tenth book discusses the unattainable and incomprehensible character of the enquiry into entities. And herein he strikingly sets forth the points concerning the nature and formation of the ant, and the passage in the Gospel, “I am the door” and “the way,” and also discusses the attribution and interpretation of the Divine names, and the episode of the children of Benjamin.
sources.answer: No. Gregory argues that anyone claiming to grasp the essence of God must first show that he can explain the real nature of the most trivial visible creature, such as the ant. Since no one can fully explain even the ant's nature, it is vain boasting to claim to have grasped by reason Him who controls all creation and surpasses all understanding.
sources.quote: But if he has not yet ascertained by his knowledge the nature of the tiny ant, how comes he to vaunt that by the apprehension of reason he has grasped Him Who in Himself controls all creation
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind attain comprehensive knowledge of the divine essence, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. No human is equal in understanding to the Lord, and the divine nature is not so small as to be compassed by human reasoning. God is greater than every token by which he may be known, and it is safer and more reverent to believe his majesty exceeds our understanding.
sources.quote: Vain, therefore, is he who maintains that it is possible to take knowledge of the divine essence, by the knowledge which puffeth up to no purpose.
sources.raw_question: Can the divine essence be comprehended by human knowledge, as Eunomius claims in defining God as 'ungenerate'?

question: Can the essence of the Son be said to be "variant" from the essence of the Father, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds to show that there is no “variance” in the essence of the Father and the Son: wherein he expounds many forms of variation and harmony, and explains the “form,” the “seal,” and the “express image.”
sources.answer: No. Things at variance are things out of harmony, and the Son, being the express image of the Father's Person, in the form of God, sealed by the Father, and displaying the Father in Himself, shows complete harmony with Him. What is in harmony is not at variance, so Eunomius's claim is absurd.
sources.quote: For if things at “variance” are not in harmony, and He Who is sealed by the Father, and displays the Father in Himself, both being in the Father, and having the Father in Himself, shows in all points His close relation and harmony
sources.raw_question: Can the essence of the Son be said to be "variant" from the essence of the Father, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds to show that there is no “variance” in the essence of the Father and the Son: wherein he expounds many forms of variation and harmony, and explains the “form,” the “seal,” and the “express image.”
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that this claim is blasphemous and refutes itself once the word "variance" is examined. In ordinary use, "variance" means a change for the worse from a natural state, as when a limb is perverted by disease. It also means the falling away of vice from virtue, or the mutually destructive opposition of contraries such as heat and cold or life and death. None of these senses can be applied to the divine essence without making one Person corrupt, evil, or at war with the other, so the assertion of variant essences cannot stand.
sources.quote: generally everything which is out of harmony with another in their observed characteristics, is said to be “at variance” with it, as health with disease, life with death, war with peace, virtue with vice, and all similar cases.
sources.raw_question: Are the essences of the Father and the Son "variant" from each other, as Eunomius claims on the ground that the names "Son" and "begotten" belong to the Son's essence itself?

question: Did the essence of the Only-begotten Son not exist before His own generation, so that there was a time when the Son was not, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, thus passing over what relates to the essence of the Son as having been already discussed, he treats of the sense involved in “generation,” saying that there are diverse generations, those effected by matter and art, and of buildings,--and that by succession of animals,--and those by efflux, as by the sun and its beam. The lamp and its radiance, scents and ointments and the quality diffused by them,--and the word produced by the mind; and cleverly discusses generation from rotten wood; and from the condensation of fire, and countless other causes.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that no new essence was begotten by the Father besides the essence contemplated in the Father Himself. To say of God the Word that 'He was not', or that non-existence preceded His existence, is a horrible blasphemy. His earlier argument, that the Word was in the Beginning together with the Father, already refutes it.
sources.quote: no new essence was begotten by the Father besides that which is contemplated in the Father Himself, and that there is no need for us to be entangled in a contest with blasphemy of this kind
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius right that the essence of the Only-begotten Son did not exist before its own generation, so that there was a time when the Son 'was not'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius takes his idea of generation from material, animal generation, where an ox or camel does not exist before it is born, and wrongly applies it to God. No one should presuppose non-existence in God, and the Son's generation from the Father shares none of the features of the lower kind of generation.
sources.quote: since an ox or an ass or a camel is not before its own generation, he thinks it proper to say even of the Only-begotten God that which the course of the lower nature presents to our view in the case of the animals
sources.raw_question: Did the essence of the Only-begotten Son not exist before His own generation, as Eunomius claims?

question: Does Eunomius's account of the Son's generation amount to treating the Son as a created being, of the same kind as creatures?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > Then, distinguishing between essence and generation, he declares the empty and frivolous language of Eunomius to be like a rattle. He proceeds to show that the language used by the great Basil on the subject of the generation of the Only-begotten has been grievously slandered by Eunomius, and so ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Eunomius uses 'generation' as a fair name for 'construction' or making. He means that the Son's essence would not have existed unless it had been constructed. That is simply the doctrine that the Lord was created, dressed in pleasant language.
sources.quote: he calls its construction “generation,” decking out his horrible blasphemy with the fairest phrase, that if “construction” is the meaning conveyed by the word “generation,” the idea of the creation of the Lord may receive a ready assent.
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius' claim that the Son's essence 'admits of generation' amount to treating the Son as a made creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > Eunomius again speaks of the Son as Lord and God, and Maker of all creation intelligible and sensible, having received from the Father the power and the commission for creation, being entrusted with the task of creation as if He were an artizan commissioned by some one hiring Him, and receiving His power of creation as a thing adventitious, ab extra, as a result of the power allotted to Him in accordance with such and such combinations and positions of the stars, as destiny decrees their lot in life to men at their nativity. Thus, passing by most of what Eunomius had written, he confutes his blasphemy that the Maker of all things came into being in like manner with the earth and with angels, and that the subsistence of the Only-begotten differs not at all from the genesis of all things, and reproaches Him with reverencing neither the Divine mystery nor the custom of the Church, nor following in his attempt to discover godliness any teacher of pious doctrine, but Manichæus, Colluthus, Arius, Aetius, and those like to them, supposing that Christianity in general is folly, and that the customs of the Church and the venerable sacraments are a jest, wherein he differs in nothing from the pagans, who borrowed from our doctrine the idea of a great God supreme over all. So, too, this new idolater preaches in the same fashion, and in particular that baptism is “into an artificer and creator,” not fearing the curse of those who cause addition or diminution to the Holy Scriptures. And he closes his book with showing him to be Antichrist.
sources.answer: Yes. By describing the Son's coming into being the same way he describes earth and angels, which came to be when before they were not, Eunomius admits that what is said of every created mode of generation and essence is no different from what is said of the divine subsistence of the Only-begotten. This openly degrades the Maker of all to the level of what he made.
sources.quote: he acknowledges that that which is predicated of every mode of generation and essence in nowise differs from the description of the Divine subsistence of the Only-begotten
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's claim that created essences vary according to the operations of their Maker show that he puts the Son's generation in the same class as the coming into being of creatures?

question: Since Eunomius admits the Son is begotten and naturally called 'Son', does this contradict and undermine his claim that the Son is a creature or 'product'?
synthesis: Both passages are from Gregory of Nyssa, and they agree. Eunomius's admission that the Son is begotten and naturally 'Son' cannot stand alongside his calling the Son a creature, so the creature claim must be rejected. In both, the enemy's own testimony is turned into a witness for the truth.

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then shows, from the instance of Adam and Abel, and other examples, the absence of alienation of essence in the case of the “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: The claim that 'Son' naturally belongs to the Only-begotten should be accepted, and the 'creature' or 'product' language rejected. Two mutually contradictory statements cannot both be true. The reader must therefore reject the impious one and keep the orthodox one. In this way even the enemy's own voice bears witness to the truth.
sources.quote: should assent to that only which is of orthodox tendency, which confesses that the appellation of “Son” naturally attaches to the Only-begotten God
sources.raw_question: Since Eunomius says the Son must be called 'Son' by nature because He is begotten, yet also calls Him a creature or 'product', which of these two incompatible claims should be accepted?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Then he ends the book with an exposition of the Divine and Human names of the Only-Begotten, and a discussion of the terms “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: Yes. Eunomius appeals to "natural order" to justify calling the Son a product of generation because he is begotten. Yet he also turns the Son's natural names into metaphors so as to call him a creature. One of these arguments must fail. By testifying that the Son is begotten, Eunomius, as an enemy whose witness carries extra weight, also testifies that the Son is not created.
sources.quote: since Eunomius bears witness that the Only-begotten God is begotten (and the evidence of enemies is of additional value for establishing the truth), he surely testifies also, by saying that He is begotten, to the fact that He is not created.
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's admission that the Only-begotten is begotten, and properly called a "product of generation," undermine his claim that the Son is a creature?

question: Is Eunomius's principle that the manner of the Son's likeness to the Father must follow the manner of his generation a valid rule?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The observations made by watching Providence are sufficient to give us the knowledge of sameness of Being.
sources.answer: No. The principle is unintelligible and proves too much. Most animals born by parturition share the same manner of generation. By this logic men, dogs and camels would all resemble one another, which is absurd.
sources.quote: we shall find that this sweeping and unqualified assertion of his establishes, by virtue of this similarity of birth, a mutual resemblance between men, dogs, camels,
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius right that the manner of the Son's likeness to the Father must follow the manner of his generation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His dictum that 'the manner of the likeness must follow the manner of the generation' is unintelligible.
sources.answer: No. Gregory argues the principle is unintelligible, since it is impossible to say what a 'manner of generation' means (figure, impulse, time, place, etc.), and birth and the thing born are different ideas altogether. In animal births and in crafted products alike, the thing produced is never likened to the manner of its production, so the rule fails even in sensible instances.
sources.quote: Birth is one thing: the thing born is another: they are different ideas altogether. No one with any sense would deny that what he says is perfectly untrue in the case of animal births.
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius's principle that 'the manner of the likeness must follow the manner of the generation' a valid rule for determining whether the Son is like the Father?

question: Can Eunomius legitimately call the Son's essence a "product of creation" or "product of making" on the ground that it exists by the Father's operation, without first proving that the Son is created?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: No. Eunomius simply assumes, without any proof, that the Son exists by a constructive operation of the Father, yet this is exactly the point in dispute. Whether the Father's essence begat the Son or made Him as one of the external things that accompany His nature is what has to be shown. As long as that premise is unproved, every inference he builds on it is worthless.
sources.quote: What reasoning showed us that the Son exists by any constructive operation, and that the nature of the Father remains inoperative with regard to the Personal existence of the Son?
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's essence rightly be called a "product of making" and "product of creation" because it exists by the operation of the Father, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He again shows Eunomius, constrained by truth, in the character of an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, confessing as most proper and primary, not only the essence of the Father, but the essence also of the Only-begotten.
sources.answer: No. Calling the Son a 'product of creation' is the very point that separates the Church from heresy. Anyone claiming his view is truer must first establish that the Lord is created on an incontrovertible basis and then proceed by inference. He should not lay down a disputed matter as if it were acknowledged fact.
sources.quote: Who knows not that what separates the Church from heresy is this term, “product of creation,” applied to the Son?
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate for Eunomius simply to assert that the Son's essence admits the name 'product of creation' without proving that the Son is created?

question: If the difference between the Father's light and the Son's light corresponds to the opposition between ungenerate and generate, does it follow that the Son is not light at all?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then referring to the blasphemy of Eunomius, which had been refuted by the great Basil, where he banished the Only-begotten God to the realm of darkness, and the apology or explanation which Eunomius puts forth for his blasphemy, he shows that his present blasphemy is rendered by his apology worse than his previous one; and herein he very ably discourses of the “true” and the “unapproachable” Light.
sources.answer: Yes, that absurdity follows from Eunomius's premise, which shows the premise is blasphemous. Since generation and ungeneracy are contradictory and mutually exclusive rather than differing by degree, a matching difference between the two lights would exclude the Son from light altogether. What is other than light has affinity with its contrary, so Eunomius would in effect banish the Only-begotten to darkness.
sources.quote: it will be logically concluded that the Son is not henceforth to be conceived as Light, as he is excluded alike from ungeneracy itself, and from the light which accompanies that condition
sources.raw_question: If the difference between the Father's light and the Son's light corresponds to the difference between ungenerate and generate, does it follow that the Son is not light at all?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then, again discussing the true Light and unapproachable Light of the Father and of the Son, special attributes, community and essence, and showing the relation of “generate” and “ungenerate,” as involving no opposition in sense, but presenting an opposition and contradiction admitting of no middle term, he ends the book.
sources.answer: It would follow that the Son is not light at all but darkness, which exposes the absurdity of the Eunomian position. Since contradictories share nothing in common, if Eunomius applies the same divergence to the Light as to generate and ungenerate, then placing 'light' on one side forces 'darkness' onto the other. Gregory does not grant this inferiority, but shows that Eunomius' own premise leads to this impious conclusion.
sources.quote: if “light” be placed on the same side as one of the two contradictories, the remaining place in the figure must of course be assigned to “darkness,” the necessity of the antithesis arranging the term of light over against its opposite
sources.raw_question: If the Son as Generate Light were inferior to the Father as Ungenerate Light in the way the generate is opposed to the ungenerate, what would follow about the Son's being Light?

question: How does the Son differ from creatures in essence, and is He one in nature with the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is Offspring of the Father's essence, the Framer through whom other things are framed, and the Radiance, Word, Image and Wisdom of the Father, while things originate serve below the Triad. Therefore He is different in kind and essence from creatures and proper to the Father's essence and one in nature with it.
sources.quote: therefore the Son is different in kind and different in essence from things originate, and on the contrary is proper to the Father’s essence and one in nature with it
sources.raw_question: Is the Son different in essence from creatures and one in nature with the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: Creatures are unlike the Maker in essence and external to him. They are made by the Word at God's grace and will, and so they can cease to be if he pleases. The Son is proper to the Father's essence, so it is irreligious to say he came from nothing, was adventitious, or could cease to be. Saying so impairs the perfection and fullness of the Father's essence.
sources.quote: other things, according to the nature of things originate, are without likeness in essence with the Maker; but are external to Him, made by the Word at His grace and will, and thus admit of ceasing to be
sources.raw_question: How does the Son differ from creatures in his relation to the Father's essence?

question: If the Son has all that belongs to the Father, does it follow absurdly that one Person is both begetter and begotten, Father and Son at once?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: No. The supposed absurdity actually supports the truth: the Son has and is all that the Father is except being Father, and the Father exhibits all that the Son is except being Son. The Persons are distinguished only by the relations of Father and Son, while sharing the whole nature, so there is no confusion of begetter and begotten.
sources.quote: For we too say that He who has all that belongs to His own Father is all that He is, save being Father, and that He who has all that belongs to the Son exhibits in Himself the Son in His completeness, save being Son
sources.raw_question: If the Son has all that belongs to the Father, does it follow absurdly that the Father is both begetter and begotten, His own Father and Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: No. Rather, Eunomius's reductio supports the truth. The Son has all that belongs to the Father, and is all that the Father is, except being Father. Since "he that hath seen the Son seeth the Father," the Father begat another self without passing out of himself, while still appearing in his fulness in the Son.
sources.quote: For we too say that He who has all that belongs to His own Father is all that He is, save being Father, and that He who has all that belongs to the Son exhibits in Himself the Son in His completeness, save being Son
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that the Son is truly of the Father imply the absurdity that one Person is both begetter and begotten, Father and Son at once?

question: Does Paul's confession of 'one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ' teach two Gods (or two Lords) or a single solitary Person in God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Neither. Paul's carefully chosen words reject oneness of person while not dividing the unity of Godhead. He who is not one person cannot multiply into two Gods, and they who are not two Gods cannot be understood as one single person.
sources.quote: he has guarded himself by those specially appropriate words from being understood to mean two Gods or a solitary God: for while he rejects oneness of person he yet does not divide the unity of Godhead
sources.raw_question: Does confessing 'one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ' teach either two Gods or a single solitary Person in God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Each is both Lord and God, yet the creed admits neither two Gods nor two Lords. Each is one, and yet neither is sole. In naming them, Paul set forth one God within the one Lord Christ and one Lord within the one God the Father, so that there is Lordship in God and Godhead in the Lord.
sources.quote: for one God the Father and one Christ the Lord, since Each is both Lord and God, do not yet admit in our creed either two Gods or two Lords. So then Each is one, and though one, neither is sole.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing one God and one Lord mean that Father and Son are two Gods or two Lords?

question: Does Jesus' saying 'I and the Father are one' teach that God is a single solitary person, with 'Son' merely another name for the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It teaches not a solitary God but a unity of Godhead that the Son's birth does not break. God can be born only of God, and he who is born God of God must be all that God is. So the text shows one nature shared by two, not one person.
sources.quote: go to prove not a solitary God, but a unity of the Godhead unbroken by the birth of the Son: for God can be born only of God, and He that is born God of God must be all that God is
sources.raw_question: Does Jesus' saying 'I and the Father are One' teach that God is a single solitary person, or something else?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The words reveal unity without solitude: Father and Son are truly Two. Yet no second nature came into being through the Son's true birth, so the unity of the divine nature is indistinguishable while the Son remains truly Son.
sources.quote: They were spoken that in this unity we might see neither difference nor solitude; for They are Two, and yet no second nature came into being through that true birth and generation.
sources.raw_question: Does "I and the Father are one" mean that God is a single solitary person, with "Son" merely another name for the Father?

question: Do the many Scripture texts that call the Father 'God' absolutely, or 'the one God', prove that the Son is not strictly and essentially God, one God with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 20: Whether the Doctor need have cited 300 teats, *wide of the purpose, to prove what nobody denies, namely, a subordination, in some sense, of the Son to the Fathe
sources.answer: No. Waterland calls them very good texts with an excellent meaning, since they show a subordination that nobody denies. They would only bear on the dispute if it were proved that all subordination implies inferiority of nature. Inferring from them that the Son is not one God with the Father is Dr. Clarke's own strained and remote inference. That inference is not warranted by Scripture or by Catholic antiquity, and it contradicts both.
sources.quote: The Doctor’s insinuating from the 300 texts (which style the Father God absolutely, or the one God) that the Son is not strictly and essentially God, not one God with the Father, is a strained and remote inference of his own;
sources.raw_question: Do the many Scripture texts that call the Father God absolutely, or the one God, prove that the Son is not strictly and essentially God with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Waterland holds that inferring the Son's non-deity from texts styling the Father God absolutely is a strained and remote inference of Dr. Clarke's own. It is not warranted by Scripture nor countenanced by Catholic antiquity, but is contradictory to both.
sources.quote: is a strained and remote inference of his own; not warranted by Scripture, nor countenanced by Catholic antiquity; but contradictory to both.
sources.raw_question: Do the many Scripture texts that call the Father 'God' absolutely or 'the one God' prove that the Son is not strictly and essentially God, one God with the Father?

question: Is John's calling the Son "the Word" merely a figure of speech?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. It is no figure of speech. John himself, in the Apocalypse, presents the one who rides the white horse, clothed in a vesture dipped in blood, and says "His name is called the Word of God," confirming that the Word is a real name of the Son who was from the beginning and has now been sent forth.
sources.quote: For John indeed speaks of the Word, but it is by a figure of speech. Nay, it is by no figure of speech.
sources.raw_question: Is John's calling the Son "the Word" merely a figure of speech?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. In the Apocalypse John names the rider whose vesture is dipped in blood "the Word of God." That blood-sprinkled vesture symbolises the flesh through which the impassible Word came under suffering. So the Word who was from the beginning is truly the Son who was sent forth and became incarnate.
sources.quote: For John indeed speaks of the Word, but it is by a figure of speech. Nay, it is by no figure of speech.
sources.raw_question: Is the designation of the Son as "the Word" in John's Gospel merely a figure of speech?

question: Does the Holy Spirit reveal the things of God in the same way as the Father and the Son do?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as God reveals what is His, so the Son and the Spirit reveal the things of God. Our knowledge proceeds from one Spirit through one Son to one Father, and from the Father through the Son to the Spirit comes goodness, sanctification and eternal power. Where the work is one, there can be no distinction of power.
sources.quote: For our knowledge proceeds from one Spirit, through one Son to one Father; and from one Father through one Son to one Holy Spirit is delivered goodness and sanctification and the sovereign right of eternal power.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit reveal the things of God in the same way as the Father and the Son do?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul, chosen by Christ, was taught by the Spirit and received the Spirit which is of God so as to know the things given by God. The Spirit thus knows God and reveals the things of God as the Son also does, and from this unity of operation the unity of the Three is inferred.
sources.quote: he shows both that the Holy Spirit knows God, and has revealed to us the things which are of God, as the Son also has revealed them.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit reveal the things of God equally with the Son and the Father?

question: If the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well, in what sense does he proceed principally from the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: The Son's being a source of the Spirit's procession is itself something he receives from the Father. As the Father has in himself that the Spirit proceeds from him, so he has given to the Son that the same Spirit proceeds from him. Since the Son has from the Father whatever he has, he has from the Father that the Spirit proceeds from him too; hence the Spirit proceeds from the Father principally, yet in common from both.
sources.quote: For if the Son has of the Father whatever He has, then certainly He has of the Father, that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from Him.
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well, how is the Spirit still said to proceed from the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Holy Spirit is Called Love, and Whether He Alone is So Called. That the Holy Spirit is in the Scriptures Properly Called by the Name of Love.
sources.answer: Yes, the Spirit proceeds from the Son also, but principally from the Father. The Father gave the Son even this, not as to one already existing who lacked it. Whatever he gave the Word he gave by begetting him, so he begot the Son in such a way that the common Gift proceeds from him too.
sources.quote: But the Father gave Him this too, not as to one already existing, and not yet having it; but whatever He gave to the only-begotten Word, He gave by begetting Him.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Son as well as from the Father, and in what sense does he proceed 'principally' from the Father?

question: If the Holy Spirit proceeds from both the Father and the Son, why did Christ say only that the Spirit 'proceedeth from the Father' (John 15:26)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: Because the Son habitually refers what is his own to the One from whom he himself is. Just as he said his doctrine was not his own but the Father's, so in saying the Spirit proceeds from the Father he does not deny that the Spirit proceeds from himself.
sources.quote: Why, think you, except as He is wont to refer to Him, that also which is His own, from whom also He Himself is?
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit proceeds from both the Father and the Son, why did the Son say only that the Spirit proceeds from the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What It is that Suffices Here to Solve the Question Why the Spirit is Not Said to Be Begotten, and Why the Father Alone is Unbegotten. What They Ought to Do Who Do Not Understand These Things.
sources.answer: Because the Son habitually refers to the Father even what is His own, since He Himself is from the Father. Just as He called His doctrine 'not mine own, but His that sent me,' so in saying the Spirit proceeds from the Father He does not deny that the Spirit proceeds from Himself as well.
sources.quote: Why, think you, except as He is wont to refer to Him, that also which is His own, from whom also He Himself is?
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit proceeds from both the Father and the Son, why did Christ say only that the Spirit 'proceedeth from the Father'?

question: Since the Holy Spirit is from both the Father and the Son, should he be called the Son of both?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: No, that would be most absurd. He would be the Son of both only if both had begotten him, which is abhorrent to sound minds. The Spirit of both is not begotten of both but proceeds from both.
sources.quote: Therefore the Spirit of both is not begotten of both, but proceeds from both.
sources.raw_question: Since the Holy Spirit is from both the Father and the Son, should he be called the Son of both?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What It is that Suffices Here to Solve the Question Why the Spirit is Not Said to Be Begotten, and Why the Father Alone is Unbegotten. What They Ought to Do Who Do Not Understand These Things.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit is a kind of consubstantial communion of Father and Son. He is not their offspring, so it is unthinkable to call him the Son of both.
sources.quote: since the Spirit of both is a kind of consubstantial communion of Father and Son, He is not called, far be it from us to say so, the Son of both.
sources.raw_question: Since the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both Father and Son, should he be called the Son of both?

question: Why is the third Person of the Trinity specially called 'Holy Spirit' when the Father and the Son are also spirit and holy?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: Because he is a certain unutterable communion of the Father and the Son. He is specially called what they are called in common, since both Father and Son are spirit and holy. Thus a name suitable to both signifies the communion of both, and he is the gift of both.
sources.quote: Therefore the Holy Spirit is a certain unutterable communion of the Father and the Son; and on that account, perhaps, He is so called, because the same name is suitable to both the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Why is the third Person of the Trinity specially called by the name 'Holy Spirit', which applies to Father and Son in common?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: Because he is common to both the Father and the Son, he is specially called by the name of what both are in common. Both Father and Son are Spirit and both are holy, so the one common to both bears that shared name as his proper name.
sources.quote: And yet it is not to no purpose that He is specially called the Holy Spirit; for because He is common to both, He is specially called that which both are in common.
sources.raw_question: Why is the third Person specially called 'Holy Spirit' when the Father and the Son are also spirit and holy?

question: Do believers have communion distinctly with each Person of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—rather than only with God in general?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. The saints have distinct communion with the Father, distinctly with the Son, and distinctly with the Holy Spirit. Scripture plainly shows this, sometimes naming Father and Son jointly, sometimes the Son alone, sometimes the Spirit alone, and assigns gifts, access, and worship distinctly to each person.
sources.quote: That the saints have distinct communion with the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit (that is, distinctly with the Father, and distinctly with the Son, and distinctly with the Holy Spirit)
sources.raw_question: Do believers have communion distinctly with each person of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—rather than only with God in general?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Every grace by which the soul goes out to God, and every act of worship or obedience, is directed distinctly to the Father, the Son and the Spirit. Since these are the very ways in which we hold communion with God, that communion is had with each Person distinctly.
sources.quote: there is no grace whereby our souls go forth unto God, no act of divine worship yielded unto him, duty or obedience performed, but they are distinctly directed unto Father, Son, and Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Do believers have communion with each Person of the Trinity distinctly?

question: Does the fact that the Holy Spirit is not the Father of the Son (nor Only-begotten) imply that the Spirit is subject and subordinate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: No. That the Spirit is not the Father of the Only-begotten is something no one ever doubted. Nothing compels the conclusion that whoever is not Father must therefore be subject. Eunomius builds his impiety on irrelevant and unconnected statements.
sources.quote: For what compels the conclusion, that if He be not Father, He must be subject?
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's not being the Father of the Son, or not being Only-begotten, prove that the Spirit is subject and subordinate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: No. The inference would hold only if "Father" meant the same as "despot" or sovereign, so that authority were part of the concept of fatherhood. But "Father" signifies merely the relation to the Son and involves no conception of absolute sovereignty or authority. Therefore the Spirit's not being Father of the Son says nothing about His being subject to the Father.
sources.quote: But if by “Father” is implied merely His relation to the Son, and no conception of absolute sovereignty or authority is involved by the use of the word, how does it follow, from the fact that the Spirit is not the Father of the Son, that the Spirit is subject to the Father?
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Holy Spirit is not the Father of the Son imply that the Spirit is subject and subordinate to the Father?

question: How does the Holy Spirit lead believers to knowledge of the Son and the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: Just as the Father is seen in the Son, the Son is seen in the Spirit. By the Spirit's illumination we behold the Son, the "Brightness of the glory" of God. Through the Son as "Express Image" we are led up to the Father, whose Image and Seal He is.
sources.quote: we behold the “Brightness of the glory” of God by means of the illumination of the Spirit, and by means of the “Express Image” we are led up to Him of whom He is the Express Image and Seal, graven to the like.
sources.raw_question: How does the Holy Spirit lead believers to knowledge of the Son and the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Definitive conceptions about the Spirit which conform to the teaching of the Scriptures.
sources.answer: The Spirit, like the sun, enables the purified eye to see the Son, the image of the invisible God, in the Spirit himself. In seeing that image, the believer beholds the unspeakable beauty of the archetype, the Father. Knowledge of God therefore moves through the Spirit to the Image and on to the Archetype.
sources.quote: And He, like the sun, will by the aid of thy purified eye show thee in Himself the image of the invisible, and in the blessed spectacle of the image thou shalt behold the unspeakable beauty of the archetype.
sources.raw_question: What role does the Holy Spirit play in our knowledge of the Son and the Father?

question: Is the Holy Spirit the mutual love or communion common to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Holy Spirit Also is Equal to the Father and the Son in All Things.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is something common to Father and Son, the one through whom the Begotten is loved by the Begetter and loves Him in return. This communion is consubstantial and co-eternal, and though it might be called friendship, it is more aptly called love.
sources.quote: Therefore the Holy Spirit, whatever it is, is something common both to the Father and Son. But that communion itself is consubstantial and co-eternal
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit the mutual love or communion common to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Holy Spirit is Called Love, and Whether He Alone is So Called. That the Holy Spirit is in the Scriptures Properly Called by the Name of Love.
sources.answer: Yes. According to Scripture the Holy Spirit is neither of the Father alone nor of the Son alone but of both. This intimates a mutual love with which the Father and the Son reciprocally love one another.
sources.quote: the Holy Spirit, according to the Holy Scriptures, is neither of the Father alone, nor of the Son alone, but of both; and so intimates to us a mutual love, wherewith the Father and the Son reciprocally love one another.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being the Spirit of both the Father and the Son indicate that he is the mutual love of the Father and the Son?

question: If the Holy Spirit is called Lord, does that imply there are three Lords alongside the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XV. Though the Spirit be called Lord, three Lords are not thereby implied; inasmuch as two Lords are not implied by the fact that the Son in the same manner as the Father is called Lord in many passages of Scripture; for Lordship exists in the Godhead, and the Godhead in Lordship, and these coincide without division in the Three Persons.
sources.answer: No. Just as calling both the Father and the Son Lord does not produce two Lords, so confessing the Spirit as Lord does not produce three Lords. Lordship is one because the Godhead is one, and Lordship and Godhead coincide without division in the three Persons.
sources.quote: So, as we do not say that there are two Lords, when we so style both the Father and the Son, so, too, we do not say that there are three Lords, when we confess the Spirit to be Lord.
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit is called Lord, does that imply there are three Lords?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIV. Besides the evidence adduced above, other passages can be brought to prove the sovereignty of the Three Persons. Two are quoted from the Epistles to the Thessalonians, and by collating other testimonies of the Scriptures it is shown that in them dominion is claimed for the Spirit as for the other Persons. Then, by quotation of another still more express passage in the second Epistle to the Corinthians, it is inferred both that the Spirit is Lord, and that where the Lord is, there is the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Calling the Son Lord does not imply two Lords, since Christ warned against serving two lords while calling both the Father and himself Lord. Where the Lordship is one, there are not several Lords, for the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Lordship coincides with the one Godhead without division in the Three Persons, as the Law teaches: 'the Lord thy God is one Lord.'
sources.quote: For there are not two Lords where the Lordship is but one, for the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and so there is one Lord.
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit is called Lord, does that imply three Lords alongside the Father and the Son?

question: If the Son is derived from the Father as a creature, can that derivation (unity of principle) make him one God with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. On the Arian supposition the plea of unity of principle is absurd. If coming from the Father as a creature made the Son one God with the Father, then angels, men, and even inanimate things would also be one God with the Father. The opponents themselves do not claim that anything makes the Son one God with the Father.
sources.quote: if his being of, or from, the Father, in this sense, makes him one God with the Father, it will follow, that angels, or men, or even things inanimate, are one God with the Father also.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is a creature of the Father, can his being from the Father make him one God with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. If being from the Father as a creature made the Son one God with the Father, then angels, men and even inanimate things would also be one God with the Father. On the Arian scheme, therefore, nothing can make the Son one God with the Father, and that departs from the ancients on the main point.
sources.quote: else, can make him one God with the Father. Which is enough to shew, how very widely you differ from the ancients, in the main point of all,
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's being derived from the Father as a creature (unity of principle) make him one God with the Father?

question: Are the Father and the Son two Gods, or one solitary God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Neither. Believing that the Father and the Son are two Gods is sin. Asserting that they are one solitary God is sacrilege. They are one God but not one Person, and their unity lies in sameness of kind: God from God.
sources.quote: It is sin to believe that Father and Son are two Gods, sacrilege to assert that Father and Son are one solitary God, blasphemy to deny the unity, consisting in sameness of kind, of God from God.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and the Son two Gods, or one solitary God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Neither. They are not two Gods merely putting on a semblance of unity in work and word. Nor is God solitary, since the Son Himself worked, spoke and was seen as God in the works, words and sight of God.
sources.quote: They are not two Gods, Who in their working and words and manifestation put on a semblance of unity. Neither is He a solitary God.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and Son two Gods, or is God a solitary person?

question: Was the Son of God created out of nothing, or did He not exist before He was born?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. He is born from the Father, Who really is, and the Father is the cause of His existence. A birth from Him Who truly is cannot have its origin in what is not. So the Son was neither born out of nothing nor ever non-existent before His birth.
sources.quote: Further, He Who is born from Him Who really is, cannot be understood to have been born from that which was not: since He Who really is, is the cause of His existing, and His birth cannot have its origin in that which is not.
sources.raw_question: Was the Son of God born out of nothing?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The claim that he did not exist before he was born is a concession to worldly philosophers. The Son has no origin external to God and was not created out of nothing, but is truly born from God.
sources.quote: to demonstrate that He has no origin external to God, and was not created out of nothing, but is the Son, born from God.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God not exist before he was born, or was he created out of nothing?

question: Can the Son consistently be called 'very Son' and 'Only-begotten' while also being called 'not uncreate', that is, a creature, as Eunomius's creed says?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: No. If what is not uncreate can be called 'very Son', then the heaven, the sun and every creature could also be called 'very Son'. And all things that come into being are in brotherhood with one another as far as their coming into being goes. So a created Son could not be uniquely 'Only-begotten'.
sources.quote: For if it is meet to call Him Who is not uncreate “very Son,” then of course the heaven is “very Son;” for it too is “not uncreate.”
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be called 'very Son' and 'Only-begotten' if he is 'not uncreate', as Eunomius says?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that adding 'not uncreate' perverts what the creed has just confessed. It is meant to stop readers from grasping the natural meaning of 'Son'. The pious-sounding opening phrases work only as a bait that sugars over the poison of making the Son a creature.
sources.quote: he immediately adds the words, “not uncreate,” lest if the natural significance of the term “Son” were apprehended by his readers, any pious conception concerning Him might find place in their minds
sources.raw_question: Can the Son consistently be confessed as 'very Son' and 'Only-begotten God' while also being called 'not uncreate', that is, a creature, as Eunomius's creed does?

question: Can the Son be Only-begotten and also created as the 'beginning' of all things, first among creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. If He were created as the beginning of all things, He would no longer be alone but one among those coming after Him, as Reuben was firstborn yet not only-begotten. A beginning shares the nature of what follows it, so He would merely be part of creation. Since He is Only-begotten, 'beginning of ways' must refer to His office in the flesh, not His essence.
sources.quote: if He is Only-begotten, how becomes He ‘beginning of the ways?’ for of necessity, if He was created a beginning of all things, He is no longer alone, as having those who came into being after Him.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be both Only-begotten and created as the 'beginning' of all things in the sense of being first among creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. Whoever is created as a beginning of all things is no longer alone, because others come into being after him and share his nature. Reuben was first in time but not only-begotten, since he was one in nature among those born after him.
sources.quote: if He is Only-begotten, how becomes He ‘beginning of the ways?’ for of necessity, if He was created a beginning of all things, He is no longer alone, as having those who came into being after Him.
sources.raw_question: Is being Only-begotten compatible with being the first-created beginning of all creatures?

question: Can the name 'Holy Spirit' (or 'Son') be said of the whole Trinity, or only of one Person within it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: The Trinity cannot in any way be called the Son, but it can in its entirety be called Holy Spirit. Since 'God is a Spirit' and God is holy, and both Father and Son are spirit and holy, the one God who is the Trinity can be called holy spirit. Yet the Holy Spirit as a distinct Person is named so relatively, as the Spirit of the Father and of the Son.
sources.quote: Neither can the Trinity in any wise be called the Son, but it can be called, in its entirety, the Holy Spirit, according to that which is written, “God is a Spirit;”
sources.raw_question: Can the whole Trinity be called 'Son' or 'Holy Spirit'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > In Relative Things that are Reciprocal, Names are Sometimes Wanting.
sources.answer: It is said of one Person within the Trinity, not of the Trinity itself. The Spirit is referred relatively to the Father and the Son as their gift, so that we say 'the gift of the giver and the giver of the gift.'
sources.quote: we have said that the Holy Spirit is so called relatively, not the Trinity itself, but He who is in the Trinity
sources.raw_question: Is 'Holy Spirit' as a relative name said of the whole Trinity or of one Person within it?

question: If 'Holy Spirit' is a relative name, why can we say 'the Holy Spirit of the Father' and 'of the Son' but not 'the Father of the Holy Spirit' or 'the Son of the Holy Spirit'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: In many relatives no designation exists by which the related terms correspond mutually in name. We cannot say 'the Father of the Holy Spirit' lest the Spirit be thought his Son, nor 'the Son of the Holy Spirit' lest the Spirit be thought his Father. Lacking a reciprocal name does not undo the relation, as with 'earnest', which is clearly relative.
sources.quote: For we speak of the Holy Spirit of the Father; but, on the other hand, we do not speak of the Father of the Holy Spirit, lest the Holy Spirit should be understood to be His Son.
sources.raw_question: Why do we say 'the Holy Spirit of the Father' but not 'the Father of the Holy Spirit', if the name is relative?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > In Relative Things that are Reciprocal, Names are Sometimes Wanting.
sources.answer: Because saying so would wrongly imply the Spirit is the Father's son or the Son's father. The lack of a reciprocal name does not refute the relative character of the term. Many relatives lack a name by which the related terms correspond to each other in words. So we speak of the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, but not the reverse.
sources.quote: For we speak of the Holy Spirit of the Father; but, on the other hand, we do not speak of the Father of the Holy Spirit, lest the Holy Spirit should be understood to be His Son.
sources.raw_question: If 'Holy Spirit' is a relative name, why can we not say 'the Father of the Holy Spirit' or 'the Son of the Holy Spirit' as we say 'the Holy Spirit of the Father' and 'of the Son'?

question: What role does the Holy Spirit play in uniting believers to Christ and giving them communion with God in the Church?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIV.—Recapitulation of the various arguments adduced against Gnostic impiety under all its aspects. The heretics, tossed about by every blast of doctrine, are opposed by the uniform teaching of the Church, which remains so always, and is consistent with itself.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit is the means of communion with Christ, given to the Church as breath was given to Adam, so that all its members may be made alive. He is the earnest of incorruption, the confirmation of faith, and the ladder of ascent to God. Where the Church is, there is the Spirit, and where the Spirit is, there is the Church and every grace.
sources.quote: the Holy Spirit, the earnest of incorruption, the means of confirming our faith, and the ladder of ascent to God
sources.raw_question: What role does the Holy Spirit play in the Church and in believers' communion with Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVII.—The apostles teach that it was neither Christ nor the Saviour, but the Holy Spirit, who did descend upon Jesus. The reason for this descent.
sources.answer: The Spirit is the 'water from heaven' that makes the many one in Christ Jesus, just as dough cannot become one loaf without liquid. Our bodies receive unity through the laver of baptism and our souls through the Spirit, and both are needed for the life of God. Without this rain from above we could bear no fruit unto life.
sources.quote: so, in like manner, neither could we, being many, be made one in Christ Jesus without the water from heaven.
sources.raw_question: What role does the Holy Spirit play in uniting believers to Christ and to God?

question: Did the Father suffer any loss, lessening or division of his substance in begetting the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. Hilary points to the virgin birth: Mary bore Christ complete in his human body without any loss of her own completeness. Piety requires us to regard as possible with God what His power made possible in a human being, so the Father begets the Son without loss.
sources.quote: Surely piety requires that we should regard as possible with God a thing which we see became possible through his power in the case of a human being
sources.raw_question: Did the Father suffer any loss or division of his substance in begetting the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The Son was begotten by no lessening of the Father or subtraction from His Substance; He who possesses all things begot an all-possessing Son, perfect Offspring of perfect Parent, not emanating but inherent in the whole Divinity.
sources.quote: the Sun was begotten by no lessening of the Father or subtraction from His Substance, but that He Who possesses all things begot an all-possessing Son
sources.raw_question: Did the begetting of the Son involve any lessening of the Father or subtraction from His substance?

question: If 'first-born of all creation' meant the Son was the first creature, would that be consistent with the Son being the one through whom all other things were made?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: Yes. In that sense the first-born would share the essence of the creatures born after him. He would differ from them only by priority in time and would contribute nothing to their birth. Someone else would then give being both to him and to the rest, which contradicts John's statement that all things were made by him.
sources.quote: For if He is first-born, He differs from those born after Him only by priority in time, while there must be some one else by Whom the power to be at all is imparted alike to Him and to the rest.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is 'first-born of all creation' in the sense of being the first among creatures, does that conflict with the claim that all things were made by him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then again admirably discusses the term πρωτότοκος as it is four times employed by the Apostle.
sources.answer: No. On the Eunomian view the Father made the Son, and the Son made all else. They call the Father the 'Father' of the Being he created, not his 'first-born'. By the same reasoning the Son should be called 'father' of his creatures rather than first-born, which leaves the title improper and superfluous in their scheme.
sources.quote: as the same relation existing in both cases towards the things created, logically gives rise to the same appellation.
sources.raw_question: If the Son were a creature made first, through whom all other things were made, would it be consistent to call him the 'first-born' of creation?

question: In what sense, if any, is the Father 'before' the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He who asserts that the Father is 'prior' to the Son with any thought of an interval must perforce allow that even the Father is not without beginning.
sources.answer: Only in the order of causation, not in time. The Father should be conceived as before the Son solely as cause. The Father's life must not be thought of as a separate life lived before the Son's generation, since that would bring in an interval and, with it, a beginning for the Father.
sources.quote: let it suffice on the ground of causation only to conceive of the Father as before the Son; and let not the Father’s life be thought of as a separate and peculiar one before the generation of the Son
sources.raw_question: In what sense, if any, is the Father 'before' the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He who asserts that the Father is 'prior' to the Son with any thought of an interval must perforce allow that even the Father is not without beginning.
sources.answer: Only on the ground of causation, not of time. Since the Father must be confessed to be without beginning, we must not fix a point for the Son's life that cuts him off from a prior separate life of the Father. The Father's life should not be thought of as a peculiar life before the Son's generation, lest an interval be introduced that destroys the Father's own eternity.
sources.quote: let it suffice on the ground of causation only to conceive of the Father as before the Son; and let not the Father’s life be thought of as a separate and peculiar one before the generation of the Son
sources.raw_question: In what sense, if any, may the Father be conceived as 'before' the Son?
