question: Did the early Fathers who spoke of a 'temporal generation' of the Son (His coming forth to create the world) mean that the Son began to exist at that time?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Athenagoras's passage shows their genuine sense: the Word always existed eternally in God, who was eternally rational. A temporal 'generation' therefore did not mean the Word was made or began to be. Rightly understood, this tells equally against Sabellians and Arians, as Bishop Bull demonstrated.
sources.quote: plainly shewing the true and genuine sense of such Fathers as spoke of a temporal generation, and being of equal force both against Sabeilians and Arians
sources.raised_by_detail: Petavius, Sandius, Gilbert Clerke, Dr. Whitby
sources.raw_question: Did Fathers who spoke of a 'temporal generation' of the Son mean that the Son began to exist at that time?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. The Arians exploited this language to claim that this was the Son's first production and that he did not exist before he was begotten. But the eternal existence of the Logos was universally taught, even by those who asserted a temporal generation. The Nicene Fathers therefore anathematised the claim that the Son did not exist before he was begotten.
sources.quote: the Arians might have known that the eternal existence of the Λόγος was universally taught, and even by those who asserted a temporal generation.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that some early Fathers called the Son's coming forth to create the world his 'generation' show that the Son did not exist before that point?

question: Is the Son the Father's own natural Word and Wisdom, or is He called Word and Wisdom only nominally, by partaking of another Word and Wisdom in God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. To say so introduces many words and wisdoms against God's oneness and reduces the Son to a mere name, so that He would be Son only because of those made sons and would have but a semblance of being in our notions. The Son is the Father's proper and natural Word and Wisdom, begotten of His essence.
sources.quote: these men introduce, after their private notions, many images and wisdoms and words, and say that the Father’s proper and natural Word is other than the Son, by whom He even made the Son
sources.raw_question: Is the Son called Word and Wisdom only notionally, while the Father's true natural Word and Wisdom is something other than the Son by which He made the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: He is the very and only Word of the Father, not a Word in name only. To posit another word and wisdom beside him, by which he was originated, makes him a mere partaker and second to it. That is blasphemy rather than a fitting statement about God.
sources.quote: that He is the Father’s Word, or that there is another word beside Him, and that by this other He was originated, and by another wisdom; and that He is only named Wisdom and Word, and is become a partaker of this wisdom, and second to it?
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the Father's own Word and Wisdom, or is he only called Word and Wisdom by partaking of another Word and Wisdom in God?

question: Why do we call the Father, Son and Holy Spirit 'three persons' (or 'three substances'), and does this imply a difference of essence among them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Preface.—The Conclusion of What Has Been Said Above. The Rule to Be Observed in the More Difficult Questions of the Faith.
sources.answer: No. The terms are used not to signify any difference of essence. They are used so that we have some single word with which to answer if someone asks, 'Three what?'
sources.quote: they are called three persons, or three substances, not in order that any difference of essence may be understood, but that we may be able to answer by some one word, should any one ask what three, or what three things?
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father, Son and Holy Spirit 'three persons' or 'three substances' imply a difference of essence among them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: These terms are used out of the needs of speech. They give us a single word with which to answer when someone asks what the three are, whom we truly confess to be three: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: the words were so used through the needs of speech, that there might be one term by which to answer, when it is asked what the three are, whom we truly confess to be three
sources.raw_question: Why do we say 'one essence, three persons' (or, with some Greeks, 'three substances') of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit?

question: If the Son is eternal and coexists with the Father, does that make him the Father's brother rather than his Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: No. The Church does not say only that he is eternally with the Father. It also confesses him to be the Son begotten from the Father. One who is begotten cannot be the brother of the one who begets, and the Word cannot be the brother of him whose Word he is.
sources.quote: if, while we say that He is eternal, we also confess Him to be Son from the Father, how can He that is begotten be considered brother of Him who begets?
sources.raw_question: If the Son is eternal and coexists with the Father, does that make him the Father's brother rather than his Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Objection, that the Son's eternity makes Him coordinate with the Father, introduces the subject of His Divine Sonship, as a second proof of His eternity. The word Son is introduced in a secondary, but is to be understood in real sense. Since all things partake of the Father in partaking of the Son, He is the whole participation of the Father, that is, He is the Son by nature; for to be wholly participated is to beget.
sources.answer: No. Brotherhood would require both to be generated from some pre-existing origin, but the Father and Son were not; the Father is the origin of the Son and begat him. Since we confess the eternal one to be Son from the Father, the begotten cannot be brother of the one who begets, and the Word cannot be brother of him whose Word he is.
sources.quote: For the Father and the Son were not generated from some pre-existing origin, that we may account Them brothers, but the Father is the Origin of the Son and begat Him
sources.raw_question: If the Son is eternal and coexists with the Father, does that make the Son the Father's brother rather than his Son?

question: Does the Son's being called the radiance (and image) of the Father's glory prove that he is eternal?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: Yes. Light is never seen without the brightness of its radiance, so if the Father is everlasting Light and the Son is His radiance, it is senseless to say 'there was once when He was not' or 'before His generation He was not.'
sources.quote: for when did man see light without the brightness of its radiance, that he may say of the Son, ‘There was once, when He was not,’ or ‘Before His generation He was not.’
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being called the radiance of the Father's glory prove that he is eternal?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: Yes. When light exists, its radiance exists with it; when a subsistence exists, so does its full expression. Likewise, as long as the Father was, his Truth, the Son, was always in him. To make time the measure of the Image is to say Truth was once not in God, which is sin. God's Image is not drawn from outside but begotten by God himself.
sources.quote: For if the Son was not before His generation, Truth was not always in God, which it were a sin to say; for, since the Father was, there was ever in Him the Truth, which is the Son
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being the Image, Radiance, Expression and Truth of the Father show that he is eternal?

question: Does Scripture ascribe eternity to the Son of God in the same terms it uses of God the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. Micah foretells one born at Bethlehem whose goings forth are from everlasting. The Word was in the beginning with God, and Christ takes the incommunicable name I AM. In Revelation he calls himself Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, which is the strongest assertion that eternity past and to come belongs to him.
sources.quote: Bethlehem was the predicted birthplace into our world of One “whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ascribe eternity to the Son of God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father is called God "from everlasting to everlasting" and "the first and the last," and the same is said of Christ: his goings forth are "from everlasting" (Mic. 5:2), his throne as God is "forever and ever" (Heb. 1:8), and he calls himself "the first and the last" (Rev. 1:17). Setting these texts side by side shows that the Son shares the Father's eternal Deity.
sources.quote: Whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting. – Mic. 5:2. Unto the Son, he saith, thy throne, O God, is forever and ever. – Heb. 1:8. I am the first and the last.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ascribe eternity to Jesus Christ in the same terms it uses of God the Father?

question: Does the Son's eternity (and so necessary existence) imply that he is self-existent?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Waterland grants that an eternal Son exists necessarily. He denies, and says the opponent cannot prove, that necessary existence entails self-existence. The Son can be necessarily existent as eternally derived from the Father without being self-existent.
sources.quote: You argue that, if the Son be eternal, he is necessarily existing; which I allow: and if necessarily existing, then self-ewistent ; which I ‘deny; and you cannot prove.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is eternal and therefore necessarily existing, does it follow that he must be self-existent, so that his eternity must be denied?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Eternity and self-existence are distinct. The Son is eternal yet born, not unborn, as Novatian guards with 'non innatum, sed natum'. Alexander of Alexandria likewise warned that 'eternal' must not be mistaken for 'self-existent', against both Sabellian and Arian misconstructions.
sources.quote: There might be some then, as well as now, who knew not how to distinguish between ETERNITY and SELF-EXISTENCE. The Sabellians in particular might pretend that the Son, being e¢ernal, must be the self-existent Father himself.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being eternal imply that he is self-existent, and so the Father himself?

question: Is the Son equal to the Father in eternity, power and all the Father's properties, given that He is derived from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: Yes. As the Father is God, Spirit and Light, so is the Son, as God from God and Light from Light. We must count the Only-begotten as the Father's equal in eternity and might. At the same time we confess that He is from God and keep the unbegotten Father above all rivalry.
sources.quote: to set the unbegotten Father above all rivalry, and count the Only-begotten Son as His equal in eternity and might, confessing concerning God the Son that He is from God
sources.raw_question: Is the Son equal to the Father in eternity and power, given that He is derived from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. As the form and image of the invisible God, the Only-begotten is equal to the Father in all the Father's properties, through the fulness of true Godhead in himself. He is equal in power and honour. Just as the Father is always Father, the Son is always Son.
sources.quote: in all things which are properties of God the Father is equal to Him by virtue of the fulness of true Godhead in Himself.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son equal to the Father in all the Father's properties, including eternity?

question: Does the baptismal formula in Matthew 28:19 show that the Holy Spirit is a distinct divine person equal with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is joined with the Father and the Son in one series without any note of distinction as to personality. On the Socinian view the text would read 'in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the virtue or efficacy of the Father,' an absurd expression. Joining a quality to acknowledged persons, where they are considered as persons, makes no sense.
sources.quote: To join a quality with acknowledged persons, and that in such things and cases as wherein they are proposed under a personal consideration, is a strange kind of mystery.
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula in Matthew 28:19 show that the Holy Spirit is a person equal with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. In Matthew 28:19 the Spirit is placed in the same rank and order as the Father and the Son. This is done without the least note of difference from them as to an interest in personality. One so placed alongside the other divine persons must be a distinct divine person.
sources.quote: He is placed in the same rank and order, without any note of difference or distinction as to a distinct interest in the divine nature (that is, as we shall see, personality) with the other divine persons.
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula in Matthew 28:19 show that the Holy Spirit is a distinct divine person?

question: Does the baptismal formula show that the Holy Spirit is co-ordinate with the Father and the Son rather than numbered under them?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who say that the Holy Ghost is not to be numbered with, but numbered under, the Father and the Son. Wherein moreover there is a summary notice of the faith concerning right sub-numeration.
sources.answer: Yes. The name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is delivered in like manner, so by the co-ordination of words in baptism the Spirit relates to the Son as the Son relates to the Father. Since the Spirit is co-ordinate with the Son and the Son with the Father, the Spirit is also co-ordinate with the Father. With all three names ranked in one co-ordinate series, there is no room to connumerate some and subnumerate another.
sources.quote: according to the co-ordination of words delivered in baptism, the relation of the Spirit to the Son is the same as that of the Son to the Father
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula show that the Holy Spirit stands in the same relation to the Son as the Son does to the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who say that the Holy Ghost is not to be numbered with, but numbered under, the Father and the Son. Wherein moreover there is a summary notice of the faith concerning right sub-numeration.
sources.answer: Yes. In 'the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost' the Spirit stands with the Son exactly as the Son stands with the Father. If the Spirit is co-ordinate with the Son and the Son with the Father, the Spirit is co-ordinate with the Father too. Applying sub-numeration to the Son would also revive the blasphemies of unlike substance, lower rank and later origin.
sources.quote: according to the co-ordination of words delivered in baptism, the relation of the Spirit to the Son is the same as that of the Son to the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula show that the Holy Spirit is co-ordinate with the Father and the Son rather than numbered under them?

question: Does the doxology "glory to the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit" mean anything different from "to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit"?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That Scripture uses the words “in” or “by,” ἐν, cf. note on p. 3, in place of “with.” Wherein also it is proved that the word “and” has the same force as “with.”
sources.answer: No. "With" has the same force as the conjunction "and", since both keep the names joined. "Paul and Silvanus and Timothy" means exactly the same as "Paul with Timothy and Silvanus". So the doxology "with the Spirit" agrees with the baptismal formula of the Lord.
sources.quote: The Lord says “The Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost.” If I say the Father and the Son with the Holy Ghost shall I make, any difference in the sense?
sources.raw_question: Does saying "the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit" mean anything different from the scriptural "the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit"?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Of the origin of the word “with,” and what force it has. Also concerning the unwritten laws of the church.
sources.answer: No. As far as sense goes the two are the same. The "and" comes from the Lord's own words and cannot be rejected, so its equivalent "with" can also be accepted. The Apostle uses the conjunction and the preposition indifferently when joining the names, showing it makes no difference to their connection.
sources.quote: the Apostle uses either word indifferently,—saying at one time “in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God;” at another “when ye are gathered together, and my Spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus,”
sources.raw_question: Is saying "glory to the Father and to the Son with the Holy Spirit" different in sense from "glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit"?

question: Why is the Son called the Word of God rather than the Thought of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Great is the Unlikeness Between Our Word and the Divine Word. Our Word Cannot Be or Be Called Eternal.
sources.answer: Calling Him the Thought of God would suggest that something in God is revolved, now taking on a form and now losing it. The Son must be understood as the simple form itself, containing nothing formable that could also be unformed. Where Scripture speaks of God's thoughts, it uses a loose mode of speech, just as it speaks of God's forgetfulness, which strictly does not exist in Him.
sources.quote: Wherefore that Word of God is in such wise so called, as not to be called a thought of God, lest we believe that there is anything in God which can be revolved
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son called the Word of God rather than the Thought of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Our Word is Never to Be Equalled to the Divine Word, Not Even When We Shall Be Like God.
sources.answer: Because calling him God's thought would imply something in God that revolves, receiving, losing, and recovering form. Our thought, attaining to what we know and formed by it, is our word, but the divine Word must be understood without any thought on God's part. He is the simple form itself, with nothing formable that could also be unformed.
sources.quote: That Son of God, then, is not called the Thought of God, but the Word of God. For our own thought, attaining to what we know, and formed thereby, is our true word.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son of God called the Word of God rather than the Thought of God?

question: If Eunomius treats 'without end' and 'ungenerate' as convertible terms, must he admit that the Son, who is without end, is also ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Eunomius says God is ungenerate because he is without end, and without end because he is ungenerate, which makes the terms wholly convertible. He also admits the Son is without end. By parity of reasoning he must then grant that the Son is ungenerate, which overturns his own doctrine that ungeneracy is the divine essence belonging to the Father alone.
sources.quote: If, then, by reason of His being without end He is ungenerate, and the being without end and ungenerate are convertible terms, and he admits that the Son also is without end, by a parity of reasoning he must necessarily admit that the Son is ungenerate
sources.raw_question: If Eunomius treats 'without end' and 'ungenerate' as convertible terms, must he admit that the Son, who is without end, is also ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, by Eunomius' own reasoning it would follow, which exposes his position as self-refuting. He says God is ungenerate because He is without end and without end because ungenerate, making the terms wholly convertible. Since he admits the Son is without end, parity of reasoning forces him to admit the Son is ungenerate, which destroys his argument that ungeneracy distinguishes the Father's essence from the Son's.
sources.quote: and he admits that the Son also is without end, by a parity of reasoning he must necessarily admit that the Son is ungenerate, if (as he has said) His being without end and His being without beginning are identical in meaning.
sources.raw_question: If 'ungenerate' and 'without end' are convertible terms, as Eunomius claims, does it follow that the Son, who is without end, is also ungenerate?

question: Does Scripture teach that the Holy Spirit is the gift of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: Yes. In John 7, Christ promises rivers of living water to those who believe, and the evangelist explains that this water is the Spirit whom believers would receive. In John 4, Christ tells the Samaritan woman that if she knew the gift of God she would ask and receive living water. Since the living water is the Holy Spirit and that water is called the gift of God, the Spirit is the gift of God.
sources.quote: Because this living water, then, as the evangelist has explained to us, is the Holy Spirit, without doubt the Spirit is the gift of God
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture call the Holy Spirit the gift of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: Yes. Many testimonies, especially in Acts, unanimously call the Holy Spirit the gift of God: Peter promises the gift of the Holy Spirit at baptism, rebukes Simon Magus for thinking to buy the gift of God, and reports that God gave the Gentiles the like gift. He is the gift of God insofar as He is given to those who by Him love God.
sources.quote: there are many other testimonies of the Scriptures, which unanimously attest that the Holy Spirit is the gift of God, in so far as He is given to those who by Him love God.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that the Holy Spirit is the gift of God?

question: Is the grace given by the Father (and the Son) the same as the grace given by the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XII. The peace and grace of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one, so also is Their charity one, which showed itself chiefly in the redemption of man. Their communion with man is also one.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul's greeting speaks of one grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, yet peace is named as the fruit of the Spirit, and Peter promises the grace of the Holy Spirit at baptism. Hence grace comes from the Spirit as from the Father and the Son, since all divine grace is in the Spirit.
sources.quote: So grace comes also of the Holy Spirit as of the Father and the Son. For how can there be grace without the Spirit, since all divine grace is in the Spirit?
sources.raw_question: Is the grace and peace given by the Father and the Son the same as that given by the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: Yes. Because God speaks of pouring forth His own Spirit, we understand that the grace of the Father is the same as that of the Holy Spirit. This one grace is distributed to the hearts of each without division or loss.
sources.quote: By which we understand that the grace of God the Father is the same as that of the Holy Spirit, and that without any division or loss it is divided to the hearts of each.
sources.raw_question: Is the grace given by God the Father the same as the grace given by the Holy Spirit?

question: Does 'The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He hath seen the Father doing' (John 5:19) show that the Son lacks the Father's omnipotence?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. 'Nothing of Himself' means that, in accordance with His birth, the Father prompts His actions; but since whatever the Father does the Son does likewise, He subsists as nothing less than God and by the Father's omnipotent nature residing in Him can do all the Father does.
sources.quote: He subsists as nothing less than God, and by the Father’s omnipotent nature residing in Him, can do all that God the Father does.
sources.raw_question: Does 'The Son can do nothing of Himself' show that the Son lacks the Father's omnipotence?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary rejects this along with the other texts the heretics cite. Christ's words must be explained by their circumstances and by the distinction between gradual revelation and full expression of his nature. Exposed in this way, they leave his true Godhead unimpaired.
sources.quote: Christ’s true Godhead is no whit impaired because, to form the mystery of the Gospel faith, the birth and Name of Christ were revealed gradually
sources.raw_question: Does 'The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He hath seen the Father doing' show that the Son's power is limited and not omnipotent?

question: Are the Father, Son and Holy Spirit one beginning or three beginnings in relation to creation?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > How the Word Beginning (Principium) is Spoken Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: One. Each, asked about singly, is truly God, yet together they are one God. Hence God is called one Beginning with respect to the creature, not two or three beginnings.
sources.quote: Therefore, God is spoken of as one Beginning in respect to the creature, not as two or three beginnings.
sources.raw_question: Are Father, Son and Holy Spirit three beginnings of creation or one?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Father and the Son the Only Beginning (Principium) of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: One beginning. In respect to the creature, the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one Beginning, just as they are one Creator and one God.
sources.quote: But the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one Beginning in respect to the creature, as also one Creator and one God.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father, Son and Holy Spirit one beginning or three beginnings in relation to creation?

question: Can the human mind comprehend the eternal birth of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. With only the ordinary resources of unaided reason, the human mind is powerless to grasp an eternal birth. Through the study of things Divine, however, people come to apprehend mysteries beyond the range of common thought. This enables them to refute the claim that birth implies prior non-existence.
sources.quote: The mind of men is powerless with the ordinary resources of unaided reason to grasp the idea of an eternal birth, but they attain by study of things Divine to the apprehension of mysteries which lie beyond the range of common thought.
sources.raw_question: Can unaided human reason grasp the idea of an eternal birth of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. What precedes eternity still eludes comprehension even when eternity itself is grasped. The believer should not try to master the origin of the Only-begotten. When the struggle with ambiguities of language and thought ceases, the one certainty of His birth remains.
sources.quote: If anything exist which precedes eternity, it will be something which, when eternity is comprehended, still eludes comprehension. And this something is Thine, and is Thy Only-begotten
sources.raw_question: Can the eternal birth of the Son, which is before times eternal, be comprehended by the human mind?

question: Should we believe in the Son's eternal generation even though human reason cannot comprehend how it occurs?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. In nature itself we know many effects whose causes we cannot understand: the heavens, the sea, the growth of seeds, even our own minds. In these, reverence supplies faith where ignorance is natural. So ignorance of the mode of the Son's origin should not weaken faith in God's omnipotence; we hold only the revealed fact that He was born.
sources.quote: And since in what concerns myself I recognise Thee, ignorant as I am, so recognising Thee I will not in what concerns Thee cherish a feebler faith in Thy omnipotence, because I do not understand.
sources.raw_question: Should we believe in the Son's eternal generation even though human reason cannot comprehend how it occurs?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. Although birth before all times is foreign to earthly nature and beyond our understanding, we must confess within the limits set by the preaching of Apostles and Prophets and believe God's declarations about Himself rather than human conceptions.
sources.quote: We may grant that for anything to be born before times eternal is not the way of human nature, nor a matter which we can understand; and yet in this we believe God’s declarations about Himself.
sources.raw_question: Must we believe in the eternal birth of the Son even though human reason cannot conceive a birth outside of time?

question: Does Christ's saying that the Comforter would not come unless He went away imply that the Son is unequal to or less than the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: No. It was said not because of any inequality between the Word and the Spirit, but because the visible presence of the Son of man hindered the disciples. While they gazed on the form of a servant they thought only what they saw to be Christ, so that form had to be removed from their eyes. Only then could they perceive His equality with the Father.
sources.quote: But this is said, not on account of any inequality of the Word of God and of the Holy Spirit, but as though the presence of the Son of man with them would be a hindrance to the coming of Him
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that the Comforter will not come unless he goes away imply that the Son is unequal to or less than the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > All are Sometimes Understood in One Person.
sources.answer: No. The saying reflects no inequality between the Word and the Holy Spirit; rather, the visible presence of the Son of man was a hindrance because the disciples, gazing on the form of a servant, thought that alone to be Christ. The Spirit did not empty Himself taking the form of a servant as the Son did, so the servant-form had to be removed from their eyes.
sources.quote: But this is said, not on account of any inequality of the Word of God and of the Holy Spirit, but as though the presence of the Son of man with them would be a hindrance to the coming of Him
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that the Comforter would not come unless He went away imply that the Holy Spirit is greater than the Son, or the Son unequal to the Spirit?

question: Does the Holy Spirit distribute his spiritual gifts by his own sovereign choice and freedom?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit distributes these privileges as he will and has their sovereign disposal. Recognising this prepares believers to pray to him for them.
sources.quote: remember that he distributes them as he will, that he hath the sovereign disposal of them; and they will be prepared for this duty.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit have sovereign disposal over the spiritual gifts and privileges he distributes?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. To distribute (diairein) as he will adds choice, judgment and freedom of will to mere operation. He gives one thing or degree to one person and another to another. This keeps the saints dependent on his sovereignty. Likewise, he is said to "give" utterance, which means he gives freely.
sources.quote: He that distributes variously, doth it with choice, and judgment, and freedom of will.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit act with sovereign choice and freedom in distributing his gifts?

question: Does ascribing the fullest majesty and divinity to the Son diminish the glory of God the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The majesty of the Son is glory to the Father, for the Source must be glorious from which One worthy of such glory comes. The Son has nothing except by virtue of His birth, so all the glory inherent in the Son is reflected back to the Father who begot so great a Son.
sources.quote: the majesty of the Son is glory to the Father; the Source must be glorious from which He Who is worthy of such glory comes. The Son has nothing but by virtue of His birth
sources.raw_question: Does ascribing the fullest majesty and divinity to the Son diminish the glory of God the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The majesty of the Son is itself glory to the Father, because the Source from which One worthy of such glory comes must itself be glorious. The Son has nothing except by virtue of His birth from the Father, so all the glory inherent in the Son is reflected back to the Father who begot a Son so great.
sources.quote: the majesty of the Son is glory to the Father; the Source must be glorious from which He Who is worthy of such glory comes. The Son has nothing but by virtue of His birth; the Father shares all veneration received by that birthright.
sources.raw_question: Does ascribing full majesty and divinity to the Son of God take away from the glory of God the Father?

question: Do the Father, Son and Holy Spirit work separately or indivisibly?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > What the Doctrine of the Catholic Faith is Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: They work indivisibly. As they are indivisible in substance, so they are indivisible in operation. This is so even though certain manifestations, such as the incarnation, the dove and the Father's voice, are proper to one Person.
sources.quote: the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as they are indivisible, so work indivisibly
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, Son and Holy Spirit work separately or indivisibly?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > A Difficulty, How We are Justified in the Blood of the Son of God.
sources.answer: No. The Father, the Son and the Spirit of both work all things equally and harmoniously. Yet it remains true that we are justified in the blood of Christ in particular. We are also reconciled to God by the death of his Son.
sources.quote: Therefore together both the Father and the Son, and the Spirit of both, work all things equally and harmoniously; yet we are justified in the blood of Christ, and we are reconciled to God by the death of His Son.
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit work separately or with differing wills in the work of salvation?

question: Does calling Christ the 'Well-beloved' Son signify that he is the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: It signifies that he is Only-begotten. 'Well-beloved' and 'Only-begotten' are the same, as in 'This is My Well-beloved Son.' The title shows that he alone is from the Father, not that the Father hates others. In the same way God called Isaac Abraham's 'well-beloved' son, meaning his only son from Sara.
sources.quote: For not as wishing to signify His love towards Him did He say ‘Well-beloved,’ as if it might appear that He hated others, but He made plain thereby His being Only-begotten, that He might shew that He alone was from Him.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'Well-beloved' merely express the Father's love, or does it signify that he is Only-begotten?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: Yes. Even Greek usage treats 'well-beloved' as equivalent to 'only-begotten'. Homer calls Telemachus, the only son of Ulysses, 'well-beloved'. The one who is the only son of his father is therefore called well-beloved.
sources.quote: Therefore he who is the only son of his father is called well-beloved.
sources.raw_question: Does calling Christ the 'Well-beloved' Son signify that he is the Only-begotten Son?

question: Is God's Wisdom and Word merely a quality or attribute in the Father, rather than the subsisting Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: No. If Wisdom and Word were a quality in God, the Father's nature would be compounded of essence and quality. Since all quality inheres in essence, the indivisible Divine Monad would be split into essence and accident, which is a dishonourable absurdity.
sources.quote: for it will issue in this, that God is compounded of essence and quality. For whereas all quality is in essence, it will clearly follow that the Divine Monad, indivisible as it is, must be compound, being severed into essence and accident.
sources.raw_question: Could the Son be God's Wisdom and Word merely as a quality or attribute in the Father rather than as a subsisting Person?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: No. If Wisdom were a quality in the Father, God would be compound. If the Father were himself Very Wisdom in the sense that excludes a distinct Son, he would prove to be his own Son and Father. God is not compounded of Word, Wisdom and Power but is generative of them, and they are the one Son.
sources.quote: This is One Son, who is Word, Wisdom, Power; for God is not compounded of these, but is generative of them.
sources.raw_question: Is the Wisdom of God a quality in the Father, or the Father's own Very Wisdom, rather than the Son?

question: Is it better and more accurate to call God 'Father' than 'Unoriginate'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: Yes. 'Unoriginate' names God only from His works, as Maker and Framer, and is a word of the Greeks who do not know the Son. 'Father' names God from the Son and implies Him, and in knowing the Word one also knows that all things were made through Him. 'Father' is also simple, scriptural and given by the Lord Himself, who taught us to pray 'Our Father'.
sources.quote: he who calls God Father, names Him from the Word; and knowing the Word, he acknowledges Him to be Framer of all, and understands that through Him all things have been made.
sources.raw_question: Is it better to call God 'Father' than 'Unoriginate'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: Yes. 'Unoriginate' names God only from his works, signifying the things that came to be through the Word, whereas 'Father' names him from the Son. As the Word surpasses originated things, so calling God Father surpasses calling him Unoriginate.
sources.quote: it is more pious and more accurate to signify God from the Son and call Him Father, than to name Him from His works only and call Him Unoriginate
sources.raw_question: Is it more accurate and pious to call God 'Father' than to call him 'Unoriginate'?

question: Does Scripture teach that the Son received his being from the Father by an act of will and pleasure preceding him?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. No Scripture speaks of the Word's being 'by will.' Scripture everywhere speaks of the Word's eternal being: 'This is My beloved Son,' 'My heart uttered a good Word,' 'In the beginning was the Word,' 'in Thy light shall we see light,' the Radiance of Glory, the form of God, the Image of the invisible God. A precedent will is ascribed in Scripture only to originate things, which once were not.
sources.quote: For whence bring they ‘by will and pleasure?’ or from what Scripture? let them say, who are so suspicious in their words and so inventive of irreligion.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that the Son received his being from the Father by an act of will and pleasure?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. Scripture everywhere speaks of the being of the Word ('He was', Image, Radiance) but never of His being 'by will' or of His making. A precedent will and pleasure is applied in Scripture only to things originate, which by nature once were not and afterwards came to be, as the Psalms show of God's works.
sources.quote: All everywhere tell us of the being of the Word, but none of His being ‘by will,’ nor at all of His making
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that the Son of God came into being 'by will and pleasure' of the Father, as a will preceding Him?

question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers deny or teach the coeternity and consubstantiality of the Son with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. At most, the Ante-Nicene writers said things that Dr. Clarke believes, by his own inference, would destroy the Son's consubstantiality. The writers themselves never admitted that inference and expressly and constantly disowned it. Clarke's citations therefore yield only concessions, and his conclusion does not follow from them.
sources.quote: though, at the same time, those writers admitted no such consequence ; but expressly and constantly disowned it.
sources.raw_question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers deny the coeternity and consubstantiality of the Son with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: Yes. Consubstantiality implies coeternity. Besides this, Bishop Bull produced more than twenty direct Ante-Nicene testimonies for the Son's coeternity, and no writer of note plainly contradicts them.
sources.quote: That the Son is not coeternal with the Father. Consubstantiality implies coeternity: besides that the aforementioned learned Prelate has given us numerous direct testimonies for it from the Ante-Nicene Fathers, above twenty of them
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's consubstantiality with the Father imply that he is coeternal with the Father, and did the Ante-Nicene Fathers teach his coeternity?

question: Was the Son produced by an 'energy' of the Father that follows him and stands between Father and Son, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in assuming, to account for the existence of the Only-Begotten, an 'energy' that produced Christ's Person.
sources.answer: No. If an energy following the Father produced the Son, then that energy, not the Almighty, would be the real Father of the Lord, and the Son would be a son in name only, a bastard intruding into relationship with the Father. Gregory illustrates Eunomius' view with a shoemaker's leather-cutter that cuts a circle equal to its span, showing how it degrades the Son into a measured product of a tool.
sources.quote: It is this, then, that is the real Father of our Lord. And why do we go on talking of the Almighty as the Father, if it was not He, but an energy belonging to the things which follow Him externally that produced the Son
sources.raw_question: Was the Son produced by a particular 'energy' that follows God the Father and is commensurate with the Son as its work, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Discussion as to the exact nature of the 'energies' which, this man declares, 'follow' the being of the Father and of the Son.
sources.answer: No. Such an energy would be a go-between that belongs to neither the first being nor the second. It would be separate from the Father because it is only the exercise of his nature and not the nature itself. It would also be separate from the Son because what results is an active being, not a mere energy. Since an energy cannot be thought of apart from the one who exercises it, this scheme of energies producing the Son and Spirit falls apart.
sources.quote: like a sort of go-between to both, and neither coalescing with the nature of the first, nor combining with the second: separated from the first because it is not its very nature, but only the exercise of its nature
sources.raw_question: Is it coherent to say, with Eunomius, that the Son was produced by an energy of the Father that stands between them as an intermediary?

question: Should thanks and honour for salvation be given equally to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son accomplished the Father's will that all men should be saved, and the Father's good will became operative through the Son, who is his power. Therefore those who receive the preaching of the Cross should honour the Father and the Son alike.
sources.quote: the same grace should be a cause of equal thankfulness to the Son and to the Father
sources.raw_question: Should the Father and the Son be honoured and thanked equally for our salvation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: Equally to both. The grace of salvation comes from the Father and the Son together, and gratitude is owed only to benefactors. Excluding the Father would make him unworthy of thanks. Since 'he that honoureth the Son honoureth the Father,' both should be honoured alike.
sources.quote: the same grace should be a cause of equal thankfulness to the Son and to the Father
sources.raw_question: Should thanks for salvation be given to the Son alone, or equally to the Father and the Son?

question: Why did Christ give the names "Father, Son, and Holy Spirit" in the baptismal formula rather than other scriptural names for God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Because these titles are better able to lead us to faith about the Self-Existent. Christ passed over the many other divine names found in the Law, the Prophets and the Historical Books. He declared that holding to "Father, Son, and Holy Ghost" is enough to apprehend Him Who is absolutely Existent. Each of these titles, understood in its natural sense, is a rule of truth.
sources.quote: our Master Christ passes by all these and commits to us these titles as better able to bring us to the faith about the Self-Existent
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ give the names "Father, Son, and Holy Ghost" in the baptismal formula rather than other scriptural names for God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Because 'Father' is a relative term that connotes the Son along with itself. Confessing the eternal Father therefore includes the right faith about the eternal Son. This keeps the Father from being thought of as ever destitute of the excellences that are His own.
sources.quote: delivers to us as part of our profession of faith the title of “Father” as better suited to indicate the truth, being a title which, as has been said, by its relative sense connotes with itself the Son
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ hand down the name 'Father' in the baptismal formula rather than other names expressing the divine excellence?

question: Does Scripture apply the preposition 'of whom' (ek, 'from whom') to the Son and the Holy Spirit, or is it reserved for the Father alone?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That v: not found “of whom” in the case of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is the head "from whom" the whole body grows, and "of his fulness have all we received." Likewise "of" is used of the Spirit, as in "shall of the spirit reap life everlasting" and "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." So the phrase is not reserved to the Father.
sources.quote: from whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture use "of whom" (ἐκ) in reference to the Son and the Holy Spirit, and not only the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That v: not found “of whom” in the case of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.answer: Scripture applies "of whom" to the Son and the Spirit as well. Christ is the head from whom the whole body grows, of his fulness we all receive, and virtue goes out of him; likewise of the Spirit one reaps life everlasting, what was conceived in Mary is of the Holy Ghost, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit. So "of whom" is used in diverse manners and is not a mark peculiar to the Father.
sources.quote: Similarly we have frequently observed “of whom” used of the Spirit. “He that soweth to the spirit,” it is said, “shall of the spirit reap life everlasting.”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture apply the preposition "of whom" (ek, 'from whom') to the Son and the Holy Spirit, or is it reserved for the Father alone?

question: Do the different prepositions Scripture uses of the Father ('of whom'), the Son ('through whom') and the Holy Spirit ('in whom') show that the three differ in nature?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > The origin of the heretics' close observation of syllables.
sources.answer: No. Basil traces this claim to a sophism of Aetius: things unlike in nature are expressed in unlike terms, and things expressed in unlike terms are unlike in nature. He treats the argument as a covert attack on true religion. Its point is to read a difference of nature into a difference of wording, and it does so by insisting that the phrases are never interchanged. He adds that the scheme is borrowed from heathen philosophy's classification of causes, which is incompatible with the truth.
sources.quote: Their pertinacious contention is to show that the mention of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost is unlike, as though they will thence find it easy to demonstrate that there is a variation in nature.
sources.raw_question: Do the different prepositions Scripture uses of the Father ('of whom'), the Son ('by/through whom') and the Holy Spirit ('in whom') show that the three differ in nature?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That there is no distinction in the scriptural use of these syllables.
sources.answer: No. This allotment of phrases comes from heathen philosophy. The opponents apply it inconsistently: they follow pagan usage for the Son and Spirit but switch to apostolic usage when speaking of the Father. Its real outcome is absurd and impious. It makes the Son differ in nature from the Father as a tool differs from a craftsman, and makes the Spirit differ as place or time differs from tools and those who use them.
sources.quote: There is one nature of Cause; another of Instrument; another of Place. So the Son is by nature distinct from the Father, as the tool from the craftsman
sources.raw_question: Does assigning 'of whom' to the Father alone, 'through whom' to the Son, and 'in whom' to the Spirit show that the three differ in nature?

question: Should the Holy Spirit be described as being "in" the Father and the Son, or "with" them?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: "With" is the more fitting term. The Spirit's essential existence before the ages and His ceaseless abiding with Father and Son require titles expressing eternal conjunction. "With" signifies co-existence of things mutually inseparable, as fire co-exists with heat and life with the soul, whereas "in" suits a grace that comes and goes in creatures.
sources.quote: in relation to the Father and the Son it is more consistent with true religion to assert Him not to be in but to be with.
sources.raw_question: Should the Holy Spirit be described as being "in" the Father and the Son, or "with" them?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. In relation to created beings the Spirit is said to be "in" them, since His grace comes and goes, but in relation to the Father and Son it is more consistent with true religion to say He is "with" them. His eternal existence and ceaseless abiding with Father and Son demand words expressing inseparable, congenital fellowship, as life co-exists with the soul.
sources.quote: while in relation to the Father and the Son it is more consistent with true religion to assert Him not to be in but to be with.
sources.raw_question: Should the Holy Spirit be said to be "in" the Father and the Son in the same way He is "in" creatures?

question: Is the unity between the Father and the Son only a unity of will, like the believer's union with God through obedience and devotion?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. The heretics wrongly use our union with God as a model of mere obedience and devout will. Even our own union with Christ is natural, not merely moral: through the sacrament of the Body and Blood the Son abides in us after the flesh, and we are united in Him corporeally and inseparably. This points to the true and natural unity of the Son with the Father.
sources.quote: the heretics falsely maintain that the union between Father and Son is one of will only, and make use of the example of our own union with God, as though we were united to the Son and through the Son to the Father by mere obedience and a devout will
sources.raw_question: Is the unity between the Father and the Son only a unity of will, like the believer's union with God through obedience and devotion?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Hilary argues that Christ is in believers not merely by agreement of will but by verity of nature, through his assumed flesh communicated in the sacrament. Since our unity with the Father rests on the Father being in Christ and Christ in us, whoever denies the Father is naturally in Christ must also deny that Christ is naturally in us; the natural unity received in the sacrament is the sign of a perfect natural unity.
sources.quote: Whosoever then shall deny that the Father is in Christ naturally must first deny that either he is himself in Christ naturally, or Christ in him, because the Father in Christ and Christ in us make us one in Them.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who bring forward a unity of will between Father and Son
sources.raw_question: Is the unity between the Father and the Son only a unity of will, as the unity of believers with God is sometimes described?

question: Does a difference among the works produced indicate a difference in the energies that produced them, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that the same energies produce the same works, and that variation in the works indicates variation in the energies.
sources.answer: No. God's single energy of command, His sole will, gave existence to all things in the world, yet the things produced are vastly different from one another. If difference of works implied difference of energies, everything made by that one command would have to be of one type, which is contrary to fact.
sources.quote: How, then, when such vast differences are seen coming from that one energy of command, can this man shut his eyes to realities, and declare that the difference of works indicates difference of energies?
sources.raw_question: Does variation in the works produced indicate variation in the energies that produce them, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that the same energies produce the same works, and that variation in the works indicates variation in the energies.
sources.answer: No. God's single energy of command, his sole will, gave existence to everything in the world, yet the things made are vastly different: light and heavy, still and moving. If differing works required differing energies, everything made by God's one command would have to be of one type. Since it is not, the inference from unlike works to unlike energies fails.
sources.quote: How, then, when such vast differences are seen coming from that one energy of command, can this man shut his eyes to realities, and declare that the difference of works indicates difference of energies?
sources.raw_question: Does a difference among works indicate a difference in the energies that produced them, as Eunomius claims?

question: If, as Eunomius holds, a maker's nature indicates the nature of what it makes, and the Son is made by the Father, does it follow that the Son's nature is known from the Father's and is therefore like it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > There is no Word of God that commands such investigations: the uselessness of the philosophy which makes them is thereby proved.
sources.answer: It would follow that the Son's nature is known through the Father's, so the Son would be like the Father, which is the Church's doctrine. Gregory argues that Eunomius's own premise, if followed consistently, leads to the Church's teaching: whoever observed the Father's nature would thereby know the Son's. Eunomius's own assumptions therefore defeat his claim that the Son is unlike the Father.
sources.quote: For if the maker’s nature is an indication of the thing made, as he affirms, and if, according to his school, the Son is something made by the Father, anyone who has observed the Father’s nature would have certainly known thereby that of the Son
sources.raw_question: If, as Eunomius holds, the maker's nature reveals the nature of the thing made, and the Son is made by the Father, what follows about the Son's nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The observations made by watching Providence are sufficient to give us the knowledge of sameness of Being.
sources.answer: Yes, and so Eunomius's own premises lead to the Church's doctrine. If the worker's nature is a sign of what he works, anyone who has observed the Father's nature would thereby know the Son's. His principle therefore undermines his claim of the Son's unlikeness.
sources.quote: if the maker’s nature is an indication of the thing made, as he affirms, and if, according to his school, the Son is something made by the Father, anyone who has observed the Father’s nature would have certainly known thereby that of the Son
sources.raw_question: If, as Eunomius holds, a maker's nature indicates the nature of what it makes and the Son is something made by the Father, does it follow that the Son's nature is known from the Father's?

question: In what sense can the Son be said to be less than himself, and even less than the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > By What Rule in the Scriptures It is Understood that the Son is Now Equal and Now Less.
sources.answer: Only according to the form of a servant. He is less than himself because he "emptied himself." He is less than the Spirit because sin against the Son of man is forgiven but blasphemy against the Spirit is not. He also worked miracles by the Spirit and was anointed and sent because the Spirit of the Lord was upon him.
sources.quote: and He is less than Himself, because it is said of Him, He emptied Himself;”[^121] and He is less than the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: In what sense can the Son be said to be less than himself and less than the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Less Than the Father, and Than Himself.
sources.answer: In the form of a servant he is less than himself, and in the form of God he is greater than himself. He emptied himself and took the form of a servant without losing the form of God. So the same only-begotten Son is less in the one form and equal to the Father in the other. This shows that his being 'less' concerns the assumed humanity, not his divine nature.
sources.quote: is there any one who cannot perceive that He Himself in the form of God is also greater than Himself, but yet likewise in the form of a servant less than Himself?
sources.raw_question: In what sense can the Son be said to be less than himself?

question: Is it Sabellianism to hold that the one God is one Person only, namely the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
