sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds that making the one God one Person only, namely the Father, is the very essence of Sabellianism and the doctrine for which Paul of Samosata was condemned. Praxeas, Noetus and Sabellius, unable to conceive how one substance could be more than one Person, made one single Hypostasis the one God under three names.
sources.quote: I again tell you, that this is the very essence of Sabellianism, and the doctrine of ° Paul of Samosata, (as hath been observed to you above,) and for which he was condemned by the Church.
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that the one God is a single Person amount to Sabellianism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds it Sabellian to say there is but one who is God, one Person rather than one nature. The same applies to making the Godhead a single Hypostasis: a Father without his substantial Word and Spirit eternally and essentially subsisting with him and from him.
sources.quote: it is Sabellianism to say, that there is but one who is God, one Person only, instead of one nature: or to suppose the Godhead to be but one single Hypostasis
sources.raw_question: Is it Sabellianism to hold that the one God is one Person only, namely the Father?

question: If eternity means having neither beginning nor end, must the Son either be ungenerate or not be eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: No. The Father is conceived as before the Son only in the order of causation, with no interval of time before the Son's subsistence. The eternal nature of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit admits no 'when,' since where time is not, the 'when' is abolished. So the Son is eternal without being ungenerate.
sources.quote: if, in conceiving of the Father before the Son on the single score of causation, we inserted any mark of time before the subsistence of the Only-begotten, the belief which we have in the Son’s eternity might with reason be said to be endangered.
sources.raw_question: If eternity means having neither beginning nor end, must the Son either be ungenerate or not be eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: No. The Father is conceived as before the Son only on the score of causation, not by any mark of time, so the Son's eternity is not endangered. Where time is not, the 'when' is annihilated, and the Son, always appearing with the thought of the Father, is always found in existence.
sources.quote: if, in conceiving of the Father before the Son on the single score of causation, we inserted any mark of time before the subsistence of the Only-begotten, the belief which we have in the Son’s eternity might with reason be said to be endangered.
sources.raised_by_detail: some one amongst even very religious people
sources.raw_question: If eternity means having neither beginning nor end, must one either deny the Son's eternity or make the Son ungenerate?

question: How is Christ's grace communicated to believers, and what role does the Holy Spirit play in it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: Christ, having been vested with fulness, appoints the Spirit to take of that fulness and give it to believers. The Spirit takes from what is in Christ and actually bestows it, in the name of the Lord Jesus, on those he is sent to sanctify.
sources.quote: The Spirit takes of that fulness that is in Christ, and in the name of the Lord Jesus bestows it actually on them for whose sanctification he is sent.
sources.raw_question: What role does the Holy Spirit play in communicating Christ's grace to believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Grace is really communicated by Christ sending the Holy Ghost to regenerate believers and to create habitual grace and its daily supplies in their hearts. Christ's satisfaction and merit are the moral procuring cause that makes all grace his to dispose of, and the Spirit is sent by Christ as mediator, God and man, to work it in his people as he sees needful.
sources.quote: The real communication of grace is by Christ sending the Holy Ghost to regenerate us, and to create all the habitual grace, with the daily supplies thereof, in our hearts, that we are made partakers of.
sources.raw_question: How is grace really communicated from Christ to believers, and what role does the Holy Spirit play in it?

question: If, as Eunomius holds, names are immutably bound to the things they signify, does Scripture's calling the Son "God" mean there is no difference in Godhead between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > He then declares that the close relation between names and things is immutable, and thereafter proceeds accordingly, in the most excellent manner, with his discourse concerning “generated” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory turns Eunomius' own principle against him. If the connection of names with things is fixed, and Scripture truly calls the Only-begotten "God," then no difference in the conception of Godhead can be found between Father and Son, since the name is common to both.
sources.quote: he cannot apprehend any difference in respect of the conception of Godhead between the Father and the Son, seeing that this name is common to both
sources.raw_question: If, as Eunomius holds, names are immutably bound to the things they signify, does the fact that Scripture calls the Son "God" mean there is no difference in Godhead between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: No; it implies the opposite. Since Scripture truly calls the Only-begotten 'God', and names are fixed to their subjects, the shared name of Godhead means no difference in the conception of Godhead between Father and Son can be apprehended. The Son also shares many other names with the Father without divergence of meaning.
sources.quote: he cannot apprehend any difference in respect of the conception of Godhead between the Father and the Son, seeing that this name is common to both
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's principle that 'the close relation of names to things is immutable' imply a difference of Godhead between the Father and the Son?

question: Is the Son begotten by the Father's will (as a product of His good pleasure) or by the Father's nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. The Son is not a work of good pleasure but the Living Counsel and Offspring in truth and nature, as radiance from light. To make Him a work of will is to bring the doctrine of Valentinus into the Church; Scripture shows the Word in the Father's heart and the Son in the Father, which leaves no room for a precedent will.
sources.quote: Therefore call not the Son a work of good pleasure; nor bring in the doctrine of Valentinus into the Church; but be He the Living Counsel, and Offspring in truth and nature, as the Radiance from the Light.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God a product of the Father's good pleasure or will, rather than begotten from the Father's nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: By nature. Human fathers do not become parents by previous counsel; begetting is proper to their nature, and what they beget is like themselves, not like their good pleasure. Since the Arians argue about the Godhead in a human way, the human instance refutes them: the Son is begotten not by will but in nature and truth.
sources.quote: What we beget, is like, not our good pleasure, but like ourselves; nor become we parents by previous counsel, but to beget is proper to our nature; since we too are images of our fathers.
sources.raw_question: Does the analogy of human fathers show that the Son is begotten by will or by nature?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be grieved by believers, and if so, how?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is grieved by our disobedience, so his glory lies in our bringing forth fruit. He dwells in believers as in his temple, which therefore must not be defiled.
sources.quote: The Spirit is glorified also by it. He is grieved by our disobedience, Eph. iv. 30; and therefore his glory is in our bringing forth fruit. He dwells in us, as in his temple; which is not to be defiled.
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be grieved and glorified, and does he personally indwell believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture commands believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 4:30), as one would grieve a loving friend. As to sanctification, he is grieved when believers walk in unholiness while he is working holiness in them. As to consolation, he is grieved when they seek their joy in creatures rather than in him. He is also grieved when, through darkness and unbelief, they refuse the comforts he offers.
sources.quote: what can grieve a loving and tender friend more than to oppose him and slight him when he is most intent about our good, — and that a good of the greatest consequence to us.
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be grieved by believers, and if so, how?

question: Can it be said of the Son, as of the Father, that there is no God beside Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. The Father attributes absolute Divinity to the Son by saying 'there is no God beside Thee,' just as he says it of himself. It is peculiar to the Son that there is no God beside Him and peculiar to the Father that there is no God apart from Him. These are exact equivalents that must not be separated.
sources.quote: It is the peculiar characteristic of the Son of God that there is no God beside Him; the peculiar characteristic of God the Father that there is no God apart from Him.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son share the Father's exclusive divine prerogative that there is no God beside Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says of the Son, 'there is no God beside Thee,' so the same exclusive divinity is ascribed to both as exact equivalents. It is the peculiar characteristic of the Son that there is no God beside Him, and of the Father that there is no God apart from Him; what is perfectly matched should not be separated.
sources.quote: It is the peculiar characteristic of the Son of God that there is no God beside Him; the peculiar characteristic of God the Father that there is no God apart from Him.
sources.raw_question: Can it be said of the Son, as of the Father, that there is no God beside Him?

question: Does the command that all should honour the Son as they honour the Father prove that the Son is of the same nature as the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. Judgment was given so that the Son would receive honour equal to the Father's, and whoever dishonours the Son dishonours the Father also. Since the Son equals the Father in work, power, honour, and the punishment of those who deny him, his nature cannot differ from the Father's.
sources.quote: How, after this proof, can we imagine that the nature given Him by birth is different from the Father’s, when He is the Father’s equal in work, in power, in honour, in the punishment awarded to gainsayers?
sources.raw_question: Does the command that all should honour the Son as they honour the Father prove that the Son's nature is the same as the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. Only things of the same nature are equal in honour, and equality of honour shows there is no separation between those honoured. Since he who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father, the honour of Christ is one and the same as, and inseparable from, the honour of God.
sources.quote: It is only things of the same nature that are equal in honour; equality of honour denotes that there is no separation between the honoured.
sources.raw_question: Does the command that all should honour the Son even as they honour the Father imply that the Son is of the same nature as the Father?

question: Could the Father's "unapproachable" light be unapproachable to, or alien from, the Son's true and good light?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then referring to the blasphemy of Eunomius, which had been refuted by the great Basil, where he banished the Only-begotten God to the realm of darkness, and the apology or explanation which Eunomius puts forth for his blasphemy, he shows that his present blasphemy is rendered by his apology worse than his previous one; and herein he very ably discourses of the “true” and the “unapproachable” Light.
sources.answer: No. "Unapproachable" rightly means remote from its opposite, evil. To make it mean alienation from good would make God alien from and at enmity with Himself, at once good and opposed to good. This is impossible, because good is akin to good.
sources.quote: But if he were to say that “unapproachable” signified alienation from good, he would suppose nothing else than that God was alien from, and at enmity with, Himself, being at the same time good and opposed to good. But this is impossible: for the good is akin to good.
sources.raw_question: Could the Father's light be "unapproachable" in the sense of being inaccessible to the Son's light, which is good and true?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then referring to the blasphemy of Eunomius, which had been refuted by the great Basil, where he banished the Only-begotten God to the realm of darkness, and the apology or explanation which Eunomius puts forth for his blasphemy, he shows that his present blasphemy is rendered by his apology worse than his previous one; and herein he very ably discourses of the “true” and the “unapproachable” Light.
sources.answer: No. If the Father's light rejected the truth, it would be associated with falsehood, because among contradictories the absence of the better entails the presence of its opposite. To read 'unapproachable' as alienation from good would make God at enmity with Himself, which is impossible since good is akin to good. So the one Light does not diverge from the other.
sources.quote: For if it were to reject the truth it would of course be associated with falsehood. For the nature of contradictories is such that the absence of the better involves the presence of its opposite.
sources.raw_question: Could the Father's unapproachable light be unapproachable to, or alien from, the Son's true light?

question: When theologians call God 'ungenerate' and 'indestructible', are they bestowing these attributes on Him or only ascribing them?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Basil merely says that whatever in the divine essence transcends the measurable distances of the ages in either direction is marked by distinctive names, so that distinct conceptions are signified by distinct names. Calling what is anterior to all beginning 'ungenerate' and what has no limit 'indestructible' describes God; it confers nothing on Him.
sources.quote: whatever in the Divine essence transcends the measurable distances of the ages in either direction is called by certain distinctive names
sources.raw_question: When theologians call God 'ungenerate' and 'indestructible' in relation to the ages, are they bestowing or lending these attributes to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. To bestow is to give something one possesses that another lacks, whereas to ascribe is to designate by a name what another already has. Basil's words ascribe indestructibility to God; they do not confer it, so the charge that human conception lends God His attributes or primacy is false.
sources.quote: For that man bestows who possesses something which another has not, while that man ascribes who designates with a name what another has.
sources.raw_question: When theologians ascribe names such as 'indestructible' or 'ungenerate' to God, are they bestowing these attributes on Him?

question: If 'ungenerate' and 'indestructible' are applied to God by human conception with reference to the ages, does it follow that indestructibility does not belong to God's essential nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Only things that can be added to or subtracted from a nature are foreign to it; indestructibility is not adventitious but always belongs to God, who is always what He is and receives no increase or addition of properties. Naming this attribute by reference to the ages does not make it any less essential to Him.
sources.quote: If, then, the indestructibility which we ascribe to God were adventitious, and did not always belong to Him, or might cease to belong to Him, he might be justified in his calumnious attack.
sources.raw_question: If God is called indestructible and ungenerate by the faculty of conception with reference to the ages, does that mean indestructibility is not part of God's essential nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Only what can be added to or taken from a nature is foreign to it, and indestructibility is not adventitious but always belongs to God. God always is what He is, receiving no addition of properties, so naming His indestructibility by conception with reference to the ages does not deny that it is of His essential nature.
sources.quote: if it is always the same, and our contention is, that God is always what He is, and that He receives nothing by way of increase or addition of properties, but continues always in whatsoever is conceived and called good
sources.raw_question: If 'ungenerate' and 'indestructible' are applied to God by human conception, from looking to past and future ages, does it follow that indestructibility does not belong to God by His nature?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's role in the conception of Christ in Mary's womb prove that the Holy Spirit is Creator?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, as well as the Father and the Son, is pointed out in holy Scripture as Creator, and the same truth was shadowed forth even by heathen writers, but it was shown most plainly in the Mystery of the Incarnation, after touching upon which, the writer maintains his argument from the fact that worship which is due to the Creator alone is paid to the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Matthew says Mary was found with child "of" (ex) the Holy Spirit. What is "of" someone comes either from his substance or from his power. The Spirit was not changed into flesh and bones, so the Virgin conceived by His operation and power. That creative act proves He is Creator.
sources.quote: If as of her substance, was the Spirit, then, changed into flesh and bones? Certainly not. But if the Virgin conceived as of His operation and power, who can deny that the Holy Spirit is Creator?
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's role in the conception of Christ in Mary's womb show that the Holy Spirit is Creator?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, as well as the Father and the Son, is pointed out in holy Scripture as Creator, and the same truth was shadowed forth even by heathen writers, but it was shown most plainly in the Mystery of the Incarnation, after touching upon which, the writer maintains his argument from the fact that worship which is due to the Creator alone is paid to the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord whom the angels serve was begotten by the Holy Spirit coming upon the Virgin, as Matthew and Luke testify. So the birth from the Virgin is the work of the Spirit. Since He was conceived of the Spirit's operation and power, not His substance, the Spirit must be Creator, and nothing can be said that He did not make, angels included.
sources.quote: since the Lord Himself, Whom the Angels serve, was begotten by the Holy Spirit coming upon the Virgin
sources.raw_question: Does the conception of Christ by the Holy Spirit prove that the Spirit is Creator?

question: Can the Father's being be known first and then used to infer the nature of the Son, as Eunomius proposes, or is the Father known only through the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His dictum that 'the manner of the likeness must follow the manner of the generation' is unintelligible.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son reveals him, so knowledge of the Father comes only through the Son. Eunomius ignores this and proceeds in reverse, presuming the Father's being is more readily comprehensible than the Son's, which contradicts the divine utterances he claims to know accurately.
sources.quote: ignoring the fact that it is not possible to approach to a knowledge of the Father except through the Son. “No man knoweth the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son shall reveal Him[^167].”
sources.raw_question: Can the nature of the Father be known first and then used to infer the nature of the Son, as Eunomius proposes by reasoning from the Begetter's being to the 'manner of generation'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He declares falsely that 'the manner of the generation is to be known from the intrinsic worth of the generator'.
sources.answer: Yes, and this is self-defeating for Eunomius. Scripture teaches that the Father can be known only through the Son. By treating the Father's being as more readily grasped and reasoning from it to the Son, Eunomius ignores this teaching. He also unwittingly reverses his own claim that the Son is inferior.
sources.quote: He goes back, for instance, to the begetting being, and from thence takes a survey of the begotten
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's method of inferring the Son's nature from the Father's being imply that the Father is more knowable than the Son?

question: What is the status of Matthew 28:19 for the doctrine of the Trinity: is it where the doctrine originates, or Jesus' own direct announcement of a doctrine already presupposed?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The doctrine is already presupposed there. What the passage records is the Founder's authoritative announcement of the Trinity as the God of Christianity, in one of His most solemn declarations.
sources.quote: We are not witnessing here the birth of the doctrine of the Trinity; that is presupposed.
sources.raw_question: Is Matthew 28:19 the point where the doctrine of the Trinity originates?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. By 'the Son' Jesus meant Himself with distinct personality, which implies the equally distinct personality of the Father and Holy Ghost. Ascribing this threefold Name to Jehovah is a direct ascription of threefold personality to the God of Israel. This is not the birth of the doctrine, which is presupposed, but its authoritative announcement by Christianity's Founder.
sources.quote: This is a direct ascription to Jehovah the God of Israel, of a threefold personality, and is therewith the direct enunciation of the doctrine of the Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Is Matthew 28:19 a direct enunciation of the doctrine of the Trinity by Jesus Himself?

question: Does Eunomius's reasoning from differences of works to differences of producing energies prove that the Son and the Holy Spirit differ in essence or rank from one another and from the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His elaborate account of degrees and differences in 'works' and 'energies' within the Trinity is absurd.
sources.answer: No. The comparison is irrelevant and inconsistent with Eunomius's own system. Scripture teaches that the heavens, angels, stars, and man are all the work of One. In Eunomius's theology, by contrast, the Son is the work of an energy following the first Being and the Spirit is the work of that work, so the analogy compares unlike processes. It would only support him if creation were produced in a chain, each thing from the one before, which no one holds.
sources.quote: since he grants that it was all made by One (unless he wishes to contradict Scripture downright), while he describes the production of the Persons after a different fashion, what connexion is there between this newly imported view and what went before?
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's claim that differences between created works (angels, stars, heavens, man) reflect differences between producing energies prove that the Son and the Spirit are graded beneath the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that the same energies produce the same works, and that variation in the works indicates variation in the energies.
sources.answer: No, it would prove the opposite. On Eunomius's own premises the Son is the work of the Father and the Spirit the work of the Son. Since the Father and the Son work in the same manner, the principle would require the beings produced by those energies to be the same. So there is no gulf between the being of the Son and the being of the Spirit, and Eunomius's own words confirm their essential union.
sources.quote: the likeness in manner of the Father’s and the Son’s energies will demonstrate the sameness of these beings who each result from them.
sources.raw_question: If Eunomius's principle that like energies produce like works were granted, would it prove an essential difference between the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Can the Wisdom of God, which is the Son, be something created, given that Christ is called the Power and Wisdom of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. If the Wisdom of God were created, God would have His Wisdom as something imported and acquired afterward, which He did not have at first. But God has nothing in Himself as created or imported; the Son, who is God's Wisdom, Power, Life and Truth, is always in the Father, so the Father is never void of good.
sources.quote: For if the Wisdom of God is created (and Christ is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God), God, it would follow, has His Wisdom as a thing imported, receiving afterwards, as the result of making, something which He had not at first.
sources.raw_question: Can the Wisdom of God (the Son) be a created thing, given that Christ is called the Power and Wisdom of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. God over all has nothing in Himself as created or imported, neither power nor wisdom nor word; Christ is the Power and Wisdom of God. If Wisdom were created, God would have received afterwards what He did not have at first, and the Father's bosom would once have been void of the Son, which is impious.
sources.quote: For if the Wisdom of God is created (and Christ is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God), God, it would follow, has His Wisdom as a thing imported, receiving afterwards, as the result of making, something which He had not at first.
sources.raw_question: Can the Wisdom of God, which is the Son, be something created in God?

question: Does the Holy Spirit come as the believer's Comforter willingly and out of his own love, or only because he is sent?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: He comes willingly, out of his own great love and infinite condescension. He knew beforehand that believers would grieve him, provoke him and quench his motions, yet he chose to come as their comforter. He distributes as he will and works as he pleases, which shows that he acts as a free and loving agent. This love of the Spirit is the head and source of all believers' communion with him.
sources.quote: Now, this is his own great love and infinite condescension. He willingly proceedeth or comes forth from the Father to be our comforter.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit come as Comforter willingly and out of his own love, or only because he is sent?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Yes. The Holy Ghost, in his infinite love and kindness, has condescended to be the believer's comforter, and he does so willingly, freely and powerfully. This love should move believers to holiness so as not to grieve him.
sources.quote: The Holy Ghost, in his infinite love and kindness towards me, hath condescended to be my comforter; he doth it willingly, freely, powerfully.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit act as the believer's comforter willingly and out of his own love?

question: Could the Son be equal to the Father in some divine attributes, such as power, but unequal in others, such as wisdom or eternity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Same Argument Continued.
sources.answer: No. Just as the virtues of the human mind are inseparable, so that men equal in courage must be equal in prudence (otherwise one's courage would be less prudent), much more in God's simple substance are the attributes inseparable. Hence inequality in any one thing signifying the substance would mean inequality in all, and equality in one entails equality in all.
sources.quote: For if you say that such and such men are equal in courage, but that one of them is greater in prudence, it follows that the courage of the other is less prudent, and so neither are they equal in courage
sources.raw_question: Could the Son be equal to the Father in one divine attribute (such as power) but unequal in another (such as wisdom)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > That the Unity of the Essence of the Father and the Son is to Be Gathered from the Words, ‘We are One.’ The Son is Equal to the Father Both in Wisdom and in All Other Things.
sources.answer: No. Power that is less wise is not equal power, and wisdom that is less powerful is not equal wisdom. Likewise, greatness that is less eternal is not equal greatness. So if the Son were unequal in anything, he would be equal in nothing. Scripture says he 'thought it not robbery to be equal with God,' so he is equal in every one thing, and therefore in all that is said of his substance.
sources.quote: It remains, therefore, that if He is not equal in anything, He is not equal in all.
sources.raw_question: Could the Son be equal to the Father in some divine attributes, such as power, but unequal in others, such as wisdom or eternity?

question: Must the doxology giving glory to the Father and the Son "with the Holy Spirit" be rejected because the phrase lacks written authority in Scripture?
synthesis: Both passages are from Basil of Caesarea, and both answer no on the ground of unwritten tradition. One passage stresses that most of the Church's mysteries are received without written authority and cites Paul's command to hold fast traditions. The other argues that even the baptismal confession of faith rests on unwritten tradition, so opponents must be consistent, and adds that "with" comes from the Fathers and is backed by argument.

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: No. Most of the Church's mysteries are received without written authority, so this one should be received along with them. Basil holds it apostolic to abide by unwritten traditions, citing Paul's praise for keeping the ordinances delivered and his command to hold fast traditions taught by word or epistle.
sources.quote: But if the greater number of our mysteries are admitted into our constitution without written authority, then, in company with the many others, let us receive this one. For I hold it apostolic to abide also by the unwritten traditions.
sources.raised_by_detail: opponents of the doxology "with the Spirit" (Pneumatomachi)
sources.raw_question: Must the doxology "glory to the Father with the Son, with the Holy Spirit" be rejected because it lacks written authority in Scripture?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Of the origin of the word “with,” and what force it has. Also concerning the unwritten laws of the church.
sources.answer: No. Many practices and even the very form of the confession of faith in Father, Son and Holy Spirit rest on unwritten tradition. If opponents reject the doxology for lacking written authority, they must likewise produce written evidence for the confession of faith. The word "with" comes from the Fathers, is preserved in unperverted churches, and is strongly supported by argument.
sources.quote: If they deprecate our doxology on the ground that it lacks written authority, let them give us the written evidence for the confession of our faith and the other matters which we have enumerated.
sources.raw_question: Is the doxology "glory to the Father and to the Son with the Holy Spirit" illegitimate because the phrase lacks written authority in Scripture?

question: Did the Son come into being by an act of the Father's will that existed before Him?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. If will came first in the Father, then 'I in the Father' would not be true. Even if the Son were in the Father, he would hold only a second place, since the will in which he subsisted came before him. He would then be one of the things that come into being by will, and could not be Lord over the servants.
sources.quote: for if will precedes in the Father, the Son’s words are not true, ‘I in the Father;’ or even if He is in the Father, yet He will hold but a second place
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent with the Son's words 'I in the Father' to hold that a will existed in the Father before the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: Yes, that absurdity would follow. God's will concerning all things is in His Word, in whom He makes and begets again; so if the Son too came by will, the will concerning Him would reside in some other Word through whom He came to be. Since there is no other Word, but all things came through Him, the Son is not by will.
sources.quote: For if He too came to be as you maintain, by will, it follows that the will concerning Him consists in some other Word, through whom He in turn comes to be
sources.raw_question: If the Son came into being by the Father's will, would there need to be another Word before Him?

question: Did the Son of God begin to exist only when he was born as man, so that Christ had no existence before the incarnation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: No. The Word existed in the beginning with God, by whom all things were made, and was always present with mankind; at the time appointed by the Father he was united to his own workmanship by becoming man. The Son did not begin to exist at the incarnation, but being with the Father from the beginning, he then commenced afresh the line of human beings.
sources.quote: For I have shown that the Son of God did not then begin to exist, being with the Father from the beginning; but when He became incarnate, and was made man, He commenced afresh the long line of human beings
sources.raised_by_detail: those who say, "If our Lord was born at that time, Christ had therefore no previous existence"
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Christ was born at a particular time in history imply that the Son of God had no existence before then?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVII.—The apostles teach that it was neither Christ nor the Saviour, but the Holy Spirit, who did descend upon Jesus. The reason for this descent.
sources.answer: No. The Son of God did not begin to exist at his birth, because he was with the Father from the beginning. In the time the Father appointed he was united to his own workmanship and became man. At the incarnation he recapitulated the human race, so that what was lost in Adam, the image and likeness of God, might be recovered in Christ.
sources.quote: For I have shown that the Son of God did not then begin to exist, being with the Father from the beginning; but when He became incarnate, and was made man, He commenced afresh the long line of human beings
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God begin to exist only when he was born as man, so that Christ had no previous existence?

question: Can the Son of God consistently be called both begotten (a 'product of generation') and a created thing (a 'product of making' or 'creation')?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Then he ends the book with an exposition of the Divine and Human names of the Only-Begotten, and a discussion of the terms “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. The terms differ widely in sense: a work is what a craftsman makes, a son is what a father begets, and no sane person calls a work a son or a son a work. So if the Only-begotten is a Son he is not a creature, and if he were created he would be alien to the title "Son," just as heaven, sea and earth are not called sons.
sources.quote: if He is a Son, that He is not to be called a “product of creation,” and if He is created, that He is alien from the appellation of “Son,” just as heaven and sea and earth, and all individual things, being things created, do not assume the name of “Son.”
sources.raw_question: Can the Son of God consistently be called both a "product of generation" (begotten) and a "product of making" or "creation"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds again to discuss the impassibility of the Lord's generation; and the folly of Eunomius, who says that the generated essence involves the appellation of Son, and again, forgetting this, denies the relation of the Son to the Father: and herein he speaks of Circe and of the mandrake poison.
sources.answer: No. Gregory treats it as an evident contradiction to say that the same Person was begotten and is a thing created. On this view something would be closely connected with the name 'Son' and yet foreign to what 'Son' means. Being truly begotten as Son excludes being a creature.
sources.quote: For what could be clearer than this contradiction—than to say that the same Person was begotten and is a thing created, and that something is closely connected with the name of “Son,” and, again, is alien from the sense of “Son”?
sources.raw_question: Can the same Person, the Son of God, coherently be called both begotten and a created thing ('product of making' and 'product of creation')?

question: Why is the Holy Spirit said to proceed rather than to be begotten?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What It is that Suffices Here to Solve the Question Why the Spirit is Not Said to Be Begotten, and Why the Father Alone is Unbegotten. What They Ought to Do Who Do Not Understand These Things.
sources.answer: If the Spirit were called a Son, He would be the Son of both Father and Son, which is absurd. No one is son of two except of a father and a mother, and nothing of that kind may be imagined between God the Father and God the Son.
sources.quote: if He, too, was called a Son, He would certainly be called the Son of both, which is most absurd, since no one is son of two, save of father and mother
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit said to proceed rather than to be born or begotten?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What It is that Suffices Here to Solve the Question Why the Spirit is Not Said to Be Begotten, and Why the Father Alone is Unbegotten. What They Ought to Do Who Do Not Understand These Things.
sources.answer: Because the birth of the Word differs from the procession of the Gift of God. If the Spirit were begotten of the Father, he would be the Son's brother; so the only-begotten Son did not say the Spirit is begotten, but that he proceeds from the Father.
sources.quote: the only-begotten Son did not say that the Holy Spirit is begotten of the Father, otherwise He would be His brother, but that he proceeds from Him.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit said to proceed from the Father rather than to be begotten of the Father?

question: Can the Father be called the 'greater' God and the Son a 'lesser' God without contradicting the declaration that the Lord God is one Lord?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 1: Whether all other beings, besides the one Supreme God, be not excluded by the texts of Isaiah, (to which many more might be added ;) and consequently, whether C
sources.answer: No. A greater and a lesser God make two Gods. Scripture says 'The Lord thy God is one Lord' and 'There is none other besides me,' not 'none other equal to me.' Following Augustine against Maximin, one must either confess that Father and Son are one Lord God or plainly deny that Christ is Lord God at all.
sources.quote: We shall answer you as often, that the greater and the “less make two.
sources.raw_question: Can calling the Father 'greater' and the Son 'less' reconcile Christ's divinity with the confession that the Lord God is one Lord?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 1: Whether all other beings, besides the one Supreme God, be not excluded by the texts of Isaiah, (to which many more might be added ;) and consequently, whether C
sources.answer: No. Following Augustine against Maximin, a greater and a lesser God make two Gods, whereas Scripture says not 'Thy greater Lord God is one Lord' but 'The Lord thy God is one Lord.' So one must either acknowledge that Father and Son are together one Lord God, or plainly deny that Christ is Lord God at all.
sources.quote: Either therefore ‘acknowledge that Father and Son are one Lord God; or in ‘* plain terms deny that Christ is Lord God at all>.”
sources.raised_by_detail: Maximin, the Arian Bishop; Dr. Clarke
sources.raw_question: Can the Father be the 'greater' God and the Son a 'lesser' God without contradicting the Old Testament declaration that the Lord God is one Lord?

question: If God was ungenerate before man existed, must the name 'ungenerate' also be prior to man rather than a human invention? Or, conversely, does the name's human origin make God's ungeneracy a mere conception?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. By Eunomius' own premises the opposite follows. Creation is later than the Creator, and man comes last in creation. Speech belongs to man, and 'ungeneracy' is a noun, a part of speech. So whoever grants that the Divine nature is prior to man must grant that the name invented to express it came later. Speech could no more be exercised before speakers existed than farming before farmers.
sources.quote: it follows that he who admits that the Divine nature was anterior to man must at the same time admit that the name invented by man to express that nature was itself later in being.
sources.raw_question: If God existed as ungenerate before the creation of man, must the name 'ungenerate' itself also be prior to man rather than a human invention?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. God existed and remains ungenerate independently of all speech, silence, or thought, before creation itself; only the verbal form expressing this fact is posterior and of human devising. No one claims God is a mental conception, so Eunomius's proof that God existed ungenerately before man does nothing to show the name is identical with the essence.
sources.quote: independently of all exercise of speech, or silence, or thought, and before the very idea of creation, God was and remains ungenerate
sources.raw_question: If the name 'ungenerate' is a product of human conception, does it follow that God was not ungenerate before humans named him, or that God himself is a mere conception?

question: Does the Son partake of something from the Father (whether external to the Father or distinct from the Son's own essence), or is the Son Himself what is partaken of the Father's essence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Objection, that the Son's eternity makes Him coordinate with the Father, introduces the subject of His Divine Sonship, as a second proof of His eternity. The word Son is introduced in a secondary, but is to be understood in real sense. Since all things partake of the Father in partaking of the Son, He is the whole participation of the Father, that is, He is the Son by nature; for to be wholly participated is to beget.
sources.answer: No. If it were external, the Son would partake not of the Father but of that thing, would no longer be second after the Father, and would be son of that thing; this contradicts the Father calling him 'My Beloved Son'. If it were from the Father's essence but other than the Son's essence, there would be something intermediate between the Father and the Son. Hence what is from the Father's essence and proper to him is entirely the Son.
sources.quote: it follows that what is partaken is not external, but from the essence of the Father. And as to this again, if it be other than the essence of the Son, an equal extravagance will meet us
sources.raw_question: If the Son partakes of the Father, could what he partakes of be something external to the Father or distinct from the Son's own essence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Objection, that the Son's eternity makes Him coordinate with the Father, introduces the subject of His Divine Sonship, as a second proof of His eternity. The word Son is introduced in a secondary, but is to be understood in real sense. Since all things partake of the Father in partaking of the Son, He is the whole participation of the Father, that is, He is the Son by nature; for to be wholly participated is to beget.
sources.answer: The Son is Himself what is partaken from the Father; He partakes of nothing. What is from the Father's essence and proper to Him is entirely the Son, and to say God is wholly participated is the same as to say He begets. Hence, when we partake of the Son through the Spirit, we are said to partake of God.
sources.quote: this shews that the Son Himself partakes of nothing, but what is partaken from the Father, is the Son; for, as partaking of the Son Himself, we are said to partake of God
sources.raw_question: Is the Son something that partakes of the Father, or is He Himself what is partaken of the Father?

question: Does the Son's being a Son in the proper sense require division and a separate existence from the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. The Son may be a Son in a proper sense without division and without a separate existence. This is what is meant by interior generation.
sources.quote: he may be a Son in a proper sense, and in our sense, without division, and without a separate existence; and the name for this is interior generation
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being a Son in the proper sense imply division and a separate existence from the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. The Son may be a Son in a proper sense without division and without separate existence, which is what the Catholics call interior generation. Scripture nowhere says Father and Son must have a separate existence; that claim rests only on reasoning from the nature of things.
sources.quote: alleging that he may be a Son in a proper sense, and in our sense, without division, and without a separate existence; and the name for this is interior generation.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being a Son in the proper sense require division and a separate existence from the Father?

question: Does the Son's birth from the Father involve division, severance or diminution of the Father's substance?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The Son exists not by division but by birth; He is not a segment cut off and incomplete, but an Offspring born and therefore perfect. Birth involves no diminution of the Begetter, and the Father, by the immutability of His nature, retains undiminished what the Son receives.
sources.quote: He is not a segment cut off, and so incomplete, but an Offspring born, and therefore perfect; for birth involves no diminution of the Begetter, and has the possibility of perfection for the Begotten.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from the Father involve division or diminution of the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The Father who begat is without passions, and the Son born is the Image of the invisible God who testifies that the Father is in Him and He in the Father, so there is no severance.
sources.quote: It is no rending or severance, for He that begat is without passions, and He that was born is the Image of the invisible God and bears witness, The Father is in Me and I in the Father
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from the Father involve a rending or division of the Father's substance?

question: Do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit each have a distinct work of love in salvation that aims at the believer's holiness?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen distinguishes the electing love of the Father, the purchasing love of the Son, and the operative love of the Spirit. The holiness of believers is an eminent end of each Person's peculiar work. The Father chooses us to be holy. The Son gave himself to purify a people zealous of good works. The Spirit prepares us for obedience, enables it, and brings forth its fruits.
sources.quote: the peculiar dispensation of Father, Son, and Spirit, in the business of exalting the glory of God in our salvation, — of the electing love of the Father, the purchasing love of the Son, and the operative love of the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, Son, and Spirit each have a distinct work of love in salvation, all aimed at the believer's holiness?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Holiness is an eminent immediate end of the distinct dispensation of each Person: the Father's electing love chooses us that we should be holy, the Son gave himself to redeem and purify a peculiar people, and the Spirit's whole work is preparing and enabling us for obedience and bringing forth its fruits. Therefore the whole work of the Trinity for us and in us makes obedience necessary.
sources.quote: it is an eminent immediate end of the distinct dispensation of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, in the work of our salvation
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit each have a distinct role in the work of salvation that aims at the believer's holiness?

question: Why does Christ pray that the disciples 'may be one as we are one' rather than saying that they are one with him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > That the Unity of the Essence of the Father and the Son is to Be Gathered from the Words, ‘We are One.’ The Son is Equal to the Father Both in Wisdom and in All Other Things.
sources.answer: Because the disciples' unity is a likeness, not an identity of nature with the Son. Christ nowhere says that we are one with himself in the way he is one with the Father. He speaks of the disciples being one among themselves, as he and the Father are one. Augustine thinks this is deliberate, preserving the unique substantial unity of the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: He has nowhere said, that we are also one with Himself, but, “that they maybe one as we also are one.”
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ pray that the disciples 'may be one as we are one' rather than saying they are one with him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Same Argument Continued.
sources.answer: Because He wished to show His own Godhead as consubstantial with the Father. Although He could have said that He and the church are one person as head and body, He reserved 'we are one' for the consubstantial parity of nature He shares with the Father, as in 'I and my Father are one.' He wills believers to be one in their own kind, in Him, not to be one thing with Him in the way He is one with the Father.
sources.quote: but in order to show His own Godhead consubstantial with the Father (for which reason He says in another place, “I and my Father are one”[^500]), in His own kind, that is, in the consubstantial parity of the same nature
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ pray that believers be one 'as we are one' rather than saying 'I and they are one'?

question: Do the names "Father" and "Son" imply that there was a time when the Father existed alone, before the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. Such a conception cannot outweigh Scripture. Scripture says the Saviour's goings-forth have been from everlasting, and Christ calls himself "the first and the last," the formula of divine self-existence. By analogy, the sun never existed without its radiance, so one Person is not before another except in order and relation.
sources.quote: do you conceive that the very names “the Father, the Son” imply a certain point in duration beyond which the Father inhabited eternity alone? Your conception cannot countervail the assertion of Scripture, that the goings-forth of the Saviour have been from everlasting
sources.raw_question: Do the names "Father" and "Son" imply that there was a time when the Father existed alone, before the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. Our conceptions drawn from human fatherhood cannot override Scripture, which declares that the Saviour's goings-forth have been from everlasting and records Christ applying to himself the formula of divine self-existence, 'I am the first and the last.' The analogy of the sun and its beams suggests how one may be generated by another without being preceded by it in time, being prior only in order and relation.
sources.quote: Your conception cannot countervail the assertion of Scripture, that the goings-forth of the Saviour have been from everlasting; or the words of Christ himself, adopting the formula which declares the Divine self-existence from eternity to eternity, “I am the first and the last.”
sources.raw_question: Do the names 'Father' and 'Son' imply that there was a point in time before which the Father existed alone without the Son?

question: Does 'the end' in 1 Corinthians 15:24, when Christ delivers the kingdom to the Father, mean the dissolution or annihilation of Christ or his reign?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. An end is not a dissolution but a final perfection. Christ is called the end of the law, yet he came to fulfil the law, not to destroy it. Likewise all things move toward an end that is rest in their completed perfection, not their abolition. So the end in this text cannot mean the annihilation of Christ.
sources.quote: is not the end of the law, so far from being its dissolution, the very opposite, namely its final perfection?
sources.raw_question: Does the 'end' in 1 Corinthians 15:24 mean that Christ ceases to exist when he delivers the Kingdom to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The end means the final perfection and ultimate condition, not abolition. Christ is the end of the law yet came to fulfil it, not destroy it, so 'end' signifies consummation. If the end meant dissolution, the blessed and the wicked would share a common annihilation, which would make both the hope of the saints and the punishment of the wicked meaningless.
sources.quote: is not the end of the law, so far from being its dissolution, the very opposite, namely its final perfection?
sources.raw_question: Does 'the end' (when Christ delivers the kingdom to the Father in 1 Corinthians 15:24) mean a dissolution or annihilation of Christ's reign?

question: Does the title 'Son of God' applied to Christ express a true Sonship rather than an adoptive or customary name, as John's statement of purpose (John 20:31) shows?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. If believing He is the Christ were enough, John would not add 'the Son of God'. Since salvation requires confessing Him as the Son, the name must express the truth rather than be a customary appendage from adoption. It is the confession of the Son, not of a creature, that saves.
sources.quote: If it be sufficient for salvation to believe that He is the Christ, why does he add The Son of God?
sources.raw_question: Does John's statement of his purpose, that we may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, show that the name 'Son' expresses a true sonship and not an adoptive title?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: It expresses true Sonship. John states that his Gospel was written so that men may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; if belief in Christ alone sufficed he would not add 'the Son of God'. Since confessing the Sonship is essential to salvation, the name cannot be a mere appendage from adoption but must express the truth.
sources.quote: then assuredly the name of Son is not attached to Christ as a customary appendage due to adoption, seeing that it is essential to salvation. If then salvation consists in the confession of the name, must not the name express the truth?
sources.raw_question: Is the title "Son of God" applied to Christ merely as an adoptive or customary name, or does it express a true Sonship?

question: Does the Genesis creation account teach that the world was created through the Son of God, the Word?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > It Is, Moreover, Proved by Moses in the Beginning of the Holy Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. Moses shows God commanding light, heaven, waters, land and living things into being, and the one present to God by whom these commanded works were made can be none other than the one by whom all things were made, as John says. Moses thus teaches the same as John, who received it from him.
sources.quote: He shows that none other was then present to God—by whom these works were commanded that they should be made—than He by whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made.
sources.raw_question: Does the Genesis creation account teach that the world was created through the Son of God, the Word?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again from the Gospel He Proves Christ to Be God.
sources.answer: Yes. When Moses shows God commanding light, heaven, waters, land and living things, no one else was present to God then except the one by whom all things were made, namely the Word. Moses thus teaches what John later says: in the beginning the Word was with the Father, and the Word was God.
sources.quote: He shows that none other was then present to God—by whom these works were commanded that they should be made—than He by whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made.
sources.raw_question: Does the creation account in Genesis show that the Son, the Word of God, was present with God and created all things?

question: Does using the titles 'Son' and 'Only-begotten' of Christ guarantee orthodox belief in His deity, if the speaker means by them a created being?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then clearly and skilfully criticises the doctrine of the impossibility of comparison with the things made after the Son, and exposes the idolatry contrived by Eunomius, and concealed by the terminology of “Son” and “Only-begotten,” to deceive his readers.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius keeps the names but empties them, changing their meaning to express creation. In this way he hides a doctrine that presents a creature for worship, which is idolatry. Piety is tested by what the titles signify and by belief in the heart, not by the sound of the words.
sources.quote: leaving only the name, and changing the signification of it to express creation, he at once sets up his idolatry, and fraudulently hides its reproach.
sources.raw_question: Does using the titles 'Son' and 'Only-begotten' of Christ guarantee an orthodox belief in His deity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then clearly and skilfully criticises the doctrine of the impossibility of comparison with the things made after the Son, and exposes the idolatry contrived by Eunomius, and concealed by the terminology of “Son” and “Only-begotten,” to deceive his readers.
sources.answer: No. Piety is not tested by the sound of a word but by what is believed in the heart; one must look to the mind of those who use the words of the faith. Eunomius keeps the name of Son but changes its signification to express creation, thereby concealing idolatry under a pious name.
sources.quote: leaving only the name, and changing the signification of it to express creation, he at once sets up his idolatry, and fraudulently hides its reproach
sources.raw_question: Does using the titles "Son" and "Only-begotten" for Christ guarantee orthodox faith, if the speaker means by them a created being?

question: Does the Son's final subjection to the Father, so that God may be all in all, require any change in the divine nature of the Only-begotten God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. He is God, the name of full and perfect divinity, and that God be all in all is a Mystery, not a necessity. Even in assuming the form of a servant Christ abode in the form of God without change, emptying Himself while remaining master of Himself; the 'all in all' concerns the promotion of the assumed humanity.
sources.quote: But neither is it necessary for the Only-begotten God that He should change. He is God, and that is the name of full and perfect divinity.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's subjection and becoming 'all in all' require any change in the Only-begotten God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The Only-begotten is God, which names full and perfect divinity, so nothing can be added to him. That God is to be all in all is a Mystery of the dispensation, not a necessity of his nature. The subjection is therefore a dispensation only, and his nature does not change, for he abides still in the Father in whom he always was.
sources.quote: All is therefore a dispensation only, and not a change of His nature; for He abides still in Him, in Whom He ever was.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's final subjection to the Father, so that God may be all in all, mean that the Only-begotten God must undergo a change in his divine nature?

question: Does the fact that Scripture says "the Lord" rather than "God" appeared to Abraham show that it was specifically the Son who appeared?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: No. The Son seems to be called Lord as though the name were appropriated to him, as in "one Lord Jesus Christ." But God the Father is also called Lord in many places, as in "The Lord hath said unto me, Thou art my Son." So the title alone does not settle which person appeared to Abraham.
sources.quote: But since it is found that God the Father also is called Lord in many places,—for instance, “The Lord hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten Thee;”
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Scripture says "the Lord" rather than "God" appeared to Abraham show that it was the Son who appeared?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: No. Although the title "Lord" seems appropriated to the Son, as in Paul's "one Lord Jesus Christ," Scripture also calls the Father Lord and the Holy Spirit Lord. Hence the word "Lord" alone does not show whether one person of the Trinity appeared to Abraham or God the Trinity itself.
sources.quote: therefore, neither here does it appear plainly whether it was any person of the Trinity that appeared to Abraham, or God Himself the Trinity
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold the Son was visible in his own substance before the Incarnation
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Scripture says "the Lord appeared to Abraham" (rather than "God appeared") show that it was specifically the Son who appeared?

question: Why was the doctrine of the Trinity not revealed in the Old Testament?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Because revelation in word had to wait upon revelation in fact. The Trinity was revealed in the redemptive acts of sending the Son and the Spirit, and the times were not ripe until the fullness of time came for those acts. A Trinity revealed as a mere abstract truth, unconnected with manifested fact, would have been foreign to God's method in Scripture. The traditional reason, that Israel first had to be grounded in God's unity, carries only a little way.
sources.quote: the times were not ripe for the revelation of the Trinity in the unity of the Godhead until the fullness of the time had come for God to send forth His Son unto redemption, and His Spirit unto sanctification
sources.raw_question: Why was the doctrine of the Trinity not revealed in the Old Testament?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Chiefly because its revelation depended on the unfolding of redemption. While it is partly true that the Old Testament first had to fix the unity of God firmly before plurality could safely be spoken of, the real reason is that the time was not ripe until God sent his Son for redemption and his Spirit for sanctification; the revelation in word had to wait on the revelation in fact.
sources.quote: the times were not ripe for the revelation of the Trinity in the unity of the Godhead until the fullness of the time had come for God to send forth His Son unto redemption, and His Spirit unto sanctification.
sources.raw_question: Why was the Trinity not revealed in the Old Testament?

question: Is there a middle position between Sabellianism and Tritheism for those who hold that Christ is essentially God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds that Scripture, compared with itself, shows that the divine unity is not a unity of Person, yet never speaks of two Gods. It follows that there is a true medium: one God with more Persons than one in the same Godhead. Dr. Clarke's denial of any such medium rests on a bare philosophical maxim that he never proves. It does not come from Scripture or antiquity.
sources.quote: These considerations (with many others too long to recite) convinee us that there is a medium (saving the Son’s essential divinity) between Sabellianism and Tritheism.
