sources.raw_question: Is there a medium position between Sabellianism and Tritheism for those who hold that Christ is essentially God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: Yes. Dr. Clarke's maxim that there is no such middle position is not learned from Scripture or Catholic antiquity. It is a mere philosophical assumption used to try Scripture and the Fathers. Persons united without separate existence can be one God without being one Person, and Scripture and the Fathers support such a medium.
sources.quote: it is not from Scripture, or from Catholic antiquity, that the Doctor has learned this maxim, of xo medium (for such as believe Christ to be essentially God) between Sabellianism and Tritheism.
sources.raw_question: Is there a middle position between Tritheism and Sabellianism for those who hold that Christ is essentially God?

question: Do the Holy Spirit's sinlessness and power to forgive sin show that he is not a creature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVIII. As he purposes to establish the Godhead of the Holy Spirit by the points already discussed, St. Ambrose touches again on some of them; for instance, that He does not commit but forgives sin; that He is not a creature but the Creator; and lastly, that He does not offer but receives worship.
sources.answer: Yes. Every creature is by nature capable of sin, and only the eternal Godhead is free from sin and undefiled. Moreover, one who forgives sins cannot himself be guilty of sin, so the Spirit is without sin and therefore not a creature.
sources.quote: For every creature is exposed to the capability of sin, and the eternal Godhead alone is free from sin and undefiled.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's sinlessness prove that He is not a creature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IX. The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ, and the oil of gladness; and why Christ Himself is not the ointment, since He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It is not strange that the Spirit should be called Ointment, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. And there is no confusion between them, since Christ alone suffered death, Whose saving cross is then spoken of.
sources.answer: Yes. No angel or archangel forgives sin; only the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit do. No one who has power to forgive sin can be unable to avoid it. So the Spirit, who forgives sin, is not liable to sin as creatures are, and he shares the Godhead.
sources.quote: The Spirit could not be liable to sin, Who rather forgives sin. Does an Angel forgive? Does an Archangel? Certainly not, but the Father alone, the Son alone, and the Holy Spirit alone.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's power to forgive sin show that he is not liable to sin and so is not a creature but God?

question: Does the verb 'create' in Scripture always denote bringing something into being in its essence, or can it refer to renewal?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. Scripture uses 'He created' for renewal and renovation, not for bringing an essence into being. David's 'Create in me a clean heart' did not ask for a different heart but for renewal, and Paul's 'new man created in righteousness' means the life of virtue, not a new essence. So the single word 'He created' must be distinguished from calling something a 'creature' by nature.
sources.quote: the single word ‘He created’ does not simply denote the essence and mode of generation, David shews in the Psalm
sources.raw_question: Does the verb 'created' in Scripture always denote that the thing spoken of has a created essence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture uses 'create' for renovation as well as for origination. 'Create in me a clean heart' does not ask for a different heart but for renewal. 'The new man created in righteousness' means the virtuous life, not a newly made essence. So 'He created me' need not denote the essence or mode of generation.
sources.quote: the single word ‘He created’ does not simply denote the essence and mode of generation
sources.raw_question: Can the verb 'create' in Scripture refer to renewal rather than to bringing something into being in its essence?

question: In Proverbs 8, why does Wisdom say it was 'created' for the beginning of God's ways if it was also established and begotten before the ages?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Because what was established and begotten before the ages was created anew from the commencement of the ages for the beginning of God's ways and works. Wisdom calls itself begotten before all things so that 'established' would not seem to mean less than birth. So creation from the beginning of the ages must be distinguished from the birth that precedes the ages and all things.
sources.quote: Because that which was established before the ages was created anew from the commencement of the ages for the beginning of the ways of God and for His works.
sources.raw_question: Why does Wisdom in Proverbs 8 say it was 'created' if it was also begotten before all things and established before the ages?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: They are distinct: the establishing is prior to the ages and is to be understood as prior to the creation, while the creation for the beginning of God's ways and works comes after the commencement of the ages. The phrase 'established before the ages' was added so that no one would subordinate the infinite birth to conditions of time.
sources.quote: since the establishing is before the ages, but the creation for the beginning of the ways and for the works of God is after the commencement of the ages.
sources.raw_question: In Proverbs 8, how is Wisdom's being 'established before the ages' related to its being 'created for the beginning of the ways' of God?

question: Does Proverbs 8:25 ('before all hills He begets me') show that the Son is an offspring rather than a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Yes. The verse was added so that no one would think the true Wisdom is a creature by nature. Wisdom is said to be begotten before all creation, so He is not created together with the works according to essence. If He was 'created for the works' yet exists before them, He is in being before He was created. He is therefore not a creature by nature but an Offspring.
sources.quote: For if He was created ‘for the works,’ yet is before them, it follows that He is in being before He was created. He is not then a creature by nature and essence, but as He Himself has added, an Offspring.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:25 ('before all hills He begets me') show that the Son is an offspring rather than a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Yes. Creatures are from without and are works of the Maker, whereas an offspring is not from without nor a work but from the Father and proper to His Essence. Had the Son been a creature, Scripture would not have said 'He begets me.'
sources.quote: For had He been a creature, He had not said, ‘He begets me,’ for the creatures are from without, and are works of the Maker; but the Offspring is not from without nor a work, but from the Father, and proper to His Essence.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's statement that Wisdom says 'He begets me' (Proverbs 8:25) show that the Son is not a creature?

question: Can traces of the Trinity be discerned in created things, including the human mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Of the Attributes Assigned by Hilary to Each Person. The Trinity is Represented in Things that are Made.
sources.answer: Yes. Everything made by divine skill shows unity, form and order: each thing is some one thing, is fashioned in some form, and seeks or keeps some order. Since the Creator is understood through the things that are made, these traces point to the Trinity. The Trinity is the supreme source of all things, the most perfect beauty and the most blessed delight.
sources.quote: When therefore we regard the Creator, who is understood by the things that are made we must needs understand the Trinity of whom there appear traces in the creature, as is fitting.
sources.raw_question: Can traces of the Trinity be discerned in created things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > God, Although Incomprehensible, is Ever to Be Sought. The Traces of the Trinity are Not Vainly Sought in the Creature.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture teaches that the invisible things of God are clearly seen through the things that are made, and the Book of Wisdom rebukes those who did not know the Maker from His works. So it was not vain to seek, step by step through various created trinities up to the mind of man, traces of the highest Trinity.
sources.quote: that no one of the faithful may think me vainly and emptily to have sought first in the creature, step by step through certain trinities, each of their own appropriate kind, until I came at last to the mind of man, traces of that highest Trinity
sources.raised_by_detail: one of the faithful who might think the search vain
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to seek traces of the Trinity in created things and in the human mind?

question: Does 'In the beginning' in John 1:1 refer to the beginning of the preaching of the gospel rather than the beginning of all things?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. On that reading the text says only that he was when he was, which is empty. 'In the beginning' used absolutely in Scripture never bears such a sense. The text, moreover, places the Word's making of all things in the beginning, whereas the Socinians' 'new creation' happened mostly after Christ's ascension.
sources.quote: That is, he was when he was, — no doubt of it! And is not this a notable way of interpreting of Scripture
sources.raw_question: Does 'In the beginning was the Word' in John 1:1 refer to the beginning of the gospel when John the Baptist preached Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Wherever Scripture uses the phrase, it denotes the beginning of all things, eternity, or existence before creation (Gen 1:1; Prov 8:23; Heb 1:10). It is never used absolutely for the beginning of the gospel. Mark 1:1 speaks of "the beginning of the gospel," not "in the beginning" absolutely. Read the Socinian way, the verse would also become an empty tautology: he was when he was.
sources.quote: Wherever these words are else used in the Scripture, they denote the beginning of all things, or eternity absolutely, or an existence preceding their creation.
sources.raw_question: Does "In the beginning" in John 1:1 refer to the beginning of the preaching of the gospel rather than the beginning of all things?

question: Does 'the Word was with God' in John 1:1 merely mean that the Word was known only to God before John the Baptist preached him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Such a sense is uncouth and says nothing singular, since countless things are known to God. It is also false, for Christ was known to Gabriel, the angels at his birth, the heavenly host, Mary, Joseph, Zacharias, Elisabeth, Simeon, Anna and John the Baptist. The interpretation is extorted from the words against their proper meaning.
sources.quote: So that the sense pretended to be wrung out and extorted from these words, against their proper meaning and intendment, is indeed false and frivolous, and belongs not at all unto them.
sources.raw_question: Does 'the Word was with God' in John 1:1 merely mean that the Word was known to God alone before John the Baptist preached him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. This uncouth sense says nothing distinctive, since the same could be said of countless things. It is also false. Christ was known to Gabriel, to the angels who appeared to the shepherds, and to the heavenly host who came to worship him.
sources.quote: Concerning how many things may the same be affirmed? Besides, it is absolutely false. He was known to the angel Gabriel, who came to his mother with the message of his incarnations Luke i. 35.
sources.raw_question: Does "the Word was with God" in John 1:1 mean merely that the Word was known only to God before John the Baptist preached him?

question: Does calling the Holy Spirit 'a thing that has been given' in time conflict with His being co-eternal with the Father and the Son, or imply change in God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said of God in Time, is Said Relatively, Not Accidentally.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit is a gift eternally, but becomes a thing actually given only in time. What is predicated of Him in time is predicated relatively to the creatures who receive Him. It is not a change in His eternal being.
sources.quote: For the Spirit is a gift eternally, but a thing that has been given in time.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit being called 'a thing that has been given' in time conflict with His being co-eternal with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whether the Holy Spirit Was a Gift Before as Well as After He Was Given.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit is a Gift eternally and a thing that has been given in time. Terms said of God in time are said relatively, not of His substance, and they imply no change in God. Similarly, God is called 'Lord' only once there is a creature to serve Him.
sources.quote: For the Spirit is a gift eternally, but a thing that has been given in time.
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit, who is co-eternal with the Father and Son, is called something that exists in time (a thing that has been given), does that make Him temporal or mean that God changes?

question: In which part or function of the human mind does the image of God reside?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > How Man is the Image of God. Whether the Woman is Not Also the Image of God. How the Saying of the Apostle, that the Man is the Image of God, But the Woman is the Glory of the Man, is to Be Understood Figuratively and Mystically.
sources.answer: No. It is found in the rational mind, in which the knowledge of God can exist. Since the new man is renewed to the knowledge of God after the image of his Creator, the image belongs to the part of the mind capable of knowing God.
sources.quote: not according to the body, nor indiscriminately according to any part of the mind, but according to the rational mind, wherein the knowledge of God can exist.
sources.raw_question: Is the image of God found indiscriminately in any part of the human mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > How Man is the Image of God. Whether the Woman is Not Also the Image of God. How the Saying of the Apostle, that the Man is the Image of God, But the Woman is the Glory of the Man, is to Be Understood Figuratively and Mystically.
sources.answer: The image of God resides in the mind as it contemplates and consults eternal truth, not in the part directed to the cognition of temporal and corporeal things. The mind is the more formed after God's image the more it extends itself to the eternal; hence the man's uncovered head signifies this unrestrained turning to the eternal, while the woman's covering signifies the restraint needed by the lower, temporal cognition.
sources.quote: on that side on which it beholds and consults truth, here also it is the image of God, but on that side whereby it is directed to the cognition of the lower things, it is not the image of God.
sources.raw_question: In which part or function of the human mind does the image of God reside?

question: Does the image of God remain in man even when it is defaced or obscured?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Image of God is to Be Sought in the Immortality of the Rational Soul. How a Trinity is Demonstrated in the Mind.
sources.answer: Yes. Reason in the soul may be torpid, small or great, but the soul is never anything other than rational or intellectual. Man is made in God's image in that he is able to use reason to understand and behold God. So from the moment the soul began to exist, the image always is, whether it is almost worn away, obscured, or bright.
sources.quote: whether this image be so worn out as to be almost none at all, or whether it be obscure and defaced, or bright and beautiful, certainly it always is
sources.raw_question: Does the image of God in man always remain, even when reason is torpid or the image is defaced?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Apostle Says that God is Now Seen by Us Through a Glass.
sources.answer: Yes. Even the obscure form is the image of God, and in it we are created as men, better than other animals. Human nature, the most excellent created thing, is transformed from a defaced form into a beautiful one when justified by its Creator; indeed the more the fault is condemned, the more the nature is praised.
sources.quote: since the obscure form, too, is the image of God; and if an image, then assuredly also “glory,” in which we are created as men, being better than the other animals.
sources.raw_question: Does the image of God remain in human nature even when it is defaced by ungodliness?

question: Is the Son rightly called the image and seal of the energy of the Almighty rather than the express image of the Father's Person?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. Paul says the Son is "the express image" not of God's energy but "of His Person," and the Brightness of His glory. To make Him a seal of an energy turns God into an energy rather than a Person and places the Son third after the Father, with an energy in between.
sources.quote: Is God then an energy, not a Person? Surely Paul when expounding this very truth says He is “the express image,” not of His energy, but “of His Person.”
sources.raw_question: Is the Son rightly called the "seal of the energy" of the Almighty rather than the express image of the Father's Person?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. An energy has no independent existence; it is only exertion in the one acting and ceases when the action stops, as running ceases when the feet stop. To make the Son the likeness of an impersonal, non-existent energy is to make Him non-existent, and it sets that energy between Him and the Father, ranking Him third. Scripture instead calls Him God the Word, and the express image of the Father's person, not of His energy.
sources.quote: So he speaks of the Son as the similitude of the impersonal, and that which is like the non-existent surely has itself no existence at all.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son rightly described as 'the image and seal of the energy of the Almighty'?

question: Can anything stand as an intermediary between God the Father and the Son, His own form, express image, and brightness?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. Nothing can be conceived as intermediate between God and His own form, between the Person and His express image, or between glory and its brightness. The relation is immediate, so no energy can stand between Father and Son.
sources.quote: What is there intermediate between God and His own form? and Whom does the Person employ as mediator with His own express image? and what can be conceived as coming between the glory and its brightness?
sources.raw_question: Can anything mediate between God the Father and His own form, image, or brightness, the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. Scripture calls the Son the brightness of the Father's glory and the express image of His person. Nothing can come between a glory and its brightness, or between God and His own form. Eunomius's mediating 'energy' wrongly makes the Son third after the Father.
sources.quote: What is there intermediate between God and His own form? and Whom does the Person employ as mediator with His own express image? and what can be conceived as coming between the glory and its brightness?
sources.raw_question: Is there anything intermediate between God the Father and the Son, His own form and express image?

question: Are the Father and the Son each wisdom singly, and yet together one wisdom and one essence rather than two?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > The Father and the Son are Together One Wisdom, as One Essence, Although Not Together One Word.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father and the Son together are one essence, one greatness, one truth and one wisdom. Wisdom is said of God with respect to substance, and in the divine simplicity to be is the same as to be wise. So because they are one essence they are one wisdom, while each singly is wisdom of wisdom, as essence of essence.
sources.quote: Whence the Father and Son together are one wisdom, because one essence, and singly wisdom of wisdom, as essence of essence.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and the Son together one wisdom and one essence?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is Wisdom of wisdom, as He is Light of light and God of God. Each singly is light, God and wisdom, yet both together are one light, one God and one wisdom.
sources.quote: therefore the Father also singly is wisdom, and the Son singly is wisdom. And as both together are one light and one God, so both are one wisdom.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and the Son each wisdom singly, and yet together one wisdom rather than two?

question: If the Father and the Son are together one wisdom and one essence, are they also together one Word?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > The Father and the Son are Together One Wisdom, as One Essence, Although Not Together One Word.
sources.answer: No. 'Word' is said relatively, of the one whose Word it is, just as 'Son' is said in relation to the Father. The Son is the Word in that he is the Son, and the Father and Son together are not one Son. Therefore they are not together one Word, since for God to be is not the same as to be the Word.
sources.quote: Inasmuch, therefore, as the Father and the Son together are certainly not one Son, it follows that the Father and the Son together are not the one Word of both.
sources.raw_question: If the Father and the Son are one wisdom, are they also together one Word?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: No. They are together one essence, greatness, truth and wisdom, because these are said essentially. "Word" is said relatively, like "Son," and the Father and the Son are not together one Son. So the Son is the Word not insofar as He is wisdom, but as wisdom that is born.
sources.quote: But the Father and Son both together are not one Word, because both together are not one Son.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and the Son together one Word, just as they are together one wisdom and one essence?

question: Could God have created human beings perfect from the very beginning, and if not, does this imply a lack of power in God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIX.—Man is endowed with the faculty of distinguishing good and evil; so that, without compulsion, he has the power, by his own will and choice, to perform God’s commandments, by doing which he avoids the evils prepared for the rebellious.
sources.answer: No. A creature only lately made cannot at once be perfect or immortal. He must first hold the rank of a man, and afterwards partake of the glory of God. Man does not make God; God makes man. So man must yield himself to the Maker's hand, which completes its work in due time, until the King takes pleasure in his beauty.
sources.quote: For it must be that thou, at the outset, shouldest hold the rank of a man, and then afterwards partake of the glory of God. For thou dost not make God, but God thee.
sources.raw_question: Could God have made human beings perfect and divine from the very first moment of their creation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVIII.—Why man was not made perfect from the beginning.
sources.answer: God could have, since all things are possible to Him, but man could not receive perfection, being newly created and thus infantile. Created things must be inferior to their Creator from the very fact of their later origin, and what is not uncreated falls short of the perfect. The limitation therefore lies in the creature, not in any impossibility or deficiency in God.
sources.quote: so also it was possible for God Himself to have made man perfect from the first, but man could not receive this [perfection], being as yet an infant.
sources.raw_question: Could God have created man perfect from the beginning, and if not, does this imply a lack of power in God?

question: If all three Persons are love, why is the Holy Spirit specially called Love?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: There is no greater gift of God than love, and no greater gift of God than the Holy Spirit, so it fits that he is love. Also, the love by which Father and Son love each other shows their communion. So it is fitting that the Spirit, who is common to both, should be specially called love.
sources.quote: if the love by which the Father loves the Son, and the Son loves the Father, ineffably demonstrates the communion of both, what is more suitable than that He should be specially called love, who is the Spirit common to both?
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit specially called love?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Holy Spirit is Called Love, and Whether He Alone is So Called. That the Holy Spirit is in the Scriptures Properly Called by the Name of Love.
sources.answer: For the same reason the Son is specially called Wisdom although Father and Spirit are also wisdom. A term common to all can be appropriated to one Person on account of the distinction of the Persons. Since the Spirit is the common Gift and Spirit of both, it is most fitting that he be specially called Love. The following chapter compares how 'the Law' names all of Scripture and also specially the books of Moses.
sources.quote: If, then, any one of the three is to be specially called Love, what more fitting than that it should be the Holy Spirit?
sources.raw_question: If all three Persons are love, why is the Holy Spirit specially called Love?

question: Could the world have been made by angels or by some lesser being, even against the will of the supreme God, rather than by God himself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VIII.—Created things are not a shadow of the Pleroma.
sources.answer: No. It is impious and foolish to say that so great a creation was formed by angels or by some production ignorant of the true God. That would place such a work within God's own territory, whether with or without his consent. God, who contains all things, is himself the Creator.
sources.quote: For it is equally impious and infatuated to affirm that so great a creation was formed by angels, or by some particular production ignorant of the true God in that territory which is His own.
sources.raw_question: Could the world have been made by angels or by some lesser being ignorant of the true God, rather than by God himself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter II.—The world was not formed by angels, or by any other being, contrary to the will of the most high God, but was made by the Father through the Word.
sources.answer: No. If angels made so great a creation against God's will, they would be more powerful than God, or God would be careless, inferior, or indifferent to what happens among his own possessions. Such conduct could not be ascribed even to a capable man, much less to God.
sources.quote: This would imply that angels were more powerful than God; or if not so, that He was either careless, or inferior, or paid no regard to those things which took place among His own possessions
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who say the world was formed by angels
sources.raw_question: Could angels or some other maker have formed the world against the will of the supreme God?

question: When God the Father begot the Son, did He make one who already existed or one who did not yet exist?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections to the Foregoing Proof. Whether, in the generation of the Son, God made One that was already, or One that was not.
sources.answer: The question is badly framed. Applied to God and His Word, it really asks whether God was ever without Reason, or whether the Light was ever without its ray. The Father who is has always had His Word with Him as the proper offspring of His substance. Since the Father is eternal, His Radiance, the Word, is eternal too, and was not added later.
sources.quote: Has the Father ‘who is’ made the Word ‘who is not,’ or has He ever with Him His Word, as the proper offspring of His substance?
sources.raw_question: When God begot the Son, did He make, from nothing, a Son who did not previously exist, or one who already existed?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections to the Foregoing Proof. Whether, in the generation of the Son, God made One that was already, or One that was not.
sources.answer: The question is senseless, but the answer is that the eternal Father has from Himself His eternal Word. Since the Father always is, His Radiance, the Word, always is. The Word was not added after not being, nor was the Father ever without Reason. The question is as foolish as asking of the sun whether it made a radiance that was or one that was not, because it imagines the offspring to be external to the one who begets.
sources.quote: whereas God is, He was eternally; since then the Father is ever, His Radiance ever is, which is His Word. And again, God who is, hath from Himself His Word who also is
sources.raw_question: In begetting the Son, did God the Father make one who already existed or one who did not yet exist?

question: Will Christ continue to intercede with the Father for believers as Mediator after he has delivered the kingdom to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to God, Even the Father. The Kingdom Having Been Delivered to God, Even the Father, Christ Will Not Then Make Intercession for Us.
sources.answer: No. Once he has brought believers to the contemplation of God, he will no longer make intercession for us as Mediator and Priest. Christ signifies this when he says that in that day he will not pray the Father for us, because the Father himself loves us.
sources.quote: then, since the kingdom will have been delivered up to God, even the Father, He will no more make intercession for us.
sources.raw_question: Will Christ continue to intercede for us as Mediator after he has delivered the kingdom to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to God, Even the Father. The Kingdom Having Been Delivered to God, Even the Father, Christ Will Not Then Make Intercession for Us.
sources.answer: No. Christ intercedes now as Mediator, in the form of a servant. Once believers are brought to face-to-face sight, he will no longer pray the Father for them. He himself signifies this when he says, "I say not unto you, that I will pray the Father for you: for the Father Himself loveth you."
sources.quote: then, since the kingdom will have been delivered up to God, even the Father, He will no more make intercession for us.
sources.raw_question: Will Christ continue to make intercession to the Father for believers after the kingdom has been delivered up?

question: Does the Incarnation of the Word show that human flesh is capable of salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIV.—Unless the flesh were to be saved, the Word would not have taken upon Him flesh of the same substance as ours: from this it would follow that neither should we have been reconciled by Him.
sources.answer: Yes. If the flesh could not be saved, the Word of God would never have become flesh, and if the blood of the righteous were not to be required, the Lord would not have had blood. Christ was made flesh and blood after the manner of the original formation, so that He might save in His own person at the end what had perished in Adam at the beginning.
sources.quote: For if the flesh were not in a position to be saved, the Word of God would in no wise have become flesh.
sources.raw_question: Does the Incarnation of the Word show that human flesh is capable of salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIII.—In the dead who were raised by Christ we possess the highest proof of the resurrection; and our hearts are shown to be capable of life eternal, because they can now receive the Spirit of God.
sources.answer: Yes. If the flesh could not be saved, the Word of God would never have become flesh. Paul uses "flesh and blood" of Christ both to establish his human nature and to confirm the salvation of our flesh.
sources.quote: For if the flesh were not in a position to be saved, the Word of God would in no wise have become flesh.
sources.raw_question: Does the Word of God becoming flesh show that human flesh can be saved?

question: Is the Son of God under the dominion or sovereignty of the Father's essence, and is there any scriptural or logical proof of this?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory challenges Eunomius to name any evangelist, process of dialectic, premises, or logical consequence that demonstrates the Only-begotten God is under dominion. Eunomius merely reiterates the assertion without proof, so the claim of the Father's essence ruling over the Son is unsupported.
sources.quote: What evangelist is the patron of this doctrine? What process of dialectic conducts us to it. What premises support it? What line of argument ever demonstrated by any logical consequence that the Only-begotten God is under dominion?
sources.raw_question: Is there any scriptural or logical proof that the Father's essence has dominion or sovereignty over the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory says no evangelist, premise or line of logical argument has ever shown that the Only-begotten God is under dominion. Eunomius merely restates the claim without proof.
sources.quote: What premises support it? What line of argument ever demonstrated by any logical consequence that the Only-begotten God is under dominion?
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God under the dominion of the Father's essence?

question: Can one consistently grant that the Son exists while denying him the title "the Existent"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Denying the title of the Existent amounts to denying essential being, and if the Son did not exist one could not argue whether he is like or unlike the Father. If his existence is granted, it is vain to haggle over the word while conceding the substance, for what exists cannot be separated from the conception of existence.
sources.quote: For that which does not exist is of course neither like anything else, nor unlike. But while granting that He is existent he forbids Him to be so called.
sources.raw_question: Can one consistently grant that the Son exists while denying him the title "the Existent"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. The only opposite of 'the Existent' is the nonexistent. To exclude the Son from that title is in effect to place him outside the pale of existence, which is 'playing the Jew' and robbing Christian doctrine of the Person of the Only-begotten. If Eunomius really granted the Son existence, he would not quarrel over the word.
sources.quote: who knows not that the only opposite to the “Existent” is the nonexistent? so that he who contrasts the Son with the Existent, is clearly playing the Jew
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be denied the title 'the Existent' while still being granted real existence?

question: Does holding that the names for God are devised by human conception (epinoia) diminish reverence toward God or imply that God depends on human naming?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. This mental operation exists so that we may think about what God has done. It does no harm to reverent ideas of God, and the name used for the faculty does not matter.
sources.quote: What harm, then, is done to our reverential ideas of God by this mental operation, instituted with a view to our thinking upon the things done, and which we call conception
sources.raw_question: Does applying names to God through human conception (epinoia) diminish reverence toward God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The Supreme Being has no need of words delivered by voice and tongue, so men naming God as each comes to conceive Him after birth does no wrong to the Deity. Indeed, since God's nature is simply perfect, lacking nothing necessary and possessing nothing unnecessary, it is profane to assign to Him naming as though it were a necessity of His being.
sources.quote: a Being Whose nature is neither lacking nor redundant, but simply perfect, neither fails to possess anything that is necessary, nor possesses what is not necessary.
sources.raw_question: If names for God are invented by human reasoning (epinoia), does it follow that God depends on human naming or that names are anterior to those who utter them?

question: Did God create all things freely, or under some necessity or the influence of another being?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VIII.—Answer to an objection, arising from the words of Christ (Matt. vi. 24). God alone is to be really called God and Lord, for He is without beginning and end.
sources.answer: God made all things freely and as he pleased. David testifies that God in heaven and earth has made whatever he pleased; creation is God's sovereign act through his Word, not the product of a lesser power.
sources.quote: But that He did Himself make all things freely, and as He pleased, again David says, “But our God is in the heavens above, and in the earth; He hath made all things whatsoever He pleased.”
sources.raw_question: Did God create the world freely, or through some necessity or intermediary agency?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter I.—There is but one God: the impossibility of its being otherwise.
sources.answer: He created freely. God created all things of His own free will, influenced by no one. He is the only God, the only Lord, the only Creator, and the only Father, who contains all things and commands them into existence.
sources.quote: nor that, influenced by any one, but of His own free will, He created all things, since He is the only God, the only Lord, the only Creator, the only Father
sources.raw_question: Did God create all things freely, or under the influence of some other being?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's making intercession for us prove that the Spirit is inferior in dignity to God?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: No. Scripture also says that the Only-begotten, who is at the right hand of God, makes intercession for us. The Spirit's loving kindness in dwelling in us, teaching and guiding us must not be turned into a ground for thinking less of Him.
sources.quote: But have you never heard concerning the Only-begotten that He “is at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us”?
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit's intercession for us prove He is inferior in dignity to God?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says the same of the Only-begotten Son, who is at the right hand of God and also makes intercession for us, so intercession cannot imply inferiority of nature. To turn the Spirit's loving kindness toward us into a ground for lowering his dignity would be extreme unfairness and ingratitude.
sources.quote: But have you never heard concerning the Only-begotten that He “is at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us”?
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's making intercession for us prove that the Spirit is inferior in dignity to God, as a suppliant is inferior to a benefactor?

question: How can Christ's saying 'The Father is greater than I' be reconciled with His statements of unity with the Father, such as 'I and the Father are one' and 'I am in the Father, and the Father is in Me'?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: The mutual indwelling reveals the divinity of the Begotten of God, while 'greater' expresses the Son's acknowledgment of the Father's authority as His Author. Both are spoken in agreement with His unity with the Father and the nature He has by birth.
sources.quote: The One is in the Other: recognise, then, the divinity of God, the Begotten of God: the Father is greater than He: perceive, then, His acknowledgment of the Father’s authority.
sources.raw_question: How can 'The Father is greater than I' be reconciled with 'I am in the Father, and the Father is in Me'?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: The two sayings refer to different aspects of the same act. The Father is greater when he gives the Name above every name. The Son and the Father are one when every tongue confesses that Jesus is Lord in the glory of God the Father.
sources.quote: When, then, is the Father greater than the Son? Surely, when He gives Him the Name above every name. And on the other hand, when is it that the Son and the Father are one?
sources.raw_question: How can 'The Father is greater than I' be reconciled with 'I and the Father are one'?

question: Are the names Son, Word and Image said of the Son relatively to the Father rather than in respect to Himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > How the Word Beginning (Principium) is Spoken Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is called Son, Word and Image relatively, and in all these names He is referred to the Father. The Father, however, is called by none of these names.
sources.quote: He is called also relatively the Word and the Image. And in all these appellations He is referred to the Father, but the Father is called by none of them.
sources.raw_question: Are the names Son, Word and Image said of the Son relatively to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: No. Nothing could be more absurd than calling the Son image in respect to Himself. Image and Word are relative names that refer to the Father. All relative terms are said reciprocally.
sources.quote: But what can be more absurd than that He should be called image in respect to Himself?
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be called 'Image' or 'Word' in respect to Himself rather than relatively to the Father?

question: Does ascribing supreme and proper being to the Father alone imply that the Son and Holy Spirit do not really exist?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He did wrong, when mentioning the Doctrines of Salvation, in adopting terms of his own choosing instead of the traditional terms Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. On Gregory's reading, it amounts in effect to a denial of their real subsistence. What is denied proper being must be described by the opposite terms, as improperly said to be. Showing that something is not properly said to be is a proof that it does not really subsist. So Eunomius confesses the Son and Spirit in words but secretly sets aside real belief in their distinct personality.
sources.quote: How can that to which a proper being is denied be said to really exist? When we deny proper being to it, we must perforce affirm of it all the opposite terms.
sources.raw_question: Does ascribing 'supreme and proper being' to the Father alone imply that the Son and Holy Spirit do not really exist?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in making the being of the Father alone proper and supreme, implying by his omission of the Son and the Spirit that theirs is improperly spoken of, and is inferior.
sources.answer: It amounts to denying that the Son and the Spirit exist at all, which is the Jewish doctrine and a denial of the gospel. What does not properly exist is called existent only nominally, as a portrait is called a man without being one. What does not properly exist is the same as the non-existent.
sources.quote: What does not properly exist is the same thing as the non-existent.
sources.raw_question: What follows from saying that only the Father's being is proper being, and that the Son's and the Spirit's being is not?

question: If, as Eunomius says, the Father begat the Son when He chose, does it follow that the Son came into being after the Father, or is the Son eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He then ingeniously shows that the generation of the Son is not according to the phrase of Eunomius, “The Father begat Him at that time when He chose, and not before:” but that the Son, being the fulness of all that is good and excellent, is always contemplated in the Father; using for this demonstration the support of Eunomius' own arguments.
sources.answer: Yes. God always chooses what is good and His power coincides with His choice. Therefore, if He begat the Son when He chose, the Son must always be with the Father. The word 'before' also has a temporal sense, and it has no meaning in reference to the Lord, who was before times and ages.
sources.quote: For if, as our opponent says, “He begat the Son at that time when He chose,” and if He always chose that which is good, and His power coincided with His choice, it follows that the Son will be considered as always with the Father
sources.raw_question: If, as Eunomius says, the Father begat the Son when He chose, does it follow that the Son is eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He then ingeniously shows that the generation of the Son is not according to the phrase of Eunomius, “The Father begat Him at that time when He chose, and not before:” but that the Son, being the fulness of all that is good and excellent, is always contemplated in the Father; using for this demonstration the support of Eunomius' own arguments.
sources.answer: No. Since the Father always chooses what is good and His power always coincides with His choice, the Son, who is the fulness of good, must be considered as always with the Father. Eunomius's own premise therefore establishes the Son's eternal coexistence with the Father.
sources.quote: if He always chose that which is good, and His power coincided with His choice, it follows that the Son will be considered as always with the Father
sources.raw_question: If the Father begat the Son 'when He chose,' as Eunomius says, does it follow that the Son came into being after the Father?

question: Does calling the Holy Spirit "the Spirit of Truth" make him subordinate to, or a possession of, Christ who is the Truth?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: No. God is called a "God of righteousness," yet no one thinks God is a possession of righteousness. Christ also immediately adds that the Spirit of Truth "proceedeth from the Father." Scripture says this of nothing in creation, so it marks something proper to uncreated being.
sources.quote: It is plain then that that, from share in which all creation is excluded, is something special and peculiar to uncreated being.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Holy Spirit "the Spirit of Truth" make him a subordinate possession of Christ, who is the Truth?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: No. Scripture calls God "a God of righteousness," yet no one concludes that God is a possession of righteousness, so the genitive does not imply subjection. Moreover, the Lord immediately adds that the Spirit of Truth "proceedeth from the Father," which directs us to a loftier interpretation befitting the Deity.
sources.quote: without being aware that God is called a God of righteousness; and we certainly do not understand thereby that God is a possession of righteousness
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Holy Spirit "the Spirit of Truth" imply that the Spirit is subject to, or a possession of, Christ who is the Truth?

question: Does the fact that the Old Testament speaks of the 'Word' while the New Testament speaks of the 'Son' show that the Son came into being later than the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No. Setting the Testaments against one another is the device of Manichees and Jews. If dating followed the Testament in which a text is written, then 'I and the Father are One' and 'Only-begotten' would also be later. In any case the Old Testament speaks of the Son often, for example in Psalm 2, Psalm 110 (109), Proverbs and Daniel. If antiquity comes from the Old Testament, the Son is ancient.
sources.quote: If then from the Old be ancientness, ancient must be the Son, who is clearly described in the Old Testament in many places.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Old Testament speaks of the 'Word' while the New speaks of the 'Son' show that the Son came later than the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. By the same reasoning the Paraclete, never named in the Old Testament, would be later than and distinct from the Holy Spirit, which is absurd. The Spirit is one and the same, then and now, and in the same way the Word and the Son are one and the same.
sources.quote: He then who dares distinguish between Word and Son, let him distinguish between Spirit and Paraclete; but if the Spirit cannot be distinguished, so neither can the Word, being also Son and Wisdom and Power.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who distinguish Word and Son
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the title 'Son' is mostly used in the New Testament show that the Son came into being later than the Word of the Old Testament?

question: Is it safer to err by honouring the Son too much than by honouring him too little?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 30: Whether, supposing the case doubtful, it be not a wise man’s part to take the safer side; rather to think too highly, than too meanly of our blessed Saviour ; r
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture gives many express cautions against failing in honour to the Son but none against honouring him too much. We are told to honour the Son even as we honour the Father, and that dishonouring the Son dishonours the Father, but never that the Father resents excessive honour paid to the Son.
sources.quote: we have many express cautions given us in Seripture, not to be wanting in our respects and services towards God the Son; but have no particular cautions against honouring him
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture warn more against honouring the Son too little than against honouring him too much?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 30: Whether, supposing the case doubtful, it be not a wise man’s part to take the safer side; rather to think too highly, than too meanly of our blessed Saviour ; r
sources.answer: Yes. Anyone who errs by honouring the Son too much has honoured only one whom the Father delights to honour, and may hope for pardon. The Arian who has blasphemed and degraded his Redeemer on speculative grounds has no comparable plea.
sources.quote: If they happened to carry their respect too high, yet it was towards those only whom the Father principally delighteth to honour; and towards. whom an ingenuous, grateful, and well-disposed mind can hardly ever think he can pay too much.
sources.raw_question: If the deity of Christ is doubtful, is it safer to risk honouring the Son too highly than too meanly?

question: Do the doctrine of the Trinity and the doctrine of the person (Deity) of Christ stand or fall together, so that denying one undermines the other?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Preface
sources.answer: Yes. Early heretics such as the Gnostics, Valentinians, Marcionites, Manichees and Cerinthus based their errors on unbelief of both the Trinity and the person of Christ. John's prologue declaring Christ's eternal Deity settles the controversy about both, for they stand and fall together.
sources.quote: the foundation of all whose abominations lay in their misapprehensions of the being of God, their unbelief of the Trinity and person of Christ
sources.raw_question: Are the doctrine of the Trinity and the doctrine of the person of Christ bound together, so that denying one undermines the other?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Preface
sources.answer: Yes. Owen treats the controversy about the Trinity and about the person of Christ as a single controversy. Opposing Christ's person is therefore opposing the Trinity, and the scriptural determination of the one settles the other.
sources.quote: this controversy about the Trinity and person of Christ (for they stand and fall together) should be so eminently and expressly determined, as it were, immediately from heaven?
sources.raw_question: Do the doctrine of the Trinity and the doctrine of the person (Deity) of Christ stand or fall together?

question: Does Scripture's comparison of the Holy Spirit to water flowing from a fount imply that the Spirit is less than the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XVI. The Holy Spirit is that large river by which the mystical Jerusalem is watered. It is equal to its Fount, that is, the Father and the Son, as is signified in holy Scripture. St. Ambrose himself thirsts for that water, and warns us that in order to preserve it within us, we must avoid the devil, lust, and heresy, since our vessels are frail, and that broken cisterns must be forsaken, that after the example of the Samaritan woman and of the patriarchs we may find the water of the Lord.
sources.answer: No. Although images from creatures are unsuitable to the Godhead, Scripture forestalls this inference by calling the Spirit not merely water but a river, indeed an abundant river of overflowing greatness that never fails. So no difference in greatness can be drawn from the comparison.
sources.quote: let them learn that not only is the Holy Spirit called Water, but also a River, as we read: “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water. But this He said of the Spirit, Whom they were beginning to receive, who were about to believe in Him.”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's comparison of the Holy Spirit to water flowing from a fount imply that the Spirit is smaller or less than the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XV. The Holy Spirit is Life equally with the Father and the Son, in truth whether the Father be mentioned, with Whom is the Fount of Life, or the Son, that Fount can be none other than the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Comparisons taken from creatures do not suit the Godhead. Scripture also calls the Spirit not only water but a river, "rivers of living water," and so equal to its Fount.
sources.quote: let them learn that not only is the Holy Spirit called Water, but also a River, as we read: “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water. But this He said of the Spirit,
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit is called the water that flows from a Fount, does that make the Spirit lesser than the Father and the Son?

question: Is the Creator of the world the one supreme God and Father of Jesus Christ, or is there a higher God above the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter IX.—There is but one Creator of the world, God the Father: this the constant belief of the Church.
sources.answer: The Creator of the world is the one true God and Father; no higher God exists above him. Even the heretics acknowledge the Creator, all the Scriptures proclaim him, the Lord teaches of this Father in heaven and no other, and the Church received this tradition from the apostles. By contrast, the 'Father' the Gnostics posit above the Creator has no witnesses at all.
sources.quote: This God, then, being acknowledged, as I have said, and receiving testimony from all to the fact of His existence, that Father whom they conjure into existence is beyond doubt untenable, and has no witnesses [to his existence].
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of the world the one supreme God and Father, or is there a higher God above the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XXII.—Deviations of heretics from the truth.
sources.answer: The Creator, the God of the patriarchs, is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and there is no other God, first principle, power or pleroma above him. This is the rule of truth that there is one God Almighty who made all things by his Word out of nothing.
sources.quote: He [who] is the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, above whom there is no other God, nor initial principle, nor power, nor pleroma,—He is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of the world, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the same as the Father of Jesus Christ, or is there a higher God or principle above him?

question: If Scripture ascribes to the Son the same divine attributes and titles it gives the one true God, does it follow that the Son is the same one God as the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: Yes. We know who the one God is only by the marks and characters Scripture gives of him; if these are equally applied to more than one Person, the honour goes with the attributes, and the attributes infer an equality of nature and substance. Hence each Person having divine attributes is God, and since God is one, the same God.
sources.quote: if divine attributes belong to each Person, each Person must be God; and if God, since God is one, the same God.
sources.raw_question: If the same divine characteristics that Scripture applies to the one true God are applied also to the Son, does it follow that the Son is the same one God as the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: Yes. The same characteristics are ascribed to both: searching all hearts, being the First and the Last, Alpha and Omega, King of kings and Lord of lords, the mighty God, and Lord over all. Waterland argues that if divine attributes belong to each Person, each Person must be God. Since God is one, each must then be the same God.
sources.quote: In a word; if divine attributes belong to each Person, each Person must be God; and if God, since God is one, the same God.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ascribe the same divine attributes and titles to the one God and to the Son, and what does this imply about the Son?

question: In what sense is the Son subordinate to the Father according to orthodox doctrine?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: The Son is subordinately wise, good and powerful in that he is from the Father: wisdom from wisdom, light from light, God from God. Yet his attributes remain strictly divine and his perfections infinite, so the subordination is of origin, not of nature.
sources.quote: I allow the second Person to be subordinately wise, good, powerful, &e. That is not the question between us: he is sapientia de sapientia; as lumen de lumine, and Deus de Deo.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Son subordinate to the Father according to orthodox doctrine?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: Only as a Son to a Father, in point of original. He is equal in every respect except as a Son can be equal to a Father, the Father being head and fountain, yet of the same nature, power, substance, and perfections, subsisting inseparably in and from the Father, and therefore one God with him.
sources.quote: that he was subordinate as a Son ; equal in every respect, but as a Son can be equal to a Father ,; inferior, in point of original, (the Father being head and fountain of all,) but still of the same nature, power, substance, and perfections
sources.raw_question: In what sense, according to the early Fathers, is the Son subordinate to the Father?

question: Can the human mind comprehend the mode of the Son's generation from the Father?
synthesis: Both passages are from Hilary of Poitiers, and both answer no: the Son's generation is indescribable and beyond human understanding. In one he adds that devout effort to penetrate the mystery still profits the seeker. In the other he stresses that unaided reason is silenced, so we must reverently accept the words of John, who was taught on the Lord's bosom.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. Scripture asks 'Who shall declare His generation?' and only the Father knows the Son and the Son the Father; the incomprehensible is begotten of the incomprehensible. Yet devout effort to penetrate the mystery profits the seeker even if he never reaches the goal.
sources.quote: Incomprehensible is begotten of Incomprehensible, for none else knows Them, but Each knows the Other; Invisible is begotten of Invisible
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind comprehend the mode of the Son's generation from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. Unaided reason is baffled and silenced before the generation the prophet calls indescribable, and 'the darkness comprehended Him not.'
