Only John, taught on the Lord's bosom, could express the mystery, so we must accept his words reverently as God's oracles and confess Father and Son whose majesty defies expression and perception.
sources.quote: The language of unaided reason was baffled and silenced; the Fisherman who lay on the bosom of the Lord was taught to express the mystery.
sources.raw_question: Can human reason by its own power comprehend and express the generation of the Son?

question: Are the mind, its self-knowledge, and its self-love related to each other as parts making up a whole?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: No. A part does not embrace the whole of which it is a part, but when the mind knows and loves itself perfectly, its knowledge and its love each extend through the whole of the mind. Therefore knowledge and love are not parts of the mind, nor are the three equal parts composing one whole.
sources.quote: But no part embraces the whole, of which it is a part; whereas, when the mind knows itself as a whole, that is, knows itself perfectly, then the knowledge of it extends through the whole of it
sources.raw_question: Are the mind, its self-knowledge, and its self-love related to each other as parts making up a whole?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: No. No part embraces the whole of which it is a part. But when the mind knows itself perfectly, its knowledge extends through the whole of it, and when it loves itself perfectly, its love extends through the whole of it. So they are not related as parts to a whole.
sources.quote: But no part embraces the whole, of which it is a part; whereas, when the mind knows itself as a whole, that is, knows itself perfectly, then the knowledge of it extends through the whole of it
sources.raw_question: Are the mind's self-love and self-knowledge parts that make up the mind as a whole?

question: In what way are mind, knowledge, and love, though one in essence, mutually in one another without confusion, each in each and all in all?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: Yes. When the mind knows and loves itself, a trinity remains: mind, love, and knowledge, not confounded by any commingling. Each is severally in itself and all are mutually in all. The mind that loves is in love, love is in the knowledge of the one who loves, and knowledge is in the mind.
sources.quote: this trinity is not confounded together by any commingling: although they are each severally in themselves and mutually all in all, or each severally in each two, or each two in each. Therefore all are in all.
sources.raw_question: Do the mind, its knowledge, and its love, though one in essence, remain distinct by being mutually in one another without confusion?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > That These Three are Several in Themselves, and Mutually All in All.
sources.answer: The mind that loves is in love, love is in the knowledge of the lover, and knowledge is in the mind that knows; each is in the other two and each two in each one. All are in all because the mind loves and knows itself wholly and knows its love wholly and loves its knowledge wholly, when these are perfect.
sources.quote: the mind loves itself as a whole, and knows itself as a whole, and knows its own love wholly, and loves its own knowledge wholly, when these three things are perfect in respect to themselves
sources.raw_question: In what way are mind, knowledge, and love mutually in one another, each in each two and all in all?

question: If the texts of Isaiah declaring that there is no God besides the Lord exclude every person other than the Father, does it follow that Christ is no God at all unless he is included in the one Supreme God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Preface
sources.answer: Yes, unless Christ shares the one Supreme Godhead. Comparing Isaiah's declarations that there is no God beside the Lord with texts calling the Word God and Christ God over all, Waterland argues that if the Son is at all excluded by the Isaiah texts he is altogether excluded and is no God at all. Since Scripture plainly calls him God, he must be included in the one Supreme God rather than be a second, inferior god.
sources.quote: That if the Son be at all excluded by those texts in the first column, he is altogether excluded, and is no God at
sources.raw_question: Do the texts of Isaiah declaring that there is no God besides the Lord exclude Christ from being God unless he is the same with the Supreme God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 1: Whether all other beings, besides the one Supreme God, be not excluded by the texts of Isaiah, (to which many more might be added ;) and consequently, whether C
sources.answer: Yes, on the Arian scheme it would follow. If the Son is excluded by those texts, he is wholly excluded: he cannot be the same God (since on Clarke's principles he is not the same Person), nor another God (since the texts exclude any other). Being neither the same God nor another God, he would be no God at all, and the only escape is that he is included in the one Supreme God.
sources.quote: He cannot, upon your principles, be the same God, because he is not the same Person: he cannot be another God, because excluded by those texts. If therefore he be neither the same God, nor another God; it must follow, that he is no God.
sources.raw_question: If the Isaiah texts declaring 'there is no God besides me' exclude every person other than the Father, does it follow that Christ is no God at all?

question: Does Isaiah's 'there is no God besides me' exclude only other supreme or equal gods, leaving room for inferior deities such as a subordinate divine Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 1: Whether all other beings, besides the one Supreme God, be not excluded by the texts of Isaiah, (to which many more might be added ;) and consequently, whether C
sources.answer: No. The text says absolutely that there is no other God, not merely no other Supreme God, so there is no ground for the restriction. Moreover, that reading would have allowed subordinate worship of Baal, Ashtaroth and the gods of the nations without idolatry, excusing Solomon and the Samaritans. And since the real danger was never belief in many supreme gods but worship of inferior deities, the texts must exclude inferior divinities too.
sources.quote: It is not said, there is no other Supreme God besides me ; but absolutely, no other.
sources.raw_question: Does 'there is no God besides me' in Isaiah mean only that there is no other Supreme God, leaving room for inferior deities?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 1: Whether all other beings, besides the one Supreme God, be not excluded by the texts of Isaiah, (to which many more might be added ;) and consequently, whether C
sources.answer: No. The text does not say 'there is none other equal to me' but 'there is none other besides me,' so it excludes every other God absolutely, not merely rival supreme ones. Hence Christ must either be included in the one God of Israel or excluded altogether with the nominal deities.
sources.quote: nor is it said, There is none other equal tome; but the “ words are, There is none other besides me.
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah's 'There is none other besides me' exclude only beings equal to the Supreme God, leaving room for a subordinate divine Son?

question: What error was the Nicene phrase 'from the substance of the Father' chiefly meant to exclude: the Son's being made from some other matter, or his being made from nothing?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: Chiefly the Arian claim that the Son was made from nothing. Since the Son was neither from another substance nor from nothing, and the Fathers rejected any division of substance, they must have held the Son to be of the same undivided, individual substance with the Father.
sources.quote: If therefore the Son, according to the Nicene Fathers, was not from any other substance besides the Father’s, nor from nothing ; it is very plain that (unless they supposed a division of substance, which they absolutely reject) they supposed the Son to be of the same undivided, or individual substance with the Father.
sources.raw_question: In saying the Son is 'from the substance of the Father', what did the Nicene Fathers chiefly intend to exclude?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: Chiefly the Arian claim that the Son was made from nothing. The idea that the Son was formed from some pre-existing substance, as Adam from dust, was too silly for anyone to hold, and the Arians themselves disowned it, teaching rather that the Son was the first thing made out of nothing.
sources.quote: The Nicene Fathers designed, chiefly, to guard against the supposition of the Son's being from nothing, which was what the Arians insisted upon
sources.raw_question: What was the chief error the Nicene Creed's phrase 'from the substance of the Father' was meant to exclude: the Son's being made from some other matter, or his being made from nothing?

question: If the Son is sent by himself as well as by the Father, since the Incarnation is a work of the whole Trinity, how can it still be said that the Father sent him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: In the same way that Scripture says both that the Father sanctified and delivered up the Son and that the Son sanctified and delivered up himself. The will of the Father and the Son is one and their working is indivisible. So the Incarnation, in which the Son is said to be sent, was wrought by one and the same operation of Father and Son, with the Holy Spirit included.
sources.quote: Because the will of the Father and the Son is one, and their working indivisible. In like manner, then, let him understand the incarnation and nativity of the Virgin, wherein the Son is understood as sent
sources.raw_question: If the Son is sent by himself as well as by the Father (since the Incarnation is a work of the whole Trinity), how can it still be said that the Father sent him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: The will of the Father and the Son is one and their working is indivisible. The incarnation, in which the Son is sent, was therefore wrought by one operation of Father and Son together. Similarly, Scripture says both that the Father sanctified and delivered up the Son and that the Son sanctified and delivered up himself.
sources.quote: Because the will of the Father and the Son is one, and their working indivisible.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is sent also by himself, how can the Father be said to have sent him?

question: Did the one God create and order all things, and did he do so through his Word?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXII.—That one God was the author of both Testaments, is confirmed by the authority of a presbyter who had been taught by the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. The one God made all things by the Word, as Moses shows in God's speaking light into being, as the Gospel states that all things were made by Him and without Him nothing was made, and as Paul confesses one God and Father above all and through all.
sources.quote: But if any one believes in [only] one God, who also made all things by the Word, as Moses likewise says, “God said, Let there be light: and there was light;”
sources.raw_question: Did the one God create all things through the Word?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Yes. There is one God, the Creator, who made and ordered all things by His Word and His Wisdom. This Creator is the same God who gave this world to the human race. No other or lower demiurge made the world.
sources.quote: There is therefore one God, who by the Word and Wisdom created and arranged all things; but this is the Creator (Demiurge) who has granted this world to the human race
sources.raw_question: Did one God create and arrange all things, and if so, by what means?

question: Is the Creator of the world a lesser being produced from a defect or apostasy from a higher God, as the Valentinians claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Preface.
sources.answer: No. The Maker and Framer of the world is the one God, and to say he originated from a defect or apostasy is blasphemy above all other heresies. Irenaeus has already shown that the Creator is God alone and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
sources.quote: they represent that the Maker and Framer, who is one God, as I have shown, was produced from a defect or apostasy.
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of the world a lesser being produced from a defect or apostasy, as the Valentinians claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: No. The Valentinians confess one God the Father from whom all things come, yet they make the Former of all things the fruit of a defect. That contradicts their own confession of unity. The one God the Father is himself the Maker of all things.
sources.quote: they do indeed confess with the tongue one God the Father, and that all things derive their existence from Him, but do at the same time maintain that He who formed all things is the fruit of an apostasy or defect.
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of all things the product of a defect or apostasy from a higher God, as the Valentinians held?

question: How is God the Father made known, and what role does the Son play in revealing him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: The Father is revealed and made manifest only through his Word, who is his Son. Only those to whom the Son reveals him know the Father, as Scripture teaches.
sources.quote: through His Word, who is His Son, through Him He is revealed and manifested to all to whom He is revealed; for those [only] know Him to whom the Son has revealed Him.
sources.raw_question: How is God the Father known, and what role does the Son play in revealing him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: God is declared through the Son, who is in the Father and has the Father in himself. The Father bears witness to the Son, and the Son announces the Father, as Isaiah writes: "I too am witness, saith the Lord God, and the Son whom I have chosen."
sources.quote: Therefore God has been declared through the Son, who is in the Father, and has the Father in Himself —He who is, the Father bearing witness to the Son, and the Son announcing the Father.
sources.raw_question: How is God made known through the relation of the Father and the Son?

question: Did God himself impose names on created things that are naturally fitted to their natures, so that divine wisdom is displayed in the names themselves?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory argues that the same object, such as the heaven, is called by many different names among different nations (Greek, Hebrew, Roman, Syrian, etc.), and no one language can claim to bear the uniquely fitting divinely imposed word. Names are therefore inventions of the human rational faculty, and Eunomius has merely borrowed Plato's Cratylus theory and made it a church doctrine.
sources.quote: Which of these, then, tell me, is the appropriate word wherein the great wisdom of God is manifested? If you prefer the Greek to the rest, the Egyptian haply will confront you with his own.
sources.raw_question: Did God himself impose names on created things that are precisely suited to their natures, so that divine wisdom is displayed in the names themselves?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. This is a theory borrowed from Plato's Cratylus, not a Church doctrine. The same created thing, such as the firmament, receives different names in different languages, Heaven, Samaim, cœlum and others, which shows names are human conventions rather than divinely fitted labels.
sources.quote: For by how many appellations, say, is the created firmament called according to the varieties of language? For we call it Heaven, the Hebrew calls it Samaim, the Roman cœlum
sources.raw_question: Is the divine wisdom displayed in the names of created things, as though each name were naturally fitted to its object?

question: Do divine attributes such as life, wisdom, power, goodness and blessedness belong to the whole Trinity or to each Person individually?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What Universal Nature Teaches Us Concerning God.
sources.answer: They belong to both. Whatever is worthily said of God in this way applies to the whole Trinity, which is one God, and also to each of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In the nature in which they are mutually equal, none is mortal, changeable, or corporeal, and none can be denied to be most powerful, good, and blessed.
sources.quote: applies to the whole Trinity, which is one God, and to the several Persons in that Trinity
sources.raw_question: Do the attributes known of God by natural reason, such as life, wisdom, and goodness, belong to the whole Trinity or to each Person separately?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Difficult It is to Demonstrate the Trinity by Natural Reason.
sources.answer: Yes. Whatever is worthily said of God in this way applies both to the whole Trinity, which is one God, and to each of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. No one would dare say that any Person is not living, lacks intelligence, or is mortal or changeable, nor deny that each is most powerful, righteous, good and blessed, since in that nature they are mutually equal.
sources.quote: applies to the whole Trinity, which is one God, and to the several Persons in that Trinity
sources.raw_question: Do the divine attributes such as living, wise, powerful, good and blessed belong to the whole Trinity and also to each Person of the Trinity individually?

question: When Scripture speaks of God 'generating' creation, does this imply place, time, material, or instruments as in human making?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He further shows the operations of God to be expressed by human illustrations; for what hands and feet and the other parts of the body with which men work are, that, in the case of God, the will alone is, in place of these. And so also arises the divergence of generation; wherefore He is called Only-begotten, because He has no community with other generation such as is observed in creation, but in that He is called the “brightness of glory,” and the “savour of ointment,” He shows the close conjunction and co-eternity of His Nature with the Father.
sources.answer: No. Scripture calls God's formative power 'generation' because divine language must descend to our lowliness, but it excludes place, time, preparation of material, instruments and the like. Creation's material, place and time had their existence in the power of His will alone, as the psalm says, "He spake and they were begotten."
sources.quote: neither place nor time nor preparation of material, nor the co-operation of instruments, nor the purpose in the things produced, but it leaves these out of sight, and greatly and loftily claims for God the generation of the things that are
sources.raw_question: When Scripture speaks of God 'generating' creation, does this imply place, time, material, or instruments as in human making?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: No. Scripture uses the language of generation because it must stoop to our low capacity, but it strips away time, place, matter, instruments, and design. It teaches instead that the power of God's will served in place of all these, as in 'He spake the word and they were made.'
sources.quote: affirming that the power of God’s will served for material substance, place, time and all such circumstances
sources.raw_question: When Scripture calls God's act of creation a 'generation', does it imply time, place, matter, or instruments in God?

question: Can the divine essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit be visible in itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > In How Many Ways the Creature is to Be Taken by Way of Sign. The Eucharist.
sources.answer: No. Whatever is visible is also changeable, though not everything changeable is visible (thoughts, memories, wills are changeable but invisible). Since the divine essence is in no way changeable, it is even less in any way visible in its proper self.
sources.quote: Since there are no doubt some things changeable, yet not visible, as are our thoughts, and memories, and wills, and the whole incorporeal creature; but there is nothing that is visible that is not also changeable.
sources.raw_question: Can the divine essence of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit be visible in itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: No. The divine essence is in no way changeable, and whatever is visible is also changeable; therefore the essence of the Trinity can in no way be visible in its proper self.
sources.quote: the essence of God, wherein we understand, in proportion to our measure, in however small a degree, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, since it is in no way changeable, can in no way in its proper self be visible.
sources.raw_question: Can the essence of God, in which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are understood, be visible in itself?

question: Is the Holy Spirit a distinct divine person, rather than merely a quality, power or virtue of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: He is a distinct divine person. He is placed in the same order with the Father and Son without any note of difference as to personality, bears names proper only to a divine person, has personal properties, is the voluntary author of divine operations, and is the proper object of divine worship. If these do not demonstrate a divine, intelligent substance, nothing expressed in words could be understood.
sources.quote: The sum is that the Holy Ghost is a divine, distinct person, and neither merely the power or virtue of God, nor any created spirit whatever.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a distinct divine person, rather than merely the power or virtue of God or a created spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Scripture says the Spirit comes, comforts, teaches, guides, spoke by the prophets, searches the deep things of God, works as he wills, appoints ministers, and can be grieved and sinned against. To say all this while requiring us to believe he is only a quality would make Scripture deceptive and leave nothing certain in it. So we must acknowledge the Spirit to be a substance, a person, God, yet distinct from the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: we must acknowledge the Holy Ghost to be a substance, a person, God; yet distinct from the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be merely a quality or power of God operating in certain works, rather than a distinct divine person?

question: Does the single common operation of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit show that their divine power is one rather than diverse?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIV. Each Person of the Trinity is said in the sacred writings to be Light. The Spirit is designated Fire by Isaiah, a figure of which Fire was seen in the bush by Moses, in the tongues of fire, and in Gideon's pitchers. And the Godhead of the same Spirit cannot be denied, since His operation is the same as that of the Father and of the Son, and He is also called the light and fire of the Lord's countenance.
sources.answer: Yes. Where the effect of the working in all is one, there can be no severance of power. So the shared operation shows not diversity but the unity of the divine power.
sources.quote: By which evidence we infer not a diversity but the unity of the divine power. For how can there be a severance of power, where the effect of the working in all is one?
sources.raw_question: Does a single common operation of Father, Son and Holy Spirit imply a unity of divine power rather than a diversity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter II. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are One in counsel.
sources.answer: Yes. The Three have one work, one judgment, one temple, one life-giving, one sanctification, and one kingdom. Given all this, their power and might cannot fail to be one.
sources.quote: For how should not the power and might be one, when the work is one, the judgment one, the temple one, the life-giving one, the sanctification one, and the kingdom also of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit one?
sources.raw_question: Does the unity of operation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit prove that their power and might are one?

question: Does Scripture ascribe omniscience and incomprehensibility to the Son, as it does to the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter tells him without qualification, "Lord, Thou knowest all things." Christ says that no one knows the Son but the Father, and no one knows the Father but the Son. He who knows the Father is omniscient, and he who is known only by the Father is incomprehensible.
sources.quote: He who knows the Father is omniscient; He who is known only by the Father is incomprehensible.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ascribe omniscience and incomprehensibility to the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter tells Christ without qualification, "Lord, Thou knowest all things," and Christ says no one knows the Son but the Father and no one knows the Father but the Son. He who knows the Father is omniscient, and He who is known only by the Father is incomprehensible. Scripture also calls Christ's riches unsearchable and says all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him.
sources.quote: In this passage both the omniscience and incomprehensibility of Christ are declared by himself. He who knows the Father is omniscient; He who is known only by the Father is incomprehensible.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ascribe omniscience and incomprehensibility to Jesus Christ as it does to the Father?

question: Is it lawful to use non-scriptural terms such as 'essence', 'substance', 'person', or 'hypostasis' in explaining the doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes; it is not only lawful but necessary, provided no other things are taught than Scripture contains. Denying this would deny all interpretation of Scripture, since if we may not express the sense of its words we may not even conceive it in our minds, which would make Scripture useless.
sources.quote: we may lawfully, nay, we must necessarily, make use of other words, phrases, and expressions, than what are literally and syllabically contained in the Scripture, but teach no other things.
sources.raw_question: Is it lawful to use non-scriptural terms such as 'essence', 'person', or 'hypostasis' in explaining the doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Though faith does not absolutely need such terms, the church has used them in all ages to defend faith against sophisms and to help believers grow in explicit understanding. Such words are proper when they are of the same import as Scripture's own expressions, include nothing of imperfection, and only declare what is necessarily included in or consequent upon what is revealed.
sources.quote: Some of these words, indeed, are not used in the Scripture; but whereas they are of the same importance and signification, and none of them include any thing of imperfection, they are properly used in the declaration of the unity of the Godhead.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to use non-scriptural terms such as 'essence', 'substance', and 'person' in explaining the doctrine of the Trinity?

question: If the Son is generated or derived from the Father, must he be a distinct individual substance from the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. It is sufficient to say that what is generated must be a distinct individual Person, not a distinct individual substance. The whole difficulty lies in the undefined sense of "individual substance," which the objector never defines.
sources.quote: No; but we think it sufficient to say, that it must be a distinct individual Person. All the difficulty here lies in fixing and determining the sense of the words individual substance.
sources.raised_by_detail: Dr. Clarke's defender (Dr. Whitby/the Modest Pleader)
sources.raw_question: If the Son is generated or derived from the Father, must he be a distinct individual substance from the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. It is enough to say that what is derived must be a distinct individual Person, not a distinct substance. The whole difficulty depends on the undefined sense of 'individual substance', and the objector should define his terms.
sources.quote: No; but we think it sufficient to say, that it must be a distinct individual Person.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is derived from the Father, must he be a distinct individual substance?

question: Does Scripture calling the Son a 'servant' or using creaturely terms of Him show that He is not the Father's natural, genuine Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. Ordinary usage shows that such names do not cancel a known nature. Bathsheba and Nathan called Solomon David's 'servant', yet he remained David's son by nature and heir. So scriptural terms like 'servant' or 'made' must be read in light of the Son's confessed nature.
sources.quote: Nor did they mind calling the son a servant, for while David heard it, he recognised the ‘nature,’ and while they spoke it, they forgot not the ‘genuineness,’
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'servant' or using creaturely terms of Him deny that He is a natural, genuine Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. Solomon was called David's 'servant' by Bathsheba and Nathan, yet he was David's son by nature. In the same way, the Son can be called servant without denying that He is proper to the Father and from Him. Such terms can also be referred to His humanity, since He was made man.
sources.quote: let not any on this account deny that He is proper to the Father and from Him; but, as in the case of Solomon and David, let them have a right idea of the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture calling the Son a 'servant' show that He is not the Father's proper, natural Son?

question: Does God's declaration in Isaiah, 'There is no God beside Me,' mean that the Father alone is God, excluding the Godhead of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The Father himself also says to another, 'There is no God beside Thee.' If 'beside Me' excluded the Son, the Father's saying 'beside Thee' would be meaningless, since a solitary Being cannot address himself this way. So the text does not support a solitary Father.
sources.quote: what sense can you assign to the solemn declaration of God the Father, There is no God beside Thee, if your explanation of There is no God beside Me be a denial of the Godhead of the Son?
sources.raw_question: Does 'There is no God beside Me' (Isaiah) mean the Father alone is God, excluding the Son's Godhead?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The Father never sought the 'majesty of isolation' the heretics attribute to Him, and He repudiates the use of these words to deny the Godhead of the Son begotten from Himself. In the same passage He attributes absolute divinity to the Son: 'there is no God beside Thee.' To deny the Son's divinity does not augment the Father's glory but slights the Father by refusing to reverence the Son.
sources.quote: He repudiates your officious interpretation which would twist His words, There is no other God beside Me, into a denial of the Godhead of the Son Whom He begot from Himself.
sources.raw_question: Does God's declaration in Isaiah, 'There is no other God beside Me,' exclude the Godhead of the Son?

question: How is the love of God the Father received by believers so as to have communion with him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: It is received by faith; receiving it is believing it. Communion consists in giving and receiving, and God has revealed his love so fully that it may be believed. Christ's words 'Ye believe in God' refer to the Father, and what is believed in him is his love, since God is love.
sources.quote: How, then, is this love of the Father to be received, so as to hold fellowship with him? I answer, By faith. The receiving of it is the believing of it.
sources.raw_question: How is the love of God the Father received by believers so as to have communion with him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. Merely contemplating the Father's love is useless for communion unless it is received by faith. The believer must believe the Father's love for himself, accept God's witness to it, assent to it with the mind, embrace it with the will, and fill the affections with it. Only then is the sweetness of that love truly his.
sources.quote: We do not hold communion with him in any thing, until it be received by faith.
sources.raw_question: Can a believer have communion with God the Father in his love without receiving that love by faith?

question: Can the Ungenerate Father and the Generate Son differ or be opposed in essence the way fire differs from water?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > Thereafter he discusses the divergence of names and of things, speaking, of that which is ungenerate as without a cause, and of that which is non-existent, as the Scindapsus, Minotaur, Blityri, Cyclops, Scylla, which never were generated at all, and shows that things which are essentially different, are mutually destructive, as fire of water, and the rest in their several relations. But in the case of the Father and the Son, as the essence is common, and the properties reciprocally interchangeable, no injury results to the Nature.
sources.answer: No. Fire and water are mutually destructive, and each is destroyed in the other. If the Father and Son differed in that way, their natures would be incompatible, and one would consume the other if they were in each other. Yet the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son without destruction. They also share goodness, wisdom, power and incorruptibility, so the analogy is blasphemous and false.
sources.quote: their nature will be, by this reasoning, incompatible and incommunicable, and the one would be consumed by the other, if both should be found to be mutually inclusive or co-existent.
sources.raw_question: Can the Ungenerate (Father) and the Generated (Son) differ in essence the way fire differs from water?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > Thereafter he discusses the divergence of names and of things, speaking, of that which is ungenerate as without a cause, and of that which is non-existent, as the Scindapsus, Minotaur, Blityri, Cyclops, Scylla, which never were generated at all, and shows that things which are essentially different, are mutually destructive, as fire of water, and the rest in their several relations. But in the case of the Father and the Son, as the essence is common, and the properties reciprocally interchangeable, no injury results to the Nature.
sources.answer: No. Things essentially opposed, like fire and water, destroy each other when one is in the other, yet the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son without either being destroyed or consumed. So the mutual indwelling of Father and Son refutes Eunomius' claim that their essences differ like fire and water.
sources.quote: How then is the Son “in the Father” without being destroyed, and how does the Father, coming to be “in the Son,” remain continually unconsumed, if, as Eunomius says, the special attribute of fire, as compared with water, is maintained in the relation of the Generate to the Ungenerate?
sources.raw_question: Are the natures of the Ungenerate Father and the Generate Son opposed to one another in the way fire is opposed to water?

question: Does the name "Godhead" (or any other name used of God) signify the divine nature or essence itself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. Following Scripture, the divine nature is unnameable and unspeakable; every term, whether coined by human custom or handed down in Scripture, explains our conceptions of the divine nature but does not include the signification of that nature itself. By any term we use, some one of its surroundings is made known, not the nature itself.
sources.quote: every term either invented by the custom of men, or handed down to us by the Scriptures, is indeed explanatory of our conceptions of the Divine Nature, but does not include the signification of that nature itself
sources.raised_by_detail: "Most men" who hold that "Godhead" is a proper name of the divine nature
sources.raw_question: Does the word "Godhead" (or any other name used of God) signify the divine nature or essence itself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. The divine nature is unlimited and incomprehensible, and what is absolutely infinite is not limited in any respect, not even by a name. The Deity is above every name, and 'Godhead' is a name. The same thing cannot both be a name and be above every name.
sources.quote: we say that the Deity is above every name: and “Godhead” is a name. Now it cannot be that the same thing should at once be a name and be accounted as above every name.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who oppose us with the assertion that we are not to conceive 'Godhead' as an operation
sources.raw_question: Can the name 'Godhead' strictly express the divine nature itself?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being 'sent' make Him a ministering creature like the Seraph or other angels who are sent?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XI. The Spirit is sent to all, and passes not from place to place, for He is not limited either by time or space. He goes forth from the Son, as the Son from the Father, in Whom He ever abides: and also comes to us when we receive. He comes also after the same manner as the Father Himself, from Whom He can by no means be separated.
sources.answer: No. The Seraph is sent to one person, to minister and perform what is commanded, and passes from place to place because he does not fill all things. The Spirit is sent to all, works a mystery, divides as He wills, and is the one who fills even the Seraph.
sources.quote: The Seraph is sent to minister, the Spirit works a mystery. The Seraph performs what is commanded, the Spirit divides as He wills. The Seraph passes from place to place, for he does not fill all things, but is himself filled by the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being 'sent' make Him like the Seraph or other angelic ministers who are sent?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter X. That the Spirit forgives sin is common to Him with the Father and the Son, but not with the Angels.
sources.answer: No. The Seraph is sent to one person, but the Spirit is sent to all. The Seraph is sent to minister and does what he is commanded, while the Spirit works a mystery and distributes gifts as he wills. The Seraph also moves from place to place, but the Spirit fills all things.
sources.quote: The Spirit, also, is indeed said to be sent, but the Seraph to one, the Spirit to all. The Seraph is sent to minister, the Spirit works a mystery.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that both the Seraph and the Holy Spirit are said to be "sent" make the Spirit a ministering creature like the angels?

question: Can the Son's generation be both by necessity of the Father's nature and by the Father's will, or are these inconsistent?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: They are consistent. The Son may be generated with the Father's will and consent in the same sense in which the Father is wise, good and just necessarily yet not against his will. Dr. Clarke wrongly set the two against each other. His own authorities, such as the Council of Sirmium, Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, asserted both, and denied only a necessity that would be against or force the Father's will. Will in the sense of consent or approbation differs from arbitrary will, meaning free choice of what might otherwise not be, and generation by arbitrary will would make the Son a creature.
sources.quote: There is a sober, Catholic sense, in which the Son may be acknowledged to be by, or from, the will of the Father, and yet may be a necessary emanation also.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's generation be both by the will of the Father and a necessary emanation, or are these inconsistent?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. The generation of the Son may be by necessity of nature without excluding the concurrence or approbation of the Father's will. Will in the sense of consent, approbation and acquiescence must be distinguished from arbitrary will, the free choice of what might otherwise not be. Only the first applies to the Son's generation.
sources.quote: the generation of the Son may be by necessity of nature, without excluding the concurrence or approbation of the will. And therefore will (i. e. consent, approbation, acquiescence) is one thing; and arbitrary will (that is, free choice of what might otherwise not be) is another.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's generation be by necessity of the Father's nature while still involving the Father's will?

question: Does the Son's prayer to be glorified by the Father (John 17:1) show that the Son is weak or inferior in Godhead?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. The prayer "Father, glorify Thy Son" is completed by "that the Son may glorify Thee," so the Son returns glory for glory. Neither Father nor Son was ever in want, yet each gives to the other. This exchange of glory demonstrates the one power of the single Godhead dwelling in both.
sources.quote: the prayer for glory to be given and to be paid back is neither a robbery of the Father nor a depreciation of the Son, but a demonstration of the power of one Godhead resident in Both.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's prayer to be glorified by the Father (John 17) show that the Son lacks power or is inferior in Godhead?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The Son asks to be glorified precisely so that he may in turn glorify the Father who glorifies him. His prayer for glory aims at the Father being glorified by granting it, which is no mark of weakness.
sources.quote: Do you call Him weak because He asks to be glorified? So be it, if He does not ask to be glorified in order that He may Himself glorify Him by Whom He is glorified.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's asking the Father to glorify him (John 17:1) show that the Son is weak or inferior?

question: In what sense is the Holy Spirit called 'the Spirit of adoption'?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Because by the Spirit we are moved out of our natural state as children of wrath and adopted as children of God. By receiving the Spirit of our Father we become the children of our Father.
sources.quote: By the Spirit we are put into another capacity, and are adopted to be the children of God, inasmuch as by receiving the Spirit of our Father we become the children of our Father.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit called 'the Spirit of adoption'?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: The Spirit is the Spirit of adoption either because he is given to the adopted to assure them of the Father's adopting love, or because he confers the privilege of adoption itself (John 1:12). Galatians 4:6 is not opposed to this, since God may send the Spirit of supplication into our hearts because we are sons and yet we may still be adopted by his Spirit.
sources.quote: Neither is that opposite hereunto which we have, Gal. iv. 6; for God may send the Spirit of supplication into our hearts, because we are sons, and yet adopted by his Spirit.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Holy Spirit called the 'Spirit of adoption', and does Galatians 4:6 (God sends the Spirit because we are sons) contradict the idea that we are adopted by the Spirit?

question: Could a creature, by becoming man, have joined humanity to God and accomplished salvation if the Son were a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. A creature cannot join creatures to God, since it itself needs one to join it to God; nor can a part of creation be creation's salvation, since it needs salvation itself. Therefore the Father sent His own Son, who, being other than all creatures, took created flesh and offered it to death for all.
sources.quote: for a creature had not joined creatures to God, as seeking itself one to join it; nor would a portion of the creation have been the creation’s salvation, as needing salvation itself.
sources.raw_question: Could a creature have joined humanity to God and accomplished salvation if the Son were a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. If the Word were a creature, man would have remained what he was, not joined to God, since a work cannot join a work to the Creator, and like cannot succour like when both need help. Only the proper Word of God taking flesh perfects and restores mankind with greater grace.
sources.quote: For if, being a creature, He had become man, man had remained just what he was, not joined to God; for how had a work been joined to the Creator by a work?
sources.raw_question: Could a creature, by becoming man, have joined humanity to God and saved it?

question: What is the inner word of the human mind, and in what way is it an image of the divine Word?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Word of God is in All Things Equal to the Father, from Whom It is.
sources.answer: The inner word is somewhat like the Word of God, though only in an enigma. It has neither sound nor the thought of sound and belongs to no language, and it is born of our knowledge, just as the divine Word is born of the Father's knowledge. Augustine stresses that its unlikeness to the divine Word must also be considered.
sources.quote: is in some sort like, in this enigma, to that Word of God which is also God; since this too is born of our knowledge, in such manner as that also is born of the knowledge of the Father
sources.raw_question: In what way is the human inner word an image of the divine Word?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Academic Philosophy.
sources.answer: It is a true word begotten from the knowledge stored in memory. It comes before all sound and before any thought of sound, and it belongs to no language. It is most like the thing known, because the sight of thinking arises from the sight of knowledge. It has nothing of its own but is wholly derived from the knowledge from which it is born, provided it is true, that is, springs from things known.
sources.quote: when it is a word belonging to no tongue, but is a true word concerning a true thing, having nothing of its own, but wholly derived from that knowledge from which it is born
sources.raw_question: What is the inner word of the human mind, and how is it begotten from knowledge, as an image bearing on the divine Word?

question: Can a distinction between a supreme God and a subordinate or inferior true God be used to describe Christ's divinity, and does Scripture warrant it?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 4: Whether, supposing the Scripture-notion of God to be no more than that of the Author and Governor of the universe, or whatever it be, the admitting of another t
sources.answer: No. Scripture nowhere intimates two true Gods or distinguishes a sovereign and an inferior Deity, and nothing warrants adding 'supreme' where Scripture says absolutely there is but one God. If two Gods existed, the early Fathers argued against polytheism on a false principle, the angel's maxim to John and Christ's reply to the devil would be defective, and the Old Testament declarations of unity insignificant. Scripture's design was to exclude lesser dependent divinities, not merely other supremes.
sources.quote: where does the Scripture give you the least intimation of two true Gods? Where does it furnish you with any ground for the distinction of a sovereign and an inferior Deity?
sources.raw_question: Is there scriptural warrant for distinguishing a supreme God from a subordinate or inferior true God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. Scripture recognizes only one God, so a second, subordinate God would introduce polytheism; and nothing can properly be God that is not supreme, since supremacy presupposes all the essential properties of the one true God. An inferior God is God only improperly or figuratively, so the distinction resolves into 'a God and no God.' Arguments for Christ being a subordinate God are therefore really arguments that he is not God at all.
sources.quote: so that at length your famed distinction of a supreme and subordinate God, resolves into a God and no God.
sources.raw_question: Is the distinction between a supreme God and a subordinate God a coherent way to describe Christ's divinity?

question: Does applying many names with different meanings to God (wise, just, good, eternal) make God composite, or must those names all mean the same thing to preserve His simplicity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Our knowledge of God is gathered from various conceptions, but this does not mean the Deity is composed of these elements or fills out His essence by participating in them. Just as one human soul can be skilled in geometry, astronomy, medicine and grammar without becoming composite, and without those terms collapsing into one meaning, so God can bear many distinct names without losing simplicity.
sources.quote: If, then, the human mind, with all such terms applied to it, is not injured as regards its simplicity, how can any one imagine that the Deity, when He is called wise, and just, and good, and eternal, and all the other Divine names, must, unless all these names are made to mean one thing, become of many parts
sources.raw_question: Does applying many names with different meanings to God (wise, just, good, eternal) make God composite or compromise His simplicity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Each divine name has its own peculiar meaning, and distinct meanings applied to one simple subject do not divide it, as the different sciences ascribed to one soul show. Making all names identical in meaning would also lead to absurdities, such as making 'Father' equivalent to 'indestructible' or 'Creator'.
sources.quote: it is within the bounds of possibility that the idea of each of these sciences should be associated with one soul, without that soul thereby becoming composite, or, on the other hand, without all those terms for sciences blending into one meaning
sources.raw_question: Must all the names of God mean exactly the same thing in order to preserve divine simplicity?

question: Does saying that the Son came into being by the goodness of the Father adequately describe the Son's origin?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: No. Every creature (mankind, animals and plants) arose from the goodness of its Maker. To say this of the Son therefore puts him on a level with the meanest creatures. It grants him only a property common to all things.
sources.quote: But to say that the Son came into being by the goodness of the Father is nothing else than to put Him on a level with the meanest objects of creation.
sources.raw_question: Does saying that the Son came into being by the goodness of the Father adequately describe the Son's origin?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: No, not as a distinguishing account of the Son. Everything that exists, from humankind to plants and animals, owes its origin to its Maker's goodness. Ascribing the Son's existence to the Father's goodness therefore grants Him only what is common to all creatures and ranks Him with the meanest of them.
sources.quote: A property, then, which reason discerns to be common to all things, Eunomius is so kind as to allow to the Eternal Son!
sources.raw_question: Is it fitting to say the Son came into being by the goodness of the Father?

question: Does Christ's having glory with the Father before the world was (John 17:5) prove that he pre-existed the world and is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again from the Gospel He Proves Christ to Be God.
sources.answer: Yes. No one can possess glory unless he first exists to keep it. Christ had glory with the Father before the foundation of the world, so he existed before the world. A mere man comes after the world, so Christ is not man only but God.
sources.quote: For no one could possess anything, unless he himself should first be in existence to keep anything. But now Christ has the glory before the foundation of the world; therefore He Himself was before the foundation of the world.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer for the glory he had with the Father before the world was prove that he pre-existed the world and is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Truth is Proved from the Sacred Writings of the New Covenant.
sources.answer: Yes. The Word came down from heaven without flesh and ascended again as the Son of man with the flesh he had assumed. There he received the glory he had before the foundation of the world. Having such glory before the world existed proves him to be God.
sources.quote: it at length receives that glory which in being shown to have had before the foundation of the world, it is most manifestly proved to be God
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's having glory with the Father before the world was prove that he is God?

question: Can Christ's pre-mundane glory in John 17:5 be explained as glory only in God's predestination rather than real pre-existence?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again from the Gospel He Proves Christ to Be God.
sources.answer: No. The text does not say 'predestination', and adding to Scripture is forbidden. Christ existed in substance before the world as the Word by whom all things were made. Moreover, if his glory were only predestined, he would be predestined after Adam, Abel, Noah and others, which would make him inferior to men. In truth he is greater and more ancient even than the angels.
sources.quote: And thus, predestination being set aside, seeing it is not so laid down, Christ was in substance before the foundation of the world. For He is “the Word by which all things were made, and without which nothing was made.”
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold Christ to be only man
sources.raw_question: Can Christ's pre-mundane glory in John 17:5 be explained as glory only in God's predestination rather than real pre-existence?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again from the Gospel He Proves Christ to Be God.
sources.answer: No. The text does not say "in predestination," and adding to Scripture is forbidden, so that gloss may not be introduced. Setting it aside, Christ existed in substance before the world, since he is the Word by whom all things were made.
sources.quote: And thus, predestination being set aside, seeing it is not so laid down, Christ was in substance before the foundation of the world.
sources.raw_question: Can Christ's having glory with the Father before the foundation of the world (John 17:5) be explained as merely predestined glory rather than real pre-existence?

question: When the Trinity is called three persons in one essence, is 'essence' related to the persons as a genus or species is to its members?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: No. If essence were a genus, it would be predicated in the plural along with its species: three horses are also three animals, never one animal. So we would have to speak of three essences. Moreover, a single essence, like a single animal, has no species. Therefore the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are not three species of one essence.
sources.quote: I do affirm, that if essence is a genus, then a single essence has no species; just as, because animal is a genus, a single animal has no species. Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three species of one essence.
sources.raised_by_detail: some who think essence is the genus and substance or person the species
sources.raw_question: Is the divine essence related to the three persons as a genus is to its species, so that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are three species of one essence?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: No. The terms are used not according to genus or species but somewhat as of a common matter, like three statues of one gold. Yet even the gold analogy is not taken as genus and species, since a species never extends beyond its individuals nor beyond the definition of its genus, whereas gold extends beyond the statues.
sources.quote: We do not therefore use these terms according to genus or species, but as if according to a matter that is common and the same.
sources.raw_question: When we say the Trinity is three persons and one essence, is 'essence' being used as a genus or species of which the persons are instances?

question: Is the Son of God rightly called "good," or does that title belong to the Father alone?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He also ingeniously shows from the passage of the Gospel which speaks of “Good Master,” from the parable of the Vineyard, from Isaiah and from Paul, that there is not a dualism in the Godhead of good and evil, as Eunomius' ally Marcion supposes, and declares that the Son does not refuse the title of “good” or “Existent,” or acknowledge His alienation from the Father, but that to Him also belongs authority over all things that come into being.
sources.answer: Yes. In the parable of the labourers in the vineyard the just judge says 'Is thine eye evil because I am good?', and since distributing recompense is the judge's function and the Father has committed all judgment to the Son, it is the Son who speaks and claims goodness.
sources.quote: all the disciples of the Gospel agree that the Only-begotten God is Judge; “for the Father,” He saith, “judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son.”
sources.raw_question: Does the Son claim the title 'good' for Himself in Scripture?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > The eleventh book shows that the title of “Good” is due, not to the Father alone, as Eunomius, the imitator of Manichæus and Bardesanes, alleges, but to the Son also, Who formed man in goodness and loving-kindness, and reformed him by His Cross and Death.
sources.answer: The Son is truly good. Gregory argues that denying His goodness is the worst charge one could bring against the Eunomians. The Son, though in the form of God and equal with God, humbled Himself to human nature purely out of love for man. Gregory also points out that whoever is not good must bear the opposite name, which is blasphemy against Christ.
sources.quote: For what more bitter charge could one invent against them for malice than that of denying that He is good “Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God,”
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God rightly called "good," or does that title belong to the Father alone?

question: Is the Trinity something contained in the one God, as three faculties are in one man, or is the Trinity itself the one God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Great the Unlikeness is Between the Image of the Trinity Which We Have Found in Ourselves, and the Trinity Itself.
sources.answer: The Trinity is itself the one God, not something in God. Its indivisibility is so great that, although three men cannot be called one man, the Trinity both is said to be and is one God. Unlike man's image, which has three things but is one person, the Trinity is three persons: the Father of the Son, the Son of the Father, and the Spirit of both.
sources.quote: nor is that Trinity in one God, but it is one God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Trinity something contained in the one God, or is the Trinity itself the one God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Augustin Dwells Still Further on the Disparity Between the Trinity Which is in Man, and the Trinity Which is God. The Trinity is Now Seen Through a Glass by the Help of Faith, that It May Hereafter Be More Clearly Seen in the Promised Sight Face to Face.
sources.answer: The Trinity is itself one God, not something contained in or belonging to one God. Whereas memory, understanding and love belong to one man without being the man, in the Highest Trinity the three are one God. Such is the divine indivisibility that, while three men cannot be called one man, the three Persons both are said to be and are one God.
sources.quote: in that, there both is said to be and is one God, nor is that Trinity in one God, but it is one God.
sources.raw_question: Is the divine Trinity 'in' one God as three faculties are in one man, or is the Trinity itself one God?

question: Does rephrasing the Arian formula as 'He was not before His generation,' without the word 'time,' differ from 'there was once when the Son was not' and so avoid placing the Son within time?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: No. Dropping the word 'time' only deceives the simple. Saying 'there was when He was not' or 'He was not before His generation' still means that times preceded him, so the formula carries the same temporal sense.
sources.quote: For you still simply mean times, when you say, ‘There was when He was not,’ and ‘He was not before His generation.’
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian formula 'There was when He was not,' which omits the word 'time,' avoid placing the Son within time?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: No. Both formulas mean the same thing: each implies that there is a time before the Word. So the softer phrasing does not avoid the error of placing the Son within time.
sources.quote: And your other, ‘The Son was not before His generation,’ is equivalent to saying, ‘There was once when He was not,’ for both the one and the other signify that there is a time before the Word.
sources.raw_question: Is the Arian formula 'The Son was not before His generation' different from saying 'there was once when the Son was not'?

question: Did the Son become God or receive life and full powers only at some point after His birth from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Neither. He was born as Life and became God by virtue of his birth, not afterwards. There are not two elements in him, one inborn and one later conferred, and no interval between birth and maturity.
