Born Living from Living, True from True, Perfect from Perfect, he possessed his powers and knew his Godhead from his birth.
sources.quote: Moreover God, the Son of God, became God by virtue of His birth, not after He was born.
sources.raw_question: Was the Son made life after his birth, or did he become God some time after being born?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The Son was born as Life, not made life after His birth; there are not two elements in Him, one inborn and one later conferred, and no interval between birth and maturity. He became God by virtue of His birth, born Living from Living, Perfect from Perfect, in full possession of His powers and conscious of His Godhead from His birth.
sources.quote: Moreover God, the Son of God, became God by virtue of His birth, not after He was born. Being born the Living from the Living, the True from the True, the Perfect from the Perfect, He was born in full possession of His powers.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son become God or receive life and full powers only at some point after His birth from the Father?

question: Can the mind's presence to itself properly be called memory, given that memory is usually thought to concern only things past?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether Memory is Also of Things Present.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as memory in things past is what makes them available to be recalled, so in a thing present, such as the mind to itself, that which makes the mind at hand to itself is not unreasonably called memory. Even ordinary usage confirms this: Virgil says Ulysses did not forget himself, meaning he remembered himself, though he was present to himself.
sources.quote: so in a thing present, as the mind is to itself, that is not unreasonably to be called memory, which makes the mind at hand to itself, so that it can be understood by its own thought, and then both be joined together by love of itself.
sources.raised_by_detail: Cicero's division of prudence into memory, understanding, forethought
sources.raw_question: Can the mind's presence to itself properly be called memory, given the objection that memory concerns only things past?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How a Trinity is Produced by the Mind Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself.
sources.answer: Yes. Memory can be of things present. Even ordinary literary usage speaks this way: when Virgil says Ulysses did not forget himself, he means Ulysses remembered himself while being present to himself. So the mind, ever present to itself, can rightly be said to remember itself.
sources.quote: For when Virgil said that Ulysses did not forget himself, what else did he mean, except that he remembered himself?
sources.raised_by_detail: those following Cicero's division of prudence
sources.raw_question: Can the mind properly be said to remember itself when it is always present to itself, given that memory is usually thought to concern only things past?

question: Does the Holy Spirit come to believers by his own will, or merely because he is sent by the Father and the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: It involves his own will. Faith sees the agreement of the Spirit's will with the gift of the Father and the Son. The Spirit's willingness reflects the distinct operation of the Deity in his person, while the gift reflects the economy of the whole Trinity in salvation. His coming is also his own condescension in love to accept their authoritative delegation.
sources.quote: the conjunction and accord of his will with the gift of Father and Son; the one respecting the distinct operation of the Deity in the person of the Holy Ghost; the other, the economy of the whole Trinity
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit's coming to believers merely the passive result of being sent, or does it involve his own will?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: He comes by his own will as well as by Christ's sending. The text says both 'he will come' and 'I will send him.' So there is not only Christ's mission but also the Spirit's own will in his coming; his own will is in his work.
sources.quote: So that there is not only the mission of Christ, but the will of the Spirit, in his coming: "He will come," — his own will is in his work.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit come by his own will, or merely because he is sent by Christ?

question: Does the New Testament, including the subordination of the Son and the Spirit in their redemptive functions, give compelling evidence that they are subordinate to the Father in their eternal modes of subsistence?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Hardly. If such subordination and derivation are not implied by the names "Son" and "Spirit," compelling New Testament evidence for them will be hard to find. Subordination is clearly expressed only in the Persons' modes of operation in redemption and in God's dealings with the world.
sources.quote: If, however, the subordination of the Son and Spirit to the Father in modes of subsistence and their derivation from the Father are not implicates of tbeir designation as Son and Spirit, it will be hard to find in the New Testament compelling evidence of their subordination and derivation.
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament give compelling evidence that the Son and Spirit are subordinate to the Father in their mode of subsistence?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No, not necessarily. Warfield argues that subordination in modes of operation may just as well rest on a voluntary agreement among the Persons, the Covenant of Redemption, by which each freely takes a distinct function in redemption. So subordination in modes of subsistence should not be assumed without definite evidence of it.
sources.quote: these relations of subordination in modes of operation may just as well be due to a convention, an agreement, between the Persons of the Trinity – a “Covenant” as it is technically called – by virtue of which a distinct function in the work of redemption is voluntarily assumed by each.
sources.raw_question: Does the subordination of the Son and the Spirit in their redemptive functions prove that they are subordinate to the Father in their eternal modes of subsistence?

question: Should natural reason and philosophical principles decide the doctrine of the Trinity, or Scripture and antiquity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: Scripture and antiquity should decide it. The subject is sublime and beyond comprehension, and we have no intrinsic evidence or ideas from which to build certain conclusions. Divine revelation is all in all here. Reason's proper use is to find the true sense of revelation, not to speculate from the nature of a thing we hardly know. Doing that follows mere conceits rather than reason.
sources.quote: The subject is sublime, and above comprehension. We have no intrinsic evidence, no ideas, to build any thing certainly upon. atrinsic evidence, divine revelation, is here all in all; and the only proper use of our rational faculties, is to inquire into the true and genuine sense of it.
sources.raw_question: Should natural reason and philosophical principles decide the doctrine of the Trinity, or Scripture and antiquity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: Only if it reached clear and evident demonstration, and it has not. Waterland grants that neither Scripture nor the Fathers could stand against genuine demonstration. However, the opponents offer only presumptions and conjectures, which carry no such weight.
sources.quote: neither Scripture nor Fathers can add force to, if concurring; nor, if reclaiming, be able to stand against, clear and evident demonstration. But demonstration is the thing wanting
sources.raw_question: Can philosophical reasoning alone settle the doctrine of the Trinity apart from Scripture and the Fathers?

question: Do the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit give the same spiritual gifts, such as apostleship, healings and tongues?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XIII. Prophecy was not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Spirit; the authority and operation of the latter on the apostles is signified to be the same as Theirs; and so we are to understand that there is unity in the three points of authority, rule, and bounty; yet need no disadvantage be feared from that participation, since such does not arise in human friendship. Lastly, it is established that this is the inheritance of the apostolic faith from the fact that the apostles are described as having obeyed the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. God set apostles, prophets and teachers and gave healings and tongues, which were shown earlier to be given by the Spirit. Christ likewise ordained apostles and promised healings and tongues. No single human receives all gifts, but the power of the Trinity, which is lavish of all graces, has no such limitation.
sources.quote: So, then, the Spirit gives the same gifts as the Father, and the Son also gives them.
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit give the same spiritual gifts, such as apostleship, healings and tongues?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XIII. Prophecy was not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Spirit; the authority and operation of the latter on the apostles is signified to be the same as Theirs; and so we are to understand that there is unity in the three points of authority, rule, and bounty; yet need no disadvantage be feared from that participation, since such does not arise in human friendship. Lastly, it is established that this is the inheritance of the apostolic faith from the fact that the apostles are described as having obeyed the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father sets apostles, prophets and teachers and gives healings and tongues; Christ, sending the apostles, promised the same signs of healing and new tongues; and Paul says that through the Spirit are given healings, tongues and prophecy. So the Spirit gives the same gifts as the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: So, then, the Spirit gives the same gifts as the Father, and the Son also gives them.
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit give the same spiritual gifts, such as healings and tongues?

question: Is the Christ of the New Testament the same Christ promised by the Creator in the Old Testament?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Further, that the Same Rule of Truth Teaches Us to Believe, After the Father, Also in the Son of God, Jesus Christ Our Lord God, Being the Same that Was Promised in the Old Testament, and Manifested in the New.
sources.answer: Yes. The Christ we read of as promised in the Old Testament is manifested in the New, fulfilling its shadows and figures. Both the ancient prophecies and the Gospels testify that he is the son of Abraham and of David. Genesis, Moses and Isaiah foretell his birth, healings, passion, resurrection, session at the Father's right hand, and judgment.
sources.quote: we read of as having been promised in the Old Testament, and we observe to be manifested in the New, fulfilling the shadows and figures of all the sacraments, with the presence of the truth embodied
sources.raw_question: Is the Christ of the New Testament the same one who was promised in the Old Testament?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That Jesus Christ is the Son of God and Truly Man, as Opposed to the Fancies of Heretics, Who Deny that He Took Upon Him True Flesh.
sources.answer: He is the Christ promised by the Creator in the Old Testament. The things predicted of Him were fulfilled, and those fulfilled had been predicted. A Christ who rejects the Creator's world, man, and law has no testimony of prophecy and comes to what is not his own, which shows he has nothing of his own.
sources.quote: Christ was not to be expected in the Gospel in any other wise than as He was promised before by the Creator, in the Scriptures of the Old Testament; especially as the things that were predicted of Him were fulfilled
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who reject the Old Testament (Marcionites)
sources.raw_question: Is the Christ of the Gospel the same Christ promised by the Creator in the Old Testament, or a different Christ sent by another god?

question: If the Son and the Holy Spirit possessed goodness only by participation rather than by essence, could they properly be called good?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. Just as iron heated by fire is not called fire, a being that only receives good from outside cannot properly be named good; it would be something other than good which at times has the good and at times lacks it. Before participation it would not have been good, and if separated it would again be other than good, so goodness would not be eternally and essentially in it.
sources.quote: that in the case of the Life-giving Power good does not reside in It essentially, but is imparted to it only, it will become impossible to call it properly good
sources.raw_question: If the Son and the Holy Spirit possess goodness only by participation rather than essentially, can they properly be called good?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. Their nature would then be one thing in itself and only acquire goodness from outside, as iron takes on heat from fire while remaining iron. Such goodness would not be eternal or essential, so they could not properly be called good. The divine nature would then need goodness rather than impart it, for no one can give what he does not possess.
sources.quote: A man who thinks this will be proving that their nature is one thing in itself, and becomes something else by virtue of its participation in this beauty or its opposite: as happens with iron for example
sources.raw_question: If the Son and the Spirit possessed goodness only by participation rather than by essence, could they properly be called good?

question: Does the Arian formula that the Son is 'a creature, but not as one of the creatures' succeed in distinguishing the Son from, and raising him above, the rest of creation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: No. The qualifier is an empty pretence, because every creature is unlike every other: light is not as night, the sun not as the moon, Angels not as Thrones, yet all are creatures, each in its own essence. Saying the Son is 'not as one of the creatures' therefore says nothing about him that could not be said of any creature, and the Arians still count him among the creatures. Either he is excepted from the works and confessed as Creator and Son by nature, or he is simply one creature among others.
sources.quote: For is any one of the creatures just what another is, that ye should predicate this of the Son as some prerogative?
sources.raised_by_detail: Arius and his party, in their letter to Alexander
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian formula that the Son is 'a creature, but not as one of the creatures' succeed in giving the Son a real prerogative above creation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: No. Every creature differs from every other creature and excels others in some respect, as star differs from star in glory, so the formula would apply to each creature equally. Mere superiority by comparison does not remove one from the class of creatures. Either the Son is excepted from the works as Creator and Son by nature, or he shares the same condition as the rest.
sources.quote: For though the Son excel the rest on a comparison, still a creature He is nevertheless, as they are; since in those which are by nature creatures one may find some excelling others.
sources.raw_question: Can the Arian formula that the Son is 'a creature but not as one of the creatures' distinguish the Son from other creatures?

question: Does the simplicity of the divine nature disprove the doctrine of the Trinity or show that it involves plurality or composition in God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Our idea of divine simplicity is imperfect, general, and obscure, and it is drawn chiefly from defective metaphysics rather than Scripture. When asked whether extension, plurality, or diversity is consistent with it, our ideas prove inadequate. So disputants explain it differently to suit their own schemes.
sources.quote: Scripture says little of it: we have took it chiefly from metaphysics, which are short and defective.
sources.raw_question: Does the doctrine of divine simplicity provide a clear standard for judging whether the Trinity involves plurality or composition in God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: No, not as an objection Clarke's party can use. Dr. Clarke himself has broken through the objection from simplicity by supposing extended parts in God. His solution serves the Trinitarians equally well, so it cannot be pressed against them alone.
sources.quote: The simplicity of the divine nature, for instance, is one of the strongest and most popular objections: but the learned Doctor has broke through it; and has contrived a solution, a very good one, both for himself and us
sources.raw_question: Does the simplicity of the divine nature disprove the doctrine of the Trinity?

question: Can each divine Person be called simple while the Persons differ in degrees of dignity, so that the Father is perfectly simple and the Son and Spirit less so?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His acknowledgment that the Divine Being is 'single' is only verbal.
sources.answer: No. The qualifier is either superfluous, if the Persons share a common dignity, or a device to grade simplicity according to a supposed declension in worth. That grading would make the Son partly composite and the Spirit more so, since imperfect simplicity cannot escape being composite, which contradicts the acknowledged simplicity of the Divine Nature.
sources.quote: Just as imperfect goodness must be owned to share in some measure in the reverse disposition, so imperfect simplicity cannot escape being considered composite.
sources.raw_question: Is it correct to say each divine Being is simple 'as estimated by its dignity,' so that the Father is perfectly simple and the Son and Spirit progressively less so?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His acknowledgment that the Divine Being is 'single' is only verbal.
sources.answer: No. Simplicity in the Holy Trinity admits of no degrees; a potency without parts or composition cannot contain differences of more and less. Whoever posits differences in size, goodness, strength, or wisdom must think of qualities incident in a subject and so cannot escape the idea of composition.
sources.quote: For who does not know that, to be exact, simplicity in the case of the Holy Trinity admits of no degrees.
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to call each divine Being 'simple' while also holding that they differ in degrees of greater and lesser dignity?

question: Does the Father need spoken words to communicate His will to the Son, or does the Son need verbal instruction to know the Father's will?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Signifying thoughts by words is a property of bodily nature, and even embodied humans can convey their minds without voice by nods or gestures. All the more, the immaterial and intangible Father needs no perishable words to make His will known to the Son, who is likewise immaterial.
sources.quote: can it be that in the case of the immaterial, and intangible, and, as Eunomius says, the Supreme and first Being, there is any need of words to indicate the thought of the Father and to make known His will to the Only-Begotten Son
sources.raw_question: Does the Father need vocal speech or words to communicate His will to the Only-Begotten Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Since the Son has in himself all that is the Father's, including the Father himself, he must have the whole of the Father's will within him. Being himself the Word of the Father in the highest sense, he cannot require a second word for instruction.
sources.quote: He needs not, therefore, to know the Father's will by word, being Himself the Word of the Father, in the highest acceptation of the term.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son need to be instructed by spoken words from the Father in order to know the Father's will?

question: Why is knowing or seeing the Son the same as knowing the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Objection, that the Son's eternity makes Him coordinate with the Father, introduces the subject of His Divine Sonship, as a second proof of His eternity. The word Son is introduced in a secondary, but is to be understood in real sense. Since all things partake of the Father in partaking of the Son, He is the whole participation of the Father, that is, He is the Son by nature; for to be wholly participated is to beget.
sources.answer: Because the Son is the Father's proper offspring from His essence. The thought and comprehension of the Son is therefore knowledge of the Father; He is the Father's Expression and Image, in whom the Father is contemplated and known, so that whoever looks on Him looks on the Father.
sources.quote: the thought and comprehension of the Son, is knowledge concerning the Father, because He is His proper offspring from His essence
sources.raw_question: Why does seeing or knowing the Son amount to knowing the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: No. Knowledge of the Father through the Son and knowledge of the Son from the Father are one and the same knowledge. That is why the whole earth is filled with the knowledge of him.
sources.quote: the knowledge of Father through Son and of Son from Father is one and the same
sources.raw_question: Is knowing the Father a different knowledge from knowing the Son?

question: Is the Son the product of an 'energy' of God that precedes him, rather than being begotten from the Father himself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in assuming, to account for the existence of the Only-Begotten, an 'energy' that produced Christ's Person.
sources.answer: No. An energy that has no existence of its own cannot give real being to anything, for what is born from an existent necessarily exists, while what comes from the non-existent necessarily does not. What is not self-existent cannot generate another. So deriving the Son from an unsubstantial energy reduces him to a non-entity and in effect denies the Saviour's deity, leaving only his name.
sources.quote: For as that which has its birth from an existence necessarily exists, so that which is evolved from the non-existent necessarily does the very contrary. When anything is not self-existent, how can it generate another?
sources.raw_question: If the Son were produced by an 'energy' that follows God rather than being born from the Father himself, would the Son have real existence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The blasphemy of these heretics is worse than the Jewish unbelief.
sources.answer: No. Gregory treats the idea of an energy prior to the Son, of which the Son is the work and product, as an invention and an insult to the Only-begotten. Even the Jews never dared to say such a thing. The doctrine reduces the Son from one generated from the Father to something made.
sources.quote: they invent an ‘energy’ prior to the personality of the Son and say that He is its work and product: a thing which the Jews hitherto have not dared to say.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the work and product of an 'energy' of God that exists prior to the Son's own personal existence?

question: If, as Eunomius claims, divine beings are known only through the works produced by their energies, how can the Holy Spirit's nature be known when Eunomius assigns no work to the Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: It cannot, on Eunomius' premise. No substantiated work of the Spirit exists in his scheme, so the Spirit's nature would be unknowable. And since the Spirit is supposed to reveal the Son, the Son would also be left unknown, hidden in the obscurity of what is meant to give evidence of Him.
sources.quote: If you insist that these beings are perceived by their energies, you must confess that the Spirit’s nature is imperceptible; you cannot infer His nature from any energy put forth by Him to carry on the continuity.
sources.raw_question: If beings are known only through their works, how can the Holy Spirit's being be known, given that Eunomius assigns no work to the Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: No, on Eunomius's own premise the Spirit's nature would be unknowable. Eunomius holds that the Father is shown in the Son as His work and the Son in the Spirit, but he assigns no substantiated work to the Spirit. So there is no energy from which the Spirit's being could be inferred. By his own rule, then, the Spirit's nature must be confessed imperceptible.
sources.quote: If you insist that these beings are perceived by their energies, you must confess that the Spirit’s nature is imperceptible; you cannot infer His nature from any energy put forth by Him to carry on the continuity.
sources.raw_question: If, as Eunomius claims, the divine beings are known through the works produced by their energies, can the nature of the Holy Spirit be known?

question: Is the Father's love for believers caused or grounded in anything lovely or deserving in them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No. The Father's love goes before not only our love but anything lovely in us. Rom. 5:8 shows he commended his love toward us while we were yet sinners, and sin removes every moving cause of love. He loves us not because we are better than others but because he himself is infinitely good.
sources.quote: Not only when we have done no good, but when we are in our blood, doth he love us; — not because we are better than others, but because himself is infinitely good.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's love for believers caused or occasioned by anything lovely in them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. He loves them because he wills to, and there is nothing in them for which they should be loved. A love that is eternally prior to their existence must be absolutely free with respect to their well-being. Its freeness is what gives it its value.
sources.quote: He loves us because he will; there was, there is, nothing in us for which we should be beloved.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's love for believers grounded in anything in them that deserves it?

question: Is the Son of God a creature or work, or an offspring proper to the Father's essence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: No. The Arians treat them as the same, writing 'generated or made.' Athanasius rejects this and holds that the Son is Son by nature, not a work. Every creature, however excellent, has a nature that comes to be and is created. The Son, by contrast, is proper to the Father.
sources.quote: For ye say that an offspring is the same as a work, writing ‘generated or made.’
sources.raw_question: Are 'offspring' and 'work' the same thing when applied to the Son of God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: He is not a creature or work but an offspring proper to the Father's essence. Scripture presents him as the very, natural and genuine Son, the only-begotten Wisdom and only Word of God, and therefore very God, one in essence with the Father.
sources.quote: Very Son of the Father, natural and genuine, proper to His essence, Wisdom Only-begotten, and Very and Only Word of God is He; not a creature or work, but an offspring proper to the Father’s essence.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God a creature or work, or an offspring proper to the Father's essence?

question: If God creates all things out of nothing through his Word, can the Word himself be among the things created out of nothing?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: No. If the Word were among the non-existent things that are called into being, another Word would be needed through whom he was called, and so on. Since God creates through him, the Word is the Creator's own Word and Wisdom. He is the proper offspring of the Father's essence and is in the Father.
sources.quote: But if He calls into existence things which existed not by His proper Word, then the Word is not in the number of things non-existing and called; or we have to seek another Word, through whom He too was called
sources.raw_question: If God creates things from nothing through his Word, can the Word himself be among the things made?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: No. If God calls non-existent things into being by His proper Word, the Word cannot be among the things called into being, or else one would need another Word through whom He was made. The one through whom God creates is not himself among things created, but is the Word of the Creator God, proper offspring of the Father's essence.
sources.quote: But if He calls into existence things which existed not by His proper Word, then the Word is not in the number of things non-existing and called; or we have to seek another Word, through whom He too was called
sources.raw_question: If God creates all things out of nothing through His Word, can the Word Himself be one of the things created out of nothing?

question: Is the Son merely an instrument that God created in order to make the world?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. Scripture deliberately does not say 'He created me to make works', lest the Son seem an instrument made for our sake, as the irreligious Arians claim. The Son is the Offspring of the Father, not a tool fashioned for creation.
sources.quote: nor, ‘He created Me to make works,’ lest, on the other hand, according to the perverseness of the irreligious, He should seem as an instrument made for our sake.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son merely an instrument created by God for the purpose of making the world?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections to the Foregoing Proof. Whether, in the generation of the Son, God made One that was already, or One that was not.
sources.answer: No. This Arian view makes the Maker weak, as if He lacked the power to make the universe by Himself. On this view He would need an external tool, like a carpenter who cannot work without adze and saw. It would also make the one who supplies the need superior to the one who needs it, which is irreligious.
sources.quote: You rather prove the weakness of the Maker, if He had not power of Himself to make the universe, but provided for Himself an instrument from without, as carpenter might do or shipwright
sources.raw_question: Did God need to create the Son out of nothing as an instrument through which to make the universe?

question: If the Son (the Word) were a creature, by what Word, Hand and Wisdom of God would he himself have been made?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: The question shows the Word cannot be a work. All things that came to be were made by the Hand and Wisdom of God, and Scripture says all things were made through the Word and consist in him. Therefore the Son is himself the Hand and Wisdom of God through whom works are made, not one of the works.
sources.quote: it is very plain that the Son cannot be a work, but He is the Hand of God and the Wisdom.
sources.raw_question: If the Word were a creature, by what Hand and Wisdom of God would he himself have been made?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: The question exposes an absurdity, so the Son is not a creature. All works were made through the Word and Wisdom of God. If the Son is that very Word and Wisdom through whom all things come to be, He cannot be among the works or things originate. He is the Offspring of the Father.
sources.quote: For if the Son be a creature, by what word then and by what wisdom was He made Himself? for all the works were made through the Word and the Wisdom
sources.raw_question: If the Son were a creature, by what Word and Wisdom would He himself have been made?

question: Is the Father whom Christ reveals the same God as the Creator proclaimed in the Old Testament, or a different, higher or lesser god as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVII.—There is but one Lord and one God, the Father and Creator of all things, who has loved us in Christ, given us commandments, and remitted our sins; whose Son and Word Christ proved Himself to be, when He forgave our sins.
sources.answer: He is the same Creator. The God to whom we were debtors, having transgressed His commandment, is the one Christ teaches us to address in prayer as Father; He is called Father in respect of love, Lord in respect of power, and Maker in respect of wisdom. An unknown Father who gives no commandment could not be the one against whom we sinned and who forgives our debts.
sources.quote: Now this being is the Creator (Demiurgus), who is, in respect of His love, the Father; but in respect of His power, He is Lord; and in respect of His wisdom, our Maker and Fashioner
sources.raw_question: Is the Father whom Christ reveals the same being as the Creator God of the Old Testament, or an unknown higher Father as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXV.—The fraud, pride, and tyrannical kingdom of Antichrist, as described by Daniel and Paul.
sources.answer: They are one and the same God. Christ confirmed Daniel's prophecy of the end when he spoke of the abomination of desolation "spoken of by Daniel the prophet." The angel Gabriel, who interpreted Daniel's visions, is the archangel of the Creator, and he also announced the incarnation of Christ to Mary. So one God sent the prophets, promised the Son, and called us into knowledge of himself. That God is the Father whom Christ made manifest.
sources.quote: that there is one and the same God the Father, who was declared by the prophets, but made manifest by Christ.
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who distinguished the Demiurge from the Father
sources.raw_question: Is the God proclaimed by the Old Testament prophets the same God as the Father whom Christ revealed, or is the Creator a different and lesser god?

question: Did the Son of God lose or give up His divine attributes by taking human flesh in the Incarnation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Although He condescended to take our flesh, He was not stripped of His own attributes. As the Only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth, He fully possesses His own divine attributes and is truly endowed with ours.
sources.quote: He, the Only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth, is fully possessed of His own attributes and truly endowed with ours
sources.raw_question: Did the Son lose His divine attributes by taking human flesh?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. Being invisible, bodiless and incomprehensible as Son of God, He took on as much matter and lowliness as was needed to come within our perception. This was a condescension to our weakness, not a surrender of His own attributes.
sources.quote: It was a condescension to our feebleness rather than a surrender of His own proper attributes.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God give up His divine attributes by taking a body in the Incarnation?

question: Does the orthodox doctrine of three divine Persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) amount to Tritheism, belief in three Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. Catholics do not hold three absolute, original, coordinate divinities as the Marcionites did. Nor do they separate the Persons as the Arians do, or hold a merely specific unity like that of two men. They acknowledge one God the Father, the head and fountain of all, with his coessential and coeternal Son and Spirit. The three are one in nature, knowledge, presence, operation and energy, distinct without division and united without confusion.
sources.quote: one head and fountain of all, the three divine Persons being one in nature, one in knowledge, in presence, in operation, and energy ; never separate, never asunder; distinct without division, united without confusion.
sources.raw_question: Is the Catholic doctrine of three divine Persons Tritheism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. Neither Scripture nor antiquity gives just ground for the charge; the early Church treated those who pressed it (Praxeas, Noetus, Sabellius, Paul of Samosata, Arius) as heretics. The charge was historically brought by Jews, pagans and heretics, while the primitive Catholic Church never thought the doctrine Tritheism and condemned those who did.
sources.quote: We have seen then that there is no just ground from Scripture or antiquity to charge our doctrine with Tritheism.
sources.raised_by_detail: Praxeas, Noetus, Sabellius, Paul of Samosata, Arius
sources.raw_question: Does the orthodox doctrine of three divine Persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) amount to Tritheism, belief in three Gods?

question: Does God give honourable names to weak or lowly things without the corresponding dignity, so that a name shared by the Father and the Son need not imply a shared nature or dignity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. God is called a God of truth and a righteous Lord, so He cannot give false names that pervert the truth of things. To invest weak things with empty honourable names would be deceit, and to grant the name while withholding the honour would be jealousy, and neither can belong to God. Scripture shows God naming things as they are, as when Christ calls the blessed "blessed" and the cursed "cursed."
sources.quote: But how can He be a God of truth Who gives false names to things, and Who perverts the truth in the meanings of their names? Again, He is called by him a righteous Lord
sources.raw_question: Does God give names to things that do not correspond to their true nature, bestowing honourable titles on weak things without the corresponding dignity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. God names and distinguishes His creatures as they truly are, by appropriate names that convey their real nature, not by names contrary to it. Scripture calls Noah righteous, Abraham faithful, Moses meek and Job blameless because they were so. It never gives honourable titles to the wicked or to the lowest creatures. Swapping names against their natural meaning is what drunkards and madmen do, and Isaiah pronounces woe on those who call darkness light. To credit God with such naming would make the God of truth a deceiver.
sources.quote: But God judges and distinguishes His creatures as they are in nature and truth, not by names contrary to them, but by such appropriate appellations as may give the clearest idea of their meaning.
sources.raw_question: Does God bestow honourable names on the weakest creatures without the corresponding dignity, and lowly names on superior beings without their inferiority, so that a shared name (such as one shared by the Father and the Son) need not imply a shared nature or dignity?

question: How can the true Holy Spirit, the Comforter, be distinguished from a false spirit claiming to be him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No. The work of the true Comforter is to glorify Christ, the one who sends him. A spirit that claims to be all and dismisses 'him that suffered at Jerusalem' is evidently false, whatever its pretence, because it does not glorify the Christ who spoke to the apostles.
sources.quote: This is not the Comforter. His work is to glorify Christ, — him that sends him. And this is an evident sign of a false spirit, whatever its pretence be, if it glorify not that Christ
sources.raised_by_detail: those claiming an inner spirit replaces the historical Christ
sources.raw_question: Can a spirit that sets itself up in place of the historical Christ be the true Holy Spirit, the Comforter?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: By his effects, which a false spirit contradicts. The Holy Ghost sheds abroad God's love in the heart and gives joy, peace, hope, and the boldness of children as a Spirit of adoption. He is also a Spirit of prayer. A spirit that brings bondage and terror, treats others with cruelty, and claims to lift men above prayer is therefore not the Comforter Christ promised.
sources.quote: There is scarce any one thing that more evidently manifesteth the spirit whereby some are now acted not to be the Comforter promised by Christ, than this, — that he is a spirit of bondage and slavery in them in whom he is
sources.raw_question: How can the true Holy Spirit, the Comforter, be distinguished from a false spirit claiming to be him?

question: Can a saving knowledge of God's nature and properties be obtained apart from Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. True wisdom consists mainly in knowing God, his nature and properties. That knowledge is wholly hidden in Christ, in whom the attributes are revealed, exercised, and made effectual for our salvation. So it cannot be obtained except through him.
sources.quote: our wisdom, consisting, in a main part of it, in the knowledge of God, his nature, and his properties, this lies wholly hid in Christ, nor can possibly be obtained but by him.
sources.raw_question: Can a saving knowledge of God's nature and properties be obtained apart from Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Knowledge of God's justice outside Christ only produces terror. Knowledge of his patience and goodness is despised and does not lead to repentance. Knowledge of his eternal power and Godhead from creation is held captive under unrighteousness and does not lead people to glorify him. Saving and comforting knowledge of God's attributes is laid up in Christ and manifested by him alone.
sources.quote: There is no saving knowledge of any property of God, nor such as brings consolation, but what alone is to be had in Christ Jesus, being laid up in him, and manifested by him.
sources.raw_question: Can any property of God be known savingly and with consolation apart from Christ?

question: What did the risen Christ mean by telling Mary 'Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father' (John 20:17), especially given that he invited the disciples to handle him before his ascension?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The One Death and Resurrection of The Body of Christ Harmonizes with Our Double Death and Resurrection of Body and Soul, to the Effect of Salvation. In What Way the Single Death of Christ is Bestowed Upon Our Double Death.
sources.answer: The two sayings signify different things. 'Touch me not' is a mystery of our inner resurrection: not to touch Christ until he has ascended means not to think of Christ after a fleshly manner. 'Handle me and see' gives a type of the resurrection of our outward body. It would be absurd to claim that men touched him before he ascended and women only after.
sources.quote: For not to touch Christ, unless when He had ascended to the Father, means not to have thoughts of Christ after a fleshly manner.
sources.raw_question: Why did the risen Christ tell Mary 'Touch me not, for I am not yet ascended to my Father' while inviting the disciples to handle him before his ascension?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > All are Sometimes Understood in One Person.
sources.answer: Touch, as it were, sets a limit to conception, and Christ did not want the thought of the heart directed toward Him to be confined to what He visibly seemed to be. His 'ascension to the Father' means His appearing as He is, equal to the Father, which is the sight that suffices us.
sources.quote: For touch, as it were, puts a limit to their conception, and He therefore would not have the thought of the heart, directed towards Himself, to be so limited as that He should be held to be only that which He seemed to be.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean by telling Mary 'Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father'?

question: In Augustine's trinity of the outer man, are the image retained in memory and the image formed in the mind's eye during recollection one thing or two?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > The Unity of the Three Takes Place in Thought, Viz. Of Memory, of Ternal Vision, and of Will Combining Both.
sources.answer: They are two, though they appear to be one. They seem single because they are exceedingly alike. Only the judgment of reason shows them to be distinct. The likeness in the memory remains even after the mind's eye turns away to something else, while the inner vision exists only as long as the mind looks at the memory.
sources.quote: yet it so seems to be one and single, that it can only be discovered to be two by the judgment of reason
sources.raw_question: Are the image retained in memory and the image formed in the mind's eye during recollection one thing or two?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Different Modes of Conceiving.
sources.answer: Yes, they are distinct. The memory can retain only as many bodily forms as were actually seen, and of the size and kind they were seen, whereas conception, though drawn from memory, can multiply and vary those forms without end. So one remembers a single round sun of a given size but can conceive two or many, larger or smaller, square or green. This shows that the remembered form and the vision of the one remembering are two terms, which the will joins as a third.
sources.quote: what the memory stores up and retains is a different thing from that which is thence copied in the conception of the man who remembers, although, when both are combined together, they appear to be one and the same
sources.raw_question: In Augustine's analogy of a trinity in the outer man, is the image stored in memory a different thing from the image formed in the mind's conception when we remember, even though the two seem to be one?

question: Was Christ subject to a special 'law of the mediator' distinct from the general law of God binding all people?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Yes. Besides the moral law, there was a peculiar law of the mediator which concerned Christ alone and contained duties not for our imitation. His laying down his life was obedience to this law, as he received the commandment from the Father to lay down his life and take it again.
sources.quote: There was a peculiar law of the mediator, which respected himself merely, and contained all those acts and duties of his which are not for our imitation.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ subject to a special 'law of the mediator' distinct from the general law of God given to all men?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Yes. Besides the laws common to us, there was a peculiar law of the mediator, containing duties not meant for our imitation, such as laying down his life and taking it again by the Father's commandment. Hence some things he did as a man under the law in general, like praying for his persecutors, and some as mediator, like praying for his elect only.
sources.quote: As mediator, he received this peculiar command of his Father, that he should lay down his life, and take it again; and he was obedient thereunto.
sources.raw_question: Was there a law peculiar to Christ as mediator, distinct from the law binding all people?

question: Is obedience properly ascribed to Jesus Christ in his work as mediator, even though he is the Son of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture ascribes obedience to Christ as mediator both in name and in substance: though he were a Son, he learned obedience, was obedient unto death, offered himself up, is called the Father's servant, and came to do the will of him that sent him. He did all this willingly and cheerfully in obedience to God.
sources.quote: That obedience is properly ascribed unto Jesus Christ as mediator, the Scripture is witness, both as to name and thing Heb. v. 8, “Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience,” etc.
sources.raw_question: Is obedience properly ascribed to Jesus Christ in his work as mediator, even though he is the Son of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture ascribes obedience to Christ as mediator both by name and in substance: though he were a Son, he learned obedience, and he was obedient unto death. He offered himself up and is called the Father's servant. He came to do the will of the one who sent him, and he did it willingly and cheerfully.
sources.quote: That obedience is properly ascribed unto Jesus Christ as mediator, the Scripture is witness, both as to name and thing Heb. v. 8, “Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience,” etc.
sources.raw_question: Is it proper to ascribe obedience to Christ as mediator, even though he is the Son?

question: Was Christ's active obedience to the law needed merely to make him a fit sacrifice for sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: No. Christ was already fully fit to be an offering through the hypostatic union and his habitual grace. Had he died earlier, there would still have been perfect innocence and holiness and infinite worth from the dignity of his person. So his long life of perfect obedience must have served some special purpose for our salvation, namely being reckoned to us.
sources.quote: he answered all types, and was every way ἱκανός (fit to be made an offering for sin), by his union and habitual grace.
sources.raw_question: Was the purpose of Christ's active obedience merely to make him fit to be an offering for sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: No. His habitual righteousness alone made him a fit sacrifice, so that had he suffered immediately after his incarnation he would have been a fit offering. Therefore his subsequent obedience must have another use beyond fitting him for oblation.
sources.quote: therefore, doubtless, his following obedience hath another use besides to fit him for an oblation, for which he was most fit without it.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's active obedience to the law needed merely to make him a fit sacrifice?

question: Did Christ perform his obedience to the law for himself or on behalf of believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: It was performed for believers, not for himself. Christ was made under the law, subject to its commands, not for his own sake but to redeem us so that we might receive adoption as sons. He himself testified that he sanctified, or dedicated, himself for their sakes, and from eternity he intended all he did to be for our acceptance with God.
sources.quote: He was made under the law; that is, in that condition that he was obnoxious to the will and commands of it. And why was this? to what end? for himself? No; but to redeem us is the aim of all that he did
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's active obedience to the law performed for his own benefit or for the benefit of believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: For believers, in their stead. Galatians 4:4-5 joins his being made of a woman and made under the law as both having the end of redeeming those under the law. Since he was not incarnate nor made under the law for himself, he did not yield obedience for himself; it was all for us.
sources.quote: If Christ were not incarnate nor made under the law for himself, he did not yield obedience for himself; it was all for us, for our good.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ perform his obedience to the law for himself or on behalf of believers?

question: Can the believer's own holiness or obedience serve as the cause, matter, condition, or ground of justification before God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. Holiness is neither the cause, the matter, nor the condition of justification. It is, however, the way God has appointed for believers to walk in to obtain salvation. None reach eternal life without walking in that way, for without holiness no one shall see God.
sources.quote: Though it be neither the cause, matter, nor condition of our justification, yet it is the way appointed of God for us to walk in for the obtaining of salvation.
sources.raw_question: Is holiness the cause, matter, or condition of a believer's justification before God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. Owen holds that the two have entirely different places and uses, and that making them do the same work would make them inconsistent. Christ's righteousness is imputed as the ground on which we are accepted and counted righteous, as truly as Adam would have been by perfect righteousness of his own. Our obedience pleases God but is not the righteousness on which we are justified. This is why those who make our obedience the cause of justification all deny the imputation of Christ's obedience.
sources.quote: The righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, as that on the account whereof we are accepted and esteemed righteous before God, and are really so, though not inherently.
sources.raw_question: Can Christ's imputed obedience and the believer's own obedience both serve as the ground on which a person is justified before God?

question: Is God's statement 'I will not give my glory to another' (Isaiah 42:8) compatible with the view that the Son is a second, subordinate God who shares divine glory?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 4: Whether, supposing the Scripture-notion of God to be no more than that of the Author and Governor of the universe, or whatever it be, the admitting of another t
sources.answer: No. God's peculiar glory is to be truly God and to be acknowledged as such to the exclusion of other Gods, not merely to be the supreme independent cause of all things. If another God and Governor of the universe existed, he would share God's glory, even if unequally. Reading the text as 'I will keep the greater share' would make it consistent with polytheism, since many pagans gave highest honour to a supreme God while admitting inferior deities as partners.
sources.quote: Now I thought it was his peculiar glory to be truly God, and to be acknowledged as such, exclusive of other Gods.
sources.raw_question: Is God's statement 'I will not give my glory to another' (Isaiah 42:8) compatible with admitting the Son as a second, inferior God who shares divine glory?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 4: Whether, supposing the Scripture-notion of God to be no more than that of the Author and Governor of the universe, or whatever it be, the admitting of another t
sources.answer: Yes. God's peculiar glory is to be truly God and acknowledged as such, exclusive of other Gods, not merely to be the one supreme independent cause. The jealous God of the Old Testament regards it as the highest indignity to admit partners and sharers with him, so a distinct inferior God sharing divine titles contradicts these texts.
sources.quote: Now I thought it was his peculiar glory to be truly God, and to be acknowledged as such, exclusive of other Gods.
sources.raw_question: Does God's statement in Isaiah that he will not give his glory to another create a difficulty for the view that the Son is a subordinate God?

question: When God begins in time to be called our Father through regeneration, does any change occur in God's substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said of God in Time, is Said Relatively, Not Accidentally.
sources.answer: No. Our substance is changed for the better when we become His sons. He begins at that point to be called our Father without any change in His own substance. What is newly said of God in time is said relatively, according to an accident of the creature and not of God.
sources.quote: Our substance therefore is changed for the better, when we become His sons; and He at the same time begins to be our Father, but without any change of His own substance.
sources.raw_question: When God begins to be our Father through regeneration, does His substance change?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said of God in Time, is Said Relatively, Not Accidentally.
sources.answer: No. When we are regenerated by grace and become sons of God, our substance is changed for the better, and God at the same time begins to be called our Father, but without any change of His own substance. The new title describes a new relation that arises from a change in us, not in Him.
sources.quote: Our substance therefore is changed for the better, when we become His sons; and He at the same time begins to be our Father, but without any change of His own substance.
sources.raw_question: When God begins in time to be called our Father through regeneration, does any change occur in God's substance?

question: If the Son's existence had a beginning in time like creatures, would he also have to have a middle and an end, making him mortal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. A beginning, in the created sense, necessarily brings with it what follows it: a midst and an end. Wisdom names beginning, midst and end together. So whoever gives the Son a temporal beginning must also, in effect, give him an end and set limits on the infinite Nature. This would make the Deity mortal, which is impious and absurd. Therefore the supposition of a beginning that leads to it must be rejected.
sources.quote: if we assume in the Nature of the Only-begotten, according to the heretical dogma, some beginning of existence defined by a certain mark of time, the book of Wisdom will by no means allow us to refrain from subjoining to the “beginning” a “midst” and an “end” also.
sources.raw_question: If the Son's existence had a beginning in time like creatures, would he also have to have a middle and an end, making him mortal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes, which shows the premise is absurd. Admitting one property of creation in the Divine essence forces one to attach the rest of the sequence, as confessing someone a man entails 'animal' and 'rational.' A beginning in this sense is the beginning of what follows it, so a temporal beginning of the Only-begotten would entail a middle and end.
sources.quote: if we should understand any of the properties of creation to be present in the Divine essence, it will no longer be open to us to refrain from attaching to that pure Nature the rest of the list of the attributes contemplated therein
sources.raw_question: If the Son's existence had a beginning like creation, would He also have to have a middle and an end?

question: When Scripture calls Moses, magistrates, angels, or idols "gods," does that show they are properly God, in a subordinate sense or by sharing some divine attribute such as dominion?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. They are called gods only by figure, because they resemble God in some particular, such as dominion, giving commands from above, or a sublime habitation. Moses was "a God unto Pharaoh" only as standing in God's place in that one respect. Otherwise we might as properly say "God David" as "King David."
sources.quote: If by the same figure of speech, by way of allusion and resemblance, any thing be called God, because resembling God in one or more particulars; we are not to conclude, that it is properly and truly God.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture calls Moses, magistrates, or angels "gods," does that make them properly God in a subordinate sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. Such beings are called gods only figuratively, by allusion to some imperfect resemblance to God in a particular respect, such as dominion, commanding from above, or receiving worship. To infer that any of them is properly God is to make the whole out of a part, reasoning fallaciously from what is said in a qualified sense to what is said absolutely (a dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter).
sources.quote: To argue from hence, that any of them is properly God, is making the whole of a part ; and reasoning fallaciously, a dicto secundum quid, as the schools speak, ad dictum simpliciter.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Scripture calls angels, magistrates, Moses, or idols "gods" show that a being can be properly God by sharing some divine attribute such as dominion?

question: When someone comes to love a person or thing known only by report or praise, does he love something unknown?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > No One at All Loves Things Unknown.
sources.answer: No. He pictures an imaginary form drawn from things he already knows and is stirred to love by that. If the real thing turns out unlike that picture, he begins to love it only once he learns it. If it turns out like the picture, he still did not love an unknown form, because he had known it in that likeness.
sources.quote: yet certainly not even then did he love a form he did not know, since he had known it in that likeness
sources.raw_question: When a person comes to love someone he has only heard praised, does he love something unknown?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Love of the Studious Mind, that Is, of One Desirous to Know, is Not the Love of a Thing Which It Does Not Know.
sources.answer: No. When a thing's reputation for beauty inflames desire, the mind already knows the genus of bodily beauty from frequent experience, so the object is not wholly unknown. When we love a good man whose face we never saw, we love him from knowledge of his virtues, which we know abstractly in the truth itself.
sources.quote: But when we love a good man whose face we never saw, we love him from the knowledge of his virtues, which virtues we know [abstractly] in the truth itself.
sources.raw_question: When someone comes to love a beautiful thing or a good person known only by report, does he love something wholly unknown?

question: Does Paul's assigning ministrations to 'the same Lord' and workings to 'the same God' in 1 Corinthians 12 show that Christ and God are not one and the same divine Being?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. The members who minister are the same members who work, and all of them make up the one body of Christ. Though God is said to have set them in the Church, Paul also says grace is given 'according to the measure of the gift of Christ.' Christ therefore ordains them too, and the unity is preserved.
sources.quote: Clearly these are the Church’s agents of ministry and work of whom the body of Christ consists; and God has ordained them.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's assigning ministrations to 'the Lord' and workings to 'God' mean he did not understand one and the same divine Being in both?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. The same members of Christ's body are both ministering and working members, and the gifts God ordained in the Church are elsewhere said to be given by Christ who ascended.
