So the gifts of ministration are Christ's while also being God's, showing one and the same Being in both ministrations and operations.
sources.quote: Are not then the gifts of ministration Christ’s, while they are also the gifts of God?
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's assigning ministrations to 'the same Lord' and workings to 'the same God' in 1 Corinthians 12 show that the Lord (Christ) and God are not one in nature?

question: Are Christ's divine works and his human acts and sufferings done by one and the same subject, the Word, or by two different agents?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: Yes. When the flesh suffered, the Word was not external to it, and when he did the Father's works, he did them in the body itself. He stretched out his hand humanly but stopped Peter's mother-in-law's fever divinely. He used human spittle but opened the blind man's eyes divinely. He called Lazarus with a human voice but raised him as God.
sources.quote: in the case of Lazarus, He gave forth a human voice as man; but divinely, as God, did He raise Lazarus from the dead
sources.raw_question: Did Christ perform divine works and human acts as one and the same agent?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: By one. When he acts divinely through the instrument of his body, he does so as God. When he speaks or suffers humanly, it is because he bore flesh and became man. Right faith recognises what is proper to each nature while confessing that both are done by the one Word.
sources.quote: For if we recognise what is proper to each, and see and understand that both these things and those are done by One, we are right in our faith, and shall never stray.
sources.raw_question: Are Christ's divine works and his human acts and sufferings done by two different subjects, or by one?

question: Does the Son's knowing the Father imply that he also knows the day and hour of the end?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes. The same Son who is said not to know the day is said to know the Father, since 'no one knows the Father save the Son.' Whoever knows the Father knows the whole creation all the more, and its end with it. Also, whatever the Father determines is determined through the Son.
sources.quote: For that Son whom He declares not to know the day, Him He declares to know the Father; for ‘No one,’ He says, ‘knoweth the Father save the Son.’
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's knowing the Father imply that He knows the day of the end?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes. The same Son said to be ignorant of the day is declared to know the Father, since no one knows the Father save the Son. He who knows the Father must much more know the whole creation and its end. Otherwise knowledge of the lower creation would be greater than knowledge of the Father, which is absurd.
sources.quote: He who knows the Father, much more knows the whole of the creation; and in that whole, its end.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's knowing the Father imply that he also knows the day and hour of the end?

question: Why did Christ in Mark 13:32 say that the angels and the Son do not know the day, without mentioning the Holy Spirit, and what does this silence show about the Son's knowledge?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Spirit knows the day, the Word, from whom the Spirit receives, must know it all the more. His silence about the Spirit also makes clear that 'not the Son' refers to His human ministry.
sources.quote: first that if the Spirit knew, much more must the Word know, considered as the Word, from whom the Spirit receives
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's silence about the Holy Spirit in Mark 13:32 show that the Son knows the day as the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: His silence about the Spirit was a double intimation. First, if the Spirit knows the day, much more must the Word know it, since the Spirit receives from the Word. Second, by omitting the Spirit He made clear that 'not the Son' referred to His human ministry, not His Godhead.
sources.quote: first that if the Spirit knew, much more must the Word know, considered as the Word, from whom the Spirit receives; and next by His silence about the Spirit, He made it clear, that He said of His human ministry, ‘no, not the Son.’
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ in Mark 13:32 mention the angels and the Son as not knowing the day, but not mention the Holy Spirit?

question: If the ages are generate (created), does it follow that God can no longer be called ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory treats the dilemma as absurd: the existence of something generate does not abolish the Divine ungeneracy. He also turns it against Eunomius, noting that if God's ungeneracy depended on the ages, Eunomius's own distinctions between generacy and ungeneracy would collapse.
sources.quote: If, O Eunomius, something is held to be generate, we no longer hold the doctrine of the Divine ungeneracy! And pray what has become of your subtle distinctions between generacy and ungeneracy
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that the ages were created (generate) force us to deny that God is ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. It is absurd to suppose that something else being generate removes God's ungeneracy. The argument also turns against Eunomius' own system. On his reasoning the Father would not be dissimilar in essence in respect of generacy, and holding His ungeneracy would reduce Him to non-existence.
sources.quote: If, O Eunomius, something is held to be generate, we no longer hold the doctrine of the Divine ungeneracy!
sources.raw_question: If the ages are generate (created), does it follow that God can no longer be called ungenerate?

question: Is God ungenerate (and whatever else He is) by His own nature, rather than by comparison with the ages or relation to created things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory denies that anyone in his party says ungeneracy is gained by God through comparison with something else. When they speak of God's life as extending beyond the ages, they do not make the ages the source of his being without beginning. Eunomius's argument therefore attacks a position no one holds.
sources.quote: Who is there that says that to Him Who hath no beginning ungeneracy is added as an acquisition through comparison with something else? Neither such a word nor such a sense will be found in any writings of ours.
sources.raw_question: Is God's ungeneracy an attribute added to him by comparing him with the ages?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, and no one disputes it. Whatever God is, He is in His own nature, not by comparison with the ages or any other existing thing. Even if neither ages nor any creature had been made, God would be no less what we believe Him to be, needing nothing created to constitute Him. Eunomius' claim therefore proves nothing peculiar for his position.
sources.quote: so that supposing neither ages, nor any other created thing, had been made, God would no less be what we believe Him to be, being in no need of the ages to constitute Him what He is.
sources.raw_question: Is God ungenerate, just, almighty and Father by His nature rather than by contrast with the ages or relation to created things?

question: Do the many titles of Christ (Bread, Light, Way, etc.) signify the Son's essence, or are they names formed by human conception from his various operations?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They are formed by conception from His operations, not indicative of His essence. As corn is one in substance yet called seed, fruit, and food according to its various properties, so the Lord is in Himself what He essentially is, but takes different names according to each notion produced in us by His operations. Many appellations can thus properly attach to the one Son of God, who is one in respect of the underlying force.
sources.quote: our Lord is in respect to Himself what He is essentially, but when named according to the differences of His operations, He has not one appellation in all cases, but takes a different name according to each notion produced in us from the operation
sources.raw_question: Do the many titles of Christ (Bread, Light, Way, etc.) signify the Son's essence, or are they names formed by human conception from his various operations?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The question is not who ascribed the names but what they mean, whether they denote essence or derive from operations by conception. If Eunomius grants they are names, it does no harm to the doctrine of conception that the Lord gave them to Himself, just as asking who named Isaac does not answer what the name 'Isaac' means.
sources.quote: For the question was not, who ascribed them, but about the meaning of the names, whether they denote essence, or whether they are derived from His operations by the process of conception.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Christ applied titles such as Bread or Light to Himself prove that those names are not products of human conception?

question: Can the human mind have an eternal or perpetual inner word, as God has an eternal Word, given that it always knows certain things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Great is the Unlikeness Between Our Word and the Divine Word. Our Word Cannot Be or Be Called Eternal.
sources.answer: No. Although the soul always lives and always knows that it lives, it is not always thinking of its life or of that knowledge. Since our true inner word is spoken only in actual thought, and thought is not eternal, God alone can be understood to have a Word that is eternal and co-eternal with Himself.
sources.quote: if there can be in the mind any knowledge that is eternal, while the thought of that knowledge cannot be eternal, and any inner and true word of ours is only said by our thought, then God alone can be understood to have a Word that is eternal, and co-eternal with Himself.
sources.raw_question: Can a human mind have an eternal inner word, even about things it always knows, such as that it is alive?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Great is the Unlikeness Between Our Word and the Divine Word. Our Word Cannot Be or Be Called Eternal.
sources.answer: No. A word is formed in the vision of thought and takes the full likeness of the knowledge it is born from. A merely formable, not-yet-formed something in the mind lacks that form. Calling it a word only because it could become one is like naming a thing by what it may later be.
sources.quote: But how is that a word which is not yet formed in the vision of the thought? How will it be like the knowledge of which it is born, if it has not the form of that knowledge, and is only now called a word because it can have it?
sources.raw_question: Can the mind's mere capacity to think what it knows count as a perpetual word, making the human word as eternal as its knowledge?

question: Do the prophets, apostles, or Christ ever give the name God or Lord to any being other than the one true God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VII.—Reply to an objection founded on the words of St. Paul (2 Cor. iv. 4). St. Paul occasionally uses words not in their grammatical sequence.
sources.answer: No. Once the misreading of 2 Corinthians 4:4 is removed, it is clear that neither the prophets nor the apostles ever named another God or called another Lord except the true and only God. Even Moses, though given as a god before Pharaoh, is not properly called Lord or God by the prophets, but is called God's faithful servant.
sources.quote: it is clearly proved that neither the prophets nor the apostles did ever name another God, or call [him] Lord, except the true and only God.
sources.raw_question: Do the prophets and apostles ever give the name God or Lord to any being other than the one true God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VIII.—Answer to an objection, arising from the words of Christ (Matt. vi. 24). God alone is to be really called God and Lord, for He is without beginning and end.
sources.answer: No. Neither the prophets nor the apostles named another God or called any other Lord, and the Lord himself still less, as when he distinguished Caesar as Caesar from God as God. Apparent counter-examples, such as "two masters" or "the god of this world," are rightly read so that the title is not given to another.
sources.quote: neither the prophets nor the apostles did ever name another God, or call [him] Lord, except the true and only God.
sources.raw_question: Do the prophets, apostles, or Christ ever give the title God or Lord to anyone other than the one true God?

question: When Christ says in John 14:10 that he speaks 'not of Myself,' does he deny that he is a distinct Person, his Sonship, or his possession of the Divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The pronoun 'I' shows that he speaks as a real subject who exists and abides in the Divine substance. Saying 'not of Myself' points to his birth as God from God the Father. So the saying affirms both that he is a distinct Person and that he is one in nature with the Father who dwells in him.
sources.quote: When He says, The words that I speak unto you I speak not of Myself, He neither suppresses His personality, nor denies His Sonship, nor conceals the presence in Himself of His Father’s Divine nature.
sources.raw_question: When Christ says 'The words that I speak unto you I speak not of Myself,' does he deny that he is a distinct Person or deny his own Sonship?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. In saying 'I' he shows that he exists and speaks as abiding in the Divine substance, and in speaking 'not of Myself' he bears witness to his birth from God the Father. So the words show both that there is not one Person only, since he does not speak of himself, and that Father and Son are not divided, since the One speaks through the voice of the Other.
sources.quote: There cannot be one Person only, for He speaks not of Himself; and, conversely, They cannot be separate and divided when the One speaks through the voice of the Other.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement in John 14:10 that he speaks 'not of Myself' deny that the Son is a distinct Person or that he possesses the Divine nature?

question: On what basis does Christ the Son possess and dispense the fulness of grace to believers, and what is the Father's role in it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: It pleased the Father that all fulness should dwell in him. The dispensation of that fulness is committed to him as the reward of his obedience and sacrificial death. With this fulness he also received authority to communicate it, as from a purchased treasury.
sources.quote: And upon what account he hath the dispensation of that fulness to him committed you may see, Phil. ii. 8–11.
sources.raw_question: On what basis does Christ the Son hold and dispense the fulness of grace to believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: The Father, by covenant with the Son, invests him with all the grace he purchased, so that all fulness dwells in him. This includes both the ability and the right to give eternal life to the elect. He holds it as head (having the Spirit without measure), as a common person entrusted on our behalf, and in a legal sense because his mediation founds the dispensation of grace.
sources.quote: The Father actually invests him with all the grace whereof, by compact and agreement, he hath made a purchase (as he received the promise of the Spirit)
sources.raw_question: How does Christ come to possess the fulness of grace he gives to believers, and what is the Father's role in it?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be placed in an intermediate rank that is neither servant nor master but simply 'free'?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: No. This view wrongly applies to God's ineffable nature the shifting degrees of rank found in human life. Among men no one is a slave by nature: men become slaves through conquest, poverty or a father's disposition. So such human categories cannot settle the Spirit's rank.
sources.quote: endeavour to apply to the ineffable nature of God that common custom of human life whereby the difference of degrees is variable, not perceiving that among men no one is a slave by nature
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit neither servant nor master but simply 'free', in an intermediate rank?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who maintain that the Spirit is in the rank neither of a servant nor of a master, but in that of the free.
sources.answer: No. Among all existent beings there is no nature that neither rules nor is ruled; every creature serves God, while whatever is above creation shares in God's royalty. Hence if the Spirit is a creature he serves with all the rest, and if he is above creation he reigns with God; there is no third 'free' middle category, and to conceive the Spirit so is blasphemy.
sources.quote: Among all existent beings no such nature is to be found. To entertain such a conception of the Spirit is obvious blasphemy. If He is a creature of course He serves with all the rest, for “all things,” it is said “are thy servants,”
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be placed in an intermediate rank that is neither servant nor master but simply 'free'?

question: Was Jesus Christ a mere man begotten by Joseph, or the incarnate Word of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: No. He is Emmanuel, born of the Virgin, the Word of God made man. Those who hold him to be a mere man remain in the bondage of the old disobedience, because they are not joined to the Word. The Word became the Son of man so that man, taken into the Word, might become a son of God and attain incorruptibility.
sources.quote: For it was for this end that the Word of God was made man, and He who was the Son of God became the Son of man, that man, having been taken into the Word, and receiving the adoption, might become the son of God.
sources.raised_by_detail: Ebionites (those who say He was a mere man begotten by Joseph)
sources.raw_question: Was Christ a mere man begotten by Joseph, rather than the incarnate Word of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XIX.—Jesus Christ was not a mere man, begotten from Joseph in the ordinary course of nature, but was very God, begotten of the Father most high, and very man, born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: No. Those who hold this remain in the bondage of the old disobedience and in death, not joined to the Word of God nor receiving liberty through the Son. Scripture calls him, in his own right beyond all men, God, Lord, King Eternal and the Incarnate Word, which it would not do if he were a mere man like others.
sources.quote: Now, the Scriptures would not have testified these things of Him, if, like others, He had been a mere man.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who assert He was a mere man begotten by Joseph (Ebionites)
sources.raw_question: Was Jesus Christ a mere man begotten by Joseph in the ordinary course of nature?

question: Does the Son's existing by reason of the Father mean that he does not appropriate being, or the title 'the Existent', treated as a dignity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. No one in ordinary usage has ever called being a dignity: whatever subsists is said to "be," and "being" is formed from "be." Even granting the term, to say the Son does not appropriate being means He is alien from being. What is alien from being is nonexistent, so Eunomius' claim implies the absurdity that the Son does not exist.
sources.quote: He therefore Who does not “appropriate” being is obviously alien from being: and He Who is alien from being is nonexistent.
sources.raw_question: Is "being" rightly called a "dignity" that the Son does not appropriate because he exists by reason of the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. Eunomius treats being as a mere "dignity" and argues that because the Father's essence is supreme over the Son, it draws the idea of the Existent away from the Son. Gregory finds this absurd. It is like saying that a man bought with money does not exist in himself but only in his purchaser, as though his personal existence were swallowed up by his owner. To deny the Son the title "Existent" amounts to saying that God the Word does not exist, and Gregory says this deserves tears rather than refutation.
sources.quote: This is much the same as if one were to say that he who is bought for money, in so far as he is in his own existence, is not the person bought, but the purchaser
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being from the Father ("by reason of the Father") mean that the Son does not possess the dignity or title of "the Existent"?

question: Does the Holy Spirit possess everything that belongs to God the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIX. Having proved above that the Spirit abides and speaks in the prophets, St. Ambrose infers that He knows all things which are of God, and therefore is One with the Father and the Son. This same point he establishes again from the fact that He possesses all that God possesses, namely, Godhead, knowledge of the heart, truth, a Name above every name, and power to raise the dead, as is proved from Ezekiel, and in this He is equal to the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son has all things that the Father has, as He said: "All things which the Father hath are Mine." Therefore the Spirit, who has what Christ has, has what God has.
sources.quote: So, then, the Spirit has that which Christ has, and therefore what God has, for all things which the Father has the Son also has
sources.raw_question: Does having what Christ has mean that the Holy Spirit has everything that God the Father has?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is named with the Father and the Son in baptism and is invoked in the oblations. He is proclaimed with them by the Seraphim and dwells with them in the saints. He inspires the prophets, so that Scripture is called God-inspired because God inspires what the Spirit has spoken. Those who deny this are challenged to say what He lacks or cannot do.
sources.quote: How, then, does He not possess all that pertains to God, Who is named by priests in baptism with the Father and the Son, and is invoked in the oblations
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who deny the Spirit's divinity
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit possess everything that belongs to God?

question: Does the phrase 'of which' or 'of whom' in Scripture always indicate the material out of which something is made?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > The systematic discussion of syllables is derived from heathen philosophy.
sources.answer: No. Scripture does sometimes use 'of which' for material, for example the ark of incorruptible wood or the man of the earth. More characteristically, however, it uses the phrase of the Supreme Cause, as in 'One God, of whom are all things.' So the phrase cannot be fixed to a single meaning in order to establish a difference of nature.
sources.quote: the phrase “of which” does not always and absolutely, as they suppose, indicate the material, but it is more in accordance with the usage of Scripture to apply this term in the case of the Supreme Cause
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'of which' or 'of whom' in Scripture always indicate the material out of which something is made?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That there is no distinction in the scriptural use of these syllables.
sources.answer: No. Scripture more usually applies 'of whom' to the Supreme Cause, as in 'One God, of whom are all things' and 'All things of God.' It does sometimes use the phrase for material, as with the ark made of wood or the man formed of clay. So the phrase does not have one fixed meaning.
sources.quote: the phrase “of which” does not always and absolutely, as they suppose, indicate the material, but it is more in accordance with the usage of Scripture to apply this term in the case of the Supreme Cause
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'of which' (or 'of whom') in Scripture always indicate the material out of which something is made?

question: If beings are generated from God and share his substance, must they all share his impassibility, or can some be passible while he remains impassible?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus argues that if the generated beings are like their Author in substance, they must remain impassible forever as he is. If instead they are of a different, passible substance, there is no explaining where such a dissimilar substance came from within the incorruptible Pleroma. So one cannot hold both that the emanations are consubstantial with an impassible Father and that one of them suffers passion.
sources.quote: Now, if the beings generated by the Father be similar to their Author, then those who have been produced must remain for ever impassible, even as is He who produced them
sources.raw_question: If beings are generated by a Father and share his substance, must they also share his impassibility?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: No. Whatever is produced from the same source and is of the same substance must share the same nature, so either all are passible along with their producer or all remain impassible forever. Irenaeus uses this against the Valentinians: if the Æons came forth like rays from the sun, the passion of the youngest Æon would either be impossible or would implicate the Father himself.
sources.quote: since all are of the same substance and sprung from the same source, all must either be capable of passion along with Him who produced them, or all will remain impassible for ever.
sources.raw_question: If beings are produced from God and share the same substance with him, can some of them be passible while others remain impassible?

question: Is the Son Son of God by nature, or by grace and participation as others are sons of God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: A son by nature is a real offspring from the essence of the parent, as Isaac was to Abraham or radiance to the sun. Sons by virtue and grace have only an acquired grace in place of nature and are something other than the gift itself. Because of this, they can lose the Spirit and be disinherited when they change, and be restored on repentance. The true Son cannot be such a son by grace.
sources.quote: For what is from another by nature, is a real offspring, as Isaac was to Abraham, and Joseph to Jacob, and the radiance to the sun; but the so called sons from virtue and grace, have but in place of nature a grace by acquisition
sources.raw_question: What is the difference between being a son of God by nature and being a son of God by grace or participation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: He is these by nature and according to essence. He alone is very Son and very God from very God, not receiving these prerogatives as a reward for virtue. He is Offspring of the Father's essence, and so, like the unalterable Father, the Word is also unalterable.
sources.quote: not receiving these prerogatives as a reward for His virtue, nor being another beside them, but being all these by nature and according to essence
sources.raw_question: Is the Son Son and God by nature, or by participation and as a reward for virtue?

question: What authority does the consensus of the Church Fathers have in interpreting Scripture on the Trinity: is it infallible, or does it still carry weight?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 28: Whether it be at all probable, that the primitive Church should mistake in so material a point as this is; or that the whole stream of Christian writers should
sources.answer: No. Waterland denies that the Church after the Apostles was infallible; all the Fathers together are worth less than any one inspired writer. Still, he holds that the concurring judgment of antiquity is the safest comment on Scripture. It should not be rejected wherever the words of Scripture can properly bear that sense.
sources.quote: we believe the concurring judgment of antiquity to be, though not infallible, yet the safest comment upon Scripture
sources.raw_question: Does appealing to the Fathers' consensus on the Trinity mean treating their interpretation of Scripture as infallible as Scripture itself?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: Yes. It does not by itself determine an article of faith, but it is a strong presumptive proof that the opposing interpretation of Scripture is wrong. It is so strong that perhaps only clear and evident demonstration should overrule it. Modern interpreters are fallible men with the same human reason, far removed from the age of inspiration, and so are at least as likely to err as the ancient universal Church.
sources.quote: No; but it is a strong presumptive proof, that his interpretation of Scripture is not the true one: a proof so considerable, that I know not whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration ought to overrule it.
sources.raw_question: If the Fathers' authority cannot determine an article of faith, does their unanimous agreement against an interpretation of Scripture on the Trinity carry any weight?

question: Are the mind, its knowledge of itself, and its love of itself of one and the same essence (and equal to one another)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: Because the mind loves itself and knows itself. These three so exist that the mind is neither loved nor known by any other thing. Since nothing outside the mind supplies the knowing or the loving, the three must be of the same essence.
sources.quote: since the mind itself loves itself, and itself knows itself; and these three so exist, as that the mind is neither loved nor known by any other thing at all. These three, therefore, must needs be of one and the same essence
sources.raw_question: Why must the mind, its knowledge, and its love be of one and the same essence?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three Things Which are Found in Love Must Be Considered.
sources.answer: Yes. When the mind wills itself to be just as much as it is, the will is on a par with the mind and the love equals the lover. Love and mind are both spirit, not body, yet they are not two spirits or two essences but one spirit and one essence.
sources.quote: Yet love and mind are not two spirits, but one spirit; nor yet two essences, but one: and yet here are two things that are one, he that loves and love
sources.raw_question: Is the mind's love of itself equal to the mind, and of one essence with it?

question: Is God properly called a 'substance' (a subject in which qualities inhere), or is He more fittingly called an 'essence'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > In God, Substance is Spoken Improperly, Essence Properly.
sources.answer: No. 'Substance' properly names a subject in which accidents such as color or shape exist, which can be lost without the thing ceasing to be. If God were a substance in that sense, something would be in Him as in a subject and He would not be simple. So God is called substance only improperly.
sources.quote: If, I say, God subsists so that He can be properly called a substance, then there is something in Him as it were in a subject, and He is not simple
sources.raw_question: Can God be properly called a 'substance' in the sense of a subject in which qualities inhere?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > God the Only Unchangeable Essence.
sources.answer: Yes. God is without doubt a substance, or better an essence, since essence is named from being, as wisdom from being wise. And none is more truly than He who said to Moses, "I am that I am" and "He who is hath sent me unto you."
sources.quote: He is, however, without doubt, a substance, or, if it be better so to call it, an essence, which the Greeks call οὐσία. For as wisdom is so called from the being wise, and knowledge from knowing; so from being comes that which we call essence.
sources.raw_question: Is God rightly called a substance or essence (ousia)?

question: Does the phrase 'He created me for the works' (Proverbs 8:22) refer to the Son's coming into being, or to something that happened to one who already existed?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: Yes, if 'created' referred to His essence, He would be later than the works, which already existed for His sake; this contradicts that He is before all things and that all things were made through Him and consist in Him. Therefore 'He created' must refer to something later than Himself, namely His taking flesh.
sources.quote: unless ‘He created’ relates to something later than Himself, He will seem later than the works, finding them on His creation already in existence before Him, for the sake of which He is also brought into being.
sources.raw_question: If the Son was created 'for the works,' would that make Him later than the works He is created for, contradicting His being before all things?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: Creatures are made first so that they may exist, and only afterwards do they receive a task. Adam was made a man before he was commanded to work, Noah before the ark, and Moses before he governed the people. Since the Word is said to be created for a purpose, the text describes a commission given to one who already existed. 'In the beginning was the Word,' and he was afterwards sent for the works.
sources.quote: For Adam was created, not that He might work, but that first he might be man; for it was after this that he received the command to work.
sources.raw_question: Why does the phrase 'for the works' show that the Son's 'creation' is not his coming into being, when ordinary creatures are first made simply to exist?

question: Does the use of the preposition 'through' (dia) for the Son's role in creation show that the Son is only an instrumental and not an efficient cause of creation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. The preposition dia with a genitive is frequently used in Scripture and church writers for the efficient cause, as much as hypo or ek, so the argument from prepositions is trifling, as Basil showed against Aetius. In Romans 11:36 'through him' is said of God; if this is the Father, the argument would make the Father merely instrumental too, and if it is understood of several Persons, it proves a Trinity in Unity.
sources.quote: The preposition διὰ, with a genitive after it, is frequently used, as well in Seripture, as in ecclesiastical writers, to express the efficient cause, as much as ὑπὸ, or ἐκ, or πρὸς, or any other.
sources.raw_question: Does the use of the preposition 'through' (dia) for the Son's role in creation prove that the Son is only an instrumental and not an efficient cause of creation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. A ministering cause is not opposed to an efficient one, and dia with the genitive is frequently used in Scripture and church writers for the efficient cause. Basil exposed this argument of Aetius long ago, and Romans 11:36 uses 'through him' of God, so the argument would make the Father merely instrumental too, or else the text proves a Trinity.
sources.quote: The preposition διὰ, with a genitive after it, is frequently used, as well in Seripture, as in ecclesiastical writers, to express the efficient cause, as much as ὑπὸ, or ἐκ, or πρὸς, or any other.
sources.raw_question: Does the distinction between 'through him' (dia) and 'by him' (hypo) show that the Son is only an instrumental, not an efficient, cause of creation?

question: Is the God whom the apostles proclaimed the same God as the Creator of heaven and earth who gave the law to Moses and was announced by the prophets?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter I.—The apostles did not commence to preach the Gospel, or to place anything on record until they were endowed with the gifts and power of the Holy Spirit. They preached one God alone, Maker of heaven and earth.
sources.answer: Yes. All the Gospel writers and apostles declared one God, Creator of heaven and earth, announced by the law and the prophets. They also declared one Christ, the Son of God. There is therefore no separate higher God distinct from the Creator, and no division of Christ.
sources.quote: These have all declared to us that there is one God, Creator of heaven and earth, announced by the law and the prophets; and one Christ the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the God whom the apostles and Gospels proclaimed the same God as the Creator of heaven and earth announced by the law and the prophets, with one Christ as his Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XV.—Refutation of the Ebionites, who disparaged the authority of St. Paul, from the writings of St. Luke, which must be received as a whole. Exposure of the hypocrisy, deceit, and pride of the Gnostics. The apostles and their disciples knew and preached one God, the Creator of the world.
sources.answer: Yes. The apostles confessed as Lord God the very Creator of heaven and earth, who spoke with Moses, gave him the law and called the patriarchs. They knew no other God. This refutes the Gnostic claim that the Creator is an inferior being distinct from the highest God.
sources.quote: they (the apostles) confessed as the Lord God Him who was the Creator of heaven and earth, who also spoke with Moses, gave to him the dispensation of the law, and who called the fathers; and that they knew no other.
sources.raw_question: Is the God the apostles confessed the same as the Creator of heaven and earth who spoke with Moses and gave the law?

question: Do Christ's weeping, hunger and thirst show that he was subject to all the weaknesses and affections of human nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The one who wept also raised the dead, the one who thirsted gave rivers of living water, and the one who hungered withered the fig tree by his word, so his nature could not be overcome by these needs. His weeping was not for himself, and his thirst and hunger needed no water or food. He conformed to bodily habits to prove the reality of his body, as a concession to our customs and not to his own necessity.
sources.quote: He conformed to the habits of the body to prove the reality of His own body, to satisfy the custom of human bodies by doing as our nature does. When He ate and drank, it was a concession, not to His own necessities, but to our habits.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's weeping, hunger and thirst show that he was subject to all the weaknesses and affections of human nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The One who wept raised the dead, the One who thirsted gave rivers of living water, and the One who hungered could wither a tree by His word. He took on these customs of the body to prove that His body was real, as a concession to human habits and not out of need.
sources.quote: He conformed to the habits of the body to prove the reality of His own body, to satisfy the custom of human bodies by doing as our nature does.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's weeping, hunger and thirst prove that He was subject to all the weaknesses and affections of human nature?

question: Is the Apostle Paul inconsistent when he speaks of Christ sometimes in exalted divine terms and sometimes in lowly human terms?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: No. Paul's argument is directed to one aim: he proclaims the union of the Human with the Divine while discerning in each its proper nature. The human weakness is changed for the better by communion with the imperishable, while the Divine power is not abased by contact with the lowly nature. So he calls Christ both "man" and "God" and "mediator," so that the suffering of the Cross is not attributed to the imperishable nature.
sources.quote: while he everywhere proclaims the combination of the Human with the Divine, he none the less discerns in each its proper nature
sources.raw_question: Is the Apostle Paul inconsistent when he speaks of Christ sometimes in lowly human terms and sometimes as divine?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: No. Paul's argument is directed to one aim: he proclaims the combination of the Human with the Divine while discerning in each its proper nature. He applies exalted names to the divine nature and lowly names to the human nature, so his opposing statements are not false but adapt to each nature the terms that belong to it.
sources.quote: let no one think that the divine Apostle is divided against himself in contradiction, and affords by his own utterances matter for their contentions on either side to those who dispute upon the doctrines
sources.raw_question: Does Paul contradict himself when he speaks of Christ sometimes in exalted divine terms and sometimes in lowly human terms?

question: Is the God who tells Abraham he has blessed Ishmael the same Person as the Angel of the Lord who promised Hagar to multiply Ishmael?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. Both speak of Ishmael, and both promise to multiply him. In addressing Abraham, the Speaker says "I have blessed him," which repeats the blessing already given to Hagar. That attests that it is the same Speaker. So God and the Angel of God are one, and the Angel of God is God the Son of God.
sources.quote: Thus God and the Angel of God are One; He Who is the Angel of God is also God the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the God who spoke to Abraham about Ishmael the same Person as the Angel of the Lord who spoke to Hagar?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. When God says to Abraham, 'I have blessed him,' there is no change from the Person indicated before; He shows that He Himself had already given the blessing. Scripture proceeds consistently from mystery to clear revelation, beginning with the Angel of God and revealing that it was God Himself who spoke.
sources.quote: This is no change from the Person indicated before; He shews that it was He Who had already given the blessing.
sources.raw_question: Is the God who tells Abraham he has blessed Ishmael the same Person as the Angel who earlier promised Hagar to multiply Ishmael?

question: What does Christ mean by 'My doctrine is not mine, but His that sent me', and does it imply that the Son is inferior to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > That Some Ways of Speaking Concerning the Son are to Be Understood According to Either Rule.
sources.answer: No. It can be read of the form of a servant, or of the form of God, in which it signifies only that the Son is from the Father. In the form of God the Son is himself the doctrine, so the saying means "I am not from myself, but from Him who sent me." It thus expresses origin, not inequality.
sources.quote: it is so to be understood as if it were, I am not from myself, but from Him who sent me
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "My doctrine is not mine, but His that sent me" imply that the Son is inferior to the Father in his divine nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: He calls it his own in one relation and not his own in another. According to the form of God it is his own; according to the form of a servant it is not. The phrase also sends us back to the Word itself, since the doctrine of the Father is the Word of the Father, the only Son.
sources.quote: According to the form of God, His own; according to the form of a servant, not His own.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ call his doctrine both his own and not his own in "My doctrine is not mine, but His that sent me"?

question: Since God is a Trinity, should God be called 'triple' or 'threefold'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > No Addition Can Be Made to the Nature of God.
sources.answer: No. God is a Trinity rather than triple. 'Triple' would imply that the three together are greater than each alone, as happens with things that grow by addition. But each Person is perfect and the three together are perfect, so nothing is added by their union.
sources.quote: But whether it be the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, He is perfect, and God the Father the Son and the Holy Spirit is perfect; and therefore He is a Trinity rather than triple.
sources.raw_question: Should God be called 'triple' or 'threefold' rather than a Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > God is a Trinity, But Not Triple (Triplex).
sources.answer: No. If God were triple, the Father alone or the Son alone would be less than the Father and Son together. But each Person alone is as great as the three together, because the divine perfection cannot be increased by addition, unlike bodies, which grow by union. So God is a Trinity but not threefold.
sources.quote: Neither, since He is a Trinity, is He therefore to be thought triple (triplex) otherwise the Father alone, or the Son alone, will be less than the Father and Son together.
sources.raw_question: Since God is a Trinity, should God be called triple (triplex), as though composed of three parts?

question: How can the Son, who gives and sends the Holy Spirit as his own, be said to be anointed with the Spirit or to act through the Spirit?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: It is not the Word as Word who is anointed, but the flesh he assumed, which is anointed in him and by him. The Lord says the Spirit is his, takes of what is his, and is sent by him. So the Word gives the Spirit as God and receives it only as man, so that the sanctification given to him as man may pass from him to all men.
sources.quote: it is not the Word, considered as the Word and Wisdom, who is anointed with the Spirit which He Himself gives, but the flesh assumed by Him which is anointed in Him and by Him
sources.raw_question: How can the Word be anointed with the Holy Spirit when the Spirit is his own and he is the one who sends the Spirit?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: He says this in respect of His manhood, not His Godhead. Just as He said He cast out demons by the Spirit of God because human nature is not equal to that by itself, so He said 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me' because He had become flesh. This shows that it is we who need the Spirit's grace for sanctification and power.
sources.quote: the Giver of the Spirit, refused not to say, ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He hath anointed Me,’ in respect of His having become flesh
sources.raw_question: How can the Son, who gives the Holy Spirit, be said to be anointed with the Spirit or to act through the Spirit?

question: Why does the human mind find it hard to accept that the three divine Persons together are no greater than any one of them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > It is Shown by Reason that in God Three are Not Anything Greater Than One Person.
sources.answer: Because carnal perception grasps created true things in its own way but cannot discern the truth itself by which they are created. In bodies, magnitude differs from reality, so more bodies make more bulk. If the mind could see the truth itself, this teaching would be clearer to it than corporeal light.
sources.quote: which carnal perception does not receive, for no other reason except because it perceives as it can the true things which are created, but cannot discern the truth itself by which they are created
sources.raw_question: Why does the human mind find it hard to accept that three divine Persons are not greater than one?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: Because the natural man can only think in terms of bulk and space, with bodily images flitting through his mind. Until purified of this, he should believe in one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, without thinking one greater, better or different than another.
sources.quote: For he cannot think except under the conditions of bulk and space, either small or great, since phantasms or as it were images of bodies flit about in his mind.
sources.raw_question: Why do people find it hard to understand that the three divine persons together are no greater than each singly?

question: If the Son and the Spirit are products of the Father's will rather than of his nature, can their ranked order be called an order inherent in the divine being?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: No. An order inherent in things belongs to natural necessity, as heat to fire; works of will have only an order resulting afterward from the motive or utility of the agent. Since Eunomius makes the Son and Spirit works of purpose, not nature, he has no grounds for calling their subordination an inherent order.
sources.quote: There is all the difference in the world between the accomplishment of an act of the will, and that of a mechanical law of nature. Heat is inherent in fire, splendour in the sunbeam, fluidity in water, downward tendency in a stone, and so on.
sources.raw_question: If the Son and Spirit are products of the Father's will rather than of nature, can their rank be called an order inherent in the matter?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: No. Order in things done by choice, like building a house or sailing with cargo, is not inherent in the operations but follows afterwards from the motive or the usefulness of the result. Eunomius makes the Son the work of the Father and the Spirit the work of the Son, done by purpose and not by nature. So he has no grounds for calling this work of will an 'order inherent in the matter.'
sources.quote: what grounds has he for declaring that this work of a will is an ‘order inherent in the matter,’
sources.raw_question: If the Son and the Spirit are products of the Father's will rather than of his nature, can their ranked order be called an order 'inherent' or 'connatural' in the divine being?

question: Is the Holy Spirit, together with the Father and the Son, the author of spiritual regeneration (the new birth and new life of grace)?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is no less the author of spiritual creation or regeneration than the Father and the Son. The excellence of that creation, and wherein it consists. How we are to understand holy Scripture, when it attributes a body or members to God.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ himself testifies that we are born again of the Spirit, and Scripture attributes the new creation to the Father and the Son as well, showing one divine operation. The Spirit is the Author of the new man created after the image of God, so He shares the creative work of the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: It is then clear that the Holy Spirit is also the Author of the grace of the Spirit, since we are created according to God, that we may be made the sons of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit, together with the Father and the Son, the author of spiritual regeneration (the new birth by grace)?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VI. To those who object that according to the words of Amos the Spirit is created, the answer is made that the word is there understood of the wind, which is often created, which cannot be said of the Holy Spirit, since He is eternal, and cannot be dissolved in death, or by an heretical absorption into the Father. But if they pertinaciously contend that this passage was written of the Holy Spirit, St. Ambrose points out that recourse must be had to a spiritual Interpretation, for Christ by His coming established the thunder, that is, the force of the divine utterances, and by Spirit is signified the human soul as also the flesh assumed by Christ. And since this was created by each Person of the Trinity, it is thence argued that the Spirit, Who has before been affirmed to be the Creator of all things, was the Author of the Incarnation of the Lord.
sources.answer: Yes. As the Father and the Son create, so the Holy Spirit creates us according to the mystery of grace, as in "we are His workmanship created in Christ Jesus in good works." Christ also testifies that we are born again of the Spirit. The Spirit is therefore the author of spiritual regeneration, making us sons of God.
sources.quote: And as the Father creates, so too does the Son create, and so too the Holy Spirit creates, as we read in the words of Paul
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit, along with the Father and the Son, the Creator of believers' new life of grace?

question: Is the human faculty of 'conception' (epinoia) merely a source of empty fictions without meaning, as Eunomius claims, or is it a genuine means of discovering truth?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It is a genuine means of discovering truth. Gregory defines conception as the method by which we discover what is unknown, proceeding from a first perception to what adjoins and follows from it until the inquiry is complete. All the sciences, from geometry and arithmetic to ontology and speculation about sublime objects, as well as the practical arts of life, have been discovered by this faculty. It may even be judged the most precious faculty given to us by Providence.
sources.quote: conception is the method by which we discover things that are unknown, going on to further discoveries by means of what adjoins to and follows from our first perception with regard to the thing studied.
sources.raw_question: Is the human faculty of 'conception' (epinoia) merely a source of empty fictions without sense or meaning, as Eunomius claims, or is it a genuine means of discovering truth?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius travesties conception by reducing it to sounds without meaning and fanciful combinations like centaurs. In truth conception is the method by which we discover unknown things, advancing from first perceptions to further discoveries, and it is the source of the sciences and arts.
sources.quote: conception is the method by which we discover things that are unknown, going on to further discoveries by means of what adjoins to and follows from our first perception with regard to the thing studied.
sources.raw_question: Is 'conception' (epinoia) merely a faculty for empty or monstrous fictions, so that names arising from it are meaningless?

question: Do Paul's statements that "God spared not His own Son" and "God sent His own Son" show that the Son's divine nature suffered in the Passion?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > The sixth book shows that He Who came for man's salvation was not a mere man, as Eunomius, falsely slandering him, affirmed that the great Basil had said, but the Only-begotten Son of God, putting on human flesh, and becoming a mediator between God and man, on Whom we believe, as subject to suffering in the flesh, but impassible in His Godhead; and demonstrates the calumny of Eunomius.
sources.answer: No. These phrases only seem to refer the Passion to the Divine Nature. Paul himself explains the mystery more clearly elsewhere. He everywhere attributes the dispensation of the Passion to the human element in Christ, so sound doctrine must not be abandoned because of such phrases.
sources.quote: even if some wrest to the support of the opposite doctrine the words of the Apostle, “God spared not His own Son,” and, “God sent His own Son,” and other similar phrases which seem to refer, in the matter of the Passion, to the Divine Nature
sources.raised_by_detail: some who wrest the Apostle's words
sources.raw_question: Do Paul's statements that "God spared not His own Son" and "God sent His own Son" show that the divine nature of the Son underwent the Passion?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > The sixth book shows that He Who came for man's salvation was not a mere man, as Eunomius, falsely slandering him, affirmed that the great Basil had said, but the Only-begotten Son of God, putting on human flesh, and becoming a mediator between God and man, on Whom we believe, as subject to suffering in the flesh, but impassible in His Godhead; and demonstrates the calumny of Eunomius.
sources.answer: No. Gregory says Paul himself explains the mystery more clearly by consistently attributing the Passion to the human element in Christ. Paul writes "by man came death," that sin was condemned "in the flesh," not in the Godhead, and that Christ was "crucified through weakness" (the flesh) yet "liveth by power" (the divine nature). So the Man tasted death while the immortal nature did not.
sources.quote: For he everywhere attributes to the Human element in Christ the dispensation of the Passion
sources.raw_question: Do texts like "God spared not His own Son" and "God sent His own Son" show that the Son's divine nature suffered in the Passion?

question: When Chrysostom (and Basil) say the Son is one with the Father 'in power' (κατὰ δύναμιν), do they mean only a lesser unity of agreement or authority, or an essential unity and equality of power and essence?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 31: Whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration, on the side of Arianism, ought to move a wise and good man, against so great appearances of truth o
sources.answer: It means essential equality of power. For Chrysostom, being one in power (κατὰ δύναμιν) is the same as being equal in power or ability, and essentially so. One Person with infinite power and another with only finite power could not properly be called one in power. So Chrysostom's explication contradicts Dr. Clarke's reading rather than supporting it.
sources.quote: One having infinite and the other only finite power, could not, according to Chrysostom, be properly said to be one, κατὰ δύναμιν, in power.
