sources.raw_question: In Chrysostom's interpretation, does the Son's being 'one in power' with the Father mean only some lesser agreement or unity of power, or essential equality of power?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: They mean a unity of essence. Dr. Clarke quotes Chrysostom selectively, but Chrysostom's following words say that if the power is the same, the essence is plainly the same too. So δύναμις here means the same inherent, essential, omnipotent power, not a merely delegated or shared authority.
sources.quote: shew that he meant by δύναμις, not the same authority, but the same inherent, essential, omnipotent power.
sources.raw_question: When Chrysostom and Basil say the Father and Son are one 'according to power' (κατὰ δύναμιν), do they mean only a unity of authority, or a unity of essence?

question: Does 'even as' (καθὼς) in John 5:23, 'that all men should honour the Son even as they honour the Father', imply equal honour to the Son, or only a general similarity of honour?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: It implies equal honour. Waterland grants καθὼς can signify only general similitude, but his argument does not rest on the particle alone: in John 5 Christ draws a parallel between the Father and himself and between their works, grounding his claim to honour on it, and he does so in answer to the charge of making himself equal with God. The context therefore fixes the meaning as equality of honour.
sources.quote: our blessed Lord, in that chapter, draws a parallel between the Father and himself, between the father’s works and his own, founding thereupon his title to honour; which sufficiently intimates what καθὼς means
sources.raw_question: Does the word καθὼς ('even as') in John 5:23, 'that all men should honour the Son even as they honour the Father', imply equal honour to the Son, or only a general similitude of honour?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: Equal honour is meant. The argument does not rest on the particle by itself, since καθὼς can indicate general likeness. Christ draws a parallel throughout the chapter between the Father's works and his own and grounds his claim to honour on it. He says this in reply to the charge of making himself equal with God, which shows that καθὼς here implies equality.
sources.quote: our blessed Lord, in that chapter, draws a parallel between the Father and himself, between the father’s works and his own, founding thereupon his title to honour; which sufficiently intimates what καθὼς means
sources.raw_question: Does the word "even as" (καθὼς) in John 5:23 mean only a general similarity between the honour given to the Son and to the Father, rather than an equal honour?

question: If 'simple' and 'ungenerate' meant the same thing, would the Son, being God and therefore simple, also have to be called ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, and this shows the Eunomian equation is absurd. The Son, being God, is simple, since God is free from all composition. So if simplicity meant ungeneracy, the Eunomians would have to either deny the Son's Godhead by making him composite or attribute ungeneracy to him as well.
sources.quote: they draw upon themselves one of two absurd alternatives, either denying the Godhead of the Only-begotten, or attributing ungeneracy to Him also.
sources.raw_question: If 'simple' and 'ungenerate' meant the same thing, would the Son, being simple, also have to be called ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Absurdity would follow either way. The Eunomians would have to deny the Son's Godhead by making him composite, or else attribute ungeneracy to him as well. The Son is by nature simple, as anything that is God must be. So if 'simple' meant 'ungenerate', the Son's simplicity would be ungeneracy, which the Eunomians themselves reject.
sources.quote: they draw upon themselves one of two absurd alternatives, either denying the Godhead of the Only-begotten, or attributing ungeneracy to Him also.
sources.raw_question: If simplicity and ungeneracy were the same, what would follow for the Son, who is also God and simple?

question: At Jesus' baptism, did a separate heavenly being called Christ descend upon the man Jesus, so that Christ and Jesus are two different beings?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IX.—One and the same God, the Creator of heaven and earth, is He whom the prophets foretold, and who was declared by the Gospel. Proof of this, at the outset, from St. Matthew’s Gospel.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus denies that Christ came down upon Jesus at that time, or that Christ is one and Jesus another. The Word of God is himself Jesus: he took flesh and was anointed by the Spirit from the Father. In this way he was made Jesus Christ, as Isaiah foretold.
sources.quote: For Christ did not at that time descend upon Jesus, neither was Christ one and Jesus another: but the Word of God
sources.raw_question: Was the Christ who descended at Jesus' baptism a separate being from Jesus?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IX.—One and the same God, the Creator of heaven and earth, is He whom the prophets foretold, and who was declared by the Gospel. Proof of this, at the outset, from St. Matthew’s Gospel.
sources.answer: No. Christ did not descend upon Jesus at the baptism, nor is Christ one and Jesus another. The Word of God, Saviour of all and ruler of heaven and earth, who is Jesus, took flesh and was anointed by the Spirit from the Father, and so was made Jesus Christ.
sources.quote: For Christ did not at that time descend upon Jesus, neither was Christ one and Jesus another: but the Word of God—who is the Saviour of all, and the ruler of heaven and earth, who is Jesus
sources.raw_question: At Jesus' baptism, did a separate heavenly being called Christ descend upon a man named Jesus, so that Christ and Jesus are two different beings?

question: Since the title 'Lord' (Kyrios) is sometimes applied to mere men in the New Testament, does calling Jesus 'Lord' still count as evidence of his deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Kyrios is the word the Septuagint uses for Jehovah, and the Jews used its equivalent Adonai in place of the divine name. Of its 737 New Testament uses, only 18 refer to men, and almost never in a sense implying worship. In 665 cases it is applied indiscriminately to the Father or the Son. Its general usage therefore marks Christ as the divine Lord, and pointing to the few human uses is trifling.
sources.quote: it is the word by which Jehovah is uniformly translated by the Septuagint, even in Exodus 6:3; and further, that standing by itself in the New Testament, it designates in multiplied passages the Infinite Father.
sources.raw_question: Since "Lord" (Kyrios) is sometimes used of men, does calling Jesus "Lord" in the New Testament carry any weight as evidence of his deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. The human uses are of a quite different kind: in scarcely any of them is there the remotest possibility of Divine worship being intended, and many are plural. Christ, by contrast, is called Lord in hundreds of passages in which, as Lord, he is believed in, served and worshipped, so the comparison is trifling.
sources.quote: Now it is trifling with this question to assert that the passages adduced in the second column, invalidate all the proof to be derived from the hundreds of passages in which Jesus Christ is called Lord, and as Lord is believed in, served, and worshiped.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the title 'Lord' (kyrios) is sometimes applied to mere men in the New Testament invalidate the argument for Christ's deity from his being called Lord?

question: Does Hebrews 3:1-2, which says Jesus was "made" Apostle and High Priest, imply that the Son's existence had a beginning or was created?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: No. The Son became High Priest not in that He was in the beginning as the Word and God, equal with God, but in that He emptied Himself in the form of a servant and offered Himself as a sacrifice for us. He became High Priest many generations later, after the order of Melchisedech, so "made" refers to the dispensation, not His pretemporal existence.
sources.quote: not in that He was in the beginning, being the Word and God, and being in the form of God, and equal with God, but in that He emptied Himself in the form of the servant, and offered an oblation and sacrifice for us
sources.raw_question: Does the statement in Hebrews that Jesus was "made" an Apostle and High Priest imply that the Son's existence had a beginning?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: No. By "made," Paul does not declare the first existence of the Only-begotten. He means the grace of priestly appointment given to the one who offered his own blood as propitiation for sins. Christ became High Priest in the dispensation, when he emptied himself in the form of a servant, not in that he was in the beginning as the Word and God.
sources.quote: he does not by the word “made” declare the first existence of the Only-begotten, but says “made” with the intention of representing that grace which is commonly spoken of in connection with the appointment of priests
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 3:1-2, which says Jesus was "made" Apostle and High Priest, teach that the Son's existence was created?

question: Can a created being be the cause of humanity's salvation, or must the Saviour be the uncreated God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > He shows the falsehood of Eunomius' calumnious charge that the great Basil had said that “man was emptied to become man,” and demonstrates that the “emptying” of the Only-begotten took place with a view to the restoration to life of the Man Who had suffered.
sources.answer: The Saviour must be the uncreated God. The created was saved by the uncreated God, and any pious judge will reject the view that refers the cause of our salvation to a creature. On the Eunomian view a servant would merely come among servants, rather than the Master being mingled with the servant to free them.
sources.quote: he who says that the created was saved by the uncreated God, or he who refers the cause of our salvation to the creature? Surely the judgment of pious men is not doubtful.
sources.raw_question: Can a created being be the cause of humanity's salvation, or must the Saviour be the uncreated God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > He shows the falsehood of Eunomius' calumnious charge that the great Basil had said that “man was emptied to become man,” and demonstrates that the “emptying” of the Only-begotten took place with a view to the restoration to life of the Man Who had suffered.
sources.answer: Salvation must come from the uncreated God. Created and uncreated differ as dominion differs from slavery: the uncreated God rules for ever, while all created things serve Him. Pious judges would therefore side with the one who says the created was saved by the uncreated God, not with the one who makes a creature the cause of salvation.
sources.quote: he who says that the created was saved by the uncreated God, or he who refers the cause of our salvation to the creature? Surely the judgment of pious men is not doubtful.
sources.raw_question: Can a created Son be the one who saves created human nature, or must salvation come from the uncreated God?

question: Did the Post-Nicene Fathers depart from the Ante-Nicene Fathers in their doctrine of the Son and his relation to the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. Both groups taught the same doctrine. Each taught the Son's subordination to the Father as head and fountain, and his real personal distinction from the Father. Each also taught that he is uncreated, eternal, Creator, and one God with the Father. It is a misrepresentation to quote only the earlier Fathers for the first set of points and to credit only the later Fathers with the second. The Post-Nicene Fathers simply preserved the faith once delivered.
sources.quote: though nothing is more evident than that they varied not a tittle, in any material point of doctrine, from their predecessors; but only preserved, as became them, with an upright zeal, the true faith of Christ
sources.raw_question: Did the Post-Nicene Fathers depart from the Ante-Nicene Fathers' doctrine about the Son, either by adding his eternity and consubstantiality or by dropping his subordination and personal distinction from the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. Epiphanius and Cyril of Jerusalem used the same reasoning against the Sabellians that prevailed before Nicaea. In no material point of doctrine did they vary from their predecessors. Supposed differences rest on a text or two read differently, or on ignorance and negligence in comparing the writers.
sources.quote: I have added to the number two Post-Nicene writers, Epiphanius and the elder Cyril; which are enough to shew, that the same way of reasoning against the Sabellians (which prevailed before the Nicene Council) obtained likewise afterwards.
sources.raw_question: Did the Post-Nicene Fathers depart from the Ante-Nicene Fathers in their doctrine of the Son's unity with the Father?

question: In what sense does the human flesh of Christ become Christ and Lord?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: It is transformed by its commixture with the Word into what it was not by nature. Just as He who knew no sin became sin to take away the world's sin, so the flesh which received the Lord becomes Christ and Lord; God is manifested in the flesh because the Word was made flesh, and the flesh is made divine because it became Christ and Lord.
sources.quote: so on the other hand the flesh which received the Lord becomes Christ and Lord, being transformed by the commixture into that which it was not by nature
sources.raw_question: In what sense does the human flesh of Christ become Christ and Lord?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: By being mingled with the Godhead. The flesh in which God was manifested first fulfilled the mystery of death. It was then transformed by this commixture into what is exalted and divine, and so changed into what the Word who appeared in it already was. The Word himself does not become anything new, since he is already the fulness of all good.
sources.quote: is transformed by commixture to that which is exalted and Divine, becoming Christ and Lord, being transferred and changed to that which He was, Who manifested Himself in that flesh
sources.raw_question: How does the crucified human flesh of Christ come to be 'Lord and Christ'?

question: How does the Holy Spirit glorify Christ according to John 16:14?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: He glorifies Christ by revealing to believers the excellencies and desirableness of Christ's person. He also shows them "the things of Christ": his love and grace, and the fruits of his death, resurrection and intercession, such as pardon, justification and adoption. In this way he communicates the grace of both Christ's person and his office.
sources.quote: He glorifies Christ by revealing his excellencies and desirableness to believers, as the “chiefest of ten thousand, — altogether lovely,” and then he shows them of the things of Christ
sources.raw_question: How does the Holy Spirit glorify Christ according to John 16:14?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: The Spirit's work is to glorify the Son, not himself. He does this by taking the things of Christ (his love, kindness, grace, and purchase) and showing them to believers, making the suffering Christ glorious and highly esteemed in their hearts. A spirit that aims at its own glory and despises the historical Christ thereby shows it is not the Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: Wherefore the Holy Ghost is sent, and his work is to glorify the Son. But now, as I said, we have a spirit come forth whose whole business is to glorify himself; whereby we may easily know whence he is.
sources.raw_question: What is the proper work of the Holy Spirit in relation to Christ according to John 16:14?

question: Why is it so difficult for the human mind to know God through itself as God's image?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Infirmity of the Human Mind.
sources.answer: Because of sin. The mind is involved in penal darkness and burdened by the corruptible body that presses down the soul. This evil is inflicted for no demerit other than sin, so the remedy is to follow the Lamb that takes away the sins of the world.
sources.quote: were they not involved in penal darkness, and burdened with the corruptible body that presses down the soul. And for what demerit save that of sin is this evil inflicted on them?
sources.raw_question: Why does the human mind struggle so much to reach certain knowledge of God and of itself as God's image?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Of the Term ‘Enigma,’ And of Tropical Modes of Speech.
sources.answer: Because the sight is enigmatic: we do not see what we cannot help seeing. No one fails to see his own thought, yet no one truly beholds his thought with inner sight. If sight were easy, Scripture would not speak of an enigma. So it should not surprise us that we must labor to see God this way.
sources.quote: For we should not hear of an enigma in this place if sight were easy. And this is a yet greater enigma, that we do not see what we cannot but see.
sources.raw_question: Why is it so difficult to see God even through the image of God in our own minds?

question: Is it right to say that the Father alone is 'really existent', excluding the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next skilfully confutes the partial, empty and blasphemous statement of Eunomius on the subject of the absolutely existent.
sources.answer: No. Real existence is opposed only to apparent or unreal existence, like a dream image or a painted man; so to deny it to the Son is to deny that he exists at all, which is the Jewish opinion. Moreover the Son is He Who Is, who named himself Existent to Moses with 'I am that I am', as Eunomius himself admits that it was the Son who appeared to Moses.
sources.quote: let them be content not to deprive of real existence Him Who is, Who in the Divine appearance to Moses gave Himself the name of Existent, when He said, “I am that I am:”
sources.raw_question: Is it right to predicate real existence (being 'really existent') of the Father alone, excluding the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next skilfully confutes the partial, empty and blasphemous statement of Eunomius on the subject of the absolutely existent.
sources.answer: No. Real existence is opposed only to unreal or apparent existence, such as a dream image or a painted man. Unless one holds, with the Jews, that the Only-begotten does not exist at all, one cannot deny him real existence. He is the One who named himself "I am that I am" to Moses, which Eunomius himself admits.
sources.quote: But if they do not deny the existence of the Maker of all things, let them be content not to deprive of real existence Him Who is, Who in the Divine appearance to Moses gave Himself the name of Existent
sources.raw_question: Is it right to say that the Father alone is "really existent"?

question: Was the Son distinctly worshipped before his resurrection, for example by the patriarchs, or only afterwards?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: It counts as distinct worship. According to the Christian Church it was paid to the Person appearing, who was the Person of the Son, and he did not refuse it. Since he received it in his own Person, he was then distinctly worshipped.
sources.quote: since the Son received that worship in his own Person, (according to the ancients,) it must be said, he was then distinctly worshipped, and in his own right, as being truly God.
sources.raw_question: Was the worship the patriarchs supposedly paid to the Son 'distinct' worship, or only worship of God in general?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No, not in the sense Dr. Clarke's party intends. Waterland holds that this claim is untrue and does not agree with the views of the ancient Church.
sources.quote: That the Son had not distinct worship paid him till after his resurrection. ‘This, in the sense wherein you understand it, is not true
sources.raw_question: Was distinct worship paid to the Son only after his resurrection?

question: Can we know that God exists without knowing what God's essence is?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as we see the heavens and do not doubt their existence yet cannot define their nature, so with the Creator we know that He exists but must confess ignorance of His essential nature. Knowledge of existence does not imply comprehension of essence.
sources.quote: even so, with regard to the Creator of the world, we know that He exists, but of His essential nature we cannot deny that we are ignorant.
sources.raw_question: Can we know that God exists without knowing what God's essence is?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: That God is, but not what He is or how. The disciple of the Gospels and Prophets believes that He Who is, is, learning this from the sacred writers, from the harmony of visible things, and from the works of Providence. He leaves the question of what and how God is aside as unprofitable speculation, and so opens no door to falsehood.
sources.quote: But the disciple of the Gospels and of Prophecy believes that He Who is, is; both from what he has learnt from the sacred writers, and from the harmony of things which do appear, and from the works of Providence.
sources.raw_question: What can a believer know about God if not His essence?

question: Can we legitimately reason about the Son's nature and generation from what we observe in created nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. The ultimate division of all that exists is between created and uncreated, and these admit no intermixture in their distinguishing properties. So we must not conceive both by similar terms or look for the same distinguishing marks in each. The names of the Son involve communion with the Father and transcend creation.
sources.quote: The ultimate division of all that exists is made by the line between “created” and “uncreated,”
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to reason about the Son's nature from what we observe in creation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He further shows that the pretemporal generation of the Son is not the subject of influences drawn from ordinary and carnal generation, but is without beginning and without end, and not according to the fabrications constructed by Eunomius, in ignorance of His power, from the statements of Plato concerning the soul and from the sabbath rest of the Hebrews.
sources.answer: No. Even the creation of the universe was measured by time, by ordered days and nights, as Moses' cosmogony shows. But even Eunomius admits the Lord was before the times of the ages, so the temporal pattern of created things cannot apply to the Son's generation.
sources.quote: there ran the measure of time, meted out in a certain order and arrangement by stated days and nights, for each of the things that came into being: and this even our adversaries’ statement does not admit with regard to the being of the Only-begotten
sources.raw_question: Can nature, including the creation of the universe, serve as a trustworthy guide to understanding the divine generation of the Son?

question: Can temporal expressions such as "then He willed" or "then He begot" be properly applied to the Divine Nature, implying that the Son's generation took place at a point in time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > The ninth book declares that Eunomius' account of the Nature of God is, up to a certain point, well stated. Then in succession he mixes up with his own argument, on account of its affinity, the expression from Philo's writings, “God is before all other things, which are generated,” adding also the expression, “He has dominion over His own power.” Detesting the excessive absurdity, Gregory strikingly confutes it.
sources.answer: No. Temporal expressions have no force when applied to the Divine Nature, which is not measured by quantity or interval. Creation may have a beginning in time, but God Himself is not extended through intervals. Speaking of a time at which God deferred the Son's generation, as though he did not yet think it good to become a Father, is therefore groundless.
sources.quote: What was the intervening cause of delay, for which God deferred the generation of the Only-begotten, not thinking it good as yet to become a Father?
sources.raw_question: Can temporal expressions such as "He then willed" or "He then begat" be properly applied to the Divine Nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > The ninth book declares that Eunomius' account of the Nature of God is, up to a certain point, well stated. Then in succession he mixes up with his own argument, on account of its affinity, the expression from Philo's writings, “God is before all other things, which are generated,” adding also the expression, “He has dominion over His own power.” Detesting the excessive absurdity, Gregory strikingly confutes it.
sources.answer: No. Temporal adverbs are fitting for the creation, which received a beginning in time by the Creator's good pleasure. But the Divine Nature is not measured by quantity or interval, and before the ages there was no interval. So temporal language about God's own being is void, and to imagine the Divine Nature as extended through intervals is the error of the 'new wisdom'.
sources.quote: since no conception of interval is present to our minds in regard to that Divine Nature which is not measured by quantity or by interval, the force of temporal expressions must surely be void.
sources.raw_question: Can temporal expressions such as 'then He willed' or 'then He begot' be properly applied to the Divine Nature itself, implying the Son's generation took place at a point in time?

question: Whom do the Scriptures properly call God and Lord?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Preface.
sources.answer: Scripture calls no one God except the Father of all, the Son, and those who have received the adoption. So the Son is called God together with the Father. The heretics' invented Æons and gods are not named God by the Spirit, the apostles, or the Lord.
sources.quote: have shown that there is none other called God by the Scriptures except the Father of all, and the Son, and those who possess the adoption.
sources.raw_question: Whom do the Scriptures properly call God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter I.—The Lord acknowledged but one God and Father.
sources.answer: Only the one God who rules over all, together with his Word, and, in a derived sense, those who receive the Spirit of adoption. The Spirit announced no other God or Lord besides these, and the apostles named no one else as God or Lord. Believers are those who believe in the one true God and in Jesus Christ his Son.
sources.quote: no other God or Lord was announced by the Spirit, except Him who, as God, rules over all, together with His Word, and those who receive the Spirit of adoption
sources.raw_question: Who is included among those whom Scripture rightly calls God and Lord?

question: Can a created or originated being be the true Image of the unoriginate God, in which the Father is seen?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: No. The originated has no likeness to the unoriginate. If a creature were the image in which the Father is seen, the Unoriginate would become the image of creatures. That would equate creatures with God and deny the Unoriginate by measuring Him with His works.
sources.quote: For what likeness has the originated to the unoriginate? (one must not weary of using repetition;) for if they will have it that the one is like the other, so that he who sees the one beholds the other, they are like to say that the Unoriginate is the image of creatures
sources.raw_question: Can a created or originated being be the true image of the unoriginate God, so that whoever sees it sees the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: No. The Father sees himself in his Image and delights in it, as the Son says, 'I was His delight.' There was never a time when the Father did not see himself in his Image or lacked delight. The Maker cannot see himself in a created essence, for such as the Father is, such must the Image be.
sources.quote: how should the Maker and Creator see Himself in a created and originated essence? for such as is the Father, such must be the Image.
sources.raw_question: Could a created, originated being be the true Image of God in which the Father sees himself and delights?

question: Must Christians affirm both Christ's humanity and his divinity together, or is it enough to confess only one of them?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And Indeed that Christ Was Not Only Man, But God Also; That Even as He Was the Son of Man, So Also He Was the Son of God.
sources.answer: Both must be believed. Since Scripture speaks of both in Christ, the faith is true only when it is complete. If one of the two is dropped and only the other, the less important one, is accepted, the rule of truth is thrown into confusion. Such boldness does not bring salvation but endangers it by overthrowing the faith.
sources.quote: Wherefore as both are read of in Christ, let both be believed; that so finally the faith may be true, being also complete.
sources.raw_question: Should Christians believe both Christ's humanity and his divinity, or is it enough to confess only one of them?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is Again Confirmed in Christ by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: Both must be affirmed together. If he were only before every creature, his humanity would be taken away. If he were only man, his divinity, which is before every creature, would be denied. The two are joined and linked in him, which is why he is the Mediator between God and man, uniting God and man in himself.
sources.quote: For if He is only before every creature, humanity is taken away from Him; but if He is only man, the divinity which is before every creature is interfered with.
sources.raw_question: Must Christ's divinity and humanity both be affirmed together, or can either be held alone?

question: Can human learning by itself remove the spiritual blindness and ignorance that came upon humanity through the curse for sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. The proper aim of learning is to undo part of the curse of sin, but it cannot reach that aim. Whatever light it yields is not spiritualized or restored to living with God, so the wisest philosophers became fools. True light comes only from Jesus Christ, the true Light.
sources.quote: is not in the least measure by it spiritualized, or brought into that order of living to God, and with God, wherein at first it lay. This is wholly beyond its reach.
sources.raw_question: Can human learning by itself recover the true, spiritual knowledge of God lost through sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. The darkness is a penal curse, and only Christ, who was made a curse for us and on whom all our sins met in punishment, removes what is penal. The most learned person without Christ is as much under the curse of blindness as the simplest. Greater mental ability without Christ only strengthens the mind's enmity against God and raises high thoughts against Christ.
sources.quote: The curse is only removed in him who was made a curse for us. Every thing that is penal is taken away only by him on whom all our sins did meet in a way of punishment
sources.raw_question: Can intellectual learning remove the spiritual blindness and ignorance that came upon humanity as a curse for sin?

question: If the Son is the product of the Father's energy, must the Son's essence be something passive, acted upon like created matter, and does this show that he is not the result of an energy?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, and therefore the Son is not the product of an energy. Whatever an energy produces must be susceptible of being acted upon, otherwise it would resist and nothing would result. So Eunomius faces a dilemma: either the Son is passive like a creature, or he does not exist. Both are impious, so the truth is that the Son exists without being acted upon and is very God of very God, shining forth from the Father from everlasting.
sources.quote: For if He verily exists, and is not subject to be acted upon, it is plain that He is not the result of an energy, but is proved to be very God of very God the Father, without liability to be acted upon, beaming from Him and shining forth from everlasting.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is the product of the Father's energy, must the Son's essence be something passive, capable of being acted upon like created matter?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, it would follow, and so he is not the result of an energy. A productive energy cannot subsist without something to work on, as a smith needs material. If Fatherhood is an energy, the Son must be either a passive subject moulded by it or else not exist at all, and both alternatives are impious. Since the Son truly exists and is not subject to being acted upon, he is not the effect of an energy but very God of very God, shining forth from the Father everlastingly.
sources.quote: For if He verily exists, and is not subject to be acted upon, it is plain that He is not the result of an energy, but is proved to be very God of very God the Father, without liability to be acted upon, beaming from Him and shining forth from everlasting.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is the product of the Father's energy, must the Son be a passive material acted upon, and does this show that he is not the result of an energy?

question: Is the God who spoke through the Old Testament prophets the same God revealed in the Gospel and from whom Christ came, or did the prophets come from another God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: The same God. The truly spiritual man, interpreting every prophecy in reference to the Lord's dispensation, knows always the same God and does not maintain that the prophets were sent from another God or that their prophecies came from different sources. To claim otherwise is to blaspheme the Father and set aside his dispensations.
sources.quote: nor dishonours the prophets, by maintaining that they were [sent] from another God [than he worships], or again, that their prophecies were derived from different sources.
sources.raw_question: Is the God who spoke through the Old Testament prophets the same God revealed in the Gospel, or did the prophets come from another God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XXVII.—Doctrines of Cerdo and Marcion.
sources.answer: Yes. The prophets announced the Lord's coming beforehand. Paul quotes the prophetic writings for exactly this purpose, which is why Marcion had to remove those quotations from Paul's epistles. So Jesus does not come from a God above the Creator in order to abolish the law and the prophets.
sources.quote: those passages from the prophetical writings which the apostle quotes, in order to teach us that they announced beforehand the coming of the Lord
sources.raw_question: Did the Old Testament prophets foretell the coming of Christ, so that Christ came from the same God who spoke through them rather than abolishing their God's works?

question: Are human beings sons of God by nature, or are they first creatures and then sons by adoption and grace?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Men are creatures by nature and become sons only afterward by grace. God first made them and then, out of lovingkindness, 'begat' them, calling them sons. They become sons by receiving the Spirit of His Son, who is Son by nature.
sources.quote: But this is God’s kindness to man, that of whom He is Maker, of them according to grace He afterwards becomes Father also; becomes, that is, when men, His creatures, receive into their hearts, as the Apostle says, ‘the Spirit of His Son, crying, Abba, Father.’
sources.raw_question: Are human beings sons of God by nature, or are they first creatures and then sons by grace?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: By adoption and grace. Men are creatures by nature and God is first their Maker; He afterwards becomes their Father when they receive the Spirit of His Son crying 'Abba, Father.' John says they 'become' children because they are not sons by nature, yet 'were begotten' because they receive the name of son.
sources.quote: first he says ‘become,’ because they are not called sons by nature but by adoption; then he says ‘were begotten,’ because they too had received at any rate the name of son.
sources.raw_question: Are human believers sons of God by nature or by adoption and grace?

question: Did Christ rise from the dead in the substance of real flesh?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VII.—Inasmuch as Christ did rise in our flesh, it follows that we shall be also raised in the same; since the resurrection promised to us should not be referred to spirits naturally immortal, but to bodies in themselves mortal.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ rose in the substance of flesh, as shown by his pointing out to his disciples the marks of the nails and the wound in his side, which are tokens of the flesh that rose. Because Christ rose in this way, Paul's promise that God will raise us by his power refers to our flesh as well.
sources.quote: In the same manner, therefore, as Christ did rise in the substance of flesh, and pointed out to His disciples the mark of the nails and the opening in His side
sources.raw_question: Did Christ rise from the dead in the substance of real flesh?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXI.—The preservation of our bodies is confirmed by the resurrection and ascension of Christ: the souls of the saints during the intermediate period are in a state of expectation of that time when they shall receive their perfect and consummated glory.
sources.answer: Yes. After tarrying in the lower parts of the earth, he rose in the flesh. He even showed the print of the nails to his disciples, and only then ascended to the Father.
sources.quote: then afterwards rising in the flesh, so that He even showed the print of the nails to His disciples, He thus ascended to the Father
sources.raw_question: Did Christ rise from the dead in the flesh, with a real body?

question: Is Christ's love for his people unchangeable, as God's love is?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ's love is like himself, and he is unchangeably the same, so his love never alters. Hebrews 1:10-12, which speaks of the Creator who remains while the heavens perish, is applied to Christ: 'he is the same, and his years fail not.' He is the Lord who changes not, and whom he loves he loves to the end. His love never had a beginning and will never have an ending.
sources.quote: Jesus Christ is still the same; and so is his love.
sources.raw_question: Is the love of Jesus Christ unchangeable in the same way that God's love is unchangeable?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Our love changes as we change, but Christ's love is like himself, and he is always the same. Hebrews 1:10-12 applies to Christ the unchanging Creator who remains while the heavens perish, so his love never fails. Whom he loves, he loves to the end.
sources.quote: Jesus Christ is still the same; and so is his love.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's love for his people unchangeable?

question: Since the Father himself is light and life, does that avoid the conclusion that darkness existed before the Son, if the Son came into being later?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory agrees darkness never was, but only because the Light never 'was not': the light is always in the light. If, as the heretics hold, the generated light came into existence later than the ungenerate light, then that created light must have come forth out of darkness. A distinct interval of darkness would then lie between the eternal light and the later one.
sources.quote: But this is just what I say, that darkness never was; for the light never “was not,” for “the light,” as the prophecy says, “is always in the light.”
sources.raw_question: Since the Father is himself light and virtue, does that remove the need to suppose darkness existed before the Only-begotten Light came to be?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory's point is precisely that darkness never was, because the Light never 'was not.' As the prophecy says, the light is always in the light. If the generated light is made distinct from and later than the eternal ungenerate light, the absurdity returns.
sources.quote: But this is just what I say, that darkness never was; for the light never “was not,” for “the light,” as the prophecy says, “is always in the light.”
sources.raw_question: Since the Father himself is light and life, does that avoid the conclusion that darkness existed before the Son existed?

question: If the Son, the true Light, were made by the Father at a later time, would that imply that darkness (and the opposites of truth, life and good) preceded him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. A later light would be made only for some use, and the one use of light is to disperse prevailing gloom. Uncreated light exists by reason of itself, but created light comes into being by reason of something else. So a Son 'made' later implies darkness preceded him, which is beyond all impiety.
sources.quote: the one use of light is that of the dispersion by its means of the prevailing gloom. Now the light which exists without creation is what it is by nature by reason of itself; but the created light clearly comes into being by reason of something else.
sources.raw_question: If the Son, as Light, were created at a later time, would his creation presuppose a preceding darkness?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes, on the heretics' premises. The Son is the true Light, Truth, Life and Good. These have contraries with no middle term, so the absence of one entails the presence of the other, as darkness preceded created light. A creator also makes what is lacking. So a Son made later implies that the Father was first without light, truth and good, and hence in their opposites. This absurdity shows the Son is eternal.
sources.quote: we must say that He was surrounded by darkness instead of Light, by falsehood instead of truth, by death instead of life, by evil instead of good
sources.raw_question: If the Father made the Son at a time when he willed, does it follow that before the Son existed the Father was surrounded by darkness, falsehood, death and evil?

question: How should the lofty and the lowly statements Scripture makes about Christ be interpreted?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > The sixth book shows that He Who came for man's salvation was not a mere man, as Eunomius, falsely slandering him, affirmed that the great Basil had said, but the Only-begotten Son of God, putting on human flesh, and becoming a mediator between God and man, on Whom we believe, as subject to suffering in the flesh, but impassible in His Godhead; and demonstrates the calumny of Eunomius.
sources.answer: Each statement should be assigned to the nature it fits: the human ones to the humanity, the lofty ones to the Godhead. Titles such as Light, Power, Life, Truth, and Creator of all belong to God the Word. Pain, sleep, need, nails, blood, and burial belong to the flesh joined to the Word. The attributes of the flesh may not be attributed to the Word, nor those of the Godhead to the flesh.
sources.quote: we assign every particular phrase accordingly to one or other of these Natures which we conceive in the mystery, that which is human to the Humanity, that which is lofty to the Godhead
sources.raw_question: How should the lofty and the lowly statements the Gospels make about Christ be interpreted?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: Scripture speaks of the one Christ formed of the house (the Humanity) and of the Wisdom which built it (the Divinity), applying fitting terms to each. As in the Gospels, the lofty and divine phraseology indicates the Godhead and the humble and lowly language indicates the Manhood, so a lowly term like "created" need not apply to the divine Wisdom.
sources.quote: employs the more lofty and divine phraseology to indicate the Godhead, and that which is humble and lowly to indicate the Manhood
sources.raw_question: How should lofty and lowly statements about Wisdom or Christ in Scripture be distinguished in their reference?

question: Does the fact that the Son suffered on the Cross show that he is inferior in essence to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius wrongly treats the surpassing act of power by which the Son was able to undergo the Passion as evidence of weakness. Nothing that acts according to its own nature is wonderful, but what overpasses the limits of its nature is especially admired; so the Cross manifests the superabundance of the Son's power by means external to his nature, not an inferior essence.
sources.quote: Eunomius makes the suffering of the Cross to be a sign of divergence in essence, in the sense of inferiority, considering, I know not how, the surpassing act of power, by which He was able to perform this, to be an evidence of weakness
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Son suffered on the Cross show that he is inferior in essence to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: No. Both sides hold the Passion as part of the faith. The orthodox honour the God manifested by the Cross even as the Father is honoured. It is Eunomius's party that treats the Cross as shameful: they find the Passion a hindrance to glorifying the Only-begotten equally with the Father, and they rank the Son lower because the reproach of the Cross falls on him alone. So the charge of being ashamed of the Cross recoils on the accuser.
sources.quote: we hold it necessary to honour, even as the Father is honoured, the God Who was manifested by the Cross, and they find the Passion a hindrance to glorifying the Only-begotten God equally with the Father that begat Him
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's suffering on the Cross make him inferior to the Father, so that those who honour the Son equally with the Father are really ashamed of the Cross?

question: Does 'the world' that the Word made in John 1:10 refer to the church or the new creation under the gospel rather than to the created world?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. The text says the world he made did not know him. The church did know him and acknowledged him to be the Son of God, since that confession is its very foundation. So the world in this verse cannot mean the church or the new state under the gospel.
sources.quote: But the world they intend did know him: for the church knew him, and acknowledged him to be the Son of God; for that was the foundation that it was built upon.
sources.raw_question: Can 'the world' that the Word made and came into in John 1:10 be the church, or the new state of things under the gospel?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. The world that the Word made is the same world he came into and which 'knew him not.' But the world the Socinians have in mind, the church, did know him. The church acknowledged him to be the Son of God, and that confession was its very foundation. So their reading contradicts the text.
sources.quote: But the world they intend did know him: for the church knew him, and acknowledged him to be the Son of God; for that was the foundation that it was built upon.
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:10, 'He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not,' refer to the new creation of the church through the apostles' preaching of the gospel rather than to the creation of the world?

question: Do the scriptural titles of Christ such as Son, Word, Wisdom, Power, Image and Radiance show that he is eternal and proper to the Father's essence rather than a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Yes. Anyone who hears of a son conceives of what is proper to the father's essence. From the original faith that God has a Son, Word, Wisdom, Power, Image and Radiance, it follows at once that he always exists, is from the Father, is like him, and is the eternal offspring of his essence. No idea of creature or work is involved; 'He is a creature' is a later sowing of tares.
sources.quote: from which it at once follows that He is always; that He is from the Father; that He is like; that He is the eternal offspring of His essence; and there is no idea involved in these of creature or work
sources.raw_question: Do the names Son, Word, Wisdom, Image and Radiance applied to Christ imply that he is eternal and of the Father's essence rather than a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Yes. These passages proscribe the Arian heresy and signify the eternity of the Word and that he is not foreign but proper to the Father's essence. No one ever saw light without radiance, no one can say the expression differs from the subsistence, and only one who has lost his mind could think God was ever without Reason and Wisdom.
sources.quote: All these passages proscribe in every light the Arian heresy, and signify the eternity of the Word, and that He is not foreign but proper to the Father's Essence. For when saw any one light without radiance?
sources.raw_question: Do the scriptural titles of the Son such as Radiance, Expression of the Father's subsistence, Word, Wisdom and Power show that the Son is eternal and proper to the Father's essence?

question: Is it legitimate to inquire how God begets the Son and what the manner of the divine generation is?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. The manner of the Son's generation is ineffable, proper to God's nature, and known only to the Father and the Son. Asking it is as irreligious as asking where and how God is. One perplexed should keep silent and believe rather than disbelieve what is written.
sources.quote: it is better in perplexity to be silent and believe, than to disbelieve on account of the perplexity
sources.raw_question: May we inquire how God begets the Son, or why God's Word is not like our word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. The manner of the Son's generation is ineffable, proper to God's nature, and known only to the Father and the Son; demanding it be explained in words is like asking where God is or of what nature the Father is, which is irreligious and measures God by our infirmity.
sources.quote: since a thing ineffable and proper to God’s nature, and known to Him alone and to the Son, this he demands to be explained in words
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to inquire how God begets the Son and what the manner of the divine generation is?

question: Can God the Father's love for believers change, increase, diminish or be withdrawn, for example because of their failures?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No, not in itself. God's love is the eternal purpose and act of his will, and it is no more changeable than God himself. It had no beginning, will have no end, and cannot be heightened or lessened by anything in us. It varies only in its fruits, such as graces and comforts, and in its manifestation to our hearts by the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: The love of God in itself is the eternal purpose and act of his will. This is no more changeable than God himself: if it were, no flesh could be saved
sources.raw_question: Can God the Father's love for his people increase or diminish?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. Though believers change every day, his love does not change. If any provocation could turn it away, it would have ceased long ago. This unchangeableness is what carries the Father into his infinite patience and forbearance toward them.
sources.quote: Though we change every day, yet his love changeth not. Could any kind of provocation turn it away, it had long since ceased.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father's love for believers be changed or withdrawn because of their failures?

question: In inquiring into the Trinity, should one begin with Scripture and faith before seeking rational understanding?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner This Work Proposes to Discourse Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine says he must first show from the authority of Holy Scripture whether the faith is so, and only then offer reasonings to the arguers. Proper order begins from faith. The Church's piety is a medicine that heals the mind's feebleness so it can perceive unchangeable truth and not fall rashly into false opinion.
sources.quote: First, however, we must demonstrate, according to the authority of the Holy Scriptures, whether the faith be so.
sources.raw_question: In inquiring into the Trinity, should one begin with Scripture and faith before rational demonstration?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Conclusion of the Book with a Prayer, and an Apology for Multitude of Words.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine directs his inquiry by the rule of faith drawn from Scripture, seeking to see with the understanding what he already believed. He describes the search as continuing, praying for strength to seek God's face ever more and to find Him more and more.
sources.quote: Directing my purpose by this rule of faith, so far as I have been able, so far as Thou hast made me to be able, I have sought Thee, and have desired to see with my understanding what I believed
sources.raw_question: Should the doctrine of the Trinity be accepted by faith first, before it is sought through understanding?

question: Can a person who professes Christianity but lives in worldliness, unholiness and sin truly have communion with God the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. Owen holds that many who bear the name of Christians hold communion with their lusts and the world, not with God. Communion with the Father is shown in holiness and obedience, so walking with God is a matter of power, not outward form. Of such professors it is truer to say that God is not in all their thoughts than that they have communion with him.
sources.quote: Do not many very evidently hold communion with their lusts and with the world, and yet would be thought to have a portion and inheritance among them that are sanctified?
sources.raw_question: Can a person who professes Christianity but lives in worldliness and sin truly have communion with God the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. Communion with the Father is wholly inconsistent with loose walking, because God is a consuming fire and holiness becomes his presence, so an unclean spirit cannot draw near to him. Scripture says that whoever claims fellowship with him while walking in darkness lies, and whoever claims to know him without keeping his commandments is a liar. The love of the Father is itself a powerful motive to holiness.
sources.quote: Communion with the Father is wholly inconsistent with loose walking.
sources.raw_question: Can a person truly have communion with God the Father while living in unholiness and sin?

question: Does the Son's taking mortal flesh mean that the Father alone, and not the Son, has immortality?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Entire Trinity Invisible.
sources.answer: No. If the Son is called mortal because he took our flesh, then it is not the Father alone who has immortality, for the Word through whom all things were made also has it. The Son did not lose his immortality by taking mortal flesh. Not even the human soul dies along with the body.
sources.quote: For He did not therefore lose His immortality, because He took mortal flesh; seeing that it could not happen even to the human soul, that it should die with
sources.raised_by_detail: those who understand 'who only hath immortality' of the Father alone
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's taking mortal flesh mean that the Father alone, without the Son, has immortality?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Against Those Who Believed the Father Only to Be Immortal and Invisible. The Truth to Be Sought by Peaceful Study.
sources.answer: No. The Word, by whom all things were made, did not lose his immortality by taking mortal flesh. Not even the human soul dies with the body, as the Lord teaches. Moreover, the Holy Spirit never took flesh. So if mortality came only from flesh, the Spirit would be immortal, and the text could not apply to the Father alone.
sources.quote: For He did not therefore lose His immortality, because He took mortal flesh; seeing that it could not happen even to the human soul, that it should die with the body
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's taking mortal flesh mean that the Father alone, and not the Son, has immortality?

question: What does Luke's genealogy of Christ, running backward from the Lord to Adam, signify?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXII.—Christ assumed actual flesh, conceived and born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: Luke runs the genealogy backward to show that Christ regenerated the ancient fathers into the life of God, and not they him. Christ, the First-begotten of the dead, receives the fathers into his bosom and gives them new life. The order of the list therefore shows that he is the source of their new life, not merely their descendant.
sources.quote: Wherefore also Luke, commencing the genealogy with the Lord, carried it back to Adam, indicating that it was He who regenerated them into the Gospel of life, and not they Him.
sources.raw_question: Why does Luke's genealogy of Jesus begin with the Lord and run backward to Adam?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXII.—Christ assumed actual flesh, conceived and born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: Luke's genealogy traces the Lord's generation back to Adam through seventy-two generations, connecting the end with the beginning. This signifies that Christ has summed up in himself all nations dispersed from Adam onward. He also sums up all languages and generations of men, together with Adam himself.
sources.quote: implying that it is He who has summed up in Himself all nations dispersed from Adam downwards, and all languages and generations of men, together with Adam himself
sources.raw_question: What does Luke's genealogy of Christ, traced back to Adam, signify?

question: What does Luke's genealogy, ending 'Adam, which was the son of God,' show about God being ungenerate, that is, having no father or cause?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Luke traces Christ's fleshly lineage back to Adam and calls him 'the son of God' because Adam had no earthly father. This makes it plain that God, from whom Adam came, does not have His subsistence from another. To be the son of no one is to be without cause, and that is what 'ungenerate' means. Being son of someone is not a man's essence, so being ungenerate is likewise not God's essence.
sources.quote: makes it obvious to every reader’s intelligence with regard to the Deity, that He, from Whom Adam was, has not Himself His subsistence from another, after the likeness of the human lives just given.
sources.raw_question: How does Luke's genealogy ending with Adam as 'the son of God' illustrate the meaning of 'ungenerate' as applied to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It shows that God is the son of no one, that is, he has no father. Each name in the catalogue refers to a father preceding the person named, so Luke's list is plainly a list of fathers. When it reaches God it stops, so the implied word 'father' may be added to the confession that the Ungenerate is from no one. No father can be named for the Ungenerate, since if one could be, he would not be ungenerate.
sources.quote: What says our great Basil? That the Ungenerate One is from no father. For the conclusion to be drawn from the mention of fathers in the preceding genealogy permits the word father, even in the silence of the evangelist, to be added to this confession of faith.
sources.raw_question: What does Luke's genealogy, ending 'Adam, which was the son of God,' imply about God having a father?

question: Did Christ's Godhead undergo change or separation when his soul was separated from his body in his Passion and death?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: No. His Godhead is immutably the same before the Incarnation, in the flesh, and after the Passion. In his death the Godhead separated the soul from the body for a season. Yet it was never itself separated from either of them, and it then rejoined them.
sources.quote: For His Godhead, alike before taking flesh and in the flesh and after His Passion, is immutably the same, being at all times what It was by nature, and so continuing for ever.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ's Godhead undergo change or separation in his Passion and death?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
