sources.answer: No. His Godhead is immutably the same before taking flesh, in the flesh, and after the Passion. In death it severed the soul from the body for a season without being separated from either. It then reunited them as the first-fruits of the resurrection.
sources.quote: For His Godhead, alike before taking flesh and in the flesh and after His Passion, is immutably the same, being at all times what It was by nature, and so continuing for ever.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ's Godhead undergo change when His human soul was separated from His body in death?

question: Is the God who made the promise to Abraham the same God who acts through Jesus Christ to bring believers into the kingdom, or a different God as Marcion claimed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VIII.—Vain attempts of Marcion and his followers, who exclude Abraham from the salvation bestowed by Christ, who liberated not only Abraham, but the seed of Abraham, by fulfilling and not destroying the law when He healed on the Sabbath-day.
sources.answer: No. The God who promised Abraham is the same God who, through Jesus Christ, brings Abraham and his seed, the Church, into the kingdom of heaven. Christ himself says that many will recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom. So those who invent another God besides the God of the promise blaspheme God and shut themselves out of the kingdom.
sources.quote: those who disallow his salvation, and frame the idea of another God besides Him who made the promise to Abraham, are outside the kingdom of God, and are disinherited from [the gift of] incorruption
sources.raw_question: Is the God who made the promise to Abraham a different God from the one who brings believers into the kingdom of heaven through Jesus Christ, as Marcion claimed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VII.—Recapitulation of the foregoing argument, showing that Abraham, through the revelation of the Word, knew the Father, and the coming of the Son of God. For this cause, he rejoiced to see the day of Christ, when the promises made to him should be fulfilled. The fruit of this rejoicing has flowed to posterity, viz., to those who are partakers in the faith of Abraham, but not to the Jews who reject the Word of God.
sources.answer: Yes. He is one and the same God, who called Abraham and gave him the promise. As Creator, He prepares through Christ lights in the world, namely believers from among the Gentiles. These fulfil the promise that Abraham's seed would be as the stars of heaven.
sources.quote: He is therefore one and the same God, who called Abraham and gave him the promise. But He is the Creator, who does also through Christ prepare lights in the world
sources.raw_question: Was the God who made the promise to Abraham the same God who acts through Christ in the Church?

question: Can things be predicated relatively of one another and yet each exist as a substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: Yes. Part and whole are said relatively, since every part belongs to some whole and a whole is a whole by having its parts. Yet both part and whole are bodies, so they also exist substantially. Likewise mind, knowledge, and love are both referred to one another and exist substantially.
sources.quote: But since both part and whole are bodies, these things are not only predicated relatively, but exist also substantially.
sources.raw_question: Can things be predicated relatively to one another and yet also exist as substances?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: Yes. Love and knowledge are said relatively to the lover and knower, yet each exists in its own substance. This is unlike color, which has no substance of its own. It is like two friends, who are substances as men but are called friends relatively.
sources.quote: but as two friends are also two men, which are substances, while they are said to be men not relatively, but friends relatively.
sources.raw_question: Can things be predicated relatively of one another and yet each exist as a substance?

question: Can God's pardoning mercy toward sinners be known apart from Jesus Christ, for example from nature or creation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Pardoning mercy comes by Christ alone and is wholly treasured up in him and revealed by him. Had God not set forth Christ, neither angels nor men could have apprehended that there was any such grace of pardoning mercy in God's nature. Adam, having sinned, had no reserve for mercy but hid himself.
sources.quote: Had not God set forth the Lord Christ, all the angels in heaven and men on earth could not have apprehended that there had been any such thing in the nature of God as this grace of pardoning mercy.
sources.raw_question: Can God's pardoning mercy toward sinners be known apart from Jesus Christ, for example from nature or creation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Pardoning mercy comes by Christ alone and is wholly treasured up in him and revealed by him. Adam, after sinning, had no hope of mercy and hid himself. Pardoning mercy is God's free acceptance of a sinner on the basis of satisfaction made to his justice in Christ's blood. No discovery of it is consistent with God's glory except as related to that satisfaction.
sources.quote: Pardoning mercy is God’s free, gracious acceptance of a sinner upon satisfaction made to his justice in the blood of Jesus; nor is any discovery of it, but as relating to the satisfaction of justice, consistent with the glory of God.
sources.raw_question: Can God's pardoning mercy be known apart from Christ?

question: Is the doctrine of Christ's satisfaction undermined because the word 'satisfaction' does not occur in Scripture?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: No. The word is not found in Scripture literally or syllabically, but the thing it signifies is asserted there beyond all modest contradiction. Neither Hebrew nor Greek has a word that exactly matches it, yet both Testaments use equivalent words and phrases that express the very thing meant. These include kopher and pidyon in the Old Testament and lutron, antilutron, apolutrosis and hilasmos in the New.
sources.quote: it is not so ῥητῶς, or syllabically, — but it is κατὰ τὸ πρᾶγμα ἀναντιῤῥήτως; the thing itself intended is asserted in it, beyond all modest contradiction.
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine of Christ's satisfaction undermined by the fact that the word 'satisfaction' does not occur in Scripture?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Owen grants that the term belongs to the explanation of the truth rather than to its express revelation, and he will not contend about the word. Yet it properly expresses the great effect of Christ's death, and it follows as the natural conclusion of what Scripture expressly declares.
sources.quote: It does, indeed, properly express and connote that great effect of the death of Christ which, in the cause before us, we plead for.
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine of Christ's 'satisfaction' invalidated because the word 'satisfaction' does not appear expressly in Scripture?

question: Is it unjust or unworthy of God to punish the innocent Christ and require satisfaction rather than simply pardoning?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. To pardon sinners becomes God's grace, and to do it through Christ also becomes his holiness and righteousness. Christ was personally innocent, but was made sin for us and, as mediator and surety, answered for the sins of those he saved; and sin truly deserves punishment in God's justice.
sources.quote: The Lord Christ was personally innocent; but “he who knew no sin was made sin for us,” 2 Cor. v. 21.
sources.raw_question: Is it unjust or unworthy of God to punish the innocent Christ and require satisfaction for sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. To pardon sinners becomes God's goodness and grace, and to do it through Christ becomes his holiness and righteousness as well. Christ was personally innocent but was made sin for us, and as mediator and surety of the covenant he answered for the sins of those he undertook to save, giving himself a ransom.
sources.quote: To pardon sinners, is a thing becoming the goodness and grace of God; to do it by Christ, that which becomes them, and his holiness and righteousness also
sources.raw_question: Is it unworthy of God to punish the innocent Christ or require satisfaction for sin rather than simply pardoning?

question: Is God's vindictive justice against sin revealed more clearly in Christ's sufferings than in the law, providence, the curse on creation, and past judgments such as the fall of the angels?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. God has shown his anger against sin through the law, through providence, through casting down the fallen angels, and through destroying Sodom. Yet his justice shines far more clearly in Christ. There it appears that justice could not be turned away from sinners without a propitiation, and the penalty laid on Christ displays it most gloriously.
sources.quote: cannot but discover much of God’s vindictive justice and his anger against sin. But far more clear doth this shine into us in the Lord Christ
sources.raw_question: Is God's vindictive justice against sin revealed more clearly in Christ than in the law, providence, and past judgments?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. The cursed world and the damned angels give some insight, but they are nothing compared with seeing the Son, the wisdom and power of God and always beloved of the Father, fear, tremble, sweat, pray and die on the cross because our sins met upon him. This, above all things, manifests the severity of God's justice.
sources.quote: To see him who is the wisdom of God, and the power of God, always beloved of the Father; to see him, I say, fear, and tremble, and bow, and sweat, and pray, and die
sources.raw_question: Is God's vindictive justice revealed more clearly in Christ's sufferings than in the curse on creation and the fall of the angels?

question: Should obscure or ambiguous passages of Scripture be interpreted in light of clear passages rather than by other ambiguities or used to build doctrine?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter X.—Perverse interpretations of Scripture by the heretics: God created all things out of nothing, and not from pre-existent matter.
sources.answer: No. No question can be solved by means of another question that itself awaits solution. Ambiguities and enigmas must be resolved by what is manifest, consistent and clear.
sources.quote: no question can be solved by means of another which itself awaits solution; nor, in the opinion of those possessed of sense, can an ambiguity be explained by means of another ambiguity, or enigmas by means of another greater enigma
sources.raw_question: Can obscure or ambiguous passages of Scripture be explained by appeal to other ambiguities or greater enigmas?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVII.—Proper mode of interpreting parables and obscure passages of Scripture.
sources.answer: Obscure parables must not be used to construct doctrine; they should be interpreted by what Scripture states clearly and unambiguously. If everyone interprets parables by private inclination, no one will possess the rule of truth, and there will be as many conflicting systems as interpreters. Interpreting them by the clear texts keeps the body of truth entire and harmonious.
sources.quote: For in this way no one will possess the rule of truth; but in accordance with the number of persons who explain the parables will be found the various systems of truth, in mutual opposition to each other
sources.raw_question: Should obscure parables and ambiguous passages of Scripture be used to establish doctrine about God, or should they be interpreted in light of clear passages?

question: Could Christ have become God through his exaltation, such as by receiving the Spirit, working miracles, rising from the dead and receiving all power?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: No. The question concerns Christ's nature, whereas these things concern his state and condition. Exaltation no more changes his nature than his humiliation, poverty and death did; just as Melchizedek's priesthood would not make him more than a man by nature.
sources.quote: But all men see that the inquiry is about the nature of Christ, and this answer is about his state and condition. Now this changes not his nature on the one hand, no more than his being humbled, poor, and dying, did on the other.
sources.raw_question: Could Christ become God by degrees through receiving the Spirit, working miracles, rising from the dead and receiving all power?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. To be made God in the proper sense is absolutely impossible. The opponents themselves can only say he was made God in an improper sense, which contradicts the plain affirmation that the Word was God in the beginning.
sources.quote: he was made God, and that not properly, which is absolutely impossible, but in an improper sense!
sources.raw_question: Could a being properly be made God, so that Christ became God through exaltation?

question: Is the inner word of the mind the same as the spoken word or other outward sign (sound, gesture, letter) used to communicate it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > We Conceive and Beget the Word Within, from the Things We Have Beheld in the Eternal Truth. The Word, Whether of the Creature or of the Creator, is Conceived by Love.
sources.answer: No. The word stays within the speaker. Voice or another bodily sign is only applied to it as a ministry, so that something similar may be produced in the hearer's mind. The outward sign serves the inner word, which never leaves the speaker.
sources.quote: we apply to the word, remaining within us, the ministry of the voice or of some bodily sign, that by some kind of sensible remembrance some similar thing may be wrought also in the mind of him that hears
sources.raw_question: Is the inner word of the mind the same thing as the spoken word or outward sign used to communicate it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Concerning the Word of the Mind, in Which We See the Word of God, as in a Glass and an Enigma.
sources.answer: They are only signs. The inner word is neither Greek nor Latin nor of any tongue. To make it known to others, a sound is offered to the ear or a nod to the eye, and letters are signs of spoken words, which are themselves signs of our thoughts. Peter's beckoning to the beloved disciple in John 13 shows that a gesture is a way of speaking to the sight.
sources.quote: letters have been invented that we might be able to converse also with the absent; but these are signs of words, as words themselves are signs in our conversation of those things which we think.
sources.raw_question: Are spoken sounds, gestures, and written letters the word itself, or only signs of the inner word?

question: Does communion with Christ, in which believers exchange their sins for his righteousness by faith, make repentance unnecessary or license sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. This communion produces quite other effects than those supposed. It casts out only legal, servile repentance full of dread, while its very foundation is a deep daily consideration of sin's guilt and vileness, which cannot coexist with a lack of godly sorrow; so it promotes gospel repentance rather than hindering it.
sources.quote: the foundation of this communion is laid in that which they suppose it overthrows.
sources.raw_question: Does the exchange of our sins for Christ's righteousness make repentance unnecessary and license sin so that grace may abound?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. Owen grants that this communion casts out a legal repentance full of dread, terror and self-love. It cannot hinder gospel repentance, which is godly sorrow for sin and turning from it, arising from faith, love and abhorrence of sin with respect to Father, Son and Spirit. The very foundation of this communion is a deep, daily sense of sin's guilt and vileness. A heart continually filled with self-abhorrence for sin cannot be a stranger to godly sorrow.
sources.quote: Here is the mistake, — the foundation of this communion is laid in that which they suppose it overthrows.
sources.raw_question: Does communion with Christ, in which believers bring their sins to him and receive his righteousness by faith, make repentance unnecessary?

question: What does Christ's statement in John 5:19 that the Son does 'whatsoever' the Father does, and does them 'likewise', reveal about the Son's true birth and His unity of nature with the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: 'Whatsoever' and 'the same' show that the Son does all the Father's works and none outside them, so He shares the one divine nature. 'Likewise' shows that the works are done in the manner of Another, which rules out isolation and proves a true birth. Thus Father and Son possess an indivisible Divinity without being confused.
sources.quote: Two truths are combined in one proposition; that His works are done likewise proves His birth; that they are the same works proves His nature.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's saying that the Son does 'whatsoever' the Father does 'likewise' (John 5:19) prove both the Son's true birth and His unity of nature with the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: It reveals both the Son's true birth and his unity of nature with the Father. That the works are the same proves the Son shares the one Divine nature, so none of his acts are different from or outside the Father's. That they are done 'likewise', in imitation of Another, proves he does not work in isolation but is born from the Father. Thus two truths are combined in one proposition.
sources.quote: Two truths are combined in one proposition; that His works are done likewise proves His birth; that they are the same works proves His nature.
sources.raw_question: What does the statement in John 5:19 that the Son does 'whatsoever' the Father does, and does them 'likewise', reveal about the Son's relation to the Father?

question: Does the phrase 'Christ died for our sins' imply that he bore their punishment as a substitute and made satisfaction for them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Yes. Predicates are regulated by their subjects, and it would be absurd to say someone dies in the stead of sins. So dying for sins can only mean bearing or answering for the sins of the sinner in whose stead one dies.
sources.quote: it is ridiculous to say that one dies in the stead of sins, the meaning can be no other but the bearing or answering of the sins of the sinner in whose stead any one dies.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'Christ died for our sins' show substitution even more clearly than 'Christ died for us'?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Yes. Owen argues that Christ died not only for us but for our sins. The phrase can only mean either bearing their punishment or expiating their guilt, and either sense implies the whole doctrine of satisfaction. He says anyone who can give the words another sense would be as great as Apollo, the author of the ambiguous oracles of old.
sources.quote: he so died for us as that he also died for our sins; that is, either to bear their punishment or to expiate their guilt (for other sense the words cannot admit)
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's dying for our sins imply that he bore their punishment and made satisfaction for them?

question: Was Christ properly a priest and his death a proper, real sacrifice for sin, rather than only metaphorically so?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes, it was a proper propitiatory sacrifice. Scripture expressly calls it an offering and sacrifice and calls Christ a priest, never intimating these are spoken only metaphorically. Moreover, the real legal sacrifices of the old law were instituted as types of Christ's sacrifice, and it would be strange for true sacrifices to represent something that was not itself a true sacrifice.
sources.quote: And it is nowhere intimated, much less expressed, that these things are not spoken properly, but metaphorically only.
sources.raw_question: Was the death of Christ a proper, real sacrifice for sin rather than merely a metaphorical one?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Christ was properly a priest, and his death was a proper propitiatory sacrifice. Scripture expressly says he offered himself as a sacrifice and calls him a priest, and it nowhere says this is meant only metaphorically. The real sacrifices of the old law were types of his sacrifice, and real types cannot represent something unreal. Making everything metaphorical would leave a merely metaphorical redemption, justification and salvation.
sources.quote: It is expressly called so in the Scripture; wherein he is said to “offer himself, to make his soul an offering, to offer himself a sacrifice,”
sources.raw_question: Was Christ properly a priest, and was his death a proper sacrifice, or were these only metaphorical, with his sacrifice consisting in his appearing in heaven?

question: Was Christ's death, like human death, a punishment for sin?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: No. For fallen humans, death is punishment because the spirit, having willingly left God, must leave the body against its will. Christ's spirit did not leave his flesh against his will but because he willed, when he willed, and as he willed, which shows his death came through no punishment of sin.
sources.quote: the spirit of the Mediator showed how it was through no punishment of sin that He came to the death of the flesh, because He did not leave it against His will, but because He willed, when He willed, as He willed.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's bodily death a punishment for sin, as human death is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Devil the Mediator of Death, Christ of Life.
sources.answer: No. We came to death through sin, but Christ came to it through righteousness. Therefore our death is the punishment of sin, while His death was made a sacrifice for sin. As Mediator of life, He met us at the end we had reached, but not by the way we had come.
sources.quote: For we, indeed, came to death through sin; He through righteousness: and, therefore, as our death is the punishment of sin, so His death was made a sacrifice for sin.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's death, like ours, a punishment for his own sin?

question: What is required for a sinner's acceptance with God, and is the removal of guilt through Christ's death sufficient by itself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: No. Removing guilt only takes away the cause of quarrel; the old quarrel may be laid aside without new friendship begun. One may be not a sinner and yet not righteous enough to have a right to the kingdom of heaven, as Adam had no right to life merely by innocence but had to 'do this' and live. A positive righteousness must also be reckoned to us.
sources.quote: The old quarrel may be laid aside, and yet no new friendship begun; we may be not sinners, and yet not be so far righteous as to have a right to the kingdom of heaven.
sources.raw_question: Is the removal of the guilt of sin through Christ's death sufficient by itself to complete a sinner's acceptance with God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Two things are required. First, satisfaction must be made for our disobedience and God must be atoned toward us, which could only happen by undergoing the penalty of the law. Christ's death does this, since God made him sin and a curse for us. By it we are absolved from guilt, from the sentence of the law and from God's wrath. Second, the righteousness of the law must be fulfilled, which Christ does by his life.
sources.quote: That satisfaction be made for our disobedience, — for whatever we had done which might damage the justice and honour of God; and that God be atoned towards us: which could no otherwise be, but by undergoing the penalty of the law.
sources.raw_question: What is required for a sinner's acceptance with God, and how does the death of Christ provide it?

question: Can God's attributes, such as Ungeneracy, Fatherhood, Power and Goodness, be ordered in a temporal sequence, so that God first had one and later acquired another?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. Humans acquire accomplishments one after another in time, but this cannot be said of God. All God's attributes, Fatherhood, Ungeneracy, Power, Imperishability, Goodness and the rest, form one compact whole with no interval of time between them. So it is blasphemy not to attribute Fatherhood to God always.
sources.quote: then it would not be so manifestly absurd to think that one of His names has precedence of another name, and to talk of His being first Ungenerate, and after that having become Father.
sources.raw_question: Can God's attributes, such as ungeneracy and Fatherhood, be acquired in a temporal sequence, so that one name of God precedes another?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. All attributes that piety ascribes to God are held together in one compact whole, and none can be separated from the others by any interval of time as preceding or following. Every adorable attribute in Him is simultaneously expressed in His everlastingness, since time and measurement have no place in the Eternal.
sources.quote: You cannot take one of these and separate it in thought from the rest by any interval of time, as if it preceded or followed something else; no sublime or adorable attribute in Him can be discovered, which is not simultaneously expressed in His everlastingness.
sources.raw_question: Can God's attributes (Ungeneracy, Fatherhood, Power, Goodness, etc.) be ordered in a temporal sequence, so that God first had one and later acquired another?

question: Does the fact that the invisible God appeared to the prophets, and in different forms, mean that the God they saw was a different God from the invisible Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter X.—Unity of the faith of the Church throughout the whole world.
sources.answer: Irenaeus affirms that the invisible God did manifest Himself to the prophets, not under one form but differently to different individuals. This variety does not imply different gods; explaining its reason belongs to the deeper understanding of the one faith.
sources.quote: understand for what reason God, though invisible, manifested Himself to the prophets not under one form, but differently to different individuals
sources.raw_question: How can God, who is invisible, have appeared to the prophets in different forms?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: No. The heretics who say this misunderstand what prophecy is. Prophecy foretells things to come, so the prophets announced beforehand that God would be seen by men. The God they spoke of is the one God and Father, who is incomprehensible in His greatness but lets Himself be seen out of His love.
sources.quote: they did not, as some allege, [proclaim] that He who was seen by the prophets was a different [God], the Father of all being invisible. Yet this is what those [heretics] declare, who are altogether ignorant of the nature of prophecy.
sources.raw_question: Was the God seen by the prophets a different God from the invisible Father of all?

question: Does the 'mission' or sending of the Word by the Father mean that God the Word changed place or moved from one location to another?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. God does not change place like creatures, since he fills heaven and earth. Scripture calls the Word's union with the Man a 'mission' because through that union the invisible nature was made known to men through the visible flesh.
sources.quote: For God changes not place, like us who are hidden in places, when in the fashion of our littleness He displays Himself in His existence in the flesh; for how should He, who fills the heaven and the earth?
sources.raw_question: Does the 'mission' or sending of the Word by the Father mean that God the Word changed place or moved from one location to another?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. God, who fills heaven and earth, does not move from place to place as we do. 'Mission' is the name given to the Word's uniting with the man, through whom the invisible nature is made known to men through the visible. Hence 'the Father that sent Me' means the Word's presence in the flesh.
sources.quote: For God changes not place, like us who are hidden in places, when in the fashion of our littleness He displays Himself in His existence in the flesh; for how should He, who fills the heaven and the earth?
sources.raw_question: Does the 'mission' or 'sending' of the Word imply that God changes place?

question: Is the word 'God' in Scripture always a relative word of office, or is its metaphysical sense (the supreme self-existent divine nature) its principal and ordinary sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 24: Whether Gal. iv. 8. may not be enough to determine the dispute betwiat us; since it obliged the Doctor to confess, that Christ as by nature truly God, as truly
sources.answer: Yes. The opponent himself concedes it may be the principal sense, though not the only one, and Clarke denies this only for prudential reasons. If the metaphysical sense is ever meant when 'God' is said of the Father, there is no reason it should not always be meant of him. It would then be the ordinary sense, giving good grounds to read it the same way when 'God' is said of the Son.
sources.quote: if the metaphysical sense be ever intended, when the word God is spoken of the Father, no good reason can be assigned why it should not be so always, when spoken of the same Person
sources.raw_question: Is the metaphysical sense of 'God' (a supreme self-existent Being) the principal sense of the word in Scripture?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 24: Whether Gal. iv. 8. may not be enough to determine the dispute betwiat us; since it obliged the Doctor to confess, that Christ as by nature truly God, as truly
sources.answer: No. Dr. Clarke's claim that 'God' is always a relative word of office has no proof or ground. If the metaphysical sense is ever intended when 'God' is said of the Father, there is no reason it should not always be meant of him. And if that is the usual scriptural sense, it is fair to argue that the same sense is meant when 'God' is said of the Son in like circumstances.
sources.quote: if the metaphysical sense be ever intended, when the word God is spoken of the Father, no good reason can be assigned why it should not be so always, when spoken of the same Person
sources.raw_question: Is the word 'God' in Scripture always a relative word of office rather than ever carrying a metaphysical sense of the divine nature?

question: Does Christ's calling himself "the door" and "the way" (John 10:9, John 14:6) prove that the essence of God can be comprehended by human beings?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > The tenth book discusses the unattainable and incomprehensible character of the enquiry into entities. And herein he strikingly sets forth the points concerning the nature and formation of the ant, and the passage in the Gospel, “I am the door” and “the way,” and also discusses the attribution and interpretation of the Divine names, and the episode of the children of Benjamin.
sources.answer: No. The Gospel text speaks of entering, being saved, going in and out, and finding pasture, each of which has its own distinct meaning, and none of them can properly be identified with knowledge of the divine essence. Taking them all as signifying the essence would make the simple, uncompounded Godhead composed of incompatible elements. The titles describe Christ's saving work for us, not a grasp of the Father's essence.
sources.quote: For assuredly one cannot, by uttering all these phrases that disagree one with another in signification, intend to indicate by incompatible terms that Essence which is simple and uncompounded.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's calling himself "the door" and "the way" (John 10:9, John 14:6) prove that the essence of God the Father can be comprehended by human beings?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > The tenth book discusses the unattainable and incomprehensible character of the enquiry into entities. And herein he strikingly sets forth the points concerning the nature and formation of the ant, and the passage in the Gospel, “I am the door” and “the way,” and also discusses the attribution and interpretation of the Divine names, and the episode of the children of Benjamin.
sources.answer: No. Gregory replies that the Gospel does not admit this meaning; Christ says that whoever enters by him 'shall be saved, and shall go in and out and find pasture,' which speaks of salvation and nourishment, not of comprehending the divine essence.
sources.quote: “Since then,” he says, “the Lord was named ‘a door,’ it follows from hence that the essence of God may be comprehended by man.” But the Gospel does not admit of this meaning.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's calling himself 'the door' and 'the way' imply that the essence of God can be comprehended by man?

question: Could humanity be saved by anyone less than God (by its own power, a mere man, or an angel), or must the Saviour be God himself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XX.—God showed himself, by the fall of man, as patient, benign, merciful, mighty to save. Man is therefore most ungrateful, if, unmindful of his own lot, and of the benefits held out to him, he do not acknowledge divine grace.
sources.answer: Salvation must come from the Lord himself, not from a mere man nor from an angel. Isaiah announces that neither an elder nor an angel, but the Lord himself will save his people because he loves them. Since angels are without flesh and a mere man cannot save, the Saviour must be God who also comes in flesh.
sources.quote: “Neither an elder, nor angel, but the Lord Himself will save them because He loves them, and will spare them: He will Himself set them free.”
sources.raw_question: Could humanity be saved by a mere man or by an angel, or must the Saviour be the Lord God himself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XX.—God showed himself, by the fall of man, as patient, benign, merciful, mighty to save. Man is therefore most ungrateful, if, unmindful of his own lot, and of the benefits held out to him, he do not acknowledge divine grace.
sources.answer: Only by God. The Lord himself, Emmanuel born of the Virgin, is the sign of salvation, because people could not be saved by their own instrumentality. Paul confesses that no good dwells in his flesh and names the grace of Jesus Christ as deliverer. Isaiah says God 'will come Himself, and will save us.'
sources.quote: the Lord Himself, who is Emmanuel from the Virgin, is the sign of our salvation, since it was the Lord Himself who saved them, because they could not be saved by their own instrumentality
sources.raw_question: Can human beings be saved by their own power, or must the Saviour be God himself?

question: Does the shedding of Christ's blood by itself cleanse believers from the pollution of sin, or must that blood also be applied (sprinkled), and what role does the Holy Spirit play in this?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: It must also be applied. Owen distinguishes the shedding of blood, without which there is no remission, from the sprinkling of blood, without which there is no actual purification. Hebrews compares Christ's blood to sacrificial blood as offered, which is its purchase, and also as sprinkled, which is its application unto holiness.
sources.quote: The eyeing of the blood of Christ as shed will not of itself take away pollution.
sources.raw_question: Does the shedding of Christ's blood by itself purify the believer from the pollution of sin, or must that blood also be applied?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Both, in different ways. The cleansing of believers' natures, persons and duties is grounded wholly in Christ's death. It is accomplished meritoriously by the shedding of his blood and efficiently by its sprinkling. That sprinkling comes from the communication of the Holy Ghost, whom Christ purchased for us and promises to us. The Spirit is the pure water with which we are sprinkled.
sources.quote: meritoriously, this work is done, by the shedding of the blood of Christ; efficiently, by its sprinkling. The sprinkling of the blood of Christ proceedeth from the communication of the Holy Ghost; which he promiseth to us, as purchased by him for us.
sources.raw_question: How does the death of Christ cleanse believers from sin: by the shedding of his blood, by its sprinkling, or both, and what role does the Holy Spirit play?

question: Does Christ, by his blood, only atone for and justify believers from the guilt of sin, or does he also purify and sanctify them from its defilement?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: He does both. He makes them not only accepted but acceptable, not only purchasing love for them but making them lovely; he came by water and blood. Justification flows from his life and death as a propitiatory sacrifice, sanctification from his death as a purchase and his life as an example.
sources.quote: He doth not only justify his saints from the guilt of sin, but also sanctify and wash them from the filth of sin.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ only justify believers from the guilt of sin, or does he also sanctify them from its defilement?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: It does both. As offered, it was a sacrifice of atonement; as poured out, it was also a sacrifice of purification. It fulfils all the typical rites of fleshly cleansing, so it has a spiritually cleansing and sanctifying power in itself. That is why Zechariah calls it a fountain opened for sin and uncleanness, able to cleanse from all sin and finally present the saints holy and without blemish.
sources.quote: It was a sacrifice not only of atonement, as offered, but also of purification, as poured out.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's blood only a sacrifice of atonement for guilt, or does it also purify and sanctify believers from the defilement of sin?

question: Does the phrase 'From the womb, before the morning star I begat Thee' imply that God has bodily members or begets through a physical process, and what does it teach about the Son's origin?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: It does not imply that God has bodily members. God uses language taken from bodily functions to help human understanding. The phrase teaches that the Only-begotten was truly born of the Father's own Godhead in a divine, ineffable sense, and was not created out of nothing.
sources.quote: Thus, when He says, From the womb, He is teaching us that His Only-begotten was, in the Divine sense, born, and did not come into existence by means of creation out of nothing.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'I bore Thee from the womb before the morning star' imply that God has bodily members, and what does it teach about the Son's origin?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. God is Spirit, not composed of parts, and subject to no natural necessity; the image of the womb is a concession to our weak understanding, given not to describe the manner of the birth but to declare the fact of generation. It enlightens the mind without making God subject to bodily causes.
sources.quote: He instructed our understanding by an example from causes which work among us: not to give an example of the manner of birth, but to declare the fact of generation; not that the example might prove Him subject to necessity, but that it might enlighten our mind.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's saying 'From the womb, before the morning star I begat Thee' imply that God has bodily parts or begets through a physical process?

question: Does Scripture reveal the Holy Spirit as God and a proper object of faith and worship?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Scripture must reveal the Spirit as the object of our faith, worship and obedience because of the divine excellencies that alone justify religious worship and the hope of reward. Owen maintains that Scripture does this fully: it reveals the Spirit's divine existence, divine excellencies and divine operations, and in this faith can rest.
sources.quote: this is done to the utmost satisfaction in the revelation that is made of the divine existence, divine excellencies, and divine operations of the Spirit
sources.raw_question: What must Scripture reveal about the Holy Spirit to establish that he is God and a proper object of faith and worship?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture reveals that he is peculiarly to be believed in and may peculiarly be sinned against, since blasphemy against him is unforgivable. He is also the great author of all grace in believers and of order in the church. This marks him as God and the object of divine worship.
sources.quote: Moreover, it is revealed that he is peculiarly to be believed in, and may peculiarly be sinned against, [as] the great author of all grace in believers and order in the church.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a proper object of faith and worship, one who can be sinned against?

question: When early Fathers such as Tertullian and Theophilus say the Son appeared and spoke 'in the name' or 'by the authority' of God the Father, do they mean he was only the Father's representative rather than truly God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: They meant that the Son acted under the character common to the Godhead, not under his own distinct character as Son, Messiah or Mediator. That character has since been reserved in a special way to the Father. The Son could rightly bear it because, as Son of God, he is truly God and Almighty in his own right. So the title "Lord God" belonged to him as much as "Messiah" did later.
sources.quote: Christ therefore, in these, or the like texts, is not represented under his own peculiar character; but under such a character as is common to the Godhead, to the Father and him too.
sources.raw_question: What did Fathers such as Theophilus and Tertullian mean in saying that the Son appeared and spoke "in the person" or "in the name" of God the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. The next words, 'with us Christ is also understood in the person of Christ', show that Christians receive him under the Messiah character in addition to the common divine character. Formerly he was adored as strictly and truly God, consubstantial with the Father, and not merely as the Father's representative.
sources.quote: not merely as representative of God the Father, or as invested with his authority, but as strictly and truly God, consubstantial with God the Father
sources.raw_question: Does Tertullian's statement that the Son who appeared was God 'by the authority and name' of the Father mean he was only God representatively, not truly God?

question: If Christ were merely the natural son of Joseph, could he be greater than Solomon, Jonah, or David?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: No. Had he been generated from the same human seed as these men and merely been their descendant, there would be no ground for his being greater than them. That Christ claims to be greater than Solomon and Jonah, and that he blessed Peter for confessing him the Son of the living God, shows he was not the son of Joseph.
sources.quote: For if He were the son of Joseph, how could He be greater than Solomon, or greater than Jonah, or greater than David, when He was generated from the same seed, and was a descendant of these men?
sources.raw_question: If Christ were merely the natural son of Joseph, could he be greater than Solomon, Jonah, or David?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: No. Born of the same seed as these men and descended from them, He could not be greater than them. Nor would Peter have been called blessed for confessing Him the Son of the living God.
sources.quote: For if He were the son of Joseph, how could He be greater than Solomon, or greater than Jonah, or greater than David, when He was generated from the same seed, and was a descendant of these men?
sources.raw_question: If Christ were the son of Joseph, could He be greater than Solomon, Jonah or David?

question: Did Christ fear to suffer His Passion?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Christ rebuked Peter as 'Satan' when he deprecated the Passion, went forth to meet His captors, and proclaimed His willingness to suffer. One who presses toward something cannot be said to fear it, since whatever we fear we avoid.
sources.quote: Do the godless say He feared? But He proclaimed with His own lips His willingness to suffer.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ fear to suffer His Passion?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. His words cannot signify fear if his actions show confidence. He sharply rebuked Peter as 'Satan' for trying to turn him from the Passion. He went out to meet the armed band, and they fell back before his majesty.
sources.quote: Do you suppose, heretic, that the Lord of glory feared to suffer? Why, when Peter made this error through ignorance, did He not call him ‘Satan’ and a ‘stumbling-block?’
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who deny Christ is God
sources.raw_question: Did Christ fear his suffering, as heretics claim on the basis of certain of his words?

question: Did God appear to Abraham in his own substance, while appearing to Moses only through an angel?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: No. Genesis itself shows that the Lord who appeared to Abraham at Mamre was seen in three men, who must be confessed to be angels. Scripture's silence about an angel in some passages does not prove that God appeared in His own substance.
sources.quote: how will they be able to explain that God was seen in three men, except they confess that they were angels, as that which follows also shows?
sources.raw_question: Did God appear to Abraham in His own substance, even though He appeared to Moses through an angel?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: No. The same mode of appearance holds for both: though Genesis says "the Lord appeared" to Abraham without mentioning an angel, the narrative shows angels were the means. At Mamre the Lord was seen in three men, who must be confessed to be angels. At the sacrifice of Isaac, the voice that speaks for God is expressly called "the angel of the Lord."
sources.quote: will they therefore venture to say that the vision and voice granted to Moses was wrought by an angel because it is so written, but that God appeared and spake in His own substance to Abraham because there is no mention made of an angel?
sources.raw_question: Did God appear to Abraham in his own substance, while appearing to Moses only through an angel?

question: Is everything said of God said according to His substance, or are some things said of God relatively?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Argument of the Arians is Refuted, Which is Drawn from the Words Begotten and Unbegotten.
sources.answer: No. Not everything said of God is said according to substance, though nothing is said of him according to accident. If the Arians insist that everything is said according to substance, Scripture's statements of oneness and equality would establish the consubstantiality they deny. Once they admit that some things are said not according to substance, terms like begotten and unbegotten can be understood in that way.
sources.quote: Or if this is not said according to substance, then something is said of God not according to substance, and therefore we are no longer compelled to understand unbegotten and begotten according to substance.
sources.raw_question: Is everything that is said of God said according to substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance.
sources.answer: Not everything is said according to substance. Some predicates, such as good and great, are said of God in respect to Himself and so according to substance. Others are said relatively, in respect to something not Himself: He is called Father in respect to the Son, and Lord in respect to the creature that serves Him.
sources.quote: some things are also predicated of Him relatively, i.e. not in respect to Himself, but to something not Himself, as He is called Father in respect to the Son, and Lord in respect to the creature that serveth Him
sources.raw_question: Is everything said of God said according to His substance, or are some things said of God relatively?

question: Does the Israelites' being 'baptized unto Moses' put that baptism on a par with Christian baptism into the Spirit, or lessen the grace given in it?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Objection that some were baptized unto Moses and believed in him, and an answer to it; with remarks upon types.
sources.answer: No. The baptism unto Moses was the baptism of the law, a shadow and type, and Scripture commonly uses "Moses" to mean the law. A type foreshadowing the reality does not diminish the reality, so the rich gift of regeneration through the Spirit is not lessened by its shadow.
sources.quote: So then, even if men were baptized unto Moses, it does not follow that the grace given of the Spirit in baptism is small.
sources.raw_question: Does being 'baptized unto Moses' imply that the grace of the Holy Spirit given in Christian baptism is small?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Objection that some were baptized unto Moses and believed in him, and an answer to it; with remarks upon types.
sources.answer: No. The two have only the name in common. The sea gave no remission of sins, renewal of life, or spiritual gift. Those baptized unto Moses did not die and rise with Christ or put on the new man.
sources.quote: Why then do you compare baptisms which have only the name in common, while the distinction between the things themselves is as great as might be that of dream and reality
sources.raw_question: Is baptism unto Moses comparable in reality to Christian baptism into the Spirit?

question: Does the meaning of an act of religious worship depend on the worshipper's inward intention, so that worship given to a creature regarded only as a creature could be innocent, or is its meaning fixed by God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: It is fixed by God, not by the worshipper's intention. To suppose that worship takes its quality from the worshipper's meaning is to begin at the wrong end. God has not left us free to make worship high or low at discretion. Out of pity for human weakness and to prevent confusion, he has made all religious worship his own, so it is sovereign of course. It signifies the divinity and sovereignty of its object, and giving it to a creature is idolatry.
sources.quote: You imagine that acts of religious worship are to derive their signification and quality from the ¢utention and meaning of the worshippers ; whereas the very reverse of it is the truth. Their meaning and signification is fixed and determined by God himself
sources.raw_question: Does the meaning of an act of religious worship depend on the worshipper's intention, or is it fixed by God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. When the Lycaonians would have sacrificed to Paul and Barnabas, the apostles did not tell them to correct their intentions; they forbade the sacrifice altogether. The angel in Revelation likewise told John to worship God, and Christ told the Devil that all religious worship belongs to God. Worship is not equivocal, and a right intention cannot make it lawful to offer it to creatures.
sources.quote: did not tell them that sacrifice was of equtvocal meaning; and that they might proceed in it, provided only that they would rectify their intentions, and consider them as apostles only; but they forbade them to sacrifice to them at all.
sources.raw_question: Does the meaning of an act of worship depend on the inward intention of the worshipper, so that worship directed to a creature becomes innocent if the creature is regarded only as a creature?

question: What is the relation between faith and understanding in inquiring into God and the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > In What Way We Must Inquire Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: Faith is the starting point and understanding is what is sought. In matters to be believed, authority must be held fast; in matters to be understood, truth must be sought out. So one may doubt without unbelief and affirm without rashness. Knowledge begun from faith will be perfected only after this life.
sources.quote: Let us doubt without unbelief of things to be believed; let us affirm without rashness of things to be understood: authority must be held fast in the former, truth sought out in the latter.
sources.raw_question: What is the relation between faith and understanding in inquiring into the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > God, Although Incomprehensible, is Ever to Be Sought. The Traces of the Trinity are Not Vainly Sought in the Creature.
sources.answer: Faith seeks and understanding finds, as the prophet says, "Unless ye believe, ye shall not understand." Yet understanding still seeks the God whom it finds. Man has understanding precisely so that he may seek after God.
sources.quote: Faith seeks, understanding finds; whence the prophet says, “Unless ye believe, ye shall not understand.” And yet, again, understanding still seeks Him, whom it finds
sources.raw_question: What is the relation between faith and understanding in seeking God?

question: Can the testimonies of the early Church Fathers count as genuine proof of what the Church believed about the Trinity, or is Scripture the only admissible proof?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: They are genuine proofs, though inferior and collateral to Scripture. Just as we can prove the opinions of ancient philosophical sects from their extant books, we can prove the faith of early Christians from the books they left. So the Fathers give a real, at least probable, proof of a matter of fact, namely what the Church believed from the beginning.
sources.quote: The proof from Church-writers is an additional, inferior proof; but still a proof it is, probable at least, of something, as to fact ; and not barely an dllustration of a dogma, or doctrine.
sources.raw_question: Can the testimonies of the early Church Fathers count as genuine proof of what the Church believed about the Trinity, or are they mere illustrations of doctrine?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: They may be admitted as inferior or collateral proofs. Scripture remains the stronger and authentic proof. But the Church writers give additional, probable evidence of what the Church believed from the beginning, just as surviving books show what philosophical sects held. They do not determine articles of faith on their own, yet they are a strong presumptive proof that an interpretation contrary to them is not the true one.
sources.quote: The proof from Church-writers is an additional, inferior proof; but still a proof it is, probable at least, of something, as to fact ; and not barely an dllustration of a dogma, or doctrine.
sources.raw_question: In matters of faith about the Trinity, may the testimonies of the Church Fathers be admitted as any kind of proof, or is Scripture the only admissible proof?

question: Was Christ, the Word of God, present and active among the righteous of the Old Testament before his incarnation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXV.—Both covenants were prefigured in Abraham, and in the labour of Tamar; there was, however, but one and the same God to each covenant.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is present with all those who were from the beginning approved by God, because God granted them His Word to be present with them. Thus patriarchs and prophets sowed the word concerning Christ, and they rejoice together with the Church in Christ's kingdom.
sources.quote: in the kingdom of Christ, who is present with all those who were from the beginning approved by God, who granted them His Word to be present with them.
sources.raw_question: Was the Word of God (Christ) present with the righteous of the Old Testament before the incarnation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXI.—Abraham’s faith was identical with ours; this faith was prefigured by the words and actions of the old patriarchs.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ, through his patriarchs and prophets, was even then prefiguring and announcing future things. He fulfilled his part in advance in God's dispensations and trained his inheritance to obey God. This is why the patriarchs' actions carry meaning, since with God nothing is without purpose.
sources.quote: who at that time, indeed, by means of His patriarchs and prophets, was prefiguring and declaring beforehand future things, fulfilling His part by anticipation in the dispensations of God
sources.raw_question: Was Christ the Word already active in the Old Testament before his incarnation?

question: Is Christ's sonship founded solely on his miraculous conception by the Virgin Mary and his incarnation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Those who refer the generation only to the incarnation are clearly condemned by Scripture, many passages of which cannot be accounted for by the miraculous conception alone. Moreover, all Christian writers from Barnabas and Clement of Rome to Nicaea unanimously speak of a higher, antecedent sonship, and generally ground worship of Christ upon it. The birth from the Virgin belongs rather to his condescension than to the supreme excellence of his sonship.
sources.quote: many places whereof can never fairly be accounted for by the miraculous conception solely: besides that from Barnabas and Clemens Romanus, down to the Counceil of Nice, all the Christian writers speak unanimously of a higher, antecedent sonship
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's sonship founded solely on his miraculous conception by the Virgin Mary?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Those who interpret the generation as referring to the incarnation alone stand clearly condemned by Scripture. Many Scripture passages cannot fairly be explained by the miraculous conception alone. All Christian writers from Barnabas and Clement of Rome down to Nicaea speak unanimously of a higher, prior sonship, and generally base the Son's worship on it.
sources.quote: such as interpret the generation of the Jast only, stand, I think, "clearly condemned by Scripture ; many places whereof can never fairly be accounted for by the miraculous conception solely
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's sonship be referred only to his miraculous conception and incarnation?

question: Why does the human mind err about its own nature, mistaking itself for something corporeal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Why the Soul is Enjoined to Know Itself. Whence Come the Errors of the Mind Concerning Its Own Substance.
sources.answer: Love is so strong that the mind drags along the bodily things it has long loved, even when it turns to think of itself. It cannot carry the bodies themselves into its incorporeal nature, so it forms images of them out of its own substance. Then it binds itself so closely to these images that it takes itself to be the very things they picture.
sources.quote: such is the strength of love, that the mind draws in with itself those things which it has long thought of with love, and has grown into them by the close adherence of diligent study, even when it returns in some way to think of itself
sources.raw_question: Why does the mind err about its own substance, mistaking itself for something corporeal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > How the Soul Inquires into Itself. Whence Comes the Error of the Soul Concerning Itself.
sources.answer: Because the mind dwells with love on corporeal things, their images cohere with it so closely that it cannot separate them from itself. When it tries to think of itself alone, it fancies itself to be that without which it cannot think of itself, namely those bodily images. This confusion is its uncleanness and the source of its error.
sources.quote: And herein consists its uncleanness; since, while it strives to think of itself alone, it fancies itself to be that, without which it cannot think of itself.
sources.raw_question: Why does the human mind err about its own nature, for example by imagining itself to be something bodily?

question: Did the Spirit's descent on Christ at his baptism in the Jordan promote, reward, or perfect the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: No. It was not a promotion of the Word but was for our sanctification. Because Christ bore our body, the descent was really a descent upon us, so that we might share His anointing and become temples of the Spirit. When He was washed and received the Spirit as man, we were washed in Him and made recipients of the Spirit through Him.
sources.quote: it is very plain that the Spirit’s descent on Him in Jordan was a descent upon us, because of His bearing our body. And it did not take place for promotion to the Word
sources.raw_question: Did the Spirit's descent on Christ at the Jordan promote or perfect the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: No. The descent took place because the Word bore our body, so it was a descent upon us for our sanctification, not a promotion of the Word. When the Lord as man was washed in Jordan, we were washed in him. When he received the Spirit, we through him were made recipients of it.
sources.quote: it is very plain that the Spirit’s descent on Him in Jordan was a descent upon us, because of His bearing our body. And it did not take place for promotion to the Word, but again for our sanctification
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit's descent upon Christ at his baptism in the Jordan show that the Word was promoted or rewarded with the Spirit?

question: If the Holy Spirit is the divine love rather than the divine understanding, how can understanding be attributed to the Spirit as a Person?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is the love of the understanding both objectively and subjectively: God loves the understanding, and the understanding flows out in love, so it is not a blind love. Because the whole divine essence flows out and subsists in this act, the Son (the divine understanding) is in the Spirit, so the Spirit may truly be said to know and search all things, even the deep things of God.
sources.quote: The understanding is so in the Spirit that the Spirit may be said to know, as the Spirit of God is truly and perfectly said to know and to search all things, even the deep things of God.
sources.raw_question: Can understanding be predicated of the Holy Spirit if the Spirit is the divine love rather than the divine understanding?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: The Spirit has understanding because the three Persons mutually indwell one another. The Son, who is the divine understanding, is in the Spirit, just as the Spirit is in the Father and the Son. Likewise the Father understands because the Son is in Him, and loves because the Spirit is in Him. Moreover, this love is the love of the understanding, both in what it loves and in where it comes from, so it is not a blind love.
sources.quote: the Holy Ghost or the Divine essence subsisting is Divine, but understands because the Son the Divine Idea is in Him.
sources.raw_question: If a person is something with understanding and will, how can the Holy Spirit, identified with divine love, be a Person who has understanding?

question: Did the Ante-Nicene writers hold that the Son is the Lord God, Jehovah, the only God and the God of Israel who appeared and spoke in the Old Testament?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Yes. The Ante-Nicene writers generally understood these Old Testament texts of Christ, so the second Person is Jehovah, the Mighty God, the only God besides whom there is no God. Yet this is not exclusive of the Father, any more than the Father's being such excludes the Son; together they are the one Supreme God.
sources.quote: All this, I say, Christ is, according to the doctrine of those early times: not exclusive of the Father, any more than the Father is such, exclusive of the Son; but together with the Father
