sources.raw_question: According to the Ante-Nicene writers, is the Son the 'Lord God', 'Jehovah', 'Only God' and 'God of Israel' spoken of in Old Testament texts?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Yes. The Ante-Nicene writers in general applied Old Testament texts that certainly speak of the God of the Jews to the Person of Christ. Examples include the theophanies to Adam, Abraham, Jacob and Moses, the divine name "I Am," and the Jehovah texts of the Psalms and Isaiah. Waterland argues this proves that, in their doctrine, the second Person is the Lord God Almighty, Jehovah, and the God besides whom there is no other. He is so together with the Father, not to the exclusion of the Father.
sources.quote: It is well known, that they ever looked upon the Son, as the God of the Jews, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
sources.raw_question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers hold that the Son was the God of the Jews, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who appeared and spoke in the Old Testament?

question: Does the unforgivability of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit show that the Holy Spirit cannot be counted among created things?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: Yes. No one thinks that injuring a creature cannot be forgiven in any way. Yet Christ says blasphemy against the Holy Ghost will never be forgiven. Since an offence against him is avenged by eternal punishment, he is above all things and not one of them.
sources.quote: certainly it follows from this that the Holy Spirit cannot be reckoned amongst all things, but that He is above all things, an offence against Whom is avenged by eternal punishment.
sources.raw_question: Does the unforgivable sin of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit show that he cannot be numbered among created things?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: Yes. No one would think that injuring a creature could never be forgiven, yet the Lord says blasphemy against the Spirit is never forgiven, here or hereafter. An offence avenged by eternal punishment shows that the Spirit is not among "all things" but above all things.
sources.quote: certainly it follows from this that the Holy Spirit cannot be reckoned amongst all things, but that He is above all things, an offence against Whom is avenged by eternal punishment.
sources.raw_question: Does the unforgivability of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit show that the Holy Spirit cannot be counted among created things?

question: Did the Word in becoming man assume a complete human nature, including a human soul as well as a body?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > The second book declares the Incarnation of God the Word, and the faith delivered by the Lord to His disciples, and asserts that the heretics who endeavour to overthrow this faith and devise other additional names are of their father the devil.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ was made like us in all things except sin, taking upon Himself manhood in its entirety, with soul and body. He did so so that our salvation might be accomplished by means of both.
sources.quote: He was like us in all things, in that He took upon Him manhood in its entirety with soul and body, so that our salvation was accomplished by means of both
sources.raw_question: Did the Word in becoming man assume a complete human nature, including a human soul as well as a body?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: No. Christ came to seek and save what was lost, and what was lost was the whole man, soul and body, so He took the whole sheep and left no part of our nature unassumed. Scripture nowhere says the Creator took flesh without a soul. On the contrary, it speaks of His soul and calls Him a man, which means soul and body together.
sources.quote: carries home on His shoulders the whole sheep, not its skin only, that He may make the man of God complete, united to the deity in body and in soul.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word in becoming man assume only a human body without a human soul, as Eunomius claimed?

question: Does the finitude of the created world show that creating requires only finite power, so that a creature could create?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. The opponent confuses infinite extent of power (reaching infinitely many things) with infinite degree of power. Granted that if creation were infinite in extent the world would be infinite, this is irrelevant; the real question is whether producing out of nothing even a single small thing is an act proper to God alone, exceeding any finite power.
sources.quote: The question is, whether the creating, that is, producing out of nothing, any one single thing, however small in extent, be not an act proper to God only; exceeding any finite power ἢ incommunicable to any creature.
sources.raised_by_detail: Dr. Clarke's defender (the 'Country Clergyman' / Dr. Whitby's school)
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the created world is finite in extent show that the power needed to create it was only finite, so that a creature could create?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. If that reasoning held, even the Father could never give proof of infinite power, and St. Paul's argument from creation to God's eternal power and Godhead would be inconclusive. The objection confuses extent of power ad intra (degree) with extent ad extra (exercise): an infinite degree of power may be needed to create even a grain of sand, though the outward act reaches only to the thing made.
sources.quote: It may require an infinite degree of power to create a grain of sand ; though the eatent of that outward act reaches no further than the thing created.
sources.raw_question: Does the finitude of the created world show that creating does not require infinite power?

question: Is God's giving of himself as an all-sufficient God, to be enjoyed by creatures as their blessedness, revealed in creation or only in Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Only in Christ. Creation shows God's sufficiency to communicate goodness in its outward effects, since he made all things good and perfect in their kind. But God's giving himself as an all-sufficient God, to be enjoyed and to make creatures blessed, is revealed alone in Christ. In Christ he is a Father and a God in covenant, who promises to give himself to believers as their exceeding great reward.
sources.quote: his giving himself as an all-sufficient God, to be enjoyed by the creatures, to hold out all that is in him for the satiating and making them blessed, — that is alone discovered by and in Christ.
sources.raw_question: Is God's giving of himself to be enjoyed by creatures as their blessedness revealed in creation, or only in Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Only in Christ. Creation shows God's all-sufficiency to communicate goodness, since he made all things good and perfect in their kind. But his giving himself to be enjoyed as an all-sufficient God, satisfying and blessing his creatures, is discovered only by and in Christ. In Christ he is a Father and a God in covenant, who promises to give himself as their exceeding great reward.
sources.quote: his giving himself as an all-sufficient God, to be enjoyed by the creatures, to hold out all that is in him for the satiating and making them blessed, — that is alone discovered by and in Christ.
sources.raw_question: Is God's all-sufficiency to be enjoyed by his creatures discovered in creation, or only in Christ?

question: Did Christ save sinners by substituting himself in their place and suffering what they deserved?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Yes. Both classical usage of 'dying for another' and the nature of the act show that one who offers to die for a guilty person substitutes himself to bear what that person deserved. The apostle himself appeals to this common human notion in Romans 5:7-8. Owen holds that denying this sense of Christ's sufferings would, so far as he can see, overthrow the whole gospel.
sources.quote: let an appeal be made to the common reason and understandings of all men, whether the intention of this his dying for another be not, that he substitutes himself in his stead, to undergo what he should have done
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says Christ died 'for' sinners, does this mean he substituted himself in their place to undergo what they should have suffered?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. By God's appointment the incarnate Son put himself in the room of those he was to save. Scripture says he was made sin for us, became a curse for us, and died the just for the unjust. Owen says these expressions undeniably show substitution in suffering, which is what is meant by his satisfaction.
sources.quote: All these expressions undeniably evince a substitution of Christ as to suffering in the stead of them whom he was to save; which, in general, is all that we intend by his satisfaction
sources.raw_question: Did Christ save sinners by substituting himself and suffering in their place?

question: Can Christ be truly called God by office and authority without being God by nature and 'the most high God', as the Socinians claim?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. 'Most high God' is not a title distinguishing one god among others but a descriptive attribute of the one true God denoting his sovereignty. To say Christ is God but not the most high God is the same as saying he is God but not the true God, which places him among false gods; whereas Scripture calls him 'over all, God blessed for ever.'
sources.quote: To say, then, that Christ indeed is God, but not the most high God, is all one as to say he is God, but not the most holy God, or not the true God; and so they have brought their Christ into the number of false gods
sources.raw_question: Can Christ be truly called God by office and authority, though not God by nature and not 'the most high God', as the Socinians claim?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Owen calls this pretence empty and vain. The title 'most high God' (Gen. 14) expresses God's sovereignty and dominion. Like God's other attributes, it describes the one divine subject rather than marking out some higher God. So whoever is truly God is the most high God, and there is no lesser deity by office in subordination to him.
sources.quote: Now, as other attributes of God, it is not distinctive of the subject, but only descriptive of it. So are all other excellencies of the nature of God.
sources.raw_question: Can Christ be truly God by office and exaltation without being the most high God by nature, as the Socinians claim?

question: Is God's Mind distinct from God the Father, so that treating it as separate (with its own origin) would make God a compound being?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: Yes. In God, thought is Logos and Logos is Mind, and Mind comprehending all things is the Father Himself, so God thinks exactly what He speaks. To give God's mind a special origin makes God one thing and the original Mind another. That is to declare Him a compound being.
sources.quote: He, therefore, who speaks of the mind of God, and ascribes to it a special origin of its own, declares Him a compound Being, as if God were one thing, and the original Mind another.
sources.raw_question: Does assigning God's Mind a separate origin of its own make God a compound being?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: No. The Father of all is not compound. Nous is the Father, and the Father is Nous. So whatever is ascribed to his Mind is ascribed to the Father himself, and passion attributed to his Mind would be passion in the Father.
sources.quote: For the Father of all is not to be regarded as a kind of compound Being, who can be separated from his Nous (mind), as I have already shown; but Nous is the Father, and the Father Nous.
sources.raw_question: Is God the Father a compound being who can be separated from his own Mind (Nous)?

question: Does Genesis 1:6-7 ('God said, Let there be a firmament... and God made the firmament') distinguish two Persons, the God who speaks and the God who makes, and is that distinction one of Person only or also of nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. The words "Let there be a firmament" show the Father speaking, while "And it was so... God made" reveals a distinct Agent who executes. God from Whom are all things gives the order, and God through Whom are all things carries it out, matching the Apostle's confession of one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ. Both are confessed under the one Name of God.
sources.quote: God, from Whom are all things, gives the order for creation which God, through Whom are all things, executes. Under one and the same Name we confess Him Who gave and Him Who fulfilled the command.
sources.raw_question: Does the Genesis account of creation ("God said, Let there be a firmament... and God made the firmament") distinguish two Persons, God from Whom and God through Whom all things are made?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Only in Person. The text makes no difference of power or nature and does not change the name. Under the one title 'God' it presents the One who speaks and the One who creates. Its language thus teaches the true Godhead of the Creator rather than taking it away.
sources.quote: it introduces no other distinction than that of Person. It indicates no difference of power or nature, and makes no change of name. Under the one title of God it reveals, first, the thought of Him Who spoke, and then the action of Him Who created.
sources.raw_question: Does Genesis 1:6-7 ('God said, Let there be a firmament... and God made the firmament') distinguish the speaker and the maker in nature or only in Person?

question: Who speaks the words of Deuteronomy, 'See, see that I am God, and there is no God beside Me': the Father alone or the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No, they are spoken by God the Only-begotten. The sense of the passage and the Apostle show this whole discourse is the Son's. Paul applies the words 'Rejoice, O ye nations, with His people' from the same song to Christ, the root of Jesse.
sources.quote: That godless heresy must not assign these words to God, the unbegotten Father, is clear by the sense of the passage and by the evidence of the Apostle who, as we have already stated, has taught us to understand this whole discourse as spoken by God the Only-begotten.
sources.raw_question: Are the words 'See, see that I am God, and there is no God beside Me' in Deuteronomy spoken by the Father alone?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: The Only-begotten Son. The sense of the passage and the Apostle's testimony show it. The Apostle refers the words "Rejoice, O ye nations, with His people" from the same discourse to Christ, the root of Jesse in whom the Gentiles hope. So the whole discourse must be understood as spoken by God the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: That godless heresy must not assign these words to God, the unbegotten Father, is clear by the sense of the passage and by the evidence of the Apostle who, as we have already stated, has taught us to understand this whole discourse as spoken by God the Only-begotten.
sources.raw_question: Who is the speaker of Deuteronomy's words "See, see that I am God, and there is no God beside Me": the unbegotten Father or the Only-begotten Son?

question: Is Christ the only source of all spiritual revelation, wisdom, and saving knowledge of God given to believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. All spiritual revelation is by Christ, who is the true Light that lightens every man, the Day-spring and Sun, so that no light can be but by him. As Mediator he makes known to his friends everything the Father has committed to him to be revealed.
sources.quote: All spiritual revelation is by Christ. He is “the true Light, that lighteth every man that comes into the world,” John i. 9.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ the source of all spiritual revelation and saving knowledge of God given to believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. Colossians 2:3 states that in Christ are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. There is no wisdom without the knowledge of God, and that knowledge is shut up in Christ. So true wisdom can be obtained only from him. In him we see the glory of God.
sources.quote: The sum of what is contended for is asserted in terms, Col. ii. 3, “In him are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.”
sources.raw_question: Is all true wisdom and knowledge, including the saving knowledge of God, found only in Christ?

question: Is Christ present in believers, through receiving his flesh in the Eucharist, by a true union of nature or only by agreement of will?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Christ is in believers naturally. The Word was truly made flesh, and believers truly receive his flesh in the sacrament, so he abides in them by nature. Since the Father in Christ and Christ in us make us one, whoever denies that the Father is naturally in Christ must also deny that Christ is naturally in us.
sources.quote: Whosoever then shall deny that the Father is in Christ naturally must first deny that either he is himself in Christ naturally, or Christ in him
sources.raw_question: Is Christ in believers through a true union of nature or only through agreement of will, and what does this show about how the Father is in Christ?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: By nature. Christ says his flesh is meat indeed and his blood drink indeed, and that whoever eats and drinks abides in him and he in them. Since it is verily flesh and blood, receiving it makes Christ dwell in us naturally and us in him.
sources.quote: As to the verity of the flesh and blood there is no room left for doubt. For now both from the declaration of the Lord Himself and our own faith, it is verily flesh and verily blood.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ present in believers through the Eucharist by nature or only by agreement of will?

question: Is the habitual grace of Christ's human nature infinite?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Not absolutely infinite, since it belongs to a created nature. Yet compared to any other creature it is as the water of the sea to the water of a pond, because the Spirit was given to him without measure.
sources.quote: This habitual grace of Christ, though not absolutely infinite, yet, in respect of any other creature, it is as the water of the sea to the water of a pond or pool.
sources.raw_question: Is the habitual grace of Christ's human nature infinite?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: No. It is created grace inherent in a created, finite nature. Christ had all kinds of grace and all degrees of grace, full to the utmost capacity of a limited nature. Yet the Spirit, the fountain of grace, was given to him without measure, and the Father willed all fulness to dwell in him.
sources.quote: It is created grace that I intend; and therefore I speak of the kinds of it: it is grace inherent in a created nature, not infinite; and therefore I speak of the degrees of it.
sources.raw_question: Is the grace in Christ's human nature infinite?

question: Is the grace in Christ's human nature, however full, sufficient by itself to supply sinners' needs, or must it come from its union with his Deity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Because created grace, however full, is limited, and only infinite grace can meet sinners' needs. Owen grants that Christ's human nature had a fulness of grace far above the angels, yet as created it was finite. If it were separated from the Deity, it could supply nothing except in a moral way. Because his humanity is inseparably united to the infinite fountain of the Deity, there is all-sufficient grace in Christ.
sources.quote: yet it was not properly an infinite fulness, — it was a created, and therefore a limited fulness.
sources.raw_question: Why must the grace believers receive from Christ come from his Deity and not only from his human nature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: It must be united to his Deity. The fulness of grace in Christ's human nature, though above the measure of angels, was created and therefore limited, not properly infinite. Considered as separated from the Deity, the multitude of guilty souls drawing on it would exhaust it, and it could afford supply only in a moral way. Because the conduit of his humanity is inseparably united to the infinite fountain of the Deity, the grace in Christ is bottomless.
sources.quote: yet it was not properly an infinite fulness, — it was a created, and therefore a limited fulness. If it could be conceived as separated from the Deity, surely so many thirsty, guilty souls
sources.raw_question: Is the grace in Christ's human nature, however full, sufficient by itself to supply sinners' needs, or must it be united to his Deity?

question: Can God's intelligence have been emitted outside God, as a ray goes out from the sun?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. Whatever is sent forth from a place must pass into some other place. That would require something more ancient than God's intelligence, able to receive and contain it, just as the air must exist before the sun's ray enters it. But nothing exists beyond, or at a distance from, God into which He could send such a ray.
sources.quote: But what existence was there more ancient than the intelligence of God, into which they maintain it was sent forth? And what a vast region that must have been which was capable of receiving and containing the intelligence of God!
sources.raw_question: Can God's intelligence have been emitted outside God, as a ray goes out from the sun?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. Anything sent forth must pass into somewhere else. That would require a space or receiving medium more ancient than God's intelligence and large enough to contain it, just as the air must exist before the sun's ray. That is absurd.
sources.quote: they will indicate that there was something in existence, into which the intelligence of God was sent forth, capable of containing it, and more ancient than itself.
sources.raw_question: Can God's intelligence be emitted like a ray from the sun into some space beyond Him?

question: Do exclusive words like 'alone' or 'only', when applied to one divine Person (e.g. 'the Father alone'), separate that Person from or exclude the others?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > God is a Trinity, But Not Triple (Triplex).
sources.answer: Yes, in a qualified sense. The Father and Son are always with each other, and neither is ever alone. But just as the Trinity is called God alone even though it is always with holy spirits and souls, because they are not God with Him, so the Father is called the Father alone. This is not because He is separate from the Son but because the two together are not the Father.
sources.quote: so we call the Father the Father alone, not because He is separate from the Son, but because they are not both together the Father.
sources.raw_question: Is it proper to speak of 'the Father alone' or 'the Son alone' when the Father and the Son are always inseparably together?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. Even if the Father had been named, the Son would not be excluded. Likewise the Son, speaking as Wisdom, says 'I alone compassed the circuit of heaven' without thereby separating the Father from Himself.
sources.quote: For neither has the Son separated the Father from Himself, because He Himself, speaking elsewhere with the voice of wisdom (for He Himself is the Wisdom of God), says, “I alone compassed the circuit of heaven.”
sources.raw_question: Would words like 'only' or 'alone' applied to the Father necessarily exclude the Son?

question: Is the indestructibility of the Son the same as the indestructibility of the Father, or does the Father possess it differently or in a higher degree?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. There is a single notion of indestructibility that applies to the Father and the Son alike. The Father's indestructibility differs in no respect from the Son's. Eunomius wrongly speaks of the Father's indestructibility as though it did not belong to the Son, who is the True Life.
sources.quote: there is but one single notion in indestructibility, considered in reference to the Father and to the Son alike, and that the indestructibility of the Father differs in no respect from that of the Son
sources.raw_question: Is the indestructibility of the Father different from the indestructibility of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It is the same. Indestructibility admits no degrees, neither remission nor intension, so it has one single notion whether attributed to the Father or the Son. To be incapable of dissolution means precisely the same thing of whatever subject it is said; hence the Son shares fully in the Father's indestructibility and cannot be shown inferior on this ground.
sources.quote: that the indestructibility of the Father differs in no respect from that of the Son, no difference as to indestructibility being observable either in remission and intension, or in any other phase of the process of destruction
sources.raw_question: Is the indestructibility of the Son the same as the indestructibility of the Father, or does the Father possess it in a higher degree?

question: What does the statement that God the Father has 'sealed' the Son of Man (John 6:27) reveal about the Son's nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It means the Son displays in Himself the whole form of the Father's nature, as a seal's impression reproduces the whole figure. The analogy is imperfect, since seals involve matter, differing natures and an act of impression. Yet it shows that the Son, who gives the food of eternal life, possesses the fulness of the Father's form, displaying nothing but the form of the God who sealed Him.
sources.quote: so that what God had sealed should display in itself none other than the form of the God Who sealed it
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that the Son of Man was sealed by God the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It reveals that the Son possesses within Himself the whole fulness of the Father's form and nature. A seal reproduces in its impression the whole figure engraved on it, so what God sealed displays none other than the form of the God who sealed it. Christ used this to show that He had the power to give food unto eternal life.
sources.quote: in that He possessed within Himself all the fulness of His Father’s form, even of the God Who sealed Him: so that what God had sealed should display in itself none other than the form of the God Who sealed it.
sources.raw_question: What does the statement that the Father has 'sealed' the Son (John 6:27) reveal about the Son's nature?

question: Does the doctrine of the divine monarchy (one sole rule) exclude a real plurality of distinct divine Persons, as Praxeas argued?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. Following Tertullian, Waterland holds that monarchy signifies only one sole authority or rule, which does not require that the ruler have no son or not administer it through others. A monarch's rule is not divided or ended by taking his son as partner; and in the other sense of one principle, the Trinity also preserves unity of principle. So both senses guard the Trinity against Praxeas.
sources.quote: Here, he says, it signifies only one authority ; and he shews that, taken in that sense, it was no just objection against a Trinity of Persons.
sources.raw_question: Does the doctrine of the divine monarchy (one sole rule) exclude a real Trinity of distinct Persons, as Praxeas argued?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. As Tertullian argued against Praxeas, monarchia signifies only one sole authority, and a monarchy does not cease to be one because the ruler has a Son who shares and administers it. Having maintained both unity of principle and unity of authority, the doctrine of the Trinity is guarded against the Praxean objection.
sources.quote: Here, he says, it signifies only one authority ; and he shews that, taken in that sense, it was no just objection against a Trinity of Persons.
sources.raw_question: Does the doctrine of a single divine monarchy exclude a plurality of divine Persons?

question: Does the Son share the Father's royal throne, or is He excluded from it as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: The Son shares the Father's throne. Scripture repeatedly says that Christ sits at the right hand of God, and there are many such passages. Eunomius denies that the Son is enthroned with the Father only because he has not learnt these texts.
sources.quote: has not yet heard, “Seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God,” and many similar passages
sources.raw_question: Does the Son share the Father's royal throne, or is He excluded from it as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says plainly and many times that Christ sits at the right hand of God. Eunomius denies that the Son is enthroned with the Father only because he has never learnt these passages.
sources.quote: Seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's claim that the Father has none who shares His royal throne exclude the Son from the Father's throne?

question: Is the name Jehovah incommunicable, belonging to the one true God alone?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: Yes. If Jehovah signifies the eternal, immutable God, the name must be incommunicable, since there is but one God. Conversely, if the name is incommunicable, it can signify nothing but that one God to whom alone it is applied. The two points support and confirm each other.
sources.quote: for if Jehovah signify the eternal, immutable God, it is manifest that the name is incommunicable, since there is but one God
sources.raw_question: Is the name Jehovah incommunicable, belonging to the one true God alone?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: Yes. Several texts show that Jehovah is the incommunicable name of the one true God. This confirms the previous point: if Jehovah signifies the eternal, immutable God, it must be incommunicable since there is but one God; and if it is incommunicable, it can signify only that one God to whom it is applied.
sources.quote: for if Jehovah signify the eternal, immutable God, it is manifest that the name is incommunicable, since there is but one God; and if the name be incommunicable, then Jehovah can signify nothing but that one God to whom, and to whom only, it is applied.
sources.raw_question: Is the name Jehovah incommunicable, belonging only to the one true God?

question: Does Christ's promise that whoever keeps his word shall never see death (John 8:51) prove that he is God and not merely a man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: Yes. Never seeing death is immortality, which belongs to and is the fruit of divinity. Immortality cannot arise from what is mortal, so a merely mortal man could not grant it; since Christ's word gives immortality, he is God.
sources.quote: For every man is mortal; and immortality cannot be from that which is mortal. Therefore from Christ, as a mortal man, immortality cannot arise.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's promise that whoever keeps his word shall never see death (John 8:51) prove his divinity?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: Yes. A mortal cannot make another immortal, yet Christ's word not only announces but actually bestows immortality. Since immortality is the fruit of divinity, he who gives it proves himself God by offering what he could not give if he were only man.
sources.quote: certainly He is not man only who gives immortality, which if He were only man He could not give; but by giving divinity by immortality, He proves Himself to be God by offering divinity, which if He were not God He could not give.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's promise that whoever keeps his word shall never see death show that Christ is God and not merely a man?

question: When Scripture says of God 'Become my strong rock' or 'The Lord became a defence,' does the word 'become' imply that the one described had a beginning of being?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. If these texts are applied to the Son, the sacred writers ask one who is not originate to become a defence to them, which refers to His incarnate presence when He bore our sins. If they are applied to the Father, the Arian reasoning would force them to call God originate, which is absurd. Such words denote succour given to the needy, not a beginning of being.
sources.quote: nor do the words of Scripture in question, ‘Become,’ and ‘He became,’ denote beginning of being, but that succour which was given to the needy. For God is always, and one and the same
sources.raw_question: Since Scripture says of God 'Become my strong rock' and 'The Lord became a defence,' does the word 'become' imply that the one it describes had a beginning of being?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. God is always one and the same, without beginning and unoriginate. When the saints say God 'became' or ask him to 'become' something to them, they mean the succour and salvation that come to them from God through his Word, not any original becoming of God's essence. Ordinary human usage confirms this: one who says 'Such a one became a refuge to me' speaks of the benefit received, not of the benefactor's coming into existence.
sources.quote: they do not denote any original becoming, for God is without beginning and unoriginate, but the salvation which is made to be unto men from Him.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says of God 'Become my strong rock' or 'The Lord became a defence,' does the word 'become' imply that God the Father had a beginning of being?

question: How can God be loved before He is fully known, given that no one seems able to love what he does not know?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Our Love of the Righteous is Kindled from Love Itself of the Unchangeable Form of Righteousness.
sources.answer: No. Faith helps toward the knowledge and love of God, not as though He were altogether unknown or altogether unloved. It works so that He may be known more clearly and loved more steadfastly, since we already discern His unchangeable righteousness in the truth.
sources.quote: Therefore faith avails to the knowledge and to the love of God, not as though of one altogether unknown, or altogether not loved; but so that thereby He may be known more clearly, and loved more steadfastly.
sources.raw_question: Does faith lead us to know and love a God who is entirely unknown and unloved beforehand?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > God Must First Be Known by an Unerring Faith, that He May Be Loved.
sources.answer: Yes. Although we do not yet see God face to face, a mind that believes what it does not yet see can hope for and love what it believes. Faith, hope and charity exist precisely in such a mind, so He who is not yet known but is believed can be loved.
sources.quote: except in a mind believing what it does not yet see, and hoping and loving what it believes? Even He therefore who is not known, but yet is believed, can be loved.
sources.raw_question: Can God be loved before he is known by sight, given that no one seems able to love what he does not know?

question: Does confessing that there is one God require denying the economy, that is, the number and distinction of persons in the Godhead?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Everyone confesses that there is one God, but that confession does not require denying the economy, that is, the number and disposition of the persons. Unity and the economy stand together.
sources.quote: For who will not say that there is one God? Yet he will not on that account deny the economy (i.e., the number and disposition of persons in the Trinity).
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that there is one God rule out a plurality and ordering of persons (the 'economy') within God?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Everyone confesses that there is one God, but this does not mean denying the economy. The texts Noetus cites, read properly, show the Father speaking of and to the Son, who is in the Father as the Father is in Him.
sources.quote: when the Word was made incarnate and became man, the Father was in the Son, and the Son in the Father, while the Son was living among men.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing one God require denying the economy, that is, the number and distinction of persons in the Godhead?

question: Does the Father's creating through the Son (and the Son's perfecting through the Spirit) imply that the Father's operation is imperfect or that the Son's power is weak?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: No. The Father, who creates by his sole will, needs nothing from the Son, yet wills to act through the Son. The Son, who works according to the likeness of the Father, needs no co-operation, yet wills to perfect through the Spirit. Acting through another is a matter of will, not of deficiency.
sources.quote: The Father, who creates by His sole will, could not stand in any need of the Son, but nevertheless He wills through the Son; nor could the Son, who works according to the likeness of the Father, need co-operation
sources.raw_question: Does the Father create through the Son, and the Son perfect through the Spirit, because the Father's or the Son's operation is imperfect or needy?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. It shows neither imperfection in the Father nor feebleness in the Son, but the unity of their will. The phrase "through whom" confesses an antecedent Cause, the Father. It is not used to deny the Son's role as efficient Cause.
sources.quote: the fact that the Father creates through the Son neither constitutes the creation of the Father imperfect nor exhibits the active energy of the Son as feeble, but indicates the unity of the will
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's creating "through" the Son imply that the Father's creative work is imperfect or that the Son's power is weak?

question: Can the human mind come to see or know the Triune God by reasoning alone, apart from faith?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Infirmity of the Human Mind.
sources.answer: No. Faith that purifies the heart is required so that He who is now seen through a glass may later be seen face to face. Without that faith, understanding the most subtle disputes about the mind's nature accomplishes nothing except to condemn people by the witness of their own understanding.
sources.quote: And if they despise this faith that purifies the heart, what do they accomplish by understanding the most subtle disputes concerning the nature of the human mind, unless that they be condemned also by the witness of their own understanding?
sources.raw_question: Can subtle philosophical understanding of the human mind lead to the vision of the Triune God without faith?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner This Work Proposes to Discourse Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: No. The highest good is discerned only by the most purified minds. The eye of the human mind is weak and is dazzled by that transcendent light unless it is strengthened by the nourishment of the righteousness of faith. So those who demand rational accounts without faith cannot see it, and should blame their own minds rather than the truth.
sources.quote: the eye of the human mind, being weak, is dazzled in that so transcendent light, unless it be invigorated by the nourishment of the righteousness of faith
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind discern the triune God, the highest good, by unaided reasoning, apart from faith?

question: Did the Holy Spirit dwell in Christ fully, or only partially as in the prophets?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Next Teaches Us that the Authority of the Faith Enjoins, After the Father and the Son, to Believe Also on the Holy Spirit, Whose Operations He Enumerates from Scripture.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah prophesied that the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord would rest upon and fill Christ. Isaiah also speaks in the Lord's own person of being anointed by the Spirit, and David says God anointed him above his fellows. The Spirit thus abides entire in Christ, who is the source from whom the Spirit's gifts flow to others.
sources.quote: “And the Spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon Him, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill Him.”
sources.raw_question: Did the Holy Spirit dwell in Christ fully, as foretold by Isaiah's prophecy of the sevenfold Spirit resting upon him?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Next Teaches Us that the Authority of the Faith Enjoins, After the Father and the Son, to Believe Also on the Holy Spirit, Whose Operations He Enumerates from Scripture.
sources.answer: Fully. At Christ's baptism the Spirit came like a dove and abode on him, dwelling in Christ full and entire, not in any measure or portion. Christ is thus the source of the entire Spirit, from whom others draw streams of gifts. Isaiah foretold this in saying the Spirit of the Lord would rest upon him.
sources.quote: dwelling in Christ full and entire, and not maimed in any measure or portion; but with His whole overflow copiously distributed and sent forth
sources.raw_question: Did the Holy Spirit dwell in Christ only partially, as in the prophets, or fully?

question: Is baptism administered by the Arians valid when they use the names of Father, Son and Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. The Arians deny the true Father, because they deny what is from him and like his essence, and they deny the true Son, putting in his place a creature made out of nothing. They therefore baptize into Creator and creature rather than Father and Son, and their rite is empty. Using the names is not enough without the right faith.
sources.quote: For the Arians do not baptize into Father and Son, but into Creator and creature, and into Maker and work.
sources.raw_question: Is baptism given by the Arians valid when they use the Scriptural names of Father, Son and Holy Ghost?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No, it is empty and unprofitable. Consecration is given into the name of Father and Son. The Arians deny the true Son, who is from the Father's essence, and so they do not confess a true Father either. They name instead a Son of their own invention created out of nothing.
sources.quote: they do not confess a true Father, because they deny what is from Him and like His Essence, and deny also the true Son, and name another of their own framing as created out of nothing
sources.raw_question: Is baptism administered by the Arians valid, given that they name the Father and the Son?

question: In what sense can eternal things be said to have been, to be, and to be about to be, and does this imply that they change over time?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > What is the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge. The Worship of God is the Love of Him. How the Intellectual Cognizance of Eternal Things Comes to Pass Through Wisdom.
sources.answer: They neither have been nor shall be in a temporal sense; they simply are. They are said to have been, to be, and to be about to be only because of the eternity in which they exist, without any changeableness of times. They abide as intelligible realities in incorporeal nature, not fixed in a place as bodies are.
sources.quote: those things belong, which neither have been, nor shall be, but are; and on account of that eternity in which they are, are said to have been, and to be, and to be about to be, without any changeableness of times
sources.raw_question: In what sense do eternal things, the objects of wisdom, "have been" and "will be"?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > What is the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge. The Worship of God is the Love of Him. How the Intellectual Cognizance of Eternal Things Comes to Pass Through Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. Past, present and future tenses are applied to eternal things only because of their eternity, without any changeableness of times. They did not exist in a way that ceases, and they will not exist in a way that implies they are not yet. They always have had and always will have that very absolute being.
sources.quote: For neither have they been in such way as that they should cease to be, nor are they about to be in such way as if they were not now; but they have always had and always will have that very absolute being.
sources.raw_question: If eternal things are said to have been, to be, and to be about to be, does that imply they change over time?

question: Does worshipping a created being as God, as Eunomius' view of the Son implies, lead logically to polytheism and the deification of all creation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > The fifth book promises to speak of the words contained in the saying of the Apostle Peter, but delays their exposition. He discourses first of the creation, to the effect that, while nothing therein is deserving of worship, yet men, led astray by their ill-informed and feeble intelligence, and marvelling at its beauty, deified the several parts of the universe. And herein he excellently expounds the passage of Isaiah, “I am God, the first.”
sources.answer: Religion collapses into polytheism and idolatry. Once divinity is granted to one creature that is no higher in nature than others, nothing stops the same reasoning from passing step by step to each neighbouring creature until all things are deified. The author points to the heathen as evidence: having wondered at the parts of nature, they deified them one after another, as with Bel and the seven spheres.
sources.quote: the Divine element, once recognized in creation, will become a stepping-stone to the like conception in the case of that which is next contemplated, and that again for the next in order
sources.raw_question: What follows if a created God, with no natural prerogative above the rest of creation, is worshipped, as Eunomius' view implies?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > The fifth book promises to speak of the words contained in the saying of the Apostle Peter, but delays their exposition. He discourses first of the creation, to the effect that, while nothing therein is deserving of worship, yet men, led astray by their ill-informed and feeble intelligence, and marvelling at its beauty, deified the several parts of the universe. And herein he excellently expounds the passage of Isaiah, “I am God, the first.”
sources.answer: Yes. Once the Divine is recognized in any created thing, nothing stops the conception of Deity from passing to the next created thing and so on through all creation. The heathen show this: having deified the highest parts of creation, they extended the same error by logical sequence to the spheres, the elements, and everything useful to life. Had reverencing creation been held unlawful from the start, they would not have fallen into polytheism.
sources.quote: had the act of reverencing the creation been from the beginning even to them a thing evidently unlawful, they would not have been led astray into this deceit of polytheism
sources.raw_question: Does worshipping a created being as God (as Eunomius's view of the Son implies) lead logically to polytheism and the deification of all creation?

question: Is God's love in giving his only Son to save the world inconsistent with Christ's making satisfaction to God's offended justice?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. God's love in giving his Son is the scriptural foundation of the doctrine, and Christ's making satisfaction to God's justice is the doctrine itself, not an absurd consequence. The phrase 'God stood off in high displeasure' is not scriptural; the point is that God's righteousness and law required the penalty to be borne.
sources.quote: That God so loved the world as to give his only Son to save it, is the expression of the Scripture, and the foundation of the doctrine whose truth we contend for.
sources.raw_question: Is it inconsistent to say that God so loved the world that he gave his Son, and yet that Christ gave himself as satisfaction to offended justice?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. That God so loved the world as to give his only Son is the very foundation of the doctrine of satisfaction, not a contradiction of it. That Christ offered himself to make atonement and satisfy God's justice is the doctrine itself, not an absurd consequence. The phrase 'God stood off in high displeasure' is neither Scriptural nor suited to divine perfections; what is meant is that God's righteousness and law required the punishment due to sin to be undergone.
sources.quote: That God so loved the world as to give his only Son to save it, is the expression of the Scripture, and the foundation of the doctrine whose truth we contend for.
sources.raw_question: Is God's love in giving his only Son to save the world inconsistent with Christ's making satisfaction to God's offended justice?

question: Is the outward gospel offer of Christ's righteousness enough by itself for believers to receive it, or must Christ also send the Holy Spirit to make them partakers of it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: The outward offer is not enough; Christ must send his Holy Spirit. The declaratory tenders of the gospel are precious, but Christ knows the condition of his people in this world, and if he did not effectually invest them with his righteousness, all would be lost. So he sends his Spirit to quicken them, to make the dead hear his voice, and to work in them whatever is required to make them partakers of his righteousness.
sources.quote: He sends them his Holy Spirit, to quicken them, John vi. 63, to cause them that are “dead to hear his voice,” John v. 25; and to work in them whatever is required of them, to make them partakers of his righteousness
sources.raw_question: Is the outward gospel offer of Christ's righteousness enough by itself for believers to receive it, or must Christ also send the Holy Spirit to make them partakers of it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. The declaratory offers are precious, and rejecting them brings death. But Christ knows that the outward letter alone cannot enable anyone to receive his righteousness. So he also sends his Holy Spirit to quicken the spiritually dead and to work in them whatever is required, and in this way he effectually gives them his righteousness.
sources.quote: the Lord Christ knows that the outward letter, though never so effectually held out, will not enable any of his for that reception of his righteousness which is necessary to interest them therein
sources.raw_question: Are the gospel's outward offers and conditional promises enough by themselves to make believers partakers of Christ's righteousness?

question: Can true wisdom concerning God be found in worldly learning and civil prudence, or is it found only in Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Owen holds that God rejects both as of no use for true wisdom. Citing 1 Corinthians 1:19-20, he says God brings the understanding of the prudent to nothing and makes the wisdom of the world foolish.
sources.quote: but God rejecteth both these, as of no use at all to the end and intent of true wisdom indeed.
sources.raw_question: Do civil prudence or human learning count as true wisdom concerning God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It is found only in Christ. Worldly wisdom and learning fall short even of their own particular ends, and even when joined and improved to the utmost they cannot reach the true general end of wisdom, as Solomon shows in Ecclesiastes. Since these are the most excellent things below, wisdom is not to be sought anywhere else on earth. The crown of wisdom therefore belongs to Christ, in whom all wisdom is laid up and is attained only by an interest in him.
sources.quote: it cannot but be to no purpose to seek for it in any thing else below, these being amongst them incomparably the most excellent; and therefore, with one accord, let us set the crown of this wisdom on the head of the Lord Jesus.
sources.raw_question: Can true and solid wisdom be found in worldly learning and civil prudence, or is it found only in the Lord Jesus Christ?

question: If Christ is God and Christ died, does it follow that God died, or else that Christ is not God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And that It Does Not Follow Thence, that Because Christ Died It Must Also Be Received that God Died; For Scripture Sets Forth that Not Only Was Christ God, But Man Also.
sources.answer: No. The argument would hold only if Scripture said Christ were God alone, but Scripture teaches he is both God and man. Since the Word was made flesh, what died in Christ was the human nature, while the divinity, being immortal and impassible, remained uncorrupted. So Christ's death neither implies that God died nor disproves his divinity.
sources.quote: But when Scripture determines, as we have frequently shown, that He is not only God, but man also, it follows that what is immortal may be held to have remained uncorrupted.
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who deny Christ is God
sources.raw_question: If Christ is God and Christ died, does it follow that God died, or else that Christ is not God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That These Have Therefore Erred, by Thinking that There Was No Difference Between the Son of God and the Son of Man; Because They Have Ill Understood the Scripture.
sources.answer: No. The argument would hold only if Scripture said Christ were God alone. Scripture teaches he is both God and man, so what is immortal remained uncorrupted. The divinity is impassible while the human weakness suffers.
sources.quote: But when Scripture determines, as we have frequently shown, that He is not only God, but man also, it follows that what is immortal may be held to have remained uncorrupted.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold Christ to be man only
sources.raw_question: If Christ is God and Christ died, does it follow that God died?

question: Was it the Son, the Word of God, who appeared to Moses and said, "I have come down to deliver them" from Egypt?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XII.—It clearly appears that there was but one author of both the old and the new law, from the fact that Christ condemned traditions and customs repugnant to the former, while He confirmed its most important precepts, and taught that He was Himself the end of the Mosaic law.
sources.answer: Yes. The one who says to Moses 'I have come down to deliver them' is the Word. From the beginning it was customary for the Word of God to ascend and descend in order to save those in affliction. The Son was therefore active in the giving of the old dispensation.
sources.quote: it being customary from the beginning with the Word of God to ascend and descend for the purpose of saving those who were in affliction
sources.raw_question: Was it the Word of God, the Son, who appeared to Moses and said he had come down to deliver Israel from Egypt?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son speaks these words to Moses, for it is he who descended and ascended for the salvation of men.
sources.quote: And again, when the Son speaks to Moses, He says, “I am come down to deliver this people.” For it is He who descended and ascended for the salvation of men.
sources.raw_question: Was it the Son who spoke to Moses, saying "I am come down to deliver this people"?

question: Does Scripture's calling the speaker at the burning bush an "Angel" show that the Son is merely a messenger of the Existent and not the Existent Himself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. This confirms rather than contradicts the orthodox view: Moses called the Self-Existent "Angel" so that the words would not be referred to the Father alone, and then shows that this Angel is the Self-Existent Himself. Thus "Angel" signifies the Son as interpreter of the Father's will, while "Existent" signifies His close relation to the Father.
sources.quote: after first calling Him “Angel,” teach us in the words that follow that He is none other than the Self-Existent Himself, that the mystery concerning the Christ might be foreshown
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's calling the speaker at the burning bush an "Angel" show that the Son is merely a messenger of the Existent and not the Existent Himself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No; it confirms that He is. The prophet called the Self-Existent 'Angel' to reveal the mystery of Christ, so that the words would not be referred to the Father alone, as they would be if only the title 'Existent' appeared. As our word is the messenger of the mind's movements, so the true Word is the messenger of the Father while being Himself the Existent.
sources.quote: the prophet, wishing to make manifest to men the mystery concerning Christ, called the Self-Existent “Angel,” that the meaning of the words might not be referred to the Father, as it would have been if the title of “Existent” alone had been found throughout the discourse.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's mention of an angel's voice conveying the Existent's words to Moses show that the Son is not Himself the Existent?

question: Is the Father whom Jesus Christ confesses as 'Lord of heaven and earth' the Creator of the world, or some higher god such as the Gnostic Bythus or the god of Marcion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter II.—Proofs from the plain testimony of Moses, and of the other prophets, whose words are the words of Christ, that there is but one God, the founder of the world, whom Our Lord preached, and whom He called His Father.
sources.answer: He is the Creator of heaven and earth. Christ explicitly calls His Father 'Lord of heaven and earth,' which is the same title Moses, David and Isaiah give to the God who made heaven and earth. The Gnostic Bythus and the Marcionite god are inventions, while the law itself proclaims that the Lord God is one God.
sources.quote: or shall it be (what is really the case) the Maker of heaven and earth, whom also the prophets proclaimed,—whom Christ, too, confesses as His Father,— whom also the law announces
sources.raw_question: Is the Father whom Jesus Christ confesses as 'Lord of heaven and earth' the Creator of the world, or some higher god such as the Gnostic Bythus or the god of Marcion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter I.—The Lord acknowledged but one God and Father.
sources.answer: He confesses the Maker of heaven and earth as his Father. He says, 'I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth,' which identifies his Father with the Creator whom Moses, David and Isaiah proclaimed. He does not mean any invented Bythus, Mother, or Marcionite god.
sources.quote: Again, our Lord Jesus Christ confesses this same Being as His Father, where He says: “I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth.”
sources.raw_question: Whom does Jesus Christ confess as his Father: the Creator of heaven and earth, or some higher being such as the Gnostic Bythus?

question: When the Old Testament speaks of 'God and God' or 'Lord and Lord', does it imply that only one is true God and the other is God only in name?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. The Law never speaks of one true God and one not true; it calls both by the strict name God, which expresses their nature, and also speaks of God as One. Since man is created after the image of both jointly, sound reason forces the conclusion that each is true God.
sources.quote: It begins by speaking of Them first by their strict name of God; then it attributes true Godhead to Both in common. For when man, Their creature, is created after the image of Both, sound reason forces the conclusion that Each of Them is true God.
sources.raw_question: Does the Old Testament Law's speaking of 'God and God' and of 'Our image' allow the Arian distinction that the Father is true God while the Son is God only in name?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. These terms admit no difference in name or nature, since the name is a test of the nature and the nature a clue to the name. The Law reveals the Son as a distinct Person (in creation, in making man in the joint image, in the Lord judging Sodom from the Lord, in the Angel who is God) while clearly stating that they are Two without casting doubt on the true Godhead of either.
sources.quote: while the Law states clearly that They are Two, it casts no shadow of doubt upon the true Godhead of either.
sources.raw_question: When the Old Testament speaks of 'God and God' or 'Lord and Lord', does it imply that one is true God and the other is not?

question: Does rendering Philippians 2:6 as 'he did not affect (or assume) to be honoured as God' undermine the proof of Christ's true divinity from that text, for example by implying that he had no divine honour before his exaltation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
