sources.answer: No. Even granting the reading about not assuming to be honoured, it refers only to the time of his humiliation and says nothing of what he had before. John 17:5 shows that after his exaltation he received no greater glory than he had with the Father before the world was. His glory was only eclipsed during his humiliation.
sources.quote: It is very clear from John xvii. 5. that our blessed Saviour was to have no greater glory after his exaltation and ascension, than he had “ before the world was.
sources.raw_question: Does Philippians 2:6 show that Christ did not take divine honour until after his humiliation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Waterland is willing to grant his opponent that rendering. The weight of the argument lies in the preceding words, 'being in the form of God', which still signify that Christ was truly God and yet humbled himself.
sources.quote: for the stress of the cause does not seem so much to lie in the interpretation of those words, as of the words foregoing, viz. ὃς ἐν μορφῇ Θεοῦ ὑπάρχων.
sources.raised_by_detail: Dr. Clarke's school (Waterland's opponent, citing Grotius, Tillotson, Whitby, Clarke)
sources.raw_question: Does translating Philippians 2:6 as 'he did not affect to be honoured as God' undermine the proof of Christ's divinity from that text?

question: Who was the God who appeared visibly to the Old Testament saints, given that Scripture says no man has seen God at any time?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: It was the Son, the Divine Word. Since Scripture says no man has seen the Father at any time and that the only-begotten Son has declared him, yet the one who appeared as angel or man is called God and Jehovah, that being must be the Son. Therefore the Word is Jehovah God.
sources.quote: This glorious being was not God the Father, for no man hath seen him at any time. But He is declared to be Jehovah and God. Are we not compelled to acknowledge that He was the Divine Word, the Son
sources.raw_question: Who was the God who appeared visibly to the Old Testament saints, given that no man can see God and live?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: The appearances were of the Son. The theophanies, combined with the declaration that no man has seen God, are inexplicable on any other hypothesis, and are decisive when the New Testament assures us that it was the glory of the Lord Jesus that they saw. Thus Christ is God Jehovah who appeared.
sources.quote: the appearances of God Jehovah to the Old Testament saints, combined with the declaration "No man hath seen God at any time," are utterly inexplicable on any other hypothesis, and are absolutely decisive when the New Testament assures us, it was the glory of the Lord Jesus they saw
sources.raw_question: How can God have appeared to Old Testament saints when Scripture says no man has seen God at any time?

question: If Christ has fully satisfied God's justice for sins, does God still have a basis to command faith, repentance, and obedience?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Christ's satisfaction does not release the creature from its dependence on God or from the duty it owes him. That duty follows necessarily from the creature's relation to God, whether or not sin is satisfied for. God may therefore justly prescribe obedience suited to his own nature, holiness and will.
sources.quote: Christ’s satisfaction for sins acquits not the creature of that dependence on God, and duty which he owes to God, which (notwithstanding that) God may justly, and does prescribe unto him, suitable to his own nature, holiness, and will.
sources.raw_question: If Christ has fully satisfied God's justice for all sins, does God lose the right to command godliness and obedience?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Christ's satisfaction does not release the creature from its dependence on God and the duty it owes him. Obedience is a necessary consequence of the relation in which we stand to God, required whether sin is satisfied for or not, and God regulates it by his prescriptions of faith, repentance, and new obedience.
sources.quote: Christ’s satisfaction for sins acquits not the creature of that dependence on God, and duty which he owes to God, which (notwithstanding that) God may justly, and does prescribe unto him, suitable to his own nature, holiness, and will.
sources.raw_question: If Christ has fully satisfied God's justice for sins, is there any remaining basis for God to command faith, repentance, and obedience?

question: Can the Trinity be proven by reason from the claim that God's perfect self-representation must be an actual second divine reality (the argument of Keckermann and Lessing)?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Such arguments, as advanced by Keckermann and Lessing, prove too much. If God's self-representation must have the same reality as God to be perfect, then his representations of everything else must also have objective reality, which would mean the eternal co-existence of all God can conceive, and that is open pantheism.
sources.quote: It is obvious that arguments like this prove too much. If God’s representation of Himself, to be perfect, must possess the same kind of reality that He Himself possesses, it does not seem easy to deny that His representations of everything else must possess objective reality.
sources.raw_question: Does God's perfect self-consciousness require that his representation of himself be an actual second divine reality, thereby proving the Trinity by reason?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The argument proves too much: if God's representation of Himself must have the same objective reality as God to be perfect, then His representations of everything else would also have objective reality, which amounts to the eternal co-existence of all God can conceive, that is, open pantheism.
sources.quote: It is obvious that arguments like this prove too much. If God’s representation of Himself, to be perfect, must possess the same kind of reality that He Himself possesses, it does not seem easy to deny that His representations of everything else must possess objective reality.
sources.raw_question: Can the Trinity be rationally proven from the claim that God's perfect self-representation must be an actual duplication of God (the argument of Keckermann and Lessing)?

question: Why does Scripture freely use 'men' in the plural but use the word 'God' only in the singular, and does its plural usage of 'men' establish that a shared nature may properly be called plural?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. Scripture uses the prevailing custom of speech without laying down rules about the propriety of words, since no harm comes from it in that case. Where truth is at risk, however, Scripture is exact. It uses 'God' only in the singular so as not to suggest different natures in the divine essence.
sources.quote: it does not lay down a law as to the propriety of using the words in one way or another, nor does it say these things by way of giving us instruction about phrases, but uses the word according to the prevailing custom
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's use of 'men' in the plural establish that it is correct to call a shared nature plural?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: Because the plural 'men' misleads no one into thinking there are many human natures, whereas a plural 'Gods' would risk introducing the idea of different natures in the divine essence. Where truth is at risk, Scripture is not indifferent in its wording. So it studiously keeps 'God' singular, as in 'the Lord our God is one Lord.'
sources.quote: But the word “God” it employs studiously in the singular form only, guarding against introducing the idea of different natures in the Divine essence by the plural signification of “Gods.”
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture freely use 'men' in the plural but use the word 'God' only in the singular?

question: Were the dove and the fiery tongues in which the Holy Spirit appeared united to him in one person, as the Word united human nature to himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Creature is Not So Taken by the Holy Spirit as Flesh is by the Word.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit did not beatify the dove, the wind or the fire. Nor did he join them for ever to himself and his person in unity, as the Word did with the flesh taken from the Virgin Mary. These forms appeared for a time to signify him and then passed away.
sources.quote: For the Spirit did not beatify the dove, or the wind, or the fire, and join them for ever to Himself and to His person in unity and “fashion.”
sources.raw_question: Did the Holy Spirit unite the dove and the fire to his person, as the Word united human nature to himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Of the Sensible Showing of the Holy Spirit, and of the Coeternity of the Trinity. What Has Been Said, and What Remains to Be Said.
sources.answer: No. The subservient creature manifested the Spirit's substance, co-eternal and unchangeable with the Father and Son, by temporal motions and forms, but it was not united so as to be one person with Him. No one could say the creature through which the Spirit appeared as a dove or tongues is the Holy Spirit in the way the Son of God is the man born of the virgin.
sources.quote: while it was not united so as to be one person with Him, as the flesh was which the Word was made
sources.raw_question: Was the dove or the fiery tongues by which the Holy Spirit appeared united with the Spirit into one person, as the flesh was united with the Word?

question: When Christ says he has received glory or power, does this mean the divine Word lacked them beforehand, or did he already possess them?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: No. Receiving, needing and being ignorant belong to man, and since the Word became man, these things are said of Him humanly, for the flesh's sake. The Giver should not be treated as receiver nor the Dispenser to others as needy, which would divide the Word from the Father as imperfect.
sources.quote: wherefore do we consider the Giver as receiver, and the Dispenser to others do we suspect to be in need, and divide the Word from the Father as imperfect and needy, while we strip human nature of grace?
sources.raw_question: When Christ says he has received glory or power, does this mean the divine Word lacked these and was in need?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: Yes. He was always Lord of all, since all things were made by Him, and He was the Lord of glory who had glory with the Father before the world was. Before the resurrection He rebuked Satan, cast out demons, forgave sins, raised the dead and gave sight to the blind, not waiting to receive power but already possessing it.
sources.quote: Thus we must acknowledge this once for all, that nothing which He says that He received, did He receive as not possessing before; for the Word, as being God, had them always
sources.raw_question: Did Christ already possess the glory and power he speaks of receiving before he received them?

question: May human reason set the limits of faith by measuring what is possible for God, including concerning Christ, according to natural reason?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Faith rejects judging Christ by natural reason. The Apostle warns against philosophy and the rudiments of the world, because in Christ dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily, and His immeasurable eternity and omnipotence baffle the utmost efforts of the earthly mind. The work of the Infinite can only be grasped by an infinite intelligence.
sources.quote: It will not confine God within the limits which barred our common reason, nor judge after the rudiments of the world concerning Christ, in Whom dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily
sources.raw_question: Can human philosophical reason determine what is possible for God concerning Christ, or should faith reject judging Christ by the limits of natural reason?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Those who made their own feeble nature the measure of God's might and reduced divine knowledge to ordinary reason undertook to improve on God's teaching. The true work of religion is a service of obedience to revelation, not confining the infinite within human comprehension.
sources.quote: who made their own feeble nature the measure of the might of God’s nature
sources.raw_question: May human reason fix the limits of faith by reducing knowledge of God's nature to the measure of ordinary reason?

question: How can the distinction of three divine Persons (hypostases) be confessed while preserving the Monarchy, the single source and rule, of God?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: The hypostases are acknowledged as distinct and ordered. Knowledge rises from the Spirit through the Son to the Father. Conversely, natural goodness, inherent holiness and royal dignity extend from the Father through the Only-begotten to the Spirit. This order both acknowledges the hypostases and preserves the true dogma of the Monarchy.
sources.quote: the natural Goodness and the inherent Holiness and the royal Dignity extend from the Father through the Only-begotten to the Spirit. Thus there is both acknowledgment of the hypostases and the true dogma of the Monarchy is not lost.
sources.raw_question: How can confessing three hypostases be reconciled with the monarchy (single source and rule) of God?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: Christians worship "God of God." This confesses the distinction of Persons while abiding by the Monarchy. One form, united in the invariableness of the Godhead, is beheld in the Father and in the Only-begotten, so the theology is not split into a divided plurality.
sources.quote: Worshipping as we do God of God, we both confess the distinction of the Persons, and at the same time abide by the Monarchy. We do not fritter away the theology in a divided plurality
sources.raw_question: How can the distinction of divine Persons be confessed while keeping the Monarchy (the single rule and source) of God?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being named second or third in order, after the Son, imply that he is inferior in dignity?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: No. If what is second were inferior to what is first, then Scripture's 'second man, the Lord from heaven' would be inferior to the 'first man' of the earth. Likewise the spiritual, which comes afterward, would be inferior to the natural. Both conclusions are absurd, so order of naming does not imply inferior rank.
sources.quote: If then the second is subnumerated to the first, and the subnumerated is inferior in dignity to that to which it was subnumerated, according to you the spiritual is inferior in honour to the natural, and the heavenly man to the earthy.
sources.raw_question: Does being second in order imply being inferior in dignity, so that the Spirit is lesser for being named after the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who say that the Holy Ghost is not to be numbered with, but numbered under, the Father and the Son. Wherein moreover there is a summary notice of the faith concerning right sub-numeration.
sources.answer: No. If sub-numeration simply meant being counted second, rank would depend on the counter's whim, since one could just as easily start by counting the brass coin before the gold. Order of counting therefore shows nothing about the worth of what is counted.
sources.quote: But if the sub-numeration belongs to the one which is numbered second, then it is in the power of the counter to begin by counting the brass coin.
sources.raw_question: Does being named second in a series, as the Holy Spirit is named after the Father and Son, imply inferiority?

question: Does Scripture's language that God laid our iniquities on Christ and that he 'bore our sins' mean that Christ underwent the punishment due to our sins?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Yes. Christ bore our iniquities because the Lord made the iniquity of us all meet on him (Isa. 53:6), which the Septuagint renders as God delivering him up to our sins, meaning to be punished for them. He was made sin for us and bore our sins in his own body on the tree, so the chastisement of our peace was upon him in his sufferings.
sources.quote: “The Lord gave him up, or delivered him unto our sins;” that is, to be punished for them, for other sense the words can have none.
sources.raw_question: Does the way Scripture describes God laying our iniquities on Christ confirm that Christ was punished for our sins?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: It means that he underwent the punishment due to our sins. The Hebrew word sabal means to carry a weight on the shoulders, and when used of sin it always means undergoing sin's punishment, as in Lamentations 5:7, 'we have borne their iniquities.' There is no just reason to invent a new sense for the same words when they are spoken of Christ.
sources.quote: And it is never used with respect unto sin, but openly and plainly it signifies the undergoing of the punishment due unto it.
sources.raw_question: What does Scripture mean when it says that Christ 'bore our sins' or 'bore the iniquities' of many?

question: If Scripture says all things, including the world, were made by Christ, can he be merely a man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Truth is Proved from the Sacred Writings of the New Covenant.
sources.answer: No. A mere man comes after all things and so could have made nothing. Scripture says all things were made by Christ, so he must be before all things. Being prior to all things, he is God as well as man.
sources.quote: He is either before all things, since all things were by Him, and so He is justly God; or because He is man He is subsequent to all things, and justly nothing was made by Him.
sources.raw_question: If all things were made by Christ, can he be merely a man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > The Author Prosecutes the Same Argument.
sources.answer: No. The world was not made by a man; man was formed after the world. So if the world was made by Christ and he came to his own, he must be God as well as man.
sources.quote: If Christ was only man, how is the world said to have been made by Him, when the world was not by man, but man was ordained after the world?
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold Christ is only man
sources.raw_question: If Scripture says the world was made by Christ, can Christ be merely a man?

question: Why are human beings who share the same occupation counted as many, while the Persons of the Trinity who share the Godhead are not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: Among men, each worker's action is separate from the others'. Each rhetorician, for example, pleads on his own account, so his operation is distinct from theirs and they are properly called many. The divine Persons do not act in this separated way, so the ground for plural counting is missing in God.
sources.quote: since among men the action of each in the same pursuits is discriminated, they are properly called many, since each of them is separated from the others within his own environment, according to the special character of his operation
sources.raw_question: Why are human beings who share the same occupation counted as many, while the Persons of the Trinity who share the Godhead are not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: Because each of them works separately at his own task. For example, each rhetorician pleads on his own account and has no share in the others' individual actions. Since each man's action is distinct, each is set apart from the others by the special character of his own work, and so they are rightly called many.
sources.quote: each of them is separated from the others within his own environment, according to the special character of his operation.
sources.raw_question: Why are human beings who share the same occupation properly counted as many?

question: Do the Gospel statements that Christ was troubled, wept, and prayed that the cup pass from Him prove that the Son is not truly God and Word of the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Twelfthly, Matthew xxvi. 39; John xii. 27, &c. Arian inferences are against the Regula Fidei, as before. He wept and the like, as man. Other texts prove Him God. God could not fear. He feared because His flesh feared.
sources.answer: No. Being troubled and weeping are properties of human nature, which the Word took on in suffering flesh; they belong to the flesh, not to the Word's Godhead. Far from diminishing Him, they make it the greater wonder that the Word should be in such a suffering flesh and yet refrain from stopping His enemies, though He was able, being the one who hindered some from dying and raised others from the dead.
sources.quote: which do but make it the greater wonder, that the Word should be in such a suffering flesh, and neither prevented those who were conspiring against Him, nor took vengeance of those who were putting Him to death, though He was able
sources.raw_question: Do the Gospel statements that Christ 'was troubled' and 'wept' prove that the Word is not truly God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Twelfthly, Matthew xxvi. 39; John xii. 27, &c. Arian inferences are against the Regula Fidei, as before. He wept and the like, as man. Other texts prove Him God. God could not fear. He feared because His flesh feared.
sources.answer: No. These affections were not proper to the Word as Word but belonged to the flesh in which the Word was; He said these things only after the Word became flesh, that is, humanly. Just as the body's advance is called His because the body was His own, so the troubling and weeping are ascribed to Him on account of His flesh.
sources.quote: But these affections were not proper to the nature of the Word, as far as He was Word; but in the flesh which was thus affected was the Word
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's weeping, being troubled, and praying that the cup pass away prove that the Son is not truly God and Word of the Father?

question: Could Christ have feared death?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Christ drove away the terrors of death from his Apostles and urged them toward martyrdom. He promised life to those who lose their life for him and told them not to fear those who kill the body. It is unreasonable that he who rewards with life those who die for him should himself dread death.
sources.quote: If to die for Him is life, what pain can we think He had to suffer in the mystery of death, Who rewards with life those who die for Him?
sources.raw_question: Could Christ have feared death, given his own teaching to his disciples about death and martyrdom?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Death could not be terrible to his body, for the Holy One was not to see corruption and he would raise the temple of his body within three days. Nor could it be terrible to his spirit, for it is absurd that Christ should fear hell while Lazarus rejoiced in Abraham's bosom. Fear is incompatible with a willingness to die and the power to live again.
sources.quote: He cannot fear death Whose power and purpose in dying is to die but for a moment: fear is incompatible with willingness to die, and the power to live again, for both of these rob death of his terrors.
sources.raw_question: Could Christ have feared death either in his body or in his spirit, even though he died willingly?

question: Does Revelation 22:1, where the river of life proceeds from the throne of God and of the Lamb, show that the Son shares the Father's throne and is coordinate with the Father as a source of blessing?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: Yes. The river, the joy of the Holy Ghost, flows equally and coordinately from the eternal Father and the eternal Son. The Lamb standing 'as it had been slain' in the midst of the throne shows that the glorified Christ still bears the traces of his crucifixion.
sources.quote: the perennial and transparent stream of felicity – the joy of the Holy Ghost – flows equally and coordinately from the eternal Father and the eternal Son
sources.raw_question: Does the river of life proceeding 'out of the throne of God and of the Lamb' (Rev. 22:1) show that the Son shares the Father's throne and is equally a source of blessing?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: Yes. The passage teaches that the stream of felicity, the joy of the Holy Ghost, flows equally and coordinately from the eternal Father and the eternal Son. This is so even though Revelation 5:6 shows that Christ glorified still bears the marks of his crucifixion.
sources.quote: the perennial and transparent stream of felicity – the joy of the Holy Ghost – flows equally and coordinately from the eternal Father and the eternal Son
sources.raw_question: Does Revelation 22:1, where the river of life proceeds from the throne of God and of the Lamb, show the Son as coordinate with the Father?

question: Is the faith by which one believes the same thing as the content that is believed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Faith a Thing of the Heart, Not of the Body; How It is Common and One and the Same in All Believers. The Faith of Believers is One, No Otherwise than the Will of Those Who Will is One.
sources.answer: No. What is believed concerns things said to be, to have been, or to be about to be. The faith by which they are believed is in the mind of the believer and is visible only to him. Faith is impressed on each heart from one doctrine, yet that doctrine is distinct from the faith it produces.
sources.quote: But that which is believed is a different thing from the faith by which it is believed. For the former is in things which are said either to be, or to have been or to be about to be; but the latter is in the mind of the believer
sources.raw_question: Is the faith by which one believes the same thing as the content that is believed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Trinity Which is the Image of God is Now to Be Sought in the Noblest Part of the Mind.
sources.answer: No. Faith is not what is believed but that by which it is believed. The things believed lie outside the mind, while faith exists within it. The things believed are believed, whereas faith itself is seen inwardly.
sources.quote: For faith is not that which is believed, but that by which it is believed; and the former is believed, the latter seen.
sources.raw_question: Is faith the same as the things that are believed?

question: What distinguishes God's creating a thing from a creature's bringing it about by applying external causes?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > God Alone Creates Those Things Which are Changed by Magic Art.
sources.answer: God alone makes and governs the creature from the innermost and highest point of causation. Angels, men or animals only apply operations from without, according to the powers God assigned to them. Such operations draw out causes already woven by God into the elements, so that things emerge at this time or in that way.
sources.quote: it is one thing to make and administer the creature from the innermost and highest turning-point of causation, which He alone does who is God the Creator; but quite another thing to apply some operation from without
sources.raw_question: What is the difference between God's creating a thing and a creature's bringing it about by applying external causes?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Original Cause of All Things is from God.
sources.answer: God alone makes and administers the creature from the innermost and highest point of causation, as the one with whom the measure, number and weight of all things primarily rests. Creatures only apply adventitious causes from without, according to the powers God assigned them, so that what is already contained in the hidden causes of the world may come forth at this or that time. The world is pregnant with causes, but these are created only from the highest unchangeable essence.
sources.quote: He only is the creator who is the chief former of these things. Neither can any one be this, unless He with whom primarily rests the measure, number, and weight of all things existing; and He is God the one Creator
sources.raw_question: What distinguishes God's creative causation from the causal operations of creatures?

question: Can a human being be saved and inherit the kingdom of God without the indwelling Spirit of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter IX.—Showing how that passage of the apostle which the heretics pervert, should be understood; viz., “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.”
sources.answer: No. The Spirit of the Father is what purifies man, gives him life and raises him up to the life of God. Flesh without the Spirit is dead and cannot possess the kingdom. For this reason the apostle urges believers to keep the Spirit through faith and chaste living, so that they do not lose the kingdom.
sources.quote: Inasmuch, therefore, as without the Spirit of God we cannot be saved, the apostle exhorts us through faith and chaste conversation to preserve the Spirit of God, lest, having become non-participators of the Divine Spirit, we lose the kingdom of heaven
sources.raw_question: Can a human being be saved and inherit the kingdom of God without the indwelling Spirit of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter X.—By a comparison drawn from the wild olive-tree, whose quality but not whose nature is changed by grafting, he proves more important things; he points out also that man without the Spirit is not capable of bringing forth fruit, or of inheriting the kingdom of God.
sources.answer: No. Man without the engrafting of the Spirit remains in his old condition as mere flesh and blood, like a wild olive that is useless and cast into the fire. It is the indwelling Spirit of the Father who raised Christ that will quicken our mortal bodies and makes us sons of God.
sources.quote: so also man, if he does not receive through faith the engrafting of the Spirit, remains in his old condition, and being [mere] flesh and blood, he cannot inherit the kingdom of God.
sources.raw_question: Can a human being bear fruit in righteousness and inherit the kingdom of God without the Spirit of God?

question: In Irenaeus's passage contrasting made man with 'the agennetos God', does agennetos mean 'unbegotten' (applying to the Father alone) or 'unmade' (including the Son and Spirit)?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: It means 'unmade' or uncreated. The word stands in deliberate contrast with 'gennetos' (made) man, and the old Latin translation renders it 'infecti Dei'. Read this way, the term covers the whole Trinity rather than excluding the Son.
sources.quote: the Doctor translates ἀγεννήτου, unbegotten, instead of unmade; not observing the antithesis, between γεννητὸς ἄνθρωπος, and ἀγεννήτου Θεοῦ
sources.raw_question: In Irenaeus's phrase 'the agennetos God', does agennetos mean 'unbegotten', which would apply to the Father alone, or 'unmade', which would include the Son and Spirit?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No, it means 'unmade' or uncreated. The passage sets up an antithesis between γεννητὸς ἄνθρωπος (made man) and ἀγεννήτου Θεοῦ (unmade God), and the old Latin translation renders it infecti Dei. Rendering it 'unbegotten', and reading 'God' where the text has 'the Father', distorts the sentence so that it seems to deny the Son is God.
sources.quote: the Doctor translates ἀγεννήτου, unbegotten, instead of unmade; not observing the antithesis, between γεννητὸς ἄνθρωπος, and ἀγεννήτου Θεοῦ, nor attending to infecti Dei, in the old translation
sources.raw_question: Should ἀγέννητος, as applied to God in Irenaeus's passage contrasting God with made man, be translated 'unbegotten' rather than 'unmade'?

question: Can the created things of this world properly be called images of the Valentinian Æons in the Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VII.—Created things are not the images of those Æons who are within the Pleroma.
sources.answer: No. The Gnostics hold that their thirty Æons share one nature with equal and similar properties, while creation contains many thousands of species, opposed in nature and destroying one another. An image must correspond to its archetype, so they would have to posit good and evil, gentle and fierce Æons, which their own system denies.
sources.quote: be the images and likenesses of the thirty Æons of the Pleroma, if indeed, as they declare, these being possessed of one nature, are of equal and similar properties, and exhibit no differences [among themselves]?
sources.raw_question: Can the manifold, mutually opposed things of creation be images of thirty supposedly equal and similar Gnostic Æons in the Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VII.—Created things are not the images of those Æons who are within the Pleroma.
sources.answer: No. Things that share neither the fashion nor the shape of the Æons cannot properly be called their images or likenesses. Also, a correspondence in number would require the Æons above to match the creation below in number and production. Yet the Valentinians count only thirty Æons and claim that the vast multitude of created things are images of them, which is absurd.
sources.quote: For how can the things which have neither the fashion nor shape of those [above] be their images?
sources.raw_question: Can the created things of this world be called images of the Valentinian Æons in the Pleroma on the basis of number and order of production rather than shape or form?

question: Is Christ a mere man distinct from God the Word, as Paul of Samosata taught, or is he the divine Word himself made one with the man born of Mary?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. The Word speaks of 'My body,' not of a Christ besides himself; the Word is the chrism and the Man who receives it is united with him, so he could not be called Christ apart from the Word. God the Word himself is Christ from Mary, God and Man, one and the same, not some other Christ.
sources.quote: Therefore God the Word Himself is Christ from Mary, God and Man; not some other Christ but One and the Same; He before ages from the Father, He too in the last times from the Virgin
sources.raw_question: Is Christ a man distinct from God the Word, so that the Word anointed a separate human Christ alongside himself, as Paul of Samosata taught?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: Christ is the divine Word made one in Mary with the man from Mary, and must be considered in both ways. The Word fashioned for himself a house in her womb, as Wisdom 'builded herself an house.' To say 'Why dost thou, being a man, make thyself God?' is the Jews' position, and the Samosatene is their disciple.
sources.quote: Let us then consider Christ in both ways, the divine Word made one in Mary with Him which is from Mary. For in her womb the Word fashioned for Himself His house
sources.raw_question: Is Christ a mere man, as Paul of Samosata taught, or is he the divine Word made one with the man born of Mary?

question: Can there be a void or region of shadow outside the supreme God that his light does not reach, or would such a void undermine his claim to fill and contain all things?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VIII.—Created things are not a shadow of the Pleroma.
sources.answer: No. If such a region existed, the Father's light would be weak and limited. It would fail and come to an end where nothing even hinders it. Then the Father could not be called the fulness of all things. Since the Father exists beforehand and fills all things, his light cannot fail and end in a vacuum.
sources.quote: Let them then no longer declare that their Bythus is the fulness of all things, if indeed he has neither filled nor illuminated that which is vacuum and shadow
sources.raw_question: Can there be a void or region of shadow that the light of the supreme Father does not reach?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter III.—The Bythus and Pleroma of the Valentinians, as well as the God of Marcion, shown to be absurd; the world was actually created by the same Being who had conceived the idea of it, and was not the fruit of defect or ignorance.
sources.answer: Yes. If there is a vacuity beyond the Pleroma, that vacuum is shown to be greater than the Pleroma itself. It is also inconsistent to say God contains all things within himself while the creation was formed by some other being in a region outside him.
sources.quote: If indeed, as they affirm, he has something subjacent and beyond himself, which they style vacuity and shadow, this vacuum is then proved to be greater than their Pleroma.
sources.raw_question: If the supreme God (the Valentinian Bythus) has a void or shadow lying beyond and beneath him, does that undermine his claim to contain all things?

question: Were the Old Testament appearances in which God was said to appear to the fathers wrought by angels through the creature rather than by God's own substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: Yes. The words and bodily appearances given to the fathers before the incarnation were wrought by angels, either speaking or acting in the person of God, as the prophets did, or assuming from the creature a form in which God might be shown figuratively. Augustine holds this established both by probable reason and by the authority of Scripture.
sources.quote: those words and bodily appearances which were given to these ancient fathers of ours before the incarnation of the Saviour, when God was said to appear, were wrought by angels
sources.raw_question: Were the Old Testament appearances in which God was said to appear to the fathers wrought by angels rather than by God's own substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: They were wrought through the creature, by the ministry of angels, as God's dispensation suited to the times. Even if we cannot discern how angels produced them, Scripture's authority, especially Hebrews, teaches that both the visible things and the word itself were wrought by angels, and on account of the people of God.
sources.quote: all those appearances to the fathers, when God was presented to them according to His own dispensation, suitable to the times, were wrought through the creature.
sources.raw_question: How were the Old Testament appearances of God to the fathers brought about?

question: Can believers open their hearts to Christ in prayer by their own power, or do they need the Holy Spirit's help?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: They need the Spirit's assistance; of themselves they cannot do it. Romans 8:26-27 teaches that we know not what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit helps our infirmities and intercedes for us. All attempts at communion with God without the supplies and effectual working of the Spirit of supplications are of no value.
sources.quote: All endeavours, all attempts for communion with God, without the supplies of the Spirit of supplications, without his effectual working in the heart, is of no value, nor to any purpose.
sources.raw_question: Can believers truly open their hearts to Christ in prayer by their own power, or do they need the assistance of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: They need the Spirit's help, because by ourselves we cannot do it. The Spirit of Jesus helps our infirmities and intercedes for us according to the will of God. Every attempt at communion with God without the Spirit of supplications is of no value.
sources.quote: Assistance for the work; for of ourselves we cannot do it. And this the saints have by the Spirit of Jesus, Rom. viii. 26, 27
sources.raw_question: Can believers open their hearts to Christ in prayer by their own power, or do they need the Holy Spirit's help?

question: Can sinners approach God the Father, or have any duty accepted by him, apart from Christ's mediation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. The way of access to God that humanity had at creation was shut by sin, and Christ has consecrated a new and living way through his flesh for believers alone. None comes to the Father but by him, and through him believers have access in one Spirit unto the Father; others who pray outside him come not near God.
sources.quote: Christ only is the way to the throne of grace; none comes to God but by him. “By him we have an access in one Spirit unto the Father,” Eph. ii. 18.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's mediation the only way by which sinners can approach God the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Out of Christ, God is a consuming fire and we are like dry stubble, so every approach to him apart from Christ only harms us. Agreement with God exists in Christ's blood alone. No duty is accepted unless it is done on that account, and through Christ alone we have access to the Father.
sources.quote: out of him God on his part is a consuming fire, — we are as stubble fully dry, yet setting ourselves in battle array against that fire: if we are brought together we are consumed.
sources.raw_question: Can sinners approach God or have any duty accepted by him apart from Christ?

question: Does Luke 2:52, which says Jesus advanced in wisdom and stature, show that the Son as the divine Word was imperfect or a creature capable of growth?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: No. If Jesus were a mere man, advance would fit Him, but that is the doctrine of Paul of Samosata. Since He is God bearing flesh, equal to God and ever in the Father, there is nothing beyond the Father into which He could advance. The Word did not advance as Word; He is said to advance humanly, because advance belongs to man.
sources.quote: But if He be God bearing flesh, as He truly is, and ‘the Word became flesh,’ and being God descended upon earth, what advance had He who existed equal to God?
sources.raw_question: Does Luke 2:52, 'Jesus advanced in wisdom and stature', prove that the Son as the Word is a creature capable of growth?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: No. The Word, considered as Word, is perfect from the perfect Father, needs nothing, and is the one by looking at whom all others advance; being One and Only in the Father, he has no room to reach forward. The advance spoken of belongs to the manhood, which advanced in Wisdom, not to Wisdom itself.
sources.quote: It was not then the Word, considered as the Word, who advanced; who is perfect from the perfect Father, who needs nothing, nay brings forward others to an advance; but humanly is He here also said to advance, since advance belongs to man
sources.raw_question: Does Luke 2:52's statement that Jesus advanced in wisdom imply that the Son of God, as the divine Word, was imperfect and grew in wisdom?

question: Is the Holy Spirit the ointment, or 'oil of gladness', with which Christ was anointed, even if the 'ointment poured forth' is taken to mean Christ Himself?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IX. The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ, and the oil of gladness; and why Christ Himself is not the ointment, since He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It is not strange that the Spirit should be called Ointment, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. And there is no confusion between them, since Christ alone suffered death, Whose saving cross is then spoken of.
sources.answer: Yes. The Psalm speaks of God anointing Christ with the oil of gladness, and Peter says God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit; Christ Himself says 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He hath anointed Me.' Therefore the Spirit is the ointment of Christ.
sources.quote: But when the Son of God Himself says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He hath anointed Me,” He points out the ointment of the Spirit. Therefore the Spirit is the ointment of Christ.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit the 'oil of gladness' or ointment with which Christ was anointed?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IX. The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ, and the oil of gladness; and why Christ Himself is not the ointment, since He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It is not strange that the Spirit should be called Ointment, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. And there is no confusion between them, since Christ alone suffered death, Whose saving cross is then spoken of.
sources.answer: No. Even if the Name of Jesus is understood as the ointment poured out, Peter's statement that the Lord Jesus was anointed with the Holy Spirit plainly shows that the Spirit too is called ointment.
sources.quote: certainly when the Apostle Peter says that the Lord Jesus was anointed with the Holy Spirit, it is without doubt plain that the Spirit also is called ointment.
sources.raw_question: If the 'ointment poured out' is taken to mean Christ Himself rather than the Spirit, does it follow that the Holy Spirit is not called ointment?

question: How far can God's patience and forbearance be known from his providence, apart from Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Only dimly. Providence shows that God does not punish immediately and that he does good to men. Yet this knowledge is dark, has proved a snare, and is always accompanied by the revelation of his wrath, so men can only fluctuate and tremble. In Christ, God's nature is revealed as love, secured by covenant and by an atonement that satisfies his justice. So we need not fear that his justice will interfere with his patience.
sources.quote: with that revelation of forbearance which we have in Christ, there is also a discovery of the satisfaction of his justice and wrath against sin; so that we need not fear any actings from them to interfere with the works of his patience
sources.raw_question: Can God's patience and forbearance be truly known from his providence, apart from Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: By cursing the earth and showing signs of anger, God reveals his wrath against sin. Yet he does not immediately destroy all things, and he continues to do good, giving rain and fruitful seasons. In this way he bears witness to his patience and forbearance toward all. Even so, this gives the world only an obscure glimpse of God.
sources.quote: yet not proceeding immediately to destroy all things, he hath manifested his patience and forbearance to all.
sources.raw_question: How does God's providence reveal his patience and forbearance?

question: In Exodus 33, what do the 'face' and the 'back parts' of God that Moses could and could not see signify?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > How the Back Parts of God Were Seen. The Faith of the Resurrection of Christ. The Catholic Church Only is the Place from Whence the Back Parts of God are Seen. The Back Parts of God Were Seen by the Israelites. It is a Rash Opinion to Think that God the Father Only Was Never Seen by the Fathers.
sources.answer: The back parts signify Christ's flesh, in which he was born of the Virgin, died, and rose again; the face signifies the form of God in which he is equal with God. The back parts may be so called because of the posteriority of mortality or because he took flesh late, near the end of the world. The face, the manifestation of the wisdom of God, no one can see and live.
sources.quote: His “back parts” are to be taken to be His flesh, in which He was born of the Virgin, and died, and rose again
sources.raw_question: In Exodus 33, what are the 'back parts' and the 'face' of God that Moses was told he could and could not see?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > In What Manner Moses Saw God.
sources.answer: The words 'Thou canst not see my face... no man shall see my face, and live' show that the divine substance was withheld from Moses. As prefiguring Christ, the 'back parts' are His flesh, in which He was born, died and rose again. The 'face' is the form of God, in which He is equal with God, and no one can see it and live.
sources.quote: that His “back parts” are to be taken to be His flesh, in which He was born of the Virgin, and died, and rose again
sources.raw_question: What do the 'face' and the 'back parts' of God in Exodus 33 signify?

question: Does Paul's phrase 'the god of this world' in 2 Corinthians 4:4 imply a lesser god of this world distinct from the supreme God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VII.—Reply to an objection founded on the words of St. Paul (2 Cor. iv. 4). St. Paul occasionally uses words not in their grammatical sequence.
sources.answer: No. Paul uses transposition of words (hyperbaton), so the verse should be read 'In whom God hath blinded the minds of them of this world that believe not.' Paul does not say 'the God of this world' as if recognising another beyond Him, but confesses the one true God as God, and 'of this world' qualifies the unbelievers, who will not inherit the future age of incorruption.
sources.quote: For Paul does not say, “the God of this world,” as if recognising any other beyond Him; but he confessed God as indeed God. And he says, “the unbelievers of this world,” because they shall not inherit the future age of incorruption.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's phrase 'the god of this world' in 2 Corinthians 4:4 show that there is a lesser god of this world distinct from a higher God beyond all principality?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: No. Paul often transposes words, and the verse should be read as 'God hath blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this world.' Paul does not acknowledge any god beyond the one true God. They are called unbelievers 'of this world' because they will not inherit the future age of incorruption.
sources.quote: For Paul does not say, “the God of this world,” as if recognising any other beyond Him; but he confessed God as indeed God.
sources.raw_question: Does 2 Corinthians 4:4, 'the god of this world hath blinded the minds,' imply a lesser god of this world distinct from the supreme God?

question: What stands above the human mind in the order of natures?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Mind Loves God in Rightly Loving Itself; And If It Love Not God, It Must Be Said to Hate Itself. Even a Weak and Erring Mind is Always Strong in Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself. Let It Be Turned to God, that It May Be Blessed by Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Him.
sources.answer: It is so placed in the order, not of place but of natures, that nothing is above it except God. Because it is the image of God, it has the capacity to cleave to Him whose image it is.
sources.quote: For it is so reckoned in the order, not of place, but of natures, as that there is none above it save Him.
sources.raw_question: Where does the human mind stand in the order of natures relative to God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > God is Above the Mind.
sources.answer: God, a nature not created but creating. If we truly seek anything above the rational mind, what we find is the uncreated Creator. The question that follows is whether this God is the Trinity.
sources.quote: If, then, we seek anything that is above this nature, and seek truly, it is God,—namely, a nature not created, but creating.
sources.raw_question: What is it that stands above the nature of the human mind?

question: How should a believer seek Christ when his felt presence and communion are withdrawn?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: It is done in two parts. First, the soul searches itself for the cause of Christ's absence, since his departure is never without provocation. Once the fault is found, it turns on it with indignation. Second, it applies itself to the promises of the covenant, where Christ is graciously offered, to find his favour there again.
sources.quote: hath two parts:— searching of our own souls for the cause of his absence; secondly, searching the promises for his presence.
sources.raw_question: How should a believer seek Christ when his felt presence and communion are withdrawn?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: They should not give up, but resolutely cast off their dull state and diligently use every means God has appointed, especially the public ordinances of worship. The chief thing believers look for in every ordinance is Christ himself, and they find refreshment only as far as they find him there.
sources.quote: Indeed, the great inquiry the souls of believers make, in every ordinance, is after Christ. So much as they find of him, so much sweetness and refreshment have they, and no more.
sources.raw_question: What should a believer do when they no longer sense Christ's presence in private prayer and meditation?

question: Was Adam formed by the Word of God, the 'hand of God', and does that same hand continue to form humanity?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. Adam was formed by the hand of God, which Irenaeus identifies as the Word of God, since all things were made by him. So the same Word who formed Adam later recapitulates Adam in himself.
sources.quote: was formed by the hand of God, that is, by the Word of God, for “all things were made by Him,”
sources.raw_question: Was Adam formed by the Word of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVI.—Since our bodies return to the earth, it follows that they have their substance from it; also, by the advent of the Word, the image of God in us appeared in a clearer light.
sources.answer: Yes. The hand of God by which Adam was fashioned is the same that forms us now and was plainly shown when the Lord made eyes for the blind man from clay. This one hand works from the beginning to the end, preparing us for life and perfecting the work after God's image and likeness.
sources.quote: And thus was the hand of God plainly shown forth, by which Adam was fashioned, and we too have been formed
sources.raw_question: Is the Word (Son) the 'hand of God' that formed Adam and continues to form humanity?

question: Did the ante-Nicene writers who spoke of the Son's temporal or voluntary procession thereby deny his eternity, divinity and consubstantiality with the Father, as later Catholic writers held them?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. They differed only in how they expressed the same doctrine. All agreed that the Person of the Son was eternal, coeval and consubstantial with the Father, and all acknowledged a temporal, voluntary procession. The only question was whether the name 'sonship' should be given to the Word's eternal coexistence or to the later procession.
sources.quote: The question was not whether the hypostasis, or Person, of the Son was from all eternity, coeval with the Father, and consubstantial with him; in that they all perfectly agreed.
sources.raw_question: Did the ante-Nicene writers who spoke of a temporal procession of the Son disagree in doctrine with later Catholic writers about his eternity and consubstantiality?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Writers like Justin, Athenagoras, Theophilus, Tertullian, Tatian, Novatian and Hippolytus called the Son's coming forth to create the world voluntary. Yet they held him God, not produced from nothing as creatures are, because he had always existed in and with the Father before coming forth. They also asserted the eternity and consubstantiality of the Logos.
sources.quote: was not produced ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, (as all creatures are;) therefore he was God, having ever existed, before his coming forth, in and with the Father.
sources.raw_question: Did the ante-Nicene writers who called the Son's coming forth voluntary thereby deny his eternity and divinity?

question: In what spirit and manner do God's adopted children obey him, as distinct from those who obey out of fear and bondage?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: Adopted children obey from love and do so willingly. Having grasped God's love, they are carried by love to give themselves to him who is love. Through the Spirit of adoption they walk in light and delight rather than in fear and bondage. They yield themselves cheerfully as a living sacrifice, under a law stripped of its condemning power by Christ's blood.
sources.quote: From an apprehension of love, they are effectually carried out by love to give up themselves unto him who is love.
sources.raw_question: What motive and manner of obedience distinguish God's adopted children from those who obey out of fear?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: It is a spiritual largeness of heart. By it God's children go forth to all holy obedience freely, willingly and genuinely, without fear, terror or constraint. This is because they have the Spirit of adoption, who is opposed to the spirit of bondage. They are adopted by Christ through the Spirit.
sources.quote: is a spiritual largeness of heart, whereby the children of God do freely, willingly, genuinely, without fear, terror, bondage, and constraint, go forth unto all holy obedience in Christ.
sources.raw_question: What is the positive liberty that adopted children enjoy within God's family, as opposed to the spirit of bondage?

question: Does Scripture teach that ultimate trust may be placed in any creature, or only in God the Creator, given its contrast between the nature of man and the nature of God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 2. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, detaches our ultimate confidence from man the creature, and attaches it to God the Creator; – by contrasting the sinfulness and feebleness of mortal man with the goodness and omnipotence of the Eternal Jehovah: by direct prohibition and precept: by exhibiting the holy Jealousy of God.
sources.answer: It sets man's weakness beside God's perfections, point by point. Man is of yesterday, ignorant, unable to do the least thing, mortal like grass, unrighteous and deceitful in heart. God is everlasting and all-knowing, can do all things, alone has immortality, is alone holy and good, and is light without darkness. Because man is a creature who has his being in God, and God has life in Himself, Scripture's design is to make us rest our confidence on God and not on man.
sources.quote: by contrasting the sinfulness and feebleness of mortal man with the goodness and omnipotence of the Eternal Jehovah
sources.raw_question: How does Scripture's contrast between the nature of man and the nature of God show that God alone is the proper object of ultimate trust?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 2. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, detaches our ultimate confidence from man the creature, and attaches it to God the Creator; – by contrasting the sinfulness and feebleness of mortal man with the goodness and omnipotence of the Eternal Jehovah: by direct prohibition and precept: by exhibiting the holy Jealousy of God.
sources.answer: Only in God the Creator. Scripture repeatedly contrasts the frailty and mortality of man with the eternity and creative power of God, and forbids trusting in princes or the son of man. Its explicit commands with one voice require that our faith and hope be in God.
sources.quote: I need not multiply passages to prove that the explicit commands of Scripture with one consentient voice require in the words of St. Peter, that our “faith and hope be in God.”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that ultimate trust for salvation may be placed in any creature, or only in God the Creator?

question: Does a person become 'spiritual' by having the flesh cast away, or by receiving the Spirit of God while remaining in the flesh?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VIII.—The gifts of the Holy Spirit which we receive prepare us for incorruption, render us spiritual, and separate us from carnal men. These two classes are signified by the clean and unclean animals in the legal dispensation.
sources.answer: No. Being spiritual comes from receiving the Spirit, not from casting away the flesh. Paul's readers still had flesh, yet they had received the Spirit of God. The spiritual man is our own substance, the union of flesh and spirit, receiving the Spirit of God.
sources.quote: This, however, does not take place by a casting away of the flesh, but by the impartation of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does becoming "spiritual" through the indwelling Spirit of God mean casting away the flesh and becoming an incorporeal spirit?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VI.—God will bestow salvation upon the whole nature of man, consisting of body and soul in close union, since the Word took it upon Him, and adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, of whom our bodies are, and are termed, the temples.
sources.answer: By partaking of the Spirit of God, not by losing the flesh. Those whom the apostle calls 'perfect' and 'spiritual' are those who have received the Spirit, as shown by the prophetic gifts and tongues in the Church. If the flesh were removed, what remained would not be a spiritual man but only the spirit of a man, or the Spirit of God. The perfect man is the union of body, soul, and the outpoured Spirit.
sources.quote: they being spiritual because they partake of the Spirit, and not because their flesh has been stripped off and taken away, and because they have become purely spiritual.
sources.raw_question: Does a person become 'spiritual' or 'perfect' by having the flesh stripped away, or by partaking of the Spirit of God?

question: By what righteousness was the devil conquered in the work of redemption, and how was he conquered by it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Man Was to Be Rescued from the Power of the Devil, Not by Power, But by Righteousness.
sources.answer: He was conquered by the righteousness of Jesus Christ. The devil found nothing worthy of death in Christ, yet he killed Him. It is therefore just that those the devil held as debtors should be set free by believing in Him whom he slew without any debt. So Christ's innocent blood was shed for the remission of sins.
sources.quote: Because, when he found in Him nothing worthy of death, yet he slew Him. And certainly it is just, that we whom he held as debtors, should be dismissed free by believing in Him whom he slew without any debt.
sources.raw_question: By what righteousness was the devil conquered, and how was he conquered by it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Unobligated Death of Christ Has Freed Those Who Were Liable to Death.
sources.answer: By the righteousness of Jesus Christ. The devil found nothing in Christ worthy of death and yet slew him. It is therefore just that those whom the devil held as debtors should be set free by believing in Him whom he slew without any debt, and so we are said to be justified in Christ's blood.
