sources.quote: Because, when he found in Him nothing worthy of death, yet he slew Him. And certainly it is just, that we whom he held as debtors, should be dismissed free by believing in Him whom he slew without any debt.
sources.raw_question: By what righteousness was the devil conquered in the work of redemption, and how?

question: How could early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr consistently teach that God alone is to be worshipped while also worshipping Christ?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: They were consistent because they taught that the Son is God. Justin says God alone is to be worshipped, yet constantly teaches that the Son is God and worships Father, Son and prophetic Spirit. Athenagoras holds that only the Creator is to be worshipped, yet teaches that all things were created by the Son.
sources.quote: Very true: but then he constantly teaches us that the Son is God; and therefore might consistently say, that the Son is to be S worshipped
sources.raw_question: How could early Christian writers consistently teach that God alone is to be worshipped while also worshipping Christ?

sources.answer: Yes. Justin held that God alone is to be worshipped, but he constantly taught that the Son is God. Therefore he could consistently say the Son is to be worshipped and, for the whole Church, that Christians worship Father, Son, and prophetic Spirit.
sources.quote: “ God “alone is to be worshipped.” Very true: but then he constantly teaches us that the Son is God; and therefore might consistently say, that the Son is to be S worshipped
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent for early Christian writers like Justin Martyr to teach that God alone is to be worshipped while also worshipping the Son?

question: What does the command in Psalm 99:5 to "worship His footstool" mean, given that the Law commands that God alone is to be worshipped?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: No. The footstool cannot be taken in a human sense, since God has no body and is beyond measure, and the earth as a creature may not be worshipped. Rather, the footstool signifies the earth which Christ assumed, that is, His flesh, which is adored in the mysteries and which the apostles adored in the risen Lord. So the prophet does not command creaturely worship against the Law.
sources.quote: by footstool is understood earth, but by the earth the Flesh of Christ, which we this day also adore in the mysteries, and which the apostles, as we said above, adored in the Lord Jesus
sources.raw_question: Does the command in Psalm 99:5 to "worship His footstool" contradict the Law's command that God alone is to be worshipped?

Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: The footstool signifies the flesh of Christ, the earth the Lord took up in the Incarnation. God has no body needing a footstool, and the earth as a creature may not be worshipped. Christ's flesh is adored in the mysteries, as the apostles adored it in the risen Lord, because Christ is not divided.
sources.quote: And so, by footstool is understood earth, but by the earth the Flesh of Christ, which we this day also adore in the mysteries, and which the apostles, as we said above, adored in the Lord Jesus
sources.raw_question: What does 'worship His footstool' (Psalm 99:5) mean, given that only God may be worshipped?

question: Who are the 'hands of God' by which man was formed in God's likeness, according to Irenaeus?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXVIII.—The distinction to be made between the righteous and the wicked. The future apostasy in the time of Antichrist, and the end of the world.
sources.answer: The hands of God are the Son and the Holy Spirit. Man was moulded at the beginning by these hands and so was made after the image and likeness of God. The Son and the Spirit thus act together with the Father as the one Creator of humanity.
sources.quote: man, having been moulded at the beginning by the hands of God, that is, of the Son and of the Spirit, is made after the image and likeness of God
sources.raw_question: Who are the 'hands of God' by which man was formed in the beginning, according to Irenaeus?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VI.—God will bestow salvation upon the whole nature of man, consisting of body and soul in close union, since the Word took it upon Him, and adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, of whom our bodies are, and are termed, the temples.
sources.answer: Man was made by the Father through the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are the Father's 'hands.' Irenaeus treats the Son and Spirit as the agents through whom the Father fashions his handiwork. The whole man, not merely a part of him, was formed by them after the likeness of God, and God is glorified by conforming that handiwork to His own Son.
sources.quote: For by the hands of the Father, that is, by the Son and the Holy Spirit, man, and not [merely] a part of man, was made in the likeness of God.
sources.raw_question: By whom was man made in the likeness of God, according to Irenaeus's description of the Son and the Holy Spirit as the 'hands of the Father'?

question: In 2 Thessalonians 2:4, what does Paul mean when he says the man of sin exalts himself 'above all that is called God' — does this include the true God, or imply other true gods?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: No. Paul refers to those who are called gods by people who do not know God, namely idols. The Father of all is called God and truly is God, and Antichrist will be lifted up not above Him but above those that are called gods but are not.
sources.quote: For the Father of all is called God, and is so; and Antichrist shall be lifted up, not above Him, but above those which are indeed called gods, but are not.
sources.raw_question: In 2 Thessalonians 2:4, when Paul says Antichrist exalts himself 'above all that is called God,' does this include the Father, the true God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXV.—The fraud, pride, and tyrannical kingdom of Antichrist, as described by Daniel and Paul.
sources.answer: No. The phrase refers to idols, which men call gods but which are not really gods. Antichrist will set aside these idols and present himself as the only idol, in order to be adored as God, so that those who now worship the devil through many idols serve him through one.
sources.quote: he is lifted up above all that is called God, or that is worshipped—that is, above every idol —for these are indeed so called by men, but are not [really] gods
sources.raw_question: In 2 Thessalonians 2:4, when Paul says the man of sin exalts himself 'above all that is called God, or that is worshipped,' does he mean that there are other true gods?

question: Do Isaiah 63:10-14, compared with Numbers 14:11 and Deuteronomy 32:12, prove that the Holy Spirit is Jehovah?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah says Israel vexed God's Holy Spirit, while Numbers and Deuteronomy say it was Jehovah who was provoked and who alone led them. Since the one provoked was both the Holy Spirit and Jehovah, the Spirit is Jehovah.
sources.quote: Here we learn that the One provoked was the Holy Spirit, and was Jehovah. Therefore the Spirit is Jehovah.
sources.raw_question: Does a comparison of Isaiah 63 with the Pentateuch show that the Holy Spirit whom Israel provoked in the wilderness is Jehovah?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah says Israel vexed his Holy Spirit and that the Spirit led them and caused them to rest, while Numbers says it was Jehovah whom the people provoked and Deuteronomy says Jehovah alone led them. The One provoked and leading was both the Holy Spirit and Jehovah; therefore the Spirit is Jehovah.
sources.quote: Here we learn that the One provoked was the Holy Spirit, and was Jehovah. Therefore the Spirit is Jehovah.
sources.raw_question: Do Isaiah 63:10-14, compared with Numbers 14:11 and Deuteronomy 32:12, prove that the Holy Spirit is Jehovah?

question: Did the righteous of the Old Testament, such as David, receive forgiveness of sins through Christ in the same way as Christians do?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVII—The sins of the men of old time, which incurred the displeasure of God, were, by His providence, committed to writing, that we might derive instruction thereby, and not be filled with pride. We must not, therefore, infer that there was another God than He whom Christ preached; we should rather fear, lest the one and the same God who inflicted punishment on the ancients, should bring down heavier upon us.
sources.answer: Yes. Nathan was sent to David so that David, by condemning himself, might obtain mercy and forgiveness from Christ. In his penitential psalm David waited for the coming of the Lord, who washes and cleanses the man bound by sin. So the same Lord who saves Christians was the source of pardon for the saints of old.
sources.quote: in order that he, passing sentence upon and condemning himself, might obtain mercy and forgiveness from Christ
sources.raw_question: Was Christ already active in the Old Testament, granting forgiveness of sins to the righteous such as David?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVII—The sins of the men of old time, which incurred the displeasure of God, were, by His providence, committed to writing, that we might derive instruction thereby, and not be filled with pride. We must not, therefore, infer that there was another God than He whom Christ preached; we should rather fear, lest the one and the same God who inflicted punishment on the ancients, should bring down heavier upon us.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord descended to the regions beneath the earth, preached His advent there, and remitted the sins of the righteous, prophets and patriarchs who hoped in Him, just as He does for us. No one is justified of himself, but only by the advent of the Lord, and His death brought healing and remission to those of former times.
sources.quote: the righteous men, the prophets, and the patriarchs, to whom He remitted sins in the same way as He did to us
sources.raw_question: Did the righteous of the Old Testament receive remission of sins through Christ in the same way as Christians do?

question: When we love a righteous person such as the Apostle Paul, through what do we love him, and what does this reveal about our knowledge of righteousness?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Our Love of the Righteous is Kindled from Love Itself of the Unchangeable Form of Righteousness.
sources.answer: We love Paul because we believe his life conformed to a form of righteousness that we already behold inwardly, or rather above ourselves, in the truth itself. We do not learn how God's ministers ought to live from hearsay; we see it in the unchangeable truth. Unless we loved that steadfast form above all, we would not love Paul for conforming to it.
sources.quote: But we do not believe that the ministers of God ought so to live because we have heard it from any one, but because we behold it inwardly within ourselves, or rather above ourselves, in the truth itself.
sources.raw_question: Why do we love a righteous person such as the Apostle Paul when we read of his life, and what does this reveal about our knowledge of righteousness?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: We love the righteous man through the form and truth of righteousness which we discern within ourselves. But that form itself can be loved only from itself. Nothing else is like it, through which we might come to love it while it is unknown, because it alone is such as it is. If we did not love that form at all, we would not love the righteous man either. Yet while we are not righteous, we love it too little to become righteous.
sources.quote: The man therefore who is believed to be righteous, is loved through that form and truth which he who loves discerns and understands within himself; but that very form and truth itself cannot be loved from any other source than itself.
sources.raw_question: When we love a person we believe to be righteous, through what do we love him, and can the form of righteousness itself be loved through anything else?

question: Does beholding the form of righteousness make a mind righteous, and if not, how does it become righteous?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: No. Those who can see and define a righteous mind are not thereby righteous themselves. They become righteous by cleaving to the very form they behold, so that they are shaped by it. One can cleave to that form only by loving it, and so live righteously, owing no one anything but to love one another.
sources.quote: except by cleaving to that very same form itself which they behold, so that from thence they may be formed and may be righteous minds
sources.raw_question: Does beholding the form of righteousness make a mind righteous, and if not, how does it become righteous?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: By cleaving to the very form of righteousness which it beholds within itself, and cleaving to it by love. Seeing what a righteous mind is does not make one righteous; one must be formed by that form, so as not only to discern righteousness but to live righteously, owing no man anything but to love one another.
sources.quote: And whence will they be able to be so, except by cleaving to that very same form itself which they behold, so that from thence they may be formed and may be righteous minds
sources.raw_question: How can a mind that is not yet righteous become righteous, according to Augustine's account of the inner form of righteousness?

question: Does God's hardening of Pharaoh's heart show that the God of the Old Testament is different from the good God revealed in the Gospel?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXIX.—Refutation of the arguments of the Marcionites, who attempted to show that God was the author of sin, because He blinded Pharaoh and his servants.
sources.answer: No. One and the same God blesses believers and blinds those who reject Him. The blindness is the result of their own refusal of the light, just as the sun, God's creature, dazzles weak eyes while it gives light to others. Christ Himself spoke in parables so that unbelievers 'seeing may not see,' so the God who hardened Pharaoh is the same God at work in the Gospel.
sources.quote: For one and the same God [that blesses others] inflicts blindness upon those who do not believe, but who set Him at naught; just as the sun, which is a creature of His, [acts with regard] to those who, by reason of any weakness of the eyes cannot behold his light
sources.raw_question: Does God's hardening of Pharaoh's heart make God the author of sin, or show that the God of the Old Testament differs from the good God revealed by Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVIII.—Those persons prove themselves senseless who exaggerate the mercy of Christ, but are silent as to the judgment, and look only at the more abundant grace of the New Testament; but, forgetful of the greater degree of perfection which it demands from us, they endeavour to show that there is another God beyond Him who created the world.
sources.answer: No. The Lord himself in the Gospel speaks in parables so that unbelievers seeing may not see, fulfilling Isaiah. One and the same God blesses believers with fuller illumination and inflicts blindness on those who set him at naught, as the sun blinds weak eyes while illuminating others.
sources.quote: For one and the same God [that blesses others] inflicts blindness upon those who do not believe, but who set Him at naught
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that God hardened Pharaoh's heart show that the Old Testament God is different from the God of the Gospel?

question: Does the prophecy in Isaiah 65 about blessing and swearing by "the true God" refer to the Son as true God, rather than to the Father speaking of himself?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. Read with its whole context, the prophecy describes as true God the very Speaker who appeared to those who did not seek him and spread out his hands all day to a gainsaying people. That Speaker is Christ, who made himself known to the Gentiles and stretched out his hands on the cross. So the one who is blessed and sworn by as true God is the Son.
sources.quote: Could a dishonest attempt to suppress the truth be more completely exposed, or the Speaker be more distinctly revealed as true God, than here?
sources.raw_question: Does the prophecy in Isaiah 65 that God's servants 'shall bless the true God' and 'swear by the true God' refer to the Son as true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. The Apostle Paul in Romans 10 interprets these same prophecies as referring to the Lord's passion and to the times of the Gospel. He applies them to Israel's unbelief toward the Lord who came in the flesh. No one has a better claim than Paul to interpret the prophet, since Paul was caught up to heaven and given revelation, so the Son is their Author and true God.
sources.quote: He interprets all these prophecies as allusions to the passion of the Lord and to the times of Gospel faith, when he is reproving the unbelief of Israel, which will not recognise that the Lord is come in the flesh.
sources.raw_question: Could the words of Isaiah 65 about the true God be the Father speaking of himself rather than prophecies concerning the Son?

question: Did the Apostle Paul apply Isaiah's prophecy about the true God to Christ with inspired understanding, or was he merely interpreting the prophet's words at random?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: He cited it rightly, because the prophecy itself shows whom it concerns. At the beginning of that very utterance Isaiah adores the God he has seen, and the Evangelist testifies that Isaiah saw the glory of the Only-begotten. So Apostle, Evangelist and Prophet agree that the true God of the prophecy is the Son.
sources.quote: The Apostle, the Evangelist, the Prophet combine to silence your objections.
sources.raw_question: Did the Apostle Paul cite Isaiah's prophecy about the true God (blessing and swearing by Him) with real inspired understanding, or was he merely interpreting another man's book at random?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. The same prophecy opens with Isaiah confessing that he has seen no God except the one addressed. John's Gospel says Isaiah saw the glory of the Only-begotten and spoke of him. So Prophet, Evangelist, and Apostle agree that the God of this prophecy is the Son.
sources.quote: And if you, in your heresy, do not know that it was God the Only-begotten Whom the prophet saw in that glory, listen to the Evangelist:—These things said Esaias, when he saw His glory, and spake of Him
sources.raw_question: Was Paul merely interpreting Isaiah's words at random, without prophetic inspiration, when he applied them to Christ?

question: Do the Scriptures (the prophets, Christ, and the apostles) teach or legitimately support the Valentinian Gnostic system of the Pleroma and its aeons?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter III.—Texts of Holy Scripture used by these heretics to support their opinions.
sources.answer: No. The Gnostics only appear to find their system in Scripture because they twist its good words through perverse interpretations and deceitful expositions, exploiting texts that can be drawn into various senses. The safeguard against being led away by such readings is a steadfast faith in one God, the Father Almighty, and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
sources.quote: lead away captive from the truth those who do not retain a stedfast faith in one God, the Father Almighty, and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: Do the parables and allegories of Scripture (the law, prophets, evangelists and apostles) legitimately support the Valentinian Gnostic doctrine of the Pleroma and its aeons?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter VIII.—How the Valentinians pervert the Scriptures to support their own pious opinions.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus says that the prophets did not announce this system, the Lord did not teach it, and the apostles did not deliver it. The Valentinians draw their views from sources other than the Scriptures. They then try to attach Scripture to their scheme afterwards, so that it will not seem to lack all support.
sources.quote: Such, then, is their system, which neither the prophets announced, nor the Lord taught, nor the apostles delivered, but of which they boast that beyond all others they have a perfect knowledge.
sources.raw_question: Is the Valentinian Gnostic system of Aeons, the Pleroma and Achamoth taught by the prophets, by Christ, or by the apostles?

question: Since Jehovah alone is God and will not give his glory to another, can Jesus Christ rightly receive the same trust, worship, and love as Jehovah?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture presents the Son as personally distinct from the Father yet in wondrous union with him. All divine attributes are ascribed to him. He claims and receives, without protest and as his just right, equal trust, adoration, love, and service with Jehovah, who will not give his glory to another.
sources.quote: who claims and receives, without protest, yea, as his just and inalienable right, equal trust, adoration, love, and service, with him who says, “I am Jehovah, my Name is Jealous, and my glory will I not give to another.”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture require the same ultimate trust, worship, and love toward Jesus Christ as toward Jehovah, who will not give his glory to another?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes, because he is himself Jehovah. Scripture ascribes all the divine attributes to Jesus Christ, who claims equal adoration and equal trust as being himself Jehovah, our God and Saviour. So resting on Christ is resting on God.
sources.quote: Scripture declares that all these Divine attributes, belong to Jesus Christ, who claims equal adoration and equal trust, as being himself Jehovah, our God and Saviour.
sources.raw_question: Since Scripture says Jehovah alone is God and is jealous of his attributes and of our trust, can Christ rightly receive equal adoration and trust?

question: Can God, who is over all, be subject to necessity, so that something happens with his permission but against his will?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter V.—This world was not formed by any other beings within the territory which is contained by the Father.
sources.answer: No. If he could not prevent it, he would be weak and powerless. If he could and yet allowed it against his will, he would be a hypocrite and a slave of necessity. But God over all is free and independent. To say otherwise makes necessity greater and more kingly than God.
sources.quote: It is not seemly, however, to say of Him who is God over all, since He is free and independent, that He was a slave to necessity, or that anything takes place with His permission, yet against His desire
sources.raw_question: Could God permit something without approving of it, as if yielding to some necessity?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter V.—This world was not formed by any other beings within the territory which is contained by the Father.
sources.answer: No. God over all is free and independent, so it is unfitting to call him a slave to necessity or to say anything occurs by his permission against his desire. Otherwise necessity would be greater and more kingly than God, since whatever has the most power is superior to all others. If the Gnostics' Father (Bythus) merely tolerates what he cannot oppose, like the Homeric Jupiter, he is shown to be the slave of necessity and fate, not God.
sources.quote: It is not seemly, however, to say of Him who is God over all, since He is free and independent, that He was a slave to necessity, or that anything takes place with His permission, yet against His desire
sources.raw_question: Can God, who is over all, be subject to necessity or fate, so that things happen with his permission but against his will?

question: Does the exalted Christ share in the sufferings and afflictions of his people, so that their afflictions are in some sense his own?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ both grieves with his people in friendly condolence and supplies them with gracious help. As the angel of the Lord, he intercedes for Jerusalem as one intimately affected with its condition, and he declares that what is done to his people is done to him.
sources.quote: He speaks as one intimately affected with the state and condition of poor Jerusalem; and therefore he hath bid all the world take notice that what is done to them is done to him
sources.raw_question: Does the exalted Christ actually share in the sufferings and afflictions of his people?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is afflicted in all his people's afflictions. Afflictions that consist in persecution belong to Christ in the first place and to believers only by participation. This is why believers are said to fill up the measure of Christ's afflictions.
sources.quote: yea, it seems that all our afflictions (at least those of one sort, — namely, which consist in persecutions) are his in the first place, ours only by participation.
sources.raw_question: Are the persecutions believers suffer in some sense Christ's own afflictions?

question: Does Christ take vengeance on the adversaries of his people, and in what ways?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. When no one else comes to the relief of his people, Christ himself undertakes to avenge them. He does this temporally on persons and nations, by making examples of eminent opposers and by judgments on the persecuting world. He does it finally through eternal vengeance on the adversaries of his beloved.
sources.quote: In that he doth and will, in the winding up of the matter, so sorely revenge the quarrel of their sufferings upon their enemies. He avenges his elect that cry unto him; yea, he doth it speedily.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ avenge the sufferings of his people on their enemies?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ avenges his beloved both in time and in eternity. In time he does so by making eminent opposers examples, as he did with Pharaoh, and by pouring out the vials of his wrath on the antichristian world. In eternity he pleads with their adversaries in eternal vengeance. This shows that he abounds in pity and compassion toward his people.
sources.quote: In eternal vengeance will he plead with the adversaries of his beloved, Matt. xxv. 41–46; 2 Thess. i. 6; Jude 15. It is hence evident that Christ abounds in pity and compassion towards his beloved.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ take vengeance on the adversaries of his people, and in what ways?

question: In 1 John 5:20, does "This is the true God, and eternal life" refer to Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The same person is called both the true God and eternal life, and John himself at the start of the epistle gives the title "Eternal Life" to Christ (1 John 1:2). Since Jehovah is called the true and living God in Jeremiah 10:10, this proves that Jesus Christ is Jehovah, very and eternal God.
sources.quote: the same person is here most evidently spoken of as ‘the true God and Eternal Life’. It will be granted that a writer is the best interpreter of his own phraseology.
sources.raw_question: In 1 John 5:20, does "This is the true God, and eternal life" refer to Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. St. John declares of Christ that he is the true God and eternal life. This matches the prophet's confession that Jehovah is the true God, and so identifies Christ as Jehovah.
sources.quote: that of him St. John declares, "this is the true God and eternal life."
sources.raw_question: Does 1 John 5:20, "This is the true God and eternal life," refer to Jesus Christ?

question: Does salvation and the mystery of godliness consist only in correct doctrine, apart from the confession of the Names of Father, Son and Holy Spirit and participation in the sacraments?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > Eunomius again speaks of the Son as Lord and God, and Maker of all creation intelligible and sensible, having received from the Father the power and the commission for creation, being entrusted with the task of creation as if He were an artizan commissioned by some one hiring Him, and receiving His power of creation as a thing adventitious, ab extra, as a result of the power allotted to Him in accordance with such and such combinations and positions of the stars, as destiny decrees their lot in life to men at their nativity. Thus, passing by most of what Eunomius had written, he confutes his blasphemy that the Maker of all things came into being in like manner with the earth and with angels, and that the subsistence of the Only-begotten differs not at all from the genesis of all things, and reproaches Him with reverencing neither the Divine mystery nor the custom of the Church, nor following in his attempt to discover godliness any teacher of pious doctrine, but Manichæus, Colluthus, Arius, Aetius, and those like to them, supposing that Christianity in general is folly, and that the customs of the Church and the venerable sacraments are a jest, wherein he differs in nothing from the pagans, who borrowed from our doctrine the idea of a great God supreme over all. So, too, this new idolater preaches in the same fashion, and in particular that baptism is “into an artificer and creator,” not fearing the curse of those who cause addition or diminution to the Holy Scriptures. And he closes his book with showing him to be Antichrist.
sources.answer: No. To think piety consists in doctrines only is a mark of the pagans. Those who slight the confession of the sacred Names and treat sacramental sanctification as worthless, while placing salvation in quibbles about generate and ungenerate, transgress the doctrines of salvation.
sources.quote: to fancy that their salvation consists in quibbles about the generate and the ungenerate,—what else are they than transgressors of the doctrines of salvation?
sources.raw_question: Does salvation and piety consist only in correct doctrine, such as reasoning about the generate and the ungenerate, apart from the sacraments and the confession of the Divine Names?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > Eunomius again speaks of the Son as Lord and God, and Maker of all creation intelligible and sensible, having received from the Father the power and the commission for creation, being entrusted with the task of creation as if He were an artizan commissioned by some one hiring Him, and receiving His power of creation as a thing adventitious, ab extra, as a result of the power allotted to Him in accordance with such and such combinations and positions of the stars, as destiny decrees their lot in life to men at their nativity. Thus, passing by most of what Eunomius had written, he confutes his blasphemy that the Maker of all things came into being in like manner with the earth and with angels, and that the subsistence of the Only-begotten differs not at all from the genesis of all things, and reproaches Him with reverencing neither the Divine mystery nor the custom of the Church, nor following in his attempt to discover godliness any teacher of pious doctrine, but Manichæus, Colluthus, Arius, Aetius, and those like to them, supposing that Christianity in general is folly, and that the customs of the Church and the venerable sacraments are a jest, wherein he differs in nothing from the pagans, who borrowed from our doctrine the idea of a great God supreme over all. So, too, this new idolater preaches in the same fashion, and in particular that baptism is “into an artificer and creator,” not fearing the curse of those who cause addition or diminution to the Holy Scriptures. And he closes his book with showing him to be Antichrist.
sources.answer: No. Christ himself taught that one must be born again of water and the Spirit and must eat his flesh and drink his blood, so the mystery of godliness is ratified by confessing the Divine Names of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and salvation is confirmed by participating in the sacraments. Correct doctrine alone is not enough, since outsiders often debate doctrine and even hit on the truth while remaining strangers to the faith.
sources.quote: are persuaded that the mystery of godliness is ratified by the confession of the Divine Names—the Names of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, and that our salvation is confirmed by participation in the sacramental customs and tokens
sources.raw_question: Does the mystery of godliness consist only in exactness of doctrine, rather than in the confession of the Names of Father, Son and Holy Spirit and in the sacraments?

question: Can God's works in creation or his attributes, such as justice, holiness and patience, considered apart from Christ, show sinners a way to approach God in peace or bring them comfort and salvation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: No. No work God has made and no attribute he has revealed gives the least light about how sinners might approach him in peace. The manifestation of pardoning grace, which is the only door into communion, is committed to Christ alone. He purchased and dispenses that grace and reveals it from the bosom of the Father.
sources.quote: Not any work that God had made, not any attribute that he had revealed, could give the least light into such a dispensation.
sources.raw_question: Can God's works in creation or his revealed attributes show sinners a way to approach God in peace?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Considered nakedly, apart from Christ, God's justice makes sinners flee and hide, his patience hardens them, and his holiness deters them from approaching him. Knowledge of God's properties becomes saving and consoling only when we see that God has glorified all of them in a way of doing us good, which he has done in Jesus Christ alone.
sources.quote: Under this naked consideration of the properties of God, justice will make men fly and hide, Gen. iii.; Isa. ii. 21, xxxiii. 15, 16; — patience, render them obdurate, Eccles. viii. 11.
sources.raw_question: Can knowledge of God's attributes such as justice, holiness, and patience, considered apart from Christ, bring sinners comfort or salvation?

question: Can the woman healed of a twelve-year issue of blood (or the twelfth apostle) serve as a numerical type of the suffering Aeon of the Valentinian Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIII.—The woman who suffered from an issue of blood was no type of the suffering Æon.
sources.answer: No. In the Valentinian scheme eleven Aeons stayed impassible and only the twelfth suffered. The woman, by contrast, suffered for eleven years and was healed in the twelfth. The pattern is therefore reversed, and she cannot be a figure of their twelfth Aeon.
sources.quote: But since she suffered during eleven years, and [all that time] obtained no cure, but was healed in the twelfth year, in what way can she be a type of the twelfth of the Æons
sources.raw_question: Does the healing of the woman with the issue of blood in her twelfth year typify the suffering of the twelfth Aeon of the Valentinian Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XX.—Futility of the arguments adduced to demonstrate the sufferings of the twelfth Æon, from the parables, the treachery of Judas, and the passion of our Saviour.
sources.answer: No. The numbers do not even correspond. Judas is agreed by all to be twelfth of the twelve named apostles. By the Gnostics' own system, however, the suffering Æon was produced not twelfth but in the thirtieth place. So the twelfth cannot be the type of the thirtieth.
sources.quote: How, then, can Judas, the twelfth in order, be the type and image of that Æon who occupies the thirtieth place?
sources.raw_question: Can the woman healed of a twelve-year issue of blood, or the twelfth apostle, be used as numerical types of a Gnostic Æon in the Pleroma?

question: How was Christ's human nature kept free from original sin, even though he was born of a woman descended from sinful ancestors?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: By the sanctifying work of the Holy Ghost from the instant of conception. The portion of the virgin's substance from which he was made was sanctified by the Spirit, so that what was born should be a holy thing. This sanctification accompanied both the separation of his bodily substance in the womb and the union of soul and body, so he is 'holy, harmless, undefiled.'
sources.quote: He was “made of a woman,” Gal. iv. 4; but that portion whereof he was made was sanctified by the Holy Ghost, that what was born thereof should be a holy thing.
sources.raw_question: How was Christ's human nature kept free from the pollution of original sin though he was born of a woman?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ was the spotless Lamb of God, holy, harmless and undefiled from the womb, as befits our high priest. Adam and the angels had spotless purity, but they came immediately from God's hand. Christ, by contrast, was born of a sinner, from a line in which all were infected, and from a nature that was both defiled and guilty. That his human nature should come from this source free from both guilt and pollution is to be adored.
sources.quote: That the human nature of Christ should be derived from hence free from guilt, free from pollution, this is to be adored.
sources.raw_question: Was the human nature of Christ free from sin, even though he descended from sinful ancestors?

question: Is the Valentinian teaching that the Saviour was formed from the combined excellences or gifts of all the Æons a genuine Christian revelation about Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIV.—Valentinus and his followers derived the principles of their system from the heathen; the names only are changed.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus says it brings forward nothing new, since it merely repeats Hesiod's myth of Pandora, recast so that the Saviour becomes 'All-gifted.' The doctrine is pagan poetry with the names changed, not a truth about Christ.
sources.quote: as to their saying that the Saviour was formed out of all the Æons, by every one of them depositing, so to speak, in Him his own special flower, they bring forward nothing new that may not be found in the Pandora of Hesiod.
sources.raw_question: Is the Valentinian teaching that the Saviour was formed out of all the Æons, each depositing its own special excellence in him, a genuine revelation about Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXI.—The twelve apostles were not a type of the Æons.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus treats it as a borrowing from pagan myth. Hesiod's Pandora, the 'gift of all,' and Pindar's tale of Pelops, whose flesh was reassembled by all the gods, express the same idea. Those who teach such a Saviour therefore show themselves to be of the same family and spirit as the pagan poets, not as the apostles.
sources.quote: Respecting this being the poet Hesiod has strikingly expressed himself, styling him Pandora —that is, “The gift of all”—for this reason, that the best gift in the possession of all was centred in him.
sources.raw_question: Is the Valentinian teaching that the Saviour was compounded from the collected gifts of all the Æons a revealed Christian mystery?

question: Does the application of Isaiah 40:3 ("Prepare ye the way of Jehovah") to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus prove that Christ is Jehovah?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah says the voice in the wilderness prepares the way of Jehovah, our God, and Matthew identifies that voice with John the Baptist. John undeniably prepared the way for Christ. Therefore Christ is Jehovah, our God.
sources.quote: Now John Baptist’s voice, without controversy, was heard in the wilderness, preparing the way for Christ. Therefore, Christ is Jehovah, our God.
sources.raw_question: Does the application of Isaiah 40:3 ("Prepare ye the way of Jehovah") to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus prove that Christ is Jehovah?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah says the voice in the wilderness prepares the way of Jehovah, our God. Matthew applies this to John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Christ. An inspired interpretation of an inspired text therefore identifies Christ as Jehovah.
sources.quote: Now John Baptist’s voice, without controversy, was heard in the wilderness, preparing the way for Christ. Therefore, Christ is Jehovah, our God.
sources.raw_question: Does the fulfilment of Isaiah 40:3 in John the Baptist's ministry show that Christ is Jehovah?

question: Does the visible object produce the bodily sense of sight itself, or does it only produce a form in that sense, so that vision is distinct from the sense?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Certain Trinity in the Sight. That There are Three Things in Sight, Which Differ in Their Own Nature. In What Manner from a Visible Thing Vision is Produced, or the Image of that Thing Which is Seen. The Matter is Shown More Clearly by an Example. How These Three Combine in One.
sources.answer: It produces only the form, not the sense. The sense exists before anything is perceived and remains after the object is removed, like water that remains when the impressed body is withdrawn. What the object produces is its own likeness in the sense, which ceases when the object is taken away.
sources.quote: we cannot, indeed, say that a visible thing produces the sense; yet it produces the form, which is, as it were, its own likeness, which comes to be in the sense, when we perceive anything by seeing.
sources.raw_question: Does the visible object produce the sense of sight itself, or only a form in the sense?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Certain Trinity in the Sight. That There are Three Things in Sight, Which Differ in Their Own Nature. In What Manner from a Visible Thing Vision is Produced, or the Image of that Thing Which is Seen. The Matter is Shown More Clearly by an Example. How These Three Combine in One.
sources.answer: Vision is distinct from the sense: it is the sense as informed from without by the object perceived. The sense already exists in the living subject before it sees anything. Otherwise we would not differ from the blind when our eyes are closed or we are in darkness. The visible body does not make the sense to be sense; it forms it so as to be vision.
sources.quote: And what plainly is vision itself other than perception informed by that thing which is perceived?
sources.raw_question: Is vision the same thing as the bodily sense of sight, or is vision produced in that sense by the visible object?

question: How can we know that seeing involves an image of the object formed in the sense, distinct from the object itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Certain Trinity in the Sight. That There are Three Things in Sight, Which Differ in Their Own Nature. In What Manner from a Visible Thing Vision is Produced, or the Image of that Thing Which is Seen. The Matter is Shown More Clearly by an Example. How These Three Combine in One.
sources.answer: Reason infers it, even though sense cannot separate the two because they are so closely united. Augustine compares a ring pressed into a fluid: no image remains when it is withdrawn, yet reason sees that a form was produced there while the ring was present. In the same way, the image in vision is real even though it does not remain once the object is gone.
sources.quote: But we rationally infer that we could not have sensation at all, unless some similitude of the body seen was wrought in our own sense.
sources.raw_question: If we cannot perceive any difference between the form of a seen body and the image of it in our sense, how can we know that a distinct image is formed in the sense?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Certain Trinity in the Sight. That There are Three Things in Sight, Which Differ in Their Own Nature. In What Manner from a Visible Thing Vision is Produced, or the Image of that Thing Which is Seen. The Matter is Shown More Clearly by an Example. How These Three Combine in One.
sources.answer: Afterimages and double vision show it. After gazing at a light and closing the eyes, fading colors, even the shapes of window lattices, remain as traces of the form that was wrought in the sense. Also, a single lamp flame appears doubled when the rays of the two eyes do not meet. This could not happen unless an image like the thing were produced in each sense.
sources.quote: unless some image, precisely like the thing we perceive, were produced in our sense, the appearance of the flame would not be doubled according to the number of the eyes
sources.raw_question: What experiential evidence shows that seeing involves an image of the object formed in the sense, distinct from the object itself?

question: In what ways does Christ help and show compassion to believers who are under temptation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Christ gives grace for help in time of need. He fortifies the heart with a habitual bent against the sin to which a person is most exposed, as with Joseph. By a strong impulse of actual grace he can also recover a soul from the very brink of sin, as with David. The following context adds that he removes temptations, supplies fresh grace, and gives wisdom to use temptations well.
sources.quote: Christ sometimes, by some strong impulse of actual grace, recovers the soul from the very borders of sin.
sources.raw_question: In what ways does Christ give believers seasonable help against temptation to sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Christ helps tempted believers in several ways. He sometimes takes the temptation away entirely, rebuking Satan so that the believer hears no more of it. He supplies fresh grace as temptations grow, as he told Paul that his grace was sufficient. He gives wisdom to put temptations to holy use, and he relieves with mercy and pardon those who are overcome, so that they do not sink utterly.
sources.quote: By one, more, or all of these ways, doth the Lord Jesus manifest his conjugal tenderness and compassion towards the saints, in and under their temptations.
sources.raw_question: In what ways does Christ show compassion to believers who are under temptation?

question: Should Isaiah 7:14 be translated 'Behold, a young woman shall conceive' (as Theodotion and Aquila rendered it) rather than 'Behold, a virgin shall conceive'?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: No. The reading 'virgin' is the correct one. It stands in the Greek translation made by the Jews themselves long before the Lord's coming, so it cannot be suspected of being a Christian invention. Those who now offer new translations do so only because they are refuted from the received Scriptures.
sources.quote: But it was interpreted into Greek by the Jews themselves, much before the period of our Lord’s advent, that there might remain no suspicion that perchance the Jews, complying with our humour, did put this interpretation upon these words.
sources.raised_by_detail: Theodotion the Ephesian and Aquila of Pontus, Jewish proselytes, followed by the Ebionites
sources.raw_question: Should Isaiah 7:14 be translated 'Behold, a young woman shall conceive' (as Theodotion and Aquila rendered it) rather than 'Behold, a virgin shall conceive'?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: No. The Lord promised a sign from the height or the depth, but there would be no sign in a young woman conceiving by a man, since that happens to all women who bear children. The unlooked-for salvation required an unlooked-for birth from a virgin, worked by God and not by man.
sources.quote: For what great thing or what sign should have been in this, that a young woman conceiving by a man should bring forth,—a thing which happens to all women that produce offspring?
sources.raw_question: Should Isaiah 7:14 be read as "a young woman shall conceive," making Christ the son of Joseph, as Theodotion, Aquila and the Ebionites hold?

question: How does the Holy Spirit's anointing (unction) teach believers and preserve them from being led into error?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: It makes truth sweet and joyful to the soul. Knowing a truth in its power, sweetness and gladness is the great security that the soul will hold on to it. Those who find no more sweetness in truth than in error will readily exchange one for the other.
sources.quote: They will readily change truth for error, who find no more sweetness in the one than in the other.
sources.raw_question: Why does the Holy Spirit's teaching by anointing preserve believers from being led into error?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: The Spirit's unction teaches believers the love of God in Christ and makes gospel truth sweet, giving joy and gladness of heart in what they know of God. This experienced sweetness is the great preservative of the soul in the truth, for those who find no more sweetness in truth than in error will readily exchange one for the other.
sources.quote: Indeed, to know any truth in the power, sweetness, joy, and gladness of it, is that great security of the soul’s constancy in the preservation and retaining of it. They will readily change truth for error, who find no more sweetness in the one than in the other.
sources.raw_question: What does the anointing (unction) of the Holy Spirit teach believers, and how does it preserve them from error?

question: If Christ's death fully procured reconciliation and satisfied for the elect, why do they remain under the curse of the law until their conversion rather than being delivered immediately?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Reconciliation is fully purchased by Christ's death. However, Father, Son, and Spirit determined that the elect would come into actual possession of it in a particular way and order, so that the whole Trinity would be glorified. Their deliverance is no less fully procured or freely given than if they had been taken to heaven at once. The timing serves the praise of God's glorious grace.
sources.quote: only this way of our deliverance and freedom is fixed on, that the whole Trinity may be glorified thereby
sources.raw_question: If Christ's death fully procured reconciliation with God, why are the elect not delivered from the curse of the law immediately upon his death?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes, they are personally and legally exposed to the curse until their appointed deliverance. But the curse does not hold them with its original purpose of being carried out on them. It is kept in place as a design of love, to bring them to know Christ and be accepted with God for his sake. Once that is accomplished, the obligation ceases.
sources.quote: but not at all with its primitive intention of execution upon them, but as it is a means appointed to help forward their acquaintance with Christ, and acceptance with God, on his account.
sources.raw_question: Are the elect, before their conversion, really under the curse of the law even though Christ has satisfied for them?

question: Does calling the one who appeared in the burning bush the 'Angel' of God show that he was not truly God by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. 'Angel' names His office, not His nature. The same one speaks as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and as 'I Am that I Am,' the absolute God. So the Angel of God is God in the full sense and not God by adoption.
sources.quote: He is manifested as Angel; that is His office, not His nature. The name which expresses His nature is given you as God; for the Angel of God is God.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the one who appeared in the burning bush the 'Angel' of God show that he was not true God by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. 'Angel' names his office, not his nature; the name expressing his nature is God, for the Angel of God is God. The same one who appears as Angel speaks from the bush as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and as 'I Am that I Am'.
sources.quote: He is manifested as Angel; that is His office, not His nature. The name which expresses His nature is given you as God; for the Angel of God is God.
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'Angel of God' given to the one who appeared in the burning bush show that he is not truly God?

question: Does the confusion of tongues at the tower of Babel show that God himself created human languages?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. At Babel God is described as confounding an existing language, not creating languages. Afterwards the scattered peoples adopted different forms of speech and named the same things differently. So human language remains the invention of the human mind.
sources.quote: not even there is God spoken of as creating men’s languages, but as confounding the existing one, that all might not hear all
sources.raw_question: Does the confusion of tongues at Babel show that God created human languages?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Scripture does not say God created men's languages at Babel but that He confounded the existing one so that all might not hear all. After the dispersion, men themselves adopted various forms of speech, agreeing in their knowledge of things but differing in the names they gave them. So human language remains an invention of the human mind.
sources.quote: not even there is God spoken of as creating men’s languages, but as confounding the existing one, that all might not hear all
sources.raw_question: Does the confusion of tongues at the tower of Babel show that God himself created human languages?

question: Do the Son's works in creating and redeeming humanity show that He is good?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > The eleventh book shows that the title of “Good” is due, not to the Father alone, as Eunomius, the imitator of Manichæus and Bardesanes, alleges, but to the Son also, Who formed man in goodness and loving-kindness, and reformed him by His Cross and Death.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son formed man from soulless dust into a Godlike image. He then took the form of a servant out of love for man, bore the sufferings due to sin, and gave himself as a ransom. One who does these things cannot be denied the title "good."
sources.quote: is He not good, Who when thou wast soulless dust invested thee with Godlike beauty, and raised thee up as an image of His own power endowed with soul?
sources.raw_question: Is the Son shown to be good by his works of creating and redeeming humanity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > The eleventh book shows that the title of “Good” is due, not to the Father alone, as Eunomius, the imitator of Manichæus and Bardesanes, alleges, but to the Son also, Who formed man in goodness and loving-kindness, and reformed him by His Cross and Death.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son formed man from soulless dust, gave him Godlike beauty, and made him an image of His own power. For man's sake He took the form of a servant, bore the sufferings due to sin, gave Himself as a ransom, and became a curse and sin for us. Such benefits prove His goodness, and denying it repays the Lord with ingratitude.
sources.quote: Is He not good, Who for thy sake took on Him the form of a servant, and for the joy set before Him did not shrink from bearing the sufferings due to thy sin, and gave Himself a ransom for thy death
sources.raw_question: Do the Son's works in creating and redeeming humanity show that He is good?

question: Can it coherently be said, as Eunomius claims, that God "has dominion over His own power," as though God were distinct from His power and could hold back the generation of the Son until a chosen time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > The ninth book declares that Eunomius' account of the Nature of God is, up to a certain point, well stated. Then in succession he mixes up with his own argument, on account of its affinity, the expression from Philo's writings, “God is before all other things, which are generated,” adding also the expression, “He has dominion over His own power.” Detesting the excessive absurdity, Gregory strikingly confutes it.
sources.answer: No. If God is something other than His power, then power is mastered by what is not power, which is absurd. If God is power and has another power in Himself by which He masters the first, then God is divided against Himself, double-natured or composite, with one power urging disorder and another restraining it. Neither alternative fits the simple Divine Nature.
sources.quote: Such is Eunomius’ God: a being with double nature, or composite, dividing Himself against Himself, having one power out of harmony with another, so that by one He is urged to disorder, and by the other restrains this discordant motion.
sources.raw_question: Can it coherently be said that God "has dominion over His own power," so as to hold back the generation of the Son until a chosen time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > The ninth book declares that Eunomius' account of the Nature of God is, up to a certain point, well stated. Then in succession he mixes up with his own argument, on account of its affinity, the expression from Philo's writings, “God is before all other things, which are generated,” adding also the expression, “He has dominion over His own power.” Detesting the excessive absurdity, Gregory strikingly confutes it.
sources.answer: No. If God were something other than His power and ruled over it as over something else, then that which is not power would be overcoming power. That is absurd, because what is other than power is not power at all. Gregory adds that the phrase is borrowed from Philo, which shows the affinity between Eunomius' doctrine and Jewish reasoning.
sources.quote: Is He something else than His own power, and Lord of a power that is something else than Himself? Then power is overcome by the absence of power.
sources.raw_question: Does it make sense to say, with Eunomius, that God 'has dominion over His own power,' as if God were something distinct from His power?

question: Are Jesus, Christ, the Saviour, the Word and the Only-begotten separate beings, as the Valentinians taught, or one and the same Lord?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Preface.
sources.answer: No. Dividing Jesus from Christ, Christ from the Saviour, the Saviour from the Word, and the Word from the Only-begotten is blasphemy against our Lord. These names refer to one and the same Lord. The apostles, who were eye-witnesses and ministers of the word, held no such opinions and warned believers to shun them.
sources.quote: They utter blasphemy, also, against our Lord, by cutting off and dividing Jesus from Christ, and Christ from the Saviour, and again the Saviour from the Word, and the Word from the Only-begotten.
sources.raw_question: May Jesus, Christ, the Saviour, the Word and the Only-begotten be treated as separate beings, as the Valentinians teach?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: No. Scripture speaks of these as one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. By dividing them into separate productions with separate origins, the Valentinians confess the unity of God with their tongues while in their real opinion they hold many deities. Their teaching therefore falls away from the doctrine of one God and one Lord.
sources.quote: their tongues alone, forsooth, have conceded the unity [of God], while their [real] opinion and their understanding (by their habit of investigating profundities) have fallen away from [this doctrine of] unity, and taken up the notion of manifold deities
sources.raw_question: Are the Only-begotten, the Word, Christ and the Saviour separate beings, each with its own origin, as the Valentinians taught?

question: What is the origin and nature of the Holy Spirit, and can it be fully understood?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: The Spirit is from the Father and through the Son, proceeding from the Father and sent through the Son. This truth is held by faith although the intellect cannot comprehend it. As Christ said, we hear the Spirit's voice but do not know whence it comes or whither it goes. Since the cause of His coming and going is unknown, He must not be counted among created things or limited by a time of origin.
sources.quote: so I hold fast in my consciousness the truth that Thy Holy Spirit is from Thee and through Him, although I cannot by my intellect comprehend it.
sources.raw_question: What is the origin of the Holy Spirit, and can it be fully understood?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: He is the one through whom all things exist and from whom are all things, and he is the Spirit of God, God's gift to the faithful. Since he is, is given, is possessed and is of God, his detractors should be silent. Those who reject this answer quarrel with the Apostles and Prophets, and with Father and Son, who spoke of him in the same way.
sources.quote: we answer that He it is through Whom all things exist, and from Whom are all things, and that He is the Spirit of God, God’s gift to the faithful.
sources.raw_question: What is the origin, purpose and nature of the Holy Spirit?

question: Should Christ be divided into separate parts, the Word, a soul and a body, rather than confessed as one Lord who is both God and man?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The Word was made flesh, so Jesus Christ must not be divided. We must see the God in Him without ignoring the Man, and the Man without ignoring the God. It is one and the same Lord who speaks both as man and as God.
sources.quote: To grasp this divine mystery we must see the God in Him without ignoring the Man; and the Man without ignoring the God. We must not divide Jesus Christ, for the Word was made flesh
sources.raised_by_detail: those who trisect Christ into the Word, the soul and the body
sources.raw_question: Should Christ be divided into the Word, a soul and a body, or reduced to a mere man, in order to explain His sufferings and death?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The Church does not, by a tripartite belief, tear Christ asunder into Word, body and soul, just as his seamless coat was not parted. He is one, perfectly God the Word and perfectly Christ the Man.
sources.quote: nor does it by a tripartite belief tear asunder Christ, Whose coat woven from the top throughout was not parted, dividing Jesus Christ into the Word, a body and a soul
sources.raw_question: Should Christ be understood as three parts, namely the Word, a body, and a soul?

question: Does holding that the Son purchased redemption by offering himself to God as satisfaction take away from the Father's free gift of his Son out of love for the world?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Scripture itself, through the Holy Spirit, says Christ 'obtained eternal redemption' for us, laid down his life as a ransom, and bought us with a price, so denying this is denying the gospel. The great gift of God consisted precisely in giving his Son to obtain redemption for us. In this work Christ both offered himself to God and gave himself for us.
sources.quote: In a word, the great gift of God consisted in giving his Son to obtain redemption for us.
sources.raw_question: Does holding that the Son purchased redemption by offering himself to God as satisfaction take away from the Father's free gift of his Son out of love for the world?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Scripture itself says Christ obtained eternal redemption, laid down his life as a ransom, and bought us with a price; the great gift of God consisted precisely in giving his Son to obtain redemption for us, in which Christ offered himself to God.
sources.quote: In a word, the great gift of God consisted in giving his Son to obtain redemption for us.
sources.raw_question: Does saying the Son purchased redemption by giving himself to God rob God of the glory of giving his Son out of love?

question: Does the account of God walking in the garden and Adam hiding from his face show that Adam saw God in a bodily or human form?
