sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: No. Adam may not have seen God at all. He may only have feared being seen by the one whose voice he heard and whose presence he felt. Similarly, Cain said he would hide from God's face, yet no one is compelled to say that Cain beheld God's face with bodily eyes; he only heard God's voice questioning him.
sources.quote: For what if he himself indeed could not see, but feared to be himself seen by Him whose voice he had heard, and had felt His presence as he walked?
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that Adam hid himself from the face of God prove that Adam usually saw God's face in a bodily form?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: Not necessarily. Read literally, the account seems to imply that God spoke to Adam in the appearance of a man, since he is said to walk and Adam hid from his face. But Augustine will not rashly assert this. Perhaps only words were formed for Adam to hear, and Adam may have feared being seen by one he could not himself see.
sources.quote: Yet I would not rashly assert, even if that scripture implies Paradise to have been a material place, that God could not have walked there in any way except in some bodily form. For it might be said, that only words were framed for the man to hear, without seeing any form.
sources.raw_question: Does the account of God walking in the garden and Adam hiding from his face require that God appeared to Adam in human form?

question: Was the worship Jesus received in the Gospels divine adoration, or merely the customary homage paid to men of great authority?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Though proskuneo is used in classical writers for prostrate salutation, its New Testament usage is almost universally divine homage: of about sixty occurrences, twenty-two are worship of God, fifteen of Christ, seventeen idolatrous worship condemned, and only two human salutation. Of those two, one (Matt. 18:26) involves a king typifying God, and the word is exchanged for 'besought' when the transaction is between fellow men. So by New Testament usage it is unnatural to deny that divine worship is paid to Christ, who never refused it.
sources.quote: We are, therefore, virtually reduced to one solitary instance, and taking the New Testament for our guide, it would be as unnatural to deny, that divine worship is paid to Christ
sources.raw_question: Was the worship (proskuneo) that Jesus received in the Gospels merely the customary homage paid to men of great authority rather than adoration of God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Those who worshipped Jesus also sought from him superhuman help, depending on his aid as divine aid, as the leper and the ruler did. If he were not God, he would have been bound to correct so dangerous an approach to idolatry, and he did not.
sources.quote: such humble dependence on his aid, as Divine aid, that if He were not God, he must needs have rectified so dangerous an approximation to idolatry
sources.raw_question: Do the petitions that accompanied the worship of Jesus in the Gospels show that he received divine rather than merely human homage?

question: Should human weaknesses ascribed to Christ in the Gospels, such as need or ignorance, be attributed to the Word's Godhead or to his human flesh?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: No. These things are foreign to God and belong to the manhood. His miracles done through the body, such as spitting or calling Lazarus, are God's works, not human triumphs. In the same way, human affections are imputed to the flesh, while grace and power belong to the Word.
sources.quote: let us, considering the nature of what is said and that they are foreign to God, not impute them to the Word’s Godhead, but to His manhood.
sources.raw_question: Should human weaknesses ascribed to Christ in the Gospels, such as need or ignorance, be attributed to the Word's Godhead?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: It belongs to the flesh, not the Godhead. In the Godhead there is no ignorance, but ignorance is proper to the flesh. The Word as Word knows all things before they come to be, as shown by his knowing from afar that Lazarus was dead, his knowing what was in man, and his alone knowing the Father.
sources.quote: in the Godhead indeed ignorance is not, but to the flesh ignorance is proper, as has been said.
sources.raw_question: If ignorance is ascribed to Christ, does it belong to his Godhead or to his human flesh?

question: Does the example of created things like the sky, whose prior non-existence implied no opposite, show that the Son's once not existing would not imply that evil, the opposite of the Good, existed?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. The sky has no corresponding opposite except its own non-existence, but the Son is virtue, truth and light, and to virtue vice is certainly opposed. So while the sky's absence implies nothing existed in its place, the absence of the good implies its opposite existed; whoever says the Good once was not admits, even unwillingly, that evil was.
sources.quote: to the sky there is no corresponding opposite, unless one were to say that its non-existence is opposed to its existence. But to virtue is certainly opposed that which is vicious (and the Lord is virtue)
sources.raw_question: Can the analogy of other created things, such as the sky, which had no opposite before it existed, show that the Son's non-existence would not imply the existence of an opposite evil?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. The sky has no real opposite except its own non-existence. Virtue, however, has vice as its opposite, and the Lord is virtue. So when good was not, its opposite was, and whoever says the good once was not must, even without intending it, grant that evil was.
sources.quote: to the sky there is no corresponding opposite, unless one were to say that its non-existence is opposed to its existence. But to virtue is certainly opposed that which is vicious (and the Lord is virtue)
sources.raw_question: Is the argument from the Son's non-existence to the presence of evil refuted by examples like the sky, whose earlier absence implied no opposite?

question: Did the Old Testament prophets speak some things from the highest God (the Pleroma) and others from an inferior Creator (the Demiurge), as the Valentinians claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXV.—A refutation of those who allege that the prophets uttered some predictions under the inspiration of the highest, others from the Demiurge. Disagreements of the Valentinians among themselves with regard to these same predictions.
sources.answer: No. It is irrational to suppose the Father of all lacked his own instruments to proclaim his will, as if he feared that many would be saved or was unable to prepare heralds of the Saviour's advent. Just as the Lord sent his apostles in the spirit of truth, so he did with the prophets, for the Word of God was always the same.
sources.quote: But if, at His advent, He sent forth His own apostles in the spirit of truth, and not in that of error, He did the very same also in the case of the prophets; for the Word of God was always the self-same
sources.raw_question: Did the prophets speak some things from the highest God (the Pleroma) and others from an inferior Creator (the Demiurge), as the Valentinians claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXV.—A refutation of those who allege that the prophets uttered some predictions under the inspiration of the highest, others from the Demiurge. Disagreements of the Valentinians among themselves with regard to these same predictions.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus argues that the Valentinians cannot even agree which higher Aeon a given passage comes from, and so they convict themselves by their discord over the same words. The Church, following the one true God as teacher, agrees that one and the same God, the Creator, sent all the prophets. Christ's parable of the vineyard confirms this, since the same householder who sends the servants also sends his only son.
sources.quote: For, though holding wrong opinions, they do in the meanwhile, however, convict themselves, since they are not of one mind with regard to the same words.
sources.raw_question: Did the Old Testament prophets utter some predictions under inspiration from a higher divine realm (the Pleroma) and others from a lesser creator god (the Demiurge)?

question: Did Irenaeus (or the Ante-Nicene writers generally) teach that the Son, as the divine Word, was really ignorant of the day of judgment?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus speaks of the Logos but only seems to ascribe ignorance to him, and only to an inattentive reader. He sought a safe interpretation that would neither contradict the text nor impute ignorance to the Lord. He held that the Father is 'declared to have the preference' in knowledge, not that the Son knows less. His purpose was to check the Gnostics' presumption by teaching men to leave the deep things of God to God.
sources.quote: He is sensible of the danger of ascribing any thing like ignorance to our blessed Lord, on one hand, and as sensible of the danger of contradicting the text, on the other.
sources.raw_question: Did Irenaeus ascribe real ignorance of the day of judgment to the divine Word (Logos) of Christ?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: No. The claim that all Ante-Nicene writers held this is unfounded; only Irenaeus is cited, and Bishop Bull shows that any ignorance Irenaeus ascribed to Christ concerned his human nature. Irenaeus elsewhere ascribes absolute omniscience to Christ's divine nature, describes the Son as perfectly knowing the Father, mocks the Gnostics for ascribing ignorance to their Sophia, and argues against the Valentinians that the Son, being eternal and uncreated, is omniscient. Waterland further argues that Irenaeus speaks of the Logos but does not really ascribe ignorance to him.
sources.quote: You are not eternal and uncreated, as the Son of God is; and therefore cannot pretend to be omniscient, as he is.
sources.raw_question: Did the Ante-Nicene writers, and Irenaeus in particular, teach that the Son as the divine Word was ignorant of the day of judgment?

question: Do the works Scripture ascribes to the Holy Spirit, such as leading, enlightening, healing, comforting and restoring, prove that He is God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture ascribes leading, strengthening, and enlightening to God, to the Father and the Son alike. If Eunomius means these phrases in the Psalmist's sense, they testify to the Spirit's divinity. If he does not, he sets his own opinions against the prophets and stands guilty of blasphemy.
sources.quote: If then the expressions of Eunomius are meant in accordance with the mind of the Psalmist, they are a testimony to the Divinity of the Holy Ghost
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit leads us, strengthens us to godliness, and enlightens souls, do these works prove His divinity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes. No one would ascribe any of these effects to anyone except God, and Scripture repeatedly assigns healing, conversion, comfort, and upholding the fallen to God alone. Since Eunomius himself says the Spirit does these things, his own words serve as an opponent's witness to the Spirit's deity.
sources.quote: If then heresy affirms that those things which it belongs to none save God alone to effect, are wrought by the power of the Spirit, we have in support of the truths for which we are contending the witness even of our adversaries.
sources.raw_question: Do the works of healing the sick, comforting the afflicted, and restoring the fallen, when ascribed to the Holy Spirit, prove that He is God?

question: Was the material substance of creation produced from the passions of the fallen Aeon Achamoth, as the Valentinians teach?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter X.—Perverse interpretations of Scripture by the heretics: God created all things out of nothing, and not from pre-existent matter.
sources.answer: No. The claim is incredible, impossible and untenable. The Valentinians ask where the Creator got His matter, yet never ask where their Mother got so great an amount of tears and sadness. Attributing the substance of things to the power and will of the God of all is credible and agreeable to reason.
sources.quote: For, to attribute the substance of created things to the power and will of Him who is God of all, is worthy both of credit and acceptance. It is also agreeable [to reason]
sources.raw_question: Was the material substance of creation produced from the passions of a fallen Æon (Achamoth), as the Valentinians teach?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter IV.—Account given by the heretics of the formation of Achamoth; origin of the visible world from her disturbances.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus treats it as an absurd fiction and refutes it by drawing out its consequences. Tears are all of one salty quality, so they cannot account for both salt and fresh water. To save the theory one would have to invent further fancies, such as her perspiration, and leave hot springs unexplained. This shows the system is arbitrary invention, not knowledge of how the world came to be.
sources.quote: For it is difficult, since we know that all tears are of the same quality, to believe that waters both salt and fresh proceeded from them.
sources.raw_question: Is the Valentinian teaching true that the material world was formed from the passions of Achamoth, a fallen Aeon, with liquids coming from her tears, light from her smile and bodies from her grief?

question: Did the apostles preach with imperfect knowledge, so that later teachers could improve on their doctrine?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter I.—The apostles did not commence to preach the Gospel, or to place anything on record until they were endowed with the gifts and power of the Holy Spirit. They preached one God alone, Maker of heaven and earth.
sources.answer: No. After the Lord rose from the dead, the apostles were invested with power from on high when the Holy Spirit came upon them. They were filled with all his gifts and had perfect knowledge before they went out to preach. Those who claim to improve on the apostles therefore assert something unlawful.
sources.quote: after our Lord rose from the dead, [the apostles] were invested with power from on high when the Holy Spirit came down [upon them], were filled from all [His gifts], and had perfect knowledge
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who boast themselves as improvers of the apostles
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles preach the Gospel before they possessed perfect knowledge, so that later teachers could improve on their doctrine?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. It would be ridiculous to suppose that Peter and the other apostles were imperfect and would need to become disciples of later teachers. Such teachers follow their own notions, which is why they disagree with one another. The Church, founded firmly on the apostles, keeps one and the same opinion about God and his Son.
sources.quote: But the Church throughout all the world, having its origin firm from the apostles, perseveres in one and the same opinion with regard to God and His Son.
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles lack a more perfect knowledge of God that was discovered later by heretical teachers?

question: Did Origen count the Son of God among the creatures (demiurgemata) of God, for example when he calls the Son 'eldest of all the works'?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 12: Whether the Creator of all things was not himself uncreated ; and therefore could not be ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, made out of nothing ?
sources.answer: No. Following Bishop Bull, Waterland reads the phrase as 'ancienter than all creatures,' with the superlative used comparatively. Other writers use such superlatives the same way: Eusebius calls the Son eldest of all times and ages, and Justin calls Moses eldest of the Greek wise men, without placing either among the things compared. Origen's whole drift, especially in that treatise, is against the Son being a creature. So the phrase only seems to say what the Arian reading claims, and does not say it expressly.
sources.quote: The superlative, we see, hath been used sometimes comparatively; and why not by Origen? He may only appear to say what he really does not.
sources.raw_question: When Origen calls the Son 'πρεσβύτατον πάντων τῶν δημιουργημάτων' (eldest of all the works), does he count the Son among the creatures?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. When Origen forbids honouring creatures such as the sun in place of God, he speaks of 'God, or the Son of God' as the proper object of honour. This shows that he clearly distinguishes the Son from the works of God, as he does everywhere.
sources.quote: We ought not to honour those in the place of God, or of the “ Son of God.” Which I take notice of here particularly, that you may see how clearly Origen distinguishes the Son from the δημιουργήματα Θεοῦ
sources.raw_question: Did Origen count the Son of God among the creatures (demiurgemata) of God, which may not be worshipped?

question: Could Christ have recapitulated the ancient enmity against the serpent and fulfilled the Creator's promise if he had been sent by a Father other than the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: No. The Lord could not have summed up in himself the ancient enmity against the serpent, and so fulfilled the Creator's promise, if he had come from another Father. It is one and the same God who formed us at the beginning and sent his Son at the end. For this reason Christ used the words of the law, the Father's commandment, to defeat Satan.
sources.quote: But as He is one and the same, who formed us at the beginning, and sent His Son at the end, the Lord did perform His command, being made of a woman
sources.raw_question: Could Christ have fulfilled the Creator's promise against the serpent if he had been sent by a Father other than the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: No. The Lord could not have fulfilled the promise of the Creator and performed His command if He had come from another Father. Because the God who formed us at the beginning is one and the same as the one who sent His Son at the end, the Son performed His command, destroying the adversary and perfecting man after God's image and likeness.
sources.quote: But as He is one and the same, who formed us at the beginning, and sent His Son at the end, the Lord did perform His command, being made of a woman
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who distinguish the Father from the Demiurge
sources.raw_question: Could Christ have recapitulated the ancient enmity against the serpent and fulfilled the Creator's promise if he had come from a Father other than the Creator?

question: Was the one who died for us on the cross truly the Son of God himself, rather than a mere man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XX.—God showed himself, by the fall of man, as patient, benign, merciful, mighty to save. Man is therefore most ungrateful, if, unmindful of his own lot, and of the benefits held out to him, he do not acknowledge divine grace.
sources.answer: No. Isaiah says the holy Lord remembered his dead Israel and came down to preach his salvation to those who slept in the grave. This shows that the one who died and descended to save was the Lord, not a mere man.
sources.quote: And that it was not a mere man who died for us, Isaiah says: “And the holy Lord remembered His dead Israel, who had slept in the land of sepulture; and He came down to preach His salvation to them
sources.raw_question: Was the one who died for us merely a man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul declares that we were reconciled to God 'by the death of His Son.' This shows that the same Being who was seized, suffered and shed his blood was both Christ and the Son of God. That same one rose again and was taken up into heaven.
sources.quote: He declares in the plainest manner, that the same Being who was laid hold of, and underwent suffering, and shed His blood for us, was both Christ and the Son of God, who did also rise again, and was taken up into heaven
sources.raw_question: Was the one who died for us on the cross truly the Son of God himself?

question: Is the Word who redeems lost humanity the same Word who created it in the beginning?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XV.—Proofs of the resurrection from Isaiah and Ezekiel; the same God who created us will also raise us up.
sources.answer: Yes. The hand of God that formed us at the beginning and forms us in the womb is the same one that in the last times sought us out when we were lost. He wins back his own, carries the lost sheep on his shoulders and restores it to the fold of life.
sources.quote: this hand of God which formed us at the beginning, and which does form us in the womb, has in the last times sought us out who were lost, winning back His own
sources.raw_question: Is the Word who redeems lost humanity the same Word who created humanity?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter X.—The Old Testament Scriptures, and those written by Moses in particular, do everywhere make mention of the Son of God, and foretell His advent and passion. From this fact it follows that they were inspired by one and the same God.
sources.answer: Yes. Moses indicates that the Word who founded and created the people from the beginning is the same who redeems and gives us life in the last times. Moses shows him hanging on the tree, saying, 'thy life shall be hanging before thine eyes.' Thus creator and redeemer are one Word.
sources.quote: He who from the beginning founded and created them, the Word, who also redeems and vivifies us in the last times, is shown as hanging on the tree, and they will not believe on Him.
sources.raw_question: Is the Word who created Israel from the beginning the same as the one who redeems us and was hung on the cross?

question: When early Fathers such as Tertullian say God 'brought forth' the Word (prolatus, protulit, προελθόντα), do they mean the Son was then produced into being as a new substance, rather than that an already existing Word came forth?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. The Fathers took care that no one should imagine a division of the Father's substance. Their phrase shows they meant an emanation, manifestation or procession of what already existed, not the production of a new substance.
sources.quote: demonstrate their meaning to be, that here was no production of a new substance, but an emanation, manifestation, or procession of what was before.
sources.raw_question: Does the early Fathers' teaching that the Son was 'brought forth but not separated' (prolatus, non separatus) imply that his procession produced a new substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Waterland says these terms mean the Word's coming forth or manifestation, not his production into existence. Rendering them as 'produced' (into being) is a mistranslation. Tertullian expressly rejects that sense, as do Tatian, Athenagoras and Hippolytus, who held that the Word always existed in and with the Father before coming forth.
sources.quote: here you render protulit, “ produced,” meaning “into being,” or “into a “ state of existence ;” which is not Tertullian’s sense, nor of any of the Fathers who speak of that matter.
sources.raw_question: When early Fathers such as Tertullian say God 'brought forth' (protulit, προελθόντα) the Word when he willed, do they mean the Son was produced into being at that time?

question: Did God act unjustly, as the Marcionites claimed, when he directed the Israelites to take goods from the Egyptians at the Exodus?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXX.—Refutation of another argument adduced by the Marcionites, that God directed the Hebrews to spoil the Egyptians.
sources.answer: No. The Egyptians were at every point debtors to the Israelites for their forced labour, so the Israelites took their goods more fairly than Christians, who receive property from Romans and other nations who owe them nothing. Critics who themselves live on others' goods condemn themselves by this accusation. God has ordered his dispensations so that all things turn out for good in a way consistent with justice.
sources.quote: Will it be the [Jewish] people, [who took] from the Egyptians, who were at all points their debtors; or we, [who receive property] from the Romans and other nations, who are under no similar obligation to us?
sources.raw_question: Does God's directing the Hebrews to take goods from the Egyptians prove, as the Marcionites claim, that the God of the Old Testament acted unjustly?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXX.—Refutation of another argument adduced by the Marcionites, that God directed the Hebrews to spoil the Egyptians.
sources.answer: No. The Egyptians owed the Israelites far more: their lives, because of Joseph's kindness, and wages for years of harsh slavery in which they built cities and enlarged Egyptian wealth while their masters plotted to destroy them. Taking a few things out of many was only a very small payment for heavy service, so the Israelites left poor rather than enriched. Anyone who blames them is like an unjust judge condemning a man who had been forcibly enslaved, and the objectors show they do not understand God's righteous dealings and dispensations.
sources.quote: In what way, then, did [the Israelites] act unjustly, if out of many things they took a few, they who might have possessed much property had they not served them, and might have gone forth wealthy
sources.raw_question: Did God act unjustly, as the Marcionites claimed, when he commanded the Israelites to take vessels and clothing from the Egyptians at the Exodus?

question: If God is the author of both natural events and miracles, what distinguishes a miracle from God's ordinary works?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > Diversity Alone Makes a Miracle.
sources.answer: Only their unusualness distinguishes them, not their author or kind of power. The same God who gives life to the flesh in the womb also restored souls to corpses when the dead rose. When such works happen in a regular, continuous succession they are called natural. When God brings them about in an unusual way to admonish men, they are called miracles.
sources.quote: when, for the admonition of men, they are thrust in by an unusual changeableness, then they are called miracles.
sources.raw_question: What distinguishes a miracle from a natural event, if God is the author of both?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > Why Miracles are Not Usual Works.
sources.answer: A miracle is not a different kind of divine power. It is God's ordinary working done in an unusual way: suddenly, with extraordinary speed, or against all expectation. God does this to signify something to humanity and make his power evident. Elijah's rain came when no sign of it had appeared. The Sinai thunders carried clear meaning. Changing the rod's matter into a serpent was a miracle because it was unusual, even though the matter was by nature changeable. Augustine adds that when such events run in their regular course they are called natural, and when they are inserted unusually to admonish humanity they are called miracles.
sources.quote: Yet, when He changed the same matter out of the rod of Moses into the flesh of a serpent, immediately and quickly, that change, which was unusual, although of a thing which was changeable, was a miracle.
sources.raw_question: If God works both natural events and miracles, what makes a miracle different from God's ordinary works?

question: Should the philosophers who knew something of God's eternal, unchangeable substance be trusted over Christian faith about the course of the ages and the resurrection of the flesh?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Old Philosophers are Not to Be Consulted Concerning the Resurrection and Concerning Things to Come.
sources.answer: No. Knowing that God exists as unchangeable substance does not give insight into the changing order of temporal events. The philosophers learned even the particular facts of nature from history and from other people's recorded experience, not from the eternal wisdom itself. The far future has been experienced and reported by no one, so historians cannot describe it, and the philosophers cannot grasp it with their understanding. Only those who foreknow the future, whom Christians call prophets, can speak to it.
sources.quote: Nor have those philosophers, who have profiled better than others in that high and eternal science, been able to grasp such subjects with the understanding; otherwise they would not be inquiring as they could into past things of the kind
sources.raised_by_detail: Platonist philosophers who deride belief in the resurrection of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Does the philosophers' ability to know God's high and unchangeable substance through created things qualify them to be trusted over Christian faith about the resurrection of the flesh and the future course of the ages?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In How Many Ways Things Future are Foreknown. Neither Philosophers, Nor Those Who Were Distinguished Among the Ancients, are to Be Consulted Concerning the Resurrection of the Dead.
sources.answer: No. Although they knew God through the things that are made, they did not glorify Him as God and became fools. They could not fix the mind's eye on the eternal, unchangeable nature so as to see, in the Creator's wisdom, the ages and the future perfecting of human bodies. Nor were they judged worthy to receive such things by angelic revelation, as the pious fathers were.
sources.quote: Therefore, neither concerning the successions of ages, nor concerning the resurrection of the dead, ought we to consult those philosophers, who have understood as much as they could the eternity of the Creator
sources.raw_question: Should the philosophers who grasped something of God's eternity be consulted about the course of the ages and the resurrection of the dead?

question: Does the Arian idea that a will or pleasure in God precedes the Word come from Scripture or from Valentinian Gnosticism?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: It comes from Valentinian Gnosticism. Ptolemy the Valentinian taught that the Unoriginate had Thought and Will, first thinking and then willing, and could put forth nothing until Will was added. The Arians learned from this to place will and pleasure before the Word. Scripture, by contrast, says the Son 'was' and is in the Father as His Image. It ascribes a precedent will and pleasure only to created things, as in the Psalms: 'He hath done whatsoever pleased Him.'
sources.quote: For Ptolemy the Valentinian said that the Unoriginate had a pair of attributes, Thought and Will, and first He thought and then He willed; and what He thought, He could not put forth, unless when the power of the Will was added.
sources.raw_question: Does the idea of a will in God preceding the Word come from Scripture or from Valentinian Gnosticism?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: It comes from Valentinianism, not Scripture. Ptolemy the Valentinian taught that the Unoriginate had Thought and Will, first thinking then willing, and could not put forth what he thought until Will was added; the Arians learned from this to make will precede the Word.
sources.quote: Thence the Arians taking a lesson, wish will and pleasure to precede the Word.
sources.raw_question: Is the Arian claim that will and pleasure precede the Word derived from Christian Scripture or from Valentinian Gnosticism?

question: Can the desire to search into and comprehend God the Father produce ignorance and passion in a spiritual being, as the Valentinians claimed of the Aeon Sophia?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVIII.—Sophia was never really in ignorance or passion; her Enthymesis could not have been separated from herself, or exhibited special tendencies of its own.
sources.answer: No. Meditating on the perfect Father and desiring to dwell within Him and comprehend Him cannot stain a spiritual being with ignorance or passion. It rather gives rise to perfection, impassibility, and truth, since such seeking is directed toward the source of truth itself.
sources.quote: to have a comprehension of His [greatness], could not entail the stain of ignorance or passion, and that upon a spiritual Æon; but would rather [give rise to] perfection, and impassibility, and truth.
sources.raw_question: Can the desire to search into the nature of God the Father and to comprehend and be united with Him produce ignorance and passion in a spiritual being, as the Valentinians claimed of the Aeon Sophia?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVIII.—Sophia was never really in ignorance or passion; her Enthymesis could not have been separated from herself, or exhibited special tendencies of its own.
sources.answer: No. The Valentinians admit that Sophia is superior to them and older, being in effect their grandfather. They also claim that their own search for the Father yields truth, perfection, and reconciliation. To say the same search ruined a higher, wholly spiritual being is inconsistent, foolish, and irrational.
sources.quote: how can such assertions be otherwise viewed than as totally inconsistent, foolish, and irrational?
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent for the Valentinians to hold that seeking the Father brings truth and perfection to men but brought passion and near-dissolution to the superior Aeon Sophia?

question: Does 1 John 3:2, "We shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is," refer to bodily conformity to the risen Son or to the perfecting of the mind's image of the Trinity through the full vision of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether the Sentence of John is to Be Understood of Our Future Likeness with the Son of God in the Immortality Itself Also of the Body.
sources.answer: Yes, primarily. Augustine holds that the full likeness of God will be realized in the image when it receives the full sight of God. Though the text could be read of bodily immortality, it is better understood of the image of the Trinity, since man was made after "our" image and John speaks of Him whose sons we are; that inward image renewed in knowledge is perfected by the face-to-face sight itself.
sources.quote: Hence it appears, that the full likeness of God is to take place in that image of God at that time when it shall receive the full sight of God.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 John 3:2, "we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is," refer to the perfecting of the image of God in the mind through the full vision of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > John is Rather to Be Understood of Our Perfect Likeness with the Trinity in Life Eternal. Wisdom is Perfected in Happiness.
sources.answer: It should be understood mainly of our perfect likeness to the Trinity. The immortality of the body is completed in the twinkling of an eye at the resurrection. But the inward image, renewed in the knowledge of God, is perfected only by the sight of God face to face after the judgment. John ties the likeness to seeing God, and he speaks of the One whose sons we are said to be.
sources.quote: And therefore that place too of the Apostle John must be understood rather according to this image, when he says, “We shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is;” because he spoke too of Him of whom he had said, “We are the sons of God.”
sources.raw_question: Does 1 John 3:2, "We shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is," refer to our bodily conformity to the risen Son or to the mind's likeness to the Trinity?

question: Were Christ and the Holy Spirit produced later than other beings as a result of a defect or degeneracy among the Æons?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIX.—Absurdities of the heretics as to their own origin: their opinions respecting the Demiurge shown to be equally untenable and ridiculous.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus treats the Valentinian claim that Christ and the Holy Spirit were formed later than the rest of the Æons, and only because of their ignorance and degeneracy, as impiety against Christ and the Spirit. They are not products of a defect. The Saviour is not a joint production of degenerate Æons; he proceeds from the Father.
sources.quote: but also against Christ and the Holy Spirit, affirming that they were produced on account of that defect
sources.raw_question: Were Christ and the Holy Spirit produced later than other beings, as a result of defect or degeneracy among the Æons?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Preface.
sources.answer: No. The Valentinian teaching that Christ and the Holy Spirit were emitted because of a defect, and that the Saviour was a product of Æons who themselves came from a defect, is wholly blasphemous. The Son and the Spirit are instead God's own hands, by whom he made man.
sources.quote: so have they also taught that Christ and the Holy Spirit were emitted on account of this defect, and that the Saviour was a product of those Æons who were produced from a defect
sources.raw_question: Were Christ and the Holy Spirit emitted as later products on account of a defect in the divine realm?

question: Could Christ have overcome Satan by quoting the law if the law came from an ignorant, defective or inferior god?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXII.—The true Lord and the one God is declared by the law, and manifested by Christ His Son in the Gospel; whom alone we should adore, and from Him we must look for all good things, not from Satan.
sources.answer: No. One ignorance cannot be removed by another ignorance, nor one defect by another. A strong man is conquered only by a greater power, so the law's words that conquered the devil must be the words of the superior God, the Father of the Word, not of an inferior or defective being.
sources.quote: For one ignorance cannot be done away with by means of another ignorance, any more than one defect by another defect. If, therefore, the law is due to ignorance and defect, how could the statements contained therein bring to nought the ignorance of the devil
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who attribute the law to ignorance and defect
sources.raw_question: Could Christ have overcome Satan by quoting the law if the law came from an ignorant or defective god?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: No. One ignorance cannot be removed by another ignorance, nor one defect by another defect. A strong man can be conquered only by one of greater power. So the law that defeated Satan must come from the one true God, and the Word proclaimed in the law is superior above all.
sources.quote: For if there were any other perfect Father above Him, He (Christ) would by no means have overthrown Satan by means of His words and commandments. For one ignorance cannot be done away with by means of another ignorance
sources.raw_question: Could Christ have overthrown Satan by the words of the law if the lawgiver were an ignorant or inferior God beneath some higher Father?

question: Was the devil telling the truth when he claimed to Christ that all the kingdoms of the world had been delivered to him to give to whomever he wished?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXII.—The true Lord and the one God is declared by the law, and manifested by Christ His Son in the Gospel; whom alone we should adore, and from Him we must look for all good things, not from Satan.
sources.answer: No. Satan is himself only one among created things, so creation is not subject to his power; God the Father rules over men and over him, so that not even a sparrow falls without the Father's will. Moreover the Lord calls the devil a liar from the beginning, so his claim was a proud lie.
sources.quote: For the creation is not subjected to his power, since indeed he is himself but one among created things.
sources.raw_question: Was Satan telling the truth when he claimed that all the kingdoms of the world had been delivered to him to give to whomever he wished?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXIV.—Of the constant falsehood of the devil, and of the powers and governments of the world, which we ought to obey, inasmuch as they are appointed of God, not of the devil.
sources.answer: No. The devil lied in the end just as he lied at the beginning, because it is God, not the devil, who appoints the kingdoms of this world. Scripture says the king's heart is in God's hand, that kings reign by the Word, and that there is no power but of God.
sources.quote: For it is not he who has appointed the kingdoms of this world, but God; for “the heart of the king is in the hand of God.”
sources.raw_question: Was the devil telling the truth when he claimed to Christ that all the kingdoms of the world had been delivered to him to give to whomever he wished?

question: When Christ on the cross said 'Father, into Thy hands I commend My Spirit', did these words show that He was afraid or despairing, for example fearing death and descent into Hades?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary holds that Christ had an assurance which never murmured. His commending of His soul to the Father was bound up with His confident entreaty for others, namely the prayer for pardon of His persecutors, not despair for Himself.
sources.quote: when He commended His own soul to the Father, in this was involved a prayer for the pardon of others
sources.raw_question: When Christ on the Cross said 'Father, into Thy hands I commend My Spirit', was He driven by fear and hopelessness about His own condition?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Christ's promise to the thief that he would be with him that day in Paradise shows that his nature and power could not be confined in, or made to fear, the lower world. Though he descended to Hades, he was never absent from Paradise. Bodily fear cannot touch him who is present everywhere by the power of his nature.
sources.quote: Such a nature with such power could not be shut up within the confines of the nether world, nor even subjected to fear of it.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's words on the cross, 'Father, into Thy hands I commend My Spirit,' show that he feared descending into Hades and death?

question: Does Thomas's confession 'My Lord and my God', and Christ's acceptance of it, show that Christ is truly God by nature rather than God by a title of honour?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: It was a confession of nature, not a title of honour. Thomas believed Christ was God in substance and power, and Christ himself called this act faith rather than mere reverence when he said 'because thou hast seen, thou hast believed.'
sources.quote: It was not a title of honour; it was a confession of nature. He believed that Christ was God in substance and in power.
sources.raw_question: Was Thomas's 'My Lord and my God' a title of honour or a confession of Christ's divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. A Son wholly devoted to the Father, seeking the Father's will and glory, would have rejected adoration under the name of God if it destroyed the unity of God he taught. Instead he confirmed the confession and accepted as his own the name belonging to the Father's nature.
sources.quote: Yet, in fact, He confirms this assertion of the mysterious truth, made by the believing Apostle; He accepts as His own the name which belongs to the nature of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's acceptance of Thomas's confession 'my God' show that he is truly God?

question: How does Psalm 36:9, 'With Thee is the fountain of life, and in Thy light we shall see light,' signify the Persons of the Trinity, and does the Fount signify the Father or the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIV. Each Person of the Trinity is said in the sacred writings to be Light. The Spirit is designated Fire by Isaiah, a figure of which Fire was seen in the bush by Moses, in the tongues of fire, and in Gideon's pitchers. And the Godhead of the same Spirit cannot be denied, since His operation is the same as that of the Father and of the Son, and He is also called the light and fire of the Lord's countenance.
sources.answer: It names all three Persons. With God the Father Almighty, the Fount of Life, in His Son who is the Light, we shall see the light of the Holy Spirit. The Lord shows this when He gives the Spirit, saying 'Receive ye the Holy Spirit.'
sources.quote: with Thee, O God the Father Almighty, Who art the Fount of Life, in Thy Son Who is the Light, we shall see the light of the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: How does Psalm 36:9, 'With Thee is the fount of life, and in Thy light we shall see light,' bear on the Trinity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XV. The Holy Spirit is Life equally with the Father and the Son, in truth whether the Father be mentioned, with Whom is the Fount of Life, or the Son, that Fount can be none other than the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Many take it of the Son, as the Fount of Life who is with Almighty God. Others hold that only the Father is meant. Ambrose points out that "with Thee" fits the Son, who is with the Father, as the Word was with God in the beginning. Either way, what flows from the Fount is the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: That is, the Son is with the Father; since the Word was with God, Who was in the beginning, and was with God.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who think the Father only is signified
sources.raw_question: In Psalm 36:9, "With Thee is the fountain of life," does the Fount signify the Father or the Son?

question: Who is 'the Angel who delivered me from all evil' whom Jacob joined with God when blessing his grandsons (Genesis 48:16)?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: The Word of God. Since blessing and delivering belong to none other than God, and the Lord Himself was Jacob's deliverer, the one Jacob joined to God in prayer must be God's Word. He is called 'Angel' because He alone reveals the Father.
sources.quote: evidently none other did he join to God in his prayer, than God’s Word, whom therefore he called Angel, because it is He alone who reveals the Father
sources.raw_question: Since only God blesses and delivers, whom did Jacob join with God in his prayer when he called on 'the Angel who delivered me' to bless his grandsons?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. Jacob joined no created angel to God; the Angel who delivered him from all evil was the Word of God, called the Angel of great Counsel. Delivering and blessing belong to God alone, and Jacob had earlier wrestled with and been blessed by Him whom he called God face to face.
sources.quote: he shewed that it was no created Angel, but the Word of God, whom he joined to the Father in his prayer, through whom, whomsoever He will, God doth deliver
sources.raw_question: Does Jacob's blessing invoking 'the Angel which delivered me from all evil' show that a created angel can be joined with God as a giver of blessing?

question: By what standard does the human mind judge corporeal things, or the images of them in memory and imagination, as beautiful, better, or in need of correction?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > There is One Knowledge of the Thing in the Thing Itself, and Another in Eternal Truth Itself. That Corporeal Things, Too, are to Be Judged the Rules of Eternal Truth.
sources.answer: The mind judges them by an unchangeable form of eternal truth above itself, which it perceives by rational intuition. When Augustine recalls a well-proportioned arch he saw at Carthage, memory supplies its image. But he also sees in his mind something else, by which the work pleases him and by which he would correct it if it displeased him. Particular things are therefore judged by the rules of eternal truth, not by the senses alone.
sources.quote: We judge therefore of those particular things according to that [form of eternal truth], and discern that form by the intuition of the rational mind.
sources.raw_question: By what standard does the human mind judge whether corporeal things, such as a work of architecture, are beautiful or need correcting?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > There is One Knowledge of the Thing in the Thing Itself, and Another in Eternal Truth Itself. That Corporeal Things, Too, are to Be Judged the Rules of Eternal Truth.
sources.answer: We judge by unchangeable rules of eternal truth that stand above our mind. For example, Augustine recalls the walls of Carthage, which he has seen, and imagines those of Alexandria, which he has not. When he prefers one imagined form to another on grounds of reason, the judgment of truth from above remains clear. It is not confounded by the corporeal images, even if they cloud it.
sources.quote: we are proved either to accept or reject, within ourselves, by other rules which remain altogether unchangeable above our mind, when we approve or reject anything rightly
sources.raw_question: When we judge between images of corporeal things in memory or imagination, by what standard do we judge rightly?

question: Should the unbegotten Father of all be counted as one among the Aeons produced from him, as in the Valentinian Triacontad of thirty Aeons?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XII.—The Triacontad of the heretics errs both by defect and excess: Sophia could never have produced anything apart from her consort; Logos and Sige could not have been contemporaries.
sources.answer: No. The Father of all is unproduced, unbegotten, incomprehensible and without figure. What he produced is begotten, is comprehended by him, and has a definite shape. Because he is superior to all of these, and is impassible and free from error, he cannot be numbered with them. Once he is removed from the count, the Valentinian Triacontad falls to twenty-nine.
sources.quote: For the Father of all ought not to be counted with other productions; He who was not produced with that which was produced; He who was unbegotten with that which was born
sources.raw_question: Should the unbegotten Father of all be counted alongside the beings produced from him, as the Valentinians do when they include the Propator in their thirty Aeons?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XI.—The heretics, from their disbelief of the truth, have fallen into an abyss of error: reasons for investigating their systems.
sources.answer: No. The Father of all is unproduced, unbegotten, incomprehensible and without figure, while the Aeons are produced, born, comprehended by him and have definite shape. Because he is superior to them, he ought not to be numbered with them. This is especially so since the impassible God cannot be reckoned alongside an Aeon that suffers passion and falls into error.
sources.quote: For the Father of all ought not to be counted with other productions; He who was not produced with that which was produced; He who was unbegotten with that which was born
sources.raw_question: Should the Father of all be counted as one among the Aeons, as in the Gnostic Triacontad of thirty Aeons?

question: Is the Valentinian system consistent in holding both that the paired Aeons are inseparably united and that Sophia suffered passion and produced offspring apart from her consort?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XII.—The Triacontad of the heretics errs both by defect and excess: Sophia could never have produced anything apart from her consort; Logos and Sige could not have been contemporaries.
sources.answer: No. The two claims contradict each other. If the pairs are always one, Sophia could neither suffer nor generate without her consort. If she did act apart from him, all the other pairs must also admit separation, which has been shown to be impossible. Their whole system, which derives material substance from her passion, is therefore overthrown.
sources.quote: For if Bythus is ever one with Sige, Nous with Aletheia, Logos with Zoe, and so on, as respects the rest, how could Sophia, without union with her consort, either suffer or generate anything?
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to hold that the Aeon-pairs are inseparably united, while also holding that Sophia suffered passion and gave birth apart from her consort?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XII.—The Triacontad of the heretics errs both by defect and excess: Sophia could never have produced anything apart from her consort; Logos and Sige could not have been contemporaries.
sources.answer: No. If the paired aeons are united, Sophia could not have produced a defect without union with her consort. If instead each aeon has its own separate substance, Logos and Sige could not appear in the same place. Either way the system contradicts itself.
sources.quote: Since, if they were united, how could Sophia have generated a defect without union with her consort?
sources.raw_question: Is the Valentinian system consistent in holding both that the paired aeons are united and that Sophia produced something without her consort?

question: Does the existence of changeable goods require the existence of an unchangeable good?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How God May Be Known to Be the Chief Good. The Mind Does Not Become Good Unless by Turning to God.
sources.answer: No. Changeable things are good only by participating in the good itself, and that good is the unchangeable good. Without it there would be nothing for them to participate in. To discern this good itself, apart from the things that share in it, is to discern God.
sources.quote: Wherefore there would be no changeable goods, unless there were the unchangeable good.
sources.raw_question: Could there be changeable goods if there were no unchangeable good?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How God May Be Known to Be the Chief Good. The Mind Does Not Become Good Unless by Turning to God.
sources.answer: Yes. Changeable things are good only by participation in the good itself; if one removes the particular things that are good by participation and discerns the good in itself, one has discerned God. Without the unchangeable good there would be no changeable goods.
sources.quote: Wherefore there would be no changeable goods, unless there were the unchangeable good.
sources.raw_question: Does the existence of changeable goods require the existence of an unchangeable good?

question: Are the merits by which the soul attains eternal blessedness its own achievement or God's gift?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Although the Soul Hopes for Blessedness, Yet It Does Not Remember Lost Blessedness, But Remembers God and the Rules of Righteousness. The Unchangeable Rules of Right Living are Known Even to the Ungodly.
sources.answer: Its merit is itself God's grace. The soul cannot give itself the righteousness it lost by sinning. It receives righteousness from God so that it may deserve blessedness. Hence the apostle asks what we have that we did not receive.
sources.quote: But its merit, too, is His grace, whose reward will be its blessedness; for it cannot give itself the righteousness it has lost, and so has not.
sources.raw_question: If the soul's blessedness is a reward for its merit, is that merit its own achievement or God's gift?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > There Was No Other More Suitable Way of Freeing Man from the Misery of Mortality Than The Incarnation of the Word. The Merits Which are Called Ours are the Gifts of God.
sources.answer: They are God's gifts. Faith works by love, and that love is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who is given to us. The Spirit was sent by Christ after he was glorified, when he ascended and gave gifts to men. These gifts make up our deserts.
sources.quote: Since those also which are called our deserts, are His gifts. For, that faith may work by love, “the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.”
sources.raw_question: Are the merits by which humans reach eternal blessedness their own achievements or gifts of God given through the Holy Spirit?

question: Are the virtues of prudence, fortitude, temperance and justice true virtues apart from faith?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > What the Wisdom is of Which We are Here to Treat. Whence the Name of Philosopher Arose. What Has Been Already Said Concerning the Distinction of Knowledge and Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. These virtues, by which men live in this mortal life, are true virtues only if they are referred to faith. That faith, though temporal, leads on to things eternal.
sources.quote: are not true virtues, unless they are referred to that same faith, temporal though it is, which leads on nevertheless to things eternal
sources.raw_question: Are the virtues of prudence, courage, temperance and justice true virtues apart from faith?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What Has Been Treated of in This Book. How We Have Reached by Steps to a Certain Trinity, Which is Found in Practical Knowledge and True Faith.
sources.answer: No. The just live by faith, which works by love, and the virtues must all be referred to that faith, for otherwise they cannot be true virtues. Even so, in this life they are not so perfect that remission of sins is never needed, and that remission comes only through Christ, who by his blood conquered the prince of sinners.
sources.quote: so that the virtues also themselves, by which one lives prudently, boldly, temperately, and justly, be all referred to the same faith; for not otherwise can they be true virtues
sources.raw_question: Can the virtues of prudence, fortitude, temperance and justice be true virtues apart from faith that works by love?

question: Did the same God, the Word, give both the old law of bondage and the later freedom of the Gospel?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIII.—Christ did not abrogate the natural precepts of the law, but rather fulfilled and extended them. He removed the yoke and bondage of the old law, so that mankind, being now set free, might serve God with that trustful piety which becometh sons.
sources.answer: Yes. When Christ says "I will not now call you servants," He shows that He Himself first appointed for men a bondage toward God through the law. Afterwards He conferred freedom on them. So the same Lord, the Word, is the author of both covenants.
sources.quote: He indicates in the most marked manner that it was Himself who did originally appoint for men that bondage with respect to God through the law, and then afterwards conferred upon them freedom.
sources.raw_question: Was the Word of God, Christ, the one who gave the old law of bondage as well as the later freedom of the Gospel?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIII.—Christ did not abrogate the natural precepts of the law, but rather fulfilled and extended them. He removed the yoke and bondage of the old law, so that mankind, being now set free, might serve God with that trustful piety which becometh sons.
sources.answer: Yes. The law was given to people in bondage and trained the soul through external, bodily things so that man might learn to serve God. The Word then set the soul free and extended the laws of liberty. This is one continuous divine economy, which leads to greater subjection and love toward the Liberator, not departure from Him. The same Word who first drew slaves to God afterwards made them free.
sources.quote: For the law, since it was laid down for those in bondage, used to instruct the soul by means of those corporeal objects which were of an external nature, drawing it, as by a bond, to obey its commandments, that man might learn to serve God. But the Word set free the soul
sources.raw_question: Do the old law and Christ's teaching come from the same God, given that Christ replaced bondage with freedom?

question: What does 'generation' signify, and what are the different kinds or modes of generation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, thus passing over what relates to the essence of the Son as having been already discussed, he treats of the sense involved in “generation,” saying that there are diverse generations, those effected by matter and art, and of buildings,--and that by succession of animals,--and those by efflux, as by the sun and its beam. The lamp and its radiance, scents and ointments and the quality diffused by them,--and the word produced by the mind; and cleverly discusses generation from rotten wood; and from the condensation of fire, and countless other causes.
sources.answer: Generation signifies being that results from some cause. Gregory divides the kinds by a scientific division. Some things result from matter and art, as buildings do. Some result from matter and nature, as animals do. Some arise by material efflux, as the sun's beam or a lamp's brightness, where the source remains undiminished. Lastly, an incorporeal cause can produce a generation perceived by the senses, as when the mind brings forth the word. Even unusual cases, such as animals produced from rotting wood, fall under generation by nature and matter.
sources.quote: That this name presents to us the fact of being as the result of some cause is clear to every one, and about this point there is, I suppose, no need to dispute.
sources.raw_question: What does the term 'generation' signify, and what are the different kinds of generation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: Gregory distinguishes four. There is generation from material and art, as with houses. There is generation from material and nature, as with animals born of parents. There is generation by material efflux, as with the sun and its ray or ointment and its fragrance, where the source stays undiminished. Finally there is generation from an incorporeal cause through bodily instruments, as when the mind begets the word.
sources.quote: Of things which have come into being as the results of some cause we recognize the following differences. Some are the result of material and art, as the fabrics of houses
sources.raw_question: What are the different modes of generation, i.e. of something existing as the result of a cause?

question: Is the glory of Almighty God incommunicable, so that no one else can share in it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: No. The Lord commands people to seek the glory that comes from the only God, which implies they can obtain it. Since 'every one that asketh receiveth', God's glory is clearly communicated.
