sources.quote: How then is the glory of the Almighty incommunicable, if it is even our duty to ask for the glory that cometh from the only God, and if, according to our Lord’s word, “every one that asketh receiveth[^384]?”
sources.raw_question: Is the glory of the Almighty God incommunicable?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: No. Christ commands people to seek the glory that comes from the only God, which implies they can obtain it, and he promises that everyone who asks receives. Even the glory bestowed on Moses was God's own glory. So Eunomius' claim that the Almighty's glory is incommunicable is false.
sources.quote: How then is the glory of the Almighty incommunicable, if it is even our duty to ask for the glory that cometh from the only God, and if, according to our Lord’s word, “every one that asketh receiveth?”
sources.raw_question: Is the glory of Almighty God incommunicable, so that no one else can share in it?

question: Does the rational handling of corporeal and temporal things, which humans share with animals, belong to the outer man shared with the beasts, or to the inner man, the rational mind itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Attempt is Made to Distinguish Out of the Scriptures the Offices of Wisdom and of Knowledge. That in the Beginning of John Some Things that are Said Belong to Wisdom, Some to Knowledge. Some Things There are Only Known by the Help of Faith. How We See the Faith that is in Us. In the Same Narrative of John, Some Things are Known by the Sense of the Body, Others Only by the Reason of the Mind.
sources.answer: It belongs to the inner man. Images of bodily things in memory belong to the life of the outer man. But when such things are taken up for the purpose of rational knowledge, their rational use is proper to the inner man. So it cannot rightly be said that this use is something we share with the irrational animals.
sources.quote: the rational use of those things which we have in common with irrational animals belongs to the inner man; neither can it rightly be said that this is common to us with the irrational animals.
sources.raw_question: Does the rational use of things that humans share with irrational animals belong to the outer man or to the inner man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Higher Reason Which Belongs to Contemplation, and the Lower Which Belongs to Action, are in One Mind.
sources.answer: It must come from the rational mind itself. This practical faculty is rational and is not shared with the beasts. It is drawn out of the rational substance of the mind, the same substance by which we cleave to unchangeable truth. Augustine compares this to Adam: no fitting help was found for him among the beasts, so one had to be taken from himself. In the same way, no fitting help for the contemplative mind can be found among the soul's animal parts.
sources.quote: so for that mind, by which we consult the supernal and inward truth, there is no like help for such employment as man’s nature requires among things corporeal out of those parts of the soul which we have in common with the beasts.
sources.raw_question: Can the faculty by which humans deal with corporeal and temporal things be supplied by the parts of the soul humans share with animals, or must it come from the rational mind itself?

question: Can the commandments to love God and to love one's neighbor be fulfilled separately, or does each imply the other?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > That He Who Loves His Brother, Loves God; Because He Loves Love Itself, Which is of God, and is God.
sources.answer: No. They cannot exist except together. Whoever loves his brother must love the love by which he loves him, and since God is love, whoever loves love loves God. We love God and neighbor with one and the same love, but God for God's sake and ourselves and our neighbors for God's sake.
sources.quote: For since “God is love,” he who loves love certainly loves God; but he must needs love love, who loves his brother.
sources.raw_question: Can the commandments to love God and to love one's neighbor be fulfilled separately?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Of True Love, by Which We Arrive at the Knowledge of the Trinity. God is to Be Sought, Not Outwardly, by Seeking to Do Wonderful Things with the Angels, But Inwardly, by Imitating the Piety of Good Angels.
sources.answer: Because each implies the other. He who loves God must do what God commands, and God commands love of neighbor; and he who loves his neighbor must above all love love itself, and since "God is love," he must above all love God.
sources.quote: But this, too, is because he who loves his neighbor must needs also love above all else love itself. But “God is love; and he that dwelleth in love, dwelleth in God.” Therefore he must needs above all else love God.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture often command only love of neighbor or only love of God, when the Law hangs on both commandments?

question: Can the angelic powers keep their order, holiness and worship of God without the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: No. Angels have free will and stand in equipoise between virtue and vice, so they need the Spirit's help; the fall of wicked spirits proves this. No one can confess Jesus as Lord except by the Spirit. Prophecy and the revelation of mysteries, as in Gabriel's announcements, are gifts of the Spirit, and beholding the Father's face is impossible without him. Remove the Spirit and the angelic hosts fall into disorder.
sources.quote: if by your argument you do away with the Spirit, the hosts of the angels are disbanded, the dominions of archangels are destroyed, all is thrown into confusion, and their life loses law, order, and distinctness.
sources.raw_question: Could the angels keep their order, praise God, prophesy, and behold the Father without the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: No. Just as eyes are useless in a house without light, or an army without its commander, so the high life of the heavenly powers cannot abide without the Spirit. The Seraphim's 'Holy, Holy, Holy', the praise of the hosts, and the concord of the celestial powers are all preserved only by the direction and co-operation of the Spirit.
sources.quote: All the glorious and unspeakable harmony of the highest heavens both in the service of God, and in the mutual concord of the celestial powers, can therefore only be preserved by the direction of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Can the angelic powers sustain their holiness, worship and order without the Holy Spirit?

question: How does a hypocrite's 'taste of the powers of the world to come' (Hebrews 6:5) differ from the Holy Spirit given to believers as an earnest of the inheritance?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: They differ greatly. A hypocrite may for a season take a vanishing taste of heavenly things by considering them in themselves, but the Spirit as an earnest is an abiding pledge given by God. He assures believers of those good things as provided for them in the love of God and the purchase of Christ.
sources.quote: there is a wide difference between taking a vanishing taste of it ourselves, and receiving an abiding earnest from God. To take a taste of the things of heaven, and to have them assured of God as from his love, differ greatly.
sources.raw_question: How does a hypocrite's 'taste of the powers of the world to come' (Hebrews 6:5) differ from the believer's receiving the Holy Spirit as an earnest of the inheritance?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No. 'The powers of the world to come' does not mean the joys of heaven. It means the powerful ministry and ordinances of the gospel age. Even if it did mean heavenly glory, a hypocrite's passing taste of those things differs widely from the abiding earnest God gives. That earnest assures believers of the inheritance as provided for them in the Father's love and the Son's purchase.
sources.quote: there is a wide difference between taking a vanishing taste of it ourselves, and receiving an abiding earnest from God.
sources.raw_question: Is the 'taste of the powers of the world to come' that hypocrites may have (Hebrews 6:5) the same as the Spirit's earnest of the inheritance given to believers?

question: Does God literally possess a soul, given that Scripture speaks of God's soul hating sabbaths and new moons?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Such language is a conventional expression, like speaking of God's hands, eyes or heart. A Spirit has no flesh and bones, and God who changes not cannot have bodily parts. God is a simple, complete, all-embracing nature who is not animated by an indwelling soul but is himself his own life.
sources.quote: God is therefore not quickened into life, like bodies, by the action of an indwelling soul, but is Himself His own life.
sources.raw_question: Does God possess a soul, given that Scripture speaks of God's soul hating sabbaths and new moons?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Such language is figurative, like Scripture speaking of God's hands and eyes. God is a simple and unchanging nature, so He is not quickened by a soul but is Himself His own life. For this reason the Godhead cannot lay down a soul or take it up again.
sources.quote: God could not lay it down, that is, die, or take it up again, that is, come to life.
sources.raw_question: Is it literally true that God has a soul, as Scripture suggests when it speaks of God's soul hating sabbaths?

question: Is the God who judges and casts the unworthy into outer darkness a different God from the Father who calls people to salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: No. The same King who gathers the faithful to His Son's marriage also orders the man without a wedding garment to be cast into outer darkness. One and the same God, the Father of our Lord, both calls the unworthy in kindness and judges. There is not one God who judges and another Father who saves.
sources.quote: It is not, then, one God who judges, and another Father who calls us together to salvation; nor one, forsooth, who confers eternal light, but another who orders those who have not on the wedding garment to be sent into outer darkness.
sources.raw_question: Is the God who judges and casts the unworthy into outer darkness a different being from the Father who calls people to salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: No. It is one and the same God, the Father of our Lord, who both calls the unworthy through infinite kindness and examines those called to see if they wear the wedding garment. The parable of the wedding feast shows the same King gathers guests to his Son's marriage and orders the one without the garment to be cast out, since the good and pure God will endure nothing evil in his wedding chamber.
sources.quote: It is not, then, one God who judges, and another Father who calls us together to salvation; nor one, forsooth, who confers eternal light, but another who orders those who have not on the wedding garment to be sent into outer darkness.
sources.raw_question: Is the God who judges and casts the unworthy into outer darkness a different God from the Father who calls people to salvation?

question: Do unbelievers have a true right before God to the worldly goods they possess?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: No, not a true right before God. They have a civil right that holds in human courts, but not a sanctified right that holds in God's court or in their own conscience. Believers receive their portion as re-invested in Christ and as pledges of the Father's love. Unbelievers hold goods still under the curse and will be called to account for them.
sources.quote: hence I dare say of unbelievers, they have no true right unto any thing, of what kind soever, that they do possess.
sources.raw_question: Do unbelievers have a true right to the worldly goods they possess?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: No. They have a civil right that holds against other people in human courts, but no sanctified right that holds in God's court or in their own conscience. God's original grant of the creatures to man was lost by sin and restored only for his saints. So unbelievers will answer both for how they misused these goods and for holding what was not theirs.
sources.quote: it is true they have a civil right in respect of others, but they have not a sanctified right in respect of their own souls
sources.raw_question: Do unbelievers have a true right before God to the temporal goods they possess?

question: Can the divine nature change so as to gain or lose any good it did not have before?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He then ingeniously shows that the generation of the Son is not according to the phrase of Eunomius, “The Father begat Him at that time when He chose, and not before:” but that the Son, being the fulness of all that is good and excellent, is always contemplated in the Father; using for this demonstration the support of Eunomius' own arguments.
sources.answer: No. The Divine Nature is itself the fulness of all goods and needs no addition for its perfecting. What is perfect is equally remote from addition and diminution, so the perfection of goods in God always remains the same. Nothing comes to it by change that was not with it before.
sources.quote: Now that which is perfect is equally remote from addition and from diminution; and therefore, we say that perfection of goods which we behold in the Divine Nature always remains the same
sources.raw_question: Can the Divine Nature gain or lose any good over time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Thereafter he expounds the appellation of “Son,” and of “product of generation,” and very many varieties of “sons,” of God, of men, of rams, of perdition, of light, and of day.
sources.answer: No. God is One Good in a single, uncompounded nature and is always the same. His choice never moves Him to change: He always wills what He is and is what He wills. So nothing can be added to God or taken away, as happens when a man changes his state.
sources.quote: But God, being One Good, in a single and uncompounded nature, looks ever the same way, and is never changed by the impulse of choice, but always wishes what He is, and is, assuredly, what He wishes
sources.raw_question: Can the divine nature undergo change so as to acquire something it did not have before?

question: When Christ called the Creator 'God', 'the great King', and the Temple His Father's house, was He speaking ironically while really preaching another God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter II.—Proofs from the plain testimony of Moses, and of the other prophets, whose words are the words of Christ, that there is but one God, the founder of the world, whom Our Lord preached, and whom He called His Father.
sources.answer: No. Christ is the Truth and spoke in earnest. He showed this by zealously vindicating the temple as His Father's house, driving out the money-changers. He did not blame the house or the law, but rebuked those who transgressed His Father's law.
sources.quote: For He who uttered them was Truth, and did truly vindicate His own house, by driving out of it the changers of money
sources.raw_question: Could Christ have called the Creator 'God' and 'the great King' only ironically, while really preaching another God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter II.—Proofs from the plain testimony of Moses, and of the other prophets, whose words are the words of Christ, that there is but one God, the founder of the world, whom Our Lord preached, and whom He called His Father.
sources.answer: No. Christ is Truth and spoke in earnest, as his actions show: he truly vindicated the Temple as his own house by driving out the money-changers. He would have had no reason to defend that house if he preached another God than the God of the law.
sources.quote: For He who uttered them was Truth, and did truly vindicate His own house, by driving out of it the changers of money, who were buying and selling
sources.raw_question: Were Christ's statements calling heaven God's throne and the Temple his Father's house spoken ironically, so that he was not really referring to the Creator as God?

question: According to John 10:38, what truth do Christ's works confirm, and how does it relate to His claim to be the Son of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: The works are meant to show that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. This is the same truth as "I am the Son of God" and "I and the Father are One." We must not divide the unity or separate the nature from the birth, but confess that the living God was truly born from the living God.
sources.quote: It is the same truth as is contained in I am the Son of God, and I and the Father are One. This is the nature which is His by birth; this the mystery of the saving faith, that we must not divide the unity, nor separate the nature from the birth
sources.raw_question: What does Christ say his works should lead us to believe, according to John 10:38?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: They confirm that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, which is the same truth as "I am the Son of God" and "I and the Father are One." This mutual indwelling is the nature the Son has by birth. The saving faith therefore requires that we neither divide the unity nor separate the nature from the birth.
sources.quote: It is the same truth as is contained in I am the Son of God, and I and the Father are One. This is the nature which is His by birth; this the mystery of the saving faith, that we must not divide the unity
sources.raw_question: What truth do Christ's works confirm according to John 10:38, and how does it relate to His claim to be the Son of God?

question: If Christ was already foretold by the prophets, what new thing did he bring by his coming?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: He brought every possible novelty by bringing himself, the one who had been announced. The prophets, like servants sent ahead of a king, foretold that a novelty would come to renew mankind. When the King actually came, he gave liberty and the sight of himself.
sources.quote: know ye that He brought all [possible] novelty, by bringing Himself who had been announced. For this very thing was proclaimed beforehand, that a novelty should come to renew and quicken mankind.
sources.raw_question: If Christ was already foretold by the prophets, what new thing did he bring by his coming?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIV.—Proof against the Marcionites, that the prophets referred in all their predictions to our Christ.
sources.answer: He brought every possible novelty by bringing Himself, the one who had been announced. The prophets were like servants sent ahead to prepare for a king. When the King comes and his subjects see him, hear him and receive his gifts, no sensible person asks what he has added beyond the announcement. The prophecy itself proclaimed that a novelty would come to renew and quicken mankind.
sources.quote: know ye that He brought all [possible] novelty, by bringing Himself who had been announced. For this very thing was proclaimed beforehand, that a novelty should come to renew and quicken mankind.
sources.raw_question: If everything about Christ was foretold by the prophets, what new thing did the Lord bring by his coming?

question: Does the Hebrew expression 'to bear sin' (nasa avon), used of Christ in Isaiah 53:12 ('he bare the sin of many'), mean that he underwent the punishment due to sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Yes. When nasa is used of men or sinners bearing sin, it constantly denotes bearing the punishment of sin, and no contrary instance can be produced. Texts like Numbers 14, Leviticus 19:8, Leviticus 20 and Ezekiel 18:20 show that to bear iniquity is the same as to be cut off, slain or die for it. So there is no just reason to forge a new sense when the words are spoken of Christ.
sources.quote: In the latter way, as it respects men or sinners, it constantly denotes the bearing of the punishment of sin, and gives that sense unto עָוֹן, with respect unto the guilt of sin as its cause.
sources.raw_question: Does the Hebrew expression 'to bear sin' (nasa avon), when used of Christ in Isaiah 53:12, mean that he underwent the punishment due to sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Yes. When nasa describes an act of God toward sin, it means to lift up, take away, or pardon the guilt of sin. When it describes men or sinners, it constantly means bearing the punishment of sin, with guilt as its cause. Spoken of Christ bearing the sin of many, it therefore means that he underwent that punishment.
sources.quote: In the latter way, as it respects men or sinners, it constantly denotes the bearing of the punishment of sin, and gives that sense unto עָוֹן, with respect unto the guilt of sin as its cause.
sources.raw_question: When the Hebrew verb nasa is used with sin, as in 'he bare the sin of many' (Isaiah 53:12), does it mean that Christ bore the punishment of sin?

question: How can sinful human beings have boldness and confidence to approach a holy God who is a consuming fire?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Only by the blood of Jesus Christ. By his sacrifice and atonement Christ has taken away the 'conscience of sin', meaning the dread of God's revenge for guilt. He has removed the slaying sword of the law. He now reveals God to believers not as a revenging Judge but as a tender, merciful and reconciled Father.
sources.quote: the Lord Jesus, by the sacrifice and the atonement that he hath made, hath taken away this conscience of sin; that is, a dread of revenge from God upon the account of the guilt thereof.
sources.raw_question: How can sinful human beings have confidence to approach and walk with God, who is described as a consuming fire?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It comes from the blood of Jesus. The dread and terror of God came in through sin, but in Christ we have boldness and access with confidence. We therefore draw near to God rather than standing far off like the people at Sinai.
sources.quote: This the apostle will inform us in Heb. x. 19; it is “by the blood of Jesus:” so Eph. iii. 12, “In him we have boldness, and access with confidence;”
sources.raw_question: Where does the believer's boldness to approach a holy God, who is a consuming fire, come from?

question: Could the mind love itself merely by inferring its own character from experience of other minds, without directly knowing itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Image of the Trinity in the Mind of Man Who Knows Himself and Loves Himself. The Mind Knows Itself Through Itself.
sources.answer: No; this is said most foolishly. The mind could not know another mind at all unless it first knew itself. Unlike the bodily eye, which sees other eyes but not itself, the mind does not know other minds while being ignorant of itself.
sources.quote: For whence does a mind know another mind, if it does not know itself? For the mind does not know other minds and not know itself, as the eye of the body sees other eyes and does not see itself
sources.raw_question: Could the mind love itself merely by inferring its own character from experience of other minds, without directly knowing itself?

question: Can the mind love itself without remembering and understanding itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Mind Loves God in Rightly Loving Itself; And If It Love Not God, It Must Be Said to Hate Itself. Even a Weak and Erring Mind is Always Strong in Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself. Let It Be Turned to God, that It May Be Blessed by Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Him.
sources.answer: No. The mind could not love itself if it were altogether ignorant of itself, that is, if it did not remember and understand itself. Its love of itself presupposes its memory and understanding of itself, and by this image of God it is able to cleave to Him whose image it is.
sources.quote: Now it could not love itself if it were altogether ignorant of itself, i.e. if it did not remember itself, nor understand itself by which image of God within itself it has such power as to be able to cleave to Him whose image it is.
sources.raw_question: Can the mind love itself without remembering and understanding itself?

question: Does the mind's knowledge that it lives show that it knows itself as a whole?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > How the Mind Knows Itself, Not in Part, But as a Whole.
sources.answer: Yes. A mind cannot be a mind without living, and as it is a whole mind, it lives as a whole. Since it knows that it lives, it knows itself as a whole, though it also has understanding beyond mere life, which beasts' souls lack.
sources.quote: As therefore a mind is a whole mind, so it lives as a whole. But it knows that it lives. Therefore it knows itself as a whole.
sources.raw_question: Does the mind's knowledge that it lives show that it knows itself as a whole?

question: When the mind seeks to know itself, does it already know that it is a mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > How the Mind Knows Itself, Not in Part, But as a Whole.
sources.answer: Yes. Otherwise it would not know whether it was seeking itself and might seek one thing in place of another. Since in seeking what mind is it knows it seeks itself, it knows itself to be a mind. And if it knows what it seeks and seeks itself, it already knows itself.
sources.quote: Wherefore since the mind, when it seeks to know what mind is, knows that it seeks itself, certainly it knows that itself is a mind.
sources.raw_question: When the mind seeks to know itself, does it already know that it is a mind?

question: Does the mind's knowledge that it knows other things already imply that the mind knows itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > That When the Mind Loves Itself, It is Not Unknown to Itself.
sources.answer: Yes. The mind knows what knowing is because it knows that it knows other things. What it knows is not that some other mind knows, but that it itself knows. Therefore, in knowing its own knowing, it knows itself.
sources.quote: In what way, then, does that which does not know itself, know itself as knowing anything? For it does not know that some other mind knows, but that itself does so. Therefore it knows itself.
sources.raw_question: Does the mind's knowledge that it knows other things already imply that the mind knows itself?

question: What three things can be distinguished in the act of bodily sight that form a trace of a trinity in the outer man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Certain Trinity in the Sight. That There are Three Things in Sight, Which Differ in Their Own Nature. In What Manner from a Visible Thing Vision is Produced, or the Image of that Thing Which is Seen. The Matter is Shown More Clearly by an Example. How These Three Combine in One.
sources.answer: The visible object, the vision or act of seeing, and the attention of the mind. The object can exist before it is seen. Vision exists only when the object is perceived. The attention of the mind keeps the eye's sense fixed on the object for as long as it is seen, and so joins the two together.
sources.quote: These three, then, the body that is seen, and vision itself, and the attention of mind which joins both together, are manifestly distinguishable, not only on account of the properties of each, but also on account of the difference of their natures.
sources.raw_question: What three things can be distinguished in the act of bodily sight that form a trace or image of a trinity in the outer man?

question: Why is sight chosen above the other bodily senses for finding a trace of the Trinity in the outer man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Trace of the Trinity Also In the Outer Man.
sources.answer: Because sight far surpasses the other senses and is nearest in kind to the mind's own seeing. It is also unnecessary to examine all five senses, since what holds for one holds for the rest.
sources.quote: For this bodily sense far surpasses the rest; and in proportion to its difference of kind, is nearer to the sight of the mind.
sources.raw_question: Why is sight chosen above the other bodily senses for finding a trace of the Trinity in the outer man?

question: What in the human mind corresponds to the Holy Spirit in the image of the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Of the Likeness of the Father and of the Son Alleged to Be in Our Memory and Understanding. Of the Likeness of the Holy Spirit in Our Will or Love.
sources.answer: The will, or love, or affection, which is a stronger will. Love joins the vision in memory and the vision of thought formed from it, as if joining parent and offspring. In the same way the Holy Spirit is the bond between Father and Son.
sources.quote: I have shown nothing in this enigma respecting the Holy Spirit such as might appear to be like Him, except our own will, or love, or affection, which is a stronger will
sources.raw_question: What in the human mind corresponds to the Holy Spirit in the image of the Trinity?

question: Is the trinity in the mind formed from remembered bodily images (the image in memory, the form in thought, and the will joining them) an image of God, given that its three members are of one substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: No. Its three members are indeed of one substance, but it still belongs to the outer man. It was brought into the mind from bodily objects perceived from without, so it is not the image of God.
sources.quote: But we found this trinity to pertain to the outer man, on this account, that it was introduced into the mind from bodily objects which are perceived from without.
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity in the mind formed from remembered bodily images (the image in memory, the form in thought, and the will joining them) an image of God, given that its three members are of one substance?

question: Is the image of the triune God found in the part of the human mind that deals with temporal things, or only in the part that contemplates eternal things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Trinity and the Image of God is in that Part of the Mind Alone Which Belongs to the Contemplation of Eternal Things.
sources.answer: Only in the part that contemplates eternal things. Though a kind of trinity may be found in the mind's activity directed toward temporal things, the image of God is found only in that function of the mind which belongs to the contemplation of eternal things.
sources.quote: not only a trinity may be found, but also an image of God, in that alone which belongs to the contemplation of eternal things; while in that other which is diverted from it in the dealing with temporal things, although there may be a trinity, yet there cannot be found an image of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the image of God, the triune God, found in the part of the human mind that deals with temporal things, or only in the part that contemplates eternal things?

question: In what sense are the mind, its knowledge of itself, and its love of itself an image of the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > Why Love is Not the Offspring of the Mind, as Knowledge is So. The Solution of the Question. The Mind with the Knowledge of Itself and the Love of Itself is the Image of the Trinity.
sources.answer: They are three yet one substance, and mutually equal. Knowledge is the mind's offspring and its word concerning itself. Love is a third, proceeding from the mind. The offspring is not less than the mind, because the mind knows itself according to the measure of its own being. Nor is love less, because the mind loves itself according to the measure of both its knowledge and its being.
sources.quote: there is a kind of image of the Trinity in the mind itself, and the knowledge of it, which is its offspring and its word concerning itself, and love as a third, and these three are one, and one substance
sources.raw_question: In what sense are the mind, its knowledge of itself, and its love of itself an image of the Trinity?

question: Why is the trinity formed when the mind remembers, understands, and loves itself a better image of God than trinities formed from temporal things such as faith or the virtues?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How a Trinity is Produced by the Mind Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself.
sources.answer: Because its three are not related by temporal succession or by something arising in the mind that was not there before. Faith, by contrast, arises in a mind that already existed. When the mind turns to itself in thought, a word is formed from that thought and will unites both. Here the image being sought can be recognized more clearly than before.
sources.quote: Here, then, we may recognize, more than we have hitherto done, the image of which we are in search.
sources.raw_question: Why is the trinity formed when the mind remembers, understands, and loves itself a better image of God than trinities formed from temporal things such as faith or the virtues?

question: Is the human mind, as the image of the Trinity, unchangeable like God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Mind Loves God in Rightly Loving Itself; And If It Love Not God, It Must Be Said to Hate Itself. Even a Weak and Erring Mind is Always Strong in Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself. Let It Be Turned to God, that It May Be Blessed by Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Him.
sources.answer: No. When the mind now sees itself, it sees something that is not unchangeable. Its changeableness is the ground on which it can hope to pass from wretchedness to blessedness, since an unchangeable being could become neither wretched nor blessed.
sources.quote: But now, when it sees itself, it sees something not unchangeable.
sources.raw_question: Is the human mind, as the image of the Trinity, unchangeable like God?

question: Does seeing the trinity in one's own mind amount to seeing God if one does not recognize the mind as an image of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Infirmity of the Human Mind.
sources.answer: No. Those who see the trinity in their own mind but do not believe or understand it to be an image of God see the glass but not Him who is to be seen through it. They do not even know that the glass they look at is a glass, that is, an image. Recognizing it as an image would lead them to seek through it the God whose image it is, and in some provisional way to see Him.
sources.quote: see indeed a glass, but do not so far see through the glass Him who is now to be seen through the glass, that they do not even know the glass itself which they see to be a glass, i.e. an image
sources.raw_question: Does seeing the trinity in one's own mind (memory, understanding, will) amount to seeing God, if one does not recognize the mind as an image of God?

question: Can a trinity be found in the mind's rational knowledge of temporal things, and how is it structured?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > In Opposition to the Reminiscence of Plato and Pythagoras. Pythagoras the Samian. Of the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge, and of Seeking the Trinity in the Knowledge of Temporal Things.
sources.answer: Yes, a kind of trinity can be sought there. Just as in bodily vision the seen object, the formed sight, and the will uniting them make a trinity, so in knowledge the likenesses of things stored in memory, the thought formed from them, and the will uniting the two form a trinity. Augustine defers full treatment to the next book, where he shows that memory, the recollecting gaze, and the will combine in this way.
sources.quote: we might have resemblances of bodies impressed within on the memory from which thought might be formed, while the will as a third united them
sources.raw_question: Can an image of the Trinity be found in the mind's rational knowledge of temporal things, and how would it be structured?

question: Should the image of the Trinity in the human mind be sought by treating practical reason (concerned with temporal things) and contemplative reason (concerned with eternal things) as separate parts which, with some third element, complete a trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Trinity and the Image of God is in that Part of the Mind Alone Which Belongs to the Contemplation of Eternal Things.
sources.answer: No. The mind is a single subject, distinguished into these two only by its functions, so the trinity must be sought in the whole mind without splitting off the action of reason in temporal things from contemplation of eternal things and then looking for a third element to complete the triad. A trinity would be found in the one undivided mind even if action on temporal things were withdrawn altogether.
sources.quote: when we seek the trinity in the mind, we seek it in the whole mind, without separating the action of the reason in things temporal from the contemplation of things eternal, so as to have further to seek some third thing
sources.raw_question: Should the image of the Trinity in the human mind be sought by treating the mind's practical reason (dealing with temporal things) and its contemplative reason (dealing with eternal things) as two separate parts that together, with some third thing, complete a trinity?

question: In what part of the human mind should the image of the Trinity be sought?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Trinity Which is the Image of God is Now to Be Sought in the Noblest Part of the Mind.
sources.answer: In the noblest part of the mind, by which it knows or can know God. Although the human mind is not of the same nature as God, the image of that nature than which none is better must be sought in that than which our nature has nothing better.
sources.quote: For although the human mind is not of the same nature with God, yet the image of that nature than which none is better, is to be sought and found in us, in that than which our nature also has nothing better.
sources.raw_question: In what part of the human mind should the image of the Trinity be sought?

question: Is the image of the Trinity in the human mind perfect in this present life?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Likeness of the Divine Word, Such as It Is, is to Be Sought, Not in Our Own Outer and Sensible Word, But in the Inner and Mental One. There is the Greatest Possible Unlikeness Between Our Word and Knowledge and the Divine Word and Knowledge.
sources.answer: No. The perfection of this image belongs to the future. Now we behold the glory of the Lord through a glass and are transformed from glory to glory by the Spirit. When the image is renewed to perfection, we shall be like God because we shall see Him as He is, face to face.
sources.quote: When, therefore, this image shall have been renewed to perfection by this transformation, then we shall be like God, because we shall see Him, not through a glass, but “as He is;”
sources.raw_question: Is the image of the Trinity in the human mind perfect in this present life?

question: When the mind seeks to know itself, should it search for itself as something absent?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > How the Soul Inquires into Itself. Whence Comes the Error of the Soul Concerning Itself.
sources.answer: No. The mind should not seek itself as though withdrawn from itself; it should withdraw what it has added to itself, namely the images of sensible things. It lies more deeply within than both external bodies and their images. It should turn upon itself the attention that was wandering among other things.
sources.quote: let it not seek itself as though it were withdrawn from itself; but let it withdraw that which it has added to itself.
sources.raw_question: When the mind seeks to know itself, should it search for itself as something absent?

question: Can the mind's search for itself be explained as one part of the mind that is already found seeking another part not yet found?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > How the Mind Knows Itself, Not in Part, But as a Whole.
sources.answer: No. If the found part seeks the unfound part, then no part seeks itself and the mind as a whole does not seek itself, so the mind would not be seeking itself at all. If instead the whole mind seeks itself, it is wholly present to itself and nothing of it is wanting. Either way the partial account fails, for mind cannot be absent from mind as a forgotten thing is.
sources.quote: Wherefore, since neither the mind as a whole seeks itself, nor does any part of it seek itself, the mind does not seek itself at all.
sources.raw_question: Can the mind's search for itself be explained as one part of the mind that is already found seeking another part not yet found?

question: Is man the image of the Son only, or the image of the whole Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: Man is the image of the Trinity. Genesis says "our image," which could not be said if it meant the Son, since the Son is the image of the Father alone. Man is made after the image of Father, Son, and Spirit together.
sources.quote: For how our, when the Son is the image of the Father alone?
sources.raw_question: Is man the image of the Son only, or the image of the whole Trinity?

question: Can human reason by itself grasp the mysteries of God's dispensation, or does true understanding of them depend on God's revelation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: It depends on revelation. The ear hears the words, but it is God who reveals their inner meaning to those who seek it. Understanding is God's gift and the reward of faith. Reason cannot anticipate God's revelation with its own preconceptions, so a person should be willing to correct his earlier judgments when God reveals the truth.
sources.quote: But God’s gift of understanding is the reward of faith, for through faith the infirmity of sense is recompensed with the gift of revelation.
sources.raw_question: Can human reason by itself grasp the mysteries of God's dispensation, or does true understanding of them depend on God's revelation?

question: How can the simple and incomposite divine nature be rightly described by many different names?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: The many names come from the limits of the human mind, not from any complexity in God. Unable to see God's essence clearly, the mind feels after Him in many ways, drawing ideas from His works: skill from the order of the universe, power from its wonders, and immortality from the contrast with death. We do not split the subject by these names. We believe it is one in substance while having something in common with all these ideas.
sources.quote: the human mind, grovelling on earth, and buried in this life on earth, in its inability to behold clearly the object of its search, feels after the unutterable Being in divers and many-sided ways
sources.raw_question: How can the simple and incomposite divine nature be rightly described by many different names?

question: Does the contradictory opposition between 'generate' and 'ungenerate' imply that the Son, as generate, is inferior to or a diminution of the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then, again discussing the true Light and unapproachable Light of the Father and of the Son, special attributes, community and essence, and showing the relation of “generate” and “ungenerate,” as involving no opposition in sense, but presenting an opposition and contradiction admitting of no middle term, he ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Contradictories do not differ by greater or lesser intensity but by mutual exclusion of signification, as living is not a diminution of not living but its complete opposite. Hence 'generate' is not a lessened form of 'ungenerate', and no inferiority of the Son follows from the opposition of the terms.
sources.quote: For the difference between contradictories is not one of greater or less intensity, but rests its opposition upon their being mutually exclusive in their signification
sources.raw_question: Does the contradictory opposition between 'generate' (begotten) and 'ungenerate' (unbegotten) imply that the Son, as generate, is inferior to or a diminution of the Father, as ungenerate?

question: What does 'ungenerate' properly signify, and does it belong to the Father alone?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: 'Ungenerate' signifies nothing more than 'not having come into being', which is common to all uncreated nature. Father, Son and Holy Spirit are equally uncreated, so in this sense each Person is alike unoriginate; the term does no harm to sound belief, though the dull use it as a starting-point for heresy.
sources.quote: “ungenerate” signifies nothing more than “not having come into being,” and that “not coming into being” is a common property of all that transcends created nature
sources.raw_question: What does the term 'ungenerate' properly signify, and does it belong to the Father alone?

question: If the Son has the same nature as the Father, does that mean the Father too was begotten?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Sameness of nature does not mean the Begetter was begotten, for then the Unbegotten would not be himself. It means the substance of the Begotten consists in all the elements contained in the substance of the Begetter, who is his only origin.
sources.quote: His nature is the same, not in the sense that the Begetter also was begotten—for then the Unbegotten, having been begotten, would not be Himself—but that the substance of the Begotten consists in all those elements which are summed up in the substance of the Begetter
sources.raw_question: If the Son has the same nature as the Father, does that mean the Father too was begotten?

question: If 'unbegotten' and 'begotten' each name the very essence of the Father and the Son, must the Son's attributes be opposite to the Father's?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Proof that the Anomœan teaching tends to Manichæism.
sources.answer: Yes, on the Eunomian premise. Gregory argues that since being generated and being ungenerated are contrary in conception, if each defines Being, then the marks of each nature must also be contrary, as heat belongs to fire and cold to ice. Since the ungenerate nature is good, holy, imperishable and eternal, the generated nature would have to bear the negations of these, which is absurd and blasphemous.
sources.quote: so that those qualities should be applied to the Son which are the reverse of those predicated of the Father, viz., of divinity, holiness, goodness, imperishability, eternity, and of every other quality that represents God to the devout mind
sources.raw_question: If 'unbegotten' and 'begotten' each name the very essence (Being) of the Father and the Son respectively, must the Son's attributes be opposite to the Father's?

question: Does the Only-begotten Son exist in a strict or proper sense, or, as Eunomius claims, only improperly?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. True existence is the special distinction of Godhead, as the Apostle says that whoever comes to God must believe that He is. To say the Son does not properly exist is the same as saying he does not exist at all, just as a man who "runs" in a dream does not really run though the name is applied to him; the name is given falsely. Hence Eunomius's claim abolishes the Son's deity.
sources.quote: he who does not properly exist, does not really exist at all; as, for example, he is said to “run” in a dream who in that state fancies he is exerting himself in the race
sources.raw_question: Is it true, as Eunomius claims, that the Only-begotten Son does not exist in a strict or proper sense?

question: Can the Son's essence properly be called both a "product of generation" and a "product of creation" or "product of making," as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: No. The terms have distinct meanings, and it is impossible for one nature to admit both appellations: if one is true, the other must be false. If the Son were a product of creation, he would not be a product of generation, and if he is a product of generation, he is excluded from the title of product of creation.
sources.quote: For, if one of these were true, the other would necessarily be false, so that, if the thing were a product of creation, it would not be a product of generation, and conversely, if it were called a product of generation, it would be alienated from the title of “product of creation.”
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's essence properly be called both a "product of generation" and a "product of creation" or "product of making," as Eunomius claims?

question: Does saying there is one God because there is one Father imply that the Son is of a different nature from the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. In the passage ascribed to Athanasius, the Son is God, having a sameness with the Father as a Son. He is not the Father himself but is united with the Father in nature. The two are two in number but one entire essence. Citing only the first half of this sentence misrepresents its sense.
sources.quote: not that he is the ‘‘ Father himself, but in nature united with the Father; two ““ indeed in number, but one entire essence.
sources.raw_question: Does saying there is one God because there is one Father imply that the Son is of a different nature from the Father?

question: Does refusing to call the Father, Son and Holy Spirit together one God exclude the Son and Spirit from the one Godhead?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds that to scruple at calling all three together one God manifestly excludes the Son and Holy Ghost from the one Godhead. He thinks this concession by Clarke's defender settles the dispute about Clarke's meaning against him.
sources.quote: because that would be manifestly excluding Son and Holy Ghost from the one Godhead
sources.raw_question: Does refusing to call the Father, Son and Holy Spirit together one God exclude the Son and Spirit from the one Godhead?

question: Does John 17:3, which calls the Father 'the only true God', exclude the Son and the Holy Spirit from true Godhead?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter III. As to know the Father and the Son is life, so is it life to know the Holy Spirit; and therefore in the Godhead He is not to be separated from the Father.
sources.answer: No. The same verse makes knowing Jesus Christ eternal life, just as knowing the only true God is. Knowing the Spirit is also eternal life. Since the Son and the Spirit confer the same benefit as the only true God, they cannot be separated from his honour. So Ambrose wonders why the Arians raise the question of the only true God at all.
sources.quote: Wherefore I wonder why the Arians stir the question as to the only true God. For as it is eternal life to know the only true God, so, too, is it eternal life to know Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Does John 17:3, which calls the Father 'the only true God', exclude the Son and the Holy Spirit from true Godhead?

question: Do Christ's sayings that he and the Father are one, and that whoever has seen him has seen the Father, together with related texts, show that the Father and the Son are one God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: Yes. Christ says he and the Father are one, that whoever has seen him has seen the Father, and that they are mutually in each other. He also says 'we will come and make our abode with him.' Paul asks grace from both and prays that both may direct his way. Taken together, these texts confirm that Father and Son are one God.
sources.quote: our blessed Lord has told us, that he and the Father are one; that whosoever hath seen him hath seen the Father; that he is in the Father, and the Father in him
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's sayings that he and the Father are one, and that whoever has seen him has seen the Father, support the claim that the Father and Son are one God?

question: Does 1 Corinthians 8:4-6 teach that there is only one true God, the Father, together with one Lord Jesus Christ, as distinct from the so-called gods?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul separates the so-called gods, which are not gods at all, from the one God the Father, from whom are all things. In his own person he also decidedly confesses one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things.
sources.quote: he has made a distinction, and separated those which are indeed called gods, but which are none, from the one God the Father, from whom are all things, and, he has confessed in the most decided manner in his own person, one Lord Jesus Christ.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 8:4-6 teach that there is only one true God, the Father, together with one Lord Jesus Christ, as distinct from the so-called gods?

question: Why does Paul call the one God specifically 'the Father' in 1 Corinthians 8:6?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: To prevent heretics from using the preaching of one God to deny the birth of the Son. By indicating the Father's peculiar attribute, Paul ensures that He who is God is also acknowledged as Father, which implies a Son.
sources.quote: the Apostle has set forth one God while indicating His peculiar attribute in these words, One God the Father, of Whom are all things, and we in Him, in order that He Who is God might also be acknowledged as Father.
sources.raw_question: Why does Paul call the one God specifically 'the Father' in 1 Corinthians 8:6?

question: Does the phrase 'by whom are all things' in 1 Corinthians 8:6 make the Son a subordinate instrument in creation rather than the Creator?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > The origin of the heretics' close observation of syllables.
sources.answer: No. Basil calls the Son the Creator of the universe. He exposes the heretics' reading of 'through whom' as 'subordinate agent or instrument' as an impious device. Its aim is to rank the Creator no higher in dignity than a tool, and to reduce the Spirit's contribution to that of place or time.
sources.quote: The object of all this is that the Creator of the universe may be regarded as of no higher dignity than an instrument, and that the Holy Spirit may appear to be adding to existing things nothing more than the contribution derived from place or time.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'by whom are all things' in 1 Corinthians 8:6 make the Son a subordinate instrument in creation rather than the Creator?

question: Does 1 Corinthians 8:6 ('one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things') exclude the Son from the created 'all things'?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter II. The words, “All things were made by Him,” are not a proof that the Holy Spirit is included amongst all things, since He was not made. For otherwise it could be proved by other passages that the Son, and even the Father Himself, must be numbered amongst all things, which would be similar irreverence.
sources.answer: Yes. In calling the Son the one by whom all things are, the Apostle excepts Him from all things, just as he excepted the Father. Paul used this expression with foresight, so that the impious, who had heard the Son say "That which My Father hath given Me is greater than all," would not think he had included the Son among all things.
sources.quote: for when he says: “And one Lord Jesus Christ, by Whom are all things,” he certainly excepts the Son of God from all, who also excepted the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 8:6 ("one Lord Jesus Christ, by Whom are all things") exclude the Son from the created "all things"?

question: Is God the Father himself the Word, or is 'Word' said only of the Son, and relatively?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: The Father is not himself the Word, just as he is not the Son or the image. 'Word', like 'Son' and 'image', is said relatively. The Word is the one whom the Father begat, who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made, and who is equal to the Father.
sources.quote: For He is not Himself the Word, as He is not the Son nor the image.
sources.raw_question: Is God the Father himself the Word, or is 'Word' said only of the Son, and relatively?

question: Is the Spirit's receiving from the Son something different from receiving from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Christ says the Spirit will receive of what is His, and grounds this on the fact that all things the Father has are His. Hence what is received from the Father is received from the Son, and the unity admits no difference as to from whom the Spirit receives.
sources.quote: He teaches also that what is received from the Father is yet received from Himself, because all things that the Father hath are His. Such a unity admits no difference, nor does it make any difference from whom that is received
sources.raw_question: Is the Spirit's receiving from the Son something different from receiving from the Father?

question: Does the Son's being glorified by the Spirit show that the Son is inferior to the Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit glorifies the Son, as the Father also does, and the Son in turn glorifies the Spirit. This mutual glorification flows from the unity of the eternal Light. So neither the one who glorifies nor the one who is glorified is weak or inferior.
sources.quote: He, then, is not weak who is the cause of the mutual glory through the Unity of the Eternal Light, nor is He inferior to the Spirit, of Whom this is true that He is glorified by the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being glorified by the Spirit show that the Son is inferior to the Spirit?

question: Are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit really distinct, or is the Son the same as the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: They are truly distinct. Scripture teaches with certainty that there is a Father, a Son, and a Holy Spirit. The Son is not the same as the Father, and the Holy Spirit is not the same as the Father or the Son. Sabellius fell into heresy by denying that they are three somewhats.
sources.quote: there is both Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit; and that the Son is not the same with the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the same with the Father or the Son
sources.raw_question: Are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit really distinct, or is the Son the same as the Father?

question: Could the Holy Spirit be equal to the Father and Son in some respects but not in all?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Holy Spirit Also is Equal to the Father and the Son in All Things.
sources.answer: No. In God it is not one thing to be and another to be great, good, or holy. Because of the absolute simplicity of the divine substance, whatever is equal there is equal in all things. So the Spirit is together with the Father and Son great, good, holy, and whatever else is said of the substance.
sources.quote: and if equal, equal in all things, on account of the absolute simplicity which is in that substance.
sources.raw_question: Could the Holy Spirit be equal to the Father and Son in some respects but not in all?

question: Are the Son and the Holy Spirit equal to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > By What Rule in the Scriptures It is Understood that the Son is Now Equal and Now Less.
sources.answer: Yes, according to the form of God. Neither the Son nor the Spirit is a creature, as Augustine has already shown. Therefore both are equal to the Father.
sources.quote: For both the Son and the Holy Spirit, according to the form of God, are equal to the Father, because neither of them is a creature, as we have already shown
sources.raw_question: Are the Son and the Holy Spirit equal to the Father?

question: Does the Holy Spirit share the same Name as the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIII. St. Ambrose shows from the Scriptures that the Name of the Three Divine Persons is one, and first the unity of the Name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as each is called Paraclete and Truth.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father sends the Spirit in the Son's Name. Whoever comes in the Son's Name also comes in the Father's Name, since their Name is one. Therefore the Name of the Father and the Son is also that of the Holy Spirit, the one Name under heaven by which we are saved.
sources.quote: But He Who came in the Name of the Son came also certainly in the Name of the Father, for the Name of the Father and of the Son is one.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit share the same Name as the Father and the Son?

question: Is the Holy Spirit the Spirit of the Son as well as of the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. He proceeds from the Father, as the Lord says, and the apostle calls him 'the Spirit of Christ'. Hence he is the gift of both Father and Son.
sources.quote: for He is the gift of the Father and of the Son, because “He proceeds from the Father,”[^586] as the Lord says; and because that which the apostle says, “Now, if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of His,”
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit the Spirit of the Son as well as of the Father?

question: Is the Father 'of God' in the way the Son and the Holy Spirit are?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Holy Spirit is Called Love, and Whether He Alone is So Called. That the Holy Spirit is in the Scriptures Properly Called by the Name of Love.
sources.answer: No. Only the Father is God without being of God. The Son is born of the Father and the Spirit proceeds from the Father, so 'God of God' can refer only to the Son or the Spirit.
sources.quote: For the Father only is so God as not to be of God; and hence the love that is so God as to be of God, is either the Son or the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father 'of God' in the way the Son and the Holy Spirit are?

question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed first from the Father into the Son and then from the Son, as a human child passes from father to mother?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
