sources.answer: No. If the Spirit passed from place to place, the Father and Son who send Him would also be located in a place, and the Spirit would leave them like a material body. But the Father, Son and Spirit are incorporeal and uncircumscribed, so the Spirit's coming is not local movement.
sources.quote: For if the Spirit proceeds from a place and passes to a place, both the Father Himself will be found in a place, and the Son likewise.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who say that the Spirit comes down by movement
sources.raw_question: When the Holy Spirit is said to proceed or come down, does He move from one place to another?

question: If the Holy Spirit does not move locally, in what sense does He 'come down' to us?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XI. The Spirit is sent to all, and passes not from place to place, for He is not limited either by time or space. He goes forth from the Son, as the Son from the Father, in Whom He ever abides: and also comes to us when we receive. He comes also after the same manner as the Father Himself, from Whom He can by no means be separated.
sources.answer: He seems to come down when we receive Him so that He may dwell in us; really our mind ascends to Him. His coming is not from place to place but from one work of grace to another—from giving life to sanctification, translating us from earth to heaven, slavery to a kingdom.
sources.quote: To us He seems to come down, not that He does come down, but that our mind ascends to Him.
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit does not move locally, in what sense does He 'come down' to us?

question: Does Eunomius's method of reasoning from the Father's being to the Son's nature unwittingly concede the Son's superiority rather than inferiority?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His dictum that 'the manner of the likeness must follow the manner of the generation' is unintelligible.
sources.answer: Yes. By treating the Father's being as more easily comprehended and the Son's nature as harder to grasp, he implicitly places the Son higher in incomprehensibility, contradicting his explicit assertions of the Son's inferiority.
sources.quote: establishes His superiority unconsciously in this device of his for knowing the Deity; for he assumes that the Father’s being lends itself the more readily to our comprehension, and then attempts to trace and argue out the Son’s nature from that.
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's method of reasoning from the Father's being to the Son's nature unwittingly concede the Son's superiority rather than inferiority?

question: Is Eunomius's method of knowing the Son's nature from the Father's being consistent with his own rule that beings are to be known from their works?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His dictum that 'the manner of the likeness must follow the manner of the generation' is unintelligible.
sources.answer: No. By his own definitions beings must be known from their works, and he calls the Son the work of the supreme being, so he should ascend from the Son to the Father. Yet he admits the Son has no light thrown on him and instead tries to climb to the supreme being first, abandoning his own principle.
sources.quote: Then has he forgotten his own definitions about the beings having to be known from their works? But this begotten being, which he calls the work of the supreme being, has as yet no light thrown upon it (according to him); so how can its nature be dealt with?
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius's method of knowing the Son's nature from the Father's being consistent with his own rule that beings are to be known from their works?

question: Does Eunomius's scheme of knowing the Father through the Son and the Son through the Spirit, as their 'works', actually make the Father's being known?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: No. On this scheme it shows instead that the Father's being is unknowable. If the Spirit, the supposed work of the Son, cannot be known, the Son cannot be known through Him. If the Son is hidden, the Father cannot be revealed through a being that is itself hidden. The Spirit's obscurity passes back through the Son to the Father, so the adversaries' own premises prove the Father's being unknowable.
sources.quote: this obscurity of the Spirit is transmitted by retrogression through the Son to the Father; so that in this view, even by our adversaries’ confession, the unknowableness of the Fathers being is clearly demonstrated.
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's scheme of knowing the Father through the Son and the Son through the Spirit (as their 'works') actually make the Father's being known?

question: Is the Son, as the Wisdom of God, the Creator of all things?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Yes. The Only-begotten and very Wisdom of God is Creator and Framer of all things, as Scripture says 'in Wisdom hast Thou made them all.' He is the one through whom the ages were brought to be, and so is not among the creatures.
sources.quote: Now the Only-begotten and very Wisdom of God is Creator and Framer of all things; for ‘in Wisdom hast Thou made them all,’ he says
sources.raw_question: Is the Son, as the Wisdom of God, the Creator of all things?

question: If the Son is ascribed the same divine attributes as the Father (goodness, holiness, power, wisdom), can the Son differ from the Father in essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Proof that the Anomœan teaching tends to Manichæism.
sources.answer: No. Differing things possess differing marks and like things are known by like signs. If the Anomœans attribute the same marks to the Only-begotten, they can conceive of no difference in the subject bearing those marks, so a difference of essence collapses.
sources.quote: Differing things must be regarded as possessing differing marks; like things are to be known by like signs. If, then, these men testify to the same marks in the Only-begotten, they can conceive of no difference whatever in the subject of the marks.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is ascribed the same divine attributes as the Father (goodness, holiness, power, wisdom), can the Son differ from the Father in essence?

question: Is the Holy Spirit, like the Father and the Son, the Creator of all things?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, as well as the Father and the Son, is pointed out in holy Scripture as Creator, and the same truth was shadowed forth even by heathen writers, but it was shown most plainly in the Mystery of the Incarnation, after touching upon which, the writer maintains his argument from the fact that worship which is due to the Creator alone is paid to the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit, as the Father and the Son, is Creator of all things, and the Father did nothing without the Spirit. Scripture shows the Spirit moving on the waters at the beginning, and the Psalm teaches that when God sends forth His Spirit things are made, which shows the Spirit is Creator of the whole creation and that no creature can stand without Him.
sources.quote: Not only, then, did he teach that no creature can stand without the Holy Spirit, but also that the Spirit is the Creator of the whole creation.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit, like the Father and the Son, the Creator of all things?

question: Does Scripture attribute the creation of all things to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. All things are of the one God, the Father. By the Word all things were made and created. The Spirit of God is said to have made man and to have needed no director. Thus the one Almighty Creator is our trust.
sources.quote: By him (the Word) were all things made. – John 1:3. All things were created by him, etc. – Col. 1:16.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture attribute the creation of all things to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

question: Is the Word through which God made all things at creation the Son of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: Yes. God the Father made by a word whatever he willed to make. By the right rule of faith we know that this Word is his only Son.
sources.quote: For He made all things by His word, which Word we know, by the right rule of faith, to be His only Son.
sources.raw_question: Is the Word through which God made all things at creation the Son of God?

question: If God creates all things through the Word, does it follow that the Word must be eternal?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: Yes. If God is eternally Maker and frames all things through His Word and Wisdom, then to say the Framing Word once was not is to say God was not Maker, or that the instrument by which He creates comes to Him from outside, alien and unlike in essence. Since God's creative Word is proper to Him and from Him, it cannot have had a beginning.
sources.quote: it is the same as saying, that God is not Maker, if He had not His proper Framing Word which is from Him, but that that by which He frames, accrues to Him from without, and is alien from Him, and unlike in essence
sources.raw_question: If God creates all things through the Word, does it follow that the Word must be eternal?

question: If the Word is eternal, must the things He made also be eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. The creation has the ages for its beginning, but no beginning can be conceived for the Maker of the ages, since no interval can be apprehended before the establishment of the ages. The marks distinguishing the Maker from His works are separated by a wide interval, so what is observed in creation cannot be transferred to the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: Well, the creation has the ages for its beginning, but what beginning can you conceive of the Maker of the ages?
sources.raw_question: If God the Word is eternal, must the created things He made also be eternal, since a maker begins from the time of his making?

question: If the Son did not always exist, does it follow that His birth took place in time?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. Whoever does not always exist must have begun to be after some point of time, so a non-eternal Son would have a birth after time. Since the Son is born before times eternal, His existence or non-existence cannot be fixed by temporal thought, and He must be confessed as eternally born.
sources.quote: For if the question of His existence or His non-existence can be determined under our conditions of thought, then the birth itself must be after time; for He Who does not always exist must, of necessity, have begun to be after some given point of time.
sources.raw_question: If the Son did not always exist, does it follow that His birth took place in time?

question: Does the fact that the Son was born imply that there was a time when He did not exist, as with every human being who is born?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. It is one thing to be born of someone who once was not, and another to be born of One Who always is. A human father was not always a father, since he grew from infancy to manhood and so did not always beget; but where the Father is eternal, the Son also is eternal.
sources.quote: It is, however, one thing to be born of some one who once was not, and another to be born of One Who always is.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Son was born imply that there was a time when he did not exist, as is true of every human being who is born?

question: Did the Son exist before the works for which he is said to be 'created,' and when did the need for his 'creation' arise?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: Yes, the Son existed before the works. Before the works were made the Son always was, and there was no need for him to be created. Only after the works existed and needed restoration did the Word take on this condescension, which the word 'He created' signifies.
sources.quote: For before the works were made, the Son was ever, nor was there yet need that He should be created; but when the works were created and need arose afterwards of the Economy for their restoration
sources.raw_question: Did the Son exist before the works for which he is said to be 'created,' and when did the need for his 'creation' arise?

question: Do the terms 'begotten' and 'son' signify the same thing when applied to the Son of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Addition of a Negative Does Not Change the Predicament.
sources.answer: Yes. A son is a son because he is begotten, and being a son he is certainly begotten. Hence 'unbegotten' is equivalent to 'not a son,' and both pairs belong to the predicament of relation, referring to a father or begetter.
sources.quote: by the word begotten is signified the same thing as is signified by the word son. For therefore a son, because begotten, and because a son, therefore certainly begotten.
sources.raw_question: Do the terms 'begotten' and 'son' signify the same thing when applied to the Son of God?

question: Is 'begotten' said of the Son in respect to himself, or only relatively to the one who begets him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Reply is Made to the Cavils of the Heretics in Respect to the Same Words Begotten and Unbegotten.
sources.answer: Only relatively. No one can be called begotten except in relation to something. He is a son because he is begotten, and begotten because he is a son. The relation of the begotten to the begetter is the same as the relation of son to father.
sources.quote: with a wonderful blindness, they do not perceive that no one can be said to be begotten except in relation to something. For he is therefore a son because begotten; and because a son, therefore certainly begotten.
sources.raw_question: Is 'begotten' said of the Son in respect to himself, or only relatively to the one who begets him?

question: Does the Son's being a true Son entail that he is true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. Hilary sets out to prove from the Gospels that, because the Son is true Son, he is also true God. The two are inseparable: he cannot be true God unless he is true Son, nor true Son unless he is true God.
sources.quote: Our present task is to prove from the Gospels that, because He is true Son, He is true God also. For unless He be true Son He cannot be true God, nor true God unless He be true Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being a true Son entail that he is true God?

question: Can a person truly honour God the Father while denying the full honour and deity of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Following the Lord's words, he who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent Him. Hilary holds that the Father is honoured precisely through the honour paid to the Son, so the saving faith lies in confessing both Father and Son.
sources.quote: He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent Him[^774], be setting themselves to honour the Father, through honour paid to the Son.
sources.raw_question: Can a person truly honour God the Father while denying the full honour and deity of the Son?

question: Can one truly honour the Son while denying that He shares the nature of the Father who begot Him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > Then, distinguishing between essence and generation, he declares the empty and frivolous language of Eunomius to be like a rattle. He proceeds to show that the language used by the great Basil on the subject of the generation of the Only-begotten has been grievously slandered by Eunomius, and so ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Saying the Son is not what the Father's nature is ranks the Lord of creation with the subject creation, and that is an insult, not an honour. Eunomius himself would count it insolent treatment if someone said he was not akin in nature to his own father but shared a lower nature.
sources.quote: These are they who profess to honour Him with due honour by saying that He is not that which the nature of Him that begat Him is.
sources.raw_question: Can one honour the Son while denying that He shares the nature of the Father who begat Him?

question: If the names 'Father' and 'Son' signify a real natural relationship, as Eunomius concedes, does it follow that the Son shares the Father's essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He thus shows the oneness of the Eternal Son with the Father the identity of essence and the community of nature (wherein is a natural inquiry into the production of wine), and that the terms “Son” and “product” in the naming of the Only-Begotten include a like idea of relationship.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory argues that Eunomius' own admission that the appellations indicate relationship, and that this relationship exists in the things themselves rather than in mere sounds, overthrows his doctrine. The Son would not be called Son unless the natural meaning of the name were verified, so the name proclaims community of essence between Father and Son.
sources.quote: who would deny that the very champion of blasphemy has by his own action been dragged into the advocacy of orthodoxy, overthrowing by his own means his own arguments, and proclaiming community of essence in the case of the Divine doctrines?
sources.raw_question: If, as Eunomius concedes, the names 'Father' and 'Son' signify a real natural relationship, does it follow that the Son shares the Father's essence?

question: Can Eunomius consistently hold both that the Son's generated essence and the name 'Son' make the language of relation to the Father appropriate, and that the Son has his relation to the Father who begat him 'without community'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds again to discuss the impassibility of the Lord's generation; and the folly of Eunomius, who says that the generated essence involves the appellation of Son, and again, forgetting this, denies the relation of the Son to the Father: and herein he speaks of Circe and of the mandrake poison.
sources.answer: No. Gregory argues that the two statements flatly contradict each other. The first ties the generated essence to the name 'Son' and so affirms a real relation to the Begetter, while the second denies that relation. Whoever accepts one statement must reject the other.
sources.quote: His earlier statement represented that the generated essence, and the appellation of “Son,” made such a relation of words appropriate. His present system says the contrary:—that “the Son possesses His relation to Him that begat Him without community.”
sources.raw_question: Can Eunomius consistently hold both that the Son's generated essence and the name 'Son' make the language of relation to the Father appropriate, and that the Son possesses his relation to the Father who begat him 'without community'?

question: Does the name "God" belong to the Word (the Son) equally with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next skilfully confutes the partial, empty and blasphemous statement of Eunomius on the subject of the absolutely existent.
sources.answer: Yes. The Evangelist says the Word was with God and the Word was God, so the name "God" belongs equally to the Beginning in which the Word was and to the Word. Hence, when Deity is spoken of, the Son is included no less than the Father.
sources.quote: the name “God” belongs equally to the Beginning in which the Word was, and to the Word Who was in the Beginning. For the Evangelist tells us that “the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
sources.raw_question: Does the name "God" belong to the Word (the Son) equally with the Father?

question: Is 'Father' a name proper to God in relation to the Son, and 'Son' a name proper to the Word in relation to the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Yes. 'Father' is proper to the Son, and 'Son' rather than 'creature' is proper to the Father. We are not sons by nature, but the Son who is in us is. God is our Father only through that Word in us.
sources.quote: Therefore ‘Father’ is proper to the Son; and not ‘creature,’ but ‘Son’ is proper to the Father.
sources.raw_question: Is 'Father' a name proper to God in relation to the Son, and 'Son' proper to the Word in relation to the Father?

question: Does the word 'person' adequately express what the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three of?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Three Persons Not Properly So Called [in a Human Sense].
sources.answer: No, not fully. When asked 'Three what?' human language suffers from great poverty of speech. We answer 'three persons' not because this fully expresses the reality, but so that it is not left wholly unsaid.
sources.quote: The answer, however, is given, three “persons,” not that it might be [completely] spoken, but that it might not be left [wholly] unspoken.
sources.raw_question: Does the word 'person' adequately express what the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three of?

question: If three human persons are called three men, why are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit not called three Gods?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. Saying "many men" is a harmless mistake tolerated because habit is hard to change. With the Divine nature, however, such loose usage is dangerous. Therefore we must confess one God, though the name of Godhead extends through the Holy Trinity. We should not carry over to God the error of pluralizing the name of the nature.
sources.quote: Therefore we must confess one God, according to the testimony of Scripture, “Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one Lord,” even though the name of Godhead extends through the Holy Trinity.
sources.raw_question: If Christians say "three men" of three human persons, must they also say "three Gods" of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?

question: Does the Son possess His divinity from Himself or as received from the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is in Christ, He Once More Asserts by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: He received it from the Father. The Son obtained from his own Father that he should be God and Lord of all, begotten as God in the form of God the Father. He possesses what he is because the Father gave it to him.
sources.quote: Yet He obtained this from His own Father, that He should be both God of all and should be Lord, and be begotten and made known from Himself as God in the form of God the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son possess his divinity from himself or as received from the Father?

question: If the Son were called Son because he was created, would every creature also properly be called 'son'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: Yes, that would follow, which shows the premise is absurd. If the Son had the name not from sharing the Father's nature but from being created, then the heaven, a lamb, a dog or a frog could equally be called 'Son.' Since these are not Son or God because they are external to that nature, the true Son is Son and God because he is of the very nature of the One who begat him.
sources.quote: it follows, surely, that He Who is truly Son is Son, and is confessed to be God by reason of His being of the very nature of Him that begat Him.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is called Son because he was created, would every creature also properly be called 'son'?

question: Can the Son rightly be called a 'creation' or 'creature' on the grounds that he shares other names with created things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > This third book shows a third fall of Eunomius, as refuting himself, and sometimes saying that the Son is to be called Only-begotten in virtue of natural generation, and that Holy Scripture proves this from the first; at other times, that by reason of His being created He should not be called a Son, but a “product,” or “creature.”
sources.answer: No. The names proper to the Son (God, Word, Life, Light, express Image, Brightness) are never applied to creation, and the characteristics signified by names in the created and uncreated natures are in no case common to both. So there is no community of names that could justify extending the name "creation" to the Maker; doing so misrepresents him.
sources.quote: if the characteristics which are contemplated by means of the names, in the created and in the uncreated nature, are in no case reconcilable or common to both, how can the misrepresentation of that man fail to be manifest to all
sources.raw_question: Can the Son rightly be called a "creation" or "creature" on the grounds that he shares other names with created things?

question: Is the Father called "Lord" in Scripture, or is that title reserved for the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: The Father is also called Lord in many places. In "The Lord hath said unto me, Thou art my Son" and "The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit Thou at my right hand," the one speaking as Lord is the Father. So the name is not exclusive to the Son.
sources.quote: But since it is found that God the Father also is called Lord in many places,—for instance, “The Lord hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten Thee;”
sources.raw_question: Is the Father called "Lord" in Scripture, or is that title reserved for the Son?

question: Does Scripture's interchangeable application of the title "Lord" to both the Father and the Son support the Son's deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The name is applied to the Father and the Son so interchangeably that in many places it is very hard to tell which is meant. If Christ were not God, the risk of wrongly giving Divine worship to him would therefore be very great. Scripture would not create that danger.
sources.quote: seeing that the name is applied to the Father and the Son indiscriminately, so that, in many places, the difficulty is very great of knowing whether the Eternal Father or the Lord Jesus Christ be intended, the risk of ascribing Divine worship would be imminent indeed.
sources.raw_question: Does the indiscriminate application of the title 'Lord' to both the Father and the Son support the Son's deity?

question: Can the essence of the Son be compared with or likened to created things?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. Since the Son laid the foundation of all things, He is other and different in essence from things originate, so there can be no comparison or likeness of His essence to them. Scripture contrasts the Son, addressed as begotten Son, with angels, who are made spirits and ministers.
sources.quote: But if He be other and different in essence from their nature, what comparison of His essence can there be, or what likeness to them?
sources.raw_question: Can the essence of the Son be compared with or likened to created things?

question: Does saying that the Son's essence cannot be compared with any of the things made by and after Him confer any special honour on the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then clearly and skilfully criticises the doctrine of the impossibility of comparison with the things made after the Son, and exposes the idolatry contrived by Eunomius, and concealed by the terminology of “Son” and “Only-begotten,” to deceive his readers.
sources.answer: No. Every created thing, by its own characteristic nature, is incomparable with things of a different kind: heaven with earth, stars with seas, animals with trees, rational with irrational creatures. So what Eunomius offers as a special honour to the Only-begotten could truly be said of any creature whatever, and his concession only makes his blasphemy more manifest.
sources.quote: it is this, which may be truly said of any creature you please, which is allotted by the enemies of the truth, as adequate and sufficient for His honour and glory, to the Only-begotten God!
sources.raw_question: Does saying that the Son's essence cannot be compared with any of the things made by and after Him confer any special honour on the Son?

question: Does Scripture's saying the Word was 'created' mean the Word is a creature by nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. Just as 'the Word was made flesh' means He put on flesh, and 'made sin' and 'a curse' mean He bore our sin and curse, so 'He created' means He put on a created body. God created Him for our sakes by preparing the body, that in Him we might be renewed and deified.
sources.quote: we must not conceive that the whole Word is in nature a creature, but that He put on the created body and that God created Him for our sakes, preparing for Him the created body
sources.raw_question: Does saying the Word was 'created' mean the whole Word is a creature by nature, just as 'the Word was made flesh' might seem to mean the Word became nothing but flesh?

question: Why must resurrection and exaltation be ascribed to the Word if He became flesh?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: Because if the Word truly became flesh, what happens to that flesh must be ascribed to Him, as it would be to a man. This is necessary so that the death ascribed to Him may redeem men from sin and abolish death. It is also needed so that resurrection and exaltation may, for His sake, remain secure for us.
sources.quote: if the Word became flesh, of necessity the resurrection and exaltation, as in the case of a man, must be ascribed to Him, that the death which is ascribed to Him may be a redemption of the sin of men and an abolition of death
sources.raw_question: Why must resurrection and exaltation be ascribed to the Word if He became flesh?

question: Does the fact that the Father is called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob prove that the Son is not that God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. These texts show only that the Father was the God of the Jews and of the patriarchs. They say nothing to deny that the Son was also that God. The argument would be relevant only if a text showed that the Son was not the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
sources.quote: Very right. But how does it appear that the Son was not? Could you have brought ever a text to prove, that God the Son was not God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Father is called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob prove that the Son is not that God?

question: Does the fact that the one who appeared to Abraham is called God prove that the Son is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: Yes. The one seen is called God and cannot be the Father, so he must be the Son, the Word of God made flesh, who is Christ. Christ is shown to be God in so many ways that there is no reason to hesitate to call him God.
sources.quote: Wherefore it is the Son who is seen; but the Son of God is the Word of God: and the Word of God was made flesh, and dwelt among us; and this is Christ. What in the world is the reason that we should hesitate to call Him God
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the one who appeared to Abraham is called God prove that the Son is God?

question: Does a fuller doctrine of the Trinity, which multiplies the mysteries we see in the Godhead, make our knowledge of God less clear or less true?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The more Scripture tells us about something infinitely above us, the more mysteries come into view, yet our understanding becomes clearer. A child told a little about God sees fewer mysteries than a divinity student, but knows less. Likewise, someone who looks at a plant through a microscope sees more wonders, yet gains truer knowledge. So the added mysteries show only that God has told us more than was generally noticed.
sources.quote: the things that have been observed increase the number of visible mysteries in the Godhead in no other manner than as by them we perceive that God has told us much more about it than was before generally observed
sources.raw_question: Does a fuller doctrine of the Trinity, which multiplies the mysteries we see in the Godhead, make our knowledge of God less clear or less true?

question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity more perplexing than truths that opponents of mysteries already accept, such as eternity and self-existence?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Self-existence is hardly understood, yet everyone believes it in a general way. An eternity past puzzles all philosophy, and both the 'nunc stans' and succession carry great difficulties. Nothing peculiar to the Trinity is nearly as perplexing as eternity, which those who would discard mysteries must still believe.
sources.quote: There is nothing peculiar to the doctrine of the Trinity, any thing near so perplexing as eternity is: and yet the gentlemen who are for discarding mysterzes are forced to believe it.
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity more perplexing than truths that opponents of mysteries already accept, such as eternity and self-existence?

question: Do objections against the theological explanations of the Trinity overthrow the revealed doctrine of the Trinity itself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. The opponents' principal objections are aimed merely at the explanations used to state the doctrine, not against the primitive revelation of it, which is the principal object of faith. To reject the revealed truth because of difficulties with its explanations is a preposterous and irrational procedure.
sources.quote: The objections these men principally insist upon, are merely against the explanations we use of this doctrine, — not against the primitive revelation of it, which is the principal object of our faith
sources.raw_question: Do objections against the theological explanations of the Trinity overthrow the revealed doctrine of the Trinity itself?

question: Must a Christian abandon belief in the Trinity if he cannot answer every objection raised against it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. It is a recognized rule that an opinion embraced on just grounds should not be deserted merely because one cannot answer every objection, unless the objections weigh as much as the reasons for the belief. Christians who let go of a truth for want of answers to objections could quickly be disputed into atheism.
sources.quote: if a man, on just grounds and reasons, have embraced any opinion or persuasion, he is not to desert it merely because he cannot answer every objection against it.
sources.raw_question: Must a Christian abandon belief in the Trinity if he cannot answer every objection raised against it?

question: Can Scripture answer rational objections and doubts raised against belief in the Trinity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. When doubts assail these first principles, or hold back an enquirer, the word of God, reverently consulted, gives a complete answer to every rational objection. Believers are therefore ready to give a reason for their hope. The doubter must pursue the enquiry wholeheartedly with watching and prayer, trusting God's promise that those who seek him with all their heart will find him.
sources.quote: then the word of God, reverently consulted, affords a complete answer to every, what I may call, rational objection. The armory supplies a weapon for every encounter.
sources.raw_question: Can Scripture answer rational objections and doubts raised against belief in the Trinity?

question: Is it legitimate for a believer to keep searching into the doctrine of the Trinity rather than claiming to have fully grasped it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > In What Way We Must Inquire Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine holds that no one justly faults a search into the Trinity provided the seeker is steadfast in the faith, whereas one who confidently affirms that he has comprehended it is justly faulted. Scripture bids us "seek His face evermore," and Paul says he has not yet apprehended. The disposition to seek truth is safer than presuming unknown things to be known, since perfect knowledge comes only after this life, face to face.
sources.quote: Let us therefore be thus minded, so as to know that the disposition to seek the truth is more safe than that which presumes things unknown to be known.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate for a believer to keep searching into the doctrine of the Trinity rather than claiming to have fully grasped it?

question: Can we know or explain how the Word is begotten of the Father?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. We cannot even explain our own generation, though we see its human cause every day. Scripture reveals the fact that the Word is begotten ("From the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten Thee") but not the manner. The Father keeps the account of this generation after the Spirit with himself, to reveal it to the holy ones in his own time. We should rest content with Christ's word, "That which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
sources.quote: He shows the fact that He is begotten, but reserves the question of the manner and means, to reveal it only in the time determined by Himself.
sources.raw_question: Can we know or explain how the Word is begotten of the Father?

question: Was the Word begotten of the Father by the Father's will?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: Yes. God the Father begat the Word in his good pleasure, as he willed. The generation is therefore an act of the Father's will, whose manner is not to be curiously inquired into.
sources.quote: you are asking an account of the generation of the Word, whom God the Father in His good pleasure begat as He willed.
sources.raw_question: Was the Word begotten of the Father by the Father's will?

question: Why must the Word begotten by the Father be equal to the Father in all things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Word of God is in All Things Equal to the Father, from Whom It is.
sources.answer: Because the Father begat the Word as though uttering Himself. He would not have uttered Himself wholly and perfectly if there were anything more or less in the Word than in Himself.
sources.quote: as though uttering Himself, the Father begat the Word equal to Himself in all things; for He would not have uttered Himself wholly and perfectly, if there were in His Word anything more or less than in Himself
sources.raw_question: Why must the Word begotten by the Father be equal to the Father in all things?

question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity revealed in the Old Testament?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No, not in the broad sense. Warfield says we cannot speak broadly of a revelation of the Trinity in the Old Testament, as shown by the plain fact that none who depended on the Old Testament alone ever attained to the doctrine. Yet the mystery of the Trinity underlies the Old Testament revelation and here and there almost comes into view.
sources.quote: It is a plain matter of fact that none who have depended on the revelation embodied in the Old Testament alone have ever attained to the doctrine of the Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity revealed in the Old Testament?

question: If the New Testament only alludes to the doctrine of the Trinity rather than formally teaching it, does that weaken the evidence for the doctrine?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Its testimony is all the more impressive because it is given with unstudied naturalness and simplicity. The Trinity is alluded to rather than asserted, but in a way that shows it is the determining basis of all Paul's thought about the God of redemption.
sources.quote: This is the uniform and pervasive testimony of the New Testament, and it is the more impressive that it is given with such unstudied naturalness and simplicity
sources.raw_question: If the New Testament does not formally teach the doctrine of the Trinity but only alludes to it, does that weaken the evidence for the doctrine?

question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity a speculative addition to Scripture, or a formulation of what the New Testament itself presupposes?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: It is a formulation of what the New Testament presupposes. The doctrine is nothing but the exact statement of the conception of God underlying the religion of the incarnate Son and the outpoured Spirit. The New Testament is the documentation of that religion, so the doctrine is simply 'the statement in well guarded language' of its composite fact.
sources.quote: what we mean by the doctrine of the Trinity is nothing but the formulation in exact language of the conception of God presupposed in the religion of the incarnate Son and outpoured Spirit
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity a speculative addition to Scripture, or a formulation of what the New Testament itself presupposes?

question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity explicitly stated in the New Testament, or is it only presupposed there?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: It is both. The doctrine underlies the whole New Testament as its constant presupposition and shapes its forms of expression throughout. It also comes to explicit expression now and again when occasion arises. Formal statements are relatively rare only because the New Testament writings were occasional and practical in purpose rather than doctrinal.
sources.quote: That this doctrine underlies the whole New Testament as its constant presupposition and determines everywhere its forms of expression is the primary fact to be noted.
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity explicitly stated in the New Testament, or is it only presupposed there?

question: Does the New Testament show the doctrine of the Trinity in the process of development, or as an already established belief?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: As already established. The New Testament is Trinitarian to the core, with frequent, cursory, easy and confident allusions to the Trinity; the doctrine is not so much inculcated as presupposed. It appears already made, as the fixed possession of the Christian community, and the process by which the community acquired it lies behind the New Testament.
sources.quote: The doctrine of the Trinity does not appear in the New Testament in the making, but as already made.
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament show the doctrine of the Trinity in the process of development, or as an already established belief?

question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity properly said to be revealed in the words of the New Testament?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Not strictly. Speaking exactly, the revelation was made not in word but in deed: in the incarnation of the Son and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. The Old Testament was written as preparation before this revelation and the New Testament as its product after it; the revelation itself is embodied in Christ and the Spirit.
sources.quote: The revelation itself was made not in word but in deed. It was made in the incarnation of God the Son, and the outpouring of God the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity properly said to be revealed in the words of the New Testament?

question: Does 'Let us make man after our image and likeness' (Genesis 1:26) reveal a plurality of divine Persons who are alike?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: Yes. By saying 'our likeness,' the speaker revealed the existence of more than one Being, each like the other. This supports the Son's perfect likeness to the Father without any separation of nature.
sources.quote: by those words Our likeness revealed the existence of Beings, Each like the Other
sources.raw_question: Does 'Let us make man after our image and likeness' (Genesis 1:26) reveal a plurality of divine Persons who are alike?

question: Does the plural in Genesis 1:26 show that the one God addresses is true God rather than God in name only?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. The word "Our" excludes isolation and any difference of purpose or nature between Speaker and the one addressed, and man is made in Their common image. Since nothing can be common to the true and the false, the one to whom the true God speaks and with whom He shares the image must himself be true God.
sources.quote: How is He falsely called God, to Whom the true God says, After Our own image and likeness? Our is inconsistent with isolation, and with difference either in purpose or in nature.
sources.raw_question: Does the plural in Genesis 1:26, "Let Us make man after Our own image and likeness," show that the one addressed by God is true God rather than God in name only?

question: Does the New Testament revelation of the Trinity correct the Old Testament conception of God, or only complete it?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The Old Testament revelation of God is not corrected by the fuller revelation that follows it. It is only perfected, extended and enlarged, since the mystery of the Trinity already underlay it.
sources.quote: Thus the Old Testament revelation of God is not corrected by the fuller revelation which follows it, but only perfected, extended and enlarged.
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament revelation of the Trinity correct the Old Testament conception of God?

question: Does the New Testament's fuller revelation of the Trinity make God more knowable, or only more mysterious?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Both. The New Testament has opened the nature of God more fully to our view than the Old Testament did. It has also increased the number of visible mysteries, so that God appears more wonderful and incomprehensible. The same is true of the fuller revelation of the incarnation and of Christ's satisfaction.
sources.quote: what the New Testament has revealed, tho it has more opened to our view the nature of God, yet it has increased the number of visible mysteries
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament's fuller revelation of the Trinity, compared with the Old Testament, make God more knowable or only more mysterious?

question: How does the image of light and its radiance explain the oneness of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Whatever the light enlightens, the radiance irradiates, and whatever the radiance irradiates draws its enlightenment from the light. In the same way, when the Son is seen the Father is seen, because the Son is the Father's radiance. So the Father and the Son are one.
sources.quote: So also when the Son is beheld, so is the Father, for He is the Father’s radiance; and thus the Father and the Son are one.
sources.raw_question: How does the image of light and its radiance explain the oneness of the Father and the Son?

question: Does the fact that believers' bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit show that the Spirit is not a creature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Believers' bodies are members of Christ, and it would be senseless and profane for Christ's members to be the temple of a creature inferior to Christ. Moreover, to the one whose temple our body is, we owe the service (latreia) due to God alone. Therefore the Spirit is not a creature, which is why the apostle says, "glorify God in your body."
sources.quote: But if the members of Christ are also the temple of the Holy Spirit, then the Holy Spirit is not a creature; because we must needs owe to Him, of whom our body is the temple, that service wherewith God only is to be served
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that believers' bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit show that the Spirit is not a creature?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's knowledge of God show that he shares the divine nature and is not a creature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter I. St. Ambrose commences his argument by complimenting the Emperor, both for his faith and for the restitution of the Basilica to the Church; then having urged that his opponents, if they affirm that the Holy Spirit is not a servant, cannot deny Him to be above all, adds that the same Spirit, when He said, “All things serve Thee,” showed plainly that He was distinct from creatures; which point he also establishes by other evidence.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture shuts out the fellowship of creatures from the knowledge of God but does not shut out the Spirit. The Spirit has the same knowledge as the Son, and nothing more clearly shows the unity of the Divine Power. So the Spirit is not of the fellowship of creatures.
sources.quote: He excludes, then, the fellowship and number of creatures from the knowledge of God, but by not excluding the Holy Spirit, He shows that He is not of the fellowship of creatures.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's knowledge of God show that He shares the Divine nature and is not a creature?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be a creature, given that every creature is confined within the limits of its own nature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is not a creature, seeing that He is infinite, and was shed upon the apostles dispersed through all countries, and moreover sanctifies the Angels also, to whom He makes us equal. Mary was full of the same likewise, so too, Christ the Lord, and so far all things high and low. And all benediction has its origin from His operation, as was signified in the moving of the water at Bethesda.
sources.answer: No. Every creature, even invisible ones, is bounded by the property of its own substance, but the Holy Spirit has no limited or circumscribed power. He is always in all things and everywhere, which is the property of Divinity and Lordship alone.
sources.quote: how can any one dare to call the Holy Spirit a creature, Who has not a limited and circumscribed power? because He is always in all things and everywhere, which assuredly is the property of Divinity and Lordship
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be a creature, given that every creature is confined within the limits of its own nature?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being poured forth from the mouth of God show that he is not a creature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as Wisdom proceeding from God's mouth, the Word uttered from His heart, and the Power containing the fulness of divine Majesty cannot be called created, so the Spirit poured forth from God's mouth cannot be considered created. God Himself shows their unity by speaking of the Spirit as His own Spirit which He pours forth.
sources.quote: so, too, the Spirit which is poured forth from the mouth of God cannot be considered to be created, since God Himself has shown their unity to be such that He speaks of His pouring forth of His Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being poured forth from the mouth of God show that He is not a creature?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be a creature if he was the author of Christ's Incarnation?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VI. To those who object that according to the words of Amos the Spirit is created, the answer is made that the word is there understood of the wind, which is often created, which cannot be said of the Holy Spirit, since He is eternal, and cannot be dissolved in death, or by an heretical absorption into the Father. But if they pertinaciously contend that this passage was written of the Holy Spirit, St. Ambrose points out that recourse must be had to a spiritual Interpretation, for Christ by His coming established the thunder, that is, the force of the divine utterances, and by Spirit is signified the human soul as also the flesh assumed by Christ. And since this was created by each Person of the Trinity, it is thence argued that the Spirit, Who has before been affirmed to be the Creator of all things, was the Author of the Incarnation of the Lord.
sources.answer: No. The mystery of the Incarnation is above all created things. The One who created it therefore cannot Himself be a creature.
sources.quote: How, then, can the Holy Spirit Who created the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, which is above all created things, be Himself a creature?
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be a creature if He was the author of Christ's Incarnation?

question: Does Scripture's speaking of the Holy Spirit singly, as one, show that he is not a creature?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is not ranked among the plurality of creation but spoken of singly; he is not one of many but One, as there is one Father and one Son. He is therefore as far from created nature as the singular is from compound and plural things. He is united to the Father and Son as unit has affinity with unit, joined to the one Father through the one Son and completing the Trinity.
sources.quote: He is consequently as far removed from created Nature as reason requires the singular to be removed from compound and plural bodies; and He is in such wise united to the Father and to the Son as unit has affinity with unit.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Scripture speaks of the Holy Spirit as one, singly, show that he is not a creature?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being manifested through the Son, through whom creation was made, place the Spirit among creatures?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit is distinguished from creation by his unchangeableness and his independence of all external goodness, which creatures lack by nature, as the fall of Satan shows. These very attributes that set him apart from creation constitute his relationship to the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: He is distinguished from it by His unchangeableness, and independence of all external goodness. The creation does not possess in its nature this unchangeableness
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being manifested through the Son, through whom creation was made, place the Spirit among creatures?

question: Could the Son be Son and God only by participation, as creatures are, by partaking of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Objection, that the Son's eternity makes Him coordinate with the Father, introduces the subject of His Divine Sonship, as a second proof of His eternity. The word Son is introduced in a secondary, but is to be understood in real sense. Since all things partake of the Father in partaking of the Son, He is the whole participation of the Father, that is, He is the Son by nature; for to be wholly participated is to beget.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit himself takes from the Son, so it is unreasonable to say the Son is sanctified by the Spirit. The only remaining option is that he partakes of the Father, which leads to the conclusion that he is not a participant at all but is himself what is partaken of the Father.
sources.quote: Nay, rather the Spirit Himself takes from the Son, as He Himself says; and it is not reasonable to say that the latter is sanctified by the former.
sources.raw_question: Could the Son be Son and God only by participation, as creatures are, by partaking of the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the Son's giving of the Holy Spirit prove that he is not a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: Yes. To give the Spirit with authority is not in the power of any creature or work, since the Spirit is God's Gift. Creatures are hallowed by the Spirit, but the Son is not hallowed by the Spirit and is rather its Giver to all; therefore He is true Son of the Father, not a creature.
sources.quote: For the creatures are hallowed by the Holy Spirit; but the Son, in that He is not hallowed by the Spirit, but on the contrary Himself the Giver of it to all, is therefore no creature, but true Son of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's giving of the Holy Spirit prove that He is not a creature?

question: Does the fact that the Son, being God, took part in human nature prove that he is a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No. If it did, then the text saying that the Word who was God "was seen upon earth and conversed with men" would also prove Him a creature, which is absurd. Being manifested in the flesh means the same as taking the form of a servant while in the form of God. If one of these statements does not support the blasphemy, neither does the other.
sources.quote: For in sense it is just the same to say that the Word that was in the beginning was manifested to men through the flesh, and to say that being in the form of God He put on the form of a servant
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Son, being God, took part in human nature prove that he is a creature?

question: Does Scripture reveal the essence of God or of created things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The sacred writers declare that heaven, earth, sea, and the creatures in them were created, but are silent on what each is in itself, and how and whence. Likewise, concerning God they exhort men to believe that He is and that He rewards those who seek Him. His essence they leave untouched as impossible to grasp and fruitless to the curious inquirer.
sources.quote: so, too, concerning God Himself, they exhort men to “believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of them that diligently seek Him,” but in regard to His nature, as being above every name, they neither name it nor concern themselves about it.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture reveal the essence of God or of created things?

question: In what sense is the Word 'created a beginning of ways' in Proverbs 8:22?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: The phrase refers to his becoming man for our sake, not to his divine nature. He became the beginning of the new way, so that we might walk in it through him who is 'the Way' and 'the Door' and come to know the Father. When the first way through Adam was lost to death, the Word put on created flesh, so as to be first of the new creation and open a new and living way.
sources.quote: therefore He is created ‘a beginning of ways,’ that we, walking along it and entering through Him who says, ‘I am the Way’ and ‘the Door,’ and partaking of the knowledge of the Father
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Word 'created a beginning of ways' (Proverbs 8:22)?

question: In what sense is the created wisdom in creation called a 'beginning of ways' in Proverbs 8:22?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: It is a beginning or rudiment of the knowledge of God. A person starts on this way in the fear of the Lord, then rises in thought to perceive the Framing Wisdom in creation. Through that Wisdom he perceives the Father, since whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father.
sources.quote: such wisdom becomes a sort of beginning. and, as it were, rudiments of the knowledge of God
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the created wisdom called a 'beginning of ways' in Proverbs 8:22?

question: Does Proverbs 8:25, 'before all the hills He begat Me,' teach that Wisdom was begotten rather than created?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. Lest the terms 'creation' and 'establishing' obstruct belief in the divine birth, the text immediately speaks of begetting. He Who is established before the ages is begotten before the earth, mountains and hills.
sources.quote: But now, lest the terms ‘creation’ and ‘establishing’ should be an obstacle to belief in the divine birth, these words follow, Before He made the earth, before He made firm the mountains, before all the hills He begat Me
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:25, 'before all the hills He begat Me,' teach that Wisdom was begotten rather than created?

question: Does Deuteronomy 6:4 ('the Lord thy God is one Lord') require confessing one God even though the Godhead belongs to three Persons?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture testifies that God is one, and the name of the nature should not take the mark of plurality. So although the Godhead extends through the Trinity, we confess one God.
sources.quote: Therefore we must confess one God, according to the testimony of Scripture, “Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one Lord,” even though the name of Godhead extends through the Holy Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Does Deuteronomy 6:4 ("the Lord thy God is one Lord") require confessing one God even though the Godhead belongs to three Persons?

question: Does Ephesians 4:6, 'One God and Father of all', diminish the Son's real divinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. The ancients generally understood the passage of the whole Trinity: above all as Father, through all by the Word, and in all by the Holy Ghost. In any case, the Father may reasonably be called the one or only God without the least diminution of the Son's real Divinity.
sources.quote: the Father may be reasonably called the one, or only God, without the least diminution of the Son’s real Divinity
sources.raw_question: Does Ephesians 4:6, 'One God and Father of all', diminish the Son's real divinity?

question: Why is the Holy Spirit called the 'Finger of God' in Scripture, and what does this name signify about the Spirit's relation to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter III. The same Unity may also be recognized from the fact that the Spirit is called Finger, and the Son Right Hand; for the understanding of divine things is assisted by the usage of human language. The tables of the law were written by this Finger, and they were afterwards broken, and the reason.
