Lastly, Christ wrote with the same Finger; yet we must not admit any inferiority in the Spirit from this bodily comparison.
sources.answer: It signifies the indivisible and inseparable communion of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Just as the Son is called the Right Hand of God, the Spirit is called the Finger of God. Both names, drawn from the members of one body, point to a single Godhead and a single working rather than separate powers.
sources.quote: the Spirit is also called the Finger of God, because there is an indivisible and inseparable communion between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit called the 'Finger of God' in Scripture, and what does this name signify about the Spirit's relation to the Father and the Son?

question: Does Scripture apply the terms 'hand' and 'finger' of God to both the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter V. The writer sums up the argument he had commenced, and confirms the statement that unity is signified by the terms finger and right hand, from the fact that the works of God are the same as are the works of hands; and that those of hands are the same as those of fingers; and lastly, that the term hand applies equally to the Son and the Spirit, and that of finger applies to the Spirit and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is called God's hand, as in "Hath not My Hand made all these things?" The covering hand in the cleft of the rock refers to the Incarnation. Since the Spirit is called the finger of God, the plural "fingers" signifies both Son and Spirit. Likewise "Thy hands have made me" shows sanctification received from both the Son and the Spirit.
sources.quote: it is certainly clear that Scripture used the term hand both of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture apply the terms "hand" and "finger" of God to both the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Did angels or some lesser power distant from the Father create humanity?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: No. Angels neither made nor formed us, and they had no power to make an image of God. Only the Word of the Lord could do this. The Scripture says God himself formed man and breathed into him the breath of life, so no power remote from the Father of all was involved.
sources.quote: It was not angels, therefore, who made us, nor who formed us, neither had angels power to make an image of God, nor any one else, except the Word of the Lord, nor any Power remotely distant from the Father of all things.
sources.raw_question: Did angels or some lesser power distant from the Father create humanity?

question: Does John 1:1 show that the Word is God because he is from God, the Beginning?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: Yes. 'In the Beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God,' for the Beginning was God. Since the Word is from that Beginning, therefore also 'the Word was God.'
sources.quote: ‘in’ that ‘Beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God,’ for the Beginning was God; and since He is from It, therefore also ‘the Word was God.’
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:1 show that the Word is God because He is from God, the Beginning?

question: Does the title 'God' (Theos) given to the Word in John 1:1 imply that the Word was Lord over all from the beginning?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: Yes. Even on the opponent's own view that Theos is a word of office implying dominion, the Word was Theos before the world was, and so was Lord as soon as anything existed to be Lord over. Accordingly, when he came into the world made by him, he came unto his own.
sources.quote: He was Θεὸς before the world was, by your own acknowledgment ; which being a word of office, and implying dominion, he was certainly Lord, as soon as ever there was any thing for him to be Lord over.
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'God' (Theos) given to the Word in John 1:1 imply that the Word was Lord over all from the beginning?

question: In John 1:1, 'the Word was with God', does 'God' refer to the Father alone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > What is Said of the Father and Son Together, and What Not.
sources.answer: Not necessarily. There is much reason to read "the Word" as the Son alone and "God" as the Father and the Son together. This is no stranger than saying the soul was with a man, that is, in a man, even though the soul is not the body and the man is soul and body together. So "the Word was God" may mean that the Word, which is not the Father, was God together with the Father.
sources.quote: “The Word,” which is the Son alone, “was with God,” which is not the Father alone, but God the Father and the Son together.
sources.raw_question: In John 1:1, "the Word was with God," does "God" refer to the Father alone?

question: Why does John's Gospel open with 'In the beginning was the Word' rather than speaking of the Father begetting the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: To guard untrained hearers from carnal and passionate ideas of generation. He says "Beginning" instead of "Father," "was" instead of "was begotten," and "Word" instead of "Son." Only after much purifying preparation does he name the Father and the Only-begotten, when the words can no longer sink to a polluted meaning.
sources.quote: instead of “the Father,” he speaks of “the Beginning”: instead of “was begotten,” he says “was”: and instead of “the Son,” he says “the Word”
sources.raw_question: Why does John's Gospel open with "In the beginning was the Word" rather than speaking of the Father begetting the Son?

question: Why does John call Christ 'Word' before calling him 'God' in John 1:1?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: John did this so that readers' thoughts would not turn at once to the Father, as they would have if the title God had come first. Moses' order of "Angel" before "Existent" works the same way.
sources.quote: having previously called Him “Word,” so introduces the further truth that the Word was God, that our thoughts might not at once turn to the Father
sources.raw_question: Why does John call Christ "Word" before calling Him "God" in John 1:1?

question: Can God have been perfect from the beginning if he only later became Father of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. If God was perfect from the first, he could not lack the power to be Father. If Fatherhood of such a Son was not good or fitting at the beginning, God could not rightly acquire it later. Since it is good and fitting to God's majesty to be Father of such a Son, a later Fatherhood would mean God once lacked a good thing.
sources.quote: Then how can He be perfect, while as yet unable to become Father? Or will they not deprive Him of this power, but say only that it was not fitting that there should be Fatherhood simultaneously with His existence.
sources.raw_question: Can God have been perfect from the beginning if he only later became Father of the Son?

question: Are the words 'He that seeth Me, seeth Him that sent Me' (John 12:45) spoken by the Son rather than by a Word distinct from the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: They are spoken by the Son. The one who says 'I came not to judge the world but to save it' is identified by John 3 as the Only-begotten Son whom God sent to save the world. Since the same speaker says 'He that seeth Me seeth Him that sent Me,' that speaker is the Son.
sources.quote: if He who came to save the world and not judge it is the Only-begotten Son of God, it is plain that it is the same Son who says, ‘He that seeth Me, seeth Him that sent Me.’
sources.raw_question: Are the words 'He that seeth Me, seeth Him that sent Me' (John 12:45) spoken by the Son rather than by a Word distinct from the Son?

question: Is the one speaking in John 14 ('He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father', 'I am in the Father and the Father in Me') the Son rather than some Word distinct from him?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: It is the Son. The same speaker identifies Himself as the Son by adding 'that the Father may be glorified in the Son', so the Son is He who is in the Father and in whom the Father is seen. Hence these divine attributes belong to the Son.
sources.quote: for He, the same who thus spoke, shews Himself to be the Son, by adding, ‘that the Father may be glorified in the Son.’
sources.raw_question: Is the Son speaking in John 14 ('He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father', 'I am in the Father and the Father in Me') the Son rather than some Word distinct from him?

question: If the world was made by angels or by some being other than the true God, do the faults attributed to that maker fall back on the supreme God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter V.—This world was not formed by any other beings within the territory which is contained by the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. If the world was formed within the Father's domain with his permission and good-will, then he is the real author. He would be the one who allows works of error and corruptible things to be mixed with his own eternal possessions. If it was made without his permission, then its maker would be more powerful and kingly than the Father.
sources.quote: the charges which they bring against the Demiurge, and those things which were made material and temporal, will in truth fall back on the Father
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics holding creation by angels or a Demiurge
sources.raw_question: If the world was made by angels or by some being other than the true God, do the faults attributed to that maker fall back on the supreme God?

question: In what sense can it be said that the Father 'made' the Son who already existed?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections to the Foregoing Proof. Whether, in the generation of the Son, God made One that was already, or One that was not.
sources.answer: In the Incarnation. The Father, who was, made the Son, who was, into man, for 'the Word was made flesh.' The one who was already Son of God became at the consummation of the ages also Son of Man. This holds unless one follows the Samosatene in claiming that He did not exist until He became man.
sources.quote: The Father who was, made the Son who was, for ‘the Word was made flesh;’ and, whereas He was Son of God, He made Him in consummation of the ages also Son of Man
sources.raw_question: In what sense can it be said that the Father 'made' the Son who already existed?

question: Do Paul's references to 'His Son' and 'the Son of God' (e.g. Romans 5:10, Romans 8:3, 1 Corinthians 1:9) teach that Christ is God's Son by true nature rather than by adoption or creation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. Paul consistently calls Christ God's Son and never speaks of His adoption or of His being God's creature. The name expresses the nature: because He is God's Son, the Sonship is true, and the Apostle's confession asserts the genuineness of the relation.
sources.quote: His Son, Son of God; so we read, but nothing is said of His adoption, or of God’s creature. The name expresses the nature; He is God’s Son, and therefore the Sonship is true.
sources.raw_question: Do Paul's references to 'His Son' and 'the Son of God' (e.g. Romans 5:10, Romans 8:3, 1 Corinthians 1:9) teach that Christ is God's Son by true nature rather than by adoption or creation?

question: Are the names we use for God, including the name 'God' itself, invented by human conception (epinoia) rather than directly imparted by God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, in the sense that the rational faculty God implanted in us invents words to indicate realities. The cause of our naming God is referable to God Himself, who gave us the faculty and who is by nature what He is, but the actual freedom to name things lies in our nature's conceptual power. Proof of this is that the Divine Being is not named alike by all peoples, but each interprets his idea as he thinks best.
sources.quote: And there is this one sure evidence in our favour, that the Divine Being is not named alike by all, but that each interprets his idea as he thinks best.
sources.raw_question: Are the names we use for God, including the name 'God' itself, invented by human conception (epinoia) rather than directly imparted by God?

question: Does human conception (epinoia) have independent authority over the names given to things, such that it could compete with God's authority in naming?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No, but this is because conception has no independent subsistence of its own. Only creatures governed by their own deliberate will can act with authority. Thought and conception are operations of the mind that depend on the deliberate choice of those who speak and subsist only in what is said. So Eunomius's denial that conception has 'authority' over names refutes a claim no one makes.
sources.quote: But thought and conception are an operation of the mind, which depends on the deliberate choice of those who speak, having no independent subsistence, but subsisting only in the force of the things said.
sources.raw_question: Does human thought or conception (epinoia) have independent authority over the names given to things, such that it could be said to compete with God's authority in naming?

question: How does the Word of God differ from the human inner word with respect to being formed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Great is the Unlikeness Between Our Word and the Divine Word. Our Word Cannot Be or Be Called Eternal.
sources.answer: The Word of God was never formable before being formed and was never capable of being formless. It is a simple form, simply equal to the One from whom it is, and wonderfully co-eternal with Him. The human word, by contrast, arises from something formable that we revolve in thought until it is shaped by what we know.
sources.quote: which is so in the form of God, as not to have been formable before it was formed, or to have been capable at any time of being formless, but is a simple form, and simply equal to Him from whom it is, and with whom it is wonderfully co-eternal?
sources.raw_question: How does the Word of God differ from the human inner word with respect to being formed?

question: Why can the human inner word not be called 'essence of essence' as the Word of God is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Great is the Unlikeness Between Our Word and the Divine Word. Our Word Cannot Be or Be Called Eternal.
sources.answer: Our word cannot be called essence of essence as the Word of God is, because for us to be is not the same as to know. We know many things that can be forgotten and perish from our mind while we still exist, whereas in God being and knowing are identical, so his Word, born of his knowledge, is essence from essence.
sources.quote: Because to us, to be is not the same as to know; since we know many things which in some sense live by memory, and so in some sense die by being forgotten
sources.raw_question: How is the human inner word unlike the Word of God with respect to being 'essence of essence'?

question: Is the Son visible in His divine nature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IV. The Holy Spirit is one and the same Who spake in the prophets and apostles, Who is the Spirit of God and of Christ; Whom, further, Scripture designates the Paraclete, and the Spirit of life and truth.
sources.answer: No. The Lord says the world cannot see or know the Spirit of Truth, so the Spirit is invisible. If even the Spirit cannot be seen by the world, it is absurd to think the Son is visible in His divine nature.
sources.quote: How, then, do some think that the Son is visible in His Divine Nature, when the world cannot see even the Spirit?
sources.raised_by_detail: some who think the Son is visible in His Divine Nature
sources.raw_question: Is the Son visible in His divine nature?

question: In what way is the Son the image of the invisible God: by visible form or by his divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: By nature, made known through his works. The Son is called the image of the invisible God so that he is not taken for a likeness of outward form. His exercise of divine powers, above all creating all things, shows that the Father's nature is in him. This is why the Lord said, 'If I do not the works of My Father, believe Me not': we are to see the Father in him through the Father's works.
sources.quote: He is styled the likeness of the invisible God in order that we may understand by His exercise of the powers (not the invisible attributes) of the Divine nature, that that nature is in Him.
sources.raw_question: In what way is the Son the image of the invisible God: by visible form or by his divine nature?

question: Was the dove at Christ's baptism an incarnation of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter I. Not only were the prophets and apostles sent by the Spirit, but also the Son of God. This is proved from Isaiah and the evangelists, and it is explained why St. Luke wrote that the same Spirit descended like a dove upon Christ and abode upon Him. Next, after establishing this mission of Christ, the writer infers that the Son is sent by the Father and the Spirit, as the Spirit is by the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. It was not a dove that descended but the Spirit as a dove, and Luke's 'bodily form' describes an appearance, not an incarnation. The appearance was given so that someone who could not see the Spirit might believe.
sources.quote: Luke, however, added that the Holy Spirit descended in a bodily form as a dove; you must not think that this was an incarnation, but an appearance.
sources.raw_question: Was the dove at Christ's baptism an incarnation of the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the Anomoean doctrine that the Son is unlike the Father follow logically from Arius's teaching that the Son was created out of nothing?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > A notice of Aetius, Eunomius' master in heresy, and of Eunomius himself, describing the origin and avocations of each.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory holds that Aetius did not so much invent something new as draw out the consequences of what Arius had already advanced. If the Son is a creature made from non-existence, it follows that he is unlike the Creator who brought him out of nothing. The Anomoean position is therefore the natural fruit of the Arian seed.
sources.quote: or rather he perceived the consequences of all that Arius had advanced, and so got this character of a shrewd discoverer of truths not obvious; revealing as he did that the Created, even from things non-existent, was unlike the Creator who drew Him out of nothing.
sources.raw_question: Does the Anomoean doctrine that the Son is unlike the Father follow logically from Arius's teaching that the Son was created out of nothing?

question: Can the Father and the Son together be called the Word, the Image, or the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > What is Said of the Father and Son Together, and What Not.
sources.answer: No. The Son alone is the Word, in the same way that He alone is the Image of the Father and the Son of the Father. Both together are not the Image, and both together are not the Son. These names are relative and belong to the Son only.
sources.quote: He is the Word in the same way as He is the Image, but the Father and Son are not both together the Image, but the Son alone is the Image of the Father
sources.raw_question: Can the Father and the Son together be called the Word, the Image, or the Son?

question: In what ways is the Son of God said to be sent?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: In two ways. First, He was sent visibly into this world in the incarnation, made manifest in the flesh in the fullness of time and made of a woman. Second, He is sent invisibly, but not into this world, when He is apprehended by a rational soul, in proportion to that soul's comprehension. In the second case He does not present Himself to the bodily senses.
sources.quote: But when from time to time He comes forth and is perceived by the mind of each, He is said indeed to be sent, but not into this world; for He does not appear sensibly
sources.raw_question: In what ways is the Son of God said to be sent?

question: Who sends the Son, and how is the sender related to the one sent?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: The Son is sent by the Father, the one of whom He is the Word and from whom He was begotten. The sender is the begetter and the one sent is the begotten, so the mission follows the order of origin. Since the Father and the Son are one, the sender and the sent are one, just as the begetter and the begotten are one.
sources.quote: Therefore the Word of God is sent by Him, of whom He is the Word; He is sent by Him, from whom He was begotten (genitum); He sends who begot, That is sent which is begotten.
sources.raw_question: Who sends the Son (the Word of God), and how is the sender related to the one sent?

question: Is confessing 'one only God, the Almighty' sufficient for Christian faith if the Almighty is not identified with the Father of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. Christian faith is directed to the Father. If 'Almighty' refers to the Father the phrase is orthodox. But to posit an Almighty other than the Father is Jewish teaching or Platonic speculation about a supreme maker of subordinate gods, and it is not Christian, even if one confesses an Almighty God.
sources.quote: As then in the case of the Jewish and Platonic opinions he who does not believe in God the Father is not a Christian, even though in his creed he asserts an Almighty God
sources.raw_question: Is confessing 'one only God, the Almighty' sufficient for Christian faith if the Almighty is not identified with the Father of the Son?

question: Does confessing the Father as always and unchangeably the one and only God exclude the Son from the Godhead?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next marvellously overthrows the unintelligible statements of Eunomius which assert that the essence of the Father is not separated or divided, and does not become anything else.
sources.answer: No. Gregory agrees that the Father is truly one, unchangeable and the only God. Such a confession is pious so long as one sees the Son in the Father, since without the Son the Father neither is nor is called Father. To posit a God who is not Father is the error of the Jews and the Hypsistiani, who acknowledge a Highest God but deny that He is Father, and that is not Christian faith.
sources.quote: holds fast the word of godliness, if in the Father he sees the Son, without Whom the Father neither is nor is named
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the Father as always and unchangeably the one and only God exclude the Son from the Godhead?

question: Does Eunomius's statement that the Son "legislates by the command of the Eternal God" imply that only the Father is the eternal God and that the Son is not eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: No. Since Eunomius himself admits it was the only-begotten God who spoke with Moses, contrasting the Son with "the Eternal God" wrongly puts the Lord of all in Moses' place and reserves eternity to the Father alone. The phrase is in fact borrowed from Paul's description of himself as preaching by the command of God. Applying it to the Son therefore puts the Master on the level of His servant Paul, and it gives no ground for denying that the Maker of the worlds is eternal.
sources.quote: ascribes the character of the eternal God to the Father alone, so as, by thus contrasting Him with the Eternal, to make out the only-begotten God, the Maker of the Worlds, to be not Eternal?
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's statement that the Son "legislates by the command of the Eternal God" imply that only the Father is the eternal God and that the Son is not eternal?

question: Does the image of God remain in the human mind even after it has lost its participation in God through sin?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Trinity Which is the Image of God is Now to Be Sought in the Noblest Part of the Mind.
sources.answer: Yes. Though worn out and defaced by losing participation in God, the image still remains. The mind is God's image precisely in being capable of God and able to partake of him, and that capacity is itself made possible only by its being his image.
sources.quote: For it is His image in this very point, that it is capable of Him, and can be partaker of Him; which so great good is only made possible by its being His image.
sources.raw_question: Does the image of God remain in the human mind even after it has lost its participation in God through sin?

question: Does John 1:14 identify the Word made flesh with the Only-begotten of the Father, or, as the Valentinians read it, present him as a distinct Aeon to whom the Father gave glory?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter VIII.—How the Valentinians pervert the Scriptures to support their own pious opinions.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus points out that the Valentinians alter the text. What John actually says is that the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and that we beheld His glory as of the only-begotten of the Father. The Word made flesh is himself the only-begotten of the Father.
sources.quote: But what John really does say is this: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us; and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.”
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:14 present the incarnate Word as an Aeon to whom glory was given by the Father, distinct from the Only-begotten, as the Valentinians read it?

question: Does John 1:14, "We beheld His glory, the glory as of the Only-begotten of the Father," show that the incarnate Word shares the Father's glory?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. He who looked on the incarnate Word, who was Light, Life and God, recognized the Father of glory through the glory he saw. So the incarnation reveals the Son's glory as the Father's own, rather than proving the Son inferior.
sources.quote: he who looked on the incarnate Word, Who was both Light and Life and God, recognized, through the glory which he saw, the Father of glory
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:14, "We beheld His glory, the glory as of the Only-begotten of the Father," show that the incarnate Word shares the Father's glory?

question: Do the doctrine of the Trinity and the doctrine of redemption stand or fall together?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Historically they stand or fall together: Unitarian theology is commonly joined with a Pelagian anthropology and a Socinian soteriology. Many cast off the history of redemption because they have not attained a conception of the Triune God. This close relation is why the church could not rest until it had a definite doctrine of the Trinity.
sources.quote: Accordingly, the doctrine of the Trinity and the doctrine of redemption, historically, stand or fall together. A Unitarian theology is commonly associated with a Pelagian anthropology and a Socinian soteriology.
sources.raw_question: Do the doctrine of the Trinity and the doctrine of redemption stand or fall together?

question: Does the distinction between a fount and the river flowing from it imply a difference of nature between the Father and Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XVI. The Holy Spirit is that large river by which the mystical Jerusalem is watered. It is equal to its Fount, that is, the Father and the Son, as is signified in holy Scripture. St. Ambrose himself thirsts for that water, and warns us that in order to preserve it within us, we must avoid the devil, lust, and heresy, since our vessels are frail, and that broken cisterns must be forsaken, that after the example of the Samaritan woman and of the patriarchs we may find the water of the Lord.
sources.answer: No. A river springs from its fount yet is of one nature, brightness and beauty with it. Likewise the Holy Spirit is of one substance, brightness and glory with the Father and the Son. The lowliness of the image should not lead the mind to lower things.
sources.quote: Set before yourself any river, it springs from its fount, but is of one nature, of one brightness and beauty. And do you assert rightly that the Holy Spirit is of one substance, brightness, and glory with the Son of God and with God the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the distinction between a fount and the river flowing from it imply a difference of nature between the Father and Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Is the title 'Unoriginate' applied to God in contrast to the Son, implying that the Son is originated?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: No. 'Unoriginate' is used in contrast with things originated, not with the Son. God is called Unoriginate because He is not like creatures but is their Creator and Framer through the Son, so the term distinguishes Him from the works made through the Son, not from the Son Himself.
sources.quote: the Unoriginate is specified not by contrast to the Son, but to the things which through the Son come to be. And excellently: since God is not as things originated, but is their Creator and Framer through the Son.
sources.raw_question: Is the title 'Unoriginate' applied to God in contrast to the Son, implying the Son is originated?

question: Is 'Unoriginate' a reliable term for theological argument about God and the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: No. It is unscriptural and suspicious, because it has various senses and carries the mind about to many ideas. It is also a word of the Greeks, who do not know the Son. 'Father', by contrast, is simple, scriptural and more accurate, and implies only the Son.
sources.quote: the latter is unscriptural and suspicious, because it has various senses; so that, when a man is asked concerning it, his mind is carried about to many ideas; but the word Father is simple and scriptural
sources.raw_question: Is 'Unoriginate' a reliable term for theological argument about God and the Son?

question: Does John 5:26, that the Father has given the Son to have life in himself, mean the Son existed first without life and later received it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: No. The Father did not give life to a Son already existing without life, but begat him apart from time, so that the life given by begetting is co-eternal with the Father's life.
sources.quote: not that the Father gave life to the Son already existing without life, but that He so begat Him apart from time, that the life which the Father gave to the Son by begetting Him is co-eternal
sources.raw_question: Does John 5:26, that the Father has given the Son to have life in himself, mean the Son existed first without life and later received it?

question: Are the mind, its self-knowledge, and its self-love three things that are nevertheless one?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: Yes. When the mind loves itself there are two things, the mind and its love, and when it knows itself there are two things, the mind and its knowledge; hence mind, love and knowledge are three things, and yet these three are one. This triad in the mind serves as an image of the Trinity in man.
sources.quote: Therefore the mind itself, and the love of it, and the knowledge of it, are three things (tria quædam), and these three are one; and when they are perfect they are equal.
sources.raw_question: Are the mind, its self-knowledge, and its self-love three things that are nevertheless one?

question: Under what condition are the mind, its self-love, and its self-knowledge equal to one another?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: They are equal when they are perfect. Love is imperfect if the mind loves itself less than it is (as merely as much as a body) or more than it is (as much as God). Knowledge is equal to the mind when the mind knows itself entirely and nothing else with itself, since knower and known are the same nature. Such knowledge is then neither less nor greater than the mind.
sources.quote: When, therefore, it knows itself entirely, and no other thing with itself, then its knowledge is equal to itself; because its knowledge is not from another nature, since it knows itself.
sources.raw_question: Under what condition are the mind, its self-love, and its self-knowledge equal to one another?

question: Does Romans 11:36 show that the prepositions 'of whom' and 'through whom' are of equal value, so that they cannot mark a difference of nature between the Persons?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That v: not found “of whom” in the case of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. If the verse refers to the Son, then "of whom" applies to the Son. If it refers to the Father, then "through whom" applies to the Father. Under either alternative both terms are used of one and the same Person with equal force, so they are equivalent and cannot mark a difference of nature between the Persons.
sources.quote: Under either alternative both terms, being employed of one and the same Person, will be shewn to be equivalent.
sources.raw_question: Whether Romans 11:36 refers to the Son or to the Father, are the prepositions "of whom" and "through whom" shown to be of equal value?

question: How does Romans 11:36 ('of him, through him, and to him are all things') apply to the three Persons in the work of redemption?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Our good is of God the Father, through God the Son, and in the Holy Ghost, who is himself all our good. So God is the one from whom our good is purchased, the one who purchases it, and the thing purchased. God is thus himself the portion of his people, the Alpha and Omega of redemption.
sources.quote: All our good is of God the Father, it is all through God the Son, and all is in the Holy Ghost as He is Himself all our good.
sources.raw_question: How does Romans 11:36 ('of him, through him, and to him are all things') apply to the three Persons in redemption?

question: Did the Nicene phrase 'from the substance of the Father' imply that the Son is of the same undivided substance with the Father, rather than merely of a similar kind?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: Yes. Since the Nicene Fathers held that the Son was neither from any other substance nor from nothing, and they absolutely rejected any division of substance, it follows that they supposed the Son to be of the same undivided, individual substance with the Father.
sources.quote: it is very plain that (unless they supposed a division of substance, which they absolutely reject) they supposed the Son to be of the same undivided, or individual substance with the Father.
sources.raw_question: Did the Nicene phrase 'from the substance of the Father' imply that the Son is of the same undivided substance with the Father, rather than merely of a similar kind?

question: Why did the Nicene Fathers specify that the Son is begotten 'from the substance of the Father'?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: For two reasons. First, to show that they understood the Son's generation in a proper and not a figurative sense, as the Arians did. Second, to secure the divine unity: if the Son were from outside and independent of the Father, the relation and unity of the Persons in one Godhead would be lost, and Ditheism would be unavoidable.
sources.quote: For, if the Son were ab extra, and independent of the Father ; the alliance, the relation, the unity of the Persons, in the same Godhead, had (upon their principles) been lost, and Ditheism unavoidable.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Nicene Fathers specify that the Son is begotten 'from the substance of the Father'?

question: Is the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of the Father, to be counted among the created servants of God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVII. St. Ambrose shows by instances that the places in which those words were spoken help to the understanding of the words of the Lord; he shows that Christ uttered the passage quoted from St. John in Solomon's porch, by which is signified the mind of a wise man, for he says that Christ would not have uttered this saying in the heart of a foolish or contentious man. He goes on to say that Christ is stoned by those who believe not these words, and as the keys of heaven were given to Peter for his confession of them, so Iscariot, because he believed not the same, perished evilly. He takes this opportunity to inveigh against the Jews who bought the Son of God and sold Joseph. He explains the price paid for each mystically; and having in the same manner expounded the murmuring of the traitor concerning Magdalene's ointment, he adds that Christ is bought in one way by heretics in another way by Catholics, and that those in vain take to themselves the name of Christians who sever the Spirit from the Father.
sources.answer: No. To compare the Spirit of the Father to the servants He created is the error of the Arians, which Ambrose has refuted at length. The Spirit cannot be severed from the Father and the Son, and denying this means denying Christ's own doctrine and Spirit.
sources.quote: For he knows not that he is comparing the Spirit of the Father to those servants whom He created.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of the Father, to be counted among the created servants of God?

question: Would counting the Holy Spirit among created things undermine God the Father's being over all?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter I. St. Ambrose commences his argument by complimenting the Emperor, both for his faith and for the restitution of the Basilica to the Church; then having urged that his opponents, if they affirm that the Holy Spirit is not a servant, cannot deny Him to be above all, adds that the same Spirit, when He said, “All things serve Thee,” showed plainly that He was distinct from creatures; which point he also establishes by other evidence.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit searches the deep things of God and is of God, the Spirit of His mouth. To include Him among all things would deny that the Father, whose Spirit He is, is over all and possesses fulness of perfection and perfect power.
sources.quote: For if we say that the Holy Spirit is included amongst all things, certainly when we read that the Spirit searches the deep things of God, we deny that God the Father is over all.
sources.raw_question: Would counting the Holy Spirit among created things undermine God the Father's being over all?

question: If the Incarnation was the work of both the Father and the Son, why is the Son said to be sent and the Father the sender, rather than the reverse?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Because it is the one who appeared in the flesh who is fitly said to be sent, and the one who did not appear in it is said to send. Outward visible events arise from the inward working of the spiritual nature. The human form taken belongs to the person of the Son, not the Father. So the invisible Father, together with the invisible Son, sent the Son by making him visible.
sources.quote: it is fitly said that He who appeared in that flesh was sent, and that He who did not appear in it, sent Him
sources.raw_question: If the Incarnation was the work of both the Father and the Son, why is the Son said to be sent and the Father the sender, rather than the reverse?

question: Apart from the gospel, how is God the Father known to sinners, and what does the gospel newly reveal about him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Apart from the gospel, the Father, as the fountain of the Deity, is known only as full of wrath and indignation against sin. The peculiar work of the gospel is to reveal him as love, full of love toward us.
sources.quote: whereas the Father, as the fountain of the Deity, is not known any other way but as full of wrath, anger, and indignation against sin
sources.raw_question: Apart from the gospel, how is God the Father known to sinners, and what does the gospel newly reveal about him?

question: How do the Old Testament Scriptures relate to the doctrine of God revealed by Christ?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > The second book declares the Incarnation of God the Word, and the faith delivered by the Lord to His disciples, and asserts that the heretics who endeavour to overthrow this faith and devise other additional names are of their father the devil.
sources.answer: The Law, the Prophets and the Sapiential Books give teaching about the transcendent divine nature only 'through a glass darkly'. That teaching is to be received as evidence of the truth now fully revealed. Their meaning is to be accepted reverently, in agreement with the faith set forth by the Lord of all the Scriptures.
sources.quote: “through a glass darkly” from the older Scriptures,—from the Law, and the Prophets, and the Sapiential Books, as an evidence of the truth fully revealed to us
sources.raw_question: How do the Old Testament Scriptures relate to the doctrine of God revealed by Christ?

question: Do the Old Testament Scriptures speak of Christ, and if so, in what way?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVI.—The treasure hid in the Scriptures is Christ; the true exposition of the Scriptures is to be found in the Church alone.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is the treasure hidden in the Scriptures, pointed out beforehand by types and parables. Anyone who reads the Scriptures attentively will find in them an account of Christ and a foreshadowing of the new calling. The risen Lord himself proved to the disciples from the Scriptures that Christ must suffer and enter into his glory.
sources.quote: the treasure hid in the Scriptures is Christ, since He was pointed out by means of types and parables.
sources.raw_question: Do the Old Testament Scriptures speak of Christ, and if so, in what way?

question: Does the Son's obedience to the Father's commandment imply that he lacks the Father's nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. His obedience is a free act of love, given so that the world may know he loves the Father, and it is directed to completing the mystery of his bodily passion. As the preceding context states, the obedience of humility does not dissolve the unity of his nature.
sources.quote: Then, giving obedience to the Father’s command as His only motive, He adds, But that the world may know that I love the Father, even as the Father gave Me commandment, so I do.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's obedience to the Father's commandment imply that he lacks the Father's nature?

question: Does the Son's being subjected to the Father imply a new or creaturely obedience in the Son's divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Though Christ humbled himself and was obedient, his nature knew no humiliation and his obedience was voluntary. His allegiance to the Father is eternal, while the subjection is an event in time belonging to the Dispensation of the Mystery, to be understood in view of the hope of our faith.
sources.quote: What that is must be understood in view of this same hope of our faith.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being subjected to the Father imply a new or creaturely obedience in the Son's divine nature?

question: What is the difference in meaning between 'generation' and 'creation' when applied to God's relation to the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: Generation is said of what comes from the essence itself; creation is said of things external to the nature of the maker. That is why Scripture handed down the names 'Father' and 'Son' rather than 'Creator' and 'work': to keep the Son from being treated as alien and to shut out doctrines that sever the Only-begotten from essential affinity with the Father.
sources.quote: applies the name of “generation” in the case of things generated from the essence itself, and understands that of “creation” of those things which are external to the nature of their maker
sources.raw_question: What is the difference in meaning between 'generation' and 'creation' when applied to God's relation to the Son?

question: Can an alterable Son be the true Image of the unalterable Father, such that whoever sees the Son sees the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. How the Word has free will, yet without being alterable. He is unalterable because the Image of the Father, proved from texts.
sources.answer: No. If the Son were ever changing, He could not bear the likeness of the Father's unalterableness, and we could not at all times see the Father in Him. Because he who has seen the Son has seen the Father, the Image of the unalterable God must be unchangeable.
sources.quote: how can such a one be the Father’s Image, not having the likeness of His unalterableness?
sources.raw_question: Can an alterable Son be the true Image of the unalterable Father, such that whoever sees the Son sees the Father?

question: Can the Son be the Image of the Father if He is not truly Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. To be the Image and Expression of the Father's proper substance belongs to the Son as Offspring. If He is not Son, neither is He Image, and He becomes merely an image of God's framing will like any creature.
sources.quote: so that there be neither Word, nor Wisdom, no, nor Image, of His proper substance. For if He be not Son, neither is He Image.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be the Image of the Father if He is not truly Son?

question: Does the Son's not becoming a Father show that He is unlike the Father, or that He is His true Image?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: It shows that He is the true Image. He is shown to be the Father's Expression and Image precisely by remaining what He is without change, having received from the Father to be one and the same. Since the Father is unalterable, the Image must also remain unaltered. So the Son will not become other than is proper to the Father's essence.
sources.quote: But if the Father is unalterable, and what He is that He continues, necessarily does the Image also continue what He is, and will not alter.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's not becoming a Father show that He is unlike the Father, or that He is His true Image?

question: Why does Scripture speak of the Son 'receiving' or being 'given' things from the Father if He possesses them eternally?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: To guard against Sabellianism. Because the Son has all that the Father has by exact likeness and identity, a person might conclude He is the Father. 'Was given' and 'I received' show that He is not the Father but the Father's Word and eternal Son, who has eternally what He has from the Father.
sources.quote: lest a man, perceiving that the Son has all that the Father hath, from the exact likeness and identity of that He hath, should wander into the irreligion of Sabellius, considering Him to be the Father
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture use language of the Son 'receiving' or being 'given' things from the Father if He possesses them eternally?

question: Should reasoning about the Trinity be pressed into detailed hypotheses about the manner of God's substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: No. The divine substance infinitely surpasses human comprehension, so both sides should stop at generals and confess ignorance of the manner. Pretending to explain further shows not less ignorance but greater vanity. Waterland discusses the subject only to expose the presumption of making the Trinity stand or fall by such reasoning.
sources.quote: Let us therefore be content to stop where it becomes us; ‘and frankly confess our ignorance of these things: for by pre‘tending further, we shall not discover less ignorance than before, ‘but much greater vanity.
sources.raw_question: Should reasoning about the Trinity be pressed into detailed hypotheses about the manner of God's substance?

question: Is it valid to reason about the Trinity and the divine substance using corporeal and sensible images?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. Arguing against the Trinity from the analogy of bodies is like a blind man forming notions of colour from hearing or touch and building demonstrations against sight, which would vanish once his eyes were opened. Our conceptions of the divine economy of the Three Persons are imperfect, so no certain argument can be drawn from them against the doctrine.
sources.quote: conceiving of the 7’rinity, after the manner of bodies, and reasoning from corporeal and sensible images.
sources.raw_question: Is it valid to reason about the Trinity and the divine substance using corporeal and sensible images?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's unity of will and operation with the Father prove that they share one substance?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Spirit is of one will and operation with the Father, he is also of one substance. This follows because the Creator is known by his works.
sources.quote: But if the Holy Spirit is of one will and operation with God the Father, He is also of one substance, since the Creator is known by His works.
sources.raw_question: Does unity of will and operation between the Holy Spirit and the Father prove that they share one substance?

question: Does Scripture teach that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each incomprehensible and omniscient?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. No one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father, so each is incomprehensible to creatures. The Son is addressed as knowing all things. The Spirit needs no counsellor and searches all things, even the depths of God. We therefore worship one all-seeing God.
sources.quote: No one knoweth the Son save the Father. – Matt. 11:27. Lord, thou knowest all things. – John 21:17.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each incomprehensible and omniscient?

question: Is it contradictory to say both that Christ subjects all things to himself and that God the Father subjects all things to Christ?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Just as no one comes to the Son unless the Father draws him, and no one comes to the Father except through the Son, so the work of subjection is both the Son's and the Father's. Through the birth the Father's nature abides in the Son, so what the Son does God does, and what God does in Him the Son himself does.
sources.quote: Through the birth the nature of God is abiding in the Son, and does that which He Himself does. What He does God does, but what God does in Him, He Himself does
sources.raw_question: Is it contradictory to say both that Christ subjects all things to himself and that God the Father subjects all things to Christ?

question: Is there a contradiction between Christ saying He does nothing of Himself and saying the Father does not leave Him alone because He always does what pleases the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Only on the heretical reading. If the Son's acting not of Himself meant He was merely moved by the indwelling Father, He could earn no merit by pleasing the Father, since doing what one does not do of oneself is no merit. The heretic is caught in a dilemma: if the Son is not a real agent, how does He please by His acts, and if He is, how are acts not done of Himself His own? The contradiction disappears only when both sayings are read as expressing the unity of the Father's and Son's nature.
sources.quote: The Son is either an Agent, or He is not. If He is not an Agent, how does He please by his acts? If He is an Agent, in what sense are deeds, done not of Himself, His own?
sources.raw_question: Is there a contradiction between Christ saying He does nothing of Himself and saying the Father does not leave Him alone because He always does what pleases the Father?

question: How do the Father's drawing believers to the Son and the Son's leading believers to the Father fit together?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: They are two aspects of one work. The Father is known only in the Son, who shows the Father in himself, so we cannot approach the Father in worship unless we first adore the Son; yet when we know the Son the Father draws and receives us. Each result is the work of the Son, for by his preaching of the Father the Father brings us to the Son and the Son leads us to the Father.
sources.quote: for by the preaching of the Father, Whom the Son preaches, the Father brings us to the Son, and the Son leads us to the Father.
sources.raw_question: How do the Father's drawing believers to the Son and the Son's leading believers to the Father fit together?

question: How are believers united to the Father and the Son, if not by nature as the Son is in the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: They are united through the Spirit, who is given from the Word. Since the Word is in the Father and the Spirit is the Word's own Spirit, those who receive the Spirit become one in the Word, and through Him in the Father. It is the Spirit who is in God, not we viewed in ourselves.
sources.quote: It is the Spirit then which is in God, and not we viewed in our own selves
sources.raw_question: How are believers united to the Father and the Son, if not by nature as the Son is in the Father?

question: Does Eunomius's principle that the active and the passive share one nature end up proving the Son coessential with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds again to discuss the impassibility of the Lord's generation; and the folly of Eunomius, who says that the generated essence involves the appellation of Son, and again, forgetting this, denies the relation of the Son to the Father: and herein he speaks of Circe and of the mandrake poison.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory turns Eunomius's own principle against him. If action and passion imply community of essence, and even craftsmanship involves action and passion, then whatever Eunomius calls the Son, whether 'created' or 'begotten', he thereby asserts the Son's affinity of essence with the Father. So the argument meant to make the Son alien from the Father's essence actually secures the glory of the coessential Son.
sources.quote: Thus by the very arguments whereby he seeks to prove the Lord alien from the essence of the Father, he asserts for Him intimate connexion.
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's principle that the active and the passive share one nature end up proving the Son coessential with the Father?

question: Does Eunomius's claim that the active and the passive share one nature lead to the absurdity that all creation is of one essence with its Maker?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds again to discuss the impassibility of the Lord's generation; and the folly of Eunomius, who says that the generated essence involves the appellation of Son, and again, forgetting this, denies the relation of the Son to the Father: and herein he speaks of Circe and of the mandrake poison.
sources.answer: Yes. The material shaped by a craftsman is passively affected while the craftsman acts, so making also involves action and passion. Applied consistently, Eunomius's principle would make the whole creation of one essence with God, which shows the principle is self-defeating as he uses it.
sources.quote: but also to make the whole creation of one essence with its Maker, if, as he says, the active and the passive are to be defined as mutually akin in respect of nature.
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's claim that the active and the passive share one nature lead to the absurdity that all creation is of one essence with its Maker?

question: Is there a love peculiar to the person of the Father in which he holds communion with believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen concludes that love is peculiarly held out to the saints in the person of the Father, and in this love he holds communion with them. God compares himself to every tender and loving thing, such as a father, mother, shepherd, and hen, to assure us of it.
sources.quote: There is love in the person of the Father peculiarly held out unto the saints, as wherein he will and doth hold communion with them.
sources.raw_question: Is there a love peculiar to the person of the Father in which he holds communion with believers?

question: Is the Father's love the proper ground for delighting in God and holding communion with the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. We delight in God exactly as much as we see of his love; every other discovery of God without this makes the soul fly from him. When the heart is taken up with the eminency of the Father's eternal, free and fruitful love, it is overpowered and endeared to him.
sources.quote: So much as we see of the love of God, so much shall we delight in him, and no more. Every other discovery of God, without this, will but make the soul fly from Him
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's love the proper ground for delighting in God and holding communion with the Father?

question: What does the believer's sanctification require from Christ through the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: It requires three things. The first is the Spirit of holiness dwelling in the believer. The second is a habit of holiness infused into him. The third is actual assistance for every work. Without these, believers can never, with all their might, perform any act of holiness before the Lord. Christ is entrusted with the fulness of all three, and believers draw them from him by faith.
sources.quote: [1.] Of the Spirit of holiness to dwell in them. [2.] Of a habit of holiness to be infused into them. [3.] Of actual assistance to work all their works for them
sources.raw_question: What does the believer's sanctification require from Christ through the Holy Spirit?

question: What does the Holy Spirit do in the salvation and sanctification of believers?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Next Teaches Us that the Authority of the Faith Enjoins, After the Father and the Son, to Believe Also on the Holy Spirit, Whose Operations He Enumerates from Scripture.
sources.answer: The Spirit works through baptismal water to bring about the second birth, a seed of divine generation and a pledge of the promised inheritance. He makes us God's temple and intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered. He dwells in our bodies, makes them holy, and will raise them to immortality at the resurrection, joining them to his divine eternity.
sources.quote: He it is who effects with water the second birth as a certain seed of divine generation, and a consecration of a heavenly nativity, the pledge of a promised inheritance
sources.raw_question: What does the Holy Spirit do in the salvation and sanctification of believers?

question: What does Paul mean in 2 Corinthians 3:17 by "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty"?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It means freedom from all the dread and terror that the administration of the law brought with it. By nature we have a spirit of bondage, full of tormenting fears. Christ takes this away and gives the Spirit of adoption, by which believers cry 'Abba, Father' and behave with confidence as children.
sources.quote: for “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty,” 2 Cor. iii. 17; that is, a freedom from all that dread and terror which the administration of the law brought with it.
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean in 2 Corinthians 3:17 by 'where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty'?

question: When Christ prays in John 17:5 to be glorified with the glory he had with the Father before the world was, does this imply the Son had lost or lacked divine glory?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. The Son had the fulness of the Godhead and still has it, for he is God's Son. By becoming flesh he did not lose his former being but took on what he was not. His prayer is that the human nature he assumed be raised to the glory he never renounced, so that flesh born in time might share the everlasting glory.
sources.quote: He had not lost His former being, but He had become what He was not before; He had not abdicated His own position, yet He had taken ours; He prays that the nature which He had assumed may be promoted to the glory which He had never renounced.
sources.raw_question: When Christ prays in John 17:5 to be glorified with the glory he had with the Father before the world was, does this imply the Son had lost or lacked divine glory?
