question: Is the Arian formula 'He was not before His generation,' condemned at Nicaea, a denial of the claim that the Son existed before His generation, or an argument against the Son's eternity?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: It is an argument against the Son's eternity. The formula is an enthymematic sentence, a reductio ad absurdum, that expresses the basic Arian argument from the word 'Son' to a beginning. It is not aimed at any Catholic claim that the Son existed before His generation, a view nobody in the controversy held. It corresponds to Arius's 'he who is begotten has a beginning of existence.' It is the same argument as 'He who is made him who was not,' stated in the passive voice.
sources.quote: the formula in question, when taken as an enthymematic sentence, or reductio ad absurdum, exactly expresses the main argument of the Arians, which they brought forward in so many shapes, as feeling that their cause turned upon it
sources.raw_question: Is the Arian formula 'He was not before His generation,' condemned at Nicaea, a denial of the claim that the Son existed before His generation, or an argument against the Son's eternity?

question: Do the Scripture texts teaching the Son's subordination to the Father prove that the Son is not eternal or not consubstantial with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 20: Whether the Doctor need have cited 300 teats, *wide of the purpose, to prove what nobody denies, namely, a subordination, in some sense, of the Son to the Fathe
sources.answer: No. They prove only that the Son is subordinate to the Father, which nobody denies. They do not show whether he is subordinate as a Son or as a creature. No single plain text against the Son's eternity or consubstantiality has been produced. The texts are good texts with an excellent meaning, but they are beside the point in question.
sources.quote: All that the learned Doctor proves by his 300 texts, or more, is only that the Son is subordinate to the Father: whether as a Son, or as a creature, appears not.
sources.raw_question: Do the roughly 300 Scripture texts Dr. Clarke cites on the Son's subordination prove that the Son is not eternal or not consubstantial with the Father?

question: Is it consistent to affirm that the Son is eternal while denying that he exists necessarily?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Eternity, taken in its proper sense, implies necessary existence. Clarke's scheme is therefore inconsistent in acknowledging the Son's eternity while denying his necessary existence. The opponent can escape this only by making 'eternal' mean something temporary.
sources.quote: objected the inconsistency of acknowledging the eternity of the Son, and yet denying his necessary existence : which, eéernity, I thought, inferred and implied.
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to affirm that the Son is eternal while denying that he exists necessarily, as Dr. Clarke does?

question: Does John 1:3, 'without him was nothing made,' mean the Son was only a companion at creation while another did the making, so that not all things were made through the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The Fisherman's own words 'All things were made through Him' stand firm. The Apostle confirms that all things visible and invisible, thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, are through him and in him. What was made 'not without him' was made in him and through him, for he is the Life who made creation possible.
sources.quote: Things visible and things invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers, all are through Him and in Him
sources.raw_question: Does 'without Him was nothing made' imply that the Son was only a companion at creation while another made things, so that not all things were made through the Son?

question: Does John 1:3, 'without him was not any thing made that was made,' show that the Son himself was not made?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 12: Whether the Creator of all things was not himself uncreated ; and therefore could not be ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, made out of nothing ?
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son himself were made, then not all things would have been made by him, but only the rest; yet John emphatically says nothing that was made was made without him. As Augustine says, if he was made, not all things were made by him. There is no creature of the Father's that is not also the Son's creature.
sources.quote: How can this be, if he himself was made? “ Si ipse “ factus est, non per illum sunt omnia facta, sed cetera ;” saith St. Austin.
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:3, 'without him was not any thing made that was made,' exclude the Son himself from being made?

question: Does the Spirit search out the deep things of God, even though believers know only in part?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit of the Saviour searches all things, even the deep things of God. But to us there are only diversities of gifts, and while on earth we know and prophesy in part, so difficult questions are to be left to Him who gives grace in measure.
sources.quote: For although the Spirit of the Saviour that is in Him “searcheth all things, even the deep things of God,” yet as to us “there are diversities of gifts, differences of administrations, and diversities of operations;”
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit search out the deep things of God, even though believers know only in part?

question: Is the Christ who was known by men a different being from the one who said "No man knoweth the Father, but the Son"?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VI.—Explanation of the words of Christ, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” etc.; which words the heretics misinterpret. Proof that, by the Father revealing the Son, and by the Son being revealed, the Father was never unknown.
sources.answer: No. He is one and the same. The Father made all things subject to Him, and He received testimony from all that He was very man and very God: from the Father, the Spirit, angels, creation, men, demons, the enemy, and death itself.
sources.quote: He, therefore, who was known, was not a different being from Him who declared “No man knoweth the Father,” but one and the same, the Father making all things subject to Him
sources.raw_question: Is the Christ who was known by men a different being from the one who said "No man knoweth the Father"?

question: Does the saying "No man knoweth the Father, but the Son" imply that the Father whom Christ revealed was an unknown God different from the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VII.—Recapitulation of the foregoing argument, showing that Abraham, through the revelation of the Word, knew the Father, and the coming of the Son of God. For this cause, he rejoiced to see the day of Christ, when the promises made to him should be fulfilled. The fruit of this rejoicing has flowed to posterity, viz., to those who are partakers in the faith of Abraham, but not to the Jews who reject the Word of God.
sources.answer: No. The God who called Abraham and gave him the promise is one and the same as the Creator. He was revealed through the Word from the beginning, to Abraham and Moses alike. Those who use this text to introduce another unknown Father are therefore vain.
sources.quote: Vain, therefore, are those who, because of that declaration, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” do introduce another unknown Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the saying "No man knoweth the Father, but the Son" imply that the Father Christ revealed was an unknown God different from the Creator?

question: Does Scripture identify the 'God said' of creation with the Word and Wisdom of God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Yes. 'God said' is explained in 'the Word,' as shown by texts saying God made all things in Wisdom, that the heavens were made fast by the Word of the Lord, and that there is one Lord Jesus Christ by whom are all things.
sources.quote: And ‘God said’ is explained in ‘the Word,’ for, he says, ‘Thou hast made all things in Wisdom;’ and ‘By the Word of the Lord were the heavens made fast;’
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture identify the 'God said' of creation with the Word and Wisdom of God?

question: Does Scripture distinguish the Word and Wisdom of God from the works of God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Yes. Texts like 'the Word of the Lord is true, and all His works are faithful' and 'in Wisdom hast Thou made them all' set the Word apart from the works. If the Word were a work, he too would have been made in Wisdom and Scripture would not distinguish him; instead it shows Wisdom to be Framer of the works.
sources.quote: But if the Word were a work, then certainly He as others had been made in Wisdom; nor would Scripture distinguish Him from the works
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture distinguish the Word and Wisdom of God from the works of God?

question: Can Christ be called both created and born, and if so in what sense is each true?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes, but in different respects. Apostolic faith knows in what dispensation of time Christ was created (the Incarnation) and in what eternity He was born. As God He was born God of God by a true and perfect generation, not created.
sources.quote: For it knows in what dispensation of time Christ was created, and in what eternity of times He was born. Moreover, He was born God of God, and the divinity of His true birth and perfect generation is not doubtful.
sources.raw_question: Can Christ be called both created and born, and if so in what sense is each true?

question: Is Christ a created being who holds the divine Name by gift rather than being truly born God by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary proves Christ's true Divinity from the Prophets, so that He is acknowledged as very God by inherent Godhead. That acknowledgement in turn holds believers fast to the certainty that God is One.
sources.quote: since they say that the Lord Jesus Christ, created rather than born, bears the Divine Name by gift and not by right, I have proved His true Divinity from the Prophets
sources.raw_question: Is Christ created rather than born, holding the divine Name by gift and not by right?

question: Is the believer's receiving of the Holy Spirit purely passive, or does the believer actively take part in it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: It depends on the work in view. Receiving the Spirit as the Spirit of sanctification is purely passive, as a vessel receives water: he quickens dead hearts by his almighty power. Receiving him as the Spirit of consolation requires an active power, namely faith. The world cannot receive him because it does not know him, while believers can because they do know him.
sources.quote: So that there is an active power to be put forth in his reception for consolation, though not in his reception for regeneration and sanctification. And this is the power of faith.
sources.raw_question: Is receiving the Holy Spirit purely passive, or does the believer actively take part in it?

question: In what sense is God alone said to be good, given that Christ elsewhere calls a man good?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: God alone is good in that no one sees him for sorrow and wailing, but only for salvation and true joy. Men may be called good in a lesser sense, as Christ himself does. But the vision of the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is granted only to the just, as everlasting joy that cannot be taken from them.
sources.quote: that one God, therefore, Himself, I say, is alone good, for this reason, that no one sees Him for sorrow and wailing, but only for salvation and true joy.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is God alone said to be good, given that Christ elsewhere calls a man good?

question: Does Scripture's statement that God alone is good exclude Christ from being called good?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > In Fine, Notwithstanding the Said Heretics Have Gathered the Origin of Their Error from Consideration of What is Written: Although We Call Christ God, and the Father God, Still Scripture Does Not Set Forth Two Gods, Any More Than Two Lords or Two Teachers.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says one is called good, even God, but the same Scriptures assert that Christ is good. The objectors accept both statements without concluding there are two goods. The same applies to God and Christ both being called God.
sources.quote: In the Scriptures there is one “called good, even God;” but in the same Scriptures Christ is also asserted to be good. There is not, then, if they rightly conclude, one good, but even two good.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture calling God alone good exclude Christ from being called good?

question: Does the usage of Scripture and the saints justify calling the Only-begotten Son a 'thing made' or 'creature' of the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > This third book shows a third fall of Eunomius, as refuting himself, and sometimes saying that the Son is to be called Only-begotten in virtue of natural generation, and that Holy Scripture proves this from the first; at other times, that by reason of His being created He should not be called a Son, but a “product,” or “creature.”
sources.answer: No. Gregory challenges Eunomius to name any patriarch, lawgiver, prophet, evangelist or apostle who called the Maker of all things a product and a creature; none can be found. On the contrary, almost the whole of Scripture, from Moses through the prophets and apostles, proclaims that all things were made by Him, so referring the term 'creature' for the Son to 'the use of the saints' is a misrepresentation of Scripture.
sources.quote: let him first of all show us in his statement what saints he says there are who declared the Maker of all things to be a product and a creature, and whom he follows in this audacity of phrase.
sources.raw_question: Does the usage of Scripture and the saints justify calling the Only-begotten Son a 'thing made' or 'creature' of the Father who made or created Him?

question: Can the Arian scheme say that the Son is Creator without implying two Creators, one of whom is a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 31: Whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration, on the side of Arianism, ought to move a wise and good man, against so great appearances of truth o
sources.answer: No. Waterland presents it as a dilemma the Arian cannot avoid. Either the Son is not Creator, which contradicts Scripture's ascription of creation to him. Or there are two Creators, one of them a creature, which is absurd. Only the orthodox doctrine of one Creator in Father and Son escapes the dilemma.
sources.quote: You are to prove, either that the Son is not Creator; or that there are two Creators, and one of them a creature.
sources.raw_question: Can the Arian scheme say that the Son is Creator without implying two Creators, one of whom is a creature?

question: Can the Arian scheme allow the Son to be worshipped without implying two objects of worship, one of whom is a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 31: Whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration, on the side of Arianism, ought to move a wise and good man, against so great appearances of truth o
sources.answer: No. On Arian principles one must either deny that the Son is to be worshipped at all, or admit two objects of worship, one of them a creature. Both conclusions are unacceptable, so the Arian hypothesis cannot account for the worship given to Christ.
sources.quote: You are to shew, either that the Son is not to be worshipped at all; or that there are two objects of worship, and one of them a creature.
sources.raw_question: Can the Arian scheme allow the Son to be worshipped without implying two objects of worship, one of whom is a creature?

question: Can the Arian scheme call the Son God without implying two Gods, one of whom is a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 31: Whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration, on the side of Arianism, ought to move a wise and good man, against so great appearances of truth o
sources.answer: No. The Arian must either deny that the Son is God, against Scripture, or hold that there are two Gods, one of them a creature. That second option is both polytheistic and self-contradictory. Only the orthodox doctrine, in which the Son is God with the Father in one Godhead, avoids this.
sources.quote: You are to prove, either that the Son is not God; or that there are two Gods, and one of them a creature.
sources.raw_question: Can the Arian scheme call the Son God without implying two Gods, one of whom is a creature?

question: Can there be degrees of simplicity in the divine nature of the Trinity, so that one Person is more simple than another?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His acknowledgment that the Divine Being is 'single' is only verbal.
sources.answer: No. Simplicity in the Holy Trinity admits no degrees, since there is no mixture of qualities but a potency without parts or composition. To posit less and more in God one must imagine qualities incident upon a subject, which introduces composition. Imperfect simplicity cannot escape being composite, just as imperfect goodness shares in its opposite.
sources.quote: For who does not know that, to be exact, simplicity in the case of the Holy Trinity admits of no degrees.
sources.raw_question: Can there be degrees of simplicity in the divine nature of the Trinity, so that one Person is more simple than another?

question: Can one rightly posit an essential unlikeness between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He discusses the incomprehensibility of the Divine essence, and the saying to the woman of Samaria, “Ye worship ye know not what.“
sources.answer: No. The divine nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is without figure, limit, size, or quantity. To claim to recognize a difference of unlikeness in it is to presume to grasp what is incomprehensible. Such a person 'thinketh more highly than he ought to think.'
sources.quote: recognizes a difference of unlikeness in that which is without figure, or limit, or size, or quantity (I mean in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit)
sources.raw_question: Can one rightly posit an essential unlikeness between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

question: Is there any unlikeness in divine operation between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter III. As to know the Father and the Son is life, so is it life to know the Holy Spirit; and therefore in the Godhead He is not to be separated from the Father.
sources.answer: No. The three share one work, including the work of giving eternal life. The world neither sees the Spirit, as it does not see the Father, nor knows him, as it does not know the Son. Their identical working shows they are not to be separated in the Godhead.
sources.quote: Let them say, then, wherein they think that there is an unlikeness in the divine operation.
sources.raw_question: Is there any unlikeness in divine operation between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

question: Why does John 1:1 say 'In the beginning was the Word' rather than 'became' or 'was made'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: John knew the difference between the phrases and chose 'was' so that we would understand the Word as Offspring, not measure Him by intervals, and believe the Son always and eternally exists.
sources.quote: said not, ‘In the beginning has become’ or ‘been made,’ but ‘In the beginning was the Word;’ that we might understand ‘Offspring’ by ‘was,’ and not account of Him by intervals, but believe the Son always and eternally to exist.
sources.raw_question: Why does John 1:1 say 'In the beginning was the Word' rather than 'became' or 'was made'?

question: How should scriptural statements that the Word 'became,' was 'made,' or was 'created' be read alongside John 1:1's statement that the Word was God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: They should be read as referring to the Incarnation. Because the Word was eternally with God and was God, statements of becoming describe what happened when he became man at the Father's good pleasure. This distinction between the eternal Word and his becoming flesh is enough by itself to refute the Arian reading.
sources.quote: it was when at the good pleasure of the Father the Word became man, that it was said of Him, as by John, ‘The Word became flesh;’ so by Peter, ‘He hath made Him Lord and Christ’
sources.raw_question: How should scriptural statements that the Word 'became,' was 'made,' or was 'created' be read alongside John 1:1's statement that the Word was God?

question: If 'Godhead' signifies the divine nature rather than an operation, does that nature become plural when it is contemplated in three Persons?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. No nature is diminished or increased by being contemplated in a larger or smaller number. Only things contemplated in individual circumscription, marked by body, size, place, figure, and colour, are counted by addition. What is free of such circumscription is not counted and cannot be thought of as a multitude.
sources.quote: according to true reasoning neither diminution nor increase attaches to any nature, when it is contemplated in a larger or smaller number
sources.raw_question: If 'Godhead' signifies the divine nature rather than an operation, does that nature become plural when it is contemplated in three Persons?

question: Does confessing the Father and Son as homoousion (of one substance) mean that the Father and the Son are the same Person, the Father having taken flesh and called Himself Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The Church rejects that meaning of homoousion. She confesses one God from Whom are all things and one Lord Jesus Christ through Whom are all things. She thus distinguishes the One who is Source from the One who is Agent, and the Father who is unborn from the Only-begotten Son.
sources.quote: She confesses one God from Whom are all things; she confesses one Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom are all things; One from Whom, One through Whom; One the Source of all, One the Agent through Whom all were created.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the Father and Son as homoousion (of one substance) mean that the Father and the Son are the same Person, the Father having taken flesh and called Himself Son?

question: Does homoousion imply that the Father and Son share in a prior substance that existed before both of them and was divided between them?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The Church detests and rejects this meaning. She confesses the Father as eternal and without beginning, a Majesty that has no beginning. So nothing is anterior to Him, and He is not later than some common matter.
sources.quote: In the One from Whom are all things she recognises the Majesty which has no beginning
sources.raw_question: Does homoousion imply that the Father and Son share in a prior substance that existed before both of them and was divided between them?

question: In what sense does one who sees the Son see the Father, if the Son is not the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Proves Also that the Words Spoken to Philip Make Nothing for the Sabellians.
sources.answer: The Son is the image of God the Father. He works as the Father works and imitates all the invisible Father's works. So whoever sees the Son may regard it as if he saw the Father. Seeing the divinity in this likeness trains a believer to advance toward perfect contemplation of the Father Himself.
sources.quote: the Son is an imitator of all the Father’s works, so that every one may regard it just as if he saw the Father, when he sees Him who always imitates the invisible Father in all His works.
sources.raw_question: In what sense does one who sees the Son see the Father, if the Son is not the Father?

question: Why is the Son visible while the Father is not seen?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Proves Also that the Words Spoken to Philip Make Nothing for the Sabellians.
sources.answer: The Son is the image of God and so could rightly be seen. The Father is invisible, and his vision is only promised to the pure in heart as something to come.
sources.quote: rightly also He was then seen as the Son, because He was the image of God; and the Father, because He is invisible, is promised and pointed out as to be seen by the pure in heart
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son visible while the Father is not seen?

question: How does the Son, as Image of the invisible God, relate to the Father's will?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: He is immediately and inseparably one with the Father in every movement of His will. Like a reflection in a mirror that moves only and wholly with the original, the Son as Image is conformed in all respects to the Archetype of goodness. Indeed, he is himself the Father's will, since he has in himself all that is the Father's, and even the Father himself.
sources.quote: in like manner we maintain that our Lord, the Image of the invisible God, is immediately and inseparably one with the Father in every movement of His Will.
sources.raw_question: How does the Son as Image of the invisible God relate to the Father's will?

question: Why did God reveal himself to humans through the Son as the image of the invisible God rather than directly as the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: It was to strengthen human weakness step by step. Great things are dangerous when they come suddenly, as the sudden light of the sun blinds eyes not used to it. So humanity is trained by looking on the Son, the image, so that it may one day see the Father without being struck by his overwhelming brightness.
sources.quote: For gradually and by progression human frailty was to be strengthened by the image to that glory of being able one day to see God the Father. For the things that are great are dangerous if they are sudden.
sources.raw_question: Why did God reveal himself to humans through the Son as the image of the invisible God rather than directly as the Father?

question: Must the Son be a creature made out of nothing and in time in order to protect the Father's glory from being lowered to the Son's level?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. Hilary treats this claim as an error that breaks the unity of God by assigning differences of nature where all is common to each Person. It also denies the Father by robbing the Son of His true Sonship. The Son is the Image, Wisdom and Power of God, born of Him and partaking His nature, not a creature from nothing.
sources.quote: They break up the absolute unity of God by assigning differences of nature where all is clearly common to Each; they deny the Father by robbing the Son of His true Sonship
sources.raised_by_detail: certain teachers of our present day
sources.raw_question: Must the Son be a creature made out of nothing and in time in order to protect the Father's glory from being lowered to the Son's level?

question: If the Son is not of the same substance as the Father, must he be a creature made out of nothing?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 13: Whether there can be any middle between being made out of nothing, and out of something ; that is, between being out of nothing, and out of the Father's substan
sources.answer: Yes. The Son must either be of the same undivided substance with the Father or be a creature made out of nothing. Denying the first necessarily entails the second. The opponents' appeal to the word 'individual' is an equivocation that cannot escape this disjunction, which Waterland calls as clear as a geometrical axiom.
sources.quote: you must either own the Son to be of the same wndivided substance with the Father; or else declare him a creature. If you deny the former, you must, of consequence, admit the latter
sources.raw_question: If the Son is not of the same substance as the Father, must he be a creature made out of nothing?

question: What does Christ's saying 'I am in the Father, and the Father in Me' (John 14:10) teach about the Son's eternity and his relation to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: It teaches that the Son never was not and cannot be thought apart from the Father. 'I am in the Father' comes first because the Son is of the Father and not the Father of the Son. 'The Father in Me' shows that whoever tries to go beyond the Son to something prior also goes beyond the Father. One who is in something cannot be found outside it, so the Father cannot be grasped as external to the Son.
sources.quote: he who, in his curious speculation, passes beyond the Son, passes also beyond the conception of the Father: for He who is in anything cannot be found outside of that in which He is
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's saying 'I am in the Father, and the Father in Me' (John 14:10) teach about the Son's eternity and his relation to the Father?

question: What does Christ's saying 'I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you' (John 14:20) show about how the Son is in the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It shows a graded unity through a Mediator, not a mere unity of will. The Son is in the Father through the nature of Deity, we are in him through his bodily birth, and he is in us through the sacraments. Thus we attain unity with the Father because we dwell naturally in him who dwells naturally in the Father by birth.
sources.quote: since He was in the Father through the nature of Deity, and we on the contrary in Him through His birth in the body, He would have us believe that He is in us through the mystery of the sacraments?
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's saying 'I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you' (John 14:20) show about how the Son is in the Father?

question: Does Wisdom's presence with God when He prepared the heavens (Proverbs 8:27) show only that the Son existed before created things, or that He is eternal?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: It shows He is eternal. The preparation of the heaven is not a temporal act of God but belongs to God's eternal counsel, in which created things already exist in His knowledge and power. Since Wisdom was present at this preparation, it is co-eternal with what is eternal, not merely earlier than temporal things.
sources.quote: Wisdom, in teaching that it was born before the ages, teaches that it is not merely prior to things which have been created, but is even co-eternal with what is eternal, to wit, with the preparation of the heaven
sources.raw_question: Does Wisdom's (Christ's) presence with God when He prepared the heavens (Proverbs 8) show only that the Son is prior to created things, or that He is eternal?

question: Does Wisdom's saying 'When He prepared the heaven, I was present with Him' (Proverbs 8:27) imply that the Father created the heavens without Wisdom, with the Son merely standing by?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: No. All things were created in and through Wisdom, and without it not one thing was made. The verse means that Wisdom was with the Father in essence. At the same time, condescending to created things, Wisdom stamped its own impress on the works so that the world would hold together in concord like one body.
sources.quote: in My Essence indeed I was with the Father, but by a condescension to things originate, I was disposing over the works My own impress, so that the whole world as being in one body, might not be at variance but in concord with itself.
sources.raw_question: Does Wisdom's saying 'When He prepared the heaven, I was present with Him' (Proverbs 8:27) imply that the Father created the heavens without Wisdom, with the Son merely standing by?

question: Does the Father's delight in the Son described in Proverbs 8:30 refer only to the Son as the image of the Father's own perfections, or also to the Son's love for humanity and their redemption?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Not only that. The delight is not so much the Father's absolute delight in the Son as the express image of his person. It is chiefly delight in the Son with respect to his love for the sons of men and his thoughts of their redemption. Owen argues that the order of the words requires this reading: "I was daily his delight" is joined with "My delights were with the sons of men."
sources.quote: the delight of the Father in the Son, there mentioned, is not so much his absolute delight in him as the express image of his person and the brightness of his glory, wherein he might behold all his own excellencies and perfections; as with respect unto his love and his delight in the sons of men
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's delight in the Son described in Proverbs 8:30 refer only to the Son as the image of the Father's own perfections?

question: Does the Father's eternal delight in Wisdom in Proverbs 8:30 prove that the Son is eternal and proper to the Father's essence rather than made from nothing?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Yes. God did not get his cause of rejoicing from outside himself, so the One in whom he rejoices is his own, not foreign or out of nothing. There was never a time when the Father did not rejoice. If he always rejoiced, then the One in whom he rejoiced always existed.
sources.quote: When then was it, when the Father rejoiced not? but if He ever rejoiced, He was ever, in whom He rejoiced.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's eternal delight in Wisdom (Proverbs 8:30) prove that the Son is eternal and proper to the Father's essence rather than made for our sake or from nothing?

question: Does Paul's phrase 'dwelling in light unapproachable' (1 Timothy 6:16) call God himself the unapproachable light, and how does it relate to the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then referring to the blasphemy of Eunomius, which had been refuted by the great Basil, where he banished the Only-begotten God to the realm of darkness, and the apology or explanation which Eunomius puts forth for his blasphemy, he shows that his present blasphemy is rendered by his apology worse than his previous one; and herein he very ably discourses of the “true” and the “unapproachable” Light.
sources.answer: No. Paul does not say God is the unapproachable light. He says God dwells in it, and being in something differs greatly from being that thing. The light in which the Father dwells is the Son, as the Gospel says the Father is in the Son. Since the Son is the true Light and truth is unapproachable by falsehood, the Son is the Light unapproachable in which the Father dwells.
sources.quote: For the Son is true Light, and the truth is unapproachable by falsehood; so then the Son is Light unapproachable in which the Father dwells, or in Whom the Father is.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's phrase "dwelling in light unapproachable" (1 Timothy 6:16) call God Himself the unapproachable light, and how does it relate to the Son?

question: In what sense is Christ 'the first-born among many brethren'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He further very appositely expounds the meaning of the term “Only-Begotten,“ and of the term “First born,“ four times used by the Apostle.
sources.answer: He is first-born among many brethren by leading the way in the spiritual birth by water and the Spirit. By His own baptism He drew down the Holy Spirit upon the water. In this way He became the first-born of those spiritually born again, and He calls those who share a like birth His brethren.
sources.quote: Himself led the way in this birth, drawing down upon the water, by His own baptism, the Holy Spirit; so that in all things He became the first-born of those who are spiritually born again
sources.raw_question: In what sense is Christ "the first-born among many brethren"?

question: How do Christ's titles 'first-born of every creature' and 'first-born from the dead' relate to each other?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: The first title concerns the origin of creation; the second concerns the dispensation in which he took our body. As spiritual things created in the First-born owe it to him that they abide, so human beings owe it to him that in the First-born from the dead they are born again into eternity. In this way he has the pre-eminence in all things, being both the image of God and the head of his body, the Church.
sources.quote: so that as to Him things spiritual, being created in the First-born, owe it that they abide, even so all things human also owe it to Him that in the First-born from the dead they are born again into eternity.
sources.raw_question: How do Christ's titles 'first-born of every creature' and 'first-born from the dead' relate to each other?

question: Does affirming that Christ had a true human body imply that he was only a man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And Indeed that Christ Was Not Only Man, But God Also; That Even as He Was the Son of Man, So Also He Was the Son of God.
sources.answer: No. Novatian holds that Christ was manifested in the substance of a true body, but by the association of the divinity of the Word in that very materiality he was also God according to the Scriptures. Teaching his real flesh gives no ground to those heretics who say he was a bare and solitary man.
sources.quote: we do not so express doctrine concerning the substance of His body, as to say that He is only and alone man, but so as to maintain, by the association of the divinity of the Word in that very materiality, that He was also God
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who hold Christ was man only
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that Christ had a true human body imply that he was only a man?

question: Is it reasonable to interpret the Scripture texts about the Trinity figuratively, as allusions rather than proper statements, in the name of right reason?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: To the Reader
sources.answer: No. Treating the Scripture propositions as allegory, in which nothing is properly expressed, is itself irrational, because it leaves nothing certain in anything said in words or writing. Such reading only pretends to follow right reason. The reader should instead submit to the plain and obvious sense of Scripture's propositions and testimonies, without seeking evasions for unbelief.
sources.quote: which irrational way of proceeding, leaving nothing certain in what is or may be expressed by word or writing, is covered over with a pretence of right reason; which utterly refuses to be so employed
sources.raw_question: Is it reasonable to interpret the Scripture texts about the Trinity figuratively, as allusions rather than proper statements, in the name of right reason?

question: How should the words of Scripture be interpreted when they are used in disputes about the Trinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: By the circumstances under which they were spoken, not by stringing together isolated phrases stripped of context. Words must be explained by circumstances, not circumstances forced into conformity with words, and each point must be considered in light of God's own instruction.
sources.quote: The meaning of words shall be ascertained by considering the circumstances under which they were spoken; words must be explained by circumstances not circumstances forced into conformity with words.
sources.raw_question: How should the words of Scripture be interpreted when used in disputes about the Trinity?

question: When rival interpretations of Scripture about the Trinity seem evenly matched, how should the dispute be decided if Scripture alone is the rule?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: Appeal to those who lived nearest to the inspired writers. Scripture remains the rule, but where text is matched against text and reason against reason, the concurrence of primitive saints and martyrs shows which interpretation is most probable and safest. That weight increases when the opposing view was condemned by the generality as heresy. Their judgment and practice are the safest guide until a better one is shown.
sources.quote: What can we do better, in such a case, than to appeal to those who lived nearest the times of the inspired writers! Their judgment, their decisions, and consequent practice, are at length the safest rule to go by; at least till you can shew us a better.
sources.raw_question: When rival interpretations of Scripture about the Trinity seem evenly matched, how should the dispute be decided if Scripture alone is the rule?

question: May more than one interpretation of a disputed Scripture text about the Son be used in defending the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Several explanations may be used, provided none contradicts sound doctrine or makes the Son unequal to the Father. The more such interpretations are available, the more powerfully the heretics are refuted, because more ways open for escaping their snares.
sources.quote: let us securely use it, and not one explanation only, but as many as we are able to find. For so much the more powerfully are the heretics proved wrong, the more outlets are open for avoiding their snares.
sources.raw_question: May more than one interpretation of a disputed Scripture text about the Son be used in defending the Trinity?

question: How should the human mind approach God's infinite and incomprehensible nature when considering the Trinity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: To the Reader
sources.answer: With reverence and humble adoration, according to God's own revelation of himself, not with captious and sophistical scrutiny. Owen himself adores and believes these things as they are revealed. Even when they must be defended in controversy, one should keep to the way Scripture reveals them and avoid unnecessary contentious or exotic phrases.
sources.quote: Let him bring with him a due reverence of the majesty, and infinite, incomprehensible nature of God, as that which is not to be prostituted to the captious and sophistical scanning of men of corrupt minds, but to be humbly adored
sources.raw_question: How should the human mind approach God's infinite and incomprehensible nature when considering the Trinity?

question: Where can the human mind best exercise itself to understand the incorporeal and unchangeable divine Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What It is that Suffices Here to Solve the Question Why the Spirit is Not Said to Be Begotten, and Why the Father Alone is Unbegotten. What They Ought to Do Who Do Not Understand These Things.
sources.answer: In the mind itself, which is the highest part of human nature and subject to nothing but God. Provided it is governed by the rule of faith, the mind is the best place to look, because it has been given a certain sight of invisible things and presides in judgment over what the bodily senses report.
sources.quote: the sight of the human mind can nowhere better exercise itself, so only that the rule of faith govern it, than in that which man himself has in his own nature better than the other animals
sources.raw_question: Where can the human mind best exercise itself to understand the incorporeal and unchangeable divine Trinity?

question: Does the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity teach that the Father's essence is divided into three, or that the one God changes shape to assume the guise of three persons?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next marvellously overthrows the unintelligible statements of Eunomius which assert that the essence of the Father is not separated or divided, and does not become anything else.
sources.answer: No. Gregory says no one in the Church ever said or heard that the Father is separated or divided as to His essence, becomes sometimes one and sometimes another, or assumes the guise of three persons. Eunomius is attacking a doctrine Christians do not hold, and these things cannot be inferred from what they confess. The Church judges it as impious to think the Father is split up or moulded into three persons, like clay or wax, as to call the Lord of creation a created being.
sources.quote: we say that it is equally impious and ungodly to call the Lord of the creation a created being and to think that the Father, in that He is, is separated or split up, or departs from Himself, or assumes the guise of three persons, like clay or wax moulded in various shapes
sources.raw_question: Does the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity teach that the Father's essence is divided or separated into three, or that the one God changes shape to assume the guise of three persons?

question: In worshipping God "in the Spirit and in truth," do the Father and the Holy Spirit stand in the same relation to the worshipper?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. Those who worship God the Spirit in the Spirit have the Holy Spirit as the means and God as the object of their reverence. Each of the Two stands in a different relation to the worshipper, which shows the imparted Gift is distinct from the One adored.
sources.quote: shall have the One for the means, the Other for the object, of their reverence: for Each of the Two stands in a different relation to the worshipper.
sources.raw_question: In worshipping God "in the Spirit and in truth," do the Father and the Holy Spirit stand in the same relation to the worshipper?

question: Can a sin be committed peculiarly against the Holy Spirit as a distinct Person?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. When the Spirit ought to be honoured in a particular way and is not, he is sinned against in a particular way. Acts 5:3 says Ananias lied to the Holy Ghost, not to God taken essentially, which would mean the whole Trinity. Ananias failed to honour the Spirit in the special gift he professed, and so sinned against him peculiarly.
sources.quote: Acts v. 3, Ananias is said to lie to the Holy Ghost, — not to God; which being taken essentially, would denote the whole Trinity, but peculiarly to the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: Can a sin be committed peculiarly against the Holy Spirit as a distinct Person?

question: Does the Holy Spirit act as a distinct person who appoints men to tasks and can be sinned against?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. In Acts 13:2 the Holy Ghost himself appoints and designates men to the work of preaching the gospel. He ordains believers to holiness. When men sin, they sin against him, which shows he is a personal agent with authority over believers.
sources.quote: The Holy Ghost appoints and ordains believers to works of obedience and holiness, and to work holiness in others.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit act as a distinct person who appoints men to tasks and can be sinned against?

question: Is the consolation believers receive the proper work of the Holy Spirit in particular?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that whenever Scripture mentions comfort given to the saints, it is the proper consequent of the Holy Ghost's work. The Spirit is the Paraclete and gives paraklesis (Acts 9:31). There is no comfort but from his effects, such as shedding abroad God's love and witnessing to adoption.
sources.quote: Whenever there is mention made of comfort and consolation in the Scripture given to the saints (as there is most frequently), it is the proper consequent of the work of the Holy Ghost towards them.
sources.raw_question: Is the consolation believers receive the proper work of the Holy Spirit in particular?

question: Does the Holy Spirit indwell believers chiefly as a Spirit of sanctification or as a Spirit of consolation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Chiefly, or perhaps solely, as a Spirit of sanctification. This is evident from the work he does as indwelling (quickening and sanctifying, Rom. 8:11), from the manner of his indwelling as in a temple which he makes holy (1 Cor. 6:19), and from the permanence of that indwelling, which relates to sanctification only. Yet the general notion of abiding is also ascribed to him as Comforter in John 14:16.
sources.quote: he is said to dwell in us chiefly, or perhaps solely, as he is a Spirit of sanctification: which is evident from the work he doth, as indwelling, — he quickeneth and sanctifieth
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit indwell believers chiefly as a Spirit of sanctification or as a Spirit of consolation?

question: Why is the Holy Spirit specifically named 'the Comforter'?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Because consolation is so large and comprehensive a consequence of his work that he takes his name from it for his whole work toward us. In the same way Christ is called Redeemer and Saviour from his work of redemption and salvation. So each divine Person is named by his distinctive work in the economy of grace.
sources.quote: the Holy Ghost receives his denomination, as to the whole work he hath to perform for us, from hence, — he is the Comforter; as Jesus Christ, from the work of redemption and salvation, is the Redeemer and Saviour of his church.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit specifically named 'the Comforter'?

question: Does Scripture ever speak of three persons in one God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: No. Scripture nowhere mentions three persons, nor does it call the three one person. It speaks of the person of the Lord, but never of the Lord as a person. The phrase 'three persons' is therefore a term the Church adopted, not a scriptural expression.
sources.quote: Is it because Scripture does not say three Gods? But neither do we find that Scripture anywhere mentions three persons.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ever speak of three persons in one God?

question: Why are there exactly three persons in God and not more?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Holy Spirit Also is Equal to the Father and the Son in All Things.
sources.answer: Because there is One who loves Him who is from Himself (the Father), One who loves Him from whom He is (the Son), and Love itself (the Spirit). This triad of lover, beloved, and love is complete, so they are not more than three.
sources.quote: And therefore they are not more than three: One who loves Him who is from Himself, and One who loves Him from whom He is, and Love itself.
sources.raw_question: Why are there exactly three persons in God and not more?

question: What makes the three Persons one God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: Their inseparability and the essential union of the Persons, with common essential attributes and perfections as the bonds of union. This is not the continuity of parts that makes Clarke's single Person one. Waterland claims Trinitarians can explain this union as well as Clarke explains his, and can prove it better.
sources.quote: We suppose three Persons to be one God, by their inseparability and the essential union of the Persons
sources.raw_question: What makes the three Persons one God?

question: Can a true saving knowledge of sin be had apart from Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. A saving knowledge of sin is found only in Christ. In him we see what our sins deserve and how polluting they are, since only his blood could bear or expiate them. His cross also reveals that we cannot satisfy God's justice or live up to his will.
sources.quote: A true saving knowledge of sin is to be had only in the Lord Christ: in him may we see the desert of our iniquities, and their pollution, which could not be borne or expiated but by his blood
sources.raw_question: Can a true saving knowledge of sin be had apart from Christ?

question: Does Moses' account of creation in Genesis testify to the Son as God through whom the Father created all things?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. In Genesis God commands "Let there be a firmament" and God makes it, which shows both the God from Whom and the God through Whom all things are. No obedience can be attributed to things not yet created. John identifies the one through whom all things were made as the Word who was God.
sources.quote: Here, then, you have the God from Whom, and the God through Whom.
sources.raw_question: Does Moses' account of creation testify to the Son as a God through whom the Father created?

question: Did Moses write about the Son of God, so that believing Moses requires believing in the Son as God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. Christ himself says that Moses wrote of him, so whoever believed Moses would believe in God the Son of God. Moses' whole Law, given through the Mediator, testifies to him.
sources.quote: if you believed Moses, you would believe also in God, the Son of God; unless perchance you deny that it was of Him that Moses spoke.
sources.raw_question: Did Moses write about the Son of God, so that believing Moses requires believing in the Son as God?

question: In the trinity of recollection, is the image retained in memory a true parent of the image formed in the mind's eye when one recalls something?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > There is Another Trinity in the Memory of Him Who Thinks Over Again What He Has Seen.
sources.answer: No, it is only a quasi-parent, and the formed vision only a quasi-offspring. The form in the mind's eye is indeed copied from the form in memory, but the mind's eye itself does not arise from the memory-image; it existed before we saw the body and before we committed it to memory. Since the one is not a true parent, the other is not a true offspring, though both suggest something whereby inner and truer things may appear more clearly.
sources.quote: Although therefore the form which is wrought in the mind’s eye of him who remembers, is wrought from that form which is in the memory; yet the mind’s eye itself does not exist from thence, but existed before it.
sources.raw_question: In the trinity of recollection (memory-image, mind's vision, will), is the image retained in memory a true parent of the image formed in the mind's eye when one recalls something?

question: Why does Augustine identify only two trinities in the outer man (sense perception and conception), omitting the middle stage of committing a sense-image to memory?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Species is Produced by Species in Succession.
sources.answer: Because we do not ordinarily call it 'vision' when the form in the sense is entrusted to the memory. There are two kinds of vision, one of sense perception, formed from the bodily object, and one of conception, formed from memory. The intermediate combination is nearer to the first but less like it than the third, so he declines to put it forward as a trinity.
sources.quote: But I have refrained from commending an intermediate one; because we do not commonly call it vision, when the form which comes to be in the sense of him who perceives, is entrusted to the memory.
sources.raw_question: Why does Augustine identify only two trinities in the outer man (sensuous perception and conception) rather than three, omitting the middle stage of committing a sense-image to memory?

question: In Augustine's trinity of the outer man, does the will that joins sense to object, memory to sense, and the mind's eye to memory also have the power to separate them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Different Modes of Conceiving.
sources.answer: Yes. The same will that unites these elements also disjoins them. It turns the bodily senses away from their objects through bodily movement, for example by averting or shutting the eyes, closing the mouth, or pushing a thing away. It turns the memory away from the sense by being intent on something else. And it turns the mind's eye away from memory simply by not thinking of what is stored there.
sources.quote: But that which harmonizes those things and unites them, itself also disjoins and separates them, that is, the will.
sources.raw_question: In Augustine's analogy of a trinity in the outer man, does the will, which joins the sense to the object, the memory to the sense, and the mind's eye to the memory, also have the power to separate them?

question: In Augustine's analogy of the trinity of bodily sight, can vision be called the end and rest of the will that unites the seen object and the sense?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Of What Kind We are to Reckon the Rest (Requies), and End (Finis), of the Will in Vision.
sources.answer: Only in a limited sense. Vision is the end and rest of the will only with respect to this one visible object, that is, of the will provisionally directed to seeing it. It is not the end of the man's whole will, whose end is nothing other than blessedness. Seeing something does not mean the will now wills nothing else.
sources.quote: Perhaps we can rightly call vision the end and rest of the will, only with respect to this one object [namely, the bodily thing that is visible]. For it will not will nothing else merely because it sees something which it is now willing.
sources.raw_question: In Augustine's analogy of the trinity of bodily sight, can vision be called the end and rest of the will that unites the seen object and the sense?

question: Was everything Christ did as mediator, including his obedience to the law, done on behalf of those for whom he was mediator?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen argues from Rom. 8:3-4 that God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh so that the righteousness the law required of us might be fulfilled in us. Joined with Gal. 4:4, where Christ is 'made under the law', this covers the whole of what Christ did or suffered. Scripture says all of it was for us.
sources.quote: God sent Christ as a mediator, to do and suffer whatever the law required at our hands for that end and purpose, that we might not be condemned, but accepted of God.
sources.raw_question: Was everything Christ did as mediator, including his obedience to the law, done on behalf of those for whom he was mediator?

question: Did Christ obey the general law as mediator, or only the special law of mediation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Whatever Christ did as a man under any law, he did as mediator. He became incarnate as mediator and everything he did and suffered was part of the duty he undertook in that office, though in a strict sense 'as mediator' refers only to the law of mediation.
sources.quote: whatever Christ did as a man subject to any law, he did it as mediator, because he did it as part of the duty incumbent on him who undertook so to be.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ obey the general law as mediator, or only the special law of mediation?

question: Was Christ, as God and man, obliged in his own right to obey the law of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: No. As mediator, God and man, the hypostatical union lifted him above that law, so his subjection to it was voluntary. Yet once he undertook to be mediator, obeying it was necessary, and he truly became subject to its commands. He also obeyed laws that exist only because of sin, such as the ceremonial law and John's baptism, which he did not need himself. That obedience must therefore have been for us.
sources.quote: as mediator, God and man, he was not by the institution of that law obliged unto it; being, as it were, exempted and lifted above that law by the hypostatical union
sources.raw_question: Was Christ, as God and man, obliged in his own right to obey the law of God?

question: Can God be conceived as ever existing without his wisdom and power, or as Father without a Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Reason cannot conceive a person without its express image, glory without radiance, God without wisdom, a Beginning without the Word, or a Father without a Son. These are declared to be in mutual union, so when one is removed the other disappears with it. Since Christ is the power and wisdom of God, God never existed without him.
sources.quote: for it is not possible to conceive by reason either a Person without express image, or glory without radiance, or God without wisdom, or a Maker without hands, or a Beginning without the Word, or a Father without a Son
sources.raw_question: Can God be conceived as existing without his wisdom and power, or as Father without a Son?

question: Could a god conceived as existing outside the Father's essence be true God and the Son of the only God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eighthly, John xvii. 3. and the Like. Our Lord's divinity cannot interfere with His Father's prerogatives, as the One God, which were so earnestly upheld by the Son. 'One' is used in contrast to false gods and idols, not to the Son, through whom the Father spoke. Our Lord adds His Name to the Father's, as included in Him. The Father the First, not as if the Son were not First too, but as Origin.
sources.answer: No. The texts declaring God alone were spoken even in anticipation of the Arians, so they might know that any god devised external to the Father's essence is not true God, nor the Image and Son of the Only and First.
sources.quote: whatsoever god they devise external to the Father’s Essence, he is not True God, nor Image and Son of the Only and First.
sources.raw_question: Could a god conceived as existing outside the Father's essence be true God and the Son of the only God?

question: On the alternative reading of Philippians 2:9, what exaltation is meant, and why does 'wherefore' apply?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: It signifies Christ's resurrection from the dead, not an exaltation of the Word as Word, who is most high and like his Father. 'Wherefore' gives the cause of the resurrection: though he died as man, being God and Life in the body he was exalted, so that unlike all men from Adam he could not be held by death. This parallels Peter's statement in Acts 2:24 that it was not possible he should be held by death.
sources.quote: wishing to shew, that, although as man He is said to have died, yet, as being Life, He was exalted on the resurrection
sources.raw_question: In the alternative reading of Philippians 2:9, what exaltation is meant, and why does 'wherefore' apply?

question: What is the 'name above every name' given to Christ in Philippians 2:9, and what does it show about him?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is in Christ, He Once More Asserts by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: It is the name of God. Only God is above all things, so the name that is above every name belongs to God, and it is given to the one who was in the form of God. Therefore Christ is God.
sources.quote: For He has “received a name which is above every name,” which assuredly we understand to be none other than the name of God. For since it belongs to God alone to be above all things
sources.raw_question: What is the 'name above every name' given to Christ in Philippians 2:9, and what does it show about him?

question: How can Scripture say that Christ, who is God, is anointed by 'His God' (Psalm 45:7)?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Christ is God in His own nature. The Father is called His God only in the dispensation of the anointing, that is, in respect of the servant's nature He assumed. The wording of the prophecy is chosen carefully to show both truths: God is anointed, and the one who anoints Him is His God.
sources.quote: God is anointed by His God; that is, in His own nature He is God, but in the dispensation of the anointing God is His God.
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture say that Christ, who is God, is anointed by 'His God' (Psalm 45:7)?

question: Does Psalm 45 speak of Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus counts Psalm 45 among the prophecies of Christ. It is addressed to him as 'O Most Mighty' and speaks of his anointing. In his reading, it sets forth the beauty and splendour of Christ's kingdom and the exaltation of all who are under his sway.
sources.quote: these indicated that beauty and splendour which exist in His kingdom, along with the transcendent and pre-eminent exaltation [belonging] to all who are under His sway
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 45, with 'God, Thy God, hath anointed Thee with the oil of gladness', speak of Christ?

question: Does Psalm 45's description of others as the 'fellows' or 'partakers' of the anointed one show that the Son is distinct from created things?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: Yes. The Psalmist calls the anointed one the eternal God and declares that all others partake of Him.
