If the Son were one of the things made from nothing, He would Himself be one of those who partake. Since all originate things partake of Him and are sanctified by Him in the Spirit, He is distinct from them and is the Father's true Word, Radiance and Wisdom.
sources.quote: were He one of things which come out of nothing and of things originate, He Himself had been one of those who partake.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 45's description of others as the 'fellows' or 'partakers' of the anointed one show that the Son is distinct from created things?

question: How can the unchangeable wisdom of God be present to and sustain changeable creatures?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > God Alone Creates Those Things Which are Changed by Magic Art.
sources.answer: God's wisdom is contained by no place. While remaining unchangeable itself, it abandons none of the changeable things, because every one of them is created by it. The suitable reasons by which bodies and souls affect each other exist immutably in that wisdom.
sources.quote: which, while it is itself unchangeable, yet quits not one even of those things which are changeable, because there is not one of them that is not created by itself
sources.raw_question: How can the unchangeable wisdom of God be present to and sustain changeable creatures?

question: Can a changeable rational soul participate in God's unchangeable wisdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Will of God is the Higher Cause of All Corporeal Change. This is Shown by an Example.
sources.answer: Yes. The rational soul, although changeable, can be a partaker of the unchangeable wisdom, so that it may partake of that which is in and of itself. Augustine reads the Psalm about Jerusalem, built of the saints as living stones, as saying this. There 'in and of itself' means the chief and unchangeable good, which is God, together with His wisdom and will.
sources.quote: which, therefore, although changeable, yet can be partaker of that unchangeable wisdom, so that “it may partake of that which is in and of itself;”
sources.raw_question: Can a changeable rational soul participate in God's unchangeable wisdom?

question: Does the Son's 'seeing' what the Father does (John 5:19) mean that he imitates a prior bodily pattern of works performed by the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The Son's knowledge is not imparted by the Father performing some bodily work as a pattern for the Son to copy afterwards. Rather, by the action of the divine nature the Son was born and shares the subsistence of that nature. God does not see in a bodily way but possesses by nature the vision of Omnipotence.
sources.quote: For God sees not after a bodily fashion, but possesses, by His nature, the vision of Omnipotence.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's 'seeing' what the Father does mean that he imitates a prior bodily pattern of works performed by the Father?

question: Does seeing the Son mean seeing the Father, and do the Son's works reveal the Father's Godhead?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son, as the Expression of the Father's Subsistence, preserves the Father's likeness and unvarying Image. Whoever sees him therefore sees the Father's Subsistence in him. From the Son's operation we understand the true Godhead of the Father, as Christ teaches that the Father dwelling in him does the works, and that he and the Father are one.
sources.quote: preserves the Father's likeness and unvarying Image, so that he who sees Him, sees in Him the Subsistence too, of which He is the Expression
sources.raw_question: Does seeing the Son mean seeing the Father, and do the Son's works reveal the Father's Godhead?

question: Is the Holy Spirit the only Person in the Trinity who is love?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit is not alone love in the Trinity, though he is specially called love for good reasons. In the same way he is not alone Spirit or holy, since the Father and the Son are each Spirit and holy. He is specially named by what the Father and Son share because he is common to both.
sources.quote: the Holy Spirit is not alone love in that Trinity, yet is not specially called love to no purpose, for the reasons we have alleged; just as He is not alone in that Trinity either a Spirit or holy
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit the only Person in the Trinity who is love?

question: Does the Holy Spirit make known to believers the love of the Father, considered distinctly as the first person of the Trinity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Yes. The Comforter is given to show believers that God is their Father and that he loves them. In particular, it is the Father, the first person of the Trinity considered distinctly, whose love the Spirit reveals. This is why the Spirit is so often said to come forth from the Father: he comes in pursuit of the Father's love to make it known.
sources.quote: In particular, that the Father, the first person in the Trinity, considered so distinctly, loves us. On this account is he said so often to come forth from the Father, because he comes in pursuit of his love
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit make known to believers the love of the Father, considered distinctly as the first person of the Trinity?

question: Is the question of how the one God is a Trinity a matter of whether to believe it, or of how to understand what is already believed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How There is a Trinity in the Very Simplicity of God. Whether and How the Trinity that is God is Manifested from the Trinities Which Have Been Shown to Be in Men.
sources.answer: It concerns understanding, not belief. Among the faithful the Trinity should admit no question as an object of belief. The inquiry asks whether there is a way for the understanding to see what is already believed. Augustine traces this through the trinity of lover, loved, and love that first began to dawn in the eighth book.
sources.quote: I do not say, How do we believe this? For among the faithful this ought to admit no question. But supposing there is any way by which we can see with the understanding what we believe, what is that way?
sources.raw_question: Is the question of how the one God is a Trinity a matter of whether to believe it, or of how to understand what is believed?

question: Must we believe in the Trinity before we understand it, and does it matter whether our belief about the Trinity is true?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Trinity May Be Loved Though Unknown.
sources.answer: Yes, on both counts. We seek to understand the Trinity's eternity, equality and unity as far as we are permitted, but we must believe first. That belief must be true and not feigned, because blessedness consists in enjoying that Trinity. If we believed something false about it, our hope would be worthless and our charity impure.
sources.quote: since we desire to understand the eternity, and equality, and unity of the Trinity, as much as is permitted us, but ought to believe before we understand
sources.raw_question: Must we believe in the Trinity before we understand it, and does it matter whether our belief about the Trinity is true?

question: Should the likeness of the divine Word be sought in the human spoken word, or in some other kind of human word?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Likeness of the Divine Word, Such as It Is, is to Be Sought, Not in Our Own Outer and Sensible Word, But in the Inner and Mental One. There is the Greatest Possible Unlikeness Between Our Word and Knowledge and the Divine Word and Knowledge.
sources.answer: It should be sought in the inner, mental word, not the outer word. The outer word, whether spoken aloud or silently rehearsed as imagined sound, is only a sign of the inner word. The inner word belongs to no language and precedes all signs. It is begotten from the knowledge in the mind when that knowledge is spoken inwardly as it really is.
sources.quote: the word that sounds outwardly is the sign of the word that gives light inwardly; which latter has the greater claim to be called a word.
sources.raw_question: Should the likeness of the divine Word be sought in the human spoken word, or in some other kind of human word?

question: Should words about divine things be read in a merely human sense?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Words about God must not be taken in a merely human and worldly sense, nor twisted into impious meanings. We should read what is written, understand it, and follow the demands of faith, speaking about Christ's nature in us only as he himself has taught.
sources.quote: The words in which we speak of the things of God must be used in no mere human and worldly sense, nor must the perverseness of an alien and impious interpretation be extorted from the soundness of heavenly words
sources.raw_question: Should words about divine things be read in a merely human sense?

question: What is the significance of the word order in Acts 2:36, 'Whom ye crucified, Him God made Christ and Lord'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: The order shows that the crucified one is the subject who was made Lord and Christ. Peter did not say 'Him whom God made Lord, ye crucified,' but put the crucifixion first, indicating that the exaltation concerns the human nature after the Passion, not a pre-temporal creation of the Word.
sources.quote: He did not say, “Him Whom God made Lord, ye crucified,” but, “Whom ye crucified, Him God made Christ and Lord”
sources.raw_question: What is the significance of the word order in Acts 2:36, 'Whom ye crucified, Him God made Christ and Lord'?

question: In Acts 2:36, does 'made Lord and Christ' mean that God manifested Jesus as Lord?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter himself explained the closing word 'made' at the beginning of his sermon with 'manifested,' calling Jesus 'a man manifested of God towards you by miracles.' Through the signs and wonders He was shown to be not merely man but God in a body, Lord and Christ. And Peter says He was made Lord 'towards' and 'in the midst of' us, not in general terms.
sources.quote: Consequently the term which he uses in the end, ‘made’, this He has explained in the beginning by ‘manifested,’
sources.raw_question: In Acts 2:36, does 'made Lord and Christ' mean that God manifested Jesus as Lord?

question: Does referring Acts 2:36 to Christ's humanity rather than his divine existence imply that there are two Christs or two Lords?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: No. Gregory argues that saying the demonstrative word ('this Jesus whom ye crucified') lays stress on what was human and visible in Christ gives no proof of teaching two Christs. The same one Christ is spoken of; the statement merely distinguishes the terms belonging to the Incarnation from those describing His divine existence. Eunomius cannot derive 'two Christs' from these words.
sources.quote: Does saying that the demonstrative word lays stress on that which is visible, convey the proof of maintaining “two Christs”?
sources.raw_question: Does Basil's saying that Acts 2:36 ('God made Him Lord and Christ') refers to the humanity of Christ rather than to the mode of Divine existence imply that there are two Christs or two Lords?

question: Does referring 'made' in Acts 2:36 to the Incarnation attribute salvation to an ordinary man?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: No. Peter's "made" refers to the new dispensation of the Incarnation, not to the pre-temporal existence. What was seen in the form of a servant was made, by being assumed, to be what the one who assumed it was by nature. This attributes salvation to the divine Son, not to a mere man.
sources.quote: that which was seen in the form of the servant has been made, by being assumed, to be that which He Who assumed it was in His own Nature
sources.raw_question: Does referring "made" in Acts 2:36 to the Incarnation mean that one attributes salvation to an ordinary man?

question: Does Peter's statement in Acts 10:36 that God sent the Word 'by Jesus Christ' prove that the Word and Christ are two different persons?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. Just as Christ confirms believers in his own day and is not one Christ confirming the day of another, the Father sent the Word made flesh so that, being made man, he preached by means of himself. Peter immediately adds 'This is Lord of all,' and Lord of all is the Word, so the Word and Christ are one and the same.
sources.quote: so the Father sent the Word made flesh, that being made man He might preach by means of Himself. And therefore he straightway adds, ‘This is Lord of all;’ but Lord of all is the Word.
sources.raised_by_detail: followers of the Samosatene (Paul of Samosata)
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's statement in Acts 10:36 that God sent the Word 'by Jesus Christ' prove that the Word and Christ are two different persons?

question: Does the vision of the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7 show that God the Father appeared in visible form to a prophet?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Vision of Daniel.
sources.answer: Yes, it is not unsuitably believed so. In Daniel's vision the Ancient of Days gives an everlasting kingdom to one like the Son of man, and the one who gives the kingdom to the Son is the Father, as the Psalm shows. Since both the Father giving and the Son receiving appear in visible form to the prophet, the claim that the Father never appeared to the prophets fails.
sources.quote: Behold the Father giving, and the Son receiving, an eternal kingdom; and both are in the sight of him who prophesies, in a visible form. It is not, therefore, unsuitably believed that God the Father also was wont to appear in that manner to mortals.
sources.raw_question: Does the vision of the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7 show that God the Father appeared in visible form to a prophet?

question: Does Daniel's vision of the Son of man coming to the Ancient of Days show a distinction between the Son and the Father, with the Son receiving power and glory from the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Yes. The same Word who appeared in the furnace is seen as the Son of man drawing near to the Ancient of Days. From Him the Son receives all power, glory and an everlasting kingdom. Likewise, the glory shown in John's vision is glory the Son has received from His Father.
sources.quote: this same individual beheld as the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven, and drawing near to the Ancient of Days, and receiving from Him all power and glory, and a kingdom.
sources.raw_question: Does the vision of the Son of man coming to the Ancient of Days show a distinction between the Son and the Father, with the Son receiving glory from the Father?

question: Is there a difference between gifts being given 'through the Spirit' and 'in the Spirit' in 1 Corinthians 12?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. Hilary says Paul worded this carefully because to be given through the Spirit and in the Spirit is not the same thing. A gift exercised in the Spirit is still bestowed through the Spirit. So there is one who distributes and another in whom the distribution is made.
sources.quote: in order to shew that these diverse gifts are given through the Spirit and in the Spirit (for to be given through the Spirit and in the Spirit is not the same thing)
sources.raw_question: Is there a difference between gifts being given 'through the Spirit' and 'in the Spirit' in 1 Corinthians 12?

question: Does 1 Corinthians 12:4 ('diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit') show that the one Father is expanded into Son and Spirit, as the Spirit is distributed into many gifts?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Marcellian illustration from 1 Cor. xii. 4, refuted.
sources.answer: No. The analogy is absurd. It would make the Father alone real, appearing as Father to one, Son to another and Spirit to another according to each one's need. On this view Son and Spirit would be names only and not realities.
sources.quote: the Father will be Word and Holy Spirit, to one becoming Father, to another Son, to another Spirit, accommodating himself to the need of each, and in name indeed Son and Spirit, but in reality Father only
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 12:4 ('diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit') show that the one Father is expanded into Son and Spirit, as the Spirit is distributed into many gifts?

question: Can the sufferings of Christ's flesh properly be called the sufferings of the divine Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: Yes. Because the flesh is the Word's own (the Word became flesh), the affections of the flesh are necessarily ascribed to him whose flesh it is. If the body had belonged to another man, the affections would have been attributed to that man. Yet these affections did not touch the Word according to his Godhead.
sources.quote: if the flesh is the Word’s (for ‘the Word became flesh’), of necessity then the affections also of the flesh are ascribed to Him, whose the flesh is.
sources.raw_question: Can the sufferings of Christ's flesh properly be called the sufferings of the divine Word?

question: Do the bodily sufferings ascribed to Christ affect the Word in his divine nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: No. The affections are proper to the Word only because the flesh is his own; they did not touch him according to his Godhead. Peter accordingly says Christ suffered 'for us in the flesh', not in his Godhead.
sources.quote: the affections of the body were proper to Him alone, though they did not touch Him according to His Godhead.
sources.raw_question: Do the bodily sufferings ascribed to Christ affect the Word in his divine nature?

question: Does the fact that Scripture directs supreme trust to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit prove that all three are equally God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Preface
sources.answer: Yes. The one infinite God alone claims our supreme and undivided confidence, and Scripture warrants reposing that same confidence in the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost. Therefore Father, Son and Spirit are equally God over all, the Triune Jehovah in whose name alone we trust and whom alone we adore.
sources.quote: that the same confidence is, on the warrant of Scripture, to be reposed in the Father, and in the Son, and in the Holy Ghost; and that therefore Father, Son, and Spirit are equally God over all, blessed forever
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Scripture directs supreme trust to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit prove that all three are equally God?

question: Does the supreme trust and love that Scripture's description of the Holy Spirit evokes prove that the Holy Spirit is God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is described as eternal, omnipresent, omniscient, Creator and giver of life, and author of the whole spiritual life, so believers must trust and love him supremely. Scripture nowhere forbids depending on him too absolutely, yet such homage belongs to God alone, who will not give his glory to another. Therefore the Holy Ghost is one with God and himself Jehovah.
sources.quote: Only believe these Scriptures and you must, perforce, trust and love this Divine Spirit supremely. This homage belongs to God alone, whose name is Jealous, who will not give his glory to another.
sources.raw_question: Does the supreme trust and love that Scripture's description of the Holy Spirit evokes prove that the Holy Spirit is God?

question: Is obedience part of the Son's nature, so that he could not be anything but obedient, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius's claim that the Son is obedient as a consequence of being begotten means his nature is built for obedience alone, like an instrument that can only trace the shape it was made with. But that would place the Son below even humanity. The human soul is self-determining and chooses with sovereignty over itself, whereas the Son would undergo obedience under a compulsory law of his nature.
sources.quote: what he intends to establish by these observations is something of this kind, that His obedience is part of His nature, so that not even if He willed it would it be possible for Him not to be obedient.
sources.raw_question: Is obedience part of the Son's nature, so that he could not be anything but obedient, as Eunomius claims?

question: Does it diminish the Son when Eunomius calls the Father faithful in words and works but calls the Son only obedient?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: Yes. Eunomius gives the Father faithfulness in word and deed but gives the Son only obedience, not faithfulness. Gregory treats this uneven distribution as one more sign that the impiety runs through all of Eunomius's statements, demoting the Son beneath the Father.
sources.quote: of the Son he does not assert faithfulness in word and deed, but only obedience and not faithfulness, so that his profanity extends impartially through all his statements
sources.raw_question: Does it diminish the Son when Eunomius calls the Father faithful in words and works but calls the Son only obedient?

question: Why does Christ call himself the Son of man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: He calls himself the Son of man because he sums up in himself the original man, Adam, from whom the woman was formed. As humanity went down to death through a vanquished man, so it rises to life through a victorious man. As death won its victory over us through a man, so through a man we win the victory over death.
sources.quote: in order that, as our species went down to death through a vanquished man, so we may ascend to life again through a victorious one; and as through a man death received the palm [of victory] against us, so again by a man we may receive the palm against death.
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ call himself the Son of man?

question: Why can the Father call the name of Jesus Christ His own name?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVII.—Proof that God did not appoint the Levitical dispensation for His own sake, or as requiring such service; for He does, in fact, need nothing from men.
sources.answer: For two reasons: it is the name of His own Son, and it was the Father who gave the Son, made man, for the salvation of men. Irenaeus compares a king who paints a likeness of his son. He rightly calls it his own, both because it is his son's likeness and because he made it. So the name of the Son belongs to the Father.
sources.quote: so also does the Father confess the name of Jesus Christ, which is throughout all the world glorified in the Church, to be His own, both because it is that of His Son, and because He who thus describes it gave Him for the salvation of men.
sources.raw_question: Why can the Father call the name of Jesus Christ His own name?

question: Does the context of Mark 13:32, where Christ describes what precedes the end, show that the Son knows the day of the end?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes. Right after saying 'nor the Son,' Christ tells the disciples what will come before that day. One who describes what precedes a day must know the day itself. He is like a guide who describes the road leading up to a city and so must know where the city is.
sources.quote: But He who speaks of what precedes the day, knows certainly the day also, which shall be manifested subsequently to the things foretold.
sources.raw_question: Does the context of Mark 13:32 show that the Son knows the day of the end?

question: If all that the Father has belongs to the Son, does the Son share the Father's knowledge of the last day?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son himself said that all that is the Father's is his. Knowing the day is an attribute of the Father, so the Son also knows it, having this as his own from the Father.
sources.quote: if all that is the Father’s, is the Son’s (and this He Himself has said), and it is the Father’s attribute to know the day, it is plain that the Son too knows it, having this proper to Him from the Father.
sources.raw_question: If all that the Father has belongs to the Son, does the Son share the Father's knowledge of the last day?

question: Does the mutual indwelling of Father and Son, and the Son's being the Father's Image, imply that the Son knows the day and hour?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes. Since the Son is in the Father and knows the things of the Father, he knows the day and hour that the Father knows. And as the Father's very Image, he has this likeness to the Father as well, namely knowing them.
sources.quote: if the Son be in the Father and the Father in the Son, and the Father knows the day and the hour, it is clear that the Son, being in the Father and knowing the things of the Father, knows Himself also the day and the hour.
sources.raw_question: Does the mutual indwelling of Father and Son, and the Son's being the Father's Image, imply that the Son knows the day and hour?

question: If the early Church had read the day-of-judgment texts as teaching the Son's literal ignorance, would it have used this against the Sabellians, and what does its silence show?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: Yes. Such a reading would have been the most decisive argument possible against the Sabellians, who held Father and Son to be one hypostasis. Yet the writers who opposed them, such as Tertullian against Praxeas, Hippolytus against Noetus, and Eusebius against Marcellus, never used it. This shows the early writers did not understand the texts in that way.
sources.quote: preted these two texts, as you pretend they did, there could not have been any thing more decisive against the Sabellians.
sources.raw_question: If the early Church had read the day-of-judgment texts as teaching the Son's literal ignorance, would this have been used against the Sabellians?

question: How do texts that distinguish the Father from the incarnate Christ, such as the Son's ignorance of the day of judgment, tell against the Sabellians?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: They show that the Father and the Son are spoken of as two Persons, one knowing and the other not knowing in a certain respect. The Sabellians granted that the man Christ Jesus was personally united with God. Since that union could not be with the Father, it must be with another divine Hypostasis, a real and distinct Son.
sources.quote: it is manifest that the Father and Son are there spoken of, as of two Persons; and one as Anowvng, the other as not knowing, though only in a certain respect
sources.raw_question: How do texts that distinguish the Father from the incarnate Christ, such as the Son's ignorance of the day of judgment, tell against the Sabellians?

question: Did those whom Christ raised from the dead, such as Lazarus and the widow's son, rise in the same bodies in which they had died, and what does this show about the general resurrection?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIII.—In the dead who were raised by Christ we possess the highest proof of the resurrection; and our hearts are shown to be capable of life eternal, because they can now receive the Spirit of God.
sources.answer: Yes. They rose in the identical bodies in which they had died, for otherwise the same individuals would not have risen at all. By these temporal raisings the Lord prefigured eternal things and showed that he is able to give both healing and life to his own handiwork. So his words about the future resurrection of the dead at the last trumpet should be believed.
sources.quote: For if it were not in the very same, then certainly those same individuals who had died did not rise again.
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostic deniers of the resurrection of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Did those whom Christ raised from the dead, such as Lazarus and the widow's son, rise in the same bodies in which they had died, and what does this show about the general resurrection?

question: Was Christ raised in the same body in which He died?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That Jesus Christ is the Son of God and Truly Man, as Opposed to the Fancies of Heretics, Who Deny that He Took Upon Him True Flesh.
sources.answer: Yes. The wounds of that very body prove He rose in the same bodily substance. In this way He showed in His flesh the law of our resurrection, as an example for the rest.
sources.quote: And that He was raised again in the same bodily substance in which He died, is proved by the wounds of that very body, and thus He showed the laws of our resurrection in His flesh
sources.raw_question: Was Christ raised in the same body in which He died?

question: Do terms like 'servant', 'created', 'son of man', or 'brother' applied to Christ designate the essence of the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. Such terms are proper to human constitution and signify that the Word has become man, not what His essence is. Once the incarnation is confessed, there is no difficulty in using any of them of Him.
sources.quote: All these terms happen to be proper to man’s constitution; and such as these do not designate the Essence of the Word, but that He has become man.
sources.raw_question: Do terms like 'servant', 'created', 'son of man', or 'brother' applied to Christ designate the essence of the Word?

question: Does the Word act in creation independently of the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XV.—Proofs of the resurrection from Isaiah and Ezekiel; the same God who created us will also raise us up.
sources.answer: No. The Word who forms us in the womb and formed the blind man's sight is the one who made the whole man. In doing so he carries out the will of the Father, as shown by God's words to Jeremiah about forming him in the womb.
sources.quote: For the Lord who formed the visual powers is He who made the whole man, carrying out the will of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Word act in creation independently of the Father?

question: Does the Word go forth from God for creation and later return into God, so that He is now external to the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Marcellus and his disciples, like Arians, say that the Word was, not indeed created, but issued, to create us, as if the Divine silence were a state of inaction, and when God spake by the Word, He acted; or that there was a going forth and return of the Word; a doctrine which implies change and imperfection in Father and Son.
sources.answer: No. The Lord says, 'I in the Father and the Father in Me,' so He is in the Father now as He always was. A going forth and return would mean the Word is now not what He was and will be, making Him imperfect and alterable. He is ever as He was, in the same state and respects.
sources.quote: But the Lord refutes such persons when He says, ‘I in the Father and the Father in Me;’ for so is He now as He ever was.
sources.raw_question: Does the Word go forth from God for creation and later return into God, so that He is now external to the Father?

question: What role does the Word play in creation, and how was the Word brought forth by the Father?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: The Father begat the Word as Author, fellow-Counsellor and Framer of created things, and made all things through Him. The Word was borne within God, invisible to the world, and God, uttering the voice and begetting Him as Light of Light, set Him forth as Lord of the world and made Him visible so the world could see Him and be saved.
sources.quote: as the Author, and fellow-Counsellor, and Framer of the things that are in formation, He begat the Word
sources.raw_question: What role does the Word play in creation and how was the Word brought forth by the Father?

question: Is the doctrine that each of the three divine Persons is God, and that all together are one God, a plain contradiction?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. It falls under the case of propositions whose ideas are seemingly, not really, repugnant. We know clearly what we mean in saying each Person is God, a Person having the essential divine perfections. We do not see perfectly how this is reconciled with there being one God, just as we cannot see how foreknowledge is reconciled with future contingents, yet we rightly believe both, trusting there is a real connection of the ideas beyond our faculties.
sources.quote: The belief of three Persons, every one singly God, and all together one God, seems to fall under case the fourth: the ideas are seemingly, not really, repugnant.
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine that each of the three divine Persons is God and that all together are one God a plain contradiction?

question: Can the three Persons of the Trinity be called three beings or 'things' and yet be only one being without contradiction?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: Yes. 'Being' can mean simply what exists, or what exists separately. In the first sense the Persons are three real things (as the schoolmen say, tres res), while in the second sense they are one being, una res numero, since none exists separately or independently of the others.
sources.quote: The very schoolmen themselves never scruple to call them tres res, tres entes, or the like, in that sense; though at the same time, in the other sense of being, they are all but one being, una summa res, and una res numero
sources.raw_question: Can the three Persons of the Trinity be called three beings or 'things' and yet be only one being without contradiction?

question: Is the name 'Beginning' (Principium) said of God the Father according to substance or relatively?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > How the Word Beginning (Principium) is Spoken Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: Relatively. The Father is called Father in relation to the Son, and Beginning in relation to all things which are from Him. Like 'creator' to 'creature' or 'master' to 'servant', 'Beginning' names a relation, not the divine substance.
sources.quote: He is called the Father in relation to the Son, the Beginning in relation to all things, which are from Him.
sources.raw_question: Is the name 'Beginning' (Principium) said of God the Father according to substance or relatively?

question: Is God the Father a beginning (principium) in relation to the Son within the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Father and the Son the Only Beginning (Principium) of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Since a begetter is a beginning in relation to what he begets, and the Father begets the Son, the Father is a beginning relative to the Son. This is said relatively, not according to substance.
sources.quote: if the begetter is a beginning in relation to that which he begets, the Father is a beginning in relation to the Son, because He begets Him
sources.raw_question: Is God the Father a beginning (principium) in relation to the Son within the Trinity?

question: Can the Holy Spirit rightly be called the Beginning and Creator?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > How the Word Beginning (Principium) is Spoken Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. Whatever remains within itself while producing or working something is a beginning of what it works. Scripture says the Spirit works all the spiritual gifts, and in working He remains unchanged. Moreover, He is not separated from the name of Creator.
sources.quote: we cannot deny that the Holy Spirit also is rightly called the Beginning, since we do not separate Him from the appellation of Creator: and it is written of Him that He works
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit rightly be called the Beginning and Creator?

question: Can God the Father properly be called an angel or messenger?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: No. To call the Father an angel would make Him subordinate to another whose angel He would be. The Son, by contrast, is subject to the Father and announces the Father's will. For this reason He is rightly called the Angel of Great Counsel.
sources.quote: But far be it from us to call God the Father an angel, lest He should be subordinate to another whose angel He would be.
sources.raw_question: Can God the Father properly be called an angel or messenger?

question: In what sense can the Holy Spirit rightly be called one, first, and alone?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: The Spirit is one, first and alone because He is contemplated indivisibly in the one God. He is One as being in the One, first as being in the First, and alone as being in the Only One. As a man's spirit and the man himself are one man, so the Spirit of God and God are properly one God, because the Spirit cannot be separated from Him in whom He is.
sources.quote: For as the spirit of man that is in him, and the man himself, are but one man, so also the Spirit of God which is in Him, and God Himself, would properly be termed One God, and First and Only
sources.raw_question: In what sense can the Holy Spirit rightly be called one, first, and alone?

question: Is the Word of God who became incarnate the same as the only begotten Son and Jesus Christ our Lord?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus says he has proved from John's own words that John knew one and the same Word of God. That Word is the only begotten, who became incarnate for our salvation as Jesus Christ our Lord.
sources.quote: That John knew the one and the same Word of God, and that He was the only begotten, and that He became incarnate for our salvation, Jesus Christ our Lord, I have sufficiently proved from the word of John himself.
sources.raw_question: Is the Word of God who became incarnate the same as the only begotten Son and Jesus Christ our Lord?

question: Is Christ called Lord only in a loose or nominal sense, or is He truly Lord?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: He is truly Lord. When His disciples called Him Master and Lord, He said 'ye say well, for so I am.' He thereby declared that He is Lord, not merely called Lord. He also named Himself the one Master, just as He named the one Father in heaven.
sources.quote: truly declaring Himself to be Lord, and that He is not falsely named Lord (for He says, “I am,” not “I am called”)
sources.raw_question: Is Christ called Lord only in a loose or nominal sense, or is He truly Lord?

question: How does the Son, as the Word, reveal the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: The Father reveals by the Son, His Word. If our temporal word declares both itself and its subject, much more does the Word of God. He declares the Father as He is because, as wisdom and essence, He is what the Father is.
sources.quote: For this Word so declares the Father as He is the Father; because both itself so is, and is that which is the Father, in so far as it is wisdom and essence.
sources.raw_question: How does the Son as Word reveal the Father?

question: Why is the Son revealed under names of the Father's properties such as Word, Wisdom and Power?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: To save us from concluding that the Son is alien from the Father's divine nature. These properties constituted His perfection when He came into existence by birth, yet they never deserted the Father, in Whom they remain eternally present; thus the Son, being God, is nothing else than God.
sources.quote: But it was to save us from concluding that the Son is alien from the Divine nature of His Father that He, the Only-begotten from the eternal God His Father, born as God into a substantial existence of His own, has had Himself revealed to us under these names of properties
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son revealed under names of the Father's properties such as Word, Wisdom and Power?

question: Was it the whole Trinity or only the Holy Spirit that appeared as a dove at Jesus' baptism and as tongues of fire at Pentecost?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > What the Doctrine of the Catholic Faith is Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: Only the Holy Spirit. The Trinity did not descend as a dove on Jesus at His baptism. Nor did the Trinity sit on the disciples as cloven tongues of fire at Pentecost. The Holy Spirit alone did.
sources.quote: Nor, again, that this Trinity descended in the form of a dove upon Jesus when He was baptized
sources.raw_question: Was it the whole Trinity or only the Holy Spirit that appeared as a dove at Jesus' baptism and as tongues of fire at Pentecost?

question: In the dove at Christ's baptism and the tongues of fire at Pentecost, did the Son and the Holy Spirit appear in their own divine substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: No. In the Lord born of a virgin, in the Spirit descending as a dove, and in the tongues of fire, what appeared to mortal senses was a creature formed for that purpose. It was not the substance in which the Word and the Spirit are equal and co-eternal with the Father.
sources.quote: it was not the Word of God Himself by His own substance, in which He is equal and eternal with the Father, nor the Spirit of the Father and of the Son by His own substance
sources.raw_question: In the dove at Christ's baptism and the tongues of fire at Pentecost, did the Son and the Holy Spirit appear in their own divine substance?

question: Does God know creatures because they exist, or do creatures exist because God knows them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Still Further of the Difference Between the Knowledge and Word of Our Mind, and the Knowledge and Word of God.
sources.answer: Creatures exist because God knows them, not the reverse. God was not ignorant of what he was about to create, so he created because he knew. Nor did his knowledge change when they came to be, since nothing accrued to his wisdom from them; he knew them the same way before and after creation.
sources.quote: He does not know them because they are, but they are because He knows them. For He was not ignorant of what He was about to create; therefore He created because He knew; He did not know because He created.
sources.raw_question: Does God know creatures because they exist, or do creatures exist because God knows them?

question: Is God unknowable to his creatures, or can He be known?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Both, in different respects. In His greatness, His nature and how great He is, God is unknown and invisible to everything He has made. In His love, however, He is always known through His Word, by whom He ordained all things. All things learn through the Word that there is one God the Father.
sources.quote: as regards His greatness, is indeed unknown to all who have been made by Him
sources.raw_question: Is God unknowable to his creatures, or can He be known?

question: Are things that begin to be said of God in time predicated of Him as accidents?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said of God in Time, is Said Relatively, Not Accidentally.
sources.answer: No. Whatever begins to be said of God in time, and was not said before, is said relatively. It is not said according to any accident in God, as though something happened to Him. It is said according to an accident in the creature in respect of which God begins to be called something.
sources.quote: that which begins to be spoken of God in time, and which was not spoken of Him before, is manifestly spoken of Him relatively; yet not according to any accident of God, so that anything should have happened to Him
sources.raw_question: Are things said of God that begin to be said in time predicated of Him as accidents?

question: Is Christ two persons, a God and a man, or one person who is both God and man?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: One person who is both God and man. The Word who was with God and was God (John 1:1) was himself made flesh (John 1:14), so that the mighty God is a child given to us and the holy thing born of the virgin is called the Son of God.
sources.quote: We have not been treating of two, a God and a man; but of one who is God and man.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ two persons, a God and a man, or one person who is both God and man?

question: Is the Holy Spirit himself a Fount of eternal life, and not only a stream from a fount?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XVI. The Holy Spirit is that large river by which the mystical Jerusalem is watered. It is equal to its Fount, that is, the Father and the Son, as is signified in holy Scripture. St. Ambrose himself thirsts for that water, and warns us that in order to preserve it within us, we must avoid the devil, lust, and heresy, since our vessels are frail, and that broken cisterns must be forsaken, that after the example of the Samaritan woman and of the patriarchs we may find the water of the Lord.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ says that the water he gives becomes a well springing up to everlasting life, and this well is the grace of the Spirit. So the Spirit is also the Fount of eternal life, which shows the unity of the divine greatness.
sources.quote: This well is clearly the grace of the Spirit, a stream proceeding from the living Fount. The Holy Spirit, then, is also the Fount of eternal life.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit himself a Fount of eternal life, and not only a stream from a fount?

question: Can the errors of heretics about the Trinity be blamed on Scripture, given that heretics defend their opinions from Scripture?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > What Augustin Requests from His Readers. The Errors of Readers Dull of Comprehension Not to Be Ascribed to the Author.
sources.answer: No. Heretics try to defend their false and varied opinions from the same Scriptures, but their errors cannot rightly be ascribed to the divine books. The fault lies with readers who misunderstand. Augustine applies the same principle to his own writings: readers who misread a hard and obscure subject cannot rightly charge their errors to him.
sources.quote: seeing that neither can any one, in any way, rightly ascribe the numerous and various errors of heretics to the holy testimonies themselves of the divine books; although all of them endeavor to defend out of those same Scriptures their own false and erroneous opinions
sources.raw_question: Can the errors of heretics about the Trinity be blamed on Scripture, given that heretics defend their opinions from Scripture?

question: Can the heretics' errors about God and Christ be refuted from the very Gospels they themselves use?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: Yes. Each heretical group appeals to a Gospel, and each is confuted from it. The Ebionites are refuted from Matthew, and Marcion from the parts of Luke he retains. Those who separate Jesus from Christ can be corrected from Mark, and the Valentinians from John. Because the opponents bear witness to these documents, proof drawn from them is firm and true.
sources.quote: Since, then, our opponents do bear testimony to us, and make use of these [documents], our proof derived from them is firm and true.
sources.raised_by_detail: Ebionites, Marcion, Valentinians, those separating Jesus from Christ
sources.raw_question: Can the heretics' errors about God and Christ be refuted from the very Gospels they themselves use?

question: Why does it matter that Proverbs 8 says 'He founded me' rather than 'He founded me as Word or Son' or 'He made me a foundation'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: The wording shows that the text does not speak of the origin of the Word's being. Had it said He was made or founded as Word or Son, there would seem to be a beginning of His making. Saying simply 'He founded me' shows He speaks not for His own sake but for those built upon Him.
sources.quote: He saith not, ‘He made me a foundation,’ lest He might seem to be made and to have a beginning of being, and they might thence find a shameless occasion of irreligion; but, ‘He founded me.’
sources.raw_question: Why does it matter that Proverbs 8 says 'He founded me' and not 'He founded me as Word or Son' or 'He made me a foundation'?

question: Why does Proverbs 8 give a reason ('for the works') for 'He created me' but give no reason for 'He begets me'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: Where Scripture speaks of the Word's becoming man it adds a cause, namely the need of the works, since the incarnation would not have occurred without human need. But the generation from the Father is stated absolutely, 'Before all the hills He begets me,' like 'In the beginning was the Word,' because the Word existed even if no works had been created; hence the Son is not a creature.
sources.quote: For, though no works had been created, still ‘the Word’ of God ‘was,’ and ‘the Word was God.’ And His becoming man would not have taken place, had not the need of men become a cause. The Son then is not a creature.
sources.raw_question: Why does Proverbs 8 add a reason ('for the works') to 'He created me' but no reason to 'He begets me'?

question: Is God's goodness something distinct from God that inheres in Him as in a subject?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > In God, Substance is Spoken Improperly, Essence Properly.
sources.answer: No. It is impious to say that God is a subject in relation to His own goodness, or that He is not His own goodness. Because God is simple, His being is the same as whatever is said of Him in respect to Himself, such as great, omnipotent and good.
sources.quote: But it is an impiety to say that God subsists, and is a subject in relation to His own goodness, and that this goodness is not a substance or rather essence, and that God Himself is not His own goodness
sources.raw_question: Is God's goodness something distinct from God that inheres in Him as in a subject?

question: Are goodness and righteousness two different qualities in God's nature, as they appear to be in His works?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Difficult It is to Demonstrate the Trinity by Natural Reason.
sources.answer: No. Although they differ in God's works, in God's nature righteousness is itself goodness, and goodness is itself blessedness. They are not two diverse qualities of God.
sources.quote: Certainly not; but that which is righteousness is also itself goodness; and that which is goodness is also itself blessedness.
sources.raw_question: Are goodness and righteousness two different qualities in God's nature, as they appear different in his works?

question: Since the Trinity is one essence, must it also be one substance rather than three substances?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > In God, Substance is Spoken Improperly, Essence Properly.
sources.answer: Yes. Whether God is called essence (properly) or substance (improperly), both terms are said of Him in respect to Himself, not relatively. For God, to be and to subsist are the same, so a Trinity of one essence is also one substance.
sources.quote: whence to God to be is the same thing as to subsist; and so the Trinity, if one essence, is also one substance.
sources.raw_question: Since the Trinity is one essence, must it also be one substance rather than three substances?

question: Can mind, knowledge, and love each be a substance while all three together are only one substance or essence?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > That These Three are Several in Themselves, and Mutually All in All.
sources.answer: Yes. These three are marvellously inseparable, yet each is severally a substance, and all together are one substance or essence. Their threeness lies in being mutually predicated relatively, offering an image of the divine Trinity.
sources.quote: these three things are marvellously inseparable from each other, and yet each of them is severally a substance, and all together are one substance or essence, whilst they are mutually predicated relatively
sources.raw_question: Can mind, knowledge, and love each be a substance while all three together are only one substance or essence?

question: Is Samuel Clarke's subordinationist account of the Trinity clearer and more intelligible than the orthodox doctrine?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. Clarke also affirms that each Person singly is God and that God is one, so he faces the same difficulty of how three can be one God. Each way his scheme tries to secure unity leads either to Sabellianism or to three Gods. It is therefore at least as hard to understand as the orthodox doctrine.
sources.quote: Thus the Doctor's scheme is liable to the same difficulties with the other.
sources.raw_question: Is Dr. Samuel Clarke's subordinationist account of the Trinity clearer and more intelligible than the orthodox doctrine?

question: Does the argument that, if orthodox Trinitarian doctrine is false and no middle position exists, Samuel Clarke's Arian view must be true amount to a demonstration of Arianism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 31: Whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration, on the side of Arianism, ought to move a wise and good man, against so great appearances of truth o
sources.answer: No. Waterland says the argument assumes what it should prove. It supposes that the orthodox notion is false and that there is no middle ground between Sabellianism and Arianism, and it proves neither. Supposing is not proving, and begging the question does not settle it. So nothing is actually demonstrated.
sources.quote: That is, if supposing be proving, and if begging the question be the same thing with determining it ; then something
sources.raw_question: Does the argument 'if the received (orthodox) doctrine of the Trinity is not true, and there is no middle position between it and Dr. Clarke's view, then Dr. Clarke's (Arian) view is the true doctrine' amount to a demonstration of Arianism?

question: Were the Angel who spoke with Hagar and the Man who spoke with Abraham God and Lord, unlike the two angels sent to Lot?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. The Angel who spoke with Hagar was God and Lord when he spoke of the same matter with Abraham. The Man who spoke with Abraham was also God and Lord. The two angels sent to Lot are described simply as angels and nothing more.
sources.quote: He Who was the Angel of God, when He spoke with Hagar, was God and Lord when He spoke of the same matter with Abraham; that the Man Who spoke with Abraham was also God and Lord
sources.raw_question: Was the Angel who spoke with Hagar, and the Man who spoke with Abraham, God and Lord, unlike the two angels sent to Lot?

question: Are the Father's 'commandment' and the Father's 'word' different things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. Christ calls the same thing both a word and a commandment, and that commandment is everlasting life. This identifies it with the Son, who is the Word of God and eternal life.
sources.quote: For the commandment of the Father is not one thing, and the word of the Father another; for He hath called it both a word and a commandment.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father's 'commandment' and the Father's 'word' different things?

question: How should the Father's 'commandment' to the Son be understood in a way fitting to the Godhead?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: It is not a spoken order given to a subordinate. It is a timeless transmission of will from Father to Son, like the reflection of an object in a mirror. Because the Father loves the Son and shows him all things, all that the Father has belongs to the Son at once, not little by little.
sources.quote: Let us rather, in a sense befitting the Godhead, perceive a transmission of will, like the reflexion of an object in a mirror, passing without note of time from Father to Son.
sources.raw_question: How should the Father's "commandment" to the Son be understood in a way fitting to the Godhead?

question: Is comparing parallel Scripture texts about the Father and the Son a valid way to prove the Son's coequal Deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4.
