That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as in algebra or trigonometry unknown quantities are found by combining known ones, so humble students who prayerfully compare spiritual things with spiritual will know what God has revealed. When the same attributes, majesty and claims are ascribed to both Father and Son, their coequal Deity follows. This is the more forceful because Jehovah declares he will not give his glory to another.
sources.quote: so in searching the Scriptures, those humble students who receive the words not which man’s wisdom teacheth but which the Holy Ghost teacheth, prayerfully comparing and combining them, shall know the things which are freely given to us of God.
sources.raw_question: Is comparing parallel Scripture texts about the Father and the Son a valid way to prove the Son's coequal Deity?

question: Does Novatian's statement that if Father and Son were 'found equal' they would be two Gods count as evidence against the Son's coequality with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Read in context, it means only that Father and Son are not two Gods because they are not both unoriginated or unbegotten. This was the standard Catholic reply to the charge of tritheism, used both before and after Nicaea. Rightly understood, the passage strongly supports the kind of coequality the orthodox defend.
sources.quote: There is nothing more in it than this, that Father and Son are not two Gods, because they are not both uwnoriqinated: which is the common answer made by the Catholics to the charge of Tritheism
sources.raw_question: Does Novatian's statement that if Father and Son were 'found equal' they would be two Gods count as evidence against the Son's coequality with the Father?

question: If both 'without beginning' and 'without end' are taken as defining God's essence, does that make God a composite of contradictory elements?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: Yes. Beginning and end are diametrically opposed, and contraries of opposites are themselves opposed, as dryness and moistness are opposed because fire and water are. So the negations of beginning and end would also contradict each other, and a God defined by both would be a patchwork of contradictions, which is incompatible with his simplicity.
sources.quote: they will exhibit this Deity of theirs as a combination of two contradictory and discordant things, because the contrary ideas to beginning and end reproduce on their side also the contradiction existing between beginning and end.
sources.raw_question: If both 'without beginning' and 'without end' are taken as defining God's essence, does that make God a composite of contradictory elements?

question: Why must God be without beginning and without end?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > God is Above All Things, Himself Containing All Things, Immense, Eternal, Transcending the Mind of Man; Inexplicable in Discourse, Loftier Than All Sublimity.
sources.answer: Because if God began to be at some time, He would come after something prior and be beneath it, and so be of less power and not above all things. Since He has no beginning, nothing precedes Him and He has no time; therefore He is eternal, and likewise immortal, having no ending of His completeness.
sources.quote: For this reason, therefore, He is always unbounded, because nothing is greater than He; always eternal, because nothing is more ancient than He. For that which is without beginning can be preceded by none, in that He has no time.
sources.raw_question: Why must God be without beginning and without end?

question: Do the terms 'without beginning' and 'without end' have the same meaning when applied to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. 'Without end' is common to all things whose life extends to infinity, while 'without beginning' belongs to Him alone who has no originating cause. Beginning and end are distinct notions, so their privations are not convertible, and what is common to many cannot be equated with what is proper to the Deity alone.
sources.quote: the term without end is common to all things whose life we believe capable of extension to infinity, while the term without beginning belongs to Him alone Who is without originating cause.
sources.raw_question: Do the terms 'without beginning' and 'without end' have the same meaning when applied to God?

question: Can 'beginning' and 'end' be applied to something that has no quantity or extension, such as the divine generation of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He further shows that the pretemporal generation of the Son is not the subject of influences drawn from ordinary and carnal generation, but is without beginning and without end, and not according to the fabrications constructed by Eunomius, in ignorance of His power, from the statements of Plato concerning the soul and from the sabbath rest of the Hebrews.
sources.answer: No. Only what is limited in some quantitative way can be said to begin or to stop at a limit. Time-measure separates beginning from end by the interval between them. What has no quantity and no extension cannot be measured, and the infinite cannot be defined by beginning and end.
sources.quote: But how can any one measure or treat as extended that which is without quantity and without extension? What measure can he find for that which has no quantity, or what interval for that which has no extension?
sources.raw_question: Can 'beginning' and 'end' be applied to something that has no quantity or extension, such as the divine generation of the Son?

question: Is the Son of God simple and incomposite in his essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Because the Son is himself God, and God is free from all compositeness, the Son must be believed to be simple. The meaning of 'simple' with regard to essence is one and the same for the Father and for the Son.
sources.quote: we hold that we are bound to believe that the Son of God, being Himself God, is Himself also simple, because God is free from all compositeness
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God simple and incomposite in his essence?

question: Do Christ's sayings such as 'I have not spoken of myself' and 'As the Father gave me commandment, even so I do' show that the Son lacks his own will or power of initiative?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. Christ uses such language not because he lacks deliberate purpose or power of initiation, nor because he waits for a cue from the Father. His aim is to show that his own will is joined in indissoluble union with the Father's will.
sources.quote: it is not because He lacks deliberate purpose or power of initiation, nor yet because He has to wait for the preconcerted key-note, that he employs language of this kind. His object is to make it plain that His own will is connected in indissoluble union with the Father.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's sayings such as "I have not spoken of myself" and "As the Father gave me commandment, even so I do" show that the Son lacks his own will or power of initiative?

question: Do Christ's sayings 'I can of mine own self do nothing' and 'the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works' show that he lacks divine power?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. As man, Christ is the exemplar of faith and worked his miracles not by his inherent divinity but by perfect faith in the Father's power. These words reveal the entire dependence of his human soul on God, which is consistent with his deity.
sources.quote: AS MAN working his miracles not by virtue of his Divinity ever inherent in him, but by virtue of a perfect faith in, the power of the Father
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's sayings "I can of mine own self do nothing" and "the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works" show that he lacks divine power?

question: Do Christ's sayings about being sent by the Father, doing the Father's will, and the Father bearing witness to him show that Christ is not the Father himself?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, Against the Sabellians He Proves that the Father is One, the Son Another.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ says he came to do the will of the One who sent him, that the Father is greater, and that he goes to his Father. He also counts himself and the Father as two witnesses and prays to the Father for the glory he had with him before the world. All of this distinguishes the Son from the Father as a second person.
sources.quote: Or when he finds it placed side by side with others: “Moreover, in your law it is written that the witness of two is true. I bear witness of myself, and the Father who sent me beareth witness of me?”
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's sayings in the Gospels about being sent by the Father, doing the Father's will, and the Father bearing witness to him show that Christ is not the Father himself?

question: Is the Creator of the world, whom the Valentinian Gnostics call the Demiurge, a product of defect and ignorance rather than the true God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: No. The Creator is the Father, who alone is called God and truly exists. Scripture acknowledges Him alone as God, and the Lord confesses Him alone as His own Father and knows no other. Calling Him the fruit of defect and offspring of ignorance is therefore a terrible blasphemy against the one who truly is God.
sources.quote: since the Father Himself is alone called God, who has a real existence, but whom ye style the Demiurge; since, moreover, the Scriptures acknowledge Him alone as God; and yet again, since the Lord confesses Him alone as His own Father
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of the world, whom the Valentinian Gnostics call the Demiurge, a product of defect and ignorance rather than the true God?

question: Could God, the Creator of the universe, be ignorant of something real (such as a 'spiritual seed') deposited within him, as the Valentinian Gnostics claimed of their Demiurge?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIX.—Absurdities of the heretics as to their own origin: their opinions respecting the Demiurge shown to be equally untenable and ridiculous.
sources.answer: No. Anything that has real substance and qualities, such as heat, swiftness, sweetness or brilliance, does not escape even human notice, much less the notice of God, the Maker of the universe. The only way the Creator could be ignorant of such a seed is if it had no substance or quality at all, that is, if it were a pure nonentity. So the Gnostic claim is either false or makes their seed nothing.
sources.quote: For how could he have been ignorant of it, if that seed had possessed any substance and peculiar properties? If, on the other hand, it was without substance and without quality, and so was really nothing, then, as a matter of course, he was ignorant of it.
sources.raw_question: Could God, the Creator of the universe, be ignorant of something real (such as a 'spiritual seed') deposited within him, as the Valentinian Gnostics claimed of their Demiurge?

question: Is baptism in the name of Jesus Christ alone a valid and complete baptism, even though the Father and the Holy Spirit are not named?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: Yes, provided there is belief in all Three Persons. The mystery is complete through the oneness of the Name, and the Spirit is not separated from the baptism of Christ. What is not mentioned in words is expressed in belief, as with the Ethiopian eunuch and the disciples at Ephesus.
sources.quote: when it is said, “In the Name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” the mystery is complete through the oneness of the Name, and the Spirit is not separated from the baptism of Christ
sources.raw_question: Is baptism in the Name of Jesus Christ alone a valid and complete baptism, even though the Father and the Holy Spirit are not named?

question: Does Hebrews 2:16 show that Christ took human nature rather than angelic nature, and so preferred believers above angels?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. The verb may mean 'took on him', referring to the incarnation, or 'helped', referring to its fruit. Either way, the text plainly shows Christ preferring the seed of Abraham to angels. The seed of Abraham means believers, so his esteem is for them.
sources.quote: it is all one, as to our present business: his preferring the seed of Abraham before angels, his valuing them above the other, is plainly expressed.
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 2:16 show that Christ took human nature rather than angelic nature, and so preferred believers above angels?

question: Does Hebrews 2:14-16 imply that Christ existed before he took human nature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Saying that he took part of flesh and blood, and took on the seed of Abraham, plainly affirms that he existed before taking our nature. It also affirms that his person remained one in that assumed nature.
sources.quote: this plainly affirms his pre-existence unto that assumption of our nature, and the unity of his person in it being so assumed
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 2:14-16 imply that Christ existed before he took human nature?

question: Is the Holy Spirit who dwells in believers the same thing as the habitual grace or new spiritual life produced in them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: No. Habitual grace is a created quality that has no subsistence except in the soul, and it can increase or decrease in degree. The Spirit, by contrast, dwells in believers as a free agent in a holy habitation. He is the efficient cause of holiness, not the created quality itself.
sources.quote: From the Spirit dwelling in the saints; for it is a created quality. The Spirit dwells in us as a free agent in a holy habitation.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit who dwells in believers the same thing as the habitual grace or new spiritual life produced in them?

question: Can there be wisdom without understanding, memory, and love?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God from the Trinities We Have Spoken of.
sources.answer: No. Where there is no understanding there can be no wisdom. One who remembers nothing, not even himself, cannot be wise. Where there is no love, no one would say there is any wisdom. So whatever is wisdom must have all three.
sources.quote: For where there is no understanding there can be no wisdom
sources.raw_question: Can there be wisdom without understanding, memory, and love?

question: Could the Wisdom that is God know and love other things without knowing and loving itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How There is a Trinity in the Very Simplicity of God. Whether and How the Trinity that is God is Manifested from the Trinities Which Have Been Shown to Be in Men.
sources.answer: No. It would be foolish and impious to say so. Where there is no knowledge there is no wisdom, so the Wisdom that is God must perceive and love itself.
sources.quote: Or are we, in truth, to think that the Wisdom which is God knows other things, and does not know itself; or loves other things, and does not love itself?
sources.raw_question: Could the Wisdom that is God know and love other things without knowing and loving itself?

question: If the Hebrew words for 'everlasting' can signify only a limited duration, does the Old Testament then give no certain proof of the Father's eternity either?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: Yes, on the Arian's way of reasoning it would. Waterland argues that the Arian method, which refuses to let these phrases prove the Son's eternity, equally leaves the Father's eternity unproven in the Old Testament. The appeal to Romans 1:20 does not rescue it, since aidios occurs only once more in the New Testament and there means eternal only in a limited sense (a parte post). The Arian ends up with no Scripture proof of the Father's eternity, for fear of having to admit the Son's.
sources.quote: we must contentedly go away, without any Seripture proof of the eernity of the Father, for fear it should oblige us to take in the Son’s also
sources.raw_question: If the Hebrew words for 'everlasting' can signify only a limited duration, does the Old Testament then give no certain proof of the Father's eternity either?

question: Since the Hebrew word translated 'from everlasting' in Proverbs 8:22-23 can signify a limited duration, does that passage fail to prove the eternity of the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: No. Waterland grants the word can sometimes signify limited duration, so he does not rest the argument on the word alone but on that together with other circumstances, chiefly that the same phrases are used for the eternity of God in Psalm 90:2 and 93:2. Because God chose these very phrases to express his own duration and then chose the same ones for his Son, we are taught that the Son is coeternal with him.
sources.quote: I allow your observation, that the Hebrew word may, and sometimes does, signify a limited, as well as it does, at other times, an wilimited duration. And therefore I do not lay all the stress of my argument upon the critical meaning of the word
sources.raw_question: Since the Hebrew word translated 'from everlasting' in Proverbs 8:22-23 can signify a limited duration, does that passage fail to prove the eternity of the Son?

question: Why do Paul's epistolary salutations wish grace and peace from the Father and the Son without mentioning the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Because the Holy Spirit is Himself the love and grace of the Father and the Son. The blessing wished from the Father and the Son is the Holy Spirit, so He need not be named separately as a third giver. Even in 2 Corinthians 13:14, where all three Persons are named, the blessing comes from the Father and the Son in the Holy Ghost, and the blessing from the Holy Ghost is His communication of Himself.
sources.quote: I can think of no other good account that can be given of the apostle Paul's wishing grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ in the beginning of his Epistles, without ever mentioning the Holy Ghost
sources.raw_question: Why does the apostle Paul, in the salutations of his Epistles, wish grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ without mentioning the Holy Spirit?

question: If the name Jehovah is applied to Christ, does it follow that Christ is the same one God as the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: Yes. Jehovah signifies the eternal, immutable God and is therefore incommunicable, since there is but one God; so whoever bears it properly must be that one God. Since Scripture applies it to Christ, Christ is the same one God, not the same Person as the Father but the same substance and Being, the same Jehovah revealed as more Persons than one.
sources.quote: the consequence is irresistible, that Christ is the same one God; not the same Person with the Father, to whom also the name Jehovah is attributed, but the same substance, the same Being ; in a word, the same Jehovah
sources.raw_question: If the name Jehovah is applied to Christ, does it follow that Christ is the same one God as the Father?

question: Is Christ called Jehovah in his own Person, or only as representing the Father, who alone is Jehovah in his own Person?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. Even Dr. Clarke admits the name Jehovah is given to the visible Person who represented the invisible God, not only to the Person represented. The opponent's own gloss on Hos. 1:7, that Jehovah saves 'not in his own Person', concedes that he saves by another Person whom the text expressly calls Jehovah. So the Son is Jehovah in his own Person and right.
sources.quote: “that Jehovah himself would save them, but not in his own Person.” Well then, it is by another Person, which Person the text expressly calls Jehovah.
sources.raised_by_detail: Dr. Clarke's defender (author of the Reply)
sources.raw_question: Is the Father alone Jehovah in his own Person, so that Christ is called Jehovah only as representing the Father?

question: Why is it so difficult to come to know the divine Trinity through the trinities found in the human mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God from the Trinities We Have Spoken of.
sources.answer: Because even our own mind, which is the image, is beyond our comprehension. If we cannot understand how memory, understanding and foresight work in us, still less can we grasp God's wisdom and knowledge, by which he made us. Yet this incomprehensibility should not end the search: we should seek God's face evermore. So we see God now only as in a glass, through the image that we are.
sources.quote: For I understand by myself how wonderful and incomprehensible is Thy knowledge, by which Thou madest me, when I cannot even comprehend myself whom Thou hast made!
sources.raw_question: Why is it so difficult to come to know the divine Trinity through the trinities found in the human mind?

question: Why is understanding the Trinity so difficult, and why does Scripture speak of God in such varied and puzzling ways?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Preface.
sources.answer: The difficulty has two sources. The mind strains to gaze on light unapproachable, and Scripture uses manifold and various modes of speech. Augustine holds that this difficulty is purposeful: through it the mind is roughly exercised so that it may later find sweetness when glorified by the grace of Christ.
sources.quote: wherein, as it seems to me, the mind is nothing else but roughly exercised, in order that it may find sweetness when glorified by the grace of Christ
sources.raw_question: Why is understanding the Trinity so difficult, and why does Scripture speak of God in such varied and puzzling ways?

question: Does 1 John 4:8-13 teach that the Holy Spirit is the love of God?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Verse 8 says God is love, so the divine essence subsists in love. Verses 12 and 13 make the same argument twice: in verse 12, having love dwell in us means having God dwell in us, and in verse 13 the apostle supports this by saying he has given us his Spirit. This assumes that love is God's Spirit and that God's Spirit is God. 1 John 3:24 gives the same argument.
sources.quote: In the 12th verse the apostle argues that if we have love dwelling in us we have God dwelling in us, and in the 13th verse He clears the force of the argument by this that love is God's Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 John 4:8-13 teach that the Holy Spirit is the love of God?

question: Does the argument of 1 John 4:12-13 presuppose that the Holy Spirit is God?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. The apostle argues that because we have God's Spirit dwelling in us, we have God dwelling in us. That inference only works if it is granted that God's Spirit is God.
sources.quote: Seeing we have God's Spirit dwelling in us, we have God dwelling in [in us], supposing it as a thing granted and allowed that God's Spirit is God.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 John 4:12-13 presuppose that the Holy Spirit is God?

question: Did Jesus Christ truly weep, given that God the Word cannot grieve and the divine Spirit cannot weep?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes. Hilary grants that God the Word cannot grieve and that the divine Spirit cannot weep. He still holds that Christ's weeping over Jerusalem was real, though how it happened is a mystery. The facts of Christ's human experience are certain even when their manner cannot be explained.
sources.quote: But God the Word cannot grieve, nor can the Spirit weep: nor could His soul possibly do anything before the body existed. Yet we cannot doubt that Jesus Christ truly wept
sources.raw_question: Did Jesus Christ truly weep, given that God the Word cannot grieve and the Spirit cannot weep?

question: Does a believer consciously direct faith to the Father's love at the first instant of believing, or does faith first come to the Father through Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No, not formally. We first believe in God through Christ, whom faith finds as the procuring cause of rest. But faith then passes through Christ to the Father and rests in his love.
sources.quote: It is true, as was said, we do not this formally in the first instant of believing. We believe in God through Christ, 1 Pet. i. 21; faith seeks out rest for the soul.
sources.raw_question: Does a believer consciously direct faith to the Father's love at the first instant of believing?

question: Must the believer first find love to God in himself before believing God the Father's love, or does the Father's love come first?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. Scripture teaches that the Father loved us first, not that we loved him; to make our love the ground of his love inverts this order and robs God of his glory. God loves us without cause in ourselves, and his love, received by faith, is what opens the soul to return love to him.
sources.quote: Herein is love,” saith the Holy Ghost, “not that we loved God, but that he loved us” first, 1 John iv. 10, 11. Now, thou wouldst invert this order
sources.raw_question: Does the believer's love to God come before God the Father's love to the believer, so that one must first find love in oneself before believing God's love?

question: Are God's love toward believers and believers' love toward God alike in being a love of rest and delight?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. Both are a love of rest and complacency. Zephaniah 3:17 shows God resting and rejoicing in his love: he is silent, without complaint, because his love is complete, and he will not seek another object.
sources.quote: Both these things are here assigned unto God in his love, — [^44]rest and delight.
sources.raw_question: Are God's love toward us and our love toward him alike in being a love of rest and delight?

question: Is God the Father's love toward believers a love of rest and delight (complacency), and not merely a love of willing them good?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen argues from Zephaniah 3:17 that God "rests" or is silent in his love, neither complaining of nor removing it from its object, and that he rejoices with gladness and exults with singing over those he loves. This expresses the greatest delight and complacency possible. Its contrary is shown where God is said to be "not well pleased" with those who draw back.
sources.quote: To rejoice with gladness of heart, to exult with singing and praise, argues the greatest delight and complacency possible.
sources.raw_question: Is God the Father's love toward believers a love of rest and delight (complacency), and not merely a love of willing them good?

question: Since 'a mediator is not a mediator of one,' does Christ's mediation imply that the one God is divided among the Father, Son and Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. God is one and is not divided among the Persons, because the Godhead in the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost is one. The two parties of the mediation are God and humanity, not Persons within the Godhead. The Lord therefore mediates once for all between God and men, binding man to the Deity in himself.
sources.quote: God is one, not divided among the Persons in Whom we have been taught to believe (for the Godhead in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost is one)
sources.raw_question: Since 'a mediator is not a mediator of one,' does Christ's mediation imply that the one God is divided among the Father, Son and Holy Spirit?

question: What do Christ's words in John 13:31-32, 'Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in Him... and God shall glorify Him in Himself', teach about the stages of Christ's glorification?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: They distinguish two glories. First, God is glorified in the Son of Man: the body is glorified by its association with the divine nature, so that the divine glory is seen in a human body, and this is shown in the power of the Resurrection. Second, God glorifies Him in Himself, which is still future. This means that Christ, leaving behind the Dispensation of subjection, is taken eternally into the glory of God, into the nature by which God is what He is.
sources.quote: So there is first signified the glory of the body, which it borrows from its association with the divine nature: and then follows the promotion to a fuller glory derived from an addition to the glory of the body.
sources.raw_question: What do Christ's words in John 13:31-32, 'Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in Him... and God shall glorify Him in Himself', teach about the stages of Christ's glorification?

question: In John 13:31, 'Now is the Son of Man glorified', is the glory Christ receives given to the Word in His divine nature or to His flesh?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It is given to His flesh. The glory obtained is not for the Word nor for the birth of His Godhead, but for the dispensation of His manhood born into the world. The Godhead needs no new glory. What is glorified is the humanity He assumed.
sources.quote: all the glory which He obtains is not for the Word but for His flesh: not for the birth of His Godhead, but for the dispensation of His manhood born into the world
sources.raw_question: In John 13:31, 'Now is the Son of Man glorified', is the glory received by Christ given to the Word in His divine nature or to His flesh?

question: Does the statement 'God is glorified in Him' (John 13:31) show either that Christ is God or that the Father's nature is in Christ?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes, it shows one or the other. The God glorified in the Son of Man must be either Christ glorified in the flesh or the Father glorified in Christ. If it is Christ, Christ is manifestly God. If it is the Father, the Father is glorified in the Son, which reveals the mystery of their unity and the Father's nature in Christ. Either way the heretic must confess Christ's Godhead.
sources.quote: if you allow it to be Christ, despite yourself you confess Him God; if you understand it of God the Father, you cannot deny the nature of God the Father in Christ
sources.raw_question: Does the statement 'God is glorified in Him' (John 13:31) show either that Christ is God or that the Father's nature is in Christ?

question: If Amos 4:13 is read spiritually, how should "thunders" and "spirit" be understood with reference to Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VI. To those who object that according to the words of Amos the Spirit is created, the answer is made that the word is there understood of the wind, which is often created, which cannot be said of the Holy Spirit, since He is eternal, and cannot be dissolved in death, or by an heretical absorption into the Father. But if they pertinaciously contend that this passage was written of the Holy Spirit, St. Ambrose points out that recourse must be had to a spiritual Interpretation, for Christ by His coming established the thunder, that is, the force of the divine utterances, and by Spirit is signified the human soul as also the flesh assumed by Christ. And since this was created by each Person of the Trinity, it is thence argued that the Spirit, Who has before been affirmed to be the Creator of all things, was the Author of the Incarnation of the Lord.
sources.answer: They refer to the Incarnation. Christ established the thunders by his coming, meaning the force and sound of the heavenly Scriptures that strike our minds with awe. The created "spirit" signifies the rational human soul Christ assumed, since Scripture often calls the human soul "spirit." So the passage speaks of a created human nature, not of the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: He established the thunders by His coming, that is, the force and sound of the heavenly Scriptures, by the thunder, as it were, of which our minds are struck with astonishment
sources.raw_question: If Amos 4:13 is read spiritually, how should "thunders" and "spirit" be understood with reference to Christ?

question: Is the human mind's ignorance and darkness a result of the curse for sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. Whatever we fall short of compared with the first man in innocence, whether good lost or evil added, comes from the curse for sin. The blindness, ignorance and darkness Scripture ascribes to people in their natural state include this loss of knowledge. The division of tongues was a further curse for a later rebellion.
sources.quote: Whatever we come short in of the state of the first man in innocence, whether in loss of good or addition of evil, it is all of the curse for sin.
sources.raw_question: Is the human mind's ignorance and darkness a result of the curse for sin?

question: Does the Son of God's incarnation unite humanity to God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IV.—The truth is to be found nowhere else but in the Catholic Church, the sole depository of apostolical doctrine. Heresies are of recent formation, and cannot trace their origin up to the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. Out of surpassing love for his creation, the Son of God condescended to be born of the virgin. Through himself he united man to God, then suffered, rose, and ascended in glory.
sources.quote: condescended to be born of the virgin, He Himself uniting man through Himself to God
sources.raw_question: Does the Son of God's incarnation unite humanity to God?

question: In the incarnation, did the Son of God unite himself to an already existing human person, or did the human nature subsist in the person of the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: The Son did not take an individual human person into conjunction with himself. Rather, he prevented the human nature from having its own personal subsistence and gave it subsistence in his own person, from which it has its individuation and distinction from all other persons. This is the personal union: the divine and human natures have but one personal subsistence and are one Christ.
sources.quote: preventing the personal subsistence of human nature in that flesh which he assumed, he gave it its subsistence in his own person; whence it has its individuation and distinction from all other persons whatever.
sources.raw_question: In the incarnation, did the Son of God unite himself to an already existing individual human person, or did the human nature subsist in the person of the Son?

question: Why did the Word take the form of a servant if He is Lord?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: He was made man not in order to exist, as men are clothed in flesh, but in order to sanctify the flesh. Though Lord, He took the servant's form. The whole creation, which came to be through Him, is the Word's servant.
sources.quote: men are clothed in flesh in order to be and to subsist; but the Word of God was made man in order to sanctify the flesh, and, though He was Lord, was in the form of a servant
sources.raw_question: Why did the Word take the form of a servant if He is Lord?

question: Did the Word's taking the form of a servant make Him a servant by nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: No. Though the Word in the form of God took a servant's form, the assumption of flesh did not make a servant of Him who was by nature Lord. Rather, by means of the servant's form He was made Lord of all and Christ, emancipating humanity and hallowing all by the Spirit.
sources.quote: the assumption of the flesh did not make a servant of the Word, who was by nature Lord
sources.raw_question: Did the Word's taking the form of a servant make him a servant by nature?

question: In what manner do believers hold communion with the person of Christ with respect to his personal grace?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: By way of a conjugal relation. Christ is married to believers and they to him, and this spiritual marriage is attended with suitable conjugal affections, which give fellowship with him in his personal excellencies. Scripture shows this in the spouse's words "My Beloved is mine, and I am his" and in God's promise to betroth his people to himself for ever.
sources.quote: Now, this the Scripture manifests to be by the way of a conjugal relation. He is married unto us, and we unto him; which spiritual relation is attended with suitable conjugal affections.
sources.raw_question: In what manner do believers hold communion with the person of Christ with respect to his personal grace?

question: What is the believer's part in communion with Christ with respect to his personal grace?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: It is the believer's free, willing consent to receive, embrace and submit to the Lord Jesus as husband, Lord and Saviour, to abide with him and be ruled by him for ever. Owen distinguishes the initial consent, which brings about union, from the renewed acts of consent made throughout life, which properly belong to communion. This self-resignation is completed by two things. The mind prefers Christ above all other beloveds, and the will accepts him as its only husband, Lord and Saviour.
sources.quote: On the part of the saints, it is their free, willing consent to receive, embrace, and submit unto the Lord Jesus, as their husband, Lord, and Saviour, — to abide with him, subject their souls unto him, and to be ruled by him for ever.
sources.raw_question: What is the believer's part in communion with Christ the Son with respect to his personal grace?

question: Is the 'personal grace' of Christ in which believers have communion the excellency of his Deity considered in itself, or the outward appearance of his human nature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Neither. It concerns Christ as mediator, so it is not his Deity abstracted from his office, nor the outward appearance of his humanity either on earth or in glory, which would be to know Christ after the flesh. It is the spiritual eminency and beauty of his person as vested with the office of mediation, appointed and anointed by the Father to bring home his elect.
sources.quote: the graces of the person of Christ as he is vested with the office of mediation, this spiritual eminency, comeliness, and beauty, as appointed and anointed by the Father unto the great work of bringing home all his elect unto his bosom.
sources.raw_question: Is the 'personal grace' of Christ in which believers have communion the excellency of his Deity considered in itself, or the outward appearance of his human nature?

question: Does the confession that Jesus is Lord "in the glory of God the Father" (Philippians 2:11) show that the Son possesses all that the Father is?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. The Father glorifies the Son not with an external glory but in Himself, taking Him back into the glory that belongs to the Father and which the Son had with Him before. Since the Son is confessed in the Father's own glory and is glorified in the Father Himself, He is plainly all that His Father is.
sources.quote: The Father glorifies Him, not with a glory from without, but in Himself. By taking Him back into that glory, which belongs to Himself, and which He had with Him before, the Father glorifies Him with Himself and in Himself.
sources.raw_question: Does the confession that Jesus is Lord "in the glory of God the Father" (Philippians 2:11) show that the Son possesses all that the Father is?

question: Does confessing Jesus as Lord "in the glory of God the Father" (Philippians 2:11) mean that Christ still remains in the weakness of human flesh?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Jesus, though born as man, no longer abides in the infirmity of our body but in the glory of God the Father. Because the fulness of the Godhead dwells in him bodily, the whole universe bows to him and he is head of all principalities and powers.
sources.quote: Jesus shall be confessed in the glory of God the Father, born in man, yet now no longer abiding in the infirmity of our body, but in the glory of God.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing Jesus as Lord 'in the glory of God the Father' (Philippians 2:11) mean Christ still remains in the weakness of human flesh?

question: When applied to the Son, is the Arian definition of 'God by nature' in Galatians 4:8 (exercising divine dominion universally, permanently and unalterably) a coherent reading?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 24: Whether Gal. iv. 8. may not be enough to determine the dispute betwiat us; since it obliged the Doctor to confess, that Christ as by nature truly God, as truly
sources.answer: No. Applied to the Son, the definition contradicts itself on its own terms. Universal exercise is impossible for a finite creature. Permanence conflicts with their view that the Son's kingdom will end. Unalterableness conflicts with their admission that the Son's dominion alters. Attributing such a meaning to the inspired Apostle shows him no respect.
sources.quote: if these things be so; that is, if contradictions be true, what then? Then “such a Being, or Person, is God by nature,” &c.
sources.raw_question: Is the Arian definition of 'God by nature' (exercising divine dominion universally, permanently and unalterably) a coherent reading of Galatians 4:8 when applied to the Son?

question: If Galatians 4:8 implies that Christ is God by nature, does it contradict a scheme in which the Son has a nature distinct from and inferior to God's?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 24: Whether Gal. iv. 8. may not be enough to determine the dispute betwiat us; since it obliged the Doctor to confess, that Christ as by nature truly God, as truly
sources.answer: Yes. The text obliged Clarke to confess that the Son is by nature truly God. A scheme that gives the Son a nature distinct from and inferior to God's, lacking God's most essential character, cannot stand with that text and is an express contradiction to it.
sources.quote: The Doctor, I observed, was obliged from Gal. iv. 8. to confess that the Son is dy nature truly God. From thence 1 infer, that his scheme cannot stand with that text; being an express contradiction to it.
sources.raw_question: Does Galatians 4:8, by implying that Christ is God by nature, contradict a scheme in which the Son has a nature distinct from and inferior to God's?

question: In the mutual love between God the Father and believers, is the believers' love to the Father as constant and unchanging as the Father's love to them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No. The Father's love to the saints never changes, but our love to God ebbs and flows, waning and increasing almost daily. Owen illustrates this from Peter's vow followed by his denial and from the psalmist's swings between confidence and despair. This discrepancy, alongside the agreements, further describes the mutual love in which the Father and the saints hold communion.
sources.quote: But now our love to God is ebbing and flowing, waning and increasing. We lose our first love, and we grow again in love;[^60] — scarce a day at a stand. What poor creatures are we! How unlike the Lord and his love!
sources.raw_question: In the mutual love between God the Father and believers, is the believers' love to the Father as constant and unchanging as the Father's love to them?

question: How does the Father's love toward believers differ in kind from believers' love toward the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: The Father's love is a love of bounty, theirs a love of duty. His love descends and is always communicating, like a fountain or the rain from heaven, creating goodness in its objects; and since God's power and will are commensurate, what he wills he works. Our love ascends as a child's in duty and thankfulness, consisting of rest, delight, reverence and obedience, and adds nothing to him (Job 35:5-8; Rom. 11:35; Mal. 1:6).
sources.quote: He adds to us by his love; we nothing to him by ours. Our goodness extends not unto him.
sources.raw_question: How does the Father's love toward believers differ from believers' love toward the Father?

question: Is love toward God the Father possible apart from faith in the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. We have no love toward the Father except through faith in the Son. Scripture says everyone who loves the Father loves him who is born from him.
sources.quote: For we have no love within us towards God the Father except through faith in the Son.
sources.raw_question: Is love toward God the Father possible apart from faith in the Son?

question: Is prayer and worship in Scripture directed distinctly to the Father as a person?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Believers call on the Father and Paul bows his knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, so prayer is directed to the Father as the fountain of the Deity and of all good in Christ. Paul also conjoins yet distinguishes the Father and the Son in his supplications, and blesses the God and Father of Christ in thanksgiving.
sources.quote: The workings, then, of the Spirit of grace in that duty are distinctly directed to the Father as such, as the fountain of the Deity, and of all good things in Christ
sources.raw_question: Is prayer and worship in Scripture directed distinctly to the Father as a person?

question: Is Christ's love for his people eternal?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son speaks of himself as present 'from the time that it was' (Isaiah 48:16). He is 'yesterday, today, and for ever' and is Alpha and Omega, the first and the last. His love is therefore as eternal as he is, having no beginning and no ending.
sources.quote: He himself is “yesterday, today, and for ever,” Heb. xiii. 8; and so is his love, being his who is “Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the ending,
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's love for his people eternal?

question: Is the title 'God over all' reserved to the Father, so that the Son is among the 'all things' beneath him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. The phrase 'over all' is common to the Son and the Father. The Apostle expressly ascribes it to Christ when he says that Christ came 'as concerning the flesh,' 'Who is God over all.' Contrasting the Son with the 'God over all' wrongly ranks him among created things.
sources.quote: this phrase, “over all,” as has been previously observed, is common to the Son with the Father, the Apostle having expressly ascribed such a title to Him
sources.raw_question: Is the title 'God over all' reserved to the Father, so that the Son is one of the 'all things' beneath him?

question: When Scripture says the Father put all things under the Son, does this mean the Son does not himself subject all things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: No. Philippians 3:21 says Christ is able to subdue all things to himself, and the working of the Father and the Son is indivisible. In 1 Corinthians 15:24 it is the Son who puts down all rule and authority, and the one who puts down also makes subject.
sources.quote: For the working of the Father and of the Son is indivisible.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says the Father put all things under the Son, does this mean the Son himself does not subject all things?

question: How can memory, understanding, and will be both one and three, and what is the difference between terms said of them absolutely and terms said relatively?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > In Memory, Understanding [or Intelligence], and Will, We Have to Note Ability, Learning, and Use. Memory, Understanding, and Will are One Essentially, and Three Relatively.
sources.answer: They are one in what is said of each in respect to itself, and three in what is said relatively. Life, mind, and essence are said of each absolutely, and of all together only in the singular. The names memory, understanding, and will are said relatively to something, and in these mutual relations they are three.
sources.quote: But they are three, in that wherein they are mutually referred to each other
sources.raw_question: How can memory, understanding, and will be both one and three, and what is the difference between terms said absolutely and terms said relatively of them?

question: Are memory, understanding, and will equal to one another, and how is this shown?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > In Memory, Understanding [or Intelligence], and Will, We Have to Note Ability, Learning, and Use. Memory, Understanding, and Will are One Essentially, and Three Relatively.
sources.answer: Yes. Each is equal to each and to all, because they mutually contain one another as wholes. I remember my whole memory, understanding, and will. I understand all three, and my will embraces my whole understanding and memory as I use them. Things that were not equal could not contain each other in this way.
sources.quote: while all are mutually comprehended by each, and as wholes, each as a whole is equal to each as a whole, and each as a whole at the same time to all as wholes
sources.raw_question: Are memory, understanding, and will equal to one another, and how is this shown?

question: How does the memory contain the whole of the understanding and the will?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > In Memory, Understanding [or Intelligence], and Will, We Have to Note Ability, Learning, and Use. Memory, Understanding, and Will are One Essentially, and Three Relatively.
sources.answer: Whatever I understand, I know that I understand, and whatever I will, I know that I will. Whatever I know, I remember. So I remember the whole of my understanding and the whole of my will. And nothing is so much in the memory as memory itself.
sources.quote: whatever I understand I know that I understand, and I know that I will whatever I will; but whatever I know I remember. Therefore I remember the whole of my understanding, and the whole of my will.
sources.raw_question: How does the memory contain the whole understanding and will?

question: Can the Word of God suffer death without undergoing any change in his own divine nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: Yes. The Word of God remains in himself and is in no way changeable, yet by taking upon himself a lower nature he can suffer something of a lower kind. The suffering belongs to the assumed flesh, which the devil, lacking an earthly body, cannot undergo.
sources.quote: the Word of God, remaining in Himself, and in Himself in no way changeable, may yet, through the taking upon Him of a lower nature, be able to suffer somewhat of a lower kind
sources.raw_question: Can the Word of God suffer death without undergoing change in his own divine nature?

question: Could the divine Word, as God, genuinely fear death?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Twelfthly, Matthew xxvi. 39; John xii. 27, &c. Arian inferences are against the Regula Fidei, as before. He wept and the like, as man. Other texts prove Him God. God could not fear. He feared because His flesh feared.
sources.answer: No. He who is Life itself and rescues others from death, who told others not to fear and encouraged Abraham, Moses and Joshua, could not himself be terrified of death or of mortal rulers. His voluntary surrender shows this: He did not flee but said 'I am He,' and had power to lay down His life and take it again.
sources.quote: whom had He to fear being God? or wherefore should He fear death, who was Himself Life, and was rescuing others from death?
sources.raw_question: Could the divine Word, as God, genuinely fear death?

question: Does the statement in Hebrews 7:22 that Jesus 'was made' (became) surety of a better testament imply that the Son's essence was created or came into being?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. 'Become' is said of the Son in a second sense, because He became man, just as in 'the Word became flesh' the becoming is ascribed to the created flesh. Paul knew the Son to be Son, Wisdom, Radiance and Image of the Father, so he refers 'become' to the ministry of the covenant and the pledge provided on our behalf, not to the Word's essence.
sources.quote: Paul does not signify that His essence has become, knowing, as he did, that He is Son and Wisdom and Radiance and Image of the Father; but here too he refers the word ‘become’ to the ministry of that covenant
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'Jesus was made (became) surety of a better testament' in Hebrews 7:22 imply that the Son's essence was created or came into being?

question: Why does Hebrews 7:22 call Christ the surety of a better covenant rather than of a testament, and for whom is He surety?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: Because a testament needs no surety, so the word is better rendered covenant. Christ is surety for both parties: for man, to give satisfaction, and for God, to bestow the whole grace of the promise.
sources.quote: He is the undertaker on the part of God and man also: of man, to give satisfaction; of God, to bestow the whole grace of the promise
sources.raw_question: Why does Hebrews 7:22 call Christ the surety of a better covenant rather than of a testament?

question: How does the human mind's trinity of memory, thought (inner word) and will illustrate the difference between the generation of the Son and the procession of the Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What It is that Suffices Here to Solve the Question Why the Spirit is Not Said to Be Begotten, and Why the Father Alone is Unbegotten. What They Ought to Do Who Do Not Understand These Things.
sources.answer: The inner word is born of knowledge, as an image of what memory contains, like offspring from parent. Will or love proceeds from thought, since no one wills what he is wholly ignorant of. Yet the will is not an image of the thought, because beholding is not the same as desiring or enjoying. This hints at a difference between birth, which produces an image, and procession, which does not.
sources.quote: this will proceeds indeed from thought (for no one wills that of which he is absolutely ignorant what or of what sort it is), yet is not an image of the thought: and so that there is insinuated in this intelligible thing a sort of difference between birth and procession
sources.raw_question: How does the human mind's trinity of memory, thought (inner word) and will illustrate the difference between generation and procession in God?

question: Why can the human mind not clearly see the difference between the generation of the Son and the procession of the Spirit in God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What It is that Suffices Here to Solve the Question Why the Spirit is Not Said to Be Begotten, and Why the Father Alone is Unbegotten. What They Ought to Do Who Do Not Understand These Things.
sources.answer: Because of infirmity, which iniquity has produced. The divine light shows the mind many true things, including the trinitarian image in itself. But the mind cannot look steadily at that light until it is healed by Him who forgives all its iniquities.
sources.quote: What reason, then, is there why thou canst not see that light itself with steady eye, except certainly infirmity? And what has produced this in thee, except iniquity?
sources.raw_question: Why can the human mind not clearly see the difference between the generation of the Son and the procession of the Spirit in God?

question: Does mortal flesh become immortal by its own nature or by the power of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIII.—In the dead who were raised by Christ we possess the highest proof of the resurrection; and our hearts are shown to be capable of life eternal, because they can now receive the Spirit of God.
sources.answer: By the power of God. The flesh becomes immortal and incorruptible not according to its own proper substance but through the mighty working of the Lord, who is able to clothe the mortal with immortality. God, who has given us the earnest of the Spirit, perfects us for this, so that mortality is swallowed up of life. Paul says this of the flesh, since the soul and spirit are not mortal.
sources.quote: not after its own proper substance, but after the mighty working of the Lord, who is able to invest the mortal with immortality, and the corruptible with incorruption.
sources.raw_question: Does mortal flesh become immortal by its own nature or by the power of God?

question: How does the single death of Christ free humanity from many sins and deaths?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: Because Christ's one death was preceded by no sin, it was not owed. By rendering an undue death for us, He loosed the bonds of many sins in many deaths, so that the death which was due might do us no harm. His death was the one most real sacrifice. It cleansed and abolished whatever fault had given the powers a hold over us.
sources.quote: For it was brought to pass that the bonds of many sins in many deaths were loosed, through the one death of One which no sin had preceded.
sources.raw_question: How does the single death of Christ free humanity from many sins and deaths?

question: What is the purpose of Christ's death and resurrection, the separation and reuniting of his soul and body, for human nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: It gives all human nature a beginning and an example of resurrection from the dead. Through it the corruptible puts on incorruption and the mortal puts on immortality. Our first-fruits were transformed to the divine nature by union with God, as Peter says: God made this Jesus both Lord and Christ.
sources.quote: so as to give to all human nature a beginning and an example which it should follow of the resurrection from the dead, that all the corruptible may put on incorruption, and all the mortal may put on immortality
sources.raw_question: What is the purpose of Christ's death and resurrection, the separation and reuniting of his soul and body, for human nature?

question: Does God's revelation of Himself to Moses as "He Who is" (Exodus 3:14) give a name that discloses the divine essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > After much discourse concerning the actually existent, and ungenerate and good, and upon the consubstantiality of the heavenly powers, showing the uncharted character of their essence, yet the difference of their ranks, he ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Scripture gives Moses "the Being" without a name, and the other divine names are all attributes of that Being. Anyone claiming to explain the essence must reveal its actual nature, not list its attributes. To recite "good" or "ungenerate" while staying silent on the essence is to speak in vain.
sources.quote: For every name which you may use is an attribute of the Being, but is not the Being,—“good,” “ungenerate,” “incorruptible,”—but to each of these “is” does not fail to be supplied.
sources.raw_question: Does God's revelation of Himself to Moses as "He Who is" give a name that discloses the divine essence?

question: What does the divine name 'He Who is' (Exodus 3:14) teach about God's being?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: It teaches that absolute being belongs to God. What is cannot be thought of as not being, since being and not-being are contraries and cannot both be true of the same thing. However far our thought reaches backward, it finds nothing prior to the fact that God always is.
sources.quote: we obtain the unambiguous conception that absolute being belongs to God; since that which is, cannot be thought of or spoken of as not being.
sources.raw_question: What does the divine name 'He Who is' (Exodus 3:14) teach about God's being?

question: Is the Son the 'He who is' (ho on) of Exodus 3:14, implying uncreated, necessary existence?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. Justin equates Moses' 'He who is' with the Platonists' 'that which is', meaning ever-existing and without origin, i.e. uncreated and necessarily existing; and he makes the Word, who spoke to Moses, to be 'He who is' in his own person. He grounds this on the Son's being God as God's firstborn Son.
sources.quote: it is manifest that Justin makes the Adyos to be ὁ ὧν, in his own proper person.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son 'He who is' (ho on) of Exodus 3:14, implying uncreated, necessary existence?

question: Does Christ's saying that he casts out devils by the Spirit of God, together with his saying that a divided kingdom is destroyed, show that Christ and the Holy Spirit hold the kingdom of God undivided?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XX. The river flowing from the Throne of God is a figure of the Holy Spirit, but by the waters spoken of by David the powers of heaven are intended. The kingdom of God is the work of the Spirit; and it is no matter for wonder if He reigns in this together with the Son, since St. Paul promises that we too shall reign with the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ first says that every kingdom divided against itself is destroyed. He then says that if he casts out devils by the Spirit of God, the kingdom has come. Joined together, these sayings show that the kingdom of God is held undivided by Christ and the Spirit.
sources.quote: He shows that the kingdom of God is held undivided by Himself and by the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying about casting out devils by the Spirit of God show that he and the Spirit hold the kingdom of God undivided?

question: Does Christ's casting out devils 'by the Spirit of God' show that He acts by the power of His own divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. Here 'Spirit of God' indicates the Son Himself. Christ shows that He casts out devils by the power of His own nature, and devils cannot be cast out except by the Spirit of God.
sources.quote: He shews clearly that He, by the power of His nature, casts out devils, which cannot be cast out save by the Spirit of God.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's casting out devils 'by the Spirit of God' show that He acts by His own divine nature?

question: Is the breath of life given to Adam at creation the same thing as the vivifying Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XII.—Of the difference between life and death; of the breath of life and the vivifying Spirit: also how it is that the substance of flesh revives which once was dead.
sources.answer: No. The breath of life made man an animated being and is given in common to all, but the vivifying Spirit makes man spiritual and is given only to those who tread down earthly desires. Isaiah distinguishes them, saying God gave breath to the people and Spirit to those walking upon the earth.
sources.quote: For the breath of life, which also rendered man an animated being, is one thing, and the vivifying Spirit another, which also caused him to become spiritual.
sources.raw_question: Is the breath of life given to Adam at creation the same thing as the vivifying Holy Spirit?

question: Is the Holy Spirit a created thing like the breath of life, or is the Spirit eternal and proper to God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XII.—Of the difference between life and death; of the breath of life and the vivifying Spirit: also how it is that the substance of flesh revives which once was dead.
sources.answer: The Spirit is eternal and proper to God, while breath is created and temporal. Isaiah's words 'the Spirit shall go forth from Me, and I have made every breath' attribute the Spirit as peculiar to God but present breath as something made. Since what is made differs from the one who makes it, the breath is temporal and the Spirit eternal.
sources.quote: Now what has been made is a different thing from him who makes it. The breath, then, is temporal, but the Spirit eternal.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a created thing like the breath of life, or is the Spirit eternal and proper to God?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's "hearing" imply bodily organs or that He learns what He did not know?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son.
