The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit hears by unity of substance and by the property of knowledge, not through bodily orifices. In men, hearing produces knowledge, but in God, who knows all things, knowledge comes before hearing. Even among men hearing is not always bodily, as with one who speaks in tongues. Scripture says He hears so that we may believe that He knows.
sources.quote: He hears, that is to say, by unity of substance and by the property of knowledge. For He receives not hearing by any orifices of the body, nor does the divine voice resound with any carnal measures, nor does He hear what He knows not
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's "hearing" imply bodily organs or that He learns what He did not know?

question: Does God need bodily members or organs to see, hear, and act?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And That, Although Scripture Often Changes the Divine Appearance into a Human Form, Yet the Measure of the Divine Majesty is Not Included Within These Lineaments of Our Bodily Nature.
sources.answer: No. Members are needed by men because a human design is ineffectual unless the body fulfils the thought, but God's will is itself effective: His thought is a command and His works proceed simultaneously with His will. He who is light needs no eyes, He who knows unexpressed wills needs no ears. Rather He is all eye, all ear, all hand, all foot.
sources.quote: For why should He require eyes who is Himself the light? or why should He ask for feet who is everywhere?
sources.raw_question: Does God need bodily members or organs to see, hear, and act?

question: Can 'substance' be predicated of God relatively, so that the three substances (hypostases) are distinguished by relation?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: No. That would be absurd. If subsisting were relative, as being Father or Lord is relative, then substance would no longer be substance. Everything subsists in respect to itself, and God does so all the more. Substance therefore cannot be a relative term. Augustine goes on to conclude that 'substance' is applied to God only improperly, while 'essence' applies properly.
sources.quote: But it is absurd that substance should be spoken relatively, for everything subsists in respect to itself; how much more God?
sources.raw_question: Can 'substance' be predicated of God relatively, so that the three substances (hypostases) are distinguished by relation?

question: What does the satisfaction made by Christ consist in, according to the orthodox doctrine?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: It is the voluntary obedience unto death and the suffering of Jesus Christ, God and man, in which he offered himself through the eternal Spirit as a propitiatory sacrifice. By this he fulfilled the law. As our sponsor he also bore the punishment due to us from God's justice, which was transferred to him. He thereby made perfect atonement for sin and obtained for us deliverance from death and the curse, and a right to eternal life.
sources.quote: the voluntary obedience unto death, and the passion or suffering, of our Lord Jesus Christ, God and man, whereby and wherein he offered himself through the eternal Spirit, for a propitiatory sacrifice, that he might fulfil the law
sources.raw_question: What does the satisfaction made by Christ consist in, according to the orthodox doctrine?

question: Does Scripture teach that Christ made real satisfaction to God for sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Owen argues that if Christ, by the Father's will and his own choice, was substituted for sinners, bore their sins by undergoing the curse of the law, offered himself as a propitiatory sacrifice, and paid a real price of redemption, then he made satisfaction. He then shows from Scripture that each of these things is testified. Satisfaction means nothing more than these things taken together.
sources.quote: then he made satisfaction to God for sin: for these are the things that we intend by that expression of satisfaction
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that Christ made real satisfaction to God for sin?

question: Is anything due to God's justice for sin, such that sin deserves punishment?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Denying that sin deserves punishment in God's justice is a doctrine comfortable only to those resolved to continue in sin. Scripture teaches that all our iniquities were laid on Christ, that he bore them in his body on the tree, and that his soul was made an offering for sin, making atonement.
sources.quote: The Scripture tells us that Christ paid what he took not; that all our iniquities were caused to meet upon him; that he bare them in his own body on the tree
sources.raw_question: Is anything due to God's justice for sin, such that sin deserves punishment?

question: Why does God's pardoning of sin necessarily remove its punishment?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Because guilt contains an obligation to punishment. When nasa is used of God's act toward sin, it means to lift up or take away the guilt of iniquity. Once the guilt is pardoned, the removal of the punishment necessarily follows as its consequence.
sources.quote: for God pardoning the guilt of sin, the removal of the punishment does necessarily ensue, guilt containing an obligation unto punishment
sources.raw_question: Why does God's pardoning of sin necessarily remove its punishment?

question: Did Christ make satisfaction for sin as God, as man, or as God and man?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: As God and man. Scripture says God redeemed his church with his own blood and laid down his life for us. Since Christ is one person in two natures, all his mediatory acts are acts of his person and therefore necessarily acts of him as God and man.
sources.quote: for all the mediatory acts of Christ being the acts of his person, must of necessity be the acts of him as God and man.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ make satisfaction for sin as God, as man, or as God and man?

question: Does the doctrine of Christ's satisfaction diminish the true purpose of Christ's life and death?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Every end the Socinians assign to Christ's life and death—teaching truth, confirming it by his death, giving an example—is also affirmed, belonging to his prophetical office. In addition, as priest he offered himself a sacrifice to make atonement and died in our stead, which is the principal end that gives efficacy to the rest.
sources.quote: All the ends, then, which they themselves assign of the life and death of Christ are by us granted; and the principal one, which gives life and efficacy to the rest, is by them denied.
sources.raw_question: Does the doctrine of Christ's satisfaction diminish the true purpose of Christ's life and death?

question: Does the doctrine of satisfaction deprive God of the praise due to his love?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Scripture fixes God's love principally on his sending his only begotten Son to die for us, and the greater the work he undertook, the greater our acknowledgment of his love ought to be.
sources.quote: The love and kindness of God towards us is in the Scripture fixed principally and fundamentally on his “sending of his only begotten Son to die for us.”
sources.raw_question: Does the doctrine of satisfaction deprive God of the praise due to his love?

question: Does the doctrine of satisfaction make the Son more loving than the Father, contradicting their being the same God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Scripture ascribes love to the Father in sending the Son and electing sinners, and to the Son in giving himself; there is no scale to weigh which is greater. The Father's sending was an act of will, an essential property of God, so it was also the Son's act as sharer of the same nature, though by order peculiarly the Father's. God's anger against sin flows from his essential righteousness, which does not hinder Father, Son and Spirit all acting in love toward sinners.
sources.quote: The love of the Father in sending of the Son was an act of his will; which being a natural and essential property of God, it was so far the act of the Son also, as he is partaker of the same nature
sources.raw_question: Does the doctrine of satisfaction make the Son more loving than the Father, contradicting their being the same God?

question: Does justifying sinners through Christ's righteousness compromise either God's justice or God's grace?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No, it shows both in full. A complete righteousness is provided, which satisfies justice, while grace is still shown in abundance. Toward the sinner as a person God acts with pure grace. Toward the righteousness by which the sinner is accepted, God acts with pure justice.
sources.quote: to have God’s dealing with his person all grace, and dealing with his righteousness all justice, takes up his thoughts.
sources.raw_question: Does justifying sinners through Christ's righteousness compromise either God's justice or God's grace?

question: Does God know created things because they have been made, or are they made because He knows them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Of the Attributes Assigned by Hilary to Each Person. The Trinity is Represented in Things that are Made.
sources.answer: Things are made because God knows them unchangeably, not known because they are made. God knew all things in His Word, through which He made them. So while times pass and succeed, nothing passes away or succeeds in God's knowledge.
sources.quote: For things which are created are not therefore known by God, because they have been made; and not rather have been therefore made, even although changeable, because they are known unchangeably by Him.
sources.raw_question: Does God know created things because they have been made, or are they made because He knows them?

question: Does God know and providentially determine the number and quantity of every created thing?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVI.—“Knowledge puffeth up, but love edifieth.”
sources.answer: Yes. Nothing that has been, is, or shall be made escapes God's knowledge. Through his providence each thing has received its nature, rank, number and special quantity, and nothing is produced in vain or by accident. This reflects an admirable and truly divine intellect.
sources.quote: through His providence every one of them has obtained its nature, and rank, and number, and special quantity, and that nothing whatever either has been or is produced in vain or accidentally
sources.raw_question: Does God know and providentially determine the number and quantity of every created thing?

question: What three elements make up the trinity Augustine finds in the act of recollecting or thinking of a body once seen?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > The Unity of the Three Takes Place in Thought, Viz. Of Memory, of Ternal Vision, and of Will Combining Both.
sources.answer: It is made of memory, internal vision, and the will that unites them. The memory takes the place of the outward bodily object and retains its likeness. The mind's eye is informed from that likeness, which takes the place of outward sight. The will turns the mind's gaze to the memory just as it once applied the bodily sense to the external body. When the three are combined into one, the result is called conception or thought.
sources.quote: And so that trinity is produced from memory, from internal vision, and from the will which unites both. And when these three things are combined into one, from that combination itself they are called conception.
sources.raw_question: What three elements make up the trinity that Augustine finds in the act of recollecting or thinking of a body once seen?

question: What are the three elements of the trinity Augustine finds in bodily sight, and do they share one nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Certain Trinity in the Sight. That There are Three Things in Sight, Which Differ in Their Own Nature. In What Manner from a Visible Thing Vision is Produced, or the Image of that Thing Which is Seen. The Matter is Shown More Clearly by an Example. How These Three Combine in One.
sources.answer: They are the form of the visible body, the image of it impressed on the sense (vision), and the will of the mind applying sense to the object; they differ in nature. The visible thing does not belong to the living being's nature (unless it is one's own body), vision belongs to it as wrought in body and soul together, and the will belongs to the soul alone.
sources.quote: The first of these, that is, the visible thing itself, does not belong to the nature of the living being, except when we discern our own body. But the second belongs to that nature to this extent, that it is wrought in the body, and through the body in the soul
sources.raw_question: What are the three elements of the trinity Augustine finds in bodily sight, and do they share one nature?

question: If some passages of Scripture cannot be explained, does that justify seeking another God besides the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: No. Seeking another God because of unexplained texts is the greatest impiety. Such matters should be left to God. The Scriptures are perfect because they were spoken by the Word of God and His Spirit, and our ignorance comes from our own limitation, not from any defect in them.
sources.quote: let us not on that account seek after any other God besides Him who really exists. For this is the very greatest impiety.
sources.raw_question: If some passages of Scripture cannot be explained, does that justify seeking another God besides the Creator?

question: What does Abraham's going out 'not knowing whither he went' teach about the knowledge of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Read allegorically, it shows the mind rising above sense and every conception suggested by divine names. Abraham reached the height of human knowledge of God, yet did not learn God's name. His sure token of knowing God was the belief that God is greater than any token by which he may be known.
sources.quote: he made this a sure and manifest token of the knowledge of God, viz. the belief that He is greater and more sublime than any token by which He may be known.
sources.raw_question: What does Abraham's going out 'not knowing whither he went' teach about the knowledge of God?

question: Does Christ's being born of a virgin prove that he is more than a mere man?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: No. Being born of a woman is, by Scripture and common sense, an invincible proof that he is a man, and, as born of her, no more. Scripture speaks of him as made of the seed of David according to the flesh and made of a woman.
sources.quote: Strange! that that should be an argument to prove him more than a man, which the Scripture, and all men in their right wits, grant to be an invincible reason to prove him to be a man
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's being born of a virgin prove that he is more than a mere man?

question: Does Christ's claim to know whence he came and whither he goes (John 8:14) show that he is more than a mere man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ says he will return to where he came from, namely heaven, whence he was sent. A mere man could not come from heaven and so could not return there; since Christ came from heaven, he shows himself to have come as God.
sources.quote: Moreover, by coming thence, whence as man He could not have come, He shows Himself to have come as God.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold Christ is only man
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's claim to know whence he came and whither he goes (John 8:14) show that he is more than a mere man?

question: Does God cease to be present everywhere when He is said to be present in a particular place?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Unlike bodies, which are confined to where they are, God is present everywhere and absent nowhere. Through His own things He is present in all places, and those things are none other than Himself.
sources.quote: Yet we must not think that, after a corporeal fashion, when He is in one place He ceases to be everywhere, for through His own things He is still present in all places
sources.raw_question: Does God cease to be present everywhere when He is said to be present in a particular place?

question: Can an inferior God be admitted alongside the supreme God, with worship paid to both?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. In the judgment of the ancients generally, nothing strikes more at the very foundations of religion than admitting a second, inferior God and worshipping both.
sources.quote: That an inferior God may be admitted besides the supreme, and worship paid to both. Nothing can strike more at the very fundamentals of religion than this position
sources.raw_question: Can an inferior God be admitted alongside the supreme God, with worship paid to both?

question: Can a 'more honourable' rank be posited among the divine Persons without implying a less honourable divine Person?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His elaborate account of degrees and differences in 'works' and 'energies' within the Trinity is absurd.
sources.answer: No. To speak of a 'more honourable' necessarily implies a 'less honourable.' Calling the Son and Spirit graded 'works' therefore predicates 'less precious' of a divine Person. Gregory judges this view so abominable that it hardly deserves treatment as an argument.
sources.quote: For can a ‘more honourable’ be discovered where there is not a less honourable?
sources.raw_question: Can a 'more honourable' rank be posited among the divine Persons (the Son and the Spirit as more or less honourable 'works') without implying a less honourable divine Person?

question: Is the inner 'word' of a thing its name, whether spoken or silently thought, or the image or notion of the thing in the mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: It is the image or notion in the mind. The word of Carthage is the image of it held in memory, which the mind discerns before or while uttering the name. It is not the two-syllable sound, nor that name thought over silently.
sources.quote: For its word is the image itself of it in my memory, not that sound of two syllables when Carthage is named, or even when that name itself is thought of silently from time to time
sources.raw_question: Is the inner 'word' of a thing the spoken or silently thought name, or the image or notion of the thing in the mind?

question: In Christ's substitution for sinners, was the law relaxed as to the penalty to be suffered, or only as to the person who would suffer it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Only as to the person. The substitution was voluntary on the part of God and of Christ, and it required a relaxation of the law regarding who would suffer, but not regarding what was to be suffered. If the penalty itself had been relaxed, Christ's suffering would not have been punishment properly so called. Nor could the law have been satisfied by it.
sources.quote: there was a relaxation of the law as to the persons that were to suffer, though not as to what was to be suffered.
sources.raw_question: In Christ's substitution for sinners, was the law relaxed as to the penalty to be suffered, or only as to the person who would suffer it?

question: Why was the incarnate Son of God, rather than any other, fit to be substituted in the place of sinners to bear the penalty of the law?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Because he alone had both the right and the will to dispose of himself for this office, and because the dignity of his divine person enabled him to answer the penalty that all others had incurred. Owen holds that the substitute had to be one with power over his own life who was willing to undertake the work. His sufferings could also satisfy for the guilt of many because of the worth of his person.
sources.quote: the person thus substituted was the Son of God incarnate, who had power so to dispose of himself, with will and readiness for it; and was, upon the account of the dignity of his person, able to answer the penalty which all others had incurred
sources.raw_question: Why was the incarnate Son of God, rather than any other, fit to be substituted in the place of sinners to bear the penalty of the law?

question: Did Christ fulfil and satisfy the law and its penalty on behalf of sinners?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Christ answered both the law and its penalty. God sent his Son made under the law to redeem those under the law, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by being made a curse for us.
sources.quote: That he answered the law and the penalty of it
sources.raw_question: Did Christ fulfil and satisfy the law and its penalty on behalf of sinners?

question: Could Christ have suffered a different kind of punishment from the one sinners deserved and still have satisfied for their sins?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: No. It would not have agreed with justice, and the nature of the things does not allow it. If the punishment were different, our sin could not have been the impulsive cause of his death. Nor could we have received any benefit from it.
sources.quote: Nor was it agreeable to justice, nor would the nature of the things themselves admit of it, that another punishment should be inflicted on Christ than what we had deserved
sources.raw_question: Could Christ have suffered a different kind of punishment from the one sinners deserved and still have satisfied for their sins?

question: Is it a serious error to deny that Christ, in his death, underwent the punishment due to our sins?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Yes. Such a denial overturns the great foundation of the gospel. It also openly perverts the plain words of Scripture to suit men's imaginations, and so gives no small countenance to infidelity and atheism.
sources.quote: to deny that the Lord Christ, in his death and suffering for us, underwent the punishment due to our sins, what we had deserved, that we might be delivered, as it everts the great foundation of the gospel
sources.raw_question: Is it a serious error to deny that Christ, in his death, underwent the punishment due to our sins?

question: How does Christ's death glorify both God's justice and God's truth in his threatenings, while also benefiting sinners?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: In Christ, God made all our iniquities meet upon him and did not spare him. In this way God exalted his justice against sin while freeing us from its condemnation. The threat of death (Gen. 2:17) and the curse of the law were fulfilled when Christ tasted death for us and became a curse for us. So God's truth in his threatenings is made glorious in a way that does us good.
sources.quote: He, by the grace of God, tasted death for us, Heb. ii. 9; and so delivered us who were subject to death, verse 15; and he hath fulfilled the curse, by being made a curse for us, Gal. iii. 13.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's death glorify both God's justice and God's truth in his threatenings, while also benefiting sinners?

question: How does Christ's death remove the guilt of sin that separates sinners from God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: By his death Christ bears the curse, undergoes the punishment due to us, and pays the ransom due for us, delivering us from wrath, the curse of the law, and the power of Satan. Thus his death is the sole cause of removing all ground of rejection, his sufferings being reckoned to us: made sin for us, he is made righteousness to us.
sources.quote: By his death, Christ — bearing the curse, undergoing the punishment that was due to us, paying the ransom that was due for us — delivers us from this condition.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's death remove the guilt of sin that separates sinners from God?

question: If Christ has paid for sins past, present, and to come, can God still justly punish anyone for their sins?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. The satisfaction was not made by the sinner himself. Freeing one person through another's suffering is not a natural or necessary consequence; it rests on a law-constitution or compact that fixes how the sinner comes to share in it. The appointed way is faith, so those who do not believe remain as liable to punishment as if no satisfaction had been made.
sources.quote: For the consequent of the freedom of one by the suffering of another is not natural or necessary, but must proceed and arise from a law-constitution, compact, and agreement.
sources.raw_question: If Christ has paid for sins past, present, and to come, can God still justly punish anyone for their sins?

question: How does Christ's death and resurrection relate to the dying of sin in believers, according to Romans 6?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Christ's death is both the source and the pattern of the death of sin in believers. Owen reads Romans 6 as showing that mortification flows from the death and blood of Christ, and that sin dies in us in the way Christ died for sin. He was crucified for us, and so sin is crucified in us. As he was raised so that death has no dominion over him, we are raised from sin so that it has no dominion over us.
sources.quote: He was crucified for us, and thereby sin was crucified in us; he died for us, and the body of sin is destroyed, that we should not serve sin;
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's death and resurrection relate to the dying of sin in believers, according to Romans 6?

question: Is the Son the Light that lights every man coming into the world (John 1:9), and does this show that the Son is the Word through whom all things were made?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is the Light come into the world, which unbelievers rejected. Since John says the Light was in the world and the world was made by Him, the Son is the Word through whom all things were made. Otherwise there would have to be two worlds.
sources.quote: either they will be compelled to speak of two worlds, that the one may have come into being by the Son and the other by the Word, or, if the world is one and the creation one, it follows that Son and Word are one and the same
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the Light that lights every man coming into the world, and does this show that the Son is the Word?

question: Does the Arians' use of phrases from Scripture show that their teaching about the Son is orthodox?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: No. Quoting Scripture does not make a doctrine reverent, any more than the Jews' study of the Law and Prophets makes their denial of Christ right. The devil, the author of heresies, borrows Scripture language as a cloak for his poison so as to deceive the simple. He did this with Eve, in earlier heresies, and now with Arius.
sources.quote: the devil, the author of heresies, because of the ill savour which attaches to evil, borrows Scripture language, as a cloak wherewith to sow the ground with his own poison also, and to seduce the simple
sources.raw_question: Does the Arians' use of phrases from Scripture show that their teaching about the Son is orthodox?

question: Is the Arian doctrine that the Son is a creature a novel teaching rather than the faith handed down from the fathers?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: Yes. No one had ever heard such a doctrine before, and its adherents admit they heard it now for the first time. It is therefore foreign and not from the fathers. Such newly appearing teaching is what Paul foretold: in the latter times some would depart from the sound faith, giving heed to doctrines of devils.
sources.quote: But if they themselves own that they have heard it now for the first time, how can they deny that this heresy is foreign, and not from our fathers?
sources.raw_question: Is the Arian doctrine that the Son is a creature a novel teaching rather than the faith handed down from the fathers?

question: If the Son is called God but is not proper to the Father's essence, does Arian doctrine lead to polytheism or atheism?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Yes. If the Arians deny that the Word is God, they fall into atheism toward him. If they call him God because Scripture does so, yet make him different in kind from the Father, they introduce many gods. Saying he is God only by participation, like other things, is equally irreligious, because it ranks the Word as one among all things.
sources.quote: or saying that He is God, because it so written, but not proper to the Father’s Essence, they will introduce many because of their difference of kind
sources.raw_question: If the Son is called God but is not proper to the Father's essence, does Arian doctrine lead to polytheism or atheism?

question: Can philosophical or metaphysical arguments for Arianism outweigh the evidence of Scripture and the Fathers for the Son's divinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 31: Whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration, on the side of Arianism, ought to move a wise and good man, against so great appearances of truth o
sources.answer: No. Waterland holds that if the Arians retreat to philosophy and metaphysics, which they consider their strongest ground, they will still accomplish nothing. Their arguments there would amount to conjecture after proof has failed, offering wishes where demonstrations are required. Nothing short of clear demonstration should move a reasonable person against the strong evidence of Scripture and antiquity.
sources.quote: It will be only falling to conjecture, after you fail of proof; and giving the world your wishes, when they looked for demonstrations.
sources.raw_question: Can philosophy and metaphysics supply a demonstration for Arianism that would outweigh the evidence of Scripture and the Fathers for the Son's divinity?

question: Does the fact that we can say "my God" or "the God of Israel" but not "my infinite substance" prove that "God" is a relative word of office rather than a word for substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. By the same reasoning "star" and "water" would be relative words, since we can say "the star of your god Remphan" but not "the luminous substance of Remphan." The real oddity lies in the word "substance." In the singular it denotes what is intrinsic to the thing, indeed the thing itself, so it cannot be joined to relative terms. The argument therefore proves nothing about the meaning of "God."
sources.quote: By parity of reason, we may make relative words almost as many as we please.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that we can say "my God" or "the God of Israel" but not "my infinite substance" prove that "God" is a relative word of office rather than a word for substance?

question: Why can relative terms such as "my God" or "our God" properly be joined to the word "God" but not to God taken in the metaphysical sense of substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: The full Scripture idea of God includes something relative, namely the notion of Governor and Protector. That is why relative terms can properly be joined to it. The metaphysical sense takes in only part of that idea. It considers the divine nature abstracted from any relation and leaves the relative part out, so relative terms do not properly attach to it.
sources.quote: because metaphysics take in only part of the idea, consider the nature abstracted from the relation, leaving the relative part out.
sources.raw_question: Why can relative terms such as "my God" or "our God" properly be joined to the word "God" but not to God taken in the metaphysical sense of substance?

question: Why does Scripture say God pours out 'of My Spirit' rather than simply 'My Spirit'?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: Because creatures cannot receive the fulness of the Holy Spirit, but only as much as God apportions according to His will and our capacity. As the Son emptied Himself not by losing His fulness but so as to infuse Himself according to our measure, so the Father does not pour out the Spirit wholly, yet what He pours forth abounds for all.
sources.quote: He said not Spirit, but “of My Spirit,” for we are not able to receive the fulness of the Holy Spirit, but we receive as much as our Master divides to us of His own according to His will.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture say God pours out 'of My Spirit' rather than simply 'My Spirit'?

question: If the Spirit of God is said to be 'poured out' and given in greater or lesser measure, does that show the Spirit is not a Person?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. "Spirit" sometimes denotes the gifts and influences of the Spirit, and these can be poured out and distributed. But many other passages plainly establish his personality. A writer who speaks of letting in "more or less sun" does not thereby deny that the sun exists. All these gifts are worked by "one and the self-same Spirit, dividing to every man severally as He will."
sources.quote: These graces may be poured out – these gifts distributed. But “all these worketh that one and the self-same Spirit, dividing to every man severally as He will.”
sources.raw_question: If the Spirit of God is said to be "poured out" and given in greater or lesser measure, does that show the Spirit is not a Person?

question: Does the fact that human reason cannot comprehend a divine truth show that the truth is impossible?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. To reason that way is the essence of unbelief, which measures infinity by its own petty scale and concludes that what it cannot understand must be impossible. Unbelief is incapacity engaged in argument; believers instead attribute omnipotence to the divine activities and leave to God's power the choice of the mysteries by which he saves.
sources.quote: Thus all unbelief is foolishness, for it takes such wisdom as its own finite perception can attain, and, measuring infinity by that petty scale, concludes that what it cannot understand must be impossible.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that human reason cannot comprehend a divine truth show that the truth is impossible?

question: If human reason cannot comprehend God's infinite greatness, is faith in God therefore opposed to reason?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. The fitting homage to the Creator is the conviction that His greatness is too vast for our comprehension but not for our faith. A reasonable faith is akin to reason and accepts its help, even where reason cannot cope with the vastness of eternal Omnipotence.
sources.quote: For a reasonable faith is akin to reason and accepts its aid, even though that same reason cannot cope with the vastness of eternal Omnipotence.
sources.raw_question: If human reason cannot comprehend God's infinite greatness, is faith in God therefore opposed to reason?

question: How does Colossians 2:9 ('in Christ dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily') bear on the Son's relation to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It proves Christ true and perfect God of the Father's nature, without severing him from the Father or identifying him with the Father. Because the incorporeal God dwells in him bodily, the Son begotten of God is in natural unity with the Father. Because God dwells in Christ, there must be a distinct, personal Christ born, in whom he dwells.
sources.quote: prove Him true and perfect God of His Father’s nature, neither severing Him from, nor identifying Him with, the Father
sources.raw_question: How does Paul's statement that 'in Christ dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily' bear on the Son's relation to the Father?

question: Does believers' being 'filled with all the fullness of God' (Eph. 3:19) equal the fullness of the Godhead dwelling bodily in Christ (Col. 2:9)?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Colossians 2:9 affirms the incarnate Godhead of Christ, the head of all principality and power, in whom we are complete. Ephesians 3:19 means only that believers are filled with divine goodness each in their degree, to the limit of finite capacity. This filling itself flows from knowing Christ's love.
sources.quote: The first affirms the incarnate Godhead of Christ as the One in whom (see next clause, verse 10,) we are complete, for He is the head of all principality said power.
sources.raw_question: Does believers' being 'filled with all the fullness of God' (Eph. 3:19) equal the fullness of the Godhead dwelling bodily in Christ (Col. 2:9)?

question: What does Colossians 2:9-10 mean by saying the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Christ bodily and that believers are made full in him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It means the full Godhead truly dwells in Christ, and by his assumption of our flesh we are made full in him. Believers regenerated to eternal life abide even now in the body of Christ and are made full in him. Afterwards they will be made full in themselves, when he conforms the body of our humiliation to his glorious body. This fulness of ours in him constitutes his headship over every principality and power.
sources.quote: Now, therefore, we are made full in Him, that is, by the assumption of His flesh, for in Him dwelleth the fullness of the Godhead bodily.
sources.raw_question: What does Colossians 2:9-10 mean by saying the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Christ bodily and that believers are made full in him?

question: Does whatever is produced by emanation from a source share the nature of the source that produced it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter IV.—The absurdity of the supposed vacuum and defect of the heretics is demonstrated.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus argues that if the Valentinian vacuum came from the same source as the Æons, it must be like in nature both to its producer and to its fellow products. The Gnostic system therefore ends in absurdity: their Bythus would himself be a vacuum, and the Æons, as brothers of vacuity, would lack substance.
sources.quote: if it proceeded from the same source [as they did], it must be similar in nature to Him who produced it, as well as to those along with whom it was produced.
sources.raw_question: Does whatever is produced by emanation from a source share the nature of the source that produced it?

question: Does a difference in qualities between what is generated and its source imply a difference in substance?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He thus shows the oneness of the Eternal Son with the Father the identity of essence and the community of nature (wherein is a natural inquiry into the production of wine), and that the terms “Son” and “product” in the naming of the Only-Begotten include a like idea of relationship.
sources.answer: No. Gregory's example is the moisture in the vine, which becomes wine through the natural process of ripening. Wine is distinguished from that moisture by qualities such as astringency, sweetness, or sourness, yet in substance the two are the same. Differences of quality therefore do not alter the common nature.
sources.quote: so that in substance the two are the same, but are distinguished by qualitative differences.
sources.raw_question: Does a difference in qualities between what is generated and its source imply a difference in substance?

question: Do Peter's words to Ananias and Sapphira show that the Spirit of the Lord is the same as the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IV. The Holy Spirit is one and the same Who spake in the prophets and apostles, Who is the Spirit of God and of Christ; Whom, further, Scripture designates the Paraclete, and the Spirit of life and truth.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter tells Ananias that he lied to the Holy Spirit. He then tells Sapphira that "you" (both of them) tempted the Spirit of the Lord, which shows he means the same Spirit. So the Spirit of the Lord is the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: When he says “to you,” he shows that he is speaking of the same Spirit of Whom he had spoken to Ananias.
sources.raw_question: Do Peter's words to Ananias and Sapphira show that the Spirit of the Lord is the same as the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the episode of Ananias and Sapphira show that the Holy Spirit beholds hidden things, as God does?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: Yes. Ananias hid his theft from all men, yet the Holy Spirit, present in Peter, detected his secret intent and gave Peter from Himself the power to see it. He could not have done this unless He were able to behold hidden things, so the Spirit is a true witness who exercises the divine operation of seeing.
sources.quote: gave to Peter from Himself the power of seeing the secret, while it is clear that He could not have done this had He not been able to behold hidden things
sources.raw_question: Does the episode of Ananias and Sapphira show that the Holy Spirit beholds hidden things, as God does?

question: Why did Christ heal the man born blind with clay rather than by a word alone, and what does this show about who the Son is?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XV.—Proofs of the resurrection from Isaiah and Ezekiel; the same God who created us will also raise us up.
sources.answer: It showed that he is the hand of God that moulded man at the beginning. In Genesis the Lord formed man from clay of the earth. So Christ made clay and anointed the man's eyes, and the Word, the artificer, supplied in public what had been left unformed in the womb. This reveals that the incarnate Word is the same hand that formed us at the beginning and forms us in the womb, so we should seek no other hand and no other Father.
sources.quote: For that which the artificer, the Word, had omitted to form in the womb, [viz., the blind man’s eyes], He then supplied in public, that the works of God might be manifested in him
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ heal the man born blind with clay rather than by a word alone, and what does this show about who the Son is?

question: Does Christ's healing of the man born blind symbolize that the Word was produced in ignorance of the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: No. The Valentinians read the healing of the man born blind as an emblem of an Æon produced blind by Monogenes. Irenaeus rejects this as falsely ascribing ignorance and blindness to the Word of God. He mocks it as a pretended super-celestial mystery that has no basis in right reason.
sources.quote: thus falsely ascribing ignorance and blindness to the Word of God, who, according to their own theory, holds the second [place of] production from the Propator.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's healing of the man born blind symbolize that the Word was produced in ignorance of the Father?

question: Do the plural 'rivers' of John 7:38 and the 'seven Spirits' of Revelation imply that there are many Holy Spirits?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XVI. The Holy Spirit is that large river by which the mystical Jerusalem is watered. It is equal to its Fount, that is, the Father and the Son, as is signified in holy Scripture. St. Ambrose himself thirsts for that water, and warns us that in order to preserve it within us, we must avoid the devil, lust, and heresy, since our vessels are frail, and that broken cisterns must be forsaken, that after the example of the Samaritan woman and of the patriarchs we may find the water of the Lord.
sources.answer: No. The plurality signifies the sevenfold gifts of the Spirit listed by Isaiah, which denote the fulness of all virtue. There is one River, but many channels of the Spirit's gifts.
sources.quote: One, then, is the River, but many the channels of the gifts of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Do the plural 'rivers' of John 7:38 and the 'seven Spirits' of Revelation imply that there are many Holy Spirits?

question: Does the heavenly worship of the Lamb in Revelation 5:8-14 amount to the highest divine worship rather than a lesser homage?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes, it is the highest worship. The redeemed and the angels adore the Lamb alone, the whole creation blesses the Father and the Lamb together, and the elders then worship the Eternal alone. So it cannot be called lesser worship, nor worship of the Father only, nor worship offered merely through the Son. This authorizes giving Christ the highest adoration.
sources.quote: You cannot say it is offered to the Father alone, for once the Lamb is united with the Father. Your cannot say it is offered to the Father only through the Son, for twice it is offered alone to the Lamb that was slain.
sources.raw_question: Does the heavenly worship of the Lamb in Revelation 5:8-14 amount to the highest divine worship, rather than a lesser homage or worship directed to the Father through the Son?

question: If the Catholic doctrine of the Trinity faces unanswered difficulties, should it be abandoned for Arianism or Sabellianism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. One may have sufficient reason to believe a doctrine without answering every difficulty raised against it. Of the three schemes, Catholic, Sabellian and Arian, one must be true. The right course is to weigh the difficulties of each against the others, and Arianism and Sabellianism have more and greater difficulties and cannot defend themselves.
sources.quote: In the present controversy there are three schemes, which I may call Catholic, Sabellian, and Arian: one of the three must, in the main, be true. ‘The way to know which, is to weigh and consider the difficulties attending each respectively
sources.raw_question: If the Catholic doctrine of the Trinity faces unanswered difficulties (how three can be one, how the Son is generated), should it be abandoned for Arianism or Sabellianism?

question: Can human reason alone establish that human nature is capable of a truly blessed and eternal life?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > We Say that Future Blessedness is Truly Eternal, Not Through Human Reasonings, But by the Help of Faith. The Immortality of Blessedness Becomes Credible from the Incarnation of the Son of God.
sources.answer: No. Only a few highly gifted, learned and leisured philosophers have even reached the immortality of the soul alone, and they failed to find a stable blessed life, some holding that the soul returns to misery after blessedness. It is faith, resting on divine authority rather than human reasoning, that promises the whole man, soul and body, shall be immortal and therefore truly blessed.
sources.quote: But that faith promises, not by human reasoning, but by divine authority, that the whole man, who certainly consists of soul and body, shall be immortal, and on this account truly blessed.
sources.raw_question: Can human reason alone establish that human nature is capable of a truly blessed and eternal life?

question: Does Tertullian's comparison of a king and his son administering the kingdom mean that the Father and Son are one God only by unity of authority?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. Tertullian uses the similitude only to answer the objection that several Persons would destroy the one government (monarchia), showing how authority can be one in the hands of several Persons. When he explains how Father and Son are one God, he grounds it in unity of substance and original; and he rejects a subordinate God as a pagan notion, saying the Divinity has no degrees.
sources.quote: But if you ask Tertullian how Father and Son can be reputed one God, he tells you in the 4chapter before, and in that very passage which the Doctor quotes, that it is by wnity of substance, and original.
sources.raw_question: Does Tertullian's comparison of a king on his throne and his son administering the kingdom support the idea that the Father and Son are one God by unity of authority alone?

question: Is it rationally coherent to attribute fear, weakness, pain and dishonour to Christ in His Passion?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Whatever we fear we avoid, a weak nature is prey to terror, and what dishonours always degrades. Christ pressed toward His Passion, awed the brave, stopped others' pain, and was exalted through the cross. Holding both sides involves contradictions below ordinary human intelligence.
sources.quote: On what reasonable principle, then, do you hold that our Lord Jesus Christ feared that towards which He pressed: or awed the brave, yet trembled Himself with weakness: or stopped the pain of wounds, yet felt the pain of His own
sources.raw_question: Is it rationally coherent to attribute fear, weakness, pain and dishonour to Christ in His Passion?

question: Did Christ's body and soul originate through ordinary human conception, so that his suffering must have been like ours?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. God the Word by his own act took flesh from the Virgin and joined a soul to it, so the nature of his suffering corresponded to the nature of a body and soul whose author he himself was. Mary contributed what mothers contribute, but the cause of the conception was solely the Holy Ghost, and Christ was not formed by an ordinary human conception.
sources.quote: But if through His own act He took to Himself flesh from the Virgin, and likewise by His own act joined a soul to the body thus conceived, then the nature of His suffering must have corresponded with the nature of His body and soul.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ's body and soul originate through ordinary human conception, so that his suffering must have been like ours?

question: Was Christ's human nature subject to human anxiety and fear of suffering?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. His nature was more than human and superior to the ills of earthly flesh. His body did not spring from earthly elements but was conceived by the Holy Ghost, and the power of the Most High imparted its power to it. So there was no place in him for human anxiety and trepidation.
sources.quote: There was, then, no place for human anxiety and trepidation in that nature, which was more than human. It was superior to the ills of earthly flesh; a body not sprung from earthly elements
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's human nature subject to human anxiety and fear of suffering?

question: Do believers have their right to God's inheritance by nature or only by adoption?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: Only by adoption. Owen reads Paul as arguing that because believers are no longer servants but sons, they are heirs and have right and title. Since by nature they are children of wrath, they were not born to this right. They receive it through adoption.
sources.quote: and being not born hereunto (for by nature we are the children of wrath), we have this right by our adoption.
sources.raw_question: Do believers have their right to God's inheritance by nature or only by adoption?

question: Does adoption by God give a believer a civil claim to particular earthly possessions?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: No. The right that comes through adoption is spiritual. It sanctifies whatever civil interest God's providence gives, but it does not create one. God has providentially set the civil bounds of men's inheritance, so no adopted person may claim any earthly portion he lacks civil title to.
sources.quote: This right is a spiritual right, which doth not give a civil interest, but only sanctifies the right and interest bestowed.
sources.raw_question: Does adoption by God give a believer a civil claim to particular earthly possessions?

question: What future inheritance do believers have a right to because of their adoption as children of God through Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: They are heirs with Christ of the whole salvation he purchased. This includes the promise, which is the foundation of salvation, and righteousness and holiness, which are its means. It also includes eternal glory, which is its end. As the apostle argues, 'if children, then heirs.' In sum, the Lord is their portion, and they are the Lord's inheritance.
sources.quote: Thus, then, distinguish the full salvation by Christ into the foundation of it, the promises; and the means of it, righteousness and holiness; and the end of it, eternal glory. The sons of God have a right and title to all, in that they are made heirs with Christ.
sources.raw_question: What future inheritance do believers have a right to because of their adoption as children of God through Christ?

question: Does Psalm 110:1, 'The Lord said unto my Lord,' show that the Father literally addresses the Son with spoken words and names?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. It is David himself who is the speaker, interpreting by voice and word the knowledge of mysteries given him by divine inspiration. Such utterances are recorded for the sake of hearers who could not otherwise learn what is meant.
sources.quote: And if David in the spirit speaks of something being said by the Lord to the Lord, it is David himself who is the speaker, being unable otherwise to make known to us the teaching of what is meant
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 110:1, 'The Lord said unto my Lord,' show that the Father literally addresses the Son with spoken words and names?

question: How could David, being a man, know of the converse between the Father and the Son in Psalm 110:1?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: He knew it not by his own human nature but by being "in the Spirit." No mere man could know the supercelestial converse of the Father with the Son. David declared it because the Spirit revealed it to him, as Christ himself teaches.
sources.quote: For how could any one, being but man, know the supercelestial converse of the Father with the Son? But being “in the Spirit” he said that the Lord spoke to the Lord those words which He has uttered.
sources.raw_question: How could David, being a man, know of the converse between the Father and the Son in Psalm 110 ("The Lord said unto my Lord")?

question: Does 'The Lord said unto my Lord' (Psalm 110:1) mean that the Spirit called the Son Lord, making the Spirit subordinate to the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XV. Though the Spirit be called Lord, three Lords are not thereby implied; inasmuch as two Lords are not implied by the fact that the Son in the same manner as the Father is called Lord in many passages of Scripture; for Lordship exists in the Godhead, and the Godhead in Lordship, and these coincide without division in the Three Persons.
sources.answer: No. It is David, speaking in the Spirit, who calls the Son Lord, not the Spirit. Calling the Son his Lord does not deny that the Father is also David's Lord. If one inferred that the Spirit called the Son Lord, one would by the same reasoning have to make the Son of God the Spirit's son, which is sacrilege.
sources.quote: David, not the Spirit, calls Him Lord in the Spirit. Or if they falsely infer from this that the Spirit called Him Lord, they must necessarily by a like sacrilege seem to assert that the Son of God is also the Son of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does the verse 'The Lord said unto my Lord' (Psalm 110:1) mean that the Spirit called the Son Lord, making the Spirit subordinate?

question: Does Psalm 110:1, 'The Lord said unto my Lord,' show that both the Father and the Son are truly Lord?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: Yes. The text shows the Father addressing the Son, giving him the inheritance of the nations and subjecting his enemies to him. Since the Father is truly Lord and the Son truly Lord, the Holy Spirit rightly designates both by the title Lord.
sources.quote: Since, therefore, the Father is truly Lord, and the Son truly Lord, the Holy Spirit has fitly designated them by the title of Lord.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 110:1, "The Lord said unto my Lord," show that both the Father and the Son are truly Lord?

question: Was the 'angel of the Lord' who spoke to Abraham at the sacrifice of Isaac the Son of God himself or a created angel?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: No, it was a created angel through whom the Lord spoke. The angel speaks as a prophet does, saying "By myself I have sworn, saith the Lord." It would be incongruous for the Son, if he were that angel, to speak of the Father this way. The angel is called Lord only because the Lord spoke through him.
sources.quote: Does the Son of God say of the Father, “The Lord saith,” while He Himself is that Angel of the Father?
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold the Son appeared visibly in his own substance
sources.raw_question: Was the "angel of the Lord" who appeared to Abraham the Son of God himself rather than a created angel?

question: Can the divine nature be counted or admit plurality, so that the Persons make several Gods?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIII. To those who object that Catholics, when they ascribe Godhead to the Holy Spirit, introduce three Gods, it is answered, that by the same argument they themselves bring in two Gods, unless they deny Godhead to the Son; after which the orthodox doctrine is set forth.
sources.answer: No. Plurality belongs to numbers, and the Divine Nature does not admit numbers. The unity of the Godhead therefore cannot admit plurality. Only a division of power would make several Gods, and there is none in God.
sources.quote: For how can the Unity of the Godhead admit of plurality, seeing that plurality is of numbers, but the Divine Nature does not admit numbers?
sources.raw_question: Can the divine nature be counted or admit plurality, so that the Persons make several Gods?

question: How can one distinguish what is said of God according to substance from what is said of God relatively?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whatever is Spoken of God According to Substance, is Spoken of Each Person Severally, and Together of the Trinity Itself. One Essence in God, and Three, in Greek, Hypostases, in Latin, Persons.
sources.answer: Whatever is said of God in respect to himself is said according to substance, while whatever is said in relation to something else is said relatively and does not denote substance. Because Father, Son and Holy Spirit share the same substance, substantial predicates are applied to them in the singular, not summed into a plural.
sources.quote: whatsoever is said of that most eminent and divine loftiness in respect to itself, is said in respect to substance, but that which is said in relation to anything, is not said in respect to substance, but relatively
sources.raw_question: How can one distinguish what is said of God according to substance from what is said of God relatively?

question: If the Israelites were baptized unto Moses and believed in Moses, does baptism and faith in the Holy Spirit fail to prove that the Spirit should be ranked with God?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Objection that some were baptized unto Moses and believed in him, and an answer to it; with remarks upon types.
sources.answer: No. Faith in the Spirit is the same faith as that in the Father and the Son, and baptism into the Spirit is likewise the same baptism. Faith in Moses and baptism in the cloud and sea were only a shadow and type, so they share the name with Christian baptism but differ from it as dream differs from reality.
sources.quote: Our answer is that the faith in the Spirit is the same as the faith in the Father and the Son; and in like manner, too, the baptism. But the faith in Moses and in the cloud is, as it were, in a shadow and type.
sources.raw_question: If the Israelites were baptized unto Moses and believed in Moses, does baptism and faith in the Holy Spirit fail to prove that the Spirit should be ranked with God?

question: Is there any warrant in Scripture or reason for taking the divine attributes applied to Christ in a more limited sense than those applied to the one God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: No. The expressions applied to Christ are equally general and extensive as those applied to the one God, and the opponent offers no proof of a restricted sense but only insinuates it under obscure terms.
sources.quote: what ground or warrant you have from Scripture, or right reason, for putting restrictions and limitations upon the texts applied to Christ Jesus, more than to those applied to the one God?
sources.raw_question: Is there any warrant in Scripture or reason for limiting the divine attributes applied to Christ more than those applied to the one God?

question: In what sense was all power 'given' to Christ after his resurrection if, as the Word, he was already Lord over all?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: It was given to him as God-Man, in respect of his human nature. The Word was Lord over all from the beginning, but the incarnate God-Man received that lordship only after the resurrection, receiving in one capacity what he had always enjoyed in another, so that full power was now possessed in both natures rather than in one. The human nature, previously in humiliation, was then exalted into union with the Word's dignity.
sources.quote: The Adyos, or Word, was from the beginning, Lord over all ; but the God inearnate, the Θεάνθρωτπος, or God-Man, was not so, till after the resurrection. Then he received, in that capacity, what he had ever enjoyed in another.
sources.raw_question: In what sense was all power 'given' to Christ after his resurrection if he was already Lord over all as the Word?

question: Does the scriptural proof of Christ's deity depend on textually disputed passages such as 1 John 5:7, Acts 20:28, and 1 Timothy 3:16?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Bickersteth deliberately forbears to use these three texts, since Griesbach judged them doubtful, and holds that the argument is incontrovertible without them. None of the texts he relies on are set aside by Griesbach, whom Unitarians themselves trust, so the case for Christ's deity rests on textually secure ground.
sources.quote: But to these three texts, that we may not be drawn into needless disputations, I have simply forborne to refer. The argument does not demand them. It is incontrovertible without them.
sources.raw_question: Does the scriptural proof of Christ's deity depend on disputed texts such as 1 John 5:7, Acts 20:28, and 1 Timothy 3:16?

question: Should an inquiry into the Trinity, the Divinity of Jesus Christ, and the personality of the Holy Spirit begin directly with the nature of God's Being?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 1. Introduction. Preparation of heart. Our position before God.
sources.answer: No. A prior investigation is needed first: what our relation and position before God is, as recorded in Scripture. Pursued with prayerful study of God's word, this investigation, by God's grace, awakens the disposition of mind fitted for the later inquiry into God's mysterious Being.
