sources.quote: I ask not then, my friends, that you should enquire first of all into the nature of God’s mysterious Being, the Divinity of Jesus Christ, and the personality of the Holy Spirit. There is a prior investigation which demands your earnest heed
sources.raw_question: Should an inquiry into the Trinity, the Divinity of Jesus Christ, and the personality of the Holy Spirit begin directly with the nature of God's Being?

question: What must chiefly be considered in an inquiry into the Trinity and into knowing God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Of True Love, by Which We Arrive at the Knowledge of the Trinity. God is to Be Sought, Not Outwardly, by Seeking to Do Wonderful Things with the Angels, But Inwardly, by Imitating the Piety of Good Angels.
sources.answer: True love, or rather love itself. Augustine holds that nothing else is chiefly to be regarded in this inquiry except what love is, since only true love deserves the name (otherwise it is mere desire), and since "God is love," knowing love is the path to knowing God.
sources.quote: No other thing, then, is chiefly to be regarded in this inquiry, which we make concerning the Trinity and concerning knowing God, except what is true love, nay, rather what is love.
sources.raw_question: What must chiefly be considered in an inquiry into the Trinity and into knowing God?

question: If the Arians claim that 'God is a Spirit' refers to the Father, does their erasing of the text create a dilemma for them?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter X. The Divinity of the Holy Spirit is supported by a passage of St. John. This passage was, indeed, erased by heretics, but it is a vain attempt, since their faithlessness could thereby more easily be convicted. The order of the context is considered in order that this passage may be shown to refer to the Spirit. He is born of the Spirit who is born again of the same Spirit, of Whom Christ Himself is believed to have been born and born again. Again, the Godhead of the Spirit is inferred from two testimonies of St. John; and lastly, it is explained how the Spirit, the water, and the blood are called witnesses.
sources.answer: Yes. If the phrase speaks of the Father, then erasing it amounts to denying that the Father is God. If it speaks of the Spirit, they deny the Spirit's Godhead. Either way their impiety binds them, as heathen who deny either the Father or the Spirit to be God.
sources.quote: For if you will have it that the expression is used of God the Father, you, who think it should be erased, deny, in consequence, God the Father.
sources.raw_question: If the Arians claim that 'God is a Spirit' refers to God the Father, does their erasing the text create a dilemma for them?

question: Can those who deny the Son's eternal Godhead and separate the Spirit from the Father rightly claim the name of Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVII. St. Ambrose shows by instances that the places in which those words were spoken help to the understanding of the words of the Lord; he shows that Christ uttered the passage quoted from St. John in Solomon's porch, by which is signified the mind of a wise man, for he says that Christ would not have uttered this saying in the heart of a foolish or contentious man. He goes on to say that Christ is stoned by those who believe not these words, and as the keys of heaven were given to Peter for his confession of them, so Iscariot, because he believed not the same, perished evilly. He takes this opportunity to inveigh against the Jews who bought the Son of God and sold Joseph. He explains the price paid for each mystically; and having in the same manner expounded the murmuring of the traitor concerning Magdalene's ointment, he adds that Christ is bought in one way by heretics in another way by Catholics, and that those in vain take to themselves the name of Christians who sever the Spirit from the Father.
sources.answer: No. Christ does not recognize His Name where His eternal Godhead is not confessed. A name divided from the Father and separated from the Spirit is not His Name, and those who rank the Spirit of the Father among created servants do not hold His doctrine, as calling Him 'Lord, Lord' does not suffice for entering the kingdom.
sources.quote: I do not recognize My Name where My eternal Godhead is not. That is not My Name which is divided from the Father, and separated from the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Can the Arians rightly claim the name of Christ while denying the Son's eternal Godhead and substance and separating the Spirit from the Father?

question: Does the context of Christ's discourse with Nicodemus in John 3 show that 'that which is born of the Spirit is Spirit' refers to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter X. The Divinity of the Holy Spirit is supported by a passage of St. John. This passage was, indeed, erased by heretics, but it is a vain attempt, since their faithlessness could thereby more easily be convicted. The order of the context is considered in order that this passage may be shown to refer to the Spirit. He is born of the Spirit who is born again of the same Spirit, of Whom Christ Himself is believed to have been born and born again. Again, the Godhead of the Spirit is inferred from two testimonies of St. John; and lastly, it is explained how the Spirit, the water, and the blood are called witnesses.
sources.answer: Yes. The whole tenor of the passage concerns the Spirit and regeneration by water and the Spirit. This is the same regeneration elsewhere called the laver of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit, and baptism with the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Spirit of whom we are born is the Holy Spirit, and he is declared to be God.
sources.quote: For who is he that is baptized with the Holy Spirit but he who is born again through water and the Holy Spirit? Therefore the Lord said of the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Does the context of Christ's discourse with Nicodemus in John 3 show that 'that which is born of the Spirit is Spirit' concerns the Holy Spirit?

question: Does John 3:5 say that believers are born 'of' the Spirit rather than merely 'through' the Spirit, and what follows for the Holy Spirit's divinity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter X. The Divinity of the Holy Spirit is supported by a passage of St. John. This passage was, indeed, erased by heretics, but it is a vain attempt, since their faithlessness could thereby more easily be convicted. The order of the context is considered in order that this passage may be shown to refer to the Spirit. He is born of the Spirit who is born again of the same Spirit, of Whom Christ Himself is believed to have been born and born again. Again, the Godhead of the Spirit is inferred from two testimonies of St. John; and lastly, it is explained how the Spirit, the water, and the blood are called witnesses.
sources.answer: Yes, it says 'of' (ex) the Spirit. Since 'that which is born of the Spirit' undoubtedly refers to the Holy Spirit, and Scripture says 'the Spirit is God,' it follows that the Holy Spirit is God, being the source of our spiritual birth and not a mere instrument.
sources.quote: we find each passage so written in Greek, that He said not, through the Spirit, but of the Spirit. For it stands thus: ἀμήν, ἀμήν, λέγω σοι, ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ ἐξ ὓδατος και Πνεύματος
sources.raw_question: Does the Greek of John 3:5 say that believers are born 'of' the Spirit rather than merely 'through' the Spirit, and what follows for the Holy Spirit's divinity?

question: Is the evidence for what the early Church believed about the Trinity as strong as the evidence by which we receive the canon of Scripture?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 28: Whether it be at all probable, that the primitive Church should mistake in so material a point as this is; or that the whole stream of Christian writers should
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds that the Church's doctrine is attested as well as the canon itself, and he cites Stillingfleet in support. Setting aside such a cloud of witnesses would weaken the very kind of testimony on which the canon rests.
sources.quote: What we pretend is, that we have as good proof of the doctrine of the Church, as of the canon of Scripture.
sources.raw_question: Is the evidence for what the early Church believed about the Trinity as strong as the evidence by which we receive the canon of Scripture?

question: Does the doctrine of the Trinity rest only on the testimony of the Fathers, while its opponents have Scripture on their side?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 28: Whether it be at all probable, that the primitive Church should mistake in so material a point as this is; or that the whole stream of Christian writers should
sources.answer: No. Waterland insists the orthodox have both Scripture and the Fathers. He judges the opposing view irreconcilable with the natural, grammatical sense of Scripture. Since Scripture and the ancient consensus very probably went together, whoever lacks the Fathers very probably lacks Scripture too. Athanasius, Hilary, Basil and others defended the doctrine from Scripture alone and overcame the Arians.
sources.quote: We do not appeal to the ancients, as if we could not maintain our ground, from Scripture and reason, against all opposers: this has been done over and over.
sources.raw_question: Does the doctrine of the Trinity rest only on the testimony of the Fathers, while its opponents have Scripture on their side?

question: Does rejecting the apostles' teaching about the one God and one Christ amount to rejecting Christ and the Father himself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter I.—The apostles did not commence to preach the Gospel, or to place anything on record until they were endowed with the gifts and power of the Holy Spirit. They preached one God alone, Maker of heaven and earth.
sources.answer: Yes. Whoever does not agree to these truths despises the companions of the Lord, and thereby despises Christ himself and the Father also. Irenaeus grounds this in the Lord's word that whoever hears or despises the apostles hears or despises him and the one who sent him. Such a person stands self-condemned, opposing his own salvation.
sources.quote: he despises the companions of the Lord; nay more, he despises Christ Himself the Lord; yea, he despises the Father also, and stands self-condemned
sources.raw_question: Does rejecting the apostles' teaching about the one God and one Christ amount to rejecting Christ and the Father himself?

question: Does rejecting Christ's statement "I and the Father are One" (John 10:30) amount to an attack on Christ himself, like the Jews' attempt to stone him?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVII. St. Ambrose shows by instances that the places in which those words were spoken help to the understanding of the words of the Lord; he shows that Christ uttered the passage quoted from St. John in Solomon's porch, by which is signified the mind of a wise man, for he says that Christ would not have uttered this saying in the heart of a foolish or contentious man. He goes on to say that Christ is stoned by those who believe not these words, and as the keys of heaven were given to Peter for his confession of them, so Iscariot, because he believed not the same, perished evilly. He takes this opportunity to inveigh against the Jews who bought the Son of God and sold Joseph. He explains the price paid for each mystically; and having in the same manner expounded the murmuring of the traitor concerning Magdalene's ointment, he adds that Christ is bought in one way by heretics in another way by Catholics, and that those in vain take to themselves the name of Christians who sever the Spirit from the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. When the Jews heard Christ say he and the Father are one, they took up stones to stone him. Whoever cannot accept this saying does the same: he stones Christ with the stones of unbelief. Christ can no longer be wounded in the flesh, yet he who rejoices in the Church's love is stoned by the impiety of the Arians.
sources.quote: He who cannot listen to this is a Jew; he who cannot listen to this stones Christ with the stones of his treachery, rougher than any rock, and if you believe me, he wounds Christ.
sources.raw_question: Does rejecting Christ's statement "I and the Father are One" amount to an attack on Christ himself, comparable to the Jews' stoning of him?

question: Is the relation of Fatherhood and Sonship in God an accident?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Nothing is Spoken of God According to Accident, But According to Substance or According to Relation.
sources.answer: No. An accident is something that can be gained, lost or changed. But the Father is always Father and the Son always Son, because the Son was always born and never began to be Son. Had He begun or ceased to be Son, Sonship would be an accident, but it is eternal and unchangeable.
sources.quote: But if He had begun to be at any time, or were at any time to cease to be, the Son, then He would be called Son according to accident.
sources.raw_question: Is the relation of Fatherhood and Sonship in God an accident?

question: Is the order of fatherhood and creation reversed between God's relation to men and God's relation to the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Yes. With men, God is first their Creator and afterwards becomes their Father through the indwelling Word and the Spirit of the Son. With the Word, God is first His Father by nature and only afterwards becomes His Creator and Maker, when the Word puts on created flesh and becomes man.
sources.quote: But in the case of the Word the reverse; for God, being His Father by nature, becomes afterwards both His Creator and Maker, when the Word puts on that flesh which was created and made, and becomes man.
sources.raw_question: Is the order of fatherhood and creation reversed between God's relation to men and God's relation to the Word?

question: Does Christ take delight in believers, and what does that delight consist of?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes, Christ delights exceedingly in his saints. Delight is the flowing of love and joy, the rest and complacence of the mind in a suitable good enjoyed. Scripture compares Christ's delight to that of a bridegroom on his wedding day, the purest delight people know. Zephaniah 3:17 describes every part of it: joy and exultation, rest and complacence.
sources.quote: Delight is the flowing of love and joy, — the rest and complacence of the mind in a suitable, desirable good enjoyed. Now, Christ delights exceedingly in his saints
sources.raw_question: Does Christ take delight in believers, and what does that delight consist of?

question: Does believers' delight in Christ extend to his people and his ordinances?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. To delight in someone is also to delight, for his sake, in everything that belongs to him. Christ's great interest in this world lies in his people and his ordinances. So the saints delight in one another on his account, just as Christ calls his church 'Hephzi-bah' and David says 'my delight is in them'. They also delight in his ordinances as the wisdom of God, though the world counts them foolishness.
sources.quote: This is an evidence of delight, when, for his sake whom we delight in, we also delight in every thing that belongs to him. Christ’s great interest in this world lies in his people and his ordinances
sources.raw_question: Does believers' delight in Christ extend to his people and his ordinances?

question: Is it unreasonable to say that a divine Person has understanding or love by another Person's being in Him?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Scripture gives ground for this regarding the Father: it teaches that the Son is the wisdom, reason and truth of God, so the Father is wise by His own wisdom, the Son, being in Him. Likewise understanding is in the Holy Spirit because the Son is in Him.
sources.quote: we have Scripture ground to conclude so concerning the Father's having wisdom and understanding or reason that it is by the Son's being in Him; because we are there informed that He is the wisdom and reason and truth of God
sources.raw_question: Is it unreasonable to say that a divine Person has understanding or love by another Person's being in Him?

question: Does excepting supremacy and independence from the powers communicated to the Son mean that the Son lacks infinite perfections?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 10: Whether if they (the attributes belonging to the Son) be not individually the same, they can be any thing more than faint resemblances of them, differing from t
sources.answer: No. The phrase can bear an orthodox sense: everything belonging to the Father is communicated to the Son except what is personal. The Son is excepted only in being not first in order and not unoriginate. To claim that excepting supremacy logically excludes infinite powers ties a loose expression to a strict meaning and loads it with unwarranted consequences.
sources.quote: that to the Son are communicated all things belonging to the Father, excepting only what is personal; that is, excepting that he is not the first im order; not supreme, in that sense, nor wnoriginate.
sources.raw_question: Does the exception of supremacy and independency from the powers communicated to the Son necessarily mean that the Son lacks infinite perfections?

question: Since infinite perfection cannot belong to a creature, what is really at issue when the Son is said to have 'all divine powers'?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 10: Whether if they (the attributes belonging to the Son) be not individually the same, they can be any thing more than faint resemblances of them, differing from t
sources.answer: The real question is simply whether God the Son is a creature or not. Communicating infinite perfection to a creature is admittedly a contradiction. So if the Son has all divine powers in the full sense, he cannot be a creature. On the Arian hypothesis, therefore, 'divine powers' cannot mean infinite powers.
sources.quote: it might be seen plainly what was the true state of the question: which, as appears now, is only this; whether God the Son be a creature or no.
sources.raw_question: Since infinite perfection cannot belong to a finite creature, what is the real point at issue when the Son is said to have 'all divine powers'?

question: What does Christ's calling himself the Vine and the Father the Husbandman in John 15 signify, and does it imply that the Son's divine nature is inferior to the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It refers to his assumed flesh, not to an inferiority of his divine nature. By calling himself the Vine, the source of unity for the branches, he distinguishes the humiliation of the assumed flesh from the form of the Father's majesty. Through his incarnation we are in him as branches in the vine, and so can bear fruit.
sources.quote: He separates the form of the Father’s majesty from the humiliation of the assumed flesh by calling Himself the Vine, the source of unity for all the branches, and the Father the careful Husbandman
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's calling himself the Vine and the Father the Husbandman signify in John 15?

question: Do Christ's discourses in John 15 (the vine and the husbandman, keeping the Father's commandments, hearing from the Father, being sent) show that the Son is not the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Proves Also that the Words Spoken to Philip Make Nothing for the Sabellians.
sources.answer: Yes. These sayings plainly attest that he who speaks is the Son and not the Father. The Lord would never have added them if he had meant that he was the Father or wished to be understood as the Father.
sources.quote: These things then, after the former, evidently attesting Him to be not the Father but the Son, the Lord would never have added, if He had had it in mind, either that He was the Father, or wished Himself to be understood as the Father
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's discourses in John 15 (the vine and the husbandman, keeping the Father's commandments, hearing from the Father, being sent) show that the Son is not the Father?

question: Can one escape the creation-out-of-nothing argument for the Son's divinity by professing ignorance whether God strictly creates anything out of nothing?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 13: Whether there can be any middle between being made out of nothing, and out of something ; that is, between being out of nothing, and out of the Father's substan
sources.answer: No. Such professed ignorance would imply that we cannot know whether God properly created anything at all, and would allow matter to be coeternal with God while denying eternity to the Son. An eternal Son is far better sense than an eternal non-divine substance out of which the Son is made, which is what the objection must mean.
sources.quote: An eternal Son, methinks, is much better sense than an eternal substance, not divine, and a Son made out of it; which is what you must mean, or mean nothing.
sources.raw_question: Can one escape the creation-out-of-nothing disjunction by professing ignorance whether God strictly creates anything out of nothing?

question: Did Christ suffer and offer himself as a sacrifice for any sin of his own?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. Unlike the Jewish high priests, who offered first for themselves and then for the people, Christ offered only for others. He had no sin and so could make no sacrifice for his own. The Messiah was 'cut off, but not for himself' and bore our sins in his body on the tree.
sources.quote: He had no sin, and could make no sacrifice for his own sin, which he had not, but only for others.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ suffer and offer himself as a sacrifice for any sin of his own?

question: Did Christ in his death offer himself as a sacrifice to God to make atonement for sins?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture calls his soul an offering for sin and him the Lamb of God who takes away sin. It says he gave himself as an offering and sacrifice to God, and that as high priest he made reconciliation by his own blood. Through the eternal Spirit he offered himself without spot to God, obtaining eternal redemption.
sources.quote: That he offered himself a sacrifice to God, to make atonement for our sins; and that in his death and sufferings
sources.raw_question: Did Christ in his death offer himself as a sacrifice to God to make atonement for sins?

question: Does believers' being "changed into the same image" (2 Cor 3:18) make them equal to Christ, who is "the express image of his person" (Heb 1:3)?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Hebrews 1:3 belongs to the chapter that most illustriously proves Christ's Godhead. The believer's transformation is wholly referred to beholding God's glory in the face of Jesus Christ, revealed progressively by the Lord, the Spirit, so it is a derived likeness.
sources.quote: The second refers all the transformation to the view of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, revealed progressively by the Lord, the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does believers' being "changed into the same image" (2 Cor 3:18) make them equal to Christ, who is "the express image of his person" (Heb 1:3)?

question: What is "the same image" into which believers are transformed according to 2 Corinthians 3:18?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Apostle Says that God is Now Seen by Us Through a Glass.
sources.answer: It is the image of God, the very image which we see in the mirror, which is also the glory of the Lord. Paul elsewhere calls man "the image and glory of God," showing that the image in which we are created is itself glory.
sources.quote: he assuredly means to speak of the image of God; and by calling it “the same,” he means that very image which we see in the glass, because that same image is also the glory of the Lord
sources.raw_question: What is "the same image" into which we are transformed according to 2 Corinthians 3:18?

question: In Jacob's blessing of Joseph's sons, is the one called both God and Angel God the Father or the Son?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God Also Appeared to Jacob as an Angel; Namely, the Son of God.
sources.answer: He is the Son, Christ, not the Father. The Father cannot be taken as an Angel, but Christ can be received as both God and Angel. Jacob's crossed hands, prefiguring the passion, point to Christ as the author of the blessing.
sources.quote: But yet He cannot be received as God the Father; but as God and Angel, as Christ He can be received.
sources.raw_question: Is the one called both God and Angel in Jacob's blessing God the Father or the Son?

question: Is the God who appeared to Jacob as an angel, and to whom Jacob made his vow, the Father or the Son?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God Also Appeared to Jacob as an Angel; Namely, the Son of God.
sources.answer: The Son. The one who is both God and Angel must be distinguished from the one who is called God only. A vow can be made to Him as to God, and no other angel could hold such authority. So He is Christ, the Son, God and Angel, not the Father.
sources.quote: it is manifest that it is not to be received as the Father, but as the Son, God and Angel
sources.raw_question: Is the God who appeared to Jacob as an angel the Father or the Son?

question: If the Holy Spirit cannot truly be grieved, what does the command 'Grieve not the Holy Spirit' (Ephesians 4:30) teach about him and about our sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: It teaches two things. First, the Spirit is disposed toward us like a loving, tender friend who cares about our good, and so he is said to be grieved when we fail. Second, we can do things that are fit to grieve such a friend. Our sin in doing them is no less than if he were actually grieved.
sources.quote: That we may do those things that are proper to grieve him, though he be not passively grieved; our sin being no less therein than if he were grieved as we are.
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit cannot truly be grieved, what does the command 'Grieve not the Holy Spirit' teach about him and about our sin?

question: What positive duty does the command not to grieve the Holy Spirit include, and how is keeping it a form of communion with him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: The duty is to pursue universal holiness out of regard for the love, kindness and tenderness of the Holy Ghost. According to the surrounding context of Ephesians 4, the Spirit is grieved when we fall short of the sanctification that our union with Christ requires. To make the Spirit's delight in our obedience a continual motive for holy living is the first general way of communion with him.
sources.quote: that we pursue universal holiness with regard unto, and upon the account of, the love, kindness, and tenderness, of the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: What positive duty does the command not to grieve the Holy Spirit include, and how is it a form of communion with him?

question: Why does Paul say Christ was "made of a woman" rather than "through a woman," and what does this show about Christ's flesh?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That v: not found “of whom” in the case of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.answer: Paul chose the more emphatic "of" to show that the God-bearing flesh was formed from the common lump of human nature, refuting those who thought the Lord's body was spiritual. "Through a woman" might suggest mere transit in generation, whereas "of the woman" indicates that mother and offspring share the same nature.
sources.quote: The phrase “through a woman” would be likely to give rise to the suspicion of mere transit in the generation, while the phrase “of the woman” would satisfactorily indicate that the nature was shared by the mother and the offspring.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who supposed that the body of the Lord was a spiritual body
sources.raw_question: Why does Paul say Christ was "made of a woman" rather than "through a woman," and what does this show about Christ's flesh?

question: Why does Paul say Christ was "made of a woman" rather than simply "born of a woman"?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: To testify that he was born of one parent only, without conception through human intercourse. 'Birth' points to the reality of the generation. 'Making' excludes the idea of a human father, since he was made of a virgin, though he was truly born and not made.
sources.quote: the term ‘making’ excludes the idea of a conception by means of human intercourse, it being expressly stated that He was made of a virgin, though it is equally certain that He was born and not made.
sources.raw_question: Why does Paul say Christ was 'made of a woman' rather than simply 'born of a woman'?

question: Does the maxim that 'nothing individual can be communicated' disprove the communication of the divine essence and attributes from the Father to the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: No. The word 'individual' is ambiguous: it may mean a part of a substance, a whole Person, or one essence shared by three Persons. In each sense the maxim is true but trivial, merely saying that what is incommunicable is incommunicable. Whether this or that is actually communicable, and how, remains the real question, and the maxim decides nothing about it.
sources.quote: This is only telling us, that so far, or in such respect, as any thing is supposed individual or incommunicable, it is supposed individual or incommunicable; which nobody doubts of.
sources.raw_question: Does Dr. Clarke's maxim that 'nothing individual can be communicated' disprove the communication of the divine essence and attributes from the Father to the Son?

question: Is the communication of the divine essential attributes to the Son any less intelligible than God's omnipresence as Dr. Clarke conceives it?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: No. On Clarke's own view of extended divine substance, one individual infinite wisdom must be entirely in the whole and entirely in every part. It is proper to each part yet common to all, diffused yet not multiplied. The communication of attributes among the divine Persons is at least as intelligible as this, and as consistent with the maxim. Clarke can no better explain how many parts make one Person than the orthodox can explain how three Persons make one substance.
sources.quote: here is but one individual infinite ‘wisdom, which is entirely in the whole, and entirely in every part ; proper, in some sense, to each single part, (since it can have only such attributes as inhere in it,) and yet common to all
sources.raw_question: Is the communication of the divine essential attributes to the Son any less intelligible than the omnipresence of God as Dr. Clarke conceives it?

question: Why is the Holy Spirit called Fire in Scripture, and does this point to his Godhead?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIV. Each Person of the Trinity is said in the sacred writings to be Light. The Spirit is designated Fire by Isaiah, a figure of which Fire was seen in the bush by Moses, in the tongues of fire, and in Gideon's pitchers. And the Godhead of the same Spirit cannot be denied, since His operation is the same as that of the Father and of the Son, and He is also called the light and fire of the Lord's countenance.
sources.answer: Yes, it points to his Godhead. Isaiah calls the Light of Israel a fire, and this shows the majesty of the Godhead. To sanctify belongs to the Godhead, to illuminate is the property of fire and light, and God is wont to be shown in the appearance of fire, since 'our God is a consuming Fire.'
sources.quote: since to sanctify is of the Godhead, to illuminate is the property of fire and light, and the Godhead is wont to be pointed out or seen in the appearance of fire
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit called Fire in Scripture, and does this point to his Godhead?

question: Why does Scripture call God 'Fire' in the Old Testament and 'Spirit' in the New Testament, if neither name describes his substance?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, that When God is Called a Spirit, Brightness, and Light, God is Not Sufficiently Expressed by Those Appellations.
sources.answer: These names are figures, not literal descriptions. God is called Fire in the Old Testament to strike fear into a sinful people by presenting him as Judge, and is announced as Spirit in the New Testament to attest his merciful goodness as the Renewer and Creator of those dead in sins who believe.
sources.quote: But these things are rather used as figures than as being so in fact.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture call God 'Fire' in the Old Testament and 'Spirit' in the New Testament, if neither names his substance?

question: By what means above all should knowledge of God be sought?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity.
sources.answer: Above all, by love. Scripture says that God is love, so love is the chief way to know Him. Within love itself there is also a trace of a trinity.
sources.quote: But it is urged above all, that the knowledge of God is to be sought by love, which God is said to be in the Scriptures; and in this love is also pointed out the existence of some trace of a trinity.
sources.raw_question: By what means above all should knowledge of God be sought?

question: Should knowledge of God be sought from God himself, through humility and prayer, rather than from the human mind's own inventions?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Preface.
sources.answer: Yes. The human heart gives birth to many figments, so Augustine prays that nothing pass into his writings except what the breath of God's truth has breathed into him. Such knowledge belongs to one who acknowledges his own weakness. It comes by returning along the way that the divinity of the only-begotten Son has made through his humanity. Charity, not knowledge that puffs up, is what edifies.
sources.quote: that there may pass into them only what the breath of His truth has breathed into me; cast out though I am from the sight of His eyes,[^441] and striving from afar to return by the way which the divinity of His only-begotten Son has made by His humanity
sources.raw_question: Should knowledge of God be sought from God himself, through humility and prayer, rather than from the human mind's own inventions?

question: What is the source of the perfect habitual holiness of Christ's human nature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: It followed necessarily from the grace of union of the human nature with the person of the Son, though it was effected by the free operations of the Holy Spirit. Hence what was born of the virgin was a 'holy thing', and Christ received an all-fulness of grace.
sources.quote: This he had necessarily from the grace of union; from whence it is that that which was born of the virgin was a “holy thing,” Luke i. 35. It was, I say, necessary consequentially, that it should be so; though the effecting of it were by the free operations of the Spirit
sources.raw_question: What is the source of the perfect habitual holiness of Christ's human nature?

question: Why does Scripture say that Christ received power and grace as man, if as God he already had them?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: So that the gift might be secure for humanity. A mere man who receives can lose again, as Adam did. Because the flesh received in the Word, the gift abides surely for us, and men gain power against demons and reign incorrupt as partakers of the divine nature.
sources.quote: in these passages He is said humanly to have received, that, whereas the flesh received in Him, henceforth from it the gift might abide surely for us.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture say that Christ received power and grace humanly, if as God he already had them?

question: Is the habitual grace given by Christ several distinct graces, or one principle that goes by different names?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: It is one principle. It is a single new principle of life. It gets various names according to the faculty of the soul it is in, or the object and operation it is directed to. In the understanding it is light, in the will obedience, in the affections love, and in all of them faith. Yet it remains one and the same habit of grace.
sources.quote: In the understanding, it is light; in the will, obedience; in the affections, love; in all, faith.
sources.raw_question: Is the habitual grace given by Christ several distinct graces, or one principle that goes by different names?

question: Does God have past or future in His being, so that He once was something He no longer is, or will cease to be?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Although the Soul Hopes for Blessedness, Yet It Does Not Remember Lost Blessedness, But Remembers God and the Rules of Righteousness. The Unchangeable Rules of Right Living are Known Even to the Ungodly.
sources.answer: No. God always is. He neither has been and is not, nor is and has not been. As He never will not be, so He never was not, and He is whole everywhere.
sources.quote: for He always is, nor has been and is not, nor is but has not been; but as He never will not be, so He never was not. And He is whole everywhere.
sources.raw_question: Does God have past or future in His being, so that He was something once or will cease to be?

question: Can God's intelligence be said to be emitted while still remaining within the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. Calling it an emission is then superfluous, because an emission is the manifestation of what is emitted beyond the one who emits it. Moreover, anything remaining within the Father could not be ignorant of Him. Nor could one such being know Him less than another, or fall into degeneracy, since with the Father there is no degeneracy.
sources.quote: For how could it have been sent forth if it continued within the Father? For an emission is the manifestation of that which is emitted, beyond him who emits it.
sources.raw_question: Can God's intelligence be said to be emitted while still remaining within the Father?

question: What descended upon Jesus at his baptism: a separate heavenly Christ or Saviour, as the Gnostics claim, or the Spirit of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVII.—The apostles teach that it was neither Christ nor the Saviour, but the Holy Spirit, who did descend upon Jesus. The reason for this descent.
sources.answer: The Spirit of God descended upon Jesus as a dove, not a distinct aeon called Christ or Saviour. The apostles could easily have said that Christ descended upon Jesus had they known it, but they recorded only what really happened. That this was the Spirit is confirmed by Isaiah's prophecies that the Spirit of God would rest upon Him and anoint Him.
sources.quote: But what really was the case, that did they record, [namely,] that the Spirit of God as a dove descended upon Him; this Spirit, of whom it was declared by Isaiah, “And the Spirit of God shall rest upon Him,”
sources.raw_question: What descended upon Jesus at his baptism: a separate heavenly Christ or Saviour (as the Gnostics claim), or the Spirit of God?

question: Was Christ the Saviour himself born of Mary, or did a superior Christ only descend on the man Jesus at his baptism, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: Christ the Saviour was himself born, not a man upon whom a higher Christ later descended. The angels proclaimed, "unto you is born this day a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord". If the Gnostic account were true, the angels would have lied, since by that account neither Christ nor the Saviour was born then.
sources.quote: Therefore, according to these men, the angels of the Ogdoad lied, when they said, “For unto you is born this day a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David.”
sources.raw_question: Was the Christ and Saviour born of Mary at the nativity, or did a superior Christ from the Pleroma only descend on the man Jesus at his baptism, as the Gnostics claim?

question: Does human deification require that the incarnate Son be true God by nature from the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Yes. Man would not have been deified if joined to a creature, nor brought into the Father's presence unless the one who put on the body were the Father's natural and true Word. The union was designed to unite what is human by nature to Him who is in the nature of the Godhead, so that salvation and deification might be sure.
sources.quote: For man had not been deified if joined to a creature, or unless the Son were very God; nor had man been brought into the Father’s presence, unless He had been His natural and true Word who had put on the body.
sources.raw_question: Does human deification require that the incarnate Son be true God by nature from the Father?

question: Did Christ partake of human passion?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: He did not partake of true passion, the diseased condition of the will, for He was without sin. He did share the natural attributes of humanity loosely called passions: birth, nourishment, growth, sleep, toil, hunger, pain and the dread of death. He shared none of those that lead to sin.
sources.quote: Of that, at least, which is truly passion, which is a diseased condition of the will, He was not a partaker; for it says “He did no sin, neither was guile found in His mouth”
sources.raw_question: Did Christ partake of human passion?

question: What did Christ accomplish through his passion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XX.—Futility of the arguments adduced to demonstrate the sufferings of the twelfth Æon, from the parables, the treachery of Judas, and the passion of our Saviour.
sources.answer: By his passion Christ destroyed death, dispersed error, ended corruption and destroyed ignorance. He manifested life, revealed truth and bestowed incorruption. Having suffered, he ascended on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to men. He also gave believers power to tread on serpents, scorpions and all the power of the enemy, the leader of apostasy.
sources.quote: Our Lord also by His passion destroyed death, and dispersed error, and put an end to corruption, and destroyed ignorance, while He manifested life and revealed truth, and bestowed the gift of incorruption.
sources.raw_question: What did Christ accomplish through his passion?

question: Does Paul's language of the 'new man which after God is created' support reading Christ's 'creation' as referring to his humanity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: Yes. Paul tells us to 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' and also to 'put on the new man which after God is created.' Since the garment of salvation is one, namely Christ, the created new man is Christ. He alone is properly the new man, because his birth did not follow the ordinary ways of nature. 'New man' refers to his wondrous birth, while 'Christ' looks to the divine nature blended with it, and both names belong to one Person.
sources.quote: For if the garment of salvation is one, and that is Christ, one cannot say that “the new man, which after God is created,” is any other than Christ
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's language of the 'new man which after God is created' support reading Christ's 'creation' as referring to his humanity?

question: Why does Paul say the new man is renewed both 'after God' and 'after the image of Him that created him'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How the Image of God is Formed Anew in Man.
sources.answer: "After God" makes clear that the renewal is not modeled on some other creature. "After the image of God" makes clear that the renewal takes place in that part of man where God's image is, namely the mind.
sources.quote: it is said to be after God, in order that it may not be supposed to be after another creature; and to be after the image of God, in order that this renewing may be understood to take place in that wherein is the image of God, i.e. in the mind.
sources.raw_question: Why does Paul say the new man is renewed both "after God" and "after the image of Him that created him"?

question: Does 'renewed after the image of Him that created him' (Colossians 3:10) mean that man is renewed according to some other image than the one being renewed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How the Image of God is Formed Anew in Man.
sources.answer: No. "After the image" means "in the image," just as "dead after the body" means dead in the body. So the image according to which man is renewed is the very image in his mind that is itself being renewed.
sources.quote: Let us not therefore so understand the words, “After the image of Him that created him,” as though it were a different image after which he is renewed, and not the very same which is itself renewed.
sources.raw_question: Does "renewed after the image of Him that created him" (Colossians 3:10) mean that man is renewed according to some other image than the one being renewed?

question: Does Colossians 3:9-10, on putting on the new man renewed after the image of the Creator, teach that redeemed humanity becomes the perfect image of God through union with the incarnate Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Yes. By being conformed to the glory of Christ's body, man is renewed unto the knowledge of God. He is created again in the image of the Creator after the pattern given to the first man. Leaving sin behind, he reaches the perfection of his constitution, and through godliness he is promoted to immortality as the image of his Creator.
sources.quote: Leaving sin and the old man behind, he is made a new man unto the knowledge of God, and arrives at the perfection of his constitution, since through the knowledge of his God he becomes the perfect image of God.
sources.raw_question: Does Colossians 3:9-10, on putting on the new man renewed after the image of the Creator, teach that redeemed humanity becomes the perfect image of God through union with the incarnate Son?

question: Do Ephesians 5:5, Titus 2:13 and 2 Peter 1:1, which join 'God' and 'Christ/Saviour' under one Greek article, refer to one person, Christ, as God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. By the ordinary rule of Greek construction, confirmed by New Testament usage and the Greek fathers, the two nouns refer to one and the same object, as the parallel "our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ" in 2 Peter 1:11 shows. Had the writer not meant to identify the great God and the Saviour, he would have misled his readers.
sources.quote: no person would ever have disputed the propriety, or rather necessity, of considering the two concluding nouns as referring to one and the same object.
sources.raw_question: Do Ephesians 5:5, Titus 2:13 and 2 Peter 1:1, which join 'God' and 'Christ/Saviour' under one article, refer to one person, Christ, as God?

question: If Ephesians 5:5, Titus 2:13 and 2 Peter 1:1 refer to both the Father and the Son rather than to Christ alone, do they still testify to Christ's deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Even granting this reading, the conjunction of God and Christ in one phrase would still prove Christ's deity. Associating a mere creature with the Creator in this way would confound the distinction between Creator and creature.
sources.quote: we find the conjunction of the names God and Christ, where such association would confound the distinction betwixt the Creator and his creature.
sources.raw_question: If Ephesians 5:5, Titus 2:13 and 2 Peter 1:1 refer to both the Father and the Son rather than to Christ alone, does that remove their testimony to Christ's deity?

question: Is the name Jehovah a relative term or a term of absolute signification?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: It is absolute, expressing God as he is. Scripture never says 'my Jehovah', 'your Jehovah' or 'the Jehovah of Israel', so relative terms do not suit it. Since it is sometimes rendered by Theos, the word 'God' in Scripture is also rarely a merely relative word.
sources.quote: Jehovah is a word of absolute signification. The relative terms do not suit with it, as with the other. We do not read, my Jehovah, or your Jehovah, or the Jehovah of Israel
sources.raw_question: Is the name Jehovah a relative term or a term of absolute signification?

question: Does the Son share the Father's attribute of being Almighty, contrary to Eunomius's claim?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: No. Christ made all things, all things exist and continue in him, and he holds in his hand all that the Father has. He is called "God over all" by Paul. Since he possesses all things and is sovereign over them, there is no reason he should not be Almighty.
sources.quote: If, then, He hath all things, and is sovereign over that which He hath, why is He Who is thus sovereign over all things something else and not Almighty?
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius right that the Son has no share in the Father's high estate as Almighty?

question: Is it meaningful to say, as Eunomius does, that no one 'has lot' in the Father's power, as though divine power could be obtained by allotment?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. To 'have lot' means to obtain something by casting lots, as the soldiers did for Christ's coat. But the power of Father, Son and Spirit resides in their nature. Scripture shows that each acts as He wills: the Spirit breathes where He lists, the Son quickens whom He will, and the Father has the times in His power. So no allotment or contest for power among them can be conceived, and the phrase is empty of meaning.
sources.quote: inasmuch as Their power resides in Their nature
sources.raw_question: Is it meaningful to say, as Eunomius does, that no one 'has lot' in the Father's power, as though the Son could obtain divine power by allotment?

question: Does Christ's promise that whoever believes in him shall never die show that he is more than a mere man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again from the Gospel He Proves Christ to Be God.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture pronounces accursed whoever trusts in man alone, yet Christ promises eternal life to those who believe in him. If he were only man, believing in him would bring a curse. Since faith in him instead frees from the curse and gives everlasting life, Christ is not man only but God also.
sources.quote: if he is not accursed, but rather, as it is read, destined for the attainment of everlasting life, Christ is not man only, but God also, in whom he who believes both lays aside all risk of curse
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's promise that whoever believes in him shall never die show that he is more than a mere man?

question: Can someone who holds that Christ is merely a man stay consistent once the prophecies about God's coming are applied to Christ?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That Christ is God, is Proved by the Authority of the Old Testament Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. The prophecies force them to call Christ God, either as the Father or as the Son. If they say the Son, they cannot deny that the Son of God is God. If they say the Father, they join Sabellius. Either way, the facts compel them to give up the view that Christ is a mere man.
sources.quote: whether they call Him Father or Son, from his heresy, however unwillingly, they must needs withdraw if they are accustomed to say that Christ is merely man
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold Christ a bare man
sources.raw_question: Can someone who holds that Christ is merely a man stay consistent once the prophecies about God's coming are applied to Christ?

question: If the Word who was in the beginning and was God 'became Lord,' does this mean the Godhead acquired some advancement or added grace?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: No. The divine nature lacks no good and contains all exalted majesty, so the Word did not advance in Godhead. He became Lord and Christ by bringing the human nature He assumed into participation in the Godhead, which the terms "Christ" and "Lord" signify.
sources.quote: not by arriving at any addition of grace in respect of His Godhead (for the Nature of the Godhead is acknowledged to be lacking in no good), but by bringing the Human Nature to that participation in the Godhead
sources.raw_question: If the Word who was in the beginning and was God "became Lord," does this mean the Godhead acquired some advancement or added grace?

question: Is it valid to deny Christ's supreme Deity by combining texts about his humiliation with texts about believers' exaltation?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Scripture affirms both the depth of Christ's abasement and the height of glory to which he raises his people. But to stand alternately on the lowest step of his humiliation and the highest step of his children's exaltation in order to deny his Deity is to deny the very one who stooped so low to draw us up so high. This is an ingratitude without parallel.
sources.quote: for a man to take his stand alternately on the lowest step of Christ’s humiliation, and on the highest step of his children’s exaltation, and thence to deny the Supreme Deity of him who stooped so low that He might draw us up so high
sources.raw_question: Is it valid to deny Christ's supreme Deity by combining texts about his humiliation with texts about believers' exaltation?

question: Should passages describing Christ's humiliation and humanity be interpreted in light of passages that establish his full deity, rather than the other way round?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: Yes. Having first proved from Scripture the coequal, coessential, coeternal Godhead of the Son, we stand on vantage ground from which we can safely look into his humiliation and humanity. Once his deity is acknowledged, passages speaking of his lowliness do not stumble us but display the depth of divine condescension: as we assign no limit to his glory, we assign none to the depths of his grace.
sources.quote: Now we shall not be stumbled at passages which speak of the exceeding humiliation to which He stooped. As we assign no limit to the height of his glory, we shall assign none to the depths of his grace.
sources.raw_question: Should passages describing Christ's humiliation and humanity be interpreted in light of passages that establish his full deity, rather than the other way round?

question: Do the proofs of Christ's true humanity and lowly humiliation disprove his eternal Deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. To use his humanity and humiliation as evidence against his Deity is a misreading and a base ingratitude. It is like a prisoner who argues that his benefactor Howard must be a convict because he humbled himself to tend him in his cell. Christ's lowliness, his sympathy, and his emptying of himself presuppose the glory he had with the Father before the world was. They do not refute it.
sources.quote: every generous feeling within you brands it as the basest ingratitude to allege these proofs of his humanity in disproof of his Deity, to trample on his lowliness that you may pluck the diadem from his brow
sources.raw_question: Do the proofs of Christ's true humanity and lowly humiliation disprove his eternal Deity?

question: Do the scriptural texts that affirm God is one also point to a plurality of persons in God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen claims that wherever Scripture mentions God's oneness, it also hints at a plurality of persons, either in the words themselves or in the surrounding context. Deut. 6:4 asserts the Trinity in the one divine essence. Isa. 44:6, 8 includes and expresses a plurality of persons.
sources.quote: it is nowhere mentioned in the Scripture, but that, either in the words themselves or the context of the place, a plurality of persons in that one sense is intimated
sources.raw_question: Do the scriptural texts that affirm God is one also point to a plurality of persons in God?

question: Do the expressions "right hand" and "bosom" of the Father imply that God has a body or occupies a place, with the Son seated physically below the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: No. To take these terms physically would confine God within local limits and invent form, shape and bodily posture for him. Such ideas are wholly foreign to the absolute, infinite and incorporeal God. Understood rightly, they show the Son's glory and the preeminence of his power.
sources.quote: so as at once to circumscribe God in local limits, and invent form, mould, and bodily position, all of which are totally distinct from the idea of the absolute, the infinite, and the incorporeal
sources.raw_question: Do the expressions "right hand" and "bosom" of the Father imply that God has a body or occupies a place, with the Son seated physically below the Father?

question: What does the Son's sitting at the right hand of the Father show about how the Son's Godhead relates to the Father's?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: It shows the Son's genuineness and that the Godhead of the Father is the same as the Son's. Because the Son reigns in the Father's kingdom, sits on the same throne, and is contemplated in the Father's Godhead, the Word is God, and whoever beholds the Son beholds the Father; thus there is one God.
sources.quote: For in that the Son reigns in His Father’s kingdom, is seated upon the same throne as the Father, and is contemplated in the Father’s Godhead, therefore is the Word God, and whoso beholds the Son, beholds the Father; and thus there is one God.
sources.raw_question: What does the Son's sitting at the right hand of the Father show about the relation of the Son's Godhead to the Father's?

question: Is the Son lower than the Father in place, as if seated beneath him?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: No. Place cannot be predicated of incorporeal things, and God fills all things, as the Psalmist says, so dividing 'up and down' between Father and Son is absurd and illogical.
sources.quote: The faith of the sound is that God fills all things;[^793] but they who divide their up and down between the Father and the Son do not remember even the word of the Prophet
sources.raw_question: Is the Son lower than the Father in place, as if seated beneath him?

question: Does placing the Father above and the Son below in a spatial sense degrade only the Son, or does it also dishonour the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: It dishonours the Father as well. Whatever is derogatory in such an idea applies equally to Father and Son, so whoever uses it does not lower the Son's dignity but blasphemes the Father. A Father seated in an upper place would carry all the conditions of a body. Whatever insolence is shown to the Son passes over to the Father, as the Lord teaches that he who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father.
sources.quote: whoever repeats these arguments does not take away the dignity of the Son, but does incur the charge of blaspheming the Father; for whatever audacity a man be guilty of against the Son he cannot but transfer to the Father
sources.raw_question: Does placing the Father above and the Son below in a spatial sense degrade only the Son, or does it also dishonour the Father?

question: Does Isaiah 7:14-16 teach that the child born of the virgin is both God and man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. The name Emmanuel indicates His essence, that He is God, while eating butter and honey and being called a child are tokens of a human infant. His not consenting to evil to choose the good is proper to God. The prophecy thus guards against thinking Him a mere man or God without flesh.
sources.quote: that by the fact, that He shall eat butter and honey, we should not understand that He is a mere man only, nor, on the other hand, from the name Emmanuel, should suspect Him to be God without flesh.
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah 7:14-16 teach that the child born of the virgin is both God and man?

question: What does the sign of Isaiah 7:14, that a virgin would bear a son called 'God with us', signify about Christ's descent and work?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XIX.—Jesus Christ was not a mere man, begotten from Joseph in the ordinary course of nature, but was very God, begotten of the Father most high, and very man, born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: It signifies that the one born of a virgin is God with us, who descends to the earth to seek the lost sheep, his own handiwork. He then ascends to offer the recovered human nature to his Father, becoming the first-fruits of the resurrection for the whole body.
sources.quote: one remaining a virgin could bring forth a son, and that what was thus born should be “God with us,” and descend to those things which are of the earth beneath
sources.raw_question: What does the sign of Isaiah 7:14, that a virgin would bear a son called 'God with us', signify about Christ?

question: Why are water and the Holy Spirit joined together in baptism?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Reply to the suggested objection that we are baptized “into water.” Also concerning baptism.
sources.answer: Because baptism has two ends: the destruction of the body of sin and our living unto the Spirit. The water figures death, the body being as it were buried in it, while the Spirit gives the earnest of life and renews the soul. To be born again of water and Spirit means being made dead in the water and made alive through the Spirit.
sources.quote: the water receiving the body as in a tomb figures death, while the Spirit pours in the quickening power, renewing our souls from the deadness of sin unto their original life.
sources.raw_question: Why are water and the Holy Spirit joined together in baptism?

question: Is the outward sign of water strictly necessary for salvation, given that the Spirit is the source of baptismal grace?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Reply to the suggested objection that we are baptized “into water.” Also concerning baptism.
sources.answer: Not in every case. Some martyrs died for Christ in actual fact, not merely in likeness. They needed no outward sign of water for salvation, because they were baptized in their own blood. This shows that the saving grace belongs to the Spirit rather than to the water.
sources.quote: have undergone the death for Christ’s sake, not in mere similitude, but in actual fact, and so have needed none of the outward signs of water for their salvation, because they were baptized in their own blood.
sources.raw_question: Is the outward sign of water strictly necessary for salvation, given that the Spirit is the source of baptismal grace?

question: Can anything that undergoes change properly be called eternal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
