sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Son of God Became Incarnate in Order that We Being Cleansed by Faith May Be Raised to the Unchangeable Truth.
sources.answer: No. Nothing that undergoes any degree of change is properly called eternal. Therefore we, being changeable in soul as well as in body, stand apart from eternity in the same measure that we are changeable. True immortality, incorruptibility and unchangeableness are eternity itself.
sources.quote: For that is not properly called eternal which undergoes any degree of change. Therefore, in so far as we are changeable, in so far we stand apart from eternity.
sources.raw_question: Can anything that undergoes change properly be called eternal?

question: Why does Peter's confession add 'the Son of the living God' to 'Thou art the Christ'?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: To confess Christ's nature, not merely to pay him reverence. Saying "Thou art the Christ" alone would have sufficed for reverence but would have been a hollow confession. The words "Thou art" answer the Father's "This is My Son" and declare that what is said of Christ is strictly true to his nature.
sources.quote: And so his words Thou art declare that what is asserted of Him is strictly and exactly true to His nature.
sources.raw_question: Why does Peter's confession add 'the Son of the living God' to 'Thou art the Christ'?

question: Does Peter's confession show that the Son of man who suffered is the same as Christ, the Son of the living God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: Yes. When Jesus asked who men said he, the Son of man, was, and Peter answered "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God," the Lord commended him, showing that the Son of man is the Christ. From that time the same one began to show that he himself must suffer and be crucified, and he rebuked Peter for opposing his suffering.
sources.quote: He made it clear that He, the Son of man, is Christ the Son of the living God.
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's confession show that the Son of man who suffered is the same as Christ, the Son of the living God?

question: What does Psalm 82:6-7 ("I have said, Ye are gods... But ye shall die like men") teach about human deification?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVIII.—Why man was not made perfect from the beginning.
sources.answer: It sets forth two truths at once. The first half shows the kindness of God's free gift, which calls men gods and sons of the Highest. The second half shows our weakness, since we could not sustain the power of divinity, and also that we were given power over ourselves.
sources.quote: But since we could not sustain the power of divinity, He adds, “But ye shall die like men,” setting forth both truths—the kindness of His free gift, and our weakness, and also that we were possessed of power over ourselves.
sources.raw_question: What does Psalm 82:6-7 ("I have said, Ye are gods... But ye shall die like men") teach about human deification?

question: Does Psalm 82:6-7 ("Ye are gods... but ye shall die like men") show that men are called 'god' in Scripture in the same sense as Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XIX.—Jesus Christ was not a mere man, begotten from Joseph in the ordinary course of nature, but was very God, begotten of the Father most high, and very man, born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: No. The Word speaks these words to those who have not received the gift of adoption and who despise the incarnation of the Word; they remain in mortal flesh. No son of Adam is absolutely and in every respect called God or Lord, whereas Christ is God and Lord in his own right.
sources.quote: no one of the sons of Adam is as to everything, and absolutely, called God, or named Lord.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 82:6-7 ("Ye are all the sons of the Highest, and gods; but ye shall die like men") show that being called 'god' in Scripture is open to all men in the same sense as Christ?

question: Is knowing God a matter of perceiving Him with bodily sight?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > God Must First Be Known by an Unerring Faith, that He May Be Loved.
sources.answer: No. To know God is to behold and steadfastly perceive Him with the mind. He is not a body to be searched out by carnal eyes.
sources.quote: And what is it to know God except to behold Him and steadfastly perceive Him with the mind? For He is not a body to be searched out by carnal eyes.
sources.raw_question: Is knowing God a matter of perceiving Him with bodily sight?

question: Did Christ suffer from necessity, or could he have avoided suffering?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Unobligated Death of Christ Has Freed Those Who Were Liable to Death.
sources.answer: He could have avoided it. He suffered things belonging to man because he was man. But had he been unwilling, it was in his power not to suffer, because he was also God. His humility therefore commends righteousness all the more, since it was voluntary.
sources.quote: But now He suffered for us things belonging to man, because He was man; but if He had been unwilling, it would have been in His power to not so to suffer, because He was also God.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ suffer from necessity, or could he have avoided suffering?

question: Since Scripture calls the three visitors at Mamre 'men,' does that show they were not angels?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: No. Scripture calls angels men, as when Daniel says "Behold the man Gabriel." So the three men in whom the Lord appeared to Abraham can rightly be understood as angels.
sources.quote: Were they not angels because they are called men? Let them read Daniel, saying, “Behold the man Gabriel.”
sources.raw_question: Since Scripture calls the three visitors at Mamre "men," does that show they were not angels?

question: Does the Son, as 'Angel', publish only another's word rather than being himself the Word?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. Making the Son the minister who publishes the word of the Existent implies that the Word who was in the beginning, and who was God, is not himself the Word. He would instead be the servant and 'angel' of some other Word. Gregory treats this as a profane conclusion contrary to Scripture.
sources.quote: the Word Who was in the beginning, the Word Who was God, is not Himself the Word, but is the Word of some other Word, being its minister and “angel.”
sources.raw_question: Does the Son, as 'Angel', publish only another's word rather than being himself the Word?

question: If each divine person is God and therefore infinite, does it follow that there are three infinites?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Each person is infinite as he is God, not as he is a person. Infinity, like all divine properties, belongs to the persons on account of their nature, which is one, not on account of their personality.
sources.quote: All divine properties, such as to be infinite is, belong not to the persons on the account of their personality, but on the account of their nature, which is one, for they are all natural properties.
sources.raw_question: If each divine person is God and therefore infinite, does it follow that there are three infinites?

question: If the divine persons are not infinite as persons, does the infinite God then have a finite mode of subsisting?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Finite and infinite are properties of beings, not of the manner of a thing's subsistence. The nature of each person is infinite, and each person is infinite because of that nature; of the mode of subsistence one can only say that an infinite being so subsists.
sources.quote: finite and infinite are properties and adjuncts of beings, and not of the manner of the subsistence of any thing. The nature of each person is infinite, and so is each person because of that nature.
sources.raw_question: If the divine persons as such are not infinite, does the infinite God then have a finite mode of subsisting?

question: Does the fact that a finite being cannot be one in one respect and three in another prove that the infinite God cannot be one in essence and three in persons?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. All such objections reason from what is impossible in finite things to what must be so in infinite things, which supposes that the finite can perfectly comprehend the infinite, an absurd and self-contradictory assertion. Moreover, the highest reason in matters of pure revelation is to submit the understanding to the authority of the Revealer, so these objections overthrow basic principles of reason itself.
sources.quote: All these reasonings are built upon this supposition, that that which is finite can perfectly comprehend that which is infinite, — an assertion absurd, foolish, and contradictory unto itself.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that a finite being cannot be one in one respect and three in another prove that the infinite God cannot be one in essence and three in persons?

question: Can one infinite divine Being be greater or less than another infinite Being?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His acknowledgment that the Divine Being is 'single' is only verbal.
sources.answer: No. The unlimited is not unlimited by relation to something else but escapes limitation in itself, so a reflecting mind cannot conceive one infinite as greater or less than another. If Eunomius grants the supreme Being is single, he must grant it simplicity and infinitude, excluding ranking among the Persons.
sources.quote: It is, indeed, difficult to see how a reflecting mind can conceive one infinite to be greater or less than another infinite.
sources.raw_question: Can one infinite divine Being be greater or less than another infinite Being?

question: Can there be two infinite beings?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, He is Good, Always the Same, Immutable, One and Only, Infinite; And His Own Name Can Never Be Declared, and He is Incorruptible and Immortal.
sources.answer: No. The infinite has neither beginning nor end, and what occupies the whole excludes the beginning of another. If God did not contain all that is, he would be contained within something greater and would cease to be God. Whatever contained him would then have the better claim to be God.
sources.quote: because there cannot be two infinites, as the very nature of things dictates. And that is infinite which neither has any sort of beginning nor end. For whatever has occupied the whole excludes the beginning of another.
sources.raw_question: Can there be two infinite beings?

question: Why is contempt of or opposition to the preaching of God's word described in Scripture as resisting the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Because the gift of preaching is from the Holy Spirit. He sets up the ministry in the church, separates men to it, and furnishes them with gifts for dispensing the word. So opposing or disobeying that word is resisting him. Stephen's charge that the Jews, like their fathers who persecuted the prophets, "resisted the Holy Ghost" shows this.
sources.quote: Now, the Holy Ghost is said to be resisted in the contempt of the preaching of the word; because the gift of preaching of it is from him.
sources.raw_question: Why is contempt of or opposition to the preaching of God's word described in Scripture as resisting the Holy Spirit?

question: Why is resisting the Holy Spirit's work described in Scripture as 'quenching' the Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Because the Spirit is set forth under the figure of fire. He was typified by the fire kept always burning on the altar and is called a 'Spirit of burning.' Fire is opposed by quenching, so opposing his actings is called quenching the Spirit. Likewise believers are told to 'stir up with new fire' the gifts that are in them.
sources.quote: Now, the opposition that is made to fire in its actings, is by quenching. Hence the opposition made to the actings of the Holy Ghost are called “quenching of the Spirit,”
sources.raw_question: Why is resisting the Holy Spirit's work described as 'quenching' him?

question: Does Christ's human nature have its own personal subsistence, or does it subsist in the person of the Son of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: It has no subsistence of its own. A necessary consequence of the union of the two natures in one person is that the human nature subsists in the person of the Son of God.
sources.quote: The subsistence of the human nature in the person of the Son of God, having no subsistence of its own, Luke i. 35; 1 Tim. iii. 16.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's human nature have its own personal subsistence, or does it subsist in the person of the Son of God?

question: Can the properties of Christ's divine and human natures be ascribed to his one person, as when God is said to purchase the church with his own blood?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Through the communication of attributes, the properties of either nature are spoken of the person of Christ by whatever name he is called, God or man. So Scripture can say that God purchased the church with his own blood.
sources.quote: that communication of attributes in the person, whereby the properties of either nature are promiscuously spoken of the person of Christ, under what name soever, of God or man, he be spoken of, Acts xx. 28, iii. 21.
sources.raw_question: Can the properties of Christ's divine and human natures be ascribed to his one person, as when God is said to purchase the church with his own blood?

question: Does Paul's statement that Christ 'put off the flesh' prove that Christ is more than a man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is Again Confirmed in Christ by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. A man can never be stripped of or clothed with himself, since what is put on or taken off must be something other than the one who wears it. So the one who put off the flesh and put it on again at the resurrection must be the Word of God. He was clothed with flesh at his birth and wears it like a garment.
sources.quote: And yet Christ could neither have been divested of nor invested with manhood, had He been only man: for man is never either deprived of nor invested with himself.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that Christ 'put off the flesh' prove that Christ is more than a man?

question: Does Christ's claim to be the bread of life that came down from heaven prove that he is more than a man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > The Author Prosecutes the Same Argument.
sources.answer: Yes. A mortal man cannot be the bread of eternal life. Nor could a man come down from heaven, where no perishable material exists. So the one who descended is divine.
sources.quote: when man can neither be the bread of life, he himself being mortal, nor could he have come down from heaven, since no perishable material is established in heaven?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's claim to be the bread of life that came down from heaven prove he is more than man?

question: Does Christ's statement that only he who is of God has seen God show that he is more than a man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > The Author Prosecutes the Same Argument.
sources.answer: Yes. No man has seen God. If Christ has seen God because he is of God, he means it to be understood that he is more than man.
sources.quote: but if, being of God, He has seen God, He wishes it to be understood that He is more than man, in that He has seen God.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that only he who is of God has seen God show that he is more than man?

question: Can God the Father be contained in a place or move by descending and ascending?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > It Is, Moreover, Proved by Moses in the Beginning of the Holy Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. Moses presents the Father as infinite. He is not enclosed in any place but includes every place, containing and filling all things. He therefore cannot descend or ascend.
sources.quote: not as being enclosed in any place, but as one who includes every place; nor as one who is in a place, but rather one in whom every place is, containing all things and embracing all things
sources.raw_question: Can God the Father be contained in a place or move by descending and ascending?

question: Can the divine nature of the Son undergo local motion, such as going or ascending from one place to another?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > This twelfth book gives a notable interpretation of the words of the Lord to Mary, “Touch Me not, for I am not yet ascended to My Father.”
sources.answer: No. Motion means leaving one place and occupying another. The Son, in whom all things were created and consist, contains all things, extends through all, and is confined by nothing. He therefore has no place outside Himself to pass into, since nothing is empty of the Divine fulness. Words like 'I go' express the local change of His human body.
sources.quote: while that which extends through all, and is in all, and controls all, and is confined by no existent thing, has no place to which to pass, inasmuch as nothing is void of the Divine fulness
sources.raw_question: Can the divine nature of the Son undergo local motion, such as going or ascending from one place to another?

question: In their communion with Christ, do believers value Jesus Christ above all other things and persons in the world?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. Believers esteem Christ above all the world, and neither heaven nor earth yields them anything comparable to him. Moses showed this when he counted the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, despising the best of the world for the worst of the cross. Christ himself said that whoever loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him.
sources.quote: Moses despised the very best of the world, for the worst of the cross of Christ. Indeed, himself hath told believers, that if they love any thing better than him, father or mother, they are not worthy of him.
sources.raw_question: In their communion with Christ, do believers value Jesus Christ above all other things and persons in the world?

question: Do believers value Christ even above their own lives?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul did not count his life dear so long as he could finish his course and his ministry from the Lord Jesus. Ignatius, led to martyrdom, said he would welcome anything so long as he obtained Christ. The apostles rejoiced to be shamed for his name. The martyrs' contempt of torments, sweetened by his name, has made this clear to men and angels.
sources.quote: The lives they have to live, the death they have to die, is little, is light, upon the thoughts of him who is the stay of their lives and the end of their death.
sources.raw_question: Do believers value Christ even above their own lives?

question: Does Psalm 82:1 ('God standeth in the assembly of the gods') show that Christ is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > It is Proved from the Scriptures that Christ Was Called an Angel. But Yet It is Shown from Other Parts of Holy Scripture that He is God Also.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ stood at various times in the synagogue, and so stood there as God, judging between the 'gods' whom he rebukes for accepting persons and not judging justly. If those who are reproved can be called gods, much more is he God who stands among them and judges them. And if those who 'fall like one of the princes' are still called gods, much more is he God who overcomes the prince of wickedness himself.
sources.quote: and Christ stood in the synagogue as God,—judging, to wit, between the gods, to whom He says, “How long do ye accept the persons of men?”
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 82 ("God standeth in the assembly of the gods") show that Christ is God?

question: Is Christ God only by participation, as those called 'gods' in Psalm 82:6 are, or is he true God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: He is very God, one in essence with the Father. Those to whom it was said 'I said ye are Gods' received this as a grace from the Father, only by participating in the Word through the Spirit. Christ is the one participated in, not a participant.
sources.quote: other beings, to whom He said, ‘I said ye are Gods,’ had this grace from the Father, only by participation of the Word, through the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ God only by participation, as those called 'gods' in Psalm 82:6 are, or is he very God?

question: Can the Holy Spirit dwell in a person without making that person holy?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: No. As to the essence of holiness, the Spirit cannot dwell in someone without making him holy, because the temple of God is holy. His comforting, by contrast, rests wholly on his sovereign will, so he may abide without actually comforting.
sources.quote: as to the essence of holiness, he cannot dwell in us but withal he must make us holy; for the temple of God is holy; — but as to his comforting, his actings therein are all of his sovereign will
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit dwell in a person without making that person holy?

question: Can someone have God as Father and Christ as Advocate without the Holy Spirit dwelling in them as Comforter?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. Scripture teaches that unless the Spirit of Christ is in us we are dead, reprobates and none of Christ's. So communion with the Father and the Son cannot be had apart from the Spirit. If the Spirit does not dwell in a person, God is not their Father, the Son is not their Advocate, and they have no portion in the gospel.
sources.quote: If the Spirit dwell not in you, if he be not your Comforter, neither is God your Father, nor the Son your Advocate, nor have you any portion in the gospel.
sources.raw_question: Can someone have God as Father and Christ as Advocate without the Holy Spirit dwelling in them as Comforter?

question: When Scripture calls the Spirit the 'earnest' of our inheritance, is the earnest a created grace or gift of the Spirit, or the person of the Holy Spirit himself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: It is the Spirit himself, personally considered. 'Of the Spirit' is a genitive of matter, naming the earnest itself rather than its author. This parallels Galatians 4:6, where God sends the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, and nothing but the person of the Spirit can be called the Spirit of his Son. In Ephesians 1:14 the masculine relative pronoun likewise refers to the Spirit as the earnest.
sources.quote: It is the Spirit himself, personally considered, that is said to be this earnest, 2 Cor. i. 22.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture calls the Spirit the 'earnest' of our inheritance, is the earnest some created grace or gift of the Spirit, or the person of the Holy Spirit himself?

question: Does God claim for himself alone the supreme dependence, love, worship, and service of his creatures?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 2. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, detaches our ultimate confidence from man the creature, and attaches it to God the Creator; – by contrasting the sinfulness and feebleness of mortal man with the goodness and omnipotence of the Eternal Jehovah: by direct prohibition and precept: by exhibiting the holy Jealousy of God.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture shows that the Lord claims the supreme dependence, love, worship and service of his creatures. Even those Bickersteth addresses would not deny this, and they could subscribe to the Church of England catechism's statement of our duty to believe in, fear, love, worship, and wholly trust God.
sources.quote: Further, He claims the supreme dependence, love, worship, and service of his creatures.
sources.raw_question: Does God claim for himself alone the supreme dependence, love, worship, and service of his creatures?

question: Is God alone free from sin by nature, so that every creature is by its own nature liable to sin?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IX. The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ, and the oil of gladness; and why Christ Himself is not the ointment, since He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It is not strange that the Spirit should be called Ointment, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. And there is no confusion between them, since Christ alone suffered death, Whose saving cross is then spoken of.
sources.answer: Yes. God alone is by nature free from sin, while every creature by its own nature can be liable to sin. This principle grounds the argument for the Spirit's divinity.
sources.quote: But if God alone is free from sin, certainly every creature by its own nature can be, as we have said, liable to sin.
sources.raw_question: Is God alone free from sin by nature, so that every creature is by its own nature liable to sin?

question: Does the river of living water proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb in Revelation signify the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XX. The river flowing from the Throne of God is a figure of the Holy Spirit, but by the waters spoken of by David the powers of heaven are intended. The kingdom of God is the work of the Spirit; and it is no matter for wonder if He reigns in this together with the Son, since St. Paul promises that we too shall reign with the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ himself identifies the rivers of living water flowing from the believer with the Spirit, whom those who believe in him drink. Therefore the river proceeding from the throne of God is the Holy Spirit, who is thus shown to be in the throne of God.
sources.quote: This is certainly the River proceeding from the throne of God, that is, the Holy Spirit, Whom he drinks who believes in Christ
sources.raw_question: Does the river of living water proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb in Revelation signify the Holy Spirit?

question: Do the 'waters above the heavens' that praise the Lord in Psalm 148 refer to the Holy Spirit or to the river from God's throne?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XX. The river flowing from the Throne of God is a figure of the Holy Spirit, but by the waters spoken of by David the powers of heaven are intended. The kingdom of God is the work of the Spirit; and it is no matter for wonder if He reigns in this together with the Son, since St. Paul promises that we too shall reign with the Son.
sources.answer: No. David places those waters above the heavens, not in the throne of God, and he says 'let them praise' in the plural, which shows he means not the element of water but the heavenly Powers. The river in the throne of God is distinct from these created waters.
sources.quote: Let them praise, he says, not let it praise. For if he had intended us to understand the element of water, he would certainly have said, Let it praise, but by using the plural he intended the Powers to be understood.
sources.raw_question: Do the 'waters above the heavens' that praise the Lord in Psalm 148 refer to the Holy Spirit or to the river from God's throne?

question: Does the 'living water' Christ promises in John 4 mean the same thing as the 'rivers of living water' in John 7, namely the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: Yes. The flowing rivers from the believer in John 7 correspond to the fountain springing up to eternal life within him in John 4. Because the evangelist explicitly identifies the John 7 water as the Spirit, the John 4 water is the Spirit too. Paul confirms this when he says all have been made to drink into one Spirit.
sources.quote: For that which is in the one passage, “Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water,” is in the other, “shall be in him a fountain of water springing up unto eternal life.”
sources.raw_question: Does the 'living water' Christ promises in John 4 mean the same thing as the 'rivers of living water' in John 7, namely the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the vision of Isaiah 6, read alongside John 12:41 and Acts 28:25, show that the Holy Spirit is worshipped together with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. John 12:41 shows the glory Isaiah saw was Christ's, while Acts 28:25 attributes the voice of Jehovah in that vision to the Holy Ghost. Hence the threefold 'Holy, Holy, Holy' of the seraphim and the plural 'Who will go for us?' point to the Trinity, and the angels worship the Spirit with the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: The glory of Jehovah of hosts was then revealed by Jesus Christ, and the voice of Jehovah was the utterance of the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: Does the vision of Isaiah 6, read alongside John 12:41 and Acts 28:25, show that the Holy Spirit is worshipped together with the Father and the Son?

question: Is the 'Lord of hosts' who becomes a stone of stumbling in Isaiah 8:13-14 the Son of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen notes that the New Testament applies this passage about the Lord of hosts to the Son in Luke 2:34, Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8. The one whom Israel must sanctify as the Lord of hosts is therefore Christ.
sources.quote: And he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel
sources.raw_question: Is the 'Lord of hosts' who becomes a stone of stumbling in Isaiah 8:13-14 the Son of God?

question: Is it fitting to describe the Holy Spirit as "sounding an accompaniment" to those who pray?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: No. The expression is ludicrous and meaningless. It treats the Holy Spirit like a bell or an empty cask that rings when struck by the voice of the one who prays.
sources.quote: the Holy Spirit is not a bell nor an empty cask sounding an accompaniment and made to ring by the voice of him who prays as it were by a blow?
sources.raw_question: Is it fitting to describe the Holy Spirit as "sounding an accompaniment" to those who pray?

question: How is the Holy Spirit the 'Spirit of supplication' at work in believers' prayers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Prayer is considered in two ways. As a duty God requires, it is wrought by the Spirit of sanctification, who raises the soul's faculties to perform it spiritually. As a means of communion with God, in which believers ease their hearts in the Father's bosom and taste his love, it belongs to the Spirit as Comforter.
sources.quote: The soul is never more raised with the love of God than when by the Spirit taken into intimate communion with him in the discharge of this duty; and therein it belongs to the Spirit of consolation, to the Spirit promised as a comforter.
sources.raw_question: How is the Holy Spirit the 'Spirit of supplication' at work in believers' prayers?

question: Does Ephesians 2:18 ('access through Christ by one Spirit unto the Father') make only the Father the object of worship?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. The verse distinguishes the Persons by their operations: access is to the Father, through the Son's mediation, by the Spirit's assistance. It does not distinguish them as objects of worship. The Son and Spirit are worshipped no less than the Father; what we draw near for is the Father's grace, obtained through the Son and the Spirit.
sources.quote: Here is a distinction of the persons, as to their operations, but not at all as to their being the object of our worship.
sources.raw_question: Does Ephesians 2:18 ('access through Christ by one Spirit unto the Father') make only the Father the object of worship?

question: Does Ephesians 2:18 show a distinct role for each divine Person in believers' access to God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Our access to God is through Christ, in the Spirit, and unto the Father. Here the persons are considered as engaged distinctly in accomplishing the counsel of God's will revealed in the gospel. So the distinction of persons is observed in our approaches to God as well as in grace coming from him.
sources.quote: Our access unto God (wherein we have communion with him) is δὶα Χριστοῦ, “through Christ,” ἐν Πνεύματι, “in the Spirit,” and πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα, “unto the Father;”
sources.raw_question: Does Ephesians 2:18 show a distinct role for each divine person in believers' access to God?

question: Does faith in true things perish when the things believed come to be seen?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Attempt is Made to Distinguish Out of the Scriptures the Offices of Wisdom and of Knowledge. That in the Beginning of John Some Things that are Said Belong to Wisdom, Some to Knowledge. Some Things There are Only Known by the Help of Faith. How We See the Faith that is in Us. In the Same Narrative of John, Some Things are Known by the Sense of the Body, Others Only by the Reason of the Mind.
sources.answer: It does not perish. It passes, as one would wish, into the things themselves. Once they are seen, it can no longer properly be called faith, because Hebrews defines faith as the evidence of things not seen. This differs from faith placed in falsehoods, which is driven out without blame when truth is found.
sources.quote: But faith in things that are true, passes, as one should wish it to pass, into the things themselves. For we must not say that faith perishes, when those things which were believed are seen.
sources.raw_question: Does faith in true things perish when the things believed come to be seen?

question: Why must a sinner have a righteousness in order to stand before God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Because of the holiness of God's nature, the righteousness of his government, the severity of his law, and the terror of his wrath. Since God is holy and of purer eyes than to behold iniquity, no one can hope to escape as they are by nature. A righteousness is absolutely required to appear before him.
sources.quote: If God be holy and righteous, and of purer eyes than to behold iniquity, they must have a righteousness to stand before him
sources.raw_question: Why must a sinner have a righteousness in order to stand before God?

question: Can even a believer's best duties and works be accepted by God on their own account?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. Even the saints' best prayers and duties are full of failings and imperfection, and are as a defiled cloth. An infinitely righteous God sees through all that vanity. If he dealt with us according to our best works, we would perish. So the believer refuses to rest his peace on his own performances.
sources.quote: Alas! thou hast to do with an infinitely righteous God, who looks through and through all that vanity, which thou art but little acquainted withal; and should he deal with thee according to thy best works, thou must perish.
sources.raw_question: Can even a believer's best duties and works be accepted by God on their own account?

question: Can believers cleanse themselves from the defilement of sin by their own efforts apart from communion with Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: No. Jeremiah says that even washing with nitre and much soap leaves their iniquity still marked. The remedy is to look by faith to the purifying power of Christ's blood. One moment of communion with Christ by faith does more to purge the soul and increase grace than the utmost self-effort of a thousand ages.
sources.quote: One moment’s communion with Christ by faith herein is more effectual to the purging of the soul, to the increasing of grace, than the utmost self-endeavours of a thousand ages.
sources.raw_question: Can believers cleanse themselves from the defilement of sin by their own efforts apart from communion with Christ?

question: How should Christ be valued in comparison with created goods and with one's own legal righteousness?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Christ is to be preferred infinitely above them all. He is 'the chiefest of ten thousand' and 'altogether lovely' (Song 5:10, 16), beyond comparison with any created good. Worldly lusts pass away, and legal righteousness and duties are to be counted loss and dung for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ (Phil 3:8). This constant preferring of Christ is the soul's entrance into conjugal communion with him.
sources.quote: Beloved peace, beloved natural relations, beloved wisdom and learning, beloved righteousness, beloved duties, [are] all loss, compared with Christ.
sources.raw_question: How should Christ be valued in comparison with created goods and with one's own legal righteousness?

question: How can Christ both ascend into heaven and descend from heaven, and both go to the Father and come from him?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And Indeed that Christ Was Not Only Man, But God Also; That Even as He Was the Son of Man, So Also He Was the Son of God.
sources.answer: He ascended into heaven as man, but as God he had first come down from there. Likewise he goes to the Father as man, and as the Son, in obedience to the Father, he will come down again. The two-sided statements are reconciled by referring each to his humanity or his divinity.
sources.quote: And in the same manner as He ascended as man into heaven, so as God He had first descended thence. And in the same manner as He goes as man to the Father, so as the Son in obedience to the Father He shall descend thence.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ both ascend into heaven and descend from heaven, and both go to the Father and come from him?

question: When Justin Martyr calls God alone 'agennetos', does he mean the Father's personal property of being unbegotten, so that the Son is excluded?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Justin pairs agennetos with aphthartos and aidios and opposes it to the corruptible, made and perishing, so it denotes the eternal, uncreated, immutable existence belonging to the Godhead, not the Father's personal character. Otherwise Justin would have to make the Son not only begotten but made, created and corruptible, which is absurd given his writings. The words agennetos and agenetos were used promiscuously before the Arian controversy, and the Son is properly agenetos as Ignatius, Irenaeus and Origen say.
sources.quote: Either Justin must have believed that ἀγέννητος in this latter sense is applicable to the Son, or else he must have supposed him not only γεννητὸς, but γενόμενος, δημιουργητὸς, and φθαρτὸς also
sources.raw_question: When Justin Martyr calls God alone 'agennetos' (unbegotten/ungenerated), does he mean the Father's personal property of being unbegotten, so that the Son is excluded?

question: Does Irenaeus's statement that man was made after the image of the uncreated God, with the Father designing, the Son executing and the Spirit nourishing, teach that the three Persons together are the one uncreated God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: Yes. The joint operations of the three Persons in creating man point both to their distinct personality and to their unity of essence. Irenaeus names the three Persons immediately after as an explanation of 'the uncreated God'. Elsewhere he calls the Son uncreated, calls the Son and Spirit the very self of the Father, and speaks of Father and Son together as one God. So the three are one eternal, uncreated God and one Creator.
sources.quote: the joint operations of the three divine Persons, concurring in the creation of man, are set forth in such a manner, as to intimate both the distinet personality and unity of essence.
sources.raw_question: Does Irenaeus's statement that man was made after the image of the uncreated God, with the Father designing, the Son executing and the Spirit nourishing, teach that the three Persons together are the one uncreated God?

question: Does Irenaeus's description of God as ἀγέννητος (uncreated) and perfect exclude the Son and Holy Spirit from being the uncreated God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus applies the same character of perfection (τέλειος) to the Son, and he could never include the Son and Spirit among the things 'in subjection' or falling short of perfection, which are the things that are not ἀγέννητος. So his meaning is that the three divine Persons are one eternal, uncreated God and one Creator.
sources.quote: the meaning of Irenzus, in this passage, appears to be, that the three divine Persons are one eternal, or uncreated God, as also one Creator.
sources.raw_question: Does Irenaeus's description of God as ἀγέννητος (unmade/uncreated) and perfect exclude the Son and Holy Spirit from being the uncreated God?

question: Is there a Pleroma of Æons, and an erring Æon's Enthymesis, above the Creator, as the Gnostic teachers claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter X.—Unity of the faith of the Church throughout the whole world.
sources.answer: No. True wisdom does not consist in imagining, beyond the Creator and Framer of the world, the Enthymesis of an erring Æon or a Pleroma of thirty or innumerable Æons; this is blasphemy by teachers destitute of divine wisdom. The Catholic Church holds one and the same faith in one God the Creator throughout the world.
sources.quote: nor does it consist in this, that he should again falsely imagine, as being above this [fancied being], a Pleroma at one time supposed to contain thirty, and at another time an innumerable tribe of Æons
sources.raw_question: Is there a Pleroma of Æons and an erring Æon's Enthymesis above the Creator, as the Gnostic teachers claim?

question: Can the Valentinian Gnostics give a reason why their Pleroma of Æons consists of an Ogdoad, a Decad and a Duodecad rather than some other number?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XV.—No account can be given of these productions.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus argues that since they claim the Aeons are prior to creation and creation is their image, they ought to give a reason for the Pleroma's structure from within the Pleroma itself. Yet they can only point to numerical harmonies found in creation, such as thirty days or twelve months. Those are secondary things and do not explain what they call primary. Their account therefore collapses into perplexity, whereas the Church's account of creation fits the actual order of things that have been made.
sources.quote: it behoves them to possess their principle [of being] in themselves, one which existed before creation, and not after the pattern of creation
sources.raw_question: Can the Valentinian Gnostics give a reason why their Pleroma of Aeons consists of an Ogdoad, a Decad and a Duodecad, rather than some other number?

question: Does refusing the Gnostic scheme of higher Æons show a failure to understand higher spiritual realities?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVI.—The Creator of the world either produced of Himself the images of things to be made, or the Pleroma was formed after the image of some previous system; and so on ad infinitum.
sources.answer: No. The Valentinians accuse orthodox believers of remaining in the lower Hebdomad, but the Basilidians bring the same charge against the Valentinians. Anyone could outdo both by multiplying heavens or Æons by the hours of the year, which shows the charge is arbitrary and proves nothing.
sources.quote: this very charge do the followers of Basilides bring in turn against them, inasmuch as they (the Valentinians) keep circling about those things which are below
sources.raw_question: Does refusing the Gnostic scheme of higher Æons show a failure to understand higher spiritual realities?

question: If only the Holy Spirit were love in God, would Colossians 1:13's phrase 'the Son of His love' make Christ the Son of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: Yes, it would, and that consequence is absurd. Scripture calls Christ the only-begotten Son of the Father, and the apostle speaks of 'the kingdom of the Son of His own love.' If the Spirit alone were love in God, Christ would be the Son of the Spirit as well. So the Spirit cannot be the only love in the Trinity.
sources.quote: Therefore He is the Son also of the Holy Spirit, if there is in that Trinity no love in God except the Holy Spirit. And if this is most absurd, it remains that the Holy Spirit is not alone therein love
sources.raw_question: If only the Holy Spirit were love in God, would Colossians 1:13's phrase 'the Son of His love' make Christ the Son of the Holy Spirit?

question: What does 'the Son of His love' in Colossians 1:13 mean?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: It means the Father's own beloved Son, that is, the Son of his own substance. Because God's nature is perfectly simple, the Father's love is nothing other than his nature and substance. So the 'Son of His love' is the one born of the Father's substance.
sources.quote: the words, “Son of His own love,” mean nothing else than His own beloved Son,—the Son, in short, of His own substance.
sources.raw_question: What does 'the Son of His love' in Colossians 1:13 mean?

question: Were the Old Testament appearances of angels and the deeds of the patriarchs similitudes pointing to Christ before his incarnation?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In What Manner We are Gathered from Many into One Through One Mediator.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine holds that all the things that appeared to the fathers through angelic miracles, or were done by the fathers themselves, were similitudes of the one Mediator who was to come. Their purpose was that every creature by its acts might in some way speak of that One in whom salvation would come.
sources.quote: of Him, all those things which appeared to our fathers in a sacred and mystical way by angelical miracles, or which were done by the fathers themselves, were similitudes
sources.raw_question: Were the Old Testament appearances of angels and the deeds of the patriarchs similitudes pointing to Christ before his incarnation?

question: Can one property of creatures, such as having a beginning, be ascribed to the divine essence without also ascribing the rest of the creaturely attributes that go with it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Admitting one property of a nature commits one to its other properties. Confessing someone to be a man means confessing him to be an animal and rational. In the same way, attributing a creaturely property to the divine essence forces us to attach to it all the other creaturely attributes that go with it.
sources.quote: if we should understand any of the properties of creation to be present in the Divine essence, it will no longer be open to us to refrain from attaching to that pure Nature the rest of the list of the attributes contemplated therein.
sources.raw_question: Can any property of creatures, such as having a beginning, be ascribed to the divine essence without ascribing the rest of creaturely attributes as well?

question: Can the divine nature have a beginning, middle and end as temporal creatures do?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Creation has a beginning, middle and end and extends through temporal intervals, as heaven and earth were not from eternity. The Divine Nature is limited in no respect. It is without interval, quantity or circumscription, contains all the ages, and surpasses them by its infinity. So a beginning, which belongs to creation, is alien to the uncreated nature.
sources.quote: Since, then, it belongs to the creation to have a beginning, that will be alien from the uncreated nature which belongs to the creation.
sources.raw_question: Can the Divine Nature have a beginning, middle and end like temporal creatures?

question: Is it the Holy Spirit who makes believers aware of their own spiritual wants so that they can pray rightly?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit of Christ reveals to us our own wants so that we may reveal them to Christ; no teaching short of the Spirit's can acquaint the soul with its wants, burdens, and temptations. Since sense of want is the spring of desire, without this sense given by the Holy Ghost there is neither desire nor prayer.
sources.quote: The Spirit of Christ reveals to us our own wants, that we may reveal them unto him: “We know not what we should pray for as we ought,” Rom. viii. 26
sources.raw_question: Is it the Holy Spirit who makes believers aware of their own spiritual wants so that they can pray rightly?

question: Is boldness in approaching God acceptable to him if it is taken apart from Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. There is no sin God will more severely avenge than boldness a person takes with him outside of Christ. Conversely, no grace is more acceptable to God than the boldness he grants believers in the blood of Jesus.
sources.quote: as there is no sin that God will more severely revenge than any boldness that man takes with him out of Christ; so there is no grace more acceptable to him than that boldness which he is pleased to afford us in the blood of Jesus.
sources.raw_question: Is boldness in approaching God acceptable to him if it is taken apart from Christ?

question: What does 'Thy Name is as ointment poured forth' (Song of Songs 1:3) signify about Christ, and how does it bear on the Holy Spirit's divinity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: It signifies that Christ's Name, once confined to Israel like ointment in a vase, was spread through the whole world at His coming, not by any increase of His fulness but by filling empty spaces. Being 'poured forth' marks an overflowing abundance proper to the Godhead, so what is poured forth (as the Spirit is) is not common to creatures.
sources.quote: In like manner that you may believe that that which is shed abroad cannot be common to the creatures but peculiar to the Godhead, the name of the Son is also poured forth
sources.raw_question: What does 'Thy Name is as ointment poured forth' signify about Christ, and how does it bear on the Spirit's divinity?

question: Does the promise in Genesis 3:15 about the seed of the woman refer to Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: Yes. From that time the One who would be born of a woman, namely the Virgin, after the likeness of Adam, was preached as keeping watch for the serpent's head. Paul identifies this seed in Galatians as the one to whom the promise was made and as the Son God sent forth, made of a woman.
sources.quote: For from that time, He who should be born of a woman, [namely] from the Virgin, after the likeness of Adam, was preached as keeping watch for the head of the serpent.
sources.raw_question: Does the promise in Genesis 3:15 about the seed of the woman refer to Christ?

question: Who is the 'seed of Abraham' to whom God's promises were made?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXII.—In that flesh in which the saints have suffered so many afflictions, they shall receive the fruits of their labours; especially since all creation waits for this, and God promises it to Abraham and his seed.
sources.answer: Abraham's seed is Christ, and with Him the Church, which receives adoption to God through the Lord. Those who are of faith, the justified, including the Gentiles, are Abraham's children and are blessed with faithful Abraham. Irenaeus cites John the Baptist, who said God can raise children to Abraham from stones, and Paul's teaching in Galatians.
sources.quote: For his seed is the Church, which receives the adoption to God through the Lord, as John the Baptist said
sources.raw_question: Who is the 'seed of Abraham' to whom God's promises were made?

question: What is God's purpose in the patience he shows toward sinners outside of Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Its purpose is to leave them inexcusable, so that God's power and wrath against sin may be shown in their destruction. Scripture calls it suffering them to walk in their own ways and winking at their ignorance, which is a dreadful judgment because of where it ends. Like the river Phasis, it is sweet at the top and bitter at the bottom.
sources.quote: It was but to leave them inexcusable, that his power and wrath against sin might be manifested in their destruction.
sources.raw_question: What is God's purpose in the patience he shows toward sinners outside of Christ?

question: What is the purpose of God's patience and forbearance as exercised in Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Its purpose is to save those toward whom God exercises it and bring them to himself. As 2 Peter 3:9 says, he is long-suffering toward us so that our repentance and salvation may be accomplished. It is God's sworn course, in wisdom and goodness, that we will not be destroyed despite our sins, and so it is a source of the greatest consolation. Its treasures are hidden in Christ, and no one gains spiritual benefit from it without learning it in him.
sources.quote: the end of that patience and forbearance of God which is exercised in Christ, and discovered in him to us, is the saving and bringing into God those towards whom he is pleased to exercise them
sources.raw_question: What is the purpose of God's patience and forbearance as exercised in Christ?

question: Does the Word of God in the form of God have a face and back parts, so that his face is invisible while his back is visible, as Exodus 33 might seem to say?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > How the Back Parts of God Were Seen. The Faith of the Resurrection of Christ. The Catholic Church Only is the Place from Whence the Back Parts of God are Seen. The Back Parts of God Were Seen by the Israelites. It is a Rash Opinion to Think that God the Father Only Was Never Seen by the Fathers.
sources.answer: No. Both the face and the back appeared visibly only in the form of a servant, that is, in Christ's flesh. In the form of God, the Word and Wisdom of God has no front and back as a human body has. Nor is he changed in place or time by any appearance or motion.
sources.quote: far be it from us to think that the Word of God and the Wisdom of God has a face on one side, and on the other a back, as a human body has, or is at all changed either in place or time by any appearance or motion.
sources.raw_question: Does the Word of God in the form of God have a face and back parts, so that his face is invisible while his back is visible, as Exodus 33 might seem to say?

question: What is signified by God covering Moses with his hand and then removing it so that Moses sees his back parts (Exodus 33)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > How the Back Parts of God Were Seen. The Faith of the Resurrection of Christ. The Catholic Church Only is the Place from Whence the Back Parts of God are Seen. The Back Parts of God Were Seen by the Israelites. It is a Rash Opinion to Think that God the Father Only Was Never Seen by the Fathers.
sources.answer: It signifies that many Israelites, of whom Moses was a figure, failed to recognize Christ before his passion. After his resurrection they believed, as though the hand had been taken from their eyes. They saw his back parts, that is, his risen body, when Peter preached that Christ had to suffer and rise again.
sources.quote: many Israelites, of whom Moses was then a figure, believed in the Lord after His resurrection, as if His hand had been taken off from their eyes, and they now saw His back parts.
sources.raw_question: What is signified by God covering Moses with his hand and then removing it so that Moses sees his back parts?

question: Why was Moses allowed to see God's back parts only as God 'passed by' (Exodus 33)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > How the Back Parts of God Were Seen. The Faith of the Resurrection of Christ. The Catholic Church Only is the Place from Whence the Back Parts of God are Seen. The Back Parts of God Were Seen by the Israelites. It is a Rash Opinion to Think that God the Father Only Was Never Seen by the Fathers.
sources.answer: Because what saves and justifies us is faith in Christ's resurrection, which was his 'passing over' from this world to the Father. Pascha means Passover, or passing by, so the back parts are rightly seen in his passing. Even his enemies grant that his flesh died, but believers hold that it rose. In it they hope for the redemption of their own bodies as members of the Head.
sources.quote: Thence it is that He would not have His back parts seen, unless as He passed by, that His resurrection may be believed.
sources.raw_question: Why was Moses allowed to see God's back parts only as God 'passed by'?

question: By what distinguishing marks can true Godhead be recognized?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVIII. As he purposes to establish the Godhead of the Holy Spirit by the points already discussed, St. Ambrose touches again on some of them; for instance, that He does not commit but forgives sin; that He is not a creature but the Creator; and lastly, that He does not offer but receives worship.
sources.answer: God is known by four marks: He is without sin, He forgives sin, He is Creator and not creature, and He receives rather than gives worship. Each is grounded in Scripture: only God forgives sins, the Creator is set against the creature as God blessed for ever, and worship is due to the Lord God alone.
sources.quote: God is known by these marks: either that He is without sin; or that He forgives sin; or that He is not a creature but the Creator; or that He does not give but receives worship.
sources.raw_question: By what distinguishing marks can true Godhead be recognized, according to Ambrose?

question: Is eternity, without beginning or end, a necessary mark of true Godhead?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture marks true Godhead by the words "I am He that is," so only what is eternal and infinite in being, always the same, is truly divine. To say God formerly was not, or will cease to be, mutilates the idea of eternity by cutting it short with non-existence on one side or the other, and both claims are equally godless.
sources.quote: We think it right, then, to believe that to be alone truly Divine which is represented as eternal and infinite in respect of being; and all that is contemplated therein is always the same, neither growing nor being consumed
sources.raw_question: Is eternity, without beginning or end, a necessary mark of true Godhead?

question: Is true existence a distinguishing mark of the Godhead?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Since the Apostle says that whoever comes to God must believe that He is, true being belongs especially to God. So to deny the Son true being is to deny that he is God.
sources.quote: “He that cometh unto God,” says the Apostle, “must believe that He is.” Accordingly, true existence is the special distinction of Godhead.
sources.raw_question: Is true existence a distinguishing mark of the Godhead?

question: Does the "anointing" in 1 John 2:27, which teaches all things and is truth, refer to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. The teaching unction there is not only true but truth itself, and that can only be the Holy Spirit of God. So the Spirit too teaches believers, being given that we might know what God has freely given us.
sources.quote: That teaching unction which is not only true, but truth itself, is only the Holy Spirit of God: so that he teacheth also
sources.raw_question: Does 1 John 2:27's "anointing" that teaches all things and is truth refer to the Holy Spirit?

question: According to 1 John 2:20, 27 and Isaiah 11:2, what is the chief work of the Holy Spirit's anointing of believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Its chief work is teaching. Isaiah 11 lists the Spirit's gifts to Christ as wisdom, understanding, counsel and knowledge. Wherever believers' anointing is mentioned, it is tied to producing these same qualities, so the anointing teaches them the mind and will of God. This fulfils Christ's promise that the Comforter would teach believers and guide them into all truth.
sources.quote: This of teaching us the mind and will of God, in the manner wherein we are taught it by the Spirit, our comforter, is an eminent part of our unction by him
sources.raw_question: What is the chief work of the Holy Spirit's anointing of believers, according to 1 John 2:20, 27 and Isaiah 11:2?

question: How does Christ's work as Mediator of life correspond to the devil's role as mediator of death?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > As Christ is the Mediator of Life, So the Devil is the Mediator of Death.
sources.answer: They are exact opposites. The devil through pride led man through pride to death, while Christ through lowliness led man back through obedience to life; the devil fell by being lifted up and cast down those who consented to him, while Christ was raised up by being abased and lifted up those who believed in Him. Our reconciliation with the Creator thus comes through the Mediator of life, as our alienation came through the mediator of death.
sources.quote: For as the devil through pride led man through pride to death; so Christ through lowliness led back man through obedience to life.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's work as Mediator of life correspond to the devil's role as mediator of death?

question: In what sense is the devil a mediator of death, bringing about humanity's double death?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Devil the Mediator of Death, Christ of Life.
sources.answer: The devil persuaded humanity to sin and so cast them down into death. He himself died only in the spirit, through ungodliness, and not in the flesh. Yet by persuading humans to ungodliness, he used his single death to bring about their double death: the death of the spirit and the deserved death of the flesh.
sources.quote: Of this way the devil was the mediator, the persuader to sin, and the caster down into death. For he, too, applied his one death to work out our double death.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the devil a mediator of death, bringing about humanity's double death?

question: Why could the devil not be a true mediator of life, as Christ is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: Because the devil, being dead in the spirit, can neither share in our death nor rise again from his own. He could apply his single death to our double one, but he could not provide a single resurrection to renew us. Christ, alive in the spirit, raised His own dead flesh. As the true Mediator of life, He cast the devil out of believers' spirits.
