sources.quote: He then who being alive in the spirit raised again His own flesh that was dead, the true Mediator of life, has cast out him, who is dead in the spirit and the mediator of death
sources.raw_question: Why could the devil not be a true mediator of life, as Christ is?

question: Is redemption by Christ owed to us, or is it given graciously by God, who needs nothing from us?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter II.—When Christ visited us in His grace, He did not come to what did not belong to Him: also, by shedding His true blood for us, and exhibiting to us His true flesh in the Eucharist, He conferred upon our flesh the capacity of salvation.
sources.answer: It is righteous with respect to the apostasy but gracious toward us. We gave him nothing beforehand and he needs nothing from us; rather we need fellowship with him. So he graciously poured himself out to gather us into the bosom of the Father.
sources.quote: For we have given nothing to Him previously, nor does He desire anything from us, as if He stood in need of it; but we do stand in need of fellowship with Him.
sources.raw_question: Is redemption by Christ owed to us, or is it given graciously by God, who needs nothing from us?

question: Did Christ redeem sinners by paying a price or ransom for their redemption?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture plainly teaches that Christ redeemed us by paying a ransom. He gave his life as a ransom for many. Believers are said to be bought with a price, and that price was not silver or gold but his own precious blood.
sources.quote: That he redeemed us by paying a price, a ransom, for our redemption:— Mark x. 45, “The Son of man came to give his life a ransom for many.”
sources.raw_question: Did Christ redeem sinners by paying a price or ransom for their redemption?

question: Are the eternal reasons by which the human mind judges bodily things located above the human mind, or do they belong to the mind itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Man Alone of Animate Creatures Perceives the Eternal Reasons of Things Pertaining to the Body.
sources.answer: They are above the human mind, yet something of our own is joined to them. If they were not above the mind, they would not be unchangeable. But unless something of our own were attached to them, we could not use them as measures for judging bodily things. For example, we judge bodies by the rule of dimensions and figures, which the mind knows to remain unchangeably.
sources.quote: it is the part of the higher reason to judge of these corporeal things according to incorporeal and eternal reasons; which, unless they were above the human mind, would certainly not be unchangeable
sources.raw_question: Are the eternal reasons by which the human mind judges bodily things located above the human mind, or do they belong to the mind itself?

question: Is the mind's knowledge of bodies the same kind of knowledge as its grasp of the eternal reasons by which it judges them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > There is One Knowledge of the Thing in the Thing Itself, and Another in Eternal Truth Itself. That Corporeal Things, Too, are to Be Judged the Rules of Eternal Truth.
sources.answer: No. Bodies are known through the bodily senses when present, or through images in memory or imagination when absent. The reasons and the beautiful skill behind such forms are grasped by simple intelligence, which reaches what is above the eye of the mind. These are two distinct modes of knowing.
sources.quote: figuring in the mind after one fashion the images of bodies, or seeing bodies through the body; but after another, grasping by simple intelligence what is above the eye of the mind
sources.raw_question: Is the mind's knowledge of bodies the same kind of knowledge as its grasp of the eternal reasons by which it judges them?

question: Can a person coherently doubt that he lives, remembers, understands, wills, thinks, knows and judges?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Every Mind Knows Certainly Three Things Concerning Itself—That It Understands, that It Is, and that It Lives.
sources.answer: No. The act of doubting itself shows each of these. If a man doubts, he lives. He remembers why he doubts, understands that he doubts, wishes to be certain, thinks, knows that he does not know, and judges that he ought not to assent rashly. So whoever doubts anything else cannot doubt these, since without them he could not doubt at all.
sources.quote: Whosoever therefore doubts about anything else, ought not to doubt of all these things; which if they were not, he would not be able to doubt of anything.
sources.raw_question: Can a person coherently doubt that he lives, remembers, understands, wills, thinks, knows and judges?

question: Is a person's knowledge of his own will, such as willing to be happy or willing not to be deceived, certain against skeptical doubt?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Academic Philosophy.
sources.answer: Yes. It would be impudent to tell someone who says 'I will to be happy' that he may be deceived. Whether or not he is mistaken about other things, he is not mistaken in knowing that he wills not to be deceived. This knowledge, too, can be reflected upon to infinity.
sources.quote: when beyond doubt, whereinsoever he may be deceived, he is nevertheless not deceived in thinking that he wills not to be deceived.
sources.raw_question: Is a person's knowledge of his own will, such as willing to be happy or willing not to be deceived, certain against skeptical doubt?

question: Can a person truly know something false?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Concerning the Word of the Mind, in Which We See the Word of God, as in a Glass and an Enigma.
sources.answer: Only in the sense of knowing that it is false. Whatever is known must be true, otherwise it would not be known. To know that something is false is to know a truth, because it is true that the thing is false.
sources.quote: For no one knows what is false, except when he knows it to be false; and if he knows this, then he knows what is true: for it is true that that is false.
sources.raw_question: Can a person truly know something false?

question: Why was it fitting that Christ, the second Adam, be born of a virgin rather than begotten by a human father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: Because the recapitulation required an analogy of origin with the first Adam. Adam was formed by the Word of God from untilled, virgin soil and had no human father. So the Word, summing up Adam in himself, had to be formed as man by God from the virgin Mary. If Adam had been born of human seed, it would be reasonable to say the second Adam was begotten of Joseph.
sources.quote: But if the former was taken from the dust, and God was his Maker, it was incumbent that the latter also, making a recapitulation in Himself, should be formed as man by God, to have an analogy with the former as respects His origin.
sources.raw_question: Why was it fitting that Christ, the second Adam, be born of a virgin rather than begotten by a human father?

question: Since Adam also was not born of human seed, does Christ's virgin birth make him no more than a second Adam?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > The Author Prosecutes the Same Argument.
sources.answer: No. Adam, the first-formed man, was not born of seed either. But he was not formed by the joining of the Word and flesh. Christ is not merely of David's seed but is the Word made flesh who dwelt among us, which no mere man is.
sources.quote: For although the Protoplast was not born of seed, yet neither was the Protoplast formed of the conjunction of the Word and the flesh.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's virgin birth make him no more than a second Adam, since Adam also was not born of human seed?

question: Did Justin Martyr teach the strict coeternity of the Son with the Father, despite speaking of the Son being begotten in time to create the world?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. Justin applies to the Son the same observation he makes of the Father, that he properly has no name, only titles from what he did in time. He also calls him emphatically the Son and says he coexisted (συνὼν) with the Father before the world, though begotten or sent forth in time to create the universe. Together these show that Justin, like Athenagoras, held the Son's strict coeternity.
sources.quote: These considerations convince me, that Justin as well as Athenagoras taught the strict cocternity of the Son; which is equally true of all the other writers.
sources.raw_question: Did Justin Martyr teach the strict coeternity of the Son with the Father, even though he speaks of the Son being begotten in time to create the world?

question: Does Justin Martyr teach that the Son receives all his titles (Son, Wisdom, Angel, God, Lord, Word) simply from being begotten of the Father by the Father's will?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Waterland says Clarke's reading runs directly contrary to the whole tenor of Justin's Dialogue and to the words immediately before the passage he cites. Justin says the Son has these titles from two things together: his being begotten of the Father, and his ministering to the Father's will. Neither ground alone accounts for all the titles.
sources.quote: It is not from his being begotten of the Father that he hath all these titles ; but from that, and his administering to his Father’s will.
sources.raw_question: Does Justin Martyr teach that the Son receives all his titles (Son, Wisdom, Angel, God, Lord, Word) simply from being begotten of the Father by the Father's will?

question: Does Justin Martyr teach that Christ is God by the Father's will?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Justin means that it was the Father's good pleasure that the Son should also take the office of an angel, not merely be God. His being God was necessary, since he is God's Son and of the same nature. Only being both God and angel depended on the Father's good pleasure.
sources.quote: That he was God, was a Υ necessary thing, as he was God's Son, of the same nature with him: but that he should be both; i.e. God and an angel too; this was entirely owing to God's good pleasure.
sources.raised_by_detail: Dr. Whitby and Dr. Clarke's defender
sources.raw_question: Does Justin Martyr teach that Christ is God by the Father's will?

question: How does the death of Christ confirm the truth of a future universal judgment?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It gives abundant assurance of it. In the death of Christ God punished and condemned sin in the flesh of his own Son before men, angels and devils; he could have no conceivable reason to lay such a load on his Son unless he will certainly reckon with mankind for all their works. Christ's death is thus a solemn exemplar of the last judgment.
sources.quote: The death of Christ is a most solemn exemplar of the last judgment. Those who own him to be the Son of God, will not deny a judgment to come.
sources.raw_question: How does the death of Christ confirm the truth of a future universal judgment?

question: How does Christ's resurrection give assurance of the coming judgment?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: By raising Christ from the dead, God has given faith and assurance of the judgment to all people. In doing so he publicly appointed Christ as the judge of all, in and by whom he will judge the world in righteousness.
sources.quote: he hath given faith and assurance of this thing to all, by raising Christ from the dead, having appointed him to be the judge of all; in whom and by whom he will judge the world in righteousness.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's resurrection give assurance of the coming judgment?

question: What is the source of the spiritual liberty that believers enjoy as adopted children of God, and how is it related to Christ and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: All true spiritual liberty comes from the Spirit of adoption, who is the Spirit of Christ given to believers by Christ because they are sons. The same Spirit anointed the Lord Jesus to proclaim liberty to captives. Where this Spirit is, there is liberty. Any other supposed liberty is licentiousness.
sources.quote: “where the Spirit of the Lord is” (that is, the Spirit of Christ, given to us by him because we are sons), “there is liberty,” 2 Cor. iii. 17. All spiritual liberty is from the Spirit of adoption; whatever else is pretended, is licentiousness.
sources.raw_question: What is the source of the spiritual liberty that believers enjoy as adopted children of God, and how is it related to Christ and the Holy Spirit?

question: How do adopted children of God regard God as the object of their obedience, in contrast to those under bondage?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: They regard him as a Father who is desirable, not terrible. By the Spirit of sons they call him Father and see God in Christ as worthy of all obedience and also as all-sufficient to satisfy the soul. Others treat him as an austere master and bury their talents.
sources.quote: In all their approaches to God, they eye him as a Father; they call him Father, Gal. iv. 6, not in the form of words, but in the spirit of sons.
sources.raw_question: How do adopted children of God regard God as the object of their obedience, in contrast to those under bondage?

question: How does God regard a creature receiving the ultimate trust and homage that belong to God alone?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 2. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, detaches our ultimate confidence from man the creature, and attaches it to God the Creator; – by contrasting the sinfulness and feebleness of mortal man with the goodness and omnipotence of the Eternal Jehovah: by direct prohibition and precept: by exhibiting the holy Jealousy of God.
sources.answer: God regards it with holy jealousy and pronounces a curse on it. In Isaiah 42:8 he declares that he will not give his glory to another. Jeremiah 17:5-8 curses the man who trusts in man and blesses the man who trusts in the Lord. These verses gather up the concurrent testimony of the whole of Scripture, from Genesis to Revelation.
sources.quote: Thus saith the Lord, cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the Lord
sources.raw_question: How does God regard a creature receiving the ultimate trust and homage that belong to God alone?

question: Does the Christian confession of the Trinity amount to polytheism, as pagans allege?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. Scripture's illustration is not three suns but the sun and its radiance, so there is one light and one origin. The Word has no other manner of godhead than that of the only God, because he is born from him; hence Christians do not introduce three origins or three Fathers as Marcion and Manichaeus did.
sources.quote: we do not introduce three Origins or three Fathers, as the followers of Marcion and Manichæus; since we have not suggested the image of three suns, but sun and radiance. And one is the light from the sun in the radiance
sources.raw_question: Does the Christian confession of the Trinity amount to polytheism, as pagans allege?

question: Is the Church's refusal to speak of 'three Gods' adequately explained as merely a way to avoid resembling pagan polytheism?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. That answer might satisfy simple people, but it does not solve the difficulty. Objectors demand that one either deny the Godhead of the three Persons or else call them three Gods. Meeting that demand requires a fuller reasoned account of why the shared Godhead is not numbered in the plural.
sources.quote: this answer is not such as to furnish any solution of the difficulty
sources.raw_question: Is the Church's refusal to speak of 'three Gods' adequately explained as merely a way to avoid resembling pagan polytheism?

question: Why did God permit humanity to fall under the power of Satan rather than preventing it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XX.—God showed himself, by the fall of man, as patient, benign, merciful, mighty to save. Man is therefore most ungrateful, if, unmindful of his own lot, and of the benefits held out to him, he do not acknowledge divine grace.
sources.answer: God was long-suffering, foreseeing the victory that would be granted to man through the Word. As with Jonah swallowed by the whale, God permitted man to be swallowed by the author of transgression not so that he would perish, but so that, receiving an unhoped-for salvation, he might rise from the dead and glorify God with unceasing gratitude.
sources.quote: so also, from the beginning, did God permit man to be swallowed up by the great whale, who was the author of transgression, not that he should perish altogether when so engulphed
sources.raw_question: Why did God permit humanity to fall under the power of Satan rather than preventing it?

question: Does the fact that Christ yielded to the devil in His sufferings show that the devil was superior to the Lord?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: No. The devil only thought himself superior because the Lord, made a little lower than the angels, yielded to him in the flesh. The devil had power only over the mortal element Christ had received from us. Where he could do anything, there he was conquered in every respect, and his inward power over us was slain.
sources.quote: wherein he received outwardly the power of slaying the Lord in the flesh, therein his inward power, by which he held ourselves, was slain
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Christ yielded to the devil in His sufferings show that the devil was superior to the Lord?

question: Why could Christ conquer the devil when Adam was conquered by him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Why the Son of God Took Man Upon Himself from the Race of Adam, and from a Virgin.
sources.answer: Adam was only man, and he fell because he proudly lusted to be a god. Christ was both man and God, and he conquered in humility. God did not merely govern that Man as he governs the saints, but bore him as Son. This was so done that whoever glories should glory in the Lord.
sources.quote: For he who was conquered was only man; and he was therefore conquered, because he lusted proudly to be a god. But He who conquered was both man and God
sources.raw_question: Why could Christ conquer the devil when Adam was conquered by him?

question: Did the earliest Christian writers teach that God alone is to be worshipped?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: Yes. Justin Martyr says Christians worship God alone and none but God ought to be worshipped. Athenagoras says they worship the Creator, not his powers. Theophilus says no one ought to be worshipped but God alone, and Tatian refuses to worship God's works. Tertullian likewise says Christians worship one God, the Creator of all things from nothing.
sources.quote: Theophilus says, “I will honour the king, but I will not “ worship him. 91 will worship God, the real and true God: “no one ought to be worshipped but God alone.”
sources.raw_question: Did the earliest Christian writers teach that God alone is to be worshipped?

question: If offspring of the same substance as their source could suffer passion or ignorance, would the source itself have to share in that passion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus says that what comes forth from a source shares its substance, so the offspring must either all remain impassible or the Father himself must participate in passion. A torch kindled later cannot have a different kind of light from the one before it. On the Valentinian view, then, the Propator would be ignorant of himself, which is absurd.
sources.quote: since they are of the same substance with the Author of their production, they must either all remain for ever impassible, or their Father Himself must participate in passion
sources.raw_question: If offspring of the same substance as their source could suffer passion or ignorance, would the source itself have to share in that passion?

question: Can a being of the same substance as the divine source it comes from suffer passion, change, or dissolution by being joined with that source?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVIII.—Sophia was never really in ignorance or passion; her Enthymesis could not have been separated from herself, or exhibited special tendencies of its own.
sources.answer: No. A substance brought into contact with what shares its nature is not destroyed but continues and increases, as fire does in fire, spirit in spirit, water in water, and light in light. Only contraries suffer and are destroyed when they meet. So an Æon consubstantial with the Pleroma, which is itself of the Father, could never have undergone change. Fear, passion and dissolution belong to embodied beings, not to spiritual beings among whom light is diffused.
sources.quote: If, therefore, this Æon was produced by the Pleroma of the same substance as the whole of it, she could never have undergone change, since she was consorting with beings similar to and familiar with herself, a spiritual essence among those that were spiritual.
sources.raw_question: Can a being that is of the same substance as the divine source it comes from suffer passion, change, or dissolution by being joined with it?

question: Are the attributes ascribed to Christ 'divine' only in the loose sense of being powers derived from God, as a king's authority might be called divine?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: No. Properly, divine powers are those proper to God alone, as angelical powers are peculiar to angels. To call anything derived from God 'divine' is an improper use of the word; the attributes in the texts are strictly divine.
sources.quote: Angelical powers are such as are peculiar to angels; and divine powers such as are proper to God only
sources.raw_question: Are the attributes ascribed to Christ merely 'divine' in the sense of being powers derived from God, as a king's authority might be called divine?

question: Can strictly divine attributes be communicated to a creature, so that Christ could possess all communicable divine powers while still being a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: No. The attributes in the texts are strictly divine and therefore incommunicable to any creature; speaking of 'communicable divine powers' clogs the question with an improper restriction.
sources.quote: I contend, that the attributes in the text are strictly divine ; and therefore incommunicable to any creature.
sources.raw_question: Can strictly divine attributes be communicated to a creature, so that Christ could have 'all communicable divine powers' while being a creature?

question: Does human sin hinder a person's ability to perceive truths about God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 1. Introduction. Preparation of heart. Our position before God.
sources.answer: Yes. The plague of sin, whose diagnosis we seek, itself impairs our perceptive faculties. Revelations of our own corruption are distasteful to the natural heart. Therefore we must lay aside prejudice and pride and come to God's word humbly, as a little child.
sources.quote: to reflect that the plague, the diagnosis of which we would learn, itself impairs our perceptive faculties. Here then, let us humble ourselves as a little child.
sources.raw_question: Does human sin hinder a person's ability to perceive truths about God?

question: Is human sin superficial and partial, or radical and universal?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 1. Introduction. Preparation of heart. Our position before God.
sources.answer: It is both radical and universal. It pervades human life from conception to the grave and comes from within the heart. None have escaped it, for all have sinned and come short of the glory of God.
sources.quote: This evil of sin is not superficial, but radical. It pervades human life from the cradle to the grave.
sources.raw_question: Is human sin superficial and partial, or radical and universal?

question: When Irenaeus calls the Son and the Spirit the 'hands' of the Father, does he mean only that they carry out the Father's will, as a man's hands carry out his will?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. In the same passage Irenaeus calls them the Father's own offspring and own figure, and says all the angels serve and do obeisance to them. That is far higher than merely executing a will. The Fathers took the 'hands' expression from Scripture but meant much more by it: the same as by dynamis or virtus, the mighty power of God and God himself.
sources.quote: True, Irenzeus, and many other of the Fathers, used that expression, which they took from Scripture ; but they understood a great deal more by it; the same as by Pdvvapts, or virtus, the mighty power of God, and God himself.
sources.raw_question: When Irenaeus calls the Son and the Spirit the 'hands' of the Father, does he mean only that they carry out the Father's will, as a man's hands carry out his will?

question: Is believing in Christ's miracles sufficient reverence toward him without confessing his divine generation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The heretics confess all the miracles—lepers cleansed, the blind given sight, the dead raised—and still perish. Right faith requires confessing the truth about the Son's generation, not just his works.
sources.quote: The heretics confess all this, and perish.
sources.raw_question: Is believing in Christ's miracles sufficient reverence toward him without confessing his divine generation?

question: Does the promise that believers will do 'greater works' than Christ diminish the evidence of his miracles for his divine claims?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Christ's own works are appealed to as proof of his right to be the Shepherd and the Messiah. The believers' works are performed only through faith in him: 'he that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also.'
sources.quote: In the latter, all the miracles, as He had just stated, are wrought by faith in him, “he that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also.”
sources.raw_question: Does the promise that believers will do 'greater works' than Christ diminish the evidence of his miracles for his divine claims?

question: Did the Jews' charge of blasphemy show that Christ's claim to be the Son of God was a claim to divinity?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Yes. Had He called Himself a creature or a work, they would not have been startled, since angels had appeared among their fathers. But they recognized that the title 'Son' is not the mark of a creature but of Godhead and the Father's nature.
sources.quote: since He called Himself Son, they perceived that such was not the note of a creature, but of Godhead and of the Father’s nature
sources.raw_question: Did the Jews' charge of blasphemy show that Christ's claim to be Son of God was a claim to divinity?

question: When Christ answered the charge of blasphemy by citing Scripture's calling men 'gods' (John 10:34-36), was he denying that he is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: No. He was confirming that he is God. If those who received the words of God are called gods, much more is he God, since he is superior to all of them as the one the Father sanctified and sent.
sources.quote: By which words He did not deny Himself to be God, but rather He confirmed the assertion that He was God.
sources.raw_question: When Christ answered the charge of blasphemy by citing Scripture's calling men "gods," was he denying that he is God?

question: Do the scriptural texts about Christ's death, resurrection, and delivering up the Kingdom refer to his divine nature or to his assumed humanity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: They refer to the mystery of his body, his assumed humanity. Christ is the firstfruits of the dead as man, since 'by man came the resurrection of the dead', and he rose 'of the seed of David'. So death and resurrection belong only to the Dispensation by which Christ was flesh.
sources.quote: Here he teaches that the death and resurrection are due only to the Dispensation by which Christ was flesh.
sources.raw_question: Do the texts about Christ's death, resurrection, and delivering up the Kingdom refer to his divine nature or to his assumed humanity?

question: Are attributes Scripture ascribes to the risen Christ, such as being seen, touched, eating, and ascending, properties of His divine nature or of His human nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > This twelfth book gives a notable interpretation of the words of the Lord to Mary, “Touch Me not, for I am not yet ascended to My Father.”
sources.answer: They belong to His human nature. The same Person who said 'God is a Spirit' told His disciples 'Handle Me', to show that the human nature can be handled while the Divinity cannot be touched. Paul told the Athenians that God is not found by touch but by contemplation and faith. What appeared and ate before the disciples was the form of a servant, not God, whom no one has seen or can see.
sources.quote: that He may show that while the Human Nature is capable of being handled the Divinity is intangible
sources.raw_question: Are attributes such as being seen, being touched, eating, and ascending, which Scripture ascribes to the risen Christ, properties of His divine nature or of His human nature?

question: Does knowledge of the nature of things depend on first learning their names?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. One does not need names to discern fire, water, or air; our perceptive and intellectual faculties, given by the Creator, grasp things directly. Names are signs added afterward by the mind to mark what it already knows, not the source of that knowledge.
sources.quote: possessing as we do in ourselves the means of discerning all of which our perception informs us
sources.raw_question: Does knowledge of the nature of things depend on first learning their names?

question: Do differences in names across languages imply differences in the understanding of the thing named?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The Hebrew and the Canaanite call heaven by different names but understand it alike. They are not led into error by the difference of sounds conveying the idea, which shows that names are conventional signs for things that exist independently.
sources.quote: The Hebrew calls Heaven by one name, the Canaanite by another, but both of them understand it alike, being in no way led into error by the difference of the sounds
sources.raw_question: Do differences in names across languages imply differences in the understanding of the thing named?

question: Does John 1:18, which calls the Only-begotten God the one "Who is in the bosom of the Father," teach that the Son is eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. The text says the Son "is" in the Father's bosom, not that He "came to be" there. Everything excellent is always present in the fountain of excellency, and the Son is beyond all excellency. Therefore He is eternally contemplated in the Father.
sources.quote: mark you, He says, “Who is in the bosom of the Father,” not “Who came to be” there.
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:18, which calls the Only-begotten God the one "Who is in the bosom of the Father," teach that the Son is eternal?

question: What does John 3:18 mean by saying that the believer in the only-begotten Son is not condemned while the unbeliever is condemned already?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXVII.—The future judgment by Christ. Communion with and separation from the divine being. The eternal punishment of unbelievers.
sources.answer: Not being condemned means not being separated from God, because the believer is united to God through faith in the Son. Being condemned already means that the unbeliever has separated himself from God of his own accord by not believing in the name of the only-begotten Son.
sources.quote: “He that believeth in Me is not condemned,” that is, is not separated from God, for he is united to God through faith.
sources.raw_question: What does John 3:18 mean by saying that the believer in the only-begotten Son is not condemned while the unbeliever is condemned already?

question: Is the righteousness of God something all people know by nature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that it is a natural notion of God that he is most righteous. Abraham appealed to it when he asked whether the Judge of all the earth will not do right. Even sinners know that God judges evildoers worthy of death. For this reason everyone convinced of immortality and judgment anxiously asks what righteousness could let them stand before this righteous God.
sources.quote: This all men are persuaded of, that God is a most righteous God; (that is a natural notion of God which Abraham insisted on, Gen. xviii. 25, “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?”)
sources.raw_question: Is the righteousness of God something all people know by nature?

question: How is God known through our love of the unchangeable form of righteousness?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Our Love of the Righteous is Kindled from Love Itself of the Unchangeable Form of Righteousness.
sources.answer: We behold in God the unchangeable form of righteousness by which we judge how a person ought to live. Love of that form makes us love righteous people, and believing in their lives kindles a more ardent love of the form itself. So the more ardently we love God, the more certainly and calmly we see Him.
sources.quote: so that the more ardently we love God, the more certainly and the more calmly do we see Him, because we behold in God the unchangeable form of righteousness, according to which we judge that man ought to live.
sources.raw_question: How is God known through our love of the unchangeable form of righteousness?

question: When a mind that is not yet righteous sees what a righteous mind is, what is it actually seeing, given that there is no other righteous mind inside it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: It sees an inner truth that is present to any mind able to behold it. The mind sees within itself what it has seen nowhere else, and sees it truly, even though it is not itself a righteous mind. Not everyone has the power to behold this truth.
sources.quote: Is that which it sees an inner truth present to the mind which has power to behold it? Yet all have not that power
sources.raw_question: When a mind that is not yet righteous sees what a righteous mind is, what is it actually seeing, given that there is no other righteous mind inside it?

question: When we love a righteous person such as the Apostle Paul, is it his human bodily nature that we love?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: No. If we loved Paul for his human kind, we would no longer love him, since his soul is now separated from his body. What we love is his righteous mind, which we believe still lives.
sources.quote: But we believe that which we love in him to be still living, for we love his righteous mind.
sources.raw_question: When we love a righteous person such as the Apostle Paul, is it his human bodily nature that we love?

question: Must a person who is not yet righteous already know what righteousness is in order to love the righteous and become righteous?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: Yes. No one wishes to be what he does not love, and to become righteous one must wish it and so love the righteous man. But no one can love what he is wholly ignorant of. Therefore even the one not yet righteous knows what a righteous man is.
sources.quote: Therefore, even he who is not yet righteous, loves the righteous man. But he cannot love the righteous man, who is ignorant what a righteous man is. Accordingly, even he who is not yet righteous, knows what a righteous man is.
sources.raw_question: Must a person who is not yet righteous already know what righteousness is in order to love the righteous and become righteous?

question: Is God composed of bodily parts or material elements that could give rise to internal conflict and passion?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > If We Regard the Anger, and Indignation, and Hatred of God Described in the Sacred Pages, We Must Remember that They are Not to Be Understood as Bearing the Character of Human Vices.
sources.answer: No. God is simple and without any corporeal commixture, constructed of no associations of bodily parts. In humans the diversity of materials of which we consist arouses corrupting anger, but this cannot subsist in God, who is wholly of His own essence, known fully only to Himself, and is called Spirit.
sources.quote: For He is simple and without any corporeal commixture, being wholly of that essence, which, whatever it be,—He alone knows,—constitutes His being, since He is called Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Is God composed of bodily parts or material elements that could give rise to internal conflict and passion?

question: Does the hardening of Pharaoh's heart cohere with God's foreknowledge, or does God arbitrarily cause unbelief?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXIX.—Refutation of the arguments of the Marcionites, who attempted to show that God was the author of sin, because He blinded Pharaoh and his servants.
sources.answer: It coheres with His foreknowledge. God knows beforehand who will not believe, so He gives them over to the unbelief and darkness they have chosen for themselves. Pharaoh would never have believed, as the Word told Moses from the bush. God's hardening therefore confirms Pharaoh in his own chosen unbelief, so that he credited the Exodus to magic or natural causes rather than to God.
sources.quote: God, knowing the number of those who will not believe, since He foreknows all things, has given them over to unbelief, and turned away His face from men of this stamp, leaving them in the darkness which they have themselves chosen for themselves
sources.raw_question: Does the hardening of Pharaoh's heart cohere with God's foreknowledge, or does God arbitrarily cause unbelief?

question: Is sanctifying grace procured for believers by Christ's mediation, that is, by his oblation and intercession?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: Yes. Faith and all grace are given 'for his sake' because Christ purchased them, and his oblation and intercession lie at the bottom of the whole dispensation of grace. His intercession is founded on his oblation, and he intercedes for exactly what he purchased, neither more nor less.
sources.quote: His oblation and intercession lie at the bottom of this dispensation. Were not grace by them procured, it would never by any one soul be enjoyed.
sources.raw_question: Is sanctifying grace procured for believers by Christ's mediation (his oblation and intercession)?

question: What role does Christ's intercession after his resurrection play in securing the grace purchased by his death?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Christ's intercession is the third source of purchased grace, carrying on and completing the work begun in his death. He rose again to continue that work, and because he ever lives to intercede he is able to save to the uttermost those who come to God by him. His intercession continues his oblation so that all its fruits are actually made over to believers.
sources.quote: He rose again to carry on the complete work of purchased grace, — that is, by his intercession; which is the third rise of it.
sources.raw_question: What role does Christ's intercession after his resurrection play in securing the grace purchased by his death?

question: Why does Isaiah 65 foretell that men will bless and swear by "the true God" rather than simply "God," as earlier prophecies did?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Because the mystery of the Incarnation would blind some to Christ's true Godhead. Since falsehood about Him was to be spread, it was necessary that the truth be stated clearly. The Jews already blessed God simply as God, so the new emphasis on "true God" in a prophecy of future times points to the Son, who is true God.
sources.quote: calling Him true God, because the mysteriousness of His Incarnation was to blind the eyes of some to His true Godhead. When falsehood was to be published abroad, it was necessary that the truth should be clearly stated.
sources.raw_question: Why does Isaiah 65 foretell that men will bless and swear by "the true God" rather than simply "God," as earlier prophecies did?

question: If the Gnostics' teaching agrees with that of pagan philosophers and poets, can it be the true and superior knowledge of God they claim it to be?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIV.—Valentinus and his followers derived the principles of their system from the heathen; the names only are changed.
sources.answer: No. Either the pagans knew the truth or they did not. If they knew it, the Saviour's descent to bring the truth would have been superfluous. If they did not know it, then the Gnostics, who speak in the same terms as those ignorant of God, are boasting of ignorance and calling it knowledge, which is the 'false knowledge' Paul warns of.
sources.quote: Did all those who have been mentioned, with whom you have been proved to coincide in expression, know, or not know, the truth? If they knew it, then the descent of the Saviour into this world was superfluous.
sources.raw_question: If the Gnostics' teaching agrees with that of pagan philosophers and poets, can it be the true and superior knowledge of God they claim it to be?

question: Why did the Word have to condescend to creatures in order for them to come into existence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Because creatures could not have endured his nature, which is the untempered splendour of the Father's own. Out of the Father's love for man, the Word supported them, took hold of them, and brought them into being. This condescension, not any shared essence with creatures, is why he is called First-born.
sources.quote: they could not have endured His nature, which was untempered splendour, even that of the Father, unless condescending by the Father’s love for man He had supported them and taken hold of them and brought them into existence
sources.raw_question: Why did the Word have to condescend to creatures in order for them to come into existence?

question: Why could creatures not come into being except through the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Because the Word is Son of God by nature, proper to the Father's essence, from Him and in Him. As light illuminates only through its radiance, so the Father works all things in the Word as by a hand and makes nothing without Him.
sources.quote: For as the light enlightens all things by its radiance, and without its radiance nothing would be illuminated, so also the Father, as by a hand, in the Word wrought all things, and without Him makes nothing.
sources.raw_question: Why could creatures not come into being except through the Word?

question: Is the Father wise by the Wisdom He begot, the Son, so that the Son is the Father's wisdom as whiteness is a quality of a white body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: No. If the Father were made wise by the Son, and to be were not the same as to be wise for Him, the Son would be His quality rather than His offspring, and the Godhead would no longer be absolutely simple. Moreover, since in God to be is to be wise, whatever makes the Father wise would also make Him to be. The begotten Wisdom would then be the begetter or creator of the Father, which is senseless.
sources.quote: But if the Father who begat wisdom is also made wise by it, and to be is not to Him the same as to be wise, then the Son is His quality, not His offspring; and there will no longer be absolute simplicity in the Godhead.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father wise by the Wisdom He begat, the Son, so that the Son is the Father's wisdom in the way whiteness is a quality of a white body?

question: How does Wisdom in itself differ from a quality such as whiteness that exists in a body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: Whiteness is not an essence but a quality in a body, and it ceases to be when the body changes color. Wisdom, by contrast, is wise in itself. When a soul that partook of wisdom becomes foolish, wisdom itself remains unchanged. So wisdom is not in the wise person the way whiteness is in a white body.
sources.quote: therefore wisdom is not in him who becomes wise by it, in the same manner as whiteness is in the body which is by it made white.
sources.raw_question: How does Wisdom in itself differ from a quality such as whiteness that exists in a body?

question: Do Christ's promises to be present wherever two or three gather and to be with his disciples always prove his omnipresence?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. He says "there am I," not "there I will be." His people may meet in ten thousand places at once, so the promise directly asserts omnipresent Deity. No one but the Divine Being who fills all things could be with the apostles and their successors in every separate region where they preach.
sources.quote: Two or three of his people (says Scott) may be thus met together in ten thousand places all over the earth at the same time, this must therefore be allowed to be a direct assertion of his omnipresent Deity.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's promises to be present wherever two or three gather and with his disciples always prove his omnipresence?

question: Could Christ's promise to be with his disciples always have been fulfilled by an invisible bodily presence rather than by his divine omnipresence?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: No. Peter says the heaven must receive him until the restitution of all things. Christ himself says, "And now I am no more in the world." His bodily presence is therefore in heaven, and his presence with his people must be divine.
sources.quote: is refuted by St. Peter, who says of him, “Whom the heaven must receive until the times of the restitution of all things” – Acts 3:21, and by Christ Himself, who says, “And now I am no more in the world”
sources.raw_question: Could Christ's promise to be with his disciples always have been fulfilled by an invisible bodily presence rather than by his divine omnipresence?

question: Does Christ sometimes withhold his presence even from believers who diligently seek him in private and public means?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. Sometimes everything fails and Christ is not found, so believers should take care not to provoke him to withdraw. Yet when all means fail and the soul waits humbly, Christ appears, so that his coming is plainly by grace. Ordinarily, though, he honours his ordinances.
sources.quote: Let them that enjoy any thing of the presence of Christ take heed what they do; if they provoke him to depart, if they lose him, it may cost them many a bitter inquiry before they find him again.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ sometimes withhold his presence even from believers who diligently seek him in both private and public means?

question: Is the abolishing of hostile powers by Christ the same thing as the subjection of his enemies?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Abolishing the enemy's power means sweeping away forever his prerogative of power and ending the rule of his kingdom, as with the devil consigned to eternal fire. Subjection, by contrast, implies obedience and allegiance, and is a proof of submission and mutability in those subjected.
sources.quote: The abolishing is not the same as the subjecting. To abolish the power of the enemy is to sweep away for ever his prerogative of power, so that by the abolition of his power is brought to an end the rule of his kingdom.
sources.raw_question: Is the abolishing of hostile powers by Christ the same thing as the subjection of his enemies?

question: Is Christ's execution of vengeance on his enemies compatible with his being lovely to believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen counts Christ's vengeance on the stubborn enemies of himself and his people among his excellencies. He calls Christ lovely and glorious in it, because by it he protects and vindicates his church. Judgment therefore takes nothing from his desirableness to the saints.
sources.quote: Lovely and glorious in the vengeance he taketh, and will finally execute, upon the stubborn enemies of himself and his people.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's execution of vengeance on his enemies compatible with his being lovely to believers?

question: What is eternal life, and does it imply that Jesus Christ is himself the one true God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: Eternal life is the sight or knowledge of God, which is not granted to the ungodly. Jesus Christ is to be known within this eternal life as the one true God, who shows himself to the godly. He will not be known only in the form of the Son of man, in which even the punished will see him.
sources.quote: And how are they to know Jesus Christ Himself also, unless as the One true God, who will show Himself to them; not as He will show Himself, in the form of the Son of man, to those also that shall be punished?
sources.raw_question: What is eternal life, and does it imply that Jesus Christ is himself the one true God?

question: Why did the Father speak from heaven at Christ's baptism to declare Him His Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: So that we would not be misled by His visible human body into failing to recognise Him as the Son. The Father willed that we should know the nature of the one who came to be baptized, and recognise as Son of God Him who appeared as Man to accomplish our salvation.
sources.quote: that by the voice of God we might recognise as the Son of God Him Who was visible as Man, to accomplish the mystery of our salvation.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Father speak from heaven at Christ's baptism to declare Him His Son?

question: Why was the command 'Hear Him' added to the Father's testimony at the Transfiguration but not at Christ's baptism?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: John the Baptist had been a prophet from the womb and already knew the truth, so he did not need the command. The Apostles received the same testimony with the addition 'Hear Him' for the instruction of believers. Its purpose is that we should listen to Christ alone, and to the Apostles who heard on our behalf.
sources.quote: He had been a prophet from the womb, and needed not the commandment, Hear Him. Yes; I will hear Him, and will hear none but Him and His Apostle, who heard for my instruction.
sources.raw_question: Why was the command 'Hear Him' added to the Father's testimony at the Transfiguration but not at Christ's baptism?

question: How does the desire involved in seeking knowledge relate to the love by which a known thing is loved?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > Why Love is Not the Offspring of the Mind, as Knowledge is So. The Solution of the Question. The Mind with the Knowledge of Itself and the Love of Itself is the Image of the Trinity.
sources.answer: They are the same will in two states. The desire or inquiry that seeks knowledge is a kind of will, though it is not yet love of the thing known. Once the thing is known, that same desire becomes love: it holds and embraces its offspring, knowledge, and unites it to its begetter, the mind. Love therefore binds together parent and offspring.
sources.quote: the same desire which led us to long for the knowing of the thing, becomes the love of the thing when known, while it holds and embraces its accepted offspring, that is, knowledge, and unites it to its begetter
sources.raw_question: How does the desire involved in seeking knowledge relate to the love by which a known thing is loved?

question: Does the hope of attaining knowledge affect how strongly the mind loves and seeks it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Love of the Studious Mind, that Is, of One Desirous to Know, is Not the Love of a Thing Which It Does Not Know.
sources.answer: Yes. The nearer a person comes in hope to attaining a capacity, the more fervently he desires it. Where there is no hope of attaining the end, he loves it lukewarmly or not at all, however clearly he sees its excellence. This is why most people study their own language rather than all languages.
sources.quote: for when any one entertains no hope of attaining his end, then he either loves lukewarmly or does not love at all, howsoever he may see the excellence of it.
sources.raw_question: Does the hope of attaining knowledge affect how strongly the mind loves and seeks it?

question: What does the case of Levi paying tithes in Abraham show about whether the Son 'was not, and then was begotten'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: It shows that even a man is not absolutely non-existent before birth, since he pre-exists in his progenitor by kinship of substance. If this holds of men, it is far more impious to say of the Divine life that the Son was not and then was begotten, since He is in the Father.
sources.quote: If, then, a man in a certain sense is not, and is then born, having existed beforehand by virtue of kinship of substance in his progenitor, according to an Apostle’s testimony, how as to the Divine life do they dare to utter the thought that He was not, and then was begotten?
sources.raw_question: What does the case of Levi paying tithes in Abraham show about whether the Son 'was not, and then was begotten'?

question: If Levi paid tithes in the loins of Abraham, why did Christ not sin in the loins of Adam and inherit the guilt of Adam's sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Christ was never federally in Adam, so Adam's sin was not imputed to him on that account. Sin was indeed imputed to Christ when he was made sin, but this happened through the covenant of the Mediator, by his voluntary undertaking. It did not come by legal imputation under Adam's covenant. Had Adam's sin been reckoned to him as a descendant of Adam, he could not have been a fit high priest 'separate from sinners.'
sources.quote: He was never federally in Adam, and so not liable to the imputation of his sin on that account.
sources.raw_question: If Levi paid tithes in the loins of Abraham, why did Christ not sin in the loins of Adam and inherit the guilt of Adam's sin?

question: Was Christ, as a descendant of Adam, liable to the imputed guilt of Adam's first sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: No. Christ was never federally in Adam and so was not liable to imputation of Adam's sin on that account. Sin was imputed to him only in the covenant of the Mediator by his voluntary undertaking, not by legal imputation in Adam's covenant. Had it been reckoned to him as Adam's descendant, he would not have been a fit high priest 'separate from sinners.'
sources.quote: it was imputed to him in the covenant of the Mediator, through his voluntary susception, and not in the covenant of Adam, by a legal imputation.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ, as a descendant of Adam, liable to the imputed guilt of Adam's first sin?

question: On what ground is Adam's first sin counted as the sin of all his descendants?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Adam was not only the natural head of mankind but also its federal head. All were in covenant with him, so his breach of that covenant is reckoned to all. This parallels the way Christ is head to believers. Whether Romans 5:12 is read 'in whom' or 'because all have sinned', the meaning is the same: that one sin is the sin of us all.
sources.quote: We were all in covenant with him; he was not only a natural head, but also a federal head unto us.
sources.raw_question: On what ground is Adam's first sin counted as the sin of all his descendants?

question: What makes a sacrifice acceptable to God: the outward correctness of the rite or the inner disposition of the offerer?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVIII.—Concerning sacrifices and oblations, and those who truly offer them.
sources.answer: The inner disposition. Sacrifices do not sanctify a man, since God stands in no need of sacrifice. It is the pure conscience of the offerer that sanctifies the sacrifice and moves God to accept it as from a friend. God respected Abel's single-minded offering but rejected Cain's because Cain's heart was divided by envy. Hypocritical offerings, like those of the Pharisees, do not deceive God.
sources.quote: Sacrifices, therefore, do not sanctify a man, for God stands in no need of sacrifice; but it is the conscience of the offerer that sanctifies the sacrifice when it is pure
sources.raw_question: What makes a sacrifice acceptable to God: the outward correctness of the rite or the inner disposition of the offerer?

question: How can Christ say both that no one can pluck the sheep from his hand and that no one can pluck them from the Father's hand?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Because the Son's hand is the Father's hand. The Son received from the Father that which is greater than all, and the one divine nature and power of the Father is in the Son. The bodily image of the hand teaches the power of the single divine nature in both, which is why Christ adds "I and the Father are one."
sources.quote: Hear, if you wish to know:—I and the Father are one. The Son’s hand is the Father’s hand.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ say both that no one can pluck the sheep from his hand and that no one can pluck them from the Father's hand?

question: Does Christ's claim that no one can pluck his sheep from his hand show that he has divine power?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. The claim is an utterance of conscious power. It confesses a free and irresistible energy that will allow no one to take his sheep, and this shows the powers of his divine nature.
sources.quote: It is the utterance of conscious power, this confession of free and irresistible energy, that will allow no man to pluck His sheep from His hand.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's claim that no one can pluck his sheep from his hand show that he has divine power?

question: In bodily sight, is vision produced by the visible object alone, or does it also require the one who sees?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Certain Trinity in the Sight. That There are Three Things in Sight, Which Differ in Their Own Nature. In What Manner from a Visible Thing Vision is Produced, or the Image of that Thing Which is Seen. The Matter is Shown More Clearly by an Example. How These Three Combine in One.
sources.answer: Vision is produced by the visible thing together with one who sees. The seer contributes the sense of seeing and the attention of looking, while the visible body alone imprints the form on the sense that is called vision. This analysis sets up the three distinct elements (object, vision, attention of mind) that Augustine uses as a trace of a trinity in the outer man.
sources.quote: Vision, then, is produced from a thing that is visible; but not from that alone, unless there be present also one who sees. Therefore vision is produced from a thing that is visible, together with one who sees
sources.raw_question: In bodily sight, is vision produced by the visible object alone, or does it also require the one who sees?

question: Does Christ, being without sin, lack true compassion toward believers whose temptations arise partly from their own sinful nature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: No. Though our temptations contain something not in Christ's, namely an inward sinful party that sides with the temptation, this increases rather than lessens his compassion. Since he succours us because we are tempted, the sorer our temptations, the readier he is to help.
sources.quote: But this is so far from taking off his compassion towards us, that, on all accounts whatever, it doth increase it; for if he will give us succour because we are tempted, the sorer our temptations are, the more ready will he be to succour us.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ, being without sin, lack true compassion toward believers whose temptations arise partly from their own sinful nature?

question: Can temptations serve a good spiritual purpose for believers, and if so, how?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. With suitable help from Christ, temptations can be turned to holy use, and chief among these uses is that believers come to know themselves. Temptation often uncovers hidden corruptions the soul never suspected. So what might be a deadly wound becomes like lancing a festered sore. Without Christ's help, however, no one can make good use of a temptation.
sources.quote: And this is from the tender care of Jesus Christ, giving them in suitable help; without which no man can possibly make use of or improve a temptation.
sources.raw_question: Can temptations serve a good spiritual purpose for believers, and if so, how?

question: Is reconciliation through Christ's death alone sufficient for believers to obtain eternal life, or is Christ's active obedience to the law also required?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Christ's obedience is also required. Reconciliation only restores us to the state of peace Adam had before his fall. Yet Adam, though under no wrath, still had to obey in order to enjoy eternal life. So after the enmity is slain, we are saved by the perfect obedience Christ yielded to God's law in his life.
