sources.quote: Notwithstanding that there was no wrath due to Adam, yet he was to obey, if he would enjoy eternal life.
sources.raw_question: Is reconciliation through Christ's death alone sufficient for believers to obtain eternal life, or is Christ's active obedience to the law also required?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be tempted or provoked by human sin, as God was tempted in the wilderness?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IX. That the Holy Spirit is provoked is proved by the words of St. Peter, in which it is shown that the Spirit of God is one and the same as the Spirit of the Lord, both by other passages and by reference to the sentence of the same Apostle on Ananias and Sapphira, whence it is argued that the union of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, as well as His own Godhead, is proved.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter's words to Sapphira, "Why have ye agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord?", show that the Holy Ghost can be tempted by our sins. So the psalm's language about God being tempted can rightly be applied to the Spirit.
sources.quote: the same Apostle Peter taught us in another place that the Holy Ghost can be tempted by our sins
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be tempted or provoked by human sin, as God was tempted in the wilderness?

question: Does Scripture's statement that the Holy Spirit was tempted in the wilderness (Hebrews 3 quoting Psalm 95) show that the Spirit is called Lord?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VIII. The aforesaid unity is proved hereby, that as the Father is said to be grieved and tempted, so too the Son. The Son was also tempted in the wilderness, where a figure of the cross was set up in the brazen serpent: but the Apostle says that the Spirit also was there tempted. St. Ambrose infers from this that the Israelites were guided into the promised land by the same Spirit, and that His will and power are one with those of the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Either one confesses the unity of Father, Son and Spirit in the divine majesty, or one must grant that the Apostle names the Spirit by the title Lord. Hebrews 3 attributes the words of Psalm 95 to the Holy Ghost, who says "your fathers tempted Me." Either way, the Spirit's divine lordship follows.
sources.quote: it is necessary that you either confess the Unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the Divine Majesty, or certainly when the writing of the Apostle says that the Spirit was tempted, it undoubtedly pointed out the Spirit by the name of Lord.
sources.raw_question: When the Lord who was tempted in the wilderness sent serpents on the Jews, does the Apostle's statement that the Holy Spirit was tempted there show that the Spirit is called Lord?

question: Does the divine life have beginning, end, increase, or decrease?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The divine beatitude is ever the same and self-dependent, not progressing by degrees, since it participates in no other life from which beginning and end could be inferred. It is life energizing in itself; increase has no place in the infinite, and the passionless nature excludes decrease.
sources.quote: it is life energizing in itself, not becoming greater or less by addition or diminution. For increase has no place in the infinite, and that which is by its nature passionless excludes all notion of decrease.
sources.raw_question: Does the divine life have beginning, end, increase, or decrease?

question: Is the divine life measured by time, or does it exist within time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: No. The divine and blessed life is not in time; time flows from it. Creation journeys from a beginning to an end through spaces of time and can be divided into beginning, middle and end, but the supreme life has no time-extension, span or measure.
sources.quote: It is not in time, but time flows from it; whereas the creation, starting from a manifest beginning, journeys onward to its proper end through spaces of time
sources.raw_question: Is the divine life measured by time or does it exist within time?

question: How does the analogy of the human soul and body show that the Word did not die when Christ's body died?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And that It Does Not Follow Thence, that Because Christ Died It Must Also Be Received that God Died; For Scripture Sets Forth that Not Only Was Christ God, But Man Also.
sources.answer: In ordinary men only the flesh dies while the immortal soul cannot be killed, as Christ taught. If even the soul, which was made by the Word, cannot be destroyed by men, much more can the Word of God not be slain. So human cruelty could only slay Christ's body, not his divinity.
sources.quote: For as the soul itself, which was made by the Word of God, is not killed by men, certainly much rather will it be believed that the Word of God cannot be destroyed.
sources.raw_question: How does the analogy of the human soul and body show that the Word did not die when Christ's body died?

question: Does Christ's saying 'Let the dead bury their dead' show that Scripture distinguishes the death of the soul from the death of the body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The One Death and Resurrection of The Body of Christ Harmonizes with Our Double Death and Resurrection of Body and Soul, to the Effect of Salvation. In What Way the Single Death of Christ is Bestowed Upon Our Double Death.
sources.answer: Yes. Burial is the proper disposal of a dead body, so the one to be buried is dead in body. Those who were to bury him are dead in soul through the impiety of unbelief. Other texts confirm this spiritual death: the call to the sleeper to rise from the dead, and the widow who 'is dead while she liveth'.
sources.quote: For burial was the fitting disposal of a dead body. But by those who were to bury it He meant those who were dead in soul by the impiety of unbelief
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'Let the dead bury their dead' show that Scripture distinguishes the death of the soul from the death of the body?

question: Is the uncreated divine nature subject to space and time as created things are?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: No. Every created thing comes into being within the background of time and space that the Creator laid down, but the all-sufficient, everlasting existence is before and above these. It has no past or future, since there is nothing beside it whose passing could make something past; all things are present to it as in an instant.
sources.quote: But the existence which is all-sufficient, everlasting, world-enveloping, is not in space, nor in time: it is before these, and above these in an ineffable way; self-contained, knowable by faith alone; immeasurable by ages; without the accompaniment of time
sources.raw_question: Is the uncreated divine nature subject to space and time as created things are?

question: Can there be a cause and something produced from it within the uncreated divine nature without any temporal separation between them?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: Yes. The faith teaches that within the uncreate divine nature there is a cause and a subsistence produced from that cause, but without separation. Since order and sequence of time belong only to the ages of creation, the relation of Father and Son involves no before and after.
sources.quote: the divine nature is to be believed uncreate (although within it, as our faith teaches, there is a cause, and there is a subsistence produced, but without separation, from the cause)
sources.raw_question: Can there be a cause and something produced from it within the uncreated divine nature without temporal separation between them?

question: How far can our faith in a revealed mystery extend beyond our ideas of it?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: It cannot extend beyond them. Believing is conceiving, so we believe confusedly where our ideas are confused, generally where they are general, and distinctly where they are distinct. Faith ends where our ideas end.
sources.quote: Such as our ideas are, such must our faith be; and we cannot believe further than we conceive, for believing is conceiving ; confusely, if ideas are confusely ; generally, if general; distinctly and adequately, if distinct and adequate.
sources.raw_question: How far can our faith in a revealed mystery extend beyond our ideas of it?

question: Should believers speculate about divine mysteries beyond the limits of human understanding?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XX.—Those pastors are to be heard to whom the apostles committed the Churches, possessing one and the same doctrine of salvation; the heretics, on the other hand, are to be avoided. We must think soberly with regard to the mysteries of the faith.
sources.answer: No. The heretics claim a knowledge of good and evil, set their own minds above the God who made them, and form opinions beyond what the understanding can reach. Believers should instead feed on all the Lord's Scriptures within the Church, but not with an uplifted mind. As the apostle says, they should be wise only as far as is fitting.
sources.quote: They therefore form opinions on what is beyond the limits of the understanding.
sources.raw_question: Should believers speculate about divine mysteries beyond the limits of human understanding?

question: Should it surprise us that we cannot fully know spiritual and heavenly things, given the limits of human knowledge?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: No. Even many ordinary things in this world are beyond our knowledge, such as the Nile's rising, the migration of birds, the tides, and the causes of rain and of the moon's phases. Only God, who made these things, can declare the truth about them. So it is fitting that revealed spiritual matters also exceed our grasp, and that God should excel all in knowledge.
sources.quote: there is no cause for wonder if this is the case with us as respects things spiritual and heavenly, and such as require to be made known to us by revelation
sources.raw_question: Should it surprise us that we cannot fully know spiritual and heavenly things, given the limits of human knowledge?

question: Can one argue from the Father's love in sending the Son for our salvation against the Son's own love, or the reverse?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. The love that saves sinners is the same love in the Father and in the Son, though acted distinctly by each. Therefore it is vain to set the Father's love against the Son's, or the Son's against the Father's.
sources.quote: That this love was the same in Father and Son, acted distinctly in the manner that shall be afterward declared; so, vain are the pretences of men, who, from the love of the Father in this matter, would argue against the love of the Son, or on the contrary.
sources.raw_question: Can one argue from the Father's love in sending the Son for our salvation against the Son's own love, or the reverse?

question: What did the exaltation of Christ consist in, and was the Word himself advanced by it?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: The exaltation was the deification of His human nature, not an advancement of the Word. What He received, He received insofar as His manhood was exalted, and this exaltation was its being deified. The Word Himself always had such exaltation, according to the Father's Godhead and perfection, which were His own.
sources.quote: For He received it as far as His man’s nature was exalted; which exaltation was its being deified. But such an exaltation the Word Himself always had according to the Father’s Godhead and perfection, which was His
sources.raw_question: What did the exaltation of Christ consist in, and was the Word himself advanced by it?

question: For whose sake is Christ said to be highly exalted, if the Word himself needed no exaltation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: He is exalted as man for our sakes. As we all died in Christ by his death, so in Christ we are exalted, raised from the dead and ascending into heaven. He is our Righteousness, and it is we who are exalted in that Righteousness.
sources.quote: as by His death we all died in Christ, so again in the Christ Himself we might be highly exalted, being raised from the dead, and ascending into heaven
sources.raw_question: For whose sake is Christ said to be highly exalted, if the Word himself needed no exaltation?

question: Does Christ remove the defilement attached even to believers' best works, so that God can accept them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Yes. Self and unbelief defile even our best duties. As high priest, Christ bears the guilt that in strict justice attaches to them and washes away their filth. He adds sweet incense to them so they may be accepted. He consumes whatever is of the flesh and keeps whatever is of the Spirit and grace.
sources.quote: the Lord Christ first, as our high priest, bears the iniquity, the guilt, and provocation, which in severe justice doth attend them, Exod. xxviii. 38; and not only so, but he washes away all their filth and defilements
sources.raw_question: Does Christ remove the defilement attached even to believers' best works, so that God can accept them?

question: Do the good works believers perform after receiving Christ contribute to their justification and acceptance with God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: No. Works done after believing are acceptable to God, and he is pleased that believers walk in them. But for the purpose for which Christ is received, justification and acceptance with God, they count no more than works done before faith. Ephesians 2:8-10 excludes even the works believers are created unto in Christ from that role. Christ alone is the believer's righteousness, and to set anything beside him for that end is unfaithfulness to him.
sources.quote: Even the works we do after believing, — those which we are created unto in Christ Jesus, those that God hath ordained that believers “should walk in them,” — as to justification and acceptance with God, (here called salvation), are excluded.
sources.raised_by_detail: professors who seek a place for their own works in acceptance with God
sources.raw_question: Do the good works believers perform after receiving Christ contribute to their justification and acceptance with God?

question: Why did the Holy Spirit in the Book of Revelation disclose only the number of Antichrist's name and not the name itself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXX.—Although certain as to the number of the name of Antichrist, yet we should come to no rash conclusions as to the name itself, because this number is capable of being fitted to many names. Reasons for this point being reserved by the Holy Spirit. Antichrist’s reign and death.
sources.answer: The number is given so that believers can recognise and avoid Antichrist when he comes, but the name is suppressed because it is not worthy to be proclaimed by the Holy Spirit. Antichrist is described as one who 'was, and is not', as if he has no real existence, and the name of what does not exist is not proclaimed. Irenaeus also suggests that if the Spirit had declared the name, Antichrist might perhaps continue for a long period.
sources.quote: the name, however, is suppressed, because it is not worthy of being proclaimed by the Holy Spirit. For if it had been declared by Him, he (Antichrist) might perhaps continue for a long period.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Holy Spirit, in the Book of Revelation, disclose only the number of Antichrist's name and not the name itself?

question: Should Christians try to work out Antichrist's name from the number 666 given in Revelation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXX.—Although certain as to the number of the name of Antichrist, yet we should come to no rash conclusions as to the name itself, because this number is capable of being fitted to many names. Reasons for this point being reserved by the Holy Spirit. Antichrist’s reign and death.
sources.answer: No, not with confidence. Many names, such as Evanthas, Lateinos and Teitan, add up to the number, so guessing leaves the question unresolved. Out of fear of God and zeal for truth it is safer to wait for the prophecy to be fulfilled. If the name had needed to be revealed in the present time, the one who saw the apocalyptic vision would have announced it.
sources.quote: It is therefore more certain, and less hazardous, to await the fulfilment of the prophecy, than to be making surmises, and casting about for any names that may present themselves
sources.raw_question: Should Christians try to determine Antichrist's name from the number 666 given in Revelation?

question: Does someone who memorizes the words of the Christian faith without understanding them have a trinity of the inner man in his mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What Has Been Treated of in This Book. How We Have Reached by Steps to a Certain Trinity, Which is Found in Practical Knowledge and True Faith.
sources.answer: No. He has a kind of trinity: the sounds held in memory, the mind's vision formed from them in recollection, and the will joining the two. Yet it belongs to the outer man, because he deals only with images of bodily things, namely sounds perceived by hearing.
sources.quote: Yet we should by no means say that the man in so doing busies himself with a trinity of the interior man, but rather of the exterior; because he remembers, and when he wills, contemplates as much as he wills, that alone which belongs to the sense of the body
sources.raw_question: Does someone who memorizes the words of the Christian faith without understanding them have a trinity of the inner man in his mind?

question: Does understanding the meaning of the articles of faith suffice for a person to live according to a trinity of the inner man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What Has Been Treated of in This Book. How We Have Reached by Steps to a Certain Trinity, Which is Found in Practical Knowledge and True Faith.
sources.answer: No. Understanding brings something of the inner man into action, but one may grasp these things while judging them false in order to refute them. The will then completes some kind of trinity, but the man does not live by it. He lives according to a trinity of the inner man only when he believes the things to be true and loves what ought to be loved, for everyone lives according to what he loves.
sources.quote: But when those things are believed to be true, and those things which therein ought to be loved, are loved, then at last the man does live according to a trinity of the inner man; for every one lives according to that which he loves.
sources.raw_question: Does understanding the meaning of the articles of faith suffice for a person to live according to a trinity of the inner man?

question: Is the Christ who descended into the lower parts of the earth the same as the Christ who ascended above the heavens?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says explicitly that 'he that descended is the same also that ascended' (Ephesians 4:9-10). Hilary takes this to mean that dead or buried, descending into Hades or ascending into heaven, it is one and the same Christ. His body lay in the grave and did not go down into Hades, yet it truly rose and ascended. So the one who descended and the one who ascended must be one subject.
sources.quote: Whether, therefore, dead or buried, descended into Hades or ascended into Heaven, all is one and the same Christ
sources.raw_question: Is the Christ who descended into the lower parts of the earth the same as the Christ who ascended above the heavens?

question: Why did Christ descend into the lower parts of the earth?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXII.—Christ did not come for the sake of the men of one age only, but for all who, living righteously and piously, had believed upon Him; and for those, too, who shall believe.
sources.answer: He descended to the righteous dead who slept in the earth, to behold their state and make known His salvation to them so that they might be saved. Irenaeus supports this from a saying he attributes to Jeremiah, that the holy Lord remembered His dead Israel and descended to them. Christ's passion is thus the arousing of His sleeping disciples.
sources.quote: in token that His passion is the arousing of His sleeping disciples, on whose account “He also descended into the lower parts of the earth,” to behold with His eyes the state of those who were resting from their labours
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ descend into the lower parts of the earth?

question: Do Christ's claims that he would raise up the destroyed temple of his body in three days and that he has power to lay down and take up his life show that he is more than a mere man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is Again Confirmed in Christ by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. No mere man could resuscitate and rebuild his own destroyed body or recover his own life. Christ could do so only because he is the Word who is from the Father and with the Father, by whom all things were made. He is therefore proved to be not man only, as son of man, but also God, as Son of God.
sources.quote: Or who says that He can again resuscitate and rebuild the destroyed temple of His body, except because He is the Word who is from the Father, who is with the Father,
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's claims that he would raise up the destroyed temple of his body in three days and that he has power to lay down and take up his life show that he is more than a mere man?

question: Whom did God send in the flesh according to Romans 8:3?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: The Word. The "own Son" whom God sent in the likeness of sinful flesh is none other than the Word, whom God called Son in view of his coming incarnation.
sources.quote: What Son of His own, then, did God send through the flesh but the Word, whom He addressed as Son because He was to become such (or be begotten) in the future?
sources.raw_question: Whom did God send in the flesh according to Romans 8:3?

question: Does Romans 8:3, which speaks of God sending his Son 'in the likeness of sinful flesh', mean that Christ's flesh was sinful flesh?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Paul says the likeness of the flesh of sin, not the flesh of sin itself. The fashion of flesh shows the truth of Christ's birth, while 'likeness of the flesh of sin' removes him from the imperfections of human weakness.
sources.quote: nor was His flesh the flesh of sin, but the likeness of the flesh of sin. Thus the fashion of flesh implies the truth of His birth, and the likeness of the flesh of sin removes Him from the imperfections of human weakness.
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 8:3, which speaks of God sending his Son 'in the likeness of sinful flesh', mean that Christ's flesh was sinful flesh?

question: Did Christ's disciples violate the law when they plucked grain on the Sabbath?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VIII.—Vain attempts of Marcion and his followers, who exclude Abraham from the salvation bestowed by Christ, who liberated not only Abraham, but the seed of Abraham, by fulfilling and not destroying the law when He healed on the Sabbath-day.
sources.answer: No. Christ justified them from the law itself, through the example of David eating the shewbread, which shows that priests may act freely. The law forbade reaping and storing grain, not eating food ready to hand when hungry. The disciples, like all the righteous, hold priestly rank and serve God, so they were blameless, just as the priests in the temple were.
sources.quote: justifying His disciples by the words of the law, and pointing out that it was lawful for the priests to act freely.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ's disciples violate the law when they plucked grain on the Sabbath?

question: Can the soul be called the creator of the body, given that it has power to affect and change corporeal substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > God Alone Creates Those Things Which are Changed by Magic Art.
sources.answer: No. However great its power to affect bodies, the soul cannot be called the creator of the body. Every cause of changeable substance, with all its measure, number and weight, arises from the intelligible and unchangeable life of God, which is above all things.
sources.quote: every cause of changeable and sensible substance, and all its measure and number and weight, by which are brought to pass both its being at all and its being of such and such a nature, arise from the intelligible and unchangeable life
sources.raw_question: Can the soul be called the creator of the body, given that it has power to affect and change corporeal substance?

question: Why does a soul that seeks its final good in bodily things come to imagine the divine as something corporeal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Lowest Degradation Reached by Degrees.
sources.answer: Because it puts its final good in things perceived through the body, it draws on the deceptive images of bodies stored within it and combines them by vain thought. As a result nothing seems divine to it unless it resembles those images. Augustine treats this as spiritual fornication: the soul is made fruitful in errors by its greed and emptied of strength by its prodigality.
sources.quote: while snatching from within the deceitful images of corporeal things, and combining them by vain thought, so that nothing seems to it to be divine, unless it be of such a kind as this
sources.raw_question: Why does a soul that seeks its final good in bodily things come to imagine the divine as something corporeal?

question: Why do some thinkers conclude that the soul is corporeal or mortal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Opinions of Philosophers Respecting the Substance of the Soul. The Error of Those Who are of Opinion that the Soul is Corporeal, Does Not Arise from Defective Knowledge of the Soul, But from Their Adding There to Something Foreign to It. What is Meant by Finding.
sources.answer: Because they cannot conceive any existence without corporeal phantasms. Asked to think of existence without bodily images, they hold it to be nothing. So they made the soul either a body or a blending of bodily elements, and therefore mortal. Those who saw it as a life opposite to body, animating living bodies, argued that it is immortal, since life cannot be without life.
sources.quote: For if you bid them conceive of existence that is without corporeal phantasms, they hold it merely nothing.
sources.raw_question: Why do some thinkers conclude that the soul is corporeal or mortal?

question: Does the definition of 'body' decide whether a soul said to be made of a 'fifth element' is corporeal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Opinions of Philosophers Respecting the Substance of the Soul. The Error of Those Who are of Opinion that the Soul is Corporeal, Does Not Arise from Defective Knowledge of the Soul, But from Their Adding There to Something Foreign to It. What is Meant by Finding.
sources.answer: Yes. If 'body' means something whose part is less than the whole in extension of place, those who make the soul of a fifth element count among the corporealists. If they call all substance, or all changeable substance, 'body' while granting that not all substance is extended in place, the dispute is only about words.
sources.quote: we need not contend with them about a question of words
sources.raised_by_detail: those who posited a fifth kind of body
sources.raw_question: Does the definition of 'body' decide whether the soul made of a 'fifth element' is corporeal?

question: Does attributing particular acts such as the Flood, the fire on Sodom, and the plagues of Egypt to the Son do justice to His divine glory?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. The Son encompasses and governs all that has been and will be, so naming two or three marvels adds nothing to His glory. Leaving out the rest instead implies a loss of it. Paul's single statement that He is "above all, and through all, and in all" already includes all such works.
sources.quote: the mention of two or three marvels does not mean the addition of glory, so much as the suppression of the rest means its deprivation or loss.
sources.raw_question: Does attributing particular acts such as the Flood, the fire on Sodom, and the plagues of Egypt to the Son do justice to His divine glory?

question: Was the Son of God himself active in the Old Testament judgments, such as the flood and the destruction of Sodom?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son of God is always one and the same. It was he who brought the deluge in Noah's day and rained fire and brimstone on Sodom and Gomorrah. He is the same one who now gives believers living water and who will judge unbelievers.
sources.quote: Since the Son of God is always one and the same, He gives to those who believe on Him a well of water[^4368] [springing up] to eternal life, but He causes the unfruitful fig-tree immediately to dry up
sources.raw_question: Was the Son of God himself active in the Old Testament judgments, such as the flood and the destruction of Sodom?

question: In Song of Songs 5:14, what do the Beloved's hands 'as gold rings set with the beryl' signify about Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: They signify all the works of Christ, the effects being named by their cause. Gold rings set with precious stones are valuable for profit and ornament, and so Christ's works are glorious, all of them fruits of wisdom, love and bounty.
sources.quote: so are the hands of Christ; that is, all his works, — the effects, by the cause. All his works are glorious; they are all fruits of wisdom, love, and bounty.
sources.raw_question: In Song of Songs 5:14, what do the Beloved's hands 'as gold rings set with the beryl' signify about Christ?

question: In Song of Songs 5:14, what does the Beloved's 'belly as bright ivory overlaid with sapphires' signify about Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: It signifies Christ's inward affections: his tender love, compassion and kindness toward his church. The word refers to the inward bowels, including the heart, not the outward bulk. In Scripture, 'bowels' ascribed to God or man mean affections.
sources.quote: It is the inward bowels, and not the outward bulk that is signified. Now, to show that by “bowels” in the Scripture, ascribed either to God or man, affections are intended, is needless.
sources.raw_question: What does the Beloved's 'belly as bright ivory overlaid with sapphires' in Song of Songs 5:14 signify about Christ?

question: In Song of Songs 3:1, is the bride's 'night' caused by some outward trouble that makes her notice Christ's absence, or by Christ's absence itself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Owen judges it to be the latter: Christ's absence makes it night. Apart from that absence, all things seem well with her, and the bed signifies ease and rest rather than tribulation. Christ is the believer's sun, so his absence brings darkness even in the midst of other comforts.
sources.quote: I rather think the latter; because, setting that aside, all things seem to be well with her. The absence of Christ will indeed make it night, dark as darkness itself, in the midst of all other glowing consolations.
sources.raw_question: In Song of Songs 3:1, does some outward trouble make the bride notice Christ's absence, or does Christ's absence itself make it night for her?

question: In Song of Songs 2:5, does the bride's being 'sick of love' mean she is fainting for lack of a sense of Christ's love under fear of God's wrath?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: No. She is not fainting for want of love under an apprehension of wrath. She is overcome by the strength of her own love for Christ, which his love has stirred up after she has tasted his sweetness in the 'banqueting-house'. Her deferred desire makes her heart sick, so she asks for strengthening grace to hold her up and for the consolations of the Holy Ghost to revive her.
sources.quote: not (as some suppose) fainting for want of a sense of love, under the apprehension of wrath; but made sick and faint, even overcome, with the mighty actings of that divine affection
sources.raw_question: In Song of Songs 2:5, does the bride's being 'sick of love' mean she is fainting for lack of a sense of Christ's love under fear of God's wrath?

question: How can lifeless things such as bodies be said to be 'life' in the Word before they were made?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > We are Made Perfect by Acknowledgement of Our Own Weakness. The Incarnate Word Dispels Our Darkness.
sources.answer: Whatever was made was not made in the Word but was life in Him. So even body, which is not life, would not have been made by the Word unless it had first been life in Him before it was made. This life is not created life like the soul, which is changeable and made. It is the unchangeable Word's own life.
sources.quote: even body, which is not life, would not have been made by Him, except it had been life in Him before it was made. For “that which was made was already life in Him;”
sources.raw_question: How can lifeless things such as bodies be said to be 'life' in the Word before they were made?

question: How and when are the soul and the body each raised from their death?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The One Death and Resurrection of The Body of Christ Harmonizes with Our Double Death and Resurrection of Body and Soul, to the Effect of Salvation. In What Way the Single Death of Christ is Bestowed Upon Our Double Death.
sources.answer: The soul is raised now, by repentance and by faith in Him who justifies the ungodly. This renewal grows day by day as the inner man is renewed. The body, the outward man, keeps decaying until death, and its resurrection is delayed until the end. Then our justification will be perfected, and God will quicken our mortal bodies by His Spirit dwelling in us.
sources.quote: For the soul is raised up again by repentance, and the renewing of life is begun in the body still mortal by faith, by which men believe on Him who justifies the ungodly
sources.raw_question: How are the soul and the body each raised from their death, and when?

question: Is the Valentinian account of the Word (Logos) being produced in a series of emanations from Bythus, Sige and Nous a genuine revelation of divine mysteries?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIV.—Valentinus and his followers derived the principles of their system from the heathen; the names only are changed.
sources.answer: No. It is a pagan theogony with new names. Irenaeus shows that it copies the comic poet Antiphanes, who had Chaos come from Night and Silence and Love from Chaos. The Valentinians simply put Bythus and Sige for Night and Silence, Nous for Chaos, and the Word for Love. Their supposed ineffable mysteries are therefore borrowed fables and not knowledge of God.
sources.quote: In place of Night and Silence they substitute Bythus and Sige; instead of Chaos, they put Nous; and for Love (by whom, says the comic poet, all other things were set in order) they have brought forward the Word
sources.raw_question: Is the Valentinian account of the Word (Logos) being produced in a series of emanations from Bythus, Sige and Nous a genuine revelation of divine mysteries?

question: Can Nous (Mind) be produced from Bythus and his Ennoea (Thought), as the Valentinians claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. Nous is the chief and highest principle and source of all understanding, while Ennoea is merely a particular movement of thought arising from Nous. So the order is reversed: Nous would be the father of Ennoea, not its offspring.
sources.quote: For Ennœa is not the daughter of Nous, as they assert, but Nous becomes the father of Ennœa.
sources.raw_question: Can Nous (Mind) be produced from Bythus and his Ennoea (Thought), as the Valentinians claim?

question: Does a philosopher's intellectual glimpse of God's unchangeable truth benefit him more than the humble Christian's faith in the cross?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > They are Proud Who Think They are Able, by Their Own Righteousness, to Be Cleansed So as to See God.
sources.answer: No. Seeing one's homeland from afar is of no use to the proud man who is ashamed to embark on the 'ship of wood', that is, the cross. The humble believer who cannot yet see the truth loses nothing, because he is actually being carried to it by that wood. Faith in the crucified Mediator, not mere contemplation, brings a person to God.
sources.quote: But of what use is it for the proud man, who on that account is ashamed to embark upon the ship of wood, to behold from afar his country beyond the sea?
sources.raw_question: Does a philosopher's intellectual glimpse of the unchangeable truth of God benefit him more than the humble Christian's faith in the cross?

question: Does the spirit in Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones (Ezekiel 37) mean the Holy Spirit rather than wind or the human life-breath?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIX. Having proved above that the Spirit abides and speaks in the prophets, St. Ambrose infers that He knows all things which are of God, and therefore is One with the Father and the Son. This same point he establishes again from the fact that He possesses all that God possesses, namely, Godhead, knowledge of the heart, truth, a Name above every name, and power to raise the dead, as is proved from Ezekiel, and in this He is equal to the Son.
sources.answer: It means the Holy Spirit. God calls it "My Spirit," which would not describe something produced by blowing. Earthly winds are partial and not universal, and the spirit by which we live is individual. Only the Holy Spirit is by nature over all and in all, as a Spirit coming from the four quarters must be.
sources.quote: But it is the nature of the Holy Spirit to be both over all and in all.
sources.raw_question: Does the spirit in Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones mean the Holy Spirit rather than wind or the human life-breath?

question: Does Ezekiel's command to prophesy to the wind in the valley of dry bones prefigure prayer to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Probably, though the author lays no stress on it. The wind (pneuma in the LXX) is plainly a type of the Spirit, since the interpretation says 'I will put my Spirit in you, and ye shall live.' So the address to the wind seems to typify prayer to the Spirit for his quickening power on dead souls.
sources.quote: to my own mind the proclamation to the wind is typical of prayer to the Spirit for his energizing power in quickening dead souls to the life of God.
sources.raw_question: Does Ezekiel's command to prophesy to the wind in the valley of dry bones prefigure prayer to the Holy Spirit?

question: Can any human authority bind the conscience of believers by laws not given by God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: No. Some claim the power to bind conscience by laws and constitutions not from God. But believers were never truly in bondage to such power. Their adoption eminently sets them free from it.
sources.quote: is the power of binding conscience by any laws and constitutions not from God, Col. ii. 20–22.
sources.raw_question: Can any human authority bind the conscience of believers by laws not given by God?

question: Can human nature or the moral law teach people that they cannot give God the obedience he requires?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Nature is proud and does not know its own impotency. The law shows what we have done wrong, but by demanding exact obedience it assumes we have the power to obey and takes no notice that we have lost it. This knowledge is found only in Christ, through whom God did what the law, weak through the flesh, could not do.
sources.quote: by requiring exact obedience of us, it takes for granted that such power is in us for that purpose: it takes no notice that we have lost it; nor doth it concern it so to do.
sources.raw_question: Can human nature or the moral law teach people that they cannot give God the obedience he requires?

question: Does Christ's bloody sweat in Gethsemane show a natural human weakness in Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Sweating blood is contrary to nature, so it was no infirmity but a work of His power reversing the law of nature. It does not support the heresy of weakness, though it does establish against the Docetists the reality of His body.
sources.quote: Nor let any one dare to impute the Sweat to a weakness, for it is contrary to nature to sweat blood. It was no infirmity, for His power reversed the law of nature.
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who assert the Son's weakness
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's bloody sweat in Gethsemane show a natural human weakness in Him?

question: Does Christ's bloody sweat in Gethsemane refute those who say His body was only apparent?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes. While the bloody sweat does not support the claim that He was weak, it establishes against the heresy that invents an apparent body the full reality of His body.
sources.quote: while it establishes against the heresy which invents an apparent body, the reality all His body
sources.raised_by_detail: Docetists (those who invent an apparent body)
sources.raw_question: Does the bloody sweat of Christ refute those who say His body was only apparent?

question: Can a being that is truly Wisdom (Sophia) be subject to ignorance, degeneracy, and passion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVIII.—Sophia was never really in ignorance or passion; her Enthymesis could not have been separated from herself, or exhibited special tendencies of its own.
sources.answer: No. Ignorance, degeneracy and passion are alien and contrary to wisdom and can never belong to it. Where foresight is lacking and the course of what is useful is unknown, wisdom does not exist. So the Valentinians must give up either the name 'Wisdom' for their Æon or the sufferings they ascribe to her.
sources.quote: For these things are alien and contrary to wisdom, nor can they ever be qualities belonging to it. For wherever there is a want of foresight, and an ignorance of the course of utility, there wisdom does not exist.
sources.raw_question: Can a being that is truly Wisdom (Sophia) be subject to ignorance, degeneracy, and passion?

question: Did Christ suffer in the twelfth month of the year, as the Gnostics claimed in order to make his passion a figure of the twelfth Aeon?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXII.—The thirty Æons are not typified by the fact that Christ was baptized in His thirtieth year: He did not suffer in the twelfth month after His baptism, but was more than fifty years old when He died.
sources.answer: No. The passover, the month in which the Lord suffered, was the first month of the year and not the twelfth, as Moses teaches. So the Gnostic reading of both the 'year' and the 'twelfth month' is false.
sources.quote: the special month in which the passover was celebrated, and in which also the Lord suffered, was not the twelfth, but the first, those men who boast that they know all things, if they know not this, may learn it from Moses.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ suffer in the twelfth month of the year, as the Gnostics claimed in order to make his passion a figure of the twelfth Aeon?

question: Does the betrayal of Christ by Judas, the twelfth apostle, serve as a type of the passion of the Gnostic twelfth Aeon (Sophia)?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XX.—Futility of the arguments adduced to demonstrate the sufferings of the twelfth Æon, from the parables, the treachery of Judas, and the passion of our Saviour.
sources.answer: No. Judas was expelled from the Twelve and never restored, Matthias being ordained in his place, whereas the Æon is said to have been restored to the Pleroma. Moreover, Judas was the betrayer and not the sufferer; it was Christ who suffered. So the supposed type does not match what it is claimed to signify.
sources.quote: How, then, could Judas, the betrayer of Him who had to suffer for our salvation, be the type and image of that Æon who suffered?
sources.raw_question: Does the betrayal of Christ by Judas, the twelfth apostle, serve as a type of the passion of the Gnostic twelfth Æon (Sophia)?

question: Was Christ's passion a real suffering, and how does it differ from the destructive 'passion' the Gnostics attribute to the Aeon Sophia?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XX.—Futility of the arguments adduced to demonstrate the sufferings of the twelfth Æon, from the parables, the treachery of Judas, and the passion of our Saviour.
sources.answer: Christ's passion was real and valid, not merely accidental, and it saved rather than endangered him. The Æon suffered dissolution while vainly seeking the Father and brought forth ignorance and formless matter. The Lord, however, was never in danger of destruction. By his own strength he restored fallen man to incorruption and brought wanderers back to knowledge of the Father and fellowship with him.
sources.quote: But the Lord, our Christ, underwent a valid, and not a merely accidental passion; not only was He Himself not in danger of being destroyed, but He also established fallen man by His own strength, and recalled him to incorruption.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's passion a real suffering, and how does it differ from the destructive 'passion' that the Gnostics attribute to the Æon Sophia?

question: Do Christ's sufferings and words on the cross, such as "My God, my God, why hast Thou forsaken Me?", signify the passions of the Aeon Sophia, as the Valentinians claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter VIII.—How the Valentinians pervert the Scriptures to support their own pious opinions.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus presents this reading as an example of how the Valentinians wrench the Lord's words from their proper connection to fit their own fictions. He calls the result "old wives' fables" patched together out of Scripture. Such texts are being made to signify something foreign to their context. They do not genuinely support the Gnostic myth of Sophia's anguish, fear and perplexity.
sources.quote: In like manner do these persons patch together old wives’ fables, and then endeavour, by violently drawing away from their proper connection, words, expressions, and parables whenever found, to adapt the oracles of God to their baseless fictions.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's sufferings and words on the cross, such as "My God, my God, why hast Thou forsaken Me?", signify the passions of the Aeon Sophia, as the Valentinians claim?

question: How does the soul fall away from God when it sees the excellent things in God's nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Why the Soul is Enjoined to Know Itself. Whence Come the Errors of the Mind Concerning Its Own Substance.
sources.answer: Instead of remaining steadfast to enjoy them, it turns from God. It wants to take these goods as its own and to be what God is by its own power, rather than to be like Him by His gift. So it slips down into lesser things that it mistakes for greater, because nothing is sufficient for it apart from God, who alone is sufficient.
sources.quote: it is turned away from Him, by wishing to appropriate those things to itself, and not to be like to Him by His gift, but to be what He is by its own
sources.raw_question: How does the soul fall away from God when it sees the excellent things that are in God's nature?

question: How does the human mind become good, and what does it lose by turning away from God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How God May Be Known to Be the Chief Good. The Mind Does Not Become Good Unless by Turning to God.
sources.answer: The mind becomes good by turning its will in love to the unchangeable good from which it has its being as a mind. Turning away from the chief good, it loses being a good mind but not being a mind, since its being a mind came from God and not from its own will; the will loses only what the will obtains.
sources.quote: For by turning itself from the chief good, the mind loses the being a good mind; but it does not lose the being a mind.
sources.raw_question: How does the human mind become good, and what does it lose by turning away from God?

question: Is picking out numbers from Scripture that happen to fit a theological system a valid way to prove that system about the divine realm?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIV.—Folly of the arguments derived by the heretics from numbers, letters, and syllables.
sources.answer: No. Every number occurs in Scripture in the utmost variety. Anyone who wished could therefore assemble an Ogdoad, a Decad, a Duodecad or any number at all and claim it as a type of his own invented system. Such selective coincidences prove nothing, especially when the most important scriptural institutions contradict the scheme.
sources.quote: every number occurs with the utmost variety in the Scriptures, so that, should any one desire it, he might form not only an Ogdoad, and a Decad, and a Duodecad, but any sort of number from the Scriptures
sources.raw_question: Is picking out numbers from Scripture that happen to fit a theological system a valid way to prove that system about the divine realm?

question: Can a doctrinal system be validly proved by collecting scattered names and expressions from Scripture and rearranging them?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter IX.—Refutation of the impious interpretations of these heretics.
sources.answer: No. Like a cento patched together from Homeric verses to tell a story Homer never wrote, such collections twist words from their natural sense; one who knows the texts and holds the rule of truth received in baptism recognises the words but restores each to its proper place, and the false system collapses.
sources.quote: collecting a set of expressions and names scattered here and there [in Scripture], they twist them, as we have already said, from a natural to a non-natural sense.
sources.raw_question: Can a doctrinal system be validly proved by collecting scattered names and expressions from Scripture and rearranging them?

question: Since God has numbered all things, should we speculate about the causes of numbers in creation, such as hairs, sparrows or stars, in order to build theological systems?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVI.—“Knowledge puffeth up, but love edifieth.”
sources.answer: No. Such labour is vain and amounts to madness. By the knowledge he imagines he has discovered, the speculator changes God himself and exalts his own opinion above the greatness of the Creator.
sources.quote: by the knowledge which he imagines himself to have discovered, he changes God Himself, and exalts his own opinion above the greatness of the Creator
sources.raw_question: Since God has numbered all things, should we speculate about the causes of numbers in creation, such as hairs, sparrows or stars, to build theological systems?

question: Did Gideon show a lack of faith in asking for further signs with the fleece after he had already received many signs?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Preface.
sources.answer: No. Gideon was speaking in mysteries, so he was not doubtful himself but careful that we should not doubt. His prayer was effectual, and he began the battle without fear because he had understood God's message. The dew on the fleece signified faith among the Jews, since God's words come down like dew.
sources.quote: But how can he seem to have asked as if doubting or wanting in faith, who was speaking in mysteries? He was not then doubtful, but careful that we should not doubt.
sources.raw_question: Did Gideon show a lack of faith in asking for further signs with the fleece after he had already received many signs?

question: Why did Gideon not wash his own feet in the dew he wrung from the fleece, and in whom is that figure fulfilled?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Preface.
sources.answer: The figure is fulfilled in Christ, not in Gideon. The prerogative of so great a mystery was reserved for the one who alone could wash away the filth of all. That one is the Son of Man, who came to minister and who washed his disciples' feet with that heavenly dew. Gideon was not great enough to claim the mystery for himself.
sources.quote: He was being waited for Who alone could wash away the filth of all. Gideon was not great enough to claim this mystery for himself
sources.raw_question: Why did Gideon not wash his own feet in the dew he wrung from the fleece, and in whom is that figure fulfilled?

question: How could the Apostle Thomas confess Christ as 'my God' without violating the commandment that the Lord God is One?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Because Thomas, enlightened by the Resurrection, understood that the Son is of the same nature as the Father. Having heard 'I and the Father are One' and 'I in the Father and the Father in Me,' he could call the Son God without proclaiming a second God, since the perfect birth of the Godhead did not bring a second God into being.
sources.quote: No longer need he fear that such a confession as his was the proclamation of a second God, a treason against the unity of the Divine nature; for it was not a second God Whom that perfect birth of the Godhead had brought into being.
sources.raw_question: How could the Apostle Thomas confess Christ as 'my God' without violating the commandment that the Lord God is One?

question: Did Christ in the new covenant abolish the laws given through Moses, or did he keep and extend some of them?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVI.—Perfect righteousness was conferred neither by circumcision nor by any other legal ceremonies. The Decalogue, however, was not cancelled by Christ, but is always in force: men were never released from its commandments.
sources.answer: Both, depending on the kind of law. The laws of bondage, which Moses gave one by one for Israel's instruction or punishment and as a sign to them, Christ cancelled by the new covenant of liberty. The natural laws common to all, summed up in the Decalogue, he increased and widened. Through adoption he grants people to know and love God the Father with the whole heart and to abstain even from the desire for evil.
sources.quote: These things, therefore, which were given for bondage, and for a sign to them, He cancelled by the new covenant of liberty. But He has increased and widened those laws which are natural, and noble, and common to all
sources.raw_question: Did Christ in the new covenant abolish the laws given through Moses, or did he keep and extend some of them?

question: Does Christ's coming abolish the law and the prophets, or fulfil them?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIV.—Proof against the Marcionites, that the prophets referred in all their predictions to our Christ.
sources.answer: It fulfils them. Christ was found to be exactly as he had been announced. If he had not fulfilled the prophets' words, they would have been proved false and not sent by the Lord. Christ himself said he came not to destroy but to fulfil, and he still fulfils in the Church the new covenant foretold by the law. Paul likewise says God's righteousness is witnessed by the law and the prophets.
sources.quote: For by His advent He Himself fulfilled all things, and does still fulfil in the Church the new covenant foretold by the law, onwards to the consummation [of all things].
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's coming abolish the law and the prophets, or fulfil them?

question: In what respects is Christ called Saviour, salutary, and salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: He is Saviour as being the Son and Word of God; salutary (bringing salvation) since he is Spirit, as it is written 'The Spirit of our countenance, Christ the Lord'; and salvation as being flesh, because the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. Thus the one Son of God, both divine and incarnate, is the content of saving knowledge.
sources.quote: For He is indeed Saviour, as being the Son and Word of God; but salutary, since [He is] Spirit; for he says: “The Spirit of our countenance, Christ the Lord.” But salvation, as being flesh
sources.raw_question: In what respects is Christ called Saviour, salutary, and salvation?

question: Since human deliverers and ministers are also called 'saviours', is Christ a saviour only in the same sense as they are?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Christ stands forth emphatically as the Author of eternal salvation. Others were either deliverers of their country from oppression or instruments, as his ministers, in the salvation of souls.
sources.quote: how infinite is the difference betwixt him who stands forth emphatically the Author of eternal salvation, and those who were deliverers of their country from oppression
sources.raw_question: Since human deliverers and ministers are also called 'saviours', is Christ a saviour only in the same sense?

question: Does the soul remember God because it recollects knowing Him in Adam or in a life before the body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Although the Soul Hopes for Blessedness, Yet It Does Not Remember Lost Blessedness, But Remembers God and the Rules of Righteousness. The Unchangeable Rules of Right Living are Known Even to the Ungodly.
sources.answer: No. The soul remembers nothing of a prior state; all of that is blotted out by forgetfulness. It can remember God because He always is and is whole everywhere, so the soul lives, moves and has its being in Him. It is reminded so that it may turn to Him as to a light that touched it even while it was turned away.
sources.quote: Not because it recollects the having known Him in Adam or anywhere else before the life of this present body, or when it was first made in order to be implanted in this body; for it remembers nothing at all of all this.
sources.raw_question: Does the soul remember God because it recollects knowing Him in Adam or in a life before the body?

question: Can people who have forgotten God be reminded of Him and turn back, or is their forgetting of God total?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How Any One Can Forget and Remember God.
sources.answer: They can be reminded. Augustine distinguishes total forgetting, where every reminder fails and one can only take another's word, from partial forgetting, where reminders recall what was not wholly blotted out of memory. Scripture says both that the nations that forget God are turned into hell and that all the ends of the world shall be reminded and turned to the Lord. So the nations had not forgotten God so completely that they could not remember Him when reminded.
sources.quote: These nations, then, will not so have forgotten God as to be unable to remember Him when reminded of Him
sources.raw_question: Can people who have forgotten God be reminded of Him and turn back, or is their forgetting of God total?

question: What does it mean for the soul to forget God and then remember Him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How Any One Can Forget and Remember God.
sources.answer: Forgetting God is like forgetting one's own life, and it turns the soul toward death, that is, hell. Remembering God when reminded is like coming to life again. The soul turns to the Lord and recovers the proper life it had forgotten. Being with God therefore depends on remembering, understanding and loving Him.
sources.quote: by forgetting God, as though forgetting their own life, they had been turned into death, i.e. into hell. But when reminded they are turned to the Lord, as though coming to life again by remembering their proper life which they had forgotten.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean for the soul to forget God and then remember Him?

question: Do the virtues of prudence, fortitude, temperance and justice cease to exist in the blessed future life?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether Justice and the Other Virtues Cease to Exist in the Future Life.
sources.answer: Not entirely. Justice is immortal and will be perfected rather than cease, since it consists in being subject to the government of God. The other three may also remain in a transformed way: prudence preferring nothing to God, fortitude cleaving to Him steadfastly, and temperance taking pleasure in no harmful defect. Only those acts of the virtues that deal with evil, such as helping the wretched or bearing troubles, will cease, because there will be no evil there.
sources.quote: but justice is immortal, and will rather then be made perfect in us than cease to be.
sources.raw_question: Do the virtues of prudence, fortitude, temperance and justice cease to exist in the blessed future life?

question: Does Christ's calling His disciples "friends" show that He is the Word of God whom Abraham followed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIII.—Christ did not abrogate the natural precepts of the law, but rather fulfilled and extended them. He removed the yoke and bondage of the old law, so that mankind, being now set free, might serve God with that trustful piety which becometh sons.
sources.answer: Yes. By making His disciples friends of God, Christ plainly declares Himself to be the Word of God. Abraham followed this same Word freely, because of the noble nature of his faith, and so became "the friend of God."
sources.quote: But when He terms His disciples “the friends of God,” He plainly declares Himself to be the Word of God, whom Abraham also followed voluntarily and under no compulsion (sine vinculis)
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's calling His disciples "friends" show that He is the Word of God whom Abraham followed?

question: Did the Word of God need Abraham's friendship, or was He already perfect before Abraham existed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIII.—Christ did not abrogate the natural precepts of the law, but rather fulfilled and extended them. He removed the yoke and bondage of the old law, so that mankind, being now set free, might serve God with that trustful piety which becometh sons.
sources.answer: He did not need it. The Word was perfect from the beginning, as His saying "Before Abraham was, I am" shows. He accepted Abraham's friendship only out of goodness, to give Abraham eternal life, because the friendship of God imparts immortality.
sources.quote: But the Word of God did not accept of the friendship of Abraham, as though He stood in need of it, for He was perfect from the beginning (“Before Abraham was,” He says, “I am”[^3959])
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God need Abraham's friendship, or was He already perfect before Abraham existed?

question: Do those redeemed by Christ still undergo death, and if so, what kind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Of the Same Subject.
sources.answer: They die only as Christ himself died for them, that is, only by the death of the flesh and not by the death of the spirit. Christ, owing no debt himself, redeemed the elect by freely pouring out his own blood. So the devil cannot deliver them to the second, eternal death.
sources.quote: should only so far die as Christ Himself died for them, i.e. only by the death of the flesh, not of the spirit.
sources.raw_question: Do those redeemed by Christ still undergo death, and if so, what kind?

question: Will Christ die again to forgive those who sin after coming to know him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVII—The sins of the men of old time, which incurred the displeasure of God, were, by His providence, committed to writing, that we might derive instruction thereby, and not be filled with pride. We must not, therefore, infer that there was another God than He whom Christ preached; we should rather fear, lest the one and the same God who inflicted punishment on the ancients, should bring down heavier upon us.
sources.answer: No. Death has no more dominion over Christ. Instead, the Son will come in the glory of the Father and require an account from His stewards. Christians should therefore fear that, if they sin after knowing Christ, they may obtain no further forgiveness and be shut out of His kingdom, just as God did not spare the natural branches.
sources.quote: but Christ shall not die again in behalf of those who now commit sin, for death shall no more have dominion over Him; but the Son shall come in the glory of the Father
sources.raw_question: Will Christ die again to forgive those who sin after coming to know him?

question: Is the teaching handed down in the Church through bishops appointed by the apostles, such as Polycarp of Smyrna, a reliable witness to Christian truth against heretics like Valentinus and Marcion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter III.—A refutation of the heretics, from the fact that, in the various Churches, a perpetual succession of bishops was kept up.
sources.answer: Yes. Polycarp was taught by apostles, spoke with many who had seen Christ, and was made bishop by apostles. He always taught only what he had received from them, which the Church hands down and which alone is true. The Asiatic Churches, his successors, and the Church at Ephesus, where John lived, all confirm this tradition. Such witnesses carry far more weight than the heretics, so the truth should be sought in the Church rather than among them.
sources.quote: having always taught the things which he had learned from the apostles, and which the Church has handed down, and which alone are true.
sources.raw_question: Is the teaching handed down in the Church through bishops appointed by the apostles, such as Polycarp of Smyrna, a reliable witness to Christian truth against heretics like Valentinus and Marcion?

question: Does the late origin of heretical teachings such as those of Valentinus and Marcion count against their claim to teach the truth about God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IV.—The truth is to be found nowhere else but in the Catholic Church, the sole depository of apostolical doctrine. Heresies are of recent formation, and cannot trace their origin up to the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. No Valentinians existed before Valentinus and no Marcionites before Marcion; each sect began with its own founder long after the apostles. Their doctrines therefore cannot trace their origin to the apostolic tradition held in the Church.
sources.quote: For, prior to Valentinus, those who follow Valentinus had no existence; nor did those from Marcion exist before Marcion
sources.raw_question: Does the late origin of heretical teachings such as those of Valentinus and Marcion count against their claim to teach the truth about God?

question: How much love should we give to God compared with ourselves and our neighbor?
