sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > That He Who Loves His Brother, Loves God; Because He Loves Love Itself, Which is of God, and is God.
sources.answer: We should love God incomparably more than ourselves, and our brother as much as ourselves. The more we love God, the more we truly love ourselves.
sources.quote: incomparably more upon God than upon ourselves, but upon our brother as much as upon ourselves; and we love ourselves so much the more, the more we love God.
sources.raw_question: How much love should we give to God compared with ourselves and our neighbor?

question: By whom was the Son given according to Isaiah 9:6, 'unto us a Son is given'?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter II. The Son and the Spirit are alike given; whence not subjection but one Godhead is shown by Its working.
sources.answer: He was given by the whole Trinity. Because the prophet does not specify who gave him, he shows that the Son was given by the grace of the Trinity: by the Father, by the Spirit (who also sent him), and by the Son, who gave himself.
sources.quote: For since the prophet has not defined by whom He was given, he shows that He was given by the grace of the Trinity
sources.raw_question: By whom was the Son given according to Isaiah 9:6, 'unto us a Son is given'?

question: Does Isaiah 9:6 teach that the child to be born is himself the mighty God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. The child born and the son given is called the mighty God, so the same one who is born as a child is the mighty God, and in that union he is the Prince of Peace, our Saviour.
sources.quote: The child that is born, the son that is given, is the mighty God; and as the mighty God, and a child born, or son given, he is the Prince of Peace
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah 9:6 teach that the child to be born is himself the mighty God?

question: What does Christ mean when he calls himself "the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys" in Song of Songs 2:1?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: It describes what Christ is to his spouse, the church. The rose stands for sweetness of savour and the lily for beauty. These are the two eminences of flowers, and both belong to Christ. The rose signifies the sweet savour of his love, his righteousness and his graces, which draw and refresh his saints. The lily signifies the comeliness and perfection of his person.
sources.quote: The two eminencies of flowers, sweetness of savour and beauty of colour, are divided between these. The rose for sweetness, and the lily for beauty
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean when he calls himself "the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys" in Song of Songs 2:1?

question: Why are Christ and his church both called by the same name, the lily, in Song of Songs 2:1-2?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: There are two reasons. First, Christ and the church are united by the indwelling of the same Spirit. Second, the saints bear a conformity and likeness to Christ, to which they are appointed. Because of this, the same image can describe both.
sources.quote: That Christ and his church are likened unto and termed the same thing (as here the lily), is, as from their union by the indwelling of the same Spirit, so from that [^87]conformity and likeness that is between them
sources.raw_question: Why are Christ and his church both called by the same name, the lily, in Song of Songs 2:1-2?

question: What does it mean that the church is "as the lily among thorns" in Christ's eyes (Song of Songs 2:2)?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: It means two things. The first is eminency: in Christ's esteem the saints excel all others as far as the lily excels the thorns. The second is trial: the rest of the world are pricking briers and grieving thorns to God's people. Even the best of them are only briers.
sources.quote: as the lily excelleth the thorns, so do the saints all others whatever, in the eye of Christ.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that the church is "as the lily among thorns" in Christ's eyes (Song of Songs 2:2)?

question: Does Daniel's stone "cut out without hands" signify that Christ's human birth came about without a human father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. "Without hands" means His coming was not by the work of human hands: Joseph took no part, and Mary alone co-operated with God's plan. The stone derives its existence from the power and wisdom of God. His advent in human nature was therefore by the will of God, not of a man.
sources.quote: So, then, we understand that His advent in human nature was not by the will of a man, but by the will of God.
sources.raw_question: Does Daniel's stone "cut out without hands" signify that Christ's human birth came about without a human father?

question: Who is the stone cut out without hands in Daniel's vision of Nebuchadnezzar's image, and what does it accomplish?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXVI.—John and Daniel have predicted the dissolution and desolation of the Roman Empire, which shall precede the end of the world and the eternal kingdom of Christ. The Gnostics are refuted, those tools of Satan, who invent another Father different from the Creator.
sources.answer: It is Christ. He will destroy the temporal kingdoms, symbolized by the iron and clay feet and ten toes, which stand for the ten kings. In their place He will introduce the eternal kingdom of the God of heaven, which is the resurrection of the just. Because the great God foretold this through Daniel and confirmed it by His Son, the passage shows that one God stands behind both prophecy and fulfilment.
sources.quote: if Christ is the stone which is cut out without hands, who shall destroy temporal kingdoms, and introduce an eternal one, which is the resurrection of the just
sources.raw_question: Who is the stone cut out without hands in Daniel's vision of Nebuchadnezzar's image?

question: In what sense are the water, the blood, and the Spirit of 1 John 5 said to be one?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VI. Although we are baptized with water and the Spirit, the latter is much superior to the former, and is not therefore to be separated from the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: They are one in the mystery, not in nature. The water witnesses to burial, the blood to death, and the Spirit to life; any grace in the water comes not from the nature of water but from the presence of the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: One in the mystery, not in nature. The water, then, is a witness of burial, the blood is a witness of death, the Spirit is a witness of life.
sources.raw_question: In what sense are the water, the blood, and the Spirit said in 1 John to be one?

question: In what sense are the Spirit, the water and the blood of 1 John 5 three witnesses, and are they equal witnesses?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter X. The Divinity of the Holy Spirit is supported by a passage of St. John. This passage was, indeed, erased by heretics, but it is a vain attempt, since their faithlessness could thereby more easily be convicted. The order of the context is considered in order that this passage may be shown to refer to the Spirit. He is born of the Spirit who is born again of the same Spirit, of Whom Christ Himself is believed to have been born and born again. Again, the Godhead of the Spirit is inferred from two testimonies of St. John; and lastly, it is explained how the Spirit, the water, and the blood are called witnesses.
sources.answer: Each bears witness through a distinct office in the sacrament: the Spirit renews the mind and makes us children by adoption, the water of the font washes us, and the blood of the Lord redeems us. So there is one invisible and one visible testimony in a spiritual sacrament. Although the fullness of the sacrament is in each, their offices differ, so their witness is not equal.
sources.quote: For the Spirit made us children by adoption, the water of the sacred Font washed us, the blood of the Lord redeemed us.
sources.raw_question: In what sense are the Spirit, the water and the blood of 1 John 5 three witnesses, and are they equal witnesses?

question: How are eternity, truth, and love related to one another in the being of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Preface.
sources.answer: In God they are not separate qualities. Each one qualifies and includes the others. Truth is eternal and love is eternal; love is true and eternity is true; eternity is loved and truth is loved. This shows the unchangeable unity of the divine essence.
sources.quote: since there truth is eternal, love eternal; and there love is true, eternity true; and there eternity is loved, and truth is loved
sources.raw_question: How are eternity, truth, and love related to one another in the being of God?

question: How does faith relate to truth, and how does it lead to eternal life?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Son of God Became Incarnate in Order that We Being Cleansed by Faith May Be Raised to the Unchangeable Truth.
sources.answer: Truth stands to faith as eternity stands to what has a beginning. We now believe in things done in time for our sake, and that faith cleanses us. When faith comes to sight it becomes truth, and eternity then possesses our changed mortality. Eternal life consists in knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent.
sources.quote: when our faith by seeing shall come to be truth, then eternity shall possess our now changed mortality.
sources.raw_question: How does faith relate to truth, and how does it lead to eternal life?

question: Can angels know of themselves whether a sinner has truly repented, or does Christ reveal it to them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: Angels cannot of themselves know a sinner's true repentance. Repentance is wrought in the heart, which only Jesus Christ can open and know. Christ reveals it to the angels when he commits such a person to their care, so that they rejoice over the sinner and serve him.
sources.quote: the angels cannot of themselves absolutely know the true repentance of a sinner in itself; it is a work wrought in that cabinet which none hath a key unto but Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Can angels know of themselves whether a sinner has truly repented, or does Christ reveal it to them?

question: Could the angels know God's wisdom in redemption by Christ before it was revealed in the gospel?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. According to Ephesians 3:10, principalities and powers could not gain the least acquaintance with it until God revealed it by gathering a church of sinners. 1 Peter 1:12 adds that the angels, who know all God's works so well, still long to look into these things. This shows how far the wisdom of the gospel goes beyond the wisdom shown in creation.
sources.quote: principalities and powers, that very angels themselves, could not in the least measure get any acquaintance with it, until God, by gathering of a church of sinners, did actually discover it
sources.raw_question: Could the angels know God's wisdom in redemption by Christ before it was revealed in the gospel?

question: Does Isaiah 53 show that Christ's sufferings were a vicarious atonement rather than the sufferings of a merely innocent man?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah 53 says not only that the servant was bruised for our iniquities but that it pleased the Lord to bruise him. It also says the Lord laid on him the iniquity of us all and made his soul an offering for sin. If Jesus were only a sinless man offering no vicarious atonement, a holy and just God would be causing a perfectly innocent being to suffer, which cannot be.
sources.quote: If Jesus were only a spotless, sinless man, offering no vicarious atonement, how was it that a holy and just Good – we will not say permitted such sufferings to light upon a perfectly innocent being, – but Himself caused him to suffer.
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah 53 show that Christ's sufferings were a vicarious atonement rather than the sufferings of a merely innocent man?

question: Does the suffering servant of Isaiah 53, in bearing the sins of all mankind, show that he is more than a mere man?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. He bears the whole load, dies in enduring it, and then triumphs over death as Redeemer, Mediator and Advocate. Bearing the accumulated guilt of all generations points to more than a mere man. The author therefore prays that this chapter, which brought life to the Ethiopian eunuch, will lead readers to believe in the Divinity of the Son of God.
sources.quote: Can He endure the burden? He can: He dies in the endurance. His soul is made an offering for sin. But death is swallowed up in victory.
sources.raw_question: Could the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 bear the sins of all mankind, and what does this imply about his nature?

question: What does Christ give to the believer when he gives himself in the marriage covenant?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: He gives himself freely with all his excellencies, righteousness, graces and eminencies, to be the soul's Saviour, head and husband for ever. Because he is righteousness, he is
sources.quote: Because he is righteousness, he is “The Lord our Righteousness,” Jer. xxiii. 6. Because he is the wisdom of God, and the power of God, he is “made unto us wisdom,” etc., 1 Cor. i. 30.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ give to the believer when he gives himself in the marriage covenant?

question: What does Christ require of sinners for him to engage himself to them in the marriage covenant?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Only their consent to accept him. Christ is fitted for this role by his person as mediator and by the grace he has purchased. He offers himself in the gospel promises and convinces sinners of his good-will and all-sufficiency. When they consent, he binds himself to be theirs for ever.
sources.quote: upon their consent to accept of him, — which is all he requires or expects at their hands, — he engageth himself in a marriage covenant to be theirs for ever.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ require of sinners for him to engage himself to them in the marriage covenant?

question: Was Daniel's discernment in the judgment of Susanna the work of the Holy Spirit's divine power?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VI. The Spirit rebukes just as do the Father and the Son; and indeed judges could not judge without Him, as is shown by the judgments of Solomon and Daniel, which are explained in a few words, by the way; and no other than the Holy Spirit inspired Daniel.
sources.answer: Yes. Daniel could never have discovered the elders' adultery and lie without the Spirit of God. Exposing concealed inward feelings through his voice was nothing other than the operation of divine power, given when the Lord raised up the Holy Spirit in him.
sources.quote: it was none other than the operation of divine power, that his voice should make them whose inward feelings were concealed to be known.
sources.raw_question: Was Daniel's discernment in the judgment of Susanna the work of the Holy Spirit's divine power?

question: In the story of Susanna, does "God raised up the Holy Spirit of a young youth" refer only to Daniel's human spirit rather than to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VI. The Spirit rebukes just as do the Father and the Son; and indeed judges could not judge without Him, as is shown by the judgments of Solomon and Daniel, which are explained in a few words, by the way; and no other than the Holy Spirit inspired Daniel.
sources.answer: No. Further on Scripture shows that Daniel received the Holy Spirit and therefore prophesied. The king advanced him because the Holy Spirit of God was in him, and he was set over others because an excellent Spirit was in him.
sources.quote: lest any one should perhaps think that, as the Scripture says, “God raised up the Holy Spirit of a young youth,” the Spirit in him was that of a man, not the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Does "God raised up the Holy Spirit of a young youth" in Susanna mean only Daniel's human spirit and not the Holy Spirit?

question: How can Christ say the Father has borne witness of Him when the Jews had never heard the Father's voice nor seen His form (John 5:36-38)?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: The Father's testimony is the very works that Christ performs. Since the working of the Son is itself the Father's testimony, the same nature must be operative in Christ by which the Father testifies. Hence the Son who works and the Father who testifies through those works are shown to possess one inseparable nature through the birth.
sources.quote: since, therefore, the working of the Son is the Father’s testimony, it follows of necessity that the same nature was operative in Christ, by which the Father testifies of Him.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ say the Father has borne witness of Him when the Jews had never heard the Father's voice nor seen His form (John 5:36-38)?

question: Does the voice from heaven at Christ's baptism contradict Christ's statement that the Jews had never heard the Father's voice (John 5:37)?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. That voice was heard by John in the desert, not by the dwellers in Jerusalem. The witness Christ appeals to is a greater witness than John's, namely the works the Father gave Him to accomplish.
sources.quote: It is no longer the witness given to John, who heard the voice from heaven, but a witness greater than that of John.
sources.raw_question: Does the voice from heaven at Christ's baptism contradict Christ's statement that the Jews had never heard the Father's voice?

question: Are those who rejected Christ excused because they never heard the Father's voice or saw His form (John 5:37-38)?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The Father's testimony was not hidden, since Christ's works are the Father's testimony. They failed to hear and see the Father because they did not believe the Son He sent. Had they believed, they would have heard the voice of God, seen His form and had His word in them.
sources.quote: if they had believed Him, they would have heard the voice of God, and seen the form of God, and His word would have been in them
sources.raw_question: Are those who rejected Christ excused because they never heard the Father's voice or saw His form?

question: Can Judas's fall from among the apostles be read as a type of the Valentinian Enthymesis, which was separated from the Æon and later restored to the Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XX.—Futility of the arguments adduced to demonstrate the sufferings of the twelfth Æon, from the parables, the treachery of Judas, and the passion of our Saviour.
sources.answer: No. In the Valentinian story the Enthymesis is separated, given shape by Christ, and finally received back into the Pleroma and united to the Saviour. Judas, by contrast, was cast away once for all and never returned to the number of the disciples, since Matthias was chosen to take his place. The Lord pronounced woe upon him, said it would have been better had he never been born, and called him the son of perdition. The supposed image therefore has no analogy to what it is claimed to represent.
sources.quote: But Judas having been once for all cast away, never returns into the number of the disciples; otherwise a different person would not have been chosen to fill his place.
sources.raw_question: Can Judas's fall from among the apostles be read as a type of the Valentinian Enthymesis, which was separated from the Æon and later restored to the Pleroma?

question: Can Judas and Matthias serve as types of the Valentinian triad of the Æon, her Enthymesis, and her passion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XX.—Futility of the arguments adduced to demonstrate the sufferings of the twelfth Æon, from the parables, the treachery of Judas, and the passion of our Saviour.
sources.answer: No. The Valentinians distinguish three things: the Æon, which is restored; her Enthymesis, which acquires form; and her passion, which becomes matter once separated. Judas and Matthias are only two persons. Two cannot be types of three, so the proposed correspondence of numbers fails.
sources.quote: Since, therefore, there are thus these three, the Æon, her Enthymesis, and her passion, Judas and Matthias, being only two, cannot be the types of them.
sources.raw_question: Can Judas and Matthias serve as types of the Valentinian triad of the Æon, her Enthymesis, and her passion?

question: Was whatever the Old Testament called 'glory' either Christ himself or a type of Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. Simeon sums it up by calling Christ God's salvation and Israel's glory (Luke 2:30-32). Owen concludes that whatever was called the glory of old was either Christ or a type of him, such as Noah, whom Lamech received as a type of Christ and of salvation by him.
sources.quote: Old Simon sums up the whole: Christ is God’s salvation, and Israel’s glory, Luke ii. 30, 31; and whatever was called the glory of old, it was either himself or a type of him.
sources.raw_question: Was whatever the Old Testament called 'glory' either Christ himself or a type of Christ?

question: Did the Old Testament prophets foretell two advents of Christ, one in humility and one in glory?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: Yes. All the prophets announced two advents. In the first he became a suffering man, rode on an ass's foal, was the rejected stone and was led as a sheep to the slaughter. In the second he will come on the clouds in judgment, burning the chaff with unquenchable fire. The Jews err in not recognising the first advent.
sources.quote: nor are willing to understand that all the prophets announced His two advents
sources.raw_question: Did the Old Testament prophets foretell two advents of Christ, one in humility and one in glory?

question: Are human souls saved because of their nature and substance, or because of righteousness and faith?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIX.—Refutation of the views of the heretics as to the future destiny of the soul and body.
sources.answer: By righteousness and faith, not by nature. If all souls reached the place of rest simply because they are souls, then faith would be altogether superfluous, and so would the Saviour's descent into the world. The Valentinians themselves admit that only the souls of the righteous reach that place while the souls of the impious remain in the fire. That admission concedes that salvation depends on righteousness rather than on substance.
sources.quote: For if it is on account of their nature that all souls attain to the place of enjoyment, and all belong to the intermediate place simply because they are souls, as being thus of the same nature with it, then it follows that faith is altogether superfluous
sources.raw_question: Are human souls saved because of their nature and substance, or because of righteousness and faith?

question: If righteousness saves the soul, does it also save the body, so that bodies will rise to immortality?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIX.—Refutation of the views of the heretics as to the future destiny of the soul and body.
sources.answer: Yes. Righteous acts are performed in bodies, so bodies share in righteousness just as souls do. If righteousness saved some of the substances that took part in it but not others, it would be either powerless or unjust. The resurrection of bodies therefore follows even from the Gnostics' own premises.
sources.quote: For it is manifest that those acts which are deemed righteous are performed in bodies.
sources.raw_question: If righteousness saves the soul, does it also save the body, so that bodies will rise to immortality?

question: Are the God who makes the chaff and the God who makes the wheat, and who separates them in judgment, different beings?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IV.—Answer to another objection, showing that the destruction of Jerusalem, which was the city of the great King, diminished nothing from the supreme majesty and power of God, for that this destruction was put in execution by the most wise counsel of the same God.
sources.answer: No. The one who makes the chaff and the one who makes the wheat are not different persons but one and the same, and he is also the one who judges and separates them. The Creator and the Judge revealed in Christ are a single God.
sources.quote: For He who makes the chaff and He who makes the wheat are not different persons, but one and the same, who judges them, that is, separates them.
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who separate the Creator from the Father of Christ
sources.raw_question: Are the God who makes the chaff and the God who makes the wheat, and who separates them in judgment, different beings?

question: If God makes both wheat and chaff, is God responsible when a man becomes 'chaff' and is condemned?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IV.—Answer to another objection, showing that the destruction of Jerusalem, which was the city of the great King, diminished nothing from the supreme majesty and power of God, for that this destruction was put in execution by the most wise counsel of the same God.
sources.answer: No. Wheat and chaff are irrational and are made what they are by nature. Man, however, is rational, like God, free in his will and with power over himself. He is therefore the cause of his own becoming wheat or chaff, and he is justly condemned when he lives irrationally and opposes God's righteousness.
sources.quote: man, being endowed with reason, and in this respect like to God, having been made free in his will, and with power over himself, is himself the cause to himself, that sometimes he becomes wheat, and sometimes chaff.
sources.raw_question: If God makes both wheat and chaff, is God responsible when a man becomes 'chaff' and is condemned?

question: Does Psalm 68:17-18, which speaks of God ascending on high and leading captivity captive, refer to Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen notes that Paul applies this psalm to the Son in Ephesians 4:8-10. The Lord God of Sinai who ascended is the same person who first descended and then ascended above all heavens to fill all things, namely Christ.
sources.quote: He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens that he might fill all things.”
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 68:17-18, which speaks of God ascending on high and leading captivity captive, refer to Christ?

question: What is the "captivity" that Christ "led captive" when he ascended, according to Ephesians 4:8?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: The captivity is the devil himself. Christ conquered him and bound him first by the bonds of righteousness and then by those of might. In this way Christ rescued from him those who were to become members of the Head, and from them his house, the Church, is built up.
sources.quote: The devil himself, therefore, is called captivity, which He led captive who ascended up on high, and gave gifts to men, or received gifts in men.
sources.raw_question: What is the "captivity" that Christ "led captive" when he ascended, according to Ephesians 4:8?

question: Does the Song of Moses show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit all worked in the crossing of the Red Sea?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IV. To those who contend that the Spirit because He is called the Finger is less than the Father, St. Ambrose replies that this would also tend to the lessening of the Son, Who is called the Right Hand. That these names are to be referred only to the Unity, for which reason Moses proclaimed that the whole Trinity worked in the passage of the Red Sea. And, indeed, it is no wonder that the operation of the Spirit found place there, where there was a figure of baptism, since the Scripture teaches that the Three Persons equally sanctify and are operative in that sacrament.
sources.answer: Yes. Moses confesses the Father and the Son, whose Right Hand He is, when he sings that God's Right Hand dashed the enemy in pieces. He also confesses the Spirit, by whom God covered the Egyptians with the sea and divided the water. This signifies the unity of the Godhead, not an inequality in the Trinity.
sources.quote: Thou didst send Thy Spirit and the sea covered them, and the water was divided by the Spirit of Thine anger.” By which is signified the unity of the Godhead, not an inequality of the Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Does the Song of Moses show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit all worked in the crossing of the Red Sea?

question: If all people will blessedness, why do they disagree so widely about what blessedness is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Will to Possess Blessedness is One in All, But the Variety of Wills is Very Great Concerning that Blessedness Itself.
sources.answer: The disagreement is not because anyone is unwilling to have blessedness but because not all know it. If all knew it, some would not place it in goodness of mind, others in bodily pleasure, and others in both. People place the blessed life in whatever thing most delights them.
sources.quote: not that any one is unwilling to have it, but that all do not know it. For if all knew it, it would not be thought by some to be in goodness of mind; by others, in pleasure of body
sources.raw_question: If all people will blessedness, why do they disagree so widely about what blessedness is?

question: Can people know what blessedness is while disagreeing only about where it is to be found?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Will to Possess Blessedness is One in All, But the Variety of Wills is Very Great Concerning that Blessedness Itself.
sources.answer: No. Blessedness is not a place in this world one could travel to. The question where it is, is already contained in the question what it is. If it lies in bodily pleasure, then whoever enjoys that pleasure is blessed. So those who define it differently either both know or both do not know what it is.
sources.quote: as if the question where blessedness is were not implied in the question what it is.
sources.raw_question: Can people know what blessedness is while disagreeing only about where it is to be found?

question: Is the image the Holy Spirit stamps on believers his own likeness only, or also the image of the Father and the Son, and does it bring believers into fellowship with the Spirit himself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: The Spirit communicates his own likeness, which is also the image of the Father and the Son. In doing so he brings believers into fellowship with himself. Our likeness to him gives us boldness with him, and when the image of Christ appears in us, we have communion with the Spirit in it.
sources.quote: Thus, then, the Holy Ghost communicates unto us his own likeness; which is also the image of the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Is the image the Holy Spirit stamps on believers his own likeness only, or also the image of the Father and the Son, and does it bring believers into fellowship with the Spirit himself?

question: Is the mental trinity in man (mind, its self-knowledge, and its self-love) identical with the man himself, as the Trinity is identical with God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God from the Trinities We Have Spoken of.
sources.answer: No. The three in man are in such a way in him that they are not themselves man; they are the chief things in man but belong to man or are in man. Whether man is defined as a rational mortal animal or as a rational substance of mind and body, these three are only part of him, located in the mind, which is itself only what is chief in the soul.
sources.quote: But these three are in such way in man, that they are not themselves man. For man, as the ancients defined him, is a rational mortal animal. These things, therefore, are the chief things in man, but are not man themselves.
sources.raw_question: Is the mental trinity in man (mind, its self-knowledge, and its self-love) identical with the man himself, as the Trinity is identical with God?

question: Is the Trinity in God something belonging to God but not itself God, as the mental trinity belongs to man without being man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God from the Trinities We Have Spoken of.
sources.answer: No. The Trinity of which man is the image is nothing else in its totality than God, and nothing else in its totality than the Trinity. Nothing pertains to the nature of God that does not pertain to the Trinity, so the Trinity is not a part or possession of God but God himself.
sources.quote: But that Trinity of which he is the image is nothing else in its totality than God, is nothing else in its totality than the Trinity. Nor does anything pertain to the nature of God so as not to pertain to that Trinity
sources.raw_question: Is the Trinity in God something belonging to God but not itself God, as the mental trinity belongs to man without being man?

question: When the mind begets knowledge of itself by thinking of itself, does that mean it was previously unknown to itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How a Kind of Trinity Exists in the Mind Thinking of Itself. What is the Part of Thought in This Trinity.
sources.answer: No. The mind already knew itself in the way things kept in memory are known while one is not thinking of them. In the same way, a man knows letters even while he is thinking of something else.
sources.quote: the mind does not so beget this knowledge of itself, when it beholds itself as understood by conception, as though it had before been unknown to itself; but it was known to itself
sources.raw_question: When the mind begets knowledge of itself by thinking of itself, does that mean it was previously unknown to itself?

question: Can the Trinity be known through created things, especially the human mind as the image of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Against Eunomius, Saying that the Son of God is the Son, Not of His Nature, But of His Will. Epilogue to What Has Been Said Already.
sources.answer: Yes, in part. God's invisible things can be understood through the things he has made. This holds especially for the rational creature made after his image, whose memory, understanding and will act as a mirror in which the Trinity may be glimpsed. Whoever sees these three in his mind, through which even the eternal nature can be recollected, beheld and desired, finds an image of the highest Trinity.
sources.quote: they might discern as far as they could, if they could, the Trinity which is God, in our own memory, understanding, will
sources.raw_question: Can the Trinity be known through created things, especially the human mind as the image of God?

question: Why should one look for a likeness of the Trinity in the perishing outer man if only the inner man is renewed after the image of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight.
sources.answer: Because we are mortal and fleshly, we handle visible things more easily than intelligible ones. So a trace of the Trinity in the outer man, though less express, may be easier to discern. The outer man is also rightly called man because it bears some likeness to the inner man. It is not, however, the image of God in the way the inner man is, which the apostle says is renewed in the knowledge of God.
sources.quote: Let us seek, then, so far as we can, in that which perishes, some image of the Trinity, if not so express, yet perhaps more easy to be discerned.
sources.raw_question: Why should one look for a likeness of the Trinity in the perishing outer man if only the inner man is renewed after the image of God?

question: Why is the image of the Trinity in the mind better seen in memory, intelligence, and will together than in memory alone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Thing is Made Plain by an Example. In What Way the Matter is Handled in Order to Help the Reader.
sources.answer: Within the mind's inner self-knowledge, the three are always together, so the image might seem to belong to memory alone. But a word cannot exist without a thought, since we think all that we say, even by the inner word that belongs to no language. So the image is better discerned in the three together. Intelligence is the understanding in thought that is formed from what lies in memory, like an offspring from its parent. Will, or love, joins that offspring and parent and is common to both.
sources.quote: because in this case a word cannot be without a thought (for we think all that we say, even if it be said by that inner word which belongs to no separate language), this image is rather to be discerned in these three things, viz. memory, intelligence, will
sources.raw_question: Why is the image of the Trinity in the mind better seen in memory, intelligence, and will together than in memory alone?

question: Does the mental triad of memory, understanding, and will in the human mind map onto the Trinity so that the Father is the memory, the Son the understanding, and the Holy Spirit the love of all three Persons?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God from the Trinities We Have Spoken of.
sources.answer: No. In man we remember only by memory, understand only by understanding, and love only by will, but no one should dare say the Father understands only through the Son or loves only through the Holy Spirit. Each divine Person has all three for Himself, so memory, understanding and love in God are not distributed among the Father, Son and Spirit as separate faculties.
sources.quote: But in that Trinity, who would dare to say that the Father understands neither Himself, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, except by the Son, or loves them except by the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Does the mental triad of memory, understanding, and will in the human mind map onto the Trinity so that the Father is the memory, the Son the understanding, and the Holy Spirit the love of all three Persons?

question: How can each member of the mental trinity (mind, knowledge, love) exist in itself and not merely in relation to the others?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > That These Three are Several in Themselves, and Mutually All in All.
sources.answer: Each is predicated both relatively and in respect to itself. The mind is called mind in respect to itself, though knowing or loving relatively; knowledge is itself known and knowing, since the knowledge by which the mind knows itself is not unknown to itself; and love is loved, but only by love, that is, by itself.
sources.quote: since love too is loved, yet cannot be loved with anything except with love, that is with itself. So these things are severally in themselves.
sources.raw_question: How can each member of the mental trinity (mind, knowledge, love) exist in itself and not merely in relation to the others?

question: Can the Trinity be seen directly and clearly in this present life, or only indirectly?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are.
sources.answer: Only indirectly. In this life the Trinity is seen as by a mirror and in an enigma, because it is seen through the image of God which we ourselves are. That likeness is obscure and hard to discern, and perfect contemplation of the Trinity is reserved for the blessed life promised to us.
sources.quote: But this Trinity, as he shows, is here seen by us as by a mirror and in an enigma, in that it is seen by means of the image of God, which we are, as in a likeness that is obscure and hard of discernment.
sources.raw_question: Can the Trinity be seen directly and clearly in this present life, or only indirectly?

question: Is there an image of the Trinity in the human mind, and are its members equal and of one essence?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
sources.answer: Yes. Man is the image of God with respect to his mind. In the mind there is a trinity: the mind, the knowledge by which it knows itself, and the love by which it loves itself and its knowledge. These three are mutually equal and of one essence, and a still clearer trinity appears as memory, understanding and will.
sources.quote: the mind, and the knowledge whereby the mind knows itself, and the love whereby it loves both itself and its knowledge of itself; and these three are shown to be mutually equal, and of one essence
sources.raw_question: Is there an image of the Trinity in the human mind, and are its members equal and of one essence?

question: Can the human mind know itself only in part while remaining ignorant of itself in another part?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > How the Mind Knows Itself, Not in Part, But as a Whole.
sources.answer: No. Whatever the mind knows, it knows as a whole, not by one part of it; so when it knows anything about itself, it knows itself as a whole. Since it knows that it knows something, and can only know as a whole, it knows itself as a whole.
sources.quote: I do not say, it knows wholly; but what it knows, it as a whole knows. When therefore it knows anything about itself, which it can only know as a whole, it knows itself as a whole.
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind know itself only in part while remaining ignorant of itself in another part?

question: Was man created in the image of the whole Trinity or in the image of only one divine Person?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > John is Rather to Be Understood of Our Perfect Likeness with the Trinity in Life Eternal. Wisdom is Perfected in Happiness.
sources.answer: Man was made after the image of the Trinity. Genesis says "Let us make man after our image and likeness," not "after my image" or "after thy image." The plural shows that the image belongs to the Trinity as a whole, not to a single Person.
sources.quote: we believe,—and, after the utmost search we have been able to make, understand,—that man was made after the image of the Trinity, because it is not said, After my, or After thy image.
sources.raw_question: Was man created in the image of the whole Trinity or in the image of only one divine Person?

question: Does the human mind know itself, as the basis for finding a trinity in it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Image of God is to Be Sought in the Immortality of the Rational Soul. How a Trinity is Demonstrated in the Mind.
sources.answer: Yes. The mind knows nothing so well as what is close to it, and nothing is closer to the mind than itself. This self-knowledge, already proved in Book 10, is the starting point for finding a trinity in the mind.
sources.quote: the mind of man knows itself. For the mind knows nothing so much as that which is close to itself; and nothing is more close to the mind than itself.
sources.raw_question: Does the human mind know itself, as the basis for finding a trinity in it?

question: Why is it hard to tell apart the mind's memory of itself from its understanding of itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Mind is an Image of the Trinity in Its Own Memory, and Understanding, and Will.
sources.answer: Because the two are very closely joined, and neither comes before the other in time. So they look like one thing called by two names rather than two things. The mind always knows and remembers itself, but it does not always think of itself as separate from what it is not. This makes the distinction hard to see.
sources.quote: where these two things are very closely conjoined, and one is not preceded by the other by any time at all, it looks as if they were not two things, but one called by two names
sources.raw_question: Why is it hard to tell apart the mind's memory of itself from its understanding of itself?

question: Can the trinitarian structure of the mind be shown more clearly through things the mind receives in time than through its timeless knowledge of itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Mind is an Image of the Trinity in Its Own Memory, and Understanding, and Will.
sources.answer: Yes, it can be set out more clearly that way, even for slower minds. When the mind comes in time to remember, see, and love what it did not before, the three acts can be seen as distinct. In the mind's constant self-knowledge, by contrast, they blur together. This is why Augustine next looks at trinities drawn from bodily sense and memory.
sources.quote: while it remembers what it did not remember before, and sees what it did not see before, and loves what it did not love before
sources.raw_question: Can the trinitarian structure of the mind be shown more clearly through things the mind receives in time than through its timeless knowledge of itself?

question: Do the three Persons of the Trinity have three distinct understandings?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Theologians have not supposed three distinct understandings in the three Persons, but one and the same understanding. That one understanding is the Son, and it is shared by the Father and the Spirit because the Son indwells them.
sources.quote: divines have not been wont to suppose that these three had three distinct understandings, but all one and the same understanding.
sources.raw_question: Do the three Persons of the Trinity have three distinct understandings?

question: When the human mind knows and loves itself, does it thereby know and love something unchangeable?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > There is One Knowledge of the Thing in the Thing Itself, and Another in Eternal Truth Itself. That Corporeal Things, Too, are to Be Judged the Rules of Eternal Truth.
sources.answer: No. The human mind that knows and loves itself does not know and love anything unchangeable. Each person's own particular mind undergoes changes at successive times, whereas the truth by which the mind is defined generally consists in an unchangeable eternity.
sources.quote: But when the human mind knows itself and loves itself, it does not know and love anything unchangeable
sources.raw_question: When the human mind knows and loves itself, does it thereby know and love something unchangeable?

question: Do the three faculties of the mind's trinitarian image (memory, understanding, love) each contain the others?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Of the Likeness of the Father and of the Son Alleged to Be in Our Memory and Understanding. Of the Likeness of the Holy Spirit in Our Will or Love.
sources.answer: Yes. Understanding and love are found in memory. Memory and love are in understanding, since thought returns to a thing only by remembering it and cares to return only by loving it. Love too cannot love rightly without knowing what it desires, which requires memory and understanding. Each faculty is thus present in the others.
sources.quote: for the gaze of our thought does not return to anything except by remembering it, and does not care to return unless by loving it
sources.raw_question: Do the three faculties of the mind's trinitarian image (memory, understanding, love) each contain the others?

question: Can the Trinity be seen face to face in this life through the image of God in the mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Of the Likeness of the Father and of the Son Alleged to Be in Our Memory and Understanding. Of the Likeness of the Holy Spirit in Our Will or Love.
sources.answer: No. The mental image shows the Trinity only by likeness in an enigma, in a small degree and by conjecture, not face to face. The likeness also includes a great unlikeness.
sources.quote: not indeed so that the thing might be seen face to face, but that it might be seen by this likeness in an enigma,
sources.raw_question: Can the Trinity be seen face to face in this life through the image of God in the mind?

question: Is the trinity in the human mind an adequate image of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and why study it at all?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three Things Which are Found in Love Must Be Considered.
sources.answer: It is an inadequate image, yet it is truly an image, since man is made in God's image. Augustine examines it because our feeble mind can consider it more familiarly and easily than heavenly things themselves. He also asks for divine illumination to see this image in ourselves.
sources.quote: We are not yet speaking of heavenly things, nor yet of God the Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit, but of that inadequate image, which yet is an image, that is, man; for our feeble mind perhaps can gaze upon this more familiarly and more easily.
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity in the human mind an adequate image of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and why study it at all?

question: How does the trinity found in recollection (memory-image, inner vision, will) differ from the trinity found in bodily sight (body seen, vision, will)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > How This Unity Comes to Pass.
sources.answer: In bodily sight the three are united though they are of diverse natures, since the external body, the sense, and the will are different kinds of things. In recollection the three — the image in memory, the vision of the one thinking, and the will joining them — are of one and the same substance, because the whole takes place within and the whole is one mind. The structure is analogous: the memory-image stands to the mind's eye as the body stands to bodily sense, and the will unites both in each case.
sources.quote: in order that here too a certain unity may take place of three things, not now distinguished by diversity of nature, but of one and the same substance; because this whole is within, and the whole is one mind.
sources.raw_question: How does the trinity found in recollection (memory-image, inner vision, will) differ from the trinity found in bodily sight (body seen, vision, will)?

question: Can the Creator, and his being the Trinity, be known by studying created things and by reason as well as by Scripture?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > God is Above the Mind.
sources.answer: Yes, to a degree. Augustine leads the reader through things that are made so that he may know the One who made them. He aims to show that God is the Trinity both to believers, by the authority of Scripture, and to those who understand, by reason as far as possible. The limits of this, his "if we can," will become clear once the inquiry begins.
sources.quote: it is now our business to demonstrate not only to believers, by authority of divine Scripture, but also to such as understand, by some kind of reason, if we can
sources.raw_question: Can the Creator, and his being the Trinity, be known by studying created things and by reason as well as by Scripture?

question: Can the finite human mind comprehend or define God's infinite nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. God's greatness so far surpasses the powers of the minds He made that however hard the limited mind strains to define Him, the gap between the finite and the boundless infinite does not shrink.
sources.quote: however far the limited mind of man might strain in the hazardous effort to define Him, the gap was not lessened between the finite nature which struggled and the boundless infinity that lay beyond its ken
sources.raw_question: Can the finite human mind comprehend or define God's infinite nature?

question: Can a finite, created mind attain complete knowledge of the infinite God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. Finite minds cannot conceive the Infinite; a being that depends on another for its existence cannot perfectly know either its Creator or itself. Its powers are bounded and its origin lies outside itself, so it possesses none of its faculties perfectly, and any claim to perfect knowledge is an empty boast.
sources.quote: Finite minds cannot conceive the Infinite; a being dependent for its existence upon another cannot attain to perfect knowledge either of its Creator or of itself
sources.raw_question: Can a finite, created mind attain complete knowledge of the infinite God?

question: Can the human mind comprehend whether God's foreknowledge is the same as his memory and his understanding?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God from the Trinities We Have Spoken of.
sources.answer: No. We cannot even comprehend how memory enables our own foresight, as when we recite a song, so in such infirmity of mind we cannot comprehend how these are related in God. He does not consider each thing in turn but sees all in one eternal vision. We must confess with the Psalmist that such knowledge is too high for us.
sources.quote: can comprehend whether the foresight of God is the same as His memory and His understanding, who does not regard in thought each several thing, but embraces all that He knows in one eternal and unchangeable and ineffable vision?
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind comprehend whether God's foreknowledge is the same as his memory and his understanding?

question: Can human reason, philosophy, or moral virtue by its own power attain true knowledge of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Our nature cannot raise itself to contemplate heavenly things, and we must learn from God what to think of God. Moses was trained in all the wisdom of Egypt and acted righteously, yet did not know God until God revealed His name from the bush. So in speaking of God we must keep to the terms in which He has revealed Himself.
sources.quote: We must learn from God what we are to think of God; we have no source of knowledge but Himself.
sources.raw_question: Can human reason, philosophy, or moral virtue by its own power attain true knowledge of God?

question: Can the substance of God be expressed in human language or grasped by human understanding?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, that When God is Called a Spirit, Brightness, and Light, God is Not Sufficiently Expressed by Those Appellations.
sources.answer: No. God as he is in himself can neither be declared by human discourse, nor received by human ears, nor gathered by human perceptions. If even the things God has prepared for those who love him surpass eye, ear and heart, much more does the one who promises them exceed the mind and nature of man.
sources.quote: For that which is, according to what it is, can neither be declared by human discourse, nor received by human ears, nor gathered by human perceptions.
sources.raw_question: Can the substance of God be expressed in human language or grasped by human understanding?

question: Can human reason grasp God by comprehending part of Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. God is everywhere wholly present and undivided, so what we seem to grasp is bound up with His entirety. It is not even a part, since a part implies division and God cannot be divided. Reason cannot cope with Him because there is no point of contemplation outside Him.
sources.quote: For a part implies division, a whole is undivided, and God is everywhere and wholly present wherever He is.
sources.raw_question: Can human reason grasp God by comprehending part of Him?

question: Can the name 'God' be used as an indication of the divine nature of the one who bears it?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. The name and nature correspond, so the name is a test of the nature and the nature a clue to the name; hence whom the Law calls God has the character, power, and attributes of God.
sources.quote: we can use the name as a test of the nature, and the nature as a clue to the name.
sources.raw_question: Can the name 'God' be used as an indication of the divine nature of the one who bears it?

question: Can the human mind directly understand the substance of God, or must it first be purified and nourished by faith?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > This Work is Written Against Those Who Sophistically Assail the Faith of the Trinity, Through Misuse of Reason. They Who Dispute Concerning God Err from a Threefold Cause. Holy Scripture, Removing What is False, Leads Us on by Degrees to Things Divine. What True Immortality is. We are Nourished by Faith, that We May Be Enabled to Apprehend Things Divine.
sources.answer: It must first be purified. The ineffable substance of God can only be seen by a cleansed mind. Until that cleansing is achieved, believers must be nourished by faith and led by ways suited to their capacity, so that they become able to grasp it.
sources.quote: it is necessary, therefore, to purge our minds, in order to be able to see ineffably that which is ineffable; whereto not having yet attained, we are to be nourished by faith
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind directly understand the substance of God, or must it first be purified and nourished by faith?

question: Can the human mind fully comprehend the nature of God, and what happens when it tries to go beyond its limits?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. A lower nature cannot understand the principle of a higher, and whatever falls within a limited consciousness is itself limited, so the divine power exceeds human capacity. As with gazing at the sun, those who strain beyond what is granted lose even what they could have seen. We can understand what God grants to our apprehension if we are content with the possible.
sources.quote: A lower nature cannot understand the principle of a higher: nor can Heaven’s mode of thought be revealed to human conception, for whatever is within the range of a limited consciousness, is itself limited.
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind fully comprehend the nature of God, and what happens when it tries to go beyond its limits?

question: Can God receive any increase or progress in fulness, so that the Son's subjection (1 Corinthians 15:28) makes God more complete by becoming 'all in all'?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. God received His being from no one, nothing is prior to or outside Him, and all things are of Him, through Him and in Him, so there is nothing from which He could gain addition. He is eternally Himself and unchangeable, as He says, 'I am and I change not.' Hence the subjection of the Son does not perfect God; He remains God as He ever was.
sources.quote: The subjection of the Son will not therefore make God to be all in all, nor will any cause perfect Him, from Whom and through Whom and in Whom are all causes.
sources.raw_question: Can God receive any increase or progress in fulness, so that the Son's subjection (1 Corinthians 15:28) makes God more complete by becoming 'all in all'?

question: Does a negative term like "ungenerate" reveal the divine essence, or only tell us what not to think about God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > After much discourse concerning the actually existent, and ungenerate and good, and upon the consubstantiality of the heavenly powers, showing the uncharted character of their essence, yet the difference of their ranks, he ends the book.
sources.answer: It only guides us as to what we must not think about the subject. Likewise, calling God "judge" or "patient" teaches one of his attributes and not his essence. Through the negative predicate of being ungenerate, God's essential being remains as unexplained as before.
sources.quote: we do not by this negative predication understand the subject, but are guided as to what we must not think concerning the subject, while what He essentially is remains as much as ever unexplained.
sources.raw_question: Does a negative term like "ungenerate" reveal the divine essence, or only tell us what not to think about God?

question: Can Eunomius divide the nature of the Father and the Son on the basis of differing names like "ungenerate" and "generated"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > After much discourse concerning the actually existent, and ungenerate and good, and upon the consubstantiality of the heavenly powers, showing the uncharted character of their essence, yet the difference of their ranks, he ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius would first have to name the essence itself before dividing the Nature by the divergence of appellations, and he cannot. The definition of "being" differs from that of "being in some particular way," and the names have no separate existence. His technical skill with names is therefore in vain.
sources.quote: Let him then first disclose to us the names of the essence, and then divide the Nature by the divergence of the appellations;—so long as what we require remains unexplained, it is in vain that he employs his scientific skill upon names
sources.raw_question: Can Eunomius divide the nature of the Father and the Son on the basis of differing names like "ungenerate" and "generated"?

question: Does defining God's essence as ungeneracy (being unbegotten) lead to absurd consequences?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Beginning and end are distinct, with an extension between them. If the privation of a beginning is itself God's essence, then his Life would subsist only in being without beginning and would not extend by nature to being without end. And if both privations are each an essence, each would be exactly what its term means and no more. Then being without beginning would not imply being without end, so Eunomius' own absurdity falls on his own view.
sources.quote: if any one allow the privation of the first of these to be essence, he must suppose His Life to be only half subsisting in this being without beginning, and not to extend further, by virtue of His nature, to the being without end
sources.raw_question: Does defining God's essence as ungeneracy (being unbegotten) lead to absurd consequences?

question: Does a difference in names such as 'generate' and 'ungenerate' prove that the Father and the Son differ in essence, as Eunomius argues?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > Thereafter he discusses the divergence of names and of things, speaking, of that which is ungenerate as without a cause, and of that which is non-existent, as the Scindapsus, Minotaur, Blityri, Cyclops, Scylla, which never were generated at all, and shows that things which are essentially different, are mutually destructive, as fire of water, and the rest in their several relations. But in the case of the Father and the Son, as the essence is common, and the properties reciprocally interchangeable, no injury results to the Nature.
sources.answer: No. Gregory grants that wholly incommunicable names indicate different natures, but the names proper to the Divine Nature (God, just, incorruptible, good, wise) are applied equally to the Father and the Son. So by Eunomius' own principle, the community of names shows a common essence, and his argument actually testifies that there is no divergence of nature.
sources.quote: if the divergent character of appellations indicates difference of natures, the community of names will surely show the common character of the essence.
sources.raw_question: Does a difference in names such as 'generate' and 'ungenerate' prove that the Father and the Son differ in essence, as Eunomius argues?

question: Can 'Ungenerate' (the negation of beginning) be treated as constituting God's very being or essence, while 'Endless' is treated as external to it, as Eunomius holds?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: No. Both negations are conceptions of one and the same thing, God's eternity, so there is no reason to place one within God's being and banish the other outside it; either both belong to the definition of being or neither does. If one must be preferred on human reckoning, the unending would have the better claim, since the future is valued above the past. Moreover, if being is confined to unbegottenness alone, the definition is curtailed by half.
sources.quote: The two are our conceptions of the same thing; and, therefore, either both should be admitted to the definition of being, or, if the one is to be judged inadmissible, the other should be rejected also.
sources.raw_question: Can 'Ungenerate' (the negation of beginning) be treated as constituting God's very being or essence, while 'Endless' is treated as external to it, as Eunomius holds?

question: Is "Ungenerate" the uniquely proper name expressing the essence of God the Father, or could other names signify Him equally well?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > He says that all things that are in creation have been named by man, if, as is the case, they are called differently by every nation, as also the appellation of “Ungenerate” is conferred by us: but that the proper appellation of the Divine essence itself which expresses the Divine Nature, either does not exist at all, or is unknown to us.
sources.answer: Other names could serve equally well. "Ungenerate" is a term we applied to the Father, and no harm to signifying the Subject results if the same concept is expressed as "First Cause," "Father of the Only-begotten," or "existing without cause." So it is not a name that captures the divine essence itself.
sources.quote: For it is allowable instead of speaking of Him as “Ungenerate,” to call Him the “First Cause” or “Father of the Only-begotten,” or to speak of Him as “existing without cause,”
