sources.raw_question: Is "Ungenerate" the uniquely proper name expressing the essence of God the Father, or could other names signify Him equally well?

question: If the term 'ungenerate' signified the essence of God the Father rather than his being without origin, would any word remain to express that the Father is without origin?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. If 'ungenerate' is taken to denote the divine nature, there is no other word left to express that the Father was not generated, so the Father's being without origin drops out of their teaching altogether. Their argument thus excludes the very term they claim to prize.
sources.quote: For inasmuch as according to them the term ungenerate does not mean without origin, but indicates the Divine nature, their argument will be found to exclude it altogether, and the term ungenerate slips out of their teaching in respect to God.
sources.raw_question: If the term 'ungenerate' signified the essence of God the Father rather than his being without origin, would any word remain to express that the Father is without origin?

question: Does treating 'ungenerate' as a name for the divine essence rather than a distinguishing property of the Father lead to Sabellianism?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Once the distinction between generated and ungenerate is removed from signifying the Persons, the Father must be held identical with the Son. The Eunomians must therefore either return to taking the term as marking a difference of personal attributes, or side with Sabellius and the 'Son-Fathers'.
sources.quote: For it is impossible that the difference of the persons should be without confusion, unless there be a distinction between generated and ungenerate.
sources.raw_question: Does treating 'ungenerate' as a name for the divine essence rather than a distinguishing property of the Father lead to Sabellianism?

question: If the title 'Father' conveys the same meaning as 'Ungenerate' (that the Father is from no cause), does it thereby cease to signify the Father's relation to the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that 'Father' in one signification means the same as Ungenerate, yet it also brings with it, as a relative bound to it, the notion of the Only-begotten. Sharing a meaning in one point does not mean two words coincide in every point. Eunomius's syllogism, that a word conveying non-generation cannot also convey having begotten a Son, is a fallacy, like arguing that bread made of flour can no longer be food.
sources.quote: so in the contemplation of the Almighty a reverent mind would not deny that by the title of Father is meant that He is without generation, as well as that in another meaning it represents His relationship to the Son.
sources.raw_question: If the title 'Father' conveys the same meaning as 'Ungenerate' (that the Father is from no cause), does it thereby cease to signify the Father's relation to the Son?

question: Should 'Ungenerate' be preferred over 'Father' as the chief name for God the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. Following Basil, Gregory says 'Ungenerate' may well be set aside because it is nowhere found in Scripture and is the foundation of Eunomius's blasphemy. 'Father' carries the same meaning of being from none. It also brings with it the notion of the Son.
sources.quote: as nowhere found in Scripture, and as forming the alphabet of Eunomius’ blasphemy, may very well be suppressed, when we have the word Father meaning the same thing
sources.raw_question: Should 'Ungenerate' be preferred over 'Father' as the chief name for God the Father?

question: Can the divine nature be captured and defined by the single term "ungenerate" (agennetos), as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Trying to include the inconceivable nature of God in the few syllables of "ungenerate" is childish labour at impossibilities, like children trying to grasp a sunbeam. God cannot be included by human reasoning under one single term, and no sacred writer taught such a definition of the divine essence.
sources.quote: they set themselves to include the inconceivable nature of God in the few syllables of the term “ungenerate,” and applaud their own folly, and imagine God to be such that human reasoning can include Him under one single term
sources.raw_question: Can the divine nature be captured and defined by the single term "ungenerate" (agennetos), as Eunomius claims?

question: Does defining God's essence as "ungenerate" lead to denying that the Only-begotten Son is truly God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, it leads there, which shows the premise is false. Because the Eunomians make "ungenerate" the whole of God's essence, their premises compel them to conclude that God the Only-begotten is not what He is called, namely God. The faulty claim to comprehend the divine essence thus issues in blasphemy against the Son.
sources.quote: And on this account they declare that they have apprehended that God the Only-begotten is not what He is called. For to this conclusion they are compelled by their premises.
sources.raw_question: Does defining God's essence as "ungenerate" lead to denying that the Only-begotten Son is truly God?

question: Does the fact that the Father is unbegotten and the Son begotten mean they are not one essence?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > The Father and the Son are Together One Wisdom, as One Essence, Although Not Together One Word.
sources.answer: No. The names Father and Son, unbegotten and begotten, express only their relative attributes, not their essence. So the distinction of the Father from the Son does not divide the essence: both together are one wisdom and one essence, in which to be is the same as to be wise.
sources.quote: they are not therefore not one essence, because the Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Father, or because the Father is un-begotten, but the Son is begotten: since by these names only their relative attributes are expressed.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Father is unbegotten and the Son begotten mean they are not one essence?

question: Is the Son equally divine with the Father, given that he is begotten?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. The perfect birth engendered perfect God, so both are equally divine and the One who is God does not differ from the Other. The birth is perfect precisely because the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily in God born of God.
sources.quote: Both so equally divine, as a perfect birth engendered perfect God. And the birth exists thus in its perfection, because the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily in God born of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son equally divine with the Father, given that he is begotten?

question: Is Eunomius consistent in calling the Son a "product of generation" while arguing that all generation involves passion?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: No. If generation is inseparably linked with passion, then whatever is free from passion is also free from generation, so Eunomius's argument would prove the Son was not generated at all. Yet he insists the Son must be called a "product of generation"; he thus contradicts himself, affirming generation in name while denying it in conception.
sources.quote: if these things, passion and generation, are considered as conjoined, He that has no share in the one would not have any participation in the other. How then does he call Him a “product” by reason of His generation, of Whom he tries to show by the arguments he now uses, that He was not generated?
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius consistent in calling the Son a "product of generation" while arguing that all generation involves passion?

question: Do negative or privative names applied to God (incorruptible, passionless, unblamable, etc.) give knowledge of what God's essence is?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. They are true of God and form a catalogue of evils from which God is separate, but they tell us what God is not, not what He is. Just as describing man as not lifeless, not winged and not four-footed says nothing false yet gives no positive definition, so such predicates show under what conditions we may conceive God, not His essence.
sources.quote: We learn from them what it is not; but what it is, the force of the words does not indicate.
sources.raw_question: Do negative or privative names applied to God (incorruptible, passionless, unblamable, etc.) give knowledge of what God's essence is?

question: Does Eunomius' claim that the Son is like the Father 'with an especial likeness', but not as Father to Father, nor as Ungenerate to Ungenerate, nor as Son to Son, establish a real likeness?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. By each of these negations Eunomius forbids us to conceive any likeness in the Son to the Father. He thus subverts the meaning of 'like' and demonstrates unlikeness under the name of likeness. His distinctions are also pointless, since no one supposes 'Father' and 'Son' to suggest two Fathers or two Sons.
sources.quote: So it is that he follows up his own statements, and conducts his demonstration of likeness by establishing unlikeness.
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius' claim that the Son is like the Father 'with an especial likeness', but not as Father to Father, nor as Ungenerate to Ungenerate, nor as Son to Son, establish a real likeness?

question: What follows if 'generation' is treated as an essence separate from the Father, from which the Son derives his being?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > He then shows the eternity of the Son's generation, and the inseparable identity of His essence with Him that begat Him, and likens the folly of Eunomius to children playing with sand.
sources.answer: Absurdities follow. Generation would take the Father's place, giving the Son two fathers: the Unbegotten, a Father in name only, and 'generation', which acts as the real Father. Alternatively, if the Father has no part in the Son's generation, the Son would have to be self-begotten. Both conclusions are absurd, so Eunomius's view collapses.
sources.quote: If, then, the Father is alien from the generation of the Son, they either invent for the Son another Father under the name of “generation,” or in their wisdom make out the Son to be self-begotten and self-generated.
sources.raw_question: What follows if 'generation' is treated as an essence separate from the Father, from which the Son derives his being?

question: Do privative divine names such as 'imperishable' or 'indestructible' signify the very essence of God rather than the absence of destruction?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. 'Imperishable' signifies that which is not receptive of destruction, and so it negates destruction. If indestructibility were not the negation of destruction, it would have to assert something incongruous with itself, because when one opposite is removed the other comes in its place. Eunomius's claim that such terms name the essence itself is folly.
sources.quote: If, that is, indestructibility is not the negation of destruction, it must be the assertion of something incongruous with itself; for it is the very nature of opposites that, when you take away the one, you admit the other to come in in its place.
sources.raw_question: Do privative divine names such as 'imperishable' or 'indestructible' signify the very essence of God rather than the absence of destruction?

question: Does the Son's birth from the Father compel believers to acknowledge two Gods?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The Son subsists through a birth from the divine nature, yet he keeps the unity in his name. The confession declares Father and Son One both in nature and in name, so the Son has the divine name precisely as a result of his birth.
sources.quote: this birth of the Son does not compel loyal believers to acknowledge two Gods, since our confession declares that Father and Son are One, both in nature and in name.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from the Father compel believers to acknowledge two Gods?

question: Does Eunomius's claim that the Son's essence is produced 'without intervention' and 'preserves its relation to its Generator, Maker, and Creator' express orthodox doctrine?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: No. By calling the Father 'Maker' and 'Creator,' Eunomius shows that his 'without intervention' means only that the Son was the first creature made directly, like a hammer forged by the smith's hands without a tool and then used to make everything else. This makes the Son a made instrument external to God's nature, which pollutes the orthodox sense of the phrase.
sources.quote: as one might say that the hammer is mediate between the smith and the nail, but its own making is “without intervention,” because, when tools had not yet been found out by the craft, the hammer came first from the craftsman’s hands
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's claim that the Son's essence is produced 'without intervention' and 'preserves its relation to its Generator, Maker, and Creator' express orthodox doctrine?

question: Does the Son's birth from the Father produce a second God of a different nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Because the birth transmits the nature of God, it is not the issuing forth of another God with a different nature. By virtue of his birth the Son abides in the mystery of the one God.
sources.quote: the birth transmitting with it, as it did, the nature of God is not the issuing forth of another God with a different nature
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from the Father produce a second God of a different nature?

question: Why should 'Ungenerate' be singled out above all other divine names to define God's nature, when the other names apply equally to Father and Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: It should not. There are many names that may reverently be applied to the Deity, and all fit both Persons equally. Eunomius ignores them because they show what Father and Son share, and fastens on 'Ungenerate' alone. Even Eunomius's party admits the Son's likeness to the Father in everything else that is conceived of God.
sources.quote: there are such a number of names which with reverence may be applied to the Deity, and all of them suitable to both Persons equally, he pays no attention to anyone of them, because these others indicate that in which Both participate
sources.raw_question: Why should 'Ungenerate' be singled out above all other divine names to define God's nature, when the other names apply equally to Father and Son?

question: Can a negative term like 'Ungenerate' define and embrace the whole substance of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: No. A negation is logically secondary to the assertion it denies, just as ignorance presupposes knowledge and passionlessness presupposes passion. 'Generation' asserts a reality and 'Ungeneracy' denies it, so the word 'Generation' is conceptually prior. A merely negative and secondary term therefore cannot define the Father's whole substance. This argument concerns only the order of the words and does not place the Son before the Father, who is truly prior in conception as the Faith teaches.
sources.quote: So Generation signifies the assertion of some reality or some idea; while Ungeneracy signifies its negation; so that there is every reason that Generation must be thought of first.
sources.raw_question: Can a negative term like 'Ungenerate' define and embrace the whole substance of God?

question: Can 'unbegotten' or 'without beginning' alone define the essence of God, as Eunomius claimed?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: No. Eternity is completed only by negating both a beginning and an end, so if God's being is confined to the absence of beginning alone, the definition is manifestly imperfect and curtailed by half, lacking the absence of end as an essential element.
sources.quote: if they confine God’s being to the one, their definition of this being will be manifestly imperfect and curtailed by half; it is thought of only by the absence of beginning
sources.raw_question: Can 'unbegotten' or 'without beginning' alone define the essence of God, as Eunomius claimed?

question: Does the Son's being personally distinct from the Father, or called 'another' than the Father, prove that he has a different essence?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Distinction of persons in an infinite substance does not prove difference of essence. That one essence can have only one person may hold for finite substances, but not for the infinite divine substance.
sources.quote: That in one essence there can be but one person, may be true where the substance is finite and limited, but has no place in that which is infinite.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being personally distinct from the Father, or called 'another' than the Father, prove that he has a different essence?

question: Is the Son of God very God, with a nature identical to the Father's, by virtue of his birth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. Hilary says he has shown from the Law that God and God are distinct and that very God is in very God. From the evangelists and apostles he has shown the perfect and true birth of the Only-begotten God. A perfect birth passes on the Begetter's own nature, so the Son is very God and of a nature identical with the Father's.
sources.quote: we then shewed from the teaching of evangelists and apostles the perfect and true birth of the Only-begotten God; and lastly, we pointed out in the due course of our argument that the Son of God is very God, and of a nature identical with the Father’s
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God very God, with a nature identical to the Father's, by virtue of his birth?

question: If being ungenerated is the essence of the Father and being generated is the essence of the Son, as Eunomius holds, must the Son possess attributes contrary to the Father's?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Proof that the Anomœan teaching tends to Manichæism.
sources.answer: Yes. Every subject is known by its own characteristic marks, and different subjects cannot share their defining marks without losing their distinction. The ungenerated God is good, holy, just, immortal and unchangeable. If generated and ungenerated are opposed essences, the generated one would have to bear the contrary marks. This revives the Manichaean opposition of good and evil. If instead the opponents grant the Son the same marks, they can conceive no difference of nature at all.
sources.quote: Differing things must be regarded as possessing differing marks; like things are to be known by like signs. If, then, these men testify to the same marks in the Only-begotten, they can conceive of no difference whatever in the subject of the marks.
sources.raw_question: If being ungenerated is the essence of the Father and being generated is the essence of the Son, as Eunomius holds, must the Son possess attributes contrary to the Father's?

question: Does God's being simple, incomposite, and without quantity or magnitude prove that God's essence is ungeneracy?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Simplicity has nothing to do with being ungenerate. The Only-begotten is generated, yet he is also simple, without parts, incomposite, and unlimited by quantity and magnitude. These attributes are therefore common to Father and Son and cannot establish that ungeneracy is the divine essence.
sources.quote: What has the notion of simplicity to do with the idea of ungenerate? For not only is the Only-begotten generated, but, without controversy, He is simple also.
sources.raw_question: Does God's being simple, incomposite, and without quantity or magnitude prove that God's essence is ungeneracy?

question: Since begetting and being begotten (or being begotten and being unbegotten) are different, does it follow that the Father and the Son are different substances?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance.
sources.answer: No. The heretics' argument assumes that everything predicated of God is predicated according to substance, but this is false. Some things, like 'Father' and 'begotten', are said of God relatively, in respect to something else, not in respect to Himself, so a difference in such predicates does not mark a difference of substance.
sources.quote: it follows, that to beget and to be begotten, or to be begotten and unbegotten, being diverse, are diverse substances; whereas it is here demonstrated that not everything predicated of God is predicated according to substance
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics arguing from their own reason (Arians/Eunomians)
sources.raw_question: Since begetting and being begotten (or being begotten and being unbegotten) are different, does it follow that the Father and the Son are different substances?

question: Can the generation of the Son be identical with the Son's essence, if Eunomius says the Son's essence 'admits of the generation'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > Then, distinguishing between essence and generation, he declares the empty and frivolous language of Eunomius to be like a rattle. He proceeds to show that the language used by the great Basil on the subject of the generation of the Only-begotten has been grievously slandered by Eunomius, and so ends the book.
sources.answer: No. On Eunomius' own wording the two cannot be the same. If generation were the essence, saying the essence 'admits of generation' would mean the essence admits of the essence, which is absurd. That which is received cannot be the same as that which receives it. So Eunomius contradicts his own constant claim that the generation is the essence.
sources.quote: He understands, then, the generation to be one thing, and the essence to be another, which “admits of generation”: for that which is taken cannot be the same with that which admits it.
sources.raw_question: Can the generation of the Son be identical with the Son's essence, if Eunomius says the Son's essence 'admits of the generation'?

question: Is being generate or ungenerate the same thing as the divine essence itself, as Eunomius held?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then shows, from the instance of Adam and Abel, and other examples, the absence of alienation of essence in the case of the “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. Eunomius himself speaks of a 'generated essence'. That phrase separates the notion of generation from the notion of essence. So neither generation nor ingeneracy constitutes the essence; they are distinguishing attributes considered within it.
sources.quote: neither absence of generation, nor generation, can any longer be supposed to constitute the essence, but the essence must be taken separately, and its being, or not being begotten, must be conceived separately
sources.raw_question: Is being generate or ungenerate the same thing as the divine essence itself, as Eunomius held?

question: Is the absence of generation (ungeneracy) the definition of God the Father's substance?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Ungeneracy indicates something that is absent from the Father, and a sign of what is absent cannot be His substance. Just as the name 'man' applies equally to Adam (ungenerated) and Abel (generated) without the nature changing, the manner of coming into existence does not define the nature.
sources.quote: this name of the nature is not altered either by the fact that Abel passed into existence by generation, or by the fact that Adam did so without generation
sources.raw_question: Is the absence of generation (ungeneracy) the definition of God the Father's substance?

question: If imperishability and ungeneracy mean the same thing, as Eunomius claims, must the imperishable Son also be ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, which shows the claim is untenable. Even the Eunomians admit the Son is imperishable. So if the two terms are equivalent, the Son would be ungenerate. Eunomius must therefore either grant that ungeneracy differs from imperishability, or blaspheme by making the Son perishable to avoid calling Him ungenerate.
sources.quote: therefore, by Eunomius’ argument, the Son also is ungenerate, if imperishability and ungeneracy are to mean the same thing.
sources.raw_question: If imperishability and ungeneracy mean the same thing, as Eunomius claims, must the imperishable Son also be ungenerate?

question: Does the begotten naturally resemble the one who begets it, and what does this imply for the Son's likeness to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His dictum that 'the manner of the likeness must follow the manner of the generation' is unintelligible.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory holds that it is probable in itself and observed in nature that the begotten resembles the begetter. Eunomius refuses to admit this because, if the offspring were allowed to be like the parent, his whole argument for the unlikeness of the Son to the Father would collapse as groundless.
sources.quote: If he allowed the offspring to be like the parent, his laboured store of arguments to prove the unlikeness of the Beings would be refuted as evanescent and groundless.
sources.raw_question: Does the begotten naturally resemble the one who begets it, and what does this imply for the Son's likeness to the Father?

question: Did God the Father beget the Son at some point when He chose, having not been Father before?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He then ingeniously shows that the generation of the Son is not according to the phrase of Eunomius, “The Father begat Him at that time when He chose, and not before:” but that the Son, being the fulness of all that is good and excellent, is always contemplated in the Father; using for this demonstration the support of Eunomius' own arguments.
sources.answer: No. The Divine Nature is always the same and is itself the fulness of all good, so it never lacks any good or later chooses something it did not always regard as good. Since the Son is the fulness of all good, He is at all times contemplated in the Father, whose nature is perfection in all good. To say the Father later chose to have a Son attributes change and addition to the unchangeable God.
sources.quote: The Divine Nature, then, is never void of good: but the Son is the fulness of all good: and accordingly He is at all times contemplated in that Father Whose Nature is perfection in all good.
sources.raw_question: Did God the Father beget the Son at some point when He chose, having not been Father before?

question: Does defining the divine essence as unbegottenness (ingeneracy), as Eunomius does, give true knowledge of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He discusses the incomprehensibility of the Divine essence, and the saying to the woman of Samaria, “Ye worship ye know not what.“
sources.answer: No. To limit the Deity by the absence of generation is like the Samaritans limiting Him by place. Such 'new Samaritans' worship what they do not know, because God's infinity exceeds every meaning and comprehension that names can supply.
sources.quote: In supposing the Deity to be limited by the absence of generation, as it were by some local limit, ‘ye worship ye know not what,’
sources.raw_question: Does defining the divine essence as unbegottenness (ingeneracy), as Eunomius does, give true knowledge of God?

question: Is Eunomius consistent in calling the Son "first-born of all creation" while also calling Him "Only-begotten, having no brother"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: No. When Eunomius wants to make the Son's essence common with creation, he calls Him "first-born of all creation." That puts all creatures in brotherhood with Him, since a first-born is first-born of those begotten like himself. Yet when he wants to separate the Spirit from the Son, he calls the Son brotherless. He thus uses the terms opportunistically and inconsistently.
sources.quote: for assuredly the first-born is not the first-born of those otherwise begotten, but of those begotten like Himself
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius consistent in calling the Son "first-born of all creation" while also calling Him "Only-begotten, having no brother"?

question: If Eunomius admits that the Son is truly begotten and properly called 'product of generation', can he consistently deny that the Son shares the essence of the Father who begat Him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Thereafter he expounds the appellation of “Son,” and of “product of generation,” and very many varieties of “sons,” of God, of men, of rams, of perdition, of light, and of day.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius himself says the generated essence and the name 'Son' make the term 'product of generation' appropriate, which means the name rests on a real natural relation. One cannot then treat it like metaphorical sonship ('child of wrath', 'son of day'), where no actual begetting occurs and only the will gives rise to the name. A real generation implies essential kinship with the begetter.
sources.quote: If, then, he confesses that such a relation of words is made appropriate by the fact that the Son is really a “product of generation,” how is it opportune to assign such a rationale of names, alike to those which are used inexactly by way of metaphor
sources.raw_question: If Eunomius admits that the Son is truly begotten and properly called 'product of generation', can he consistently deny that the Son shares the essence of the Father who begat Him?

question: If the Son is called a 'product' (gennema) of the Father, as Eunomius calls him, does this term imply a difference of essence between the Son and the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He thus shows the oneness of the Eternal Son with the Father the identity of essence and the community of nature (wherein is a natural inquiry into the production of wine), and that the terms “Son” and “product” in the naming of the Only-Begotten include a like idea of relationship.
sources.answer: No. The term 'product' is used only where there is natural community between product and source: wine is the product of the vine, not of the oak, and the 'generation of vipers' are snakes, not sheep. Wine is in substance the same moisture that is in the vine, differing only in quality. So even the adversaries' word teaches the Son's kinship in essence with him who produced him.
sources.quote: we do not call wine the “product” of the oak, nor the acorn the “product” of the vine, but we use the word only if there is some natural community between the “product” and that from which it comes.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is called a 'product' (gennema) of the Father, as Eunomius calls him, does this term imply a difference of essence between the Son and the Father?

question: Does Eunomius validly show that 'product of generation' means the same as 'product of making' and 'product of creation'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: No. He groups 'product of generation' with two terms that are equivalent, both implying something external to the maker, so that readers will assume the third is equivalent too. This is fraud, not demonstration, because a true demonstration shows what is unknown from what is acknowledged.
sources.quote: For that only is called demonstration which shows what is unknown from what is acknowledged
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius validly show that 'product of generation' means the same as 'product of making' and 'product of creation'?

question: Is there a supremacy of order of the Father over the Son, and does it imply inequality of nature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: There is a supremacy of order rightly understood: the Father as Father is supreme and the Son as Son subordinate, the Son being the second Person, not the first. But this does not imply inequality of nature or essence, and Waterland doubts it implies any inequality of honour. Because the two Persons share one undivided nature, the case differs widely from one separate man acting under another.
sources.quote: The Father, as Father, is supreme; and the Son, as Son, subordinate. We pretend not to make the Son the first, but the second Person of the Godhead.
sources.raw_question: Is there a supremacy of order of the Father over the Son, and does it imply inequality of nature?

question: Is the Son of Man a different person from the Son of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The Son of Man is not one and the Son of God another. He Who is Son of God is Himself also Son of Man. So when God is said to be glorified in the Son of Man, He is glorified in one who is also Son of God.
sources.quote: since the Son of Man is not one and the Son of God another, but He Who is Son of God is Himself also Son of Man
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of Man a different person from the Son of God?

question: Is 'ungeneracy' God's essence, the supreme attribute in which the divine life glories above all others?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. That the first cause has its subsistence from no superior cause is a true and praiseworthy conception, but to judge it superior to other aspects of the Divine nature and say God glories in it alone has no support except Eunomius' own fancy. Ungeneracy is one conception among others framed by reverent thought, not the essence itself.
sources.quote: But if one should judge it to be superior to other aspects of the Divine nature, and so should say that God, exulting and rejoicing in this alone, glories in it, as of paramount excellence, one would find support only from the Muse by whom Eunomius is inspired
sources.raw_question: Is 'ungeneracy' God's essence, the supreme attribute in which the divine life glories above all others?

question: Does the fact that the Father is Unbegotten and the Son Begotten mean that the Son's nature is inferior to or different from the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The two terms seem opposed in meaning, but the Begotten cannot be excluded from the nature of the Unbegotten, because there is no one else from whom he could derive his substance. Being born of God, he is in the form of God. He does not share the Father's prerogative of being unbegotten, yet he has received from the Unbegotten God the nature of divinity.
sources.quote: though by their very signification, ‘Unbegotten’ and ‘Begotten’ seem to be opposed, yet the Begotten cannot be excluded from the nature of the Unbegotten, for there is none other from whom He could derive His substance.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Father is Unbegotten and the Son Begotten mean that the Son's nature is inferior to or different from the Father's?

question: Do the terms 'cause' and 'caused' (or 'unbegotten' and 'begotten') signify a difference of nature between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. They indicate a difference in the manner of existence, not of nature, since no one would define 'cause' and 'nature' the same way. Saying that the Son does not exist without generation, and the Father does not exist by generation, does not divide the nature.
sources.quote: in speaking of “cause,” and “of the cause,” we do not by these words denote nature (for no one would give the same definition of “cause” and of “nature”), but we indicate the difference in manner of existence.
sources.raw_question: Do the terms 'cause' and 'caused' (or 'unbegotten' and 'begotten') signify a difference of nature between the Father and the Son?

question: Does the Father undergo change or diminution by begetting the Son, and is the Son's birth an emanation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The birth is not by way of emanation but results from an act of power. God has the power of giving birth but not of suffering change. His nature is capable of increase, not diminution, because He continues in and shares the life of the Son, to whom He gave a nature like and inseparable from His own.
sources.quote: God has the power of giving birth but not of suffering change. His nature is capable of increase, not of diminution
sources.raw_question: Does the Father undergo change or diminution by begetting the Son, and is the Son's birth an emanation?

question: Is the Son separated from the Father's nature by the event of His birth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The Son, the Living born from the Living, is not separated by His birth from the nature that begat Him. The Father gave Him in birth a nature like and inseparable from His own, and the Father continues to share the Son's life.
sources.quote: And that Son, the Living born from the Living, is not separated by the event of His birth from the nature that begat Him.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son separated from the Father's nature by the event of His birth?

question: Does teaching a subordination of order among the Father, Son and Holy Spirit imply a subordination or inferiority of nature in the Son and Spirit?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. Waterland holds that the Church's public forms teach a subordination of order only, not any inferiority of nature. Dr. Clarke wrongly treats the first as if it implied the second, and so claims the Liturgy supports his doctrine. That claim rests only on a consequence of his own making, which the forms themselves do not contain.
sources.quote: but does not find any subordination or inferiority of nature; which is his principle.
sources.raw_question: Does teaching a subordination of order among the Father, Son and Holy Spirit imply a subordination or inferiority of nature in the Son and Spirit?

question: Did the Son's birth from God diminish the Father's divinity or make the Son something other than God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. In being born God from God, the Son withdrew nothing from the Divinity of His Author nor was He born other than God. He became God not by a new beginning of Deity but by birth from the existing God, so the birth involves neither impoverishment of the Begetter nor inferiority of the Begotten.
sources.quote: She is assured that the birth of God involves neither impoverishment of the Begetter nor inferiority of the Begotten.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son's birth from God diminish the Father's divinity or make the Son something other than God?

question: Can Eunomius consistently hold that the Son is called Son by natural generation and also that, being created, he should be called a "product" or "creature" rather than a Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > This third book shows a third fall of Eunomius, as refuting himself, and sometimes saying that the Son is to be called Only-begotten in virtue of natural generation, and that Holy Scripture proves this from the first; at other times, that by reason of His being created He should not be called a Son, but a “product,” or “creature.”
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that once natural order and the testimony of Scripture together establish the natural meaning of "Son," any assertion contrary to them is plainly a fight against the truth itself. Eunomius's later reduction of the Son to a thing made and created contradicts the premises he himself laid down, so he refutes himself before any opposing argument is brought.
sources.quote: it is clear, that to assert anything contrary to these, is nothing else than manifestly to fight against the truth itself.
sources.raw_question: Can Eunomius consistently hold that the Son is called Son by natural generation and also that, being created, he should be called a "product" or "creature" rather than a Son?

question: Is the Son unalterable as the Father is, or alterable in nature like the creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: He is unalterable, like the Father. Athanasius treats the Arian claim that the Son is alterable as part of a blasphemous heresy that makes speculations against him who is. As the proper offspring of the Father's essence and very God, the Son shares the Father's nature rather than the changeable nature of creatures.
sources.quote: Wonderful this heresy, not plausible even, but making speculations against Him that is, that He be not, and everywhere putting forward blasphemy for reverent language!
sources.raw_question: Is the Son unalterable as the Father is, or alterable in nature like the creatures?

question: Does a distinction of Persons or the Son's subordination as Son imply a difference of nature or essential inequality between Father and Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. To argue so is a petitio principii, assuming that distinction of persons equals difference of nature and that subordination as Son implies essential disparity, which can never be shown. The opponent's arguments prove only that the Son is not the Father or first Person, which is true but beside the point.
sources.quote: that a distinction of persons is the same with a difference of nature; and that a subordination of the Son, as a Son, to the Father, implies an essential disparity and inequality betwixt them; which you can never make out.
sources.raw_question: Does a distinction of Persons or the Son's subordination as Son imply a difference of nature or essential inequality between Father and Son?

question: What does the title 'Father' properly signify about the relation of the Father to the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: It signifies only that the Only-begotten is not without a source but has his cause of being from the Father. It does not imply passion, need of nature's help, or extension in time. A beginning of the Son's subsistence cannot be calculated, because there is no sign of one.
sources.quote: will allow to the title ‘Father’ only the meaning that the Only-begotten is not Himself without a source, but derives from That the cause of His being
sources.raw_question: What does the title 'Father' properly signify about the relation of the Father to the Only-begotten Son?

question: What does the title 'Son' signify about the Only-begotten once its bodily connotations are removed?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: It signifies community of nature with the Father. Scripture borrows the human word 'Son' but excludes matter, passions, time, and place from it. What remains is only the close affinity and genuine relationship of the Son's manifestation from the Father.
sources.quote: But when all such material, temporal and local existence is excluded from the sense of the term “Son,” community of nature alone is left
sources.raw_question: What does the title 'Son' signify about the Only-begotten once its bodily connotations are removed?

question: If all that the Father has belongs to the Son, does it follow that the Son is ungenerate or that the Father is generated?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. The Son has all the things of the Father but is not Father, and all the things of the Son are in the Father but He is not Son. The 'all' does not erase the distinguishing relations of ungeneracy and generation.
sources.quote: For the Son has all the things of the Father; but He is not Father: and again, all the things of the Son are to be observed in the Father, but He is not a Son.
sources.raw_question: If all that the Father has belongs to the Son, does it follow that the Son is ungenerate or that the Father is generated?

question: Does divine simplicity rule out God's being first Ungenerate and later Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: Yes. God is not a compound; whatever He is is the whole of Him. If He were first Ungenerate and afterwards Father, the whole of Him would be both older and younger than the whole of Him, which is absurd; nothing in Him is older or younger.
sources.quote: we must remember God is not a compound; whatever He is is the whole of Him
sources.raw_question: Does divine simplicity rule out God's being first Ungenerate and later Father?

question: Do different names necessarily signify different essences, as Eunomius argues in order to show the Father and Son differ in nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: No. Quoting Basil, Gregory notes that Peter and Paul have different names, yet all men share one essence. Names do not indicate essence. They indicate the properties that mark the particular individual, so different names do not prove different natures.
sources.quote: For the appellations of Peter and Paul, and, generally speaking, of men, are different, while the essence of all is one
sources.raw_question: Do different names necessarily signify different essences, as Eunomius argues in order to show the Father and Son differ in nature?

question: Are the terms 'incomposite' (simple) and 'ungenerate' synonymous when applied to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. 'Incomposite' signifies the simplicity of the subject, its freedom from admixture or composition. 'Ungenerate' signifies that the subject is without origin. These meanings are not convertible and cannot be substituted for each other, even though both are predicated of one subject.
sources.quote: the terms incomposite and ungenerate are not the same thing, for the former represents the simplicity of the subject, the other its being without origin, and these expressions are not convertible in meaning, though both are predicated of one subject.
sources.raw_question: Are the terms 'incomposite' (simple) and 'ungenerate' synonymous when applied to God?

question: If Eunomius calls both the essence of the Father and the essence of the Only-begotten 'most proper,' does this imply that Father and Son share the same essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He again shows Eunomius, constrained by truth, in the character of an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, confessing as most proper and primary, not only the essence of the Father, but the essence also of the Only-begotten.
sources.answer: Yes. Eunomius himself elsewhere grants that things bearing the same appellations do not differ in nature, and no one signifies things differing in nature by identity of names. So by calling both essences 'most proper' he unwittingly bears witness that the definition of essence in Father and Son is one, much as Caiaphas foretold the Passion without knowing what he said.
sources.quote: it is surely for this reason, that the definition of essence in Father and Son is one, that he says that the one is “most proper,” and that the other also is “most proper.”
sources.raw_question: If Eunomius calls both the essence of the Father and the essence of the Only-begotten 'most proper,' does this imply that Father and Son share the same essence?

question: Is it because the Father is incorruptible that His begetting does not divide His essence, implying that corruptible begetters do divide their essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: No. If incorruptibility alone prevented division in begetting, every corruptible begetter would divide his essence and beget himself. But Adam and Abraham, though corruptible, begot sons without their essence being split into fractions among their descendants; otherwise Adam's essence would have been used up long before Abraham. So the reasoning is absurd: generation as such does not divide nature.
sources.quote: if Adam was corruptible, to whom the word was spoken, “Dust thou art and unto dust shalt thou return,” then, according to Eunomius’ reasoning, he certainly divided his essence, being cut up among those who were begotten of him
sources.raw_question: Is it because the Father is incorruptible that His begetting does not divide His essence, implying that corruptible begetters do divide their essence?

question: Is the Son called absolutely the one true God in Scripture, or is that title reserved for the Father alone?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: The Son is so called. Irenaeus observes that Scripture never calls anyone absolutely God or Lord besides the only true God, yet immediately notes that both Father and Son are so called by the same Scriptures; hence he regarded the Son as the only true God as well as the Father.
sources.quote: He observes, that the Holy Scriptures never call any person absolutely God or Lord, besides the only true God ; and yet presently after takes notice, that both Father and Son are by the same Scriptures absolutely so called.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son called absolutely the one true God in Scripture, or is that title reserved for the Father alone?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's share in the kingdom show that he is of one nature, lordship and power with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XX. The river flowing from the Throne of God is a figure of the Holy Spirit, but by the waters spoken of by David the powers of heaven are intended. The kingdom of God is the work of the Spirit; and it is no matter for wonder if He reigns in this together with the Son, since St. Paul promises that we too shall reign with the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Because the Spirit shares the kingdom with the Father and the Son, and does so by nature rather than by grace, he is of one nature with them, of one Lordship, and of one power.
sources.quote: The Holy Spirit, therefore, shares in the kingdom with the Father and the Son, and He is of one nature with Them, of one Lordship, and also of one power.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's share in the kingdom show that he is of one nature, lordship and power with the Father and the Son?

question: Does the distinction between the Person of the Father and the Person of the Son in texts about the one God prove that the Son is not the one God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. The texts do distinguish the Persons, since both are named separately, and that tells against the Sabellians, who make one Person of two. It shows nothing further unless one can prove that there is no good reason to call the Father the only God other than excluding the Son. That negative proposition has not been proved.
sources.quote: unless you can prove this negative proposition, that no sufficient reason can be assigned for styling the Father the only God, without supposing that the Son is excluded.
sources.raw_question: Does the distinction between the Person of the Father and the Person of the Son in texts about the one God prove that the Son is not the one God?

question: Does Christ's statement 'I and the Father are One' (John 10:30) mean that the Son is the Father himself, as Sabellius held?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No. When the Jews took 'One' in a Sabellian sense, Christ explained it by saying 'I am the Son of God' and 'the Father is in Me and I in the Father.' The unity lies not in one being the other but in the Son's being in the Father and the Father in the Son. Thus Sabellius is overthrown by 'I am the Son,' not 'the Father.'
sources.quote: the union and the inseparability lay, not in This being That, with which It was One, but in His being in the Father and the Father in the Son
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement 'I and the Father are One' (John 10:30) mean that the Son is the Father himself, as Sabellius held?

question: Does Christ's saying "I and my Father are one" prove that he is truly God and not a mere man?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: Yes. Novatian argues that no mere man could have spoken these words. Christ alone spoke them from a consciousness of his divinity, and so he is rightly called God. Origen likewise holds that because Father and Son are one, Christians worship one God in worshipping both the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: you may please to observe, how absurd he thinks it would have been for any mere man to
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "I and my Father are one" prove that he is truly God and not a mere man?

question: Is Sabellius right that the Son is merely an extension of the Father, one Person who is both Father and Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. Hilary rejects this view. By making one and the same Person Son to Himself and also Father, Sabellius turns the faith into a matter of words rather than reality, and so denies the real distinction that the Names convey.
sources.quote: Sabellius, for instance, makes the Son an extension of the Father, and the faith in this regard a matter of words rather than of reality, for he makes one and the same Person, Son to Himself and also Father.
sources.raw_question: Is Sabellius right that the Son is merely an extension of the Father, one Person who is both Father and Son?

question: What does Christ's saying 'I and the Father are One', together with 'the Father is in Me, and I in the Father', teach about the Son's nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: It teaches that the Son shares one indissoluble Divine nature with the Father, and that He has it by birth from God. Christ grounds the oneness in His being Son of God, and the mutual indwelling guards against imagining that birth brings a difference of nature. Thus His Divinity is His by nature and by right, not something alien raised to Godhead.
sources.quote: to guard them, at the same time, from imagining that the birth involves a difference of nature, He crowns His argument with the words, Believe the works, that the Father is in Me, and I in the Father.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's saying 'I and the Father are One', together with 'the Father is in Me, and I in the Father', teach about the Son's nature?

question: Does Christ's saying 'I and the Father are one' mean that the Father and Son are one being divided into two parts?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Unless Father and Son are two in name only, or as parts and so each imperfect, or two gods, they are coessential, one in Godhead, and the Son from the Father.
sources.answer: No. If the one were divided into two, what is divided would have to be a body, and neither part would be perfect, since each would be a part and not a whole. So the unity of Father and Son cannot be that of parts of a divided whole.
sources.quote: Now if the one is divided into two, that which is divided must need be a body, and neither part perfect, for each is a part and not a whole.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'I and the Father are one' mean that the Father and Son are one being divided into two parts?

question: Does John 10:30, "I and my Father are one," express only a unity of will and consent between Father and Son, or also a unity of substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: It expresses both. There is a unity of concord and harmonious love, but it is founded upon unity of substance, and the text expresses both the unity itself and its foundation. The Fathers who stressed unity of consent against the Sabellians presupposed equality of nature, as Paul and Apollos could be one in will only because both were truly men.
sources.quote: there is an unity bof concord, and harmonious love, founded upon unity of substance: and the words, “1 and my Father are one,” express both the unity itself, and the foundation of it.
sources.raw_question: Does John 10:30, "I and my Father are one," express only a unity of will and consent between Father and Son, or also a unity of substance?

question: Does the unity expressed in 'I and the Father are One' and 'I in the Father and the Father in Me' collapse the Father and Son into one person, as Sabellius taught?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: No. The texts show the identity of Godhead and unity of essence, but not one thing twice named. They are two, because the Father is Father and not also Son, and the Son is Son and not also Father. Yet the nature is one, since the offspring is the image of its parent.
sources.quote: But They are two, because the Father is Father and is not also Son, and the Son is Son and not also Father; but the nature is one;
sources.raw_question: Does the unity expressed in 'I and the Father are One' and 'I in the Father and the Father in Me' collapse the Father and Son into one person, as Sabellius taught?

question: Does confessing the Godhead of the Holy Spirit introduce three Gods?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XII. From the fact that St. Paul has shown that the light of the Godhead which the three apostles worshipped in Christ is in the Trinity, it is made clear that the Spirit also is to be worshipped. It is shown from the words themselves that the Spirit is intended by the apostles. The Godhead of the same Spirit is proved from the fact that He has a temple wherein He dwells not as a priest, but as God: and is worshipped with the Father and the Son; whence is understood the oneness of nature in Them.
sources.answer: No. Where the Godhead is understood as one, one God is spoken of; calling the Son God does not make two Gods, so neither does calling the Spirit God make three. Objectors who think 'God' names one person rather than one nature would have to either admit two Gods or deny the Son is God.
sources.quote: lest you should make three Gods. God forbid; for where the Godhead is understood as one, one God is spoken of. For neither when we call the Son God do we say there are two Gods.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the Godhead of the Holy Spirit introduce three Gods?

question: In what sense are the Father and the Son 'one' according to John 10:30, given that Sabellius was condemned?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: They are one not as one thing divided into two parts, nor as one thing twice named (as Sabellius held), but as two Persons with one nature. The Father is Father and not also Son, and the Son is Son and not also Father, yet the nature is one because the offspring is the image of its parent and all that is the Father's is the Son's.
sources.quote: But They are two, because the Father is Father and is not also Son, and the Son is Son and not also Father; but the nature is one; (for the offspring is not unlike its parent, for it is his image)
sources.raw_question: In what sense are the Father and the Son 'one' according to John 10:30, given that Sabellius was condemned?

question: How did the Sabellian view of Father and Son differ from the Church's view that they are one in essence?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: The Sabellians not only made Father and Son one in essence, as the Church also did. They went further and made them one subject or hypostasis, so that the distinction between them was merely nominal, not real. The Church held one substance but a real distinction of Persons.
sources.quote:
The Sabellians did

not only make Father and Son one

im essence, (as the Church did also,)
sources.raw_question: How did the Sabellian view of Father and Son differ from the Church's view that they are one in essence?

question: Do texts such as 'I and the Father are One' and 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father' teach only an agreement of will between Father and Son, rather than a unity of nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Where unity of nature is proclaimed, agreement of will naturally follows. But the heretics put forward mere harmony of will in order to set aside the unity of nature that comes from the birth. Paul cuts this off: the bodily indwelling of the incorporeal God in Christ teaches the strict unity of their nature.
sources.quote: where the unity of nature is proclaimed the agreement of will cannot be denied; but in order to set aside that unity which follows from the birth, they profess merely a relationship of mutual harmony
sources.raw_question: Do texts such as 'I and the Father are One' and 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father' teach only an agreement of will between Father and Son, rather than a unity of nature?

question: What do Christ's sayings "I and the Father are one," "He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father," and "the Father is in Me, and I in the Father" show about the Son's relation to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: They show His birth, His unity of nature with the Father, and His indivisibility from Him. The name Father signifies His birth, and the Father is known in knowing the Son. Those who see Him see the Father, which shows one nature. Mutual indwelling shows He is indivisible from the Father.
sources.quote: He avows the unity of nature, when those who see Him see the Father. He bears witness that He is indivisible from the Father, when He dwells in the Father Who dwells in Him.
sources.raw_question: What do Christ's sayings "I and the Father are one," "He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father," and "the Father is in Me, and I in the Father" show about the Son's relation to the Father?

question: How do the individual words of 'I and the Father are One' show both the distinction and the unity of Father and Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: 'I' and 'Father' name two substantive Beings, so the Persons are real. 'One' declares that their nature is essentially the same in both. 'Are' forbids us to confound them together. Taken together, 'are one' teaches that the unity of the Two results from a birth.
sources.quote: For I and Father are the names of substantive Beings; One is a declaration of Their nature, namely, that it is essentially the same in Both; are forbids us to confound Them together
sources.raw_question: How do the individual words of 'I and the Father are One' show both the distinction and the unity of Father and Son?

question: Does confessing the unity of the Godhead from John 10:30 ('I and the Father are one') mean that God is a solitary Person who called Himself 'Father' as divine and 'I' as man?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Hilary rejects the charge that his teaching makes the Unbegotten God descend into the Virgin and speak of Himself as two persons, human and divine. The Father and Son are one not by giving a double name to one Person but by a true begetting and being begotten. God is not solitary because He is one.
sources.quote: that the Two are One, not by the giving of a double name to one Person, but by a true begetting and being begotten
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the unity of the Godhead from John 10:30 ('I and the Father are one') mean that God is a solitary Person who called Himself 'Father' as divine and 'I' as man?

question: If Scripture says there is one Lord, does confessing Christ as Lord produce two Lords?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > In Fine, Notwithstanding the Said Heretics Have Gathered the Origin of Their Error from Consideration of What is Written: Although We Call Christ God, and the Father God, Still Scripture Does Not Set Forth Two Gods, Any More Than Two Lords or Two Teachers.
sources.answer: No. Even the objectors do not doubt that Christ is Lord, yet they do not think this destroys the scriptural truth that there is one Lord. So the confession of Christ's lordship stands alongside the oneness of the Lord. This shows their two-Gods inference is faulty.
sources.quote: they do not doubt absolutely that He is Lord; therefore, if their reasoning be true, here are already two Lords. How, then, is it true according to the Scriptures, there is one Lord?
sources.raw_question: If Scripture says there is one Lord, does confessing Christ as Lord produce two Lords?

question: Does Christ's saying "He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father" prove that the Father and Son are one indistinguishable Person, as Sabellius held?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. That the Father is seen in the Son proves the Son's divinity, not the denial of His birth. The birth is precisely the mode in which the unity of nature of Father and Son is revealed to us, so the text shows sameness of nature, not identity of Person.
sources.quote: For the fact that the Father is seen in the Son is a proof of the Son’s Divinity, not a disproof of His birth.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father" prove that the Father and Son are one indistinguishable Person, as Sabellius held?

question: Does "I and the Father are One" teach that the Father and Son are a single solitary Person or Power?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The conjunction "and" shows more than one Person is meant, and the plural "are" requires a plurality of subjects. "One" signifies that the two Persons share one nature, which is compatible with a birth. Thus "One" excludes difference of nature while "are" excludes identity of Person.
sources.quote: The use of the conjunction and shews clearly that more than one Person is signified; and are requires a plurality of subject. Moreover, the One is not incompatible with a birth.
sources.raw_question: Does "I and the Father are One" teach that the Father and Son are a single solitary Person or Power?

question: Are the Father and the Son 'one' (John 10:30) merely because the Son agrees with the Father in will, judgment and teaching?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. If agreement of will and doctrine made the Son one with the Father, then angels, Powers, Thrones, and even sun, moon and stars, which all obey God's will, would equally be sons, one with the Father, and his Image and Word. But Scripture calls the Son alone Only-begotten, Word, Wisdom and Image. So the oneness and likeness must be referred to the Son's very essence.
sources.quote: it follows forthwith that the Angels too, and the other beings above us, Powers and Authorities, and Thrones and Dominions, and what we see, Sun and Moon, and the Stars, should be sons also, as the Son
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and the Son 'one' (John 10:30) merely because the Son agrees with the Father in will, judgment and teaching?

question: Does Christ's comparison of the disciples' unity to his unity with the Father ("that they may be one, as we are one") show that the Father and Son are one only in will, like believers?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. "As" (kathōs) often signifies a general similitude rather than exact equality. Hippolytus admits a parallel in concord but shows that the union of God and Christ is infinitely more perfect, because the Son is the living, substantial mind of the Father. God and Christ are one by an infinitely higher union resting on an infinitely higher foundation.
sources.quote: You need not be told, that καθὼς often signifies, not an exact equality, but a general similitude*: the remark is just; and, as it is at other times urged against us, so let me here claim the benefit of it.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's comparison of the disciples' unity to his unity with the Father ("that they may be one, as we are one") show that the Father and Son are one only in will, like believers?

question: Does "I and my Father are one" prove that the Father and the Son are the same person, as Noetus and the Sabellians claimed?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. Christ said "we are one," not "I am one," so that we neither estrange the Son from the Father nor merge them into a Son-Father. The Fathers point to his prayer that the disciples be one: Peter and John could not be one by being confounded into a single person, so the unity is not a confusion of persons.
sources.quote: Οὐκ εἶπε ἐγὼ καὶ 6 πατὴρ ἕν εἶμι, GAN’ ἐγὼ καὶ 6 πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν, ἵνα μήτε ἀπαλλοτριώσωμεν, μήτε συναλοιφὴν υἱοπατορίας ἐργασώμεθα.
sources.raw_question: Does "I and my Father are one" prove that the Father and the Son are the same person, as Noetus and the Sabellians claimed?

question: Is confessing that God is One inconsistent with confessing the Son as God from God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
