sources.answer: No. Hilary holds that one can set forth God from God and at the same time confess one true God. This neither ascribes singleness of Person to the one God nor adds a second Deity: we confess neither an isolated God nor two Gods.
sources.quote: We have set forth God from God, and at the same time confessed One true God; shewing that this presentation of the faith neither falls short of the truth by ascribing singleness of Person to the One true God, nor adds to the faith by asserting the existence of a second Deity.
sources.raw_question: Is confessing that God is One inconsistent with confessing the Son as God from God?

question: Does Christ's oneness with the Father mean that the Son is the Father himself?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: No. Christ is God, but God in such a way that he is the Son, not the Father. He said he was sent, that he did good works from the Father, and he called himself the Son of God, so that he would not be understood to be the Father.
sources.quote: He is God, therefore, but God in such a manner as to be the Son, not the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's oneness with the Father mean that the Son is the Father himself?

question: Does confessing that the Son is eternal with the Father mean believing in two Eternals?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: No. The Son is not eternal on his own as a second independent eternal being. He is the Father's true Son by nature, co-existing in the Father's own eternity. Being the Father's Image and Radiance, inseparable from him, he has the Father's eternity, and there never was a time when he was not.
sources.quote: ye will no longer reproach us with holding two Eternals, but ye will yourselves acknowledge that the Lord is God’s true Son by nature, and not as merely eternal, but revealed as co-existing in the Father’s eternity.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing that the Son is eternal with the Father mean believing in two Eternals?

question: How does John 10:30, 'I and My Father are one,' refute both Sabellius and Arius?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: By naming a Father, the Son shows that he is not himself the first cause and is distinct from the Father. This leaves Sabellius no ground for confusing the Persons. By asserting oneness, he declares their common nature, so Arius cannot claim the two natures are foreign to each other. The verse thus guards the faith against error on either side.
sources.quote: Sabellius has no ground for his confusion of the individuality of each Person, when the Only-begotten has so distinctly marked Himself off from the Father in those words, “I and My Father;” and Arius finds no confirmation
sources.raw_question: How does John 10:30, 'I and My Father are one,' refute both Sabellius and Arius?

question: If the Spirit's hearing proves His weakness, would the same argument also make the Son inferior?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: Yes, the argument would equally injure the Son, which shows it is invalid. The Son also says "As I hear I judge" and "The Son can do nothing but what He seeth the Father doing." Yet the Son is one with the Father by natural substance, and what is one in substance cannot be separated. So the Son does only what He hears from the Father because His operation is inseparable from the Father's, not because He is weak.
sources.quote: But if you contend that this is an argument for the weakness of the Holy Spirit, and for a kind of likeness to the lowliness of the body, you will also make it an argument to the injury of the Son
sources.raw_question: If the Spirit's hearing proves His weakness, would the same argument also make the Son inferior?

question: If the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are each called a person and so are called three persons, why are they not called three Gods, since each is also called God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: Because Scripture forbids saying three Gods, while it does not forbid saying three persons. Scripture names neither three persons nor one person, so 'three persons' was allowed only because speaking and reasoning required it and Scripture does not contradict it. To say three Gods would contradict 'Hear, O Israel; the Lord thy God is one God.'
sources.quote: it was lawful through the mere necessity of speaking and reasoning to say three persons, not because Scripture says it, but because Scripture does not contradict it: whereas, if we were to say three Gods, Scripture would contradict it
sources.raw_question: If the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are each called a person and so are called three persons, why are they not called three Gods, since each is also called God?

question: If the Son (divine understanding) is in the Holy Spirit, does the Son proceed from the Spirit?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The Son is in the Spirit, but not as proceeding from Him, because the understanding must be considered prior in the order of nature to the will or love, both in creatures and in the Creator. The understanding is in the Spirit as flowing out in Him, not as originating from Him.
sources.quote: the Son is in the Holy Spirit tho it does not proceed from Him by reason ( of the fact) that the understanding must be considered as prior in the order of nature to the will or love or act
sources.raw_question: If the Son (divine understanding) is in the Holy Spirit, does the Son proceed from the Spirit?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be separated from the Father and the Son in Christian worship?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Outside the Spirit one cannot worship at all, and once in Him one cannot sever Him from God, just as light cannot be divorced from the objects it makes visible. The Image of the invisible God can be seen only by the Spirit's enlightenment. The cause of vision is necessarily seen together with what is seen.
sources.quote: If you remain outside the Spirit you will not be able even to worship at all; and on your becoming in Him you will in no wise be able to dissever Him from God;—any more than you will divorce light from visible objects.
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be separated from the Father and the Son in Christian worship?

question: Is there more than one sense in which the Holy Spirit is said to 'proceed' from the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Yes, there are two. One procession is natural or hypostatic: the Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son and so receives his substance and personality. The other is economical or dispensatory: his going forth to carry on the work of grace.
sources.quote: in which respect he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeding from both eternally, so receiving his substance and personality
sources.raw_question: Is there more than one sense in which the Holy Spirit is said to 'proceed' from the Father?

question: Are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit distinguished from one another by their mutual relations?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture reveals the Father as Father of the Son, the Son as Son of the Father, and the Spirit as Spirit of both, and it is in respect of these mutual relations that they are distinct. In the fuller explication, these mutual respects are their peculiar properties giving the manner of their subsistence.
sources.quote: and that, in respect of this their mutual relation, they are distinct from each other.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit distinguished from one another by their mutual relations?

question: Is the Holy Spirit separated from the Father and the Son when He proceeds from them?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XI. The Spirit is sent to all, and passes not from place to place, for He is not limited either by time or space. He goes forth from the Son, as the Son from the Father, in Whom He ever abides: and also comes to us when we receive. He comes also after the same manner as the Father Himself, from Whom He can by no means be separated.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son is not separated from either, for He is the Spirit of the Father's mouth. This inseparability proves both His eternity and the unity of the Godhead.
sources.quote: The Holy Spirit also, when He proceeds from the Father and the Son, is not separated from the Father nor separated from the Son. For how could He be separated from the Father Who is the Spirit of His mouth?
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit separated from the Father and the Son when He proceeds from them?

question: Does the Holy Spirit come to believers separately from the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XI. The Spirit is sent to all, and passes not from place to place, for He is not limited either by time or space. He goes forth from the Son, as the Son from the Father, in Whom He ever abides: and also comes to us when we receive. He comes also after the same manner as the Father Himself, from Whom He can by no means be separated.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit comes as the Father comes, for where the Father is there is the Son, and where the Son is there is the Spirit. Christ says the Father and He will come and make their abode with the believer, and the Father does not come bodily; so in the Spirit's coming is the full presence of Father and Son.
sources.quote: The Spirit, then, so comes as does the Father, for where the Father is there is also the Son, and where the Son is there is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit, therefore, is not to be supposed to come separately.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit come to believers separately from the Father and the Son?

question: Is the Holy Spirit the Spirit of both the Father and the Son, and co-equal and co-eternal with both?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine calls the Holy Spirit the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. By his own substance the Spirit is equal and co-eternal with both, just as the Word is equal and eternal with the Father.
sources.quote: nor the Spirit of the Father and of the Son by His own substance, in which He Himself also is equal and co-eternal with both
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit the Spirit of both the Father and the Son, and co-equal and co-eternal with both?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be separated from the Father and the Son, given his role in sealing and sanctifying believers?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VI. Although we are baptized with water and the Spirit, the latter is much superior to the former, and is not therefore to be separated from the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. Through the Spirit we are sealed by God, attain to the image and likeness of God, and become partakers of the divine nature, so no one can dare to separate him from the Father and the Son. One who imparts the divine image and nature must share in the divine nature.
sources.quote: Who, then, can dare to say that the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, since through Him we attain to the image and likeness of God, and through Him, as the Apostle Peter says, are partakers of the divine nature?
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be separated from the Father and the Son, given his role in sealing and sanctifying believers?

question: Does Christ's sending of the Holy Spirit imply that the Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son's sending of the Holy Ghost argues the Spirit's personal procession from the Son too. Because this was a deep mystery, Christ taught it gradually. First he said he would pray the Father to give the Comforter (John 14:16). Then he said the Father would send him in Christ's name (John 14:26). Next, 'I will send him from the Father' (John 15:26). Finally, absolutely, 'I will send him' (John 16:7).
sources.quote: The business of sending the Holy Ghost by Christ — which argues his personal procession also from him, the Son — was a deep mystery, which at once they could not bear; and therefore he thus instructs them in it by degrees.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's sending of the Holy Spirit imply that the Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father?

question: Does the Son have from Himself, or from the Father, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from Him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What It is that Suffices Here to Solve the Question Why the Spirit is Not Said to Be Begotten, and Why the Father Alone is Unbegotten. What They Ought to Do Who Do Not Understand These Things.
sources.answer: From the Father. The Son, who is God of God, receives from the Father both His divine nature and the fact that the Spirit proceeds from Him. So the Spirit has from the Father Himself that He proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father.
sources.quote: From Him, certainly, from whom the Son had his Divine nature, for He is God of God, He has also, that from Him too proceeds the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Does the Son have from Himself, or from the Father, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from Him?

question: Are the Father and the Son also called 'Spirit' in Scripture?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IX. The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ, and the oil of gladness; and why Christ Himself is not the ointment, since He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It is not strange that the Spirit should be called Ointment, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. And there is no confusion between them, since Christ alone suffered death, Whose saving cross is then spoken of.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord says 'God is Spirit' of the Father, and Jeremiah says 'The Spirit before our face, Christ the Lord.' Whatever is not a created body is spirit, so both Father and Son are Spirit; hence it is no wonder the Spirit is given a further name like ointment.
sources.quote: So, then, both the Father is Spirit and Christ is Spirit, for that which is not a created body is spirit
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and the Son also called 'Spirit' in Scripture?

question: Are the Son and the Holy Spirit omnipresent, as the Father is?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord fills heaven and earth. Christ promises "Lo, I am with you alway." The Psalmist asks "Whither shall I go from thy Spirit?" These show the one omnipresent God in whom we live and move.
sources.quote: Lo, I am with you alway. – Matt. 28:20. 3. Whither shall I go from thy Spirit? – Psa. 139:7.
sources.raw_question: Are the Son and the Holy Spirit omnipresent, as the Father is?

question: Why is the Holy Spirit not called a Son, given that he also comes forth from the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Father and the Son the Only Beginning (Principium) of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Because the Spirit came forth not as born but as given. He was neither born like the Only-begotten nor made so as to be born into adoption by grace like us. Therefore the name 'Son' does not apply to him.
sources.quote: For the Spirit came forth, not as born, but as given; and so He is not called a son, because He was neither born, as the Only-begotten, nor made
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit not called a Son, given that he also comes forth from the Father?

question: Why is the Holy Spirit called both the Spirit of God and 'our' Spirit, while the Son is called the Son of the Father only and not our Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Father and the Son the Only Beginning (Principium) of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: What is born is referred only to the one who begets it, so the Son is the Son of the Father alone. What is given is referred both to the giver and to the receivers. So the Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and Son who give him, and also ours who receive him, just as 'the salvation of the Lord' is also our salvation.
sources.quote: but that which is given is referred both to Him who gave, and to those to whom He gave; and so the Holy Spirit is not only the Spirit of the Father and of the Son who gave Him, but He is also called ours
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit called both the Spirit of God and 'our' Spirit, while the Son is called the Son of the Father only and not our Son?

question: How can the Holy Spirit be both the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of the Son, given that He proceeds from the Father but receives from the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: The Spirit of Truth proceeds from the Father, and He is sent by the Son and receives from the Son. All things that the Father has belong to the Son. So the One who receives from the Son is the Spirit of God and at the same time the Spirit of Christ, of the nature of both.
sources.quote: But all things that the Father hath are the Son’s, and for this cause He Who receives from Him is the Spirit of God but at the same time the Spirit of Christ.
sources.raw_question: How can the Holy Spirit be both the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of the Son, given that He proceeds from the Father but receives from the Son?

question: Must every name applied to the divine Nature be applied equally to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory proceeds to discuss the relative force of the unnameable name of the Holy Trinity and the mutual relation of the Persons, and moreover the unknowable character of the essence, and the condescension on His part towards us, His generation of the Virgin, and His second coming, the resurrection from the dead and future retribution.
sources.answer: Yes. The single 'name' in the baptismal formula signifies one Nature common to the three. Whatever term our understanding devises to indicate the undefiled Nature of Godhead must therefore be predicated alike of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: that name should be applied alike to Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, whether it be “the Good” or “the Incorruptible,”
sources.raw_question: Must every name applied to the divine Nature be applied equally to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the indwelling of the Father, Son, and Spirit together in believers show that they share one nature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XII. From the fact that St. Paul has shown that the light of the Godhead which the three apostles worshipped in Christ is in the Trinity, it is made clear that the Spirit also is to be worshipped. It is shown from the words themselves that the Spirit is intended by the apostles. The Godhead of the same Spirit is proved from the fact that He has a temple wherein He dwells not as a priest, but as God: and is worshipped with the Father and the Son; whence is understood the oneness of nature in Them.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father abides in us through the Spirit He has given, and different natures cannot abide together in this way; so Father, Son, and Spirit abide in one subject through the oneness of the same nature. Hence we are not many temples but one temple of one Power.
sources.quote: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit abide in one and the same [subject] through the oneness of the same nature.
sources.raw_question: Does the indwelling of the Father, Son, and Spirit together in believers show that they share one nature?

question: Why is the Father said to send the Holy Spirit, and why does Christ send the Spirit "from the Father"?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Life-giving power belongs eminently to the Father by way of original authority. So when the quickening Spirit is sent, the Father is said to send him (John 14:26), or Christ sends him from the Father (John 15:26). Christ is also said to send the Spirit himself, but on another account (John 16:7).
sources.quote: Life-giving power is, in respect of original authority, invested in the Father by the way of eminency; and therefore, in sending of the quickening Spirit, Christ is said to do it from the Father, or the Father himself to do it.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Father said to send the Holy Spirit, and why does Christ send the Spirit "from the Father"?

question: If Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together are one God, does the Father become only a third part of God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. The objection wrongly imagines God in terms of extension and sensible images. As Augustine teaches, there is no division of parts in the unity of the Godhead. One Person is not a part of the Trinity, two are not greater than one, and all three are not greater than each singly, because divine greatness is spiritual, not bodily.
sources.quote: you seem to consider every thing under the notion of extension, and sensible images. A reverential silence may well become us in so awful a subject, in which imagination has nothing to do
sources.raw_question: If Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together are one God, does the Father become only a third part of God?

question: Does the fact that the Son was sent by the Father imply that the Son is not equal to the Father in nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What Has Been Treated of in This Book. How We Have Reached by Steps to a Certain Trinity, Which is Found in Practical Knowledge and True Faith.
sources.answer: No. Augustine recalls that in the fourth book he explained why and how Christ was sent by the Father in the fullness of time. He did so specifically to refute those who claim that the one who sends and the one who is sent cannot be equal in nature. The sending concerns the work of redemption in time, not an inequality of nature.
sources.quote: that I might show why and how Christ was sent in the fullness of time by the Father, on account of those who say that He who sent and He who was sent cannot be equal in nature
sources.raised_by_detail: those who say that He who sent and He who was sent cannot be equal in nature
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Son was sent by the Father imply that the Son is not equal to the Father in nature?

question: Does the Son's acknowledgment of receiving everything from the Father imply inferiority of His divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Christ carefully pairs acknowledgment of His birth with claims to unity of nature: He speaks not from Himself yet whoever sees Him sees the Father; the Father gave to Him yet He and the Father are one; judgment is given Him yet He claims equal honour. His receiving confesses His origin, while the unity is a property of the nature derived from that origin.
sources.quote: To say that the Father gave, is a confession that He received His origin: but the unity of Himself with the Father is a property of His nature derived from that origin.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's acknowledgment of receiving everything from the Father imply inferiority of His divine nature?

question: Does calling the Holy Spirit the instrument ('sword') of the Word imply that the Spirit is inferior to the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VII. The Son Himself does not judge or punish without the Spirit, so that the same Spirit is called the Sword of the Word. But inasmuch as the Word is in turn called the Sword of the Spirit, the highest unity of power is thereby recognized in each.
sources.answer: No. Scripture also calls the Word the 'sword of the Spirit', so each is said to be the sword of the other. This mutual description shows there is no inequality between them. Rather, there is a unity of nature and oneness of power in both.
sources.quote: Since, then, the Sword of the Word is the Holy Spirit, and the Sword of the Holy Spirit is the Word of God, there is certainly in Them oneness of power.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Holy Spirit the instrument ('sword') of the Word imply that the Spirit is inferior to the Son?

question: If the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one substance, how are they distinct from one another?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > What the Doctrine of the Catholic Faith is Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: They are distinguished by their relations of origin. The Father has begotten the Son, so the Father is not the Son. The Son is begotten by the Father, so the Son is not the Father. The Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son but the Spirit of both, and is co-equal with them.
sources.quote: although the Father hath begotten the Son, and so He who is the Father is not the Son; and the Son is begotten by the Father, and so He who is the Son is not the Father
sources.raw_question: If the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one substance, how are they distinct from one another?

question: Is the Holy Spirit one with the Father and the Son because He knows all the things of God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIX. Having proved above that the Spirit abides and speaks in the prophets, St. Ambrose infers that He knows all things which are of God, and therefore is One with the Father and the Son. This same point he establishes again from the fact that He possesses all that God possesses, namely, Godhead, knowledge of the heart, truth, a Name above every name, and power to raise the dead, as is proved from Ezekiel, and in this He is equal to the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as the Father and Son are One because the Son has all that the Father has, so the Spirit is one with them because He knows all the things of God. Whoever has all things that God has cannot fail to be God.
sources.quote: so too the Spirit is one with the Father and the Son, because He too knows all the things of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit one with the Father and the Son because He knows all the things of God?

question: Does the Spirit's being sent by both the Father and the Son prove that he eternally proceeds from both?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit's outward relation to the Father and the Son in their working (ad extra) proves his inward relation to them in personal procession (ad intra).
sources.quote: this relation ad extra (as they call it) of the Spirit unto the Father and the Son, in respect of operation, proves his relation ad intra, in respect of personal procession
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit's being sent by both the Father and the Son prove that he eternally proceeds from both?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's taking on the work of Comforter imply that he is inferior to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: No. It is a voluntary condescension in the order of working, like the Son's taking on the work of Redeemer. It is done by his own will, not forced on a subordinate being.
sources.quote: The condescension of the Holy Ghost in this order of working, this dispensation, to proceed from the Father and the Son, as to this work; to take upon him this work of a Comforter, as the Son did the work of a Redeemer
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's taking on the work of Comforter imply that he is inferior to the Father and the Son?

question: Is it safe to separate the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in our faith and doctrine?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the baptism in the name of the Father alone is sufficient.
sources.answer: No. In baptism, separating the Spirit from the Father and the Son endangers the one baptizing and does nothing for the one baptized. It follows that tearing the Spirit away from the Father and the Son in belief cannot be safe either.
sources.quote: If then in baptism the separation of the Spirit from the Father and the Son is perilous to the baptizer, and of no advantage to the baptized, how can the rending asunder of the Spirit from Father and from Son be safe for us?
sources.raw_question: Is it safe to separate the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in our faith and doctrine?

question: If the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each holy, are there three Holies?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: No. The Father, Son and Spirit are each holy, but there is one Holy God and one Lord. True holiness belonging to the Divine Nature is one, just as the true Godhead is one.
sources.quote: the Father is holy, the Son is holy, and the Spirit is holy, but they are not three Holies; for there is one Holy God, one Lord.
sources.raw_question: If the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each holy, are there three Holies?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be separated from the Father and the Son, given that no one can confess Jesus as Lord except in the Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XI. The Spirit is sent to all, and passes not from place to place, for He is not limited either by time or space. He goes forth from the Son, as the Son from the Father, in Whom He ever abides: and also comes to us when we receive. He comes also after the same manner as the Father Himself, from Whom He can by no means be separated.
sources.answer: No. Since no one can call Jesus Lord except in the Holy Spirit, we cannot even name or proclaim the Son without the Spirit. Even the angels' proclamation of Jesus as Lord shows the Spirit operating in them.
sources.quote: But who can separate the Spirit from the Father and the Son, since we cannot even name the Father and the Son without the Spirit?
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be separated from the Father and the Son, given that no one can confess Jesus as Lord except in the Spirit?

question: Can the Father, Son and Holy Spirit be called three Fathers, three Sons, or three Holy Spirits, in the way that three people who are mutually friends can be called three friends?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: No. 'Friends' is a relative name that applies mutually, so each can be called a friend of the others. In the Trinity the relative names are not shared. Only the Father is father, and he is father of the Son alone, not of two. Neither the Father nor the Spirit is the Son, and the Spirit, called the gift of God, is neither Father nor Son.
sources.quote: But this is not the case in the Trinity, since the Father only is there father; and not Father of two, but of the Son only. Neither are they three Sons, since the Father there is not the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father, Son and Holy Spirit be called three Fathers, three Sons, or three Holy Spirits, in the way that three people who are mutually friends can be called three friends?

question: Is the Holy Spirit himself divine Power, as the Father and the Son are?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter II. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are One in counsel.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit promised through Joel is the same "promise of the Father" that Christ says will endue the disciples "with power from on high." So the one promised is himself Power. Luke also describes the Spirit coming down at Pentecost with great power.
sources.quote: He, then, Who was promised to us is Himself Power, as in the Gospel the same Son of God declared
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit himself divine Power, as the Father and the Son are?

question: How is the Holy Spirit given to believers in relation to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVII.—The apostles teach that it was neither Christ nor the Saviour, but the Holy Spirit, who did descend upon Jesus. The reason for this descent.
sources.answer: The Son receives the Spirit as a gift from the Father and Himself bestows the Spirit on those who partake of Him. The Lord sends the Holy Spirit upon all the earth and confers the Comforter on the Church. The Spirit then joins us to God, offering the first-fruits of the nations to the Father.
sources.quote: The Lord, receiving this as a gift from His Father, does Himself also confer it upon those who are partakers of Himself, sending the Holy Spirit upon all the earth.
sources.raw_question: How is the Holy Spirit given to believers in relation to the Father and the Son?

question: Is the doctrine that believers have distinct communion with each of the three Persons of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) a new and novel teaching?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: To the reader.
sources.answer: No. The prefacer (Daniel Burgess) holds that distinct fellowship with each Person of the Trinity is an established truth rather than a new-fangled one. He cites Samuel Clarke's sermon on 1 John 1:7, which notes a distinct fellowship with each Person. He also cites Lewis Stuckley, who calls it a glorious truth attested by God and solemnly owned by the first and best age of Christianity. He directs doubters to the second chapter of Owen's treatise for the proof.
sources.quote: It is a most glorious truth, though considered but by a few, that believers have, or may have, distinct communion with the three persons, Father, Son, and Spirit. This is attested by the finger of God, and solemnly owned by the first and best age of Christianity.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who take the doctrine of distinct communion to be new-fangled
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine that believers have distinct communion with each of the three Persons of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) a new and novel teaching?

question: Do the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit equally possess power to do whatever they will?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture attributes sovereign will and power to each Person. The Spirit breathes where He will and works all in all as He will. The Son made all things, did whatever He pleased, and quickens whom He will. The Father holds the times, and so all things done in time, in His own power.
sources.quote: it has been demonstrated that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit alike are in a position of power to do what They will
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit equally possess power to do whatever they will?

question: From whom does the Holy Spirit proceed?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit proceeds from Father and Son. For this reason he must be confessed along with them, and his existence should not even be a matter of dispute.
sources.quote: There is no need to speak, because we are bound to confess Him, proceeding, as He does, from Father and Son
sources.raw_question: From whom does the Holy Spirit proceed?

question: Does the use of 'Holy Spirit' to describe the Father or the Son cast doubt on the Holy Spirit as a distinct third Name?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The term may be applied to the Father or the Son, since each is spirit and holy, and this raises no objection. Hilary also warns that a text like 'God is Spirit' must be read by its context and aim. It must not be used to deny the Name, work and gift of the Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: No objection need be raised to this; whether it be Father or Son, He is Spirit, and He is holy.
sources.raw_question: Does the use of 'Holy Spirit' to describe the Father or the Son cast doubt on the Holy Spirit as a distinct third Name?

question: Why does Scripture say the Father is greater than the Son but never that the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit, if both the Son and the Spirit are said to be sent?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Creature is Not So Taken by the Holy Spirit as Flesh is by the Word.
sources.answer: Because the creature in which the Holy Spirit appeared was not assumed in the way the Son assumed human nature. The Son took the form of a servant into the unity of his person, and in respect of that form he is called less. The Spirit's visible signs were never joined to his person, so nothing in him gives grounds for calling him less than the Father.
sources.quote: It is, then, for this reason nowhere written, that the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit is less than God the Father, because the creature in which the Holy Spirit was to appear was not taken in the same way as the Son of man was taken
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture say the Father is greater than the Son but never that the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit, if both the Son and the Spirit are said to be sent?

question: Is the Holy Spirit almighty and all-seeing like the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXII. In proof of the Unity in Trinity the passage of Isaiah which has been cited is considered, and it is shown that there is no difference as to its sense amongst those who expound it of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Spirit. If He Who was crucified was Lord of glory, so, too, is the Holy Spirit equal in all things to the Father and the Son, and the Arians will never be able to diminish His glory.
sources.answer: Yes. Like the Father and the Son, the Spirit is free from stain and almighty. Solomon in the Book of Wisdom calls Him all-powerful and all-surveying, so the Spirit enjoys honour and glory.
sources.quote: as the Father and the Son, so, too, the Spirit is free from stain and Almighty, for Solomon called Him in Greek παντοδύναμον, πᾶνέπίσχοπον , because He is Almighty and beholds all things
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit almighty and all-seeing like the Father and the Son?

question: If the Son and the Spirit are said to be inferior in being, what reason can be given for this inferiority?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: None that stands. Eunomius gives no reason why the Son should be inferior in being, since being and energy are found in the same characteristics and attributes. If instead being and energy mean different things, he cannot prove a claim about being by appealing to energy. Either way his argument for the Son's inferior being fails.
sources.quote: why the Son is inferior on the score of being, when both this being and energy are to be discovered in the same characteristics and attributes
sources.raw_question: If the Son and the Spirit are said to be inferior in being, what reason can be given for this inferiority?

question: Is the Son inferior to the Holy Spirit, given that He spoke as if acting by the Spirit's power?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: No. He spoke of Himself as inferior only as man and for the exposure of the Jews' blasphemy. To the disciples He showed His Godhead and equality with the Spirit by giving the Spirit, saying 'Receive ye the Holy Ghost,' 'I send Him,' and 'He shall glorify Me.'
sources.quote: intimating that He was not inferior but equal to the Spirit, He gave the Spirit and said, ‘Receive ye the Holy Ghost,’ and ‘I send Him,’ and ‘He shall glorify Me,’
sources.raw_question: Is the Son inferior to the Holy Spirit, given that He spoke as if acting by the Spirit's power?

question: Can it be said from Scripture that things are "of" the Son and "of" the Holy Spirit, as they are said to be "of" the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IX. A passage of St. Paul abused by heretics, to prove a distinction between the Divine Persons, is explained, and it is proved that the whole passage can be rightly said of each Person, though it refers specially to the Son. It is then proved that each member of the passage is applicable to each Person, and as to say, of Him are all things is applicable to the Father, so may all things are through Him and in Him also be said of Him.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says the whole body grows from Christ the Head and that of His fulness we have all received. It also says that he who sows in the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap eternal life, and that what was born of Mary is of the Holy Spirit. So, as all things are of the Father, all things can also be said to be of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.quote: So, then, as we read that all things are of the Father, so, too, that all things can be said to be of the Son, through Whom are all things; and we are taught by proof that all things are of the Spirit in Whom are all things.
sources.raw_question: Can it be said from Scripture that things are "of" the Son and "of" the Holy Spirit, as they are said to be "of" the Father?

question: Is the Holy Spirit omnipresent?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Psalm 139:7-8 asks where one could go from God's Spirit, and the Spirit's distinct personality has already been shown, so this text establishes the omnipresence of a divine Person. It is also self-evident from his simultaneous work in countless hearts throughout the universe.
sources.quote: Having proved his distinct personality, this establishes his omnipresence: which truth is indeed self-evident, from the simultaneous work he is carrying on in ten thousand thousand hearts throughout the universe.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit omnipresent?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's performing the same operations as the Father and the Son prove that he shares their nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as whatever shines and warms exactly as fire does is itself fire, so if the Spirit does the works of the Father, such as quickening and working man's salvation, he has the same power and nature. Eunomius himself admits the Spirit quickens like the Father and Son, so from identity of operations the Spirit is not alien from their nature.
sources.quote: For just as, if anything should perform the functions of fire, shining and warming in precisely the same way, it is itself certainly fire, so if the Spirit does the works of the Father, He must assuredly be acknowledged to be of the same nature with Him.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's performing the same operations as the Father and the Son prove that he shares their nature?

question: Do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit exist in succession or separation within the divine substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Of the Sensible Showing of the Holy Spirit, and of the Coeternity of the Trinity. What Has Been Said, and What Remains to Be Said.
sources.answer: No. In their proper substance the three are one and the very same, above all creation, without temporal motion and without any interval of time or place. They are at once one and the same from eternity to eternity, like eternity itself. Only in our words, which are bodily sounds, are they named separately and one after another.
sources.quote: in their proper substance wherein they are, the three are one, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the very same, by no temporal motion, above the whole creature, without any interval of time and place
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit exist in succession or separation within the divine substance?

question: Is the Holy Spirit the Spirit of the Son and sent by the Son, just as he is the Spirit of the Father poured out by God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The Old Testament has God saying 'I will pour out my Spirit,' and the Spirit is called 'the Spirit of your Father.' The New Testament likewise has Christ say 'I will send the Comforter.' It calls the Spirit 'the Spirit of Christ' and 'the Spirit of his Son,' and says Christ 'shed forth' the Spirit. The Son therefore stands in the same relation to the Spirit as the Father, which shows his coequal deity.
sources.quote: I will send the Comforter unto you. – John 16:7. Spirit of Christ. – Rom. 8:9. The Spirit of his Son. Gal. 4:6. He hath shed forth this. – Acts 2:33.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit the Spirit of the Son and sent by the Son, just as he is the Spirit of the Father poured out by God?

question: Does the gift of the Holy Spirit come from the Son as well as from the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Preface.
sources.answer: Yes. Ambrose addresses Christ and says that the divine gift is "Thy gift and that of the Father." He cites the prophetic promise "I will pour out of My Spirit upon all flesh" as spoken by Christ through the prophets. The outpouring of the Spirit is therefore a common gift of the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: it is, O Lord, Thy gift and that of the Father, as Thou hast spoken by the prophets, saying: “I will pour out of My Spirit upon all flesh
sources.raw_question: Does the gift of the Holy Spirit come from the Son as well as from the Father?

question: If Father, Son and Holy Ghost are one God, in what respect must they be one and in what respect three?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: They must be one in essence and three in distinct subsistences. Owen argues these are the only respects in which it is possible for them to be one and three, so this follows necessarily and unavoidably from Scripture's revelation that the three are one God.
sources.quote: they are one in essence (wherein alone it is possible they can be one), and three in their distinct subsistences (wherein alone it is possible they can be three)
sources.raw_question: If Father, Son and Holy Ghost are one God, in what respect must they be one and in what respect three?

question: Are the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit merely one and the same person under different names, as modalists claim?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Conclusion of the Book with a Prayer, and an Apology for Multitude of Words.
sources.answer: No. If God were himself Father, Son and Holy Spirit as a single person, Scripture would not say that God sent his Son. Nor would the Only-begotten say that the Father will send the Spirit in his name, or that he himself will send the Spirit from the Father. Sending implies a real distinction between the one who sends and the one who is sent.
sources.quote: if Thou, O God, wert Thyself the Father, and wert Thyself the Son, Thy Word Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit your gift, we should not read in the book of truth, “God sent His Son;”
sources.raw_question: Are the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit merely one and the same person under different names, as modalists claim?

question: Can the scriptural phrase 'Spirit of God' refer to the Father or to the Son, and not only to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. Hilary holds that 'Spirit of God' is used of Either, Father and Son, as well as of the Paraclete. The Father is meant where Christ says the Spirit of the Lord is upon Him and anoints Him, and the Son is meant where Christ casts out devils 'in the Spirit of God', that is, by the power of His own nature. The Paraclete is meant in Joel's prophecy fulfilled at Pentecost.
sources.quote: the Son of God is revealed under the title Spirit of God in order that we may understand the presence of the Father in Him, and that the term Spirit of God may be employed to indicate Either
sources.raw_question: Can the scriptural phrase 'Spirit of God' refer to the Father or to the Son, and not only to the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the fact that the Holy Spirit is both the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ prove that the Father and the Son are one in nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit who dwells in us is a single Being of one nature, and He is both the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ. Therefore the Son's nature must be identical with the Father's. Their natures could differ only if the Spirit that is of God could be shown not to be the Spirit of Christ as well.
sources.quote: we must regard the nature of the Son as identical with that of the Father, since the Holy Spirit Who is both the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of God is proved to be a Being of one nature
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Holy Spirit is both the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ prove that the Father and the Son are one in nature?

question: Should the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit be called three greatnesses or three who are great, or rather one who is great?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Those Things Which Belong Absolutely to God as an Essence, are Spoken of the Trinity in the Singular, Not in the Plural.
sources.answer: One who is great, not three greatnesses or three greats. Just as we do not say three essences, we do not say three greatnesses, because for God to be and to be great are the same thing. Since greatness belongs to God's essence, and the essence is one, the greatness of the Trinity is one and is predicated in the singular.
sources.quote: And, therefore, as we do not say three essences, so neither do we say three greatnesses; for it is the same thing to God to be, and to be great.
sources.raw_question: Should the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit be called three greatnesses or three who are great, or rather one who is great?

question: If the Father and the Son are each called Jehovah, Creator, God, and object of worship, does it follow that there are two Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. Scripture gives both Persons the same titles, powers and worship, yet it never speaks of two Gods, two Creators or two worships. It constantly asserts that God is one. The obvious conclusion is that Father and Son are both one God. Otherwise ditheism would be unavoidable.
sources.quote: The obvious conclusion, from these premises, is, that they are both one God, (otherwise indeed Ditheism is unavoidable,) and thus the Scripture-notion of unity is of more Persons than one in the same Godhead.
sources.raw_question: If the Father and the Son are each called Jehovah, Creator, God, and object of worship, does it follow that there are two Gods?

question: Can the Son be both God's Offspring and a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. No one says that he begets what he creates, nor calls his own proper offspring creatures. Since Scripture calls the Son Offspring and Only-begotten, he cannot be a creature.
sources.quote: For if He is Offspring, how call ye Him creature? for no one says that He begets what He creates, nor calls His proper offspring creatures
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be both God's Offspring and a creature?

question: If the Father and the Son are distinct and both are called God, does that introduce two Gods, so that Christ must be a mere man for God to remain one?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > In Fine, Notwithstanding the Said Heretics Have Gathered the Origin of Their Error from Consideration of What is Written: Although We Call Christ God, and the Father God, Still Scripture Does Not Set Forth Two Gods, Any More Than Two Lords or Two Teachers.
sources.answer: No. Novatian turns the argument back on its makers. They themselves admit Christ is Lord although Scripture says there is one Lord. By their own reasoning that would yield two Lords, yet they do not think it does. Likewise, calling the Son God alongside the Father does not overthrow the scriptural confession that God is one.
sources.quote: What, then, do they think of Christ?—that He is Lord, or that He is not Lord at all? But they do not doubt absolutely that He is Lord; therefore, if their reasoning be true, here are already two Lords.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who contend that Christ is man only
sources.raw_question: If the Father and the Son are distinct and both are called God, does that introduce two Gods, so that Christ must be a mere man for God to remain one?

question: Did the early Church Fathers teach that the Father and the Son are one God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus, Athenagoras, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Hippolytus, Lactantius and finally Eusebius asserted it, and the post-Nicene writers contended for it generally. They judged, rightly, that the Son's divinity could not otherwise be secured while avoiding polytheism.
sources.quote: They thought that the divinity of the Son could not be otherwise secured, and Polytheism at the same time avoided, than by asserting Father and Son to be one God; and they thought right.
sources.raw_question: Did the early Church Fathers teach that the Father and the Son are one God?

question: Does the distinction between Father and Son mean that their divinity differs in kind, so that there are two Gods?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. There is a real distinction because they are Father and Son, but their Godhead is not different in kind; both are one, God of God, One God Only-begotten of One God Unbegotten. They are not two Gods but One of One, and not two Unbegotten, since the Son is born of the Unborn.
sources.quote: There is a distinction, for They are Father and Son; not that Their Divinity is different in kind, for Both are One, God of God, One God Only begotten of One God Unbegotten. They are not two Gods, but One of One
sources.raw_question: Does the distinction between Father and Son mean that their divinity differs in kind, so that there are two Gods?

question: Was the Son of God born of God or created out of nothing with a nature different in kind from the Divine?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: He was born, not created. The opponents' aim is to show a creation from non-existence, but Christ's words that what is born of the Spirit is Spirit show that, since God is Spirit, nothing alien can be in the One born from Him. Thus his birth constitutes him perfect God.
sources.quote: For, since God is a Spirit, it is clear that in One born from Him there can be nothing alien or different from that Spirit from which He was born. Thus the birth of God constitutes Him perfect God.
sources.raw_question: Was the Son of God born of God or created out of nothing with a nature different in kind from the Divine?

question: Is the Son either a second God or the sole God alongside the confession of one God the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Neither. Because the nature of the one God is in Him by birth, He cannot be a God of a different kind, and His birth requires a perfect Sonship. Hence He can neither be separated from God nor merged into God, being neither a second God nor the solitary God.
sources.quote: He declared Himself, by the nature which is His by birth, neither a second God, nor the sole God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son either a second God or the sole God alongside the confession of one God the Father?

question: Is the Son a creature made by God, or did he come forth from the Father by birth?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: He was not created but came forth from the Father. In his ineffable and mysterious birth or procession, the Word himself testifies throughout the Gospel that the Father is his Father, not his Creator. He is therefore not a work of God but the Son of God.
sources.quote: the Very Father was a father, not a creator, of Himself, and that He was not a work of God, but Son of God?
sources.raw_question: Is the Son a creature made by God, or did he come forth from the Father by birth?

question: Was the Son of God brought into being out of nothing, by an act of creation, rather than born from God the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Because the Son was born from God, he was not born from nothing or from things non-existent. His birth was the birth of the eternally living divine nature, and by that birth he shared in the nature of his Source. Hilary holds that the Arian formulas are meant to lead step by step to the blasphemy that Christ is born out of nothing by a divine act of creation.
sources.quote: God, since He was born from God, was assuredly not born from nothing, nor from things non-existent. His birth was that of the eternally living nature.
sources.raw_question: Was the Son of God brought into being out of nothing, by an act of creation, rather than born from God the Father?

question: If the Son derives his being from the Father's free, arbitrary choice, does that make him a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. To make the Son's being depend on the Father's will in the sense of free choice of what might otherwise not have been is the same thing as making him a creature. The opponent's attempt to prove this is therefore a denial of the Son's divinity.
sources.quote: You endeavour to prove, that the Son derives his being from the wi// of the Father, in this latter sense; which is the same thing with the making him a creature.
sources.raw_question: If the Son derives his being from the Father's free, arbitrary choice, does that make him a creature?

question: Is the Son of God a second God alongside the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. He is God from God by nature and by birth, since the source of His Godhead is God. Yet He is not a second God, because the truth in Him is nothing other than the truth of God. God is in God, and beside Him there is no God.
sources.quote: He is God from God by nature and by birth, for the Source of His Godhead is God. And, again, He is not a second God, for no other is likened unto Him; the truth that is in Him is nothing else than the truth of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God a second God alongside the Father?

question: Can the Creator through whom all things were made be Himself a creature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Human reason rejects calling the Creator a creature, since creation comes into being through the Creator. Moreover, if He were a creature He would share the creature's subjection to vanity, expectation, corruption and bondage that Paul describes.
sources.quote: In the first place our human intelligence repudiates this statement that the Creator is a creature; since creation comes to exist by means of the Creator.
sources.raw_question: Can the Creator through whom all things were made be Himself a creature?

question: Does worshipping and believing in the Son amount to worshipping a second God alongside the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: No. Since the Godhead is one, he who believes in the Son believes in the Father, and he who worships the Son worships the Father in Him. There is therefore one faith, one honour and one worship, paid to the one God.
sources.quote: for one is the Godhead; and therefore one the honour and one the worship which is paid to the Father in and through the Son. And he who thus worships, worships one God
sources.raw_question: Does worshipping and believing in the Son amount to worshipping a second God alongside the Father?

question: Does the Son's being God in the strict sense imply that there are two Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Father and Son, by a most intimate and ineffable union of substance, will, power, presence and operation (called perichoresis), may be one God. The objection that two divine Persons cannot be one God is not drawn from Scripture but only from conjectures about the nature of a thing of which the objector has no adequate idea.
sources.quote: we answer, that Father and Son, by a most intimate and ineffable union of swdstance, will, power, presence, operation, ὅσο. (which we call zepuχώρησις,) may be one God.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being God in the strict sense imply that there are two Gods?

question: May the Son be worshipped jointly with the Father as one God, and also distinctly as a Person?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: Yes, in both ways. Because the Son is truly God and Creator, he may be worshipped jointly with the Father as one Godhead. He may also be worshipped distinctly as one Person of the Godhead.
sources.quote: he may be worshipped ; either jointly with the Father, as one τὸ Θεῖον, or distinctly, as one Person of the Godhead.
sources.raw_question: May the Son be worshipped jointly with the Father as one God, and also distinctly as a Person?

question: If whatever the Father makes the Son also makes, can the Son be the Father's creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: No. If the Son were the Father's work, then, since the Father's works are the Son's works too, the Son would create himself, which is absurd and impossible. Therefore, because he works the things of the Father, he is himself neither a work nor a creature.
sources.quote: then either He will work His own self, and will be His own creator (since what the Father worketh is the Son’s work also), which is absurd and impossible
sources.raw_question: If whatever the Father makes the Son also makes, can the Son be the Father's creature?

question: Does the Son's being derived or generated from the Father make him a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 13: Whether there can be any middle between being made out of nothing, and out of something ; that is, between being out of nothing, and out of the Father's substan
sources.answer: No. Derivation understood in the Catholic sense, as eternal generation, does not make the Son a creature. What makes a being a creature is being out of nothing, so that it now is and once was not. Waterland's argument turns on the words 'out of nothing', not on derivation as such.
sources.quote: Does not my argument turn upon the words, out of nothing ? Point me out any being so derived, a being which now is, and once was not ; and deny him to be a creature,if you can.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being derived or generated from the Father make him a creature?

question: What makes the Father and the Son a unity rather than two separate Gods?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: They are a unity because they are interdependent, and their interdependence is proved by their being One from One. The Father gives the Son his own nature in begetting him, and the Son receives only that nature. So one and the same Divine nature exists in both, and each dwells in the other.
sources.quote: because They are interdependent They form an unity; and that They are interdependent is proved by Their being One from One
sources.raw_question: What makes the Father and the Son a unity rather than two separate Gods?

question: Did Christ or the Father ever teach that the Son was created or made rather than born?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Nowhere did the Lord tell His disciples that His birth was a creation or making, and the Father never testified to Him as anything but a Son. Since disciples may not go beyond their master, it would be rash to call the Son made; Scripture instead calls Him the Son born of the Father.
sources.quote: the Father never bore witness to Him as being aught else but a Son, nor did the Son profess that God was aught else than His own true Father, assuredly affirming that He was born, not made nor created
sources.raw_question: Did Christ or the Father ever teach that the Son was created or made rather than born?

question: Does being 'born from' God, as 1 John says of the Son, mean the same as being created by God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The Evangelist says the Son is born from the Father, and the heretic cannot more correctly teach that he was created. To turn birth into creation is to make the Apostle a liar.
sources.quote: What, I ask, is the meaning of being born from Him? Can it mean, perchance, being created by Him? Does the Evangelist lie in saying that He was born from God, while the heretic more correctly teaches that He was created?
sources.raw_question: Does being 'born from' God, as 1 John says of the Son, mean the same as being created by God?

question: How can Father and Son be two and yet have only one Divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Each subsists in such a way that neither exists apart from the Other. They are Two through birth given and received, and so only one Divine nature exists. The Father loses nothing by being in the Son, and the Son receives his whole Sonship from the Father.
