sources.quote: For Each subsists in such wise as not to exist apart from the Other, since They are Two through birth given and received, and therefore only one Divine nature exists.
sources.raw_question: How can Father and Son be two and yet have only one Divine nature?

question: Do the Proverbs call the Son a creature or an Offspring?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: Offspring. The Proverbs say 'He created' but call the Son 'Offspring,' acknowledging what is proper to Him by nature: that He is the Only-begotten Wisdom and Framer of creatures. 'He created' refers not to His essence but to His becoming a beginning of ways. No one begets what he creates or calls his proper offspring creatures.
sources.quote: For the Proverbs say ‘He created,’ but they call not the Son creature, but Offspring
sources.raw_question: Do the Proverbs call the Son a creature or an Offspring?

question: Can the whole Trinity be called 'Father'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: Not properly, only perhaps metaphorically in respect to the creature. The one Lord our God of Deuteronomy, which includes Son and Spirit, is rightly called our Father because he regenerates us by grace and adopts us as sons. But the Trinity is not Father in the way the First Person is Father of the Son.
sources.quote: the Trinity cannot in the same way be called the Father, except perhaps metaphorically, in respect to the creature, on account of the adoption of sons.
sources.raw_question: Can the whole Trinity be called 'Father'?

question: How is the name 'Holy Spirit' a relative name, and where is its relation most apparent?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit is referred both to the Father and to the Son, being the Spirit of both. The relation is not obvious in the name 'Holy Spirit' itself, but is apparent when he is called the Gift of God, for gift and giver are spoken of relatively in reciprocal reference. He is the gift of the Father, from whom he proceeds, and of the Son, being called the Spirit of Christ.
sources.quote: But the relation is not itself apparent in that name, but it is apparent when He is called the gift of God;
sources.raw_question: How is the name 'Holy Spirit' a relative name, and where is its relation most apparent?

question: Does calling the Son the Image of the Father imply that the Son is inferior to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Of the Attributes Assigned by Hilary to Each Person. The Trinity is Represented in Things that are Made.
sources.answer: No. An image that perfectly fills the measure of its original is equal to it. The Son is the perfect Image, with prime equality and likeness, differing in nothing and unequal in no respect.
sources.quote: For if an image perfectly fills the measure of that of which it is the image, then the image is made equal to that of which it is the image, not the latter to its own image.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son the Image of the Father imply that the Son is inferior to the Father?

question: Is the Holy Spirit rightly identified as Love, just as the Word of God is identified as the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > Why Love is Not the Offspring of the Mind, as Knowledge is So. The Solution of the Question. The Mind with the Knowledge of Itself and the Love of Itself is the Image of the Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine takes it as settled by the truth that, just as no Christian doubts that the Word of God is the Son, the Holy Spirit is love. He makes this the premise for investigating why love, unlike knowledge, is not said to be begotten. On this basis the triad of mind, its knowledge and its love becomes an image of Father, Son and Spirit.
sources.quote: assuming, however, that the truth itself has persuaded us, that as no Christian doubts the Word of God to be the Son, so that the Holy Spirit is love
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit rightly identified as Love, just as the Word of God is identified as the Son?

question: Does denying the eternal existence of the Son, who is the 'brightness' and 'express image' of the Father, logically entail denying the eternal existence of the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Brightness and glory, image and person, wisdom and God are correlatives joined together. To abolish one is to abolish the other, just as saying a lamp's ray 'is not' means the lamp has gone out. So if the Son was not, neither was the Father, whose power, wisdom, image and brightness the Son is.
sources.quote: so that when the Son is said not to be, thereby is also maintained as a necessary consequence the non-existence of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does denying the eternal existence of the Son, who is the 'brightness' and 'express image' of the Father, logically entail denying the eternal existence of the Father?

question: Can Eunomius consistently hold that the Son had a beginning while holding that the Father's essence is unoriginate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. If the Son 'was not,' logic forces one of two absurdities: either God does not exist at all, which is atheism, or God's being was not unoriginate and eternal. The Eunomians would refuse atheism, so they must give up their claim that the Father's essence is unoriginate. That undoes their syllogisms built on the opposition of 'Generated' and 'Ungenerate.'
sources.quote: either that we should say that God does not exist at all, or that we should say that His being was not unoriginate, let them choose which they like of the two courses before them
sources.raw_question: Can Eunomius consistently hold that the Son had a beginning while holding that the Father's essence is unoriginate?

question: Is the Son in the Father by nature, or by some condition or example, as believers are?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: The Son is in the Father simply and by nature, as His own Word and Radiance. For believers, to whom this is not natural, an image and example is needed, which is why the word 'as' is applied to us and not to Him.
sources.quote: the Son Himself, simply and without any condition is in the Father; for this attribute He has by nature; but for us, to whom it is not natural, there is needed an image and example
sources.raw_question: Is the Son in the Father by nature, or by some condition or example, as believers are?

question: Is the Son in the Father by participating in the Holy Spirit, as believers are?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. The Son does not receive or merely partake of the Spirit; He supplies the Spirit to all. The Spirit does not unite the Word to the Father but receives from the Word, so the Son is in the Father in a different way from us.
sources.quote: the Son does not merely partake the Spirit, that therefore He too may be in the Father; nor does He receive the Spirit, but rather He supplies It Himself to all; and the Spirit does not unite the Word to the Father
sources.raw_question: Is the Son in the Father by participating in the Holy Spirit, as believers are?

question: Does Clarke's analogy of a king and his son ruling with one authority show that the Father and Son, as two distinct beings, are not two Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 4: Whether, supposing the Scripture-notion of God to be no more than that of the Author and Governor of the universe, or whatever it be, the admitting of another t
sources.answer: No. If the king's son is not a king, he cannot truly be called king. If he is, there are two kings. Likewise, if the Son is not God in the Scripture sense, he cannot truly be called God. If he is truly God, then on Clarke's view of two distinct beings there are plainly two Gods, against the texts of Isaiah.
sources.quote: So if the Son be not God in the Scripture-notion of God, he cannot truly be called God ; and then how is the Doctor consistent with Scripture, or with himself?
sources.raw_question: Does Clarke's analogy of a king and his son ruling with one authority show that the Father and Son, as two distinct beings, are not two Gods?

question: Can the Son's divine name, nature, power and self-revelation be treated separately from His birth from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The Son's birth includes all of them, because they belong to Him by the very fact that He is born. So the argument about His birth cannot keep these other points back for separate discussion.
sources.quote: For His birth involves all these, and they are His by the fact that He is born.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's divine name, nature, power and self-revelation be treated separately from His birth from the Father?

question: Is God's being 'Lord' eternal to Him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said of God in Time, is Said Relatively, Not Accidentally.
sources.answer: No. To be Lord is not eternal to God, because lord and servant are correlatives. If God were Lord from eternity, the creature would also have to be a servant from eternity. Since the creature is not eternal, God's lordship over man, over Israel, or over a particular tree began in time.
sources.quote: Behold! to be the Lord, is not eternal to God; otherwise we should be compelled to say that the creature also is from eternity
sources.raw_question: Is God's being 'Lord' eternal to Him?

question: Is the Son the Power of God itself or merely the seal of the Father's power?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: The Son is the Power of God itself. Paul calls the Son "the Power of God." When Eunomius calls Him only "the seal of a power," he is presuming to correct the Apostle.
sources.quote: Paul says that the Son is “the Power of God”; Eunomius calls Him “the seal of a power,” not the Power.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the Power of God itself or merely the seal of the Father's power?

question: Does Scripture teach that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is truly God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > In Fine, Notwithstanding the Said Heretics Have Gathered the Origin of Their Error from Consideration of What is Written: Although We Call Christ God, and the Father God, Still Scripture Does Not Set Forth Two Gods, Any More Than Two Lords or Two Teachers.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture lays down clear marks of Christ's divinity, and these must not be rejected. To reject them would corrupt Scripture's authority and the integrity of the faith. The proofs are that 'the Word was God', that 'the Word was made flesh', Thomas's confession 'My Lord and my God', and Paul's description of Christ as 'over all, God blessed for evermore'.
sources.quote: we ought by no means to reject those marks of Christ’s divinity which are laid down in the Scriptures, that we may not, by corrupting the authority of the Scriptures, be held to have corrupted the integrity of our holy faith.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is truly God?

question: Does Scripture's teaching that God is love and that we know we abide in God because he has given us of his Spirit show that the Holy Spirit is God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says God is love and love is of God, and that we abide in God and he in us, knowing it because he has given us of his Spirit. Hence the Spirit himself, who is this love given to us, is God who is love.
sources.quote: and that hereby we know this, because He has given us of His Spirit, then the Spirit Himself is God, who is love.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's teaching that God is love and that we know we abide in God because he has given us of his Spirit show that the Holy Spirit is God?

question: Is the Father's love something distinct from his divine nature or substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: No. God's nature is ineffably simple, so the love in the Father is nothing else than his very nature and substance.
sources.quote: For the love in the Father, which is in His ineffably simple nature, is nothing else than His very nature and substance itself
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's love something distinct from his divine nature or substance?

question: Does affirming the unity of Father and Son amount to the Sabellian error of making the Father and the Son one Person divided into two?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Sabellius cuts one indivisible Person into two parts, one of which enters the Virgin's womb, so there is no real birth of a second Person. The Church confesses a true birth and rejects the confusion of two Persons in one, while still holding the divine unity. The Arians condemn Sabellius in order to deny any point of union between Father and Son, but the true faith is Two Persons in One God.
sources.quote: But we confess a birth; we reject this confusion of two Persons in One, while yet we cleave to the Divine unity.
sources.raw_question: Does affirming the unity of Father and Son amount to the Sabellian error of making the Father and the Son one Person divided into two?

question: Why does the Son's being 'God from God' imply that Father and Son are one in nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Because the Son was truly born of God, so he can draw his substance from no source other than the divine. Since he continues to draw his being from God as he did at first, he remains true God for ever. Having no nature and no origin other than the divine, he is one with the Father.
sources.quote: we hold that God from God means unity of nature; for that Being, Who, by a true birth from God, became God, can draw His substance from no other source than the Divine.
sources.raw_question: Why does the Son's being 'God from God' imply that Father and Son are one in nature?

question: Since a human mother has no son before giving birth, does it follow that the Son of God did not exist before His generation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections to the Foregoing Proof. Whether, in the generation of the Son, God made One that was already, or One that was not.
sources.answer: No. The argument wrongly likens God to men. We do not conclude that God needs materials to create because an architect does, or that God is in place because men are. In the same way, God begets not as men beget but as God. Our idea of God transcends such human conditions in begetting just as it does in creating.
sources.quote: creates not as man creates, but yet creates as God, it is plain that He begets also not as men beget, but begets as God.
sources.raw_question: Since a human mother has no son before giving birth, does it follow that the Son of God did not exist before His generation?

question: Does the existence of the Father imply the existence of a true Son in whom the Father is revealed?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Yes. Because there is a Father, there is a Son. In that Son the Father is made known to us, which gives certainty that the Son is born the Only-begotten and is very God.
sources.quote: Because there is a Father we know that there is a Son; in that Son the Father is manifested to us, and hence our certainty that He is born the Only-begotten and that He is very God.
sources.raw_question: Does the existence of the Father imply the existence of a true Son in whom the Father is revealed?

question: Does the Son's being in the Father mean he shares every attribute of the Father, including eternity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is in the Father not in one respect only but altogether, in all that the Father is conceived to be. So he is incorruptible in the Father's incorruptibility, good in his goodness, and powerful in his might. By the same reasoning, being in the Father's eternity, he is eternal, without beginning or end.
sources.quote: being in the Father, He is not in Him in one respect only, but He is in Him altogether, in respect of all that the Father is conceived to be.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being in the Father mean he shares every attribute of the Father, including eternity?

question: Since the Father is the principium (source) of the Son, does it follow that the Son is not eternal?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. The argument equivocates on 'principium' and so has four terms. If principium means a beginning in time, the claim that the Son has one is false. If it means a source in some other sense, it is false that whatever has a principium is not eternal. The sun's light is coeval with the sun, and thought with an always-thinking mind, though each has a principium.
sources.quote: If principium be understood in respect of time, the minor is not true: if it be taken in any other sense, the major is not true: so that both cannot be true.
sources.raw_question: Since the Father is the principium (source) of the Son, does it follow that the Son is not eternal?

question: Does the claim that the Father was always Father prove that the Son is eternal?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. To say the Father was never without the Son is the most express statement of the Son's eternity. It is absurd to say the Father was ever not a Father, and that amounts to the same thing as saying the Son once was not. Novatian ('ne Pater non semper sit Pater') and Dionysius of Alexandria both argue in this way.
sources.quote: He plainly supposes it absurd to say, that the Father was ever no Father, or, which comes to the same, that ever the Son was not.
sources.raw_question: Does the claim that the Father was always Father prove that the Son is eternal?

question: Does the Son's being called the Power of God show that He is co-eternal with the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IV. To those who contend that the Spirit because He is called the Finger is less than the Father, St. Ambrose replies that this would also tend to the lessening of the Son, Who is called the Right Hand. That these names are to be referred only to the Unity, for which reason Moses proclaimed that the whole Trinity worked in the passage of the Red Sea. And, indeed, it is no wonder that the operation of the Spirit found place there, where there was a figure of baptism, since the Scripture teaches that the Three Persons equally sanctify and are operative in that sacrament.
sources.answer: Yes. There can be no perfection without power. If the Power of God ever did not exist, then the Father would at some time have lacked perfection and been only half perfect in His own Substance. That is impious to say. Therefore the Son, who is the Power of God, always existed with the Father.
sources.quote: For when did the Power of God not exist? But if they think that at any time the Power of God existed not, they will say that at some time Perfection existed not in God the Father
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being called the Power of God show that He is co-eternal with the Father?

question: Does Scripture give a sufficient revelation that the Son of God is eternally God in the same way as the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that the testimony of John 1 alone, once vindicated from Socinian glosses, is a pledge of the full confirmation the other testimonies can give. He concludes that Scripture fully and sufficiently reveals the Son's eternal Deity, and reveals him to be God as the Father is.
sources.quote: It appears, then, that there is a full, sufficient revelation made in the Scripture of the eternal Deity of the Son of God; and that he is so, as is the Father also.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture give a sufficient revelation that the Son of God is eternally God in the same way as the Father?

question: Is the Son equal to the Father in every divine property, neither exceeding nor falling short of Him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: Yes. We should believe of the Son everything we behold in the Father, because They are One and each is conceived in the other. The Son neither overpasses the Father nor is inferior to Him. Nor is He altered or subject to change in any divine or excellent property.
sources.quote: because They are One, and in the one is conceived the other, not overpassing Him, not inferior to Him, not altered or subject to change in any Divine or excellent property
sources.raw_question: Is the Son equal to the Father in every divine property, neither exceeding nor falling short of Him?

question: Does God's eternal Fatherhood imply the eternity of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father is always Father, and the title of father cannot be justified unless there is a son to make it true. Hence the Son must always be thought of along with the Father, and nothing in the Father precedes our apprehension of the Son by any interval.
sources.quote: The Father therefore is always Father; and seeing that the Son must always be thought of along with the Father (for the title of father cannot be justified unless there is a son to make it true), all that we contemplate in the Father is to be observed also in the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does God's eternal Fatherhood imply the eternity of the Son?

question: Is the Holy Spirit called 'Power' in the same sense as the Father and the Son, so that He is not inferior to them?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter I. The Spirit is the Lord and Power; and in this is not inferior to the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. As the Father is Power and the Son is Power, so the Holy Spirit is Power. Christ is called 'the Power of God'; the Father is called Power, at whose right hand the Son sits; and the Lord Himself named the Spirit Power when He said 'Ye shall receive Power when the Holy Spirit cometh upon you.'
sources.quote: For as the Father is Power, so, too, the Son is Power, and the Holy Spirit is Power.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit called 'Power' in the same sense as the Father and the Son, so that He is not inferior to them?

question: Does the case against the Son's eternal generation, argued from reason alone, ultimately depend on denying that God's essence is above human comprehension?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds that the controversy, managed on mere reason, terminates in the single question whether God's essence is above comprehension. The Catholics affirmed it is incomprehensible, while the Eunomians consistently denied it; anyone who argues from the nature of the thing against the Son's generation must either take shelter in that bold denial or give up those arguments.
sources.quote: this controversy, managed upon the foot of mere reason, terminates at length in that single question, Whether the essence of God be above comprehension, or no. The Catholics stood up for the affirmative
sources.raw_question: Does the case against the Son's eternal generation, argued from reason alone, ultimately depend on denying that God's essence is above human comprehension?

question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit share one and the same will, calling, and command, or does each Person have a separate will?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter X. Being about to prove that the will, the calling, and the commandment of the Trinity is one, St. Ambrose shows that the Spirit called the Church exactly as the Father and the Son did, and proves this by the selection of SS. Paul and Barnabas, and especially by the mission of St. Peter to Cornelius. And by the way he points out how in the Apostle's vision the calling of the Gentiles was shadowed forth, who having been before like wild beasts, now by the operation of the Spirit lay aside that wildness. Then having quoted other passages in support of this view, he shows that in the case of Jeremiah cast into a pit by Jews, and rescued by Abdemelech, is a type of the slighting of the Holy Spirit by the Jews, and of His being honoured by the Gentiles.
sources.answer: They share one and the same will, calling, and giving of commands, just as their operation is one. Ambrose shows this in the calling of the Church: the Father called the Gentiles through the prophets, Christ chose Paul to bear His name to the nations, and the Spirit likewise called and sent Paul and Barnabas. One calling is ascribed to each Person, so the will of the Trinity is one.
sources.quote: not only is the operation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit everywhere one but also there is one and the same will, calling, and giving of commands, which one may see in the great and saving mystery of the Church.
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit share one and the same will, calling, and command, or does each Person have a separate will?

question: Is the Son, who took the form of a servant and became incarnate, equal with God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory proceeds to discuss the relative force of the unnameable name of the Holy Trinity and the mutual relation of the Persons, and moreover the unknowable character of the essence, and the condescension on His part towards us, His generation of the Virgin, and His second coming, the resurrection from the dead and future retribution.
sources.answer: Yes. Being in the form of God, the Son thought it not robbery to be equal with God. He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became incarnate of the Virgin. He redeemed us by his blood as a ransom and will come in the Father's glory to judge.
sources.quote: For He “being in the form of God thought it not robbery to be equal with God, but made Himself of no reputation, and took upon Him the form of a servant,”
sources.raw_question: Is the Son, who took the form of a servant and became incarnate, equal with God?

question: Is the Spirit by whom the gifts are distributed the same Person as the Spirit in whom they are distributed?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Hilary says Paul refutes this view by saying it is 'the same God Who worketh all things in all.' So there is one who distributes and another in whom the distribution is given. Yet it is always God who works all these things, in such a way that Christ works and the Son in His working performs the Father's work.
sources.quote: So there is one Who distributes and another in Whom the distribution is vouchsafed. Yet know that it is always God Who worketh all these things, but in such a way that Christ works, and the Son in His working performs the Father’s work.
sources.raw_question: Is the Spirit by whom the gifts are distributed the same Person as the Spirit in whom they are distributed?

question: Is Eunomius consistent in claiming to know God's essence while challenging others to define the nature of the ages?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that God's essence is unapproachable and incomprehensible to human beings. One who claims to define it on his own authority should be the one to explain the ages. His demand for an answer from others shows presumption rather than real knowledge.
sources.quote: For it is he who professes to know the essence of God, defining on his own authority what is unapproachable and incomprehensible by man.
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius consistent in claiming to know God's essence while challenging others to define the nature of the ages?

question: Did the Father create the Son in the same way the creation was made through the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: No. Such a supposition denies the Godhead of the Only-begotten, reducing him to a creature. Since worshipping the creature rather than the Creator is the mark of idolatry, a created Son could not rightly be worshipped.
sources.quote: the Father created Him in like manner as the creation was made by the Son,—then we retract our former statement, because such a supposition is a denial of the Godhead of the Only-begotten.
sources.raw_question: Did the Father create the Son in the same way the creation was made through the Son?

question: Can one consistently worship the Son while denying that he shares the Father's nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: No. Whoever severs the Son from the Father's nature must either refuse to worship the Son, lest he worship an alien God, or else worship a creature, which is idolatry, merely giving the name of Christ to an idol.
sources.quote: he who severs the Son from the nature of the Father either absolutely disallows the worship of the Son, that he may not worship an alien God, or bows down before an idol
sources.raw_question: Can one consistently worship the Son while denying that he shares the Father's nature?

question: Does saying that we speak 'in the Holy Spirit' imply that the Spirit is subordinate, as an instrument?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VIII. St. Ambrose examines and refutes the heretical argument that because God is said to be glorified in the Spirit, and not with the Spirit, the Holy Spirit is therefore inferior to the Father. He shows that the particle in can be also used of the Son and even of the Father, and that on the other hand with may be said of creatures without any infringement on the prerogatives of the Godhead; and that in reality these prepositions simply imply the connection of the Three Divine Persons.
sources.answer: No. Paul also says we speak 'in Christ,' and Christ is not lessened by this; likewise 'No man saith Lord Jesus, except in the Holy Spirit' signifies a connection of grace, not subjection of the Spirit. It is faith that commends a syllable, not a syllable that prejudices faith.
sources.quote: So, then, in this place not any subjection of the Holy Spirit, but a connection of grace is signified.
sources.raw_question: Does saying that we speak 'in the Holy Spirit' imply that the Spirit is subordinate, as an instrument?

question: Do the prepositions 'in' and 'with' differ in a way that separates the Spirit from the Father and Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VIII. St. Ambrose examines and refutes the heretical argument that because God is said to be glorified in the Spirit, and not with the Spirit, the Holy Spirit is therefore inferior to the Father. He shows that the particle in can be also used of the Son and even of the Father, and that on the other hand with may be said of creatures without any infringement on the prerogatives of the Godhead; and that in reality these prepositions simply imply the connection of the Three Divine Persons.
sources.answer: No. Both are conjunctive particles, and the Apostle uses them indifferently. A conjunction by its nature joins rather than divides; if it divided it would not be called a conjunction.
sources.quote: For each is a conjunctive particle, and conjunction does not cause separation, for if it divided it would not be called a conjunction.
sources.raw_question: Do the prepositions 'in' and 'with' differ in a way that separates the Spirit from the Father and Son?

question: If Eunomius holds that immortality is the very essence of God the Father, does it follow that the Son, being likewise immortal, shares the same essence as the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory presses a dilemma: Eunomius must either deny that the Son's essence is immortality, in which case by the logic of contradictories he makes the Son's essence death, or affirm it, in which case Father and Son are both immortality. Since immortality admits no internal difference, no difference of essence can then be found between Father and Son, by the opponents' own premise.
sources.quote: If the nature of the Father and the nature of the Son are equally immortality, and if immortality does not divide itself by any manner of difference, then it is confessed by our foes themselves, that on the score of essence no manner of difference is discoverable between the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: If Eunomius holds that immortality is the very essence of God the Father, does it follow that the Son, being likewise immortal, shares the same essence as the Father?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being Creator prove that He is God of one Godhead with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVIII. As he purposes to establish the Godhead of the Holy Spirit by the points already discussed, St. Ambrose touches again on some of them; for instance, that He does not commit but forgives sin; that He is not a creature but the Creator; and lastly, that He does not offer but receives worship.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul contrasts the creature with "the Creator, Who is God blessed for ever," and Hebrews says "He that created all things is God." Nothing has been created apart from Father, Son and Holy Spirit. So the opponents must either name something made without the Spirit or confess Him one Godhead with the Father and Son.
sources.quote: Let them, therefore, either say what it is which has been created without the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, or let them confess that the Spirit also is of one Godhead with the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being Creator prove that He is God of one Godhead with the Father and the Son?

question: When Scripture says the Son is 'from God' (from Himself), does this mean the Son is from some other source, from nothing, or truly from the Father's own nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: The Son is truly from the Father's own nature. 'From Himself' cannot mean 'from some one else', because the Son's Godhead has no source other than God. It cannot mean 'from nothing', because it names the nature from which He is born. Nor does it make the Son identical with the Father, since the text says 'from Himself', not 'Himself', and so shows they are related as Father and Son.
sources.quote: It is not “From some one else,” for it is From Himself; that is, His Godhead has no other source than God. It is not “From nothing,” for it is From Himself; a declaration of the nature from which His birth is.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says the Son is 'from God' (from Himself), does this mean the Son is from some other source, from nothing, or truly from the Father's own nature?

question: Did Christ exist before the worlds, or did he begin to exist only as man?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Christ existed before the worlds. His activity is from everlasting, as the opponents of Sabellius rightly prove against Sabellius and Hebion. The Church confesses him as very God of very God, born before the worlds and born in after times as man.
sources.quote: the Lord Jesus Christ is very God of very God, born before the worlds and born in after times as man.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ exist before the worlds, or did he begin to exist only as man?

question: Does the birth of the Son introduce a duality of Gods into the Godhead?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. The unity of God is consistent with the birth of the Son. The birth involves no duality in the Godhead, and Christ's being true God is shown without breach of the mysterious unity.
sources.quote: the eighth book is taken up with the proof of the unity of God, shewing that this unity is consistent with the birth of the Son, and that the birth involves no duality in the Godhead.
sources.raw_question: Does the birth of the Son introduce a duality of Gods into the Godhead?

question: Do texts saying believers are 'one' (Acts 4:32, 1 Cor 3:8, John 17:20-21) show that the Father and Son are one only in will and mind, not in Divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary calls this plea helpless and absurd. Read in their true sense, these texts point to the reality of the Divine birth rather than reducing the unity of Father and Son to agreement of will.
sources.quote: a unity of will and mind, not of Divinity, is expressed. From a consideration of the true sense of these texts we shew that they involve the reality of the Divine birth
sources.raw_question: Do texts saying believers are 'one' (Acts 4:32, 1 Cor 3:8, John 17:20-21) show that the Father and Son are one only in will and mind, not in Divinity?

question: Is the Spirit of the Father the same as the Holy Spirit, given that Scripture also calls angels spirits?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IV. The Holy Spirit is one and the same Who spake in the prophets and apostles, Who is the Spirit of God and of Christ; Whom, further, Scripture designates the Paraclete, and the Spirit of life and truth.
sources.answer: Yes. In Matthew, Christ says the Spirit of the Father speaks in persecuted believers, and in Luke the same promise is attributed to the Holy Spirit. So the two are one. Although angels and many other beings are called spirits, the Spirit of God is only one.
sources.quote: So, although many are called spirits, as it is said: “Who maketh His Angels spirits,” yet the Spirit of God is but one.
sources.raw_question: Is the Spirit of the Father the same as the Holy Spirit, given that Scripture also calls angels spirits?

question: Does the distinct communication of grace by each divine Person imply that believers have distinct communion with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Grace is communicated distinctly from the several Persons of the Deity. It follows that the saints must hold distinct communion with each of them. This confirms what was already shown from the fact that all worship and obedience are distinctly directed to Father, Son, and Spirit.
sources.quote: there being such a distinct communication of grace from the several persons of the Deity, the saints must needs have distinct communion with them.
sources.raw_question: Does the distinct communication of grace by each divine Person imply that believers have distinct communion with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

question: In what sense is God the Father also the Lord of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Only through the Dispensation of the Incarnation. The Father is Father in the generation of the Only-begotten, but Lord only where the other is a servant; the Son was not a servant by nature at first but became one by assuming manhood. Thus the Father is Lord on the same grounds as the Son is servant.
sources.quote: The Son was not at the first a servant by nature, but afterwards began to be by nature something which He was not before. Thus the Father is Lord on the same grounds as the Son is servant.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is God the Father also the Lord of the Son?

question: Is it a sound argument that unity excludes a second, so that the Father and the Son, being Two, cannot be One God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. The argument is the world's wisdom, which is folly with God. Scripture itself teaches both that God is One and that there is God and God. Moses and the Gospels confirm one another, so the unity of God and the Godhead of the Son stand together.
sources.quote: For the Gospels tell us that Moses taught the truth when he proclaimed that God is One; and Moses by his proclamation of One God confirms the lesson of the Gospels, which tell of God and God.
sources.raw_question: Is it a sound argument that unity excludes a second, so that the Father and the Son, being Two, cannot be One God?

question: What makes a thing 'true', and does that bear on whether the Son is true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: The truth, or genuineness, of a thing is a matter of its nature and powers. True wheat, for example, is known by its natural properties and uses. So whether the Son is true God must be judged by whether He has the divine nature and powers.
sources.quote: It is clear that the truth, or genuineness, of a thing is a question of its nature and its powers.
sources.raw_question: What makes a thing 'true', and does that bear on whether the Son is true God?

question: Should the name 'generation' or 'sonship' refer to the Word's eternal existence from the Father or to his temporal procession to create?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Both usages can be true when rightly explained. Tertullian and Hippolytus called the temporal going forth the 'perfect nativity' of the Word. Other Fathers saw this way of speaking was open to abuse, since the Word could properly be called Son in respect of his eternal existence in and from the Father as root and cause. They therefore called that eternal existence 'generation' and the later going forth a condescension or manifestation.
sources.quote: they chose to give that the name of generation : and to call the other two fcondescensions, manifestations, proceeding forth, or the like.
sources.raw_question: Should the name 'generation' or 'sonship' refer to the Word's eternal existence from the Father or to his temporal procession to create?

question: If both the Father and the Son are called the Beginning, are there two beginnings of creation?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > How the Word Beginning (Principium) is Spoken Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: No. The Father and the Son together are one beginning with respect to the creature. They are so as one Creator and one God, so naming each 'Beginning' does not multiply principles of creation.
sources.quote: we do not speak of two beginnings of the creature; since both the Father and the Son together is one beginning in respect to the creature, as one Creator, as one God.
sources.raw_question: If both the Father and the Son are called the Beginning, are there two beginnings of creation?

question: Since it is good to be the Father of such a Son, does God's goodness imply that the Father always had the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. What is naturally good was never absent from God, and there is no cause, neither lack of power nor weakness of will, by which the good could fail to be always present with Him who is good. Hence the Father, always willing the good and having the power for it, always possessed the Son.
sources.quote: That it is irreverent to believe that what is naturally good was not in God: for that he saw no cause by which it was probable that the good was not always present with Him Who is good, either for lack of power or for weakness of will.
sources.raw_question: Since it is good to be the Father of such a Son, does God's goodness imply that the Father always had the Son?

question: Do the names 'Father, Son, and Holy Spirit' in Matthew 28:19 reveal the mutual relations of the Trinitarian Persons, such as subordination or derivation of being?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Not as certainly as commonly supposed. These designations are characteristic only of Jesus and John, not preserved by the New Testament writers at large, and the implications usually drawn from them do not certainly lie in them. In Semitic usage sonship denotes likeness, so 'Son' asserts equality with the Father rather than subordination, any implication of derivation being very distant.
sources.quote: the implications with respect to the mutual relations of the Trinitarian Persons, which are ordinarily derived from these designations, do not so certainly lie in them as is commonly supposed.
sources.raw_question: Do the names 'Father, Son, and Holy Spirit' in Matthew 28:19 reveal the mutual relations of the Trinitarian Persons, such as subordination or derivation of being?

question: Is a begotten son something external to his father, like a possession acquired from without?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: No. A son by nature is not acquired from outside like a house or possession, which passes from one owner to another; he is from the father himself, proper and similar to his essence, and the father is wholly in him while remaining himself. So likewise the Word is simply from the Father, not from without.
sources.quote: For things which are from without are possessions, and pass from one to another; but my son is from me, proper and similar to my essence, not become mine from another, but begotten of me
sources.raw_question: Is a begotten son something external to his father, like a possession acquired from without?

question: Is the Word of God eternal and co-existent with the Father rather than made from nothing?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: Yes. Since the Son is admitted to be a natural offspring from the Father and not from without, and nothing can restrain God from always being Father, the Word is ever co-existent with Him. Natural examples such as the sun and its radiance or a fountain and its stream show an offspring always existing with its source; to deny this of God would make Him inferior to created things.
sources.quote: it follows that the Word is from Him and is ever co-existent with Him, through whom also the Father caused that all things which were not should be.
sources.raw_question: Is the Word of God eternal and co-existent with the Father rather than made from nothing?

question: Does Scripture's calling Christ "the wisdom of God" show that the Son is God's eternal idea of Himself?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. God's wisdom or knowledge is the same as His perfect and eternal idea. So if Scripture teaches that Christ is God's wisdom, it teaches that He is God's perfect idea. Christ is called the wisdom of God in the New Testament, and He speaks under the name of Wisdom in Proverbs, especially chapter 8.
sources.quote: If we are taught in the Scripture that Christ is the same with God's wisdom or knowledge, then it teaches us that He is the same with God's perfect and eternal idea.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's calling Christ "the wisdom of God" show that the Son is God's eternal idea of Himself?

question: Does the fact that creatures have a beginning of existence prove that the Son of God also had a beginning and was not always with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. The Divine essence and the created nature must not be judged in the same way. None of the other marks of creation appear in the Maker of creation. So the creation's having a beginning is no proof that the Son, who is Wisdom, Power, Light and Life, was not always in the Father. Eunomius is wrong to use creaturely attributes to separate the Only-begotten from the Father's eternity.
sources.quote: For as none other of the marks which characterize the creation appears in the Maker of the creation, so neither is the fact that the creation has its existence from some beginning a proof that the Son was not always in the Father
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that creatures have a beginning of existence prove that the Son of God also had a beginning and was not always with the Father?

question: Is the Father's eternal Word like a human spoken or thought word that unfolds in time?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. A human word that makes a sound or is thought before being spoken is completed in spaces of time, but the Word of God is eternal. It speaks to us by enlightening us about itself and about the Father.
sources.quote: yet not as a word producing a sound proceeds from the mouth, or is thought before it is pronounced. For this word is completed in certain spaces of time, but that is eternal
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's eternal Word like a human spoken or thought word that unfolds in time?

question: Was God called 'ungenerate' or 'Father' before any creatures existed, so that divine names precede created conception?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius' claim makes it seem that God, if unnamed, would be ignorant or forgetful of Himself, which is absurd. Neither the Son, nor the Spirit, nor incorporeal powers need names to know God, so there was no naming of God before creatures; names are a device arising from human need.
sources.quote: as being afraid lest, His name not being uttered among creatures as yet unborn, He should be ignorant or forgetful of Himself, through ignorance of His own nature because of His name being unspoken
sources.raw_question: Was God called 'ungenerate' or 'Father' before any creatures existed, so that divine names precede created conception?

question: Is the Holy Spirit given to us in the same way as the Son was given?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: Yes. As the Son was given ('unto us a Son is given'), so the grace of the Spirit is given, and indeed the Spirit Himself is given, as Romans 5:5 says. Christ first led captivity captive so that freed hearts could receive Him, and then poured forth the good gift.
sources.quote: for as the Son was given, of Whom it is written: “Unto us a Child is born, unto us a Son is given;” so, too, is the grace of the Spirit given.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit given to us in the same way as the Son was given?

question: Does the Holy Spirit have goodness in Himself as the source of goodness, as the Father and the Son do?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: Yes. As the Father and the Son have goodness, so does the Holy Spirit, since He is the Source and Principle of goodness. The Apostle names goodness among the fruit of the Spirit. Since a good tree brings forth good fruit, He whose fruit is goodness must be good.
sources.quote: For as the Father and the Son have, so too the Holy Spirit also has goodness. And the Apostle also taught this when he said: “Now the fruit of the Spirit is peace, love, joy, patience, goodness.”
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit have goodness in Himself as the source of goodness, as the Father and the Son do?

question: How can God be one while the Father, Son and Spirit are distinct?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: There is one form of Godhead, and it is in the Word. The one God, the Father, exists by himself as above all, appears in the Son as pervading all things, and acts in the Spirit in all things through the Word. Thus God is confessed as one through the Triad. This is more religious than the heretics' godhead of many kinds and parts.
sources.quote: For there is but one form of Godhead, which is also in the Word; and one God, the Father, existing by himself according as He is above all, and appearing in the Son according as He pervades all things
sources.raw_question: How can God be one while the Father, Son and Spirit are distinct?

question: If the Son is created from nothing like the world, differing from creatures only in order of precedence, must he share the same nature as the world?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He convicts Eunomius of having used of the Only-begotten terms applicable to the existence of the earth, and thus shows that his intention is to prove the Son to be a being mutable and created.
sources.answer: Yes, and this is a blasphemous consequence. Where the definition of essence is the same, the nature is not different, as Peter and John share one nature. So if the Lord were of the same kind as the parts of the world, he would be subject to whatever belongs to them, and would pass away with heaven and earth.
sources.quote: knowing that where the definition of things is the same neither is their nature different. For as the definition of the essence of Peter and John and other men is common and their nature is one
sources.raw_question: If the Son is created from nothing like the world, differing from creatures only in order of precedence, must he share the same nature as the world?

question: If Peter, James and John share one human nature and are rightly called three men, why should the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who share one divine nature, not be called three Gods?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: Calling many individuals who share one nature "many men" is itself a customary abuse of language. Gregory compares it to saying "many human natures." The term "man" names the common nature, not the individual as such, so the nature remains one even when the persons are many. On this view there is no inconsistency in confessing three Persons and yet one Godhead, and so not three Gods.
sources.quote: but the man in them all is one; since, as has been said, the term “man” does not belong to the nature of the individual as such, but to that which is common.
sources.raw_question: If Peter, James and John share one human nature and are rightly called three men, why should the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who share one divine nature, not be called three Gods?

question: If God begot the Son willingly, does it follow that the Son is Son by will and not by nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Against Eunomius, Saying that the Son of God is the Son, Not of His Nature, But of His Will. Epilogue to What Has Been Said Already.
sources.answer: No. The heretic's question can be turned back on him by asking whether the Father is God willingly or unwillingly. If unwillingly, God would be miserable, which is madness to believe. If willingly, then by the same reasoning God would be God by will and not by nature. The dilemma therefore proves nothing against the Son's being Son by nature.
sources.quote: demanded of him in turn, whether God the Father was God willingly or unwillingly; in order that if he answered unwillingly, that misery would follow
sources.raw_question: If God begot the Son willingly, does it follow that the Son is Son by will and not by nature?

question: Does the Holy Spirit possess Godhead as the Father and the Son do?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIX. Having proved above that the Spirit abides and speaks in the prophets, St. Ambrose infers that He knows all things which are of God, and therefore is One with the Father and the Son. This same point he establishes again from the fact that He possesses all that God possesses, namely, Godhead, knowledge of the heart, truth, a Name above every name, and power to raise the dead, as is proved from Ezekiel, and in this He is equal to the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father has Godhead, and the fulness of the Godhead dwells in the Son. Scripture also says "The Spirit of God is in my nostrils," showing that the Spirit has Godhead too.
sources.quote: God the Father has Godhead, and the Son, too, in Whom dwells the fulness of the Godhead, has it, and the Spirit has it
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit possess Godhead as the Father and the Son do?

question: If the Son is God from God, does the Christian confession of Father and Son introduce two Gods or two first principles?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: No. The Word, being Son of the One God, is referred back to Him from whom He is, so Father and Son are two while the Monad of the Godhead remains indivisible. There is one Beginning of Godhead and hence a true Monarchy, because the Son is not another self-subsisting beginning nor produced externally, but the own Son, Word and Wisdom existing from the one Beginning.
sources.quote: so that Father and Son are two, yet the Monad of the Godhead is indivisible and inseparable. And thus too we preserve One Beginning of Godhead and not two Beginnings, whence there is strictly a Monarchy.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is God from God, does the Christian confession of Father and Son introduce two Gods or two first principles?

question: How are the texts 'I and the Father are one', 'I am in the Father and the Father in Me', and 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father' related?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: They carry one and the same sense. Whoever understands that the Son and Father are one knows that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son, since the Son's Godhead is the Father's; and so he sees that whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father, for the Father's Godhead is contemplated in the Son.
sources.quote: there is one and the same sense in these three passages. For he who in this sense understands that the Son and the Father are one, knows that He is in the Father and the Father in the Son
sources.raw_question: How are the texts 'I and the Father are one', 'I am in the Father and the Father in Me', and 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father' related?

question: In what distinct way does the Holy Spirit contribute to the believer's spiritual quickening, as compared with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: The Spirit quickens by way of immediate efficacy. Romans 8:11 says the Father who raised Christ will quicken our mortal bodies "by his Spirit that dwelleth in you," so the Spirit is the one who directly and immediately effects the work, while the Father's quickening is authoritative and the Son's is mediatory.
sources.quote: and the Spirit’s immediate efficacy, — “He shall do it by the Spirit that dwelleth in you.”
sources.raw_question: In what distinct way does the Holy Spirit contribute to the believer's spiritual quickening, as compared with the Father and the Son?

question: Does assigning a particular aspect of communion to one Person of the Trinity exclude the other Persons from that same communion?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: No. When a thing is assigned as peculiar to one Person, the other Persons are not excluded from communion with the soul in that very thing. The point is only that the communion is held with that one Person principally, immediately and by way of eminency.
sources.quote: I do not exclude the other persons from communion with the soul in the very same thing. Only this, I say, principally, immediately, and by the way of eminency, we have, in such a thing, or in such a way, communion with some one person
sources.raw_question: Does assigning a particular aspect of communion to one Person of the Trinity exclude the other Persons from that same communion?

question: Do the prepositions "in Him," "through Him," and "with Him" used of Christ in creation imply different or lesser roles for the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: No. Scripture uses them as equivalent: all things were made in Him and through Him, and Wisdom was with the Father in creating. These expressions signify one and the same in all respects, uniting the Son to the Father rather than separating Him, so by parity "in Spirit" unites the Spirit with God in worship.
sources.quote: These words, “in Him” and “with Him,” have this force, that by them is understood one and like in all respects, not contrary.
sources.raw_question: Do the prepositions "in Him," "through Him," and "with Him" used of Christ in creation imply different or lesser roles for the Son?

question: Does the fact that the Spirit of God is also the Spirit of Christ prove that Christ is God by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
