sources.answer: Yes. Whatever is of God is also of Christ, and whatever is of Christ is also of God. So Christ cannot be anything different from what God is. Christ is therefore God, one Spirit with God.
sources.quote: And so since what is of God is also of Christ, and what is of Christ is also of God, Christ cannot be anything different from what God is. Christ, therefore, is God, one Spirit with God.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Spirit of God is also the Spirit of Christ prove that Christ is God by nature?

question: Does the Son's generation from the Father involve a division or severance of the Father's substance?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The Son is perfect from the perfect and whole from the whole, and there is no division because each is in the other and the fulness of the Godhead is in the Son. The life of the living God is in the living Christ.
sources.quote: The Son is perfect from Him that is perfect, for He is whole from Him that is whole. This is no division or severance, for Each is in the Other, and the fulness of the Godhead is in the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's generation from the Father involve a division or severance of the Father's substance?

question: If the Word is from God, are the Father and the Son two, and in what sense are they one?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: They are two, yet one. That which is from another is distinct from that from which it is, so Father and Son are two. They are one because the Son is not from outside but is begotten of God. If the names belonged to the same subject, cause and effect, begetter and begotten, would be identical. That is the absurdity of Sabellius.
sources.quote: But if it be unseemly so to say, Father and Son must be two; and they are one, because the Son is not from without, but begotten of God.
sources.raw_question: If the Word is from God, are the Father and the Son two, and in what sense are they one?

question: Do Christ's words to Mary, "Touch me not, for I am not yet ascended to my Father... my God and your God" (John 20:17), prove that the Son is inferior to the Father, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > This twelfth book gives a notable interpretation of the words of the Lord to Mary, “Touch Me not, for I am not yet ascended to My Father.”
sources.answer: No. Eunomius's reading was invented only to destroy the glory of the Only-begotten. The true reading takes in the aim of the dispensation for mankind. It was not the intangible, immutable and invisible God who gave Mary this command, but the moving, visible and tangible human nature of Christ. The words therefore speak of Christ's humanity and of our reconciliation, not of any degradation of the Son's divinity.
sources.quote: it was not the intangible, immutable, and invisible God, but the moving, visible, and tangible nature which is proper to humanity, that gave command to Mary to minister the word to His disciples
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's words to Mary, "Touch me not, for I am not yet ascended to my Father... my God and your God" (John 20:17), prove that the Son is inferior to the Father, as Eunomius claims?

question: Can one ask whether the Holy Spirit had already proceeded from the Father before the Son was born, or only proceeded from both after the Son's birth?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: No. Such questions are impossible in the Godhead, where nothing begins in time to be perfected in a later time. Unlike the human mind, where will precedes the found notion and love then proceeds from both, in God there are no distinct times, no sooner and later.
sources.quote: These things it is absolutely impossible to ask in this case, where nothing is begun in time, so as to be perfected in a time following.
sources.raw_question: Can one ask whether the Holy Spirit had already proceeded from the Father before the Son was born, or only proceeded from both after the Son's birth?

question: Does the Son's calling the Father 'Lord' after the incarnation deny the eternity of His Godhead?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. Just as we, calling the Lord Father by grace, do not deny our natural servitude, so the Son, calling the Father Lord on taking the servant's form, does not lose the eternity of His Godhead. He did this out of love for man, so that we, servants by nature, receiving the Spirit of the Son, might call God Father by grace.
sources.quote: so when the Son, on taking the servant’s form, says, ‘The Lord created me a beginning of His ways,’ let them not deny the eternity of His Godhead, and that ‘in the beginning was the Word,’
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's calling the Father 'Lord' after the incarnation deny the eternity of His Godhead?

question: When the Holy Spirit takes of what is the Son's, does He receive from a creature, and does He receive something other than what is the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No to both. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God and does not receive of a creature; what He takes of the Son He takes also of the Father, because all that the Father has belongs equally to the Son. All things of the Father are the Spirit's.
sources.quote: the Holy Spirit takes of His, but takes also of the Father’s: and if He receives of the Father’s, He receives also of His.
sources.raw_question: When the Holy Spirit takes of what is the Son's, does He receive from a creature, and does He receive something other than what is the Father's?

question: Is the Son's likeness to the Father the same kind of likeness as man's creation in the image and likeness of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. The likeness of man to God spoken of in Genesis 1:26 is not the likeness between Father and Son. To apply it would make the Only-begotten God identical with man, which not even Eunomius would hold.
sources.quote: but I do not suppose that Eunomius would discern this kind of likeness between the Father and the Son, so as to make out the Only-begotten God to be identical with man
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's likeness to the Father the same kind of likeness as man's creation in the image and likeness of God?

question: Is saying that the Son came to be by the Father's will and pleasure equivalent to saying that the Son once was not and is a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Athanasius holds that the phrase 'the Son came to be at the Divine will,' as used by the Arians, carries the same meaning as 'Once He was not,' 'out of nothing,' and 'He is a creature.' The Arians adopted the language of 'will' because they were ashamed of their earlier phrases, but they still intend the same heresy. If a believer used the phrase in simplicity with right intention it might be tolerated, but in heretical mouths it is a disguise.
sources.quote: For he who says, ‘The Son came to be at the Divine will,’ has the same meaning as another who says, ‘Once He was not,’ and ‘The Son came to be out of nothing,’ and ‘He is a creature.’
sources.raw_question: Is saying that the Son came to be by the Father's will and pleasure equivalent to saying that the Son once was not and is a creature?

question: Did the Son begin to be Son at some point, so that the Father became Father at a time?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Nothing is Spoken of God According to Accident, But According to Substance or According to Relation.
sources.answer: No. The Son was always born and never began to be the Son. Therefore the Father never began or ceases to be Father.
sources.quote: but because the Son was always born, and never began to be the Son
sources.raw_question: Did the Son begin to be Son at some point, so that the Father became Father at a time?

question: According to Novatian, how can the Father be called the one God while the Son is also truly God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: Because the Son is so intimately one with the Father by communion of substance that he is reckoned to the Father and is not another God from him. All recurs to one head and fountain, the Father. The divinity sent forth to the Son returns again to the Father through communion of substance. So it is all one divinity, or divine substance, of the Father in both.
sources.quote: the Son is so intimately one with him, as to be reckoned, in a manner, to him, and not another God from him. It is all but one divinity, or divine substance, of the Father in both.
sources.raw_question: According to Novatian, how can the Father be called the one God while the Son is also truly God?

question: When Athanasius denies that Christ is 'the only God' against the Sabellians, does he mean that the Son is not the only God in any sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. Athanasius denies only that Christ is the Father, or the only God in the Sabellian sense. The plain translation shows this. A man may therefore believe the Son to be the only God without being a Sabellian.
sources.quote: a man may believe the Son to be the only God, without being a Sabellian.
sources.raw_question: When Athanasius denies that Christ is 'the only God' against the Sabellians, does he mean that the Son is not the only God in any sense?

question: Does 1 Corinthians 15:24-28, where all things are subjected to the Son except the one who subjected them, show that the Son and the Father are distinct?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: Yes. Since all things are put under the Son except the Father who put them under him, the Son is Lord of all and the Father is Lord of the Son. In this way one God is manifested, to whom all things are made subject together with Christ.
sources.quote: He is Lord of all, and the Father is Lord of Him, that in all there might be manifested one God, to whom all things are made subject together with Christ
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 15:24-28, where all things are subjected to the Son except the one who subjected them, show that the Son and the Father are distinct?

question: In what sense is it true that the Son, whose existence comes from generation, did not exist before his generation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > He then shows the eternity of the Son's generation, and the inseparable identity of His essence with Him that begat Him, and likens the folly of Eunomius to children playing with sand.
sources.answer: It is true only if 'generation' means the Father. To be father is the same as to have begotten, so paternity and generation are identical. Read this way, the statement means that he whose existence is from the Father was not before the Father, which is sound. Read as an independent generation separated from the Father, the statement is unintelligible.
sources.quote: Since then to be father is the same as to have begotten, if any one shifts the words from one form of speech to the other, paternity will be shown to be identical with generation.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is it true that the Son, whose existence comes from generation, did not exist before his generation?

question: Did the Nicene Fathers teach only a specific (generic) consubstantiality of the Son with the Father, such as one man has with another?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: No. The word homoousios expresses their sense but not their whole sense: it signifies equality of nature, which was chiefly to be insisted on against the Arians. But the Fathers added qualifying clauses (God of God, Light of Light, of the substance of the Father, without division) to guard against tritheism and preserve the unity of the undivided substance.
sources.quote: The word ὁμοούσιος expresses their sense; but not their whole sense, in that article. It expresses an eguality of nature, and signifies that the Son is as truly equal in nature to the Father, as one man is egual to another
sources.raw_question: Did the Nicene Fathers teach only a specific (generic) consubstantiality of the Son with the Father, such as one man has with another?

question: If the Son were merely homoousios with the Father in the way one human person is with another, would Father and Son be two Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: Yes. Homoousios is necessary for the Son to be God in the strict sense, but it is not alone sufficient for Father and Son to be one God; bare specific consubstantiality like that of two men would make two Gods. Hence the Nicene Fathers stressed both coequality and the undivided substance, guarding equally against Arianism and Tritheism.
sources.quote: 4Opoodσιος the Son must be, or he could not be God at all, in the strict sense ; and yet if he was barely ὁμοούσιος, like as one human person is to another, the fwo would be two Gods.
sources.raw_question: If the Son were merely homoousios with the Father in the way one human person is with another, would Father and Son be two Gods?

question: Does the fact that the Son is not the same individual Person from whom he was begotten imply that his substance is divided from the Father's?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: No. It is true that the Son is not that Person from whom he proceeded, but the substance may nevertheless be undivided, which is all that Catholics mean by individual substance. Dr. Clarke wrongly equates 'individual substance' with individual hypostasis or Person.
sources.quote: it is very true, that the Son is not that Person, from whom, or of whom, he proceeded: but the substance might be wndivided notwithstanding ; which is all that any Catholic means by individual substance.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Son is not the same individual Person from whom he was begotten imply that his substance is divided from the Father's?

question: Does the Son's equality with God require that He share the identical nature of the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. The Evangelist himself judges that the Son made Himself equal with God, and equality can exist only through identity of nature. What is begotten can only derive what it is from its source. It therefore cannot be foreign to the one who begets it.
sources.quote: equality cannot exist except by identity of nature. The begotten cannot derive what it is save from its source and the thing generated cannot be foreign to that which generates it
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's equality with God require that He share the identical nature of the Father?

question: If the Son is eternal because God is always Father, must creatures also be eternal because God is always Maker?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: No. A work is external to the maker's nature and is made when he wills, so one may be called Maker before any works exist. A son, however, is the proper offspring of the essence and is not subject to will, and no one can be or be called father unless a son exists.
sources.quote: a work is external to the nature, but a son is the proper offspring of the essence; it follows that a work need not have been always, for the workman frames it when he will; but an offspring is not subject to will, but is proper to the essence
sources.raw_question: If the Son is eternal because God is always Father, must creatures also be eternal because God is always Maker?

question: Are the Father, Son and Holy Spirit each properly persons, given that the Son is identified as the divine understanding and the Spirit as the divine love?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. All three are persons because each has understanding and will. The Father has them as the Son and Spirit are in Him and proceed from Him; the Son as He is understanding and the Spirit is in Him and proceeds from Him; the Spirit as He is the divine will and the Son is in Him.
sources.quote: All the Three are Persons for they all have understanding and will.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father, Son and Holy Spirit each properly persons, given that the Son is identified as the divine understanding and the Spirit as the divine love?

question: How can the Son be begotten by the Father and the Spirit proceed from Father and Son, yet all three be co-eternal?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: On Edwards's account the Son is God's eternal idea or understanding of Himself and the Spirit is the eternal love flowing between them, so these processions are not temporal events but necessary acts of the divine nature. Hence begetting and procession are compatible with co-eternity, and the Spirit's procession from both Father and Son is illustrated.
sources.quote: Hereby we see how that it is possible for the Son to be begotten by the Father and the Holy Ghost to proceed from the Father and Son, and yet that all the Persons should be Co-etemal.
sources.raw_question: How can the Son be begotten by the Father and the Spirit proceed from Father and Son, yet all three be co-eternal?

question: Can the Father, Son and Holy Spirit be one God merely because all three exercise one and the same authority, if they are three distinct Beings?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. On Clarke's scheme the three are distinct Beings. A shared authority cannot make three distinct Beings individually one God, because that would amount to saying three Persons are one Person.
sources.quote: That is hard to conceive how three distinct Beings, according to the Doctor's scheme, can be individually one God, that 1s, three Persons one Person.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father, Son and Holy Spirit be one God merely because all three exercise one and the same authority, if they are three distinct Beings?

question: Do believers have distinct communion and fellowship with the Holy Spirit as a Person when they are comforted by Christ's promises?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. In this work of the Spirit believers have communion and fellowship with him in particular. When the soul feels a promise warming and relieving it, it ought to know that the Holy Ghost is there. Recognising him in his work adds to its joy and leads it into fellowship with him.
sources.quote: No sooner doth the soul begin to feel the life of a promise warming his heart, relieving, cherishing, supporting, delivering from fear, entanglements, or troubles, but it may, it ought, to know that the Holy Ghost is there
sources.raw_question: Do believers have distinct communion and fellowship with the Holy Spirit as a Person when they are comforted by Christ's promises?

question: Are the Father and the Son one Supreme God by being one Person, or in some other way?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: They are one Supreme God not by being one Person, but by being one in substance, power, and perfection. Waterland rejects the insinuation that his view collapses into a unity of Person, holding that the unity lies in substance.
sources.quote: Father and Son both are the one Supreme God: not one in Person, as you frequently and groundlessly insinuate, but in substance, power, and perfection.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and the Son one Supreme God by being one Person, or in some other way?

question: Does the statement that all things are of God and through the Son (1 Cor 8:6) separate the Holy Spirit from the operation of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: No. If that text excluded the Spirit, then Romans 9:5, which calls Christ "over all, God blessed for ever," would by the same reasoning set Christ above the Father, which is impious. The Father is not one among the crowd of his creatures. Over all creation stands the Godhead of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, which rules and is worshipped, while creation serves and worships.
sources.quote: The whole creation is below, over all is the Godhead of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The former serves, the latter rules; the former is subject, the latter reigns
sources.raised_by_detail: those who deny the Spirit's deity
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that all things are of God and through the Son (1 Cor 8:6) separate the Holy Spirit from the operation of the Father and the Son?

question: Would denying that the Son and Holy Spirit always coexist with the Father detract from the Father's glory and goodness?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is the Father's glory, and the Spirit is the Son's glory. To strip the Almighty of the Son and Spirit would leave a God removed from every good and godlike deed and thought. So whatever in the Trinity is supposed not to coexist with the Father would diminish God himself.
sources.quote: if following out this heresy any thought could be entertained of stripping the Almighty of the glory of the Son and Holy Ghost, it would end in nothing else than in a God manifestly removed from every deed and thought that was good and godlike.
sources.raw_question: Would denying that the Son and Holy Spirit always coexist with the Father detract from the Father's glory and goodness?

question: If the Father is greater because he gives, is the Son less because he receives?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The Giver is greater, but the Receiver is not less, because what is given to him is to be one with the Giver. He is confessed as Lord in the glory of God the Father. The prerogative of giving shows the Father greater, while the confession of the gift shows that the Two are One.
sources.quote: The Giver is greater: but the Receiver is not less, for to Him it is given to be one with the Giver.
sources.raw_question: If the Father is greater because he gives, is the Son less because he receives?

question: Can the Son be confessed as a God of a second or lower order than God the Father without falling into error?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Making the Only-begotten a God of the second order by assigning different grades of divinity amounts to professing two Gods, which is a damning profession of impiety. Such teaching estranges the Son from the power and nature of God the Father, which He truly possesses.
sources.quote: in either case a damning profession of impiety, whether one profess two Gods by making different grades of divinity; or else deny divinity altogether to Him Who drew His nature by birth from God.
sources.raised_by_detail: teachers who preach not God but a creature
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be confessed as a God of a second or lower order than God the Father without falling into error?

question: Does affirming the Son as true God mean believing in two true Gods?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The Apostolic faith forbids two true Gods, because nothing foreign to the nature of the one God can be equal to it. There would be two Gods only if a true God of another kind existed outside the nature of the only true God. The Son, however, possesses the same nature by virtue of his birth.
sources.quote: if there exists outside the nature of the only true God a true God of another kind, not possessing by virtue of His birth the same nature with Him.
sources.raw_question: Does affirming the Son as true God mean believing in two true Gods?

question: Does the Son's sharing the Father's eternity show that his likeness to the Father is perfect, as in "He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
sources.answer: Yes. Because the Son shares the Father's eternity along with all his attributes, there is no divergence at all between the Likeness and the one whose Likeness he is. This is why Christ's saying is true that whoever has seen him has seen the Father.
sources.quote: in this respect, more especially, is seen the complete absence of divergence in the Likeness, as compared with Him Whose Likeness He is. And herein is His saying found true
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's sharing the Father's eternity show that his likeness to the Father is perfect, as in "He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father"?

question: Does the Son acquire existence by being generated, so that generation marks his coming into being?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: No. Eunomius claims the Son acquired existence by being generated, but no sound philosophy supports this. 'Generated' signifies only that the Son was begotten of the Father as cause. Because his existence is bound to the Father's eternal Existence, he was both begotten and always was, and there was no moment when he did not exist.
sources.quote: not agreeing with us that Generated is to be used only because the Son was generated, and Ungenerate because the Father exists without having been generated; but affirming that he thinks the former has acquired existence by having been generated
sources.raw_question: Does the Son acquire existence by being generated, so that generation marks his coming into being?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being sent, given, and poured out show that he is a created servant or merely an impersonal power of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: No. Scripture gives him personal properties in this very work, especially that he himself 'proceeds' of his own accord. This shows his personality and liberty, against those who make him an inferior created spirit or merely God's power.
sources.quote: that this Spirit were altogether an inferior, created spirit, a mere servant, as some have blasphemed, nor yet merely and principally, as to his personality, the virtue of God, as some have fancied
sources.raised_by_detail: those who make the Spirit a created servant or merely the virtue of God
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being sent, given, and poured out show that he is a created servant or merely an impersonal power of God?

question: Is it consistent for Eunomius to find unlikeness only between the Father and the Son while ignoring the great diversity within the created world?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that the same energies produce the same works, and that variation in the works indicates variation in the energies.
sources.answer: No. The world is full of dissimilar things: light and heavy, still and moving, hot and cold, and countless animals and plants. All of these come from one divine command. Eunomius's principle would require a universal likeness in creation, so applying it selectively to make the Son unlike the Father is arbitrary.
sources.quote: Can it be that he does see here a universal likeness, and detects unlikeness only between the Father and the Son?
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent for Eunomius to find unlikeness only between the Father and the Son while ignoring the great diversity within the created world?

question: Does God need words or names in order to know and distinguish things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Humans need verbal notation to keep their memory of absent things unconfused, but to God all things are present within His penetrating vision and He needs no memory. His own wisdom and power hold the nature of all things distinct and unconfused, so names exist for our sake, not His.
sources.quote: But to God all things are present, nor does He need memory, all things being within the range of His penetrating vision. What need, then, in His case, of parts of speech
sources.raw_question: Does God need words or names in order to know and distinguish things?

question: Is Eunomius' concern to avoid passion in God the real reason he denies the Son's generation from the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius does not actually see passion in the divine and incorruptible nature. He uses his pretended caution about passion so that the Maker of all creation may be counted part of creation. His real aim is to deny the Only-begotten God.
sources.quote: to the end that the Maker of all creation may be accounted a part of creation, he builds up these arguments in order to a denial of the Only-begotten God, and uses his pretended caution about passion to help him in his task
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius' concern to avoid passion in God the real reason he denies the Son's generation from the Father?

question: Does St. Paul's statement 'to us there is but one God, the Father' exclude the Son's being God, and does it tell more against the orthodox or against the Arians?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: It tells more against the Arians than against the orthodox. The Arians make the Son a second God, God to us in the same relative sense in which Paul uses the word, and so plainly contradict him. The orthodox make the Son essentially the same one God. Both sides need a distinction to read the text, and the orthodox distinction is older and better warranted. The Son is tacitly included because he partakes of the same divine nature.
sources.quote: Whether, think you, do we, who make him essentially the same God with that one, and suppose but one God in all, more flatly contradict St. Paul; or you, who make ¢wo Gods, and in the same relative sense, in which St. Paul is supposed to use the word God?
sources.raw_question: Does St. Paul's statement 'to us there is but one God, the Father' exclude the Son's being God, and does it tell more against the orthodox or against the Arians?

question: Does Scripture require that the Son receive the same honour as the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His elaborate account of degrees and differences in 'works' and 'energies' within the Trinity is absurd.
sources.answer: Yes. The evangelist's words 'that all may honour the Son, as they honour the Father' are a law establishing equality of honour. Whoever assigns more honour to the Father and less to the Son annuls both the law and its Giver.
sources.quote: This utterance (and such an utterance is a law to us) makes a law of this equality in honour: yet this man annuls both the law and its Giver
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture require that the Son receive the same honour as the Father?

question: Since honouring God means loving him with the whole heart, can the Son be honoured less than the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His elaborate account of degrees and differences in 'works' and 'energies' within the Trinity is absurd.
sources.answer: No. Reverence for God is at bottom love and the confession of his perfections. The command to honour the Son as the Father stands in place of the command to love God with all the heart and strength. No one can love the Son with the whole heart yet honour him only by half, so nothing can exceed the honour due to him.
sources.quote: No one can say that we ought to love Him with all our heart and strength, but to honour Him only with half.
sources.raw_question: Since honouring God means loving him with the whole heart, can the Son be honoured less than the Father?

question: When Christ answered the rich young man 'Why callest thou Me good? None is good save one, God,' was He denying that He Himself is good or that He is God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Christ did not repudiate the name 'good' but rebuked the unbelief of the youth who addressed Him merely as a human teacher of the law. By adding 'None is good save one, God' He showed how He may rightly be called good, namely as God. He then performed the functions of divine goodness by opening heavenly treasures and offering Himself as guide, so His words and actions at that moment were those of the one God.
sources.quote: None is good, save one, God, not repudiating the name of good, if it be given to Him as God.
sources.raw_question: When Christ answered the rich young man 'Why callest thou Me good? None is good save one, God,' was He denying that He Himself is good or that He is God?

question: Does the Son's not being ungenerate mean that he is not God, as Eunomius' claim that God is never called "Son" or "generate" implies?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > He then declares that the close relation between names and things is immutable, and thereafter proceeds accordingly, in the most excellent manner, with his discourse concerning “generated” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. Gregory exposes the argument as blasphemy resting on an illegitimate inversion. The valid converse of "no generated thing is ungenerate" is "nothing naturally ungenerate is generate," not "God is not generate." By swapping "God" in for "ungenerate," Eunomius ranks the Son with all generated things and shuts him out from being God. This contradicts Scripture's witness that the Word in the beginning was God.
sources.quote: by his premise that no generated thing is ungenerate, and his inference that God is not generated, he clearly shuts out the Only-begotten God from being God, laying down that because He is not ungenerate, neither is He God
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's not being ungenerate mean that he is not God, as Eunomius' claim that God is never called "Son" or "generate" implies?

question: Do privative names such as 'immortal' and 'indestructible' signify that death and destruction are absent from God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Every conceivable thing is either absent from something or present in it, as with light and darkness or life and death. To deny that 'immortal' signifies the absence of death is therefore to imply that death is present in God. That would make Eunomius' God mortal and subject to destruction. Ordinary usage confirms this reading: we call a man 'sound' because disease is absent from him, and 'unmutilated' because he has no mutilation.
sources.quote: If, then, Eunomius denies that God can be called immortal by reason of the absence of death, he will plainly prove the presence of death in Him, and so deny any immortality in the case of the universal Deity.
sources.raw_question: Do privative names such as 'immortal' and 'indestructible' signify that death and destruction are absent from God?

question: If 'First-born of all creation' meant the Son were a creature in essence, what would follow about his relation to irrational and lifeless things?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: It would make him the brother and fellow of beings without reason and life, since these are also parts of creation. A first-born is first only in time and is the same in kind with the rest. That conclusion is so irreligious that it refutes the Arian reading.
sources.quote: let them reflect that they will be conceiving Him as brother and fellow of the things without reason and life. For of the whole creation these also are parts
sources.raw_question: If 'First-born of all creation' meant the Son were a creature in essence, what would follow about his relation to irrational and lifeless things?

question: Does the Son's birth from the Father give the Son the Father's own power, authority and nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. Through the mystery of the birth, the Son's power, authority and nature are the Father's. As the Father's image he reproduces all that is in the Father. He is the reality as well as the image, since a perfect birth produces a perfect image.
sources.quote: Through the Mystery of the birth the Son’s power is the power of the Father, His authority the Father’s authority, His nature the Father’s nature.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from the Father give the Son the Father's own power, authority and nature?

question: In what ways do believers have communion with the Holy Spirit, and how do these correspond to his person and works?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: There are three general ways, each stated negatively in Scripture but each containing a positive duty: not grieving him, not quenching him, and not resisting him. These match three things in the Spirit. Not grieving answers to his person dwelling in us, not quenching to the actings and motions of his grace, and not resisting to his working in Christ's ordinances and gifts.
sources.quote: 1. Not to grieve him, in respect of his person dwelling in us. 2. Not to quench him, in respect of the actings and motions of his grace. 3. Not to resist him, in respect of the ordinances of Christ
sources.raw_question: In what ways do believers have communion with the Holy Spirit, and how do these correspond to his person and works?

question: If the Son came into being by the Father's will like the creatures, would there have to be another Word through whom He was made?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. That would follow, which shows the Arian position to be absurd. All things that the Father wills come to be through the Word, so if the Son were by will there would have to be another Word before Him. Scripture knows of no such Word, and positing one leads to an endless series and to polytheism.
sources.quote: If then there is another Word of God, then be the Son originated by a word; but if there be not, as is the case, but all things by Him have come to be, which the Father has willed
sources.raw_question: If the Son came into being by the Father's will like the creatures, would there have to be another Word through whom He was made?

question: Is the Holy Spirit owed the same faith, worship and obedience as the Father and the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Baptism into his name binds us to believe in him, obey him and worship him, just as it binds us to the Father and the Son. He also commands that the church's ministers be set apart to himself, as in Acts 13:2, which takes in all the church's religious worship.
sources.quote: For our being baptized into his name, is our solemn engagement to believe in him, to yield obedience to him, and to worship him, as it puts the same obligation upon us to the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit owed the same faith, worship and obedience as the Father and the Son?

question: Does Scripture's calling the Son of God the 'true Light' prove that the Son is true God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIV. Each Person of the Trinity is said in the sacred writings to be Light. The Spirit is designated Fire by Isaiah, a figure of which Fire was seen in the bush by Moses, in the tongues of fire, and in Gideon's pitchers. And the Godhead of the same Spirit cannot be denied, since His operation is the same as that of the Father and of the Son, and He is also called the light and fire of the Lord's countenance.
sources.answer: Yes. Since John says God is Light, and the Evangelist calls the Son 'the true Light which lighteth every man,' it follows without doubt that the Son of God is true God. Being Light pertains to the power of God.
sources.quote: So, then, since God is Light, and the Son of God the true Light, without doubt the Son of God is true God.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's calling the Son of God the 'true Light' prove that the Son is true God?

question: Does the Son's being called the Brightness of eternal Light imply that he shines with a radiance unlike the Father's, or only for a time?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIV. Each Person of the Trinity is said in the sacred writings to be Light. The Spirit is designated Fire by Isaiah, a figure of which Fire was seen in the bush by Moses, in the tongues of fire, and in Gideon's pitchers. And the Godhead of the same Spirit cannot be denied, since His operation is the same as that of the Father and of the Son, and He is also called the light and fire of the Lord's countenance.
sources.answer: No. The Son is the Brightness of the Father, the eternal Light. He is always with the Father and always shines, not with an unlike radiance but with the same radiance. This also proves that the Father is Light.
sources.quote: Who both is always with the Father, and always shines, not with unlike but with the same radiance.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being called the Brightness of eternal Light imply that he shines with a radiance unlike the Father's, or only for a time?

question: Does the unity of Father and Son imply a solitary God, as the modalists hold?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The saying 'He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father Which hath sent Him' shows that the Son is distinct, because he is sent and is not the Father. A unity constituted through birth cannot be solitary. Solitude has only a single occupant, whereas such a unity implies the conjunction of two.
sources.quote: an unity constituted through birth cannot be solitary; for solitude can have but a single occupant, while an unity constituted through birth implies the conjunction of Two.
sources.raw_question: Does the unity of Father and Son imply a solitary God, as the modalists hold?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's work as Comforter warrant a distinct, particular communion of believers with the Holy Spirit himself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen sets out to show how believers hold particular communion with the Holy Ghost as the Comforter promised by Christ. He holds that this communion is prepared for by rightly valuing the Spirit's work of consolation: what he comforts us against, what he comforts us with, and the principle from which he acts.
sources.quote: I come to show how we hold particular communion with the Holy Ghost, as he is promised of Christ to be our comforter
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's work as Comforter warrant a distinct, particular communion of believers with the Holy Spirit himself?

question: Can the Son be a creature made out of nothing and still rightly be called the Son of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. If the Son were an arbitrary creation like other beings, there would be no reason to call him Son. To say he was made from nothing makes him a bastard rather than the true and only Son. The names Father and Son are given by God to indicate realities, so they must be taken in their plain sense: a Father who begot and a Son truly born of his nature.
sources.quote: Since He is the true and only Son, let us not make Him a bastard by asserting that He was made out of nothing.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be a creature made out of nothing and still rightly be called the Son of God?

question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each possess their own self-determining will according to Scripture?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture ascribes a will to each: the Father works all things after the counsel of his own will, the Son wills to reveal the Father and says "Father, I will," and the Spirit divides gifts to each as He wills. Yet believers rest on the will of the one Lord who alone is Jehovah.
sources.quote: Dividing to every one severally as He wills (βούλεται). 1 Cor. 12:11.
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each possess their own self-determining will according to Scripture?

question: Does Scripture explicitly call the Holy Spirit good?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: Yes. For those who want express statements and not only works, David says, "Let Thy good Spirit lead me forth in the right way." The Spirit is full of goodness.
sources.quote: let them hear that the Holy Spirit is good, for David said: “Let Thy good Spirit lead me forth in the right way.”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture explicitly call the Holy Spirit good?

question: Why does it matter whether the Son is truly begotten of the Father rather than a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds again to discuss the impassibility of the Lord's generation; and the folly of Eunomius, who says that the generated essence involves the appellation of Son, and again, forgetting this, denies the relation of the Son to the Father: and herein he speaks of Circe and of the mandrake poison.
sources.answer: Because the whole of Christian hope is at stake. Denying the truly begotten Son would amount to agreeing with the Jews. Worshipping the Son as a creature would mean falling into the idolatry of the heathen. Only the true doctrine avoids both errors.
sources.quote: that we may neither agree with the doctrine of the Jews by a denial of the verily begotten Son, nor be involved in the downfall of the idolaters by the adoration of the creature
sources.raw_question: Why does it matter whether the Son is truly begotten of the Father rather than a creature?

question: What does the title 'Son' signify about Christ's relation to God the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: It signifies a true, real and natural relationship to the Almighty. Just as 'Son of Man' marks his kinship with his mother according to the nature of the flesh, 'Son' marks his natural connexion with the Father.
sources.quote: so also by the title of Son he expresses His true and real relationship to the Almighty, by that name of Son showing this natural connexion
sources.raw_question: What does the title 'Son' signify about Christ's relation to God the Father?

question: Does the Father's willing the existence of the Son imply that the Son came into being after the Father, separated from Him by an interval?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He then discusses the “willing” of the Father concerning the generation of the Son, and shows that the object of that good will is from eternity, which is the Son, existing in the Father, and being closely related to the process of willing, as the ray to the flame, or the act of seeing to the eye.
sources.answer: No. Just as a flame endowed with choice would at once will its radiance and the radiance would at once exist, so the Father's act of will concerning the Son does not delay or separate the Son's existence. We apprehend simultaneously the eternal existence of the Father, His will concerning the Son, and the Son Himself. The movement of choice is no hindrance to the dignity of the Son's existence.
sources.quote: you will not, by confessing the good act of will as existing in the Father, separate by that act of will the Son from the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's willing the existence of the Son imply that the Son came into being after the Father, separated from Him by an interval?

question: Is God's begetting of the Son prior to His creating by will, and why?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: Yes. What is by nature lies above and before what is by will. If God makes external things that were not by willing them, much more is He first Father of an Offspring from His own essence. The Word comes first and creation second, since the one who disposes is prior to the things disposed.
sources.quote: God’s creating is second to His begetting; for Son implies something proper to Him and truly from that blessed and everlasting Essence; but what is from His will, comes into consistence from without
sources.raw_question: Is God's begetting of the Son prior to His creating by will, and why?

question: Do different effects (such as the Son and the Spirit as distinct works) require correspondingly different energies in the producer, so that Eunomius can infer degrees of being among the Father, Son and Spirit from differences of their 'energies'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that Scripture teaches all things were made by the single word of God's command, and the vast diversity of created things shows that one divine energy produces varied effects. Eunomius's principle that varied works need varied energies is a bare assertion, no better than telling dreams, and cannot ground a ranking of the divine Persons.
sources.quote: Or because differences of products imply differences of producers, as if it were impossible that different effects should be produced by similar energies?
sources.raw_question: Do different effects (such as the Son and the Spirit as distinct works) require correspondingly different energies in the producer, so that Eunomius can infer degrees of being among the Father, Son and Spirit from differences of their 'energies'?

question: Does the equality of love with wisdom in God prove that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Holy Spirit Also is Equal to the Father and the Son in All Things.
sources.answer: Yes. If love were less than wisdom in God, wisdom would be loved less than it deserves. So love must be equal to wisdom, so that wisdom is loved according to its being. Since wisdom (the Son) is equal to the Father, the Spirit as love is also equal.
sources.quote: For if love is less great therein [i.e. in God] than wisdom, then wisdom is loved in less degree than according to what it is; love is therefore equal, in order that wisdom may be loved according to its being
sources.raw_question: Does the equality of love with wisdom in God prove that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son?

question: Is the Holy Spirit the unity of Father and Son by participation or by gift from a superior?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Holy Spirit Also is Equal to the Father and the Son in All Things.
sources.answer: Neither. The Father and Son keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace not by participation and not by the gift of any superior, but by their own essence. Creatures are commanded to imitate this unity by grace.
sources.quote: through whom, not by participation, but by their own essence, neither by the gift of any superior, but by their own, they are “keeping the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace;”
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit the unity of Father and Son by participation or by gift from a superior?

question: Is the Holy Spirit inseparable from the Father and the Son in every operation?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: Yes. In every operation the Spirit is closely conjoined with and inseparable from the Father and the Son. Scripture shows that God works the operations and the Lord the administrations, while the Spirit is present of His own will distributing the gifts, so all three act together.
sources.quote: in every operation the Spirit is closely conjoined with, and inseparable from, the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit inseparable from the Father and the Son in every operation?

question: Are 'generate' and 'ungenerate' the most fitting names for expressing the Divine essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > Thereafter he discusses the divergence of names and of things, speaking, of that which is ungenerate as without a cause, and of that which is non-existent, as the Scindapsus, Minotaur, Blityri, Cyclops, Scylla, which never were generated at all, and shows that things which are essentially different, are mutually destructive, as fire of water, and the rest in their several relations. But in the case of the Father and the Son, as the essence is common, and the properties reciprocally interchangeable, no injury results to the Nature.
sources.answer: No. If the divine essence is to be named, it should be by lofty names like good, incorruptible, just and wise, which belong strictly to the Nature beyond understanding. 'Generated' is shared even with dogs and frogs. 'Ungenerate' is also applied to non-existent things like the Minotaur, Scylla or the Chimaera, which never came into being at all. These terms are equivocal and so cannot define God's essence.
sources.quote: “good” and “incorruptible,” “just” and “wise,” and all such terms as these are strictly applicable only to that Nature which passes all understanding, whereas “generated” exhibits community of name with even the inferior forms of the lower creation.
sources.raw_question: Are 'generate' and 'ungenerate' the most fitting names for expressing the Divine essence?

question: Does the Son's role as the one 'through whom' blessings come from the Father mean the Son is a mere instrument or servant carrying out detailed commissions?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. Basil denies that the Son used assistance or was entrusted with each work by detailed commission, since that would be menial and unworthy of the divine dignity. Rather the Word is full of the Father's excellences and does all things according to the likeness of the One who begat Him, fulfilling the Father's creative will, not discharging slavish service.
sources.quote: We are not to suppose that He used assistance in His action, or yet was entrusted with the ministry of each individual work by detailed commission, a condition distinctly menial and quite inadequate to the divine dignity.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's role as the one 'through whom' blessings come from the Father mean the Son is a mere instrument or servant carrying out detailed commissions?

question: Does calling the Son's generation 'eternal' involve equivocation, given that the word 'generation' is used of the Son in a sense different from human generation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. 'Generation' is a word of latitude with more than one sense, and the Church has used it for fifteen hundred years in a proper sense, following Tertullian's rule that every origin is a parent. It is not the same as human generation, but human generation is not the measure and standard of all generation.
sources.quote: True, it is not the same with human generation. But who will pretend that human is to be the measure and standard of all generation?
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son's generation 'eternal' involve equivocation, given that the word 'generation' is used of the Son in a sense different from human generation?

question: If Father, Son, and Holy Spirit all work jointly in creation, redemption, and sanctification, why is creation attributed especially to the Father, redemption to the Son, and sanctification to the Spirit?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: Because Infinite Wisdom has chosen, for great ends, to attribute each work to one Person rather than another. All three are jointly concerned in each work, yet the Father may be called Creator, the Son Redeemer, and the Holy Ghost Sanctifier in an emphatic sense. The distinct worship of each Person among men began when these titles were revealed. This is a matter of how the works are ascribed. It does not mean only one Person is involved.
sources.quote: yet it may seem good to Infinite Wisdom, for great ends and reasons, to attribute each respectively to one Person rather than another; so that the Father may be emphatically Creator, the Son Redeemer, the Holy Ghost Sanctifier
sources.raw_question: If Father, Son, and Holy Spirit all work jointly in creation, redemption, and sanctification, why is creation attributed especially to the Father, redemption to the Son, and sanctification to the Spirit?

question: According to 1 John 1:3, do believers truly have communion with God, and is that communion with both the Father and the Son Jesus Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Yes. The apostle asserts with emphatic, almost oath-like force that the fellowship of believers is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. So the saints have a real, holy and spiritual communion with God. Though this fellowship looked mean and contemptible to a carnal view, it is honourable, glorious and desirable. How it relates distinctly to the Father and to the Son is to be opened later.
sources.quote: This being so earnestly and directly asserted by the apostle, we may boldly follow him with our affirmation, — namely, “That the saints of God have communion with him.”
sources.raw_question: According to 1 John 1:3, do believers truly have communion with God, and is that communion with both the Father and the Son Jesus Christ?

question: Why does the oneness of wisdom in the Trinity imply that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one essence and one God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: Because in the Trinity to be is the same as to be wise, so one wisdom entails one essence. Likewise, in the Trinity it is not one thing to be and another to be God. Therefore the three are one God.
sources.quote: because in the Trinity to be is the same as to be wise, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, are one essence. Neither in the Trinity is it one thing to be and another to be God
sources.raw_question: Why does the oneness of wisdom in the Trinity imply that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one essence and one God?

question: Does the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 ascribe a threefold personality to the one God of Israel?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Jesus gives Jehovah a new Name for His community, the threefold Name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost. By "the Son" He meant Himself, with all the distinct personality that implies, and this carries with it the equally distinct personality of the Father and the Spirit. That is a direct ascription of threefold personality to Jehovah, and so a direct statement of the doctrine of the Trinity.
sources.quote: This is a direct ascription to Jehovah the God of Israel, of a threefold personality, and is therewith the direct enunciation of the doctrine of the Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 ascribe a threefold personality to the one God of Israel?

question: Does Jesus deny that he is good or divine in asking the rich young ruler 'Why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is God'?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. The ruler saw him only as a human teacher and put his own good works on the same level, so Christ refused homage built on false assumptions. The stress falls on 'why', which was meant to expose the man's self-ignorance and self-righteousness. The ruler unknowingly knelt before Jehovah our righteousness, whose goodness is perfect.
sources.quote: The Lord refused such homage. It was founded on false assumptions. Its acceptance would have strengthened a yet unhumbled self-righteousness. "Why," he asked, "why callest thou me good?" The stress is on the "why".
sources.raw_question: Does Jesus deny that he is good or divine in asking the rich young ruler 'Why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is God'?

question: Is there any name, specific or generic, that properly answers the question 'three what?' about the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: No. When we look for a special or general name to cover the three, none comes to mind. This is because the super-eminence of the Godhead surpasses the power of ordinary speech. God is more truly thought than he is spoken of, and exists more truly than he is thought.
sources.quote: and no such name occurs to the mind, because the super-eminence of the Godhead surpasses the power of customary speech
sources.raw_question: Is there any name, specific or generic, that properly answers the question 'three what?' about the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Since there is no difference of essence among the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, should they be named by a specific name rather than a generic one, and is 'person' such a specific name?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: They ought to have a specific name, but none is to be found, and 'person' is not one. Only a difference of nature forces us to use a merely generic name, as with a laurel, a myrtle and an olive. Where there is no difference of essence, a specific name is required. 'Person', however, is a generic name, since it is applied even to man despite the vast difference between man and God.
sources.quote: But here, where there is no difference of essence, it is necessary that these three should have a specific name, which yet is not to be found. For person is a generic name, insomuch that man also can be so called
sources.raw_question: Since there is no difference of essence among the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, should they be named by a specific name rather than a generic one, and is 'person' such a specific name?

question: Is Christ God only in name rather than in nature, so that the Father is greater by nature and the Son a creature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. The Son is born truly from God and so shares the very nature of the one true God. He is therefore very God and not a creature of a different nature. Christ's own sayings affirm a unity of nature with the Father.
sources.quote: we declare the true nativity of Only-begotten God from God the Father, because that through this He was both very God and not alien from the nature of the One very God
sources.raw_question: Is Christ God only in name rather than in nature, so that the Father is greater by nature and the Son a creature?

question: Does being less than the Father necessarily mean the Son has a nature alien from the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
