sources.answer: No. Hilary rejects the Arian inference from the Father being greater to a difference of natures. The perfect birth gives the Son the Father's own nature, without difference, so that the two are one God.
sources.quote: He Who is not one person with Him Who is, is yet so free from difference from Him that They Two are One God
sources.raw_question: Does being less than the Father necessarily mean the Son has a nature alien from the Father's?

question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit share one divine counsel?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter II. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are One in counsel.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah calls the Holy Spirit "the Spirit of Counsel and of Power," just as the Son is called the Angel of great counsel, which shows that the counsel of Father, Son, and Spirit is one. This counsel is not deliberation about doubtful matters. It concerns things foreknown and determined.
sources.quote: so, too, is the Holy Spirit the Spirit of Counsel, that you may know that the Counsel of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is One
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit share one divine counsel?

question: When Scripture says God alone stretched out the heavens (Job 9:8; Isaiah 44:24), does the word "alone" exclude the Son from being Creator or from being the one God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. According to Athanasius, whom Waterland cites as expressing the general sense of the pre-Nicene Catholics, the Word is included in the one who is said to be alone. The heavens were made by the Word, yet God says "I alone" made them. So the Son is understood to be with the alone God. In the "one, alone, and first" the Word is comprehended, as radiance is implied in light.
sources.quote: we are undoubtedly to understand, that in the one, alone, and “ first, is comprehended the Word, as effulgency, ἀπαύγασμα, is ‘implied in light.”
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says God alone stretched out the heavens (Job 9:8; Isaiah 44:24), does the word "alone" exclude the Son from being Creator or from being the one God?

question: Does calling Christ 'the beginning of the creation of God' (Rev. 3:14) imply that he was the first thing created?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Every other use of ἀρχή in the Apocalypse is the Lord's title 'the beginning and the end.' So in Rev. 3:14 it refers to his preexistent eternity. It declares him the origin or originator, the First Cause of God's creation.
sources.quote: it regards the preexistent eternity, the “from everlasting” of the Lord, and as such declares him to be the beginning, or origin, or originator, or precisely as we say, the First Cause of the creation of God.
sources.raw_question: Does calling Christ 'the beginning of the creation of God' (Rev. 3:14) imply that he was the first thing created?

question: Does the Son's handing over the kingdom to the Father and becoming subject to him (1 Cor. 15:24-28) mean that Christ's kingdom and supremacy will end?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. The subjection concerns Christ as the second Man and federal Head of the church. His mediatorial pleading will cease once sin and death are abolished, and he will forever keep the Father's commandments as our Representative. Yet Scripture also says his kingdom shall have no end and his throne is forever. He shares a real and undivided supremacy with the Father, and the love of God will always be manifested through him.
sources.quote: a time will come when He will no longer exercise his mediatorial office, by pleading the virtue of his blood for penitent sinners (seeing that sin and death are forever abolished)
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's handing over the kingdom to the Father and becoming subject to him (1 Cor. 15:24-28) mean that Christ's kingdom and supremacy will end?

question: Does Paul's confession of 'one God the Father' exclude the Son from Godhead, since oneness seems not to admit partnership?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Paul names one God as Father precisely so that the Son's birth cannot be denied, and adds one Lord Jesus Christ because faith in the Father alone does not suffice for salvation. In 'one God and one Lord' he utters the mystery of an indivisible unity. Moreover, if being 'one God' denied Christ Godhead, then Christ being 'one Lord' would deny the Father Lordship, which is absurd.
sources.quote: he has uttered the mystery of that indivisible and indissoluble unity and faith in the words one God and one Lord.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's confession of 'one God the Father' exclude the Son from Godhead, since oneness seems not to admit partnership?

question: Does the same Spirit working in both the Father and the Son prove the unity of Father and Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. Since the Spirit of God is the same as the Spirit of Christ, and one Spirit works and divides gifts in the ministration of the Lord and the working of God, those whose properties are those of one cannot but be one.
sources.quote: They cannot but be one Whose properties are those of one; since in the same Lord the Son, and in the same God the Father, one and the same Spirit distributing in the same Holy Spirit accomplishes all things
sources.raw_question: Does the same Spirit working in both the Father and the Son prove the unity of Father and Son?

question: Can the Son be denied an identical nature with the Father while still being called the one Lord?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Unless the Son is one Lord through unity of the Spirit with the Father, there would be no room for God the Father also to be Lord. The one lordship therefore requires an identical nature.
sources.quote: For unless through unity of the Spirit He is one Lord room will not be left for God the Father to be Lord.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who preach the Only-begotten God is a creature
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be denied an identical nature with the Father while still being called the one Lord?

question: Did Christ become Son only in time through his Incarnation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Paul teaches that all things are through Him, which shows that His timeless infinity was creating all things before time began. He therefore existed as Son before the Incarnation.
sources.quote: let him who holds the Son to have become Son in time and by His Incarnation, learn that through Him are all things and we through Him, and that His timeless Infinity was creating all things before time was
sources.raw_question: Did Christ become Son only in time through his Incarnation?

question: Does affirming that the Word is eternally in the Beginning make the Father and the Word two separate beginnings?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: No. The beginning is one, and in it the Word is discerned indivisibly, completely united to the Father. Holding this guards against heresy's use of the term 'ungenerate' to divide the Son from the Father.
sources.quote: For the beginning is most assuredly one, wherein is discerned, indivisibly, that Word Who is completely united to the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that the Word is eternally in the Beginning make the Father and the Word two separate beginnings?

question: Is the Son truly the very Life, or only a 'generate life' distinct from and lesser than the Father's 'ungenerate life'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: The Son is the very Life. Eunomius calls Him 'life' but adds 'generate' to set Him against the 'ungenerate' life. This quietly denies that the Son is the very Life, so it is poison mixed into sound terms.
sources.quote: when he speaks of the “life” as “generate” he makes a reservation by the implied opposition to the “ungenerate” life, and does not affirm the Son to be the very Life.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son truly the very Life, or only a 'generate life' distinct from and lesser than the Father's 'ungenerate life'?

question: Should believers honour the Son as they honour the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that saints who do not honour Christ as they honour the Father are of all men the most unworthy. Indeed the great solemn worship of the Christian church consists in ascribing glory and dominion to the Lord Jesus, as seen in the doxologies of Revelation.
sources.quote: If they honour him not as they honour the Father, they are, of all men, the most unworthy.
sources.raw_question: Should believers honour the Son as they honour the Father?

question: Is there any interval of time or place in which the Son can be said not to have existed?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: No. There is no place in which He was not, since He is in the Father, and no time, since the Lord was before all times. No vacancy of substance or conception can be found by which the Father's life would surpass that of the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: When was it, then, that the Son was not? In what category shall we detect His non-existence? In place? There is none. In time? Our Lord was before all times; and if so, when was He not?
sources.raw_question: Is there any interval of time or place in which the Son can be said not to have existed?

question: Does the title 'Father' in God imply temporal priority of the Father over the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: No. The name Father signifies only that the Only-begotten derives the cause of His being from the Father, not a temporal precedence. The name conveys both Persons equally, so the Son is inevitably implied whenever the Father is named.
sources.quote: This name in fact conveys the two Persons equally; the idea of the Son is inevitably suggested by that word.
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'Father' in God imply temporal priority of the Father over the Son?

question: Does the oneness of the divine working of Father, Son, and Spirit imply a oneness of their Name?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIII. St. Ambrose shows from the Scriptures that the Name of the Three Divine Persons is one, and first the unity of the Name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as each is called Paraclete and Truth.
sources.answer: Yes. No one could deny the oneness of Name who sees the oneness of working. Ambrose adds that Scripture's plain testimony makes argument unnecessary, because the baptismal command names all three in one Name.
sources.quote: Who, then, would dare to deny the oneness of Name, when he sees the oneness of the working.
sources.raw_question: Does the oneness of the divine working of Father, Son, and Spirit imply a oneness of their Name?

question: Do the Son and the Holy Spirit share a oneness of power and presence?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIII. St. Ambrose shows from the Scriptures that the Name of the Three Divine Persons is one, and first the unity of the Name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as each is called Paraclete and Truth.
sources.answer: Yes. Both are called Paraclete, and with the oneness of Name goes a oneness of power: where the Paraclete Spirit is, there the Son is too. The Spirit is promised to be with the faithful for ever, and the Son promises to be with the apostles always. So their presence is one and indivisible.
sources.quote: Therefore the Son and the Spirit are one, the Name of the Trinity is one, and the Presence one and indivisible.
sources.raw_question: Do the Son and the Holy Spirit share a oneness of power and presence?

question: Does the fact that Scripture describes the Son's duration (Proverbs 8) in the same phrases it uses for God's own eternity (Psalm 90) show that the Son is coeternal with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland does not rest on the force of any single phrase, which might bear a limited sense, but on several phrases applied equally to both. Since God chose these phrases as the most significant to express his own duration, and then chose the very same to express his Son's duration, we are taught to believe the Son is coeternal with him.
sources.quote: considering that God had made choice of them, as most significant to express his own duration; and again made choice of the very same, out of many others, to express his Son’s duration too, we might from thence be taught to believe that the Son is coeternal with him.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Scripture describes the Son's duration (Proverbs 8) in the same phrases it uses for God's own eternity (Psalm 90) show that the Son is coeternal with the Father?

question: Was the Son of God made by the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says all things that were made were made by the Son. If the Father had made the Son, then something made would not have been made by the Son, since the Son did not make himself. So the Son was not made, but makes all things together with the Father.
sources.quote: Because if the Father made even the Son, whom certainly the Son Himself did not make, then all things were not made by the Son; but all things were made by the Son: therefore He Himself was not made
sources.raw_question: Was the Son of God made by the Father?

question: If the Son were a creature brought into being from nothing, why would all other things be made through Him alone rather than directly by God's same command?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: There would be no reason, which shows the Son is not a creature. God is not wearied by commanding nor unequal in strength to make all things, so if the Son came into being at God's bare command, all things could have come to be at that same command. That Scripture makes all things through the Word and places Him with the Father, not among 'all things', shows He is not one of the originated things.
sources.quote: For God is not wearied by commanding, nor is His strength unequal to the making of all things, that He should alone create the only Son, and need His ministry and aid for the framing of the rest.
sources.raw_question: If the Son were a creature brought into being from nothing, why would all other things be made through Him alone rather than directly by God's same command?

question: When Scripture says 'all things' were made through the Word, is the Son Himself included among the 'all things'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: No. When 'all things' are spoken of, only originated things are meant. Scripture places the Word with the Father as the one in whom providence and salvation for all are wrought by the Father. If all that is originate comes to be through the Son, He cannot be called one of the originated things.
sources.quote: if all that is originate comes to be through the Son, we must not call Him one of the originated things
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says 'all things' were made through the Word, is the Son Himself included among the 'all things'?

question: If the Son was created as an instrument so that God could create other creatures through him, does it follow that the Son exists for the sake of creatures rather than creatures for the sake of the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: Yes, on the Arian premise. That is exactly why the premise is absurd and irreligious. If the Word was made as an instrument for our need, then he was constituted from our need and owes thanks to us, as the woman was made for the man. But the truth is the reverse: the Word was not made for us, rather we for him, and in him all things were created. Even if God had never made anything, the Word would still have been with God.
sources.quote: God’s Word was made, as you must hold, not that He might be; but as an instrument for our need, so that not we from Him, but He is constituted from our need. Are not men who even conceive such thoughts, more than insensate?
sources.raw_question: If the Son was created as an instrument so that God could create other creatures through him, does it follow that the Son exists for the sake of creatures rather than creatures for the sake of the Son?

question: Is the single title 'Ungenerate' sufficient by itself to express God's eternity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: No. Eternity must be expressed by two titles, 'Ungenerate' and 'Endless,' because each states only one negation. 'Endless' indicates no end but says nothing of a beginning, while 'Unoriginate' expresses being beyond a beginning but leaves the question of an end doubtful; dropping either mars the meaning.
sources.quote: for it is impossible with either one of them singly to express the notion residing in each of the two
sources.raw_question: Is the single title 'Ungenerate' sufficient by itself to express God's eternity?

question: Could the Son rightly bear the titles 'Lord God' and 'God of Abraham' in his own right, or only as a stand-in for the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: In his own right. As Son of God he was really God, and as Son of the Almighty he was Almighty in his own right, as Tertullian says. So he could justly bear the style 'Lord God' while acting in that capacity, just as he later bore the titles Mediator and Messiah.
sources.quote: As Son of God, he was really God; and as Son of the Almighty, he was Almighty, in his own right, as P Tertullian expresses it
sources.raw_question: Could the Son rightly bear the titles 'Lord God' and 'God of Abraham' in his own right, or only as a stand-in for the Father?

question: Do names such as Understanding and Light describe God adequately?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. They are fitting, but God is above all these properties and cannot be described. He is an Understanding that comprehends all things, yet unlike human understanding, and Light, yet unlike the light we know. We use these terms out of love, but His greatness exceeds them.
sources.quote: He is, however, above [all] these properties, and therefore indescribable.
sources.raw_question: Do names such as Understanding and Light describe God adequately?

question: Does "all things were made by Him" in John 1:3 include the material creation we live in, or only higher spiritual beings such as the Gnostic Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: It includes our material creation. The Gnostics cannot restrict "all things" to beings within their Pleroma. If the Pleroma contains all things, then this creation is not outside it. If this creation were outside, the Pleroma would not be "all things." John settles the matter by saying that the world was made by Him and that He came to His own.
sources.quote: "All things," he says, "were made by Him;" therefore in "all things" this creation of ours is [included], for we cannot concede to these men that [the words] "all things" are spoken in reference to those within their Pleroma.
sources.raw_question: Does "all things were made by Him" in John 1:3 include the material creation we live in, or only higher spiritual beings such as the Gnostic Pleroma?

question: Does the Son's receiving something from the Father mean he received it after his birth, or that he is inferior in nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. He received it at his birth, not after it, so it is truly from Another and yet belongs to his nature from the start. By saying no one can pluck the sheep from the Father's hand, he forbids us to think he is different in kind from the Giver or does not eternally share his nature.
sources.quote: And He Who received it, received it at His birth, not after His birth, and yet it came to Him from Another, for He received it
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's receiving something from the Father mean he received it after his birth, or that he is inferior in nature?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's omnipresence distinguish His nature from that of created angels?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > The glorifying of the enumeration of His attributes.
sources.answer: Yes. Angels and other created powers are each in a circumscribed place, so the angel with Cornelius was not simultaneously with Philip. The Spirit, however, operated at the same time in Habakkuk, Daniel, Jeremiah and Ezekiel and fills the world, so His nature must be all-embracing, not confined to places like the angels'.
sources.quote: But what nature is it becoming to assign to Him who is omnipresent, and exists together with God? The nature which is all-embracing, or one which is confined to particular places, like that which our argument shews the nature of angels to be? No one would so say.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's omnipresence distinguish His nature from that of created angels?

question: Can the baptismal formula (Matthew 28:19) and the apostolic benediction (2 Corinthians 13:14) be read consistently with the view that Jesus was merely a man and the Holy Spirit merely an influence?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. On that view the baptismal formula would mean baptizing into "the Father, an exalted man, and an influence of the Father." The benediction would mean "the grace of a creature, the love of the Creator, and the communion of creative energy." Reason and conscience refuse to believe that Scripture sanctions such confusion between God and man, and between a person and an abstraction.
sources.quote: Your reason and conscience alike, refuse to believe that this inextricable confusion betwixt God and man, between a person and an abstraction, is sanctioned by Scripture.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who insist on the mere humanity of Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Can the baptismal formula (Matthew 28:19) and the apostolic benediction (2 Corinthians 13:14) be read consistently with the view that Jesus was merely a man and the Holy Spirit merely an influence?

question: Does the fact that the Son was given (as well as sent) by the Father imply that the Son is subject to the Father in his Godhead?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter II. The Son and the Spirit are alike given; whence not subjection but one Godhead is shown by Its working.
sources.answer: No. The Son also gave himself, as Paul says, and he cannot be subject to himself according to his Godhead. His being given was an act of grace, not a sign of subjection, so being given cannot indicate subjection in the Godhead.
sources.quote: inasmuch as the Son Himself gave Himself, He could not be subject to Himself according to His Godhead. Therefore that He was given could not be a sign of subjection in the God-head.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who argue the Son is subject because he was sent
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Son was given (as well as sent) by the Father imply that the Son is subject to the Father in his Godhead?

question: What does the fact that both the Son and the Holy Spirit are sent and given show about their relation to each other in the Godhead?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter II. The Son and the Spirit are alike given; whence not subjection but one Godhead is shown by Its working.
sources.answer: It shows that they share one Godhead. Scripture says the Spirit is given by the Father (John 14:16; 1 Thessalonians 4:8; Isaiah 42:5), just as the Son is given (Isaiah 42:6). Those who have a oneness of action have a oneness of Godhead. So being sent and given points to unity, not to inferiority.
sources.quote: Since, then, the Son is both sent and given, and the Spirit also is both sent and given, They have assuredly a oneness of Godhead Who have a oneness of action.
sources.raw_question: What does the fact that both the Son and the Holy Spirit are sent and given show about their relation to each other in the Godhead?

question: Does the Paraclete's receiving from Christ what he declares prove that Christ is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again from the Gospel He Proves Christ to Be God.
sources.answer: Yes. A mere man could give nothing to the Paraclete, since man receives knowledge, including knowledge of the future, from the Paraclete. So if Christ were only man, either his statement would be false or the order would be reversed. Because Christ does not deceive, the Paraclete truly receives from him, and this proves Christ's divinity.
sources.quote: if Christ were only man, Christ would receive from the Paraclete what He should say, not the Paraclete receive from Christ what He should declare
sources.raw_question: Does the Paraclete's receiving from Christ what he declares prove that Christ is God?

question: Why are negative or privative names such as 'unbeginning', 'incorporeal', and 'imperishable' applied to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: To separate the Supreme Being from the conditions of created things. Everything we comprehend involves extension, spatial capacity, bounding by beginning and end, or qualities of change and suffering; so we use terms denying these of God. Such names tell us what God is not, but do not disclose what He essentially is.
sources.quote: in order that the Supreme Being may not appear to have any connection whatever with things below, we use, with regard to His nature, ideas and phrases expressive of separation from all such conditions
sources.raw_question: Why are negative or privative names such as 'unbeginning', 'incorporeal', and 'imperishable' applied to God?

question: If the Son is to be worshipped along with the Father, does it follow that the Son is equally and truly God with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: Yes. Worship is offered to the Father not for his personal properties but for his essential perfections, which set him apart from creatures. If the Son is worshipped too, he must have all the same essential perfections and be as far removed from creatures as the Father. So Scripture, by giving worship to both, gives the Son equal divine honour.
sources.quote: it is very manifest, that if the Son is to be worshipped too, he is equally God, and true God, with the Father; has all the same essential excellencies and perfections which the Father hath
sources.raw_question: If the Son is to be worshipped along with the Father, does it follow that the Son is equally and truly God with the Father?

question: Does attributing equal divine honour to the Son make him absolutely equal with the Father in a way that contradicts Scripture and reason?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: It depends on what 'absolutely equal' means. If it means the Son would also be the first Person, the inference is denied. If it means the Son is equal in every respect for which worship is due, being equally divine, eternal, immutable, wise and powerful, this is granted. The subordination or order of Persons within the one Godhead is a separate matter, and those inner relations may never be fully comprehended.
sources.quote: If you mean by absolutely equal, that the Son must be the jirst Person, as well as the Father, I deny your inference: if any thing else, I allow it to be true.
sources.raw_question: Does attributing equal divine honour to the Son make him absolutely equal with the Father in a way that contradicts Scripture and reason?

question: Does 1 John show that the Son existed eternally with the Father before becoming man?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: Yes. John says the Eternal Life 'was with the Father' (not 'became'), and at the end of the Epistle identifies the Son Jesus Christ as 'the True God and Eternal Life.' Since the Life was with the Father and the Son is the Life, and the Word likewise 'was with God,' the Son is the Word who is ever with the Father.
sources.quote: While he says here that ‘the Life,’ not ‘became,’ but ‘was with the Father,’ in the end of his Epistle he says the Son is the Life
sources.raw_question: Does 1 John show that the Son existed eternally with the Father before becoming man?

question: Can there have been times or ages before the Son existed?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: No. The ages themselves were made through the Word, and without him nothing was made. So time could not have existed before the Word had appeared, and to imagine times before the Son is incoherent.
sources.quote: for how did time or age at all subsist when the Word, as you say, had not appeared, ‘through’ whom ‘all things have been made and without’ whom ‘not one thing was made?’
sources.raw_question: Can there have been times or ages before the Son existed?

question: Is the Son's divinity a foreign nature, a created addition, or a portion separated from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. It is not a foreign nature, nor something added to God by creation, nor born by a partition of God. By a perfect birth He is begotten perfect God, so that nothing of the Godhead is lacking in Him.
sources.quote: This says nothing of a nature foreign to Himself, or added by creation to God, or born into Godhead by a partition of God, but it betokens the divinity of One Who by a perfect birth is begotten perfect God
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's divinity a foreign nature, a created addition, or a portion separated from the Father?

question: If the Son were a creature, would His incarnation really be a self-emptying from a higher to a lower nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > He shows the falsehood of Eunomius' calumnious charge that the great Basil had said that “man was emptied to become man,” and demonstrates that the “emptying” of the Only-begotten took place with a view to the restoration to life of the Man Who had suffered.
sources.answer: No. Since "creature" is one common name for all things that came from nothing, a created Son becoming man would merely move from one created kind to another of similar dignity. He would in effect be "emptied" to become what He already was. There would be no descent from the transcendent to the lowly. Only if the Son is uncreated does the incarnation mean the immutable God coming into mutable nature out of love for man.
sources.quote: so that if He is created, and man is created, He was “emptied,” to use Eunomius’ phrase, to become Himself, and changed His place, not from the transcendent to the lowly, but from what is similar in kind
sources.raw_question: If the Son were a creature, would His incarnation really be a self-emptying from a higher to a lower nature?

question: Was the Son in the form of a servant before His incarnation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > He shows the falsehood of Eunomius' calumnious charge that the great Basil had said that “man was emptied to become man,” and demonstrates that the “emptying” of the Only-begotten took place with a view to the restoration to life of the Man Who had suffered.
sources.answer: No. Gregory flatly denies ever teaching this and calls the charge as absurd as saying the sun is misty or water dry. The true Son was in the glory of the Father. To ascribe the form of a servant to Him before the incarnation would insult the eternal glory of the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: How could one who says distinctly that the true Son was in the glory of the Father, insult the eternal glory of the Only-begotten by conceiving it to have been “in the form of a servant”?
sources.raw_question: Was the Son in the form of a servant before His incarnation?

question: Must a Christian be able to explain how Father, Son and Holy Spirit are each God and yet one God before believing it?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 20: Whether the Doctor need have cited 300 teats, *wide of the purpose, to prove what nobody denies, namely, a subordination, in some sense, of the Son to the Fathe
sources.answer: No. The first Christians simply believed that the Father, Son and Holy Ghost, in whose name they were baptized and whom they worshipped, were equally divine and all one God. They did not trouble themselves about the manner of it. In the same way, most people believe both that God foreknows everything and that man is free, without knowing how to reconcile the two.
sources.quote: so, probably, the plain honest Christians believed every Person to be God, and all but one God ; and troubled not their heads with any nice speculations about the modus of it.
sources.raw_question: Must a Christian be able to explain how Father, Son and Holy Spirit are each God and yet one God before believing it?

question: Why is the Holy Spirit so often said to come forth from the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Because in his saving work he comes in pursuit of the Father's love. He comes forth from the Father to make that love known to the hearts of believers, so that they may be comforted and established. His coming from the Father therefore serves to reveal the Father's love.
sources.quote: On this account is he said so often to come forth from the Father, because he comes in pursuit of his love, and to acquaint the hearts of believers therewith, that they may be comforted and established.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit so often said to come forth from the Father?

question: Does Christ's saying that all things the Father has are His (John 16:15) show only a unity of will between Father and Son, or a unity of nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It shows a unity of nature. All that the Father has belongs to the Son, and all that the Son has belongs to the Father (John 17:10). The one Godhead therefore exists in both through generation. Heretics may not reduce this to a mere agreement of will.
sources.quote: The nature in all respects maintains its law, and because Both are One that same Godhead is signified as existing in Both through generation and nativity
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that all things the Father has are His (John 16:15) show only a unity of will between Father and Son, or a unity of nature?

question: Does Romans 8:9-11 show that the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of God are one and the same Spirit?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. Paul calls the Spirit dwelling in believers both the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ. He also calls it the Spirit of Him who raised Christ from the dead. So the Spirit of Christ cannot be separated from the Spirit of God, and the passage teaches the unity of nature of Father and Son.
sources.quote: when the Spirit of Christ that dwelleth in us is the Spirit of God, and when the Spirit of Christ Who was raised from the dead is yet the Spirit of God Who raises Christ from the dead
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 8:9-11 show that the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of God are one and the same Spirit?

question: Does Paul's statement that Christ is the power and wisdom of God have to be denied or qualified in order to keep the Father wise and powerful?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: No. Denying that Christ is the power and wisdom of God would shamelessly and impiously resist the apostle. Saying instead that the Father is not the Father of His own power and wisdom is no less impious, since then He would not be the Father of Christ. The text must therefore be kept, and the difficulty resolved some other way.
sources.quote: either we must say that Christ is not the power of God and the wisdom of God, and so shamelessly and impiously resist the apostle; or we must acknowledge that Christ is indeed the power of God and the wisdom of God, but that His Father is not the Father of His own power and wisdom, which is not less impious
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that Christ is the power and wisdom of God have to be denied or qualified in order to keep the Father wise and powerful?

question: Does the Son possess all of the Father's power, and does this mean the power is transferred from the Father to the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: The Son possesses all the Father's power, but nothing is transferred away from the Father. The power remains in the Father and at the same time resides in the Son. As heir of all things, maker of the ages, and the express image of the Father's person, the Son has everything the Father has.
sources.quote: not that the right is transferred from the Father to the Son, but that it at once remains in the Father and resides in the Son
sources.raw_question: Does the Son possess all of the Father's power, and does this mean the power is transferred from the Father to the Son?

question: How does the mutual indwelling of the Father and the Son show that the Son has the Father's full power?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: The Son has the whole Father in Himself, not merely a part of Him. Whoever has the Father entirely necessarily has His power as well. Likewise, the Son who is in the Father is there with all His own might. So mutual indwelling entails a full sharing of power.
sources.quote: For He has in Himself all the Father, and not merely a part of Him: and He Who has Him entirely assuredly has His power as well.
sources.raw_question: How does the mutual indwelling of the Father and the Son show that the Son has the Father's full power?

question: Is the Holy Spirit omnipresent, so that his being sent is also a sending to where he already was?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. God cannot be anywhere without his own Spirit, so if God is everywhere, his Spirit is also everywhere. The Psalmist confirms this when he speaks of God's omnipresence by asking where he could go from God's Spirit. Therefore the Spirit too was sent to where he already was.
sources.quote: But He cannot be anywhere without His own Spirit. Therefore, if God is everywhere, His Spirit also is everywhere. Therefore, the Holy Spirit, too, was sent thither, where He already was.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit omnipresent, so that his being sent is also a sending to where he already was?

question: In his birth from the Father, did the Son receive newly created attributes, or the Father's own eternal divine properties?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: He received the Father's own properties. Because his was a true birth, the Son received not things newly created but what was and remains the permanent possession of God. Thus God was born and began to exist out of, and together with, the properties of God.
sources.quote: received, because His was a true birth, not things new-created but things which were and are the permanent possession of God.
sources.raw_question: In his birth from the Father, did the Son receive newly created attributes, or the Father's own eternal divine properties?

question: Did the Son's generation from the Father take place in time?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Hilary has always maintained a birth existing outside time. He calls it a timeless and ineffable generation that transcends human understanding.
sources.quote: we have always maintained the birth existing out of time
sources.raw_question: Did the Son's generation from the Father take place in time?

question: Is God eternally Father, or was there a time when He was without His Son, Word and Wisdom?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: God is eternally Father as well as eternally God. Hilary will never assert that the Father was ever without His Wisdom, Power and Word, the Only-begotten. Unlike our own word and wisdom, which are products of our activity, the Son is the absolute generation of perfect God and can never be separated from the Father. The context adds that to posit the Father without the Son would charge Him either with imperfection or with superfluousness.
sources.quote: I will confess Thee to be not only eternally God, but also eternally Father.
sources.raw_question: Is God eternally Father, or was there a time when He was without His Son, Word and Wisdom?

question: What does the statement that the Son was born 'before times eternal' reveal about Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: It reveals two things. First, that the Father is the Source of the Son's being. Second, it is sufficient to confirm the Son's infinity, since He is born before times eternal. This birth before eternity eludes comprehension, yet it shows the Son to be eternal.
sources.quote: Yet His birth is only so far shewn as to make manifest the fact that Thou art the Source of His being; yet sufficiently to confirm our belief in His infinity, inasmuch as it is related that He was born before times eternal.
sources.raw_question: What does the statement that the Son was born 'before times eternal' reveal about Him?

question: Does Scripture explicitly reveal that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, or is this only an inference?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Scripture explicitly reveals it. Although their oneness necessarily follows from the doctrine of the one God, Scripture particularly declares that "these three are one" so that the distinct consideration of the three does not draw us away from the one. These testimonies are fewer than those for other heads of the doctrine but are clear and sufficient for faith on the plain meaning of the words.
sources.quote: for the confirmation of our faith, and that we may not, by the distinct consideration of the three be taken off from the one, it is particularly declared that “these three are one;” that one, the one and same God.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture explicitly reveal that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, or is this only an inference?

question: Can believing in a Son who is a creature, unlike the Father in essence, join a person to the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. A creature can give no help toward union with God. Someone who believes in one who is unlike and foreign to the Father in essence does not have the Father's own Son by nature, the one who is in the Father and in whom the Father is. Such a person therefore remains destitute and stripped of the Godhead.
sources.quote: believing in one unlike and foreign to the Father in essence, to the Father they will not be joined, not having His own Son by nature, who is from Him, who is in the Father
sources.raw_question: Can believing in a Son who is a creature, unlike the Father in essence, join a person to the Father?

question: In what order does the human mind come to know the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > A passing repetition of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: It rises from the Spirit, through the Son, to the Father. The mind passes from one like Person to another like Person. The Lord shines in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, since no one can know Jesus as Lord except by the Spirit. Then the God over all is found through the Lord, because the invisible Archetypal Good can only be known exactly in its image.
sources.quote: so that the Cause of all things, which is Our Lord, shines in our hearts by means of the Holy Spirit; (for it is impossible, as the Apostle says, that the Lord Jesus can be truly known, “except by the Holy Spirit”)
sources.raw_question: In what order does the human mind come to know the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Is the Holy Spirit later in time than the Son, or less divine than the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > A passing repetition of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit is a Light separated by no interval of time from the offspring Light. It shines forth through the Son while tracing its being to the Primal Light, and does everything light does. Qua light there is no difference between them, since the Spirit lacks nothing, though it is counted after the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: There is, indeed, no difference between one light and another light, qua light, when the one shows no lack or diminution of illuminating grace
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit later in time than the Son, or less divine than the Father and the Son?

question: What must be believed about the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit before one tries to understand the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > In What Way We Must Inquire Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: That the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one God, Creator and Ruler of all creation. Yet the Father is not the Son, and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son. They are a trinity of persons related to one another and a unity of equal essence. This is held by faith and then sought to be understood through prayer.
sources.quote: let us believe that the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one God, the Creator and Ruler of the whole creature; and that the Father is not the Son, nor the Holy Spirit either the Father or the Son, but a trinity of persons mutually interrelated, and a unity of an equal essence.
sources.raw_question: What must be believed about the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit before one tries to understand the Trinity?

question: Is the Son's eternal generation from the Father the same thing as his being sent?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: No. The Son is not properly said to be sent in that He is begotten of the Father. He is sent either when the Word made flesh appeared to the world, or when from time to time He is perceived by the mind of each person. What is born from eternity is eternal, but what is sent from time to time is what each person apprehends.
sources.quote: The Son, therefore, is not properly said to have been sent in that He is begotten of the Father; but either in that the Word made flesh appeared to the world
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's eternal generation from the Father the same thing as his being sent?

question: Does Christ's saying to Philip, "He that sees Me sees also the Father," show that the apostles knew and saw the Father in the Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XIII—Refutation of the opinion, that Paul was the only apostle who had knowledge of the truth.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord bore witness that in Himself the apostles had both known and seen the Father, because He is in the Father and the Father in Him. The Father is truth, so denying that the apostles knew the truth contradicts Christ's own testimony.
sources.quote: To these men, therefore, did the Lord bear witness, that in Himself they had both known and seen the Father (and the Father is truth).
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying to Philip, "He that sees Me sees also the Father," show that the apostles knew and saw the Father in the Son?

question: Is Christ the Son and Word of the Creator of the world, through whom creation is made fruitful?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVIII.—Concerning sacrifices and oblations, and those who truly offer them.
sources.answer: Yes. The heretics cannot consistently call the eucharistic bread and cup the body and blood of their Lord unless they confess Him to be the Son of the Creator. He is the Creator's Word, through whom trees bear fruit, springs flow and the earth yields its grain. Created bread and wine can be His body and blood only because creation belongs to Him.
sources.quote: if they do not call Himself the Son of the Creator of the world, that is, His Word, through whom the wood fructifies, and the fountains gush forth, and the earth gives “first the blade, then the ear, then the full corn in the ear.”
sources.raw_question: Is Christ the Son and Word of the Creator of the world, through whom creation is made fruitful?

question: Does the text "Thou art great: Thou art God alone" refer to the Father alone, excluding the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whatever is Spoken of God According to Substance, is Spoken of Each Person Severally, and Together of the Trinity Itself. One Essence in God, and Three, in Greek, Hypostases, in Latin, Persons.
sources.answer: No. It is said not of the Father alone, as the heretics perversely suppose, but of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together, because the Trinity is one God and one great.
sources.quote: For it is not written of the Father alone, as they perversely suppose, but of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, “Thou art great: Thou art God alone.”
sources.raw_question: Does the text "Thou art great: Thou art God alone" refer to the Father alone, excluding the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the Son of God come into being by the Father's will and good pleasure, as creatures and callings do?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says creatures, Paul's apostleship and our calling come by God's will, and all things came into being through the Word. The Word is therefore outside the things made by will. He is himself the Living Counsel of the Father by which they were made. So he cannot be made 'by good pleasure and will' like everything else.
sources.quote: How then can the Word, being the Counsel and Good Pleasure of the Father, come into being Himself ‘by good pleasure and will,’ like every one else?
sources.raw_question: Does the Son of God come into being by the Father's will and good pleasure, as creatures and callings do?

question: If the Son came to be by a will of the Father, does that imply another Word before him through whom he was made, leading to an infinite regress?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son came to be through the Father's counsel, there must be another Word or Christ through whom he came to be, as Valentinus taught. That one too must come into being through someone. The series runs on without limit, so the heresy ends in polytheism and endless madness.
sources.quote: And though they fashion another, yet assuredly he too comes into being through some one; and so, while we are thus reckoning up and investigating the succession of them, the many-headed heresy of the Atheists is discovered to issue in polytheism
sources.raw_question: If the Son came to be by a will of the Father, does that imply another Word before him through whom he was made, leading to an infinite regress?

question: Is the Son the offspring of the Father's will or of the Father's essence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: Of the Father's essence. Hebrews calls him the Radiance and Expression of the Father's Subsistence, not of his will. The Father's essence does not exist by will. So what is proper to that essence is not from will either, since the Offspring must be such as the Subsistence is.
sources.quote: the Apostle proclaims the Son to be the own Radiance and Expression, not of the Father’s will, but of His Essence Itself
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the offspring of the Father's will or of the Father's essence?

question: Are the titles 'Son' and 'Father' applied to Christ and God merely titles of adoption and of dignity, or do they express a real relation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: They express a real relation and are literal truths. God does not speak to deceive; the Father says 'This is My Son' and the Son says 'My Father', and the pronoun 'My' indicates genuine belonging. Hence the Fatherhood of the Father and the Sonship of the Son are what they are in name.
sources.quote: God does not speak in order to deceive. The Fatherhood of the Father, the Sonship of the Son, are literal truths.
sources.raw_question: Are the titles 'Son' and 'Father' applied to Christ and God merely titles of adoption and of dignity, or do they express a real relation?

question: Do the scriptural titles 'Son', 'Only-begotten', and 'of the Father' show that Christ truly shares the Father's nature rather than being a 'First created' work?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > Then, distinguishing between essence and generation, he declares the empty and frivolous language of Eunomius to be like a rattle. He proceeds to show that the language used by the great Basil on the subject of the generation of the Only-begotten has been grievously slandered by Eunomius, and so ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes. The title 'Son' plainly declares a true relation to the Father. John, Paul and the other saints proclaim words of truth that point to close affinity. Only if Christ were neither begotten nor a Son, but came into being through some energy, would it follow that he cannot share God's essence. So long as the Gospel calls him Son and Only-begotten, Eunomius' sophisms are empty.
sources.quote: For while the title of “Son” speaks aloud the true relation to the Father, who is so foolish that, while John and Paul and the rest of the choir of the Saints proclaim these words,—words of truth, and words that point to the close affinity
sources.raw_question: Do the scriptural titles 'Son', 'Only-begotten', and 'of the Father' show that Christ truly shares the Father's nature rather than being a 'First created' work?

question: Does Eunomius's definition of the Son's generation (not by extension, flux, division, growth or change, but by the mere will of the Generator) suffice to distinguish the Son from created things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He convicts Eunomius of having used of the Only-begotten terms applicable to the existence of the earth, and thus shows that his intention is to prove the Son to be a being mutable and created.
sources.answer: No. Gregory substitutes "earth" for "Son" in the definition and shows every clause applies equally to the earth's coming into being. God did not produce the earth by extension, division, growth or alteration, but by his will alone. So the definition marks the Son as one of the creatures, and Eunomius calls him "Son" in name only.
sources.quote: Is there anything in what we have said that does not apply to the existence of the earth? I think no one would say so
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's definition of the Son's generation (not by extension, flux, division, growth or change, but by the mere will of the Generator) suffice to distinguish the Son from created things?

question: Can the Son be a creature who differs from other creatures only by being made first, as an instrument through which the rest are made?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He convicts Eunomius of having used of the Only-begotten terms applicable to the existence of the earth, and thus shows that his intention is to prove the Son to be a being mutable and created.
sources.answer: No. Gregory treats this as heresy. On that view the Son would be like a smith's tongs and hammer: made before the other ironwork but of the same iron. He would then differ from his works only in order, not in nature. Gregory rejects any theology that places the Lord on the same level of nature as the things he made.
sources.quote: Such is the theology of heresy touching the Son,—to imagine that there is no difference between the Lord Himself and the things that were made by Him, save the difference in respect of order.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be a creature who differs from other creatures only by being made first, as an instrument through which the rest are made?

question: Is it true, as Eunomius claims, that the same energy (operation) always produces the same kind of works?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that the same energies produce the same works, and that variation in the works indicates variation in the energies.
sources.answer: No. Experience refutes it: fire's single energy of heating melts bronze, hardens mud, destroys wax, and spares the salamander; the sun's same warmth makes one plant grow and withers another; a single act of nourishment forms every diverse part of the body; and the same hand-movement builds shrines, makes coats, digs wells or murders. So one energy can yield widely differing results.
sources.quote: The energy of fire is always one and the same; it consists in heating: but what sort of agreement do its results show? Bronze melts in it; mud hardens; wax vanishes
sources.raw_question: Is it true, as Eunomius claims, that the same energy (operation) always produces the same kind of works?

question: Does Scripture present the Holy Spirit, as it does the Son, as an object of the Father's love?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Scripture never says God loves the Holy Spirit and never gives Him epithets of love. The Son, by contrast, is called God's Elect, the Beloved, and the one in whom God is well pleased, as if no other person shared the Father's love. Scripture also has no command to love or delight in the Spirit, and no mutual friendship between the Spirit and the other Persons, though such commands are frequent concerning the other Persons.
sources.quote: God is never said to love the Holy Ghost nor are any epithets that betoken love anywhere given to Him, tho so many are ascribed to the Son, as God's Elect, The Beloved, He in Whom God's soul delights
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture present the Holy Spirit, as it does the Son, as an object of the Father's love?

question: Is there any real opposition or diversity of attributes between God the Father and God the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > Thereafter he discusses the divergence of names and of things, speaking, of that which is ungenerate as without a cause, and of that which is non-existent, as the Scindapsus, Minotaur, Blityri, Cyclops, Scylla, which never were generated at all, and shows that things which are essentially different, are mutually destructive, as fire of water, and the rest in their several relations. But in the case of the Father and the Son, as the essence is common, and the properties reciprocally interchangeable, no injury results to the Nature.
sources.answer: No. Every exalted attribute (goodness, wisdom, justice, providence, power, incorruptibility) is predicated alike of each. Moreover each has his strength in the other: the Father makes all things through the Son, and the Son works all things in himself as the Power of the Father. Unlike earth and air, black and white, or circle and triangle, nothing in one is what the other is not.
sources.quote: One goodness, wisdom, justice, providence, power, incorruptibility,—all other attributes of exalted significance are similarly predicated of each, and the one has in a certain sense His strength in the other
sources.raw_question: Is there any real opposition or diversity of attributes between God the Father and God the Only-begotten Son?

question: If Eunomius' principle that a single simple life must have one and the same expression is applied to the Son, does it follow that the Son must also be called ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, by Eunomius' own premises. The Son too is a single, simple, uncompounded life with no other subject reality besides it, and the Father's substance is likewise a single life admitting no variation. Things coinciding in idea must bear the same name, so if the Father's simple life is named ungeneracy, the Son's identical simple life must be named so too, which shows Eunomius' reasoning is absurd.
sources.quote: if the simplicity and incompositeness of the Father’s life has ungeneracy for its name, in like manner for the Son’s life the same idea will necessarily have to be attached to the same utterance
sources.raw_question: If Eunomius' principle that a single simple life must have one and the same expression is applied to the Son, does it follow that the Son must also be called ungenerate?

question: Is God the Creator of words (names), or of the things which our words signify?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Of things. Just as the heavens declare God's glory without voice in Psalm 19, the same Holy Spirit teaching through Moses says the fiat preceded creation to show that creation has a Lord and is not spontaneous, not that God created words. God is the Creator of things made known to us by the signification of our words.
sources.quote: we are not told that God is the Creator of words, but of things made known to us by the signification of our words.
sources.raw_question: Is God the Creator of words (names), or of the things which our words signify?

question: In what does the believer's communion with God consist?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: It consists in God's communicating himself to believers and their returning to him what he requires and accepts. This mutual giving and receiving flows from the union believers have with God in Jesus Christ. It takes place in a holy and spiritual manner while God and the saints walk together in a covenant of peace ratified in Christ's blood.
sources.quote: Our communion, then, with God consisteth in his communication of himself unto us, with our returnal unto him of that which he requireth and accepteth, flowing from that union which in Jesus Christ we have with him.
sources.raw_question: In what does the believer's communion with God consist?

question: Is the believer's communion with God complete in this life, or does it differ from communion in glory?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: It is incomplete in this life. Communion with God is twofold. The perfect and complete form is the full enjoyment of God's glory and total self-giving to him as our final end, which comes when we see him as he is. The initial and incomplete form is the first-fruits and dawning of that perfection, which believers have now in grace.
sources.quote: Initial and incomplete, in the first-fruits and dawnings of that perfection which we have here in grace; which only I shall handle.
sources.raw_question: Is the believer's communion with God complete in this life, or does it differ from communion in glory?

question: Does affirming the unity of Godhead of Father, Son and Spirit necessarily imply the Godhead of the Spirit, and vice versa?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IX. That the Holy Spirit is provoked is proved by the words of St. Peter, in which it is shown that the Spirit of God is one and the same as the Spirit of the Lord, both by other passages and by reference to the sentence of the same Apostle on Ananias and Sapphira, whence it is argued that the union of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, as well as His own Godhead, is proved.
sources.answer: Yes. Whichever of the two one confesses, the other is contained in it, because the unity upholds the Godhead and the Godhead the unity. To confess one is in effect to confess both.
sources.quote: Whichever you say, you will have said each in God, for both the Unity upholds the Godhead and the Godhead the Unity
sources.raw_question: Does affirming the unity of Godhead of Father, Son and Spirit necessarily imply the Godhead of the Spirit, and vice versa?

question: Is the Eunomian claim to know the divine essence (as ungenerate) credible, given that they cannot even explain the nature of the heavens?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
