sources.answer: No. Those who boast of knowing God's essence should first explain inferior things like the body of the heavens and the mechanism of the stars' motion; yet speculation on these quickly ends in perplexity and infinite regress. If created things exceed our comprehension, much more does the Creator's essence.
sources.quote: boasting as they do that they know these things, let them first tell us about the things of inferior nature; what they think of the body of the heavens
sources.raw_question: Is the Eunomian claim to know the divine essence (as ungenerate) credible, given that they cannot even explain the nature of the heavens?

question: If imperishability and immortality are the very essence of God, does it follow that the Father and the Son share one essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. If imperishability is the essence, and the Son is imperishable and immortal as the Father is, then imperishability is also the Son's essence. Since there is no difference between the two imperishabilities, one essence differs from the other in no way, the nature in both being equally a stranger to corruption.
sources.quote: one essence will differ from the other essence in no way at all, seeing that in both equally the nature is a stranger to any corruption.
sources.raw_question: If imperishability and immortality are the very essence of God, does it follow that the Father and the Son share one essence?

question: Is the Only-begotten Son owed the same honour, glory and worship as God the Father, or is calling him God an empty title?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: The Son is owed all honour, glory and worship. The faith held in common by all believers places every hope of salvation in Christ. He is the Author of life who does the works of the Father, as the Lord says in the Gospel, and he falls short of no excellence. The Eunomian claim that the term 'God' applied to him is empty of grandeur is a perversion born of jealousy of the Lord's honour.
sources.quote: all honour and glory and worship being due to the Only-begotten God as the Author of life, Who doeth the works of the Father, as the Lord Himself saith in the Gospel
sources.raw_question: Is the Only-begotten Son owed the same honour, glory and worship as God the Father, or is calling him God an empty title?

question: Does the Son's being begotten mean that his life had a beginning and that he is inferior to the unbegotten Father in essence, power and dignity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The Eunomian argument that the begotten must be younger, finite and inferior to the begetter is a sophistical inference drawn from the opposition between 'generate' and 'ungenerate.' It is wrapped in seductive fallacies so that hearers will draw the impious conclusion themselves. Stripped of its plausible dress, the claim that the Father only later became Father, and that the Son lacks the perfection of life, horrifies any believer.
sources.quote: after saying that the Only-begotten God is not the same in essence with the true Father, and after sophistically inferring this from the opposition between generate and ungenerate, they work in silence to the conclusion
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being begotten mean that his life had a beginning and that he is inferior to the unbegotten Father in essence, power and dignity?

question: Is the Son of God the image after which man was created, and did he become man in order to display that likeness?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: Yes. Man was created after the image of the Son of God. In these last days the Son displayed that likeness by becoming man and taking his own ancient handiwork into his own nature.
sources.quote: the Son of God was made man, assuming the ancient production [of His hands] into His own nature
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God the image after which man was created, and did he become man in order to display that likeness?

question: Is the Son related to the Father as a part to a whole?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: No. The Son, the Right Hand and Power of God, does not depend on the Father as a part upon a whole. He is truly from the Father and yet is contemplated in His own individual existence.
sources.quote: not in the sense of depending upon Him as a part upon a whole, but as being indeed from Him, and yet contemplated in individual existence
sources.raw_question: Is the Son related to the Father as a part to a whole?

question: Can the divine Word (the Son) be false or lie, as a human inner word can be false through deception or lying?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Great is the Unlikeness Between Our Word and the Divine Word. Our Word Cannot Be or Be Called Eternal.
sources.answer: No. Our word can be false when we are deceived or when we willingly lie, but the Word which is God cannot. It does nothing except what it sees the Father do and speaks not of itself but has from the Father all it speaks, and its great might is precisely that it cannot lie, since in it there is no 'yea and nay' but only 'yea yea, nay nay.'
sources.quote: the great might of that Word is that it cannot lie, because there cannot be there “yea and nay,” but “yea yea, nay nay.”
sources.raw_question: Can the divine Word (the Son) be false or lie, as a human inner word can be false through deception or lying?

question: Can a human inner word be eternal as the Word of God is co-eternal with the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Great is the Unlikeness Between Our Word and the Divine Word. Our Word Cannot Be or Be Called Eternal.
sources.answer: No. Even knowledge that is always present to the mind, such as knowing that one lives, is not always actually thought, and our inner word is spoken only in thought. Since thought of that knowledge cannot be eternal, God alone can be understood to have a Word that is eternal and co-eternal with Himself.
sources.quote: then God alone can be understood to have a Word that is eternal, and co-eternal with Himself.
sources.raw_question: Can a human inner word be eternal as the Word of God is co-eternal with the Father?

question: Is the Son of God the Word through whom the one God, Creator of heaven and earth, founded all things?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXIV.—The conversion of the Gentiles was more difficult than that of the Jews; the labours of those apostles, therefore who engaged in the former task, were greater than those who undertook the latter.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus states that the apostolic preaching to the Gentiles taught worship of the one God, Creator and Framer of all creation, and that His Son is His Word, by whom He founded all things. This same Word became a man among men in the last times, so the Creator's own Word, not a lesser being, is the agent of both creation and redemption.
sources.quote: to worship one God, the Creator of heaven and earth, and the Framer of the whole creation; and that His Son was His Word, by whom He founded all things; and that He, in the last times, was made a man among men
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God the Word through whom the one God, Creator of heaven and earth, founded all things?

question: If the names "Father" and "Son" express a natural relation, does that relation signify diversity of essence or community of essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He thus shows the oneness of the Eternal Son with the Father the identity of essence and the community of nature (wherein is a natural inquiry into the production of wine), and that the terms “Son” and “product” in the naming of the Only-Begotten include a like idea of relationship.
sources.answer: Community of essence. Names have relation or affinity only through what they signify, so if Eunomius admits that "Son" has a natural relation to "Father," the relation lies in the things themselves. To claim the affinity signifies diversity is "downright madness," since unrelated things could not preserve a conformable order in their names. Thus Eunomius unwittingly argues for community of essence.
sources.quote: If, on the other hand, he should say that these appellations signify relationship, he will necessarily appear in the character of an advocate of the community of essence
sources.raw_question: If the names "Father" and "Son" express a natural relation, does that relation signify diversity of essence or community of essence?

question: Is the Son's generation from the Father a bodily process of division, extension, emanation or transfusion of one nature into another?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. God is from God by Divine power and by the secret working of the one nature. That nature brings into existence, by birth, a nature one with itself. There is no division, extension, emanation or transfusion from nature into nature.
sources.quote: God from God, not by division or extension or emanation, but by the operation of a nature which brings into existence, by means of birth, a nature One with itself.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's generation from the Father a bodily process of division, extension, emanation or transfusion of one nature into another?

question: Is the Father's fatherhood eternal and co-existent with his Deity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen argues that the one we worship as God is the Father, and his fatherhood must be as eternal as his Deity. Anyone who is not the Father, or was not Father from eternity, is not God to us. To deny the eternal Son is therefore to lose the Father as well, as 2 John 9 shows.
sources.quote: So that he who is not the Father, who was not so from eternity, whose paternity is not equally co-existent unto his Deity, is not God unto us.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's fatherhood eternal and co-existent with his Deity?

question: Does the Son's being the Father's agent in creating the universe prove he is inferior to the Father in nature and powers?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. The Father is primarily and the Son secondarily or immediately Author of the world, which implies a subordination of order but not of nature. Far from proving inferiority, sharing the work of creation is rather a convincing argument that the Son is equal to the Father in nature and powers.
sources.quote: The Father is primarily, and the Son secondarily, or immediately, Author of the world; which is so far from proving that he is wferior, in nature or powers, to the Father, that it is rather a convincing argument that he is egual in both.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being the Father's agent in creating the universe prove he is inferior to the Father in nature and powers?

question: Does the unity of authority between the Father and the Son, if they are two distinct Beings, prevent them from being two Gods, as a king and his son administering his government are not two kings?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. If the king's son is not a king, he cannot truly be called king; if he is, there are two kings. Likewise, if the Son is not God in the Scripture-notion he cannot truly be called God, but if he is truly God as a distinct being, then on Dr. Clarke's hypothesis there are two Gods as plainly as one and one are two, and the exclusive texts of Isaiah stand against that notion.
sources.quote: But if the Son be truly God, there are two Gods upon the Doctor's hypothesis, as plainly as that one and one are two: and so all the texts of Isaiah cited above, besides others, stand full and clear against the Doctor's notion.
sources.raw_question: Does the unity of authority between the Father and the Son, if they are two distinct Beings, prevent them from being two Gods, as a king and his son administering his government are not two kings?

question: Can the nature of divine generation be inferred from the passions involved in bodily generation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: No. The mystery of theology and the physiology of unstable bodies are separated by a wide interval. One must not frame the account of things above from things below. The Son is known to be from the Father, but not from passion.
sources.quote: Surely truth answers you on his behalf, that the mystery of theology is one thing, and the physiology of unstable bodies is another.
sources.raw_question: Can the nature of divine generation be inferred from the passions involved in bodily generation?

question: Does the Son's having things 'from the Father' mean the Father also has His attributes from another?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: No. The Father has all things from no one, while the Son has them from the Father. This order of origin does not mean the Son ever lacked what He has.
sources.quote: all things which He says that He has received, He has always, yet has from the Father; and the Father indeed not from any, but the Son from the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's having things 'from the Father' mean the Father also has His attributes from another?

question: Does God's being ungenerate depend on His being called 'ungenerate' by human beings?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. To be and to be called are not convertible terms: God is by nature what He is, and is named by us only as the poverty of our nature allows. His ungenerate existence is not the result of His being called ungenerate; rather the name results from the existence. So naming Him by a human-devised term does Him no harm.
sources.quote: For His ungenerate existence is not the result of His being called ungenerate, but the name is the result of the existence.
sources.raw_question: Does God's being ungenerate depend on His being called 'ungenerate' by human beings?

question: For whose sake were names for God, such as 'ungenerate', devised: for God's or for ours?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: For ours. Words exist to teach about the things they signify, and only ignorance needs teaching. The Divine nature comprehends all knowledge and is above all teaching. God did not attach the term ungeneracy to Himself to instruct Himself, since He who knows all things needs no syllables to learn His own nature. Names are human labels for our conceptions of Him.
sources.quote: it follows that names were invented to denote the Supreme Being, not for His sake, but for our own. For He did not attach the term ungeneracy to His nature in order that He Himself might be instructed.
sources.raw_question: For whose sake were names for God, such as 'ungenerate', devised: for God's or for ours?

question: Do Old Testament texts saying God is 'One,' 'Only,' and 'beside Me there is no God' disprove that the Son is God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eighthly, John xvii. 3. and the Like. Our Lord's divinity cannot interfere with His Father's prerogatives, as the One God, which were so earnestly upheld by the Son. 'One' is used in contrast to false gods and idols, not to the Son, through whom the Father spoke. Our Lord adds His Name to the Father's, as included in Him. The Father the First, not as if the Son were not First too, but as Origin.
sources.answer: No. These texts are not said with reference to the Son but to deny the falsely called gods invented by men. God, caring for mankind, recalls those who wandered to idols, so that He may condemn things which are not and convert all men to Himself. The Son is not a rival to the Father, so such words are not uttered against Him.
sources.quote: for not with reference to the Son is it thus written, but for the denial of those falsely called gods, invented by men.
sources.raw_question: Do Old Testament texts saying God is 'One,' 'Only,' and 'beside Me there is no God' disprove that the Son is God?

question: Is the believer's communion with God the Father and the Son tied to walking in holiness?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Walking in the light of new obedience is the way of fellowship with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ, and true peace and rest are found only there. Separation or alienation from God brings no peace, only darkness, wandering and confusion.
sources.quote: He that walks in the light of new obedience, he hath communion with God, and in his presence is fulness of joy for ever; without it, there is nothing but darkness, and wandering, and confusion.
sources.raw_question: Is the believer's communion with God the Father and the Son tied to walking in holiness?

question: Does the Son's being from the Father, and so second to Him, mean the Son can be separated from the Father or is less than true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. The Son is second because He is from the Father, but He is the Father's own, begotten in the unity of His nature. He is true God, acknowledged after the Father and yet with Him, and so the Father cannot be separated from Him. He is no portion, extension or empty name.
sources.quote: For since He is from Thee, He is second to Thee; yet since He is Thine, Thou art not to be separated from Him.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being from the Father, and so second to Him, mean the Son can be separated from the Father or is less than true God?

question: What is the foundation of believers' communion with the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit's mission, his being sent by Jesus Christ to be the believers' Comforter. For this reason Owen first sets out the whole economy or dispensation of the Spirit's sending. He grounds this chiefly in Christ's promise in John 16:7.
sources.quote: The foundation of all our communion with the Holy Ghost consisting in his mission, or sending to be our comforter, by Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: What is the foundation of believers' communion with the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the Son's being said to do nothing of himself and to receive all from the Father count against his being honoured equally with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. The Father is admittedly the fountain of all, from whom the Son derives his essence and powers in an ineffable manner. That derivation is such that the Son is one with the Father, so it does not lessen his title to equal honour.
sources.quote: the Father is the fountain of all, from whom the Son derives, in an ineffable manner, his essence and powers, so as to be one with him
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being said to do nothing of himself and to receive all from the Father count against his being honoured equally with the Father?

question: Can the Son be either self-existent or unborn, given that He is the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. He who exists through birth does not exist of Himself, and He who is the Son cannot be unborn. The very name Son implies that He comes to exist only by being born, so He is neither made nor unbegotten.
sources.quote: He does not exist of Himself, Who exists through birth; nor is He not born, Who is the Son; nor can He, Who is the Son, come to exist otherwise than by being born, because He is the Son.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be either self-existent or unborn, given that He is the Son?

question: Does the Son's assumption of the form of a servant permanently estrange Him from the form of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The Father glorifies the servant's form in Himself so that it becomes for ever the form of God. The servant's form is honoured in Him in whose form it is glorified, so the Son resumes all He had with the Father before.
sources.quote: that the assumption of the servant’s form should not estrange from Him the nature of the form of God, but that God should glorify in Himself the form of the servant, that it might become for ever the form of God
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's assumption of the form of a servant permanently estrange Him from the form of God?

question: Is the Son the Word and doctrine of the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: Yes. The doctrine of the Father is the Word of the Father, which is the only Son. So when Christ refers his teaching to the Father, he is referring us to himself as the Word, not to something other than himself.
sources.quote: For the doctrine of the Father is the Word of the Father, which is the Only Son.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the Word and doctrine of the Father?

question: Does listing "product of generation" together with "product of making" and "product of creation" show that these terms mean the same thing when applied to the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: No. Naming things together does not merge their meanings. When Paul lists wood, hay, stubble, gold, silver, and precious stones, we count them together yet recognize the nature of each separately. In the same way, the intelligent hearer passes from the sounds to the sense and sees that "product of creation" means one thing and "product of generation" another.
sources.quote: we reckon up summarily the number of things he mentions, and yet do not fail to recognize separately the nature of each of the substances named. So here, too, when “product of generation” and “product of making” are named together, we pass from the sounds to the sense
sources.raw_question: Does listing "product of generation" together with "product of making" and "product of creation" show that these terms mean the same thing when applied to the Son?

question: Can the Son stand in a single relation to God that is at once the relation of offspring to begetter and of product to maker?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: No. Relative terms are always linked to their proper correlatives and never to something heterogeneous. "Son" implies a father, "slave" a master, and "maker" a work, so "product of generation" is linked to a generator and "product of creation" to a creator. It is contrary to nature for one thing to be split into different relations: the Son is properly related to the Father, while a product of making is related to its maker.
sources.quote: with the “product of generation,” surely, is linked the generator, and with the “product of creation” the creator; and we must certainly, if we are not prepared by a substitution of names to introduce a confusion of things, preserve for each of the relative terms that which it properly connotes.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son stand in a single relation to God that is at once the relation of offspring to begetter and of product to maker?

question: Does ascribing Godhead to the Holy Spirit mean that Christians worship three Gods?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIII. To those who object that Catholics, when they ascribe Godhead to the Holy Spirit, introduce three Gods, it is answered, that by the same argument they themselves bring in two Gods, unless they deny Godhead to the Son; after which the orthodox doctrine is set forth.
sources.answer: No. Where the Godhead is understood as one, one God is spoken of. The Spirit is included in the unity of the Godhead, and it is not unity but a division of power that makes plurality. So confessing the Spirit's Godhead no more yields three Gods than confessing the Son's yields two.
sources.quote: we exclude not the Holy Spirit from the Unity of the Godhead, and do not assert but deny that there are three Gods, because it is not unity but a division of power which makes plurality.
sources.raised_by_detail: Macedonians / opponents of the Spirit's Godhead
sources.raw_question: Does ascribing Godhead to the Holy Spirit mean that Christians worship three Gods?

question: Did the Apostles believe Jesus Christ to be Son of God by nature and birth, or only in name and by adoption?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: By nature and birth. Hilary sets out to show that the Apostles' faith confirms what the Father's witness and the Son's self-revelation teach. Their confession rested on his having gone forth from God, which they took as a birth of the divine nature. It did not rest merely on his title or his mission.
sources.quote: the Apostles believed our Lord Jesus Christ to be the Son of God, not merely in name but in nature, not by adoption but by birth.
sources.raw_question: Did the Apostles believe Jesus Christ to be Son of God by nature and birth, or only in name and by adoption?

question: Is there a temporal sequence in the Trinity such that the Son was born of the Father first and the Holy Spirit proceeded afterwards?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: No. In the Highest Trinity which is God there are no intervals of time, so it cannot even be inquired whether the Son was born first and the Spirit proceeded afterwards. Whoever can understand the generation of the Son from the Father without time should also understand the procession of the Spirit from both without time.
sources.quote: in that Highest Trinity which is God, there are no intervals of time, by which it could be shown, or at least inquired, whether the Son was born of the Father first and then afterwards the Holy Spirit proceeded from both
sources.raw_question: Is there a temporal sequence in the Trinity such that the Son was born of the Father first and the Holy Spirit proceeded afterwards?

question: Does Christ's giving of the Holy Spirit prove that Christ is God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: Yes. Only God gives the Holy Spirit. The apostles did not give Him themselves but prayed that He might come on those on whom they laid hands. Even Simon Magus asked only that those he laid hands on might receive the Spirit. Therefore He who gives God must be God, and great indeed.
sources.quote: How, therefore, is He not God, who gives the Holy Spirit? Nay, how great a God is He who gives God! For no one of His disciples gave the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's giving of the Holy Spirit prove that Christ is God?

question: If ungeneracy, indestructibility and being are identical in God, does it follow that the generate Son is destructible and without being?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, on Eunomius' premise, which is why the premise must be rejected. Since Eunomius must call the Son generate, the Son would lack ungeneracy. He would then also lack indestructibility and being, and so be excluded from the Godhead. Because this conclusion is manifest perdition, the terms must instead be taken to have distinct meanings.
sources.quote: our new God-maker is clearly convicted of regarding the Son created by Him as destructible, by his not regarding Him as ungenerate, and not only so, but altogether without being
sources.raw_question: If ungeneracy, indestructibility and being are identical in God, does it follow that the generate Son is destructible and without being?

question: Does the Son's excelling other creatures in degree show that he can be a creature and yet Lord and Creator of the rest?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: No. Among creatures some excel others, as star differs from star in glory, but this never makes some lords and others servants, or some efficient causes through whom the others come to be. All creatures share a nature that is created and that confesses its Framer. Since the Son is Creator and Lord, he must be excepted from the works and confessed as Son by nature.
sources.quote: yet it follows not for all this that some are lords, and others servants to the superior, nor that some are efficient causes, others by them come into being, but all have a nature which comes to be and is created
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's excelling other creatures in degree show that he can be a creature and yet Lord and Creator of the rest?

question: Does calling Christ God, alongside the Father, contradict Scripture's teaching that God is one and imply two Gods?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > In Fine, Notwithstanding the Said Heretics Have Gathered the Origin of Their Error from Consideration of What is Written: Although We Call Christ God, and the Father God, Still Scripture Does Not Set Forth Two Gods, Any More Than Two Lords or Two Teachers.
sources.answer: No. Novatian turns the charge back on the objectors: Scripture says there is one Lord, yet they confess Christ is Lord; it says one Master is Christ, yet Paul is called a master; it says one is good, God, yet Christ is called good. If these do not break the unity of Lord, Master and good, then by the same reasoning the truth that God is one is not obstructed by Christ also being declared God.
sources.quote: on the same reasoning, let them understand that, from the fact that God is one, no obstruction arises to the truth that Christ also is declared to be God.
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who charge the orthodox with saying there are two Gods
sources.raw_question: Does calling Christ God, alongside the Father, contradict Scripture's teaching that God is one and imply two Gods?

question: What is the ground of the mutual indwelling of the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: The Son's true generation from the Father. The Father dwells in the Son because the Son was truly begotten from Him. The Son dwells in the Father because of the nature given to Him in His abiding birth. Hilary says the Gospels and the words of Christ Himself teach this.
sources.quote: how Thou dwellest in Him, by virtue of His true generation from Thyself, and He in Thee, because of the nature given in His abiding birth from Thee.
sources.raw_question: What is the ground of the mutual indwelling of the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father?

question: Did the Father withhold any divine perfection from the Son in begetting Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The Father is omnipotent, so in begetting the Son He exerted His full omnipotence, and to doubt this would deny His omnipotence. He is also good, so He grudged the Only-begotten no good gift. Therefore all that is the Father's is the Son's, and all that is the Son's is the Father's.
sources.quote: Nothing is impossible with Thee, and I doubt not that in begetting Thy Son Thou didst exert Thy full omnipotence. To doubt it would be to deny that Thou art omnipotent.
sources.raw_question: Did the Father withhold any divine perfection from the Son in begetting Him?

question: Does asserting that the Son and Spirit are lesser Beings than the Father imply that the Godhead is composite?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His acknowledgment that the Divine Being is 'single' is only verbal.
sources.answer: Yes. Whoever detects greater and smaller Beings in the Divine Nature must posit more or less of goodness, wisdom or power, thereby distinguishing subject from quality and making a composite, heterogeneous Deity. A Being truly single is identical with goodness rather than possessing it, and admits no greater or less. So Eunomius grants simplicity only in appearance while really proving composition.
sources.quote: if any one says that he detects Beings greater and smaller in the Divine Nature, he is unconsciously establishing a composite and heterogeneous Deity
sources.raw_question: Does asserting that the Son and Spirit are lesser Beings than the Father imply that the Godhead is composite?

question: Is the Holy Spirit subsequent in existence to the Son, so that the Son was ever without the Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: No. Through the Son and yet with Him, the Spirit is found at once in closest union. The Spirit has the same cause of His being, the God over all, as the Only-begotten Light, and has shone forth in that Light. He is divisible neither by duration nor by an alien nature from the Father or the Son.
sources.quote: not subsequent in existence to the Son, as if the Son could be thought of as ever having been without the Spirit; but Himself also owning the same cause of His being, i.e. the God over all, as the Only-begotten Light
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit subsequent in existence to the Son, so that the Son was ever without the Spirit?

question: Is it right to say there was a time when the Son was not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: No. Saying so partitions the indivisible and inserts a false idea of time into the creative Source of the universe. The Son's everlastingness is included in the Father's ungeneracy. Any interval imagined between them would fix a beginning for the life of the Almighty, which is a monstrous supposition.
sources.quote: so that it can in no kind of way be right to partition the indivisible, and to insert, by declaring that there was a time when the Author of all existence was not, this false idea of time into the creative Source of the Universe.
sources.raw_question: Is it right to say there was a time when the Son was not?

question: What does Paul mean in 1 Corinthians 15 when he says the Son will be subject to the Father so that God may be all in all?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXVI.—Men shall be actually raised: the world shall not be annihilated; but there shall be various mansions for the saints, according to the rank allotted to each individual. All things shall be subject to God the Father, and so shall He be all in all.
sources.answer: It refers to the Son yielding up his work to the Father in due time. After the Son has reigned and put all enemies, including death, under his feet, he hands over his accomplished work, the Father who subjected all things to him is excepted from that subjection, and God becomes all in all.
sources.quote: in due time the Son will yield up His work to the Father, even as it is said by the apostle, “For He must reign till He hath put all enemies under His feet. The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.”
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean in 1 Corinthians 15 when he says the Son will be subject to the Father so that God may be all in all?

question: Does making the Son equal to God the Father compromise God's unity and pre-eminence?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. If any being not born from God were equal to him, God would admit a partner, lose his pre-eminence and cease to be One. But the Son is born from God's own nature, so what is like and equal to God is God's own and not external to him. It even heightens the Father's glory that he begot Omnipotence without severing it from himself.
sources.quote: On the other hand, there is no insult in making His own true Son His equal. For then that which is like Him is His own; that which is compared with Him is born from Himself; the Power that can do His own works is not external to Him.
sources.raw_question: Does making the Son equal to God the Father compromise God's unity and pre-eminence?

question: Does the relation of Sender and Sent between the Father and the Son contradict the Son's true divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Sender and Sent is simply another expression for Father and Son and concerns the order of revelation, not inferiority in the Son himself. The Only-begotten by his birth possesses true divinity from the Unbegotten Father, so that from One comes an indivisible unity.
sources.quote: This revelation of Them as Sender and as Sent is but another expression for Father and Son; not contradicting the true Divine nature of the Son, nor cancelling His possession of the Godhead as His birthright.
sources.raw_question: Does the relation of Sender and Sent between the Father and the Son contradict the Son's true divine nature?

question: Can a difference in kind between the Son and the Holy Spirit be inferred when they share identical divine properties?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit alike possess life-giving power, which the Gospel ascribes also to the Spirit. They are alike incorruptible, immutable, free of evil, good, right, guiding, and working all in all as He wills. Identity in these respects cannot yield difference in kind. The Church holds one power, goodness, essence, and glory in the three, differing only in the Persons.
sources.quote: If one may discern alike in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit the properties of being incorruptible, immutable, of admitting no evil, of being good, right, guiding, of working all in all as He wills, and all the like attributes, how is it possible by identity in these respects to infer difference in kind?
sources.raw_question: Can a difference in kind between the Son and the Holy Spirit be inferred when they share identical divine properties?

question: How do the Spirit, Son and Father share in the one work by which God is revealed and man is saved?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: God the Father is shown forth through all these operations. The Spirit works, the Son ministers, and the Father approves. Irenaeus reads Paul's "same Spirit," "same Lord" and "same God which worketh all in all" as the inspired explanation of Hosea's "multiplied visions."
sources.quote: for God the Father is shown forth through all these [operations], the Spirit indeed working, and the Son ministering, while the Father was approving, and man’s salvation being accomplished.
sources.raw_question: How do the Spirit, Son and Father share in the one work by which God is revealed and man is saved?

question: If the Son is Eternal from Eternal, does it follow that he is Ungenerate from Ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: No. Confessing that the Son comes from the Father banishes all idea of ungeneracy from him. The very thought of him as Son brings with it the thought of the Father inseparably joined to him. So he is eternal, being without temporal intervals, yet not ungenerate, being bound by generation to the Father's ungeneracy.
sources.quote: in confessing His ‘coming from the Father’ he has banished all ideas of Ungeneracy as regards the Only-begotten; and there will be then no danger in pronouncing Him Eternal and yet not Ungenerate.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is Eternal from Eternal, does it follow that he is Ungenerate from Ungenerate?

question: Does the Son's deriving existence from the Father make him later than the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: No. The Son derives existence from the Father but is not substantially after him. The priority of the Father is only that of cause, not of time, because extensions in time find no admittance in the eternal life.
sources.quote: For as the Son is bound to the Father, and, while deriving existence from Him, is not substantially after Him
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's deriving existence from the Father make him later than the Father?

question: Can one consistently hold that the Son had a beginning of being while denying that his kingship had a beginning?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Arians date the Son's beginning earlier than Marcellus, &c.
sources.answer: No. Whoever ascribes to the Son a beginning of being plainly ascribes to him also a beginning of reigning, since one cannot reign before one exists. So the Eusebians who deny a beginning to his kingdom while granting a beginning to his being confess what they deny.
sources.quote: he who ascribes to the Son a beginning of being, very plainly ascribes to Him also a beginning of reigning; so blind are they, confessing what they deny
sources.raw_question: Can one consistently hold that the Son had a beginning of being while denying that his kingship had a beginning?

question: Does the Holy Spirit exercise the same power of rebuking as the Father and the Son, and does this show a oneness of divine power?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VI. The Spirit rebukes just as do the Father and the Son; and indeed judges could not judge without Him, as is shown by the judgments of Solomon and Daniel, which are explained in a few words, by the way; and no other than the Holy Spirit inspired Daniel.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture ascribes rebuking to the Father (Psalm 6:1), to the Lord in Psalm 50, and to the Holy Spirit, whom the Son says will rebuke the world concerning sin, righteousness and judgment. Since the same action is ascribed to each, the oneness of power extends to all three, and we should not reject like words when asserting this oneness.
sources.quote: the oneness of power extends so far that the Spirit rebukes, as the Father rebukes, and as the Son rebukes.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit exercise the same power of rebuking as the Father and the Son, and does this show a oneness of divine power?

question: Does 1 Timothy 2:5 ("one God and one mediator... the man Christ Jesus") and John 17:3 ("the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent") exclude Christ from being God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. If the Son became incarnate to be a mediator between God and man, one with God by eternal essence and one with us by assumed humanity, there is no other way the relationship could be expressed. These texts describe his mediatorial office as man, not a denial of his deity.
sources.quote: that we might have a mediator betwixt us and God, one with God by reason of his eternal essence, one with us by reason of the humanity He deigned to assume
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Timothy 2:5 ("one God and one mediator... the man Christ Jesus") and John 17:3 ("the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent") exclude Christ from being God?

question: Is the Son merely an extension of the Father into human flesh, so that the Father was himself born as his own Son and Begetter and Begotten are identical?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary rejects the modalist view that God extended himself into the Virgin and was born as his own Son. God born of God cannot be the same as his Father, since he is his Son. The faith confesses God the Father and God the Son united but not confounded.
sources.quote: We will not admit Their identity nor allow, as a compromise, that Christ is God in some imperfect sense; for God, born of God, cannot be the same as His Father, since He is His Son
sources.raw_question: Is the Son merely an extension of the Father into human flesh, so that the Father was himself born as his own Son and Begetter and Begotten are identical?

question: Does confessing a true birth of God the Son from the Father compromise monotheism by introducing more gods than one?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Divinely taught, Christians confess neither two Gods nor a solitary God. The Son, born of God, is not the same person as the Father, yet he cannot be different in nature. So the unity of God is preserved without confounding Father and Son.
sources.quote: But we, divinely taught to confess neither two Gods nor yet a solitary God, will adduce the evidence of the Gospels and the prophets for our confession of God the Father and God the Son, united, not confounded, in our faith.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing a true birth of God the Son from the Father compromise monotheism by introducing more gods than one?

question: Can the Son be God only in some imperfect or figurative sense, being different in nature from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary refuses the compromise that Christ is God in an imperfect sense. A true birth from God means the Son cannot be different in nature from the one who begets him. Calling him God merely as a figure of speech is a fraud against the faith.
sources.quote: for God, born of God, cannot be the same as His Father, since He is His Son, nor yet can He be different in nature
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be God only in some imperfect or figurative sense, being different in nature from the Father?

question: Does Scripture use the same language ('made', 'created') for the Son as it does for creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. Scripture consistently applies 'made' and 'created' to creatures (Genesis 1:1, Psalm 119:73) but 'begat', 'begets', 'uttered' and 'was' to the Son (Psalm 2:7, Psalm 45:1, John 1:1). This consistent difference of phrasing shows Scripture recognises the difference between the Offspring and things made.
sources.quote: Nor did David say in the Psalm, ‘Thy hands have “begotten me,”’ but ‘made me and fashioned me,’ everywhere applying the word ‘made’ to the creatures. But to the Son contrariwise; for he has not said ‘I made,’ but ‘I begat,’
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture use the same language ('made', 'created') for the Son as it does for creatures?

question: When Christ says that only one is good, namely God, does he disclaim for himself the titles "good" and "Existent"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. Nothing in Christ's saying that the Father alone is good shows the Son disclaiming the title "Existent." Eunomius's jump from goodness to authority and existence is a non sequitur that does not hold together as a syllogism. Gregory had already argued that "one" here does not exclude the Son, who is one with the Father. To deny the Son either existence or goodness is a lamentable impiety.
sources.quote: Where in this does the Son disclaim the title of “Existent”?
sources.raw_question: When Christ says that only one is good, namely God, does he disclaim for himself the titles "good" and "Existent"?

question: Does authority over all created things belong to the Son, or does it belong to the Father alone?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: It belongs to the Son. Gregory says Eunomius brings "authority" into the argument with no connection to the context. He judges the claim that authority over all things that come into being does not belong to the Son to be among Eunomius's grievous errors, calling for "tears" and "a wail of mourning." The Son, as Creator, holds authority over what he made.
sources.quote: and to make out that the authority over all things that come into being does not belong to him,—this calls for our tears, and for a wail of mourning
sources.raw_question: Does authority over all created things belong to the Son, or does it belong to the Father alone?

question: If the Father first willed to have a Son and then became a Father, does the Father's will introduce an interval making the Son posterior to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He then discusses the “willing” of the Father concerning the generation of the Son, and shows that the object of that good will is from eternity, which is the Son, existing in the Father, and being closely related to the process of willing, as the ray to the flame, or the act of seeing to the eye.
sources.answer: No. The will of the Father does not come between Father and Son as an interval. In God's simple and all-powerful nature, willing and possessing what is willed are simultaneous. His eternal good will is never conceived apart from its object, and nothing can hinder its fulfilment.
sources.quote: nor does the “willing” separate the Son from the Father, coming in between them as a kind of interval
sources.raw_question: If the Father first willed to have a Son and then became a Father, does the Father's will introduce an interval making the Son posterior to the Father?

question: Does Christ's confession of God as Father separate the Son from God or make the Father single and solitary?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Neither. In confessing the Father, Christ never separates Himself from the divine unity. In placing Himself in unity with the Father, He never makes God single and solitary. By the word 'Father' He proclaims His relationship to God and includes Himself in the honour due to God.
sources.quote: The Only-begotten God does not, therefore, separate Himself from God when He confesses God the Father; but, proclaiming by the word “Father” His relationship to God, He includes Himself in the honour due to God.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's confession of God as Father separate the Son from God or make the Father single and solitary?

question: Is Christ as 'the Wisdom and Power of God' merely an inward activity or property of the Father rather than a substantial being?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. These names of inward forces indicate a nature possessing a true substantial existence through birth. What has by birth an existence of its own cannot be a property, since a property is inherent in another and has no independent existence. The names are used to show the Son is not alien from the Father's divine nature.
sources.quote: For an object, which has by birth an existence of its own, cannot be regarded as a property; a property is necessarily inherent in some being and can have no independent existence.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ as 'the Wisdom and Power of God' merely an inward activity or property of the Father rather than a substantial being?

question: In what sense is it true that the Father does not "impart" glory to the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: It is true only because the Son already has the glory by nature. Strictly, "impart" applies to someone whose glory comes from outside and is not part of his own nature. Father and Son share one and the same nature, and the Son has the Father dwelling in him entirely. So he needs no one to impart each attribute to him, since none of the Father's attributes is withdrawn from him.
sources.quote: where one and the same nature is observed in both Persons, He Who is as regards nature all that the Father is believed to be stands in no need of one to impart to Him each several attribute
sources.raw_question: In what sense is it true that the Father does not "impart" glory to the Son?

question: In what sense is the Only-begotten properly and truly called Son of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Thereafter he expounds the appellation of “Son,” and of “product of generation,” and very many varieties of “sons,” of God, of men, of rams, of perdition, of light, and of day.
sources.answer: He is called Son of God properly in both senses, by nature and by will. A man may be truly a son by nature but called a son only loosely because of his choices. In God, nature and will are never separated. His nature contains the good and His choice never departs from what is best, so the name 'Son' applies to Him without any looseness and shows His kinship of nature with the Father.
sources.quote: so that He is in both respects properly and truly called Son of God, since His nature contains the good, and His choice also is never severed from that which is more excellent, so that this word is employed, without inexactness, as His name.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Only-begotten properly and truly called Son of God?

question: If the names "Son" and "product of generation" express a natural relation to the Father who begets, does this prove that the Son is of the same essence as the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Thereafter he expounds the appellation of “Son,” and of “product of generation,” and very many varieties of “sons,” of God, of men, of rams, of perdition, of light, and of day.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory argues that if, as Eunomius himself admits, the natural relation to the Father is established by the appellation "Son" and "product of generation," then the mutual relation of names grounded in nature proves kinship, indeed identity of essence. Eunomius' own phrase thus contradicts both the truth and itself when he denies essential kinship.
sources.quote: no one could longer doubt that the mutual relation of the names which is established by nature is a proof of their kindred, or rather of their identity of essence
sources.raw_question: If the names "Son" and "product of generation" express a natural relation to the Father who begets, does this prove that the Son is of the same essence as the Father?

question: Since Scripture calls people "children of wrath," "son of perdition," and "sons of God" without any community of nature, does the title "Son" applied to Christ fail to establish that he shares the Father's nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Thereafter he expounds the appellation of “Son,” and of “product of generation,” and very many varieties of “sons,” of God, of men, of rams, of perdition, of light, and of day.
sources.answer: No. Scripture uses "son" in two senses: sometimes from nature (sons of men, sons of rams, sons of Eli), sometimes adventitiously by choice (sons of Belial, children of God, children of light). The figurative usages arise from the difference of human will, since human nature is inclined to vice or virtue. Eunomius himself grounds the Son's title in his being truly begotten, so it is the natural sense that applies, which implies essential kinship with the Begetter.
sources.quote: The divine Scripture knows how to use the word “Son” in both senses, so that in some cases such an appellation is derived from nature, in others it is adventitious and artificial.
sources.raised_by_detail: one contending on behalf of the Eunomians
sources.raw_question: Since Scripture calls people "children of wrath," "son of perdition," and "sons of God" without any community of nature, does the title "Son" applied to Christ fail to establish that he shares the Father's nature?

question: Is it correct to set 'Son' in opposition to 'Ungenerate' rather than to 'Father' when distinguishing the Persons of the Trinity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: No. The proper correlative opposition is between Father and Son, and generate and ungenerate; Eunomius should have said 'Very Son, not Father.' Substituting 'ungenerate' for 'Father' severs the Father from the relationship to the Son naturally implied by the title, and so places the Son on a level with all created things which stand opposed to the ungenerate.
sources.quote: he ought, if he had any concern for truth, to have avoided diverting his phrase from the due sequence of relationship, and to have said, “Very Son, not Father”?
sources.raw_question: Is it correct to set 'Son' in opposition to 'Ungenerate' rather than to 'Father' when distinguishing the Persons of the Trinity?

question: Does the Son's being truly from the Father mean that he possesses all that belongs to the Father's nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He thus shows the oneness of the Eternal Son with the Father the identity of essence and the community of nature (wherein is a natural inquiry into the production of wine), and that the terms “Son” and “product” in the naming of the Only-Begotten include a like idea of relationship.
sources.answer: Yes. Whatever has its existence from something by way of generation is of the same kind as its source. Therefore the Son is of the essence of the one who generated him, not of anything external to that nature. If he is truly from the Father, he is not alien from anything that belongs to the Father.
sources.quote: And if He is truly from Him, He is not alien from all that belongs to Him from Whom He is, as in the other cases too it was shown that all that has its existence from anything by way of generation is clearly of the same kind
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being truly from the Father mean that he possesses all that belongs to the Father's nature?

question: Does denying that the Son's essence was made lead to the absurdity of the Son, already in servant's form, taking the form of a servant?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No; the absurdity falls on Eunomius instead. Whoever holds that the Son is uncreated shows he is no servant by nature, so his taking the form of a servant is real humiliation. It is Eunomius, calling the Son a created servant of the Father before the Incarnation, who has Him pass from servitude to servitude.
sources.quote: Thus one who asserts that He, being a servant, took upon Him our form, is surely the man who transfers the Only-begotten from servitude to servitude.
sources.raw_question: Does denying that the Son's essence was made lead to the absurdity of the Son, already in servant's form, taking the form of a servant?

question: Should the Son be called the servant of the Father, under his dominion before the Incarnation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No. Holding that the Son has uncreated being proves that He is no servant. Only on the Eunomian view that the Son is a creature does He become subject to the Father as a servant before taking the servant's form. That view makes the self-emptying of Philippians 2 meaningless.
sources.quote: he who claims for Him uncreated being, and thereby proves that He is no servant, or you, rather, who continually cry that the Son is the servant of the Father
sources.raw_question: Should the Son be called the servant of the Father, under his dominion before the Incarnation?

question: Does the account of Christ's baptism show that the Holy Spirit is distinct from the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. At the baptism the Father speaks from heaven, the Son stands present in his humanity, and the Spirit visibly descends like a dove. These three simultaneous agents compel us to say that the descending Spirit is distinct both from the baptized Saviour and from the approving Father.
sources.quote: we are compelled to say, that the descending Spirit is distinct from the baptized Saviour, and from the approving Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the account of Christ's baptism show that the Holy Spirit is distinct from the Father and the Son?

question: Is it the Eunomian position, which makes the Son a creature, that actually implies the Son can be called Ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: Yes. Since some things come into existence by birth and others by being fashioned, a thing that is made and not begotten can be called 'ungenerate' in one sense of the term, looking only to the idea of generation. By defining the Lord as a creature and denying his real generation from the Father, the Eunomians themselves make the Only-begotten nameable as Ungenerate.
sources.quote: So, my very learned sirs, it is in your view, not ours, when it is thus followed out, that the Only-begotten can be named Ungenerate
sources.raw_question: Is it the Eunomian position, which makes the Son a creature, that actually implies the Son can be called Ungenerate?

question: Is the doxology "with the Spirit" an unnecessary novelty with no sanction in Scripture or church usage, so that it should be rejected in favour of "in the Spirit"?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Of the origin of the word “with,” and what force it has. Also concerning the unwritten laws of the church.
sources.answer: No. Basil undertakes to trace the origin of the word "with," explain its force, and show that it agrees with Scripture. He also argues that practices without written authority, received from apostolic tradition, have the same force in matters of true religion as written teaching. Lacking an explicit written source is therefore no ground for rejecting a usage.
sources.quote: It remains for me to trace the origin of the word “with;” to explain what force it has, and to shew that it is in harmony with Scripture.
sources.raw_question: Is the doxology "with the Spirit" an unnecessary novelty with no sanction in Scripture or church usage, so that it should be rejected in favour of "in the Spirit"?

question: Does baptism in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit show that the Holy Spirit receives worship equal with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Baptism is a solemn act of worship and entire consecration to the one in whose name we are baptized. As a 'stipulation' of a good conscience toward God, it presupposes the presence or knowledge of the party to whom the engagement is made. It therefore implies the Spirit's cognizance and acceptance equally with the Father's, and by Christ's command adoring homage is paid to the Spirit together with the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: Here again we have, by our Lord’s express command, adoring homage paid to the Holy Ghost in union with the Father and himself, at this sacred profession of every Christian’s faith.
sources.raw_question: Does baptism in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit show that the Holy Spirit receives worship equal with the Father and the Son?

question: Does calling the Son 'the Angel of God' show that he is a Person distinct from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. The title Angel of God reveals that he is no self-contained and solitary Being, since he is sent as the Angel of another. Yet when he is called Lord and God he receives the full title due to his nature. He is no less God for being God's Angel, and no less the Angel for being God.
sources.quote: When He is styled the Angel of God, the fact is revealed that He is no self-contained and solitary Being: for He is the Angel of God. When He is designated Lord and God, He receives the full title which is due to His nature and His name.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'the Angel of God' show that he is a Person distinct from the Father?

question: Is the Son God by nature, born from the Father, or only by adoption and the gift of a name, like other sons of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: He is God by nature, as the true Son. The Church confesses one Only-begotten Son of God, through Whom all things were made, and recognises in Him a might coequal with His Source. Father and Son are jointly supreme in creating and in ruling creation. This excludes the heretics' view that He is an adopted creature called God.
sources.quote: in the One through Whom are all things she recognises a might coequal with His Source; for Both are jointly supreme in the work of creation and in rule over created things
sources.raw_question: Is the Son God by nature, born from the Father, or only by adoption and the gift of a name, like other sons of God?

question: If the man assumed were the Only-begotten Son, what relation would the Word then have to the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: The Word would have no coherent place. As the Father is one, so the Only-begotten from Him is one; so the Word would either come second, below the Only-begotten, or, if above Him, would have to be the Father Himself. Moreover Scripture assigns seeing and knowing the Father and saving the world to the Son, leaving the Word nothing above the man unless the Word is the Son.
sources.quote: Either one must say that He comes second, or, if He be above the Only-begotten, He must be the Father Himself. For as the Father is One, so also the Only-begotten from Him is One
sources.raw_question: If the man assumed were the Only-begotten Son, what relation would the Word then have to the Father?

question: Can the Son's essence be at once a 'product of generation,' a 'product of making,' and a 'product of creation' while keeping an undivided relation to God as Generator, Maker and Creator?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
