sources.answer: No. Relative terms each have their proper correlative: the begotten is related to the begetter, the thing made to its maker. It is contrary to nature that a single thing should be split into different relations, so Eunomius's mixing of these titles confuses things by substituting names.
sources.quote: For it is contrary to nature, that a single thing should be split up into different relations. But the Son is properly related to the Father, and that which is begotten to him that begat it, while the “product of making” has its relation to its “maker”
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's essence be at once a 'product of generation,' a 'product of making,' and a 'product of creation' while keeping an undivided relation to God as Generator, Maker and Creator?

question: Does attributing generation to God imply passion or corruption in the divine nature, as Eunomius fears?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: No. Even among humans not all generation involves passion: material generation does, but spiritual generation is pure and incorruptible, since what is begotten of the Spirit is spirit. Eunomius himself reasons from human examples, so he should infer the passionless character of the divine generation from this spiritual mode. His fear is one 'where no fear is.'
sources.quote: not all generation exists by way of passion, but that that which is material is by passion, while that which is spiritual is pure and incorruptible, (for that which is begotten of the Spirit is spirit and not flesh
sources.raw_question: Does attributing generation to God imply passion or corruption in the divine nature, as Eunomius fears?

question: Does calling God 'ungenerate' as a privative term imply that generation naturally belongs to God and that He has been deprived of it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory denies that anyone has ever held that generation belongs naturally to the ungenerate God, so that God becomes ungenerate by losing a natural condition. He says such a view could only come from a madman. Eunomius invents this position so that he has something to refute, and so he misrepresents what the orthodox mean when they speak of ungeneracy by way of privation.
sources.quote: as to say, in so many words, that generation belongs naturally to the ungenerate God, but that, deprived of this natural condition, He becomes ungenerate instead of generated?
sources.raw_question: Does calling God 'ungenerate' as a privative term imply that generation naturally belongs to God and that He has been deprived of it?

question: If God's life is both without beginning and without end, must 'ungeneracy' (unbegottenness) and 'indestructibility' mean the same thing?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Though the divine life is one and continuous, the terms 'unbeginning' and 'unending' each have their own meaning: one denies a beginning, the other an end. Their difference of meaning produces no division in the subject, so the unity of the life does not require the identity of the terms, as Eunomius claims.
sources.quote: nor yet is the one name the same in meaning as the other; the one points to the absence of beginning, the other to the absence of end, and yet there is no division produced in the subject
sources.raw_question: If God's life is both without beginning and without end, must 'ungeneracy' (unbegottenness) and 'indestructibility' mean the same thing?

question: Do Christ's sayings that He is in the Father, one with the Father, and that whoever sees Him sees the Father show His true divine Sonship?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ calls men to believe His works, so that they may know that He is in the Father and the Father in Him, that He and the Father are one, and that to see Him is to see the Father. These texts refute the Arians from every part of Scripture and show Him to be God and God's Son.
sources.quote: yet believe the works, that ye may know that “I am in the Father and the Father in Me,” and “I and the Father are one,” and “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father.”
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's sayings that He is in the Father, one with the Father, and that whoever sees Him sees the Father show His true divine Sonship?

question: Does saying that God begets a Son from His own essence imply affection (passion) or division of the divine essence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Objection, that the Son's eternity makes Him coordinate with the Father, introduces the subject of His Divine Sonship, as a second proof of His eternity. The word Son is introduced in a secondary, but is to be understood in real sense. Since all things partake of the Father in partaking of the Son, He is the whole participation of the Father, that is, He is the Son by nature; for to be wholly participated is to beget.
sources.answer: No. No one would call God's being participated an affection or division of His essence, and to be participated is the same as to beget. Therefore what is begotten is neither affection nor division of the blessed essence, and it is not incredible that God should have a Son, the Offspring of His own essence.
sources.quote: therefore that which is begotten is neither affection nor division of that blessed essence. Hence it is not incredible that God should have a Son, the Offspring of His own essence
sources.raw_question: Does saying that God begets a Son from His own essence imply affection (passion) or division of the divine essence?

question: If believers are said to have communion peculiarly with one Person of the Trinity (e.g., the Father) in some particular thing, are the other Persons excluded from communion with the soul in that same thing?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No. Communion in a given thing is with one Person principally, immediately and by way of eminency, and with the other Persons secondarily and by consequence. The reason is that no Person, as a Person, is the prime object of divine worship except as identified with the one divine nature or essence.
sources.quote: I do not exclude the other persons from communion with the soul in the very same thing. Only this, I say, principally, immediately, and by the way of eminency, we have, in such a thing, or in such a way, communion with some one person
sources.raw_question: If believers are said to have communion peculiarly with one Person of the Trinity (e.g., the Father) in some particular thing, are the other Persons excluded from communion with the soul in that same thing?

question: Do all three Persons of the Trinity concur in producing an act of communion such as faith, even when that act is directed toward one Person?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. Every act of communion with any Person receives influence from every Person. Faith is given by the Father (Eph. 2:8), who reveals the gospel (Matt. 11:25). It is purchased and increased by the Son (Phil. 1:29; Luke 17:5). It is wrought in us by the Spirit's mighty power (Eph. 1:19-20).
sources.quote: Look, by what act soever we hold communion with any person, there is an influence from every person to the putting forth of that act.
sources.raw_question: Do all three Persons of the Trinity concur in producing an act of communion such as faith, even when that act is directed toward one Person?

question: In what do believers peculiarly and eminently have communion with God the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: In love: free, undeserved and eternal love. The Father peculiarly fixes this love on the saints, and they are to eye it in him, receive it from him and return love to him. Owen supports this from 1 John 4:8-10, where 'God' is taken personally for the Father, who is distinguished from the Son he sends. That love is antecedent to the sending of Christ.
sources.quote: I come now to declare what it is wherein peculiarly and eminently the saints have communion with the Father; and this is love, — free, undeserved, and eternal love.
sources.raw_question: In what do believers peculiarly and eminently have communion with God the Father?

question: Can God truly be called Father if the Son is not of the same substance and nature as Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. A son is not truly a son when begetter and begotten do not share the same properties, and one whose being is different from and unlike the father's is no son. So denying that the Son is Son by nature also strips the Father of His fatherhood. God is Father only because He has begotten in the Son His own substance and nature.
sources.quote: Yet in what sense is God a Father (as He is), if He have not begotten in His Son that same substance and nature which are His own?
sources.raw_question: Can God truly be called Father if the Son is not of the same substance and nature as Him?

question: Do the names Father, Son and Holy Spirit in Scripture imply real realities corresponding to them, or are they mere words open to any interpretation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: They imply real realities. The name Father involves sonship, and the naming of the Holy Ghost requires that He exist. Fatherhood cannot be separated from the Father, nor sonship from the Son. Heresy lies in the sense an expositor arbitrarily assigns, not in the text, and heretics empty the terms of meaning even though the Names remain to witness to the truth.
sources.quote: When we hear the name Father, is not sonship involved in that Name? The Holy Ghost is mentioned by name; must He not exist?
sources.raw_question: Do the names Father, Son and Holy Spirit in Scripture imply real realities corresponding to them, or are they mere words open to any interpretation?

question: Does Dr. Clarke's view that the Father is the supreme God and the Son a subordinate God, one God under another, avoid positing two Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. Waterland argues that one God under another God makes two Gods, just as one king under another king makes two kings. A petty king under a supreme king is easy to conceive, but the two are still two kings, or else one of them is no king, contrary to the supposition. So a supreme and a subordinate God are either two Gods, or one of them is not God at all.
sources.quote: However, if there had been one king under another king, there would have been two kings. The same I say for one God under another God ; they make two Gods.
sources.raw_question: Does Dr. Clarke's view that the Father is the supreme God and the Son a subordinate God, one God under another, avoid positing two Gods?

question: In 1 Corinthians 15:24-28, what is the final purpose toward which the Son's delivering of the Kingdom and his subjection to the Father are ordered?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Their purpose is that God may be all in all. Hilary reads the passage as a chain of causes. The end comes when the Kingdom is delivered, which follows the abolition of all powers, which follows his reign until all enemies are subdued. The subjection itself is caused by the goal that God be all in all. So the end is that God is all in all, not the loss or weakening of Christ.
sources.quote: But the cause of the subjection is none other than that God may be all in all; and therefore the end is that God is all in all.
sources.raw_question: In 1 Corinthians 15:24-28, what is the final purpose toward which the Son's delivering of the Kingdom and his subjection to the Father are ordered?

question: Why does Eunomius's objection to referring Christ's Passion to his human nature serve his claim that the Son differs in essence from the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > The sixth book shows that He Who came for man's salvation was not a mere man, as Eunomius, falsely slandering him, affirmed that the great Basil had said, but the Only-begotten Son of God, putting on human flesh, and becoming a mediator between God and man, on Whom we believe, as subject to suffering in the flesh, but impassible in His Godhead; and demonstrates the calumny of Eunomius.
sources.answer: Because there are only two options: either the Godhead or the humanity suffered. If he rejects the humanity as the subject of suffering, he makes the Son's Godhead passible. Since the Father stays wholly impassible, the Son's suffering nature would then differ in essence from the Father's. Eunomius thus uses passibility, alongside the begotten/unbegotten contrast, to prove the Son is unlike the Father in essence.
sources.quote: For if, according to their statement, the Godhead of the Son suffers, while that of the Father is preserved in absolute impassibility, then the impassible Nature is essentially different from that which admits passion.
sources.raw_question: Why does Eunomius's objection to referring Christ's Passion to his human nature serve his claim that the Son differs in essence from the Father?

question: Was the Son made by the Father in order to create the other creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: No. Even with the Son existing, the Father is still seen to work, as Christ says, 'My Father worketh hitherto and I work.' If the Son had been made to do the making after Him, yet the Father still works, the making of such a Son would be superfluous.
sources.quote: Nor hath He made the Son for the making of things created; for behold, though the Son exists, still the Father is seen to work
sources.raw_question: Was the Son made by the Father in order to create the other creatures?

question: If being without end implied being ungenerate, would ungeneracy, which Eunomius calls the Father's essence, become shared by all immortal creatures and make them consubstantial with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, and this absurdity refutes the identification. If whatever is without end is so ungenerately, then angels, archangels, human souls, and even the devil and his demons, whose life extends to infinity, would share ungeneracy and so be consubstantial with the Father. Otherwise immortality would have to be denied to all of them.
sources.quote: your much-talked-of ungeneracy, which you say is the only characteristic of the Father’s essence, will be found to be shared with whatever is immortal, and to be making all things consubstantial with the Father
sources.raw_question: If being without end implied being ungenerate, would ungeneracy, which Eunomius calls the Father's essence, become shared by all immortal creatures and make them consubstantial with the Father?

question: Does the statement that the Son was glorified by the Father before the worlds prove that the Son is eternal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: Yes. In Scripture, "before the worlds" means the same as "from all eternity," since prophecy uses the phrase to describe God's own eternity. What is glorified must already exist, because the non-existent cannot be glorified. So whoever says the Son was glorified before the worlds affirms, even as an opponent, that the Son existed eternally.
sources.quote: If then to exist before the worlds is beyond all beginning, he who confers glory on the Son before the worlds, does thereby assert His existence from eternity before that glory: for surely it is not the non-existent, but the existent which is glorified.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that the Son was glorified by the Father before the worlds prove that the Son is eternal?

question: Does saying the Son is glorified by the Holy Spirit together with every rational and generated being reduce the Spirit to a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: Yes, and Gregory rejects that conclusion. Eunomius's phrase places the Holy Spirit's glorifying of the Lord on the same footing as that of angels, heavens and all the creatures the psalm summons to praise. This erases any distinction between the Spirit and created things and makes the Spirit one of the angelic host. Gregory calls this a blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: so that there is no distinction between the Holy Spirit and all that comes into being; if, that is, the Holy Spirit glorifies the Lord in the same sense as all the other existences enumerated by the prophet
sources.raw_question: Does saying the Son is glorified by the Holy Spirit together with every rational and generated being reduce the Spirit to a creature?

question: Does the generation of the Son from the Father, like fire kindled from fire, involve any division or separation of the Father's nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. When one flame is kindled from another, nothing is cut off from the first, yet there is light from light; the first lives on in the second and the second dwells in the first. So the Son's birth involves no division, and the two remain one in nature, since it is logically impossible to distinguish them in nature.
sources.quote: For no portion has been cut off from the nature of the first flame, and yet there is light from light. Does not the first flame live on in the second, which owes its existence, though not by division, to the first?
sources.raw_question: Does the generation of the Son from the Father, like fire kindled from fire, involve any division or separation of the Father's nature?

question: Do the names 'Father' and 'Son' imply each other, so that confessing one involves confessing the other?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. Without a son none can be a father, and a son cannot exist except from a father. Therefore in confessing the Father the faith confesses the Son, and in believing in the Son it believes in the Father.
sources.quote: For the name of Father involves that of Son, since without having a son none can be a father. Evidence of the existence of a son is proof that there has been a father
sources.raw_question: Do the names 'Father' and 'Son' imply each other, so that confessing one involves confessing the other?

question: Is the relation between the Father and the Son in the Godhead a partnership between two, or a unity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: It is a unity, not a partnership. Scripture teaches that Father and Son do not share the Godhead as partners, because they are one in it. The Lord taught this Himself in saying "I and the Father are one" and "he that hath seen Me hath seen the Father."
sources.quote: do not see between the Father and the Son a partnership of Godhead, but unity, inasmuch as the Lord hath taught us this by His own words
sources.raw_question: Is the relation between the Father and the Son in the Godhead a partnership between two, or a unity?

question: Is the Holy Spirit 'of God' in the same sense in which all created things are said to be 'of God'?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit is 'of God' not as all things are of God by creation, but by proceeding out of God. This proceeding is not by generation like the Son's, but as Breath of His mouth, which proves the Spirit's natural communion with God.
sources.quote: not indeed in the sense in which “all things are of God,” but in the sense of proceeding out of God, not by generation, like the Son, but as Breath of His mouth.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit 'of God' in the same sense in which all created things are said to be 'of God'?

question: What role does the Holy Spirit play in our knowledge of God and of Christ the Image?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: The Spirit of knowledge gives believers, in Himself, the power to behold the Image of the invisible God. He does not show it from outside but leads within Himself to full knowledge. No one can say Jesus is Lord except 'by' (not merely 'through') the Spirit. So the way of knowledge runs from the one Spirit through the one Son to the one Father.
sources.quote: Thus the way of the knowledge of God lies from One Spirit through the One Son to the One Father
sources.raw_question: What role does the Holy Spirit play in our knowledge of God and of Christ the Image?

question: Does the incomparability of the Father's nature mean the Son has a lower and weaker nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The Son is the living image of the living God and the perfect form of the Father's nature. He could not be the true image unless He possessed the Father's whole glory and nature. A weak, sinful, bodily, describable or fictitious Son could not be the image of an omnipotent, good, incorporeal, ineffable and true God.
sources.quote: Who is not truly the image of God unless He possesses the perfect glory of the Father’s blessedness: and reproduces in its exactitude the likeness of His whole nature.
sources.raw_question: Does the incomparability of the Father's nature mean the Son has a lower and weaker nature?

question: In what sense is the Son the Image of the Father, and is he an image like a painted or carved likeness that differs in nature from its original?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: The Son is the living Image of the Living Father. He is not a lifeless copy that merely imitates its original. He is one in kind with the Father, of a nature in no way different, and so he possesses the same power. At the same time, his being Image indicates that the Father is his Origin.
sources.quote: For the Son is in such a sense the Image, as to be One in kind with the Father, and yet to indicate that the Father is His Origin.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Son the Image of the Father, and is he an image like a painted or carved likeness that differs in nature from its original?

question: Does the Son's being the Image of God imply that he is unlike the Father or inferior to him in power?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Because the Son born of the Father has a nature in no way different from the Father's, he possesses the power of that same nature. His likeness to the Father is indelibly his because the powers of the divine nature are inalienably his own. His being Image only shows that the Father is the Author of his birth.
sources.quote: The Son that is born of the Father has a nature in no wise different from His; and, because His nature is not different, He possesses the power of that nature which is the same as His own.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being the Image of God imply that he is unlike the Father or inferior to him in power?

question: In the form of a servant, is the incarnate Son less than the Holy Spirit and even less than himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > There is a Double Rule for Understanding the Scriptural Modes of Speech Concerning the Son of God. These Modes of Speech are of a Threefold Kind.
sources.answer: Yes. In the form of a servant the Son is less than the Father, and also less than the Holy Spirit. He is even less than himself, not than what he once was but than what he still is, because taking the form of a servant did not remove the form of God.
sources.quote: not only less than the Father, but also less than the Holy Spirit; and not only so, but less even than Himself,—not than Himself who was, but than Himself who is
sources.raw_question: In the form of a servant, is the incarnate Son less than the Holy Spirit and even less than himself?

question: Can the question whether the Son existed before His generation be meaningfully asked, as it can of men?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: No. A man may in a sense exist before his generation, as Levi was in the loins of Abraham, but the Son's generation coincides with His being from the beginning. Hence, as Gregory says, the question is irrelevant rather than the answer difficult, just as asking it of the Father ('is He too before His generation?') would be idle.
sources.quote: I say that the question is irrelevant, not the answer difficult.
sources.raw_question: Can the question whether the Son existed before His generation be meaningfully asked, as it can of men?

question: If the Son was not before His generation, would it follow that He is a creature and that Truth was not always in God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: Yes, if the formula were true of Him, since not being before generation is proper to creatures. Athanasius uses this as a reductio to show the formula cannot be said of the Son, whose generation is eternal; otherwise God would once have been without His Truth.
sources.quote: How is He not in the number of the creatures, if, as they say, He was not before His generation? for it is proper to the creatures and works, not to be before their generation.
sources.raw_question: If the Son was not before His generation, would it follow that He is a creature and that Truth was not always in God?

question: Is the Father's priority of order inconsistent with the Son being God in the full and proper sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. A priority of order does not entail a subordinate nature. As Adam was prior to Seth, yet Seth was man in the same sense as Adam, so the Father may be first in order while the Son is God in no lesser sense.
sources.quote: There is no inconsistency in admitting a priority of order, and yet denying the Son to be God in a subordinate or improper sense.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's priority of order inconsistent with the Son being God in the full and proper sense?

question: Does the ascription of creation to the Word prove that he is the one true God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: Yes. Creation is an indisputable mark of the one true God, the distinguishing character by which he is known and for which he claims all worship. Since creation of all things is ascribed to the Word, he is God in the strict and proper sense.
sources.quote: Creation is an indisputable mark of the one true God; the distinguishing character by which he was to be known, and for which he was to be reverenced above all Gods
sources.raw_question: Does the ascription of creation to the Word prove that he is the one true God?

question: Should the three Persons of the Trinity be imagined as three bodies joined together in space, so that three are greater than one?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Every Corporeal Conception Must Be Rejected, in Order that It May Be Understood How God is Truth.
sources.answer: No. We must not picture any touching or embrace in local space, or any compact conjunction like the fabled three-bodied Geryon. Any conception that is greater in three than in each singly, and less in one than in two, must be rejected without doubt. Rejecting it rejects everything corporeal.
sources.quote: let whatsoever may occur to the mind, that is of such sort as to be greater in three than in each singly, and less in one than in two, be rejected without any doubt; for so everything corporeal is rejected.
sources.raw_question: Should the three Persons of the Trinity be imagined as three bodies joined together in space, so that three are greater than one?

question: Does the Scripture's saying that the Holy Spirit can be grieved show that he is a person?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Yes. Being grieved is a personal affection, so the Spirit is said to be grieved in respect of his person. Being 'quenched', by contrast, refers to his actings and operations. He is 'delighted with our obedience' and 'grieved at our evils', which is how a person responds, not an impersonal power.
sources.quote: not immediately, in respect of his person (in which regard he is said to be grieved, which is a personal affection)
sources.raw_question: Does the Scripture's saying that the Holy Spirit can be grieved show that he is a person?

question: Does Scripture distinguish sharply between the prepositions 'in' and 'with', so that a doctrinal difference can be built on them?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VIII. St. Ambrose examines and refutes the heretical argument that because God is said to be glorified in the Spirit, and not with the Spirit, the Holy Spirit is therefore inferior to the Father. He shows that the particle in can be also used of the Son and even of the Father, and that on the other hand with may be said of creatures without any infringement on the prerogatives of the Godhead; and that in reality these prepositions simply imply the connection of the Three Divine Persons.
sources.answer: No. Scripture often uses one where the other is meant, as 'I will enter into Thy house in whole burnt-offerings' means 'with', and 'He brought them forth in silver and gold' means 'with silver and gold'. Hence no lessening of honour to the Godhead can be deduced from the expression used.
sources.quote: we often find in holy Scripture the one inserted and the other understood, as it is written: “I will enter into Thy house in whole burnt-offerings,” that is, “with whole burnt-offerings;”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture distinguish sharply between the prepositions 'in' and 'with', so that a doctrinal difference can be built on them?

question: How can the Son be from eternity if he is begotten of the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Generation as Word or Radiance does not involve a before and an after. Reason is always present with the one whose reason it is, and proper to his essence. So the Expression of the Father's subsistence always exists alongside him.
sources.quote: For we see that reason is ever, and is from him and proper to his essence, whose reason it is, and does not admit a before and an after.
sources.raw_question: How can the Son be from eternity if he is begotten of the Father?

question: If the Son is from the Father's essence, must he be a part of the Father, so that the Father's essence is divided and no longer whole?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. The sun's radiance is proper to it, yet the sun's essence is not divided or impaired; the essence stays whole and the radiance is perfect and whole. Likewise the Son is begotten from the Father, not from outside him, while the Father remains whole. If even created and irrational things have offspring that are not parts and involve no passion, it is madness to ascribe division to the immaterial God.
sources.quote: the radiance from the sun is proper to it, and the sun's essence is not divided or impaired; but its essence is whole and its radiance perfect and whole
sources.raw_question: If the Son is from the Father's essence, must he be a part of the Father, so that the Father's essence is divided and no longer whole?

question: Does the uniqueness of the Word, compared with the many ministers God uses, show that the Son is not a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: Yes. God has many ministers: archangels, thrones, prophets, apostles, and Moses with Aaron, Joshua and the judges. If the Son were a creature and minister, there would be many such sons. But the creatures are many while the Word is one. So the Son differs from all creatures and is proper to the Father: one Word of the one Father and one Image of the one God.
sources.quote: while the creatures are many, the Word is one, any one will collect from this, that the Son differs from all, and is not on a level with the creatures, but proper to the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the uniqueness of the Word, compared with the many ministers God uses, show that the Son is not a creature?

question: Does Scripture's use of 'creation' language for the Son prove that His divine birth is a creation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. The 'creation' of which Scripture speaks dates from the commencement of the ages and belongs to the saving dispensation. His birth is without end and before the ages. No prophet, apostle or oracle ever called the birth of His eternal divinity a creation, so this saving economy cannot be turned against His eternal birth.
sources.quote: The creation, of which you speak, dates from the commencement of the ages; but His birth is without end, and before the ages.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's use of 'creation' language for the Son prove that His divine birth is a creation?

question: Is a true generation (birth) of the Son incompatible with the Son's being of the same divine nature as the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Birth is the very way the unity of nature between Father and Son is manifested; the Son who was in the form of God reveals the form of God exactly. Because there is no difference of nature between them, knowledge of each is conditioned by knowledge of the other.
sources.quote: Thus our knowledge of Each of Them is conditioned by our knowledge of the Other, for there is no difference of nature between them
sources.raw_question: Is a true generation (birth) of the Son incompatible with the Son's being of the same divine nature as the Father?

question: Does saying the Son was begotten 'before all time' or 'before the ages' mean he is strictly eternal, or only that he existed before created time?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: It means strictly eternal. In the ancient writers 'tempus' signifies duration in the widest sense, not time in the restricted sense that the Arians later gave it in order to evade the Catholic meaning. Whatever is before all time has always been, and so it admits no point at which it was not.
sources.quote: Tempus here manifestly signifies duration, in the largest sense; not time, in the restrained sense, as the Arians afterwards understood it.
sources.raw_question: Does saying the Son was begotten 'before all time' or 'before the ages' mean he is strictly eternal, or only that he existed before created time?

question: Does "I and the Father are one" mean only that the Father and Son are one in will?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. It would be absurd to suppose the Lord could not say what he meant or did not mean what he said. He could have said "one in will" if that were his meaning. This passage is not a parable, so its meaning must not be sought outside the plain sound of the words, which point to a unity of divinity.
sources.quote: But this passage concerning the unity, of which we are speaking, does not allow us to look for the meaning outside the plain sound of the words.
sources.raw_question: Does "I and the Father are one" mean only that the Father and Son are one in will?

question: Does the uninterrupted conjunction of the Son with the Father imply the Son's eternity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He further shows that the pretemporal generation of the Son is not the subject of influences drawn from ordinary and carnal generation, but is without beginning and without end, and not according to the fabrications constructed by Eunomius, in ignorance of His power, from the statements of Plato concerning the soul and from the sabbath rest of the Hebrews.
sources.answer: Yes. If nothing intervenes between Father and Son, there is no interval in which the Son was not; confessing this unbroken conjunction testifies to his eternity. And since the Word that was in the beginning is absent from no place, time or creature, the claim that the Lord 'once was not' is excluded.
sources.quote: For in confessing that the conjunction of the Son with the Father is not interrupted by anything, He clearly testifies to His eternity.
sources.raw_question: Does the uninterrupted conjunction of the Son with the Father imply the Son's eternity?

question: Can the title 'Ungenerate' follow God while the ungenerate being itself is identified with God's essence, so that the name and the being are separated?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The thing that follows is not the same as the thing that it follows.
sources.answer: No. A title either fits the being or it does not. If it is inappropriate, it cannot represent the being. If, as Eunomius says, the being is fittingly defined by the title 'Ungenerate,' the two cannot then be parted. Making the name follow one thing and the being another is incoherent: the same term would both precede God as His definition and follow Him like a stranger.
sources.quote: If the title is inappropriate to the being, then how can the being be represented by the title; but if, as he himself phrases it, the being is fittingly defined by the title of Ungenerate, how can there be any parting of them after that?
sources.raw_question: Can the title 'Ungenerate' follow God while the ungenerate being itself is identified with God's essence, so that the name and the being are separated?

question: Does the term 'Ungenerate' contain the whole content of the Godhead, so that the faith stands or falls with it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The thing that follows is not the same as the thing that it follows.
sources.answer: No. Gregory mocks Eunomius for giving this one name 'the whole contents of godhead,' as if worship needed nothing else and the faith were endangered without it. In the following section he explains that 'Ungenerate' expresses only one aspect of God's eternity: that His life has no beginning. It does not define the divine essence.
sources.quote: he gives to it the whole contents of godhead; as if there will be nothing wanting in our adoration, if God be so named; and as if the whole system of our faith will be endangered, if He is not?
sources.raw_question: Does the term 'Ungenerate' contain the whole content of the Godhead, so that the faith stands or falls with it?

question: Can some divine names be used both absolutely and relatively, such as 'Father' applied to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: Yes. Some nouns are absolute, others are relative, and some can be turned either way according to the speaker's intention. Thus 'God' and 'Father' can be said absolutely, as in 'Abba, Father', or relatively, as in 'Our Father' or 'the Lord our God'. The relative use does not diminish the absolute meaning.
sources.quote: some nouns are absolute and out of all relation, others express some relationship. Of these last, again, there are some which incline, according to the speaker’s wish, either way
sources.raw_question: Can some divine names be used both absolutely and relatively, such as 'Father' applied to God?

question: On what ground is the Holy Spirit ranked together with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Statement of the reason why in the writings of Paul the angels are associated with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: The ground is natural fellowship with God. The Spirit is not named for the convenience of the moment, as witnesses are. Nor is he added by human invention; the Lord himself invited him into that rank.
sources.quote: But the Spirit is ranked together with God, not on account of the emergency of the moment, but on account of the natural fellowship; is not dragged in by us, but invited by the Lord.
sources.raw_question: On what ground is the Holy Spirit ranked together with the Father and the Son?

question: Does Paul's phrase 'one Lord, Jesus Christ' in 1 Corinthians 8:6 identify Christ with the one Jehovah of the Shema?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul takes the very words of the Septuagint ('one Lord') to which the Jews clung as the foundation of God's unity, as in Deuteronomy 6:4 and Zechariah 14:9. He then applies them to Jesus Christ. This amounts to an explicit declaration that Christ is the Eternal Jehovah.
sources.quote: Here the apostle uses the very words to which the Jews clung with such tenacity, as establishing the fundamental truth of the Unity of God; and adapting the very words of the common version, the Septuagint, applies them to Jesus Christ.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's phrase 'one Lord, Jesus Christ' in 1 Corinthians 8:6 identify Christ with the one Jehovah of the Shema?

question: If the Son is consubstantial with the Father, must he be so either individually (which would be Sabellianism) or specifically (which would be Tritheism)?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Waterland treats this dilemma as a sophism that leaves out the Catholic doctrine, which is neither Sabellianism nor Tritheism. Clarke presents only the two extremes and Arianism, keeping the Catholic middle position out of sight. Arguments of the same form could just as easily be brought against God's omnipresence, eternity, prescience and even self-existence. So this way of reasoning would undermine far more than the Trinity.
sources.quote: how easy it would be to match this syllogism, or sophism, with others of the like kind, . against omnipresence, eternity, prescience, and even self-ewistence
sources.raw_question: If the Son is consubstantial with the Father, must he be so either individually (which would be Sabellianism) or specifically (which would be Tritheism)?

question: Can the Son be really distinct from the Father and strictly divine only if he is coordinate with the Father in every respect, so that otherwise he must be a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Waterland says Clarke simply takes this for granted everywhere without proving it. Being Son and second Person excludes full coordination in order, yet it does not make the Son a creature. The claim reduces to a philosophical question that would need clear demonstration, and only presumptions and conjectures are offered.
sources.quote: God the Son cannot be really distinct, and strictly divine too, unless he be coordinate, in all respects, with the Father; which would be contrary to the supposition of his being a Son, and second Person.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be really distinct from the Father and strictly divine only if he is coordinate with the Father in every respect, so that otherwise he must be a creature?

question: If glorifying another implied superiority, would the Holy Spirit have to be considered greater than both the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Glorification of the Son by the Father Does Not Prove Inequality.
sources.answer: Yes, and this absurdity refutes the principle. The Spirit glorifies the Son whom the Father glorifies, yet Scripture nowhere says the Spirit is glorified by the Father or the Son; so on the objectors' reasoning the Spirit would outrank both, which they themselves would reject. Glorification therefore cannot measure rank among the Persons.
sources.quote: Truly let them beware lest the Holy Spirit be thought greater than both, because He glorifies the Son whom the Father glorifies, while it is not written that He Himself is glorified either by the Father or by the Son.
sources.raw_question: If glorifying another implied superiority, would the Holy Spirit have to be considered greater than both the Father and the Son?

question: Does the Holy Spirit personally call and equip ministers of the gospel?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. The whole work of the ministry depends on the Holy Spirit. He calls people to that work, and they are set apart to him. He also gives them the gifts and abilities they need to carry it out.
sources.quote: He calls men to that work, and they are separated unto him, Acts xiii. 2; he furnisheth them with gifts and abilities for that employment, 1 Cor. xii. 7–10.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit personally call and equip ministers of the gospel?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being said to 'hear' from the Father imply that the Spirit is subordinate or obedient to the Father, given that the Father also is said to hear the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: No. The Father himself is said to hear the Son, as when Christ says 'Father, I thank Thee that Thou heardest Me' and 'I knew that Thou hearest Me always,' though he had spoken nothing aloud beforehand. So the hearing among the divine Persons is not the hearing of a subject obeying an order. It signifies their eternal unity, and the Spirit's hearing is to be understood in the same way.
sources.quote: And I knew that Thou hearest Me always.”[^1204] Therefore the hearing is not that of subject obedience, but of eternal Unity.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being said to 'hear' from the Father imply that the Spirit is subordinate or obedient to the Father, given that the Father also is said to hear the Son?

question: If the Son's eternity is described in Scripture in the same phrases as the Father's, does it follow that the Son is coeternal with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: Yes. The proof of the Son's eternity stands on the same footing in Scripture as the proof of the Father's and is expressed in equally strong words. Whoever refuses this inference must equally doubt the Father's eternity from the same texts, since the same descriptions are applied to both as if on purpose to teach their coeternity.
sources.quote: the proof of the Son’s eternity stands upon the same foot, in Seripture, with the proof of the Mather’s ; and is expressed in as strong words.
sources.raw_question: If the Son's eternity is described in Scripture in the same phrases as the Father's, does it follow that the Son is coeternal with the Father?

question: Do 'begetter' and 'unbegotten' express the same notion when both are said of God the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Reply is Made to the Cavils of the Heretics in Respect to the Same Words Begotten and Unbegotten.
sources.answer: No. The Father is understood as begetter under one notion and as unbegotten under another. 'Begetter' is said in relation to the begotten, that is, the Son. Nothing makes someone a father because he is unbegotten, nor unbegotten because he is a father; among humans, those who are begotten also beget.
sources.quote: And therefore any one is understood to be a begetter under one notion, but understood to be unbegotten under another. For though both are said of God the Father, yet the former is said in relation to the begotten, that is to the Son
sources.raw_question: Do 'begetter' and 'unbegotten' express the same notion when both are said of God the Father?

question: In what sense can created things be called 'generate' or sons of God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: Only by participation, not by nature. Things originate are God's handiwork and cannot be called generate in their own nature; they are said to be generated only because, after their making, they partake of the generate Son in the Spirit.
sources.quote: they partake of the generate Son, and are therefore said to have been generated also, not at all in their own nature, but because of their participation of the Son in the Spirit
sources.raw_question: In what sense can created things be called 'generate' or sons of God?

question: Does the Eunomian maxim 'If the Son was, He has not been begotten, and if He has been begotten, He was not' show that the Only-begotten passed from nothing into being and that there was a time when He was not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
sources.answer: No. Gregory calls this transition of the Only-begotten from nothing into being a godless doctrine that only superficially persuades weaker minds. True Godhead, as revealed in 'I am He that is,' is eternal and infinite in being, always the same, so to say that God formerly was not, or now is but once was not, cuts eternity short by non-existence. Asserting that the Son at some time did not exist is therefore a denial of His true Godhead.
sources.quote: For this reason we declare the maintenance of their doctrine as to the non-existence at some time of Him Who truly is, to be a denial and rejection of His true Godhead
sources.raw_question: Does the Eunomian maxim 'If the Son was, He has not been begotten, and if He has been begotten, He was not' show that the Only-begotten passed from nothing into being and that there was a time when He was not?

question: Does the Son, as the Word of the Father, have more or less in substance than the Father who begets Him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Of the Likeness of the Father and of the Son Alleged to Be in Our Memory and Understanding. Of the Likeness of the Holy Spirit in Our Will or Love.
sources.answer: No. The Word has nothing either more or less in substance than is in the Father. The Father begot the Word truly, not lyingly, so the Word fully expresses all that the Father has in His substance.
sources.quote: God His Word Himself, who Himself has nothing either more or less in substance than is in Him, who, not lyingly but truly, hath begotten the Word
sources.raw_question: Does the Son, as the Word of the Father, have more or less in substance than the Father who begets Him?

question: Does asserting one true God, against the Arians, imply the Sabellian view that the Father and the Son are one Person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Hilary insists that the assertion of the One true God must give no cover to the Sabellian heresy that the Father is one Person with the Son. Nor does it support the denial of the Son's Godhead drawn from God's unity. The Law speaks of God and God as Two, while affirming the true Godhead of each.
sources.quote: I shall take care that in our assertion of the One true God I give no cover to the Sabellian heresy that the Father is one Person with the Son
sources.raw_question: Does asserting one true God, against the Arians, imply the Sabellian view that the Father and the Son are one Person?

question: Does the fact that the Son prays to the Father show that the Son is inferior to the Father in his divine nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to God, Even the Father. The Kingdom Having Been Delivered to God, Even the Father, Christ Will Not Then Make Intercession for Us.
sources.answer: No. The Son prays only in so far as he is less than the Father, that is, in the form of a servant. As equal with the Father, he grants together with the Father. Praying and granting therefore belong to his two different forms. They are not two ranks within the Godhead.
sources.quote: For indeed He “prays,” in so far as He is less than the Father; but as He is equal with the Father, He with the Father grants.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Son prays to the Father show that the Son is inferior to the Father in his divine nature?

question: Does the title 'Only-begotten' in John's Gospel show that Christ is Son by nature rather than by adoption?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. John judged that the name 'Son' alone might not set forth His true divinity distinctly enough, so he added 'Only-begotten' to mark Christ's difference from all others. This removes any basis for an imaginary adoption, since being the Only-begotten is proof positive of His right to the name of Son.
sources.quote: Hence he not only calls Him the Son, but adds the further designation of the Only-begotten, and so cuts away the last prop from under this imaginary adoption.
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'Only-begotten' in John's Gospel show that Christ is Son by nature rather than by adoption?

question: If Eunomius's reasoning about the Father's life and substance is applied to the Son, does it lead to the absurd conclusion that the Son's substance is ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory turns Eunomius's own argument back on him. The Son is also a "Life thoroughly single," with no subject reality besides His life. By Eunomius's method, then, the Son's substance would equally be reduced to ungeneracy, which exposes the argument as a delusion.
sources.quote: let us examine whether, by employing the same method by which he, in the case of the Father, has brought the definition of the substance to ungeneracy, we may not equally bring the substance of the Son to ungeneracy.
sources.raw_question: If Eunomius's reasoning about the Father's life and substance is applied to the Son, does it lead to the absurd conclusion that the Son's substance is ungenerate?

question: Does the Arian confession of 'One true God' imply that true Godhead belongs exclusively to the Father and excludes the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Hilary holds that the heretics deliberately placed 'One God' before 'One true God' so that truth would seem confined to the Father alone and the Son detached from the name and nature of God. But Moses, in proclaiming the unity of God, also meant to assert the Son's divinity. Hilary undertakes to show that the One true God is upheld in the two Persons of Father and Son.
sources.quote: the heretics have ingeniously contrived this arrangement of first naming One God and then One true God, in order to detach the Son from the name and nature of God; since the thought must suggest itself that, truth being inherent in the One God, it must be strictly confined to Him.
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian confession of 'One true God' imply that true Godhead belongs exclusively to the Father and excludes the Son?

question: Does the Son's role in the creation of the world prove that he is true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. All things were made through the Son, and made out of nothing. The power to bring the non-existent into being at will belongs only to the divine nature. The Son therefore lacks no element of true Godhead, since he possesses both the nature and the power of God.
sources.quote: If all things are through Him, and all were made out of nothing, and none otherwise than through Him, in what element of true Godhead is He defective, Who possesses both the nature and the power of God?
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's role in the creation of the world prove that he is true God?

question: How does the Son's obedience to the Father bear on the unity of God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: The Son's obedience shows the one God the Father. Although the Son is himself God, by obeying the Father in all things he declares the Father as the one from whom he drew his beginning. His obedience therefore displays the Father as the single source and does not set up a rival divinity.
sources.quote: Thus making Himself obedient to His Father in all things, although He also is God, yet He shows the one God the Father by His obedience, from whom also He drew His beginning.
sources.raw_question: How does the Son's obedience to the Father bear on the unity of God?

question: Is the Father alone unbegotten and without beginning, as distinct from the Son?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: Yes. Only God the Father is unborn and is beyond any beginning. He is therefore the beginning of the Son and of all creatures. The Son, being born, comes from him who has no beginning and so shows the Father to be that beginning.
sources.quote: For since that is the beginning to other creatures which is unborn,—which God the Father only is, being beyond a beginning of whom He is who was born,—while He who is born of Him reasonably comes from Him who has no beginning
sources.raw_question: Is the Father alone unbegotten and without beginning, as distinct from the Son?

question: By what means is divinity shared between the Father and the Son without dividing the one God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: It is shared by communion of substance. The power of divinity is sent forth from the Father alone and is given and extended to the Son, so the Son is shown to be God. That same divinity is then returned and reflected back to the Father through the communion of substance, so the Father is proved to be the one God and the source of the Son.
sources.quote: The true and eternal Father is manifested as the one God, from whom alone this power of divinity is sent forth, and also given and directed upon the Son, and is again returned by the communion of substance to the Father.
sources.raw_question: By what means is divinity shared between the Father and the Son without dividing the one God?

question: Why were names such as 'ungenerate' devised for God, and for whose benefit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They were devised by human mental conception for our sake, not God's. God, knowing all things, needs no words to instruct him about his own nature; we stamp our ideas of what may reverently be thought about him with words and syllables, as labels of our mental processes, so as to express them clearly.
sources.quote: we have stamped our different ideas with certain words and syllables, labelling, as it were, our mental processes with verbal formulæ to serve as characteristic notes and indications
sources.raw_question: Why were names such as 'ungenerate' devised for God, and for whose benefit?

question: Why could humanity receive the Holy Spirit only through the incarnate Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: Because the Spirit is the Son's own, it was fitting that the Spirit be given through Him, and we could receive it only when the Word became man. His flesh was first sanctified in Him, and since He as man received for its sake, we securely receive the Spirit's grace out of His fulness.
sources.quote: for the flesh being first sanctified in Him, and He being said, as man, to have received for its sake, we have the sequel of the Spirit grace, receiving ‘out of His fulness.’
sources.raw_question: Why could humanity receive the Holy Spirit only through the incarnate Son?

question: Does calling the Son 'subordinate' to the Father imply that the Son is inferior in nature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 13: Whether there can be any middle between being made out of nothing, and out of something ; that is, between being out of nothing, and out of the Father's substan
sources.answer: No. Catholics call the Son subordinate only in a subordination of order, as Son and second Person. The Arians take the same word to mean an inferiority of nature. The verbal agreement hides a difference as wide as that between a dependent creature and the eternal God.
sources.quote: We say, the Son is subordinate, meaning it of a subordination of order, as is just and proper: you also lay hold of the word subordinate, and seem wonderfully pleased with it ; but understanding by it, an inferiority of nature.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'subordinate' to the Father imply that the Son is inferior in nature?

question: Must Scripture state expressly that "all things are of the Son" or "of the Spirit" before these expressions can be applied to them?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IX. A passage of St. Paul abused by heretics, to prove a distinction between the Divine Persons, is explained, and it is proved that the whole passage can be rightly said of each Person, though it refers specially to the Son. It is then proved that each member of the passage is applicable to each Person, and as to say, of Him are all things is applicable to the Father, so may all things are through Him and in Him also be said of Him.
sources.answer: No. Scripture does not expressly say that "all things are through the Father" either, so the demand works against the objector as well. Since the expressions are shown to suit each Person, all things are of Him through whom all things are, and in Him. This is because every creature exists by the one will, operation and power of the Trinity.
sources.quote: But perhaps some one may say, Show me that we can read expressly that all things are of the Son, or that all things are of the Spirit. But I reply, Let them also show that it is written that all things are through the Father.
sources.raw_question: Must Scripture state expressly that "all things are of the Son" or "of the Spirit" before these expressions can be applied to them?

question: Is God both Wise and his own Wisdom, and both Father and Word, as one and the same person?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Unless Father and Son are two in name only, or as parts and so each imperfect, or two gods, they are coessential, one in Godhead, and the Son from the Father.
sources.answer: No. That is the view of the Gentiles, and it would be unfitting for God to be his own Father. The divine teaching distinguishes Father and Son, Wise and Wisdom, God and Word. Yet it always guards the Son as indivisible, inseparable and indissoluble from the Father.
sources.quote: For the Same is not, as the Gentiles hold, Wise and Wisdom, or the Same Father and Word; for it were unfit for Him to be His own Father
sources.raw_question: Is God both Wise and his own Wisdom, and both Father and Word, as one and the same person?

question: What analogy illustrates how the Father and the Son can be two yet one?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Unless Father and Son are two in name only, or as parts and so each imperfect, or two gods, they are coessential, one in Godhead, and the Son from the Father.
sources.answer: The analogy of a fire and the radiance coming from it. These are two in being and in appearance. Yet they are one, because the radiance is from the fire indivisibly.
sources.quote: let the fire and the radiance from it be a similitude of man, which are two in being and in appearance, but one in that its radiance is from it indivisibly.
sources.raw_question: What analogy illustrates how the Father and the Son can be two yet one?

question: What is a divine person, and how are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit distinguished?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: A divine person is the divine essence subsisting in a special manner on account of a special property. Father, Son, and Spirit are three hypostases distinctly subsisting in the same essence; for example, the Father is the divine essence with the property of begetting the Son, subsisting as Father.
sources.quote: a divine person is nothing but the divine essence, upon the account of an especial property, subsisting in an especial manner.
sources.raw_question: What is a divine person, and how are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit distinguished?

question: Does Scripture require that the Son pre-existed in a divine nature before his incarnation, so that he cannot be a mere man?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen says the view that Christ was only a man, held by Paul of Samosata and Photinus, was plainly folly. Even the Arians saw that they might as well deny the whole Scripture as deny the Son a pre-existence in a divine nature before his incarnation.
sources.quote: they had as good deny the whole Scripture as not grant unto him a pre-existence in a divine nature antecedent to his incarnation
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture require that the Son pre-existed in a divine nature before his incarnation, so that he cannot be a mere man?
