question: Does Origen's reading of John 10:30 as unity of consent show that he denied a substantial unity between Father and Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. Authors do not always state their whole mind, and Origen was chiefly guarding against the Sabellian abuse of the text. In that same place he inferred that Father and Son are one God and one object of worship, which on his principles implies the Son's uncreated nature and substantial unity with the Father. His added phrases, "brightness of glory" and "express image of his person," point the same way.
sources.quote: he made so much use of the text, as from thence to infer, that Father and Son are one God, and one object of worship
sources.raw_question: Does Origen's reading of John 10:30 as unity of consent show that he denied a substantial unity between Father and Son?

question: Does Athanasius's statement that the Father is 'the one God, and the only one, and the first' exclude the Son from being the one, only, and first God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. Waterland argues that Athanasius's phrase 'not to exclude the Son' means the Son is not excluded from being the one, only and first God together with the Father. Athanasius himself explains that the Son is also 'first', being the fulness of the Godhead of the first and only God. So the passage, rightly understood, supports the Son's full deity rather than conceding subordination.
sources.quote: Οὐκ εἰς ἀναίρεσιν, literally, is, not to exclude the Son: plainly meaning not to exclude him from being the one God, and the only one, and the first, together with the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does Athanasius's statement that the Father is 'the one God, and the only one, and the first' exclude the Son from being the one, only, and first God?

question: Can the Son be said to be 'eternally begotten' while 'eternal' is not meant in its strict and proper sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. 'Eternal,' 'always,' and similar words are plain words. In this question they should either not be used at all or be used in their true and proper sense. Clarke explained his 'eternally begotten' as meaning only 'without any limitation of time' within the Father's duration, not strict eternity. Using the word that way is equivocation and does not admit the Son's real eternity.
sources.quote: The words eternal, always, or the like, are plain English words, and should either not be used in this case at all, or used in their true and proper sense.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be said to be 'eternally begotten' while 'eternal' is not meant in its strict and proper sense?

question: Does Scripture teach that the Son is eternal and always coexistent with the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture never says the Son 'once was not'; it uses 'always' and 'eternal' of him. John says 'In the beginning was the Word', the Apocalypse speaks of 'Who is and who was and who is to come', and Paul calls Christ 'God blessed for ever'. No one can strip 'who is' and 'who was' of eternity.
sources.quote: no holy Scripture has used such language of the Saviour, but rather ‘always’ and ‘eternal’ and ‘coexistent always with the Father.’
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that the Son is eternal and always coexistent with the Father?

question: Does Scripture treat the Holy Spirit as the sum of all good things given to believers?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. In Scripture, 'good things' and 'the Holy Spirit' are used as synonymous expressions: Matthew 7:11 promises the Holy Spirit to those who ask. The living water of John 4 and John 7 is said to mean the Spirit. The river of the water of life in Revelation 22 is the Holy Ghost, the sum of happiness in the next world. The Spirit is also the earnest of the purchased inheritance and the Spirit of promise, which gives force to Paul's question in Galatians 3:2.
sources.quote: The Holy Ghost is the sum of all good things. Good things and the Holy Spirit are synonymous expressions in Scripture: (Matt. 7:11) "How much more shall your Heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask Him."
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture treat the Holy Spirit as the sum of all good things given to believers?

question: Is saying the Son exists 'by will' equivalent to saying 'once He was not'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Counselling precedes things which once were not, so to say 'by will' places time before the Son just as 'once He was not' does. But the Word coexists with the Father and is Framer of creatures, so counsel cannot precede the Everlasting; otherwise all things would not be through Him.
sources.quote: since it is all one to say ‘By will’ and Once He was not,’ let them make up their minds to say, ‘Once He was not,’
sources.raw_question: Is saying the Son exists 'by will' equivalent to saying 'once He was not'?

question: Do the baptismal Names Father, Son and Holy Spirit convey real information about the divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Yes. God Himself assigned the Names Father, Son and Holy Ghost, and they are our information of the Divine nature. Inquiry pushed beyond them becomes ineffable and incomprehensible, so the Names must be held to their proper meaning, including their connotation of divine character.
sources.quote: He has assigned the Names—Father, Son and Holy Ghost,—which are our information of the Divine nature.
sources.raw_question: Do the baptismal Names Father, Son and Holy Spirit convey real information about the divine nature?

question: Is Eunomius consistent in using the Father's energy and works to know the Father's being, but using the Father's being to know the being of the Son, whom he calls an energy or a product of energy?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He vainly thinks that the doubt about the energies is to be solved by the beings, and reversely.
sources.answer: No. Gregory points out that Eunomius reverses his method at will: for the Father he argues from energy and work up to the being, but for the Only-begotten he argues down from the producer's being. Since the Father's being is itself the thing in question and unknown, it cannot serve as the clear starting-point for knowing the Son.
sources.quote: when the inquiry is about the being of the Only-begotten, whether Eunomius calls Him an energy or a product of the energy (for he does both), then he tells us that the question may be easily solved by looking at the being of His producer!
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius consistent in using the Father's energy and works to know the Father's being, but using the Father's being to know the being of the Son, whom he calls an energy or a product of energy?

question: Are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each love, and are they three loves or one love?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Holy Spirit is Called Love, and Whether He Alone is So Called. That the Holy Spirit is in the Scriptures Properly Called by the Name of Love.
sources.answer: Each is love, and all together are one love, not three. This parallels how each is Wisdom yet all are one wisdom, and how each is God yet all are one God. In God's simple substance, he who has love is the love he has.
sources.quote: I know not why both the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit should not be called Love, and all together one love, just as both the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit is called Wisdom, and all together not three, but one wisdom.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each love, and are they three loves or one love?

question: Is the Son, who appeared to Moses in the bush, God only by adoption or by name rather than true God by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No, he is true God absolutely. The Angel speaking from the bush is eternally the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and he declares himself 'He that is', which gives full assurance that he is God in the absolute sense, not by adoption.
sources.quote: And, lest you insinuate that the name is His only by adoption, it is the absolute God Who speaks to Moses.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son, who appeared to Moses in the bush, God only by adoption or by name rather than true God by nature?

question: What distinct roles do the Father, Son and Holy Spirit have in creating and perfecting man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVIII.—Why man was not made perfect from the beginning.
sources.answer: The Father plans everything well and gives commands. The Son carries these out and performs the work of creating. The Spirit nourishes and increases what is made. Through this ordered working, man is formed after the image and likeness of the uncreated God and progresses toward perfection.
sources.quote: the Father planning everything well and giving His commands, the Son carrying these into execution and performing the work of creating, and the Spirit nourishing and increasing [what is made]
sources.raw_question: What distinct roles do the Father, Son and Holy Spirit have in creating and perfecting man?

question: Is it improper to call the Holy Spirit specially 'Love' when the Father and the Son can also be called love?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Holy Spirit is Called Love, and Whether He Alone is So Called. That the Holy Spirit is in the Scriptures Properly Called by the Name of Love.
sources.answer: No. Many names are used both universally and specially, as 'the Law' sometimes means the whole Old Testament and sometimes only what Moses gave, and 'the Prophets' sometimes includes the Psalms and sometimes excludes them. So the Spirit can be specially called Love though all three are love. In the same way the Son is specially called Wisdom though Father and Spirit are also wisdom.
sources.quote: I have said so much, lest any one should think that it was therefore unsuitable for us to call the Holy Spirit Love, because both God the Father and God the Son can be called Love.
sources.raw_question: Is it improper to call the Holy Spirit specially 'Love' when the Father and the Son can also be called love?

question: Does the title "Only-begotten" show that the Son's generation is unlike all other generation, so that He did not begin to exist?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. "Only-begotten" by its very meaning marks something unique that has nothing in common with other begetting. If the Son shared the features of ordinary generation, He would be like a brother to other begotten things and would no longer be only-begotten. Not existing before one's generation belongs to all things that come about by ordinary generation, so it does not apply to the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: But non-existence before generation is proper to all things that exist by generation: therefore this is foreign to the special character of the Only-begotten
sources.raw_question: Does the title "Only-begotten" show that the Son's generation is unlike all other generation, so that He did not begin to exist?

question: If the creation has a beginning without thereby limiting the Father's everlasting life, why cannot the Son likewise have a beginning in time without limiting it, so that either the creation is everlasting or the Son is later than the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: The comparison fails because the Son belongs to the uncreated divine nature, which is above creation, not to the created order. Creation alone is subject to temporal extension and sequence; the divine nature, though containing a cause and a subsistence produced from it without separation, is beyond all before and after. One could only argue as the objector does if something above creation could be shown to have a time-interval, which no one admits.
sources.quote: If he could point to anything above Creation which has its origin marked by any interval of time, and it were acknowledged possible by all to think of any time-interval as existing before Creation, he might have occasion for endeavouring to destroy by such attacks that everlastingness of the Son
sources.raw_question: If the creation has a beginning without thereby limiting the Father's everlasting life, why cannot the Son likewise have a beginning in time without limiting it, so that either the creation is everlasting or the Son is later than the Father?

question: If the Son were a creature, could his lordship over the rest of creation be legitimate rather than a kind of usurpation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Proof that the Anomœan teaching tends to Manichæism.
sources.answer: No. If the Son were created, he would share the same natural rank as the rest of creation, and his rule over his fellow creatures would be an arbitrary division of equals into masters and slaves, a usurpation. Legitimate dominion rests on a superiority of nature, as man ruled the brutes only because his reason set him above them. So the Son's rule over all things requires that he be a true Son of the divine nature, ruling by virtue of a superior nature.
sources.quote: That were like a usurpation, viz. not to assign the command to a superiority of Being, but to divide a creation that retains by right of nature equal privileges into slaves and a ruling power, one part in command, the other in subjection
sources.raw_question: If the Son were a creature, could his lordship over the rest of creation be legitimate rather than a kind of usurpation?

question: How are the roles of the Father and the Son distinguished in the work of creation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: The Father is the Cause, acting by His command. The Son executes what is commanded and sets things in order. The distinction between the Persons is marked by the work assigned to each: creation is identified with the Father's word of command, "Let us make," while the Son is the One through Whom it is arranged.
sources.quote: The Father, by His commands, is the Cause; the Son, by His execution of the things commanded, sets in order. The distinction between the Persons is marked by the work assigned to Each.
sources.raw_question: How are the roles of the Father and the Son distinguished in the work of creation?

question: If the Word is from God, must the Word also be called the Son of God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: Yes. Whatever exists from something is the son of that from which it is. Since the Word is from God, it is absurd to name Him Word yet deny that He is Son. Only if the Word were not from God could one reasonably deny His sonship.
sources.quote: For if the Word be not from God, reasonably might they deny Him to be Son; but if He is from God, how see they not that what exists from anything is son of him from whom it is?
sources.raised_by_detail: those who separate Word and Son
sources.raw_question: If the Word is from God, must the Word also be called the Son of God?

question: If God is Father of the Word, does it follow that the Word is Son of the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: Yes. Father and Son are correlative terms: one is and is called father whose son another is, and one is and is called son whose father another is. So if God is Father of Christ, the Word is necessarily Son.
sources.quote: for one is and is called father, whose is the son; and one is and is called son of another, whose is the father. If then God is not Father of Christ, neither is the Word Son
sources.raw_question: If God is Father of the Word, does it follow that the Word is Son of the Father?

question: Has the Father always been Father and the Son always been Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son were a work, God might begin to be Father toward Him as toward other creatures. But the Son is not a work, so the Father was ever Father and the Son ever Son.
sources.quote: If then the Son too were a work, well might God begin to be a Father towards Him as others; but if the Son is not a work, then ever was the Father and ever the Son
sources.raw_question: Has the Father always been Father and the Son always been Son?

question: Does being begotten 'before the earth, mountains and hills' mean merely that the Son is prior to these things, so that He is first in time but not eternal?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. More is meant than said: things existing in time cannot express eternity, and even angels precede the earth, so being merely prior to earth would be nothing remarkable. To be only antecedent to temporal things would place the Son in the same relation to time as they; rather He surpasses by the eternity of His infinity all things.
sources.quote: we cannot maintain that He came, indeed, first in time, yet was not infinite, inasmuch as the only privilege bestowed upon Him was a birth prior to things temporal.
sources.raw_question: Does being begotten 'before the earth, mountains and hills' mean merely that the Son is prior to these things, so that He is first in time but not eternal?

question: Does the generation of bodies on earth, which involves passion and the communication of material essence, tell us what the Son's generation from the Father is like?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: No. The word "generation" is used both of the divine, simple, immaterial life and of material existence subject to passion, so the two must be sharply distinguished. Bodily generation is material and brought about by passion. What is bodiless, without form and free from material mixture is alien from every condition that admits passion. Eunomius's account of earthly generation therefore deserts the real question, which is the pre-temporal, passionless existence of the Only-begotten from the Father.
sources.quote: As the speculation is two-fold, concerning that life which is Divine, simple, and immaterial, and concerning that existence which is material and subject to passion, and as the word “generation” is used of both, we must needs make our distinction sharp and clear
sources.raw_question: Does the generation of bodies on earth, which involves passion and the communication of material essence, tell us what the Son's generation from the Father is like?

question: Is the generation of the Only-begotten Son a temporal event, or does it lie before all time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: It is pre-temporal. Gregory says no one would deny that the existence proposed for consideration regarding the Only-begotten God is pre-temporal existence. That existence is exalted and unspeakable, and by it He is believed to be of the Father. This is why the generation cannot be measured by the conditions of temporal, fleshly birth.
sources.quote: Now, no one, I suppose, would deny that with regard to the Only-begotten God, it is pre-temporal existence that is proposed for the consideration of Eunomius’ discourse.
sources.raw_question: Is the generation of the Only-begotten Son a temporal event, or does it lie before all time?

question: Do the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit give life by separate works, or is their life-giving one single operation?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IV. The Holy Spirit gives life, not in a different way from the Father and the Son, nor by a different working.
sources.answer: It is one single operation, not separate works. God himself quickens through the Spirit. Paul says that he who raised Christ from the dead will quicken our mortal bodies because of his Spirit who dwells in us. So there is a oneness of quickening among Father, Son and Spirit.
sources.quote: that you may understand that the quickening of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is no separate work, read how there is a oneness of quickening also, since God Himself quickens through the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit give life by separate works, or is their life-giving one single operation?

question: In asking for and receiving the Holy Spirit, do believers have communion with each of the three divine Persons distinctly?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. In asking for the Holy Ghost, believers have communion with the Father in his love, from which the Spirit is sent. They have communion with the Son in his grace, by which the Spirit is obtained for them. They also have communion with the Spirit himself, because he voluntarily condescends to this dispensation. So every request for the Holy Ghost implies closing with all three Persons in their distinct roles.
sources.quote: we have communion with the Father in his love, whence he is sent; and with the Son in his grace, whereby he is obtained for us; so with himself, on the account of his voluntary condescension to this dispensation
sources.raw_question: In asking for and receiving the Holy Spirit, do believers have communion with each of the three divine Persons distinctly?

question: Is it possible to worship the Son or call upon the Father apart from the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That they who deny the Spirit are transgressors.
sources.answer: No. It is impossible to worship the Son save by the Holy Ghost, and impossible to call upon the Father save by the Spirit of adoption. Therefore one who denies the Spirit has no part in true worship.
sources.quote: it is impossible to worship the Son, save by the Holy Ghost; impossible to call upon the Father, save by the Spirit of adoption.
sources.raw_question: Is it possible to worship the Son or call upon the Father apart from the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the Father's begetting of the Son make the Son inferior in eternity, perfection, or glory?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. So long as the Father begat and did not create the Son, all is safe: the eternity, perfections, and glory of both are one. Begetting implies sameness of nature, not creaturely dependence.
sources.quote: very well; so long as he did not create him, all is safe: the eternity, the perfections, the glory of both are one.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's begetting of the Son make the Son inferior in eternity, perfection, or glory?

question: Can one who always exists be begotten, or does the Son's being begotten imply there was a time when he was not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: The Son can be begotten and yet never have begun to exist. The question arises from carrying the human use of words over to God: human generation involves time, place, passion and passage from non-existence to existence, but none of these belong to the Eternal. Divine generation is cleared of all temporal notions, so the Son exists by generation yet never begins to be.
sources.quote: It is in fact a constant question amongst his pupils, “How can He who (always) is be begotten?” This comes, I take it, of not weaning oneself from the human application of words, when we have to think about God.
sources.raw_question: Can one who always exists be begotten, or does the Son's being begotten imply there was a time when he was not?

question: Does Eunomius's confession that the Son is 'begotten' amount to saying the Son is created?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: Yes, in Eunomius's usage, and Gregory rejects it. Eunomius transfers the sense of generation to mean creation, as shown by his calling the Son one who 'came into being' and 'not uncreate'. Gregory treats this as evident blasphemy arising from untrained confusion about the meaning of 'generation', and sets out to distinguish its modes.
sources.quote: That he transfers, then, the sense of generation to indicate creation is plain from his expressly calling Him created, when he speaks of Him as “coming into being” and “not uncreate”.
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's confession that the Son is 'begotten' amount to saying the Son is created?

question: Is love peculiarly ascribed to the Father as distinct from the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. In the benediction of 2 Corinthians 13:14, the apostle distributes distinct things to the distinct persons: grace to Christ, fellowship to the Spirit, and love to the Father. Romans 5:5-8 likewise distinguishes God, whose love it is, from the Spirit who sheds it abroad and from the Son who is sent from that love. The Father is also called "the God of love."
sources.quote: Ascribing sundry things unto the distinct persons, it is love that he peculiarly assigns to the Father.
sources.raw_question: Is love peculiarly ascribed to the Father as distinct from the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Why did Christ speak of himself absolutely, without giving reasons, in sayings like 'I and the Father are one'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: He spoke of Himself absolutely so that He would not seem secondary to the things for which He was made. A being made for a purpose is subordinate to that purpose, since without it he would not have come into being. So Paul was subordinate to the Gospel he was set apart for, and John the Baptist to the Lord whose way he prepared. The Word is subordinate to no such reason.
sources.quote: not setting down in every case the reason, nor the wherefore, lest He should seem second to those things for which He was made. For that reason would needs take precedence of Him, without which not even He Himself had come into being.
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ speak of himself absolutely, without giving reasons, in sayings like 'I and the Father are one'?

question: Should the human connotations of the word 'father', such as passion and temporal interval, be applied to God the Father's generation of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then shows, from the instance of Adam and Abel, and other examples, the absence of alienation of essence in the case of the “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. One must lay aside all material conceptions associated with carnal fatherhood and form a conception befitting the Divine nature that expresses only the reality of the relationship. Since human fatherhood includes a notion of interval as well as bodily passion, both must be rejected in the Divine generation, so that it is free from passion and from interval.
sources.quote: it would be well, in the case of the Divine generation, to reject, together with bodily pollution, the notion of interval also, that so what properly belongs to matter may be completely purged away
sources.raw_question: Should the human connotations of the word 'father', such as passion and temporal interval, be applied to God the Father's generation of the Son?

question: Does saying the Son 'once was not' dishonour only the Son, or also the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then shows, from the instance of Adam and Abel, and other examples, the absence of alienation of essence in the case of the “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: It dishonours the Father equally. The Father is Father of Life, Truth, Wisdom, Light, Power and all that the Only-begotten is, so to say the Son once was not is to say the Father was once without His Light, Power and Wisdom, a destitution of all good in the Father. Thus the Lord's word is fulfilled that he who despises the Son despises Him that sent Him.
sources.quote: Thus the assertion made by your doctrine that the Son “once was not,” establishes nothing else than a destitution of all good in the case of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does saying the Son 'once was not' dishonour only the Son, or also the Father?

question: Did Christ himself teach us to name God as 'Father' rather than as 'Unoriginate'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord, knowing whose Son he was, spoke of himself as being in the Father and one with the Father, and he never called the Father Unoriginate. In teaching us to pray, he told us to say 'Our Father, which art in heaven', not 'O God Unoriginate'.
sources.quote: He says not, ‘When ye pray, say, O God Unoriginate,’ but rather, ‘When ye pray, say, Our Father, which art in heaven.’
sources.raw_question: Did Christ himself teach us to name God as 'Father' rather than as 'Unoriginate'?

question: Does Christ send the Holy Spirit to believers to remain with them in his place?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ himself says he sends the Spirit for this purpose (John 16:7). In Tertullian's phrase, the Spirit acts as Christ's vicar, abiding with believers for ever to accomplish all Christ's purposes toward them. The Spirit dwells in them to keep them blameless for Christ, so Owen calls him the 'holy substitute of the Lord Jesus Christ.'
sources.quote: In cherishing that Spirit, that holy Comforter, which Christ sends to us, to abide with us in his room and stead. He tells us that he sends him to that purpose, John xvi. 7.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ send the Holy Spirit to believers to remain with them in his place?

question: For what main purposes does Christ send the Holy Spirit to believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: For two main ends: their sanctification and their consolation. All the Spirit's particular acts, such as purging, teaching, anointing, sealing and establishing, can be referred to these two. As the Spirit of holiness he is holy in himself and works holiness in believers (Titus 3:5). As the Comforter he gives them peace and joy.
sources.quote: There be two main ends for which Christ sends his Spirit to believers:— (1.) For their sanctification; (2.) For their consolation: to which two all the particular acts of purging, teaching, anointing, and the rest that are ascribed to him, may be referred.
sources.raw_question: For what main purposes does Christ send the Holy Spirit to believers?

question: Is the claim that the Son is not consubstantial with the Father consistent with the teaching of the Ante-Nicene Fathers?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. This claim is directly opposite to all antiquity. It is the leading position of Clarke's scheme, on which the whole controversy turns. Bishop Bull's collected testimonies, and Waterland's own further observations, show that the early Fathers taught the Son's consubstantiality.
sources.quote: That the Son is not consubstantial with God the Father. You are directly opposite to all antiquity in this your leading position, on which the rest hang, and on which the controversy turns.
sources.raw_question: Is the claim that the Son is not consubstantial with the Father consistent with the teaching of the Ante-Nicene Fathers?

question: Does the identity of the divine attributes in the Father and the Son prove that they share the same nature or being?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He declares falsely that 'the manner of the generation is to be known from the intrinsic worth of the generator'.
sources.answer: Yes. Characters inseparable from a being are an index of the subject that has them. Since the Father and the Son are found to have the same characters, their identity of being is shown most clearly. If, as the Eunomians argue, a variation in a single name proves an alien being, then identity in countless names should all the more prove community of nature.
sources.quote: For if the variation in a single name is to be held to be the index of an alien being, how much more should the identity of these countless names avail to prove community of nature!
sources.raw_question: Does the identity of the divine attributes in the Father and the Son prove that they share the same nature or being?

question: Does John's calling Jesus Christ God's 'true Son' exclude the view that he is a creature bearing the divine name by adoption?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. John, by the knowledge granted him, calls the Son of God true, eternal life and our resurrection. Asserting his creation and adoption and denying his birth turns Father, Son, nature and truth into lies. For whoever holds that the Son is not true, there is neither eternal life nor resurrection.
sources.quote: The Apostle, by that most excellent knowledge that was granted him, speaks of the Son of God as true. You assert His creation, proclaim His adoption, deny His birth.
sources.raw_question: Does John's calling Jesus Christ God's 'true Son' exclude the view that he is a creature bearing the divine name by adoption?

question: Can the Son of God be a creature made out of nothing, of whom it can be said 'he was not before his generation'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. Being God, the Son cannot be a work, and it is impious to call him a creature. The phrases 'out of nothing' and 'it was not before its generation' belong only to creatures and works. The Son is not from nothing and is not counted among originated things.
sources.quote: for, being God, He cannot be a work, and it is impious to call Him a creature, and it is of creatures and works that we say, ‘out of nothing,’ and ‘it was not before its generation’
sources.raw_question: Can the Son of God be a creature made out of nothing, of whom it can be said 'he was not before his generation'?

question: What kind of communion do believers have with God: one of shared nature, shared condition, or actions?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: It is in actions and is voluntary, not natural or of shared state. Communion can be in a common nature, a common condition, or joint actions, but communion with God cannot be natural and must be by consent. Nor is it joint action upon a third party; it is a mutual return of actions from God to us and from us to him.
sources.quote: It cannot be natural; it must be voluntary and by consent. It cannot be of state and conditions; but in actions.
sources.raw_question: What kind of communion do believers have with God: one of shared nature, shared condition, or actions?

question: How are the Father, Son and Holy Spirit distinguished in their activity while remaining one God?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: They are distinguished by order of operation within one economy. The Father decrees, commands and wills. The Son executes, obeys and does. The Spirit gives understanding and manifests. The Father is above all, the Son through all, and the Spirit in all, and this economy of harmony is referred back to the one God.
sources.quote: It is the Father who commands, and the Son who obeys, and the Holy Spirit who gives understanding: the Father who is above all, and the Son who is through all, and the Holy Spirit who is in all.
sources.raw_question: How are the Father, Son and Holy Spirit distinguished in their activity while remaining one God?

question: What does the baptismal command in Matthew 28:19 show about how God is to be worshipped?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: It shows that the Father wills to be worshipped only through Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Anyone who omits any one of the three fails to glorify God perfectly. It is through this Trinity that the Father is glorified.
sources.quote: And by this He showed, that whosoever omitted any one of these, failed in glorifying God perfectly. For it is through this Trinity that the Father is glorified.
sources.raw_question: What does the baptismal command in Matthew 28:19 show about how God is to be worshipped?

question: Can a creature brought into being out of nothing truly be God's own Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. A creature cannot be God's own Son, so if Christ were a creature He would be lying in calling Himself the Son of God. Hence those who make Christ a creature in effect make Him Antichrist, since the Father, the Son, Peter, John and Paul all proclaim Him God's own Son, never a creature from nothing.
sources.quote: For they who hold that Christ is but a creature, must regard Christ as Antichrist, since a creature cannot be God's own Son, and therefore He must lie in calling Himself the Son of God.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who describe the Son as a creature out of nothing
sources.raw_question: Can a creature brought into being out of nothing truly be God's own Son?

question: If Scripture compels us to acknowledge Father, Son and Holy Spirit as three, in what sense is God still one?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: God is one with respect to power, but threefold with respect to the economy. Scripture forces acknowledgment of God the Father Almighty, Christ the Son who being God became man, and the Holy Spirit as three; yet the unity of God is preserved because His power is one, while the threefold manifestation belongs to the economy.
sources.quote: let him know that His power is one. As far as regards the power, therefore, God is one. But as far as regards the economy there is a threefold manifestation
sources.raw_question: If Scripture compels us to acknowledge Father, Son and Holy Spirit as three, in what sense is God still one?

question: Does the Son's being born of the Father imply that there was a time when the Son did not exist, as Arius argued?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Son, According to the Apostle, is the Power and Wisdom of the Father. Hence the Reasoning of the Catholics Against the Earlier Arians. A Difficulty is Raised, Whether the Father is Not Wisdom Himself, But Only the Father of Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. Arius failed to understand that for God even being born is from all eternity, so the Son is co-eternal with the Father. Brightness produced by fire is co-eval with the fire, and it would be co-eternal if the fire were eternal.
sources.quote: not understanding that even to be born is, to God, from all eternity; so that the Son is co-eternal with the Father, as the brightness which is produced and is spread around by fire is co-eval with it
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being born of the Father imply that there was a time when the Son did not exist, as Arius argued?

question: If the Father is wise only by the Wisdom he begot, must he also be great, good, eternal and omnipotent only by attributes he begot?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Son, According to the Apostle, is the Power and Wisdom of the Father. Hence the Reasoning of the Catholics Against the Earlier Arians. A Difficulty is Raised, Whether the Father is Not Wisdom Himself, But Only the Father of Wisdom.
sources.answer: Yes, the same reasoning would extend to all of these. The Father would then not be his own greatness, goodness, eternity or omnipotence, but would have each only through what is born of him. Augustine presents this as the troubling consequence of holding that the Father is not wisdom itself.
sources.quote: why is He not the begetter also of His own greatness, and of His own goodness, and of His own eternity, and of His own omnipotence; so that He is not Himself His own greatness
sources.raw_question: If the Father is wise only by the Wisdom he begot, must he also be great, good, eternal and omnipotent only by attributes he begot?

question: Does Scripture directly call the Holy Spirit God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. In Acts 5 Peter charges Ananias with lying to the Holy Ghost and then says he has lied not to men but to God, so the Spirit is directly called God. And this cannot be explained, as the Socinians do with the Son, as a title gained by exaltation to an office or authority.
sources.quote: He is directly affirmed to be, and is called, “God,” Acts v. 3, 4; which the Socinians will not say is by virtue of an exaltation unto an office or authority, as they say of the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture directly call the Holy Spirit God?

question: How is the Holy Spirit related to believers in the distribution of spiritual gifts?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: As a whole is to its parts. Believers are members of one another with differing gifts, completing the Body of Christ in the unity of the Spirit, and we are individually in the Spirit as parts in a whole, since we were all baptized into one body in one Spirit.
sources.quote: And as parts in the whole so are we individually in the Spirit, because we all “were baptized in one body into one spirit.”
sources.raw_question: How is the Holy Spirit related to believers in the distribution of spiritual gifts?

question: If the Father is something other than the Ungenerate, as Eunomius holds, can the Son still be called the Son of the Ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. On that view the Son, who relates to the Father alone, would be estranged from the Ungenerate and could not be Son of both. That would follow if the Father is something other than the Ungenerate and his title does not include that meaning. So Eunomius must either admit that Father and Ungenerate are the same, which means he mocked the orthodox view without cause, or cut the Son off from all relation to the Ungenerate.
sources.quote: either the Father is the same as the Ungenerate (which is necessary in order that the Son of the Father may be Son of the Ungenerate as well); and then our doctrine has been ridiculed by him without reason; or, the Father is something different to the Ungenerate
sources.raw_question: If the Father is something other than the Ungenerate, as Eunomius holds, can the Son still be called the Son of the Ungenerate?

question: Does separating 'Father' from 'Ungenerate' undermine the Eunomian argument for the Son's unlikeness to the Father, which rests on Ungeneracy?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Father is other than the Ungenerate, logic points to a generated Father, since what exists but not without generation has a generated substance. Then the Ungeneracy on which Eunomians build vanishes. With it goes their proof that the Son is unlike the Father, so their own reasoning dissolves their position.
sources.quote: logic inevitably points to a “generated Father;” for that which exists, but does not exist without generation, must have a generated substance.
sources.raw_question: Does separating 'Father' from 'Ungenerate' undermine the Eunomian argument for the Son's unlikeness to the Father, which rests on Ungeneracy?

question: Did God first exist as Ungenerate and only later become Father by begetting the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. Just as God was never not good or powerful, it is blasphemy to say Fatherhood came to Him later. God is always identical with Himself and does not change by addition; so if He is Father now, He always was and always will be Father. Ungenerate and Father are never found parted from each other.
sources.quote: Just, then, as we cannot say that God was ever not good, or powerful, or imperishable, or immortal, in the same way it is a blasphemy not to attribute to Him Fatherhood always, and to say that that came later.
sources.raw_question: Did God first exist as Ungenerate and only later become Father by begetting the Son?

question: Does the Son's obedience to the Father who sent him dissolve his unity of nature with the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The obedience of humility does not dissolve the unity of his nature. He became obedient unto death, yet after death he is above every name. Receiving that Name restores to him equality of form and does not impair the divinity of the Father who gives it.
sources.quote: He pays to the Father the tribute of obedience to the will of Him Who sent Him, but the obedience of humility does not dissolve the unity of His nature: He becomes obedient unto death, but, after death, He is above every name
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's obedience to the Father who sent him dissolve his unity of nature with the Father?

question: How does the Holy Spirit make believers acquainted with the Father's love and their sonship?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: The Spirit, sent into believers' hearts crying 'Abba, Father', persuades them of their sonship and acceptance with God as Father. From this follows the inference that they are heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ. So the Spirit assures them of their right to the inheritance.
sources.quote: This is the use, then, we have of it, — even the Spirit persuading us of our sonship and acceptation with God our Father.
sources.raw_question: How does the Holy Spirit make believers acquainted with the Father's love and their sonship?

question: Can 'in Us' in John 17:21 also mean believers are united by the power of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Yes, alternatively. 'In Us' can mean that believers are made one in the power of the Father and the Son, since without God such unity is impossible. Scripture uses this idiom, as in 'In God will we do great acts' and 'In Thee will we tread down our enemies'.
sources.quote: the words ‘in Us’ may mean the same as saying, that in the power of the Father and the Son they may be one, speaking the same things; for without God this is impossible.
sources.raw_question: Can 'in Us' in John 17:21 also mean believers are united by the power of the Father and the Son?

question: Is the creation of the world, which Scripture ascribes to God, also ascribed to the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture describes the world as heaven, earth, the sea and all in them, made by God (Acts 4:24). The making of this same world is expressly assigned to the Son in Hebrews 1:10: "Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth." John 1:10 likewise says the world was made by him.
sources.quote: that is, the world, the making whereof is expressly assigned unto the Son, Heb. i. 10, “Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth; and the heavens are the works of thine hands.”
sources.raw_question: Is the creation of the world, which Scripture ascribes to God, also ascribed to the Son?

question: Can Eunomius' claim that only the Ungenerate is indestructible 'not by reason of any energy' establish a difference of nature between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Only if the Son were destructible would a divergence of natures follow. But if neither is subject to destruction, and pure indestructibility has no degrees, then no ground remains for saying the Father cannot be compared with the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: But if neither is subject to destruction,—and no degrees are to be found in pure indestructibility,—how does he show that the Father cannot be compared with the Only-begotten Son
sources.raw_question: Can Eunomius' claim that only the Ungenerate is indestructible 'not by reason of any energy' establish a difference of nature between the Father and the Son?

question: Does the baptismal command of Matthew 28:19 show that God is a Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Conclusion of the Book with a Prayer, and an Apology for Multitude of Words.
sources.answer: Yes. The Truth would not command baptism in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit unless God were a Trinity. Since each of the three is named in that one formula, the formula itself testifies to the three Persons.
sources.quote: For the Truth would not say, Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, unless Thou wast a Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Does the baptismal command of Matthew 28:19 show that God is a Trinity?

question: If Eunomius holds that the essence of the Son is called "Spirit" and Scripture calls God (the Father) "Spirit," does his own principle about names prove that the Father and Son share one essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory turns Eunomius' own rule against him. Eunomius teaches that divergent essences have divergent names, and that where there is one and the same name, the thing signified is one. Since he calls the Son's essence "Spirit" and the Gospel calls God "Spirit," the identical name shows there is no difference in essence between Father and Son.
sources.quote: Since then, according to their account, the essence of the Father and that of the Son are both called “Spirit,” hereby is clearly proved the absence of any difference in essence.
sources.raw_question: If Eunomius holds that the essence of the Son is called "Spirit" and Scripture calls God (the Father) "Spirit," does his own principle about names prove that the Father and Son share one essence?

question: Since the Son is equal in essence to the Father, does likeness to the Son entail likeness to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Why This Opinion is to Be Rejected.
sources.answer: Yes. Pious faith teaches that the Son is like the Father by equality of essence. Therefore whatever is made in the likeness of the Son must also be made in the likeness of the Father.
sources.quote: if a pious faith teaches us, as it does, that the Son is like the Father after an equality of essence, then that which is made in the likeness of the Son must needs also be made in the likeness of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Since the Son is equal in essence to the Father, does likeness to the Son entail likeness to the Father?

question: Does Scripture use 'begat' and 'created' as interchangeable terms, so that being begotten of God is the same as being made by Him?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. When Scripture wishes to signify a son, it uses 'begat,' not 'created'; begetting signifies a Son while making signifies works. Texts like Deuteronomy 32 and Malachi place 'made' or 'created' first and 'begat' or 'Father' afterwards precisely to distinguish what men are by nature from what they receive by grace.
sources.quote: generally, when Scripture wishes to signify a son, it does so, not by the term ‘created,’ but undoubtedly by that of ‘begat.’
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture use 'begat' and 'created' as interchangeable terms, so that being begotten of God is the same as being made by Him?

question: Does being begotten 'before all' make the Word merely the first or beginning of created things?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. The text does not say 'He begat me as a beginning' but 'before all He begat me.' What is before all is other than all, including the beginning of all. Since all things were made together at one command, no creature precedes another. So the Word is other than the creatures.
sources.quote: But He who is before all is not a beginning of all, but is other than all; but if other than all (in which ‘all’ the beginning of all is included), it follows that He is other than the creatures
sources.raw_question: Does being begotten 'before all' make the Word merely the first or beginning of created things?

question: Is Jesus Christ the Son of God only by adoption, so that his calling God "My Father" is a title rather than the literal truth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Throughout the Gospels Christ consistently confesses His humility. It would be absurd to think that the same Christ makes a presumptuous, baseless claim when He calls God His Father. To grant Him the name of Son by adoption only is to accuse Him of claiming what is not His own.
sources.quote: But what else is it than such an accusation, if we allow to Jesus Christ the name of Son by adoption only? Do we not charge Him, when He calls God His Father, with daring to make a baseless claim?
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who hold an adoptive sonship
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus Christ the Son of God only by adoption, so that his calling God "My Father" is a title rather than the literal truth?

question: Is the Son coeternal with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: Yes. Consubstantiality implies coeternity, so if the Son is of one substance with the Father he must be eternal with him. Bishop Bull also collected more than twenty direct testimonies to the Son's coeternity from the Ante-Nicene Fathers, and no writer of any note plainly contradicts them.
sources.quote: That the Son is not coeternal with the Father. Consubstantiality implies coeternity
sources.raw_question: Is the Son coeternal with the Father?

question: Does the title 'God', when used absolutely in Scripture, always signify the Father alone?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. This runs directly against the stream of antiquity. Among other evidence, the ancients applied to the Son Old Testament texts in which God is spoken of absolutely. Their habit of usually meaning the Father when they say 'God' absolutely is easily accounted for and does not exclude the Son.
sources.quote: application of Scripture texts, of the Old Testament, in which God is spoken of absolutely, to the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'God', when used absolutely in Scripture, always signify the Father alone?

question: Does the Fathers' acknowledgment of the Son's subordination to the Father support the view that the Son is a lesser, non-consubstantial being?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. It is true that both Ante-Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers allowed a subordination, but this is beside the point. No certain conclusion in favour of Clarke's hypothesis can be drawn from it, as Clarke himself seems to recognize.
sources.quote: allowed a subordination ; which is very true, but not at all pertinent ; nor can any consequence be certainly drawn from it, in favour of the Doctor’s hypothesis
sources.raw_question: Does the Fathers' acknowledgment of the Son's subordination to the Father support the view that the Son is a lesser, non-consubstantial being?

question: Does the worship Christ appointed give believers communion with the Father as well as with the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen says Christ's ordinances and the whole spiritual worship he appointed are the means by which his people draw near and have communion with him and his Father. Communion with the Son in his appointed worship is at the same time communion with the Father.
sources.quote: Lovely in all his ordinances, and the whole of that spiritually glorious worship which he hath appointed to his people, whereby they draw nigh and have communion with him and his Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the worship Christ appointed give believers communion with the Father as well as with the Son?

question: Is the Holy Spirit eternally with the Father and the Son, or added to the Godhead as an accretion?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: The Spirit belongs to God eternally and not by way of accretion. There is no gap between Wisdom and the Spirit of Wisdom, or between Truth and the Spirit of Truth. As the Son is eternally contemplated in the Father, so the Spirit is contemplated with Him, being the Spirit of all that the Son is and is called.
sources.quote: we see of necessity that the good and holy Spirit must belong to Him, not by way of accretion.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit eternally with the Father and the Son, or added to the Godhead as an accretion?

question: Since Scripture calls some created things 'everlasting' (Psalm 24:7, 'ye everlasting gates'), is the Son shown to be Lord merely because he is eternal?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. sources.quote: is proved to be Lord not so much from His eternity, as in that He is God’s Son; for being the Son, He is inseparable from the Father, and never was there when He was not, but He was always
sources.raw_question: Since Scripture calls some created things 'everlasting' (Psalm 24:7, 'ye everlasting gates'), is the Son shown to be Lord merely because he is eternal?

question: If the divine nature is simple and without degrees, how are the Father, Son and Holy Spirit distinguished from one another?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: The Persons are distinguished not by quantity or degree but by the peculiar, incommunicable characteristics of each Person. All three share invariableness through their common uncreatedness. They are differentiated by the unique character of each: the Father as ungenerate, the Son as Only-begotten, and the Spirit as neither of these.
sources.quote: as possessing invariableness by virtue of its common attribute of uncreatedness, but differentiated by the unique character of each Person
sources.raw_question: If the divine nature is simple and without degrees, how are the Father, Son and Holy Spirit distinguished from one another?

question: If God is simple and without composition, must His title 'Ungenerate' name His very nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. 'Incomposite' and 'ungenerate' are not convertible terms, though both are predicated of the one subject. The first signifies freedom from composition and the second signifies being without origin. So the simplicity of the Godhead does not require that its nature be called ungeneracy.
sources.quote: the terms incomposite and ungenerate are not the same thing, for the former represents the simplicity of the subject, the other its being without origin, and these expressions are not convertible in meaning
sources.raw_question: If God is simple and without composition, must His title 'Ungenerate' name His very nature?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's working according to his own will in distributing gifts show that he is a person rather than an impersonal power?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is said to work all these things, dividing to every man severally as he will, and to work according to will is the inseparable property of a person. The same phrase is used expressly of God himself, so the text evinces the Spirit's personality.
sources.quote: for to work according to will is the inseparable property of a person, and is spoken expressly of God, Eph. i. 11
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's working according to his own will in distributing gifts show that he is a person rather than an impersonal power?

question: Does the Father and Son's sending of the Holy Spirit take away the Spirit's freedom in his works?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: No. In the economy of salvation the acting of no one person prejudices the freedom of any other. The Father's free sending of the Son does not remove the Son's free laying down of his life. The Son's satisfaction does not remove the freedom of the Father's grace in pardoning. In the same way, the Spirit's being sent does not derogate from his freedom, and he gives freely what he gives.
sources.quote: so the Father’s and Son’s sending of the Spirit doth not derogate from his freedom in his workings, but he gives freely what he gives
sources.raw_question: Does the Father and Son's sending of the Holy Spirit take away the Spirit's freedom in his works?

question: Why does Scripture use 'Spirit of God' for both Father and Son with respect to their mutual indwelling?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: To prevent us from thinking that the Son is in the Father, or the Father in the Son, in a merely bodily way. A body confined to one place cannot be elsewhere. God, however, is a living Force of infinite power, present everywhere. He manifests His whole self through what is His own, and what is His own is nothing other than Himself.
sources.quote: lest we should believe that the Son was present in the Father or the Father in the Son in a merely corporeal manner, that is, lest God might be thought to abide in one position and exist nowhere else apart from Himself
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture use 'Spirit of God' for both Father and Son with respect to their mutual indwelling?

question: Is the oneness of Father and Son in John 10:30 merely a oneness of will or moral likeness, rather than of nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: No. The oneness refers to what belongs to them in their actual being. Moral excellences such as mercy can be shared by creatures who imitate God, yet saints are not thereby one with God, because what differs in nature cannot be 'one' with it. In the Father and Son, community of nature and community of will run together into one. If the Son were united only in will and divided in nature, he could not truly testify to his oneness with the Father.
sources.quote: That which is not in every respect the same, cannot be ‘one’ with him whose nature thus varies from it.
sources.raw_question: Is the oneness of Father and Son in John 10:30 merely a oneness of will or moral likeness, rather than of nature?

question: Are the Father and Son one by two beings being joined together, or in some other way?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: They are not two made one. The One is from the Other, and they are a Unity because what is in both is the same. Each is therefore in the Other.
sources.quote: The One is from the Other, and they Two are a Unity; not Two made One, yet One in the Other, for that which is in Both is the same.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and Son one by two beings being joined together, or in some other way?

question: Does the Son's universal power belong to him as given by the Father rather than as originating in himself?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, Against the Sabellians He Proves that the Father is One, the Son Another.
