sources.answer: Yes. Scripture shows the Son born of the Father, the one by whom all things were made. He always has power over all things, but as delivered, granted and permitted to him by the Father.
sources.quote: that He always has power over all things, but as delivered, as granted, as by the Father Himself permitted to Him
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's universal power belong to him as given by the Father rather than as originating in himself?

question: Is the claim 'He was not before He was born' a valid description of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. It is a verbal quibble. Saying something once was not places it within time and thought, which would make thought and time prior to the Son's birth. But he was born before times eternal, so his birth is prior to all thought. He is from the Eternal yet has always been: not ingenerate, yet never non-existent.
sources.quote: There is no room for the verbal quibble, “He was not, before He was born.” For if He is within the range of our thought, in the sense that He was not before He was born, then both our thought and time are prior to His birth
sources.raw_question: Is the claim 'He was not before He was born' a valid description of the Son?

question: Is the name 'Ungenerate' identical with God's glory, so that because God's glory is prior to all creation the name must be too?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory grants that God's glory transcends all ages and creation, but denies that anyone has proved the appellation is identical with the glory. Nothing follows for Eunomius's argument from the priority of God's glory, since the name and the glory are different things.
sources.quote: “Yes, but this name is His glory,” he says. But pray tell us, in order that we may assent to this statement, who has proved that the appellation is identical with the glory?
sources.raw_question: Is the name 'Ungenerate' identical with God's glory, so that because God's glory is prior to all creation the name must be too?

question: Did God engraft the name 'Ungeneracy' in human minds by a law of creation as the name of the Father's essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. What is natural to humanity appears with our nature at its first formation and continues in all its posterity, like seeds from the first creation. Yet no one from Adam onward ever uttered this word until Eunomius. It is therefore a bastard invention sprung from tares, not from the good seed God sowed in our nature.
sources.quote: it is plain that it is a bastard invention, that has sprung up from the seed of tares, not from that good seed which God has sown, to use evangelic words, in the field of our nature.
sources.raw_question: Did God engraft the name 'Ungeneracy' in human minds by a law of creation as the name of the Father's essence?

question: Is eternity implied in every title given to God the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: Yes. The First Father is presupposed before all existence, has nothing previous to Himself and no end in which He will cease. He transcends any beginning and end by the infinitude of His life, so whatever His title, eternity is implied with it.
sources.quote: He transcends the limit of any end, the idea of any beginning, by the infinitude of His life; whatever be His title, eternity must be implied with it.
sources.raw_question: Is eternity implied in every title given to God the Father?

question: Can there have been a time when the Son, as image of the Father, did not exist?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Origen argued that since the Son is the resemblance of the Father there could not have been a time when he was not; the image of an eternal original and the radiance of eternal light must exist always.
sources.quote: that since he is the resemblance of his Father, there could “μοί have been a time when he was not.”
sources.raw_question: Can there have been a time when the Son, as image of the Father, did not exist?

question: Can it reasonably be denied that the Holy Spirit reigns together with Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XX. The river flowing from the Throne of God is a figure of the Holy Spirit, but by the waters spoken of by David the powers of heaven are intended. The kingdom of God is the work of the Spirit; and it is no matter for wonder if He reigns in this together with the Son, since St. Paul promises that we too shall reign with the Son.
sources.answer: No, such a denial is foolish. The Apostle promises that even we shall reign with Christ, so the Spirit all the more reigns with him. Yet the manner differs: we reign by adoption and grace, while the Spirit reigns by power and by nature.
sources.quote: what is more foolish than for any one to deny that the Holy Spirit reigns together with Christ when the Apostle says that even we shall reign together with Christ
sources.raw_question: Can it reasonably be denied that the Holy Spirit reigns together with Christ?

question: What does Christ mean when He says the Holy Spirit "shall not speak from Himself"?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: It means the Spirit does not speak without the participation of the Father and the Son. The Spirit is not divided or separated from them but speaks what He hears. He speaks the truth and breathes wisdom, never apart from the Father, because He is the Spirit of God. The Trinity speaks nothing external to Itself.
sources.quote: “He shall not speak from Himself,” that is, not without the participation of the Father and Myself. For the Spirit is not divided and separated, but speaks what He hears.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean when He says the Holy Spirit "shall not speak from Himself"?

question: Is there any difference in time, order, or kind between the works of the Father and the works of the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: No. The Son says "The works which I do He doeth," and "whatsoever things He doeth, the Son likewise doeth the same." The will, working and power of Father and Son are therefore the same. Neither Person acts before or after the other; there is one result of one operation.
sources.quote: So that the action of neither Person is before or after that of the Other, but the same result of one operation.
sources.raw_question: Is there any difference in time, order, or kind between the works of the Father and the works of the Son?

question: Is it legitimate to find the Trinity in the Old Testament, or does this read New Testament ideas back into it?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: It is legitimate. Doing so is not reading New Testament ideas back into the Old Testament text but reading that text under the illumination of the New Testament revelation. Warfield likens the Old Testament to a chamber richly furnished but dimly lit. Bringing in light adds nothing that was not already there; it only reveals what was there.
sources.quote: This is not an illegitimate reading of New Testament ideas back into the text of the Old Testament; it is only reading the text of the Old Testament under the illumination of the New Testament revelation.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to find the Trinity in the Old Testament, or does this read New Testament ideas back into it?

question: Can anything be said of God properly, rather than metaphorically, by human speech?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Those Things Which Belong Absolutely to God as an Essence, are Spoken of the Trinity in the Singular, Not in the Plural.
sources.answer: Augustine allows it only with hesitation. He holds that absolute attributes are said of God properly and not by similitude. Yet he qualifies this: if indeed anything can be spoken of God properly by the mouth of man.
sources.quote: not metaphorically and by similitude, but properly, if indeed anything can be spoken of Him properly, by the mouth of man.
sources.raw_question: Can anything be said of God properly, rather than metaphorically, by human speech?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's work of sanctifying the saints show that He shares the holiness of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Sanctifying is said truly of the Father and the Son as well, for the Holy One makes holy those in whom He dwells, just as the Good One makes men good. Since the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are alike holy and good, the Spirit's sanctifying work places Him with them rather than below them.
sources.quote: For those in whom the Holy One dwells, He makes holy, even as the Good One makes men good. And the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are holy and good, as has been shown.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's work of sanctifying the saints show that He shares the holiness of the Father and the Son?

question: Is it adequate to describe the Holy Spirit merely as a guide leading people to the mystery of baptism?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: No. That description could equally be said of Apollos, who watered what Paul planted by baptizing those Paul had instructed. To speak this way puts on a level with a human minister the Spirit who Himself perfects men through baptism.
sources.quote: Thus he places on a level with Apollos that Spirit Who perfects men through baptism.
sources.raw_question: Is it adequate to describe the Holy Spirit merely as a guide leading people to the mystery of baptism?

question: When Christians pray to the Father and close in the name of Jesus Christ, is the Son also being invoked and worshipped?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is invoked no less than the Father at the beginning of the prayer, because the Father is invoked as God and every Person is God. Christ is named at the close as mediator, not as mediator to himself but to the whole Trinity.
sources.quote: the Son is no less invocated and worshipped in the beginning than the Father, though he be peculiarly mentioned as mediator in the close, — not as Son to himself, but as mediator to the whole Trinity
sources.raw_question: When Christians pray to the Father and close in the name of Jesus Christ, is the Son also being invoked and worshipped?

question: Is the formal reason for worshipping the Holy Spirit his role as Comforter, or his deity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: His deity. Just as the Son is worshipped because he is God, not because of his mediation, the Spirit is worshipped because he is God. His being our Comforter is a powerful motive to worship him, but it is not the formal ground of that worship.
sources.quote: so the formal reason of our worshipping the Holy Ghost is not his being our comforter, but his being God; yet his being our comforter is a powerful motive thereunto.
sources.raw_question: Is the formal reason for worshipping the Holy Spirit his role as Comforter, or his deity?

question: Could God the Father be said to be sent by the Son or the Holy Spirit if he appeared visibly through a creature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Of the Sensible Showing of the Holy Spirit, and of the Coeternity of the Trinity. What Has Been Said, and What Remains to Be Said.
sources.answer: No. It would be most absurd to say so, because the Son is begotten by the Father and the Spirit proceeds from him. Sending follows the order of origin, and the Father has no origin from another Person.
sources.quote: it would be most absurd to say that He was sent either by the Son, whom He begot, or by the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from Him
sources.raw_question: Could God the Father be said to be sent by the Son or the Holy Spirit if he appeared visibly through a creature?

question: Is God called Father in respect to Himself or in relation to another?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: In relation to another. What God is, is said in respect to Himself. He is called Father in relation to the Son, and Lord in relation to the creature that serves Him. So He begets relatively and rules relatively.
sources.quote: that which He is, is spoken in respect to Himself, but He is called Father in relation to the Son, and Lord in relation to the creature which serves Him
sources.raw_question: Is God called Father in respect to Himself or in relation to another?

question: If the Son were created as 'a beginning of the ways' (Proverbs 8:22), what would follow about his nature relative to the rest of creation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: He would be of the same kind as the creatures he began, and not Lord over them. A beginning is of the same nature as what follows from it, as Reuben was firstborn yet one among his brothers, or as the first part of a city belongs to the city. So the Word would merely be one part of creation, with the same Maker and Lord as the rest, which contradicts his being Only-begotten and Lord.
sources.quote: If then the Lord is in such sense created as a ‘beginning’ of all things, it would follow that He and all other things together make up the unity of the creation, and He neither differs from all others
sources.raw_question: If the Son were created as 'a beginning of the ways' (Proverbs 8:22), what would follow about his nature relative to the rest of creation?

question: In what sense is the Word called 'a beginning of ways' in Proverbs 8:22, given that he is not by nature a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: He is the 'beginning of ways' as the incarnate Lord who opens a new way after the first way through Adam was lost. Since the way through Adam ended in death, the Word put on created flesh at the Father's will to quicken it and open a new and living way through his flesh. He thus becomes the beginning of the new creation, the Way that we now follow.
sources.quote: Therefore from love to man none other than the Lord, the ‘beginning’ of the new creation, is created as ‘the Way,’ and consistently says, ‘The Lord created me a beginning of ways for His works;’
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Word called 'a beginning of ways' in Proverbs 8:22, given that he is not by nature a creature?

question: What does 'for His works' mean in Proverbs 8:22 ('The Lord created me a beginning of His ways, for His works')?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: It means the perfect Word took an imperfect body in order to complete God's work, man, which the transgression had left wanting and dead. By paying the debt in our place, he supplied what man lacked, namely immortality and the way to paradise. Saying 'the Lord created me for the works' is the same as Christ's saying that the Father gave him the works to perfect. The following context makes clear that he received these works at his incarnation, not before.
sources.quote: for it is all one to say, ‘The Father hath given me the works,’ and ‘The Lord created me for the works.’
sources.raw_question: What does 'for His works' mean in Proverbs 8:22 ('The Lord created me a beginning of His ways, for His works')?

question: Should Proverbs 8:22 ('The Lord created me a beginning of His ways') be interpreted literally, or as figurative proverbial speech?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: It must be interpreted as proverbial, figurative speech. Proverbs do not speak plainly but put forth their meaning latently, as Christ himself indicated when he contrasted speaking in proverbs with speaking openly. So one must inquire into the person speaking and unfold the hidden sense religiously, lest a naked literal reading lead away from the truth.
sources.quote: since, however, these are proverbs, and it is expressed in the way of proverbs, we must not expound them nakedly in their first sense, but we must inquire into the person, and thus religiously put the sense on it.
sources.raw_question: Should Proverbs 8:22 ('The Lord created me a beginning of His ways') be interpreted literally, or as figurative proverbial speech?

question: Should Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways," be read as referring to the eternal divine nature of Christ the Wisdom of God, or to his Incarnation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: It refers to the Incarnation. Reading it of the divine nature makes the Creator and Lord of all a thing made and places him on a level with the creation that is in bondage. Reading it of the Incarnation keeps the right proportion between what befits the Divinity and what befits the Humanity. Paul supports this: he speaks of creation in connection with the "new man," and of creative power in connection with the true Wisdom.
sources.quote: whether that which declares the Creator and Lord of all to have been made, and places Him on a level with the creation that is in bondage, or that rather which looks to the Incarnation, and preserves the due proportion with regard to our conception alike of the Divinity and of the Humanity
sources.raw_question: Should Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways," be read as referring to the eternal divine nature of Christ the Wisdom of God, or to his Incarnation?

question: How can Wisdom (the Son) be both born of God before the ages and 'created for the beginning of the ways of God' (Proverbs 8:22) without contradiction?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: The birth before the ages is an eternal, endless generation, while the 'creation' from the commencement of the ages refers to a dispensation in which the Son serves as the creative cause for God's ways and works. The two are not the same event: one concerns His eternal divinity, the other His temporal manifestations in created form for human salvation.
sources.quote: where there is a birth before the commencement of the ages, there is the eternity of an endless generation: but where the same birth is represented as a creation from the commencement of the ages, for the ways of God and for His works, it is applied as the creative cause
sources.raw_question: How can Wisdom (the Son) be both born of God before the ages and 'created for the beginning of the ways of God' (Proverbs 8:22) without contradiction?

question: Does Proverbs 8:22's statement that Wisdom was 'created' for the beginning of God's ways mean the same as its being born before all things?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Birth precedes causation, whereas creation takes place through causation. Being created for the beginning of God's ways relates to time employed in action. Being born before the ages has no relation to time. So the word 'creation' does not reduce the Son's eternal birth to a creaturely origin.
sources.quote: For birth cannot be understood to denote creation, since the birth precedes causation, but the creation takes place through causation.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22's statement that Wisdom was 'created' for the beginning of God's ways mean the same as its being born before all things?

question: Does the Arian reading of Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created me in the beginning of His ways," prove that the Son was created?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > This third book shows a third fall of Eunomius, as refuting himself, and sometimes saying that the Son is to be called Only-begotten in virtue of natural generation, and that Holy Scripture proves this from the first; at other times, that by reason of His being created He should not be called a Son, but a “product,” or “creature.”
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that its godly sense is clear to careful readers, so it does the doctrine of the faith no harm. In Scripture a "proverb" is not meant in its evident sense but points to a hidden meaning, like the dark and obscure sayings the Gospel calls proverbs. The verse therefore cannot simply be read literally as Wisdom admitting it was created.
sources.quote: It is universally admitted that the name of “proverb,” in its scriptural use, is not applied with regard to the evident sense, but is used with a view to some hidden meaning
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian reading of Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created me in the beginning of His ways," prove that the Son was created?

question: Does the sequence in Proverbs 8, where Wisdom is first "created," then "set up," then "begotten," fit a literal account of the making of a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. A creature is not first created, then set up, and only afterwards begotten. No account that keeps to the common and obvious sense can explain this order, which shows the passage must be interpreted rather than read at face value.
sources.quote: What new order of the formation of a creature is this? First it is created, and after that it is set up, and then it is begotten.
sources.raw_question: Does the sequence in Proverbs 8, where Wisdom is first "created," then "set up," then "begotten," fit a literal account of the making of a creature?

question: Does Proverbs' statement that Wisdom (Christ) was 'created for the beginning of the ways of God' mean the same thing as the Son's being born before all ages?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Birth and creation are distinct ideas: the birth precedes all causation and has no relation to time, whereas creation takes place through causation and relates to time employed in action. Since Scripture affirms both a birth before the ages and a creation for the beginning of God's ways, the 'creation' cannot be read as denoting the Son's generation.
sources.quote: Is it possible that to be created for the beginning of the ways of God and for His works, means the same as to be born before all things? No: one of these ideas relates to time employed in action, but the other bears a sense which has no relation to time.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs' statement that Wisdom (Christ) was 'created for the beginning of the ways of God' mean the same thing as the Son's being born before all ages?

question: Does the text 'The Lord created me for the beginning of His ways' in Proverbs 8 refer to the Son's eternal generation or to something else?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: It refers to a dispensation beginning with the ages, not to the eternal generation. Wisdom introduces it by promising to recount 'things which are from of old,' i.e. things dating from the beginning of the ages, which are posterior to that beginning. Hence the 'creation' concerns Christ's role as the Way for God's works and men, not His birth before the ages.
sources.quote: Thus Wisdom’s teaching concerns not a generation declared to precede the ages, but a dispensation which began with the ages themselves.
sources.raw_question: Does the text 'The Lord created me for the beginning of His ways' in Proverbs 8 refer to the Son's eternal generation or to something else?

question: Do Proverbs 8:22 ('The Lord created me'), Hebrews 1:4 ('being made so much better than the Angels'), Hebrews 3:2 ('faithful to Him that made Him') and Acts 2:36 ('God hath made him Lord and Christ') prove that the Word of God is a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. The Arians misread these texts by imposing their heresy on them. Anyone who confesses that 'the Word became flesh' must interpret such language of the Saviour's incarnate, embodied presence, not of the Word's divine nature. To accept the Incarnation and still read these texts as making the Word a creature is inconsistent.
sources.quote: either let them rightly interpret the words of Scripture, of the embodied presence of the Saviour, or, if they deny their sense, let them deny that the Lord became man at all.
sources.raw_question: Do Proverbs 8:22 ('The Lord created me'), Hebrews 1:4 ('being made so much better than the Angels'), Hebrews 3:2 ('faithful to Him that made Him') and Acts 2:36 ('God hath made him Lord and Christ') prove that the Word of God is a creature?

question: Does Proverbs 8:22 speak of the Word's divine essence and eternal generation, or of his incarnation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: It speaks of his manhood and the Economy toward us, not of his Godhead or his eternal generation from the Father. Wisdom itself gives the meaning in a parallel expression: 'Wisdom made herself a house.' That house is the human body Wisdom took to become man, which agrees with John's 'The Word was made flesh.'
sources.quote: not as signifying the Essence of His Godhead, nor His own everlasting and genuine generation from the Father, has the Word spoken by Solomon, but on the other hand His manhood and Economy towards us.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8:22 speak of the Word's divine essence and eternal generation, or of his incarnation?

question: How should the mountains, depths, springs and hills of Proverbs 8:24-25, before which Wisdom is begotten, be applied to the Word?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: They are to be taken tropically, following the usage of Scripture. David calls righteousness the "mountains of God," God's judgments "deeps," the teachers of the Churches "fountains," and guilelessness "hills." So the One who was created as man for our sakes is born in us before these virtues, so that their creation may also take place in us.
sources.quote: Before these therefore is born in us He Who for our sakes was created as man, that of these things also the creation may find place in us.
sources.raw_question: How should the mountains, depths, springs and hills of Proverbs 8:24-25, before which Wisdom is begotten, be applied to the Word?

question: Does calling the Son 'faithful' in Hebrews 3:2 mean that He exercised faith like other creatures and received the reward of faith?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. Scripture uses 'faithful' in two senses: 'believing,' which belongs to man, and 'trustworthy,' which belongs to God, as when Moses and Paul call God faithful. Applied to the Son it means that, being Son of the true God, He is trustworthy and to be believed in all He says and does, remaining unalterable in His human economy.
sources.quote: they acknowledged two senses of the word ‘faithful’ in Scripture, first ‘believing,’ then ‘trustworthy,’ of which the former belongs to man, the latter to God.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'faithful' in Hebrews 3:2 mean that He exercised faith like other creatures and received the reward of faith?

question: Does the phrase 'who was faithful to Him that made Him' in Hebrews 3:2 refer to the essence or eternal generation of the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. The context concerns the Son as 'Apostle and High Priest of our profession,' offices He took on only when the Word became flesh and offered Himself. So 'made' signifies His descent to mankind and His High-priesthood, which did 'become,' not His essence or natural generation, for the Word is not made but makes.
sources.quote: Not then as wishing to signify the Essence of the Word nor His natural generation from the Father, did the Apostle say, ‘Who was faithful to Him that made Him’—(perish the thought! for the Word is not made, but makes)
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'who was faithful to Him that made Him' in Hebrews 3:2 refer to the essence or eternal generation of the Word?

question: What does Hebrews 3:2 mean in calling Christ 'faithful' to him that made him?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: 'Faithful' here means trustworthy and unchangeable, not that the Son came to believe as a creature does. Just as God is faithful because He is ever the same and does not change, the Son is faithful as ever the same, deceiving neither in His essence nor in His promise. Even when made man, Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever.
sources.quote: therefore His Son is ‘faithful,’ being ever the same and unchanging, deceiving neither in His essence nor in His promise
sources.raw_question: What does Hebrews 3:2 mean in calling Christ 'faithful' to him that made him?

question: Does calling Christ 'faithful' in Hebrews mean that He has faith in someone, as believers do?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. He is faithful because He deserves to be believed in all He says and does. He also offered a faithful sacrifice that lasts forever, unlike the sacrifices of the Law that passed away. And He holds an unchanging high priesthood without succession and keeps His promises, just as Peter calls God a 'faithful Creator.'
sources.quote: faithful, not as sharing faith with us, nor as having faith in any one as we have, but as deserving to receive faith in all He says and does
sources.raw_question: Does calling Christ 'faithful' in Hebrews mean that He has faith in someone, as believers do?

question: Why can the uncreated Wisdom of God speak of being 'created' for God's works in Proverbs 8:22?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Because an impress and image of Wisdom is created in us and in all the works, the true Wisdom takes to Himself what belongs to His own impress. Just as Christ says 'He that receiveth you receiveth Me' because His impress is in us, so He speaks in His own person of what is created in the works, though He Himself is Creator.
sources.quote: whereas He is not Himself created, being Creator, yet because of the image of Him created in the works, He says this as if of Himself.
sources.raw_question: Why can the uncreated Wisdom of God speak of being 'created' for God's works in Proverbs 8:22?

question: Do the words 'He created me', 'He formed me' and 'He set me' (Proverbs 8:22, Isaiah 49:5) denote the beginning of the Son's being or essence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: No. The three terms have the same meaning and signify not His beginning of being but His beneficent renovation of us, i.e. His taking manhood. The Son Himself taught that He existed before, saying 'Before Abraham came to be, I am,' and Wisdom says 'when He prepared the heavens, I was present with Him.' He exists first and is formed afterwards, so the forming refers to the Economy in the flesh.
sources.quote: 'He created' then and 'He formed' and 'He set,' having the same meaning, do not denote the beginning of His being, or of His essence as created, but His beneficent renovation which came to pass for us.
sources.raw_question: Do the words 'He created me', 'He formed me' and 'He set me' (Proverbs 8:22, Isaiah 49:5) denote the beginning of the Son's being or essence?

question: Why does Proverbs 8:22 say the Lord created Wisdom 'for the works,' and what does the added phrase show?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: The phrase 'for the works' gives the reason for the creation, showing that it signifies His becoming man for the renovation of the works. Being other than the works and their Framer, it befitted Him to take on their renovation, so that, He being created for us, all things might be created anew in Him. The works are evidently later than Himself.
sources.quote: For when He said 'He created,' He forthwith added the reason, naming 'the works,' that His creation for the works might signify His becoming man for their renovation.
sources.raw_question: Why does Proverbs 8:22 say the Lord created Wisdom 'for the works,' and what does the added phrase show?

question: Is it consistent to read 'He created' in David and Paul as renewal but to read it of the Son's essence in Proverbs 8:22?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. It is evidently unfair to understand 'He created' as renewal when David and Paul use it, yet as essence when the Lord uses it. Likewise the Arians read 'Wisdom built her an house' allegorically yet take 'He created' literally in the same book. Consistency requires the same figurative reading.
sources.quote: Indeed is it not evidently unfair in you, when David and Paul say ‘He created,’ then indeed not to understand it of the essence and the generation, but the renewal; yet, when the Lord says ‘He created’ to number His essence with the creatures?
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to read 'He created' in David and Paul as renewal but to read it of the Son's essence in Proverbs 8:22?

question: Should the sayings that Wisdom speaks in her own person in Proverbs 8, including the context of 'The Lord created me', be read according to their obvious literal sense?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that a careful reader will accept none of these phrases without scrutiny. Read literally, the surrounding clauses lead to absurd conclusions. So they must be read in a deeper, spiritual sense. Since 'The Lord created me' is written in close connection with these clauses, prudent readers should not take it absolutely and without examination either.
sources.quote: Now every one will see that the considerate reader will receive none of the phrases quoted without scrutiny according to the obvious sense.
sources.raw_question: Should the sayings that Wisdom speaks in her own person in Proverbs 8, including the context of 'The Lord created me', be read according to their obvious literal sense?

question: Can the Wisdom of Proverbs 8:22 be a creature made along with other things without contradicting John's teaching that all things were made through the Word?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. John teaches that all created things are the work of the Word. If God made Wisdom together with all other things, then all things would not be made through her, and she would herself be counted among the things that were made. Therefore John's theology excludes the reading that Wisdom is a creature.
sources.quote: For it is not possible that the theology of John should be esteemed true, which recites that all created things are the work of the Word, if in this passage He Who created Wisdom be believed to have made together with her all other things also.
sources.raw_question: Can the Wisdom of Proverbs 8:22 be a creature made along with other things without contradicting John's teaching that all things were made through the Word?

question: In what sense is the Holy Spirit the 'Use' or 'Gift' in the Trinity, and is He begotten?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Of the Attributes Assigned by Hilary to Each Person. The Trinity is Represented in Things that are Made.
sources.answer: The Spirit is the love, delight and blessedness of the union between the Father and His Image, which Hilary calls 'Use.' He is not begotten. He is the sweetness of the begetter and the begotten, and He fills all creatures according to their capacity, so that they keep their proper order.
sources.quote: is the Holy Spirit in the Trinity, not begotten, but the sweetness of the begetter and of the begotten, filling all creatures according to their capacity
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Holy Spirit the 'Use' or 'Gift' in the Trinity, and is He begotten?

question: Did the prophets of the Old Testament speak from a different god than the Father of Jesus Christ, as the Gnostics claimed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: No. In the parable of the wicked husbandmen Christ shows one and the same Householder who sends at one time his servants (the prophets) and at another his Son. Therefore the Father from whom the Son was sent is the same from whom the servants were sent, and Christ never says the prophets spoke from another god or another essence.
sources.quote: From that Father, therefore, from whom the Son was sent to those husbandmen who slew Him, from Him also were the servants [sent].
sources.raw_question: Did the prophets of the Old Testament speak from a different god than the Father of Jesus Christ, as the Gnostics claimed?

question: Can human beings know God, and if so, in what respect?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIV.—Recapitulation of the various arguments adduced against Gnostic impiety under all its aspects. The heretics, tossed about by every blast of doctrine, are opposed by the uniform teaching of the Church, which remains so always, and is consistent with itself.
sources.answer: Yes, but only in a limited way. Out of love and infinite kindness God has come within reach of human knowledge. We cannot know His greatness or His essence, which no one has measured or handled. We can know that He who made us, breathed life into us, and nourishes us through creation is the only true God.
sources.quote: knowledge, however, not with regard to His greatness, or with regard to His essence—for that has no man measured or handled
sources.raw_question: Can human beings know God, and if so, in what respect?

question: By what means does the one God create and sustain all things?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIV.—Recapitulation of the various arguments adduced against Gnostic impiety under all its aspects. The heretics, tossed about by every blast of doctrine, are opposed by the uniform teaching of the Church, which remains so always, and is consistent with itself.
sources.answer: God establishes all things by His Word and binds them together by His Wisdom. The Creator who formed man and breathed life into him works through His Word and Wisdom. So creation is the work of the one true God with His Word and Wisdom, not of an inferior being.
sources.quote: establishing all things by His Word, and binding them together by His Wisdom— this is He who is the only true God
sources.raw_question: By what means does the one God create and sustain all things?

question: Does the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies others, himself need sanctification?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter V. The writer sums up the argument he had commenced, and confirms the statement that unity is signified by the terms finger and right hand, from the fact that the works of God are the same as are the works of hands; and that those of hands are the same as those of fingers; and lastly, that the term hand applies equally to the Son and the Spirit, and that of finger applies to the Spirit and the Son.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit needs no sanctification but abounds in it, and so he sanctifies each person. His majesty is so great that he is as inseparable from God the Father as the finger is from the body.
sources.quote: what wonder is it if He Who Himself needs no sanctification, but abounds therewith, sanctifies each man
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies others, himself need sanctification?

question: Is the Father robbed of His Godhead or oneness if the Son shares the Godhead?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. God is still God if His Son shares the Godhead, because the case is that of God from God, One from One. The Father remains One because the God who is the Son is from Him.
sources.quote: God is not robbed, He is still God, if His Son share the Godhead. For the case is that of God from God, of One from One, of God Who is One because God is from Him.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father robbed of His Godhead or oneness if the Son shares the Godhead?

question: Is the trinity of memory, inner vision and will in thought more unified in substance than the trinity of outward bodily sight?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > The Unity of the Three Takes Place in Thought, Viz. Of Memory, of Ternal Vision, and of Will Combining Both.
sources.answer: Yes. In the inner trinity there is no longer any diversity of substance. The sensible body, which is wholly distinct from the nature of the living being, is absent, and all three elements now belong to the soul itself. The outer trinity, by contrast, joined the external body with the bodily sense.
sources.quote: And in these three there is no longer any diversity of substance. For neither is the sensible body there, which is altogether distinct from the nature of the living being
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity of memory, inner vision and will in thought more unified in substance than the trinity of outward bodily sight?

question: Can the human mind, as the image of God, legitimately be used to investigate questions about the Trinity, such as why the Holy Spirit is not begotten?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > Why Love is Not the Offspring of the Mind, as Knowledge is So. The Solution of the Question. The Mind with the Knowledge of Itself and the Love of Itself is the Image of the Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine holds that by questioning the lower image in the rational creature, whose nature answers us in a more familiar way, we can train our mental vision and then direct it from the enlightened creature to the unchangeable light. Since man is made after the image of the Trinity, the mind's relations of knowing and loving offer an analogy for the supreme Trinity.
sources.quote: from a lower image, in which our own nature itself as it were answers, upon being questioned, in a way more familiar to ourselves, we may be able to direct a more practised mental vision from the enlightened creature to the unchangeable light
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind, as the image of God, legitimately be used to investigate questions about the Trinity, such as why the Holy Spirit is not begotten?

question: If Proverbs 8 is read as saying that the same Lord who created Wisdom (the Son) also made the inhabited and uninhabited land, does this contradict John 1:3, which says all things were made by the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: Yes, on the literal reading. If one and the same Lord creates both Wisdom and the particular things of creation, then the Son would not be the maker of all things. That would set Proverbs against the Gospel. The Arian literal reading therefore makes John speak falsely and must be rejected.
sources.quote: For if one and the same Lord creates both Wisdom (which they advise us to understand of the Son), and also the particular things which are included in the Creation, how does the sublime John speak truly, when he says that all things were made by Him?
sources.raw_question: If Proverbs 8 is read as saying that the same Lord who created Wisdom (the Son) also made the inhabited and uninhabited land, does this contradict John 1:3, which says all things were made by the Son?

question: Do texts saying that power was 'given' to Christ, or that God 'highly exalted' him, show that the Son was in want and therefore not truly God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > When the Word and Son hungered, wept, and was wearied, He acted as our Mediator, taking on Him what was ours, that He might impart to us what was His.
sources.answer: No. The Word was never in want and did not come into being; such gifts were received by him as Mediator in his humanity, not because he needed them. They were given to man through the Word, and are said to be given to him because they were given on his account. The mere Word did not need them, and mere man was not worthy of them.
sources.quote: For the Word was never in want, nor has come into being; nor again were men sufficient to minister these things for themselves, but through the Word they are given to us; therefore, as if given to Him, they are imparted to us.
sources.raw_question: Do texts saying that power was 'given' to Christ, or that God 'highly exalted' him, show that the Son was in want and therefore not truly God?

question: Why did the Word of God become man and Mediator between God and men?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > When the Word and Son hungered, wept, and was wearied, He acted as our Mediator, taking on Him what was ours, that He might impart to us what was His.
sources.answer: So that he might give the things of God to us and offer ours to God. He took our human affections in order to annul them, and he received God's gifts so that they might pass on to us. Because man is united to the Word, man receives through him what he could not receive by his own nature.
sources.quote: For this was the reason of His becoming man, that, as being given to Him, they might pass on to us
sources.raw_question: Why did the Word of God become man and Mediator between God and men?

question: Do the Scripture declarations that there is only one God exclude only other supreme, independent deities, or also lesser, inferior, dependent divinities?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 4: Whether, supposing the Scripture-notion of God to be no more than that of the Author and Governor of the universe, or whatever it be, the admitting of another t
sources.answer: They exclude inferior and dependent divinities as well. The reason of the thing and the whole drift and design of Scripture was to exclude not only other supreme deities, which few were foolish enough to posit, but also lesser, dependent gods. Scripture never adds 'supreme' to its statements of God's unity, and never hints at a distinction between a sovereign and an inferior Deity.
sources.quote: the drift, scope, and design of the Scripture seems plainly to have been to exclude not other Supremes only, or other independent Deities, (which few have been weak enough to suppose,) but other lesser, inferior, and dependent Divinities?
sources.raw_question: Do the Scripture declarations that there is only one God exclude only other supreme, independent deities, or also lesser, inferior, dependent divinities?

question: In Augustine's image of the Trinity in the human mind, how does the mind come to have an inner 'word', and does that word leave the mind when it is begotten?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > We Conceive and Beget the Word Within, from the Things We Have Beheld in the Eternal Truth. The Word, Whether of the Creature or of the Creator, is Conceived by Love.
sources.answer: The mind beholds in the eternal truth the form of things and conceives from it true knowledge, which is a word within us. By speaking inwardly we beget this word, yet once born it does not depart from us. This begetting that stays within is a likeness of the Father's begetting of the Word.
sources.quote: we have the true knowledge of things, thence conceived, as it were as a word within us, and by speaking we beget it from within; nor by being born does it depart from us.
sources.raw_question: In Augustine's image of the Trinity in the human mind, how does the mind come to have an inner 'word', and does that word leave the mind when it is begotten?

question: Does the Son's being before all things make him the beginning of creation as to his essence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. What is the beginning of all is counted in the number of all. Since the Son is alone First and Son, he is not such a beginning in essence. He therefore differs in essence and nature from creatures, and is the Image of the only true God.
sources.quote: if He be before all, as indeed He is, and is Himself alone First and Son, it does not follow that He is beginning of all things as to His Essence, for what is the beginning of all is in the number of all.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being before all things make him the beginning of creation as to his essence?

question: Does Scripture class the Son among the creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. David rebukes those who think of the Lord as like any among the gods or sons of God. Baruch says no other shall be reckoned with God. The One creates and the rest are created, and the Son is the Father's own Word through whom all things were made.
sources.quote: Hence He is not classed with creatures in Scripture, but David rebukes those who dare even to think of Him as such, saying, ‘Who among the gods is like unto the Lord?’
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture class the Son among the creatures?

question: If Christ existed before all creation, must he be divine rather than a creature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Creator and creatures make up the whole range of beings, so the pre-existent Word must be one or the other. He cannot have been a creature existing before any creature was made, so his pre-existence must be in the divine nature.
sources.quote: who know that Creator and creatures take up the whole nature of beings. One of them he must be; and it may be well supposed that he was not a creature before the creation of any.
sources.raw_question: If Christ existed before all creation, must he be divine rather than a creature?

question: Does proving any pre-existence of Christ before his incarnation refute the Socinian view of his person?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. The Socinians flatly deny any pre-existence of Christ before his incarnation. Granting any such pre-existence would therefore overthrow their whole heresy on this point, even before eternity itself is proven.
sources.quote: we prevail against our adversaries, if we prove any pre-existence of Christ unto his incarnation; which, as they absolutely deny, so to grant it would overthrow their whole heresy in this matter.
sources.raw_question: Does proving any pre-existence of Christ before his incarnation refute the Socinian view of his person?

question: How does John 1:1-3 relate to Genesis 1:1, and what does that relationship show about the Word?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: John's opening is an exposition of Genesis 1:1. Genesis says God created all things in the beginning; John says the Word was in the beginning and made all things. Even if 'beginning' is limited to creation, this shows the Word's personal pre-existence before all creation and his role as Creator.
sources.quote: There it is asserted that in the beginning God created all things; here, that the Word was in the beginning, and made all things.
sources.raw_question: How does John 1:1-3 relate to Genesis 1:1, and what does that relationship show about the Word?

question: Does the statement that the Holy Spirit "shall not speak of Himself, but whatsoever He shall hear, that shall He speak" show that the Holy Spirit is less than the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Some Things Concerning the Holy Spirit are to Be Understood According to the One Rule Only.
sources.answer: No. The words belong to the Spirit as proceeding from the Father, signifying his origin, not inferiority. Just as the Son's saying he can do nothing of himself does not make him less but shows he is of the Father, so this saying does not make the Spirit less.
sources.quote: so it is not brought to pass that the Holy Spirit is less, because it is said of Him, “For He shall not speak of Himself, but whatsoever He shall hear, that shall He speak;” for the words belong to Him as proceeding from the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that the Holy Spirit "shall not speak of Himself, but whatsoever He shall hear, that shall He speak" show that the Holy Spirit is less than the Father?

question: Are the three divine Persons one in essence in the same way that an individual man with his trinity of mind, knowledge and love is one person?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God from the Trinities We Have Spoken of.
sources.answer: No. In man the three belong to a single person, so the mental trinity is found within one person. In God, by contrast, there are Three Persons who are of one essence, so the unity of the Trinity is not the unity of a single person as in each individual man. This is a key way the image falls short of what it images.
sources.quote: and the Three Persons are of one essence, not as each individual man is one person.
sources.raw_question: Are the three divine Persons one in essence in the same way that an individual man with his trinity of mind, knowledge and love is one person?

question: Can the Son be the seal or likeness of the Father's works when all created things are the works of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. All things visible and invisible are the work of the Son, so no works of the Father remain apart from His for the Son to copy. If Eunomius says the Son is Himself a work of the Father, he falls into the absurdity that the same Person is at once a work and the likeness of a work. No Scripture calls Him the "seal of the Father's works."
sources.quote: All things visible and invisible are the work of the Son: in the visible are included the whole world and all that is therein; in the invisible, the supramundane creation.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be the seal or likeness of the Father's works when all created things are the works of the Son?

question: Is the Son the image of words and counsels of the Father that exist prior to Him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. The Father has no other Word than the Son, who is the Word in the absolute and primary sense, and no counsels apart from the Wisdom of God, which is the Son. The Son has the whole Father in Himself and is wholly in the Father. He is therefore all things in the Father, not the copy of things discerned in the Father before Him.
sources.quote: Himself is all things in the Father, and does not come to be the image and seal and likeness of certain other things discerned in the Father prior to Himself.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the image of words and counsels of the Father that exist prior to Him?

question: Can a creature, or anything that had a beginning, be truly called God or act as Creator, so that the Son could be an inferior God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus, cited approvingly, allows no creature or anything with a beginning to be justly called God. He treats an inferior God as a contradiction and denies that any creature can create. Yet he calls the Son truly God, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, and Creator of men, angels and all things.
sources.quote: allows no creature, nothing that had a beginning, to be justly called God; ylooks upon the notion of an inferior God as a contradiction; does not Zadmit that any creature can create
sources.raw_question: Can a creature, or anything that had a beginning, be truly called God or act as Creator, so that the Son could be an inferior God?

question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers generally believe the Son to be of an eternal, uncreated, immutable and strictly divine substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds that this, and not some narrower formula, is the real question between Bishop Bull and the Arians. Bull maintained the affirmative and, in the judgment of most learned men at home and abroad, proved it unanswerably. The Examiner himself had formerly granted as much and should not have hidden or disguised it.
sources.quote: Whether the Ante-Nicene Fathers, in general, believed the Son to be of an eterna/, wncreated, immutable, and strictly divine substance, or no? Bishop Bull maintained the affirmative
sources.raw_question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers generally believe the Son to be of an eternal, uncreated, immutable and strictly divine substance?

question: Does Scripture teach that there is only one God, the maker of heaven and earth?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > In Fine, Notwithstanding the Said Heretics Have Gathered the Origin of Their Error from Consideration of What is Written: Although We Call Christ God, and the Father God, Still Scripture Does Not Set Forth Two Gods, Any More Than Two Lords or Two Teachers.
sources.answer: Yes. The Church knows, reads, believes and maintains that God is one, who made heaven and earth, and that there is no other. Scripture states this repeatedly: 'I am God, and there is none beside me', 'Thou art God alone', 'God alone is good', and 'God is one'.
sources.quote: For we both know, and read, and believe, and maintain that God is one, who made the heaven as well as the earth, since we neither know any other, nor shall we at any time know such, seeing that there is none.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that there is only one God, the maker of heaven and earth?

question: Is the Son's generation from the Father a spatial extension or prolongation of the divine substance?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. It is a begetting, not a prolongation in space or an extension. The unity of light with light is a unity of nature, not unbroken material continuation. God is immutable and has no material elements, so his begetting cannot be understood in bodily terms.
sources.quote: The birth of the Only-begotten Son from God is not a prolongation in space, but a begetting; not an extension, but Light from Light. For the unity of light with light is a unity of nature, not unbroken continuation.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's generation from the Father a spatial extension or prolongation of the divine substance?

question: What can be one with the Father in the sense of John 10:30?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: Only what is from the Father, that is, the Son. Christ referred the sense of 'are One' to his being the Son of God, showing that oneness with the Father belongs to the one who is begotten from Him.
sources.quote: For nothing is one with the Father, but what is from Him. What is that which is from Him but the Son?
sources.raw_question: What can be one with the Father in the sense of John 10:30?

question: Is it consistent for Christians to worship the Son if, as the Arians claim, the Son is a creature and a work?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: No. Christian teaching calls people away from worshipping the creation. Telling them to abandon creature-worship and then worship a creature and a work is self-contradictory and was never taught. Worship of the Son therefore requires that he not be a creature.
sources.quote: who told them, ‘Abandon the worship of the creation, and then draw near and worship a creature and a work?’
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent for Christians to worship the Son if, as the Arians claim, the Son is a creature and a work?

question: Why must Christ, as mediator, be both truly human and truly divine?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
