sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: Because a mediator must reach both parties. Like Jacob's ladder, whose foot rests on earth while its top reaches heaven, Christ is one with us by the humanity he assumed and one with God by his eternal essence. The texts on his humanity and those on his Godhead together form the grace of our salvation.
sources.quote: As combined with the revelations of his essential Godhead, they form that inimitable grace which is our salvation. The foot of the ladder must rest on earth, as the top of it reaches to heaven.
sources.raw_question: Why must Christ, as mediator, be both truly human and truly divine?

question: Does Scripture call the Holy Spirit 'Lord', and does the Samson narrative show this?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter I. The Spirit is the Lord and Power; and in this is not inferior to the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. In the account of Samson, the Spirit of the Lord is said to go with him, and after he was shaven it is said 'the Lord departed from him'; He Who went with him is the same Who departed, so the Spirit of the Lord is Himself called Lord. The Apostle confirms this when he says 'The Lord is the Spirit.'
sources.quote: You see, then, that He Who went with him, Himself departed from him. The Same is, then, the Lord, Who is the Spirit of the Lord, that is, he called the Spirit of God, Lord
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture call the Holy Spirit 'Lord', and does the Samson narrative show this?

question: Is the Son's unity with the Father ('I and the Father are One') the same kind of union that believing creatures have when they 'attach themselves' to the Lord (Deuteronomy 4:4)?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: No. Creatures, being external and foreign by nature, are attached to God from without and by free choice as they make moral advance. The Word, by contrast, is in the Father as being His own, so his oneness is by nature, not by adhesion. This difference shows that the Son of God is not a creature.
sources.quote: The Word then is in the Father as being His own; but things originate, being external, are attached, as being by nature foreign, and attached by free choice.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's unity with the Father ('I and the Father are One') the same kind of union that believing creatures have when they 'attach themselves' to the Lord (Deuteronomy 4:4)?

question: How does the human inner word, as an image of the Son, differ from the Son as image of the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Likeness of the Divine Word, Such as It Is, is to Be Sought, Not in Our Own Outer and Sensible Word, But in the Inner and Mental One. There is the Greatest Possible Unlikeness Between Our Word and Knowledge and the Divine Word and Knowledge.
sources.answer: The human word is the word of an image that is made by God, not born of God. The Son is the image that is born, like the Father in substance in all things. A true human word, in which exactly what is in the knowledge is in the word and nothing else, comes as near as possible to that begotten likeness. Yet it remains greatly unlike it.
sources.quote: this likeness of the image that is made, approaches as nearly as is possible to that likeness of the image that is born, by which God the Son is declared to be in all things like in substance to the Father.
sources.raw_question: How does the human inner word, as an image of the Son, differ from the Son as image of the Father?

question: When Christ delivers up the kingdom to God the Father (1 Cor 15:24), are the Son and the Holy Spirit excluded from that kingdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to God, Even the Father. The Kingdom Having Been Delivered to God, Even the Father, Christ Will Not Then Make Intercession for Us.
sources.answer: No. Christ will deliver up the kingdom to God, even the Father, without himself or the Holy Spirit being excluded. Delivering up the kingdom means bringing believers to the contemplation of God, and that contemplation is of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together.
sources.quote: Our Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, will so deliver up the kingdom to God, even the Father, Himself not being thence excluded, nor the Holy Spirit, when He shall bring believers to the contemplation of God
sources.raw_question: When Christ delivers up the kingdom to God the Father (1 Cor 15:24), are the Son and the Holy Spirit excluded from that kingdom?

question: Is the incarnate Son more truly 'another substance' from the Father, or is his manhood more truly another substance from the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to God, Even the Father. The Kingdom Having Been Delivered to God, Even the Father, Christ Will Not Then Make Intercession for Us.
sources.answer: It is rather the manhood in the Son that is another substance from the Son, not the Son that is another substance from the Father. Augustine compares this to a human being: the bodily nature is more another substance from one's soul, even within the same man, than another man's soul is from one's own soul.
sources.quote: it is rather to be said that the manhood in the Son is another substance [from the Son], than that the Son in the Father [is another substance from the Father]
sources.raw_question: Is the incarnate Son more truly 'another substance' from the Father, or is his manhood more truly another substance from the Son?

question: How is the inner word of the mind generated, and how does it relate to the knowledge from which it is born, as an image of the Word's generation?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Concerning the Word of the Mind, in Which We See the Word of God, as in a Glass and an Enigma.
sources.answer: When we speak what is true, that is, what we know, a word is necessarily born from the knowledge which the memory retains. This word is altogether of the same kind as the knowledge from which it is born. The thought formed by the thing we know is the word we speak in the heart.
sources.quote: there is born from the knowledge itself which the memory retains, a word that is altogether of the same kind with that knowledge from which it is born.
sources.raw_question: How is the inner word of the mind generated, and how does it relate to the knowledge from which it is born, as an image of the Word's generation?

question: Does the title 'Father' reveal the essence of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory proceeds to discuss the relative force of the unnameable name of the Holy Trinity and the mutual relation of the Persons, and moreover the unknowable character of the essence, and the condescension on His part towards us, His generation of the Virgin, and His second coming, the resurrection from the dead and future retribution.
sources.answer: No. The name 'Father' does not present the essence but only indicates the Father's relation to the Son. By the relative force of the term, confessing the Father also declares the majesty of the Son.
sources.quote: it is plain that the title of Father does not present to us the Essence, but only indicates the relation to the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'Father' reveal the essence of God?

question: How is the Holy Spirit implied in the confession of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory proceeds to discuss the relative force of the unnameable name of the Holy Trinity and the mutual relation of the Persons, and moreover the unknowable character of the essence, and the condescension on His part towards us, His generation of the Virgin, and His second coming, the resurrection from the dead and future retribution.
sources.answer: Confessing the Father as absolutely existent declares, by the relative force of the term, the Son. The Son in turn implies in close union with himself the Spirit of Life and Truth, since the Son is himself Life and Truth. Thus the Father, Son, and Spirit are confessed together in inseparable relation.
sources.quote: the Son, as has been said, implying in close union with Himself the Spirit of Life and Truth, inasmuch as He is Himself Life and Truth.
sources.raw_question: How is the Holy Spirit implied in the confession of the Father and the Son?

question: Does Scripture teach that we should believe in or baptize into 'the one and only true God' rather than into the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as Eunomius' creed claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory proceeds to discuss the relative force of the unnameable name of the Holy Trinity and the mutual relation of the Persons, and moreover the unknowable character of the essence, and the condescension on His part towards us, His generation of the Virgin, and His second coming, the resurrection from the dead and future retribution.
sources.answer: No. The Gospels read in the churches contain no command to believe in or baptize into 'the one and only true God.' The command is to baptize into the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. Eunomius' formula therefore perverts the Lord's own exposition of the faith.
sources.quote: They cannot manage to show where in the Gospels the Lord said that we should believe on “the one and only true God:” unless they have some new Gospel.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that we should believe in or baptize into 'the one and only true God' rather than into the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as Eunomius' creed claims?

question: Should the consubstantiality of Father, Son and Spirit be described as specific or as numerical unity of substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: Neither term exactly fits, nor perhaps any other we can think of, and the label does not matter. What matters is that the consubstantiality is proper and not figurative. It preserves the unity without destroying the distinct personality of the Persons.
sources.quote: As to the question, whether it shall be called specific or numerical, | am in no pain about it. Neither of the names exactly suits it; nor perhaps any other we can think on.
sources.raw_question: Should the consubstantiality of Father, Son and Spirit be described as specific or as numerical unity of substance?

question: Should the doctrine of the Trinity and the deity of Christ be settled chiefly by appeal to Scripture rather than to human authorities?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Preface
sources.answer: Yes. Although the author used other writers, he holds that our appeal must ultimately be to one Book. He let Scripture lead him and built his case by gathering Bible evidence alone. He trusts the word of God, as the sword of the Spirit, to convince those who deny Christ's Godhead.
sources.quote: I therefore suffered Scripture as it were to lead me by the hand: until by compiling and illustrating Bible evidence alone, my little essay swelled to nearly its present dimensions.
sources.raw_question: Should the doctrine of the Trinity and the deity of Christ be settled chiefly by appeal to Scripture rather than to human authorities?

question: Does Scripture show the Holy Spirit to have independent authority and power, rather than being a subject creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. The prophet calls the Spirit "good," "right," and "guiding," and "guiding" signifies a power of control. The apostle says the Spirit works all in all as He wills. The Lord tells Nicodemus that "the Spirit breatheth where He willeth," which shows the Spirit's independent power and operation.
sources.quote: even so the apostle ascribes independent authority to the dignity of the Spirit, when he affirms that He works all in all as He wills
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture show the Holy Spirit to have independent authority and power, rather than being a subject creature?

question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers believe that the Son of God is omniscient?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: Yes. Ignatius says nothing is hid from the Lord. Clement of Alexandria calls the Son all mind, all light, all eye of the Father, knowing all things, and says ignorance cannot affect him. Origen studiously seeks interpretations that clear the Word of literal ignorance of the day of judgment.
sources.quote: all mind, all “light, all eye of his Father, beholding all things, hearing “all things, knowing all things.
sources.raw_question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers believe that the Son of God is omniscient?

question: Can the Father's essence "attract to itself" the conception of the Existent so that existence is drawn away from the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. If it means the Father attracts his own existence, this is superfluous, since he already possesses it. If it means the Son's existence is drawn to the Father, it is unintelligible how existence could be wrenched from one who exists and passed to another; this would either collapse into Sabellius's error or absurdly separate the Existent from existence.
sources.quote: If, on the other hand, his meaning is that the existence of the Son is attracted by the Father, I cannot make out how existence is to be wrenched from the Existent, and to pass over to Him Who “attracts” it.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father's essence "attract to itself" the conception of the Existent so that existence is drawn away from the Son?

question: Does the Son exist in himself as a distinct person, or is he merely an aspect of the Father's personal existence as Sabellius taught?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: The Son exists in himself. Gregory counts it an error of Sabellius to suppose the Son lacks his own existence and is merely painted onto the Father's personal existence. He presents this as an absurdity into which Eunomius's language about attracting existence would fall.
sources.quote: Can he be dreaming of the error of Sabellius, as though the Son did not exist in Himself, but was painted on to the personal existence of the Father?
sources.raw_question: Does the Son exist in himself as a distinct person, or is he merely an aspect of the Father's personal existence as Sabellius taught?

question: Is it legitimate to glorify God by joining the divine names with "and" (Father and Son and Holy Spirit) instead of "with"?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That Scripture uses the words “in” or “by,” ἐν, cf. note on p. 3, in place of “with.” Wherein also it is proved that the word “and” has the same force as “with.”
sources.answer: Yes. Basil accepts the formula "Father and Son and Holy Ghost" without objection, because it is the form taught in the Gospel's baptismal command. Like "with", it coordinates the Spirit with the Father and the Son. It is exactly this coordination that his opponents refuse.
sources.quote: if any one likes, in the ascription of praise, to couple the names by the syllable “and,” and to give glory, as we have taught in the Gospel, in the formula of baptism, Father and Son and Holy Ghost, be it so: no one will make any objection.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to glorify God by joining the divine names with "and" (Father and Son and Holy Spirit) instead of "with"?

question: Do the names Scripture gives to Christ, such as Door, Bread, Way, Vine, Shepherd, Light, signify the nature or essence of the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. None of these names represents the nature, Godhead, or peculiar character of the Son's essence. If they did, the divine nature would be multiform and complex, since Bread, Lion, Axe and Water each have their own distinct definition not shared by the others. Yet they are not idle or unmeaning, since nothing in God's words is idle.
sources.quote: Does Eunomius affirm that the words are indicative of His nature itself? If so, he asserts that the Divine nature is multiform, and that the variety which it displays in what is signified by the names is very complex.
sources.raw_question: Do the names Scripture gives to Christ, such as Door, Bread, Way, Vine, Shepherd, Light, signify the nature or essence of the Only-begotten Son?

question: Is the Son (the Word) the Creator who made all things without needing external assistance?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is the Power and Wisdom of God, by whom all things visible and invisible were made, and his will alone suffices to give subsistence to things, for his will is power. He upholds all things by the word of his power and needs no instrument or matter.
sources.quote: For what instrument and what matter could He Who upholds all things by the word of His power need in upholding the constitution of existing things by His almighty word?
sources.raw_question: Is the Son (the Word) the Creator who made all things without needing external assistance?

question: Is it inappropriate to say that Christ or God is 'with' the Holy Spirit, as if this joined the Spirit too closely to the Godhead?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VIII. St. Ambrose examines and refutes the heretical argument that because God is said to be glorified in the Spirit, and not with the Spirit, the Holy Spirit is therefore inferior to the Father. He shows that the particle in can be also used of the Son and even of the Father, and that on the other hand with may be said of creatures without any infringement on the prerogatives of the Godhead; and that in reality these prepositions simply imply the connection of the Three Divine Persons.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says creatures are 'with Christ' and Christ wills us to be with Him; it would be absurd that we can be with Christ while the Spirit cannot. Paul even says 'my spirit with the power of the Lord Jesus,' so the Lord who comes together with us would not disdain to be with the Spirit.
sources.quote: or does our state avail more than the grace of the Spirit, so that we can be with Christ and the Holy Spirit cannot?
sources.raw_question: Is it inappropriate to say that Christ or God is 'with' the Holy Spirit, as if this joined the Spirit too closely to the Godhead?

question: Can the Son have a true relationship of generation to the Father while His nature remains free from passion?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory rejects Eunomius's claim that true relationship to the Father and exemption from passion cannot coincide in God. The Son's generation is pure, divine and passionless; John shows this by naming Him Son of God while purging the proclamation of passion, speaking of "Beginning," "was," and "Word" instead of Father, begotten and Son, so that affinity is expressed without passion.
sources.quote: it is not possible that the two things, the true relationship to the Father, and exemption of His nature from passion, should be found to coincide in God, but that, if there were no passion, there would be no generation
sources.raw_question: Can the Son have a true relationship of generation to the Father while His nature remains free from passion?

question: In what respect are believers the brethren of Christ, the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Only in respect of His flesh and the Dispensation in which He suffered, not in respect of His divinity. The Psalm has Him say 'I will declare Thy name unto My brethren' as 'a worm and no man', and Paul calls Him firstborn among many brethren in the same sense as firstborn from the dead, which concerns His body. As Only-begotten He is unique and has no brethren.
sources.quote: Thus God has brethren according to His flesh, for the Word became flesh and dwelt amongst us: but the Only-begotten Son, unique as the Only-begotten, has no brethren.
sources.raw_question: In what respect are believers the brethren of Christ, the Only-begotten Son?

question: Does 'no one knows the Father except the Son' imply that the Son has a greater knowledge than the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Scripture adds more about the Son revealing, not because he has more than the Father, but so that he would not be thought to have less. The Son knows the Father exactly as the Father knows the Son.
sources.quote: He said more concerning the Son, not because He has more than the Father, but lest He should be supposed to have less.
sources.raw_question: Does 'no one knows the Father except the Son' imply that the Son has a greater knowledge than the Father?

question: Is the Father distinct from the Creator God, a higher deity revealed only secretly through parables and enigmas, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVII.—Proper mode of interpreting parables and obscure passages of Scripture.
sources.answer: No. Scripture clearly proclaims that one only God formed all things by His Word, and creation itself testifies that one Being made and governs it. The Gnostics themselves admit nothing is said openly in Scripture about their separate Father, since they claim the Saviour taught it privately through enigmas and parables; seeking God from such uncertain sources while deserting what is certain is building on sand.
sources.quote: they proclaim that one only God, to the exclusion of all others, formed all things by His word, whether visible or invisible, heavenly or earthly, in the water or under the earth
sources.raw_question: Is the Father distinct from the Creator God, a higher deity revealed only secretly through parables and enigmas, as the Gnostics claim?

question: Does the order of creation itself testify that there is only one God who made the world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVII.—Proper mode of interpreting parables and obscure passages of Scripture.
sources.answer: Yes. The very system of creation to which we belong testifies, through what we observe, that one Being made and governs it. Those who ignore this clear demonstration blind themselves and each invent a God of their own.
sources.quote: the very system of creation to which we belong testifies, by what falls under our notice, that one Being made and governs it
sources.raw_question: Does the order of creation itself testify that there is only one God who made the world?

question: Does the Son's statement 'I went forth from the Father and am come' show that His divinity is derived from the Father by birth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. To go out from the Father means that He had a birth, and that the Father and no other gave Him that birth. By these words the Son testifies that the One from whom He came forth is the Author of His being.
sources.quote: He went out from the Father; that is, He had a birth, and the Father, and no other, gave Him that birth. He bears witness that He, from Whom He declares that He came forth, is the Author of His being.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's statement 'I went forth from the Father and am come' show that His divinity is derived from the Father by birth?

question: Is glory due to the Holy Spirit in such a way that He should be exalted in doxologies?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit's communion with the Father and the Son already testifies to His rank, and His titles, His operations and His gifts to all creation show the sublimity of His nature. Rather than fearing to honour Him excessively, we should fear that even the highest names we can conceive let our thoughts about Him fall too low.
sources.quote: With these thoughts before us are we to be afraid of going beyond due bounds in the extravagance of the honour we pay? Shall we not rather fear lest
sources.raw_question: Is glory due to the Holy Spirit in such a way that He should be exalted in doxologies?

question: What do the names the Spirit shares with the Father and the Son (Spirit, holy, good, upright, Paraclete) show about His nature?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: They show His natural and close relationship to the Father and the Son. He is called Spirit as God is Spirit, holy and good as the Father and Son are, and Paraclete like the Only-begotten. His goodness is His essence, and His uprightness comes from the immutability of His substance. These common titles can only come from shared nature.
sources.quote: Thus names are borne by the Spirit in common with the Father and the Son, and He gets these titles from His natural and close relationship. From what other source could they be derived?
sources.raw_question: What do the names the Spirit shares with the Father and the Son (Spirit, holy, good, upright, Paraclete) show about His nature?

question: Does the Holy Spirit speak and act as an inferior or servant, or with divine authority?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: With divine authority. The Spirit sends and commands, saying "I have sent them" and "Separate me Barnabas and Saul." These are not the words of an inferior, of one in dread, or of a slave.
sources.quote: Are these the words of an inferior, or of one in dread? “Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.” Does a slave speak thus?
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit speak and act as an inferior or servant, or with divine authority?

question: Could the Father be seen in the Son if the Son were unlike the Father in nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The Father is seen in the Son, which could not happen if God were a lonely Being, nor if the Father were unlike the Son. The Father is made visible through the Son only because they are one and alike in nature.
sources.quote: For the Father is seen in the Son, and this could be the case neither if He were a lonely Being, nor yet if He were unlike the Son.
sources.raw_question: Could the Father be seen in the Son if the Son were unlike the Father in nature?

question: Is the divine work of teaching believers ascribed to each Person of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—severally?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Teaching is a comprehensive instance that covers the whole communication of grace, and Scripture assigns it to each Person. The Father teaches and draws to Christ (John 6:45). The Son is the one Master whom the Father commands us to hear (Matt 23:10). The Spirit, as Comforter and anointing, teaches all things (John 14:26; 1 John 2:27).
sources.quote: I shall give only one instance, which is very comprehensive, and may be thought to comprise all other particulars; and this is teaching.
sources.raw_question: Is the divine work of teaching believers ascribed to each Person of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—severally?

question: In what way does the manner in which Father, Son, and Holy Spirit communicate grace differ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: The Father communicates grace by way of original authority. The Son does so by communicating from a treasury he purchased. The Spirit does so by way of immediate efficacy. Romans 8:11 shows all three concurring distinctly in our quickening: the Father raises, the work is done through Christ's death, and the indwelling Spirit effects it.
sources.quote: the Father doth it by the way of original authority; the Son by the way of communicating from a purchased treasury; the Holy Spirit by the way of immediate efficacy.
sources.raw_question: In what way does the manner in which Father, Son, and Holy Spirit communicate grace differ?

question: Is the love of the Father toward humanity the same love as that of the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XII. The peace and grace of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one, so also is Their charity one, which showed itself chiefly in the redemption of man. Their communion with man is also one.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ says that whoever loves him will be loved by the Father and by himself. The Son's love appears in offering himself and redeeming us by his blood, and the same love is in the Father, who so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son.
sources.quote: The same love which is the Father’s is also the Son’s. For He Himself said: “He that loveth Me shall be loved of My Father, and I will love him.”
sources.raw_question: Is the love of the Father toward humanity the same love as that of the Son?

question: Did the Holy Spirit share with the Father and the Son in giving the Son for humanity's redemption?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XII. The peace and grace of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one, so also is Their charity one, which showed itself chiefly in the redemption of man. Their communion with man is also one.
sources.answer: Yes. Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted, so the loving Spirit also gave the Son of God. This love of God is shed abroad by the Spirit and is the Spirit's fruit, so the love of Father, Son and Spirit is one.
sources.quote: For it is written: “Then was Jesus led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.” So, too, the loving Spirit gave the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: Did the Holy Spirit share with the Father and the Son in giving the Son for humanity's redemption?

question: If Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the only true God, does it follow that they are all the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. The phrase 'the only true God' can be used sometimes in a personal sense, meaning the Father, and sometimes in an essential sense, meaning the whole Godhead. Once that is granted, the inference has no force.
sources.quote: But if the only true God may be sometimes used in a personal, sometimes in an essential sense, there is no force in this reasoning.
sources.raw_question: If Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the only true God, does it follow that they are all the Father?

question: Can the Holy Spirit rightly be called a servant of God?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says the servant does not know what his lord does. Yet the Spirit knows the things of God, as the spirit of a man knows what is in him. His knowledge of God's inner things rules out his being a servant.
sources.quote: Do you call the Spirit a servant? But, it is said, “the servant knoweth not what his Lord doeth,” and yet the Spirit knoweth the things of God, as “the spirit of man that is in him.”
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit rightly be called a servant of God?

question: Is human flesh capable of salvation and incorruption, given that the Gnostics deny it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter II.—When Christ visited us in His grace, He did not come to what did not belong to Him: also, by shedding His true blood for us, and exhibiting to us His true flesh in the Eucharist, He conferred upon our flesh the capacity of salvation.
sources.answer: Yes. If the flesh were not saved, the Lord did not redeem us with his blood and the Eucharist would not be communion in his body and blood. Since our flesh is nourished by the Eucharist, which is Christ's body and blood, and is a member of him, it can receive eternal life, and it will rise by the Word's gift to the Father's glory.
sources.quote: how can they affirm that the flesh is incapable of receiving the gift of God, which is life eternal, which [flesh] is nourished from the body and blood of the Lord, and is a member of Him?
sources.raw_question: Is human flesh capable of salvation and incorruption, given that the Gnostics deny it?

question: Why does 1 John 1:3 speak of fellowship with the Father and the Son but not with the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Because our fellowship with the Father and the Son consists in sharing the Holy Spirit with them. The Spirit is not named as a third party to the fellowship because He is the common good that is shared. Elsewhere Paul likewise wishes grace from the Father and the Son without naming the Spirit, because the Spirit is Himself that love and grace.
sources.quote: We are said to have fellowship with the Son and not with the Holy Ghost, because therein consists our fellowship with the Father and the Son, even in partaking with them of the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: Why does 1 John 1:3 speak of fellowship with the Father and the Son but not with the Holy Spirit?

question: If the Son is life but not eternal life, what follows about the Word who is called Life?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > He then wonderfully displays the Eternal Life, which is Christ, to those who confess Him not, and applies to them the mournful lamentation of Jeremiah over Jehoiakim, as being closely allied to Montanus and Sabellius.
sources.answer: It leads to absurdity. Life that is not eternal is temporary, and temporary life is shared by irrational animals. If the Word is that kind of life, then either irrational animals are rational or the Word (Reason) must be called irrational. Otherwise Christ's saying "I am the life" would be false, so the Son must be eternal life.
sources.quote: Why, either that irrational animals are rational, or that the Reason must be confessed to be irrational.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is life but not eternal life, what follows about the Word who is called Life?

question: Does the Fathers' teaching that the Son remained in the Father after proceeding prove his full divinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. They declared that, though the Son proceeded from the Father, he was still in the Father. Combined with the maxim that nothing is in God but what is God, this puts the Son's divinity beyond reasonable doubt.
sources.quote: their declaring that, though he proceeded from the Father, he was still in the Father, (taken together with the tmaxim, that “ nothing is in God but what is “ God,”) sets the matter beyond all reasonable scruple.
sources.raw_question: Does the Fathers' teaching that the Son remained in the Father after proceeding prove his full divinity?

question: Does the Son of God exist only 'by participation' in the self-existent God, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Making divine sons 'by participation' in the divine nature is the work of poets and myth-makers. They invent figures such as Dionysus, Hercules and Minos by mixing the superhuman with human bodies. The opinion carries within itself the evidence of its own folly and profanity.
sources.quote: every one who possesses a spark of practical sagacity is not unaware that it is only poets and moulders of mythology who father sons “by participation” upon the Divine Being.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son of God exist only 'by participation' in the self-existent God, as Eunomius claims?

question: Is the Father the source or beginning of the whole Godhead, even though the Spirit proceeds from both Father and Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father is the principium of the whole deity. The Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, is therefore referred back to the one from whom the Son was born.
sources.quote: He, therefore, who proceeds from the Father and from the Son, is referred back to Him from whom the Son was born (natus).
sources.raw_question: Is the Father the source or beginning of the whole Godhead, even though the Spirit proceeds from both Father and Son?

question: Since Christ is truly God, should he be identified as God the Father himself?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And This is So Manifest, that Some Heretics Have Thought Him to Be God the Father, Others that He Was Only God Without the Flesh.
sources.answer: No. This view, held by certain heretics (modalists), is contrary to the truth of the Scriptures. Reason and the proportion of the Scriptures show Christ to be God, but as the Son of God, born of God, not as the Father.
sources.quote: when reason and the proportion of the heavenly Scriptures show Christ to be God, but as the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Since Christ is truly God, should he be identified as God the Father himself?

question: Did the New Testament writers regard the order 'Father, Son, Spirit' of Matthew 28:19 as essential to the doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Apparently not. Neither Paul nor the other writers preserve that order; the reverse order occasionally appears (perhaps climactically), and the order is very variable, with the most formal enumeration in 2 Corinthians 13:14 running Lord, God, Spirit. If they thought the essence of the doctrine lay in this order, we would expect some suggestion of it in their numerous allusions.
sources.quote: But the order is very variable; and in the most formal enumeration of the three Persons, that of II Cor. xiii. 14, it stands thus: Lord, God, Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Did the New Testament writers regard the order 'Father, Son, Spirit' of Matthew 28:19 as essential to the doctrine of the Trinity?

question: Does knowing God make the human mind like God, and if so, is it equal to God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > That the Image or Begotten Word of the Mind that Knows Itself is Equal to the Mind Itself.
sources.answer: Knowing God makes us like Him, but not equal to Him. We do not know Him to the extent of His own being. Knowledge of God that is loved becomes a word and a kind of likeness of God. Yet that knowledge is of a lower kind, because it exists in a lower nature: the mind is creature and God is Creator.
sources.quote: in so far as we know God, we are like Him, but not like to the point of equality, since we do not know Him to the extent of His own being.
sources.raw_question: Does knowing God make the human mind like God, and if so, is it equal to God?

question: Does the Arian claim that the Father alone, being supreme, is the one God preserve both the Son's divinity and monotheism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. If supremacy alone makes a Person God, then the Son, not being supreme, is no God at all on Arian principles; if he is nevertheless God, then Father and Son are two Gods. The scheme cannot escape this dilemma, and so it either retracts the Son's divinity or falls into polytheism.
sources.quote: If supremacy only makes a Person God, the Son is no God, upon your principles: or, if he is God notwithstanding, then Father and Son are two Gods.
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian claim that the Father alone, being supreme, is the one God preserve both the Son's divinity and monotheism?

question: Does refusing to admit two supreme Gods clear a scheme of a supreme and a subordinate God from the charge of polytheism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. The pagan polytheists, the idolatrous Samaritans and others condemned in Scripture for polytheism did not hold two supreme Gods either. Admitting a greater and a lesser God, a supreme and an inferior, is polytheism by Scripture's standard and by that of the Catholic Church before and after Nicaea.
sources.quote: You can say only this: that you do not admit two supreme Gods. This is very true: no more did the Pagan Polytheists, nor the idolatrous Samaritans, nor others condemned in Scripture for Polytheism.
sources.raw_question: Does refusing to admit two supreme Gods clear a scheme of a supreme and a subordinate God from the charge of polytheism?

question: If the Son's attributes are not individually the same as the Father's, can they be more than faint resemblances differing from the Father's as finite from infinite?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 10: Whether if they (the attributes belonging to the Son) be not individually the same, they can be any thing more than faint resemblances of them, differing from t
sources.answer: No. The Son's attributes are not a finite copy of the Father's. Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son the brightness of the Father's glory and the express image of his Person. Waterland, following all antiquity, takes this to mean the resemblance between Father and Son is complete and perfect. A finite-infinite difference would set them infinitely apart from any such perfect likeness, so quoting this text actually argues against the Arian hypothesis.
sources.quote: The inference we draw from this text, consonant to all antiquity, is, that the resemblance between Father and Son is complete and perfect ; and that therefore they do not differ as finite and inJinite
sources.raw_question: If the Son's attributes are not individually the same as the Father's, can they be more than faint resemblances differing from the Father's as finite from infinite?

question: Does the analogy of human sons, who are born after their fathers, show that the Son of God must have come into existence after the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: No. If the Arians draw from human examples that generation implies time, they should equally draw from them that generation implies that the offspring is natural and proper to the parent's essence. The point of the analogy is connaturality, not temporal succession; the human parent precedes his son only because his nature restrains him, which does not apply to God.
sources.quote: If then they assume from human examples that generation implies time, why not from the same infer that it implies the Natural and the Proper, instead of extracting serpent-like from the earth only what turns to poison?
sources.raised_by_detail: Arians questioning 'silly women' about whether they had a son before begetting him
sources.raw_question: Does the analogy of human sons, who are born after their fathers, show that the Son of God must have come into existence after the Father?

question: Does the Son need to obtain power by some allotment or share, such that the Father alone has power without anyone sharing in it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. The Son upholds all things by the word of his power, does what he wills by the power of his command, and his power is commensurate with his will. All things were made by him and consist in him, so it is absurd to imagine him waiting to receive power by allotment.
sources.quote: He Whose power lags not behind His will and Whose will is the measure of His power
sources.raw_question: Does the Son need to obtain power by some allotment or share, such that the Father alone has power without anyone sharing in it?

question: Do titles such as Almighty, God of Gods, Lord of Lords and Most High, which are proper to the Father, also belong to the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. All terms of highest significance are proper to the Father. But all that is the Father's is also the Son's, so these titles are rightly said of the Son too.
sources.quote: all terms of highest significance are proper to the Father. But all that is the Father’s is the Son’s also; so that, on this understanding, we admit this phrase too.
sources.raw_question: Do titles such as Almighty, God of Gods, Lord of Lords and Most High, which are proper to the Father, also belong to the Son?

question: Can the human mind be present to its own view (in its own sight) other than by actually thinking of itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How a Kind of Trinity Exists in the Mind Thinking of Itself. What is the Part of Thought in This Trinity.
sources.answer: No. Thought matters so much that nothing is in the mind's sight except what is being thought of. Even the mind, by which we think everything else, comes into its own sight only by thinking of itself.
sources.quote: not even the mind itself, whereby we think whatever we do think, can be in its own sight otherwise than by thinking of itself
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind be present to its own view (in its own sight) other than by actually thinking of itself?

question: If we grant that the Son of God has a beginning of being, what follows about his other attributes?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: The other attributes of creation would come in along with it. To grant the Son a beginning would let the rest of creation's marks, such as mutability, be attributed to him as well. That is why his being must not be bounded by any beginning: he is truly unchangeable life, not a mere participant in life.
sources.quote: nor to circumscribe the being of the Son of God by any beginning, lest, if this be granted, the other attributes of creation should enter in together with our acknowledgment of this one
sources.raw_question: If we grant that the Son of God has a beginning of being, what follows about his other attributes?

question: In what sense is Christ 'made unto us wisdom' by God, if as Son He is the uncreated, begotten Wisdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: He is made wisdom for us in time. We turn to Him at some particular time so as to remain with Him for ever, and He was made wisdom by being made man, the Word made flesh. As eternal Wisdom He is begotten, not made.
sources.quote: But the Son is “by God made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification;” because we turn ourselves to Him in time, that is, from some particular time, that we may remain with Him for ever.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is Christ 'made unto us wisdom' by God, if as Son He is the uncreated, begotten Wisdom?

question: Is the Holy Spirit owed praise and thanksgiving for applying redemption, just as the Son is praised for accomplishing it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. As Revelation 1:5-6 gives glory to the Son for redeeming us, the like praises are due to the Spirit, by whom redemption is made effectual. He undertook our consolation with no less infinite love than the Son undertook our redemption.
sources.quote: And are not the like praises and blessings due to him by whom the work of redemption is made effectual to us? who with no less infinite love undertook our consolation than the Son our redemption.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit owed praise and thanksgiving for applying redemption, just as the Son is praised for accomplishing it?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being sent by the Father and the Son make his work of comforting merely imposed rather than voluntary and loving?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit is sent by the Father and Son for this purpose, yet he willingly condescended to the office of comforter. His love was in it, and he freely engaged in the work, so believers owe him thanks for his own love and kindness.
sources.quote: Considering his free engagement in this work, his coming forth from the Father to this purpose, his mission by the Son, and condescension therein, his love and kindness
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being sent by the Father and the Son make his work of comforting merely imposed rather than voluntary and loving?

question: Can the Father's being 'supreme' and the Son's being lower be understood as a difference of place?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He did wrong, when mentioning the Doctrines of Salvation, in adopting terms of his own choosing instead of the traditional terms Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Differences in space cannot apply to intellectual and spiritual being. Local position is a property of material things, while the immaterial is confessedly removed from the idea of locality. So the Father cannot be placed on a peak with the Son seated lower down in the hollows.
sources.quote: Local position is a property of the material: but the intellectual and immaterial is confessedly removed from the idea of locality.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father's being 'supreme' and the Son's being lower be understood as a difference of place?

question: Do the Son and the Holy Spirit need names or titles in order to know God the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The Only-begotten is in the Father and sees the Father in Himself, so He needs no name or title to make the Father known. Likewise the Holy Spirit searches the deep things of God and does not come to know the divine mystery through a nominal appellation. Names are therefore not required within the Godhead for mutual knowledge.
sources.quote: God the Only-begotten, Who is in the Father, and Who seeth the Father in Himself, is in no need of any name or title to make Him known
sources.raw_question: Do the Son and the Holy Spirit need names or titles in order to know God the Father?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's knowledge of the deep things of God distinguish Him from creatures?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Proof of the absurdity of the refusal to glorify the Spirit, from the comparison of things glorified in creation.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit knows the deep things of God, while the creature receives the manifestation of ineffable things only through the Spirit. He is the source of revelation, not a recipient of it.
sources.quote: He knows “The deep things of God;” the creature receives the manifestation of ineffable things through the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's knowledge of the deep things of God distinguish Him from creatures?

question: If the Son shares in the Godhead, must He also share in the goodness that belongs to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He also ingeniously shows from the passage of the Gospel which speaks of “Good Master,” from the parable of the Vineyard, from Isaiah and from Paul, that there is not a dualism in the Godhead of good and evil, as Eunomius' ally Marcion supposes, and declares that the Son does not refuse the title of “good” or “Existent,” or acknowledge His alienation from the Father, but that to Him also belongs authority over all things that come into being.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ Himself attests that the name of goodness belongs to God, and prophets, evangelists and apostles proclaim the Godhead of the Only-begotten. So whoever partakes of the Godhead must partake of the goodness too. Only if the Son were excluded from the title of God could He be thought alien from the title "good."
sources.quote: how is it possible that He Who is partaker of the Godhead should not be partaker of the goodness too?
sources.raw_question: If the Son shares in the Godhead, must He also share in the goodness that belongs to God?

question: Did the Ante-Nicene Church believe that the Son is consubstantial (of one substance) with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: Yes. Almost all the Fathers, expressly or implicitly, asserted the Son's consubstantiality with the Father. They unanimously held that the Son was not of any created or mutable substance but strictly divine, and so closely allied to the Father's Person that the Son's substance could justly be called the Father's substance, both being one.
sources.quote: They unanimously maintained that the Son was not of any created or mutable substance, but strictly divine; and so closely and nearly allied to the Father’s Person, (in a mysterious way above comprehension,) that the substance of the Son might be justly called the Father's substance, both being one.
sources.raw_question: Did the Ante-Nicene Church believe that the Son is consubstantial (of one substance) with the Father?

question: Is making the Father and the Son one Person, as Noetus did, a legitimate way of holding both the unity of God and the full divinity of Christ?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. The Noetians, unable otherwise to reconcile Christ's divinity with God's unity, made Father and Son one Person and so became Patripassians. The Church condemned Noetus as weak and rash, keeping both the real distinction of Persons and the one Godhead.
sources.quote: they had no way of solving the difficulty, but by making Father and Son one Person, and, in consequence, were Patripassians.
sources.raw_question: Is making the Father and the Son one Person, as Noetus did, a legitimate way of holding both the unity of God and the full divinity of Christ?

question: Does the Arian claim 'We say not two Unoriginates' avoid the charge of believing in two Gods?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. The phrase itself implies two Gods of different natures, one originate and one unoriginate. The Arians then differ from the Greeks only in number: the Greeks worship one unoriginate and many originate gods, the Arians one unoriginate and one originate. In both cases the originate god is a creature worshipped instead of the Creator.
sources.quote: in their very professing ‘We say not two Unoriginates,’ they imply two Gods, and these with different natures, one originate and one Unoriginate
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian claim 'We say not two Unoriginates' avoid the charge of believing in two Gods?

question: Did the Word of God in the incarnation merely come into a man, as he came to the prophets and saints, or did he actually become man?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: He became man; he did not merely come into a man. When the Word came to the saints of old, it was never said that he was born when they were born or that he suffered when they suffered. If he had only dwelt in a man as in the prophets, nothing would have been strange about it, and the Jews would not have been scandalised. But Scripture says the Word 'became flesh.'
sources.quote: And He became man, and did not come into man; for this it is necessary to know, lest perchance these irreligious men fall into this notion also
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God in the incarnation merely come into a man, as he came to the prophets and saints, or did he actually become man?

question: Can the Eunomians consistently hold that the Son is a creature and also worship him as God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He convicts Eunomius of having used of the Only-begotten terms applicable to the existence of the earth, and thus shows that his intention is to prove the Son to be a being mutable and created.
sources.answer: No. They attribute to the Son what is true of creation: made from nothing, consisting by God's will, alien to the Maker's essence, and serving the Maker. So whatever they predicate of him they must predicate of creation. Either they deify the elements of the world, as the Greeks do, or they deny the Son's Godhead and refuse him worship. The only escape is the orthodox confession that he is uncreated and therefore truly God.
sources.quote: For either the elements of the world must be Divine, according to the foolish belief of the Greeks, or the Son must not be worshipped.
sources.raw_question: Can the Eunomians consistently hold that the Son is a creature and also worship him as God?

question: Does the Father exist as Father, coexisting with the Son, by the same necessity of nature by which he exists at all?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland asserts that by the same absolute necessity of nature by which the Father exists, he exists as Father. He therefore necessarily coexists with his coessential Son, who proceeds from him. The generation of the Son is thus natural and necessary, not a contingent act of will.
sources.quote: I shall not scruple to assert, that by the same absolute necessity of nature that the Father exists, he exists as a Father; and coexists with his coessential Son proceeding from him.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father exist as Father, coexisting with the Son, by the same necessity of nature by which he exists at all?

question: Does holding that the Son exists necessarily alongside the Father make the Son self-existent or unoriginate?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: No. The objector must prove that it does, not merely assert it. Unbegotten and begotten, unoriginate and proceeding, are different ideas. The Son can exist necessarily and eternally while still being begotten of and proceeding from the Father.
sources.quote: If you say, this supposes the Son self-canstent, or unoriginate; I desire it may not be said only, but proved.
sources.raw_question: Does holding that the Son exists necessarily alongside the Father make the Son self-existent or unoriginate?

question: Can it please the Son of God to give him honour he never claimed, and is it no detraction to refrain from calling him what he is not?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 30: Whether, supposing the case doubtful, it be not a wise man’s part to take the safer side; rather to think too highly, than too meanly of our blessed Saviour ; r
sources.answer: These objections beg the question. The case is supposed to be doubtful whether the Son has claimed such honour or who he really is. Under such doubt it is better to give him what he may not require than to defraud him of what he does.
sources.quote: In such a case, it may be better to give him what he does not require, than to defraud him of what he does: it is safer and more prudent to run the risk of one, than of the other.
sources.raw_question: Can it please the Son of God to give him honour he never claimed, and is it no detraction to refrain from calling him what he is not?

question: Do Christ's 'I am' sayings signify that the Son is eternal and without beginning?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord says 'I am the Truth,' not 'I became the Truth,' and always speaks in the present 'I am' (the Shepherd, the Light, Lord and Master). Coming from the Word and Wisdom of the Father about Himself, this language signifies that the Son is eternal and without beginning.
sources.quote: ‘I am the Truth,’ not ‘I became the Truth;’ but always, ‘I am,—I am the Shepherd,—I am the Light,’
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's 'I am' sayings signify that the Son is eternal and without beginning?

question: Is the Son of God the Son of the Father's will rather than of the Father's nature or substance, as Eunomius claimed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Against Eunomius, Saying that the Son of God is the Son, Not of His Nature, But of His Will. Epilogue to What Has Been Said Already.
sources.answer: No. The Son is Son by nature, born of the Father's substance. Eunomius's view makes the will by which God begot the Son something accidental to God, as when we will something we did not will before. Such change belongs to our changeable nature and must not be believed of God.
sources.quote: he alleged that He was not the Son of His own nature or substance or essence, but the Son of the will of God; so as to mean to assert that the will by which he begot the Son was something accidental [and optional] to God
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God the Son of the Father's will rather than of the Father's nature or substance, as Eunomius claimed?

question: Is the Holy Spirit true in the same sense that God is true?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIX. Having proved above that the Spirit abides and speaks in the prophets, St. Ambrose infers that He knows all things which are of God, and therefore is One with the Father and the Son. This same point he establishes again from the fact that He possesses all that God possesses, namely, Godhead, knowledge of the heart, truth, a Name above every name, and power to raise the dead, as is proved from Ezekiel, and in this He is equal to the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Being true is an attribute of God. The Spirit is the Spirit of Truth, and John calls Him the Truth as he calls the Son. In Psalm 43, "Thy light and Thy truth" refers to the Son and the Spirit, so if the Son is the light, the Spirit is the Truth.
sources.quote: If you consider that in this passage the Son is the light, then the Spirit is the Truth, or if you consider the Son to be the Truth, then the Spirit is the light.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit true in the same sense that God is true?

question: Is God's Word merely a spoken sound or utterance, like a human word, rather than an essential, subsisting Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: No. The Word is an essential and subsisting Word, the true Son, not a sound that dissolves. If He were not essential, God would be speaking into the air and would have a body no differently from men; but since God is not man, neither is His Word subject to human infirmity.
sources.quote: For were He not essential, God will be speaking into the air, and having a body, in nothing differently from men; but since He is not man, neither is His Word according to the infirmity of man.
sources.raw_question: Is God's Word merely a spoken sound or utterance, like a human word, rather than an essential, subsisting Word?

question: Is God Himself identical with Very Wisdom and Very Word, so that 'Son' and 'Word' are only names for the Father, as Sabellius held?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: No. If God were Himself Very Wisdom and Word with no distinct subsisting Son, He would be His own Father and Son, begetting and begotten by Himself, and the titles would be idle and empty. That is the absurdity of Sabellius; rather the Son is truly an Offspring from the Father, so that the Father is truly Father and the Son truly Son.
sources.quote: if as a quality, the absurdity has been shewn; but if God is that Very Wisdom, then it is the absurdity of Sabellius; therefore He is so, as an Offspring in a proper sense from the Father Himself, according to the illustration of light.
sources.raw_question: Is God Himself identical with Very Wisdom and Very Word, so that 'Son' and 'Word' are only names for the Father, as Sabellius held?

question: Does denying the deity of Christ also dishonour God the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And Indeed that Christ Was Not Only Man, But God Also; That Even as He Was the Son of Man, So Also He Was the Son of God.
sources.answer: Yes. To call the one through whom all things were created, and to whom the Father delivered all things, merely a man denies him divine authority. Novatian argues that this contempt recoils on the Father too, since it implies that God the Father could not beget God the Son.
sources.quote: For this contempt of the heretics will recoil also upon God the Father, if God the Father could not beget God the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does denying the deity of Christ also dishonour God the Father?

question: Does being the Son of God make Christ truly God, just as being the Son of man makes him truly man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And Indeed that Christ Was Not Only Man, But God Also; That Even as He Was the Son of Man, So Also He Was the Son of God.
sources.answer: Yes. Nature itself prescribes that one who is of man must be believed to be man. By the same principle, he who is of God must be believed to be God. Scripture calls him both Son of God and Son of man, so he is both, and denying one side would logically endanger the other.
sources.quote: For as nature itself has prescribed that he must be believed to be a man who is of man, so the same nature prescribes also that He must be believed to be God who is of God
sources.raw_question: Does being the Son of God make Christ truly God, just as being the Son of man makes him truly man?

question: Why are the same attributes said of the Son as of the Father, except the name 'Father'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same.
