They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: Because they are one and the Godhead is one, and the Son is the proper Offspring of the Father's Essence. Hence Scripture calls the Son God, Almighty, Lord, Light, and forgiver of sins, and the Son says all that the Father has is His.
sources.quote: since they are one, and the Godhead itself one, the same things are said of the Son, which are said of the Father, except His being said to be Father
sources.raw_question: Why are the same attributes said of the Son as of the Father, except the name 'Father'?

question: Does honoring or worshipping the Son as the Father's Image amount to worshipping the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. As with an Emperor's exact image, which shows his very shape so that one who worships the image worships the Emperor in it, the Son is the Father's exact Image. Therefore the Godhead and propriety of the Father is the Son's very Being, and the Father is seen and honoured in Him.
sources.quote: Accordingly he who worships the image, in it worships the Emperor also; for the image is his form and appearance.
sources.raw_question: Does honoring or worshipping the Son as the Father's Image amount to worshipping the Father?

question: Since the names 'Fount' and 'River' are applied interchangeably to the Father, the Son and the Spirit, what does this show about their greatness?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XVI. The Holy Spirit is that large river by which the mystical Jerusalem is watered. It is equal to its Fount, that is, the Father and the Son, as is signified in holy Scripture. St. Ambrose himself thirsts for that water, and warns us that in order to preserve it within us, we must avoid the devil, lust, and heresy, since our vessels are frail, and that broken cisterns must be forsaken, that after the example of the Samaritan woman and of the patriarchs we may find the water of the Lord.
sources.answer: It shows the unity of the divine greatness. The Spirit is called a Fount, so Christ cannot be denied to be a Fount. The Father says he comes 'like a river of peace,' and the Son is the River of life. Because the same titles pass among the Persons, no difference of greatness can be inferred from them.
sources.quote: You observe, then, from His words that the unity of the divine greatness is pointed out, and that Christ cannot be denied to be a Fount even by heretics, since the Spirit, too, is called a Fount.
sources.raw_question: Since the names 'Fount' and 'River' are applied interchangeably to the Father, the Son and the Spirit, what does this show about their greatness?

question: Is the trinity that Augustine finds in knowledge (scientia), as distinct from wisdom (sapientia), properly called the image of God in man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God.
sources.answer: No. Although this trinity belongs to the inner man and not to the outer man we share with the beasts, it is not yet to be called or thought of as the image of God. The reason is that it lies in knowledge, the lower of the two faculties distinguished from wisdom, so the image of the Trinity must be sought in something higher.
sources.quote: points out a kind of trinity, of a peculiar sort, in that which is properly called knowledge, and which is the lower of the two; and this trinity, although it certainly pertains to the inner man, is still not yet to be called or thought an image of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the trinity that Augustine finds in knowledge (scientia), as distinct from wisdom (sapientia), properly called the image of God in man?

question: Is Christ Lord by divine nature or merely by a title of adoption?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: By divine nature. No one can call Jesus Lord except in the Holy Spirit. Whoever holds Christ to be Lord through His divine nature has the Spirit. Whoever calls Him a creature who is Lord only by adoption, as one of a common class with a familiar name, does not truly say He is the Lord and lacks the Spirit.
sources.quote: If thou holdest that Christ is Lord through His Divine nature, thou hast the Holy Spirit. But if He be Lord merely by a name of adoption thou lackest the Holy Spirit, and art animated by a spirit of error
sources.raw_question: Is Christ Lord by divine nature or merely by a title of adoption?

question: Can one rightly claim God as Father while not loving or confessing the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Christ condemns those who claim God as Father but do not love Him, since he who hates the Son hates the Father also. All who have God for Father through faith have Him so through the same faith that confesses Jesus Christ as Son of God.
sources.quote: none can be devoted to the Father save those who love the Son
sources.raw_question: Can one rightly claim God as Father while not loving or confessing the Son?

question: If the Son is granted some substantial existence but denied proper or complete existence, does he really exist at all?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in making the being of the Father alone proper and supreme, implying by his omission of the Son and the Spirit that theirs is improperly spoken of, and is inferior.
sources.answer: No, denying the Son proper existence amounts to denying that he exists at all. Just as something lacking any property of man is not a man, whatever is denied complete and proper existence is not shown to subsist by a partial affirmation. Proving its incomplete being proves its total effacement. So Eunomius must either deny the Son's existence outright or admit his full being.
sources.quote: in every thing whose complete and proper existence is denied, the partial affirmation of its existence is no proof of its subsisting at all; the demonstration, in fact, of its incomplete being is a demonstration of its effacement in all points
sources.raw_question: If the Son is granted some substantial existence but denied proper or complete existence, does he really exist at all?

question: Can the time of the Son's birth from the Father be stated, and does uncertainty about it cast doubt on the fact?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: The time of the Son's birth cannot be told, yet it would be impious to doubt the fact of it. The generation is certain though its time is beyond expression.
sources.quote: I cannot tell the time of the Son’s birth; it were impious not to be certain of the fact.
sources.raw_question: Can the time of the Son's birth from the Father be stated, and does uncertainty about it cast doubt on the fact?

question: If the Son received the name 'Son' and worship only after his obedience unto death, what was he before the incarnation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: The Arian view leaves only two options. Either he was something other than God, Son and Word and later shared in these for his virtue, or he did not exist before and is merely a man. The second is the view of Paul of Samosata and the Jews, not of the Church. Both options are absurd, because Scripture shows the Son as Creator and as worshipped before the incarnation.
sources.quote: either He was something else beside these, and afterwards became partaker of them for His virtue's sake, as we have said; or they must adopt the alternative (may it return upon their heads!) that He was not before that time, but is wholly man by nature and nothing more.
sources.raw_question: If the Son received the name 'Son' and worship only after his obedience unto death, what was he before the incarnation?

question: Does Scripture show that the Son possessed glory and received worship before his incarnation and exaltation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: Yes. All things were made through him, and the Father delighted in him. Abraham worshipped him in the tent, Moses at the bush, and Daniel saw myriads ministering to him. He himself spoke of the glory he had with the Father before the world was. So he was ever Lord of glory and the Highest, and was not promoted by his descent.
sources.quote: how did the Son Himself make mention of that His glory before and above the world, when He said, ‘Glorify Thou Me, O Father, with the glory which I had with Thee before the world was.’
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture show that the Son possessed glory and received worship before his incarnation and exaltation?

question: Could the Word of God have subsisted by himself and then been joined to the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: No. If the Word subsisted of himself and is God, there would be two Beginnings (two first principles), and the Word would not be the Father's own, being not of the Father but of himself. Since there is one Father and not two, there is one Beginning, and from that One the Son.
sources.quote: If the former, I mean if He subsisted by Himself and is God, then there are two Beginnings; and moreover, as is plain, He is not the Father’s own, as being not of the Father, but of Himself.
sources.raw_question: Could the Word of God have subsisted by himself and then been joined to the Father?

question: Is it enough to say that the Word merely exists with God, without calling him the Father's Offspring?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: No. Refusing the scriptural term 'Offspring' and treating the Word as simply joined to the Father makes God a being of double nature. It introduces a twofold essence in which neither is Father of the other. The same holds for the Power of God.
sources.quote: For not granting that the Word is from the Monad, but simply as if He were joined to the Father, he introduces a twofold essence, and neither of them Father of the other.
sources.raw_question: Is it enough to say that the Word merely exists with God, without calling him the Father's Offspring?

question: Does God's never being without Wisdom or Word prove that the Son is eternal and not from nothing?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: Yes. God is not wisdom-less or word-less, which would be absurd. If he had Word and Wisdom from outside, someone must have given them to him first, and before that he lacked them. If he has them from himself, the Word is not from nothing and never 'was not', since he whose Image he is exists for ever. Arians are refuted from the very notion of a Father.
sources.quote: But if from Himself, it is plain that the Word is not from nothing, nor once was not; for He was ever; since He of whom He is the Image, exists ever.
sources.raw_question: Does God's never being without Wisdom or Word prove that the Son is eternal and not from nothing?

question: Does the very relation signified by the names "Father" and "Son" exclude any variance between them?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds to show that there is no “variance” in the essence of the Father and the Son: wherein he expounds many forms of variation and harmony, and explains the “form,” the “seal,” and the “express image.”
sources.answer: Yes. No relation is more closely fitted together than that of Son to Father: when one name is spoken the other is connoted, and neither can be conceived without the other. Saying "the Son is variant from Him Who begat Him" therefore shows the absurdity of the claim more clearly.
sources.quote: even if both of these names be not spoken, that which is omitted is connoted by the one that is uttered, so closely is the one implied in the other, and concordant with it
sources.raw_question: Does the very relation signified by the names "Father" and "Son" exclude any variance between them?

question: What does the image of a seal and its wax impression show about the Son as the "express image" of the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds to show that there is no “variance” in the essence of the Father and the Son: wherein he expounds many forms of variation and harmony, and explains the “form,” the “seal,” and the “express image.”
sources.answer: It shows that the Son corresponds perfectly to the Father. Wax stamped by a signet fits back into the engraving exactly, while a foreign pattern does not fit. The Son, being the express image sealed by the Father, matches the Father's essence in every point and is not out of harmony with it.
sources.quote: But He Who is “in the form of God” has been formed by no impression different from the Father, seeing that He is “the express image” of the Father’s Person
sources.raw_question: What does the image of a seal and its wax impression show about the Son as the "express image" of the Father?

question: If the Father's essence is good, what does it imply to say that the Son's essence is at variance with it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds to show that there is no “variance” in the essence of the Father and the Son: wherein he expounds many forms of variation and harmony, and explains the “form,” the “seal,” and the “express image.”
sources.answer: It implies that the Son differs from the good itself, and so would be contrary to goodness. To say the Only-begotten's nature varies from the Father's good essence is in effect to set the Son opposite to the good. Gregory points to this to expose the impiety hidden in Eunomius's language.
sources.quote: he who says that the nature of the Only-begotten is at “variance” with the good essence of the Father, clearly has in view variation in the good itself.
sources.raw_question: If the Father's essence is good, what does it imply to say that the Son's essence is at variance with it?

question: Why does the Son call the Father 'Lord' in Proverbs 8:22 if He is the Father's proper Son, and does this make Him a servant by nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: He is not a servant by nature; He names the Father Lord because He took the servant's form. As Word from the Father it befits Him to call God Father, but having taken a servant's form to finish the work, He names Him Lord. He shows this distinction in the Gospel: 'I thank Thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth.'
sources.quote: yet here He names the Father Lord; not that He was servant, but because He took the servant’s form.
sources.raw_question: Why does the Son call the Father 'Lord' in Proverbs 8:22 if He is the Father's proper Son, and does this make Him a servant by nature?

question: For what purpose was the Son of God sent into the world?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son.
sources.answer: Christ died for sinners so that we would be convinced how great God's love for us is, and also what kind of people we are whom he loved. The Word also came in the flesh to cleanse us, so that we could contemplate God and cleave to him.
sources.quote: by Christ’s dying for sinners, we were to be convinced how great is God’s love for us, and also what manner of men we are whom He loved. That the Word came in the flesh, to the purpose also of enabling us to be so cleansed as to contemplate and cleave to God.
sources.raw_question: For what purpose was the Son of God sent into the world?

question: When the prepositions 'of whom' and 'through whom' are used in deliberate contrast for the Father and the Son, do they show a difference in nature or power between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. Even in contrast they may signify only a real distinction of Persons, as Basil observes, or a certain priority of order proper to the first Person. That is all any Catholic writer ever drew from the distinction. Romans 11:36 itself uses them in contrast of the one God.
sources.quote: they may signify only a real distinction of Persons, as ™ St. Basil well observes; or some priority of order proper to the first Person: this is all the use which any Catholic writer ever pretended to make of the distinction.
sources.raw_question: When the prepositions 'of whom' and 'through whom' are used in deliberate contrast for the Father and the Son, do they show a difference in nature or power between the Father and the Son?

question: What do 'of Him,' 'through Him,' and 'in Him' signify when applied to the Son as Creator?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IX. A passage of St. Paul abused by heretics, to prove a distinction between the Divine Persons, is explained, and it is proved that the whole passage can be rightly said of each Person, though it refers specially to the Son. It is then proved that each member of the passage is applicable to each Person, and as to say, of Him are all things is applicable to the Father, so may all things are through Him and in Him also be said of Him.
sources.answer: 'Of Him' means the nature of everything comes from His will and He is the Author of all things. 'Through Him' means the establishment and continuance of all things is His gift. 'In Him' means all creatures, by longing and unspeakable love, look to Him as the Author of their life and Giver of their graces.
sources.quote: What is “of Him”? That the nature of everything is of His will, and He is the Author of all things which have come into being. “Through Him” means what? That the establishment and continuance of all things is His gift.
sources.raw_question: What do 'of Him,' 'through Him,' and 'in Him' signify when applied to the Son as Creator?

question: Does the Son learn the Father's knowledge or will the Father's will by question and command, or are they His by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: They are His by nature. Receiving His whole being from the Father, He received all that belongs to God's being, His knowledge and will, so that it is the property of His nature to will and know exactly as the Father does. 'I came not to do Mine own will' expresses His birth, while 'Father, I will' shows He wills the same.
sources.quote: What the Father knows, the Son does not learn by question and answer; what the Father wills, the Son does not will by command.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son learn the Father's knowledge or will the Father's will by question and command, or are they His by nature?

question: Does the difference between being Father and being Son imply that the Father and the Son are different substances?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Nothing is Spoken of God According to Accident, But According to Substance or According to Relation.
sources.answer: No. 'Father' and 'Son' are said not according to substance but according to relation, since each is so called only in reference to the other. So although to be Father and to be Son are different, their substance is not different.
sources.quote: Wherefore, although to be the Father and to be the Son is different, yet their substance is not different; because they are so called, not according to substance, but according to relation
sources.raw_question: Does the difference between being Father and being Son imply that the Father and the Son are different substances?

question: Does Athanasius' statement that the Word has no other divinity but that of the only God mean the Son's divinity is a lesser, derived divine power?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. The true construction is that the Word has no other kind of divinity than that of the only God, because he is begotten of him. This means the Godhead of Father and Son is all one. Glossing 'divinity' as 'divine power' contradicts both Athanasius' ordinary sense of θεότης and the context.
sources.quote: The plain meaning is, that the Godhead of Father and Son is all one: directly contrary to what the Doctor cites the passage for.
sources.raw_question: Does Athanasius' statement that the Word has no other divinity but that of the only God mean the Son's divinity is a lesser, derived divine power?

question: Can the Father's being be called supreme in the sense of possessing more goodness or power than the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in making the being of the Father alone proper and supreme, implying by his omission of the Son and the Spirit that theirs is improperly spoken of, and is inferior.
sources.answer: No. Good is limited only by its opposite, so a nature incapable of change for the worse is unlimited in goodness, and the unlimited is the infinite. Since the divine nature of the Son and Spirit is unalterable (as even the opponents allow), it is infinite in goodness and power, and excess and defect cannot be posited in the infinite, because excess is conceived only by comparing limits.
sources.quote: But to suppose excess and defect in the infinite and unlimited is to the last degree unreasonable: for how can the idea of infinitude remain, if we posited increase and loss in it?
sources.raw_question: Can the Father's being be called supreme in the sense of possessing more goodness or power than the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Does God's power, authority and sovereignty depend on his being the one who invented the words or names by which things are signified?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The true power and sovereignty of God do not consist in syllables; otherwise any inventor of words could claim equal honour with God. God's power over all is witnessed by the ages, the beauty of the universe, the heavenly luminaries, the wonders of land and sea, and the angelic powers, not by the coining of names.
sources.quote: For the true power, and authority, and dominion, and sovereignty of God do not, we think, consist in syllables. Were it so, any and every inventor of words might claim equal honour with God.
sources.raw_question: Does God's power, authority and sovereignty depend on his being the one who invented the words or names by which things are signified?

question: Did the Ante-Nicene writers interpret the texts calling the Father the one God so as to exclude the Son from being one God with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. They declared the contrary and proclaimed Father and Son to be one God. When they called the Father autotheos and the Son subordinate, 'God of God', they did not mean what Clarke means. For Clarke this means that only the Father is necessarily existing and strictly divine and the Son is an inferior being, which the ancients would have rejected with abhorrence.
sources.quote: No certainly: they declare the contrary, and proclaim Father and Son to be one God.
sources.raw_question: Did the Ante-Nicene writers interpret the texts calling the Father the one God so as to exclude the Son from being one God with the Father?

question: Does deriving the Son from an intermediate 'energy' undermine the doctrine that all things were created through the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in assuming, to account for the existence of the Only-Begotten, an 'energy' that produced Christ's Person.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son owes his being to a prior energy, then another personality prior to him has been invented, and the authorship of the world would have to be referred to it. The Son's role as Creator, the Word through whom all things were made, would then have no foundation.
sources.quote: another personality, prior to Him, has been invented by our neologian, to which the authorship of the world must be referred, because the Son Himself derives His being according to them from that ‘energy.’
sources.raw_question: Does deriving the Son from an intermediate 'energy' undermine the doctrine that all things were created through the Son?

question: Does the Divine Nature of the Word change when it is united with flesh?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: No. The Divine Nature is always one and the same and keeps the same mode of existence. It is the flesh which, when mixed with the Divine, no longer stays within its own limitations and properties but is taken up into what is transcendent.
sources.quote: the Divine Nature is always one and the same, and with the same mode of existence, while the flesh in itself is that which reason and sense apprehend concerning it, but when mixed with the Divine no longer remains in its own limitations and properties
sources.raw_question: Does the Divine Nature of the Word change when it is united with flesh?

question: Does Christ's saying 'I go to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God' refute Noetus's claim that the Son is the Father himself?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ confesses the Father to be his Father and his God. If Christ were the Father, there would be no father to whom he could go away, as the Gospel says he does. Abandoning the Gospel for Noetus's view would be obeying men rather than God.
sources.quote: If then, Noetus ventures to say that He is the Father Himself, to what father will he say Christ goes away according to the word of the Gospel?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'I go to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God' refute Noetus's claim that the Son is the Father himself?

question: Why does Scripture attribute human words and expressions to God as speaker?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Because the Holy Spirit addresses us in our own language, adapting to our capacity, as at Pentecost each heard in his native tongue. Since human nature is deaf to higher truths, God's grace spoke through the prophets in our familiar modes of expression. This leads us toward higher truths by descending to our limited comprehension.
sources.quote: we should remember that the Holy Spirit is addressing us in language of our own
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture attribute human words and expressions to God as speaker?

question: If Christ applies His various names to Himself with no first or second among them, does it follow that the names of Christ are not products of human conception (epinoia)?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Following Basil's example of corn, which is one thing in substance yet is called seed, fruit and food according to its properties, Christ is in Himself what He is essentially. However, He receives different names according to the different notions His various operations produce in us. The plurality of His names therefore arises from our conception of His operations, not from a ranking of the names by accuracy.
sources.quote: Similarly, says he, our Lord is in respect to Himself what He is essentially, but when named according to the differences of His operations, He has not one appellation in all cases, but takes a different name according to each notion produced in us from the operation.
sources.raw_question: If Christ applies His various names to Himself with no first or second among them, does it follow that the names of Christ are not products of human conception (epinoia)?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's proceeding from the Father show that the Spirit is uncreated?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord never said that any created thing, visible or invisible, including thrones, principalities and powers, proceeds from the Father. What all creation is excluded from sharing must be special and peculiar to uncreated being.
sources.quote: It is plain then that that, from share in which all creation is excluded, is something special and peculiar to uncreated being.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's proceeding from the Father show that the Spirit is uncreated?

question: Is it adequate to describe the Holy Spirit as "the Guide of godliness" whom we believe in along with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: No. If believing in the Spirit means believing in whatever guides us to godliness, then Paul, Barnabas, Timothy, the prophets, apostles, pastors and teachers would all have equal honour with the Holy Spirit. Each of them has been a guide to godliness, which makes the description absurd as a statement of the Spirit's dignity.
sources.quote: all the prophets and lawgivers and patriarchs, heralds, evangelists, apostles, pastors, and teachers, have equal honour with the Holy Spirit, as they have been “guides to godliness”
sources.raw_question: Is it adequate to describe the Holy Spirit as "the Guide of godliness" whom we believe in along with the Father and the Son?

question: In respect of bodily immortality, are believers conformed to the image of the whole Trinity or only to the image of the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether the Sentence of John is to Be Understood of Our Future Likeness with the Son of God in the Immortality Itself Also of the Body.
sources.answer: Only to the image of the Son. Of the Trinity, the Son alone took a body, died and rose in it, and carried it to heaven; Scripture and sound faith say of Him alone that "the Word was made flesh." So the immortal body we shall have conforms us to the Son, the first-born from the dead, and not to the Father or the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: being conformed in this respect not to the image of the Father or of the Holy Spirit, but only of the Son, because of Him alone is it read and received by a sound faith, that “the Word was made flesh.”
sources.raw_question: In respect of bodily immortality, are believers conformed to the image of the whole Trinity or only to the image of the Son?

question: Since the Father sent the Son by a word, and the Son is the Word of the Father, was the Son's sending the work of both the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Whether the Father commanded, requested or suggested, it was done by a word, and the Word of God is the Son himself. So the sending was the work of both the Father and his Word, and the Son was sent by the Father and by the Son.
sources.quote: since the Father sent Him by a word, His being sent was the work of both the Father and His Word; therefore the same Son was sent by the Father and the Son, because the Son Himself is the Word of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Since the Father sent the Son by a word, and the Son is the Word of the Father, was the Son's sending the work of both the Father and the Son?

question: If the Holy Spirit is said to be sent through visible corporeal forms such as the dove and the fire, does this make the Spirit less than the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > A Doubt Raised About Divine Appearances.
sources.answer: No. The Son is called less than the Father because of the form of a servant, which was joined to the unity of his person. The corporeal forms by which the Spirit was shown were not united to him in this way. They appeared for a time to show what was needed and then ceased to be, so they imply no inferiority in the Spirit.
sources.quote: because that form of a servant inhered in the unity of the person of the Son, but those corporeal forms appeared for a time, in order to show what was necessary to be shown, and then ceased to be
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit is said to be sent through visible corporeal forms such as the dove and the fire, does this make the Spirit less than the Father?

question: Would the Son's not always existing with the Father detract from God, in a way that creatures' not always existing does not?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: Yes. That creatures did not always exist does not disparage the Maker, since He has the power to frame them whenever He wills. But for the Offspring not to be ever with the Father would disparage the perfection of the Father's essence. Since the Father always is, what is proper to His essence, His Word and Wisdom, must always be.
sources.quote: but for the offspring not to be ever with the Father, is a disparagement of the perfection of His essence.
sources.raw_question: Would the Son's not always existing with the Father detract from God, in a way that creatures' not always existing does not?

question: Does the mind know itself through imagined images, as it knows bodies, or through its own inward presence to itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Every Mind Knows Certainly Three Things Concerning Itself—That It Understands, that It Is, and that It Lives.
sources.answer: Through inward presence. The mind thinks of fire, air and bodies through an imaginary phantasy drawn from things touched by the bodily senses. But it knows that it lives, remembers, understands and wills by a true inward presence, since nothing is more present to it than itself. If it were some body, it would think that body in this inward way rather than by phantasy; and once it attaches nothing imagined to itself, what remains is itself.
sources.quote: but by some inward, not feigned, but true presence (for nothing is more present to it than itself); just as it thinks that itself lives, and remembers, and understands, and wills.
sources.raw_question: Does the mind know itself through imagined images, as it knows bodies, or through its own inward presence to itself?

question: Is the Creator of heaven and earth the one only God and Father, or is there a higher God, a second God (as Marcion taught), or a Pleroma of Aeons above him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: The Creator is the one only God and Father. He made all things freely and by his own power, his will being the substance of all things. He contains all things but is contained by none, and there is no one beside or above him. There is no mother, no second God as Marcion imagined, no Pleroma, Bythus, or unnameable Aeon.
sources.quote: there is no one besides Him, or above Him, neither has He any mother, as they falsely ascribe to Him; nor is there a second God, as Marcion has imagined
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of heaven and earth the one only God and Father, or is there a higher God, a second God (as Marcion taught), or a Pleroma of Aeons above him?

question: Is the mind's certain self-knowledge limited to a few items, or can it be multiplied without end by reflection?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Academic Philosophy.
sources.answer: It can be multiplied without end. Someone who knows he is alive can also know that he knows it, and then know that he knows both, and so on. He cannot count or state that infinite number, but he grasps with perfect certainty that the series is both true and innumerable.
sources.quote: he comprehends this at least, and with perfect certainty, viz. that this is both true and so innumerable that he cannot truly comprehend and say its infinite number.
sources.raw_question: Is the mind's certain self-knowledge limited to a few items, or can it be multiplied without end by reflection?

question: If 'one God' necessarily means only one Person, what follows for the deity of the Son and Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: There are only two possible conclusions. Either the Father alone is that one Person, which is downright Sabellianism. Or the three Persons are three Gods. Clarke's identification of 'one God' with one Person therefore cannot avoid one of these errors.
sources.quote: either that the Father ts that one Person, and none else, which is downright Sabellianism ; or that the three Persons are three Gods.
sources.raw_question: If 'one God' necessarily means only one Person, what follows for the deity of the Son and Holy Spirit?

question: On Dr. Clarke's principles, how can it be true both that each Person of the Trinity is God and that there is only one God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: It cannot be true without contradiction. Clarke holds that dominion and authority make God to be God, and that 'God' in Scripture is a relative word of office meaning personal dominion. If such dominion belongs to three Persons, those three must on his principles be three Gods. Clarke's defender also never explains how three Gods could be one God.
sources.quote: if dominion and authority, such as make any Person truly God, be lodged in three Persons ; those three Persons, upon the Doctor’s principles, must be three Gods.
sources.raw_question: On Dr. Clarke's principles, how can it be true both that each Person of the Trinity is God and that there is only one God?

question: Does John 5 teach both the Son's equality of nature with the Father and his real distinction from the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: Yes. Following Hilary, the drift of Christ's words is to declare equality of nature and Sonship together: no inferior nature could be capable of having all things, and a Son could have them only as communicated. So the passage refutes both Arians, who deny equality of nature, and Sabellians, who deny real distinction.
sources.quote: No inferior nature could be capable of having all things; nor could a Son have them but as communicated. So that, in the whole, it is directly opposite to such as either disown an equality of nature, or a real distinction
sources.raw_question: Does John 5 teach both the Son's equality of nature with the Father and his real distinction from the Father?

question: In what senses is the Son said to be 'generated', and which of these generations is the proper one that makes him the only-begotten and a distinct Person from the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Waterland distinguishes a threefold generation of the Son. The first and most proper is his eternal existing in and of the Father, as the eternal Word of the eternal Mind; chiefly by this he is the only-begotten and a Person distinct from the Father. The second is his coming forth, in time, to create the world. The third is his birth of the Virgin. The second and third are condescensions rather than generations in the strict sense.
sources.quote: The first and most proper filzation and generation, is his eternally existing in and of the Father; the eternal Adyos, of the eternal mind. In respect of this, chiefly, he is the only begotten, and a distinct Person from the Father.
sources.raw_question: In what senses is the Son said to be 'generated', and which of these generations is the proper one that makes him the only-begotten and a distinct Person from the Father?

question: In what sense is the Son called 'firstborn of every creature', and does his coming forth to create the world mean he was separated from the Father or first began to exist?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: The title belongs to his second generation: his voluntary condescension, in time, of coming forth from the Father to create the world. In this respect he is firstborn of, or before, all creatures. This coming forth was a manifestation, not a beginning of existence. Nor was he ever separated or divided from the Father.
sources.quote: His second generation was his condescension, manifestation, coming forth, as it were, from the Father (though never separated or divided from him) to create the world: this was in time, and
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Son called 'firstborn of every creature', and does his coming forth to create the world mean he was separated from the Father or first began to exist?

question: Is it legitimate to call the Father the "Maker" or "Creator" of the Son, the Son a "creature" or "product," and the Holy Spirit the "creature of a creature," instead of using the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Christ himself delivered the names Father, Son and Holy Spirit in the baptismal formula as the rule of faith. To substitute terms like "Maker," "creature," or "product of a product" is to pretend to correct God the Word, and it amounts to a denial and violation of the Godhead revealed in that formula.
sources.quote: all such fancies we term a denial and violation of the Godhead revealed to us in this doctrine
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to call the Father the "Maker" or "Creator" of the Son, the Son a "creature" or "product," and the Holy Spirit the "creature of a creature," instead of using the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?

question: In what sense is God one, and in what sense is He not one?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: God is one in essence and distinguished in the attributes that mark the Persons. The Lord ordained that we look to one Name because the essence is one. Yet our faith is distinguished into belief in the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost. Thus God is divided without separation and united without confusion.
sources.quote: In regard to essence He is one, wherefore the Lord ordained that we should look to one Name: but in regard to the attributes indicative of the Persons, our belief in Him is distinguished
sources.raw_question: In what sense is God one, and in what sense is He not one?

question: If the Son had a beginning, would the Father once have lacked His own Wisdom, Power, Life and Truth?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes, and that conclusion is absurd and impious. Scripture calls the Son the Power, Wisdom, Truth, Light and Life of God. If the Son did not exist, these too would not have existed, and the Father's bosom would have been empty of such excellences. So the Son must be eternal with the Father.
sources.quote: For if the Son, as the Scripture saith, is the Power of God, and Wisdom, and Truth, and Light, and Sanctification, and Peace, and Life, and the like, then before the Son existed, according to the view of the heretics, these things also had no existence at all.
sources.raw_question: If the Son had a beginning, would the Father once have lacked His own Wisdom, Power, Life and Truth?

question: Why did God the Word appear in the flesh, with respect to human knowledge of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > The second book declares the Incarnation of God the Word, and the faith delivered by the Lord to His disciples, and asserts that the heretics who endeavour to overthrow this faith and devise other additional names are of their father the devil.
sources.answer: He came so that people would no longer form opinions about the Self-existent from their own vague conjectures. Instead they would believe the true 'mystery of godliness', God manifested in the flesh, as it was delivered by the Word Himself to His Apostles. The faith is therefore neither of men nor by men, but from Christ Himself.
sources.quote: that men might no longer have opinions according to their own notions about the Self-existent, formulating into a doctrine the hints that come to them from vague conjectures, but that we might be convinced that God has truly been manifested in the flesh
sources.raw_question: Why did God the Word appear in the flesh, with respect to human knowledge of God?

question: Do the same energies always produce the same works, so that different works prove different energies in the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: No. One and the same energy produces different results in different subjects. Fire's single energy of heating melts bronze, hardens mud and makes wax vanish. The sun's single warming power makes one plant grow and withers another. So difference in works does not prove difference in the energies.
sources.quote: The energy of fire is always one and the same; it consists in heating: but what sort of agreement do its results show? Bronze melts in it; mud hardens; wax vanishes
sources.raw_question: Do the same energies always produce the same works, so that different works prove different energies in the Father and the Son?

question: Is it legitimate to deny true divinity to the Son, treating him as a creature rather than God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The Son drew His nature by birth from God the Father, so to deny Him divinity, or to preach a creature in place of God, is impious. Such preaching is the corrupt doctrine of the last days foretold by the Apostle, which estranges the Only-begotten God from the power and nature of the Father.
sources.quote: that preaching alone rules among their crowd of doctors which estranges the Only-begotten God from the power and nature of God the Father, and makes Him in our faith either a God of the second order, or not a God at all
sources.raised_by_detail: teachers who preach not God but a creature
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to deny true divinity to the Son, treating him as a creature rather than God?

question: Can one hold that the Word had a substantive existence of his own and was only afterwards united to the Father without positing two first principles (Origins) in God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus C. Introductory to the Fourth Discourse against the Arians.
sources.answer: No. Such a view involves two ἀρχαί, two independent Origins, in the Godhead. The only ways out are to collapse into the Sabellian idea of a two-natured God or to accept the true solution: the eternal divine generation of the Son from the Father, which preserves one Origin while keeping the Son distinct.
sources.quote: he taxes with the consequence of involving two ᾽Αρχαί a view that the Word had a substantive existence and was then united to the Father
sources.raw_question: Can one hold that the Word had a substantive existence of his own and was only afterwards united to the Father without positing two first principles (Origins) in God?

question: Does the eternity of Christ's Kingdom imply the eternity of his Person?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus C. Introductory to the Fourth Discourse against the Arians.
sources.answer: Yes. Each implies the other. It is therefore inconsistent to defend the eternity of Christ's Kingdom, as Eusebius did against Marcellus, while defending those who deny the eternity of his Person. It is equally inconsistent to deny the Son any pre-existence while indignantly rejecting the Arian formulas.
sources.quote: The eternity of Christ’s Kingdom and of His Person implied each in the other.
sources.raw_question: Does the eternity of Christ's Kingdom imply the eternity of his Person?

question: If the Only-begotten Son is truly God, must he also be eternal, with no time when he did not exist?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
sources.answer: Yes. Whoever is believed to be God must be believed eternal, for God, if he now is, always was, and if he once was not, he does not now exist at all as God. The Evangelist's repeated "was" in John's prologue removes any suspicion of non-existence. Since even the heretics confess the Son is the Only-begotten God, they must grant his eternity.
sources.quote: For God, as we have often said, if He now is, also assuredly always was, and if He once was not, neither does He now exist at all.
sources.raw_question: If the Only-begotten Son is truly God, must he also be eternal, with no time when he did not exist?

question: Why does God not explicitly except the Son when he says 'there is none other besides me'?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Because naming the Son as an exception would have separated him and made him 'another' or alien to God. Excepting him out of others would imply he belongs among the others. Tertullian's analogy: if the sun said 'there is no sun besides me except my ray,' the exception would be absurd, since the ray is reckoned as included in the sun.
sources.quote: suppose he had said, There is none other “ besides me, except my Son; he would in effect have declared ἐς him to be another, (or aliene,) by excepting him in that “ manner out of others.
sources.raw_question: Why does God not explicitly except the Son when he says 'there is none other besides me'?

question: Did the early Christians who confessed one God, the Father, exclude the Son from that one God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Athenagoras, after proving there is but one God, the Father, immediately adds that Christians also acknowledge the Son of God. This shows the Son is comprehended in the one God, and he calls the Son the Mind and Word of the Father, uncreated and eternal.
sources.quote: aS much as to say, we comprehend and include the Son in that one God; we are always to be understood with this reserve, or 7salvo, to the divinity of the Son
sources.raw_question: Did the early Christians who confessed one God, the Father, exclude the Son from that one God?

question: Is the presence of the Holy Spirit as Comforter better for believers than the bodily presence of Christ would be?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Yes. Once Christ has fulfilled the one sacrifice for sin he was to offer, the Spirit's presence as a comforter, sent by Christ for the purposes for which he was promised, is better and more profitable for believers than any bodily presence of Christ could be.
sources.quote: is better and more profitable for believers than any corporeal presence of Christ can be, now he hath fulfilled the one sacrifice for sin which he was to offer.
sources.raw_question: Is the presence of the Holy Spirit as Comforter better for believers than the bodily presence of Christ would be?

question: Does John 15:26 ('who proceedeth from the Father') refer to the Spirit's eternal procession or to his being sent in time?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: It refers chiefly to his economical procession, his being sent by Christ after the ascension. The text ties his proceeding to a particular work, testifying of Christ, and that work cannot belong to his eternal procession. It is like God 'coming out of his place' (Isa. 26:21), which means a new work and not any change in God, or like Christ's 'coming forth from God.'
sources.quote: it is in reference to a peculiar work that he is said to proceed, — namely, to testify of Christ: which cannot be assigned to him in respect of his eternal procession, but of his actual dispensation
sources.raw_question: Does John 15:26 ('who proceedeth from the Father') refer to the Spirit's eternal procession or to his being sent in time?

question: Does John 15:26, by naming only the Father, deny that the Spirit proceeds from the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: No. Naming the Father alone is part of Christ's step-by-step teaching of this mystery to his disciples. Elsewhere Christ says the same about himself: 'I will send him' (John 16:7).
sources.quote: The single mention of the Father in this place, and not of the Son, belongs to the gradation before mentioned, whereby our Saviour discovers this mystery to his disciples. He speaks as much concerning himself, John xvi. 7.
sources.raw_question: Does John 15:26, by naming only the Father, deny that the Spirit proceeds from the Son?

question: How do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit each take part in giving the Spirit as Comforter?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: The Father is the fountain, through the purpose of his electing love. The Son asks the Father for the Spirit, and that asking includes his merit and purchase. The Holy Spirit then willingly proceeds. This order supports believers' distinct communion with the Father in love, the Son in grace, and the Spirit in consolation.
sources.quote: First, there is the πρόθεσις of the Father, or the purpose of his love, the fountain of all; then the ἐρώτησις, the asking of the Son, John xiv. 16, which takes in his merit and purchase; whereunto follows ἐκπόρευσις, or willing proceeding of the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: How do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit each take part in giving the Spirit as Comforter?

question: If human beings impose names on things, does that make humans of higher authority than God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Scripture shows humans naming things without presumption: Pharaoh's daughter named Moses, mothers named the patriarchs, and places were named by men, yet God Himself used these names. The Divine nature does not depend on words for its evidence to itself, and God's sovereignty does not consist in syllables.
sources.quote: from which we may learn that men may notify the meaning of things by words without presumption, and that the Divine nature does not depend on words for its evidence to itself
sources.raw_question: If human beings impose names on things, does that make humans of higher authority than God?

question: Does learning from Scripture that Christ is the Son of God force us to understand "Son" in its earthly sense?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: No. Gregory confesses the Lord as Son because the voice from heaven proclaimed him so. Yet he is not dragged down by the name to its earthly meaning. He knows the Son is from the Father, and he does not know him to be from passion.
sources.quote: Yet, though I was taught that He is the Son, I was not dragged down by the name to the earthly significance of “Son,” but I both know that He is from the Father and do not know that He is from passion.
sources.raw_question: Does learning from Scripture that Christ is the Son of God force us to understand "Son" in its earthly sense?

question: When the Church professed three Hypostases against Sabellius, did it mean three divine substances?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. The Church professed three Hypostases only in the sense of three Persons, and always professed one eternal, uncreated substance. Sabellius was not censured for holding one substance. He was censured for making one Hypostasis, or Person, with three names. The objector exploits the ambiguity of 'hypostasis' to build a fallacy.
sources.quote: The Church never professed three Hypostases in any other sense, but as they mean three Persons ; nor would Sabellius have been censured for holding one Hypostasis only, had he meant one substance.
sources.raw_question: When the Church professed three Hypostases against Sabellius, did it mean three divine substances?

question: Can the Son and the Holy Spirit be described as 'works' of differing worth, such that one energy in the Godhead is more honourable than another?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His elaborate account of degrees and differences in 'works' and 'energies' within the Trinity is absurd.
sources.answer: No. To speak of a 'more honourable' work within the Trinity necessarily implies a 'less honourable' one, and nothing that we believe of the Trinity can be called 'less precious.' Eunomius's claim that the energies producing the Son and Spirit rank higher or lower is profane and not even worth arguing against as if it were a real argument.
sources.quote: For can a ‘more honourable’ be discovered where there is not a less honourable?
sources.raw_question: Can the Son and the Holy Spirit be described as 'works' of differing worth, such that one energy in the Godhead is more honourable than another?

question: Does the Son share the Father's incomprehensible nature, signified by the name 'above every name'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: Yes. The name 'above every name,' which alone represents God's proper nature, is also granted to the Only-begotten, because all that the Father has belongs to the Son.
sources.quote: the single name of being ‘Above every name’; which is granted to the Only-begotten also, because “all that the Father hath is the Son’s.”
sources.raw_question: Does the Son share the Father's incomprehensible nature, signified by the name 'above every name'?

question: Does the Son acquire knowledge from the Father by asking and receiving answers, advancing from ignorance to knowledge?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The Son's nature, abiding in mysterious unity with the Father, received its whole being from Him along with its origin, including the Father's knowledge and will. What the Father knows the Son does not learn by question and answer; it is the property of His nature to know exactly as the Father knows.
sources.quote: What the Father knows, the Son does not learn by question and answer; what the Father wills, the Son does not will by command.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son acquire knowledge from the Father by asking and receiving answers, advancing from ignorance to knowledge?

question: Does John 1:1 exclude any time when the Only-begotten did not exist?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
sources.answer: Yes. John guards his statement in every way so that non-existence finds no access to the Son. By repeating "was" (He was in the beginning, was with God, was God), he shows the Word was always all good things and never at any time failed to be. If the Only-begotten is God, He must be eternal.
sources.quote: guards his own statement in every way, so that the conception of non-existence shall find no access to Him Who is
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:1 exclude any time when the Only-begotten did not exist?

question: Should the Only-begotten Son be counted among "all things that have come into being" when they are contrasted with God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > He then declares that the close relation between names and things is immutable, and thereafter proceeds accordingly, in the most excellent manner, with his discourse concerning “generated” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. Gregory faults Eunomius for setting all generated things against God without making any special distinction for the Only-begotten Godhead of the Son. In Gregory's view the Son's begetting does not place him among creatures, for the Word who was in the beginning is God.
sources.quote: without making any special distinction for the Only-begotten Godhead of the Son as compared with the rest of the “generated,” but makes his opposition of “all things that have come into being” to “God” without discrimination
sources.raw_question: Should the Only-begotten Son be counted among "all things that have come into being" when they are contrasted with God?

question: Is God the Father, the Son (Word), or the Holy Spirit changeable in what he is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > In How Many Ways the Creature is to Be Taken by Way of Sign. The Eucharist.
sources.answer: No. Augustine confidently affirms, by the grace of the Spirit sent from above, that neither the Father, nor His Word, nor His Spirit, which together are the one God, is in any way changeable in regard to that which He is and whereby He is what He is.
sources.quote: I dare to say confidently, that neither God the Father, nor His Word, nor His Spirit, which is the one God, is in any way changeable in regard to that which He is
sources.raw_question: Is God the Father, the Son (Word), or the Holy Spirit changeable in what he is?

question: Does the revelation of the Father to those whom the Son chooses (Matt 11:27) mean that believers know the Father as the Son does?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. The Son's knowledge is joined with his unlimited inheritance of all things. The believers' knowledge is finite: it is granted to babes, with the Son as the efficient cause of it.
sources.quote: their finite knowledge of the Father is granted through the Son, as the efficient cause
sources.raw_question: Does the revelation of the Father to those whom the Son chooses (Matt 11:27) mean that believers know the Father as the Son does?

question: Does John 10:29-30 ('no one is able to snatch them out of My Father's hand; I and the Father are One') show the unity of power of Father, Son and Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: Yes. Ambrose has already shown that the Holy Spirit is the Hand of the Father. The Hand of the Father is therefore the same as the Hand of the Son, since the same Spirit is the Spirit of both. So whoever receives eternal life in the name of the Trinity is not torn from the Father, from the Son, or from the Spirit.
sources.quote: the same is certainly the Hand of the Father which is the Hand of the Son, since the Same is the Spirit of the Father Who is the Spirit of the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does John 10:29-30 ('no one is able to snatch them out of My Father's hand; I and the Father are One') show the unity of power of Father, Son and Spirit?

question: Is it possible that the Son of God might not have existed?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. To say the Son might not have been is an irreligious presumption reaching to the Father's Essence, as though what is His own might not have been. It is the same as saying the Father might not have been good. As the Father is always good by nature, so He is always generative by nature.
sources.quote: For it is the same as saying, ‘The Father might not have been good.’ And as the Father is always good by nature, so He is always generative by nature
sources.raw_question: Is it possible that the Son of God might not have existed?

question: How does the analogy of light and its radiance show that the Son is generated by nature and not by a prior act of will?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
