sources.answer: In light there is no will preceding its radiance. The radiance is light's natural offspring, at the pleasure of the light that begets it, but not by will and consideration. Likewise the Son is the Father's natural Offspring, and Father and Son have mutual love and good pleasure in nature and truth.
sources.quote: there is no will preceding radiance in the light, but it is its natural offspring, at the pleasure of the light which begat it, not by will and consideration, but in nature and truth
sources.raw_question: How does the analogy of light and its radiance show that the Son is generated by nature and not by a prior act of will?

question: Could God's "Let Us make man" in Genesis 1:26 be addressed to a being of a different nature from God, such as an angel?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. "Us" and "Our" are just as inconsistent with addressing a stranger who has nothing in common with the Speaker as they are with soliloquy. The phrase "our image" (not "our images") proves that both share one nature. The text therefore shows neither an isolated God nor one God in two dissimilar Persons.
sources.quote: Both words, Us and Our are inconsistent with the notion of a solitary God speaking to Himself, and equally inconsistent with that of the address being made to a stranger who has nothing in common with the Speaker.
sources.raw_question: Could God's "Let Us make man" in Genesis 1:26 be addressed to a being of a different nature from God, such as an angel?

question: Was the Word Son and God before he was called First-born of creation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Yes. Before creation he was the Son through whom creation came to be. Before he was called First-born of the whole creation, the Word was already with God and was God. The title First-born therefore belongs to him later, because of creation.
sources.quote: as before the creation He was the Son, through whom was the creation, so also before He was called the First-born of the whole creation, not the less was the Word Himself with God and the Word was God
sources.raw_question: Was the Word Son and God before he was called First-born of creation?

question: Can the Father be called anything in respect to His own substance, or is everything said of Him said only relatively to the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: The Father must be something in respect to Himself. Just as there can be no master unless there is first a man, some substance, to be called master relatively, so if the Father were not something in respect to Himself there would be no one to be spoken of relatively at all. Both Father and Son are substance, and both are one substance.
sources.quote: Wherefore, if the Father also is not something in respect to Himself then there is no one at all that can be spoken of relatively to something.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father be called anything in respect to His own substance, or is everything said of Him said only relatively to the Son?

question: Why was it expedient for believers that Christ's bodily presence be replaced by the presence of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Because the Spirit makes Christ's promises effective for comfort in a way they were not while Christ was bodily present. While Christ was with the disciples, his promises had little effect on their hearts. When the Spirit came, he filled those promises with joy. This work belongs peculiarly to the Spirit by virtue of his office, and was reserved for him so that he also might be glorified.
sources.quote: That which was his peculiar work, which belonged to him by virtue of his office, that he also might be glorified, was reserved for him.
sources.raw_question: Why was it expedient for believers that Christ's bodily presence be replaced by the presence of the Holy Spirit?

question: Is it necessary for salvation to confess that Christ Jesus is both truly God and truly man?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. The knowledge of the Eternal is given in the same confession that gives eternal life, and whoever is ignorant that Christ was very God as well as very man cannot know his own life. Denying either his divinity or his real flesh is equally perilous, as Christ himself warned that he will deny before the Father those who deny him before men.
sources.quote: He does not, he cannot know his own life, who is ignorant that Christ Jesus was very God, as He was very man. It is equally perilous, whether we deny that Christ Jesus was God the Spirit, or that He was flesh of our body
sources.raw_question: Is it necessary for salvation to confess that Christ Jesus is both truly God and truly man?

question: If the Son has the individual attributes of God the Father, must the Son be the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: No. The Son has the Father's individual attributes as much as he has the individual essence, without being the Father. Denying this makes the Son a mere creature. So the real question is whether the Son is God or a creature.
sources.quote: On the contrary, I affirm, that he hath the individual attributes of God the Father, as much as he has the individual essence: for otherwise he must be a creature only
sources.raw_question: If the Son has the individual attributes of God the Father, must the Son be the Father?

question: Does the title 'Comforter' in John 16 show that the Holy Spirit is a divine person?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. 'Comforter' is a personal title, and the passage says he will come and will do various things, which marks him as a person. Because he is the Comforter of all God's people, the name can belong only to a divine person.
sources.quote: A personal appellation this is also; and because he is the Comforter of all God’s people, it can be the name of none but a divine person.
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'Comforter' in John 16 show that the Holy Spirit is a divine person?

question: Can the divine works ascribed to the Holy Spirit, such as creation, inspiring prophecy, and regeneration, be attributed to a mere quality or power?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. These are personal operations performed by will. They cannot reasonably be assigned, consistently and uniformly, to a quality or virtue. The Spirit, as God with omniscience, omnipotence, life, understanding and will, acts according to wisdom, choice and power.
sources.quote: Now, all these are personal operations, and cannot, with any pretence of sobriety or consistency with reason, be constantly and uniformly assigned unto a quality or virtue.
sources.raw_question: Can the divine works ascribed to the Holy Spirit, such as creation, inspiring prophecy, and regeneration, be attributed to a mere quality or power?

question: Is the Wisdom who speaks in Proverbs 8 to be identified with Christ, the Lord of the Gospels?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory identifies the Wisdom of Proverbs with the Lord, who is the Wisdom of the Gospel. The Lord promises the kingdom of heaven to the poor in spirit, and these are the kings who reign by Wisdom. Gregory also says that man was first appointed ruler over his 'land' by the Word.
sources.quote: the poor in spirit, whose possession is the kingdom of heaven, as the Lord promises, Who is the Wisdom of the Gospel
sources.raw_question: Is the Wisdom who speaks in Proverbs 8 to be identified with Christ, the Lord of the Gospels?

question: Does the Father's having given all judgment to the Son mean the Son is a lesser being, or does it show his Sonship together with unity of nature with the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: It shows both his birth and his unity of nature. Only a nature altogether one with the Father's could possess all things, while a Son can possess nothing except by gift. So the gift of all judgment teaches both that he is truly born and that he is fully divine.
sources.quote: The statement that all judgment is given teaches both His birth and His Sonship; for only a nature which is altogether one with the Father’s could possess all things; and a Son can possess nothing, except by gift.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's having given all judgment to the Son mean the Son is a lesser being, or does it show his Sonship together with unity of nature with the Father?

question: Can a nature born from God contain any element of a substance different from the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Everything conveyed to the Son in his birth must be contained in the nature from which that birth comes. A nature springing from one nature only must be entirely one with its parent nature.
sources.quote: Into His nature no element of any substance different in kind from that of His Author is introduced, for a nature which springs from one nature only must be entirely one with that nature which is its parent.
sources.raw_question: Can a nature born from God contain any element of a substance different from the Father's?

question: Should we deny the Son's birth from the Father because we cannot comprehend how it happened?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. Disbelief based on our inability to understand the works of God is impious. It wrongly makes the limits of our understanding into the limits of reality. Believers should hold to the names Scripture gives and to the Son's own declaration about himself, being content with the written word.
sources.quote: Hold fast the Names which teach the truth, hold fast the Son’s declaration of Himself.
sources.raw_question: Should we deny the Son's birth from the Father because we cannot comprehend how it happened?

question: Does Scripture attribute the giving of the divine law to the Son and the Holy Spirit as well as to the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture speaks of the law of the Lord, the law of Christ and the law of the Spirit of life. It also says holy men spoke as moved by the Holy Ghost. Since James says there is one lawgiver, the three are that one Legislator.
sources.quote: The word of One Legislator is the believer’s rule. There is One lawgiver who is able to save. – James 4:12.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture attribute the giving of the divine law to the Son and the Holy Spirit as well as to the Father?

question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each dwell in believers, and does this mean three divine guests?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Each dwells in believers, yet the contrite heart receives one divine guest. God says "I will dwell in them," Christ dwells in hearts by faith, and the Spirit dwells with and in believers. These are not three separate indwellers but the one high and lofty One who inhabits eternity.
sources.quote: The contrite heart receives One Divine guest.
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each dwell in believers, and does this mean three divine guests?

question: What does it show when Scripture ascribes the same attributes, works and names to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: It shows that the three share one Godhead, so that the three are one God. They have the same divine attributes and the same divine names. Their mind, will and heart are personally distinct but act in harmony in the same divine acts.
sources.quote: have the same Divine attributes, concur with a mind, and will, and heart personally independent, but unitedly harmonious in the same Divine acts, and are addressed by the same Divine names
sources.raw_question: What does it show when Scripture ascribes the same attributes, works and names to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

question: Is the Holy Spirit's goodness acquired, as a creature's is, or imparted from himself?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: It is imparted. The Spirit does not receive from creatures but is received by them. He is not sanctified but sanctifies, so his goodness is not acquired.
sources.quote: Good, then, is the Spirit, but good, not as though acquiring but as imparting goodness. For the Holy Spirit does not receive from creatures but is received; as also He is not sanctified but sanctifies
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit's goodness acquired, as a creature's is, or imparted from himself?

question: Is the Holy Spirit a creature, given that the whole invisible creation, including the angels, receives his grace?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: No. All creation outside the Trinity acquires and receives the Spirit's grace rather than imparting it, so the Spirit stands apart from creation. Those who associate him with the Father and the Son cannot consistently hold him a creature, for where sanctification is one, the nature is one.
sources.quote: But if they do not think that He should be separated from the Father and the Son, they do not consider Him to be a creature, for where the sanctification is one the nature is one.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a creature, given that the whole invisible creation, including the angels, receives his grace?

question: Is the conclusion that Father, Son, and Spirit are one in essence and three in subsistence as much divine revelation as the scriptural statement that they are one God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Whatever necessarily follows from a revealed truth is true in the same kind as its source. Since Scripture reveals Father, Son, and Spirit to be one God, and they can be one only in essence and three only in distinct subsistences, these consequences are no less divine revelation.
sources.quote: seeing it necessarily and unavoidably follows thereon that they are one in essence (wherein alone it is possible they can be one), and three in their distinct subsistences (wherein alone it is possible they can be three)
sources.raw_question: Is the conclusion that Father, Son, and Spirit are one in essence and three in subsistence as much divine revelation as the scriptural statement that they are one God?

question: Should the language of Proverbs 8 about Wisdom be read literally?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. It is parabolic and metaphorical, as the context shows. Expressions like God setting his throne upon the winds cannot be understood literally of the immaterial, incomprehensible and formless Deity. So these words carry a deeper meaning and give no ground for thinking the Lord was created.
sources.quote: What is this throne of the immaterial, incomprehensible, and formless Deity? Who could possibly understand all this in a literal sense?
sources.raw_question: Should the language of Proverbs 8 about Wisdom be read literally?

question: Is the Son a product of the Father's will, or is He Himself the Father's living Will and essential energy?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: He is Himself the Father's living Will. God's will is effective, and His Word is the effective Framer of all things. So the Word must be the living Will of the Father, an essential energy and a real Word in whom all things consist, not something produced from without by will.
sources.quote: that Word must surely be the living Will of the Father, and an essential energy, and a real Word, in whom all things both consist and are excellently governed
sources.raw_question: Is the Son a product of the Father's will, or is He Himself the Father's living Will and essential energy?

question: How can 'There is no God beside Thee' be true if God dwells within the Son, so that there seem to be two Gods?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Indweller and indwelt are distinguished only in Person, not in nature. God cannot reside in a nature alien to His own. He abides in One born from Himself, so God is in God because God is from God, and there is no second, different God.
sources.quote: The words distinguish the Indweller from Him in Whom He dwells, but it is a distinction of Person only, not of character. God is in Him, and He, in Whom God is, is God.
sources.raw_question: How can 'There is no God beside Thee' be true if God dwells within the Son, so that there seem to be two Gods?

question: Is the love of God the Father the fountain from which all other gracious dispensations to believers flow?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen argues that the Father's love is to be looked on as the fountain of all following gracious dispensations. Titus 3:4-6 speaks of the kindness and love of God the Father appearing and being shed on us abundantly through Jesus Christ, and this love is the hinge of the saints' recovery from their former sinful condition.
sources.quote: his love ought to be looked on as the fountain from whence all other sweetnesses flow. Thus the apostle sets it out, Tit. iii. 4, “After that the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared.”
sources.raw_question: Is the love of God the Father the fountain from which all other gracious dispensations to believers flow?

question: Does Scripture itself speak of God's eternity in terms of past and future?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. David speaks of God as King 'before the ages', looking backward to the past. Moses says He reigns 'from generation to generation for evermore', looking to the future. Both teach that every conceivable duration is encompassed by the infinite divine nature. If Basil's way of speaking divides the ages, Scripture must be accused of the same.
sources.quote: so that we are taught by both that every duration conceivable is environed by the Divine nature, bounded on all sides by the infinity of Him Who holds the universe in His embrace
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture itself speak of God's eternity in terms of past and future?

question: Does the Son receive the power of executing judgment as one inferior to the Father, which would undermine his equality with the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: No. As the Son of God equal to the Father, he does not receive this power but has it with the Father in secret. He receives it only as Son of man, so that the good and the bad may see him judging.
sources.quote: For inasmuch as the Son of God is equal to the Father, He does not receive this power of executing judgment, but He has it with the Father in secret; but He receives it, so that the good and the bad may see Him judging
sources.raw_question: Does the Son receive the power of executing judgment as one inferior to the Father, which would undermine his equality with the Father?

question: Do apparent contradictions in Scripture about the Son's divinity undermine belief in Christ's Godhead?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 1. Introduction. Preparation of heart. Our position before God.
sources.answer: No. The author admits that apparent contradictions once troubled him greatly and that the Tempter can misuse Scripture, as he did with Christ. Yet through study of the Bible and prayer, the very truths around which his doubts had gathered became his strongest supports. Rightly examined, Scripture confirms the Divinity of the Son.
sources.quote: those very truths around which skeptical doubts had once clustered most thickly, became the strongest bulwarks to which, when assailed on other points, I used to resort.
sources.raw_question: Do apparent contradictions in Scripture about the Son's divinity undermine belief in Christ's Godhead?

question: Is the Son's birth from God like a human birth, involving division, diminution, efflux or change in the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. God is not born from God by the ordinary process of human childbirth; it is One from One without partition, withdrawing, lessening, efflux, extension or change. It is the birth of living nature from living nature, so pure that it may better be called a proceeding forth than a birth.
sources.quote: For it is One from One; no partition, or withdrawing, or lessening, or efflux, or extension, or suffering of change, but the birth of living nature from living nature.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's birth from God like a human birth, involving division, diminution, efflux or change in the Father?

question: Is Christ the dispenser of the Holy Spirit and of the grace of sanctification to believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ, upon his intercession, is granted to make effectual all the fruits of his purchase for the sanctification of his people, and this is actually accomplished by the Spirit, whom he gives out. From him believers receive the Spirit to dwell in them, the new principle of life, and actual assistance for every duty.
sources.quote: They look upon him as, in his own Spirit, he is the only dispenser of the Spirit and of all grace of sanctification and holiness.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ the dispenser of the Holy Spirit and of the grace of sanctification to believers?

question: Did God the Creator form the world from his own conception, or did he copy it from archetypes supplied by some higher being?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VII.—Created things are not the images of those Æons who are within the Pleroma.
sources.answer: God formed the world from his own conception. If the Creator copied models furnished by others, then whoever supplied the models must also have received them from someone above him. This leads to an infinite regress of images and gods, unless we fix our minds on one Artificer and one God who formed created things of Himself. Irenaeus adds that it is absurd to grant mere men the power to invent useful things while denying God the power to create forms by himself.
sources.quote: the talk about images, as about gods, will extend to infinity, if we do not at once fix our mind on one Artificer, and on one God, who of Himself formed those things which have been created.
sources.raw_question: Did God the Creator form the world from his own conception, or did he copy it from archetypes supplied by some higher being?

question: Can the Father, Son and Holy Spirit stand in an unbroken series and unalterable relation to one another if they differ in essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: No. An unalterable relation and series can only exist among those united in being; if they are separated by essential unlikeness, they are alien entities and no true series or relationship can hold between them. Eunomius contradicts himself by claiming both an unbroken connexion and essential unlikeness.
sources.quote: Either, as our own doctrine insists, they are united in being, and then they really preserve an unalterable relation to each other; or else they stand apart in essential unlikeness, as he fancies.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father, Son and Holy Spirit stand in an unbroken series and unalterable relation to one another if they differ in essence?

question: If the Holy Spirit is the love between Father and Son, is He a mere relation or quality rather than a substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Holy Spirit Also is Equal to the Father and the Son in All Things.
sources.answer: No, He is a substance. God is a substance, and Scripture says "God is love". So the love that is the Spirit is itself substance, and if it were nothing or not substance, neither could God be love or be substance.
sources.quote: And this is also a substance, since God is a substance, and “God is love,” as it is written.
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit is the love between Father and Son, is He a mere relation or quality rather than a substance?

question: Does Job 33:4, "The Spirit of God hath made me," show that the Holy Spirit is divine and Creator rather than a creature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, as well as the Father and the Son, is pointed out in holy Scripture as Creator, and the same truth was shadowed forth even by heathen writers, but it was shown most plainly in the Mystery of the Incarnation, after touching upon which, the writer maintains his argument from the fact that worship which is due to the Creator alone is paid to the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. In one short verse Job shows the Spirit to be both divine and Creator. If the Spirit is Creator, He cannot be a creature. The Apostle sharply separates Creator from creature when he condemns those who "served the creature rather than the Creator."
sources.quote: If, then, the Spirit is Creator, He is certainly not a creature, for the Apostle has separated the Creator and the creature, saying: “They served the creature rather than the Creator.”
sources.raw_question: Does Job 33:4, "The Spirit of God hath made me," show that the Holy Spirit is divine and Creator rather than a creature?

question: Does the worship or service Christians give to the Holy Spirit prove that He is God and Creator?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, as well as the Father and the Son, is pointed out in holy Scripture as Creator, and the same truth was shadowed forth even by heathen writers, but it was shown most plainly in the Mystery of the Incarnation, after touching upon which, the writer maintains his argument from the fact that worship which is due to the Creator alone is paid to the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul condemns serving the creature and teaches that service is owed to the Creator alone. Yet he says "we are the circumcision who serve the Spirit of God." So the Spirit must be the Creator, to be venerated with the honour due to the eternal Godhead, since God alone is to be served.
sources.quote: without doubt he plainly shows that the Holy Spirit is Creator, and is to be venerated with the honour due to the eternal Godhead; for it is written: “Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and Him only shalt thou serve.”
sources.raw_question: Does the worship or service Christians give to the Holy Spirit prove that He is God and Creator?

question: Does the glory the Father gives the Son, which the Son gives to believers (John 17:22), show that the unity in question is a unity of will?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Will is an emotion of the mind, while glory is an ornament of nature. What the Son gives believers is the glory received from the Father, not will. If will had been given, faith would carry no reward, since a will imposed by necessity would also force faith upon us.
sources.quote: Now I ask whether glory is identical with will, since will is an emotion of the mind while glory is an ornament or embellishment of nature.
sources.raw_question: Does the glory the Father gives the Son, which the Son gives to believers (John 17:22), show that the unity in question is a unity of will?

question: Since men were called 'gods' (John 10:35), is the Word called God in John 1:1 only in a lower, official sense?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. The context of John 1 requires 'God' to be applied to the Word in the same sense as to the Father just before and after: the Word is essentially God, the Creator of all. John 10:35 grants a lower official sense in which mortal men were called gods. It sets this against the Messiah's divine Sonship.
sources.quote: the context compels us to understand (Θεος) God, when applied to the Word, in the same sense as when immediately before and after applied to the Father: the Word is essentially God, the Creator of all
sources.raw_question: Since men were called 'gods' (John 10:35), is the Word called God in John 1:1 only in a lower, official sense?

question: What does the 'finger of God' signify in Scripture?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Of the Appearance on Sinai. Whether the Trinity Spake in that Appearance or Some One Person Specially.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit. Augustine says the Gospel teaches us that the name 'finger of God' signifies the Holy Spirit, which supports linking the Law written by God's finger with the Spirit.
sources.quote: written upon tables of stone with the finger of God, by which name we know the Holy Spirit to be signified in the Gospel
sources.raw_question: What does the 'finger of God' signify in Scripture?

question: By what means does the mind know itself, since it is incorporeal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Image of the Trinity in the Mind of Man Who Knows Himself and Loves Himself. The Mind Knows Itself Through Itself.
sources.answer: The mind knows itself through itself. Just as it gains knowledge of bodily things through the bodily senses, it gains knowledge of incorporeal things through itself. Since the mind is incorporeal, it knows itself directly through itself, and this self-knowledge is the ground of its self-love.
sources.quote: As the mind, then, itself gathers the knowledge of corporeal things through the senses of the body, so of incorporeal things through itself. Therefore it knows itself also through itself, since it is incorporeal
sources.raw_question: By what means does the mind know itself, since it is incorporeal?

question: Is the Son only nominally a Word or only notionally a Son, or is He an eternally existing Son coessential with the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Marcellus and his disciples, like Arians, say that the Word was, not indeed created, but issued, to create us, as if the Divine silence were a state of inaction, and when God spake by the Word, He acted; or that there was a going forth and return of the Word; a doctrine which implies change and imperfection in Father and Son.
sources.answer: He exists eternally and is coessential with the Father. There was never a time when God was silent and then spoke. There is ever a Father and a Son who is His Word, not a Word in name alone nor a Son in notion only.
sources.quote: there is ever a Father, and a Son who is His Word, not in name alone a Word, nor the Word in notion only a Son, but existing coessential with the Father
sources.raw_question: Is the Son only nominally a Word or only notionally a Son, or is He an eternally existing Son coessential with the Father?

question: Does the Son's identity of essence with the Father imply identity of power and operation?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son is without variation in essence from the Father, He is also without variation in power, and those whose power is equal have operations equal in all ways. Since Christ is the power and wisdom of God, all things are made through Him.
sources.quote: For if in essence He is without variation, so also is He without variation in power. And of those whose power is equal, the operation also is in all ways equal.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's identity of essence with the Father imply identity of power and operation?

question: Does a hierarchy of one supreme God with subordinate, graded powers beneath him agree with Christian doctrine about the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > Eunomius again speaks of the Son as Lord and God, and Maker of all creation intelligible and sensible, having received from the Father the power and the commission for creation, being entrusted with the task of creation as if He were an artizan commissioned by some one hiring Him, and receiving His power of creation as a thing adventitious, ab extra, as a result of the power allotted to Him in accordance with such and such combinations and positions of the stars, as destiny decrees their lot in life to men at their nativity. Thus, passing by most of what Eunomius had written, he confutes his blasphemy that the Maker of all things came into being in like manner with the earth and with angels, and that the subsistence of the Only-begotten differs not at all from the genesis of all things, and reproaches Him with reverencing neither the Divine mystery nor the custom of the Church, nor following in his attempt to discover godliness any teacher of pious doctrine, but Manichæus, Colluthus, Arius, Aetius, and those like to them, supposing that Christianity in general is folly, and that the customs of the Church and the venerable sacraments are a jest, wherein he differs in nothing from the pagans, who borrowed from our doctrine the idea of a great God supreme over all. So, too, this new idolater preaches in the same fashion, and in particular that baptism is “into an artificer and creator,” not fearing the curse of those who cause addition or diminution to the Holy Scriptures. And he closes his book with showing him to be Antichrist.
sources.answer: No. This is the pagan scheme of a great God above lesser powers ranked by superiority and inferiority. The Eunomian teaching, which ranks the Son as a creature under the Father, simply repeats that scheme and is therefore a new idolatry.
sources.quote: some of them hold that there is some one great God preeminent above the rest, and acknowledge some subject powers, differing among themselves in the way of superiority or inferiority
sources.raw_question: Does a hierarchy of one supreme God with subordinate, graded powers beneath him agree with Christian doctrine about the Son?

question: Does calling the Father and Son one 'individual' substance commit Trinitarians to making Father and Son one Person?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. The opponent's argument rests on misconstruing the word 'individual' in his own sense. Trinitarians do not take it in that sense, since they do not suppose Father and Son to be one Person.
sources.quote: All you have to say turns only upon your misconstruction of, I should say eguévocation in, the word individual ; which, you must needs know, we understand not in your sense of it
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father and Son one 'individual' substance commit Trinitarians to making Father and Son one Person?

question: Are the presence and grace of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit one or three?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XI. The Spirit is sent to all, and passes not from place to place, for He is not limited either by time or space. He goes forth from the Son, as the Son from the Father, in Whom He ever abides: and also comes to us when we receive. He comes also after the same manner as the Father Himself, from Whom He can by no means be separated.
sources.answer: One. Ambrose concludes from the joint coming and indwelling of the three that their presence and grace is one, something so heavenly and divine that the Son gives thanks to the Father for revealing it to babes.
sources.quote: We have proved, then, that the presence and the grace of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one
sources.raw_question: Are the presence and grace of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit one or three?

question: Is the trinitarian baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 unauthentic because of its 'high theology' and universalism?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The external evidence is overwhelmingly against excluding it, and the internal evidence is just as decisive. Matthew's Jesus elsewhere speaks universally and of His church, and after Matthew 11:27 nothing loftier remained to be attributed to Him. Moreover, all the New Testament writers think in trinitarian terms, and that universal conviction requires some such teaching from Jesus Himself.
sources.quote: The universal possession by His followers of so firm a hold on such a doctrine requires the assumption that some such teaching as is here attributed to Him was actually contained in Jesus’ instructions to His followers.
sources.raised_by_detail: critics of the genuineness of Matt. 28:19
sources.raw_question: Is the trinitarian baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 unauthentic because of its 'high theology' and universalism?

question: Can unaided human reason attain certain knowledge of divine things such as the Trinity, or is revelation and faith required?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Unaided reason cannot attain it. Our minds are born with clouded vision and are penned within an impassable ignorance concerning divine things. Only the study of God's revelation raises the soul to comprehension, and submission to faith leads to a certainty beyond the reach of unassisted reason. Hence Hilary prays for the Spirit who guided the Prophets and Apostles, so that he may read their words in the sense they intended.
sources.quote: the study of Thy revelation elevates our soul to the comprehension of sacred truth, and submission to the faith is the path to a certainty beyond the reach of unassisted reason
sources.raw_question: Can unaided human reason attain certain knowledge of divine things such as the Trinity, or is revelation and faith required?

question: Does the oneness of God the Father mean that the Son cannot be truly begotten of him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. God's being One does not rule out the Son's true birth from him. The Son is born of the Father from everlasting. The Father is therefore to be proclaimed as God yet not solitary.
sources.quote: We may not say that He is not begotten of Thee, because Thou art One.
sources.raw_question: Does the oneness of God the Father mean that the Son cannot be truly begotten of him?

question: Are philosophical difficulties sufficient grounds for denying the Son's full divinity, such as the claims that generation implies division or that necessary generation implies compulsion?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 30: Whether, supposing the case doubtful, it be not a wise man’s part to take the safer side; rather to think too highly, than too meanly of our blessed Saviour ; r
sources.answer: No. Reasoning from such fancies and conjectures is unbecoming Christians, who have Scripture as the only source of satisfaction in these matters. Rejecting revealed truth because we cannot comprehend how three Persons exist, or why the Father begets the Son, shows too little reverence for God's unsearchable nature and too high an opinion of ourselves.
sources.quote: To go upon our own fancies and conjectures, in a thing of this kind, is only betraying too little reverence for the tremendous and unsearchable nature of God, and too high an
sources.raw_question: Are philosophical difficulties sufficient grounds for denying the Son's full divinity, such as the claims that generation implies division or that necessary generation implies compulsion?

question: Is the term 'the Word' in John's prologue a title for Jesus Christ the Messiah?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture is its own best interpreter, and the same apostle, writing of Christ's advent, says that his name is called the Word of God. The contemporary Jewish usage of Philo, who described the Divine Word as Son of God, Image of God and instrument of creation, further shows the name would have been understood by John's readers.
sources.quote: But Scripture is its own best interpreter. And this same apostle, writing in after years of the advent of Christ, says, “He was clothed in a vesture dipped in blood, and his name is called the Word of God.”
sources.raw_question: Is the term 'the Word' in John's prologue a title for Jesus Christ the Messiah?

question: Must the Son be self-existent or unoriginate in every sense in order to be strictly and essentially God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Waterland calls this Dr. Clarke's leading fallacy. He cites Alexander of Alexandria's teaching that eternity and necessary existence are not the same as being unbegotten. The Son can therefore be eternal and necessarily existent while still being begotten of the Father.
sources.quote: diametrically opposite to the Doctor’s leading principle, or rather fallacy, which runs through his performance, viz. That the Son cannot be strictly and essentially God, unless he be self-existent, or unoriginate in every sense.
sources.raw_question: Must the Son be self-existent or unoriginate in every sense in order to be strictly and essentially God?

question: Is eternal life given by knowing the Father alone, apart from the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. Bare knowledge of the true God does not give life. Christ adds the knowledge of himself as the one sent, so the believer's hope of life rests on both. The true God is inseparable from the Son, whose name follows in the creed.
sources.quote: It is life to know the true God; but the bare knowledge of Him does not give it. What, then, does He add? And Jesus Christ Whom Thou hast sent.
sources.raw_question: Is eternal life given by knowing the Father alone, apart from the Son?

question: If there is only one God, does confessing Christ as God contradict monotheism by introducing a second God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. The true birth of the Only-begotten from God the Father makes Him very God, yet not alien from the nature of the one God. Because the birth makes Him God and the nature in Him is that of one God of God, He is neither denied Godhead nor described as another God.
sources.quote: because while the birth made Him God, the nature within him of one God of God did not separate Him off as another God
sources.raw_question: If there is only one God, does confessing Christ as God contradict monotheism by introducing a second God?

question: Is the Holy Spirit a sharer in, or arbiter of, the divine counsel?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter II. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are One in counsel.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture calls baptism the counsel of God, since the Pharisees despised God's counsel by not being baptized. Ambrose has already shown that the Spirit is the Lord of baptism. Just as there is no baptism without the Spirit, the counsel of God is not without the Spirit.
sources.quote: it is quite clear that as there can be no baptism without the Spirit, so, too, the counsel of God is not without the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a sharer in, or arbiter of, the divine counsel?

question: Should the search for an image of the Trinity in love proceed from bodily loves to the mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > There are Three Things in Love, as It Were a Trace of the Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. To find something purer, one must tread down the flesh and ascend to the mind, since what the mind loves in a friend is the mind; there too the triad of lover, beloved and love appears. From there one must ascend further toward the things above, as far as is given to man.
sources.quote: But that we may drink in something more pure and clear, let us tread down the flesh and ascend to the mind. What does the mind love in a friend except the mind?
sources.raw_question: Should the search for an image of the Trinity in love proceed from bodily loves to the mind?

question: If the Son is the Jehovah and "only God" of the Old Testament, does that make the Father and the Son one Person, or exclude the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. The Son is the one God not to the exclusion of the Father, any more than the Father is to the exclusion of the Son. He is so together with the Father. Father and Son are both the one Supreme God, one in substance, power, and perfection, but not one in Person.
sources.quote: not exclusive of the Father, any more than the Father is such, exclusive of the Son; but together with the Father: that is, Father and Son both are the one Supreme God: not one in Person
sources.raw_question: If the Son is the Jehovah and "only God" of the Old Testament, does that make the Father and the Son one Person, or exclude the Father?

question: Do texts such as 'the head of Christ is God' and 'Christ is God's' prove that the Son is inferior in nature to the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. They describe Jesus as man, the federal Head of the church, ascending to his God and Father and doing the Father's will as our surety. Other texts in the same Scripture show that Christ and the Father are one, each in the other, and that he is head of the church with undivided supremacy. The same principle applies to every passage cited for the Son's subordination.
sources.quote: we learn that Christ and his Father are one, that He has a real and undivided supremacy, that his kingdom shall never wax old, his glory never pale, his royalty never pass away
sources.raw_question: Do texts such as 'the head of Christ is God' and 'Christ is God's' prove that the Son is inferior in nature to the Father?

question: Is belief in one God the Father alone sufficient for salvation without faith in the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Paul added 'one Lord Jesus Christ' because bare belief in one God the Father would not suffice; saving faith consists in confessing both one God and one Lord, as Christ said that whoever sees and believes on the Son has eternal life.
sources.quote: inasmuch as this bare belief in one God the Father would not suffice for salvation, he added, And one, our Lord Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Is belief in one God the Father alone sufficient for salvation without faith in the Son?

question: Can one confess Jesus as Lord and God without the gifts of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. No one can call Jesus Lord except in the Holy Spirit; through the word of wisdom Christ is understood to be Lord, through the word of knowledge we speak what we know, and through faith we believe He is God. Heretics, lacking understanding, lack these gifts.
sources.quote: And no one can call Jesus Lord but in the Holy Spirit, because but through this word of wisdom Christ could not be understood to be Lord
sources.raw_question: Can one confess Jesus as Lord and God without the gifts of the Holy Spirit?

question: Why is the Holy Spirit not more prominently set forth in Scripture as an object of worship, if he is truly God coequal with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Because of a divine equipoise in the parts the Three sustain in our salvation. The Father's love and the Son's grace are displayed preeminently in Scripture, while the Spirit's personal glories, though affirmed and his worship enjoined, are less shown to view. This relative seclusion is fully compensated by the abundant scriptural evidence of his inward, subjective work in believers, whose glory exceeds as much as his visible majesty is concealed.
sources.quote: his worship is enjoined, but it is comparatively withdrawn from observation: when, however, we look into the subjective work carried on by him, there is an amplitude and plenitude of evidence from Holy Writ which entirely compensates any seclusion of his visible majesty.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit not more prominently set forth in Scripture as an object of worship, if he is truly God coequal with the Father and the Son?

question: What does Scripture clearly teach about the Holy Spirit's person and Godhead?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Scripture clearly teaches that the Holy Spirit is distinct from the Father and the Son and is an intelligent person. It ascribes to him divine attributes such as eternal self-existence, omnipresence, infinite wisdom and foreknowledge, absolute freedom and goodness, and creative, providential and spiritual power, any one of which proves his Godhead. He is joined with the Father and Son in divine offices, worshipped and glorified with them, and called Jehovah and God.
sources.quote: attributes any one of which would prove his Godhead – are assigned to him; that He is associated in Divine offices with the Father and the Son; that He with them is worshipped and glorified; that He is Jehovah and God
sources.raw_question: What does Scripture clearly teach about the Holy Spirit's person and Godhead?

question: Is not knowing a thing the same as not thinking of it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Thing is Made Plain by an Example. In What Way the Matter is Handled in Order to Help the Reader.
sources.answer: No. A person can know something without thinking of it, as when an expert in several fields thinks of one and still knows the others. It would be absurd to say that such a musician does not understand or love music merely because he is not now thinking of it.
sources.quote: But can we rightly say, This musician certainly knows music, but he does not now understand it, because he is not thinking of it; but he does now understand geometry, for of that he is now thinking? Such an assertion, as far as appears, is absurd.
sources.raw_question: Is not knowing a thing the same as not thinking of it?

question: Why does Augustine illustrate the mental trinity with examples where the begetter comes before the begotten in time, even though the mind's memory, understanding, and will are always together?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Thing is Made Plain by an Example. In What Way the Matter is Handled in Order to Help the Reader.
sources.answer: He does so for teaching purposes. It is easier to distinguish things that happen one after another, where the parent comes before the offspring by an interval of time. Recollection shows how thought is formed from memory and something is begotten when a man conceives. This helps readers grasp the inner trinity, in which the three always exist together and have done so since they began to exist.
sources.quote: because it is easier to distinguish things that take place at successive times, and where the parent precedes the offspring by an interval of time
sources.raw_question: Why does Augustine illustrate the mental trinity with examples where the begetter comes before the begotten in time, even though the mind's memory, understanding, and will are always together?

question: Is the Son's likeness and oneness with the Father merely a likeness in doctrine, teaching, and will, rather than a likeness of essence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. The likeness and oneness must be referred to the very Essence of the Son. If the Son were like the Father only in doctrines, He would have nothing beyond creatures, the Father would be Father in name only, and the Son would not be an exact Image; Paul too taught like the Saviour yet was not like Him in essence.
sources.quote: the likeness and the oneness must be referred to the very Essence of the Son; for unless it be so taken, He will not be shown to have anything beyond things originate
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's likeness and oneness with the Father merely a likeness in doctrine, teaching, and will, rather than a likeness of essence?

question: If the Son is altogether what the Father is, why is the Son not the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Word of God is in All Things Equal to the Father, from Whom It is.
sources.answer: The Son is in all things like and equal to the Father, God of God, Essence of Essence, yet He is not the Father because one is Son and the other is Father. The distinction lies in the relation of begetting and being begotten, not in any difference of essence.
sources.quote: is altogether that which the Father is, yet is not the Father, because the one is Son, the other is Father
sources.raw_question: If the Son is altogether what the Father is, why is the Son not the Father?

question: Is the Father of Jesus Christ the same God who created Adam, or should Christians look for another Father beyond the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVI.—Since our bodies return to the earth, it follows that they have their substance from it; also, by the advent of the Word, the image of God in us appeared in a clearer light.
sources.answer: The Father of Christ is the same Creator. There is one and the same Father whose voice is present with His handiwork from beginning to end, and the Lord showed this by forming eyes from the same earth from which Adam was made. Therefore we should not seek another Father, another substance of our formation, or another hand of God besides the one that fashioned Adam.
sources.quote: we should therefore not seek after another Father besides Him, nor [look for] another substance from which we have been formed, besides what was mentioned beforehand, and shown forth by the Lord
sources.raw_question: Is the Father of Jesus Christ the same God who created Adam, or should Christians look for another Father beyond the Creator?

question: In whose image was man created, and why was that image not clearly shown before the Incarnation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVI.—Since our bodies return to the earth, it follows that they have their substance from it; also, by the advent of the Word, the image of God in us appeared in a clearer light.
sources.answer: Man was created after the image of the Word, who was then still invisible, so the image was declared but not actually shown, and man easily lost the likeness. When the Word became flesh He showed the image truly by becoming Himself what was His image. He also restored the likeness securely, making man like the invisible Father through the visible Word.
sources.quote: for the Word was as yet invisible, after whose image man was created, Wherefore also he did easily lose the similitude.
sources.raw_question: In whose image was man created, and why was that image not clearly shown before the Incarnation?

question: If the Son and the Holy Spirit each fully possess wisdom, memory, understanding and love, from where do they have this?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God from the Trinities We Have Spoken of.
sources.answer: They have it from their origin. The Son has it from the Father, of whom He is born, as wisdom begotten of wisdom. The Holy Spirit, as wisdom proceeding from wisdom, has it from that whence He proceeds. So their full possession of these does not erase their order of origin.
sources.quote: And because the Holy Spirit also is wisdom proceeding from wisdom, He too has not the Father for a memory, and the Son for an understanding, and Himself for love
sources.raw_question: If the Son and the Holy Spirit each fully possess wisdom, memory, understanding and love, from where do they have this?

question: Can the Arian avoid the charge of two Gods by saying the Father and Son are not two supreme beings?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 4: Whether, supposing the Scripture-notion of God to be no more than that of the Author and Governor of the universe, or whatever it be, the admitting of another t
sources.answer: No. They would still be two Authors and Governors of the universe, and each such is by the Arian's own definition a God. If instead 'supreme' must be added to the definition of God, then a non-supreme Author and Governor is not God at all, and the Arian 'ungods' the Son, taking away with one hand what he gave with the other.
sources.quote: Or admitting that supreme must be added to Author and Governor, to make a true definition of God, then Author and Governor of the universe, without supreme, is not sufficient to denominate a person God; and so you wngod the second Person
sources.raw_question: Can the Arian avoid the charge of two Gods by saying the Father and Son are not two supreme beings?

question: In the mental trinity of mind, knowledge, and love, are the three confounded or mingled together so as to lose their distinctness?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > That These Three are Several in Themselves, and Mutually All in All.
sources.answer: No. When the mind knows and loves itself, a trinity remains of mind, love, and knowledge, and it is not confounded by any commingling. Each is severally in itself, yet all are mutually in all, so they remain three while being inseparable.
sources.quote: there remains a trinity: mind, love, knowledge; and this trinity is not confounded together by any commingling: although they are each severally in themselves and mutually all in all
sources.raw_question: In the mental trinity of mind, knowledge, and love, are the three confounded or mingled together so as to lose their distinctness?

question: Since Christ says he will send the Holy Spirit in one place and that the Father will send the Spirit in another, does each saying exclude the other Person from sending the Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. Each text is phrased as if only one Person sends, yet neither denies the other. This illustrates the rule that what is said of one Person in the Trinity is also said of all, because of their inseparable working.
sources.quote: in this Trinity, what is said of each is also said of all, on account of the indivisible working of the one and same substance.
sources.raw_question: Since Christ says he will send the Holy Spirit in one place and that the Father will send the Spirit in another, does each saying exclude the other Person from sending the Spirit?

question: How should 'As the Father hath life in himself, so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself' be understood?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: It means the Father begat the Son to be unchangeable life, which is eternal life. It does not mean the Son existed without life and then received it. In that the Son is, he is life, since he is identical with what he has.
sources.quote: Therefore “He gave to the Son to have life in Himself” means, He begat the Son to be unchangeable life, which is life eternal.
sources.raw_question: How should 'As the Father hath life in himself, so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself' be understood?

question: Does teaching that the Son is created yet possessed of power equal to the uncreated Father lead to Manichaean dualism?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Proof that the Anomœan teaching tends to Manichæism.
sources.answer: Yes. The created and the uncreate are diametrically opposed. If both are ranked as First Causes with equal and inexhaustible power, they will be set against each other, and the primacy between them will become doubtful. So the Anomoean assertion of diminution in the divine being introduces two opposed leading principles, as the Manichees teach.
sources.quote: They will find, therefore, that assertion of diminution (in the Divine being) is the beginning of Manichæism; for their teaching organizes a discord within that being, which comes to two leading principles
sources.raw_question: Does teaching that the Son is created yet possessed of power equal to the uncreated Father lead to Manichaean dualism?

question: Does John 1:14 distinguish the Word from the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. John speaks of the Word becoming flesh and of 'glory as of the Only-begotten' as one and the same subject, attesting their identity. The glory meant is not that of the flesh but of the Word. The case parallels Christ's 'the Paraclete, which is the Holy Ghost', where one and the same is named.
sources.quote: so Word is not one, and Son another, but the Word is Only-Begotten; for He says not the glory of the flesh itself, but of the Word.
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:14 distinguish the Word from the Only-begotten Son?

question: Does the fact that Scripture attributes prophetic inspiration both to the Holy Spirit and to the Lord God of Israel prove the Spirit is God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says the Holy Ghost spoke by Isaiah and moved holy men, while it also says the Lord God of Israel spoke by his prophets and that all Scripture is inspired by God. The same work ascribed to both shows the Spirit is the Lord God of Israel.
sources.quote: The Spirit, therefore, is God, yea, the Lord God of Israel.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Scripture attributes prophetic inspiration both to the Holy Spirit and to the Lord God of Israel prove the Spirit is God?

question: Does the interchange in Scripture of the names and works of God with those of the Holy Spirit (new birth, miracles, comfort, being lied to, being tempted, indwelling a temple) prove the Spirit's Deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6.
