That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Being born of the Spirit and of God, the Spirit's wonders and Jehovah who alone does wonders, the Comforter and the God of all comfort, lying to the Holy Ghost being lying to God, tempting the Spirit and tempting the Lord God, and believers being the temple of the Spirit and of the living God all interchange the same names and offices. Hence the Eternal Spirit is Jehovah, the living God; in one word, He is God.
sources.quote: observing the way in which the names and offices of God and of the Holy Spirit are interchanged, we conclude that this same Eternal Spirit is Jehovah, the God of Israel, the Lord God, the Lord of Lords, the God of Gods, the living God
sources.raw_question: Does the interchange in Scripture of the names and works of God with those of the Holy Spirit (new birth, miracles, comfort, being lied to, being tempted, indwelling a temple) prove the Spirit's Deity?

question: Does divine simplicity mean that every name applied to God, such as 'Creator' or 'Maker', must define his essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. If simplicity turned every name into a definition of the essence, the Father's essence would have to be 'creation' and 'making', which is absurd. Just as the essence of the builder is not the thing built, ungeneracy is not the essence of the Ungenerate.
sources.quote: For as the essence of the builder is not the thing built, no more is ungeneracy the essence of the Ungenerate.
sources.raw_question: Does divine simplicity mean that every name applied to God, such as 'Creator' or 'Maker', must define his essence?

question: Can the human mind measure or comprehend God's greatness so as to posit something beyond Him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIX.—Earthly things may be the type of heavenly, but the latter cannot be the types of others still superior and unknown; nor can we, without absolute madness, maintain that God is known to us only as the type of a still unknown and superior being.
sources.answer: No. God cannot be measured in the heart and is incomprehensible in the mind; if man cannot grasp even the fulness of His hand, which holds heaven and earth, he cannot know so great a God. Those who imagine another Pleroma and Father beyond Him act as though they had measured God, which is madness.
sources.quote: But if man comprehends not the fulness and the greatness of His hand, how shall any one be able to understand or know in his heart so great a God?
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind measure or comprehend God's greatness so as to posit something beyond Him?

question: Does Paul's statement that there is one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ divide Godhead from Lordship, making the Father alone God and the Son alone Lord?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Hilary holds that in Christ the Lord there is also God, and in God the Father there is also Lord, so the Two together are the unity which is God and the unity which is Lord. Reason shows something would be imperfect in God unless He were Lord, and in the Lord unless He were God. Hence both are implied under either name and neither exists apart from the unity.
sources.quote: since in Christ the Lord there was also God, and in God the Father there was also Lord, and They Two are that unity which is God, and They Two are also that unity which is the Lord
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that there is one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ divide Godhead from Lordship, making the Father alone God and the Son alone Lord?

question: Does affirming that the Son is God compromise the truth that God is One?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The adversaries imagine that confessing the Son as God means deserting the unity of God. They fail to see that God's not being alone is consistent with His unity. Though God is One, He is not solitary.
sources.quote: Our adversaries are blind to the fact that His assertion that He is not alone is consistent with unity; that though He is One He is not solitary.
sources.raised_by_detail: Those who charge that the doctrine teaches two Gods
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that the Son is God compromise the truth that God is One?

question: Is the Sabellian understanding of God's unity, which denies any distinction of the Son, correct?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Hilary means to proclaim God's unity in the sense of the Law, Prophets and Apostles. He denies that God is One in the Sabellian sense, which swallows up the Son. He also rejects the opposite error of teaching two Gods.
sources.quote: If I withstand him, and deny that, in the Sabellian sense, God is One a fresh heresy is ready to receive me, pointing out that I teach the existence of two Gods.
sources.raw_question: Is the Sabellian understanding of God's unity, which denies any distinction of the Son, correct?

question: Is the birth of Jesus Christ from the Virgin Mary his only birth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Hilary rejects as a pestilent doctrine the Photinian teaching that Christ's only birth was from the Virgin. As established earlier, the Son is truly born from God, not merely born of Mary.
sources.quote: Pannonia upholds her pestilent doctrine that the only birth of Jesus Christ was from the Virgin.
sources.raw_question: Is the birth of Jesus Christ from the Virgin Mary his only birth?

question: Does Christ's coming in his Father's Name show that the Father and Son share one Name and one Godhead?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIII. St. Ambrose shows from the Scriptures that the Name of the Three Divine Persons is one, and first the unity of the Name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as each is called Paraclete and Truth.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ said he came in his Father's Name, not in a name of his own. This reveals that the Godhead and Majesty are one. By contrast, Antichrist comes in his own name, which shows that oneness of the divine Name must be taught, not difference.
sources.quote: Christ came in the oneness of the Name, but Antichrist will come in his own name
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's coming in his Father's Name show that the Father and Son share one Name and one Godhead?

question: Does the shared Name of the Son and the Spirit imply, as Sabellians hold, that the Son is the Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIII. St. Ambrose shows from the Scriptures that the Name of the Three Divine Persons is one, and first the unity of the Name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as each is called Paraclete and Truth.
sources.answer: No. Christ called the Spirit "another Paraclete," so that no one would think the Son is also the Spirit. The oneness lies in the Name, not in a Sabellian confusion of the Persons. The Son is one Paraclete and the Spirit is another.
sources.quote: And He said well “another,” that you might not suppose that the Son is also the Spirit, for oneness is of the Name, not a Sabellian confusion of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does the shared Name of the Son and the Spirit imply, as Sabellians hold, that the Son is the Spirit?

question: Is the Holy Spirit called "the Truth" itself, as the Son is, and not only "the Spirit of Truth"?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIII. St. Ambrose shows from the Scriptures that the Name of the Three Divine Persons is one, and first the unity of the Name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as each is called Paraclete and Truth.
sources.answer: Yes. John's epistle says, "the Spirit is Truth," just as the Son says, "I am the Way, the Truth, and the Life." The shared title of Truth is a further sign of the oneness of Name between the Son and the Spirit.
sources.quote: Not only, then, is the Spirit called the Spirit of Truth, but also the Truth, as the Son is also declared to be the Truth
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit called "the Truth" itself, as the Son is, and not only "the Spirit of Truth"?

question: Does Tatian's statement that at creation the Word 'becomes the first-born work of the Father' mean that the Son is a creature, or that He was generated at the time of creation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: No. Tatian says the Word became a 'work,' not a Son, at creation, so he teaches no generation at that time. Being counted the first of the works was the Word's condescension (συγκατάβασις), as the type of the works. Creatures were to be raised to adoption and called sons, so for that purpose He stooped to creation and was called a work. Tatian's use of ἀρχή points to the text in which Wisdom is 'created a beginning of ways unto the works.'
sources.quote: It was His great condescension, συγκατάβασις, to be accounted the first of the works, as being their type; that as they were to be raised to an adoption and called sons, so He for that purpose might stoop to creation, and be called a work.
sources.raised_by_detail: Newman, against Bull's interpretation of Tatian
sources.raw_question: Does Tatian's statement that at creation the Word 'becomes the first-born work of the Father' mean that the Son is a creature, or that He was generated at the time of creation?

question: Did Christ remain equal with God even while he appeared in the form of a servant?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen argues that although Christ once appeared in the form of a servant, he still "thought it not robbery to be equal with God" (Phil. 2:6). His humiliation did not remove his divine majesty, and in that majesty he dwells in light inaccessible.
sources.quote: And though he once appeared in the form of a servant, yet then “he thought it not robbery to be equal with God,” Phil. ii. 6.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ remain equal with God even while he appeared in the form of a servant?

question: If the Holy Spirit is not a creature, does it follow that he is very God, equal to and consubstantial with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Men are also called gods, so being called "God" alone does not prove full deity. But whatever is not a creature is very God. Therefore the Spirit is absolutely equal with the Father and the Son, consubstantial and co-eternal in the unity of the Trinity.
sources.quote: But if not a creature, then not only God (for men likewise are called gods), but also very God; and therefore absolutely equal with the Father and the Son, and in the unity of the Trinity consubstantial and co-eternal.
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit is not a creature, does it follow that he is very God, equal to and consubstantial with the Father and the Son?

question: Does the Arian view that God created the Son only in order to create us imply that the Father never willed the Son for his own sake, and that the Son becomes superfluous once creation exists?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: Yes. On their view God took counsel about us and willed us first, forming the Son only afterwards as a means. So the Father would have had no will for the Son himself, and the Son would have no precedence with God over us. Once the creatures for whom he was made exist, such an instrument becomes superfluous. Athanasius regards this conclusion as plainly irreligious, and so as refuting the premise.
sources.quote: perchance the Father had not even a will for the Son at all; for not as having a will for Him, did He create Him, but with a will for us, He formed Him for our sake
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian view that God created the Son only in order to create us imply that the Father never willed the Son for his own sake, and that the Son becomes superfluous once creation exists?

question: Is the unity of the Father and the Son as one God grounded merely in their sharing one authority or dominion, as Dr. Clarke claimed?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. The Fathers distinguished unity of authority from unity of Godhead; God and his angels share one authority, yet the angels are not thereby Gods. The Fathers resolved the unity of Godhead into unity of substance and original: one Head, Root, Fountain and Father, not in authority only but in substance, since the Son is derived from the Father's substance.
sources.quote: there is but one Head, Root, Fountain, Father of all; not in respect of authority only, but of substance also
sources.raw_question: Is the unity of the Father and the Son as one God grounded merely in their sharing one authority or dominion, as Dr. Clarke claimed?

question: Is resolving the divine unity into the Son's Sonship or the Father's being sole principle different from resolving it into unity of substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No, they come to the same thing. Fathers such as Justin, Athanasius, Hilary, Basil, and moderns like Pearson and Bull resolved the unity into Sonship or unity of principle, which amounts to communion of substance, since the Son is from the Father's substance. None excluded the Son from being one God with the Father in nature, substance and perfection.
sources.quote: all of them, somewhere or other, are known to resolve it into Sonship, or unity of principle; either of which comes to the same with the former.
sources.raw_question: Is resolving the divine unity into the Son's Sonship or the Father's being sole principle different from resolving it into unity of substance?

question: Are the only-begotten Son, the Christ, the Word, and the Saviour one and the same person, and is he God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: Yes. He is one and the same: Saviour of those who are saved, Lord of those under authority, and God of all things that have been formed. He is the only-begotten of the Father, the announced Christ, and the Word of God, who became incarnate in the fulness of time. At that point the Son of God became the Son of man.
sources.quote: the God of all those things which have been formed, the only-begotten of the Father, Christ who was announced, and the Word of God, who became incarnate when the fulness of time had come
sources.raw_question: Are the only-begotten Son, the Christ, the Word, and the Saviour one and the same person, and is he God?

question: Is it possible to hold a saving faith in the only true God while denying that Christ is true God and calling him a creature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Christ is united with the only true God the Father in what Christians believe and confess. Believing in the only true God without Christ is no faith at all, so denying Christ's true deity overturns the faith that brings eternal life.
sources.quote: what faith is it, pray, to deny Him to be true God, and to call Him a creature, when it is no faith to believe in the only true God without Christ?
sources.raw_question: Is it possible to hold a saving faith in the only true God while denying that Christ is true God and calling him a creature?

question: Is the God who made the promise to Abraham the same God who calls the Gentiles through his Son Jesus Christ, or is the God of the Gospel a different deity from the God of the Old Testament?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IX.—One and the same God, the Creator of heaven and earth, is He whom the prophets foretold, and who was declared by the Gospel. Proof of this, at the outset, from St. Matthew’s Gospel.
sources.answer: They are one and the same God. Irenaeus argues that Matthew presents John the Baptist preaching repentance in reference to the God who promised Abraham, without declaring any other God. He adds that the prophets foretold the forerunner, and the Gospel announces his coming. Hence the Father of our Lord is the very God who promised through the prophets.
sources.quote: There is therefore one and the same God, the Father of our Lord, who also promised, through the prophets, that He would send His forerunner
sources.raw_question: Is the God who made the promise to Abraham the same God who calls the Gentiles through his Son Jesus Christ, or is the God of the Gospel a different deity from the God of the Old Testament?

question: Was the world made by the Word of God, or by angels or a lower Demiurge?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: By the Word of God. Marcion holds that the Word came to things belonging to another. Some Gnostics credit angels with making the world, and the Valentinians credit a Demiurge produced from the Mother. Against all of these, the Gospel plainly affirms that the world was made by the Word who was in the beginning with God, and that He came to His own things.
sources.quote: while the Gospel affirms plainly, that by the Word, which was in the beginning with God, all things were made, which Word, he says, "was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
sources.raw_question: Was the world made by the Word of God, or by angels or a lower Demiurge?

question: What does it mean to give glory to God, and how does this apply to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > The glorifying of the enumeration of His attributes.
sources.answer: Giving glory is nothing else than enumerating the wonders that belong to the one glorified. We glorify even the Father and the Only-begotten Son only by recounting their wonders as far as we are able. So simply recounting the Spirit's attributes and benefits is the fullest possible glorification of Him, in the same way as for the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: For not even in the case of the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the Only begotten Son, are we capable of giving Them glory otherwise than by recounting, to the extent of our powers, all the wonders that belong to Them.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean to give glory to God, and how does this apply to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: If the Gnostics posit a higher god above the Creator, would that higher god be superior to the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. Even granting another god above the Creator, a comparison of the works done by each would show the Creator superior, since by deeds the better one appears. Because the heretics can adduce no works of their supposed higher father, the Creator is shown to be God alone.
sources.quote: For by deeds the better man appears, as I have already remarked; and, inasmuch as these men have no works of their father to adduce, the latter is shown to be God alone.
sources.raw_question: If the Gnostics posit a higher god above the Creator, would that higher god be superior to the Creator?

question: Did the one God make all things directly through his Word, or through angels or intermediate powers separate from him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XXII.—Deviations of heretics from the truth.
sources.answer: God made all things through his own Word, not through angels or powers separated from him. Scripture states that the heavens were established by the Word of the Lord and that all things were made by him, without exception. God needs none of these intermediaries, but by his Word and Spirit makes, disposes and governs all things.
sources.quote: these eternal things He did not make by angels, or by any powers separated from His Ennœa. For God needs none of all these things, but is He who, by His Word and Spirit, makes, and disposes, and governs all things
sources.raw_question: Did the one God make all things directly through his Word, or through angels or intermediate powers separate from him?

question: Are the names of things, including divine titles like "Ungenerate," imposed by human beings rather than given by nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > He says that all things that are in creation have been named by man, if, as is the case, they are called differently by every nation, as also the appellation of “Ungenerate” is conferred by us: but that the proper appellation of the Divine essence itself which expresses the Divine Nature, either does not exist at all, or is unknown to us.
sources.answer: Yes. Eunomius himself argues that Peter and Paul's names were man-made because they could be changed; by the same premise, since earth, sky, sea and all things are named differently by every nation, all names are imposed by us. "Generate" and "Ungenerate" are no exception, since they too vary across languages.
sources.quote: Now if all things are so, surely the Generate and the Ungenerate are not exceptions, for even they are among the things that change their name.
sources.raw_question: Are the names of things, including divine titles like "Ungenerate," imposed by human beings rather than given by nature?

question: Is there any name known to us that expresses the divine nature or essence itself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > He says that all things that are in creation have been named by man, if, as is the case, they are called differently by every nation, as also the appellation of “Ungenerate” is conferred by us: but that the proper appellation of the Divine essence itself which expresses the Divine Nature, either does not exist at all, or is unknown to us.
sources.answer: No. We are taught that God exists, but a name able to comprehend the unspeakable and infinite Nature either does not exist at all or is unknown to us. Scripture teaches that Abraham and Moses could not know the Name, that no one has seen or can see God, that His light is unapproachable, and that His greatness has no end. Language compares to the divine nature as a cupped hand compares to the whole sea.
sources.quote: We are taught the fact of Its existence, while we assert that an appellation of such force as to include the unspeakable and infinite Nature, either does not exist at all, or at any rate is unknown to us.
sources.raw_question: Is there any name known to us that expresses the divine nature or essence itself?

question: Since Scripture's many names for the Only-begotten (stone, vine, door, light, shepherd) are not taken in their ordinary sense, should the name 'Son' likewise not be taken as signifying a real community of nature with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Then he ends the book with an exposition of the Divine and Human names of the Only-Begotten, and a discussion of the terms “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. 'Son' is unlike the other names because it alone is spoken with reference to the Father who begat Him. Names like vine, shepherd or physician describe His providential work toward creatures and would not apply if there were no beneficiaries. 'Son of the Father' is not such a name. Eunomius's inference treats the Son's name as an empty sound in order to avoid its witness to the community of essence, and it does not follow.
sources.quote: we assert that none of the other names is closely connected with the reference to Him that begat Him.
sources.raw_question: Since Scripture's many names for the Only-begotten (stone, vine, door, light, shepherd) are not taken in their ordinary sense, should the name 'Son' likewise not be taken as signifying a real community of nature with the Father?

question: Should scriptural names of Christ such as axe, light, vine or stone be understood in their literal, material sense?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Then he ends the book with an exposition of the Divine and Human names of the Only-Begotten, and a discussion of the terms “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. It would be absurd to think that what is incorporeal, immaterial, simple and without figure is shaped according to the apparent senses of these names. We transfer their meaning to something befitting the Divine nature. He is called these things without being any of them according to the definition of His nature.
sources.quote: it would be a most absurd thing to think that what is incorporeal and immaterial, simple, and without figure, should be fashioned according to the apparent senses of these names
sources.raw_question: Should scriptural names of Christ such as axe, light, vine or stone be understood in their literal, material sense?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be said to be 'subject' to the Father and the Son in any scriptural sense of 'subjection' without blasphemy?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Examination of the meaning of 'subjection:' in that he says that the nature of the Holy Spirit is subject to that of the Father and the Son. It is shewn that the Holy Spirit is of an equal, not inferior, rank to the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. Scripture uses 'subjection' for the subjection of brute creatures to man, for the conquest of rebels in war, and for the Son's (as Mediator sharing humanity) subjection to the Father. If the Spirit were subject as the Son is, He would rank with the Son, not below Him; if as brutes to man, or as a conquered rebel, the claim is plainly blasphemous.
sources.quote: whichever it is I do not see how he can avoid the inevitable crime of blasphemy: whether he says the Spirit is subject in the manner of the brute creation, as fish and birds and sheep, to man, or were to fetch Him a captive to a superior power
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be said to be 'subject' to the Father and the Son in any scriptural sense of 'subjection' without blasphemy?

question: Since the Fathers usually styled the Father 'the Almighty' (ὁ παντοκράτωρ), does it follow that the Son is not Almighty?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. It is true that the Father was ordinarily or emphatically called ὁ παντοκράτωρ, but this is beside the point. It does not show that the ancients denied the title to the Son. They expressly applied it to the Son in Revelation 1:8 and in other texts.
sources.quote: without proving any thing more than that the Father was ordinarily or emphatically styled ὁ παντοκράτωρ, which is true, but not pertinent
sources.raw_question: Since the Fathers usually styled the Father 'the Almighty' (ὁ παντοκράτωρ), does it follow that the Son is not Almighty?

question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity an added burden on the intellect, or does it help our conception of God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: It helps rather than burdens. Although the idea is difficult in itself, it resolves the deepest and most persistent difficulties in conceiving God as an infinite moral Being. Conceiving God as Trinity gives new fullness, richness and force to the idea of a self-conscious, loving God. Once someone has conceived God as Trinity, they can never again be satisfied with a monadistic conception.
sources.quote: it does not come to us as an added burden upon our intelligence; it brings us rather the solution of the deepest and most persistent difficulties in our conception of God as infinite moral Being
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity an added burden on the intellect, or does it help our conception of God?

question: Is the term 'person' predicated of God the Father relatively (in relation to the Son and Holy Spirit) or in respect to Himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: In respect to Himself. We do not speak of the Father as 'the person of the Son', as we would with relative terms like friend or neighbour. When we speak of the person of the Father we mean nothing other than the substance of the Father, that is, the Father Himself. Just as for God to be is the same as to be God, great or good, so for Him to be is the same as to be a person.
sources.quote: so also the person of the Father is not anything else than the Father Himself; for He is called a person in respect to Himself, not in respect to the Son, or the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Is the term 'person' predicated of God the Father relatively (in relation to the Son and Holy Spirit) or in respect to Himself?

question: If 'person' is said of God absolutely, like 'God' and 'essence', why do Christians speak of three persons in the Trinity rather than one person, while saying one God and one essence rather than three?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: The plural is used out of linguistic necessity rather than strict propriety. Having confessed that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are three, we need some single word to answer the question 'three what?'. 'Persons' serves that purpose, so that we are not left entirely silent.
sources.quote: unless it be because we wish some one word to serve for that meaning whereby the Trinity is understood, that we might not be altogether silent, when asked, what three, while we confessed that they are three?
sources.raw_question: If 'person' is said of God absolutely, like 'God' and 'essence', why do Christians speak of three persons in the Trinity rather than one person, while saying one God and one essence rather than three?

question: Is the one divine essence a species shared by the three persons as individuals, in the way Abraham, Isaac and Jacob share the species 'man'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: No, not properly. One man cannot be subdivided into several men, so on this model one essence could not be divided into three persons. Augustine instead says the terms are used not according to genus or species but as of a common and identical 'matter'. The comparison is three statues made of the same gold: three statues, one gold. Yet the gold is neither a genus nor a species of the statues.
sources.quote: not as man is subdivided into Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, so can one man also be subdivided into several single men; for this is altogether impossible, since one man is already a single man. Why then is one essence subdivided into three substances or persons?
sources.raw_question: Is the one divine essence a species shared by the three persons as individuals, in the way Abraham, Isaac and Jacob share the species 'man'?

question: Does Scripture call the Son 'God' in the full sense, such as 'great God' and 'God over all'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He also ingeniously shows from the passage of the Gospel which speaks of “Good Master,” from the parable of the Vineyard, from Isaiah and from Paul, that there is not a dualism in the Godhead of good and evil, as Eunomius' ally Marcion supposes, and declares that the Son does not refuse the title of “good” or “Existent,” or acknowledge His alienation from the Father, but that to Him also belongs authority over all things that come into being.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul calls Christ 'God over all, blessed for ever' in Romans, 'the great God and our Saviour' in Titus, and says 'God was manifest in the flesh' to Timothy. These texts, together with the prophets, demonstrate on every side that the Only-begotten is God.
sources.quote: who gives the Lord the appellation not only of “God,” but of “great God” and “God over all,”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture call the Son 'God' in the full sense, such as 'great God' and 'God over all'?

question: Does the word 'one' in 'none good but one' refer to the Father alone so as to separate Him from the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He also ingeniously shows from the passage of the Gospel which speaks of “Good Master,” from the parable of the Vineyard, from Isaiah and from Paul, that there is not a dualism in the Godhead of good and evil, as Eunomius' ally Marcion supposes, and declares that the Son does not refuse the title of “good” or “Existent,” or acknowledge His alienation from the Father, but that to Him also belongs authority over all things that come into being.
sources.answer: No. Although 'one' ordinarily signifies not being coupled with anything else, in the case of Father and Son it does not imply isolation, since Christ says 'I and the Father are one'. So in predicating goodness of 'one', the Lord claimed goodness for Himself as one with the Father in nature.
sources.quote: in all other cases, it is true, the term “one” carries with it the signification of not being coupled with anything else, but in the case of the Father and the Son “one” does not imply isolation.
sources.raw_question: Does the word 'one' in 'none good but one' refer to the Father alone so as to separate Him from the Son?

question: Can human reason comprehend the manner in which the Son is born from God the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. The powers of God, including the Birth of the Son, exceed the methods of human reason, yet faith is convinced of them by the sure evidence of God's action. Christ's miracles, such as turning water into wine, show a real result whose mode baffles sight and sense while God's power is plainly manifest. So we should believe the Birth on God's testimony rather than reject it because we cannot explain how it happens.
sources.quote: Such powers are there in God; powers which the methods of our reason cannot comprehend, but of which our faith, on the sure evidence of His action, is convinced.
sources.raw_question: Can human reason comprehend the manner in which the Son is born from God the Father?

question: Did Christ pray only that the Father be glorified, so that glory belongs to the Father alone and not to the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. In John 17 Christ prays 'glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee,' and asks for the glory he had with the Father before the world was. This shows he was concerned for his own glory as well as his Father's, and that the honour of either redounds to both.
sources.quote: Father, the hour is come, glorify thy Son, that thy Son also ‘“‘ may glorify thee.” How familiar, how equally concerned, as well for his own, as his Father’s glory.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ pray only that the Father be glorified, so that glory belongs to the Father alone and not to the Son?

question: Is the Father alone the object of Christian prayer, or may Christ also be invoked and worshipped?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: Christ may also be invoked and worshipped. He is sometimes invoked distinctly and personally, and grace and peace are implored from him together with the Father in many New Testament places. He is worshipped by men, by angels and by the whole creation, and eternal glory and dominion are ascribed to him as to the Father. The earliest Christian writers held the same view and worshipped Christ in practice.
sources.quote: He is to be worshipped and adored, as well as the Father, by men, by dangels, by the ¢whole creation. Gloryand dominion for ever and ‘ever are fascribed to him, as well as to the Father.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father alone the object of Christian prayer, or may Christ also be invoked and worshipped?

question: What order among the Father, Son and Holy Spirit does the Spirit's work of glorifying Christ reflect?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: The Spirit's work follows the order of the divine dispensations. Everything springs from the Father's love. The Son came to glorify the Father and, having finished redemption, was to be glorified with the Father. The Holy Ghost is then sent to glorify the Son by showing believers Christ's love, grace and purchase. A spirit that seeks its own glory inverts this order.
sources.quote: The fountain of all being and lying in the Father’s love, the Son came to glorify the Father.
sources.raw_question: What order among the Father, Son and Holy Spirit does the Spirit's work of glorifying Christ reflect?

question: How should scriptural statements about the Son be interpreted when it is unclear whether they refer to his assumed human nature (form of a servant) or to his being from the Father though equal to him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > That Some Ways of Speaking Concerning the Son are to Be Understood According to Either Rule.
sources.answer: Such passages may without danger be understood according to either rule. Where it cannot be discerned which rule applies, both readings are orthodox: one refers the text to the Son's lesser status as having taken the creature, the other to his being equal yet of the Father.
sources.quote: if this is in such way doubtful, that which it really is can neither be explained nor discerned, then such passages may without danger be understood according to either rule
sources.raw_question: How should scriptural statements about the Son be interpreted when it is unclear whether they refer to his assumed human nature (form of a servant) or to his being from the Father though equal to him?

question: When Scripture says the Father "hath given life to the Son," does this mean the Son received life as something distinct from himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > That Some Ways of Speaking Concerning the Son are to Be Understood According to Either Rule.
sources.answer: No. In the form of God the Son is not one thing and his life another; the life itself is the Son. So "He hath given life to the Son" means nothing other than "He hath begotten the Son, who is life." Likewise, giving doctrine to the Son means begetting the Son, who is doctrine.
sources.quote: as the text, “He hath given life to the Son,” is no otherwise to be understood than, He hath begotten the Son, who is life
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says the Father "hath given life to the Son," does this mean the Son received life as something distinct from himself?

question: Does Scripture treat Christian love as the same thing as the indwelling Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes, or at least as the Spirit's first and most natural breathing and acting in the soul. Many texts join or interchange love and the Spirit: 'fellowship of the Spirit' with 'comfort of love', 'love of the Spirit', 'love in the Spirit', and God's love 'shed abroad... by the Holy Ghost'. In Galatians 5, Paul first says love keeps liberty from turning to biting and devouring. He then restates the same point as 'walk in the Spirit.'
sources.quote: The Scripture seems in many places to speak of love in Christians as if it were the same with the Spirit of God in them, or at least as the prime and most natural breathing and acting of the Spirit in the soul.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture treat Christian love as the same thing as the indwelling Holy Spirit?

question: Can the family-triad view of the image of the Trinity be saved by saying the woman was already in Adam's side and the son in his loins when man was created in God's image?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Why This Opinion is to Be Rejected.
sources.answer: No. If that were the point, Scripture, in saying 'God made man after the image of God,' should have named the son along with male and female to complete the trinity. Yet it specifies only 'male and female,' which shows the image is not meant as a triad of father, mother and son.
sources.quote: Certainly, in order to complete the image of the Trinity, it ought to have added also son, although still placed in the loins of his father, as the woman was in his side.
sources.raw_question: Can the family-triad view of the image of the Trinity be saved by saying the woman was already in Adam's side and the son in his loins when man was created in God's image?

question: Can the term "ungenerate" (agennetos) be justified as a name denoting the essence of God if only Scripturally sanctioned terms are allowed?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. No sacred writer hands down "ungenerate" as a term for the divine essence, so by Eunomius's own test it would have to be erased from his writings. If he accepts it for the sense it carries, then "conception" must equally be accepted for its sense; either both are excluded or both retained.
sources.quote: How, then, can you lay down the law that the Divine essence should be denoted by the word “ungenerate”—a term which none of the sacred writers can be shown to have handed down to us?
sources.raw_question: Can the term "ungenerate" (agennetos) be justified as a name denoting the essence of God if only Scripturally sanctioned terms are allowed?

question: If the Son is really subordinate to the Father, does that refute the Son's consubstantiality with the Father, on the ground that one individual substance cannot be subordinate to itself?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 20: Whether the Doctor need have cited 300 teats, *wide of the purpose, to prove what nobody denies, namely, a subordination, in some sense, of the Son to the Fathe
sources.answer: No. The objection assumes that consubstantiality means personal identity, a notion the Querist never held. It trades on an ambiguous use of 'individual'. By the same trick one could argue that Clarke's own omnipresent substance, being in heaven and filling all things, is greater and less than itself, remote from itself, containing and contained. The objector would answer that his meaning of 'individual' had been misread, and the same answer serves for the Querist.
sources.quote: The Querist never had such a notion as that of personal consubstantiality, which is ridiculous in the sound, and contradiction in sense
sources.raised_by_detail: Clarke's defender (Jackson), replying for Dr. Clarke
sources.raw_question: If the Son is really subordinate to the Father, does that refute the Son's consubstantiality with the Father, on the ground that one individual substance cannot be subordinate to itself?

question: What does the Holy Spirit make known to believers concerning God the Father in his work as Comforter?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: He acquaints believers with the Father's love, specifically that the Father, the first person of the Trinity considered distinctly, loves them. Christ grounds the consolation the Comforter brings in the words "The Father himself loveth you" (John 16:27). By persuading believers of the Father's eternal and unchangeable love, the Spirit fills them with consolation, so that communion with the Father in his love comes about through the Spirit's operation.
sources.quote: In particular, that the Father, the first person in the Trinity, considered so distinctly, loves us.
sources.raw_question: What does the Holy Spirit make known to believers concerning God the Father in his work as Comforter?

question: Is the Christ who took the form of a servant a different person from the one who existed in the form of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. It was not another, different Person who emptied himself and took the form of a servant. Through the mystery of the Dispensation, the same Person is both in the form of God and in the form of a servant. The two forms remain distinct: obedience unto death does not belong to the form of God.
sources.quote: Yet it was not another and a different Person Who emptied Himself and Who took the form of a servant. To take anything cannot be predicated of some one who is not, for he only can take who exists.
sources.raw_question: Is the Christ who took the form of a servant a different person from the one who existed in the form of God?

question: Why is it harder to distinguish the three members of the inner trinity of recollection than those of the trinity of bodily sight?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > There is Another Trinity in the Memory of Him Who Thinks Over Again What He Has Seen.
sources.answer: Because in the inner trinity all three share the likeness and equality of the same nature and substance. In bodily sight the body, the sense, and the will differ in nature and are easily discerned, but the trinity of recollection, though introduced from without, is transacted wholly within, with no part outside the nature of the mind; so the will unites the two as one and they can be distinguished only by reason.
sources.quote: the likeness and equality of the same nature and substance cause this difficulty of distinguishing
sources.raw_question: Why is it harder to distinguish the three members of the inner trinity of recollection than those of the trinity of bodily sight?

question: What is the relation of the Spirit of truth to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: The Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father and is sent from the Father by the Son. Because all things the Father has are the Son's, whatever the Spirit receives, He receives from the Son.
sources.quote: For the Spirit of truth proceedeth from the Father and is sent from the Father by the Son.
sources.raw_question: What is the relation of the Spirit of truth to the Father and the Son?

question: Does confessing that there is only one God and that Christ is God require the conclusion that Christ is the Father himself and that the Father suffered?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Noetus argued that since God is one and Christ is God, Christ must be the Father, so the Father suffered. Hippolytus replies that the Scriptures do not present the matter this way. Their real meaning must be drawn out against this interpretation.
sources.quote: If therefore I acknowledge Christ to be God, He is the Father Himself, if He is indeed God; and Christ suffered, being Himself God; and consequently the Father suffered, for He was the Father Himself.” But the case stands not thus
sources.raw_question: Does confessing that there is only one God and that Christ is God require the conclusion that Christ is the Father himself and that the Father suffered?

question: Do the Father and the Son share one common glory, so that the doxology can be offered to the Father with the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that it is not proper for “with whom” to be said of the Son, and that the proper phrase is “through whom.”
sources.answer: Yes. The fathers taught that the glory of the Father and the Son is common, and they were following the sense of Scripture. Scripture calls the Son the brightness of the glory and the image of the archetype. Brightness is always thought of together with glory, and an image together with its archetype.
sources.quote: What our fathers said, the same say we, that the glory of the Father and of the Son is common; wherefore we offer the doxology to the Father with the Son.
sources.raw_question: Do the Father and the Son share one common glory, so that the doxology can be offered to the Father with the Son?

question: Can the Son be separated from the Father in thought or in nature, given that he is called the "brightness" of God's glory and the "image"?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that it is not proper for “with whom” to be said of the Son, and that the proper phrase is “through whom.”
sources.answer: No. The Son is always and everywhere together with the Father, as brightness is with glory and an image with its archetype. Even the close connection of their names forbids separating them, and the nature of the things themselves forbids it far more.
sources.quote: the Son always and everywhere together with the Father; nor does even the close connexion of the names, much less the nature of the things, admit of separation.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be separated from the Father in thought or in nature, given that he is called the "brightness" of God's glory and the "image"?

question: Is the Holy Spirit one of the created things that serve God, or is He above all things?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter I. St. Ambrose commences his argument by complimenting the Emperor, both for his faith and for the restitution of the Basilica to the Church; then having urged that his opponents, if they affirm that the Holy Spirit is not a servant, cannot deny Him to be above all, adds that the same Spirit, when He said, “All things serve Thee,” showed plainly that He was distinct from creatures; which point he also establishes by other evidence.
sources.answer: He is above all things, not among them. Scripture says "All things serve Thee," and it was the Spirit Himself who spoke this through the prophet, saying not "We serve" but "serve Thee," thereby excepting Himself from serving. Since all things serve and the Spirit does not serve, He is not included among all things.
sources.quote: He did not say, We serve, but, “serve Thee,” that you might believe that He Himself is excepted from serving. So, then, since all things serve, and the Spirit does not serve, the Holy Spirit is certainly not included amongst all things.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit one of the created things that serve God, or is He above all things?

question: Does 'All things were made through Him' wrongly include the Unbegotten Father among things made through the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The added clause 'without Him was nothing made' shows that the Son was not alone in the work. One through whom the work was done is distinguished from Another without whom it was not done. This restores the Father as Author while giving him the Son as Companion.
sources.quote: He through Whom the work was done is One; He without Whom it was not done is Another: a distinction is drawn between Creator and Companion.
sources.raw_question: Does 'All things were made through Him' wrongly include the Unbegotten Father among things made through the Son?

question: Can essence itself be predicated relatively, so that the Father's very being is said only in relation to the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: No. If essence were spoken relatively, essence would not be essence but would only signify a relation. Everything said relatively presupposes something that is a substance in respect to itself. A master is first a man, and a beast of burden is first a horse. So if the Father were nothing in respect to Himself, there would be nothing to be spoken of relatively at all.
sources.quote: Wherefore, if the Father also is not something in respect to Himself then there is no one at all that can be spoken of relatively to something.
sources.raw_question: Can essence itself be predicated relatively, so that the Father's very being is said only in relation to the Son?

question: Is everything said of the Father said only relatively to the Son, while the Son alone is spoken of both in respect to Himself and relatively to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: No. In no way may we think that the Father cannot be called anything in respect to His own substance. That would leave the Son, called great greatness and powerful power, as substantial in Himself while the Father is merely relative. Such an asymmetry is absurd, because relative terms presuppose substance.
sources.quote: But in no way may we think, in like manner, that the Father cannot be called anything in respect to His own substance, but that whatever He is called, He is called in relation to the Son
sources.raw_question: Is everything said of the Father said only relatively to the Son, while the Son alone is spoken of both in respect to Himself and relatively to the Father?

question: Can the Word be counted as included in the Father's name in the baptismal formula, so that the Word need not be the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No. If the Word were tucked into the Father's name, the Spirit could equally be, as if he were not distinct from the Father. Then the Man would be named after the Father and the Spirit after the Man. The divine Monad would expand into a Tetrad of Father, Word, Son and Holy Spirit instead of a Triad, which is absurd.
sources.quote: the Monad, instead of dilating into a Triad, dilates according to them into a Tetrad, Father, Word, Son, and Holy Ghost.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who separate the Word from the Son
sources.raw_question: Can the Word be counted as included in the Father's name in the baptismal formula, so that the Word need not be the Son?

question: Is the Son the Word and the assumed Man taken together, so that the Word was not Son before the incarnation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No. If the Word is Son because of the flesh, then the flesh is the Son, with all the absurdities already shown. If the flesh is called Son because of the Word, then the Word was Son before the flesh. If their union makes the Son, some prior cause of the union makes the Son, and so the Son again precedes the flesh.
sources.quote: But if the flesh is called Son because of the Word, then even before the flesh the Word certainly, being such, was Son.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who say Word and Man together are the Son
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the Word and the assumed Man taken together, so that the Word was not Son before the incarnation?

question: Does the Old Testament calling people 'sons of God' before the incarnation show that the Word was Son before he became man?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: Yes. Men are sons only because of the true Son. Scripture calls the ancients sons long before the incarnation: 'I begat sons,' the sons of God in Noah's time, and 'Is not He thy Father?' So the true Son, for whose sake they were sons, already existed before his coming among us.
sources.quote: Therefore there was also that True Son, for whose sake they too were sons.
sources.raw_question: Does the Old Testament calling people 'sons of God' before the incarnation show that the Word was Son before he became man?

question: Was the Son sent by the Father alone, or also by the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: He was sent by the Holy Spirit as well. The Father did not make the Son of a woman without his own Spirit. The Gospels say plainly that the Holy Ghost came upon Mary and that she was with child of the Holy Ghost. Isaiah also has Christ say that the Lord God and his Spirit have sent him.
sources.quote: Moreover, He could not be sent by the Father without the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Was the Son sent by the Father alone, or also by the Holy Spirit?

question: Should the Son be worshipped and glorified together with the Father in the doxology?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is joined with the Father in nature, in glory and in dignity. The Lord taught that whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father. Refusing the Son a share in the doxology, as if he deserved only a lower rank of honour, is rash and contrary to true religion.
sources.quote: to refuse to worship and glorify with the Father him who in nature, in glory, and in dignity is conjoined with him?
sources.raw_question: Should the Son be worshipped and glorified together with the Father in the doxology?

question: Can two distinct persons rightly be called "one" without being the same person, as with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Skilfully Replies to a Passage Which the Heretics Employed in Defence of Their Own Opinion.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says that he who plants and he who waters are one, though Paul and Apollos are clearly different persons with different offices. Persons divided by personhood can be one through having the same mind, judgment, and faith, and so the Father and Son are one in agreement while remaining two persons.
sources.quote: For when two persons have one judgment, one truth, one faith, one and the same religion, one fear of God also, they are one even although they are two persons: they are the same, in that they have the same mind.
sources.raw_question: Can two distinct persons rightly be called "one" without being the same person, as with the Father and the Son?

question: Does confessing that the Son is born from the Father's own nature imply that the pre-existing God (the Father) ceased to be himself and was then born as the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The abiding God was not born; rather, God was born from the abiding God. The Son's birth is itself evidence that its Author goes on existing. So the Son, though he is God, is not the same as the pre-existing God, and the Arian charge that orthodoxy makes the Father turn into the Son is a senseless caricature.
sources.quote: The abiding God was not born, but God was born from the abiding God; the nature bestowed in that birth was the very nature of the Begetter.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing that the Son is born from the Father's own nature imply that the pre-existing God (the Father) ceased to be himself and was then born as the Son?

question: Is the Son God by nature, or can he be called God without being God by nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next skilfully confutes the partial, empty and blasphemous statement of Eunomius on the subject of the absolutely existent.
sources.answer: The Son is God by nature. Whoever is not God by nature is not God at all, and Paul says those who serve beings that are by nature no gods do not serve God. Christians serve 'the living and true God', and the one they serve is Jesus Christ, whom Paul gladly calls his master and to whom every knee bows. So Christ must be the living and true God by nature.
sources.quote: We then, who no longer serve them which by nature are no Gods, have come to the knowledge of Him Who by nature is God, to Whom every knee boweth
sources.raw_question: Is the Son God by nature, or can he be called God without being God by nature?

question: Are the Word, the Only-begotten, the Life, the Light, the Saviour, the Christ and the Son of God in John's Gospel one and the same person, or distinct beings?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter IX.—Refutation of the impious interpretations of these heretics.
sources.answer: They are one and the same. John, proclaiming one God Almighty and one Jesus Christ the Only-begotten through whom all things were made, declares that this same one is the Son of God, Former of all things, true Light, Creator, and he who came to his own and became flesh. The heretics wrongly multiply another Monogenes, another Logos, another Saviour and another Christ.
sources.quote: since Logos, and Monogenes, and Zoe, and Phōs, and Soter, and Christus, and the Son of God, and He who became incarnate for us, have been proved to be one and the same
sources.raw_question: Are the Word, the Only-begotten, the Life, the Light, the Saviour, the Christ and the Son of God in John's Gospel one and the same person, or distinct beings?

question: In what sense is the Son the image of the Father, and does the Father act through Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: The Son is the living copy of the living nature, the impression of the divine seal, and is undistinguished from God in power and kind. His works, words and form are no other than the Father's. Because the image by nature possesses its author's nature, the Father works, speaks and appears through His natural image.
sources.quote: since the image by nature possesses the nature of its author, the Author also has worked and spoken and appeared through His natural image
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Son the image of the Father, and does the Father act through Him?

question: When Christ prays to be glorified, does this show that His divine nature lacked glory?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The glorifying is not of His divine nature but of the lower nature He assumed. He asks for the glory He had with God before the world was made.
sources.quote: Nor, when He asks that He may be glorified, is it in any way a glorifying of His divine nature, but of the lower nature He assumed
sources.raw_question: When Christ prays to be glorified, does this show that His divine nature lacked glory?

question: Does the analogy of the human word and wisdom show that the Son, called the Word and Wisdom of God, is a mere activity or property of the Father rather than a distinct begotten Person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Our word, wisdom and power are products of our own free inward activity. God's Word, Wisdom and Power is the absolute generation of perfect God. The names of the Father's eternal properties show the Son to be born of Him and inseparable from Him.
sources.quote: For although we have a word and wisdom and power of our own, the product of our free inward activity, yet Thine is the absolute generation of perfect God, Who is Thy Word and Wisdom and Power
sources.raw_question: Does the analogy of the human word and wisdom show that the Son, called the Word and Wisdom of God, is a mere activity or property of the Father rather than a distinct begotten Person?

question: Do the mutual acts of knowing and loving among the Father, Son, and Spirit show that they are really distinct?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Their relational distinction is the foundation of distinct actings, some of which have one person as the object of another's act. Those who know, love, and delight in each other must be distinct, and Scripture presents them to faith that way.
sources.quote: They which thus know each other, love each other, delight in each other, must needs be distinct; and so are they represented unto our faith.
sources.raw_question: Do the mutual acts of knowing and loving among the Father, Son, and Spirit show that they are really distinct?

question: Can someone who denies the Son still truly have the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. The Son is the Wisdom springing from the Fountain of Wisdom, the radiance that must be contemplated together with its light. So those who reject the Son, as the Jews did in saying 'We have no king but Caesar', have not the Father either.
sources.quote: Whence the Jews, as denying the Son as well as they, have not the Father either; for, as having left the ‘Fountain of Wisdom,’ as Baruch reproaches them, they put from them the Wisdom springing from it
sources.raw_question: Can someone who denies the Son still truly have the Father?

question: Does the Son's being caused by the Father mean that he came into existence after the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > A passing repetition of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. He is like the sun's ray, whose cause is in the sun but whose existence is simultaneous with it, not a later addition. Better still, he is like another sun shining forth from the Ungenerate sun at the same moment we conceive of the first. He is equal to it in beauty, power, lustre and every other respect.
sources.quote: like the ray co-existent with the sun, whose cause indeed is in the sun, but whose existence is synchronous with the sun, not being a later addition, but appearing at the first sight of the sun itself
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being caused by the Father mean that he came into existence after the Father?

question: Since Scripture says "God is love," must love be attributed either to the Holy Spirit properly or else to the Father, the Son or the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > In What Way We Must Inquire Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture's authority that "God is love" cannot be resisted, so love belongs to God. The question under inquiry is whether the Holy Spirit is properly that most excellent love. If he is not, then love is to be attributed to the Father, the Son, or the Trinity itself.
sources.quote: our wish is to see whether the Holy Spirit is properly that love which is most excellent which if He is not, either the Father is love, or the Son, or the Trinity itself
sources.raw_question: Since Scripture says "God is love," must love be attributed either to the Holy Spirit properly or else to the Father, the Son or the Trinity?

question: Should the name "Son" applied to Christ be interpreted metaphorically, like the names "Stone," "Shepherd," "Light," or "Vine"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Then he ends the book with an exposition of the Divine and Human names of the Only-Begotten, and a discussion of the terms “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. The title "Son" is not to be interpreted in the same manner as the other names. Names like vine, shepherd, and physician arise from Christ's providential dealings with creatures, whereas "Son" belongs to a class of names that express his relation to the Father. Its natural sense, being of the same essence as the one who begat him, is already the loftiest sense available, so there is nothing higher to transfer it to.
sources.quote: our argument has sufficiently shown that it is not proper to interpret the title of “Son” in like manner with the other names
sources.raw_question: Should the name "Son" applied to Christ be interpreted metaphorically, like the names "Stone," "Shepherd," "Light," or "Vine"?

question: If the name "Son" were given a more exalted, non-literal sense, could any meaning be higher than being of the Father's own nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Then he ends the book with an exposition of the Divine and Human names of the Only-Begotten, and a discussion of the terms “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. Divine names drawn from ordinary life are always to be raised to a loftier sense, never a lower one. Yet nothing is more exalted than the nature of the Father, since the divine majesty transcends all height. To reject the natural relation to the Father therefore lowers the meaning of "Son" instead of raising it. The proper and highest sense is that the Son is of the same essence as the one who begat him.
sources.quote: let them tell us whether they know, in their secret wisdom, anything more exalted than the nature of the Father, that, in raising the Only-begotten God to this level, they should lift Him also above His relation to the Father
sources.raw_question: If the name "Son" were given a more exalted, non-literal sense, could any meaning be higher than being of the Father's own nature?

question: Is the Holy Spirit to be invoked and worshipped in prayer as the Father and the Son are?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
