sources.answer: Yes. Because the Holy Ghost is God, he is no less to be invoked, prayed to and called on than the Father and the Son. Owen says he has proved this elsewhere.
sources.quote: Now the Holy Ghost, being God, is no less to be invocated, prayed to, and called on, than the Father and Son; as elsewhere I have proved.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit to be invoked and worshipped in prayer as the Father and the Son are?

question: Is the Creator of the world the one supreme God, or is he the product of a defect beneath some higher God or Pleroma, as the Valentinian Gnostics teach?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Preface.
sources.answer: The Creator is the one God, not the fruit of any defect, and there is nothing above or after Him. God must contain all things in His immensity and be contained by no one. If anything existed beyond Him, He would lack it and so would not be the Pleroma, the Fulness of all. He would then have a beginning, middle and end relative to what lies outside Him, which is absurd.
sources.quote: I proved also that there is one God, the Creator, and that He is not the fruit of any defect, nor is there anything either above Him, or after Him.
sources.raised_by_detail: Valentinians and Gnostics descended from Simon Magus
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of the world the one supreme God, or is he the product of a defect beneath some higher God or Pleroma, as the Valentinian Gnostics teach?

question: What does it mean for the Son to be sent, as distinct from being born?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: For the Son, to be born means to be from the Father. To be sent means to be known to be from the Father. The mission is therefore the temporal manifestation of His eternal origin, and it implies no inequality, because sender and sent are one.
sources.quote: For as to be born, in respect to the Son, means to be from the Father; so to be sent, in respect to the Son, means to be known to be from the Father.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean for the Son to be sent, as distinct from being born?

question: Is the Son as incomprehensible as the Father, and does he know the Father as the Father knows him?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. God cannot be found out by searching, and his ways are "past finding out" (anexichniastoi). In the same way no one knows the Son but the Father, and Christ's riches are called by the same word, "unsearchable." The Son also knows the Father just as the Father knows him. This mutual and exclusive knowledge shows the Son's divine, infinite nature.
sources.quote: No man knoweth the Son but the Father. – Matt. 11:27. – Even so know I the Father. – John 10:15. The unsearchable (ανεξιχνίαστον) riches of Christ.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son as incomprehensible as the Father, and does he know the Father as the Father knows him?

question: Does the designation "Spirit of God" imply that the Holy Spirit is subordinate to or derived from God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. In the Old Testament "Spirit of God" or "Spirit of Jehovah" is the executive name of God, designating God from the point of view of his activity. It therefore imports identity with God, and there is no reason to think the term changed its essential meaning in the New Testament.
sources.quote: is just the executive name of God — the designation of God from the point of view of His activity – and imports accordingly identity with God
sources.raw_question: Does the designation "Spirit of God" imply that the Holy Spirit is subordinate to or derived from God?

question: Does John 5:18 show that Jesus' claim to be God's Son was a claim to equality with God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. The point lies in the word "own." Jesus called God his own Father in the real sense, not figuratively as when Israel was called God's son, and this was rightly understood as claiming to be all that God is. To be God's own Son is to be exactly like God, that is, "equal with God."
sources.quote: To be the Son of God in any sense was to be like God in that sense; to be God’s own Son was to be exactly like God, to be “equal with God.”
sources.raw_question: Does John 5:18 show that Jesus' claim to be God's Son was a claim to equality with God?

question: Do doxologies that join the Holy Spirit to the Father and Son with "with" and those that use "and" express different doctrines?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: No. Some of the ancient Fathers joined the Spirit in the doxology by the preposition "with" and others by the conjunction "and." Neither group was ever thought to diverge from true religion. Both forms rank the Spirit together with the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: Of these some coupled the word in the doxology by the preposition, others by the conjunction, but were in no case supposed to be acting divergently,—at least so far as the right sense of true religion is concerned.
sources.raw_question: Do doxologies that join the Holy Spirit to the Father and Son with "with" and those that use "and" express different doctrines?

question: Does confessing three hypostases in God divide the Godhead, as the Sabellians object?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: No. Following Dionysius of Alexandria, Basil holds that the hypostases are three whether the Sabellians like it or not. Denying the three would destroy the divine Trinity altogether. The Trinity is "most divine" after the Unity, so the three hypostases do not undo God's oneness.
sources.quote: If by the hypostases being three they say that they are divided, there are three, though they like it not. Else let them destroy the divine Trinity altogether.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing three hypostases in God divide the Godhead, as the Sabellians object?

question: Did the Son's taking on human weaknesses in the incarnation make his divine nature weak or changeable?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. God, born man, took on the weaknesses of humanity without reducing his unchangeable nature to a weak one, for he assumed flesh within that unchangeable nature. He who was God became man, but as man he never ceased to be God. So he uses human language and human ways without any loss to his divinity.
sources.quote: He, Who was God is man, but, being man, has not ceased to remain God.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son's taking on human weaknesses in the incarnation make his divine nature weak or changeable?

question: Is it unworthy of God to adapt His speech to human languages and capacities?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. It fits God's love for man to adapt speech to the hearers' capacity for their profit. So the divine power divided itself into many tongues at Pentecost, and Paul suited his words to his hearers. Such adaptation only makes sense, however, when there are hearers to benefit.
sources.quote: For that His speech should have some adaptation to the capacity of the hearers, with a view to their profit, no one would conceive to be unworthy of God’s love to man
sources.raw_question: Is it unworthy of God to adapt His speech to human languages and capacities?

question: Does the mutual knowledge between Father and Son, and the delivering of all things to the Son, show that they share equal power and nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. All things are delivered to the Son without exception, and only the Father knows the Son and only the Son knows the Father. Equal might and an equal mutual knowledge hidden from us show that they are truly what their names declare: wielders of the same omnipotence, shrouded in the same impenetrable mystery.
sources.quote: If They possess an equal might; if They share an equal mutual knowledge, hidden from us; if these names of Father and Son express the relation between Them, then, I demand, are They not in truth what They are in name, wielders of the same omnipotence
sources.raw_question: Does the mutual knowledge between Father and Son, and the delivering of all things to the Son, show that they share equal power and nature?

question: Is 'admitting generation into its own essence' something peculiar to the Only-begotten that sets him apart from creatures?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > Then, distinguishing between essence and generation, he declares the empty and frivolous language of Eunomius to be like a rattle. He proceeds to show that the language used by the great Basil on the subject of the generation of the Only-begotten has been grievously slandered by Eunomius, and so ends the book.
sources.answer: No. In Eunomius' sense it is not peculiar to the Son at all. Heaven, earth, sea and even the humble-bee and the gnat exist by being made, and so they admit generation into themselves. Eunomius' argument therefore puts the Only-begotten on the same level as the smallest creatures. Any proof he offers for the Son's alienation from the Father would hold equally for every individual creature.
sources.quote: It is therefore acknowledged by his own writings, that by them the essence of the Only-begotten is placed on the same level with the smallest parts of the creation
sources.raw_question: Is 'admitting generation into its own essence' something peculiar to the Only-begotten that sets him apart from creatures?

question: Does the claim that the Son did not exist before His own generation establish anything distinctive about the Son, or does it reduce Him to the level of creatures?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > After this, fearing to extend his reply to great length, he passes by most of his adversary's statements as already refuted. But the remainder, for the sake of those who deem them of much force, he briefly summarizes, and refutes the blasphemy of Eunomius, who says of the Lord also that He is what animals and plants in all creation are, non-existent before their own generation; and so with the production of frogs; alas for the blasphemy!
sources.answer: It reduces Him to the level of the lowest creatures. Gregory argues that not existing before one's own formation is common to every part of creation: frogs, worms, beetles and blades of grass. Eunomius, quoting no Scripture but relying on his own dialectic, labours to prove of the Only-begotten God what is already acknowledged of any chance creature, thereby placing Him on a level with the meanest created things. Eunomius also cannot show that the Son was ever separated from the Father in any way.
sources.quote: Not a frog, not a worm, not a beetle, not a blade of grass, nor any other of the most insignificant objects, existed before its own formation
sources.raw_question: Does the claim that the Son did not exist before His own generation establish anything distinctive about the Son, or does it reduce Him to the level of creatures?

question: Do philosophical objections that the Trinity involves contradictions (for example, that one individual divine substance cannot be wholly in several places or Persons) succeed against the doctrine, or do they prove too much?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: They prove too much. Waterland holds that this kind of reasoning about matters infinitely beyond human comprehension is fancy rather than reasoning. The same style of argument would equally overthrow God's omnipresence and other attributes, so it is as strong for atheism as against the Trinity, and it would reason God out of his attributes and the reasoner out of his faith.
sources.quote: You may go on, till you reason, in a manner, God out of his attributes, and yourself out of your faith; and not know at last where to stop. For, indeed, all arguments, of this kind, are as strong for atheism, as they are against a Trinity
sources.raw_question: Do philosophical objections that the Trinity involves contradictions (for example, that one individual divine substance cannot be wholly in several places or Persons) succeed against the doctrine, or do they prove too much?

question: In explaining a Christian doctrine such as the Trinity, should one rely chiefly on Scripture rather than on abstract reasoning about the nature of the thing?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Preface
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds up Bishop Bull's method as the right one. Bull examined Scripture more than the abstract nature and reason of the thing. He chose texts by their real sense, not their sound, and explained them naturally without straining. He also stated the full force of texts that seemed to tell against him and answered them solidly, without subtle glosses.
sources.quote: his way was to examine carefully into Scripture, more than into the nature and reason of the thing abstractedly considered.
sources.raw_question: In explaining a Christian doctrine such as the Trinity, should one rely chiefly on Scripture rather than on abstract reasoning about the nature of the thing?

question: Is God to blame for not making human beings gods (perfect) from the very beginning rather than first making them mere men?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVIII.—Why man was not made perfect from the beginning.
sources.answer: No. Those who blame God for this ascribe to Him the weakness of their own created nature and fail to distinguish the uncreated God from a creature of today. God chose the gradual course out of pure benevolence, so that no one could accuse Him of grudgingness: man must first be what he was created, a man subject to passions, and only afterwards be made a god.
sources.quote: For we cast blame upon Him, because we have not been made gods from the beginning, but at first merely men, then at length gods; although God has adopted this course out of His pure benevolence, that no one may impute to Him invidiousness or grudgingness.
sources.raw_question: Is God to blame for not making human beings gods (perfect) from the very beginning rather than first making them mere men?

question: Does the case of the ungenerated Adam and the generated Abel show that being generated or ungenerated changes a being's essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then shows, from the instance of Adam and Abel, and other examples, the absence of alienation of essence in the case of the “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. Adam existed without generation and Abel was generated, yet both bear the same essential name 'man'. Things whose essences differ cannot share the same essential name. So Adam and Abel have one essence and are distinguished only by individual attributes. Adam did not generate another essence; he generated another self.
sources.quote: For Adam and Abel are both one so far as the definition of their nature is concerned, but are distinguished one from the other without confusion by the individual attributes observed in each of them.
sources.raw_question: Does the case of the ungenerated Adam and the generated Abel show that being generated or ungenerated changes a being's essence?

question: Does confessing the Father and the Son as consubstantial (homoousios) commit one to believing in two independent, causeless first principles?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: No. The charge of two causeless beings would follow only if the Faith preached two natures alien to each other in being, as the Anomoean school does. Orthodox faith acknowledges one nature with differences of Person, the Father believed in and the Son glorified, so it cannot be represented as preaching two First Causes.
sources.quote: But if, as is the case, we acknowledge one nature with the differences of Person, if, while the Father is believed in, the Son also is glorified, how can such a Faith be misrepresented by our opponents as preaching Two First Causes?
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the Father and the Son as consubstantial (homoousios) commit one to believing in two independent, causeless first principles?

question: Was the world through which Christ accomplished salvation created by angels or by an ignorant demiurge rather than by God's own Word?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVIII.—God the Father and His Word have formed all created things (which They use) by Their own power and wisdom, not out of defect or ignorance. The Son of God, who received all power from the Father, would otherwise never have taken flesh upon Him.
sources.answer: No. The world is God's own creation, made by the Word according to the Father's will, not by angels, apostasy, defect, ignorance, Prunicus, or any maker ignorant of the Father. John's Gospel testifies that all things were made by the Word and that the world was made by Him and is His own.
sources.quote: this world belongs to Him, and was made by Him, according to the Father’s will, and not by angels; nor by apostasy, defect, and ignorance; nor by any power of Prunicus, whom certain of them also call “the Mother;”
sources.raw_question: Was the world through which Christ accomplished salvation created by angels or by an ignorant demiurge rather than by God's own Word?

question: Does the mutual indwelling of the Father and the Son mean that whatever bears the Son also bears the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVIII.—God the Father and His Word have formed all created things (which They use) by Their own power and wisdom, not out of defect or ignorance. The Son of God, who received all power from the Father, would otherwise never have taken flesh upon Him.
sources.answer: Yes. Because the Lord said 'I am in the Father, and the Father in Me,' anything that bore the Son would be bearing the Father and the Son together. This is why only God's own creation, sustained invisibly by the Father, could visibly bear His Word.
sources.quote: when the Lord declared, “For I am in the Father, and the Father in Me,”
sources.raw_question: Does the mutual indwelling of the Father and the Son mean that whatever bears the Son also bears the Father?

question: Does God's use of human speech in addressing people show that speech belongs to the divine nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. A man who talks with a deaf person by signs is not himself deaf. Likewise we direct animals by clucking and whistling, yet that is not our own language. In the same way God uses speech by way of accommodation to reach us, and we must not attribute speech to Him on that account.
sources.quote: just as we cannot call a man deaf who converses with a deaf man by means of signs,—his only way of hearing,—so we must not suppose speech in God because of His employing it by way of accommodation in addressing man
sources.raw_question: Does God's use of human speech in addressing people show that speech belongs to the divine nature?

question: Is it unfitting for God to use human language because human nature is prone to evil?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. For our sakes God did not refuse even to be made sin and a curse, and in His love He came to share not only our good but our evil. If He took part in our evil, there is no reason He should refuse to share in speech, the noblest of our gifts.
sources.quote: And if He was partaker in our evil, why should He refuse to be partaker in speech, the noblest of our gifts?
sources.raw_question: Is it unfitting for God to use human language because human nature is prone to evil?

question: Is the Father, as a distinct Person, to be regarded peculiarly as the fountain and spring of love toward believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. It is God's will that he be eyed as benign, loving and unchangeable, and that peculiarly as the Father, the great fountain of all gracious communications and fruits of love. This revelation of God as Father is what Christ came to declare.
sources.quote: that peculiarly as the Father, as the great fountain and spring of all gracious communications and fruits of love. This is that which Christ came to reveal, — God as a Father, John i. 18
sources.raw_question: Is the Father, as a distinct Person, to be regarded peculiarly as the fountain and spring of love toward believers?

question: Does the Eunomian teaching that the Son's essence is unlike the Father's lead to Manichaean dualism?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Proof that the Anomœan teaching tends to Manichæism.
sources.answer: Yes, and to something worse. Like Manes, they make a contrariety of Being between natures, so that opposite to the good Father stands a nature contrary to the good. But they go further, making the good God the very cause and maker of this opposite nature, so that evil derives from the good itself, which is more horrible than Manichaeism.
sources.quote: not only that the opposite to the good subsists, but that this contrary comes from the good itself. I declare this to be more horrible even than the irrationality of the Manichees.
sources.raw_question: Does the Eunomian teaching that the Son's essence is unlike the Father's lead to Manichaean dualism?

question: Does saying that something accrues to God, as distinct from His essence, make God composite, so that every divine name must signify His essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Gregory turns the dilemma back on Eunomius. If anything accruing to God makes Him composite, then Fatherhood too must belong to the essence. God would then be Father by nature, and the Son could not be excluded from this essential relationship. If instead Fatherhood accrues outside the substance without marring simplicity, then ungeneracy may likewise mean something outside the essence.
sources.quote: for it will not be possible, if God is essentially Father, to exclude the Son from a relationship to Him thus essential.
sources.raw_question: Does saying that something accrues to God, as distinct from His essence, make God composite, so that every divine name must signify His essence?

question: Is God the Father by nature, and if so, does the Son share in that essential relationship?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes, on Eunomius' own premise that nothing accrues to God without compositeness. Fatherhood would then belong to His essence just as imperishability and immortality do. Because God is essentially Father, the Son must be admitted to partake of that intimate nature.
sources.quote: he certainly cannot eject the Fatherhood either from the essence, but must confess that He is Father by His nature as much as He is imperishable and immortal
sources.raw_question: Is God the Father by nature, and if so, does the Son share in that essential relationship?

question: Is it compatible with the Son's being born that He always existed?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. Faith, argument and thought conclude that the Lord Jesus both was born and always existed. As it is the Father's property to exist without birth, so it is the Son's property to exist always through birth.
sources.quote: As it is a property of God the Father to exist without birth, so also it must belong to the Son to exist always through birth.
sources.raw_question: Is it compatible with the Son's being born that He always existed?

question: Does the Son share in the manner of existence of creatures, so that He too has a beginning?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. If the Son had communion with the creation in other respects, one might say He shares its manner of existence. But none of the names Scripture gives the Only-begotten belongs to creation: being in the beginning with God, being God, life, light, brightness of glory, express image, being in the Father. Therefore He has no communion with creation in the manner of His existence either.
sources.quote: But if the creation has no share in such things as are all those which we learn concerning the Son, we must surely of necessity say that in this matter also He has no communion with it.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son share in the manner of existence of creatures, so that He too has a beginning?

question: What is the true faith regarding the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit and their distinct roles?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: The true believer has full faith in one God Almighty, from whom are all things. He believes in the Son of God, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and who became man through the dispensations. He also holds firmly to the Spirit of God, who gives knowledge of the truth, set forth the dispensations of the Father and the Son, and dwells with every generation according to the Father's will.
sources.quote: he has a full faith in one God Almighty, of whom are all things; and in the Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, by whom are all things, and in the dispensations connected with Him
sources.raw_question: What is the true faith regarding the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit and their distinct roles?

question: Can the human mind fully understand the words and deeds of Christ?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. We know the Lord's deeds and words and are not ignorant of them, yet they cannot be comprehended. The facts are real, but the divine power behind them remains a mystery.
sources.quote: We know the deeds and words of our Lord, yet we know them not: we are not ignorant of them, yet they cannot be understood. The facts are real, but the power behind them is a mystery.
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind fully understand the words and deeds of Christ?

question: Does the Son's exercising the same providence over the universe as the Father show that the Son shares the Father's nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The observations made by watching Providence are sufficient to give us the knowledge of sameness of Being.
sources.answer: Yes. Will follows the bent of nature, so sameness of purpose shows communion of nature. If the Son were unlike the Father, he would not purpose the same good things and would be shut out from providence. Scripture says the Son does what he sees the Father doing, so the identity of their providential works proves a common nature.
sources.quote: But if, while the Father is provident for the Universe, the Son is equally provident for it (for ‘what He sees the Father doing that also the Son does’), this sameness of their purposes exhibits a communion of nature in those who thus purpose the same things.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's exercising the same providence over the universe as the Father show that the Son shares the Father's nature?

question: Can one uphold the unity of God while confessing a true God the Father and a lesser, unlike God the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. To link true and false, genuine and base, like and unlike under a pretended devotion to God's unity is incoherent. The Father is God and the Son is God, with one true Godhead, and no other God is likened to Him.
sources.quote: Why link together, in pretended devotion to the unity of God, true and false, base and genuine, unlike and unlike? The Father is God and the Son is God.
sources.raw_question: Can one uphold the unity of God while confessing a true God the Father and a lesser, unlike God the Son?

question: If the Son is a creature, does the incarnation remain a marvel?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: No. If the Son is created and man is also created, nothing wonderful happens, since created nature merely comes to be in itself. The participation of the created with the created is no 'change of the Right Hand.' The marvel of the incarnation depends on the uncreated Nature entering the passible creature.
sources.quote: For if, as their doctrine asserts, He is created, and man is created also, the wonder of the doctrine disappears, and there is nothing marvellous in what is alleged, since the created nature comes to be in itself
sources.raw_question: If the Son is a creature, does the incarnation remain a marvel?

question: Can the mind exist separately from its self-love and self-knowledge, as friends can be separated?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: No. The lover and love, or the knower and knowledge, cannot exist apart, unlike friends who may be separated or even cease to be friends. If the love by which the mind loves itself ceases, the mind at the same time ceases to love itself. The case is similar with knowledge. They are also more inseparable than a head and the thing that has it, which can be cut apart.
sources.quote: But if the love with which the mind loves itself ceases to be, then the mind also will at the same time cease to love.
sources.raw_question: Can the mind exist separately from its self-love and self-knowledge, as friends can be separated?

question: Does the doctrine that the Father is eminently styled the one God and that the Son is subordinate imply that the Son is not essentially God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. Waterland grants both that the Father is eminently called the one God and that the Son is subordinate, but denies the consequence Dr. Clarke draws from them. The Doctor spends his effort proving what nobody disputes, while the real point of difference is left unproved and rests only on an assumed philosophical principle.
sources.quote: He need not have told us so often that the Father is eminently styled the one God, or that the Son is subordinate. We allow all that: the consequence which he draws from it, and covertly insinuates to his reader, is the thing we doubt of.
sources.raw_question: Does the doctrine that the Father is eminently styled the one God and that the Son is subordinate imply that the Son is not essentially God?

question: What do the scriptural images of the Son as 'brightness of glory', 'savour of ointment', and 'breath of God' teach about the Son's generation, given that material efflux involves dispersion and loss?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory again discusses the generation of the Only-Begotten, and other different modes of generation, material and immaterial, and nobly demonstrates that the Son is the brightness of the Divine glory, and not a creature.
sources.answer: They teach only that the Son is of the Father and exists together with Him, with no interval between them. All material notions are excluded: breath does not imply dispersion into air, fragrance does not imply the ointment's quality passing away, and effulgence does not imply rays flowing off a body. As with creation and the term 'Son', the images admit no time, matter, place, or affection.
sources.quote: by such a mode of generation is indicated this alone, that the Son is of the Father and is conceived of along with Him, no interval intervening between the Father and Him Who is of the Father
sources.raw_question: What do the scriptural images of the Son as 'brightness of glory', 'savour of ointment', and 'breath of God' teach about the Son's generation, given that material efflux involves dispersion and loss?

question: Is there any God above or besides the Creator who made heaven and earth?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: No. Through David the Holy Spirit warns that some will despise the One who formed us, who is God alone. He means to say: besides or above Him there is no other God to whom we should rather stretch out our hands.
sources.quote: See that ye do not err; besides or above Him there is no other God, to whom ye should rather stretch out [your hands], thus rendering us pious and grateful towards Him who made, established, and [still] nourishes us.
sources.raw_question: Is there any God above or besides the Creator who made heaven and earth?

question: Is the doxology "to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit" found word for word in Scripture, so that the opponents can claim exclusive scriptural warrant for it?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That Scripture uses the words “in” or “by,” ἐν, cf. note on p. 3, in place of “with.” Wherein also it is proved that the word “and” has the same force as “with.”
sources.answer: No. The separate clauses can be found, but nowhere in this combination. If the opponents demand exact conformity to what is written, they must produce exact references. If they allow liturgical custom, they cannot deny the same privilege to the form "with the Spirit".
sources.quote: You may indeed find each of these clauses separately, but they will nowhere be able to show them to us arranged in this conjunction. If, then, they want exact conformity to what is written, let them give us exact references.
sources.raw_question: Is the doxology "to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit" found word for word in Scripture, so that the opponents can claim exclusive scriptural warrant for it?

question: Does Adam and Abel's sharing one human nature, despite their different modes of origin, show that the Father and Son can share one essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He thus shows the oneness of the Eternal Son with the Father the identity of essence and the community of nature (wherein is a natural inquiry into the production of wine), and that the terms “Son” and “product” in the naming of the Only-Begotten include a like idea of relationship.
sources.answer: Yes. Adam was not generated as Abel was, yet as regards the definition of essence they were the same, and Abel's generation produced no change in the essence. By analogy, the Son's generation does not make his nature diverse from the Father's.
sources.quote: he that was not generated after a like sort was yet, so far as concerns the definition of essence, the same with him that was generated, and Abel’s generation did not produce any change in the essence
sources.raw_question: Does Adam and Abel's sharing one human nature, despite their different modes of origin, show that the Father and Son can share one essence?

question: Does Jesus' description of the Holy Spirit as 'another Advocate' in John 14 show that the Spirit is a Person distinct from the Son?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. The Son makes request of the Father, and the Father in response gives an Advocate who is 'another' than the Son and is sent in the Son's name. This sharply distinguishes the Spirit from Our Lord as a distinct Person, so the interrelations of distinct Persons extend to the Spirit as well as to the Father and Son.
sources.quote: The Father, Son and Spirit are constantly distinguished from one another — the Son makes request of the Father, and the Father in response to this request gives an Advocate, “another” than the Son, who is sent in the Son’s name.
sources.raw_question: Does Jesus' description of the Holy Spirit as 'another Advocate' in John 14 show that the Spirit is a Person distinct from the Son?

question: Can the God who is in the Son be divided from the Son, so that the Father and the Son are classed as separate Gods each after his kind?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Isaiah declares a name and a nature inseparably joined, a union perfect in title and in fact. God is in God, and beside him there is no God. Heresy therefore cannot divide the indwelling God from the God in whom he dwells, nor make the Son a second God.
sources.quote: Let heresy, if it can, divide the God within from the God within Whom He is, and classify, Each after His kind, the members of that mystic union.
sources.raw_question: Can the God who is in the Son be divided from the Son, so that the Father and the Son are classed as separate Gods each after his kind?

question: Why does the Old Testament mainly speak of the Spirit being 'poured out' rather than being 'sent' by the Father and the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Because under the Old Testament the mystery of the Father and the Son, and the Spirit's commission and delegation from them, were not yet clearly revealed. So the Spirit's communication was chiefly described by the image of pouring out. This image is drawn from water and probably signifies chiefly efficacy and plenty.
sources.quote: And this was the chief expression of his communication under the Old Testament; the mystery of the Father and the Son, and the matter of commission and delegation being then not so clearly discovered.
sources.raw_question: Why does the Old Testament mainly speak of the Spirit being 'poured out' rather than being 'sent' by the Father and the Son?

question: By what acts of faith do believers receive the Holy Spirit as comforter?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: By three acts. First, faith looks on the Spirit as promised in the covenant and waits on that promise. Second, it asks for him in prayer in Christ's name. Third, it cherishes him by attending to his motions. Faith regards him as purchased by Christ and promised by the Father.
sources.quote: We do it by faith, looking on him as purchased by Jesus Christ, and promised of the Father; we seek him at the hands of God, and do receive him.
sources.raw_question: By what acts of faith do believers receive the Holy Spirit as comforter?

question: Does Christ's saying that goodness belongs to God alone imply that the title "good" belongs to the Father alone and not to the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > The eleventh book shows that the title of “Good” is due, not to the Father alone, as Eunomius, the imitator of Manichæus and Bardesanes, alleges, but to the Son also, Who formed man in goodness and loving-kindness, and reformed him by His Cross and Death.
sources.answer: No. Gregory argues that if Eunomius means only the empty name, he absurdly grants the Father a mere sound. If he means the reality of goodness, he is reviving the Manichaean heresy. Restricting goodness to the Father excludes the Only-begotten from good, which no Christian can accept.
sources.quote: He says that the Father alone is worthy of the title of “good,” that to Him alone such a name is due, on the plea that even the Son Himself agrees that goodness belongs to Him alone.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that goodness belongs to God alone imply that the title "good" belongs to the Father alone and not to the Son?

question: If goodness belongs to the Father alone, what follows for the moral character of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > The eleventh book shows that the title of “Good” is due, not to the Father alone, as Eunomius, the imitator of Manichæus and Bardesanes, alleges, but to the Son also, Who formed man in goodness and loving-kindness, and reformed him by His Cross and Death.
sources.answer: It follows that the Son would be the opposite of good, that is, evil. Goodness and badness destroy each other, so the absence of one is the presence of the other. Every act of will tends either toward good or against it, and only inanimate things stay neutral. So denying the Son goodness implicitly calls him evil, which is a Manichaean blasphemy.
sources.quote: For as health and disease, even so goodness and badness exist on terms of mutual destruction, so that the absence of the one is the presence of the other.
sources.raw_question: If goodness belongs to the Father alone, what follows for the moral character of the Son?

question: Why was Christ's bodily departure 'expedient' or advantageous for his disciples?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Christ's departure was for their profit, because only on that condition would the Comforter come and be sent to them. The presence of the Holy Ghost with believers as Comforter is better and more profitable than any bodily presence of Christ, now that Christ has fulfilled his one sacrifice for sin.
sources.quote: the presence of the Holy Ghost with believers as a comforter, sent by Christ for those ends and purposes for which he is promised, is better and more profitable for believers than any corporeal presence of Christ can be
sources.raw_question: Why was Christ's bodily departure 'expedient' or advantageous for his disciples?

question: Does Scripture teach that God is one, and can this also be known by reason?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that God's oneness can be firmly proven by the light of reason, but it is also revealed in Scripture as an object of faith. He cites Deut. 6:4 and Isa. 44:6, 8 as plain testimonies that God is one, and only one.
sources.quote: I know that this may be uncontrollably evinced by the light of reason itself, unto as good and quiet an assurance as the mind of man is capable of in any of its apprehensions whatever
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that God is one, and can this also be known by reason?

question: Can those who deny the Son's eternal pre-existence consistently confess that the Father is God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Owen argues that the Father is called Father only in relation to the Son. If the Son did not exist before his birth from the Virgin, there was no God the Father before that time. A God who is not eternally Father is not the true God whom Christians worship.
sources.quote: if this Son had no pre-existence in his divine nature before he was born of the Virgin, there was no God the Father seventeen hundred years ago, because there was no Son
sources.raw_question: Can those who deny the Son's eternal pre-existence consistently confess that the Father is God?

question: Did Jesus Christ pre-exist in the form of God before his incarnation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen argues that Christ is God as well as man, and existed in the form of God before becoming incarnate. The incarnation came about through Christ's own voluntary acts, and acting in that way requires that he already existed in another nature.
sources.quote: as God, he did pre-exist in the form of God before his incarnation, which was effected by voluntary actings of his own, — which could not be without a pre-existence in another nature
sources.raw_question: Did Jesus Christ pre-exist in the form of God before his incarnation?

question: Is Jesus Christ to be worshipped as God on account of his own divine excellencies?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that Scripture presents Christ as God, to be served, worshipped, believed in and obeyed as God. This rests on his own divine excellencies, and believing it is necessary as a matter of faith based on divine testimony.
sources.quote: he is proposed, declared, and revealed unto us in the Scripture to be God, that is to be served, worshipped, believed in, obeyed as God, upon the account of his own divine excellencies
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus Christ to be worshipped as God on account of his own divine excellencies?

question: Does Scripture's ascription of creation to the Son prove his true divinity, given that creatorship marks the one supreme God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: Yes. The Son was and is endowed with creative powers, as the texts plainly show and Catholic antiquity unanimously confirms. Since the title of Creator is the distinguishing character of the one supreme God throughout Scripture, the Son shares in what belongs to the one God.
sources.quote: That the Son was and is endowed with creative powers, is plain from these texts, and others which might be added ; and is confirmed by the unanimous suffrage of Catholic antiquity.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's ascription of creation to the Son prove his true divinity, given that creatorship marks the one supreme God?

question: Can one avoid the charge of holding two Gods by saying the Father is supreme and the Son is a subordinate God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. Since the Arian scheme expressly maintains that a subordinate being may be properly and truly God, calling the Son a subordinate but true God still yields two real and true Gods, one supreme and one inferior. To deny two Gods would require denying that any subordinate being is truly God, which overturns the very principle on which they assert the Son's divinity.
sources.quote: I do not charge you with asserting two supreme Gods; but I do charge you with holding two Gods, one supreme, another inferior ; two real and true Gods, according to the Scripture-notion of the word God, as explained by yourself.
sources.raw_question: Can one avoid the charge of holding two Gods by saying the Father is supreme and the Son is a subordinate God?

question: Is the Son, through whom all things were made, inferior in power to the Father, from whom all things are?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The Church recognizes beginningless majesty in the One from whom are all things. In the One through whom are all things she recognizes a might coequal with his Source. Both are jointly supreme in the work of creation and in rule over created things.
sources.quote: in the One through Whom are all things she recognises a might coequal with His Source; for Both are jointly supreme in the work of creation and in rule over created things
sources.raw_question: Is the Son, through whom all things were made, inferior in power to the Father, from whom all things are?

question: Does calling the Son homoousios with the Father deny the Son's birth, or imply that the Father's substance was diminished by begetting him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The Son abides forever in the substance in which he was begotten from the Father. The birth of the Son did not diminish anything of the substance in which the Father abides. The Fathers who used homoousios meant no such defects, and the term does not negate the nativity of the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: the Son abides ever in that substance wherein He was begotten from the Father, and that the birth of His Son has not diminished ought of that Substance wherein the Father was abiding
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son homoousios with the Father deny the Son's birth, or imply that the Father's substance was diminished by begetting him?

question: Is the Father's committing all judgment to the Son meant in the same sense as his giving the Son to have life in himself, that is, as a way of describing the Son's eternal begetting?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: No. If it were meant in that sense, Scripture would not say "The Father judgeth no man." Insofar as the Father has begotten the Son equal to himself, he judges with him. So the text refers to the form of the Son of man that will appear in the judgment, as with the exaltation in Philippians.
sources.quote: For in respect to this, that the Father hath begotten the Son equal to Himself, He judges with Him.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's committing all judgment to the Son meant in the same sense as his giving the Son to have life in himself, that is, as a way of describing the Son's eternal begetting?

question: In the trinity of the mind remembering, understanding, and loving itself, is memory prior in time to understanding and will, as it is when we recall external things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How a Trinity is Produced by the Mind Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself.
sources.answer: No. With external things, retaining them in memory comes before seeing them in recollection and before will joins the two. The mind, however, is not adventitious to itself and is not set up in its own memory after it comes to know itself. From the moment it began to be, it has never ceased to remember, understand, and love itself, so there is no temporal priority among the three.
sources.quote: from the time when it began to be, it has never ceased to remember, to understand, and to love itself, as we have already shown.
sources.raw_question: In the trinity of the mind remembering, understanding, and loving itself, is memory prior in time to understanding and will, as it is when we recall external things?

question: Is the Son 'after' the Father in time?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: No. The Son, as Maker of the ages, cannot hold a second place in time, since no interval intervenes in the natural conjunction of Father and Son. Father and Son are conceived together by their very relation, and temporal priority is measured by distance from the present, which cannot be applied to a life transcending all time and ages.
sources.quote: in time no one is so devoid of sense as to assert that the Maker of the ages holds a second place, when no interval intervenes in the natural conjunction of the Father with the Son.
sources.raised_by_detail: Pneumatomachi / opponents who say the Son is after the Father
sources.raw_question: Is the Son 'after' the Father in time?

question: Does the mutual relation of 'Father' and 'Son' imply that they must be conceived together rather than one after the other?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: Yes. Father and Son are mutually conceived of in accordance with the relationship subsisting between them, so it is impossible even by human analogy to think of the Son as later than the Father.
sources.quote: Father and Son are mutually conceived of in accordance with the relationship subsisting between them
sources.raw_question: Does the mutual relation of 'Father' and 'Son' imply that they must be conceived together rather than one after the other?

question: Should glory be given to the Father only 'through' the Son and not 'with' the Son, on the ground that the Son is subordinate?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: No. The opponents' claim that 'with him' expresses equality while 'through him' denotes subordination rests on the false premise that the Son is after the Father; since the Son is not after the Father in time, place or dignity, the doxology may rightly be completed to the Son together with the Father.
sources.quote: Hence it follows that glory should be ascribed to the Father “through him,” but not “with him;” inasmuch as “with him” expresses equality of dignity, while “through him” denotes subordination.
sources.raw_question: Should glory be given to the Father only 'through' the Son and not 'with' the Son, on the ground that the Son is subordinate?

question: Does "the Word was with God" imply that the Word is as infinite as God the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. The whole being of the Word is with the whole being of God, so the Word is as great as God. If God's infinity exceeds limit, the Word contemplated with Him is likewise not bounded by limits or measures. No part of the Father's Godhead is destitute of the Word.
sources.quote: “The Word was with God”—the whole being of the Word, assuredly, with the whole being of God. Therefore, as great as God is, so great, clearly, is the Word also that is with Him
sources.raw_question: Does "the Word was with God" imply that the Word is as infinite as God the Father?

question: Does the Son's being 'heir of all things' and receiving all things show that He is a creature or that He is the true Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: It shows He is the true Son. If all things are delivered to Him, He is other than all those things received. If He were one of all things, He could not be heir of all, but would receive only His share as the Father willed. Being heir of all, He alone is the Son, proper to the Father's essence.
sources.quote: For if He were one of all, then He were not ‘heir of all,’ but every one had received according as the Father willed and gave. But now, as receiving all things, He is other than them all, and alone proper to the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being 'heir of all things' and receiving all things show that He is a creature or that He is the true Son?

question: How does the analogy of light and its radiance explain the Son receiving all things from the Father without having once lacked them?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: If radiance said the light had given it all places to enlighten, it would not mean it once lacked this. It would mean that it is proper to the light and that all things of the light are its own. So, and much more, with the Son: He has all things always, yet from the Father.
sources.quote: yet, in saying this, it does not imply that it once had not, but it means, ‘I am proper to the light, and all things of the light are mine;’ so, and much more, must we understand in the instance of the Son.
sources.raw_question: How does the analogy of light and its radiance explain the Son receiving all things from the Father without having once lacked them?

question: Is the Son a creature, even if exalted above all other creatures as their Creator and Lord, as Arianism taught?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Warfield calls Arianism the Logos-Christology running to seed. Against it the church asserted its settled faith in a Triune God who is one in being, with three consubstantial Persons subsisting in that unity. This faith, which rests on the absolute Deity of Christ, was proclaimed at Nicaea.
sources.quote: the church was thus prepared to assert its settled faith in a Triune God, one in being, but in whose unity there subsisted three consubstantial Persons
sources.raw_question: Is the Son a creature, even if exalted above all other creatures as their Creator and Lord, as Arianism taught?

question: Is the Son self-existent (autotheos), God of himself, rather than deriving his deity from the Father?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Warfield approves Calvin's reassertion of the attribute of self-existence for the Son. Calvin made this point in the interests of the true Deity of Christ, which Warfield calls the constant motive of all Trinitarian thought. He counts it a chief contribution to the exact statement of the doctrine of the Triune God.
sources.quote: it fell to Calvin, in the interests of the true Deity of Christ – the constant motive of the whole body of Trinitarian thought – to reassert and make good the attribute of self-existence (autotheotos) for the Son
sources.raw_question: Is the Son self-existent (autotheos), God of himself, rather than deriving his deity from the Father?

question: Is there any interval separating the life of the Father from the life of the Son, such that God deferred becoming a Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > The ninth book declares that Eunomius' account of the Nature of God is, up to a certain point, well stated. Then in succession he mixes up with his own argument, on account of its affinity, the expression from Philo's writings, “God is before all other things, which are generated,” adding also the expression, “He has dominion over His own power.” Detesting the excessive absurdity, Gregory strikingly confutes it.
sources.answer: No. Nothing can be placed between the Father's life and the Son's life, since there is no time, space, or extension in the Divine Nature. When pressed on every side, Eunomius himself must admit that the interval does not exist at all. Gregory concludes that the Son is always contemplated in the Father.
sources.quote: When he is driven in all directions he is himself forced to admit that the interval does not exist at all.
sources.raw_question: Is there any interval separating the life of the Father from the life of the Son, such that God deferred becoming a Father?

question: Would worshipping the Son as a subordinate, non-supreme God be idolatry if the Son is not included in the one Supreme God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 1: Whether all other beings, besides the one Supreme God, be not excluded by the texts of Isaiah, (to which many more might be added ;) and consequently, whether C
sources.answer: Yes. The Isaiah texts and the first commandment direct all worship and trust to the one God alone, in opposition to every other person or thing. If the Son is excluded from that one God, he is at best a nominal God. Worship of him and reliance upon him would then be idolatry, just like worship of angels, men, or heathen gods.
sources.quote: all worship of him, and reliance upon him, will be idolatry, as much as the worship of angels, or men, or of the Gods of the Heathen would be.
sources.raw_question: Would worshipping the Son as a subordinate, non-supreme God be idolatry if the Son is not included in the one Supreme God?

question: In what sense is the Father said to be the 'God' of the Son, Jesus Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: It is a covenant expression. The Father became the Son's God by reason of the covenant of redemption the Son entered into with him. It does not describe the Son's relation to the Father apart from that undertaking.
sources.quote: Hence the Father became to be his God; which is a covenant expression
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Father said to be the 'God' of the Son, Jesus Christ?

question: Since God spoke the words 'Beside Me there is no God' through His Word, can those words be meant to deny the Word's deity?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eighthly, John xvii. 3. and the Like. Our Lord's divinity cannot interfere with His Father's prerogatives, as the One God, which were so earnestly upheld by the Son. 'One' is used in contrast to false gods and idols, not to the Son, through whom the Father spoke. Our Lord adds His Name to the Father's, as included in Him. The Father the First, not as if the Son were not First too, but as Origin.
sources.answer: No. Everything God says or does He says and does in the Word; the Word of the Lord came to the prophet. It would be absurd to think God traduces and denies His own Word through that very Word, so these sayings concern things foreign to Him and not from Him.
sources.quote: nor is there a thing which God says or does, but He says and does it in the Word. Not then with reference to Him is this said, O Christ’s enemies, but to things foreign to Him and not from Him.
sources.raw_question: Since God spoke the words 'Beside Me there is no God' through His Word, can those words be meant to deny the Word's deity?

question: Is the outer, bodily man an image of God in the same way the inner man (the mind) is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Trace of the Trinity Also In the Outer Man.
sources.answer: No. Augustine seeks only a trace of the Trinity in the outer man, not an image of God in the same manner. The apostle teaches that it is the inner man that is renewed in the knowledge of God after the image of Him who created him, while the outer man perishes.
sources.quote: Let us try, then, if we can, to discover in this outer man also, some trace, however slight, of the Trinity, not that itself also is in the same manner the image of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the outer, bodily man an image of God in the same way the inner man (the mind) is?

question: Why should one look for analogies of the Trinity in bodily sense perception if the true image of God lies in the mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Trace of the Trinity Also In the Outer Man.
sources.answer: Because mortal and fleshly human beings handle visible things more easily and familiarly than intelligible things. The mind, though spiritual, keeps falling back on bodies. So the argument must be suited to this weakness by drawing likenesses from outward bodily things, in order to point more readily to the inward spiritual reality. The trinity found there may be less express but easier to discern.
sources.quote: if we would endeavor at any time to distinguish more aptly, and intimate more readily, the inward spiritual thing, we must take examples of likenesses from outward things pertaining to the body
sources.raw_question: Why should one look for analogies of the Trinity in bodily sense perception if the true image of God lies in the mind?

question: If 'unoriginate' means 'not a work but existing always,' is the Son unoriginate as well as the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: Yes. In Asterius's sense, the Son must be called unoriginate just as the Father is. He is not among things originated nor a work, but has ever been with the Father.
sources.quote: then they must constantly be told that the Son as well as the Father must in this sense be called unoriginate. For He is neither in the number of things originated, nor a work, but has ever been with the Father
sources.raw_question: If 'unoriginate' means 'not a work but existing always,' is the Son unoriginate as well as the Father?

question: What did 'the name' of God mean to Jesus' Hebrew hearers, and why does it matter for understanding the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: To the Hebrew the name was not a mere external symbol but the adequate expression of the innermost being of its bearer, so that the Name of Jehovah was virtually equivalent to God Himself. Hence baptizing 'into the name of' the Father, Son and Spirit is language charged with high meaning: those baptized are placed under God's own Name as His possession.
sources.quote: For the Hebrew did not think of the name, as we are accustomed to do, as a mere external symbol; but rather as the adequate expression of the innermost being of its bearer.
sources.raw_question: What did 'the name' of God mean to Jesus' Hebrew hearers, and why does it matter for understanding the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19?

question: Are even the holy angels commanded to worship the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. Unfallen beings are bound to adore him because of the divine offices and perfections he holds. Scripture gives this command directly: "Let all the angels of God worship Him."
sources.quote: Thus far we might argue with unfallen beings, and thus might urge those holy intelligences who left not their first estate, to obey the Divine command, (Heb. 1:6) “Let all the angels of God worship Him.”
sources.raw_question: Are even the holy angels commanded to worship the Son?

question: Why does the Son reveal the Father from the beginning of history, and what is his role in revelation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Because the Son was with the Father from the beginning, he is the one who declares the Father. He showed prophetic visions, gifts, ministrations and the Father's glory in ordered succession at fitting times. In this way the Word became the dispenser of the Father's grace, revealing God to men and presenting man to God.
sources.quote: Therefore the Son of the Father declares [Him] from the beginning, inasmuch as He was with the Father from the beginning
sources.raw_question: Why does the Son reveal the Father from the beginning of history, and what is his role in revelation?

question: Does Christ's prayer 'glorify Thou Me with Thine own self, with the glory which I had with Thee before the world was' (John 17:5) show that the Son is inseparable from the nature of the only true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. The Father needed no glory, so the prayer means the Son asks to be glorified with the Father Himself, reinstated in the unity of nature He had by divine birth. Those who deny Christ remained in God's nature or think Him separable from the only true God cannot explain this prayer.
sources.quote: Does any one deny that Christ remained in the nature of God or believe Him separable and distinct from the only true God? Let him tell us what is the meaning of this prayer.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who deny Christ remained in the nature of God
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer 'glorify Thou Me with Thine own self, with the glory which I had with Thee before the world was' (John 17:5) show that the Son is inseparable from the nature of the only true God?

question: Does saying 'once the Son was not' imply that God was once without his Word and Wisdom?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Objection, that the Son's eternity makes Him coordinate with the Father, introduces the subject of His Divine Sonship, as a second proof of His eternity. The word Son is introduced in a secondary, but is to be understood in real sense. Since all things partake of the Father in partaking of the Son, He is the whole participation of the Father, that is, He is the Son by nature; for to be wholly participated is to beget.
sources.answer: Yes. Since 'Son' means what is generated from the Father, namely his Word, Wisdom and Radiance, to say the Son once was not is to say God was once without his proper Word and Wisdom, the Light without radiance, the Fountain barren and dry. Even assigning intervals before the Son without naming 'time' still implies times and imputes to God an absence of Reason.
sources.quote: they rob God of His Word, like plunderers, and openly predicate of Him that He was once without His proper Word and Wisdom, and that the Light was once without radiance, and the Fountain was once barren and dry
sources.raw_question: Does saying 'once the Son was not' imply that God was once without his Word and Wisdom?

question: Are "Generator," "Maker," and "Creator" three equivalent names for God's relation to the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: No. The three names express only two concepts, because making and creating are the same, while generating is distinct from both. No argument has been offered to show that making is the same as generation. So long as the ordinary meaning of the words holds, one nature cannot be divided between the conception of a product of making and that of a product of generation.
sources.quote: For to make is the same as to create, but generation is another thing distinct from those spoken of.
sources.raw_question: Are "Generator," "Maker," and "Creator" three equivalent names for God's relation to the Son?

question: Why did the Spirit of God descend on Christ at his baptism, and whose Spirit was it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IX.—One and the same God, the Creator of heaven and earth, is He whom the prophets foretold, and who was declared by the Gospel. Proof of this, at the outset, from St. Matthew’s Gospel.
sources.answer: It was the Spirit of the Father, the same God who had promised through the prophets that he would anoint him.
