It descended so that we might receive from the abundance of Christ's anointing and be saved. This ties the God of the prophets to the Father who anoints the Son in the Gospel.
sources.quote: Therefore did the Spirit of God descend upon Him, [the Spirit] of Him who had promised by the prophets that He would anoint Him, so that we, receiving from the abundance of His unction, might be saved.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Spirit of God descend on Christ at his baptism, and whose Spirit was it?

question: Is the work of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in the apostles one single operation?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XIII. Prophecy was not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Spirit; the authority and operation of the latter on the apostles is signified to be the same as Theirs; and so we are to understand that there is unity in the three points of authority, rule, and bounty; yet need no disadvantage be feared from that participation, since such does not arise in human friendship. Lastly, it is established that this is the inheritance of the apostolic faith from the fact that the apostles are described as having obeyed the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Galatians 2:8 says the same one worked in Peter and in Paul, so the Spirit who worked in Paul also worked in Peter. Peter testifies that God the Father worked in him, and Christ chose him. Denying that this is one operation would absurdly imply that Christ's operation alone was too weak to establish Peter and needed the others added to it.
sources.quote: The operation, then, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one, unless perchance you, who deny the oneness of the same operation upon the Apostle, think this
sources.raw_question: Is the work of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in the apostles one single operation?

question: Why did Eunomius deny that Christ had a human soul, and what does this have to do with the Son's deity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: Eunomius denied the soul so that Christ's lowlier sayings, uttered in His humanity, would have to be attributed to the Godhead itself. That would make the Son's divine nature appear inferior. Gregory replies that because the Lord assumed a full humanity with a soul, those humble statements belong to the manhood. Christ's Godhead remains immutably the same before, during and after the flesh.
sources.quote: Their object in such a malignant perversion of the true doctrine, is to show that the less exalted statements, which our Lord utters in His humanity, are to be thought to have issued from the Godhead Itself
sources.raw_question: Why did Eunomius deny that Christ had a human soul, and what does this have to do with the Son's deity?

question: Does the Son's being 'like as Son to Father' indicate kinship of nature with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: Yes. The phrase indicates kinship in nature, as Scripture shows in the case of Seth, who was in the likeness of Adam. Eunomius concedes the phrase but empties it by redefining the Son as the image of the Father's energy.
sources.quote: But although such a phrase indicates kinship in nature, as the inspired Scripture attests in the case of Seth and Adam
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being 'like as Son to Father' indicate kinship of nature with the Father?

question: Why does the New Testament allude to the Trinity rather than teach it formally and explicitly?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Because the Trinity had already been revealed in the actual events of redemption, so it was the common property of all Christians. The apostles therefore spoke out of a shared Trinitarian consciousness rather than instructing believers in something they already held. As a result, New Testament allusions show how the authoritative teachers conceived a Trinity that everyone already believed.
sources.quote: It is because the revelation, having been made in the actual occurrences of redemption, was already the common property of all Christian hearts.
sources.raw_question: Why does the New Testament allude to the Trinity rather than teach it formally and explicitly?

question: Was the One who revealed Himself to Moses as "the Existent" (I AM) the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: Yes. Since Moses begged not to be led by an angel and the One speaking consented to go with the people Himself, the Existent who spoke is the Son. To deny this is either to say the Only-begotten never appeared to Moses or to exclude the Son from Israel's deliverance, which amounts to adopting Jewish doctrine.
sources.quote: either that the Only-begotten God on no occasion appeared to Moses, or that the Son is Himself the “Existent,” from Whom the word came to His servant
sources.raw_question: Was the One who revealed Himself to Moses as "the Existent" (I AM) the Only-begotten Son?

question: Does the word 'God' name a single person or the one divine nature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIII. To those who object that Catholics, when they ascribe Godhead to the Holy Spirit, introduce three Gods, it is answered, that by the same argument they themselves bring in two Gods, unless they deny Godhead to the Son; after which the orthodox doctrine is set forth.
sources.answer: It names the one nature. Because there is one God, one Godhead and oneness of power are understood. So the Father, Son and Spirit can each be confessed as God without multiplying Gods. Taking 'God' as the name of one person is the objectors' error.
sources.quote: For according to our opinion, because there is one God, one Godhead and oneness of power is understood.
sources.raw_question: Does the word 'God' name a single person or the one divine nature?

question: Is it consistent to say that nothing exists between or before the Father and the Son, yet that the Son came into being when He was not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He further shows that the pretemporal generation of the Son is not the subject of influences drawn from ordinary and carnal generation, but is without beginning and without end, and not according to the fabrications constructed by Eunomius, in ignorance of His power, from the statements of Plato concerning the soul and from the sabbath rest of the Hebrews.
sources.answer: No. Gregory agrees nothing is intermediate between Father and Son, but Eunomius contradicts himself by affirming an immediate connection while denying its continuity. Since 'then' and 'when' and 'was not once' imply time, and time did not exist before the Son, the Son's existence must be eternal.
sources.quote: speaking of the immediate character of the connection while refusing to admit its continuity, and conceiving that nothing was before the Son and having some suspicion that the Son was while yet contending that He came into being when He was not
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to say that nothing exists between or before the Father and the Son, yet that the Son came into being when He was not?

question: If the Holy Spirit is included among "all things" because He is not expressly excepted in John 1:3, must the Son also be counted among creatures because of 1 Corinthians 8:6 and similar texts?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter II. The words, “All things were made by Him,” are not a proof that the Holy Spirit is included amongst all things, since He was not made. For otherwise it could be proved by other passages that the Son, and even the Father Himself, must be numbered amongst all things, which would be similar irreverence.
sources.answer: Yes, the opponents' reasoning would require it, which shows the reasoning is absurd. 1 Corinthians 8:6 says all things are of the Father, and Romans 11:36 says all things are of God, without excepting the Son. By the same logic one could not even separate the Father from all things, since all things are of the Father just as they are by the Son. Yet Paul goes on to say "one Lord Jesus Christ, by Whom are all things," which clearly excepts the Son as he excepted the Father. In the same way, failing to name an exception does not place the Spirit among creatures.
sources.quote: they who think that the Holy Spirit ought to be numbered amongst all things, because they read that all things were made by the Son, must needs also think that the Son is to be numbered amongst all things, because they read: “All things are of God.”
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit is included among "all things" because He is not expressly excepted in John 1:3, must the Son also be counted among creatures because of 1 Corinthians 8:6 and similar texts?

question: Is it reasonable to dispute technical terms like 'substance' and 'person' in Trinitarian doctrine before settling whether the Father, Son and Spirit are each God and God is one?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. One must first grant or deny the revealed thing itself, that God is one and that Father, Son and Spirit are each God. If it is granted, the manner of expressing it may be debated; if denied, disputing the manner is madness, since of that which is not there is neither manner, property, adjunct nor effect.
sources.quote: it is a plain madness to dispute of the manner of any thing, and the way of expressing it, whilst the thing itself is denied to have a being; for of that which is not, there is neither manner, property, adjunct, nor effect
sources.raw_question: Is it reasonable to dispute technical terms like 'substance' and 'person' in Trinitarian doctrine before settling whether the Father, Son and Spirit are each God and God is one?

question: Can there be degrees of 'less' perfection among the divine Persons, so that the Son is less good than the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. If a Person is perfect, no abatement can be conceived, and it is absurd to speak of less perfection; if his participation in good is imperfect, he would be an indigent being busy satisfying his own want. Then Providence, judgment, and the Dispensation of the Only-begotten would be fictions, since he would have to abandon care of the universe to look after his own good.
sources.quote: If it is in a state of perfection, no abatement of that can be conceived, and it is absurd to talk of less of perfection.
sources.raw_question: Can there be degrees of 'less' perfection among the divine Persons, so that the Son is less good than the Father?

question: Can Eunomius consistently hold both that God gives every thing a name suited to its nature and that the Son's lofty names do not show his real dignity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory says this either is nonsense or contradicts itself. If God fits names to their subjects, Eunomius cannot also argue that God gives lofty names to lowly things without their sharing that dignity. Nor can he argue that God gives humble names to lofty things. So his attempt to empty the Son's exalted titles of meaning collapses under his own theory of divine naming.
sources.quote: For if he now professes that God affixes names suitable to their subjects, why does he argue, as we have seen that God bestows lofty names on things without honour, not allowing them a share in the dignity which their names indicate
sources.raw_question: Can Eunomius consistently hold both that God gives every thing a name suited to its nature and that the Son's lofty names do not show his real dignity?

question: By what means can human beings investigate the substance of God, including the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Preface.
sources.answer: Through both Scripture and the created world. Augustine says he will search out the substance of God 'whether through His Scripture or through the creature.' Both are set before us for contemplation so that God, who inspired the one and created the other, may be sought and loved.
sources.quote: For both of these are set forth for our contemplation to this end, that He may Himself be sought, and Himself be loved, who inspired the one, and created the other.
sources.raw_question: By what means can human beings investigate the substance of God, including the Trinity?

question: Do the orthodox equivocate when they call the Son's generation 'generation', since it differs from human generation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. 'Generation' is a word with more than one sense, and the Church uses it in a proper sense that has prevailed for fifteen hundred years, following Tertullian's rule that every origin is a parent. It is not the same as human generation, but human generation is not the measure and standard of all generation. 'Eternal' is likewise meant in its strict and proper sense.
sources.quote: We use it in the sense which has prevailed in the Church fifteen hundred years; and in a proper sense, according to the . rule of Tertullian, Omnis origo parens est.
sources.raw_question: Do the orthodox equivocate when they call the Son's generation 'generation', since it differs from human generation?

question: Is the Son 'God in God' through a mingling or confusion of the Father and the Son, or through nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Through nature, without mingling or confusion. The Father is God in God because the Divinity that is the Father's own dwells in Him who is from the Father. That indwelling follows from the Son's true generation, not from any blending of the two.
sources.quote: I learnt that Thou art God in God, by no mingling or confusion but by Thy very nature, since the Divinity which is Thyself dwells in Him Who is from Thee.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son 'God in God' through a mingling or confusion of the Father and the Son, or through nature?

question: If the Father dwells in the Son, are the Father and the Son one and the same Person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The doctrine of the perfect birth shows that the Indwelt and the Indweller are not one Person. Yet the Father truly dwells in the Son who is from Him. So the unity of nature does not erase the distinction of Persons.
sources.quote: But the true doctrine of the perfect birth revealed that Thou, the Indwelt, and Thou, the Indweller, are not One Person, yet that Thou dost dwell in Him Who is from Thee.
sources.raw_question: If the Father dwells in the Son, are the Father and the Son one and the same Person?

question: Is the Son, as God's Wisdom, begotten from God and like Him, or something foreign to Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: He is begotten from God and like Him. The creation of the world shows that God is wise. His Wisdom, who is like Him, must therefore have been begotten from Himself. Nothing in Him who is God from God is anything other than the Father's own.
sources.quote: The creation of the world is sufficient evidence to me that Thou art wise; and I am sure that Thy Wisdom, Who is like Thee, must have been begotten from Thyself.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son, as God's Wisdom, begotten from God and like Him, or something foreign to Him?

question: Is the Son called God and Son only by adoption and favour, as the Arians claim, rather than by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Hilary says the true faith of the Evangelists and Apostles recognises Christ as the true Son of God by nature, not by adoption. The name of God belongs to Him by absolute right, not as a title shared with others. Every work and word of Christ goes beyond the power of those who merely bear the title of sons.
sources.quote: recognise Him Who is the true Son of God, not by adoption but by nature.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son called God and Son only by adoption and favour, as the Arians claim, rather than by nature?

question: Can there be any difference of being among the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit if all three are uncreated?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: No. In the pre-temporal world there is no difference on the score of being. It is not possible to see differences when comparing the uncreate with the uncreate, and the Holy Spirit too has been shown to be uncreate.
sources.quote: There are no intervals in that pre-temporal world: and difference on the score of being there is none. It is not even possible, comparing the uncreate with the uncreated, to see differences
sources.raw_question: Can there be any difference of being among the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit if all three are uncreated?

question: In what order do the saved ascend to God with respect to the Spirit, the Son and the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXVI.—Men shall be actually raised: the world shall not be annihilated; but there shall be various mansions for the saints, according to the rank allotted to each individual. All things shall be subject to God the Father, and so shall He be all in all.
sources.answer: They ascend through the Spirit to the Son, and through the Son to the Father. Irenaeus reports this as the teaching of the presbyters, the disciples of the apostles, about the gradation and arrangement of the saved.
sources.quote: also that they ascend through the Spirit to the Son, and through the Son to the Father, and that in due time the Son will yield up His work to the Father
sources.raw_question: In what order do the saved ascend to God with respect to the Spirit, the Son and the Father?

question: In what does the believer's communion with the person of Christ under the image of marriage consist?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: It consists in two things: a mutual resignation of Christ and the soul to one another, and the mutual conjugal affections that follow from it. Some elements are common to Christ and the saints and some are peculiar to each, as the nature of the relation requires. Christ makes himself over to the soul with all the love and care of a husband, and the soul gives itself wholly to Christ in loving obedience.
sources.quote: The whole may be reduced unto these two heads:— [1.] A mutual resignation of themselves one to the other; [2.] Mutual, consequential, conjugal affections.
sources.raw_question: In what does the believer's communion with the person of Christ under the image of marriage consist?

question: Is the Son from nothing, so that once he was not, as Arius claimed?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Marcellian illustration from 1 Cor. xii. 4, refuted.
sources.answer: No. Athanasius says Arius 'raves' in this, just as Sabellius does at the opposite extreme. The Son is truly from the Father and has always been Son and Word; he is not lately come to be.
sources.quote: Arius then raves in saying that the Son is from nothing, and that once He was not
sources.raw_question: Is the Son from nothing, so that once he was not, as Arius claimed?

question: Can a Son created out of nothing be a true image or likeness of the God who brought things into being from nothing?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: No. A thing made out of nothing cannot be like the One who made what was nothing into being. It falls short of Him by having once not existed and by belonging among originated things. To call the Son 'Image' merely as a name, without likeness of essence, makes Him no image or expression at all.
sources.quote: For what is the likeness of what is out of nothing to Him who brought what was nothing into being? or how can that which is not, be like Him that is, being short of Him in once not being
sources.raw_question: Can a Son created out of nothing be a true image or likeness of the God who brought things into being from nothing?

question: Why does the Son alone make the invisible Father known?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Only the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has seen God. He has declared Him, so all things learn through Him that there is one God the Father. The following context adds that the Son reveals the Father from the beginning because He was with the Father from the beginning.
sources.quote: for all things learn through His Word that there is one God the Father, who contains all things, and who grants existence to all
sources.raw_question: Why does the Son alone make the invisible Father known?

question: Is the Holy Spirit eternal, and how is the Spirit related in order to the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: The Spirit is eternal in the same way as the Son; the only difference lies in the place assigned in order. The Only-begotten is conceived as before the Spirit's subsistence only in the theoretical light of a cause, not in time. When the thought of cause is set aside, the Trinity shows no discord with itself.
sources.quote: so again the Holy Spirit is in touch with the Only-begotten, Who is conceived of as before the Spirit’s subsistence only in the theoretical light of a cause
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit eternal, and how is the Spirit related in order to the Son?

question: Is the Son called 'Word' only notionally, or is the Word called 'Son' only notionally, or are both titles true by nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Arians date the Son's beginning earlier than Marcellus, &c.
sources.answer: Both titles are true by nature, and to make either one merely notional is groundless. The Eusebians confess a Son but make 'Word' a mere name for him. The Marcellians confess the Word but make 'Son' a mere name. Both positions are equally without footing.
sources.quote: Eusebius and his fellows, confessing a Son, deny that He is the Word by nature, and would have the Son called Word notionally; and the others confessing Him to be Word, deny Him to be Son
sources.raised_by_detail: Eusebius and his fellows; followers of Marcellus
sources.raw_question: Is the Son called 'Word' only notionally, or is the Word called 'Son' only notionally, or are both titles true by nature?

question: Should the doxology to the Son use "through him" or "with him," and when is each phrase appropriate?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: Both phrases are appropriate, but they express different things. "Through him" fits his saving roles, especially as Door and Way, and expresses his grace toward us. "With him" expresses his own proper dignity: as God and Son he is glorified together with the Father, since every knee bows at his name to the glory of the Father.
sources.quote: Wherefore we use both terms, expressing by the one His own proper dignity, and by the other His grace to usward.
sources.raw_question: Should the doxology to the Son use "through him" or "with him," and when is each phrase appropriate?

question: When the Son became incarnate and emptied himself, did he empty himself of his Godhead?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. The Son emptied himself not of his Godhead, which is impossible, but of his glory, and took human nature into mysterious union with his divine nature so that God and man make one Christ. He is thus one with God by eternal essence and one with us by assumed humanity.
sources.quote: should empty himself, not of his Godhead, which were impossible, but of his glory, and take our human nature into mysterious union with his Divine nature, so that God and man make one Christ
sources.raw_question: When the Son became incarnate and emptied himself, did he empty himself of his Godhead?

question: Can the trinity in the image of God be investigated soundly by human effort alone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Image of God is to Be Sought in the Immortality of the Rational Soul. How a Trinity is Demonstrated in the Mind.
sources.answer: No. It must be sought with the aid of Him who made us after His own image. Otherwise we can neither investigate it soundly nor reach any result according to the wisdom that comes from Him.
sources.quote: Let us seek, then, in this image of God a certain trinity of a special kind, with the aid of Him who Himself made us after His own image. For no otherwise can we healthfully investigate this subject
sources.raw_question: Can the trinity in the image of God be investigated soundly by human effort alone?

question: Are analogies drawn from created things adequate descriptions of God's nature and the Son's birth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. There can be no true comparison between God and earthly things. Analogies are aids to the weakness of human understanding rather than descriptions of God. They suggest the meaning sought rather than exhausting it, so they should not be condemned for imperfection.
sources.quote: We must therefore regard any comparison as helpful to man rather than as descriptive of God, since it suggests, rather than exhausts, the sense we seek.
sources.raw_question: Are analogies drawn from created things adequate descriptions of God's nature and the Son's birth?

question: Does Deuteronomy 32, which says God both 'made' and 'begat' Israel, show that 'offspring' and 'work' mean the same thing, so that the Son can be called a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. Moses places 'bought' and 'made' first and 'begat' last so that the sentence carries its own interpretation: 'made' denotes what men are by nature, works and things made, while 'begat' denotes God's lovingkindness afterward calling them sons by grace. So the terms are not indifferent, and the passage gives no ground for calling the Son a work.
sources.quote: for in the word ‘made’ he accurately denotes what belongs to men by nature, to be works and things made; but in the word ‘begat’ he shews God’s lovingkindness exercised towards men after He had created them.
sources.raw_question: Does Deuteronomy 32, which says God both 'made' and 'begat' Israel, show that 'offspring' and 'work' mean the same thing, so that the Son can be called a creature?

question: Is the Son's essence controlled by or under the dominion of the Father, making Him a kind of slave?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Being subject and controlled is the very mark of a slave, and a slave cannot by nature be Lord. Scripture, however, declares Christ to be the one Lord. Christ Himself accepts the title Lord as true ('I am,' not 'I am called'), and we are commanded to honour Him as the Father is honoured. Eunomius' view has no support in Scripture.
sources.quote: For we recognize no other mark of a slave than to be subject and controlled. The slave is assuredly a slave, but the slave cannot by nature be Lord, even though the term be applied to Him by inexact use.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's essence controlled by or under the dominion of the Father, making Him a kind of slave?

question: Why is the mind's love of itself not plainly felt, even though it always exists?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Mind is an Image of the Trinity in Its Own Memory, and Understanding, and Will.
sources.answer: Because love is most noticeable when need reveals it. What the mind loves in this case is itself, and that is always at hand. So no sense of lack brings the love to awareness, even though the mind always loves itself.
sources.quote: love itself is not so plainly felt to exist when the sense of need does not disclose it, since what is loved is always at hand
sources.raw_question: Why is the mind's love of itself not plainly felt, even though it always exists?

question: Is the Son derived from the Father by partition, extension or procession, or in some other way?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: He is derived by none of these but by birth. He is born of the Father as Son of Father, ineffably and incomprehensibly, and retains the fulness of the Godhead from which and in which he was born. He is therefore true, infinite and perfect God, and if any of this were lacking there would not be the fulness that was pleased to dwell in him.
sources.quote: confess also the Son a Son by no partition or extension or procession, but born of Him, as Son of Father, ineffably and incomprehensibly, and retaining the fulness of that Godhead
sources.raw_question: Is the Son derived from the Father by partition, extension or procession, or in some other way?

question: Does the eternal, immediate conjunction of the Son with the Father mean the Father begot the Son without choice, by mere necessity of nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He then discusses the “willing” of the Father concerning the generation of the Son, and shows that the object of that good will is from eternity, which is the Son, existing in the Father, and being closely related to the process of willing, as the ray to the flame, or the act of seeing to the eye.
sources.answer: No. The immediate conjunction does not exclude the Father's willing. The good will that is always present in the divine nature is directed toward the Son and is not forced out by the inseparable union. So generation involves will without involving any delay.
sources.quote: Neither does this immediate conjunction exclude the “willing” of the Father, in the sense that He had a Son without choice, by some necessity of His Nature
sources.raw_question: Does the eternal, immediate conjunction of the Son with the Father mean the Father begot the Son without choice, by mere necessity of nature?

question: Does Christ's statement 'I am in the Father and the Father in Me' mean that the Father and the Son fill each other like empty vessels, so that each is incomplete without the other?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: No. The mutual indwelling of Father and Son is not a matter of one filling the emptiness of the other, as happens with bodies and vessels. To claim that would be irreligious, because each is complete and perfect in himself. The Father is full and perfect, and the Son is the Fulness of Godhead.
sources.quote: They are not therefore, as these suppose, discharged into Each Other, filling the One the Other, as in the case of empty vessels, so that the Son fills the emptiness of the Father and the Father that of the Son
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement 'I am in the Father and the Father in Me' mean that the Father and the Son fill each other like empty vessels, so that each is incomplete without the other?

question: If the Son is truly, properly, and by nature God, must he be the same God as the one supreme God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 24: Whether Gal. iv. 8. may not be enough to determine the dispute betwiat us; since it obliged the Doctor to confess, that Christ as by nature truly God, as truly
sources.answer: Yes. Since there is but one God, whoever is truly God must be the same with the only true God. Being properly God means his substance is properly divine, and being God by nature means he has the same nature as the one God. The Arian attempt to affirm these phrases while denying identity of nature only strains the words into a sense they cannot bear.
sources.quote: Then, say I, he must be the same with the one supreme God, because there is but one. If he is truly so, he is the same with the only true God; if properly so, his substance is properly divine; if by nature so, he has the same zature with the one God.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is truly, properly, and by nature God, must he be the same God as the one supreme God?

question: Does the wide acceptance of a doctrine about the Son of God, such as the claim that He is a creature, count as evidence that it is true?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Hilary rejects the idea that the number of people holding an opinion proves it correct. A deluded multitude merely assumes its size proves its views right, and so a falsehood that has won general credence is boldly claimed to be established truth.
sources.quote: It assumes that its size is evidence of the correctness of its opinions; and thus a falsehood which has found general credence is boldly asserted to have established its truth.
sources.raw_question: Does the wide acceptance of a doctrine about the Son of God, such as the claim that He is a creature, count as evidence that it is true?

question: Is the title 'Son' applied to Christ metaphorically, in the way that people become 'children of light' or 'children of God' by moral choice?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Thereafter he expounds the appellation of “Son,” and of “product of generation,” and very many varieties of “sons,” of God, of men, of rams, of perdition, of light, and of day.
sources.answer: No. Metaphorical sonship by choice belongs only to natures on the border between virtue and vice, which can move from one state to the other and change their names accordingly. God has no contraries in Him and does not change from an inferior state, so the Only-begotten did not gain the more honourable name by moral improvement. He has the name of what He is by nature.
sources.quote: But where contraries have no place, one could no longer say that the word “Son” is applied metaphorically, in like manner as in the case of those who by choice appropriate the title to themselves.
sources.raw_question: Is the title 'Son' applied to Christ metaphorically, in the way that people become 'children of light' or 'children of God' by moral choice?

question: Do the apparent difficulties in the incarnation of the Son of God amount to real contradictions?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. The incarnation has seeming, not real, repugnancies. Our ideas of it are general and confused rather than particular, so we believe it as far as those ideas reach.
sources.quote: There are some seeming, not real repugnancies; and the ideas we have of it are general and confuse, not particular nor special.
sources.raw_question: Do the apparent difficulties in the incarnation of the Son of God amount to real contradictions?

question: Does Matthew 11:27 ('No man knoweth the Father but the Son') mean that the true God was unknown to everyone before Christ's coming, so that the God of the prophets is not the Father of Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VI.—Explanation of the words of Christ, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” etc.; which words the heretics misinterpret. Proof that, by the Father revealing the Son, and by the Son being revealed, the Father was never unknown.
sources.answer: No. The Gnostics alter the text to the past tense ('No man knew') to make it teach that the true God was unknown before the advent, but the evangelists give it in the present. Christ spoke it to reveal himself as the Word who imparts knowledge of the Father and to rebuke the Jews who rejected the Word, not to deny that the prophets' God is his Father.
sources.quote: they explain it as if the true God were known to none prior to our Lord’s advent; and that God who was announced by the prophets, they allege not to be the Father of Christ.
sources.raw_question: Does Matthew 11:27 ('No man knoweth the Father but the Son') mean that the true God was unknown to everyone before Christ's coming, so that the God of the prophets is not the Father of Christ?

question: What is the relation between the Father and the Son in the work of revelation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VI.—Explanation of the words of Christ, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” etc.; which words the heretics misinterpret. Proof that, by the Father revealing the Son, and by the Son being revealed, the Father was never unknown.
sources.answer: The Son performs the Father's good pleasure: the Father sends and the Son is sent and comes. Knowledge of the Son comes through the Father's good pleasure, and knowledge of the Father through the Son's revealing; the Father reveals the Son so that through him the Father might be manifested to all.
sources.quote: But the Son performs the good pleasure of the Father; for the Father sends, and the Son is sent, and comes.
sources.raw_question: What is the relation between the Father and the Son in the work of revelation?

question: Does the Apostle Paul use the title 'first-born' of Christ in one single sense?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then again admirably discusses the term πρωτότοκος as it is four times employed by the Apostle.
sources.answer: No. Paul uses the name four times in different senses: 'first-born of all creation,' 'first-born among many brethren,' 'first-born from the dead,' and, without qualification, 'first-begotten' in Hebrews. Each passage must therefore be interpreted separately. One cannot argue from the general sense of 'first-born' (one of the same kind as those born after him) to a conclusion about the Son's essence.
sources.quote: Four times the name of “first-born” or “first-begotten” is used by the Apostle in all his writings: but he has made mention of the name in different senses and not in the same manner.
sources.raw_question: Does the Apostle Paul use the title 'first-born' of Christ in one single sense?

question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each distinctly appoint believers to obedience?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Our obedience rests on the sovereign will of God as Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. The Father ordains it (Ephesians 2:10). The Son ordains it as mediator (John 15:16). The Holy Ghost appoints believers to works of holiness and designs men for the work of preaching (Acts 13:2).
sources.quote: Our universal obedience and good works are indispensably necessary, from the sovereign appointment and will of God; Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each distinctly appoint believers to obedience?

question: Can Dr. Clarke avoid tritheism by saying the Persons are no more three Gods than each is 'the God and Father of all, who is above all', the Apostle's definition of the one supreme God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. The reply works only if no one can be God who is not the supreme God. Yet Clarke labours to show that the Son, though not supreme, is truly God. If he adopts the Apostle's definition instead, it means none but the Father is God, which strikes out the Son and Holy Ghost from the Trinity.
sources.quote: But this is not to the purpose; unless no one can be God, that is not the supreme God. If the Doctor says that, he contradicts himself strangely
sources.raw_question: Can Dr. Clarke avoid tritheism by saying the Persons are no more three Gods than each is 'the God and Father of all, who is above all', the Apostle's definition of the one supreme God?

question: If the Son were created, would he be a servant by nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says all things serve God, and the whole creation is in servitude. Being created is a mark proper to servitude. So a created Son would be a fellow-servant with all creatures, lowered into servitude by sharing in creation.
sources.quote: by the peculiar attributes of servitude is marked that which is by nature servile, and to be created is an attribute proper to servitude.
sources.raw_question: If the Son were created, would he be a servant by nature?

question: Is the divine operation of providence and superintendence divided among the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit so that each Person performs a separate act of his own?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. The power of superintendence is one, issuing from the Father as from a spring, brought into operation by the Son, and perfected by the power of the Spirit. No operation is performed by one Person apart from the others; the work is directed by the Trinity but not severed into three according to the number of Persons.
sources.quote: issuing from the Father as from a spring, brought into operation by the Son, and perfecting its grace by the power of the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Is the divine operation of providence and superintendence divided among the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit so that each Person performs a separate act of his own?

question: Is there any interval of time or delay in the movement of the divine will from the Father through the Son to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. Every good thing is brought to perfection in the power of the Spirit through the Only-begotten God without mark of time or distinction. There is no delay, either existing or conceivable, in the motion of the divine will from the Father, through the Son, to the Spirit.
sources.quote: since there is no delay, existent or conceived, in the motion of the Divine will from the Father, through the Son, to the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Is there any interval of time or delay in the movement of the divine will from the Father through the Son to the Holy Spirit?

question: Is there significance in the Son of God becoming man in the sixth age of the human race?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Ratio of the Single to the Double Comes from the Perfection of the Senary Number. The Perfection of The Senary Number is Commended in the Scriptures. The Year Abounds in The Senary Number.
sources.answer: Yes. Man was first made in the image of God on the sixth day of creation. Fittingly, the Son of God was made the Son of man in the sixth age to re-create us after that image. The five earlier ages run from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, and then through Matthew's three divisions. The Lord's nativity began the sixth age, which continues until the hidden end of time.
sources.quote: And the Son of God came and was made the Son of man, that He might re-create us after the image of God, in the sixth age of the human race.
sources.raw_question: Is there significance in the Son of God becoming man in the sixth age of the human race?

question: Does the revelation of the Holy Spirit as a distinct divine Person support the coequal deity of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. If Scripture reveals a third, distinct from the Father and the Son, who is personal, has divine attributes, is worshipped in parity with them, and is called Jehovah, this gives strong collateral evidence that plurality in unity is possible. It therefore also supports the possibility of the coequal Deity of the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: what strong collateral evidence of the possible plurality in unity, and therefore of the possible coequal Deity of the Father and of the Son, we shall obtain, if another be revealed in Scripture
sources.raw_question: Does the revelation of the Holy Spirit as a distinct divine Person support the coequal deity of the Father and the Son?

question: Is the evidence for the Holy Spirit's deity weaker because it is more inward or subjective than the evidence for the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. The evidence is more subjective, because the Spirit's peculiar office is to quicken and foster the hidden life within, but it is no less conclusive. In the analogy of the sun, its light and its heat, the orb and its radiance are seen while the warmth is only felt. Yet the warmth is manifested in the life it spreads through creation, and its existence is self-demonstrating.
sources.quote: the vital warmth is felt, not seen, and is only manifested in the life it transfuses through creation. The proof of its real existence is self-demonstrating.
sources.raw_question: Is the evidence for the Holy Spirit's deity weaker because it is more inward or subjective than the evidence for the Father and the Son?

question: Can the Father be called "the only true God" in contrast to the Son, as Eunomius's creed implies?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next skilfully confutes the partial, empty and blasphemous statement of Eunomius on the subject of the absolutely existent.
sources.answer: No. The contrast between "true God" and others is legitimate only against idols, which are called gods equivocally. Truth is opposed only to falsehood and God only to what is not God. Since the Son is the Truth, is God, and is in and one with the Father, there is no room for such a contrast between Father and Son.
sources.quote: But if the contrast is one with the Only-begotten God, let our sages learn that truth has its opposite only in falsehood, and God in one who is not God.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father be called "the only true God" in contrast to the Son, as Eunomius's creed implies?

question: Does Holy Scripture reveal or define the essence of the Divine nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Scripture's names for God teach things about Him (His power, immutability, being without cause or limit), but His essence, being beyond human intellect and speech, it leaves untouched. It forbids inquiry into things too deep for us and commands that the essence be revered in silence, so no doctrine of the Divine nature is found anywhere in Revelation.
sources.quote: But His very essence, as not to be conceived by the human intellect or expressed in words, this it has left untouched as a thing not to be made the subject of curious enquiry, ruling that it be revered in silence
sources.raw_question: Does Holy Scripture reveal or define the essence of the Divine nature?

question: Should believers recognise the Holy Spirit personally as the author of his particular works in them, so as to have distinct communion with him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit's peculiar effects include bringing Christ's promises to remembrance, glorifying Christ, shedding abroad God's love, witnessing, sealing, anointing, confirming adoption and assisting supplication. The wisdom of faith is to find and meet the Comforter in all these, neither losing their sweetness by being in the dark about their author nor failing to make him the returns he is owed.
sources.quote: Here is the wisdom of faith, — to find out and meet with the Comforter in all these things; not to lose their sweetness, by lying in the dark [as] to their author, nor coming short of the returns which are required of us.
sources.raw_question: Should believers recognise the Holy Spirit personally as the author of his particular works in them, so as to have distinct communion with him?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being beyond the grasp of the world's knowledge, like the Father and the Son, show that He shares their divine nature?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Establishment of the natural communion of the Spirit from His being, equally with the Father and the Son, unapproachable in thought.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ uses the same language of the Spirit as He does of the Father and of Himself: the world has not known the Father, the world will see the Son no more, and the world cannot receive the Spirit because it neither sees nor knows Him. Being unapproachable in thought in the same way as the Father and the Son shows the surpassing excellence of the Spirit's nature and His natural communion with them.
sources.quote: the surpassing excellence of the nature of the Spirit is to be learned not only from His having the same title as the Father and the Son, and sharing in their operations, but also from His being, like the Father and the Son, unapproachable in thought.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being beyond the grasp of the world's knowledge, like the Father and the Son, show that He shares their divine nature?

question: Does the Son possess the Father's attributes by grace or participation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: No. What is said of the Father is also said of the Son, not because it accrues to Him by grace or participation. It is said because the Son's very Being is the proper Offspring of the Father's Essence.
sources.quote: not as accruing to His Essence by grace or participation, but because the very Being of the Son is the proper Offspring of the Father’s Essence
sources.raw_question: Does the Son possess the Father's attributes by grace or participation?

question: Are the works done by the Son in the Incarnation the Father's works?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is the Form of the Father's Godhead, which wrought the works. So when God was in Christ reconciling the world, the Son's works were the Father's works.
sources.quote: what things the Son then wrought are the Father’s works, for the Son is the Form of that Godhead of the Father, which wrought the works
sources.raw_question: Are the works done by the Son in the Incarnation the Father's works?

question: Can there be a God superior to the Creator who made and contains the world, as some (e.g., Gnostic) teachers claim?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > God is Above All Things, Himself Containing All Things, Immense, Eternal, Transcending the Mind of Man; Inexplicable in Discourse, Loftier Than All Sublimity.
sources.answer: No. God contains all things in the bosom of perfect greatness and power, having nothing vacant beyond Himself, so there is no room left for any superior God. Since He contains all things, there could be nothing beyond Him.
sources.quote: And over all these things He Himself, containing all things, having nothing vacant beyond Himself, has left room for no superior God, such as some people conceive.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who conceive a superior God (Gnostics/Marcionites)
sources.raw_question: Can there be a God superior to the Creator who made and contains the world, as some (e.g., Gnostic) teachers claim?

question: Do the divine names given to the Son (Word, God, Life, Light, Truth, express Image, Brightness) show that He differs in nature from creation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > This third book shows a third fall of Eunomius, as refuting himself, and sometimes saying that the Son is to be called Only-begotten in virtue of natural generation, and that Holy Scripture proves this from the first; at other times, that by reason of His being created He should not be called a Son, but a “product,” or “creature.”
sources.answer: Yes. None of the things made is ever called by these names proper to Deity, whereas the Son is in the beginning, with God, and is God, Word, Life, Light, Image and Brightness. Since the names signify characteristics not shared between created and uncreated nature, He who is these things is by nature other than the creation.
sources.quote: then it is clear that He Who is these things is by nature something else besides the creation, which neither is nor is called any of these things.
sources.raw_question: Do the divine names given to the Son (Word, God, Life, Light, Truth, express Image, Brightness) show that He differs in nature from creation?

question: Can the Son rightly be given the name 'creature' when Scripture says the whole creation is in bondage?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > This third book shows a third fall of Eunomius, as refuting himself, and sometimes saying that the Son is to be called Only-begotten in virtue of natural generation, and that Holy Scripture proves this from the first; at other times, that by reason of His being created He should not be called a Son, but a “product,” or “creature.”
sources.answer: No. Paul teaches that all creation is in bondage, whereas the Only-begotten rules with His power for ever and has the pre-eminence in all things. To call Him a creature is to apply the name of servitude to the Lord and reduce Him to the servile nature.
sources.quote: who dares to apply the name of servitude to Him Who, as the Psalmist declares, “ruleth with His power for ever,” and to bring Him Who, as the Apostle says, “in all things hath the pre-eminence,” to a level with the servile nature
sources.raw_question: Can the Son rightly be given the name 'creature' when Scripture says the whole creation is in bondage?

question: Does homoousion mean that the Son came from a cutting off or partition of the Father's substance, making God divisible and changeable?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The Church recognises God as Spirit, impassible and indivisible. The Lord taught that a spirit has neither flesh nor bones, so God cannot suffer bodily division or loss. The Son's sharing the Father's substance therefore involves no severing or diminution of the Father.
sources.quote: In the Spirit she recognises God as Spirit, impassible and indivisible, for she has learnt from the Lord that Spirit has neither flesh nor bones
sources.raw_question: Does homoousion mean that the Son came from a cutting off or partition of the Father's substance, making God divisible and changeable?

question: Does Paul's statement that "he that planteth and he that watereth are one" (1 Corinthians 3:8) show a unity of mere will that could model the unity of Father and Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Hilary argues that the planter and the waterer are one because both were born again in one baptism and serve one regenerating baptism. They are one through the same thing, so they are one by nature and not only by will. They have been made the same thing and minister the same power.
sources.quote: So they who are one through the same thing are one also by nature, not only by will, inasmuch as they themselves have been made the same thing and are ministers of the same thing and the same power.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that "he that planteth and he that watereth are one" (1 Corinthians 3:8) show a unity of mere will that could model the unity of Father and Son?

question: Are the Word of God and the Son of God one and the same, given that Scripture says the world was made both by the Word and by the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: Yes. Since the Son is the true Light who was in the world and through whom the world was made, and the Evangelist says all things were made by the Word, one must either posit two worlds, one made by the Son and one by the Word, or admit that, the world and creation being one, Son and Word are one and the same Creator before all creation.
sources.quote: For either they will be compelled to speak of two worlds, that the one may have come into being by the Son and the other by the Word, or, if the world is one and the creation one, it follows that Son and Word are one and the same before all creation
sources.raised_by_detail: those who distinguish the Word from the Son (Marcellus/Photinus party)
sources.raw_question: Are the Word of God and the Son of God one and the same, given that Scripture says the world was made both by the Word and by the Son?

question: Because John wrote 'In the beginning was the Word' rather than 'In the beginning was the Son', should the attributes of the Word be denied to the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No. Since all things came to be by the Son as by the Word, it is identical to say 'In the beginning was the Son.' If the Word's attributes are denied to the Son, then by parity the Son's attributes, such as 'I and the Father are One', being in the Father's bosom, and revealing the Father, would have to be denied to the Word, which the objectors would not accept.
sources.quote: But if because John did not say, ‘In the beginning was the Son,’ they shall maintain that the attributes of the Word do not suit with the Son, it at once follows that the attributes of the Son do not suit with the Word.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who distinguish the Word from the Son (Marcellus/Photinus party)
sources.raw_question: Because John wrote 'In the beginning was the Word' rather than 'In the beginning was the Son', should the attributes of the Word be denied to the Son?

question: Is the man (the flesh from Mary) whom the Word assumed, rather than the Word, the Only-begotten Son of God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No. If so, the man born of Abraham's seed forty-two generations later would have existed before Abraham, the flesh from Mary would have made the world, and one who is himself part of the world would save the world, all of which are absurd. Scripture ascribes to the Son being one with the Father, being in His bosom, pre-existence, creating and saving the world, which cannot belong to a mere man.
sources.quote: And is it not absurd to say, as they do, that one who came of the seed of Abraham after two and forty generations, should exist before Abraham came to be?
sources.raised_by_detail: those who distinguish the Word from the Son (Marcellus/Photinus party)
sources.raw_question: Is the man (the flesh from Mary) whom the Word assumed, rather than the Word, the Only-begotten Son of God?

question: If Christ is God the Only-begotten, does it follow that God is not one?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary holds that the whole evidence of the Law and the Prophets shows it is impious to assert the unity of God in a way that excludes the Godhead of Christ. He calls it treason to argue that Christ's being God the Only-begotten destroys the oneness of God. The Scriptures teach neither two gods nor one isolated God.
sources.quote: the treason of alleging that if Christ be God the Only-begotten, then God is not one
sources.raised_by_detail: the heretics whose creed is examined in Book IV
sources.raw_question: If Christ is God the Only-begotten, does it follow that God is not one?

question: Does the fact that Jesus accepted worship, while apostles and angels refused it, show that he is God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. When the same homage, described by the same word, was offered to a man or angel, as by Cornelius to Peter or by John to his angelic guide, it was immediately rebuked and redirected to the Creator. Jesus was worshipped again and again and never refused it, and those who worshipped him sought divine aid from him; were he not God, he would have had to correct so dangerous an approach to idolatry.
sources.quote: the action was immediately rebuked, and the worship straightway diverted from the creature to the Creator.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Jesus accepted worship, while apostles and angels refused it, show that he is God?

question: Is the wisdom of God the same as God himself, and how does it relate to the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > What the Wisdom is of Which We are Here to Treat. Whence the Name of Philosopher Arose. What Has Been Already Said Concerning the Distinction of Knowledge and Wisdom.
sources.answer: Yes. The wisdom of God is without doubt God himself, since his only-begotten Son is called the wisdom of God. Augustine therefore distinguishes this divine Wisdom, which is God, from the wisdom of man that he now treats.
sources.quote: not the wisdom of God, which without doubt is God, for His only-begotten Son is called the wisdom of God
sources.raw_question: Is the wisdom of God the same as God himself, and how does it relate to the Son?

question: Is the Holy Spirit the author of all Scripture?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: Yes. Everything the divine Scripture says is an utterance of the Holy Spirit, which is why it is called "given by inspiration of God." Paul introduces Isaiah's words with "well did the Holy Spirit prophesy" and the Psalm with "as saith the Holy Spirit." Christ likewise says that David spoke "in the Spirit."
sources.quote: that all things the Divine Scripture says are utterances of the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit the author of all Scripture?

question: Is the Son called Word, Wisdom, and Power merely by derivation from created things (rational, wise, and powerful beings), rather than by his own nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. If he were Word only because of rational creatures, Wisdom only because of wise ones, and Son only because of those made sons, he would be none of these things in himself. He would then have only a semblance of being, decorated with names borrowed from us, and might even exist only in our notions. This empties God's Word into a mere name. The Son is Son because he is begotten of the Father and proper to his Essence.
sources.quote: And then after all what is He? for He is none of these Himself, if they are but His names: and He has but a semblance of being, and is decorated with these names from us.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son called Word, Wisdom, and Power merely by derivation from created things (rational, wise, and powerful beings), rather than by his own nature?

question: Is the Son who is the Offspring of the Father's essence the same as the Wisdom, Word, Brightness and Image of the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Objection, that the Son's eternity makes Him coordinate with the Father, introduces the subject of His Divine Sonship, as a second proof of His eternity. The word Son is introduced in a secondary, but is to be understood in real sense. Since all things partake of the Father in partaking of the Son, He is the whole participation of the Father, that is, He is the Son by nature; for to be wholly participated is to beget.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Offspring of the Father's essence is the Son, we must be certain that the same is the Wisdom and Word through whom the Father creates all things. He is also the Brightness by which He enlightens all things, and the Image in whom He is known. Hence He and the Father are one, and He is the Christ in whom all things are redeemed.
sources.quote: the same is the Wisdom and Word of the Father, in and through whom He creates and makes all things; and His Brightness too, in whom He enlightens all things
sources.raw_question: Is the Son who is the Offspring of the Father's essence the same as the Wisdom, Word, Brightness and Image of the Father?

question: Is it reasonable for finite human beings to reject the doctrine of the Trinity because the inner Being of God exceeds their comprehension?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. When a finite being seeks to know the Infinite, God's self-revelation always involves a greater self-concealment, so mystery is to be expected. Just as we rebuke the unlearned peasant who argues from ignorance against science, the angels, who see farther than we, would rebuke us for refusing to credit God's simple revelations about his own mysterious Being because of our preconceived notions.
sources.quote: surely those blessed spirits would rebuke us, if we, through preconceived notions of our own, refused to credit the simple revelations of God regarding his own mysterious Being.
sources.raw_question: Is it reasonable for finite human beings to reject the doctrine of the Trinity because the inner Being of God exceeds their comprehension?
