question: Are truth, holiness, and goodness ascribed equally to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father is true, holy, righteous, and good. The Son is the truth, the Holy One and the Just, and the good Shepherd. The Spirit is truth, the holy one, and good. Yet God only is holy, which points to one Lord in three.
sources.quote: I am ... the truth. – John 14:6. The holy One and the just (τον άγιον και τον δίκαιον). – Acts 3:14. The good Shepherd. – John 10:11.
sources.raw_question: Are truth, holiness, and goodness ascribed equally to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

question: When the Son is called 'like' the Father, could this be the deceptive kind of likeness in which things different in nature only appear similar, as a statue resembles a living creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. That kind of likeness rests on accidental resemblances such as form, colour, sound or taste between things that differ in nature, and it deceives the senses. Gregory holds that no one could find such deceptive similarity in him who is the Truth.
sources.quote: Nay, surely he cannot be so infatuated as to discover deceptive similarity in Him Who is the Truth.
sources.raw_question: When the Son is called 'like' the Father, could this be the deceptive kind of likeness in which things different in nature only appear similar, as a statue resembles a living creature?

question: Does 1 John 1:3's phrase "with the Father, and with his Son" distinguish the Father and the Son or unite them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: It does both. The particle "and" both distinguishes and unites the Father and the Son in the believer's fellowship. John 14:23 likewise shows Father and Son together making their abode with the soul.
sources.quote: The particle “and” is both distinguishing and uniting.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 John 1:3's phrase "with the Father, and with his Son" distinguish the Father and the Son or unite them?

question: Does the order of Proverbs 8 (the creation of "the beginning of the ways" followed by the founding of the ages) support reading the passage of Christ's Incarnation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: Yes. If "the beginning of the ways" had not been created among us, the foundation of the ages to come would not have been laid. Christ became "the Father of the age to come" only because, as Isaiah says, a Child was born to us. So first came the virgin birth and the Passion, and then the foundation of the Faith, which is Christ, was laid.
sources.quote: For if the “beginning of the ways” had not been created among us, the foundation of those ages for which we look would not have been laid; nor would the Lord have become for us “the Father of the age to come,” had not a Child been born to us
sources.raw_question: Does the order of Proverbs 8 (the creation of "the beginning of the ways" followed by the founding of the ages) support reading the passage of Christ's Incarnation?

question: In what sense can Wisdom, who is Christ, be said to be "begotten" as described in Proverbs 8?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: Wisdom is begotten in the faithful through faith. He is present in those who have received him but is not yet begotten in unbelievers. Faith, as Paul teaches, is the foundation by which wisdom is begotten in believers. Through this begetting the virtues and gifts of the Spirit, which Scripture figuratively calls "mountains" and "hills," are wrought in each soul.
sources.quote: Wisdom is begotten in the faithful, and the saying is found true. For He Who is in those who have received Him, is not yet begotten in the unbelieving.
sources.raw_question: In what sense can Wisdom, who is Christ, be said to be "begotten" as described in Proverbs 8?

question: How can Scripture say both that the Father made all things and that nothing came into being without the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: Both statements are true because the Son is the Power of the Father, and the operation of a power is referred to the one whose power it is. Therefore all the works of the Son are works of the Father, and the whole world and its parts are the Father's works because they are works of His Power.
sources.quote: for the operation of the Power bears relation to Him Whose Power It is. Thus, since the Son is the Power of the Father, all the works of the Son are works of the Father.
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture say both that the Father made all things and that nothing came into being without the Son?

question: Did the Nicene Fathers teach a middle position in which the Son is 'from the substance of the Father' without being of the same undivided substance with him?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 13: Whether there can be any middle between being made out of nothing, and out of something ; that is, between being out of nothing, and out of the Father's substan
sources.answer: No. The Nicene Fathers explain themselves in the Creed and its anathemas, declaring the Son to be no creature and not a different God from the Father, but of the same undivided substance with him, 'God of God, Light of Light,' consubstantial yet a distinct Person.
sources.quote: determining the Son to be no creature, nor a different God from the Father; but of the same undivided substance with him, “ God of God, Light of Light,” consubstantial with him, and a distinct Person from him.
sources.raw_question: Did the Nicene Fathers teach a middle position in which the Son is 'from the substance of the Father' without being of the same undivided substance with him?

question: Does making the Son a creature also lead to error about the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Yes. If the Giver of the Spirit is subjected to creation, change and non-existence, it is no wonder that the doctrine of the Spirit is also corrupted. Such teachers deny the Holy Ghost, blind to the facts that we possess Him and that Christ gave Him.
sources.quote: What wonder that their doctrine of the Holy Ghost should be different from ours, when they presume to subject the Giver of that Holy Ghost to creation, and change, and non-existence.
sources.raised_by_detail: certain teachers of our present day
sources.raw_question: Does making the Son a creature also lead to error about the Holy Spirit?

question: Why does every human birth imply that the one born previously did not exist?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Every human birth implies prior non-existence, both in respect of time and in respect of cause. Time already existed before the person was born, so there was a 'yesterday' when he was not. His existence also comes from parents who themselves once did not exist, not from any cause within himself. Even Adam was formed from earth made out of nothing, and after time had begun.
sources.quote: And these facts hold good of the origin of everything relating to man: all receive a beginning, previously to which they had not been: firstly, as we have explained, in respect of time, and then in respect of cause.
sources.raw_question: Why does every human birth imply that the one born previously did not exist?

question: Does Christ's prayer to be glorified, answered by the Father's voice from heaven, show the Son's dependence on the Father for glory?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Christ said the voice came not for his sake but for the bystanders. The Father's answer was granted to the ignorance of the hearers, not to a need of the Son for glory.
sources.quote: The answer of the Glorifier is granted not to the prayer for glory, but to the ignorance of the bystanders
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer to be glorified, answered by the Father's voice from heaven, show the Son's dependence on the Father for glory?

question: Does the Son's "coming out" from the Father mean that he is separated from the Father's nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The coming out is not a separation but a birth, and by that birth the nature of God the Father continues in the Son. For this reason Christ says that even when the disciples leave Him He is not alone, because the Father is with Him in power and unity of nature, abiding in Him, speaking in His words and working in His works.
sources.quote: He would shew that the “coming out” is not a separation from God the Father, but a birth, which by His being born continues in Him the nature of God the Father
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's "coming out" from the Father mean that he is separated from the Father's nature?

question: How does the combination of Scripture's teaching that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each God with its teaching that there is only one God establish the doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: The two truths, revealed with equal clearness, together require that the Three subsist in one infinite divine essence called Jehovah. Neither truth may be set aside for the other. Combined, they yield one God in three Persons, Father, Son and Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: The combination of these truths establishes the doctrine of the Holy Trinity, for “these Three must together subsist in one infinite Divine essence, called Jehovah or God;
sources.raw_question: How does the combination of Scripture's teaching that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each God with its teaching that there is only one God establish the doctrine of the Trinity?

question: Does calling Wisdom (the Son) an 'emanation issuing from the glory of the Almighty' imply that the Son is of a different substance from the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: No. What issues and that from which it issues are of one and the same substance. The Son does not issue as water from an opening in earth or stone, but as light issues from light.
sources.quote: For there, that which issues, and that from which it issues, is of one and the same substance. For it does not issue as water issues from an aperture of earth or of stone, but as light issues from light.
sources.raw_question: Does calling Wisdom (the Son) an 'emanation issuing from the glory of the Almighty' imply that the Son is of a different substance from the Father?

question: Why is 'brightness of light' a better expression than 'light of light' for the Son's relation to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: It guards against the idea that the light which issues is dimmer than its source. Hearing of brightness, one more easily believes the source shines by means of it than that it shines less. No heretic has claimed the begetting light is less, so Scripture addresses only the opposite error.
sources.quote: But it is preferable to say, “the brightness of light,” rather than” the light of light;” lest that which issues should be thought to be darker than that from which it issues.
sources.raw_question: Why is 'brightness of light' a better expression than 'light of light' for the Son's relation to the Father?

question: Is a supreme God together with a subordinate God really two Gods, or can one of them fail to be God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: They are two Gods, or else one of them is no God. Waterland does not deny that one ruler can be subordinate to another. He insists only that a great king and a little king make two kings. Likewise, a supreme and a subordinate God make two Gods, unless the subordinate one is not truly God.
sources.quote: But what I insist upon is this: that a great king and a little king make two kings; or else one of them is no king, contrary to the supposition.
sources.raw_question: Is a supreme God together with a subordinate God really two Gods, or can one of them fail to be God?

question: Does the rule of faith require belief in the Holy Spirit in addition to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Next Teaches Us that the Authority of the Faith Enjoins, After the Father and the Son, to Believe Also on the Holy Spirit, Whose Operations He Enumerates from Scripture.
sources.answer: Yes. The order of reason and the authority of the faith, both in the arrangement of the creed's words and in Scripture, direct us after the Father and the Son to believe also on the Holy Spirit. He was promised by the prophet Joel and given by Christ to the Church.
sources.quote: the order of reason, and the authority of the faith in the disposition of the words and in the Scriptures of the Lord, admonish us after these things to believe also on the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Does the rule of faith require belief in the Holy Spirit in addition to the Father and the Son?

question: What works does Scripture attribute to the Holy Spirit in the Church?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Next Teaches Us that the Authority of the Faith Enjoins, After the Father and the Son, to Believe Also on the Holy Spirit, Whose Operations He Enumerates from Scripture.
sources.answer: The Spirit strengthened the apostles to endure chains and tortures. He marked out the Gospel sacraments and enlightened them in divine things. He places prophets in the Church, instructs teachers, directs tongues, gives powers and healings, works wonders, grants discernment of spirits and powers of government, and orders all the charismata. In this way he perfects the Church everywhere.
sources.quote: This is He who places prophets in the Church, instructs teachers, directs tongues, gives powers and healings, does wonderful works, offers discrimination of spirits, affords powers of government
sources.raw_question: What works does Scripture attribute to the Holy Spirit in the Church?

question: If God created the Son for the purpose of creating us, does the Son exist for our sake rather than we for His?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: Yes, on the Arian premise, which shows its absurdity. The Son would be made as an instrument for our need, so that He would owe thanks to us and have no precedence over us with God; God would have counselled about us first and formed the Son only for our sake. Such thoughts are irreligious and insensate.
sources.quote: the Son appears rather to have been for us brought to be, than we for Him; for we were not created for Him, but He is made for us
sources.raw_question: If God created the Son for the purpose of creating us, does the Son exist for our sake rather than we for His?

question: Did God literally pronounce names for created things (such as seed, herb and tree) with audible words at creation, as Eunomius claims from Genesis?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Taking the Genesis account by the bare letter is Judaizing, since the Christian is a disciple of the Spirit, not the letter. If God literally uttered syllables, He would need vocal organs (windpipe, tongue, lips, teeth), which would make Him bodily. Names are instead the product of the rational faculty God implanted in man.
sources.quote: If, then, he abides by the bare letter, and so far Judaizes, and has yet to learn that the Christian is a disciple not of the letter but of the Spirit (for the letter killeth, says the Apostle, but the Spirit giveth life)
sources.raw_question: Did God literally pronounce names for created things (such as seed, herb and tree) with audible words at creation, as Eunomius claims from Genesis?

question: Is it impious, or a denial of Providence, to hold that human words were invented by the rational faculty God gave to man rather than given directly by God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Basil does not deny that God created man rational. He ascribes the invention of words to the logical faculty God implanted in human nature, so Providence remains the ultimate source. The literal alternative leads to a bodily, perishable God.
sources.quote: while we do not deny man’s having been created a rational being by God, we ascribe the invention of words to the logical faculty implanted by God in man’s nature
sources.raw_question: Is it impious, or a denial of Providence, to hold that human words were invented by the rational faculty God gave to man rather than given directly by God?

question: Does the Son possess a life that is not extraneous, not composite, and immortal and imperishable in itself, as Eunomius ascribes to the ungenerate God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture teaches this of the Only-begotten as well, since He says 'I am the Life'; life was not brought upon Him from without. His life is neither composite nor admits difference, and by virtue of that life He is immortal and so imperishable, for what is stronger than death cannot be corrupted. To deny this is to oppose St. John openly.
sources.quote: For life was not brought in from without upon the Son either (for He says, “I am the Life”), nor is His Life either composite, nor does it admit difference, but by virtue of that life itself He is immortal
sources.raw_question: Does the Son possess a life that is not extraneous, not composite, and immortal and imperishable in itself, as Eunomius ascribes to the ungenerate God?

question: Is it illegitimate to use bodily analogies to make the doctrine of the Trinity intelligible?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Hilary rejects the heretical objection that a doctrine needing bodily analogies is suspect. Such analogies are aids to grasping the faith, not standards of comparison for the Divine majesty. God Himself uses them in His self-revelation, so reverence and reason justify using bodily instances as a clue to the invisible.
sources.quote: These illustrations, I repeat, must only be used as aids to apprehension of the faith, not as standards of comparison for the Divine majesty. Our method is that of using bodily instances as a clue to the invisible.
sources.raw_question: Is it illegitimate to use bodily analogies to make the doctrine of the Trinity intelligible?

question: Does Scripture ever describe the Holy Spirit as worshipping God, as it describes angels worshipping the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVIII. As he purposes to establish the Godhead of the Holy Spirit by the points already discussed, St. Ambrose touches again on some of them; for instance, that He does not commit but forgives sin; that He is not a creature but the Creator; and lastly, that He does not offer but receives worship.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says "Let all the Angels of God worship Him" of the Son, but nowhere says "Let the Spirit worship Him." The Spirit cannot worship because He is not among the servants and ministers. Rather, together with the Father and the Son, He has the service of the just under Him.
sources.quote: For how can He worship Who is not amongst servants and ministers, but, together with the Father and the Son, has the service of the just under Him
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ever describe the Holy Spirit as worshipping God, as it describes angels worshipping the Son?

question: If the Father has no sharer in His Godhead, must the Son either be denied to be God or be a second God of a different nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: Gregory turns this into a dilemma against Eunomius. If the Father's deity cannot be shared with the Son, then either the Son is not God at all, which denies the God Christians worship, or the Son is God but of a different nature from the true God, which introduces a plurality of Gods divided by their natures. Both alternatives are equally impious. The orthodox position escapes the dilemma because Father and Son share one nature.
sources.quote: Let him choose which of these he will,—either to deny the Godhead of the Son, or to introduce into his creed a plurality of Gods. For whichever of these he chooses, it is all one as regards impiety
sources.raw_question: If the Father has no sharer in His Godhead, must the Son either be denied to be God or be a second God of a different nature?

question: Does 'the Finger of God' in Luke 11:20 refer to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter III. The same Unity may also be recognized from the fact that the Spirit is called Finger, and the Son Right Hand; for the understanding of divine things is assisted by the usage of human language. The tables of the law were written by this Finger, and they were afterwards broken, and the reason. Lastly, Christ wrote with the same Finger; yet we must not admit any inferiority in the Spirit from this bodily comparison.
sources.answer: Yes. In the parallel passage of another Gospel, Christ says he casts out devils 'by the Spirit of God' where Luke has 'by the Finger of God.' So Scripture itself interprets the Finger as the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: For in the same place in another book of the Gospel He named the Spirit of God, as you find: “But if I by the Spirit of God cast out devils.”
sources.raw_question: Does 'the Finger of God' in Luke 11:20 refer to the Holy Spirit?

question: Would dividing the substance of the Godhead among the Father, Son and Spirit, or multiplying its powers, contradict the unity of God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter III. The same Unity may also be recognized from the fact that the Spirit is called Finger, and the Son Right Hand; for the understanding of divine things is assisted by the usage of human language. The tables of the law were written by this Finger, and they were afterwards broken, and the reason. Lastly, Christ wrote with the same Finger; yet we must not admit any inferiority in the Spirit from this bodily comparison.
sources.answer: Yes. The image of hand and finger shows that whoever severed the unity of substance and multiplied its powers would divide the eternal Godhead more than our own body is divided. Yet the eternity of the same Godhead is one. The Godhead and its working are one in Father, Son and Spirit.
sources.quote: the fulness of the eternal Godhead would seem to be divided far more than this body of ours, if any one were to sever the unity of Substance, and multiply Its powers, whereas the eternity of the same Godhead is one
sources.raw_question: Would dividing the substance of the Godhead among the Father, Son and Spirit, or multiplying its powers, contradict the unity of God?

question: Does calling the Father 'alone good, alone omnipotent, alone immortal' exclude the Son, Jesus Christ, from these divine attributes?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Hilary holds that such 'pious praise' is used by the heretics to exclude Christ from the blessedness proper to God, leaving Him in weakness and death while the Father reigns alone. But the Son, by a true birth from the Father, inherits the same virtue of nature as the Begetter. What is natural to the Father is therefore also His.
sources.quote: Does it not deny in Christ a natural origin from God the Father, in the fear lest He should be thought to inherit by a birth, which bestows upon the Begotten the same virtue of nature as the Begetter
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father 'alone good, alone omnipotent, alone immortal' exclude the Son, Jesus Christ, from these divine attributes?

question: What does Paul's calling Christ 'the image of the invisible God' and 'the form of God' show about the Son's nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: It shows that the Son has the full divine nature, even invisibility. Paul calls Him the image and form of God without reservation, not a part of the image. If Christ's substance were discernible, He could not be the image of an invisible nature.
sources.quote: Christ is the image of the invisible God even in respect of His invisibility: for if the substance of Christ were discernible how could He be the image of an invisible nature?
sources.raw_question: What does Paul's calling Christ 'the image of the invisible God' and 'the form of God' show about the Son's nature?

question: Does the statement that 'there shall be none other likened unto Him' imply that the Son is a second god alongside the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The words forbid us to liken the Son to some second deity. He is God from God, born from no alien being, with nothing new or created in Him. Therefore, when Israel hears that its God is one, this means the Father and the Son are one altogether, not by confusion of Person but by unity of substance.
sources.quote: the revelation means that God the Father and God the Son are One altogether, not by confusion of Person but by unity of substance. For the prophet forbids us, because God the Son is God, to liken Him to some second deity.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that 'there shall be none other likened unto Him' imply that the Son is a second god alongside the Father?

question: Does making the Son the product of an energy rather than born from the Father collapse into Jewish unbelief about Christ?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in assuming, to account for the existence of the Only-Begotten, an 'energy' that produced Christ's Person.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son is born from some unsubstantial energy and not from the Father, he must be thought not merely inferior to the Father. The doctrine then ends in pure Judaism, because it denies the true deity and real subsistence of the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: If, that is, the Son was born, not from the Father, but from some unsubstantial ‘energy,’ He must be thought of as not merely inferior to the Father, and this doctrine must end in pure Judaism.
sources.raw_question: Does making the Son the product of an energy rather than born from the Father collapse into Jewish unbelief about Christ?

question: Can the being of the Son (or the Spirit) be said to fall short of the Father's being by some measurable degree of deficiency?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. The divine nature has no quantity or size, so there is no method by which one could measure how far the Only-begotten supposedly falls short of perfection. Eunomius's claim of a 'shortness' in the Son's being treats the divine like a measurable body. Gregory says that making the Son and Spirit comparatively less may sound like a slight profanity, but on close examination it is the height of blasphemy.
sources.quote: they discover in His being a certain shortness in the way of deficiency, though they do not tell us by what method they measure that which is devoid of quantity and size
sources.raw_question: Can the being of the Son (or the Spirit) be said to fall short of the Father's being by some measurable degree of deficiency?

question: How can Scripture describe the Son of God as both equal to the Father and less than the Father without contradiction?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > There is a Double Rule for Understanding the Scriptural Modes of Speech Concerning the Son of God. These Modes of Speech are of a Threefold Kind.
sources.answer: The Son is equal to the Father according to the form of God, in which he is, and less than the Father according to the form of a servant, which he took. This is the canonical rule taught by Scripture and Catholic interpreters. Taking the form of a servant did not cause him to lose the form of God.
sources.quote: the Son of God is both understood to be equal to the Father according to the form of God in which He is, and less than the Father according to the form of a servant which He took
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture describe the Son of God as both equal to the Father and less than the Father without contradiction?

question: Is there a third way Scripture speaks of the Son, one that shows neither his inferiority nor his equality but only that he is from the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > There is a Double Rule for Understanding the Scriptural Modes of Speech Concerning the Son of God. These Modes of Speech are of a Threefold Kind.
sources.answer: Yes. Besides texts showing equality, such as John 10:30, and texts showing lesserness in the form of a servant, such as John 14:28, some texts only indicate that the Son is from the Father. Examples are 'as the Father hath life in Himself, so hath He given to the Son' and 'the Son can do nothing of Himself'. These declare his birth, not his inequality.
sources.quote: some are so put, as to show Him at that time neither as less nor as equal, but only to intimate that He is of the Father
sources.raw_question: Is there a third way Scripture speaks of the Son, one that shows neither his inferiority nor his equality but only that he is from the Father?

question: Did the orthodox Fathers hold the contrary formula that the Son 'was before His generation'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: No. Athanasius, Gregory Nazianzen and Hilary hold that neither 'He was before His generation' nor 'He was not before His generation' applies to the Son; the question is unmeaning and irrelevant, because in His case being begotten is concurrent with existence and from the beginning. Athanasius' conditional phrases ('if the Son was not before His generation') mean only 'if the formula could be applied'.
sources.quote: In His case, to be begotten is concurrent with existence and is from the beginning
sources.raw_question: Did the orthodox Fathers hold the contrary formula that the Son 'was before His generation'?

question: Must whatever comes into existence from one person, so as to be another person, be called that person's son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Opinion Which Devises an Image of the Trinity in the Marriage of Male and Female, and in Their Offspring.
sources.answer: No. Scripture shows this in the creation of the woman: Eve came into existence from the man's person, yet she is not called his daughter. In the same way, the Lord says the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, and yet the Spirit is not a son. Procession of one person from another is therefore not always generation.
sources.quote: that what so comes into existence from some person as to make another person, cannot in every case be called a son; since the person of the woman came into existence from the person of the man, and yet she is not called his daughter
sources.raw_question: Must whatever comes into existence from one person, so as to be another person, be called that person's son?

question: Should a bodily analogy for the divine Persons, such as calling the Holy Spirit the Father's spouse, be rejected simply because it suggests carnal conception and birth?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Opinion Which Devises an Image of the Trinity in the Marriage of Male and Female, and in Their Offspring.
sources.answer: No. In the supreme spiritual things there is nothing corruptible or born in time, so bodily associations should not disturb sober judgment. Avoiding an empty disgust must not lead into pernicious error. One should learn to find traces of spiritual things in corporeal ones without carrying the defects of lower things upward. No one blushes, for example, to choose wisdom as a wife, even though the word is feminine.
sources.quote: Let him accustom himself so to find in corporeal things the traces of things spiritual, that when he begins to ascend upwards from thence, under the guidance of reason, in order to attain to the unchangeable truth itself
sources.raw_question: Should a bodily analogy for the divine Persons, such as calling the Holy Spirit the Father's spouse, be rejected simply because it suggests carnal conception and birth?

question: Does the Father's calling the Son "beloved" at his baptism show that divine love is a love of rest and acquiescence?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. When the Father calls his Son "beloved" (agapētos) in Matthew 3:17, he adds by way of explanation "in whom I am well pleased" (en hō eudokēsa), that is, "in whom I rest well pleased." The love is thereby glossed as rest and satisfaction in its object. Owen notes the same link in the Hebrew words for love of desire and love of acquiescence, both of which are applied to God.
sources.quote: when God calls his Son ἀγαπητόν, “beloved,” Matt. iii. 17, he adds, as an exposition of it, ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα, “in whom I rest well pleased.”
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's calling the Son "beloved" at his baptism show that divine love is a love of rest and acquiescence?

question: Is the saints' love for God the Father, by which they have communion with him, likewise a love of rest and delight?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. Their love bears an analogy to God's love. The soul makes God its rest, gathering itself from all other beloveds to rest in him alone, and it delights in him more than in life with all its enjoyments. Owen cites Psalm 116:7, Psalm 73:25 and Psalm 63:3 for this.
sources.quote: Thus the soul gathers itself from all its wanderings, from all other beloveds, to rest in God alone, — to satiate and content itself in him; choosing the Father for his present and eternal rest.
sources.raw_question: Is the saints' love for God the Father, by which they have communion with him, likewise a love of rest and delight?

question: Are necessary existence and self-existence the same thing, so that a necessarily existing Son would have to be self-existent?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Aristotle and the later Platonists held that the world and inferior deities proceed by emanation from a superior cause without temporal production. They thought these beings necessary but not self-existent. The Christian Church has always believed something similar of the Logos, who exists necessarily from the Father but is not self-existent. So the ideas are distinct, and in the judgment of much of mankind one does not even imply the other.
sources.quote: that is, they believed them to be necessary, but not selfexistent. Something like this has been constantly believed by the Christian Church, in respect of the Adyos
sources.raw_question: Are necessary existence and self-existence the same thing, so that a necessarily existing Son would have to be self-existent?

question: Does the use of the verb 'made' about Christ in Scripture justify classing the Word among created things?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: No. If catching at stray expressions like 'He made' sufficed, one would have to call the Word the heaven, the earth, the sun and every made thing, as Genesis uses 'made' of these. The Arians would thus resemble the Stoics, ranking God's Word with each work. Such terms must be understood not of His Godhead but by investigating their reason and manner.
sources.quote: they should come in time to call the Word the heaven, and the Light which took place on the first day, and the earth, and each particular thing that has been made
sources.raw_question: Does the use of the verb 'made' about Christ in Scripture justify classing the Word among created things?

question: What blessings of salvation does Scripture attribute to the work of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Reply to the suggested objection that we are baptized “into water.” Also concerning baptism.
sources.answer: Through the Holy Spirit come all the goods of salvation. These are restoration to paradise, ascent into the kingdom, adoption as sons, and freedom to call God Father. They also include sharing in Christ's grace, being children of light, and sharing in eternal glory. In short, the Spirit brings every "fulness of blessing" in this world and the next. What we have now is only the earnest and first fruits of the full fulfilment to come.
sources.quote: Through the Holy Spirit comes our restoration to paradise, our ascension into the kingdom of heaven, our return to the adoption of sons, our liberty to call God our Father, our being made partakers of the grace of Christ
sources.raw_question: What blessings of salvation does Scripture attribute to the work of the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the Apostle's confession of 'one Lord' (Christ) and 'one God and Father' in Ephesians 4 mean that the Father and Son are one by a union of person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Lord and God are each one not by union of person but by distinction of properties. It is the property of each to be one, the Father in His Fatherhood and the Son in His Sonship, and this very individuality of each constitutes the mystery of His union with the other.
sources.quote: Lord and God are each one, not by union of person but by distinction of properties: for, on the one hand, it is the property of Each to be one, whether of the Father in His Fatherhood, or of the Son in His Sonship
sources.raw_question: Does the Apostle's confession of 'one Lord' (Christ) and 'one God and Father' in Ephesians 4 mean that the Father and Son are one by a union of person?

question: Does Scripture ever say that God the Father was sent?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Appearance to Lot is Examined.
sources.answer: No. Scripture speaks of the Son and of the Holy Spirit as being sent, but nowhere says the Father was sent; this is why a sent pair of divine persons is best understood as the Son and the Spirit.
sources.quote: For we find nowhere in the Scriptures that the Father was sent.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ever say that God the Father was sent?

question: Does Paul's use of the same word 'form' for both the 'form of God' and the 'form of a servant' show that Christ truly possessed both natures?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes. Using the one word 'form' for both natures compels us to recognise that He truly had both. To take the form of a servant is to be born a man, and to be in the form of God is to be God. He is God by His eternal nature and man by the plan of grace, and the word has its true meaning in both cases.
sources.quote: The use of the one word ‘form’ to describe both natures compels us to recognise that He truly possessed both.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's use of the same word 'form' for both the 'form of God' and the 'form of a servant' show that Christ truly possessed both natures?

question: What happened to the human body the Son assumed when it was united with his divine nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: It was transformed into what the assuming nature is. The body in which he suffered, being mingled with the Divine Nature, was made by that commixture to be divine and incorruptible. So the assumption of our lowly nature casts no low idea on the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: even the body in which He underwent His Passion, by being mingled with the Divine Nature, was made by that commixture to be that which the assuming Nature is.
sources.raw_question: What happened to the human body the Son assumed when it was united with his divine nature?

question: Is Eunomius right to teach that the Son once did not exist and is a creature, a work and a servant rather than truly Son, Creator and Lord?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > All his insulting epithets are shewn by facts to be false.
sources.answer: No. Gregory says this is not a trivial falsehood but a misstatement of Truth itself. The Son always is, so it is false to say he once was not. He is truly a Son and not merely so called. He is the Creator, not a creature or a work, and the Lord who essentially rules, not a servant to be ranked with subject beings.
sources.quote: He asserts that One who always is once was not; he demonstrates that One who is truly a Son is falsely so called; he defines the Creator to be a creature and a work;
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius right to teach that the Son once did not exist and is a creature, a work and a servant rather than truly Son, Creator and Lord?

question: Can the Word in John 1:1 be called God merely in a relative sense of dominion or office over creatures?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. The Word is said to be God 'in the beginning', before creation, when there were no creatures. He could have no relation or dominion over things not yet made, so he cannot be God there in the sense of dominion or office, but must be God in the proper sense.
sources.quote: He could have no relation to the creatures before they were made ; no dominion over them when they were not: and therefore could not be God in the sense of dominion or office.
sources.raw_question: Can the Word in John 1:1 be called God merely in a relative sense of dominion or office over creatures?

question: Does the Son, regarded as the Father's work, reveal the Father's being, and does the Spirit, regarded as the Son's work, reveal the Son's nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: No, not on Eunomius' own premises. A work is commensurate only with the energy that produced it, just as a smith's skill shows only as far as making a gimlet requires. The energy, extended into its work, reveals neither its own full nature nor the being of the agent. So the Son as a 'work' would show only the energy, and the Father's being would stay in the dark. The same holds for the Spirit and the Son.
sources.quote: the energy, while it extends itself into its work, does not reveal therein the nature either of itself or of the agent who exerts it.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son, regarded as the Father's work, reveal the Father's being, and does the Spirit, regarded as the Son's work, reveal the Son's nature?

question: Do the 'all things' made by the Word in John 1:3 refer only to the things of the gospel, such as the preaching of the apostles and the new state of the church?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. The words illustrate the divine nature of the Word by his divine work of creation, since he that built all things is God. The 'all things' are expressly said to be the world and everything in heaven and earth. Nothing in these verses mentions the gospel or its preaching, which John treats only afterward. The Socinian gloss turns 'all things' into some things, 'made' into mended, and 'in the beginning' into afterwards.
sources.quote: The words are a plain illustration of the divine nature of the Word, by his divine power and works, as the very series of them declares. He was God, and he made all things
sources.raw_question: Do the 'all things' made by the Word in John 1:3 refer only to the things of the gospel, such as the preaching of the apostles and the new state of the church?

question: Since human sons come into being after their fathers, how can the Son of God always exist with the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Human analogies of time do not apply to God, because the offspring is such as the one who begets. Man is begotten in time and so begets in time. God is not as man but exists eternally, so his Word also exists everlastingly with the Father, as radiance with light.
sources.quote: For such as he that begets, such of necessity is the offspring; and such as is the Word’s Father, such must be also His Word.
sources.raw_question: Since human sons come into being after their fathers, how can the Son of God always exist with the Father?

question: Is the Son of God a distinct object of saving faith, so that believers trust in him directly and not merely assent that he is the Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen distinguishes believing that Christ is the Son of God, which is an assent to the Father's testimony about him, from believing on him. Believing on him is a divine, supernatural faith fixed on the Son as Son, the same faith by which we believe in the Father. Scripture presses this distinct affixing of faith and confidence on the Son again and again (John 14:1; 3:16, 18, 36; 6:29).
sources.quote: Believe also, act faith distinctly on me; faith divine, supernatural, — that faith whereby you believe in God, that is, the Father.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God a distinct object of saving faith, so that believers trust in him directly and not merely assent that he is the Christ?

question: Does John 5:23 establish that the Son is to receive the same honour and worship as the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen calls this text the foundation of the whole teaching that faith and worship are directed to the Son. All men are to honour the Son even as they honour the Father. Whoever withholds that honour from the Son does not honour the Father who sent him.
sources.quote: The foundation of the whole is laid, John v. 23, “That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him.”
sources.raw_question: Does John 5:23 establish that the Son is to receive the same honour and worship as the Father?

question: Is the Holy Spirit the immediate author of the grace and good motions in believers, so that they may have distinct communion with him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit acts in believers by stirring up the grace they have received and by bringing new supplies of grace from Jesus Christ. All good motions and all striving against sin are to be considered by faith as coming from him in a particular way. Believers have communion with him when they recognise his mind and goodwill in these workings and respond with care and reverence.
sources.quote: we have communion with the Holy Ghost, when we can consider him by faith as the immediate author of all supplies, assistance, and the whole relief we have by grace; of all good actings, risings, motions in our hearts
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit the immediate author of the grace and good motions in believers, so that they may have distinct communion with him?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be said to be 'with' Christ, given that Paul claims to be with Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VIII. St. Ambrose examines and refutes the heretical argument that because God is said to be glorified in the Spirit, and not with the Spirit, the Holy Spirit is therefore inferior to the Father. He shows that the particle in can be also used of the Son and even of the Father, and that on the other hand with may be said of creatures without any infringement on the prerogatives of the Godhead; and that in reality these prepositions simply imply the connection of the Three Divine Persons.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul did not fear to say of himself that he would be with Christ, and it was through the Spirit that he was made worthy of this. It is therefore absurd to deny of the Spirit what a creature claims for himself.
sources.quote: Do you deny that the Spirit, through Whom the Apostle was made worthy of being with Christ, is with Christ?
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be said to be 'with' Christ, given that Paul claims to be with Christ?

question: Does John 17:3, which makes eternal life consist in knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent, show that Christ is more than a created prophet?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. If Christ were only an angelic or human prophet revealing the Father, it would be incredible for knowledge of him to be placed on the same level as knowledge of God. Yet Scripture makes knowing Christ equally essential to the life of the soul and equally necessary to sustain it. Second Peter 1:2 says the same.
sources.quote: is it credible that the intimate heart-knowledge of the expositor should be put on the same level with the knowledge of God, as equally essential to the life of the soul
sources.raw_question: Does John 17:3, which makes eternal life consist in knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent, show that Christ is more than a created prophet?

question: Is there any substance intermediate between God and creatures, such that the Son could be neither creature nor of God's substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. Every substance that is not God is a creature, and everything that is not a creature is God. So if the Son is not a made substance, as John 1:3 proves, He must be of one substance with the Father.
sources.quote: For all substance that is not God is creature; and all that is not creature is God.
sources.raw_question: Is there any substance intermediate between God and creatures, such that the Son could be neither creature nor of God's substance?

question: Does the contrast 'they shall perish, but Thou remainest' in Hebrews 1:11 show that the Son is eternal and never was not?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: Yes. 'They shall perish' expresses the nature of creatures, which came from nothing and witness that they once were not, though by grace they do not perish. 'Thou remainest' shows that the Son lacks the capacity of perishing and has eternal duration, so it is foreign to Him to say 'He was not before His generation' and proper to Him always to be with the Father.
sources.quote: it is foreign to Him to have it said, ‘He was not before His generation,’ but proper to Him to be always, and to endure together with the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the contrast 'they shall perish, but Thou remainest' in Hebrews 1:11 show that the Son is eternal and never was not?

question: Does God's declaration "I am God, and there is none beside me" exclude the gods of the heathen and the conceptions of heretics?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God is the Founder of All Things, Their Lord and Parent, is Proved from the Holy Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. By saying there is none beside Him and that He will not give His majesty to another, God excludes all heathens and heretics with their figments. What is made by a workman's hand or feigned by a heretic's intellect is not God. He is not God whose existence depends on a workman.
sources.quote: that He may exclude all heathens and heretics with their figments; proving that that is not God who is made by the hand of the workman, nor that which is feigned by the intellect of a heretic.
sources.raw_question: Does God's declaration "I am God, and there is none beside me" exclude the gods of the heathen and the conceptions of heretics?

question: What does it mean that all things are "of Him, and through Him, and in Him"?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God is the Founder of All Things, Their Lord and Parent, is Proved from the Holy Scriptures.
sources.answer: All things are of God because they exist by His command. They are through Him because they are ordered by His word. They are in Him because all things return to His judgment, being recalled to Him when they await liberty after corruption is done away.
sources.quote: For all things are by His command, because they are of Him; and are ordered by His word as being through Him; and all things return to His judgment
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that all things are "of Him, and through Him, and in Him"?

question: Does affirming that the Son is eternal as the Word, Wisdom and Power of God by itself establish his eternal generation as Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Not strictly. Someone might hold that the Son is eternal as the Logos while his sonship began later, so such a statement is not a fully clear authority for eternal generation unless it says 'eternal as a Son.' Still, there is hardly any reasonable doubt in the case of Dionysius of Rome, because he made the Father the Head, Root and Origin of the Logos.
sources.quote: He might be supposed eternal, as the Λόγος, and his sonship commence afterwards.
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that the Son is eternal as the Word, Wisdom and Power of God by itself establish his eternal generation as Son?

question: Could the Son be ignorant of the Father's thoughts because, as a weaker nature, he cannot penetrate the stronger nature of the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Material analogies of dense and rare, heavy and light must be cast aside, and God born of God must be measured by his own divine claims. Even the Spirit searches the deep things of God, and the Son says that whoever has seen him has seen the Father, that he is in the Father and the Father in him, and that he and the Father are one. So he does not differ in nature from the Father and is not separate from him.
sources.quote: But let us cast aside these empty illustrations of material things, and measure God born of God, Spirit of Spirit, by His own powers and not by earthly conditions.
sources.raw_question: Could the Son be ignorant of the Father's thoughts because, as a weaker nature, he cannot penetrate the stronger nature of the Father?

question: Does the Son's mutual indwelling with the Father show that he shares the Father's nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. If names that correspond to realities convey true information, then he who is seen in another by the eye of understanding is not different in nature from that other. The Son is not different in kind, since he abides in the Father and the Father in him. Nor is he separate, since both are one in an indivisible nature.
sources.quote: He Who is seen in Another by the eye of understanding is not different in nature from that Other; not different in kind, since He abides in the Father, and the Father in Him; not separate, since Both are One.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's mutual indwelling with the Father show that he shares the Father's nature?

question: In what sense is the Son the mirror or image of the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Not as a reflection produced by the splendour of a nature outside himself. He is a living nature indistinguishable from the Father's living nature, derived wholly from the whole of the Father's. He has the Father in him because he is the Only-begotten, and he abides in the Father because he is God.
sources.quote: He is the mirror, not as the image reflected by the splendour of a nature outside Himself, but as being a living nature, indistinguishable from the Father’s living nature, derived wholly from the whole of His Father’s
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Son the mirror or image of the Father?

question: Can the Father and Son be one in will if they differ in nature and in knowledge?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Separable natures cannot be one in will, because a diversity of kind and nature draws them into diversities of will and judgment. Omniscience and nescience are opposites, and there can be no unity of will between ignorance and knowledge. So the opponents' own unity-of-will reading requires that the Son not be ignorant of what the Father knows.
sources.quote: There can be no unity of will between ignorance and knowledge. Omniscience and nescience are opposites, and opposites cannot be of the same will.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father and Son be one in will if they differ in nature and in knowledge?

question: How can Christ be called 'the first-born of every creature' if he were only a man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is Again Confirmed in Christ by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: He cannot be, if he were only a man, because man comes after every creature. He is the first-born of every creature because, according to his divinity, the Word proceeded from the Father before every creature. That same Word then became flesh and took on human nature, which comes after every creature. So the title proves his divine pre-existence, and the heretics cannot show that Christ the mere man was first-born of all creation.
sources.quote: how could He be the first-born of every creature, unless because according to His divinity the Word proceeded from the Father before every creature?
sources.raw_question: How can Christ be called 'the first-born of every creature' if he were only a man?

question: Does Hebrews 1 present Christ as truly divine rather than a creature exalted above the angels?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. In a passage written to show Christ's superiority to prophets and angels, where any exaggerated view of his dignity would be corrected, the writer describes him in divine terms. He is the brightness of God's glory and the express image of his person, the one who upholds all things and made the worlds. Angels worship him, he is addressed as God on an everlasting throne, and he is the unchanging Lord who laid the foundation of the earth.
sources.quote: The innumerable company of angels are his worshippers. He is seated on the everlasting throne. He is the only-begotten Son of the Father. He is addressed as God. He is adored as the immutable, immortal Jehovah.
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1 present Christ as truly divine rather than a creature exalted above the angels?

question: Does Christ's being made lower than the angels, suffering and being tempted, as described in Hebrews 2, contradict the divine majesty ascribed to him in Hebrews 1?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. The same epistle presents both. In chapter 2 he is made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, takes flesh and blood, and is made like his brethren. In chapter 1 his transcendent majesty as God and immutable Jehovah is declared. His humiliation belongs to his taking our nature and does not diminish his deity.
sources.quote: In the following chapter, we find this wonderful Saviour made a little lower than the angels, for the suffering of death, perfected through suffering, taking part of flesh and blood, in all things made like unto his brethren
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's being made lower than the angels, suffering and being tempted, as described in Hebrews 2, contradict the divine majesty ascribed to him in Hebrews 1?

question: Is self-existence (being unbegotten or underived) an essential attribute of God, so that the Son must be self-existent to be God by nature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 24: Whether Gal. iv. 8. may not be enough to determine the dispute betwiat us; since it obliged the Doctor to confess, that Christ as by nature truly God, as truly
sources.answer: No. Unbegottenness is a negative and relative notion, a personal character of the Father, not an essential attribute of the divine nature. Following Augustine, what is said relatively does not denote substance. Necessary existence is the essential character, and it belongs equally to Father and Son. If that is what is meant by self-existence, then it belongs to both.
sources.quote: Necessary-existence is an essential character, and belongs equally to Lather and Son: if that be what you mean by self-eaistence, then that also belongs to both.
sources.raw_question: Is self-existence (being unbegotten or underived) an essential attribute of God, so that the Son must be self-existent to be God by nature?

question: Does the Son's prayer "Father, glorify me" prove that the Father is greater than the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Glorification of the Son by the Father Does Not Prove Inequality.
sources.answer: No. The Holy Spirit also glorifies the Son, so if glorifying proved superiority the Spirit would be greater than the Son, which the objectors do not accept. Moreover the Son also glorifies the Father, so if the glorifier is greater, those who mutually glorify each other must be equal. The argument therefore yields equality, not inferiority.
sources.quote: But if he who glorifies is greater than he whom he glorifies, let them allow that those are equal who mutually glorify each other. But it is written, also, that the Son glorifies the Father; for He says, “I have glorified Thee on the earth.”
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's prayer "Father, glorify me" prove that the Father is greater than the Son?

question: Does denying any difference of nature among the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit lead to a mixture and confusion of the Persons?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. The nature is confessed to be invariable, but the difference of cause and caused is not denied. By that difference alone one Person is distinguished from another: one is the Cause, and another is of the Cause. So the Persons remain distinct without confusion.
sources.quote: while we confess the invariable character of the nature, we do not deny the difference in respect of cause, and that which is caused, by which alone we apprehend that one Person is distinguished from another
sources.raw_question: Does denying any difference of nature among the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit lead to a mixture and confusion of the Persons?

question: Does the Son's mediating role in the Spirit's origin cut the Holy Spirit off from a natural relation to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. The interposition of the Son guards the Son's own attribute of being Only-begotten. It does not shut out the Spirit from his relation by way of nature to the Father.
sources.quote: the interposition of the Son, while it guards His attribute of being Only-begotten, does not shut out the Spirit from His relation by way of nature to the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's mediating role in the Spirit's origin cut the Holy Spirit off from a natural relation to the Father?

question: Does calling the Father 'unbegotten' tell us what the divine essence is?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. 'Unbegotten' teaches only the mode in which the Father exists, not what he is. The question of existence is one question and the question of the mode of existence is another. A farmer who says whether a tree was planted or grew by itself states how it exists but leaves its nature unexplained.
sources.quote: when we learn that He is unbegotten, we are taught in what mode He exists, and how it is fit that we should conceive Him as existing, but what He is we do not hear in that phrase.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father 'unbegotten' tell us what the divine essence is?

question: Do texts saying that power was given to the Son, or that he asks the Father to glorify him, show that the Son lacked power and glory by nature and is therefore inferior to the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: No. He says these things humanly, because of the body. As God he always had the power and glory; he receives them as man, and he who glorifies others asks to be glorified in order to show that he has a flesh needing these things. Because the flesh that receives is his own, he is said himself to receive.
sources.quote: He says that He has received power, as man, which He ever had as God, and He says, ‘Glorify Me,’ who glorifies others, to shew that He hath a flesh which has need of these things.
sources.raw_question: Do texts saying that power was given to the Son, or that he asks the Father to glorify him, show that the Son lacked power and glory by nature and is therefore inferior to the Father?

question: Since the Spirit distributes gifts according to his own will and the Father works all in all, must the Father and the Spirit share one will?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father works all in all, so he works the things the Spirit works, and the Spirit divides these according to his own will. Then either the Spirit acts against the Father's will, which is absurd, or the Father wills the same as the Spirit. One is therefore compelled to confess the oneness of the divine will and operation.
sources.quote: you must of necessity confess the oneness of the divine will and operation, even if you do it unwillingly, and, if not with the heart, at least with the mouth.
sources.raw_question: Since the Spirit distributes gifts according to his own will and the Father works all in all, must the Father and the Spirit share one will?

question: Is the chief gift of sanctification that believers receive from Christ the indwelling of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is made our sanctification by procuring for us the Spirit of sanctification. Our renewing is the work of the Holy Ghost, who is shed on us through Christ alone.
