Paul in Romans 8 chiefly insists that the prime gift of sanctification is the Spirit's indwelling and our following his guidance.
sources.quote: the prime and principal gift of sanctification that we receive from Christ, is the indwelling of the Spirit, and our following after the guidance hereof
sources.raw_question: Is the chief gift of sanctification that believers receive from Christ the indwelling of the Holy Spirit?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's power to forgive sins show that he shares the divinity of the Father and the Son rather than being a creature like the angels?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter X. That the Spirit forgives sin is common to Him with the Father and the Son, but not with the Angels.
sources.answer: Yes. Forgiving sin belongs to the Father alone, the Son alone, and the Holy Spirit alone; no angel or archangel forgives sin. Since the Spirit forgives sin, he shares a power proper to God, which places him with the Father and Son and not among created beings.
sources.quote: Does an Angel forgive? Does an Archangel? Certainly not, but the Father alone, the Son alone, and the Holy Spirit alone.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's power to forgive sins show that he shares the divinity of the Father and the Son rather than being a creature like the angels?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be liable to sin, as creatures are?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter X. That the Spirit forgives sin is common to Him with the Father and the Son, but not with the Angels.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit forgives sin, and one who has power to forgive sin cannot be unable to avoid it. Since every creature is by nature liable to sin and God alone is free from sin, the Spirit's sinlessness shows his Godhead.
sources.quote: The Spirit could not be liable to sin, Who rather forgives sin.
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be liable to sin, as creatures are?

question: Does the confession in Deuteronomy that 'the Lord thy God is One' and the phrase 'the true God' in Isaiah prove that the Son of God bears the name of God only and not the divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Hilary accepts that there is One true God, but holds that the One true God is confessed in the nature of the Son as well. The heretics keep the words of the faith while perverting their sense, using the confession of one true God to deny the Son's true Godhead.
sources.quote: We recognise One God, and Him true God. The name of God has no dangers for our confession, which proclaims that in the nature of the Son there is the One true God.
sources.raw_question: Does the confession in Deuteronomy that 'the Lord thy God is One' and the phrase 'the true God' in Isaiah prove that the Son of God bears the name of God only and not the divine nature?

question: If the Son is truly born as God, can he be God in name only and not true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. If his birth were in name only, one could deny his true right to the name. But if he is truly born as God, he must be true God by virtue of that birth. No being can alter its own essential nature, so admitting the fact of his divine birth entails admitting his true Godhead.
sources.quote: If His birth be in name, not in nature, then you are justified in denying His true right to the name; but if He be truly born as God, how then can He fail to be true God by virtue of His birth?
sources.raw_question: If the Son is truly born as God, can he be God in name only and not true God?

question: Could God have used a created intermediary as the instrument of creation, as the Arians suppose the Son to be?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: No. If a creature could frame creatures, every creature could have heard God's command 'Become' and been framed directly, so no intermediary Word would be needed. Scripture does not say this, and it could not be so. Making the Word a created instrument of creation copies the Gnostics Valentinus, Marcion and Basilides, who held that angels create.
sources.quote: And if this pleases you, what is the need of the Word, seeing that things inferior can be brought to be by things superior?
sources.raw_question: Could God have used a created intermediary as the instrument of creation, as the Arians suppose the Son to be?

question: Does 'Only-begotten Son' mean merely 'perfect creature of God,' as the Arians claimed?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. John described the Only-begotten Son as God, not as a perfect creature. By adding 'which is in the bosom of the Father' he anticipated such blasphemous designations, and he had heard the Lord Himself speak of the Only-begotten Son given by the Father.
sources.quote: And first let us see whether the word mean, as you assert, a perfect creature of God; Only-begotten being equivalent to perfect, and Son a synonym for creature. But John described the Only-begotten Son as God, not as a perfect creature.
sources.raw_question: Does 'Only-begotten Son' mean merely 'perfect creature of God,' as the Arians claimed?

question: Does God's giving of His Only-begotten Son as proof of His love for the world show that the Son is His own true Son rather than a creature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. If God had given only a creature made from nothing on behalf of creatures made from nothing, it would be a cheap and petty sacrifice and a poor assurance of His love. Gifts of price are the evidence of affection, and the greatness of the surrender shows the greatness of the love. So the proof of God's love is that He gave His own Only-begotten Son, with true Sonship, not creation or adoption.
sources.quote: Gifts of price are the evidence of affection: the greatness of the surrender of the greatness of the love. God, Who loved the world, gave not an adopted Son, but His own, His Only-begotten.
sources.raw_question: Does God's giving of His Only-begotten Son as proof of His love for the world show that the Son is His own true Son rather than a creature?

question: If the Father who commands creation is true God, must the Son who executes that command also be true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. Only the divine nature has the power to carry out a word of creation. If the word spoken was truly divine, the deed done was truly divine as well. It would be incoherent to say true Godhead was present in the One's speech but absent from the Other's action.
sources.quote: How then is He not true God, Who creates, if He is true God, Who commands? If the word spoken was truly Divine, the deed done was truly Divine also.
sources.raw_question: If the Father who commands creation is true God, must the Son who executes that command also be true God?

question: Does the groaning of the whole creation for deliverance show that the Son is not a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son were a creature he would groan with the rest and need someone to bring adoption and freedom to himself. But he is the one who gives sonship and freedom to all, as he says 'if the Son shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed'; so he is true Son by nature, not a creature.
sources.quote: For if He were creature, He too would be one of those who groan, and would need one who should bring adoption and deliverance to Himself as well as others.
sources.raw_question: Does the groaning of the whole creation for deliverance show that the Son is not a creature?

question: Is the Son, because Scripture calls him an 'Angel', of the same nature as the angels and as far below the Divine Nature as angels are below him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. The Apostle proclaims that every angelic nature is subject to the Lord, citing the command that all the angels of God worship the first-begotten and the address 'Thy throne, O God, is for ever.' Angels are 'ministering spirits' and 'a flame of fire,' terms that mark the subordinate nature, while the Son is distinguished by the name of Godhead. To degrade the Lord of angels to the rank of an angel contradicts the whole apostolic argument for his unapproachable majesty.
sources.quote: how the Apostle proclaims that every angelic nature is subject to the Lord, and in witness of his doctrine invokes the sublime utterances of the prophets
sources.raw_question: Is the Son, because Scripture calls him an 'Angel', of the same nature as the angels and as far below the Divine Nature as angels are below him?

question: Is denying that the Son will ever cease to be logically tied to denying that the Son ever 'was not'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. To ascribe non-existence to the Son at any point, past or future, is the same impiety as calling immortal life mortal or truth a lie. As no death cuts short His endless life, so looking back no period of non-existence bounds it, so that He who really is has no community with what is not.
sources.quote: He, accordingly, who refuses to allow that He will at some future time cease to be, will also refuse to allow that He “once was not,” avoiding, according to our view, the same impiety on either hand
sources.raw_question: Is denying that the Son will ever cease to be logically tied to denying that the Son ever 'was not'?

question: Can a term expressing a mere mental conception (epinoia) be distinguished from a term expressing God's essence by the fact that it perishes with the voice that utters it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Every spoken word equally dissolves into the air once uttered, so if vanishing with the voice marked a term as a mere conception, every term, including "ungenerate" itself, would be a mere conception. The sense of words is not preserved in the air but is engraved on the hearer's memory, whether true or false, and written letters can equally record substantial and non-substantial objects of thought. Eunomius' definition of conception is therefore baseless.
sources.quote: he may as well at once call every term a mere conception, inasmuch as no substance remains in any term subsequent to its utterance
sources.raw_question: Can a term expressing a mere mental conception (epinoia) be distinguished from a term expressing God's essence by the fact that it perishes with the voice that utters it?

question: In what sense is the Son 'not unoriginate' and 'not independent' of the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 13: Whether there can be any middle between being made out of nothing, and out of something ; that is, between being out of nothing, and out of the Father's substan
sources.answer: The Son is not unoriginate only in the sense that he is not the head or fountain, not the first Person of the Trinity. He is not independent only in that he is second in order and has no separate existence from the Father, being coessentially and coeternally one with him. These words do not mean that the Son had a beginning in time. Nor do they mean that he depends on the Father's will for his existence.
sources.quote: We say, not unoriginate, meaning that he is not the head or fountain, not the first Person of the Trinity: you take up the very same word, and zealously contend that the Son is not unoriginate; understanding it in respect of time, or duration.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Son 'not unoriginate' and 'not independent' of the Father?

question: Should the difficulty of comprehending the Trinity and eternal generation outweigh the testimony of Scripture that the Son is God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 13: Whether there can be any middle between being made out of nothing, and out of something ; that is, between being out of nothing, and out of the Father's substan
sources.answer: No. These doctrines are too sublime for men or even angels to comprehend. Yet a few specious difficulties do not outweigh the many unanswerable objections to the Arian scheme. Nor do they outweigh the united voice of Scripture and antiquity, which everywhere proclaims the Son to be Creator, Preserver and very and eternal God.
sources.quote: points too sublime for men, or, it may be, angels to comprehend. But why must these be thought to weigh down the many and unanswerable objections against your own scheme
sources.raw_question: Should the difficulty of comprehending the Trinity and eternal generation outweigh the testimony of Scripture that the Son is God?

question: Are the Son and the Holy Spirit created servants of the Father, ranked among the angels?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VII.—Recapitulation of the foregoing argument, showing that Abraham, through the revelation of the Word, knew the Father, and the coming of the Son of God. For this cause, he rejoiced to see the day of Christ, when the promises made to him should be fulfilled. The fruit of this rejoicing has flowed to posterity, viz., to those who are partakers in the faith of Abraham, but not to the Jews who reject the Word of God.
sources.answer: No. The Son and the Holy Spirit, the Word and Wisdom, are the Father's own offspring and similitude, not creatures among His servants. All the angels serve them and are subject to them.
sources.quote: whom all the angels serve, and to whom they are subject
sources.raw_question: Are the Son and the Holy Spirit created servants of the Father, ranked among the angels?

question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each sanctify, and is their sanctification one?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IV. To those who contend that the Spirit because He is called the Finger is less than the Father, St. Ambrose replies that this would also tend to the lessening of the Son, Who is called the Right Hand. That these names are to be referred only to the Unity, for which reason Moses proclaimed that the whole Trinity worked in the passage of the Red Sea. And, indeed, it is no wonder that the operation of the Spirit found place there, where there was a figure of baptism, since the Scripture teaches that the Three Persons equally sanctify and are operative in that sacrament.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture attributes sanctification to the Father, as when 'the God of peace sanctify you' and 'Father, sanctify them in the truth'. It attributes sanctification to the Son, who was made our sanctification. It also attributes it to the Spirit, in 'sanctification of the Spirit'. Yet the sanctification is one, just as baptism and the grace of the sacrament are one.
sources.quote: So, then, the Father sanctifies, the Son also sanctifies, and the Holy Spirit sanctifies; but the sanctification is one, for baptism is one, and the grace of the sacrament is one.
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each sanctify, and is their sanctification one?

question: Does the Son's being 'made' sanctification for us imply a change in His divine nature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IV. To those who contend that the Spirit because He is called the Finger is less than the Father, St. Ambrose replies that this would also tend to the lessening of the Son, Who is called the Right Hand. That these names are to be referred only to the Unity, for which reason Moses proclaimed that the whole Trinity worked in the passage of the Red Sea. And, indeed, it is no wonder that the operation of the Spirit found place there, where there was a figure of baptism, since the Scripture teaches that the Three Persons equally sanctify and are operative in that sacrament.
sources.answer: No. He was made sanctification 'unto us', meaning for our benefit. This does not mean He changed what He was. It means He sanctified us in the flesh.
sources.quote: But He was made so unto us, not that He should change that which He was, but that He might sanctify us in the flesh.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being 'made' sanctification for us imply a change in His divine nature?

question: Can creatures be adopted as sons or deified apart from the true Son and Word of God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. Adoption is impossible apart from the real Son, since no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom he reveals him. Likewise, those called gods are so called because the Word of God came to them. So all who are sons and gods became so through the Word, and he must therefore be before them all and be Son and God by nature.
sources.quote: for adoption there could not be apart from the real Son, who says, ‘No one knoweth the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal Him.’
sources.raw_question: Can creatures be adopted as sons or deified apart from the true Son and Word of God?

question: Since the Son is the Creator of all things, must the Son himself be uncreated?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 12: Whether the Creator of all things was not himself uncreated ; and therefore could not be ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, made out of nothing ?
sources.answer: Yes. Dr. Whitby/the opponent himself admits that the Creator of all things must be uncreated, and Scripture teaches that the Son created all things; therefore the Son is uncreated. The premises are the opponent's own, and the conclusion follows necessarily.
sources.quote: You admit (p. 60.) that “the Creator of all things must be “himself uncreated.” Well then; the Son is Creator of all things; therefore he is wncreated.
sources.raw_question: Since the Son is the Creator of all things, must the Son himself be uncreated?

question: Does the 'Scripture-sense' of the word 'creature' mean only things brought into being by the Logos, so that the Son could be called uncreated in that narrow sense while still being produced out of nothing?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 12: Whether the Creator of all things was not himself uncreated ; and therefore could not be ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, made out of nothing ?
sources.answer: No. To make the whole Scripture account of creation (including the agent through whom it was wrought) part of the meaning of the single word 'creature' is like saying 'temple' means only something built by Solomon. The Jews, who drew their notion of creation from Scripture, did not understand the word this way, and John's statement that all things were made 'by him' would be a mere tautology if 'made' already implied 'made by the Logos'.
sources.quote: It was perfectly needless, if your pretence be true, to insert, by dim; because, in the “ς Scripture-sense” of the word, it was implied, and the addition of it only renders it tautology.
sources.raised_by_detail: Dr. Clarke's defender (the Modest Plea author)
sources.raw_question: Does the 'Scripture-sense' of the word 'creature' mean only things brought into being by the Logos, so that the Son could be called uncreated in that narrow sense while still being produced out of nothing?

question: Is the Son the work of the Father and the Holy Spirit the work of the Son, so that each divine Person is produced by the preceding one in a chain?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no reason for distinguishing a plurality of beings in the Trinity. He offers no demonstration that it is so.
sources.answer: No. Even in the created order no one would say that the sun is the work of the heavens, the moon of the sun, and so on, since all created things are the work of one God, of whom are all things. If such a chain of production cannot be affirmed of creatures, still less can it be affirmed of the transcendent existences, so that the second is a work of the first and the third a work of the second.
sources.quote: none would venture to affirm that, while the heavens are the work of God, the sun is that of the heavens, and the moon that of the sun, and the stars that of the moon, and other created things that of the stars: seeing that all are the work of One
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the work of the Father and the Holy Spirit the work of the Son, so that each divine Person is produced by the preceding one in a chain?

question: If the generation of the Son is modelled on animal generation, can the Son have a nature different from and inferior to the Father's?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no reason for distinguishing a plurality of beings in the Trinity. He offers no demonstration that it is so.
sources.answer: No. In natural generation the offspring are of the same type as their progenitors, because nature runs on through each generation. Eunomius is therefore inconsistent. He appeals to production of one from another and at the same time gives the offspring strange and uninherited qualities. That makes the Son a bastard relative to His Father's nature, against the law of nature.
sources.quote: for such productions are of the same type as their progenitors: whereas he assigns to the members of his succession strange and uninherited qualities
sources.raw_question: If the generation of the Son is modelled on animal generation, can the Son have a nature different from and inferior to the Father's?

question: Is Eunomius's argument that the energies and works of the divine Beings are of first and second rank a valid proof that the Son and Spirit are inferior in nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His acknowledgment that the Divine Being is 'single' is only verbal.
sources.answer: No. The argument starts from data not granted—namely that each is a separate being with its own dignity—and then constructs a blasphemy by mere logic upon that premise. A statement made at random and without proof from Scripture or human reasoning is an 'old woman's tale' and proves nothing.
sources.quote: it starts from data that are not granted, and then it constructs by mere logic a blasphemy upon them. It attempts no demonstration that could attract towards such a conception of the doctrine
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius's argument that the energies and works of the divine Beings are of first and second rank a valid proof that the Son and Spirit are inferior in nature?

question: Would interpreting Christ's pre-mundane glory as predestination absurdly make Christ inferior to other men?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again from the Gospel He Proves Christ to Be God.
sources.answer: Yes. If his glory were only predestined, Christ would be predestined last of all, after Adam, Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham and many others. That would make him inferior to men, though he is in fact better, greater and more ancient than the angels themselves. So the predestination reading fails, and his proper divinity must be acknowledged.
sources.quote: And on these terms Christ is discovered to be inferior to other men, although He is really found to be better and greater, and more ancient than the angels themselves.
sources.raw_question: Would interpreting Christ's pre-mundane glory as predestination absurdly make Christ inferior to other men?

question: Do John's saying 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father' and Paul's calling Christ 'the image of the invisible God' teach the same faith?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. Diversity in preaching does not divide the one faith; Paul neither forgot nor concealed the meaning of the Lord's words but restated it by calling the Son the image of the invisible God. Both teach that the Father is seen in the Son because the Son shares the Father's nature.
sources.quote: But has Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, forgotten or kept back the meaning of the Lord’s words, when he says, Who is the image of the invisible God?
sources.raw_question: Do John's saying 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father' and Paul's calling Christ 'the image of the invisible God' teach the same faith?

question: Can the Son be the image of the invisible God if he is a bodily, finite likeness of a different nature from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. A likeness must repeat the form of what it resembles, and a finite, bodily shape cannot represent the infinite and invisible God. Scripture teaches that both Christ and God are Spirit, so those who give the Son a different nature cannot explain how he is the likeness of the invisible God.
sources.quote: If they confine this Christ the Spirit within the bounds of shape and body, such a corporeal Christ will not be the likeness of the invisible God, nor will a finite limitation represent that which is infinite.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who will have a nature of a different sort in the Son
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be the image of the invisible God if he is a bodily, finite likeness of a different nature from the Father?

question: Do Christ's sayings that the Son does whatever the Father does, and has life in himself as the Father does, show the Son is divine?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > The Author Prosecutes the Same Argument.
sources.answer: Yes. A man cannot do works like God's heavenly works. Nor can a man have life in himself after the pattern of the Father, since man is made of mortal material and not glorious in eternity. These sayings prove the Son is more than man.
sources.quote: when man cannot have life in him after the example of God the Father, because he is not glorious in eternity, but made with the materials of mortality?
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's sayings that the Son does whatever the Father does, and has life in himself as the Father does, show the Son is divine?

question: Does describing the Son as begotten 'before all ages' or 'timelessly' distinguish a position from Arianism if strict coeternity is denied?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. Arius's chief objection was to the strict eternity or coeternity of the Son. Arius himself used nearly the same phrases ('timelessly,' 'before times and before ages,' 'before all ages'). Such language is therefore compatible with saying there was a time when the Son was not. Without consubstantiality and coeternity, there is no real middle way that raises the Son's divinity above the Arian view.
sources.quote: the principal thing which stuck with him was the τὸ ἀΐδιον, or συναΐδιον, the strict edernity or coeternity of the Son. As to other lesser matters, he would easily have compounded with the Catholics
sources.raw_question: Does describing the Son as begotten 'before all ages' or 'timelessly' distinguish a position from Arianism if strict coeternity is denied?

question: Can human birth serve as an exact model for understanding the Son's birth from God the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Analogies from human experience do not apply perfectly to divine mysteries; they serve only as a ladder by which we rise toward an apprehension of God's majesty. A birth involving intercourse, conception, time and travail gives no clue to the divine manner; we must accept that the Son was truly born and be content with that.
sources.quote: analogies drawn from human experience are not of perfect application to the mysteries of Divine power; that their only value is that this comparison with material objects imparts to the spirit such a notion of heavenly things
sources.raw_question: Can human birth serve as an exact model for understanding the Son's birth from God the Father?

question: Does the mental trinity formed by faith persist after faith has passed away, because we will still remember, recollect, and will regarding the faith we once had?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > A Difficulty Removed, Which Lies in the Way of What Has Just Been Said.
sources.answer: No. The trinity formed when we recollect past faith is a different trinity from the one formed by present faith. The present one is produced by the thing itself actually present in the believer's mind, whereas the later one is produced by an image or trace of a past thing left in memory. Augustine illustrates this with bodily vision: when a seen object has perished, the trinity formed from its remembered image differs from the trinity of actual sight, because the former was produced by a present object and the latter by its image.
sources.quote: For that which now is, is wrought by the thing itself, actually present and attached to the mind of one who believes; but that which shall then be, will be wrought by the imagination of a past thing left in the memory of one who recollects.
sources.raw_question: Does the mental trinity formed by faith persist after faith has passed away, because we will still remember, recollect, and will regarding the faith we once had?

question: Is the Arian claim that 'there was once when the Son was not' coherent, given what the 'once' could refer to?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: No. If the 'once' refers to the Father, it is impious, since the Father is ever and cannot be signified by 'once'; if it refers to the Son, it is absurd, since the Son cannot both be and not be. The only remaining meaning is that there was a time before the Word, which Scripture never says.
sources.quote: But if ye say that the Son was once, when He Himself was not, the answer is foolish and unmeaning. For how could He both be and not be?
sources.raw_question: Is the Arian claim that 'there was once when the Son was not' coherent, given what the 'once' could refer to?

question: In what order do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit act in bringing divine love to believers in salvation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Divine love begins with the Father, is carried on by the Son, and is communicated by the Spirit. The Father designs, the Son purchases, and the Spirit effectually works. Our participation runs the other way: the Spirit gives us an actual interest in the Son's blood, and through that we are accepted with the Father. So believers ascend to the Father's love through the Spirit's work and the Son's blood.
sources.quote: The emanation of divine love to us begins with the Father, is carried on by the Son, and then communicated by the Spirit; the Father designing, the Son purchasing, the Spirit effectually working: which is their order.
sources.raw_question: In what order do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit act in bringing divine love to believers in salvation?

question: Is the Creator (Demiurge) truly God and Father by nature, or is he called God only by courtesy, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter I.—The Lord acknowledged but one God and Father.
sources.answer: The Creator is truly God and Father. The Spirit, the apostles, and above all the Lord himself announced no other God or Lord than the one who rules over all with his Word, and the Lord commanded us to confess as Father only the one God in the heavens. The Gnostic claim that their invented being is God by nature while the Demiurge is God merely 'verbo tenus' is therefore shown to be false.
sources.quote: those things are clearly shown to be false which these deceivers and most perverse sophists advance, maintaining that the being whom they have themselves invented is by nature both God and Father; but that the Demiurge is naturally neither God nor Father
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator (Demiurge) truly God and Father by nature, or is he called God only by courtesy, as the Gnostics claim?

question: Did the Word's becoming flesh and dying diminish the glory of his Godhead?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. Even as man called Jesus he remains what he ever was and has the whole creation bending the knee to him. His incarnation and death were 'to the glory of God the Father.' It is the Father's glory that lost and dead man should be found, made alive, and become God's temple.
sources.quote: the Word’s becoming flesh, and undergoing death in flesh, has not happened against the glory of His Godhead, but ‘to the glory of God the Father.’
sources.raw_question: Did the Word's becoming flesh and dying diminish the glory of his Godhead?

question: Was the created world made by a lower power such as the Gnostic Achamoth or the Demiurge, or by the one God through His Word?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XXI.—The views of redemption entertained by these heretics.
sources.answer: It was made by the one God through His Word. The rule of truth holds that there is one God Almighty who made all things by His Word and Spirit, out of nothing, without exception, visible and invisible alike. He did not make them by angels or by powers separated from Him, for God needs none of these, and there is no God, principle, power or pleroma above Him. He is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
sources.quote: The rule of truth which we hold, is, that there is one God Almighty, who made all things by His Word, and fashioned and formed, out of that which had no existence, all things which exist.
sources.raw_question: Was the created world made by a lower power such as the Gnostic Achamoth or the Demiurge, or by the one God through His Word?

question: Did the Father deliberate or counsel beforehand about begetting the Son, as He does about creating the world?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. God counsels to make things which once were not and come from external causes, but His own Word begotten from Him by nature He did not counsel about beforehand. Rather it is in the Word that the Father makes and frames whatever else He counsels, as James says He begat us of His will 'with the Word of truth.'
sources.quote: but His own Word begotten from Him by nature, concerning Him He did not counsel beforehand; for in Him the Father makes, in Him frames, other things whatever He counsels
sources.raw_question: Did the Father deliberate or counsel beforehand about begetting the Son, as He does about creating the world?

question: What is the proper relation between Scripture and the Church's creeds concerning doctrines such as the Trinity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: The Church teaches and Scripture proves. Creeds and articles are valuable when they can be proved by most certain warrants of Scripture, and they give needed stability. This is shown by the shifting opinions of Unitarian congregations on vital articles of faith. Articles received because they are demonstrable from Scripture are beyond all price.
sources.quote: To the Church then, has her all-wise Founder left the office of teaching – to the Scriptures, that of proving the Christian doctrine
sources.raw_question: What is the proper relation between Scripture and the Church's creeds concerning doctrines such as the Trinity?

question: Is the Holy Spirit absolutely free and independent in his action?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture calls him God's 'free Spirit.' It says he blows where he wills and divides gifts 'as he willeth.' Where he is, there is liberty.
sources.quote: He is absolutely free and independent.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit absolutely free and independent in his action?

question: Is the Holy Spirit the almighty Creator, with wisdom and power of his own?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah 40:12-14 asks 'Who hath directed the Spirit of the Lord, or being his counsellor, hath taught him?' within a description of creation. This presents an intelligent Creator inferior to none, whose counsel is underived and whose omnipotence is inherent. It also casts light on Genesis 1:2, where the Spirit of God moved on the waters.
sources.quote: No words could express more plainly an intelligent Creator, inferior to none, whose wisdom was his own, whose counsel was underived, whose omnipotence was inherent.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit the almighty Creator, with wisdom and power of his own?

question: Does the account of creation show that God Himself gave names to the things He created, rather than Adam?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The inspired testimony says the various kinds of animals were named by Adam, and Eunomius's contrary reading impugns Scripture. Paul, speaking by the Spirit, is a more trustworthy interpreter, and he teaches that Adam points prophetically to Christ.
sources.quote: a man who openly impugns the words of the inspired testimony, and who by his false interpretation of the word would fain prove that the various kinds of animals were not named by Adam
sources.raw_question: Does the account of creation show that God Himself gave names to the things He created, rather than Adam?

question: If the Son is truly generated and Only-begotten, is it consistent to speak of Him in terms of 'the operation of a maker', as Eunomius does?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then clearly and skilfully criticises the doctrine of the impossibility of comparison with the things made after the Son, and exposes the idolatry contrived by Eunomius, and concealed by the terminology of “Son” and “Only-begotten,” to deceive his readers.
sources.answer: No. What is generated is correlative to the one who generates, so the Only-begotten is correlative to the Father. Whoever looks to the truth sees alongside the Son not the operation of a maker but the nature of Him who begat Him. To couple 'the operation of the maker' with the Son's essence contradicts calling Him generated and Only-begotten. It treats Him like plants, seeds, or stones in the order of creation.
sources.quote: That which is generated is correlative to the generator, and the Only-begotten, surely, by consequence, to the Father; and he who looks to the truth beholds, in co-ordination with the Son, not “the operation of the maker,” but the nature of Him that begat Him.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is truly generated and Only-begotten, is it consistent to speak of Him in terms of 'the operation of a maker', as Eunomius does?

question: Can doubts about the divine energies be resolved by knowledge of the divine beings, while knowledge of those beings is in turn obtained from the energies, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He vainly thinks that the doubt about the energies is to be solved by the beings, and reversely.
sources.answer: No. Gregory argues this is circular: proof of anything doubted must proceed from well-known truths, but here both the being and the energy are equally unknown. If the being were already comprehended, the energy would not be needed to reach it; if it is not comprehended, it cannot settle doubts about the energy.
sources.quote: The proof of anything that is doubted must be made by means of well-known truths; but when there is an equal uncertainty about both the objects of our search, how can Eunomius say that they are comprehended by means of each other
sources.raw_question: Can doubts about the divine energies be resolved by knowledge of the divine beings, while knowledge of those beings is in turn obtained from the energies, as Eunomius claims?

question: In God's simple nature, is God's love something distinct from God's substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Holy Spirit is Called Love, and Whether He Alone is So Called. That the Holy Spirit is in the Scriptures Properly Called by the Name of Love.
sources.answer: No. In that simple and highest nature, substance is not one thing and love another. Substance itself is love and love itself is substance, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. As an unchangeable and simple substance, God is what he has.
sources.quote: in that simple and highest nature, substance should not be one thing and love another, but that substance itself should be love, and love itself should be substance
sources.raw_question: In God's simple nature, is God's love something distinct from God's substance?

question: How can one affirm that both the Father and the Son are God without either teaching two Gods or teaching a solitary, isolated God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: By confessing God as One yet not alone. Father and Son are one in name, nature, and kind of divinity, so there is no difference of Godhead and no second God; yet there is no confusion of Persons, so God is not a lonely, solitary Deity. The proof of the Son's deity must avoid both errors at once.
sources.quote: It shall manifest God as One yet not alone; but in its care to avoid the error of making Him lonely it shall not fall into the error of denying His unity.
sources.raw_question: How can one affirm that both the Father and the Son are God without either teaching two Gods or teaching a solitary, isolated God?

question: Can the Father and the Son both be Jehovah if they are not one individual being?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: Yes. The objection merely plays on the word 'individual' and attacks no one, since the orthodox do not claim the Father and Son are one individual person. Antiquity constantly held that the Son is Jehovah in his own Person and right, as the coessential Son of God.
sources.quote: it is nothing but playing with the word individual, and disputing against nobody : either take the word in our sense of it, or pretend not that you oppose us.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father and the Son both be Jehovah if they are not one individual being?

question: Is the Son the exact image of the Father's essence, so that seeing the Son is seeing the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: Yes. He is the expression of the Father's Person, Light from Light, Power, and very Image of the Father's essence. The Lord confirms this by saying, 'He that hath seen Me, hath seen the Father.' This is against the Arian claim that the Son neither sees nor knows the Father perfectly.
sources.quote: For He is the expression of the Father’s Person, and Light from Light, and Power, and very Image of the Father’s essence. For this too the Lord has said, ‘He that hath seen Me, hath seen the Father.’
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the exact image of the Father's essence, so that seeing the Son is seeing the Father?

question: In what sense can the Word be properly called Son: in respect of his eternal existence from the Father, or only in respect of his coming forth to create the world?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Primarily and chiefly in respect of his eternal existence from the Father. Waterland holds that the Word is Son as partaking of the same divine substance from all eternity, and also Son secondarily in going forth to create the world and in becoming man. Later Fathers therefore gave the name 'generation' to the eternal existence from the Father, and called the other two condescensions or manifestations.
sources.quote: Son of the Father, as partaking of the same divine substance from all eternity; !going out from the Father to create the world; and, lastly, condescending to become man: Son, in all these respects, but primarily and chiefly in respect of the first.
sources.raw_question: In what sense can the Word be properly called Son: in respect of his eternal existence from the Father, or only in respect of his coming forth to create the world?

question: Is there any scriptural basis for affirming inequality between the Son and the Holy Spirit in divine attributes?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: No. All the attributes befitting the Godhead are predicated equally of the Son and the Spirit in Scripture, so nothing warrants assigning the Spirit excess or defect; Eunomius asserts the Spirit's inferiority nakedly, without argument.
sources.quote: since all these are by Holy Scripture predicated equally of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, can he inform us wherein he discerns inequality to exist
sources.raw_question: Is there any scriptural basis for affirming inequality between the Son and the Holy Spirit in divine attributes?

question: Is it consistent to hold both that the Son is one of the things made and that 'all things were made by Him'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Proof that the Anomœan teaching tends to Manichæism.
sources.answer: No. If the Son is one of the things made, then either he made himself, which is absurd, or he must be withdrawn from the 'all.' In that case the statement that all things were made by him is false, because removing even one thing makes 'all' untrue. Therefore Scripture's teaching that he made all things excludes his being a creature.
sources.quote: Either He must have made Himself, for that text to be true, and so this unreasonableness which they have devised to harm our Faith will recoil with all its force upon themselves
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to hold both that the Son is one of the things made and that 'all things were made by Him'?

question: Do the plural words "Us" and "Our" in Genesis 1:26 show that God was not a solitary, isolated Being at creation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. The words "Us" and "Our" cannot be used by an isolated being speaking to himself, nor to a stranger with nothing in common with the speaker. They therefore reveal that there is neither one isolated God nor one God in two dissimilar Persons.
sources.quote: these two words Us and Our reveal that there is neither one isolated God, nor yet one God in two dissimilar Persons; and our confession must be framed in harmony with the second as well as with the first truth.
sources.raised_by_detail: the blasphemers who assert Moses proclaims the solitude of God
sources.raw_question: Do the plural words "Us" and "Our" in Genesis 1:26 show that God was not a solitary, isolated Being at creation?

question: Does the singular "image" in "Let Us make man after Our image" show that the divine Persons share one nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says "our image", not "our images", so the image after which man is made belongs to Both in common. This proves there is one nature possessed by Father and Son, and no difference in kind between the Godhead of the One and of the Other.
sources.quote: For the words our image—not our images—prove that there is one nature possessed by Both.
sources.raw_question: Does the singular "image" in "Let Us make man after Our image" show that the divine Persons share one nature?

question: Does God's command to Noah, "for after the image of God made I man," support a distinction of divine Persons?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. In it God again distinguishes the likeness, the creature, and the Creator. He could have said "after My image" without inaccuracy. Instead He says "after the image of God," to remove more fully all doubt about whether God is a solitary Being.
sources.quote: But for the more perfect removal of all doubt as to whether God be, or be not, a solitary Being, when He made man He made him, we are told, After the image of God.
sources.raw_question: Does God's command to Noah, "for after the image of God made I man," support a distinction of divine Persons?

question: Does Proverbs 8, where Wisdom says "I was with Him, setting them in order," show that the Son shared in the work of creation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. Wisdom, confessed to be Christ, was begotten before the worlds. Wisdom was not only present with the Father but set creation in order, so the Father did not work in isolation. Wisdom also rejoiced in the Father's joy over the finished world, as His partner in their conjoint labour.
sources.quote: There is with God Wisdom, begotten before the worlds; and not only present with Him, but setting in order, for She was with Him, setting them in order.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs 8, where Wisdom says "I was with Him, setting them in order," show that the Son shared in the work of creation?

question: If the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit work inseparably, how can the Father's voice, the Son's flesh, and the Spirit's dove each be referred to one Person separately?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Of the Sensible Showing of the Holy Spirit, and of the Coeternity of the Trinity. What Has Been Said, and What Remains to Be Said.
sources.answer: The Trinity together wrought the voice, the flesh, and the dove, yet each is referred to one Person, because the inseparable Trinity cannot be manifested inseparably by an inferior, bodily creature. Just as our spoken words must name Father, Son, and Spirit in separate intervals of time though they are one, so the visible creature shows them separably. The operation in each manifestation remains the work of the whole Trinity.
sources.quote: the Trinity together wrought both the voice of the Father, and the flesh of the Son, and the dove of the Holy Spirit, while each of these things is referred severally to each person
sources.raw_question: If the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit work inseparably, how can the Father's voice, the Son's flesh, and the Spirit's dove each be referred to one Person separately?

question: How does the analogy of memory, intellect, and will illustrate the inseparable operation of the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Of the Sensible Showing of the Holy Spirit, and of the Coeternity of the Trinity. What Has Been Said, and What Remains to Be Said.
sources.answer: When one names memory, intellect, and will, each name refers to one faculty only, yet each name is uttered by all three together, by the soul as a whole. In the same way each visible manifestation refers to one divine Person, yet all three Persons produce it. So the Trinity, inseparable in itself, is shown separably through creatures while its operation stays inseparable.
sources.quote: each name refers to each severally, but yet each is uttered by all three; for there is no one of these three names that is not uttered by both my memory and my intellect and my will together
sources.raw_question: How does the analogy of memory, intellect, and will illustrate the inseparable operation of the Trinity?

question: Do Christ's words 'I in the Father and the Father in Me' refute both the belief in two Gods and the belief in a solitary God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. The heretics would have to blot out this self-revelation of the Son before they could assert either two Gods or one God in loneliness. The mutual indwelling shows that there are two Persons sharing one Divine nature.
sources.quote: Let the heretics blot out this record of the Son’s self-revelation I in the Father and the Father in Me; then, and not till then, shall they assert that there are two Gods, or one God in loneliness.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's words 'I in the Father and the Father in Me' refute both the belief in two Gods and the belief in a solitary God?

question: Can the Holy Spirit's being 'sub-numerated' under the Father and Son be understood as the division of a common genus (God) into subordinate species or individuals?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who say that the Holy Ghost is not to be numbered with, but numbered under, the Father and the Son. Wherein moreover there is a summary notice of the faith concerning right sub-numeration.
sources.answer: No. To treat the God of the universe as a common quality existing only in thought and divided into subdivisions would be impious, since God is not an abstraction without existence in a hypostasis. Moreover, the argument defeats itself: subdivisions are of the same essence as that from which they are divided, so this sense of sub-numeration would prove the Spirit consubstantial, the opposite of what the opponents intend.
sources.quote: they are establishing the very opposite argument to their own contention. For the subdivisions are of the same essence as that from which they have been divided.
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit's being 'sub-numerated' under the Father and Son be understood as the division of a common genus (God) into subordinate species or individuals?

question: When Isaiah 45:5 ('I am God, and there is none besides me') is applied to God the Father, does it exclude the Son from being the one God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Novatian applies the text to the Father, but only in contrast to false gods. It is not set against the Son, who remains included in the one God. The Father is called the one God in a way that comprehends the consubstantial Son rather than excluding him.
sources.quote: not so as to exclude the Son from being comprehended in the one God, but in opposition to false Gods only
sources.raw_question: When Isaiah 45:5 ('I am God, and there is none besides me') is applied to God the Father, does it exclude the Son from being the one God?

question: Do the Son's receiving worship from the Church and his being present everywhere prove his true divinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Yes. Novatian, a primitive writer, argues for Christ's divinity from these very points. Being present in every place when called upon is not a property of human nature but of God. Novatian also makes the Son consubstantial with the Father, which is all Waterland means by the Son being one with the Supreme God.
sources.quote: He proves the divinity of Christ from his receiving worship of the Church, and his being every where present
sources.raw_question: Do the Son's receiving worship from the Church and his being present everywhere prove his true divinity?

question: Does the Father's being called the Son's God ("Thy God") contradict the Son's divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. "Thy God" declares the Son's birth but does not contradict His nature. It means the Son was born from the Father to share the Godhead, and the Father's being God is no obstacle to the Son's being God also.
sources.quote: That word Thy declares His birth, yet does not contradict His nature; Thy God means that the Son was born from Him to share the Godhead.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's being called the Son's God ("Thy God") contradict the Son's divine nature?

question: When is the inner word of the mind 'born', and what role does love play in its conception?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > In What Desire and Love Differ.
sources.answer: The word is conceived by love, whether of the creature or of the Creator. It is born when, having been thought out, it pleases us, whether toward sinning or toward doing right. Love's approval of the thought is therefore what brings the inner word to birth.
sources.quote: Now a word is born, when, being thought out, it pleases us either to the effect of sinning, or to that of doing right.
sources.raw_question: When is the inner word of the mind 'born', and what role does love play in its conception?

question: Is the incarnate Word a different being from God the Word, or did He take a flesh unlike ours?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Neither. He dwelt among us so that He might be known as the indwelling God, the same God the Word, and as God incarnate in no other flesh than our own. He became flesh so that our flesh might attain union with God the Word.
sources.quote: lest we should think that this incarnate Word was some other than God the Word, or that His flesh was of a body different from ours, He dwelt among us
sources.raw_question: Is the incarnate Word a different being from God the Word, or did He take a flesh unlike ours?

question: What does John mean by saying that what was made 'not without' the Word, and does this imply something was made by the Father apart from the Son's creative agency?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. What was made in Him is life, and whatever was made in Him was also made through Him, so nothing was made without Him. All things were created in Him and through Him because He was born as God the Creator and is the Life which made their creation possible.
sources.quote: That which was made in Him was certainly not made without Him; for that which was made in Him was also made through Him. All things were created in Him and through Him
sources.raw_question: What does John mean by saying that what was made 'not without' the Word, and does this imply something was made by the Father apart from the Son's creative agency?

question: In the simple divine nature, are two or three Persons greater in magnitude than one?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How There is a Trinity in the Very Simplicity of God. Whether and How the Trinity that is God is Manifested from the Trinities Which Have Been Shown to Be in Men.
sources.answer: No. God's nature has no bulk, so there is nothing in which two or three could be thought greater than one. Augustine discerned the Trinity to this extent even before seeing it clearly.
sources.quote: there was no bulk wherein we must needs think the magnitude of two or three to be more than that of one
sources.raw_question: In the simple divine nature, are two or three Persons greater in magnitude than one?

question: Why should the human mind be studied in order to understand the Trinity that is God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How There is a Trinity in the Very Simplicity of God. Whether and How the Trinity that is God is Manifested from the Trinities Which Have Been Shown to Be in Men.
sources.answer: Because man is made after the image of God, and the invisible things of God are understood through the things that are made. The mind could not yet bear the direct light of God, so it was trained on the more familiar trinities in our own mind. Yet the Trinity is rather believed than seen through these, because something remains that must be believed even though it is not beheld.
sources.quote: according to which man is made after the image of God, in order to relieve our overstrained attention
sources.raw_question: Why should the human mind be studied in order to understand the Trinity that is God?

question: Is the Eunomian doctrine of the Son as the offspring of an energy and a creature a new and strange teaching?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > Then, distinguishing between essence and generation, he declares the empty and frivolous language of Eunomius to be like a rattle. He proceeds to show that the language used by the great Basil on the subject of the generation of the Only-begotten has been grievously slandered by Eunomius, and so ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Nothing could be newer than a Son of an energy, a Father of a creature, a new God springing up from nothing, and good at variance with good. Like the Athenians who spent their time on novelties, the Eunomians invent a new god. Basil, like Paul, is falsely charged with novelty while actually preaching the truth.
sources.quote: For what could be found newer than this,—a Son of an energy, and a Father of a creature, and a new God springing up from nothing, and good at variance with good?
sources.raw_question: Is the Eunomian doctrine of the Son as the offspring of an energy and a creature a new and strange teaching?

question: Did the Son come into existence by the Father's command, as creatures did?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. He is the Only-begotten of the one God and has life in Himself just as the Father has life in Himself, which distinguishes Him from created things brought into being by command.
sources.quote: Nor did He come into existence in obedience to a command as did created things, for He is the Only-begotten of the One God; and He has life in Himself, even as He that begot Him has life
sources.raw_question: Did the Son come into existence by the Father's command, as creatures did?

question: Does the subjection of the Son in 1 Corinthians 15:28 mean that Christ's human nature will be changed into the substance of the Godhead?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: Augustine does not grant this reading. He offers instead that the text guards against thinking the human form of Christ will be transformed into the Godhead. Even if someone holds the conversion view, he must admit the change had not yet taken place when Christ said "My Father is greater than I" before his passion. So the saying still refers to the human nature, not to the Godhead.
sources.quote: such an one at any rate admits this, of which in truth there is no possible doubt, that this had not yet taken place, when the Lord said, “My Father is greater than I.”
sources.raised_by_detail: some who thought the subjection is a conversion of the creature into the Creator's substance
sources.raw_question: Does the subjection of the Son in 1 Corinthians 15:28 mean that Christ's human nature will be changed into the substance of the Godhead?

question: When the Person appearing in the Old Testament theophanies is called God and Lord, does he bear these titles in his own right as Son, or only as representing God the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: He bears them in his own right. According to Novatian, the title of God belonged to the Person of Christ himself, not to the Father whom he represented. It is given to him as God's Son and consubstantial with the Father, not merely because he has dominion and authority. This is directly opposed to the hypothesis of Dr. Clarke and his followers.
sources.quote: they are given to him in his own Person, in his own right, as God’s Son, and consubstantial with him
sources.raw_question: When the Person appearing in the Old Testament theophanies is called God and Lord, does he bear these titles in his own right as Son, or only as representing God the Father?

question: Does Christ's divinity rest on his sonship, and does that sonship imply that he shares the same divine substance as the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Yes. Justin Martyr and Novatian both trace Christ's divinity to his being the Son. They take his sonship to mean that the same divine substance is communicated to him. For Novatian, being God's Son means a communion of substance, that is, real and essential divinity, and not a title of office only.
sources.quote: he, as well as Novatian, resolves the divinity of Christ into his fsonship; and sonship into $communication of the same divine substance
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's divinity rest on his sonship, and does that sonship imply that he shares the same divine substance as the Father?

question: Did the Father create man alone, without the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Less Than the Father, and Than Himself.
sources.answer: No. In the form of God the Son made man, just as in the form of a servant he was made man. If the Father alone had made man, Scripture would not say "Let us make man in our image." Likewise, as the Word, all things were made by the Son.
sources.quote: For if the Father alone had made man without the Son, it would not have been written, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.”
sources.raw_question: Did the Father create man alone, without the Son?

question: In what particular respect do believers have distinctive (peculiar) fellowship with the Son, Jesus Christ, as distinct from the other divine Persons?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: In grace. Scripture everywhere ascribes grace to Christ by way of eminency: he came full of grace and truth, and of his fulness we all receive grace for grace. Thus believers receive all manner of grace from him, and therein hold fellowship with him.
sources.quote: that is, we have communion with him in grace; we receive from him all manner of grace whatever; and therein have we fellowship with him.
sources.raw_question: In what particular respect do believers have distinctive (peculiar) fellowship with the Son, Jesus Christ, as distinct from the other divine Persons?

question: Does denying the eternity of the Son also imply something blasphemous about God the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections to the Foregoing Proof. Whether, in the generation of the Son, God made One that was already, or One that was not.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son once was not, the Father was once without Reason and Wisdom. He would then have had to devise a Word and Wisdom for Himself from outside. So the attack on the Son rebounds as a blasphemy against the Father.
sources.quote: For this assault upon the Son makes the blasphemy recoil upon the Father; as if He devised for Himself a Wisdom, and Word, and Son from without
sources.raw_question: Does denying the eternity of the Son also imply something blasphemous about God the Father?

question: Does the worship of the Son, which is said not to terminate in the Son but in the Father, divide honour between them?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. Strictly speaking no honour is paid to either Person that does not redound to the glory of both, because of their intimate union and because both are but one God.
sources.quote: Strictly speaking, no honour is paid to either, but what redounds to the glory of both; because of their intimate union; and because both are but one God.
