sources.raw_question: Does the worship of the Son, which is said not to terminate in the Son but in the Father, divide honour between them?

question: Does the immutability and incorporeality of God rule out the Son's being truly born from God the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The Arians use the true premise that God is incorporeal and immutable as a fallacious argument against the birth of God from God, but the earlier books refuted this from the Law and the Prophets. The truths of God's immutability and incorporeality are part of the Church's faith and are wrongly turned into an engine against it; the Son is truly born from God without contradicting them.
sources.quote: They use the fact, true in itself, that God is immutable and incorporeal, as an argument against the birth of the Son from Him.
sources.raised_by_detail: authors of the Arian manifesto (Arius' letter)
sources.raw_question: Does the immutability and incorporeality of God rule out the Son's being truly born from God the Father?

question: Do patristic phrases like 'before all ages' (πρὸ πάντων τῶν αἰώνων) and 'ante tempus', applied to the Son, mean strict eternity or only priority to created time?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: They mean strict eternity. Hilary, Alexander of Alexandria, the Sardican Fathers, the Catholic bishops at Ariminum and the Constantinopolitan creed all understood them so. The Arians equivocated on 'time' and 'ages' to evade this sense while keeping the words. The plain-spoken Ante-Nicene Catholics used the phrases in their common meaning of eternity.
sources.quote: The 4Arians indeed, equivocating upon the words time and ages, eluded the Catholic sense, still retaining the Catholic expression: but the Ante-Nicene Catholics were sincere, plain, honest men
sources.raw_question: Do patristic phrases like 'before all ages' (πρὸ πάντων τῶν αἰώνων) and 'ante tempus', applied to the Son, mean strict eternity or only priority to created time?

question: Does the Son owe his existence to an act of creation, as the human race does, or to a true generation from the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The blasphemy of these heretics is worse than the Jewish unbelief.
sources.answer: He comes from a true, eternal generation from the Father, not from creation. Gregory calls the Son's birth from the Father 'grand, sublime, ineffable' and 'before the ages'. To argue that the Son exists by creation, like everything that is born, repeats the Jewish rejection of His divine birth and is in fact a worse blasphemy.
sources.quote: these men in the same way deny His grand, sublime, ineffable generation from the Father, and would prove that He owes His existence to a creation, just as the human race, and all that is born, owe theirs.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son owe his existence to an act of creation, as the human race does, or to a true generation from the Father?

question: Do names like 'Father' and 'generation' mean the same thing when applied to God as when applied to human beings?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: No. Divine and human things share names, but the meanings differ in proportion to the gulf between the subjects. Scripture applies 'householder', 'house', limbs and senses to God symbolically, with a human sound but not a human meaning. So 'Father' also hides a distinction matching the difference between God and man.
sources.quote: As, then, each one of these names has a human sound, but not a human meaning, so also that of Father, while applying equally to life divine and human, hides a distinction between the uttered meanings exactly proportionate to the difference existing between the subjects of this title.
sources.raw_question: Do names like 'Father' and 'generation' mean the same thing when applied to God as when applied to human beings?

question: Does a father who generates another produce a different essence from his own, as illustrated by Adam generating Abel?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then shows, from the instance of Adam and Abel, and other examples, the absence of alienation of essence in the case of the “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. Adam did not generate another essence besides himself but generated another self, with whom the whole definition of the begetter's essence was produced. By analogy, the Father's generating the Son does not produce an essence alien to the Father's, so 'ungenerate' and 'generate' do not imply different essences.
sources.quote: We cannot therefore properly say that Adam generated another essence besides himself, but rather that of himself he generated another self, with whom was produced the whole definition of the essence of him who generated him.
sources.raw_question: Does a father who generates another produce a different essence from his own, as illustrated by Adam generating Abel?

question: Should a defense of the Trinity begin with the scriptural revelation of the doctrine or with its philosophical explanation in terms like essence, substance and person?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: It should begin with the revelation. The plain revelation that there is one God, and that the Father, Son and Holy Ghost are each God, must first be established and believed; the explanations come after and serve only for further edification. Opponents act preposterously by attacking the explanatory terms while ignoring the revelation from which they are deduced.
sources.quote: they will always begin their opposition, not unto the revelation of it, but unto the explanation of it; which is used only for farther edification.
sources.raw_question: Should a defense of the Trinity begin with the scriptural revelation of the doctrine or with its philosophical explanation in terms like essence, substance and person?

question: Do terms like Trinity, essence, substance, person and properties have independent, original weight in the doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. They are explanatory deductions from the scriptural revelation, not of original consideration. If the revelation is confirmed, they follow of themselves and believers will not object to them; if it is rejected, they fall and no one would contend for them.
sources.quote: Let the direct, express revelations of the doctrine be confirmed, they will follow of themselves, nor will be excepted against by those who believe and receive it.
sources.raw_question: Do terms like Trinity, essence, substance, person and properties have independent, original weight in the doctrine of the Trinity?

question: What exactly must be proved from Scripture to establish the doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: That God is one; that this one God is Father, Son and Holy Ghost; and that the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Ghost is God, each to be believed in, obeyed and worshipped as first cause and last end. The only original dispute is with those who deny one of these propositions, and each can be confirmed by Scripture testimony.
sources.quote: that God is one; that this one God is Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; so that the Father is God, so also is the Son, and the Holy Ghost likewise, and, as such, are to be believed in, obeyed, worshipped, acknowledged
sources.raw_question: What exactly must be proved from Scripture to establish the doctrine of the Trinity?

question: Does the Son's unique knowledge and revelation of the Father show that he is not a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son as a work could know the Father, all works would know Him in proportion to their measure; but no originate being can see or know God. Since Christ says no one knows the Father save the Son, He differs from all originate things and alone knows the Father because He alone is proper to Him as true Son.
sources.quote: For could He, a work, possibly know the Father, then must the Father be also known by all according to the proportion of the measures of each: for all of them are works as He is.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's unique knowledge and revelation of the Father show that he is not a creature?

question: What, according to the Catholic tradition summed up by Augustine, makes Father, Son, and Holy Spirit one God while remaining three Persons?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: The same homogeneous substance together with inseparability. The sameness of substance makes each Hypostasis a res divina, truly divine. Their inseparability makes all three una substantia, one undivided or numerical substance, and so one God. Hence each Person singly is God and Almighty, yet together they are not three Gods or three Almighties but one God Almighty.
sources.quote: The same homogeneous substance, and inseparability. The first makes each Hypostasis, ves divina; the last makes all to be una substantia, wna summa res, one undivided, or individual, or numerical substance; one God.
sources.raw_question: What, according to the Catholic tradition summed up by Augustine, makes Father, Son, and Holy Spirit one God while remaining three Persons?

question: In what sense can the Son be called unoriginate, and in what sense not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He declares falsely that 'the manner of the generation is to be known from the intrinsic worth of the generator'.
sources.answer: If 'unoriginate' means deriving existence from no cause whatever, it belongs only to the Father. But origin has other meanings, such as the origin of creation, time, or order, and in these senses the Son is also beyond origin. He through whom all things were made is above creation, time and sequence. So the Son is unoriginate but not ungenerate.
sources.quote: while the Father is unoriginate and Ungenerate, the Son is unoriginate in the way we have said, though not ungenerate.
sources.raw_question: In what sense can the Son be called unoriginate, and in what sense not?

question: Is ungeneracy the only intrinsic character of the Father, so that it alone should determine our understanding of the Son's generation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He declares falsely that 'the manner of the generation is to be known from the intrinsic worth of the generator'.
sources.answer: No. If the other divine names are meaningless, listing them is pointless. But if each has its proper force, God's intrinsic dignities must be viewed in the whole list. Eunomius isolates ungeneracy only in order to establish an unlikeness between Father and Son.
sources.quote: Why do they pronounce this ‘Ungeneracy’ to be the only intrinsic character in the Father, and thrust all the rest aside? It is in order that they may establish their mischievous mode of unlikeness of Father and Son
sources.raw_question: Is ungeneracy the only intrinsic character of the Father, so that it alone should determine our understanding of the Son's generation?

question: Can Christ rightly be called a creature of God if saving faith consists in confessing him as the Son of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. If the saving name expresses the truth, there is no authority to call him a creature. Salvation comes from confessing the Son, not from confessing a creature.
sources.quote: If the name express the truth, by what authority can He be called a creature? It is not the confession of a creature, but the confession of the Son, which shall give us salvation.
sources.raw_question: Can Christ rightly be called a creature of God if saving faith consists in confessing him as the Son of God?

question: Was the Son of God sent by the Holy Spirit, as the prophets and apostles were?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter I. Not only were the prophets and apostles sent by the Spirit, but also the Son of God. This is proved from Isaiah and the evangelists, and it is explained why St. Luke wrote that the same Spirit descended like a dove upon Christ and abode upon Him. Next, after establishing this mission of Christ, the writer infers that the Son is sent by the Father and the Spirit, as the Spirit is by the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ himself read Isaiah's words "The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me... He hath sent Me to preach the Gospel" and declared them fulfilled in himself. Isaiah 48 also has the speaker say "the Lord God hath sent Me and His Spirit," which can only be the one who came from the Father to save sinners.
sources.quote: now we add what all will rightly wonder at, and not be able to doubt, that the Spirit was upon Christ; and that as He sent the Spirit, so the Spirit sent the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: Was the Son of God sent by the Holy Spirit, as the prophets and apostles were?

question: Can there be any Fulness, Principle, Power, or God above the Creator of heaven and earth?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter I.—There is but one God: the impossibility of its being otherwise.
sources.answer: No. God, as the Pleroma of all things, must contain all things in His immensity and be contained by no one. If anything existed beyond Him, it would be wanting to Him, and He would no longer be the Fulness of all nor contain all.
sources.quote: it is matter of necessity that God, the Pleroma (Fulness) of all these, should contain all things in His immensity, and should be contained by no one? But if there is anything beyond Him, He is not then the Pleroma of all
sources.raw_question: Can there be any Fulness, Principle, Power, or God above the Creator of heaven and earth?

question: Is a trusting knowledge of God the Father sufficient for salvation without acknowledging the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. There is no true knowledge of God the Father except in God the Son. Christ says no one comes to the Father but by him, and John teaches that whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, while whoever abides in the doctrine of Christ has both the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: Do you say, is not a trustful knowledge of God the Father sufficient? Scripture answers there is no true knowledge of God the Father, except in God the Son
sources.raw_question: Is a trusting knowledge of God the Father sufficient for salvation without acknowledging the Son?

question: Does denying the Godhead of the Son count as the 'denial of the Son' that Scripture condemns?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture proves the Son shares the same divine essence as the Father, so denying his Godhead is the clearest case of denying the Son. Such denial destroys the glory of his Person and empties the atonement of its virtue. It also charges the Church with idolatry and Scripture with equivocation. Whoever denies Christ's Deity does not believe the record God has given of his Son.
sources.quote: what can denial of the Son be, if to deny his Godhead be not this negation?
sources.raw_question: Does denying the Godhead of the Son count as the 'denial of the Son' that Scripture condemns?

question: Does Christ's saying to Mary, "I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God," show that the Son is a servant of God sharing no community of nature with the Father, just as the disciples do not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > This twelfth book gives a notable interpretation of the words of the Lord to Mary, “Touch Me not, for I am not yet ascended to My Father.”
sources.answer: No. The words were spoken by Him who humbled Himself to the level of human littleness, and so they do not apply to the Godhead of the Only-begotten. They are not a proof of the Son's degradation but the glad tidings of our reconciliation to God: the Father has become again the God and Father of humanity through Christ's assumed humanity.
sources.quote: Now that the words addressed to Mary are not applicable to the Godhead of the Only-begotten, one may learn from the intention with which they were uttered. For He Who humbled Himself to a level with human littleness, He it is Who spake the words.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying to Mary, "I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God," show that the Son is a servant of God sharing no community of nature with the Father, just as the disciples do not?

question: Does the fact that the same relative term 'God and Father' is used of Christ and of the disciples imply either that the disciples share the Father's essence or that the Son does not?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > This twelfth book gives a notable interpretation of the words of the Lord to Mary, “Touch Me not, for I am not yet ascended to My Father.”
sources.answer: No. The opponents' dilemma fails because the phrase refers to the Son in His assumed humanity, the first-fruits of our nature, not to His Godhead. The Father becoming 'our God and Father' is a restored relation won for humanity through Christ, not a statement about the Son's divine nature.
sources.quote: And the words are not a proof of the degradation of the Son, but the glad tidings of our reconciliation to God.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the same relative term 'God and Father' is used of Christ and of the disciples imply either that the disciples share the Father's essence or that the Son does not?

question: Is confessing Jesus as 'the Christ' sufficient for saving faith, or must one confess Him as the Son of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: One must confess Him as the Son of God. Christ asked the healed blind man 'Dost thou believe on the Son of God?' rather than 'in Christ', because heretics would confess the name Christ while denying His Sonship; so He requires faith in what is peculiar to Himself, His divine Sonship. Martha's confession of Him as Christ the Son of God is likewise called eternal life.
sources.quote: Surely, if a simple confession of Christ, leaving His nature in obscurity, were a complete expression of the faith, the terms of the question would have been, ‘Dost thou believe in Christ?’
sources.raw_question: Is confessing Jesus as 'the Christ' sufficient for saving faith, or must one confess Him as the Son of God?

question: Does calling the Word 'another' beside the Father mean there are two Gods?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. The Word is 'another' only as light from light, water from a fountain, or a ray from the sun. There is but one power, which is from the All, and the Father is the All from whom this Power, the Word, comes forth; so the Son is distinct without being a second God.
sources.quote: But when I say another, I do not mean that there are two Gods, but that it is only as light of light, or as water from a fountain, or as a ray from the sun.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Word 'another' beside the Father mean there are two Gods?

question: Is the Son alone of the Father in a way that distinguishes Him from created things?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: Yes. All things are made by the Son, but He alone is from the Father. He is the Father's mind and power which came forth into the world and was manifested as the Son of God.
sources.quote: All things, then, are by Him, and He alone is of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son alone of the Father in a way that distinguishes Him from created things?

question: Can the Son's eternity be proved from the fact that he is the power and wisdom of God, and God was never without power and wisdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Son, According to the Apostle, is the Power and Wisdom of the Father. Hence the Reasoning of the Catholics Against the Earlier Arians. A Difficulty is Raised, Whether the Father is Not Wisdom Himself, But Only the Father of Wisdom.
sources.answer: Catholics used this argument against the Arians. If the Son is God's power and wisdom, and it is senseless to say God ever lacked these, then there was no time when the Son was not. Augustine reports the argument with approval. He notes, however, that it seems to compel the conclusion that the Father is wise only through the Wisdom he begot, which he goes on to examine.
sources.quote: If the Son of God is the power and wisdom of God, and God was never without power and wisdom, then the Son is co-eternal with God the Father
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's eternity be proved from the fact that he is the power and wisdom of God, and God was never without power and wisdom?

question: Why are human beings united with one another differently from how the Son is united with the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Because like is naturally one with like: all men share one nature and so become one with each other in good disposition, but the Word is unlike us and like the Father. Hence He is one with the Father in nature and truth, while we are one only by agreement modeled on that natural unity.
sources.quote: For like things are naturally one with like; thus all flesh is ranked together in kind; but the Word is unlike us and like the Father.
sources.raw_question: Why are human beings united with one another differently from how the Son is united with the Father?

question: Does counting Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three hypostases lead to a plurality of gods?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: No. Each hypostasis is proclaimed singly: one God and Father, one Only-begotten, one Holy Spirit. They are not counted by addition from unity to multitude, so no second God arises. God says, "I am the first, and I am the last."
sources.quote: We proclaim each of the hypostases singly; and, when count we must, we do not let an ignorant arithmetic carry us away to the idea of a plurality of Gods.
sources.raw_question: Does counting Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three hypostases lead to a plurality of gods?

question: Why is the worship (doxology) given to the Father and the Son one rather than two?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: Because the sovereignty and authority over us is one, and the honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype. Since the Son is the Father's image by nature, worship of him is not a second, separate worship.
sources.quote: The sovereignty and authority over us is one, and so the doxology ascribed by us is not plural but one; because the honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype.
sources.raw_question: Why is the worship (doxology) given to the Father and the Son one rather than two?

question: Can the Only-begotten Son, through whom all things were made, be numbered among created things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. To make the Lord, whose power over all things is only-begotten, one of the things made by Him is impious and degrades His unspeakable glory. Scripture nowhere joins His pre-temporal glory with the subject creation. And John teaches that all things were made by the Word, which could not be true if He were Himself counted among the things made.
sources.quote: striving to show that the Lord Whose power over all things is only-begotten, is one of the things that were made by Him
sources.raw_question: Can the Only-begotten Son, through whom all things were made, be numbered among created things?

question: Can the Holy Spirit depart from those who have received Him?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Like health or heat in the body, the Spirit is often a variable condition in the soul, not abiding with those whose unstable will easily rejects the grace received. Saul and the seventy elders (except Eldad and Medad) illustrate this.
sources.quote: He does not abide with those who, on account of the instability of their will, easily reject the grace which they have received. An instance of this is seen in Saul,
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit depart from those who have received Him?

question: In what respects do adopted believers have fellowship with Jesus Christ through their adoption as sons of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: Adoption is the head and source of all the privileges Christ purchased, and in it believers share with Christ in many ways. They share his name as sons of God and his title as co-heirs. They are predestined to be like him, the first-born, and he is not ashamed to call them brethren. They also share in his sufferings, since every received son is scourged, and in his kingdom, since they shall reign with him.
sources.quote: fellowship in name; we are (as he is) sons of God: fellowship in title and right; we are heirs, co-heirs with Christ: fellowship in likeness and conformity; we are predestinated to be like the first-born of the family
sources.raw_question: In what respects do adopted believers have fellowship with Jesus Christ through their adoption as sons of God?

question: Did Christ begin to exist only at his birth from Mary, so that he was not pre-existent?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The Church, taught by the Apostles, recognises a birth of Christ but no beginning. The one born of Mary is the same pre-existent Son of God, not a mere man who began to exist at that moment.
sources.quote: the faith of the Church, inspired by the teaching of the Apostles, has recognised a birth of Christ, but no beginning.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ begin to exist only at his birth from Mary, so that he was not pre-existent?

question: In what capacity do believers have fellowship with the second person of the Trinity, the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Believers have fellowship with the Son as Mediator. This is the office he submitted to by dispensation for our sakes, being made of a woman and made under the law to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.
sources.quote: the fellowship we have with the second person, is with him as Mediator, — in that office whereunto, by dispensation, he submitted himself for our sakes
sources.raw_question: In what capacity do believers have fellowship with the second person of the Trinity, the Son?

question: How does 1 John 1:1-2, speaking of the "Word of Life" and the "Life which was with the Father," show that both the Father and the Son are Life?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XV. The Holy Spirit is Life equally with the Father and the Son, in truth whether the Father be mentioned, with Whom is the Fount of Life, or the Son, that Fount can be none other than the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: John uses both expressions, "Word of Life" and "Life," in order to signify that both Father and Son are Life. The "Word of Life" is the Word of God, so the phrase shows that God and his Word are both Life.
sources.quote: He said both Word of Life and Life that he might signify both the Father and the Son to be Life. For what is the Word of Life but the Word of God?
sources.raw_question: How does 1 John 1:1-2, speaking of the "Word of Life" and the "Life which was with the Father," show that both the Father and the Son are Life?

question: Does the Son's prayer to be glorified by the Father show that he lacked glory or power, since one who is about to give glory should not need to ask for it?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. Hilary admits the Father is greater, as Unbegotten, Sender, and the one who wills. But the prayer 'glorify thy Son' is completed by 'that thy Son may glorify thee,' so the Son repays the glory he receives. The Father was never in want, and the Son never needed to ask, yet each gives glory to the other. Such paradoxes are grasped by faith, not by philosophers' syllogisms.
sources.quote: Thus there is no lack of power in the Son, Who, when He has received this glory, will make His return for it in glory.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's prayer to be glorified by the Father show that he lacked glory or power, since one who is about to give glory should not need to ask for it?

question: In what sense does the Father precede the Son if the Son is always in the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: The Father precedes the Son only in a certain sense, as the one without beginning goes before the one who has an origin by being born. The Father alone knows no beginning, while the Son has an origin because he is born of that Father. This priority is one of origin, not of time, since the Son is before all time.
sources.quote: Because it is essential that He who knows no beginning must go before Him who has a beginning
sources.raw_question: In what sense does the Father precede the Son if the Son is always in the Father?

question: How is the Son related in order to creation and to the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: He is before all things but after the Father. All things come after him because they were made through him, and he proceeded from the Father, by whose will all things were made.
sources.quote: And reasonably, He is before all things, but after the Father, since all things were made by Him, and He proceeded from Him of whose will all things were made.
sources.raw_question: How is the Son related in order to creation and to the Father?

question: Is the subject-matter of John 1:1-3 the new creation by the preaching of the gospel, so that "all things were made by him" means only spiritual renewal?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. This claim is plainly false, and the words will not bear such a sense. No evidence is offered for it except further perversions of other equally clear testimonies. The text speaks of the Word making the world and all things in heaven and earth.
sources.quote: But this is plainly false; nor will the words allow any such sense, nor the contempt, nor is any thing offered to give evidence unto this corrupt perverting of the words
sources.raw_question: Is the subject-matter of John 1:1-3 the new creation by the preaching of the gospel, so that "all things were made by him" means only spiritual renewal?

question: Is God's Fatherhood toward the Son the same kind of thing as his being Creator of the world, so that both are due to an energy?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory charges that Eunomius treats Fatherhood and creative power alike as energies. If both names come from energies as their cause, their results must be homogeneous, which would make the Son a creature on a level with the world. Gregory rejects this as plainly blasphemous.
sources.quote: If, then, it is the same thing to call Him Father and Creator of the world because either name is due to an energy as its cause, the results of His energies must be homogeneous
sources.raw_question: Is God's Fatherhood toward the Son the same kind of thing as his being Creator of the world, so that both are due to an energy?

question: Does calling the Son a creature reduce him to the servile condition of creation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > This third book shows a third fall of Eunomius, as refuting himself, and sometimes saying that the Son is to be called Only-begotten in virtue of natural generation, and that Holy Scripture proves this from the first; at other times, that by reason of His being created He should not be called a Son, but a “product,” or “creature.”
sources.answer: Yes, and therefore it is impious. Paul teaches that all creation is in bondage, whereas the Son rules with his power for ever, has pre-eminence in all things, is Lord and God over all, and is the one through whom all creation was made. To apply the name "creation" to him is to bring the Lord of all down to the level of the servile nature.
sources.quote: If then on the one hand Paul proclaims aloud “the creation is in bondage,” and on the other the Only-begotten God is truly Lord and God over all, and John bears witness to the fact that the whole creation of the things that were made is by Him
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son a creature reduce him to the servile condition of creation?

question: If the name "Son" rests on natural generation, can the Son's relation to the Father be the relation of a thing made to its maker?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > This third book shows a third fall of Eunomius, as refuting himself, and sometimes saying that the Son is to be called Only-begotten in virtue of natural generation, and that Holy Scripture proves this from the first; at other times, that by reason of His being created He should not be called a Son, but a “product,” or “creature.”
sources.answer: No. Eunomius himself admits that the "order of nature" confirms the name Son because he is begotten, so the name expresses the relation of Begotten to Begetter. To turn that into the relation of thing made to maker contradicts his own definition. It also strips the name of any distinctive meaning, since that relation applies equally to a gnat or an ant.
sources.quote: how comes it that he wrests the significance of the word “Son” from its natural application, and changes the relation to “the thing made and its maker”—a relation which applies not only in the case of the elements of the universe, but might also be asserted of a gnat or an ant
sources.raw_question: If the name "Son" rests on natural generation, can the Son's relation to the Father be the relation of a thing made to its maker?

question: Does being baptized in the name of the Son and the Holy Spirit imply that they are the Lord God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Conclusion of the Book with a Prayer, and an Apology for Multitude of Words.
sources.answer: Yes. God would not bid us be baptized in the name of one who is not the Lord God. Baptism in the name of the Son and the Spirit therefore implies that they share the divinity of the Father.
sources.quote: Nor wouldest thou, O Lord God, bid us to be baptized in the name of Him who is not the Lord God.
sources.raw_question: Does being baptized in the name of the Son and the Holy Spirit imply that they are the Lord God?

question: Should the analogy that likens the Holy Spirit to a spouse of the Father and mother of the Son (the family analogy of father, mother and child as the image of the Trinity) be rejected, and on what grounds?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Why This Opinion is to Be Rejected.
sources.answer: Yes, it is to be rejected, but not because the image of the Spirit as spouse is distasteful. The reason is that Scripture shows it to be false: man was made in the image of God as an individual, the image of the whole Trinity, not in a trio of father, mother and son. The Spirit is from the Father but not as offspring and not to beget the Word.
sources.quote: We do not therefore reject this opinion, because we fear to think of that holy and inviolable and unchangeable Love, as the spouse of God the Father, existing as it does from Him, but not as an offspring in order to beget the Word
sources.raw_question: Should the analogy that likens the Holy Spirit to a spouse of the Father and mother of the Son (the family analogy of father, mother and child as the image of the Trinity) be rejected, and on what grounds?

question: Does God's being called the Fountain of wisdom and life imply that the Son, who is Wisdom and Life, is eternal?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: Yes. Since God is called the Fountain of living waters and of wisdom, life and wisdom are proper to His essence and never were without existence. The Son is this Life and Wisdom, so to say 'once the Son was not' is to say the Fountain was once dry and barren. And what does not beget from itself is no fountain; if the Fountain is eternal, the Wisdom must be eternal too.
sources.quote: truth witnessing that God is the eternal Fountain of His proper Wisdom; and, if the Fountain be eternal, the Wisdom also must needs be eternal.
sources.raw_question: Does God's being called the Fountain of wisdom and life imply that the Son, who is Wisdom and Life, is eternal?

question: Is the Son owed the same honour as the Father, and does that equal honour show that the Son is not a creature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. Being in the form of God is being equal with God, and Christ says all should honour the Son as they honour the Father. Different natures require different degrees of honour. If a creature received the Father's honour, the Father would be honoured only as a creature. Since the Son is born God from God, he is equal in honour because he is a Son and not a creature.
sources.quote: But since He is equal to God the Father, inasmuch as He is born as God from Him, He is also equal to Him in honour, for He is a Son and not a creature.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son owed the same honour as the Father, and does that equal honour show that the Son is not a creature?

question: Is believing that Jesus Christ is truly the Son of God necessary for salvation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. The only way to eternal life is the assurance that Jesus Christ, God the Only-begotten, is the Son of God, and denying this means death. Faith is demanded in the question "Dost thou believe on the Son of God?", and confessing that name brings salvation.
sources.quote: there is no other way to eternal life than the assurance that Jesus Christ, God the Only-begotten, is the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Is believing that Jesus Christ is truly the Son of God necessary for salvation?

question: Do the terms 'generate' and 'ungenerate' admit any middle term or degrees between them?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then, again discussing the true Light and unapproachable Light of the Father and of the Son, special attributes, community and essence, and showing the relation of “generate” and “ungenerate,” as involving no opposition in sense, but presenting an opposition and contradiction admitting of no middle term, he ends the book.
sources.answer: No. They are an opposite and contradictory pair admitting no middle term, like asleep/not asleep or was/was not, where the denial of one is the assertion of the other. What one expresses has nothing to do with what the other expresses in the way of more or less.
sources.quote: we conceived having been generated not as a diminution of not having been generated, but as an opposite and contradictory not admitting of any middle term
sources.raw_question: Do the terms 'generate' and 'ungenerate' admit any middle term or degrees between them?

question: Is the mutual indwelling of Father and Son a kind of reciprocal emanation, or one body contained inside another?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Bodies cannot mutually contain each other or share the perfect unity of one abiding nature. The Son's being in the Father comes from their unity in one nature through birth given and received. For Christ, to be and to be in God are the same thing. He is within the subsisting God while having a subsistence of his own.
sources.quote: this being in God is not the presence of one thing within another, as a body inside another body, but that the life and subsistence of Christ is such that He is within the subsisting God, and within Him, yet having a subsistence of His own.
sources.raw_question: Is the mutual indwelling of Father and Son a kind of reciprocal emanation, or one body contained inside another?

question: Does the doctrine that the Only-begotten Son is generated from God amount to belief in two Gods?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The doctrine of generation is guiltless of ditheism. The Son, born into the Godhead, shows in himself the very nature of the God who begot him. He is not different from or inferior to the Father, so there is one Godhead in Father and Son.
sources.quote: the doctrine of the generation of the Only-begotten is guiltless of ditheism, for the Son of God, in being born into the Godhead, manifested in Himself the nature of God His Begetter.
sources.raw_question: Does the doctrine that the Only-begotten Son is generated from God amount to belief in two Gods?

question: Does the Son's being 'sanctified' by the Father imply that he has a different and inferior nature to the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. The Father may designate, appoint, or consecrate the Son, in either his divine or human capacity, to the office of Mediator without implying an inferior nature. Or the sanctifying may refer to the human nature, which the Father sanctified by uniting it to the Logos.
sources.quote: May not the Father design, appoint, consecrate his Son, considered in either capacity, to the office of Mediator, without supposing him of a different and inferior nature to him?
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being 'sanctified' by the Father imply that he has a different and inferior nature to the Father?

question: Is Christ called God in Scripture in the same full sense as the Father, rather than in a subordinate sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is called God in as high a sense as the Father, first because he is called Jehovah, a name of absolute signification and the incommunicable name of the one true God. Texts addressed to Jehovah in the Old Testament are applied to Christ in the New, and Luke 1:16-17 calls him 'the Lord their God.'
sources.quote: Because he is called the Jehovah, which is a word of absolute signification, and is the incommunicable name of the one true God.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ called God in Scripture in the same full sense as the Father, rather than in a subordinate sense?

question: Do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit ever act separately, so that one Person has an operation peculiar to himself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. Scripture never teaches that the Father does anything by himself without the Son working with him, or that the Son has any operation apart from the Spirit. Every operation from God toward creation originates from the Father, proceeds through the Son, and is perfected in the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: every operation which extends from God to the Creation, and is named according to our variable conceptions of it, has its origin from the Father, and proceeds through the Son, and is perfected in the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit ever act separately, so that one Person has an operation peculiar to himself?

question: Since life is given by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, do we receive three lives or have three Givers of life?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. Although there are three Persons and three names, one and the same life is wrought by the Father, prepared by the Son, and depends on the will of the Spirit. Because the result is one, we do not speak of three Givers of life. In the same way we do not speak of three Good beings, or use the plural for any other divine attribute.
sources.quote: we do not consider that we have had bestowed upon us three lives, one from each Person separately; but the same life is wrought in us by the Father, and prepared by the Son, and depends on the will of the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Since life is given by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, do we receive three lives or have three Givers of life?

question: Is Christ the one who dispenses the graces and consolations of the Holy Spirit to the saints?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen speaks of the dispensations of Christ's Holy Spirit, by which the saints receive supplies of grace and consolation. He presents this as one of Christ's excellencies, alongside his dispensing of the pardon and reconciliation he purchased.
sources.quote: Lovely in all those supplies of grace and consolations, in all the dispensations of his Holy Spirit, whereof his saints are made partakers.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ the one who dispenses the graces and consolations of the Holy Spirit to the saints?

question: Can the Father be manifested without the Son, or the Son without the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: No. Neither can be manifested without the other, because they are one, as Christ says: 'My Father and I are one.' So it makes no difference whether we hear 'Show us the Son' or 'Show us the Father.'
sources.quote: it is even all one, since neither can be manifested without the other. For they are one, as He also Himself says, "My Father and I are one."
sources.raw_question: Can the Father be manifested without the Son, or the Son without the Father?

question: Is the gift of the Holy Spirit given equally to all, or in different measures to different people?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: The gift is one and is offered fully to everyone, but each person receives it according to how willing they are to receive it. It is denied to no one, and the more earnestly a person desires it, the richer it becomes for them. The Spirit remains with believers until the end of the world as the light of the mind and the pledge of future hope.
sources.quote: That Gift, which is in Christ, is One, yet offered, and offered fully, to all; denied to none, and given to each according to the measure of his willingness to receive
sources.raw_question: Is the gift of the Holy Spirit given equally to all, or in different measures to different people?

question: Is it legitimate to argue from the nature of 'all generation' in the created world to conclusions about the Son's divine generation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He further shows that the pretemporal generation of the Son is not the subject of influences drawn from ordinary and carnal generation, but is without beginning and without end, and not according to the fabrications constructed by Eunomius, in ignorance of His power, from the statements of Plato concerning the soul and from the sabbath rest of the Hebrews.
sources.answer: No. It is irreverent to make ordinary nature our teacher about the being of the Only-begotten. Bodily generation involves the union of parents, formation in the womb, travail, place and time. All of these are alien to the Divine generation. Whatever the term 'generation' means in creatures has no common ground with the unsullied Nature.
sources.quote: Is it a reverent proceeding to draw from “all generation” evidence even as to the pre-temporal generation of the Son? and ought we to put forward ordinary nature as our instructor on the being of the Only-begotten?
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to argue from the nature of 'all generation' in the created world to conclusions about the Son's divine generation?

question: Since nothing is more present to the mind than itself, how can the mind be said to seek and find itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Opinions of Philosophers Respecting the Substance of the Soul. The Error of Those Who are of Opinion that the Soul is Corporeal, Does Not Arise from Defective Knowledge of the Soul, But from Their Adding There to Something Foreign to It. What is Meant by Finding.
sources.answer: The mind does not seek itself as if it were absent to itself, for nothing is so present to the mind as the mind itself. To 'find' or 'invent' means to 'come into' what is sought. The mind finds things through itself, without bodily sense, whether the higher substance in God or the parts of the soul. Its error comes from what it adds to itself, so it must withdraw that addition rather than seek itself as though withdrawn.
sources.quote: let it not seek itself as though it were withdrawn from itself; but let it withdraw that which it has added to itself
sources.raw_question: Since nothing is more present to the mind than itself, how can the mind be said to seek and find itself?

question: Does Christ's reference to 'Him Who alone is God' (John 5:44) exclude the Son from being the only God whose glory is to be sought?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Christ gives as the reason they do not seek the glory of the only God that they reject Him and receive Antichrist. Since rejecting Him is neglecting the glory of the only God, His glory is the glory of the only God, and He does not separate Himself from it.
sources.quote: To reject Him is to neglect the glory of the only God; is not, then, His glory the glory of the only God, if to receive Him steadfastly was to seek the glory of the only God?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's reference to 'Him Who alone is God' (John 5:44) exclude the Son from being the only God whose glory is to be sought?

question: How can the Psalm say Christ "received gifts in men" while Paul says he "gave gifts to men"?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the Scriptures. By the Gift of the Holy Spirit is Meant the Gift Which is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is Specially Called Love, Although Not Only the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is Love.
sources.answer: Both are true, since both carry the authority of a divine utterance. Christ gave to men as the head gives to his members. He also received in men, as in his own members. This is shown by his saying "Saul, why persecutest thou me?" and "ye have done it unto me." So Christ both gave from heaven and received on earth.
sources.quote: He gave to men, as the head to His own members: He Himself that gave, received in men, no doubt as in His own members
sources.raw_question: How can the Psalm say Christ "received gifts in men" while Paul says he "gave gifts to men"?

question: In Athanasius's usage, when δημιούργημα (work) and δημιουργός (maker) are applied to God, do they mean the same as κτίσις (creature) and κτίσας (creator), so that calling the Son a δημιούργημα would make him a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 12: Whether the Creator of all things was not himself uncreated ; and therefore could not be ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, made out of nothing ?
sources.answer: Yes. In Athanasius's comparison between admiring the works before the craftsman and worshipping the creature rather than the Creator, δημιουργήματα and δημιουργόν correspond to κτίσει and κτίσαντα. Waterland therefore concludes that, when used of God, the first pair is equivalent to the second. On this reading, placing the Son among the δημιουργήματα would amount to calling him a creature, which Athanasius rejects.
sources.quote: words δημιουργήματα and δημιουργὸν answer, in the similitude and analogy, to κτίσει and κτίσαντα, going before.
sources.raw_question: In Athanasius's usage, when δημιούργημα (work) and δημιουργός (maker) are applied to God, do they mean the same as κτίσις (creature) and κτίσας (creator), so that calling the Son a δημιούργημα would make him a creature?

question: Does the Son's being eternal and uncreated entail that he is omniscient?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: Yes. Following Irenaeus's argument against the Valentinians, a creature who has a beginning cannot claim omniscience, but the Son, as eternal and uncreated and always coexisting with God, can. Irenaeus also holds that true Wisdom, which the Son is, cannot be ignorant of anything.
sources.quote: How then could he imagine that the true Sophia, wisdom itself, could be ignorant of any thing?
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being eternal and uncreated entail that he is omniscient?

question: Does the Son's power to forgive sins and free humanity from God's sentence show that he is not a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says pardoning iniquity is God's own doing, and originate things cannot undo sin. The Son who makes us free thus shows he is the proper Word and Image of the Father's essence, the one who at the beginning sentenced and alone remits sins.
sources.quote: the Son, who made free, has shewn in truth that He is no creature, nor one of things originate, but the proper Word and Image of the Father’s Essence, who at the beginning sentenced, and alone remitteth sins.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's power to forgive sins and free humanity from God's sentence show that he is not a creature?

question: How is the Spirit bestowed on believers through the mediation of Christ, given that the Father gives the Spirit yet Christ says he sends him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: The Father, who holds the original and sovereign dispensation, gives the Spirit upon Christ's intercession, and Christ, having received the Holy Ghost according to promise, actually sends and sheds him on his own. So the Father gives the Spirit into Christ's hand for us, and Christ bestows him.
sources.quote: Receiving, according to promise, the Holy Ghost, Acts ii. 33, he sheds him abroad on his own.
sources.raw_question: How is the Spirit bestowed on believers through the mediation of Christ, given that the Father gives the Spirit yet Christ says he sends him?

question: Does Christ's prayer to the Father, 'that they may know Thee the one true God' (John 17:3), show that the Son is not true God, as the Arians argue?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Whether One or the Three Persons Together are Called the Only God.
sources.answer: No. Augustine sets aside the Arian reading and proposes that the words may be ordered as 'That they may know Thee, and Jesus Christ whom Thou hast sent, the one true God.' On this reading the Father and the Son together are the one true God. The text therefore need not be read as confining true deity to the Father alone.
sources.quote: so that the order of the words is this, “That they may know Thee, and Jesus Christ whom Thou hast sent, the one true God?”
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer to the Father, 'that they may know Thee the one true God' (John 17:3), show that the Son is not true God, as the Arians argue?

question: Should each of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be called the one true God, and the Trinity together one true God rather than three true Gods?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Whether One or the Three Persons Together are Called the Only God.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine suggests that, in line with the Lord's testimony, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit may each be called the one true God. The Trinity itself, taken together, is likewise not three true Gods but one true God. This is because the three share one and the same substance and are absolutely equal.
sources.quote: and the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together, that is, the Trinity itself together, not three true Gods but one true God?
sources.raw_question: Should each of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be called the one true God, and the Trinity together one true God rather than three true Gods?

question: Is the analogy of a seal and its impression an adequate image of the Son's divine birth from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No, not fully. In seals there is a distinct matter, a difference of nature between die and impression, and an act of impression by which a stronger nature stamps a more yielding one. None of this applies to the divine birth. The analogy is useful only for showing that the whole form of the Father is present in the Son.
sources.quote: Yet this comparison is not adequate to exemplify the Divine birth, because in seals there is a matter, difference of nature, and an act of impression, whereby the likeness of stronger natures is impressed upon things of a more yielding nature.
sources.raw_question: Is the analogy of a seal and its impression an adequate image of the Son's divine birth from the Father?

question: Is the Son, who is in the form of God, a God of another kind than the Father, as an impression differs in material from its die?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. It is foolish to think that the one God fashions to be God, pertaining to Himself, is anything but God. Even after the Incarnation and death on the cross, every tongue confesses that Jesus is in the glory of God the Father. So He must all the more have been in the divine nature while in the form of God.
sources.quote: At this point I ask whether He Who abides as God in the form of God is a God of another kind, as we perceive in the case of seals in respect of the likenesses which stamp and those which are stamped
sources.raw_question: Is the Son, who is in the form of God, a God of another kind than the Father, as an impression differs in material from its die?

question: Is the essence of the Only-begotten Son of God comprehensible to human knowledge?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The Son is truly God, eternally being what He is called, but His essential being is beyond the reach of curiosity that would comprehend it. He makes Himself known proportionately through the greatness and beauty of His creatures, granting faith through His works but not comprehension of what He is.
sources.quote: vouchsafing to us the gift of faith by the operations of His hands, but not the comprehension of what He is
sources.raw_question: Is the essence of the Only-begotten Son of God comprehensible to human knowledge?

question: Is the Creator of the world the only God, who took the pattern of creation from himself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVI.—The Creator of the world either produced of Himself the images of things to be made, or the Pleroma was formed after the image of some previous system; and so on ad infinitum.
sources.answer: Yes. It is safer and more accurate to confess at once that God the Creator who formed the world is the only God, with no other God besides him, and that he received the model and figure of created things from himself. Every rival scheme must eventually stop at some One from whom the configuration of things proceeded, so the regress gains nothing.
sources.quote: that this God, the Creator, who formed the world, is the only God, and that there is no other God besides Him—He Himself receiving from Himself the model and figure of those things which have been made
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of the world the only God, who took the pattern of creation from himself?

question: If the Son and the Holy Spirit give the same gift of eternal life as the Father, must they share the Father's true Godhead?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter III. As to know the Father and the Son is life, so is it life to know the Holy Spirit; and therefore in the Godhead He is not to be separated from the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Giving eternal life is the greatest gift of the only true Godhead, so whoever gives it must be true God. Denying this means saying a creature can give eternal life. That would actually insult the Father, because his chief work would then be no greater than a creature's work.
sources.quote: If the knowledge of the only true God confers the same benefit as the knowledge of the Son and of the Spirit, why do you sever the Son and the Spirit from the honour of the true God, when you do not sever Him from conferring the benefit?
sources.raw_question: If the Son and the Holy Spirit give the same gift of eternal life as the Father, must they share the Father's true Godhead?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be denied a share in the glory, inheritance, and reign with Christ that Scripture promises to believers?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That our opponents refuse to concede in the case of the Spirit the terms which Scripture uses in the case of men, as reigning together with Christ.
sources.answer: No. Believers are joint heirs with Christ, will be glorified and reign with him, and will sit together in heavenly places, all of which they receive through the Spirit. It is the height of folly to refuse the Spirit any share in the glory or fellowship of God and Christ that we receive from Him, as though He were not worthy of equal honour even with us.
sources.quote: refuse to assign to the Spirit any share in the sitting together, or in the glory, or anything else which we have received from Him
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be denied a share in the glory, inheritance, and reign with Christ that Scripture promises to believers?

question: Is it consistent to be baptized into and confess the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son while ranking the Spirit as a creature or a slave?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That our opponents refuse to concede in the case of the Spirit the terms which Scripture uses in the case of men, as reigning together with Christ.
sources.answer: No. We profess belief in the Spirit, are baptized, call on Him as the Prince of Life, and received Him with the Father and Son; to then dishonour Him as part of creation and a fellow-slave contradicts our own confession. Assigning Him the rank of a subordinate is doing despite to the Spirit of grace.
sources.quote: We call upon Him as the Prince of Life, and then despise Him as a slave like ourselves. We received Him with the Father and the Son, and we dishonour Him as a part of creation.
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to be baptized into and confess the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son while ranking the Spirit as a creature or a slave?

question: Is it legitimate to expound the doctrine of the Trinity using philosophical terms such as 'Supreme and Absolute Being', 'a second Being existing through the First', and 'a third Being', in place of the names Father, Son and Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Résumé of his dogmatic teaching. Objections to it in detail.
sources.answer: No. The Lord Himself handed down the mystery of the faith in the names Father, Son and Holy Ghost. If other names had been more appropriate, the Truth Himself would have found them, and so would the apostles, their successors and the councils whose traditions the churches preserve. To replace these names is to put one's own conceptions ahead of what was handed down by the voice of God.
sources.quote: And yet if those had been the more appropriate names, the Truth Himself would not have been at a loss to discover them, nor those men either, on whom successively devolved the preaching of the mystery
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to expound the doctrine of the Trinity using philosophical terms such as 'Supreme and Absolute Being', 'a second Being existing through the First', and 'a third Being', in place of the names Father, Son and Holy Spirit?

question: If being in another denied strict existence to the Son, would it also deny strict existence to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes, which shows the argument's absurdity. The Gospel teaches that just as the Son abides in the Father, so the Father abides in the Son, so by the Eunomian reasoning the Father too would not exist absolutely.
sources.quote: For if they make out that to exist in something is an indication of not existing in the strict sense, then certainly they allow that not even the Father exists absolutely
sources.raw_question: If being in another denied strict existence to the Son, would it also deny strict existence to the Father?

question: Does Eunomius's calling the Son 'God of all things after Him' actually grant the Son true deity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. Just as Moses was called 'a god to Pharaoh' while remaining a man in nature, Eunomius makes the Son one of the angels and merely covers this error with the title of God in an equivocal sense. Such a title gives superiority of authority, not superiority of nature over the angels.
sources.quote: Eunomius, while making out the Son to be one of the angels, salves over such an error by the appellation of Godhead, in the manner expressed, allowing Him the title of God in some equivocal sense.
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius's calling the Son 'God of all things after Him' actually grant the Son true deity?

question: Does the Son's living 'through the Father' (John 6:57) imply that his nature is different from or inferior to the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Hilary argues that just as we live naturally through Christ by sharing the nature of his flesh, so the Son must naturally have the Father within himself, since he lives through the Father. His birth gives him no alien or different nature: his being is from the Father, yet no unlikeness of nature divides him from the Father.
sources.quote: His birth has not implanted in Him an alien and different nature inasmuch as His very being is from Him yet is not divided from Him by any barrier of an unlikeness of nature
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's living 'through the Father' (John 6:57) imply that his nature is different from or inferior to the Father's?

question: Was the Son begotten from pre-existent matter, from nothing, or as a portion cut off from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: None of these. He was not begotten from matter, because all things are through the Son. He was not from nothing, because He is from the Father's own self.
