He was not a piece cut or stretched off, because God is passionless and bodiless. Rather, the Father begat Him ineffably from His own unbegotten substance before time.
sources.quote: not from any pre-existent matter, for all things are through the Son; not from nothing, for the Son is from the Father’s self; not by way of childbirth, for in God there is neither change nor void
sources.raw_question: Was the Son begotten from pre-existent matter, from nothing, or as a portion cut off from the Father?

question: Does the Son's obedience and subjection to the Father prove that the Son is not the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, Against the Sabellians He Proves that the Father is One, the Son Another.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture shows the Son always obeying the Father and holding power over all things as delivered and granted by the Father. If he were the Father, Christ would have to be subjected to another God the Father, which is absurd. So his obedience is the clearest proof that he is the Son and not the Father.
sources.quote: And what can be so evident proof that this is not the Father, but the Son; as that He is set forth as being obedient to God the Father, unless, if He be believed to be the Father, Christ may be said to be subjected to another God the Father?
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's obedience and subjection to the Father prove that the Son is not the Father?

question: Does Proverbs agree with John's Gospel that the Son, as Wisdom, is the Maker of all things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: Yes. As the evangelist comprehensively proclaims the Word to be the cause and Maker of all things, so Solomon says that the individual things included in the whole were made by Wisdom: God by Wisdom established the earth and in understanding prepared the heavens. Both speak first of the eternal power and energy of Wisdom.
sources.quote: For as the latter in his comprehensive phrase proclaimed Him to be the cause and Maker of all things, so Solomon says that by Him were made those individual things which are included in the whole.
sources.raw_question: Does Proverbs agree with John's Gospel that the Son, as Wisdom, is the Maker of all things?

question: Can the Father's essence be superior to the Son's in power, greatness or honour if the Son's essence is 'most proper'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He again shows Eunomius, constrained by truth, in the character of an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, confessing as most proper and primary, not only the essence of the Father, but the essence also of the Only-begotten.
sources.answer: No. What is something only imperfectly is not that thing 'most properly.' So a superiority of the Father's essence would prove the Son's essence imperfect and therefore not proper. If the Son's essence is 'most proper,' it is perfect. When the perfect is compared with the perfect, there can be no excess or defect, because perfection is one in both, like a rule showing neither hollow nor projection.
sources.quote: For that which is whatever it is imperfectly, is not that thing “most properly,” be it nature, or power, or rank, or any other individual object of contemplation
sources.raw_question: Can the Father's essence be superior to the Son's in power, greatness or honour if the Son's essence is 'most proper'?

question: Is the Father's love for believers eternal, existing before they existed?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father fixed his love on believers before the foundation of the world, before they existed or had done any good. From eternity he laid in his own bosom a design for their happiness, and the Son rejoiced in the thought of fulfilling the Father's delight.
sources.quote: It was fixed on us before the foundation of the world. Before we were, or had done the least good, then were his thoughts upon us
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's love for believers eternal, existing before they existed?

question: Is the Son's being begotten compatible with his never having been non-existent?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. He is not ingenerate, because he is born of the Father and bears witness to the Father as the source of his being. Yet he never was non-existent, because to have always been transcends time. Since he was born of One who eternally exists, he was not born of nothing.
sources.quote: He is not ingenerate, yet never was non-existent; since to have always been transcends time, and to have been born is birth.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's being begotten compatible with his never having been non-existent?

question: How does the Son, as the Wisdom of God, reveal the Father: through creation, through the Incarnation, or both?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Through both, in succession. The same Wisdom first showed itself, and through itself the Father, by its image impressed on creatures; this is why Wisdom is said to be 'created'. Because the world did not know God by that wisdom, the true Wisdom itself became flesh and died on the cross. Having abolished death, the Word revealed himself and the Father still more fully, so that believers might be saved through faith in him.
sources.quote: it is the same Wisdom of God, which through Its own Image in the creatures (whence also It is said to be created), first manifested Itself, and through Itself Its own Father; and afterwards, being Itself the Word, has 'become flesh,'
sources.raw_question: How does the Son, as the Wisdom of God, reveal the Father: through creation, through the Incarnation, or both?

question: Is it consistent to reject the divine unity of Father and Son in 'I and the Father are one' while using Christ's tears and sufferings to rank Him among creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Twelfthly, Matthew xxvi. 39; John xii. 27, &c. Arian inferences are against the Regula Fidei, as before. He wept and the like, as man. Other texts prove Him God. God could not fear. He feared because His flesh feared.
sources.answer: No. Such readers distort 'I and the Father are one' to separate Father and Son, yet ignore His body when reading of tears and sweat, ranking among creatures the one by whom creation was made. Divine sayings should be referred to His Godhead and human sufferings to His body; doing otherwise is like the Jews ascribing God's works to Beelzebub.
sources.quote: they violently distort the sense, and separate the unity of the Father and the Son; but reading of His tears or sweat or sufferings, they do not advert to His body
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to reject the divine unity of Father and Son in 'I and the Father are one' while using Christ's tears and sufferings to rank Him among creatures?

question: Do names of God divide into absolute names, relative names, and names that can be used both ways?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: Yes. Some names such as 'imperishable,' 'everlasting,' 'immortal' are absolute and contain a complete thought about the Deity; others such as Helper or Rescuer are purely relative, losing their force without one in need; and some, like 'God,' 'good,' and 'Father,' are both absolute and relative, as when 'the Lord God' becomes 'the Lord our God' or 'Father' becomes 'Our Father'.
sources.quote: Some, on the other hand, as we have said, are both absolute, and are also amongst the words of relation; ‘God,’ for instance, and ‘good,’ and many other such.
sources.raw_question: Do names of God divide into absolute names, relative names, and names that can be used both ways?

question: Is Jesus Christ one single person who possesses both the divine and human natures without separation, or two subjects, a Son of Man and a Son of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: He is one person. There is one Jesus Christ, Son of God and Son of Man, God the Word and Man in the flesh. That one Christ suffered, died, rose, and sits at God's right hand. In his single self he holds the form of God and the form of a servant, the human and the divine, without separation or division.
sources.quote: Who possesses in His one single self, according to the Divine Plan and nature, in the form of God and in the form of a servant, the Human and Divine without separation or division.
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus Christ one single person who possesses both the divine and human natures without separation, or two subjects, a Son of Man and a Son of God?

question: Does asserting that the Father and Son are two real things or Persons amount to teaching two separate, independent substances?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. The early writers' strong expressions of distinction (two things, two powers, two lights) were meant to guard against Sabellianism, and after Arianism arose they softened them to 'Light of Light', 'Essence of Essence'. The aim throughout was to assert a real distinction of Persons without teaching three absolute, independent or separate substances, so as not to divide the substance.
sources.quote: The design of all which was, so to assert a real distinction, as not to teach three absolute, independent, or separate substances ; so to maintain the distinction of persons, as not to divide the substance.
sources.raw_question: Does asserting that the Father and Son are two real things or Persons amount to teaching two separate, independent substances?

question: Can the divine nature of the Word suffer affections such as hunger, fear and grief?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: No. The Godhead in its proper nature admits no such affections. They belonged to Christ through the human nature he assumed, a soul affected together with the body.
sources.quote: For the Godhead, in its proper nature, admits no such affections, nor is the flesh by itself involved in them, if the soul is not affected co-ordinately with the body.
sources.raw_question: Can the divine nature of the Word suffer affections such as hunger, fear and grief?

question: Do the New Testament texts calling Christ God before the world, God over all, Maker of the world, and worshipped by angels show that he is not among the excluded nominal gods, and so is the one Supreme God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is God before the world was, God over all, Maker of the world, and worshipped by angels, so he cannot be one of the nominal gods whom it would be idolatry to worship. Since every god except the one Supreme God is excluded, Christ must be the same one Supreme God. He is not the same Person as the Father but another Person in the same Godhead, so the Supreme God is more Persons than one.
sources.quote: But since all are excluded, as hath been before shewn, except the one Supreme God, it is very manifest, that he is the same with the one Supreme God. Not the same Person with the Father, as you groundlessly object to us, but another Person in the same Godhead
sources.raw_question: Do the New Testament texts calling Christ God before the world, God over all, Maker of the world, and worshipped by angels show that he is not among the excluded nominal gods, and so is the one Supreme God?

question: If Christ is God at all, must he be a different individual God from the Supreme God, the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. The objection plays on the word 'individual', taking it to mean the same individual Person. Nobody claims the Son is the same Person as the Father. The orthodox claim is only that the Son is the same Supreme God, a partaker of the same undivided Godhead.
sources.quote: Who pretends that the Son is the same Person with the Father? All we assert is, that he is the same Supreme God ; that is, partaker of the same undivided Godhead.
sources.raw_question: If Christ is God at all, must he be a different individual God from the Supreme God, the Father?

question: Was the Word already perfect Son before the incarnation?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: Not in the full sense. Before the incarnation the Word was perfect Word and only-begotten, but not yet perfect Son. God addressed him as Son because he was to become such in the future. Since the flesh has its subsistence only in the Word, the incarnate Word was manifested as one perfect Son of God.
sources.quote: For neither was the Word, prior to incarnation and when by Himself, yet perfect Son, although He was perfect Word, only-begotten.
sources.raw_question: Was the Word already perfect Son before the incarnation?

question: Do attributes such as goodness, eternity, and omnipotence, said of God in respect to himself, apply to the Trinity in the singular rather than the plural?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Those Things Which Belong Absolutely to God as an Essence, are Spoken of the Trinity in the Singular, Not in the Plural.
sources.answer: Yes. The same reasoning used for greatness holds for goodness, eternity, omnipotence, and every predicate said properly of God in respect to himself. God is these by being them, not by participation, so they are identical with his one essence. They are therefore predicated of the Trinity in the singular, as of one God.
sources.quote: Let the same be said also of the goodness, and of the eternity, and of the omnipotence of God, and, in short, of all the predicaments which can be predicated of God, as He is spoken of in respect to Himself
sources.raw_question: Do attributes such as goodness, eternity, and omnipotence, said of God in respect to himself, apply to the Trinity in the singular rather than the plural?

question: Should a philosophical maxim about what is possible in God be used as the rule for judging what Scripture teaches about the Trinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. We cannot know a priori whether there can or cannot be a plurality of Persons in one God. We can only inquire a posteriori into the fact as Scripture reveals it. If Scripture, rightly understood, shows such a medium, a pretended maxim against it carries no weight. God best knows his own nature, and Scripture rather than the light of nature is the rule.
sources.quote: We do not pretend to be wise enough to know any thing, a priori, whether there can or there cannot ; but, @ posteriori, we may inquire after fact
sources.raw_question: Should a philosophical maxim about what is possible in God be used as the rule for judging what Scripture teaches about the Trinity?

question: Is the unity of the divine Persons a specific unity, like that between two individual men?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. Waterland expressly denies that Catholics hold a specific unity such as exists between two individuals of a species. He says such a view would give colour to the charge of Tritheism. The Persons are instead coessential and inseparable, one in nature and operation.
sources.quote: we hold not a specific unity, (such as between two individuals of any species, two men, for instance.) If we did any of these, there might be some colour for the charge of Tritheism.
sources.raw_question: Is the unity of the divine Persons a specific unity, like that between two individual men?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's casting out of demons show that He is inferior, or that He is divine?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: It shows that He is divine. The only-begotten God, who commanded the devil with authority, Himself attributed His casting out of devils to the Spirit of God. The expulsion of demons therefore demonstrates the Spirit's divine and transcendent power and takes nothing from His glory.
sources.quote: the expulsion of devils is not destructive of the glory of the Spirit, but rather a demonstration of His divine and transcendent power.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's casting out of demons show that He is inferior, or that He is divine?

question: Are the lofty titles given to the Only-begotten Son, such as God, Wisdom, Power, Light, Truth and God over all, merely honorific names that do not indicate His actual divine dignity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory says that Eunomius' argument about names is meant to suggest that the Son's honour is limited to the name, and he treats this as blasphemy. Just as Daniel showed that the name of God did not really belong to the brazen image or the dragon, the divine names given to the Son must be taken to show His true nature. We should look at the truth of facts and draw His name from them, so the Son really shares the dignity those names signify.
sources.quote: although the Only-begotten is called God, and Wisdom, and Power, and Light, and the Truth, and the Judge, and the King, and God over all, and the great God, and the Prince of peace, and the Father of the world to come, and so forth, His honour is limited to the name.
sources.raw_question: Are the lofty titles given to the Only-begotten Son, such as God, Wisdom, Power, Light, Truth and God over all, merely honorific names that do not indicate His actual divine dignity?

question: Why should we not speak of three essences in God, even though Scripture does not forbid the expression?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: Because 'three essences' would suggest some difference within the absolute equality of the three. Also, in God to be is the same as to be God and to be wise. So just as we do not say three Gods or three wisdoms, we do not say three essences. The unity of the Trinity means they are called one essence.
sources.quote: because it is the same thing to Him to be God as to be, it is not right to say three essences, as it is not right to say three Gods
sources.raw_question: Why should we not speak of three essences in God, even though Scripture does not forbid the expression?

question: Are the names that are proper to individual Persons of the Trinity (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) predicated of God according to substance or relatively?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: Relatively. Whatever is specially predicated of one Person in the Trinity is not said of that Person in reference to himself, but either in mutual reference among the Persons or in respect to the creature. Hence such names signify relation, not substance, unlike 'great', 'good', 'eternal', which are said of God absolutely.
sources.quote: these are in no way said in reference to themselves in themselves, but either in mutual reference, or in respect to the creature; and, therefore, it is manifest that such things are spoken relatively, not in the way of substance.
sources.raw_question: Are the names that are proper to individual Persons of the Trinity (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) predicated of God according to substance or relatively?

question: In the Old Testament appearances of God under bodily forms, was the very essence of God seen by human eyes?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed.
sources.answer: No. The divine essence itself was never seen in itself in these appearances. God was manifested to human sight through bodily forms, either a creature formed for that purpose or angels speaking in the person of God, while the substance of God remained invisible to bodily sight.
sources.quote: according to the power given to them by the Creator; while the essence itself of God was never seen in itself.
sources.raw_question: In the Old Testament appearances of God under bodily forms, was the very essence of God seen by human eyes?

question: How does the Son's manner of speaking differ from that of the prophets, and what does it show about the Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: The Son comes from the Father with supreme authority (principali auctoritate) and so says "But I say unto you." The prophets came as servants from their Lord, delivering a message, and so said "Thus saith the Lord." This marks the Son's unique authority as Son, in contrast with the servants.
sources.quote: But the Son, as coming from the Father with supreme authority (principali auctoritate), used to express Himself thus: “But I say unto you.”
sources.raw_question: How does the Son's manner of speaking differ from that of the prophets, and what does it show about the Son?

question: Why should the analogy between the mind and the Trinity be examined through knowledge and love that arise in time, rather than through the mind's eternal self-knowledge alone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > Why Love is Not the Offspring of the Mind, as Knowledge is So. The Solution of the Question. The Mind with the Knowledge of Itself and the Love of Itself is the Image of the Trinity.
sources.answer: Because what happens in the order of time is easier to explain. Speech itself unfolds in time, so cases where knowledge or love comes into being where it did not exist before show more clearly what to say about how knowledge and love arise from the mind.
sources.quote: because to speech also itself, which must be disposed in time, that thing is easier of explanation which is comprehended in the order of time
sources.raw_question: Why should the analogy between the mind and the Trinity be examined through knowledge and love that arise in time, rather than through the mind's eternal self-knowledge alone?

question: Can God be partly a father, communicating only some of His being to the begotten Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Paternity admits of no compromise; a father is father in respect of his whole personality, and the birth proceeds from the whole of himself. Since God is not compounded of parts but simple and all-embracing, He must be Father to the Son in all that He is.
sources.quote: This name admits of no compromise: no one can be partly father, and partly not. A father is father in respect of his whole personality; all that he is is present in the child, for paternity by piecemeal is impossible
sources.raw_question: Can God be partly a father, communicating only some of His being to the begotten Son?

question: How should the Son's profession of not knowing the day and hour be understood if He is not truly ignorant?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: His profession of ignorance is a divine economy rather than real ignorance. As God in Scripture says He does not know when it is not yet the time to speak or act, so Christ's not knowing refers to the occasion of declaring knowledge, not a defect of His nature.
sources.quote: In Him are hidden all the treasures of knowledge, and so His ignorance is an economy rather than ignorance. Thus we can assign a reason for His ignorance, without the assumption that He did not know.
sources.raw_question: How should the Son's profession of not knowing the day and hour be understood if He is not truly ignorant?

question: Are the acts Christ performs through his human nature or through his divine nature the acts of one person or of two?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: They are all the acts of one person. The Son, a divine person, took human nature so that divine and human natures became one person, one Christ, God and man; hence whatever he does about our salvation is done by that one person in whom both natures are.
sources.quote: Whatever acts are ascribed unto him, however immediately performed, in or by the human nature, or in and by his divine nature, they are all the acts of that one person, in whom are both these natures.
sources.raw_question: Are the acts Christ performs through his human nature or through his divine nature the acts of one person or of two?

question: Does Christ's saying 'I am in the Father and the Father in Me' (John 14:10) mean only that his words and works were not his own but the Father's, as Asterius claimed?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: No. If that were the meaning, every prophet and saint who spoke God's words and worked miracles by God's power (David, Solomon, Moses, Elijah, Elisha, Samuel, the Apostles) could equally say 'I in the Father and the Father in me.' Christ would then be only one among many, not the one Son, Word and Wisdom of God. The text expresses something proper to the Son alone.
sources.quote: it is plain that, according to Asterius such a statement must be common to all, so that each of them is able to say, ‘I in the Father and the Father in me;’ and as a consequence that He is no longer one Son of God and Word and Wisdom
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'I am in the Father and the Father in Me' (John 14:10) mean only that his words and works were not his own but the Father's, as Asterius claimed?

question: Does the wording of John 14:10 itself show that the Son's being in the Father is unique rather than a grace shared with creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Had Christ meant a shared grace, he would have said 'I too am in the Father, and the Father is in Me too.' Instead he speaks absolutely, as one who has this by prerogative as the genuine Son. It befits him alone to say it.
sources.quote: His words would not rightly have been, ‘I in the Father and the Father in Me,’ but rather, ‘I too am in the Father, and the Father is in Me too,’
sources.raw_question: Does the wording of John 14:10 itself show that the Son's being in the Father is unique rather than a grace shared with creatures?

question: Can the Son, who is the Father's Power and Word, be said to receive power or authority from the Father in the way creatures do?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: No. To say the Power of the Father receives power is irreligious. It would imply that the Word received a word's authority and that the Son was made a son in another son. It ranks him with things made, as if he had learned like them, rather than speaking as the Son.
sources.quote: he says, lawless man, that the Power of the Father receives power, that from this his irreligion it may follow to say that in a son the Son was made a son, and the Word received a word’s authority
sources.raw_question: Can the Son, who is the Father's Power and Word, be said to receive power or authority from the Father in the way creatures do?

question: In what sense are the Son and the Father in each other (the coinherence)?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: They are in each other because the whole being of the Son is proper to the Father's essence. He is from the Father as radiance is from light and a stream from a fountain. Since the Form and Godhead of the Father is the Being of the Son, whoever sees the Son sees what is proper to the Father. Hence the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son.
sources.quote: For whereas the Form and Godhead of the Father is the Being of the Son, it follows that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son.
sources.raw_question: In what sense are the Son and the Father in each other (the coinherence)?

question: How can the Father be said to be in the Son, as the sun is in its radiance?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: The Son is what is from the Father and proper to him. The Father is in the Son as the sun is in its radiance, the thought in the word, and the fountain in the stream. Whoever contemplates the Son contemplates what is proper to the Father's essence and so knows that the Father is in him.
sources.quote: For the Father is in the Son, since the Son is what is from the Father and proper to Him, as in the radiance the sun, and in the word the thought, and in the stream the fountain
sources.raw_question: How can the Father be said to be in the Son, as the sun is in its radiance?

question: How do 2 Timothy 1:9-10 and Ephesians 1:3-5 help interpret 'before the world' in Proverbs 8 as applied to the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Paul himself interprets the Proverbs language. He speaks of grace 'given us in Christ Jesus before the world began' and of our being chosen in him 'before the foundation of the world.' This shows that what existed 'before the world' was the divine purpose and grace stored in Christ for our sake. We were chosen and predestined in him before we existed because the Son was 'founded' beforehand for that economy.
sources.quote: how at all, before men were created, did He predestinate us unto adoption, but that the Son Himself was ‘founded before the world,’ taking on Him that economy which was for our sake?
sources.raw_question: How do 2 Timothy 1:9-10 and Ephesians 1:3-5 help interpret 'before the world' in Proverbs 8 as applied to the Son?

question: Could any creature, even the Word if he were one, be created alone and first, before all other creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. Creatures come into being together according to their kind, not one first and then another. The stars and lights were all made on one day by one command, and the whole human race was involved in Adam. The invisible powers likewise came to be all at once, differing only in glory. So if the Word were a creature, he would have come to be with the other Powers and not first.
sources.quote: If then, as I have said, the Word were creature He must have been brought into being, not first of them, but with all the other Powers, though in glory He excel the rest ever so much.
sources.raw_question: Could any creature, even the Word if he were one, be created alone and first, before all other creatures?

question: What does Christ's saying 'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' teach about the relation between the Son's works and the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: It teaches that the Son's work must be regarded as the work of the Father, who works in Him all that He does. Christ used it to justify healing on the Sabbath by divine authority, and in calling God His own Father He made Himself equal with God, which the Jews rightly understood as a claim to divine equality.
sources.quote: He taught them by the same words that His work must be regarded as the work of the Father, Who was working in Him all that He wrought.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's saying 'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' teach about the relation between the Son's works and the Father's?

question: Who is meant by 'the Word' (Logos) in John 1:1-3?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Jesus Christ the Son of God. Whether he is called the Word as the eternal Wisdom of the Father or as the revealer of God's will, the context leaves no doubt: this Word came into the world, was rejected by his own, was made flesh, is named Jesus Christ, and is called the only begotten Son of the Father.
sources.quote: Jesus Christ the Son of God is intended. This is on all hands acknowledged; and the context will admit of no hesitation about it.
sources.raw_question: Who is meant by 'the Word' (Logos) in John 1:1-3?

question: Does John 8:58, 'Before Abraham was, I am,' assert Christ's real existence before Abraham, or does it mean only that Christ was destined to be the light of the world before Abraham became father of many nations?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: It asserts his real, divine pre-existence. Christ was answering the Jews' objection that he was not yet fifty and so could not have seen Abraham; any other reading turns his reply into a gross equivocation. The Jews understood him to claim deity and took up stones against him for blasphemy. The Socinian reading is absurd.
sources.quote: there be no proper sense in the words, but a gross equivocation, if the existence of Christ before Abraham was born be not asserted in them
sources.raw_question: Does John 8:58, 'Before Abraham was, I am,' assert Christ's real existence before Abraham, or does it mean only that Christ was destined to be the light of the world before Abraham became father of many nations?

question: If God begins to be called 'Lord' in time, does something happen accidentally to God's substance, making Him changeable?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said of God in Time, is Said Relatively, Not Accidentally.
sources.answer: No. Relative terms that begin to apply to God in time imply no change in His substance. The change happens only in the creature to which He is related. Money can begin to be called a price or a pledge without any change in itself. Much more can the unchangeable substance of God be called something relative to creatures without any change in Him.
sources.quote: nothing shall be understood to have happened to the substance itself of God, but only to that creature in respect to which it is predicated
sources.raw_question: If God begins to be called 'Lord' in time, does something happen accidentally to God's substance, making Him changeable?

question: Does Christ's statement that the Holy Spirit "shall receive of mine" imply that the Holy Spirit is born of Christ as Christ is born of the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Some Things Concerning the Holy Spirit are to Be Understood According to the One Rule Only.
sources.answer: No. Christ immediately explained that "All things that the Father hath are mine; therefore said I, that He shall take of mine," so the Spirit is to be understood as having of what is the Father's, just as the Son has. This is grounded in the Spirit's procession from the Father, not in a birth from the Son.
sources.quote: it remains that the Holy Spirit be understood to have of that which is the Father’s, as the Son also hath.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that the Holy Spirit "shall receive of mine" imply that the Holy Spirit is born of Christ as Christ is born of the Father?

question: Does confessing that the Son comes from the Father mean the Son did not always live with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He who asserts that the Father is 'prior' to the Son with any thought of an interval must perforce allow that even the Father is not without beginning.
sources.answer: No. Along with the 'coming from Him', the Son's 'living along with Him' must also be confessed, as Scripture teaches. This keeps the Son's life from failing when traced upward. It also leaves the Father's everlastingness untouched by any definite beginning assigned to the Son.
sources.quote: let it suffice for us, when we confess the ‘coming from Him,’ to admit also, bold as it may seem, the ‘living along with Him;’ for we are led by the written oracles to such a belief.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing that the Son comes from the Father mean the Son did not always live with the Father?

question: Did the ante-Nicene Fathers who spoke of the Word's 'procession' or 'generation' before creation think the Word was merely an impersonal attribute of the Father until then, so that the Son began to exist and was created out of nothing?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. If these Fathers had held the Word to be only an attribute or power before the procession, it would follow that the Son began to be and was a creature made out of nothing, and that procession was just another word for creation. But they expressly guard against this: Novatian distinguishes procession from creation, and Athenagoras declares the Son was not then made but existed in the Father as the Word from all eternity.
sources.quote: Athenagoras is still more express to the same purpose; °declaring that the Son was not then made, but had existed in the Father, as the Adyos, or Word, from all eternity.
sources.raw_question: Did the ante-Nicene Fathers who spoke of the Word's 'procession' or 'generation' before creation think the Word was merely an impersonal attribute of the Father until then, so that the Son began to exist and was created out of nothing?

question: If being uncreated and incorruptible is the ground of being God, must the Son share that uncreated existence in order to be truly God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. Justin makes God's being uncreated and incorruptible the very foundation on account of which he is God, so that without it one could not be God. Since Justin everywhere insists the Son is God, he must hold the Word to be uncreated and incorruptible in this sense.
sources.quote: If therefore the Λόγος be not, in this sense, ἀγέννητος and ἄφθαρτος, he is not Θεὸς, according to Justin Martyr: and yet no man is more express than Justin, every where, in making the Son Θεὸς
sources.raw_question: If being uncreated and incorruptible is the ground of being God, must the Son share that uncreated existence in order to be truly God?

question: Is saying that the Son is only 'like' God in substance (homoiousios) equivalent to denying that he is God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: Yes, according to Athanasius, whose distinction Waterland endorses. Athanasius carefully separated homoousion from homoiousion. He held that calling the Son only like God amounts to denying he is God, just as calling something only like silver or gold means it is not silver or gold.
sources.quote: He thought that to say the Son was only ike God, was as much as denying him to be God: as if we should say a thing is only like silver, therefore not silver ; or only like gold, therefore not gold.
sources.raw_question: Is saying that the Son is only 'like' God in substance (homoiousios) equivalent to denying that he is God?

question: Did the earliest ante-Nicene doxologies give glory 'to' or 'with' the Son and the Holy Spirit, or only 'through' or 'in' them?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: They gave glory 'to' and 'with' the Son and Spirit as well. Basil, the Clementine Constitutions, Polycarp's doxology, the Church of Smyrna, Clement of Alexandria and Hippolytus show 'to' or 'with' applied to the Son and Holy Ghost from the earliest times. Dismissing all of these as Athanasian forgeries in effect gives up the point.
sources.quote: can make any reasonable doubt, whether to or with were not applied in doxologies to the Son or Holy Ghost, as well as by, through, or in, by the earliest Ante-Nicene writers.
sources.raw_question: Did the earliest ante-Nicene doxologies give glory 'to' or 'with' the Son and the Holy Spirit, or only 'through' or 'in' them?

question: Does showing that the Ante-Nicene Fathers did not hold one 'numerical essence' of Father, Son and Spirit, in the sense of one Person, prove that they did not hold the Nicene doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Taking 'same numerical essence' to mean one Person is the Sabellian sense, which neither Bull nor the Fathers held. Demanding it changes the question and would require the Fathers to have professed a heresy they themselves condemned. Showing that the Fathers were not Sabellians proves nothing against Bull, since no one of sense claims they were. If the Examiner thinks such unity necessary, he should openly call Bull and the Catholic Church tritheist rather than say Bull failed to prove what he intended.
sources.quote: What does it signify to shew that they were not Sabellians? Did Bishop Bull, or does any man of sense, pretend they were ?
sources.raw_question: Does showing that the Ante-Nicene Fathers did not hold one 'numerical essence' of Father, Son and Spirit, in the sense of one Person, prove that they did not hold the Nicene doctrine of the Trinity?

question: Does the clause 'nor as if He were previously in being, and afterwards born or created afresh, to be a Son' rightly guard against error, or does it undermine the Son's eternal birth from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: It is aimed at the true faith. No one supposes that the Father ceased to be himself and was later born as the Son, since the birth itself shows that its Author continues to exist. The Son was born from the eternally living nature, not from nothing. Though distinct from the God who begat him, he shares his nature by birth. The clause is used to banish belief in this unity of nature.
sources.quote: Now who is senseless enough to suppose that the Father ceased to be Himself; that the same Person Who had previously existed was afterwards born, or created afresh, to be the Son?
sources.raw_question: Does the clause 'nor as if He were previously in being, and afterwards born or created afresh, to be a Son' rightly guard against error, or does it undermine the Son's eternal birth from the Father?

question: If the Son and the Word were distinct, would the Son be greater than the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: Yes, that would follow, which shows the distinction is absurd. The highest attributes—being One with the Father, mutual indwelling, and 'he that hath seen Me hath seen the Father'—are spoken by the Son. So either the Son is greater than the Word or the Word has nothing beyond the Son; hence the Word is the Son.
sources.quote: either that the Son is greater than the Word, or the Word has nothing beyond the Son. For what can be greater or more perfect than ‘One,’
sources.raw_question: If the Son and the Word were distinct, would the Son be greater than the Word?

question: Did the Ante-Nicene Christian writers teach that the Son of God is uncreated?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 12: Whether the Creator of all things was not himself uncreated ; and therefore could not be ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, made out of nothing ?
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds that the Ante-Nicene writers almost everywhere declare the Son uncreated by implication and consequence. Some of them, including Athenagoras, Irenaeus, Origen, Dionysius of Rome, Theognostus, Methodius and probably Hippolytus, also say it directly and in express words.
sources.quote: it is well known that they do implicitly and consequentially, almost every where, declare the Son to be wnereated.
sources.raw_question: Did the Ante-Nicene Christian writers teach that the Son of God is uncreated?

question: Which names are predicated of each divine Person individually and which belong to the Trinity as a whole?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Preface.—The Conclusion of What Has Been Said Above. The Rule to Be Observed in the More Difficult Questions of the Faith.
sources.answer: Names spoken relatively (Father, Son, Gift/Holy Spirit) belong severally to each Person, so none of them is the Trinity. But whatever is said of each Person in respect to himself, such as God, good or omnipotent, is said according to essence. It is therefore predicated in the singular of the one Trinity.
sources.quote: those things are predicated specially in the Trinity as belonging severally to each person, which are predicated relatively the one to the other, as Father and Son, and the gift of both, the Holy Spirit; for the Father is not the Trinity
sources.raw_question: Which names are predicated of each divine Person individually and which belong to the Trinity as a whole?

question: Can someone who denies the Son's true and eternal generation from the Father still hold correct beliefs about the Father, the Holy Spirit, the resurrection, and the incarnation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: No. Error about the Word corrupts the whole faith. The Son is the one who reveals the Father, and the Word is the one who supplies the Spirit. Christ is the first-begotten from the dead, and the incarnation can only be understood through the Son's genuine generation. So whoever denies the Son loses truth on all these points at once.
sources.quote: For how can he speak truth concerning the Father, who denies the Son, that reveals concerning Him? or how can he be orthodox concerning the Spirit, while he speaks profanely of the Word that supplies the Spirit?
sources.raw_question: Can someone who denies the Son's true and eternal generation from the Father still hold correct beliefs about the Father, the Holy Spirit, the resurrection, and the incarnation?

question: Are the attributes predicated of God, such as eternal, wise, and blessed, really distinct things in God's nature, so that they might constitute the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How There is a Trinity in the Very Simplicity of God. Whether and How the Trinity that is God is Manifested from the Trinities Which Have Been Shown to Be in Men.
sources.answer: No. The many attributes of God can be reduced to three and even to one, because in God's simple nature wisdom and might, life and wisdom, eternity and wisdom, blessedness and wisdom are one and the same thing. So the three attributes are not three things that could be the three Persons; the question remains how the one wisdom that is God is a trinity.
sources.quote: For if wisdom and might, or life and wisdom, can be one and the same thing in the nature of God, why cannot eternity and wisdom, or blessedness and wisdom, be one and the same thing in the nature of God?
sources.raw_question: Are the attributes predicated of God, such as eternal, wise, and blessed, really distinct things in God's nature, so that they might constitute the Trinity?

question: How do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit each figure in the believer's access to God in prayer?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Prayer is directed to the Father, through the mediation of the Son, by the assistance of the Spirit. The saints have the assistance of the Spirit, without which they are nothing, and the way of Christ's mediation, without which God cannot be approached. Thus by Christ we have access in one Spirit unto the Father.
sources.quote: The assistance of the Spirit, without which they are nothing; and the way of Christ’s mediation, without which God is not to be approached unto.
sources.raw_question: How do the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit each figure in the believer's access to God in prayer?

question: Do the biblical texts asserting the Son's inferiority and subordination to the Father, which Unitarians cite, disprove the deity of Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. The incarnation, in which the Word was made flesh, unlocks all those texts, since they speak of the Son of man in his assumed humanity. Trinitarians neither hide nor explain them away; they are essential to the faith, and, combined with the revelations of his essential Godhead, they make up the grace of salvation.
sources.quote: This unlocks all those texts on which Unitarians are wont to insist, asserting the inferiority and subordination of the Son of man to the Father. We do not hide these truths. We do not gloss them over. We do not explain them away.
sources.raw_question: Do the biblical texts asserting the Son's inferiority and subordination to the Father, which Unitarians cite, disprove the deity of Christ?

question: Can a person assent to a proposition, such as an article of faith, that he does not understand at all?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Waterland agrees with Dr. Whitby that where there is no idea there can be no assent, because assenting to nothing is the same as not assenting. He denies, however, that this applies to Christian mysteries. He goes on to distinguish cases in order to show that believing mysteries is not assent to a proposition that is wholly unintelligible.
sources.quote: For, undoubtedly, where there is no idea, there can be no assent: because assenting to nothing is the very same with not assenting.
sources.raw_question: Can a person assent to a proposition, such as an article of faith, that he does not understand at all?

question: Are Christian mysteries such as the Trinity comparable to propositions whose terms are not understood, or whose words convey no determinate meaning?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. When none of the terms are understood (as with "Mene mene tekel upharsin" before it was interpreted), there is no proposition at all, only sounds. When familiar words are put together with no determinate sense (as in "a woman ought to have power on her head because of the angels"), a person can only assent to another proposition, that whatever Scripture asserts is true. Waterland rejects as unjust any parallel between such cases and the mysteries of Christianity properly so called.
sources.quote: the justice and equity of his drawing a parallel between this and the mysteries of Christianity, properly so called, must be a mystery to as many as cannot perceive either the sense or the ingenuity of doing it
sources.raw_question: Are Christian mysteries such as the Trinity comparable to propositions whose terms are not understood, or whose words convey no determinate meaning?

question: If the Son advanced in wisdom when He became man, would that imply He was imperfect before the Incarnation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes, it would, and that is absurd. It would make the flesh a cause of perfection to the Word, rather than the Word to the flesh. Therefore the advance cannot belong to the Word as such.
sources.quote: If He advanced when He became man, it is plain that, before He became man, He was imperfect; and rather the flesh became to Him a cause of perfection, than He to the flesh.
sources.raw_question: If the Son advanced in wisdom when He became man, would that imply He was imperfect before the Incarnation?

question: Is the sanctifying and purifying of the Gentiles a work of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter X. Being about to prove that the will, the calling, and the commandment of the Trinity is one, St. Ambrose shows that the Spirit called the Church exactly as the Father and the Son did, and proves this by the selection of SS. Paul and Barnabas, and especially by the mission of St. Peter to Cornelius. And by the way he points out how in the Apostle's vision the calling of the Gentiles was shadowed forth, who having been before like wild beasts, now by the operation of the Spirit lay aside that wildness. Then having quoted other passages in support of this view, he shows that in the case of Jeremiah cast into a pit by Jews, and rescued by Abdemelech, is a type of the slighting of the Holy Spirit by the Jews, and of His being honoured by the Gentiles.
sources.answer: Yes. After the voice said, "What God hath cleansed call not thou common," the Holy Spirit came upon the Gentiles to purify them. The beasts in Peter's vision figure fallen humanity, which keeps its bestial ferocity unless it is made gentle by the Spirit's sanctification. Since this cleansing is God's work, the Spirit's operation is divine.
sources.quote: It is, then, the Holy Spirit Who has delivered us from that Gentile impurity.
sources.raw_question: Is the sanctifying and purifying of the Gentiles a work of the Holy Spirit?

question: What is the difference between a natural son and an adopted son in relation to the father, and how does it apply to the Son of God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: A son by nature is one with the one who begat him, while a son from without who is made a son is only attached to the family. The Son of God is a son by nature and so is one with the Father. Creatures who become sons are attached from without.
sources.quote: For a son which is by nature, is one with him who begat him; but he who is from without, and is made a son, will be attached to the family.
sources.raw_question: What is the difference between a natural son and an adopted son in relation to the father, and how does it apply to the Son of God?

question: How does the human inner word illustrate that God made all things through the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Likeness of the Divine Word, Such as It Is, is to Be Sought, Not in Our Own Outer and Sensible Word, But in the Inner and Mental One. There is the Greatest Possible Unlikeness Between Our Word and Knowledge and the Divine Word and Knowledge.
sources.answer: Just as God made the universe through His only-begotten Word, no human work happens unless it is first spoken in the heart. As Scripture says, a word is the beginning of every work. Also, a word can exist without any work following, but no work without a word. Likewise, the Word could have existed without creatures, but no creature could exist except through the Word.
sources.quote: as it is said of that Word, “All things were made by Him,” where God is declared to have made the universe by His only-begotten Son, so there are no works of man that are not first spoken in his heart
sources.raw_question: How does the human inner word illustrate that God made all things through the Son?

question: Can the image and likeness of God in the human soul be preserved apart from the soul's relation to God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Image of the Beast in Man.
sources.answer: No. The true honour of man is the image and likeness of God, and it is kept only while the soul stays turned toward the God who impresses it. So the less a person loves what is merely their own, the more they cleave to God and keep that image.
sources.quote: For the true honor of man is the image and likeness of God, which is not preserved except it be in relation to Him by whom it is impressed. The less therefore that one loves what is one’s own, the more one cleaves to God.
sources.raw_question: Can the image and likeness of God in the human soul be preserved apart from the soul's relation to God?

question: Can the fallen soul restore itself to the likeness of God by its own power?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Image of the Beast in Man.
sources.answer: No. Having thrown away and destroyed its strength, the soul cannot return unless its Maker, by grace, calls it to repentance and forgives its sins. Only the grace of God through Jesus Christ delivers the wretched soul from the body of this death.
sources.quote: having thrown away and destroyed its strength, it cannot return, unless by the grace of its Maker calling it to repentance, and forgiving its sins.
sources.raw_question: Can the fallen soul restore itself to the likeness of God by its own power?

question: Did the Word of God take flesh of the same substance as ours, derived from Adam, or flesh of some other substance?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIV.—Unless the flesh were to be saved, the Word would not have taken upon Him flesh of the same substance as ours: from this it would follow that neither should we have been reconciled by Him.
sources.answer: The Word took flesh of the very same substance as ours. Otherwise He would not have summed up (recapitulated) human nature in Himself, nor could He truly be called flesh, since flesh is a transmission of what was originally moulded from the dust. If another material had been needed, the Father would have moulded man from a different substance at the beginning. Christ therefore recapitulated not some other thing but the Father's original handiwork.
sources.quote: He had Himself, therefore, flesh and blood, recapitulating in Himself not a certain other, but that original handiwork of the Father, seeking out that thing which had perished.
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who deny the salvation of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God take flesh of the same substance as ours, derived from Adam, or flesh of some other substance?

question: Can any human being, such as a priest or apostle, confer the Holy Spirit by his own authority?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: No. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone; the priest only invokes and ministers. Paul did not presume to give the Spirit by his own authority but prayed that God would fill believers, and Peter confessed he could not resist God's granting of the Spirit.
sources.quote: For this is no work of man, nor gift of man; but He Who is invoked by the priest is given by God, wherein is the gift of God and the ministry of the priest.
sources.raw_question: Can any human being, such as a priest or apostle, confer the Holy Spirit by his own authority?

question: Is the substance of the Holy Spirit created?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: No. It is by the Spirit's shining in our hearts that we perceive the distance between creature and Godhead, and God speaks of no creature as He does of the Spirit when He says 'I will pour out of My Spirit.' What is poured forth from God is peculiar to the Godhead and not common to creatures.
sources.quote: Who, then, can dare to say that the substance of the Holy Spirit is created, at Whose shining in our hearts we behold the beauty of divine truth, and the distance between the creature and the Godhead
sources.raw_question: Is the substance of the Holy Spirit created?

question: Does holding one supreme God together with two inferior divine Persons, each truly called God, amount to Tritheism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: Yes. On the Arian or Clarkean scheme, one divine Person is equivalent to one God, so three divine Persons are three Gods. Asserting three Gods, whether coordinate or not, is Tritheism in the same sense in which the pagans are called polytheists. It is contrary to the first commandment, the whole tenor of Scripture, and the principles of the primitive Church.
sources.quote: One supreme and two inferior Gods, is your avowed doctrine : and, certainly, the asserting three Gods (whether coordinate or otherwise) is Tritheism; against the jirst commandment, against the whole tenor of Scripture, and the principles of the primitive Church.
sources.raw_question: Does holding one supreme God together with two inferior divine Persons, each truly called God, amount to Tritheism?

question: Does the way the pre-Nicene Catholics argued against the Sabellians show that they believed the Son to be consubstantial with the Father in the proper sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: Yes. If the early Catholics had held the Son to be a creature, not eternal, not omniscient and of limited power, they could easily have refuted the Sabellians by arguing that Creator and creature cannot be one Hypostasis. Acute writers like Tertullian, Origen and Hippolytus never pressed this decisive argument, which shows it was inconsistent with their principles. They believed the Son shared all the Father's essential perfections in common with him.
sources.quote: This argument had been irrefragable, and could not have failed of being urged and pressed home, by men of such acute parts as Tertullian, Origen, Hippolytus, and others, had it been consistent with Catholic principles
sources.raw_question: Does the way the pre-Nicene Catholics argued against the Sabellians show that they believed the Son to be consubstantial with the Father in the proper sense?

question: Can the priority of the Father as source be maintained together with the essential divinity of the Son and Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: Yes. Proper consubstantiality is the middle way between the Sabellian and Arian extremes. It keeps the Father's priority as head and fountain, while giving the Son and Spirit the same divine substance and perfections. The Son is subordinate only as a Son, inferior in point of origin but equal in nature, and so one God with the Father.
sources.quote: It is a mediwm, to preserve the priority of the Father, and withal the divinity, the essential divinity, of Son and Holy Ghost: in a word; it is the sober, middle way, between the extravagancies of both extremes.
sources.raw_question: Can the priority of the Father as source be maintained together with the essential divinity of the Son and Holy Spirit?

question: Did the Word have a real human body or only the appearance of one?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: A real body. He had a body not in appearance but in truth. It was fitting for him to put on human flesh whole, together with the affections proper to it.
sources.quote: because He had a body, not in appearance, but in truth
sources.raw_question: Did the Word have a real human body or only the appearance of one?

question: Was the Son obedient to the Father in the work of creating all things, or did he create by his own sovereign authority?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: He created by his own sovereign authority.
