Scripture nowhere teaches a list of obediences in creation; rather it attests his independent power: "He spake the word and they were made: He commanded and they were created." This refers to the one who upholds all things by the word of his power, whose will alone framed every existence.
sources.quote: every inspired Scripture attests His independent and sovereign power, saying, “He spake the word and they were made: He commanded and they were created”
sources.raw_question: Was the Son obedient to the Father in the work of creating all things, or did he create by his own sovereign authority?

question: Can the texts about the day of judgment be applied to the Son's divine nature without implying that the Word was ever ignorant?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: Yes. Basil and possibly Irenaeus understood the texts of the divine Word. Yet they were far from thinking the Word was ignorant of anything. They took the texts to ascribe original, underived knowledge to the Father. If the texts are understood of the human nature only, the difficulty vanishes entirely.
sources.quote: the texts might be understood of the Adyos, or divine nature, as Basil understands them, in the place above cited; and yet that they, who so understood them, might be far from thinking that the Adyos, or Word, was ever ignorant of any thing.
sources.raw_question: Can the texts about the day of judgment be applied to the Son's divine nature without implying that the Word was ever ignorant?

question: Does Christ's saying 'Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour' (Matt. 25:13) show who is truly ignorant of the day?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). sources.quote: He who said shortly before, ‘No one knoweth, no not the Son,’ now says not ‘I know not,’ but ‘ye know not.’
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour' (Matt. 25:13) show who is truly ignorant of the day?

question: Why did Christ say 'not the Son' rather than 'not the Son of God' in Mark 13:32?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.

sources.raw_question: Why did Christ say 'not the Son' rather than 'not the Son of God' in Mark 13:32?

question: Does the Son's professed ignorance of the day and hour show that his nature is alien from the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Christ also says that he is in the Father and the Father in him. Both statements are utterances of the same Speaker, and both must be read in light of his chosen, gradual revelation of his birth and Name. They therefore do not deny his true Godhead.
sources.quote: or between I in the Father and the Father in Me, and But of the day and hour knoweth no one, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father only

question: Is ignorance of the Son's divine birth tied to ignorance of the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. Christ demonstrates men's ignorance of God by their ignorance that he is the Son of God; they do not know who Christ is because they do not know from whom he is. None can confess the Son who denies that he was born.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The apostles attributed His not knowing to the divine plan, not to weakness, so it is wrong to conclude that He did not know because He was not God. sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes. In the Noah example, Christ said 'they knew not,' not 'I knew not.' The Saviour himself brought the flood and foretold it to Noah: 'Yet seven days and I will bring a flood.' Since he knew the day of the flood and uses it as the parallel, he also knows the day of his own coming.
sources.quote: But if in describing the day He makes use of the parallel of Noah’s time, and He did know the day of the flood, therefore He knows also the day of His own coming.
sources.raw_question: Does the comparison with Noah's flood show that the Son knows the day of his coming?

question: Since the Son gave Paul knowledge of what Paul says he did not know, does it follow that the Son himself knew the day of judgment?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes. He who gave Paul to know much rather knew Himself. Since He also foretold the events that come before the day, He knew when the day and the hour would be.
sources.quote: Therefore He who gave to Paul to know, much rather knew Himself; for since He spoke of the antecedents of the day, He also knew, as I said before, when the Day and when the Hour
sources.raw_question: Since the Son gave Paul knowledge of what Paul says he did not know, does it follow that the Son himself knew the day of judgment?

question: Is the Arian claim that the Son knows all things relating to his office consistent with his supposed ignorance of the day of judgment?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: No. The precise time of the day of judgment would seem to belong to the Son's office as much as anything, so if he were ignorant of it he could not be omniscient even in the opponent's low, office-relative sense.
sources.quote: Or how can he be so much as omniscient, in this low sense, if he knows not, or knew not, the precise time of the day of judgment; a thing which, one would imagine, should belong to his office as much as any!
sources.raw_question: Is the Arian claim that the Son knows all things relating to his office consistent with his supposed ignorance of the day of judgment?

question: In what sense are divine attributes such as omniscience ascribed to the Father first and to the Son derivatively?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: The Son's attributes are derived from the Father in the same way that his essence is, without being any less. Just as the Son is God of God and Light of Light, he is Omniscience of Omniscience. This is the meaning of St. Basil, and Waterland thinks also of Irenaeus, when they ascribe the primary knowledge to the Father as first cause of all things.
sources.quote: As the Son is God of God, and Light of Light ; so it is proper to say, Omniscience of Omniscience, &c., the attributes being derivative in the same sense as the essence is:
sources.raw_question: In what sense are divine attributes such as omniscience ascribed to the Father first and to the Son derivatively?

question: Does Dr. Clarke's distinction between the Father being God with the approbation of his will and not by an act of his will rescue the Arian argument?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 31: Whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration, on the side of Arianism, ought to move a wise and good man, against so great appearances of truth o
sources.answer: No, it recoils on the Arian. If the Father is God volens by approbation and not by an act of will, the Catholic can reply that the Father likewise had his Son with the approbation of his will and not by an act of will. The dilemma then collapses. It was the Arians, not Augustine, who first confounded approbation with an act of will.
sources.quote: Well then ; so the Father had his Son (volens) with the approbation of his will, and not by an act of his wil/: and now what becomes of your dilemma, and your olens volens?
sources.raw_question: Does Dr. Clarke's distinction between the Father being God with the approbation of his will and not by an act of his will rescue the Arian argument?

question: Is the claim that humans comprehend God's essence consistent with Scriptures saying that no one has seen God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > The tenth book discusses the unattainable and incomprehensible character of the enquiry into entities. And herein he strikingly sets forth the points concerning the nature and formation of the ant, and the passage in the Gospel, “I am the door” and “the way,” and also discusses the attribution and interpretation of the Divine names, and the episode of the children of Benjamin.
sources.answer: No. If being inside or outside the door or finding pasture meant knowing the Father's essence, Scripture could not truly say that no man has seen God or can see Him. These texts show that the essence remains beyond human sight and comprehension.
sources.quote: And how can the word hold good, “No man hath seen God at any time” and, “Whom no man hath seen nor can see” and, “There shall no man see the face of the Lord and live”
sources.raw_question: Is the claim that humans comprehend God's essence consistent with Scriptures saying that no one has seen God?

question: How does Colossians 2:9 exclude both a oneness of Persons (Sabellianism) and a belief in two different natures in Father and Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: The Godhead dwelling in Christ is neither solitary nor separable. Because the indwelling Godhead cannot also be its own dwelling-place, Father and Son are distinct, excluding a single Person; yet the fulness is held one in nature with Christ and admits no partition, excluding two different natures.
sources.quote: For the fulness of Godhead which dwells in Christ in bodily fashion is neither solitary nor separable
sources.raw_question: How does Colossians 2:9 exclude both a oneness of Persons (Sabellianism) and a belief in two different natures in Father and Son?

question: Did the visible appearances of God in the Old Testament show the divine nature as it really is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > How the Back Parts of God Were Seen. The Faith of the Resurrection of Christ. The Catholic Church Only is the Place from Whence the Back Parts of God are Seen. The Back Parts of God Were Seen by the Israelites. It is a Rash Opinion to Think that God the Father Only Was Never Seen by the Fathers.
sources.answer: No. Those visions were wrought through changeable creatures made subject to the unchangeable God. They did not manifest God properly as he is. They gave intimations suited to the causes and times of the several circumstances.
sources.quote: those visions were wrought through the changeable creature, made subject to the unchangeable God, and did not manifest God properly as He is, but by intimations such as suited the causes and times
sources.raw_question: Did the visible appearances of God in the Old Testament show the divine nature as it really is?

question: Is it appropriate to call the Son a "product of generation" (gennema)?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: No. Following Basil, Gregory says we should confess that the Son is generated without turning that conception into a coined name. Scripture properly applies the term "product of generation" to inanimate things or uses it as a figure of wickedness, so it is unfit as a name for the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: to confess that He is generated without transforming this conception into the formula of a name, so as to call Him Who is generated “a product of generation,” as this term is properly applied in Scripture to things inanimate
sources.raw_question: Is it appropriate to call the Son a "product of generation" (gennema)?

question: Does Basil's teaching that God is 'from no one' mean that the Father comes from absolute non-existence, as Eunomius charges?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius has torn an expression out of its context. Basil was explaining that 'ungenerate' means only that God does not have His subsistence from another. God is the First Cause, beyond which nothing transcends. This is a denial of any cause, not an assertion that God arose from nothing.
sources.quote: Stealing an expression from its context, from which he drags it, as from its surrounding body, into a naked isolation, he tries to carp at it by worrying the word
sources.raw_question: Does Basil's teaching that God is 'from no one' mean that the Father comes from absolute non-existence, as Eunomius charges?

question: Does the Son of God know all things, including the things the Spirit declares about the future?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit receives from the Son the very things he declares, and all that the Father has belongs to the Son. So the things thought to be unknown to the Son are in fact received from him. Zechariah also says the day of the Lord's coming is known to the Lord who comes with his saints.
sources.quote: see that those very things which you think to be unknown to the Son, the Holy Spirit received from the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son of God know all things, including the things the Spirit declares about the future?

question: Does the Holy Spirit forgive sins, and does the fact that priests forgive sins undermine this as a mark of divinity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVIII. As he purposes to establish the Godhead of the Holy Spirit by the points already discussed, St. Ambrose touches again on some of them; for instance, that He does not commit but forgives sin; that He is not a creature but the Creator; and lastly, that He does not offer but receives worship.
sources.answer: The Spirit forgives sins, as Christ said in giving the Spirit to the apostles. Men only provide the ministry. They forgive not by their own power but in the name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit: they ask, the Godhead gives. Since only God forgives sins, the Spirit who forgives is God.
sources.quote: They ask, the Godhead gives, the service is of man, the gift is of the Power on high.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit forgive sins, and does the fact that priests forgive sins undermine this as a mark of divinity?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's part in baptismal forgiveness show that He shares the power and name of God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVIII. As he purposes to establish the Godhead of the Holy Spirit by the points already discussed, St. Ambrose touches again on some of them; for instance, that He does not commit but forgives sin; that He is not a creature but the Creator; and lastly, that He does not offer but receives worship.
sources.answer: Yes. Sin is forgiven in baptism, where the operation belongs jointly to Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Spirit cannot be separated from the one name of the divine nature, so He cannot be severed from God's power either. If He is not severed from God's power, He cannot be severed from the name of God.
sources.quote: certainly He Who cannot be separated from the oneness of the name of the Nature is also incapable of being severed from the power of God. Now if He is not severed from the power of God, how is He severed from the name of God.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's part in baptismal forgiveness show that He shares the power and name of God?

question: If one excludes the Holy Spirit from the Godhead, who else could share the glory of the Godhead with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XII. From the fact that St. Paul has shown that the light of the Godhead which the three apostles worshipped in Christ is in the Trinity, it is made clear that the Spirit also is to be worshipped. It is shown from the words themselves that the Spirit is intended by the apostles. The Godhead of the same Spirit is proved from the fact that He has a temple wherein He dwells not as a priest, but as God: and is worshipped with the Father and the Son; whence is understood the oneness of nature in Them.
sources.answer: No one. Ambrose holds that the power of the Godhead can be referred to no one besides the Holy Spirit, so those who exclude the Spirit would be forced to bring in some other being to receive divine glory with the Father and the Son, which is absurd.
sources.quote: For they who exclude the Spirit must necessarily bring in another, who may with the Father and the Son receive the glory of the Godhead.
sources.raw_question: If one excludes the Holy Spirit from the Godhead, who else could share the glory of the Godhead with the Father and the Son?

question: If the Son is born from God, does this make God changeable and corporeal, as though He extended or developed a part of Himself to become the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Not every birth is an extension, and not every begetting involves a loss to the one who begets. Even in nature there are cases of life passed from one living creature to another without bodily intercourse. Above all, God has revealed the birth and the Only-begotten, so the Church confesses them without making God mutable.
sources.quote: I could bring forward instances of birth, even in natures belonging to this world, which would refute this wretched delusion that every birth must be an extension.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is born from God, does this make God changeable and corporeal, as though He extended or developed a part of Himself to become the Son?

question: Should God's own testimony about the Son's birth be accepted over human reasoning about what is fitting to the divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. God's statements about Himself must be accepted exactly as spoken, and correcting them by human reasoning is an insult to His self-revelation. If life comes through God alone, He must also be the author of the faith on which that life depends. If we doubt His witness about Himself, we cannot be sure of the life He gives.
sources.quote: For if life comes through Him alone, must not He be the Author of the faith which is the condition of that life? And if we hold Him an untrustworthy witness concerning Himself, how can we be sure of the life which is His gift?
sources.raw_question: Should God's own testimony about the Son's birth be accepted over human reasoning about what is fitting to the divine nature?

question: Does the phrase "through him" applied to Christ, as in "more than conquerors through him that loved us," imply a lowly or subordinate ministry of the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. Such phrases suggest no lowly or subordinate ministry but the succour rendered "in the power of his might." Christ himself bound the strong man and spoiled his goods, rescuing humanity by his own power.
sources.quote: But in a phrase of this kind there is no suggestion of any lowly and subordinate ministry, but rather of the succour rendered “in the power of his might.”
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase "through him" applied to Christ, as in "more than conquerors through him that loved us," imply a lowly or subordinate ministry of the Son?

question: Does Revelation 1:4-5 show the Father, Spirit, and Son jointly yet distinctly communicating grace and peace to believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. In Rev 1:4-5 grace and peace come from him who is, was, and is to come, from the seven Spirits before the throne, and from Jesus Christ. All three are joined together as the source of the same gift, yet each is mentioned distinctly in that communication. The "seven Spirits" signify the Holy Spirit as the perfect fountain of every gift.
sources.quote: The seven Spirits before the throne, are the Holy Spirit of God, considered as the perfect fountain of every perfect gift and dispensation. All are here joined together, and yet all mentioned as distinguished in their communication of grace and peace unto the saints.
sources.raw_question: Does Revelation 1:4-5 show the Father, Spirit, and Son jointly yet distinctly communicating grace and peace to believers?

question: Does the Father's giving up of the Son to death wrong the Son or contradict the Father's love?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XII. The peace and grace of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one, so also is Their charity one, which showed itself chiefly in the redemption of man. Their communion with man is also one.
sources.answer: No. The Son was willing and offered himself, so the giving involved no distress and no wrong to affection. The Father did not give him to punishment but to grace. That the Father gave the Son and the Son gave himself shows the unity of one divine love.
sources.quote: He gave one Who was willing, He gave One Who offered Himself, the Father did not give the Son to punishment but to grace.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's giving up of the Son to death wrong the Son or contradict the Father's love?

question: Does the shared peace, grace, love and communion of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit prove that they have one power and substance?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XII. The peace and grace of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one, so also is Their charity one, which showed itself chiefly in the redemption of man. Their communion with man is also one.
sources.answer: Yes. If the peace, grace, love and communion of the three are one, then their working is one. Where the working is one, the power cannot be divided nor the substance separated, for otherwise the grace of one working could not agree.
sources.quote: the working is certainly one, and where the working is one, certainly the power cannot be divided nor the substance separated.
sources.raw_question: Does the shared peace, grace, love and communion of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit prove that they have one power and substance?

question: If only one hypostasis can be the one true God, what follows for the status of the Word and the Spirit?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: On that premise, the Word and Spirit must either be mere names or, if they are real distinct persons, creatures. The Sabellians chose the first option because Scripture and tradition strongly affirm the divinity of the Word and Spirit. The Arians chose the second after Sabellianism had been exploded. Both therefore in effect remove the Son and Spirit from the one true Godhead.
sources.quote: it is manifest that the Word and Spirit must either be names only, or, if real distinct persons, creatures.
sources.raw_question: If only one hypostasis can be the one true God, what follows for the status of the Word and the Spirit?

question: Do the scriptural statements that the Holy Spirit can be grieved, resisted, vexed and angered show that he has divine authority rather than the rank of a creature or instrument?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is grieved, resisted and angered by rebellious people, and when vexed he turned to be their enemy. These passages show authoritative power. To call the Spirit an instrument, a subject, a creature or our fellow servant is blasphemy that pious ears cannot bear.
sources.quote: Are not these passages indicative of authoritative power?
sources.raw_question: Do the scriptural statements that the Holy Spirit can be grieved, resisted, vexed and angered show that he has divine authority rather than the rank of a creature or instrument?

question: Do the Bible's images for the Holy Spirit (water, fire, breath, wind, oil, being poured out or breathed forth) suggest that the Spirit is God's love rather than God's understanding?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. These metaphors fit naturally only with affection: love or joy can be said to flow out like water, to be breathed forth like breath, to be warm like fire, or to be shed abroad (Romans 5:5). It would not sound right to say that an idea, a judgment, perception or reason flows out or is breathed forth. So the Spirit is best understood as the affection, love and delight of God.
sources.quote: The affection, love or joy, may be said to flow out as water or to be breathed forth as breath or wind. But it would [not] sound so well to say that an idea or judgment flows out or is breathed forth.
sources.raw_question: Do the Bible's images for the Holy Spirit (water, fire, breath, wind, oil, being poured out or breathed forth) suggest that the Spirit is God's love rather than God's understanding?

question: Does the saints' communion with God consist in sharing the Holy Spirit, and does this confirm that the Spirit is God's love and delight?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Communion means sharing in a common good, whether excellency or happiness. The saints have fellowship with the Father and the Son by partaking of the divine nature, holiness, glory and joy. Since the Holy Spirit is God's love and joy, and so His beauty and happiness, sharing the Spirit is exactly how we share the Father's and the Son's good.
sources.quote: the Holy Ghost being the love and joy of God is His beauty and happiness, and it is in our partaking of the same Holy Spirit that our communion with God consists
sources.raw_question: Does the saints' communion with God consist in sharing the Holy Spirit, and does this confirm that the Spirit is God's love and delight?

question: Was the Lord who called to Adam in the garden, "Where art thou?", the same Word who later became incarnate?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XV.—Proofs of the resurrection from Isaiah and Ezekiel; the same God who created us will also raise us up.
sources.answer: Yes. God's coming to Adam at eventide prefigures the same Word of God coming in the last times to call man back. By means of the same voice he searched out Adam's posterity and visited them, so the Word who sought Adam is the incarnate Lord.
sources.quote: That means that in the last times the very same Word of God came to call man, reminding him of his doings, living in which he had been hidden from the Lord.
sources.raw_question: Was the Lord who called to Adam in the garden, "Where art thou?", the same Word who later became incarnate?

question: What does every mind know with certainty about itself, even when it is mistaken about what kind of thing it is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Every Mind Knows Certainly Three Things Concerning Itself—That It Understands, that It Is, and that It Lives.
sources.answer: It knows certainly that it is, that it lives, and that it understands, and also that it wills and remembers. People have held the mind to be air, fire, the brain and so on, but none of them doubted these things about themselves. The mind therefore should not add to its self-knowledge what it only thinks itself to be, but should keep what it knows.
sources.quote: yet all know that they themselves understand, and are, and live; but they refer understanding to that which they understand, but to be, and to live, to themselves.
sources.raw_question: What does every mind know with certainty about itself, even when it is mistaken about what kind of thing it is?

question: How do memory, understanding and will in the human mind relate to one another in knowing and possessing things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Every Mind Knows Certainly Three Things Concerning Itself—That It Understands, that It Is, and that It Lives.
sources.answer: The knowledge and science of many things are contained in two of the three, memory and understanding. The will must also be present so that we may enjoy or use what is known. We enjoy things the will delights in for their own sake and rests in. We use things that we refer to something else which we are to enjoy.
sources.quote: Therefore the knowledge and science of many things are contained in two of these three, memory and understanding; but will must be present, that we may enjoy or use them.
sources.raw_question: How do memory, understanding and will in the human mind relate to one another in knowing and possessing things?

question: How could texts about Christ's human nature, such as his prayers and his ignorance of the last day, prove against the Sabellians a distinct divine Person besides the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: Catholics and Sabellians both agreed that the divine nature was personally united to the man Christ Jesus. The question was whether the Father himself was that Person. Christ's speaking of the Father as another (praying to him, complaining of being forsaken, saying the Father knows what he does not) shows the Father was not personally united to Christ's humanity. So on the Sabellians' own principles another divine Hypostasis, a real Son of the Father, must be united with it.
sources.quote: It appearing therefore, from that manner of expression, that the Father was: not personally united with the human nature of Christ ; this was sufficient against the Sabellians, who allowed that the man Christ Jesus was personally united with God
sources.raw_question: How could texts about Christ's human nature, such as his prayers and his ignorance of the last day, prove against the Sabellians a distinct divine Person besides the Father?

question: Can a mystery of the Christian faith be a proposition that is unintelligible or plainly self-contradictory?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Propositions with no meaning cannot be assented to and are mere sounds, and plain contradictions are no more mysteries than plain truths are. Genuine mysteries are propositions whose ideas are only seemingly repugnant, general rather than particular, or purely intellectual. Assent can rightly be given in each of these cases.
sources.quote: plain contradictions are certainly no mysteries, any more than plain truths; as is justly observed by the learned * Dr. Clarke.
sources.raw_question: Can a mystery of the Christian faith be a proposition that is unintelligible or plainly self-contradictory?

question: Was the Spirit Christ breathed on the disciples a different Spirit from the one sent after the ascension?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: No. Only a madman would say so. The Spirit of God is one, the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, who works all in all. That he was given twice was a significant economy, not a sign of two Spirits.
sources.quote: For the veriest of madmen would not say, that it was one Spirit which He gave when He breathed on them, and another which He sent after His ascension.
sources.raw_question: Was the Spirit Christ breathed on the disciples a different Spirit from the one sent after the ascension?

question: Since things that are made begin in time, must the Son, as Maker, also begin his existence at the time when he begins making?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Time and the ages mark the beginnings of created things, but the Maker of time and of the ages cannot be measured by them. The only 'beginning' named of the Son, the 'beginning' in the Gospel, signifies the Father. The Son, who is in the Father, cannot begin his being in Him from any particular point.
sources.quote: Well, the creation has the ages for its beginning, but what beginning can you conceive of the Maker of the ages?
sources.raw_question: Since things that are made begin in time, must the Son, as Maker, also begin his existence at the time when he begins making?

question: Does affirming that Christ had a human birth and true flesh diminish his divinity, so that he should be held to be God without flesh?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And This is So Manifest, that Some Heretics Have Thought Him to Be God the Father, Others that He Was Only God Without the Flesh.
sources.answer: No. Novatian rejects the view of those who removed Christ's humanity to protect his divine dignity. Because the Son of man was taken up by God, Christ must be believed to be man as well as God.
sources.quote: other heretics have so far embraced the manifest divinity of Christ, as to say that He was without flesh, and to withdraw from Him the whole humanity which He took upon Him
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that Christ had a human birth and true flesh diminish his divinity, so that he should be held to be God without flesh?

question: Does the New Testament clearly teach that three Persons subsist in the one Godhead, each fully divine?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. To the fact that in the unity of the Godhead three Persons subsist, each with his part in salvation, the New Testament testimony is clear, consistent, pervasive and conclusive. It gives constant witness to the complete and undiminished Deity of each Person, applying the most exalted language to each in turn.
sources.quote: There is included in this testimony constant and decisive witness to the complete and undiminished Deity of each of these Persons; no language is too exalted to apply to each of them in turn
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament clearly teach that three Persons subsist in the one Godhead, each fully divine?

question: Does Paul's list of created things in Colossians 1:16 show whether the Holy Spirit is a creature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > These doctrines of our Faith witnessed to and confirmed by Scripture passages.
sources.answer: Yes, it shows that the Spirit is above creation. Paul spells out the 'all things' made by the Son, both visible and invisible, and names the classes of created intelligible beings: thrones, dominions, principalities and powers. By his silence he leaves out the Spirit. It is like listing an army's subordinate officers without naming the supreme commander, since including him among his inferiors would be an insult.
sources.quote: having traversed all the angelic and transcendental world, he stops his reckoning there, and refuses to drag down to the level of creation that which is above it. Hence there is a clear testimony in Scripture that the Holy Spirit is higher than the creation.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's list of created things in Colossians 1:16 show whether the Holy Spirit is a creature?

question: Since Paul's list also omits the Cherubim and Seraphim, does the Spirit's omission prove nothing about His being above creation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > These doctrines of our Faith witnessed to and confirmed by Scripture passages.
sources.answer: No, the objection fails, because the Cherubim and Seraphim are not really omitted. 'Thrones' is Paul's Greek name for the Cherubim, since God sits upon the Cherubim. The Seraphim are included under 'powers', as David's Psalm calls God's ministering powers, so the Spirit alone is truly left out of the catalogue of creation.
sources.quote: Under “thrones” he includes the Cherubim, giving them this Greek name, as more intelligible than the Hebrew name for them. He knew that “God sits upon the Cherubim:” and so he calls these Powers the thrones of Him who sits thereon.
sources.raw_question: Since Paul's list also omits the Cherubim and Seraphim, does the Spirit's omission prove nothing about His being above creation?

question: Why are the Father, Son and Holy Spirit counted one by one, while created spiritual beings are counted in groups?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > These doctrines of our Faith witnessed to and confirmed by Scripture passages.
sources.answer: It is a peculiarity of the Holy Trinity to be proclaimed as individuals: one Father, one Son, one Holy Ghost. Created spirits are counted in masses such as dominions, principalities and powers. This excludes any suspicion that the Holy Ghost is one of those created classes.
sources.quote: For it is a peculiarity of the Holy Trinity that it is to be proclaimed as consisting of individuals: one Father, one Son, one Holy Ghost: whereas those existences aforesaid are counted in masses
sources.raw_question: Why are the Father, Son and Holy Spirit counted one by one, while created spiritual beings are counted in groups?

question: Do positive names of God such as Creator, Almighty, Good and Judge express the divine nature itself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. They express the results of our reverent reasoning about God from His works and from Scripture, not the divine nature itself. Seeing the greatness and beauty of creation, the good in our life, and the coming judgment, we form thoughts about God and stamp each with a corresponding name. So no name is given to God apart from some distinct intuition of His operations.
sources.quote: do not afford that indication of the Divine nature itself, but only of the results of our reverent speculations about it.
sources.raw_question: Do positive names of God such as Creator, Almighty, Good and Judge express the divine nature itself?

question: Is the Holy Spirit alone sufficient for our blessedness, or must the Father and Son be added to complete it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit alone suffices for our blessedness, because He cannot be divided from the Father and the Son. Likewise the Father alone suffices and the Son alone suffices, each being inseparable from the other two. Our fullest joy is the fruition of God the Trinity, so naming any one Person implies all three.
sources.quote: He does alone so suffice, because He cannot be divided from the Father and the Son; as the Father alone is sufficient, because He cannot be divided from the Son and the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit alone sufficient for our blessedness, or must the Father and Son be added to complete it?

question: Do the Church Fathers support the notion of a supreme God and a subordinate God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. The ancients implicitly condemned it all along in their disputes with the pagans. As soon as it was started in the Church, the Catholics condemned it as reviving creature-worship and pagan polytheism. No Scripture, sound reason or good Catholic ever taught two Gods, one greater and one less.
sources.quote: Two Gods, a greater and a less, a supreme and an inferior, no Scripture, no sound reason, no good Catholic ever taught; no church would have endured.
sources.raw_question: Do the Church Fathers support the notion of a supreme God and a subordinate God?

question: Can Arians or Socinians fairly charge the Catholic doctrine of the Trinity with tritheism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. The Catholic scheme only appears chargeable with polytheism but really is not, while the Arian and Socinian schemes both appear so and are so. Even three coordinate Gods would be no more repugnant to Scripture than their plurality of Gods, great and little, created and uncreated, all receiving religious adoration. Only the Sabellian scheme is wholly clear of the appearance of polytheism, and only because it ungods the Son and annihilates the Spirit.
sources.quote: The Catholic appears chargeable, but really is not so: the Arian and Socinian both appear so, and are so; wherefore a charge of Tritheism must come from them with a very ill grace.
sources.raw_question: Can Arians or Socinians fairly charge the Catholic doctrine of the Trinity with tritheism?

question: Why do human fathers exist before their sons, and does that reason apply to God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: Human fathers precede their sons only because their nature, being temporal and weak, restrains them from begetting until they reach the proper age; otherwise the child would be ever coexistent with the parent. Nothing restrains God, who is not as man, so He is always Father of the Son. Levi's being in the loins of his great-grandfather shows the child is in a sense already present in the parent.
sources.quote: yet he too would have had his child ever coexistent with him, but that his nature was a restraint and made it impossible. For Levi too was already in the loins of his great-grandfather
sources.raw_question: Why do human fathers exist before their sons, and does that reason apply to God?

question: Must God's knowledge or view of Himself be conceived as something distinct from His mere direct existence?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. If God beholds Himself so as to delight and rejoice in Himself, He must become His own object. There must therefore be a duplicity in God: there is God and the idea of God, something answering to our reflection though without its imperfection.
sources.quote: However, if God beholds Himself so as thence to have delight and joy in Himself He must become his own object. There must be a duplicity. There is God and the idea of God
sources.raw_question: Must God's knowledge or view of Himself be conceived as something distinct from His mere direct existence?

question: Do the Scripture texts calling Christ the image and form of God support identifying the Son with God's perfect idea of Himself?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Nothing agrees better with Scripture's account of the Son as the form of God and His express and perfect image and representation. The image of the invisible God and the express image of His person is exactly what God's perfect idea of Himself would be.
sources.quote: Nothing can more agree with the account the Scripture gives us of the Son of God, His being in the form of God and His express and perfect image and representation
sources.raw_question: Do the Scripture texts calling Christ the image and form of God support identifying the Son with God's perfect idea of Himself?

question: Does the mind of an infant know itself, even though it seems wholly absorbed in sensible things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether the Mind of Infants Knows Itself.
sources.answer: Yes, it is to be believed that the infant mind knows itself, though it does not think of itself. Being intent on the novel objects of the bodily senses, it cannot be ignorant of itself, yet it is unable to turn its thought inward. Its absorption in sense is shown by how fixedly infants gaze at light, and admonition cannot redirect them since they do not yet know words.
sources.quote: it is not able indeed to be ignorant of itself, but is also not able to think of itself?
sources.raw_question: Does the mind of an infant know itself, even though it seems wholly absorbed in sensible things?

question: When a person comes to think about the nature of his own mind, does he discover something he did not previously know?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether the Mind of Infants Knows Itself.
sources.answer: No. He finds the truth only in himself, and finds not what he did not know but what he had not thought of. For if we do not know what is in our own mind, we know nothing, since we can know nothing at all except by the mind.
sources.quote: And he will find, not what he did not know, but that of which he did not think. For what do we know, if we do not know what is in our own mind
sources.raw_question: When a person comes to think about the nature of his own mind, does he discover something he did not previously know?

question: When the mind looks at itself in thought, does it see one part of itself with another part, move itself to a place before itself, or become doubled like a body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How a Kind of Trinity Exists in the Mind Thinking of Itself. What is the Part of Thought in This Trinity.
sources.answer: No. Such pictures are absurd, because they come from feigned images of bodily things, and the mind is not a body. The mind's beholding of itself belongs to its nature. It is recalled to that nature not by moving through space but by an incorporeal conversion toward itself.
sources.quote: the beholding of the mind is something pertaining to its nature, and is recalled to that nature when it conceives of itself, not as if by moving through space, but by an incorporeal conversion
sources.raw_question: When the mind looks at itself in thought, does it see one part of itself with another part, move itself to a place before itself, or become doubled like a body?

question: Is the Son the same as the Father in so far as He is the Word?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. As wisdom and essence the Word is what the Father is. But 'Word', like 'Son', is spoken relatively, and the Word is not the Father.
sources.quote: For in so far as it is the Word, it is not what the Father is; because the Word is not the Father, and Word is spoken relatively, as is also Son, which assuredly is not the Father.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the same as the Father in so far as He is the Word?

question: Why should the Trinity be confessed by the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit rather than by newly devised philosophical terms such as Eunomius's 'supreme and proper being'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He did wrong, when mentioning the Doctrines of Salvation, in adopting terms of his own choosing instead of the traditional terms Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Because the traditional names themselves convey the proper and natural relationship between Father and Son. Anyone hearing 'father' and 'son' at once recognizes their natural relation to one another. Eunomius abandons these inspired terms precisely to strip away this idea of relationship, so that it would not be understood of the Father and the Only-begotten. His new terms are devised to injure the truth.
sources.quote: every one, when the words father and son are spoken, at once recognizes the proper and natural relationship to one another which they imply. This relationship is conveyed at once by the appellations themselves.
sources.raw_question: Why should the Trinity be confessed by the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit rather than by newly devised philosophical terms such as Eunomius's 'supreme and proper being'?

question: Since the Holy Spirit is a gift of God, should He receive less honour than God the Giver?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Proof of the absurdity of the refusal to glorify the Spirit, from the comparison of things glorified in creation.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit is a gift, but a gift of life and of power. The Father also gave the Son as a free gift to mankind, yet the Son is not lightly esteemed because of this. To turn the greatness of God's loving kindness into grounds for dishonour is blasphemous ingratitude.
sources.quote: Is He on this account to be lightly esteemed? Did not God also bestow His Son as a free gift to mankind?
sources.raw_question: Since the Holy Spirit is a gift of God, should He receive less honour than God the Giver?

question: How does the mind's self-trinity of memory, understanding, and will differ from the trinities found in bodily sight or in knowledge acquired from outside?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Trinity Which is the Image of God is Now to Be Sought in the Noblest Part of the Mind.
sources.answer: Its terms are not received from outside. In bodily vision and in learned knowledge, the object is external or adventitious, and the will joins it to the perceiver. In the mind's self-knowledge, by contrast, memory does not receive its content from outside, nor does understanding find its object outside, nor does will join two things brought in from without. This interiority is why it qualifies as an image of God where the lower trinities did not.
sources.quote: The memory does not receive from without that which it is to hold; nor does the understanding find without that which it is to regard, as the eye of the body does; nor has will joined these two from without
sources.raw_question: How does the mind's self-trinity of memory, understanding, and will differ from the trinities found in bodily sight or in knowledge acquired from outside?

question: Is the Son of God a slave or servant of the Father by nature, as Eunomius held?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory argues that the Son who has all things that the Father has is Lord of all and not a slave. Slavery is dishonour, and dishonour cannot make up the brightness of the true glory, nor can the King's Son be born into slavery. As He is Light of Light and God of God, so He is Lord of Lord and King of King.
sources.quote: He who has all things that the Father has is lord of all, and not a slave. For how can the personality that owns no lord over it bear on itself the brand of slavery?
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God a slave or servant of the Father by nature, as Eunomius held?

question: Does the Arian confession that the Father alone is unborn (unbegotten) count against the Son's divinity or require any concession from orthodox believers?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. No orthodox believer supposes that the Father, who begot the Son through whom all things exist, derived His being from any other source. The very name Father reveals Him as the cause of the Son's existence while giving no hint that He descends from another. So unbegottenness is rightly left to the Father as His own special and incommunicable property, without detracting from the Son.
sources.quote: The very fact that He bears the name of Father reveals Him as the cause of His Son’s existence. That name of Father gives no hint that He who bears it is Himself descended from another
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian confession that the Father alone is unborn (unbegotten) count against the Son's divinity or require any concession from orthodox believers?

question: Can the Son of God be both slave (under the Father's dominion) and Lord over creatures at the same time, like a head servant set over fellow-servants?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. The analogy of a steward set over fellow-servants is drawn from ordinary human life and wrongly transferred to the Godhead. Because the Son's essence is simple and uncompounded, it cannot admit contrary attributes such as lordship and servitude together. If he is Lord, as the saints teach, his simplicity rules out his being a slave. If he were a slave, it would be idle to call him Lord.
sources.quote: If then the Lord is simple and uncompounded in nature, how can the conjunction of contraries be found in the subject, as would be the case if servitude mingled with lordship?
sources.raw_question: Can the Son of God be both slave (under the Father's dominion) and Lord over creatures at the same time, like a head servant set over fellow-servants?

question: Did the early Church Fathers understand John 10:30 only as a unity of love, consent and power between Father and Son, so that the Catholic use of it for unity of substance runs against the whole stream of antiquity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. The Catholics consistently used the text in two ways: against those who denied Christ's divinity, to prove his real divinity, and against the Sabellians, to prove his real distinction from the Father. Against the Sabellians they stressed unity of love and consent, because those opponents already made the unity so high as to allow only one Hypostasis. That emphasis does not exclude unity of substance, which the same writers maintained elsewhere. Waterland charges that the opponent represents the Fathers only by halves.
sources.quote: The text, which you speak of, has all along been made use of by the Catholics, in two respects ; first, in proof of our Lord’s real divinity, against: as many as denied it; and secondly, in proof of his real distinction from the Father
sources.raw_question: Did the early Church Fathers understand John 10:30 only as a unity of love, consent and power between Father and Son, so that the Catholic use of it for unity of substance runs against the whole stream of antiquity?

question: Did Tertullian interpret John 10:30 as referring to unity of substance between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: Yes. In one passage he expressly interprets the text of unity of substance, "ad substantiae unitatem, non ad numeri singularitatem." His other passage, which speaks of "unitatem," should be understood the same way once the word is construed properly. Unity of love, consent and power follows naturally from that foundation. Elsewhere Tertullian grounds the harmony of the three Persons in unity of substance.
sources.quote: he interprets the text expressly of unity of substance, in one citation: and he is to be so understood in the other, had you but thought how to construe wnitatem, as you should have done.
sources.raw_question: Did Tertullian interpret John 10:30 as referring to unity of substance between the Father and the Son?

question: Does the orthodox doctrine of 'individual' or 'numerical' consubstantiality mean that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one Person?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: No. No one who owns a Trinity holds that the three Persons are one Person, hypostasis or suppositum, and this is not the scholastic notion either. By 'individual' or 'numerical' sober Catholics meant only that the Son is strictly divine and so nearly united to the Father that the Son's substance is the Father's substance, both being one.
sources.quote: That present scholastic notion, as you call it, of three Persons being one Person, Hypostasis, or Suppositum, is nowhere present, that 1 know of, amongst any that own a Trinity
sources.raw_question: Does the orthodox doctrine of 'individual' or 'numerical' consubstantiality mean that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one Person?

question: If the Fathers held only a specific (same-kind) unity of Father and Son, would that support the Arian view that the Son is of an inferior nature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: No. Specific unity implies equality of nature, as two men of the same species are equal in nature. So even on that reading all the Fathers would be directly opposed to the view that the Son is inferior in kind, nature or substance. Either specific or individual consubstantiality refutes the Arian scheme.
sources.quote: Specific unity implies equality of nature ; as two men, specifically one with each other, are in nature equal; and so, any other two things of the same sort and kind.
sources.raw_question: If the Fathers held only a specific (same-kind) unity of Father and Son, would that support the Arian view that the Son is of an inferior nature?

question: Did the Fathers understand the unity of the divine Persons as merely specific, like three men or three suns of the same kind?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: No. The Fathers took care to deny that the Persons are one only as three separately existing human persons are. They rejected three suns as an illustration and preferred rays of one sun or streams of one fountain, to signify a closer and more substantial union than specific unity. The Persons are three hypostases yet, in Tertullian's words, of one substance.
sources.quote: nor would they allow three suns,which would be specifically one, to be a proper or suitable illustration ; but the rays of the same sun, the streams of the same fountain, and the like; all to intimate a much closer tie, a more substantial union, than specific amounts to.
sources.raw_question: Did the Fathers understand the unity of the divine Persons as merely specific, like three men or three suns of the same kind?

question: Is acknowledging that human nature is too weak to comprehend God a sign of a mind blinded by malignity, as Eunomius alleges?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > The tenth book discusses the unattainable and incomprehensible character of the enquiry into entities. And herein he strikingly sets forth the points concerning the nature and formation of the ant, and the passage in the Gospel, “I am the door” and “the way,” and also discusses the attribution and interpretation of the Divine names, and the episode of the children of Benjamin.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that confessing the weakness of human nature is the honest recognition that the divine power transcends all conception. Knowledge of hidden things must be warranted by knowledge of what is evident, and since even small creatures exceed our comprehension, admitting our limits is not blindness but truth.
sources.quote: Let him, then, who boasts that he has grasped the knowledge of real existence, disclose to us awhile the nature of the ant, and then, and not till then, let him discourse on the nature of the power that surpasses all understanding.
sources.raw_question: Is acknowledging that human nature is too weak to comprehend God a sign of a mind blinded by malignity, as Eunomius alleges?

question: Is confining the divine unity to the Father alone, excluding the Son, a valid way to preserve monotheism, as Paul of Samosata and Arius held?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. Paul of Samosata, who confined the unity to the Father only, was rejected by the Catholic bishops as a wolf, and Arius, who for the same pretext denied the Son's divinity while allowing his preexistence, followed the same erroneous line. The Church retained the faith in the Son's divinity, regarding such charges as weak and groundless.
sources.quote: was a warm, injudicious Passerter of the unity, confining it to the Father only, exclusive of the other Persons.
sources.raw_question: Is confining the divine unity to the Father alone, excluding the Son, a valid way to preserve monotheism, as Paul of Samosata and Arius held?

question: Is the Holy Spirit of the same substance as corporeal or invisible created things such as angels?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit sheds incorporeal grace on corporeal things, so He is not corporeal; and invisible creatures like Angels, Dominions and Powers receive sanctification from Him and await His grace, so He is not of their substance either. What sanctifies creatures cannot itself be one of the creatures sanctified.
sources.quote: nor, again, is He of the substance of invisible creatures, for they receive His sanctification, and through Him are superior to the other works of the universe. Whether you speak of Angels, or Dominions, or Powers, every creature waits for the grace of the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit of the same substance as corporeal or invisible created things such as angels?

question: Is the Holy Spirit capable of change, as every creature is?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: No. Every creature, including angels, is by nature changeable even if discipline keeps it from falling, but the Holy Spirit is unchangeable. He does away the faults of all and works a change to grace in others by sanctifying them, while not being changed Himself. This sets Him apart from all creatures.
sources.quote: Every creature, therefore, is capable of change, but the Holy Spirit is good and not capable of change, nor can He be changed by any fault, Who does away the faults of all and pardons their sins.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit capable of change, as every creature is?

question: Does comparing Matthew 7:11 with Luke 11:13 show that the Holy Spirit is good?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: Yes. Where Matthew says the Father gives 'good things' to those who ask, Luke says He gives 'the Holy Spirit.' So one evangelist puts good things in place of the Spirit and the other names the Spirit in place of good things. By the Lord's own judgment, then, the Spirit is that which is good.
sources.quote: the one has put good things in the place of the Holy Spirit, the other has named the Holy Spirit in the place of good things. If, then, the Holy Spirit is that which is good, how is He not good?
sources.raw_question: Does comparing Matthew 7:11 with Luke 11:13 show that the Holy Spirit is good?

question: Could God the Father ever have existed without his Word (Logos)?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. The ancients took the relation of the Word to the Father to be as close and intimate as that of thought to a mind, and held that the very name implies this. They therefore rightly concluded that the Father could never be without the Logos, any more than an eternal Mind could be without eternal thought.
sources.quote: rightly concluded that the Father could not be “Adoyos, or without the Λόγος, any more than an eternal Mind could be without eternal thoughtz
sources.raw_question: Could God the Father ever have existed without his Word (Logos)?

question: Did ante-Nicene writers who spoke of a temporal generation of the Son, such as Tertullian, Justin and Theophilus, deny that the Word is coeternal with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. These writers held the coeternity of the Word, even though they did not consider him strictly under the formality of a Son. It was their maxim that God was always endowed with his Word and never without it. In this they agreed fully with the writers before, after and alongside them, so their talk of a temporal generation does not deny the Word's eternity.
sources.quote: They asserted the coeternity of the Adyos, or Word, though not considered precisely under the formality of a Son.
sources.raw_question: Did ante-Nicene writers who spoke of a temporal generation of the Son, such as Tertullian, Justin and Theophilus, deny that the Word is coeternal with the Father?

question: What is the overall scope or rule of faith by which Scripture's statements about Christ should be interpreted?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human.
