Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: Scripture gives a double account of the Saviour. He was always God and the Son, the Father's Word, Radiance and Wisdom. Afterwards, for our sake, he took flesh of the Virgin Mary and was made man. Reading every passage in light of this double account keeps one from the Arians' misinterpretations.
sources.quote: it contains a double account of the Saviour; that He was ever God, and is the Son, being the Father’s Word and Radiance and Wisdom; and that afterwards for us He took flesh of a Virgin, Mary Bearer of God, and was made man.
sources.raw_question: What is the overall scope or rule of faith by which Scripture's statements about Christ should be interpreted?

question: Would making the Son a created nature imply that he is mutable and capable of moral change, like the angels and the devil?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He convicts Eunomius of having used of the Only-begotten terms applicable to the existence of the earth, and thus shows that his intention is to prove the Son to be a being mutable and created.
sources.answer: Yes, that is the consequence of the heretical view, and it is false. The devil was created intellectual and incorporeal, yet his created nature did not keep him from becoming evil by change. This is because a mutable essence follows the will either way. To call the Son created is therefore to make him capable of contrary dispositions, ranked with the angels.
sources.quote: Accordingly they will define the Lord as being capable even of contrary dispositions, drawing Him down as it were to a rank equal with the angels, by the conception of creation
sources.raw_question: Would making the Son a created nature imply that he is mutable and capable of moral change, like the angels and the devil?

question: If reason cannot resolve the difficulty of confessing three Persons but one God, should belief in the Trinity be abandoned?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. Even if our reasoning proves unequal to the problem, we must hold firm and unmoved the tradition received from the fathers. We should seek from the Lord the reason that defends the faith. The faith on points already determined stands whether or not an argument is found.
sources.quote: we must keep for ever, firm and unmoved, the tradition which we received by succession from the fathers, and seek from the Lord the reason which is the advocate of our faith
sources.raw_question: If reason cannot resolve the difficulty of confessing three Persons but one God, should belief in the Trinity be abandoned?

question: Since there is no medium between a being and not a being, must the Son be either a separate real being or a mere name?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: No. The maxim holds only if 'being' is used in the same sense throughout. 'Being' can mean either simply what exists or what exists separately. The Persons are each real (tres res), yet not separate, so together they are one being (una res numero). Waterland illustrates this with Clarke's own view of God's substance as the substratum of space. The substratum in the sun and that in the moon must be either two distinct beings, which leads toward two Gods, or something that is real yet not a separate being.
sources.quote: The truth of this matter, so far as I apprehend, is, that being may signify, either simply what ewists, or what exists separately.
sources.raw_question: Since there is no medium between a being and not a being, must the Son be either a separate real being or a mere name?

question: If it is doubtful whether Christ is fully divine, is it safer to think too highly of him than too meanly?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 30: Whether, supposing the case doubtful, it be not a wise man’s part to take the safer side; rather to think too highly, than too meanly of our blessed Saviour ; r
sources.answer: Yes. Though going beyond Revelation is culpable as well as falling short of it, the two faults are not equal in degree. Excessive honour to Christ out of gratitude is a pitiable failing on the right side, whereas falling short is ingratitude and blasphemy, degrading our Maker, Preserver, King and Judge to the level of creatures.
sources.quote: if we happen to fall short in our regards, there is not only ingratitude, but blasphemy in it. It is degrading and dethroning our Maker, Preserver, King, and Judge; and bringing him down to a level with his creatures.
sources.raw_question: If it is doubtful whether Christ is fully divine, is it safer to think too highly of him than too meanly?

question: Should the Son be called the will or counsel of the Father itself, rather than will of will and counsel of counsel?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Against Eunomius, Saying that the Son of God is the Son, Not of His Nature, But of His Will. Epilogue to What Has Been Said Already.
sources.answer: It is better to say counsel of counsel and will of will, just as we say substance of substance and wisdom of wisdom. Otherwise the Father would lack counsel or will in his own substance. The Son would then make the Father wise or willing, an absurdity already refuted.
sources.quote: it is better in my judgment to say counsel of counsel, and will of will, as substance of substance, wisdom of wisdom, that we may not be led into that absurdity
sources.raised_by_detail: some who wished to avoid calling the Word the Son of God's will
sources.raw_question: Should the Son be called the will or counsel of the Father itself, rather than will of will and counsel of counsel?

question: How can the Son be from the Father as a real Offspring without dividing the divine Monad?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: As light is from fire, so the Word is from God, Wisdom from the Wise, and the Son from the Father. In this way the Monad remains undivided and entire, while the Son is a truly essential and subsisting Word, not a mere notion or name.
sources.quote: For as there is light from fire, so from God is there a Word, and Wisdom from the Wise, and from the Father a Son. For in this way the Monad remains undivided and entire
sources.raw_question: How can the Son be from the Father as a real Offspring without dividing the divine Monad?

question: Should the philosophical classification of causes, which assigns 'of whom' to the maker or matter, 'through whom' to the instrument, and 'in whom' to time and place, be used to mark distinctions of nature between the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > The systematic discussion of syllables is derived from heathen philosophy.
sources.answer: No. Basil holds that these careful distinctions come from heathen philosophy and 'vain delusion.' His opponents studied and admired them and then carried them over into the simple doctrine of the Spirit. The result is to belittle God the Word and set at naught the Divine Spirit. Scripture is not bound by this pagan scheme and varies its expressions as occasion requires.
sources.quote: It is these careful distinctions, derived from unpractical philosophy and vain delusion, which our opponents have first studied and admired, and then transferred to the simple and unsophisticated doctrine of the Spirit, to the belittling of God the Word, and the setting at naught of the Divine Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Should the philosophical classification of causes, which assigns 'of whom' to the maker or matter, 'through whom' to the instrument, and 'in whom' to time and place, be used to mark distinctions of nature between the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: How does the analogy of the sun and its radiance illustrate that Father and Son are not two Gods?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: The radiance is light, not second to the sun, not a different light, nor light by participation, but the whole and proper offspring of the sun. Sun and radiance are two, yet there is one light; likewise the Son's Godhead is the Father's and therefore indivisible, so there is one God.
sources.quote: no one would say that they are two lights, but sun and radiance two, yet one the light from the sun enlightening in its radiance all things
sources.raw_question: How does the analogy of the sun and its radiance illustrate that Father and Son are not two Gods?

question: Did Jesus nevertheless openly testify to his own divine nature and his pre-existence before the incarnation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Preface
sources.answer: Yes. As occasions required, he gave plain and open testimony to his divinity and eternal pre-existence, as when he said, "Before Abraham was, I am." This assertion of Deity is precisely what most provoked the Jews to try to stone him.
sources.quote: he forbare not to give plain and open testimony to his own divine nature and eternal pre-existence unto his incarnation.
sources.raw_question: Did Jesus nevertheless openly testify to his own divine nature and his pre-existence before the incarnation?

question: When the Creator says 'I am God, and besides Me there is no other God,' is he speaking falsely out of ignorance of a higher Power, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter IX.—There is but one Creator of the world, God the Father: this the constant belief of the Church.
sources.answer: No. The Gnostics say the Creator is the fruit of a defect who does not know the Power above him, and so they accuse him of lying. Irenaeus answers that it is they who lie. By positing a god who does not exist, they blaspheme the God who truly exists, which makes them worse than the heathen.
sources.quote: Affirming that He lies, they are themselves liars, attributing all sorts of wickedness to Him; and conceiving of one who is not above this Being as really having an existence, they are thus convicted by their own views of blasphemy against that God who really exists
sources.raw_question: When the Creator says 'I am God, and besides Me there is no other God,' is he speaking falsely out of ignorance of a higher Power, as the Gnostics claim?

question: When the Father and the Son come to dwell in a believer, do two distinct Spirits indwell, or one?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: One. Paul teaches that it is not two Spirits, of God and of Christ, that are present in believers, but the Spirit of Christ which is also the Spirit of God. It is one indwelling under the mysterious semblance of a joint indwelling, since neither do two Spirits indwell nor does one differ from the other. Their coming together is therefore not as aliens associated together but in unity of nature.
sources.quote: This is no joint indwelling, it is one indwelling: yet an indwelling under the mysterious semblance of a joint indwelling, for it is not the case that two Spirits indwell, nor is one that indwells different from the other.
sources.raw_question: When the Father and the Son come to dwell in a believer, do two distinct Spirits indwell, or one?

question: Does calling the Son 'originate' amount to saying he came 'out of nothing' and 'once was not'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: Yes. When the Arians could no longer openly say 'out of nothing' and 'He was not before His generation', they adopted 'unoriginate' so that calling the Son 'originate' would convey the same ideas. Such phrases properly belong to things originated and creatures, so applying them to the Son reduces Him to a creature.
sources.quote: by saying among the simple that the Son was ‘originate,’ they might imply the very same phrases ‘out of nothing,’ and ‘He once was not;’ for in such phrases things originated and creatures are implied.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son 'originate' amount to saying he came 'out of nothing' and 'once was not'?

question: Can divine attributes be said to belong to the Father only because he possesses them primarily or originally as the self-existent cause?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: In a qualified sense, yes. Waterland admits this provided 'cause' is taken in the sober catholic sense of the Greek Fathers and 'self-existent' is understood negatively (as unoriginated), not as implying the Son's attributes are lesser in kind.
sources.quote: This I can readily admit, as well as you, provided only the word cause be interpreted to a just, sober, and catholic sense, (as the Greek writers especially have understood it,) and self: eaistent be interpreted, as it should be, negatively.
sources.raw_question: Can divine attributes be said to belong to the Father only because he possesses them primarily or originally as the self-existent cause?

question: Can attributes like omniscience or eternity belong to Christ in a 'subordinate' (restricted, limited) sense and still be the same attributes as God's?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: No. A limited omniscience or eternity is a different thing from the true attribute, so to say they belong to Christ in such a sense is in effect to deny they belong to him at all. Catholic writers meant subordination of order (wisdom from wisdom, God from God), not limited perfections.
sources.quote: omniscience, or eternity, &e. in your subordinate sense, are very different from the other ; and therefore are not the same attributes.
sources.raw_question: Can attributes like omniscience or eternity belong to Christ in a 'subordinate' (restricted, limited) sense and still be the same attributes as God's?

question: Does the Father's 'showing' the Son all that he does (John 5:20) imply that the Son is ignorant and needs instruction?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. To suppose the Only-begotten ignorant is reckless blasphemy; he already knows everything he is taught, as shown by his immediately stating what greater works will be shown him. The showing aids not ignorance in him but faith in us, teaching his true birth. The showing was part of his birth itself, the knowledge of the Father's works being imparted with that birth by the Father's love.
sources.quote: The shewing of the works is an aid, not to ignorance in Him, but to faith in us. It conveys to the Son no knowledge of things unknown, but it imparts to us the confidence to proclaim His birth
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's 'showing' the Son all that he does (John 5:20) imply that the Son is ignorant and needs instruction?

question: Does the Son's raising the dead 'as' the Father does show that the Son has equal power with the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so the Son gives life to whom he will; the power is equal because the nature is one and the same. Moreover, his giving life 'to whom He will' shows he needs no precedent to act, since to will implies a free nature with the power of omnipotence.
sources.quote: The power is equal because the nature is one and the same.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's raising the dead 'as' the Father does show that the Son has equal power with the Father?

question: Is the Son's power to give life to whom he will only a prerogative of the unbegotten Father, not possessible by one truly born?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Christ adds that the Father has given all judgment to the Son, which teaches both his birth and his Sonship: only a nature altogether one with the Father's could possess all things, and a Son possesses them by gift. The aim is that all honour the Son even as they honour the Father.
sources.quote: The statement that all judgment is given teaches both His birth and His Sonship; for only a nature which is altogether one with the Father’s could possess all things; and a Son can possess nothing, except by gift.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's power to give life to whom he will only a prerogative of the unbegotten Father, not possessible by one truly born?

question: Can one being be more or less a being than another, so that the Father has being in a higher degree than the Son and the Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in making the being of the Father alone proper and supreme, implying by his omission of the Son and the Spirit that theirs is improperly spoken of, and is inferior.
sources.answer: No. When being is taken in its plain meaning, apart from qualities like force, value, colour or reputation that gather round the subject, two existing things are equally existences. Degrees of more and less belong to accidental qualities, not to being itself, so Eunomius's ranking of a supreme and proper being above lesser beings has no basis in philosophy, Scripture, or common sense.
sources.quote: We have yet to learn that of two known existencies, which still exist, the one is more, the other less, an existence. Both are equally such, as long as they are in the category of existence
sources.raw_question: Can one being be more or less a being than another, so that the Father has being in a higher degree than the Son and the Spirit?

question: Is it fitting to call the Son 'a Being existing through the First, but after It' instead of using the scriptural name 'Son'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in making the being of the Father alone proper and supreme, implying by his omission of the Son and the Spirit that theirs is improperly spoken of, and is inferior.
sources.answer: No. The most appropriate name is the one given by the Truth himself in the Gospel, namely 'Son'. Eunomius sets aside this name so as to hide the proper character of the Son's nature, and uses his invented terms to make the Father alone supreme and proper being and to class the Son and Spirit as inferior.
sources.quote: Yet what name could be more appropriate than that which has been given by the Very Truth? He sets his views against the Gospel, and names not the Son, but ‘a Being existing through the First, but after It though before all others.’
sources.raw_question: Is it fitting to call the Son 'a Being existing through the First, but after It' instead of using the scriptural name 'Son'?

question: Did the Word gain promotion through taking flesh, or did he promote humanity by becoming man?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: He promoted humanity. Since he already had glory before the world and descended from heaven, he did not receive the names Son and God as a reward. Rather, he descended to promote the things that needed promotion. He made us sons of the Father and deified men by becoming man himself: he was God and then became man, not man who then became God.
sources.quote: He did not receive in reward the name of the Son and God, but rather He Himself has made us sons of the Father, and deified men by becoming Himself man.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word gain promotion through taking flesh, or did he promote humanity by becoming man?

question: Does the fact that the Fathers did not teach an 'individual consubstantiality' of Father and Son weaken the claim that they taught the orthodox Trinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 28: Whether it be at all probable, that the primitive Church should mistake in so material a point as this is; or that the whole stream of Christian writers should
sources.answer: No. Waterland grants that the Fathers did not assert individual consubstantiality in the objector's sense, which he regards as absurd. Admitting that they avoided an absurdity does not show they rejected the orthodox doctrine. It is like being told that they were not mad when he is arguing that they were sober.
sources.quote: You have little to object, but that the Fathers did not assert an individual consubstantiality, in your sense ; which is true ; and is no more than telling me, that they were not mad, when 1 contend that they were sober.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Fathers did not teach an 'individual consubstantiality' of Father and Son weaken the claim that they taught the orthodox Trinity?

question: Does Christ's joining Himself with the Father in "I and the Father" refute the Photinian view that Christ is a mere man?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: Yes. By coupling Himself with God the Father in one statement, Christ places Himself alongside God. This he could not do if He were merely a man.
sources.quote: He rejects the Photinian, for He joins Himself with God the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's joining Himself with the Father in "I and the Father" refute the Photinian view that Christ is a mere man?

question: Does the order of the words "I and the Father," with the Son named first, imply rank or gradation between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: No. Christ deliberately said "I and the Father" rather than "the Father and I" so that we would not wrongly infer rank from the order of words. He did this out of dutifulness and foreknowledge, not rudeness. Unity knows no order and equality knows no gradation, so the order in which divine Persons are named implies no inferiority.
sources.quote: For unity knows no order, equality knows no gradation; nor can it be laid to the Son of God that the Teacher Himself of dutifulness should offend against dutifulness by rudeness.
sources.raw_question: Does the order of the words "I and the Father," with the Son named first, imply rank or gradation between the Father and the Son?

question: Is Christ's being Son of God, rather than a creature, the central principle of the Christian faith?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter confessed Christ as the Son of the living God, and even the devil's first question was 'If thou be the Son of God.' He knew that if Christ were the Son, his tyranny would end, but if a creature, Christ would be just another descendant of Adam. The Jews also took His claim to sonship as a claim to Godhead and the Father's nature, which they would not have done had He called Himself a creature.
sources.quote: he knew that this is the truth and the sovereign principle of our faith; and that, if He were Himself the Son, the tyranny of the devil would have its end
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's being Son of God, rather than a creature, the central principle of the Christian faith?

question: Does being 'founded' imply that the Word began to exist when He was founded?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: No. A foundation stone already exists in the mountain before it is moved and laid in the earth, so being founded presupposes prior existence. The Word existed before; He was 'founded' when He took a body from Mary, being enveloped in earthly flesh for our sake.
sources.quote: Therefore the Lord also did not when founded take a beginning of existence; for He was the Word before that; but when He put on our body, which He severed and took from Mary, then He says ‘He hath founded me;’
sources.raw_question: Does being 'founded' imply that the Word began to exist when He was founded?

question: Could God have his own internal word and wisdom distinct from Christ, by which he made Christ?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: No. If Christ was made in that word, then so were all things, and that word would be the one of whom John says 'All things were made by Him'. Christ would then speak untruly in saying 'I in the Father', since another would be in the Father. 'The Word became flesh' would also be false, because Christ would be Word only in name.
sources.quote: And Christ will be found to speak untruly, ‘I in the Father,’ there being another in the Father. And ‘the Word became flesh’ is not true according to them.
sources.raw_question: Could God have his own internal word and wisdom distinct from Christ, by which he made Christ?

question: Is the God of the old covenant (patriarchs and prophets) the same God as the God of the new covenant (the Church), against those who posit two different gods?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXV.—Both covenants were prefigured in Abraham, and in the labour of Tamar; there was, however, but one and the same God to each covenant.
sources.answer: Yes. Though one people sows and another reaps, it is one God who gives seed to the sower and bread to the reaper, just as one plants and another waters but one God gives the increase. Abraham, being one man, prefigured both covenants, and in one God all things are shown forth.
sources.quote: but it is one God who bestows things suitable upon both—seed to the sower, but bread for the reaper to eat. Just as it is one that planteth, and another who watereth, but one God who giveth the increase.
sources.raw_question: Is the God of the old covenant (patriarchs and prophets) the same God as the God of the new covenant (the Church), against those who posit two different gods?

question: Why is 'essence' the proper name for God, perhaps belonging to God alone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > In God, Substance is Spoken Improperly, Essence Properly.
sources.answer: God alone truly is, because He alone is unchangeable. He declared this as His own name to Moses: "I am that I am" and "He who is hath sent me." Therefore 'essence', which is taken from 'being', is properly said of Him.
sources.quote: For He is truly alone, because He is unchangeable; and declared this to be His own name to His servant Moses, when He says, “I am that I am;”
sources.raw_question: Why is 'essence' the proper name for God, perhaps belonging to God alone?

question: When Christ calls the Father "my God and your God" (John 20:17), does the true God's becoming the God and Father of Christ's humanity mean he has become our God and Father as well?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > This twelfth book gives a notable interpretation of the words of the Lord to Mary, “Touch Me not, for I am not yet ascended to My Father.”
sources.answer: Yes. What took place in Christ's humanity is a common boon bestowed on mankind, since he is our first-fruits. Just as his body's ascension assures us that we too shall be caught up to meet the Lord, so the Father's becoming God and Father of our First-fruits assures us that he has become our God and Father too, since we shall come where Christ entered as our forerunner.
sources.quote: when we hear that the true God and Father has become the God and Father of our First-fruits, we no longer doubt that the same God has become our God and Father too
sources.raw_question: When Christ calls the Father "my God and your God" (John 20:17), does the true God's becoming the God and Father of Christ's humanity mean he has become our God and Father as well?

question: Is the holiness of Christ's human nature a necessary consequence of the hypostatical union?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Yes, in a secondary sense. The one primary necessary effect of the hypostatical union is the subsistence of the human nature in the person of the Son, yet it was also necessary that what was so united to him be completely holy.
sources.quote: although there be but one primary necessary effect of the hypostatical union (which is the subsistence of the human nature in the person of the Son of God), yet that he that was so united to him should be a “holy thing,” completely holy, was necessary also
sources.raw_question: Is the holiness of Christ's human nature a necessary consequence of the hypostatical union?

question: Does the Son's being called God's 'child' (pais) imply that He is a servant or creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. The term 'child' does not imply servitude, since Isaac was called Abraham's child and the Shunamite's son was called young child, though both were true sons.
sources.quote: But if, because He was called child, they idly talk, let them know that both Isaac was named Abraham’s child, and the son of the Shunamite was called young child.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being called God's 'child' (pais) imply that He is a servant or creature?

question: If Christ is called God only in a relative sense (as Moses, magistrates and angels are called gods in Scripture), can one still properly speak of Christ's Divinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Preface
sources.answer: No. Nobody speaks of the Divinity of Moses, magistrates or angels though they are called gods, so if Christ is God only relatively there is no reason to speak of his Divinity rather than theirs. The Church has always used 'divinity' in the strict and proper sense; to keep the name while giving up the thing is equivocation, and one should rather speak only of Christ's Mediatorship or Kingship. The only true Divinity is the strict one; the other, falsely so called, is really none.
sources.quote: If Christ be God, in the relative sense only, why should we speak of his Divinity, more than of the other? The Christian Church has all along used the word divinity, in the strict and proper sense
sources.raised_by_detail: Anonymous author of the Apology for Dr. Clarke's Preface
sources.raw_question: If Christ is called God only in a relative sense (as Moses, magistrates and angels are called gods in Scripture), can one still properly speak of Christ's Divinity?

question: Should the patristic language that the Father commands creation and the Son executes it be taken as implying a real inferiority of the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. Such language is not to be interpreted strictly according to the letter but economically and in a manner befitting God. Its design was to keep alive a sense of the real distinction of Persons, to teach the indivisible unity and coessentiality of all Three as one Creator, and to show that this unity resolves into unity of principle, the Father being the one Head, Root and Fountain.
sources.quote: The design of all was; 1. Τὸ keep up a more lively sense of a real distinction of Persons. 2. To teach us the indivisible unity and coessentiality of all Three, as of one! Creator.
sources.raw_question: Should the patristic language that the Father commands creation and the Son executes it be taken as implying a real inferiority of the Son?

question: Is the Son merely the instrument through whom the Father works in creation rather than the Artificer himself?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IX. A passage of St. Paul abused by heretics, to prove a distinction between the Divine Persons, is explained, and it is proved that the whole passage can be rightly said of each Person, though it refers specially to the Son. It is then proved that each member of the passage is applicable to each Person, and as to say, of Him are all things is applicable to the Father, so may all things are through Him and in Him also be said of Him.
sources.answer: No. The heretics make the Son an instrument alien in nature from the worker, but an instrument being alien from its author would make the Son alien from the Father's nature, which is false. All things are through the Son in such a way that they are also of Him and in Him, and Isaiah's description of the Artificer of all, cited by Paul, refers to the Son.
sources.quote: so that they declare that the Son is not so much the Artificer as the instrument of the work
sources.raw_question: Is the Son merely the instrument through whom the Father works in creation rather than the Artificer himself?

question: Does saying that all things are 'of' God the Father mean that creation was made out of God's own nature as its matter?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IX. A passage of St. Paul abused by heretics, to prove a distinction between the Divine Persons, is explained, and it is proved that the whole passage can be rightly said of each Person, though it refers specially to the Son. It is then proved that each member of the passage is applicable to each Person, and as to say, of Him are all things is applicable to the Father, so may all things are through Him and in Him also be said of Him.
sources.answer: No. Opponents claim matter came forth from God's nature as a chest is made from wood, but all things are of the Father not as if of matter. 'Of Him' means that the nature of everything comes from His will and He is the Author of all that has come into being.
sources.quote: all things are so of God the Father, that God the Father has suffered no loss because all things are either through Him or in Him, and yet all things are not of Him as if of matter
sources.raw_question: Does saying that all things are 'of' God the Father mean that creation was made out of God's own nature as its matter?

question: Does the Father communicate with the Son by speaking after silence, as with bodily speech, so that the Son passes from ignorance to knowledge?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. God is simple, without parts or variability, and needs none of the bodily apparatus of speech. Voices from heaven were uttered for our sake, not the Son's. Christ has no ignorance to be removed nor knowledge not His own before the Father speaks; human terms are used only to reach our understanding.
sources.quote: We have established this point to exclude the idea that after silence God spoke to the Son, or after ignorance the Son began to know.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father communicate with the Son by speaking after silence, as with bodily speech, so that the Son passes from ignorance to knowledge?

question: Can the Son's likeness to the Father be a deceptive or accidental resemblance between things really different in kind, like a brass coin resembling a gold one?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. Such deceptive similarity, where things different in kind appear alike by accidental resemblance, cannot be found in the Son, who is the Truth itself. To attribute that kind of likeness to Him would be infatuation.
sources.quote: Can it possibly be such a form of “likeness” as this, that he is continually attributing to the Son? Nay, surely he cannot be so infatuated as to discover deceptive similarity in Him Who is the Truth.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's likeness to the Father be a deceptive or accidental resemblance between things really different in kind, like a brass coin resembling a gold one?

question: If nothing in God is accidental, must everything predicated of God be predicated according to substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Nothing is Spoken of God According to Accident, But According to Substance or According to Relation.
sources.answer: No. Some things are said of God according to relation, as Father in relation to the Son and Son in relation to the Father. Such relative terms are neither substantial predicates nor accidents.
sources.quote: For it is said in relation to something, as the Father in relation to the Son and the Son in relation to the Father, which is not accident
sources.raw_question: If nothing in God is accidental, must everything predicated of God be predicated according to substance?

question: If no sacred writer states that the names of Christ (Door, Bread, Way, Vine, Shepherd, Light) arise from human conception (epinoia), does that prove they are not conceptions?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. If silence in Scripture proved something forbidden, then by the same reasoning Scripture's not forbidding it would prove it permitted. Since no sacred writer forbids regarding these names as products of conception, and Christ is indeed called by them, Eunomius' argument fails.
sources.quote: For if he maintains that its not being mentioned is a proof that it is forbidden, by a parity of reasoning he must admit that its not being forbidden is an argument that it is permitted.
sources.raw_question: If no sacred writer states that the names of Christ (Door, Bread, Way, Vine, Shepherd, Light) arise from human conception (epinoia), does that prove they are not conceptions?

question: Does the Fathers' teaching that the Father alone is unbegotten or unoriginate imply that the Son is only an inferior God or no God at all?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. Waterland grants that the Fathers made such concessions and says Catholics are ready to make the same ones. Dr. Clarke never shows any real logical connection between them and his conclusion. He only relies on a verbal resemblance and puts an Arian construction on Catholic expressions that the Fathers meant in a high sense.
sources.quote: the Fathers asserted the first Person only to be begotten, or unoriginate; therefore they must of consequence make the Son no more than an inferior God, or no God.
sources.raw_question: Does the Fathers' teaching that the Father alone is unbegotten or unoriginate imply that the Son is only an inferior God or no God at all?

question: Does positing a producing 'energy' between the Father and the Son displace the Son and the Holy Spirit from their rank in the Trinity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in assuming, to account for the existence of the Only-Begotten, an 'energy' that produced Christ's Person.
sources.answer: Yes. With a mediating energy in second place, the Son would rank third rather than next after the Almighty. By the same sequence the Holy Spirit would fall to the fifth place, since another energy following the Only-Begotten would intervene before the Spirit.
sources.quote: The Holy Spirit also according to this sequence will be found not in the third, but in the fifth place, that ‘energy’ which follows the Only-Begotten, and by which the Holy Spirit came into existence necessarily intervening between them.
sources.raw_question: Does positing a producing 'energy' between the Father and the Son displace the Son and the Holy Spirit from their rank in the Trinity?

question: If the 'energy' that produced the Son is said to be unsubstantial, can it produce and contain a substantial Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in assuming, to account for the existence of the Only-Begotten, an 'energy' that produced Christ's Person.
sources.answer: No. Non-being cannot follow being, and what is not a substance cannot produce a substance. Whatever is produced from and contained by an unreality must itself be a non-entity, because opposites cannot contain opposites, as fire cannot contain water nor non-being contain being. So this option would reduce the Son to nothing.
sources.quote: that which is produced from and is contained by an unreality can itself be conceived of as nothing else but a non-entity. Opposites, in the nature of things, cannot be contained by opposites
sources.raw_question: If the 'energy' that produced the Son is said to be unsubstantial, can it produce and contain a substantial Son?

question: Are God's intelligence, word, and other attributes distinct parts within Him, one prior to another?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. God is simple: just as He is all vision and all hearing, seeing in the same manner as He hears, so He is all intelligence and all word, and His Nous is His Logos. Even this remains an inadequate conception of the Father, but it is far more fitting than imagining a sequence of emissions.
sources.quote: Just as he does not err who declares that God is all vision, and all hearing (for in what manner He sees, in that also He hears; and in what manner He hears, in that also He sees)
sources.raw_question: Are God's intelligence, word, and other attributes distinct parts within Him, one prior to another?

question: Is Basil's account of conception (epinoia), as a more minute and accurate investigation following a first idea of a thing, refuted by cases of thought where no first and second notion can be distinguished?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Basil did not define all thought and conception this way; he described one subdivision of the objects of conception and left sensible readers to reason from the part to the whole. Just as defining an animal by the example of man is not wrong merely because winged or aquatic animals differ, the existence of another species of conception does not make Basil's description of the first one erroneous.
sources.quote: it is no refutation of Basil’s statement to say that it is improperly so called in one case because there is another species. Accordingly, even if another species come under consideration, it by no means follows that the one previously given is erroneously so called.
sources.raw_question: Is Basil's account of conception (epinoia), as a more minute and accurate investigation following a first idea of a thing, refuted by cases of thought where no first and second notion can be distinguished?

question: If generation is an operation, can it be alien from God the Father while belonging to the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > He then shows the eternity of the Son's generation, and the inseparable identity of His essence with Him that begat Him, and likens the folly of Eunomius to children playing with sand.
sources.answer: No. Every operation is connected equally with its product and its producer. So if generation is an operation, it belongs to the Father who begets as much as to the Son who is begotten, and it cannot be separated from its author.
sources.quote: If he conceives it to be an operation, it is clearly equally connected with its result and with its author, as in every kind of production one may see the operation alike in the product and the producer
sources.raw_question: If generation is an operation, can it be alien from God the Father while belonging to the Son?

question: When the Father and the Son come to make their abode with the one who loves them, is the Holy Spirit excluded or does He depart to give place to greater Persons?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > All are Sometimes Understood in One Person.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says the Spirit abides with and in believers and is given to abide with them for ever, so He will not depart when the Father and the Son come. He dwells in the same abode with them eternally, since He does not come without them nor they without Him.
sources.quote: He will not therefore depart when the Father and the Son come, but will be in the same abode with them eternally; because neither will He come without them, nor they without Him.
sources.raw_question: When the Father and the Son come to make their abode with the one who loves them, is the Holy Spirit excluded or does He depart to give place to greater Persons?

question: When Scripture affirms something of one divine Person by name, are the other Persons thereby excluded?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > All are Sometimes Understood in One Person.
sources.answer: No. Some things are affirmed separately of each Person to intimate the Trinity, but the other Persons are not excluded, because of the unity of the Trinity and the one substance and Godhead of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: in order to intimate the Trinity, some things are separately affirmed, the Persons being also each severally named; and yet are not to be understood as though the other Persons were excluded, on account of the unity of the same Trinity
sources.raw_question: When Scripture affirms something of one divine Person by name, are the other Persons thereby excluded?

question: Is it acceptable to confess an eternal Word (a distinct, consubstantial person) rather than an eternal Son, referring the Son's generation to his manifestations at creation and incarnation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: It is tolerable but not the safer course. Provided the Word is held to be a distinct person consubstantial with God, the only harm lies in the words being liable to misconstruction or offence. Still, the safer way is to follow the most general and approved manner of expression (eternal generation) along with the ancient faith, as the surest means of preserving both.
sources.quote: there seems to be no further harm in it, than what lies in the words, and their liableness to be misconstrued, or to give offence.
sources.raw_question: Is it acceptable to confess an eternal Word (a distinct, consubstantial person) rather than an eternal Son, referring the Son's generation to his manifestations at creation and incarnation?

question: Does being born of the Spirit, which makes people children of God, show that the Holy Spirit is divine?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord expressly ascribes the birth of the children of God to the Spirit, saying that what is born of the Spirit is spirit. Since those born of the Spirit are called children of God, the Spirit's begetting of God's children attests the Spirit's Divinity.
sources.quote: For thus He expressly ascribes the birth of the children of God to the Spirit, saying, that as that which is born of the flesh is flesh, so that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does being born of the Spirit, which makes people children of God, show that the Holy Spirit is divine?

question: Could angels or a Demiurge who created the world have been ignorant of the Supreme God, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VI.—The angels and the Creator of the world could not have been ignorant of the Supreme God.
sources.answer: No. Since they would be God's property, his creatures, and contained by him, they must have known him. He may be invisible to them because of his superiority, but he cannot be unknown because of his providence and dominion over them; they must know their Ruler and that their Creator is Lord of all.
sources.quote: He might indeed have been invisible to them on account of His superiority, but He could by no means have been unknown to them on account of His providence.
sources.raw_question: Could angels or a Demiurge who created the world have been ignorant of the Supreme God, as the Gnostics claim?

question: If only the Son knows the Father and those to whom the Son reveals him, can creatures have any natural knowledge of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VI.—The angels and the Creator of the world could not have been ignorant of the Supreme God.
sources.answer: Yes, at least in part. Although full knowledge of the Father comes through the Son's revelation, all beings know that there is one God, Lord of all. Reason implanted in their minds moves them to this, and God's mighty invisible essence gives all a deep perception of his omnipotent greatness.
sources.quote: yet all [beings] do know this one fact at least, because reason, implanted in their minds, moves them, and reveals to them [the truth] that there is one God, the Lord of all.
sources.raw_question: If only the Son knows the Father and those to whom the Son reveals him, can creatures have any natural knowledge of God?

question: Can God be known to exist and to rule without being seen?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VI.—The angels and the Creator of the world could not have been ignorant of the Supreme God.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus compares this to subjects of the Roman empire who have never seen the emperor but know who rules because they experience his rule. Likewise demons and all creatures tremble at the invocation of God's name without having seen him, and even dumb animals yield to it.
sources.quote: shall not those who live under the empire of the Romans, although they have never seen the emperor, but are far separated from him both by land and sea, know very well, as they experience his rule, who it is that possesses the principal power in the state?
sources.raw_question: Can God be known to exist and to rule without being seen?

question: Is the God who made the world by his Word the same as the Supreme God over all, or a lesser Demiurge?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VI.—The angels and the Creator of the world could not have been ignorant of the Supreme God.
sources.answer: He is the same Supreme God. All things are subject to his name, just as they are to the name of the Lord, because he made and established all things by his Word. It was no other than he who formed the world, which is why all beings fear the invocation of their Creator.
sources.quote: so must they also be to His who made and established all things by His word, since it was no other than He who formed the world.
sources.raw_question: Is the God who made the world by his Word the same as the Supreme God over all, or a lesser Demiurge?

question: Did the Father utter a new word in time in order to send the eternal Son into the flesh?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. To think so would be impious. The time at which the Word was to be made flesh was set eternally, without time, in the Word and Wisdom of God himself. The order of times is in God's eternal wisdom without time. Only the appearing in the flesh, 'made of a woman', happened in time.
sources.quote: for the order of times is in the eternal wisdom of God without time.
sources.raw_question: Did the Father utter a new word in time in order to send the eternal Son into the flesh?

question: How should Christ's words 'Neither came I of myself' be understood if the Son also sends himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: They are spoken according to the form of a servant, that is, his human nature. The saying 'I judge no man' is to be read in the same way. They do not deny that the Son, as God, shares in his own sending.
sources.quote: Why, therefore, does He say, “Neither came I of myself?” This, we may now say, is said according to the form of a servant, in the same way as it is said, “I judge no man.”
sources.raw_question: How should Christ's words 'Neither came I of myself' be understood if the Son also sends himself?

question: Why does Scripture call the second Person both 'Son' and 'Word,' 'Wisdom' and 'Radiance'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: To convey both his true origin from the Father's essence and the manner of that generation. 'Son' heralds that he is the natural and true offspring of the Father's essence. 'Word,' 'Wisdom' and 'Radiance' guard against thinking of that offspring humanly, teaching that the generation is impassible, eternal and worthy of God.
sources.quote: it also calls Him Word, Wisdom, and Radiance; to teach us that the generation was impassible, and eternal, and worthy of God.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture call the second Person both 'Son' and 'Word,' 'Wisdom' and 'Radiance'?

question: Does the human analogy of a word show that the Word of God is an affection or part of the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: No. Even a human word is neither an affection of the speaker nor a part of his mind, though men are passible and divisible. Much less should passions and parts be imagined in the immaterial and indivisible God, so the Word is begotten without affection.
sources.quote: they will find that the word which they put forth is neither an affection of them nor a part of their mind.
sources.raw_question: Does the human analogy of a word show that the Word of God is an affection or part of the Father?

question: Why does God, who always had the power to create, not create eternally?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: Although God always had the power to make, created things lack the capacity to be eternal. They come from nothing and so did not exist before their origination, and they could not coexist with the ever-existing God. God made them when He saw it was good for them and they were able to abide, much as He sent His Word only at the consummation of the ages. Prying into this is itself presumptuous, for no one has known the mind of the Lord.
sources.quote: although God always had the power to make, yet the things originated had not the power of being eternal
sources.raw_question: Why does God, who always had the power to create, not create eternally?

question: Does knowing something truly require knowing its substance, so that the mind's self-knowledge is knowledge of its own substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Every Mind Knows Certainly Three Things Concerning Itself—That It Understands, that It Is, and that It Lives.
sources.answer: Yes. Nothing is rightly said to be known while its substance is unknown. Hence when the mind knows itself it knows its own substance, and when it is certain about itself it is certain about its substance.
sources.quote: But nothing is at all rightly said to be known while its substance is not known. And therefore, when the mind knows itself, it knows its own substance
sources.raw_question: Does knowing something truly require knowing its substance, so that the mind's self-knowledge is knowledge of its own substance?

question: Were the Old and New Testaments given by one and the same God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXII.—That one God was the author of both Testaments, is confirmed by the authority of a presbyter who had been taught by the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. All the apostles taught that there were two testaments for two peoples, but one and the same God appointed both for the benefit of those who were to believe in Him. A presbyter taught by the apostles reasoned likewise that both were truly from one God.
sources.quote: all the apostles taught that there were indeed two testaments among the two peoples; but that it was one and the same God who appointed both for the advantage of those men
sources.raised_by_detail: Those who separate the God of the Old Testament from the God of the New
sources.raw_question: Were the Old and New Testaments given by one and the same God?

question: Are the three divine Persons equal in honor even though the Father is the source from whom the Son and Spirit proceed?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Besides the common honor that each is God, each has a peculiar honor that is equal. The Father is the author of perfect wisdom, but the Son is that wisdom itself; the Father and Son are fountains of excellency, holiness and happiness, but the Spirit is that excellency, holiness and happiness itself. Being the thing itself is as great an honor as being its source.
sources.quote: The honor of the Father and the Son is that they are infinitely excellent, or that from them infinite excellency proceeds; but the honor of the Holy Ghost is equal for He is that Divine excellency and beauty itself.
sources.raw_question: Are the three divine Persons equal in honor even though the Father is the source from whom the Son and Spirit proceed?

question: Do the Persons of the Trinity have equal concern and deserve equal glory in the work of redemption?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Glory belongs to the Father for giving His Son and to the Son for giving Himself out of love for the world. Equal glory is due to the Holy Spirit, because He is that very love of the Father and Son toward the world, so as much as they are glorified by their love, so much is the Spirit glorified.
sources.quote: But there is equal glory due to the Holy Ghost for He is that love of the Father and the Son to the world.
sources.raw_question: Do the Persons of the Trinity have equal concern and deserve equal glory in the work of redemption?

question: Is the image of God in the human mind renewed all at once in the moment of conversion and baptism?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How the Image of God in the Mind is Renewed Until the Likeness of God is Perfected in It in Blessedness.
sources.answer: No. Baptism removes the cause of infirmity at once by forgiving all sins, but the healing of the infirmity itself happens gradually as the image is renewed day by day. Augustine compares this to being freed from fever versus regaining strength, or removing a weapon versus healing the wound. Psalm 103 distinguishes 'who forgiveth all thine iniquities' from 'healeth all thine infirmities.'
sources.quote: the first cure is to remove the cause of infirmity, and this is wrought by the forgiving of all sins; but the second cure is to heal the infirmity itself, and this takes place gradually by making progress in the renewal of that image
sources.raw_question: Is the image of God in the human mind renewed all at once in the moment of conversion and baptism?

question: Is the difficulty of the Trinity solved by saying that the Son and Holy Spirit are not God in the Scripture sense of the word?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. This cuts the knot instead of untying it. In effect it denies that Scripture presents the Son and Spirit as divine Persons at all, so it abandons the doctrine rather than explaining it.
sources.quote: But this is cutting the knot, instead of untying it ; and is in effect to say, they are not set forth as
sources.raw_question: Is the difficulty of the Trinity solved by saying that the Son and Holy Spirit are not God in the Scripture sense of the word?

question: Does the fact that a name fits the thing it designates show that the name has a divine origin?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Humans such as bathing-attendants coin names that appropriately designate the articles they use, like foot-baths and towels, yet no one credits them with divine honours for it. Fitness of a name thus proves only human rational invention, and to ascribe such naming to God is to give him a dignity not above that of tradesmen.
sources.quote: no one invests them with Divine honours for the invention of such names as foot-baths, depilatories, towels, and the like—words which appropriately designate the articles in question.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that a name fits the thing it designates show that the name has a divine origin?

question: How can human beings receive adoption as sons of God through the incarnation of the Word?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: Only because the Word was made flesh and entered into communion with us. Through the Son we receive the fellowship that belongs to him, and so share in sonship. He also passed through every stage of life, restoring communion with God to all.
sources.quote: For, in what way could we be partaken of the adoption of sons, unless we had received from Him through the Son that fellowship which refers to Himself, unless His Word, having been made flesh, had entered into communion with us?
sources.raw_question: How can human beings receive adoption as sons of God through the incarnation of the Word?

question: Did God have to teach the first humans the names of things, as a teacher teaches words, for them to know and speak of realities?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. God, by implanting reason in human nature, endowed man with all rational faculties, which work by themselves on their natural objects, just as the eye needs no one to name colours. The intellect looks out on realities and affixes a verbal sign to each so its knowledge is not confused. Moses confirms this when he records that God brought the animals to Adam to see what he would call them, and Adam gave the names.
sources.quote: we maintain that the intellectual faculty, made as it was originally by God, acts thenceforward by itself when it looks out upon realities, and that there be no confusion in its knowledge, affixes some verbal note to each several thing
sources.raw_question: Did God have to teach the first humans the names of things, as a teacher teaches words, for them to know and speak of realities?

question: Does Scripture teach that one can rightly be baptized in the Holy Spirit, and does this show a single working of Father, Son and Spirit in baptism?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ says "ye shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit" and the Apostle says we were all baptized into one Spirit. The work is one because the mystery is one, and the baptism is one because there was one death for the world. There is therefore a oneness of working that cannot be separated among the Persons.
sources.quote: The work is one, for the mystery is one; the baptism one, for there was one death on behalf of the world; there is, then, a oneness of working, a oneness of setting forth, which cannot be separated.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that one can rightly be baptized in the Holy Spirit, and does this show a single working of Father, Son and Spirit in baptism?

question: What does John 5:18, where the Jews sought to kill Jesus for calling God his own Father and making himself equal with God, show about Christ's nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: It shows his true birth and equality of nature with the Father. The Evangelist explains the Jews' motive, proving Christ's nature was plainly revealed to them: by calling God his own Father he declared a birth of nature from nature, and thereby equality with God.
sources.quote: Was not His clearly a birth of nature from nature, when He published the equality of His nature by speaking of God, by name, as His own Father?
sources.raw_question: What does John 5:18, where the Jews sought to kill Jesus for calling God his own Father and making himself equal with God, show about Christ's nature?

question: Is the equality of Father and Son compatible with their being one solitary person (confusion) or with a difference of nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Neither. Equality cannot exist where there is confusion any more than where there is difference. Equality, like that of an image, requires two who are distinct yet without diversity of nature, so it excludes both isolation and diversity.
sources.quote: Thus equality, as of the image, is incompatible with isolation and with diversity; for equality cannot dwell with difference, nor yet in solitude.
sources.raw_question: Is the equality of Father and Son compatible with their being one solitary person (confusion) or with a difference of nature?

question: Should the title 'Son' be restricted to the man Jesus (or to the Word only as incarnate), as distinct from the eternal Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus C. Introductory to the Fourth Discourse against the Arians.
sources.answer: No. Scripture identifies the Son with the Word. That identification refutes all three alternatives: that 'Son' means merely the man Christ (as Photinus held), the union of Word and man, or the Word only as incarnate (as Marcellus held). The Old Testament passages alleged in support of these views also fail to establish them.
sources.quote: The Scriptural identification of Son and Word refutes the restriction of the former title to the man Jesus.
sources.raw_question: Should the title 'Son' be restricted to the man Jesus (or to the Word only as incarnate), as distinct from the eternal Word?

question: Can the divine energy, as Eunomius claims, 'follow' the divine being as something external, the way heat follows fire or an accident inheres in a subject?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Discussion as to the exact nature of the 'energies' which, this man declares, 'follow' the being of the Father and of the Son.
