sources.answer: No. Gregory denies that God's being is something heterogeneous and composite with energy contained in it like an accident in a subject, or produced by natural necessity as heat from fire. If instead the energy is a free, voluntary activity, it cannot be called an external consequence that 'follows' the being. Agent and energy are conceived together and cannot be separated so that one is left behind by itself.
sources.quote: Still I do not think that he would affirm that we should consider the being of God to be something heterogeneous and composite, having the energy inalienably contained in the idea of itself, like an ‘accident’ in some subject-matter
sources.raw_question: Can the divine energy, as Eunomius claims, 'follow' the divine being as something external, the way heat follows fire or an accident inheres in a subject?

question: Can the Arians consistently hold that the Son is a creature while ascribing to him the work of creating the world?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. In ascribing creation to a creature the Arians innovated in the faith, copied the Gnostics, and exposed their cause; if they meant to make the Son a mere creature, they should have denied him creative power and read the texts metaphorically as the Socinians later did. Their admission instead shows how strongly Scripture and tradition ran for the Son's creating, which implies his divinity.
sources.quote: Since they resolved to make a creature only, of the Son of God, they should not have allowed him any power of creating; but should have interpreted all those texts which speak in favour of it, as the Socinians have done since, of a metaphorical creation.
sources.raw_question: Can the Arians consistently hold that the Son is a creature while ascribing to him the work of creating the world?

question: Is it orthodox to say that the Son's generation from the Father is 'without intervention,' with nothing between Father and Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: Yes, if properly meant. Orthodox doctrine confesses so close a connection of the Son with the Father that no interval at all intervenes, not even the dimensionless instant of the present in time. Taken this way, 'without intervention' expresses the orthodox conjunction of the Son with the Father, since anything separated by any interval would cease to be immediate.
sources.quote: we too confess the close connection and relation of the Son with the Father, so that there is nothing inserted between them which is found to intervene in the connection of the Son with the Father, no conception of interval
sources.raw_question: Is it orthodox to say that the Son's generation from the Father is 'without intervention,' with nothing between Father and Son?

question: Does the Shema's confession 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord' exclude Christ from being Lord?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Christ, without violating the law's faith, teaches that he is Lord because he has his being by a natural birth from the substance of the incorporeal God. He is one born of one, and the nature of the one Lord makes him Lord by nature, so he is included in the confession of the one Lord rather than severed from it.
sources.quote: He is one, born of one, and the nature of the one Lord has made Him by nature Lord.
sources.raw_question: Does the Shema's confession 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord' exclude Christ from being Lord?

question: Does the real generation of the Son diminish either the Father's lordship or make the Son less than Lord?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Neither. Because the generation is real, the Father keeps his authority and the Son receives the full nature. The Only-begotten is not separated from the one Lord, since he derives his nature as Lord from him.
sources.quote: because the generation is real, neither is the Father degraded from being Lord, nor is the Son born less than Lord. The Father retains His authority, the Son obtains His nature.
sources.raw_question: Does the real generation of the Son diminish either the Father's lordship or make the Son less than Lord?

question: Is the Son's being "of the Father" compatible with his having no beginning of days?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > The eighth book very notably overthrows the blasphemy of the heretics who say that the Only-begotten came from nothing, and that there was a time when He was not, and shows the Son to be no new being, but from everlasting, from His having said to Moses, “I am He that is,” and to Manoah, “Why askest thou My name? It also is wonderful”;--moreover David also says to God, “Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail;” and furthermore Isaiah says, “I am God, the first, and hereafter am I:” and the Evangelist, “He was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God:”--and that He has neither beginning nor end: --and he proves that those who say that He is new and comes from nothing are idolaters. And herein he very finely interprets “the brightness of the glory, and the express image of the Person.”
sources.answer: Yes. The Father's eternity means never taking being from non-existence and never ending in non-existence. The Son has all that is the Father's, so he is in the Father's unoriginateness and has "no beginning of days." He is at once "of the Father" and contemplated within the Father's eternity.
sources.quote: so, being in the unoriginateness of the Father, has, as the Apostle says, “no beginning of days,” but at once is “of the Father,” and is regarded in the eternity of the Father
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's being "of the Father" compatible with his having no beginning of days?

question: Can the Son be the same God as the Father without being the same Person, as against Praxeas and Sabellius?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Yes. Tertullian, writing against Praxeas, asserts the Son to be the same God with the Father without making him the same Person. He maintains the distinction of Persons while keeping the Catholic doctrine of unity of substance, avoiding both the modalist extreme and its opposite.
sources.quote: He takes care so to assert the Son to be. the same God with the Father, as not to make him the same Person: and on the other hand, while he maintains the distinction of Persons, he does not forget to keep up the true Catholic doctrine of the unity of substance.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be the same God as the Father without being the same Person, as against Praxeas and Sabellius?

question: Are the Father and the Son one by divine appointment, creation, or agreement of will, or by a birth of nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: They are one by a birth of nature. God loses nothing in begetting the Son from Himself. Their unity shows in shared acts: no one plucks out of the Son's hand what is not plucked out of the Father's; to know or see the Son is to know or see the Father; the Father speaks and works in the Son; each is in the other. To be created and to be born differ, as do to will and to be able, and to agree and to abide.
sources.quote: It is not through any mysterious appointment of God that they are one, but through a birth of nature, for God loses nothing in begetting Him from Himself.
sources.raw_question: Are the Father and the Son one by divine appointment, creation, or agreement of will, or by a birth of nature?

question: If concord alone is not the bond of unity between the Father and the Son, does that imply they are at variance?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. The orthodox do not deny that the Father and the Son are of one mind. They are one in nature, honour and power, and a single nature cannot will contrary things. Their unanimity therefore follows from their unity of nature rather than constituting it.
sources.quote: The Father and the Son are one in nature, honour, power, and the same nature cannot will things that are contrary.
sources.raw_question: If concord alone is not the bond of unity between the Father and the Son, does that imply they are at variance?

question: Does the Holy Spirit produce joy in believers directly, or only through their reasoning about God's love?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: He does both, and either way it is his own work. Sometimes he works joy immediately, infusing gladness without any reasoning, as when John the Baptist leapt in the womb. The soul then rises from this joy to consider God's love. At other times he works mediately, through his other works such as assurance of adoption, but even then our reasoning cannot move our hearts to joy without his action.
sources.quote: it is left no less the proper work of the Spirit to do it from hence, and by the intervenience of these considerations, than to do it immediately without them
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit produce joy in believers directly, or only through their reasoning about God's love?

question: Does stressing that there is one only true God rule out the true and personal divinity of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Hilary says the Arians stress the oneness of the true God precisely in order to strip the Son of his true divinity. They also pointedly avoid ever calling the Son God. For Hilary, the one true Godhead belongs to Father and Son together.
sources.quote: They strenuously assert that there is One only, One true God, to the end that they may strip the Son of God of His true and personal Divinity.
sources.raw_question: Does stressing that there is one only true God rule out the true and personal divinity of the Son?

question: Is confessing the Son as truly born from the Father's nature the same as the Valentinian idea of a 'development' from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Hilary says the Arians label the birth of God from God a 'development' in order to discredit it as Valentinian. The Church's faith knows nothing of Valentinus's imaginary development or his aeons. It confesses one God the Father and one Jesus Christ, who is God born from God.
sources.quote: It knows none but One God the Father, from Whom are all things, and One Jesus Christ, our Lord, through Whom are all things, Who is God born from God.
sources.raw_question: Is confessing the Son as truly born from the Father's nature the same as the Valentinian idea of a 'development' from the Father?

question: How can the word 'God' be applied both to the Father alone and to the three Persons together?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: Waterland says the word 'God' is sometimes taken personally and sometimes essentially. When the Father is called the one God, the word is meant personally. This distinguishes him from the Son and Spirit without excluding them, and it marks his priority of order as Fountain of all. When God is said to be three Persons, the word refers to the divine essence. Each Person may likewise be called God in the personal sense.
sources.quote: The truth is, the Church always professed one substance; one eternal, immutable, uncreated substance; and this they understood by God. Notwithstanding, they believed the Son and Holy Spirit to be substantially God.
sources.raw_question: How can the word 'God' be applied both to the Father alone and to the three Persons together?

question: If the Word differed from us only in time, would he still rightly be called Only-begotten and the only Word and Wisdom of the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. Things of one nature share their name in common even when they differ in time, just as Adam, Paul and a newborn are all men. If the Word differed from us only in time, his titles would belong to all of us alike. But we are not Word or Wisdom, and he is not a creature or work. That is why we are all many, sprung from one, while he is the only Word.
sources.quote: But in truth neither we are Word or Wisdom, nor is He creature or work; else why are we all sprung from one, and He the Only Word?
sources.raw_question: If the Word differed from us only in time, would he still rightly be called Only-begotten and the only Word and Wisdom of the Father?

question: Does Christ's subordination to the Father in office as mediator imply inequality with the Father in nature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Distinction and inequality of office does not take away equality and sameness of nature. Just as a son of the same nature as his father may in office be his subject, so Christ may be inferior in office while equal in essence.
sources.quote: A son, of the same nature with his father, and therein equal to him, may in office be his inferior, — his subject.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's subordination to the Father in office as mediator imply inequality with the Father in nature?

question: Does the Son share the Father's divine titles, such as good, incorruptible, just, judge, merciful and eternal, in the same sense as the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > He then declares that the close relation between names and things is immutable, and thereafter proceeds accordingly, in the most excellent manner, with his discourse concerning “generated” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory says there is a long list of names expressing majesty of nature and power that the Son shares with the Father without divergence of meaning. None of these names is applied to him with any reservation. Eunomius ignores this whole list and fixes on the single pair "generate" and "ungenerate."
sources.quote: there is a long list of names in which the Son shares, without divergence of meaning, the appellations of the Father,—“good,” “incorruptible,” “just,” “judge,” “long-suffering,” “merciful,” “eternal,” “everlasting,”
sources.raw_question: Does the Son share the Father's divine titles, such as good, incorruptible, just, judge, merciful and eternal, in the same sense as the Father?

question: Does the apostle Paul's speaking of baptism "into Christ" alone, without naming the Father and the Holy Spirit, show that invoking all three names in baptism is unnecessary?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the baptism in the name of the Father alone is sufficient.
sources.answer: No. Naming Christ is itself a confession of the whole Trinity, because "Christ" means "the Anointed". The name therefore implies the God who anointed, the Son who was anointed, and the Spirit who is the anointing. Peter, Isaiah and the Psalmist all describe Christ's anointing in these terms.
sources.quote: For the naming of Christ is the confession of the whole, shewing forth as it does the God who gave, the Son who received, and the Spirit who is, the unction.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who assert that the baptism in the name of the Father alone is sufficient
sources.raw_question: Does the apostle Paul's speaking of baptism "into Christ" alone, without naming the Father and the Holy Spirit, show that invoking all three names in baptism is unnecessary?

question: How are faith and baptism related, and why must both name the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the baptism in the name of the Father alone is sufficient.
sources.answer: Faith and baptism are two kindred and inseparable ways of salvation. Faith is perfected through baptism, and baptism is established through faith. Both are completed by the same three names. We are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit just as we believe in them: the confession comes first, and baptism then seals our assent.
sources.quote: For as we believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost, so are we also baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost
sources.raw_question: How are faith and baptism related, and why must both name the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together?

question: Can one validly infer equality between God and a creature from the use of identical phrases about both in Scripture?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Scripture sometimes uses the same phrase for a prerogative of God and for a privilege of a believer: "With God all things are possible" and "All things are possible to him that believeth", or "Be ye perfect as your Father is perfect." No one would deny God's omnipotence or ascribe omnipotence to the believer because of this. A bare resemblance of words proves nothing.
sources.quote: Would you, because of the sameness of the terms employed, deny the omnipotence of God, or ascribe omnipotence to the believer?
sources.raw_question: Can one validly infer equality between God and a creature from the use of identical phrases about both in Scripture?

question: Does Christ's love for his disciples, compared with the Father's love for the Son (John 15:9), place the disciples on the same level as Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. In John 3:35 supreme authority is assigned to Christ as heir of all things, and mankind's trust centers on him. In John 15 he urges disciples, who are defectible beings, to abide in a love from which they would fall without him, since without him they can do nothing.
sources.quote: He is urging his disciples as defectible beings, by the plea of the infinite fullness of his love towards them, infinite so far as regarded himself, to abide in that love from which without him they would assuredly fall
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's love for his disciples, compared with the Father's love for the Son (John 15:9), place the disciples on the same level as Christ?

question: Is the threefold distinction among the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit compatible with the undiminished unity of the one God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Christians everywhere understood that the one God whom they worshipped included the three within His undiminished unity. The activities of the three relative to one another are conceived as distinctly personal.
sources.quote: included within His undiminished unity the three: God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, whose activities relatively to one another are conceived as distinctly personal
sources.raw_question: Is the threefold distinction among the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit compatible with the undiminished unity of the one God?

question: What is wrong with saying the Son came into being 'of will' by a will preceding His generation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: It implies two errors. First, it implies that once the Son was not. Second, it implies an inclination two ways, so that the Father could have not willed the Son. Placing will and consideration between the Father and the Word is the Valentinian doctrine of a precedent will and is madness.
sources.quote: For to say, ‘Of will He came to be,’ in the first place implies that once He was not; and next it implies an inclination two ways, as has been said, so that one might suppose that the Father could even not will the Son.
sources.raw_question: What is wrong with saying the Son came into being 'of will' by a will preceding His generation?

question: Must one confess Father and Son in order rightly to know the one true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. Heresy's distorted mind cannot know the One true God. Father and Son must be confessed before God can be apprehended as One and true, since the unity rests on God being from the nature of God.
sources.quote: We must confess Father and Son before we can apprehend God as One and true.
sources.raw_question: Must one confess Father and Son in order rightly to know the one true God?

question: Could Christ as mediator, even in his highest exaltation, be the one said to be 'equal to God' in Philippians 2:6?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: No. Nothing but that which is infinite is equal to the infinite. Christ considered as mediator, even in his greatest glory, is not equal to God. The equality therefore belongs to him as truly divine.
sources.quote: Now, nothing but God is equal to God. Not Christ as he is mediator, in his greatest glory, — nothing but that which is infinite, is equal to that which is infinite.
sources.raw_question: Could Christ as mediator, even in his highest exaltation, be the one said to be 'equal to God' in Philippians 2:6?

question: Was the incarnation itself, the Son's very taking of flesh, a humiliation of the person of the Son of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. The very taking of flesh was a condescension and debasing of the Son's person, and it could not be otherwise. If God humbles himself even to behold things in heaven and earth (Psalm 113:6), then taking our nature into personal union with himself is an inconceivable abasement.
sources.quote: In the very taking of flesh, there was a condescension, a debasing of the person of the Son of God; it could not be without it.
sources.raw_question: Was the incarnation itself, the Son's very taking of flesh, a humiliation of the person of the Son of God?

question: Does divine simplicity mean that in God to be and to be wise are the same thing?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: Yes. The Godhead is absolutely simple essence, so in God to be is the same as to be wise. Wisdom there is therefore the same as essence, just as being is to essence what being wise is to wisdom.
sources.quote: And since in the Divine simplicity, to be wise is nothing else than to be, therefore wisdom there is the same as essence.
sources.raw_question: Does divine simplicity mean that in God to be and to be wise are the same thing?

question: Can isolated sayings of Christ, such as 'None is good save one, God' or 'The Father is greater than I', be used on their own to deny his divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The heretics quote single detached sayings and hold back the sequel that explains them or the incidents that prompted them. They fail to distinguish the occasions of the words or to read them in light of the Gospel mysteries. The meaning of words must be sought in the context before and after them.
sources.quote: keeping back either the sequel which explains or the incidents which prompted them, though the meaning of words must be sought in the context before or after them
sources.raw_question: Can isolated sayings of Christ, such as 'None is good save one, God' or 'The Father is greater than I', be used on their own to deny his divinity?

question: What is the difference between something that comes from the Father by will and the Son who comes from the Father by nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: What comes by will is made, begins to be, and is external to the maker, like a house a man builds by counsel. What comes by nature is the proper offspring of the parent's essence and not external to him, like a son a man begets. So the Son is proper to the Father's essence, and the Father does not deliberate about Him, lest He seem to deliberate about Himself.
sources.quote: A man by counsel builds a house, but by nature he begets a son; and what is in building began to come into being at will, and is external to the maker; but the son is proper offspring of the father’s essence
sources.raw_question: What is the difference between something that comes from the Father by will and the Son who comes from the Father by nature?

question: Is God good and merciful by His will or by His nature, and what does this imply for the Father's begetting of the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: God is good by nature, not by will. If He were good by will, He would have begun to be good and could fail to be good, since choosing implies an inclination two ways. Yet this natural goodness is not imposed on Him by necessity. So much more truly is He Father of the Son by nature and not by will.
sources.quote: But if it be unseemly to speak of necessity in the case of God, and therefore it is by nature that He is good, much more is He, and more truly, Father of the Son by nature and not by will.
sources.raw_question: Is God good and merciful by His will or by His nature, and what does this imply for the Father's begetting of the Son?

question: Does the Father Himself exist as the result of His own counsel and will?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. To ask this is unseemly and self-destructive, since merely hearing God's Name tells us He is He that Is. In the same way, hearing the Name of the Word is enough to know that God, who is not by will, has His own Word by nature and not by will.
sources.quote: He who is God not by will, has not by will but by nature His own Word
sources.raw_question: Does the Father Himself exist as the result of His own counsel and will?

question: Are the prepositions "from whom" and "through whom" strictly fixed in meaning so that they can always be distinguished to rank the divine Persons?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That v: not found “of whom” in the case of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Scripture frequently interchanges them even outside theology: Adam says he gotten a man "through God" meaning from God, Joseph says interpretation is "through God," and Paul says Christ was "made from a woman" though elsewhere man is "through the woman." Since the terms are transferred between the same subjects, they cannot be invariably distinguished to find fault with true religion.
sources.quote: Since, therefore, the term “from whom” is transferred to the identical subjects in the case of which “through whom” is decided to be properly used, with what consistency can these phrases be invariably distinguished one from the other
sources.raised_by_detail: Aetius and his followers (the opponents of the passage)
sources.raw_question: Are the prepositions "from whom" and "through whom" strictly fixed in meaning so that they can always be distinguished to rank the divine Persons?

question: Is the Holy Spirit, rather than our natural abilities, the source of the spiritual comfort believers receive from Christ's promises?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. Applying our natural abilities to remember and consider Christ's promises yields no success. When the Comforter undertakes the work, it is done effectually. All the peace and joy received from anything Christ did or promised belongs to the Spirit's dispensation, and he works this powerfully, voluntarily and freely.
sources.quote: whatever peace, relief, comfort, joy, supportment, we have at any time received from any work, promise, or thing done by Christ, it all belongs to this dispensation of the Comforter.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit, rather than our natural abilities, the source of the spiritual comfort believers receive from Christ's promises?

question: Can faith in the Son survive if his existence is held to be improper or unsubstantial?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Whoever says the Only-begotten God does not properly exist, or does not exist at all, plainly removes all faith in Him from his creed. No one can believe in or turn to something non-existent, or to one whose being has been shown to be improper and unsubstantial.
sources.quote: he who dares to assert that the Only-begotten God either does not properly exist, or does not exist at all, manifestly blots out of his creed all faith in Him
sources.raw_question: Can faith in the Son survive if his existence is held to be improper or unsubstantial?

question: Since Christ is one Person, do all his sayings that express weakness or ignorance refer to his divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Heretics attribute words spoken in his human character to a weakness of his divine nature, arguing that one Person must always speak of his whole self. Because Christ's words share the same mystery as his twofold nature, they must be sorted into words as God and words as man. They must also be read according to the time they belong to: before his birth, during his mortal life, and in his glorified state.
sources.quote: These words, uttered in His human character, they falsely refer to the weakness of His divine nature; and because He was one and the same Person in all His utterances, they claim that He spoke always of His entire self.
sources.raw_question: Since Christ is one Person, do all his sayings that express weakness or ignorance refer to his divine nature?

question: Can three Persons be one individual being without contradiction?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds that three Persons may be one individual being, and that this sense of 'individual' is as reasonable as any other until opponents can fix a principle of individuation. Clarke himself makes infinitely many distant parts of extended divine substance one individual being and Person.
sources.quote: we say further, that three Persons may be one imdividual being; having, we think, a very good meaning in it.
sources.raw_question: Can three Persons be one individual being without contradiction?

question: Is the Word who became incarnate the same person as the Father, or distinct from the Father who sent him?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: He is distinct from the Father. The Father is One, and his Word is present with him. Through this Word the Father made all things, and in later times the Father sent the Word forth to save men. The Word, preached beforehand by the law and the prophets, is the one who came and was made man.
sources.quote: the Father is One, whose word is present (with Him), by whom He made all things; whom also, as we have said above, the Father sent forth in later times for the salvation of men
sources.raw_question: Is the Word who became incarnate the same person as the Father, or distinct from the Father who sent him?

question: If Christ is our brother and shares a common Father and God with us, are believers equal to the Only-begotten Son in divine substance?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Christ is our brother and fellow only in that the Word was made flesh and the man Jesus Christ is Mediator. As servant He has a common Father and God with us, and the same nature as His anointed fellows. Yet He remains at once very man and very God, God of God, so no one may count himself equal to Him in His divine substance.
sources.quote: In the mystery of the Mediatorship let Him be at once very man and very God, Himself God of God, but having a common Father and God with us in that community by which He is our brother.
sources.raw_question: If Christ is our brother and shares a common Father and God with us, are believers equal to the Only-begotten Son in divine substance?

question: When the Father gives all judgment to the Son, is judgment taken away from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Judgment is not taken from the Father, even though he does not exercise it directly. The Son's whole power of judgment proceeds from the Father's power as a gift from him.
sources.quote: Now we cannot suppose that judgment is taken away from the Father, although He does not exercise it; for the Son’s whole power of judgment proceeds from the Father’s, being a gift from Him.
sources.raw_question: When the Father gives all judgment to the Son, is judgment taken away from the Father?

question: What is the only legitimate distinction between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: The only distinction is that the Son was born. Yet he was born in such a way as to be one with his Father. Every other attribute, including work, power and honour, is shared equally.
sources.quote: And the only distinction that it is right or possible to make between Father and Son is that the Latter was born; yet born in such a sense as to be One with His Father.
sources.raw_question: What is the only legitimate distinction between the Father and the Son?

question: How does John 5 establish the Son's Sonship, his deity, his unity with the Father, and his distinction from the Father together?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: He is the Son because he can do nothing of himself. He is God because he does whatever the Father does. Father and Son are one because he is equal in honour and does the very same works. He is not the Father because he is sent.
sources.quote: He is the Son, because He can do nothing of Himself; He is God, because, whatever the Father does, He does the same; They Two are One, because He is equal in honour to the Father and does the very same works; He is not the Father, because He is sent.
sources.raw_question: How does John 5 establish the Son's Sonship, his deity, his unity with the Father, and his distinction from the Father together?

question: Was the chief purpose of the Son's revelation to make God known as Creator or to make him known as Father of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: To make him known as Father. When Christ says 'Father, I have manifested Thy Name unto men' he does not say 'Thou hast created the Creator of all the heavens.' The revelation is not of the Father shown to be God, but of God shown to be the Father of a Son truly born of him. Prophets, Incarnation, miracles and cross all serve this end.
sources.quote: Remember that the revelation is not of the Father manifested as God, but of God manifested as the Father.
sources.raw_question: Was the chief purpose of the Son's revelation to make God known as Creator or to make him known as Father of the Son?

question: Are the Son and the Holy Spirit each, like the Father, called the supreme Jehovah and "the Highest" in Scripture?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. Each by himself is the supreme Jehovah and God. Isaiah 40:3, applied in Matthew 3:3, calls Christ "Jehovah our God," and Luke 1:76 calls him "the Highest." Ezekiel calls the Spirit Jehovah God, and Luke 1:35 calls the Spirit "the Highest." Yet Deuteronomy 6:4 says there is one Jehovah.
sources.quote: The Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost are, each by himself, the supreme
sources.raw_question: Are the Son and the Holy Spirit each, like the Father, called the supreme Jehovah and "the Highest" in Scripture?

question: If the Son's generation by God cannot be like human generation because human generation involves passion, must we likewise deny that God is Creator because human making cannot supply matter as well as form?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds again to discuss the impassibility of the Lord's generation; and the folly of Eunomius, who says that the generated essence involves the appellation of Son, and again, forgetting this, denies the relation of the Son to the Father: and herein he speaks of Circe and of the mandrake poison.
sources.answer: Yes, the reasoning would cut both ways. Eunomius himself admits that human craftsmen do not make matter but only add form to it, so if human limitations ruled out divine generation, they would equally rule out divine creation. If he refuses to measure God's creating by human power, he must also stop slandering divine generation with human imperfections.
sources.quote: If, on the other hand, he refuses to conceive creation in the case of God according to man’s measure of power, let him also cease to slander Divine generation by human imperfections.
sources.raw_question: If the Son's generation by God cannot be like human generation because human generation involves passion, must we likewise deny that God is Creator because human making cannot supply matter as well as form?

question: Are the Son and the Holy Spirit each to be worshipped and regarded as first cause, sovereign Lord, and last end just as the Father is?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Since Scripture reveals that the Son is the one true God, and likewise the Holy Ghost, each is to be believed in, worshipped, obeyed, and lived unto exactly as the Father is. The purpose of this revelation is that we worship the only true God rather than our own imaginations.
sources.quote: that the Son is the one true God; and therefore is to be believed in, worshipped, obeyed, lived unto, and in all things considered by us as the first cause, sovereign Lord, and last end of all
sources.raw_question: Are the Son and the Holy Spirit each to be worshipped and regarded as first cause, sovereign Lord, and last end just as the Father is?

question: Is it a contradiction to say that the whole divine substance is communicated to the Son yet remains whole and uncommunicated in the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. The objection rests on a mistake: by the Father's substance the objector means the Father's Hypostasis or Person, and no one teaches that the Father communicated his own Person in whole or in part. So the objector refutes a doctrine nobody holds.
sources.quote: by Father’s substance, as it seems, you understand the Father’s Hypostasis, or Person ; and are proving, very elaborately, that the Father never communicated his own Hypostasis, or Person, either in whole or in part.
sources.raw_question: Is it a contradiction to say that the whole divine substance is communicated to the Son yet remains whole and uncommunicated in the Father?

question: Do objections about part and whole of the divine substance, raised against the Trinity, apply equally to God's omnipresence?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: Yes. If God's substance in heaven is only part of the substance, then only part of God and part of his infinite attributes are there. If it is the whole, then by the same reasoning it must be both confined and unconfined, diffused and undiffused. Since the objector accepts omnipresence, such reasoning proves too much and has no force against the Trinity. Waterland adds that pressed consistently it would argue as strongly for atheism.
sources.quote: For it is supposed that the whole essence or substance is diffused all over the universe, and yet remains whole and undiffused in heaven. Which, again, is ““ evidently ¢o be, and not to be, at the same time.”
sources.raw_question: Do objections about part and whole of the divine substance, raised against the Trinity, apply equally to God's omnipresence?

question: Is the God who spoke to the patriarchs and gave the Mosaic law the same God who sent Jesus Christ for our salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: Yes. The Gospel texts (Mary's Magnificat and Zacharias's prophecy) show that it was God who spoke to the fathers and instituted the law through Moses, and this same God in his goodness poured out his compassion on us in Christ. Men were taught to worship God in a new fashion, but not another god, for there is one God who justifies both circumcision and uncircumcision by faith.
sources.quote: men were taught to worship God after a new fashion, but not another god, because in truth there is but “one God, who justifieth the circumcision by faith, and the uncircumcision through faith.”
sources.raw_question: Is the God who spoke to the patriarchs and gave the Mosaic law the same God who sent Jesus Christ for our salvation?

question: What is the strongest proof that the Holy Spirit is conjoined with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: That Scripture says the Spirit has the same relation to God that a man's own spirit has to the man. As only a man's spirit within him knows the things of the man, so only the Spirit of God knows the things of God, showing the Spirit's intimate inseparability from God.
sources.quote: But the greatest proof of the conjunction of the Spirit with the Father and the Son is that He is said to have the same relation to God which the spirit in us has to each of us.
sources.raw_question: What is the strongest proof that the Holy Spirit is conjoined with the Father and the Son?

question: Does faith act immediately on the Father, or only through the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Faith does not act immediately on the Father but only through the Son. Christ is the way, and no one comes to the Father but by him; he is the high priest through whom we have access. Yet having access through Christ, believers behold and believe the Father's own love, which they are to receive as being in him, while its fruits come through Christ alone.
sources.quote: It is true, there is not an immediate acting of faith upon the Father, but by the Son. “He is the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father but by him,” John xiv. 6.
sources.raw_question: Does faith act immediately on the Father, or only through the Son?

question: Is there a trinity of one substance in the mind's recollection of things perceived by the bodily senses?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight.
sources.answer: Yes. Within the mind there is a trinity of three somewhats of one substance: the image of the bodily object held in memory, the impression formed from it when the thinker's mind's eye turns to it, and the will combining both. Unlike the trinity of external sight, these three are of one substance because all are in the mind. Still, it is said to belong to the outer man, because its content is introduced into the mind from bodily objects perceived from without.
sources.quote: a kind of trinity, in three somewhats of one substance, is observed to exist in the mind itself, as it were introduced there from those things that are perceived from without
sources.raw_question: Is there a trinity of one substance in the mind's recollection of things perceived by the bodily senses?

question: Does distinguishing God's eternity into 'without beginning' (ungenerate) and 'without end' (indestructible) divide the ages or God's life into two parts?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. These names signify the one eternity of God, which is the same from every point of view and unbroken in continuity. Because our intellect conceives things according to our own nature, it measures the eternal by a past and a future. God Himself neither leaves any interval behind nor passes on to something before Him.
sources.quote: not of course that God in His own existence leaves any interval behind, or passes on afresh to something that lies before, but because our intellect can only conceive things according to our nature
sources.raw_question: Does distinguishing God's eternity into 'without beginning' (ungenerate) and 'without end' (indestructible) divide the ages or God's life into two parts?

question: Is Dr. Clarke's notion of the Trinity free from both Sabellianism and Tritheism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. Its ground is Sabellian, since it starts from the same preliminary principles about the one God as the Sabellians, while its superstructure is Tritheistic, since it makes the Son and Spirit distinct divine beings besides the Father. The whole therefore hangs loosely together.
sources.quote: the ground is Sabellian, and the superstructure Tritheistic; and the whole contrived in such a way, as to hang loosely together.
sources.raw_question: Is Dr. Clarke's notion of the Trinity free from both Sabellianism and Tritheism?

question: Should the Trinity be rejected because we cannot understand how three can be one, or why consubstantial and coeval Persons are not coordinate (e.g. why the Father could not be begotten or sent)?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. These difficulties arise only from our imperfect and inadequate conception of things. We can see a priori why creatures of yesterday cannot search the deep things of God. It becomes them to submit their presumptions to divine revelation and be content to see through a glass darkly until they know God more perfectly.
sources.quote: You cannot understand how three can be one; you see no reason, a priori, why, if the Son and Holy Spirit be coeval and consubstantial, they should not be coordinate too
sources.raw_question: Should the Trinity be rejected because we cannot understand how three can be one, or why consubstantial and coeval Persons are not coordinate (e.g. why the Father could not be begotten or sent)?

question: Has the human mind ever been without knowledge and love of itself, the self-knowledge and self-love in which Augustine finds an image of the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > How the Soul Inquires into Itself. Whence Comes the Error of the Soul Concerning Itself.
sources.answer: No. When the mind turns its attention on itself, it sees that at no time did it ever not love itself or not know itself. Its apparent ignorance comes from loving other things together with itself and so confusing itself with them. It thinks things to be one which are in fact diverse.
sources.quote: So it will see that at no time did it ever not love itself, at no time did it ever not know itself; but by loving another thing together with itself it has confounded itself with it
sources.raw_question: Has the human mind ever been without knowledge and love of itself, the self-knowledge and self-love in which Augustine finds an image of the Trinity?

question: Why does Christ say "Marvel not at this" after saying he was given authority to judge because he is the Son of man rather than the Son of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: Because one might have expected him to say "since He is the Son of God." The wicked cannot see the Son in the form of God, yet both just and wicked must see the Judge. So he received the power as Son of man, in the form all can see when all rise from the graves.
sources.quote: whereas, it might rather have been anticipated that He would say, since He is the Son of God? But because the wicked are not able to see the Son of God as He is in the form of God equal to the Father
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ say "Marvel not at this" after saying he was given authority to judge because he is the Son of man rather than the Son of God?

question: Does Scripture show that being born of the Spirit is the same as being born of God, indicating a unity of divine operation?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is no less the author of spiritual creation or regeneration than the Father and the Son. The excellence of that creation, and wherein it consists. How we are to understand holy Scripture, when it attributes a body or members to God.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says believers are children of promise born after the Spirit, and that the new man is renewed in the spirit of the mind yet created according to God. He who is born after the Spirit is therefore born after God, which signifies the unity of the divine operation.
sources.quote: Let them hear how the Scripture has signified the unity of the divine operation. He who is renewed in the spirit of his mind has put on the new man, which is created according to God.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture show that being born of the Spirit is the same as being born of God, indicating a unity of divine operation?

question: Does Christ's command not to serve two lords conflict with calling both the Father and the Son Lord?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XV. Though the Spirit be called Lord, three Lords are not thereby implied; inasmuch as two Lords are not implied by the fact that the Son in the same manner as the Father is called Lord in many passages of Scripture; for Lordship exists in the Godhead, and the Godhead in Lordship, and these coincide without division in the Three Persons.
sources.answer: No. Christ called the Father Lord and called himself Lord, yet warned against serving two lords. This shows he did not count himself and the Father as two Lords. Where there is one Lordship, with the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, there is one Lord.
sources.quote: For there are not two Lords where the Lordship is but one, for the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and so there is one Lord.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's command not to serve two lords conflict with calling both the Father and the Son Lord?

question: Are the titles 'God' and 'Lord' distinct dignities that belong to different Persons of the Trinity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XV. Though the Spirit be called Lord, three Lords are not thereby implied; inasmuch as two Lords are not implied by the fact that the Son in the same manner as the Father is called Lord in many passages of Scripture; for Lordship exists in the Godhead, and the Godhead in Lordship, and these coincide without division in the Three Persons.
sources.answer: No. He who is God is Lord, and he who is Lord is God, because the Godhead is in the Lordship and the Lordship in the Godhead. Scripture calls the Father both Lord and God, and Thomas calls the Son 'My Lord and my God.' The title may pass from one Person to another, but the divine nature and its dignity remain unchanged.
sources.quote: He Who is God is Lord, and He Who is Lord is God, for the Godhead is in the Lordship, and the Lordship is in the Godhead.
sources.raw_question: Are the titles 'God' and 'Lord' distinct dignities that belong to different Persons of the Trinity?

question: Is it as wrong to speak of two Gods or two Lords as to speak of three Gods or three Lords?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XV. Though the Spirit be called Lord, three Lords are not thereby implied; inasmuch as two Lords are not implied by the fact that the Son in the same manner as the Father is called Lord in many passages of Scripture; for Lordship exists in the Godhead, and the Godhead in Lordship, and these coincide without division in the Three Persons.
sources.answer: Yes. To say there are three Lords or three Gods is profane, and to speak of two Lords or two Gods is equally profane. There is one God, one Lord, one Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: For as it is profane to say that there are three Lords or three Gods, so, too, is it utter profanity to speak of two Lords or two Gods
sources.raw_question: Is it as wrong to speak of two Gods or two Lords as to speak of three Gods or three Lords?

question: Do the Son's weeping, being troubled and suffering prove that He is a creature rather than true God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Twelfthly, Matthew xxvi. 39; John xii. 27, &c. Arian inferences are against the Regula Fidei, as before. He wept and the like, as man. Other texts prove Him God. God could not fear. He feared because His flesh feared.
sources.answer: No. Texts like 'I and the Father are one' are written of Him as God and show the oneness of Godhead and propriety of the Father's essence, while weeping and the like are proper to the body He took. Such bodily properties would not belong to the incorporeal Word unless He had taken a corruptible and mortal body from Mary; they are ascribed to Him together with that body, not to the Word considered as Word.
sources.quote: If then He wept and was troubled, it was not the Word, considered as the Word, who wept and was troubled, but it was proper to the flesh
sources.raw_question: Do the Son's weeping, being troubled and suffering prove that He is a creature rather than true God?

question: How does Christ make his mind known to believers, and what role does the Holy Spirit play in it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Christ reveals his mind to the saints by sending his Spirit. As 1 Corinthians 2 teaches, God reveals these things to us by his Spirit, whom we have received that we might know the things freely given us of God. The Spirit leads them into all truth, so that the apostle can conclude that we have the mind of Christ.
sources.quote: He sends us his Spirits as he promised, to make known his mind unto his saints, and to lead them into all truth.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ make his mind known to believers, and what role does the Holy Spirit play in it?

question: Do the Father and the Son possess and exercise the same life-giving power?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ says that as the Father raises the dead and quickens them, even so the Son quickens whom he will. The Son therefore brings the same grace to operation in the same way as the Father, and not otherwise.
sources.quote: If then it is even so as the Father quickeneth, and not otherwise, that the Son brings to operation the same grace
sources.raw_question: Do the Father and the Son possess and exercise the same life-giving power?

question: Is 'He that hath seen me hath seen the Father' merely the language of an ambassador, as in 'He that heareth you heareth me'?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. The first explains how knowledge of Christ himself includes knowledge of the Father, and it vindicates his claim to be the way, the truth and the life. The second only gives his messengers an ambassador's official authority, speaking in the king's place.
sources.quote: The first explains, how knowledge of himself embraces knowledge of the Father, and vindicates his claim to be the way, and the truth, and the life.
sources.raw_question: Is 'He that hath seen me hath seen the Father' merely the language of an ambassador, as in 'He that heareth you heareth me'?

question: Does the Son's mutual knowledge with the Father prove his omniscience, or is it comparable to the saints' future perfect knowledge?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: It proves omniscience. The Good Shepherd must know all his sheep thoroughly, which requires omniscience. The saints' heavenly knowledge will be perfect and unperplexed only as far as it extends, and so will merely resemble Christ's knowledge of us.
sources.quote: The good Shepherd, who is to know thoroughly all his sheep, needs omniscience; this, the first proves.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's mutual knowledge with the Father prove his omniscience, or is it comparable to the saints' future perfect knowledge?

question: Does Christ's making known to the disciples all he heard from the Father mean they share the Son's knowledge of all the Father does?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. The Father's showing the Son all things comes together with every divine claim in John 5. The disciples' knowledge is qualified by Christ's statement that he had many more things to say which they could not yet bear.
sources.quote: The second, is qualified by the quickly succeeding assurance, “I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.”
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's making known to the disciples all he heard from the Father mean they share the Son's knowledge of all the Father does?

question: Did Christ as mediator fulfil every law required of us, including laws introduced because of sin, to which he was not subject on his own account?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Yes. He was made under the law and fulfilled all righteousness: the law of nature, morally positive and ceremonial institutions, and judicial laws. He did no sin and did everything God required, so the Father was always well pleased with him.
sources.quote: Hence he is said to be “made under the law,” Gal. iv. 4; subject or obnoxious to it, to all the precepts or commands of it.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ as mediator fulfil every law required of us, including laws introduced because of sin, to which he was not subject on his own account?

question: Does John 1:3 show that our material world was made by the Word of God rather than by some other power?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter II.—The world was not formed by angels, or by any other being, contrary to the will of the most high God, but was made by the Father through the Word.
sources.answer: Yes. John says all things were made by the Word and nothing was made without Him. Our world must be included among the 'all things', so it too was made by the Word. Genesis and David's words, 'He spake, and they were made', confirm this.
sources.quote: Now, among the “all things” our world must be embraced. It too, therefore, was made by His Word, as Scripture tells us in the book of Genesis that He made all things connected with our world by His Word.
sources.raw_question: Does John 1:3 show that our material world was made by the Word of God rather than by some other power?

question: Is God good by participating in some good other than Himself, or is God goodness itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How God May Be Known to Be the Chief Good. The Mind Does Not Become Good Unless by Turning to God.
sources.answer: God is goodness itself. If we abstract from this and that particular good thing and regard the good itself, we see God, who is not good by a good other than Himself but is the good of all good. Creatures are good by participation, while God is the unchangeable good in which they participate.
sources.quote: take away this and that, and regard good itself if thou canst; so wilt thou see God, not good by a good that is other than Himself, but the good of all good.
sources.raw_question: Is God good by participating in some good other than Himself, or is God goodness itself?

question: Because Paul names the Spirit first, the Lord second and God third in 1 Corinthians 12:4-6, is the order of rank among the divine Persons reversed?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: No. The apostle simply begins according to our habits of thought. When we receive gifts, we think first of the distributer (the Spirit), then of the sender (the Son), and then lift our thoughts to the fountain and cause of the gifts (the Father).
sources.quote: It must not however be supposed because in this passage the apostle names in the first place the Spirit, in the second the Son, and in the third God the Father, that therefore their rank is reversed.
sources.raw_question: Because Paul names the Spirit first, the Lord second and God third in 1 Corinthians 12:4-6, is the order of rank among the divine Persons reversed?

question: Was the Son (Word) begotten or brought forth for our sake, in order that God might create the world through Him?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Marcellus and his disciples, like Arians, say that the Word was, not indeed created, but issued, to create us, as if the Divine silence were a state of inaction, and when God spake by the Word, He acted; or that there was a going forth and return of the Word; a doctrine which implies change and imperfection in Father and Son.
sources.answer: No. The Son was not begotten for us; rather we were brought into being for Him. If He were begotten for us, we would be the cause of His perfection and the Arians would be giving more to creatures than to the Son. His generation shows not that we were created but that He is from God, since He existed before our creation.
sources.quote: For His generation evidences, not that we were created, but that He is from God; for He was even before our creation.
sources.raw_question: Was the Son (Word) begotten or brought forth for our sake, in order that God might create the world through Him?

question: Was the Word perfect and able to create while still within God before His supposed issuing forth, and what follows either way for the claim that He was begotten in order to create?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Marcellus and his disciples, like Arians, say that the Word was, not indeed created, but issued, to create us, as if the Divine silence were a state of inaction, and when God spake by the Word, He acted; or that there was a going forth and return of the Word; a doctrine which implies change and imperfection in Father and Son.
sources.answer: Either way the claim fails. If the Word was imperfect in God and became perfect by being begotten, then we creatures are the cause of His perfection. If He was already perfect and able to make, His generation for the sake of creating is superfluous. So either He was not begotten at all, or He was begotten not for us but because He is ever from the Father.
sources.quote: so that either He has not been begotten, or He was begotten, not for us, but because He is ever from the Father.
sources.raw_question: Was the Word perfect and able to create while still within God before His supposed issuing forth, and what follows either way for the claim that He was begotten in order to create?

question: Is the Father known through a separate and peculiar operation distinct from that of the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. The Father is not discerned by a difference of operations, since whatever the Son sees the Father doing, the Son does likewise. Instead the Father is glorified through the works of the Only Begotten, and the Son's words direct our wonder at creation to the Father, so that through Him we know the Father.
sources.quote: For the Father is not regarded from the difference of the operations, by the exhibition of a separate and peculiar energy; for whatsoever things He sees the Father doing, “these also doeth the Son likewise;”
sources.raw_question: Is the Father known through a separate and peculiar operation distinct from that of the Son?

question: When the Son says He received a commandment from the Father about what to say and do, does this mean He lacks will or initiative and is a subordinate taking orders?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. Such language shows that His will is united indissolubly with the Father's, not that He lacks purpose or power of initiation. 'Commandment' should be understood in a way befitting the Godhead, as a timeless transmission of will from Father to Son, like a reflection in a mirror, not a spoken order to a subordinate.
sources.quote: Let us rather, in a sense befitting the Godhead, perceive a transmission of will, like the reflexion of an object in a mirror, passing without note of time from Father to Son.
