sources.raw_question: When the Son says He received a commandment from the Father about what to say and do, does this mean He lacks will or initiative and is a subordinate taking orders?

question: Does the apostolic council at Jerusalem over circumcision show that the apostles preached a Father of Christ different from the God of the Mosaic law?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. The apostles' letter to the Gentile believers gave them the new covenant of liberty in the Holy Spirit, but it did not proclaim another Father. The question they debated, whether the disciples still had to be circumcised, only makes sense if the God of the law and the God of the Gospel are one. So the dispute itself shows they had no idea of another god.
sources.quote: they clearly indicated, from the nature of the point debated by them, as to whether or not it were still necessary to circumcise the disciples, that they had no idea of another god.
sources.raised_by_detail: Marcionites and Gnostics who posit another Father
sources.raw_question: Does the apostolic council at Jerusalem over circumcision show that the apostles preached a Father of Christ different from the God of the Mosaic law?

question: Does the apostles' continued keeping of the Mosaic observances show that the law came from the same God who is the Father of Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter, James and John witnessed all of the Lord's actions and teaching. They still kept the Mosaic dispensation carefully, and Peter even hesitated to eat with Gentiles. They would never have done this if the Lord had taught them that there was another Father besides the one who appointed the law. Their conduct therefore shows that law and Gospel come from one and the same God.
sources.quote: scrupulously act according to the dispensation of the Mosaic law, showing that it was from one and the same God; which they certainly never would have done, as I have already said, if they had learned from the Lord [that there existed] another Father
sources.raised_by_detail: Marcionites and Gnostics who posit another Father
sources.raw_question: Does the apostles' continued keeping of the Mosaic observances show that the law came from the same God who is the Father of Jesus Christ?

question: Does the operation of beholding signified by the name "God" belong to only one Person of the Trinity, or to Father, Son and Holy Spirit alike?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: It belongs equally to all three, so none of the Persons can reasonably be excluded from the name "God." Scripture attributes seeing to the Father ("See, O God our defender"), to the Son ("Jesus, seeing their thoughts"), and to the Holy Spirit, as Peter's rebuke of Ananias shows. The power of beholding therefore extends throughout the Three Persons.
sources.quote: no one of the Persons in the Trinity could reasonably be excluded from such an appellation on the ground of the sense involved in the word. For Scripture attributes the act of seeing equally to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does the operation of beholding signified by the name "God" belong to only one Person of the Trinity, or to Father, Son and Holy Spirit alike?

question: Does the Son's saying 'I came forth from the Father and am come into the world' mean the Son left the Father or moved locally?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XI. The Spirit is sent to all, and passes not from place to place, for He is not limited either by time or space. He goes forth from the Son, as the Son from the Father, in Whom He ever abides: and also comes to us when we receive. He comes also after the same manner as the Father Himself, from Whom He can by no means be separated.
sources.answer: No. The Son's going forth is not a retiring from a place nor a separation of body from body. As Wisdom came forth from the mouth of the Most High, He remains with and in the Father, as the Word was with God and the Son is in the Father.
sources.quote: But neither when He goes forth from the Father does He retire from a place, nor is He separated as a body from a body; nor when He is in the Father is He as if a body enclosed as it were in a body.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's saying 'I came forth from the Father and am come into the world' mean the Son left the Father or moved locally?

question: Is Christ's right to worship founded only on the powers given to him after his resurrection, or did it exist before his mediatorial kingdom?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: His right to worship existed before his mediatorial kingdom. It rests on the dignity of his Person, on his creative powers, on his being God (Θεὸς) from the beginning, and on his preserving and upholding all things. To ground his title to worship only on powers received after his humiliation implies that no worship was due to him before then. That view suits Socinians or Sabellians, who make creation metaphorical, but it is inconsistent with the Arian scheme Dr. Clarke otherwise holds.
sources.quote: I found the Son’s title to worship upon the dignity of his Person ; his creative powers declared in John i. and elsewhere; his being Θεὸς from the beginning; and his preserving and upholding all things
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's right to worship founded only on the powers given to him after his resurrection, or did it exist before his mediatorial kingdom?

question: Why does Scripture speak of God using bodily and emotional language, such as wings, jealousy, or repentance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > This Work is Written Against Those Who Sophistically Assail the Faith of the Trinity, Through Misuse of Reason. They Who Dispute Concerning God Err from a Threefold Cause. Holy Scripture, Removing What is False, Leads Us on by Degrees to Things Divine. What True Immortality is. We are Nourished by Faith, that We May Be Enabled to Apprehend Things Divine.
sources.answer: Scripture adapts itself to babes, using words drawn from things that really exist so that our understanding may rise by degrees to divine things. Such expressions signify what is not literally so in God but must be said in this way. Scripture never uses terms drawn from things that do not exist at all.
sources.quote: it has borrowed many things from the spiritual creature, whereby to signify that which indeed is not so, but must needs so be said
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture speak of God using bodily and emotional language, such as wings, jealousy, or repentance?

question: What is proper to the Son that distinguishes Him from creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: It is proper to the Son to have the things of the Father. He is such that the Father is seen in Him. Through Him all things were made, and the salvation of all comes to pass and consists in Him. These are marks of the true Son, not of a creature.
sources.quote: For it is proper to the Son, to have the things of the Father, and to be such that the Father is seen in Him, and that through Him all things were made, and that the salvation of all comes to pass and consists in Him.
sources.raw_question: What is proper to the Son that distinguishes Him from creatures?

question: Does the Arian dilemma that the Father begat the Son either with his will (so the will preceded the Son, making him not eternal) or against his will (which is absurd) disprove the Son's eternity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. The Catholics answered it best by retorting the dilemma: was God the Father God with or against his will? If against, that is absurd; if with, then God would be God by will and not by nature. The retort silences the objection, since the same reasoning would undo the Father's own necessary existence.
sources.quote: One, which was the best and safest, was, by Sretorting upon the Arians the dilemma, thus: “ Was God the Father God, with “or against his will?” By this short question, that so famous objection of the Arians was effectually silenced.
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian dilemma that the Father begat the Son either with his will (so the will preceded the Son, making him not eternal) or against his will (which is absurd) disprove the Son's eternity?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's inward witness of adoption show that he has divine rather than created power?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. The soul knows his voice when he speaks, and it is too great to come from a created power. Christ's stilling of the storm with one word showed divine power to those with him. In the same way, when the Spirit stills the storms of the soul with one word, the soul recognizes his divine power and rejoices in his presence.
sources.quote: There is something too great in it to be the effect of a created power.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's inward witness of adoption show that he has divine rather than created power?

question: In Christ's Passion, did the divine nature of the Son suffer, or was the suffering confined to his human nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > The sixth book shows that He Who came for man's salvation was not a mere man, as Eunomius, falsely slandering him, affirmed that the great Basil had said, but the Only-begotten Son of God, putting on human flesh, and becoming a mediator between God and man, on Whom we believe, as subject to suffering in the flesh, but impassible in His Godhead; and demonstrates the calumny of Eunomius.
sources.answer: The suffering belonged to the body, while the saving operation belonged to God. The Godhead worked the world's salvation by means of the body that encompassed it, so that the Man tasted death while the immortal Nature did not admit the suffering of death.
sources.quote: For verily the Godhead works the salvation of the world by means of that body which encompassed It, in such wise that the suffering was of the body, but the operation was of God
sources.raw_question: In Christ's Passion, did the divine nature of the Son suffer, or was the suffering confined to his human nature?

question: Can an unchangeable, single God beget a Son from Himself, given that birth in the universe requires two parents and the changeless cannot be added to?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. Hilary calls it foolish to lay down a law for God from the pattern of created births. He affirms the true nativity of the Only-begotten from God the Father, as the Gospels declare.
sources.quote: how foolish they are in their attempts to lay down a law for God when they maintain that no birth can take place from one single being, because throughout the universe birth arises from the union of two
sources.raw_question: Can an unchangeable, single God beget a Son from Himself, given that birth in the universe requires two parents and the changeless cannot be added to?

question: Why did the Holy Spirit descend upon the Son of God made man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVII.—The apostles teach that it was neither Christ nor the Saviour, but the Holy Spirit, who did descend upon Jesus. The reason for this descent.
sources.answer: So that the Spirit might grow accustomed, in fellowship with the incarnate Son, to dwell in the human race. God had promised to pour out the Spirit on His servants in the last times. By first resting on the Son made man, the Spirit came to dwell in God's workmanship, working the Father's will in human beings and renewing them into the newness of Christ.
sources.quote: wherefore He did also descend upon the Son of God, made the Son of man, becoming accustomed in fellowship with Him to dwell in the human race, to rest with human beings, and to dwell in the workmanship of God
sources.raw_question: Why did the Holy Spirit descend upon the Son of God made man?

question: Through whom do believers receive the image and superscription of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVII.—The apostles teach that it was neither Christ nor the Saviour, but the Holy Spirit, who did descend upon Jesus. The reason for this descent.
sources.answer: Through the Holy Spirit. In the parable of the Good Samaritan, the Lord commends His fallen man to the Spirit and gives two royal denarii. By the Spirit, believers receive the image and superscription of the Father and the Son, and must make this entrusted coin fruitful for the Lord.
sources.quote: so that we, receiving by the Spirit the image and superscription of the Father and the Son, might cause the denarium entrusted to us to be fruitful
sources.raw_question: Through whom do believers receive the image and superscription of the Father and the Son?

question: Is the syllogism 'The only true God is the Father; Christ is the only true God; therefore Christ is the Father' logically valid?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No, it is a sophism. Its major premise is a particular proposition that restricts a term communicable to several, 'God', to one individual, 'the Father'. It then treats the two terms as reciprocal, which assumes the very point in question. The divine nature is singular, but it is communicated to Father, Son and Holy Ghost. For the argument to work, the premise would have to read 'Whoever is the only true God is the Father', and that can never be proved.
sources.quote: So that, though the only true God be the Father, yet every one who is true God is not the Father.
sources.raw_question: Is the syllogism 'The only true God is the Father; Christ is the only true God; therefore Christ is the Father' logically valid?

question: Do the analogies of brightness from glory and a word from the mind show how the Son can come from the Father without division?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: Yes. Glory is not diminished or divided by producing its brightness. A human word is generated from the mind without dividing it. So God the Word is generated from the Father without the Father's essence being divided, and it is irrational to deny this.
sources.quote: the word of man is generated from his mind without division, but God the Word cannot be generated from the Father without the essence of the Father being divided!
sources.raw_question: Do the analogies of brightness from glory and a word from the mind show how the Son can come from the Father without division?

question: Would Scripture, the Lord, or the apostles call anyone God or Lord absolutely who was not truly God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter V.—Christ and His apostles, without any fraud, deception, or hypocrisy, preached that one God, the Father, was the founder of all things. They did not accommodate their doctrine to the prepossessions of their hearers.
sources.answer: No. They named as Lord in his own person only God the Father ruling over all and his Son, who received dominion from the Father. Psalm 110:1 shows the Father addressing the Son as Lord, and Genesis 19:24 shows the Lord raining fire from the Lord. Psalm 45 likewise calls both the anointer and the anointed God. Both Father and Son are therefore truly Lord and God.
sources.quote: Since, therefore, the Father is truly Lord, and the Son truly Lord, the Holy Spirit has fitly designated them by the title of Lord.
sources.raw_question: Would Scripture, the Lord, or the apostles call anyone God or Lord absolutely who was not truly God?

question: When the Son works or comes to the saints, is it also the Father who works and comes?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Yes. Because the Son is the Father's own Image and Radiance, when the Son works the Father is the Worker, and when the Son comes the Father comes in Him, as Christ promised that He and the Father would come and make their abode. In the Image the Father is contemplated, as in the radiance the light is seen.
sources.quote: when the Son works, the Father is the Worker, and the Son coming to the Saints, the Father is He who cometh in the Son
sources.raw_question: When the Son works or comes to the saints, is it also the Father who works and comes?

question: Does the divine Word become passible by passing through the sufferings of the flesh?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: No. God is present in heaven, earth and sea without being any of those things. In the same way the Word passed through the sufferings of the flesh without becoming subject to passion. A physician who touches the sick is not infected, for it is he who touches the disease, not the disease him. So Christ, healing our infirmity by touch, is not thereby passible.
sources.quote: We do not say that one who touches a sick man to heal him is himself partaker of the infirmity, but we say that he does give the sick man the boon of a return to health, and does not partake of the infirmity: for the suffering does not touch him, it is he who touches the disease.
sources.raw_question: Does the divine Word become passible by passing through the sufferings of the flesh?

question: Does each divine Person possess memory, understanding, and love in Himself, and is each of these identical with that Person?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God from the Trinities We Have Spoken of.
sources.answer: Yes. Wisdom requires understanding, memory, and love. Since each Person is wisdom, each remembers, understands, and loves by His own memory, understanding, and love, and these are the Person Himself. So the triad in the highest essence is found in the Father alone, and likewise in the Son and in the Spirit.
sources.quote: for He is Himself also His own memory, His own understanding, and His own love. But that He is so comes to Him from the Father, of whom He is born.
sources.raw_question: Does each divine Person possess memory, understanding, and love in Himself, and is each of these identical with that Person?

question: Does Scripture show that the Son has a free will of his own?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. He 'quickeneth whom He will', which shows his equality with the Father in power and honour. He wills that believers be with him where he is. He reveals the Father to whomsoever he wills. All of these demonstrate a will free to bestow the knowledge of himself and of the Father.
sources.quote: Is not His will so free that He can bestow on whom He will the knowledge of Himself and His Father?
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture show that the Son has a free will of his own?

question: Does the Son's doing the Father's will mean mere obedience under external necessity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. To do another's will is more than to obey it. Obedience would imply external necessity, but doing another's will is an act of volition that requires unity with him. Through identity of nature the Son's will is the same in nature as the Father's. Wills of the same nature cannot dissent, so the Son freely wills all that the Father wills.
sources.quote: But to do is something more than to obey a will: the latter would imply external necessity, while to do another’s will requires unity with him, being an act of volition.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's doing the Father's will mean mere obedience under external necessity?

question: Can the Son be both free in will and yet have every act of his be the Father's will?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. Father and Son jointly possess a nature common to both through birth and through unity. So the Son is free of will, yet what he does willingly is an act of the Father's will. The Father wills that believers have eternal life, and the Son wills that they dwell with him, which is that same eternal life.
sources.quote: Thus Father and Son are manifestly joint Possessors of a nature common to Both through birth and common through unity: for the Son is free of will, but what He does willingly is an act of the Father’s will.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be both free in will and yet have every act of his be the Father's will?

question: Does calling God 'Father' refute those, such as Sabellius and Photinus, who deny a real Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. A father becomes a father only by having a son, so the name Father necessarily connotes the existence of the Son. The revelation of God as Father thus demonstrates the true nativity of Christ.
sources.quote: inasmuch as a father becomes a father only by having a son, this name Father necessarily connotes the existence of the Son
sources.raw_question: Does calling God 'Father' refute those, such as Sabellius and Photinus, who deny a real Son?

question: What does Christ mean by saying 'I have not spoken of myself'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: It can be understood as 'I am not born of myself.' The Son speaks the Father's word, and he is himself the Word of the Father. So in speaking the Father's word he speaks himself, as the one who has his being from the Father.
sources.quote: For if He speaks the word of the Father, then He speaks Himself, because He is Himself the Word of the Father.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean by saying 'I have not spoken of myself'?

question: Did the Son exist as Son before his birth from Mary?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: Yes. The righteous under the Old Covenant were made sons through no one other than the Son. If He were Son only after Mary, others would be sons before Him. He could then neither be 'before all' nor 'First-born', since He would come after many.
sources.quote: For unless even before Mary there were a Son who was of God, how is He before all, when they are sons before Him? and how also ‘First-born,’ if He comes second after many?
sources.raw_question: Did the Son exist as Son before his birth from Mary?

question: Does Acts 10:36, 'the Word He sent… preaching peace by Jesus Christ', show that the Word is distinct from Christ the Son, as a prophet is distinct from the Lord who speaks through him?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. The parallel is 1 Corinthians 1:7-8, where one Christ does not confirm the day of another Christ; He Himself confirms in His own day. So the Father sent the Word made flesh, that, having become man, He might preach by means of Himself. Peter immediately adds 'This is Lord of all', and Lord of all is the Word.
sources.quote: so the Father sent the Word made flesh, that being made man He might preach by means of Himself. And therefore he straightway adds, ‘This is Lord of all;’ but Lord of all is the Word.
sources.raised_by_detail: followers of the Samosatene (Paul of Samosata)
sources.raw_question: Does Acts 10:36, 'the Word He sent… preaching peace by Jesus Christ', show that the Word is distinct from Christ the Son, as a prophet is distinct from the Lord who speaks through him?

question: If the Son and corn are said to be equally unfit for comparison with the Ungenerate God, does it follow that the Son is reduced to the level of a created thing?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Things equally distant from a given object are equal to one another. So by Eunomius' reasoning the Maker of the worlds, who holds all nature in His hand, is put on a par with the most insignificant seed. This exposes the blasphemy of making the Son inferior to the Father in dignity.
sources.quote: every one knows that things equally distant from a given object are possessed of equality as regards each other, so that according to our wise theologian the Maker of the worlds, Who holds all nature in His hand, is shown to be on a par with the most insignificant seed
sources.raw_question: If the Son and corn are said to be equally unfit for comparison with the Ungenerate God, does it follow that the Son is reduced to the level of a created thing?

question: Does the human mind lose its natural memory, understanding and love of itself when it falls into sin and error?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Mind Loves God in Rightly Loving Itself; And If It Love Not God, It Must Be Said to Hate Itself. Even a Weak and Erring Mind is Always Strong in Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself. Let It Be Turned to God, that It May Be Blessed by Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Him.
sources.answer: No. Even amid the weakness and delusion caused by abandoning God, the mind cannot lose its natural memory, understanding and love of itself. This is why it is still said that man 'walketh in an image', since the trinitarian image remains in the mind even when it is disordered.
sources.quote: Yet, in the midst of these evils of weakness and delusion, great as they are, it could not lose its natural memory, understanding and love of itself.
sources.raw_question: Does the human mind lose its natural memory, understanding and love of itself when it falls into sin and error?

question: Can the spiritual and heavenly realities be themselves types of yet higher realities, so that the Creator God is merely an image of another, superior Father (as the Gnostics claim)?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIX.—Earthly things may be the type of heavenly, but the latter cannot be the types of others still superior and unknown; nor can we, without absolute madness, maintain that God is known to us only as the type of a still unknown and superior being.
sources.answer: No. It is fitting that earthly things serve as types of celestial things, both being made by the same God, so that He might adapt spiritual things to our comprehension. But to make heavenly things types of another Pleroma and God the image of another Father is folly, since it requires endless types of types and images of images and never rests on the one true God.
sources.quote: such persons will find it necessary to be continually finding out types of types, and images of images, and will never [be able to] fix their minds on one and the true God.
sources.raw_question: Can the spiritual and heavenly realities be themselves types of yet higher realities, so that the Creator God is merely an image of another, superior Father (as the Gnostics claim)?

question: Does God's revelation about Himself in Scripture use language adapted to human understanding?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. God spoke not for His own sake but for ours, tempering His language so that the weakness of our nature could grasp it. Images such as sealing are therefore accommodations that point to the truth without fully matching it.
sources.quote: God has spoken not for Himself but for us, and that He has so far tempered the language of His utterance as to enable the weakness of our nature to grasp and understand it
sources.raw_question: Does God's revelation about Himself in Scripture use language adapted to human understanding?

question: Which properties of God can be known from the work of creation, and which cannot?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Creation reveals God's power, goodness, wisdom, and all-sufficiency, his eternal power and Godhead. But it cannot reveal his patience, long-suffering, and forbearance. Since all things were made good, there was no occasion for these properties to be exercised or shown, though they are eminent properties of his nature.
sources.quote: But yet there are some properties of God which all the works of creation cannot in any measure reveal or make known; — as his patience, long-suffering, and forbearance.
sources.raw_question: Which properties of God can be known from the work of creation, and which cannot?

question: Can God's most glorious properties be known apart from Christ through creation and providence?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Creation and providence give only an obscure glimpse of God, not even his 'back parts'. Some of God's most glorious properties cannot be glimpsed at all except in Christ. Of all the rest there is no true light except by him. As Moses saw God only when placed in the rock, and that rock was Christ.
sources.quote: There are some of the most eminent and glorious properties of God (I mean, in the manifestation whereof he will be most glorious; otherwise his properties are not to be compared) that there is not the least glimpse to be attained of out of the Lord Christ
sources.raw_question: Can God's most glorious properties be known apart from Christ through creation and providence?

question: Can God's love toward sinners be known from nature or human wisdom, without Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. The only discovery God has made of love toward sinners is his sending his only begotten Son into the world, so that we might live through him. Those who studied the sun, moon, stars, and seasons learned nothing of it and were only left inexcusable. A wisdom that cannot teach that God is love is folly.
sources.quote: This is the only discovery that God hath made of any such property in his nature, or of any thought of exercising it towards sinners, — in that he hath sent Jesus Christ into the world, that we might live by him.
sources.raw_question: Can God's love toward sinners be known from nature or human wisdom, without Christ?

question: Can the Arian (Dr. Clarke's school) consistently show from reason and revelation that the Father, the God of Jews and Christians, is the eternal God in the metaphysical sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: No. On their principles every route fails. They say 'no God besides me' is not meant in the metaphysical sense. They say Jehovah signifies only one who keeps his word, not necessary existence. They say creation, being finite, does not infer an infinite subject. So reason may show that some eternal God exists, but nothing on their principles connects that God to the Father.
sources.quote: You can demonstrate that there must be some eternal God, in the metaphysical sense, as you call it, of these words: but sinee the Father, the God of Jews and Christians, has not declared, either that he is eternal, or God, in the metaphysical sense, it does not appear how he is at all concerned in it.
sources.raw_question: Can the Arian (Dr. Clarke's school) consistently show from reason and revelation that the Father, the God of Jews and Christians, is the eternal God in the metaphysical sense?

question: Can the human mind fully comprehend the divine glory of the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: No. Owen argues that in the glory of his majesty Christ dwells in light inaccessible. In the words of Job 11:7-9, we cannot by searching find out the Almighty unto perfection. Proverbs 30:2-4 asks "what is his name, and what is his Son's name," a question that shows how far the Son's glory exceeds human understanding.
sources.quote: In the glory of this majesty he dwells in light inaccessible. We “cannot by searching find out the Almighty unto perfection:
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind fully comprehend the divine glory of the Son?

question: If Scripture says all things are from the Father and also that all things were made by the Son, does it follow that the Son is equal to the Father and that their working is indivisible?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. If some things were made by the Father and others by the Son, then neither would have made all things. But Scripture says all things are by each, so the same things were made by both. Therefore the Son is equal with the Father and their working is indivisible.
sources.quote: if all things were made by the Father, and all things by the Son, then the same things were made by the Father and by the Son. The Son, therefore, is equal with the Father, and the working of the Father and the Son is indivisible.
sources.raw_question: If Scripture says all things are from the Father and also that all things were made by the Son, does it follow that the Son is equal to the Father and that their working is indivisible?

question: Can any being other than the Son, such as the Gnostics' 'Mother' or 'seed,' know the Father and reveal the truth about him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIV.—Valentinus and his followers derived the principles of their system from the heathen; the names only are changed.
sources.answer: No. The Father is truth, and Christ said, 'No one knoweth the Father but the Son.' If the Mother or her seed knew and proclaimed the truth, then on their theory the Saviour spoke falsely. Knowledge and revelation of the Father belong properly to the Son.
sources.quote: if either the Mother or her seed knew and proclaimed those things which were of the truth (and the Father is truth), then on their theory the Saviour spoke falsely when He said, “No one knoweth the Father but the Son,”
sources.raw_question: Can any being other than the Son, such as the Gnostics' 'Mother' or 'seed,' know the Father and reveal the truth about him?

question: Is it consistent to hold that God first counselled about creatures and created the Son for their sake, yet calls the Son his proper Son and Heir while calling the creatures only creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: No. The Arian scheme reverses itself. God would counsel about us first yet create the Son first, and would will us before the Mediator. He would also make more of the weak than of the strong one who could endure his direct making. If we were the primary object of God's will, we should rather be called sons. If instead he who is called Son is truly the Son, then he is the prior object of God's thought and will, and all things are made for him.
sources.quote: But we, for whose sake He made Him, ought rather to be called sons; or certainly He, who is His Son, is rather the object of His previous thoughts and of His will, for whom He makes all us.
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to hold that God first counselled about creatures and created the Son for their sake, yet calls the Son his proper Son and Heir while calling the creatures only creatures?

question: Is the Christ who suffered and rose the same as the one born of Mary, or did a heavenly Christ depart from the man Jesus before the passion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: The same one. The Gospel knows no other Son of man than the one born of Mary who suffered, and no Christ who flew away from Jesus before the passion. Christ's own words that the Son of man must suffer and rise, and John's statement that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, show that the one born is himself Jesus Christ the Son of God who suffered and rose.
sources.quote: The Gospel, therefore, knew no other son of man but Him who was of Mary, who also suffered; and no Christ who flew away from Jesus before the passion; but Him who was born it knew as Jesus Christ the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Is the Christ who suffered and rose the same as the one born of Mary, or did a heavenly Christ depart from the man Jesus before the passion?

question: Is Jesus Christ formed of two different beings, a passible Jesus and an impassible Christ who descended on him from above?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: No. Such systems divide the Lord and depart from the true God. The only-begotten Word of the Father, always present with the human race, became flesh and is himself Jesus Christ our Lord, who suffered, rose, and will return in the Father's glory. John's warning that whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ is Antichrist was written against such teachers.
sources.quote: being ignorant that His only-begotten Word, who is always present with the human race, united to and mingled with His own creation, according to the Father’s pleasure, and who became flesh, is Himself Jesus Christ our Lord, who did also suffer for us
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus Christ formed of two different beings, a passible Jesus and an impassible Christ who descended on him from above?

question: Does the fact that the Word, who is Life and Light, became incarnate prove that the Son's Light is inferior to the Light of the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: No. Being manifested in flesh does not make the true Light diverge in any degree from the Light in the Father. The Word in the flesh remains the Word, and the Light shining in darkness remains Light without taking on its contrary. Since each Light is equally inconvertible to evil and unalterable, the incarnation shows no variation of the Son's Light toward inferiority.
sources.quote: how does he show by this argument variation of the Light to inferiority, when each Light has in equal measure the property of being inconvertible to evil, and unalterable?
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Word, who is Life and Light, became incarnate prove that the Son's Light is inferior to the Light of the Father?

question: What is the content or matter of the consolation the Holy Spirit gives to believers, and how does it relate to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: The Spirit's consolations consist entirely in acquainting believers with, and communicating to them, the love of the Father and the grace of the Son. Nothing in the Father's love or the Son's grace is left out; the Spirit makes all of it a matter of comfort. So the believer's communion with the Father in his love, and with the Son in his grace, is carried on through the Spirit's operation.
sources.quote: All the consolations of the Holy Ghost consist in his acquainting us with, and communicating unto us, the love of the Father and the grace of the Son
sources.raw_question: What is the content or matter of the consolation the Holy Spirit gives to believers, and how does it relate to the Father and the Son?

question: According to the ante-Nicene Fathers, why is the Son God in his own Person?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Because he is God's Son, and he is God's Son because the divine substance was communicated to him from the Father. So, in the mind of the ancients, the Son is God and is called God in his own Person.
sources.quote: 2. That he was God in his own Person, as being Giod’s Son.
sources.raw_question: According to the ante-Nicene Fathers, why is the Son God in his own Person?

question: Why was the incarnation necessary for the redemption of man?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: God's work, man, was created perfect but became wanting and dead through sin, and it was unbecoming that God's work should remain imperfect. So the perfect Word put on an imperfect body. In it he paid the debt in our stead and supplied what man lacked, immortality and the way to paradise.
sources.quote: it was unbecoming that the work of God should remain imperfect
sources.raw_question: Why was the incarnation necessary for the redemption of man?

question: Could God beget from himself a God of a different or inferior kind?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. True divinity necessarily produces a true birth, and the one God cannot produce from himself a God of a second kind. If the Son were changed or defective, the fault would fall on the Father. It would mean the Father had failed to keep his nature constant in the birth and had brought forth something foreign to himself.
sources.quote: the outcome of true divinity must be a true birth, and that the one God could not produce from Himself a God of a second kind
sources.raw_question: Could God beget from himself a God of a different or inferior kind?

question: Are analogies such as a spring and its stream, a tree and its branch, or fire and its heat adequate to explain the unity of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. In those cases there is extension without separation: the parts do not exist of themselves, and only the whole thing has independent existence. The Only-begotten, by contrast, subsists as God through a perfect and ineffable birth. He is incorporeal offspring of an incorporeal nature, living and true God of living and true God, and inseparable from God in nature.
sources.quote: But the Only-begotten God is God, subsisting by virtue of a perfect and ineffable birth, true Scion of the Unbegotten God, incorporeal offspring of an incorporeal nature, living and true God of living and true God
sources.raw_question: Are analogies such as a spring and its stream, a tree and its branch, or fire and its heat adequate to explain the unity of the Father and the Son?

question: Why did the Word of God, called 'the salvation of God', become incarnate and visible to all flesh?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IX.—One and the same God, the Creator of heaven and earth, is He whom the prophets foretold, and who was declared by the Gospel. Proof of this, at the outset, from St. Matthew’s Gospel.
sources.answer: So that the King might be made manifest in all things. Irenaeus says the Father caused his salvation, that is his Word, to be seen by all flesh through the incarnation. Those who are to be judged must see and know their judge. Those who are to be glorified should likewise know the one who gives them glory.
sources.quote: For it is necessary that those [beings] which are judged do see the judge, and know Him from whom they receive judgment
sources.raw_question: Why did the Word of God, called 'the salvation of God', become incarnate and visible to all flesh?

question: If the Father and the Son are both confessed to be God, can one consistently call the Father 'uncreated' and the Son 'created'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: No. Just as it is folly to call one man a 'man' and another real man a 'horse', so it is folly to call one who is God 'uncreated' and another who is God 'created', since the Godhead does not admit a change of name to one expressing another kind. The creature stands to the Godhead as the irrational stands to man, unable to share the name of the superior nature. Eunomius's own maxim against misnaming thus turns against his heresy.
sources.quote: it is surely a piece of equal stupidity, when the Father is confessed to be God, and the Son is confessed to be God, to call the one ‘created’ and the other ‘uncreated,’
sources.raw_question: If the Father and the Son are both confessed to be God, can one consistently call the Father 'uncreated' and the Son 'created'?

question: Is the mind's knowledge of itself like its knowledge of absent things such as the cherubim, another person's will, or one's own face?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Mind Knows Itself, by the Very Act of Understanding the Precept to Know Itself.
sources.answer: No. The cherubim are absent and known by belief. Another person's will is known only through bodily signs, and so is believed more than understood. One's own face can be seen only in a mirror. The mind, by contrast, is immediately present to itself, so it should seek to discern itself as present, not as absent.
sources.quote: Let it not therefore seek to discern itself as though absent, but take pains to discern itself as present. Nor let it take knowledge of itself as if it did not know itself, but let it distinguish itself from that which it knows to be another.
sources.raw_question: Is the mind's knowledge of itself like its knowledge of absent things such as the cherubim, another person's will, or one's own face?

question: Why does 2 Corinthians 13:14 name the Son, the Father and the Spirit in a different order from Matthew 28:19, and what does this show?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: The change of order shows that no Person of the Trinity comes before or after another, and none is greater or less. The author takes this, with the Athanasian Creed, as a mark of the Persons' coequality. He judges these two verses sufficient to settle the controversy.
sources.quote: why this notable change of the order observed in Matt. 28:19, if not to show that “in this Trinity, none is afore or after other, none is greater or less than another?”
sources.raw_question: Why does 2 Corinthians 13:14 name the Son, the Father and the Spirit in a different order from Matthew 28:19, and what does this show?

question: Is confessing Jesus as Lord a matter of human reasoning alone?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. The question of Christ's deity is not a merely intellectual problem to be solved by human analysis. No one can say that Jesus is the Lord except by the Holy Ghost, so the inquirer must depend on the Spirit of truth to glorify Christ and reveal him.
sources.quote: is no mere intellectual problem, to be grasped by the power of human reason, and to be solved by the skill of human analysis: for “that no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost.”
sources.raw_question: Is confessing Jesus as Lord a matter of human reasoning alone?

question: Is the Word of God on the side of the Creator rather than among created things?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VIII.—Answer to an objection, arising from the words of Christ (Matt. vi. 24). God alone is to be really called God and Lord, for He is without beginning and end.
sources.answer: Yes. All things were made by the Word, so he is distinguished from the things made and cannot be compared to any of them. Since the Creator alone, together with his Word, is properly called God and Lord, the Word shares the divine title that belongs to the Creator and that no creature may claim.
sources.quote: But the things established are distinct from Him who has established them, and what have been made from Him who has made them.
sources.raw_question: Is the Word of God on the side of the Creator rather than among created things?

question: Is the Holy Spirit (the Paraclete) less than Christ because he receives from Christ?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again from the Gospel He Proves Christ to Be God.
sources.answer: Yes, in this economy. Novatian argues that the Paraclete would not receive from Christ unless he were less than Christ. He therefore calls Christ greater than the Paraclete, and he treats this very subordination as a powerful testimony to Christ's divinity.
sources.quote: Christ is greater than the Paraclete, because the Paraclete would not receive from Christ unless He were less than Christ
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit (the Paraclete) less than Christ because he receives from Christ?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being named third in the baptismal formula prove that He is inferior in nature and dignity to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Examination of the meaning of 'subjection:' in that he says that the nature of the Holy Spirit is subject to that of the Father and the Son. It is shewn that the Holy Spirit is of an equal, not inferior, rank to the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. By that reasoning the Father would be inferior to the Son, since Scripture often names the Lord first and the Father second or even third. Order of mention follows a particular reason of sequence, not a difference of dignity or nature.
sources.quote: By the same reasoning he should make the Father inferior to the Son, since the Scripture often places the name of our Lord first, and the Father Almighty second.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being named third in the baptismal formula prove that He is inferior in nature and dignity to the Father and the Son?

question: Is the Holy Spirit a work produced by the Father as cause and by the Son as artificer, and thus subject to them?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Examination of the meaning of 'subjection:' in that he says that the nature of the Holy Spirit is subject to that of the Father and the Son. It is shewn that the Holy Spirit is of an equal, not inferior, rank to the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius opposes the arrangement of Scripture by separating the Spirit from the equality with the Father and Son and the natural connexion which the Lord Himself pronounces, numbering Him among 'subjects' and calling Him a work of both Persons without even explaining what 'subjection' means.
sources.quote: He separates off that equality with the Father and the Son of His proper and natural rank and connexion which our Lord Himself pronounces, and numbers Him with ‘subjects’
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a work produced by the Father as cause and by the Son as artificer, and thus subject to them?

question: When some Ante-Nicene Fathers call the Father αὐτόθεος and the Son 'subordinate' or 'God of God', do they mean, as Dr. Clarke does, that only the Father necessarily exists and is strictly divine, while the Son is a different and inferior being?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. Clarke agrees with the Fathers only while he speaks in general terms that Catholics and Arians can both accept. When he explains what he means by αὐτόθεος and 'subordinate', namely that the Father alone necessarily exists and that the Son is another Being inferior in kind, in effect a creature, he contradicts all the ancients. The same Fathers understood the texts as consistent with the Son's consubstantiality and coeternity.
sources.quote: the Father only is necessarily existing and strictly divine ; the Son another Being, inferior in kind, (or, what comes to the same, a creature,) directly contrary to all the ancients.
sources.raw_question: When some Ante-Nicene Fathers call the Father αὐτόθεος and the Son 'subordinate' or 'God of God', do they mean, as Dr. Clarke does, that only the Father necessarily exists and is strictly divine, while the Son is a different and inferior being?

question: Do rational arguments for the Trinity have value even though they cannot demonstrate it?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Once revelation has given the doctrine, such reasoning shows that the Trinitarian conception of God is superior to that of an abstract monad. In this way it lends important rational support to the doctrine. It does not prove the Trinity, but it supports what faith already holds.
sources.quote: It carries home to us in a very suggestive way the superiority of the Trinitarian conception of God to the conception of Him as an abstract monad, and thus brings important rational support to the doctrine of the Trinity, when once that doctrine has been given us by revelation.
sources.raw_question: Do rational arguments for the Trinity have value even though they cannot demonstrate it?

question: Do Christ's sorrow, his prayer that the cup pass, his cry of dereliction and his commending of his spirit prove that he lacks the passionless divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary holds that these words were recorded by the Lord himself as evidences of his true majesty. They must be set beside his contrary words of confidence, such as 'Henceforth ye shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power' and 'Today shalt thou be with Me in Paradise.' The heretics fix on words belonging to his earthly ministry and ignore those that assert his Deity.
sources.quote: I am compelled to prove that this is a blasphemous misinterpretation, and that these things were put on record by the Lord Himself as evidences of His true and absolute majesty.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's sorrow, his prayer that the cup pass, his cry of dereliction and his commending of his spirit prove that he lacks the passionless divine nature?

question: Why is it not enough, in defending the Son's divinity, simply to set out the proofs from faith without refuting the heretics' arguments?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Arguments we have not tested may mislead us about the meaning of our own words. The faith must therefore also be established by exposing the hollowness and absurdity of the opponents' proofs.
sources.quote: Arguments which we have not tested may delude us into a misapprehension of the meaning of our own words, unless we take the offensive by exposing the hollowness of the enemy’s proofs
sources.raw_question: Why is it not enough, in defending the Son's divinity, simply to set out the proofs from faith without refuting the heretics' arguments?

question: Does Christ give grace, pardon and the Spirit to believers sparingly or abundantly, and why do believers sometimes lack these supplies?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Christ gives abundantly. The fullness of God dwells in him so that believers may receive from it. He abundantly pardons, pours out the Spirit richly, and gives an abundance of grace. Any lack lies in believers themselves, because supplies from Christ fail only when faith fails to receive them.
sources.quote: If in any things, then, we are straitened, it is in ourselves; Christ deals bountifully with us.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ give grace, pardon and the Spirit to believers sparingly or abundantly, and why do believers sometimes lack these supplies?

question: To which nature of Christ should Peter's words 'God made Him Lord and Christ' be referred?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: To the Humanity. Scripture itself ascribes increase to the Lord in respect of his humanity (Luke 2:52), so it is reasonable that the lowly human nature was raised to majesty through communion with the Divine. He who was assumed was made Lord from servant, King from subject, and received the Name above every name.
sources.quote: He Who was, by being assumed, elevated from Man to the Divinity, being one thing and becoming another, is strictly and truly said to have become Christ and Lord.
sources.raw_question: To which nature of Christ should Peter's words 'God made Him Lord and Christ' be referred?

question: Can the weakness of the flesh or the nature of created things prevent God from giving bodies eternal life?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter V.—The prolonged life of the ancients, the translation of Elijah and of Enoch in their own bodies, as well as the preservation of Jonah, of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, in the midst of extreme peril, are clear demonstrations that God can raise up our bodies to life eternal.
sources.answer: No. God is not subject to created things; created things are subject to God, and all things obey his will. The long lives of the patriarchs, Jonah's deliverance from the whale, and the youths' rescue from the furnace show that God's power overrides natural limits. As the Lord says, what is impossible with men is possible with God.
sources.quote: Neither the nature of any created thing, therefore, nor the weakness of the flesh, can prevail against the will of God. For God is not subject to created things, but created things to God
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics denying the salvation of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Can the weakness of the flesh or the nature of created things prevent God from giving bodies eternal life?

question: Does being filled with the Holy Spirit amount to being filled with the will of God, and does this show there is no difference of will between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is not a creature, seeing that He is infinite, and was shed upon the apostles dispersed through all countries, and moreover sanctifies the Angels also, to whom He makes us equal. Mary was full of the same likewise, so too, Christ the Lord, and so far all things high and low. And all benediction has its origin from His operation, as was signified in the moving of the water at Bethesda.
sources.answer: Yes. The Apostle prays that believers be filled with the knowledge of God's will in spiritual understanding, and it is God who puts His Holy Spirit in our hearts. So whoever has the Holy Spirit is filled with the will of God. Ambrose concludes from this that there is no difference of will between the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: Therefore if he who has the Holy Spirit is filled with the will of God, there is certainly no difference of will between the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does being filled with the Holy Spirit amount to being filled with the will of God, and does this show there is no difference of will between the Father and the Son?

question: Should Christians give the Lord Jesus Christ the same honour and worship that they give to God the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Saints who fail to honour Christ as they honour the Father are of all men the most unworthy. Scripture shows the church and the heavenly host ascribing glory, dominion and worship to the Lamb, and the great solemn worship of the Christian church consists in assigning honour and glory to the Lord Jesus.
sources.quote: If they honour him not as they honour the Father, they are, of all men, the most unworthy.
sources.raw_question: Should Christians give the Lord Jesus Christ the same honour and worship that they give to God the Father?

question: Does the phrase 'the Only-begotten Son which is in the bosom of the Father' show that the Son always existed, and is he the 'Right Hand' of God in the Psalms?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son being in the Father's bosom shows he ever was; and since the Psalm speaks of God's Right Hand in his bosom, the Hand is the Son, through whom the Father made all things and led out his people. The 'Well-beloved' Hand that was changed is the one the Father calls 'My Beloved Son.'
sources.quote: Therefore if the Hand is in the bosom, and the Son in the bosom, the Son will be the Hand, and the Hand will be the Son, through whom the Father made all things
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'the Only-begotten Son which is in the bosom of the Father' show that the Son always existed, and is he the 'Right Hand' of God in the Psalms?

question: Does Scripture apply phrases like 'once was not,' 'before it came to be,' and 'when' to the Son, or only to creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > That the Son is Eternal and Increate. These attributes, being the points in dispute, are first proved by direct texts of Scripture. Concerning the 'eternal power' of God in Rom. i. 20, which is shewn to mean the Son. Remarks on the Arian formula, 'Once the Son was not,' its supporters not daring to speak of 'a time when the Son was not.'
sources.answer: Only to creatures. Athanasius collects texts (Genesis on the plants 'before' they were, Deuteronomy 'when the Most High divided,' Jeremiah 'before I formed thee') showing these temporal phrases are used of originated things, while 'ever' and 'I am' are used of the Word. Hence the Arian formulas, borrowed from creaturely language, are alien to the Word.
sources.quote: Thus it appears that the phrases ‘once was not,’ and ‘before it came to be,’ and ‘when,’ and the like, belong to things originate and creatures, which come out of nothing, but are alien to the Word.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture apply phrases like 'once was not,' 'before it came to be,' and 'when' to the Son, or only to creatures?

question: Does the Father reconcile the world in and through Christ, and what does this show about the unity of Father and Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Yes. The Father reconciles in the Son's reconciliation, just as He works in His works and speaks in His words. This shows that the Father abides in the Son through a like nature, restoring the world to Himself through and in Him.
sources.quote: because the Father abiding in Him through a like nature restored the world to Himself by reconciliation through and in Him.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father reconcile the world in and through Christ, and what does this show about the unity of Father and Son?

question: Did the Son's birth deprive the Father of any of His completeness, or leave the Son lacking it?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Being One of One and Whole of Whole, the Son did not by His birth take away the Father's completeness. By right of that birth He possesses the same completeness in Himself.
sources.quote: being One of One, Whole of Whole, God and Son, He has neither by His birth deprived the Father of His completeness, nor failed to possess the same completeness in Himself by right of His birth.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son's birth deprive the Father of any of His completeness, or leave the Son lacking it?

question: What does the opening of John's Gospel teach about the Son's relation to the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: It teaches the Son's original, effectual and glorious generation from the Father. John declares that in the beginning the Word was with God and was God, and that all things were made by Him. For this reason John's Gospel is full of confidence, because such is the Son's divine person.
sources.quote: For that according to John relates His original, effectual, and glorious generation from the Father, thus declaring, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
sources.raw_question: What does the opening of John's Gospel teach about the Son's relation to the Father?

question: Do patristic phrases describing the unity of Father and Son as 'agreement' (συμφωνία) or 'power' (δυνάμει), as in Athenagoras and the Council of Antioch, imply only a moral unity of will rather than a unity of substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. Such expressions must be read alongside the same writers' explicit statements of consubstantiality. Athenagoras is clear elsewhere for consubstantiality, and Hippolytus and Chrysostom explain the meaning of his δυνάμει. The Council of Antioch's 'agreement' is explained by Hilary in light of the Fathers' teaching that the Holy Spirit is, as it were, the bond of the Trinity. Augustine likewise confesses an incomparable agreement of will and undivided charity in the Three while still saying that this Trinity is one God.
sources.quote:
Athenagoras’s δυνάμει may be rightly interpreted by Hippolytus before cited ; or by Chrysostom ; or by himself, in several places

where he is clear for the consubstantiality.
sources.raw_question: Do patristic phrases describing the unity of Father and Son as 'agreement' (συμφωνία) or 'power' (δυνάμει), as in Athenagoras and the Council of Antioch, imply only a moral unity of will rather than a unity of substance?

question: Is the Son, according to the form of God, identical with his attributes such as life and doctrine rather than possessing them as something other than himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > That Some Ways of Speaking Concerning the Son are to Be Understood According to Either Rule.
sources.answer: Yes. According to the form of God the Son is not one thing and his life another, nor one thing and his doctrine another. The life itself is the Son, and the doctrine itself is the Son.
sources.quote: as the Son is not one and His life another, but the life itself is the Son; so the Son is not one and His doctrine another, but the doctrine itself is the Son
sources.raw_question: Is the Son, according to the form of God, identical with his attributes such as life and doctrine rather than possessing them as something other than himself?

question: Do the Holy Spirit's name 'Comforter' and the biblical phrase 'joy in the Holy Ghost' support the view that the Spirit is God's joy and delight?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Comforting and delighting God's people is an office of the Spirit, which is why he is called the Comforter. This fits well with the Spirit being God's own joy and delight. Acts 13:52, 'filled with joy and with the Holy Ghost', means they were filled with spiritual joy.
sources.quote: But how well doth this agree with the Holy Ghost being God's joy and delight, (Acts 13:52) "And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Ghost"
sources.raw_question: Do the Holy Spirit's name 'Comforter' and the biblical phrase 'joy in the Holy Ghost' support the view that the Spirit is God's joy and delight?

question: Is it illegitimate to apply names to Christ (such as homonyms drawn from analogy) that arise from human conception rather than from explicit Scriptural teaching?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius's own objection relies on terms like "analogy" and "homonyms" which no Scripture teaches and which are themselves products of the thinking faculty, so he uses the very principle he attacks. Words formed by conception are legitimately used for the sense they convey.
