sources.quote: For he makes war against our principle of words being formed by the operation of conception, and would endeavour to establish, by the aid of words formed on that very principle, that it is unlawful to use them.
sources.raw_question: Is it illegitimate to apply names to Christ (such as homonyms drawn from analogy) that arise from human conception rather than from explicit Scriptural teaching?

question: Can the distinction between subordination of order and inferiority of nature be dismissed on the ground that 'nature' and 'essence' are obscure metaphysical notions?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 20: Whether the Doctor need have cited 300 teats, *wide of the purpose, to prove what nobody denies, namely, a subordination, in some sense, of the Son to the Fathe
sources.answer: No. The plea is not true, and it does not meet the argument. It is also inconsistent coming from Clarke, who builds heavily on 'self-existence', a metaphysical term that is itself equivocal and obscure. Waterland calls this dodge an evasion into a mist of words.
sources.quote: which is neither true, nor to the purpose, nor consistently pleaded by one who builds so much upon seélf-existence, a metaphysical term
sources.raw_question: Can the distinction between subordination of order and inferiority of nature be dismissed on the ground that 'nature' and 'essence' are obscure metaphysical notions?

question: Should Christ's weaknesses and lowly sayings be ascribed to an infirmity in his divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Heretics mislead the unlearned by attributing to the form of God what belongs only to the form of the servant. Christ's words and deeds can always be sorted into two kinds, because the true faith confesses Jesus Christ as Word and flesh, God and Man.
sources.quote: We can always safely distinguish the two kinds of utterances, since the only true faith lies in the confession of Jesus Christ as Word and flesh, that is, God and Man.
sources.raw_question: Should Christ's weaknesses and lowly sayings be ascribed to an infirmity in his divinity?

question: Is there one trinity of recollection in the mind, or as many trinities as there are acts of remembrance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > There is Another Trinity in the Memory of Him Who Thinks Over Again What He Has Seen.
sources.answer: There are as many trinities as there are remembrances, since each has the stored memory, the conceived vision, and the uniting will. Yet one may also speak of a single trinity generally, taking all stored bodily species as one unity and the mind's vision as another, joined by the will. Because the mind's eye cannot see everything at once, these trinities succeed one another and are innumerable, though not infinite, being limited by what memory has stored.
sources.quote: There are, then, as many trinities of this kind as there are remembrances; because there is no one of them wherein there are not these three things
sources.raw_question: Is there one trinity of recollection in the mind, or as many trinities as there are acts of remembrance?

question: Does the phrase 'Spirit of God' denote God's nature itself or merely something belonging to God's nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Hilary insists that the two must be distinguished, because a nature is not the same as a thing belonging to it, just as a man differs from what belongs to a man. In what follows he argues that 'Spirit of God' can denote Father or Son and so expresses the very excellence of the divine nature. It is used of each so that the mutual indwelling of Father and Son is not thought of as corporeal.
sources.quote: For a nature is not identical with a thing belonging to it, just as neither is a man identical with what belongs to a man, nor fire with what belongs to fire itself
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'Spirit of God' denote God's nature itself or merely something belonging to God's nature?

question: Is it true that the Father himself became Christ, was born, suffered, and raised himself?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Hippolytus calls this a rash and audacious dogma and says flatly, "it is not so," because the Scriptures say otherwise. The Church's confession, voiced by the presbyters, is that the Son suffered, died, rose, and sits at the right hand of the Father. This distinguishes the Son who suffered from the Father.
sources.quote: the Father is Himself Christ, Himself the Son, Himself was born, Himself suffered, Himself raised Himself. But it is not so.
sources.raw_question: Is it true that the Father himself became Christ, was born, suffered, and raised himself?

question: Are the angels holy by nature in the same way the Holy Spirit is holy?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: No. The heavenly powers are not holy by nature; if they were, there would be no difference between them and the Holy Spirit. Their sanctification is external to their substance and comes through communion with the Spirit, in proportion to their excellence. Basil compares this to a branding-iron, which is conceived together with the fire and yet is distinct from it.
sources.quote: The powers of the heavens are not holy by nature; were it so there would in this respect be no difference between them and the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Are the angels holy by nature in the same way the Holy Spirit is holy?

question: How is Christ's anointing with the Holy Spirit related to the anointing believers receive from the Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Christ has the fulness of the Spirit, and believers' measure is communicated from it. Being 'anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows' is the same as God's not giving the Spirit by measure to him. Christ is therefore anointed above believers, who receive the Spirit by measure, so that he has the pre-eminence. Because the same Spirit dwells in him and in them, believers share in his offices of king, priest and prophet.
sources.quote: We, who have the Spirit by measure, are anointed with the “oil of gladness;” Christ hath the fulness of the Spirit, whence our measure is communicated: so he is anointed above us, “that in all things he may have the pre-eminence.”
sources.raw_question: How is Christ's anointing with the Holy Spirit related to the anointing believers receive from the Spirit?

question: Do the Holy Spirit's being sent by the Son, receiving from Him, and guiding into truth show that the Spirit is merely a minister like a human teacher, rather than God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory argues that if these were the whole account of the Spirit, they would describe nothing above a human teacher. Being sent, receiving, announcing, teaching and suggesting the truth all belong to the present pastors and teachers of the Church. Eunomius' list therefore fails to express the Spirit's true dignity, which belongs to One who breathes where He wills and works all in all.
sources.quote: All these things, which Eunomius is good enough to allow to the Holy Spirit, belong to the present pastors and teachers of the Church,—to be sent, to receive, to announce, to teach, to suggest the truth.
sources.raw_question: Do the Holy Spirit's being sent by the Son, receiving from Him, and guiding into truth show that the Spirit is merely a minister like a human teacher, rather than God?

question: Is the Holy Spirit merely the highest of the creatures made by the Son, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory calls the phrase "surpassing all the creatures of the Son" profane, because it gives the Spirit only a relative superiority among created things. Such a ranking produces confusion when applied to One who "breatheth where He willeth" and "worketh all in all." These are divine attributes, not those of a creature.
sources.quote: with his addition of his profane phrase, “surpassing all the creatures of the Son,” he produces turbid confusion by assigning to Him Who “breatheth where He willeth,” and “worketh all in all,” a mere superiority in comparison with the rest of created things.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit merely the highest of the creatures made by the Son, as Eunomius claims?

question: Did the Only-begotten Son, in suffering the passion, feel pain in his divine nature as ordinary men do?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. He suffered the attacks of all our infirmities in his body, but bore them in the power of his own nature, just as at his birth he did not lose his omnipotent nature. He had a body which could feel pain, but his nature could not feel pain, because his origin was not human but by conception of the Holy Ghost. It is a mistaken human judgment to think he felt pain merely because he suffered.
sources.quote: So too He felt pain for us, but not with our senses; He was found in fashion as a man, with a body which could feel pain, but His nature could not feel pain
sources.raw_question: Did the Only-begotten Son, in suffering the passion, feel pain in his divine nature as ordinary men do?

question: Was Christ's passion and death a necessity imposed on his nature, showing infirmity, or a free act of divine power?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: It was a free act of divine power. Paul describes the death of Christ as stripping off his flesh, nailing the bond of ordinances to the cross, and triumphing over principalities and powers in himself. Hence the passion was a free gift, a mystery, a display of power and boldness, and a triumph, not subjection to necessity, force, fear or disgrace. The accompanying signs, such as the earthquake and the darkened sun, confirm that as man he suffered but as God he triumphed.
sources.quote: to distort into the dishonourable charge of natural weakness, what was an act of free-will, a mystery, a display of power and boldness, a triumph?
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's passion and death a necessity imposed on his nature, showing infirmity, or a free act of divine power?

question: Is the statement 'the Word was God' consistent with the prophetic teaching that God is One?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Yes. John's 'He was in the beginning with God' shows the Word is eternal, is God and more than a voice, and is with God so that his identity is neither swallowed up in the Father's nor encroaches on it. He is present with the One Unbegotten God as God, his One and Only-begotten Son.
sources.quote: that He is with God proves that He neither encroaches nor is encroached upon, for His identity is not swallowed up in that of Another
sources.raw_question: Is the statement 'the Word was God' consistent with the prophetic teaching that God is One?

question: Is it one thing for God the Father to be and another thing for Him to be wise?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: No. Distinguishing being from being wise fits the soul, which is sometimes unwise and sometimes wise. The soul is changeable by nature and not absolutely simple. God is perfectly simple, so in Him to be and to be wise are not different.
sources.quote: a thing usually understood of the soul, which is at some times unwise, at others wise; as being by nature changeable, and not absolutely and perfectly simple
sources.raw_question: Is it one thing for God the Father to be and another thing for Him to be wise?

question: Can the Word make others sons of God without being the Son himself?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No. Something that is not a son cannot make sons, especially when there is a father. If the Word makes sons for himself, he would be Father. If he makes them for the Father, he must be that Son through whom the rest are made sons.
sources.quote: For how could a being make other sons, not being himself a son, especially when there was a father?
sources.raw_question: Can the Word make others sons of God without being the Son himself?

question: How can God be called the Father of believers, and how does this differ from his being Christ's own Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: God is properly the Father of the Son alone, which is why Christ says 'My Father' and 'I came from the Father.' God is called our Father only because the Son, by taking our flesh, dwells in us through his Spirit and calls on his own Father in us. Where the Son is not in someone's heart, God cannot be called that person's Father.
sources.quote: Therefore the Son in us, calling upon His own Father, causes Him to be named our Father also. Surely in whose hearts the Son is not, of them neither can God be called Father.
sources.raw_question: How can God be called the Father of believers, and how does this differ from his being Christ's own Father?

question: Since the Son was already in the world, how can he be said to have been sent into the world?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Son and Holy Spirit are Not Therefore Less Because Sent. The Son is Sent Also by Himself. Of the Sending of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: He was sent to where he already was. John says that he was in the world and that the world was made by him, and that he also came unto his own. As God he fills heaven and earth, so his sending cannot mean moving to a place where he was absent.
sources.quote: if He was sent into the world, because He came forth from the Father, then He both came into the world and was in the world. He was sent therefore thither, where He already was.
sources.raw_question: Since the Son was already in the world, how can he be said to have been sent into the world?

question: Do the scriptural titles of the Holy Spirit ("Spirit of God," "Spirit of truth," "Holy Spirit") indicate that the Spirit belongs to the supreme divine nature rather than to creation?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Definitive conceptions about the Spirit which conform to the teaching of the Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. Basil argues that the titles of the Spirit compel the hearer to raise his conception to the supreme nature. The name "spirit" is proper to what is incorporeal, immaterial and indivisible, as Christ shows in saying "God is a spirit." Hence on hearing of the Spirit one cannot conceive a circumscribed, changeable nature like a creature.
sources.quote: On our hearing, then, of a spirit, it is impossible to form the idea of a nature circumscribed, subject to change and variation, or at all like the creature.
sources.raw_question: Do the scriptural titles of the Holy Spirit ("Spirit of God," "Spirit of truth," "Holy Spirit") indicate that the Spirit belongs to the supreme divine nature rather than to creation?

question: How can the Holy Spirit be wholly present to each person and also everywhere, shared by many without being divided or diminished?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Definitive conceptions about the Spirit which conform to the teaching of the Scriptures.
sources.answer: The Spirit is simple in essence but various in powers. Like a sunbeam, it is wholly present to each recipient as though given to him alone, yet it is wholly everywhere. It is divided without suffering and shared without ceasing to be entire. What each person receives is limited by the capacity of that person's nature, not by the Spirit's power.
sources.quote: in essence simple, in powers various, wholly present in each and being wholly everywhere; impassively divided, shared without loss of ceasing to be entire, after the likeness of the sunbeam
sources.raw_question: How can the Holy Spirit be wholly present to each person and also everywhere, shared by many without being divided or diminished?

question: What does the Holy Spirit's indwelling accomplish in believers, and does it include being made God?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Definitive conceptions about the Spirit which conform to the teaching of the Scriptures.
sources.answer: The Spirit makes believers spiritual by fellowship with himself, as a sunbeam makes transparent bodies shine with their own brightness. From this come foreknowledge, understanding of mysteries, abiding in God, and likeness to God. Highest of all is the being made God, a work that shows the Spirit's divine greatness and dignity.
sources.quote: Shining upon those that are cleansed from every spot, He makes them spiritual by fellowship with Himself.
sources.raw_question: What does the Holy Spirit's indwelling accomplish in believers, and does it include being made God?

question: Was God the Father unknown before the Son's incarnation, so that the words "to whomsoever the Son shall reveal Him" refer only to revelation beginning with Christ's birth from Mary?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VI.—Explanation of the words of Christ, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” etc.; which words the heretics misinterpret. Proof that, by the Father revealing the Son, and by the Son being revealed, the Father was never unknown.
sources.answer: No. The phrase "shall reveal" applies indifferently to all time, not to the future alone. The Son has been present with His own handiwork from the beginning and has always revealed the Father, to whom He wills, when He wills, and as the Father wills.
sources.quote: For “shall reveal” was said not with reference to the future alone, as if then [only] the Word had begun to manifest the Father when He was born of Mary, but it applies indifferently throughout all time.
sources.raw_question: Was God the Father unknown before the Son's incarnation, so that the words "to whomsoever the Son shall reveal Him" refer only to revelation beginning with Christ's birth from Mary?

question: Can anyone attain knowledge of God apart from the Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VI.—Explanation of the words of Christ, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” etc.; which words the heretics misinterpret. Proof that, by the Father revealing the Son, and by the Son being revealed, the Father was never unknown.
sources.answer: No. The Son administers all things for the Father from beginning to end. He is the knowledge of the Father, while the knowledge of the Son is in the Father and has been revealed through the Son. Without Him no one can know God.
sources.quote: For the Son is the knowledge of the Father; but the knowledge of the Son is in the Father, and has been revealed through the Son
sources.raw_question: Can anyone attain knowledge of God apart from the Son?

question: Does the Word reveal the Creator through creation, the law and the prophets, as well as through the incarnation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VI.—Explanation of the words of Christ, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” etc.; which words the heretics misinterpret. Proof that, by the Father revealing the Son, and by the Son being revealed, the Father was never unknown.
sources.answer: Yes. Through creation the Word reveals God the Creator, and through the world He reveals the Maker of the world. Through the law and the prophets He preached both Himself and the Father, and finally He showed forth the Father by becoming visible. All men are addressed alike, though not all believe.
sources.quote: For by means of the creation itself, the Word reveals God the Creator; and by means of the world [does He declare] the Lord the Maker of the world
sources.raw_question: Does the Word reveal the Creator through creation, the law and the prophets, as well as through the incarnation?

question: How does the human mind lose its vision of eternal things, which is where the image of God lies?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Turning Aside from the Image of God.
sources.answer: It loses that vision when the lower reason, the part entrusted with temporal things, slides too far into outward things. The higher, 'masculine' part of counsel consents to this and fails to restrain it. Then the head itself, 'eating with his spouse that which was forbidden,' is cut off from the light of eternal truth. Fallen people then cover this nakedness with good words that lack the fruit of good works, as Adam and Eve covered themselves with leaves.
sources.quote: that vision of eternal things is withdrawn also from the head himself, eating with his spouse that which was forbidden, so that the light of his eyes is gone from him
sources.raw_question: How does the human mind lose its vision of eternal things, which is where the image of God lies?

question: Does Christ's statement that the Father sanctified him and sent him into the world show that he is the Son and not the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Skilfully Replies to a Passage Which the Heretics Employed in Defence of Their Own Opinion.
sources.answer: Yes. One who receives sanctification from another and is sent by another cannot be that other; had he been the Father he would have given sanctification and sent rather than received and been sent. Otherwise the Father would be subjected to another God, so being sanctified and sent proves him to be the Son.
sources.quote: In receiving, then, sanctification from the Father, He is inferior to the Father. Now, consequently, He who is inferior to the Father, is not the Father, but the Son; for had He been the Father, He would have given, and not received, sanctification.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that the Father sanctified him and sent him into the world show that he is the Son and not the Father?

question: When Christ answered the charge of making himself God, did he identify himself as the Father or as the Son of God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Skilfully Replies to a Passage Which the Heretics Employed in Defence of Their Own Opinion.
sources.answer: As the Son of God. He explained the ground of his claim by saying "I am the Son of God," plainly testifying that he is the Son and not the Father; to call Christ the Father contradicts his own testimony.
sources.quote: Therefore if He plainly testifies that He is the Son of God, and not the Father, it is an instance of great temerity and excessive madness to stir up a controversy of divinity and religion
sources.raw_question: When Christ answered the charge of making himself God, did he identify himself as the Father or as the Son of God?

question: Do the biblical phrases 'from Him', 'from the womb', and 'I went out from the Father and am come' imply that the Father is compound, divisible, changeable or bodily if the Son is from his substance?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. These are God's own words about himself and must be accepted as spoken. 'From Himself' means the Son's Godhead has no source other than God: it is neither from someone else nor from nothing, and it marks a relation of Father and Son. 'From the womb' borrows bodily language to show that the birth is real, not because God has bodily members. The birth is also not a spatial extension but Light from Light.
sources.quote: It is not "From some one else," for it is From Himself; that is, His Godhead has no other source than God. It is not "From nothing," for it is From Himself; a declaration of the nature from which His birth is.
sources.raw_question: Do the biblical phrases 'from Him', 'from the womb', and 'I went out from the Father and am come' imply that the Father is compound, divisible, changeable or bodily if the Son is from his substance?

question: Does calling the Father alone eternal and without end imply that the Son is perishable and temporary?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next skilfully confutes the partial, empty and blasphemous statement of Eunomius on the subject of the absolutely existent.
sources.answer: Yes. That is the implication of Eunomius's claim, and it is why the claim is impious. Whatever is neither everlasting nor without end belongs to a perishable and mortal nature. So whoever predicates eternity and unendingness of the one God while excluding the Son makes the Son perishable and temporary. That view is unworthy of the Godhead of the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: he who predicates “unendingness” of the one and only God, and does not include the Son in the assertion of “unendingness” and “eternity,” maintains by such a proposition, that He Whom he thus contrasts with the eternal and unending is perishable and temporary.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father alone eternal and without end imply that the Son is perishable and temporary?

question: Did the Word of God take real human flesh from Adam's stock, or only a specially formed animal (psychic) body?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter IX.—Refutation of the impious interpretations of these heretics.
sources.answer: He took real flesh. The heretics say the Saviour assumed an animal body formed by a special dispensation to be visible and palpable, but flesh is what God formed of old for Adam out of the dust, and it is this that John declares the Word became.
sources.quote: But flesh is that which was of old formed for Adam by God out of the dust, and it is this that John has declared the Word of God became.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God take real human flesh from Adam's stock, or only a specially formed animal (psychic) body?

question: Does believing in one God require either two Gods of different kinds or a solitary God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Neither. There are not two Gods different in kind, nor is God solitary. The Son is indicated in the Father's name and exists in the Father, whose name and nature are in Him. The Father by His name implies the Son and abides in Him, since a son cannot be spoken of or exist except as born of a father.
sources.quote: neither are there two Gods, different in kind, in our faith, nor is God solitary because He is one
sources.raw_question: Does believing in one God require either two Gods of different kinds or a solitary God?

question: Is it a sufficient ground for holding Christ to be only man that he had a fleshly birth?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: No. Like the Jews who 'judged after the flesh,' those who take Christ's carnal birth as his only birth overlook his descent from heaven. Since no man can come from heaven, he who descended thence must be God.
sources.quote: holding that the carnal birth of Christ was the only one, believed that Christ was nothing else than man; not considering this point, that as man could not come from heaven
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold Christ is only man
sources.raw_question: Is it a sufficient ground for holding Christ to be only man that he had a fleshly birth?

question: Is the analogy of the sun and its ray adequate for describing the Son's relation to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > A passing repetition of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: Not fully. Gregory says we need not be slaves to the image, since its inadequacy could give critics a handle against the faith. A ray is less than the sun, so he corrects the image: the Son is another sun, an offspring of the Ungenerate sun, like it in every way.
sources.quote: it will not be a ray of the sun that we shall perceive, but another sun blazing forth, as an offspring, out of the Ungenerate sun
sources.raw_question: Is the analogy of the sun and its ray adequate for describing the Son's relation to the Father?

question: Is the Holy Spirit counted among the three Persons only because of order, rather than because of any inferiority?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > A passing repetition of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is beheld together with the Father and the Son and is counted after them, but by its complete perfection it is part of the highest light. By its own power it gives those able to partake of it access to the light seen in the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: is beheld along with the Father and the Son, though counted after them, and by its own power gives access to the light that is perceived in the Father and Son
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit counted among the three Persons only because of order, rather than because of any inferiority?

question: Can a kind of trinity be found in the human mind when the words of the Christian faith are committed to memory?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine says there is a kind of trinity here. First, the sounds of the words are stored in the memory, even when the person is not thinking of them. Second, the mind's eye of recollection is formed from them when he thinks of them. Third, the will joins the two together when he thinks and remembers.
sources.quote: there is in the mind a kind of trinity, since there are, first, in the memory the sounds of the words, and this even when the man is not thinking of them; and next, the mind’s eye of his recollection is formed thereupon when he thinks of them
sources.raw_question: Can a kind of trinity be found in the human mind when the words of the Christian faith are committed to memory?

question: In what way do created things, including past and future ones, exist in the Word of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > We are Made Perfect by Acknowledgement of Our Own Weakness. The Incarnate Word Dispels Our Darkness.
sources.answer: They exist in the Word simultaneously, potentially and unchangeably. In the Word they neither have been nor shall be, but only are. There they are life and one being and one life, because the Word is the one unchangeable truth by which all things were made.
sources.quote: all things are simultaneously therein, potentially and unchangeably; not only those things which are now in this whole creation, but also those which have been and those which shall be. And therein they neither have been, nor shall be, but only are
sources.raw_question: In what way do created things, including past and future ones, exist in the Word of God?

question: Does the Son's assumption of flesh in the Incarnation mean a weakening or dishonouring of his divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The Apostle teaches that the Dispensation of the flesh is the 'mystery of great godliness,' not the dishonour of God. This mystery was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit and received up in glory. The justification in the Spirit removes any idea of fleshly weakness. What looks like infirmity and necessity is in truth mystery and godliness.
sources.quote: what room does our faith leave for any to think that the secret of the Dispensation of godliness is the enfeebling of the divinity, when through the assumption of glory is to be confessed the mystery of great godliness?
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's assumption of flesh in the Incarnation mean a weakening or dishonouring of his divinity?

question: If Christ says in John 14:16 that the Father will give the Comforter, how can he also say in John 15:26 and 16:7 that he himself sends the Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: Both are true in different respects. The original and sovereign dispensation of the Spirit is in the Father's hand, and he gives the Spirit upon Christ's intercession. But the Spirit is not bestowed on us immediately; he is given into Christ's hand for us. So, as to the actual bestowing, Christ receives the Spirit from the Father and sends him to his saints himself.
sources.quote: not being bestowed immediately on us, but, as it were, given into the hand of Christ for us, he affirms that (as to actual collation or bestowing) he sends him himself
sources.raw_question: If Christ says in John 14:16 that the Father will give the Comforter, how can he also say in John 15:26 and 16:7 that he himself sends the Spirit?

question: Does Moses' use of the words 'fruit' and 'seed' before these were created show that God himself gave things their names?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Moses teaches that the thing underlying these names, wheat or other produce, grows and reproduces by the will of the Creator. He does not teach that God coined the words. The thing is produced by the divine will, not the name.
sources.quote: And by the Divine will the thing is produced, not the name
sources.raw_question: Does Moses' use of the words 'fruit' and 'seed' before these were created show that God himself gave things their names?

question: Could God have spoken in human words and language before the creation of the world?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Before creation there was no hearer, and no bodily element in which an articulate voice could sound. God is incorporeal, and no national language yet existed. The heavenly voices at the Jordan and the Transfiguration were formed by God in the air, in the hearers' own language, for their sake. That only confirms that divine speech is an accommodation to created hearers.
sources.quote: before the creation of the world, inasmuch as there was no one to hear the word, and no bodily element capable of accentuating the articulate voice, how can he who says that God used words give any air of probability to his assertion?
sources.raw_question: Could God have spoken in human words and language before the creation of the world?

question: If the Holy Spirit is God and may be prayed to directly, how can we consistently also ask the Father and the Son to give the Spirit to us?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: The two kinds of prayer consider the Spirit in different respects. When we pray to the Spirit himself, we consider him as essentially God over all, blessed for evermore. When we pray to the Father and Son for him, we consider him as under their mission and delegation in the economy of salvation. Both are fitting answers to how God has revealed himself.
sources.quote: In our prayers that are directed to himself, we consider him as essentially God over all, blessed for evermore; we pray for him from the Father and Son, as under this mission and delegation from them.
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit is God and may be prayed to directly, how can we consistently also ask the Father and the Son to give the Spirit to us?

question: Is the Holy Spirit given to believers for their comfort as a free gift of grace or as something they earn?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: As a free gift. Scripture constantly says he is given and received as a gift, and what is of gift is free. He is received by the gospel, not by the law, that is, of mere grace. His workings are called charismata, free donations, and he is freely bestowed in respect of consolation as well as sanctification.
sources.quote: Hence the Spirit is said to be received by the gospel, not by the law, Gal. iii. 2; that is, of mere grace, and not of our own procuring.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit given to believers for their comfort as a free gift of grace or as something they earn?

question: What is said of God the Father as such, apart from what He shares with the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > What is Said of the Father and Son Together, and What Not.
sources.answer: Only relative terms. Nothing is said of the Father as such except what is said in relation to the Son: that He is His Father, begetter, or beginning. Whatever else is said of Him is said with the Son, or rather in the Son.
sources.quote: if nothing is spoken of the Father as such, except that which is spoken of Him in relation to the Son, that is, that He is His father, or begetter, or beginning
sources.raw_question: What is said of God the Father as such, apart from what He shares with the Son?

question: Can the Gnostics' 'Mother' (Achamoth), or the Gnostics themselves as spiritual beings, be the source of the spiritual creation instead of the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: No. They have no proof that spiritual things came from the Mother's travail, and they admit that the Creator, not the Mother, is lord of all creation. They cannot create even a fly or a gnat except by the natural law God set from the beginning. They are not even lords of their own bodies, which suffer pain against their will, so they cannot claim to be spiritual while denying that to the Creator of all.
sources.quote: these men cannot create even a fly, or a gnat, or any other small and insignificant animal, without observing that law by which from the beginning animals have been and are naturally produced by God
sources.raw_question: Can the Gnostics' 'Mother' (Achamoth), or the Gnostics themselves as spiritual beings, be the source of the spiritual creation instead of the Creator?

question: How can Christ's human weaknesses (birth, weeping, hunger, suffering, abandonment, death) be reconciled with his divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Each human weakness is accompanied, according to the Scriptures, by a sign of divine power. He was born of a Virgin but conceived of the Holy Ghost; he hungered but cursed the fruitless tree by divine power; he complained of abandonment yet at that moment received the thief into Paradise; he died but rose and sits at God's right hand. Confessing both together according to the Scriptures is the safe faith.
sources.quote: Christ hungered; but according to the Scriptures, He used His power as God against the tree which bore no fruit, when He had no food.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ's human weaknesses (birth, weeping, hunger, suffering, abandonment, death) be reconciled with his divinity?

question: How do the Father and the Son each act in bringing the apostles to the knowledge of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XIII—Refutation of the opinion, that Paul was the only apostle who had knowledge of the truth.
sources.answer: The Son leads them to the Father, and the Father reveals the Son to them. Peter's confession came not from flesh and blood but from the Father in heaven. Paul likewise was an apostle by Jesus Christ and God the Father, and so were the rest. The two Persons therefore work together in a reciprocal revelation.
sources.quote: the Son indeed leading them to the Father, but the Father revealing to them the Son.
sources.raw_question: How do the Father and the Son each act in bringing the apostles to the knowledge of God?

question: Do Scripture's statements that Christ is unchangeable and almighty place him on a level with God the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Jehovah says "I change not" and "I am the Almighty God." Of Christ it is said that he is "the same yesterday, today, and forever," and he calls himself "the Almighty." Moreover, whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise, which shows the Son has the same omnipotence.
sources.quote: I am ... the Almighty. Rev. 1:8. Whatsoever things He doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise. – John 5:19.
sources.raw_question: Do Scripture's statements that Christ is unchangeable and almighty place him on a level with God the Father?

question: Does 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 show that the Holy Spirit is God himself rather than a being subordinate to God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. The passage presents the Spirit as the substrate of the divine self-consciousness, the principle of God's knowledge of himself. As a man's spirit is his very life, so the Spirit of God is God's very life-element, God himself in the innermost essence of his being. He therefore cannot be thought subordinate to God or derived from him.
sources.quote: Here the Spirit appears as the substrate of the Divine self-consciousness, the principle of God’s knowledge of Himself: He is, in a word, just God Himself in the innermost essence of His Being.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 show that the Holy Spirit is God himself rather than a being subordinate to God?

question: Why is the Son Lord of all while creation is in bondage?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: The Son is Lord because he is one with the Father's Lordship. Creation is in bondage because it is outside the Oneness of the Father. Once it was not, and it was brought into being.
sources.quote: but He is Lord of all, because He is one with the Father’s Lordship; and the creation is all in bondage, since it is external to the Oneness of the Father
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son Lord of all while creation is in bondage?

question: Is the Son's right to religious worship founded on the power and authority given to him after his resurrection, or on his personal dignity and essential perfections?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: It is founded on his personal dignity and essential perfections. Even if distinct worship of Christ in fact began only after his resurrection, he always had the same right and title to it; the right simply could not take effect until it was clearly revealed. Likewise, God the Father always had a right to worship, though it could not take place until he made himself known.
sources.quote: the worship due to him is not founded merely upon the power and authority supposed to have been given him after his resurrection; but upon his personal dignity and essential perfections.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's right to religious worship founded on the power and authority given to him after his resurrection, or on his personal dignity and essential perfections?

question: Was the Son worshipped before his incarnation, for example by the patriarchs and the Jewish Church?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: Yes, Waterland inclines to think so. Irenaeus says expressly that the Logos was worshipped of old together with the Father. All the Ante-Nicene Fathers held that the one who appeared to the patriarchs and gave the law was the second Person of the Trinity. Eusebius and Athanasius, though opposed in party, agreed that Abraham, Moses and the Jewish Church worshipped the Son.
sources.quote: I incline to think that worship, distinct worship, was paid to the Son, long before his incarnation.
sources.raw_question: Was the Son worshipped before his incarnation, for example by the patriarchs and the Jewish Church?

question: Does the Son's acceptance of worship from the patriarchs in his Old Testament appearances prove his divinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: Yes. The patriarchs worshipped the Person who appeared to them, taking him to be the God of the universe, to whom all worship rightly belongs. Had he not been what they took him for, he should have refused that worship, as the angel in Revelation refused St. John's. Since he received it in his own Person, he was worshipped distinctly and in his own right, as truly God.
sources.quote: Had he not been what they took him for, he should have rejected that worship, as the angel in the Revelations rejected the worship which St. John would have offered him.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's acceptance of worship from the patriarchs in his Old Testament appearances prove his divinity?

question: Is the Son related to the Father merely as a spoken word is related to the speaker, lacking substantive divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The Only-begotten is God the Word, existing with God in the beginning and abiding in the form of God. To make him a mere utterance of God's voice deprives him of substantive divinity. It is this eternal God the Word who was himself born as Christ the Man.
sources.quote: With a view to deprive of substantive divinity the Only-begotten God, Who was God the Word with God in the beginning, they make Him merely the utterance of the voice of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son related to the Father merely as a spoken word is related to the speaker, lacking substantive divinity?

question: Are Christ and Jesus two distinct beings, such that an impassible heavenly Christ descended upon the man Jesus and left him before the passion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: No. Paul knew no other Christ than him who was born, suffered, was buried and rose again, and he consistently uses the name Christ when speaking of the passion, human nature and death. This shows that the impassible Christ did not descend upon Jesus, but that he himself, being Jesus Christ, suffered for us.
sources.quote: indicating that the impassible Christ did not descend upon Jesus, but that He Himself, because He was Jesus Christ, suffered for us; He, who lay in the tomb, and rose again, who descended and ascended
sources.raw_question: Are Christ and Jesus two distinct beings, such that an impassible heavenly Christ descended upon the man Jesus and left him before the passion?

question: How does the name "Christ" point to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: The name Christ implies one who anoints, one who is anointed, and the unction itself. The Father is the one who anoints, the Son is the one anointed, and the Spirit is the unction, as Isaiah shows: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because He hath anointed me."
sources.quote: And it is the Father who anoints, but the Son who is anointed by the Spirit, who is the unction
sources.raw_question: How does the name "Christ" point to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: What do the works Christ performs prove about his relation to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: They prove that he was sent by the Father, which shows his sonlike obedience and the Father's authority. Because these works are equal to the Father's own, they also attest his equality with the Father. Such works could not be done by anyone other than the one the Father sent.
sources.quote: We have the Father’s witness to His Sonship; by works, equal to the Father’s, the Son bears witness to His own equality with the Father.
sources.raw_question: What do the works Christ performs prove about his relation to the Father?

question: Does Scripture teach that Christ pre-existed as God and descended from heaven to become man?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: Yes. The Bible records Christ's descent from above. The Word, who in the beginning was with God and was God, was made flesh. He came down from heaven and proceeded forth from God, leaving the glory he had with the Father before the world was. Being originally in the form of God, he emptied himself and took the form of a servant.
sources.quote: that being originally (υπάρχων) in the form of God, He emptied himself, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that Christ pre-existed as God and descended from heaven to become man?

question: If the Son had a beginning, would the Trinity itself have come into being by addition from an original Monad?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: Yes, and this is absurd. If the Word was not with the Father from everlasting, then a Monad came first and became a Triad by addition, deficient before the Son and complete afterward. The knowledge of God would then grow over time, which is impious.
sources.quote: for if the Word is not with the Father from everlasting, the Triad is not everlasting; but a Monad was first, and afterwards by addition it became a Triad
sources.raw_question: If the Son had a beginning, would the Trinity itself have come into being by addition from an original Monad?

question: If the doctrine of God as Trinity is true now, must it have been true eternally?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: Yes. If the doctrine of God is now perfect in a Triad and this is the true religion, it must always have been so. Otherwise the good and the truth would be later additions. Either the Triad is eternal, or it is not truly a Triad now either.
sources.quote: For if the doctrine of God is now perfect in a Triad, and this is the true and only Religion, and this is the good and the truth, it must have been always so, unless the good and the truth be something that came after
sources.raw_question: If the doctrine of God as Trinity is true now, must it have been true eternally?

question: Does dishonouring the Son by calling Him a creature also dishonour the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: Yes. To say of the Word seated by the Father that 'once He was not' does not glorify the Lord but the reverse. Whoever dishonours the Son dishonours also the Father.
sources.quote: Such statements do not glorify and honour the Lord, but the reverse; for he who dishonours the Son, dishonours also the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does dishonouring the Son by calling Him a creature also dishonour the Father?

question: Does Christ's prayer 'not as I will, but as Thou wilt' show that the Son's will is opposed to or distinct in nature from the Father's will?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. By his prayer for the cup's removal he expressed fellowship with human anxiety, while associating himself with the will he shares inseparably with the Father. As Man he prays for men, but as God from God his will is in unison with the Father's effectual will.
sources.quote: as Man He prays for men that the cup may pass away, but as God from God, His will is in unison with the Father’s effectual will.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's prayer 'not as I will, but as Thou wilt' show that the Son's will is opposed to or distinct in nature from the Father's will?

question: Given the Eunomian principle that things sharing attributes share a nature, what follows from saying the Son, like creatures, did not exist before His generation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > After this, fearing to extend his reply to great length, he passes by most of his adversary's statements as already refuted. But the remainder, for the sake of those who deem them of much force, he briefly summarizes, and refutes the blasphemy of Eunomius, who says of the Lord also that He is what animals and plants in all creation are, non-existent before their own generation; and so with the production of frogs; alas for the blasphemy!
sources.answer: By the Eunomians' own principle, it would follow that the Son shares the nature of dogs, fleas and snakes. Eunomius held that not existing before generation is equivalent in fact and meaning to not being ungenerate. Gregory replies that the same is true of a dog: its not existing before its generation is equivalent to its not being ungenerate. If shared attributes imply a shared nature, Eunomius's argument would make the Son of one nature with the meanest creatures. The absurdity of that conclusion exposes the falsity of his premise.
sources.quote: if, in accord with the definition they have so often laid down, all things that share in attributes share also in nature, and if it is an attribute of the dog, and of the rest severally, not to exist before generation
sources.raw_question: Given the Eunomian principle that things sharing attributes share a nature, what follows from saying the Son, like creatures, did not exist before His generation?

question: Does the long survival of the doctrine of the Trinity count against the claim that it is a gross contradiction of common sense and reason?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: Yes, it is an additional confirmation. The doctrine has survived every attack of argument and also severe persecution. Neither force nor self-interest brought it in or upheld it. People do not generally embrace contradictions out of whim when truth and consistency are as easily had, so its universal acceptance tells against the charge of absurdity.
sources.quote: This is to me an additional confirmation, that the doctrine we profess is no such gross imposition upon the common sense and reason of mankind, as is pretended. It was neither force nor interest that brought it in
sources.raw_question: Does the long survival of the doctrine of the Trinity count against the claim that it is a gross contradiction of common sense and reason?

question: Is saying 'He created me' equivalent to saying 'I am a creature'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: No. Wisdom says with cautious exactness only 'He created me.' It does not say 'I am a creature' or 'created me that I might have being.' Things with a created essence are called creatures. The bare verb 'created,' however, can denote something coming to pass in a person without making that person a creature in nature and essence.
sources.quote: this mere term ‘He created’ does not necessarily signify the essence or the generation, but indicates something else as coming to pass in Him of whom it speaks, and not simply that He who is said to be created, is at once in His Nature and Essence a creature
sources.raw_question: Is saying 'He created me' equivalent to saying 'I am a creature'?

question: Could the Word of God have existed even if no creature had ever existed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Likeness of the Divine Word, Such as It Is, is to Be Sought, Not in Our Own Outer and Sensible Word, But in the Inner and Mental One. There is the Greatest Possible Unlikeness Between Our Word and Knowledge and the Divine Word and Knowledge.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine draws the likeness from the human word: a word of ours can exist without any work following, but no work can exist unless a word precedes. So the Word of God could have existed though no creature existed, whereas no creature could exist except through that Word by whom all things are made.
sources.quote: just as the Word of God could have existed though no creature existed, but no creature could exist unless by that Word by which all things are made
sources.raw_question: Could the Word of God have existed even if no creature had ever existed?

question: Can the Son rightly speak of something belonging to His image or impress as though it were Himself?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ said to Saul, 'Why persecutest thou Me?', speaking of the Church, which bore His image, as if He Himself were persecuted. In the same way the true Wisdom can say 'The Lord created me' of His impress created in the works. A king's son might likewise say 'I am made in the works' because his name is stamped on them, without meaning that his own essence is created.
sources.quote: when Saul was persecuting the Church, in which was His impress and image, He said, as if He were Himself under persecution, ‘Saul, why persecutest thou Me?’
sources.raw_question: Can the Son rightly speak of something belonging to His image or impress as though it were Himself?

question: Is there a real distinction between the uncreated God and created man, such that man cannot be like God from the outset?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVIII.—Why man was not made perfect from the beginning.
sources.answer: Yes. Only the Uncreated is perfect, and man, as a creature only just made, cannot at once sustain the power of divinity. Those who deny any distinction between the uncreated God and man are more irrational than dumb animals, which simply give thanks for being what they were created to be.
sources.quote: they who are more destitute of reason than dumb animals [insist] that there is no distinction between the uncreated God and man, a creature of to-day.
sources.raw_question: Is there a real distinction between the uncreated God and created man, such that man cannot be like God from the outset?

question: Does Ignatius's statement that Christ is Son of God 'according to the will and power of God' prove that the Son exists by the Father's arbitrary choice?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. The phrase admits several other readings: that the Son is the offspring of God's will and power, meaning no more than God of God; that he is begotten by God's eternal will; that he exists with God's approbation, as God acquiesces in his own wisdom and goodness; or that it refers to his coming forth to create the world rather than his generation in the highest sense. So little or nothing can be proved from it.
sources.quote: From these four particulars, you may perceive how little you can be able to prove from that passage in Ignatius.
sources.raw_question: Does Ignatius's statement that Christ is Son of God 'according to the will and power of God' prove that the Son exists by the Father's arbitrary choice?

question: In Ignatius's phrase, is Christ called Son of God only with respect to his incarnation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. The sonship 'according to the will and power of God' is set against his being of David 'according to the flesh', so it must mean a higher sonship. The ancients consistently read 'according to the flesh' as referring to his birth of the Virgin, in contrast to a prior sonship in his divine nature before the world. Ignatius elsewhere says the Son was with the Father before the ages and is his eternal Word.
sources.quote: I can by no means think that the Son is here called vids Θεοῦ, in respect of his incarnation; which was really his nativity κατὰ σάρκα, to which this other is opposed, and which must therefore be understood of some higher sonship.
sources.raw_question: In Ignatius's phrase, is Christ called Son of God only with respect to his incarnation?

question: Does it follow logically from the homoousion that one of two ungenerate beings is brought down by generation to the rank of Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: No. No teacher or hearer of such a doctrine exists in the Church, and Eunomius shows no article of faith from which it strictly follows. To speak of Father and Son and yet imagine two ungenerate beings, one coming into being through the other, is an absurdity of his own invention, a fight with shadows.
sources.quote: when there is not, and never can be such a doctrine in the Church, when neither a teacher of it nor a hearer of it is to be found, and the absurdity cannot be shown, either, to be the strict logical consequence of anything
sources.raw_question: Does it follow logically from the homoousion that one of two ungenerate beings is brought down by generation to the rank of Son?

question: Does Philippians 2:5-7 teach that Christ is truly God as well as truly man?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. The same Christ is said to be in the form of God and equal with God, and also to have taken the form of a servant. The opponents admit the second clause expresses true humanity. So the first clause, stated just as plainly, must express true deity.
sources.quote: That his being truly a man is expressed in these words our adversaries deny not; and we therefore believe that the same Jesus Christ is God also, because that is no less plainly expressed.
sources.raw_question: Does Philippians 2:5-7 teach that Christ is truly God as well as truly man?

question: How is the Son of God begotten within the Godhead?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: By a reflex act of God's knowledge. God's first knowledge is His knowledge of everything possible. Then God views and knows Himself, and so knows His own knowledge, and in this the Son is begotten. This knowledge of knowledge, an idea of an idea, is nothing else than God's idea or knowledge repeated.
sources.quote: Then comes a reflex act of knowledge and His viewing Himself and knowing Himself and so knowing His own knowledge and so the Son is begotten. There is such a thing in God as knowledge of knowledge, an idea of an idea.
sources.raw_question: How is the Son of God begotten within the Godhead?

question: Was the world made especially for the Son of God?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. God made the world for Himself out of love to Himself, but He loves Himself only in a reflex act, by viewing Himself. When God makes something for Himself, He sets Himself before Himself as its end, which is to have an idea of Himself. To make the world for the Godhead so viewed is to make it for the Godhead begotten, that is, for the Son.
sources.quote: to make the world for the Godhead thus viewed and understood is to make the world for the Godhead begotten and that is to make the world for the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Was the world made especially for the Son of God?

question: If all the names applied to God mean the same thing, as Eunomius claims, does it follow that God has always been Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Since 'Father' is one of the names applied to the Divine Nature, and Eunomius holds that all such names coincide in meaning, 'Father' would mean the same as 'indestructible'. Then God would be always Father as He is always indestructible. Eunomius must either admit the eternal Fatherhood or abandon his claim that the divine names have a single signification.
sources.quote: if the meaning of indestructible and Father is exactly the same, He will be believed to be, just as He is always indestructible, so likewise always Father
sources.raw_question: If all the names applied to God mean the same thing, as Eunomius claims, does it follow that God has always been Father?

question: Can God's eternal power and Godhead be known from the created world?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Nothing exists by chance; there is a cause on whom all nature depends. As the Apostle says, His eternal power and godhead are clearly seen through creation, and the order of the heavens leads us to imagine the beauty of the invisible Archetype.
sources.quote: since, as saith the Apostle, His eternal power and godhead are understood, being clearly seen through the creation of the world, therefore all creation and, before all, as saith the Scripture, the system of the heavens, declare the wisdom of the Creator
sources.raw_question: Can God's eternal power and Godhead be known from the created world?

question: What return does the Father require from believers in communion with him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Mainly love. God loves first so that he may be loved in return, commanding the heart and love of the whole soul. When the soul sees God as love and delights in him as such, it has communion with him in love.
sources.quote: When the soul sees God, in his dispensation of love, to be love, to be infinitely lovely and loving, rests upon and delights in him as such, then hath it communion with him in love.
sources.raw_question: What return does the Father require from believers in communion with him?

question: Is the baptismal confession of the Names of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit something through which grace is actually given?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > Eunomius again speaks of the Son as Lord and God, and Maker of all creation intelligible and sensible, having received from the Father the power and the commission for creation, being entrusted with the task of creation as if He were an artizan commissioned by some one hiring Him, and receiving His power of creation as a thing adventitious, ab extra, as a result of the power allotted to Him in accordance with such and such combinations and positions of the stars, as destiny decrees their lot in life to men at their nativity. Thus, passing by most of what Eunomius had written, he confutes his blasphemy that the Maker of all things came into being in like manner with the earth and with angels, and that the subsistence of the Only-begotten differs not at all from the genesis of all things, and reproaches Him with reverencing neither the Divine mystery nor the custom of the Church, nor following in his attempt to discover godliness any teacher of pious doctrine, but Manichæus, Colluthus, Arius, Aetius, and those like to them, supposing that Christianity in general is folly, and that the customs of the Church and the venerable sacraments are a jest, wherein he differs in nothing from the pagans, who borrowed from our doctrine the idea of a great God supreme over all. So, too, this new idolater preaches in the same fashion, and in particular that baptism is “into an artificer and creator,” not fearing the curse of those who cause addition or diminution to the Holy Scriptures. And he closes his book with showing him to be Antichrist.
