sources.answer: Yes. Through the revered Names the power of the new, divine birth distributes grace to those who come in faith. The sacramental tokens secure spiritual blessings and protect believers from the assaults of the evil one, so treating them as useless amounts to mocking the mystery, as pagans do.
sources.quote: he despises the revered Names, by which the power of the more Divine birth distributes grace to them who come for it in faith
sources.raw_question: Is the baptismal confession of the Names of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit something through which grace is actually given?

question: Does the Spirit come from the Word, so that whatever the Spirit has, He has from the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Yes. The Word gives the Spirit, and the Spirit is given from the Word. Therefore the Son cannot have come to be in the Father by participating in the Spirit, as the Arians suggest. Rather, the Spirit is in the Word, who is in the Father.
sources.quote: For since the Word is in the Father, and the Spirit is given from the Word, He wills that we should receive the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit come from the Word, so that whatever the Spirit has, He has from the Son?

question: Is the division of all existing things into created and uncreated nature exhaustive, so that the Son must belong to one or the other?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > The fifth book promises to speak of the words contained in the saying of the Apostle Peter, but delays their exposition. He discourses first of the creation, to the effect that, while nothing therein is deserving of worship, yet men, led astray by their ill-informed and feeble intelligence, and marvelling at its beauty, deified the several parts of the universe. And herein he excellently expounds the passage of Isaiah, “I am God, the first.”
sources.answer: Yes. Our conception of existences is divided into just two: the creation and the uncreated Nature. The Son must therefore be either uncreated, and so worthy of worship, or a creature, and so excluded from worship.
sources.quote: Seeing, then, that our conception of existences is divided into two, the creation and the uncreated Nature
sources.raw_question: Is the division of all existing things into created and uncreated nature exhaustive, so that the Son must belong to one or the other?

question: How does Christ's saying 'by their fruits ye shall know them' bear on whether the Son and the Father share one nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The observations made by watching Providence are sufficient to give us the knowledge of sameness of Being.
sources.answer: It shows that fruit reveals the character of the tree, since good fruit does not come from a bad tree. Providence is the fruit here, and it shows no difference between the Father and the Son. So we detect a single nature from which it springs, even though the persons from whom it comes are distinct.
sources.quote: so when the fruit, Providence, presents no difference, we detect a single nature from which that fruit has sprung, even though the trees be different from which the fruit is put forth.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's saying 'by their fruits ye shall know them' bear on whether the Son and the Father share one nature?

question: Is the wisdom by which the human mind becomes wise the same as the wisdom by which God is wise?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Trinity in the Mind is the Image of God, in that It Remembers, Understands, and Loves God, Which to Do is Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. Man's true wisdom is called God's because it comes from God, the mind being wise by participation in the supreme Light, not by its own light. But God is not wise by partaking of himself as the mind is wise by partaking of God; it is like the righteousness of God, which means both God's own righteousness and that which he gives in justifying the ungodly.
sources.quote: Yet not so of God, as is that wherewith God is wise. For He is not wise by partaking of Himself, as the mind is by partaking of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the wisdom by which the human mind becomes wise the same as the wisdom by which God is wise?

question: Is human wisdom true wisdom when it is merely the mind's own, apart from worship of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Trinity in the Mind is the Image of God, in that It Remembers, Understands, and Loves God, Which to Do is Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. Wisdom is the worship of God, and the mind is wise only by participating in the supreme Light. Wisdom that is merely human is vain; it is true wisdom only because it is also of God.
sources.quote: For this wisdom of man is so called, in that it is also of God. For then it is true wisdom; for if it is human, it is vain.
sources.raw_question: Is human wisdom true wisdom when it is merely the mind's own, apart from worship of God?

question: Does the orthodox confession that the immutable divine Word took flesh imply, as Eunomius charges, that Christ 'was emptied to become Himself'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: No. The orthodox confess that the immutable, uncreated Nature put on the created and perishable, which is a genuine change from majesty to lowliness. It is rather Eunomius's view, which makes the Son created like man, that reduces the incarnation to a transition from like to like, the created coming to be in the created. So the charge properly falls back on Eunomius himself.
sources.quote: For it is not one who confesses that the immutable Nature has put on the created and perishable, who speaks of the transition from like to like, but one who conceives that there is no change from the majesty of Nature to that which is more lowly.
sources.raw_question: Does the orthodox confession that the immutable divine Word took flesh imply, as Eunomius charges, that Christ 'was emptied to become Himself'?

question: When early Fathers such as Hippolytus and Theophilus speak of the Word being 'begotten' just before creation, do they teach that the Son's generation is not eternal, as Arianism holds?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: Not necessarily. Read literally and stripped of figure, such language would amount to Arianism. Bishop Bull's explanation, however, is that this generation is metaphorical. On this view the real, eternal generation is pictured by events in the economy of time, such as the Resurrection and the Nativity. The Word's going forth to create the worlds is one such event.
sources.quote: the γέννησις which S. Hippolytus and other writers spoke of, was but a metaphorical generation, the real and eternal truth being shadowed out by a succession of events in the economy of time
sources.raw_question: When early Fathers such as Hippolytus and Theophilus speak of the Word being 'begotten' just before creation, do they teach that the Son's generation is not eternal, as Arianism holds?

question: Why is the Son called simply 'God' when speaking to Abraham, but first 'Angel of God' when speaking to Hagar?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: The distinction of Persons first had to be made, through the title 'Angel of God,' as a safeguard against the delusion that God is a solitary Being. Once that distinction was established, his true and unqualified name 'God' could safely be used.
sources.quote: For when the distinction of Persons had first been made, as a safeguard against the delusion that God is a solitary Being, then His true and unqualified name could safely be uttered.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son called simply 'God' when speaking to Abraham, but first 'Angel of God' when speaking to Hagar?

question: Why can knowledge of a body be greater than the body, while the mind's knowledge of itself is not greater than the mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: Knowledge is a kind of life in the reason of the knower. Any life is greater than any body in power, so knowledge of a body exceeds the body. But when the mind knows itself, the same mind both knows and is known. Its self-knowledge therefore does not rise above itself.
sources.quote: For knowledge is a kind of life in the reason of the knower, but the body is not life; and any life is greater than any body, not in bulk, but in power.
sources.raw_question: Why can knowledge of a body be greater than the body, while the mind's knowledge of itself is not greater than the mind?

question: Does Jesus' claim in John that he and the Father are one imply a oneness of essential being rather than mere agreement of will?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Jesus not only declares that he and the Father are one with a unity of mutual interpenetration, so that to see him is to see the Father, but removes all doubt about the essential nature of this oneness by asserting his eternity, his co-eternity with God, and his eternal participation in the divine glory.
sources.quote: He removes all doubt as to the essential nature of His oneness with the Father by explicitly asserting His eternity (“Before Abraham was born, I am,” Jn. viii. 58), His co-eternity with God
sources.raw_question: Does Jesus' claim in John that he and the Father are one imply a oneness of essential being rather than mere agreement of will?

question: Does the Son's identity of being with the Father leave room for a real personal distinction between them?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. The very sayings that assert the Son's coming out of God use stressed pronouns to emphasize his personal distinctness from the Father. Jesus' characteristic language implies both a unity that is identity of Being and a distinction of Person. That distinction allows for love between them and for action and reaction upon one another.
sources.quote: a form of expression which combines a clear implication of a unity of Father and Son which is identity of Being, and an equally clear implication of a distinction of Person between them
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's identity of being with the Father leave room for a real personal distinction between them?

question: What does Jesus' repeated statement that he was sent by the Father show about the relation between Father and Son?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: It shows a distinction of Person between them. Jesus continually represents himself both as sent by God and as having come forth from the Father, in John and in the Synoptics alike. This mutual action implies, if not exteriority, then certainly a high measure of exteriorization between Father and Son.
sources.quote: He continually represents Himself as on the one hand sent by God, and as, on the other, having come forth from the Father
sources.raw_question: What does Jesus' repeated statement that he was sent by the Father show about the relation between Father and Son?

question: Why is Christ alone fitted to be mediator between God and humanity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Because he is one with God and one with us, and these two are united in one person. Being both God and man in the unity of one person gives him the ability and universal fitness for the office of mediator or umpire, and in this he is the power and wisdom of God.
sources.quote: Thus is he fitted for a mediator, a days-man, an umpire between God and us, — being one with him, and one with us, and one in himself in this oneness, in the unity of one person.
sources.raw_question: Why is Christ alone fitted to be mediator between God and humanity?

question: Can the human mind remain steadily in contemplation of eternal, unchangeable truth?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > What is the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge. The Worship of God is the Love of Him. How the Intellectual Cognizance of Eternal Things Comes to Pass Through Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. Few attain to these truths at all, and those who do cannot abide in them. The mind's eye is driven back, so the result is a transitory thought of a thing that is not transitory. That thought is stored in memory through instruction so the mind can return to it. If it is wholly forgotten, teaching can lead the mind back to the same unchanging truth, which is found just as it was.
sources.quote: he himself who attains to them does not abide in them, but is as it were repelled by the rebounding of the eye itself of the mind, and so there comes to be a transitory thought of a thing not transitory
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind remain steadily in contemplation of eternal, unchangeable truth?

question: Does Paul's list of created powers (dominions, principalities, powers) omit the Holy Spirit because the Spirit is merely one unlisted creature among others?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > These doctrines of our Faith witnessed to and confirmed by Scripture passages.
sources.answer: No. Paul counts creatures in masses, by classes like "dominions" and "principalities", whereas the Trinity is peculiarly proclaimed as individuals: one Father, one Son, one Holy Ghost. His silence about the Spirit in cataloguing creation excludes any suspicion that the Spirit is one of those ranks. Paul deliberately refrains from mentioning the divine mysteries when speaking of lower beings.
sources.quote: For it is a peculiarity of the Holy Trinity that it is to be proclaimed as consisting of individuals: one Father, one Son, one Holy Ghost: whereas those existences aforesaid are counted in masses
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's list of created powers (dominions, principalities, powers) omit the Holy Spirit because the Spirit is merely one unlisted creature among others?

question: Are there degrees of greater and less among the Persons of the Trinity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > These doctrines of our Faith witnessed to and confirmed by Scripture passages.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit, like the Only-begotten, is above creation and shares in the supreme and absolutely perfect nature. What is infinite and perfect cannot be regarded as in any way 'less.' Introducing degrees curtails the divine infinitude and contracts its perfection, which is what the heretic Eunomius attempts.
sources.quote: cannot be regarded as in any way a ‘less,’ although this teacher of heresy attempt to curtail its infinitude by introducing the idea of degrees
sources.raw_question: Are there degrees of greater and less among the Persons of the Trinity?

question: Do the presentation of Jesus in the Temple and the words of Simeon and Anna show that the Father of Christ is the same God who gave the Mosaic law?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: Yes. Luke himself calls the One who appointed the legal dispensation "Lord". Simeon and Anna glorified that same God on seeing Christ, calling the child God's salvation. By all these one God is shown, who reveals the new covenant through the advent of His Son.
sources.quote: Now by all these one God is shown forth, revealing to men the new dispensation of liberty, the covenant, through the new advent of His Son.
sources.raw_question: Do the presentation of Jesus in the Temple and the words of Simeon and Anna show that the Father of Christ is the same God who gave the Mosaic law?

question: Do Christ's bodily healings show that human flesh is able to receive life and salvation from him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XII.—Of the difference between life and death; of the breath of life and the vivifying Spirit: also how it is that the substance of flesh revives which once was dead.
sources.answer: Yes. Healing would be pointless, and only a temporary benefit, if the healed parts could not attain salvation. The flesh received healing from the Word, so it can also receive the life that flows from him. Life comes through healing and incorruption through life, and the one who heals also gives life and incorruption to his own handiwork.
sources.quote: Or how can they maintain that the flesh is incapable of receiving the life which flows from Him, when it received healing from Him? For life is brought about through healing, and incorruption through life.
sources.raised_by_detail: opponents who deny the salvation of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's bodily healings show that human flesh is able to receive life and salvation from him?

question: Does Methodius teach that the Son was made or had a beginning, or does he teach the Son's eternal generation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: He teaches eternal generation. Methodius not only asserts the eternal generation of the Son but guards it against the objection from 'This day have I begotten thee,' explaining that text not of any temporal generation, which he does not allow, but of a temporal manifestation to the world of the one already existing before the ages.
sources.quote: nothing can be clearer than that passage of Methodius for the eternal generation of the Son; which he does: not only assert, but guards it against the objection from that text, (“This day have I begotten thee,”)
sources.raw_question: Does Methodius teach that the Son was made or had a beginning, or does he teach the Son's eternal generation?

question: Does the fact that the Old Testament Scriptures testify of Christ show that the Old Testament and Christ come from one and the same God and Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter X.—The Old Testament Scriptures, and those written by Moses in particular, do everywhere make mention of the Son of God, and foretell His advent and passion. From this fact it follows that they were inspired by one and the same God.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ said the Scriptures testify of him, and they could only do so if they came from the same Father who was instructing men beforehand about the advent of his Son and the salvation he would bring. So the God of the law is the Father of Christ, against those who separate them.
sources.quote: How therefore did the Scriptures testify of Him, unless they were from one and the same Father, instructing men beforehand as to the advent of His Son, and foretelling the salvation brought in by Him?
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Old Testament Scriptures testify of Christ show that the Old Testament and Christ come from one and the same God and Father?

question: How does speaking of the Son as "with" the Father refute Sabellius's denial of distinct persons?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That Scripture uses the words “in” or “by,” ἐν, cf. note on p. 3, in place of “with.” Wherein also it is proved that the word “and” has the same force as “with.”
sources.answer: Like "and", "with" shows the distinction of the hypostases, as in "I and my Father are one". One cannot be "with" oneself, so saying the Son is with the Father exhibits two distinct hypostases. At the same time it shows that their fellowship cannot be separated.
sources.quote: For to say that the Son is with the Father is to exhibit at once the distinction of the hypostases, and the inseparability of the fellowship.
sources.raw_question: How does speaking of the Son as "with" the Father refute Sabellius's denial of distinct persons?

question: Is the Son of God the creator of the whole world, and thus infinitely greater than creation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. The heavens, earth and supramundane nature are the true works of Him who sojourned in the flesh, and the Maker of all things created by the fiat of His will is infinitely greater than all. Hence no account, still less a human one, can contain all that might be said of the Lord of Creation.
sources.quote: learn that these are the true works of Him Who sojourned for thee in the flesh,
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God the creator of the whole world, and thus infinitely greater than creation?

question: How can the coming of the Holy Spirit be described in John 14 as the coming of the Son, and even of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Because the three Persons, though distinct, are also one. The oneness of the three is kept so firmly in view that the coming of 'another Advocate' is spoken of without embarrassment as Christ's own coming (vv. 18-21) and as the coming of Father and Son (v. 23). When the Spirit comes, Christ comes in Him, and with Christ the Father comes too. Both the distinction and the identity among the Persons must be allowed for.
sources.quote: There is a sense, then, in which, when Christ goes away, the Spirit comes in His stead; there is also a sense in which, when the Spirit comes, Christ comes in Him; and with Christ’s coming the Father comes too.
sources.raw_question: How can the coming of the Holy Spirit be described in John 14 as the coming of the Son, and even of the Father and the Son?

question: Does the Spirit's receiving His whole commission from the Son (John 16) take away from the Father?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. In John 16 the Spirit is sent by the Son to complete and apply the Son's work, and He takes of the Son's things, which parallels the Son's relation to the Father. This is no derogation of the Father, because all that the Father has belongs to the Son. To speak of the things of the Son is therefore to speak of the things of the Father.
sources.quote: receiving His whole commission from the Son – not, however, in derogation of the Father, because when we speak of the things of the Son, that is to speak of the things of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit's receiving His whole commission from the Son (John 16) take away from the Father?

question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity weakened as a biblical doctrine because Jesus' discourses in John presuppose it rather than formally state it?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The doctrine is not formulated in these discourses, but it is presupposed throughout them. In terms of probative force, being presupposed is even better than being formulated. The reader is kept in continual contact with three Persons who each act as distinct persons and yet are, in a deep underlying sense, one.
sources.quote: it certainly is presupposed in them, and that is, considered from the point of view of their probative force, even better.
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine of the Trinity weakened as a biblical doctrine because Jesus' discourses in John presuppose it rather than formally state it?

question: Does the Spirit promised in John 14:17 refer to the Spirit as sanctifier or as comforter?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: As comforter. The close of the verse shows this, because the Spirit is said already to be in the disciples at the very time he is promised to them. He was in them as the Spirit of quickening and sanctification while being promised to them as the Spirit of comfort.
sources.quote: He was in them as a Spirit of quickening and sanctification when promised to them as a Spirit of comfort and consolation, to abide with them for that purpose.
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit promised in John 14:17 refer to the Spirit as sanctifier or as comforter?

question: Who is the Comforter whom Christ promises to send in John 16:7?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: The Comforter is the Holy Ghost. Christ had already declared him in John 15:26 to be 'the Spirit of truth,' that is, the Holy Ghost, who reveals all truth to the sons of men.
sources.quote: He is Πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας, "the Spirit of truth;" that is, the Holy Ghost, who revealeth all truth to the sons of men.
sources.raw_question: Who is the Comforter whom Christ promises to send in John 16:7?

question: Does the Gospel of John's statement 'the Spirit is God' refer to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter X. The Divinity of the Holy Spirit is supported by a passage of St. John. This passage was, indeed, erased by heretics, but it is a vain attempt, since their faithlessness could thereby more easily be convicted. The order of the context is considered in order that this passage may be shown to refer to the Spirit. He is born of the Spirit who is born again of the same Spirit, of Whom Christ Himself is believed to have been born and born again. Again, the Godhead of the Spirit is inferred from two testimonies of St. John; and lastly, it is explained how the Spirit, the water, and the blood are called witnesses.
sources.answer: Yes. The same Evangelist shows elsewhere that he writes of the Holy Spirit, as in 1 John where the Spirit bears witness and is truth. So the passage on being born of the Spirit and the statement that the Spirit is God together show that the Holy Spirit is God.
sources.quote: since one ought not to doubt that “that which is born of the Spirit” is written of the Holy Spirit; there is no doubt but that the Holy Spirit also is God, according to that which is written, “the Spirit is God.”
sources.raw_question: Does the Gospel of John's statement 'the Spirit is God' refer to the Holy Spirit?

question: Is unity of authority the same thing as unity of Godhead?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. They are distinct things: God and his angels share one authority, yet that does not make the angels Gods, nor would there still be only one God if they were. Unity of Godhead between Father and Son rests on unity of substance and origin, not merely shared government.
sources.quote: Unity of authority, and unity of Godhead, are, with Tertullian, distinct things, however you may please to confound them: God and his angels have, according to him, one authority; but he does not therefore say, that the angels are Gods
sources.raw_question: Is unity of authority the same thing as unity of Godhead?

question: Does confessing the eternity of the Son make his birth from the Father impossible?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The Church confesses the Father as eternal and without beginning, and the Son as having his beginning from eternity. The Son is not unoriginated or self-originated, but receives his birth from the eternity of the Father who is unbegotten from everlasting. Eternity and birth are therefore compatible.
sources.quote: She confesses the Father eternal and without beginning; she confesses also that the Son’s beginning is from eternity. Not that He has no beginning, but that He is Son of the Father Who has none
sources.raw_question: Does confessing the eternity of the Son make his birth from the Father impossible?

question: Where does a 'word' appear in the trinity of the mind, as an analogy for the Son as Word?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How a Trinity is Produced by the Mind Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself.
sources.answer: A word arises when the mind is turned to itself by thought. It is formed from thought itself, with will uniting the remembering mind and the word. In this way a trinity emerges in which a word can now be discerned, which makes it a closer image of God.
sources.quote: when it is turned to itself by thought, there arises a trinity, in which now at length we can discern also a word; since it is formed from thought itself, will uniting both.
sources.raw_question: Where does a 'word' appear in the trinity of the mind, as an analogy for the Son as Word?

question: When 1 Corinthians 1:24 calls Christ "the wisdom of God," does it refer to him as the essential, eternal Wisdom of the Father or to him as crucified?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It refers to Christ as crucified, not to his essential Wisdom as the eternal Son. Owen grants that the Son is called Wisdom in his eternal character in Proverbs 8:22-23. In 1 Corinthians 1, however, the context (verse 23) shows Paul means Christ crucified. In him God sets forth all the wisdom by which he manifests himself and saves sinners.
sources.quote: not the essential Wisdom of God, as he is the eternal Son of the Father (upon which account he is called “Wisdom” in the Proverbs, chap. viii. 22, 23); but as he is crucified, verse 23.
sources.raw_question: When 1 Corinthians 1:24 calls Christ "the wisdom of God," does it refer to him as the essential, eternal Wisdom of the Father or to him as crucified?

question: Can human beings come to know God by themselves, or only through God's Word?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter V.—The author returns to his former argument, and shows that there was but one God announced by the law and prophets, whom Christ confesses as His Father, and who, through His word, one living God with Him, made Himself known to men in both covenants.
sources.answer: Only through God's Word. Since it was impossible, without God, to come to a knowledge of God, God teaches men through His Word to know Him. His self-declarations in the prophets are therefore not boastful but instructive.
sources.quote: since it was impossible, without God, to come to a knowledge of God, He teaches men, through His Word, to know God.
sources.raw_question: Can human beings come to know God by themselves, or only through God's Word?

question: Can the mind conceive of anything prior to the Son's generation, such that the Father is more remote than the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: No. Thought is wholly impotent to go beyond the generation of the Lord; John confines the conception by 'In the beginning was the Word,' since thought cannot travel outside 'was' nor imagination beyond 'beginning.' Hence true religion teaches us to think of the Son together with the Father.
sources.quote: For thought cannot travel outside “was,” nor imagination beyond “beginning.”
sources.raw_question: Can the mind conceive of anything prior to the Son's generation, such that the Father is more remote than the Son?

question: Do the scriptural titles of Christ as power, wisdom, image and brightness of God show his equality of glory with the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Issue joined with those who assert that the Son is not with the Father, but after the Father. Also concerning the equal glory.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is the power and wisdom of God, the image of the invisible God, the brightness of his glory, and the one the Father sealed by engraving Himself on Him; these are proclamations of the majesty of the Only Begotten and the equality of his glory, as are 'He that hath seen me hath seen the Father' and 'honour the Son even as they honour the Father.'
sources.quote: Let them learn that “Christ is the power of God and wisdom of God,” and that “He is the image of the invisible God” and “brightness of his glory,”
sources.raw_question: Do the scriptural titles of Christ as power, wisdom, image and brightness of God show his equality of glory with the Father?

question: Does "the Word was God" teach that the Word is truly God and not something other than God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. John first says where the Word was, then with whom He was, and finally what He is. This Word, who was in the Beginning and with God, was not anything other than God but was Himself God. He is the one by whom all things were made, and He is life and true light.
sources.quote: For this Word, that was in the Beginning, and was with God, was not anything else besides God, but was also Himself God.
sources.raw_question: Does "the Word was God" teach that the Word is truly God and not something other than God?

question: What does John 5:26, 'As the Father hath life in Himself, so hath He given to the Son,' teach about the Son's eternity and likeness to the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: 'Hath given' signifies that the Son is not the Father. 'So' shows the Son's natural likeness and propriety to the Father. If the Son once lacked life, the Father once lacked it too, since the Son has it as the Father does. But it is irreligious to say the Father ever lacked it, so the Son has always had it, though from the Father.
sources.quote: Now from the words ‘Hath given,’ He signifies that He is not the Father; but in saying ‘so,’ He shews the Son’s natural likeness and propriety towards the Father. If then once the Father had not, plainly the Son once had not
sources.raw_question: What does John 5:26, 'As the Father hath life in Himself, so hath He given to the Son,' teach about the Son's eternity and likeness to the Father?

question: Can God's works or the bare letter of Scripture give a saving knowledge of God without Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. The knowledge of God gained from his works is weak and imperfect. The letter of the word, though it is light like the sun, does not save us because of our blindness, just as sunlight cannot help someone who has no eyes. Christ must give us an understanding and open our minds to understand the Scriptures.
sources.quote: as that knowledge of God which we have by his works is but very weak and imperfect, so that which we have by the word, the letter of it, by reason of our blindness, is not saving to us if we have no other help
sources.raw_question: Can God's works or the bare letter of Scripture give a saving knowledge of God without Christ?

question: Does the Son's calling Himself God make Him a rival to the Father who draws worship away from Him?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eighthly, John xvii. 3. and the Like. Our Lord's divinity cannot interfere with His Father's prerogatives, as the One God, which were so earnestly upheld by the Son. 'One' is used in contrast to false gods and idols, not to the Son, through whom the Father spoke. Our Lord adds His Name to the Father's, as included in Him. The Father the First, not as if the Son were not First too, but as Origin.
sources.answer: No. Unlike Absalom or Adonijah toward David, the Son glorified not Himself but the Father: He said none is good save one, God; cited 'the Lord our God is One Lord'; came to do the Father's will; and taught that whoever honours Him honours the Father. He who knows the Son knows and sees the Father in Him, so the Son leads to the Father rather than away.
sources.quote: if the Son on coming, glorified not Himself but the Father, saying to one who came to Him, ‘Why callest thou Me good? none is good save One, that is, God;’
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's calling Himself God make Him a rival to the Father who draws worship away from Him?

question: Is the fulness of grace and of the Spirit committed to Christ so that all grace is given out to believers from him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: Yes. Like Joseph over Egypt's granaries, Christ has been given charge of all the stores of the kingdom of heaven. The Father has gathered all things together under him as head, so that everything might be dispensed to the saints from him. All treasures and all fulness are in him, and he has the Spirit without measure.
sources.quote: as one in whom it hath pleased the Father to gather all things unto a head, Eph. i. 10, that from him all things might be dispensed unto them. All treasures, all fulness, the Spirit not by measure, are in him
sources.raw_question: Is the fulness of grace and of the Spirit committed to Christ so that all grace is given out to believers from him?

question: Is the flesh excluded from salvation, as the heretics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Preface.
sources.answer: No. The flesh is truly God's workmanship, and the Son of God carried out the whole dispensation of mercy on its behalf. Denying the salvation of the flesh goes together with blaspheming the Creator.
sources.quote: they blaspheme the Creator, and disallow the salvation of God’s workmanship, which the flesh truly is; on behalf of which I have proved, in a variety of ways, that the Son of God accomplished the whole dispensation
sources.raw_question: Is the flesh excluded from salvation, as the heretics claim?

question: If only the Father is unoriginate in the sense of 'having no father,' does it follow that the Son is a thing originated or a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: No. In this sense only the Father is unoriginate, but that does not make the Son originated. The Word is such as He is who begat Him. So the Image of the unoriginate God is not originated but an Offspring, His Word and Wisdom.
sources.quote: For to say that God is in this sense Unoriginate, does not shew that the Son is a thing originated, it being evident from the above proofs that the Word is such as He is who begat Him.
sources.raw_question: If only the Father is unoriginate in the sense of 'having no father,' does it follow that the Son is a thing originated or a creature?

question: Does the title 'Creator' properly belong to Christ?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. Since all things were created through the Lord Christ, Creator is His proper name and He holds both the reality and the title of creative power. Melchisedec, Hosea, and Peter all witness to God as Creator, and these are referred to the Son, so the name of the work should not be applied to its Maker.
sources.quote: For through the Lord Christ all things were created; and therefore it is His proper name that He should be the Creator.
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'Creator' properly belong to Christ?

question: Are the Word and the Spirit, once sent forth, reabsorbed into the Father, so that God alternates between forms?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VI. To those who object that according to the words of Amos the Spirit is created, the answer is made that the word is there understood of the wind, which is often created, which cannot be said of the Holy Spirit, since He is eternal, and cannot be dissolved in death, or by an heretical absorption into the Father. But if they pertinaciously contend that this passage was written of the Holy Spirit, St. Ambrose points out that recourse must be had to a spiritual Interpretation, for Christ by His coming established the thunder, that is, the force of the divine utterances, and by Spirit is signified the human soul as also the flesh assumed by Christ. And since this was created by each Person of the Trinity, it is thence argued that the Spirit, Who has before been affirmed to be the Creator of all things, was the Author of the Incarnation of the Lord.
sources.answer: No. This view fails to distinguish the Holy Spirit and makes God one being changing himself into various forms. Rather, the distinction of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit always abides unchangeably and preserves the unity of their power.
sources.quote: whereas the distinction between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit always abiding and unchangeable, preserves the Unity of its power.
sources.raw_question: Are the Word and the Spirit, once sent forth, reabsorbed into the Father, so that God alternates between forms?

question: Does the Old Testament direct the saving faith of believers toward the Son of God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. From the seed of the woman in Genesis to the Sun of righteousness in Malachi, the promises and prophecies fix the hopes of all mankind for salvation on him. Among these are Job's living Redeemer, the angel of the burning bush, and the Begotten Son and eternal Priest of the Psalms. They also include Isaiah's Emmanuel, named the Mighty God and Father of Eternity, and Jeremiah's Lord our righteousness.
sources.quote: on Him, from age to age the faith of every believer was fastened, by promise and by prophecy.
sources.raw_question: Does the Old Testament direct the saving faith of believers toward the Son of God?

question: Why does the Word preserve the Father's invisibility while still revealing God to men?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: He does both for man's good. He keeps the Father invisible so that man never comes to despise God and always has something toward which to advance. He reveals God through many dispensations so that man does not fall away from God entirely and cease to exist. The life of man consists in beholding God, and the revelation of the Father through the Word gives life to those who see him.
sources.quote: preserving at the same time the invisibility of the Father, lest man should at any time become a despiser of God, and that he should always possess something towards which he might advance
sources.raw_question: Why does the Word preserve the Father's invisibility while still revealing God to men?

question: Was the Father's nature affected when the Son assumed flesh?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The Father's nature, with which the Son was in natural unity, was not affected by the assumption of flesh. Only the Son, in respect of the humanity assumed in this temporal change, stood in need of being restored to the unity of the divine nature.
sources.quote: But the Father’s nature, with which He was in natural unity, was not affected by this assumption of flesh
sources.raw_question: Was the Father's nature affected when the Son assumed flesh?

question: What is the significance of Christ saying 'the glory which I had with Thee' rather than 'when I was with Thee' in John 17:5?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: 'When I was with Thee' would mean only dwelling beside the Father, but 'which I had with Thee' teaches the mystery of His nature, a shared possession of the Father's glory. Likewise 'Glorify Me with Thyself' differs from 'Glorify Me': He asks not for a separate glory of His own but to be glorified in unity with the Father.
sources.quote: When I was with Thee would signify, “when I dwelt by Thy side:” but which I had with Thee teaches the Mystery of His nature.
sources.raw_question: What is the significance of Christ saying 'the glory which I had with Thee' rather than 'when I was with Thee' in John 17:5?

question: Does "He that believeth on me, believeth not on me, but on Him that sent me" separate the Son from the Father or deny that the Son is an object of faith?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. It means that whoever believes on Christ does not believe on the visible creature he took, lest our hope rest in a creature. Instead he believes on the one who took that creature in order to cleanse our hearts by faith, so that we might see him as equal to the Father. Christ did not separate himself from the one who sent him. He meant that men should believe on him just as they believe on the Father, to whom he is equal.
sources.quote: He certainly did not mean Himself to be separated from the Father, that is, from Him that sent Him; but that men might so believe on Himself, as they believe on the Father, to whom He is equal.
sources.raw_question: Does "He that believeth on me, believeth not on me, but on Him that sent me" separate the Son from the Father or deny that the Son is an object of faith?

question: Is the Son the whole participation of the Father, so that to be wholly participated is the same as to beget?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Objection, that the Son's eternity makes Him coordinate with the Father, introduces the subject of His Divine Sonship, as a second proof of His eternity. The word Son is introduced in a secondary, but is to be understood in real sense. Since all things partake of the Father in partaking of the Son, He is the whole participation of the Father, that is, He is the Son by nature; for to be wholly participated is to beget.
sources.answer: Yes. What is from the Father's essence and proper to him is entirely the Son, and it is all one to say God is wholly participated and that he begets. Thus the Son partakes of nothing, while all creatures, partaking of the Son through the Spirit, are said to partake of God and the divine nature.
sources.quote: we are driven to say that what is from the essence of the Father, and proper to Him, is entirely the Son; for it is all one to say that God is wholly participated, and that He begets
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the whole participation of the Father, so that to be wholly participated is the same as to beget?

question: Can the Father be known by bypassing the Son and investigating the being of the Begetter directly?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His dictum that 'the manner of the likeness must follow the manner of the generation' is unintelligible.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius abandons knowledge from works and tries to rise to the supreme being directly, contradicting his own principle that beings are known from their works. Scripture teaches that no one approaches knowledge of the Father except through the Son.
sources.quote: ignoring the fact that it is not possible to approach to a knowledge of the Father except through the Son.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father be known by bypassing the Son and investigating the being of the Begetter directly?

question: Did the Son of God lose his eternity or his co-eternity with the Father by becoming the Son of man and taking a beginning in time?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Son of God Became Incarnate in Order that We Being Cleansed by Faith May Be Raised to the Unchangeable Truth.
sources.answer: No. The Truth, co-eternal with the Father, took a beginning from earth when the Son of God became the Son of man, yet he so undertook our mortality as not to lose his own eternity. He took up our faith and our temporal condition in order to lead us on to his own truth and eternity.
sources.quote: the Truth itself, co-eternal with the Father, took a beginning from earth, when the Son of God so came as to become the Son of man, and to take to Himself our faith, that He might thereby lead us on to His own truth, who so undertook our mortality, as not to lose His own eternity.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God lose his eternity or his co-eternity with the Father by becoming the Son of man and taking a beginning in time?

question: Is it one and the same God, acting through the Word, who revealed himself in both the Old Testament and the New?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XI.—The old prophets and righteous men knew beforehand of the advent of Christ, and earnestly desired to see and hear Him, He revealing himself in the Scriptures by the Holy Ghost, and without any change in Himself, enriching men day by day with benefits, but conferring them in greater abundance on later than on former generations.
sources.answer: Yes. The Scriptures testify of Christ only because all things were always revealed to believers by one and the same God through the Word. The Word at one time conversed with his creature, at another gave the law, reproved, exhorted, freed and adopted man, and at the proper time bestowed an incorruptible inheritance.
sources.quote: all things had ever been revealed and shown to believers by one and the same God through the Word; He at one time conferring with His creature, and at another propounding His law
sources.raw_question: Is it one and the same God, acting through the Word, who revealed himself in both the Old Testament and the New?

question: Did the Son at his coming reveal a different Father from the God proclaimed by the prophets?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XI.—The old prophets and righteous men knew beforehand of the advent of Christ, and earnestly desired to see and hear Him, He revealing himself in the Scriptures by the Holy Ghost, and without any change in Himself, enriching men day by day with benefits, but conferring them in greater abundance on later than on former generations.
sources.answer: No. The same person announced by the prophets, Jesus Christ, is the one who came. So the Father is the same one the prophets proclaimed, and the Son spread knowledge of the Father preached from the beginning, not of another Father. From this same Father he brought liberty to those who serve him.
sources.quote: it is plain that the Father also is Himself the same who was proclaimed by the prophets, and that the Son, on His coming, did not spread the knowledge of another Father, but of the same who was preached from the beginning
sources.raw_question: Did the Son at his coming reveal a different Father from the God proclaimed by the prophets?

question: Do texts such as "My Father is greater than I" and "the head of Christ is God" prove an eternal subordination of the Son to the Father within the Trinity?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No, they cannot safely be pressed that far. Several New Testament doctrines may fully explain these passages: the Son's humiliation for His earthly work, the Two Natures in His incarnate Person, and the Covenant of Redemption. This makes it extremely difficult to read them as statements about eternal relations. It is illegitimate to use them to impair the Son's complete identity with the Father in Being and complete equality in powers, which the New Testament everywhere presupposes.
sources.quote: the difficulty of interpreting subordinationist passages of eternal relations between the Father and Son becomes extreme.
sources.raw_question: Do texts such as "My Father is greater than I" and "the head of Christ is God" prove an eternal subordination of the Son to the Father within the Trinity?

question: If the Word of God were a work (creature), would He be among the works that God brings into judgment, and what does this show about His nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: Yes, if He were a work He would have to be judged, which is absurd, so He is not a work. Scripture says God will bring every work into judgment, yet the Son is not among those on trial but is Himself the Judge of all works. The Judge cannot be on trial nor the Lawgiver judged by law; hence it is clearer than the sun that the Son is the Father's Word, in whom all works come to be and come into judgment.
sources.quote: if God shall bring the works one and all into judgment, but the Son is not in the number of things put on trial, but rather is Himself the Judge of works one and all, is not the proof clearer than the sun, that the Son is not a work
sources.raw_question: If the Word of God were a work (creature), would He be among the works that God brings into judgment, and what does this show about His nature?

question: Must the mind come to know itself indirectly, as bodily eyes see themselves only in a mirror or as we picture absent people from report?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > That When the Mind Loves Itself, It is Not Unknown to Itself.
sources.answer: No. Nothing can be more present to the mind than itself, so it is absurd that it should know other minds and not itself. The analogy of eyes seeing themselves only in looking-glasses cannot be applied to the contemplation of incorporeal things. If it were true, the mind would never find itself.
sources.quote: For eyes can never see themselves except in looking-glasses; and it cannot be supposed in any way that anything of that kind can be applied also to the contemplation of incorporeal things, so that the mind should know itself, as it were, in a looking-glass.
sources.raw_question: Must the mind come to know itself indirectly, as bodily eyes see themselves only in a mirror or as we picture absent people from report?

question: If the Son suffered because his nature necessarily made him subject to passion, would humans owe him any gratitude for the Incarnation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He then again charges Eunomius with having learnt his term ἀγεννησία from the hieroglyphic writings, and from the Egyptian mythology and idolatry, and with bringing in Anubis, Osiris, and Isis to the creed of Christians, and shows that, considered as admitting His sufferings of necessity and not voluntarily, the Only-begotten is entitled to no gratitude from men: and that fire has none for its warmth, nor water for its fluidity, as they do not refer their results to self-determining power, but to necessity of nature.
sources.answer: No. Nobody gives thanks for what happens by necessity, however useful it is. We do not thank fire for its warmth or water for flowing downhill, because these follow from their natures. If the Son's benefit came from a natural compulsion rather than from his own authoritative and free power, Eunomius's view leaves him owed no thanks. Gregory treats this as a reductio of the view.
sources.quote: For we neither thank fire for its warmth nor water for its fluidity, as we refer these qualities to the necessity of their several natures
sources.raw_question: If the Son suffered because his nature necessarily made him subject to passion, would humans owe him any gratitude for the Incarnation?

question: Since all ordinary generation ceases at some end, must the generation of the Son of God also be bounded by a beginning and an end?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He further shows that the pretemporal generation of the Son is not the subject of influences drawn from ordinary and carnal generation, but is without beginning and without end, and not according to the fabrications constructed by Eunomius, in ignorance of His power, from the statements of Plato concerning the soul and from the sabbath rest of the Hebrews.
sources.answer: No. Beginning and end are limits of extension, and only things circumscribed quantitatively can begin or cease at a limit. The Divine Nature is without quantity and extension, hence without limit, and so infinite; it is idle to circumscribe the infinite by beginning and ending.
sources.quote: Now the Divine Nature is without extension, and, being without extension, it has no limit; and that which is limitless is infinite, and is spoken of accordingly. Thus it is idle to try to circumscribe the infinite by “beginning” and “ending”
sources.raw_question: Since all ordinary generation ceases at some end, must the generation of the Son of God also be bounded by a beginning and an end?

question: If God is indestructible by his very essence, does the Son lack this and the other divine attributes by essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Every attribute of God, such as justice, goodness, eternity, incapacity for evil and infinite perfection, belongs to the very essence of the Son as well. No divine virtue is acquired. All good springs from the divine nature and is seen in it.
sources.quote: what other conceivable attribute of God does not attach to the very essence of the Son, as justice, goodness, eternity, incapacity for evil, infinite perfection in all conceivable goodness?
sources.raw_question: If God is indestructible by his very essence, does the Son lack this and the other divine attributes by essence?

question: Do the Evangelists' words, such as "All things were made by Him," come from the Holy Spirit speaking through them?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter II. The words, “All things were made by Him,” are not a proof that the Holy Spirit is included amongst all things, since He was not made. For otherwise it could be proved by other passages that the Son, and even the Father Himself, must be numbered amongst all things, which would be similar irreverence.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord Himself said, "it will not be you that speak, but the Spirit of your Father that speaketh in you," showing that the Spirit of God spoke in the Evangelists. So when John wrote "All things were made by Him," it was the Spirit speaking. He said "all things were made," not that He Himself was among the things made.
sources.quote: although the Spirit of God speaking in John said: “All things were made by Him,” and said not we were all things which were made
sources.raw_question: Do the Evangelists' words, such as "All things were made by Him," come from the Holy Spirit speaking through them?

question: If each person is God and God subsists in three persons, does it follow that each person contains three persons or three Gods?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. The argument equivocates on 'God': in 'each person be God' the divine nature is meant, while in 'that God subsist' a singular person is meant. Stated properly, that the nature of God subsists in three persons, the inference that each person contains three persons is plainly absurd.
sources.quote: The collusion of this sophism consists in that expression, “be God” and “that God.” In the first place the nature of God is intended; in the latter, a singular person.
sources.raw_question: If each person is God and God subsists in three persons, does it follow that each person contains three persons or three Gods?

question: Can 'greater and less' among the divine Persons be understood in a material or quantitative sense?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. To do so would introduce quality, distance, weight, figure and all that makes up a body into the Divine Nature, and whatever is compound must also admit dissolution. It is monstrous to find a smaller and larger in what is sizeless and not concrete.
sources.quote: A teaching so monstrous, which dares to discover a smaller and a larger in what is sizeless and not concrete lands us in these and suchlike conclusions
sources.raw_question: Can 'greater and less' among the divine Persons be understood in a material or quantitative sense?

question: Can the true faith about God and Christ be known and kept without written Scriptures?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IV.—The truth is to be found nowhere else but in the Catholic Church, the sole depository of apostolical doctrine. Heresies are of recent formation, and cannot trace their origin up to the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. Many barbarian nations who believe in Christ have salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit, without paper or ink. They preserve the apostolic tradition, and that tradition guards them so firmly that they refuse even to listen to heretical teaching.
sources.quote: having salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit, without paper or ink, and, carefully preserving the ancient tradition
sources.raw_question: Can the true faith about God and Christ be known and kept without written Scriptures?

question: Is proving that the Word is not a 'work' (thing made) also a proof that he is not a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: Yes. To call something a work and to call it a creature are the same thing, so whatever shows the Word is no work equally shows that he is no creature. Athanasius therefore treats Proverbs 8:22 ('The Lord created me') as already answered in principle, though he examines it separately because the Arians constantly cite it.
sources.quote: For it is the same to say work or creature, so that the proof that He is no work is a proof also that He is no creature.
sources.raw_question: Is proving that the Word is not a 'work' (thing made) also a proof that he is not a creature?

question: Can the essence of the uncreated God be known by distinctive marks or attributes?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: No. The divine nature is above beginning and presents no marks of its inmost nature; it is known only through the impossibility of perceiving it. Its most special characteristic is that it is too high for any distinctive attribute, and it is known by faith alone.
sources.quote: It is above beginning, and presents no marks of its inmost nature: it is to be known of only in the impossibility of perceiving it. That indeed is its most special characteristic, that its nature is too high for any distinctive attribute.
sources.raw_question: Can the essence of the uncreated God be known by distinctive marks or attributes?

question: Should the Son and the Holy Spirit be placed among created things or above creation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: Above creation. Creation differs in essence from its Maker and lies within time and space. The Only-begotten and the Holy Spirit belong to the uncreated, pre-temporal existence, so they are not to be looked for in the creation but believed to be above it.
sources.quote: We have shewn, then, by what we have said that the Only-begotten and the Holy Spirit are not to be looked for in the creation but are to be believed above it
sources.raw_question: Should the Son and the Holy Spirit be placed among created things or above creation?

question: Is the God who created man and promised the earth to the fathers the same God who fulfils the promises of the kingdom of his Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXVI.—Men shall be actually raised: the world shall not be annihilated; but there shall be various mansions for the saints, according to the rank allotted to each individual. All things shall be subject to God the Father, and so shall He be all in all.
sources.answer: Yes. In creation, the promise to the fathers, the resurrection of the just and the kingdom, the same God the Father is shown. He fashioned man, frees creation from bondage, and fulfils the promises for his Son's kingdom.
sources.quote: the same God the Father is manifested, who fashioned man, and gave promise of the inheritance of the earth to the fathers, who brought it (the creature) forth [from bondage] at the resurrection of the just, and fulfils the promises for the kingdom of His Son
sources.raw_question: Is the God who created man and promised the earth to the fathers the same God who fulfils the promises of the kingdom of his Son?

question: Can any creature be equal or like to God in power?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. No creature or nature external to God is comparable to him in might, and comparing anything outside him to God insults his majesty. Only the Son, born from God himself, can without blasphemy be likened and equalled to him.
sources.quote: No creature is equal or like to God, no nature external to His is comparable in might to Him; it is only the Son, born from Himself, Whom we can without blasphemy liken and equal to Him.
sources.raw_question: Can any creature be equal or like to God in power?

question: Does Christ's human birth and bodily humility count against recognising him as God's Son by divine birth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The divinely born Son performs every divine work through the humanity he assumed, so the works themselves witness to his divine sonship. If people will not believe the Man, they should believe the works, which are plainly God's works done by the Son of God.
sources.quote: Why should the mystery of His human birth hinder our recognition of His birth as God, when He that is Divinely born fulfils every Divine task by the agency of that Manhood which He has assumed?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's human birth and bodily humility count against recognising him as God's Son by divine birth?

question: Is the Word who appeared in the incarnation the same Word of God who was at work before he was manifested?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: Yes. The spiritual interpreter always acknowledges the same Word of God, even though he has only now been manifested to us. The whole sequence of prophecy displays one continuous work of the Son of God across both covenants.
sources.quote: knowing always the same God, and always acknowledging the same Word of God, although He has [but] now been manifested to us
sources.raw_question: Is the Word who appeared in the incarnation the same Word of God who was at work before he was manifested?

question: If the Word went forth from the Father only temporarily and then withdrew back into him, would creation cease to exist?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Marcellian illustration from 1 Cor. xii. 4, refuted.
sources.answer: Yes, it would follow, and this shows the view is absurd. The Word came forth so that we might be created. If he withdrew back into the Father, he would be as he was before, and we would no longer exist, just as we did not exist then. Creation depends on the abiding, real existence of the Word.
sources.quote: for if the Word came forth that we might be created, and when He was come forth, we were, it is plain that when He retires into the Father, as they say, we shall be no longer.
sources.raw_question: If the Word went forth from the Father only temporarily and then withdrew back into him, would creation cease to exist?

question: Does the Son's being called the 'Angel of God' (as in the appearance to Hagar) imply a lower nature than the Father's?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. The title Angel, meaning Messenger, signifies his office, not his nature; the same being is also called God, which proves his nature truly divine. Scripture shows that titles like angel or minister describe function, as in 'Who maketh His angels spirits'.
sources.quote: the title of Angel informs us of His office, not of His nature.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being called the 'Angel of God' (as in the appearance to Hagar) imply a lower nature than the Father's?

question: Does the Son's being called "Only-begotten," with no brother begotten with Him, prove that the Holy Spirit is alien in essence from the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Scripture teaches that we should not call the Spirit the Son's brother. But it nowhere teaches that the Spirit is not homogeneous with the Son. Eunomius uses "Only-begotten" not to deny the Son brethren, since he elsewhere makes all creation His brethren. He uses it as a device to sever the Spirit from essential union with the Son. That is heretical knavery.
sources.quote: It is true that we learn from Holy Scripture not to speak of the Holy Ghost as brother of the Son: but that we are not to say that the Holy Ghost is homogeneous with the Son, is nowhere shown in the divine Scriptures.
