sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being called "Only-begotten," with no brother begotten with Him, prove that the Holy Spirit is alien in essence from the Son?

question: Must the Son, as the true Image of the Father, possess all the Father's attributes such as eternity, immortality, lordship and creatorship?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father is eternal, immortal, powerful, light, King, Lord and Creator, and these must all be in the Image if it is true that he who has seen the Son has seen the Father. If the Son were originate and not eternal, he would not be a true Image of the Father.
sources.quote: These attributes must be in the Image, to make it true that he ‘that hath seen’ the Son ‘hath seen the Father.’
sources.raw_question: Must the Son, as the true Image of the Father, possess all the Father's attributes such as eternity, immortality, lordship and creatorship?

question: Are human fathers and sons fathers and sons in the proper sense, as the divine Father and Son are?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: No. Among men the son becomes a father in his turn, so neither stays fixed in his character. A man is son of his father and father of his son. Only in the Godhead is the Father properly and always Father and the Son properly and always Son.
sources.quote: Thus it belongs to the Godhead alone, that the Father is properly father, and the Son properly son, and in Them, and Them only, does it hold that the Father is ever Father and the Son ever Son.
sources.raw_question: Are human fathers and sons fathers and sons in the proper sense, as the divine Father and Son are?

question: Is asking why the Son does not beget a son as reasonable as asking why the Father had no father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: The two questions stand or fall together, and both are impious. Whoever asks why the Son does not beget must also ask why the Father had no father. As the Father is ever Father and could never become Son, so the Son is ever Son and could never become Father.
sources.quote: he who asks why the Son is not to beget a son, must inquire why the Father had not a father. But both suppositions are unseemly and full of impiety.
sources.raw_question: Is asking why the Son does not beget a son as reasonable as asking why the Father had no father?

question: Is the Son's title to worship founded only on the mediatorial power given him after his resurrection?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: No. The divine Logos was always our King and God and had the same title to worship as the Father, though it was less clearly revealed. His enthronement after the resurrection only declared his dignity more solemnly and invested him as God-man with the authority he always had as God, adding the new title of Redeemer. His right to worship rests on his personal dignity and essential perfections.
sources.quote: his enthronization, after his resurrection, was nothing more than declaring the dignity of his person more solemnly, and investing him as ἢ Giod-man, in his whole person, with the same power and authority, which, as God, he always had
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's title to worship founded only on the mediatorial power given him after his resurrection?

question: How do the Father, Son and Holy Spirit each take part in bringing humanity to see God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Each has a distinct role in one work. God was seen prophetically through the Spirit, is seen adoptively through the Son, and will be seen paternally in the kingdom. The Spirit prepares man in the Son, the Son leads him to the Father, and the Father gives incorruption for eternal life.
sources.quote: the Spirit truly preparing man in the Son of God, and the Son leading him to the Father, while the Father, too, confers [upon him] incorruption for eternal life
sources.raw_question: How do the Father, Son and Holy Spirit each take part in bringing humanity to see God?

question: Can human learning and philosophy, such as that of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, bring a person to true spiritual knowledge of God without Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Whatever light learning uncovers is small, uncertain and contentious, and it cannot be made spiritual or ordered to living to God. The apostle says those who relied on it 'became fools,' and Socrates died sacrificing a cock to Asclepius. Christ alone is 'the true Light,' and no one has true light except what comes immediately from him; without him even the most learned remain natural men who do not perceive the things of God.
sources.quote: Jesus Christ alone is “the true Light,” that lighteth us, John i. 9. And there is not any that hath any true light, but what is immediately from him.
sources.raw_question: Can human learning and philosophy, such as that of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, bring a person to true spiritual knowledge of God without Christ?

question: Does Isaiah's saying 'I am the first... no God was before Me, and no God shall be after Me' show that there is no priority or posteriority within the Trinity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > The fifth book promises to speak of the words contained in the saying of the Apostle Peter, but delays their exposition. He discourses first of the creation, to the effect that, while nothing therein is deserving of worship, yet men, led astray by their ill-informed and feeble intelligence, and marvelling at its beauty, deified the several parts of the universe. And herein he excellently expounds the passage of Isaiah, “I am God, the first.”
sources.answer: Yes. Whatever comes after God is creation, and what is before God is nothing, which is not God. So the Divine Nature is one, continuous with itself and indivisible. Though it is declared in Trinity, nothing in it is older or more recent than anything else.
sources.quote: the Divine Nature is one, continuous with Itself and indiscerptible, not admitting in Itself priority and posteriority, though it be declared in Trinity
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah's saying 'I am the first... no God was before Me, and no God shall be after Me' show that there is no priority or posteriority within the Trinity?

question: If the Son is the speaker in Isaiah's 'none hath been before Me', does the verse prove the Son's eternity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > The fifth book promises to speak of the words contained in the saying of the Apostle Peter, but delays their exposition. He discourses first of the creation, to the effect that, while nothing therein is deserving of worship, yet men, led astray by their ill-informed and feeble intelligence, and marvelling at its beauty, deified the several parts of the universe. And herein he excellently expounds the passage of Isaiah, “I am God, the first.”
sources.answer: Yes. On that reading, 'None hath been before Me' clearly shows that the One contemplated 'in the Beginning' shares in the eternity of the Beginning. Either way the orthodox doctrine is upheld, and anything 'after' God is shown to be a creature.
sources.quote: the phrase, “None hath been before Me,” will be a clear intimation that He Whom we contemplate “in the Beginning” is apprehended together with the eternity of the Beginning
sources.raw_question: If the Son is the speaker in Isaiah's 'none hath been before Me', does the verse prove the Son's eternity?

question: Can those who say the Word of God is non-subsistent and the Son only a name consistently condemn those who say 'once the Son was not'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Arians date the Son's beginning earlier than Marcellus, &c.
sources.answer: No. Those who give the Son no real being at all are worse than those who at least grant him existence in time. By censuring the Arians they confess what they themselves deny, namely that the Son truly exists.
sources.quote: they who give Him no being at all, are angry with those who at least grant Him to be in time. Thus these also confess what they deny
sources.raw_question: Can those who say the Word of God is non-subsistent and the Son only a name consistently condemn those who say 'once the Son was not'?

question: Does Scripture's ascribing to the Holy Spirit the same grieving that it ascribes to the Lord God show that the Spirit shares one divine nature with the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VIII. The aforesaid unity is proved hereby, that as the Father is said to be grieved and tempted, so too the Son. The Son was also tempted in the wilderness, where a figure of the cross was set up in the brazen serpent: but the Apostle says that the Spirit also was there tempted. St. Ambrose infers from this that the Israelites were guided into the promised land by the same Spirit, and that His will and power are one with those of the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Ezekiel and David say the Lord, the Most High, was grieved by the people, while Isaiah and Paul say the Holy Spirit was grieved. Since the same offence is directed at God and at the Spirit, Scripture shows the unity of the Spirit with God.
sources.quote: Again, whereas Isaiah says of the Jews themselves: “But they believed not, but grieved the Holy Spirit;” David says of God: “They grieved the Most High in the desert, and tempted God in their hearts.”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's ascribing to the Holy Spirit the same grieving that it ascribes to the Lord God show that the Spirit shares one divine nature with the Father?

question: Does the created world offer any intimation of a Trinity in unity that counts against the claim that the doctrine is contrary to reason?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Learned men have shown by various instances that the works of creation present some expression and resemblance of a Trinity in unity. It is therefore most unreasonable to call contrary to reason what many objects of rational consideration in some measure present to our minds.
sources.quote: There is so great an intimation made of such an expression and resemblance of a Trinity in unity in the very works of the creation
sources.raw_question: Does the created world offer any intimation of a Trinity in unity that counts against the claim that the doctrine is contrary to reason?

question: Does every created thing bear some likeness of God, and is every likeness of God also an image of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > The Trinity of the Outer Man, or of External Vision, is Not an Image of God. The Likeness of God is Desired Even in Sins. In External Vision the Form of the Corporeal Thing is as It Were the Parent, Vision the Offspring; But the Will that Unites These Suggests the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Every thing that is good has some likeness of the supreme good, since God, being supremely good, made all things very good. But not every likeness is an image: only that is the image of God which is copied from Him in all points, between which and God no other nature is interposed.
sources.quote: No doubt every thing in the creatures which is in any way like God, is not also to be called His image; but that alone than which He Himself alone is higher.
sources.raw_question: Does every created thing bear some likeness of God, and is every likeness of God also an image of God?

question: Is the bodily object a true parent of the vision formed in the sense, so that the vision is a true offspring?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > The Trinity of the Outer Man, or of External Vision, is Not an Image of God. The Likeness of God is Desired Even in Sins. In External Vision the Form of the Corporeal Thing is as It Were the Parent, Vision the Offspring; But the Will that Unites These Suggests the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. The object is only a quasi-parent and the vision a quasi-offspring. The vision is not wholly born from the object, because something else, the sense of the seer, must be applied to the object for the vision to be formed.
sources.quote: But it is not a true parent; whence neither is that a true offspring; for it is not altogether born therefrom, since something else is applied to the bodily thing in order that it may be formed from it
sources.raw_question: Is the bodily object a true parent of the vision formed in the sense, so that the vision is a true offspring?

question: Does the humble, infant condition of Christ at his birth mean that he was not truly God or forfeited divine majesty?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The inward reality differs from the outward appearance: the Magi worship him, angels praise him, a star and the prophetic Spirit minister around him. Thus the glory of his Majesty is not forfeited when he assumes the lowliness of flesh; he is God with us, Emmanuel.
sources.quote: There are coarse swaddling clothes; God is being worshipped. The glory of His Majesty is not forfeited when He assumes the lowliness of flesh.
sources.raw_question: Does the humble, infant condition of Christ at his birth mean that he was not truly God or forfeited divine majesty?

question: How can Christ during his earthly life be recognized as both man and God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: He was man by virtue of the flesh he had taken, and God by the evidence of the works he did. Throughout his life in human form he performed the works of God, and his acts of power and healing show his deity.
sources.quote: He was man by virtue of the flesh He had taken, God by the evidence of the works He did.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ during his earthly life be recognized as both man and God?

question: Must the image of God in the human soul be something that endures forever rather than something transient?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > There is a Kind of Trinity in the Holding, Contemplating, and Loving of Faith Temporal, But One that Does Not Yet Attain to Being Properly an Image of God.
sources.answer: Yes. The soul's nature is immortal and never ceases to be from its creation. Its best possession, being made after the image of its Creator, cannot fail to endure along with that immortality. So the image must be sought in what will exist always, not in faith, which will pass away.
sources.quote: We must find then what may be fittingly called the image of God, not in the holding, contemplating, and loving that faith which will not exist always, but in that which will exist always.
sources.raw_question: Must the image of God in the human soul be something that endures forever rather than something transient?

question: Would the Son still share the unity of the divine nature if His works were not really His own but only prompted by the Father dwelling in Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. If His deeds were not His own and He were merely moved to act by the indwelling Father, He would not be in the unity of the divine nature. The Son's real agency, shown in doing what pleases the Father, is required for His natural unity with the Father, not opposed to it.
sources.quote: But He would not be in the unity of the divine nature, if the deeds which He does, and wherein He pleases, were not His own, and He were merely prompted to action by the Father abiding in Him.
sources.raw_question: Would the Son still share the unity of the divine nature if His works were not really His own but only prompted by the Father dwelling in Him?

question: Is God unchangeable while creatures are changeable?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Will of God is the Higher Cause of All Corporeal Change. This is Shown by an Example.
sources.answer: Yes. God is the chiefest and unchangeable good, 'in and of itself'. Creatures are changed by Him while He remains the same, as the Psalm sings: 'Thou shalt change them, and they shall be changed; but Thou art the same.'
sources.quote: For “in and of itself,” in that place, is understood of that chiefest and unchangeable good, which is God, and of His own wisdom and will.
sources.raw_question: Is God unchangeable while creatures are changeable?

question: How can the Trinity of three Persons be more indivisible than the human image, which is only one person?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Augustin Dwells Still Further on the Disparity Between the Trinity Which is in Man, and the Trinity Which is God. The Trinity is Now Seen Through a Glass by the Help of Faith, that It May Hereafter Be More Clearly Seen in the Promised Sight Face to Face.
sources.answer: In God the three are always and unchangeably equal in the nature of the Deity, with no time when it was not or was otherwise. In the human mind the three are not separated in place, yet they are unequal in magnitude. Memory, understanding or love may each exceed the others in different people. So the one-person image is more divided than the three-person Trinity, which Augustine calls ineffably wonderful.
sources.quote: For that [Trinity], in the nature of the Divinity, or perhaps better Deity, is that which it is, and is mutually and always unchangeably equal: and there was no time when it was not, or when it was otherwise
sources.raw_question: How can the Trinity of three Persons be more indivisible than the human image, which is only one person?

question: Will the human image of the Trinity, once healed and perfected by grace, become equal to the divine Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Augustin Dwells Still Further on the Disparity Between the Trinity Which is in Man, and the Trinity Which is God. The Trinity is Now Seen Through a Glass by the Help of Faith, that It May Hereafter Be More Clearly Seen in the Promised Sight Face to Face.
sources.answer: No. Even when memory, understanding and love are healed and mutually equal, the creature remains what has been changed by grace. It cannot be equalled to the Creator, who by nature cannot change.
sources.quote: not even then will that thing which by grace will not be changed, be made equal to that which by nature cannot change, because the creature cannot be equalled to the Creator
sources.raw_question: Will the human image of the Trinity, once healed and perfected by grace, become equal to the divine Trinity?

question: Do the divine attributes and offices Scripture ascribes to the Son (omnipresence, immutability, creation, final judgment) prove his deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture assigns to the Son equally with the Father that he is first and last, omnipresent, immutable, almighty, holy, Creator, Preserver, Governor, Searcher of hearts and final Judge. One possessing such properties and offices must be God, and since there are not two Gods, the Son is one with God.
sources.quote: Now, One possessing such properties and fulfilling such offices, must needs be God. But there are not two Gods. Therefore the Son is one with God, and is God.
sources.raw_question: Do the divine attributes and offices Scripture ascribes to the Son (omnipresence, immutability, creation, final judgment) prove his deity?

question: In what does communion with the person of Christ in the conjugal relation consist?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Partly in what Christ and the saints share and partly in what is proper to each. The whole of it falls under two heads. The first is a mutual resignation, or making over, of their persons one to the other, which is the first act of communion. The second is the mutual conjugal affections that follow from it.
sources.quote: The whole may be reduced unto these two heads:— [1.] A mutual resignation of themselves one to the other; [2.] Mutual, consequential, conjugal affections.
sources.raw_question: In what does communion with the person of Christ in the conjugal relation consist?

question: Is the Word of God something that was ever formable or formless before being formed, like a human mental word?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Our Word is Never to Be Equalled to the Divine Word, Not Even When We Shall Be Like God.
sources.answer: No. The divine Word is simple form, never formable, formless, formed, or reformed. It is eternal and unchangeable substance. A creature that is formable can at best be perfectly formed, but it can never equal that simplicity.
sources.quote: that simplicity wherein there is not anything formable, which has been formed or reformed, but only form; and which being neither formless nor formed, itself is eternal and unchangeable substance.
sources.raw_question: Is the Word of God something that was ever formable or formless before being formed, like a human mental word?

question: How do measure, number, and weight correspond to the elements of the trinity found in sense perception and memory?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Number, Weight, Measure.
sources.answer: Measure belongs to the memory and to the things from which visions are copied, since each has a fixed limit. Number belongs to the visions themselves, because one object yields many visions. Weight resembles the will, which unites and regulates these and draws desire toward its object. This triad reflects God, who has ordered all things in measure, number, and weight.
sources.quote: measure appears in the memory, number in the vision of things
sources.raw_question: How do measure, number, and weight correspond to the elements of the trinity found in sense perception and memory?

question: Do technical terms such as person, hypostasis, homoousios and perichoresis add new knowledge about the Trinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. They do not enlarge our views or add to our ideas. Their purpose is to fix and secure the plain fundamental truth that Father, Son and Holy Ghost are all strictly divine and uncreated, yet not three Gods but one God. The notion itself cannot be improved without new revelation.
sources.quote: The design of these terms is not to enlarge our views, or to add any thing to our stock of ideas; but to secure the plain fundamental truth, that Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are all strictly divine

sources.answer: Yes. Through the unity of their nature the Father is heard, manifested and possessed in the Son, who is the expression of the Father since He was sent from Him. Christ therefore makes no difference of nature between Himself and the Father.

sources.answer: No. On those principles the Son is a finite creature, so he can exercise divine power and dominion only partially. sources.answer: Yes, ordinarily. The mind keeps the power of distinguishing the bodily thing left outside from the image of it held within. The exception is when images are projected so that they seem to be perceived outside rather than thought within, as happens to people who are asleep, mad, or in a trance.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Hilary says the Arians borrow the opening words of the orthodox confession only as a semblance of truth. question: Is the God whom Christ proclaims an 'unknown God' who cannot be known at all?

sources.answer: No. Whatever is known even by a few is not unknown, and the Gnostics themselves claim to know him. sources.answer: No. The word God is taken sometimes essentially and sometimes personally. When one Person is called God, he is a divine Hypostasis having the Godhead. sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?

question: If the Son is the Maker of all intelligible being, is that intelligible being created or uncreated, and what follows for the Son's own nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > Eunomius again speaks of the Son as Lord and God, and Maker of all creation intelligible and sensible, having received from the Father the power and the commission for creation, being entrusted with the task of creation as if He were an artizan commissioned by some one hiring Him, and receiving His power of creation as a thing adventitious, ab extra, as a result of the power allotted to Him in accordance with such and such combinations and positions of the stars, as destiny decrees their lot in life to men at their nativity. Thus, passing by most of what Eunomius had written, he confutes his blasphemy that the Maker of all things came into being in like manner with the earth and with angels, and that the subsistence of the Only-begotten differs not at all from the genesis of all things, and reproaches Him with reverencing neither the Divine mystery nor the custom of the Church, nor following in his attempt to discover godliness any teacher of pious doctrine, but Manichæus, Colluthus, Arius, Aetius, and those like to them, supposing that Christianity in general is folly, and that the customs of the Church and the venerable sacraments are a jest, wherein he differs in nothing from the pagans, who borrowed from our doctrine the idea of a great God supreme over all. So, too, this new idolater preaches in the same fashion, and in particular that baptism is “into an artificer and creator,” not fearing the curse of those who cause addition or diminution to the Holy Scriptures. And he closes his book with showing him to be Antichrist.
sources.answer: Eunomius's claim leads to a dilemma. If the intelligible being the Son makes is uncreated, then he falsely ascribes to the Son the making of the uncreated Nature. If it is created and the Son belongs to intelligible being, then the Son becomes his own Maker. Unless the uncreated Son is set apart from the intelligible nature he creates, nothing remains to distinguish Creator from creature.
sources.quote: What does he suppose this “being” to be? created? or uncreated? For if he confesses Jesus to be Lord, God, and Maker of all intelligible being, it necessarily follows, if he says it is uncreated, that he speaks falsely, ascribing to the Son the making of the uncreated Nature.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is the Maker of all intelligible being, is that intelligible being created or uncreated, and what follows for the Son's own nature?

Thus, passing by most of what Eunomius had written, he confutes his blasphemy that the Maker of all things came into being in like manner with the earth and with angels, and that the subsistence of the Only-begotten differs not at all from the genesis of all things, and reproaches Him with reverencing neither the Divine mystery nor the custom of the Church, nor following in his attempt to discover godliness any teacher of pious doctrine, but Manichæus, Colluthus, Arius, Aetius, and those like to them, supposing that Christianity in general is folly, and that the customs of the Church and the venerable sacraments are a jest, wherein he differs in nothing from the pagans, who borrowed from our doctrine the idea of a great God supreme over all. So, too, this new idolater preaches in the same fashion, and in particular that baptism is “into an artificer and creator,” not fearing the curse of those who cause addition or diminution to the Holy Scriptures. sources.answer: No. To say the Son was 'entrusted' with creation by the Father makes him like Bezaleel, who was commissioned by Moses to build the tabernacle. It implies the Son's creative power was adventitious, so that before the commission he had neither the will nor the power to act. Such language degrades the Lord to a hired craftsman and is profane.

question: Does the Son come into being from non-existence in the same way that earth and angels did?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > Eunomius again speaks of the Son as Lord and God, and Maker of all creation intelligible and sensible, having received from the Father the power and the commission for creation, being entrusted with the task of creation as if He were an artizan commissioned by some one hiring Him, and receiving His power of creation as a thing adventitious, ab extra, as a result of the power allotted to Him in accordance with such and such combinations and positions of the stars, as destiny decrees their lot in life to men at their nativity. Thus, passing by most of what Eunomius had written, he confutes his blasphemy that the Maker of all things came into being in like manner with the earth and with angels, and that the subsistence of the Only-begotten differs not at all from the genesis of all things, and reproaches Him with reverencing neither the Divine mystery nor the custom of the Church, nor following in his attempt to discover godliness any teacher of pious doctrine, but Manichæus, Colluthus, Arius, Aetius, and those like to them, supposing that Christianity in general is folly, and that the customs of the Church and the venerable sacraments are a jest, wherein he differs in nothing from the pagans, who borrowed from our doctrine the idea of a great God supreme over all. So, too, this new idolater preaches in the same fashion, and in particular that baptism is “into an artificer and creator,” not fearing the curse of those who cause addition or diminution to the Holy Scriptures. And he closes his book with showing him to be Antichrist.
sources.answer: No. Applying the same description to earth, angels and the Maker of all is absurd. If the same thing is predicated of the earth and its Lord, one must either make a god of the earth or degrade the Lord to the earth's level. sources.quote: Surely if he thinks it fit to predicate the same of earth and its Lord, he must either make a god of the one, or degrade the other to a level with it.

question: Can there be a subordinate or inferior being that is properly God alongside the supreme God, as Christ is held to be on the Arian view?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland

sources.answer: No. Nothing can be properly God that is not supreme, since supremacy presupposes all the essential properties of the true God. An inferior God is God only improperly, by figure. question: Can the doctrine of the Trinity be called a Biblical doctrine even though the term "Trinity" and its technical definition do not appear in Scripture?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. The sense of Scripture is Scripture, and it is better to preserve the truth of Scripture than its words. The doctrine lies in Scripture "in solution," given in fragmentary allusions rather than formulated definition; assembling these into their organic unity is not departing from Scripture but entering more thoroughly into its meaning.
sources.quote: The doctrine of the Trinity lies in Scripture in solution; when it is crystallized from its solvent it does not cease to be Scriptural, but only comes into clearer view.

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The Trinity is incapable of proof from reason, and there are no analogies to it in nature, not even in man's spiritual nature made in God's image. In His trinitarian mode of being God is unique, so nothing in the universe can help us comprehend Him in this respect.
sources.quote: In His trinitarian mode of being, God is unique; and, as there is nothing in the universe like Him in this respect, so there is nothing which can help us to comprehend Him.
sources.raw_question: Are there analogies in nature or in the human soul that can prove or help us comprehend the Trinity?

question: Does Christ's promise of 'another Comforter', fulfilled at Pentecost, show that the Holy Spirit is distinct from the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. Within the same song the speaker is the God who is to be glorified by the angels of God, and that is God the Only-begotten. The Father and the Son are one God because no difference of nature separates the One from the One who is his offspring.
sources.quote: God is to be glorified by the Angels of God, and He says, For I am the Lord, and there is no God beside Me. For He is God the Only-begotten
sources.raw_question: Does the statement 'I am the Lord, and there is no God beside Me' in Moses' song exclude the Son from being God?

question: How can the Unoriginate Father and the Only-begotten Son each be unique and yet be one God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Each title is exclusive in its own character. 'Unoriginate' admits no sharer, and neither does 'Only-begotten', so each stands single and alone. Yet they are one God, because no gulf of difference of nature lies between the One and his offspring in the eternal Godhead.
sources.quote: And so They Two are One God, for between the One, and the One Who is His offspring there lies no gulf of difference of nature in the eternal Godhead.
sources.raw_question: How can the Unoriginate Father and the Only-begotten Son each be unique and yet be one God?

question: Does Moses' confession of one God teach that God dwells in solitude, as a single Person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The passages draw a definite line between the Unbegotten and the Begotten. They teach that angels and sons of God worship him who is God's Angel and Son, so we must not dream of God as solitary.
sources.quote: we are taught not to dream of God as dwelling in solitude, when angels and sons of God shall worship Him, Who is God’s Angel and His Son.
sources.raw_question: Does Moses' confession of one God teach that God dwells in solitude, as a single Person?

question: Does calling the Holy Spirit the 'oil of gladness' show that the Spirit cannot be classed among creatures?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IX. The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ, and the oil of gladness; and why Christ Himself is not the ointment, since He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It is not strange that the Spirit should be called Ointment, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. And there is no confusion between them, since Christ alone suffered death, Whose saving cross is then spoken of.
sources.answer: Yes. Oil by its nature will not mingle with other liquids but rises and separates, signifying that the Spirit cannot be mixed in with creatures. Corporeal things cannot be mingled with incorporeal, nor created with uncreated, so the attempts of heretics to rank the Spirit among creatures fail.
sources.quote: since of a truth corporeal things cannot be mingled with in corporeal, nor things created with uncreated?
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Holy Spirit the 'oil of gladness' show that the Spirit cannot be classed among creatures?

question: Why did the Son of God take on a human nature that He was not?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IX. The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ, and the oil of gladness; and why Christ Himself is not the ointment, since He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It is not strange that the Spirit should be called Ointment, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. And there is no confusion between them, since Christ alone suffered death, Whose saving cross is then spoken of.
sources.answer: He took on what He was not to hide what He was, so that He might be tempted in it and that human nature might be redeemed. Through what He was not He calls us to what He was, and on the cross in His flesh the temptations of our flesh die.
sources.quote: For He took on Him that which He was not that He might hide that which He was; He hid that which He was that He might be tempted in it, and that which He was not might be redeemed
sources.raw_question: Why did the Son of God take on a human nature that He was not?

question: Is God able to make mortal, corruptible bodies incorruptible and immortal, even though this goes beyond their nature?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIX.—Refutation of the views of the heretics as to the future destiny of the soul and body.
sources.answer: Yes. God is superior to nature. Because he is good, he is disposed to show kindness. Because he is mighty, he is able to do so. Because he is rich and perfect, he can fully carry out his purpose. So when he raises bodies that preserved righteousness, he will make them incorruptible.
sources.quote: For God is superior to nature, and has in Himself the disposition [to show kindness], because He is good; and the ability to do so, because He is mighty; and the faculty of fully carrying out His purpose, because He is rich and perfect.
sources.raw_question: Is God able to make mortal, corruptible bodies incorruptible and immortal, even though this goes beyond their nature?

question: When we call God Light, Strength, or Majesty, do these names declare God's very essence?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > God is Above All Things, Himself Containing All Things, Immense, Eternal, Transcending the Mind of Man; Inexplicable in Discourse, Loftier Than All Sublimity.
sources.answer: No. Such names describe His creature, His power, or His honour rather than Himself. Whatever we declare of Him unfolds some condition or power of His rather than God Himself; we best grasp what God is by recognizing that He cannot be understood in quality or quantity.
sources.quote: Whatever in any respect you might declare of Him, you would rather be unfolding some condition and power of His than Himself.
sources.raw_question: When we call God Light, Strength, or Majesty, do these names declare God's very essence?

question: Does the phrase 'God hath highly exalted Him' show that it was the Son and not the Father who became flesh?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says God exalted and gave to Him in order to show that it is not the Father who became flesh. Rather, it is the Father's Word who became man, who receives from the Father after the manner of men, and who is exalted by Him. The text therefore marks the distinction between Father and Son against any confusion of the Persons.
sources.quote: that herein moreover he may show that it is not the Father that hath become flesh, but it is His Word, who has become man, and receives after the manner of men from the Father, and is exalted by Him
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'God hath highly exalted Him' show that it was the Son and not the Father who became flesh?

question: Can the creative act in Genesis 1:27 be attributed to the Father alone, so as to deny the Son's role in creating man?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. It must be borne in mind that all things are through the Son. Heretical ingenuity may not twist the passage into an action of the Father alone, so it is the Son through whom man is made after the Father's image.
sources.quote: He must bear constantly in mind that all things are through the Son; heretical ingenuity must not, for its own purposes, twist this passage into action on the part of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Can the creative act in Genesis 1:27 be attributed to the Father alone, so as to deny the Son's role in creating man?

question: Can the Holy Spirit's abiding in believers show that He is eternal and unlike any creature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says God abides in us by the Spirit, and what abides always is unchanged, and what suffers no change is eternal. Creatures, by contrast, are liable to fault and therefore subject to change, and what is changeable cannot be eternal. So the Spirit has nothing in common with creatures, since He is eternal and every creature is temporal.
sources.quote: there cannot therefore be anything in common between the Spirit and the creature, because the Spirit is eternal, but every creature is temporal.
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit's abiding in believers show that He is eternal and unlike any creature?

question: Can the saying of Christ 'I in the Father and the Father in Me' be grasped at all by human understanding, given that it is beyond comprehension?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Yes, in a measure, by faith equipped with reason. Hilary holds that the saying is in itself beyond comprehension. Yet it is brought within the range of faith's understanding by considering the greatest instances of God's power. We may not doubt God's word about Himself, nor suppose that devout reason cannot apprehend His might.
sources.quote: neither may we doubt God’s Word concerning Himself, nor can we suppose that the devout reason is incapable of apprehending His might
sources.raw_question: Can the saying of Christ 'I in the Father and the Father in Me' be grasped at all by human understanding, given that it is beyond comprehension?

question: Is the true divine Sonship of Jesus Christ adequately attested, or is it open to dispute?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: It is fully attested, and Christ left no excuse for ignorance of it. Hilary proves it by the witness of the Father, by Christ's own assertion, by the preaching of the Apostles, and by the faith of believers. He adds the cries of devils, the contradiction of the Jews (which is itself a confession), and the recognition of the heathen.
sources.quote: that Divine Sonship of Jesus Christ, which is the object of their most strenuous denial, we prove by the witness of the Father, by Christ’s own assertion, by the preaching of Apostles, by the faith of believers
sources.raw_question: Is the true divine Sonship of Jesus Christ adequately attested, or is it open to dispute?

question: Is the Holy Spirit also the Lord of glory?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXII. In proof of the Unity in Trinity the passage of Isaiah which has been cited is considered, and it is shown that there is no difference as to its sense amongst those who expound it of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Spirit. If He Who was crucified was Lord of glory, so, too, is the Holy Spirit equal in all things to the Father and the Son, and the Arians will never be able to diminish His glory.
sources.answer: Yes. One is the vision, one the right to command, one the glory of Father, Son and Spirit. Moreover the Lord of glory who was crucified was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, so the Spirit cannot be denied that title.
sources.quote: One, then, is the vision, one the right to command, one the glory. Do we deny that the Holy Spirit is also the Lord of glory when the Lord of glory was crucified
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit also the Lord of glory?

question: Is the Son's obedience a necessity of His nature, such that He could not disobey even if He willed to?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: No. If the Son obeyed only because He was so constituted, like an instrument that can only trace the figure built into it, He would be below even humanity. Our souls are self-determining and choose freely, whereas such a Son would merely undergo obedience under a compulsory law of His nature. That notion is profane.
sources.quote: He on the contrary exercises, or rather experiences, obedience under the constraint of a compulsory law of His nature, while His nature suffers Him not to disobey, even if He would.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's obedience a necessity of His nature, such that He could not disobey even if He willed to?

question: Do Christ's words in the same discourse show that He is distinct from the Father rather than identical with Him?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Proves Also that the Words Spoken to Philip Make Nothing for the Sabellians.
sources.answer: Yes. In the same discourse Christ says He goes to the Father, will ask the Father to send another Comforter, and that "we" will come and abide. He also says the Father is greater than He, the Father is the husbandman, and the Father sent Him. Christ would never have added these things if He meant to be understood as the Father. They plainly attest that He is the Son, not the Father.
sources.quote: These things then, after the former, evidently attesting Him to be not the Father but the Son, the Lord would never have added, if He had had it in mind, either that He was the Father, or wished Himself to be understood as the Father
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's words in the same discourse show that He is distinct from the Father rather than identical with Him?

question: Does Scripture teach that there are other Words or Wisdoms of God besides the Son, with Christ as only the first of many created powers?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. Scripture's plural 'words' of God are precepts and commands spoken through the one true Word, and Christ himself distinguishes them from himself. They are not offspring, framers of the world, or images of God. Scripture testifies to one Word, Only-Begotten, made flesh, through whom all things were made. Other Wisdoms are an invention like the Manichees' second god, supported by neither work nor testimony.
sources.quote: For certainly such words are not offsprings or sons, nor are there so many words that frame the world, nor so many images of the One God, nor so many who have become men for us
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that there are other Words or Wisdoms of God besides the Son, with Christ as only the first of many created powers?

question: If the Son is Himself the Father's Will and Counsel, can He have come into being by a prior act of will or counsel?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. If He is Will Himself, it is unseemly to place counsel within Will, for then the Word would come into being in a word, the Son in a son, and Wisdom in a wisdom. Nothing was in the Father before the Word; rather, will is in the Word, and through Him the objects of will are carried into effect.
sources.quote: For the Son is the Father’s All; and nothing was in the Father before the Word; but in the Word is will also, and through Him the objects of will are carried into effect
sources.raw_question: If the Son is Himself the Father's Will and Counsel, can He have come into being by a prior act of will or counsel?

question: Did the Father make the Son, who is Truth, at a time when the Son did not exist?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. The Father is the fountain of light, truth and all good. He shed forth from himself the Only-begotten Light of truth, by which the glory of his Person is expressly imaged. So the claim that the Son was a later addition to God by way of creation is refuted at every point.
sources.quote: the Father of truth did not make the truth at a time when it was not; but, being the fountain of light and truth, and of all good, He shed forth from Himself that Only-begotten Light of truth
sources.raw_question: Did the Father make the Son, who is Truth, at a time when the Son did not exist?

question: Why are human affections such as suffering ascribed to the impassible Word at all, if they do not belong to his divine nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: Because the flesh he put on is truly his own body. The affections are proper to the flesh, and the flesh is proper to the Saviour. So they are rightly said of him, while he himself remains unchanged in his impassible nature.
sources.quote: in nature the Word Himself is impassible, and yet because of that flesh which He put on, these things are ascribed to Him, since they are proper to the flesh, and the body itself is proper to the Saviour.
sources.raw_question: Why are human affections such as suffering ascribed to the impassible Word at all, if they do not belong to his divine nature?

question: Can the Son, as proper Offspring of the Father's essence, be called a work out of nothing or said not to have existed before His generation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Objection, that the Son's eternity makes Him coordinate with the Father, introduces the subject of His Divine Sonship, as a second proof of His eternity. The word Son is introduced in a secondary, but is to be understood in real sense. Since all things partake of the Father in partaking of the Son, He is the whole participation of the Father, that is, He is the Son by nature; for to be wholly participated is to beget.
sources.answer: No. Since He is the Offspring proper to the Father's essence, it is perilous to call Him a work out of nothing or to say He was not before His generation. Whoever says this blasphemes the Father Himself, because he really thinks of the Father what he falsely imagines of His Offspring.
sources.quote: For he who thus speaks of that which is proper to the Father’s essence, already blasphemes the Father Himself; since he really thinks of Him what he falsely imagines of His offspring.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son, as proper Offspring of the Father's essence, be called a work out of nothing or said not to have existed before His generation?

question: In what sense is Christ called 'Mediator' in Scripture: is he a mediator of doctrines and of the Law, as Eunomius says, or a mediator between God and humanity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: Christ is the one mediator between God and humanity, not a mediator of doctrines or of the Law. Humanity had revolted, been enslaved to sin and alienated from the true Life. The Lord became man while remaining God, complete in both natures, and so united humanity indissolubly to God. Through the first-fruits he assumed, the whole lump of humanity is potentially united to God.
sources.quote: becomes Man while still remaining God, being both God and Man in the entirety of the two several natures, and thus humanity was indissolubly united to God, the Man that is in Christ conducting the work of mediation
sources.raw_question: In what sense is Christ called 'Mediator' in Scripture: is he a mediator of doctrines and of the Law, as Eunomius says, or a mediator between God and humanity?

question: In what sense can the Son rightly be said to be 'like' the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: He is like the Father in the way Seth was like Adam, who begat a son in his own likeness and image. In that kind of likeness the two are not different in nature. The impress and type imply a community of nature, so this sense of likeness is acceptable.
sources.quote: For in this case the nature of the two objects which are alike is not different, and the impress and type imply community of nature.
sources.raw_question: In what sense can the Son rightly be said to be 'like' the Father?

question: Can there be any medium (such as a voice or air) between God the Father and the Son through which the Father's speech reaches the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Any medium would have to be either created or uncreated; it cannot be created because the Word existed before creation, and it cannot be uncreated because apart from the Divine nature nothing is uncreate, the Only-begotten alone being generated and the Father alone ungenerate. Moreover a medium with its own nature would divide Father from Son. So truth obliges us to conclude there is no medium between them.
sources.quote: Generated we have learnt the Only-begotten (and Him alone) to be. Except the Father, none is ungenerate. Truth, therefore, obliges us to the conclusion that there is no medium between the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Can there be any medium (such as a voice or air) between God the Father and the Son through which the Father's speech reaches the Son?

question: Could the Father's spoken words before creation have been addressed to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The Holy Spirit, being God, needs no instruction by speech, for he searches all things, even the deep things of God. Since God needs not address himself, the Son needs no words, and creation did not yet exist, there was no audience for audible divine speech.
sources.quote: But neither does the Holy Spirit require instruction by speech, for being God, as saith the Apostle, He “searcheth all things, yea the deep things of God.”
sources.raw_question: Could the Father's spoken words before creation have been addressed to the Holy Spirit?

question: Did the Son of God begin to exist only from Mary, with 'the Word' meaning merely a spoken voice?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. Hilary rejects Hebion's teaching that Christ was first man and then God. The Virgin received into herself One already existing, Who was in the beginning God the Word dwelling with God. The Word is the nature of the pre-existent Only-begotten God, not just the sound of an uplifted voice.
sources.quote: declares that the Virgin did not receive into herself One previously existent, Who had been in the beginning God the Word dwelling with God
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God begin to exist only from Mary, with 'the Word' meaning merely a spoken voice?

question: Is Christ fully God, possessing the whole fulness of the Godhead?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says in Him dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily; and since this fulness is in Christ, our being raised in Him reveals the Father joining to raise us in Him. Therefore we must confess Christ Jesus is none other than God in all the fulness of the Deity.
sources.quote: we must confess that Christ Jesus is none other than God in all the fulness of the Deity
sources.raw_question: Is Christ fully God, possessing the whole fulness of the Godhead?

question: Does each Person of the Trinity possess only a part of the divine essence?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. The divine essence is indivisible. Each of the Three therefore possesses not a part or portion of it but the whole fullness of the essential Godhead. Together, in a unity of nature, they are one eternal Jehovah.
sources.quote: as this essence must be indivisible, each of them must possess not a part or portion of it, but the, whole fullness or perfection of the essential Godhead
sources.raw_question: Does each Person of the Trinity possess only a part of the divine essence?

question: Does calling the Son an emanation from the Omnipotent mean that the Son is not himself omnipotent?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: No. Shortly afterward the same text says of Wisdom, 'being but one, she can do all things.' Whoever can do all things is omnipotent, so the Son who issues from the Almighty is himself almighty.
sources.quote: for soon after it is said of it, “And being but one, she can do all things.” But who is omnipotent, unless He who can do all things?
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Son an emanation from the Omnipotent mean that the Son is not himself omnipotent?

question: Does the fact that salvation comes through baptism in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit require believers to keep confessing the Spirit as undivided from the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who say that it is not right to rank the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. We are saved by rebirth through the grace of baptism, and that salvation is established through the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. To give up the form of teaching received at baptism would move us further from salvation and break the confession we made. So the Spirit must be kept undivided from the Father and the Son, both in the confession of faith and in worship.
sources.quote: after recognising that this salvation is established through the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost, shall we fling away “that form of doctrine” which we received?
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that salvation comes through baptism in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit require believers to keep confessing the Spirit as undivided from the Father and the Son?

question: Must doctrine about the Holy Spirit be proven by written Scripture alone, or does the unwritten tradition of the Fathers also carry authority?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who say that it is not right to rank the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: The unwritten tradition also carries authority. Basil faults his opponents for demanding written proof while dismissing the Fathers' unwritten tradition as worthless. He sees this as an attempt to overturn apostolic tradition and so undermine the foundation of faith in Christ.
sources.quote: they clamour for written proof, and reject as worthless the unwritten tradition of the Fathers.
sources.raw_question: Must doctrine about the Holy Spirit be proven by written Scripture alone, or does the unwritten tradition of the Fathers also carry authority?

question: Is the belief that the Father and the Son together are one God a late invention of the Scholastic writers?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. Waterland says that the so-called Scholastic writers are as old as Tertullian, Irenaeus and Athenagoras, which reaches back almost to the middle of the second century. From that time onward the Father and the Son were called, and believed to be, one God. This is the Catholic doctrine, which has held for at least fifteen centuries.
sources.quote: The reader should be told, that those Scholastic writers are as old as Tertullian, Ireneeus, or Athenagoras; which brings it up almost to the middle of the second century.
sources.raw_question: Is the belief that the Father and the Son together are one God a late invention of the Scholastic writers?

question: Is the lower, active kind of knowledge (scientia), considered apart from contemplative wisdom, properly an image of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Concerning the Word of the Mind, in Which We See the Word of God, as in a Glass and an Enigma.
sources.answer: No. Wisdom and knowledge together belong to one mind and together form one image of God. When the lower, active knowledge is treated separately it is not to be called an image of God, although some likeness of the Trinity can still be found in it.
sources.quote: But when we treat of the lower of the two distinctly and separately, then it is not to be called an image of God, although even then, too, some likeness of that Trinity may be found in it
sources.raw_question: Is the lower, active kind of knowledge (scientia), considered apart from contemplative wisdom, properly an image of God?

question: What does it mean that God 'hath glorified Him in Himself' (John 13:32), and does it show that Christ is true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes, it shows that Christ is very God. The Father does not glorify Himself. Rather, He glorifies in Himself the God who was glorified in man, taking the nature He glorifies into the glory of His own nature. Because He glorifies Christ in Himself, Christ is not outside Him. This proves that the God whom He glorifies is in Him.
sources.quote: since the God, Who glorifies the God glorified in man, glorifies Him in Himself, He proves that the God Whom He glorifies is in Himself, for He glorifies Him in Himself
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that God 'hath glorified Him in Himself' (John 13:32), and does it show that Christ is true God?

question: In Christ's glorification, is the assumed servant's form taken into the form and glory of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. The servant's form He assumed is in turn assumed into the form of God. The Father restores to Christ, in Himself, the glory which He had with Him before He emptied Himself. Christ is thus united with God's self both in the form of the servant and in the nature belonging to His divine birth.
sources.quote: now that the servant’s form, which He assumed, is in turn assumed into the form of God, God Who is glorified in man is glorified in Himself
sources.raw_question: In Christ's glorification, is the assumed servant's form taken into the form and glory of God?

question: In what sense can Christ say 'The Lord created me' if believers are created in Him?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: Because believers are created in Him and bear in His body the 'one new man,' He who bears them in Himself is spoken of as if Himself created. Just as He is called infirm, sin, and a curse for bearing our infirmities and sins without being so Himself, so by creating us in Him He may say 'He created me' though not a creature.
sources.quote: But if in Him the twain are created, and these are in His body, reasonably then, bearing the twain in Himself, He is as if Himself created; for those who were created in Himself He made one, and He was in them, as they.
sources.raw_question: In what sense can Christ say 'The Lord created me' if believers are created in Him?

question: Does Christ's coming "in the glory of the Father" at the Judgment show that the Son shares the Father's nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. Different glories indicate different natures, as with the sun and the moon, whose glories differ because their natures differ. When the Son says He will appear in the Father's own glory, that identity of glory shows that Father and Son have a common nature.
sources.quote: so He Who foretold of Himself that He would appear in the glory of the Father indicated by the identity of glory their community of nature
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's coming "in the glory of the Father" at the Judgment show that the Son shares the Father's nature?

question: Is it legitimate to reason about God by means of human language and comparisons taken from visible things?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter III. The same Unity may also be recognized from the fact that the Spirit is called Finger, and the Son Right Hand; for the understanding of divine things is assisted by the usage of human language. The tables of the law were written by this Finger, and they were afterwards broken, and the reason. Lastly, Christ wrote with the same Finger; yet we must not admit any inferiority in the Spirit from this bodily comparison.
sources.answer: Yes, within limits. It is often convenient to estimate things above us from our own words, and to infer invisible things from visible ones. The Apostle says the invisible things of God are understood through the things that are made. But divine things must not be compared carnally with bodily things.
sources.quote: For oftentimes it is convenient to estimate from our own words those things which are above us, and because we cannot see those things we draw inferences from those which we can see.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to reason about God by means of human language and comparisons taken from visible things?

question: Is the Holy Spirit's glorifying of Christ the same as the glory that creatures give to God?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: No. Glory given from outside is twofold: servile glory, as a servant honours his master, which creatures give; and intimate glory, as a son honours his father, which the Spirit gives. The Spirit glorifies Christ as Spirit of truth and wisdom, showing the truth in Himself. As Paraclete He manifests in His own dignity the majesty of Him from whom He proceeded.
sources.quote: Of these two the one, the servile, is given by the creature; the other, which may be called the intimate, is fulfilled by the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit's glorifying of Christ the same as the glory that creatures give to God?

question: Why does Scripture speak of the Father's and the Son's love for believers but never of the Holy Spirit's love for the Father, the Son, or the saints?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Because the Holy Spirit is Himself the love of the Father and the Son. Christ promises that He and the Father will love believers without mentioning the Holy Ghost, since the Spirit is that love. For the same reason Scripture never says the Spirit loves the Father or the Son, or that they love the Spirit.
sources.quote: Christ promises that He and the Father will love believers (John 14:21,23), but no mention is made of the Holy Ghost, and the love of Christ and the love of the Father are often distinctly mentioned, but never any mention of the Holy Ghost's love.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture speak of the Father's and the Son's love for believers but never of the Holy Spirit's love for the Father, the Son, or the saints?
