question: How should the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each be understood as subsisting within the one Godhead?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: The Father is the Deity subsisting in the prime, unoriginated and most absolute manner, the Deity in its direct existence. The Son is the Deity generated by God's understanding, that is, by God's idea of Himself, and subsisting in that idea. The Holy Spirit is the Deity subsisting in act, the divine essence flowing out and breathed forth in God's infinite love to and delight in Himself. The whole divine essence truly subsists in both the divine idea and the divine love, so these are properly distinct Persons.
sources.quote: The Son is the Deity generated by God's understanding, or having an idea of Himself and subsisting in that idea. The Holy Ghost is the Deity subsisting in act, or the Divine essence flowing out and breathed forth in God's Infinite love to and delight in Himself.
sources.raw_question: How should the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each be understood as subsisting within the one Godhead?

question: Does the mutual indwelling Christ describes between Himself and the Father ('I am in the Father and the Father in me') apply to all three Persons of the Trinity?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. There is such an ineffable union among the Persons that each is in the others, has communion in the others, and is as it were predicable of the others. So the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, the Holy Ghost is in the Father and the Father in the Holy Ghost, and the Holy Ghost is in the Son and the Son in the Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: they are, after an ineffable and inconceivable manner, One in Another, so that One hath Another and they have communion in One Another and are as it were predicable One of Another
sources.raw_question: Does the mutual indwelling Christ describes between Himself and the Father ('I am in the Father and the Father in me') apply to all three Persons of the Trinity?

question: Does Christ's taking on human nature and its weaknesses prove that His divinity is inferior?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. He who was in the form of God took the form of a servant. The servant's form must not be used to dishonour the form of God, which includes the fulness of divinity. Instead one must distinguish the occasions and mysteries of the Incarnation. As begotten of God He had divine omnipotence, and as born of the Virgin He had a complete humanity, so He remained in the nature of God while abiding in a real body.
sources.quote: As begotten of God He possessed the nature of divine omnipotence, as born of the Virgin He had a perfect and entire humanity. Though He had a real body, He subsisted in the nature of God
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's taking on human nature and its weaknesses prove that His divinity is inferior?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's sanctifying work rest on a righteousness of our own?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit's whole work of preparing and enabling us for obedience is done in opposition to any righteousness of our own, whether preceding obedience or made up by it.
sources.quote: And this he doth in opposition to a righteousness of our own, either before it or to be made up by it, Tit. iii. 5.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's sanctifying work rest on a righteousness of our own?

question: In his sacrifice, did Christ offer only his body, or his whole human nature including his soul?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: His whole human nature. The body prepared for him, which he offered, stands for his entire humanity, because Scripture says his soul was also made an offering for sin. This is why he is said to offer himself, and he did so willingly, having the law of this obedience written in his heart.
sources.quote: And that body he offered, Heb. x. 10; — that is, his whole human nature; for “his soul” also was made “an offering for sin,” Isa. liii. 10
sources.raw_question: In his sacrifice, did Christ offer only his body, or his whole human nature including his soul?

question: What follows for the Holy Spirit if, as Eunomius teaches, the Spirit is formed by a second energy that follows the Son, who was himself produced by an energy?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in assuming, to account for the existence of the Only-Begotten, an 'energy' that produced Christ's Person.
sources.answer: The Spirit's real existence is lost too. If the first energy is unreal, its product the Son is unreal, and the second energy that follows this product, together with the Spirit it forms, is still further removed from reality. The Spirit then descends from a lineage of unrealities. The doctrine thus amounts to denying that anything really exists after the Ingenerate God, reducing the Son and Spirit to shadowy fictions without any actual subsistence.
sources.quote: it consists in nothing less than in denying that after the Ingenerate God there is any real existence: and their doctrine advances into shadowy and unsubstantial fictions, where there is no foundation of any actual subsistence.
sources.raw_question: What follows for the Holy Spirit if, as Eunomius teaches, the Spirit is formed by a second energy that follows the Son, who was himself produced by an energy?

question: Could anyone other than the Word of God reveal the things of the Father to humanity?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter I.—Christ alone is able to teach divine things, and to redeem us: He, the same, took flesh of the Virgin Mary, not merely in appearance, but actually, by the operation of the Holy Spirit, in order to renovate us. Strictures on the conceits of Valentinus and Ebion.
sources.answer: No. Only the Father's own proper Word has the power to reveal the things of the Father, for no other being has known the mind of the Lord or been his counsellor. Moreover, we could learn only by the Word becoming man, so that we might see and hear our Teacher and imitate him.
sources.quote: For no other being had the power of revealing to us the things of the Father, except His own proper Word. For what other person “knew the mind of the Lord,” or who else “has become His counsellor?”
sources.raw_question: Could anyone other than the Word of God reveal the things of the Father to humanity?

question: What are the respective roles of the Spirit and of the incarnate Word in uniting God and man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter I.—Christ alone is able to teach divine things, and to redeem us: He, the same, took flesh of the Virgin Mary, not merely in appearance, but actually, by the operation of the Holy Spirit, in order to renovate us. Strictures on the conceits of Valentinus and Ebion.
sources.answer: The Lord poured out the Spirit of the Father for the union and communion of God and man. Through the Spirit he imparts God to men, and through his own incarnation he attaches man to God. In this way he bestows immortality through communion with God.
sources.quote: has also poured out the Spirit of the Father for the union and communion of God and man, imparting indeed God to men by means of the Spirit, and, on the other hand, attaching man to God by His own incarnation
sources.raw_question: What are the respective roles of the Spirit and of the incarnate Word in uniting God and man?

question: Did Christ appear as a man only in seeming, as the Docetists and Valentinians claimed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter I.—Christ alone is able to teach divine things, and to redeem us: He, the same, took flesh of the Virgin Mary, not merely in appearance, but actually, by the operation of the Holy Spirit, in order to renovate us. Strictures on the conceits of Valentinus and Ebion.
sources.answer: No. If he only seemed to be a man, the invisible Spirit could not truly have rested upon him, and there would be no truth in him. His appearance would also be only a prophetic vision, so his real advent would still be awaited. He must truly have had flesh and blood from Mary, summing up Adam's formation in himself, in order to redeem us.
sources.quote: But if He did appear as a man, when He was not a man, neither could the Holy Spirit have rested upon Him,—an occurrence which did actually take place—as the Spirit is invisible; nor, [in that case], was there any degree of truth in Him
sources.raw_question: Did Christ appear as a man only in seeming, as the Docetists and Valentinians claimed?

question: When God the Father is said to speak, does he speak by a temporal, audible word or by the co-eternal Word, the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of the Trinity by Itself is Wisdom. With What Difficulty, or in What Way, the Proposed Question is to Be Solved.
sources.answer: Properly, the Father speaks by the co-eternal Word whom he begat, by whom he always and unchangeably utters himself. That Word is not one that is uttered, sounds and passes away. God's words in time are produced in creatures and pass away, and they are set aside here. Because the Father speaks by this Word, in speaking he is understood not singly but together with the Word, without whom he does not speak.
sources.quote: by the Word which is equal to Himself, by whom He always and unchangeably utters Himself.
sources.raw_question: When God the Father is said to speak, does he speak by a temporal, audible word or by the co-eternal Word, the Son?

question: In what kind of being do differences of 'more and less' properly apply, and do they apply to the uncreated divine nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: Differences of more and less properly belong to the sensible world, where they consist in quantity, quality and other properties perceived by the bodily senses. In created intelligible beings, greater and less is measured only by how far each participates in the good. The uncreate intelligible nature is good in its own essence and simple, so it is far removed from such distinctions. Therefore greater and less cannot be ascribed to the divine Persons.
sources.quote: In the Sensible world, then, is found everything that we comprehend by our organs of bodily sense, and in which the differences of qualities involve the idea of more and less, such differences consisting in quantity, quality, and the other properties.
sources.raw_question: In what kind of being do differences of 'more and less' properly apply, and do they apply to the uncreated divine nature?

question: When Scripture speaks of the Holy Spirit as 'ours', does it mean the human spirit by which we exist?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Father and the Son the Only Beginning (Principium) of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. The human spirit by which we exist is the spirit of a man in him. The Holy Spirit is ours in another way, as something received so that we might be holy, just as we pray 'Give us this day our bread.' We received our own spirit so that we might be, and the Holy Spirit so that we might be holy.
sources.quote: But that is one thing, which we have received that we might be; another, that which we have received that we might be holy.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture speaks of the Holy Spirit as 'ours', does it mean the human spirit by which we exist?

question: What does it mean for the Son to 'see' the Father working?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > There is a Double Rule for Understanding the Scriptural Modes of Speech Concerning the Son of God. These Modes of Speech are of a Threefold Kind.
sources.answer: For the Son, being born of the Father is nothing else than seeing the Father. Seeing him work is nothing else than working with him. He does not work from himself because he is not from himself. His seeing is therefore his eternal generation, not an act of learning by observation.
sources.quote: For to be of the Father, that is, to be born of the Father, is to Him nothing else than to see the Father; and to see Him working, is nothing else than to work with Him
sources.raw_question: What does it mean for the Son to 'see' the Father working?

question: Is it legitimate to treat the Son's 'generation' as equivalent to 'making' or 'creation', as Arius does?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: No. Arius himself interprets generation as making, creation, or founding, which shows the formula is an Arian argument rather than a Catholic statement. To call One God and yet rank Him among creatures 'made' is incoherent; the Son is the Framer of things that have a beginning, His offspring and not a creature.
sources.quote: Who is there in all mankind, Greek or Barbarian, who ventures to rank among creatures One whom he confesses the while to be God
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to treat the Son's 'generation' as equivalent to 'making' or 'creation', as Arius does?

question: Does Christ's cleansing of the Temple show that the God of the Mosaic law is the same as the Father whom Christ preached?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter II.—Proofs from the plain testimony of Moses, and of the other prophets, whose words are the words of Christ, that there is but one God, the founder of the world, whom Our Lord preached, and whom He called His Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ called the Temple his house and reproved only those who misused it and broke the law. He did not condemn the house or the law, which he came to fulfil. This shows that the law was his Father's law and not that of some other God.
sources.quote: that He might point out the transgressors of His Father’s law; for neither did He bring any accusation against the house, nor did He blame the law, which He had come to fulfil
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's cleansing of the Temple show that the God of the Mosaic law is the same as the Father whom Christ preached?

question: Do 'I and the Father are one,' Thomas's 'My Lord and my God,' and Romans 9:5 show that Christ is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Truth is Proved from the Sacred Writings of the New Covenant.
sources.answer: Yes. No mere man could truly say 'I and the Father are one,' yet Christ said it out of the consciousness of his divinity. Thomas, instructed in all the proofs of Christ's divinity, called him Lord and God. Paul calls Christ 'over all, God blessed for evermore.'
sources.quote: whereas this word can be true of no man, “I and the Father are one,” Christ alone declared this word out of the consciousness of His divinity
sources.raw_question: Do 'I and the Father are one,' Thomas's 'My Lord and my God,' and Romans 9:5 show that Christ is God?

question: Does seeing Christ in the flesh justify calling him man only?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Truth is Proved from the Sacred Writings of the New Covenant.
sources.answer: No. The flesh shows that he is man, but his works, such as creating all things, show that he is God. When both aspects are considered, both truths must be believed.
sources.quote: For how can you say that He is man only, when you see Him also in the flesh, unless because when both aspects are considered, both truths are rightly believed?
sources.raised_by_detail: those who say Christ is merely man
sources.raw_question: Does seeing Christ in the flesh justify calling him man only?

question: Does Moses teach that God laid down the laws of human speech by assigning names to things before creating those who would use them?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The writings of Moses contain the account of creation, genealogies, history, legislation and regulations of worship and life, but no enactment concerning verbs and nouns. Eunomius cannot produce any such text, and to make the invention of words the essential point of piety is folly, neglecting the far greater grounds on which God is to be praised.
sources.quote: But, if he says that there was any legislative enactment in regard to words, let him point it out, and I will hold my tongue.
sources.raw_question: Does Moses teach that God laid down the laws of human speech by assigning names to things before creating those who would use them?

question: If Eunomius concedes that 'God is the most highly exalted of all goods,' does it follow that the Son is also the most highly exalted of all goods, equal to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > The ninth book declares that Eunomius' account of the Nature of God is, up to a certain point, well stated. Then in succession he mixes up with his own argument, on account of its affinity, the expression from Philo's writings, “God is before all other things, which are generated,” adding also the expression, “He has dominion over His own power.” Detesting the excessive absurdity, Gregory strikingly confutes it.
sources.answer: Yes. John proclaims that the Word was with God and was God, so whatever is predicated of God belongs to the Only-begotten. Since the same superlative phrase is applied to the Father, and a superlative admits no diminution or addition by comparison, the Son cannot be less exalted than the Father.
sources.quote: as this phrase is also applied to the Father, the superlative force of “most highly exalted” admits of no diminution or addition by way of comparison.
sources.raw_question: If Eunomius concedes that 'God is the most highly exalted of all goods,' does it follow that the Son is also the most highly exalted of all goods, equal to the Father?

question: Does a right confession of God as Father depend on a right confession of Christ as the Son by true generation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Yes. If Christ is Son only by appellation or a creature, then God is Father only by authority or as Creator of the universe, not by generation. Thus our confession of one God the Father depends on faith in one Lord Christ, and those who make Christ created rather than begotten preach another God the Father who is Creator, not Begetter.
sources.quote: for on our faith in one Lord Christ depends our confession of one God the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does a right confession of God as Father depend on a right confession of Christ as the Son by true generation?

question: Was the Son of Man a separate person, inspired by God the Word as a prophet is inspired, or are the Son of Man and the Son of God one and the same Christ?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: They are one and the same Christ. The whole Son of Man is the whole Son of God. It is ridiculous to preach, besides the Word made flesh, another person inspired by the Word as a prophet is. He was born not to be two separate beings but so that He Who was God before He was Man might be God and Man.
sources.quote: for the whole Son of Man is the whole Son of God), how ridiculous is it to preach besides the Son of God, the Word made flesh, another I know not whom, inspired, like a prophet, by God the Word
sources.raw_question: Was the Son of Man a separate person, inspired by God the Word as a prophet is inspired, or are the Son of Man and the Son of God one and the same Christ?

question: Is the Christ who was born, died, rose again and is in heaven the same Person as the One who existed in the form of God and descended from heaven?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes. He cannot be separated from Himself across these diverse mysteries. The One who took the form of a servant is none other than He who was in the form of God. The One who died is the One who was born, the One who rose is the One who died, and the One in heaven is the One who descended from heaven.
sources.quote: He Who died was the same as He Who was born: He Who rose again as He Who died; He Who is in heaven as He Who rose again; lastly, He Who is in heaven as He Who before descended from heaven.
sources.raw_question: Is the Christ who was born, died, rose again and is in heaven the same Person as the One who existed in the form of God and descended from heaven?

question: Does the crucified Son share the same throne and glory with the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture teaches that the God who was in the beginning was afterwards seen on earth and conversed with men. He became a ransom for our death and loosed death's bonds by his resurrection. Being on the same throne and in the same glory with his Father, he will judge all, and he is comprehensible only by himself, the Father and the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: being on the same throne and in the same glory with His own Father, will in the day of judgment give sentence upon those who are judged
sources.raw_question: Does the crucified Son share the same throne and glory with the Father?

question: Does the Ante-Nicene Fathers' observation that the article (ὁ Θεός) is generally reserved for the Father imply that the Son is not God in the proper sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. The title ὁ Θεός, understood as Αὐτόθεος (God unoriginated), was reserved to the Father as the distinguishing personal character of the first Person, acknowledging only his prerogative as Father. Since it may also signify any Person truly and essentially God, it is sometimes properly applied to the Son, and the Fathers applied many Old Testament texts with the article to Christ.
sources.quote: the title of ὁ Θεὸς, being understood in the same sense with Αὐτόθεος, was, as it ought to be, generally reserved to the Father, as the distinguishing personal character of the first Person of the Holy Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Does the Ante-Nicene Fathers' observation that the article (ὁ Θεός) is generally reserved for the Father imply that the Son is not God in the proper sense?

question: Is it fitting to hold that the Almighty Father produced a Son and Spirit inferior to Himself, so that a lesser result shows a greater power?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: No. No one could allow that a great and powerful cause is to be looked for in small results. Making God produce inferior works implies either that He could not establish His own perfection in what comes from Him, which makes His power fall short of His will, or that He withheld perfection out of envy. Envy cannot be attributed to the Blessed Deity.
sources.quote: But who really could ever allow that a cause that is great and powerful is to be looked for in this smallness of results? As if God was unable to establish His own perfection in anything that comes from Him
sources.raw_question: Is it fitting to hold that the Almighty Father produced a Son and Spirit inferior to Himself, so that a lesser result shows a greater power?

question: Is God's Word like a human word: syllables that signify the speaker's will and then pass away?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. A human word lacks life and power and passes away because man, who utters it, has his nature from nothing. God's Word is not a pronounced sound or a command but the perfect offspring of the perfect, as radiance from light. He is living, powerful and discerning, and he is God as God's Image.
sources.quote: But God’s Word is not merely pronounced, as one may say, nor a sound of accents, nor by His Son is meant His command; but as radiance of light, so is He perfect offspring from perfect
sources.raw_question: Is God's Word like a human word: syllables that signify the speaker's will and then pass away?

question: Is the Word of God himself God and the agent through whom all things are made?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Yes. As God's Image and perfect offspring he is God, as Scripture says 'the Word was God.' Unlike man's word, which accomplishes nothing so that man must work with his hands, God's Word is living and powerful. He is Framer of all, and nothing can be made without him.
sources.quote: He is then Framer of all, ‘and without Him was made not one thing,’ nor can anything be made without Him.
sources.raw_question: Is the Word of God himself God and the agent through whom all things are made?

question: Does Paul's warning 'if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die' forbid living in the body?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter X.—By a comparison drawn from the wild olive-tree, whose quality but not whose nature is changed by grafting, he proves more important things; he points out also that man without the Spirit is not capable of bringing forth fruit, or of inheriting the kingdom of God.
sources.answer: No. Paul himself was in the flesh when he wrote; he does not prohibit living in the flesh but cuts away the lusts of the flesh which bring death, and says those who through the Spirit mortify the works of the flesh shall live.
sources.quote: he does not prohibit them from living their lives in the flesh, for he was himself in the flesh when he wrote to them; but he cuts away the lusts of the flesh, those which bring death upon a man.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's warning 'if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die' forbid living in the body?

question: In Ephesians 1:17, why does Paul call God 'the God of our Lord Jesus Christ' but 'the Father of glory'?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Because the two titles refer to the two natures of Christ. Where Christ is spoken of as Jesus, that is, in the servant's form He took on, God is His God; where the glory of Christ, His divinity, is spoken of, God is His Father. The Greek articles make this distinction clearer than the Latin.
sources.quote: Where the glory of Christ is concerned, God is His Father; where Christ is Jesus, there the Father is His God.
sources.raw_question: In Ephesians 1:17, why does Paul call God 'the God of our Lord Jesus Christ' but 'the Father of glory'?

question: Is it accurate to say the Fathers taught that the Son 'was produced' by the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. The authors being translated give no warrant for the phrase 'was produced'. It conveys to the English reader a low idea of the Son, namely the idea of a creature, which the Fathers did not intend.
sources.quote: he uses frequently, without any warrant from the authors he translates; and for no other reason, that I can see, but because it is apt to convey a low idea
sources.raw_question: Is it accurate to say the Fathers taught that the Son 'was produced' by the Father?

question: Do the heavenly doxologies in Revelation show that the Father and the Son are jointly the object of divine worship?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. In Revelation 1:5-6 glory and dominion are ascribed for ever to the one who washed us in his own blood. In Revelation 5 every creature gives blessing, honour, glory and power both to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb. The Father and the Son are thus held out jointly, yet distinctly, as the adequate object of all divine worship for ever.
sources.quote: The Father and the Son (he that sits upon the throne, and the Lamb) are held out jointly, yet distinctly, as the adequate object of all divine worship and honour, for ever and ever.
sources.raw_question: Do the heavenly doxologies in Revelation show that the Father and the Son are jointly the object of divine worship?

question: Is the divine worship given to Christ owed to him as Mediator or as God the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: It is owed to him as God, as the Son, not as Mediator. Owen holds that divine worship cannot be given without idolatry to anyone who is not God by nature. So Christ, though he is our Mediator, receives this worship on account of his divine sonship.
sources.quote: This, then, is the due of our Mediator, though as God, as the Son, — not as Mediator.
sources.raw_question: Is the divine worship given to Christ owed to him as Mediator or as God the Son?

question: What does the analogy of a human word teach about the Word of God, and where does the analogy fail?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: As our word is proper to us and from us and not an external work, so God's Word is proper to God and from Him and is not a work. But unlike human words, which are many, successive and pass away as their speakers change, God's Word is one, unchanging and enduring forever, otherwise we would have to suppose God to be a man.
sources.quote: so also God’s Word is proper to Him and from Him, and is not a work; and yet is not like the word of man, or else we must suppose God to be man
sources.raw_question: What does the analogy of a human word teach about the Word of God, and where does the analogy fail?

question: Does Paul's calling Christ 'God's power' and 'God's wisdom' without the article mean that the Father's eternal Power and Wisdom are something other than Christ, of which Christ is merely one created instance among many powers, like the locust?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. Asterius's reading makes the Son one of many created powers and compares Him to the locust and caterpillar, which is portentous; moreover, by positing an unoriginate Wisdom coexisting with the Father besides the Son, Asterius himself falls into holding two Unoriginates, the very charge he levels against the orthodox.
sources.quote: Is not this portentous, to say that Wisdom coexists with the Father, yet not to say that this is the Christ, but that there are many created powers and wisdoms, of which one is the Lord whom they go on to compare to the caterpillar and locust?
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's calling Christ 'God's power' and 'God's wisdom' without the article mean that the Father's eternal Power and Wisdom are something other than Christ, of which Christ is merely one created instance among many powers, like the locust?

question: When the Holy Spirit is given and pours love into believers, does only the Spirit dwell in them, or the whole Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > No Gift of God is More Excellent Than Love.
sources.answer: The whole Trinity. The Holy Spirit, who is love, sheds abroad the love of God in our hearts. By that love the whole Trinity dwells in us, so the Spirit's being given brings the indwelling of Father, Son and Spirit together.
sources.quote: Love, therefore, which is of God and is God, is specially the Holy Spirit, by whom the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts, by which love the whole Trinity dwells in us.
sources.raw_question: When the Holy Spirit is given and pours love into believers, does only the Spirit dwell in them, or the whole Trinity?

question: Did the ante-Nicene Fathers attribute the work of creation to the Son as truly as to the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: Yes. The ancients ascribed creation equally to both, differing only in that, for the Father's dignity as first Person, he was supposed to give the fiat and the Son to execute it. As to real power or efficiency the Son is as truly Creator, and writers from Barnabas to Nicaea (Athenagoras, Tatian, Irenaeus, Clement, Origen, Hippolytus) style him Creator in the fullest terms.
sources.quote: A man must be a very stranger to the ancients, who can make any question whether they attributed the work of creation to the Son, as much as to the Father. They ascribed it equally to both
sources.raw_question: Did the ante-Nicene Fathers attribute the work of creation to the Son as truly as to the Father?

question: Does the Son's work of creation prove his eternal power and Godhead?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: Yes. Applying St. Paul's argument that created things manifest the Creator's eternal power and Godhead, Waterland holds creating to be sufficient proof of the Son's eternal power and Godhead, from which infinite power follows by necessary inference.
sources.quote: I shall be content, if creating be allowed a sufficient proof of the Son’s eternal power and Godhead ; since it brings me directly to the point I aim at: besides, that infinite power will come in of course afterwards
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's work of creation prove his eternal power and Godhead?

question: Do Christ's words in John 14 about the Father and himself loving the believer and making their abode with him show that the Son is equal with God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. In these words the love of the Father and of the Son is an equal privilege, their access to the believer's soul is shared, and their indwelling is a single combined dwelling. No created being could speak this way. The passage therefore obliges us to confess that Jesus made himself equal with God.
sources.quote: The love of the Father and of the Son is represented as an equal privilege, – the access of the Father and of his Son to the soul of the obedient believer is a common access
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's words in John 14 about the Father and himself loving the believer and making their abode with him show that the Son is equal with God?

question: Since God led Israel out of Egypt and gave the Law through Moses, a mere man, does it follow that creatures could be brought into being through a created Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: No. Moses was not sent to frame the world or to call into being things that did not exist. He was only a minister of words to the people and to Pharaoh. Ministering belongs to originate beings as servants, but framing and creating belong to God alone and to his proper Word and Wisdom.
sources.quote: to minister is of things originate as of servants, but to frame and to create is of God alone, and of His proper Word and His Wisdom.
sources.raw_question: Since God led Israel out of Egypt and gave the Law through Moses, a mere man, does it follow that creatures could be brought into being through a created Son?

question: Does ascribing to the Holy Spirit care and forethought for all things show that the Spirit is God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes. To care and take thought for all belongs to God alone, as David says, 'I am poor and needy, but the Lord careth for me.' Hence Eunomius' description of the Spirit as caring for all agrees with orthodoxy and confesses the Spirit's divinity.
sources.quote: For in fact it belongs to God alone to care and to take thought for all, as the mighty David has expressed it, “I am poor and needy, but the Lord careth for me.”
sources.raw_question: Does ascribing to the Holy Spirit care and forethought for all things show that the Spirit is God?

question: Did the created forms in which the Son appeared in the Old Testament constitute His true divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. The variety of forms, angel, then man, then fire, shows that none of them is His natural form as God. The burning bush that was not consumed shows that the created form gave Him an outward guise without embodying His nature, and He could lay that form aside by the same power by which He assumed it.
sources.quote: in order that you might learn to believe that this created nature was to provide Him with an outward guise, not to embody the reality of His nature.
sources.raw_question: Did the created forms in which the Son appeared in the Old Testament constitute His true divine nature?

question: Why does the Church refuse to admit a difference of essence between the Father and the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: To admit different essences would be polytheism. If the Godheads differed in essence, they would fall under the conception of number, and that would bring in many gods. The Church therefore teaches that the Only-begotten is essentially God, very God of the essence of the very God.
sources.quote: does not admit the difference of essences, in order that the Godheads may not, by divergence of essence, fall under the conception of number (for this is nothing else than to introduce polytheism into our life)
sources.raw_question: Why does the Church refuse to admit a difference of essence between the Father and the Only-begotten Son?

question: Is the Son a true Son by nature, begotten from the Father's essence, or a Son by adoption of a Father so called only falsely?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: He is a true Son by nature. The Church believes that the Only-begotten truly exists by generation from Him Who is, and is not adopted. He is not alienated from the essence of Him that begat Him.
sources.quote: not adopted by a Father falsely so called, but existing according to nature, by generation from Him Who is, not alienated from the essence of Him that begat Him
sources.raw_question: Is the Son a true Son by nature, begotten from the Father's essence, or a Son by adoption of a Father so called only falsely?

question: Must the orthodox doctrine of the Son's true divinity be proven by constructive reasoning, or does the burden of proof lie on those who deny it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: The burden lies on the innovators. The orthodox confession is sufficiently proved by the tradition handed down from the apostles and the saints who followed them, like an inheritance. Those who change the doctrine to a novelty need abundant arguments. Their unproved claims cannot outweigh the teaching of the evangelists and apostles.
sources.quote: it is enough for proof of our statement, that the tradition has come down to us from our fathers, handed on, like some inheritance, by succession from the apostles and the saints who came after them.
sources.raw_question: Must the orthodox doctrine of the Son's true divinity be proven by constructive reasoning, or does the burden of proof lie on those who deny it?

question: Can God, who cannot be seen with the eyes, be known by human reason, and if so how?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God is the Founder of All Things, Their Lord and Parent, is Proved from the Holy Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes, indirectly. Since we cannot see God with our eyes, we rightly learn of Him from the greatness, power and majesty of His works. As Paul says, His invisible things, His eternal power and godhead, are understood from the things that are made. So the mind, learning hidden things from manifest ones, considers the greatness of the Architect.
sources.quote: And since by the gaze of our eyes we cannot see Him, we rightly learn of Him from the greatness, and the power, and the majesty of His works.
sources.raw_question: Can God, who cannot be seen with the eyes, be known by human reason, and if so how?

question: In what sense is God called both Lord and Parent of all things?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God is the Founder of All Things, Their Lord and Parent, is Proved from the Holy Scriptures.
sources.answer: God is the Creator of all things. He is called Lord on account of His power and Parent on account of His discipline. Scripture shows Him as the one who spoke and all things were made.
sources.quote: God, the Creator of all things—Lord on account of His power, Parent on account of His discipline
sources.raw_question: In what sense is God called both Lord and Parent of all things?

question: Do the words 'then' and 'when' in Scripture and ordinary speech denote time, so that applying them to the Son's generation would place it in time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He further shows that the pretemporal generation of the Son is not the subject of influences drawn from ordinary and carnal generation, but is without beginning and without end, and not according to the fabrications constructed by Eunomius, in ignorance of His power, from the statements of Plato concerning the soul and from the sabbath rest of the Hebrews.
sources.answer: Yes. Both sound common usage and Scripture use these parts of speech to signify time, as in 'then shall they say among the heathen,' 'when I sent you,' and 'then shall the kingdom of heaven be likened.' Hence to say the Son was generated 'when' the Father willed is to imply a temporal origin, which cannot apply where time did not yet exist.
sources.quote: “then” and “when” have a sense which specially and properly refers to the denoting of time, according to the common use of men who speak soundly, and according to their signification in Scripture.
sources.raw_question: Do the words 'then' and 'when' in Scripture and ordinary speech denote time, so that applying them to the Son's generation would place it in time?

question: Does the Holy Spirit build and unite the Church in the same way that Christ does?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter X. Being about to prove that the will, the calling, and the commandment of the Trinity is one, St. Ambrose shows that the Spirit called the Church exactly as the Father and the Son did, and proves this by the selection of SS. Paul and Barnabas, and especially by the mission of St. Peter to Cornelius. And by the way he points out how in the Apostle's vision the calling of the Gentiles was shadowed forth, who having been before like wild beasts, now by the operation of the Spirit lay aside that wildness. Then having quoted other passages in support of this view, he shows that in the case of Jeremiah cast into a pit by Jews, and rescued by Abdemelech, is a type of the slighting of the Holy Spirit by the Jews, and of His being honoured by the Gentiles.
sources.answer: Yes. The Apostle Peter declared that the Church was built by the Holy Spirit, since God bore witness by giving the Gentiles the Holy Spirit just as He gave Him to the Jews, making no distinction between them. Just as Christ is the Cornerstone who joins both peoples into one, the Holy Spirit makes no distinction between the hearts of each people but unites them. The calling of the Church is therefore a common work of the Son and the Spirit.
sources.quote: as Christ is the Cornerstone, Who joined together both peoples into one, so, too, the Holy Spirit made no distinction between the hearts of each people, but united them.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit build and unite the Church in the same way that Christ does?

question: Should divine names such as 'Good,' 'Holy,' 'Saviour,' and 'Judge' be applied to the Trinity in the singular or in the plural?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: In the singular. Just as the divine nature is called one nature, it is called in the singular by all its other names. This holds whether these names are taken to signify nature or operation, and Gregory declines to dispute that point.
sources.quote: as it is called one nature, so it is called in the singular by all its other names, “God,” “Good,” “Holy,” “Saviour,” “Just,” “Judge,” and every other Divine name conceivable
sources.raw_question: Should divine names such as 'Good,' 'Holy,' 'Saviour,' and 'Judge' be applied to the Trinity in the singular or in the plural?

question: Is it consistent to call God the Father incorporeal and unspeakable while describing him as opening his mouth to utter the Word?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XV.—Sige relates to Marcus the generation of the twenty-four elements and of Jesus. Exposure of these absurdities.
sources.answer: No. Marcus names the one he calls unnameable, expounds the one he calls unspeakable, and searches out the one he calls unsearchable. He makes the Father, whom he holds to be without body or form, open his mouth like an organized bodily being, which contradicts his own premises.
sources.quote: declares that He whom thou maintainest to be destitute of body and form, opened His mouth and sent forth the Word, as if He were included among organized beings
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to call God the Father incorporeal and unspeakable while describing him as opening his mouth to utter the Word?

question: Does the Holy Spirit work by command, as a servant obeying another's orders?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XII. After proof that the Spirit is the Giver of revelation equally with the Father and the Son, it is explained how the same Spirit does not speak of Himself; and it is shown that no bodily organs are to be thought of in Him, and that no inferiority is to be supposed from the fact of our reading that He hears, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son, and indeed even to the Father, since He hears the Son. The Spirit then hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that He revealed Him to the prophets and apostles, by which the Unity of operation of the Three Persons is inferred; and, since the Spirit does the same works as the Father, the substance of each is also declared to be the same.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit works voluntarily, free in his own will, and not as the servant of another's power. Scripture says he divides the gifts 'as He will.' He does not obey as one who has been told what to do; as the giver, he is the controller of his own gifts.
sources.quote: Nor does He work in accordance with a command, as he who hears in bodily fashion, but voluntarily, as being free in His own will, not the servant of the power of another.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit work by command, as a servant obeying another's orders?

question: How does knowledge of one's own individual mind differ from general knowledge of what the human mind is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > There is One Knowledge of the Thing in the Thing Itself, and Another in Eternal Truth Itself. That Corporeal Things, Too, are to Be Judged the Rules of Eternal Truth.
sources.answer: Knowledge of one's own individual mind is seen only by oneself, and others can only believe one's report of it. General or specific knowledge of the human mind is seen in the truth itself, which others can also gaze upon and so recognize and approve. The former is changeable, while the latter rests in unchangeable eternity.
sources.quote: each sees a thing in himself, in such way that another person may believe what he says of it, yet may not see it; but another [sees a thing] in the truth itself, in such way that another person also can gaze upon it
sources.raw_question: How does knowledge of one's own individual mind differ from general knowledge of what the human mind is?

question: Should scriptural phrases such as 'He became' and 'He was made' be applied to the Word's divine nature or to His humanity?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: To His humanity. Eternal being belongs to the Word, as in 'In the beginning was the Word.' Becoming and being made are proper to man. Since 'the Word became flesh,' it is fitting to say of Him as man that He was faithful to Him that made Him, meaning that the Father made Him man and sent Him as High Priest.
sources.quote: for as it is proper to the Word to have it said of Him, 'In the beginning was the Word,' so it is proper to man to 'become' and to be 'made.'
sources.raw_question: Should scriptural phrases such as 'He became' and 'He was made' be applied to the Word's divine nature or to His humanity?

question: Does the Son's being called 'faithful' point to His unchangeableness, as with the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: Yes. God is faithful because He is ever the same and does not change. Therefore His Son is faithful too, being ever the same and unchanging, deceiving neither in His essence nor in His promise. Even when made man, Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.
sources.quote: therefore His Son is 'faithful,' being ever the same and unchanging, deceiving neither in His essence nor in His promise
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being called 'faithful' point to His unchangeableness, as with the Father?

question: Does Christ's saying 'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' (John 5:17) show the eternal existence of the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: Yes. The word 'hitherto' shows the Word's eternal existence in the Father. It is proper to the Word to work the Father's works and not to be external to him.
sources.quote: And the word ‘hitherto’ shews His eternal existence in the Father as the Word; for it is proper to the Word to work the Father’s works and not to be external to Him.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' (John 5:17) show the eternal existence of the Word?

question: Does the creation of man in Genesis 1:26-27 prove that Christ is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > It Is, Moreover, Proved by Moses in the Beginning of the Holy Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. Since the Son is the one by whom all things were made, he is also the one by whom man was made. Scripture calls the maker of man God, who made man in the image of God. Since the Word who made man became flesh as Christ, Christ is God.
sources.quote: But God made man in the image of God; He is therefore God who made man in the image of God; therefore Christ is God
sources.raw_question: Does the creation of man in Genesis 1:26-27 prove that Christ is God?

question: Is God's life identical with God's substance, given that God is simple?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory agrees with Eunomius here. In a simple being no addition may be conceived, and we cannot divide him into a side that communicates and a side that is communicated, so whatever the life is, that is the substance. Gregory calls this "excellent" philosophy, but denies that it lets Eunomius identify ungeneracy with the substance.
sources.quote: The life, he says, is not a different thing from the substance; no addition may be thought of in connection with a simple being, by dividing our conception of him into a communicating and communicated side
sources.raw_question: Is God's life identical with God's substance, given that God is simple?

question: By what criterion can we judge whether something, such as the Son of God, is truly what it is called?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: By its nature and powers. Hilary compares this to true wheat, which is known to be true because it grows, is ground to flour, and yields the nature and uses of bread. Natural powers are therefore the evidence of truth, and this is the test he applies to the Son.
sources.quote: It is clear that the truth, or genuineness, of a thing is a question of its nature and its powers.
sources.raw_question: By what criterion can we judge whether something, such as the Son of God, is truly what it is called?

question: Does the Son's role as Creator and upholder of all things imply that he knows when creation will end?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes. Whatever the Father has determined, including the day and hour, is determined through the Son, since nothing comes to be or is determined except through him. As Framer of the universe, he knows its nature, magnitude and limits, and its period is included in these. So he knows when each thing and all things together will end.
sources.quote: if already the day and the hour be determined by the Father, it is plain that through the Son are they determined, and He knows Himself what through Him has been determined
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's role as Creator and upholder of all things imply that he knows when creation will end?

question: If God can create without passion, can he also beget the Son without passion?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds again to discuss the impassibility of the Lord's generation; and the folly of Eunomius, who says that the generated essence involves the appellation of Son, and again, forgetting this, denies the relation of the Son to the Father: and herein he speaks of Circe and of the mandrake poison.
sources.answer: Yes. If one judges God by human conditions, one would have to deny both begetting and creating to him, since humans do neither without passion. Consistency requires either rejecting both or admitting both to be impassible in God: if he creates without labour or matter, he also begets without labour or flux.
sources.quote: for if He creates without labour or matter, He surely also begets without labour or flux.
sources.raw_question: If God can create without passion, can he also beget the Son without passion?

question: Since human craftsmen only shape existing matter and cannot supply it, does that limitation of earthly making mean God cannot properly be called Creator, just as Eunomius rejects true divine generation because of the limits of bodily generation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds again to discuss the impassibility of the Lord's generation; and the folly of Eunomius, who says that the generated essence involves the appellation of Son, and again, forgetting this, denies the relation of the Son to the Father: and herein he speaks of Circe and of the mandrake poison.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius himself admits that men do not make materials but only add form to matter, yet he does not deny that God is Creator. By the same reasoning, if he refuses to measure divine creation by human power, he must also stop slandering divine generation by human imperfections.
sources.quote: If, on the other hand, he refuses to conceive creation in the case of God according to man’s measure of power, let him also cease to slander Divine generation by human imperfections.
sources.raw_question: Since human craftsmen only shape existing matter and cannot supply it, does that limitation of earthly making mean God cannot properly be called Creator, just as Eunomius rejects true divine generation because of the limits of bodily generation?

question: When Basil interprets texts of the Father and Son being one as referring to power, does he mean the Son is merely united with the Father in power (as Dr. Clarke holds), or equal and identical in power?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: Basil means the Son is equal and the very same in power. His words are "equal and the very same with respect of power," and Clarke's dropping of "equal" in translation turns a statement repugnant to his hypothesis into an apparent concession. Agreement in the word "power" is not agreement in the idea.
sources.quote: Basil’s words are ἴσου καὶ ταυτοῦ κατὰ δύναμιν ; that is, equal and the very same with respect of power. The Doctor drops equal, which would have discovered Basil’s meaning
sources.raw_question: When Basil interprets texts of the Father and Son being one as referring to power, does he mean the Son is merely united with the Father in power (as Dr. Clarke holds), or equal and identical in power?

question: If all things are subjected to the Son as God, how is the Father still the one God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: The Father subjects all things to the Son, so the Son is Lord and God of all else. Yet the Son, together with everything subjected to him, is himself subject to the Father. He refers everything he has received back to the Father and returns the whole authority of his divinity to him. In this way the Father remains the one God from whom this power of divinity proceeds.
sources.quote: For all things being subjected to Him as the Son by the Father, while He Himself, with those things which are subjected to Him, is subjected to His Father, He is indeed proved to be Son of His Father; but He is found to be both Lord and God of all else.
sources.raw_question: If all things are subjected to the Son as God, how is the Father still the one God?

question: Are memory, understanding, and will in the human mind three substances or one substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > In Memory, Understanding [or Intelligence], and Will, We Have to Note Ability, Learning, and Use. Memory, Understanding, and Will are One Essentially, and Three Relatively.
sources.answer: They are one substance. They are not three lives or three minds but one life and one mind, and so not three substances but one. Each is called life, mind, and essence in respect to itself, and such terms are said of the three together in the singular.
sources.quote: Since, then, these three, memory, understanding, will, are not three lives, but one life; nor three minds, but one mind; it follows certainly that neither are they three substances, but one substance.
sources.raw_question: Are memory, understanding, and will in the human mind three substances or one substance?

question: Can anyone know God the Father apart from the Son, the Word?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VII.—Recapitulation of the foregoing argument, showing that Abraham, through the revelation of the Word, knew the Father, and the coming of the Son of God. For this cause, he rejoiced to see the day of Christ, when the promises made to him should be fulfilled. The fruit of this rejoicing has flowed to posterity, viz., to those who are partakers in the faith of Abraham, but not to the Jews who reject the Word of God.
sources.answer: No. No one can know God without the goodwill of the Father and the agency of the Son. The Son reveals the Father to whom He wills. Christ's words "no man cometh unto the Father but by Me" show that the Father is known by the Son, that is, by the Word. The Jews departed from God because they imagined they could know the Father by Himself, without the Word.
sources.quote: neither without the goodwill of the Father nor without the agency of the Son, can any man know God
sources.raw_question: Can anyone know God the Father apart from the Son, the Word?

question: Is the fulness of the Godhead present in the Father and the Holy Spirit as well as in Christ, with one shared operation?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IV. To those who contend that the Spirit because He is called the Finger is less than the Father, St. Ambrose replies that this would also tend to the lessening of the Son, Who is called the Right Hand. That these names are to be referred only to the Unity, for which reason Moses proclaimed that the whole Trinity worked in the passage of the Red Sea. And, indeed, it is no wonder that the operation of the Spirit found place there, where there was a figure of baptism, since the Scripture teaches that the Three Persons equally sanctify and are operative in that sacrament.
sources.answer: Yes. The fulness of the Godhead that dwells bodily in Christ dwells also in the Father and in the Holy Spirit. As there is a unity of the Godhead, so there is a unity of operation.
sources.quote: the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily in Christ, which dwells also in the Father, and dwells in the Holy Spirit; and that, as there is a unity of the Godhead, so also is there a unity of operation.
sources.raw_question: Is the fulness of the Godhead present in the Father and the Holy Spirit as well as in Christ, with one shared operation?

question: If Scripture says many things are done "through" the Father, does that make the Father less, in the way heretics argue "through" makes the Son less?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IX. A passage of St. Paul abused by heretics, to prove a distinction between the Divine Persons, is explained, and it is proved that the whole passage can be rightly said of each Person, though it refers specially to the Son. It is then proved that each member of the passage is applicable to each Person, and as to say, of Him are all things is applicable to the Father, so may all things are through Him and in Him also be said of Him.
sources.answer: No. Scripture speaks of Paul as an apostle through the will of God and of Christ rising by the glory of God, and it uses "through" of the Father in other places too. No one would conclude from this that the Father is less. So the same reasoning cannot be used to lower the Son.
sources.quote: Is, then, the Father less because we read that many things are in the Son and of the Son, and find in the heavenly Scriptures very many things done or given through the Father?
sources.raw_question: If Scripture says many things are done "through" the Father, does that make the Father less, in the way heretics argue "through" makes the Son less?

question: Does Scripture speak of things being done "through" the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IX. A passage of St. Paul abused by heretics, to prove a distinction between the Divine Persons, is explained, and it is proved that the whole passage can be rightly said of each Person, though it refers specially to the Son. It is then proved that each member of the passage is applicable to each Person, and as to say, of Him are all things is applicable to the Father, so may all things are through Him and in Him also be said of Him.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says God has revealed things to us through His Spirit, that the good deposit is kept through the Holy Spirit, and that believers are strengthened through Him. It also says the word of wisdom is given through Him, that through Him we mortify the deeds of the flesh, and that our mortal bodies are quickened through His indwelling. The Spirit therefore shares the same expressions used of the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: But in like manner we also read of many things done through the Spirit, as you find: “But God hath revealed them to us through His Spirit;”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture speak of things being done "through" the Holy Spirit?

question: Is creation the work of the Father alone, or of the whole Trinity together?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IX. A passage of St. Paul abused by heretics, to prove a distinction between the Divine Persons, is explained, and it is proved that the whole passage can be rightly said of each Person, though it refers specially to the Son. It is then proved that each member of the passage is applicable to each Person, and as to say, of Him are all things is applicable to the Father, so may all things are through Him and in Him also be said of Him.
sources.answer: It is the work of the whole Trinity. Every creature exists by the will, through the operation and in the power of the Trinity. Scripture shows this in "Let Us make man after Our image" and in the heavens being established by the Word of the Lord and their power by the Spirit of His mouth.
sources.quote: For every creature exists both of the will, and through the operation and in the power of the Trinity, as it is written: “Let Us make man after Our image and likeness;”
sources.raw_question: Is creation the work of the Father alone, or of the whole Trinity together?

question: Can many different names with distinct meanings (immaterial, without anger, immutable, incorporeal, invisible, formless, true, just) be predicated of God without implying division or contradiction in the divine nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. There are numberless ways of thinking about the Divine Life, each expressed by a term with its own peculiar meaning, and all are properly said of the one simple God. A difference in meaning between, say, truth and justice does not make them opposed in God, nor does denying one meaning to a term entail its contrary.
sources.quote: there are numberless other ways of thinking about the Divine Life, each one of which is announced by an expressive sound with a peculiar meaning of its own.
sources.raw_question: Can many different names with distinct meanings (immaterial, without anger, immutable, incorporeal, invisible, formless, true, just) be predicated of God without implying division or contradiction in the divine nature?

question: Does Eunomius' own premise that 'endless' and 'imperishable' have distinct meanings lead to absurdity when turned against him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. If the two terms mean one thing, Eunomius supports Gregory's position; if they differ, then by his own method neither could be said of the other, so the unending would be perishable and the imperishable terminable. Gregory adopts this sportive retort to break through Eunomius' sophistry.
sources.quote: neither will he grant that the imperishable is unending, nor that the unending is imperishable, but the unending will be perishable, and the imperishable will be terminable.
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius' own premise that 'endless' and 'imperishable' have distinct meanings lead to absurdity when turned against him?

question: Is the Son truly and fully living God, given that He has life 'through the Father'?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. That which is born from the living God could not be other than living.
