When Christ says the Father has given the Son to have life in Himself, He testifies that the Son has life to the fullest extent as the Father's gift. Receiving life from the Father therefore does not lessen the Son's life.
sources.quote: For as the Father hath life in Himself, so hath He given to the Son also to have life in Himself, He bore witness that life, to the fullest extent, is His gift from the living God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son truly and fully living God, given that He has life 'through the Father'?

question: How far can human birth serve as an analogy for the Son's generation from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Only partially. Human analogies give real but incomplete light. In human birth the begetter remains bound up with the begotten, who abides in the begetter. But human birth is weak: it comes from two unlike natures, is sustained by lifeless substances, and is subject to decay, so it falls short of the perfect divine birth.
sources.quote: It is inadequate as a parallel to the perfect birth of God the Only-begotten; for humanity is born in weakness and from the union of two unlike natures
sources.raw_question: How far can human birth serve as an analogy for the Son's generation from the Father?

question: Is it valid to argue that the Son and the Spirit are created by taking it as a premise that each divine being is the work of the one before it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no reason for distinguishing a plurality of beings in the Trinity. He offers no demonstration that it is so.
sources.answer: No. Every proof must begin from plain, undeniable axioms and reach the unknown through legitimate syllogisms. Whether the Son and Spirit are created or uncreated is the very point the Church and the Anomoeans dispute. Assuming it as a premise proves the obscure by the obscure, a case of the blind leading the blind. The conclusion drawn from it, that the Son is alien and unlike the Father in being, is equally unsupported.
sources.quote: The reasoner, therefore, who makes what ought to be the object of inquiry itself a premiss of his demonstration is only proving the obscure by the obscure, and illusion by illusion.
sources.raw_question: Is it valid to argue that the Son and the Spirit are created by taking it as a premise that each divine being is the work of the one before it?

question: Can reasoning by analogy from created things establish truths about the transcendent divine nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no reason for distinguishing a plurality of beings in the Trinity. He offers no demonstration that it is so.
sources.answer: Not reliably. Conjecturing about the transcendent from lower existences is not altogether sound, though such an error might be pardonable. Eunomius's claim cannot claim even this excuse, because it has no analogy in creation at all.
sources.quote: such conjecturing about the transcendent from lower existences would not be altogether sound, though the error in arguing from natural phenomena to the incomprehensible might then be pardonable
sources.raw_question: Can reasoning by analogy from created things establish truths about the transcendent divine nature?

question: In what respect is God said to be one in the doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: God's oneness concerns his nature, being, substance, or essence. Scripture speaks of the 'Godhead' of God and of being God 'by nature', which is his essence with its necessary excellencies such as eternity, immensity, and omnipotence. This one essence is absolutely the same in Father, Son, and Spirit, since none can be God except by this divine nature.
sources.quote: This one nature, substance, or essence, being the nature, substance, or essence of God, as God, is the nature, essence, and substance of the Father, Son, and Spirit; one and the same absolutely in and unto each of them
sources.raw_question: In what respect is God said to be one in the doctrine of the Trinity?

question: If each divine person is a distinct principle of operation, are the external works of the Trinity divided among three agents?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Each person, having the understanding, will, and power of God, is a distinct principle of operation. Yet since all their actions outside the Godhead are actions of God, they are undivided and are the works of one and the same God.
sources.quote: each person having the understanding, the will, and power of God, becomes a distinct principle of operation; and yet all their actings ad extra being the actings of God, they are undivided
sources.raw_question: If each divine person is a distinct principle of operation, are the external works of the Trinity divided among three agents?

question: Did Novatian understand "I and my Father are one" as mere unity of love and consent, excluding unity of nature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. Novatian took the text to speak of unity of love, but with equality of nature presupposed. He thought it absurd for a mere man to say these words, and he resolved all unity of consent and love into unity of substance and principle.
sources.quote: Novatian did conceive the text to speak of unity of love, &c. but equality of nature presupposed: for even Paul and Apollos were not of a different nature; one was as truly man as the other
sources.raw_question: Did Novatian understand "I and my Father are one" as mere unity of love and consent, excluding unity of nature?

question: When Athanasius calls the Father 'the true God, who truly exists,' does he imply the Father is more strictly God than the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. The phrase means the Father really and truly is God, in contrast to the heathen idols that have no real existence or are not divine. Athanasius was exhorting pagans to turn from idols to the living God, not comparing the Father with Christ, and he says the same of the Son elsewhere in that treatise.
sources.quote: This is no more than Athanasius would have said of the Son; and Zindeed has said, (in other words,) in that very treatise
sources.raw_question: When Athanasius calls the Father 'the true God, who truly exists,' does he imply the Father is more strictly God than the Son?

question: Can things that are identical in being still be distinct in personal characteristics, and how does this apply to the Trinity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His acknowledgment that the Divine Being is 'single' is only verbal.
sources.answer: Yes. Things identical on the score of being do not agree equally in definition on the score of personality: Peter, James, and John are the same as beings, each being a man, yet differ in the characteristics of their personalities. So the three divine Persons share one being while differing by their recognized personal characteristics.
sources.quote: things that are identical on the score of being will not all agree equally in definition on the score of personality. For instance, Peter, James, and John are the same viewed as beings, each was a man
sources.raw_question: Can things that are identical in being still be distinct in personal characteristics, and how does this apply to the Trinity?

question: Are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit three distinct beings or substances differing in nature, magnitude, and rank of dignity, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His acknowledgment that the Divine Being is 'single' is only verbal.
sources.answer: No. The Church teaches that faith must not be divided among a plurality of beings, but that there is no difference of being in the three Persons. Eunomius merely assumes as an axiom, without proof from Scripture or reason, that each has a different substantial being; this is an unproved impiety that never can be proved.
sources.quote: the Church teaches that we must not divide our faith amongst a plurality of beings, but must recognize no difference of being in three Subjects or Persons
sources.raw_question: Are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit three distinct beings or substances differing in nature, magnitude, and rank of dignity, as Eunomius claims?

question: Can God be known, given that his greatness is immeasurable?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: God cannot be known as regards his greatness, since the Father cannot be measured. But as regards his love, which leads us to God through his Word, those who obey him come to learn that there is so great a God, who by himself established, adorned and contains all things.
sources.quote: As regards His greatness, therefore, it is not possible to know God, for it is impossible that the Father can be measured; but as regards His love (for this it is which leads us to God by His Word)
sources.raw_question: Can God be known, given that his greatness is immeasurable?

question: Does God have a beginning or an end in time?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXI. Isaiah was sent by the Spirit, and accordingly the same Spirit was seen by him. What is meant by the revolving wheels, and the divers wings, and how since the Spirit is proclaimed Lord of Sabaoth by the Seraphim, certainly none but impious men can deny Him this title.
sources.answer: No. God has neither beginning nor end, and the whole course of times and seasons rests in Him. The Seraphim's wings veiling His face and feet signify that we must not ask after the secrets of His beginning or end, for there is neither.
sources.quote: Ask not after the secrets of His beginning or His end, for there is neither. You have the present, but you must praise Him, not question.
sources.raw_question: Does God have a beginning or an end in time?

question: When Scripture ascribes the same appointment of apostles to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, does this mean the operation is divided among them like shares in a jointly held property?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XIII. Prophecy was not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Spirit; the authority and operation of the latter on the apostles is signified to be the same as Theirs; and so we are to understand that there is unity in the three points of authority, rule, and bounty; yet need no disadvantage be feared from that participation, since such does not arise in human friendship. Lastly, it is established that this is the inheritance of the apostolic faith from the fact that the apostles are described as having obeyed the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. There is one authority, one appointment and one giving. Splitting the work as if the Persons, like human co-owners, feared legal prejudice to their rights is a narrow and paltry notion. The same appointment is ascribed to each because their power and operation are one.
sources.quote: There is, then, unity of authority, unity of appointment, unity of giving.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture ascribes the same appointment of apostles to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, does this mean the operation is divided among them like shares in a jointly held property?

question: Is the unity of will and power among the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit merely an agreement of affection, like the unity of human friends?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XIII. Prophecy was not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Spirit; the authority and operation of the latter on the apostles is signified to be the same as Theirs; and so we are to understand that there is unity in the three points of authority, rule, and bounty; yet need no disadvantage be feared from that participation, since such does not arise in human friendship. Lastly, it is established that this is the inheritance of the apostolic faith from the fact that the apostles are described as having obeyed the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Even human friends united by love are called "a second self," so the oneness of Majesty in the Trinity must be far greater. By their same operation and divine power, not just unity but identity (ταυτότης) is expressed. Their sameness of will and power is not from affection but inheres in the substance of the Trinity.
sources.quote: to have the same will and the same power does not arise from the affection of the will, but inheres in the substance of the Trinity
sources.raw_question: Is the unity of will and power among the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit merely an agreement of affection, like the unity of human friends?

question: Does the apostles' obedience to the Holy Spirit's commands show that the Spirit has divine authority?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XIII. Prophecy was not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Spirit; the authority and operation of the latter on the apostles is signified to be the same as Theirs; and so we are to understand that there is unity in the three points of authority, rule, and bounty; yet need no disadvantage be feared from that participation, since such does not arise in human friendship. Lastly, it is established that this is the inheritance of the apostolic faith from the fact that the apostles are described as having obeyed the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. In Acts, Paul, Barnabas and all the apostles obeyed the Spirit's command to separate Barnabas and Saul and ordained those He named. This shows the authority of the One who commands, and that honouring the Spirit's authority is the inheritance of apostolic faith.
sources.quote: Paul and Barnabas obeyed the commands of the Holy Spirit. And all the apostles obeyed, and forthwith ordained those whom the Spirit had ordered to be separated
sources.raw_question: Does the apostles' obedience to the Holy Spirit's commands show that the Spirit has divine authority?

question: Does the creation of things visible and invisible, including thrones, powers and dominions, by and in Christ prove that he is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > The Author Prosecutes the Same Argument.
sources.answer: Yes. The heavenly powers existed before man, so they could not have been made by a man. Since they were created by Christ, he is more than man.
sources.quote: how are “visible things and invisible, thrones, powers, and dominions,” said to be created by Him and in Him; when the heavenly powers could not have been made by man, since they must needs have been prior to man?
sources.raw_question: Does the creation of things visible and invisible, including thrones, powers and dominions, by and in Christ prove that he is God?

question: Does rejecting Valentinus's doctrine that the Son is a 'development' (emanation) of the Father require denying that the Son is truly born of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The Church rejects Valentinus's fantasy of æons and a development produced by a secret act of will, but she still confesses that the Son is God truly born from God. The Arians use the condemnation of Valentinus as a cloak to destroy faith in the true birth, exploiting the fact that every birth looks to human faculties like a development.
sources.quote: they think to cast discredit upon the birth of God from God by calling it a “development,” as though it were a form of the Valentinian heresy.
sources.raw_question: Does rejecting Valentinus's doctrine that the Son is a 'development' (emanation) of the Father require denying that the Son is truly born of God?

question: Does condemning the Manichæan idea of birth by division of substance require rejecting the Son's birth and the unity of substance between Father and Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The Arians wrongly condemn all birth along with birth by severance, and abolish the unity of substance because heretics held it divisible. But the Church, taught by the Only-begotten that Father and Son are One and that the fulness of the Godhead dwells in the Son, confesses a true, undivided birth and worships the Son as rightful Possessor of true Divinity.
sources.quote: She has learnt from God the Only-begotten these truths, that Father and Son are One, and that in the Son the fulness of the Godhead dwells.
sources.raw_question: Does condemning the Manichæan idea of birth by division of substance require rejecting the Son's birth and the unity of substance between Father and Son?

question: Should what is said of God be understood by analogy with visible, changeable, and mortal things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What the Author Entreats from God, What from the Reader. In God Nothing is to Be Thought Corporeal or Changeable.
sources.answer: No. Whatever is said of a nature that is unchangeable, invisible, absolutely living and self-sufficient must not be measured by the standards of things that are visible, changeable, mortal, or not self-sufficient.
sources.quote: whatever is said of a nature, unchangeable, invisible and having life absolutely and sufficient to itself, must not be measured after the custom of things visible, and changeable, and mortal, or not self-sufficient
sources.raw_question: Should what is said of God be understood by analogy with visible, changeable, and mortal things?

question: Does God have bodily attributes such as shape, color, spatial extension, parts, or local motion?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What the Author Entreats from God, What from the Reader. In God Nothing is to Be Thought Corporeal or Changeable.
sources.answer: No. The best thing in our own nature, the intellect, has no outlines of form, colors, spatial size, distance of parts, or movement through place. Whatever is absent from our best part should not be looked for in God, who is far better than that best of ours.
sources.quote: What, therefore, we do not find in that which is our own best, we ought not to seek in Him who is far better than that best of ours
sources.raw_question: Does God have bodily attributes such as shape, color, spatial extension, parts, or local motion?

question: Do all the names applied to God signify in the same way, or do some signify what is present in God and others what is absent from Him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They do not signify uniformly. Some express qualities inherent in God, as "just" signifies that justice is in Him, while others express what is not in Him, as "incorruptible" signifies that corruption is absent. Both kinds yield true knowledge about God.
sources.quote: for some of them express qualities inherent in God, and others qualities that are not, as when we say that He is just or incorruptible
sources.raw_question: Do all the names applied to God signify in the same way, or do some signify what is present in God and others what is absent from Him?

question: Is there a real difference in meaning between affirmative and negative names of God, such as calling Him "good" versus "unsusceptible of evil," or "immortal" versus "ever living"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Such pairs signify one and the same thing, though one appears as an affirmation and the other as a negation. By a change of the things signified, a property can be expressed in negative form and vice versa, and the orthodox conception of the object stays fixed.
sources.quote: For it amounts to the same, whether we speak of God as unsusceptible of evil, or whether we call Him good; whether we confess that He is immortal, or say that He ever liveth.
sources.raw_question: Is there a real difference in meaning between affirmative and negative names of God, such as calling Him "good" versus "unsusceptible of evil," or "immortal" versus "ever living"?

question: Is calling God "without cause" or "ungenerate" consistent with calling Him the First Cause of all things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. There is no contradiction in sense. To say He has no primal cause and to say He is First Cause of all, or alone exists ungenerately, both declare that God is the prime Ruler and Cause of all. The words differ in form, but their meaning is the same.
sources.quote: when we speak of God as the First Cause of all things, or again, when we speak of Him as without cause, we are guilty of no contradiction in sense
sources.raw_question: Is calling God "without cause" or "ungenerate" consistent with calling Him the First Cause of all things?

question: When Christ names 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord' as the chief commandment, does He exclude Himself from the nature and worship of the one God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Although by the word 'only' He seems to disclaim the divine nature for Himself, He places Himself within the unity of the Father's nature without destroying belief in one God. His following question about David calling Christ 'Lord' shows that the confession of the one God, rightly understood, includes the Son by the nature of His birth. The Scribe missed this mystery of the law.
sources.quote: nevertheless, without destroying the belief in one God, He places Himself in the unity of the Father’s nature.
sources.raw_question: When Christ names 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord' as the chief commandment, does He exclude Himself from the nature and worship of the one God?

question: How does the Son procure the Holy Spirit for believers, and what is the Spirit's role in applying purchased grace?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: By his intercession Christ procures the Holy Spirit for believers. The Spirit then actually confers and bestows on them all the grace Christ purchased. Christ promised that he would do this in John 14:16, where he says he will ask the Father to give another Comforter. So the Son's mediation and the Spirit's application work together in giving believers the fruits of redemption.
sources.quote: He procureth the Holy Spirit for us, effectually to collate and bestow all this purchased grace upon us. That he would do this, and doth it, for us, we have his engagement, John xiv. 16.
sources.raw_question: How does the Son procure the Holy Spirit for believers, and what is the Spirit's role in applying purchased grace?

question: When the apostles confess the Creator as God, Lord and Father, do they contradict Christ's command to call only one being Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter I.—The Lord acknowledged but one God and Father.
sources.answer: No, since the Creator is the one God and Father. On the Gnostic view, however, the apostles would be transgressors of Christ's command, and Jesus himself would be the author of their transgression. That conclusion is absurd. Christ's command to call only one being Father therefore obliges us to confess the Creator as our Father.
sources.quote: inasmuch as He commanded that one Being should be called Father, thus imposing upon them the necessity of confessing the Creator as their Father
sources.raw_question: When the apostles confess the Creator as God, Lord and Father, do they contradict Christ's command to call only one being Father?

question: Do the redeemed depend equally on the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in redemption, and what is each Person's role?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes, the dependence is equal. The Father appoints and provides the Redeemer, accepts the price, and grants what is purchased. The Son is the Redeemer and is himself the price. The Holy Ghost communicates the thing purchased by communicating himself, and he is the thing purchased.
sources.quote: the Son is the Redeemer by offering Himself and is the price; and the Holy Ghost immediately communicates to us the thing purchased by communicating Himself, and He is the thing purchased.
sources.raw_question: Do the redeemed depend equally on the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in redemption, and what is each Person's role?

question: Is the Holy Spirit himself the sum of what Christ purchased for believers?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Galatians 3:13-14 says Christ was made a curse so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit. Communion with God, God's love and favor, holiness (which is love to God), and spiritual joy all consist in partaking of the Holy Ghost. Our blessedness is partaking of Christ's fullness, which is the Spirit given to him without measure.
sources.quote: The sum of all that Christ purchased for men was the Holy Ghost: (Gal. 3:13,14) "He was made a curse for us... that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith."
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit himself the sum of what Christ purchased for believers?

question: Does the fact that Christ was worshipped even before the incarnation show that the Son is truly divine and not exalted to divinity by reward?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture shows his Name invoked and worshipped before he became man. His Name endures before the sun, and the angels worship him. So he could not be receiving as a reward a worship and exaltation he always had as the Most High.
sources.quote: how is He exalted, being before His exaltation the Most High? or how did He receive the right of being worshipped, who before He now received it, was ever worshipped?
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Christ was worshipped even before the incarnation show that the Son is truly divine and not exalted to divinity by reward?

question: Is Asterius right that if it befits God to make things at His pleasure, then the Son as first Offspring should also be said to come to be by will?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. Asterius's argument presupposes that the Son is an offspring like other offsprings and the same as a thing made, which is irreligious. His own conclusion that works are by will and pleasure only applies to the Son if the Son is a work; since the Son is other than all things, 'by will' must not be applied to Him.
sources.quote: In spite of the Sophist having introduced abundant irreligion in his words, namely, that the Offspring and the thing made are the same, and that the Son is one offspring out of all offsprings that are
sources.raw_question: Is Asterius right that if it befits God to make things at His pleasure, then the Son as first Offspring should also be said to come to be by will?

question: Does the comparison in 1 Corinthians 2:11 between the spirit of man and the Spirit of God show that the Spirit is merely a quality of God's nature, as consciousness is of the human mind?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. The first clause, 'God hath revealed them to us by his Spirit,' implies a personal distinction. One could not say that a man makes anything known to others by his consciousness. (The author is quoting P. Smith.)
sources.quote: which clearly implies a personal distinction for it could not be said that a man makes anything known to others by his consciousness.
sources.raw_question: Does the comparison in 1 Corinthians 2:11 between the spirit of man and the Spirit of God show that the Spirit is merely a quality of God's nature, as consciousness is of the human mind?

question: Is the Holy Spirit infinitely good and holy, as the source of truth and holiness?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The Old Testament calls him God's 'good Spirit' and emphatically 'the Holy Spirit of God.' Christ and the apostles use 'Holy Spirit' as his distinctive name. He is also called the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of holiness, as the fountain of truth and goodness.
sources.quote: He is likewise called the Spirit of truth, and the Spirit of holiness, as the fountain of verity and goodness.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit infinitely good and holy, as the source of truth and holiness?

question: Is it legitimate for theologians to make doctrinal pronouncements about Father, Son and Holy Spirit that go beyond the explicit words of Scripture?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Yes, under necessity. Because heretics keep the Names of the baptismal formula while emptying them of meaning, the Church must, without adding to the appointed form, set a limit to their interpretation by emphasising the truth the Names convey. Hilary undertakes this reluctantly, with a prayer for pardon, promising to accept whatever conclusion God indicates.
sources.quote: Since their malice, inspired by the devil’s cunning, empties the doctrine of its meaning while it retains the Names which convey the truth, we must emphasise the truth which those Names convey.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate for theologians to make doctrinal pronouncements about Father, Son and Holy Spirit that go beyond the explicit words of Scripture?

question: Were invisible spiritual beings such as angels, archangels, principalities and powers made by the one God the Creator, or by some other spiritual source?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: They were made by the one God, the Creator. The authoritative Scriptures, the Lord, Moses and the prophets declare that all things visible and invisible were made by one God. The Gnostics cannot even describe these beings' nature, number or ranks, which shows they were not made by them.
sources.quote: we prove from the authoritative Scriptures that all the things which have been mentioned, visible and invisible, have been made by one God.
sources.raw_question: Were invisible spiritual beings such as angels, archangels, principalities and powers made by the one God the Creator, or by some other spiritual source?

question: Is the Son one with the Father and equal to God, against those who mock his divine Sonship?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Yes. Christ says he came out from the Father, is in the Father's bosom, that he and the Father are One, and that he is in the Father and the Father in him. To those who, like the Jews, are angered at his making himself equal with God, the answer is his own: believe his works, that the Father is in him and he in the Father.
sources.quote: They must hear, I came out from the Father and The Son in the Father’s bosom, and I and the Father are One, and I in the Father, and the Father in Me.
sources.raised_by_detail: preachers whose apostleship is of the newest fashion
sources.raw_question: Is the Son one with the Father and equal to God, against those who mock his divine Sonship?

question: Why did the Son of God become incarnate of the Virgin?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: For the sake of mankind. By his own divine power he formed his Body from the Virgin and took human nature to himself. His aim was that a hallowed Body of all humanity might come into being, in which all mankind would be hidden in him and he in turn reproduced in all.
sources.quote: that so through that Body which He was pleased to assume all mankind might be hid in Him, and He in return, through His unseen existence, be reproduced in all.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Son of God become incarnate of the Virgin?

question: Can the nature of a created work be known by contemplating the nature of its divine Maker?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He vainly thinks that the doubt about the energies is to be solved by the beings, and reversely.
sources.answer: No. Gregory takes the sky as an example: contemplating God as immaterial, invisible, formless, ungenerate, everlasting and unchangeable gives no knowledge of the sky's substance. So the principle that a product is known from the being of its producer fails even for God's undoubted works.
sources.quote: How will the contemplation of the Maker of the sky procure a solution of the question, immaterial, invisible, formless, ungenerate, everlasting, incapable of decay and change and alteration, and all such things, as He is.
sources.raw_question: Can the nature of a created work be known by contemplating the nature of its divine Maker?

question: Is the Father the memory, the Son the understanding, and the Holy Spirit the love of all three Persons, so that each performs only one of these acts for the others?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Holy Spirit is Called Love, and Whether He Alone is So Called. That the Holy Spirit is in the Scriptures Properly Called by the Name of Love.
sources.answer: No. Each Person and all together have all three in his own nature. The Father does not depend on the Son to understand or on the Spirit to love. In God these are not distinct things as they are in us, but one thing equivalent to all, like wisdom.
sources.quote: but rather in this way, that both all and each have all three each in His own nature. Nor that these things should differ in them, as in us memory is one thing, understanding another, love or charity another
sources.raw_question: Is the Father the memory, the Son the understanding, and the Holy Spirit the love of all three Persons, so that each performs only one of these acts for the others?

question: Do Christ's expressions of sorrow and fear in his Passion prove that the Son has a nature inferior to God the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Hilary holds that the texts the heretics cite ("My soul is sorrowful," "let this cup pass," "why hast Thou forsaken Me," "into Thy hands I commend My Spirit") do not show that the Son was subject to fear or sorrow on his own account. The heretics misuse these words of the faith to deny his equality and likeness to God. Hilary then argues that Christ had nothing to fear, so these words cannot show weakness in his divine nature.
sources.quote: Now first of all, before we shew from these very texts, that He was subject to no infirmity of fear or sorrow on His own account, let us ask, "What can we find for Him to fear, that the dread of an unendurable pain should have seized Him?"
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's expressions of sorrow and fear in his Passion prove that the Son has a nature inferior to God the Father?

question: Do the conflicting heresies of Sabellius, Arius, and Photinus, by refuting one another, actually confirm the Church's doctrine of the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. Each heresy is right in part: Sabellius proves Christ's divinity from His works, the Arians grant that He is Son, and Photinus maintains His manhood. Their mutual refutations thus vindicate the Church's faith that the Son truly exists (against Sabellius), is God by nature (against Arius), and created the universe before His human birth (against Photinus).
sources.quote: the Church, whose faith is based upon the teaching of Evangelists and Apostles, holds fast, against Sabellius, her assertion that the Son exists; against Arius, that He is God by nature; against Photinus, that He created the universe.
sources.raw_question: Do the conflicting heresies of Sabellius, Arius, and Photinus, by refuting one another, actually confirm the Church's doctrine of the Son?

question: How can God create changeable and temporal things without himself undergoing change or temporal movement?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > This Work is Written Against Those Who Sophistically Assail the Faith of the Trinity, Through Misuse of Reason. They Who Dispute Concerning God Err from a Threefold Cause. Holy Scripture, Removing What is False, Leads Us on by Degrees to Things Divine. What True Immortality is. We are Nourished by Faith, that We May Be Enabled to Apprehend Things Divine.
sources.answer: God fashions changeable things and creates temporal things without any change or temporal motion in himself. Augustine holds this is part of what makes God's substance difficult to contemplate and know fully, and it is not something the unpurified mind can yet grasp directly.
sources.quote: who fashions things changeable, yet without any change in Himself, and creates things temporal, yet without any temporal movement in Himself
sources.raw_question: How can God create changeable and temporal things without himself undergoing change or temporal movement?

question: If Christ obeyed the law perfectly for believers, are believers no longer bound to obey the law?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: No, they are still bound to obey, though not in the same way. As Christ's death frees us from death only as penal, yet we still die, so his obedience frees us from obeying in our own strength and as a means to earn eternal life under the covenant 'Do this, and live.' We remain bound to obedience as a way of walking with God, not as a way of working to come to him.
sources.quote: we are not freed from obedience, as a way of walking with God, but we are, as a way of working to come to him
sources.raw_question: If Christ obeyed the law perfectly for believers, are believers no longer bound to obey the law?

question: Does the fact that human conceptual thought (epinoia) can invent fictions and monsters show that it is unable to reach truth or useful knowledge?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The capacity of conception to invent unrealities shows that it can also discover what is profitable and true. The elective faculty of the soul is given to incline us to good, and its occasional abuse for evil does not prove it never inclines to good. In the same way, conception's bias toward vain things proves that it can also serve what is beneficial.
sources.quote: so the bias of conception towards what is vain and unprofitable does not prove its inability for what is profitable, but, on the contrary, is a demonstration of its not being unserviceable for what is beneficial and necessary to the mind
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that human conceptual thought (epinoia) can invent fictions and monsters show that it is unable to reach truth or useful knowledge?

question: Does defining God as the one self-existent, underived, independent, supreme Being exclude the Son from being God, since the Son is derived?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 24: Whether Gal. iv. 8. may not be enough to determine the dispute betwiat us; since it obliged the Doctor to confess, that Christ as by nature truly God, as truly
sources.answer: No. That definition has long been used by believers in the Trinity without any such consequence. It defines the divine nature in the abstract, apart from the distinction of Persons. In it, 'self-existent', 'underived' and 'independent' are essential rather than personal characters, meaning necessarily-existing, uncreated, immutable and all-sufficient. Taken as personal characters, the definition would describe only the Person of the Father, not the Godhead.
sources.quote: there the words self-existent, underived, independent, are not considered as personal, but essential characters. Necessarily-existing, uncreated, immutable, all-sufficient, are what they mean in that definition
sources.raw_question: Does defining God as the one self-existent, underived, independent, supreme Being exclude the Son from being God, since the Son is derived?

question: Is the eternal Word of the Father a different Logos from the Word who was begotten, so that the eternal Word is only an impersonal attribute and the begotten Word a created substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Waterland rejects this Arian salvo of a twofold Logos as directly contrary to all antiquity, which gives no support to any such notion. The Catholic doctrine from the beginning was of one eternal Logos who is distinct from the Father and consubstantial with him. This same Logos went forth to create and later became man.
sources.quote: the former being only the Father's own proper Word, and no substantial thing; the latter a created substance, directly contrary to all antiquity, which has nothing to countenance any such notion of a twofold Λόγος.
sources.raw_question: Is the eternal Word of the Father a different Logos from the Word who was begotten, so that the eternal Word is only an impersonal attribute and the begotten Word a created substance?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's acting according to the good pleasure of the Son imply his subordination, or does it indicate unity of essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: It indicates unity of essence. Gregory accepts that the Spirit works according to the Son's good pleasure, but the community of nature means Father, Son, and Spirit have one will; the Spirit's willing what seems good to the Son shows community of will, which points to unity of essence.
sources.quote: the will of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost is one, and thus, if the Holy Spirit wills that which seems good to the Son, the community of will clearly points to unity of essence.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's acting according to the good pleasure of the Son imply his subordination, or does it indicate unity of essence?

question: Does denying that the Son was made 'out of nothing,' while still not affirming his consubstantiality and coeternity, place Dr. Clarke on a middle way between orthodoxy and Arianism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. Many ancient Arians did exactly the same thing. They indignantly rejected the charge of making the Son a creature, with the reserve that he was not a creature 'like other creatures.' They also often denied, or even anathematized, the claim that the Son was 'out of nothing.' So this is not a middle way but a copy of Arian evasion.
sources.quote: But herein he only copies after many of the ancient Arians; who, when accused by the Catholics of making the Son a creature, rejected the charge with great disdain
sources.raw_question: Does denying that the Son was made 'out of nothing,' while still not affirming his consubstantiality and coeternity, place Dr. Clarke on a middle way between orthodoxy and Arianism?

question: Does God's calling Israel 'My firstborn son' show that the phrase 'This is My beloved Son' need not imply a true birth of Christ from God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Israel is said to be born only in the sense that it is made, as Scripture says 'a people which shall be born, whom the Lord hath made'; it is a son by adoption and in title, not by generation. 'My beloved Son' is the language of birth, while 'My firstborn son' is the language of choice from among the nations and adoption by an act of will.
sources.quote: For where there is birth, there we see, My beloved Son; but where there is a choice from among the nations, and adoption through an act of will, there is My firstborn son.
sources.raw_question: Does God's calling Israel 'My firstborn son' show that the phrase 'This is My beloved Son' need not imply a true birth of Christ from God?

question: If the Word were someone other than the Son, would the Word have to be either the Father or inferior to the Son, given that the Son is 'in the bosom of the Father'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is in the bosom of the Father, and nothing is before Him who is in the Father. So a Word distinct from the Son is either the Father, in whom the Son is, or else external to the Father, since only one, the Only-begotten Son, is in the bosom. Hence the eternal Son must be the Word.
sources.quote: For not both the Word and the Son are in the bosom, but one must be, and He the Son, who is Only-begotten.
sources.raw_question: If the Word were someone other than the Son, would the Word have to be either the Father or inferior to the Son, given that the Son is 'in the bosom of the Father'?

question: Would separating the Word from the Son make the Son superior to the Word, since 'no one knoweth the Father save the Son'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says only the Son knows the Father, not 'the Word.' If the Word were another than the Son, either the Word would not know the Father, or the saying 'no one knows' would be false. The same holds for 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father' and 'I and the Father are One,' which are spoken by the Son. Therefore the Son and the Word are the same.
sources.quote: for ‘no one knoweth the Father save the Son,’ not the Word. Either then the Word does not know, or if He knows, it is not true that ‘no one knows.’
sources.raw_question: Would separating the Word from the Son make the Son superior to the Word, since 'no one knoweth the Father save the Son'?

question: What do Christ's hunger, weariness, tears, sweat of blood, and the blood and water from his side show about his humanity?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXII.—Christ assumed actual flesh, conceived and born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: They show that he had real flesh derived from the earth through Mary. A body not taken from Mary would not need earthly food, would not hunger after fasting, or grow weary, or weep, or bleed. All these are tokens of the flesh that he recapitulated in himself. Otherwise his descent into Mary would also have been superfluous.
sources.quote: For all these are tokens of the flesh which had been derived from the earth, which He had recapitulated in Himself, bearing salvation to His own handiwork.
sources.raw_question: What do Christ's hunger, weariness, tears, sweat of blood, and the blood and water from his side show about his humanity?

question: Does Scripture call anyone God and Lord absolutely and in his own person other than the Father and his Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: No. The Lord, the Holy Spirit and the apostles never named anyone God definitely and absolutely unless he were truly God, and named no one Lord in his own person except God the Father ruling over all and his Son, who received dominion from the Father over all creation. Since both are truly Lord, the Spirit fitly gives both that title.
sources.quote: nor would they have named any one in his own person Lord, except God the Father ruling over all, and His Son who has received dominion from His Father over all creation
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture call anyone God and Lord absolutely and in his own person other than the Father and his Son?

question: Is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ the same as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the only true God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: Yes. The author prays to the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. He confesses him as maker of heaven and earth, ruler over all, and the only and true God, above whom there is no other God.
sources.quote: Lord God of Abraham, and God of Isaac, and God of Jacob and Israel, who art the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ the same as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the only true God?

question: Is the Holy Spirit one who receives life (is quickened) or one who gives life (quickens)?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IV. The Holy Spirit gives life, not in a different way from the Father and the Son, nor by a different working.
sources.answer: The Spirit gives life. Scripture says, "The letter killeth, but the Spirit giveth life." The Spirit is therefore not among the servants who are quickened. He quickens as the Father and the Son do, and this shows his divine majesty.
sources.quote: Let us then see whether the Spirit is quickened, or Himself quickens. Now it is written: “The letter killeth, but the Spirit giveth life.” So, then, the Spirit quickens.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit one who receives life (is quickened) or one who gives life (quickens)?

question: When we conceive bodily things from someone else's narrative rather than from our own recollection, does the trinity of memory, mental vision, and uniting will still apply?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Different Modes of Conceiving.
sources.answer: Yes. At first it seems that the mind does not turn back to memory and so the trinity is not completed. On closer consideration, however, we could not understand the narrator unless we already remembered, by kind, the individual things he describes, such as mountains, timber, and olive trees. So all conception of bodily things goes back to memory, which sets the limit and measure of what the mind can picture.
sources.quote: But if we consider the matter more carefully, even in this case, the limit of the memory is not overstepped. For I could not even understand the narrator, if I did not remember generically the individual things of which he speaks
sources.raw_question: When we conceive bodily things from someone else's narrative rather than from our own recollection, does the trinity of memory, mental vision, and uniting will still apply?

question: Are the trinities of thought arising from the things held in memory infinite in number?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Different Modes of Conceiving.
sources.answer: No. They are innumerable but not infinite. Because the mind cannot view everything in memory at once, these trinities follow one another in succession and become extremely numerous. Their number is still fixed and finite, since it does not go beyond the things stored in memory. 'Innumerable' is said not only of infinite things but also of finite things that exceed anyone's power to count.
sources.quote: For we not only call infinite things innumerable, but also those, which, although finite, exceed any one’s power of reckoning.
sources.raw_question: Are the trinities of thought arising from the things held in memory infinite in number?

question: Is the Holy Spirit's office as Comforter merely imposed on him by the Father and the Son, or does he take it up willingly?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: He takes it up willingly. The Spirit is delegated by the Father and the Son to be our Comforter, yet he condescends to this delegation. For that reason believers have communion with the Spirit himself, on account of his voluntary condescension to the dispensation.
sources.quote: consider him as he condescends to this delegation of the Father and the Son to be our comforter, and ask him daily of the Father in the name of Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit's office as Comforter merely imposed on him by the Father and the Son, or does he take it up willingly?

question: Can sins be committed against the Holy Spirit personally, so that repenting of them is part of communion with him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Believers may grieve the Spirit as to his person, quench him as to the motion of his grace, and resist him in his ordinances. Humbling ourselves before him for these failings is part of our communion with him, and it is a fitting ground of godly sorrow and of indignation against sin.
sources.quote: That we have grieved him as to his person, quenched him as to the motion of his grace, or resisted him in his ordinances, is to be mourned for
sources.raw_question: Can sins be committed against the Holy Spirit personally, so that repenting of them is part of communion with him?

question: Does Scripture ascribe to Christ the infinite goodness and holiness that belong to God alone?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says none is good but God and none is holy but Jehovah. Yet Jesus calls himself the Good Shepherd, the absolutely good one. He is called the Holy One and the Just, the one who knew no sin, holy, harmless and undefiled, and full of grace and truth.
sources.quote: Jesus says, “I am the Good Shepherd,” (ο ποιμην ο καλός) the absolutely good one.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ascribe to Christ the infinite goodness and holiness that belong to God alone?

question: Do the eternity, infinity and beauty that natural reason ascribes to the Creator also belong to the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Yes. Hilary learnt from John's prologue that the eternity, infinity and beauty which reason attributes to the Creator belong also to God the Only-begotten. The Son therefore shares the divine attributes of the Father.
sources.quote: the eternity and infinity and beauty which, by the light of natural reason, it had attributed to its Creator belonged also to God the Only-begotten
sources.raw_question: Do the eternity, infinity and beauty that natural reason ascribes to the Creator also belong to the Only-begotten Son?

question: Should sayings in the Book of Proverbs be interpreted according to their literal, obvious sense when they are used to establish doctrine about God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. In Scripture a 'proverb' is a form of speech that, through one set of ideas presented on the surface, points to something hidden and teaches indirectly. Solomon's preface says the book is meant to help the reader 'understand a parable and a dark saying' and speaks of words that reveal their aim 'by a turn.' A reasonable reader will therefore examine even the seemingly clear passages for an underlying mystical meaning, and obscure passages need even closer scrutiny.
sources.quote: a reasonable man will not receive any passage cited from this book, be it never so clear and intelligible at first sight, without examination and inspection; for assuredly there is some mystical contemplation underlying even those passages which seem manifest.
sources.raw_question: Should sayings in the Book of Proverbs be interpreted according to their literal, obvious sense when they are used to establish doctrine about God?

question: Is the Son of God bounded by time or of limited duration?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. He is free from time and unlimited in duration, since all things, including time, were made by Him, and He could not be confined within a limit He Himself created.
sources.quote: One free from time, unlimited in duration, since by Him all things were made, and, indeed, He could not be confined within a limit created by Himself.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God bounded by time or of limited duration?

question: Does Luke 1:35, which calls the holy thing born of Mary 'the Son of God', prove that the human flesh born of Mary is itself the Son of God, so that Christ is man only?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That These Have Therefore Erred, by Thinking that There Was No Difference Between the Son of God and the Son of Man; Because They Have Ill Understood the Scripture.
sources.answer: No. The angel adds the conjunction 'also' ('therefore also that Holy Thing'), showing that the flesh born of Mary is Son of God only consequently and secondarily. Primarily the Son of God is the Word of God, incarnate by the Spirit who came upon Mary. The angel thus set down a distinction rather than confusing the two.
sources.quote: so as to make it plain that that Holy Thing which is born of her—that is, that substance of flesh and body—is not the Son of God primarily, but consequently, and in the secondary place
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold Christ to be man only (adoptionists)
sources.raw_question: Does Luke 1:35, which calls the holy thing born of Mary 'the Son of God', prove that the human flesh born of Mary is itself the Son of God, so that Christ is man only?

question: How does the human nature born of Mary come to be called the Son of God if it is not Son of God by nature?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That These Have Therefore Erred, by Thinking that There Was No Difference Between the Son of God and the Son of Man; Because They Have Ill Understood the Scripture.
sources.answer: By being assumed into union with the Word, who is the legitimate Son of God from God himself. The Word takes the Son of man to himself and by this association makes him Son of God, which by nature he was not. So the original cause of the name lies in the divine Son, and the man has only a derived continuance of the name.
sources.quote: For He is the legitimate Son of God who is of God Himself; and He, while He assumes that Holy Thing, and links to Himself the Son of man, and draws Him and transfers Him to Himself
sources.raw_question: How does the human nature born of Mary come to be called the Son of God if it is not Son of God by nature?

question: Does Scripture use prepositional phrases such as 'of which', 'through which' and 'in which' with fixed technical meanings, as pagan philosophy does?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That there is no distinction in the scriptural use of these syllables.
sources.answer: No. Scripture uses these expressions, but the freedom of the Spirit is not bound to the pettiness of pagan classifications. Scripture varies its expressions as each occasion and circumstance requires, so no strict rule about these syllables can be drawn from it.
sources.quote: we absolutely deny that the freedom of the Spirit is in bondage to the pettiness of Paganism. On the contrary, we maintain that Scripture varies its expressions as occasion requires, according to the circumstances of the case.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture use prepositional phrases such as 'of which', 'through which' and 'in which' with fixed technical meanings, as pagan philosophy does?

question: Can a trinity be discerned in the divine Wisdom, which is God, by considering how that Wisdom knows and loves itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How There is a Trinity in the Very Simplicity of God. Whether and How the Trinity that is God is Manifested from the Trinities Which Have Been Shown to Be in Men.
sources.answer: Yes. Since God is Wisdom, and Wisdom cannot lack knowledge or fail to know and love itself, we find a trinity: wisdom, the knowledge wisdom has of itself, and its love of itself. This parallels the trinity in man of mind, the mind's knowledge of itself, and its love of itself.
sources.quote: then behold we have a trinity,—to wit, wisdom, and the knowledge wisdom has of itself, and its love of itself.
sources.raw_question: Can a trinity be discerned in the divine Wisdom, which is God, by considering how that Wisdom knows and loves itself?

question: Could something in God be called accidental if it cannot be lost but can increase or decrease, as the soul's life is greater when it is wise and less when it is foolish?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Accidental Always Implies Some Change in the Thing.
sources.answer: No. Increase and decrease are themselves a kind of change. God remains altogether unchangeable, so nothing in Him can grow greater or less. Therefore not even this weaker sense of accident applies to God.
sources.quote: nothing of this kind, either, happens to God, because He remains altogether unchangeable.
sources.raw_question: Could something in God be called accidental if it cannot be lost but can increase or decrease, as the soul's life is greater when it is wise and less when it is foolish?

question: If nothing accidental is said of God, must everything said of God, such as 'unbegotten' and 'begotten,' be said according to substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Accidental Always Implies Some Change in the Thing.
sources.answer: No. In creatures, whatever is not said according to substance is said according to accident. In God, however, some things are said relatively, as Father in relation to Son and Son in relation to Father. These relations are not accidents, because the Father is always Father and the Son is always Son, never having begun to be Son. So a difference between begetting and being begotten does not imply a difference of substance.
sources.quote: For it is said in relation to something, as the Father in relation to the Son and the Son in relation to the Father, which is not accident; because both the one is always Father, and the other is always Son
sources.raw_question: If nothing accidental is said of God, must everything said of God, such as 'unbegotten' and 'begotten,' be said according to substance?

question: Does Basil's teaching on the term "Son" dishonour the divine generation by importing human notions, as Eunomius charges?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > Then, distinguishing between essence and generation, he declares the empty and frivolous language of Eunomius to be like a rattle. He proceeds to show that the language used by the great Basil on the subject of the generation of the Only-begotten has been grievously slandered by Eunomius, and so ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Basil distinguishes two senses in the word "Son": being formed by passion, and true relationship to the begetter. He excludes the first, carnal sense from divine discourse and keeps only the second, which testifies to the glory of the Only-begotten. It is rather Eunomius who dishonours the Son, by ranking the Creator of all things with the lower creation.
sources.quote: Who, then, dishonours the generation of the Son by human notions? He who sets far from the Divine generation what belongs to passion and to man, and joins the Son impassibly to Him that begat Him?
sources.raw_question: Does Basil's teaching on the term "Son" dishonour the divine generation by importing human notions, as Eunomius charges?

question: Is the Son's generation from the Father passionless?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > Then, distinguishing between essence and generation, he declares the empty and frivolous language of Eunomius to be like a rattle. He proceeds to show that the language used by the great Basil on the subject of the generation of the Only-begotten has been grievously slandered by Eunomius, and so ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes. In speaking of God, the passionate and carnal sense of sonship is set aside. All that remains is the true relationship to the begetter, so the Son is joined impassibly to the Father who begat Him.
sources.quote: while by the word “Son” two things are signified, the being formed by passion, and the true relationship to the begetter, he does not admit in discourses upon things divine the former sense, which is unseemly and carnal
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's generation from the Father passionless?

question: Could the interval by which the Father is supposedly prior to the Son be an infinite interval rather than a bounded one?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He who asserts that the Father is 'prior' to the Son with any thought of an interval must perforce allow that even the Father is not without beginning.
sources.answer: No. An infinite interval by its nature extends without bound in either direction, so it could not be limited above by the Father and below by the Son. To call it infinite would annul the very conception of Father and Son and of anything connecting them. Therefore anyone holding the Father prior must posit a definite, bounded interval, which leads to a beginning of the Father.
sources.quote: he would annul thereby the very conception of Father and Son and the thought of anything connecting them, as long as this infinite were limited on neither side
sources.raw_question: Could the interval by which the Father is supposedly prior to the Son be an infinite interval rather than a bounded one?

question: Can the Father's life exceed the Son's life in duration in the future rather than the past?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He who asserts that the Father is 'prior' to the Son with any thought of an interval must perforce allow that even the Father is not without beginning.
sources.answer: No. Even the opponents grant that both Father and Son are imperishable, so no excess of the Father's life can lie in the future. The supposed excess must therefore lie in the past, and as a definite interval it requires a starting-point for the Father's existence.
sources.quote: they will allow that this interval of excess cannot be in the future, for that Both are imperishable, even the foes of the truth will grant.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father's life exceed the Son's life in duration in the future rather than the past?

question: Can human language adequately express what God the Father is, given attributes like self-existence, immortality, and invisibility?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. Terms like self-existent, self-originating, immortal, incomprehensible and invisible are acknowledgments of His glory and sketches of our thought, but each, taken by human analogy, falls short or even implies something false. Perfect knowledge of God is to be sure we must not be ignorant of Him yet unable to describe Him; belief, apprehension and worship stand in place of definition.
sources.quote: Thus our confession of God fails through the defects of language; the best combination of words we can devise cannot indicate the reality and the greatness of God.
sources.raw_question: Can human language adequately express what God the Father is, given attributes like self-existence, immortality, and invisibility?

question: Does holding that names are produced by human conception (epinoia) commit one to Epicurean atomism or to Aristotle's denial of providence over earthly things, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory treats the charge as absurd. Attributing words that express things to the reasoning faculty in human nature has nothing to do with Epicurus' doctrine of atoms, empty space and chance generation. Nor does it amount to Aristotle's restriction of providence. Eunomius' linking of these views shows his lack of understanding, not any real kinship of doctrine.
sources.quote: If we ascribe words expressive of things to the logical faculty in our nature, we thereby stand convicted of holding the Epicurean doctrine of indivisible bodies, and combinations of atoms, and the collision and rebound of particles, and so on.
sources.raw_question: Does holding that names are produced by human conception (epinoia) commit one to Epicurean atomism or to Aristotle's denial of providence over earthly things, as Eunomius claims?

question: Does the absence of Scriptural examples of holy men inventing new words prove that words and names were appointed by God himself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Human nature was complete and self-sufficient in reason and thought from the very first. It therefore needed no special saints to supply new names. Failing to cite such instances proves nothing about God having fixed particular syllables and words.
sources.quote: But if from the very first man’s nature existed self-sufficing and complete for all purposes of reason and thought, why should any one, in order to establish this doctrine of conception, humour them so far as to seek for instances where holy men initiated sounds or names?
sources.raw_question: Does the absence of Scriptural examples of holy men inventing new words prove that words and names were appointed by God himself?

question: Does denying that poets invented their words honour God by making him the author of all human vocabulary?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
