sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory ridicules the idea. It is no honour to God to credit him with poetic coinages such as Homer's words for clashing, twanging or shouting. Poets use such expressions by their own licence, not by some mysterious divine initiation.
sources.quote: What a generous concession does he make to God in investing Him with the inventions of the poetic faculty, so that God may thereby seem to men more sublime and august
sources.raw_question: Does denying that poets invented their words honour God by making him the author of all human vocabulary?

question: How does the Holy Spirit's work as sanctifier differ from his work as comforter?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: As sanctifier, the Spirit comes with power to conquer an unbelieving heart. As comforter, he comes with sweetness to be received by a believing heart. This is why his consolation can be offered and yet refused, as when David's soul "refused to be comforted."
sources.quote: the Spirit as a sanctifier comes with power, to conquer an unbelieving heart; the Spirit as a comforter comes with sweetness, to be received in a believing heart.
sources.raw_question: How does the Holy Spirit's work as sanctifier differ from his work as comforter?

question: Does the apostolic practice of praying and giving thanks to God through Jesus Christ show that the Son is not equal to the Father or not to be equally honoured?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. Because the Son stands to us in the particular character of Mediator, besides what he has in common with the Father, prayers are generally offered through him rather than to him. Yet prayers are also rightly offered directly to him and he is joined with the Father in doxologies, as the ancient Church did.
sources.quote: as the Son stands to us under the particular character of Mediator, besides what he is in common with the Father, our prayers, igenerally, are to be
sources.raw_question: Does the apostolic practice of praying and giving thanks to God through Jesus Christ show that the Son is not equal to the Father or not to be equally honoured?

question: Does referring everything to the Father as first Person and Fountain of all imply two worships, supreme and inferior?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. All worship is one acknowledgment of one and the same essential excellency, considered primarily in the Father and derivatively in the Son. The Persons are personally distinguished but undivided in substance and essentially one.
sources.quote: being all but one acknowledgment of one and the same essential excellency and perfection, considered primarily in the Father, and derivatively in the Son; who, though personally distinguished; are in substance undivided, and essentially one.
sources.raw_question: Does referring everything to the Father as first Person and Fountain of all imply two worships, supreme and inferior?

question: Is the Father's love for the elect a result of Christ's purchase or antecedent to it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: It is antecedent to it. In 1 John 4:9-10 the Father's love is presented as the cause of his sending the Son to be the propitiation. That love therefore comes before all benefits received through Christ, even though its whole fruit is made out only by Christ.
sources.quote: This love, I say, in itself, is antecedent to the purchase of Christ, although the whole fruit thereof be made out alone thereby
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's love for the elect a result of Christ's purchase or antecedent to it?

question: Why does Scripture speak of God in human, anthropomorphic terms if God is not like that?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And That, Although Scripture Often Changes the Divine Appearance into a Human Form, Yet the Measure of the Divine Majesty is Not Included Within These Lineaments of Our Bodily Nature.
sources.answer: Because the prophet spoke of God in parables suited to the stage of faith, not as God is but as the people could receive Him. Such language is to be imputed to the limits of the people, not to God. Just as the tabernacle and temple did not contain God, the limitation lies in the people's perception, not in God.
sources.quote: It is not therefore God who is limited, but the perception of the people is limited; nor is God straitened, but the understanding of the reason of the people is held to be straitened.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture speak of God in human, anthropomorphic terms if God is not like that?

question: Is there a reason or purpose for which the Son exists as Word, as there is for created things?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: No. The Son is the Father's Radiance, and as the Father is but not for any reason, we must not seek a reason for the Radiance. If He had been made for some purpose, that purpose would take precedence over Him and He would be subordinate to it. He is subordinate to no reason for being Word except that He is the Father's Offspring and Only-begotten Wisdom.
sources.quote: For He is the Father's Radiance; and as the Father is, but not for any reason, neither must we seek the reason of that Radiance.
sources.raw_question: Is there a reason or purpose for which the Son exists as Word, as there is for created things?

question: What makes the man Christ Jesus to be a man, and what makes him that particular man?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: The union of soul and body made him a man. What made him that man, without which he would not be that man, is that both soul and body subsist united in the person of the Son of God. His human nature therefore has no subsistence of its own apart from the Son.
sources.quote: That which made the man Christ Jesus to be a man, was the union of soul and body; that which made him that man, and without which he was not the man, was the subsistence of both united in the person of the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: What makes the man Christ Jesus to be a man, and what makes him that particular man?

question: Why does Hebrews 1:2-3 describe the Son as heir of all things, maker of the worlds, and express image of the Father's person before saying that he purged our sins?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: To show that only one possessing this divine dignity could purge sins. The one who purged our sins is the very Son by whom the world was made and the brightness of the Father's glory. He alone was able to do it.
sources.quote: It was he that purged our sins, who was the Son and heir of all things, by whom the world was made, — the brightness of his Father’s glory, and express image of his person; he did it, he alone was able to do it.
sources.raw_question: Why does Hebrews 1:2-3 describe the Son as heir of all things, maker of the worlds, and express image of the Father's person before saying that he purged our sins?

question: Can it be piously said that God once existed by himself without the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then shows, from the instance of Adam and Abel, and other examples, the absence of alienation of essence in the case of the “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. God is not believed to be Father of a Being such that God could be said to have existed alone without it, because the Son is the Father's Light, Life, Truth and Power. Positing a time without the Son would make God once lacking light and power, which is absurd.
sources.quote: for He is not believed to be the Father of a Being such that it may be piously asserted that God once existed by Himself without that Being.
sources.raw_question: Can it be piously said that God once existed by himself without the Son?

question: Do believers hold a distinct communion with the Son, Jesus Christ, as shown in the Song of Songs?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that the whole Song of Songs describes the communion between Christ and his saints. In it Christ gives them refreshment, delight, safety under the banner of his love, and support and comfort in his embrace. To rest in the arms of Christ's love under his constant support and refreshment is plainly to hold communion with him. The relations between Christ and his saints also require such communion.
sources.quote: In brief, this whole book is taken up in the description of the communion that is between the Lord Christ and his saints
sources.raw_question: Do believers hold a distinct communion with the Son, Jesus Christ, as shown in the Song of Songs?

question: Are truths that necessarily follow from what Scripture reveals about the Trinity themselves matters of divine revelation, equally with what is directly stated?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. From truth nothing can follow but what is true, and in the same kind of truth as its source; so whatever is included in or rightly collected from a revealed assertion is itself divine revelation. Thus since Scripture reveals Father, Son and Holy Ghost to be one God, the consequences that they are one in essence and three in subsistences are no less revealed.
sources.quote: For how far soever the lines be drawn and extended, from truth nothing can follow and ensue but what is true also; and that in the same kind of truth with that which it is derived and deduced from.
sources.raw_question: Are truths that necessarily follow from what Scripture reveals about the Trinity themselves matters of divine revelation, equally with what is directly stated?

question: Is it coherent to call the Son 'a creature, but not as one of the creatures' because he excels them in glory?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: No. If He was not before His generation, He has precisely what is proper to all creatures: not existing before origination and subsisting from nothing. Excelling others in glory is merely the ordinary difference found among all creatures, so the formula is unmeaning and blasphemous.
sources.quote: for it is proper to the creatures and works not to be before their origination, and to subsist out of nothing, even though they excel other creatures in glory
sources.raw_question: Is it coherent to call the Son 'a creature, but not as one of the creatures' because he excels them in glory?

question: Does the weakness and corruptibility of human flesh show that God cannot raise it from the dead to incorruption?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter III.—The power and glory of God shine forth in the weakness of human flesh, as He will render our body a participator of the resurrection and of immortality, although He has formed it from the dust of the earth; He will also bestow upon it the enjoyment of immortality, just as He grants it this short life in common with the soul.
sources.answer: No. Those who dwell on the infirmity of the flesh ignore the power of God who raises it. If God could not give life to what is mortal and bring the corruptible back to incorruption, He would not be a God of power. His power is shown by His forming man from the dust in the first place.
sources.quote: For if He does not vivify what is mortal, and does not bring back the corruptible to incorruption, He is not a God of power.
sources.raised_by_detail: those denying the resurrection of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Does the weakness and corruptibility of human flesh show that God cannot raise it from the dead to incorruption?

question: Is the manner of a generation to be known from the intrinsic worth of the one who generates, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He declares falsely that 'the manner of the generation is to be known from the intrinsic worth of the generator'.
sources.answer: No. Taken as a general rule, it would mean there are as many manners of generation as there are differences of worth among parents (Jew, Greek, slave, free, rich, poor), which is absurd. Even granting that man is separated by intrinsic character from brutes, nature brings both into being in the same way, by generation; so difference of dignity does not dictate the manner of birth.
sources.quote: nature brings man and the brute into the world in just the same way, i.e. by generation.
sources.raw_question: Is the manner of a generation to be known from the intrinsic worth of the one who generates, as Eunomius claims?

question: If the Word were a work, would He be brought into judgment along with all other works?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: He would have to be, which shows He cannot be a work. Ecclesiastes says God will bring every work into judgment. The Son is not among those judged; He is Himself the Judge and Lawgiver of all works. Therefore He is not a work but the Father's Word.
sources.quote: if God shall bring the works one and all into judgment, but the Son is not in the number of things put on trial, but rather is Himself the Judge of works one and all, is not the proof clearer than the sun, that the Son is not a work
sources.raw_question: If the Word were a work, would He be brought into judgment along with all other works?

question: In what sense was Christ anointed and sent by the Spirit, so that the Spirit is said to be 'upon' him?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter I. Not only were the prophets and apostles sent by the Spirit, but also the Son of God. This is proved from Isaiah and the evangelists, and it is explained why St. Luke wrote that the same Spirit descended like a dove upon Christ and abode upon Him. Next, after establishing this mission of Christ, the writer infers that the Son is sent by the Father and the Spirit, as the Spirit is by the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Christ spoke as the Son of Man when he said "The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me." He was anointed and sent to preach the Gospel according to his humanity, not according to his Godhead.
sources.quote: And rightly did He say “upon Me,” because He was speaking as the Son of Man. For as the Son of Man He was anointed and sent to preach the Gospel.
sources.raw_question: In what sense was Christ anointed and sent by the Spirit, so that the Spirit is said to be 'upon' him?

question: Why is it reasonable to say of created things 'it was not before it was born' but not of the Son of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Because all time falls within human knowledge and imagination, and every creature has antecedent time before its origin, as a city was preceded by a time when it was not founded. But in the birth of God there is nothing that is not before times eternal, so no prior time exists in which He could be said not to have been.
sources.quote: since in things of God, that is to say, in regard to the birth of God, there is nothing that is not before time eternal: it is illogical to use of Him the phrase “before He was born,”
sources.raw_question: Why is it reasonable to say of created things 'it was not before it was born' but not of the Son of God?

question: Is God good, and how can his goodness be known?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, He is Good, Always the Same, Immutable, One and Only, Infinite; And His Own Name Can Never Be Declared, and He is Incorruptible and Immortal.
sources.answer: Yes, God alone is rightly called good. The whole created world witnesses to it, since he would not have ordained the world unless he were good. Because "everything was very good," the things he made prove that their Maker is good, and the work of a good Ordainer cannot be other than good.
sources.quote: Him alone the Lord rightly declares good, of whose goodness the whole world is witness; which world He would not have ordained if He had not been good.
sources.raw_question: Is God good, and how can his goodness be known?

question: Can God change, increase, or suffer loss?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, He is Good, Always the Same, Immutable, One and Only, Infinite; And His Own Name Can Never Be Declared, and He is Incorruptible and Immortal.
sources.answer: No. Change from one thing to another is a kind of partial death, so a changing God would appear mortal. Any increase would imply he once lacked some perfection, and any loss would imply mortality. Hence God says, "I am God, I change not."
sources.quote: For increasing argues beginning, as well as losses prove death and perishing. And therefore He says, “I am God, I change not;”
sources.raw_question: Can God change, increase, or suffer loss?

question: Can God's proper name be declared or expressed?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, He is Good, Always the Same, Immutable, One and Only, Infinite; And His Own Name Can Never Be Declared, and He is Incorruptible and Immortal.
sources.answer: No. A name signifies what can be comprehended of a thing's nature, but God cannot be grasped even by the understanding. What is beyond the intellect must also be beyond the meaning of any name. The names God uses are not his proper appellation but significations given so that people may seek his mercy.
sources.quote: Whence it results that God’s own name also cannot be declared, because He cannot be conceived.
sources.raw_question: Can God's proper name be declared or expressed?

question: How are God's incorruptibility and immortality related?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, He is Good, Always the Same, Immutable, One and Only, Infinite; And His Own Name Can Never Be Declared, and He is Incorruptible and Immortal.
sources.answer: Each implies the other. Because God is incorruptible he is immortal, and because he is immortal he is incorruptible. They are mutually connected and together extend to eternity, since he suffers neither loss nor ending.
sources.quote: For because He is incorruptible, He is therefore immortal; and because He is immortal, He is certainly also incorruptible,
sources.raw_question: How are God's incorruptibility and immortality related?

question: Does John's statement that the Word was with God and was God imply that Christians worship two Gods?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Hippolytus says he will not speak of two Gods but of one God, yet of two Persons and a third economy, the grace of the Holy Spirit. The Father is one, but there are two Persons because there is also the Son, and a third, the Holy Spirit, and this ordered economy of harmony is led back to one God.
sources.quote: Would one say that he speaks of two Gods? I shall not indeed speak of two Gods, but of one; of two Persons however, and of a third economy (disposition), viz., the grace of the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: Does John's statement that the Word was with God and was God imply that Christians worship two Gods?

question: Can one rightly think of the one God without believing in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Hippolytus says we cannot otherwise think of one God except by truly believing in Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Jews glorified the Father but did not recognise the Son. The disciples recognised the Son but not yet in the Holy Spirit, and so they denied Him.
sources.quote: And we cannot otherwise think of one God, but by believing in truth in Father and Son and Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Can one rightly think of the one God without believing in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Was it the Word, rather than the Father himself, who was sent and manifested among men?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: Yes. Jeremiah speaks of seeing the Word, and Hippolytus says the Word of God alone is visible, so this visible Word must have been sent, and no one other than the Word was sent. Peter confirms this when he says God sent His Word to Israel through the preaching of Jesus Christ. The one made manifest is the Word of the Father, whom the Father sent.
sources.quote: When he speaks of seeing the Word, I must believe that this visible (Word) has been sent. And there was none other (sent) but the Word.
sources.raw_question: Was it the Word, rather than the Father himself, who was sent and manifested among men?

question: Would the Father's begetting many divine attributes such as greatness, goodness and eternity mean he has many co-eternal sons?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > The Son, According to the Apostle, is the Power and Wisdom of the Father. Hence the Reasoning of the Catholics Against the Earlier Arians. A Difficulty is Raised, Whether the Father is Not Wisdom Himself, But Only the Father of Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. It does not follow that naming many attributes yields many sons, just as calling Christ both power and wisdom does not make two sons. In God the power is the wisdom and the wisdom is the power, and likewise greatness and the other attributes are one and the same.
sources.quote: For that certainly is the power which is the wisdom, and that is the wisdom which is the power; and in like manner, therefore, of the rest also
sources.raw_question: Would the Father's begetting many divine attributes such as greatness, goodness and eternity mean he has many co-eternal sons?

question: What should someone do if they cannot understand the equality and distinction of the Persons of the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: They should hold it by faith until understanding is given. Augustine cites the prophet: "If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not understand." Faith comes before understanding.
sources.quote: And if this cannot be grasped by the understanding, let it be held by faith, until He shall dawn in the heart who says by the prophet, “If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not understand.”
sources.raw_question: What should someone do if they cannot understand the equality and distinction of the Persons of the Trinity?

question: In Scripture, does the comparative word 'as' (e.g. 'merciful as your Father') imply equality of nature between the things compared?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. Just as 'be not like horse' does not make us beasts, 'be merciful as your Father' and 'be perfect as your Father' do not make us equal to God, which is impossible for creatures made from nothing. Such comparisons set a pattern for imitation, according to our own nature.
sources.quote: not that we might become as God, did He say, ‘Be ye merciful as your Father,’ but that looking at His beneficent acts, what we do well, we might do
sources.raw_question: In Scripture, does the comparative word 'as' (e.g. 'merciful as your Father') imply equality of nature between the things compared?

question: Why does Christ set the unchangeable unity of the Father and Son as a pattern for human concord?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Because what is natural and unchangeable is a safe model for changeable human conduct. Since the Father and Son's oneness is indivisible and never changes, looking to it lets men keep their agreement true, firm and indissoluble, just as Christ's own meekness is offered for imitation, not equality.
sources.quote: this imitation of natural conditions is especially safe for man, as has been said; for, since they remain and never change, whereas the conduct of men is very changeable, one may look to what is unchangeable by nature
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ set the unchangeable unity of the Father and Son as a pattern for human concord?

question: Does the baptism of Jesus reveal the Trinity?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. All four evangelists record it, and in it the three Persons appear in a dramatic picture that strongly emphasizes the Deity of each. The Spirit descends visibly from the opened heavens, and the Father's voice declares Jesus his beloved Son. Care seems to have been taken that the Son's advent into the world should also be the revelation of the Triune God, preparing men's minds for the divine redemption.
sources.quote: the three Persons are thrown up to sight in a dramatic picture in which the Deity of each is strongly emphasized.
sources.raw_question: Does the baptism of Jesus reveal the Trinity?

question: Does Jesus' claim in Matthew 11:27 that only he knows the Father and only the Father knows him imply equality with God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Jesus' Sonship is unique and involves an absolute community between Father and Son in knowledge and power. The verse declares a perfect mutual knowledge between them that no one else shares.
sources.quote: which involves an absolute community between the two in knowledge, say, and power
sources.raw_question: Does Jesus' claim in Matthew 11:27 that only he knows the Father and only the Father knows him imply equality with God?

question: Are Jesus, Christ, the Only-begotten, the Word, and the Saviour distinct beings, as the Gnostics teach, or one and the same person?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: They are one and the same. Irenaeus holds that those who divide Jesus, Christ, the Only-begotten, the Word and the Saviour into different beings are outside the Christian dispensation, multiplying gods and dividing the Son of God. John's warning against every spirit that 'separates Jesus Christ' and his statement that 'the Word was made flesh' show that the one Jesus Christ is the incarnate Word.
sources.quote: Their doctrine is homicidal, conjuring up, as it does, a number of gods, and simulating many Fathers, but lowering and dividing the Son of God in many ways.
sources.raw_question: Are Jesus, Christ, the Only-begotten, the Word, and the Saviour distinct beings, as the Gnostics teach, or one and the same person?

question: Why does Paul say both that God raised 'Jesus' from the dead and that he raised 'Christ' from the dead?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: Paul foresaw through the Spirit that false teachers would divide the Lord's person. By using both names of the one raised, he removed any pretext for separating Jesus from Christ. The lesson is that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is one and the same.
sources.quote: Do not err, [he says to all:] Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is one and the same, who did by suffering reconcile us to God, and rose from the dead; who is at the right hand of the Father
sources.raw_question: Why does Paul say both that God raised 'Jesus' from the dead and that he raised 'Christ' from the dead?

question: Is worship offered to the Father "in the Spirit" an indication that the Spirit is the true place of worship?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. The spiritual burnt offering is the sacrifice of praise, and it is offered in the Holy Spirit, which is the special place of true worship chosen by God; this is learned from the Lord's words that true worshippers worship the Father in spirit and in truth.
sources.quote: And in what place do we offer it? In the Holy Spirit. Where have we learnt this? From the Lord himself in the words “The true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth.”
sources.raw_question: Is worship offered to the Father "in the Spirit" an indication that the Spirit is the true place of worship?

question: Does the orthodox (Basilian) position hold that the Only-begotten Son is ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Calling the Son ungenerate is as absurd and blasphemous as calling the Father begotten. When we say "Father" we imply a Son, and when we say "Son" we mean he truly is what he is called, shed forth by generation from the ungenerate Light; so the charge is a calumny.
sources.quote: if, when we use the name “Son,” we declare that He really is what He is called, being shed forth by generation from the ungenerate Light, how can the calumny of those who persist that we say the Only-begotten is ungenerate fail to be manifest?
sources.raw_question: Does the orthodox (Basilian) position hold that the Only-begotten Son is ungenerate?

question: Are Jesus and Christ two distinct beings, as the Gnostics (Valentinians) teach, or is the incarnate Son of God one and the same Lord Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVII.—The apostles teach that it was neither Christ nor the Saviour, but the Holy Spirit, who did descend upon Jesus. The reason for this descent.
sources.answer: Jesus Christ is one and the same. The Only-begotten Son, the Word of the Father, became incarnate in man for man's sake and fulfilled all the conditions of human nature, remaining one and the same Lord, as the Lord himself testifies, the apostles confess and the prophets announce. Therefore the Gnostic teachings that divide the Lord's person into Christ and Jesus, or into many Christs, are proved false.
sources.quote: our Lord Jesus Christ being one and the same, as He Himself the Lord doth testify, as the apostles confess, and as the prophets announce,—all the doctrines of these men who have invented putative Ogdoads and Tetrads, and imagined subdivisions [of the Lord’s person], have been proved falsehoods
sources.raw_question: Are Jesus and Christ two distinct beings, as the Gnostics (Valentinians) teach, or is the incarnate Son of God one and the same Lord Jesus Christ?

question: Did God the Word become the soul of Christ's body, so that the Word was absorbed into a human soul and ceased to be God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The Church's faith does not absorb the Word in body and soul; Christ is perfectly God the Word and perfectly Christ the Man. To say the Word turned into a soul by self-humiliation would mean the Word ceased to be God, which is an irreverent and ill-grounded theory.
sources.quote: nor, on the other hand, does it absorb the Word in body and soul. To it He is perfectly God the Word, and perfectly Christ the Man.
sources.raw_question: Did God the Word become the soul of Christ's body, so that the Word was absorbed into a human soul and ceased to be God?

question: Is it an indignity to the Son, or a denial of his equality, that the Unbegotten God is his Father and the source of his being?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. His only-begotten birth from the Unbegotten is what gives him the divine nature. He is not the source of his own being, nor did he bring himself out of nothing. As a living nature born from a living nature, he possesses that nature's power, and by honouring the Father he bears witness to the birth he received.
sources.quote: Or is it an indignity to the Only-begotten God, that the Unbegotten God is His Father, seeing that His Only-begotten birth from the Unbegotten gives Him the Only-begotten nature?
sources.raw_question: Is it an indignity to the Son, or a denial of his equality, that the Unbegotten God is his Father and the source of his being?

question: Are the Holy Spirit and Life inseparable, so that wherever one is, the other is also?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XV. The Holy Spirit is Life equally with the Father and the Son, in truth whether the Father be mentioned, with Whom is the Fount of Life, or the Son, that Fount can be none other than the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord says, "The words which I speak unto you are Spirit and Life." Where the Spirit is, Life is; and where Life is, the Holy Spirit is.
sources.quote: for where the Spirit is, there also is Life; and where Life is, is also the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Are the Holy Spirit and Life inseparable, so that wherever one is, the other is also?

question: Did the New Testament writers regard their Trinitarian conception of God as a departure from or innovation upon the God of the Old Testament?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. They understood themselves as worshipping and proclaiming just the God of Israel, stressing his unity as strongly as the Old Testament. They applied Old Testament passages to Father, Son and Spirit indifferently without misgiving, conceiving Jehovah himself as at once Father, Son and Spirit, and felt no incongruity between their Triune God and the God of the Fathers.
sources.quote: They do not, then, place two new gods by the side of Jehovah as alike with Him to be served and worshipped; they conceive Jehovah as Himself at once Father, Son and Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Did the New Testament writers regard their Trinitarian conception of God as a departure from or innovation upon the God of the Old Testament?

question: What is the relation between the revelation of the Trinity and the work of redemption?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: The revelation of the Trinity was incidental to and the inevitable effect of accomplishing redemption. Those who knew the Father who gave his Son, the Son who gave himself for them, and the Spirit who dwelt in them, knew the Triune God and could not think of God otherwise. The doctrine is the modification wrought in the conception of the one God by his complete self-revelation in the redemptive process, and so had to wait upon that process's completion.
sources.quote: The doctrine of the Trinity, in other words, is simply the modification wrought in the conception of the one only God by His complete revelation of Himself in the redemptive process.
sources.raw_question: What is the relation between the revelation of the Trinity and the work of redemption?

question: Is the Son of God born of the Father as a spoken word, a sound of voice, or as a substantial divine power?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: He is a substantial power, not a mere sound. The Word is not received in the sound of struck air or a voice from the lungs, but is acknowledged in the substance of the power put forth by God. The mysteries of this divine nativity are known to no apostle, prophet, angel or creature, but only to the Son.
sources.quote: who is not received in the sound of the stricken air, or in the tone of voice forced from the lungs, but is acknowledged in the substance of the power put forth by God
sources.raw_question: Is the Son of God born of the Father as a spoken word, a sound of voice, or as a substantial divine power?

question: Does Christ's exclusive knowledge of the Father prove that he is from the Father by true birth rather than by creation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. Christ says he alone knows the Father because he is from him; but if being 'from God' meant being created, all creatures are from God and should likewise know the Father, yet none do. Since the knowledge is peculiar to the Son, his being from the Father must also be peculiar to him, which can only be a true birth from God's nature. Thus a unique knowledge results from a unique birth.
sources.quote: For the reason why He alone knows God is that He alone is from God. You observe, then, a knowledge, which is peculiar to Himself, resulting from a birth which also is peculiar to Himself.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's exclusive knowledge of the Father prove that he is from the Father by true birth rather than by creation?

question: Does the Son's being 'from God' date only from his sending or Advent in the flesh?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. In saying 'I am from Him, and He hath sent Me' Christ makes two distinct statements in logical sequence: first he is born of the Father, then he is sent. This wording debars the heretical assumption that his origin from God began at the Incarnation.
sources.quote: to debar heresy from the violent assumption that His being from God dates from the time of His Advent. The Gospel revelation of the mystery proceeds in a logical sequence; first He is born, then He is sent.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being 'from God' date only from his sending or Advent in the flesh?

question: Was the Only-begotten Son made out of nothing?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Christ tells the unbelievers they do not know whence he is; but if he were from nothing, his origin would be known definitely, as 'out of nothing' is a piece of definite knowledge. Their ignorance of his origin shows that he springs from the unknown Father, the Sender, and so is born of God rather than made from nothing. None who thinks him from nothing can understand that he was born.
sources.quote: If we can say of a thing that it came into existence out of nothing, then we are not ignorant of its origin; we know that it was made out of nothing, and this is a piece of definite knowledge.
sources.raised_by_detail: the blasphemers who say all things are from nothing
sources.raw_question: Was the Only-begotten Son made out of nothing?

question: Does Isaiah 49:5, 'who formed me from the womb to be His servant, to gather together Jacob,' show that the Son had a beginning of existence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: No. He is formed not into existence but in order to gather the tribes, which existed before he was formed. As 'He created' in Proverbs parallels 'He formed' in Isaiah, both are said after 'the Word was' and refer to his taking manhood.
sources.quote: See here too, He is formed, not into existence, but in order to gather together the tribes, which were in existence before He was formed.
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah 49:5, 'who formed me from the womb to be His servant, to gather together Jacob,' show that the Son had a beginning of existence?

question: What role does the will play in uniting the mind's eye with an image held in memory, so that a threefold unity results?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > How This Unity Comes to Pass.
sources.answer: The will is what moves the mind's eye to and fro and joins it, once informed, to the image. When the will turns wholly from the senses to the inner image, the likeness becomes so exact that even reason cannot tell whether a body is seen outside or only thought within. Desire and fear both direct the will, and the stronger they are, the more distinctly the eye is informed.
sources.quote: that will which moves to and fro, hither and thither, the eye that is to be informed, and unites it when formed, shall have wholly converged to the inward phantasy
sources.raw_question: What role does the will play in uniting the mind's eye with an image held in memory, so that a threefold unity results?

question: Do the saints or the Scriptures call the Son a slave, a creature, or something made?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > This third book shows a third fall of Eunomius, as refuting himself, and sometimes saying that the Son is to be called Only-begotten in virtue of natural generation, and that Holy Scripture proves this from the first; at other times, that by reason of His being created He should not be called a Son, but a “product,” or “creature.”
sources.answer: No. Gregory challenges Eunomius or anyone on his behalf to produce a single such phrase from the inspired Scriptures. No such phrase or thought can be found there, so the "use of the saints" Eunomius claims to follow does not exist.
sources.quote: Let him, or some other on his behalf, produce to us one such phrase, and we will hold our peace.
sources.raw_question: Do the saints or the Scriptures call the Son a slave, a creature, or something made?

question: When we hear a proper name such as "Peter," does the name signify the essence or the individual's distinguishing properties?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: It signifies the properties. Basil, quoted by Gregory, says that the name "Peter" does not make us understand the essence or material substratum. It impresses on us the conception of the properties we contemplate in him. Men are identical in most respects and differ only in the special properties seen in individuals.
sources.quote: Thus, when we hear of Peter, we do not by the name understand the essence (and by ‘essence’ I here mean the material substratum), but we are impressed with the conception of the properties which we contemplate in him.
sources.raw_question: When we hear a proper name such as "Peter," does the name signify the essence or the individual's distinguishing properties?

question: Does saying that someone 'became' Lord over others imply that he himself came into existence then?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: No. One who becomes Lord of others comes into possession of beings already existing; so the Word, Framer of all and everlasting King, gained possession of us when He became man. The phrase signifies the after-subjection of all things to Him, not that His essence is a work, just as 'the Lord became a refuge' does not mean God is originate but that His beneficence becomes toward us.
sources.quote: Peter’s language evidently does not signify that the Essence of the Word is a work, but the after-subjection of all things, and the Saviour’s Lordship which came to be over all.
sources.raw_question: Does saying that someone 'became' Lord over others imply that he himself came into existence then?

question: Why was it necessary that redemption be accomplished by one who is Lord by nature rather than by a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: Because, having been created by the Son, if we were redeemed by another we would name another Lord and fall into the Arian and pagan folly of serving the creature rather than the all-creating God. Hence the Redeemer must be the Lord by nature.
sources.quote: it was fitting that the redemption should take place through none other than Him who is the Lord by nature, lest, though created by the Son, we should name another Lord
sources.raw_question: Why was it necessary that redemption be accomplished by one who is Lord by nature rather than by a creature?

question: In what sense is the Word 'created a beginning of the ways for works'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: He is so called because He became man. The Word is first eternally begotten and other than all things. Afterwards He is said to be created when He put on created flesh. In this way, as 'Beginning' and 'First-born from the dead,' He has the preeminence in all things.
sources.quote: the Word, being other than all things and before all, afterwards is created ‘a beginning of the ways for works,’ because He became man
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Word 'created a beginning of the ways for works'?

question: Does the Arian inference from 'become' to 'originate' in the case of the Son lead logically to the absurd conclusion that the Father is also originate?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: Yes. The same terms 'become' and 'He became' are applied in Scripture to God the Father, so if the Arians reasoned consistently they would have to affirm that God is originate. Since this is unthinkable for the faithful, the inference itself must be rejected for the Son as well.
sources.quote: for the course of their argument carries them on to conjecture the same things concerning the Father, as they devise concerning His Word.
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian inference from 'become' to 'originate' in the case of the Son lead logically to the absurd conclusion that the Father is also originate?

question: Should the names "Father" and "Son" in Scripture, such as "This is My Son" and "My Father," be read in their plain meaning or given some other sense?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: They must be read in their plain meaning. No hint of any other meaning is given. The pronoun "My" shows that what follows belongs to the speaker. To empty these words of their sense contradicts both the Father and the Son, and amounts to saying that God lied about Himself.
sources.quote: The pronoun My indicates that the noun which follows belongs to the speaker. What right, I demand, have you heretics to suppose it otherwise?
sources.raw_question: Should the names "Father" and "Son" in Scripture, such as "This is My Son" and "My Father," be read in their plain meaning or given some other sense?

question: Does Scripture's ascription of all divine attributes to Christ establish his unity and equality with the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Since there is one God and none else, a being who possesses all the attributes of essential Deity cannot be a second, lesser being; therefore the ascription of these attributes to the Son establishes his unity and equality with the Father.
sources.quote: not only does Scripture ascribe to Christ all the attributes of essential Deity and thus, seeing there is one God and none else, establish the unity and equality of the Son with the Father
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's ascription of all divine attributes to Christ establish his unity and equality with the Father?

question: Does the Father do his works in the Son only by his own omnipotent energy, without the Son possessing the Divine nature himself?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Christ added 'Believe Me, that I am in the Father, and the Father in Me' to rule out this reading. The Father works in the Son, but the Son also does the Father's works because he possesses the Divine nature as his birthright. That the Father dwells in the Son shows the Father is not alone. That the Father works through the Son shows the Son is not an alien to him.
sources.quote: lest we should believe and say that the Father works in the Son through His own omnipotent energy, and not through the Son’s possession, as His birthright, of the Divine nature
sources.raw_question: Does the Father do his works in the Son only by his own omnipotent energy, without the Son possessing the Divine nature himself?

question: Does the Apostle's statement that all things are of the Father and through the Son, without mentioning the Holy Spirit, exclude the Spirit from the divine work of creation?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: No. Scripture often asserts the power of the Holy Spirit in passages that say nothing of the Father or the Son, leaving them to be understood, so silence about one Person does not exclude Him. What is referred to one Person is also attributed to each, because the Name and the Power of the Three are one.
sources.quote: in how many passages will he find the power of the Holy Spirit asserted, in which Scripture has stated nothing concerning either the Father or the Son, but has left it to be understood?
sources.raw_question: Does the Apostle's statement that all things are of the Father and through the Son, without mentioning the Holy Spirit, exclude the Spirit from the divine work of creation?

question: When a divine operation is attributed to one Person of the Trinity, is it to be understood as the work of that Person alone?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: No. Any divine operation, whether it is ascribed to the Father, the Son or the Holy Spirit, belongs to all Three. Just as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, the love of God is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit. One who is blessed in Christ is blessed in the Name of all Three, because the Name is one and the Power one.
sources.quote: when any divine operation, whether of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit, is treated of, it is not referred only to the Holy Spirit, but also to the Father and the Son
sources.raw_question: When a divine operation is attributed to one Person of the Trinity, is it to be understood as the work of that Person alone?

question: Is a baptism that names the Father, Son and Holy Spirit valid if the person denies or lessens the power of one of the Three?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: No. Baptism is complete only if one confesses the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and to deny One is to overthrow the whole. Even if all Three are named, lessening the power of any of them makes the whole mystery empty.
sources.quote: although you name the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and lessen the power of either the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, the whole mystery is made empty
sources.raw_question: Is a baptism that names the Father, Son and Holy Spirit valid if the person denies or lessens the power of one of the Three?

question: If the Holy Spirit is excluded from the Father's and Son's work because 1 Corinthians 8:6 does not mention Him, does it follow that Christ, called 'over all, God blessed for ever,' is set above the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: Yes, the same reasoning would lead there, and that conclusion is impious, so the reasoning must be rejected. The Father is not counted among 'all things' as if He were one of the crowd of His own creatures. The whole creation is below, and over all is the Godhead of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, which rules and is worshipped by all.
sources.quote: The whole creation is below, over all is the Godhead of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit is excluded from the Father's and Son's work because 1 Corinthians 8:6 does not mention Him, does it follow that Christ, called 'over all, God blessed for ever,' is set above the Father?

question: Does Jesus's appeal in John 10:35-36 to men being called 'gods' prove that he himself is God only in a subordinate or improper sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. Jesus had only insinuated his true deity, and when the Jews charged him with blasphemy he appealed to their Law (Psalm 82:6) merely to show that applying the title God is not always blasphemy, neither affirming nor denying the higher sense. He left the point undecided and kept insinuating his divinity, which enraged them further so that they sought again to seize him. The text therefore yields no inference that he is God only improperly.
sources.quote: he appeals to their Law, in order to shew, that it is not always blasphemy to make one’s self God, or to apply the title of God even to mortal men, and men inferior to himself, considered only as man.
sources.raw_question: Does Jesus's appeal in John 10:35-36 to men being called 'gods' prove that he himself is God only in a subordinate or improper sense?

question: Does Hebrews 1:8-9, where the Son, being called God, has another as his God, prove that the Son is God only in a subordinate sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. Following Hilary, the Father being his God may signify only his subordination as Son, or as God of God, without any inferiority of nature: the Father is his God because he is God by being begotten of him. Alternatively, and probably, the text refers to his human nature, in which case the objection has no weight.
sources.quote: This may signify only his subordination, as a * Son, or as God of God, without any inferiority of nature. The “ Father is his God, as he is God by being begotten of him.”
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1:8-9, where the Son, being called God, has another as his God, prove that the Son is God only in a subordinate sense?

question: Does Scripture contradict itself when it says God judges all the earth but also that the Father judges no man, and does this make Father and Son two judges?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No contradiction. The Father judges all the earth through the Son, to whom he has committed all judgment, and the Son's judgment conforms to the Father's will. So the Father is at once Judge of all and judges no man. Father and Son are neither two judges, nor is either excluded from the authority to judge.
sources.quote: one could not properly say either that They are two judges, or that one of Them is excluded from the authority and power implied in judgment
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture contradict itself when it says God judges all the earth but also that the Father judges no man, and does this make Father and Son two judges?

question: Why does Scripture sometimes name only the Father, or only the Son, as the object of our future blessedness?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: It does so because the Persons are indivisible. Naming one alone is enough, since the one cannot be had without the others. The following context applies the same reasoning to the Holy Spirit. Each Person alone suffices for our blessedness because he cannot be divided from the other two, and our fullness of joy is the enjoyment of God the Trinity.
sources.quote: Finally, on account of this very indivisibility, it suffices that sometimes the Father alone, or the Son alone, should be named, as hereafter to fill us with the joy of His countenance.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture sometimes name only the Father, or only the Son, as the object of our future blessedness?

question: Can the human mind in this life understand why the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father, is not a Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Question Why the Holy Spirit is Not Begotten, and How He Proceeds from the Father and the Son, Will Only Be Understood When We are in Bliss.
sources.answer: Not adequately. In this life reasoning fails to explain it; Augustine admits that whenever he tried to illustrate it through the created image in the human mind, adequate expression failed him, and even his understanding reached only effort, not accomplishment. In the life of bliss the saints will see it without difficulty. There they will see it by contemplation rather than by discursive inquiry.
sources.quote: Nor shall we be inquiring into anything by a mind that reasons, but shall discern by a mind that contemplates, why the Holy Spirit is not a Son, although He proceeds from the Father.
sources.raw_question: Can the human mind in this life understand why the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father, is not a Son?

question: Does Scripture teach that the diverse spiritual gifts (wisdom, knowledge, faith, healings, prophecy, tongues) all come from one and the same Holy Spirit, and what does this show about the Spirit?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Yes. Hilary cites Paul's teaching that there are diversities of gifts, ministrations and workings, but the same Spirit, the same Lord and the same God, and that the one and same Spirit works all these. He holds that this passage, together with Paul's words on adoption and on confessing Jesus as Lord, clearly defines the Spirit's origin, action and powers. He says no doubt about the Spirit can remain after such a clear statement.
sources.quote: Here we have a statement of the purpose and results of the Gift; and I cannot conceive what doubt can remain, after so clear a definition of His Origin, His action and His powers.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that the diverse spiritual gifts (wisdom, knowledge, faith, healings, prophecy, tongues) all come from one and the same Holy Spirit, and what does this show about the Spirit?

question: If every generation comes to an end, must the Son's generation from the Father also have had a beginning and an end?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He further shows that the pretemporal generation of the Son is not the subject of influences drawn from ordinary and carnal generation, but is without beginning and without end, and not according to the fabrications constructed by Eunomius, in ignorance of His power, from the statements of Plato concerning the soul and from the sabbath rest of the Hebrews.
sources.answer: No. Generation that begins and ends is a kind of extension, and all extension is measured by time. Since time has no place in the pretemporal generation of the Only-begotten, no point can be fixed where it begins or where it ceases. It is therefore uninterrupted and without beginning or end.
sources.quote: as time (by which we mark both the end of birth and its beginning) is excluded, it would be vain, in the case of the uninterrupted generation, to entertain the idea of end or beginning
sources.raw_question: If every generation comes to an end, must the Son's generation from the Father also have had a beginning and an end?

question: Do the imperfect statutes of the Mosaic law (the 'statutes that were not good') show that the law was given by a different God from the God whom Christians worship?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XV.—At first God deemed it sufficient to inscribe the natural law, or the Decalogue, upon the hearts of men; but afterwards He found it necessary to bridle, with the yoke of the Mosaic law, the desires of the Jews, who were abusing their liberty; and even to add some special commands, because of the hardness of their hearts.
sources.answer: No. The burdensome ordinances were a servitude suited to Israel's own wish after they turned to the golden calf and longed for Egypt. They did not cut Israel off from God; they placed the people under a yoke of bondage. Ezekiel and Stephen both show that the same God gave this law, adapted to the people's condition.
sources.quote: pointing out plainly, that the law being such, was not given to them by another God, but that, adapted to their condition of servitude, [it originated] from the very same [God as we worship].
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics/Marcionites who ascribed the law to another God
sources.raw_question: Do the imperfect statutes of the Mosaic law (the 'statutes that were not good') show that the law was given by a different God from the God whom Christians worship?

question: Is it consistent with one and the same God that He grants concessions to human weakness in both the Old and New Testaments?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XV.—At first God deemed it sufficient to inscribe the natural law, or the Decalogue, upon the hearts of men; but afterwards He found it necessary to bridle, with the yoke of the Mosaic law, the desires of the Jews, who were abusing their liberty; and even to add some special commands, because of the hardness of their hearts.
sources.answer: Yes. In the New Testament Paul gives precepts 'by permission, not by commandment' because of human infirmity and incontinence, so that people do not despair and fall away from God. So it is no wonder that the same God allowed similar indulgences in the Old Testament. He did this to draw His people toward salvation, keep them from idolatry, and teach them to love Him with the whole heart.
sources.quote: it ought not to be wondered at, if also in the Old Testament the same God permitted similar indulgences for the benefit of His people
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent with one and the same God that He grants concessions to human weakness in both the Old and New Testaments?

question: What does it mean that the Son 'comes in His Father's name', and does it show He shares the divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It means He comes in the name of God. It shows He is not Himself the Father, yet is of the same divine nature, for as Son and God it is natural for Him to come in the Father's name. Rejecting Him is why the love of God is not in them, and He gives life as God does.
sources.quote: He comes in the name of the Father: that is, He is not Himself the Father, yet is in the same divine nature as the Father: for as Son and God it is natural for Him to come in the name of the Father.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that the Son 'comes in His Father's name', and does it show He shares the divine nature?

question: Does the Son's delivering the kingdom to the Father mean that the Son loses or surrenders his rule?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The Father delivered all things and all authority to the Son without ceasing to possess them, so delivery does not imply forfeiture. By the same reasoning the Son does not lose what he delivers to the Father. Only the Dispensation explains how one possesses what was delivered while the other keeps what he gave.
sources.quote: But if the Father did not cease to possess that which He delivered, neither does the Son surrender that which He delivers.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's delivering the kingdom to the Father mean that the Son loses or surrenders his rule?

question: Why did Christ in Acts 1:7 say 'It is not for you to know' rather than repeat that the Son does not know?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be.
