He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: After the resurrection His flesh had put off mortality and been deified. It no longer befitted Him to answer according to the flesh when ascending, so He taught in a divine manner. His words imply 'I know, but it is not for you to know,' which shows that the Son, as the Word, knew the day.
sources.quote: For now the flesh had risen and put off its mortality and been deified; and no longer did it become Him to answer after the flesh when He was going into the heavens; but henceforth to teach after a divine manner
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ in Acts 1:7 say 'It is not for you to know' rather than repeat that the Son does not know?

question: What benefit to believers came from Christ declaring that the Son, as man, did not know the day of the end?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: It protects believers against deceivers. If demons disguised as angels, or Antichrist claiming to be Christ, should speak about the end, believers would disbelieve them. It also keeps people watchful: not knowing the end, or the day of their own death, keeps them ready day by day instead of neglecting themselves in the meantime.
sources.quote: For who, knowing the day of the end, would not be dilatory with the interval? but, if ignorant, would not be ready day by day?
sources.raw_question: What benefit to believers came from Christ declaring that the Son, as man, did not know the day of the end?

question: What is the difference in meaning between glorifying God "in" the Holy Spirit and glorifying God "with" the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Of the origin of the word “with,” and what force it has. Also concerning the unwritten laws of the church.
sources.answer: They are complementary, not opposed. "In" expresses the truth relative to ourselves, announcing the grace that is in us, while "with" proclaims the fellowship of the Spirit with God and so expresses the Spirit's dignity. Therefore both are rightly used in giving glory.
sources.quote: The preposition “in” states the truth rather relatively to ourselves; while “with” proclaims the fellowship of the Spirit with God. Wherefore we use both words, by the one expressing the dignity of the Spirit; by the other announcing the grace that is with us.
sources.raw_question: What is the difference in meaning between glorifying God "in" the Holy Spirit and glorifying God "with" the Holy Spirit?

question: Is the gift of the Holy Spirit to believers, as a Spirit of grace and holiness, something purchased by Christ's death?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit, as a Spirit of grace, holiness and consolation to us, is the great promise of the new covenant, and all the fruits of that covenant are the purchase of Christ's blood. Christ as mediator and surety both satisfied for sin and procured the promise, so the Spirit promised in the covenant is part of his purchase.
sources.quote: Now the Spirit, as unto us a Spirit of grace, holiness, and consolation, is of the purchase of Christ. It is upon the matter, the great promise of the new covenant
sources.raw_question: Is the gift of the Holy Spirit to believers, as a Spirit of grace and holiness, something purchased by Christ's death?

question: What rule of faith should guide the interpretation of Gospel texts about Christ, so that sayings about his weakness are not misread?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: Scripture should be read according to the scope of the Christian faith, which gives a double account of the Saviour. He was always God and the Son, the Father's Word, Radiance and Wisdom. Afterwards, for our sake, he took flesh from the Virgin Mary and became man. The Arians do not know this scope, and so they misinterpret the Gospel texts and stumble.
sources.quote: it contains a double account of the Saviour; that He was ever God, and is the Son, being the Father’s Word and Radiance and Wisdom; and that afterwards for us He took flesh of a Virgin, Mary Bearer of God, and was made man.
sources.raw_question: What rule of faith should guide the interpretation of Gospel texts about Christ, so that sayings about his weakness are not misread?

question: Does the title "Lord" applied to the Only-begotten signify his essence, as Eunomius claims, or his dignity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: It signifies dignity (lordship), not essence. Eunomius simply renames "Lordship" as "essence" and tries to prove it from 2 Corinthians 3:17. Paul, however, never said "the Lord is essence" but "the Lord is the Spirit," so the argument proves nothing unless "Spirit" means essence, which it does not.
sources.quote: Well, if it had been said by Paul, “Now the Lord is essence,” we too would have concurred in his argument. But seeing that the inspired writing on the one side says, “the Lord is the Spirit,” and Eunomius says on the other, “Lordship is essence,”
sources.raw_question: Does the title "Lord" applied to the Only-begotten signify his essence, as Eunomius claims, or his dignity?

question: Would attributing less goodness to the Son or the Holy Spirit than to the Father imply some admixture of evil in them?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: Yes. Whoever introduces the notion of less good into any member of the Trinity must admit some admixture of the opposite quality in whatever falls short of the good. It is blasphemous to imagine this in the Only-begotten or in the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: the man who introduces the notion of less of good into any of the things believed to be in the Holy Trinity must admit thereby some admixture of the opposite quality in that which fails of the good
sources.raw_question: Would attributing less goodness to the Son or the Holy Spirit than to the Father imply some admixture of evil in them?

question: If Christ in the form of a servant is in the glory of God the Father, what does that imply about His state before the Incarnation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It implies that in the form of God He was in the very nature of God. 'In the glory of God' means being in the divine nature. If the incarnate Jesus exists in that glory, then Christ the Spirit before taking flesh certainly abode in the nature of God.
sources.quote: If then, when His form had become that of a slave He abides in such glory, how, I ask, did He abide when in the form of God?
sources.raw_question: If Christ in the form of a servant is in the glory of God the Father, what does that imply about His state before the Incarnation?

question: Would attributing ignorance of the day of judgment to the Son make Him of an imperfect nature, subject to a power stronger than Himself?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes, and this is why the attribution must be rejected. It would make the Lord of glory a discordant and imperfect nature, subject to the necessity of coming yet ignorant of when, and would make God weaker than the power of ignorance which robbed Him of knowledge. The Son born as God cannot possess an imperfect knowledge.
sources.quote: This would make God weaker than the power of ignorance, which took from Him the prerogative of knowledge.
sources.raw_question: Would attributing ignorance of the day of judgment to the Son make Him of an imperfect nature, subject to a power stronger than Himself?

question: Could the Father have withheld from the Son the knowledge of the day of judgment while granting Him knowledge of His passion?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. That would impute defect and malice to the Father, as though He defrauded His beloved Only-begotten of foreknowledge and granted prescience of His death but not of His glory. Such human fickleness cannot be ascribed to God; the Father denies nothing to the Son, since God is love and wholly Father, communicating all that He is to the Son.
sources.quote: or ascribe to Him such taint of human fickleness, that the Father should deny anything to the Son, or the Son, Who was born as God, should possess an imperfect knowledge.
sources.raw_question: Could the Father have withheld from the Son the knowledge of the day of judgment while granting Him knowledge of His passion?

question: Does distinguishing the Light of the Father from the Light of the Son by special attributes, while holding the Light to be common, make God composite?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then, again discussing the true Light and unapproachable Light of the Father and of the Son, special attributes, community and essence, and showing the relation of “generate” and “ungenerate,” as involving no opposition in sense, but presenting an opposition and contradiction admitting of no middle term, he ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Community and specific difference are not the essence itself but accompanying conceptions and attributes, so their conjunction does not render the subject composite. The essence by itself remains what it is in nature, and the simple divine Nature, having nothing to do with quantity, admits no composition or multiplicity of parts merely because some attributes contemplated in it are special and others common.
sources.quote: For our statement does not hereby violate the simplicity of the Godhead, since community and specific difference are not essence, so that the conjunction of these should render the subject composite
sources.raw_question: Does distinguishing the Light of the Father from the Light of the Son by special attributes, while holding the Light to be common, make God composite?

question: Does Eunomius' own calling of the Son "true Light" and the Father "unapproachable Light" imply the very composition he charges against the orthodox?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then, again discussing the true Light and unapproachable Light of the Father and of the Son, special attributes, community and essence, and showing the relation of “generate” and “ungenerate,” as involving no opposition in sense, but presenting an opposition and contradiction admitting of no middle term, he ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes, on his own principles. By giving both the common name "light," and holding that names fit underlying realities and that things with the same name cannot differ in nature, he acknowledges their community. His adding "unapproachable" and "true" then separates that common nature by specific differences. So he must either give up his premises or stop charging the orthodox with what his own language contains.
sources.quote: Accordingly, by the use of a common name, they recognize the identity of the objects signified, since they have already declared that the natures of those things which have the same name cannot be different.
sources.raw_question: Does Eunomius' own calling of the Son "true Light" and the Father "unapproachable Light" imply the very composition he charges against the orthodox?

question: Does Christ's being called Jehovah in his own Person prove that he is God in the strict and proper sense rather than in a relative or improper sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: Yes. Jehovah is a word of absolute signification expressing the divine nature or essence, and it is the incommunicable name of the one true God. Since it is applied to Christ, it follows that he is the same one God: not the same Person as the Father, but the same substance and Being, the same Jehovah revealed as more Persons than one.
sources.quote: since it appears that Christ is, in his own proper Person, called Jehovah, a word of absolute signification, expressing the Divine nature or essence, it must follow, that he is God, strictly so called, and not in the relative or improper sense, as is pretended.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's being called Jehovah in his own Person prove that he is God in the strict and proper sense rather than in a relative or improper sense?

question: Did the apostles call anyone God or Lord other than the one true God the Father and His Word?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XV.—Refutation of the Ebionites, who disparaged the authority of St. Paul, from the writings of St. Luke, which must be received as a whole. Exposure of the hypocrisy, deceit, and pride of the Gnostics. The apostles and their disciples knew and preached one God, the Creator of the world.
sources.answer: No. The preachers of the truth gave the names God and Lord only to the one true God the Father and to His Word, who has pre-eminence in all things. They did not recognise the further deities or powers that the Gnostics posit. So the Word shares the titles of God and Lord with the Father, and no other being does.
sources.quote: termed no one else God, or named him Lord, except the only true God the Father, and His Word, who has the pre-eminence in all things
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles call anyone God or Lord other than the one true God the Father and His Word?

question: What kind of proof would be needed before a reasonable Christian should give up the received doctrine of the Trinity in favour of Arianism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 31: Whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration, on the side of Arianism, ought to move a wise and good man, against so great appearances of truth o
sources.answer: Nothing less than a strict demonstration. Waterland means a chain of clear reasoning that starts from a plain, undoubted axiom and descends by necessary deductions to its conclusion. On the orthodox side stand Scripture, the agreed judgment and practice of the primitive Church, and centuries of supreme adoration paid to Christ, and dread of blasphemy forbids lightly withdrawing that worship. Without such a demonstration these reasons must and ought to sway modest, conscientious people.
sources.quote: a chain of clear reasoning, beginning from some plain and undoubted axiom, and regularly descending by necessary deductions, or close connection of ideas, till you come at your conclusion.
sources.raw_question: What kind of proof would be needed before a reasonable Christian should give up the received doctrine of the Trinity in favour of Arianism?

question: Can the Son consistently be said both not to exist in the strict sense and to be of a composite, non-simple nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. The two claims contradict each other: what is non-existent cannot be called composite, and what is composite cannot be denied existence. Eunomius's opponents must choose one alternative, and their combining both shows their blasphemy grasping at every godless notion.
sources.quote: For one of two alternatives they must choose: if they predicate of Him non-existence they cannot speak of Him as composite, or if they affirm Him to be composite they cannot rob Him of existence.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son consistently be said both not to exist in the strict sense and to be of a composite, non-simple nature?

question: Is the Spirit of Him who raised Christ from the dead a different Spirit from the Spirit of the Christ who was raised?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. The Spirit of the Father, who raised Christ, is no other than the Spirit of Christ, who was raised. When Christ dwells in us, it is not two Spirits that dwell in us but one indwelling Spirit, who is both God's and Christ's. This shows that Father and Son are one in nature.
sources.quote: He is the Spirit of Him Who raised Christ from the dead; but this is no other than the Spirit of Christ Who was so raised.
sources.raw_question: Is the Spirit of Him who raised Christ from the dead a different Spirit from the Spirit of the Christ who was raised?

question: Does the Son's oneness of nature with the Father, together with his dependence on the Father as cause, avoid positing two first principles as in Manichaeism?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ's words teach both the Son's dependence on a cause and the identity of his nature with the Father's. This avoids two diverse principles in the category of cause. If the Son were created yet ranked as a first cause alongside the uncreate, Manichaean dualism would be brought into the Church.
sources.quote: and so the supposition of two diverse principles in the category of Cause is avoided, and there is no loophole for the Manichæan heresy to enter.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's oneness of nature with the Father, together with his dependence on the Father as cause, avoid positing two first principles as in Manichaeism?

question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers hold the eternity and consubstantiality of the Son, or do their principles show them to be on the side of Dr. Clarke's subordinationist view?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: They held the eternity and consubstantiality of the Son and were plainly anti-Arian. Even if Clarke believes their premises imply his conclusions, they should be judged by the consequences they drew themselves, not by disputable consequences drawn for them. They expressly rejected Clarke's consequences and constantly affirmed the Son's eternity and consubstantiality, so they belong to the orthodox side and not to his.
sources.quote: constantly affirming the eternity and consubstantiality of the Son, (the very points of difference between us and the Doctor,) it is plain and obvious to common sense, that the Doctor has no just claim or title to them
sources.raw_question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers hold the eternity and consubstantiality of the Son, or do their principles show them to be on the side of Dr. Clarke's subordinationist view?

question: Can human reason grasp truths about God, such as the mutual indwelling of Father and Son, that seem to contradict the laws of the natural world?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: Human reason cannot solve or find an analogy for such divine truths unaided. Yet reasoning based on divine verities can still establish its conclusions, even when they seem contrary to the laws of the universe. What man cannot understand, God can be.
sources.quote: reasoning based upon Divine verities can establish its conclusions, even though they seem to contradict the laws of the universe
sources.raw_question: Can human reason grasp truths about God, such as the mutual indwelling of Father and Son, that seem to contradict the laws of the natural world?

question: Does Solomon's speech about Wisdom in Proverbs contain prophecy about the Incarnation of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: Yes. Wisdom given by divine illumination cannot come without the gift of prophecy, since perfect wisdom includes knowledge of the future; and Solomon claims his wisdom and words come from God. Hence in this part of Proverbs he is prophetically moved and delivers the mystery of the Incarnation.
sources.quote: So we may see in this passage also Solomon prophetically moved, and delivering to us in its fulness the mystery of the Incarnation
sources.raw_question: Does Solomon's speech about Wisdom in Proverbs contain prophecy about the Incarnation of the Son?

question: Is the Father's love for believers only something purchased by the blood of Christ, or does it originate in the Father himself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: It originates in the Father himself. Christ's blood is the only way by which the Father's love is communicated, but the free fountain and spring of all is in the bosom of the Father. Eternal life was with the Father and is manifested to us, so believers should regard the Father himself as love, not as one made kind only by the Son's purchase.
sources.quote: It is true, that alone is the way of communication; but the free fountain and spring of all is in the bosom of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's love for believers only something purchased by the blood of Christ, or does it originate in the Father himself?

question: In what ways does a believer's faith actually exercise communion with Christ concerning acceptance with God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Chiefly in three ways. The first is meditation: the soul dwells now on its own sinfulness and now on Christ's righteousness, and in times of special burden it goes over the whole work and takes up the peace Christ has won. The second is studying the gospel promises, which set out the excellence and fulness of Christ's righteousness and the exchange made in God's love. The third is daily prayer.
sources.quote: Especially on great occasions, when grieved and burdened by negligence, or eruption of corruption, then the soul goes over the whole work, and so drives things to an issue with God, and takes up the peace that Christ hath wrought out for him.
sources.raw_question: In what ways does a believer's faith actually exercise communion with Christ concerning acceptance with God?

question: If human reason cannot fully explain the visible created order (the heavens, stars, earth), can it comprehend the essence of God who made it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The lower creation that falls under our senses already transcends human knowledge, so the One who by His mere will made the worlds is all the more beyond our apprehension. Only He who made all things in wisdom can give an account of creation, and we understand creation's origin by faith. To think the incomprehensible can be comprehended is vanity and lying madness.
sources.quote: If, then, the lower creation which comes under our organs of sense transcends human knowledge, how can He, Who by His mere will made the worlds, be within the range of our apprehension?
sources.raw_question: If human reason cannot fully explain the visible created order (the heavens, stars, earth), can it comprehend the essence of God who made it?

question: Is it a holy thing and part of Providence that the names of realities, such as 'Ungenerate' for God, are imposed from above by God rather than by humans?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The Prophets never called God by this name of Ungeneracy. God himself did not name the animals he had formed but gave the power of naming to Adam. If naming from above were the holy way, God's own handing of naming to Adam would be unholy, which is absurd.
sources.quote: How, too, is it that the Deity Himself never knew of this kind of holiness, when He did not give names from above to the animals which He had formed, but gave away this power of name-giving to Adam?
sources.raw_question: Is it a holy thing and part of Providence that the names of realities, such as 'Ungenerate' for God, are imposed from above by God rather than by humans?

question: Does Basil's statement that Paul in Philippians 2 sets forth the terms of the Incarnation rather than the mode of the divine existence imply that a man emptied himself to become man, or that the form of the servant existed before time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > He shows the falsehood of Eunomius' calumnious charge that the great Basil had said that “man was emptied to become man,” and demonstrates that the “emptying” of the Only-begotten took place with a view to the restoration to life of the Man Who had suffered.
sources.answer: No. Gregory says there is no connection between the two claims. To say that the Apostle points to the dispensation of the Passion rather than to the mode of the divine existence does not mean the Man born of Mary existed before the coming in the flesh. The charge is a calumny that truth itself refutes.
sources.quote: He is not setting forth to us the mode of the Divine existence, but the terms which belong to the Incarnation.
sources.raw_question: Does Basil's statement that Paul in Philippians 2 sets forth the terms of the Incarnation rather than the mode of the divine existence imply that a man emptied himself to become man, or that the form of the servant existed before time?

question: In the Incarnation, is the Son an immutable, uncreated nature entering mutable creation, or a created being coming to what is kindred with himself?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > He shows the falsehood of Eunomius' calumnious charge that the great Basil had said that “man was emptied to become man,” and demonstrates that the “emptying” of the Only-begotten took place with a view to the restoration to life of the Man Who had suffered.
sources.answer: The Son is immutable and uncreated, and He came to be in what is mutable in order to change it for the better. Gregory argues that Eunomius' view, which makes the Son created, means He came only to what was homogeneous with Himself. On that view He was "emptied" to become what He already was, changing from like to like rather than descending from the transcendent to the lowly. That would ascribe our salvation to a creature rather than to the uncreated God.
sources.quote: he does say that He, being Himself created, came to that which was kindred and homogeneous with Himself, not coming from a transcendent nature to put on the lowlier nature by reason of His love to man, but becoming that very thing which He was.
sources.raw_question: In the Incarnation, is the Son an immutable, uncreated nature entering mutable creation, or a created being coming to what is kindred with himself?

question: Does God's delight in the sons of men after finishing the world (Proverbs 8:31) mean that joy was added to God from his creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: No. God's delight is not something added to him. He rejoices in his works because he sees them made after his own Image. So even this rejoicing is on account of the Son, in whom the Father sees himself.
sources.quote: For even thus He had delight, not because joy was added to Him, but again on seeing the works made after His own Image; so that even this rejoicing of God is on account of His Image.
sources.raw_question: Does God's delight in the sons of men after finishing the world (Proverbs 8:31) mean that joy was added to God from his creatures?

question: Why does Augustine seek trinities in the human mind before contemplating the Trinity that is God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What Has Been Treated of in This Book. How We Have Reached by Steps to a Certain Trinity, Which is Found in Practical Knowledge and True Faith.
sources.answer: To ascend by steps. By seeking a trinity of its own kind in the inner man, in knowledge and wisdom, as earlier in the outer man, the mind is exercised in lower things. It may then come, in its small measure, to contemplate the Trinity which is God, though only in a riddle and as through a glass.
sources.quote: in order that we may come, with a mind more practised in these lower things, to the contemplation of that Trinity which is God, according to our little measure, if indeed, we can even do this, at least in a riddle and as through a glass
sources.raw_question: Why does Augustine seek trinities in the human mind before contemplating the Trinity that is God?

question: Is confessing Christ as Lord with the mouth sufficient if one does not believe in the heart that he is God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then clearly and skilfully criticises the doctrine of the impossibility of comparison with the things made after the Son, and exposes the idolatry contrived by Eunomius, and concealed by the terminology of “Son” and “Only-begotten,” to deceive his readers.
sources.answer: No. The Son must first be believed in the heart unto righteousness and then confessed with the mouth unto salvation. Those who say in their hearts that he is not God, even though they confess him as Lord with their mouths, are corrupt and abominable, as the prophet says.
sources.quote: those who say in their hearts that He is not God, even though with their mouths they confess Him as Lord, are corrupt and became abominable
sources.raw_question: Is confessing Christ as Lord with the mouth sufficient if one does not believe in the heart that he is God?

question: Why can human reason not comprehend the eternal God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Because our knowledge extends only to what is placed before the senses or is posterior in time to the origin of our faculties. Reason cannot project itself into a time before it existed, and even within its limits it lacks certain knowledge of cause and effect; much less can it grasp what existed before it in eternity. God is eternal and unlimited, so His whole being is a depth we cannot examine or penetrate.
sources.quote: How much less then can it go back behind the time when it had its origin, and comprehend with its perception things which existed before it in the realms of eternity?
sources.raw_question: Why can human reason not comprehend the eternal God?

question: Does Paul's preaching of 'Christ crucified' as 'the power of God and the wisdom of God' imply a division between a crucified Jesus and a divine Christ?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Hilary argues that Paul does not divide Christ into a crucified Jesus and a separate Christ who is God's power and wisdom. The same Christ Jesus who was crucified is the power and wisdom of God. This identity is a hidden mystery, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but known to faith by the gift of the Spirit.
sources.quote: Is Christ divided here so that Jesus the crucified is one, and Christ, the power and wisdom of God, another?
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's preaching of 'Christ crucified' as 'the power of God and the wisdom of God' imply a division between a crucified Jesus and a divine Christ?

question: Does attributing incorruptibility to the Father alone imply that the Son is corruptible?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: Yes, on Eunomius's reasoning, which shows its impiety. By ascribing incorruptibility to the Father alone, he places everything after the Father, including the Son, in the category of the corruptible by opposition. He thereby would also subject the Son to all the absurdities he says only the incorruptible escapes, such as having His essence divided and being His own father and son.
sources.quote: when he asserted incorruptibility of the Father alone, he places all things which are considered after the Father in the category of corruptible, by virtue of opposition to the incorruptible, so as to make out even the Son not to be free from corruption
sources.raw_question: Does attributing incorruptibility to the Father alone imply that the Son is corruptible?

question: Is Christ the one who was present with Israel in the Old Testament, so that its law and types point to Him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIV.—If God demands obedience from man, if He formed man, called him and placed him under laws, it was merely for man’s welfare; not that God stood in need of man, but that He graciously conferred upon man His favours in every possible manner.
sources.answer: Yes. The Word himself conferred benefits on Israel and drew up for them a law suited to every class of people. Paul says "the rock was Christ," and the ceremonies of the law were types that led the people from earthly things to heavenly ones and from figures to realities. God needed none of these ceremonies, being always full of all good.
sources.quote: And the Word, passing through all those [men], did liberally confer benefits upon His subjects, by drawing up in writing a law adapted and applicable to every class [among them].
sources.raw_question: Is Christ the one who was present with Israel in the Old Testament, so that its law and types point to Him?

question: Does Gregory of Nyssa deny that the Father is ungenerate and that the Son is generated?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > After much discourse concerning the actually existent, and ungenerate and good, and upon the consubstantiality of the heavenly powers, showing the uncharted character of their essence, yet the difference of their ranks, he ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory affirms that the Father exists without generation and that the Only-begotten God is generated. What he denies is that these terms disclose what either Person is in his own nature.
sources.quote: we do not intend to deny that the Father exists without generation, and we have no intention of refusing to agree to the statement that the Only-begotten God is generated;—on the contrary the latter has been generated, the former has not been generated.
sources.raw_question: Does Gregory of Nyssa deny that the Father is ungenerate and that the Son is generated?

question: Why must "is" be understood with every divine name, such as "just," "incorruptible," or "ungenerate"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > After much discourse concerning the actually existent, and ungenerate and good, and upon the consubstantiality of the heavenly powers, showing the uncharted character of their essence, yet the difference of their ranks, he ends the book.
sources.answer: "Is" points to the underlying subject of which each name is predicated. Without it the epithets would be purposeless and unreal, having no subject to rest on. This shows that each name is an attribute contemplated in the Being and not the Being itself. Gregory illustrates this with David's description of God as "a righteous judge, strong and patient."
sources.quote: if “is” were not understood with each of the epithets included in the phrase, the enumerations of the appellations will seem purposeless and unreal, not having any subject to rest upon
sources.raw_question: Why must "is" be understood with every divine name, such as "just," "incorruptible," or "ungenerate"?

question: Is the flesh that Christ quickens by the Spirit the same substance that died, or something else?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XII.—Of the difference between life and death; of the breath of life and the vivifying Spirit: also how it is that the substance of flesh revives which once was dead.
sources.answer: It is the same substance of flesh. Just as the Lord sought the very sheep that was lost, it is not one thing which dies and another which is quickened. The flesh that lost the breath of life is what the Lord came to quicken, so that as all die in Adam, all may live in Christ by receiving the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: For it is not one thing which dies and another which is quickened, as neither is it one thing which is lost and another which is found, but the Lord came seeking for that same sheep which had been lost.
sources.raw_question: Is the flesh that Christ quickens by the Spirit the same substance that died, or something else?

question: Can the human flesh of Christ subsist on its own, apart from the Word?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. The flesh has its subsistence in the Word, so it could not subsist by itself apart from him. Hence one perfect Son of God was manifested, not two.
sources.quote: Nor could the flesh subsist by itself apart from the Word, because it has its subsistence in the Word.
sources.raw_question: Can the human flesh of Christ subsist on its own, apart from the Word?

question: Is it possible to worship one Person of the Trinity without worshipping the whole Trinity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. The divine nature is the reason and cause of all worship, and that nature is common to all three Persons. So whichever Person is worshipped, he is worshipped as God, and in each act of adoration all three are adored and worshipped.
sources.quote: The divine nature is the reason and cause of all worship; so that it is impossible to worship any one person, and not worship the whole Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Is it possible to worship one Person of the Trinity without worshipping the whole Trinity?

question: What does the sending of a divine Person signify, if not inferiority?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Of the Sensible Showing of the Holy Spirit, and of the Coeternity of the Trinity. What Has Been Said, and What Remains to Be Said.
sources.answer: Sending signifies either the visible manifestation through a created form or the order of origin within the Godhead. It points to the one sent being from the sender, not to any lesser substance. This is shown by the fact that, even if the Father appeared visibly, he could not be said to be sent. That is because he is from no one, whereas the Son is begotten of him and the Spirit proceeds from him.
sources.quote: even if God the Father had willed to appear visibly through the subject creature, yet it would be most absurd to say that He was sent either by the Son, whom He begot, or by the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from Him
sources.raw_question: What does the sending of a divine Person signify, if not inferiority?

question: Why is the consolation given by the Holy Spirit everlasting and strong?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: It is everlasting because it rises from everlasting things: eternal love, eternal redemption, and an everlasting inheritance. It is strong because it comes from him who is strong. Perishing comforts arise only from perishing things.
sources.quote: abiding consolation, which we have by the Holy Ghost, is from things everlasting:— everlasting love, eternal redemption, an everlasting inheritance.
sources.raw_question: Why is the consolation given by the Holy Spirit everlasting and strong?

question: Why did the Church adopt the terms 'three persons' or 'three substances' for the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: Out of the need to speak at length against the errors of heretics. The terms were not meant to signify diversity in God but to deny that God is a single solitary one. 'One essence' conveys the unity, and 'three persons' or 'substances' conveys the Trinity. Some term for 'three somewhats' had to be found, because denying any three was the heresy of Sabellius.
sources.quote: by which names it did not intend diversity to be meant, but singleness to be denied: that not only unity might be understood therein from the being called one essence, but also Trinity from the being called three substances or persons
sources.raw_question: Why did the Church adopt the terms 'three persons' or 'three substances' for the Trinity?

question: Are God's attributes, as manifested in Christ, powerful enough to bring believers to the everlasting enjoyment of God despite every obstacle?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. God gathers the whole covenant of grace into the promise "I will be your God," so that all his attributes become ours, and he declares himself "God Almighty" (all-sufficient), able to remove every difficulty and pardon every sin. This covenant is ratified and confirmed only in Christ's blood, so it is in Christ alone that God is all-sufficient to anyone, and Christ saves to the uttermost those who come to God by him.
sources.quote: in him only is God an all-sufficient God to any, and an exceeding great reward. And hence Christ himself is said to “save to the uttermost them that come to God by him,”
sources.raw_question: Are God's attributes, as manifested in Christ, powerful enough to bring believers to the everlasting enjoyment of God despite every obstacle?

question: Is faith something perceived by the bodily senses, and can one person see faith in another?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Faith a Thing of the Heart, Not of the Body; How It is Common and One and the Same in All Believers. The Faith of Believers is One, No Otherwise than the Will of Those Who Will is One.
sources.answer: No. Faith comes by hearing, yet it is not a sound, a colour, or a bulk; it is a thing of the heart, not of the body. Each person sees his own faith within himself, but he only believes that faith is present in another. He believes this more firmly the more he knows its fruits, which faith works by love. Faith can also be feigned, or wrongly thought to be present where it is not.
sources.quote: Therefore every one sees his own faith in himself; but does not see, but believes, that it is in another; and believes this the more firmly, the more he knows the fruits of it, which faith is wont to work by love.
sources.raw_question: Is faith something perceived by the bodily senses, and can one person see faith in another?

question: In the Son as Word and Image, are being, living and understanding distinct things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Of the Attributes Assigned by Hilary to Each Person. The Trinity is Represented in Things that are Made.
sources.answer: No. In the Son there is prime and absolute life and intellect, for whom to be, to live and to understand are one and the same. He is the perfect Word, lacking nothing, one from one.
sources.quote: to whom it is not one thing to live, another to understand, but to understand is to live, and is to be, and all things are one: as though a perfect Word
sources.raw_question: In the Son as Word and Image, are being, living and understanding distinct things?

question: When Scripture says God 'tells the number of the stars', does it mean that God gains knowledge of things by counting them as humans do?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Counting is how those who lack information measure quantity, and God, who knew all things before he created them, needs no arithmetic to inform him. Scripture uses this language to suit our understanding. It teaches from the part to the whole that nothing unknown to us, however vast, escapes God's knowledge.
sources.quote: For to measure quantity by number is the part of those who want information. But He Who knew all things before they were created needs not number as His informant.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says God 'tells the number of the stars', does it mean that God gains knowledge of things by counting them as humans do?

question: Can Christ's active obedience be counted as part of his sufferings?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: No. Doing and suffering belong to different categories and cannot coincide. Nearly every act of Christ's obedience was accompanied by suffering. Still, considered as willing obedience, it is formally distinct from his sufferings and is called his active righteousness.
sources.quote: Doing is one thing, suffering another; they are in diverse predicaments, and cannot be coincident.
sources.raw_question: Can Christ's active obedience be counted as part of his sufferings?

question: Do the many different names and titles for God in the prophets indicate more than one God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: No. The prophets did not announce one God and then another, but one and the same God under various aspects and many titles. The variety of titles reflects the richness of the Father's attributes, not a plurality of gods.
sources.quote: For the prophets did not announce one and another God, but one and the same; under various aspects, however, and many titles. For varied and rich in attribute is the Father
sources.raw_question: Do the many different names and titles for God in the prophets indicate more than one God?

question: What does Christ's joining of His own name with the Father's in John 17:3 show about His nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eighthly, John xvii. 3. and the Like. Our Lord's divinity cannot interfere with His Father's prerogatives, as the One God, which were so earnestly upheld by the Son. 'One' is used in contrast to false gods and idols, not to the Son, through whom the Father spoke. Our Lord adds His Name to the Father's, as included in Him. The Father the First, not as if the Son were not First too, but as Origin.
sources.answer: It shows that He is of the Father's nature and is true Offspring of the true Father. Had He been a creature He would not have ranked Himself with His Creator. John confirms this in his Epistle, calling the Son 'the True God and eternal life.'
sources.quote: by adding Himself to the Father, He has shewn that He is of the Father’s nature; and He has given us to know that of the True Father He is True Offspring.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's joining of His own name with the Father's in John 17:3 show about His nature?

question: Does God's saying 'I the First and I the Last' support the Arian view that the Son is not first?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eighthly, John xvii. 3. and the Like. Our Lord's divinity cannot interfere with His Father's prerogatives, as the One God, which were so earnestly upheld by the Son. 'One' is used in contrast to false gods and idols, not to the Son, through whom the Father spoke. Our Lord adds His Name to the Father's, as included in Him. The Father the First, not as if the Son were not First too, but as Origin.
sources.answer: No; it rather exposes their error. If 'First' meant ranking God with the things after Him, it would make God precede His works only in time, which is irreligious. Rather it means He is from none, none is before Him, and He is Origin and Cause of all, against Gentile fables.
sources.quote: if it is in order to prove that He is not from any, nor any before Him, but that He is Origin and Cause of all things, and to destroy the Gentile fables, that He has said ‘I the First,’
sources.raw_question: Does God's saying 'I the First and I the Last' support the Arian view that the Son is not first?

question: Since God is perfect Father, must the Son possess all the properties of the Father, including foreknowledge?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. God is simple essence without parts, so as Father He must be Father to the Begotten in all that He Himself is; the perfect birth of the Son makes Him perfect Father. Hence the Son must possess all the Father's properties, and to deny Him one of them, such as prescience, is almost to deny Him all of them.
sources.quote: So, if He is proper Father to the Son, the Son must possess all the properties of the Father. Yet how can this be, if the Son has not the quality of prescience, if there is anything from His Author, which is wanting in His birth?
sources.raw_question: Since God is perfect Father, must the Son possess all the properties of the Father, including foreknowledge?

question: Does the conditional form "If I declare to you the things that happen day by day... the Lord created me" show that Wisdom's being created cannot be meant in a literal, absolute sense?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: Yes. Read literally, the conditional would mean that if Wisdom did not declare the daily things, she would not have been created. That is absurd. So "created" here is tied to a condition and must be understood differently from the plain sound of the syllables.
sources.quote: For he who says, “If I declare, I was created,” leaves you by his silence to understand, “I was not created, if I do not declare.”
sources.raw_question: Does the conditional form "If I declare to you the things that happen day by day... the Lord created me" show that Wisdom's being created cannot be meant in a literal, absolute sense?

question: Does the fact that God gave his only begotten Son to suffer for sin reveal the true demerit of sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. The correction of a slave shows a fault, of a son a great provocation, but of an only son the greatest imaginable. Since God laid sin on the Son of his love and spared him not, it is clear that sin's demerit is such that God cannot let the least sin go unpunished; if he would have spared any, he would have spared his only Son.
sources.quote: Never was sin seen to be more abominably sinful and full of provocation, than when the burden of it was upon the shoulders of the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that God gave his only begotten Son to suffer for sin reveal the true demerit of sin?

question: Can Christ coherently be said to be more than a mere man if he has no divine nature, as the Socinian catechism claims?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: No. If Christ has no nature but that of man, he is as to his nature a mere man and nothing more. The Socinian denial that he is 'purus homo' while also denying his divine nature is incoherent and merely gives a colour to their error, since most of their disputes aim to prove him a mere man.
sources.quote: For to us it seems, that if Christ has no other nature but that of man, he is as to his nature purus homo, a mere man, and no more.
sources.raw_question: Can Christ coherently be said to be more than a mere man if he has no divine nature, as the Socinian catechism claims?

question: Does Christ's receiving gifts from the Father and praying for his disciples (John 17) imply that he is inferior to the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > When the Word and Son hungered, wept, and was wearied, He acted as our Mediator, taking on Him what was ours, that He might impart to us what was His.
sources.answer: No. He receives as an intercessor receives, not out of need but for the sake of those he intercedes for. He took on himself what is ours and gave to us what he received, and he thanks the Father by referring our gifts to himself.
sources.quote: For every one interceding for another, receives the gift in his own person, not as needing, but on his account for whom he intercedes.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's receiving gifts from the Father and praying for his disciples (John 17) imply that he is inferior to the Father?

question: In 1 Corinthians 15:48-49, what do 'the image of the earthy' and 'the image of the heavenly' mean?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter IX.—Showing how that passage of the apostle which the heretics pervert, should be understood; viz., “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.”
sources.answer: The earthy is what God fashioned, that is, the flesh. The heavenly is the Spirit. Without the celestial Spirit people walked in the oldness of the flesh and disobeyed God. By receiving the Spirit they walk in newness of life and obey God, so that the flesh takes on the quality of the Spirit.
sources.quote: What, therefore, is the earthly? That which was fashioned. And what is the heavenly? The Spirit.
sources.raw_question: In 1 Corinthians 15:48-49, what do 'the image of the earthy' and 'the image of the heavenly' mean?

question: Is it acceptable to Christ that believers daily come to him laying their sins on him and receiving his righteousness in exchange?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Nothing delights Christ more than that his saints continually hold communion with him in this giving of sins and receiving of righteousness. It honours him by ascribing to him the work of mediation for which he came, bearing our iniquities, and it endears believers to him so that he has the pre-eminence in their hearts.
sources.quote: There is not any thing that Jesus Christ is more delighted with, than that his saints should always hold communion with him as to this business of giving and receiving.
sources.raw_question: Is it acceptable to Christ that believers daily come to him laying their sins on him and receiving his righteousness in exchange?

question: Does someone instructed only by the Hebrew prophets already know God the Father, so that only the coming of the Son is new to him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXIII.—The patriarchs and prophets by pointing out the advent of Christ, fortified thereby, as it were, the way of posterity to the faith of Christ; and so the labours of the apostles were lessened inasmuch as they gathered in the fruits of the labours of others.
sources.answer: Yes. The Ethiopian eunuch, taught by the prophets, was not ignorant of God the Father or of the right way of life. He lacked only knowledge of the coming of the Son of God, and once he learned it he needed nothing more than baptism. So the God proclaimed by the prophets is the same Father whose Son Christ is.
sources.quote: he was not ignorant of God the Father, nor of the rules as to the [proper] manner of life, but was merely ignorant of the advent of the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Does someone instructed only by the Hebrew prophets already know God the Father, so that only the coming of the Son is new to him?

question: Could one avoid saying that God became Lord in time by arguing that He is Lord of time itself, which did not begin in time?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said of God in Time, is Said Relatively, Not Accidentally.
sources.answer: No. Even granting that point about time, God's lordship over man, who was made in time, plainly began in time. So did His lordship over each of us, over the people of Israel, and over newly grown trees or crops. Being Lord of matter differs from being Lord of a nature newly made from it.
sources.quote: Certainly to be the Lord of man happened to God in time.
sources.raw_question: Could one avoid saying that God became Lord in time by arguing that He is Lord of time itself, which did not begin in time?

question: How does the one Son of God relate to the one Father in the final judgment?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XL.—One and the same God the Father inflicts punishment on the reprobate, and bestows rewards on the elect.
sources.answer: The Son acts as the one Judge carrying out what the Father has prepared. The Father prepared both the kingdom for the righteous and the furnace for the wicked, while the Son receives the worthy into the kingdom and commissions His angels to cast the guilty into the fire, according to God's command. The unity of the Son's judging work therefore shows the unity of the Father who sent Him.
sources.quote: The Father, therefore, who has prepared the kingdom for the righteous, into which the Son has received those worthy of it, is He who has also prepared the furnace of fire, into which these angels commissioned by the Son of man shall send those persons
sources.raw_question: How does the one Son of God relate to the one Father in the final judgment?

question: Did Basil reject the unity of essence between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Basil argued only against unity of Person, which would be Sabellianism, not against unity of essence. Clarke's reading confuses the two.
sources.quote: he misrepresents Basil as declaring against unity of essence, where the good Father intended nothing but against unity of Person.
sources.raw_question: Did Basil reject the unity of essence between the Father and the Son?

question: If the Arians used the same lofty expressions about Christ's divinity as the Ante-Nicene Fathers, does it follow that the Fathers meant no more by those expressions than the Arians did?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. The Arians were practised at dissembling and used such words while meaning little by them. They also adopted these high expressions only by degrees, once their doctrine proved too shocking in plain terms and they needed Catholic language. The Ante-Nicene Fathers were under no such temptation. They were plain, open men who meant what they said and expected to be understood accordingly.
sources.quote: But it can never be shewn that the Ante-Nicene Fathers were under any such temptation; or that they affected to speak otherwise than they really meant, or than they would be generally understood.
sources.raw_question: If the Arians used the same lofty expressions about Christ's divinity as the Ante-Nicene Fathers, does it follow that the Fathers meant no more by those expressions than the Arians did?

question: How should a believer treat truths about the Trinity that the intellect has not yet grasped?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Preface.—The Conclusion of What Has Been Said Above. The Rule to Be Observed in the More Difficult Questions of the Faith.
sources.answer: What has not yet been made clear to the intellect must still not be loosened from the firmness of faith. One should also pray that God open the understanding and remove the inclination to dispute. In that way the mind may discern the truth, which has neither bulk nor movement.
sources.quote: preserving the while this rule, that what has not yet been made clear to our intellect, be nevertheless not loosened from the firmness of our faith
sources.raw_question: How should a believer treat truths about the Trinity that the intellect has not yet grasped?

question: How are believers made one and reconciled to God through Christ the Mediator?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In What Manner We are Gathered from Many into One Through One Mediator.
sources.answer: By believing in Christ, who died sinless in the flesh for us and is now risen, and by rising again with him in spirit through faith. In this way we are justified by being made one in the one righteous One. Cleansed now by faith and later renewed by sight, we are reconciled to God through him as Mediator, so that we cleave to, feast upon, and continue in the One.
sources.quote: that we should be justified by being made one in the one righteous One
sources.raw_question: How are believers made one and reconciled to God through Christ the Mediator?

question: Does Christ's resurrection give believers grounds to hope for their own bodily resurrection?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In What Manner We are Gathered from Many into One Through One Mediator.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine says we should not despair of our own resurrection in the flesh. The one Head has gone before us, the many members, and has already risen in the flesh.
sources.quote: we should not despair of our own resurrection in the flesh itself, when we consider that the one Head had gone before us the many members
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's resurrection give believers grounds to hope for their own bodily resurrection?

question: How does the creature's relation to goodness differ from God's?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: The Godhead lacks no conceivable good, while the creature reaches excellence only by participating in what is better than itself. The creature is therefore always beginning anew, advancing without end. Each good it gains becomes the starting point for a further ascent, as Paul says of reaching forth to what lies before. The divine nature, being always unchanged, admits no contrary. Creatures, being on the boundary line, can incline either way.
sources.quote: For to the Godhead it properly belongs to lack no conceivable thing which is regarded as good, while the creation attains excellence by partaking in something better than itself
sources.raw_question: How does the creature's relation to goodness differ from God's?

question: In what sense is the incarnation, "the Word was made flesh," an act of condescension by God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: In becoming man, the eternal Word performed a majestic condescension that nothing can equal. As the following context explains, he did not empty himself of his Godhead, which is impossible, but of his glory, taking human nature into union with his divine nature so that God and man make one Christ.
sources.quote: “The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.” There is a majestic condescension in these few words that nothing can equal. He was made man.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the incarnation, "the Word was made flesh," an act of condescension by God?

question: Does the phrase 'the right hand of the Power of God' show that the Father is called Power?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter I. The Spirit is the Lord and Power; and in this is not inferior to the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. The one at whose right hand the Son sits is the Father, as Psalm 110 says, 'The Lord said unto My Lord, Sit Thou on My right hand'; so when Christ speaks of sitting at the right hand of the Power of God, He names the Father Power.
sources.quote: He certainly named the Father Power, at Whose right hand the Son sits, as you read: “The Lord said unto My Lord, Sit Thou on My right hand.”
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'the right hand of the Power of God' show that the Father is called Power?

question: Is the divine nature no more mysterious than the nature of God's creatures?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Waterland calls the assertion that the divine nature is no more mysterious than that of creatures shocking and a bold paradox. He says Socinians and Eunomians are forced into it only to keep their position consistent, which counts against the position rather than for it.
sources.quote: Some of our English Socinians have expressed themselves as roundly, upon this head, as any of the ancient Arians or Eunomians; declaring the divine nature to be no more mysterious than that of his creatures. Such assertions are shocking
sources.raw_question: Is the divine nature no more mysterious than the nature of God's creatures?

question: Could God later appoint some other being or creature to be worshipped besides himself?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. The exclusion of all other objects of worship is made unchangeable for all time. Isa. 43:10 says no God was formed before or after him. Deuteronomy says even miracles cannot give credit to anyone introducing another object of worship. The angel did not say "Worship God, and whom God shall appoint."
sources.quote: miracles could not be sufficient to give credit to any one who should pretend to introduce another object of worship, or to set up another god, beside the one supreme God. All creatures whatever are hereby effectually precluded from receiving any religious homage and adoration.
sources.raw_question: Could God later appoint some other being or creature to be worshipped besides himself?

question: Do the reasons Scripture gives for worshipping God alone exclude all creatures?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: Yes. The Old Testament grounds God's exclusive claim to worship in his being Jehovah. He is Creator, Sustainer and Preserver of all things, with no God before or after him. These are properties no creature can share.
sources.quote: the reasons which God insists upon and inculeates, in the Old Testament, why he, and he alone, in opposition to all others, is to be worshipped, are such as exclude all creatures.
sources.raw_question: Do the reasons Scripture gives for worshipping God alone exclude all creatures?

question: Can the Son, who is Wisdom and the Power of God and the giver of grace, advance in wisdom and grace as Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: No. The Word already is Word, Wisdom, Son and God's Power. Angels and men become perfect by partaking of Him. He who supplies perfection and grace to others, and to whom angels ministered at His birth, cannot advance later than they. Wisdom cannot advance in wisdom.
sources.quote: How then does He who to others supplies perfection, Himself advance later than they?
sources.raw_question: Can the Son, who is Wisdom and the Power of God and the giver of grace, advance in wisdom and grace as Word?

question: Is resisting the Holy Spirit's grace the same as resisting God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter X. Being about to prove that the will, the calling, and the commandment of the Trinity is one, St. Ambrose shows that the Spirit called the Church exactly as the Father and the Son did, and proves this by the selection of SS. Paul and Barnabas, and especially by the mission of St. Peter to Cornelius. And by the way he points out how in the Apostle's vision the calling of the Gentiles was shadowed forth, who having been before like wild beasts, now by the operation of the Spirit lay aside that wildness. Then having quoted other passages in support of this view, he shows that in the case of Jeremiah cast into a pit by Jews, and rescued by Abdemelech, is a type of the slighting of the Holy Spirit by the Jews, and of His being honoured by the Gentiles.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter recognized that the message and the grace given to the Gentiles came from the Spirit. Yet he said, "who was I that I should resist God?" This shows that the operation of the Spirit is a divine operation and that the Spirit is God.
sources.quote: Peter, when sent by the Spirit, did not wait for the command of God the Father, but acknowledged that that message was from the Spirit Himself, and the grace that of the Spirit Himself
sources.raw_question: Is resisting the Holy Spirit's grace the same as resisting God?
