question: Does the threefold repetition of Peter's vision signify the Trinity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter X. Being about to prove that the will, the calling, and the commandment of the Trinity is one, St. Ambrose shows that the Spirit called the Church exactly as the Father and the Son did, and proves this by the selection of SS. Paul and Barnabas, and especially by the mission of St. Peter to Cornelius. And by the way he points out how in the Apostle's vision the calling of the Gentiles was shadowed forth, who having been before like wild beasts, now by the operation of the Spirit lay aside that wildness. Then having quoted other passages in support of this view, he shows that in the case of Jeremiah cast into a pit by Jews, and rescued by Abdemelech, is a type of the slighting of the Holy Spirit by the Jews, and of His being honoured by the Gentiles.
sources.answer: Yes. Ambrose holds that the vision appearing three times expressed the operation of the Trinity. The same pattern appears in baptism, with its threefold question and threefold confession. It also appears in Peter's threefold profession of love, which loosed the guilt of his threefold denial.
sources.quote: Notice, also, that the appearance of the mystery three times repeated expressed the operation of the Trinity. And so in the mysteries the threefold question is put, and the threefold answer made
sources.raw_question: Does the threefold repetition of Peter's vision signify the Trinity?

question: Does the scriptural language of 'applying oneself' to God (Deuteronomy 13:4) describe the Son's relation to the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: No. What is applied is applied from without, so such language suits creatures, who are external to God. The Son is not applied or attached to the Father but co-exists with Him as His own.
sources.quote: And the Son is not attached to the Father, but co-exists with Him; whence also Moses says again in the same Deuteronomy, ‘Ye shall obey His voice, and apply yourselves unto Him;’ but what is applied, is applied from without.
sources.raw_question: Does the scriptural language of 'applying oneself' to God (Deuteronomy 13:4) describe the Son's relation to the Father?

question: Is the Word of God in John 1 the same as the 'word of God' preached by prophets and apostles?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Likeness of the Divine Word, Such as It Is, is to Be Sought, Not in Our Own Outer and Sensible Word, But in the Inner and Mental One. There is the Greatest Possible Unlikeness Between Our Word and Knowledge and the Divine Word and Knowledge.
sources.answer: No. The preached word is called God's word because the doctrine it delivers is divine, though it is spread in human languages. What is sought here is the Word of whom it is said 'the Word was God,' 'all things were made by Him,' and 'the Word became flesh.'
sources.quote: which is therefore called the word of God, because the doctrine that is delivered is not human, but divine
sources.raw_question: Is the Word of God in John 1 the same as the 'word of God' preached by prophets and apostles?

question: Is the Father invisible while the Son and Spirit are visible, because the Father appeared only to a dreaming Daniel while Moses saw his visions awake?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Vision of Daniel.
sources.answer: No. Moses did not see the Word, the Wisdom of God, or the Spirit with fleshly eyes, for even the human spirit cannot be seen. Men who sleep are still men, so the Father's appearing in a dream would already contradict 'no man hath seen'. Moreover, he who can fashion a bodily likeness to signify himself in dreams can also fashion a bodily creature to signify himself to people who are awake.
sources.quote: When men sleep, are they then not men? Or cannot He, who can fashion the likeness of a body to signify Himself through the visions of dreamers, also fashion that same bodily creature to signify Himself to the eyes of those who are awake?
sources.raw_question: Is the Father invisible while the Son and Spirit are visible, because the Father appeared only to a dreaming Daniel while Moses saw his visions awake?

question: Does the appearance of three men to Abraham at Mamre count against the view that the Father never appeared to people who were awake?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Vision of Daniel.
sources.answer: Yes. Abraham was awake and serving his guests when Scripture says 'The Lord appeared unto Abraham'. Three men appeared, none of them more prominent, more glorious, or acting with more authority than the others. This tells against confining the appearances to the Son or the Spirit alone.
sources.quote: what do they say of our father Abraham, who was certainly awake and ministering, when, after Scripture had premised, “The Lord appeared unto Abraham,” not one, or two, but three men appeared to him
sources.raw_question: Does the appearance of three men to Abraham at Mamre count against the view that the Father never appeared to people who were awake?

question: Can we determine which Person of the Trinity appeared in each Old Testament theophany?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Vision of Daniel.
sources.answer: Not rashly, and only where the context gives probable indications. The divine nature, substance or essence cannot be seen bodily. We must believe that by means of creatures made subject to God, not only the Son or the Holy Spirit but also the Father may have given intimations of himself to the senses through a bodily form.
sources.quote: we may not rashly affirm which person of the Trinity appeared to this or that of the fathers or the prophets in some body or likeness of body, unless when the context attaches to the narrative some probable intimations on the subject.
sources.raw_question: Can we determine which Person of the Trinity appeared in each Old Testament theophany?

question: If Christ's flesh was sinless, does that mean it was of a different substance from ours?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIV.—Unless the flesh were to be saved, the Word would not have taken upon Him flesh of the same substance as ours: from this it would follow that neither should we have been reconciled by Him.
sources.answer: No. Christ's flesh differs from ours in that it committed no sin and no deceit was found in His soul, but it is not of another substance. Reconciliation requires that the very thing which was at enmity be reconciled. Had the Lord taken flesh from another substance, He would not have reconciled to God the flesh that had become hostile through transgression.
sources.quote: For that thing is reconciled which had formerly been in enmity. Now, if the Lord had taken flesh from another substance, He would not, by so doing, have reconciled that one to God which had become inimical through transgression.
sources.raw_question: If Christ's flesh was sinless, does that mean it was of a different substance from ours?

question: How do Christ's flesh and blood reconcile humanity to God the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIV.—Unless the flesh were to be saved, the Word would not have taken upon Him flesh of the same substance as ours: from this it would follow that neither should we have been reconciled by Him.
sources.answer: By communion with Himself. The Lord reconciled man to the Father by reconciling us to Himself through the body of His own flesh and redeeming us by His own blood. His righteous flesh reconciled the flesh held in bondage to sin and brought it into friendship with God. The apostle testifies in every Epistle that we are saved through Christ's flesh and blood.
sources.quote: by means of communion with Himself, the Lord has reconciled man to God the Father, in reconciling us to Himself by the body of His own flesh, and redeeming us by His own blood
sources.raw_question: How do Christ's flesh and blood reconcile humanity to God the Father?

question: How does Christ's reception of the Spirit differ from ours?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: Upon us the Spirit is poured out in measure, but upon the Lord Jesus in the form of man the Spirit descended and abode, so that the fulness of the Spirit abides in Him for ever. No one besides Christ is capable of receiving the Spirit wholly.
sources.quote: Around us is the liberality of the Giver in abundant provision, in Him abides for ever the fulness of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's reception of the Spirit differ from ours?

question: Can the Spirit poured forth from the mouth of God be considered created?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: No. Just as the Wisdom proceeding from God's mouth and the Word uttered from His heart cannot be called created, neither can the Spirit poured forth from God's mouth. God shows their unity by calling Him 'His' Spirit, so the grace of the Father and of the Spirit is the same.
sources.quote: so, too, the Spirit which is poured forth from the mouth of God cannot be considered to be created, since God Himself has shown their unity to be such that He speaks of His pouring forth of His Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Can the Spirit poured forth from the mouth of God be considered created?

question: In 1 Corinthians 12, what does Paul mean by the 'manifestation of the Spirit' given for what is profitable?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It is the Spirit's gift made visible through the diverse miraculous workings Paul lists. These gifts fulfil the 'promise of the Father' Christ told the apostles to await in Jerusalem. Wisdom, knowledge, faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues and interpretation each make the gift of the Spirit apparent for the profit of believers.
sources.quote: Thus in all these things distributed to each one to profit withal there is the manifestation of the Spirit, the gift of the Spirit being apparent through these marvellous advantages bestowed upon each.
sources.raw_question: In 1 Corinthians 12, what does Paul mean by the 'manifestation of the Spirit' given for what is profitable?

question: Why does it matter for salvation and worship that Christ's sufferings are ascribed to the true Son rather than to a creature or a mere man?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: So that the triumph and the grace come from the Lord himself. Those to whom the sufferings are ascribed are also those to whom the victory belongs. In this way Christians worship no one other than God. They invoke no originate thing or ordinary man, but the natural and true Son from God made man, who remains Lord and God.
sources.quote: we invoke no originate thing, no ordinary man, but the natural and true Son from God, who has become man, yet is not the less Lord and God and Saviour.
sources.raw_question: Why does it matter for salvation and worship that Christ's sufferings are ascribed to the true Son rather than to a creature or a mere man?

question: Is the Son's obedience, as described by Paul in Philippians 2:8, an eternal attribute of his divine nature or something belonging to the time of his incarnation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: It belongs to the incarnation, not to his divine nature. Paul says once for all that he "became obedient" when he came in the form of a servant, emptied and humbled himself in human likeness, to accomplish redemption by the cross. He became obedient for our sakes, to heal human disobedience by his own obedience. Likewise he became "sin" and "a curse" not by nature but by the dispensation of his love for man.
sources.quote: then it was that for our sakes He was made obedient, even as He became “sin” and “a curse” by reason of the dispensation on our behalf, not being so by nature, but becoming so in His love for man.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's obedience, as described by Paul in Philippians 2:8, an eternal attribute of his divine nature or something belonging to the time of his incarnation?

question: Is God to be grasped through rational reasoning about his essence or through faith?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > The tenth book discusses the unattainable and incomprehensible character of the enquiry into entities. And herein he strikingly sets forth the points concerning the nature and formation of the ant, and the passage in the Gospel, “I am the door” and “the way,” and also discusses the attribution and interpretation of the Divine names, and the episode of the children of Benjamin.
sources.answer: Through faith. Faith is the only thing within the compass of our observation. Those who try to measure the incomprehensible by reasoning are like the sons of Benjamin, skilled archers aiming at useless targets who ignored the law and were destroyed. One should give up idle labour about the incomprehensible and hold to the gain found by faith alone.
sources.quote: rather to drop their idle labour about the incomprehensible, and not to lose the gain that is ready to their hand, which is found by faith alone.
sources.raw_question: Is God to be grasped through rational reasoning about his essence or through faith?

question: How are the many scriptural names of Christ properly applied to him, if not as names of his essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They are applied by 'conception' (epinoia), the mental faculty that names God according to his various operations. As the Lord provided for human life in various forms, each kind of his beneficence is fittingly marked by a distinct name. His provident care and working for us passes over into the mould of a name. So the Divine Being is called by various names according to the variety of his operations.
sources.quote: as our Lord provided for human life in various forms, each variety of His beneficence is suitably distinguished by His several names, His provident care and working on our behalf passing over into the mould of a name.
sources.raw_question: How are the many scriptural names of Christ properly applied to him, if not as names of his essence?

question: Does the fact that no sacred writer says Christ's names were given by conception prove that such an account is forbidden?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. If silence proved a thing forbidden, then by parity of reasoning the absence of any prohibition would prove it permitted. No sacred writer forbids regarding these names as the result of conception or calls that view blasphemous.
sources.quote: For if he maintains that its not being mentioned is a proof that it is forbidden, by a parity of reasoning he must admit that its not being forbidden is an argument that it is permitted.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that no sacred writer says Christ's names were given by conception prove that such an account is forbidden?

question: Is God's life without beginning one and the same as his life without end, or are they distinct lives?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They are one and the same life. Gregory holds that the Divine life is one, continuous, infinite and eternal, and no limit bounds it before the ages or after them. Even Eunomius ends up admitting that the same life is without beginning and without end.
sources.quote: For this is just what we say; that the Divine life is one and continuous in itself, infinite and eternal, in no wise bounded by any limit to its infinity.
sources.raw_question: Is God's life without beginning one and the same as his life without end, or are they distinct lives?

question: Does it follow from the Old Testament appearances of Christ or the Holy Spirit that God the Father never appeared in any visible form to the patriarchs and prophets?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > How the Back Parts of God Were Seen. The Faith of the Resurrection of Christ. The Catholic Church Only is the Place from Whence the Back Parts of God are Seen. The Back Parts of God Were Seen by the Israelites. It is a Rash Opinion to Think that God the Father Only Was Never Seen by the Fathers.
sources.answer: No. Many appearances happened in which neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit was expressly named. Yet probable interpretations give some intimations about which Person was meant. So it is too rash to say the Father never appeared in visible forms. Augustine goes on to point to Daniel's vision of the Ancient of Days giving the kingdom to the Son of man.
sources.quote: so that it would be too rash to say that God the Father never appeared by any visible forms to the fathers or the prophets.
sources.raw_question: Does it follow from the Old Testament appearances of Christ or the Holy Spirit that God the Father never appeared in any visible form to the patriarchs and prophets?

question: How does Christ's assuming human nature as first-fruits make God the Father and God of all humanity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He further very appositely expounds the meaning of the term “Only-Begotten,“ and of the term “First born,“ four times used by the Apostle.
sources.answer: Christ took up the first-fruits of human nature and in himself presented it to the true God and Father. The blessing is therefore secured for human nature as a whole: "if the first-fruits be holy, the lump also is holy." Wherever Christ the first-fruits is, there also are those who are Christ's.
sources.quote: Since, then, the first-fruits made the true God to be its God, and the good Father to be its Father, the blessing is secured for human nature as a whole
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's assuming human nature as first-fruits make God the Father and God of all humanity?

question: By whom is the purifying blood of Christ actually applied to the soul so that the believer is made holy?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: It is applied by the Spirit, whom Christ alone dispenses. Upon Christ's intercession it is granted to him to make the fruits of his purchase effectual. Christ's Spirit sprinkles the blood on souls and creates holiness in them, and faith rests in expectation of Christ giving out the Spirit for these ends.
sources.quote: They look upon him as, in his own Spirit, he is the only dispenser of the Spirit and of all grace of sanctification and holiness.
sources.raw_question: By whom is the purifying blood of Christ actually applied to the soul so that the believer is made holy?

question: Could some external cause or necessity prevent the supreme God from giving life to bodies without compromising his supremacy and freedom?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter IV.—Those persons are deceived who feign another God the Father besides the Creator of the world; for he must have been feeble and useless, or else malignant and full of envy, if he be either unable or unwilling to extend external life to our bodies.
sources.answer: No. Any cause that restrained God from exercising his benevolence would be superior to him. His benevolence would then be weak, and he would be the slave of necessity rather than a free agent with his will under his own control. Bodies are clearly capable of receiving life, since they live as long as God pleases, so nothing on their side can be the obstacle.
sources.quote: their Father shall be the slave of necessity and that cause, and not therefore a free agent, having His will under His own control.
sources.raw_question: Could some external cause or necessity prevent the supreme God from giving life to bodies without compromising his supremacy and freedom?

question: Is God the Father of Christ in the same way that He is Father of all creatures?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. God is Christ's Father in two ways: by the birth of God the Word, which belongs to Him as with God in the beginning, and by the constitution of His flesh, since God is Father of all flesh. But God is Father of all flesh not in the same way that He is Father to God the Word.
sources.quote: God was His Father both by the birth of God the Word, and by the constitution of His flesh: for God is the Father of all flesh, though not in the same way that He is Father to God the Word.
sources.raw_question: Is God the Father of Christ in the same way that He is Father of all creatures?

question: Can the First Cause of the universe itself depend on any prior cause?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. If a cause were found to depend on something else, it would not be a first cause. Therefore, if God is the First Cause of the universe, nothing whatever transcends Him.
sources.quote: But if any such cause be found dependent on something else, then it is not a first cause. Therefore, if God is the First Cause of the Universe, there will be nothing whatever transcending this cause of all things.
sources.raw_question: Can the First Cause of the universe itself depend on any prior cause?

question: Can it be shown from Scripture that the Holy Spirit is without sin, as it is said of the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVIII. As he purposes to establish the Godhead of the Holy Spirit by the points already discussed, St. Ambrose touches again on some of them; for instance, that He does not commit but forgives sin; that He is not a creature but the Creator; and lastly, that He does not offer but receives worship.
sources.answer: Yes. Wisdom 7 calls the Spirit in Wisdom "undefiled," and Scripture would be lying about the Son as much as about the Spirit if this were not trusted. Since only God is without sin, the sinless Spirit is God.
sources.quote: The Scripture says He is undefiled, has it lied concerning the Son, that you should believe it to have lied concerning the Spirit?
sources.raw_question: Can it be shown from Scripture that the Holy Spirit is without sin, as it is said of the Son?

question: Does 2 Corinthians 4:6 ('God, who commanded light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts') refer to the Holy Spirit and thereby call the Spirit God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XII. From the fact that St. Paul has shown that the light of the Godhead which the three apostles worshipped in Christ is in the Trinity, it is made clear that the Spirit also is to be worshipped. It is shown from the words themselves that the Spirit is intended by the apostles. The Godhead of the same Spirit is proved from the fact that He has a temple wherein He dwells not as a priest, but as God: and is worshipped with the Father and the Son; whence is understood the oneness of nature in Them.
sources.answer: Yes. Ambrose argues that since the verse speaks of the glory of God (the Father) in the face of Jesus Christ, the remaining agent who 'shined in our hearts' must be the Holy Spirit, since no other can be venerated with the Father and the Son. Thus the Apostle calls the Spirit God, and those who deny the Spirit's Godhead must confess it.
sources.quote: it remains that “He who said that light should shine out of darkness, and shine in our hearts,” be understood to be the Holy Spirit, for we cannot venerate any other with the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does 2 Corinthians 4:6 ('God, who commanded light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts') refer to the Holy Spirit and thereby call the Spirit God?

question: Does the fact that believers are called the temple of the Holy Spirit prove the Spirit's Godhead?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XII. From the fact that St. Paul has shown that the light of the Godhead which the three apostles worshipped in Christ is in the Trinity, it is made clear that the Spirit also is to be worshipped. It is shown from the words themselves that the Spirit is intended by the apostles. The Godhead of the same Spirit is proved from the fact that He has a temple wherein He dwells not as a priest, but as God: and is worshipped with the Father and the Son; whence is understood the oneness of nature in Them.
sources.answer: Yes. Only God has a temple; a creature has no true temple. Scripture says believers are the temple of God because the Spirit dwells in them, and that our members are temples of the Holy Spirit, so the Spirit is God.
sources.quote: Now God has a temple, a creature has no true temple. But the Spirit, Who dwelleth in us, has a temple.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that believers are called the temple of the Holy Spirit prove the Spirit's Godhead?

question: Is the Son merely a mask or a name taken on by a single divine Person who also calls himself the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The Son, who is the Truth, does not deceive us with a theatrical change of names and appearances. He is not one solitary Being who sometimes poses as his own Son and sometimes calls himself the Father. The Father is truly the Father and the Son is truly the Son.
sources.quote: He is not a solitary Being, now posing as His own Son, and again calling Himself the Father; tricking out one unchanging nature with varying names. Far removed from this is the plain honesty of the words. The Father is the Father, and the Son is the Son.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son merely a mask or a name taken on by a single divine Person who also calls himself the Father?

question: Should we speak about God's nature in our own words, or keep to the words God has given in Scripture?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: We should keep to the words God has given. Only the Word of God gives us grounds to reason about divine things; anything else about the Godhead is dark and dangerous. Whoever uses other words either shows his own ignorance or leaves his readers confused. Where Scripture seems obscure, the fault lies in our own reason and our lack of faith.
sources.quote: If any man propose to express what is known in other words than those supplied by God, he must inevitably either display his own ignorance, or else leave his readers’ minds in utter perplexity.
sources.raw_question: Should we speak about God's nature in our own words, or keep to the words God has given in Scripture?

question: Can one substance or being be more than one real person or hypostasis?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland calls the contrary claim, that one substance can be only one real person, the fundamental principle of heresy. Sabellius and Arius both started from it, as Nestorius and Eutyches started from the parallel assumption that two natures could not make one Person. Catholics deny the principle and hold that three real Persons are one divine being.
sources.quote: Both agree in the fundamental principle of heresy, that one substance, or being, can be only one real person, or hypostasis.
sources.raw_question: Can one substance or being be more than one real person or hypostasis?

question: Did Christ, in redeeming humanity, come to what belonged to another God (the creator) rather than to his own creation, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter II.—When Christ visited us in His grace, He did not come to what did not belong to Him: also, by shedding His true blood for us, and exhibiting to us His true flesh in the Eucharist, He conferred upon our flesh the capacity of salvation.
sources.answer: No. Those who say God came to things not his own make his advent unrighteous, as though he coveted another's property. Rather, the Word came to his own handiwork, man made after God's image and likeness, taking possession of his own righteously and graciously rather than snatching another's property by stratagem.
sources.quote: restoring to His own handiwork what was said [of it] in the beginning, that man was made after the image and likeness of God; not snatching away by stratagem the property of another, but taking possession of His own in a righteous and gracious manner.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ, in redeeming humanity, come to what belonged to another God (the creator) rather than to his own creation, as the Gnostics claim?

question: In what way does human knowledge of bodily things differ from that of animals, given that animals also sense and remember bodily things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Man Alone of Animate Creatures Perceives the Eternal Reasons of Things Pertaining to the Body.
sources.answer: Humans exercise reason upon what the senses supply, and animals do not. Animals perceive, remember and pursue or avoid bodily things. Only humans deliberately commit things to memory and revive them by recollection. Only humans combine imagined images and distinguish what merely resembles the true from the true. Above this, the higher reason judges bodily things by incorporeal and eternal reasons.
sources.quote: these acts, and the like, although performed in reference to things sensible, and those which the mind has deduced through the bodily senses, yet, as they are combined with reason, so are not common to men and beasts.
sources.raw_question: In what way does human knowledge of bodily things differ from that of animals, given that animals also sense and remember bodily things?

question: Can the believing mind rise above the generation of the Son and reach the Father beyond the Son's life, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > He then wonderfully displays the Eternal Life, which is Christ, to those who confess Him not, and applies to them the mournful lamentation of Jeremiah over Jehoiakim, as being closely allied to Montanus and Sabellius.
sources.answer: No. Such a view makes the Only-begotten something the mind can climb over, leaving God the Word, who was in the beginning, below it as if he were a creature with a beginning. It also imagines a region where the Only-begotten God is not, which is grovelling and earthly thinking about the Son's Person.
sources.quote: will leave God the Word, Who was in the beginning, below itself, just as it has left below it all other things, and itself comes to be in Him in Whom God the Word was not
sources.raw_question: Can the believing mind rise above the generation of the Son and reach the Father beyond the Son's life, as Eunomius claims?

question: Does cutting the Son off from the Father's nature also cut him off from eternal life?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > He then wonderfully displays the Eternal Life, which is Christ, to those who confess Him not, and applies to them the mournful lamentation of Jeremiah over Jehoiakim, as being closely allied to Montanus and Sabellius.
sources.answer: Yes. On the Eunomian view, eternal life is seen in the Father's essence alone, so alienating the Son from that nature removes him from eternal life. Gregory holds that this is a manifest rejection of faith in the Lord. Those whose hope in Christ reaches only to temporal life are, as Paul says, most miserable.
sources.quote: if these people see eternal life in the essence of the Father alone, and if by alienating the Son from the Nature of the Father they also cut Him off from eternal life, what is this but a manifest denial and rejection of the faith in the Lord?
sources.raw_question: Does cutting the Son off from the Father's nature also cut him off from eternal life?

question: Did the ante-Nicene writers apply the word "God" to the Son in a strict and proper sense, or only in a loose or relative sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: In the strict and proper sense. Novatian argued that the one appearing could not be an angel because he was called God, a title never granted to angels in that sense. He did allow that angels are loosely called gods, but he meant the title in a higher sense when he applied it to the Son. The ancients in general knew nothing of Clarke's relative sense of the word.
sources.quote: here he plainly signifies that the word God, when applied to the Son, is to be understood in the strict and proper sense: and thus the ancients in general understood it.
sources.raw_question: Did the ante-Nicene writers apply the word "God" to the Son in a strict and proper sense, or only in a loose or relative sense?

question: Is everything that is eternal necessarily unbegotten (ingenerate)?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Whatever always exists is eternal, but not everything eternal is unborn. That which is born from eternity eternally has the character of having been born, whereas the unborn is both ingenerate and eternal; so eternity and being begotten are compatible in the Son.
sources.quote: But nevertheless, not everything which is eternal is also not born; since that which is born from eternity has eternally the character of having been born
sources.raw_question: Is everything that is eternal necessarily unbegotten (ingenerate)?

question: Since all human beings who are born once did not exist, must the same hold for the Son of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. It is one thing to be born of someone who once was not, and another to be born of One who always is. A human father was not always a father and so did not always beget, but where the Father is eternal, the Son is eternal; if fatherhood is co-eternal with the Father, sonship is co-eternal with the Son.
sources.quote: It is, however, one thing to be born of some one who once was not, and another to be born of One Who always is.
sources.raw_question: Since all human beings who are born once did not exist, must the same hold for the Son of God?

question: Should Christians answer questions about the Son's generation using philosophical syllogisms, or avoid reason altogether?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Neither simply. Paul warns against philosophy and vain deceit, since syllogistic sophistry can trap the simple into conceding what undermines faith; yet faith is not meant to be bare and devoid of reason. Believers must refute, not merely avoid, human reasonings, using spiritual weapons and heavenly wisdom to cast down arguments raised against God.
sources.quote: The Apostle did not leave us a faith which was bare and devoid of reason; for although a bare faith may be most mighty to salvation, nevertheless, unless it is trained by teaching
sources.raw_question: Should Christians answer questions about the Son's generation using philosophical syllogisms, or avoid reason altogether?

question: Do the human attributes of Christ recorded in the Gospels (receiving power, fear and trouble before the passion, growing in wisdom, asking questions, praying, being forsaken, not knowing the Day) prove that the Son is a creature rather than the Father's true Son, Word, Wisdom and Power by nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: No. Athanasius holds that these sayings belong to the Saviour's human attributes, because the Word did not merely come into a man but became man. He therefore truly had the acts and affections of the flesh while remaining the Father's own Word. He says the Arian argument repeats the Jews' unbelief. The Jews reasoned that a Son of God would not have endured the Cross, and the Arians reason that one who suffered such things cannot be proper to the Father's essence. Both forget the Son's paternal Godhead.
sources.quote: Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh.
sources.raw_question: Do the human attributes of Christ recorded in the Gospels (receiving power, fear and trouble before the passion, growing in wisdom, asking questions, praying, being forsaken, not knowing the Day) prove that the Son is a creature rather than the Father's true Son, Word, Wisdom and Power by nature?

question: Can unaided human logic settle what may be affirmed about the divine unity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Human logic is fallacy before the counsels of God, limited by the feebleness of natural reason. It must recognise its own poverty and seek Divine wisdom before it can understand.
sources.quote: But human logic is fallacy in the presence of the counsels of God, and folly when it would cope with the wisdom of heaven; its thoughts are fettered by its limitations, its philosophy confined by the feebleness of natural reason.
sources.raw_question: Can unaided human logic settle what may be affirmed about the divine unity?

question: Did Tertullian teach that the Son in his highest, divine capacity was ignorant of the day of judgment?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Tertullian understood the Son's ignorance only in respect of his humanity, just as he did the other lowly things listed in the same paragraph, such as the cry of dereliction, which he expressly calls the voice of the man, not of the Word. His teaching elsewhere that the Son is of one undivided substance with the Father puts this beyond doubt.
sources.quote: No reasonable doubt can be made, but that Tertullian understood the Son’s being ignorant, &c. in respect only of his humanity, as well as he understood the other things, mentioned together with it in the same paragraph.
sources.raw_question: Did Tertullian teach that the Son in his highest, divine capacity was ignorant of the day of judgment?

question: Does the subjection of human nature to Christ at the resurrection mean that our nature ceases to exist?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. This subjection is a passing from one nature into another. Our nature ceases only in its present character and is changed into the form of Christ's glorious body. 'Ceasing' here means promotion to something higher, not an end of being.
sources.quote: But by ‘ceasing’ is implied not an end of being, but a promotion into something higher.
sources.raw_question: Does the subjection of human nature to Christ at the resurrection mean that our nature ceases to exist?

question: Can the existence of God as first cause be demonstrated a priori?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. When resolved into plainer terms, the claim means there is a cause prior to the first cause, which is a manifest contradiction.
sources.quote: The eaistence of ὦ first cause is demonstrable, a priori: as it lies under these terms, it seems reducible to case the second; as being sound without sense. But resolve it into this; There is a cause prior to the first; and then the irepugnancy appears.
sources.raw_question: Can the existence of God as first cause be demonstrated a priori?

question: Can necessity of existence be, in order of nature, the antecedent cause or ground of God's existence?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Necessity is a property, and to say a property is naturally antecedent to, and the ground and cause of, the subject that supports it is a manifest contradiction.
sources.quote: A property is, im order of nature, antecedent to, and. the ground and cause of the subject which supports vt ; and the contradiction is manifest.
sources.raw_question: Can necessity of existence be, in order of nature, the antecedent cause or ground of God's existence?

question: When Christ calls himself 'the Beginning' in John 8:25, does he mean he is the beginning of the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > How the Word Beginning (Principium) is Spoken Relatively in the Trinity.
sources.answer: No. By saying he was the Beginning, Christ meant to show himself as Creator. He is the beginning of the creature, just as the Father is the beginning of the creature because all things are from Him.
sources.quote: But is He, pray, the Beginning of the Father? For He intended to show Himself to be the Creator when He said that He was the Beginning
sources.raw_question: When Christ calls himself 'the Beginning' in John 8:25, does he mean he is the beginning of the Father?

question: Can a single relational name like 'Father' carry more than one meaning at once, such as having no cause and having a Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: Yes. Relational names are not confined to one idea of relationship. 'Emperor' signifies both being masterless and ruling over subjects, and it does not lose the second meaning because it has the first. Likewise 'Father' signifies both being without cause and being related to the Son.
sources.quote: the word emperor, in fact, is midway between these two conceptions, and at one time indicates masterlessness, at another the ruling over lower orders.
sources.raw_question: Can a single relational name like 'Father' carry more than one meaning at once, such as having no cause and having a Son?

question: Does saying that God the Father has no father (comes 'from no one') amount to saying that God comes from absolute nonentity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Basil's statement means only that the Ungenerate One is from no father, the word 'father' being implied by the genealogy in Luke, which is a list of fathers. Eunomius illegitimately converts 'no one' into 'nothing at all' and then into 'absolute nonentity.' His syllogism also rebounds on himself: he too must answer that no one is the Father of the Ungenerate, so by his own rule he would be making God come from nonentity.
sources.quote: Whereas, you have transformed “no one” into “nothing at all,” and again “nothing at all” into “absolute nonentity,” thereby concocting that fallacious syllogism of yours.
sources.raw_question: Does saying that God the Father has no father (comes 'from no one') amount to saying that God comes from absolute nonentity?

question: Is the human soul a simple nature like God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > How God is a Substance Both Simple and Manifold.
sources.answer: No. The soul is simpler than the body, because it is not spread out in space but is whole in the whole body and whole in each part. Yet in itself it is manifold. Being skillful, intelligent or retentive of memory are different things in it, as are desire, fear, joy and sadness. These are found some without others, and in greater or lesser degree.
sources.quote: since in the soul also it is one thing to be skillful, another to be indolent, another to be intelligent, another to be of retentive memory
sources.raw_question: Is the human soul a simple nature like God?

question: Can anything changeable be truly simple, and is any creature simple?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > How God is a Substance Both Simple and Manifold.
sources.answer: No. Nothing simple is changeable, and every creature is changeable. Therefore no creature, bodily or spiritual, is truly simple. Only the unchangeable divine substance is simple.
sources.quote: it is manifest that its nature is not simple, but manifold. For nothing simple is changeable, but every creature is changeable.
sources.raw_question: Can anything changeable be truly simple, and is any creature simple?

question: How does Christ make peace between God and sinners?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: In four ways. He removes the cause of the enmity, which is sin and the curse of the law, by atoning for iniquity and being made a curse for us. He destroys the devil, who would prolong the enmity. He makes reconciliation with God by his blood, turning away wrath. Finally, he slays our own enmity, so that we receive the atonement and gain access to the Father.
sources.quote: He takes out of the way the cause of the enmity that was between God and us, — sin and the curse of the law.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ make peace between God and sinners?

question: Does our lack of a name appropriate to God's nature diminish God's glory?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. This inability reflects the poverty of our own nature and is itself evidence of God's glory. As the Apostle teaches, the only name naturally appropriate to God is to believe Him to be 'above every name'. That He transcends every effort of thought and every name proves His ineffable majesty.
sources.quote: the only name naturally appropriate to God is to believe Him to be “above every name.”
sources.raw_question: Does our lack of a name appropriate to God's nature diminish God's glory?

question: Does Christ's promise to ask the Father to send 'another Comforter' imply that the Son alone was not sufficient for the disciples?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: No. The words might seem to imply the Son's insufficiency, but each Person suffices because each is inseparable from the others. The sending of another Comforter does not reveal any deficiency in the Son, any more than texts about the Spirit exclude the Son.
sources.quote: But it may perhaps seem, further, as if the words, “And I will pray the Father, and He shall give you another Comforter,” were so said as if the Son alone were not sufficient.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's promise to ask the Father to send 'another Comforter' imply that the Son alone was not sufficient for the disciples?

question: Does the statement that the Spirit of truth 'will guide you into all truth' mean the Son does not teach all truth, or that the Spirit supplies what the Son could not teach?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: No. If that reasoning held, the opponents would have to say the Holy Spirit is greater than the Son, contrary to their own claim that the Son is less. The text does not say the Spirit alone teaches, so the Son is understood to teach together with Him. Such texts attribute to one Person what belongs to the inseparable Trinity.
sources.quote: Pray, therefore, is the Son here excluded, as if He did not teach all truth, or as if the Holy Spirit were to fill up that which the Son could not fully teach?
sources.raised_by_detail: those who call the Son less
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that the Spirit of truth 'will guide you into all truth' mean the Son does not teach all truth, or that the Spirit supplies what the Son could not teach?

question: Can there be only one intelligent being or person who is absolutely infinite in all respects, so that the Son cannot be infinite as the Father is?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 10: Whether if they (the attributes belonging to the Son) be not individually the same, they can be any thing more than faint resemblances of them, differing from t
sources.answer: No, this is not proven. The objector merely asserts it without any proof. He also admits that two immense, omnipresent beings are possible. If one person's infinite presence does not exclude another's, then one person's infinite power, wisdom and goodness do not exclude another's. Two persons infinite in all respects are as easily conceived as two infinite in any one respect.
sources.quote: And why not as well two Persons infinitely perfect in all other respects, as well as presence?
sources.raw_question: Can there be only one intelligent being or person who is absolutely infinite in all respects, so that the Son cannot be infinite as the Father is?

question: Must two persons with the same individual nature coincide and become one person?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 10: Whether if they (the attributes belonging to the Son) be not individually the same, they can be any thing more than faint resemblances of them, differing from t
sources.answer: No. The objection only holds if 'same individual nature' is taken to mean 'same person', and the orthodox do not use the phrase that way. They hold that more persons than one share the same individual nature. Read rightly, the objection says nothing more than that two persons cannot be one person without becoming one person. That is true but irrelevant.
sources.quote: It is very certain they do not understand the phrase of the same individual nature, as you, who make it equivalent to the same Person, understand it: for they assert more persons than one to have the same individual nature.
sources.raw_question: Must two persons with the same individual nature coincide and become one person?

question: Should God's infinity be understood as infinite spatial extension?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 10: Whether if they (the attributes belonging to the Son) be not individually the same, they can be any thing more than faint resemblances of them, differing from t
sources.answer: Waterland suspends judgment. He does not find it asserted in Scripture or generally held by the Fathers. He also finds it open to rational difficulties he cannot answer, and thinks such questions are too high for our faculties. Even so, anyone who admits two infinitely extended beings cannot reasonably object to the one infinity of three infinite Persons.
sources.quote: such intricate questions are too high for us, and are what our facul-
sources.raw_question: Should God's infinity be understood as infinite spatial extension?

question: If being above all rule, unchangeable and undefiled is ascribed to the Father alone, what follows about the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: It follows that the Son and Spirit would be variable, corruptible and subject to change. This is implied by the very contrast with the Father. But the divine nature, which is above all rule, is constituted by Father, Son and Spirit. Making the Son and Spirit changeable makes them unfit objects of reverence and so destroys faith in them.
sources.quote: If he assigns this property to the Father alone, and if he affirms Him alone to be free from variableness and change, and if he says that He alone is undefiled, the inference that we are meant to draw is plain
sources.raw_question: If being above all rule, unchangeable and undefiled is ascribed to the Father alone, what follows about the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Is the Spirit who rested on the Old Testament prophets the same Spirit who rests on the Christian Church?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: Yes. The Church suffers persecution in a new fashion, just as the ancient prophets did, because the self-same Spirit rests upon her as rested upon them. This continuity of the one Spirit across both covenants supports Irenaeus's claim that one God is the author of both Testaments.
sources.quote: inasmuch as she does indeed, in a new fashion, suffer persecution from those who do not receive the word of God, while the self-same spirit rests upon her
sources.raw_question: Is the Spirit who rested on the Old Testament prophets the same Spirit who rests on the Christian Church?

question: Is God's perfect idea of Himself truly God, so that by thinking of Himself God begets the Son?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. God understands His own essence with perfect clearness, fullness and strength, and in that essence there is no distinction of substance and act. So the idea God has of Himself is absolutely Himself, the divine nature and essence again. Thereby another Person is begotten who is infinite, eternal, almighty and the very same God.
sources.quote: This representation of the Divine nature and essence is the Divine nature and essence again: so that by God's thinking of the Deity must certainly be generated.
sources.raw_question: Is God's perfect idea of Himself truly God, so that by thinking of Himself God begets the Son?

question: In what sense can the Holy Spirit be called the 'Sword of the Word'?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VII. The Son Himself does not judge or punish without the Spirit, so that the same Spirit is called the Sword of the Word. But inasmuch as the Word is in turn called the Sword of the Spirit, the highest unity of power is thereby recognized in each.
sources.answer: The Spirit is the Sword of the Word because Christ slays Antichrist with the Spirit of His mouth. Christ also said He came to bring a sword, since He came to give the Spirit. So the two-edged sword in His mouth is the grace of the Spirit.
sources.quote: For He came that He might give the Spirit; and so there is in His mouth a two-edged sword, which is in truth the grace of the Spirit. So the Spirit is the Sword of the Word.
sources.raw_question: In what sense can the Holy Spirit be called the 'Sword of the Word'?

question: Does Ephesians 6:17, 'the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God', prove that the Son and the Spirit are equal in nature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VII. The Son Himself does not judge or punish without the Spirit, so that the same Spirit is called the Sword of the Word. But inasmuch as the Word is in turn called the Sword of the Spirit, the highest unity of power is thereby recognized in each.
sources.answer: Yes. Here the Word is called the sword of the Holy Spirit, which reverses the image in which the Spirit is the sword of the Word. Ambrose cites the text so that we may know there is no inequality between them, but unity of nature.
sources.quote: And that you may know that there is no inequality but unity of nature, the Word also is the Sword of the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Does Ephesians 6:17, 'the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God', prove that the Son and the Spirit are equal in nature?

question: Does Acts 5:3, where Ananias lies to the Holy Ghost, show that the Holy Spirit as a distinct person can be peculiarly sinned against?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Ananias is said to have lied to the Holy Ghost, not to God taken essentially, which would denote the whole Trinity, but peculiarly to the Spirit. He should have honoured the Spirit in the special gift he professed, and failing this he sinned peculiarly against him; where the Spirit ought to be peculiarly honoured and is not, he is peculiarly sinned against.
sources.quote: Ananias is said to lie to the Holy Ghost, — not to God; which being taken essentially, would denote the whole Trinity, but peculiarly to the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: Does Acts 5:3, where Ananias lies to the Holy Ghost, show that the Holy Spirit as a distinct person can be peculiarly sinned against?

question: Is God's sovereign authority and power a fitting account of the cause of the Father's begetting the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Sovereign authority and power is what accounts for the creation of the universe, its elements, and even beasts and creeping things. To assign the same cause to the begetting of the Only-begotten reduces Him to the level of creatures, which is unbecoming.
sources.quote: the most becoming cause for God’s begetting the Son was His sovereign authority and power, which may be said not only in regard to the universe and its elements, but in regard to beasts and creeping things
sources.raw_question: Is God's sovereign authority and power a fitting account of the cause of the Father's begetting the Son?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's life-giving work show that He belongs to the Godhead?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Proof of the absurdity of the refusal to glorify the Spirit, from the comparison of things glorified in creation.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture attributes giving life to the Father, to the Son, and equally to the Spirit. The Spirit quickens together with the Father and the Son, so He cannot be cut off from His quickening power and ranked with lifeless created nature.
sources.quote: How then shall we alienate the Spirit from His quickening power, and make Him belong to lifeless nature?
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's life-giving work show that He belongs to the Godhead?

question: Does calling the Holy Spirit "the Comforter" (Paraclete), as Eunomius does instead of "Holy Spirit," set the Spirit below the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: No. Scripture applies the title Comforter to the Father, the Son and the Spirit alike. David and Paul say the Father comforts. John's epistle names the Son an advocate, and Christ's promise of "another Comforter" implies he is one himself. So Eunomius cannot lower the Spirit's glory by giving him a title the Father and Son also bear.
sources.quote: he has not been able, even though he wished it, to belittle the glory of the Spirit by ascribing to Him the very attribute which Holy Scripture refers also to the Father and to the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Holy Spirit "the Comforter" (Paraclete), as Eunomius does instead of "Holy Spirit," set the Spirit below the Father and the Son?

question: Whichever sense of παρακαλεῖν (to beseech or to comfort) is meant by "Paraclete," does the title separate the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: No. Scripture assigns both senses to the divine nature. Paul uses the word for God's healing comfort ("God, Who comforteth those that are cast down"). He also uses it for beseeching ("as though God did beseech you by us"). In either meaning, the Spirit shares the title with the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: in whatever way you understand the title “Paraclete,” when used of the Spirit, you will not in either of its significations detach Him from His community in it with the Father and the Son.
sources.raw_question: Whichever sense of παρακαλεῖν (to beseech or to comfort) is meant by "Paraclete," does the title separate the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son?

question: Do scriptural statements that God is the only true, only wise, only good, only Potentate and alone immortal exclude the Son from possessing truth, wisdom, goodness, power and immortality?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. Hilary charges that the heretics insert the word 'alone' as a barrier to cut the Son off from these attributes. But if these attributes belonged to the Father only, it would follow that the Son has neither truth nor wisdom, and is bodily, visible, ill-disposed, feeble and mortal. That conclusion is absurd and impious, so the texts cannot mean to exclude the Son.
sources.quote: if we suppose that these attributes reside in the Father only, and not in the Son also, then we must believe that God the Son has neither truth nor wisdom; that He is a bodily being compact of visible and material elements
sources.raw_question: Do scriptural statements that God is the only true, only wise, only good, only Potentate and alone immortal exclude the Son from possessing truth, wisdom, goodness, power and immortality?

question: Is the essence of the Only-begotten simple or composite?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Simple. Anyone who held him to be multiform and made up of parts could not even grant him the name of Deity. Such a view would drag the doctrine of Christ down to bodily and material conceptions.
sources.quote: If they think that He is some multiform thing, made up of many parts, assuredly they will not concede Him even the name of Deity, but will drag down their doctrine of the Christ to corporeal and material conceptions
sources.raw_question: Is the essence of the Only-begotten simple or composite?

question: Could the Son be a slave by nature and called Lord only in name?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. To say so openly would be a self-confessed impiety needing no refutation, as a man who accuses himself of murder needs no further evidence brought against him. Christ himself says "I am" Lord, not "I am called" Lord. His lordship is therefore not a mere name.
sources.quote: But if they affirm that He is one, and is called the other, that He is by nature slave and Lord in name alone, let them boldly utter this declaration and relieve us from the long labour of answering them.
sources.raw_question: Could the Son be a slave by nature and called Lord only in name?

question: Why should the consent of the early Church be considered alongside Scripture in settling the doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: The consent of the early Church, together with Scripture, gives greater security that Scripture is being interpreted correctly. The universal Church, as far back as records reach, agrees with the main of the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity. Waterland therefore appeals to the Fathers as well as to Scripture.
sources.quote: To them we appeal, as well as to the Scriptures, that, together with Scripture, we may be the more secure that we follow the true interpretation.
sources.raw_question: Why should the consent of the early Church be considered alongside Scripture in settling the doctrine of the Trinity?

question: How could God have been revealed to Moses and the patriarchs if the Son did not exist before the incarnation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: He could not have been. The Father is known only through the Son, as it is written, 'he to whomsoever the Son will reveal Him.' Yet God says he was plainly revealed to the house of Eli's father. Therefore there must already have been a Son to reveal him, and the Son existed before the incarnation.
sources.quote: But if God was revealed, there must have been a Son to reveal, as He says Himself, ‘And he to whomsoever the Son will reveal Him.’
sources.raw_question: How could God have been revealed to Moses and the patriarchs if the Son did not exist before the incarnation?

question: Can the Old Testament texts about the Son be read as merely prophetic of the future while the texts about the Word are read as referring to the eternal past?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No. Both sets of texts must be read the same way. If 'Thou art My Son' refers to the future, so does 'By the Word of the Lord were the heavens established.' Likewise, if 'From the womb' refers to something human, so does 'From the heart.' But if what is from the heart is eternal, then what is from the womb is eternal too.
sources.quote: For if ‘Thou art My Son’ refer to the future, so does ‘By the Word of the Lord were the heavens established;’
sources.raw_question: Can the Old Testament texts about the Son be read as merely prophetic of the future while the texts about the Word are read as referring to the eternal past?

question: Does God the Father acquire his knowledge, as humans do, through bodily senses, testimony of others, or messengers?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Still Further of the Difference Between the Knowledge and Word of Our Mind, and the Knowledge and Word of God.
sources.answer: No. God has no body and needs no messengers or witnesses, since his own perfection enables him to know all things he knows. The angels "bring him word" not that he may learn, but that they may learn from him by consulting his truth about their own works.
sources.quote: or has stood in need of messengers or witnesses that He might know them? Certainly not; since His own perfection enables Him to know all things that He knows.
sources.raw_question: Does God the Father acquire his knowledge, as humans do, through bodily senses, testimony of others, or messengers?

question: Would numbering the Son under the Father (sub-numeration) imply that the Son is of unlike substance, lower rank, and later origin than the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who say that the Holy Ghost is not to be numbered with, but numbered under, the Father and the Son. Wherein moreover there is a summary notice of the faith concerning right sub-numeration.
sources.answer: Yes. Basil holds that applying sub-numeration to the Son revives the impious doctrine of unlikeness of substance, lowliness of rank, and coming into being in later time. By this one term all the blasphemies against the Only-begotten would be set circling again, which he says he has refuted elsewhere.
sources.quote: If, on the other hand, you apply this sub-numeration also to the Son, you revive what is the same impious doctrine, the unlikeness of the substance, the lowliness of rank, the coming into being in later time
sources.raw_question: Would numbering the Son under the Father (sub-numeration) imply that the Son is of unlike substance, lower rank, and later origin than the Father?

question: Can the charge of Tritheism be sustained from reason or the nature of the thing, apart from Scripture?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: Any such pretence is of very slight moment. The divine nature is best known from Revelation rather than from speculation, and Revelation teaches a real Trinity in one God.
sources.quote: If there be any pretence from the nature and reason of the thing itself, it is of very slight moment. The divine nature is best known from Revelation
sources.raw_question: Can the charge of Tritheism be sustained from reason or the nature of the thing, apart from Scripture?

question: Does Scripture ascribe to Jesus Christ the searching of human hearts, which the Old Testament reserves to God alone?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Solomon says that God, 'even Thou only,' knows the hearts of all the children of men.
