Yet the risen Christ declares that all the churches shall know that He is the one who searches the reins and hearts. An attribute Scripture limits to God alone is claimed by Christ, and this shows His coequal Deity with the Father.
sources.quote: All the churches shall know that I am He that searcheth the reins and hearts. – Rev. 2:23.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ascribe to Jesus Christ the searching of human hearts, which the Old Testament reserves to God alone?

question: How can Christ be called 'Lord of all' when the Old Testament says there shall be one Lord, whose name alone is Jehovah?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Christ is called 'Lord of all' because He shares the one universal lordship of Jehovah; He is not a second, rival Lord. Zechariah and the Psalms say there is one Lord, whose name alone is Jehovah, most high over all the earth. The New Testament likewise says there is 'but one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things,' and that He is Lord of all with a name above every name. The sole sovereignty of Jehovah is thus ascribed to Christ.
sources.quote: To us there is but one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by Him. – 1 Cor. 8:6.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ be called 'Lord of all' when the Old Testament says there shall be one Lord, whose name alone is Jehovah?

question: Why does Scripture's command to love God imply that the mind also remembers and understands God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Mind Loves God in Rightly Loving Itself; And If It Love Not God, It Must Be Said to Hate Itself. Even a Weak and Erring Mind is Always Strong in Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself. Let It Be Turned to God, that It May Be Blessed by Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Him.
sources.answer: Because love presupposes the other two. No one loves what he does not remember or what he is wholly ignorant of, so where love of God is commanded, memory and understanding of God are understood by consequence. Thus the image of the trinity in the mind (memory, understanding, love) is directed toward God through love.
sources.quote: For in it, those other two [namely, memory and understanding] are understood by consequence, inasmuch as no one loves that which he does not remember, or of which he is wholly ignorant.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture's command to love God imply that the mind also remembers and understands God?

question: Is the grace of believers' acceptance with God the work of one divine Person only, or of all three Persons of the Trinity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: It is the work of all three Persons, each in a distinct way. It is the great product of the Father's righteousness, wisdom, love and grace; the fruit of the Son's love and condescension; and the great discovery of the Holy Ghost in revealing the mystery of the gospel.
sources.quote: The great product it is of the Father’s righteousness, wisdom, love, and grace; — the great and astonishable fruit of the love and condescension of the Son; — the great discovery of the Holy Ghost in the revelation of the mystery of the gospel.
sources.raw_question: Is the grace of believers' acceptance with God the work of one divine Person only, or of all three Persons of the Trinity?

question: Is human incorruptibility or immortality something man possesses by nature?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XX.—God showed himself, by the fall of man, as patient, benign, merciful, mighty to save. Man is therefore most ungrateful, if, unmindful of his own lot, and of the benefits held out to him, he do not acknowledge divine grace.
sources.answer: No. Incorruptibility is a gift received from God, not man's own by nature. To think otherwise is the error Satan induced, making man boast as if he were naturally like God. Through the fall and redemption man learns that he is mortal and weak, while God is so powerful as to confer immortality on what is mortal.
sources.quote: supposing that the incorruptibility which belongs to him is his own naturally, and by thus not holding the truth, should boast with empty superciliousness, as if he were naturally like to God
sources.raw_question: Is human incorruptibility or immortality something man possesses by nature?

question: Can the individual divine attributes, such as omniscience and ubiquity, be communicated to another without the divine essence in which they subsist?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: No. The individual divine attributes are inseparable from the individual divine nature and cannot be communicated without it. Waterland notes that his opponent concedes this, which clarifies that Dr. Clarke's talk of the Son receiving 'all divine powers' cannot mean the very individual attributes of the Father apart from his essence.
sources.quote: You agree with me, that the individual divine attributes cannot be communicated without the individual nature in which they subsist.
sources.raw_question: Can the individual divine attributes, such as omniscience and ubiquity, be communicated to another without the divine essence in which they subsist?

question: What does Paul's language of "height, depth, breadth and length" in Ephesians signify about the power of the Crucified Christ?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: Gregory reads it as describing the figure of the Cross. The upper arm is height, the lower arm is depth, and the cross-beam is length and breadth. Through this figure Paul shows that things in heaven, things under the earth, and all the bounds of what exists are ruled and held together by Christ. The Cross therefore displays his universal divine power.
sources.quote: all the furthest bounds of the things that are, are ruled and sustained by Him Who gave an example of this unspeakable and mighty power in the figure of the Cross
sources.raw_question: What does Paul's language of "height, depth, breadth and length" in Ephesians signify about the power of the Crucified Christ?

question: Does the Holy Spirit share God's prerogative of searching the hearts of men?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIX. Having proved above that the Spirit abides and speaks in the prophets, St. Ambrose infers that He knows all things which are of God, and therefore is One with the Father and the Son. This same point he establishes again from the fact that He possesses all that God possesses, namely, Godhead, knowledge of the heart, truth, a Name above every name, and power to raise the dead, as is proved from Ezekiel, and in this He is equal to the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. God searches the hearts and reins, and the Son knew men's thoughts. The Spirit reveals to the prophets the secrets of others' hearts. It is no wonder that He searches the hidden things of man, since He searches even the deep things of God.
sources.quote: And why do we wonder if He searches the hidden things of man Who searches even the deep things of God?
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit share God's prerogative of searching the hearts of men?

question: Does the Holy Spirit share God's prerogative of raising the dead?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIX. Having proved above that the Spirit abides and speaks in the prophets, St. Ambrose infers that He knows all things which are of God, and therefore is One with the Father and the Son. This same point he establishes again from the fact that He possesses all that God possesses, namely, Godhead, knowledge of the heart, truth, a Name above every name, and power to raise the dead, as is proved from Ezekiel, and in this He is equal to the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father and the Son raise and quicken the dead, and Paul says God will quicken our mortal bodies through His Spirit. Ezekiel shows the Spirit breathing life into the dry bones. The likeness of this work to Christ's raising of the dead at His Passion shows the oneness of divine power.
sources.quote: Do we not in the likeness of what is done recognize the oneness of the divine power?
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit share God's prerogative of raising the dead?

question: Does the fact that Israel believed in Moses, a mere man, show that belief in the Holy Spirit is no proof of the Spirit's divinity?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Objection that some were baptized unto Moses and believed in him, and an answer to it; with remarks upon types.
sources.answer: No. If the opponents' reasoning held, it would rather weaken faith in God Himself, since Scripture says the people "believed the Lord and his servant Moses," joining Moses with God, not with the Spirit. Moses was a type of Christ the Mediator, so faith in Moses is referred to the Lord, and faith in the Lord is not made a trifle because it was foreshadowed through Moses.
sources.quote: belief in Moses not only does not show our belief in the Spirit to be worthless, but, if we adopt our opponents’ line of argument, it rather weakens our confession in the God of the universe.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Israel believed in Moses, a mere man, show that belief in the Holy Spirit is no proof of the Spirit's divinity?

question: Does Scripture distinguish between sovereign and inferior religious vows or oaths, so that lesser ones may be directed to creatures?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. Scripture says nothing of sovereign and inferior, absolute and relative vows. Swearing by God's name is plain and well understood. Any swearing that falls short of sovereign respect would be little better than profaneness.
sources.quote: We read nothing of sovereign and inferior, absolute and relative vows; that we should imagine supreme vows to be appropriate to God, inferior permitted to angels, or idols or to any creature.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture distinguish between sovereign and inferior religious vows or oaths, so that lesser ones may be directed to creatures?

question: Why was it fitting that God's Lordship be shown and redemption accomplished through the Word made flesh rather than through a mere man?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: Because if a mere man were our Lord, we would become worshippers of man. Since men would not acknowledge God through His Word, God showed His Lordship in man by having the Word Himself become flesh, so that in Jesus we acknowledge as Lord both the Son and through Him the Father.
sources.quote: But to do this by a mere man beseemed not; lest, having man for our Lord, we should become worshippers of man.
sources.raw_question: Why was it fitting that God's Lordship be shown and redemption accomplished through the Word made flesh rather than through a mere man?

question: Did Jesus teach that he is the divine Son of God and not a mere man, according to John 10:35-36?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ taught the Jews that God had come among them: if Scripture calls 'gods' those to whom the word of God came, he whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world is not blaspheming in calling himself the Son of God.
sources.quote: and the rest of the Jews that God was come among them, saying, ‘If He called them gods to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken, say ye of Him whom the Father hath sanctified
sources.raw_question: Did Jesus teach that he is the divine Son of God and not a mere man, according to John 10:35-36?

question: Does the Holy Spirit stand above every creature, including the angels?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XVI. The Holy Spirit is that large river by which the mystical Jerusalem is watered. It is equal to its Fount, that is, the Father and the Son, as is signified in holy Scripture. St. Ambrose himself thirsts for that water, and warns us that in order to preserve it within us, we must avoid the devil, lust, and heresy, since our vessels are frail, and that broken cisterns must be forsaken, that after the example of the Samaritan woman and of the patriarchs we may find the water of the Lord.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit rises above every creature. He waters the heavenly Jerusalem and flows more abundantly among the Thrones, Dominions, Powers, Angels and Archangels, gladdening them with the fertility of his sanctification. Creatures receive sanctification from the Spirit, so the Spirit is the sanctifier rather than one of the sanctified.
sources.quote: how much more does the Spirit, rising above every creature, when He touches the as it were low-lying fields of our minds, make glad that heavenly nature of the creatures with the larger fertility of His sanctification.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit stand above every creature, including the angels?

question: Does generation of spiritual beings as separate individuals, in the way one man is born from another, imply bodily rather than spiritual existence?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus argues that such separate generation means each being is wholly separated from the others. Each would have its own shape, its own sphere of action and a particular size. These are qualities characteristic of a body, not of a spirit. So those who teach such production cannot call their Pleroma spiritual.
sources.quote: each having a distinct shape of his own, and a definite sphere of action, while each one of them, too, is formed of a particular size, —qualities characteristic of a body, and not of a spirit
sources.raw_question: Does generation of spiritual beings as separate individuals, in the way one man is born from another, imply bodily rather than spiritual existence?

question: Does Romans 8:11 show all three Persons of the Trinity distinctly concurring in the work of quickening believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. In this one verse all three are comprised, each with a distinct concurrence. The Father quickens authoritatively, since he raised Christ and will quicken us. The Son quickens mediatorially, since it is done through Christ's death. The Spirit quickens by immediate efficacy, as the one who dwells in us. This distinct concurrence proves that believers have distinct communion with each Person.
sources.quote: Here are all three comprised, with their distinct concurrence unto our quickening. Here is the Father’s authoritative quickening, — “He raised Christ from the dead, and he shall quicken you;” and the Son’s mediatory quickening
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 8:11 show all three Persons of the Trinity distinctly concurring in the work of quickening believers?

question: Is God bound by the laws of nature, so that what is impossible in nature is impossible for Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. We must set no bounds to God's boundless majesty and power, nor tie the Lord of nature down to nature's laws. What seems impossible to human apprehension is no limit on the Creator.
sources.quote: setting no bounds to boundless majesty and power, nor tying the Lord of nature down to nature’s laws
sources.raw_question: Is God bound by the laws of nature, so that what is impossible in nature is impossible for Him?

question: When God is called 'Almighty' and 'Lord of the Powers', is the Son included among the things over which God is Almighty and Lord?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: No. The Father has power and mastery over all things by the Word, and the Son rules the Father's kingdom and has power over all as His Word and Image. So the Son is not reckoned among the 'all', and God is called Almighty and Lord with reference to the things that come to be through the Son.
sources.quote: it is quite plain that neither here is the Son reckoned among that all, nor is God called Almighty and Lord with reference to Him, but to those things which through the Son come to be
sources.raw_question: When God is called 'Almighty' and 'Lord of the Powers', is the Son included among the things over which God is Almighty and Lord?

question: Does the Arian use of the word 'unoriginate' to dishonour the Son also dishonour the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture teaches that whoever honours the Son honours the Father, and whoever dishonours the Son dishonours the Father. Using 'unoriginate' to class the Son as originated therefore dishonours the Father as well, though the term itself has a good and religious sense.
sources.quote: they, in their own heresy, bring it forth for the dishonour of the Son, not having read that he who honoureth the Son honoureth the Father, and he who dishonoureth the Son, dishonoureth the Father
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian use of the word 'unoriginate' to dishonour the Son also dishonour the Father?

question: Since the exercise of divine attributes is finite, does their possession by Christ fail to prove an infinite subject?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: No. It is a contradiction to speak of a finite exercise of eternity or omniscience, and they can only be possessed by an infinite subject. Nor must infinite power be finite in its exercise, as though God could not perform an act infinitely exceeding any finite power.
sources.quote: 1 understand not what you mean by the ewercise of eternity and omniscience, which are two of those attributes; nor how it can be finite, without an express contradiction; nor how either of them can be exercised, whatever you mean by it, but by an infinite subject.
sources.raw_question: Since the exercise of divine attributes is finite, does their possession by Christ fail to prove an infinite subject?

question: Is the scriptural evidence for Christ's deity enough on its own to bring a person to embrace it with the heart?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Cordially embracing the truth of Christ's deity requires the convincing power of the Holy Ghost. The arguments are like the altar prepared on Carmel, which still needed fire from heaven. God must reveal his Son, draw people to him, and shine in their hearts.
sources.quote: But cordially to embrace this, needs I know the convincing power of the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: Is the scriptural evidence for Christ's deity enough on its own to bring a person to embrace it with the heart?

question: Is the Son from the Father by His advent (mission) or by His birth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: By His birth. The one and only reason Christ gives for loving the Son is His origin from the Father, which is His birth, not His coming. So love for the Father is possible only to those who believe the Son is truly from Him.
sources.quote: The Son, therefore, is from the Father, not by His Advent, but by His birth; and love for the Father is only possible to those who believe that the Son is from Him.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son from the Father by His advent (mission) or by His birth?

question: Does John 16:27-28 show that the Son's going forth from God implies He is God by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. The words must be taken in the strictest literal sense. Only God could go forth from God, that is, come into existence by birth from Him, so His nature is exactly what His birth gave Him. 'Went forth from God' refers to His nature and birth. 'Came from the Father into this world' refers to His incarnation.
sources.quote: for what being but God could go forth from God, that is, could enter upon existence by birth from Him?
sources.raw_question: Does John 16:27-28 show that the Son's going forth from God implies He is God by nature?

question: If God hides himself and his ways are past finding out, can human beings attain real knowledge of God's being, including the doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 1. Introduction. Preparation of heart. Our position before God.
sources.answer: Yes, sufficiently for salvation, though not exhaustively. God's self-revelation necessarily contains mysteries beyond our finite capacities. Yet God did not tell the seed of Jacob to seek him in vain. So all necessary and saving knowledge is promised to the humble student, since the Lord has respect to the lowly.
sources.quote: there must be in the self-revelation of Him, whose ways are past finding out, mysteries beyond the reach and range of our finite capacities, all necessary and saving knowledge is promised to the humble student
sources.raw_question: If God hides himself and his ways are past finding out, can human beings attain real knowledge of God's being, including the doctrine of the Trinity?

question: If we are born again by the Holy Spirit, can it be doubted that we are born of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter X. The Divinity of the Holy Spirit is supported by a passage of St. John. This passage was, indeed, erased by heretics, but it is a vain attempt, since their faithlessness could thereby more easily be convicted. The order of the context is considered in order that this passage may be shown to refer to the Spirit. He is born of the Spirit who is born again of the same Spirit, of Whom Christ Himself is believed to have been born and born again. Again, the Godhead of the Spirit is inferred from two testimonies of St. John; and lastly, it is explained how the Spirit, the water, and the blood are called witnesses.
sources.answer: No. Christ himself was both born and born again of the Holy Spirit. It is folly to confess the Spirit's role in Christ's birth, which is peculiar to God, while denying his role in regeneration, which is common to men. The Greek text also reads 'of' (ἐξ) the Spirit, not merely 'through' the Spirit. Since we are born of the Spirit and 'the Spirit is God,' the Holy Spirit is God.
sources.quote: I ask, however, why, if there be no doubt that we are born again by the Holy Spirit, there should be any doubt that we are born of the Holy Spirit, since the Lord Jesus Himself was both born and born again of the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: If we are born again by the Holy Spirit, can it be doubted that we are born of the Holy Spirit?

question: Why must the Word that is in God be the Only-begotten Christ and not a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: The Word in God cannot be a creature or out of nothing. If a Word is in God, he must be Christ, who says 'I am in the Father and the Father in Me'. He is therefore the Only-begotten, since no other was begotten from God. God has the Word as an Offspring according to the nature of his own Essence, and through him frames, creates and governs all things.
sources.quote: but if once a Word be in God, then He must be Christ who says, ‘I am in the Father and the Father in Me,’ who also is therefore the Only-begotten, since no other was begotten from Him.
sources.raw_question: Why must the Word that is in God be the Only-begotten Christ and not a creature?

question: Would God be without his work if he were without a Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is God's Offspring through whom he works, so a God without a Son would be without work. All things came to be by the Word and Wisdom and continue by his ordinance.
sources.quote: if God be without Son, then is He without Work; for the Son is His Offspring through whom He works
sources.raw_question: Would God be without his work if he were without a Son?

question: Would commingling or confusing three things of one essence destroy their trinity and their mutual relations?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: Yes. If they were confounded by commingling, they could not be three in any way, nor could they be referred to one another. Augustine compares three rings made from one gold: as separate rings they are a trinity of rings yet one gold, related to one another by similarity. If melted together, the trinity disappears and they are no longer three things of gold at all.
sources.quote: if they were confounded together as it were by a commingling, they could not be in any way three, neither could they be mutually referred to each other.
sources.raw_question: Would commingling or confusing three things of one essence destroy their trinity and their mutual relations?

question: Is the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son timeless, like the generation of the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: Yes. Whoever can understand the generation of the Son from the Father without time should also understand the procession of the Spirit from both without time. Just as generation gives the Son essence without beginning, procession from both gives the Spirit essence without beginning, without any change of nature.
sources.quote: let him who can understand the generation of the Son from the Father without time, understand also the procession of the Holy Spirit from both without time.
sources.raw_question: Is the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son timeless, like the generation of the Son?

question: Since the Holy Spirit is not begotten, should he be called unbegotten?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: No. Calling him unbegotten might suggest two Fathers in the Trinity, or two who are not from another. Only the Father is not from another, and so he alone is called unbegotten, a term used not in Scripture but by disputants.
sources.quote: For the Father alone is not from another, and therefore He alone is called unbegotten, not indeed in the Scriptures, but in the usage of disputants
sources.raw_question: Since the Holy Spirit is not begotten, should he be called unbegotten?

question: Does Psalm 86:16, 'Give Thy strength unto Thy Child, and help the Son of Thine handmaid,' distinguish the Son of God from created sons?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22. Proverbs are of a figurative nature, and must be interpreted as such. We must interpret them, and in particular this passage, by the Regula Fidei. 'He created me' not equivalent to 'I am a creature.' Wisdom a creature so far forth as Its human body. Again, if He is a creature, it is as 'a beginning of ways,' an office which, though not an attribute, is a consequence, of a higher and divine nature. And it is 'for the works,' which implied the works existed, and therefore much more He, before He was created. Also 'the Lord' not the Father 'created' Him, which implies the creation was that of a servant.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit marks a distinction between the one natural and true Child of God and the sons of the handmaid, that is, of originate nature. The One as Son has the Father's might, whereas the rest need salvation.
sources.quote: For the natural and true child of God is one, and the sons of the handmaid, that is, of the nature of things originate, are other. Wherefore the One, as Son, has the Father’s might; but the rest are in need of salvation.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 86:16, 'Give Thy strength unto Thy Child, and help the Son of Thine handmaid,' distinguish the Son of God from created sons?

question: Does Scripture always speak of creation in the 'softer' form that God created through Christ, keeping the full title of Creator of the universe for the Father alone?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. This misrepresents Scripture, which does not consistently follow that softer language. In John 1:3 and 1:10, Colossians 1:16 and Hebrews 1:10 creation is ascribed directly to the Son. In none of these texts can a merely instrumental sense be fixed from any necessary force of the preposition dia.
sources.quote: They do it not in John i. 3, 10, Coloss. i. 16, Heb. i. 10. Neither can that construction be ascertained, in any one of these texts, from any necessary force of the preposition διά.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture always speak of creation in the 'softer' form that God created through Christ, keeping the full title of Creator of the universe for the Father alone?

question: Can 'of Him, through Him, and in Him' rightly be said of God the Father too?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IX. A passage of St. Paul abused by heretics, to prove a distinction between the Divine Persons, is explained, and it is proved that the whole passage can be rightly said of each Person, though it refers specially to the Son. It is then proved that each member of the passage is applicable to each Person, and as to say, of Him are all things is applicable to the Father, so may all things are through Him and in Him also be said of Him.
sources.answer: Yes. 'Of Him' fits because the operative Wisdom (the Son) is of Him. 'Through Him' fits because all things were made through His Wisdom, and 'in Him' because He is the Fount of substantial Life in whom we live and move and have our being.
sources.quote: “Through Him,” because all things were made through His Wisdom. “In Him,” because He is the Fount of substantial Life, in Whom we live and move and have our being.
sources.raw_question: Can 'of Him, through Him, and in Him' rightly be said of God the Father too?

question: Under what condition would 'Father' and 'Son' be predicated of God according to substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Nothing is Spoken of God According to Accident, But According to Substance or According to Relation.
sources.answer: Only if each were called Father or Son in relation to Himself rather than to the other. But the Father is called Father only because He has a Son, and the Son is called Son only because He has a Father. The terms are reciprocal, so they are not substantial predicates.
sources.quote: because the Father is not called the Father except in that He has a Son, and the Son is not called Son except in that He has a Father, these things are not said according to substance
sources.raw_question: Under what condition would 'Father' and 'Son' be predicated of God according to substance?

question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers interpret the first chapter of John as making the Father the one supreme God and the Word another, inferior God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. That is Clarke's real interpretation, but the Ante-Nicene writers did not read the text that way. They understood such texts to be consistent with the Son's consubstantiality and coeternity, so it is absurd to claim them for Clarke's reading.
sources.quote: Do the AnteNicene writers interpret the first of St. John, so as to make the Father one God supreme; the Word another God, an inferior God besides him?
sources.raw_question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers interpret the first chapter of John as making the Father the one supreme God and the Word another, inferior God?

question: Do the Prophets and Apostles actually apply to Christ names such as Shepherd, Well, Stone, Axe, Light and Bread?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. David calls the Lord one who shepherds and the Well of life, and speaks of the Stone the builders rejected. John the Baptist names the Lord's power to uproot evil an Axe, and John calls Him the true Light. Paul saw the Light that said 'I am Jesus', and Christ Himself took the manna as a type of Himself, the true Bread from heaven. Eunomius' denial thus shows his ignorance of Scripture.
sources.quote: None of the Prophets or Apostles has spoken of our Lord as Bread, or a Stone, or a Fountain, or an Axe, or Light, or a Shepherd! What, then, saith David, and of whom? “The Lord shepherds me.”
sources.raw_question: Do the Prophets and Apostles actually apply to Christ names such as Shepherd, Well, Stone, Axe, Light and Bread?

question: When Christ promises 'I will manifest myself to him' without mentioning the Father, is the Father excluded from that manifestation?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > All are Sometimes Understood in One Person.
sources.answer: No. Because the Father and the Son are one and each is in the other, when the Son is manifested the Father is also manifested, and vice versa. Christ's answer to Judas confirms this, for He says 'we will come unto him, and make our abode with him.'
sources.quote: because it is true, “I and my Father are one,” when the Father is manifested, the Son also, who is in Him, is manifested; and when the Son is manifested, the Father also, who is in Him, is manifested.
sources.raw_question: When Christ promises 'I will manifest myself to him' without mentioning the Father, is the Father excluded from that manifestation?

question: Is Christ's revealing his mind and secrets to believers evidence of his delight in them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. People unbosom themselves only to a bosom friend, and there is no greater evidence of delight in close communion than revealing one's heart. Christ makes known to his friends everything he has heard from his Father, and he enables them to reveal their hearts to him. This shows his great delight in them.
sources.quote: Christ reveals his secrets, his mind, unto his saints, and enables them to reveal the secrets of their hearts to him, — an evident demonstration of great delight.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's revealing his mind and secrets to believers evidence of his delight in them?

question: Did the orthodox Fathers who called the Son's eternal generation an act of the Father's will thereby deny that the Son is eternal in the strict sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Dr. Clarke's authorities do not show that those Fathers who asserted eternal generation thought it arbitrary or something that might have been otherwise, nor that those who held a voluntary, temporary procession denied the Logos's eternal pre-existence in the Father. Hence none of his citations prove that the Fathers understood 'eternal' in a loose sense.
sources.quote: or that those who expressly asserted an eternal generation, believed also that it was an arbitrary thing, and might have been otherwise, (which I suppose is the Doctor’s sense of an “ act of the “ will,”) then he will do something.
sources.raw_question: Did the orthodox Fathers who called the Son's eternal generation an act of the Father's will thereby deny that the Son is eternal in the strict sense?

question: Was the Father inactive and uninvolved while the Son carried out the work of salvation in the Incarnation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: No. Christ himself said that the One who sent him is with him and that the Father dwelling in him does the works. Our salvation would not have been wrought had not the Father's good will proceeded to actual operation for us through his own power, which is the Son.
sources.quote: our salvation would not have been wrought, had not the good will of the Father proceeded to actual operation for us through His own power. And we have learnt from the Scripture that the Son is the power of the Father
sources.raw_question: Was the Father inactive and uninvolved while the Son carried out the work of salvation in the Incarnation?

question: Did the Holy Spirit come into being from the only God, the Father, through the Only-begotten Son acting as an instrument?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: No. No evangelist, apostle or prophet teaches this, and Eunomius cannot deduce it from any scriptural premise. On the contrary, every inspired Scripture attests the Divinity of the Spirit.
sources.quote: What shadow of such a notion did he find in Scripture, that he ventures upon this assertion?
sources.raw_question: Did the Holy Spirit come into being from the only God, the Father, through the Only-begotten Son acting as an instrument?

question: How can believers now bear "the image of the heavenly" (1 Corinthians 15:49) if bodily immortality is still future?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether the Sentence of John is to Be Understood of Our Future Likeness with the Son of God in the Immortality Itself Also of the Body.
sources.answer: They bear it now in faith and hope, not yet in sight or in fact. Mortal after Adam, we hold by true faith and sure hope that we shall be immortal after Christ, since Paul is speaking there of the resurrection of the body.
sources.quote: For so can we now bear the same image, not yet in sight, but in faith; not yet in fact, but in hope.
sources.raw_question: How can believers now bear "the image of the heavenly" (1 Corinthians 15:49) if bodily immortality is still future?

question: What is the meaning of "My Father worketh even until now, and I work" (John 5:17) for the relation between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It means that the Father works in the Son at the very moment the Son works. The Son's present words and deeds are the working of the Father's nature within Him. Since all things are through and in the Son, the Father's work is done in the Son, as John 14:10 states. The added "And I work" shows that whatever the Father works, the Son also works.
sources.quote: The Father works in Him while He works; without doubt, then, He works along with the working of the Father
sources.raw_question: What is the meaning of "My Father worketh even until now, and I work" (John 5:17) for the relation between the Father and the Son?

question: Does the shared working of the Father and Son mean they are merged into a single Person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. When Christ says that the Father works and He also works, He sets forth two who work. Their union does not merge them into one Person. This guards the faith against confining itself to the Father alone.
sources.quote: if the Father works, and the Son works, no union exists between them, which merges them into a single Person
sources.raw_question: Does the shared working of the Father and Son mean they are merged into a single Person?

question: Can the Father's communication of divine powers and attributes to the Son and Spirit, without communicating the substance, make the three one God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: No. The idea falls into a dilemma. If the Son and Spirit have distinct attributes and a divinity of their own, then on Clarke's principle they are distinct Gods, related to the Father as finite to infinite and creature to Creator. If they have no divinity except the Father's, which is inseparable from his essence, they have no distinct essence and become mere names. Communicating attributes without substance is even harder to conceive than communicating both together.
sources.quote: a communication of divine powers and attributes, without the substance, being as hard to conceive, nay, much harder, than a communication of both together
sources.raw_question: Can the Father's communication of divine powers and attributes to the Son and Spirit, without communicating the substance, make the three one God?

question: Could a creature be commissioned to do all things that the Creator does, and in the same manner?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No, it would be very odd and strange. To say a creature has commission to do everything the Father does, and do it in the same manner (homoiōs), sounds harsh and too presumptuous for a creature. Verse 20, where the Father shows the Son all things that he does, confirms that the Son's powers are coextensive with the Father's, which fits equality of nature.
sources.quote: For, after all, it must be thought very odd and strange for a creature to be commissioned or empowered to do all things that the Creator doth ; and to do them ὁμοίως in the same manner
sources.raw_question: Could a creature be commissioned to do all things that the Creator does, and in the same manner?

question: Why does comfort from Christ's promises vary so much, both for the same believer at different times and between different believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Because the Holy Spirit distributes as he wills. Consolation depends on his sovereign will and is not bound to any fixed rule or procedure. So one person finds every promise sweet in great distress and finds none in a small trial, while others taste little comfort all their days. Faith therefore waits on the Spirit for the right time.
sources.quote: The reason is, Πνεῦμα διαιρεῖ καθὼς βούλεται, — the Spirit distributes as he will. And so with divers persons: to some each promise is full of life and comfort; others taste little all their days, — all upon the same account.
sources.raw_question: Why does comfort from Christ's promises vary so much, both for the same believer at different times and between different believers?

question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers hold the eternal generation of the Son, even though they seldom use that phrase?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland grants they are sparing in the term but not in the thing itself. They all held the eternity of the Word and the distinction of Persons, together with consubstantiality and unity of principle. Taken together, these amount to everything meant by eternal generation.
sources.quote: The eternity of the Word, or Adyos, and the distinction of Persons, they all held; together with the consubstantiality, and unity of principle; which together are as much as can be meant by efernal generation.
sources.raw_question: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers hold the eternal generation of the Son, even though they seldom use that phrase?

question: Does Hebrews 1:6, where the angels are commanded to worship the Son, support the Son's true divinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: Yes. The angels are ordered to worship the Son, the text applies to him what Psalm 97 says of Jehovah, and Scripture and antiquity appropriate worship to God alone. So the text proves the Son is Jehovah and rightly adored.
sources.quote: the angels are there ordered to worship the Son; and that that text is a proof of the Son’s being Jehovah (see Psalm xevii.) and that worship is appropriated to God only
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1:6, where the angels are commanded to worship the Son, support the Son's true divinity?

question: What in Hebrews 1 shows why the Son is capable of receiving worship and adoration?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: His divine, eternal, uncreated nature. The chapter says he made the worlds, is the brightness of the Father's glory and the express image of his Person, and upholds all things by the word of his power. These are strong expressions of his divinity, which give him the justest claim to the worship of men and angels.
sources.quote: Strong and lively expressions of his divine, eternal, uncreated nature; such as might give him the justest claim to the worship and adoration of men and angels.
sources.raw_question: What in Hebrews 1 shows why the Son is capable of receiving worship and adoration?

question: Is the Saviour a different being from the Word and Only-begotten of God, produced by the Æons rather than proceeding from the Father of all?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIX.—Absurdities of the heretics as to their own origin: their opinions respecting the Demiurge shown to be equally untenable and ridiculous.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus rejects the multiplication of 'another Monogenes', 'another Word', 'another Christ' and 'another Saviour'. He rejects especially the claim that the Saviour did not proceed from the Father of all but was a joint production of degenerate Æons. Such a doctrine is intolerable to anyone with even a small share of truth.
sources.quote: and another Saviour, who, they say, did not proceed from the Father of all, but was a kind of joint production of those Æons who were formed in [a state of] degeneracy
sources.raw_question: Is the Saviour a different being from the Word and Only-begotten of God, produced by the Æons rather than proceeding from the Father of all?

question: Can the Son's perfections be called infinite but not absolutely infinite, as if there were a limited kind of infinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 10: Whether if they (the attributes belonging to the Son) be not individually the same, they can be any thing more than faint resemblances of them, differing from t
sources.answer: No. Infinity cannot be divided into absolute and limited kinds, or into infinity and not-infinity. Words should keep their proper meaning. If the Arian will neither call the Son's perfections infinite nor limit them, the honest word is 'indefinite', so that readers can see where the parties really differ.
sources.quote: as if infinity were of two sorts, absolute and limited; or might be rightly divided into infinity and not infinity.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's perfections be called infinite but not absolutely infinite, as if there were a limited kind of infinity?

question: Was the Christ whom the Jews saw a mere phantasm, or a real human being of flesh and blood?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXII.—The thirty Æons are not typified by the fact that Christ was baptized in His thirtieth year: He did not suffer in the twelfth month after His baptism, but was more than fifty years old when He died.
sources.answer: He was a real human being of flesh and blood. The Jews described the age they actually saw in him, because what they beheld was not an apparition but an actual body that aged like other men.
sources.quote: For what they saw, that they also expressed; and He whom they beheld was not a mere phantasm, but an actual being
sources.raw_question: Was the Christ whom the Jews saw a mere phantasm, or a real human being of flesh and blood?

question: What does the Holy Spirit's role as witness of the Son, and as distributor of gifts, show about his rank?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: It shows that he is above all things, not among them. A witness knows all things, as God the Father is a witness, and Hebrews joins the Spirit's distributions to God's testimony. He who divides as he wills is above all, since dividing gifts belongs to the worker, not to the work. So the Spirit is to be reckoned with the Father and the Son, not numbered with the crowd of creatures.
sources.quote: He who divides as he will is certainly above all, not amongst all, for to divide is the gift of the worker, not an innate part of the work itself.
sources.raw_question: What does the Holy Spirit's role as witness of the Son, and as distributor of gifts, show about his rank?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: Yes. All the strength of things in heaven and on earth comes from the Spirit, so he is above all things. He who is above all does not serve. He who does not serve is free, and he who is free has the prerogative of lordship.
sources.quote: He, then, Who is above all things certainly does not serve; He Who serves not is free; He Who is free has the prerogative of lordship.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit possess lordship rather than servitude?

question: How can natural reason determine the attributes of God the Creator?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What Universal Nature Teaches Us Concerning God.
sources.answer: By ranking perfections and attributing the higher to the Creator. Reason sees that the living is better than the non-living, the understanding than the non-understanding, the immortal than the mortal, the unchangeable than the changeable, and the incorporeal than the corporeal. Since the Creator must be placed above created things, he must live in the highest sense, understand all things, and be immortal, incorruptible, and unchangeable. He is also an incorporeal spirit, most powerful, righteous, beautiful, good, and blessed.
sources.quote: since without doubt we place the Creator above things created, we must needs confess that the Creator both lives in the highest sense, and perceives and understands all things, and that He cannot die, or suffer decay, or be changed
sources.raw_question: How can natural reason determine the attributes of God the Creator?

question: Does true birth produce a nature equal to that of its source?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Yes. Equality consists in the absence of difference, and birth can only bring into existence a nature without difference from its origin. Hence birth is the only possible origin of true equality between Son and Father.
sources.quote: And this is the only possible origin of true equality; birth can only bring into existence a nature equal to its origin.
sources.raw_question: Does true birth produce a nature equal to that of its source?

question: Can there be a 'before' and a 'more honourable' among the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > It will not do to apply this conception, as drawn out above, of the Father and Son to the Creation, as they insist on doing: but we must contemplate the Son apart with the Father, and believe that the Creation had its origin from a definite point.
sources.answer: No. The Father exists before the ages and is always in glory, and the pre-temporal Son is his glory. The Spirit is likewise always contemplated with the Father and the Son. A 'before' cannot exist in what is timeless, nor a 'more honourable' in what is essentially all honourable. Ranking one Person above another simply dishonours the other.
sources.quote: what training could have led this man of learning to declare that there is a ‘before’ in what is timeless, and a ‘more honourable’ in what is all essentially honourable
sources.raw_question: Can there be a 'before' and a 'more honourable' among the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as Eunomius claims?

question: Does the fact that the Father gave Jesus 'the Name above every name' after his humiliation prove that the Son is unequal to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. The giving of the Name belongs to the mystery of the humility he assumed: by taking the servant's form his form was changed, and the gift restores to him the equality of form he had. What is given is something pertaining to God, and granting it to the receiving nature does not impair the divinity of the giving nature.
sources.quote: The birth of His humanity brought to Him a new nature, and His form was changed in His humility, by the assumption of a servant’s form, but now the giving of the Name restores to Him equality of form.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Father gave Jesus 'the Name above every name' after his humiliation prove that the Son is unequal to the Father?

question: Does the unity of God consist merely in the one God, the Father, making and governing the world through the Son and the Holy Spirit, as Dr. Clarke glosses Gregory Nazianzen?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. Governing the world through the Son and Spirit is a true notion, but it does not account for the divine unity, and it is not Gregory's account of it. Gregory keeps one God by referring the Son and Holy Ghost to one cause without composition or confusion. He also asserts one and the same movement and will of the Godhead, together with sameness of essence.
sources.quote: Here is not a syllable about the one God’s governing the world by his Son and his Spirit; which, though a true notion, is not sufficient to account for the wnity
sources.raw_question: Does the unity of God consist merely in the one God, the Father, making and governing the world through the Son and the Holy Spirit, as Dr. Clarke glosses Gregory Nazianzen?

question: Is the visible world God's only creation?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Novatian, with the View of Treating of the Trinity, Sets Forth from the Rule of Faith that We Should First of All Believe in God the Father and Lord Omnipotent, the Absolute Founder of All Things. The Works of Creation are Beautifully Described. Man's Free-Will is Asserted; God's Mercy in Inflicting Penalty on Man is Shown; The Condition After Death of the Souls of the Righteous and Unrighteous is Determined.
sources.answer: No. Above the firmament God ordained angels, spiritual powers, thrones and countless heavens. Beneath the earth there are also ordered powers, including a place where the souls of the just and unjust await judgment. So this world seems rather the latest than the only work of God, which shows the Artificer's greatness.
sources.quote: so that this world, immense as it is, might almost appear rather as the latest, than the only work of corporeal things
sources.raw_question: Is the visible world God's only creation?

question: Are 'Word', 'Son' and 'Wisdom' merely an accidental grace or habit of virtue in some essence, able to be added or taken away?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. How the Word has free will, yet without being alterable. He is unalterable because the Image of the Father, proved from texts.
sources.answer: No. That view is not the faith of Christians, because it denies that He is truly Word, Son and Wisdom of God. What alters and changes cannot be true, yet the Lord says 'I am the Truth.' It would be sin to say that an alterable word and changeable wisdom was begotten from the unalterable essence.
sources.quote: For what alters and changes, and has no stay in one and the same condition, how can that be true? whereas the Lord says, ‘I am the Truth.’
sources.raw_question: Are 'Word', 'Son' and 'Wisdom' merely an accidental grace or habit of virtue in some essence, able to be added or taken away?

question: Is the doctrine that the divine Monad expands (dilatation) into the Word and contracts again compatible with real personal distinctions in the Godhead?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus C. Introductory to the Fourth Discourse against the Arians.
sources.answer: No. The Marcellian doctrine of πλατυσμός and συστολή denies true personal distinctions in the Godhead. It therefore leads inevitably to Sabellianism.
sources.quote: The doctrine of divine dilatation and contraction denies true personal distinctions in the Godhead.
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine that the divine Monad expands (dilatation) into the Word and contracts again compatible with real personal distinctions in the Godhead?

question: Could perfect obedience to the law from now on make up for sins already committed?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. All have already sinned, so a debt stands against them for the past that future obedience cannot answer. Consulted about that past account, the law offers no direction or consolation. It only pronounces the sentence of death, and there is no escaping it.
sources.quote: This they are sufficiently sensible of, that although they could for the time to come fulfil the whole law, yet there is a score, a reckoning, upon them already, that they know not how to answer for.
sources.raw_question: Could perfect obedience to the law from now on make up for sins already committed?

question: How does Christ give his peace to his disciples, and how is this related to the sending of the Holy Spirit as Comforter?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Christ gives his peace only by bestowing the Comforter on them. In John 14 the promise of peace follows directly on the promise of the Comforter. The peace of Christ is the soul's sense of its acceptance with God in friendship, which Christ purchased by removing the enmity and which the Spirit applies.
sources.quote: Nor doth Christ otherwise leave his peace, or give his peace unto them, but by bestowing the Comforter on them.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ give his peace to his disciples, and how is this related to the sending of the Holy Spirit as Comforter?

question: Does Paul's statement that "the life of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh" refer to the resurrection of the physical body of flesh?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIII.—In the dead who were raised by Christ we possess the highest proof of the resurrection; and our hearts are shown to be capable of life eternal, because they can now receive the Spirit of God.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul speaks of the body that is delivered to death for Jesus' sake, and the only substance that is put to death for confessing God is the flesh. So the mortal flesh in which Jesus' life is manifested can only be the body of flesh, and it will be raised.
sources.quote: In what other mortal flesh, therefore, can life be understood as being manifested, unless in that substance which is also put to death on account of that confession which is made of God?
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that "the life of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh" refer to the resurrection of the physical body of flesh?

question: When Scripture compares people to animals or tells them to be 'as' something, does it mean they should become that thing in nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. Scripture customarily uses things of nature as images to illustrate human moral conduct. 'Be ye not like to horse and mule' and 'wise as serpents and harmless as doves' do not mean we become beasts, serpents or doves, which our nature does not allow. They mean we should avoid one creature's irrational motions and imitate another's wisdom or meekness. So comparisons with 'as' signify imitation, not sameness of nature.
sources.quote: And He said this, not that we may become in nature beasts of burden, or become serpents and doves; for He hath not so made us Himself, and therefore nature does not allow of it
sources.raw_question: When Scripture compares people to animals or tells them to be 'as' something, does it mean they should become that thing in nature?

question: Why can no one see the 'face' of God, the form of God, and live?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > How the Back Parts of God Were Seen. The Faith of the Resurrection of Christ. The Catholic Church Only is the Place from Whence the Back Parts of God are Seen. The Back Parts of God Were Seen by the Israelites. It is a Rash Opinion to Think that God the Father Only Was Never Seen by the Fathers.
sources.answer: Either because the face-to-face vision belongs to the life after death and resurrection, when we shall see Him as He is, or because, even now, the more we spiritually understand the wisdom of God, the more we die to carnal affections and to the world. In either case, seeing the divine form requires a kind of death to this mortal life.
sources.quote: in whatever degree we spiritually understand the wisdom of God, by which all things were made, in that same degree we die to carnal affections
sources.raw_question: Why can no one see the 'face' of God, the form of God, and live?

question: Is making satisfaction for sin by undergoing punishment a different thing from expiating sin by a propitiatory sacrifice?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: No. Where sin is the cause and God is the one offended, satisfaction by bearing punishment and expiation by propitiatory sacrifice are only two ways of describing the same thing. Owen shows this from ancient practice, where a person devoted to die for the people was regarded as an expiatory sacrifice that turned away divine wrath.
sources.quote: For where sin is the cause, and God is the object respected; the making of satisfaction by undergoing punishment, and expiating of sin by a propitiatory sacrifice, are but various expressions of the same thing.
sources.raw_question: Is making satisfaction for sin by undergoing punishment a different thing from expiating sin by a propitiatory sacrifice?

question: Does the command 'Believe in God, believe also in Me' support a unity in which God is a single solitary person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. While the words show that the Son is God, they also exclude an irreligious unity, because they distinguish two objects of belief. The exhortation therefore forbids thinking of God as alone in solitude.
sources.quote: Yet He excludes the suggestion of a unity contrary to religion, for the exhortation Believe in God, believe in Me also, forbids us to think of Him as alone in solitude.
sources.raw_question: Does the command 'Believe in God, believe also in Me' support a unity in which God is a single solitary person?

question: Do the Scriptures that describe Christ's humanity, birth, life and death thereby deny his deity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Asserting his humanity no more denies his deity than asserting his deity with its essential properties denies his humanity; both natures are affirmed.
sources.quote: The Scriptures, asserting the humanity of Christ, with the concernments thereof, as his birth, life, and death, do no more thereby deny his Deity than, by asserting his Deity, with the essential properties thereof, they deny his humanity.
sources.raw_question: Do the Scriptures that describe Christ's humanity, birth, life and death thereby deny his deity?

question: When Scripture says God worked in and by Christ, does this mean Christ was only an instrument and not himself the divine agent?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Such language about God working in and by Christ as mediator denotes the Father's sovereign appointment of what was to be done, not the Father's immediate efficiency in doing the things themselves.
sources.quote: God working in and by Christ as he was mediator, denotes the Father’s sovereign appointment of the things mentioned to be done, — not his immediate efficiency in the doing of the things themselves.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says God worked in and by Christ, does this mean Christ was only an instrument and not himself the divine agent?

question: Should Christians expect to resolve every question raised by Scripture, or must some questions be left to God both now and in the age to come?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: Some questions must be left to God, not only in this life but also in the world to come. Even in creation some things are known only to God, so there is no ground for complaint if the same holds for the spiritual matters of Scripture. God will forever teach and man will forever learn, which is why faith, hope and charity endure. Leaving such questions to God keeps faith unharmed and lets all Scripture be seen to agree.
sources.quote: we must leave others in the hands of God, and that not only in the present world, but also in that which is to come, so that God should for ever teach, and man should for ever learn the things taught him by God?
sources.raw_question: Should Christians expect to resolve every question raised by Scripture, or must some questions be left to God both now and in the age to come?

question: Is the Logos produced from the Father at a third remove, as a product separated from God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
