sources.answer: No. Ranking the Logos third in production from the Father shows ignorance of His greatness and separates the Logos far from God. God's thought is Logos and Logos is Mind, so the Word is not a distant emanation.
sources.quote: So, again, with respect to Logos, when one attributes to him the third place of production from the Father; on which supposition he is ignorant of His greatness; and thus Logos has been far separated from God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Logos produced from the Father at a third remove, as a product separated from God?

question: Are any of Christ's distinctive titles and attributes, such as only-begotten Son, First and Last, omnipresent, omniscient, Creator, and Jehovah, ever ascribed to saints in Scripture?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. No saint is anywhere called the only-begotten Son, the First and the Last, eternal, omnipresent, omniscient, infinitely good, the creator and preserver of all things, or Jehovah. These are incommunicable prerogatives, so the proof of Christ's Godhead is incontrovertible even if the disputed passages are set aside.
sources.quote: Where is any saint said to be the only-begotten Son of God, the First and the Last, from everlasting, the same yesterday today and forever, omnipresent, omniscient, infinitely good, the creator and preserver of all things
sources.raw_question: Are any of Christ's distinctive titles and attributes, such as only-begotten Son, First and Last, omnipresent, omniscient, Creator, and Jehovah, ever ascribed to saints in Scripture?

question: Is it right to lower the dignity of the Holy Spirit, given that his very name is 'Holy'?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: No. Nothing is more worthy to say of God than to call Him holy. The Spirit's name is itself the praise of God. The Seraphim praise the Spirit as holy in the same way as the Father and the Son, so to derogate from the Spirit is to derogate from the praise of God.
sources.quote: consider from this fact also whether one ought at all to derogate from the Holy Spirit, whose Name is the praise of God.
sources.raw_question: Is it right to lower the dignity of the Holy Spirit, given that his very name is 'Holy'?

question: How does John 10:30 refute both the Sabellians and the Arians?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVI. The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and so They are honoured in the same Trisagion: nor can we speak more worthily of God than by calling Him Holy; whence it is clear that we must not derogate from the dignity of the Holy Spirit. In Him is all which pertains to God, since in baptism He is named with the Father and the Son, and the Father has given to Him to be greater than all, nor can any one deprive Him of this. And so from the very passage of St. John which heretics used against His dignity, the equality of the Trinity and the Unity of the Godhead is established. Lastly, after explaining how the Son receives from the Father, St. Ambrose shows how various heresies are refuted by the passage cited.
sources.answer: 'I and the Father' refutes the Sabellians, because it makes the Son one and the Father another. 'Are One' refutes the Arians, because it asserts one substance. 'We are One' means one substance, not one Person. Saying 'I and the Father' rather than 'the Father and I' shows that unity knows no order and equality no gradation.
sources.quote: For unity knows no order, equality knows no gradation
sources.raw_question: How does John 10:30 refute both the Sabellians and the Arians?

question: Is the Father's good pleasure towards the Son matched by a corresponding good pleasure of the Son towards the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. By the same good pleasure with which the Son is the object of the Father's pleasure, the Father is the object of the Son's love, pleasure and honour. There is one good pleasure from Father in Son, so that the Son is contemplated in the Father and the Father in the Son. Such language signifies genuineness of nature and likeness of Essence, not a precedent will.
sources.quote: one is the good pleasure which is from Father in Son, so that here too we may contemplate the Son in the Father and the Father in the Son.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's good pleasure towards the Son matched by a corresponding good pleasure of the Son towards the Father?

question: Does the statement that no one has seen God at any time contradict the claim that Isaiah saw God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. No one has seen the Father, but the Only-begotten, who is in the Father's bosom and declares Him, is God and was seen. So the One seen is true God, though none dare say the Father was seen.
sources.quote: Isaiah did see God; even though it is written, No one hath seen God at any time, save the Only-begotten Son Who is in the bosom of the Father; He hath declared Him, it was God Whom the prophet saw.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that no one has seen God at any time contradict the claim that Isaiah saw God?

question: Can one confess the Father as the only true, wise and immortal God while holding that the Son is an adopted Son of a different substance, God only by title?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Such a confession only pretends to keep the truth while denying it. Making the Son a creature of different substance, God by adoption and not by nature, strips Him of all the attributes heaped on the Father in lonely majesty. The Son is born from God to be God.
sources.quote: they attach to Him a Son different in substance, not born from God to be God, but adopted through creation to be a Son, having the name of God not by nature, but as a title received by adoption
sources.raw_question: Can one confess the Father as the only true, wise and immortal God while holding that the Son is an adopted Son of a different substance, God only by title?

question: Does 1 Corinthians 6:17, 'He that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit,' imply that the Lord becomes greater through the union?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > No Addition Can Be Made to the Nature of God.
sources.answer: No. The one joined to the Lord becomes greater, because he becomes better. The Lord does not become greater, since in such a union the lesser gains from the greater and not the reverse.
sources.quote: “He,” then, “that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit:” but yet the Lord does not therefore become greater, although he who is joined to the Lord does so.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 6:17, 'He that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit,' imply that the Lord becomes greater through the union?

question: Why is the Son called 'First-born' at all, if not because he is from the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: He is called First-born not because of his origin from the Father, which is why he is Only-begotten, but because of his condescension to creation. He is 'First-born among many brethren' through kinship of the flesh, 'First-born from the dead' because resurrection comes from him and after him, and 'First-born of creation' because through him creation is adopted and will be freed from corruption. Hebrews 1:6 ties the title to his being brought into the world.
sources.quote: the Son is the Father’s ‘Only-begotten,’ because He alone is from Him, and He is the ‘First-born of creation,’ because of this adoption of all as sons
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son called 'First-born' at all, if not because he is from the Father?

question: Does Ephesians 4:30 ('Grieve not the Holy Spirit of God') refer to the Holy Spirit as a distinct person rather than an impersonal influence?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Yes. The text intends the person of the Holy Ghost. This appears from the emphatic Greek phrasing with a double article, 'That Holy Spirit', and from the personal work assigned to him in the same verse, sealing believers to the day of redemption, which is the proper work of the Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: That it is the person of the Holy Ghost which is here intended, is evident, —
sources.raw_question: Does Ephesians 4:30 ('Grieve not the Holy Spirit of God') refer to the Holy Spirit as a distinct person rather than an impersonal influence?

question: What does Christ's promise in John 14:26 that the Holy Spirit will bring to remembrance all that he said mean with respect to the apostles' writing of Scripture?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: It means the Holy Spirit would, by immediate efficacy and inspiration, bring Christ's words to the apostles' minds so they could infallibly write and preach them as a rule of faith. Their natural memory was insufficient for this, since they forgot or might forget much. Prophecy comes not from private conception or remembrance, but from men borne along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21).
sources.quote: what they did retain, in a natural way of remembrance, was not a sufficient foundation to them to write what they so remembered for a rule of faith to the church.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's promise in John 14:26 that the Holy Spirit will bring to remembrance all that he said mean with respect to the apostles' writing of Scripture?

question: Was the Holy Spirit already a Gift before there was anyone to whom He could be given, or did He become a Gift only when He was actually given to creatures?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whether the Holy Spirit Was a Gift Before as Well as After He Was Given.
sources.answer: The Spirit was a Gift eternally, even before there was anyone to receive Him. A gift differs from a thing that has been given: a gift can exist before it is given, but it is only called 'given' once it has been given. So the Spirit is eternally a Gift, and is 'given' only in time.
sources.quote: For there is a difference in meaning between a gift and a thing that has been given. For a gift may exist even before it is given; but it cannot be called a thing that has been given unless it has been given.
sources.raw_question: Was the Holy Spirit already a Gift before there was anyone to whom He could be given, or did He become a Gift only when He was actually given to creatures?

question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed in time, only when He is given to creatures, or does He proceed eternally?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whether the Holy Spirit Was a Gift Before as Well as After He Was Given.
sources.answer: He proceeds eternally, not in time. If He proceeded only when He was given, He could not proceed before there was someone to receive Him, and then His very being would depend on creatures. Instead He proceeds from eternity in such a way that He is capable of being given. He is therefore co-eternal with the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: Does the Holy Spirit proceed always, and proceed not in time, but from eternity, but because He so proceeded that He was capable of being given, was already a gift even before there was one to whom He might be given?
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed in time, only when He is given to creatures, or does He proceed eternally?

question: Just as the Son's being born gives Him not only His relative identity as Son but also His very being, does the Holy Spirit's procession give Him His very substance as well as His relative identity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whether the Holy Spirit Was a Gift Before as Well as After He Was Given.
sources.answer: Yes. By being born the Son has not only His relative name of Son but His very substance, so that He exists at all. In the same way, the Spirit's procession gives Him His being absolutely. For this reason His procession cannot depend on His being given in time, or His very existence would hang on creatures.
sources.quote: just as the Son, by being born, not only has this, that He is a Son, which is said relatively, but His very substance absolutely, so that He is.
sources.raw_question: Just as the Son's being born gives Him not only His relative identity as Son but also His very being, does the Holy Spirit's procession give Him His very substance as well as His relative identity?

question: Is it credible that God could be born as a man and still remain God, given that this goes against our ordinary experience of nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. Natural things grow by increase and never shrink back into what they were before. So when the higher nature is born into the lower, it is reasonable to expect that the lower is raised into the higher, not that the higher is lessened. Taking on our nature was no gain for God, but it promoted man: he did not give up his divinity but conferred divinity on man.
sources.quote: for when the higher nature is born into the lower, it is credible that the lower should also be born into the higher.
sources.raw_question: Is it credible that God could be born as a man and still remain God, given that this goes against our ordinary experience of nature?

question: Does Acts 5 call the Holy Spirit God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. The one called the Holy Ghost in verse 3 and the Spirit of the Lord in verse 9 is called God in verse 4. That is the name of a divine person. The Socinians themselves will not call anyone God unless he is a person. They also cannot invent an office by which the Spirit became God without admitting he is a person.
sources.quote: He who is termed the “Holy Ghost,” verse 3, and the “Spirit of the Lord,” verse 9, is called also “God,” verse 4. Now, this is the name of a divine person, on one account or other.
sources.raw_question: Does Acts 5 call the Holy Spirit God?

question: Is the doxology to Christ in Revelation 1:5-6 the same divine adoration as the doxology to God in 1 Peter 5:11?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Opponents admit that Peter's doxology to the God of all grace is adoration of the infinite God. John's doxology to him who washed us in his blood uses words identical in Greek and English. Consistency therefore requires granting the same adoration to Christ, and shows the Father and the Saviour to be one indivisible Jehovah.
sources.quote: The words both in Greek and English are identical; the adoration is the same; and the Beings worshipped – the God of all grace, and the bleeding ) Saviour – are one indivisible Jehovah.
sources.raw_question: Is the doxology to Christ in Revelation 1:5-6 the same divine adoration as the doxology to God in 1 Peter 5:11?

question: Does the presence of the Spirit's grace, shown in signs such as the fiery tongues at Pentecost, prove the Godhead of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIV. Each Person of the Trinity is said in the sacred writings to be Light. The Spirit is designated Fire by Isaiah, a figure of which Fire was seen in the bush by Moses, in the tongues of fire, and in Gideon's pitchers. And the Godhead of the same Spirit cannot be denied, since His operation is the same as that of the Father and of the Son, and He is also called the light and fire of the Lord's countenance.
sources.answer: Yes. Wherever the grace of the Spirit is, there the manifestation of the Godhead appears, as in the fiery tongues at Pentecost. Therefore no one can doubt the Spirit's Godhead.
sources.quote: Who, then, can doubt of the Godhead of the Holy Spirit, since where the grace of the Spirit is, there the manifestation of the Godhead appears.
sources.raw_question: Does the presence of the Spirit's grace, shown in signs such as the fiery tongues at Pentecost, prove the Godhead of the Holy Spirit?

question: Does Christ's crying to the Father on the cross and commending his spirit to him show that the Son is distinct from the Father, even though inseparable from him?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: Yes. The one who is inseparable from the Father nevertheless cries to the Father and commends his spirit to him. This shows that the Son is a distinct person who addresses the Father, while remaining inseparable from him.
sources.quote: And He who is inseparable from the Father cries to the Father, and commends to Him His spirit
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's crying to the Father on the cross and commending his spirit to him show that the Son is distinct from the Father, even though inseparable from him?

question: Was it the Son, the Word, who appeared in the theophanies of the Old Testament and in John's visions, such as the fourth figure in the furnace in Daniel?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Yes. The Word appeared in many figures, suited to the purposes of His dispensations. He was the fourth figure in the furnace who was "like to the Son of God," the stone cut without hands, and the Son of man who receives the kingdom from the Ancient of Days. In Revelation He is the one like the Son of man, the Lamb, and the rider called the Word of God.
sources.quote: not in one figure, nor in one character, did He appear to those seeing Him, but according to the reasons and effects aimed at in His dispensations, as it is written in Daniel.
sources.raw_question: Was it the Son, the Word, who appeared in the theophanies of the Old Testament and in John's visions, such as the fourth figure in the furnace in Daniel?

question: In Christ's anointing with the Spirit, was the eternal Word anointed, or only the human nature He assumed?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: The human nature only. The Word, God with God in the beginning, needed no anointing with the Spirit and power of God, since He was Himself the Spirit and power of God. The prophecy also places the anointing in time, after His divine birth. So what was anointed was the whole nature of the servant that He assumed, and in this our manhood was sanctified in Christ.
sources.quote: It was then not the begotten Word, God with God in the beginning, Who was anointed, but that nature in God which came to Him through the dispensation later than His divinity
sources.raw_question: In Christ's anointing with the Spirit, was the eternal Word anointed, or only the human nature He assumed?

question: Why could the Old Testament prophecies about the Son of God's coming in human nature not be clearly understood before his advent?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVI.—The treasure hid in the Scriptures is Christ; the true exposition of the Scriptures is to be found in the Church alone.
sources.answer: Every prophecy is full of enigmas and ambiguities to men until it is fulfilled. Once the predicted event comes to pass, the prophecy gains a clear and certain exposition. Daniel was therefore told to seal the book until the time of consummation. For this reason the law read by Jews who lack the explanation of Christ's advent seems like a fable, while Christians read it as a treasure brought to light by the cross.
sources.quote: For every prophecy, before its fulfilment, is to men [full of] enigmas and ambiguities. But when the time has arrived, and the prediction has come to pass, then the prophecies have a clear and certain exposition.
sources.raw_question: Why could the Old Testament prophecies about the Son of God's coming in human nature not be clearly understood before his advent?

question: Can a human being who loves God come to see God and hear his Word?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVI.—The treasure hid in the Scriptures is Christ; the true exposition of the Scriptures is to be found in the Church alone.
sources.answer: Yes. The Scriptures, read in light of Christ, proclaim beforehand that the man who loves God will arrive at such excellency as to see God and hear his Word. By hearing God's discourse he will be glorified so greatly that others cannot look on the glory of his face. This is what Daniel foretold when he said the wise will shine like the brightness of the firmament.
sources.quote: proclaiming beforehand that the man who loves God shall arrive at such excellency as even to see God, and hear His word, and from the hearing of His discourse be glorified
sources.raw_question: Can a human being who loves God come to see God and hear his Word?

question: Can believers rightly bear and benefit spiritually from their afflictions apart from the consolations of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: No. Owen holds that there is no due management or improvement of any affliction, to God's glory and the soul's benefit, except by the consolations of the Holy Ghost. Those who seek relief elsewhere either despise God's correction or faint under it, and lose the benefit of their trials. Christ's promise to his suffering disciples was precisely to send the Spirit as Comforter.
sources.quote: there is no management nor improvement of any affliction, but merely and solely by the consolations of the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: Can believers rightly bear and benefit spiritually from their afflictions apart from the consolations of the Holy Spirit?

question: If the world was formed by lesser beings within the domain contained by the supreme Father, does any defect or darkness in it reflect on the Father himself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter V.—This world was not formed by any other beings within the territory which is contained by the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. If a void, dark, formless region exists within the Father, then either everything within him is lucid and full, or his light must be accused of being unable to illuminate what is within himself. Claiming the world is the fruit of defect and error therefore places defect and error inside the Father's own bosom.
sources.quote: they will be compelled either to acknowledge all those things which are within the Father, lucid, full, and energetic, or to accuse the light of the Father as if He could not illuminate all things
sources.raw_question: If the world was formed by lesser beings within the domain contained by the supreme Father, does any defect or darkness in it reflect on the Father himself?

question: Does believing in three coequal divine Persons divide the believer's trust and worship among three gods?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. Our trust is not scattered or confused by the coequal Godhead of the three. The Gospel opens access to God through the revelation of the Father in Christ by the Spirit. In that way we rest on, worship and love one God.
sources.quote: our trust is not dispersed or confused by this coequal Godhead of the Sacred Three
sources.raw_question: Does believing in three coequal divine Persons divide the believer's trust and worship among three gods?

question: Why does Paul pray for grace 'from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' together, and what does this show about the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: It shows that the Son is indivisible from the Father and that the grace given by Them is one and the same. The Father gives it, but the gift comes through the Son. When the Son is said to give it, it is the Father who supplies it through and in the Son.
sources.quote: For thus the blessing was secure, because of the Son’s indivisibility from the Father, and for that the grace given by Them is one and the same.
sources.raw_question: Why does Paul pray for grace 'from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' together, and what does this show about the Father and the Son?

question: Does seeing an angel amount to seeing God the Father, in the way that seeing the Son does?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. Someone who sees an angel knows he has seen an angel and not God, and the angel himself confesses that he has been sent. Scripture keeps the cases apart: Zacharias saw an angel, Isaiah saw the Lord; Manoah and Gideon saw angels, Moses and Abraham saw God. By contrast, whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father Himself.
sources.quote: And neither he who saw God, beheld an Angel, nor he who saw an Angel, considered that he saw God; for greatly, or rather wholly, do things by nature originate differ from God the Creator.
sources.raw_question: Does seeing an angel amount to seeing God the Father, in the way that seeing the Son does?

question: What rules should govern the theological explication of the Trinity beyond the bare scriptural propositions?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Two: it must tend directly to the ends of the revelation itself, enlightening the mind, strengthening faith against opposition, and directing worship; and it must affirm nothing that could beget undue apprehensions of God or our obedience. Such explication covers how God is one in essence, subsists in three persons, and how the persons are distinguished by their properties.
sources.quote: That nothing be affirmed or taught herein that may beget or occasion any undue apprehensions concerning God, or our obedience unto him
sources.raw_question: What rules should govern the theological explication of the Trinity beyond the bare scriptural propositions?

question: Does Paul's saying 'whether in the body I know not' (2 Cor. 12:2) show that a speaker who says 'I know not' may in fact know, and what does this imply for Christ's 'not even the Son'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: It shows that one can say 'I know not' while knowing. Paul knew how he was caught up, since Christ within him revealed all things, yet said 'I know not' for good reasons. If Paul knew by Christ's revelation, much more does Christ Himself know though He says 'I know not'; the Arians are inconsistent in granting Paul knowledge but denying it to the Lord.
sources.quote: For if since Christ was within him, Paul knew that of which he says, ‘I know not,’ does not much more Christ Himself know, though He say, ‘I know not?’
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's saying 'whether in the body I know not' (2 Cor. 12:2) show that a speaker who says 'I know not' may in fact know, and what does this imply for Christ's 'not even the Son'?

question: Can an act of will and a natural operation coexist without one delaying the other, as an analogy for the Father's will and the Son's generation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He then discusses the “willing” of the Father concerning the generation of the Son, and shows that the object of that good will is from eternity, which is the Son, existing in the Father, and being closely related to the process of willing, as the ray to the flame, or the act of seeing to the eye.
sources.answer: Yes. In the eye, seeing is an operation of nature and the will to see is an impulse of choice, yet the choice causes no delay to sight; they are interexistent, the natural operation concurring with the choice. So in the divine Nature, will concerning the Son and the Son's existence come together simultaneously.
sources.quote: perception naturally belongs to the eye, and the willing to see produces no delay in respect to actual sight, but one wills that it should have vision, and immediately what he wills is
sources.raw_question: Can an act of will and a natural operation coexist without one delaying the other, as an analogy for the Father's will and the Son's generation?

question: How do differences of reward among the saints relate to the gift of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: The differing glories of the saints are measured gifts of the Spirit's grace. Spiritual glory is distributed to each in proportion to how nobly he has lived, so that those sealed by the Spirit who preserve undiminished His first fruits receive greater reward, as the 'many mansions' and the stars differing in glory show.
sources.quote: the crown of the righteous is the grace of the Spirit, bestowed in more abundant and perfect measure in that day, when spiritual glory shall be distributed to each in proportion as he shall have nobly played the man
sources.raw_question: How do differences of reward among the saints relate to the gift of the Holy Spirit?

question: Is the divine essence fruitful, so that God is by nature a Father, or barren as the Arians hold?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: The divine essence is fruitful. To call it barren is to make it like a light that does not shine or a dry fountain. It is absurd to grant God a framing energy toward creatures while denying Him a natural generative fruitfulness.
sources.quote: For if the Divine Essence be not fruitful itself, but barren, as they hold, as a light that lightens not, and a dry fountain, are they not ashamed to speak of His possessing framing energy?
sources.raw_question: Is the divine essence fruitful, so that God is by nature a Father, or barren as the Arians hold?

question: Was the world we belong to formed by some power other than the supreme Father, such as angels who do not know him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXI.—Recapitulation and application of the foregoing arguments.
sources.answer: No. It is not plausible that any being other than the Father of all formed our creation. The view that the Father contains all things while some lesser power or ignorant angels made the world is refuted by the arguments already given. Those arguments apply equally to Saturninus, Basilides, Carpocrates and the other Gnostics.
sources.quote: when I showed that it is not a probable supposition that any other being than the Father of all formed that creation to which we belong
sources.raised_by_detail: Saturninus, Basilides, Carpocrates and other Gnostics
sources.raw_question: Was the world we belong to formed by some power other than the supreme Father, such as angels who do not know him?

question: Is the Creator of the world the one and only God and Father of all, or an inferior being produced through defect and ignorance?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXI.—Recapitulation and application of the foregoing arguments.
sources.answer: The Creator alone is God and Father of all. Irenaeus applies all his arguments about the Creator against heretics in general. He rejects ascribing the Creator's origin to defect and ignorance as blasphemy against the one who is Maker, Sustainer and Lord.
sources.quote: And all that has been said respecting the Creator (Demiurge) to show that he alone is God and Father of all
sources.raw_question: Is the Creator of the world the one and only God and Father of all, or an inferior being produced through defect and ignorance?

question: How does faith in Christ's incarnation relate to belief in his equality with the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: The godly receive the Son as made less than the Father for their sakes, in the form of a servant. Through this they believe him equal to the Father in the form of God. Christ reinforces this by saying that as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself.
sources.quote: who so receive Him, as made for their sakes less than the Father, in the form of a servant, that they believe Him equal to the Father, in the form of God
sources.raw_question: How does faith in Christ's incarnation relate to belief in his equality with the Father?

question: Do the Son's titles in Scripture, such as Judge, King and object of worship, stand or fall together with his true Godhead?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. The divine names cannot be true of him in one case and false in another; they follow one another. If he is truly God, then he is truly Judge and King and rightly worshipped. That is exactly why denying his true Godhead overthrows every honour due to him, which is what the Eunomian argument is quietly aiming at.
sources.quote: if He be truly God, it follows that He is Judge and King, and that His several attributes are such as they are described, while, if His godhead be falsely asserted, neither will the truth hold respecting any of His other attributes
sources.raw_question: Do the Son's titles in Scripture, such as Judge, King and object of worship, stand or fall together with his true Godhead?

question: If the Son's birth from God is ineffable and cannot be defined in words, how can we be certain of it?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: We are certain through faith in the Son's own teaching. Though our apprehension of this truth cannot be put into words, the Son's revelation that He went forth from God gives it the certainty of an assured faith.
sources.quote: though our apprehension of this truth, which is ineffable, cannot be defined in words, yet the teaching of the Son, as He reveals to us that He went forth from God, imparts to it the certainty of an assured faith.
sources.raw_question: If the Son's birth from God is ineffable and cannot be defined in words, how can we be certain of it?

question: Does Scripture testify clearly enough to the Godhead of Christ, the eternal Son of God, to make it an object of faith?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen gathers many texts that ascribe to Christ divine names, creation, judgment, omniscience, eternity and worship, and identify him with the LORD of the Old Testament. He judges these testimonies to be as clear and unquestionable as those that prove there is a God at all. Anyone who receives Scripture as God's infallible word and considers them with a conscience must see that they sufficiently set forth this article of faith.
sources.quote: the testimonies given to the Godhead of Christ, the eternal Son of God, are every way as clear and unquestionable as those are which testify to the being of God, or that there is any God at all
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture testify clearly enough to the Godhead of Christ, the eternal Son of God, to make it an object of faith?

question: Is the Father's being alone supreme, with the Son's being dependent and the Spirit's more dependent still, as though the divine Beings differ in extent or size?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: No. Gregory ridicules the idea that the divine Beings are greater or less, like casks nested inside each other, since this attributes degrees of size to Beings that are illimitable. Nor is the Only-begotten circumscribed as the effect of an energy accompanying the Father.
sources.quote: Or because these Beings are to be thought of as of greater or less extent, the smaller included within and surrounded by the larger, like casks put one inside the other, inasmuch as he detects degrees of size within Beings that are illimitable?
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's being alone supreme, with the Son's being dependent and the Spirit's more dependent still, as though the divine Beings differ in extent or size?

question: Are the divine titles of the Son and the Spirit gifts granted to them by favour, or do they belong to them by nature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XV. Though the Spirit be called Lord, three Lords are not thereby implied; inasmuch as two Lords are not implied by the fact that the Son in the same manner as the Father is called Lord in many passages of Scripture; for Lordship exists in the Godhead, and the Godhead in Lordship, and these coincide without division in the Three Persons.
sources.answer: They belong by nature. The titles are not contributions gathered from bounty but free-will gifts of natural love. The unity keeps each Person's special property, and the special properties are bound together in unity.
sources.quote: For they are not [as it were] contributions gathered from bounty, but free-will gifts of natural love; for both Unity has its special property, and the special properties are bound together in unity.
sources.raw_question: Are the divine titles of the Son and the Spirit gifts granted to them by favour, or do they belong to them by nature?

question: Is understanding the doctrine of Scripture in the letter the same as truly knowing the mind of Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. There is a wide difference between knowing the letter of scriptural doctrine and truly knowing Christ's mind. The natural man does not receive the things of God. True knowledge comes only by a special unction from Christ, the Holy One, given to believers.
sources.quote: There is a wide difference between understanding the doctrine of the Scripture as in the letter, and a true knowing the mind of Christ. This we have by special unction from Christ
sources.raw_question: Is understanding the doctrine of Scripture in the letter the same as truly knowing the mind of Christ?

question: Is the Father superior in dignity to the Son because the Son carried out the work of mercy while the Father remained inactive in it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: No. It is absurd to judge the inoperative to be superior to the operative in a benevolent work. Moreover, the Father was not inactive in the dispensation, since every good has its origin from the Father. Christ says 'He that sent Me is with Me' and 'The Father that dwelleth in Me, He doeth the works'.
sources.quote: They judge that which is ineffective for a benevolent purpose to be superior to that which is operative.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father superior in dignity to the Son because the Son carried out the work of mercy while the Father remained inactive in it?

question: Are the visible manifestations of God in the Old Testament signs of the Father only, or of the Son and Holy Spirit as well?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Of the Appearance on Sinai. Whether the Trinity Spake in that Appearance or Some One Person Specially.
sources.answer: They signify the whole invisible God, not only the Father but also the Son and the Holy Spirit. All such sensible things are exhibited through a subject creature to signify the invisible and intelligible God, of whom, through whom and in whom are all things.
sources.quote: exhibited through the creature made subject in order to signify the invisible and intelligible God, not only the Father, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Are the visible manifestations of God in the Old Testament signs of the Father only, or of the Son and Holy Spirit as well?

question: Should the soul love particular good things or God as the good itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How God May Be Known to Be the Chief Good. The Mind Does Not Become Good Unless by Turning to God.
sources.answer: God, the good itself, is to be loved. The good the soul must seek is not one it rises above by judging. It is one to which it cleaves by loving, and this can be nothing but God.
sources.quote: For the good that must be sought for the soul is not one above which it is to fly by judging, but to which it is to cleave by loving; and what can this be except God?
sources.raw_question: Should the soul love particular good things or God as the good itself?

question: What absurdities follow if the Word's generation is tied to creation and His return to God ends that generation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Marcellus and his disciples, like Arians, say that the Word was, not indeed created, but issued, to create us, as if the Divine silence were a state of inaction, and when God spake by the Word, He acted; or that there was a going forth and return of the Word; a doctrine which implies change and imperfection in Father and Son.
sources.answer: His return would close His generation, so He that was begotten would again be unbegotten. God would fall silent again, and creation, which exists by the Word's outgoing, would cease to exist. It would then be pointless for creation to come into being or for God to speak at all. God would either be silent forever or beget again and devise new creations without end.
sources.quote: For if His progression be generation, His return will be the close of that generation, for when He has come to be in God, God will be silent again.
sources.raw_question: What absurdities follow if the Word's generation is tied to creation and His return to God ends that generation?

question: Does the Son's creating and sustaining of all things require time or bodily instruments?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. The Son upholds all things by the word of His power, works not by bodily agency or hands, and acts faster than any light, motion or thought. All nature follows Him in obedient and unforced consent, so His works are accomplished without lapse of time.
sources.quote: For what extent of time is needed by Him who “upholds all things by the word of His power,” and works not by bodily agency, nor requires the help of hands to form and fashion
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's creating and sustaining of all things require time or bodily instruments?

question: From what does the name "Godhead" (theotes) or "God" (theos) derive its meaning?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: It derives from an operation, namely beholding or surveying (thea). Since we name God from His known operations, and one of these is the activity whereby He surveys and oversees all things, discerns our thoughts and sees what is invisible, He is called theos as the beholder. The name therefore signifies an operation, not the nature itself.
sources.quote: we suppose that Godhead, or θεότης, is so called from θέα, or beholding, and that He who is our θεατής or beholder, by customary use and by the instruction of the Scriptures, is called θεός, or God
sources.raw_question: From what does the name "Godhead" (theotes) or "God" (theos) derive its meaning?

question: If all things exist within God, can some of them be ignorant of Him while others know Him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. Whatever is within the Father who fills all things must partake of Him equally, as figures formed in water all partake of water. So ignorance has no place among them. This destroys the Gnostic account of degeneracy and of matter arising from passion and ignorance.
sources.quote: so must those also who are within Him all equally partake of the Father, ignorance having no place among them.
sources.raw_question: If all things exist within God, can some of them be ignorant of Him while others know Him?

question: Why does Scripture sometimes seem to ground Christ's title to worship in what he has done for us rather than in what he is in himself?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: Because moral agents are moved most strongly by reasons that concern themselves, just as we love God "because he first loved us." The essential dignity of Christ's Person is the true ground of honour and worship. His offices toward us are the reasons that chiefly move our wills to give that worship. Scripture teaches both his absolute and his relative dignity, so that we know what honour is due to him and have every motive to give it.
sources.quote: The essential dignity of Christ’s Person is really the ground and foundation of honour and esteem, (and consequently of worship, the highest expression of both,) which ought always to bear proportion to the intrinsic excellency of the object
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture sometimes seem to ground Christ's title to worship in what he has done for us rather than in what he is in himself?

question: Could a mere creature have been entrusted with the work of redeeming mankind?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: Very probably not, even if a creature had the abilities for it. So great and endearing a charge would draw to the redeemer more love and esteem than is consistent with our duty to God and with Scripture's rules about how we treat creatures. Christ's office toward us therefore points back to the prior excellence of the Person who could do such things.
sources.quote:
no creature what-

ever (supposing him to have suitable abilities) could have been intrusted with so great and so endearing a charge
sources.raw_question: Could a mere creature have been entrusted with the work of redeeming mankind?

question: Can fallen human beings, by nature and since the entrance of sin, have any communion with God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: No. Since sin entered, no one has communion with God by nature. God is light, life and love, while sinners are darkness, dead and at enmity with him, and two cannot walk together unless they are agreed. Sinners are without Christ, without hope and without God in the world, alienated from the life of God. Sin so lost our first interest in God that we have no power in ourselves to return.
sources.quote: He is life, we are dead, — he is love, and we are enmity; and what agreement can there be between us?
sources.raw_question: Can fallen human beings, by nature and since the entrance of sin, have any communion with God?

question: Is Christ's kingdom and government eternal?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Like solid gold, his rule has both splendour and duration. Scripture declares that his throne is for ever and ever and that of the increase of his government there shall be no end. It is an everlasting kingdom that shall never be destroyed, for he must reign until all his enemies are subdued.
sources.quote: It is durable, yea, eternal, — solid gold. “His throne is for ever and ever,” Ps. xlv. 6
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's kingdom and government eternal?

question: Do the texts that stress Christ's humanity and subordination count against his Deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Following Coleridge, the author holds that these very texts refute those who deny his Deity. A mere man could not, without absurd presumption, solemnly declare that God the Father was greater than he. Nor could a mere man be 'made flesh', or show humility by being made in the likeness of man.
sources.quote: How could a mere man without absurd presumption, solemnly announce that God the Father was greater than He? How could He be made flesh?
sources.raw_question: Do the texts that stress Christ's humanity and subordination count against his Deity?

question: Should the knowledge and discoveries humans reach through the faculty of conception be ascribed to God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture, in God's answer to Job, says that God set man over the arts and gave woman skill in weaving. He did this not by visible teaching but by endowing human nature with the faculty of conceiving and discovering. By the law of causation, whatever conception discovers is rightly ascribed to the Author of that faculty, just as the human art of healing is rightly called a gift of God.
sources.quote: And by the law of causation, whatever is discovered and established by conception must be ascribed to Him Who is the Author of that faculty.
sources.raw_question: Should the knowledge and discoveries humans reach through the faculty of conception be ascribed to God?

question: How can Scripture say that God "only hath immortality" when the human soul is also immortal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > This Work is Written Against Those Who Sophistically Assail the Faith of the Trinity, Through Misuse of Reason. They Who Dispute Concerning God Err from a Threefold Cause. Holy Scripture, Removing What is False, Leads Us on by Degrees to Things Divine. What True Immortality is. We are Nourished by Faith, that We May Be Enabled to Apprehend Things Divine.
sources.answer: True immortality is unchangeableness, which no creature can possess and which belongs to the Creator alone. The soul is immortal only in a certain manner. This is confirmed by texts teaching that in God there is no variableness and that He remains the same while creatures change.
sources.quote: Scripture would not say “only hath,” unless because true immortality is unchangeableness; which no creature can possess, since it belongs to the creator alone.
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture say that God "only hath immortality" when the human soul is also immortal?

question: How do the Father and the Son glorify each other?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: The Father glorified the Son by giving him all things. The Son glorified the Father when all things were made through him and when he made the Father known. All the Son's glory is the Father's glory, because everything he has is the Father's gift. The glory of the Begotten therefore redounds to the Begetter.
sources.quote: For the glory of Him who executes a charge redounds to the glory of Him Who gave it, the glory of the Begotten to the glory of the Begetter.
sources.raw_question: How do the Father and the Son glorify each other?

question: Does love contain a threefold structure that can serve as a trace or likeness of the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > There are Three Things in Love, as It Were a Trace of the Trinity.
sources.answer: Yes. Love is always of someone who loves, and by love something is loved, so there are three things: the lover, the beloved, and love itself. Augustine offers this triad as a starting-point or 'hinge' for seeking an image of the Trinity, though he insists it is not yet the thing sought but only shows where to look for it.
sources.quote: But love is of some one that loves, and with love something is loved. Behold, then, there are three things: he that loves, and that which is loved, and love.
sources.raw_question: Does love contain a threefold structure that can serve as a trace or likeness of the Trinity?

question: Why is it necessary both that the Word's flesh be truly human and that the Word be truly Son of God by nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Both are equally required for our salvation. We could not be freed from sin and the curse unless the flesh the Word assumed were truly human, since we would have nothing in common with what was foreign; and we could not be deified unless the Word were by nature from the Father. So denying the Son's natural deity is as damaging as Valentinus's denial of true flesh.
sources.quote: for in neither case had it been of profit to us men, whether the Word were not true and naturally Son of God, or the flesh not true which He assumed.
sources.raw_question: Why is it necessary both that the Word's flesh be truly human and that the Word be truly Son of God by nature?

question: Why is the mind's love of itself not called an offspring begotten by the mind, as its knowledge of itself is, even though the mind is the principle of both?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > Why Love is Not the Offspring of the Mind, as Knowledge is So. The Solution of the Question. The Mind with the Knowledge of Itself and the Love of Itself is the Image of the Trinity.
sources.answer: Because love is not 'brought forth' or discovered in the way knowledge is. Knowledge is the result of an inquiry that finds its object, and what is found is like an offspring born; love, by contrast, proceeds from the mind as its principle but is the very desire that precedes and leads to that bringing forth. So love proceeds rather than being begotten, which offers an analogy for the Spirit's procession as distinct from the Son's generation.
sources.quote: that desire by which knowledge is conceived and brought forth, cannot rightly be called the bringing forth and the offspring
sources.raw_question: Why is the mind's love of itself not called an offspring begotten by the mind, as its knowledge of itself is, even though the mind is the principle of both?

question: Does Paul's joining of the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ as givers of grace and peace show the oneness of Father and Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Yes. One and the same grace comes from the Father in the Son, as the light of sun and radiance is one. In praying for the Thessalonians Paul wrote 'may He direct', not 'may they direct', showing it is not a double grace from two sources but the Father giving through the Son.
sources.quote: For he has not said, ‘May they direct,’ as if a double grace were given from two Sources, This and That, but ‘May He direct,’ to shew that the Father gives it through the Son
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's joining of the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ as givers of grace and peace show the oneness of Father and Son?

question: If 'God' in Scripture means the Author and Governor of the universe, does admitting the Son as a second Author and Governor distinct in being from the Father amount to admitting a second God contrary to Isaiah's declarations of one God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 4: Whether, supposing the Scripture-notion of God to be no more than that of the Author and Governor of the universe, or whatever it be, the admitting of another t
sources.answer: Yes. Substituting the definition 'Author and Governor of the universe' for 'God' in Isaiah's texts ('there is no Author and Governor beside me') sets them in direct contradiction with texts calling the Word Author and Governor (John 1:1, Rom 9:5). Two such Authors and Governors conceived as separate beings are plainly two Gods, the difference being only that of putting the definition for the thing defined.
sources.quote: two Authors and Governors of the universe, whom you suppose two distinct separate Beings, are as plainly two Gods, as if it were said so in terms. For indeed there is no difference more than that of putting the definition for the thing defined.
sources.raw_question: If 'God' in Scripture means the Author and Governor of the universe, does admitting the Son as a second Author and Governor distinct in being from the Father amount to admitting a second God contrary to Isaiah's declarations of one God?

question: When Christ says the seats at his right and left are prepared by his Father, does this mean the Son himself does not prepare them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. What is prepared by the Father is prepared also by the Son, because he and the Father are one. In the Trinity what is said of each is also said of all, on account of the indivisible working of the one substance, so the Son with the Father prepares seats of glory for whom he will.
sources.quote: But that which is prepared by His Father is prepared also by the Son Himself, because He and the Father are one.
sources.raw_question: When Christ says the seats at his right and left are prepared by his Father, does this mean the Son himself does not prepare them?

question: Is Christ only a part of the believer's acceptance with God, or the whole of it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Christ is the whole of it. Owen argues that Christ is made of God unto us wisdom and righteousness, so he is not merely one part of our acceptation but all of it, which most tends to his honour in the hearts of believers.
sources.quote: Not that he is this or that part of our acceptation with God; but he is all, — he is the whole.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ only a part of the believer's acceptance with God, or the whole of it?

question: Was Christ exalted by God the Father on account of his suffering and work of redemption?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Whether the 'wherefore' of Philippians 2:9 signifies causality or only consequence, it is evident that on account of his suffering, and as its end, Christ was exalted by God to unspeakable pre-eminence, dignity and authority, as God had promised. Hence after purging our sins he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.
sources.quote: Whether that word “wherefore” denotes a connection of causality or only a consequence, this is evident, that on the account of his suffering, and as the end of it, he was honoured and exalted of God to an unspeakable pre-eminence, dignity, and authority
sources.raw_question: Was Christ exalted by God the Father on account of his suffering and work of redemption?

question: Should the things Christ says humanly after the Incarnation be ascribed to His manhood rather than to the Word's divinity?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ did not say He was ignorant when the heavens were made or when He was with the Father before the Incarnation. He said it only after 'the Word became flesh.' So what He says humanly after becoming man is reasonably ascribed to His manhood, while knowing what was made belongs properly to the Word.
sources.quote: On this account it is reasonable to ascribe to His manhood everything which, after He became man, He speaks humanly.
sources.raw_question: Should the things Christ says humanly after the Incarnation be ascribed to His manhood rather than to the Word's divinity?

question: Does the Word, as Creator of all things, know the end of all things?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Yes. The works are His, so the Word knows the beginning of each and the limit of its existence. Knowing the beginning and end of each thing, He surely knows the general and common end of all.
sources.quote: And knowing of each the beginning and the end, He knows surely the general and common end of all.
sources.raw_question: Does the Word, as Creator of all things, know the end of all things?

question: Are God's justice and mercy in conflict when he lays our sins on Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
