sources.answer: No. In causing our iniquities to meet on Christ, not sparing him but delivering him up for us, God declared his justice while exercising grace, so there is a blessed harmony of the highest justice and most excellent mercy. Since God's attributes are essentially one in him, his wisdom ensures their effects are never contrary.
sources.quote: there was a blessed harmony in the highest Justice and most excellent grace and mercy
sources.raw_question: Are God's justice and mercy in conflict when he lays our sins on Christ?

question: Can He who is be begotten, as the Eunomians ask?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: Yes, in the proper sense. He who is in the Ungenerate was generated from Him and derives His source from Him, yet no 'when' of His beginning can be named. He was both begotten and always was: generation from the Father on the score of causation, but no moment of non-existence by virtue of His everlasting life. This is not the sense of Nicodemus's question about a second birth of one already existing.
sources.quote: He was both begotten and was, evincing on the score of causation generation from the Father, but by virtue of His everlasting life repelling any moment of non-existence.
sources.raw_question: Can He who is be begotten, as the Eunomians ask?

question: Can the Arian scheme give a satisfactory account of the Scripture texts that declare the unity of God and call the Son God, Creator, and an object of worship?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 31: Whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration, on the side of Arianism, ought to move a wise and good man, against so great appearances of truth o
sources.answer: No. All the texts the Arians bring against the Catholic doctrine have already been weighed, and solutions are ready for them. The Arians, by contrast, have yet to give a tolerable account of several texts, especially those declaring the unity of God and proclaiming the Son to be God, Creator, and worthy of adoration.
sources.quote: you are yet to seek how to give a tolerable account of several texts; those, especially, which declare the wnity of God, and proclaim the Son to be God, Creator, and object of worship and adoration.
sources.raw_question: Can the Arian scheme give a satisfactory account of the Scripture texts that declare the unity of God and call the Son God, Creator, and an object of worship?

question: Is there a difference between Christ being 'begotten' and being 'brought forth' from the womb?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: Yes. Begetting concerns the primary foundation of being, while bringing forth is only the production of what already exists. Scripture keeps these apart: He is begotten before the morning star, but drawn from the womb, which happened at night, whereas His bodily conception at the Annunciation is not said to be at night.
sources.quote: to beget differs from bringing forth; for begetting involves the primary foundation, but to bring forth is nothing else than the production of what exists.
sources.raw_question: Is there a difference between Christ being 'begotten' and being 'brought forth' from the womb?

question: Does John chapter 5 express as fully as possible the Son's real subordination to and dependence on the Father, as a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. Had Christ been a mere creature charged with blasphemy for making himself equal with God, he would have repudiated the thought and said he was only God's creature acting by God's power, as the apostles did. Instead he again called himself Son of God and claimed he could do whatever the Father does: work on the sabbath, give life, raise the dead and judge the world. He therefore claimed the same right to the same honour.
sources.quote: being charged with blasphemy, in making himself equal with God, he might have expressed his abhorrence of such a thought ; and have told them that he pretended to be nothing more than a creature of God’s, sent upon God’s errand
sources.raw_question: Does John chapter 5 express as fully as possible the Son's real subordination to and dependence on the Father, as a creature?

question: Does the fact that God manifested his attributes in Christ mean he will actually use them for the good of every person?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. It does not follow absolutely, because countless people perish despite God's manifestation of himself in Christ. In addition, God has committed the exercise of all his properties into Christ's hand. Christ manages them on behalf of believers as the captain of their salvation.
sources.quote: Though he hath made them all glorious in a way that may tend to our good, yet it doth not absolutely follow that he will use them for our good
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that God manifested his attributes in Christ mean he will actually use them for the good of every person?

question: In what sense does Christ, the Son, have the exercise of God's attributes committed to him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Christ glorified the Father in all his attributes, and the Father has now committed their exercise to him on behalf of those who believe. Scripture accordingly calls Christ 'the power of God, and the wisdom of God' and 'the Lord our Righteousness.' Whatever good is in God's righteousness, love, mercy, and all-sufficiency, Christ dispenses it, since God is 'in him, reconciling the world unto himself.'
sources.quote: Christ having glorified his Father in all his attributes, he hath now the exercise of them committed to him, that he might be the captain of salvation to them that do believe
sources.raw_question: In what sense does Christ, the Son, have the exercise of God's attributes committed to him?

question: Is it blasphemous to say that God's essence, like the Only-begotten Son or like corn, admits of a variety of conceptions (names derived from different operations and relations)?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory treats Basil's comparison as legitimate and turns the charge back on Eunomius. In Gregory's view the real blasphemy is Eunomius' own: he holds it equally absurd to compare the Ungenerate God with corn and with the Son. That puts the Only-begotten on a level with a seed.
sources.quote: he declares that even in like manner the most holy essence of God admits of the same variety of conception.
sources.raw_question: Is it blasphemous to say that God's essence, like the Only-begotten Son or like corn, admits of a variety of conceptions (names derived from different operations and relations)?

question: What role does Christ the Lord play in bringing the righteous to share in the glory of God the Father in the coming kingdom?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXV.—He contends that these testimonies already alleged cannot be understood allegorically of celestial blessings, but that they shall have their fulfilment after the coming of Antichrist, and the resurrection, in the terrestrial Jerusalem. To the former prophecies he subjoins others drawn from Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the Apocalypse of John.
sources.answer: Christ is the mediator through whom the saints are gradually accustomed to the Father's glory. In the kingdom the righteous grow stronger by seeing the Lord, and through Him they become accustomed to partaking in the glory of God the Father. They also enjoy communion with the holy angels and union with spiritual beings.
sources.quote: the righteous shall reign in the earth, waxing stronger by the sight of the Lord: and through Him they shall become accustomed to partake in the glory of God the Father
sources.raw_question: What role does Christ the Lord play in bringing the righteous to share in the glory of God the Father in the coming kingdom?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's anointing and empowering of Christ for redemption prove the Spirit's own Deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Once the Godhead of Christ is proved, the Spirit's anointing of this infinite Saviour for all the work of redemption shows the Spirit's own divine infinitude, since none but God could empower God.
sources.quote: the very fact of the Holy Spirit anointing this infinite Saviour for all the work of redemption proves his own Divine infinitude; – for who but God could empower God?
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's anointing and empowering of Christ for redemption prove the Spirit's own Deity?

question: Does Exodus show that the Father and the Son share the same Name, "Lord"?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIII. St. Ambrose shows from the Scriptures that the Name of the Three Divine Persons is one, and first the unity of the Name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as each is called Paraclete and Truth.
sources.answer: Yes. In Exodus the Lord says he will call the Lord by his own Name before Moses. The Lord thus calls the Lord by his Name, so "Lord" is the Name of both the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: So, then, the Lord said that He would call the Lord by His Name. The Lord, then, is the Name of the Father and of the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does Exodus show that the Father and the Son share the same Name, "Lord"?

question: Does the worship (latreia) that Christians pay to the Holy Spirit prove that the Spirit is not a creature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture forbids giving to any creature the service (latreia) due to God alone, which is why those who give it to images are called idolaters. Yet the saints render this service to the Spirit, as Philippians 3:3 says in the Greek, "we who serve the Spirit of God." Therefore the Holy Spirit is not a creature.
sources.quote: then assuredly the Holy Spirit is not a creature, to whom such a service is paid by all the saints; as says the apostle, “For we are the circumcision, which serve the Spirit of God,”
sources.raw_question: Does the worship (latreia) that Christians pay to the Holy Spirit prove that the Spirit is not a creature?

question: Would it be beneath God's dignity to create lesser creatures directly, so that He would commit their making to the Son as an assistant?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: No. There is no pride in God. Christ teaches that the Father's providence reaches sparrows, the grass of the field and the hairs of the head. If it is not unworthy of God to exercise providence over such small things, it is not unworthy of Him to make them, and He is Maker of what He provides for through His proper Word.
sources.quote: If then it be not unworthy of God to exercise His Providence, even down to things so small, a hair of the head, and a sparrow, and the grass of the field, also it was not unworthy of Him to make them.
sources.raw_question: Would it be beneath God's dignity to create lesser creatures directly, so that He would commit their making to the Son as an assistant?

question: Can love love itself as love without loving some object beyond itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > That He Who Loves His Brother, Loves God; Because He Loves Love Itself, Which is of God, and is God.
sources.answer: No. Love that loves nothing is not love, so love loves itself as love only by loving itself as loving something. It is like a word, which shows itself to be a word only by showing that it signifies something.
sources.quote: so love also loves indeed itself, but except it love itself as loving something, it loves itself not as love.
sources.raw_question: Can love love itself as love without loving some object beyond itself?

question: Does the comparison of a king sharing his rule with his son support the view that the Son is a lesser being than the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. Athenagoras and Tertullian used the similitude only to illustrate the one government common to Father and Son, not the unity of Godhead. If anything, the comparison of a king and his son argues an equality of nature, contrary to Clarke's tenets.
sources.quote: (which however would argue an equality of nature, contrary to your tenets.)
sources.raw_question: Does the comparison of a king sharing his rule with his son support the view that the Son is a lesser being than the Father?

question: How do the Father and the Son relate in carrying out the plan of salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: The Father foreknows all things, and the Son accomplishes them in their proper order and season. This is why Christ told Mary at Cana that his hour had not yet come, and why no one could seize him before the time the Father had foreknown. Paul likewise says God sent his Son when the fulness of time came. The Son thus fulfils the Father's will as Saviour, Lord, and God of all created things.
sources.quote: For all these things were foreknown by the Father; but the Son works them out at the proper time in perfect order and sequence.
sources.raw_question: How do the Father and the Son relate in carrying out the plan of salvation?

question: Does Christ's reply to the Jews citing 'Ye are gods' (Psalm 82:6) mean that He claimed to be God only in the same nominal sense as holy men?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Christ first shows the absurdity of the charge of blasphemy, since the Law gave the name 'gods' to confessed men, so a man bearing the title is no blasphemy. But He excels them, having been sanctified by the Father and sent into the world, and He proclaims Himself the Son of God. His argument as a whole proves that He is Son of God in name, in nature and by birth.
sources.quote: if other men may use this name without blasphemy, there can obviously be no blasphemy in its use by the Man Whom the Father has sanctified
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's reply to the Jews citing 'Ye are gods' (Psalm 82:6) mean that He claimed to be God only in the same nominal sense as holy men?

question: Does Christ's being 'sanctified' and 'appointed Son of God with power' imply that He is merely a man elevated to the title of god?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The sanctification refers to His being hallowed as the Son, as Paul says of the Son made of the seed of David according to the flesh and declared Son of God with power. Christ speaks of Himself as Man because the Son of God is also Son of Man. Yet He excels all others who bear the name 'gods', and His Sonship is grounded in a true birth.
sources.quote: He excels them, in that He has been hallowed to be the Son, as the blessed Paul says, who teaches us of this sanctification
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's being 'sanctified' and 'appointed Son of God with power' imply that He is merely a man elevated to the title of god?

question: Does the statement that John was 'a man sent from God' (John 1:6) belong to the same kind of knowledge as the statement that there was a man named John?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Attempt is Made to Distinguish Out of the Scriptures the Offices of Wisdom and of Knowledge. That in the Beginning of John Some Things that are Said Belong to Wisdom, Some to Knowledge. Some Things There are Only Known by the Help of Faith. How We See the Faith that is in Us. In the Same Narrative of John, Some Things are Known by the Sense of the Body, Others Only by the Reason of the Mind.
sources.answer: No. That there was a man named John is a temporal fact known through our common notion of human nature, gained from bodily sight, self-knowledge, and speech. Believers and unbelievers think of it in the same way. That he was 'sent from God' is held only by faith; those without faith either doubt it or mock it. Yet anyone who does not deny God can still think, as far as he is able, what God is and what it is to be sent from God.
sources.quote: But that which is there also, viz. “sent from God,” they who hold at all, hold by faith; and they who do not hold it by faith, either hesitate through doubt, or deride it through unbelief.
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that John was 'a man sent from God' (John 1:6) belong to the same kind of knowledge as the statement that there was a man named John?

question: Is it right to describe God as producing Thought, Mind and Word in succession, the way these arise in a human soul?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. Such a series of emissions belongs to men, who are compound beings of body and soul. Applying it to God gives the Father of all human affections and passions and shows ignorance of God. Scripture teaches that God is not like men and His thoughts are not like men's thoughts.
sources.quote: they ascribe those things which apply to men to the Father of all, whom they also declare to be unknown to all
sources.raw_question: Is it right to describe God as producing Thought, Mind and Word in succession, the way these arise in a human soul?

question: Can God's Mind or Word be sent forth from God by emission so as to become separate from Him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. Even in humans, understanding does not arise by emission and is not separated from the living person. Much more will the mind of God, who is all understanding, never be separated from Himself, and nothing in Him can be produced as if by a different being. Emission would make God compound and corporeal and would split His intelligence into parts.
sources.quote: much more will the mind of God, who is all understanding, never by any means be separated from Himself; nor can anything [in His case] be produced as if by a different Being.
sources.raw_question: Can God's Mind or Word be sent forth from God by emission so as to become separate from Him?

question: Is the mystery of God one of simple singleness or of multiplicity of gods?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Neither. There is no second God springing from God with a nature of his own, so the mystery is not multiplicity. Nor does God remain a single Person, because the Son's true birth teaches us to confess God as Father.
sources.quote: The mystery of God consists neither in simplicity, nor in multiplicity: for neither is there another God, Who springs from God with qualities of His own nature, nor does God remain as a single Person
sources.raw_question: Is the mystery of God one of simple singleness or of multiplicity of gods?

question: Did the prophets, apostles, and Christ acknowledge any God or Lord other than the supreme God, the Father, together with his Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IX.—One and the same God, the Creator of heaven and earth, is He whom the prophets foretold, and who was declared by the Gospel. Proof of this, at the outset, from St. Matthew’s Gospel.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus holds that the prophets and apostles confessed the Father and the Son and named no other as God or Lord. He also says the Lord himself taught that the Father is the only God and ruler of all. Christians, as their disciples, must follow this testimony.
sources.quote: the prophets and the apostles confessing the Father and the Son; but naming no other as God, and confessing no other as Lord
sources.raw_question: Did the prophets, apostles, and Christ acknowledge any God or Lord other than the supreme God, the Father, together with his Son?

question: Can a being be both truly God and created?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: No. Created and uncreated essences cannot be expressed by the same terms, because the attributes of the one are not found in the other: Godhead is not found in the creature, nor createdness in the Godhead. If he is God he is not created, and if created he is not God. A creature called 'God' bears only the empty name, as a horse given a man's name is still not a man.
sources.quote: so neither is Godhead discoverable in the creature, nor the attribute of being created in the Godhead: but if He be God He is certainly not created, and if He be created He is not God
sources.raw_question: Can a being be both truly God and created?

question: Does the 'mediator' in whose hand the Law was ordained through angels (Galatians 3:19) refer to an angel or to Christ?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: It refers to Christ. The Law was ordered through angels in Christ's own hand. Paul shows elsewhere that the one Mediator between God and men is the man Christ Jesus, not any angel, in so far as he deigned to be made man.
sources.quote: he does not mean any one of the angels as a mediator, but the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, in so far as He deigned to be made man
sources.raw_question: Does the 'mediator' in whose hand the Law was ordained through angels (Galatians 3:19) refer to an angel or to Christ?

question: Is the Father sovereign over the Son and the Holy Spirit in the way a ruler is set over those who are ruled?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: No. A ruler is needed only by a mutable nature, which must be kept by help from above from turning to evil. The divine nature of the Son and Spirit is incapable of evil, unchangeable and eternally permanent. It therefore needs no ruler, since it is itself the ruler of all creation.
sources.quote: If, on the other hand, the Divine nature is incapable of evil, unchangeable, unalterable, eternally permanent, to what end does it stand in need of a ruler
sources.raw_question: Is the Father sovereign over the Son and the Holy Spirit in the way a ruler is set over those who are ruled?

question: Could the "seven spirits" from whom John invokes grace and peace be abstract powers or angels rather than an intelligent divine Person?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. It is inconceivable that John would pray to seven abstractions, in parity with the Father and the Son, for grace and peace, so they denote a willing intelligence. They cannot be angels, because the worship of angels is expressly forbidden.
sources.quote: for to imagine that St. John prays to seven abstractions in parity with the Father and the Son for grace and peace is inconceivable.
sources.raw_question: Could the "seven spirits" from whom John invokes grace and peace be abstract powers or angels rather than an intelligent divine Person?

question: Does ὁ Θεὸς in John 1:1 carry the meaning of Jehovah?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: Yes, it may reasonably be thought so. The Septuagint frequently renders Jehovah by Θεὸς, and St. John follows that rendering, as comparing John 6:45 with Isaiah 54:13 shows. This further proves the word is to be understood absolutely, not relatively.
sources.quote: we may reasonably think that ὁ Θεὸς, in the text, is of the same signification with Jehovah : which is a further proof, that it is to be understood absolutely, and not relatively
sources.raw_question: Does ὁ Θεὸς in John 1:1 carry the meaning of Jehovah?

question: Does the absence of the Greek article before Θεὸς when applied to the Word in John 1:1 show that the Word is God only in an inferior or different sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. By the same argument, Θεὸς without the article in four other places in the same chapter (verses 6, 12, 13, 18) would not mean the one true God, so the remark proves too much or nothing. Θεὸς without the article confessedly means as much as with it in many places. At most the article marks the Father's eminent personal distinction, not a change in the sense of the word.
sources.quote: Θεὸς without the article, in many places, confessedly means as much as Θεὸς with the article ; which is enough for our purpose.
sources.raw_question: Does the absence of the Greek article before Θεὸς when applied to the Word in John 1:1 show that the Word is God only in an inferior or different sense?

question: Why can only the Creator, together with his Word, properly be called God and Lord, and not any created being?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VIII.—Answer to an objection, arising from the words of Christ (Matt. vi. 24). God alone is to be really called God and Lord, for He is without beginning and end.
sources.answer: Because the Creator is uncreated, without beginning or end, lacking nothing, self-sufficient, and the giver of existence to all else. Created things have a beginning, are liable to dissolution, and depend on their maker, so they must bear a different name. Hence only he who made all things, together with his Word, is properly termed God and Lord, and creatures cannot rightly take the Creator's title.
sources.quote: so that He indeed who made all things can alone, together with His Word, properly be termed God and Lord: but the things which have been made cannot have this term applied to them
sources.raw_question: Why can only the Creator, together with his Word, properly be called God and Lord, and not any created being?

question: Can any text be interpreted against Christ's divinity in the strict sense while still claiming the support of the ancient Fathers?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. There is no text that Clarke can urge for his doctrine and against the Catholic one while also showing that the ancients agree with him. As soon as a text is interpreted directly against Christ's strict divinity, the interpreter leaves the ancients entirely. This holds for John 12:41, Acts 7:30-32 and John 10:30 as much as for the rest.
sources.quote: As soon as ever you interpret any text directly against the divinity of Christ, as understood by us in the strict sense, you go off entirely from the ancients, and go on by yourselves.
sources.raw_question: Can any text be interpreted against Christ's divinity in the strict sense while still claiming the support of the ancient Fathers?

question: How can three things of different substance, such as the visible object, vision, and will, form a unity in the act of seeing?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Certain Trinity in the Sight. That There are Three Things in Sight, Which Differ in Their Own Nature. In What Manner from a Visible Thing Vision is Produced, or the Image of that Thing Which is Seen. The Matter is Shown More Clearly by an Example. How These Three Combine in One.
sources.answer: They coalesce so closely that the object's form and the image in the sense can scarcely be distinguished even by reason. The will binds them, applying the sense to the object to be informed and keeping it fixed there once informed. Thus diverse things are tempered into a kind of unity, a trace of trinity in the outer man.
sources.quote: Although then the substances of these three are so different, yet they coalesce into such a unity that the two former can scarcely be distinguished, even with the intervention of the reason as judge
sources.raw_question: How can three things of different substance, such as the visible object, vision, and will, form a unity in the act of seeing?

question: Is a perfect image of God, lacking nothing that makes God God, thereby itself God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. To the claim that there is nothing in the Deity that lacks a counterpart in its image, the reply is: except the Deity itself. The image lacks objective reality, and that is exactly what it would need to be a second Deity.
sources.quote: it is enough to respond – except the Deity itself. What is wanting to the image to make it a second Deity is just objective reality.
sources.raw_question: Is a perfect image of God, lacking nothing that makes God God, thereby itself God?

question: Is Christ to be obeyed and honoured as God, equal with the Father, so that believers direct their obedience to him in the same way as to the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. Believers regard Christ as God, equal with his Father, to whom all honour and obedience is due. We are to honour the Son as we honour the Father, and Scripture shows him receiving the same praise as the One on the throne. So in all their obedience the saints have a special regard to Christ.
sources.quote: They consider him as God, equal with his Father, to whom all honour and obedience is due. So Rev. v. 13.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ to be obeyed and honoured as God, equal with the Father, so that believers direct their obedience to him in the same way as to the Father?

question: Does distinguishing Christ's divine and human natures mean holding two Christs or two Lords, or glorifying a mere man as having suffered for the world?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: No. Gregory denies holding two Christs or two Lords, denies being ashamed of the Cross, and denies that a mere man suffered for the world. The one Word who was in the beginning became, in the man He assumed, Lord and Christ.
sources.quote: that we neither hold two Christs nor two Lords, that we are not ashamed of the Cross, that we do not glorify a mere man as having suffered for the world
sources.raw_question: Does distinguishing Christ's divine and human natures mean holding two Christs or two Lords, or glorifying a mere man as having suffered for the world?

question: Can the Divine Nature of the Son advance or receive any increase in dignity, such as becoming Lord or King?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No. The Divine Nature always remains the same, above all augmentation and incapable of diminution. Only a childish mind would suppose the Divinity passes on to perfection by addition. God the Word is always King, always Lord, always God and Most High, by nature and not by advancement.
sources.quote: since the Divine Nature, whatever it is believed to be, always remains the same, being above all augmentation and incapable of diminution, we are absolutely compelled to refer his saying to the Humanity.
sources.raw_question: Can the Divine Nature of the Son advance or receive any increase in dignity, such as becoming Lord or King?

question: Do Psalm texts such as 'I am established as king by Him' and 'Be Thou Lord in the midst of Thine enemies' imply that the Son came into existence when made king or Lord?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No. The establishment of his kingdom signifies advance to dignity, not the formation of his essence. The one who bids him 'be Lord' does not command something non-existent to come into being, but grants rule over the disobedient to one who already is.
sources.quote: As, then, the establishment of His kingdom does not signify the formation of His essence, but the advance to His dignity, and He Who bids Him “be Lord” does not command that which is non-existent to come into being
sources.raw_question: Do Psalm texts such as 'I am established as king by Him' and 'Be Thou Lord in the midst of Thine enemies' imply that the Son came into existence when made king or Lord?

question: Why can divine names be applied to Christ's humanity and human names to his Godhead?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: Because of the unspeakable mixture and conjunction of human littleness with divine greatness in one Person. Through this union great and divine names properly apply to the humanity, and the Godhead is spoken of by human names. The same Person who has the Name above every name is worshipped by all creation under the human name of Jesus.
sources.quote: For it is the same Person who both has the Name which is above every name, and is worshipped by all creation in the human Name of Jesus.
sources.raw_question: Why can divine names be applied to Christ's humanity and human names to his Godhead?

question: If the Son is born of the Father alone, must He be only a part of the Father, so that neither Father nor Son is perfect?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. Hilary rejects this as the wisdom of the world, which God has made foolish. Such logic assumes that birth requires two parents and that begetting divides and diminishes the begetter, but God's omnipotence is not bound by these conclusions. The Church rightly confesses God from God, True from True, Perfect from Perfect, One from One. The feeding of the five thousand shows God producing new portions while the loaf grows no smaller, so God's working need not involve any loss in its source.
sources.quote: who contradict our proclamation of God from God, True from True, Perfect from Perfect, One from One, as though we taught things impossible. They pin their faith to certain conclusions which they have reached by process of logic
sources.raw_question: If the Son is born of the Father alone, must He be only a part of the Father, so that neither Father nor Son is perfect?

question: Does the fact that the Holy Spirit presides over God's blessings show that the Spirit's working is divine?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is not a creature, seeing that He is infinite, and was shed upon the apostles dispersed through all countries, and moreover sanctifies the Angels also, to whom He makes us equal. Mary was full of the same likewise, so too, Christ the Lord, and so far all things high and low. And all benediction has its origin from His operation, as was signified in the moving of the water at Bethesda.
sources.answer: Yes. God Himself testifies that He puts His Spirit upon the seed and His blessings upon the children, linking the Spirit to all divine blessing. No blessing can be full except through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, so nothing is more divine than the Spirit's working.
sources.quote: What, then, is more divine than the working of the Holy Spirit, since God Himself testifies that the Holy Spirit presides over His blessings
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Holy Spirit presides over God's blessings show that the Spirit's working is divine?

question: Was Christ begotten by Joseph, as the Ebionites claim, rather than born of a virgin?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: No. To say He was begotten by Joseph destroys God's marvellous dispensation and sets aside the testimony of the prophets, which came from God. God Himself was made man and gave the sign of the Virgin. The apostles testify that before Joseph came together with Mary she was found with child of the Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: The Ebionites, following these, assert that He was begotten by Joseph; thus destroying, as far as in them lies, such a marvellous dispensation of God, and setting aside the testimony of the prophets which proceeded from God.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ begotten by Joseph, as the Ebionites claim, rather than born of a virgin?

question: Do the prophecies foretell that the one born of the Virgin is both God and man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. God was made man, and the Lord Himself saved us, giving us the sign of the Virgin. The prophecies, faithfully translated, compel belief in the coming of the Son of God.
sources.quote: God, then, was made man, and the Lord did Himself save us, giving us the token of the Virgin.
sources.raw_question: Do the prophecies foretell that the one born of the Virgin is both God and man?

question: Do memory, understanding, and love in the human mind act for themselves as distinct agents, or is it the one person who acts through them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Great the Unlikeness is Between the Image of the Trinity Which We Have Found in Ourselves, and the Trinity Itself.
sources.answer: It is the one person who acts through them. The man himself remembers by memory, understands by understanding, and loves by love. Even when love remembers or understands, it does so by the person's memory and understanding, not its own. So the three are possessions of one person rather than three subjects.
sources.quote: In brief, by all these three things, it is I that remember, I that understand, I that love, who am neither memory, nor understanding, nor love, but who have them.
sources.raw_question: Do memory, understanding, and love in the human mind act for themselves as distinct agents, or is it the one person who acts through them?

question: How can the pardon of sinners be consistent with God's justice, faithfulness and truth, which demand the destruction of sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Through the righteousness revealed in Christ, all of God's properties are glorified in the pardon, justification and acceptance of sinners. The sinner fears his safety cannot be had without loss to God's honour, but Christ has really borne the punishment due to sin. He has answered God's justice as fully as the sinner's own damnation would have done.
sources.quote: they plainly see that all the properties of God are exceedingly glorified in the pardon, justification, and acceptance of poor sinners
sources.raw_question: How can the pardon of sinners be consistent with God's justice, faithfulness and truth, which demand the destruction of sin?

question: What does Scripture signify by speaking of the Son as coming from God's 'womb' or 'heart' while speaking of creatures as made by God's 'hand'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: It signifies that the Son is God's proper and genuine offspring, while creatures have a beginning of being as works. God makes and creates the world, but begets the Son from himself as Word or Wisdom; as we have offspring from the womb but make our works by the hand.
sources.quote: For the one God makes and creates; but Him He begets from Himself, Word or Wisdom. Now ‘womb’ and ‘heart’ plainly declare the proper and the genuine
sources.raw_question: What does Scripture signify by speaking of the Son as coming from God's 'womb' or 'heart' while speaking of creatures as made by God's 'hand'?

question: Can the Son be a real but inferior, created God alongside the one Supreme God, consistently with Isaiah's monotheistic texts?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. The texts of Isaiah are purposely designed to exclude all inferior as well as coordinate gods, as Isaiah 43:10 says no God was formed before or after him. So the Son must either be entirely excluded from deity, making him a merely nominal God, or not excluded at all, in which case he is comprehended in and one with the one Supreme God.
sources.quote: he must either be entirely excluded, or not at all: and if he be not excluded, he is comprehended in the one Supreme God, and is one with him
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be a real but inferior, created God alongside the one Supreme God, consistently with Isaiah's monotheistic texts?

question: Did Christ come into being from non-existence like the elements of the world?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. The elements of the world came into being out of nothing. Christ's existence did not begin in the non-existent, nor did He ever begin to exist; He took from the beginning a beginning which is eternal.
sources.quote: Christ’s continuity of existence did not begin in the non-existent, nor did He ever begin to exist, but He took from the beginning a beginning which is eternal.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ come into being from non-existence like the elements of the world?

question: Did the Son of God suffer only in appearance (Docetism)?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: No. If he did not truly suffer, we would owe him no thanks, and he would be misleading us by urging us to endure what he never endured himself. We would then be above our Master. Rather, the Word of God the Father truly became the Son of man, fought and conquered, and through obedience undid disobedience.
sources.quote: For if He did not truly suffer, no thanks to Him, since there was no suffering at all; and when we shall actually begin to suffer, He will seem as leading us astray
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God suffer only in appearance (Docetism)?

question: How can one test whether a spirit claiming to be the Holy Spirit is the Spirit promised by Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: By trying it against the effects Christ promised the Holy Ghost would produce. The true Spirit brings to remembrance and gives understanding of Christ's words as written in Scripture, for guidance and consolation. A spirit that decries the written word and pretends to new revelations of its own is not the Spirit Christ promised.
sources.quote: he shall bring to our remembrance, and give us understanding of the words of Christ in the Scripture, for our guidance and consolation. Is this, now, the work of the spirit which is abroad in the world, and perverteth many? Nothing less.
sources.raw_question: How can one test whether a spirit claiming to be the Holy Spirit is the Spirit promised by Christ?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's work in believers today lead them away from Scripture through new revelations?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit brought Christ's words to the apostles' remembrance so that they could write the Scriptures, and he does the same work in believers to the end of the world by opening those written words. A spirit that leads men away from the written word, where all of God's work and Christ's promises are recorded, is a false spirit.
sources.quote: His business is, to decry the things that Christ hath spoken which are written in the word; to pretend new revelations of his own; to lead men from the written word
sources.raised_by_detail: enthusiasts pretending new revelations by the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's work in believers today lead them away from Scripture through new revelations?

question: Is it a mark of a false spirit to speak of Christ only 'in the Spirit' while denying that he has come in the flesh?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. Talking of Christ in the Spirit only, and denying him to be come in the flesh, is the very character of the false spirit the apostle warns against. The true Spirit glorifies the Christ who suffered for us. The false spirit despises this Christ as a 'Christ without us' and seeks its own glory.
sources.quote: now, he talks of Christ in the Spirit only, and denies him to be come in the flesh, — the proper character of the false spirit we are warned of, 1 John iv. 1.
sources.raw_question: Is it a mark of a false spirit to speak of Christ only 'in the Spirit' while denying that he has come in the flesh?

question: Does the risen Christ's saying 'Handle Me and see' show that the Word and the flesh he assumed are one subject rather than two?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: Yes. He did not say 'this' or 'this man whom I have taken,' but 'Me.' He speaks of his own side and hands as one who is whole man and God together. So the union of God the Word with the flesh is confirmed by the Word himself.
sources.quote: And He did not say, ‘This,’ or ‘this Man which I have taken to Me,’ but ‘Me.’
sources.raw_question: Does the risen Christ's saying 'Handle Me and see' show that the Word and the flesh he assumed are one subject rather than two?

question: Could Genesis 1:27 omit the son because it is a summary statement and no son had yet been born?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Why This Opinion is to Be Rejected.
sources.answer: No. The Holy Spirit could easily have included the son in that brief summary while narrating his birth later. Scripture did exactly this with the woman, naming her in the summary although it narrates her formation from Adam's side only afterwards.
sources.quote: As if the Holy Spirit could not have comprehended this, too, in that brief statement, while about to narrate the birth of the son afterwards in its own place
sources.raw_question: Could Genesis 1:27 omit the son because it is a summary statement and no son had yet been born?

question: Can the Only-begotten Word become something good that He was not before, such as becoming Lord or Christ?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No. The Only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father and is Word, King and Lord, needs to become nothing good, since He is Himself the fulness of all good things. What 'becomes' Christ and Lord is the flesh He assumed, not the Word Himself.
sources.quote: needs not to become anything that is good, seeing that He is Himself the fulness of all good things? What then is that, by changing into which He becomes what He was not before?
sources.raw_question: Can the Only-begotten Word become something good that He was not before, such as becoming Lord or Christ?

question: Is the Spirit's work of comfort to be valued in the same way Scripture teaches us to value Christ's redemption?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture raises our estimation of redemption by stressing that Christ acted freely and out of love toward sinners and enemies. In the same way, the Spirit proceeds freely from the Father to comfort people who are froward and provoking. Since nothing is valuable but what comes from love and good-will, the Spirit's comfort deserves the same high valuation.
sources.quote: May we not hence, also, have a valuation of the dispensation of the Spirit for our consolation? He proceeds to that end from the Father; he distributes as he will, works as he pleaseth.
sources.raw_question: Is the Spirit's work of comfort to be valued in the same way Scripture teaches us to value Christ's redemption?

question: Is a name that expresses a 'mere conception' unfit to be applied to God because such a name dissolves and passes away when it is spoken?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Every spoken word ceases to exist once it is uttered, as the breath of the voice disperses into the air. If vanishing with utterance marked a mere conception, every term would be a mere conception, including 'ungeneracy' itself, which Eunomius exempts from the products of conception. His criterion is therefore empty.
sources.quote: he may as well at once call every term a mere conception, inasmuch as no substance remains in any term subsequent to its utterance.
sources.raw_question: Is a name that expresses a 'mere conception' unfit to be applied to God because such a name dissolves and passes away when it is spoken?

question: Can God's essence admit accidents, as created substances do?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > God the Only Unchangeable Essence.
sources.answer: No. Other substances admit accidents by which they are changed in greater or lesser degree, but no such accident can belong to God. God is therefore the only unchangeable substance or essence.
sources.quote: But there can be no accident of this kind in respect to God; and therefore He who is God is the only unchangeable substance or essence
sources.raw_question: Can God's essence admit accidents, as created substances do?

question: Can a sound doctrine of Christ be built on only one class of Scripture passages, such as those that stress God's oneness?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Noetus uses only one set of texts. In this he is as one-sided as Theodotus, who used other texts to make Christ a mere man. Both misunderstand, because Scripture taken as a whole refutes them. Misreading by heretics is no reason to reject the texts; their misinterpretation should be refuted and the true meaning explained.
sources.quote: they make use only of one class of passages; just in the same one-sided manner that Theodotus employed when he sought to prove that Christ was a mere man. But neither has the one party nor the other understood the matter rightly
sources.raw_question: Can a sound doctrine of Christ be built on only one class of Scripture passages, such as those that stress God's oneness?

question: If blasphemy against the Son of Man can be forgiven but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit cannot, does this mean the Spirit has a dignity different from the Son's?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: No. The dignity of the Son and the Spirit is one and common, so an offence against either is the same. The forgivable sin concerns thinking too lightly of Christ's visible human body, which can be pardoned through faith. Denying the dignity, majesty and eternal power of the Spirit is the fulness of sacrilege.
sources.quote: Is an offence against the Son different from one against the Holy Spirit? For as their dignity is one, and common to both, so too is the offence.
sources.raw_question: If blasphemy against the Son of Man can be forgiven but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit cannot, does this mean the Spirit has a dignity different from the Son's?

question: Does the contrast between idolatry of the heavenly host and confessing the Holy Spirit show that the Spirit is a proper object of worship?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: Yes. The Jews were deprived of divine protection for worshipping the host of heaven, which is created. Yet whoever worships and confesses the Holy Spirit is accepted by God, and whoever does not confess Him is convicted of sacrilege. Therefore the Spirit is not a creature but is rightly worshipped as God.
sources.quote: For if the Jews because they worshipped the host of heaven were deprived of divine protection, whilst he who worships and confesses the Holy Spirit is accepted of God
sources.raw_question: Does the contrast between idolatry of the heavenly host and confessing the Holy Spirit show that the Spirit is a proper object of worship?

question: In what different ways does the Holy Spirit teach people?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: In three ways. First, through conviction and illumination, by which he teaches many in the world through preached word. Second, through sanctification, by which he gives believers a new understanding and a saving knowledge of the gospel. Third, through consolation, by which he makes what believers know of God's will sweet and joyful, especially the love of God in Christ.
sources.quote: A teaching by the Spirit of consolation; — making sweet, useful, and joyful to the soul, the discoveries that are made of the mind and will of God in the light of the Spirit of sanctification.
sources.raw_question: In what different ways does the Holy Spirit teach people?

question: Does "No man hath seen God at any time" (John 1:18) exclude the Holy Spirit from seeing God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter I. St. Ambrose commences his argument by complimenting the Emperor, both for his faith and for the restitution of the Basilica to the Church; then having urged that his opponents, if they affirm that the Holy Spirit is not a servant, cannot deny Him to be above all, adds that the same Spirit, when He said, “All things serve Thee,” showed plainly that He was distinct from creatures; which point he also establishes by other evidence.
sources.answer: No. The verse rules out creatures, but the Spirit searches the deep things of God, knows the things of God, and is of God, so He has seen God. Because He is excepted from the "no one," He stands apart from all creatures and is above all.
sources.quote: So, since it is laid down that no one has seen God at any time, whereas the Holy Spirit has seen Him, clearly the Holy Spirit is excepted. He, then, is above all Who is excluded from all.
sources.raw_question: Does "No man hath seen God at any time" (John 1:18) exclude the Holy Spirit from seeing God?

question: If believers are made righteous with Christ's own righteousness, does it follow that they are as righteous as Christ himself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: No. The righteousness is inherent in Christ and properly his own, whereas it is only imputed or freely given to us. More importantly, Christ did not work that righteousness for himself but for us, so no comparison can be made. We can only say that we are completely righteous with the righteousness he wrought for us.
sources.quote: Christ was not righteous with that righteousness for himself, but for us; so that here can be no comparison
sources.raw_question: If believers are made righteous with Christ's own righteousness, does it follow that they are as righteous as Christ himself?

question: Under what aspects does Scripture present the death of Christ, and what effect corresponds to each?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Scripture presents it in three ways: as a price, a sacrifice and a penalty. As a price, its effect is redemption. As a sacrifice, its effect is reconciliation or atonement. As a penalty, its effect is satisfaction.
sources.quote: In the first regard, its proper effect is redemption; in the second, reconciliation or atonement; in the third, satisfaction;
sources.raw_question: Under what aspects does Scripture present the death of Christ, and what effect corresponds to each?

question: Does being called a 'searcher' imply that the Holy Spirit is inferior to God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Scripture calls the Father a searcher of hearts and reins and the Son a searcher of mind and thoughts. No inferior searches the inward things of his superior, since knowing hidden things belongs to divine power alone; so 'searching' signifies that nothing escapes Him, in the Spirit as in the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: Whence it is clear that no inferior searches the inward things of his superior, for to know hidden things is of the divine power alone.
sources.raw_question: Does being called a 'searcher' imply that the Holy Spirit is inferior to God?

question: If the Word and the Son were different beings, would Christian salvation and baptism have any connection with the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Since the Word is from God, He must be Son. Since the Son is from everlasting, He must be the Word; else either He is superior to the Word, or the Word is the Father. Texts of the New Testament which state the unity of the Son with the Father; therefore the Son is the Word. Three hypotheses refuted--1. That the Man is the Son; 2. That the Word and Man together are the Son; 3. That the Word became Son on His incarnation. Texts of the Old Testament which speak of the Son. If they are merely prophetical, then those concerning the Word may be such also.
sources.answer: No connection would remain, which shows the Word must be the Son. Scripture commands belief not in 'the Word' but in the Son for eternal life, and baptism, in which the whole faith is lodged, is given in the name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. If the Word were not the Son, the Word would have no share in baptism and could not be said to be with the Father in it.
sources.quote: If then, as they hold, the Word is one and the Son another, and the Word is not the Son, Baptism has no connection with the Word.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who separate the Word from the Son (Marcellian/Photinian view)
sources.raw_question: If the Word and the Son were different beings, would Christian salvation and baptism have any connection with the Word?

question: What attributes belong to the Holy Spirit's nature, and do they show that the Spirit is uncreated?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Definitive conceptions about the Spirit which conform to the teaching of the Scriptures.
sources.answer: The Spirit has the attributes of deity, which no creature has. Basil describes the Spirit as an intelligent essence, infinite in power and unlimited in magnitude, not measured by time. The Spirit perfects others but lacks nothing, gives life without needing restoration, does not grow by additions, and is self-established, omnipresent, and the origin of sanctification. All of these mark the Spirit off from creatures.
sources.quote: perfecting all other things, but Itself in nothing lacking; living not as needing restoration, but as Supplier of life; not growing by additions; but straightway full, self-established, omnipresent, origin of sanctification
sources.raw_question: What attributes belong to the Holy Spirit's nature, and do they show that the Spirit is uncreated?

question: Does the Holy Spirit come near to the soul by moving through space?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Definitive conceptions about the Spirit which conform to the teaching of the Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit is incorporeal, so a bodily approach to it is impossible. Union with the Spirit comes when the soul withdraws from the passions that estranged it from God. Once purified and restored to its natural beauty, the restored image, the soul can draw near to the Paraclete.
sources.quote: Now the Spirit is not brought into intimate association with the soul by local approximation. How indeed could there be a corporeal approach to the incorporeal?
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit come near to the soul by moving through space?

question: When God tells Jacob to make a sacrifice to the God who appeared to him at Bethel, does this distinction between the God speaking and the God who appeared imply that the Son is not true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Both bear the one name of God, which indicates one nature, so no difference of nature separates them. It is God who was seen and God who speaks about the God who was seen; the Son who teaches reverence for the Father cannot fall beneath Himself so as to be other than true God.
sources.quote: What difference of nature separates the Two, when Both bear the one name which indicates the one nature? It is God Who was seen; it is also God Who speaks about God Who was seen.
sources.raw_question: When God tells Jacob to make a sacrifice to the God who appeared to him at Bethel, does this distinction between the God speaking and the God who appeared imply that the Son is not true God?

question: When Genesis says 'God said, Let there be light,' does it mean the Father gave orders to the Word as to a subordinate under-worker who heard and then carried them out?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. Such hearing and obeying is proper to creatures and unseemly to attribute to the Word, who is Framer and Maker and the Father's own Will. Scripture records no question or answer, only 'Let it be' and 'it was,' because the Father is in the Word and the Word in the Father; 'He said' signifies the will for our sake, and 'it was so' the work done through the Word.
sources.quote: And He spoke, not that, as in the case of men, some under-worker might hear, and learning the will of Him who spoke might go away and do it; for this is what is proper to creatures, but it is unseemly so to think or speak of the Word.
sources.raw_question: When Genesis says 'God said, Let there be light,' does it mean the Father gave orders to the Word as to a subordinate under-worker who heard and then carried them out?

question: What is the significance of the neuter "one" (unum) in "I and the Father are one"?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Skilfully Replies to a Passage Which the Heretics Employed in Defence of Their Own Opinion.
sources.answer: The neuter "one" signifies a unity of concord and association, not a numerical unity of person. Had it been masculine it would denote one person; the neuter refers to agreement, identity of judgment, and loving association between Father and Son, while the distinction remains that the Father is not the Son.
sources.quote: For one placed in the neuter, intimates the social concord, not the personal unity. He is said to be one neuter, not one masculine, because the expression is not referred to the number
sources.raw_question: What is the significance of the neuter "one" (unum) in "I and the Father are one"?

question: Is the Jesus who suffered and dwelt among us the very Word of God, or a later Saviour distinct from the Word?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter IX.—Refutation of the impious interpretations of these heretics.
sources.answer: Jesus who suffered is himself the Word of God. John sums up what he said of the Word by stating "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us"; and the Word of the Father who descended is the same who ascended, the Only-begotten Son of the only God made flesh by the Father's good pleasure. The heretics' claim that the Word never left the Pleroma contradicts this.
sources.quote: Learn then, ye foolish men, that Jesus who suffered for us, and who dwelt among us, is Himself the Word of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Jesus who suffered and dwelt among us the very Word of God, or a later Saviour distinct from the Word?

question: Does declaring the Father to be prior to the subsistence of the Son lead to an absurdity, given that all ages were made by the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His elaborate account of degrees and differences in 'works' and 'energies' within the Trinity is absurd.
sources.answer: Yes. Since all ages and all duration of time were created after the Son and by the Son, anyone who places the Father prior to the Son's subsistence in effect makes the Son later than the things the Son himself made. This is plainly absurd, so the Father cannot be prior to the Son in time.
sources.quote: he who declares the Father to be ‘prior’ to the subsistence of the Son declares nothing short of this, viz., that the Son is later than the things made by the Son
sources.raw_question: Does declaring the Father to be prior to the subsistence of the Son lead to an absurdity, given that all ages were made by the Son?

question: Why is the prerogative of fixing the day of judgment reserved to the Father rather than given to the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
