sources.answer: It is reserved to show, against the Sabellians, that the Father's authority is without birth or beginning. The Son's birth cannot make Him unbegotten, so this prerogative of unbegotten authority belongs to the Father alone. This marks a distinction of Persons, not a lower degree of divinity in the Son.
sources.quote: It is to demonstrate against the Sabellian heretics that the Father’s authority is without birth or beginning, that this prerogative of unbegotten authority is not granted to the Son
sources.raw_question: Why is the prerogative of fixing the day of judgment reserved to the Father rather than given to the Son?

question: Are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit distinct intelligent and voluntary principles of operation, and not merely modes or names?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture reveals them as distinct, living, divine, intelligent, voluntary, and omnipotent principles of working. They act both in internal acts toward one another and in outward acts directed to creation, which Scripture expresses abundantly. Anyone bound to believe Scripture must therefore believe in one God, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: there is one God, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; which are divine, distinct, intelligent, voluntary, omnipotent principles of operation and working
sources.raw_question: Are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit distinct intelligent and voluntary principles of operation, and not merely modes or names?

question: Is the grace given to believers given by the Father alone, or by the Father in and through the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: It is one grace given from the Father in the Son. Paul shows this by greeting the churches with grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ together, and Christ promises that he and the Father will come and make their abode in the believer. As light cannot be without its radiance, the Father is never present or giving without the Son.
sources.quote: And the grace given is one, given from the Father in the Son, as Paul writes in every Epistle, ‘Grace unto you, and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.’
sources.raw_question: Is the grace given to believers given by the Father alone, or by the Father in and through the Son?

question: Why did Christ command his disciples to teach before baptizing into the Name of Father, Son and Holy Ghost?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: So that right faith might follow upon learning, and the consecration of baptism might come together with that faith. Merely saying 'O Lord' does not give baptism. Only one who has the right faith along with the Name gives true baptism.
sources.quote: our Saviour also did not simply command to baptize, but first says, ‘Teach;’ then thus: ‘Baptize into the Name of Father, and Son, and Holy Ghost;’ that the right faith might follow upon learning
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ command his disciples to teach before baptizing into the Name of Father, Son and Holy Ghost?

question: Does sharing one common essence (consubstantiality) imply that the things sharing it must be corporeal and subject to corruption, so that calling the Son consubstantial with the Father would make God bodily and corruptible?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > After much discourse concerning the actually existent, and ungenerate and good, and upon the consubstantiality of the heavenly powers, showing the uncharted character of their essence, yet the difference of their ranks, he ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Bodies are corrupted not because they share one essence but because they are compound in nature. The idea of compound nature is distinct from that of common essence. Human souls are countless yet share one essence and are free from bodily corruption, so consubstantiality does not entail corruptibility.
sources.quote: bodies are corrupted and dissolved, not because they have the same essence one with another, but because of their possessing a compound nature. The idea of the compound nature is one, that of the common nature of their essence is another
sources.raw_question: Does sharing one common essence (consubstantiality) imply that the things sharing it must be corporeal and subject to corruption, so that calling the Son consubstantial with the Father would make God bodily and corruptible?

question: Does the Son rule over the universe by an arbitrary grant of power or by virtue of his own superior nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > A passing repetition of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: By virtue of his superior nature. If the Son is held to be of the divine nature without admixture, everything fits together: he is maker of all things and King of the universe, set above it not by a capricious act of power but by the nature he possesses.
sources.quote: that He is King of the universe, set above it not by an arbitrary act of capricious power, but ruling by virtue of a superior nature
sources.raw_question: Does the Son rule over the universe by an arbitrary grant of power or by virtue of his own superior nature?

question: If the Son is a cause of creation alongside the Father, are there then several first causes divided by different substances?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > A passing repetition of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. Because Father, Son and Spirit are alike in substance, there is one Godhead, one Cause, one Power over all things. The First Cause is not split by any unlikeness of substance into separate first causes.
sources.quote: the one First Cause, as taught by us, is not divided by any unlikeness of substance into separate first causes, but one Godhead, one Cause, one Power over all things is believed in
sources.raw_question: If the Son is a cause of creation alongside the Father, are there then several first causes divided by different substances?

question: Is the seal of the Holy Spirit in baptism primarily bodily or spiritual?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VI. Although we are baptized with water and the Spirit, the latter is much superior to the former, and is not therefore to be separated from the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Spiritual. Though visibly sealed in the body, we are truly sealed in our hearts, so that the Spirit may portray in us the likeness of the heavenly image. The prophet confirms this, saying the light of God's countenance is impressed upon us and gladness put in the heart.
sources.quote: For although we were visibly sealed in our bodies, we are in truth sealed in our hearts, that the Holy Spirit may portray in us the likeness of the heavenly image.
sources.raw_question: Is the seal of the Holy Spirit in baptism primarily bodily or spiritual?

question: If the world was formed within the Father's domain as the fruit of defect and error, does that place defect and error within God himself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter IV.—The absurdity of the supposed vacuum and defect of the heretics is demonstrated.
sources.answer: Yes, and this shows the Gnostic theory is absurd. Those who say creation within the Pleroma was the product of defect and the work of error thereby introduce defect and error into the Pleroma and into the bosom of the Father. Such a conclusion contradicts the perfection they themselves ascribe to the Father.
sources.quote: when they maintain that these things were the fruit of defect and the work of error, they do moreover introduce defect and error within the Pleroma, and into the bosom of the Father.
sources.raw_question: If the world was formed within the Father's domain as the fruit of defect and error, does that place defect and error within God himself?

question: Is God alone unchangeable in nature, and the highest of eternal things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > What is the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge. The Worship of God is the Love of Him. How the Intellectual Cognizance of Eternal Things Comes to Pass Through Wisdom.
sources.answer: Yes. Nothing among eternal things is more excellent than God, whose nature alone is unchangeable. For this reason the worship of God (piety) is the proper object of wisdom.
sources.quote: And what is there in eternal things more excellent than God, of whom alone the nature is unchangeable?
sources.raw_question: Is God alone unchangeable in nature, and the highest of eternal things?

question: What role does Christ play in the continuing work of the Holy Spirit in believers after their first regeneration?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: Christ sends the Spirit, and he does so not only at first. He gives the first enduing of the heart with the Spirit and also continual supplies of the Spirit. He draws forth more effectual operations of the indwelling Spirit, who does in the saints all that Christ himself has to do for them. This happens because the Father always hears Christ's intercession.
sources.quote: not only in respect of the first enduing of our hearts with his Holy Spirit, but also of the continual supplies of it, drawing forth and exciting more effectual operations and actings of that indwelling Spirit
sources.raw_question: What role does Christ play in the continuing work of the Holy Spirit in believers after their first regeneration?

question: How can the various divine names given to the Only-begotten in Scripture be classified?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Then he ends the book with an exposition of the Divine and Human names of the Only-Begotten, and a discussion of the terms “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: They fall into two classes. One class indicates his lofty and unspeakable glory. The other indicates the variety of his providential dispensation toward creatures. Names like vine, shepherd, and physician would not apply if there were no beneficiaries of his care. Names like Son, Word, Wisdom, Power, and Right Hand are relative names that name him together with the Father, apart from the objects of the dispensation.
sources.quote: It is possible to make a twofold division of the signification of the Divine names, as it were by a scientific rule: for to one class belongs the indication of His lofty and unspeakable glory; the other class indicates the variety of the providential dispensation
sources.raw_question: How can the various divine names given to the Only-begotten in Scripture be classified?

question: Does the diversity of human languages show that names were not imposed by God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. The natures God created, such as fire, air and water, are the same for all people. Names imposed by God would likewise be the same for all. Yet names differ across countless languages while the things remain the same, so names are a human imposition.
sources.quote: the imposition of names, if applied to things by God, would have been the same for all. But, in point of fact, while the nature of things as constituted by God remains the same, the names which denote them are divided by so many differences of language
sources.raw_question: Does the diversity of human languages show that names were not imposed by God?

question: What is the relation between the Holy Spirit's mission by the Father and the Son and his eternal procession within the Trinity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: The mission of the Spirit by the Father and the Son answers to the order of the persons' subsistence in the Trinity. It reflects his procession from them both. It also reflects the order the persons voluntarily agreed to for accomplishing our salvation.
sources.quote: This mission of the Holy Ghost by the Father and the Son, as it answers the order of the persons’ subsistence in the blessed Trinity, and his procession from them both
sources.raw_question: What is the relation between the Holy Spirit's mission by the Father and the Son and his eternal procession within the Trinity?

question: Why is the sin against the Holy Spirit uniquely unpardonable?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Because the Spirit acts not only in his own name but in the name and authority of the Father and Son who send him. To sin against him is therefore to sin against all the authority of God, all the love of the Trinity, and the utmost condescension of each person to our salvation. It is a sin against the summing-up of the love of Father, Son and Spirit.
sources.quote: to sin against him is to sin against all the authority of God, all the love of the Trinity, and the utmost condescension of each person to the work of our salvation.
sources.raw_question: Why is the sin against the Holy Spirit uniquely unpardonable?

question: If the Father and Son are God only together, how can the Creed say the Son is "God of God, Light of Light"?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > What is Said of the Father and Son Together, and What Not.
sources.answer: The phrase may be a brief way of teaching that the Son is co-eternal with the Father. It would mean God who is not the Son without the Father, from God who is not the Father without the Son. Read this way, the Begetter did not precede the one He begot.
sources.quote: so that, when it is said, God which is not the Son without the Father, and of God which is not the Father without the Son, it may be perfectly understood that the Begetter did not precede that which He begot.
sources.raw_question: If the Father and Son are God only together, how can the Creed say the Son is "God of God, Light of Light"?

question: Does Scripture ascribe omnipresence to Christ as it does to God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. God says he fills heaven and earth and will be with his people and not fail them. Christ likewise ascended "that He might fill all things" and promises, "Lo, I am with you alway." The attribute of filling all things belongs to God alone, so it witnesses to Christ's Deity.
sources.quote: He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that He might fill all things. – Eph. 4:10. Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. – Matt. 28:20.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture ascribe omnipresence to Christ as it does to God?

question: Are the divine holiness, truth, and everlasting sovereignty ascribed to God also ascribed to Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. God is "the Holy One of Israel" and "a God of truth," and Christ is "the Holy One and the Just," "the Truth," and "without sin." God is "King of kings, and Lord of lords" with an everlasting kingdom, and Christ bears the same title and holds an everlasting dominion.
sources.quote: King of kings, and Lord of lords. – Rev. 19:16. His dominion is an everlasting dominion ... and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed. – Dan. 7:14.
sources.raw_question: Are the divine holiness, truth, and everlasting sovereignty ascribed to God also ascribed to Christ?

question: Can someone who denies Christ's Deity consistently hold that Old Testament texts describing Jehovah refer to the Messiah?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. In every case the witness in these texts is said to be of God, or of the Lord Jehovah. So anyone who denies Christ's Deity would contradict himself by applying any of them to the Messiah. For the author, the fact that some of these texts primarily refer to the Son therefore strengthens their testimony rather than weakening it.
sources.quote: no one who denied the Deity of Christ could maintain that a single passage there adduced designates the Messiah, without contradicting himself.
sources.raw_question: Can someone who denies Christ's Deity consistently hold that Old Testament texts describing Jehovah refer to the Messiah?

question: Did early Fathers who held unsound views about the Holy Spirit still treat the Spirit as an object of worship?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: Yes, in many places. Origen did not always think soundly about the Spirit. Yet he used the doxology "with the Holy Ghost" and spoke of the Godhead of the adorable Trinity and of the Godhead of the Holy Spirit. Basil sees this as tradition's power moving men to speak rightly even against their own opinions.
sources.quote: Thus I apprehend, the powerful influence of tradition frequently impels men to express themselves in terms contradictory to their own opinions.
sources.raw_question: Did early Fathers who held unsound views about the Holy Spirit still treat the Spirit as an object of worship?

question: Why is knowledge of the day of Christ's coming withheld from believers?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It is withheld to encourage perseverance, not to deceive. Certain knowledge might breed negligence, while uncertainty keeps minds alert and always watching in hope. In the same way a householder guards against a thief whose hour he does not know.
sources.quote: The ignorance is, therefore, a means not to delude, but to encourage in perseverance.
sources.raw_question: Why is knowledge of the day of Christ's coming withheld from believers?

question: In Matthew 16:16-17, did the Father reveal to Peter only the name 'Son of God' or the Son's divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: The divine nature. Peter had often heard Christ call himself the Son and speak of the Father, so the name was not new to him and announcing it would earn no honour. What the Father revealed, and what flesh and blood cannot attain, was that Christ is to be believed truly Son of God, possessing the Divine nature.
sources.quote: Was it only the Divine name; was it not rather the Divine nature that was revealed to Peter? If it were the name, he had heard it often from the Lord, proclaiming Himself the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: In Matthew 16:16-17, did the Father reveal to Peter only the name 'Son of God' or the Son's divine nature?

question: Is Christ a creature made out of nothing?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The faith revealed by the Father teaches that we must not imagine a false Christ, a creature made from nothing, but must confess him the Son of God truly possessing the Divine nature. Peter was blessed precisely for confessing the Son of God, so calling Christ a creature distorts his confession and denies his apostleship and faith.
sources.quote: even the knowledge that we must not imagine a false Christ, a creature made out of nothing, but must confess Him the Son of God, truly possessed of the Divine nature.
sources.raised_by_detail: lying bishop of the new apostolate
sources.raw_question: Is Christ a creature made out of nothing?

question: Why does God's greatness not multiply into three greatnesses even though each divine Person is great?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whatever is Spoken of God According to Substance, is Spoken of Each Person Severally, and Together of the Trinity Itself. One Essence in God, and Three, in Greek, Hypostases, in Latin, Persons.
sources.answer: Because in God it is not one thing to be and another to be great; to be is the same as to be great. Since there are not three essences, there are not three greatnesses, but one essence and one greatness.
sources.quote: For inasmuch as to God it is not one thing to be, and another thing to be great, but to Him it is the same thing to be, as it is to be great; therefore, as we do not say three essences, so we do not say three greatnesses
sources.raw_question: Why does God's greatness not multiply into three greatnesses even though each divine Person is great?

question: If God's will is his Wisdom and the Son is that Wisdom, what follows from saying the Son is 'by will'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: It would mean that Wisdom came to be in wisdom, a Son was made in a Son, and the Word was created through the Word. That is absurd, unworthy of God, and contrary to Scripture.
sources.quote: he who says that the Son is ‘by will,’ says virtually that Wisdom has come into being in wisdom, and the Son is made in a son, and the Word created through the Word
sources.raw_question: If God's will is his Wisdom and the Son is that Wisdom, what follows from saying the Son is 'by will'?

question: What are the 'words of God' recorded by Moses and the prophets, if God does not speak a human language?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They are indications of the divine will that flashed in various ways on the pure minds of the holy men, according to the measure of grace each received. Moses ascribed them to God as speech because his hearers were still childish in their knowledge of God. Speaking this way gave a clear picture of God's will and made the hearers more obedient through awe at the speaker's authority.
sources.quote: are indications of the Divine will, flashing forth, now in one way, now in another, on the pure intellect of those holy men, according to the measure of the grace of which they were partakers
sources.raw_question: What are the 'words of God' recorded by Moses and the prophets, if God does not speak a human language?

question: Is the Christ who was crucified distinct from an impassible superior Saviour, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. The apostles preached that the very one the Jews fastened to the cross was Christ the Son of God, their eternal King. Had the crucified one not been the true Saviour, the Jews' sin would have been far less, yet the apostles charged them directly with slaying the Lord.
sources.quote: He whom the Jews had seen as a man, and had fastened to the cross, should be preached as Christ the Son of God, their eternal King
sources.raw_question: Is the Christ who was crucified distinct from an impassible superior Saviour, as the Gnostics claim?

question: Would a Son made from nothing make the Trinity consist of unlike and alien natures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son is not proper offspring of the Father's essence but came from nothing, then a thing originated is ranked and worshipped with the Creator. The Triad would then be unlike itself, made of strange and alien essences, with an originated consistence. But the Triad is one eternal Godhead with one glory.
sources.quote: Nay, what is more serious still, the Triad is discovered to be unlike Itself, consisting of strange and alien natures and essences.
sources.raw_question: Would a Son made from nothing make the Trinity consist of unlike and alien natures?

question: Is the Trinity one indivisible Godhead, or may it be divided into different natures with the Son ranked among creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: It is one eternal Godhead in a Triad, with one glory, and it may not be divided. The Triad is Creator and Framer, so the Son cannot be ranked with servile beings made from nothing. Introducing an originated Triad belongs to the Greeks. Christians guard the unity of the Godhead as indivisible and confess the Son as eternal like the Father.
sources.quote: the Triad is not originated; but there is an eternal and one Godhead in a Triad, and there is one Glory of the Holy Triad. And you presume to divide it into different natures
sources.raw_question: Is the Trinity one indivisible Godhead, or may it be divided into different natures with the Son ranked among creatures?

question: Did Christ's knowledge of Peter's coming denial come from his divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord, knowing by his Divine Nature what would come to pass, foretold Peter's triple denial, so that we might learn from Peter how the others too were offended.
sources.quote: But the Lord knowing by His Divine Nature what should come to pass, answered that Peter would deny Him thrice
sources.raw_question: Did Christ's knowledge of Peter's coming denial come from his divine nature?

question: How does the human word's being the beginning of every work resemble the Word of God through whom all things were made?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Likeness of the Divine Word, Such as It Is, is to Be Sought, Not in Our Own Outer and Sensible Word, But in the Inner and Mental One. There is the Greatest Possible Unlikeness Between Our Word and Knowledge and the Divine Word and Knowledge.
sources.answer: As all things were made by God through His only-begotten Son, so no human work exists unless a word is first spoken in the heart. That word is a true beginning of good work only when it is begotten from true knowledge of working good, so that what is in the knowledge is also in the word. Otherwise the word is a lie, and what comes from it is sin.
sources.quote: And a word is true when it is begotten from the knowledge of working good works, so that there too may be preserved the “yea yea, nay nay;”
sources.raw_question: How does the human word's being the beginning of every work resemble the Word of God through whom all things were made?

question: Is there a created wisdom in creatures that is distinct from the uncreated Wisdom who is the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture speaks of wisdom in the world and of many wise men, and Sirach says God poured wisdom out on all His works. This outpouring is not the essence of the very Wisdom and Only-begotten but the wisdom imaged in the world. It is created in the works and is not itself creative.
sources.quote: this outpouring is a note, not of the Essence of the Very Wisdom and Only-begotten, but of that wisdom which is imaged in the world
sources.raw_question: Is there a created wisdom in creatures that is distinct from the uncreated Wisdom who is the Son?

question: Does saving faith in Christ depend on correctly imagining his bodily appearance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > God Must First Be Known by an Unerring Faith, that He May Be Loved.
sources.answer: No. Christ's countenance in the flesh is imagined in countless different ways, though it was one, whatever it was, and these imaginings may be far from the reality. What is wholesome in our faith is that we think of him according to the general notion of human nature implanted in us. This notion lets us truly believe that God was made man.
sources.quote: Nor in our faith which we have of our Lord Jesus Christ, is that wholesome which the mind imagines for itself, perhaps far other than the reality, but that which we think of man according to his kind
sources.raw_question: Does saving faith in Christ depend on correctly imagining his bodily appearance?

question: Who comes closer to positing two First Causes: one who affirms the Son's real generation from the Father, or one who denies that the Son is truly begotten?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: The one who denies real generation. Whoever says the Son exists but not by generation would sooner make Him a First Cause. Whoever holds that the Son's distinguishing mark is subsisting by generation from the Father cannot think the Son ungenerate. Indeed, the Eunomian view of the Son as a creature not truly begotten makes Him 'ungenerate' in one sense of that word.
sources.quote: whereas the second, making the representative sign of the Person of the Only-begotten to consist in subsisting generatively from the Father, cannot by any possibility be drawn into the error of supposing the Son to be Ungenerate.
sources.raw_question: Who comes closer to positing two First Causes: one who affirms the Son's real generation from the Father, or one who denies that the Son is truly begotten?

question: In what sense do believers have communion with Christ in the grace he purchased, such that Scripture says they were crucified, buried, and raised with him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Believers are said to do with Christ what he did because of the compact between Christ as mediator and the Father. That compact lays a sure foundation for communicating the fruits of his actions to those in whose place he acted. In sharing those fruits, they are counted as having done the same things with him: crucified, dead, buried, quickened, and raised together with him.
sources.quote: In the actings of Christ, there is, by virtue of the compact between him as mediator, and the Father, such an assured foundation laid of the communication of the fruits of those actings unto those in whose stead he performed them
sources.raw_question: In what sense do believers have communion with Christ in the grace he purchased, such that Scripture says they were crucified, buried, and raised with him?

question: Did Christ's obedience as mediator go beyond the moral law that applies to every creature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ could have been perfectly holy by obeying only the moral law of creation, as the angels are. Yet he also submitted to every law and ordinance introduced because of sin. On his own account he was not subject to these, but it became him to fulfil all righteousness. His obedience was therefore a universal conformity, as mediator, to the whole will of God.
sources.quote: he submitted himself also to every law or ordinance that was introduced upon the occasion of sin, which, on his own account, he could not be subject to, it becoming him to “fulfil all righteousness,”
sources.raw_question: Did Christ's obedience as mediator go beyond the moral law that applies to every creature?

question: Is the essence of God changeable in any respect, whether in eternity, truth, or will?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Preface.
sources.answer: No. The essence by which God is has nothing changeable at all, neither in eternity, nor in truth, nor in will. Bodies change in place and time. The thoughts of our spirits change in time and in a sort of place. Even our mind's reasonings change in time. God's being admits none of these kinds of change.
sources.quote: For the essence of God, whereby He is, has altogether nothing changeable, neither in eternity, nor in truth, nor in will
sources.raw_question: Is the essence of God changeable in any respect, whether in eternity, truth, or will?

question: How are the roles of Father, Word, and Spirit distinguished in the formula 'one God and Father, who is above all, and through all, and in all'?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVIII.—God the Father and His Word have formed all created things (which They use) by Their own power and wisdom, not out of defect or ignorance. The Son of God, who received all power from the Father, would otherwise never have taken flesh upon Him.
sources.answer: The Father is above all and is the Head of Christ. The Word is through all things and is the Head of the Church. The Spirit is in us all and is the living water the Lord gives to those who rightly believe. In this way one God the Father is declared, acting together with His Word and Spirit.
sources.quote: The Father is indeed above all, and He is the Head of Christ; but the Word is through all things, and is Himself the Head of the Church; while the Spirit is in us all, and He is the living water
sources.raw_question: How are the roles of Father, Word, and Spirit distinguished in the formula 'one God and Father, who is above all, and through all, and in all'?

question: Who gives the Holy Spirit to creatures, and by whose will?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVIII.—God the Father and His Word have formed all created things (which They use) by Their own power and wisdom, not out of defect or ignorance. The Son of God, who received all power from the Father, would otherwise never have taken flesh upon Him.
sources.answer: The Word, who is borne by the Father, grants the Spirit to all as the Father wills. The Father bears both the creation and His Word at once. The Word gives to some in the manner of creation and to others in the manner of adoption, that is, generation from God.
sources.quote: For the Father bears the creation and His own Word simultaneously, and the Word borne by the Father grants the Spirit to all as the Father wills.
sources.raw_question: Who gives the Holy Spirit to creatures, and by whose will?

question: What is the role of Christ the mediator in bringing believers to the love of the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Christ is the only way to the Father and the procuring cause of rest for the soul, but faith does not stop in him. Through Christ faith gains access to the Father and finds that he is love, having a purpose of love toward us from eternity, all cause of anger being removed. So the soul is brought by Christ into the bosom of God and rests in his love.
sources.quote: This is presented to it by Christ, the mediator, as the only procuring cause. Here it abides not, but by Christ it hath an access to the Father, Eph. ii. 18, — into his love
sources.raw_question: What is the role of Christ the mediator in bringing believers to the love of the Father?

question: Is communion with God as Father distinct from obedience to him as sovereign and lawgiver?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. Universal obedience belongs to communion with God as God, our sovereign, lawgiver and rewarder. Communion with him as Father, revealed in Christ as love, is carried on in love. This love is a particular delight and resting in the Father, not only the love that animates moral obedience.
sources.quote: as he is the Father, our Father in Christ, as revealed unto us to be love, above and contrary to all the expectations of the natural man; so it is in love that we have this intercourse with him.
sources.raw_question: Is communion with God as Father distinct from obedience to him as sovereign and lawgiver?

question: Is it legitimate to posit another God above the Creator as the true Father, regarding the Creator as imperfect?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVI.—“Knowledge puffeth up, but love edifieth.”
sources.answer: No. Those who conjure up another God as the Father are blasphemous against their own God. There is no greater conceit than for anyone to imagine he is better and more perfect than the One who made and fashioned him and gave him the breath of life. Such people fall away from the love of God through a pretence of knowledge.
sources.quote: Now there can be no greater conceit than this, that any one should imagine he is better and more perfect than He who made and fashioned him, and imparted to him the breath of life
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to posit another God above the Creator as the true Father, regarding the Creator as imperfect?

question: What distinguishes uncreated divine nature from created nature such that the creature cannot comprehend God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Created nature is limited, confined within boundaries set by its Maker, and extended in degrees of time and space. Uncreated nature is bounded only by infinity and transcends all notion of degree. Hence the interval between them is wide and insurmountable, and the finite cannot take in the infinite.
sources.quote: wide and insurmountable is the interval that divides and fences off uncreated from created nature. The latter is limited, the former not.
sources.raw_question: What distinguishes uncreated divine nature from created nature such that the creature cannot comprehend God?

question: Does a believer's being 'in God' depend on keeping the Holy Spirit, so that a person who falls away is no longer in God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Yes. Believers are in God only because the Spirit is in them. If a fallen sinner repents, the grace remains for those who are willing. If he does not, he is no longer in God, because the Spirit has left him and he is in the power of whatever he has subjected himself to. Saul's case shows this: the Spirit of God departed from him and an evil spirit afflicted him.
sources.quote: otherwise he who has fallen is no longer in God (because that Holy Spirit and Paraclete which is in God has deserted him)
sources.raw_question: Does a believer's being 'in God' depend on keeping the Holy Spirit, so that a person who falls away is no longer in God?

question: Does Scripture permit worship to be given to any created thing?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > The fifth book promises to speak of the words contained in the saying of the Apostle Peter, but delays their exposition. He discourses first of the creation, to the effect that, while nothing therein is deserving of worship, yet men, led astray by their ill-informed and feeble intelligence, and marvelling at its beauty, deified the several parts of the universe. And herein he excellently expounds the passage of Isaiah, “I am God, the first.”
sources.answer: No. The divine word declares as a law, throughout almost the whole of Scripture, that no created thing deserves man's worship. Moses, the Tables, the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels and the apostolic decrees all alike forbid reverencing the creation, and even a single divine word has full force to establish this truth.
sources.quote: Moses, the Tables, the Law, the Prophets that follow, the Gospels, the decrees of the Apostles, all alike forbid the act of reverencing the creation.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture permit worship to be given to any created thing?

question: How do Christ's being greater than Solomon and Jonah and his being David's Lord show that he is more than a mere man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: They show he cannot be of the same merely human substance as those men. One who was of the same substance as Solomon, Jonah, and David could not be greater than them or be David's Lord. So Christ must be of a higher nature, namely the Son of God.
sources.quote: And how could He (Christ) have been greater than Solomon, or greater than Jonah, or have been the Lord of David, who was of the same substance as they were?
sources.raw_question: How do Christ's being greater than Solomon and Jonah and his being David's Lord show that he is more than a mere man?

question: Did the incarnate Son of Man have a real human soul as well as a body?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is confessed as God the Word, yet the Son of Man was composed of a soul and a body. The angel's words to Joseph prove this, speaking of those who sought 'the soul of the child.'
sources.quote: we know that the Son of Man was composed of a soul and a body: compare the angel’s words to Joseph
sources.raw_question: Did the incarnate Son of Man have a real human soul as well as a body?

question: When Christ says he lays down his life and takes it up again (John 10:17-18), can this mean that God the Word died?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The body cannot lay down the soul, since the body is quickened by the soul and cannot receive a command from the Father. To say God the Word laid aside his soul would mean God died and lay lifeless, which is impossible. Rather, God raises up the temple of his body, so God was neither dead nor buried.
sources.quote: God then was neither dead nor buried
sources.raw_question: When Christ says he lays down his life and takes it up again (John 10:17-18), can this mean that God the Word died?

question: Can we reason from like operations to a like nature in beings that transcend our comprehension, such as the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The observations made by watching Providence are sufficient to give us the knowledge of sameness of Being.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as similar brightness and warmth lead us to recognize fire, equal and similar effects cannot come from causes of an alien nature. As the observed phenomena relate to each other, so do their subjects: opposed effects show opposed natures, and like effects show like natures. So equal providential power in the Father and the Son lets us infer their common nature.
sources.quote: we feel that causes of an alien nature cannot be detected in these equal and similar effects. As the observed phenomena are to each other, so will the subjects of those phenomena be
sources.raw_question: Can we reason from like operations to a like nature in beings that transcend our comprehension, such as the Father and the Son?

question: Can the Right Hand of the uncreated Father be created, and does the Son's generation compromise His eternity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: No to both. The Right Hand of the Highest is such as the Highest is: Uncreated of Uncreated, Good of Good, Eternal of Eternal. His being in the Father by way of generation does not prejudice His eternity. To call the Right Hand of the uncreated Nature created belongs only to Eunomius and his followers.
sources.quote: Uncreated of Uncreated, Good of Good, Eternal of Eternal without prejudice to Its eternity by Its being in the Father by way of generation
sources.raw_question: Can the Right Hand of the uncreated Father be created, and does the Son's generation compromise His eternity?

question: According to Jesus' words in John, where did the Son come from in coming into the world?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: He came forth from out of God himself. This was not merely from God's presence or from fellowship with God, and it shows that his eternal home is in the depths of the Divine Being.
sources.quote: not merely from the presence of God (xvi. 30; cf. xiii. 3) or from fellowship with God (xvi. 27; xvii. 8), but from out of God Himself (viii. 42; xvi. 28)
sources.raw_question: According to Jesus' words in John, where did the Son come from in coming into the world?

question: Does the fulness of grace that Christ communicates to believers reside in his human nature considered in itself, or in the person of the mediator, God and man?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: It lies in the person of the mediator, God and man, not in the human nature considered in itself. Grace is not stored in the human nature and parcelled out by participation; rather it becomes Christ's morally, by compact, through his satisfaction and merit, to be bestowed by him as mediator, the only begotten Son made flesh.
sources.quote: did not, doth not, lie in the human nature, considered in itself; but in the person of the mediator, God and man.
sources.raw_question: Does the fulness of grace that Christ communicates to believers reside in his human nature considered in itself, or in the person of the mediator, God and man?

question: Is a human inner word true merely because it corresponds to the thing spoken of, and when is it false?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Great is the Unlikeness Between Our Word and the Divine Word. Our Word Cannot Be or Be Called Eternal.
sources.answer: No. A word is true only if it is born of a thing that is known. So even a statement that matches reality is not a true word if we do not know it, and our word is false not only when we lie but when we are deceived. When we doubt or lie, we still have a true word about the doubt or the lie itself, because we know that we doubt or lie.
sources.quote: they are yet not true in respect to our word, because a word is not true unless it is born of a thing that is known
sources.raw_question: Is a human inner word true merely because it corresponds to the thing spoken of, and when is it false?

question: Why is the scriptural evidence for worship offered to the Holy Spirit often circumstantial rather than direct, and does this weaken the case for his deity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: It does not weaken it; it is what we should expect a priori. In the economy of redemption the Spirit's office is to kindle in us the spirit of grace and supplication, to intercede with us, and to enable us to pray to the Father as sons. Hence prayer is ordinarily through the Spirit, yet Scripture still shows divine worship rendered to him.
sources.quote: I admit that in some of the cases the evidence is rather circumstantial than direct. But this we should have a priori expected; for in the economy of redemption it is the office of the Holy Ghost to kindle in us the spirit of grace, and of supplications
sources.raw_question: Why is the scriptural evidence for worship offered to the Holy Spirit often circumstantial rather than direct, and does this weaken the case for his deity?

question: When the Son or the Holy Spirit is sent, or when God appears visibly, does only one Person of the Trinity act, or does the whole Trinity work together?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: The whole Trinity works indivisibly in each sending or appearance. The three Persons are equal in all things and share one nature that is unchangeable, invisible and omnipresent. Therefore no sending or appearance is the work of one Person in isolation from the others.
sources.quote: but that the Trinity, being in all things equal, and alike in its own nature unchangeable and invisible and omnipresent, works indivisibly in each sending or appearance.
sources.raw_question: When the Son or the Holy Spirit is sent, or when God appears visibly, does only one Person of the Trinity act, or does the whole Trinity work together?

question: Is Christ's wisdom and understanding infinite, unlike even the perfected knowledge of creatures?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is the wisdom of God's eternal wisdom itself, and his understanding is infinite. Creaturely knowledge, even when made perfect, remains finite and limited. His knowledge has no spot of darkness and no foil of limitedness.
sources.quote: but most glorious [is he] in his sight and wisdom: he is the wisdom of God’s eternal wisdom itself; his understanding is infinite.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's wisdom and understanding infinite, unlike even the perfected knowledge of creatures?

question: Does the fact that early Christian writers distinguish God from Christ and call the Father 'God' absolutely show that they denied the Son's divinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Post-Nicene writers do exactly the same, and nobody scruples calling the Father God absolutely even today, so the usage is consistent with orthodox belief in the Son's divinity. It therefore proves nothing against it.
sources.quote: the Ante-Nicene writers distinguish God from Christ, (that is, the Father from the Son,) and call the Father God absolutely : now, since the Post-Nicene writers do so too, and since nobody scruples it, even at this day
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that early Christian writers distinguish God from Christ and call the Father 'God' absolutely show that they denied the Son's divinity?

question: Does Christ intercede with the Father only for believers' sins, or also for their sufferings?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Christ intercedes for their sufferings as well as their sins. The Father always hears him. Every deliverance, recovery of health or relief from evil that believers receive is given on account of Christ's intercession, not dispensed by common providence. Failing to see this is why believers value their mercies too little.
sources.quote: Christ intercedeth on our behalf, not only in respect of our sins, but also our sufferings; and when the work of our afflictions is accomplished, we shall have the relief he intercedes for. The Father always hears him
sources.raw_question: Does Christ intercede with the Father only for believers' sins, or also for their sufferings?

question: Does the New Testament's consistent answer to 'What must I do to be saved?', namely faith in Jesus Christ, show that Christ is the object of a trust proper to God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. From the angel's message to Joseph to John's doxology in Patmos, the New Testament replies plainly, "Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ and thou shalt be saved." Christ presents himself to fallen and lost sinners as able to raise them from sin and make them a royal priesthood reigning forever. Only an utterance like Mary's, "My spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour," does justice to his claims, so he is owed the trust due to God the Saviour.
sources.quote: No utterance but one like Mary’s satisfies his claims: “My spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.”
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament's consistent answer to 'What must I do to be saved?', namely faith in Jesus Christ, show that Christ is the object of a trust proper to God?

question: Is it necessary to know the substance of created things, or of God, in order to benefit from them and rightly relate to them?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. We know the elements only so far as they serve our life, not their substance, and lose nothing by this ignorance; likewise Scripture omits idle inquiry into substance as superfluous and unnecessary.
sources.quote: Wherefore Holy Scripture omits all idle inquiry into substance as superfluous and unnecessary.
sources.raw_question: Is it necessary to know the substance of created things, or of God, in order to benefit from them and rightly relate to them?

question: Do Jesus' discourses in John teach that the Son and the Spirit are God while maintaining that there is only one God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. There is never any question in them that there is but one God. Yet the Son sent by God not only represents God but is God, and the Spirit sent by the Son is also Himself God. The Son and Spirit are clearly distinct Persons, and it is equally clear that the Son of God is God the Son and the Spirit of God is God the Spirit.
sources.quote: There is but one God – there is never any question of that – and yet this Son who has been sent into the world by God not only represents God but is God, and this Spirit whom the Son has in turn sent unto the world is also Himself God.
sources.raw_question: Do Jesus' discourses in John teach that the Son and the Spirit are God while maintaining that there is only one God?

question: Is it legitimate to apply human distinctions of slave and free to the divine nature when discussing the rank of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who maintain that the Spirit is in the rank neither of a servant nor of a master, but in that of the free.
sources.answer: No. Among men no one is a slave by nature; slavery arises from conquest, poverty, or a dispensation for the benefit of the unwise, so these degrees are variable and accidental. Applying such changeable human customs to the ineffable nature of God insults the doctrines concerning the divine nature.
sources.quote: endeavour to apply to the ineffable nature of God that common custom of human life whereby the difference of degrees is variable, not perceiving that among men no one is a slave by nature.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to apply human distinctions of slave and free to the divine nature when discussing the rank of the Holy Spirit?

question: Does confessing that the Word was made flesh entail preaching two Words, one who was in the beginning and one who was made flesh?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius himself confesses from John that the Word who was in the beginning was made flesh, yet no one charges him with teaching two Words, because the Word who appeared in the flesh is identical with the Word who was with God. Likewise distinguishing the dispensation in the flesh from the Divine power in itself does not make two Christs.
sources.quote: for he knows, surely, that the Word is identical with the Word, He who appeared in the flesh with Him Who was with God.
sources.raw_question: Does confessing that the Word was made flesh entail preaching two Words, one who was in the beginning and one who was made flesh?

question: Is goodness in God a nature-property, so that whoever does not share the Father's nature cannot properly be called good?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > The eleventh book shows that the title of “Good” is due, not to the Father alone, as Eunomius, the imitator of Manichæus and Bardesanes, alleges, but to the Son also, Who formed man in goodness and loving-kindness, and reformed him by His Cross and Death.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father has goodness not as something acquired but in his nature. On the heretics' view the Son does not share the Father's nature, so he would be cut off from both the essence and the title of "good." This shows the impiety of denying the Son's consubstantiality.
sources.quote: If the Father alone is good, having goodness not as a thing acquired, but in His nature, and if the Son, as heresy will have it, does not share in the nature of the Father, then he who does not share the good essence of the Father is of course at the same time excluded
sources.raw_question: Is goodness in God a nature-property, so that whoever does not share the Father's nature cannot properly be called good?

question: Does the ancient language of the Son 'ministering' or 'serving' in creation disparage the Son's dignity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. It is no more a disparagement of the Son than it is of the Father to be represented as having the counsel and help of two other Persons. Such expressions are to be read economically and in a manner befitting God, not literally. Their purpose is to express the real distinction of Persons, the unity of all Three as one Creator, and the unity of principle in the Father as fountain.
sources.quote: This need not be thought any greater disparagement to the dignity of the Son, than it is, on the other hand, a disparagement to the dignity of the Father to be represented as having the counsel and assistance of two other Persons
sources.raw_question: Does the ancient language of the Son 'ministering' or 'serving' in creation disparage the Son's dignity?

question: In the mind's inner word, is the word conceived the same as the word born when the will rests in the knowledge of spiritual things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > In the Love of Spiritual Things the Word Born is the Same as the Word Conceived. It is Otherwise in the Love of Carnal Things.
sources.answer: Yes. When the will finds rest in knowledge itself, as in the love of spiritual things, the word conceived and the word born are the very same. For example, one who perfectly knows and loves righteousness is already righteous, even without outwardly acting through bodily members.
sources.quote: But the word conceived and the word born are the very same when the will finds rest in knowledge itself, as is the case in the love of spiritual things.
sources.raw_question: In the mind's inner word, is the word conceived the same as the word born when the will rests in the knowledge of spiritual things?

question: In inquiring into the Trinity, should a theologian's writings carry the same authority as canonical Scripture, and by what standard should they be corrected?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > Preface.
sources.answer: No. Augustine says that what is found in canonical Scripture must be believed without hesitation, even if one did not believe it before. A theologian's writings should be held only where the reader has understood with certainty what he did not hold as certain before. Any correction of such writings must come from the divine text or from unanswerable reason, not from the corrector's own opinion or skill in argument.
sources.quote: Do not be willing to yield to my writings as to the canonical Scriptures; but in these, when thou hast discovered even what thou didst not previously believe, believe it unhesitatingly
sources.raw_question: In inquiring into the Trinity, should a theologian's writings carry the same authority as canonical Scripture, and by what standard should they be corrected?

question: How does the sun serve as an image of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: The Father is like the sun's inner constitution. The Son is like the brightness and glorious form of its disk as it appears to us. The Spirit is like the sun's action. Its inner heat stands for God's infinite love to himself and happiness in himself. Its emitted beams, which warm and enliven the world, stand for God communicating himself.
sources.quote: The Spirit as it is God's Infinite love to Himself and happiness in Himself, is as the internal heat of the Sun, but as it is that by which God communicates Himself, it is as the emanation of the sun's action, or the emitted beams of the sun.
sources.raw_question: How does the sun serve as an image of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit?

question: Does God order the whole visible creation to typify spiritual things?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Edwards affirms that the visible creation, being but the shadow of being, is made and ordered by God to typify and represent spiritual things. He holds this not as a mere hypothesis but as Divine truth established by Scripture.
sources.quote: the whole visible creation which is but the shadow of being is so made and ordered by God as to typify and represent spiritual things
sources.raw_question: Does God order the whole visible creation to typify spiritual things?

question: When Scripture calls Christ 'made' or 'created' (Galatians 4:4, Ephesians 4:24), does this refer to his divine nature or to his human birth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: It refers to his human birth. The Apostle names the true birth of the flesh conceived in the Virgin a creating and a making, because then the nature and form of our created being was born. This was not the birth of the divinity but the creating of the flesh, so the new man is created according to God who was born before the ages.
sources.quote: This was not the birth of the divinity, but the creating of the flesh; the new Man taking the title of the race, and being created according to God Who was born before the ages.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture calls Christ 'made' or 'created' (Galatians 4:4, Ephesians 4:24), does this refer to his divine nature or to his human birth?

question: In what capacity did Christ act when he undertook and accomplished reconciliation with God by his death?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: He acted as a common, public person standing in the place of those for whom he suffered. That is why Scripture calls him the mediator who gave himself a ransom, the surety of the better covenant, and one given for a covenant of the people. He is the second Adam, who brings righteousness to his spiritual seed as the first Adam brought sin to his natural seed.
sources.quote: was constituted and considered as a common, public person, in the stead of them for whose reconciliation to God he suffered. Hence he is the “mediator between God and man,” 1 Tim. ii. 5
sources.raw_question: In what capacity did Christ act when he undertook and accomplished reconciliation with God by his death?

question: Does 1 Corinthians 1:30, which says Christ is "made unto us wisdom," imply that Christ was created?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Christ is "made" wisdom to us by God's ordination and appointment, not by creation. He is our wisdom in two ways. He teaches us wisdom as the great prophet of the church. And in knowing him we come to know the wisdom of God.
sources.quote: He is made, not by creation, but ordination and appointment, wisdom unto us; not only by teaching us wisdom (by a metonymy of the effect for the cause), as he is the great prophet of his church
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 1:30, which says Christ is "made unto us wisdom," imply that Christ was created?

question: Were the Son and the Father known to Abraham before the incarnation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter V.—The author returns to his former argument, and shows that there was but one God announced by the law and prophets, whom Christ confesses as His Father, and who, through His word, one living God with Him, made Himself known to men in both covenants.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ said Abraham rejoiced to see His day. As a prophet, Abraham saw in the Spirit the Lord's coming and passion, and he followed the Word as a pilgrim. He also knew the Lord's Father, having learned from the Word and believed Him as the maker of heaven and earth. Therefore the claim that the true God was unknown before Christ's advent is false.
sources.quote: The Lord, therefore, was not unknown to Abraham, whose day he desired to see; nor, again, was the Lord’s Father, for he had learned from the Word of the Lord, and believed Him
sources.raw_question: Were the Son and the Father known to Abraham before the incarnation?

question: How does Abraham's offering of Isaac relate to God the Father's offering of His Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter V.—The author returns to his former argument, and shows that there was but one God announced by the law and prophets, whom Christ confesses as His Father, and who, through His word, one living God with Him, made Himself known to men in both covenants.
sources.answer: It prefigures it. Abraham, following the Word's command, willingly offered his only-begotten and beloved son. This was so that God might be pleased to offer His own beloved and only-begotten Son as a sacrifice for the redemption of all Abraham's seed.
sources.quote: delivered up, as a sacrifice to God, his only-begotten and beloved son, in order that God also might be pleased to offer up for all his seed His own beloved and only-begotten Son, as a sacrifice for our redemption.
sources.raw_question: How does Abraham's offering of Isaac relate to God the Father's offering of His Son?

question: How does the name "Word" help us conceive the Son's origin from the Father without passion?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: A human word proceeds from the mind without any intervention of passion. So, on hearing of the divine Word, we should conceive of one who is from another, without conceiving of passion.
