sources.quote: For as thy word proceeds from thy mind, without requiring the intervention of passion, so here also, in hearing of the Word, thou shalt conceive that which is from something, and shalt not conceive passion.
sources.raw_question: How does the name "Word" help us conceive the Son's origin from the Father without passion?

question: How does the Father's giving the Son 'to have life in Himself' bear on the Spirit's procession from the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > What It is that Suffices Here to Solve the Question Why the Spirit is Not Said to Be Begotten, and Why the Father Alone is Unbegotten. What They Ought to Do Who Do Not Understand These Things.
sources.answer: The Spirit is life, just as the Father and the Son are life. As the Father, having life in Himself, gave the Son to have life in Himself, so He also gave the Son that life, the Spirit, should proceed from Him as it proceeds from the Father.
sources.quote: as the Father, while He has life in Himself, has given also to the Son to have life in Himself; so has He given also to Him that life should proceed from Him, as it also proceeds from Himself
sources.raw_question: How does the Father's giving the Son 'to have life in Himself' bear on the Spirit's procession from the Son?

question: Do texts saying the Father 'hath given all things' into the Son's hand (Matthew 11:27; John 3:35) imply that the Son once lacked these prerogatives?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: No. The Son eternally has what the Father has, since 'All that the Father hath are Mine'; because the Father has them always, what the Son has, being the Father's, was always in the Son. Such texts are spoken not because He once lacked them but because, while He has them eternally, He has them from the Father.
sources.quote: not then because once He had them not, did He say this, but because, whereas the Son hath eternally what He hath, yet He hath them from the Father.
sources.raw_question: Do texts saying the Father 'hath given all things' into the Son's hand (Matthew 11:27; John 3:35) imply that the Son once lacked these prerogatives?

question: Can a person love something of which he is wholly ignorant?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Love of the Studious Mind, that Is, of One Desirous to Know, is Not the Love of a Thing Which It Does Not Know.
sources.answer: No. Augustine holds that love always presupposes some knowledge of its object, even if that knowledge is only partial or generic. Even the eager desire of a student to learn what he does not yet know depends on some prior impression or knowledge of the thing desired, so that what is utterly unknown can in no way be loved.
sources.quote: So it is that the studious zeal of those who learn is kindled: for that of which any one is utterly ignorant, he can in no way love.
sources.raw_question: Can a person love something of which he is wholly ignorant?

question: Does the traditional Nicene language of eternal generation and procession imply a real subordination of the Son and Spirit to the Father?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Warfield treats this language as a remnant of the Logos-Christology carried into church terminology. Nicaea guarded the language against the subordinationism inherent in that Christology. The Athanasian Creed's stress on the equality of the three Persons (homoousia) practically pushes these suggestions of derivation and subordination out of sight. The principle of equalization must still be vigorously reasserted against any tendency to over-emphasize them.
sources.quote: the principle of the equalization of the three Persons, which was already the dominant motive of the Nicene Creed – the homoousia – is so strongly emphasized as practically to push out of sight, if not quite out of existence, these remanent suggestions of derivation and subordination
sources.raw_question: Does the traditional Nicene language of eternal generation and procession imply a real subordination of the Son and Spirit to the Father?

question: Could there be something in God, whether an independent existence or a non-subsistent condition, that God restrained from begetting the Son until a due time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > The ninth book declares that Eunomius' account of the Nature of God is, up to a certain point, well stated. Then in succession he mixes up with his own argument, on account of its affinity, the expression from Philo's writings, “God is before all other things, which are generated,” adding also the expression, “He has dominion over His own power.” Detesting the excessive absurdity, Gregory strikingly confutes it.
sources.answer: No. If the thing restrained were quiescent, it would need no one to master it. If it were a separate existence besides God, it could not be in God. If it were a condition without existence of its own, then it simply is not, and what is not can neither be held under dominion nor be set free. So there is no restrained power delaying the generation of the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: for that which has no existence of its own is not: and that which is not, is neither under dominion, nor set free from it.
sources.raw_question: Could there be something in God, whether an independent existence or a non-subsistent condition, that God restrained from begetting the Son until a due time?

question: How does Christ remove the enmity between God and sinners so that they can walk with God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Christ removes the enmity in four ways. He takes away its cause, sin and the curse of the law, by making atonement and being made a curse for us; he destroys the devil who would widen the breach; he makes reconciliation with God by his blood, turning away the wrath due to us; and he slays the enmity on our side, so that we receive the atonement and lay down our hostility to God.
sources.quote: He takes out of the way the cause of the enmity that was between God and us, — sin and the curse of the law. He makes an end of sin, and that by making atonement for iniquity
sources.raw_question: How does Christ remove the enmity between God and sinners so that they can walk with God?

question: Is saving acquaintance with God, especially knowledge of him as love and pardoning mercy, possible only through the revelation of Jesus Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. God dwells in unapproachable light, and no one has ever seen him except through Christ's revelation. The Son reveals the Father, gives the understanding by which we know him that is true, and is the true Light that enlightens all who are enlightened. The Pharisees, despite their claimed knowledge, had never heard God's voice nor seen his shape. Knowledge of God as love and grace exists only in Christ.
sources.quote: There is no acquaintance with God, as love, and full of kindness, patience, grace, and pardoning mercy (on which knowledge of him alone we can walk with him), but only in Christ
sources.raw_question: Is saving acquaintance with God, especially knowledge of him as love and pardoning mercy, possible only through the revelation of Jesus Christ?

question: In what sense can it be said that Christ was created, without denying his eternal deity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: Christ was created in his human nature at the Incarnation, since the nature of flesh is created. By partaking of it in all points as we do, yet without sin, he was created when he became man. But this creation was "after God," in a new manner and not according to human wont, being of the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest.
sources.quote: For the nature of flesh is created: and by partaking in it in all points like as we do, yet without sin, He was created when He became man: and He was created “after God,” not after man
sources.raw_question: In what sense can it be said that Christ was created, without denying his eternal deity?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being given, sent, bestowed and promised to men show that he cannot be God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. These expressions were never offered as proof of his deity, but they do prove he is a person, an intelligent voluntary agent, since a mere power or quality cannot properly be sent or given. And one who is God, equal in nature with the Father, may be promised, sent and given because of the gracious arrangement in which he has taken on the office of comforter and sanctifier.
sources.quote: He who is God, equal in nature and being with the Father, may be promised, sent, and given, with respect unto the holy dispensation and condescension wherein he has undertaken the office of being our comforter and sanctifier.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being given, sent, bestowed and promised to men show that he cannot be God?

question: Do Scripture's references to the Spirit being divided, distributed or imparted to people show that the Spirit is an impersonal, divisible power?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. When these terms are viewed from the side of those who receive them, they refer only to the works, gifts, operations and effects of the Spirit, not to his being. The rule is given in 1 Corinthians 12:11: the Spirit works them in whom he will and as he will, which itself shows a personal agent.
sources.quote: denote only works, gifts, operations, and effects of the Spirit; the rule whereof is expressed, 1 Cor. xii. 11. He works them in whom he will, and as he will.
sources.raw_question: Do Scripture's references to the Spirit being divided, distributed or imparted to people show that the Spirit is an impersonal, divisible power?

question: Does Paul assert the full deity of Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. No expression is too strong for Paul in asserting Christ's Godhead. He calls Him 'our great God' and 'God over all,' and declares that the fullness of the Godhead, everything that constitutes Godhead, dwells in Him.
sources.quote: no expression is too strong for him to use in order to assert the Godhead of Christ: He is “our great God” (Tit. ii. 13); He is “God over all” (Rom. ix. 5)
sources.raw_question: Does Paul assert the full deity of Jesus Christ?

question: How is an enigma related to an allegory as a figure of speech in Scripture?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Of the Term ‘Enigma,’ And of Tropical Modes of Speech.
sources.answer: An enigma is one species of allegory: an obscure allegory. Every enigma is an allegory, but not every allegory is an enigma. An allegory is a trope in which one thing is understood from another, and it may be plain, as in 1 Thessalonians 5. An enigma is dark, like "The horseleech had three daughters." Paul's allegory of Abraham's two sons was an enigma until it was explained.
sources.quote: so every enigma is an allegory, but every allegory is not an enigma. What then is an allegory, but a trope wherein one thing is understood from another?
sources.raw_question: How is an enigma related to an allegory as a figure of speech in Scripture?

question: What does the Hebrew name Jesus signify about the Lord?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIV.—Folly of the arguments derived by the heretics from numbers, letters, and syllables.
sources.answer: It signifies the Lord who contains heaven and earth. Irenaeus says that, according to the learned among the Hebrews, the name is made up of two and a half letters. It is therefore a word whose meaning concerns the Lord's embrace of all creation, not a numerical code for Aeons.
sources.quote: Jesus, which is a word belonging to the proper tongue of the Hebrews, contains, as the learned among them declare, two letters and a half,[^3154] and signifies that Lord who contains heaven and earth;
sources.raw_question: What does the Hebrew name Jesus signify about the Lord?

question: Does God's command to Jacob to build an altar 'unto God that appeared unto thee' show two distinct Persons who are both truly God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. God speaks and demands honour for God, referring to Another than Himself, so the Persons are not confused. Both bear their true Name of God, asserting their shared majesty, while the words declare their several existence.
sources.quote: It is God Who speaks, and God of Whom He speaks. Their majesty is asserted by the combination of Both under Their true Name of God, while the words plainly declare Their several existence.
sources.raw_question: Does God's command to Jacob to build an altar 'unto God that appeared unto thee' show two distinct Persons who are both truly God?

question: Is it a genuine contradiction for Scripture to affirm and deny the same thing of Christ, as in "I will not judge" and "I will judge"?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: No. Such sayings are true because they are said of Christ in different relations, one according to the form of God and one according to the form of a servant. Both forms belong to one and the same person, who is both Son of God and Son of man. That is why even the Lord of glory can be said to be crucified.
sources.quote: How can this be true, unless He has called it His own in one relation; not His own, in another?
sources.raw_question: Is it a genuine contradiction for Scripture to affirm and deny the same thing of Christ, as in "I will not judge" and "I will judge"?

question: Are the three elements of bodily sight (the object seen, the vision, and the mind's attention) of one and the same nature or substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Certain Trinity in the Sight. That There are Three Things in Sight, Which Differ in Their Own Nature. In What Manner from a Visible Thing Vision is Produced, or the Image of that Thing Which is Seen. The Matter is Shown More Clearly by an Example. How These Three Combine in One.
sources.answer: No. They differ not only in their properties but in their very natures. The visible body is a separable thing outside us. The sense and the vision belong to the nature of the living subject who sees. The attention is an act of the mind alone, as mind differs from body.
sources.quote: In these three, then, not only is there an evident distinction, but also a diverse nature.
sources.raw_question: Are the three elements of bodily sight (the object seen, the vision, and the mind's attention) of one and the same nature or substance?

question: Is the Holy Spirit, and not only the Father and the Son, the author of prophecy?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XIII. Prophecy was not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Spirit; the authority and operation of the latter on the apostles is signified to be the same as Theirs; and so we are to understand that there is unity in the three points of authority, rule, and bounty; yet need no disadvantage be feared from that participation, since such does not arise in human friendship. Lastly, it is established that this is the inheritance of the apostolic faith from the fact that the apostles are described as having obeyed the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Hebrews says God spoke in the prophets, Wisdom (the Son) says he will send prophets, and Paul lists prophecy among the gifts given through the one Spirit. Therefore prophecy comes through Father, Son and Spirit alike, so the office and the grace are one.
sources.quote: Therefore, according to the Apostle, prophecy is not only through the Father and the Son, but also through the Holy Spirit, and therefore the office is one, and the grace one.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit, and not only the Father and the Son, the author of prophecy?

question: Do the Scripture passages that speak of the Son's subordination as man contain any warning against trusting or loving Christ too much, as one would expect if he were only a creature?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. If Christ were not God, the Scriptures that ascribe divine perfections to him would have needed constant caveats against worshipping and trusting him. Yet the passages affirming his subordination as man contain no such warning, not even the faintest hint that one could love or trust him too much. Instead, contemplating his humiliation raises confidence and affection to the highest pitch, so that believers adore him supremely.
sources.quote: Now I ask, do the passages affirming his subordination as man, contain that caveat? – or anything like such a warning? – or any, even the faintest intimation of the possibility of loving him too much, or trusting in him too entirely? You must confess they do not.
sources.raw_question: Do the Scripture passages that speak of the Son's subordination as man contain any warning against trusting or loving Christ too much, as one would expect if he were only a creature?

question: How does God differ from created man with respect to change and growth?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XI.—The old prophets and righteous men knew beforehand of the advent of Christ, and earnestly desired to see and hear Him, He revealing himself in the Scriptures by the Holy Ghost, and without any change in Himself, enriching men day by day with benefits, but conferring them in greater abundance on later than on former generations.
sources.answer: God makes and is always the same, while man is made and must have beginning, middle, addition and increase. God is perfect in all things, equal and similar to himself, all light, all mind, all substance and the fount of all good. Man advances toward God, and God never stops conferring benefits on him.
sources.quote: God indeed makes, but man is made; and truly, He who makes is always the same; but that which is made must receive both beginning, and middle, and addition, and increase.
sources.raw_question: How does God differ from created man with respect to change and growth?

question: If the human soul is capable of sin, could a sinless Christ assume one?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: Yes. The soul is not itself sin, though it can admit sin through being ill-advised. Christ, tempted in all points yet without sin, took the soul and sanctified it by union with Himself, so that the whole lump might be holy along with the first-fruits.
sources.quote: Now the soul is not sin though it is capable of admitting sin into it as the result of being ill-advised: and this He sanctifies by union with Himself for this end, that so the lump may be holy along with the first-fruits.
sources.raw_question: If the human soul is capable of sin, could a sinless Christ assume one?

question: Can there be many gods or creators each ruling a separate territory, or must there be one God who contains all things?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter I.—There is but one God: the impossibility of its being otherwise.
sources.answer: There must be one God who contains all things. If there were many unlimited creators and gods bordering on one another, each would be shut up within its own territory and contained from without by some greater being. Each would then possess only a small part compared with the rest and would lack much, so none of them would truly be God.
sources.quote: For it must be either that there is one Being who contains all things, and formed in His own territory all those things which have been created, according to His own will; or, again, that there are numerous unlimited creators and gods
sources.raw_question: Can there be many gods or creators each ruling a separate territory, or must there be one God who contains all things?

question: What is the fundamental proof that God is a Trinity?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: The fundamental proof is Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit themselves, revealed in fact in the incarnation of the Son and the outpouring of the Spirit. All evidence that Christ is God manifested in the flesh, and that the Spirit is a divine Person, is therefore evidence for the Trinity. So the whole New Testament, which is saturated with such evidence, testifies to the Trinity, not merely the scattered explicit allusions.
sources.quote: In a word, Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit are the fundamental proof of the doctrine of the Trinity.
sources.raw_question: What is the fundamental proof that God is a Trinity?

question: Is the believers' right to created things the same kind of right that Christ has as heir of all things?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: No. Christ's right is sovereign and supreme, to do what he will with his own. The saints' right is subordinate, and they must give account for how they use what they have. Christ's right is that of the Lord of the house; theirs is that of servants.
sources.quote: The right of Christ is the right of the Lord of the house; the right of the saints is the right of servants.
sources.raw_question: Is the believers' right to created things the same kind of right that Christ has as heir of all things?

question: Does Isaiah's calling Christ "the Angel of mighty counsel" prove that the Son is a lesser being than God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. In that prophecy the title clearly refers to the dispensation of His humanity, since it speaks of a Child born and a Son given. It therefore concerns the Incarnation, not His divine nature.
sources.quote: For there, in clear and uncontrovertible terms, there is indicated by the prophecy the dispensation of His Humanity
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah's calling Christ "the Angel of mighty counsel" prove that the Son is a lesser being than God?

question: Does David's description of Christ being "established King" on Sion imply that the Son was not King before?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. David speaks with an eye to the dispensation: the Lord's humiliation to the estate of a servant was taken up and absorbed into the majesty of His Kingdom, not that He was ever not a King.
sources.quote: not as though He were not a King, but in the view that the humiliation to the estate of a servant to which the Lord submitted by way of dispensation, was taken up and absorbed into the majesty of His Kingdom
sources.raw_question: Does David's description of Christ being "established King" on Sion imply that the Son was not King before?

question: Can any name express the essence of the Son as "the Existent"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. As the Existent He has no name that could give knowledge of His essence, since He transcends every power of names to express. That is why the Apostle says His name is "above every name": not one name ranked highest among comparable names, but because He who truly is surpasses all naming.
sources.quote: not as though it were some one name preferred above all others, though still comparable with them, but rather in the sense that He Who verily is is above every name
sources.raw_question: Can any name express the essence of the Son as "the Existent"?

question: Is it inconsistent for the Apostle to say that the Father raised Christ when Christ says he raises himself?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Christ declares himself God and the Resurrection his own work by saying he has power to take up his life again and will raise the temple of his body. Yet he refers everything to his Father's command. Since Christ is the power and wisdom of God, whatever Christ does, God himself does. So Christ was raised by the working of God, because he worked the Father's works with a nature indistinguishable from God's.
sources.quote: for whatever Christ does, the power and the wisdom of God does: and whatever the power and the wisdom of God does, without doubt God Himself does, Whose power and wisdom Christ is.
sources.raw_question: Is it inconsistent for the Apostle to say that the Father raised Christ when Christ says he raises himself?

question: Does attributing to the Son a capacity to suffer, and denying it to the Father, actually lower the Son below the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He then again charges Eunomius with having learnt his term ἀγεννησία from the hieroglyphic writings, and from the Egyptian mythology and idolatry, and with bringing in Anubis, Osiris, and Isis to the creed of Christians, and shows that, considered as admitting His sufferings of necessity and not voluntarily, the Only-begotten is entitled to no gratitude from men: and that fire has none for its warmth, nor water for its fluidity, as they do not refer their results to self-determining power, but to necessity of nature.
sources.answer: No. By Eunomius's own reasoning it would rather raise the Son above the Father. Had the Son been incapable of suffering, as they say the Father is, human nature would have stayed in its misery, with no one to lift it to incorruption. Since one who has the power to act for good deserves more honour than one powerless for good, the quibble meant to diminish the Only-begotten ends up exalting him.
sources.quote: the cunning of these quibblers, by the very means which it employs in its attempt to destroy the majesty of the Only-begotten God, does but raise men’s conceptions of Him to a grander and loftier height
sources.raw_question: Does attributing to the Son a capacity to suffer, and denying it to the Father, actually lower the Son below the Father?

question: If every divine person has its own substance, must three persons mean three substances and therefore three Gods?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Each person has its own substance in that the one substance of the Deity is the substance of each person, so the substance remains one. But no person has a distinct substance of its own, because the substance of all three is the same.
sources.quote: Every person has distinctly its own substance, for the one substance of the Deity is the substance of each person, so it is still but one; but each person has not its own distinct substance, because the substance of them all is the same
sources.raw_question: If every divine person has its own substance, must three persons mean three substances and therefore three Gods?

question: Can a divine Person who needs to receive goodness from a superior be the source who imparts goodness to creatures?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. If the Divine Nature in the Son or Spirit only participates in goodness, it would itself need goodness rather than transmit it, for no one can give another what he does not possess. Such a being would be occupied with supplying its own want and could not help inferiors.
sources.quote: the Divine Nature cannot be apprehended as transmissive of good, but rather as itself needing goodness: for how can one impart to another that which he does not himself possess?
sources.raw_question: Can a divine Person who needs to receive goodness from a superior be the source who imparts goodness to creatures?

question: Is there any consistent middle position between the orthodox doctrine of the Son's consubstantiality and Arianism, such as Semi-Arianism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: No. Waterland holds there is no medium between orthodoxy and Arianism, because there is no medium between God and creature, between unmade and made. Semi-Arianism, so understood, is nonsense and contradiction, and whoever disowns consubstantiality, rightly understood, is really as much an Arian as Eunomius or Arius. The only 'middle way' is to suspend judgment, not to hold a third doctrine.
sources.quote: There is certainly no medium betwixt orthodoay and Arianism, (for *Semi-Arianism, if so understood, is perfect nonsense and contradiction,) there being no medium between God and creature, between unmade and made.
sources.raw_question: Is there any consistent middle position between the orthodox doctrine of the Son's consubstantiality and Arianism, such as Semi-Arianism?

question: Why did the First-begotten Word, the Father's offspring, descend to and become joined with the human creature?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXVI.—Men shall be actually raised: the world shall not be annihilated; but there shall be various mansions for the saints, according to the rank allotted to each individual. All things shall be subject to God the Father, and so shall He be all in all.
sources.answer: So that the creature might be brought to perfection by being joined to the Son. The Word descends to what was moulded so that it might be contained by him, and the creature in turn contains the Word, rises above the angels, and is made after the image and likeness of God. There is one Son who accomplished his Father's will, and one human race in which these mysteries are carried out.
sources.quote: that His offspring, the First-begotten Word, should descend to the creature (facturam), that is, to what had been moulded (plasma), and that it should be contained by Him; and, on the other hand, the creature should contain the Word, and ascend to Him
sources.raw_question: Why did the First-begotten Word, the Father's offspring, descend to and become joined with the human creature?

question: Do Abraham, Moses, the prophets and the Lord Jesus derive from one and the same source, or did the Old Testament figures come from a different essence than Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter II.—Proofs from the plain testimony of Moses, and of the other prophets, whose words are the words of Christ, that there is but one God, the founder of the world, whom Our Lord preached, and whom He called His Father.
sources.answer: They are all from one essence. In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, the Lord teaches that those who obey Moses and the prophets will believe in the Son of God whom they preached. Moses and the prophets announced the Son's coming, so they belong to the same divine economy as the Lord. Those who assign them to another essence scoff at the truth.
sources.quote: He shows that all are from one essence, that is, Abraham, and Moses, and the prophets, and also the Lord Himself, who rose from the dead
sources.raw_question: Do Abraham, Moses, the prophets and the Lord Jesus derive from one and the same source, or did the Old Testament figures come from a different essence than Christ?

question: Does it matter for theological meaning whether language allows a single negative word like 'unbegotten' or requires a phrase like 'not begotten'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Addition of a Negative Does Not Change the Predicament.
sources.answer: No. The usage of a language does not decide the matter; we must consider the meaning of the things themselves. Latin allows 'ingenitus' but not 'infilius,' and 'inimicus' but not 'invicinus,' yet 'non filius' and 'non genitus' mean the same. Thus the form 'unbegotten' does not make it a substantial predicate distinct from 'not begotten.'
sources.quote: we must not consider what the usage of our own language either allows or does not allow, but what clearly appears to be the meaning of the things themselves.
sources.raw_question: Does it matter for theological meaning whether language allows a single negative word like 'unbegotten' or requires a phrase like 'not begotten'?

question: Do the acts of the Angel who appeared to Hagar prove that he is true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. He promises to multiply Ishmael into a great people and many nations, which is not within an angel's power but is the power of God. Whoever possesses the true power of God cannot be refused true divinity.
sources.quote: Is this, I ask, within an angel’s power? If not, and this is the power of God, why do you refuse true Divinity to Him Who, on your own confession, has the true power of God?
sources.raw_question: Do the acts of the Angel who appeared to Hagar prove that he is true God?

question: Is it true that no worship is due to the Son for creating the world because creation is not an act of dominion and he created only ministerially, as angels serve only instrumentally?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: No. If creation is no ground of worship because it is not dominion, the same reasoning would apply to the Father, for creating is one thing and ruling another. Yet Scripture makes creation the distinguishing ground of worship, so that no one who had no hand in creating has any title to worship. Antiquity agrees, and the claim that the Son created only ministerially was refuted earlier.
sources.quote: Seripture makes creation the ground and reason of worship, in so particular and distinguishing a manner, that no person whatever, that had not a hand in creating, has any right or title to worship, upon Scripture-principles
sources.raw_question: Is it true that no worship is due to the Son for creating the world because creation is not an act of dominion and he created only ministerially, as angels serve only instrumentally?

question: How can Scripture say both that the pure in heart shall see God and that no one can see God and live?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: The two sayings concern different respects. In His greatness and wonderful glory no one can see God, because the Father is incomprehensible. In His love, kindness and power, God grants those who love Him the sight of Himself. What is impossible for men is possible for God.
sources.quote: But in respect to His greatness, and His wonderful glory, “no man shall see God and live,” for the Father is incomprehensible; but in regard to His love, and kindness, and as to His infinite power, even this He grants to those who love Him
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture say both that the pure in heart shall see God and that no one can see God and live?

question: Can human beings see God by their own natural powers?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: No. Man does not see God by his own powers. God is seen when He pleases, by whom He wills, when He wills and as He wills. He who is boundless and invisible made Himself visible and comprehensible to believers.
sources.quote: For man does not see God by his own powers; but when He pleases He is seen by men, by whom He wills, and when He wills, and as He wills.
sources.raw_question: Can human beings see God by their own natural powers?

question: What does the Father's giving the Son power over all flesh to give eternal life show about the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It shows both the Fatherhood of the Giver and the Divinity of the Receiver. What is given is the Father's own property: power to bestow eternal life and to change the corruptible into the incorruptible. So this power is natural and congenital to the Son, and it does not separate him from his Author.
sources.quote: postulates the Fatherhood of the Giver and the Divinity of the Receiver: for by giving is signified that the One is the Father, and in receiving the power to give eternal life, the Other remains God the Son.
sources.raw_question: What does the Father's giving the Son power over all flesh to give eternal life show about the Father and the Son?

question: Are God's attributes such as power, eternity and providence things God possesses as extraneous to himself?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. We should not think God possesses these as something external to himself. Rather, by these qualities God himself is expressed in terms partly comprehensible to our senses.
sources.quote: not that we should think that He possesses these as something extraneous to Himself, but that by these His qualities He Himself has been expressed in terms partly comprehensible by our sense.
sources.raw_question: Are God's attributes such as power, eternity and providence things God possesses as extraneous to himself?

question: Does Psalm 139:7, "Whither shall I go from Thy Spirit?", show that the Holy Spirit is omnipresent and therefore divine?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is not a creature, seeing that He is infinite, and was shed upon the apostles dispersed through all countries, and moreover sanctifies the Angels also, to whom He makes us equal. Mary was full of the same likewise, so too, Christ the Lord, and so far all things high and low. And all benediction has its origin from His operation, as was signified in the moving of the water at Bethesda.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says this of the Spirit and never of any Angel, Dominion or Power. Angels were sent to few, but the Spirit was poured on whole peoples at once and is unseen. What is shed on many at once is divine, while what is seen and held by individuals is corporeal.
sources.quote: Who, then, can doubt that that is divine which is shed upon many at once and is not seen; but that that is corporeal which is seen and held by individuals?
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 139:7, "Whither shall I go from Thy Spirit?", show that the Holy Spirit is omnipresent and therefore divine?

question: Is the Holy Spirit able to make human beings equal to the Angels?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is not a creature, seeing that He is infinite, and was shed upon the apostles dispersed through all countries, and moreover sanctifies the Angels also, to whom He makes us equal. Mary was full of the same likewise, so too, Christ the Lord, and so far all things high and low. And all benediction has its origin from His operation, as was signified in the moving of the water at Bethesda.
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord promised, "Ye shall be as the Angels in heaven." Since the Spirit made the Angels what they are, he can by the same grace raise men's lower nature to equality with them.
sources.quote: He Who made those Angels in the Spirit will by the same grace make men also equal to the Angels.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit able to make human beings equal to the Angels?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's filling of all things show that he shares in the divine dominion and power?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is not a creature, seeing that He is infinite, and was shed upon the apostles dispersed through all countries, and moreover sanctifies the Angels also, to whom He makes us equal. Mary was full of the same likewise, so too, Christ the Lord, and so far all things high and low. And all benediction has its origin from His operation, as was signified in the moving of the water at Bethesda.
sources.answer: Yes. Filling heaven and earth belongs to the Lord, and Scripture says the Spirit of the Lord fills the whole world and is poured on all flesh. No creature or Angel can be said to do this. Therefore the Spirit shares the dominion and divine power.
sources.quote: If, then, it is the Lord Who fills heaven and earth, Who can judge the Holy Spirit to be without a share in the dominion and divine power, seeing that He has filled the world
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's filling of all things show that he shares in the divine dominion and power?

question: Does the statement that Jesus was "full of the Holy Spirit" prove the Spirit's divinity, or was it said only of Christ's flesh?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is not a creature, seeing that He is infinite, and was shed upon the apostles dispersed through all countries, and moreover sanctifies the Angels also, to whom He makes us equal. Mary was full of the same likewise, so too, Christ the Lord, and so far all things high and low. And all benediction has its origin from His operation, as was signified in the moving of the water at Bethesda.
sources.answer: It proves the Spirit's divinity. Only one possessing the same fulness could fill Christ, who fills all things. Even if the objection is made that this was said according to the flesh, Scripture still says independently that the Spirit of the Lord filled the whole world, just as the Lord fills all things.
sources.quote: Who, then, except one who possessed the same fulness could fill Him Who fills all things?
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that Jesus was "full of the Holy Spirit" prove the Spirit's divinity, or was it said only of Christ's flesh?

question: What is the distinguishing mark of the Divine nature that separates it from created existence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > The fifth book promises to speak of the words contained in the saying of the Apostle Peter, but delays their exposition. He discourses first of the creation, to the effect that, while nothing therein is deserving of worship, yet men, led astray by their ill-informed and feeble intelligence, and marvelling at its beauty, deified the several parts of the universe. And herein he excellently expounds the passage of Isaiah, “I am God, the first.”
sources.answer: The uncreated nature never begins to be and never ceases to be. Scripture teaches us to regard all created existence as outside the Divine nature and to worship the uncreated Nature alone. Isaiah expresses this mark when God says that no God was before Him and none shall be after Him.
sources.quote: to worship and revere that uncreated Nature alone, Whose characteristic and token is that it never either begins to be or ceases to be
sources.raw_question: What is the distinguishing mark of the Divine nature that separates it from created existence?

question: Does saying that grace and access to the Father come "through" the Son (as in Romans 1:5 and 5:2) detract from the Son's glory or imply he is inferior to the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. Confessing the grace the Son works toward us is not a detraction from his glory. Rather, recounting his benefits is a proper reason for glorifying him. "Through him" describes the good gifts passing from the Father to us, and our being brought to the Father through Christ.
sources.quote: Is then the confession of the grace wrought by Him to usward a detraction from His glory? Is it not truer to say that the recital of His benefits is a proper argument for glorifying Him?
sources.raised_by_detail: opponents who use "through whom" to diminish the Son
sources.raw_question: Does saying that grace and access to the Father come "through" the Son (as in Romans 1:5 and 5:2) detract from the Son's glory or imply he is inferior to the Father?

question: Do the many scriptural titles of Christ, such as Shepherd, King, Door, Way and Rock, describe his divine nature?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. Scripture uses two kinds of names for Christ. Some names describe his nature: Son, true Son, only begotten God, Power, Wisdom and Word. The other titles, such as Shepherd, Physician, Door and Rock, set forth the various kinds of saving work he does out of tenderness toward each creature's particular need. So these functional titles say nothing about his being lesser in nature.
sources.quote: And these titles do not set forth His nature, but, as I have remarked, the variety of the effectual working which, out of His tender-heartedness to His own creation, according to the peculiar necessity of each, He bestows upon them that need.
sources.raw_question: Do the many scriptural titles of Christ, such as Shepherd, King, Door, Way and Rock, describe his divine nature?

question: Is Christ faithful in the same way Moses was faithful, as a creature believing God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. Moses, a man by nature, became faithful by believing God who spoke to him through the Word. Christ is faithful as Son over the house, its Builder, Lord and Framer, being God in flesh, not a creature within creation.
sources.quote: the Word was not as one of things originate in a body, nor as creature in creature, but as God in flesh, and Framer of all and Builder in that which was built by Him
sources.raw_question: Is Christ faithful in the same way Moses was faithful, as a creature believing God?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's calling God's promised rest "My rest," and condemning the unbelievers by the same oath, show that the Spirit has one will and power with the Father?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VIII. The aforesaid unity is proved hereby, that as the Father is said to be grieved and tempted, so too the Son. The Son was also tempted in the wilderness, where a figure of the cross was set up in the brazen serpent: but the Apostle says that the Spirit also was there tempted. St. Ambrose infers from this that the Israelites were guided into the promised land by the same Spirit, and that His will and power are one with those of the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. God promised rest to the Jews, yet the Spirit calls that rest His own. God condemned the people so that they could not enter the land, and the Spirit condemned them by the same decree: "If they shall enter into My rest." One decree shows one Will and one Power.
sources.quote: the Spirit condemns them by the same decree: “If they shall enter into My rest.” It is, then, the decree of one Will, the excellency of one Power.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's calling God's promised rest "My rest," and condemning the unbelievers by the same oath, show that the Spirit has one will and power with the Father?

question: In what sense is the human soul immortal, if it can suffer its own kind of death?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Image of God is to Be Sought in the Immortality of the Rational Soul. How a Trinity is Demonstrated in the Mind.
sources.answer: The soul is called immortal only with a qualification. It has its proper death when it lacks the blessed life, which is its true life. Yet it is called immortal because it never ceases to live with some life or other, even when it is most miserable.
sources.quote: the soul too has its proper death, when it lacks a blessed life, which is to be called the true life of the soul; but it is therefore called immortal, because it never ceases to live with some life or other
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the human soul immortal, if it can suffer its own kind of death?

question: Is a doctrine about God that is above human reason thereby contrary to reason?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Many things are above reason as it exists in men without being against it, as countless instances even in finite and temporary things show. Indeed everything concerning the being and properties of God is above our comprehension, since we cannot by searching find out the Almighty to perfection.
sources.quote: Many things are above reason, — that is, as considered in this or that subject, as men, — which are not at all against it.
sources.raw_question: Is a doctrine about God that is above human reason thereby contrary to reason?

question: What does the ongoing power of the name of Jesus Christ in the Church's miracles show about Christ's incarnate works and his relation to the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXII.—Further exposure of the wicked and blasphemous doctrines of the heretics.
sources.answer: It shows that the incarnate Christ truly acted by God's power and according to the Father's will. Healing and other benefits come through the name of Jesus Christ, never through the names of Simon, Menander or Carpocrates. From this it is clear that when Christ became man he held fellowship with his own creation. It is also clear that he truly did all things through the power of God, according to the will of the Father of all, as the prophets foretold.
sources.quote: did all things truly through the power of God, according to the will of the Father of all, as the prophets had foretold
sources.raw_question: What does the ongoing power of the name of Jesus Christ in the Church's miracles show about Christ's incarnate works and his relation to the Father?

question: If the Son once 'was not,' was the bosom of the Father empty, and what would that imply about the Father's perfection?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: The Arian claim implies an absurdity. Either the bosom was full, in which case the Son filled it and so always existed, or it was empty, in which case the Father would have gained perfection by augmentation, passing from void and deficiency to fulness. Since God cannot be perfected by addition, the Son must always have been in the Father's bosom.
sources.quote: they do nothing else than assert of Him perfection by way of augmentation, in the sense that He passed from the state of void and deficiency to the state of fulness and perfection
sources.raw_question: If the Son once 'was not,' was the bosom of the Father empty, and what would that imply about the Father's perfection?

question: How can God justly punish a substitute when the law binds the sinner himself to punishment?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: God as supreme ruler does not set aside the act of the law but dispenses with its immediate object, substituting another sufferer in place of those principally liable. In this way the law's demand for the punishment of sin is satisfied and justice is exalted, yet the sinner is saved. The substitute was the incarnate Son of God. He had power to dispose of himself, and the dignity of his person made him able to bear the penalty all others deserved.
sources.quote: God, as the supreme ruler, dispenses, not with the act of the law, but the immediate object, and substitutes another sufferer in the room of them who are principally liable unto the sentence of it
sources.raw_question: How can God justly punish a substitute when the law binds the sinner himself to punishment?

question: Does the Son's saying 'I am sent' make Him a ministering servant like the angels?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: No. Angels minister and say 'I am sent unto thee' as servants, and they are commanded to worship the Son. The Son says 'I am sent' in human fashion, but as Word and Image He also says 'I am in the Father, and the Father in Me' and 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father.' What we behold in that Image are the Father's own works.
sources.quote: but the Son, though He say in human fashion, ‘I am sent,’ and comes to finish the work and to minister, nevertheless says, as being Word and Image, ‘I am in the Father, and the Father in Me;’
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's saying 'I am sent' make Him a ministering servant like the angels?

question: Is it meaningful to deny that God is separated from His own essence or that His essence is divided from Him?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next marvellously overthrows the unintelligible statements of Eunomius which assert that the essence of the Father is not separated or divided, and does not become anything else.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that the phrase has no real sense, because nothing can stay in existence once separated from its own essence. Nor can anything's essence be divided off and set apart from it, or a being leave what it is and become something outside itself. So Eunomius's denial is empty sound and says nothing against the Church's doctrine.
sources.quote: For how does any one remain in existence when separated from his own essence? or how is the essence of anything divided and displayed apart?
sources.raw_question: Is it meaningful to deny that God is separated from His own essence or that His essence is divided from Him?

question: Is belief in God as Father essential to Christian faith, as distinct from belief in a supreme God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He next marvellously overthrows the unintelligible statements of Eunomius which assert that the essence of the Father is not separated or divided, and does not become anything else.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory says the Jews and the Hypsistiani acknowledge a Highest or Almighty God but do not admit that He is Father. A Christian, by contrast, must believe in the Father, and so in the Son as well. Whoever does not believe in the Father is no Christian at all.
sources.quote: they acknowledge that there is a God Whom they term the Highest or Almighty, but do not admit that he is Father; while a Christian, if he believe not in the Father, no Christian at all
sources.raw_question: Is belief in God as Father essential to Christian faith, as distinct from belief in a supreme God?

question: Does the Holy Spirit truly exist as part of the Christian confession of faith?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Yes. He exists because he is given, received and retained by believers, and he is joined with Father and Son in the confession of faith. He cannot be excluded from a true confession of Father and Son; to remove him mars the whole faith. The Apostle's words that God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts and that we are sealed in him confirm this.
sources.quote: He does exist, inasmuch as He is given, received, retained; He is joined with Father and Son in our confession of the faith, and cannot be excluded from a true confession of Father and Son
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit truly exist as part of the Christian confession of faith?

question: Does the mutual glorification of Father and Son in John 17 imply any increase or augmentation of the Godhead of either?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. The exchange of glory means only the praise rendered by men for the knowledge of God granted to those who had been ignorant of Him. The Father, from whom are all things, lacked nothing, and the Son, in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwells, was lacking in nothing.
sources.quote: This exchange of glory, given and received, implies no augmentation of the Godhead, but means the praises rendered for the knowledge granted to those who had lived in ignorance of God.
sources.raw_question: Does the mutual glorification of Father and Son in John 17 imply any increase or augmentation of the Godhead of either?

question: Can analogies from created things, such as flame and its radiance or the eye and seeing, illustrate how the Father's will in begetting the Son involves no delay?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He then discusses the “willing” of the Father concerning the generation of the Son, and shows that the object of that good will is from eternity, which is the Son, existing in the Father, and being closely related to the process of willing, as the ray to the flame, or the act of seeing to the eye.
sources.answer: Yes, though imperfectly. No created likeness fully suffices. Still, if a flame had choice, its will that its radiance shine and the radiance itself would be simultaneous with its kindling. Likewise, seeing and the will to see occur without delay. So confessing the Father's will does not separate the Son from the Father.
sources.quote: you will not, by confessing the good act of will as existing in the Father, separate by that act of will the Son from the Father
sources.raw_question: Can analogies from created things, such as flame and its radiance or the eye and seeing, illustrate how the Father's will in begetting the Son involves no delay?

question: Does the analogy of memory, understanding and love in one human person imply that God is only one person?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Augustin Dwells Still Further on the Disparity Between the Trinity Which is in Man, and the Trinity Which is God. The Trinity is Now Seen Through a Glass by the Help of Faith, that It May Hereafter Be More Clearly Seen in the Promised Sight Face to Face.
sources.answer: No. The human image has three things but is one person, whereas in God there are three persons: the Father of the Son, the Son of the Father, and the Spirit of both. The image therefore differs from its exemplar on this point, though it bears some unequal likeness.
sources.quote: Nor, again, as that image in the case of man has these three things but is one person, so is it with the Trinity; but therein are three persons
sources.raw_question: Does the analogy of memory, understanding and love in one human person imply that God is only one person?

question: Does the Valentinian system itself, in which the Mother (Achamoth) used the Demiurge to make images of the Pleroma, imply that the Demiurge is superior to the 'spiritual' Gnostics?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: Yes. By their own account the Mother made all things, visible and invisible, through the Demiurge as her agent. She did nothing through the spiritual seed, which stayed idle and useless. No one forms images of important beings through an inferior agent rather than a superior one. So on their own reasoning the Creator is superior and they are 'wretchedly inferior', like an abortion fit for no work.
sources.quote: for she would by no means form the images of such important beings through means of an inferior, but by a superior, agent.
sources.raw_question: Does the Valentinian system itself, in which the Mother (Achamoth) used the Demiurge to make images of the Pleroma, imply that the Demiurge is superior to the 'spiritual' Gnostics?

question: How does a believer come to know that God the Father loves him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: By believing it as revealed. Though the knowledge of God's love is carried on by spiritual sense and experience, it is received purely by faith; our knowing of it is our believing of what God, who is truth, has declared. To refuse it is to make God a liar.
sources.quote: though it be carried on by spiritual sense and experience, yet it is received purely by believing. Our knowing of it, is our believing of it as revealed.
sources.raw_question: How does a believer come to know that God the Father loves him?

question: Can the doctrine of three Persons in one God be believed if we have only a general and inadequate idea of it, just as with God's eternity and omnipresence?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture gives only general, confused ideas of God's eternity and omnipresence, and we believe them only as far as we apprehend them. The same holds for three Persons each truly God yet one God. Scripture makes this evident and we apprehend it in general as clearly as eternity or omnipresence. The particular modus of the union and distinction remains as secret as how God foresees future contingents.
sources.quote: The same is the case of three Persons, every one truly God, and all but one God ; so far evident: from Scripture, and apprehended, in the general, as fully and clearly (perhaps more so) as eternity, omnipresence, or the like.
sources.raw_question: Can the doctrine of three Persons in one God be believed if we have only a general and inadequate idea of it, just as with God's eternity and omnipresence?

question: Must ordinary Christians settle questions such as whether the divine union is individual or specific, or whether each Person is self-existent, in order to believe the Trinity rightly?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Whoever believes simply and in general, as Scripture lays it down, that the three are divine and yet one God believes enough. Such questions are difficult trifles, mostly verbal or vain. They concern common Christians only so far as they must guard against subtleties invented to perplex a plain Scripture truth.
sources.quote: He that believes this simply, and in the general, as laid down in Scripture, believes enough; and need never trouble his head with nice questions
sources.raw_question: Must ordinary Christians settle questions such as whether the divine union is individual or specific, or whether each Person is self-existent, in order to believe the Trinity rightly?

question: Is the Son in the Father only in the sense in which Scripture says of all creatures, 'In Him we live and move and have our being'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: No. The Son comes from the Fount of the Father and is himself the Life, in which all things are quickened and consist. The Life does not live in another life, otherwise it would not be Life. Rather, he gives life to all things, so his being in the Father differs entirely from that of creatures.
sources.quote: else it would not be Life, but rather He gives life to all things.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son in the Father only in the sense in which Scripture says of all creatures, 'In Him we live and move and have our being'?

question: Should believers accept the Lord's words about the Father and Son simply, rather than requiring elaborate proof?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Seventhly, John xiv. 10. Introduction. The doctrine of the coinherence. The Father and the Son Each whole and perfect God. They are in Each Other, because their Essence is One and the Same. They are Each Perfect and have One Essence, because the Second Person is the Son of the First. Asterius's evasive explanation of the text under review; refuted. Since the Son has all that the Father has, He is His Image; and the Father is the One God, because the Son is in the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. On hearing the Lord's own words it would suffice to believe at once, because simple faith is better than an elaborate process of persuasion. Explanation becomes necessary only because heretics distort the text, and it is given to protect the faithful.
sources.quote: It were sufficient indeed, on hearing only words which are the Lord’s, at once to believe, since the faith of simplicity is better than an elaborate process of persuasion
sources.raw_question: Should believers accept the Lord's words about the Father and Son simply, rather than requiring elaborate proof?

question: Does Eusebius's use of Hebrews 1:3 to call the Father and the Son 'two substances, two things, and two powers' contradict the individual consubstantiality of Father and Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Eusebius wrote against the Sabellians, before the sense of these terms was fixed, and he meant only that the Father is not the Son but really distinct from him. In this he signified no more than the Church means by two Persons. Other Catholic writers, such as Pierius and Alexander of Alexandria, used similar language. Such strong expressions guarded against Sabellianism and were later softened to avoid suggesting separate, independent substances.
sources.quote: there may be nothing in all this, which signifies more than what the Catholic Church has always meant by two persons; and what all must affirm, who believe a real Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Does Eusebius's use of Hebrews 1:3 to call the Father and the Son 'two substances, two things, and two powers' contradict the individual consubstantiality of Father and Son?

question: Can dominion over creatures be what makes God to be God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 24: Whether Gal. iv. 8. may not be enough to determine the dispute betwiat us; since it obliged the Doctor to confess, that Christ as by nature truly God, as truly
sources.answer: No. If dominion made God to be God, one would have to ask what God was before the creatures were made. It would follow that he only became God when he created the universe and began to rule it. On Clarke's principles the Father could also cease to be God by letting all things fall back into nothing, which is absurd.
sources.quote: I need only ask here, what was God before the creatures were made? Or did he then commence Grod, by nature, when he created the universe, and began to have dominion over it?
sources.raw_question: Can dominion over creatures be what makes God to be God?

question: Does Dr. Clarke's own treatment of John 1:1 show that 'God' is not always a word of office?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 24: Whether Gal. iv. 8. may not be enough to determine the dispute betwiat us; since it obliged the Doctor to confess, that Christ as by nature truly God, as truly
sources.answer: Yes. To explain why the Word is called God before the creation, Clarke has to abandon his notion of dominion. He appeals instead to the Son's being in the form of God, to his sharing divine power and glory, or to his partaking of the Father's divinity. This gives Clarke's own authority against his claim that 'God' is always a word of office. He should also have explained in what sense the Father was God before creation.
sources.quote: So that now we have the Doctor’s own authority for contradicting him, if he tells us again, that the word God is always a word of office.
sources.raw_question: Does Dr. Clarke's own treatment of John 1:1 show that 'God' is not always a word of office?

question: When the human mind attaches itself closely to images of bodily things and thinks itself to be such a thing, does it actually become corporeal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
