sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Opinion Which the Mind Has of Itself is Deceitful.
sources.answer: No. The mind is conformed to these images only by thinking it is such a thing, not by actually being it. Its error is that it binds itself so lovingly and intimately to images of bodies that it takes itself to be the very bodily thing whose image it holds, not merely an image. This matters for Augustine's search for an image of the Trinity in the mind, because the mind's true nature must be distinguished from the bodily images it carries.
sources.quote: For so it is conformed to them to some extent, not by being this, but by thinking it is so: not that it thinks itself to be an image, but outright that very thing itself of which it entertains the image.
sources.raw_question: When the human mind attaches itself closely to images of bodily things and thinks itself to be such a thing, does it actually become corporeal?

question: In John 10:18, who is it that lays down His soul and takes it up again, given that God cannot die and a body cannot raise itself?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Neither the Godhead as such nor the body by itself. God cannot die, and the body cannot take its soul up again of itself, because Christ said of the temple of His body, 'I will raise it up.' So it is God who raises the temple of His body. Laying down and taking up the soul belong to the one Christ, who is both God and man.
sources.quote: Thus it is God Who raises up the temple of His body. And Who lays down His soul to take it again? The body does not take it up again of itself: it is raised up by God.
sources.raw_question: In John 10:18, who is it that lays down His soul and takes it up again, given that God cannot die and a body cannot raise itself?

question: Was Moses given the divine nature when God made him 'a god to Pharaoh'?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. He was made a god in Pharaoh's sight through the wonders he wrought, being feared and entreated, chastising and healing. It is one thing to be appointed a god and another to be God; Moses lacked the nature and name in which God consists.
sources.quote: It is one thing to be appointed a god; it is another thing to be God. He was made a god to Pharaoh; he had not that nature and that name wherein God consists.
sources.raw_question: Was Moses given the divine nature when God made him 'a god to Pharaoh'?

question: If God pours out his Spirit on all flesh, can he withhold his glory from the only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He explains the phrase “The Lord created Me,” and the argument about the origination of the Son, the deceptive character of Eunomius' reasoning, and the passage which says, “My glory will I not give to another,” examining them from different points of view.
sources.answer: No. God did not grudge a share in his own Spirit to all flesh, as Joel and Peter testify. Much less, then, would he refuse his glory to the Son who is in the Father's bosom and has all that the Father has.
sources.quote: He then Who did not grudge the partaking in His own Spirit to all flesh,—how can it be that He does not impart His own glory to the only-begotten Son, Who is in the bosom of the Father, Who has all things that the Father has?
sources.raw_question: If God pours out his Spirit on all flesh, can he withhold his glory from the only-begotten Son?

question: Can a person rationally believe a mystery like the generation of the Son of God when his ideas of it are only general and confused?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: Yes. We have real ideas of the Son's generation (equality of nature, reference to a fountain, eternal reference, inseparability), though they are general, confused, and partly figurative. We understand enough to make it properly an article of belief, so no one can reject it as meaningless. Our faith keeps pace with our ideas, believing in part what is revealed in part.
sources.quote: Nevertheless we understand enough (though we can imagine little) to make it properly an article of belief; and no man can reasonably pretend to reject it, as having no meaning, or carrying no idea at all with it.
sources.raw_question: Can a person rationally believe a mystery like the generation of the Son of God when his ideas of it are only general and confused?

question: Does the Lord Jesus acknowledge any God other than the one Father and Creator proclaimed by the law and the prophets?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XI.—The heretics, from their disbelief of the truth, have fallen into an abyss of error: reasons for investigating their systems.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus says the Lord's own words show that he acknowledges one Father, the Creator of the world and Fashioner of man, who was proclaimed by the law and the prophets. He knows no other God, and this One is truly God over all. This rules out the Gnostic claim that a higher unknown God stands above the Creator.
sources.quote: He acknowledges one Father and Creator of the world, and Fashioner of man, who was proclaimed by the law and the prophets, while He knows no other, and that this One is really God over all
sources.raw_question: Does the Lord Jesus acknowledge any God other than the one Father and Creator proclaimed by the law and the prophets?

question: How is the doctrine of the Trinity related to the Christian's experience of salvation?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: The Trinity is rooted in the threefold divine causality of salvation and is echoed in every redeemed consciousness. Though the believer could not construct the doctrine from his experience alone, the elements of that experience are interpreted and ordered only by the Trinity: Fatherly love sending a Redeemer, redeeming love executing redemption, saving love applying it. Without the doctrine the Christian life would be thrown into confusion and given an air of unreality.
sources.quote: If he could not construct the doctrine of the Trinity out of his consciousness of salvation, yet the elements of his consciousness of salvation are interpreted to him and reduced to order only by the doctrine of the Trinity
sources.raw_question: How is the doctrine of the Trinity related to the Christian's experience of salvation?

question: What principles determined and guided the church's formulation of the doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Two principles: the church's profound conviction of the absolute Deity of Christ, which was the determining impulse, and the Baptismal Formula of Matthew 28:19, which supplied the guiding ground-plan for baptismal confessions and rules of faith. Every attempt to formulate the doctrine of God was tested by these two, until a statement was reached doing justice to the New Testament revelation and Christian experience.
sources.quote: It was by these two fundamental principia — the true Deity of Christ and the Baptismal Formula — that all attempts to formulate the Christian doctrine of God were tested
sources.raw_question: What principles determined and guided the church's formulation of the doctrine of the Trinity?

question: If Christ paid our debt to God with what was his own, is the debt merely transferred, so that sinners now owe the Son what they once owed the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Christ paid his own, but not for himself. When one is accepted in the place of another and his payment is accepted, all law and reason require that the original debtor be discharged. What we now owe the Son is not that debt but praise, thankfulness and obedience. Our actual discharge comes on the terms appointed by the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: When a debt is so transferred as that one is accepted in the room and obliged to payment in the stead of another, and that payment is made and accepted accordingly, all law and reason require that the original debtor be discharged.
sources.raw_question: If Christ paid our debt to God with what was his own, is the debt merely transferred, so that sinners now owe the Son what they once owed the Father?

question: How has the Father revealed himself to all people?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VI.—Explanation of the words of Christ, “No man knoweth the Father, but the Son,” etc.; which words the heretics misinterpret. Proof that, by the Father revealing the Son, and by the Son being revealed, the Father was never unknown.
sources.answer: By making his Word visible to all. The Father revealed the Son so that through him he might be manifested to all, and the Word, having become visible, declared both the Father and the Son to all; hence God's righteous judgment falls on those who saw but did not believe.
sources.quote: The Father therefore has revealed Himself to all, by making His Word visible to all; and, conversely, the Word has declared to all the Father and the Son, since He has become visible to all.
sources.raw_question: How has the Father revealed himself to all people?

question: In Ephesians 2:10, is 'God' meant personally as the Father, as distinct from Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen reads the text as speaking of the Father personally. Christ is mentioned there in his role as mediator, so the God who prepared good works for us is the Father.
sources.quote: The Father is spoken of personally, Christ being mentioned as mediator.
sources.raw_question: In Ephesians 2:10, is 'God' meant personally as the Father, as distinct from Christ?

question: If dominion and authority are what make God to be God, as Dr. Clarke holds, does it follow that three Persons each having such dominion are three Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: Yes, on Clarke's principles. If the word God signifies personal dominion, and each of the three Persons has that dominion which suffices to make a Person truly God, then three divine Persons are exactly three Gods. Clarke must therefore either profess three Gods or deny that the Son and Holy Ghost are God.
sources.quote: Because three divine Beings, or Persons, is exactly the same, in other words, with three Gods, upon his principles; and because every one of the three is supposed to have personal dominion
sources.raw_question: If dominion and authority are what make God to be God, as Dr. Clarke holds, does it follow that three Persons each having such dominion are three Gods?

question: Does Athanasius understand the title 'first-born of every creature' as a figurative birth or going-forth of the Son from the Father at the creation of the world?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: No. Athanasius says Scripture nowhere calls the Son 'first-born of God'; it calls him Only-begotten, Word and Wisdom, and these names express his relation to the Father. 'First-born' refers only to creatures. It names his condescension at creation, by which he became the Prototype of all creation. It does not name any generation of the Son, even a figurative one.
sources.quote: Nowhere in the Scriptures,’ he says, ‘is He called πρωτότοκος τοῦ Θεοῦ, first-born of God, nor creature of God, but Only-begotten, Word, Wisdom, have their relation to the Father, and are proper to Him.
sources.raw_question: Does Athanasius understand the title 'first-born of every creature' as a figurative birth or going-forth of the Son from the Father at the creation of the world?

question: Why was it fitting that God become a righteous man in order to intercede with God for sinners?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > How We are Rendered Apt for the Perception of Truth Through the Incarnate Word.
sources.answer: Because the sinner is not congruous to the righteous, but man is congruous to man. By joining to us the likeness of His humanity, Christ took away the unlikeness of our unrighteousness. By sharing our mortality He made us partakers of His divinity.
sources.quote: Wherefore God, made a righteous man, interceded with God for man the sinner. For the sinner is not congruous to the righteous, but man is congruous to man.
sources.raw_question: Why was it fitting that God become a righteous man in order to intercede with God for sinners?

question: Does the plurality of individuals sharing one nature, such as Peter, James, and John, multiply that nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. Gold cut into many staters remains one gold; the number applies to the coins, not to the material. In the same way Peter, James, and John are many, yet the man in them is one. Speaking of 'many men' is a loose custom of speech.
sources.quote: As, then, the golden staters are many, but the gold is one, so too those who are exhibited to us severally in the nature of man, as Peter, James, and John, are many, yet the man in them is one.
sources.raw_question: Does the plurality of individuals sharing one nature, such as Peter, James, and John, multiply that nature?

question: What does Paul mean in 1 Corinthians 15 when he says the body is 'sown an animal body' and 'raised a spiritual body'?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VII.—Inasmuch as Christ did rise in our flesh, it follows that we shall be also raised in the same; since the resurrection promised to us should not be referred to spirits naturally immortal, but to bodies in themselves mortal.
sources.answer: He means that dead bodies, which once shared in life and then lost it, are raised through the Holy Spirit's agency and become spiritual bodies. They are spiritual because by the Spirit they have perpetual life, not because they cease to be bodies. The language applies to corpses, not to the soul or the spirit.
sources.quote: then, rising through the Spirit’s instrumentality, they become spiritual bodies, so that by the Spirit they possess a perpetual life
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean in 1 Corinthians 15 when he says the body is 'sown an animal body' and 'raised a spiritual body'?

question: Does 1 Peter 1:2 present the sanctifying Spirit as distinct from the Father and from Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The saints are elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through the sanctification of the Spirit, unto the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ. Just as the bleeding Saviour is distinct from the predestinating Father, the sanctifying Spirit is himself distinct.
sources.quote: as the bleeding Saviour is distinct from the predestinating Father, so the sanctifying Spirit is himself distinct.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Peter 1:2 present the sanctifying Spirit as distinct from the Father and from Christ?

question: Does our ignorance of the substance of created things count as a loss, and does Scripture concern itself with such inquiries into substance?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. We know created things through the senses only so far as we need them for living. Ignorance of their substance is no loss: one who uses fire fares no worse than one who studies its nature. So Scripture omits idle inquiry into substance as superfluous.
sources.quote: Wherefore Holy Scripture omits all idle inquiry into substance as superfluous and unnecessary.
sources.raw_question: Does our ignorance of the substance of created things count as a loss, and does Scripture concern itself with such inquiries into substance?

question: Does "the love of the Father" in 1 John 2:15 mean the Father's love for us or our love for the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Our love for the Father. The Father is set as the object of our love in opposition to the world, which competes for our affections; "the Father" denotes the object, not the efficient cause, of the love in question. This love of him as Father is what Malachi calls his honour.
sources.quote: The Father denotes the matter and object, not the efficient cause, of the love inquired after.
sources.raw_question: Does "the love of the Father" in 1 John 2:15 mean the Father's love for us or our love for the Father?

question: Does the early Fathers' description of the Word as conversing and taking counsel with the Father before creation show that the Word was a distinct Person?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. The Fathers describe the Logos as always with God, conversing with him and assisting in council. Such language would be improper of a mere attribute, since one cannot properly be said to consult with one's own attribute; it must denote distinct personality.
sources.quote: It would be very improper to say that God was ¢7m, or with one of his attributes, or consulted with it: all such expressions must denote a distinct personality.
sources.raw_question: Does the early Fathers' description of the Word as conversing and taking counsel with the Father before creation show that the Word was a distinct Person?

question: Does Tertullian's distinction between 'ratio' (eternal reason) and 'sermo' (the Word as person) mean the Son was not eternally a Person?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Tertullian connects both in one, treating them as the selfsame hypostasis under different capacities and names before and after the procession: eternal as ratio, afterwards sermo and Son. The distinction is one of capacity, not of a different subject coming into being.
sources.quote: It was one and the same hypostasis; once ratio, (according to this writer,) and as such, eternal; afterwards sermo, and as such, !@ Son.
sources.raw_question: Does Tertullian's distinction between 'ratio' (eternal reason) and 'sermo' (the Word as person) mean the Son was not eternally a Person?

question: When the Holy Spirit appeared as a dove or as fire, was the Spirit himself changed into those forms?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Creature is Not So Taken by the Holy Spirit as Flesh is by the Word.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit's nature is not mutable, so he was not turned into one form and then another, as water is changed into ice. The creature was changed at the command of the Creator, who remains immutable in himself. It served to signify and manifest him in a way fit for mortal men.
sources.quote: Nor, again, is the nature of the Holy Spirit mutable and changeable; so that these things were not made of the creature, but He himself was turned and changed first into one and then into another, as water is changed into ice.
sources.raw_question: When the Holy Spirit appeared as a dove or as fire, was the Spirit himself changed into those forms?

question: If Christ can be called the Lamb or the Rock, why can the Holy Spirit not likewise be called a dove or fire?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Creature is Not So Taken by the Holy Spirit as Flesh is by the Word.
sources.answer: Because the cases differ. The Lamb was seen in a prophetic vision through spiritual images, not by bodily eyes. The rock, Jacob's stone and Isaac were already-existing things that were later given a signifying role. The dove and fire, by contrast, came into being suddenly simply in order to signify, like the burning bush and the pillar in the wilderness.
sources.quote: A particular significative action was added to those already existing things; they did not, as that dove and fire, suddenly come into being in order simply so to signify.
sources.raw_question: If Christ can be called the Lamb or the Rock, why can the Holy Spirit not likewise be called a dove or fire?

question: Does unwritten apostolic tradition carry the same authority in matters of faith and worship as written Scripture?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Of the origin of the word “with,” and what force it has. Also concerning the unwritten laws of the church.
sources.answer: Yes. Basil teaches that some of the Church's beliefs and practices come from written teaching and others were handed down "in a mystery" by apostolic tradition, and both have the same force for true religion. To reject unwritten customs would wound the Gospel in its vitals. Practices such as the sign of the cross, triple immersion, the words of the eucharistic invocation, and the renunciation of Satan have no written source yet are universally received.
sources.quote: others we have received delivered to us “in a mystery” by the tradition of the apostles; and both of these in relation to true religion have the same force.
sources.raw_question: Does unwritten apostolic tradition carry the same authority in matters of faith and worship as written Scripture?

question: Is the God whom the apostles preached the same God who appeared to Abraham and spoke with Moses?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. In his speech Stephen announces the God of glory who appeared to Abraham, promised him the land, and gave him the covenant of circumcision. He is the God who was with Joseph and the patriarchs and spoke with Moses. The apostolic preaching is therefore continuous with the God of the Old Testament.
sources.quote: And the rest of his words announce the same God, who was with Joseph and with the patriarchs, and who spake with Moses.
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who separate the Old Testament God from the God of the apostles
sources.raw_question: Is the God whom the apostles preached the same God who appeared to Abraham and spoke with Moses?

question: How does Scripture's unqualified 'they are one' differ from qualified expressions like 'one body' or 'one spirit'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > That the Unity of the Essence of the Father and the Son is to Be Gathered from the Words, ‘We are One.’ The Son is Equal to the Father Both in Wisdom and in All Other Things.
sources.answer: Qualified expressions can describe a unity formed from things different in nature. 'He who is joined to a harlot is one body' and 'he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit' add a qualifier because two different things are joined into one. The human spirit and God's Spirit differ in nature, and God's Spirit is blessed without man's, but man's cannot be blessed without God. Unqualified 'one' signifies sameness of nature.
sources.quote: For the spirit of man and the Spirit of God are different in nature; but by being joined they become one spirit of two different spirits
sources.raw_question: How does Scripture's unqualified 'they are one' differ from qualified expressions like 'one body' or 'one spirit'?

question: Is Christ Jesus, the Son of God, rightly confessed as God and as the one to whom all creation bows?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter X.—Unity of the faith of the Church throughout the whole world.
sources.answer: Yes. The apostolic faith confesses Christ Jesus as Lord, God, Saviour and King. According to the will of the invisible Father, every knee in heaven, on earth and under the earth is to bow to him and every tongue confess him.
sources.quote: to Christ Jesus, our Lord, and God, and Saviour, and King, according to the will of the invisible Father, “every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth
sources.raw_question: Is Christ Jesus, the Son of God, rightly confessed as God and as the one to whom all creation bows?

question: Who is able to behold and know the Holy Spirit, and on what condition?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Establishment of the natural communion of the Spirit from His being, equally with the Father and the Son, unapproachable in thought.
sources.answer: Only the saints, through purity of heart. Christ, who taught purity of life, gave His disciples the power to behold and contemplate the Spirit, because they were made clean through His word. Isaiah also says the Spirit is given to those who trample down earthly things and rise above them.
sources.quote: the Lord, who by His teaching bore witness to purity of life, gives to His disciples the power of now both beholding and contemplating the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Who is able to behold and know the Holy Spirit, and on what condition?

question: Does the Son's interceding with the Father as Mediator show that he is inferior to the Father in Godhead?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In What Manner Christ Wills that All Shall Be One in Himself.
sources.answer: No. The Son intercedes with the Father in that he is man, having taken humanity upon himself. Yet he remains equal to the Father through the unity of the Godhead. Even while praying he did not conceal that he was God, one with the Father.
sources.quote: equal to the Father through the unity of the Godhead, and partaker with us by the taking upon Him of humanity, interceding for us with the Father in that He was man,
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's interceding with the Father as Mediator show that he is inferior to the Father in Godhead?

question: Can Scripture's account of God speaking with Adam in Paradise determine whether the Father, or only the Son and Holy Spirit, can appear to human eyes through a visible creature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: No. Augustine judges that this question is not discoverable from that testimony of Scripture. It is not even evident that Adam habitually saw God with his bodily eyes, and the text leaves open what kind of eyes were opened when he and Eve ate the forbidden fruit.
sources.quote: the thing itself, so far as concerns this testimony of Scripture, where God spake with man, is, in my judgment, not discoverable, because it does not evidently appear even whether Adam usually saw God with the eyes of his body
sources.raw_question: Can Scripture's account of God speaking with Adam in Paradise determine whether the Father, or only the Son and Holy Spirit, can appear to human eyes through a visible creature?

question: Must the heavenly voices saying "This is my beloved Son" and "I have both glorified, and will glorify again" be understood as the Father's alone, rather than the Holy Spirit's or the Trinity's?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: Yes. Jesus cannot be believed or understood to be the Son of the Holy Spirit, or his own Son, so "This is my beloved Son" can be said only by the Father. The voice saying "I have both glorified" answers Christ's prayer "Father, glorify thy Son." That prayer could be addressed only to the Father, not to the Holy Spirit, whose Son he was not.
sources.quote: For Jesus can neither be believed nor understood to be the Son of the Holy Spirit, or even His own Son.
sources.raw_question: Must the heavenly voices saying "This is my beloved Son" and "I have both glorified, and will glorify again" be understood as the Father's alone, rather than the Holy Spirit's or the Trinity's?

question: In "And the Lord God said to Adam," should the speaker be understood as a single person of the Trinity or as the Trinity itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: Nothing forbids taking it as the Trinity itself. Unlike the baptismal and transfiguration voices, nothing in this text restricts the speaker to one person, so no reason can be given why the Trinity should not be understood. If only words and sounds were produced, the passage might also be read as manifesting the Father, as with the voices from heaven in the Gospels.
sources.quote: But here, where it is written, “And the Lord God said to Adam,” no reason can be given why the Trinity itself should not be understood.
sources.raw_question: In "And the Lord God said to Adam," should the speaker be understood as a single person of the Trinity or as the Trinity itself?

question: Does Paul's phrase "the spirit of your mind" (Ephesians 4:23) refer to two distinct things, the mind and a spirit belonging to it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How the Image of God is Formed Anew in Man.
sources.answer: No. All mind is spirit, but not all spirit is mind, so Paul uses "the spirit of the mind" to name the kind of spirit that is mind. The phrase works like "the body of the flesh," which names the body that is flesh, since many bodies have no flesh.
sources.quote: he does not intend to be understood of two things, as though mind were one, and the spirit of the mind another; but he speaks thus, because all mind is spirit, but all spirit is not mind.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's phrase "the spirit of your mind" (Ephesians 4:23) refer to two distinct things, the mind and a spirit belonging to it?

question: Can the Spirit that is God be renewed, as the human mind is renewed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How the Image of God is Formed Anew in Man.
sources.answer: No. God is Spirit, but that Spirit cannot be renewed, because it cannot grow old. Only created spirit, such as the human mind, undergoes renewal.
sources.quote: For there is a Spirit also that is God, which cannot be renewed, because it cannot grow old.
sources.raw_question: Can the Spirit that is God be renewed, as the human mind is renewed?

question: Can fallen human beings, by their own power, cease from sinning against God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. In the fallen state all people continue in sin against God and cannot of themselves do otherwise. Scripture declares that there is none righteous, none that seeks God, and none that does good.
sources.quote: That in this state all men continue in sin against God, nor of themselves can do otherwise
sources.raw_question: Can fallen human beings, by their own power, cease from sinning against God?

question: How can the Son both give grace from the Father and himself be said to receive that same grace?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: He gives as the Word and receives as the Son of Man. Everything the Father gives, He gives through the Son, so as Word the Son bestows grace and exaltation. Yet because the Son of God became Son of Man, He is said, after the manner of men, to receive these gifts. This is because His body is truly His own and is a natural recipient of grace.
sources.quote: as Word, He gives from the Father, for all things which the Father does and gives, He does and supplies through Him; and as the Son of Man, He Himself is said after the manner of men to receive what proceeds from Him
sources.raw_question: How can the Son both give grace from the Father and himself be said to receive that same grace?

question: In what sense is the correlation of 'thing made' with 'maker' and 'creature' with 'creator' legitimate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > This third book shows a third fall of Eunomius, as refuting himself, and sometimes saying that the Son is to be called Only-begotten in virtue of natural generation, and that Holy Scripture proves this from the first; at other times, that by reason of His being created He should not be called a Son, but a “product,” or “creature.”
sources.answer: It is legitimate when applied to the actual creation, visible and invisible, which was made by the Lord. Thus angels are things made by Him and the world is His creature. But applying this correlation to the Only-begotten as made by the Father is illegitimate, and as mere grammar about relative terms it is a triviality.
sources.quote: since the Lord is the Maker of angels, the angel is assuredly a thing made by Him that made him: and since the Lord is the Creator of the world, clearly the world itself and all that is therein are called the creature of Him that created them.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the correlation of 'thing made' with 'maker' and 'creature' with 'creator' legitimate?

question: Is there any medium or interval separating the Father from the Son through which communication could pass?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Voice needs a medium such as air, and any medium would have to be either created or uncreate. It cannot be created, since the Word existed before creation, and nothing besides the Divine nature is uncreate. So there is no medium between Father and Son; they are inseparably united through identity of will.
sources.quote: Truth, therefore, obliges us to the conclusion that there is no medium between the Father and the Son. But where separation is not conceived of the closest connection is naturally implied.
sources.raw_question: Is there any medium or interval separating the Father from the Son through which communication could pass?

question: Did Christ undergo birth, suffering and death by necessity of human nature, or by his own divine power and will?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: By his own will and power, yet truly as man. He passed through all the circumstances of our nature but bore them by the power of his own divine nature: he was the cause of his own birth, willed to suffer what he could not suffer, and died though he lives for ever. Yet he also did these things as man, for he was really born, suffered and died.
sources.quote: He was Himself the cause of His birth, He willed to suffer what He could not suffer, He died though He lives for ever. Yet God did all this not merely through man, for He was born of Himself, He suffered of His own free will, and died of Himself.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ undergo birth, suffering and death by necessity of human nature, or by his own divine power and will?

question: Is the oneness of believers "in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28) a unity of will or a unity that comes from the sacrament of baptism?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: It comes from the sacrament. Hilary argues that people of different races, conditions and sexes are one because they have one baptism and have all put on one Christ. Agreement of minds adds nothing to explain a unity that is grounded in the nature of one baptism.
sources.quote: What, therefore, will a concord of minds avail here when they are one in that they have put on one Christ through the nature of one baptism?
sources.raw_question: Is the oneness of believers "in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28) a unity of will or a unity that comes from the sacrament of baptism?

question: Is man created after one image shared by the Father and the Son, or after two distinct images?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: After one image. Man is made in the common image of Father and Son, who are One in name and One in nature. Hence the image cannot be split into true and false parts, for the Two are One, and man is the one copy of Their one image.
sources.quote: The Two are One in name and One in nature. It is only one image after which man is made.
sources.raw_question: Is man created after one image shared by the Father and the Son, or after two distinct images?

question: Does Hebrews 9:13-14 teach that the Holy Spirit is eternal?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: Yes. The Apostle says that Christ offered Himself without spot to God "through the eternal Spirit." Therefore the Spirit is eternal.
sources.quote: how much more the blood of Christ, Who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself without spot to God?”[^914] Therefore the Spirit is eternal.
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 9:13-14 teach that the Holy Spirit is eternal?

question: Does the Old Testament's teaching on the unity of God prove that the true God is a single Person, so that the Son has no true birth from Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. The heretics claim the Law proves that the true God is of one Person, and they use this to deny Christ's birth. Hilary answers from the Law and the Prophets that there are not two gods, nor one isolated true God. This keeps faith in the divine unity intact without denying the birth of Christ, which is the evidence of His origin.
sources.quote: from the Law and the Prophets I demonstrate that there are not two gods, nor one isolated true God, neither perverting the faith in the Divine unity nor denying the birth of Christ
sources.raw_question: Does the Old Testament's teaching on the unity of God prove that the true God is a single Person, so that the Son has no true birth from Him?

question: Can the Arians lower the Holy Spirit from His fellowship with the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXII. In proof of the Unity in Trinity the passage of Isaiah which has been cited is considered, and it is shown that there is no difference as to its sense amongst those who expound it of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Spirit. If He Who was crucified was Lord of glory, so, too, is the Holy Spirit equal in all things to the Father and the Son, and the Arians will never be able to diminish His glory.
sources.answer: No. The strength of the heavens comes from the Spirit, so dragging Him down would overturn them. To drag Him down one would first have to lay hands on God, because the Spirit is God, who searches the deep things of God.
sources.quote: If thou choose to drag Him down, thou must first lay hands on God, for the Spirit is God. But how wilt thou drag Him down, Who searcheth the deep things of God?
sources.raw_question: Can the Arians lower the Holy Spirit from His fellowship with the Father and the Son?

question: Does saying the Son was eternally obedient 'in words' imply that other words stand prior to Him who is the Word?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: Yes, and this shows the doctrine is absurd. To make the Word obedient to words is to place other words before Him who is truly the Word. These words would act as intermediaries between the Beginning and the Word that was in the Beginning, conveying commands to Him. This makes a chain of mediating words between the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: Thou makest the Word obedient to words, and supposest other words prior to Him Who is truly the Word, and another Word of the Beginning is mediator between the Beginning and the Word that was in the Beginning
sources.raw_question: Does saying the Son was eternally obedient 'in words' imply that other words stand prior to Him who is the Word?

question: Did the Word become incarnate in order to gain things he lacked before, so that he was promoted because of the body?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: No. On that view the Word would owe thanks to the body and be promoted by it rather than the body by Him, which Athanasius calls a Judaic notion. He came to redeem and deify mankind, so the gifts He mentions pertained to the flesh in which He spoke.
sources.quote: For on this shewing He seems rather to be Himself promoted because of the body, than the body promoted because of Him. But this notion is Judaic.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word become incarnate in order to gain things he lacked before, so that he was promoted because of the body?

question: Are all the attributes ascribed to God (justice, wisdom, power, goodness, incorruptibility) synonymous terms with a single meaning because God is simple?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. If every divine name meant the same thing, Scripture would be pointless in giving God many titles such as Judge, righteous, powerful, long-suffering, true and merciful. Each title has its own peculiar sense, while all of them refer to one simple subject. Making them all convertible would destroy the meaning of words.
sources.quote: why do the Scriptures vainly assign various names to the Divine nature, calling God a Judge, righteous, powerful, long-suffering, true, merciful and so on?
sources.raw_question: Are all the attributes ascribed to God (justice, wisdom, power, goodness, incorruptibility) synonymous terms with a single meaning because God is simple?

question: Do distinct divine attributes, such as 'incorporeal' and 'just', conflict with one another or divide God's unity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. These terms are not opposites like life and death, which cannot exist in the same subject. Each has its own significance yet implies no opposition to the others. They can therefore all be truly said of the one simple God without dividing Him.
sources.quote: What opposition, for instance, is there between “incorporeal” and “just,” even though the words do not coincide in meaning: and what hostility is there between goodness and invisibility?
sources.raw_question: Do distinct divine attributes, such as 'incorporeal' and 'just', conflict with one another or divide God's unity?

question: Should Scripture be read only according to its literal sense, or does a spiritual meaning lie beneath the letter?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: A spiritual meaning lies beneath the letter. The divine intention is hidden under the body of Scripture as under a veil, and a merely literal reading can become a "doctrine of death." Those who turn to what the mind contemplates find the glory beneath the letter, which Paul calls "the Lord, which is the Spirit."
sources.quote: the Divine intention lies hid under the body of the Scripture, as it were under a veil, some legislative enactment or some historical narrative being cast over the truths that are contemplated by the mind
sources.raw_question: Should Scripture be read only according to its literal sense, or does a spiritual meaning lie beneath the letter?

question: Does affirming that the Word coexists eternally with the Father imply that there are two Unoriginates?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: The Arians cannot press this charge without condemning themselves. Asterius himself speaks of God's 'Unoriginate Wisdom' coexisting with him. So the Arians incur the very charge they rashly bring against the orthodox. By their own confession, that coexisting Wisdom must be the Son.
sources.quote: when they hear us say that the Word coexists with the Father, forthwith murmur out, ‘Are you not speaking of two Unoriginates?’ yet in speaking themselves of ‘His Unoriginate Wisdom,’ do not see that they have already incurred themselves the charge
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that the Word coexists eternally with the Father imply that there are two Unoriginates?

question: When Christ says 'God is a Spirit', does the term 'Spirit' fully express the substance of God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, that When God is Called a Spirit, Brightness, and Light, God is Not Sufficiently Expressed by Those Appellations.
sources.answer: No. Christ spoke of God in a way his hearers could receive, intending that something more be understood than merely that God is a Spirit. Just as God is called Love and Light without those names declaring his substance, so calling him Spirit does not state all that he is; it leads the mind upward to conjecture that God is something even greater.
sources.quote: so that reasonably also, when He is called a Spirit, it is not all that He is which is so called
sources.raw_question: When Christ says 'God is a Spirit', does the term 'Spirit' fully express the substance of God?

question: If 'spirit' were taken as the very substance of God, would that make God a creature?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, that When God is Called a Spirit, Brightness, and Light, God is Not Sufficiently Expressed by Those Appellations.
sources.answer: Yes. Every spirit is a creature, so to identify God's substance as spirit would make God something made. Likewise, taking God literally to be fire would describe something ordained rather than its ordainer.
sources.quote: Finally, if you receive the Spirit as the substance of God, you will make God a creature. For every spirit is a creature. And therefore, then, God will be made.
sources.raw_question: If 'spirit' were taken as the very substance of God, would that make God a creature?

question: When Scripture says Christ hungered, thirsted, did not know, feared, and suffered, does this mean the Word of God suffers or is passible in his divine nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: No. Following 1 Peter 4:1, all such affections are to be understood as undergone 'for us in the flesh,' not in his Godhead. They are proper by nature to the flesh, not to the Word, who is impassible by nature; yet they are ascribed to him because the body in which they occur is his own.
sources.quote: For on this account has the Apostle himself said, ‘Christ then having suffered,’ not in His Godhead, but ‘for us in the flesh,’ that these affections may be acknowledged as, not proper to the very Word by nature, but proper by nature to the very flesh.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture says Christ hungered, thirsted, did not know, feared, and suffered, does this mean the Word of God suffers or is passible in his divine nature?

question: Do the human weaknesses of the Saviour prove that the Son is a creature, as the Arians argue?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: No. The Arians look only at what is human in the Saviour and conclude that he is a creature, which is a low view of the Word drawn from what belongs to the flesh. By the same faulty reasoning, looking only at his divine works, they would have to deny that his body was originated and side with the Manichees. Rightly understood, 'the Word became flesh,' and these texts have a correct interpretation within the scope of the faith.
sources.quote: This then is what happens to God’s enemies the Arians; for looking at what is human in the Saviour, they have judged Him a creature.
sources.raw_question: Do the human weaknesses of the Saviour prove that the Son is a creature, as the Arians argue?

question: How does Scripture lead us to the doctrine of the Trinity in Unity, given that God reveals himself by his names, attributes, and acts?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: God is known by his names, attributes, and acts, and Scripture, while asserting that God is one, ascribes the same names, attributes, and acts to Three, as far as personal distinction allows. No fourth divine one is ever intimated, an intimate union is affirmed between Father, Son, and Spirit, and Christians are baptized into the one Name of all three. Together these lead swiftly and irresistibly to the Trinity in Unity.
sources.quote: if combined with assertions that God is one, we find Three revealed in Scripture to whom the same names, attributes, and acts are ascribed, the same so far as a personal distinction allows; if we look vainly for any fourth Divine one
sources.raw_question: How does Scripture lead us to the doctrine of the Trinity in Unity, given that God reveals himself by his names, attributes, and acts?

question: What does it mean to say the Father and the Son are 'connected' if God is spiritual and not bodily?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: It means they are in all respects inseparable, not corporeally joined. In a spiritual nature connection is the union and blending of spirit with spirit through identity of will, so there is no divergence of will between Father and Son.
sources.quote: For in the case of a spiritual nature the term connection does not mean corporeal connection, but the union and blending of spiritual with spiritual through identity of will.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean to say the Father and the Son are 'connected' if God is spiritual and not bodily?

question: Does Christ's 'emptying himself' (Philippians 2:7) in being born prove that he is not a mere man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is in Christ, He Once More Asserts by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. A mere man is increased and enriched by being born, not emptied, since he comes to be what he was not before. Christ's emptying makes sense only if the divine Word, already existing, took on humanity and held back its real strength. In this way it humbled itself to bear injuries, reproaches and things unworthy of it.
sources.quote: But if Christ is emptied in being born, in taking the form of a servant, how is He man only? Of whom it could more truly have been said that He was enriched, not emptied, at the time that He was born
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's 'emptying himself' (Philippians 2:7) in being born prove that he is not a mere man?

question: Does Christ's obedience to the Father even unto death prove that he is only a man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is in Christ, He Once More Asserts by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. His obedience to the Father does not make him man only. The higher features of the same passage proclaim his divinity: being in the form of God, emptying himself, receiving the name above every name, and universal worship. So Christ is shown to be both Lord and God.
sources.quote: consequently He is not man only, from the fact that He became obedient to the Father, even to death, yea, the death of the cross; but, moreover, from the proclamation by these higher matters of the divinity of Christ
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who hold Christ is man only
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's obedience to the Father even unto death prove that he is only a man?

question: Is the appearance of God in human form to the Patriarchs (e.g. to Abraham) inconsistent with His having a true divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. These merciful self-revelations are in no way inconsistent with His true heavenly nature; He assumed a semblance of manhood to foreshadow His future birth as Man. God remained unchanged whether seen in the appearance or born in the reality of manhood, and the saints saw through the guise by faith.
sources.quote: His merciful and mysterious self-revelations are in no wise inconsistent with His true heavenly nature; and His faithful saints never fail to penetrate the guise He has assumed in order that faith may see Him.
sources.raw_question: Is the appearance of God in human form to the Patriarchs (e.g. to Abraham) inconsistent with His having a true divine nature?

question: Do Christ's birth, growth, suffering, and death on the Cross show that He is not truly God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. He took these capacities upon Himself as additions to His nature, which He had not possessed in His divine nature, and so acquired them without loss of His true Divinity. He ceased not to be God when He became Man; rather, becoming what He was not while remaining what He was is itself an exercise of the omnipotence proper to true God.
sources.quote: Thus He acquired them without loss of His true Divinity, and ceased not to be God when He became Man; when He, Who is God eternally, became Man at a point in time.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's birth, growth, suffering, and death on the Cross show that He is not truly God?

question: Did the Son undergo the Passion because of a weakness in His nature, implying He is inferior in essence to the impassible Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: No. The Son entered upon the dispensation of the Passion by the power of His will, not by weakness of nature, as countless Gospel passages show. What took place was not really 'passion' but love of men, and the saving of the lost is good. So it cannot be used to separate the Son from the Father, who also saved men from death by His own Power, which is Christ.
sources.quote: That He entered upon the dispensation of the Passion not by weakness of nature but by the power of His will, one might bring countless passages of the Gospel to show
sources.raw_question: Did the Son undergo the Passion because of a weakness in His nature, implying He is inferior in essence to the impassible Father?

question: Do the Old Testament prophecies of the Messiah give him divine names such as 'the mighty God' and 'Jehovah'?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen cites two prophecies. Isaiah 9:6 names the child born to us 'The mighty God, The everlasting Father'. Jeremiah 23:5-6 calls the righteous Branch raised up to David 'Jehovah our Righteousness'. The promised Messiah therefore bears the incommunicable names of God.
sources.quote: and this is his name whereby he shall be called, Jehovah our Righteousness.”
sources.raw_question: Do the Old Testament prophecies of the Messiah give him divine names such as 'the mighty God' and 'Jehovah'?

question: Is a single Person of the Trinity, considered as a Person, the prime object of divine worship?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No. A Person is worshipped as identified with the nature or essence of God, not as a Person considered by itself. This is why communion with one Person carries communion with the others by consequence.
sources.quote: for the person, as the person, of any one of them, is not the prime object of divine worship, but as it is identified with the nature or essence of God
sources.raw_question: Is a single Person of the Trinity, considered as a Person, the prime object of divine worship?

question: Is it consistent to plead ignorance about how creatures come into existence while confidently asserting that the Son's generation was temporal?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 13: Whether there can be any middle between being made out of nothing, and out of something ; that is, between being out of nothing, and out of the Father's substan
sources.answer: No. Waterland charges that the objector claims ignorance where knowledge is easy, yet positively affirms the Son's generation to be temporal and denies he existed before it, matters far less within our knowledge. Such inconsistency carries its own confutation.
sources.quote: presuming to make the generation of the Son of God temporal; and determining it ἰὼ contradiction to predicate existence of him before his generation. Such things as these carry their own confutation with them
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to plead ignorance about how creatures come into existence while confidently asserting that the Son's generation was temporal?

question: Does Christ's praying to the Father, as at the raising of Lazarus, prove that the Son needed help from the Father and is inferior?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Christ himself said he knew the Father always heard him and prayed because of the multitude, so that they might believe the Father sent him. The prayer availed him nothing; he was not in want of help, but we were in want of teaching.
sources.quote: He prayed then for us, that we may know Him to be the Son; the words of prayer availed Him nothing, but He said them for the advancement of our faith. He was not in want of help, but we of teaching.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's praying to the Father, as at the raising of Lazarus, prove that the Son needed help from the Father and is inferior?

question: What are the distinct roles of the Father and of Christ when believers ask the Father in Christ's name?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: The Father is approached as the fountain of the promised blessings. Christ is the procurer of them by his mediation and purchase, and in him all the promises are yea and amen. To ask in Christ's name is therefore to rest all hope of receiving on Christ's mediation while addressing God as Father.
sources.quote: This it is to ask the Father in Christ’s name, — God as a father, the fountain; and Christ as the procurer of them.
sources.raw_question: What are the distinct roles of the Father and of Christ when believers ask the Father in Christ's name?

question: How did the sending of Wisdom (the Son) in the incarnation differ from its earlier sendings to angels, patriarchs and prophets?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: Before, Wisdom was sent to be with men or in them, entering holy souls and making them friends of God and prophets, and filling the angels. In the fullness of time it was sent neither to fill angels nor merely to dwell in men, but so that the Word itself should be made man. Wisdom is sent in one way to be with man and in another way to be man.
sources.quote: But she is sent in one way that she may be with man; she has been sent in another way that she herself may be man.
sources.raw_question: How did the sending of Wisdom (the Son) in the incarnation differ from its earlier sendings to angels, patriarchs and prophets?

question: Does the analogy of the Persian 'king of kings', who had other kings under him, show that the Father and a subordinate Son can both be called God without there being two Gods?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 5: Whether Dr. Olarke’s pretence, that the authority of Father and Son being one, though they are two distinct Beings, makes them not to be two Gods, as a king upo
sources.answer: No. Waterland poses a dilemma. Either the subordinate rulers really were kings of Persia, in which case there was more than one king of Persia, or they were not, in which case they should not be called so. In the same way, either there are two Authors and Governors of the universe, that is two Gods, or there are not. If there are, Clarke should not deny it; if there are not, he should not affirm the title of both.
sources.quote: either there are two Authors and Governors of the uni- — verse, that is, two Gods; or there are not: if there are, why do you deny it of either?
sources.raw_question: Does the analogy of the Persian 'king of kings', who had other kings under him, show that the Father and a subordinate Son can both be called God without there being two Gods?

question: Is thinking a kind of inner speech, so that the mind forms a word in the heart?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Concerning the Word of the Mind, in Which We See the Word of God, as in a Glass and an Enigma.
sources.answer: Yes. Whoever thinks speaks in his heart, even when no words are uttered aloud. Scripture explains 'saying within themselves' as 'thinking'. Wisdom says 'they said, thinking', and Luke says 'they thought, saying'. Christ also answers what the scribes 'said within themselves' by asking 'What think ye?' This inner word grounds the analogy to the divine Word.
sources.quote: For although there were no words spoken, at any rate, he who thinks speaks in his heart.
sources.raw_question: Is thinking a kind of inner speech, so that the mind forms a word in the heart?

question: Are the inner speech of the mind and the mind's inner sight two different acts?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Concerning the Word of the Mind, in Which We See the Word of God, as in a Glass and an Enigma.
sources.answer: No. Outwardly, through the body, speech and sight are different things. When we think inwardly, they are one, just as seeing and hearing are one in the mind. This is why the Gospel says Jesus 'saw' the thoughts the scribes 'said' within themselves. True thoughts are both speech of the heart and sight arising from knowledge.
sources.quote: For when these things are done outwardly by means of the body, then speech and sight are different things; but when we think inwardly, the two are one
sources.raw_question: Are the inner speech of the mind and the mind's inner sight two different acts?

question: Can God the Father be said to come from a particular place, or is he limited to a location?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That Christ is God, is Proved by the Authority of the Old Testament Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. To say the Father comes from a place would mean he is excluded from that place and bounded within the narrow limits of some dwelling. That is unworthy of the Almighty and amounts to the sacrilegious heresy of Sabellius.
sources.quote: then God the Father comes from a place, from which place, moreover, He is thus excluded, and He is bounded within the straitnesses of some abode
sources.raw_question: Can God the Father be said to come from a particular place, or is he limited to a location?

question: Would the claim that God taught a created Son to create imply jealousy or weakness in God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: Yes. It implies jealousy, since God would not have taught many framers as He has many angels, and weakness, since He could not make by Himself but needed a fellow-worker. But God lacks nothing, as He says 'I am full.'
sources.quote: these insensate men are ascribing jealousy and weakness to God;—jealousy, in that He has not taught many how to frame
sources.raw_question: Would the claim that God taught a created Son to create imply jealousy or weakness in God?

question: Does attributing audible speech to God imply that God has a body and is therefore corruptible?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Articulate speech needs vocal organs shaped in some form, and form is a bodily limitation. All bodies are composite, and what is composite is subject to dissolution, which is destruction. So Eunomius's speaking God would end in destruction, which is absurd.
sources.quote: For each adaptation of the vocal organs must be in some form or other, and form is a bodily limitation. Further, we know very well that all bodies are composite, but where you see composition you see also dissolution
sources.raw_question: Does attributing audible speech to God imply that God has a body and is therefore corruptible?

question: When God appeared to the patriarchs such as Abraham and Moses, was the divine substance itself seen?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: No. God appears through a changeable and visible creature that is subject to his power. He himself remains in his own substance, which is unchangeable and invisible. Whatever bodily eyes saw was a created form, not the divine nature.
sources.quote: through the changeable and visible creature, subjected to Himself, while He Himself remains in Himself and in His own substance, in which He is unchangeable and invisible
sources.raw_question: When God appeared to the patriarchs such as Abraham and Moses, was the divine substance itself seen?

question: Is Christ divided from the Father, and what follows for the believer who denies the unity of the Godhead in the Trinity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter III. The same Unity may also be recognized from the fact that the Spirit is called Finger, and the Son Right Hand; for the understanding of divine things is assisted by the usage of human language. The tables of the law were written by this Finger, and they were afterwards broken, and the reason. Lastly, Christ wrote with the same Finger; yet we must not admit any inferiority in the Spirit from this bodily comparison.
sources.answer: No, Christ is not divided but is one with the Father. Whoever fails to believe the unity of Godhead in the Trinity has the table of his heart broken. The coherence of his soul is lessened.
sources.quote: Is Christ divided? He is not divided, but is one with the Father; and let no one separate you from Him.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ divided from the Father, and what follows for the believer who denies the unity of the Godhead in the Trinity?

question: Could Christ have been sorrowful from fear of the cross?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The martyrs forgot to fear terrible things in the zeal of their faith. Christ would have remained God upon the cross even if conceived with our sinful origin, and he was to judge the world and reign for ever. He could not forget such a reward and tremble with dishonourable fear.
sources.quote: should Christ be sorrowful from fear of the cross, Christ, Who even if He had been conceived with our sinful origin, would have been still God upon the cross, Who was to judge the world and reign for ever and ever?
sources.raw_question: Could Christ have been sorrowful from fear of the cross?

question: How does Christ's bearing of punishment in our place produce satisfaction to God's justice?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Justice asks no more than a punishment proportional to the offence. Christ voluntarily took our persons as mediator and bore that punishment in our stead. Because the righteous Judge accepted this substitution, satisfaction to God properly follows.
