sources.quote: His substituting himself in our room being allowed of by the righteous Judge, satisfaction to him doth thence properly ensue.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's bearing of punishment in our place produce satisfaction to God's justice?

question: Should Christians attempt to determine by speculation the questions Scripture leaves undeclared, such as how the Son was begotten or how God produced matter?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: No. Following the Son's own example in ascribing knowledge of the day of judgment to the Father, we should reserve greater questions to God. We know only in part, so we should not form endless conjectures about God but leave such knowledge in His hands.
sources.quote: If, then, the Son was not ashamed to ascribe the knowledge of that day to the Father only, but declared what was true regarding the matter, neither let us be ashamed to reserve for God those greater questions which may occur to us.
sources.raw_question: Should Christians attempt to determine by speculation the questions Scripture leaves undeclared, such as how the Son was begotten or how God produced matter?

question: Did God produce the substance of matter, and can we know how He did so?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: God produced matter, since Scripture teaches that He holds supremacy over all things. But whence or how He produced it Scripture nowhere declares, so we should not conjecture but leave that knowledge to God.
sources.quote: But whence or in what way He produced it, neither has Scripture anywhere declared; nor does it become us to conjecture
sources.raw_question: Did God produce the substance of matter, and can we know how He did so?

question: Is each Person of the Trinity a part of God, as the extended parts of the divine substance would be on Clarke's account of omnipresence?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: No. Clarke makes the substrata parts of God, each infinitely perfect yet only a part. Trinitarians more consistently hold the three Persons equal in all respects, none of them singly a part of God, but each perfect God.
sources.quote: We, more consistently, suppose three Persons equal, in all respects; none of them singly part of God; but every one perfect God.
sources.raw_question: Is each Person of the Trinity a part of God, as the extended parts of the divine substance would be on Clarke's account of omnipresence?

question: Does the Son merely imitate the Father's works, like a painter copying another's pictures, or does he do the same works with the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > There is a Double Rule for Understanding the Scriptural Modes of Speech Concerning the Son of God. These Modes of Speech are of a Threefold Kind.
sources.answer: He does the same works with the Father. The Son neither does other things in the same way, as a copying painter does, nor the same things in a different way, as the body expresses what the mind thought. Scripture says 'these same things' and 'likewise'. The working of Father and Son is therefore indivisible and equal, though it is from the Father to the Son.
sources.quote: He has said both “these same things,” and “likewise;” and hence the working of both the Father and the Son is indivisible and equal, but it is from the Father to the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son merely imitate the Father's works, like a painter copying another's pictures, or does he do the same works with the Father?

question: Does the doctrine that Christ made satisfaction for sin contradict the teaching that everyone must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive according to their deeds?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. All must indeed appear before Christ's judgment seat. Woe at that day will belong to those who cannot plead the atonement of Christ's blood, together with evidence of their interest in it through faith and obedience. The judgment therefore confirms the need for the satisfaction and does not undercut it.
sources.quote: woe will be unto them at the great day who are not able to plead the atonement made for their sins by the blood of Christ, and an evidence of their interest therein by their faith and obedience
sources.raw_question: Does the doctrine that Christ made satisfaction for sin contradict the teaching that everyone must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive according to their deeds?

question: Was the Mosaic law the cause of the Jews' unbelief in Christ, as though it came from a God opposed to the Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter II.—Proofs from the plain testimony of Moses, and of the other prophets, whose words are the words of Christ, that there is but one God, the founder of the world, whom Our Lord preached, and whom He called His Father.
sources.answer: No. The law never hindered anyone from believing in the Son of God. Instead it was a pedagogue leading to Christ, and it urged belief in him. It taught that the old wound of the serpent could be healed only by believing in him who is lifted up on the tree. Unbelief came from those who despised God and broke the law.
sources.quote: Let them not therefore ascribe to the law the unbelief of certain [among them]. For the law never hindered them from believing in the Son of God; nay, but it even exhorted them so to do
sources.raw_question: Was the Mosaic law the cause of the Jews' unbelief in Christ, as though it came from a God opposed to the Son?

question: Does the Father love the Son only as his eternal Son, or also as mediator?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Both. The Father loves the Son first and by way of eminence as his eternal Son, the delight of his soul before the foundation of the world. He also loves him as mediator, the means by which his love is conveyed to believers.
sources.quote: not only as his eternal Son, — as he was the delight of his soul before the foundation of the world, Prov. viii. 30, — but also as our mediator, and the means of conveying his love to us
sources.raw_question: Does the Father love the Son only as his eternal Son, or also as mediator?

question: Is the idea of eternity the same as the idea of necessary existence?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Eternity is simply duration without beginning and without end, while necessary existence is a distinct idea. Some have even held that God could have created the world from all eternity, which shows the ideas can be separated. Eternity may, in sound reasoning, imply necessary existence, but if the two were the same idea it would be nonsense to say one implies the other.
sources.quote: The idea of eternity is neither more nor less than duration without beginning and without end.
sources.raw_question: Is the idea of eternity the same as the idea of necessary existence?

question: When John says Jesus was 'making Himself equal with God,' does it mean Christ became God or fashioned Himself into God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: No. The Lord did not then fashion Himself to be God, and a made God is inconceivable. Rather, He manifested His deity through His works, as He said, 'believe My works, that ye may know that I am in the Father, and the Father in Me.'
sources.quote: For the Lord did not then fashion Himself to be God, nor indeed is a made God conceivable, but He manifested it by the works
sources.raw_question: When John says Jesus was 'making Himself equal with God,' does it mean Christ became God or fashioned Himself into God?

question: Did Christ first begin to be Lord and King at His incarnation and crucifixion?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: No. He was Lord and King everlasting before He became man, as Abraham's worship, Genesis 19:24, Psalm 110:1 and Psalm 45:6 show. What began was His showing of His Lordship and its extension over the disobedient, a Lordship over us that came about when He redeemed all by the Cross. To hold otherwise revives the teaching of Paul of Samosata.
sources.quote: He who is now displayed as Lord and King, does not then begin to be King and Lord, but begins to shew His Lordship, and to extend it even over the disobedient.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ first begin to be Lord and King at His incarnation and crucifixion?

question: How does Isaac's blessing of Jacob show that the word 'made' need not refer to a being's essence or coming into existence?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: Isaac told Esau 'I have made him thy lord' over thirty years after Jacob's birth, meaning not Jacob's essence or origin but his subsequent authority over his brother. If the Arians do not read 'made' as denoting origin even of Jacob, a creature, it is worse madness to read it so of the Son of God, who is no creature.
sources.quote: For Isaac said ‘Become’ and ‘I have made,’ signifying neither the coming into being nor the essence of Jacob (for after thirty years and more from his birth he said this); but his authority over his brother
sources.raw_question: How does Isaac's blessing of Jacob show that the word 'made' need not refer to a being's essence or coming into existence?

question: Is Christ everlastingly Lord and King, or did He only become Lord at some point?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: He is everlasting Lord and King. Being Son of God He must be like the Father, and being like Him He is certainly Lord and King, as He says 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father.' He ever was and is Lord of all, having all that is the Father's; His being 'made' Lord refers to His manhood among us.
sources.quote: For He ever was and is, as Son, so also Lord and Sovereign of all, being like in all things to the Father, and having all that is the Father’s
sources.raw_question: Is Christ everlastingly Lord and King, or did He only become Lord at some point?

question: Is Christ's satisfaction a physical act of one of his natures, or something else?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: It is the apotelesma or effect of his actions, not a physical act of either nature. Satisfaction is the dignity of what Christ did and suffered in reference to its end. Each nature acts distinctly according to its own properties, yet the immediate act of either nature is the act of the one person, from whom it has its dignity.
sources.quote: satisfaction is in it looked on as a real act or operation of one or the other nature in Christ, when it is the apotelesma or effect of the actings, the doing and suffering of Christ
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's satisfaction a physical act of one of his natures, or something else?

question: Does the doctrine of satisfaction imply that God was compelled to save men in this way?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. The whole salvation of men depends on a free, sovereign act of God's will exercised in infinite wisdom, holiness and grace. God, freely purposing to save, did so in a way becoming his holy nature and righteous law; and 'uncontrollable' properly concerns actions, not natures.
sources.quote: The whole business of the salvation of men, according unto this doctrine, depends on a mere free, sovereign act of God’s will, exerting itself in a way of infinite wisdom, holiness, and grace.
sources.raw_question: Does the doctrine of satisfaction imply that God was compelled to save men in this way?

question: Can someone who confesses Christ in name but denies that He is truly Son by generation and God by nature hold the one faith of the one baptism?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Christ is one Lord in the truth of the confession only if He is Son, God, unchangeable, and eternally possessed of Sonship and Godhead. Whoever preaches Him otherwise preaches another Christ and is outside the one faith of the one baptism. Whatever is not the one faith is not faith at all.
sources.quote: He who preaches Christ other than He is, that is, other than Son and God, preaches another Christ. Nor is he in the one faith of the one baptism
sources.raw_question: Can someone who confesses Christ in name but denies that He is truly Son by generation and God by nature hold the one faith of the one baptism?

question: Is calling Christ 'God' by name sufficient, given that Scripture allows the name 'god' to be given to many?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Some call Christ God in name only, since religion permits speaking of more gods than one, but true confession requires that He be God by nature, sharing the divine nature. Christ must be one Lord not in name but in confession, Son by generation and not by appellation.
sources.quote: Another will call Him, but not think Him, God on the ground that religion allows us to speak of more Gods than One
sources.raw_question: Is calling Christ 'God' by name sufficient, given that Scripture allows the name 'god' to be given to many?

question: From where did Christ's human soul come: from human parents, from some alien source, or from God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: From God alone. Even in ordinary birth the soul is never derived from the parents, and since the Virgin received the flesh of Christ from God alone, it is far more certain that the soul of that body came from God alone. The Word assumed the soul from Himself, just as He assumed the body by His own act.
sources.quote: If, then, the Virgin received from God alone the flesh which she conceived, far more certain is it that the soul of that body can have come from God alone.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who deny the Word became flesh
sources.raw_question: From where did Christ's human soul come: from human parents, from some alien source, or from God?

question: Do Christ's sorrow unto death and His power to lay down His soul and take it up again show that His soul came from some source other than the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. God the Word became man without departing from the mystery of His own nature. The Holy Ghost, who is the Author of His body's conception, is also the source of His humanity, so there is no need for an alien origin of His soul.
sources.quote: they want to derive it from some alien source, and not from the Holy Ghost, the Author of His body’s conception: for God the Word became man without departing from the mystery of His own nature.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's sorrow unto death and His power to lay down His soul and take it up again show that His soul came from some source other than the Holy Spirit?

question: Is it the orthodox who hold the Son equal to the Father, or the Eunomians who deny it, that are truly ashamed of the Cross?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: The Eunomians. The orthodox, even after the Passion, worship the Son equally with the Father. Eunomius, by contrast, ranks the Father above the Son precisely because the shame of the Cross touches the Son and not the Father, and so he makes the Passion a reason to deny the Son equal glory.
sources.quote: Who then is it who is ashamed of the Cross? he who, even after the Passion, worships the Son equally with the Father, or he who even before the Passion insults Him
sources.raw_question: Is it the orthodox who hold the Son equal to the Father, or the Eunomians who deny it, that are truly ashamed of the Cross?

question: Did the Word, considered as the Word, gain anything or receive grace and promotion through the Incarnation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. The Word of God is without want and full, so he gained nothing from us for his own promotion; rather we were promoted from him. The worship of the incarnate Jesus as God's Son shows that not the Word as Word, but we, received this grace, since through relationship to his Body we become God's temple and sons.
sources.quote: And He indeed has gained nothing from us for His own promotion: for the Word of God is without want and full; but rather we were promoted from Him
sources.raw_question: Did the Word, considered as the Word, gain anything or receive grace and promotion through the Incarnation?

question: If the Word is God in a higher sense than any nominal god and is not excluded with the nominal gods, must he be included in the one Supreme God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture's exclusive statements exclude all nominal gods besides the one God; the Word is called God in a higher sense than nominal gods and is not excluded with them, so he is comprehended in the one Supreme God and is therefore coeternal and coessential with the Father.
sources.quote: since he is not excluded with the nominal Gods, he is included and comprehended in the one Supreme God ; and consequently is coeternal and coessential with the Father.
sources.raw_question: If the Word is God in a higher sense than any nominal god and is not excluded with the nominal gods, must he be included in the one Supreme God?

question: When a person receives the Holy Spirit, does his human nature or substance change, or only the quality of his works?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter X.—By a comparison drawn from the wild olive-tree, whose quality but not whose nature is changed by grafting, he proves more important things; he points out also that man without the Spirit is not capable of bringing forth fruit, or of inheriting the kingdom of God.
sources.answer: Only the quality changes, not the substance. As the engrafted wild olive does not lose the substance of its wood but bears different fruit and receives a new name, so the man who receives the Spirit of God does not lose the substance of flesh but changes the quality of his works and is called a spiritual man.
sources.quote: he certainly does not lose the substance of flesh, but changes the quality of the fruit [brought forth, i.e.,] of his works, and receives another name
sources.raw_question: When a person receives the Holy Spirit, does his human nature or substance change, or only the quality of his works?

question: Does the fact that the Father is called the God of our Lord Jesus Christ imply that Christ has a lower order of divinity than the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. God is Christ's God not as though Christ possessed a different order of divinity, but in respect of the Dispensation by which He was born a servant of the Virgin. He was begotten God of the Father, so God is His Father because He is God of God, and God is His God because He is flesh of the Virgin.
sources.quote: God is His God but not as possessing a different order of divinity from His. He was begotten God of the Father, and born a servant by the Dispensation
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Father is called the God of our Lord Jesus Christ imply that Christ has a lower order of divinity than the Father?

question: In what sense are believers the brethren and fellows of Christ, so that His Father and God is also theirs?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Only in respect of His assumed flesh. No one is fellow to the Only-begotten God the Word, but we are counted His brethren and fellows because He was born into the body. So the message to His brethren in John 20:17 concerns the Dispensation of the flesh and does not degrade His divinity.
sources.quote: No one is fellow to the Only-begotten Christ, God the Word: but we know that we are His fellows by the assumption which made Him flesh.
sources.raw_question: In what sense are believers the brethren and fellows of Christ, so that His Father and God is also theirs?

question: If the Arians confess that the only true God is also the only righteous Judge, does the Son's role as Judge of the earth show that he is true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. The Lord who rains from the Lord is called by Abraham the Judge of all the earth who will not slay the righteous with the wicked. The Arians themselves have confessed that the only righteous Judge is the only true God. So they must either deny the Son his judgeship or admit his true Divinity.
sources.quote: You must deprive the Son of His judgeship before you can deprive Him of His true Divinity.
sources.raw_question: If the Arians confess that the only true God is also the only righteous Judge, does the Son's role as Judge of the earth show that he is true God?

question: Are the three divine Persons distinct sources of their being, or only distinct sources of the gifts they give to us?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: They are distinct fountains of dispensations to us, not distinct sources of being in themselves. The Persons are revealed as acting distinctly when they communicate good things to believers. Owen explicitly denies that this distribution implies distinct origins of being within the Deity.
sources.quote: points at distinct rises and fountains (though not of being in themselves, yet) of dispensations unto us.
sources.raw_question: Are the three divine Persons distinct sources of their being, or only distinct sources of the gifts they give to us?

question: Does God have many words, wisdoms and images, or only one?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Only one. Since God is One, it is fitting that His Image, Word and Wisdom be one also, existing always the same, not before or after another, as Scripture says the Word of God endures forever.
sources.quote: For it was fitting, whereas God is One, that His Image should be One also, and His Word One and One His Wisdom
sources.raw_question: Does God have many words, wisdoms and images, or only one?

question: Are Christ's mediatorial actions the actions of a mere man or of one who is both God and man?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: All of Christ's actings on behalf of believers are the actings of one who is God and man in one person. This one person is the single principle of all his operations as mediator. Believers are therefore to believe in and obey this Son of God, God and man, so that they may have eternal life.
sources.quote: that Jesus Christ is God and man in one person; and that all his actings in their behalf are the actings of him who is God and man
sources.raw_question: Are Christ's mediatorial actions the actions of a mere man or of one who is both God and man?

question: In what sense was the Father called Creator 'primarily' or 'eminently' if the Son is also Creator?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: Only in order, not in power. The Father, as first Person, was conceived as issuing the orders or fiat for creation and the Son as executing it; hence the title is eminently the Father's for his majesty as first Person, while the Son is as truly and properly Creator in real efficiency.
sources.quote: From hence we may easily understand in what sense the title of Creator was 5 primarily or eminently attributed to the Father; and yet, as to any real power or efficiency, the Son is as truly and properly Creator
sources.raw_question: In what sense was the Father called Creator 'primarily' or 'eminently' if the Son is also Creator?

question: Does Hebrews 1:10 ('Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth') refer to the Son rather than to God the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: Yes. The verse begins with 'and thou', naturally continuing the address to the Son in the preceding verse; the author's scope is to exalt the Son above angels, for which creating the world is most fitting; it explains verse 2 where the Son made the worlds; it shows he is Jehovah and no ministering spirit; a sudden reference to God's immutability would be abrupt and irrelevant; and antiquity everywhere calls the Son Creator.
sources.quote: The verse begins with καὶ σὺ, which -properly refers to the same who was spoken of immediately before, in the second Person. The σοῦ preceding and σὺ following, answer to each other.
sources.raised_by_detail: a late writer, Examination of Dr. Bennet on the Trinity
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 1:10 ('Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth') refer to the Son rather than to God the Father?

question: Do the apostles' interchangeable descriptions of themselves as servants of God or of Jesus Christ imply that Christ's authority is equal to the Father's?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. An earthly envoy who styled himself now the emperor's servant and now the chancellor's would be thought to compromise the emperor's supremacy, even though the two are men of the same nature. The apostles draw no distinction at all between God and Christ as the source of their commission. This shows that the original authority of the two is equal.
sources.quote: But no distinction is drawn in this celestial commission: – Is not then the original authority equal?
sources.raw_question: Do the apostles' interchangeable descriptions of themselves as servants of God or of Jesus Christ imply that Christ's authority is equal to the Father's?

question: What does describing a church as being 'in God the Father and in the Lord Jesus Christ' imply about the Son?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: It implies that the Father and the Son are equally the Rock of salvation. The Thessalonian church's spiritual standing is placed in the Father and the Son alike, without distinction. That would be inconsistent if the Son were a creature.
sources.quote: Was then their spiritual status equally, indiscriminately consistent in the Father and the Son? Then to that church the Father and the Son were equally the Rock of their salvation.
sources.raw_question: What does describing a church as being 'in God the Father and in the Lord Jesus Christ' imply about the Son?

question: If created nature could not bear to be made directly by God, so that a mediating Word was needed, how could the Word himself, if he were a creature, endure being made directly by God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: He could not, so the Arian theory refutes itself. If the Word, being of originate nature, could endure God's immediate hand, then all creatures could, and no mediator would be needed. If no originate thing can endure it, then neither could the Word, since they call him one of the originate things.
sources.quote: for it follows either that, if He could endure it, all could endure it, or, it being endurable by none, it was not endurable by the Word, for you say that He is one of originate things.
sources.raw_question: If created nature could not bear to be made directly by God, so that a mediating Word was needed, how could the Word himself, if he were a creature, endure being made directly by God?

question: Does the existence of single created things such as one sun and one earth show that the Word could be unique and still be a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: No. Each created thing is one in its own essence, but none is adequate by itself for the service committed to it. The sun, moon and stars share one common office of lighting, each supplying what the others lack. All creatures together form one body, the world, like members of each other. To make the Word such a part would make him an insufficient piece of the universe, which is irreligious, so he is not among originate things.
sources.quote: everything that is brought to be, is one in its own essence; but for the ministry and service committed to it, by itself it is not adequate nor sufficient alone.
sources.raw_question: Does the existence of single created things such as one sun and one earth show that the Word could be unique and still be a creature?

question: Does the phrase 'whom no man hath seen, nor can see' in 1 Timothy 6:16 count against applying the passage to the Son, since men saw Christ?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. It can be applied to Christ according to His divinity. The Jews saw and crucified Him in the flesh, but His divinity cannot be seen by human sight at all. It is seen only by a sight by which those who see are no longer men but beyond men.
sources.quote: His divinity can in no wise be seen by human sight, but is seen with that sight with which they who see are no longer men, but beyond men.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'whom no man hath seen, nor can see' in 1 Timothy 6:16 count against applying the passage to the Son, since men saw Christ?

question: When early writers such as Novatian say that the Father 'precedes' the Son or 'must go before' him, do they mean a priority in time?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Such phrases can only mean a priority of nature or order, not of time or duration, and all Catholics agreed on this. Novatian himself says the Son is before all time and always in the Father, so the 'preceding' he speaks of cannot be temporal. Novatian's own wording ('etiam ipso tempore') shows he regarded temporal posteriority as only a lower kind of posteriority, distinct from posteriority in order of nature.
sources.quote: Mark the force of the words, etiam ipso; intimating that posteriority in time is a low degree of ool ged and that a thing might
sources.raw_question: When early writers such as Novatian say that the Father 'precedes' the Son or 'must go before' him, do they mean a priority in time?

question: Does Novatian's talk of a voluntary procession or nativity of the Son mean that the Son's generation was only temporal?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Novatian holds both a first and a second nativity. He supposes that the Son existed, and existed as Son, before the procession, which is the voluntary nativity he speaks of. Any temporal procession is therefore additional to an eternal generation and does not replace it.
sources.quote: As he supposes the Son existing before the procession, (which is the voluntary nativity he speaks of,) and preexisting as a'!Son, he cannot be understood otherwise.
sources.raw_question: Does Novatian's talk of a voluntary procession or nativity of the Son mean that the Son's generation was only temporal?

question: How can an act such as the Father's sending of the Son be both common to the divine Persons and proper to one Person?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Because the will is an essential property of the one divine nature, an act of will is the act of each Person who shares that nature; yet in respect of order it is eminently and peculiarly ascribed to one Person, as the sending is to the Father.
sources.quote: though eminently, and in respect of order, it was peculiarly the act of the Father
sources.raw_question: How can an act such as the Father's sending of the Son be both common to the divine Persons and proper to one Person?

question: How do Christ's two natures work together in his work of mediation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: The single person, God and man, is the agent and the principle giving life and efficacy to the whole work. Both natures, distinctly considered, are what operates, each working according to its own proper operation. The one effect produced arises from all of these and relates to them all.
sources.quote: The execution of his office of mediation in his single person, in respect of both natures: wherein is considerable, ὁ ἐνεργῶν, — the agent, Christ himself, God and man.
sources.raw_question: How do Christ's two natures work together in his work of mediation?

question: Why did Christ, as mediator, receive the Spirit without measure from the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: So that he would have all fulness for the work of salvation and could supply all who are his, grace for grace. The Father pleased that all fulness should dwell in him. Had it been given to him by measure, believers would have exhausted it.
sources.quote: Had it been given to him by measure, we had exhausted it.
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ, as mediator, receive the Spirit without measure from the Father?

question: Is the Maker of heaven and earth the one and only God Almighty, or was he produced by a defect within a higher divine realm, as the Valentinian Gnostics (Marcosians) claimed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XVI.—Absurd interpretations of the Marcosians.
sources.answer: The Maker of heaven and earth is the only God Almighty, besides whom there is no God. Irenaeus calls the opposite claim, that the Creator was the product of a third defect, impious beyond all impiety. It is a doctrine to be detested and its holders shunned.
sources.quote: who assert that the Maker of heaven and earth, the only God Almighty, besides whom there is no God, was produced by means of a defect, which itself sprang from another defect
sources.raw_question: Is the Maker of heaven and earth the one and only God Almighty, or was he produced by a defect within a higher divine realm, as the Valentinian Gnostics (Marcosians) claimed?

question: What is adoption, as the privilege believers receive through Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: Adoption is the authoritative translation of a believer, by Jesus Christ, from the family of the world and Satan into the family of God. With it comes investiture in all the privileges and advantages of that family. It requires that the person belonged by right to another family and had no right of his own to God's family. It also requires that he be legally translated by sovereign authority, freed from his former obligations, and given full rights as if born a son.
sources.quote: adoption is the authoritative translation of a believer, by Jesus Christ, from the family of the world and Satan into the family of God, with his investiture in all the privileges and advantages of that family.
sources.raw_question: What is adoption, as the privilege believers receive through Christ?

question: In the Incarnation, what does it mean that the Godhead 'empties' itself, and what happens to the human nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: The Godhead empties itself so as to come within the capacity of human nature, while the human nature is renewed by becoming divine through its commixture with the Divine. The divine nature is not diminished; rather the human is raised and transformed by the divine.
sources.quote: The Godhead “empties” Itself that It may come within the capacity of the Human Nature, and the Human Nature is renewed by becoming Divine through its commixture
sources.raw_question: In the Incarnation, what does it mean that the Godhead 'empties' itself, and what happens to the human nature?

question: How was Christ's flesh raised after the Passion, and by what power?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: By the power of his own Godhead. As air submerged in water rushes upward and carries water with it, the true Life that underlay the flesh rose after the Passion and drew the flesh with it from corruption to incorruptibility. Like hidden fire in wood blazing up, he rekindled his life by his own divine power.
sources.quote: when the true Life that underlay the flesh sped up, after the Passion, to Itself, the flesh also was raised up with It, being forced upwards from corruption to incorruptibility by the Divine immortality
sources.raw_question: How was Christ's flesh raised after the Passion, and by what power?

question: Why does the deity of Christ matter for the sinner's assurance of pardon and grace?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Only an infinite God can supply grace enough for sinners, so if Christ were a mere man there would not be sufficient grace. Scripture grounds the sinner's peace on the fact that his Maker and Redeemer is the Lord of hosts and the God of the whole earth. Owen therefore warns against those who would rob believers of the Deity of Christ.
sources.quote: Take heed of them who would rob you of the Deity of Christ. If there were no more grace for me than what can be treasured up in a mere man, I should rejoice [if] my portion might be under rocks and mountains.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who would rob you of the Deity of Christ
sources.raw_question: Why does the deity of Christ matter for the sinner's assurance of pardon and grace?

question: Does Christ's saying 'As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you' (John 15:9) show that his love is more than the love of a mere man?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ's love in his human nature, however intense and tender, cannot as such be infinite, eternal, or absolutely unchangeable in itself. If it were only that, it could not be compared with and equalled to the Father's divine love in eternity, fruitfulness and unchangeableness. Yet Christ equates his love with the Father's, which implies that it is divine.
sources.quote: His love could not be compared with and equalled unto the divine love of the Father, in those properties of eternity, fruitfulness, and unchangeableness
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you' (John 15:9) show that his love is more than the love of a mere man?

question: What does the promise contain, of which God's adopted children are said to be heirs?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: It is the promise God made in Christ from the foundation of the world, later renewed and confirmed by his oath. It contains deliverance from all the evil that the guilt of sin and the dominion of Satan brought. It also invests believers with all spiritual blessings in Christ. Hence the Holy Ghost calls it a 'promise of the eternal inheritance.'
sources.quote: It contains a deliverance from all the evil which the guilt of sin and dominion of Satan had brought upon them, with an investiture of them in all spiritual blessings in heavenly things in Christ Jesus.
sources.raw_question: What does the promise contain, of which God's adopted children are said to be heirs?

question: Does Paul's naming of the elect angels alongside God and Christ in 1 Timothy 5:21 show that being enumerated with the Father and the Son does not imply equal rank, so that the Spirit's being named with them proves nothing?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Statement of the reason why in the writings of Paul the angels are associated with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. The angels are mentioned in a different way: they are called as witnesses, fellow-slaves and faithful witnesses of the truth. The Spirit is invoked as Lord of life. Paul calls the angels to witness because they will be present with the Lord at the judgment. He is preparing proofs for himself before that tribunal, not ranking them with God.
sources.quote: It follows that the mention of the Spirit and that of angels are not made under like conditions. The Spirit is called on as Lord of life, and the angels as allies of their fellow-slaves and faithful witnesses of the truth.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's naming of the elect angels alongside God and Christ in 1 Timothy 5:21 show that being enumerated with the Father and the Son does not imply equal rank, so that the Spirit's being named with them proves nothing?

question: Could a created being, itself a fellow-slave, be the one who frees us, makes us sons of God, and gives us life?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Statement of the reason why in the writings of Paul the angels are associated with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. A fellow-slave might serve as a witness. But only one who has natural kinship with God can make us free, adopt us as sons, and quicken us from death. One who is alien to God cannot make us kin with God, and one under the yoke of slavery cannot free us. Since the Spirit does these things, he cannot be a creature like the angels.
sources.quote: For how can we be made kin with God by one who is an alien? How can we be freed by one who is himself under the yoke of slavery?
sources.raw_question: Could a created being, itself a fellow-slave, be the one who frees us, makes us sons of God, and gives us life?

question: Can Dr. Clarke consistently hold that the Son is truly God by nature while also denying him self-existence, which Clarke calls the most essential character of God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 24: Whether Gal. iv. 8. may not be enough to determine the dispute betwiat us; since it obliged the Doctor to confess, that Christ as by nature truly God, as truly
sources.answer: No. If self-existence is the most essential character of God, then the Son, who on Clarke's own admission lacks it, cannot be truly and by nature God. Nothing can be truly and by nature man without the essential character of man, and the same holds for God. Clarke is therefore saying and unsaying, playing fast and loose with words.
sources.quote: If se/f-existence be the most essential character of God, it seems to .me to follow, that the Son, who by the Doctor’s confession wants that character, cannot be truly and by nature God, any more than any thing can be truly and by nature man
sources.raw_question: Can Dr. Clarke consistently hold that the Son is truly God by nature while also denying him self-existence, which Clarke calls the most essential character of God?

question: Since Scripture calls men, idols, the devil and even the belly 'gods', can the Son be God only in such a subordinate sense?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 24: Whether Gal. iv. 8. may not be enough to determine the dispute betwiat us; since it obliged the Doctor to confess, that Christ as by nature truly God, as truly
sources.answer: No. St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 8:5-6 shows that the Son is not to be reckoned among the nominal gods, and the Arians themselves admit this. If the Son is God at all, he is a real God. Scripture does not permit us to profess two real and true Gods. So if he is truly, properly and by nature God, he must be the same as the one supreme God and share the same nature.
sources.quote: But, I think, St. Paul hath sufficiently intimated, (1 Cor. viii. 5,6.) that the Son is not to be reckoned among the nominal Gods; besides that you yourselves confess it. If he be God at all, he is a veal one
sources.raw_question: Since Scripture calls men, idols, the devil and even the belly 'gods', can the Son be God only in such a subordinate sense?

question: Why is it necessary for our salvation that the gifts of grace be received by the incarnate Word rather than by a mere man?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: So that the grace might be secure and irrevocable. A mere man who receives can lose again, as Adam received and lost. When the Lord receives and the grant is lodged in him, the grace remains sure for humanity. If the Word had received these things for his own sake as God, humanity would gain nothing from them.
sources.quote: For while mere man receives, he is liable to lose again (as was shewn in the case of Adam, for he received and he lost), but that the grace may be irrevocable, and may be kept sure by men, therefore He Himself appropriates the gift
sources.raw_question: Why is it necessary for our salvation that the gifts of grace be received by the incarnate Word rather than by a mere man?

question: If the Word is the image of the Father yet is made of letters and syllables, does it follow that the Father is also composed of letters and syllables?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XV.—Sige relates to Marcus the generation of the twenty-four elements and of Jesus. Exposure of these absurdities.
sources.answer: Yes, on Marcus's theory, and that shows the theory is absurd. Since Marcus says the Word is like its Author and bears the image of the invisible, a Word made of thirty elements and four syllables would require that the Father of all also consist of thirty elements and four syllables.
sources.quote: It will follow, then, according to thy theory, that the Father of all, in accordance with the likeness of the Word, consists of thirty elements and four syllables!
sources.raw_question: If the Word is the image of the Father yet is made of letters and syllables, does it follow that the Father is also composed of letters and syllables?

question: Can human beings remedy their own sinfulness by their own power?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 1. Introduction. Preparation of heart. Our position before God.
sources.answer: No. The author holds that the evil of sin, so far as man is concerned, cannot cure itself. Scripture asks who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean and answers that no one can. Like the Ethiopian who cannot change his skin, those used to doing evil cannot make themselves good.
sources.quote: This evil is not self-remedial; but so far as lies in man, incurable. Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one.
sources.raw_question: Can human beings remedy their own sinfulness by their own power?

question: How can Scripture say that God was seen by Abraham when it also says that no man can see God and live?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: The one seen was not the Father, who has never been seen, but the Son. Since Scripture cannot lie, God truly was seen; yet since the Father is invisible, the God who appeared must be the Son, who is accustomed to descend and to be seen because he descends.
sources.quote: Whence it may be understood that it was not the Father who was seen, seeing that He never was seen; but the Son, who has both been accustomed to descend, and to be seen because He has descended.
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture say that God was seen by Abraham when it also says that no man can see God and live?

question: Is it strictly correct to speak of several individuals who share one human nature as "many men"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. Calling those undivided in nature by the plural of their common nature is a customary abuse of language, equivalent to saying "many human natures." The term "man" signifies the common nature, not the individual; individuals are distinguished by proper names and peculiar attributes, while the nature remains one.
sources.quote: the practice of calling those who are not divided in nature by the very name of their common nature in the plural, and saying they are “many men,” is a customary abuse of language
sources.raw_question: Is it strictly correct to speak of several individuals who share one human nature as "many men"?

question: How can persons be counted as many while the nature they share is spoken of as one?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: Persons are separated by the peculiar attributes seen in each, and when combined they are presented by means of number. The nature is common and is not divided among them. Just as "a people" or "an army" is spoken of in the singular though it contains many, "man" may properly be called one even when many individuals share it.
sources.quote: as we speak of a people, or a mob, or an army, or an assembly in the singular in every case, while each of these is conceived as being in plurality, so according to the more accurate expression, “man” would be said to be one
sources.raw_question: How can persons be counted as many while the nature they share is spoken of as one?

question: How can believers become one, given that they cannot be one in themselves?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Same Argument Continued.
sources.answer: They become one only in Christ the Mediator, not in themselves. Their sinful desires and uncleannesses divide them from one another, so they must be cleansed through the Mediator. They are then made one by sharing a nature equal to the angels, and by a common will directed to the same blessedness, fused by charity into one spirit.
sources.quote: since they could not be so in themselves, separated as they are one from another by divers pleasures and desires and uncleannesses of sin; whence they are cleansed through the Mediator, that they may be one[^502] in Him
sources.raw_question: How can believers become one, given that they cannot be one in themselves?

question: Are 'Father' and 'Son' mutual relations of the same kind as 'friend' and 'neighbor', where the same term applies to both sides?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Reply is Made to the Cavils of the Heretics in Respect to the Same Words Begotten and Unbegotten.
sources.answer: No. Friends and neighbors are named relative to one another with the same term, so the same friendship or neighborhood is in both. The Son, however, is called Son relative to the Father, not relative to a son. The relation is therefore not the same on both sides, and the Son's equality with the Father cannot lie in the relation itself.
sources.quote: Since Father and Son are not so called in relation to each other in the same way as friends and neighbors are; for a friend is so called relatively to his friend, and if they love each other equally, then the same friendship is in both
sources.raw_question: Are 'Father' and 'Son' mutual relations of the same kind as 'friend' and 'neighbor', where the same term applies to both sides?

question: Does teaching that God's love is unchangeable encourage people to sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No. The doctrine of grace may be twisted into wantonness, but the principle of grace itself cannot be. No one who has truly tasted God's love can seriously make this objection. God's hatred of sin in a person is consistent with his accepting that person and appointing them to eternal life.
sources.quote: He never tasted of the love of God that can seriously make this objection. The doctrine of grace may be turned into wantonness; the principle cannot.
sources.raw_question: Does teaching that God's love is unchangeable encourage people to sin?

question: Can right love or will exist without knowledge, so that the analogue of the Holy Spirit lacks memory and understanding?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Of the Likeness of the Father and of the Son Alleged to Be in Our Memory and Understanding. Of the Likeness of the Holy Spirit in Our Will or Love.
sources.answer: No. A right will must know what to desire and what to avoid. It therefore has a kind of knowledge of its own, which cannot exist without memory and understanding. Love would not know what to love rightly unless it knew what it desired.
sources.quote: Are we to say that our will, when it is right, knows not what to desire, what to avoid? Further, if it knows, doubtless then it has a kind of knowledge of its own, such as cannot be without memory and understanding.
sources.raw_question: Can right love or will exist without knowledge, so that the analogue of the Holy Spirit lacks memory and understanding?

question: Does the fact that all creation praises its Framer and the Truth show that the Word is not a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: Yes. The whole earth hymns, blesses and fears the Truth and its Framer. The Word is that Framer, and he says, 'I am the Truth.' He is therefore celebrated by all things as Creator rather than standing among them. It follows that he is not a creature but alone proper to the Father.
sources.quote: it follows that the Word is not a creature, but alone proper to the Father, in whom all things are disposed, and He is celebrated by all, as Framer
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that all creation praises its Framer and the Truth show that the Word is not a creature?

question: When Christ says "the Father Himself loveth you," does he exclude himself and the Holy Spirit from that love?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to God, Even the Father. The Kingdom Having Been Delivered to God, Even the Father, Christ Will Not Then Make Intercession for Us.
sources.answer: No. For the most part each Person of the Trinity is so named that the other Persons may also be understood. So "the Father Himself loveth you" implies by consequence that the Son and the Holy Spirit love us too.
sources.quote: for the most part each Person of the Trinity is so named, that the other Persons also may be understood.
sources.raw_question: When Christ says "the Father Himself loveth you," does he exclude himself and the Holy Spirit from that love?

question: Why does Christ say he will "declare" the Father plainly, and what does this indicate about the Son's relation to the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to God, Even the Father. The Kingdom Having Been Delivered to God, Even the Father, Christ Will Not Then Make Intercession for Us.
sources.answer: He uses "declare" because he is the Father's Word. Declaring the Father plainly means showing the Father openly in face-to-face sight, rather than through similitudes as now.
sources.quote: For He says, I will “declare” to you, because He is His word.
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ say he will "declare" the Father plainly, and what does this indicate about the Son's relation to the Father?

question: Does the promise that the Father will love us at the end imply that God does not love us now?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to God, Even the Father. The Kingdom Having Been Delivered to God, Even the Father, Christ Will Not Then Make Intercession for Us.
sources.answer: No. God loves us now, since he spared not his own Son but delivered him up for us all. But God loves us as we shall be, not as we are. He loves us in order that we may become such as he keeps eternally. We arrive at that state through faith leading to sight.
sources.quote: not that He does not now love us, who spared not His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all; but God loves us, such as we shall be, not such as we are
sources.raw_question: Does the promise that the Father will love us at the end imply that God does not love us now?

question: Does Peter's confession of Christ as the Son of God, on which the Church is founded, exclude the view that Christ is a creature made from nothing and Son only by adoption?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. Hilary argues that the faith confessing Christ as the Son of God, and that faith only, received in Peter every blessing, the keys and the Church's foundation. A confession of Christ as a perfect creature adopted as Son was never revealed to Peter and would have been rebuked, since even Peter's lesser defect of faith was sternly condemned. Therefore the creature-confession holds not the keys of the Church and is neither the Church's nor Christ's faith.
sources.quote: then perforce the faith which proclaims Him a creature, made out of nothing, holds not the keys of the Church and is a stranger to the apostolic faith and power. It is neither the Church’s faith, nor is it Christ’s.
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's confession of Christ as the Son of God, on which the Church is founded, exclude the view that Christ is a creature made from nothing and Son only by adoption?

question: Do different names applied to God (such as "unbeginning" and "life") necessarily mean either different realities or the same meaning?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Gregory replies that the various terms used of God each keep their own meaning without dividing or opposing one another in the single subject. "Unbeginning" means that God's life was not given by another; it does not mean the same thing as "life" or "substance." Eunomius's argument, as Gregory sums it up, comes down to the claim that the most varied names do not differ in meaning, and Gregory rejects that claim.
sources.quote: But the upshot of all he says is this; that there is no difference in the meaning of the most varied names.
sources.raw_question: Do different names applied to God (such as "unbeginning" and "life") necessarily mean either different realities or the same meaning?

question: How is the guilt of past sin removed so that a sinner can appear before God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Only through Christ's atoning sacrifice. Christ expiates former iniquities, satisfies for sin, and procures remission; God set him forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood. This alone is our righteousness as to the removal of guilt, so that none can condemn those in Christ.
sources.quote: He expiates former iniquities, he satisfies for sin, and procures remission of it.
sources.raw_question: How is the guilt of past sin removed so that a sinner can appear before God?

question: Does Romans 5:10 distinguish between what Christ's death and Christ's life accomplish for believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen reads it as teaching that Christ's death reconciled us, while his life, namely the actual obedience he yielded to the whole law, is the righteousness by which we are saved, provided we are found in him with the righteousness which is of God by faith.
sources.quote: His death reconciled us; then are we saved by his life. The actual obedience which he yielded to the whole law of God, is that righteousness whereby we are saved
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 5:10 distinguish between what Christ's death and Christ's life accomplish for believers?

question: Does Christian spiritual rebirth show that some generation can be free from passion?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds again to discuss the impassibility of the Lord's generation; and the folly of Eunomius, who says that the generated essence involves the appellation of Son, and again, forgetting this, denies the relation of the Son to the Father: and herein he speaks of Circe and of the mandrake poison.
sources.answer: Yes. The generation "from above" that leads to the blessed life is not "of blood and of the will of the flesh" and lacks flux, change, and growth, and even the opponents admit it exists without passion. Hence generation as such does not imply passion, and much less does generation in the incorruptible divine Nature.
sources.quote: the other kind is believed to be from God, and heavenly, and, as the Gospel says, “from above,” which excludes the passions of flesh and blood?
sources.raw_question: Does Christian spiritual rebirth show that some generation can be free from passion?

question: If the Son were like the Father only in doctrine and teaching, would he truly be the Father's exact Image?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. On that view the Son would resemble the Father's doctrines rather than the Father himself. The Father would be Father in name only, and the Son would lack any propriety or likeness to the Father. Paul taught like the Saviour yet was not like him in essence, so likeness of teaching does not establish likeness of essence. The Son is like the Father as a son is to a father and as radiance is to the sun.
sources.quote: If then in respect to the doctrines and the teaching the Son is like the Father, then the Father according to them will be Father in name only, and the Son will not be an exact Image
sources.raw_question: If the Son were like the Father only in doctrine and teaching, would he truly be the Father's exact Image?

question: Does sharing the name 'angel' with created messengers prove that the Son is the same in nature as they are?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. Eunomius' principle that things sharing a name cannot differ in nature would make Christ no greater than John the Baptist, who is also called God's angel, and would put his deity on a level with that of Moses. Moses was called a god to the Egyptians yet remained a man and a servant. Scripture uses distinctive terms to separate the angelic nature from the supreme power of Godhead.
sources.quote: by giving Him the same name as the angels, trying to establish that He no wise differs from them in nature: for he has often previously said that all those things which share the same name cannot be different in nature
sources.raw_question: Does sharing the name 'angel' with created messengers prove that the Son is the same in nature as they are?

question: In 2 Corinthians 3:18, does "beholding" (speculantes) the glory of the Lord mean looking as in a mirror or looking from a watch-tower?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Apostle Says that God is Now Seen by Us Through a Glass.
sources.answer: It means seeing by means of a mirror. The Latin is ambiguous between "speculum" (mirror) and "specula" (watch-tower), but the Greek words are wholly distinct, and it is plain the apostle meant the word to come from "speculum."
sources.quote: it is quite plain that the apostle, in using the word “speculantes” in respect to the glory of the Lord, meant it to come from “speculum,” not from “specula.”
sources.raw_question: In 2 Corinthians 3:18, does "beholding" (speculantes) the glory of the Lord mean looking as in a mirror or looking from a watch-tower?

question: What does "from glory to glory" in 2 Corinthians 3:18 mean, and by whom is this transformation brought about?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
