sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Apostle Says that God is Now Seen by Us Through a Glass.
sources.answer: Chiefly it means from the glory of creation to the glory of justification, though it may also mean from the glory of faith to that of sight, or from being sons of God to being like Him when we see Him as He is. The addition "as by the Spirit of the Lord" shows the transformation is conferred by the grace of God.
sources.quote: And therefore he has added, “from glory to glory:” from the glory of creation to the glory of justification.
sources.raw_question: What does "from glory to glory" in 2 Corinthians 3:18 mean, and by whom is this transformation brought about?

question: Will Christ judge the world by his human nature or by his divine nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: He will judge as the Son of man, appearing in the human form, yet not by human power but by the divine power whereby he is the Son of God. Christ himself says the Son of man will come in his glory with all nations gathered before him, so the man will judge. Yet the judging is done by divine power, just as the Lord of glory was crucified though crucifixion belongs to the flesh.
sources.quote: Wherefore He will judge as the Son of man, yet not by human power, but by that whereby He is the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Will Christ judge the world by his human nature or by his divine nature?

question: Did the Old Testament patriarchs such as Abraham know God the Father, and if so, through whom did they receive that knowledge?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VII.—Recapitulation of the foregoing argument, showing that Abraham, through the revelation of the Word, knew the Father, and the coming of the Son of God. For this cause, he rejoiced to see the day of Christ, when the promises made to him should be fulfilled. The fruit of this rejoicing has flowed to posterity, viz., to those who are partakers in the faith of Abraham, but not to the Jews who reject the Word of God.
sources.answer: Yes. Abraham knew the Father through the Word, who made heaven and earth, and confessed Him to be God. All who have known God from the beginning and foretold Christ's advent received that revelation from the Son Himself, who was later made visible and passible in the last times.
sources.quote: how all who have known God from the beginning, and have foretold the advent of Christ, have received the revelation from the Son Himself; who also in the last times was made visible and passible
sources.raw_question: Did the Old Testament patriarchs such as Abraham know God the Father, and if so, through whom did they receive that knowledge?

question: How do future events exist in the wisdom of God before they happen in time?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In How Many Ways Things Future are Foreknown. Neither Philosophers, Nor Those Who Were Distinguished Among the Ancients, are to Be Consulted Concerning the Resurrection of the Dead.
sources.answer: In the Creator's wisdom the revolutions of the ages already were, and always were. In the created world, by contrast, they were only about to be and did not yet exist. Seeing them requires the mind to fix its eye on the eternity of the spiritual and unchangeable nature, which the proud philosophers could not do.
sources.quote: those revolutions of the ages, which in that wisdom were already and were always, but here were about to be so that as yet they were not
sources.raw_question: How do future events exist in the wisdom of God before they happen in time?

question: Was the Son first a man who later became God and Son as a reward, or was he God who became man?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: He was God and then became man, in order to deify us. If he were only called Son and God upon becoming man, he would be called so later than Israel, Moses and others who were called sons and gods, which contradicts Scripture's teaching that all things are through him and that he is before all and first-born of all creation.
sources.quote: Therefore He was not man, and then became God, but He was God, and then became man, and that to deify us
sources.raw_question: Was the Son first a man who later became God and Son as a reward, or was he God who became man?

question: When Paul says Christ was 'highly exalted' after the Passion, is the Son exalted as God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then returning to the words of Peter, “God made Him Lord and Christ,” he skilfully explains it by many arguments, and herein shows Eunomius as an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, and concludes the book by showing that the Divine and Human names are applied, by reason of the commixture, to either Nature.
sources.answer: No. Nothing is higher than the Divine height, so God cannot be exalted to it. What was exalted was the lowliness of the humanity. The word indicates that the assumed Man was assimilated to and united with the exalted state of the Divine Nature.
sources.quote: For what height is there more sublime than the Divine height, that he should say God was exalted thereunto? But he means that the lowliness of the Humanity was exalted
sources.raw_question: When Paul says Christ was 'highly exalted' after the Passion, is the Son exalted as God?

question: Did Simeon recognize the infant Jesus, born of Mary, as Christ himself, the Son of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: Yes. Holding the infant in his arms, Simeon confessed that this child born of Mary was Christ himself, the Son of God, the light of all and the glory of Israel. The child was already doing Christ's works, removing ignorance and imparting knowledge, so he was Christ from birth, not a man on whom Christ later descended.
sources.quote: confessing thus, that the infant whom he was holding in his hands, Jesus, born of Mary, was Christ Himself, the Son of God, the light of all, the glory of Israel itself
sources.raw_question: Did Simeon recognize the infant Jesus, born of Mary, as Christ himself, the Son of God?

question: Can the Holy Spirit rightly be called Lord of Sabaoth (Lord of hosts or powers)?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXI. Isaiah was sent by the Spirit, and accordingly the same Spirit was seen by him. What is meant by the revolving wheels, and the divers wings, and how since the Spirit is proclaimed Lord of Sabaoth by the Seraphim, certainly none but impious men can deny Him this title.
sources.answer: Yes. The Seraphim proclaim Him Lord of Sabaoth in Isaiah's vision, and only the impious can deny that the Spirit is Lord of powers. He is the one who distributes whatever powers He Himself wills, which shows His sovereign lordship.
sources.quote: Therefore the Holy Spirit is also the Lord of Sabaoth. Unless perchance the Teacher Whom Christ chose pleases not the impious, or they can deny that the Holy Spirit is the Lord of powers, Who gives whatever powers He Himself wills.
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit rightly be called Lord of Sabaoth (Lord of hosts or powers)?

question: Should we curiously investigate God's nature, or rather praise Him?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXI. Isaiah was sent by the Spirit, and accordingly the same Spirit was seen by him. What is meant by the revolving wheels, and the divers wings, and how since the Spirit is proclaimed Lord of Sabaoth by the Seraphim, certainly none but impious men can deny Him this title.
sources.answer: We should praise Him, not question. If we cannot even understand how the Seraphim could both stand and fly, we cannot expect to comprehend God, whom we have not seen. The Seraphim praise with unwearied voices, teaching us always to praise God rather than inquire into Him.
sources.quote: If we cannot understand this, how is it that we want to understand God, Whom we have not seen?
sources.raw_question: Should we curiously investigate God's nature, or rather praise Him?

question: Does the Epistle to the Hebrews show that the Old Testament word was spoken by angels, in contrast to the New Testament word spoken by the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: Yes. Hebrews contrasts "the word spoken by angels" with the salvation "which at the first began to be spoken by the Lord," showing that as the Old Testament word was spoken by angels, so the New is spoken by the Son. Because it says "by angels" in the plural, it gives a plainer testimony than texts mentioning a single angel, which some take to be the Son.
sources.quote: demonstrating by plain consequence that as at that time the word was spoken by the angels, so now by the Son
sources.raw_question: Does the Epistle to the Hebrews show that the Old Testament word was spoken by angels, in contrast to the New Testament word spoken by the Son?

question: Is the Son a portion or severed part of the Father's substance, as Manichæus taught?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The Church knows nothing of the Son as a portion; she knows Him as whole God from whole God, One from One, not severed but born. Manichæus's notion of a piece of God's substance cut off and appearing in the flesh is blasphemy.
sources.quote: She knows Him as whole God from whole God, as One from One, not severed but born.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son a portion or severed part of the Father's substance, as Manichæus taught?

question: Does a believer's own religious righteousness, zeal and spiritual privileges keep any value as a ground of acceptance once Christ is known?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: No. Owen reads Paul in Philippians 3 as counting all his spiritual privileges and law-righteousness as loss and dung compared with Christ. Once Christ is known in his excellency, these things, taken without him, lose their beauty, and the soul puts them away as defiled. It confesses that its righteousness and glory are in the Lord Jesus alone.
sources.quote: when once Christ appears to the soul, when he is known in his excellency, all these things, as without him, have their paint washed off, their beauty fades, their desirableness vanisheth
sources.raw_question: Does a believer's own religious righteousness, zeal and spiritual privileges keep any value as a ground of acceptance once Christ is known?

question: Why does the Gospel of John follow its promise that believers become sons of God with the statement that the Word was made flesh?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > We Say that Future Blessedness is Truly Eternal, Not Through Human Reasonings, But by the Help of Faith. The Immortality of Blessedness Becomes Credible from the Incarnation of the Son of God.
sources.answer: To keep human weakness from despairing of so great an excellence. If the Son of God by nature became Son of man through mercy, it becomes far more credible that sons of men by nature should become sons of God by grace and dwell in God. The Son shared our mortality to convince us that we may share His immortality.
sources.quote: how much more credible is it that the sons of men by nature should be made the sons of God by the grace of God, and should dwell in God
sources.raw_question: Why does the Gospel of John follow its promise that believers become sons of God with the statement that the Word was made flesh?

question: Can knowing that God transcends knowledge itself count as a kind of knowledge of God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. The mind gains knowledge partly by reasoning and partly from its very inability to discern God, for it is a sort of knowledge to know that what is sought transcends knowledge. From the properties that are or are not in Him, the mind sees that what is removed from all evil and contains all good is ineffable and incomprehensible.
sources.quote: finding that it is a sort of knowledge to know that what is sought transcends knowledge
sources.raw_question: Can knowing that God transcends knowledge itself count as a kind of knowledge of God?

question: Does the phrase 'God gave Him the Name above every name' mean that the Son received worship or grace he did not possess before?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. Even before he became man he was worshipped by the angels and all creation, as being proper to the Father. As man he is said to receive what as God he always had, so that the grant of grace might reach us. The Word was not impaired by taking a body; rather he deified what he put on.
sources.quote: as Christ died and was exalted as man, so, as man, is He said to take what, as God, He ever had, that even such a grant of grace might reach to us.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'God gave Him the Name above every name' mean that the Son received worship or grace he did not possess before?

question: Does Christ's promise that the Spirit would come and lead the disciples into all truth set the Spirit's power above that of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIV. Besides the evidence adduced above, other passages can be brought to prove the sovereignty of the Three Persons. Two are quoted from the Epistles to the Thessalonians, and by collating other testimonies of the Scriptures it is shown that in them dominion is claimed for the Spirit as for the other Persons. Then, by quotation of another still more express passage in the second Epistle to the Corinthians, it is inferred both that the Spirit is Lord, and that where the Lord is, there is the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Christ said the Spirit would make the disciples, who were like little children, into stronger men by spiritual growth. But he said this not to put the Spirit's power in first place. He said it to show that fulness of strength consists in the knowledge of the Trinity.
sources.quote: this He laid down not that He might set the power of the Spirit in the first place, but that He might show that the fulness of strength consists in the knowledge of the Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's promise that the Spirit would come and lead the disciples into all truth set the Spirit's power above that of the Father and the Son?

question: Would an explicit scriptural statement of the Trinity have settled all controversy about the Godhead of Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Not certainly. Such a text would have been exposed to manuscript variations and disputes like any other. Even if it were as clear as the opening of St. John's Gospel, those unconvinced by that passage would probably remain unconvinced, because saving faith is the gift of God, not the product of a proof-text.
sources.quote: But even if the text were as impregnable as the opening of St. John’s Gospel, I doubt whether it would have convinced such minds as remain unconvinced of the Godhead of Christ, after weighing those transparent declarations.
sources.raw_question: Would an explicit scriptural statement of the Trinity have settled all controversy about the Godhead of Christ?

question: Does the Holy Spirit hold power over natural life and death?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says the Spirit of God made man. When God sends forth his Spirit, creatures are created, and the grass withers when the Spirit of the Lord blows on it. So the issues of life and death are in his hands.
sources.quote: In his hands are the issues of life and death.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit hold power over natural life and death?

question: Is the Holy Spirit the author of the whole spiritual life in believers, including the future resurrection?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. He regenerates the soul dead in sin, teaches prayer, and dwells in believers as his temple. He produces his fruits, seals them for redemption, sanctifies them into the divine image, and bears witness that they are God's children. As the one who quickened Christ, he will quicken their mortal bodies at the last day.
sources.quote: And by him, as the One who quickened Christ our Head, will God quicken our mortal bodies at the last day.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit the author of the whole spiritual life in believers, including the future resurrection?

question: In what sense is the Father self-existent and the source of all things?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: The Father is the origin of all existence, acting in and through Christ, and unlike everything else He does not draw His being from outside but possesses it from and in Himself. He is unbegotten, everlasting and inherently eternal, and He is anterior to time, since time is His creation.
sources.quote: In contrast to all else He is self-existent. He does not draw His being from without, but possesses it from Himself and in Himself.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Father self-existent and the source of all things?

question: Do the Arian-type heretics' teachings divide the unity of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Yes, and wrongly. By assigning differences of nature to Father and Son they divide the indivisible and dissolve the perfect unity of God. Such teaching also presumes to make laws for Omnipotence and to limit Infinity.
sources.quote: who pervert the truth, darken the light, divide the indivisible, rend the scatheless, dissolve the perfect unity
sources.raw_question: Do the Arian-type heretics' teachings divide the unity of God?

question: If the Creator made spiritual and holy beings, can he himself be of a merely animal (non-spiritual) nature?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: No. Since the Creator produced spiritual and holy beings, he who produced spiritual beings cannot himself be of an animal nature. This overthrows the Gnostic system that ranks the Creator below spiritual beings.
sources.quote: If, on the other hand, these were made by the Creator, as was really the case, and are of a spiritual and holy character, then it follows that He who produced spiritual beings is not Himself of an animal nature
sources.raw_question: If the Creator made spiritual and holy beings, can he himself be of a merely animal (non-spiritual) nature?

question: How can two things be distinct by relation and yet one in essence, as illustrated by lover and love in the mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three Things Which are Found in Love Must Be Considered.
sources.answer: Lover and love are said relatively, each referred to the other. Take away the lover and there is no love; take away love and there is no lover. Insofar as they are referred to one another they are two. But 'mind' and 'spirit' express essence, not relation, so each is spirit and both together are one spirit and one mind. This shows how relative terms distinguish while essential terms unite, as in the Trinity.
sources.quote: And therefore, in so far as they are mutually referred to one another, they are two; but whereas they are spoken in respect to themselves, each are spirit, and both together also are one spirit; and each are mind, and both together one mind.
sources.raw_question: How can two things be distinct by relation and yet one in essence, as illustrated by lover and love in the mind?

question: Since Christ's death was an act of his own free will, could death have held any terror for him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Human death comes upon us from outside or through the decay of age. Christ instead had power to lay down his life and take it up again. He bowed his head and gave up his Spirit of his own will. Because death was in his own power, it held no terror for him.
sources.quote: But if He died of His own will, and through His own will gave back His Spirit, death had no terror; because it was in His own power.
sources.raw_question: Since Christ's death was an act of his own free will, could death have held any terror for him?

question: How are God's power, wisdom and goodness shown in creation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVIII.—Why man was not made perfect from the beginning.
sources.answer: All three are displayed together. His power and goodness appear in His freely calling into being things that did not previously exist. His wisdom appears in making created things parts of one harmonious whole. His ungrudging goodness is further shown in granting them growth and long existence.
sources.quote: His power and goodness [appear] in this, that of His own will He called into being and fashioned things having no previous existence; His wisdom [is shown] in His having made created things parts of one harmonious and consistent whole
sources.raw_question: How are God's power, wisdom and goodness shown in creation?

question: Can the Holy Spirit as third person be derived from the self-consciousness argument for the Trinity?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Not convincingly. Every attempt to construct the Trinity rationally from self-consciousness treats the third hypostasis as a standing puzzle. It reaches the Spirit only by a very artificial solution.
sources.quote: The discovery of the third hypostasis – the Holy Spirit -remains meanwhile, to all these attempts rationally to construct a Trinity in the Divine Being, a standing puzzle which finds only a very artificial solution.
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit as third person be derived from the self-consciousness argument for the Trinity?

question: Why did Paul present Christ to immature believers as crucified rather than in his divine equality with the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > This Work is Written Against Those Who Sophistically Assail the Faith of the Trinity, Through Misuse of Reason. They Who Dispute Concerning God Err from a Threefold Cause. Holy Scripture, Removing What is False, Leads Us on by Degrees to Things Divine. What True Immortality is. We are Nourished by Faith, that We May Be Enabled to Apprehend Things Divine.
sources.answer: He did it out of accommodation to their weakness. All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid in Christ, but carnal believers, who are babes in Christ, cannot yet bear solid food. So Paul commended Christ to them through the human infirmity in which he was crucified, not through the divine virtue in which he is equal to the Father.
sources.quote: not by that divine virtue wherein He is equal to the Father, but by that human infirmity whereby He was crucified
sources.raw_question: Why did Paul present Christ to immature believers as crucified rather than in his divine equality with the Father?

question: Does the 'obedience of one' in Romans 5:19 refer only to Christ's passive obedience (his sufferings and death)?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: No. It is set against Adam's disobedience, which was an active transgression, so the opposing righteousness must be an active fulfilment of the law. Obedience in its own nature denotes actions conformable to the law, and Christ came to fulfil the law (Matthew 5:17) for us.
sources.quote: The fault was an active transgression of the law, and the obedience opposed to it must be an active accomplishment of it.
sources.raw_question: Does the 'obedience of one' in Romans 5:19 refer only to Christ's passive obedience (his sufferings and death)?

question: Is the faith in one God the Father, the incarnation of the Son of God and the gift of the Spirit held in common by the whole Church, and does that common confession mark it as true over against the heretics?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XX.—Those pastors are to be heard to whom the apostles committed the Churches, possessing one and the same doctrine of salvation; the heretics, on the other hand, are to be avoided. We must think soberly with regard to the mysteries of the faith.
sources.answer: Yes. The Church throughout the world holds the sure tradition received from the apostles. All its members receive one and the same God the Father, the same dispensation of the Son's incarnation and the same gift of the Spirit. The heretics, by contrast, are later in date and scattered in disagreeing opinions. This worldwide agreement in one way of salvation shows that the Church's preaching is true and steadfast.
sources.quote: since all receive one and the same God the Father, and believe in the same dispensation regarding the incarnation of the Son of God, and are cognizant of the same gift of the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Is the faith in one God the Father, the incarnation of the Son of God and the gift of the Spirit held in common by the whole Church, and does that common confession mark it as true over against the heretics?

question: What do the scriptural titles Son, brightness, God, express image and form of God show about the Son's divinity?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Together they establish the Son's perfect divinity. "Son" shows His close kinship of nature with the Father. "Brightness" shows that He is joined to and inseparable from the Father. "God," applied to both, shows their complete equality. "Express image" shows that the Son lacks none of the Father's greatness, and "form of God" shows His complete identity in all the marks of Godhead.
sources.quote: by the appellation of “God,” applied alike to the Father and the Son, their absolute equality, while the “express image,” contemplated in reference to the whole Person of the Father, marks the absence of any defect in the Son’s proper greatness
sources.raw_question: What do the scriptural titles Son, brightness, God, express image and form of God show about the Son's divinity?

question: Is an explicit profession of the Son's 'eternal generation' essential to orthodoxy, or is the eternal personal existence of the Word what really matters?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: The essential point is the eternal existence of the Logos as a real subsisting person, in and of the Father. Waterland says an explicit profession of eternal generation might have been dispensed with, provided that point is secured, because it comes to the same thing. On this all sound Catholics agreed, and to dispute it was counted heresy. He adds that the safer course is still to keep the received language.
sources.quote: an explicit profession of eternal generation might have been dispensed with ; provided only that the eternal existence of the Adyos, as a real subsisting person, in, and of ™the Father, which comes to the same thing, might be secured.
sources.raw_question: Is an explicit profession of the Son's 'eternal generation' essential to orthodoxy, or is the eternal personal existence of the Word what really matters?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's being the first-produced work of the Son, prior to other creatures, prove that he surpasses them in nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: No. If priority in production made something superior, irrational animals would be superior to man, Cain to Abel, and the plants of the third day to the stars of the fourth. Since no one accepts these conclusions, temporal priority proves nothing about excellence of nature, and Eunomius's ground for exalting the Spirit above creatures (while still counting him a creature) is senseless.
sources.quote: So there is no sense in our author’s contention that the nature of the Holy Spirit is superior to that of the creatures that came into being subsequently, on the ground that He came into being before they did.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's being the first-produced work of the Son, prior to other creatures, prove that he surpasses them in nature?

question: If the Son was made, as Dr. Clarke's principles imply, can we conceive of a time when the Son did not exist?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 15: Whether he also must not, of consequence, affirm of the Son, that there was a time when he was not, since God must ewist before the creature; and therefore 1s a
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son was made at all, then he was made in time like any angel or archangel. We not only can but must conceive of countless ages, an eternity a parte ante, before he came into being. Replacing the word 'time' with 'duration' does not remove this consequence.
sources.quote: We can conceive, and must conceive, that there were millions and millions of ages backwards; an eternity, ὦ parte ante, before he came into being.
sources.raw_question: If the Son was made, as Dr. Clarke's principles imply, can we conceive of a time when the Son did not exist?

question: Does teaching that the Word of God is a creature who once did not exist amount to turning from the true Word to a non-existent fiction?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Extracts from the Thalia of Arius. Arius maintains that God became a Father, and the Son was not always; the Son out of nothing; once He was not; He was not before his generation; He was created; named Wisdom and Word after God's attributes; made that He might make us; one out of many powers of God; alterable; exalted on God's foreknowledge of what He was to be; not very God; but called so as others by participation; foreign in essence from the Father; does not know or see the Father; does not know Himself.
sources.answer: Yes. The Word of God truly and eternally is. Arius rejects this Word and invents in his place a Son who 'once was not,' a Word of his own making that does not exist. Athanasius reads Hosea's complaint that the people 'turn away to nothing' as describing this: abandoning the Word who is for an imagined one is falling to what is nothing.
sources.quote: For to turn away from the Word of God, which is, and to fashion to themselves one that is not, is to fall to what is nothing.
sources.raw_question: Does teaching that the Word of God is a creature who once did not exist amount to turning from the true Word to a non-existent fiction?

question: Does God's power being made perfect in weakness refer to the flesh?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter III.—The power and glory of God shine forth in the weakness of human flesh, as He will render our body a participator of the resurrection and of immortality, although He has formed it from the dust of the earth; He will also bestow upon it the enjoyment of immortality, just as He grants it this short life in common with the soul.
sources.answer: Yes. The weakness in which the power of the life-giver is perfected is the flesh, which shares in God's constructive wisdom and power. So the flesh's frailty is no obstacle to God giving it life.
sources.quote: But if the power of Him who is the bestower of life is made perfect in weakness —that is, in the flesh—
sources.raw_question: Does God's power being made perfect in weakness refer to the flesh?

question: By what means were the words and visible appearances before the incarnation that foreshadowed Christ produced?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Of the Sensible Showing of the Holy Spirit, and of the Coeternity of the Trinity. What Has Been Said, and What Remains to Be Said.
sources.answer: God produced them through the angels. Augustine holds that he has shown this sufficiently from the testimonies of Scripture. The angelic nature could foreshadow the person of Christ but could not take it on.
sources.quote: I reply that God wrought those things by the angels; and this I have also shown sufficiently, as I think, by testimonies of the Holy Scriptures
sources.raw_question: By what means were the words and visible appearances before the incarnation that foreshadowed Christ produced?

question: Is the deepest wisdom of God known from creation, providence and the law, or is it hidden in and revealed only by Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: The depth of God's wisdom is hidden in and revealed only by Christ. God does show infinite wisdom in creation, providence and his law, but the wisdom Paul marvels at in Romans 11:33 belongs to God's design carried out in Christ and revealed in the gospel. That is why Christ is called the wisdom of God, and why the gospel is called God's hidden and manifold wisdom.
sources.quote: “The depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God,” Rom. xi. 33; — that is only hid in and revealed by Christ.
sources.raw_question: Is the deepest wisdom of God known from creation, providence and the law, or is it hidden in and revealed only by Christ?

question: What does Christ's self-description in John 14:6 as the Way, the Truth and the Life teach about how we come to the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: The way to the Father is through the Son. These names show the method Christ appointed for our salvation: as the Way he guides us to the Truth, and the Truth establishes us in the Life. Hilary then asks whether this way is simply obedience to Christ's teaching or faith that the Father's Godhead dwells in him. He says the question must be settled from the force of the words that follow, which reveal the Father's nature dwelling in the Son.
sources.quote: As the Way, He will guide us to the Truth; the Truth will establish us in the Life.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's self-description in John 14:6 as the Way, the Truth and the Life teach about how we come to the Father?

question: What distinguishes a true sonship by birth from an adoptive sonship?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Adoptive sonship is imputed, not real: the adopted son was something else before he became a son and so was not always a son. In birth the father's ownership comes first and then his love, while in adoption the son is first made a firstborn and then owned. Hence there is no true and complete birth where sonship is imputed.
sources.quote: Accordingly there is no true and complete birth where sonship is imputed rather than real: since it is not doubtful that that people, which is born into a state of sonship, is also made.
sources.raw_question: What distinguishes a true sonship by birth from an adoptive sonship?

question: Why does it matter for salvation that the Word was made truly what we are, body and soul?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXII.—Christ assumed actual flesh, conceived and born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: Because otherwise his suffering would accomplish nothing great. Man consists of a body taken from the earth and a soul receiving spirit from God, and the Word was made this. In doing so he recapitulated his own handiwork in himself, bringing salvation to it.
sources.quote: But every one will allow that we are [composed of] a body taken from the earth, and a soul receiving spirit from God. This, therefore, the Word of God was made, recapitulating in Himself His own handiwork
sources.raw_question: Why does it matter for salvation that the Word was made truly what we are, body and soul?

question: Who is meant in Psalm 82, "God stood in the congregation of the gods," and who are the "gods" there?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: The Father and the Son are meant, together with those who have received adoption, who are the Church. The Church is the synagogue of God, which God, that is the Son himself, has gathered. The "gods" are those to whom it is said, "Ye are gods, and all sons of the Most High," namely those who have received the grace of adoption by which they cry "Abba, Father."
sources.quote: He [here] refers to the Father and the Son, and those who have received the adoption; but these are the Church.
sources.raw_question: Who is meant in Psalm 82, "God stood in the congregation of the gods," and who are the "gods" there?

question: When Scripture calls idols "gods," does it acknowledge them as gods in any real sense?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: No. Scripture never calls them gods absolutely, but always with an addition that shows they are no gods at all, such as "gods of the heathen," "other gods," "idols of demons," or gods that will perish. It uses the word only so that we may know of whom it speaks.
sources.quote: it does not, as I have already remarked, declare them as gods in every sense, but with a certain addition and signification, by which they are shown to be no gods at all.
sources.raw_question: When Scripture calls idols "gods," does it acknowledge them as gods in any real sense?

question: Can people who do not share in the promised Holy Spirit have true consolation, in either affliction or prosperity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. Without the Spirit, people must bear their troubles in their own natural strength. That resolve is mostly outward show, and at best it is a contending with God, who sends affliction to disturb their security. Any comfort they draw from God's supposed care is like a hungry man's dream. Their prosperity, as Solomon found, is vanity and vexation of spirit, like a crackling of thorns under the pot.
sources.quote: They have no true consolation or comfort, be their estate and condition what it will.
sources.raw_question: Can people who do not share in the promised Holy Spirit have true consolation, in either affliction or prosperity?

question: Is Christ himself the only way and medium of communion between God and believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ declares, "I am the way; and no man comes to the Father but by me," so the way he prepared is no other than himself. All love, kindness and mercy from God to us come through him, and all our love, faith and obedience return to God through him. All other paths lead down to death and to walking contrary to God.
sources.quote: He is the medium of all communication between God and us. In him we meet, in him we walk. All influences of love, kindness, mercy, from God to us, are through him
sources.raw_question: Is Christ himself the only way and medium of communion between God and believers?

question: Is the ascription of divine attributes to Christ confined to a few obscure texts?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: No. All the essential attributes of Godhead are ascribed to Christ by a general consensus of the inspired writers, not in one or two obscure passages. Many more proof texts could be added.
sources.quote: Here then we have all the essential attributes
sources.raw_question: Is the ascription of divine attributes to Christ confined to a few obscure texts?

question: Do the divine attributes ascribed to Christ require believers to trust, love and adore him as God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ fills toward us the offices of God: he made us, sustains us, watches us, and will judge us. If we believe this testimony, we must confide in him, love him and adore him. Nothing short of entire reliance and supreme love answers his claims.
sources.quote: The offices He fills towards you are those of God. And He is so unutterably good and gracious. What remains? If you believe this testimony, you must confide in him – you must love him – you must adore him.
sources.raw_question: Do the divine attributes ascribed to Christ require believers to trust, love and adore him as God?

question: Is there anything contrary to reason in confessing God born of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Hilary saw nothing contrary to reason in God of God, since the Son was revealed as having been in the beginning God with God. This shows the Son existing eternally alongside the Father as God.
sources.quote: Nor yet did my soul perceive anything contrary to reason in God of God, since He was revealed as having been in the beginning God with God.
sources.raw_question: Is there anything contrary to reason in confessing God born of God?

question: Does becoming a son of God come by inheritance or compulsion, or by free choice through faith?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: By free choice through faith. Sonship to God is a possibility rather than a compulsion. The divine gift is offered to all, but it is no inevitable heredity; it is a prize awarded to a willing choice, through a birth of faith rather than of the flesh.
sources.quote: this sonship to God is not a compulsion but a possibility, for, while the Divine gift is offered to all, it is no heredity inevitably imprinted but a prize awarded to willing choice
sources.raw_question: Does becoming a son of God come by inheritance or compulsion, or by free choice through faith?

question: What is the order of the divine dispensations among the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit with respect to glory?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Each Person glorifies the other in an ordered way. All flows from the fountain of the Father's love, and the Son came to glorify the Father, seeking not his own glory. Having finished redemption, the Son was to be glorified with the Father with the glory he had before the world was. The Holy Ghost is then sent to glorify the Son, so a spirit that glorifies itself inverts this divine order.
sources.quote: The fountain of all being and lying in the Father’s love, the Son came to glorify the Father. He still says, “I seek not mine own glory, but the glory of him that sent me.”
sources.raw_question: What is the order of the divine dispensations among the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit with respect to glory?

question: How did the early Fathers answer the objection that the Son's generation divides or diminishes the Father's substance?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: They denied any division or diminution of the Father's substance, but never denied the ground of the objection by comparing the Son to a created being. They illustrated the mystery by light kindled from light, the sun and its rays, fountain and streams, stock and branch, all instances of the same specific nature, signifying proper consubstantiality.
sources.quote: they only deny any division. or diminution of the Father's substance, and illus- — trate, as well as they are able, so sublime a mystery, by one light kindled, as it were, from another ; by the sun and its rays ; by fountain and streams; stock and branch
sources.raw_question: How did the early Fathers answer the objection that the Son's generation divides or diminishes the Father's substance?

question: Does God's love for us precede our love for him and anything lovely in us?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father's love is antecedent: 'not that we loved God, but that he loved us' (1 John 4:10). By nature we are haters of God, while he is by nature a lover of men, so all mutual love must begin on his side. It also precedes anything lovely in us, since Christ died for us while we were yet sinners (Rom. 5:8); he loves us not because we are better than others but because he himself is infinitely good.
sources.quote: Yea, we are by nature θεοστυγεῖς, Rom. i. 30, — haters of God. He is in his own nature φιλάνθρωπος, — a lover of men; and surely all mutual love between him and us must begin on his hand.
sources.raw_question: Does God's love for us precede our love for him and anything lovely in us?

question: If Christ were only a creature, would worshipping him be idolatry, even though it is far better than worshipping heathen idols?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: Yes. Worshipping Christ is indeed much preferable to pagan worship, just as worshipping saints and angels is. But such acts, though not equally culpable, are equally idolatry and breaches of the first Commandment. Whatever love and gratitude a creature might deserve, it cannot rise to worship, which belongs to God alone.
sources.quote: The worship even of saints and angels is much preferable to Pagan worship. But still they are both equally, though not equally culpable, idolatry ; and are breaches of the first Commandment.
sources.raw_question: If Christ were only a creature, would worshipping him be idolatry, even though it is far better than worshipping heathen idols?

question: Does God's command to worship Christ free the Arians from the charge of idolatry if they hold that Christ is a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. Because the primary and perpetual law is that God alone is to be worshipped, any worship inconsistent with that law is idolatrous, whether in practice or in principle. The Arians obey a Scripture command but not on Scripture principles. They perform a Christian duty on the pagan foundation of creature-worship and polytheism, and so they stand charged with idolatry.
sources.quote: the Arians, following a Scripturecommand, but not upon Scripture-principles, and practising a Christian duty upon a Pagan foundation of creature-worship, and polytheism, stand charged with idolatry.
sources.raw_question: Does God's command to worship Christ free the Arians from the charge of idolatry if they hold that Christ is a creature?

question: What does Christ mean by promising that the Comforter will abide with the disciples "for ever" (John 14:16)?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: The promise is made in contrast to Christ's own bodily presence, which lasted only a short time. Christ assures the disciples that the Spirit will not merely visit them briefly as he did. The coming of the Spirit is the last dispensation, and no other is to be expected. The Comforter does all the remaining work and will never depart.
sources.quote: He is promised to abide with the disciples for ever, in opposition to the abode of Christ. Christ, in the flesh, had been with them for a little while, and now was leaving them
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean by promising that the Comforter will abide with the disciples "for ever" (John 14:16)?

question: Does the Holy Spirit ever completely and universally leave a believer without consolation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: No. A believer may be darkened, refuse comfort, and actually feel none. Yet radically he keeps a foundation of consolation that will be drawn out in due time. God's promises to restore comfort, as in Isaiah 57:18, mean that such people had less comfort than they needed, not that they had none at all.
sources.quote: I deny that ever the Holy Spirit doth absolutely and universally leave a believing soul without consolation.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit ever completely and universally leave a believer without consolation?

question: In the incarnation, is the divinity changed into the creature or the humanity changed into God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Less Than the Father, and Than Himself.
sources.answer: Neither. The form of God took the form of a servant, so that the one Christ is both God, because of God who takes, and man, because of the man who is taken. The divinity does not cease to be divinity by becoming creature. Nor does the creature become divinity and cease to be creature.
sources.quote: the Divinity is not changed into the creature, so as to cease to be Divinity; nor the creature into Divinity, so as to cease to be creature.
sources.raw_question: In the incarnation, is the divinity changed into the creature or the humanity changed into God?

question: Does 1 Corinthians 12:3, 'No man can say that Jesus is the Lord but by the Holy Ghost,' show that faith in the Son depends on the Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That they who deny the Spirit are transgressors.
sources.answer: Yes. Basil cites it to prove that confession of the Son as Lord is only possible through the Spirit, so that rejecting the Spirit removes the very ground of faith in the Son, and consequently in the Father whom the Son reveals.
sources.quote: For none “can say that Jesus is the Lord but by the Holy Ghost,”
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 12:3, 'No man can say that Jesus is the Lord but by the Holy Ghost,' show that faith in the Son depends on the Spirit?

question: Is it legitimate to ask 'when, where, and whether' the Son was made, as one might ask of a created thing?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections to the Foregoing Proof. Whether, in the generation of the Son, God made One that was already, or One that was not.
sources.answer: No. Such questions treat what comes from the Father as external to Him, the way someone might wrongly treat the sun's radiance as external to the sun. To call the natural offspring a work and say 'he was not before his generation' is madness. It conceives of the Father's Word as outside Him.
sources.quote: it is to conceive of the Word of the Father as external to Him, and to idly call the natural offspring a work, with the avowal, ‘He was not before His generation.’
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to ask 'when, where, and whether' the Son was made, as one might ask of a created thing?

question: Did the Father give the Son, as divine Son, dominion over us, implying a derived and lesser authority?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: Not as divine Son. This cannot be proved unless it is understood of Christ considered as God-man or Mediator.
sources.quote: That is more than you can prove; unless you understand it of Christ, considered as God-man, or Mediator.
sources.raw_question: Did the Father give the Son, as divine Son, dominion over us, implying a derived and lesser authority?

question: Should the ancient doxologies, such as glory to the Father through the Son, be read as excluding the Son and Spirit from proper divine worship?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. The ancient doxologies differed in form but had one meaning, to be understood according to the prevailing primitive doctrine. The Arians were the first to wrest some of them to favour creature-worship or exclude the Son and Spirit, and the Catholics answered by asserting their true sense and using less equivocal forms.
sources.quote: They were different in form, but had all one meaning ; the same which I have shewn you from the primitive writers. The Arians were the first who interpreted some of them to such a sense
sources.raw_question: Should the ancient doxologies, such as glory to the Father through the Son, be read as excluding the Son and Spirit from proper divine worship?

question: Is the Son's nature limited or measured by the amount of the productive power that brought Him into being, so that He falls short of perfection?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The blasphemy of these heretics is worse than the Jewish unbelief.
sources.answer: No. Gregory rejects the idea of enclosing the Son within the limits of a power that made Him, calling it a cloak devised to muffle Him up in. The divine being has no quantity or size, so it cannot be measured to show how far the Only-begotten falls short of perfection. Making the Son's being less than the Father's is, when strictly tested, the height of blasphemy.
sources.quote: though they do not tell us by what method they measure that which is devoid of quantity and size
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's nature limited or measured by the amount of the productive power that brought Him into being, so that He falls short of perfection?

question: Can the Father be considered 'older' than the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Answer to the question he is always asking, “Can He who is be begotten?”
sources.answer: No. 'Older' and 'younger' involve intervals of time, and time does not enter the Eternal life. Once time is mentally abstracted from divine generation, all such notions of priority in age disappear with it.
sources.quote: ‘Older’ and ‘younger’ and all such notions are found to involve intervals of time; and so, when you mentally abstract time in general, all such indications are got rid of along with it.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father be considered 'older' than the Son?

question: How can Christ say in John 16:26 that he will not pray the Father for the disciples, when in John 14:16 he says he will pray the Father for them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Christ will pray the Father to send the Spirit and the fruits of the Father's love. The Father's love itself, however, needs no intercession to procure it, for the Father himself loves them. Christ's words remove the disciples' fear that he must win the Father's love for them.
sources.quote: I will pray the Father to send you the Spirit, the Comforter, and with him all the gracious fruits of his love; but yet in the point of love itself, free love, eternal love, there is no need of any intercession for that
sources.raw_question: How can Christ say in John 16:26 that he will not pray the Father for the disciples, when in John 14:16 he says he will pray the Father for them?

question: How can one tell in Scripture whether a statement refers to the Son's Godhead or to his human origination?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: When Scripture speaks of the Son's fleshly origination it adds the cause for which He became man. When it speaks of His Godhead, it uses simple, absolute language without giving a reason. So John 1:1 gives no 'wherefore', but 'the Word was made flesh' adds 'and dwelt among us'. Likewise Philippians 2 gives no reason for 'being in the form of God', but adds one once He took the form of a servant.
sources.quote: when it signifies the fleshly origination of the Son, it adds also the cause for which He became man; but when he speaks or His servants declare anything of His Godhead, all is said in simple diction, and with an absolute sense, and without reason being added.
sources.raw_question: How can one tell in Scripture whether a statement refers to the Son's Godhead or to his human origination?

question: Must the Word (Logos) who comes forth from the Father be perfect and impassible?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father is perfect and impassible Mind. Therefore the Logos who springs from him must also be perfect and impassible, and so must whatever proceeds from him that is of the same substance. It is impious to ascribe passion and ignorance to the Father of all, and so it is impious to ascribe them to his Wisdom or Word.
sources.quote: It necessarily follows, therefore, both that he who springs from Him as Logos, or rather that Nous himself, since he is Logos, must be perfect and impassible
sources.raw_question: Must the Word (Logos) who comes forth from the Father be perfect and impassible?

question: In what way was the Word 'made flesh': by being changed into flesh, by appearing in the likeness of flesh, or by assuming a human nature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: By assuming a human nature. The Word did not convert himself into flesh, nor merely appear in the outward shape of flesh. He took the holy thing born of the virgin into personal union with himself.
sources.quote: not by a conversion of itself into flesh; not by appearing in the outward shape and likeness of flesh; but by assuming that holy thing that was born of the virgin, Luke i. 35, into personal union with himself.
sources.raw_question: In what way was the Word 'made flesh': by being changed into flesh, by appearing in the likeness of flesh, or by assuming a human nature?

question: Can a creature act as the agent through whom God brings things from nothing into being?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: No. No creature can make what is not into what is; angels, sun, and man can at most arrange existing materials. Only God creates from nothing, so the Word through whom all things were made cannot be a creature, and God is a Maker, not merely an artificer working on materials.
sources.quote: And if through Him He creates and makes, He is not Himself of things created and made; but rather He is the Word of the Creator God
sources.raw_question: Can a creature act as the agent through whom God brings things from nothing into being?

question: If the Son were merely the most glorious creature, how would Scripture describe him?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Chapter XVI.--Introductory to Proverbs viii. 22, that the Son is not a Creature. Arian formula, a creature but not as one of the creatures; but each creature is unlike all other creatures; and no creature can create. The Word then differs from all creatures in that in which they, though otherwise differing, all agree together, as creatures; viz. in being an efficient cause; in being the one medium or instrumental agent in creation; moreover in being the revealer of the Father; and in being the object of worship.
sources.answer: It would compare Him favourably with other works, calling Him greater than archangels or brighter than the sun. Instead Scripture presents Him as the Father's own proper and only Son, which shows He is not a superior creature but different in kind.
sources.quote: But he is not in fact thus referred to; but the Father shews Him to be His own proper and only Son, saying, ‘Thou art My Son,’ and ‘This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’
sources.raw_question: If the Son were merely the most glorious creature, how would Scripture describe him?

question: Did the generality of Christian writers before the Council of Nicaea side with Dr. Clarke's view against the Son's coeternity and consubstantiality with the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. They agreed with Clarke only so far as allowing a subordination of the Son to the Father, which the Church of England also allows; on the main points of difference, eternity and consubstantiality, they were clearly against him. Clarke's quotations never determine against the Son's coeternity and consubstantiality, and Athanasius already told the Arians that all reputable earlier writers were against them.
sources.quote: they have not plainly, nor at all determined against the coeternity and consubstantiality of the Son, the pommts in question; and therefore can’ do the Doctor no service
sources.raw_question: Did the generality of Christian writers before the Council of Nicaea side with Dr. Clarke's view against the Son's coeternity and consubstantiality with the Father?

question: What constitutes the native dignity of God, and is it found in the Son as well as the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He declares falsely that 'the manner of the generation is to be known from the intrinsic worth of the generator'.
sources.answer: God's native dignity consists in godhead itself, wisdom, power, goodness, justice, mercy, truth, creativeness, invisibility, everlastingness and every other quality Scripture names to magnify his glory. Every one of these is properly and inalienably found in the Son. The only difference recognized between them concerns unoriginateness, in the sense of existing from no cause.
sources.quote: we affirm that everyone of them is properly and inalienably found in the Son, recognizing difference only in respect of unoriginateness
sources.raw_question: What constitutes the native dignity of God, and is it found in the Son as well as the Father?

question: Does affirming that the Son is unoriginate amount to claiming that the Son is ungenerate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He declares falsely that 'the manner of the generation is to be known from the intrinsic worth of the generator'.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that anyone who maintains the Son is ungenerate is no less impious than an Anomoean. The Son has an origin with respect to his subsistence from the Father. He is unoriginate only with respect to creation, time and order.
sources.quote: let no carping critic attack this statement as if we were attempting to exhibit the Very Son as ungenerate; for we hold that one who maintains that is no less impious than an Anomœan.
sources.raw_question: Does affirming that the Son is unoriginate amount to claiming that the Son is ungenerate?

question: Can one describe the Father and Son as Creator and creature while still truly confessing the Father and the Son and avoiding the charge of denying them?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Scripture calls him antichrist who denies the Father and the Son. A confession in which all of Christ's attributes are spurious and nominal denies the true Son. He who denies the Son lacks the Father, and he who confesses the Son has the Father too, which leaves no room for adoptive names.
sources.quote: He that denies the Son is destitute of the Father; he that confesses and has the Son has the Father also. What room is there here for adoptive names? Does not every word tell of the Divine nature?
sources.raw_question: Can one describe the Father and Son as Creator and creature while still truly confessing the Father and the Son and avoiding the charge of denying them?

question: Is it consistent to read 'servant' of Solomon as compatible with natural sonship, yet read creaturely terms of Christ as proof that He is a work?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: No. Doing so applies 'diverse weights,' interpreting one case fairly while forcing the other into blasphemy. Consistency requires reading titles like 'Offspring,' 'Word,' and 'Wisdom' as signifying natural generation. Creaturely terms should be referred to His humanity, not used to deny the Word.
sources.quote: forthwith drop down to the notion of His being by nature a work, and deny the Word; and this, though it is possible, from His having been made man, to refer all these terms to His humanity?
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to read 'servant' of Solomon as compatible with natural sonship, yet read creaturely terms of Christ as proof that He is a work?

question: When asking whether Christ is a creature or work, should one first settle whether He is Son, Word, and Wisdom?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: Yes. Once it is shown that He is Son, Word, and Wisdom, the idea that He is a work collapses at once. A work could never be Son and Word, and the Son could never be a work; the two are mutually exclusive.
sources.quote: For a work could never be Son and Word; nor could the Son be a work.
sources.raw_question: When asking whether Christ is a creature or work, should one first settle whether He is Son, Word, and Wisdom?

question: Does the Spirit's being 'upon' Christ mean the Spirit is over Christ in his Godhead?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter I. Not only were the prophets and apostles sent by the Spirit, but also the Son of God. This is proved from Isaiah and the evangelists, and it is explained why St. Luke wrote that the same Spirit descended like a dove upon Christ and abode upon Him. Next, after establishing this mission of Christ, the writer infers that the Son is sent by the Father and the Spirit, as the Spirit is by the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. According to the Godhead the Spirit is not upon Christ but in him. As the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, so the Spirit is in both the Father and the Son. The Trinity is over all things, not over itself; it is in itself.
sources.quote: He is, then, not over Christ according to the Godhead of Christ, for the Trinity is not over Itself, but over all things: It is not over Itself but in Itself.
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit's being 'upon' Christ mean the Spirit is over Christ in his Godhead?

question: When Hebrews calls Christ's covenant, sacrifice, hope and promises 'better', does it mean better in degree within the same kind, or different in nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature.
