The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: Different in nature. The Apostle consistently ascribes 'better' to the Lord, who is better than and other than originated things. So the sacrifice, hope and promises through Him are better not merely as great compared with small, but as differing in nature, because the One who conducts this economy is above created things.
sources.quote: not merely as great compared with small, but the one differing from the other in nature, because He who conducts this economy, is ‘better’ than things originated.
sources.raw_question: When Hebrews calls Christ's covenant, sacrifice, hope and promises 'better', does it mean better in degree within the same kind, or different in nature?

question: Why must God be one and without equal?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, He is Good, Always the Same, Immutable, One and Only, Infinite; And His Own Name Can Never Be Declared, and He is Incorruptible and Immortal.
sources.answer: Whatever is God must be the Highest, and the Highest must be without any equal. That which has no peer must therefore be alone and one. Moreover, there cannot be two infinites, as the very nature of things dictates.
sources.quote: For whatever can be God, must as God be of necessity the Highest. But whatever is the Highest, must certainly be the Highest in such sense as to be without any equal.
sources.raw_question: Why must God be one and without equal?

question: Did the Old Testament prophets speak under the inspiration of different gods?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXV.—Refutation of Basilides, and of the opinion that the prophets uttered their predictions under the inspiration of different gods.
sources.answer: No. All the prophets proclaimed one God and Lord, the very Maker of heaven and earth and of everything in them. They also announced the coming of His Son. The Gnostic claim that different gods inspired them is therefore overthrown by what the prophets themselves taught.
sources.quote: all the prophets proclaimed one God and Lord, and that the very Maker of heaven and earth, and of all things which are therein; while they moreover announced the advent of His Son
sources.raw_question: Did the Old Testament prophets speak under the inspiration of different gods?

question: Does the recording of the sins of Old Testament saints show that the God of the Old Testament is a different God from the Father preached by Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVII—The sins of the men of old time, which incurred the displeasure of God, were, by His providence, committed to writing, that we might derive instruction thereby, and not be filled with pride. We must not, therefore, infer that there was another God than He whom Christ preached; we should rather fear, lest the one and the same God who inflicted punishment on the ancients, should bring down heavier upon us.
sources.answer: No. The sins of the ancients were written down for our instruction, so that we might know that our God and theirs is one, and that sins do not please Him even when committed by men of renown. Paul's account in 1 Corinthians shows that the same God judged the fathers in the wilderness and now judges Christians.
sources.quote: that we might know, in the first place, that our God and theirs is one, and that sins do not please Him although committed by men of renown
sources.raised_by_detail: Marcionites/Gnostics who posit a degenerate Creator distinct from the Father
sources.raw_question: Does the recording of the sins of Old Testament saints show that the God of the Old Testament is a different God from the Father preached by Christ?

question: Does denying the divinity of Christ remove the saving efficacy of his work?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. Unbelief in the Son's divinity drains all saving efficacy from his work. Those who profess such unbelief therefore reject the only name under heaven by which people must be saved.
sources.quote: those who professedly disbelieve his divinity, seeing that such unbelief extracts all saving efficacy from his work, are rejecting the only name under heaven given among men whereby we must be saved
sources.raw_question: Does denying the divinity of Christ remove the saving efficacy of his work?

question: What is communion, in general terms?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Communion is the mutual communication of good things in which the persons holding it delight, grounded on some union between them. Jonathan and David illustrate it: their souls were united in love, and they then mutually communicated all the issues of that love. In spiritual communion the union is most excellent and the things communicated most precious.
sources.quote: Now, communion is the mutual communication of such good things as wherein the persons holding that communion are delighted, bottomed upon some union between them.
sources.raw_question: What is communion, in general terms?

question: Does faith in Christ as a creature have saving value?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Christ requires faith in Himself not as a creature but as the Son of God, and that confession alone is eternal life; so the one who denies the Son has no source from which to hope for life.
sources.quote: What is the profit of faith in the Son of God, if it be faith in a creature, when He requires of us faith in Christ, not the creature, but the Son, of God.
sources.raw_question: Does faith in Christ as a creature have saving value?

question: How can Christ, who was born of Abraham's line, truthfully say "Before Abraham was, I am"?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: Only if he is also God. No one can exist before the person from whom he takes his origin. So if Christ were merely a man descended from Abraham, his claim would be false and deceptive. Since he does not deceive, he must be God and must have existed before Abraham.
sources.quote: Either, therefore, He says what is not true, and deceives, if He was not before Abraham, seeing that He was of Abraham; or He does not deceive, if He is also God, and was before Abraham.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ, who was born of Abraham's line, truthfully say "Before Abraham was, I am"?

question: Is nearness to or distance from God a matter of place?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: No. One approaches God by likeness and withdraws from Him by unlikeness, not by intervals of place. This is why Scripture speaks of being renewed and of imitating God.
sources.quote: For approach to God is not by intervals of place, but by likeness, and withdrawal from Him is by unlikeness.
sources.raw_question: Is nearness to or distance from God a matter of place?

question: Is the Holy Spirit merely the power, virtue or efficacy of God (a quality in God) rather than a personal substance, as the Socinians claim?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Scripture ascribes to the Holy Spirit knowledge, will and works done 'as he will,' which can only belong to an intelligent, voluntary agent having being, life and will. If such frequently repeated ascriptions do not prove a personal subsistence, Scripture would have been written to mislead us about what we must rightly believe on pain of eternal ruin.
sources.quote: He is an intelligent, voluntary, divine agent; he knows, he works as he will: which things, if, in their frequent repetition, they are not sufficient to evince an intelligent agent, a personal subsistence, that has being, life, and will
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit merely the power, virtue or efficacy of God (a quality in God) rather than a personal substance, as the Socinians claim?

question: Does the annunciation of Jesus' birth reveal the three Persons of the Trinity as divine Persons?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. In Luke 1:35 the Holy Ghost is the active agent of the conception, and that same effect is also ascribed to the power of the Most High. The child is named the Son of God. Matthew's account likewise brings the three Persons into view and twice intimates the Deity of the child: he will save his people from their sins, and his name is Immanuel, God-with-us.
sources.quote: Here the Holy Ghost is the active agent in the production of an effect which is also ascribed to the power of the Most High, and the child thus brought into the world is given the great designation of “Son of God.”
sources.raw_question: Does the annunciation of Jesus' birth reveal the three Persons of the Trinity as divine Persons?

question: Did a heavenly, impassible Christ descend upon the man Jesus at baptism and fly away from him before the suffering?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: No. If one suffered while the other stayed impassible, and one was born while the other descended and departed, there would be two, not one. Paul, however, knew one Christ Jesus who was both born and suffered: we are baptized into Christ Jesus's death, and Christ died for the ungodly. The one who suffered and shed his blood is the same who rose and sits at God's right hand.
sources.quote: For if, in truth, the one suffered, and the other remained incapable of suffering, and the one was born, but the other descended upon him who was born, and left him again, it is not one, but two, that are shown forth.
sources.raw_question: Did a heavenly, impassible Christ descend upon the man Jesus at baptism and fly away from him before the suffering?

question: Must the Son share the Father's unalterableness if He is like the Father and has all that the Father has?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: Yes. God's Word is ever in one state, as the Father is. He could not be like the Father, nor could all that is the Father's be the Son's, if He lacked the Father's unalterableness and unchangeableness. The Image must have the same nature as its Father.
sources.quote: since how is He like the Father, unless He be thus? or how is all that is the Father’s the Son’s also, if He has not the unalterableness and unchangeableness of the Father?
sources.raw_question: Must the Son share the Father's unalterableness if He is like the Father and has all that the Father has?

question: If Scripture also says the Father loves righteousness and hates iniquity, does reading such words of the Son as signs of mutability lead to absurdity?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says the same of the Father, for example 'The Righteous Lord loveth righteousness' and 'Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.' If the Arians read these words of the Son as implying alterability, they must also conceive the Father as alterable. Both should be read the same way: God, as judge, loves and takes the righteous to Himself and withdraws from the bad, and so does His Image.
sources.quote: Let them then expound those former words as these latter; for the former also are written of the Image of God: else, misinterpreting these as those, they will conceive that the Father too is alterable.
sources.raw_question: If Scripture also says the Father loves righteousness and hates iniquity, does reading such words of the Son as signs of mutability lead to absurdity?

question: Can a person who has not received the Holy Spirit possess true peace with God and in their own soul?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. True and solid peace is an effect of the Holy Ghost in the hearts of believers, so those who are not partakers of him have no such peace. Whatever quiet they have rests on false grounds: darkness or ignorance, a treacherous conscience, self-righteousness and vain hope, which will not avail them when the Lord deals with them.
sources.quote: True and solid peace being an effect of the Holy Ghost in the hearts of believers (as hath been declared), they who are not made partakers of him have no such peace.
sources.raw_question: Can a person who has not received the Holy Spirit possess true peace with God and in their own soul?

question: Can non-existence at any time be attributed to the Son, given that Scripture calls him Life, Light, and Truth?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Since Scripture teaches that the Only-begotten is the Prince of Life, the very life, light and truth, it is absurd and impious to join to Him Who really is the opposite conception of non-existence, whether before formation or after dissolution. To say so is like saying immortal life is mortal or light is darkness.
sources.quote: we say that it is absurd and impious to contemplate, in conjunction with Him Who really is, the opposite conception, whether of dissolution tending to corruption, or of non-existence before formation
sources.raw_question: Can non-existence at any time be attributed to the Son, given that Scripture calls him Life, Light, and Truth?

question: Does Scripture direct believers to seek God's edification through faith rather than through speculative inquiry into divine mysteries?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes. Paul charged Timothy to avoid fables and endless genealogies that minister questionings, since the edification of God is in faith. He thereby limits human reverence to faithful worship of the Almighty and does not let our weakness strain to see what only dazzles.
sources.quote: The edification of God, he says, is in faith: he limits human reverence to the faithful worship of the Almighty, and does not suffer our weakness to strain itself in the attempt to see what only dazzles the eye.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture direct believers to seek God's edification through faith rather than through speculative inquiry into divine mysteries?

question: Did the incarnate Son cease to be the immeasurable God while He was an infant and grew as a boy?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The Infant wails yet is in heaven, and the Boy grows yet remains ever the immeasurable God. He is as He ever was, yet He was not ever what He is, since He took on manhood without losing His Godhead.
sources.quote: The Infant wails but is in Heaven: the Boy grows but remains ever the immeasurable God.
sources.raw_question: Did the incarnate Son cease to be the immeasurable God while He was an infant and grew as a boy?

question: Can sin die in a person apart from Christ, or is the mortification of sin found only in Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Sin can die outwardly apart from Christ, but its root dies only in Christ. Christless men may stop acting on sin because their bodies fail or because indulging it no longer serves their interest, yet sin is never more alive than then. The daily decay of sin's strength, principle and power in the soul is found only in Christ. Of itself sin does not die but grows to eternity.
sources.quote: But there is a dying of it as to the root, the principle of it, — the daily decaying of the strength, power, and life of it; and this is to be had alone in Christ.
sources.raw_question: Can sin die in a person apart from Christ, or is the mortification of sin found only in Christ?

question: Does sin serve any end beyond dishonouring God and displaying his vindictive justice?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. In Christ, sin is made to serve the praise of God's glorious grace in pardoning it. In its own nature sin only dishonours God and ruins the creature, and the law reveals only one further end: the display of God's punishing justice. In Christ, God has arranged that what tended only to his dishonour serves his infinite glory, so that he is known as a God who pardons iniquity.
sources.quote: God having taken order in Christ that that thing which tended merely to his dishonour should be managed to his infinite glory
sources.raw_question: Does sin serve any end beyond dishonouring God and displaying his vindictive justice?

question: Why did Christ undergo human birth, growth, hunger, weariness, tears, and the sufferings of the passion?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: These things were ordained to assure us that in Christ there is pure, true humanity. The shame of the cross was his, not ours; we are spared the scourge and the spitting.
sources.quote: These things were ordained for our assurance that in Christ is pure man. But the shame of the cross is not ours; we are not sentenced to the scourge, nor defiled by spitting.
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ undergo human birth, growth, hunger, weariness, tears, and the sufferings of the passion?

question: Does 1 John 3:24 teach that God's indwelling in believers is by the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. The apostle argues validly that because we have the Spirit, God dwells in us and we in him, since God's dwelling in us is by that Spirit and our interest in him comes from the Spirit. The argument holds in itself, even when a believer does not feel it, for the Spirit gives a sense of it as he pleases.
sources.quote: "We have of the Spirit; therefore he dwells in us, and we in him:" because, indeed, his dwelling in us is by that Spirit, and our interest in him is from thence.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 John 3:24 teach that God's indwelling in believers is by the Holy Spirit?

question: In what sense are creatures 'far' from God if God is everywhere present?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Creatures are far from God not in place but in nature. Nothing is distant from God locally, since He is everywhere, but all things differ from Him in nature. Hence believers can be one only distantly as the Son is in the Father.
sources.quote: distantly not in place but in nature; for in place nothing is far from God, but in nature only all things are far from Him
sources.raw_question: In what sense are creatures 'far' from God if God is everywhere present?

question: Does the Father's declaration 'This is My Son' at the Transfiguration reveal the Son's nature or merely confer a title?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: It reveals his nature. The words 'This is My Son' disclose what he is, while 'Hear Him' summons us to receive his teaching; and the Son never claims less than this designation. His sonship is genuine, not a name of favour.
sources.quote: The Father’s words, This is My Son, reveal His nature; those which follow, Hear Him, are a summons to us to listen to the mystery and the faith which He came down from heaven to bring
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's declaration 'This is My Son' at the Transfiguration reveal the Son's nature or merely confer a title?

question: If the Father is all-sufficient, why does he create through the Son and why is the Son named with him in baptism?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: The Son is not named because the Father lacks anything, nor by accident. As God's own Word, Wisdom and Radiance, the Son is always with the Father, so whatever the Father gives he necessarily gives in the Son, as light shines in its radiance. Where the Father is or is named, there the Son must be also.
sources.quote: the Son is named with the Father, not as if the Father were not all-sufficient, not without meaning, and by accident; but, since He is God’s Word and own Wisdom, and being His Radiance, is ever with the Father
sources.raw_question: If the Father is all-sufficient, why does he create through the Son and why is the Son named with him in baptism?

question: If the Son says 'My Father formed and created me for His works,' does that imply he is a servant or one of the works?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: No. Athanasius compares a king's son who puts on the dress of captured servants in order to rescue them. Asked why, the son would say his father formed him for this task. He would not mean he is a servant, or speak of his origin, but of the charge later given him. In the same way the Lord, having put on our flesh, speaks of his commission and not of his being.
sources.quote: he neither implies that he is a servant nor one of the works, nor speaks of the beginning of His origination, but of the subsequent charge given him over the works
sources.raw_question: If the Son says 'My Father formed and created me for His works,' does that imply he is a servant or one of the works?

question: Does the Son's being 'set as King upon Sion' (Psalm 2:6) or 'set over the works' (Psalm 8:6) mean his reign or existence began then?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: No. When he shone in the body upon Sion he did not begin to exist or to reign, because he is God's Word and everlasting King. He let his kingdom shine in a human way in order to redeem humanity from sin and bring it under the Father's Kingdom. Likewise he was set over things that already existed and needed restoration.
sources.quote: He had not His beginning of existence or of reign, but being God’s Word and everlasting King, He vouchsafed that His kingdom should shine in a human way in Sion
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's being 'set as King upon Sion' (Psalm 2:6) or 'set over the works' (Psalm 8:6) mean his reign or existence began then?

question: What is the difference between man possessing the image of God and receiving the similitude (likeness) of God, and what role does the Holy Spirit play?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VI.—God will bestow salvation upon the whole nature of man, consisting of body and soul in close union, since the Word took it upon Him, and adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, of whom our bodies are, and are termed, the temples.
sources.answer: The image is present in man's bodily formation, but the likeness comes only through the Spirit. A man who lacks the Spirit is of an animal nature and carnal. He has the image in his formation but does not receive the similitude through the Spirit, so he remains imperfect. When the Spirit is joined to the soul and united to God's handiwork, the man becomes spiritual and perfect, made in both the image and the likeness of God.
sources.quote: possessing indeed the image [of God] in his formation (in plasmate), but not receiving the similitude through the Spirit; and thus is this being imperfect.
sources.raw_question: What is the difference between man possessing the image of God and receiving the similitude (likeness) of God, and what role does the Holy Spirit play?

question: Is the Holy Spirit a servant or slave rather than a sharer in divine lordship, as the Pneumatomachi hold?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Proof from Scripture that the Spirit is called Lord.
sources.answer: No. Paul calls those in whom the Spirit dwells the temple of God, and he would never honour the quarters of a slave with the title of temple. Likewise he calls Scripture God-inspired because it was written by the Spirit's inspiration, which is not the language of one belittling the Spirit.
sources.quote: Could he ever have brooked to honour with the title of “temple” the quarters of a slave? How can he who calls Scripture “God-inspired,” because it was written through the inspiration of the Spirit, use the language of one who insults and belittles Him?
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit a servant or slave rather than a sharer in divine lordship, as the Pneumatomachi hold?

question: Do believers have a real, distinct communion of mutual love with God the Father himself, even though the world despises them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. However lowly the world thinks of them, the saints have close, spiritual fellowship with the Father in an interchange of love: they receive his love and return love to him. This makes them, though misjudged, the truly great and noble on earth, as Paul describes believers as unknown yet well known, poor yet possessing all things.
sources.quote: Truly their fellowship is with the Father: let men think of it as they please, they have close, spiritual, heavenly refreshing, in the mutual communication of love with the Father himself.
sources.raw_question: Do believers have a real, distinct communion of mutual love with God the Father himself, even though the world despises them?

question: When Christ is said to become Lord at the incarnation, does he become Lord more than before or begin to be Lord?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: No. Just as God, when 'becoming a God and defence' to people, does not become God more than before but becomes to those in need what He ever is, so Christ, being by nature everlasting Lord, does not then begin to be Lord. What He ever is, He is made according to the flesh; we began to have Him for our Lord.
sources.quote: Nor did He then begin to be, but we began to have Him for our Lord.
sources.raw_question: When Christ is said to become Lord at the incarnation, does he become Lord more than before or begin to be Lord?

question: Did the man Christ merit, by prior good works, to be united with the Word and become the Son of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Other Advantages of the Incarnation.
sources.answer: No. The man Christ obtained by no precedent merits that he should be joined in such unity with the true God and become one person with the Son. From the moment he began to be man he was also God, as it is said, "The Word was made flesh." In this way the grace of God is commended to us without prior merits.
sources.quote: not even He Himself obtained by any precedent merits that He should be joined in such great unity with the true God, and should become the Son of God, one Person with Him; but from the time when He began to be man, from that time He is also God
sources.raw_question: Did the man Christ merit, by prior good works, to be united with the Word and become the Son of God?

question: How does the invisible and inaccessible God bring help to people who call on him, and what role does the Word play in this?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: God, being invisible and inaccessible to originated things, shines forth in love for mankind with his beneficence, which he exercises through and in his own proper Word. Every defence that comes to anyone through the Son is rightly called God having 'become' a help to that person, because the succour comes from God himself through the Word.
sources.quote: the Invisible, being a lover of man, shines forth upon them with His beneficence, which He exercises through and in His proper Word.
sources.raw_question: How does the invisible and inaccessible God bring help to people who call on him, and what role does the Word play in this?

question: Is the Holy Spirit involved in the creation of the angels, who were perfect from the moment of their creation?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: Yes. Even for beings who are not gradually perfected but are perfect from creation, the Holy Spirit is present in their creation. He confers on them the grace flowing from Him for the completion and perfection of their essence, showing he is inseparable from the Father and Son in creation.
sources.quote: there is in creation the presence of the Holy Spirit, who confers on them the grace that flows from Him for the completion and perfection of their essence.
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit involved in the creation of the angels, who were perfect from the moment of their creation?

question: Would rejecting the plain scriptural statements that Christ is God violate ordinary rules of interpretation?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. To reject the positive assertions that Christ is God, the great God our Saviour, in whom dwells the fullness of the Godhead bodily, would violate the rules of common sense applied to every other classical work. Resting on these declarations is relying on the exact meaning the inspired writers intended.
sources.quote: if he rejected the positive assertions that Christ is God, the great God our Saviour, in whom dwelleth all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, he would be violating those rules of sound common sense which he must apply, to interpret every other classical work
sources.raw_question: Would rejecting the plain scriptural statements that Christ is God violate ordinary rules of interpretation?

question: What does 'Believe Me' in John 14:11 refer back to, and what does it teach about seeing the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: It answers the request 'Shew us the Father' and confirms the disciples' faith with a command to believe. Christ goes beyond 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father.' He teaches us to contemplate the Father in the Son while remembering that the Son is in the Father.
sources.quote: What means this, Believe Me? Clearly it refers back to the previous, Shew us the Father. Their faith—that faith which had demanded that the Father should be shewn—is confirmed by this command to believe.
sources.raw_question: What does 'Believe Me' in John 14:11 refer back to, and what does it teach about seeing the Father?

question: Is the Son the efficient cause of the universe and of all created beings?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland judges that denying the Son's role as efficient cause of all created things is contrary to all the ancients, whose testimonies he has already cited.
sources.quote: That the Son is not efficient cause of the universe, and of all created beings. This I take to be contrary to all the ancients.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the efficient cause of the universe and of all created beings?

question: Did earlier Christian tradition regard the Holy Spirit as an object of worship and as possessing Godhead?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: Yes. Basil cites Origen's Commentary on John, which speaks of one who yields himself 'to the God-head of the adorable Trinity.' He also cites Origen's exposition of Romans, which speaks of 'the Godhead of the Holy Spirit.' These show the Spirit being given worship along with the Father and Son.
sources.quote: It is, if I am not mistaken, in the Sixth Book of his Commentary on the Gospel of St. John that he distinctly makes the Spirit an object of worship.
sources.raw_question: Did earlier Christian tradition regard the Holy Spirit as an object of worship and as possessing Godhead?

question: Does ancient popular worship praise the Holy Spirit together with the Father and the Son, and was this ever counted as impious?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: Yes, it does, and it was never counted impious. The ancient thanksgiving at the lighting of the evening lamps, whose author is unknown, praises 'Father, Son, and God's Holy Spirit,' and no one has ever reckoned those who say it guilty of impiety. The Hymn of Athenogenes, left by the martyr before his death by fire, likewise shows the martyrs' mind concerning the Spirit.
sources.quote: no one has ever reckoned guilty of impiety those who say “We praise Father, Son, and God’s Holy Spirit.”
sources.raw_question: Does ancient popular worship praise the Holy Spirit together with the Father and the Son, and was this ever counted as impious?

question: Can the human soul attain knowledge of God by its natural faculties alone, without the gift of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. Hilary teaches that the soul has an innate faculty for apprehending God, but without the Spirit received through faith it lacks the light of knowledge. He compares it to the eye, which cannot work without light, and the ear, which cannot work without sound. The faculty is present but unused and unexperienced. The Spirit is received so that we may know the things given to us by God.
sources.quote: So, too, the soul of man, unless through faith it have appropriated the gift of the Spirit, will have the innate faculty of apprehending God, but be destitute of the light of knowledge.
sources.raw_question: Can the human soul attain knowledge of God by its natural faculties alone, without the gift of the Holy Spirit?

question: Do the conditions of bodily birth, such as passion, place and time, apply to the Father's begetting of the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He further shows that the pretemporal generation of the Son is not the subject of influences drawn from ordinary and carnal generation, but is without beginning and without end, and not according to the fabrications constructed by Eunomius, in ignorance of His power, from the statements of Plato concerning the soul and from the sabbath rest of the Hebrews.
sources.answer: No. These affections are things no one would transfer to the Divine Nature. If any one of them were admitted, all the rest would necessarily come in with it. To keep the Divine generation free of passion, we must not attribute to it even extension measured by intervals.
sources.quote: things which are all equally alien from the Divine generation of the Only-begotten: for if any one of these things were admitted, the rest will of necessity all enter with it.
sources.raw_question: Do the conditions of bodily birth, such as passion, place and time, apply to the Father's begetting of the Son?

question: Is the Son's generation like the making of an artifact, which has a beginning and an end?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He further shows that the pretemporal generation of the Son is not the subject of influences drawn from ordinary and carnal generation, but is without beginning and without end, and not according to the fabrications constructed by Eunomius, in ignorance of His power, from the statements of Plato concerning the soul and from the sabbath rest of the Hebrews.
sources.answer: No. Making something needs material, place, time, preparation and the power of a craftsman. These fix the product's beginning and end, since gathering the material is itself the beginning and is tied to place and time. None of these conditions has any share in the pretemporal generation of the Only-begotten God. So no beginning or end of that generation can be calculated from them.
sources.quote: no one could say that these things have any participation in the pretemporal generation of the Only-begotten God, so that, by the aid of the things now under consideration, we are able to calculate, with regard to that generation, any beginning or end.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's generation like the making of an artifact, which has a beginning and an end?

question: Does the word "until" in "He must reign, until He hath put all enemies under His feet" (1 Corinthians 15:25) imply that Christ will cease to reign afterward?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: No. "Until" is used here as in Psalm 112:8, "He shall not be afraid, until He see His desire upon His enemies," where the person is obviously not afraid afterward either. The word marks a point reached without implying a reversal after it. Only careless readers eager for controversy are deceived by it.
sources.quote: Neither do they perceive that this is said in the same way as that other text, “His heart is established: He shall not be afraid, until He see His desire upon His enemies.” For He will not then be afraid when He has seen it.
sources.raw_question: Does the word "until" in "He must reign, until He hath put all enemies under His feet" (1 Corinthians 15:25) imply that Christ will cease to reign afterward?

question: Did the Son of God truly become incarnate and come visibly into the world he had made, or was his coming only apparent?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIX.—A comparison is instituted between the disobedient and sinning Eve and the Virgin Mary, her patroness. Various and discordant heresies are mentioned.
sources.answer: He truly became incarnate. The Lord came openly to his own things and sustained them through the creation he himself upholds. Those who reject his incarnation, or who say he was begotten by Joseph and not born of a virgin, are ignorant of the dispensation by which he took human nature. In denying it they speak against their own salvation.
sources.quote: That the Lord then was manifestly coming to His own things, and was sustaining them by means of that creation which is supported by Himself
sources.raised_by_detail: Docetists and those holding Jesus was begotten by Joseph
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God truly become incarnate and come visibly into the world he had made, or was his coming only apparent?

question: Does Christ's statement that Lazarus' sickness is 'for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified' show that the Son's glory is God's glory?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. The death of Lazarus, which is glorious to God, glorifies the Son of God, so the Son's glory is the glory of God and He is one in nature with the Father through His birth. Yet the distinction is preserved, since He is still confessed as the Son of God who is glorified.
sources.quote: Is there any doubt that the glory of the Son of God is the glory of God, when the death of Lazarus, which is glorious to God, glorifies the Son of God?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's statement that Lazarus' sickness is 'for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified' show that the Son's glory is God's glory?

question: Does Christ's humbling himself and becoming obedient unto death mean that his divine nature was humiliated?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. Although he humbled himself, his nature knew no humiliation. His obedience was voluntary, since he became obedient by the act of humbling himself, as the Only-begotten God obeying the Father within the Dispensation.
sources.quote: Although He humbled Himself, His nature knew no humiliation: though He was obedient, it was a voluntary obedience, for He became obedient by humbling Himself.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's humbling himself and becoming obedient unto death mean that his divine nature was humiliated?

question: Can Scripture say someone 'knows' or 'does not know' something when it means causing others to know or withholding knowledge from them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and the Hour Which the Father Knows. Some Things Said of Christ According to the Form of God, Other Things According to the Form of a Servant. In What Way It is of Christ to Give the Kingdom, in What Not of Christ. Christ Will Both Judge and Not Judge.
sources.answer: Yes. When God tells Abraham 'Now I know that thou fearest God', it means 'now I have caused thee to know it'. Paul said he knew nothing among the Corinthians except Christ crucified because they could not receive higher things, yet he spoke wisdom among the perfect. Scripture speaks in the ordinary idioms men use, because it speaks to men.
sources.quote: For a man is said not to know what he hides, after that kind of speech, after which a ditch is called blind which is hidden.
sources.raw_question: Can Scripture say someone 'knows' or 'does not know' something when it means causing others to know or withholding knowledge from them?

question: What attributes or activities show the Holy Spirit's divine status?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory then makes an explanation at length touching the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: The Spirit is a princely Spirit and a quickening Spirit. He is the controlling and sanctifying force of all creation, working all in all as He wills. These marks place Him with the Godhead rather than among creatures.
sources.quote: That Spirit is indisputably a princely Spirit, a quickening Spirit, the controlling and sanctifying force of all creation, the Spirit that “worketh all in all” as He wills.
sources.raw_question: What attributes or activities show the Holy Spirit's divine status?

question: Did the divine nature of the Only-begotten suffer on the Cross?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: No. Paul calls Christ both "man" and "God" and "mediator between God and men" so that impassibility is ascribed to the divine nature and the Passion to the human nature. The Divine is not polluted by its condescension; it makes the human element subject to suffering while working, through its divine power, the resurrection of what suffered.
sources.quote: to the end that no one should connect the suffering of the Cross with the imperishable nature, he gives in other words a fairly distinct correction of such an error
sources.raw_question: Did the divine nature of the Only-begotten suffer on the Cross?

question: Does the judging work of the Son show that the Father exercises providence over all and has given humans free choice?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXVII.—The future judgment by Christ. Communion with and separation from the divine being. The eternal punishment of unbelievers.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son's coming reaches all alike, but it serves to judge and to separate believers from unbelievers, who accept or reject his doctrine by their own choice. This shows that the Father made all people in a like condition, each with free choice and understanding. It also shows that the Father has regard to all things and exercises providence over all.
sources.quote: it is manifest that His Father has made all in a like condition, each person having a choice of his own, and a free understanding; and that He has regard to all things, and exercises a providence over all
sources.raw_question: Does the judging work of the Son show that the Father exercises providence over all and has given humans free choice?

question: Why does Christ promise to pray the Father to send the Spirit but not to pray for the Father's love toward the disciples?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: Because the Father's eternal love is not the fruit but the fountain of Christ's purchase, whereas the Spirit is a fruit of it. What Christ as mediator asks of the Father for us is part of what he purchased, so he intercedes for the Spirit but not for the Father's love.
sources.quote: he will not pray the Father for his love unto them, because the eternal love of the Father is not the fruit but the fountain of his purchase: but the Spirit, that is a fruit
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ promise to pray the Father to send the Spirit but not to pray for the Father's love toward the disciples?

question: Why is the Holy Spirit not mentioned in John 17:3, where the Father and Jesus Christ are named?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Whether One or the Three Persons Together are Called the Only God.
sources.answer: The Spirit is understood there even though he is not named. He is the harmony by which the Father and the Son cleave together so that both are one. So whenever the One who cleaves to the One is named, that bond of harmony is implied. Paul similarly seems to pass over the Spirit in 'ye are Christ's, and Christ is God's,' yet the Spirit is understood there too.
sources.quote: whenever we name One who cleaves to One by a harmony so great that through this harmony both are one, this harmony itself must be understood, although it is not mentioned?
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit not mentioned in John 17:3, where the Father and Jesus Christ are named?

question: Can degrees of greater and less be attributed to the uncreated divine nature in the way they apply to created intelligible beings?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: No. Created intelligible nature has more or less excellence according to its participation in the First Good and its free inclination toward good or evil. The uncreated nature does not possess the good by acquisition or participation but is good in its own essence, simple, uniform and incomposite, and so it is far removed from such distinctions of degree.
sources.quote: it does not possess the good by acquisition, or participate only in the goodness of some good which lies above it: in its own essence it is good, and is conceived as such: it is a source of good, it is simple, uniform, incomposite
sources.raw_question: Can degrees of greater and less be attributed to the uncreated divine nature in the way they apply to created intelligible beings?

question: How can the analogy of the sun, its light and its heat illustrate the eternal generation of the Son, and does any creaturely image adequately represent the Trinity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: The sun generates its beams, yet the sun never existed without radiance nor radiance without warmth, so one is not before another but only in order and relation. Still, the analogy offers only a faint resemblance, since no creature can adequately image the Creator, as God asks, 'To whom then will ye liken God?'
sources.quote: But no creature can adequately image forth the Creator, who asks “To whom then will ye liken God, or what likeness will ye compare unto him?”
sources.raw_question: How can the analogy of the sun, its light and its heat illustrate the eternal generation of the Son, and does any creaturely image adequately represent the Trinity?

question: Is it impossible for three subsistences to exist in one eternal divine essence?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No, we have no grounds to assert such an impossibility. We cannot find out the Almighty to perfection, and we do not even understand the essence of created things: white light appears simple yet science shows three constituent lights subsisting in it. If an ignorant man would wrongly deny plurality in light's unity, much more should we refrain from denying it in God, whom we know only as He reveals himself.
sources.quote: The unity of that pure white light was not so simple as he affirmed. More constituents than one subsist in its ethereal essence.
sources.raw_question: Is it impossible for three subsistences to exist in one eternal divine essence?

question: Does Christ's knowledge of future thoughts and of who would betray Him show that His nature has foreknowledge of the future?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. John testifies that Jesus knew from the beginning who would not believe and who would betray Him, so His nature perceives the unborn future and passions still dormant. It is incredible that a nature which foresees what belongs to others would not know what is through and within itself.
sources.quote: By its virtue His nature could perceive the unborn future, and foresee the awakening of passions yet dormant in the mind: do you believe that it did not know what is through itself, and within itself?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's knowledge of future thoughts and of who would betray Him show that His nature has foreknowledge of the future?

question: Can the divine beings be grasped through their works while those works are in turn grasped through the beings, as Eunomius proposes?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: No, this reasoning is circular. When both the being and the energy are equally unknown, neither can serve to prove the other. A doubt can only be resolved by means of well-known truths. If the being were already comprehended, there would be no need to reason from the energy to reach it. If it is not comprehended, it cannot settle any doubt about the energy.
sources.quote: The proof of anything that is doubted must be made by means of well-known truths; but when there is an equal uncertainty about both the objects of our search, how can Eunomius say that they are comprehended by means of each other
sources.raw_question: Can the divine beings be grasped through their works while those works are in turn grasped through the beings, as Eunomius proposes?

question: Could the world have been made by subordinate beings in God's own territory, or outside it, without his will?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter II.—The world was not formed by angels, or by any other being, contrary to the will of the most high God, but was made by the Father through the Word.
sources.answer: No. If the world were made beyond God, God would be enclosed by something beyond him and would have an end. If it were made within his own domain by beings under his power against his will, that would wrongly imply that he did not see or know what happens among his own possessions.
sources.quote: the Supreme God will be enclosed by that which is beyond Him, in which also it will be necessary that He should find His end.
sources.raw_question: Could the world have been made by subordinate beings in God's own territory, or outside it, without his will?

question: If angels or a demiurge made the world with God's consent, as Basilides says, who is truly the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter II.—The world was not formed by angels, or by any other being, contrary to the will of the most high God, but was made by the Father through the Word.
sources.answer: The Father. If the work was done with God's will and knowledge, his will is the cause, because whoever prepared the causes of a work is its author. We say a man cut the wood, not the axe he made. In the same way, the Father of all is declared the Former of the world, not the angels.
sources.quote: Wherefore, we do not say that it was the axe which cut the wood, or the saw which divided it; but one would very properly say that the man cut and divided it who formed the axe and the saw
sources.raw_question: If angels or a demiurge made the world with God's consent, as Basilides says, who is truly the Creator?

question: Is the Word through whom the Father creates a lesser intermediary like the Gnostic demiurge?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter II.—The world was not formed by angels, or by any other being, contrary to the will of the most high God, but was made by the Father through the Word.
sources.answer: No. The Word is God's own Word, a Word that never wearies, and not some power far inferior to God and ignorant of the Father. Through this Word God himself formed all things and gave each its fitting nature.
sources.quote: while He formed all things that were made by His Word that never wearies.
sources.raw_question: Is the Word through whom the Father creates a lesser intermediary like the Gnostic demiurge?

question: Does the Holy Spirit give grace and consolation only by moral persuasion and arguments, or by working effectually himself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: He works effectually himself. Scripture says the Spirit "worketh" (energei) these things. He does not merely propose arguments or moral motives and leave us to use them as we can. He himself effects what he communicates of grace and consolation.
sources.quote: It is not by proposing this or that argument to us, persuading us by these or those moral motives or inducements alone, leaving us to make use of them as we can; but he works effectually himself
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit give grace and consolation only by moral persuasion and arguments, or by working effectually himself?

question: Does Christ's coming reveal another Father besides the Creator, and will the perfected state reveal yet another Father, Christ or Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IX.—There is but one author, and one end to both covenants.
sources.answer: No. Christ confers greater gifts but does not change God or proclaim another Father. In perfection we will see the same Father we now desire to see, the same Christ born of the Virgin who suffered, and the same Holy Spirit who now cries 'Abba, Father' in us. Progress consists in fuller enjoyment of the same God's gifts, face to face rather than through a glass.
sources.quote: we have not been taught another God besides the Framer and the Maker of all, who has been pointed out to us from the beginning; nor another Christ, the Son of God, besides Him who was foretold by the prophets.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's coming reveal another Father besides the Creator, and will the perfected state reveal yet another Father, Christ or Holy Spirit?

question: Does Exodus 6:3, saying God was not known to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob by the name Jehovah, mean the patriarchs did not know God as the eternal, immutable Creator under that name?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. The patriarchs certainly knew and worshipped him as the true, eternal, immutable God under the name Jehovah. The most probable solution is to read the clause as a question: 'Was I not also known unto them by my name Jehovah?', a reading supported by some Greek writers and the Arabic version. In any case so obscure a text cannot ground a special meaning of Jehovah against the best critics.
sources.quote: the words, in the latter part of the text, ought to be understood by way of interrogation, thus: But by my name Jehovah was 1 not also known unto them?
sources.raw_question: Does Exodus 6:3, saying God was not known to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob by the name Jehovah, mean the patriarchs did not know God as the eternal, immutable Creator under that name?

question: Should one be cautious about praising the Holy Spirit too highly, limiting speech about Him to exact proportion?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That our opponents refuse to concede in the case of the Spirit the terms which Scripture uses in the case of men, as reigning together with Christ.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit passes all understanding and exposes speech's natural inability to approach His dignity, so we should rather bewail our weakness in expressing gratitude. As Wisdom says, exalt Him as much as you can, for He will still exceed it; and blasphemy against the Holy Ghost has no forgiveness.
sources.quote: He “passes all understanding,” and convicts speech of its natural inability even to approach His dignity in the least degree
sources.raw_question: Should one be cautious about praising the Holy Spirit too highly, limiting speech about Him to exact proportion?

question: Does Christ's humble act of washing feet as a servant conflict with his being God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Preface.
sources.answer: No. Christ acts in both respects: as a servant he washes the disciples' feet, and as God he sends the dew of the Spirit from heaven. He himself affirms that he is rightly called Master and Lord even while performing the servant's task.
sources.quote: How great is that excellence! As a servant, Thou dost wash the feet of Thy disciples; as God, Thou sendest dew from heaven.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's humble act of washing feet as a servant conflict with his being God?

question: Was the one who sent Moses the Existent (the Father), while the Son was merely the 'Angel of the Existent' through whom He spoke, as Eunomius claimed?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: No. Scripture itself refutes this: Moses begged that the people not be led by an angel but by the Lord Himself, and the One speaking with him consented to go with them as guide. Hence the One who revealed Himself by the title 'the Existent' is the Only-begotten God, not an angel subordinate to the Existent.
sources.quote: if Moses begs that the people may not be led by an angel, and if He Who was discoursing with him consents to become his fellow-traveller and the guide of the army, it is hereby manifestly shown that He Who made Himself known by the title of “the Existent” is the Only-begotten God.
sources.raw_question: Was the one who sent Moses the Existent (the Father), while the Son was merely the 'Angel of the Existent' through whom He spoke, as Eunomius claimed?

question: What does the prologue of John's Gospel reveal about God that natural reason could not attain, particularly concerning the Word?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: It reveals that the Creator is God of God: the Word was God and was with God in the beginning, and all things were made through Him. It also reveals that the Word became flesh and showed the glory of the Only-begotten from the Father. In this teaching the soul goes beyond its natural capacities and learns more about God than it had imagined. In the following section, the eternity, infinity and beauty that reason had ascribed to the Creator are seen to belong also to the Only-begotten.
sources.quote: Here the soul makes an advance beyond the attainment of its natural capacities, is taught more than it had dreamed concerning God. For it learns that its Creator is God of God; it hears that the Word is God and was with God in the beginning.
sources.raw_question: What does the prologue of John's Gospel reveal about God that natural reason could not attain, particularly concerning the Word?

question: Do Old Testament texts such as "Let us make man in our image" and "The Lord rained fire from the Lord" show that the Son is a person distinct from the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, Against the Sabellians He Proves that the Father is One, the Son Another.
sources.answer: Yes. In "Let us make man" the Father speaks to the Son, and in the Sodom text one Lord acts from another Lord. Likewise "Thou art my Son" and "The Lord said unto my Lord" are spoken by one person to another, which shows the Son to be second after the Father.
sources.quote: For who does not acknowledge that the person of the Son is second after the Father, when he reads that it was said by the Father, consequently to the Son, “Let us make man in our image and our likeness;”
sources.raw_question: Do Old Testament texts such as "Let us make man in our image" and "The Lord rained fire from the Lord" show that the Son is a person distinct from the Father?

question: Is God able to give each individual human body its own proper soul, or must souls be recycled from body to body?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXIII.—Absurdity of the doctrine of the transmigration of souls.
sources.answer: God gives each body its own proper soul. God is not so poor or lacking in resources that He cannot confer a proper soul on each body, just as He gives each body its special character. Souls therefore do not need to pass from one body to another.
sources.quote: For God is not so poor or destitute in resources, that He cannot confer its own proper soul on each individual body, even as He gives it also its special character.
sources.raw_question: Is God able to give each individual human body its own proper soul, or must souls be recycled from body to body?

question: Does considering Christ 'in two ways' (as divine Word and as man) introduce a division into the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. Even if Christ is considered in two ways, this is without any division of the Word, as John says 'the Word became flesh.' Scripture speaks of Christ in both ways, for example calling Christ God's power and wisdom, while he remains one.
sources.quote: And even if He be considered in two ways, still it is without any division of the Word, as when the inspired John says, ‘And the Word became flesh, and dwelt among us.’
sources.raw_question: Does considering Christ 'in two ways' (as divine Word and as man) introduce a division into the Word?

question: Is Christ a mere man, or a prophet like those through whom the Word was sent?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. The Word is the maker of man, who took enfeebled man into himself to renew and divinize him, so he cannot be reckoned with the apostles and prophets whom he himself sent. Being made one with the Word, Christ is rightly called Christ and Son of God, as the prophet foretold and the Father declared at the Jordan.
sources.quote: And how can Christ be called a mere man? on the contrary, being made one with the Word, He is with reason called Christ and Son of God
sources.raw_question: Is Christ a mere man, or a prophet like those through whom the Word was sent?

question: Who was the Lord who appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre and was received as a guest?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: It was God the Son. If it were the Father, the Father would be visible, which He is not. If it were a mere angel, an angel would be called God, which is not usual. To give the Father His proper invisibility and the angel his proper inferiority, the one seen must be the Son, who is God. He thereby anticipated sacramentally His future life among Abraham's descendants.
sources.quote: in order that His proper invisibility may be restored to the Father, and the proper inferiority be remitted to the angel, it was only God the Son, who also is God, who was seen by Abraham
sources.raw_question: Who was the Lord who appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre and was received as a guest?

question: What role does the Spirit of God play in bringing the human body into the kingdom of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter IX.—Showing how that passage of the apostle which the heretics pervert, should be understood; viz., “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.”
sources.answer: The Spirit of God is the living heir who inherits the mortal parts of man, which rot in the earth, and translates them into the kingdom of heaven. Christ died so that his freed slaves might become heirs when the Spirit possesses them by inheritance. To lose the Spirit is therefore to lose life.
sources.quote: What, therefore, is it that lives? The Spirit of God, doubtless. What, again, are the possessions of the deceased? The various parts of the man, surely, which rot in the earth. But these are inherited by the Spirit when they are translated into the kingdom of heaven.
sources.raw_question: What role does the Spirit of God play in bringing the human body into the kingdom of God?

question: Does the Father love all people with the same saving love?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. His love is distinguishing: he has not loved all the world in this way, as shown in "Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated." He sets his love on some and passes by millions from whom they do not differ by nature.
sources.quote: He hath not thus loved all the world: “Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.”
sources.raw_question: Does the Father love all people with the same saving love?

question: Do the Gospels ascribe to the Only-begotten Son the same absolute, eternal being that Moses ascribes to God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. The Gospels testify to the very property declared by Moses as belonging to God Only-begotten. They say that in the beginning was the Word, that the Word was with God, that he was the true Light, that he is in the bosom of the Father, and that Christ is God over all.
sources.quote: that very quality the Gospels testify to be a property of God Only-begotten; since in the beginning was the Word, and since the Word was with God
