sources.raw_question: Do the Gospels ascribe to the Only-begotten Son the same absolute, eternal being that Moses ascribes to God?

question: What does the term "variance" mean when applied to things, and why does this matter for describing the relation of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds to show that there is no “variance” in the essence of the Father and the Son: wherein he expounds many forms of variation and harmony, and explains the “form,” the “seal,” and the “express image.”
sources.answer: Gregory gives three senses of "variance." The first is a body or condition perverted from its natural health. The second is the inferior compared with the excellent, as vice compared with virtue. The third is contraries that are mutually opposed and destructive, as heat and cold. Each sense implies disharmony, degradation, or conflict, so in every case "variance" marks something lacking agreement with another. Analyzing the word this way exposes what is blasphemous in ascribing variance to the divine essences.
sources.quote: The term “variance” is used, in the inexact sense sanctioned by custom, of bodies, when, by palsy or any other disease, any limb is perverted from its natural co-ordination.
sources.raw_question: What does the term "variance" mean when applied to things, and why does this matter for describing the relation of the Father and the Son?

question: If every divine attribute can be predicated both of the whole Trinity and of each Person, how can the Trinity be discerned or demonstrated from the attributes of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Difficult It is to Demonstrate the Trinity by Natural Reason.
sources.answer: It is very difficult, and the attributes alone do not show it. Since they all apply equally to the Trinity and to each Person, Augustine first reduces the many predicates to a few (eternal, wise, blessed) and then to one, wisdom. He then asks what force of reasoning could show how this one thing, wisdom, is a trinity, acknowledging that the Trinity is not plainly manifest through such predicates.
sources.quote: If, then, these things, and all others of the kind, can be predicated both of the Trinity itself, and of each several one in that Trinity, where or how shall the Trinity manifest itself?
sources.raw_question: If every divine attribute can be predicated both of the whole Trinity and of each Person, how can the Trinity be discerned or demonstrated from the attributes of God?

question: Is God's life something distinct from God's essence, so that God lives by a life he receives from outside himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Difficult It is to Demonstrate the Trinity by Natural Reason.
sources.answer: No. What is called life in God is his very essence and nature. God lives only by the life which he is to himself. This life is not like a tree's or a beast's; it perceives and understands all things by mind, not by body.
sources.quote: For that which is called life in God, is itself His essence and nature. God, therefore, does not live, unless by the life which He is to Himself.
sources.raw_question: Is God's life something distinct from God's essence, so that God lives by a life he receives from outside himself?

question: Do the terms eternal, immortal, incorruptible and unchangeable mean different things when said of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Difficult It is to Demonstrate the Trinity by Natural Reason.
sources.answer: No. In God they are one and the same. True immortality belongs only to one whose nature admits no change, and true eternity is that by which God is unchangeable, without beginning or end, and therefore incorruptible. This is why Scripture says he 'only hath immortality.'
sources.quote: It is one and the same thing, therefore, to call God eternal, or immortal, or incorruptible, or unchangeable
sources.raw_question: Do the terms eternal, immortal, incorruptible and unchangeable mean different things when said of God?

question: When God is called a good, wise spirit, does 'spirit' name God's substance while 'good' and 'wise' name qualities of that substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Difficult It is to Demonstrate the Trinity by Natural Reason.
sources.answer: No. In God's ineffable and simple nature, whatever seems to be said according to quality must be understood according to substance or essence. So 'spirit' and 'good' are both said of God according to substance. The many names of God are not unequal but are many names for one thing.
sources.quote: For whatever seems to be predicated therein according to quality, is to be understood according to substance or essence. For far be it from us to predicate spirit of God according to substance, and good according to quality; but both according to substance.
sources.raw_question: When God is called a good, wise spirit, does 'spirit' name God's substance while 'good' and 'wise' name qualities of that substance?

question: Why can the many divine attributes be reduced to eternal, wise and blessed when seeking the Trinity in God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How Difficult It is to Demonstrate the Trinity by Natural Reason.
sources.answer: Because in God each group of attributes names one thing, so one term can stand for each group. 'Wise' is chosen over life, power and beauty because beasts have life and bodies have beauty, and Scripture ranks wisdom above strength. 'Blessed' is chosen over spirit, righteous and good because even in men nothing can be blessed without also being just, good and a spirit.
sources.quote: Although these four are not to be called unequal in speaking of God; for they are four names, but one thing.
sources.raw_question: Why can the many divine attributes be reduced to eternal, wise and blessed when seeking the Trinity in God?

question: Is the one who suffered human weaknesses the same person as the one who performed divine works, and what does this show about the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Twelfthly, Matthew xxvi. 39; John xii. 27, &c. Arian inferences are against the Regula Fidei, as before. He wept and the like, as man. Other texts prove Him God. God could not fear. He feared because His flesh feared.
sources.answer: Yes, it is the same person. He who wept and hungered is He who raised Lazarus, turned water into wine and gave sight to the blind. By permitting His body to suffer He showed that, though impassible God, He had taken passible flesh, while His works show Him to be the Word of God in the Father.
sources.quote: how He who did the works is the same as He who shewed that His body was passible by His permitting it to weep and hunger, and to shew other properties of a body.
sources.raw_question: Is the one who suffered human weaknesses the same person as the one who performed divine works, and what does this show about the Son?

question: Are the three divine persons formed 'out of' the divine essence as three statues are made out of the same gold?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: No. We say three persons of the same essence, or three persons one essence, but not three persons out of the same essence. That would make essence one thing and person another, as gold and statue differ. Also, unlike gold, nothing of the divine essence exists besides the Trinity, leaving no remainder.
sources.quote: but we do not say three persons out of the same essence, as though therein essence were one thing, and person another, as we can say three statues out of the same gold
sources.raw_question: Are the three divine persons formed 'out of' the divine essence as three statues are made out of the same gold?

question: Could there be further persons of the divine essence besides Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as other men can share the same human nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: No. Three men can be said to be out of the same nature because other such men could also exist from it. But in the essence of the Trinity no other person whatever can exist from the same essence; there is nothing of that essence besides the Trinity.
sources.quote: But in that essence of the Trinity, in no way can any other person whatever exist out of the same essence.
sources.raw_question: Could there be further persons of the divine essence besides Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as other men can share the same human nature?

question: Does the incomprehensibility of God described in Romans 11:33-36 also apply to the Son, so that the Son does not know the Father's mind?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. The inscrutability applies to us men only, not to Him through Whom are all things, the Angel of mighty Counsel. The Son himself said that no one knows the Father save the Son, so He shares the Father's knowledge and counsel.
sources.quote: But all this applies to us men only, and not to Him, through Whom are all things, the Angel of mighty Counsel
sources.raw_question: Does the incomprehensibility of God described in Romans 11:33-36 also apply to the Son, so that the Son does not know the Father's mind?

question: Does 1 Corinthians 2:8, saying the rulers 'crucified the Lord of Glory', show that the one crucified is the divine Lord himself?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes. Paul does not split Christ into a Lord of Glory and a crucified Jesus. He says the rulers of this world crucified the Lord of Glory because they did not know the hidden wisdom of God. He confirms this when he determines to know nothing but Jesus Christ and him crucified.
sources.quote: Does he divide Christ into a Lord of Glory and a crucified Jesus? Nay, rather, he contradicts this most foolish and impious idea
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 2:8, saying the rulers 'crucified the Lord of Glory', show that the one crucified is the divine Lord himself?

question: According to Romans 8:33-34, are the Christ who died, the Christ who rose, the Christ at God's right hand, and the Christ who intercedes the same person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes. Paul's chain of statements names a single subject: the Christ who died is the one who was raised, sits at God's right hand, and intercedes for us. Hilary further asks whether the Christ who condemns is not also the God who justifies. One cannot distinguish them without blaspheming the hidden mystery.
sources.quote: Is He Who intercedes for us other than He Who is at the right hand of God? Is not He Who is at the right hand of God the very same Who rose again? Is He Who rose again other than He Who died?
sources.raw_question: According to Romans 8:33-34, are the Christ who died, the Christ who rose, the Christ at God's right hand, and the Christ who intercedes the same person?

question: Does human service or obedience add anything to God or benefit Him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIV.—If God demands obedience from man, if He formed man, called him and placed him under laws, it was merely for man’s welfare; not that God stood in need of man, but that He graciously conferred upon man His favours in every possible manner.
sources.answer: No. Service rendered to God profits Him nothing, because He is rich, perfect, and in need of nothing. He asks for service only so that, being good and merciful, He may give life, incorruption and glory to those who serve Him. People enlightened by light add nothing to the light; they only receive from it, and the same holds for those who serve God.
sources.quote: service [rendered] to God does indeed profit God nothing, nor has God need of human obedience; but He grants to those who follow and serve Him life and incorruption and eternal glory
sources.raw_question: Does human service or obedience add anything to God or benefit Him?

question: When the disciples followed Christ, did they add to the Son's glory, or did they receive glory from Him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIV.—If God demands obedience from man, if He formed man, called him and placed him under laws, it was merely for man’s welfare; not that God stood in need of man, but that He graciously conferred upon man His favours in every possible manner.
sources.answer: They received glory from Him. Christ said, "Ye have not chosen Me, but I have chosen you," which shows the disciples did not glorify Him by following. Rather, in following the Son of God they were glorified by Him. His prayer that they might behold His glory expresses His wish that they share in it, not any boasting.
sources.quote: indicating that they did not glorify Him when they followed Him; but that, in following the Son of God, they were glorified by Him.
sources.raw_question: When the disciples followed Christ, did they add to the Son's glory, or did they receive glory from Him?

question: Is the kingdom of God the work of the Holy Spirit, so that it is fitting for the Spirit to be in God's throne?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XX. The river flowing from the Throne of God is a figure of the Holy Spirit, but by the waters spoken of by David the powers of heaven are intended. The kingdom of God is the work of the Spirit; and it is no matter for wonder if He reigns in this together with the Son, since St. Paul promises that we too shall reign with the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says the kingdom of God is righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. So it is no wonder that the Spirit is in the throne of God, since the kingdom itself is his work.
sources.quote: what wonder is it if the Holy Spirit is in the throne of God, since the kingdom of God itself is the work of the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Is the kingdom of God the work of the Holy Spirit, so that it is fitting for the Spirit to be in God's throne?

question: How does the Holy Spirit's reigning with Christ differ from believers' reigning with Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XX. The river flowing from the Throne of God is a figure of the Holy Spirit, but by the waters spoken of by David the powers of heaven are intended. The kingdom of God is the work of the Spirit; and it is no matter for wonder if He reigns in this together with the Son, since St. Paul promises that we too shall reign with the Son.
sources.answer: Believers reign with Christ by adoption and grace. The Spirit reigns by power and by nature. His share in the kingdom is therefore not a creaturely gift but belongs to him as divine.
sources.quote: But we by adoption, He by power; we by grace, He by nature.
sources.raw_question: How does the Holy Spirit's reigning with Christ differ from believers' reigning with Christ?

question: Does Paul's command to 'put off the old man' mean rejecting the substance of the flesh?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XII.—Of the difference between life and death; of the breath of life and the vivifying Spirit: also how it is that the substance of flesh revives which once was dead.
sources.answer: No. Paul means laying aside our former manner of life and the lusts of the flesh, not God's handiwork. If he meant the body itself, suicide would be required. He also says that to live in the flesh is the fruit of his work, so he did not despise the flesh.
sources.quote: he did not surely contemn the substance of flesh in that passage where he said, “Put ye off the old man with his works;” but he points out that we should lay aside our former conversation
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's command to 'put off the old man' mean rejecting the substance of the flesh?

question: What is the visible fruit of the work of the invisible Holy Spirit in man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XII.—Of the difference between life and death; of the breath of life and the vivifying Spirit: also how it is that the substance of flesh revives which once was dead.
sources.answer: The salvation of the flesh. The Spirit renders the flesh mature and capable of incorruption, and once it pervades a man within and without it never leaves him.
sources.quote: For what other visible fruit is there of the invisible Spirit, than the rendering of the flesh mature and capable of incorruption?
sources.raw_question: What is the visible fruit of the work of the invisible Holy Spirit in man?

question: Was it the Father himself who came down from heaven and became incarnate, as Noetus claims?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. It was the Father's power, the Word, that came down from heaven, not the Father himself. Christ says, "I came forth from the Father, and am come." The one who comes forth from the Father, and is begotten of him, is the Word.
sources.quote: in reality the Father’s power, which is the Word, came down from heaven, and not the Father Himself. For thus He speaks: “I came forth from the Father, and am come.”
sources.raw_question: Was it the Father himself who came down from heaven and became incarnate, as Noetus claims?

question: Is it certain, as Dorner argues, that traces of the Trinity must exist in the Old Testament because any living idea of God must be Trinitarian?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Not certain; Warfield calls it a 'nice question.' The doctrine was not revealed there. Still, someone who already knows the doctrine may fairly see indications of it in certain Old Testament expressions and events. The strongest of these are the appearances of the Angel of Jehovah.
sources.quote: Whether there really exist traces of the idea of the Trinity in the Old Testament, however, is a nice question. Certainly we cannot speak broadly of the revelation of the doctrine of the Trinity in the Old Testament.
sources.raw_question: Is it certain, as Dorner argues, that traces of the Trinity must exist in the Old Testament because any living idea of God must be Trinitarian?

question: Do the New Testament writers think their doctrine of Father, Son and Spirit is a departure from the Old Testament God of Israel?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. They felt no incongruity between their doctrine of the Trinity and the Old Testament conception of God. They stressed God's unity as strongly as the Old Testament does. They conceived Jehovah Himself as at once Father, Son and Spirit rather than placing new gods beside Him.
sources.quote: They do not, then, place two new gods by the side of Jehovah as alike with Him to be served and worshipped; they conceive Jehovah as Himself at once Father, Son and Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Do the New Testament writers think their doctrine of Father, Son and Spirit is a departure from the Old Testament God of Israel?

question: Is God great by participating in a greatness distinct from himself, as a great house or mountain is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Those Things Which Belong Absolutely to God as an Essence, are Spoken of the Trinity in the Singular, Not in the Plural.
sources.answer: No. If God were great by partaking of a greatness other than himself, that greatness would be greater than God, but nothing is greater than God. Therefore God is great by that greatness which he himself is; he is his own greatness.
sources.quote: otherwise that will be a greatness greater than God, whereas there is nothing greater than God; therefore, He is great with that greatness by which He Himself is that same greatness.
sources.raw_question: Is God great by participating in a greatness distinct from himself, as a great house or mountain is?

question: Is the formal object of divine worship the divine Persons considered precisely in their personal relations, or the divine essence?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: It is the divine essence. Owen agrees with the schoolmen that the formal reason of worship does not lie in the Persons considered under what constitutes their personality, namely their relations to one another. The proper object of invocation is God's essence in its infinite excellency, majesty and causality as first cause of all things. This is common to all three Persons and belongs to each as God, not formally as a Person.
sources.quote: The proper and peculiar object of divine worship and invocation is the essence of God, in its infinite excellency, dignity, majesty, and its causality, as the first sovereign cause of all things.
sources.raw_question: Is the formal object of divine worship the divine Persons considered precisely in their personal relations, or the divine essence?

question: Is it right to pray to the Trinity by repeating the same petition separately to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as in the Litany?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. Owen calls it groundless, if not impious. It assumes that one Person is worshipped and not another, when each is worshipped as God. It also treats the same request as three distinct acts expecting three separate grants, although all the works of the Trinity toward creatures are indivisible.
sources.quote: Hence is that way of praying to the Trinity, by the repetition of the same petition to the several persons (as in the Litany), groundless, if not impious. It supposeth that one person is worshipped, and not another, when each person is worshipped as God
sources.raw_question: Is it right to pray to the Trinity by repeating the same petition separately to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as in the Litany?

question: When a work appropriated to one divine Person, such as the Spirit, leads us to worship him, is that Person worshipped to the exclusion of the others?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. The concurrence of the other Persons in that work is never excluded. Worship directed to the Spirit as God is equally directed to the Father and the Son, so the whole Godhead is worshipped.
sources.quote: when any work of the Holy Ghost (or any other person), which is appropriated to him (we never exclude the concurrence of other persons), draws us to the worship of him, yet he is not worshipped exclusively, but the whole Godhead is worshipped.
sources.raw_question: When a work appropriated to one divine Person, such as the Spirit, leads us to worship him, is that Person worshipped to the exclusion of the others?

question: Can a supposed spiritual experience that brings no comfort be attributed to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. Owen holds that all the Spirit's effects bring consolation, at least in the root if not in the ripe fruit. Whatever lacks this is not of the Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: whatever we have in the kinds of the things before mentioned that brings not consolation with it, in the root at least, if not in the ripe fruit, is not of the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: Can a supposed spiritual experience that brings no comfort be attributed to the Holy Spirit?

question: Is Abraham excluded from the salvation and inheritance bestowed by Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter VIII.—Vain attempts of Marcion and his followers, who exclude Abraham from the salvation bestowed by Christ, who liberated not only Abraham, but the seed of Abraham, by fulfilling and not destroying the law when He healed on the Sabbath-day.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit, speaking through many and through Paul, testifies that Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness. The Lord also testifies to Abraham by raising up children to him and by placing him in the kingdom of heaven. Abraham's seed, the Church, receives the adoption and the inheritance promised to him.
sources.quote: God, who introduces, through Jesus Christ, Abraham to the kingdom of heaven, and his seed, that is, the Church, upon which also is conferred the adoption and the inheritance promised to Abraham
sources.raw_question: Is Abraham excluded from the salvation and inheritance bestowed by Christ?

question: Does the natural conscience of all people give them a knowledge of sin and of God's displeasure against it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes, but only dimly. Conscience by nature tells people what is good and evil and that those who do such things are worthy of death. Since every nation keeps some sense of a Deity as the rewarder of good and evil, every nation also has some sense of sin, as its sacrifices show. Yet this knowledge is obscure and mostly concerns the greater sins.
sources.quote: there is no nation but hath a sense of sin, and the displeasure of God for it. For this is the very first notion of God in the world, that he is the rewarder of good and evil.
sources.raw_question: Does the natural conscience of all people give them a knowledge of sin and of God's displeasure against it?

question: Does the formula 'of whom, and through whom, and to whom are all things' denote an undistinguished unity or many gods?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Of the Attributes Assigned by Hilary to Each Person. The Trinity is Represented in Things that are Made.
sources.answer: Neither. The phrases are not used indiscriminately, as if marking a unity without distinctions. Nor do they denote many gods, since the text goes on 'to Him be glory,' in the singular. God is one, yet a Trinity.
sources.quote: Neither are we to take the words, “of whom, and through whom, and to whom are all things,” as used indiscriminately [i.e., to denote a unity without distinctions]; nor yet to denote many gods
sources.raw_question: Does the formula 'of whom, and through whom, and to whom are all things' denote an undistinguished unity or many gods?

question: Is what is incomprehensible to human beings also beyond God's knowledge?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says God numbers the stars, which are too many for us to count. This shows that all things, however far above human understanding, are embraced by God's wisdom. We must not suppose that God takes note of things by the measure of human knowledge.
sources.quote: we must not imagine God to take note of things by the measure of human knowledge, but that all things, however incomprehensible and above human understanding, are embraced by the knowledge of the wisdom of God
sources.raised_by_detail: many who think what is incomprehensible to themselves is incomprehensible to God
sources.raw_question: Is what is incomprehensible to human beings also beyond God's knowledge?

question: Does the passage in Exodus about God covering Moses with his hand in the cleft of the rock refer to Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter V. The writer sums up the argument he had commenced, and confirms the statement that unity is signified by the terms finger and right hand, from the fact that the works of God are the same as are the works of hands; and that those of hands are the same as those of fingers; and lastly, that the term hand applies equally to the Son and the Spirit, and that of finger applies to the Spirit and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Ambrose reads it as referring to the mystery of the Incarnation. The eternal Power of God, who is the Son as God's hand, took on itself the covering of a body.
sources.quote: which refers to the mystery of the Incarnation, because the eternal Power of God took on Itself the covering of a body
sources.raw_question: Does the passage in Exodus about God covering Moses with his hand in the cleft of the rock refer to Christ?

question: What does Christ's sitting at the right hand of God (Mark 16:19) show about the relation of the Son to the God of the prophets?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: It shows that the God at whose right hand the Son sits is the same God who spoke in the prophets. Mark's account fulfils Psalm 110, "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit Thou on My right hand." So the God and Father of Christ is one and the same God, announced by the prophets and handed down by the Gospel.
sources.quote: He was received up into heaven, and sitteth on the right hand of God;”[^3427] confirming what had been spoken by the prophet: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit Thou on My right hand
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's sitting at the right hand of God (Mark 16:19) show about the relation of the Son to the God of the prophets?

question: Why is the Son, like the Father, ineffable?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: Because the Son is the Only-begotten Image of the Unbegotten Father. As the Father is ineffable because Unbegotten, the Son is ineffable because Only-begotten; since we form our idea of an image and of what it represents by the same means, and our faculties deal only with visible things, the invisible Image is as beyond our grasp as the original.
sources.quote: For even as the Father is ineffable because He is Unbegotten, so is the Son ineffable because He is the Only-begotten, since the Begotten is the Image of the Unbegotten.
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son, like the Father, ineffable?

question: Does Colossians 2:2-3, saying all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ, show that the Son is not ignorant of the day of judgment?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. A part is not the whole; if the Son did not know the day, all the treasures of knowledge would not be in Him. But all are in Him, so He is not ignorant of the day. They are hidden in Him as in a mystery, but hidden does not mean wanting.
sources.quote: If the Son does not know the day, all the treasures of knowledge are not in Him; but He has all the treasures of knowledge in Him, therefore He is not ignorant of the day.
sources.raw_question: Does Colossians 2:2-3, saying all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ, show that the Son is not ignorant of the day of judgment?

question: Was the imputation of sin to Christ forced upon him, or did the Son voluntarily assume it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It was voluntary. Sin was imputed to the dear Son of God's bosom upon his own voluntary assumption of it, as he said to the Father, "Lo, I come to do thy will," and all our iniquities met on him.
sources.quote: If sin be imputed to the dear Son of his bosom, as upon his own voluntary assumption of it it was (for he said to his Father, “Lo, I come to do thy will,” and all our iniquities did meet on him)
sources.raw_question: Was the imputation of sin to Christ forced upon him, or did the Son voluntarily assume it?

question: Did God the Father delight in the sufferings of his Son, or why did he require them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: He did not delight in them, for God does not afflict willingly. He required only that his law be fulfilled, his justice satisfied, and his wrath atoned for sin, and nothing less than Christ's sufferings would accomplish this; had a cheaper rate sufficed, Christ's blood would not have been required.
sources.quote: only he required that his law be fulfilled, his justice satisfied, his wrath atoned for sin; and nothing less than all this would bring it about.
sources.raw_question: Did God the Father delight in the sufferings of his Son, or why did he require them?

question: Did the one who suffered on the cross, being God's equal, merely undergo a light trial because of his divine strength?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Though he was the fellow of the Lord of hosts, the mighty one, the wisdom and power of God, his sufferings made him tremble, sweat blood, cry and wrestle; God bruised him, forsook him, made him sin and a curse. Sin brought him who was the Son of God, equal unto God, God blessed for ever, into the form of a servant and slew the Lord of life.
sources.quote: It brought him who was the Son of God, equal unto God, God blessed for ever, into the form of a servant, who had not where to lay his head.
sources.raw_question: Did the one who suffered on the cross, being God's equal, merely undergo a light trial because of his divine strength?

question: How do believers come to be in God and God in them?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Through the gift of the Spirit. Since the Spirit given to us is God's Spirit, having the Spirit we are counted as being in God and God in us. Apart from the Spirit we are strange and distant from God, and by participating in the Spirit we are knit into the Godhead, keeping it through true confession.
sources.quote: we, apart from the Spirit, are strange and distant from God, and by the participation of the Spirit we are knit into the Godhead; so that our being in the Father is not ours, but is the Spirit’s which is in us
sources.raw_question: How do believers come to be in God and God in them?

question: Could the Son have come to be in the Father through participation of the Spirit and moral improvement of conduct?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. Even entertaining this thought is an excess of irreligion. The Son gives to the Spirit, and whatever the Spirit has, He has from the Word, so the Son cannot be advanced into the Father through the Spirit.
sources.quote: For He, as has been said, gives to the Spirit, and whatever the Spirit hath, He hath from the Word.
sources.raw_question: Could the Son have come to be in the Father through participation of the Spirit and moral improvement of conduct?

question: Do Christ's hunger, weeping, weariness and cry of 'Eloi, Eloi' show that the Word is weak by nature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > When the Word and Son hungered, wept, and was wearied, He acted as our Mediator, taking on Him what was ours, that He might impart to us what was His.
sources.answer: No. These are our human affections, which he took from us in the body he bore. He took our infirmities without being infirm, and he hungered without hungering in his own nature as Word. He offered these to the Father, interceding for us, so that in him they might be abolished.
sources.quote: For as He takes our infirmities, not being infirm, and hungers not hungering, but sends up what is ours that it may be abolished
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's hunger, weeping, weariness and cry of 'Eloi, Eloi' show that the Word is weak by nature?

question: Why was it necessary that our eternal life be founded in the Word, who is before the ages, rather than in some created being?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Earthly human beings were not of themselves capable of eternal life. Only because life and salvation were prepared beforehand in the eternal Word, through whom the ages were made, can we outlive the passing visible world and abide forever in Christ.
sources.quote: Nor in any other way was it fitting that our life should be founded, but in the Lord who is before the ages, and through whom the ages were brought to be; that, since it was in Him, we too might be able to inherit that everlasting life.
sources.raw_question: Why was it necessary that our eternal life be founded in the Word, who is before the ages, rather than in some created being?

question: How does the Spirit of God relate to the weakness of the flesh in a person who receives him, as in Christ's saying that 'the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak'?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter IX.—Showing how that passage of the apostle which the heretics pervert, should be understood; viz., “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.”
sources.answer: The strength of the Spirit absorbs the weakness of the flesh. The person becomes spiritual rather than carnal through fellowship with the Spirit. A living man is formed from both: living because he partakes of the Spirit, and man because of the substance of flesh. This is why martyrs despise death, through the Spirit's readiness and not through the flesh's infirmity.
sources.quote: and from both of these is formed a living man,—living, indeed, because he partakes of the Spirit, but man, because of the substance of flesh.
sources.raw_question: How does the Spirit of God relate to the weakness of the flesh in a person who receives him, as in Christ's saying that 'the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak'?

question: Is Christ dishonoured when people rely on their own repentance or duties to bear away their sins?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ's work in the world was to bear our iniquities and lay down his life as a ransom, so to ascribe this to repentance, duties, or any other means takes his work out of his hands. The greatest dishonour to Christ is to think to get rid of sins any other way than by him.
sources.quote: What greater dishonour, then, can be done to the Lord Jesus, than to ascribe this work to any thing else, — to think to get rid of our sins [by] any other way or means?
sources.raw_question: Is Christ dishonoured when people rely on their own repentance or duties to bear away their sins?

question: Does daily laying sins upon Christ by faith mean that Christ suffers or dies again?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. Christ does not die or suffer any more; rather, as the faith of the Old Testament saints made present what had not yet come to pass, so faith now makes present what was accomplished long ago. This is what it is to know Christ crucified.
sources.quote: Not as though he died any more, or suffered any more; but as the faith of the saints of old made that present and done before their eyes [which had] not yet come to pass, Heb. xi. 1, so faith now makes that present
sources.raw_question: Does daily laying sins upon Christ by faith mean that Christ suffers or dies again?

question: Do the prophecies of Isaiah, such as the virgin bearing Emmanuel and the Spirit-anointed preacher, refer to Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXIII.—The patriarchs and prophets by pointing out the advent of Christ, fortified thereby, as it were, the way of posterity to the faith of Christ; and so the labours of the apostles were lessened inasmuch as they gathered in the fruits of the labours of others.
sources.answer: Yes. The angel told Joseph that Mary was the virgin Isaiah had foretold, who would give birth to Emmanuel, conceived of the Holy Spirit. At Capernaum the Lord himself read Isaiah's prophecy of the one anointed by the Spirit of the Lord and declared that it was fulfilled in their hearing. This showed that He was the one Isaiah had foretold.
sources.quote: pointing out that it was she who was the virgin mentioned by Isaiah beforehand, who should give birth to Emmanuel
sources.raw_question: Do the prophecies of Isaiah, such as the virgin bearing Emmanuel and the Spirit-anointed preacher, refer to Jesus Christ?

question: How can the righteousness by which believers are accepted be a righteousness of works and yet be received entirely by grace?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: It is both, in different respects. In itself Christ's righteousness is a righteousness of works, because he fully performed what the law required. But it is given to us freely, not at all because of our own works. Scripture says plainly that it is 'by grace, and no more of works.'
sources.quote: It is of mere grace that it is bestowed on us, it is not at all of works; though it be in itself a righteousness of works, yet to us it is of mere grace.
sources.raw_question: How can the righteousness by which believers are accepted be a righteousness of works and yet be received entirely by grace?

question: How can a holy and righteous God accept a sinful and unclean person without contradicting his own nature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Through the righteousness of Christ, which shows God's infinite wisdom. The sinner knows God is holy and cannot see how God and a sinner could be at peace. In Christ crucified, 'the wisdom of God,' the difficulty is removed and the two are reconciled.
sources.quote: But in the righteousness of Christ doth a world of wisdom open itself, dispelling all difficulties and darkness, and manifesting a reconciliation of all this.
sources.raw_question: How can a holy and righteous God accept a sinful and unclean person without contradicting his own nature?

question: Does greater theological intelligence or skill entitle a teacher to conceive of a God higher than the Creator of the universe, or of another Christ or Only-begotten?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter X.—Unity of the faith of the Church throughout the whole world.
sources.answer: No. Differences in intelligence do not change the subject-matter of the faith, which is one and the same; no one should conceive of another God besides the Framer, Maker and Preserver of the universe, nor another Christ or Only-begotten. Superior skill consists rather in explaining more clearly the meaning of parables and God's dispensation within the one rule of faith.
sources.quote: should conceive of some other God besides Him who is the Framer, Maker, and Preserver of this universe, (as if He were not sufficient for them), or of another Christ, or another Only-begotten
sources.raw_question: Does greater theological intelligence or skill entitle a teacher to conceive of a God higher than the Creator of the universe, or of another Christ or Only-begotten?

question: Is it one and the same God who made both temporal and eternal, heavenly and earthly things, and who gave the various covenants?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter X.—Unity of the faith of the Church throughout the whole world.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus treats it as part of the one faith that one and the same God made some things temporal and some eternal, some heavenly and others earthly, and gave more than one covenant to mankind; the skilled teacher's task is only to explain why, not to posit different gods.
sources.quote: set forth why it is that one and the same God has made some things temporal and some eternal, some heavenly and others earthly
sources.raw_question: Is it one and the same God who made both temporal and eternal, heavenly and earthly things, and who gave the various covenants?

question: Does Scripture itself cause the modalist and psilanthropist heresies by saying both that God is one and that Christ is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > In Fine, Notwithstanding the Said Heretics Have Gathered the Origin of Their Error from Consideration of What is Written: Although We Call Christ God, and the Father God, Still Scripture Does Not Set Forth Two Gods, Any More Than Two Lords or Two Teachers.
sources.answer: No. The heavenly Scriptures never deceive. Both truths are plainly written and must be held together with fitting reverence and sound argument. Any scandal arises from human error and the heretics' presumption, not from any fault in Scripture.
sources.quote: not assuredly by the fault of the heavenly Scriptures, which never deceive; but by the presumption of human error, whereby they have chosen to be heretics.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture itself cause the modalist and psilanthropist heresies by saying both that God is one and that Christ is God?

question: Why are absolute attributes such as greatness, goodness and wisdom predicated of God according to his essence?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Preface.—The Conclusion of What Has Been Said Above. The Rule to Be Observed in the More Difficult Questions of the Faith.
sources.answer: In God, to be is the same as to be great, good or wise. Such attributes are therefore not accidents added to the divine being but are the essence itself. So whatever is said of a Person in respect to himself is said of the one essence.
sources.quote: For they are thus spoken of according to essence, since in them to be is the same as to be great, as to be good, as to be wise
sources.raw_question: Why are absolute attributes such as greatness, goodness and wisdom predicated of God according to his essence?

question: Why was it fitting that many things should proclaim the one Mediator, Christ?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In What Manner We are Gathered from Many into One Through One Mediator.
sources.answer: Because humanity had fallen away from the one true and supreme God and become distracted by and attached to many things. It was therefore needful, by God's merciful decree, that those same many things should proclaim and witness to the One who was to come. Freed from the burden of the many, we would then come to the One.
sources.quote: it was needful, by the decree and command of God in His mercy, that those same many things should join in proclaiming the One that should come
sources.raw_question: Why was it fitting that many things should proclaim the one Mediator, Christ?

question: Since souls and angels have a beginning yet live forever, could the Son likewise have a beginning yet endure everlastingly?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. The parallel fails because the Godhead differs from creation in its proper attributes. Creatures live by participating in life and attain excellence by sharing in something better than themselves, so they could cease to live if that participation ceased. The Son is life itself and needs no life from outside. So what holds of creatures gives no reason to cancel the Son's eternity.
sources.quote: But if He is the very life, and needs not to have life in Himself ab extra, while all other things are not life, but are merely participants in life, what constrains us to cancel, by reason of what we see in creation, the eternity of the Son?
sources.raw_question: Since souls and angels have a beginning yet live forever, could the Son likewise have a beginning yet endure everlastingly?

question: If some people never reach perfection, is God's creative skill or calling at fault?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIX.—Man is endowed with the faculty of distinguishing good and evil; so that, without compulsion, he has the power, by his own will and choice, to perform God’s commandments, by doing which he avoids the evils prepared for the rebellious.
sources.answer: No. The cause of imperfection lies in the person who did not obey, not in God who called him. Those invited to the marriage who refused shut themselves out of the royal supper. God's power is not defective, for He can raise up children to Abraham from stones. Likewise, light does not fail because some people blind themselves.
sources.quote: The skill of God, therefore, is not defective, for He has power of the stones to raise up children to Abraham;
sources.raw_question: If some people never reach perfection, is God's creative skill or calling at fault?

question: Does God compel the unwilling to accept His saving work, or are human beings free agents?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIX.—Man is endowed with the faculty of distinguishing good and evil; so that, without compulsion, he has the power, by his own will and choice, to perform God’s commandments, by doing which he avoids the evils prepared for the rebellious.
sources.answer: God compels no one; human beings are free agents. Like light, God never enslaves anyone by necessity. Those who turn away from the light given by the Father do so by their own fault, because they were created free and have power over themselves.
sources.quote: nor, again, does God exercise compulsion upon any one unwilling to accept the exercise of His skill.
sources.raw_question: Does God compel the unwilling to accept His saving work, or are human beings free agents?

question: Is the honouring of Christ as Lord and Redeemer by a believer a work peculiar to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit reveals the good things of the covenant which the Father provided and the Son purchased, and so Christ is magnified in believers' hearts. No soul glorifies Christ upon a sense of his redemption except as a peculiar effect of the Holy Ghost, since no one can say Jesus is Lord but by the Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: A soul doth never glorify or honour Christ upon a discovery or sense of the eternal redemption he hath purchased for him, but it is in him a peculiar effect of the Holy Ghost as our comforter.
sources.raw_question: Is the honouring of Christ as Lord and Redeemer by a believer a work peculiar to the Holy Spirit?

question: Does Scripture appropriate religious worship and adoration to the one supreme God alone, so that no other being may receive it?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: Yes. Exod. 20:3-5, Deut. 6:13 and 10:20 forbid all acts of religious worship to any being besides the one supreme God, and Christ himself explains this as "him only shalt thou serve." Scripture gives neither rule nor example for worshipping any creature, and all relevant texts are full and clear for the worship of God only.
sources.quote: All acts of religious worship are forbidden to be offered to any other being, besides the one supreme God: to him they are appropriated, to him only.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture appropriate religious worship and adoration to the one supreme God alone, so that no other being may receive it?

question: When God asked Adam 'Where art thou?' and Cain 'Where is Abel thy brother?', does this show that God was ignorant, and does it bear on how the Son can ask questions while knowing the answer?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: No. To hold that God asked because He was ignorant is the Manichaean error; God asked while knowing. Since it was the Son in whom God then inquired, there is nothing strange in the same Son, now clad in flesh, inquiring of the disciples as man while knowing.
sources.quote: the Son, in whom God then inquired, that same Son who now is clad in flesh, inquires of the disciples as man?
sources.raw_question: When God asked Adam 'Where art thou?' and Cain 'Where is Abel thy brother?', does this show that God was ignorant, and does it bear on how the Son can ask questions while knowing the answer?

question: Does Peter's vision in Acts 10 show that the Holy Spirit is the Lord who commands with divine authority?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter X. Being about to prove that the will, the calling, and the commandment of the Trinity is one, St. Ambrose shows that the Spirit called the Church exactly as the Father and the Son did, and proves this by the selection of SS. Paul and Barnabas, and especially by the mission of St. Peter to Cornelius. And by the way he points out how in the Apostle's vision the calling of the Gentiles was shadowed forth, who having been before like wild beasts, now by the operation of the Spirit lay aside that wildness. Then having quoted other passages in support of this view, he shows that in the case of Jeremiah cast into a pit by Jews, and rescued by Abdemelech, is a type of the slighting of the Holy Spirit by the Jews, and of His being honoured by the Gentiles.
sources.answer: Yes. The voice Peter answered as "Lord" is identified by Scripture as the Spirit, who then says, "I have sent thee." Since the One who formed the mystery also made it known, the Spirit clearly shows His own lordship and power. Peter did not wait for a command from God the Father; he acknowledged that the message and the grace came from the Spirit Himself.
sources.quote: But the Scripture declares Who that Lord was, for He Whom he had answered spoke to him when he answered. And the following words show the Spirit clearly revealed, for He Who formed the mystery made known the mystery.
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's vision in Acts 10 show that the Holy Spirit is the Lord who commands with divine authority?

question: Where in the human mind can one find a likeness, however dim, of the divine Word spoken of in John 1:1?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Concerning the Word of the Mind, in Which We See the Word of God, as in a Glass and an Enigma.
sources.answer: In the inner word of the mind, which exists before it is uttered in sound and even before the images of its sounds are considered in thought. Whoever can understand such a word, which belongs to no national language, can see through a glass and in an enigma some likeness of the Word who was in the beginning with God and was God.
sources.quote: whoever, I say, is able to understand this, is able now to see through this glass and in this enigma some likeness of that Word of whom it is said, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
sources.raw_question: Where in the human mind can one find a likeness, however dim, of the divine Word spoken of in John 1:1?

question: In Peter's statement that Christ was "exalted by the right hand of God," is it the Divinity or the Humanity of Christ that was exalted?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: The Humanity. God, being the Highest, has no need to be exalted, so only the lowly element, which is the Humanity, can be raised up. Its exaltation consisted in its becoming Lord and Christ.
sources.quote: Who then was “exalted”? He that was lowly, or He that was the Highest? and what else is the lowly, but the Humanity? what else is the Highest, but the Divinity? Surely, God needs not to be exalted, seeing that He is the Highest.
sources.raw_question: In Peter's statement that Christ was "exalted by the right hand of God," is it the Divinity or the Humanity of Christ that was exalted?

question: Who is "the right hand of God" that exalted the crucified Jesus?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > A remarkable and original reply to these utterances, and a demonstration of the power of the Crucified, and of the fact that this subjection was of the Human Nature, not that which the Only-Begotten has from the Father. Also an explanation of the figure of the Cross, and of the appellation “Christ,” and an account of the good gifts bestowed on the Human Nature by the Godhead which was commingled with it.
sources.answer: The Right Hand of God is the Lord Himself, the Word by whom all things were made. It raised the Man united with It to Its own height and made Him what It is by nature, namely Lord and King, that is, Christ.
sources.quote: the Right Hand of God, that made all things that are, (which is the Lord, by Whom all things were made, and without Whom nothing that is subsists,) Itself raised to Its own height the Man united with It, making Him also to be what It is by nature.
sources.raw_question: Who is "the right hand of God" that exalted the crucified Jesus?

question: Does the fact that the love of God is shed abroad through the Holy Spirit show that the Spirit is not a created work?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VIII. The Holy Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each person, since there is no one besides Christ capable of receiving Him wholly. Charity is shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, Who, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing common with creatures; and He, inasmuch as He is said to proceed from the mouth of God, must not be classed with creatures, nor with things divisible, seeing He is eternal.
sources.answer: Yes. As God sheds forth of the Spirit, so the love of God is shed abroad through the Spirit, showing unity of operation and grace between God and the Spirit. The Spirit is thus the dispenser and plenteous Fount of divine love, not a work.
sources.quote: in order that we may understand that the Holy Spirit is not a work, Who is the dispenser and plenteous Fount of the divine love.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the love of God is shed abroad through the Holy Spirit show that the Spirit is not a created work?

question: Did the ancient Fathers teach that only equality between Father and Son would make them two Gods, and that the Son's real subordination is what saves the Church from polytheism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. Athanasius, Hilary and Basil, whom the opponent cites, repeatedly condemned the Arian doctrine as polytheism and paganism. When they appealed to unity of principle to answer the charge of Tritheism, they were defending the Catholic doctrine, which already held equality of nature. They were not defending an inferior, created Son.
sources.quote: Not your doctrine, not the Arian doctrine; but the Catholic doctrine. For since equality of nature and unity of principle too, are both requisite; the Catholics admitting the former (as their adversaries well knew)
sources.raw_question: Did the ancient Fathers teach that only equality between Father and Son would make them two Gods, and that the Son's real subordination is what saves the Church from polytheism?

question: Could humanity have been deified and freed from death if the Word had only acted upon or healed human nature from outside, without taking flesh as his own?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: No. Unless the Word's divine works were done through the body, man would not have been deified. Unless the properties of the flesh were ascribed to the Word, man would not have been fully delivered from them. Even holy men such as Jeremiah and John the Baptist remained mortal, for death reigned even over those who had not sinned. Only the Word appropriating the flesh destroys corruption, so that people rise immortal.
sources.quote: if the works of the Word’s Godhead had not taken place through the body, man had not been deified; and again, had not the properties of the flesh been ascribed to the Word, man had not been thoroughly delivered from them
sources.raw_question: Could humanity have been deified and freed from death if the Word had only acted upon or healed human nature from outside, without taking flesh as his own?

question: Why is the eternal Word, who gives others their origin, said to have been born of Mary?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: Because the flesh born of Mary, the Bearer of God, is his own. He is said to be born so that he may transfer our origin into himself. Then we no longer return to earth as mere earth but, knit into the Word from heaven, are carried to heaven by him.
sources.quote: He Himself is said to have been born, who furnishes to others an origin of being; in order that He may transfer our origin into Himself
sources.raw_question: Why is the eternal Word, who gives others their origin, said to have been born of Mary?

question: Where does the boundary lie between the 'outer man' and the 'inner man' in the human being, and does the outer man consist of the body alone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Of What Kind are the Outer and the Inner Man.
sources.answer: The outer man is whatever we have in the mind in common with the beasts, not merely the body. It includes the body together with the life that gives it vigor, the bodily senses that perceive outward things, and even the recollection of images of sensed things stored in memory. In all these we do not differ from the beasts except in upright bodily posture.
sources.quote: For whatever we have in the mind common with the beasts, thus much is rightly said to belong to the outer man. For the outer man is not to be considered to be the body only
sources.raw_question: Where does the boundary lie between the 'outer man' and the 'inner man' in the human being, and does the outer man consist of the body alone?

question: Is true teaching about God a secret mystery to be passed on only to an elite who can pay for it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter IV.—Account given by the heretics of the formation of Achamoth; origin of the visible world from her disturbances.
sources.answer: No. The Gnostics' 'profound mysteries' are taught privately and for a high price. This marks them as unlike the Lord's doctrine, which he commanded to be given as freely as it was received. Truth from Christ is public and freely given, whereas these hidden doctrines are pursued only by those in love with falsehood.
sources.quote: For these doctrines are not at all similar to those of which our Lord said, “Freely ye have received, freely give.”
sources.raw_question: Is true teaching about God a secret mystery to be passed on only to an elite who can pay for it?

question: Can Eunomius's claim that the Holy Spirit was "once for all made subject" be sustained in any of the senses Scripture gives to "subjection"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He proceeds to discuss the views held by Eunomius, and by the Church, touching the Holy Spirit; and to show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are not three Gods, but one God. He also discusses different senses of “Subjection,” and therein shows that the subjection of all things to the Son is the same as the subjection of the Son to the Father.
sources.answer: No. Scripture uses "subjection" for irrational beasts, captives of war, servants, unruly children, and people saved by submitting to God. None of these can apply to the Spirit. Saving subjection in particular is sought by those who need life, like the sick seeking healing. The Spirit gives life to all things and needs no salvation, so Eunomius's claim rests on neither Scripture nor sound reasoning.
sources.quote: But of what life does the Holy Spirit, that quickeneth all things, stand in need, that by subjection He should obtain salvation for Himself?
sources.raw_question: Can Eunomius's claim that the Holy Spirit was "once for all made subject" be sustained in any of the senses Scripture gives to "subjection"?

question: Why was it necessary for Christ to be born of a woman in order to defeat Satan?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: Because the enemy would not have been fairly vanquished unless a man born of a woman conquered him. Satan first gained the advantage over man by means of a woman, so justice required that a man born of a woman, from the Virgin, be the one to overcome him.
sources.quote: For indeed the enemy would not have been fairly vanquished, unless it had been a man [born] of a woman who conquered him. For it was by means of a woman that he got the advantage over man at first
sources.raw_question: Why was it necessary for Christ to be born of a woman in order to defeat Satan?

question: How did the Catholic Fathers answer the Arian dilemma by asking whether the Father is God willingly or unwillingly?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 31: Whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration, on the side of Arianism, ought to move a wise and good man, against so great appearances of truth o
sources.answer: They turned the Arians' weapon on them. Athanasius, Gregory Nazianzen, Cyril and Augustine asked whether the Father is God against his will or with his will. 'Against his will' is absurd, and 'with his will' would, by the Arians' own reasoning, make the Father prior to himself. So the dilemma proves nothing about the Son's posteriority.
sources.quote: if they had said volens, with his will; then, by their own argument, they made the Father prior to himself.
sources.raw_question: How did the Catholic Fathers answer the Arian dilemma by asking whether the Father is God willingly or unwillingly?

question: Does a symmetrical and consistent rational theory about God guarantee that one has solved the mystery of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. We must not trust human intellect so blindly as to think we know the objects of our thought completely just because we have formed a consistent theory. The mind's knowledge is limited to the range of its perception and shares the weakness of its dependent existence.
sources.quote: we must not repose so blind a confidence in human intellect as to imagine that we have complete knowledge of the objects of our thought, or that the ultimate problem is solved as soon as we have formed a symmetrical and consistent theory
sources.raw_question: Does a symmetrical and consistent rational theory about God guarantee that one has solved the mystery of God?

question: What does Paul mean in 1 Corinthians 1 by calling the wisdom of the world foolishness and the preaching of the cross the power of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
