sources.answer: He means that human wisdom, bounded by its own narrow horizon, judges divine truth to be foolish. The real foolishness lies in that human wisdom, which demands signs and reasons from God as the condition of belief. Christ crucified, an offence to Jews and folly to Greeks, is the Power and Wisdom of God. What seems weak and foolish in the things of God surpasses all earthly thought and power.
sources.quote: There is no foolishness in the things of God; the foolishness lies in that human wisdom which demands of God, as the condition of belief, signs and wisdom.
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean in 1 Corinthians 1 by calling the wisdom of the world foolishness and the preaching of the cross the power of God?

question: How does a person know that faith is present in his own heart, given that faith concerns things not seen?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Attempt is Made to Distinguish Out of the Scriptures the Offices of Wisdom and of Knowledge. That in the Beginning of John Some Things that are Said Belong to Wisdom, Some to Knowledge. Some Things There are Only Known by the Help of Faith. How We See the Faith that is in Us. In the Same Narrative of John, Some Things are Known by the Sense of the Body, Others Only by the Reason of the Mind.
sources.answer: He sees it directly within himself, not as bodies are seen or imagined, nor as another's soul is conjectured. Faith is held fast by most certain knowledge, and conscience proclaims it. So although we believe what we cannot see, faith in absent and unseen things is itself present and seen within us.
sources.quote: Faith is not so seen in the heart in which it is, by him whose it is; but most certain knowledge holds it fast, and conscience proclaims it.
sources.raw_question: How does a person know that faith is present in his own heart, given that faith concerns things not seen?

question: Should the formation of the world be ascribed to God alone, or can it be attributed to some other agent or to a pre-existing vacuum and shadow?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter IV.—The absurdity of the supposed vacuum and defect of the heretics is demonstrated.
sources.answer: To God alone. One may ask about the reason for God's dispensation, but the making of the world must not be credited to any other. All things were prepared beforehand by God to be made as they were made, and shadow and vacuity must not be invented as sources of creation.
sources.quote: the formation of the world is not to be ascribed to any other. And all things are to be spoken of as having been so prepared by God beforehand, that they should be made as they have been made
sources.raw_question: Should the formation of the world be ascribed to God alone, or can it be attributed to some other agent or to a pre-existing vacuum and shadow?

question: If something exists unproduced and self-generated, must it be equal in age, nature and honour with the supreme Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter IV.—The absurdity of the supposed vacuum and defect of the heretics is demonstrated.
sources.answer: Yes. Anything must either be produced by another or be self-generated. Whatever is self-generated would be as old as the Father of all and of the same nature and honour with him. A self-existent vacuum would therefore rival the supreme God, which is absurd.
sources.quote: it must have sprang from and been generated by itself, and in that case it will be equal in point of age to that Bythus who is, according to them, the Father of all
sources.raw_question: If something exists unproduced and self-generated, must it be equal in age, nature and honour with the supreme Father?

question: Could a supreme God allow a defect or a rival creator to arise within his own domain against his will and correct it only later?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter IV.—The absurdity of the supposed vacuum and defect of the heretics is demonstrated.
sources.answer: No. Such a God would be degenerate for allowing a stain in his own bosom and permitting another to create against his will. Whoever can later remedy a defect could have prevented it from the start. If things could not have been made otherwise at first, they could never be rectified afterward.
sources.quote: For he who can afterwards rectify a defect, and does, as it were, wash away a stain, could at a much earlier date have taken care that no such stain should, even at first, be found among his possessions.
sources.raw_question: Could a supreme God allow a defect or a rival creator to arise within his own domain against his will and correct it only later?

question: Can there be a supreme good God and Father distinct from and higher than the Creator who refuses to give life to human bodies?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter IV.—Those persons are deceived who feign another God the Father besides the Creator of the world; for he must have been feeble and useless, or else malignant and full of envy, if he be either unable or unwilling to extend external life to our bodies.
sources.answer: No. Such a Father would be either powerless, if he cannot quicken bodies, and so less perfect than the Creator who does quicken them, or envious and malignant, if he can but will not. Either way he cannot be the truly good and supreme God. The Creator, who vivifies the whole man and promises the body's resurrection, is shown to be the more powerful and truly good God.
sources.quote: If, on the one hand, it is because he cannot, he is, upon that supposition, not a powerful being, nor is he more perfect than the Creator; for the Creator grants, as we must perceive, what He is unable to afford.
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who posit another Father beyond the Creator
sources.raw_question: Can there be a supreme good God and Father distinct from and higher than the Creator who refuses to give life to human bodies?

question: Is it a mark of divine goodness to give life only to things already immortal by nature, such as soul and spirit, and not to the mortal body?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter IV.—Those persons are deceived who feign another God the Father besides the Creator of the world; for he must have been feeble and useless, or else malignant and full of envy, if he be either unable or unwilling to extend external life to our bodies.
sources.answer: No. Giving life to what is immortal by nature, where life is always present, is no real benefaction. True goodness gives life to what needs help in order to live. A God who leaves the body to fall under death is careless rather than benevolent.
sources.quote: He feigns to be the quickener of those things which are immortal by nature, to which things life is always present by their very nature; but he does not benevolently quicken those things which required his assistance
sources.raw_question: Is it a mark of divine goodness to give life only to things already immortal by nature, such as soul and spirit, and not to the mortal body?

question: Can the bodily imagination grasp everything that reason knows, such as the infinity of number or the infinite divisibility of bodies?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > The Imagination Also Adds Even to Things We Have Not Seen, Those Things Which We Have Seen Elsewhere.
sources.answer: No. Imagination can enlarge or shrink images only within the measure supplied by memory, such as the greatest spaces or smallest particles we have seen. Reason goes further and announces the infinity of number and the infinite divisibility of atoms, but imagination cannot follow it there. So we picture no bodily thing except what we remember or what we build from things remembered.
sources.quote: And reason, indeed, proceeds still beyond, but phantasy does not follow her; as when reason announces the infinity of number also, which no vision of him who conceives according to corporeal things can apprehend.
sources.raw_question: Can the bodily imagination grasp everything that reason knows, such as the infinity of number or the infinite divisibility of bodies?

question: Does the Holy Spirit dwell in His temple as a priest or minister, or as God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XII. From the fact that St. Paul has shown that the light of the Godhead which the three apostles worshipped in Christ is in the Trinity, it is made clear that the Spirit also is to be worshipped. It is shown from the words themselves that the Spirit is intended by the apostles. The Godhead of the same Spirit is proved from the fact that He has a temple wherein He dwells not as a priest, but as God: and is worshipped with the Father and the Son; whence is understood the oneness of nature in Them.
sources.answer: As God. He does not dwell as a priest or minister but as the Lord who dwells in His holy temple, just as the Father and the Son dwell in believers and make their abode with them.
sources.quote: But He does not dwell in the temple as a priest, nor as a minister, but as God
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit dwell in His temple as a priest or minister, or as God?

question: Is the God who in the New Testament 'raises up children unto Abraham from the stones' the same God who in the Old Testament promises to gather the saved from all nations?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXIV.—He fortifies his opinions with regard to the temporal and earthly kingdom of the saints after their resurrection, by the various testimonies of Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, and Daniel; also by the parable of the servants watching, to whom the Lord promised that He would minister.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus argues that the Church is the seed of Abraham, and that the prophetic promises of gathering from all nations show that the one who raises up children to Abraham in the New Testament is the same Lord who speaks in the Old Testament. Jeremiah's prophecy of the Lord gathering His people from every region confirms that one and the same God is at work in both covenants.
sources.quote: that we may know that He who in the New Testament “raises up from the stones children unto Abraham,” is He who will gather, according to the Old Testament, those that shall be saved from all the nations
sources.raised_by_detail: implicitly against the Gnostics who separated the God of the Old Testament from the God of the New
sources.raw_question: Is the God who in the New Testament 'raises up children unto Abraham from the stones' the same God who in the Old Testament promises to gather the saved from all nations?

question: Was Sabellius right that the works of Christ were the works of true God, even though he denied that it was the Son who worked them?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: Partly. Sabellius rightly maintained that the works done in Christ were those of true God, and the Church shares his victory over those who call Christ a creature. But he erred in denying that it was the Son who worked, recognising true God but not God the Son in this activity.
sources.quote: Sabellius denies that it was the Son who was working, and he is wrong; but he proves his case triumphantly when he alleges that the work done was that of true God.
sources.raw_question: Was Sabellius right that the works of Christ were the works of true God, even though he denied that it was the Son who worked them?

question: Does Christ's condescending care for humanity, signified by humble titles like Physician, lower our estimate of his divine dignity?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. His care should rather strike us with amazement at both his mighty power and his love for humanity. Nothing in creation sets forth the excellency of his might so well as that the incomprehensible God could impassibly, through flesh, come into conflict with death to free us from suffering.
sources.quote: And shall this His care for us degrade to meanness our thoughts of Him? Or, on the contrary, shall it smite us with amazement at once at the mighty power and love to man of the Saviour
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's condescending care for humanity, signified by humble titles like Physician, lower our estimate of his divine dignity?

question: Are the Spirit of Life, the Paraclete, and the Spirit of Truth the same as the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IV. The Holy Spirit is one and the same Who spake in the prophets and apostles, Who is the Spirit of God and of Christ; Whom, further, Scripture designates the Paraclete, and the Spirit of life and truth.
sources.answer: Yes. The one Paul calls the Spirit of Life is the one the Lord calls the Paraclete and the Spirit of Truth. The same Gospel later has the Lord say "Receive the Holy Spirit," which shows that the Spirit of Truth is the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: Him, then, Whom the Apostle called the Spirit of Life, the Lord in the Gospel named the Paraclete, and the Spirit of Truth
sources.raw_question: Are the Spirit of Life, the Paraclete, and the Spirit of Truth the same as the Holy Spirit?

question: What role does the Holy Spirit play in the establishment of the angelic powers?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: The heavenly powers were established by the Spirit, and their establishment means their inability to fall away from good. From the Spirit they derive their close relationship to God, their inability to change to evil, and their continuance in blessedness.
sources.quote: For it is from the Spirit that the powers derive their close relationship to God, their inability to change to evil, and their continuance in blessedness.
sources.raw_question: What role does the Holy Spirit play in the establishment of the angelic powers?

question: Do the Spirit's works in salvation history (Christ's advent, miracles, remission of sins, adoption, resurrection) show His divine dignity?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit is forerunner of Christ's advent and inseparable from His incarnate presence. Miracles, exorcisms and remission of sins come through Him, closeness to God and adoption come through Him, and resurrection and renewal are His operation. The magnitude of these operations reveals the sublimity of His nature.
sources.quote: Is it Christ’s advent? The Spirit is forerunner. Is there the incarnate presence? The Spirit is inseparable.
sources.raw_question: Do the Spirit's works in salvation history (Christ's advent, miracles, remission of sins, adoption, resurrection) show His divine dignity?

question: Does the Spirit's guiding of God's people imply that He renders only humble service?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: No. Scripture testifies that leading God's people is the work of God himself, as in "Thou leddest thy people like a flock." So when Christ promises that the Comforter will guide into all truth, this must not be misread as a lowly function.
sources.quote: And pray do not again understand by this guidance some humble service, for the Word witnesses that it was the work of God
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit's guiding of God's people imply that He renders only humble service?

question: Do the Spirit's indwelling, teaching and guiding of believers show that he is a lesser being serving us?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be glorified.
sources.answer: No. These are benefits of his loving kindness and give no reason to give up the right and holy opinion about him. Making the benefactor's kindness a ground for dishonouring him is ingratitude.
sources.quote: For to make the loving kindness of your benefactor a ground of ingratitude were indeed a very extravagance of unfairness.
sources.raw_question: Do the Spirit's indwelling, teaching and guiding of believers show that he is a lesser being serving us?

question: Why did God permit human bodies to die and decay if he intended to raise them?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter II.—When Christ visited us in His grace, He did not come to what did not belong to Him: also, by shedding His true blood for us, and exhibiting to us His true flesh in the Eucharist, He conferred upon our flesh the capacity of salvation.
sources.answer: So that we would not be puffed up as though we had life from ourselves. By learning by experience that our eternal duration comes from God's power and not our nature, we come to know both God and ourselves truly, since strength is made perfect in weakness.
sources.quote: learning by experience that we possess eternal duration from the excelling power of this Being, not from our own nature, we may neither undervalue that glory which surrounds God as He is, nor be ignorant of our own nature
sources.raw_question: Why did God permit human bodies to die and decay if he intended to raise them?

question: Does Psalm 36:7-9 show that God's loving-kindness is the same thing as the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. In the psalm, God's precious loving-kindness, the fatness of His house, the river of His pleasures, the fountain of life and God's light are all one thing. Christ Himself teaches that the spiritual fountains and rivers of living water are the Holy Spirit (John 4:14; 7:38-39). The river of God's pleasures is also the same as the river of the water of life in Revelation 22:1, which flows from the throne of God and the Lamb. So the Spirit is God's loving-kindness and delight.
sources.quote: But Christ Himself expressly teaches us that by spiritual fountains and rivers of water of life is meant the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 36:7-9 show that God's loving-kindness is the same thing as the Holy Spirit?

question: Is it the Word of God who forms human beings in the womb?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XV.—Proofs of the resurrection from Isaiah and Ezekiel; the same God who created us will also raise us up.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus cites God's words to Jeremiah, "Before I formed thee in the womb, I knew thee," and Paul's statement that God separated him from his mother's womb. He then argues that the same Word who forms us in secret showed himself openly by forming sight for the man born blind.
sources.quote: As, therefore, we are by the Word formed in the womb, this very same Word formed the visual power in him who had been blind from his birth; showing openly who it is that fashions us in secret
sources.raw_question: Is it the Word of God who forms human beings in the womb?

question: Do the varied forms in which the Son appeared to the patriarchs, and the Spirit as dove and fire, prove that the Son and Spirit are in their own substance visible, changeable, and therefore mortal?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Against Those Who Believed the Father Only to Be Immortal and Invisible. The Truth to Be Sought by Peaceful Study.
sources.answer: No. God, whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, never appeared to bodily eyes except through a corporeal creature made subject to his power. The divine substance itself stays invisible and unchangeable. The changing appearances belong to the creatures God used, not to the substance of the Son or Spirit. Those who argue otherwise cannot even grasp the invisible substance of the soul.
sources.quote: who deny that God, whether the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, ever appeared to bodily eyes, unless through the corporeal creature made subject to His own power
sources.raised_by_detail: those who believed the Father only to be immortal and invisible
sources.raw_question: Do the varied forms in which the Son appeared to the patriarchs, and the Spirit as dove and fire, prove that the Son and Spirit are in their own substance visible, changeable, and therefore mortal?

question: Does Jeremiah's curse on Jechoniah show that Christ could not have been begotten by Joseph if he is to be the Davidic king?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. Matthew's genealogy shows Joseph descends from Joachim and Jechoniah, whose seed Jeremiah declared disinherited from David's throne. The Holy Spirit foresaw the doctrines of evil teachers and spoke these words so that it might be known Christ was not born of Joseph's seed. Instead, according to God's promise, the eternal King was raised up from David's belly through the Virgin.
sources.quote: that they may learn that from his seed—that is, from Joseph—He was not to be born but that, according to the promise of God, from David’s belly the King eternal is raised up
sources.raw_question: Does Jeremiah's curse on Jechoniah show that Christ could not have been begotten by Joseph if he is to be the Davidic king?

question: Did Irenaeus hold that the Word (Logos), considered in his divine nature, was capable of suffering?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus only taught that the Logos suffered in the flesh, being constantly united to the man Christ Jesus and not deserting the human nature in the passion. His aim against the heretics was to show that the suffering Redeemer had to be both God and man; one might as well say he held the Logos as such was visible and changed into a frail man.
sources.quote: All that Irenzeus intended to prove against the heretics was, that the Λόγος was constantly united to the man Christ Jesus, and did not desert the human nature in the passion, it being Snecessary that the suffering Redeemer should be both God and man
sources.raw_question: Did Irenaeus hold that the Word (Logos), considered in his divine nature, was capable of suffering?

question: What is meant by Christ's conquest of death as the last enemy in 1 Corinthians 15:26?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: It is the resurrection of the dead. When the corruption of death is halted, our quickened nature becomes heavenly and eternal, as Paul says that the corruptible must put on incorruption. So the subjection of Christ's enemies ends in the conquest of death, and immortal life follows.
sources.quote: This victory over death is nothing else than the resurrection from the dead: for when the corruption of death is stayed, the quickened and now heavenly nature is made eternal
sources.raw_question: What is meant by Christ's conquest of death as the last enemy in 1 Corinthians 15:26?

question: Must we understand precisely how a doctrine like divine omnipresence works before we can believe it?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. We have a general, confused idea of omnipresence and mean something by it, so we can assent as far as our ideas reach. We have no notion of the particular manner, so we are not obliged to believe any particular mode. Any particular mode we fix on brings seeming inconsistencies.
sources.quote: We have a general confuse idea of it, and mean something by it. The particular manner how it is, we have no notion of; and therefore are not obliged to believe any particular modus.
sources.raw_question: Must we understand precisely how a doctrine like divine omnipresence works before we can believe it?

question: Does our inability to imagine God or spiritual beings prevent us from rationally assenting to propositions about them?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. Ideas of God, angels and souls are ideas of pure intellect that imagination can hardly grasp. Provided we understand the terms, our inability to imagine them is no hindrance to assent.
sources.quote: our not being able to imagine, provided we do but understand, is no hinderance to our assent
sources.raw_question: Does our inability to imagine God or spiritual beings prevent us from rationally assenting to propositions about them?

question: Is it reasonable to believe scriptural statements about God whose meaning we grasp only in general terms, such as 'the pure in heart shall see God'?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: Yes. Phrases like seeing God, or the pleasures at God's right hand, convey real though general and confused ideas, and we assent as far as those ideas reach. Our faith can go no further than our perception, and no more is expected of us.
sources.quote: Having no more than a general confuse perception, our faith in such points can rise no higher, or reach no further; nor can more be expected of us.
sources.raw_question: Is it reasonable to believe scriptural statements about God whose meaning we grasp only in general terms, such as 'the pure in heart shall see God'?

question: When Fathers such as Hippolytus and Athenagoras place the Son's procession after the beginning of creation, does that deny his prior existence or his role in creating?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. These writers clearly believed in the Son's prior existence, and that things were first created by him as well as afterwards adorned and ordered. Assigning the work of adornment to the Son alludes to his titles Word, Wisdom and Light. The whole Trinity was understood to create in concert, and such statements rest on belief in a coessential, coeternal Trinity.
sources.quote: And yet nothing is plainer than that @all these writers believed the prior existence of the Son; and that things were at first created by him, as well as afterwards adorned and regulated.
sources.raw_question: When Fathers such as Hippolytus and Athenagoras place the Son's procession after the beginning of creation, does that deny his prior existence or his role in creating?

question: Is the resurrection of the dead a real, bodily rising, or should it be understood allegorically?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXV.—He contends that these testimonies already alleged cannot be understood allegorically of celestial blessings, but that they shall have their fulfilment after the coming of Antichrist, and the resurrection, in the terrestrial Jerusalem. To the former prophecies he subjoins others drawn from Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the Apocalypse of John.
sources.answer: It is real. Since it is truly God who raises man, man truly rises from the dead and not allegorically. As he rises actually, he will also actually be disciplined beforehand for incorruption in the times of the kingdom. This prepares him to receive the glory of the Father and to dwell truly in the city of God.
sources.quote: For as it is God truly who raises up man, so also does man truly rise from the dead, and not allegorically, as I have shown repeatedly.
sources.raw_question: Is the resurrection of the dead a real, bodily rising, or should it be understood allegorically?

question: Does the fact that some heretics identified Christ with God the Father, or denied his flesh, serve as evidence that Scripture teaches Christ is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And This is So Manifest, that Some Heretics Have Thought Him to Be God the Father, Others that He Was Only God Without the Flesh.
sources.answer: Yes. Novatian argues that a substantial proof can be gathered even from adversaries: the divinity of Christ is so manifest in Scripture that some heretics, overwhelmed by it, exaggerated it into calling him the Father himself, and others into denying his humanity. Though these views are false, they testify that Christ's divinity is plainly declared.
sources.quote: it is so far manifest that He is declared in the Scriptures to be God, that many heretics, moved by the magnitude and truth of this divinity, exaggerating His honours above measure, have dared to announce or to think Him not the Son, but God the Father Himself.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that some heretics identified Christ with God the Father, or denied his flesh, serve as evidence that Scripture teaches Christ is God?

question: Did Christ suffer only in outward appearance because he was by nature impassible?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus sets out to show from the whole mind of the apostles that they never held such opinions. Those who teach that Christ merely appeared to suffer are condemned as agents of Satan. The one Jesus Christ, the Son of God born of the Virgin, is himself the Saviour who saves his people from their sins.
sources.quote: show that not only did they never hold any such opinions regarding Him; but, still further, that they announced through the Holy Spirit, that those who should teach such doctrines were agents of Satan
sources.raw_question: Did Christ suffer only in outward appearance because he was by nature impassible?

question: Why do Paul and most New Testament writers speak of 'God, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit' rather than, as Jesus did, of 'the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit'?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: The difference arises largely from the different relations in which the speakers stand to the Trinity. Jesus could not naturally call himself 'the Lord,' while 'the Son' expressed his consciousness of close relation and exact similarity to God. Christ was Paul's Lord, and 'Lord' became Paul's practical proper name and Divine Name for Christ, so he naturally sets him as 'Lord' beside God (his name for the Father) and the Spirit. Paul speaks as a worshipper rather than a systematizer, naming the Persons from his relations to them rather than their relations to one another.
sources.quote: He designates the Persons of the Trinity therefore rather from his relations to them than from their relations to one another. He sees in the Trinity his God, his Lord, and the Holy Spirit who dwells in him
sources.raw_question: Why do Paul and most New Testament writers speak of 'God, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit' rather than, as Jesus did, of 'the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit'?

question: What is the significance of the last judgment being carried out by Christ himself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It brings unspeakable consolation to believers and terror to the wicked. The judge is the one who loved believers and gave himself for them, and who is himself the righteousness he requires of them. He is also the one whose person, grace, worship and servants the world has reviled and despised.
sources.quote: that it shall be by him who hath loved us, and given himself for us, — who is himself the righteousness that he requires of our hands
sources.raw_question: What is the significance of the last judgment being carried out by Christ himself?

question: Can sinful humans walk in fellowship with God without a prior reconciliation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Two cannot walk together unless they are agreed, and God and natural man are in the greatest enmity: God reveals wrath, and our minds are enmity against God. God is light, life, holiness and love, while we are darkness, dead in sin, defiled and full of hatred. The foundation of agreement is laid only in Christ, who is our peace and slew the enmity on the cross.
sources.quote: The foundation, then, of this, I say, is laid in Christ, hid in Christ. “He,” saith the apostle, “is our peace; he hath made peace” for us, Eph. ii. 14, 15. He slew the enmity in his own body on the cross
sources.raw_question: Can sinful humans walk in fellowship with God without a prior reconciliation?

question: Since the Holy Spirit belongs to the invisible, immaterial order, does He subsist among the created intelligible beings?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > These doctrines of our Faith witnessed to and confirmed by Scripture passages.
sources.answer: No. Paul anticipated this inference and drew a distinct division between intelligible beings made by creation and the existence that is above creation. He listed only the created classes of invisible beings.
sources.quote: in order that none may surmise that the Spirit, because He is of the intelligible and immaterial world, on account of this connexion subsists therein) to another most distinct division into the things that have been made in the way of creation, and the existence that is above creation
sources.raw_question: Since the Holy Spirit belongs to the invisible, immaterial order, does He subsist among the created intelligible beings?

question: Is the mental image of a body inferior or superior to the body itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > That the Image or Begotten Word of the Mind that Knows Itself is Equal to the Mind Itself.
sources.answer: It is superior in one respect. Bodies are not themselves in the mind, only their likenesses, and taking the likeness for the thing is an error. Still, the image of the body in the mind is of a better sort than the body's own species, because it exists in a better nature: a living substance, the mind.
sources.quote: yet the image of the body in the mind is a thing of a better sort than the species of the body itself, inasmuch as the former is in a better nature, viz. in a living substance, as the mind is
sources.raw_question: Is the mental image of a body inferior or superior to the body itself?

question: Is all knowledge a likeness of the thing known?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > That the Image or Begotten Word of the Mind that Knows Itself is Equal to the Mind Itself.
sources.answer: Yes. All knowledge according to species is like the thing it knows. There is also knowledge according to privation, by which we speak a word only when we condemn something. That condemnation of a privation amounts to praise of the species, so the mind still holds a likeness to the known species, whether it likes the species or dislikes its privation.
sources.quote: But all knowledge according to species is like the thing which it knows. For there is another knowledge according to privation, according to which we speak a word only when we condemn.
sources.raw_question: Is all knowledge a likeness of the thing known?

question: Was the world formed by some being other than the Supreme God, such as an ignorant Demiurge working outside the Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VII.—Created things are not the images of those Æons who are within the Pleroma.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus says he has already shown two things. Nothing can exist beyond the Pleroma, the region where the Valentinians claim the images were made. And the world was formed by no one other than the Supreme God himself.
sources.quote: I have already shown that it was impossible that anything should exist beyond the Pleroma
sources.raw_question: Was the world formed by some being other than the Supreme God, such as an ignorant Demiurge working outside the Pleroma?

question: Does Christ's command "Judge not, that ye be not judged" forbid Christians from finding fault with sinners?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXX.—Refutation of another argument adduced by the Marcionites, that God directed the Hebrews to spoil the Egyptians.
sources.answer: No. It does not mean we should not reprove sinners or consent to wrongdoers. It means we should not pass unfair judgment on the dispensations of God, since God himself provides that all things turn out for good in a just way.
sources.quote: [The meaning is] not certainly that we should not find fault with sinners, nor that we should consent to those who act wickedly; but that we should not pronounce an unfair judgment on the dispensations of God
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's command "Judge not, that ye be not judged" forbid Christians from finding fault with sinners?

question: Is being 'Most High over all the earth' and 'true in words and works' a property of one divine Person only, or of Father, Son and Holy Spirit alike?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: Of all three alike. The oversight of earthly things from on high is exercised alike by Father, Son and Spirit. One cannot deny truth in words to the Son, who said 'I am the Truth', or to the Spirit of truth. Nor can one deny being 'true in works' to the Son, who does righteousness, or to the Spirit, who works all in all as he wills.
sources.quote: whichever of the Three Persons you are thinking of, He is Most High over all the earth, inasmuch as the oversight of earthly things from on high is exercised alike by the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost
sources.raw_question: Is being 'Most High over all the earth' and 'true in words and works' a property of one divine Person only, or of Father, Son and Holy Spirit alike?

question: Can a being that is changeable or untrue in words and works be a fitting object of Christian faith and worship?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. No one can rightly revere what varies, changes and decays, nor trust one who is false in words and untrue in works. Therefore the Persons in the creed, the Son and Spirit included, must possess truth and immutability.
sources.quote: For who will allow it to be right to deem that a fitting object of reverence which varies, changes, and is subject to decay?
sources.raw_question: Can a being that is changeable or untrue in words and works be a fitting object of Christian faith and worship?

question: Would a perfect reflexive idea of oneself amount to a second instance of oneself?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Suppose a man had an absolutely perfect contemplative idea of every thought and exercise of his mind at the very moment it occurred. He would really be two during that time, twice at once, because the idea he had of himself would be himself again. Edwards uses this to illustrate how God's idea of Himself can be God.
sources.quote: a man would really be two during that time, he would be indeed double, he would be twice at once. The idea he has of himself would be himself again.
sources.raw_question: Would a perfect reflexive idea of oneself amount to a second instance of oneself?

question: Is the reflexive or contemplative idea relevant to this argument the same thing as mere consciousness?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: No. A mere direct consciousness differs greatly from a reflex or contemplative view of oneself by which one delights in one's own beauty or excellency. Consciousness, if it means anything beyond the simple existence of what is in the mind, is only a power to view by reflection what passes there.
sources.quote: There is a great difference between a man's having a view of himself, reflex or contemplative idea of himself so as to delight in his own beauty or excellency, and a mere direct consciousness.
sources.raw_question: Is the reflexive or contemplative idea relevant to this argument the same thing as mere consciousness?

question: Why is Christ called the "face" or presence of God and the angel of His presence?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Because the Son is God's own perfect idea of Himself, by which God continually views His essence, as a man sees his own face in a looking glass. The Hebrew word signifies face, form or appearance, and its root means to behold. What God beholds most eminently is His own perfect image, so it is fitly called God's face, and the angel of His presence.
sources.quote: this idea is that "face of God" which God sees as a man sees his own face in a looking glass. 'Tis of such form or appearance whereby God eternally appears to Himself.
sources.raw_question: Why is Christ called the "face" or presence of God and the angel of His presence?

question: Does Christ's judging and punishing 'with the Spirit of His mouth' mean that the Son receives the Holy Spirit as a grace from outside, like a prophet?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VII. The Son Himself does not judge or punish without the Spirit, so that the same Spirit is called the Sword of the Word. But inasmuch as the Word is in turn called the Sword of the Spirit, the highest unity of power is thereby recognized in each.
sources.answer: No. When the Lord Jesus slays Antichrist with the Spirit of His mouth, this is not a grace received but the undivided unity of the divine nature. Christ cannot be without the Spirit, nor the Spirit without Christ, because the unity of the divine nature cannot be divided.
sources.quote: Yet here is not a grace received, but the unity remains undivided, since neither can Christ be without the Spirit, nor the Spirit without Christ. For the unity of the divine nature cannot be divided.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's judging and punishing 'with the Spirit of His mouth' mean that the Son receives the Holy Spirit as a grace from outside, like a prophet?

question: Must every believer work through a lengthy process of scriptural proof before believing in the Trinity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. The Bible is the poor man's book, and these things are revealed to babes. A childlike believer is convinced by a few simple texts: God as the only Saviour, the Lamb of God, and the promised Comforter. He also knows he was baptized into the name of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, so without laboured syllogisms he believes these Three are One. He does not try to fathom the mystery.
sources.quote: His Father, his Redeemer, his Sanctifier, are equally indispensable to him: and he knows that he was baptized into the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. He needs no more. Without any laboured syllogisms, he believes these Three are One.
sources.raw_question: Must every believer work through a lengthy process of scriptural proof before believing in the Trinity?

question: Why can created intellectual beings such as angels not be called eternal in the way God is, even if they do not die?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Because their emergence from non-existence shows that their nature is mutable, so separation from God (the death proper to intellectual natures) is potentially present in them. They are kept from falling into that contrary state only by the grace of Him who strengthens them, not by their own nature. What does not abide in the good by its own nature is not eternal, whereas God alone, being truly unchangeable, has immortality.
sources.quote: for their emergence from non-existence shows mutability of nature; and that to which change is in affinity is hindered from participation in the contrary state by the grace of Him Who strengthens it: it does not abide in the good by its own nature: and such a thing is not eternal
sources.raw_question: Why can created intellectual beings such as angels not be called eternal in the way God is, even if they do not die?

question: Is the distinction of the persons of the Trinity something to be imagined by the believer or something believed on the basis of revelation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: It is to be believed, not fancied. Faith in the distinct persons rests on what Scripture reveals about their distinct operations, not on imagination; believers act faith distinctly on the Holy Ghost because Scripture distinctly ascribes these effects to him.
sources.quote: faith, not imagination. The distinction of the persons in the Trinity is not to be fancied, but believed.
sources.raw_question: Is the distinction of the persons of the Trinity something to be imagined by the believer or something believed on the basis of revelation?

question: Do immaterial intellectual beings such as angels use words and names to address God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. In immaterial intellectual nature the mental energy itself is speech, needing no material instruments of communication. Being free of bodily envelopment, such natures require no words or names for themselves or for what is above them; utterances recorded of them in Scripture are given for the sake of human hearers.
sources.quote: For, in the case of immaterial intellectual nature, the mental energy is speech which has no need of material instruments of communication.
sources.raw_question: Do immaterial intellectual beings such as angels use words and names to address God?

question: If the Son were a servant, would it follow that he does not know the counsels of the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: That would follow, since Scripture says the servant does not know what his lord does. But it is false of the Son. He has in Himself all that belongs to the Father, sees all that the Father does, and has the whole Father in Himself, so nothing of the Father lies outside His knowledge. Therefore He is not a servant.
sources.quote: the Son has in Himself all that pertains to the Father, and sees all things that the Father doeth, and none of the good things that belong to the Father is outside the knowledge of the Son
sources.raw_question: If the Son were a servant, would it follow that he does not know the counsels of the Father?

question: Would making the Son a slave also make the Father a slave?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Because the Father is wholly in the Son and everything the Son has is the Father's, anyone who makes the Son a slave must drag the Father into servitude too. As Christ says, "All Mine are Thine, and Thine are Mine." The Father, who is in the Son and contains all that is the Son's, would have slavery in Himself, which is absurd.
sources.quote: For it is not possible that He Who contains in Himself all that belongs to the Son, and Who is Himself in the Son, should not also absolutely be in the slavery of the Son, and have slavery in Himself.
sources.raw_question: Would making the Son a slave also make the Father a slave?

question: If God appeared in the bush through an assumed creature called 'the Angel of the Lord,' could that Person be the Father?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Appearance in the Bush.
sources.answer: No. If a creature was assumed so that it could be seen, heard, and called the Angel (messenger) of the Lord, then the Father cannot be meant. It must be the Son or the Holy Spirit, since Scripture nowhere says the Father is sent.
sources.quote: then cannot God here be understood to be the Father, but either the Son or the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: If God appeared in the bush through an assumed creature called 'the Angel of the Lord,' could that Person be the Father?

question: Is the Father's lordship his by nature or something he acquired by election?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: It is his by nature. No one with any share of intellect would deny that the lordship of the God of all belongs to him by nature. What is simple, uncompounded and indivisible is wholly and eternally what it is. It does not become one thing after another through change.
sources.quote: For that which is by nature simple, uncompounded, and indivisible, whatever it happens to be, that it is throughout in all its entirety, not becoming one thing after another by some process of change
sources.raw_question: Is the Father's lordship his by nature or something he acquired by election?

question: Would making the Son a slave by nature imply that he is subject to fear?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Whoever is a slave by nature and works under a master's constraint cannot be free of fear. Paul witnesses to this link between bondage and fear. The Eunomians would therefore attribute fear, in a human manner, to the Son as God, which is absurd.
sources.quote: So that they will be found to attribute, after the likeness of men, the emotion of fear also to their fellow-servant God.
sources.raw_question: Would making the Son a slave by nature imply that he is subject to fear?

question: Was the whole Trinity born of the Virgin Mary, crucified, buried and raised, or only the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > What the Doctrine of the Catholic Faith is Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: Only the Son. The Catholic faith holds that it was not the Trinity that was born of Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, buried, rose again and ascended. These belong to the Son alone.
sources.quote: Yet not that this Trinity was born of the Virgin Mary, and crucified under Pontius Pilate, and buried, and rose again the third day, and ascended into heaven, but only the Son.
sources.raw_question: Was the whole Trinity born of the Virgin Mary, crucified, buried and raised, or only the Son?

question: Whose voice spoke from heaven saying "Thou art my Son" at the baptism, at the transfiguration, and in John 12:28?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > What the Doctrine of the Catholic Faith is Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: The Father's only. That word was the Father's alone, spoken to the Son, not a word of the Trinity. This holds even though Father, Son and Holy Spirit, being indivisible, work indivisibly.
sources.quote: but that it was a word of the Father only, spoken to the Son; although the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as they are indivisible, so work indivisibly
sources.raw_question: Whose voice spoke from heaven saying "Thou art my Son" at the baptism, at the transfiguration, and in John 12:28?

question: Does Arius's use of Scripture language when speaking of God show that his teaching about the Son is faithful to Scripture?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Introduction. Reason for writing; certain persons indifferent about Arianism; Arians not Christians, because sectaries always take the name of their founder.
sources.answer: No. Athanasius compares Arius to the Pharisees, who claimed zeal for the words of the Law in order to break it. Under cover of God's name they denied the Lord, charging him with blasphemy for saying 'I and the Father are one.' In the same way Arius borrows Scripture's phrases while denying the Son and counting him among the creatures. Quoting biblical wording does not make a doctrine scriptural when its content contradicts the Son's deity.
sources.quote: They, that they might transgress the Law, pretended to be anxious for the words of the Law, and that they might deny the expected and then present Lord, were hypocritical with God’s name
sources.raw_question: Does Arius's use of Scripture language when speaking of God show that his teaching about the Son is faithful to Scripture?

question: Does the divine prerogative of vengeance and wrath on the wicked belong to Christ as well as to God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. God says 'Vengeance is mine' and rains fire and brimstone on the wicked in the day of His wrath. Scripture says in the same way that the Lord Jesus will be revealed in flaming fire, taking vengeance. It also speaks of 'the great day of His wrath,' meaning the wrath of the Lamb. The divine work of final retribution is therefore Christ's.
sources.quote: The Lord Jesus shall be revealed from heaven with His mighty angels, in flaming fire, Taking vengeance on them that know not God. – 2 Thess. 1:7–8.
sources.raw_question: Does the divine prerogative of vengeance and wrath on the wicked belong to Christ as well as to God?

question: What does the complete grace of the Holy Spirit accomplish in relation to the Father's will and the image of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VIII.—The gifts of the Holy Spirit which we receive prepare us for incorruption, render us spiritual, and separate us from carnal men. These two classes are signified by the clean and unclean animals in the legal dispensation.
sources.answer: It makes us like God and accomplishes the Father's will by forming man after God's image and likeness. The earnest of the Spirit already makes us cry "Abba, Father." The full gift, given by God at the resurrection, will do far more.
sources.quote: It will render us like unto Him, and accomplish the will of the Father; for it shall make man after the image and likeness of God.
sources.raw_question: What does the complete grace of the Holy Spirit accomplish in relation to the Father's will and the image of God?

question: Is God bound by necessity, so that every substance must return to what it came from and he cannot give immortality to what is mortal or incorruption to what is corruptible?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIV.—Valentinus and his followers derived the principles of their system from the heathen; the names only are changed.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus treats this as a doctrine of the Stoics and of 'all that are ignorant of God', which the Valentinians took over when they claimed God 'can do no otherwise'. In assigning the view to those ignorant of God, he rejects the claim that God is the slave of necessity and implies that God can bestow immortality and incorruption.
sources.quote: God is the slave of this necessity, so that He cannot impart immortality to what is mortal, or bestow incorruption on what is corruptible
sources.raw_question: Is God bound by necessity, so that every substance must return to what it came from and he cannot give immortality to what is mortal or incorruption to what is corruptible?

question: Was it the teaching of the early Church before Nicaea that God the Father was always Father, so that the Son's generation is eternal?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. Alexander of Alexandria counted it among Arius's novelties that he denied the Father was always Father and held that the Word was produced in time. Alexander treats these two claims as explaining each other. Waterland traces the maxim that the Father was always Father back through Dionysius of Alexandria, Novatian, Origen and Irenaeus, close to the time of St. John. On the reasoning of that age, all who asserted the eternity of the Word implicitly held eternal generation.
sources.quote: It appears to have been a maxim in the Church at this time, that is, about the year 315, ten years before the Council of Nice, that the Father was always Father.
sources.raw_question: Was it the teaching of the early Church before Nicaea that God the Father was always Father, so that the Son's generation is eternal?

question: When ante-Nicene writers said God was never without his Logos, did they mean by the Logos only an attribute or power of the Father rather than a real Person?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. They meant a real, subsisting Person, always in and with the Father and distinct from him, even before the temporary generation they describe. Later writers, who confessedly took the Logos to be a real, eternal Person, used the very same maxim and reasoning. Moreover, these writers say that before the procession the Father was not alone, which makes little sense if they meant only his own attributes.
sources.quote: They did not mean by the Λόγος, or Word, any attribute, power, virtue, or operation of the Father; but a real, subsisting Person
sources.raw_question: When ante-Nicene writers said God was never without his Logos, did they mean by the Logos only an attribute or power of the Father rather than a real Person?

question: If the Word is a creature yet called God, must one hold two Gods and two faiths?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Yes. Such a view has one Creator God and one creature God, two Lords (unoriginate and originate), and two faiths. Worshipping one then means turning from the other, because the One cannot be seen in the Other when their natures and operations are foreign. This tends toward yet more gods.
sources.quote: they must of necessity say that there are two Gods, one Creator, the other creature, and must serve two Lords, one Unoriginate, and the other originate and a creature
sources.raw_question: If the Word is a creature yet called God, must one hold two Gods and two faiths?

question: Does John 5:37-38 show that the Word is the Form and Image of the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Yes. Christ fittingly joins 'Word' to 'Form' to show that the Word is himself the Image, Expression and Form of the Father. The Jews who did not receive him therefore did not receive the Word, who is the Form of God. Jacob saw this same Form at Penuel and received the name Israel.
sources.quote: Suitably has He joined the ‘Word’ to the ‘Form,’ to shew that the Word of God is Himself Image and Expression and Form of His Father
sources.raw_question: Does John 5:37-38 show that the Word is the Form and Image of the Father?

question: Why are human properties such as hunger, thirst, suffering and weariness attributed to the divine Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: Because the flesh was the Word's own body and he was in it, its properties are rightly said to be his. Being God, he had his own body and used it as an instrument. The Word therefore bore the flesh's infirmities as his own, while the flesh ministered to the works of the Godhead. Even so, the Word himself received no hurt.
sources.quote: And the Word bore the infirmities of the flesh, as His own, for His was the flesh; and the flesh ministered to the works of the Godhead, because the Godhead was in it, for the body was God’s
sources.raw_question: Why are human properties such as hunger, thirst, suffering and weariness attributed to the divine Word?

question: Does Romans 2:4, which says God's goodness and forbearance lead to repentance, show that God's patience outside Christ is meant to bring people to repentance?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No, not in that sense. Paul is addressing the Jews, who had the means to learn the natural tendency of the forbearance God exercises in Christ, which does lead to repentance. Alternatively, Paul is only saying in general that reason requires men to use God's goodness better than they usually do, as verse 5 charges them with hardness.
sources.quote: is spoken to the Jews, who had advantages to learn the natural tendency of that goodness and forbearance which God exercises in Christ; which, indeed, leads to repentance
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 2:4, which says God's goodness and forbearance lead to repentance, show that God's patience outside Christ is meant to bring people to repentance?

question: Can one consistently confess Christ to be God while ranking him among creatures and saying he did not exist until he was made?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: No. Athanasius holds that no one in all mankind, Greek or barbarian, would venture to call someone God and at the same time count him among creatures who was not until he was made. Such a combination is so contradictory that it would rouse universal indignation. Since the Son is confessed as Word of the Father, true Son, God from God, and 'over all blessed for ever,' the Arian claims that he is a creature with a beginning must be rejected.
sources.quote: For who is there in all mankind, Greek or Barbarian, who ventures to rank among creatures One whom he confesses the while to be God and says, that He was not till He was made?
sources.raw_question: Can one consistently confess Christ to be God while ranking him among creatures and saying he did not exist until he was made?

question: Is God's will or counsel changeable, like human willing?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Against Eunomius, Saying that the Son of God is the Son, Not of His Nature, But of His Will. Epilogue to What Has Been Said Already.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says that the counsel of the Lord abides for ever. Just as God is eternal, so his counsel is eternal and therefore as unchangeable as he is. What holds of his counsel holds of his will: the will of the Lord abides for ever.
sources.quote: as God is eternal, so is His counsel for eternity, and therefore unchangeable, as He himself is. And what is said of thoughts can most truly be said also of the will
sources.raw_question: Is God's will or counsel changeable, like human willing?

question: Was Moses a type of the Holy Spirit or of Christ?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Objection that some were baptized unto Moses and believed in him, and an answer to it; with remarks upon types.
sources.answer: Moses was a type of Christ, not of the Spirit. In the ministry of the law he typified "the Mediator between God and men," since the law was given by the hand of a mediator at the people's request that God not speak to them directly. Christ himself refers faith in Moses to himself: "Had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me."
sources.quote: Moses then is joined with God, not with the Spirit; and he was a type not of the Spirit, but of Christ.
sources.raw_question: Was Moses a type of the Holy Spirit or of Christ?

question: Did the Mosaic law forbid only 'absolute' or supreme sacrifice to other gods, leaving 'relative' or inferior sacrifice to lesser beings permitted?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. The law of Exodus 22:20 appropriated all sacrifice to God alone, not merely a supposed supreme sort. If the Arian distinction held, an idolater could have escaped condemnation by pleading that he intended only an inferior, relative sacrifice to the other gods, which is absurd.
sources.quote: you must be content to say, that not only absolute supreme sacrifice, (if there be any sense in that phrase,) but al/ sacrifice was, by the Law, appropriate to God only.
sources.raw_question: Did the Mosaic law forbid only 'absolute' or supreme sacrifice to other gods, leaving 'relative' or inferior sacrifice to lesser beings permitted?

question: Can invocation and adoration be divided into absolute and relative kinds, so that inferior adoration may be given to the Son as a lesser being?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. Prayer and adoration are acts of religious worship like sacrifice, vows and oaths. They are appropriated to God in the same manner, by the same laws, and for the same reasons. So relative prayer and prostration are as absurd as relative sacrifice. Worship given to the Son therefore cannot be an inferior kind of worship.
sources.quote: Why should not absolute and relative prayer and prostration appear as absurd as absolute and relative sacrifice, vows, oaths, or the like? They are acts and instances of religious worship, like the other; appropriated to God in the same manner
sources.raw_question: Can invocation and adoration be divided into absolute and relative kinds, so that inferior adoration may be given to the Son as a lesser being?

question: If Christ's sufferings and weaknesses prove that he is human, do his mighty works prove that he is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And Indeed that Christ Was Not Only Man, But God Also; That Even as He Was the Son of Man, So Also He Was the Son of God.
sources.answer: Yes. The inference is parallel. If infirmities are taken to prove humanity, the powers and works must equally prove divinity. To reject one inference while keeping the other is inconsistent, and would undermine the proof of his humanity as well.
sources.quote: For if His sufferings show in Him human frailty, why may not His works assert in Him divine power? For if this should not avail to assert Him to be God from His powers, neither can His sufferings avail to show Him to be man also from them.
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who hold Christ was man only
sources.raw_question: If Christ's sufferings and weaknesses prove that he is human, do his mighty works prove that he is God?

question: Do the Old Testament prophecies about the Christ show him to be a mere man descended from David, or Lord and God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: They show him to be Lord and God, immortal and the dispenser of life. David calls the coming one his own Lord, and the prophecy that the Holy One would not see corruption cannot refer to David, who died and whose sepulchre remains; it is fulfilled in Jesus' resurrection.
sources.quote: what is written of Him shews Him to be not such as you say, but rather announces Him as Lord and God, and immortal, and dispenser of life.
sources.raw_question: Do the Old Testament prophecies about the Christ show him to be a mere man descended from David, or Lord and God?

question: Did the Word suffer any loss of his Lordship by becoming man and suffering?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: No. Though made man and called Jesus, he received no loss through his human passion; rather, by becoming man he was manifested as Lord of the living and the dead.
sources.quote: For though made man, and called Jesus, as we said before, He received no loss by that human passion, but rather, in being made man, He is manifested as Lord of quick and dead.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word suffer any loss of his Lordship by becoming man and suffering?

question: Is the revelation of the Son's divine nature and personhood the first disclosure of a plurality of persons in the divine essence?

sources.author: John Owen
