sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Preface
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that the first discovery of a plurality of persons in God lies in the revelation of the divine nature and personality of the Son. Hence those Jews who opposed Christ's claim to deity may justly be regarded as the first assertors of the anti-Trinitarian unbelief now being revived.
sources.quote: the first discovery of a plurality of persons in the divine essence consists in the revelation of the divine nature and personality of the Son
sources.raw_question: Is the revelation of the Son's divine nature and personhood the first disclosure of a plurality of persons in the divine essence?

question: Does Paul's statement that 'one star differs from another star in glory' show that beings derived from one source can differ in substance or in being passible or impassible?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus reads the text as describing a difference in glory only, not in qualities, substance or capacity for passion. Beings derived alike from the Father's light must therefore all be impassible and immutable, or else all be passible together with the Father's light.
sources.quote: For if “one star differs from another star in glory,” but not in qualities, nor substance, nor in the fact of being passible or impassible
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that 'one star differs from another star in glory' show that beings derived from one source can differ in substance or in being passible or impassible?

question: Why does inquiry into the unity of the Trinity call for particular care and humility compared with other theological subjects?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > What Augustin Requests from His Readers. The Errors of Readers Dull of Comprehension Not to Be Ascribed to the Author.
sources.answer: Because no other subject carries such stakes. Error about it is more dangerous than anywhere else, inquiry into it is harder, and finding the truth about it is more profitable. Augustine therefore asks readers to inquire together with him in charity, correcting one another. He trusts God to keep him in what is certain and to reveal whatever he has gotten wrong.
sources.quote: because in no other subject is error more dangerous, or inquiry more laborious, or the discovery of truth more profitable
sources.raw_question: Why does inquiry into the unity of the Trinity call for particular care and humility compared with other theological subjects?

question: Is it legitimate to worship Christ's flesh, given that Christ is both Son of God and born of the Virgin?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is not divided but one, so when He is adored as Son of God it is not denied that He was born of the Virgin. His flesh is therefore adored together with Him, as the apostles adored Him risen in the flesh.
sources.quote: for Christ is not divided but is one; nor, when He is adored as the Son of God, is He denied to have been born of the Virgin
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to worship Christ's flesh, given that Christ is both Son of God and born of the Virgin?

question: If worship is due to the author of Christ's flesh, does it follow that the Virgin Mary is to be worshipped?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: No. Mary was the temple of God, not the God of the temple. Only He who was working in the temple, the divine Spirit, is to be worshipped.
sources.quote: Mary was the temple of God, not the God of the temple. And therefore He alone is to be worshipped Who was working in His temple.
sources.raw_question: If worship is due to the author of Christ's flesh, does it follow that the Virgin Mary is to be worshipped?

question: In what sense is the Father in Christ, so that worshipping the Father in Christ means also worshipping Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XI. The objection has been made, that the words of St. John, “The Spirit is God,” are to be referred to God the Father; since Christ afterwards declares that God is to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. The answer is, first, that by the word Spirit is sometimes meant spiritual grace; next, it is shown that, if they insist that the Person of the Holy Spirit is signified by the words “in Spirit,” and therefore deny that adoration is due to Him, the argument tells equally against the Son; and since numberless passages prove that He is to be worshipped, we understand from this that the same rule is to be laid down as regards the Spirit. Why are we commanded to fall down before His footstool? Because by this is signified the Lord's Body, and as the Spirit was the Maker of this, it follows that He is to be worshipped, and yet it does not accordingly follow that Mary is to be worshipped. Therefore the worship of the Spirit is not done away with, but His union with the Father is expressed, when it is said that the Father is to be worshipped in Spirit, and this point is supported by similar expressions.
sources.answer: The Father is in the Son not as a body in a body, since God is not a body, nor by confused mixture, but as true in true, God in God, Light in Light, the eternal Father in the co-eternal Son. This indwelling is unity of power, so Christ is jointly worshipped in the Father when the Father is worshipped in Christ, and likewise the Spirit is jointly worshipped when God is worshipped in the Spirit.
sources.quote: Not, indeed, as a body in a body, for God is not a body; nor as a confused mixture [confusus in confuso], but as the true in the true, God in God, Light in Light; as the eternal Father in the co-eternal Son.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Father in Christ, so that worshipping the Father in Christ means also worshipping Christ?

question: Are believers freed from the ceremonial law of ordinances given to Israel?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: Yes. That law was a yoke which neither the apostles nor their fathers could bear. Christ blotted out this handwriting of ordinances and nailed it to his cross. Believers must therefore stand fast in the liberty with which Christ has made them free.
sources.quote: wherefore Christ “blotted out this hand-writing of ordinances that was against them, which was contrary to them, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross,” Col. ii. 14
sources.raw_question: Are believers freed from the ceremonial law of ordinances given to Israel?

question: In what sense are believers freed from the moral law of God through Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: Believers are freed from the moral law's rigour and terror in commanding, as at Sinai. Because sin makes the law impossible to fulfil, they are freed from it as an instrument of righteousness, and are righteous by Christ's righteousness instead. They are also freed from the curse of the law, since Christ was made a curse for them. Finally, they are freed from death, Satan, sin and the world.
sources.quote: There being an impossibility of obtaining life by the law, we are exempted from it as to any such end, and that by the righteousness of Christ, Rom. viii. 3.
sources.raw_question: In what sense are believers freed from the moral law of God through Christ?

question: Is God's moral relation to humanity that of Father, Lawgiver, and Judge at once, so that sin offends him in each capacity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 1. Introduction. Preparation of heart. Our position before God.
sources.answer: Yes. God is Father, Legislator, and Judge in one, and sin violates every obligation. It wounds the heart of the eternal Father, sets at naught the wise regulations of the Lawgiver, and provokes the judicial condemnation of the righteous Judge.
sources.quote: He is Father, and Legislator, and Judge in one. Sin violates every obligation: it wounds the heart of the eternal Father.
sources.raw_question: Is God's moral relation to humanity that of Father, Lawgiver, and Judge at once, so that sin offends him in each capacity?

question: When God sends 'the operation of error' on unbelievers, is God the cause of their unbelief and condemnation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXVIII.—The distinction to be made between the righteous and the wicked. The future apostasy in the time of Antichrist, and the end of the world.
sources.answer: No. The unbelievers refused the love of God and consented to unrighteousness of their own accord. The Antichrist likewise gathers the apostasy into himself by his own will and choice. God, foreseeing all this by His prescience, sends him at the proper time so that those who did not believe the truth may be judged. The Word prepares a fitting place both for those who seek the light and for those who shun it.
sources.quote: God by His prescience foreseeing all this, and at the proper time sending such a man, “that they may believe a lie, that they all may be judged who did not believe the truth, but consented to unrighteousness;”
sources.raw_question: When God sends 'the operation of error' on unbelievers, is God the cause of their unbelief and condemnation?

question: If God cannot be comprehended, does faith have any real function?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Yes. The proper service of faith is to grasp and confess the truth that it is incompetent to comprehend its Object. Faith thus acknowledges the inexhaustible mystery rather than being rendered useless by it.
sources.quote: Not so; the proper service of faith is to grasp and confess the truth that it is incompetent to comprehend its Object.
sources.raw_question: If God cannot be comprehended, does faith have any real function?

question: Does the Word's freedom from time make him independent of God, and what does 'the Word was with God' add?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The clause 'the Word was with God' shows that the Word, existing before the beginning and unconditioned by time, exists with God. He who is absent when we seek his origin in time is present all along with the Creator of time.
sources.quote: He Who is absent when we seek for His origin in time is present all the while with the Creator of time.
sources.raw_question: Does the Word's freedom from time make him independent of God, and what does 'the Word was with God' add?

question: In the final subjection, does Christ cast off or lose his human body?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. He becomes God only, not by casting off the body but by translating and transfiguring it in glory. Humanity is added to his divinity, and he is not divested of divinity by his humanity. He is not robbed of his being through dissolution.
sources.quote: not, however, by casting off the body, but by translating it through subjection; not by losing it through dissolutions, but by transfiguring it in glory: adding humanity to His divinity, not divesting Himself of divinity by His humanity.
sources.raw_question: In the final subjection, does Christ cast off or lose his human body?

question: Why did Christ, after rebuking the disciples for sleeping, then tell them 'Sleep on now, and take your rest'?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Because His prayer for them had been answered. Having been comforted through the angel sent to watch over the Apostles, He no longer sorrowed for them and showed His certainty by bidding them sleep; the fulfilment appears when none of those given Him was lost and Peter's faith did not fail.
sources.quote: Jesus shewed His certainty that the prayer was answered when, at its close, He bade the disciples sleep on.
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ, after rebuking the disciples for sleeping, then tell them 'Sleep on now, and take your rest'?

question: Why was Christ's habitual righteousness necessary for his work as mediator?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: It made him fit to do all he had to do for us. Without complete habitual grace, given by the Spirit's presence with him, he could not have actually fulfilled the required righteousness, nor have been a perfect sacrifice without blemish answering the types.
sources.quote: So himself lays down the presence of the Spirit with him as the bottom and foundation of his going forth to his work, Isa. lxi. 1.
sources.raw_question: Why was Christ's habitual righteousness necessary for his work as mediator?

question: Is the true cleansing of the soul achieved through Christ alone as the one Mediator?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. All are gathered together from many into one by the one Mediator of life, Christ. True cleansing of the soul is wrought through him alone.
sources.quote: That all are gathered together from many into one by the one Mediator of life, viz. Christ, through Whom alone is wrought the true cleansing of the soul.
sources.raw_question: Is the true cleansing of the soul achieved through Christ alone as the one Mediator?

question: Is the Son like the Father in the way Seth was like Adam, implying community of nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: Yes. If likeness is meant in the sense in which Adam begat a son in his own likeness, that statement is acceptable. In such likeness the natures of the two are not different, and the impress and type imply community of nature.
sources.quote: For in this case the nature of the two objects which are alike is not different, and the impress and type imply community of nature.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son like the Father in the way Seth was like Adam, implying community of nature?

question: Does the power of God's will extend through spiritual creatures such as angels to produce visible, bodily effects in the corporeal creation, as in the Old Testament appearances of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > What is to Be Said Thereupon.
sources.answer: Yes. The power of God's will reaches through the spiritual creature even to visible and sensible effects in the corporeal creature. Augustine supports this from the book of Wisdom: the creature serves its Maker and is altered into all fashions at his bidding. God's wisdom 'reacheth from one end to another mightily, and sweetly doth order all things,' so it works whatever God wills everywhere.
sources.quote: For the power of the will of God reaches through the spiritual creature even to visible and sensible effects of the corporeal creature.
sources.raw_question: Does the power of God's will extend through spiritual creatures such as angels to produce visible, bodily effects in the corporeal creation, as in the Old Testament appearances of God?

question: To explain how God appeared in bodily forms in the Old Testament, must we decide whether angels take on matter from the elements like a garment or change their own bodies into those forms?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > What is to Be Said Thereupon.
sources.answer: No. Augustine says it does not matter to the present question which of these is true. As a man he cannot know by experience how angels do this, and he declines to settle it from Scripture. The real question is whether angels acted as agents in showing these appearances and sounding these words when the bodily creature was changed at the Creator's bidding.
sources.quote: But it does not signify to the present question which of these it is.
sources.raw_question: To explain how God appeared in bodily forms in the Old Testament, must we decide whether angels take on matter from the elements like a garment or change their own bodies into those forms?

question: In what different ways can created things be used to signify the person of God in the Old Testament appearances?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > In How Many Ways the Creature is to Be Taken by Way of Sign. The Eucharist.
sources.answer: God's person may be signified through an angel, or through a form ministered by an angel. That form may be an already existing body changed for the purpose, or one made for the occasion and then discarded. Likewise men such as prophets bear God's person in word and act, and things such as Jacob's stone, the brazen serpent, or the eucharistic bread are taken or made to signify.
sources.quote: When, however, that person is assumed, it is sometimes made manifest as an angel; sometimes in that form which is not an angel in his own proper being, although it is ordered and ministered by an angel.
sources.raw_question: In what different ways can created things be used to signify the person of God in the Old Testament appearances?

question: How can Christ share our humanity through birth from the Virgin and yet be free from its sins and defects?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Christ's body is unique because of its origin. He did not come into being through the passions of human conception but took the form of our body by his own power, being the source of his own humanity. So we are in him because he was born of the Virgin, while our faults are not in him because his conception was not under the defects of human conception.
sources.quote: that we might be in Him, because He was born of the Virgin, and yet our faults might not be in Him, because He is the source of His own humanity, born as man but not born under the defects of human conception.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ share our humanity through birth from the Virgin and yet be free from its sins and defects?

question: Are the properties of Christ's Godhead and of his flesh confused, so that one may say the Word came into being in the last times or that the Godhead suffered?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: No. When each is considered by itself, the properties stay unconfused. The Word is before the ages and operative, while the flesh came into being in the last times and is passible. So it cannot be said that the flesh is pretemporal, that the Word came into being lately, or that the Godhead's power suffers.
sources.quote: The flesh is of a passible, the Word of an operative nature: and neither is the flesh capable of making the things that are, nor is the power possessed by the Godhead capable of suffering.
sources.raw_question: Are the properties of Christ's Godhead and of his flesh confused, so that one may say the Word came into being in the last times or that the Godhead suffered?

question: Are divine attributes such as life, truth and incorruption produced in God in a descending order, as the Gnostic emanations of Aeons claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. These are names of perfections that always exist in God, used so far as is proper for men to speak of Him. Intelligence cannot be older than life, since intelligence is itself life; otherwise God, the intellect of all, would at some time have been without life.
sources.quote: these and such like attributes have not been produced according to a gradual scale of descent, but they are names of those perfections which always exist in God
sources.raw_question: Are divine attributes such as life, truth and incorruption produced in God in a descending order, as the Gnostic emanations of Aeons claim?

question: Did the Son delight in communion with the saints from eternity, on the basis of an agreement between the Father and the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. Proverbs 8:31, 'my delights were with the sons of men,' shows that the thoughts of communion with the saints were the joy of Christ's heart from eternity. This rested on the compact between the Father and the Son that he should save a remnant for his inheritance. His soul rejoiced in the delight he would take in them once he actually brought them into communion with himself.
sources.quote: The thoughts of communion with the saints were the joy of his heart from eternity. On the compact and agreement that was between his Father and him, that he should divide a portion with the strong, and save a remnant for his inheritance
sources.raw_question: Did the Son delight in communion with the saints from eternity, on the basis of an agreement between the Father and the Son?

question: What does the Hebrew word 'amon' in Proverbs 8:30, describing Wisdom (Christ) as being by the Father, mean?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Taken actively, it means one whom another takes into his care to bring up, and who arranges things for that person's advantage. Translations render it 'as one brought up with him,' or 'ordering/disposing all things.' Owen applies it to Christ taking his people into his care from eternity and rejoicing at the thought of carrying out that trust.
sources.quote: The word taken actively, signifies him whom another takes into his care to breed up, and disposeth of things for his advantage. So did Christ take us then into his care, and rejoiced in the thoughts of the execution of his trust.
sources.raw_question: What does the Hebrew word 'amon' in Proverbs 8:30, describing Wisdom (Christ) as being by the Father, mean?

question: What is the difference between saying the divine Persons are 'of one substance' (unius substantiae) and 'one substance' (una substantia)?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: Two men are of one and the same kind of substance but not one substance; the three divine Persons are both of one substance and one substance. The modern sense of 'consubstantial' includes both, and Augustine teaches that the three, being of one substance with no diversity of nature or will, are by ineffable conjunction one God.
sources.quote: Two men are wnius ejusdemque substantie, not una substantia. But the three Persons are not only unius substantiea, but una substantia. The modern sense of consubstantial takes in both.
sources.raw_question: What is the difference between saying the divine Persons are 'of one substance' (unius substantiae) and 'one substance' (una substantia)?

question: Did Augustine's teaching on the unity of the three Persons amount to Sabellianism?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: No. In his late work against Maximinus he teaches the three are one by unity of substance and ineffable conjunction while remaining three, and the work contains many passages against Sabellianism as well as against Arianism.
sources.quote: may shew how far St. Austin was from Sabellianism ;
sources.raised_by_detail: some who charge Augustine with Sabellianism
sources.raw_question: Did Augustine's teaching on the unity of the three Persons amount to Sabellianism?

question: Does the Son's saving work as the 'operative' Light make him superior or inferior in dignity to the Father, who supposedly remained inoperative?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: Neither premise holds. Making the Father ineffective in the work of salvation excludes him from our gratitude, since thanks are due only to benefactors. Every good, including our return to life, has its origin from the Father working through the Son, so the same grace calls for equal thankfulness to both.
sources.quote: With what right then does heresy attribute to the Son alone the gracious intervention on our behalf, and thereby exclude the Father from having any part or lot in our gratitude for its successful issue?
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's saving work as the 'operative' Light make him superior or inferior in dignity to the Father, who supposedly remained inoperative?

question: Did only the Son, and not the Father or the Holy Spirit, become incarnate, die and rise in a body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether the Sentence of John is to Be Understood of Our Future Likeness with the Son of God in the Immortality Itself Also of the Body.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine states that the Son alone in the Trinity took a body, in which He died, rose again and ascended. That is why our future bodily immortality is a likeness to the Son specifically.
sources.quote: but only to the Son, because He only in the Trinity took a body, in which He died and rose again, and which He carried with Him to heaven above.
sources.raw_question: Did only the Son, and not the Father or the Holy Spirit, become incarnate, die and rise in a body?

question: How could the Son of God, who as God could not die, undergo death in the Passion, and why?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVII. St. Ambrose shows by instances that the places in which those words were spoken help to the understanding of the words of the Lord; he shows that Christ uttered the passage quoted from St. John in Solomon's porch, by which is signified the mind of a wise man, for he says that Christ would not have uttered this saying in the heart of a foolish or contentious man. He goes on to say that Christ is stoned by those who believe not these words, and as the keys of heaven were given to Peter for his confession of them, so Iscariot, because he believed not the same, perished evilly. He takes this opportunity to inveigh against the Jews who bought the Son of God and sold Joseph. He explains the price paid for each mystically; and having in the same manner expounded the murmuring of the traitor concerning Magdalene's ointment, he adds that Christ is bought in one way by heretics in another way by Catholics, and that those in vain take to themselves the name of Christians who sever the Spirit from the Father.
sources.answer: He who was not to die because He was God died by our death, that is, in the human nature He assumed, so that we might live by His Spirit. Ambrose regards this as the fullest measure of mercy, greater even than His forgiving wrongs done to Himself, and the Mystery of the Passion as the fulfilment of faith.
sources.quote: that He Who was not to die because He was God, should die by our death, that we might live by His Spirit.
sources.raw_question: How could the Son of God, who as God could not die, undergo death in the Passion, and why?

question: Are forgiveness of sin and salvation prerogatives that Scripture assigns to God alone?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 2. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, detaches our ultimate confidence from man the creature, and attaches it to God the Creator; – by contrasting the sinfulness and feebleness of mortal man with the goodness and omnipotence of the Eternal Jehovah: by direct prohibition and precept: by exhibiting the holy Jealousy of God.
sources.answer: Yes. After man's fall, the Lord gave a deeper revelation of his goodness and grace. He revealed himself as the only Being who forgives iniquity, transgression and sin. He is the only Refuge, Saviour, Deliverer and Redeemer of his people.
sources.quote: He reveals himself as the Alone Being who forgives iniquity, transgression, and sin, as the Alone Refuge for the fugitive, as the Alone Saviour, Deliverer, and Redeemer of his people.
sources.raw_question: Are forgiveness of sin and salvation prerogatives that Scripture assigns to God alone?

question: Does the Father's love for the Son (John 5:20) imply that the Son's powers are given by free choice rather than by necessity of nature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. Love does not imply freedom of choice: God loves himself, and that love is no matter of choice. Likewise the love of his Son, his other self, need not be represented as free. The text says only that the Father loves the Son; calling it 'free love' adds to the text.
sources.quote: But why must love imply freedom? Doth not God Jove himself? And if the love of himself be no matter of choice, why must the love of his Son, his other self, be represented otherwise?
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's love for the Son (John 5:20) imply that the Son's powers are given by free choice rather than by necessity of nature?

question: Does a believer's spiritual comfort depend on outward circumstances or on the inward state of their own heart?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No. It depends on the powerful and effectual working of the Holy Ghost. That is why comfort can break through every opposition, into dungeons, flames and tribulation. When the Spirit brings Christ's promises to mind, neither Satan, sin, the world nor death can stop it.
sources.quote: their consolation or trouble depends not on any outward condition or inward frame of their own hearts, but on the powerful and effectual workings of the Holy Ghost, which by faith they give themselves up unto.
sources.raw_question: Does a believer's spiritual comfort depend on outward circumstances or on the inward state of their own heart?

question: Can Christ's promises comfort the soul by their bare letter and our meditation on them, without the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No. The promises are powerless in the bare letter, even when we consider and meditate on them as fully as we can. They come alive only when the Spirit applies them, sometimes unexpectedly and with conquering vigour. So faith deals specifically with the Holy Ghost in this work, looking up to him and waiting for him.
sources.quote: Who knows not how powerless they are in the bare letter, even when improved to the uttermost by our considerations of them, and meditation on them?
sources.raw_question: Can Christ's promises comfort the soul by their bare letter and our meditation on them, without the Holy Spirit?

question: Did the pre-Nicene Church teach that the Son is a distinct, inferior, created being subordinate to the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: No. No ancient author of reputation before Arius taught that the Son was a separate, inferior being or creature. The ancients held a subordination only in some sense, that of Son to Father. They did not hold it in Arius's sense or in the opponent's sense of an inferior nature.
sources.quote: there is not an author of reputation, among all the ancients, before Arius, that taught or maintained any such thing. A subordination, in some sense, they held; and that is all; not in Arius’s sense, not in yours.
sources.raw_question: Did the pre-Nicene Church teach that the Son is a distinct, inferior, created being subordinate to the Father?

question: Can God be superior to His works by virtue of attributes He lacks, as the negative terms used by Basil imply?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. The grandeur of the Divine Nature is recognized precisely in its not sharing the peculiarities of lower natures. If God were involved in them, He would be on a level with any individual that shares them. Being removed from them, He stands above those who possess them, just as the Sinless is superior to sinners, and being removed from evil is evidence of abounding in the best.
sources.quote: the very grandeur of the Divine Nature is recognized in this, viz. in the absence of all participation in those things which the lower natures are shown to possess.
sources.raw_question: Can God be superior to His works by virtue of attributes He lacks, as the negative terms used by Basil imply?

question: Can those who claim to be 'spiritual by nature' be saved regardless of their conduct, so that immoral actions cannot harm them, as the Valentinian Gnostics taught?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter VI.—The threefold kind of man feigned by these heretics: good works needless for them, though necessary to others: their abandoned morals.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus treats this as an error contradicted by Scripture, which assures us that those who commit such forbidden deeds 'shall not inherit the kingdom of God.' He shows the doctrine's falsity by its fruits: it leads its 'most perfect' adherents into idolatry, lust, and adultery without fear. Against their claim that good works are needed only by lesser 'animal' men, he presents the Church as guarding against sin even in thought and word out of the fear of God.
sources.quote: the “most perfect” among them addict themselves without fear to all those kinds of forbidden deeds of which the Scriptures assure us that “they who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.”
sources.raw_question: Can those who claim to be 'spiritual by nature' be saved regardless of their conduct, so that immoral actions cannot harm them, as the Valentinian Gnostics taught?

question: In what sense is the Holy Spirit said to be "in" created beings such as the saints?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: The Spirit is said to be "in" creatures because of the grace flowing from Him. He dwells in the worthy and carries out His operations "in divers portions and in divers manners." That grace naturally comes and goes, even if it abides continually in those firmly disposed to good. So "in" describes His operation in recipients, not His proper rank.
sources.quote: Where on the other hand the grace flowing from the Spirit naturally comes and goes, it is properly and truly said to exist in, even if on account of the firmness of the recipients’ disposition to good the grace abides with them continually.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Holy Spirit said to be "in" created beings such as the saints?

question: Why are created things changeable while the Son is unchangeable?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. How the Word has free will, yet without being alterable. He is unalterable because the Image of the Father, proved from texts.
sources.answer: Created things come into being from nothing, existing after not existing, and so have a changeable nature. The Son is from the Father and proper to His essence, and is therefore as unchangeable as the Father Himself.
sources.quote: for things originate, being from nothing, and not being before their origination, because, in truth, they come to be after not being, have a nature which is changeable; but the Son, being from the Father, and proper to His essence, is unchangeable
sources.raw_question: Why are created things changeable while the Son is unchangeable?

question: Are creation and redemption to be referred to the divine Nature, as a necessary process in God, or to the divine Will?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus C. Introductory to the Fourth Discourse against the Arians.
sources.answer: To the divine Will. Sabellius treated creation and redemption as the one God under successive manifestations. Marcellus treated them as the realisation of a process eternally latent in God. Both erred alike in referring to the divine Nature what the Church's theology has consistently referred to the divine Will.
sources.quote: both Marcellus and apparently Sabellius referred to the divine Nature what the theology of the Church has consistently referred to the divine Will.
sources.raw_question: Are creation and redemption to be referred to the divine Nature, as a necessary process in God, or to the divine Will?

question: Was the Son brought into existence first as an instrument or standard for creating the world, as Theognostus suggested?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then exposes argument about the “Generate,” and the “product of making,” and “product of creation,” and shows the impious nature of the language of Eunomius and Theognostus on the “immediate” and “undivided” character of the essence, and its “relation to its creator and maker.”
sources.answer: No. Whatever exists for the sake of something else is of less value than that for which it exists, as a plough is worth less than the life it serves. If the Son existed for the sake of the world, the world would be more valuable than the Lord, which is absurd. The world exists on account of Him, not He on account of it.
sources.quote: if the Lord also exists on account of the world, and not all things on account of Him, the whole of the things for the sake of which they say He exists, would be more valuable than the Lord.
sources.raw_question: Was the Son brought into existence first as an instrument or standard for creating the world, as Theognostus suggested?

question: If God foreknew the world that would come to be, does it follow that God himself is its creator rather than some lesser being?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter III.—The Bythus and Pleroma of the Valentinians, as well as the God of Marcion, shown to be absurd; the world was actually created by the same Being who had conceived the idea of it, and was not the fruit of defect or ignorance.
sources.answer: Yes. Either the supreme Father was ignorant of what would happen in the void, which would deny his prescience, or he foreknew and mentally contemplated the creation. In the latter case he who formed it beforehand in himself is the one who created it.
sources.quote: If, again, He is prescient, and contemplated mentally that creation which was about to have a being in that place, then He Himself created it who also formed it beforehand [ideally] in Himself.
sources.raw_question: If God foreknew the world that would come to be, does it follow that God himself is its creator rather than some lesser being?

question: Do texts saying the Son was sent, was made of a woman, did not do his own will, and had a doctrine not his own contradict texts calling him Creator, one with the Father, and true God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > By What Rule in the Scriptures It is Understood that the Son is Now Equal and Now Less.
sources.answer: No. The first set of texts belongs to the form of a servant, and the second to the form of God. Thus all things were made by him, he and the Father are one, and he has life in himself as the Father does. Yet as servant he was made under the law, came to do the will of the one who sent him, was sorrowful unto death, and was obedient unto the cross.
sources.quote: According to the form of God, He and the Father are one;[^127] according to the form of a servant, He came not to do His own will, but the will of Him that sent Him.
sources.raw_question: Do texts saying the Son was sent, was made of a woman, did not do his own will, and had a doctrine not his own contradict texts calling him Creator, one with the Father, and true God?

question: Is there any basis in the divine nature for degrees of honour among the divine Persons, as there are among human rulers?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His elaborate account of degrees and differences in 'works' and 'energies' within the Trinity is absurd.
sources.answer: No. Among men, honour is measured by differences of worth. But every perfection of goodness is implied in the very name of God, and the Son has no less power, glory, wisdom or love than the Father. All that is the Father's is seen in the Son, so there is no ground for revering the Father more.
sources.quote: Where there is no greater and smaller in power, or glory, or wisdom, or love, or of any other imaginable good whatever, but the good which the Son has is the Father’s also, and all that is the Father’s is seen in the Son
sources.raw_question: Is there any basis in the divine nature for degrees of honour among the divine Persons, as there are among human rulers?

question: What is required for a saving and comforting knowledge of God's attributes, and where is it found?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Three things are required. First, God must have manifested the glory of all his attributes by doing good to us. Second, he must still exercise them to the utmost on our behalf. Third, being so manifested and exercised, they must be able to bring us to the everlasting enjoyment of himself, which is our blessedness. All three lie hidden in Christ, and not even a glimpse of them can be attained outside him.
sources.quote: Now, all these three lie hid in Christ; and the least glimpse of them out of him is not to be attained.
sources.raw_question: What is required for a saving and comforting knowledge of God's attributes, and where is it found?

question: Does the command 'Be ye merciful, as your Father is merciful' mean that we creatures can become as God the Father is?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. To become as the Father is impossible for creatures brought into being out of nothing. The command means we should look to God's beneficent acts and do good for his sake. In the same way, we are called sons and gods by grace, not in nature and truth as the one only-begotten Son is.
sources.quote: to become as the Father, is impossible for us creatures, who have been brought to be out of nothing
sources.raw_question: Does the command 'Be ye merciful, as your Father is merciful' mean that we creatures can become as God the Father is?

question: What does Christ's answer to the apostles after the resurrection, that it is not theirs to know the times which the Father has set in His own authority, show about the Son's knowledge of the day?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It shows that the Son does know. The apostles asked again as though He knew, perceiving His earlier ignorance as a plan of silence, and He no longer denied knowing but said the knowledge was not theirs. The Father set the times not in His own exclusive knowledge but in His own authority, and He who was to restore the kingdom to Israel could not be ignorant of its time.
sources.quote: the Father has set the times not in His own knowledge, but in His own authority.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's answer to the apostles after the resurrection, that it is not theirs to know the times which the Father has set in His own authority, show about the Son's knowledge of the day?

question: Do the things Christ did and suffered in time belong to knowledge (scientia) or to wisdom (sapientia), and how does contemplation of the eternal Word differ?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What in the Incarnate Word Belongs to Knowledge, What to Wisdom.
sources.answer: The temporal deeds and sufferings of the incarnate Word belong to knowledge, not wisdom. The Word as such is without time and place, co-eternal with the Father and wholly everywhere, and true discourse about the Word in that respect pertains to wisdom. Thus Christ has the treasures both of wisdom and of knowledge.
sources.quote: And as the Word is without time and without place, it is co-eternal with the Father, and in its wholeness everywhere; and if any one can, and as much as he can, speak truly concerning this Word, then his discourse will pertain to wisdom.
sources.raw_question: Do the things Christ did and suffered in time belong to knowledge (scientia) or to wisdom (sapientia), and how does contemplation of the eternal Word differ?

question: Is Christ both the object of our knowledge and of our wisdom, so that we move from one to the other without leaving him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What in the Incarnate Word Belongs to Knowledge, What to Wisdom.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ implants faith concerning temporal things and shows forth the truth concerning eternal things. Through him we reach to him, stretching from knowledge to wisdom without withdrawing from the one and same Christ in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.
sources.quote: Through Him we reach on to Himself: we stretch through knowledge to wisdom; yet we do not withdraw from one and the same Christ,
sources.raw_question: Is Christ both the object of our knowledge and of our wisdom, so that we move from one to the other without leaving him?

question: Does the title 'the most high God' imply that there are other lesser gods beneath the supreme one?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Like God's other attributes, it is descriptive, not distinctive of the subject. It means only that the true God is endued with sovereign power, dominion and authority over all, not that there are other gods over whom he is highest.
sources.quote: It does not intimate that there are other gods, only he is the most high, or one over them all; but only that the true God is most high, — that is, endued with sovereign power, dominion, and authority over all.
sources.raw_question: Does the title 'the most high God' imply that there are other lesser gods beneath the supreme one?

question: Can the scriptural ascription to Christ of eternity, omnipotence, immensity and omniscience be explained as a divinity of office conferred on an exalted man?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. These properties belong necessarily and absolutely to a divine nature and essence, not to any power or authority to which a man may be exalted. To ascribe them to a mere man exalted to office implies the highest contradiction.
sources.quote: all these concern a divine nature, a natural essence, a Godhead, and not such power or authority as a man may be exalted unto; yea, the ascribing any of them to such a one, implies the highest contradiction expressible.
sources.raw_question: Can the scriptural ascription to Christ of eternity, omnipotence, immensity and omniscience be explained as a divinity of office conferred on an exalted man?

question: May divine worship rightly be given to one who is God only by office and not by nature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. The formal reason and object of religious worship is divine essential excellencies, so worshipping one who is not God by nature is idolatry. A god who did not make the heavens and earth falls under God's threat that such gods shall perish.
sources.quote: For they are divine, essential excellencies that are the formal reason and object of worship, religious and divine; and to ascribe it unto any one that is not God by nature, is idolatry.
sources.raw_question: May divine worship rightly be given to one who is God only by office and not by nature?

question: Is Christ's exaltation as mediator to dignity and authority inconsistent with his already possessing essential divine honour?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. His exaltation in office relating to the work of redemption does not conflict with the essential honour he has in himself as God blessed for ever. Though he humbled himself and was exalted in office, in nature he remained the same and did not change.
sources.quote: Though he humbled himself, and was exalted in office, yet in nature he was one and the same; he changed not.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ's exaltation as mediator to dignity and authority inconsistent with his already possessing essential divine honour?

question: Do Paul's statements that God blinds unbelievers and gives them up to a reprobate mind refer to the one true God rather than to a lesser or different deity?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXIX.—Refutation of the arguments of the Marcionites, who attempted to show that God was the author of sin, because He blinded Pharaoh and his servants.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus reads 2 Corinthians 4:4, Romans 1:28 and 2 Thessalonians 2:11 as speaking of the same God who blinds those who reject Him. In the same way, Christ's parables were meant to fulfil Isaiah's prophecy against unbelievers. Judicial blinding of the unbelieving is therefore the work of the one God of both Testaments.
sources.quote: In whom the God of this world hath blinded the minds of them that believe not, lest the light of the glorious Gospel of Christ should shine [unto them].
sources.raw_question: Do Paul's statements that God blinds unbelievers and gives them up to a reprobate mind refer to the one true God rather than to a lesser or different deity?

question: Does regarding all grace as purchased by Christ detract from the free grace of the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: No. Owen holds that it is no prejudice to the Father's free grace to view anything as the Son's purchase, because the Son's purchase itself flowed from the Father's grace. Indeed, we have no communion with Christ in receiving grace unless we regard it as his purchase.
sources.quote: It is no prejudice to the free grace of the Father, to look on any thing as the purchase of the Son; it was from that grace that he made that purchase
sources.raw_question: Does regarding all grace as purchased by Christ detract from the free grace of the Father?

question: Can we know what God was doing before He made the world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: No. The answer lies with God alone. Scripture teaches that the world was made perfect by God and had a beginning in time, but it does not reveal what God was occupied with before this. To offer guesses is foolish, rash and blasphemous, and speculating about the origin of matter risks setting aside God the Creator.
sources.quote: For that this world was formed perfect by God, receiving a beginning in time, the Scriptures teach us; but no Scripture reveals to us what God was employed about before this event.
sources.raw_question: Can we know what God was doing before He made the world?

question: Is it valid to divide the Divine into "created" and "uncreated" in the way one might divide animals into kinds?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > He then declares that the close relation between names and things is immutable, and thereafter proceeds accordingly, in the most excellent manner, with his discourse concerning “generated” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: No. The Only-begotten is proclaimed God in Scripture, so splitting the Divine into created and uncreated is as foolish as dividing "man" into "horse" and "man." Whatever is truly called God cannot be placed among created things.
sources.quote: condemn for utter folly the man who parts the Divine into created and uncreated, as he does him who divides “man” into “horse” and “man.”
sources.raw_question: Is it valid to divide the Divine into "created" and "uncreated" in the way one might divide animals into kinds?

question: Is it legitimate to argue about the worship of Christ in terms of 'honour' rather than 'religious worship'?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. 'Honour' is an ambiguous word that can mean mere respect or esteem. Substituting it for worship and adoration changes the ideas and the very state of the question. The dispute is strictly about acts of religious worship.
sources.quote: Let us keep to the terms we began with; lest, by the changing of words, we make a change of ideas, and alter the very state of the question.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to argue about the worship of Christ in terms of 'honour' rather than 'religious worship'?

question: Did the Jews of the Old Testament worship God as Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. Because they did not grasp the typical meaning of their mysteries, they did not know God the Son, so they worshipped God simply as God and not as Father. Had they worshipped Him as Father, they would also have worshipped the Son, since Father and Son are known together.
sources.quote: worshipped God simply as God, and not as Father; for, if they had worshipped Him as Father, they would have worshipped the Son also.
sources.raw_question: Did the Jews of the Old Testament worship God as Father?

question: Does the faith of the Church confess Christ to be true God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: Yes. Christians carry the new name Christ gave them in reward for loyal service, and they swear that He is true God. Every believer confesses, proclaims and is inwardly assured that Christ is true God. This fulfils Isaiah's prophecy that men would bless and swear by the true God.
sources.quote: The faith of all believers swears that Thou art God, confesses, proclaims, is inwardly assured, that Thou art true God.
sources.raw_question: Does the faith of the Church confess Christ to be true God?

question: Does Paul present the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit together as co-sources of the saving blessings given to believers?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Throughout his epistles, from the earliest (1 and 2 Thessalonians) to the latest (Titus, 2 Timothy), Paul brings the three Persons together, in the most incidental manner, as co-sources of all saving blessings. Ephesians offers a typical series of such passages. The very casualness of these references shows that a Trinitarian conception underlies his thought.
sources.quote: all three Persons, God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, are brought together, in the most incidental manner, as co-sources of all the saving blessings which come to believers in Christ
sources.raw_question: Does Paul present the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit together as co-sources of the saving blessings given to believers?

question: Does the New Testament restrict the Trinitarian distinctions to God's economic operations rather than to God's being in Himself?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The New Testament makes no effort to distinguish the ontological from the economical aspects of the Trinitarian distinctions. It shows no apparent awareness of such a distinction. Whether God is thought of in Himself or in His operations, the conception runs naturally into trinal forms.
sources.quote: Whether God is thought of in Himself or in His operations, the underlying conception runs unaffectedly into trinal forms.
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament restrict the Trinitarian distinctions to God's economic operations rather than to God's being in Himself?

question: Does Psalm 33:9, "He spake, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created," imply a Mediator distinct from the Father in creation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. The text does not say God merely willed things and they came to be. It says He spoke and commanded, which implies someone who receives and carries out the command. If creation happened by sheer will alone, there would be no office for a Mediator between God and the world awaiting creation. A solitary God giving a spoken order to Himself would be meaningless.
sources.quote: He spake, and they were made; the Scripture does not say that He willed it, and did it. He commanded, and they were created; you observe that it does not say they came into existence, because it was His pleasure.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 33:9, "He spake, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created," imply a Mediator distinct from the Father in creation?

question: Is God's superiority over lower natures recognized by His being free of the limitations those natures possess?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Such privative terms express God's freedom from the defects found in lower beings, and that freedom is precisely what shows His superiority. If 'immortal' did not mean the absence of death, either the term would be applied to God falsely or it would carry some other meaning that Eunomius cannot explain. Being free of evil and defect is evidence of abounding in the best.
sources.quote: for he from whom death is not absent is not in his essence immortal. But again; if these terms signify the absence neither of death nor of destruction, either they are applied falsely to the God overall, or else they comprise within themselves some different meaning.
sources.raw_question: Is God's superiority over lower natures recognized by His being free of the limitations those natures possess?

question: Could God have deliberated and chosen to have a Word and Wisdom so as not to be without them?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. It is madness to think God counsels and chooses so as not to be without Word and Wisdom. That would mean deliberating about what is proper to His own Essence, which amounts to deliberating about Himself. Created things come to be by favour and will, but the Son is by nature the own Offspring of God's Essence.
sources.quote: the Son is not a work of will, nor has come after, as the creation, but is by nature the own Offspring of God’s Essence
sources.raw_question: Could God have deliberated and chosen to have a Word and Wisdom so as not to be without them?

question: Do the texts in Proverbs 8:14 ('Counsel is mine') and Isaiah 9:6 ('Angel of great Counsel') show that the Son is the Father's Living Counsel rather than a product of it?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is Himself the Understanding and Power of God, yet says 'mine is understanding' and 'mine strength.' In the same way, when He says 'Mine is counsel' He is Himself the Living Counsel of the Father. As the Father's Counsel and Good Pleasure, by which all things willed come to be, He cannot Himself come to be by will.
sources.quote: so while He says, ‘Mine is counsel,’ He must Himself be the Living Counsel of the Father; as we have learned from the Prophet also, that He becomes ‘the Angel of great Counsel,’
sources.raw_question: Do the texts in Proverbs 8:14 ('Counsel is mine') and Isaiah 9:6 ('Angel of great Counsel') show that the Son is the Father's Living Counsel rather than a product of it?

question: Should we distinguish different times in Christ's existence when interpreting what he says about himself?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. It is one thing that he was God before he was man, another that he was man and God, and another that after this he was perfect man and perfect God. He speaks of himself differently before his birth, while still mortal, and as eternal. So the times and natures in the dispensation must not be confused.
sources.quote: It is one thing, that He was God before He was man, another, that He was man and God, and another, that after being man and God, He was perfect man and perfect God.
sources.raw_question: Should we distinguish different times in Christ's existence when interpreting what he says about himself?

question: Do Christ's hunger, weariness, fear, prayer and agony disprove that he is God?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Though shown to be God, he does not refuse the conditions proper to him as man. The same one who as God has a sleepless nature slumbers on a pillow. The one who strengthens believers is himself strengthened by an angel. He went through all these things for us, having been made as we are for our sakes.
sources.quote: Thus then, too, though demonstrated as God, He does not refuse the conditions proper to Him as man, since He hungers and toils and thirsts in weariness, and flees in fear, and prays in trouble.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's hunger, weariness, fear, prayer and agony disprove that he is God?

question: What do the details of John's vision of the Son of man in Revelation 1 signify about Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: They set forth aspects of His person and work. The white head shows the glory He has received from the Father. The long garment shows His priestly office, which is why Moses vested the high priest that way. The burning brass points to the end of all things, signifying the power of faith and constant prayer in view of the consuming fire to come.
sources.quote: For in these words He sets forth something of the glory [which He has received] from His Father, as [where He makes mention of] the head; something in reference to the priestly office also, as in the case of the long garment reaching to the feet.
sources.raw_question: What do the details of John's vision of the Son of man in Revelation 1 signify about Christ?

question: Does 'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' describe the activity of two unlike natures?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. It is the one divine nature working in both. In the healing of the blind man, Christ calls his own work 'the works of Him that sent Me', so the Son's work is the Father's work and God's work. The Son is engaged in the very work the Father does.
sources.quote: You see that in his case the work wrought by the Son is the Father’s work; and the Son’s work is God’s work.
sources.raw_question: Does 'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' describe the activity of two unlike natures?

question: Did the Word give the Holy Spirit to the saints even before the Incarnation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: Yes. Before becoming man, the Word dispensed the Spirit to the saints as his own: he gave it to Moses and the seventy, and through him David prayed, 'Take not thy Holy Spirit from me.' When made man, he likewise sends the Paraclete and gives the Spirit to his disciples. This shows he is the same yesterday, today and for ever.
sources.quote: as, before His becoming man, He, the Word, dispensed to the saints the Spirit as His own, so also when made man, He sanctifies all by the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Did the Word give the Holy Spirit to the saints even before the Incarnation?

question: Can angels or other creatures work together with God or give grace alongside Him, as the Son does?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. Creatures are not efficient causes but belong among things that come to be. They are separate from God, divided from Him, and other in nature. So they cannot do what God does, and they cannot give grace with Him. They are only ministering spirits and heralds of gifts that God gives through the Word.
sources.quote: being separate and divided from the only God, and other in nature, and being works, they can neither work what God works, nor, as I said before, when God gives grace, can they give grace with Him
sources.raw_question: Can angels or other creatures work together with God or give grace alongside Him, as the Son does?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's work of transforming sinners into righteous people show that he is good?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit makes good men out of the worst, does away with sin, destroys evil, pours in good gifts, and makes apostles of persecutors and priests of sinners. One who does such things cannot be denied to be good.
sources.quote: Or is the Spirit not good, Who of the worst makes good men, does away sin, destroys evil, shuts out crime, pours in good gifts, makes apostles of persecutors, and priests of sinners?
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's work of transforming sinners into righteous people show that he is good?

question: How can the Holy Spirit be beyond our reach by nature and yet be received by creatures and present everywhere?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: By nature he cannot be attained to, but because of his goodness he can be received. He is simple in substance and fills all things by his power, yet only the just partake of him. He gives of his own to each while remaining whole everywhere.
sources.quote: Who though because of His nature He cannot be attained to, yet because of His goodness can be received by us, filling all things His power, but only partaken of by the just, simple in substance, rich in virtues, present to each, dividing of His own to every one, and Himself whole everywhere.
