sources.raw_question: How can the Holy Spirit be beyond our reach by nature and yet be received by creatures and present everywhere?

question: Did the Word of God reveal himself to the Old Testament prophets only through visions and spoken words, or also through their actions?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Also through their actions. The Word was beheld by the prophets not only in visions and proclamations but in actual works. Through these he prefigured future events, so that what the prophets did typically, Christ later accomplished truly in the Church.
sources.quote: it was not by means of visions alone which were seen, and words which were proclaimed, but also in actual works, that He was beheld by the prophets, in order that through them He might prefigure and show forth future events beforehand.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God reveal himself to the Old Testament prophets only through visions and spoken words, or also through their actions?

question: Is the one who imparts or receives an essence distinct from the essence that is imparted or received?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He proceeds again to discuss the impassibility of the Lord's generation; and the folly of Eunomius, who says that the generated essence involves the appellation of Son, and again, forgetting this, denies the relation of the Son to the Father: and herein he speaks of Circe and of the mandrake poison.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory notes that Eunomius's own analysis implies this. Whoever gives or receives is other than what is given or received. So we must first conceive someone in his own separate existence, and then speak of him as giving what he has or receiving what he lacks.
sources.quote: For he that receives or imparts is surely another besides that which is given or received, so that we must first conceive some one by himself, viewed in his own separate existence
sources.raw_question: Is the one who imparts or receives an essence distinct from the essence that is imparted or received?

question: Did the Jews who sought to kill Jesus correctly understand him to be claiming Deity for himself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Preface
sources.answer: Yes. Owen says the Jews would have slain the Saviour for bearing witness to his own Deity, and that they rightly understood his meaning. Cerinthus and the Ebionites who later denied his Deity persisted in the Jews' heresy despite the evidence of that testimony.
sources.quote: persisted in the heresy of the Jews, who would have slain our Saviour for bearing witness to his own Deity, notwithstanding the evidence of that testimony, and the right apprehension which the Jews had of his mind therein
sources.raw_question: Did the Jews who sought to kill Jesus correctly understand him to be claiming Deity for himself?

question: What died in Christ when he died on the cross for us: our life or our guilt?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IX. The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ, and the oil of gladness; and why Christ Himself is not the ointment, since He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It is not strange that the Spirit should be called Ointment, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. And there is no confusion between them, since Christ alone suffered death, Whose saving cross is then spoken of.
sources.answer: Our guilt, not our life. Christ died for us so that we might live in his risen Body. He bore our sins in his own body on the tree, so that we might be freed from sin and live in righteousness.
sources.quote: For Christ died for us, that we might live in His revived Body. Therefore not our life but our guilt died in Him
sources.raw_question: What died in Christ when he died on the cross for us: our life or our guilt?

question: Does the Holy Spirit have any role in the final judgment at Christ's second coming, or is He inactive then?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: Yes, the Spirit is present and active with the Lord in the judgment. The crown of the righteous is the grace of the Spirit bestowed more abundantly and perfectly in that day, and the condemnation of sinners consists in their being deprived of the Spirit. Since the Spirit is both the prize of the righteous and the one whose withdrawal constitutes punishment, the judgment cannot be conceived as accomplished without Him.
sources.quote: How then is it possible to conceive that the judgment is accomplished without the Holy Spirit, wherein the word points out that He is Himself the prize of the righteous, when instead of the earnest is given that which is perfect
sources.raised_by_detail: some who suppose the Spirit has no functions at the Lord's appearing
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit have any role in the final judgment at Christ's second coming, or is He inactive then?

question: Does the address 'God is in Thee' imply a real distinction of Persons, against a solitary God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. 'In Thee' implies one present and addressed by the speaker. 'God is in Thee' reveals both God present and God abiding in him. Such facts are inconsistent with solitude.
sources.quote: The facts are inconsistent with solitude. In Thee implies that there was One present within range, if I may say so, of the Speaker’s voice.
sources.raw_question: Does the address 'God is in Thee' imply a real distinction of Persons, against a solitary God?

question: Why do the Scriptural data about the Word require the Catholic doctrine rather than Arian or Sabellian alternatives?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 23: Whether the Doctor's notion of the Trinity be more clear and intelligible than the other ?
sources.answer: The Arian scheme cannot stand without borrowing the Catholic principle of a human soul joined to the Word. Once that is admitted, the Sabellian scheme looks simpler and better fits the high things said of the Word. But the strong arguments for the distinct personality of the Word and Spirit then force a further Catholic principle, which completely answers all. So the Catholic doctrine is needed to make Scripture consistent.
sources.quote: the arguments for the distinet personality of the Word and Holy Spirit, bear so full and strong, that there will appear a necessity for taking in another Catholic principle; and that will completely answer all.
sources.raw_question: Why do the Scriptural data about the Word require the Catholic doctrine rather than Arian or Sabellian alternatives?

question: Is accepting or rejecting the Godhead of Jesus Christ a matter that bears on a person's eternal salvation?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 1. Introduction. Preparation of heart. Our position before God.
sources.answer: Yes. The author holds that eternal death or eternal life depends on whether this truth is rejected or cordially accepted. He grounds this in Scripture's warnings that whoever does not believe the Son, or does not abide in the doctrine of Christ, lacks life and lacks God. For this reason he calls the deity of Christ a foundation truth.
sources.quote: from a deep assurance that in the rejection or cordial acceptance of this truth are bound up the issues of eternal death or eternal life. (John 3:36; 2 John 9.)
sources.raw_question: Is accepting or rejecting the Godhead of Jesus Christ a matter that bears on a person's eternal salvation?

question: How do the Son's works, such as knowing all things without being asked, show that he went forth from God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: They show it because only one who has God's nature can do God's works. The Apostles believed He went forth from God because He both can and does perform the works of God, such as universal knowledge; His birth from God is what accounts for that omnipotence.
sources.quote: The reason why they believe that He went forth from God is that He both can, and does, perform the works of God.
sources.raw_question: How do the Son's works, such as knowing all things without being asked, show that he went forth from God?

question: Could the devil rightly claim the worship he demanded of Christ in the temptation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. Following Irenaeus, worship is owed to the Lord God alone. The devil promised things that were not his own, since the creation is not under his dominion, and he himself is only one of the creatures.
sources.quote: The system of creatures is not ** under his dominion, since he himself is one of the creatures.
sources.raw_question: Could the devil rightly claim the worship he demanded of Christ in the temptation?

question: What kind of order exists among the Persons of the Trinity according to orthodox faith?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: The order is natural and germane, such that the Persons cannot be confounded because they are divided as Persons, yet they are united in their being. Had Eunomius meant only this order of attributes in the Trinity, he would teach the same doctrine as the Church.
sources.quote: an order so ‘natural’ and ‘germane’ that the Persons cannot be confounded, being divided as Persons, though united in their being
sources.raw_question: What kind of order exists among the Persons of the Trinity according to orthodox faith?

question: Is spiritual regeneration by the Holy Spirit a greater work than bodily creation, and does this bear on the Spirit's dignity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is no less the author of spiritual creation or regeneration than the Father and the Son. The excellence of that creation, and wherein it consists. How we are to understand holy Scripture, when it attributes a body or members to God.
sources.answer: Yes. The regeneration wrought by the Spirit produces the new, heavenly man made after God's image, which no one doubts to be better than the earthly outer man. So the Spirit is Author of the more excellent creation.
sources.quote: That more excellent regeneration is then the work of the Holy Spirit; and the Spirit is the Author of that new man which is created after the image of God, which no one will doubt to be better than this outer man of ours.
sources.raw_question: Is spiritual regeneration by the Holy Spirit a greater work than bodily creation, and does this bear on the Spirit's dignity?

question: Is it coherent to say that the Father not only was not incarnate but could not have become incarnate?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: No. The claim yields a double absurdity: either taking flesh is evil, and then evil is ascribed to the Son, or it is good, and then the Father is made powerless for good. Saying only that the Father did not become incarnate would have sufficed.
sources.quote: For if to partake of our flesh is evil, then he predicates evil of the Only-begotten God; but if the lovingkindness to man was good, then he makes out the Father to be powerless for good
sources.raw_question: Is it coherent to say that the Father not only was not incarnate but could not have become incarnate?

question: Why are the Father and the Son one by nature in a way proper to them alone?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Because the Son is God from God. The Only-begotten, being from the Unbegotten, can subsist in no other nature than that of his origin. What is begotten exists in the substance of its birth, and that birth possesses no other truth of deity than the one from which it issued.
sources.quote: it is proper to the Father alone and the Son that They should be one by nature because God is from God, and the Only-begotten from the Unbegotten can subsist in no other nature than that of His origin
sources.raw_question: Why are the Father and the Son one by nature in a way proper to them alone?

question: Does believers' sharing Christ's throne (Rev. 3:21) put them on a level with the Son, whose throne is addressed as God's throne (Heb. 1:8)?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Setting the verses side by side shows an immeasurable difference. Universal supremacy belongs to Christ by right forever. Reigning with him is a favour he grants to his people.
sources.quote: the immeasurable difference betwixt the universal supremacy belonging of right to Christ forever, and the favour granted by him to his people of reigning with him
sources.raw_question: Does believers' sharing Christ's throne (Rev. 3:21) put them on a level with the Son, whose throne is addressed as God's throne (Heb. 1:8)?

question: Does the liberty of adopted children of God consist in freedom to perform or omit duties as they choose?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: No. That is a liberty stolen by slaves, not given by the Spirit to sons. The liberty of sons is an inward spiritual freedom of heart that naturally goes out in all the ways and worship of God; slaves take liberty from duty, children have liberty in duty.
sources.quote: Slaves take liberty from duty; children have liberty in duty. There is not a greater mistake in the world, than that the liberty of sons in the house of God consists in this, — they can perform duties, or take the freedom to omit them
sources.raw_question: Does the liberty of adopted children of God consist in freedom to perform or omit duties as they choose?

question: Why is the obedience of God's adopted sons joyful rather than grievous?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: Because it springs from love, which is the bottom of all their duties. Just as Jacob's hard service was not grievous because of his love for Rachel, no duty is grievous to a saint because of his love to Christ. Perfect love casts out the fear that comes from a spirit of bondage.
sources.quote: When their soul is acted to obedience by love, it expels that fear which is the issue of bondage upon the spirit.
sources.raw_question: Why is the obedience of God's adopted sons joyful rather than grievous?

question: Why does the holiness of Christ's human nature surpass that of the angels and all other creatures?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Because every other creature has the Spirit by measure, whereas the Spirit was given to Christ without measure, it pleasing the Father that all fulness should dwell in him. Other creatures subsist in created, dependent being and so have the fountain of their holiness outside themselves, but Christ's human nature subsists in the person of the Son of God and so has the fountain of its holiness in strictest unity with itself.
sources.quote: But the human nature of Christ subsists in the person of the Son of God; and so hath the bottom and fountain of its holiness in the strictest unity with itself.
sources.raw_question: Why does the holiness of Christ's human nature surpass that of the angels and all other creatures?

question: When Moses drew near to the cloud where God was, did he see the Son of God in His own substance with bodily eyes?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Of the Appearance on Sinai. Whether the Trinity Spake in that Appearance or Some One Person Specially.
sources.answer: No. The Wisdom of God cannot be seen with the eyes of the flesh, any more than the wisdom of any wise man can. Heretics who hold the Son is visible in His own substance err; the visible things were creaturely signs of the invisible God.
sources.quote: Forsooth, Moses may have seen Him with the eyes of the flesh, if not only the wisdom of God which is Christ, but even that of any man you please and howsoever wise, can be seen with the eyes of the flesh
sources.raised_by_detail: doting heretics who hold the Son visible in His own substance
sources.raw_question: When Moses drew near to the cloud where God was, did he see the Son of God in His own substance with bodily eyes?

question: Can a created mind become good by itself, or only by turning to a good other than itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How God May Be Known to Be the Chief Good. The Mind Does Not Become Good Unless by Turning to God.
sources.answer: Only by turning to a good other than itself. The mind did not make itself a mind. It becomes a good mind by an act of will, yet it cannot become good unless it turns to something it is not, namely the good it loves, seeks and obtains. If it turns away, it can only return because that good remains present to it.
sources.quote: But when it does this of set purpose, and becomes a good mind, it yet cannot attain to being so unless it turn itself to something which itself is not.
sources.raw_question: Can a created mind become good by itself, or only by turning to a good other than itself?

question: If God emitted Intelligence (Nous) as a separate being, what would follow about God's own nature?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: God would have to be a compound and corporeal being. On the Valentinian view, the emitter and the emitted would be separated from each other, which implies parts and bodily division in God. Equally, to say intelligence was sent forth from intelligence cuts God's mind asunder into parts.
sources.quote: For if He produced intelligence, then He who did thus produce intelligence must be understood, in accordance with their views, as a compound and corporeal Being; so that God, who sent forth [the intelligence referred to], is separate from it
sources.raw_question: If God emitted Intelligence (Nous) as a separate being, what would follow about God's own nature?

question: Must a being that had a beginning either have been unbegotten in order to be immortal, or else perish, so that created souls cannot endure forever?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXIV.—Souls can be recognised in the separate state, and are immortal although they once had a beginning.
sources.answer: No. God alone, the Lord of all, is without beginning and end and is always the same unchangeable Being. Everything that comes from Him has a beginning and is therefore inferior to its Maker. Yet created things such as the heavens and souls endure for long ages, even forever, because God wills that they continue. Scripture says He commanded them, they were created, and He established them forever.
sources.quote: let them learn that God alone, who is Lord of all, is without beginning and without end, being truly and for ever the same, and always remaining the same unchangeable Being.
sources.raw_question: Must a being that had a beginning either have been unbegotten in order to be immortal, or else perish, so that created souls cannot endure forever?

question: Is the soul life in itself, or does it have life only by participating in a life given by God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXIV.—Souls can be recognised in the separate state, and are immortal although they once had a beginning.
sources.answer: The soul is not life itself but shares in a life God gives it. The body is not the soul but is joined to it as long as God pleases, and in the same way the soul and its life are distinct. Scripture says the first man 'became a living soul,' showing that the soul became alive by sharing in life.
sources.quote: so the soul herself is not life, but partakes in that life bestowed upon her by God.
sources.raw_question: Is the soul life in itself, or does it have life only by participating in a life given by God?

question: Is unending life natural to human beings, or is it a gift of God's grace that the ungrateful can lose?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXIV.—Souls can be recognised in the separate state, and are immortal although they once had a beginning.
sources.answer: It is a gift of grace. Life does not come from us or from our nature; the Father gives everlasting continuance to those who are saved. Whoever keeps that life and gives thanks receives length of days forever. Whoever ungratefully rejects the Giver deprives himself of it, as the Lord indicates in asking who will give the great to those unfaithful in little.
sources.quote: For life does not arise from us, nor from our own nature; but it is bestowed according to the grace of God.
sources.raw_question: Is unending life natural to human beings, or is it a gift of God's grace that the ungrateful can lose?

question: How do the virtues of this life form a trinity in the mind now, and how will that trinity differ in the future life when those virtues have passed away?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether Justice and the Other Virtues Cease to Exist in the Future Life.
sources.answer: Now the virtues form one trinity: we hold them, look at them and love them as present. Later their acts, like faith, will be reckoned among things past. They will then form a different trinity, made of the trace they leave in memory, the true recognition of that trace, and the will joining these two as a third. So the image-trinity of memory, understanding and will continues even about things that have ceased to be.
sources.quote: since then, too, there will be a trinity, when that trace, be it of what sort it may, shall be retained in the memory, and truly recognized, and then these two be joined by will as a third.
sources.raw_question: How do the virtues of this life form a trinity in the mind now, and how will that trinity differ in the future life when those virtues have passed away?

question: What distinguishes divine wisdom from created light such as the sun or created spirits?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why the Son Chiefly is Intimated in the Scriptures by the Name of Wisdom, While Both the Father and the Holy Spirit are Wisdom. That the Holy Spirit, Together with the Father and the Son, is One Wisdom.
sources.answer: Wisdom is spiritual and unchangeable light. The sun is light but corporeal, and the spiritual creature is light but not unchangeable. Only God is both spiritual and unchangeable light.
sources.quote: But what is wisdom, except spiritual and unchangeable light? For yonder sun also is light, but it is corporeal; and the spiritual creature also is light, but it is not unchangeable.
sources.raw_question: What distinguishes divine wisdom from created light such as the sun or created spirits?

question: Do Christians who worship the Father, Son and Holy Spirit worship a different God from the Jehovah of Israel?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Israel worshipped the one only true God under the Name of Jehovah. Christians worship the same one true God under the Name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost. The Trinity is the distinguishing mark of the religion Christ founded, not a new God.
sources.quote: Israel had worshipped the one only true God under the Name of Jehovah; Christians are to worship the same one only and true God under the Name of “the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost.”
sources.raw_question: Do Christians who worship the Father, Son and Holy Spirit worship a different God from the Jehovah of Israel?

question: If the Father gave up, raised and exalted Christ, does that make Christ's death, resurrection and ascension merely passive and so show he is not God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. As man, Christ's death, resurrection and ascension were subordinate to the Father and took place at his ordination. As God, Christ gives himself, has power to lay down his life and take it again, raises his own body, and ascends in his own might. The paired texts therefore teach both his subordination as man and his Deity.
sources.quote: as God, Christ gives himself, raises himself, ascends in his own might, and as the King of glory, the Lord of hosts mighty in battle, enters the everlasting doors.
sources.raw_question: If the Father gave up, raised and exalted Christ, does that make Christ's death, resurrection and ascension merely passive and so show he is not God?

question: Can God rightly be conceived by transferring to Him ideas drawn from bodily things or from the human mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > This Work is Written Against Those Who Sophistically Assail the Faith of the Trinity, Through Misuse of Reason. They Who Dispute Concerning God Err from a Threefold Cause. Holy Scripture, Removing What is False, Leads Us on by Degrees to Things Divine. What True Immortality is. We are Nourished by Faith, that We May Be Enabled to Apprehend Things Divine.
sources.answer: No. Those who think of God as white or red, or as now forgetting and now remembering, are in error, because such properties belong to bodies or created minds, not to God. Reasoning about God by measuring the incorporeal by the corporeal, or God by the affections of the human soul, produces distorted and fallacious rules.
sources.quote: For he who thinks, for instance, that God is white or red, is in error; and yet these things are found in the body. Again, he who thinks of God as now forgetting and now remembering, or anything of the same kind, is none the less in error
sources.raw_question: Can God rightly be conceived by transferring to Him ideas drawn from bodily things or from the human mind?

question: Is it coherent to say that God has the power to generate Himself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > This Work is Written Against Those Who Sophistically Assail the Faith of the Trinity, Through Misuse of Reason. They Who Dispute Concerning God Err from a Threefold Cause. Holy Scripture, Removing What is False, Leads Us on by Degrees to Things Divine. What True Immortality is. We are Nourished by Faith, that We May Be Enabled to Apprehend Things Divine.
sources.answer: No. This error is even worse than conceiving God in bodily or psychic terms, because nothing at all, neither God nor any spiritual or bodily creature, generates its own existence. Such a conception corresponds to nothing in the Creator or in any creature.
sources.quote: But he who thinks that God is of such power as to have generated Himself, is so much the more in error, because not only does God not so exist, but neither does the spiritual nor the bodily creature; for there is nothing whatever that generates its own existence.
sources.raw_question: Is it coherent to say that God has the power to generate Himself?

question: If Christ's healings were types of events in the Pleroma, can the Gnostics apply the typology to some healings and not others?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIII.—The woman who suffered from an issue of blood was no type of the suffering Æon.
sources.answer: No. If Christ's acts were types of what happened in the Pleroma, the type must be kept consistently in every case. On that logic the woman bound eighteen years would point to an eighteenth suffering Aeon, and the man ill thirty-eight years to a thirty-eighth. The Gnostic system cannot accommodate either. To say the Saviour kept the type in some cases and not in others is absurd and inconsistent.
sources.quote: Now, it is in every way absurd and inconsistent to declare that the Saviour preserved the type in certain cases, while He did not do so in others.
sources.raw_question: If Christ's healings were types of events in the Pleroma, can the Gnostics apply the typology to some healings and not others?

question: If Scripture already proves Christ's deity by inference from his divine attributes and claims, what value do explicit statements that Christ is God add?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: They add confirmation, though not greater certainty. Just as an independent measurement that coincides with a mathematically demonstrated result further shows the reliability of the demonstration, so explicit texts state outright what other Scriptures prove demonstratively. The argument from the One Jehovah's attributes belonging to Christ is already conclusive.
sources.quote: I would then, draw into a brief compass, some few of these positive deductions. They state expressly what other Scriptures prove demonstratively.
sources.raw_question: If Scripture already proves Christ's deity by inference from his divine attributes and claims, what value do explicit statements that Christ is God add?

question: In what sense can the Son be called the product of the Father's will, according to Augustine and some early writers?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: The Father's will is God himself, just as his wisdom is God himself. Whatever is the product of God is therefore equally the product of his will and wisdom. So the Son, as the perfect image of the Father, is will of will, as he is wisdom of wisdom, light of light and God of God. On this view, being 'from the will' signifies no more than being God of God.
sources.quote: “That since the will of God is God himself, as “much as the wisdom, &c. of God is God himself; whatever is “the fruit and product of God, is the fruit and product of his “ will, wisdom, &e.
sources.raw_question: In what sense can the Son be called the product of the Father's will, according to Augustine and some early writers?

question: Does a creature united to God make God greater, as two bodies joined together form a greater body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > God is a Trinity, But Not Triple (Triplex).
sources.answer: No. Bodies increase by union, but in spiritual things, when the lesser adheres to the greater, as the creature to the Creator, only the lesser becomes greater. It becomes greater because it becomes better. He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit, yet the Lord does not thereby become greater.
sources.quote: “He,” then, “that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit:” but yet the Lord does not therefore become greater, although he who is joined to the Lord does so.
sources.raw_question: Does a creature united to God make God greater, as two bodies joined together form a greater body?

question: Is the Spirit's sealing of believers the same as his confirming the promise as irrevocable, like a seal set on a written grant?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No. Many expositors read it this way, but it does not fit the wording. Scripture says that we are sealed, not that the promise is sealed. When a deed is sealed, we say the deed is sealed, not the person who receives it.
sources.quote: It is not said that the promise is sealed, but that we are sealed; and when we seal a deed or grant to any one, we do not say the man is sealed, but the deed or grant.
sources.raw_question: Is the Spirit's sealing of believers the same as his confirming the promise as irrevocable, like a seal set on a written grant?

question: Is it legitimate to suppose that the difference among the Persons of the Trinity is as great as the difference among created things, such as between the heavens and a single man or star?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His elaborate account of degrees and differences in 'works' and 'energies' within the Trinity is absurd.
sources.answer: No. Gregory holds that supposing so wide a difference within the Holy Trinity is openly profane. The Trinity is set above creation and shares a supreme, perfect nature that admits no greater and less. Grading the Persons like ranked creatures therefore contradicts their divine perfection.
sources.quote: To suppose that within the Holy Trinity there is a difference as wide as that which we can observe between the heavens which envelope the whole creation, and one single man or the star which shines in them, is openly profane
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to suppose that the difference among the Persons of the Trinity is as great as the difference among created things, such as between the heavens and a single man or star?

question: Was it God the Father who was seen by Abraham and received as his guest?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: No. The Father is invisible and was not seen at that time. The one seen, and even touched, was the one accustomed to be seen and touched, namely the Son, Christ. Christ is therefore rightly called both Lord and God, since he was begotten of the Father as God the Word before Abraham.
sources.quote: It was not the Father, then, who was a guest with Abraham, but Christ. Nor was it the Father who was seen then, but the Son; and Christ was seen.
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who make the Father visible
sources.raw_question: Was it God the Father who was seen by Abraham and received as his guest?

question: How do Paul's texts on Christ's death and life show that death belongs to Christ's humanity and life and power to his Godhead?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > The sixth book shows that He Who came for man's salvation was not a mere man, as Eunomius, falsely slandering him, affirmed that the great Basil had said, but the Only-begotten Son of God, putting on human flesh, and becoming a mediator between God and man, on Whom we believe, as subject to suffering in the flesh, but impassible in His Godhead; and demonstrates the calumny of Eunomius.
sources.answer: Paul says Christ condemned sin "in the flesh," not "in the Godhead." "Crucified through weakness" refers to the flesh, while "liveth by power" refers to the Divine Nature. Likewise "He died unto sin" refers to the body, and "liveth unto God" refers to the Godhead. Together these establish that the Man tasted death while the immortal Nature did not suffer death.
sources.quote: so that by these words it is established that, while the Man tasted death, the immortal Nature did not admit the suffering of death
sources.raw_question: How do Paul's texts on Christ's death and life show that death belongs to Christ's humanity and life and power to his Godhead?

question: How does faith in the Son's perfect birth avoid both the error of two Gods and the error of a single solitary person?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Father and Son are one in essence but not one person. The Son, though a distinct person, has no difference of nature from the Father. Thus the Two are one God, which excludes both tritheistic division and Sabellian confusion.
sources.quote: every error, as well that of two Gods as of a single God, is abolished, since They Who are one in essence are not one person
sources.raw_question: How does faith in the Son's perfect birth avoid both the error of two Gods and the error of a single solitary person?

question: Should the Spirit's descent "with great power" at Pentecost be understood as something bodily and perceptible to the senses?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter II. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are One in counsel.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit descended in the same way that Christ is to descend, coming in the clouds with great power and majesty. The descent therefore signifies divine power and majesty, not a material event.
sources.quote: that you may not suppose that this is to be referred to bodily things and perceptible to the senses, learn that the Spirit so descended as Christ is to descend
sources.raw_question: Should the Spirit's descent "with great power" at Pentecost be understood as something bodily and perceptible to the senses?

question: What is love, considered in its own nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > There are Three Things in Love, as It Were a Trace of the Trinity.
sources.answer: Love is the love of good, and is a kind of life that couples, or seeks to couple, two things together: the one who loves and the one who is loved. This holds even in carnal loves, but is seen more purely in the mind's love for a friend's mind.
sources.quote: What, then, is love, except a certain life which couples or seeks to couple together some two things, namely, him that loves, and that which is loved?
sources.raw_question: What is love, considered in its own nature?

question: Why do some people fail to accept the truth that the Son and the Father are one?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVII. St. Ambrose shows by instances that the places in which those words were spoken help to the understanding of the words of the Lord; he shows that Christ uttered the passage quoted from St. John in Solomon's porch, by which is signified the mind of a wise man, for he says that Christ would not have uttered this saying in the heart of a foolish or contentious man. He goes on to say that Christ is stoned by those who believe not these words, and as the keys of heaven were given to Peter for his confession of them, so Iscariot, because he believed not the same, perished evilly. He takes this opportunity to inveigh against the Jews who bought the Son of God and sold Joseph. He explains the price paid for each mystically; and having in the same manner expounded the murmuring of the traitor concerning Magdalene's ointment, he adds that Christ is bought in one way by heretics in another way by Catholics, and that those in vain take to themselves the name of Christians who sever the Spirit from the Father.
sources.answer: Because Christ speaks this truth only in the heart of the wise and peaceful, not in the unquiet and foolish. The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, since they seem foolishness to him. The narrow hearts of sinners cannot take in the greatness of this faith, so the believer must open his heart to the Word.
sources.quote: He will not say this in the breast of the unquiet and foolish, for “the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness unto him.” The narrow breasts of sinners do not take in the greatness of the faith.
sources.raw_question: Why do some people fail to accept the truth that the Son and the Father are one?

question: Does Scripture present only the Father, and not the Son, as the first cause of miracles and of forgiveness?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Scripture names the Father and the Son in turn as the source. Healing is done 'by the name of thy holy child Jesus,' yet Peter says 'Jesus Christ maketh thee whole,' showing the Son as the immediate Author of healing. Likewise forgiveness is ascribed both to God for Christ's sake and to Christ himself.
sources.quote: Now the Father, now the Son, is referred to as the first cause of forgiveness.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture present only the Father, and not the Son, as the first cause of miracles and of forgiveness?

question: Could a created Word have definitively overcome the devil and freed humanity from the fear of death?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. If the Word were a creature, the devil, also a creature, would have continued the battle forever, and man, caught between the two, would always be in peril of death. Only the Framer of all things could destroy the works of the devil in the flesh and deliver man from all fear.
sources.quote: for with a creature, the devil, himself a creature, would have ever continued the battle, and man, being between the two, had been ever in peril of death, having none in whom and through whom he might be joined to God
sources.raw_question: Could a created Word have definitively overcome the devil and freed humanity from the fear of death?

question: Does the Son's birth from the Virgin by the Holy Spirit show that divine begetting can take place without passion or division?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Gregory further shows that the Only-Begotten being begotten not only of the Father, but also impassibly of the Virgin by the Holy Ghost, does not divide the substance; seeing that neither is the nature of men divided or severed from the parents by being begotten, as is ingeniously demonstrated from the instances of Adam and Abraham.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ was born by the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest without the conditions of human generation. The Spirit was not diminished, the power of the Highest was not divided, and the Virgin's incorruption was not sullied. If flesh could be born of flesh without carnal passion, it is absurd to deny that the Son can be begotten of the Father without division.
sources.quote: nor was the Virgin subject to those conditions, nor was the Spirit diminished, nor the power of the Highest divided? For the Spirit is entire, the power of the Highest remained undiminished
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's birth from the Virgin by the Holy Spirit show that divine begetting can take place without passion or division?

question: Can conclusive evidence alone produce a saving belief in the divinity of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. The understanding may be convinced while the heart rebels, because the world cannot receive the Spirit of truth and the natural man cannot know the things of the Spirit, which are spiritually discerned. Saving belief must therefore be sought in prayer, pleading Christ's promise that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask.
sources.quote: no evidence, however conclusive, can ensure a saving belief in the Divinity of the Holy Ghost. The understanding may be convinced, while the heart may rebel.
sources.raw_question: Can conclusive evidence alone produce a saving belief in the divinity of the Holy Spirit?

question: Can the divine power shared by the Father, Son and Holy Spirit be divided, as the teachings of Arius and Photinus imply?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XVI. The Holy Spirit is that large river by which the mystical Jerusalem is watered. It is equal to its Fount, that is, the Father and the Son, as is signified in holy Scripture. St. Ambrose himself thirsts for that water, and warns us that in order to preserve it within us, we must avoid the devil, lust, and heresy, since our vessels are frail, and that broken cisterns must be forsaken, that after the example of the Samaritan woman and of the patriarchs we may find the water of the Lord.
sources.answer: No. Ambrose holds that the divine power is an indivisible unity. Arius and Photinus try to separate it, and he calls this impiety that tears the Church's garment and destroys faith. Whoever takes in their teaching loses the water of the Spirit, as water spills from a cracked vessel.
sources.quote: our moth is Arius, our moth is Photinus, who rend the holy vesture of the Church with their impiety, and desiring to separate the indivisible unity of the divine power, gnaw the precious veil of faith with sacrilegious tooth.
sources.raw_question: Can the divine power shared by the Father, Son and Holy Spirit be divided, as the teachings of Arius and Photinus imply?

question: Why may one pray to receive gifts from the Father and the Son together but not from God and the angels?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Because no creature is a partner with its Maker in His givings, whereas the Son is the own Offspring of the Father's Essence. Joint prayer to Father and Son shows their oneness and the oneness of their giving, since the Father works whatever He gives through the Son. Were the Son divided in nature from the Father, the Father alone giving would suffice.
sources.quote: No one, for instance, would pray to receive from God and the Angels, or from any other creature, nor would any one say, ‘May God and the Angel give thee;’ but from Father and the Son, because of Their oneness
sources.raw_question: Why may one pray to receive gifts from the Father and the Son together but not from God and the angels?

question: Is the faith of Abraham the same faith as that of Christians who believe in Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXI.—Abraham’s faith was identical with ours; this faith was prefigured by the words and actions of the old patriarchs.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul calls Abraham both the prophet of faith and the father of Gentile believers because his faith and ours are one and the same. Abraham believed in future things as though already done because of God's promise, and we likewise, on God's promise, see by faith the inheritance laid up in the future kingdom.
sources.quote: because his faith and ours are one and the same: for he believed in things future, as if they were already accomplished, because of the promise of God
sources.raw_question: Is the faith of Abraham the same faith as that of Christians who believe in Jesus Christ?

question: Is the God of the patriarchs the same God whom Christians worship?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXI.—Abraham’s faith was identical with ours; this faith was prefigured by the words and actions of the old patriarchs.
sources.answer: Yes. The two nations foretold to Rebecca were of one and the same father, and our God, one and the same, is also the God of the patriarchs. He knows all things before they happen, which is why he could say before their birth that he loved Jacob and hated Esau.
sources.quote: Our God, one and the same, is also their God, who knows hidden things, who knoweth all things before they can come to pass
sources.raw_question: Is the God of the patriarchs the same God whom Christians worship?

question: Does Psalm 2:8 ('Ask of Me, and I will give Thee the heathen for Thine inheritance') describe the Father's promise to the Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXI.—Abraham’s faith was identical with ours; this faith was prefigured by the words and actions of the old patriarchs.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus reads it as the Father promising Christ his wages. Those wages are human beings from many nations gathered into one company of faith, prefigured by the many-coloured sheep given to Jacob as his wages.
sources.quote: the wages of Christ are human beings, who from various and diverse nations come together into one cohort of faith, as the Father promised Him
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 2:8 ('Ask of Me, and I will give Thee the heathen for Thine inheritance') describe the Father's promise to the Son?

question: Does Christ's obedience on the cross show that the God we offended in Adam is the same God as the Father Christ reveals?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVI.—Since our bodies return to the earth, it follows that they have their substance from it; also, by the advent of the Word, the image of God in us appeared in a clearer light.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ undid the disobedience committed by means of a tree through His obedience upon the tree of the cross. He would not have come to cancel disobedience against our Maker if He had proclaimed another Father. We were debtors only to Him whose commandment we transgressed at the beginning, and in the second Adam we are reconciled to that same God.
sources.quote: Now He would not have come to do away, by means of that same [image], the disobedience which had been incurred towards our Maker if He proclaimed another Father.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's obedience on the cross show that the God we offended in Adam is the same God as the Father Christ reveals?

question: How can the same Wisdom that establishes the earth and prepares the heavens also be said to be 'created for the beginning of His works'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: Because the creation spoken of is a dispensation for man's salvation. Since men forgot God's commandment through disobedience, the ever-existing Wisdom was 'created' in the Incarnation to restore them to their first estate. He thus became a new and living way for the wanderers, the beginning of ways for the works of God, that is, for men.
sources.quote: for this cause I was created, Who ever am, and need no creation in order to be; so that I am the beginning of ways for the works of God, that is for men.
sources.raw_question: How can the same Wisdom that establishes the earth and prepares the heavens also be said to be 'created for the beginning of His works'?

question: Where chiefly does Scripture locate God's love and grace in the forgiveness of sinners?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Principally in two things: God's holy eternal purpose to provide relief for lost sinners, and his sending his Son to accomplish that purpose. Scripture most eminently celebrates God's love in giving his only begotten Son as a propitiation and in Christ dying for us while we were sinners. Those who deny this remove the foundation of the gospel.
sources.quote: In his holy eternal purpose of providing a relief for lost sinners.
sources.raw_question: Where chiefly does Scripture locate God's love and grace in the forgiveness of sinners?

question: Was the devil conquered by Christ only at the resurrection, or already at the moment Christ was slain?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Of the Same Subject.
sources.answer: He was conquered precisely when he thought he had conquered, at Christ's death. Christ's blood, being that of one with no sin, was poured out for the remission of our sins. The devil had held sinners justly under the condition of death, so he could justly lose them through Christ, whom death struck undeservedly because he had no sin. The victory at the resurrection is easier to see, but the deeper victory was by righteousness on the cross.
sources.quote: It is something more, and more profound of comprehension, to see that the devil was conquered when he thought himself to have conquered, that is, when Christ was slain.
sources.raw_question: Was the devil conquered by Christ only at the resurrection, or already at the moment Christ was slain?

question: Is the Trinity, which is God, to be sought among eternal, incorporeal and unchangeable realities, and does the blessed life consist in contemplating it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine says the inquiry has advanced to the point of seeking the Trinity, which is God, in eternal, incorporeal and unchangeable things. He holds that the perfect contemplation of these things is the blessed life promised to us.
sources.quote: inquiring concerning the Trinity, which is God, in those eternal, incorporeal, and unchangeable things themselves, in the perfect contemplation of which a blessed life is promised to us.
sources.raw_question: Is the Trinity, which is God, to be sought among eternal, incorporeal and unchangeable realities, and does the blessed life consist in contemplating it?

question: Why is the Son, rather than the Father, appointed Judge of all men according to John 5:22-23?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: Judgment is committed to the Son so that the world might fully grasp his high worth and dignity and honour him as it honours the Father. The Father's personal dignity is less likely to be questioned. Committing these powers to the Son's hands secures to him the honour that is his due.
sources.quote: the execution of those powers was lodged in his hands particularly, lest the world should not be sufficiently apprehensive of his high worth, eminency, and dignity; or should not “ honour the Son even as they honour the Father.”
sources.raw_question: Why is the Son, rather than the Father, appointed Judge of all men according to John 5:22-23?

question: Does John the Baptist's bearing witness to the eternal, intelligible Light belong to the eternal order (wisdom) or to the temporal order (knowledge)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Attempt is Made to Distinguish Out of the Scriptures the Offices of Wisdom and of Knowledge. That in the Beginning of John Some Things that are Said Belong to Wisdom, Some to Knowledge. Some Things There are Only Known by the Help of Faith. How We See the Faith that is in Us. In the Same Narrative of John, Some Things are Known by the Sense of the Body, Others Only by the Reason of the Mind.
sources.answer: It belongs to the temporal order. Although the Light to which John witnessed is eternal and intelligible, the act of bearing witness to it is an action done in time. It therefore falls under knowledge of temporal things rather than under wisdom's contemplation of eternal things.
sources.quote: For to bear witness even to that which is eternal, as is that light that is intelligible, is a thing done in time.
sources.raw_question: Does John the Baptist's bearing witness to the eternal, intelligible Light belong to the eternal order (wisdom) or to the temporal order (knowledge)?

question: Is the meaning of the word "believed" in John 1:11 ("His own received Him not") known through the bodily senses or through the reason of the mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Attempt is Made to Distinguish Out of the Scriptures the Offices of Wisdom and of Knowledge. That in the Beginning of John Some Things that are Said Belong to Wisdom, Some to Knowledge. Some Things There are Only Known by the Help of Faith. How We See the Faith that is in Us. In the Same Narrative of John, Some Things are Known by the Sense of the Body, Others Only by the Reason of the Mind.
sources.answer: It is known through the reason of the mind. The sound of the word "crediderunt" reaches us through the ear, but what belief is cannot be perceived by any bodily sense. Unless we knew by the mind what believing means, we would not understand what those who did not receive Christ failed to do. By contrast, a word like "world" signifies something known through bodily sight.
sources.quote: what belief is, we do not know by any sense of the body, but by the reason of the mind
sources.raw_question: Is the meaning of the word "believed" in John 1:11 ("His own received Him not") known through the bodily senses or through the reason of the mind?

question: Does the Spirit's commissioning of Peter in his own name ("I have sent thee") show that the Spirit is a divine person with supreme authority?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. As Christ, the Angel of God's presence, showed his Deity by saying "I am the God of thy father, I will send thee," so the Spirit, saying "I have sent thee" in his own right and setting aside the ceremonial law, shows he is a divine person who acts in the Son's place and governs the church.
sources.quote: in his own right, setting aside the ceremonial law, we may safely argue this is a Divine person, who, in the absence of the Son of God, according to his promise, acts in his place and governs his church.
sources.raw_question: Does the Spirit's commissioning of Peter in his own name ("I have sent thee") show that the Spirit is a divine person with supreme authority?

question: Why is the Holy Spirit called "Spirit," a name similar to the human spirit, when this risks obscuring his personality?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: The name is not arbitrary but the only one that reveals his distinctive character, as "Son" alone describes the Eternal Word. Its likeness to our own spirit expresses his fellowship with us, his spiritual indwelling, and his witness with our spirit. This similarity testifies our union with the Comforter who renews us, as shared humanity testifies our union with the Saviour.
sources.quote: his name is no arbitrary choice; that it is the only one which would reveal to us the distinctive character of this holy Being, as the name the Son could alone describe the Eternal Word
sources.raw_question: Why is the Holy Spirit called "Spirit," a name similar to the human spirit, when this risks obscuring his personality?

question: Is the difference between Christ and any creature, even the highest angel, merely one of degree?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: No. Owen says there is still a proportion between creatures, since an angel and a worm are both creatures and agree in something. Between all the nothings of the world and the God infinitely blessed for evermore there is no proportion at all. Christ is therefore infinitely above every creature, not just greater in degree.
sources.quote: There is still a proportion between these, they agree in something; but what are all the nothings of the world to the God infinitely blessed for evermore?
sources.raw_question: Is the difference between Christ and any creature, even the highest angel, merely one of degree?

question: Was the Son created first as a medium because creation could not endure the untempered hand of the Father, as Eusebius, Arius and Asterius claimed?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: No. To say God made only the Son because making everything was too toilsome is unworthy of God, for Isaiah says the Creator neither faints nor is weary. Moreover, if the Word were originate, He too could not endure God's hand. He would then need a mediator, and that mediator another, without end, so creation could never subsist.
sources.quote: For if they shall assign the toil of making all things as the reason why God made the Son only, the whole creation will cry out against them as saying unworthy things of God
sources.raw_question: Was the Son created first as a medium because creation could not endure the untempered hand of the Father, as Eusebius, Arius and Asterius claimed?

question: Can the Father's work of framing creation be separated from the Son's work, so that the Father makes the framing and the Son makes the creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: No. The Arians wrongly distinguish between the creatures and their framing, assigning one to the Father and the other to the Son. Rather, all things must be brought to be by the Father together with the Son. Otherwise, if everything originate comes through the Son, the Son cannot be one of the originated things.
sources.quote: either all things must be brought to be by the Father with the Son, or if all that is originate comes to be through the Son, we must not call Him one of the originated things
sources.raw_question: Can the Father's work of framing creation be separated from the Son's work, so that the Father makes the framing and the Son makes the creatures?

question: Are all human beings sons of God, or only those who believe and obey him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XLI.—Those persons who do not believe in God, but who are disobedient, are angels and sons of the devil, not indeed by nature, but by imitation. Close of this book, and scope of the succeeding one.
sources.answer: In one sense all are, in another only believers. By creation all men are sons of God, since God made them all; but with respect to obedience and doctrine only those who believe in him and do his will are his sons. The disobedient, like disinherited children, remain his offspring by creation but cease to be his sons and lose the inheritance, though by repentance they may become sons of God again.
sources.quote: According to nature, then—that is, according to creation, so to speak— we are all sons of God, because we have all been created by God. But with respect to obedience and doctrine we are not all the sons of God
sources.raw_question: Are all human beings sons of God, or only those who believe and obey him?

question: Do the opening verses of John's Gospel about the eternal Word (John 1:1-5) belong to wisdom (contemplation of eternal things) rather than to knowledge of temporal things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Attempt is Made to Distinguish Out of the Scriptures the Offices of Wisdom and of Knowledge. That in the Beginning of John Some Things that are Said Belong to Wisdom, Some to Knowledge. Some Things There are Only Known by the Help of Faith. How We See the Faith that is in Us. In the Same Narrative of John, Some Things are Known by the Sense of the Body, Others Only by the Reason of the Mind.
sources.answer: Yes. The verses stating that the Word was in the beginning, was with God, was God, and made all things concern what is immutable and eternal, the contemplation of which makes us blessed. They require a contemplative life and must be discerned by the intellectual mind, so they belong to wisdom. The later verses, which join eternal things with temporal events, belong partly to knowledge.
sources.quote: require a contemplative life, and must be discerned by the intellectual mind; and the more any one has profited in this, the wiser without doubt will he become
sources.raw_question: Do the opening verses of John's Gospel about the eternal Word (John 1:1-5) belong to wisdom (contemplation of eternal things) rather than to knowledge of temporal things?

question: What does the eternity of God's life consist in, and how can it be conceived?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Explanation of 'Ungenerate,' and a 'study' of Eternity.
sources.answer: God's eternity means He is always in existence, admitting no time when He was not or will not be. It can be pictured by a circle drawn from a centre, which has no discernible beginning or end: extending thought from the present instant in every direction, we find the divine life returning upon itself in unbroken continuity, with no end and no parts. Hence God is defined as earlier than any beginning and exceeding any end.
sources.quote: He is always to be apprehended as in existence; He admits not a time when He was not, and when He will not be.
sources.raw_question: What does the eternity of God's life consist in, and how can it be conceived?

question: What does John 1:5, "the Light shined in darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not," show about the Son's nature in the incarnation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: It shows that the Light remained unapproachable by its contrary even when it was present in darkness. Had the Light been changed into its contrary or overpowered by gloom, that would support the claim that it is inferior to the Father's Light. The Gospel attests the opposite, so the Son's Light is unchanged.
sources.quote: it is attested by the Gospel that, even when it had place in darkness, the light remained unapproachable by the contrary element
sources.raw_question: What does John 1:5, "the Light shined in darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not," show about the Son's nature in the incarnation?

question: How does the Holy Spirit console a believer who is troubled by the guilt of sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: The Spirit gives the believer peace in Christ, the only refuge from guilt, as the believer flees to him. Each weapon sin uses is met by a matching work of the Spirit. Against the dread of wrath, the Spirit sheds abroad the love of God in the heart. Against the accusation by Satan and the law that we are objects of God's hatred, the Spirit bears witness with our spirits that we are God's children.
sources.quote: There is not any one engine or instrument that sin useth or sets up against our peace, but one effect or other of the Holy Ghost towards us is suited and fitted to the casting of it down.
