sources.raw_question: How does the Holy Spirit console a believer who is troubled by the guilt of sin?

question: When the Son appeared to the patriarchs in the Old Testament as 'Lord God' or 'God of Bethel', why was he not identified as the Son or Messiah?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Because he then acted under a character common to the whole Godhead, not under his own personal distinguishing character. The distinction of persons had not yet been revealed, so he bore the common title 'Lord God', which has since been reserved in a more eminent way to the Father, while Christ is now known as Son, Mediator and Messiah.
sources.quote: Christ therefore, in these, or the like texts, is not represented under his own peculiar character; but under such a character as is common to the Godhead, to the Father and him too.
sources.raw_question: When the Son appeared to the patriarchs in the Old Testament as 'Lord God' or 'God of Bethel', why was he not identified as the Son or Messiah?

question: If the Son acted in the Father's name and authority in the theophanies, must everything he did be attributed only to the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: No. Because the Son is God of God and not unoriginated, all he did is referred back to the Father as Head and Fountain, whose authority he exercised. Yet whatever is said of Christ is still to be understood of him in his own Person, not of the Father only. The same holds in the New Testament (John 10:30, 14:9, 5:30).
sources.quote: And yet whatever is said of Christ is to be understood of him in his own Person, and not of the Father only, whom he represented.
sources.raw_question: If the Son acted in the Father's name and authority in the theophanies, must everything he did be attributed only to the Father?

question: Is the Lord God whom Christ commanded alone to be worshipped and served in the temptation the same God who gave the Mosaic law?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: Yes. Beyond all doubt it is the God who gave the law, since Christ answered Satan with the words of the law, and the law itself declares the Word of God from the Father. Christ thereby identifies the lawgiver with the Father whom his disciples alone must serve, so no other Father above the Creator is to be sought.
sources.quote: Who, then, is this Lord God to whom Christ bears witness, whom no man shall tempt, whom all should worship, and serve Him alone? It is, beyond all manner of doubt, that God who also gave the law.
sources.raw_question: Is the Lord God whom Christ commanded alone to be worshipped and served in the temptation the same God who gave the Mosaic law?

question: Do Isaiah's 'My Hand made all these things' and Paul's teaching that all things are of the Father and by the Son show that the Son is distinct from creation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: Yes. The prophet's 'Hand' signifies the power of the Only-begotten, by which God over all makes everything, and Paul likewise makes all things depend on their productive cause without counting the producer among 'all things'. This teaches a difference of nature between the maker and the made. Hence, since the Son is God and all things were made by him, the Son is opposed to creation just as the Godhead is.
sources.quote: the Apostle makes the same division of entities, making all things depend upon their productive cause, yet not reckoning in the number of “all things” that which produces them
sources.raw_question: Do Isaiah's 'My Hand made all these things' and Paul's teaching that all things are of the Father and by the Son show that the Son is distinct from creation?

question: How can the mind obey the precept "Know thyself" if it must already know what "know" and "thyself" mean in order to understand the command?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Mind Knows Itself, by the Very Act of Understanding the Precept to Know Itself.
sources.answer: The mind already knows itself in the very act of understanding the precept. To obey "Know thyself" it must understand both what "know" means and what "thyself" means, and if it knows both, it knows itself. So it is bidden to do the very thing it does in understanding the command, because it is present to itself.
sources.quote: But when it is said to the mind, Know thyself; then it knows itself by that very act by which it understands the word “thyself;” and this for no other reason than that it is present to itself.
sources.raw_question: How can the mind obey the precept "Know thyself" if it must already know what "know" and "thyself" mean in order to understand the command?

question: Does knowing that all temporal things are made according to an eternal divine science enable the philosophers to read off the particular facts of creation from that science itself?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Old Philosophers are Not to Be Consulted Concerning the Resurrection and Concerning Things to Come.
sources.answer: No. The philosophers rightly prove that temporal things are made according to an eternal science. However, they do not see clearly into that science itself. Facts such as the kinds of animals, their seeds, their growth and the patterns of their lives were learned from the history of places and times, or from the written experience of others. They were not drawn from the unchangeable wisdom.
sources.quote: Have they not sought out all these things, not through that unchangeable wisdom, but through the actual history of places and times, or have trusted the written experience of others?
sources.raw_question: Does knowing that all temporal things are made according to an eternal divine science enable the philosophers to read off the particular facts of creation from that science itself?

question: Did the apostles teach that the God who called Abraham and gave the covenant of circumcision is the same God who is the Father of Jesus Christ and the Maker of all things?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. The whole range of the apostles' words and acts proclaims one and the same God who removed Abraham, promised him an inheritance, gave circumcision, called Israel out of Egypt, made all things, and is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Anyone may learn from the apostles' own words that this God is one, above whom there is no other.
sources.quote: that He was the Maker of all things, that He was the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that He was the God of glory,—they who wish may learn from the very words and acts of the apostles
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles teach that the God who called Abraham and gave the covenant of circumcision is the same God who is the Father of Jesus Christ and the Maker of all things?

question: Should what the apostles declared about God be allegorized to refer to some god other than the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. The author's earlier arguments establishing one God as Founder and Maker of all things agree with the apostles' plain teaching that there is one God, the Maker of all things. Allegorizing their statements into another god is error and blasphemy against God.
sources.quote: if any one, “doting about questions,” do imagine that what the apostles have declared about God should be allegorized, let him consider my previous statements, in which I set forth one God as the Founder and Maker of all things
sources.raw_question: Should what the apostles declared about God be allegorized to refer to some god other than the Creator?

question: What did the apostles preach about Jesus' relation to God the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: They preached that Jesus, crucified by the Jews, is the Son of God, the Judge of the living and the dead, who received an eternal kingdom from His Father; and to the Greeks they preached one God, Maker of all, and Jesus Christ His Son. Stephen likewise saw the Son of man standing at the right hand of God.
sources.quote: the Jesus who was crucified by them was the Son of God, the Judge of quick and dead, and that He has received from His Father an eternal kingdom in Israel
sources.raw_question: What did the apostles preach about Jesus' relation to God the Father?

question: Does Peter's application of Isaiah's "stone of stumbling" to Christ show that Christ is Jehovah of hosts?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah says the stone of stumbling and rock of offence is "Jehovah of hosts himself." Peter, explicitly referring to that Scripture, says this stone is Christ. Therefore Christ is Jehovah of hosts himself.
sources.quote: The stone of stumbling, as Isaiah affirms, is “Jehovah of hosts himself,” but as St. Peter interprets it (for he is referring to what is contained in the Scripture, verse 6), this stone is Christ. Therefore, Christ is Jehovah of hosts himself.
sources.raw_question: Does Peter's application of Isaiah's "stone of stumbling" to Christ show that Christ is Jehovah of hosts?

question: In the angelic appearances of the Old Testament, which Person of the Trinity was signified?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: Sometimes the Father, sometimes the Son, sometimes the Holy Spirit, and sometimes God without distinction of Person. Father, Son and Spirit were all in those angels. In every case God was shown figuratively by his own creature, not by his substance.
sources.quote: sometimes the Father, sometimes the Son, sometimes the Holy Spirit, and sometimes God, without any distinction of person, was figuratively signified by them
sources.raw_question: In the angelic appearances of the Old Testament, which Person of the Trinity was signified?

question: Is God's substance ever seen in visible appearances, or is it shown only through creatures?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: It is shown only through creatures. God appeared in visible and sensible forms by his own creature, not by his substance. Seeing his substance requires hearts to be cleansed, and the things seen and heard serve that cleansing.
sources.quote: yet by His own creature, not by His substance, in order to the seeing of which, hearts are cleansed through all those things which are seen by the eyes and heard by the ears
sources.raw_question: Is God's substance ever seen in visible appearances, or is it shown only through creatures?

question: Does the divine title "Almighty" name God's absolute nature, or does it express a relation to something that is governed?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: It is a relative title. Some divine names express God's majesty absolutely, such as immortal and invisible. Others, like Physician, Merciful and Almighty, name God's operations toward creation. As God would not be called Physician except on account of the sick, he would not be called Almighty unless creation needed someone to rule it and keep it in being.
sources.quote: so neither would He be styled Almighty, did not all creation stand in need of one to regulate it and keep it in being
sources.raw_question: Does the divine title "Almighty" name God's absolute nature, or does it express a relation to something that is governed?

question: Is "the Holy Ghost" merely a figure of speech (metonymy) for the power of God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Paul speaks of abounding in hope "through the power of the Holy Ghost," which would be a most unlikely combination if the Spirit were simply God's power. Likewise, "the love of the Spirit" parallels "the mercies of God," a plea made by a personal subject.
sources.quote: If the Spirit were a metonymy for the power of God, this would be a most unlikely combination.
sources.raw_question: Is "the Holy Ghost" merely a figure of speech (metonymy) for the power of God?

question: Does the worship that every creature gives "to him that sitteth on the throne, and unto the Lamb" allow a distinction between lesser worship of Christ and supreme worship of God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Every creature ascribes blessing, honour, glory and power to both together, without intermission or pause. This leaves no room for any distinction like the Romanists' dulia and latria. The Lamb therefore receives the same divine adoration as God on the throne.
sources.quote: therefore without the possibility of any distinction (as between the dulia and latria of the Romanists,) being drawn in their adoration
sources.raw_question: Does the worship that every creature gives "to him that sitteth on the throne, and unto the Lamb" allow a distinction between lesser worship of Christ and supreme worship of God?

question: When Christ calls the devil "the strong man," does this make the devil comparable in strength to the Lord?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VIII.—Answer to an objection, arising from the words of Christ (Matt. vi. 24). God alone is to be really called God and Lord, for He is without beginning and end.
sources.answer: No. The devil is called strong only relative to us, whom he held captive in apostasy, not absolutely. Christ shows himself the truly strong one who binds him and spoils his house; no created and subject thing can be compared to the Word of God, by whom all things were made.
sources.quote: not he alone, but not one of created and subject things, shall ever be compared to the Word of God, by whom all things were made, who is our Lord Jesus Christ.
sources.raw_question: When Christ calls the devil "the strong man," does this make the devil comparable in strength to the Lord?

question: If the Father's greatness and power are made the cause of the ignorance among lower beings, does that make the Father the author of evil?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: Yes, on the heretics' hypothesis. If ignorance is an evil and the source of all evils, and the Father's greatness is its cause, then they set the Father forth as the author of all evils. Irenaeus treats this consequence as a reductio of their system.
sources.quote: while ye maintain that the greatness and power of the Father is the cause of this ignorance, ye do thus set Him forth as the author of [all] evils.
sources.raw_question: If the Father's greatness and power are made the cause of the ignorance among lower beings, does that make the Father the author of evil?

question: Does Jonathan Edwards's argument that God's perfect idea of Himself and His perfect love of Himself constitute the Son and the Holy Spirit succeed as a rational proof of the Trinity?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The mind does not consist in its states, so the repetition of its states would not duplicate or triplicate it. God differs from His idea and His love of Himself precisely as His Being differs from His acts. What is wanting to God's self-image to make it a second Deity is objective reality.
sources.quote: Neither God’s perfect idea of Himself nor His perfect love of Himself reproduces Himself. He differs from His idea and His love of Himself precisely by that which distinguishes His Being from His acts.
sources.raw_question: Does Jonathan Edwards's argument that God's perfect idea of Himself and His perfect love of Himself constitute the Son and the Holy Spirit succeed as a rational proof of the Trinity?

question: Is the Septuagint translation of the Old Testament an inspired and trustworthy witness to prophecies about the Son of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. The seventy elders translated separately, yet all produced the same words from beginning to end, which showed that they translated by God's inspiration. The apostles agree with this translation, and the one Spirit who spoke through the prophets also guided its translators.
sources.quote: For all of them read out the common translation [which they had prepared] in the very same words and the very same names, from beginning to end, so that even the Gentiles present perceived that the Scriptures had been interpreted by the inspiration of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the Septuagint translation of the Old Testament an inspired and trustworthy witness to prophecies about the Son of God?

question: Why does human philosophy fail to recognize that the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Christ?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: Because the worldly mind judges by the laws of material elements and thinks possible only what it can see or do. Creaturely parents give their offspring the beginnings of life but are not themselves present in them. In Christ, however, the whole fulness of the Godhead is present bodily, and He is wholly all that God is, as God from God.
sources.quote: they are not themselves present as living beings in their offspring, whereas in Christ all the fulness of the Godhead is present in bodily shape.
sources.raw_question: Why does human philosophy fail to recognize that the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Christ?

question: Should Christ's humiliation, or the glory he gives his people, lessen our trust in him as God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. His humiliation was a voluntary act of divine compassion: he left the throne and the Father's bosom to gather the scattered children of God. The one who is over all, God blessed forever, took our flesh and is not ashamed to call us brethren. Both his descent and our exaltation call forth greater gratitude and trust, not less.
sources.quote: gratitude can find no words to express itself when we believe on him who, being over all, God blessed forever, partook of our flesh and blood
sources.raw_question: Should Christ's humiliation, or the glory he gives his people, lessen our trust in him as God?

question: What fundamentally distinguishes the created from the uncreated?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > He shows the falsehood of Eunomius' calumnious charge that the great Basil had said that “man was emptied to become man,” and demonstrates that the “emptying” of the Only-begotten took place with a view to the restoration to life of the Man Who had suffered.
sources.answer: The difference is that of dominion and slavery. The uncreated God rules by His power for ever, while all things in creation serve Him. The whole creation is in bondage. If the Son were created, He would be a servant by nature, and His incarnation would be a change "from servitude to servitude."
sources.quote: terms of which the divergence is marked by dominion and slavery, since the uncreated God, as the prophet says, “ruleth with His power for ever,” while all things in the creation are servants to Him
sources.raw_question: What fundamentally distinguishes the created from the uncreated?

question: Did the divine Word of God himself speak with the patriarchs before Moses, before his incarnation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: Yes. The Word of God conversed with the ante-Mosaic patriarchs in accordance with his divinity and glory. For those under the law he instituted a sacerdotal and liturgical service. Afterwards, being made man, he sent the Spirit, so that one and the same Word directs every stage of God's dealings with mankind.
sources.quote: And the Word of God Himself used to converse with the ante-Mosaic patriarchs, in accordance with His divinity and glory; but for those under the law he instituted a sacerdotal and liturgical service.
sources.raw_question: Did the divine Word of God himself speak with the patriarchs before Moses, before his incarnation?

question: How does the Holy Spirit proceed within the Godhead according to Jonathan Edwards?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit proceeds as the mutual love and delight between the Father and the Son. Once the Son subsists as God's perfect idea of Himself, a most pure act and infinitely holy energy arises between Father and Son in mutually loving each other. In this act the divine essence flows out and is breathed forth in love and joy, so the Godhead stands forth in a third manner of subsistence, the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: there proceeds a most pure act, and an infinitely holy and sacred energy arises between the Father and Son in mutually loving and delighting in each other, for their love and joy is mutual
sources.raw_question: How does the Holy Spirit proceed within the Godhead according to Jonathan Edwards?

question: Why should the Holy Spirit be identified with the divine act of will rather than with some other divine act?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Because there is no other act in God but the act of the will. The Son is God's idea or understanding of Himself, and the Spirit is the Deity in act, the essential and most perfect act of the divine nature, in which the Godhead acts to an infinite degree. That act is love and joy, which belong to the will.
sources.quote: there proceeds the third Person in the Trinity, the Holy Spirit, viz., the Deity in act, for there is no other act but the act of the will.
sources.raw_question: Why should the Holy Spirit be identified with the divine act of will rather than with some other divine act?

question: When Scripture calls the man Jesus 'anointed', 'sent' or 'appointed' (as in Acts 10:38, Acts 2:22, Acts 17:31), does this separate the man from God the Word or deny the Son's Godhead?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: No. Anointing, mission and appointment are synonymous names that the sacred writers give to the union of God the Word with the man from Mary. So Peter rightly proclaims the Godhead of the Only-begotten without separating the subsistence of the Word from the man. Peter had heard 'I and the Father are one' and could not have meant to divide them.
sources.quote: there is no discordance in the words of the sacred writers, but that they but give various names to the union of God the Word with the Man from Mary, sometimes as anointing, sometimes as mission, sometimes as appointment
sources.raw_question: When Scripture calls the man Jesus 'anointed', 'sent' or 'appointed' (as in Acts 10:38, Acts 2:22, Acts 17:31), does this separate the man from God the Word or deny the Son's Godhead?

question: How does Christ's sinless innocence relate to his shedding of blood and his bearing of imputed sin in the work of salvation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Christ was white in innocence and holiness, and he became ruddy in the blood of his offering. He was ruddy in two ways: naturally, by actually pouring out his blood, and morally, by the imputation of sin, whose colour is crimson. By his whiteness he fulfilled the law, and by his redness he satisfied justice.
sources.quote: He who was white, became ruddy for our sakes, pouring out his blood an oblation for sin. This also renders him graceful: by his whiteness he fulfilled the law; by his redness he satisfied justice.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's sinless innocence relate to his shedding of blood and his bearing of imputed sin in the work of salvation?

question: Is the Church's use of metaphysical terms such as 'homoousios', 'three hypostases' and 'generation without division' a philosophical corruption of the simple Christian faith?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 20: Whether the Doctor need have cited 300 teats, *wide of the purpose, to prove what nobody denies, namely, a subordination, in some sense, of the Son to the Fathe
sources.answer: No. Philosophy and metaphysics were called in only after heretics had started subtle difficulties. Catholics then had to meet them with their own weapons and guard the faith. For example, the Church said generation was without division only after heretics accused Catholics of asserting a division. It is the Arians whose strength lay chiefly in logical and metaphysical subtleties.
sources.quote: Philosophy and metaphysics were called in to its assistance; but not till heretics had shewn the way, and made it in a manner necessary for the Catholics to encounter them with their own weapons.
sources.raw_question: Is the Church's use of metaphysical terms such as 'homoousios', 'three hypostases' and 'generation without division' a philosophical corruption of the simple Christian faith?

question: Why does being belong most truly to God alone, as the one who is unchangeable?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > God the Only Unchangeable Essence.
sources.answer: Whatever changes does not keep its own being. Whatever can change, even if it never actually does, is able not to be what it was. So only what neither changes nor can change at all falls most truly under the category of being, and that is God.
sources.quote: that which not only is not changed, but also cannot at all be changed, alone falls most truly, without difficulty or hesitation, under the category of being.
sources.raw_question: Why does being belong most truly to God alone, as the one who is unchangeable?

question: Who is the one God from whom all things come, according to the Scriptures?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: The Father. Hippolytus says the right starting point is the truth that the Father is one God, "of whom is every family" and "by whom are all things, of whom are all things."
sources.quote: For it is right, in the first place, to expound the truth that the Father is one God, “of whom is every family,”
sources.raw_question: Who is the one God from whom all things come, according to the Scriptures?

question: Does assigning distinct causal roles in creation to Father, Son and Spirit imply three original principles or hypostases of all things?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: No. The first principle of existing things is one, namely the Father, who creates through the Son and perfects through the Spirit. The distinct roles express an order of operation from one source, not three independent origins.
sources.quote: let no one imagine me either to affirm that there are three original hypostases or to allege the operation of the Son to be imperfect. For the first principle of existing things is One, creating through the Son and perfecting through the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does assigning distinct causal roles in creation to Father, Son and Spirit imply three original principles or hypostases of all things?

question: Is there anything of which the Holy Spirit is ignorant, given that he is said to know the things of God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XI. We shall follow the example of Abdemelech, if we believe that the Son and Holy Spirit know all things. This knowledge is attributed in Scripture to the Spirit, and also to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, as also the Spirit by the Son. Also, inasmuch as we read that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit say and reveal the same things, we must acknowledge in Them a oneness of nature and knowledge. Lastly, that the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God is not a mark of ignorance, since the Father and the Son are likewise said to search, and Paul, although chosen by Christ, yet was taught by the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. He who knows the deep things of God, His counsels and hidden mysteries, knows all that is of God; and as a man's spirit knows the things of a man, so the Spirit of God knows the things of God. This also proves He is of one substance with the Father and not inferior in the fulness of the Godhead.
sources.quote: What is there that He knows not Who knows all things that are of God? For “the Spirit searcheth even the deep things of God.”
sources.raw_question: Is there anything of which the Holy Spirit is ignorant, given that he is said to know the things of God?

question: Does the parable of the two sons sent into the vineyard imply two different fathers, or one and the same Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: One and the same Father. Both sons are sent by one father into the same vineyard. One refuses and later repents, while the other promises to go and does not. The parable thus points to one Father over both peoples.
sources.quote: [this parable, I say], points out one and the same Father.
sources.raw_question: Does the parable of the two sons sent into the vineyard imply two different fathers, or one and the same Father?

question: Could the Son, who upholds all things by His word, be a being who waits to obtain His power by allotment?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He then shows the unity of the Son with the Father and Eunomius' lack of understanding and knowledge in the Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. The Son upholds all things by the word of His power, and His power never lags behind His will. Nothing comes into being or remains in being without Him. It is therefore absurd to think He must receive power by some process of allotment.
sources.quote: He Whose power lags not behind His will and Whose will is the measure of His power
sources.raw_question: Could the Son, who upholds all things by His word, be a being who waits to obtain His power by allotment?

question: Does the Holy Spirit guard orthodox faith, so that no one established in him denies that Christ is the Son of God or rejects God the Creator?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Next Teaches Us that the Authority of the Faith Enjoins, After the Father and the Son, to Believe Also on the Holy Spirit, Whose Operations He Enumerates from Scripture.
sources.answer: Yes. No one established in the Spirit calls Jesus anathema, denies Christ to be the Son of God, rejects the Creator, or teaches anything contrary to Scripture. The Spirit orders the rule of truth, overcomes heretics, and keeps the Church uncorrupt. Blasphemy against him is not forgiven in this world or the next.
sources.quote: no one has ever denied Christ to be the Son of God, or has rejected God the Creator; no one utters any words of his own contrary to the Scriptures
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit guard orthodox faith, so that no one established in him denies that Christ is the Son of God or rejects God the Creator?

question: Was the Word of God made for the sake of creatures, as an instrument by which God could frame them?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: No. The Word was not made for us; rather we were made for Him, and in Him all things were created. Even if God had chosen never to make creatures, the Word would still have been with God and the Father in Him, so His existence does not depend on creation.
sources.quote: For though it had seemed good to God not to make things originate, still had the Word been no less with God, and the Father in Him.
sources.raw_question: Was the Word of God made for the sake of creatures, as an instrument by which God could frame them?

question: How does God's commanding of creatures such as angels, Moses, or Abraham differ from His working through the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: When God commands creatures, they hear and respond with questions, as Moses and Zacharias did, and they have the Word as Mediator making known the Father's will. But when the Word Himself creates there is no question and answer, since it suffices for the Father to will and the work is done in the Word, who is the Father's Will and Wisdom.
sources.quote: But when that Word Himself works and creates, then there is no questioning and answer, for the Father is in Him and the Word in the Father; but it suffices to will, and the work is done
sources.raw_question: How does God's commanding of creatures such as angels, Moses, or Abraham differ from His working through the Word?

question: Was the human race delivered into the power of the devil justly, and on account of Adam's sin?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > All, on Account of the Sin of Adam, Were Delivered into the Power of the Devil.
sources.answer: Yes. By the justice of God in some sense the human race was delivered into the devil's power, because the sin of the first man passed originally to all his descendants through birth, and the debt of the first parents bound their whole posterity. This is foreshadowed in Genesis, where the serpent is told "Dust shalt thou eat" and man is told "Dust thou art."
sources.quote: By the justice of God in some sense, the human race was delivered into the power of the devil; the sin of the first man passing over originally into all of both sexes in their birth through conjugal union
sources.raw_question: Was the human race delivered into the power of the devil justly, and on account of Adam's sin?

question: Does Paul's phrase "by nature the children of wrath" (Ephesians 2:3) mean that human nature as God created it is evil?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > All, on Account of the Sin of Adam, Were Delivered into the Power of the Devil.
sources.answer: No. "By nature" means nature as it has been depraved by sin, not nature as it was created upright from the beginning. It is equivalent to saying that all men are "originally" under the prince of the power of the air. Every person is among the "children of unfaithfulness" before becoming a believer.
sources.quote: viz. by nature as it has been depraved by sin, not as it was created upright from the beginning
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's phrase "by nature the children of wrath" (Ephesians 2:3) mean that human nature as God created it is evil?

question: Did God actively hand man over to the devil or command it, or did He only permit it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > All, on Account of the Sin of Adam, Were Delivered into the Power of the Devil.
sources.answer: God only permitted it, though justly. When God abandoned the sinner, the author of sin immediately entered. Even so, God did not wholly abandon His creature. He continued to create, quicken and bestow good things on him, and He never removed man from the law of His own power.
sources.quote: ought not to be so understood as if God did this, or commanded it to be done; but that He only permitted it, yet that justly. For when He abandoned the sinner, the author of the sin immediately entered.
sources.raw_question: Did God actively hand man over to the devil or command it, or did He only permit it?

question: How is man rescued from the devil's power, given that sin subjected him to it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > All, on Account of the Sin of Adam, Were Delivered into the Power of the Devil.
sources.answer: Man is rescued through the remission of sins by God's merciful reconciliation. Since the commission of sins under God's just anger subjected man to the devil, it follows that the remission of sins frees him. The following chapter adds that the devil was to be overcome by God's righteousness, not by God's power.
sources.quote: If, therefore, the commission of sins through the just anger of God subjected man to the devil, doubtless the remission of sins through the merciful reconciliation of God rescues man from the devil.
sources.raw_question: How is man rescued from the devil's power, given that sin subjected him to it?

question: Does Christ's saying 'I am from above; I am not of this world' (John 8:23) prove that he is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: Yes. Every mere man is of this world and was not made in heaven, so if Christ were only man he would speak falsely in saying he is not of this world. Since he does not speak falsely, he is from above, from heaven, and therefore God.
sources.quote: He is God, therefore, who is from above, and therefore He is not of this world
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying 'I am from above; I am not of this world' (John 8:23) prove that he is God?

question: Does the statement 'corruptible bodies are of one essence' logically imply its converse, that whatever is of one essence is corruptible?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > After much discourse concerning the actually existent, and ungenerate and good, and upon the consubstantiality of the heavenly powers, showing the uncharted character of their essence, yet the difference of their ranks, he ends the book.
sources.answer: No. It is true that corruptible bodies are consubstantial with one another, but the converse does not follow. Souls share one essence and yet corruption does not attach to them because of that community of essence.
sources.quote: it is true to say, “corruptible bodies are of one essence,” but the converse statement is not true at all, if it be anything like, “this consubstantial nature is also surely corruptible,”
sources.raw_question: Does the statement 'corruptible bodies are of one essence' logically imply its converse, that whatever is of one essence is corruptible?

question: Do Paul's names for the heavenly powers (principalities, thrones, powers, mights, dominions) signify different natures or essences among the angels, as Eunomius claims?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > After much discourse concerning the actually existent, and ungenerate and good, and upon the consubstantiality of the heavenly powers, showing the uncharted character of their essence, yet the difference of their ranks, he ends the book.
sources.answer: No. The names signify operations and ranks, not diversities of essence. To rule, to exercise power and dominion, or to be someone's throne are all operations. So Paul recognizes distinctions of rank among the intelligible powers but not varieties of essence, and the argument about souls applies to every intellectual creature.
sources.quote: the sense of the names clearly shows that the Apostle recognizes in the intelligible powers distinctions of certain ranks, but does not by these names indicate varieties of essences
sources.raw_question: Do Paul's names for the heavenly powers (principalities, thrones, powers, mights, dominions) signify different natures or essences among the angels, as Eunomius claims?

question: If one wrongly attributes to one Person of the Trinity what properly belongs to another, is that as serious as saying something unworthy of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > In What Way We Must Inquire Concerning the Trinity.
sources.answer: No. Assigning to the Father something that properly belongs to the Son, the Spirit, or the whole Trinity is an error of attribution. It still says nothing unworthy of God, since the attribute belongs to God. What must be avoided is profane error: saying of the Trinity what suits the creature rather than the Creator, or what is mere empty invention.
sources.quote: we ought not to deviate into profane error, so as to say anything of the Trinity which does not suit the Creator, but rather the creature, or which is feigned outright by mere empty thought.
sources.raw_question: If one wrongly attributes to one Person of the Trinity what properly belongs to another, is that as serious as saying something unworthy of God?

question: Can there be a void or region of shadow within God (the Father), in which the created world was formed by lesser beings such as angels or the Demiurge?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter IV.—The absurdity of the supposed vacuum and defect of the heretics is demonstrated.
sources.answer: No. If the Father's light fills and illuminates everything contained within Him, there can be no unilluminated, unoccupied, dark place within Him where creation could have been made. To posit such a void would reproach the Father's light as unable to fill and illuminate what is within Himself.
sources.quote: how can any vacuum or shadow possibly exist within that territory which is contained by the Pleroma, and by the light of the Father?
sources.raw_question: Can there be a void or region of shadow within God (the Father), in which the created world was formed by lesser beings such as angels or the Demiurge?

question: What does the worship of God consist in?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > What is the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge. The Worship of God is the Love of Him. How the Intellectual Cognizance of Eternal Things Comes to Pass Through Wisdom.
sources.answer: The worship of God is the love of Him. By this love we now desire to see Him and believe and hope that we shall see Him. As we progress we see now through a glass in an enigma, but then face to face, when we shall be like Him because we shall see Him as He is.
sources.quote: And what is the worship of Him except the love of Him, by which we now desire to see Him, and we believe and hope that we shall see Him
sources.raw_question: What does the worship of God consist in?

question: What is meant by the 'life which was the light of men' in John 1:4?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > We are Made Perfect by Acknowledgement of Our Own Weakness. The Incarnate Word Dispels Our Darkness.
sources.answer: It is the light of rational minds, by which men differ from beasts and are therefore men. It is not corporeal light, which even beasts and worms see. It is the unchangeable Word, in whom we live, move and have our being, and so it is not far from any of us.
sources.quote: “the life [which] was the light of men;” the light certainly of rational minds, by which men differ from beasts, and therefore are men. Therefore not corporeal light, which is the light of the flesh
sources.raw_question: What is meant by the 'life which was the light of men' in John 1:4?

question: Did Christ die and rise again in a real sense or only nominally, given that he is the Only-begotten God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Really. Paul's phrase "according to the Scriptures" warns us to confess that Christ died and rose after a real manner, not a nominal, since the full weight of Scripture certifies it. We must understand his death in exactly the sense Scripture declares it.
sources.quote: a warning to us to confess that Christ died and rose after a real manner, not a nominal, since the fact is certified by the full weight of Scripture authority
sources.raw_question: Did Christ die and rise again in a real sense or only nominally, given that he is the Only-begotten God?

question: Should believers inquire by what power or by what division of parts within Christ he wept, suffered, died, descended and ascended?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The Apostle leaves no room for such questions as "Who wept? Who rejoiced? Who descended?" but rests faith on reverent confession. Faith trusts God's omnipotence, which human limitations cannot bound, as Abraham believed God's promise beyond human possibility.
sources.quote: He rests the merits of faith entirely on the confession of unquestioning reverence.
sources.raw_question: Should believers inquire by what power or by what division of parts within Christ he wept, suffered, died, descended and ascended?

question: Was Christ brought down from heaven to earth by some external force or agent, implying dependence on another?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Christ needed no one to ascend and bring him down; no external force drove him to earth. True religion confesses Christ not brought down but descending, and the time and manner of his coming belong to him alone, so his coming in time does not imply dependence on another.
sources.quote: it is true religion to confess Jesus Christ not brought down, but descending. The mystery both of the time and the method of His coming, belongs to Him alone.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ brought down from heaven to earth by some external force or agent, implying dependence on another?

question: Was it the Word (the Son) who gave Israel the Old Testament command to make offerings?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVIII.—Concerning sacrifices and oblations, and those who truly offer them.
sources.answer: Yes. The Word gave the people the command about oblations, even though He needed none of them, so that they might learn to serve God. Offerings are made to God through the Word. This is why the Jews, who have not received the Word, do not offer a pure sacrifice.
sources.quote: so did the Word give to the people that very precept as to the making of oblations, although He stood in no need of them, that they might learn to serve God
sources.raw_question: Was it the Word (the Son) who gave Israel the Old Testament command to make offerings?

question: Is sharing in the Holy Spirit necessary for inheriting the kingdom of heaven?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: Yes. Basil cites Irenaeus, who reads Paul's saying that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom this way: those without a share in the divine Spirit fall short of it. Those Paul calls carnal are the ones with no desire for the Spirit. Irenaeus thus calls the Spirit divine.
sources.quote: The Apostle exclaimed that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of the heavens lest we, being without share in the divine Spirit, fall short of the kingdom of the heavens.
sources.raw_question: Is sharing in the Holy Spirit necessary for inheriting the kingdom of heaven?

question: Are position, condition, place and time properly predicated of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whatever is Spoken of God According to Substance, is Spoken of Each Person Severally, and Together of the Trinity Itself. One Essence in God, and Three, in Greek, Hypostases, in Latin, Persons.
sources.answer: No. They are said of God only metaphorically and through similitudes. Examples are his dwelling between the cherubim (position), being covered with the deep as with a garment (condition), years without end (time), and being in heaven (place).
sources.quote: But position, and condition, and places, and times, are not said to be in God properly, but metaphorically and through similitudes.
sources.raw_question: Are position, condition, place and time properly predicated of God?

question: Are understanding, counsel and wisdom in God accidental habits that come and go, distinct from the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: No. Understanding and counsel are the same, and that same thing is the Lord himself, as his words in Proverbs show. To make them a passing habit in God, after the manner of men, revives Valentinus's 'Thought' and 'Will' in order to separate the Son from the Father. Scripture names the Son as God's Wisdom, Understanding, Word and Living Counsel.
sources.quote: For as strength and security are the same (for they mean one attribute), so we may say that Understanding and Counsel are the same, which is the Lord.
sources.raw_question: Are understanding, counsel and wisdom in God accidental habits that come and go, distinct from the Son?

question: What does the Father's declaration 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased' show about how the Son is from the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Objections continued, as in Chapters vii.--x. Whether the Son is begotten of the Father's will? This virtually the same as whether once He was not? and used by the Arians to introduce the latter question. The Regula Fidei answers it at once in the negative by contrary texts. The Arians follow the Valentinians in maintaining a precedent will; which really is only exercised by God towards creatures. Instances from Scripture. Inconsistency of Asterius. If the Son by will, there must be another Word before Him. If God is good, or exist, by His will, then is the Son by His will. If He willed to have reason or wisdom, then is His Word and Wisdom at His will. The Son is the Living Will, and has all titles which denote connaturality. That will which the Father has to the Son, the Son has to the Father. The Father wills the Son and the Son wills the Father.
sources.answer: It shows that the Son is Son by nature, not by will. The Father did not say 'the Son originated at My will' but simply 'My Son.' 'In whom I am well pleased' means that the Father's will about what pleases him is lodged in the Son.
sources.quote: the Father Himself said not, ‘This is the Son originated at My will,’ nor ‘the Son whom I have by My favour,’ but simply ‘My Son,’
sources.raw_question: What does the Father's declaration 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased' show about how the Son is from the Father?

question: Did the Son have a right to worship before his mediatorial kingdom began, even on Arian principles?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: Yes. Being in the form of God, being God, and being Creator, Preserver and Sustainer of all things from the beginning, he had a right to worship long before his mediatorial kingdom. So his title to worship was not founded on powers given to him later. The texts alleged for that view therefore cannot bear the weight placed on them.
sources.quote: had a right to worship, even upon your principles, (much more mine,) long before the commencing of his mediatorial hkingdom: and therefore his right and title to worship was not founded upon the powers then supposed to have been given him
sources.raw_question: Did the Son have a right to worship before his mediatorial kingdom began, even on Arian principles?

question: Was the angel of God who spoke to Jacob in a dream (Genesis 31) and said "I am God, who appeared to thee in the place of God" truly God, or merely a created angel?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God Also Appeared to Jacob as an Angel; Namely, the Son of God.
sources.answer: He was truly God as well as Angel. He declares himself to be God and refers to the vow Jacob made to Him at Bethel, and Scripture calls it the place of God, not of an angel. Since no mere angel could claim divinity and receive a vow as God, this angel must be divine.
sources.quote: If the Angel of God speaks thus to Jacob, and the Angel himself mentions and says, “I am God, who appeared unto thee in the house of God,” we see without any hesitation that this is declared to be not only an angel, but God also
sources.raw_question: Was the angel of God who spoke to Jacob in a dream (Genesis 31) and said "I am God, who appeared to thee in the place of God" truly God, or merely a created angel?

question: Did Christ receive his human soul from the Virgin Mary, as from Adam's sinful stock?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Though flesh is born of flesh, every soul is the direct work of God. Since the Virgin received from God alone the flesh she conceived, all the more the soul of that body came from God alone. Christ assumed his soul from himself, just as he assumed his body by his own act.
sources.quote: As if in receiving so much from the Virgin, He received from her His soul also; whereas though flesh is always born of flesh, every soul is the direct work of God.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ receive his human soul from the Virgin Mary, as from Adam's sinful stock?

question: Did the Word of God merely dwell in the man Jesus as the spirit of prophecy dwelt in the prophets?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The Word was made flesh: God the Word emptied himself of the form of God and became man by birth from the Virgin. He is one subject, true Son of God and true Son of Man. It is ridiculous to preach, besides the Word made flesh, another man inspired by the Word like a prophet.
sources.quote: that being true Son of God, He is indeed true Son of Man, neither the less Man because born of God, nor the less God because Man born of God.
sources.raw_question: Did the Word of God merely dwell in the man Jesus as the spirit of prophecy dwelt in the prophets?

question: Is the God whom the apostles and the early Jerusalem Church invoked as Father of Jesus Christ the same God who made heaven and earth and spoke through the prophets?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. The first Church prayed to the Lord who made heaven, earth and sea, who spoke through the Holy Spirit by David, and named Jesus as His holy Son whom He anointed. These voices of the mother Church show the apostles knew no other God than the Creator announced by the prophets, together with His Son Jesus Christ.
sources.quote: called upon the God who made heaven, and earth, and the sea,—who was announced by the prophets,— and Jesus Christ His Son, whom God anointed, and who knew no other [God]
sources.raw_question: Is the God whom the apostles and the early Jerusalem Church invoked as Father of Jesus Christ the same God who made heaven and earth and spoke through the prophets?

question: Does Scripture teach that the one sent to accomplish salvation is himself Jehovah, the eternal I AM?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture reveals a mission in which the Lord God and his Spirit send forth, and the Eternal I AM is the one sent. All the attributes, honours and rights of Jehovah are ascribed to this Sent One, Jesus, who claims equality with God as his only-begotten Son and is associated with God in every supreme office of Deity.
sources.quote: we find a wondrous mission revealed, in which the Lord God and his Spirit send forth, and the Eternal I AM is the sent One.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture teach that the one sent to accomplish salvation is himself Jehovah, the eternal I AM?

question: Why did Christ say the cup could not pass from him unless he drank it?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Because the disciples' fear and stumbling at the cup would end only when his Passion was completed. After his death the glory of his power would remove the stumbling-block of their weakness. So his sadness was ended by his death rather than caused by it.
sources.quote: after His death, the stumbling-block of the disciples’ weakness would be removed by the glory of His power.
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ say the cup could not pass from him unless he drank it?

question: If the Son shared the same definition of essence as the parts of the world, what would follow about his eternity and his right to be worshipped?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He convicts Eunomius of having used of the Only-begotten terms applicable to the existence of the earth, and thus shows that his intention is to prove the Son to be a being mutable and created.
sources.answer: Absurd consequences would follow. Where the definition of essence is the same, the nature is the same, as with Peter and John. So the Son would pass away with heaven and earth, or else the world would share in divinity. Hence either the elements are divine, as the Greeks foolishly hold, or the Son must not be worshipped.
sources.quote: For either the elements of the world must be Divine, according to the foolish belief of the Greeks, or the Son must not be worshipped.
sources.raw_question: If the Son shared the same definition of essence as the parts of the world, what would follow about his eternity and his right to be worshipped?

question: Is faith in Christ within a person's own power, or is it determined independently of human will?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVII.—Men are possessed of free will, and endowed with the faculty of making a choice. It is not true, therefore, that some are by nature good, and others bad.
sources.answer: Faith is within a person's own power. God has kept man's will free in faith as well as in works. The Lord's sayings show this: "According to thy faith be it unto thee" and "All things are possible to him that believeth." For this reason the believer has eternal life and the unbeliever remains under wrath. Christ's lament over Jerusalem, "ye would not," shows both His goodness and man's free choice.
sources.quote: Now all such expressions demonstrate that man is in his own power with respect to faith.
sources.raw_question: Is faith in Christ within a person's own power, or is it determined independently of human will?

question: Should God have created angels and men incapable of sinning, good by necessity rather than by choice?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVII.—Men are possessed of free will, and endowed with the faculty of making a choice. It is not true, therefore, that some are by nature good, and others bad.
sources.answer: No. Goodness implanted by nature without the creature's own effort would be of no consequence to it. Such creatures would neither grasp that the good is comely nor take pleasure in it. Communion with God would not be precious to them, and they would deserve no credit or crown. Those who say some beings are by nature "material" also make the Lord either powerless to do what He willed or ignorant of what He made.
sources.quote: Thus it would come to pass, that their being good would be of no consequence, because they were so by nature rather than by will, and are possessors of good spontaneously, not by choice
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who call some men by nature "material"
sources.raw_question: Should God have created angels and men incapable of sinning, good by necessity rather than by choice?

question: If the whole Trinity works inseparably, why was only the Son, and not the Father or the Holy Spirit, made flesh?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Likeness of the Divine Word, Such as It Is, is to Be Sought, Not in Our Own Outer and Sensible Word, But in the Inner and Mental One. There is the Greatest Possible Unlikeness Between Our Word and Knowledge and the Divine Word and Knowledge.
sources.answer: Only the Son, who is the Word of God, was made flesh, although the whole Trinity was the maker of that flesh. The Word became incarnate so that we might live rightly by following and imitating His example through our own word. That means having no lie either in the thought or in the work of our word.
sources.quote: not God the Father, not the Holy Spirit, not the Trinity itself, but the Son only, which is the Word of God, was made flesh; although the Trinity was the maker
sources.raw_question: If the whole Trinity works inseparably, why was only the Son, and not the Father or the Holy Spirit, made flesh?

question: Why did the true Wisdom place His impress in creation, and what does it reveal?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: It was placed there so that people might recognise the Creator, the true Wisdom of God, through the works. Recognising Him, they also know they are made after God's image, and through the Son they come to know the Father. The heavens thus declare God's glory through the wisdom created in them. This was an act of condescension by Wisdom for the framing of all things.
sources.quote: This if men have within them, they will acknowledge the true Wisdom of God; and will know that they are made really after God’s Image.
sources.raw_question: Why did the true Wisdom place His impress in creation, and what does it reveal?

question: Do the Father and the Son work in different manners, so that a difference between their operations could be inferred?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that the same energies produce the same works, and that variation in the works indicates variation in the energies.
sources.answer: No. The Father's manner of working is always the Son's, as the Lord's own words and reason show. Neither is embodied, neither works from different material, in different times or places, or with different organs. In both the bare movement of wish and will suffices, backed by creative power. Thus the Father from whom are all things and the Son by whom are all things work alike in the very form of their operation.
sources.quote: the one is not unbodied while the other is embodied, the one is not from this material, the other from that, the one does not work his will in this time and place, the other in that time and place
sources.raw_question: Do the Father and the Son work in different manners, so that a difference between their operations could be inferred?

question: Is it illegitimate to use material examples, such as Peter and Paul sharing one nature as two persons, to illustrate the unity of nature and distinction of Persons in God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > Thereafter he discusses the divergence of names and of things, speaking, of that which is ungenerate as without a cause, and of that which is non-existent, as the Scindapsus, Minotaur, Blityri, Cyclops, Scylla, which never were generated at all, and shows that things which are essentially different, are mutually destructive, as fire of water, and the rest in their several relations. But in the case of the Father and the Son, as the essence is common, and the properties reciprocally interchangeable, no injury results to the Nature.
sources.answer: No. Eunomius condemns such examples as rash, yet he himself argues for a diversity of essence from material elements like fire, water, earth and air. If material illustrations may serve to argue for difference of essence, they may equally serve, within our limited compass, to show the kindred character of the divine Nature.
sources.quote: Or are we to make concessions to you when you are establishing the diversity of essence by material aid, and to be ourselves rejected when we point out the kindred character of the Nature by means of examples within our compass?
sources.raw_question: Is it illegitimate to use material examples, such as Peter and Paul sharing one nature as two persons, to illustrate the unity of nature and distinction of Persons in God?

question: Who is meant as the 'father' of the human race in Deuteronomy 32:6, 'Is not He thy father who hath obtained thee, and formed thee, and created thee?'

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXI.—We should not hastily impute as crimes to the men of old time those actions which the Scripture has not condemned, but should rather seek in them types of things to come: an example of this in the incest committed by Lot.
sources.answer: The Word of God. Moses points to the Word as the one who begot, formed and created humanity. So the Word is the father of the human race, and the only one who can give the churches the power to bear children.
sources.quote: Now the father of the human race is the Word of God, as Moses points out when he says, “Is not He thy father who hath obtained thee [by generation], and formed thee, and created thee?”
sources.raw_question: Who is meant as the 'father' of the human race in Deuteronomy 32:6, 'Is not He thy father who hath obtained thee, and formed thee, and created thee?'

question: Can Scripture speak of declaration or speech without any literal voice, as when the heavens declare God's glory?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. The heavens proclaim the wisdom and power of their Creator through their beauty, order and motion, not by articulate speech. This instils knowledge of divine power more effectively than spoken words, and Scripture is not in error in describing it as speech.
sources.quote: This is not given in articulate speech, but by the things which are seen, and it instils into our minds the knowledge of Divine power more than if speech proclaimed it with a voice.
sources.raw_question: Can Scripture speak of declaration or speech without any literal voice, as when the heavens declare God's glory?

question: Does Paul's saying "Knowledge puffeth up, but love edifieth" condemn true knowledge of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVI.—“Knowledge puffeth up, but love edifieth.”
sources.answer: No. Paul did not mean to attack true knowledge of God, for then he would have accused himself. He aimed at those who, puffed up by a pretence of knowledge, fall away from the love of God. They think themselves perfect while setting forth an imperfect Creator.
sources.quote: not that he meant to inveigh against a true knowledge of God, for in that case he would have accused himself
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's saying "Knowledge puffeth up, but love edifieth" condemn true knowledge of God?

question: Wherever the Holy Spirit is present, is Christ also present, and wherever Christ is present, is the Holy Spirit also present?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter IX.
