That the Holy Spirit is provoked is proved by the words of St. Peter, in which it is shown that the Spirit of God is one and the same as the Spirit of the Lord, both by other passages and by reference to the sentence of the same Apostle on Ananias and Sapphira, whence it is argued that the union of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, as well as His own Godhead, is proved.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul passes from the Spirit dwelling in us directly to "if Christ be in you." He also speaks interchangeably of Christ speaking in him and of having the Spirit of God. The unity of the Persons is therefore inseparable: where any one Person is named, the whole fulness of the Trinity is present.
sources.quote: The Unity, then, is inseparable, for by the testimony of Scripture where either the Father or the Son or the Holy Spirit is designated, there is all the fulness of the Trinity.
sources.raw_question: Wherever the Holy Spirit is present, is Christ also present, and wherever Christ is present, is the Holy Spirit also present?

question: After Christ's redemption, does the devil still have power over the faithful, and can any of the elect perish with him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Remains of Death and the Evil Things of the World Turn to Good for the Elect. How Fitly the Death of Christ Was Chosen, that We Might Be Justified in His Blood. What the Anger of God is.
sources.answer: The devil is cast out of his dominion and out of the hearts of the faithful. He is allowed to act as an adversary only as far as this mortal condition permits and as God knows to be good for them. God does not let them be tempted beyond what they can bear. None of the predestinated will perish with the devil or remain under his power until death.
sources.quote: is only so far permitted to be an adversary according to the condition of this mortality, as God knows to be expedient for them
sources.raw_question: After Christ's redemption, does the devil still have power over the faithful, and can any of the elect perish with him?

question: Does the disagreement among Valentinus, Secundus and other Gnostic teachers about the origin of the Aeons, Christ and the Holy Spirit count against their doctrine?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XI.—The opinions of Valentinus, with those of his disciples and others.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus sets out their inconsistent accounts to show that, while using the same things and names, they put forward opinions that conflict with one another. Valentinus himself derives Jesus sometimes from Theletus, sometimes from Christ, and sometimes from Anthropos and Ecclesia. Such discord marks their systems as human inventions, in contrast with the one faith the Church holds everywhere.
sources.quote: how they do not agree in treating the same points, but alike, in things and names, set forth opinions mutually discordant
sources.raw_question: Does the disagreement among Valentinus, Secundus and other Gnostic teachers about the origin of the Aeons, Christ and the Holy Spirit count against their doctrine?

question: Must Christ be truly God, and not a mere man, for human beings to be saved, as against the Ebionites?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: Yes. Man cannot be saved unless it was God himself who wrought salvation on earth, and man cannot pass into God unless God first passed into man. A merely human Christ would leave humanity in its mortal generation without the new generation and adoption that only God can give.
sources.quote: how can they be saved unless it was God who wrought out their salvation upon earth? Or how shall man pass into God, unless God has [first] passed into man?
sources.raw_question: Must Christ be truly God, and not a mere man, for human beings to be saved, as against the Ebionites?

question: Could a mere man have conquered the devil, who had overcome mankind?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: No. The one who conquered him must be greater than vanquished man. The devil had overcome man and held him captive, so only someone superior to man could defeat him and set mankind free. The only one more eminent than man, who was made after God's likeness, is the Son of God, after whose image man was created.
sources.quote: But who else is superior to, and more eminent than, that man who was formed after the likeness of God, except the Son of God, after whose image man was created?
sources.raw_question: Could a mere man have conquered the devil, who had overcome mankind?

question: Could Christ have saved anyone if he had been human only in appearance, as the docetists claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: No. If Christ was only an imaginary being and not a reality, those who believe in him could receive nothing steadfast from him and could not truly share in salvation. A real salvation requires a real incarnation.
sources.quote: how can these men really be partaken of salvation, if He in whom they profess to believe, manifested Himself as a merely imaginary being?
sources.raised_by_detail: Docetists, who describe Christ as having become man only in opinion
sources.raw_question: Could Christ have saved anyone if he had been human only in appearance, as the docetists claim?

question: If all things exist in God, can a person still fail to be with God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Trinity in the Mind is the Image of God, in that It Remembers, Understands, and Loves God, Which to Do is Wisdom.
sources.answer: Yes. Everyone is in God, without whom no one can exist, but not all are with him in the sense of 'I am continually with Thee.' A person who does not remember, understand, and love God is not with him, and this is man's peculiar wretchedness.
sources.quote: For, beyond a doubt, he is not without Him in whom he is; and yet if he does not remember, and understand, and love Him, he is not with Him.
sources.raw_question: If all things exist in God, can a person still fail to be with God?

question: Is the uncreated nature that made all other natures, God, more excellent than the rational human mind made in his image?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Trinity in the Mind is the Image of God, in that It Remembers, Understands, and Loves God, Which to Do is Wisdom.
sources.answer: Yes. There is a nature not made which made all other natures, great and small. It is without doubt more excellent than the things it made, including the rational and intellectual mind of man made after its image. That nature is God.
sources.quote: There is, then, a nature not made, which made all other natures, great and small, and is without doubt more excellent than those which it has made
sources.raw_question: Is the uncreated nature that made all other natures, God, more excellent than the rational human mind made in his image?

question: Is the desire to seek and know the Father a fault that makes a spiritual being liable to passion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVIII.—Sophia was never really in ignorance or passion; her Enthymesis could not have been separated from herself, or exhibited special tendencies of its own.
sources.answer: No. The Valentinian view contradicts the Lord's command, "Seek, and ye shall find." The Lord makes his disciples perfect by their seeking and finding the Father. The heretics' Christ, by contrast, forbids the Æons to seek him. Seeking the perfect Father leads to perfection, impassibility and truth, not to ignorance or passion.
sources.quote: For the Lord renders His disciples perfect by their seeking after and finding the Father; but that Christ of theirs, who is above, has rendered them perfect, by the fact that He has commanded the Æons not to seek after the Father
sources.raw_question: Is the desire to seek and know the Father a fault that makes a spiritual being liable to passion?

question: Was Christ, after his humiliation and death, exalted and invested with universal authority?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. He who was dead now lives for ever and holds the keys of hell and death; God has made him Lord and King, crowned him with honour after he was made lower than the angels, and given him all power in heaven and earth and over all flesh. He uses this power to give eternal life to his elect and to subdue his enemies.
sources.quote: And what power over them hath our Beloved? “All power in heaven and earth,” Matt. xxviii. 18. As for men, he hath power given him “over all flesh,” John xvii. 2.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ, after his humiliation and death, exalted and invested with universal authority?

question: If God cannot forgive without satisfaction, is a finite creature who forgives freely more merciful than the infinite Creator?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Because God is essentially holy and righteous, has pledged his faithfulness in the law's sanction, and is necessarily the world's governor, forgiving without satisfaction would be imperfection in him, like lying or denying himself. Private persons forgiving private offences have no authority to exact punishment, so the comparison fails; and through satisfaction God forgives in a way of righteousness and goodness surpassing all creaturely conception.
sources.quote: the forgiving of sin without satisfaction would be no perfection in him, but an effect of impotency and imperfection, — a thing which God cannot do, as he cannot lie, nor deny himself.
sources.raw_question: If God cannot forgive without satisfaction, is a finite creature who forgives freely more merciful than the infinite Creator?

question: Who bears the burden of proof on whether two divine Persons can be so united as to be one Being, the Trinitarian or the Arian?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: The Arian bears it. Waterland affirms that such a union is possible, on grounds found in Scripture and Catholic antiquity. The opponent must prove the negative, namely that no union could make two persons one God. That would mean demonstrating an impossibility in a nature of which we have no ideas, which cannot be done.
sources.quote: It lies upon you, in this case, to prove the negative, viz. that no union whatever can make two persons one Being, one τὸ Θεῖον, one God: you are to shew the supposition to be impossible, in the nature of the thing
sources.raw_question: Who bears the burden of proof on whether two divine Persons can be so united as to be one Being, the Trinitarian or the Arian?

question: Can texts such as John 1, Acts 20:28 and John 8:58 be legitimately explained away on the principle that being and person are the same?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: No. Waterland says Dr. Clarke evades the force of these and other texts only by an unproved philosophical maxim. That maxim could be used to dispose of any number of texts, however explicit, and even the Nicene and Athanasian Creeds. This shows the Doctor's case rests not on Scripture but on vain philosophy, to which he makes Scripture yield.
sources.quote: It is not Scripture, it is not antiquity, but a philosophical principle: to which Scripture, Fathers, Councils, Creeds, every thing, must yield.
sources.raw_question: Can texts such as John 1, Acts 20:28 and John 8:58 be legitimately explained away on the principle that being and person are the same?

question: Do eternal intelligible things abide in a place as bodies do?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > What is the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge. The Worship of God is the Love of Him. How the Intellectual Cognizance of Eternal Things Comes to Pass Through Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. They abide as intelligible things in an incorporeal nature, not fixed in some place. They are present to the glance of the mind as visible things in place are present to bodily sense. Even sensible things in space and motions in time have unchanging intelligible reasons that stand apart from local space and from any passage of time.
sources.quote: And they abide, but not as if fixed in some place as are bodies; but as intelligible things in incorporeal nature, they are so at hand to the glance of the mind
sources.raw_question: Do eternal intelligible things abide in a place as bodies do?

question: Does Paul's statement 'In Adam we all die' prove that Adam himself was not saved?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIII.—Arguments in opposition to Tatian, showing that it was consonant to divine justice and mercy that the first Adam should first partake in that salvation offered to all by Christ.
sources.answer: No. Tatian uses this Pauline saying while ignoring that the same apostle teaches that where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. Grace therefore exceeds the sin that came through Adam, and it reaches Adam himself. The serpent gained nothing lasting by making man a transgressor, because he did not know God's power.
sources.quote: endeavouring from time to time to employ sayings of this kind often [made use of] by Paul: “In Adam we all die;” ignorant, however, that “where sin abounded, grace did much more abound.”
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement 'In Adam we all die' prove that Adam himself was not saved?

question: Since Revelation 4:6 says the living creatures were 'in the midst of the throne', does being in the midst of the throne imply sharing the throne and receiving worship, so that the Lamb's position proves nothing?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Following Ezekiel's parallel vision, the throne rests on a firmament upheld by the living creatures, so they appear around it while being beneath it as a support. That they did not occupy the throne or receive adoration is plain, since the Lamb appears in their midst and they fall down before him.
sources.quote: That they did not occupy the throne and receive adoration is plain; for (ch. 5:6) the Lamb appears in the midst of the living creatures, as well as in the midst of the elders; and verse 8, they, with the elders, fall down before him.
sources.raw_question: Since Revelation 4:6 says the living creatures were 'in the midst of the throne', does being in the midst of the throne imply sharing the throne and receiving worship, so that the Lamb's position proves nothing?

question: Is the believer's adoption into God's family a private act or an authoritative, legal (forensic) act?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: It is an authoritative, forensic act. Scripture says Christ gave believers 'power' or authority to become sons of God, and it describes this as being made 'meet to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light.' This is a judicial exaltation into a family where God is Father and Christ the elder brother.
sources.quote: This investing them with the power, excellency, and right of the sons of God, is a forensical act, and hath a legal proceeding in it.
sources.raw_question: Is the believer's adoption into God's family a private act or an authoritative, legal (forensic) act?

question: Does the word "with" express the eternal and uninterrupted union of Father, Son and Spirit against those who separate them by intervals of time?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That Scripture uses the words “in” or “by,” ἐν, cf. note on p. 3, in place of “with.” Wherein also it is proved that the word “and” has the same force as “with.”
sources.answer: Yes. "And" shows only that persons share a common action. "With" adds that they act in company with one another, as when Paul and Timothy are said to have sailed "with" each other. Applied to the divine persons, "with" proves their eternal fellowship and uninterrupted conjunction. It therefore defeats both Sabellius and those who separate the Son from the Father, or the Spirit from the Son, by intervals of time.
sources.quote: Thus while the word “with” upsets the error of Sabellius as no other word can, it routs also sinners who err in the very opposite direction; those, I mean, who separate the Son from the Father and the Spirit from the Son, by intervals of time.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who separate the Son from the Father and the Spirit from the Son by intervals of time
sources.raw_question: Does the word "with" express the eternal and uninterrupted union of Father, Son and Spirit against those who separate them by intervals of time?

question: If the whole world cannot contain an account of God's works, can the human mind comprehend or define the Lord of creation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. If creation cannot contain what might be said about itself, much less can human shallowness, which is next to nothing compared with the universe, contain what might be said of its Lord. David confesses this when he says his age is as nothing before God.
sources.quote: If, then, the whole creation cannot contain what might be said respecting itself (for so, according to our explanation, the great Evangelist testifies), how should human shallowness contain all that might be said of the Lord of Creation?
sources.raw_question: If the whole world cannot contain an account of God's works, can the human mind comprehend or define the Lord of creation?

question: Do the prophets and the apostles proclaim different gods, given that they preached different things to different peoples?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: No. Both proceed from one and the same God. Some announced the Lord, some preached the Father, some foretold the Son's coming, and others declared Him already present. The difference lies in their messages and audiences, not in their source.
sources.quote: the prophets were not from one God, and the apostles from another; but, [proceeding] from one and the same, some of them announced the Lord, others preached the Father, and others again foretold the advent of the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Do the prophets and the apostles proclaim different gods, given that they preached different things to different peoples?

question: What does Isaiah's text "God is in Thee, and there is no God beside Thee; Thou art God, and we knew it not, O God of Israel, the Saviour" teach about the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: It teaches the indivisible and inseparable Godhead of Father and Son. "God is in Thee" means the true nature of God the Father is present in the Son. "There is no God beside Thee" means no God exists outside him, since God dwells within him. "Thou art God" is the believer's confession of Emmanuel, so every notion of another God must be given up.
sources.quote: For when He says God is in Thee, He teaches that the true nature of God the Father is present in God the Son; for we must understand that it is the God Who is that is in Him.
sources.raw_question: What does Isaiah's text "God is in Thee, and there is no God beside Thee; Thou art God, and we knew it not, O God of Israel, the Saviour" teach about the Father and the Son?

question: Why is grieving the Holy Spirit an especially serious sin, given the Spirit's mission from the Father and the Son?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Because the Spirit comes to believers in the name, with the love, and upon the condescension of the whole Trinity. He deserves cheerful entertainment on his own account as God and for the work he comes to do, but being sent by the Father and the Son, commissioned to communicate their love and grace, makes grieving him a great aggravation of sin.
sources.quote: because he comes to us in the name, with the love, and upon the condescension, of the whole blessed Trinity. To do that which might grieve him so sent, on such an account, for that end and purpose which shall afterward be mentioned, is a great aggravation of sin.
sources.raw_question: Why is grieving the Holy Spirit an especially serious sin, given the Spirit's mission from the Father and the Son?

question: Do Scripture texts such as Paul's phrase 'to all the generations of the Æons of the Æon', 'In Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead', and 'All things are gathered together by God in Christ' teach the Valentinian system of thirty Æons and a Saviour formed from all of them?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter III.—Texts of Holy Scripture used by these heretics to support their opinions.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus says the Valentinians only appear to draw their system from Scripture. They strain the good words of revelation to fit their own wicked inventions through perverse interpretations and deceitful expositions. In this way they lead astray those who do not hold firmly to faith in one God, the Father Almighty, and one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
sources.quote: striving, as they do, to adapt the good words of revelation to their own wicked inventions. And it is not only from the writings of the evangelists and the apostles that they endeavour to derive proofs for their opinions by means of perverse interpretations and deceitful expositions
sources.raw_question: Do Scripture texts such as Paul's phrase 'to all the generations of the Æons of the Æon', 'In Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead', and 'All things are gathered together by God in Christ' teach the Valentinian system of thirty Æons and a Saviour formed from all of them?

question: Should 'Paraclete' in John 16:7 be translated 'Advocate' or 'Comforter'?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Owen prefers 'Comforter.' The word can mean either; Christ himself is called Paraclete in the sense of advocate in 1 John 2:1. The following verse, which describes the Spirit pleading Christ's cause against the world, suggests 'Advocate.' But Owen chooses to interpret the promise by its occasion, the disciples' sorrow, and so keeps 'Comforter.'
sources.quote: I shall choose rather to interpret the promise by the occasion of it, which was the sorrow of his disciples, and to retain the name of the Comforter.
sources.raw_question: Should 'Paraclete' in John 16:7 be translated 'Advocate' or 'Comforter'?

question: Did Eusebius and the ancients, in attributing creation primarily to the Father, deny the Son's proper efficiency in creation?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. Eusebius only asserts that creation is primarily attributed to the Father because of his authority as first Person, denying the Son not proper efficiency but only original efficiency. The general view of the ancients, Ante- and Post-Nicene, was that the Father as supreme ordered creation and the Son executed it, which marks the Son as second Person, not a lesser being.
sources.quote: not denying the Son’s proper efficiency, but only (if I may so call it) 9 original efficiency ; that is, making him the second and not the first Person; not Father, but Son.
sources.raw_question: Did Eusebius and the ancients, in attributing creation primarily to the Father, deny the Son's proper efficiency in creation?

question: Can God, being Spirit, suffer bodily passion or division?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. The Church recognizes God as Spirit, impassible and indivisible. She learned from the Lord that a spirit has neither flesh nor bones. This teaching guards against supposing that God could be burdened with bodily suffering and loss.
sources.quote: In the Spirit she recognises God as Spirit, impassible and indivisible, for she has learnt from the Lord that Spirit has neither flesh nor bones
sources.raw_question: Can God, being Spirit, suffer bodily passion or division?

question: Do phrases like "became subject" and the Father "delivered him up for us all" imply the Son is a passive subordinate in redemption?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. They mean that the Son has from the Father his working in goodness on behalf of men. Scripture also attributes redemption to Christ's own act: "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law" and "Christ died for us."
sources.quote: It is meant that the Son has it of the Father that He works in goodness on behalf of men.
sources.raw_question: Do phrases like "became subject" and the Father "delivered him up for us all" imply the Son is a passive subordinate in redemption?

question: Why does Christ sometimes speak with personal authority, as in "I will; be thou clean" and "But I say unto you"?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: These expressions of personal authority let us recognise him as our Master and Maker. The sayings that refer to the Father teach us about the Father of our Master and Creator. So the Son is shown to be divine author in his own right, not merely an executor.
sources.quote: in order that by these we may recognise our Master and Maker, and by the former may be taught the Father of our Master and Creator.
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ sometimes speak with personal authority, as in "I will; be thou clean" and "But I say unto you"?

question: Why is it the Son, rather than the Father, who will be seen as judge by the ungodly?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: Because the Son is also the Son of man, so he can be seen even by the ungodly. They too shall see him whom they pierced. The form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, is a sight reserved for those who love him, and it will not appear to the wicked.
sources.quote: because He is also the Son of man, so that He can be seen even by the ungodly, since they too shall see Him whom they have pierced
sources.raw_question: Why is it the Son, rather than the Father, who will be seen as judge by the ungodly?

question: Do knowable things generate knowledge, or does knowledge generate the things known?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How a Trinity is Produced by the Mind Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself.
sources.answer: Knowable things generate knowledge and are not generated by it. Whether the object exists before it is known (as sensible objects or historical facts) or begins simultaneously with the knowing (as a sound heard as it is made), the object is the source of the knowledge, not its product.
sources.quote: Yet none the less, whether preceding in time or beginning to exist simultaneously, knowable things generate knowledge, and are not generated by knowledge.
sources.raw_question: Do knowable things generate knowledge, or does knowledge generate the things known?

question: Is it beyond God's power to raise the humanity of the incarnate Son into full divine glory, when He can glorify human beings?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: No. It is absurd to think God can do for us what He cannot do in Himself. He will conform our earthly bodies to the glory of the Lord's body. Therefore He who became man in the form of a servant is not powerless to make Himself again entirely God.
sources.quote: He is not powerless to make Himself again entirely God, for without doubt He will transform us also into that which as yet we are not.
sources.raw_question: Is it beyond God's power to raise the humanity of the incarnate Son into full divine glory, when He can glorify human beings?

question: Are the Father, Son, and Spirit merely different aspects or successive moments in the life of one Divine Person, as Monarchianism held?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Warfield presents Monarchianism as an overreaction that identified the three too completely. Guided by the Baptismal Formula and the Rule of Faith, the church reached a more balanced conception: one God in being, in whose unity three consubstantial Persons subsist.
sources.quote: identified the Father, Son, and Spirit so completely that they were thought of only as different aspects or different moments in the life of the one Divine Person, called now Father, now Son, now Spirit
sources.raw_question: Are the Father, Son, and Spirit merely different aspects or successive moments in the life of one Divine Person, as Monarchianism held?

question: Are some human beings good by nature and others bad by nature, as some heretics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVII.—Men are possessed of free will, and endowed with the faculty of making a choice. It is not true, therefore, that some are by nature good, and others bad.
sources.answer: No. If some were made bad by nature and others good, the good would deserve no praise and the bad no blame, because each would simply be as they were created. In fact all men share the same nature, able both to hold fast to the good and to cast it away. That is why some are justly praised and others justly condemned.
sources.quote: But if some had been made by nature bad, and others good, these latter would not be deserving of praise for being good, for such were they created; nor would the former be reprehensible, for thus they were made [originally].
sources.raw_question: Are some human beings good by nature and others bad by nature, as some heretics claim?

question: Was Christ's work of satisfaction appointed by the Father alone, or was it also the Son's own voluntary act?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: It was both. The work proceeded from the will, purpose, and love of God the Father. It was also done by the Son's own voluntary consent, so that he both was substituted and substituted himself as mediator of the covenant in the place of sinners.
sources.quote: according to the will of the Father, and by his own counsel and choice, was substituted, and did substitute himself, as the mediator of the covenant
sources.raw_question: Was Christ's work of satisfaction appointed by the Father alone, or was it also the Son's own voluntary act?

question: What does Christ's resurrection, described with the words of Psalm 2:7 ('this day have I begotten thee'), signify about his work as mediator?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: It was the solemn declaration that Christ, as a public person, was absolved and justified. The pains of death were loosed, and he was declared to be the Son of God with power. In this the Father accepted his performance and pronounced him free of the obligation he had taken on for the elect.
sources.quote: As to solemn declaration, he was so absolved when, the “pains of death being loosed”, he was “declared to be the Son of God with power, by the resurrection from the dead;”
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's resurrection, described with the words of Psalm 2:7 ('this day have I begotten thee'), signify about his work as mediator?

question: Can God's declaration 'I alone am God' exclude His own Word, as the sun saying 'I alone am the light' would exclude its own radiance?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eighthly, John xvii. 3. and the Like. Our Lord's divinity cannot interfere with His Father's prerogatives, as the One God, which were so earnestly upheld by the Son. 'One' is used in contrast to false gods and idols, not to the Son, through whom the Father spoke. Our Lord adds His Name to the Father's, as included in Him. The Father the First, not as if the Son were not First too, but as Origin.
sources.answer: No. If the sun said 'I alone am the light of the day' to correct someone who called a painted piece of wood the cause of light, it would speak against the wooden image, not against its own radiance, which it has not outside itself. So God's 'I am Only God' is aimed at false gods, while the Word, as His radiance, is included in Him.
sources.quote: if the sun had spoken those words, he would have been setting right the error and have so spoken, not as having his radiance without him, but in the radiance shewing his own light.
sources.raw_question: Can God's declaration 'I alone am God' exclude His own Word, as the sun saying 'I alone am the light' would exclude its own radiance?

question: Why did God not declare 'I am the only God' to Adam at the beginning, even though His Word was already with Him?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eighthly, John xvii. 3. and the Like. Our Lord's divinity cannot interfere with His Father's prerogatives, as the One God, which were so earnestly upheld by the Son. 'One' is used in contrast to false gods and idols, not to the Son, through whom the Father spoke. Our Lord adds His Name to the Father's, as included in Him. The Father the First, not as if the Son were not First too, but as Origin.
sources.answer: Because there was no need before idols came in. Only when men rebelled against the truth and named gods for themselves did such words become necessary, to deny gods that were not. This shows the sayings target idolatry, not the Word who was with God from the beginning.
sources.quote: God spoke not such words to Adam at the beginning, though His Word was with Him, by whom all things came to be; for there was no need, before idols came in;
sources.raw_question: Why did God not declare 'I am the only God' to Adam at the beginning, even though His Word was already with Him?

question: How does Christ, as mediator, shelter believers from the wrath of God and give them rest?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Christ stands between the soul and God's wrath and bears that wrath himself. Under his shadow the soul rests safely, covered by the righteousness of the Lord Jesus. He also gives quiet and repose from the weariness caused by corruption, temptation and persecution, being 'as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land.'
sources.quote: When the heat of wrath is ready to scorch the soul, Christ, interposing, bears it all.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ, as mediator, shelter believers from the wrath of God and give them rest?

question: Do the letters of Paul presuppose a Trinitarian conception of God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Throughout Paul's letters, from 1 Thessalonians to 2 Timothy, redemption and all its blessings are consistently referred to a threefold Divine causation. God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit appear everywhere as joint objects of adoration and the conjunct source of all Divine operations, sometimes singly, often two together, and not infrequently all three.
sources.quote: Everywhere, throughout their pages, God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit appear as the joint objects of all religious adoration, and the conjunct source of all Divine operations.
sources.raw_question: Do the letters of Paul presuppose a Trinitarian conception of God?

question: Does Paul's strict monotheism conflict with his treating the Son and the Spirit as God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Paul's monotheism is intense and the unity of God is the first premise of his thought, yet to him the Father is no more God than Christ or the Spirit. He holds that within the unity of God's Being there is a distinction of Persons.
sources.quote: Paul’s monotheism is intense: the first premise of all his thought on Divine things is the unity of God (Rom. iii. 30; I Cor. viii. 4; Gal iii. 20; Eph. iv. 6;I Tim. ii. 5; cf. Rom. xvi. 22; I Tim. i. 17). Yet to him God the Father is no more God than the Lord Jesus Christ is God, or the Holy Spirit is God.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's strict monotheism conflict with his treating the Son and the Spirit as God?

question: Who alone sees God and makes the will of the Father known?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: The Son alone. "Israel" means a man who sees God, and no one sees God except the Son, the perfect man who alone declares the Father's will. John confirms this: no one has seen God, but the only-begotten in the Father's bosom has declared Him.
sources.quote: there is no one who sees God except the Son alone, the perfect man who alone declares the will of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Who alone sees God and makes the will of the Father known?

question: What is the best likeness through which the human mind can come to see God in this life?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Of the Term ‘Enigma,’ And of Tropical Modes of Speech.
sources.answer: The image of God that is the human mind itself is best suited to this purpose. Many likenesses could be meant by the glass and the enigma, as far as they help us understand God. But none is better adapted than that which is rightly called God's image.
sources.quote: yet nothing is better adapted to this purpose than that which is not vainly called His image.
sources.raw_question: What is the best likeness through which the human mind can come to see God in this life?

question: To whom was God speaking when he said "Let Us make man," and what does this show about the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Preface.
sources.answer: God spoke to the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are his "hands" by which man was moulded after God's likeness. So the Son and Spirit took part with the Father in the work of creation.
sources.quote: formed after the likeness of God, and moulded by His hands, that is, by the Son and Holy Spirit, to whom also He said, “Let Us make man.”
sources.raw_question: To whom was God speaking when he said "Let Us make man," and what does this show about the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Does Christ's foretelling of his disciples' persecutions bear witness to his deity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ told them beforehand so that, when the persecutions came, they would remember he had foretold them. Recalling this would support them with the consideration of his Deity and omniscience, since he knew these things before they came to pass.
sources.quote: you may be supported with the consideration of my Deity and omniscience, who told you all these things before they came to pass
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's foretelling of his disciples' persecutions bear witness to his deity?

question: According to John 5:23, is the Son's appointment as Judge of the world the only ground of the honour due to him?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. The Son was owed honour for having been God (Θεὸς) from the beginning, for creating the world, and for being the only begotten Son, which St. John treats as exceedingly glorious. The true reason Christ assigns in John 5 is that he does the same things the Father does and has the same power and authority, and so has a title to equal honour; judgment was committed to him to make that dignity manifest, not to be its sole foundation.
sources.quote: What! was there no honour due to him on account of his having been Θεὸς from the beginning ? None for his having created the world? None on account of his being the “ only begotten Son,”
sources.raw_question: According to John 5:23, is the Son's appointment as Judge of the world the only ground of the honour due to him?

question: Do the signs of weakness and lowliness recorded of Christ in Scripture prove that he was only a man and not God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And Indeed that Christ Was Not Only Man, But God Also; That Even as He Was the Son of Man, So Also He Was the Son of God.
sources.answer: No. The imperfections recorded of Christ prove his human frailty, but the majesties recorded of him equally affirm his divine power. Each lowly feature belongs to him as man, while a corresponding exalted feature belongs to him as God: as man he came after many and was inferior to others, as God he was before all and greater than all.
sources.quote: So if imperfections in Him prove human frailty, majesties in Him affirm divine power.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who hold Christ to be only man
sources.raw_question: Do the signs of weakness and lowliness recorded of Christ in Scripture prove that he was only a man and not God?

question: If Christ were a creature, would Solomon's teaching contradict Paul's condemnation of those who serve the creature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes. The Arian reading would mean Solomon calls us to adore a creature while Paul forbids serving the creature rather than the Creator. Since the same Spirit speaks in Prophets and Apostles, and Paul names Christ Creator, Christ cannot be a creature.
sources.quote: Solomon calls upon us to adore a creature, while Paul convicts those who serve a creature. And certainly these two texts do not seem to agree together, according to the blasphemous theory
sources.raw_question: If Christ were a creature, would Solomon's teaching contradict Paul's condemnation of those who serve the creature?

question: Can the Holy Spirit be said to be created repeatedly, as the wind is?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VI. To those who object that according to the words of Amos the Spirit is created, the answer is made that the word is there understood of the wind, which is often created, which cannot be said of the Holy Spirit, since He is eternal, and cannot be dissolved in death, or by an heretical absorption into the Father. But if they pertinaciously contend that this passage was written of the Holy Spirit, St. Ambrose points out that recourse must be had to a spiritual Interpretation, for Christ by His coming established the thunder, that is, the force of the divine utterances, and by Spirit is signified the human soul as also the flesh assumed by Christ. And since this was created by each Person of the Trinity, it is thence argued that the Spirit, Who has before been affirmed to be the Creator of all things, was the Author of the Incarnation of the Lord.
sources.answer: No. Winds are often created whenever they occur, but the Holy Spirit is eternal, existing before the world and moving upon the waters, so he cannot begin to be after creation. Repeated creation would imply many Holy Spirits or that he frequently dies, but the Spirit of life cannot die, so there is no reason he should be created.
sources.quote: I do not understand why He should be frequently created; unless perchance they believe that He dies frequently and so is frequently created. But how can the Spirit of life die? If, then, He cannot die, there is no reason why He should be often created.
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit be said to be created repeatedly, as the wind is?

question: What is the purpose of the Incarnation with respect to Christ's humanity and the unity of the divine nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: That man might become God: the whole Son, manhood as well as divinity, was to continue in the unity of the Father's nature. Since the Word was in the nature of God, the flesh united to the glory of the Word could also be restored to the unity of the Father's nature, which required the Father to glorify the assumed flesh with Himself.
sources.quote: For the object to be gained was that man might become God. But the assumed manhood could not in any wise abide in the unity of God, unless, through unity with God, it attained to unity with the nature of God.
sources.raw_question: What is the purpose of the Incarnation with respect to Christ's humanity and the unity of the divine nature?

question: Does the mind's attention or will to see depend on the bodily sense, so that it perishes when the eyes are lost?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Certain Trinity in the Sight. That There are Three Things in Sight, Which Differ in Their Own Nature. In What Manner from a Visible Thing Vision is Produced, or the Image of that Thing Which is Seen. The Matter is Shown More Clearly by an Example. How These Three Combine in One.
sources.answer: No. The attention is an act of the mind alone, whereas the sense works through a bodily instrument. When someone is blinded, the sense is destroyed but the mind remains the same. The desire to see continues unimpaired, which shows that the attention can neither perish nor be diminished by the loss of the bodily sense.
sources.quote: For there remains unimpaired a desire [appetitus] of seeing, whether it can be carried into effect or not.
sources.raw_question: Does the mind's attention or will to see depend on the bodily sense, so that it perishes when the eyes are lost?

question: Did the Fathers of the second century ground the unity of the Godhead on the same principle as the Nicene Fathers?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds that Bishop Bull demonstrated this. He adds that Dr. Whitby himself concedes as much in the very next page, and has left only an evasion about the term 'individual'.
sources.quote: he pretends that the Bishop has not shewn, that the Fathers of the second century resolved the unity into the same principle with the Nicene Fathers. Yet the Bishop * has shewn it, and Dr. Whitby allows as much in the very next page
sources.raw_question: Did the Fathers of the second century ground the unity of the Godhead on the same principle as the Nicene Fathers?

question: If the Word of God is divine, in what respect could the Spirit of God rest upon and anoint him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IX.—One and the same God, the Creator of heaven and earth, is He whom the prophets foretold, and who was declared by the Gospel. Proof of this, at the outset, from St. Matthew’s Gospel.
sources.answer: The Spirit rested on and anointed the Word with respect to his humanity. Because the Word was man from the root of Jesse and son of Abraham, the Spirit came on him and anointed him to preach the Gospel to the lowly. As God, however, he needed no such equipping, and did not judge according to appearance, since he himself knew what was in man.
sources.quote: For inasmuch as the Word of God was man from the root of Jesse, and son of Abraham, in this respect did the Spirit of God rest upon Him, and anoint Him to preach the Gospel to the lowly.
sources.raw_question: If the Word of God is divine, in what respect could the Spirit of God rest upon and anoint him?

question: How does divine operation differ from a servant carrying out a task, and what does this imply about the Spirit's role?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XIII. Prophecy was not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Spirit; the authority and operation of the latter on the apostles is signified to be the same as Theirs; and so we are to understand that there is unity in the three points of authority, rule, and bounty; yet need no disadvantage be feared from that participation, since such does not arise in human friendship. Lastly, it is established that this is the inheritance of the apostolic faith from the fact that the apostles are described as having obeyed the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Divine operation works by the power of command, not by performing a ministry. God does not fashion things by toil or skill: he spoke and they were made, so the effecting of the work is contained in his command. Because this royal commanding power is attributed to the Spirit, the Spirit is not a servant but shares the divine authority. The apostles are therefore ministers of Father, Son and Spirit.
sources.quote: For the divine operation works by the power of a command, not in the execution of a ministry; for God, when He works, does not fashion anything by toil or art, but “He spake and they were made.”
sources.raw_question: How does divine operation differ from a servant carrying out a task, and what does this imply about the Spirit's role?

question: Why does Scripture stress God's creative power when calling people to trust Him rather than man?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 2. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, detaches our ultimate confidence from man the creature, and attaches it to God the Creator; – by contrasting the sinfulness and feebleness of mortal man with the goodness and omnipotence of the Eternal Jehovah: by direct prohibition and precept: by exhibiting the holy Jealousy of God.
sources.answer: Because creative power proves God's infinite preeminence over all creatures, so that the Maker alone is mighty to save. If this holds for temporal deliverances, it holds much more for eternal salvation, since no man can redeem his brother but God will redeem the soul from the grave.
sources.quote: Observe, in all these passages, how much stress is laid on the creative power of God as proof of his infinite preeminence. The Maker alone is mighty to save.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture stress God's creative power when calling people to trust Him rather than man?

question: How can jealousy be attributed to God without implying a sinful or selfish passion?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 2. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, detaches our ultimate confidence from man the creature, and attaches it to God the Creator; – by contrasting the sinfulness and feebleness of mortal man with the goodness and omnipotence of the Eternal Jehovah: by direct prohibition and precept: by exhibiting the holy Jealousy of God.
sources.answer: Divine jealousy is the perfect form of a just jealousy that even among men can be good, as in Paul's godly jealousy. It springs from a true estimate of one's rightful claims and a holy indignation when they are violated. In God it is without flaw: He perfectly knows His supreme majesty, perfectly estimates the claims it has on creatures, and conceives perfect jealousy when they are set at naught.
sources.quote: He has an absolutely perfect knowledge of his own supreme majesty and goodness: He forms an absolutely perfect estimate of the claims that supremacy has on his creatures: and He conceives an absolutely perfect jealousy when those obligations are set at naught.
sources.raw_question: How can jealousy be attributed to God without implying a sinful or selfish passion?

question: How could the Old Testament prophets have desired to see Christ's advent unless they had received foreknowledge of it from the Word himself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XI.—The old prophets and righteous men knew beforehand of the advent of Christ, and earnestly desired to see and hear Him, He revealing himself in the Scriptures by the Holy Ghost, and without any change in Himself, enriching men day by day with benefits, but conferring them in greater abundance on later than on former generations.
sources.answer: They had foreknowledge because the Word himself revealed it to them. Christ says many prophets and righteous men desired to see what the disciples saw; they could only desire this if they foreknew his coming, and they could only foreknow it if they had received this knowledge from him. So all things were revealed to believers by one and the same God through the Word throughout history.
sources.quote: In what way, then, did they desire both to hear and to see, unless they had foreknowledge of His future advent? But how could they have foreknown it, unless they had previously received foreknowledge from Himself?
sources.raw_question: How could the Old Testament prophets have desired to see Christ's advent unless they had received foreknowledge of it from the Word himself?

question: Does the greater grace given in the New Testament imply a change in God or a different God from the God of the Old Testament?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XI.—The old prophets and righteous men knew beforehand of the advent of Christ, and earnestly desired to see and hear Him, He revealing himself in the Scriptures by the Holy Ghost, and without any change in Himself, enriching men day by day with benefits, but conferring them in greater abundance on later than on former generations.
sources.answer: No. The Lord remains the same and the same Father is revealed. The one and the same Lord, through his advent, gave a greater gift of grace to later generations than to those under the Old Testament. Earlier believers only heard that the King would come, while later believers see him present and share his gifts.
sources.quote: for the Lord remains the same, and the same Father is revealed; thus, therefore, has the one and the same Lord granted, by means of His advent, a greater gift of grace to those of a later period
sources.raw_question: Does the greater grace given in the New Testament imply a change in God or a different God from the God of the Old Testament?

question: How does Aaron becoming high priest illustrate the sense in which the Word 'was made' High Priest without being a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: Aaron was born a man and later became high priest by putting on the priestly garments, without changing what he was. Likewise the Word, who was in the beginning with God and was God, took earthly flesh from Mary as a robe, so that He might offer Himself as High Priest. He did not become other than Himself, but was made High Priest by putting on a created body.
sources.quote: Aaron was not born a high-priest, but a man; and in process of time, when God willed, he became a high-priest
sources.raw_question: How does Aaron becoming high priest illustrate the sense in which the Word 'was made' High Priest without being a creature?

question: What Scripture texts show that Christ had a human soul and was a complete man?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: Several texts show it. The angel told Joseph that those who sought the young Child's life (or 'soul') were dead. The Lord called Himself 'a man that hath told you the truth,' and 'man' means soul and body together. He also said He lays down His soul and takes it again. Further, Peter's reading of David says His soul was not left in hell.
sources.quote: Now by “Man” is not meant the body of a man only, but that which is composed of both, soul and body.
sources.raw_question: What Scripture texts show that Christ had a human soul and was a complete man?

question: Does calling the Father 'Almighty' mean that the Son is a subordinate subject under the Father's absolute sovereignty, a fellow-slave with creation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. Eunomius twists 'Almighty' from providential operation into arbitrary sovereignty in order to make the Son part of the subject universe. Gregory rejects this as a profane misuse of the term aimed at that very result.
sources.quote: so as to make the Son to be a part of the subject and subordinate universe, a fellow-slave with all the rest to Him Who with arbitrary and absolute sovereignty controls all alike
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Father 'Almighty' mean that the Son is a subordinate subject under the Father's absolute sovereignty, a fellow-slave with creation?

question: If there were several gods, each with his own creation, could one god rightly concern himself with another's creation without ceasing to be God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter I.—There is but one God: the impossibility of its being otherwise.
sources.answer: No. On the hypothesis of many gods, each deity would have to be content with his own possessions. Meddling in another's domain would make him unjust and rapacious, so he would cease to be what God is. Likewise, a creation that honoured another maker than its own would rightly be judged an apostate.
sources.quote: each deity will be contented with his own possessions, and will not be moved with any curiosity respecting the affairs of others; otherwise he would be unjust, and rapacious, and would cease to be what God is
sources.raw_question: If there were several gods, each with his own creation, could one god rightly concern himself with another's creation without ceasing to be God?

question: Is it consistent with God's nature to allow error to arise at the beginning and only later, as if repenting, try to destroy its results?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter V.—This world was not formed by any other beings within the territory which is contained by the Father.
sources.answer: No. It would be far better, more consistent, and more God-like for God to cut off the cause of such necessity at the very beginning. Acting afterwards as if moved by repentance, trying to root out the results once they have grown, is unworthy of God. So the Gnostic account of the Father permitting the world's formation and later correcting it is incoherent.
sources.quote: For it would have been much better, more consistent, and more God-like, to cut off at the beginning the principle of this kind of necessity, than afterwards, as if moved by repentance, to endeavour to extirpate the results of necessity
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent with God's nature to allow error to arise at the beginning and only later, as if repenting, try to destroy its results?

question: How do adopted children of God come to have a right to the things of this world after sin forfeited humanity's title to creation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: Through Christ as the second Adam and "heir of all things." Sin reversed God's original grant of creation to man, leaving man without any claim to the creatures. God then invested the whole right and title the first Adam lost in Christ, so those adopted as fellow-heirs with Christ regain a right to the things of creation.
sources.quote: To this end he invests the whole right and title of them in the second Adam, which the first had lost; he appoints him “heir of all things.”
sources.raw_question: How do adopted children of God come to have a right to the things of this world after sin forfeited humanity's title to creation?

question: Are the Christ who dies and the Christ who raises the dead two different persons, given that death belongs to the humanity and the quickening to the divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Death is attributed to the man and the quickening of the flesh to the God, each nature performing its proper function. Yet he who dies and he who raises are not two but one Person, Christ Jesus. The flesh stripped off and he who strips it off are not different from one another, since he triumphs in himself, that is, in that flesh.
sources.quote: death is attributed to the man, and the quickening of the flesh to the God, though He Who dies and He Who raises the dead to life are not two, but one Person?
sources.raw_question: Are the Christ who dies and the Christ who raises the dead two different persons, given that death belongs to the humanity and the quickening to the divinity?

question: Is Jesus Christ, whom Christians believe in after the Father, the Son of the one God who is the Founder of all things, or of some other god?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Further, that the Same Rule of Truth Teaches Us to Believe, After the Father, Also in the Son of God, Jesus Christ Our Lord God, Being the Same that Was Promised in the Old Testament, and Manifested in the New.
sources.answer: He is the Son of the one and only God, the Founder of all things. The same rule of truth that teaches belief in the one Creator God teaches belief, after the Father, in His Son Christ Jesus, the Lord our God. There is no other god whose Son he could be.
sources.quote: The same rule of truth teaches us to believe, after the Father, also on the Son of God, Christ Jesus, the Lord our God, but the Son of God—of that God who is both one and alone, to wit the Founder of all things
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus Christ, whom Christians believe in after the Father, the Son of the one God who is the Founder of all things, or of some other god?

question: What does the quickness of Christ's death on the cross show?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: It shows that his death was voluntary. Men who are crucified usually suffer a long death, which is why the thieves' legs were broken. Christ gave up his spirit immediately after his last word, which astonished those present and made Pilate marvel.
sources.quote: For they who are hung on the cross are commonly tortured by a prolonged death. Whence it was that the legs of the thieves were broken, in order that they might die directly
sources.raw_question: What does the quickness of Christ's death on the cross show?

question: Do Christ's miracles and his universal knowledge show that he went forth from God by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. Turning water into wine, multiplying the loaves, healing, raising Lazarus at a word, and knowing the hidden purposes of men without needing to ask were all done in the power and nature of God. Such works are evidence of the divine nature, and so evidence that he went forth from God. The Apostles believed he went forth from God because he can and does perform the works of God.
sources.quote: For all these things, done in the power and in the nature of God, are evidence that He must have gone forth from God.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's miracles and his universal knowledge show that he went forth from God by nature?

question: Why did Christ give the Holy Spirit twice, once on earth after the resurrection and again from heaven at Pentecost?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: In Augustine's judgment, the double gift signifies the two commandments of love. Love is shed abroad in our hearts by this Gift, so Christ gave the Spirit once on earth for love of neighbor and once from heaven for love of God. Whatever the reason, it was the same Holy Spirit given both times.
sources.quote: gave to them the Holy Spirit, once upon earth, on account of the love of our neighbor, and a second time from heaven, on account of the love of God
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ give the Holy Spirit twice, once on earth after the resurrection and again from heaven at Pentecost?

question: When was Christ anointed with the Holy Spirit: at His baptism or at the Incarnation?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Holy Spirit Twice Given by Christ. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son is Apart from Time, Nor Can He Be Called the Son of Both.
sources.answer: At the Incarnation, not at His baptism. He was anointed with a mystical, invisible unction when the Word was made flesh and human nature, without prior merits, was joined to God the Word in the Virgin's womb to become one person. It is absurd to think He received the Spirit only at about thirty. The dove at His baptism prefigured His body, the Church, in which the baptized receive the Spirit. If John was filled with the Spirit from the womb, far more so Christ, whose conception was spiritual.
sources.quote: He is to be understood to have been then anointed with that mystical and invisible unction, when the Word of God was made flesh
sources.raw_question: When was Christ anointed with the Holy Spirit: at His baptism or at the Incarnation?

question: Does the Hebrew sabbath on the seventh day, given as a memorial of God's rest from creation, prove that the Son's generation had a beginning and an end?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > He further shows that the pretemporal generation of the Son is not the subject of influences drawn from ordinary and carnal generation, but is without beginning and without end, and not according to the fabrications constructed by Eunomius, in ignorance of His power, from the statements of Plato concerning the soul and from the sabbath rest of the Hebrews.
sources.answer: No. The keeping of the sabbath has nothing to do with the question of whether the Son came into being when He was not. One might as well cite circumcision on the eighth day or the scapegoat; such Jewish observances are far removed from the eternal generation of the Son.
sources.quote: Because the Jew honours his sabbath by idleness, the fact, as he says, is proved that the Lord both had a beginning of birth and ceased being born!
sources.raw_question: Does the Hebrew sabbath on the seventh day, given as a memorial of God's rest from creation, prove that the Son's generation had a beginning and an end?

question: Would denying that Christ and the Holy Spirit are perfect in goodness by nature undermine baptism, regeneration, and the hope of resurrection?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: Yes. If Christ has no goodness of his own, baptism into him is pointless, and belief in the Holy Spirit likewise if the same is said of him. Regeneration requires a regenerating Power with infallibility and independence in its own nature, and our vile body cannot be changed by one who himself needs change by another. Faith and preaching would then be vain.
sources.quote: How are they regenerate by baptism from their mortal birth, if the regenerating Power does not possess in its own nature infallibility and independence?
sources.raw_question: Would denying that Christ and the Holy Spirit are perfect in goodness by nature undermine baptism, regeneration, and the hope of resurrection?

question: Why would a divine Person who participates in the infinite First Good never reach perfection?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: Because the First Good is infinite, participation in it is also infinite: a being deficient in good is ceaselessly drawn toward the superior nature, always grasping more yet always finding more beyond. Such a being would be always changing and never at rest in perfection, so it could not be the unchanging divine Son or Spirit.
sources.quote: The First Good is in its nature infinite, and so it follows of necessity that the participation in the enjoyment of it will be infinite also
sources.raw_question: Why would a divine Person who participates in the infinite First Good never reach perfection?

question: For whose benefit did Christ intend his suffering and oblation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: He intended it only for the good of his elect and their acceptance with God. Scripture says he loved the church and gave himself for it, and that he suffered as the just for the unjust in order to bring us to God.
sources.quote: Christ in his suffering and oblation, had his intention only upon the good of his elect, and their acceptation with God
sources.raw_question: For whose benefit did Christ intend his suffering and oblation?

question: Why is the incarnate Word called our 'First-born' and Brother, even though He became man after us?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: He became our brother through the likeness of His body. He is our first-born because, when all men were lost through Adam's transgression, His flesh was saved and set free before all others, being the Word's own body. We who are made one body with it are then saved after its pattern, and He becomes our way and door to the Father.
sources.quote: His flesh before all others was saved and liberated, as being the Word’s body; and henceforth we, becoming incorporate with It, are saved after Its pattern.
