sources.raw_question: Why is the incarnate Word called our 'First-born' and Brother, even though He became man after us?

question: On what ground should believers give obedience to the word of God as preached by ministers, and how is this communion with the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Obedience is owed to the preached word because the Holy Spirit alone furnishes men with gifts for preaching and is present with them in its power. Believers should therefore regard his authority, wisdom and goodness in the ministry and submit to the word on that account. When this consideration makes them bow before the word, they have communion with the Holy Spirit in that ordinance.
sources.quote: On this reason, I say, on this ground, is obedience to be yielded to the word, in the ministerial dispensation thereof, — because the Holy Ghost, and he alone, doth furnish with gifts to that end and purpose.
sources.raw_question: On what ground should believers give obedience to the word of God as preached by ministers, and how is this communion with the Holy Spirit?

question: Do the prophets' promises of a new covenant and a new heart imply a different God from the one who made the old covenant at Horeb?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: No. The prophecies of a new covenant announce the liberty of faith in Christ and the streams of the Holy Spirit given to God's elect. They were given so that God's people would praise him, not so that they would blaspheme the God who made these things. One and the same God makes both covenants.
sources.quote: the streams of the Holy Spirit in a dry land, to give water to the elect people of God, whom He has acquired, that they might show forth His praise, but not that they might blaspheme Him who made these things, that is, God.
sources.raw_question: Do the prophets' promises of a new covenant and a new heart imply a different God from the one who made the old covenant at Horeb?

question: If the Son were only a temporary mode of the Father, what would follow for the Son's existence and for the Incarnation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Marcellian illustration from 1 Cor. xii. 4, refuted.
sources.answer: The Son would have a beginning, since the Father would 'become' a Son and stop being called Father. The Incarnation would be in name only, with God 'made man in name, but in truth not even coming among us.' Everything that happened would be make-believe, displayed in name rather than in truth.
sources.quote: having a beginning in that He becomes a Son, and then ceasing to be called Father, and made man in name, but in truth not even coming among us
sources.raw_question: If the Son were only a temporary mode of the Father, what would follow for the Son's existence and for the Incarnation?

question: Is the God proclaimed by the Law and the Prophets, the Maker of the world, a different God from the Father of Jesus Christ, as Cerdo and Marcion taught?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XXVII.—Doctrines of Cerdo and Marcion.
sources.answer: No. The Maker of this universe is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Lord himself is recorded in the Gospel as plainly confessing that the Creator is his Father, and Paul's epistles teach that the God who made the world is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Marcion could hold his view only by cutting these passages out of Luke and out of Paul's letters.
sources.quote: setting aside a great deal of the teaching of the Lord, in which the Lord is recorded as most dearly confessing that the Maker of this universe is His Father
sources.raw_question: Is the God proclaimed by the Law and the Prophets, the Maker of the world, a different God from the Father of Jesus Christ, as Cerdo and Marcion taught?

question: If the Son is the Father's offspring and Image and like Him in all things, must the Son also beget a son, and so on without limit?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: No. The objection imports material, human ideas of generation into God. Among men and animals, a son begotten of a father who was himself a son inherits the power to become a father in turn. God is not as man. The Father is not from a father, so He does not beget one who will become a father. The Son is not begotten from a begotten father or by effluence, so He is not begotten in order to beget.
sources.quote: for the Father is not from a father; therefore doth He not beget one who shall become a father; nor is the Son from effluence of the Father, nor is He begotten from a father that was begotten; therefore neither is He begotten so as to beget.
sources.raw_question: If the Son is the Father's offspring and Image and like Him in all things, must the Son also beget a son, and so on without limit?

question: Was worship due to the Son from angels and men before his mediatorial kingdom began, on account of his being their Creator and Preserver?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: Yes. The Son created all things and upholds all things (Col. 1:16-17; Heb. 1:3), and these titles express supreme majesty, imply dominion, and mark the true God. He was also God (Theos) before the world and came 'unto his own' as their Creator and Governor, so he had a just title to worship from the foundation of the world, even on Clarke's own hypothesis.
sources.quote: Wherefore, certainly, he had a just claim and title to adoration and worship from the foundation of the world, even upon your own hypothesis.
sources.raw_question: Was worship due to the Son from angels and men before his mediatorial kingdom began, on account of his being their Creator and Preserver?

question: What does the giving of the one Holy Spirit to apostles scattered in different places show about the Spirit's nature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is not a creature, seeing that He is infinite, and was shed upon the apostles dispersed through all countries, and moreover sanctifies the Angels also, to whom He makes us equal. Mary was full of the same likewise, so too, Christ the Lord, and so far all things high and low. And all benediction has its origin from His operation, as was signified in the moving of the water at Bethesda.
sources.answer: It shows the Spirit is uncircumscribed and divine, unlike creatures. The apostles, being creatures, had to be sent to different places because they could not be everywhere at once, yet the one Spirit was given to all of them at once as indivisible grace, so the working was one in all.
sources.quote: The persons, then, were different, but the accomplishment of the working was in all one, because the Holy Spirit is one
sources.raw_question: What does the giving of the one Holy Spirit to apostles scattered in different places show about the Spirit's nature?

question: Is the holiness of the Angels a natural property of theirs rather than a gift of the Holy Spirit, so that the Spirit who sanctifies them is a fellow creature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is not a creature, seeing that He is infinite, and was shed upon the apostles dispersed through all countries, and moreover sanctifies the Angels also, to whom He makes us equal. Mary was full of the same likewise, so too, Christ the Lord, and so far all things high and low. And all benediction has its origin from His operation, as was signified in the moving of the water at Bethesda.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit who sanctifies Angels has no partnership with creatures, just as he is not human for sanctifying the apostles. If Angels' holiness were not from the Spirit, men, who receive the divine sanctification of the Spirit, would rank above Angels, which is absurd. So Angels are higher because they receive more of the Spirit's grace, and the grace given to them and to us has the same author.
sources.quote: it must be understood that the nature of Angels is higher as it receives more of the grace of the Spirit, and that the favour awarded to us and to them comes from the same author
sources.raw_question: Is the holiness of the Angels a natural property of theirs rather than a gift of the Holy Spirit, so that the Spirit who sanctifies them is a fellow creature?

question: Does saying God dilated or expanded imply that God is bodily and passible?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Such a doctrine precludes all real distinctions of personality in the Divine Nature. Illustration of the Scripture doctrine from 2 Cor. vi. 11, &c.
sources.answer: Yes. Dilatation is an affection undergone by what is dilated, which first was contracted and then becomes what it was not. Whoever ascribes dilatation to God must therefore ascribe a body to Him and represent Him as passible, which is impious; the idea is borrowed from the Stoics' God who contracts and expands with creation.
sources.quote: a man who thus should lie, must ascribe a body to God, and represent Him as passible; for what is dilatation, but an affection of that which is dilated?
sources.raw_question: Does saying God dilated or expanded imply that God is bodily and passible?

question: Was it the Holy Spirit who guided Israel through the wilderness into the promised land?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VIII. The aforesaid unity is proved hereby, that as the Father is said to be grieved and tempted, so too the Son. The Son was also tempted in the wilderness, where a figure of the cross was set up in the brazen serpent: but the Apostle says that the Spirit also was there tempted. St. Ambrose infers from this that the Israelites were guided into the promised land by the same Spirit, and that His will and power are one with those of the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Since the Spirit was tempted in the wilderness, He was also the one leading the people. Isaiah says that "the Spirit came down from the Lord and guided them." The Spirit also supplied them with the heavenly food of manna.
sources.quote: If He was tempted, He also certainly was guiding the people of the Jews into the land of promise
sources.raw_question: Was it the Holy Spirit who guided Israel through the wilderness into the promised land?

question: Is the God who spoke with Abraham, gave the Law and sent the prophets the same God and Father who in the last times sent His Son, or a different god from the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XLI.—Those persons who do not believe in God, but who are disobedient, are angels and sons of the devil, not indeed by nature, but by imitation. Close of this book, and scope of the succeeding one.
sources.answer: He is the same God. Irenaeus holds that all the words of the Lord proclaim one and the same Father, the Creator of this world. He also holds that the apostle Paul, rightly expounded, taught that it was one God the Father who spoke with Abraham, gave the law, sent the prophets beforehand, and in the last times sent His Son. This Father also conferred salvation on His own handiwork, the substance of flesh. The heretics who invoke Paul for a different god have misunderstood him.
sources.quote: it was one God the Father who spake with Abraham, who gave the law, who sent the prophets beforehand, who in the last times sent His Son, and conferred salvation upon His own handiwork
sources.raw_question: Is the God who spoke with Abraham, gave the Law and sent the prophets the same God and Father who in the last times sent His Son, or a different god from the Creator?

question: Is what we love in the divine Trinity simply that it is three, a number we already know?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Trinity May Be Loved Though Unknown.
sources.answer: No. We do know what three things are, but that is not what we love, since we could have a trinity simply by holding up three fingers. What we love in the Trinity is that it is God. Yet we have never seen or known any other God, because God is one, so we love Him only by believing.
sources.quote: We love then in the Trinity, that it is God: but we never saw or knew any other God, because God is One; He alone whom we have not yet seen, and whom we love by believing.
sources.raw_question: Is what we love in the divine Trinity simply that it is three, a number we already know?

question: In what sense is the Father glorified through the Son's earthly works?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: The Father is glorified when, through the Son's works, he is recognised as God and as Father of the Only-begotten. All praise given to the Son for the virgin birth, the cross, the conquest of death and the raising of man is praise of the Father, since the Son accomplished what the Father willed.
sources.quote: All the Father’s praise is from the Son, for every praise bestowed upon the Son is praise of the Father, since all that He accomplished is what the Father had willed.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Father glorified through the Son's earthly works?

question: If the name of God was always known through Moses, the Law and the prophets, what new name of God did the Son reveal to men?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: He revealed God as Father, Father of the Only-begotten Son. Though men always knew the name of God, they were truly ignorant of him. No one knows God unless he confesses him as Father of a true Son, born of him and retaining the full Godhead.
sources.quote: For no man knows God unless He confess Him as Father, Father of the Only-begotten Son
sources.raw_question: If the name of God was always known through Moses, the Law and the prophets, what new name of God did the Son reveal to men?

question: How does the Son's being the good show that he has always been the object of the Father's will and is joined to the Father without intermediary?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He then discusses the “willing” of the Father concerning the generation of the Son, and shows that the object of that good will is from eternity, which is the Son, existing in the Father, and being closely related to the process of willing, as the ray to the flame, or the act of seeing to the eye.
sources.answer: The Son is by nature the good, or rather beyond all good. The good never fails to be the object of the Father's will. Since God's will always possesses its object, the Son is conjoined to the Father without any intermediary, and the Father's will remains present rather than excluded.
sources.quote: Since, then, the Only-begotten God is by nature the good (or rather beyond all good), and since the good does not fail to be the object of the Father’s will
sources.raw_question: How does the Son's being the good show that he has always been the object of the Father's will and is joined to the Father without intermediary?

question: Will faith continue to exist once the soul comes to see God face to face?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > There is a Kind of Trinity in the Holding, Contemplating, and Loving of Faith Temporal, But One that Does Not Yet Attain to Being Properly an Image of God.
sources.answer: No. Faith believes what is not seen. When this pilgrimage ends and sight succeeds it, there will be no more faith but sight, which sees what was believed. The past faith will be remembered only as something past and done with.
sources.quote: For then it will be no longer faith, by which that is believed which is not seen; but sight, by which that is seen which is believed.
sources.raw_question: Will faith continue to exist once the soul comes to see God face to face?

question: Why did Christ, the Mediator of life, undergo bodily death rather than avoiding it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Devil the Mediator of Death, Christ of Life.
sources.answer: Men fear the death of the flesh, which they cannot escape, more than ungodliness, which is the death of the spirit and can be guarded against through faith. Christ underwent bodily death to show that this death is not to be feared, but rather ungodliness. In this way, as death came by one man, the resurrection of the dead also came by one man.
sources.quote: the Mediator of life, making it plain that death is not to be feared, which by the condition of humanity cannot now be escaped, but rather ungodliness, which can be guarded against through faith
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ, the Mediator of life, undergo bodily death rather than avoiding it?

question: Does reconciliation by the death of Christ mean that God the Father was angry with us and was appeased only when he saw the Son's death, while the Son was already favourable?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > A Difficulty, How We are Justified in the Blood of the Son of God.
sources.answer: No. The Father loved us before the Son died for us, indeed before the creation of the world, since he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world. He also did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us, which shows his love came first. So the death of the Son did not change a wrathful Father into a loving one.
sources.quote: But I see that the Father loved us also before, not only before the Son died for us, but before He created the world
sources.raw_question: Does reconciliation by the death of Christ mean that God the Father was angry with us and was appeased only when he saw the Son's death, while the Son was already favourable?

question: Was the Son delivered up to death by the Father against his own will?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > A Difficulty, How We are Justified in the Blood of the Son of God.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says the Father did not spare his Son but delivered him up. It also says of the Son that he "loved me, and delivered up Himself for me." The Son therefore gave himself willingly, in the same act in which the Father gave him.
sources.quote: Nor was the Son delivered up for us as it were unwillingly, the Father Himself not sparing Him; for it is said also concerning Him, “Who loved me, and delivered up Himself for me.”
sources.raw_question: Was the Son delivered up to death by the Father against his own will?

question: Does Christ take delight and honour in his marriage relation with sinners, and how does Song of Solomon 3:11 show this?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. In Song of Solomon 3:11 Christ calls others to behold him on the day of his espousals, which is both his honour and his delight. It is his coronation day, and his spouse is the crown with which he is crowned. It is also the day of the gladness of his heart. He rejoiced in it from eternity, willingly undertook the cross to gain his bride, and is crowned by believers, who are his mother and brethren.
sources.quote: It is the gladness of the heart of Christ, the joy of his soul, to take poor sinners into this relation with himself. He rejoiced in the thoughts of it from eternity, Prov. viii. 31
sources.raw_question: Does Christ take delight and honour in his marriage relation with sinners, and how does Song of Solomon 3:11 show this?

question: Can a small theological term, rightly or wrongly used, carry great weight for true religion?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Prefatory remarks on the need of exact investigation of the most minute portions of theology.
sources.answer: Yes. Basil notes that the two syllables Yea and Nay can separate Truth from a Lie, and a martyr has fulfilled the claim of true religion merely by nodding his head. Since not one jot or tittle of the law passes away, no term in theology is so small that its right or wrong use lacks great effect; such terms are small in use but great in the force of their meaning.
sources.quote: what term in theology is so small but that the effect of its weight in the scales according as it be rightly or wrongly used is not great?
sources.raw_question: Can a small theological term, rightly or wrongly used, carry great weight for true religion?

question: When the Lord went before Israel in the pillar of cloud and fire, did God appear in his own substance or through a created bodily thing?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Of the Appearance in the Pillar of Cloud and of Fire.
sources.answer: Through a created bodily thing. Augustine holds that no one could doubt that God appeared to mortal eyes by means of a corporeal creature made subject to him, not by his own substance, which remains invisible.
sources.quote: Who here, too, would doubt that God appeared to the eyes of mortal men by the corporeal creature made subject to Him, and not by His own substance?
sources.raw_question: When the Lord went before Israel in the pillar of cloud and fire, did God appear in his own substance or through a created bodily thing?

question: Can a Sabellian or Arian account of God satisfy the data of Scripture and of Christian experience of salvation?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Neither the Sabellian nor the Arian construction could meet the data of the consciousness of salvation, any more than the data of Scriptural revelation. The dissatisfied Christian consciousness kept searching the Scriptures and never rested until a valid doctrine of the Trinity gave consistent formulation to the Scriptural data.
sources.quote: Neither the Sabellian nor the Arian construction could meet and satisfy the data of the consciousness of salvation, any more than either could meet and satisfy the data of the Scriptural revelation.
sources.raw_question: Can a Sabellian or Arian account of God satisfy the data of Scripture and of Christian experience of salvation?

question: If God required full satisfaction from Christ and abated nothing, does that leave believers owing gratitude only to the Son and not to God the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. Owen treats this as a repetition of the earlier objection. God's love consisted in giving his Son to make satisfaction, and the obligation to thankfulness and obedience extends to God. Fundamental truths are not to be moved by mere exclamations.
sources.quote: Wherein the love of God in this matter consisted, and what is the obligation on us unto thankfulness and obedience, has been before also declared
sources.raw_question: If God required full satisfaction from Christ and abated nothing, does that leave believers owing gratitude only to the Son and not to God the Father?

question: Who is the seed of the woman who is to tread on the serpent's head in Genesis 3:15?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIII.—Arguments in opposition to Tatian, showing that it was consonant to divine justice and mercy that the first Adam should first partake in that salvation offered to all by Christ.
sources.answer: It is Christ, born of Mary. God placed enmity between the serpent and the woman's seed until the appointed seed came to crush the serpent's head. The prophet's words about trampling the asp, the lion and the dragon mean that Christ deprives sin and death of their power and tramples down antichrist. He also binds the old serpent and subjects him to the man who had been conquered.
sources.quote: until the seed did come appointed to tread down his head,—which was born of Mary, of whom the prophet speaks: “Thou shalt tread upon the asp and the basilisk; thou shalt trample down the lion and the dragon;”
sources.raw_question: Who is the seed of the woman who is to tread on the serpent's head in Genesis 3:15?

question: If believers are not saved by good works, why are good works necessary at all?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Because God has ordained that we should walk in them. Owen finds this in Ephesians 2:10, and it is ground enough for our obedience whatever its use. God's will that we be holy is by itself enough to make obedience our duty.
sources.quote: An assertion of the necessity of good works, notwithstanding that we are not saved by them; and that is, that God has ordained that we shall walk in them
sources.raw_question: If believers are not saved by good works, why are good works necessary at all?

question: Can the Son's power be a measured portion 'allotted from above', proportioned to the quantity of things created?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > Eunomius again speaks of the Son as Lord and God, and Maker of all creation intelligible and sensible, having received from the Father the power and the commission for creation, being entrusted with the task of creation as if He were an artizan commissioned by some one hiring Him, and receiving His power of creation as a thing adventitious, ab extra, as a result of the power allotted to Him in accordance with such and such combinations and positions of the stars, as destiny decrees their lot in life to men at their nativity. Thus, passing by most of what Eunomius had written, he confutes his blasphemy that the Maker of all things came into being in like manner with the earth and with angels, and that the subsistence of the Only-begotten differs not at all from the genesis of all things, and reproaches Him with reverencing neither the Divine mystery nor the custom of the Church, nor following in his attempt to discover godliness any teacher of pious doctrine, but Manichæus, Colluthus, Arius, Aetius, and those like to them, supposing that Christianity in general is folly, and that the customs of the Church and the venerable sacraments are a jest, wherein he differs in nothing from the pagans, who borrowed from our doctrine the idea of a great God supreme over all. So, too, this new idolater preaches in the same fashion, and in particular that baptism is “into an artificer and creator,” not fearing the curse of those who cause addition or diminution to the Holy Scriptures. And he closes his book with showing him to be Antichrist.
sources.answer: No. Such an allotment treats the Son's generation like astrological destiny, which assigns men their faculties at birth. It also confines within limits him who is above all rule, authority, dominion and every name. The Son's power is not a measured share given to him from outside.
sources.quote: there has been allotted, as though He were pent in some hollow spaces, power from on high, measured out in accordance with the quantity of things which come into being.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's power be a measured portion 'allotted from above', proportioned to the quantity of things created?

question: Is God to be sought far off in the heavens and the depths of the earth, or within us?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Of True Love, by Which We Arrive at the Knowledge of the Trinity. God is to Be Sought, Not Outwardly, by Seeking to Do Wonderful Things with the Angels, But Inwardly, by Imitating the Piety of Good Angels.
sources.answer: Within us. Since "God is Love" and humility rather than pride brings rest in him, as Christ taught saying "Learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart," there is no need to run to the heights of heaven or the depths of the earth to find him who is within us.
sources.quote: Behold, “God is Love:” why do we go forth and run to the heights of the heavens and the lowest parts of the earth, seeking Him who is within us, if we wish to be with Him?
sources.raw_question: Is God to be sought far off in the heavens and the depths of the earth, or within us?

question: In Romans 8:11, do the 'mortal bodies' that the Spirit of him who raised Jesus will quicken refer to souls, to the spirit, or to the flesh?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VII.—Inasmuch as Christ did rise in our flesh, it follows that we shall be also raised in the same; since the resurrection promised to us should not be referred to spirits naturally immortal, but to bodies in themselves mortal.
sources.answer: They refer to the flesh. The soul is the incorporeal breath of life and is not mortal, and the spirit cannot be called a mortal body. Only the moulded flesh dies and decomposes, so it alone can be the 'mortal body' that God will bring to life.
sources.quote: What therefore is there left to which we may apply the term “mortal body,” unless it be the thing that was moulded, that is, the flesh, of which it is also said that God will vivify it?
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who deny the resurrection of the flesh
sources.raw_question: In Romans 8:11, do the 'mortal bodies' that the Spirit of him who raised Jesus will quicken refer to souls, to the spirit, or to the flesh?

question: Is the God who promised through the prophet Joel to pour out his Spirit the same God who actually sent the Holy Spirit at Pentecost?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter interprets the Pentecost outpouring as the fulfilment of Joel's prophecy, so the God who promised by the prophet to send his Spirit upon all flesh is the very one who sent it. God himself is thus announced by Peter as having fulfilled his own promise, which excludes any different God behind the apostolic gospel.
sources.quote: The God, therefore, who did promise by the prophet, that He would send His Spirit upon the whole human race, was He who did send; and God Himself is announced by Peter as having fulfilled His own promise.
sources.raw_question: Is the God who promised through the prophet Joel to pour out his Spirit the same God who actually sent the Holy Spirit at Pentecost?

question: How does Peter's Pentecost sermon describe the relations between the Father, the exalted Jesus, and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Peter teaches that Jesus, exalted by the right hand of God, received from the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost. Jesus then poured forth that gift on the disciples. The one God the Father is thus the source of the Spirit's sending through the risen Christ, without any second God or divided Christ.
sources.quote: who, being exalted by the right hand of God, receiving from the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, hath shed forth this gift[^3472] which ye now see and hear.
sources.raw_question: How does Peter's Pentecost sermon describe the relations between the Father, the exalted Jesus, and the Holy Spirit?

question: Does a difference in the manner of origin, such as begetting versus making, imply a difference in nature between those who share a substance?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: No. Adam was moulded and Abel was born by copulation, yet both have the same definition of being, since each was mortal, reasoning, and capable of intuition and science. The order and manner of coming into existence make no difference to the nature. So in God, the Father and the Son differing in origin does not undermine their oneness of nature.
sources.quote: If, then, the idea of humanity in Adam and Abel does not vary with the difference of their origin, neither the order nor the manner of their coming into existence making any difference in their nature
sources.raw_question: Does a difference in the manner of origin, such as begetting versus making, imply a difference in nature between those who share a substance?

question: When the early Fathers (Theophilus, Tatian, Hippolytus, Tertullian) said God was 'not alone' before the generation of the Word, did they mean merely that God had his own attributes, or that a distinct Person was with him?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: They meant a distinct Person. Waterland argues it is hard to make sense of 'not alone' if it meant only that God had his attributes; rather, they held God was alone only with respect to things outside himself, but within himself he was not single, having the Logos always with him as a plurality.
sources.quote: Alone, indeed, they own him to have been, with respect to any thing ad eatra; but with respect to what was in himself, he was not alone; not single, but consisting of a plurality, having the Λόγος always with him.
sources.raw_question: When the early Fathers (Theophilus, Tatian, Hippolytus, Tertullian) said God was 'not alone' before the generation of the Word, did they mean merely that God had his own attributes, or that a distinct Person was with him?

question: How can Fathers who say God was not 'sermonalis' from the beginning be reconciled with those who call Christ the eternal Word of the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: By distinguishing two respects of the one Word. As inward speech from the eternal Mind, the Word was always with God; as God's agent sounding forth his wisdom in external works, he 'existed' as such only from the creation. So both statements can be understood in a sound sense.
sources.quote: The Word, as he is nward “ speech formed from the eternal Mind, was for ever with God : “ but as God’s agent to display and sound forth the wisdom of “ς God in external works, as such, he existed not till the creation
sources.raw_question: How can Fathers who say God was not 'sermonalis' from the beginning be reconciled with those who call Christ the eternal Word of the Father?

question: Can the truths contained in Scripture be proved by anything other than Scripture itself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus says that proofs of the things contained in the Scriptures can only be shown from the Scriptures themselves. This is why he gathers apostolic texts at length and asks the reader not to find his method prolix.
sources.quote: proofs [of the things which are] contained in the Scriptures cannot be shown except from the Scriptures themselves.
sources.raw_question: Can the truths contained in Scripture be proved by anything other than Scripture itself?

question: Was Christ the object of the hope, desire, and delight of believers in the Old Testament, before his incarnation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. From the foundation of the world Christ has been the hope, expectation, desire, and delight of all believers. The promise of him was what God gave Adam in his distress (Gen. 3:15), Abraham rejoiced to see Christ's day from two thousand years off (John 8:56), and Jacob comforted himself by waiting for God's salvation, meaning the one who was to save his people.
sources.quote: He hath, from the foundation of the world, been the hope, expectation, desire, and delight of all believers. The promise of him was all (and it was enough) that God gave Adam in his inexpressible distress, to relieve and comfort him
sources.raw_question: Was Christ the object of the hope, desire, and delight of believers in the Old Testament, before his incarnation?

question: What does the faith received from the apostles teach about God the Father, Christ Jesus, and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter X.—Unity of the faith of the Church throughout the whole world.
sources.answer: It confesses one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven, earth, the sea and all in them; one Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who became incarnate for our salvation; and the Holy Spirit, who proclaimed through the prophets God's dispensations. Irenaeus holds that the whole Church received this threefold confession from the apostles and their disciples and holds it everywhere.
sources.quote: [She believes] in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them; and in one Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who became incarnate for our salvation; and in the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: What does the faith received from the apostles teach about God the Father, Christ Jesus, and the Holy Spirit?

question: Can a more learned or eloquent teacher add to the faith about God and Christ, or a less able one diminish it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter X.—Unity of the faith of the Church throughout the whole world.
sources.answer: No. The faith is ever one and the same, handed down in harmony by all the Churches throughout the world. Greater ability lets one explain it more fully, but cannot change its substance. No teacher is greater than the Master.
sources.quote: For the faith being ever one and the same, neither does one who is able at great length to discourse regarding it, make any addition to it, nor does one, who can say but little diminish it.
sources.raw_question: Can a more learned or eloquent teacher add to the faith about God and Christ, or a less able one diminish it?

question: If the Trinity works indivisibly, how can a voice from heaven manifest the person of the Father alone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: The whole Trinity produces the voice, but it is produced in such a way as to manifest only the Father's person. The same is true of the human form taken from the Virgin Mary: the Trinity wrought it, yet it is the person of the Son alone. The invisible Trinity wrought the visible person of the Son alone.
sources.quote: Not that the voice could be wrought without the work of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (since the Trinity works indivisibly), but that such a voice was wrought as to manifest the person of the Father only
sources.raw_question: If the Trinity works indivisibly, how can a voice from heaven manifest the person of the Father alone?

question: Does the human nature of Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, belong to the Son alone even though it was made by the whole Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: Yes. The Trinity wrought the human form from the Virgin Mary, yet it is the person of the Son alone. The invisible Trinity jointly produced the visible person of the Son alone.
sources.quote: just as the Trinity wrought that human form from the Virgin Mary, yet it is the person of the Son alone; for the invisible Trinity wrought the visible person of the Son alone.
sources.raw_question: Does the human nature of Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, belong to the Son alone even though it was made by the whole Trinity?

question: Is the God whom the angels and sons of God are commanded to worship in Deuteronomy 32:43 the Son, and not only the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. Moses' blessing on Joseph invokes 'Him that appeared in the bush', who was the Angel of God. So the God worshipped by the sons and angels of God is the one who is himself God's Son and Angel. In any case the Father is honoured in the Son.
sources.quote: Thus God is to be worshipped by the sons of God; but God Who is Himself the Son of God. And God is to be reverenced by the angels of God; but God Who is Himself the Angel of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the God whom the angels and sons of God are commanded to worship in Deuteronomy 32:43 the Son, and not only the Father?

question: How do the virtues such as wisdom, goodness, and justice relate to God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > God is Above All Things, Himself Containing All Things, Immense, Eternal, Transcending the Mind of Man; Inexplicable in Discourse, Loftier Than All Sublimity.
sources.answer: God exceeds all of them: He is wiser than all wisdom, better than all goodness, juster than all justice. All virtues are less than He, since He is the God and Parent of all virtues, so that nothing can be compared to Him.
sources.quote: For all kinds of virtues must needs be less than Himself, who is both. God and Parent of all virtues, so that it may truly be said that God is that, which is such that nothing can be compared to Him.
sources.raw_question: How do the virtues such as wisdom, goodness, and justice relate to God?

question: Does the unity of the early believers, whose "heart and soul were one" (Acts 4:32), show that unity can be a mere agreement of will, as the Arians use it to explain the unity of Father and Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. The believers were one through faith, and that faith is one, as the Apostle teaches one faith, one Lord, one baptism, one hope and one God. They were born again into the nature of one life and eternity. So their unity is a unity of nature by regeneration, and mere unity of will does not account for it.
sources.quote: If, however, they have been begotten again into the nature of one life and eternity, then, inasmuch as their soul and heart are one, the unity of will fails to account for their case who are one by regeneration into the same nature.
sources.raw_question: Does the unity of the early believers, whose "heart and soul were one" (Acts 4:32), show that unity can be a mere agreement of will, as the Arians use it to explain the unity of Father and Son?

question: Do the Old Testament instances of prayer to the Angel of the Lord (Abraham's intercession for Sodom, Jacob's wrestling, Jacob's blessing of his grandsons) constitute direct prayer to the Son of God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The one with whom Abraham interceded and with whom Jacob wrestled was God the Son, since Hosea says Jacob 'had power with God; yea, he had power with the Angel.' Jacob's prayer to 'the Angel which redeemed me from all evil' to bless the lads is likewise addressed to the Son. In all these instances there is direct prayer to Christ.
sources.quote: It was God the Son with whom Jacob wrestled in prayer, for we are told – “he had power with God; yea, he had power with the Angel and prevailed,”
sources.raw_question: Do the Old Testament instances of prayer to the Angel of the Lord (Abraham's intercession for Sodom, Jacob's wrestling, Jacob's blessing of his grandsons) constitute direct prayer to the Son of God?

question: Do John (who says Isaiah saw the Son's glory) and Paul (who says the Holy Spirit spoke to Isaiah) contradict each other?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXII. In proof of the Unity in Trinity the passage of Isaiah which has been cited is considered, and it is shown that there is no difference as to its sense amongst those who expound it of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Spirit. If He Who was crucified was Lord of glory, so, too, is the Holy Spirit equal in all things to the Father and the Son, and the Arians will never be able to diminish His glory.
sources.answer: No. The difference is of words, not of meaning, and neither is in error. The Father is seen in the Son, as Christ said "He that seeth Me seeth the Father," and the Son is seen in the Spirit, since no one says "Lord Jesus" except in the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: There is, indeed, a difference of words, not of meaning. For though they said different things, neither was in error, for both the Father is seen in the Son
sources.raw_question: Do John (who says Isaiah saw the Son's glory) and Paul (who says the Holy Spirit spoke to Isaiah) contradict each other?

question: When Christ became obedient in His Passion, did He give up His free will and sovereign authority?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: No. The obedience Paul speaks of belongs to the incarnation, when He became flesh, a servant, a curse and sin for our sakes. Even then the Lord of glory kept His free will. He said He had power to lay down His life and take it again. He made the armed band fall back by saying 'I am He,' and He promised Paradise to the thief. So His Passion gives no ground for subordinating the King of glory to authority.
sources.quote: If then not even in the time of His Passion He is separated from His authority, where can heresy possibly discern the subordination to authority of the King of glory?
sources.raw_question: When Christ became obedient in His Passion, did He give up His free will and sovereign authority?

question: How should the saying in Peter that Christ received honour and glory, with angels made subject to him, be understood?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: 'He received' is said of Him humanly, while the subjection of the angels marks the Word's Godhead. It is like His asking where Lazarus lay as man and raising him as God.
sources.quote: As He inquired humanly, and raised Lazarus divinely, so ‘He received’ is spoken of Him humanly, but the subjection of the Angels marks the Word’s Godhead.
sources.raw_question: How should the saying in Peter that Christ received honour and glory, with angels made subject to him, be understood?

question: Why do Christ's actions in the Gospels show both divine power and human affections, often at once?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: Because He was Very God in the flesh and true flesh in the Word. Through His works He revealed Himself as Son of God and revealed His Father. Through the affections of the flesh He showed that His body was real and His own, as when He asked about Lazarus and then raised him, or said His hour had not come and then made water wine.
sources.quote: For He was Very God in the flesh, and He was true flesh in the Word. Therefore from His works He revealed both Himself as Son of God, and His own Father
sources.raw_question: Why do Christ's actions in the Gospels show both divine power and human affections, often at once?

question: Why is Christ's love able to produce the good it wishes for its objects, when human love often cannot help those it loves?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Because the love of Christ is the love of God, and so it is effectual. Human love may pity a friend but cannot relieve him, or love grace into a child. For Christ, to love is properly to will good to someone, and his willing actually brings about that good. He loves life, grace and holiness into his people, and loves them into the covenant and into heaven.
sources.quote: But now the love of Christ, being the love of God, is effectual and fruitful in producing all the good things which he willeth unto his beloved.
sources.raw_question: Why is Christ's love able to produce the good it wishes for its objects, when human love often cannot help those it loves?

question: Does God need the sacrifices, oblations and ritual obedience that the Mosaic law required of men?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVII.—Proof that God did not appoint the Levitical dispensation for His own sake, or as requiring such service; for He does, in fact, need nothing from men.
sources.answer: No. God stands in need of nothing. He commanded these observances for the sake of the people who offered them, not for His own benefit. In Psalm 50 He says that every beast of the earth and the whole world belong to Him already, and that He does not eat flesh or drink blood. Isaiah likewise has God say, "I am full."
sources.quote: the prophets indicate in the fullest manner that God stood in no need of their slavish obedience, but that it was upon their own account that He enjoined certain observances in the law
sources.raw_question: Does God need the sacrifices, oblations and ritual obedience that the Mosaic law required of men?

question: Is the impassible Word harmed by taking on human passions, and what effect does his bearing them have on humanity?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: He is not harmed; he obliterates and destroys the passions. Because human passions are changed and abolished in the Impassible, men themselves become impassible and free from them for ever. As the Lord became man by putting on a body, so men are deified by being taken to the Word through his flesh.
sources.quote: as the Lord, putting on the body, became man, so we men are deified by the Word as being taken to Him through His flesh, and henceforward inherit life ‘everlasting.’
sources.raw_question: Is the impassible Word harmed by taking on human passions, and what effect does his bearing them have on humanity?

question: How can flesh that is by nature mortal and earthly rise and become free from hunger, suffering and death?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: It can, because it has become the Word's own flesh. The Word 'carried' its affections, though he is without them, and so freed it from them. To object to the flesh's deliverance from natural corruption is in effect to object to the Word's taking the form of a servant.
sources.quote: ‘I am from earth, being by nature mortal, but afterwards I have become the Word’s flesh,’ and He ‘carried’ my affections, though He is without them; and so I became free from them
sources.raw_question: How can flesh that is by nature mortal and earthly rise and become free from hunger, suffering and death?

question: How does 1 John 5:7, on the three that bear record in heaven, show distinct communion with the Father, Word, and Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: It shows that the three bear witness as three distinct witnesses to Christ's sonship and believers' salvation. Since we must receive God's testimony as he gives it, we receive each person's testimony severally. In giving and receiving this testimony we have communion with them severally.
sources.quote: The Father beareth witness, the Son beareth witness, and the Holy Spirit beareth witness; for they are three distinct witnesses. So, then, are we to receive their several testimonies: and in doing so we have communion with them severally
sources.raw_question: How does 1 John 5:7, on the three that bear record in heaven, show distinct communion with the Father, Word, and Holy Spirit?

question: Who was the one who appeared to Abraham as a man and was worshipped by him as God and Judge?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: It was the true God, the Son of God. The one who appeared as Man was worshipped as God and proclaimed as Judge, and Abraham, worshipping with full knowledge, was not blind to the fact that it was true God he worshipped. This appearance was a type preparing for the Son's actual birth as Man.
sources.quote: for the present, we are shewing from the Law that it was true God, the Son of God, Who appeared to the Patriarchs in human form.
sources.raw_question: Who was the one who appeared to Abraham as a man and was worshipped by him as God and Judge?

question: Does the fact that Christ's history contradicts the common course of nature (the Unchangeable growing, the Impassible suffering) count against His Godhead?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No, it proves it. That the Eternal was born, the Impassible suffered, and the Living died is simply to say that He, being God, was omnipotent. There could have been no acceptance of our feeble nature unless by His omnipotent nature He came to be what He was not while remaining what He was.
sources.quote: Is not all this simply to say that He, being God, was omnipotent?
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Christ's history contradicts the common course of nature (the Unchangeable growing, the Impassible suffering) count against His Godhead?

question: Can a spiritual being that proceeds from the divine light receive its form and perfection from matter, which the Gnostics themselves call darkness and defect?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIX.—Absurdities of the heretics as to their own origin: their opinions respecting the Demiurge shown to be equally untenable and ridiculous.
sources.answer: No. If the light from the Pleroma left the seed formless and matter then perfected it, matter would prove more effective than the Father's light, which is absurd. The Gnostics also teach that the earthly is opposed to the spiritual. So a spiritual particle could not grow and be perfected among substances contrary and foreign to it.
sources.quote: then a sojourn here (which they also term darkness) would seem much more efficacious and useful than was the light of their Father.
sources.raw_question: Can a spiritual being that proceeds from the divine light receive its form and perfection from matter, which the Gnostics themselves call darkness and defect?

question: If Christ made full satisfaction for sin, does the guilty person's acquittal follow automatically ('ipso facto')?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: No. Substituting one person to suffer for another rests on a voluntary compact, and it requires a relaxation of the law as to who is punished, though not as to the punishment itself. In criminal guilt the person, not merely a debt, is principally under the obligation. So even when the substitute suffers the very same punishment, deliverance comes only on the terms fixed in the covenant. This differs from a money debt, which ceases once anyone pays it.
sources.quote: deliverance of the guilty persons cannot ensue “ipso facto,” but by the intervention of the terms fixed on in the covenant or agreement for an admittance of the substitution.
sources.raw_question: If Christ made full satisfaction for sin, does the guilty person's acquittal follow automatically ('ipso facto')?

question: Does Psalm 102:25-27, which describes the one who laid the foundations of the earth and remains unchangeable while the heavens perish, refer to the Son of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: Yes. Owen notes that the apostle explicitly declares this psalm to be spoken of the Son in Hebrews 1:10-12. The Son is therefore the creator of heaven and earth, eternal and unchangeable, which are attributes of God alone.
sources.quote: but thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end.” Declared by the apostle to be meant of the Son, Heb. i. 10–12.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 102:25-27, which describes the one who laid the foundations of the earth and remains unchangeable while the heavens perish, refer to the Son of God?

question: Does the fact that divine realities are prefigured by small, human types imply that those divine realities are themselves small?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Objection that some were baptized unto Moses and believed in him, and an answer to it; with remarks upon types.
sources.answer: No. A type is an imitative anticipation of things to come, and the divine nature is often represented by rough, shadowy outlines. One must not judge the reality by the shadow. Otherwise God's love in giving his Son would not be great because Abraham offered Isaac, and Christ's passion would not be glorious because a sheep typified it.
sources.quote: because divine things are prefigured by small and human things, it is obvious that we must not therefore conclude the divine nature to be small. The type is an exhibition of things expected, and gives an imitative anticipation of the future.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that divine realities are prefigured by small, human types imply that those divine realities are themselves small?

question: Does the text "The people believed the Lord and his servant Moses" show that faith in the Holy Spirit is no more significant than faith in a creature?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Objection that some were baptized unto Moses and believed in him, and an answer to it; with remarks upon types.
sources.answer: No. Moses is joined there with God, not with the Spirit, and he was a type not of the Spirit but of Christ the Mediator. Faith in Moses therefore points to the Lord. Our faith in Christ is not made a trifle by being foreshadowed through Moses, so neither is the grace of the Spirit given in baptism.
sources.quote: Moses then is joined with God, not with the Spirit; and he was a type not of the Spirit, but of Christ.
sources.raw_question: Does the text "The people believed the Lord and his servant Moses" show that faith in the Holy Spirit is no more significant than faith in a creature?

question: Why did the Son of God take human flesh and die on the cross?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: He took the flesh in which we sinned so that by wearing it—without sinning in it—He might forgive sins. He blotted out the sentence of death through death, renewing our race in Himself, and was nailed to the cross to abolish the curses on the world; the Immortal died so that mortals might gain eternity.
sources.quote: For He took upon Him the flesh in which we have sinned that by wearing our flesh He might forgive sins; a flesh which He shares with us by wearing it, not by sinning in it.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Son of God take human flesh and die on the cross?

question: Should Christ's becoming Son of Man and dying for us be used as an argument against his divinity?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. His dying was to assure us that he had assumed true humanity, while he remained secure of his divinity; signs on the cross like promising Paradise show him to be God the King. To turn the confession that the Son of God became man and died for us into a weapon against his divinity is godless unbelief.
sources.quote: why should we use this very confession of the Son of God that for us He became Son of Man and died as the chief weapon to deny His divinity?
sources.raw_question: Should Christ's becoming Son of Man and dying for us be used as an argument against his divinity?

question: What role does the Holy Spirit play in the prayers of believers according to Romans 8:26?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: The Spirit assists believers so that their hearts labour with desires larger than their words can express, making intercession with groans that cannot be uttered. Such a person finds his best prayers fall short of the holy desires the Spirit has conceived in him: the more he speaks, the more he finds left unspoken.
sources.quote: therefore, in and after their supplications, “the Spirit makes intercession with sighs and groans that cannot be [^235]uttered.” Some men’s words go exceedingly beyond their hearts.
sources.raw_question: What role does the Holy Spirit play in the prayers of believers according to Romans 8:26?

question: How can believers know they are praying according to the will of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: One sure way is to pray according to the promise, regulating requests by God's word of promise, as David did. Owen sets two conditions. The things asked must be viewed as promised in Christ, hoped for only through his mediation and purchase. They must also be asked for the promise's own end, which is holiness, and not to spend on our lusts.
sources.quote: When we ask what is in the promise, as it is in the promise, to this end of the promise, our supplications are according to the will of God.
sources.raw_question: How can believers know they are praying according to the will of God?

question: Must someone who truly says 'I do not know' already know what knowing is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Love of the Studious Mind, that Is, of One Desirous to Know, is Not the Love of a Thing Which It Does Not Know.
sources.answer: Yes. Anyone who confidently and truly says 'I know' or 'I do not know' must know what knowing is. Looking into himself, he distinguishes the one who knows from the one who does not. Since he knows that his statement is true, he could not know this without knowing what knowing is.
sources.quote: he also who says, I do not know, and says so confidently and truly, and knows that he says so truly, certainly knows what knowing is
sources.raw_question: Must someone who truly says 'I do not know' already know what knowing is?

question: Is the trust Christians are required to place in Christ the same as the trust they are required to place in God the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. It is one and the same trust. Christ himself says, "Believe in God: believe also in me," and he insists that all men honour the Son even as they honour the Father. He also claims to give eternal life and to raise his people at the last day, which are divine prerogatives.
sources.quote: But is this trust altogether identical with that we are required to repose in the Father? It is one and the same. He says, “Believe in God: believe also in me.”
sources.raw_question: Is the trust Christians are required to place in Christ the same as the trust they are required to place in God the Father?

question: What does the opening of Ephesians show about the place of Jesus Christ relative to God the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: It shows that Christ is the coordinate source of grace with the Father, and the one in whom every spiritual blessing comes to us. The benediction comes from God our Father and coordinately from the Lord Jesus Christ. Election, adoption, acceptance and redemption all come "in Him," so believers owe everything to Christ and must say, "O Lord, my trust is in Thee."
sources.quote: The benediction is given from God our Father, and coordinately “from the Lord Jesus Christ”.
sources.raw_question: What does the opening of Ephesians show about the place of Jesus Christ relative to God the Father?

question: Does the Word of God, in becoming flesh and being born of the Virgin as Immanuel, cease to be the Mighty God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: No. The prophets who proclaimed Immanuel born of the Virgin showed the union of the Word of God with his own workmanship: the Word became flesh and the Son of God became Son of man. Yet having become what we are, he is nevertheless the Mighty God and has a generation that cannot be declared.
sources.quote: and having become this which we also are, He [nevertheless] is the Mighty God, and possesses a generation which cannot be declared
sources.raw_question: Does the Word of God, in becoming flesh and being born of the Virgin as Immanuel, cease to be the Mighty God?

question: Do Old Testament texts that speak of God coming, such as 'God comes from the south' and 'In Judah is God known', refer to the advent of Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus reads these texts as prophecies of Christ's coming in Judea and his birth at Bethlehem. In doing so he treats the God whose coming they announce as Christ himself, who rules and feeds the people of his Father.
sources.quote: Those, again, who declare that “God comes from the south, and from a mountain thick with foliage,” announced His advent at Bethlehem
sources.raw_question: Do Old Testament texts that speak of God coming, such as 'God comes from the south' and 'In Judah is God known', refer to the advent of Christ?

question: Why did Christ, the holy Lord, undergo his sufferings and death?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: He suffered in order to save the dead. Prophecy said that 'the holy Lord remembered His own dead ones who slept in the dust, and came down to them to raise them up'. Irenaeus takes this as giving the reason for all of Christ's sufferings: to raise them up and save them.
sources.quote: “The holy Lord remembered His own dead ones who slept in the dust, and came down to them to raise them up, that He might save them,” furnished us with the reason on account of which He suffered all these things
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ, the holy Lord, undergo his sufferings and death?

question: What do Christ's promises of the Paraclete teach about how the Holy Spirit relates to the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Next Teaches Us that the Authority of the Faith Enjoins, After the Father and the Son, to Believe Also on the Holy Spirit, Whose Operations He Enumerates from Scripture.
sources.answer: The Spirit is "another Advocate" whom the Father gives at the Son's request. The Son sends him from the Father, and he proceeds from the Father. He is the Spirit of truth who guides the disciples into all truth. Christ gave him because he was departing, so as not to leave the disciples orphans without a protector.
sources.quote: When He, the Advocate, shall come, whom I shall send unto you from my Father, the Spirit of truth who proceedeth from my Father.
sources.raw_question: What do Christ's promises of the Paraclete teach about how the Holy Spirit relates to the Father and the Son?

question: Did the Son learn how to create from God as from a master craftsman, as Asterius claimed?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: No. If framing could be taught, God Himself might be Framer by science rather than nature and could lose the power. Moreover the Wisdom of God would not be Wisdom if it needed teaching; it would be an empty thing called Wisdom only by advancement and liable to unlearn. The Word does the Father's works not by teaching but because He is the Image and Wisdom of the Father.
sources.quote: if the Wisdom of God attained to frame by teaching, how is He still Wisdom, when He needs to learn? and what was He before He learned? For it was not Wisdom, if it needed teaching
sources.raw_question: Did the Son learn how to create from God as from a master craftsman, as Asterius claimed?

question: Can the Son be said to lack a share in the Father's estate or sovereignty?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: No. The Son has all things whatsoever the Father has, so speaking of a division of estate or sovereignty between them has no meaning. Such talk only demonstrates the impiety of the one who proposes it.
