sources.quote: But to speak of division of estate or sovereignty in the case of Him Who hath all things whatsoever that the Father hath, carries with it no meaning, unless it be a demonstration of the propounder’s impiety.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be said to lack a share in the Father's estate or sovereignty?

question: When did the Son become obedient, and was His Sonship connected with that obedience?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > After expounding the high estate of the Almighty, the Eternity of the Son, and the phrase “being made obedient,” he shows the folly of Eunomius in his assertion that the Son did not acquire His sonship by obedience.
sources.answer: The Son became obedient only in His incarnation. Paul says it once for all of the time when the Son emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled Himself to accomplish redemption by the cross. Obedience therefore belongs to the economy of salvation in His human nature, healing human disobedience. It is not an eternal condition of His Sonship or a relation the Son has with respect to creation.
sources.quote: For it was when He came in the form of a servant to accomplish the mystery of redemption by the cross, Who had emptied Himself, Who humbled Himself by assuming the likeness and fashion of a man
sources.raw_question: When did the Son become obedient, and was His Sonship connected with that obedience?

question: Why must the Word not be of created essence for our salvation to be effective?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22 Continued. Our Lord is said to be created 'for the works,' i.e. with a particular purpose, which no mere creatures are ever said to be. Parallel of Isai. xlix. 5, &c. When His manhood is spoken of, a reason for it is added; not so when His Divine Nature; Texts in proof.
sources.answer: If the Word were a creature by essence, He would not have been created for us, and we would not be created in Him; we would then have Him only externally, as a teacher. Then sin would not lose its reign over the flesh but remain inherent in it, whereas His dwelling in the flesh as the Word expels sin perfectly.
sources.quote: if not created in Him, we have Him not in ourselves but externally; as, for instance, as receiving instruction from Him as from a teacher. And it being so with us, sin has not lost its reign over the flesh
sources.raw_question: Why must the Word not be of created essence for our salvation to be effective?

question: Does 1 Corinthians 14:24-25, where the unbeliever falls down and worships God present among prophesying Christians, show that the Holy Spirit is worshipped?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVIII. As he purposes to establish the Godhead of the Holy Spirit by the points already discussed, St. Ambrose touches again on some of them; for instance, that He does not commit but forgives sin; that He is not a creature but the Creator; and lastly, that He does not offer but receives worship.
sources.answer: Yes. Prophecy is given by the Spirit, who abides and speaks in the prophets. The unbeliever worships God, declaring that God is truly among them. Since the One who abides and speaks in the prophets is the Spirit, it is the Spirit who is worshipped as God.
sources.quote: It is, therefore, God Who is worshipped, God Who abides and Who speaks in the prophets; but the Spirit thus abides and speaks, therefore, also, the Spirit is worshipped.
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Corinthians 14:24-25, where the unbeliever falls down and worships God present among prophesying Christians, show that the Holy Spirit is worshipped?

question: Does calling the Holy Spirit the 'Breath of God's mouth' imply that God has bodily members or that the Spirit is a transient breath?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases we preserve the pious dogma of the Monarchia. Wherein also is the refutation of them that allege that the Spirit is subnumerated.
sources.answer: No. The 'mouth' is not a bodily member, and the Spirit is not breath that dissolves. The word is used only so far as it fits God. The Spirit is a living Substance with supreme power of sanctification. The image shows His close relation to God while the mode of His ineffable existence stays safeguarded.
sources.quote: But in no way is the “mouth” a member, nor the Spirit breath that is dissolved; but the word “mouth” is used so far as it can be appropriate to God, and the Spirit is a Substance having life
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Holy Spirit the 'Breath of God's mouth' imply that God has bodily members or that the Spirit is a transient breath?

question: Does the theologians' maxim that 'everything in God is God' apply to all divine attributes, including immutability, omnipresence and authority?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: No. It holds only for real attributes, not for mere modalities. It makes no rational sense to say that God's being without change, or being everywhere, or having a right to govern creatures is God. But it is true of God's understanding and love, because the Deity subsists in them distinctly, and so they are distinct divine Persons.
sources.quote: It is a maxim amongst divines that everything that is in God is God which must be understood of real attributes and not of mere modalities.
sources.raw_question: Does the theologians' maxim that 'everything in God is God' apply to all divine attributes, including immutability, omnipresence and authority?

question: Does the disagreement among the founders of the Gnostic systems tell us anything about the truth of the Church's faith?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter IX.—Refutation of the impious interpretations of these heretics.
sources.answer: Yes. The fact that the fathers of these heretical systems differ among themselves, as if moved by different spirits of error, is an a priori proof. It shows that their theories are a tissue of falsehoods, while the truth proclaimed by the Church is immoveable. That single, unchanging faith is the one in one God the Father, one Christ Jesus the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: For this very fact forms an a priori proof that the truth proclaimed by the Church is immoveable, and that the theories of these men are but a tissue of falsehoods.
sources.raw_question: Does the disagreement among the founders of the Gnostic systems tell us anything about the truth of the Church's faith?

question: Why did Christ direct his disciples to offer to God the first-fruits of created things, such as bread and wine, if God needs nothing?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVII.—Proof that God did not appoint the Levitical dispensation for His own sake, or as requiring such service; for He does, in fact, need nothing from men.
sources.answer: Christ did so not because God stands in need of such offerings. He did it so that the disciples themselves might be neither unfruitful nor ungrateful. Taking bread and the cup, which belong to the creation, he called them his body and blood. In this way he taught the new oblation of the new covenant, which the Church offers to God throughout the world.
sources.quote: not as if He stood in need of them, but that they might be themselves neither unfruitful nor ungrateful
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ direct his disciples to offer to God the first-fruits of created things, such as bread and wine, if God needs nothing?

question: Why did Christ rebuke Philip for not knowing him, and how should the disciples have recognised the Father's Godhead in the Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: If they had truly known Christ, they would have recognised in him the Godhead of the Father's nature. His works were the peculiar works of God: walking on the waves, commanding the winds, forgiving sins, and raising the dead. He did these while in the flesh and declared himself the Son of God. The divine nature was acting through the Manhood he had assumed.
sources.quote: if they had known Him, they must have recognised in Him the Godhead which belongs to His Father’s nature. For His works were the peculiar works of God.
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ rebuke Philip for not knowing him, and how should the disciples have recognised the Father's Godhead in the Son?

question: Was Christ merely a man born by natural generation, as the Ebionites held?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter I.—Christ alone is able to teach divine things, and to redeem us: He, the same, took flesh of the Virgin Mary, not merely in appearance, but actually, by the operation of the Holy Spirit, in order to renovate us. Strictures on the conceits of Valentinus and Ebion.
sources.answer: No. The Holy Ghost came upon Mary and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, so that what was born is holy and is the Son of the Most High. This was a new kind of generation: as we inherited death by the former birth, we inherit life by this one. The Ebionites therefore reject the union of God and man.
sources.quote: who do not choose to understand that the Holy Ghost came upon Mary, and the power of the Most High did overshadow her: wherefore also what was generated is a holy thing, and the Son of the Most High God
sources.raw_question: Was Christ merely a man born by natural generation, as the Ebionites held?

question: Who are the 'hands of God' addressed in 'Let Us make man in Our image', and what do they do in the incarnation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter I.—Christ alone is able to teach divine things, and to redeem us: He, the same, took flesh of the Virgin Mary, not merely in appearance, but actually, by the operation of the Holy Spirit, in order to renovate us. Strictures on the conceits of Valentinus and Ebion.
sources.answer: The Word and the Spirit are the hands of God to whom the Father spoke at creation. Just as they formed Adam, in the last times they united with the ancient substance of Adam's formation, by the Father's good pleasure. In doing so they formed a living man re-created after the image and likeness of God.
sources.quote: For never at any time did Adam escape the hands of God, to whom the Father speaking, said, “Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness.”
sources.raw_question: Who are the 'hands of God' addressed in 'Let Us make man in Our image', and what do they do in the incarnation?

question: Could a being conceived outside the divine fullness, in ignorance, reveal true knowledge of divine mysteries and foretell Christ's passion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXV.—A refutation of those who allege that the prophets uttered some predictions under the inspiration of the highest, others from the Demiurge. Disagreements of the Valentinians among themselves with regard to these same predictions.
sources.answer: No. On the Gnostics' own premises, what lies outside the Pleroma lies outside knowledge, so seed conceived in ignorance could not declare knowledge. Nor could it foresee future events like Christ's passion. The prophecies of the passion also have no counterpart in their supposed higher Christ, who never drank gall or was pierced.
sources.quote: How, then, could that seed, which was conceived in ignorance, possess the power of declaring knowledge?
sources.raw_question: Could a being conceived outside the divine fullness, in ignorance, reveal true knowledge of divine mysteries and foretell Christ's passion?

question: Do the names devised by human thought for God serve to glorify or add honour to the divine life, as Eunomius alleges?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. To add honour to the Divine nature, which is above all honour, is beyond human infirmity; as the Psalmist says, our goods are nothing to Him. We use such names not to glory in God's life but to guide ourselves toward comprehending what is hidden, giving some notion of His attributes.
sources.quote: we do not seek to glory in it by the names we employ, but to guide our own selves by the aid of such terms towards the comprehension of the things which are hidden.
sources.raw_question: Do the names devised by human thought for God serve to glorify or add honour to the divine life, as Eunomius alleges?

question: Do we truly know what we learn through the bodily senses and through the testimony of others?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Academic Philosophy.
sources.answer: Yes. By the senses we have come to know heaven and earth, as far as their Creator has willed them to be within our knowledge. To deny knowledge gained from testimony would mean we did not know that there is an ocean, that distant cities exist, what history records, or even where and from whom we were born, which is absurd. So both our own senses and those of others add greatly to our knowledge.
sources.quote: we must confess, that not only our own senses, but those of other persons also, have added very much indeed to our knowledge
sources.raw_question: Do we truly know what we learn through the bodily senses and through the testimony of others?

question: If Scripture says "God called the light Day" and "the firmament Heaven," does it follow that names are of divine rather than human invention?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. God, who brought creation into being out of nothing, is Creator of things existing substantially, not of unsubstantial words existing only in sound. Scripture says God created the heaven and the earth, not their names, and made light, not the name Light. Things are named by human speech according to their inherent nature and qualities, in the vernacular of each race.
sources.quote: He Who brought all creation into being out of nothing is the Creator of things seen in substantial existence, not of unsubstantial words having no existence but in the sound of the voice and the lisp of the tongue.
sources.raw_question: If Scripture says "God called the light Day" and "the firmament Heaven," does it follow that names are of divine rather than human invention?

question: Is the God who creates by sovereign will, determining both what is good and the time of its being good, the Only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > The ninth book declares that Eunomius' account of the Nature of God is, up to a certain point, well stated. Then in succession he mixes up with his own argument, on account of its affinity, the expression from Philo's writings, “God is before all other things, which are generated,” adding also the expression, “He has dominion over His own power.” Detesting the excessive absurdity, Gregory strikingly confutes it.
sources.answer: Yes. Gregory accepts Eunomius' description of a Creator who acts without hindrance or compulsion and fixes the time of each thing's goodness, but notes that the gospel proclaims the Only-begotten God as the one who made all things, including the ages. So these attributes of sovereign creative authority belong to the Son.
sources.quote: But He Who made all things is, as the gospel proclaims, the Only-begotten God.
sources.raw_question: Is the God who creates by sovereign will, determining both what is good and the time of its being good, the Only-begotten Son?

question: Do the two natures of Christ combine into a single compound principle of operation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: No. The natures are so united that no third compound principle of physical acts arises; each nature acts distinctly according to its own being. In mediatory action one must distinguish the agent (the person), the immediate principles (the natures), the actions (operations of either nature), and the effect, which relates to the person who is God and man.
sources.quote: For the two natures are so united in Christ as not to have a third compound principle of physical acts and operations thence arising; but each nature acts distinctly according to its own being and properties
sources.raw_question: Do the two natures of Christ combine into a single compound principle of operation?

question: Did the devil hold humanity captive by some kind of right, and how was that right overcome?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: Yes, the devil held man as if by right, because man was seduced by his own consent and the captivity was just on account of sin. But the devil put the innocent Christ to death unjustly. By this Christ overcame him by a most just right, blotting out the handwriting and redeeming us through His righteous blood unrighteously poured out.
sources.quote: being Himself put to death, although innocent, by the unjust one acting against us as it were by just right, might by a most just right overcome him
sources.raw_question: Did the devil hold humanity captive by some kind of right, and how was that right overcome?

question: Why did Christ, the Son of God, submit to being tempted by the devil?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: He offered Himself to be tempted so that He might be a mediator who overcomes the devil's temptations. He helps us not only by giving succor but also by setting an example. The devil, being dead in the spirit, could force no entrance into Him who was alive in the spirit.
sources.quote: And to him, too, He offered Himself to be tempted, in order that He might be also a mediator to overcome his temptations, not only by succor, but also by example.
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ, the Son of God, submit to being tempted by the devil?

question: Does the worship of Jesus in his human body imply a worship distinct from worship of the one true God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ only he who is really God is worshipped; the Lord even in human body was worshipped and believed to be God's Son, and through him the Father was known, while idols and demons are brought to nought.
sources.quote: And the illusion of demons is come to nought, and He only who is really God is worshipped in the Name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
sources.raw_question: Does the worship of Jesus in his human body imply a worship distinct from worship of the one true God?

question: If Θεός with the article signifies the supreme God, do the inspired writers apply such texts to Christ?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: Yes. If the Septuagint uses Θεός without the article for subordinate gods, then the arthrous form denotes the supreme God; yet the apostles apply Old Testament texts having ὁ Θεός to Christ, as Paul does with Isaiah 45:22-23. Hence Christ is the supreme God by the opponent's own rule.
sources.quote: The inference I should draw from thence is, that when Θεὸς has the article prefixed, the supreme God is meant thereby.
sources.raw_question: If Θεός with the article signifies the supreme God, do the inspired writers apply such texts to Christ?

question: Is every act of knowledge a 'word' of the mind, or only knowledge that is loved?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > Whether Only Knowledge that is Loved is the Word of the Mind.
sources.answer: In the strict sense Augustine intends, only knowledge joined with love is the word of the mind. Things we know but dislike merely reach the point of being known and are not, properly speaking, conceived or brought forth by the mind. The word he seeks to discern as an image of the divine Word is 'knowledge together with love.'
sources.quote: A word, then, which is the point we wish now to discern and intimate, is knowledge together with love.
sources.raw_question: Is every act of knowledge a 'word' of the mind, or only knowledge that is loved?

question: How can 'No man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost' be reconciled with people who say 'Lord, Lord' without entering the kingdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > Whether Only Knowledge that is Loved is the Word of the Mind.
sources.answer: The two texts use 'saying' in different senses of 'word'. Paul means the word that is knowledge loved, and such confession comes only by the Holy Spirit. Those who merely say 'Lord, Lord' speak only in another, lesser sense of word.
sources.quote: And that which the apostle says, must be taken according to this last kind of word, “No man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost;”
sources.raw_question: How can 'No man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost' be reconciled with people who say 'Lord, Lord' without entering the kingdom?

question: Is the Christ who speaks through the prophets the same Christ who was born in the flesh?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Yes. Time and the lapse of ages make no difference to a Spirit. Christ is one and the same, whether in the body or abiding by the Spirit in the prophets. So the Psalm spoken through David is His own word about His future Dispensation.
sources.quote: Time and the lapse of ages make no difference to a Spirit. Christ is one and the same Christ, whether in the body, or abiding by the Spirit in the prophets.
sources.raw_question: Is the Christ who speaks through the prophets the same Christ who was born in the flesh?

question: Why does the principle that being equally true means being equally great apply to God but not to bodies like gold or to created souls?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Every Corporeal Conception Must Be Rejected, in Order that It May Be Understood How God is Truth.
sources.answer: Because in bodies and souls, magnitude and truth (reality) are different things, whereas God's essence is truth itself. Two pieces of gold can be equally real gold yet one greater than the other, and a soul can be truly a soul without being great. But the Trinity is truth itself, so in God to be true, to be, and to be great are the same.
sources.quote: since the essence of body and soul is not the essence of the truth [reality] itself; as is the Trinity, one God, alone, great, true, truthful, the truth.
sources.raw_question: Why does the principle that being equally true means being equally great apply to God but not to bodies like gold or to created souls?

question: Does 'receiving' Christ in John 1:12 refer only to the first act of faith by which a person is united to him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: No. It covers the solemn act by which one first closes with Christ, but also the constant frame of the soul in abiding with him and owning him. In this ongoing receiving the soul consents to take Christ on his own terms and to be saved merely by grace rather than by its own works. That ongoing consent is how communion with Christ, as to the grace of his person, is carried on.
sources.quote: This is called “receiving” of Christ, John i. 12; and is not intended only for that solemn act whereby at first entrance we close with him, but also for the constant frame of the soul in abiding with him and owning of him as such.
sources.raw_question: Does 'receiving' Christ in John 1:12 refer only to the first act of faith by which a person is united to him?

question: Did Basil teach that the Son is an effect of the Father, so that the Father has preeminence over the Son in nature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. Basil allowed that the Father is prior in order to the Son with respect to emanative causes and the things issuing from them, as fire is prior to the light streaming from it. However, he expressly denied any difference in nature or any priority of time. No Catholic ever called the Son an effect of the Father.
sources.quote: the Father “is prior in order to the Son: but as to any difference in “ nature, or priority of time, we allow no such thing.”
sources.raw_question: Did Basil teach that the Son is an effect of the Father, so that the Father has preeminence over the Son in nature?

question: When the Angel of God who appeared to the patriarchs is called God, is this only an honorary title received by adoption rather than true Godhead?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: No. The one who appeared, even under the lower guise of a man, was worshipped by Abraham as God and declared that all things are possible to him. Nothing is impossible to God alone, so he to whom all things are possible cannot fall short of true Divinity.
sources.quote: Is there any, but God alone, to Whom nothing is impossible? And He, to Whom all things are possible, does He fall short of true Divinity?
sources.raw_question: When the Angel of God who appeared to the patriarchs is called God, is this only an honorary title received by adoption rather than true Godhead?

question: How does Scripture show that the divine Persons act distinctly in giving grace to believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Scripture does this in two ways. First, the same blessing is ascribed jointly yet distinctly to all three Persons, as when grace and peace come from him who is, from the seven Spirits, and from Jesus Christ (Rev. 1:4-5). Second, the same thing is attributed singly to each Person. Owen's chief example of the second is divine teaching, which comprises the whole communication of grace.
sources.quote: When the same thing is, at the same time, ascribed jointly and yet distinctly to all the persons in the Deity, and respectively to each of them.
sources.raw_question: How does Scripture show that the divine Persons act distinctly in giving grace to believers?

question: How can Scripture say that God shed his blood, or that the Son of man was in heaven while on earth, if these belong to different natures of Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: Christ acts in each nature according to that nature's properties: as God he made and upholds all things, and as man he suffered and died. Because both natures are united in one person, the person named after one nature is said to do what he did only in the other. So God is said to redeem the church with his own blood, and the Son of man to be in heaven while on earth.
sources.quote: the person expressed by the name which he has on the account of one nature, is said to do that which he did only in the other.
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture say that God shed his blood, or that the Son of man was in heaven while on earth, if these belong to different natures of Christ?

question: If things are said to be 'in' someone, are they thereby greater than him, so that 'God reigns in the Spirit' would make the Spirit the source of God's rule?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VIII. St. Ambrose examines and refutes the heretical argument that because God is said to be glorified in the Spirit, and not with the Spirit, the Holy Spirit is therefore inferior to the Father. He shows that the particle in can be also used of the Son and even of the Father, and that on the other hand with may be said of creatures without any infringement on the prerogatives of the Godhead; and that in reality these prepositions simply imply the connection of the Three Divine Persons.
sources.answer: No, and such a conclusion would be impious. Rather, the one in whom things consist is greater, as all things consist in Christ and receive their substance from His power and cannot be compared to Him. To understand that the Spirit imparts to God the origin of His rule is impious; hence the fathers spoke of glory 'with' the Spirit to declare the unity of power of Father, Son and Spirit.
sources.quote: And the things which consist in Him cannot be compared to Him, because they receive from His power the substance whereby they consist.
sources.raw_question: If things are said to be 'in' someone, are they thereby greater than him, so that 'God reigns in the Spirit' would make the Spirit the source of God's rule?

question: Did Christ, at his death on the cross, go immediately up to the Father, or did he first descend to the place of the dead?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXI.—The preservation of our bodies is confirmed by the resurrection and ascension of Christ: the souls of the saints during the intermediate period are in a state of expectation of that time when they shall receive their perfect and consummated glory.
sources.answer: He descended to the place of the dead. For three days he dwelt where the dead were, and only afterwards rose and ascended. Irenaeus proves this from Christ's own Jonah saying, from Paul's statement that he descended into the lower parts of the earth, and from David's prophecy of deliverance from the nethermost hell. He adds the risen Lord's words to Mary that he had not yet ascended to the Father.
sources.quote: But the case was, that for three days He dwelt in the place where the dead were, as the prophet says concerning Him
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics (Valentinians) who deny the resurrection of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Did Christ, at his death on the cross, go immediately up to the Father, or did he first descend to the place of the dead?

question: Does the Arian claim that creatures need a created mediator in order to be made lead to an infinite regress of mediators?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Word were a creature, he too would need a mediator for his own making, and that mediator would need another, without end. Creation could then never come to exist, because it would always be waiting for a mediator. Yet things plainly exist, so the premise is absurd.
sources.quote: then again a fresh mediator is needed for that second, and thus tracing back and following out, we shall invent a vast crowd of accumulating mediators; and thus it will be impossible that the creation should subsist
sources.raw_question: Does the Arian claim that creatures need a created mediator in order to be made lead to an infinite regress of mediators?

question: Does attributing to the Holy Spirit the work of emboldening the faint-hearted imply that the Spirit is God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: Yes. To implant courage in the fearful belongs to none other than God, as Scripture shows when God says 'Fear not, for I am with thee' and when the Lord Himself says 'Let not your heart be troubled.' So even Eunomius' own words, against his intention, testify to the Spirit's divinity.
sources.quote: For to none other than to God does it belong to implant courage in the fearful, saying to the faint-hearted, “Fear not, for I am with thee, be not dismayed,”
sources.raw_question: Does attributing to the Holy Spirit the work of emboldening the faint-hearted imply that the Spirit is God?

question: Is it unworthy of the Father to possess judicial and rebuking power?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXV.—This world is ruled by the providence of one God, who is both endowed with infinite justice to punish the wicked, and with infinite goodness to bless the pious, and impart to them salvation.
sources.answer: No. If the Father is wise, He must test others, and testing entails judicial power; justice follows judgment and judgment executed with justice passes into wisdom. So the Father excels all wisdom precisely because He is Lord, Judge, the Just One and Ruler over all.
sources.quote: And how can they call the Father of all wise, if they do not assign to Him a judicial faculty? For if He is wise, He is also one who tests [others]; but the judicial power belongs to him who tests
sources.raw_question: Is it unworthy of the Father to possess judicial and rebuking power?

question: Do justice and goodness conflict within the one God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXV.—This world is ruled by the providence of one God, who is both endowed with infinite justice to punish the wicked, and with infinite goodness to bless the pious, and impart to them salvation.
sources.answer: No. God is good, merciful and patient and saves whom He ought, while judging those worthy of judgment; goodness does not desert Him in justice nor is His wisdom lessened. His goodness goes before and takes precedence, so He is not unmercifully just; the same God who sends sun and rain on just and unjust will judge those who abuse His bounty.
sources.quote: nor does goodness desert Him in the exercise of justice, nor is His wisdom lessened; for He saves those whom He should save, and judges those worthy of judgment.
sources.raw_question: Do justice and goodness conflict within the one God?

question: Do Christ's divine works, such as forgiving sins and raising the dead, show that he is the one God without any distinct Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The works do show Christ to be God by nature, but the revealed faith equally shows Him to be the Son, sent by the Father, through whom the worlds were made. Sabellius and the Arians each prove half the Church's faith: one that Christ is God, the other that He is the Son.
sources.quote: Sabellius displays Christ as God by the witness of the Divine nature manifested in His works; Sabellius’ antagonists confess Christ, on the evidence of the revealed faith, to be the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's divine works, such as forgiving sins and raising the dead, show that he is the one God without any distinct Son?

question: Why must the Saviour be both God and man united in one person?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Because only the union of the two natures in one person makes him a fit Saviour. By partaking of God's nature he lays his hand on God, and by partaking of ours he lays his hand on us, so he becomes an umpire between both and fills up the distance sin made. This union also gave him room enough to receive, and power enough to bear, all the wrath prepared for us.
sources.quote: He lays his hand upon God, by partaking of his nature, Zech. xiii. 7; and he lays his hand upon us, by being partaker of our nature, Heb. ii. 14, 16: and so becomes a days-man, or umpire between both.
sources.raw_question: Why must the Saviour be both God and man united in one person?

question: How could Christ's finite sufferings answer for sin that deserves infinite punishment?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: The infinity lies in different places. Sin is infinite only because of the object offended, God. Christ's punishment was infinite because of the subject who bore it, a divine person. This infinite worth arises from his personal union.
sources.quote: Sin was infinite only in respect of the object; and punishment was infinite in respect of the subject. This ariseth from his union.
sources.raw_question: How could Christ's finite sufferings answer for sin that deserves infinite punishment?

question: Why can man not discover the causes of all things that God has made?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXV.—God is not to be sought after by means of letters, syllables, and numbers; necessity of humility in such investigations.
sources.answer: Because man is infinitely inferior to God. He has received grace only in part and was created only recently. He is as far below the uncreated and unchanging God in knowledge and in the power to investigate causes as he is in being.
sources.quote: in the same proportion as he who was formed but to-day, and received the beginning of his creation, is inferior to Him who is uncreated, and who is always the same, in that proportion is he, as respects knowledge
sources.raw_question: Why can man not discover the causes of all things that God has made?

question: Do fallen human beings have any natural right or title to belong to God's family?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: No. By nature they are children of wrath, belonging to the family of sin and Satan. They are alienated from God's family and can lay no claim to anything in it. God drove Adam from the garden and barred return with a flaming sword, which shows that Adam and all in him lost every right of approaching God in any family relation.
sources.quote: Corrupted, cursed nature is not vested with the least right to any thing of God.
sources.raw_question: Do fallen human beings have any natural right or title to belong to God's family?

question: If Christ is to be 'confessed in the glory of God the Father' and God is to become all in all, who actually gains or is promoted: the divine Son or the humanity he assumed?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: The assumed humanity, and through it we, are the ones promoted. A new nature, which was not God before, began in Christ with his human birth. All that he obtains is on behalf of that nature. Believers are the gainers, since they will be conformed to the glory of the body of God. The Only-begotten himself remains nothing less than God.
sources.quote: It is, therefore, we who are the gainers, we who are promoted, for we shall be conformed to the glory of the body of God.
sources.raw_question: If Christ is to be 'confessed in the glory of God the Father' and God is to become all in all, who actually gains or is promoted: the divine Son or the humanity he assumed?

question: Does affirming two natures in Christ imply preaching two Christs, as Eunomius charged?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: No. The doctrine preaches the union of the Man with the Divinity, in which the assumed nature is made, by commixture, to be what the Word is, as a drop of vinegar mingled in the deep becomes sea. Hence there is one Christ and Lord, the humanity sharing in the power and names of the Godhead.
sources.quote: This is our doctrine, which does not, as Eunomius charges against it, preach a plurality of Christs, but the union of the Man with the Divinity
sources.raw_question: Does affirming two natures in Christ imply preaching two Christs, as Eunomius charged?

question: Do only God's adopted children have a genuine right and title to the privileges and ordinances of the church, the house of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: Yes. The church is made up of living stones, saints, and a holy people, the sons and daughters of the Lord Almighty, and all others are excluded. Unregenerate persons may creep in unawares, but they have no right or title to it. Its privileges are food for living souls, and only children are alive; all others are dead in sin.
sources.quote: It is true that oftentimes, at unawares, other persons creep into the great house of God; and so there become in it “not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and of earth,” etc., 2 Tim. ii. 20; but they only creep in
sources.raw_question: Do only God's adopted children have a genuine right and title to the privileges and ordinances of the church, the house of God?

question: Does someone who despises the Son also despise the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter X. Being about to prove that the will, the calling, and the commandment of the Trinity is one, St. Ambrose shows that the Spirit called the Church exactly as the Father and the Son did, and proves this by the selection of SS. Paul and Barnabas, and especially by the mission of St. Peter to Cornelius. And by the way he points out how in the Apostle's vision the calling of the Gentiles was shadowed forth, who having been before like wild beasts, now by the operation of the Spirit lay aside that wildness. Then having quoted other passages in support of this view, he shows that in the case of Jeremiah cast into a pit by Jews, and rescued by Abdemelech, is a type of the slighting of the Holy Spirit by the Jews, and of His being honoured by the Gentiles.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is the one whom the prophets foretold, and the prophets spoke by the Holy Spirit. Whoever despises the Son, as the Jews did, therefore also despises the Holy Spirit and the prophets, such as Isaiah and Jeremiah, through whom the Spirit spoke. Honour or dishonour shown to one of these Persons cannot be separated from the other.
sources.quote: Do not, then, like a Jew, despise the Son, Whom the prophets foretold; for you would despise also the Holy Spirit, you would despise Isaiah, you would despise Jeremiah
sources.raw_question: Does someone who despises the Son also despise the Holy Spirit?

question: Is it the Holy Spirit who transforms sinful people from a beast-like condition into a heavenly way of life?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter X. Being about to prove that the will, the calling, and the commandment of the Trinity is one, St. Ambrose shows that the Spirit called the Church exactly as the Father and the Son did, and proves this by the selection of SS. Paul and Barnabas, and especially by the mission of St. Peter to Cornelius. And by the way he points out how in the Apostle's vision the calling of the Gentiles was shadowed forth, who having been before like wild beasts, now by the operation of the Spirit lay aside that wildness. Then having quoted other passages in support of this view, he shows that in the case of Jeremiah cast into a pit by Jews, and rescued by Abdemelech, is a type of the slighting of the Holy Spirit by the Jews, and of His being honoured by the Gentiles.
sources.answer: Yes. We were once like wild beasts, the ravening wolves the Lord warned of. Through the Holy Spirit the rage of lions, the spots of leopards, the craft of foxes and the rapacity of wolves have passed away from our feelings. This is so great a grace that it changes earth into heaven, so that our conversation is now in heaven.
sources.quote: But now, through the Holy Spirit, the rage of lions, the spots of leopards, the craft of foxes, the rapacity of wolves, have passed away from our feelings
sources.raw_question: Is it the Holy Spirit who transforms sinful people from a beast-like condition into a heavenly way of life?

question: Does it matter that the Old Testament texts quoted in Hebrews 1 might originally be read otherwise, or does the apostle's use of them settle that they refer to Christ's divinity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: The apostle's use settles it. Writing as he was moved by the Holy Ghost, he cites these verses as proof texts of Christ's glory, so we have a Divine interpretation of the Divine Scriptures. Whatever one's preconceived view of these verses, that inspired interpretation governs their meaning.
sources.quote: Whatever be your preconceived view of these verses, the apostle, writing as he was moved by the Holy Ghost, adduces them as proof texts of the glory of Christ.
sources.raw_question: Does it matter that the Old Testament texts quoted in Hebrews 1 might originally be read otherwise, or does the apostle's use of them settle that they refer to Christ's divinity?

question: Is it consistent to accept God's eternity, omnipresence and foreknowledge while their manner is incomprehensible, yet reject the Trinity because its manner is incomprehensible?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. The cases are exactly alike, so the opponent is unequal and partial. He admits that the manner in which the divine attributes exist is above comprehension, yet he still believes they are real. Likewise the Trinity may be true even though its manner, or modus, is beyond comprehension.
sources.quote: Why then so unequal and partial, with respect to the Trinity, the case being exactly the same? why may not the thing be true, though the Mannmr, or modus of it, be above comprehension!
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to accept God's eternity, omnipresence and foreknowledge while their manner is incomprehensible, yet reject the Trinity because its manner is incomprehensible?

question: Is the work of the Holy Spirit essential to the Christian religion, or is it an optional addition to faith in Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: It is essential. Christ made no greater promise to his disciples than the gift of the Holy Spirit, both for their own good and for carrying on his work. In worship, obedience, consolation, sanctification and ministry the Spirit is the principle, life and soul of the whole. Without this administration of the Spirit the whole religion professed is nothing, and nothing comes of Christ's resurrection.
sources.quote: So that the whole religion we profess, without this administration of the Spirit, is nothing; nor is there any fruit without it of the resurrection of Christ from the dead.
sources.raw_question: Is the work of the Holy Spirit essential to the Christian religion, or is it an optional addition to faith in Christ?

question: What is the chief difference between the administration of the new covenant and the old?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: The chief difference is the abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit. When Christ ascended, he received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and poured him out in such an eminent way that this became the greatest and most glorious difference between the two covenants. It is also the basis on which gifts and graces are given to the church.
sources.quote: that he had received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, Act ii. 33; and that in such an eminent manner as thereby to make the greatest and most glorious difference between the administration of the new covenant and old
sources.raw_question: What is the chief difference between the administration of the new covenant and the old?

question: Can the Word of God, the Maker of all things, be enclosed in numbers or divided into syllables and letters?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XV.—Sige relates to Marcus the generation of the twenty-four elements and of Jesus. Exposure of these absurdities.
sources.answer: No. The Word is the Founder, Framer and Maker of all things and the Lord who founded the heavens. To shut him up in shifting numbers, cut him into syllables and elements, and reduce him to the number 888 debases the Creator to the level of the alphabet.
sources.quote: whilst thou shuttest up [in these] the Word of God, the Founder, and Framer, and Maker of all things; and then, again, cutting Him up piecemeal into four syllables and thirty elements
sources.raw_question: Can the Word of God, the Maker of all things, be enclosed in numbers or divided into syllables and letters?

question: Once believers have the indwelling Spirit and habitual grace, do they still need fresh influences of grace from Christ for every spiritual act?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Yes. Even with both of those gifts, Christ says that without him they can do nothing. Believers cannot live on the old stock of grace. Every new act requires new grace, as God works in us both to will and to do.
sources.quote: They cannot live and spend upon the old stock; for every new act they must have new grace.
sources.raw_question: Once believers have the indwelling Spirit and habitual grace, do they still need fresh influences of grace from Christ for every spiritual act?

question: What is the consequence of sin for humanity before God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 1. Introduction. Preparation of heart. Our position before God.
sources.answer: Death. The author says sin is fatal. God warned Adam, "dying thou shalt die," and after the fall moral and spiritual death spread through all humanity. Bodily disease and death followed. For those who die in their sins, bodily death leads to the second death in the lake of fire.
sources.quote: for sin uncleansed and unchecked is present defilement and final death
sources.raw_question: What is the consequence of sin for humanity before God?

question: Does the greater privilege Christ brings at his advent consist in revealing knowledge of another, previously unknown Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: No. The greater gift is not the revelation of another Father. It is that by his advent Christ poured out on the human race the greater gift of the same paternal grace. For this reason he justly requires more from those who receive more, and those who reject him face severer judgment than Sodom.
sources.quote: the more, however, not because He reveals the knowledge of another Father, as I have shown so fully and so repeatedly, but because He has, by means of His advent, poured upon the human race the greater gift of paternal grace
sources.raw_question: Does the greater privilege Christ brings at his advent consist in revealing knowledge of another, previously unknown Father?

question: Is a common nature such as humanity multiplied or divided when it exists in many individuals?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. The nature is one, united in itself and absolutely indivisible. It cannot be increased by addition or diminished by subtraction, and it remains one and complete even though it appears in plurality. Only the persons, distinguished by their peculiar attributes, are counted by number.
sources.quote: their nature is one, at union in itself, and an absolutely indivisible unit, not capable of increase by addition or of diminution by subtraction, but in its essence being and continually remaining one
sources.raw_question: Is a common nature such as humanity multiplied or divided when it exists in many individuals?

question: Does the Son's role as Creator of all things entitle him to religious worship, given that the Fathers restricted worship to the Creator?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: Yes. Athenagoras, Clement, and Origen taught that only the Creator and Governor of all things may be worshipped. They also taught that the Son created all things and governs the world. The Son therefore falls within the object of worship rather than among the creatures.
sources.quote: The reason is plain: the Son is "Maker and Governor of the world, and even παντοκράτωρ, according to this excellent writer.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's role as Creator of all things entitle him to religious worship, given that the Fathers restricted worship to the Creator?

question: Do the titles 'the first and the last' and 'Alpha and Omega' applied to Christ in Revelation prove that the Son is eternal?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: Yes. These phrases respect duration, as Isaiah 44:6 compared with Isaiah 43:10 shows ('Before me was there no God formed, neither shall there be after me'), and as Revelation 1:8 explains them by 'which is, and which was, and which is to come.' Since they are applied to Christ in Revelation 1:17 and 22:13, there was no God before him, and he is eternal in the strictest sense.
sources.quote: The phrase then respects duration; and it is applied to our blessed Saviour, as hath been shewn, Rev. 1. 17, xxii. 13. Therefore there was no God before him: therefore he is, in the strictest sense, eternal.
sources.raw_question: Do the titles 'the first and the last' and 'Alpha and Omega' applied to Christ in Revelation prove that the Son is eternal?

question: Does God love his people while they are sinning as much as when they obey?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes, he loves his people, though not their sinning. He does not alter the purpose of his will toward them, only the dispensations of his grace. He may rebuke, chasten and hide his face from them, and these things proceed from love as truly as his kindnesses do.
sources.quote: loves he his people in their sinning? Yes; his people, — not their sinning. Alters he not his love towards them? Not the purpose of his will, but the dispensations of his grace.
sources.raw_question: Does God love his people while they are sinning as much as when they obey?

question: Was Christ, in taking flesh, a true and real servant to the Father, and how does his earthly obedience show his esteem for believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. For believers' sakes the Son humbled and emptied himself in taking flesh, becoming a real servant to the Father and of no esteem in the world's eyes. His whole life of prayers, tears, fears, obedience and suffering, which he undertook cheerfully as his "meat and drink," consisted in fulfilling all righteousness, enduring persecution, and doing good to men, all for their sakes.
sources.quote: For their sakes he so humbled and emptied himself, in taking flesh, as to become therein a servant, — in the eyes of the world of no esteem nor account; and a true and real servant unto the Father.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ, in taking flesh, a true and real servant to the Father, and how does his earthly obedience show his esteem for believers?

question: What did Christ's death on the cross contain, and what does it reveal about his love for believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: It contained the curse of the law, the wrath of God, and the loss of God's presence. It was a fearful cup he drank so that believers might never taste it. Because he died for them while they were still sinners and enemies, no greater demonstration of love is possible. Such a death shows as high a valuation of them as Christ's heart was capable of.
sources.quote: The curse of the law was in it, the wrath of God was in it, the loss of God’s presence was in it. It was a fearful cup that he tasted of, and drank of, that they might never taste of it.
sources.raw_question: What did Christ's death on the cross contain, and what does it reveal about his love for believers?

question: Is the Word of God the same agent who acted with the human race throughout the Old Testament dispensations as in the New?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVIII.—Those persons prove themselves senseless who exaggerate the mercy of Christ, but are silent as to the judgment, and look only at the more abundant grace of the New Testament; but, forgetful of the greater degree of perfection which it demands from us, they endeavour to show that there is another God beyond Him who created the world.
sources.answer: Yes. There is one and the same God the Father and His Word, who has always been present with the human race through various dispensations, saving from the beginning those who love God and follow the Word, and judging those who forget God and transgress His word.
sources.quote: since there is one and the same God the Father, and His Word, who has been always present with the human race, by means indeed of various dispensations, and has wrought out many things, and saved from the beginning those who are saved
sources.raw_question: Is the Word of God the same agent who acted with the human race throughout the Old Testament dispensations as in the New?

question: If God saved Israel by afflicting and drowning the Egyptians, does that make the Old Testament God the cause of their sin and thus a different, lesser God than the Father of Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVIII.—Those persons prove themselves senseless who exaggerate the mercy of Christ, but are silent as to the judgment, and look only at the more abundant grace of the New Testament; but, forgetful of the greater degree of perfection which it demands from us, they endeavour to show that there is another God beyond Him who created the world.
sources.answer: No. By the same reasoning the Lord Christ would be the cause of the Jews' sin in killing him, since by his coming and the Jews' unbelief we were saved. As Israel was saved through the blindness of the Egyptians, so we are saved through that of the Jews; Christ is a savour of life to believers and of death to unbelievers, so the same pattern belongs to one God.
sources.quote: For as they were saved by means of the blindness of the Egyptians, so are we, too, by that of the Jews; if, indeed, the death of the Lord is the condemnation of those who fastened Him to the cross
sources.raw_question: If God saved Israel by afflicting and drowning the Egyptians, does that make the Old Testament God the cause of their sin and thus a different, lesser God than the Father of Christ?

question: Is the forgiveness of sins, which makes a person innocent, sufficient by itself to give a title to eternal life?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Being free of guilt makes us innocent but not obedient, and innocence alone gives no title to reward. Adam was innocent at creation but still had to keep the commandments before entering life. Therefore the whole law must also be fulfilled, which is found only in Christ's actual obedience, by whose life we are saved.
sources.quote: By taking away the guilt of sin, we are as persons innocent; but something more is required to make us to be considered as persons obedient.
sources.raw_question: Is the forgiveness of sins, which makes a person innocent, sufficient by itself to give a title to eternal life?

question: Does Hebrews 4:12-13 show that the Word of God is distinct from all creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul calls originated things 'creature' but names the Son the Word of God, before whose eyes all things are naked. The Word judges while every originated thing must give account to him, so he is other than all creatures.
sources.quote: For hence it is that He judges, but each of all things originate is bound to give account to Him.
sources.raw_question: Does Hebrews 4:12-13 show that the Word of God is distinct from all creatures?

question: Why did God implant an image of His Wisdom in creatures?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: So that what came into being might not only exist but be good, wise works worthy of God, and so that the world might recognise in it its Creator the Word and through Him the Father. Our wisdom is an image of the Son as Wisdom, as our word is an image of Him as Word, and through it we know the Father, as Paul says that God's invisible things are seen through the things made.
sources.quote: that the world might recognise in it its own Creator the Word, and through Him the Father.
sources.raw_question: Why did God implant an image of His Wisdom in creatures?

question: In what sense was our salvation 'founded' in Christ 'before the world'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: God's will and purpose for our salvation were prepared before the world in the Word, who is before the ages, and took effect when the Saviour came. Like a wise architect who provides materials for repair before building the house, God founded our renewal in Christ beforehand so that we might inherit everlasting life in Him.
sources.quote: And the will and the purpose were made ready ‘before the world,’ but have taken effect when the need required, and the Saviour came among us.
sources.raw_question: In what sense was our salvation 'founded' in Christ 'before the world'?

question: Does Justin Martyr's statement that it was not the Creator of the universe who spoke to Moses as the God of Abraham imply that the Son is not God absolutely or not Creator?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. Justin means that the divine Person who called himself God and was God was not the Person of the Father, whose ordinary character is Maker of all things, but another divine Person, God the Son. Arguing against a Jew who admitted only one divine Person, Justin aimed to prove there were two divine Persons, and the Son was really the God of Abraham.
sources.quote: that divine Person, who called himself God, and was God, was not the Person of the Father, (whose ordinary character is that of Maker of all things,) but another divine Person, viz. God the Son.
sources.raw_question: Does Justin Martyr's statement that it was not the Creator of the universe who spoke to Moses as the God of Abraham imply that the Son is not God absolutely or not Creator?

question: Does Christ as Mediator, having all creation subjected to him, compete with the Father's sole deity?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: No. Christ Jesus, the Mediator of God and men, has every creature subjected to him by his Father, inasmuch as he is God. Being found at one with the Father and abiding in his condition as one who "was heard," he proves the Father to be the one, only and true God.
sources.quote: found at one with His Father God, has, by abiding in that condition that He moreover “was heard,” briefly proved God His Father to be one and only and true God.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ as Mediator, having all creation subjected to him, compete with the Father's sole deity?

question: Why did the Word of God allow His own body to suffer?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Twelfthly, Matthew xxvi. 39; John xii. 27, &c. Arian inferences are against the Regula Fidei, as before. He wept and the like, as man. Other texts prove Him God. God could not fear. He feared because His flesh feared.
sources.answer: He came precisely so that He might suffer in the flesh. Through that suffering the flesh might thereafter be made impassible and immortal. The sufferings and troubles would end in Him and be annulled, so that men might abide incorruptible for ever as a temple of the Word.
sources.quote: for therefore did He come, as I said before, that in the flesh He might suffer, and thenceforth the flesh might be made impassible and immortal
sources.raw_question: Why did the Word of God allow His own body to suffer?

question: In what different ways can future events be foreknown, and how does true prophecy differ from mere conjecture or demonic divination?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In How Many Ways Things Future are Foreknown. Neither Philosophers, Nor Those Who Were Distinguished Among the Ancients, are to Be Consulted Concerning the Resurrection of the Dead.
sources.answer: Augustine distinguishes several ways. Some predictions are conjectures from past experience, like those of physicians, farmers or sailors. Demons, the aerial powers, foresee things already on their way, like a man on a mountain who sees someone coming far off. True prophecy comes either through holy angels, to whom God shows things by His Word and Wisdom, or through minds lifted by the Holy Spirit to behold the unchangeable causes of future things. The aerial powers hear only as much as God judges fitting.
sources.quote: by means of holy angels, to whom God shows those things by His Word and His Wisdom, wherein both things future and things past consist
sources.raw_question: In what different ways can future events be foreknown, and how does true prophecy differ from mere conjecture or demonic divination?

question: Since the Word is in the Father and like him in all things, can he be capable of any addition or higher exaltation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: No. Since God is highest of all, his Word must necessarily be highest also. Being in the Father and like the Father in all things, he is beyond the need of any addition.
sources.quote: Where then could He be exalted higher, who is in the Father and like the Father in all things? Therefore He is beyond the need of any addition
sources.raw_question: Since the Word is in the Father and like him in all things, can he be capable of any addition or higher exaltation?

question: Why did Christ use the words of the Mosaic law to defeat Satan in the temptation, and what does this show about the relation of the Son to the God of the law?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: Christ drew his means of confounding the devil from no other source than the law, using the Father's commandment as His help. This shows that the law's God is His own Father, and that the law itself declares the Word of God from the Father. The Lord God to whom Christ bears witness, whom none may tempt and whom alone all must worship, is the God who gave the law.
sources.quote: He did not draw the means of confounding him from any other source than from the words of the law, and made use of the Father’s commandment as a help towards the destruction and confusion of the apostate angel
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ use the words of the Mosaic law to defeat Satan in the temptation, and what does this show about the relation of the Son to the God of the law?

question: Does Christ's hunger after his forty-day fast show that he had a real human nature?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ hungered first so that we might perceive He was a real and substantial man, since suffering hunger when fasting belongs to a man. Secondly, His hunger gave the adversary an opportunity to attack Him, so that the corruption that came through eating in paradise could be undone by His want of food.
sources.quote: first, in order that we may perceive that He was a real and substantial man—for it belongs to a man to suffer hunger when fasting
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's hunger after his forty-day fast show that he had a real human nature?

question: Does Christ's dying, when the devil cannot die, show that Christ is inferior to the devil?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
