sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: No. The devil's inability to die comes from his lacking an earthly body, not from superiority. Christ descended into death through great mercy, by taking a lower nature. The proud who prefer the devil for this reason contradict themselves, since they count themselves better than devils though they too can die.
sources.quote: whereas they themselves are better than the devils, yet, because they bear a body of flesh, they can so die, as the devils certainly cannot die, who do not bear such a body
sources.raised_by_detail: proud men who despise the death of Christ
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's dying, when the devil cannot die, show that Christ is inferior to the devil?

question: Are attributes like wisdom, will, and immensity in each divine person by virtue of that person's personal property?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Because each person has the whole divine nature, all essential properties are in each person, but they belong to the person as God, not as that particular person. The wisdom and will of God are in the Father not as Father but because the Father is God, and likewise in the Son and Spirit.
sources.quote: The wisdom, the understanding of God, the will of God, the immensity of God, is in that person, not as that person, but as the person is God.
sources.raw_question: Are attributes like wisdom, will, and immensity in each divine person by virtue of that person's personal property?

question: What does Athanasius mean in calling the Son the 'radiance' (apaugasma) of the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: He means the Son issues or streams forth from the Father's very substance, as light from the sun. Waterland faults Clarke's rendering 'brightness of glory' for concealing this sense, which points to the Son's derivation from the Father's substance and so to his true divinity.
sources.quote: Athanasius intended to signify the Son’s isswing or streaming forth, as: it were, from the Father’s substance, as light from the sun
sources.raw_question: What does Athanasius mean in calling the Son the 'radiance' (apaugasma) of the Father?

question: Does Stephen's account in Acts show that God's appearances to the patriarchs, such as to Moses at the bush, were wrought through an angel rather than in God's own substance?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: Yes. Stephen says the God of glory appeared to Abraham. But so that no one thinks God appeared to mortal eyes as He is in Himself, Stephen adds that an angel of the Lord appeared to Moses in the bush. Yet the voice said, "I am the God of Abraham." Stephen thus speaks of both angel and Lord in the same appearance.
sources.quote: But lest any one should think that the God of glory appeared then to the eyes of any mortal in that which He is in Himself, he goes on to say that an angel appeared to Moses.
sources.raw_question: Does Stephen's account in Acts show that God's appearances to the patriarchs, such as to Moses at the bush, were wrought through an angel rather than in God's own substance?

question: Do prayer to Christ as Mediator and hope placed in him imply that Christ is God and not merely a man?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > The Author Prosecutes the Same Argument.
sources.answer: Yes. Calling on a man for salvation is condemned as ineffectual, and hope in man is declared accursed. Yet Christians pray to Christ and hope in him. Likewise, denying Christ destroys the soul, whereas a sin against a man may be forgiven. So he is not man only.
sources.quote: If Christ is only man, why is hope rested upon Him, when hope in man is declared to be accursed?
sources.raw_question: Do prayer to Christ as Mediator and hope placed in him imply that Christ is God and not merely a man?

question: Is our redemption accomplished through the real flesh and blood of the Son of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIV.—Unless the flesh were to be saved, the Word would not have taken upon Him flesh of the same substance as ours: from this it would follow that neither should we have been reconciled by Him.
sources.answer: Yes. Believers have been redeemed by the flesh of the Lord and re-established by His blood. If the Lord had not taken real flesh of our substance, He would not have reconciled to God the humanity that had become hostile through sin.
sources.quote: Remember, therefore, my beloved friend, that thou hast been redeemed by the flesh of our Lord, re-established by His blood
sources.raw_question: Is our redemption accomplished through the real flesh and blood of the Son of God?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's work in a believer come before the believer's interest in Christ's blood, or is that work itself a result of what Christ purchased?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: It is both, depending on the point of view. In itself, the Spirit's quickening and converting work is a fruit and part of what Christ purchased. In the believer's experience, the communication of the Spirit comes first, and at the same instant the believer is given an interest in Christ's blood.
sources.quote: yea, this very work of the Spirit itself is a fruit and part of the purchase of Christ. But we speak of our sense of this thing, whereunto the communication of the Spirit is antecedent.
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's work in a believer come before the believer's interest in Christ's blood, or is that work itself a result of what Christ purchased?

question: Why does recognising that an unfamiliar word is a sign, and not an empty sound, awaken the desire to know its meaning?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Love of the Studious Mind, that Is, of One Desirous to Know, is Not the Love of a Thing Which It Does Not Know.
sources.answer: Because no sign is known perfectly until it is known what it signifies. If a man knew the sound only as a sound, he would seek nothing further, since the senses have already grasped it fully. Knowing it is a sign means it is partly known but not fully known, and the more a thing is known without being fully known, the more the mind desires to know the rest.
sources.quote: The more, then, the thing is known, yet not fully known, the more the mind desires to know concerning it what remains to be known.
sources.raw_question: Why does recognising that an unfamiliar word is a sign, and not an empty sound, awaken the desire to know its meaning?

question: Which Persons of the Trinity brought about the Incarnation of Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VI. To those who object that according to the words of Amos the Spirit is created, the answer is made that the word is there understood of the wind, which is often created, which cannot be said of the Holy Spirit, since He is eternal, and cannot be dissolved in death, or by an heretical absorption into the Father. But if they pertinaciously contend that this passage was written of the Holy Spirit, St. Ambrose points out that recourse must be had to a spiritual Interpretation, for Christ by His coming established the thunder, that is, the force of the divine utterances, and by Spirit is signified the human soul as also the flesh assumed by Christ. And since this was created by each Person of the Trinity, it is thence argued that the Spirit, Who has before been affirmed to be the Creator of all things, was the Author of the Incarnation of the Lord.
sources.answer: All three. The Father created it ("The Lord created Me"; "God sent His Son, made of a woman"), the Spirit created it ("Mary was found with child of the Holy Spirit"), and the Son made His own body ("Wisdom hath made herself a house"). The Incarnation is therefore a common work of Father, Son and Spirit.
sources.quote: For as we read that the Father created the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, the Spirit too created it; and so too we read that Christ Himself created His own Body.
sources.raw_question: Which Persons of the Trinity brought about the Incarnation of Christ?

question: If Christ had recognized many fathers and gods, would he have taught his disciples to call only one being Father and God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter I.—The Lord acknowledged but one God and Father.
sources.answer: No. A good teacher would not command his disciples to confess one Father while himself acknowledging other fathers and gods in the same sense; that would make him a misleading and invidious teacher. Rather, Christ distinguished those called gods merely by word from him who is truly God, so that the disciples should not mistake one for another.
sources.quote: if the Lord had known many fathers and gods, He would not have taught His disciples to know [only] one God, and to call Him alone Father? But He did the rather distinguish those who by word merely (verbo tenus) are termed gods, from Him who is truly God
sources.raw_question: If Christ had recognized many fathers and gods, would he have taught his disciples to call only one being Father and God?

question: How does the work of redemption show the infinite worth of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: It shows his worth to be infinite. Redemption shows the infinite excellency of the Father, whose honor the Son prized so highly that he stooped infinitely low. It also shows the infinite worth of the Son, in whom the Father so delighted that he received sinners into favor for his sake. The Holy Ghost is that mutual delight of Father and Son, and the worth of a delight equals the worth of the thing delighted in, so his worth is infinite too.
sources.quote: So great as the worth of a thing delighted in is to any one, so great is the worth of that delight and joy itself which he has in it.
sources.raw_question: How does the work of redemption show the infinite worth of the Holy Spirit?

question: Why, according to Augustine, are three things involved whenever someone loves something?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three Things Which are Found in Love Must Be Considered.
sources.answer: Every act of love involves the lover, the thing loved, and love itself. Love cannot exist without something being loved, so one cannot love love except by loving a lover. Hence wherever one person loves another thing, three things are concerned.
sources.quote: when I, who make this inquiry, love anything, there are three things concerned—myself, and that which I love, and love itself. For I do not love love, except I love a lover; for there is no love where nothing is loved.
sources.raw_question: Why, according to Augustine, are three things involved whenever someone loves something?

question: When a mind loves itself, does the triad of lover, beloved, and love reduce to only two things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three Things Which are Found in Love Must Be Considered.
sources.answer: Yes. When someone loves himself, the lover and the beloved are the same, so only two things remain, the mind and its love. Love and what is loved are still two, since self-love requires that love itself be loved. It therefore does not follow that three things are found wherever love is, and the image of the Trinity must be sought further.
sources.quote: Therefore there are two things when any one loves himself—love, and that which is loved. For then he that loves and that which is loved are one. Whence it seems that it does not follow that three things are to be understood wherever love is.
sources.raw_question: When a mind loves itself, does the triad of lover, beloved, and love reduce to only two things?

question: Through what channel does the Church come to know the true doctrine of the Son of God, and does that channel carry the authority of Christ and the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Preface.
sources.answer: The Church knows the truth about the Son of God through the apostles, to whom the Lord of all gave the power of the Gospel. Their teaching carries divine authority. Christ himself said that whoever hears the apostles hears him, and whoever despises them despises him and the Father who sent him. The faith the Church received from the apostles is therefore the only true and life-giving faith, and it is the standard for refuting the heretics.
sources.quote: For the Lord of all gave to His apostles the power of the Gospel, through whom also we have known the truth, that is, the doctrine of the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Through what channel does the Church come to know the true doctrine of the Son of God, and does that channel carry the authority of Christ and the Father?

question: Did the Son of God exist before his conception in the Virgin's womb, contrary to Hebion (Ebion)?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Yes. Christ speaks of the glory he had with the Father before the world was, and John declares that in the beginning the Word was with God and was God, and that all things were made through him. Therefore his existence did not begin with his life in the flesh.
sources.quote: Let Hebion try to sap the faith, who allows the Son of God no life before the Virgin’s womb, and sees in Him the Word only after His life as flesh had begun.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God exist before his conception in the Virgin's womb, contrary to Hebion (Ebion)?

question: What roles did the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High play in Christ's conception?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit came down, hallowed the Virgin's womb and joined himself to human fleshly nature. The power of the Most High overshadowed her like a cloud, strengthening her frail body so that it could receive the procreative power of the Spirit. This shows the divine glory that accompanied the conception.
sources.quote: The Holy Ghost, descending from above, hallowed the Virgin’s womb, and breathing therein (for The Spirit bloweth where it listeth), mingled Himself with the fleshly nature of man
sources.raw_question: What roles did the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High play in Christ's conception?

question: When Christian teachers say that the mysteries of God are beyond some inquirers' grasp, does this show that the teachers are hiding their own ignorance or begrudging others knowledge?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > This Work is Written Against Those Who Sophistically Assail the Faith of the Trinity, Through Misuse of Reason. They Who Dispute Concerning God Err from a Threefold Cause. Holy Scripture, Removing What is False, Leads Us on by Degrees to Things Divine. What True Immortality is. We are Nourished by Faith, that We May Be Enabled to Apprehend Things Divine.
sources.answer: No. The difficulty lies in the inquirers' own unfitness, not in any ignorance or malice on the teachers' part. The things sought about God may exceed what they can receive, and perhaps what the teachers can fully apprehend or express. Augustine therefore promises to give the requested account, that the Trinity is one God of one substance. In doing so he aims to show that the highest good is discerned only by purified minds strengthened by faith.
sources.quote: because the eye of the human mind, being weak, is dazzled in that so transcendent light, unless it be invigorated by the nourishment of the righteousness of faith
sources.raw_question: When Christian teachers say that the mysteries of God are beyond some inquirers' grasp, does this show that the teachers are hiding their own ignorance or begrudging others knowledge?

question: Are the 'senses exercised to discern both good and evil' in Hebrews 5:14 the bodily senses we share with animals?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Opinion of Those Who Have Thought that the Mind Was Signified by the Man, the Bodily Sense by the Woman.
sources.answer: No. Those senses belong to the rational nature and pertain to the understanding. They are distinct from the fivefold bodily sense, through which corporeal species and motion are perceived by beasts as well as by us.
sources.quote: for these “senses” belong to the rational nature and pertain to the understanding; but that sense which is divided into five parts in the body
sources.raw_question: Are the 'senses exercised to discern both good and evil' in Hebrews 5:14 the bodily senses we share with animals?

question: Does Scripture call Christ Jehovah (the Lord God), for example in Luke 1:16-17?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: Yes, very probably. In Luke 1:16-17 John the Baptist turns many to 'the Lord their God' and goes 'before him'; even Dr. Clarke concedes that in strict construction 'the Lord their God' refers to Christ. Hence Christ is Lord God, Jehovah Elohim.
sources.quote: The Doctor owns that, in strictness of construction, the words (the Lord their God) must be understood of Christ. And therefore Christ is Lord God, or Jehovah Eloim, which comes to the same.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture call Christ Jehovah (the Lord God), for example in Luke 1:16-17?

question: How does the Holy Spirit, when given to human beings, enable them to love God and neighbour?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How the Holy Spirit is Called Love, and Whether He Alone is So Called. That the Holy Spirit is in the Scriptures Properly Called by the Name of Love.
sources.answer: The Spirit, being Himself love, inflames those to whom He is given with love of God and neighbour. Man has nothing from which to love God except from God. So Paul says the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost who is given to us.
sources.quote: Therefore God the Holy Spirit, who proceedeth from the Father, when He has been given to man, inflames him to the love of God and of his neighbor, and is Himself love.
sources.raw_question: How does the Holy Spirit, when given to human beings, enable them to love God and neighbour?

question: Can the dispute over the Son's nature be settled by asking what is fitting to say of one who is God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > The Importance of the Subject. The Arians affect Scripture language, but their doctrine new, as well as unscriptural. Statement of the Catholic doctrine, that the Son is proper to the Father's substance, and eternal. Restatement of Arianism in contrast, that He is a creature with a beginning: the controversy comes to this issue, whether one whom we are to believe in as God, can be so in name only, and is merely a creature. What pretence then for being indifferent in the controversy? The Arians rely on state patronage, and dare not avow their tenets.
sources.answer: Yes. Since 'the Word was God,' the whole case turns on what it is fitting to say of God: that he was or was not, eternal or from a beginning, true or by adoption, a creature or the one through whom creatures came to be. Athanasius holds that only the Catholic answers are fitting.
sources.quote: For from this one question the whole case on both sides may be determined, what is fitting to say,—He was, or He was not; always, or before His birth; eternal, or from this and from then; true, or by adoption
sources.raw_question: Can the dispute over the Son's nature be settled by asking what is fitting to say of one who is God?

question: Should the definition of God be taken from metaphysics or from Scripture, and what does a scriptural definition include?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 24: Whether Gal. iv. 8. may not be enough to determine the dispute betwiat us; since it obliged the Doctor to confess, that Christ as by nature truly God, as truly
sources.answer: Metaphysics must always stand corrected by Gospel revelation, so a scriptural definition is preferable. Melanchthon's definition is fuller and more complete. It describes God as a spiritual, intelligent, true, good, just, merciful and almighty essence. In it the eternal Father begets the coeternal Son as his image, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from Father and Son.
sources.quote: if, instead of metaphysics, (which must always be content to stand corrected by Gospel Revelation,) we choose to take our definition of God from Scripture, then that of *Melancthon, which I have put into the margin, will be more full and complete.
sources.raw_question: Should the definition of God be taken from metaphysics or from Scripture, and what does a scriptural definition include?

question: How did Fathers such as Justin Martyr and Hippolytus understand the 'generation' of the Son at the creation of the world?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: They interpreted it as a manifestation of the already existing Word, not as his first coming into being. Justin read 'this day have I begotten thee' as the Son's generation becoming known to men. Hippolytus described the Father making visible his own Word, who had previously been invisible to the created world.
sources.quote: Justin Martyr; who, in like manner, interprets generation, in the secondary sense, by manifestation. And even h Hippolytus, as before observed, explains the procession, or generation of the Son, a little after the creation, by manifestation of him.
sources.raw_question: How did Fathers such as Justin Martyr and Hippolytus understand the 'generation' of the Son at the creation of the world?

question: Is there a higher Father, distinct from the Creator, who does not judge, exercises no providence over human affairs, and approves of sins?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXVI.—John and Daniel have predicted the dissolution and desolation of the Roman Empire, which shall precede the end of the world and the eternal kingdom of Christ. The Gnostics are refuted, those tools of Satan, who invent another Father different from the Creator.
sources.answer: No. Such a Father is a satanic invention, devised by those who blame the Creator for their own apostasy and will not admit that God's judgment is just. If the Father did not judge, all persons would be equal. Christ's advent would then be pointless and absurd, since He came to separate the wheat from the tares and to send the wicked into the fire prepared by His Father.
sources.quote: If the Father, then, does not exercise judgment, [it follows] that judgment does not belong to Him, or that He consents to all those actions which take place; and if He does not judge, all persons will be equal
sources.raw_question: Is there a higher Father, distinct from the Creator, who does not judge, exercises no providence over human affairs, and approves of sins?

question: Could "Let Us make man" be explained as the Father alone speaking to Himself as if to a companion?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No, not consistently with the opponents' own confession. Hilary concedes it is possible in principle that a solitary God spoke this way. But the opponents confess that all things are from the Father and all things are through the Son. On that confession, "Let Us make" points to the Father as Source, while "God made him after the image of God" points to the Son through Whom the work was done.
sources.quote: For you have confessed that all things are from the Father, but all through the Son; and the words, Let Us make man, shew that the Source from Whom are all things is He Who spoke thus
sources.raw_question: Could "Let Us make man" be explained as the Father alone speaking to Himself as if to a companion?

question: How does God's setting forth his Son as a propitiation reveal both his justice and his grace?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It reveals both at once. Through it God is known as a God who pardons iniquity and advances the riches of his grace, which was his design. At the same time he has infinitely vindicated his justice before men, angels and devils. Believers also gain by it, being more firmly established in his favour than Adam was: they receive better grace in Christ for the grace lost in Adam.
sources.quote: He hath infinitely vindicated his justice also, in the face of men, angels, and devils, in setting forth his Son for a [^163]propitiation.
sources.raw_question: How does God's setting forth his Son as a propitiation reveal both his justice and his grace?

question: In John 14:9, how can knowing the man Jesus Christ amount to knowing the invisible, bodiless Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Because the Father's nature dwells within the Son under the flesh that he took on. Hilary asks how a knowledge of the man the Apostles saw could be a knowledge of the bodiless Father. Christ himself answers that his Father's nature dwells in him, so knowing him is knowing the Father's nature, on which the Apostles had long gazed in him.
sources.quote: Who asserts that under the flesh, which, in a mystery, He had taken, His Father’s nature dwells within Him
sources.raw_question: In John 14:9, how can knowing the man Jesus Christ amount to knowing the invisible, bodiless Father?

question: Is God's preparation of creation an act within time, involving successive thoughts or a sudden impulse in God's mind?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. God does not linger over preliminary thoughts or seek materials like a human craftsman; the heavens were established by His word and breath. Things which have a beginning in respect of their creation have no beginning in God's knowledge and power, so the whole preparation of creation is perpetual and co-eternal with God, though executed in an ordered sequence of times.
sources.quote: For everything, which there is in created things, was always with God: for although these things in respect of their creation have a beginning, nevertheless they have no beginning in respect of the knowledge and power of God.
sources.raw_question: Is God's preparation of creation an act within time, involving successive thoughts or a sudden impulse in God's mind?

question: Are Christians to love, obey and serve Christ as their Master in the same way they owe love, obedience and service to God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Love to God is shown in keeping his commandments, and Christ says, 'If ye love Me, keep my commandments.' The Lord of hosts claims to be Master and the one to be served. Christ is called the one Master, and believers are told they 'serve the Lord Christ.' This religious love and service, due to God alone, is claimed by and paid to the Son.
sources.quote: One is your Master, even Christ. – Matt. 23:8, 10. Ye serve the Lord Christ. – Col. 3:24.
sources.raw_question: Are Christians to love, obey and serve Christ as their Master in the same way they owe love, obedience and service to God?

question: If the term 'advanced' is referred to Jesus, the Word made flesh, does this impair the Son's divinity as the Father's Light?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: No. It rather shows that the Word truly became man and bore true flesh. Just as he suffered, hungered and was fatigued in the flesh, he may reasonably be said to advance in the flesh, because the flesh was his own and not external to him; yet the advance was not the Word's, nor was the flesh Wisdom, but the flesh became Wisdom's body.
sources.quote: Neither then was the advance the Word’s, nor was the flesh Wisdom, but the flesh became the body of Wisdom
sources.raw_question: If the term 'advanced' is referred to Jesus, the Word made flesh, does this impair the Son's divinity as the Father's Light?

question: Why does Luke say 'Jesus advanced' rather than 'the Word advanced'?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: Because 'Jesus' is the name by which the Lord was called when he became man, so the Evangelist signals that the advance is of the human nature. Athanasius adds that the manhood advanced in Wisdom, as Wisdom built herself a house and gave that house advancement.
sources.quote: Wherefore neither said he, ‘The Word advanced,’ but Jesus, by which Name the Lord was called when He became man; so that the advance is of the human nature
sources.raw_question: Why does Luke say 'Jesus advanced' rather than 'the Word advanced'?

question: To whom and in whose name should believers pray for the Holy Spirit, and why should they do so daily?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Believers should ask the Holy Spirit of the Father, in the name of Jesus Christ, every day, as children ask their parents for daily bread. All their grace, peace, mercy, joy and hope lie in the promise of the Spirit. These things are communicated to them by him alone.
sources.quote: In this promise, they know, lies all their grace, peace, mercy, joy, and hope. For by him so promised, and him alone, are these things communicated to them.
sources.raw_question: To whom and in whose name should believers pray for the Holy Spirit, and why should they do so daily?

question: After the fall, can sinners still walk with God by the original path of the covenant of works, or is a new way required?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: A new way is required. The path of innocence and exact holiness assigned in the covenant of works is so stopped up by sin, curses and wrath that no one can take a single step in it. Christ has consecrated a "new and living way" into the holiest, new because the old is useless and living because the old is dead.
sources.quote: This path, by sin, is so filled with thorns and briers, so stopped up by curses and wrath, that no flesh living can take one step in that path; a new way for us to walk in must be found out
sources.raw_question: After the fall, can sinners still walk with God by the original path of the covenant of works, or is a new way required?

question: Is the Son the Creator, Preserver and Governor of all things, as the Father is?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: Yes. By the Son all things visible and invisible were created, and without the Word nothing was made. He upholds all things by the word of his power. He is the supreme Governor, addressed as God whose throne is forever, God over all, King of kings, with an everlasting dominion.
sources.quote: Jesus is the Creator, for “by him (the Son of his love) were all things created that are in heaven and that are in earth, visible and invisible
sources.raw_question: Is the Son the Creator, Preserver and Governor of all things, as the Father is?

question: Is God above us in place?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > How There is a Trinity in the Very Simplicity of God. Whether and How the Trinity that is God is Manifested from the Trinities Which Have Been Shown to Be in Men.
sources.answer: No. God's unchangeable nature is above us not in place but by its own awful and wonderful excellence. It is also not far from us, being present to us by its own light.
sources.quote: not far from us, and as above us, not in place, but by its own awful and wonderful excellence
sources.raw_question: Is God above us in place?

question: What does the Sabellian charge of tritheism against the early Church imply about the Church's view of the three Persons?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: It implies the Church held the three Persons to be consubstantial in a proper, not figurative, sense. The Sabellians meant tritheism in the strictest sense, as shown by their solution of making Father, Son, and Spirit one Hypostasis, so the charge arose because the Church held a real sameness of nature, as three men share one specific nature.

sources.raw_question: What does the Sabellian charge of tritheism against the early Church imply about the Church's view of the three Persons?

question: Did the early Fathers answer the charge of tritheism by saying the Son is called God only in a loose sense, like Moses, being a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: No. They never gave that easy answer, which they must have given had they held the Son a creature. Instead they secured both the Son's divinity and God's unity by appealing to unity of substance, as Tertullian did against Praxeas.

sources.raw_question: Did the early Fathers answer the charge of tritheism by saying the Son is called God only in a loose sense, like Moses, being a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: It could not be the Father because the one appearing acted ministerially. He is called an angel, he appeared, and he took on human shape, and these things do not suit the first Person of the Trinity. The Fathers did not argue from the pure simplicity of the divine nature. They also understood the human actions ascribed to this angel figuratively, in a manner fitting God, not literally.

question: In what senses does Scripture use the word 'grace' when applied to Christ and believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: In three main senses: the grace of personal comeliness and excellency, as in Psalm 45:2; the grace of God's free favour and acceptance, by which we are saved; and the sanctifying fruits of the Spirit renewing our natures. The latter two, as received by us, are 'purchased grace', bought by Christ for us.
sources.quote: These two latter, as relating unto Christ in respect of us who receive them, I call purchased grace, being indeed purchased by him for us
sources.raw_question: In what senses does Scripture use the word 'grace' when applied to Christ and believers?

question: Did Irenaeus teach the eternal generation of the Word even though he did not use the phrase 'eternal generation'?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes, by necessary implication. Irenaeus constantly asserts the eternity of the Word and censures those who ascribe any beginning to the Word's nativity or prolation. Denying any beginning to the Word's prolation is in effect asserting an eternal prolation or generation.
sources.quote: he censures those who pretended to ascribe any beginning to the nativity of the Word; which is in effect asserting an eternal prolation, or generation
sources.raw_question: Did Irenaeus teach the eternal generation of the Word even though he did not use the phrase 'eternal generation'?

question: Was the Son of God, who carries out the new covenant, foretold by the prophets of the old covenant?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IX.—There is but one author, and one end to both covenants.
sources.answer: Yes. The new covenant was known and preached by the prophets, and He who was to carry it out according to the Father's good pleasure was also preached, revealed as God pleased, so that men might progress through believing in Him. Hence we have not been taught another Christ besides the one foretold by the prophets.
sources.quote: For the new covenant having been known and preached by the prophets, He who was to carry it out according to the good pleasure of the Father was also preached, having been revealed to men as God pleased
sources.raw_question: Was the Son of God, who carries out the new covenant, foretold by the prophets of the old covenant?

question: Did God give commandments and require love and service from man because God himself needed anything?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVI.—Perfect righteousness was conferred neither by circumcision nor by any other legal ceremonies. The Decalogue, however, was not cancelled by Christ, but is always in force: men were never released from its commandments.
sources.answer: No. God stands in need of nothing from man. The commandments profit man alone: they supply what he lacks, the friendship and glory of God, which he can obtain only by serving God.
sources.quote: these things did indeed make man glorious, by supplying what was wanting to him, namely, the friendship of God; but they profited God nothing, for God did not at all stand in need of man’s love.
sources.raw_question: Did God give commandments and require love and service from man because God himself needed anything?

question: Are Paul's prayers to "the Lord" in 1 Thessalonians 3:12-13 and 2 Thessalonians 3:5 addressed to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes, in all likelihood. In both prayers the Father and Christ are named in addition to the Lord being addressed. The thing asked for, love, is the Spirit's peculiar gift, since the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost (Rom. 5:5). So the One addressed is especially the Spirit of Love, and these are prayers directed to him.
sources.quote: In both these supplications we have the Father and Christ named besides the One to whom the prayer is addressed; may we not be assured that this One is especially the blessed Spirit of Love?
sources.raw_question: Are Paul's prayers to "the Lord" in 1 Thessalonians 3:12-13 and 2 Thessalonians 3:5 addressed to the Holy Spirit?

question: Is it harder for God to create man from nothing than to restore a decomposed body in the resurrection?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter III.—The power and glory of God shine forth in the weakness of human flesh, as He will render our body a participator of the resurrection and of immortality, although He has formed it from the dust of the earth; He will also bestow upon it the enjoyment of immortality, just as He grants it this short life in common with the soul.
sources.answer: Creation from nothing is much harder. Making an animated, rational creature out of bones, nerves and veins that did not yet exist is more difficult and incredible than reintegrating what once existed and has decomposed into its elements. So He who first gave being to what was not will much more restore those who had a former existence.
sources.quote: For He who in the beginning caused him to have being who as yet was not, just when He pleased, shall much more reinstate again those who had a former existence
sources.raw_question: Is it harder for God to create man from nothing than to restore a decomposed body in the resurrection?

question: Why does Scripture say the Spirit 'abode' upon Christ, in contrast to the prophets?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter I. Not only were the prophets and apostles sent by the Spirit, but also the Son of God. This is proved from Isaiah and the evangelists, and it is explained why St. Luke wrote that the same Spirit descended like a dove upon Christ and abode upon Him. Next, after establishing this mission of Christ, the writer infers that the Son is sent by the Father and the Spirit, as the Spirit is by the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: The Spirit inspired the prophets or acted upon them only as often as he willed. In Christ, however, he abode always.
sources.quote: because the Spirit inspired a saying or acted upon the prophets as often as He would, but abode always in Christ.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture say the Spirit 'abode' upon Christ, in contrast to the prophets?

question: Is the God who gave the Mosaic law distinguishing clean and unclean the same God who purified the Gentiles through the blood of his Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter's vision, "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common," was given to teach that the God who through the law distinguished clean from unclean is the same who purified the Gentiles through his Son's blood. The apostles did not introduce a second god distinct from the lawgiver.
sources.quote: this happened [to teach him] that the God who had, through the law, distinguished between clean and unclean, was He who had purified the Gentiles through the blood of His Son
sources.raw_question: Is the God who gave the Mosaic law distinguishing clean and unclean the same God who purified the Gentiles through the blood of his Son?

question: Does the greater punishment for neglecting the salvation spoken by the Lord, compared to transgressing the law given through angels, show that the Son differs in nature from created beings?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Son were one of the originated things, He would not be better than the angels, and disobedience to Him would not bring increased punishment, just as under the angelic ministry there was one law and one vengeance regardless of which angel spoke. Because the Word is not among originate things but is Son of the Father, He and His acts are transcendent, and so the punishment for neglecting Him is worse.
sources.quote: But if the Son were in the number of things originate, He was not better than they, nor did disobedience involve increase of punishment because of Him
sources.raw_question: Does the greater punishment for neglecting the salvation spoken by the Lord, compared to transgressing the law given through angels, show that the Son differs in nature from created beings?

question: Why is a being that is not born or made incapable of change?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover, He is Good, Always the Same, Immutable, One and Only, Infinite; And His Own Name Can Never Be Declared, and He is Incorruptible and Immortal.
sources.answer: Only things that are made or begotten undergo change. Such things once did not exist and learn to be by coming into being, so being born is itself a change. What has neither nativity nor maker has no beginning in which a cause of change could lie, and so it excludes change altogether.
sources.quote: Moreover, those things which neither have nativity nor maker, have excluded from themselves the capacity of change, not having a beginning wherein is cause of change.
sources.raw_question: Why is a being that is not born or made incapable of change?

question: Was Christ present and active among Israel in the Old Testament, as shown by Paul's statement that the rock was Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVII—The sins of the men of old time, which incurred the displeasure of God, were, by His providence, committed to writing, that we might derive instruction thereby, and not be filled with pride. We must not, therefore, infer that there was another God than He whom Christ preached; we should rather fear, lest the one and the same God who inflicted punishment on the ancients, should bring down heavier upon us.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says the fathers drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ, and that some tempted Christ and were destroyed. Irenaeus takes this to show that the same God, with Christ, dealt with the ancients and deals with us now.
sources.quote: for they drank of that spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ present and active among Israel in the Old Testament, as shown by Paul's statement that the rock was Christ?

question: Does the fact that God is love mean he will not condemn his creatures eternally?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. Such a view imagines a God of mercy only, without holy jealousy and righteousness, and that is not the God of creation, providence, or the Bible. Creation and providence show severity as well as goodness. In Scripture, divine love includes all God's attributes, righteousness as well as mercy. Christ's warning that unbelievers will die in their sins confirms this.
sources.quote: God is love indeed – but love embraces all his attributes, not mercy only, but righteousness likewise
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that God is love mean he will not condemn his creatures eternally?

question: Does a believer's confession add anything to Christ's power when He grants help?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The confession does not augment the power of Him who is the Power of God. Christ requires it so that the benefit may be the reward of faith, as with Martha before Lazarus was raised.
sources.quote: Not, indeed, that the suppliant’s confession could augment the power of Him, Who is the Power of God; but the earning was to be the reward of faith.
sources.raw_question: Does a believer's confession add anything to Christ's power when He grants help?

question: From what source do we gain knowledge of the one God and the Trinity?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: From the Holy Scriptures alone. Just as worldly wisdom is learned only by mastering the philosophers' dogmas, piety can be learned only from the oracles of God. We must believe about the Father, glorify the Son, and receive the Spirit as God wills and teaches in Scripture, not according to our own will or mind.
sources.quote: There is, brethren, one God, the knowledge of whom we gain from the Holy Scriptures, and from no other source.
sources.raw_question: From what source do we gain knowledge of the one God and the Trinity?

question: Was God, existing alone before creation, a solitary unity without any plurality?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Though nothing was contemporaneous with God and He existed alone, He nevertheless existed in plurality, for He was never without reason, wisdom, power, or counsel. All things were in Him, and He later manifested His Word at the times He determined.
sources.quote: Beside Him there was nothing; but He, while existing alone, yet existed in plurality. For He was neither without reason, nor wisdom, nor power, nor counsel.
sources.raw_question: Was God, existing alone before creation, a solitary unity without any plurality?

question: How did the prophets speak the Father's will, and what role did the Holy Spirit and the Word play?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: God gave the law and the prophets and made them speak by the Holy Spirit, so that, inspired with the Father's power, they declared the Father's counsel and will. In them the Word spoke of Himself, heralding His own future manifestation among men.
sources.quote: He made them speak by the Holy Ghost, in order that, being gifted with the inspiration of the Father’s power, they might declare the Father’s counsel and will.
sources.raw_question: How did the prophets speak the Father's will, and what role did the Holy Spirit and the Word play?

question: Does Christ's promise to give his sheep eternal life so that they never perish prove that he is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: Yes. Every man is bound by the laws of mortality and cannot keep even himself forever, much less another. Christ promises eternal salvation and truly gives what he promises, so he would be a deceiver if he were only a man. Therefore he is God.
sources.quote: But Christ promises to give salvation for ever, which if He does not give, He is a deceiver; if He gives, He is God. But He does not deceive, for He gives what He promises.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's promise to give his sheep eternal life so that they never perish prove that he is God?

question: Do the confessions of the apostles in the boat and the centurion at the Cross prove that Christ is the true Son of God by nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. The apostles, seeing wind and sea calmed at His command, confessed 'Of a truth this is the Son of God.' The centurion, an unbeliever, was convinced by the torn veil, the earthquake and the rising of the dead that Christ's nature was omnipotent. So he named Him truly the Son of God, assured of His true Divinity.
sources.quote: The deeds that were done convinced him that Christ’s nature was omnipotent; he names Him the Son of God, being assured of His true Divinity.
sources.raw_question: Do the confessions of the apostles in the boat and the centurion at the Cross prove that Christ is the true Son of God by nature?

question: If we answer the question "three what?" with "three persons" or "three substances," does this imply any inequality or separation among them?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: No. Such plural terms may be admitted for the needs of argument, but no one should imagine bulk, interval, or the least unlikeness among the three. None is less than another in any way, so there is neither confusion of persons nor a distinction that implies inequality.
sources.quote: in order that there may be neither a confusion of persons, nor such a distinction as that there should be any inequality.
sources.raw_question: If we answer the question "three what?" with "three persons" or "three substances," does this imply any inequality or separation among them?

question: What does Jesus' statement that he casts out demons by the Spirit of God reveal about his relation to the Spirit?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: It shows that Jesus employs God's own Spirit for his works, as if the activities of God were at his disposal. Luke's parallel calls this the "finger of God." Just as the Father works by the Son, the Son works by the Spirit.
sources.quote: Jesus speaks of employing the Spirit of God Himself for the performance of His works, as if the activities of God were at His disposal
sources.raw_question: What does Jesus' statement that he casts out demons by the Spirit of God reveal about his relation to the Spirit?

question: Could salvation truly be brought about by Christ if the Word of God were not himself the one who suffered?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: No. Christ truly brought in salvation because the one who suffered and reconciled us is himself the Word of God and the Only-begotten of the Father, Christ Jesus our Lord. The Word took flesh, and he will return in that same flesh, revealing the Father's glory.
sources.quote: For He did Himself truly bring in salvation: since He is Himself the Word of God, Himself the Only-begotten of the Father, Christ Jesus our Lord.
sources.raw_question: Could salvation truly be brought about by Christ if the Word of God were not himself the one who suffered?

question: Why was it fitting that Christ, the second Adam, be unalterable?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: Because the first Adam altered and through his sin death came upon all men, the second Adam had to be unalterable so that the Serpent's assault would be baffled. Just as Adam's sin reached all men, the Lord's victory over the Serpent, as man, extends its strength through all men. By taking alterable flesh while remaining the same, He condemned sin in the flesh and secured its freedom and ability to fulfil the righteousness of the law.
sources.quote: For since the first man Adam altered, and through sin death came into the world, therefore it became the second Adam to be unalterable; that, should the Serpent again assault, even the Serpent’s deceit might be baffled
sources.raw_question: Why was it fitting that Christ, the second Adam, be unalterable?

question: Does the Son's loving righteousness and hating iniquity imply that He chooses between good and evil as one capable of either?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: No. He does not love one and hate the other as one subject to law and biased to one side out of fear of falling away. Being God and the Father's Word, just and holy by nature, He is a just judge and dispenser of virtue. To say He loves righteousness means He loves and chooses the virtuous and rejects the unrighteous.
sources.quote: Therefore being just and holy by nature, on this account He is said to love righteousness and to hate iniquity; as much as to say, that He loves and chooses the virtuous, and rejects and hates the unrighteous.
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's loving righteousness and hating iniquity imply that He chooses between good and evil as one capable of either?

question: Does calling the Holy Spirit the "place" of the saints degrade Him?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: No; by this figure He is rather glorified. Scripture transfers bodily words to spiritual conceptions, even calling God a "strong place"; the Spirit is the place of contemplation where Moses saw God and the place of true worship where the sacrifice of praise is offered, as Christ said the Father is worshipped in spirit and in truth.
sources.quote: the Spirit is frequently spoken of as the place of them that are being sanctified, and it will become evident that even by this figure the Spirit, so far from being degraded, is rather glorified.
sources.raw_question: Does calling the Holy Spirit the "place" of the saints degrade Him?

question: Does Christ have two generations, one from the Father and one from the Virgin?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XIX.—Jesus Christ was not a mere man, begotten from Joseph in the ordinary course of nature, but was very God, begotten of the Father most high, and very man, born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture testifies that he had beyond all others a pre-eminent birth from the Most High Father and also a pre-eminent generation from the Virgin. Hence it speaks of him both as a man without comeliness, liable to suffering, and as the Mighty God and Judge of all.
sources.quote: that He had, beyond all others, in Himself that pre-eminent birth which is from the Most High Father, and also experienced that pre-eminent generation which is from the Virgin
sources.raw_question: Does Christ have two generations, one from the Father and one from the Virgin?

question: How could the incarnate Word suffer and be crucified while also being glorified as God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XIX.—Jesus Christ was not a mere man, begotten from Joseph in the ordinary course of nature, but was very God, begotten of the Father most high, and very man, born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: The Word remained quiescent during the temptation, dishonour, crucifixion and death, so that he could suffer as man. But in his victory, endurance, acts of kindness, resurrection and ascension, the human nature was swallowed up in the divine. He became man to be tempted and was the Word that he might be glorified.
sources.quote: the Word remaining quiescent, that He might be capable of being tempted, dishonoured, crucified, and of suffering death, but the human nature being swallowed up in it (the divine), when it conquered
sources.raw_question: How could the incarnate Word suffer and be crucified while also being glorified as God?

question: In Christ's prayer 'Father, glorify thy Son', what is meant by the hour and the glorification?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: The hour is the hour of his passion. The Father glorified the Son at the cross through the signs that accompanied his death: the sun fled, the earth quaked, the rocks were rent. These culminated in the centurion confessing that he was truly the Son of God. The outcome thus fulfilled the prayer.
sources.quote: This then is the hour in which He prays to be glorified by the Father, that He Himself may glorify the Father.
sources.raw_question: In Christ's prayer 'Father, glorify thy Son', what is meant by the hour and the glorification?

question: Which Person of the Trinity appeared in the corporeal forms and visions granted to the Old Testament saints?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > Preface.
sources.answer: It was not always the Father alone, the Son alone, or the Spirit alone. Sometimes it was the Lord God indifferently, understood as the Trinity itself. At other times it was one particular Person, as the context of the narrative indicates.
sources.quote: not only the Father, nor only the Son, nor only the Holy Spirit appeared in those ancient corporeal forms and visions, but either indifferently the Lord God, who is understood to be the Trinity itself, or some one person of the Trinity
sources.raw_question: Which Person of the Trinity appeared in the corporeal forms and visions granted to the Old Testament saints?

question: Why does God give the Holy Spirit within believers in addition to external securities such as his word, promises, covenant and oath?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: So that believers may have all the security they are capable of. Having given many securities without us, God graciously gives one within us, the Holy Spirit. He is the first-fruits of glory, the utmost pledge of God's love, and the earnest of all.
sources.quote: he is pleased also graciously to give us one within us, Isa. lix. 21, that we may have all the security we are capable of. What can more be done? He hath given us of the Holy Spirit
sources.raw_question: Why does God give the Holy Spirit within believers in addition to external securities such as his word, promises, covenant and oath?

question: Is the Father, in particular, to be regarded as the eternal fountain of the grace that comes to sinners through the blood of Jesus, and does he welcome being received in this way?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. Receiving the Father as he holds out his love to the soul gives him the honour he aims at, and it is exceedingly acceptable to him. Scripture therefore sets forth the Father's love prominently, so that it may be received. Believers should fix their hearts on the Father as the eternal source of all the rich grace that flows to sinners in Christ's blood.
sources.quote: there is nothing more acceptable unto the Father, than for us to keep up our hearts unto him as the eternal fountain of all that rich grace which flows out to sinners in the blood of Jesus.
sources.raw_question: Is the Father, in particular, to be regarded as the eternal fountain of the grace that comes to sinners through the blood of Jesus, and does he welcome being received in this way?

question: Since the body is the temple in which the Spirit of the Father dwells and is a member of Christ, can it be excluded from salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VI.—God will bestow salvation upon the whole nature of man, consisting of body and soul in close union, since the Word took it upon Him, and adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, of whom our bodies are, and are termed, the temples.
sources.answer: No. Scripture calls our body the temple of God in which the Spirit dwells, and the members of Christ. It is therefore the utmost blasphemy to claim that this temple and these members are reduced to perdition. God, who raised up the Lord, will also raise up our bodies by His power.
sources.quote: How then is it not the utmost blasphemy to allege, that the temple of God, in which the Spirit of the Father dwells, and the members of Christ, do not partake of salvation, but are reduced to perdition?
sources.raw_question: Since the body is the temple in which the Spirit of the Father dwells and is a member of Christ, can it be excluded from salvation?

question: How can the Shema's declaration that the Lord is one God be reconciled with God being a Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Conclusion of the Book with a Prayer, and an Apology for Multitude of Words.
sources.answer: God is a Trinity in such a way as to be one Lord God. The divine voice would not have said "the Lord thy God is one God" unless the Trinity were also the one Lord God. Threeness of Persons and oneness of God are therefore held together, not set against each other.
sources.quote: Nor would the divine voice have said, Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one God, unless Thou wert so a Trinity as to be one Lord God.
sources.raw_question: How can the Shema's declaration that the Lord is one God be reconciled with God being a Trinity?

question: What remains of Scripture when the 'bodily veil' of the letter is removed, according to Paul's teaching that the Lord is the Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: What remains is Lord, life and Spirit. Paul teaches that whoever turns from the letter to the Spirit no longer apprehends the bondage that slays, but the Lord who is the life-giving Spirit. The Gospel likewise says Christ's words are spirit and life, since they are divested of the bodily veil.
sources.quote: If the bodily veil of the words were removed, that which remains is Lord and life and Spirit, according to the teaching of the great Paul, and according to the words of the Gospel also.
sources.raw_question: What remains of Scripture when the 'bodily veil' of the letter is removed, according to Paul's teaching that the Lord is the Spirit?

question: Was the Son already Lord and King before he became man and suffered on the Cross?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fifthly, Acts ii. 36. The Regula Fidei must be observed; made applies to our Lord's manhood; and to His manifestation; and to His office relative to us; and is relative to the Jews. Parallel instance in Gen. xxvii. 29, 37. The context contradicts the Arian interpretation.
sources.answer: Yes. Abraham worshipped Him as Lord, Moses speaks of the Lord raining fire 'from the Lord', David says 'The Lord said unto my Lord' and 'Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever.' Hence even before becoming man He was everlasting King and Lord, being Image and Word of the Father; to deny this revives the teaching of Paul of Samosata.
sources.quote: it is plain that even before He became man, He was King and Lord everlasting, being Image and Word of the Father.
sources.raw_question: Was the Son already Lord and King before he became man and suffered on the Cross?

question: Does the Son's obedience to the Father even to death on the cross teach anything for human salvation?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Other Advantages of the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Yes. Humanity perished through disobedience, and no greater example of obedience could be given than God the Son obedient to God the Father even to the death of the cross. The reward of obedience is likewise shown in the Mediator's flesh, which rose again to eternal life.
sources.quote: For what greater example of obedience could be given to us, who had perished through disobedience, than God the Son obedient to God the Father, even to the death of the cross?
sources.raw_question: Does the Son's obedience to the Father even to death on the cross teach anything for human salvation?

question: Was the Holy Spirit present and active in Christ's incarnate life and works?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit was made an unction and was inseparably present with the very flesh of the Lord, as shown at his baptism and anointing. He led Christ into the wilderness to be tempted, was with him in casting out devils, and was bestowed by him after the resurrection when he breathed on the disciples. Thus every operation of Christ was wrought with the co-operation of the Spirit.
sources.quote: In the first place He was made an unction, and being inseparably present was with the very flesh of the Lord
sources.raw_question: Was the Holy Spirit present and active in Christ's incarnate life and works?

question: Is the ordering of the Church effected by the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: Yes. It is plain and incontestable, for apostles, prophets, teachers, miracles, healings, helps, governments and tongues are set in the Church according to the division of the gifts of the Spirit.
sources.quote: for this order is ordained in accordance with the division of the gifts that are of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Is the ordering of the Church effected by the Holy Spirit?

question: What did Christ signify by breathing on the disciples and saying 'Receive ye the Holy Ghost'?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
