sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: He was renewing man by restoring the grace that came from God's original inbreathing, which man had lost. By imparting the Spirit he gave the disciples power to remit and retain sins, showing the Spirit's work in the risen Lord's renewal of humanity.
sources.quote: restoring the grace, that came of the inbreathing of God, which man had lost
sources.raw_question: What did Christ signify by breathing on the disciples and saying 'Receive ye the Holy Ghost'?

question: Can Christ's love for the believer be increased by the believer's desire for more of it?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. Christ's love is inconceivable and cannot be increased; what the soul seeks is not more love in Christ but a fuller apprehension and manifestation of that love to itself. Hence the spouse asks for the love to be shown on Christ's arm, made evident by its fruits.
sources.quote: The soul knows, indeed, on serious thoughts, that the love of Christ is inconceivable, and cannot be increased; but it would fain work up itself to an apprehension of it
sources.raw_question: Can Christ's love for the believer be increased by the believer's desire for more of it?

question: When Philip asked 'Show us the Father, and it sufficeth us,' would seeing the Son alone have sufficed equally?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Philip could equally have said, 'Lord, show Thyself to us, and it sufficeth us.' Christ answered him that 'he that hath seen me hath seen the Father,' because the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. Seeing either one therefore satisfies us fully.
sources.quote: But he had not yet understood that he himself was able to say this very same thing in this way also: Lord, show Thyself to us, and it sufficeth us.
sources.raw_question: When Philip asked 'Show us the Father, and it sufficeth us,' would seeing the Son alone have sufficed equally?

question: Can a writer whose own views on the Holy Spirit were not sound still be a valid witness to the Church's tradition of honouring the Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word “with.”
sources.answer: Yes. Established tradition is so strong that it often leads men to speak in terms contrary to their private opinions. So even Origen, whose views on the Spirit were not always sound, reverently followed established usage and spoke of the Spirit in terms consistent with true religion.
sources.quote: Thus I apprehend, the powerful influence of tradition frequently impels men to express themselves in terms contradictory to their own opinions.
sources.raw_question: Can a writer whose own views on the Holy Spirit were not sound still be a valid witness to the Church's tradition of honouring the Spirit?

question: What does Christ's putting down all rule, authority and power (1 Corinthians 15:24) signify for our knowledge of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: It signifies that there will no longer be any need for an economy of similitudes mediated by angelic rulers, authorities and powers. Now we see through a glass, in an enigma, that is, in similitudes. Then we shall see face to face, once Christ, our hidden life, appears.
sources.quote: that is, in such wise that there shall be no more need of any economy of similitudes, by means of angelic rulers, and authorities, and powers.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's putting down all rule, authority and power (1 Corinthians 15:24) signify for our knowledge of God?

question: Does Christ's teaching on the Mosaic permission of divorce show that the God of the Old Testament is the same God Christ proclaimed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XV.—At first God deemed it sufficient to inscribe the natural law, or the Decalogue, upon the hearts of men; but afterwards He found it necessary to bridle, with the yoke of the Mosaic law, the desires of the Jews, who were abusing their liberty; and even to add some special commands, because of the hardness of their hearts.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ said Moses permitted divorce because of the people's hardness of heart, but that from the beginning it was not so. In saying this he cleared Moses as a faithful servant and acknowledged one God, the one who made male and female from the beginning. The concession came from the people's hard nature, not from a different deity.
sources.quote: thus exculpating Moses as a faithful servant, but acknowledging one God, who from the beginning made male and female, and reproving them as hard-hearted and disobedient.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's teaching on the Mosaic permission of divorce show that the God of the Old Testament is the same God Christ proclaimed?

question: When Scripture speaks of loving or praising God with the whole 'heart', does it mean the bodily organ?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Opinions of Philosophers Respecting the Substance of the Soul. The Error of Those Who are of Opinion that the Soul is Corporeal, Does Not Arise from Defective Knowledge of the Soul, But from Their Adding There to Something Foreign to It. What is Meant by Finding.
sources.answer: No. In these texts the word is carried over from the body to the soul by metaphor. It does not mean the small bodily part seen when the inner organs are laid open, as some philosophers thought the soul to be.
sources.quote: for this word by misapplication or metaphor is transferred from the body to the soul
sources.raw_question: When Scripture speaks of loving or praising God with the whole 'heart', does it mean the bodily organ?

question: Who is the 'Power' of the Father mentioned in Acts 1:7-8?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: The Son. Christ is 'God's Power and God's Wisdom.' The times are in the Father's power, that is, in the Son.
sources.quote: And what is that Power of the Father but the Son? for Christ is ‘God’s Power and God’s Wisdom.’
sources.raw_question: Who is the 'Power' of the Father mentioned in Acts 1:7-8?

question: Does God directly inflict eternal punishment on unbelievers, or does punishment consist in self-chosen separation from God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXVII.—The future judgment by Christ. Communion with and separation from the divine being. The eternal punishment of unbelievers.
sources.answer: Punishment is chiefly the separation from God that apostates choose for themselves. Communion with God is life, light and all good things, so separation from him is death, darkness and the loss of every good. God does not punish them immediately of himself; like the blind deprived of light, they suffer because they lack all good. Since the goods with God are eternal, their loss is eternal too.
sources.quote: God, however, does not punish them immediately of Himself, but that punishment falls upon them because they are destitute of all that is good. Now, good things are eternal and without end with God, and therefore the loss of these is also eternal and never-ending.
sources.raw_question: Does God directly inflict eternal punishment on unbelievers, or does punishment consist in self-chosen separation from God?

question: Is the wrath of God an emotional disturbance like human anger?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Remains of Death and the Evil Things of the World Turn to Good for the Elect. How Fitly the Death of Christ Was Chosen, that We Might Be Justified in His Blood. What the Anger of God is.
sources.answer: No. God's wrath is nothing else but just retribution, not a perturbation of the mind as in man. Scripture says that God, mastering His power, judges with calmness.
sources.quote: For the wrath of God is not, as is that of man, a perturbation of the mind; but it is the wrath of Him to whom Holy Scripture says in another place, “But Thou, O Lord, mastering Thy power, judgest with calmness.”
sources.raw_question: Is the wrath of God an emotional disturbance like human anger?

question: Why is it significant that the second Adam is God as well as man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Remains of Death and the Evil Things of the World Turn to Good for the Elect. How Fitly the Death of Christ Was Chosen, that We Might Be Justified in His Blood. What the Anger of God is.
sources.answer: The second Adam is not only man but also God. By paying for us what He did not owe, He frees us from the debts both of our first father and of ourselves. Just as the devil held all who were begotten through Adam's corrupted concupiscence, it is just that through Christ he should release all who are regenerated by His spiritual grace.
sources.quote: the other the second Adam, who is not only man, but also God, by whose payment for us of what He owed not, we are freed from the debts both of our first father and of ourselves
sources.raw_question: Why is it significant that the second Adam is God as well as man?

question: Do the human attributes of Christ, such as sleeping, weeping, asking questions and suffering on the Cross, prove that he is not the eternal Word and true God?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: No. These lowly attributes belong to the flesh that the Saviour took on himself and spoke for our sakes as man. They do not belong to his Godhead. To argue from them against his divinity is the same unbelief as the Jews who asked how a man could be God. Christians accept both his Godhead and Eternity and the human things he said and did for us.
sources.quote: Thus both parties deny the Eternity and Godhead of the Word in consequence of those human attributes which the Saviour took on Him by reason of that flesh which He bore.
sources.raw_question: Do the human attributes of Christ, such as sleeping, weeping, asking questions and suffering on the Cross, prove that he is not the eternal Word and true God?

question: If God is only the three Persons together, how can God be called the head of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:3), since Christ is himself within the Trinity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Whether One or the Three Persons Together are Called the Only God.
sources.answer: Christ here is the Word made flesh, the man who is mediator. The divine being, which the Word shares as one with the Father, is the head of that mediator. Augustine compares this to the mind being called the head of a human being, even though the whole man includes the mind. In the same way, the Word together with the Father, which together is God, can fittingly be called the head of Christ.
sources.quote: so that the very being of God, which is one to Him with the Father, is itself the head of the man who is mediator, which He is alone.
sources.raw_question: If God is only the three Persons together, how can God be called the head of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:3), since Christ is himself within the Trinity?

question: What does Paul mean by "the Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: It means the Holy Spirit coming to dwell in the mind of the faithful. Paul often calls the mind "spirit." When the mind receives the communion of the Holy Spirit, those who receive it attain the dignity of adoption. Nothing about essence is signified.
sources.quote: signifies nothing else than the Holy Spirit Which comes to be in the mind of the faithful; for in many other passages of his writings he gives the name of spirit to the mind
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean by "the Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit"?

question: What property is peculiar to the Father and not shared by the Son and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: Being ungenerate. Uncreatedness is common to the Father, the Son and the Spirit. Only the Father is also ungenerate, never having been generated any more than created, and this is peculiar to him and cannot be communicated to the other Persons.
sources.quote: While this uncreatedness is common to Him and the Son, and the Spirit, He is ungenerate as well as the Father. This is peculiar and uncommunicable, being not seen in the other Persons.
sources.raw_question: What property is peculiar to the Father and not shared by the Son and the Holy Spirit?

question: Can the one name of Jehovah comprehend a Trinity in Unity?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. Human imagination to the contrary counts for nothing against Christ's own words revealing the one divine name as 'the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost,' a single name shared by three.
sources.quote: Your imagination is as nothing in contradiction of the words of Christ revealing the one Divine name, as “the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.”
sources.raw_question: Can the one name of Jehovah comprehend a Trinity in Unity?

question: Would it be consistent with God's perfection for the supreme Father to have formed his works in a certain shape without any reason?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XV.—No account can be given of these productions.
sources.answer: No. If the Gnostics admit that their Father gave the Pleroma its shape without a reason, they must accuse him of acting vainly and thoughtlessly. That would ascribe deformity to him. Irenaeus assumes that God's works proceed from reason and wisdom, so a structure with no reason behind it reflects badly on its supposed maker.
sources.quote: their Father formed it of that figure vainly and thoughtlessly, and must ascribe to Him deformity, if He made anything without a reason
sources.raw_question: Would it be consistent with God's perfection for the supreme Father to have formed his works in a certain shape without any reason?

question: Is God the cause of the eternal darkness and punishment suffered by those who reject him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIX.—Man is endowed with the faculty of distinguishing good and evil; so that, without compulsion, he has the power, by his own will and choice, to perform God’s commandments, by doing which he avoids the evils prepared for the rebellious.
sources.answer: No. Those who flee the eternal light of God are themselves the cause of their dwelling in eternal darkness. Sunlight is not to blame when people shut themselves off from it and sit in darkness. In the same way, God's light does not cause the misery of those who turn away from it. God, foreknowing all things, simply prepared a habitation suited to their own choice.
sources.quote: so those who fly from the eternal light of God, which contains in itself all good things, are themselves the cause to themselves of their inhabiting eternal darkness, destitute of all good things
sources.raw_question: Is God the cause of the eternal darkness and punishment suffered by those who reject him?

question: Why does separation from God amount to the loss of all good and a just punishment?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIX.—Man is endowed with the faculty of distinguishing good and evil; so that, without compulsion, he has the power, by his own will and choice, to perform God’s commandments, by doing which he avoids the evils prepared for the rebellious.
sources.answer: Because all good things are with God. Whoever by their own choice flees from God therefore deprives themselves of every good. Submission to God is eternal rest, so those who flee that rest justly receive a place that matches their flight. Those who avoid the light justly dwell in darkness.
sources.quote: Now, since all good things are with God, they who by their own determination fly from God, do defraud themselves of all good things
sources.raw_question: Why does separation from God amount to the loss of all good and a just punishment?

question: Did God have no other possible way to free humanity from mortality than the incarnation of the only-begotten Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > There Was No Other More Suitable Way of Freeing Man from the Misery of Mortality Than The Incarnation of the Word. The Merits Which are Called Ours are the Gifts of God.
sources.answer: God could have used other means, since all things are equally subject to his power, but there neither was nor needed to be any more appropriate way of curing our misery. Nothing better builds up hope and frees mortals from despair of immortality than demonstrating how highly God values us and how much he loves us. The Son becoming man and bearing our evils without any desert of his own is the most manifest proof of that love.
sources.quote: not indeed that no other mode was possible to God, to whose power all things are equally subject, but that there neither was nor need have been any other mode more appropriate for curing our misery
sources.raw_question: Did God have no other possible way to free humanity from mortality than the incarnation of the only-begotten Son?

question: If the Demiurge made the world after the model of a higher spiritual realm (the Pleroma), where did the highest being get the model for that higher realm?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVI.—The Creator of the world either produced of Himself the images of things to be made, or the Pleroma was formed after the image of some previous system; and so on ad infinitum.
sources.answer: The Gnostic scheme cannot answer without either admitting the highest god formed the model from himself or positing yet another higher system. Either the intention and model of creating dwelt in the god who made the world, or one must constantly ask whence the one above received its configuration. If Bythus could impart a configuration of himself, there is no reason the Demiurge could not form the world of himself.
sources.quote: If, however, it was in the power of Bythus to impart of himself such a configuration to the Pleroma, then why may it not have been in the power of the Demiurge to form of himself such a world as exists?
sources.raw_question: If the Demiurge made the world after the model of a higher spiritual realm (the Pleroma), where did the highest being get the model for that higher realm?

question: Why can each Person of the Trinity act freely even when one Person sends another?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Because the will of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is essentially one and the same. So in the acting of any one Person there is the counsel of all and each, freely engaged. Being sent therefore never compromises the liberty of the Person sent.
sources.quote: because the will of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, is essentially the same; so that in the acting of one there is the counsel of all and each freely therein
sources.raw_question: Why can each Person of the Trinity act freely even when one Person sends another?

question: Does God's sharing a name such as "good" with men show that community of attributes is the same as identity of essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > Then, again discussing the true Light and unapproachable Light of the Father and of the Son, special attributes, community and essence, and showing the relation of “generate” and “ungenerate,” as involving no opposition in sense, but presenting an opposition and contradiction admitting of no middle term, he ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Scripture calls both God and men good, yet Divinity is not thereby humanity, nor humanity Divinity. God is named good as the fountain of goodness, while man shares the name by partaking of goodness. The special meaning in each case distinguishes what the shared term holds in common. Hence the idea of community is one thing and that of essence another.
sources.quote: For He Who is the fountain of goodness is named from it; but he who has some share of goodness also partakes in the name, and God is not for this reason composite, that He shares with men the title of “good.”
sources.raw_question: Does God's sharing a name such as "good" with men show that community of attributes is the same as identity of essence?

question: Does Christ's saying that one greater than the temple is here imply that the new dispensation belongs to a different God, opposed to the God of the temple?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IX.—There is but one author, and one end to both covenants.
sources.answer: No. 'Greater' and 'less' are only used of things of the same substance that share properties and differ in number or size, like water from water or light from light, not of things opposite and mutually repugnant. So the comparison shows that the new and old come from the same source, the new law of liberty being greater than the law of bondage.
sources.quote: greater and less are not applied to those things which have nothing in common between themselves, and are of an opposite nature, and mutually repugnant; but are used in the case of those of the same substance
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that one greater than the temple is here imply that the new dispensation belongs to a different God, opposed to the God of the temple?

question: What is the work of the Holy Spirit within believers according to Christ's promise of the Advocate?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: The Spirit, sent as another Advocate, guides believers into all truth, speaks what He hears, declares things to come, and glorifies Christ by taking of what is His. Because our feeble minds cannot comprehend the Father or the Son, and faith finds the incarnation hard to believe, the Spirit illumines that faith as the Bond of union and Source of light.
sources.quote: our faith which finds God’s incarnation hard of credence shall be illumined by the gift of the Holy Ghost, the Bond of union and the Source of light.
sources.raw_question: What is the work of the Holy Spirit within believers according to Christ's promise of the Advocate?

question: Did God, the giver of good, give human life only for it to end in death?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Immortal God has not given life only to end in death. No one can believe that the Giver of good bestowed the pleasant sense of life only to have it overcast by the gloomy fear of dying. Nature itself teaches that life is meant for progress towards immortality.
sources.quote: for none can believe that the Giver of good has bestowed the pleasant sense of life in order that it may be overcast by the gloomy fear of dying.
sources.raw_question: Did God, the giver of good, give human life only for it to end in death?

question: Can a single-nature Arian account of the Word explain both the Son's high divine titles and his human limitations, such as growing in wisdom, not knowing the day of judgment, and anguish in his agony?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 31: Whether any thing less than clear and evident demonstration, on the side of Arianism, ought to move a wise and good man, against so great appearances of truth o
sources.answer: No. Waterland argues that no single created Logos can be high enough to carry all the divine titles and attributes Scripture gives the Son. It also cannot be low enough to account for his increase in wisdom, ignorance of the day, and sorrow and agony. The Arian must either make both sets of attributes meet in the one Word, which is impossible, or borrow the orthodox scheme of two natures in Christ.
sources.quote: You are to make all to meet in the one Adyos, or Word; or else to mend your scheme by borrowing from ours.
sources.raw_question: Can a single-nature Arian account of the Word explain both the Son's high divine titles and his human limitations, such as growing in wisdom, not knowing the day of judgment, and anguish in his agony?

question: Does a creature's imitation of divine virtues such as mercy make it one with God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > The Passage where he attacks the ῾Ομοούσιον, and the contention in answer to it.
sources.answer: No. God wills us to be merciful, and saints have become kind and lowly through effort. Yet they are not thereby one with God, since such qualities lie over and above nature and can be shared by created beings. True oneness requires sameness of nature, with union of will added to it.
sources.quote: does it follow that they are therefore one with God, or united to Him by virtue of any one of them? Not so.
sources.raw_question: Does a creature's imitation of divine virtues such as mercy make it one with God?

question: Does the angel's annunciation to Mary show that the divine Word and the man born of Mary are one?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: Yes. The archangel says that the Holy One born of Mary shall be called the Son of God, which shows more clearly than any reasoning the oneness of the divine Word and the man. So it is irrational to separate the Word from the man of Mary; the Word is not sent through that man but rather himself sends in him, saying 'Go ye, teach all nations.'
sources.quote: More clearly however and indisputably than all reasoning does what was said by the Archangel to the Bearer of God herself, shew the oneness of the Divine Word and Man.
sources.raw_question: Does the angel's annunciation to Mary show that the divine Word and the man born of Mary are one?

question: Why was it the Son rather than God the Father who was seen by men in the Old Testament, and what purpose did this serve?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of Abraham is Called God; Which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No Man Hath Seen at Any Time; But of the Son in the Likeness of an Angel.
sources.answer: The Son, as the image of the invisible God, was seen so that human weakness might be gradually trained to bear the sight of God. Just as the sun rises by degrees so as not to blind eyes, so men, being accustomed to look upon the Son, may one day be able to see God the Father as He is without being struck by His sudden and intolerable brightness.
sources.quote: so that, being accustomed to look upon the Son, it may one day be able to see God the Father Himself also as He is, that it may not be stricken by His sudden and intolerable brightness
sources.raw_question: Why was it the Son rather than God the Father who was seen by men in the Old Testament, and what purpose did this serve?

question: Is a name applied 'most properly' only when it truly agrees with the nature of the thing named?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He again shows Eunomius, constrained by truth, in the character of an advocate of the orthodox doctrine, confessing as most proper and primary, not only the essence of the Father, but the essence also of the Only-begotten.
sources.answer: Yes. Common usage does not apply 'most proper' where the name does not truly fit the nature. A portrait is called 'a man' only inexactly, and Scripture calls idols, demons and the belly 'god' without the proper sense. Likewise if a real man and a portrait were counted as 'two men,' the proper meaning would not belong to both. So if the Son's nature differed from the Father's essence, both could not be called 'most proper.'
sources.quote: the general usage of men bears witness to our argument, which does not apply the term “most proper” where the name does not truly agree with the nature.
sources.raw_question: Is a name applied 'most properly' only when it truly agrees with the nature of the thing named?

question: Why does Christ promise to manifest himself to those who love him when he was already visible to people's eyes?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In What Manner the Son Was Sent and Proclaimed Beforehand. How in the Sending of His Birth in the Flesh He Was Made Less Without Detriment to His Equality with the Father.
sources.answer: Because he offered his flesh, the flesh the Word was made, to be accepted by faith. He kept back the Word himself, by whom all things were made, to be contemplated in eternity by minds cleansed by faith. The promised manifestation is therefore of his divinity, not of his visible body.
sources.quote: He was offering that flesh, which the Word was made in the fullness of time, to be accepted by our faith; but was keeping back the Word itself, by whom all things were made, to be contemplated in eternity by the mind when cleansed by faith?
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ promise to manifest himself to those who love him when he was already visible to people's eyes?

question: Why was the Son's mission accompanied by signs and testimonies throughout creation, both before and after his coming?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In What Manner the Son Was Sent and Proclaimed Beforehand. How in the Sending of His Birth in the Flesh He Was Made Less Without Detriment to His Equality with the Father.
sources.answer: These things were done in time to produce faith, by which we are cleansed so as to contemplate truth. They were either testimonies of the Son's mission or the mission itself. Since the one by whom all creation was made became a creature, the whole creation had to bear witness to him. Lowly people needed signs that seemed great to them in order to believe that he, being great, would make them great.
sources.quote: For that He was made a creature by whom the whole creation was made, must needs find a witness in the whole creation.
sources.raw_question: Why was the Son's mission accompanied by signs and testimonies throughout creation, both before and after his coming?

question: Does a law of nature cause the names of things to arise from the things themselves rather than from the choice of those who name them?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. If nature had enacted such a law, it would bind all who share the common nature, and the names given to objects would not vary. Then all mankind would speak one tongue. The actual diversity of languages shows that naming is entrusted to human choice.
sources.quote: If nature had really enacted such a law, it ought to have authority amongst all who share the common nature, just as the other things peculiar to that nature have.
sources.raw_question: Does a law of nature cause the names of things to arise from the things themselves rather than from the choice of those who name them?

question: Why do the Father and the Son rejoice in each other?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Because each sees himself in the other. The Father rejoices in seeing himself in his own Image, the Word. The Son delights in seeing himself in the Father. This is what 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father' and 'I am in the Father and the Father in Me' express.
sources.quote: And in whom does the Father rejoice, except as seeing Himself in His own Image, which is His Word?
sources.raw_question: Why do the Father and the Son rejoice in each other?

question: How can things be loved that are not known but only believed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What Has Been Treated of in This Book. How We Have Reached by Steps to a Certain Trinity, Which is Found in Practical Knowledge and True Faith.
sources.answer: No one loves what he is wholly ignorant of. When unknown things are said to be loved, they are loved by means of things that are known.
sources.quote: we found, that no one loves what he is wholly ignorant of, but that when things not known are said to be loved, they are loved from those things which are known
sources.raw_question: How can things be loved that are not known but only believed?

question: What is the first and highest cause of all corporeal appearances and motions in creation?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > God Uses All Creatures as He Will, and Makes Visible Things for the Manifestation of Himself.
sources.answer: The will of God is the first and highest cause. Bodies are governed by spirits, irrational spirits by rational ones, sinful rational spirits by pious and just ones, and these by God Himself, so that the whole creature is ruled by its Creator. Nothing happens visibly or sensibly except by command or permission of the invisible supreme Governor.
sources.quote: And so it comes to pass that the will of God is the first and the highest cause of all corporeal appearances and motions.
sources.raw_question: What is the first and highest cause of all corporeal appearances and motions in creation?

question: Can a created sign, such as words, writing, or the consecrated bread and wine, signify Christ without being identical to what it signifies?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > God Uses All Creatures as He Will, and Makes Visible Things for the Manifestation of Himself.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul preached Christ by tongue, by epistle, and by the sacrament, yet neither his tongue, the parchment, the ink, nor the sounds are called Christ's body and blood. Only what is taken from the fruits of the earth and consecrated is the sacrament. Even that is sanctified only by the Spirit of God working invisibly, though men's hands bring it to visible form. This serves as an analogy for how God manifests Himself through creatures.
sources.quote: yet is not sanctified to become so great a sacrament, except by the spirit of God working invisibly
sources.raw_question: Can a created sign, such as words, writing, or the consecrated bread and wine, signify Christ without being identical to what it signifies?

question: How can Christ be said to have been 'three days and three nights in the heart of the earth' when he was buried on the evening of the sixth day and rose at dawn on the first day of the week?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Three Days of the Resurrection, in Which Also the Ratio of Single to Double is Apparent.
sources.answer: The three days were not each whole and entire. The first day is counted as a whole from its last part and the third day from its first part. Only the middle day was a complete day of twenty-four hours, twelve of day and twelve of night. Since Christ was buried 'when the even was come', the first day cannot be made an entire day, so it is reckoned whole from its end.
sources.quote: the first day is counted as a whole from its last part, and the third day is itself also counted as a whole from its first part; but the intervening day, i.e. the second day, was absolutely a whole with its twenty-four hours
sources.raw_question: How can Christ be said to have been 'three days and three nights in the heart of the earth' when he was buried on the evening of the sixth day and rose at dawn on the first day of the week?

question: Why are the days of Christ's death and resurrection reckoned from night to light, when the days of creation were reckoned from light to night?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Three Days of the Resurrection, in Which Also the Ratio of Single to Double is Apparent.
sources.answer: The order of reckoning signifies the fall and the restoration of man. The first days of creation ran from light to night because of man's future fall. The days of Christ's passion ran from darkness to light because of man's restoration. This fits God, who commanded light to shine out of darkness, and the saying 'ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord'.
sources.quote: For as the first days of all were reckoned from light to night, on account of the future fall of man; so these on account of the restoration of man, are reckoned from darkness to light.
sources.raw_question: Why are the days of Christ's death and resurrection reckoned from night to light, when the days of creation were reckoned from light to night?

question: Are the numbers connected with Christ's death and resurrection in Scripture placed there for mystical reasons, or for no purpose?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Three Days of the Resurrection, in Which Also the Ratio of Single to Double is Apparent.
sources.answer: They have mystical reasons, and no one could sensibly hold that they are there for no purpose. For example, the forty hours from Christ's death to his resurrection match the forty days of his life on earth afterward, and forty signifies perfection in the fourfold world. The thirty-six hours from burial to resurrection show the ratio of single to double, which Augustine links to Christ's single death redeeming both our spirit and our body. Others may offer different explanations, but Augustine's are drawn from church tradition, from Scripture, and from the nature of numbers.
sources.quote: there is no one surely so foolish or so absurd as to contend that they are so put in the Scriptures for no purpose at all, and that there are no mystical reasons why those numbers are there mentioned
sources.raw_question: Are the numbers connected with Christ's death and resurrection in Scripture placed there for mystical reasons, or for no purpose?

question: Did God create Adam because He needed humanity, for example to receive glory or service?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIV.—If God demands obedience from man, if He formed man, called him and placed him under laws, it was merely for man’s welfare; not that God stood in need of man, but that He graciously conferred upon man His favours in every possible manner.
sources.answer: No. God formed Adam not because He stood in need of man but so that He might have someone on whom to confer His benefits. Even before all creation the Word glorified the Father and was glorified by Him, so God lacked no glory that creation could supply.
sources.quote: In the beginning, therefore, did God form Adam, not as if He stood in need of man, but that He might have [some one] upon whom to confer His benefits.
sources.raw_question: Did God create Adam because He needed humanity, for example to receive glory or service?

question: How does the Virgin Mary's obedience relate to Eve's disobedience in the work of salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXII.—Christ assumed actual flesh, conceived and born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: Mary's obedience undoes what Eve's disobedience caused. Eve, still a virgin though she had a husband, disobeyed and became the cause of death for herself and the whole human race. Mary, also a virgin though betrothed, obeyed and became the cause of salvation for herself and the whole race. A bond can only be loosed by reversing the process that tied it, so the knot Eve tied through unbelief was untied by Mary through faith.
sources.quote: And thus also it was that the knot of Eve’s disobedience was loosed by the obedience of Mary. For what the virgin Eve had bound fast through unbelief, this did the virgin Mary set free through faith.
sources.raw_question: How does the Virgin Mary's obedience relate to Eve's disobedience in the work of salvation?

question: Is Eunomius right that things united in the idea of their essence must exist corporeally and be subject to corruption?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > After much discourse concerning the actually existent, and ungenerate and good, and upon the consubstantiality of the heavenly powers, showing the uncharted character of their essence, yet the difference of their ranks, he ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Countless human souls share one essence, yet their consubstantial substratum is foreign to bodily corruption. Bodies decay because they are compound, not because they share an essence. So "corruptible bodies are of one essence" is true, but its converse, that a consubstantial nature is corruptible, is false.
sources.quote: bodies are corrupted and dissolved, not because they have the same essence one with another, but because of their possessing a compound nature.
sources.raw_question: Is Eunomius right that things united in the idea of their essence must exist corporeally and be subject to corruption?

question: Why does the apostle say that what is animal comes first and what is spiritual comes afterwards?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XII.—Of the difference between life and death; of the breath of life and the vivifying Spirit: also how it is that the substance of flesh revives which once was dead.
sources.answer: Because there was a necessary order. A human being first had to be fashioned and to receive a soul, and only afterwards to receive the communion of the Spirit. So the first Adam was made a living soul and the second Adam a quickening spirit.
sources.quote: For there had been a necessity that, in the first place, a human being should be fashioned, and that what was fashioned should receive the soul; afterwards that it should thus receive the communion of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Why does the apostle say that what is animal comes first and what is spiritual comes afterwards?

question: Can the origin and nature of Christ be discovered from the numerical values and letter-counts of Greek names such as 'Jesus' (888) and 'Christ the Son', as the Gnostic Marcus claimed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XV.—Sige relates to Marcus the generation of the twenty-four elements and of Jesus. Exposure of these absurdities.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus calls such letter-and-number speculation ravings and audacious falsehoods. The Greek alphabet is a late human invention: Cadmus brought sixteen letters, and others added further letters later. If divine truth were made of these letters, truth would have come into being after Cadmus and the later inventors, which is absurd.
sources.quote: Was it so, then, that until these things took place among the Greeks, truth had no existence? For, according to thee, Marcus, the body of truth is posterior to Cadmus and those who preceded him
sources.raw_question: Can the origin and nature of Christ be discovered from the numerical values and letter-counts of Greek names such as 'Jesus' (888) and 'Christ the Son', as the Gnostic Marcus claimed?

question: Can the God whom the Gnostics call unspeakable and unnameable have his hidden names and inner nature spelled out, as Marcus claims his revealer 'Sige' did?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XV.—Sige relates to Marcus the generation of the twenty-four elements and of Jesus. Exposure of these absurdities.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus answers that this is self-contradictory. Marcus's 'Sige' names the One who by his own account cannot be named. It expounds the nature of the One who is unspeakable and searches out the One who is unsearchable. The same teaching even has the bodiless and formless One open his mouth and speak.
sources.quote: who names Him that cannot be named, and expounds the nature of Him that is unspeakable, and searches out Him that is unsearchable
sources.raw_question: Can the God whom the Gnostics call unspeakable and unnameable have his hidden names and inner nature spelled out, as Marcus claims his revealer 'Sige' did?

question: Does the Old Testament contain intimations or germs of the distinctions in the Godhead that are later fully revealed in the New Testament?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. The Old Testament presents God acting through His creative Word and His Spirit as co-causes, and it tends to hypostatize the Word and the Spirit. Warfield holds that this contains at least the germ of the distinctions in the Godhead later made known in the Christian revelation. In the light of later revelation, the Trinitarian reading of such phenomena is the most natural one.
sources.quote: we must recognize in the Old Testament doctrine of the relation of God to His revelation by the creative Word and the Spirit, at least the germ of the distinctions in the Godhead afterward fully made known in the Christian revelation
sources.raw_question: Does the Old Testament contain intimations or germs of the distinctions in the Godhead that are later fully revealed in the New Testament?

question: What does the miracle of Elisha making the lost axe-head float by throwing wood into the Jordan signify about the Word of God and the cross?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVII.—There is but one Lord and one God, the Father and Creator of all things, who has loved us in Christ, given us commandments, and remitted our sins; whose Son and Word Christ proved Himself to be, when He forgave our sins.
sources.answer: It prefigures the recovery of the Word of God through the cross. As the iron was lost and recovered by means of wood, so the Word of God, which we negligently lost by means of a tree, we receive anew by the dispensation of a tree, the cross of Christ. The Word is likened to an axe, as John the Baptist and Jeremiah show.
sources.quote: By this action the prophet pointed out that the sure word of God, which we had negligently lost by means of a tree, and were not in the way of finding again, we should receive anew by the dispensation of a tree, [viz., the cross of Christ].
sources.raw_question: What does the miracle of Elisha making the lost axe-head float by throwing wood into the Jordan signify about the Word of God and the cross?

question: How does Christ's crucifixion with outstretched hands relate to the unity of the one God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVII.—There is but one Lord and one God, the Father and Creator of all things, who has loved us in Christ, given us commandments, and remitted our sins; whose Son and Word Christ proved Himself to be, when He forgave our sins.
sources.answer: The two outstretched hands of the divine person on the cross gather the two scattered peoples to one God. There were two hands because there were two peoples, but one head in the middle, just as there is one God who is above all, through all, and in us all.
sources.quote: For these were two hands, because there were two peoples scattered to the ends of the earth; but there was one head in the middle, as there is but one God, who is above all, and through all, and in us all.
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's crucifixion with outstretched hands relate to the unity of the one God?

question: Is the law of God by itself sufficient to give a person a true and thorough conviction of sin, or is this the work of the Holy Spirit sent by Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: The law is not sufficient by itself. It reveals sin's pollution and guilt clearly, but we have no eyes of our own to look into it or apply it. Christ therefore sends his Spirit to convince the world of sin. Although the Spirit makes use of the law, the work of saving conviction is the Spirit's peculiar work, so this knowledge is also hidden in Christ.
sources.quote: Not but that the glass is clear, but of ourselves we have not eyes to look into it; the rule is straight, but we cannot apply it: and therefore Christ sends his Spirit to convince the world of sin
sources.raw_question: Is the law of God by itself sufficient to give a person a true and thorough conviction of sin, or is this the work of the Holy Spirit sent by Christ?

question: Why does the cross of Christ reveal the desert of sin more clearly than anything else?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It reveals it through the dignity of the person who suffered and through the penalty he bore. God sent his only begotten Son to suffer for sin and did not spare him. Just as the punishment of an only son points to the greatest possible provocation, laying sin on the Son of God shows its utter abominableness. It also shows that God cannot let the least sin go unpunished.
sources.quote: The correction of a son argues a great provocation; that of an only son, the greatest imaginable. Never was sin seen to be more abominably sinful and full of provocation, than when the burden of it was upon the shoulders of the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: Why does the cross of Christ reveal the desert of sin more clearly than anything else?

question: Is the Christian faith of all believers one in number, or only one in kind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Faith a Thing of the Heart, Not of the Body; How It is Common and One and the Same in All Believers. The Faith of Believers is One, No Otherwise than the Will of Those Who Will is One.
sources.answer: It is one in kind, not in number. Each believer has his own faith, as Christ shows when He calls one person's faith great and another's little. Because these faiths are alike and differ in nothing, we call them one rather than many. In the same way, two people who look exactly alike are said to have one countenance, and people who will the same thing are said to have one will.
sources.quote: For it is not one in number, but in kind; yet on account of the likeness, and the absence of all difference, we rather call it one than many.
sources.raw_question: Is the Christian faith of all believers one in number, or only one in kind?

question: What did Hilary mean by attributing 'eternity' to the Father in the formula 'Eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > Of the Attributes Assigned by Hilary to Each Person. The Trinity is Represented in Things that are Made.
sources.answer: Augustine thinks Hilary meant only that the Father has no father from whom He is. The Son is from the Father, but in such a way that He exists and is co-eternal with Him, so 'eternity' does not deny the Son's eternity.
sources.quote: I do not think that he intended more by the word eternity, than that the Father has not a father from whom He is; but the Son is from the Father, so as to be, and so as to be co-eternal with Him.
sources.raw_question: What did Hilary mean by attributing 'eternity' to the Father in the formula 'Eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift'?

question: Did Christ need to die in spirit and be renewed in the inner man as sinners do?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The One Death and Resurrection of The Body of Christ Harmonizes with Our Double Death and Resurrection of Body and Soul, to the Effect of Salvation. In What Way the Single Death of Christ is Bestowed Upon Our Double Death.
sources.answer: No. He was not a sinner or ungodly, so he had no death of the soul needing renewal through repentance. He died and rose only in his mortal flesh, and in that alone he answered for both our deaths.
sources.quote: For He was not a sinner or ungodly, that, as though dead in spirit, He should need to be renewed in the inner man, and to be recalled as it were to the life of righteousness by repentance
sources.raw_question: Did Christ need to die in spirit and be renewed in the inner man as sinners do?

question: Does the parable of the wicked husbandmen show that the Creator of the world is the Father of Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: Yes. The Householder who planted the vineyard is one God the Father, who made all things by himself. The same Householder sends his only son last of all, so the Maker of the world and the Father of the Son are one and the same.
sources.quote: He clearly points out to His disciples one and the same Householder—that is, one God the Father, who made all things by Himself
sources.raw_question: Does the parable of the wicked husbandmen show that the Creator of the world is the Father of Jesus Christ?

question: Is the God of the Mosaic dispensation, with its law of bondage, the same God who calls people to adoption through Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: Yes. The God who called those of the former dispensation is the same who received those of the latter. He planted the vineyard in Adam and the fathers, let it out under Moses, and sent prophets. Last of all he sent his Son, and then gave the vineyard to the Gentiles. It is one and the same Father throughout.
sources.quote: He who at first used that law which entails bondage, is also He who did in after times [call His people] by means of adoption.
sources.raw_question: Is the God of the Mosaic dispensation, with its law of bondage, the same God who calls people to adoption through Christ?

question: Is the supreme God a being who has no contact with the human race and exercises no providence over the world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIV.—Recapitulation of the various arguments adduced against Gnostic impiety under all its aspects. The heretics, tossed about by every blast of doctrine, are opposed by the uniform teaching of the Church, which remains so always, and is consistent with itself.
sources.answer: No. A god who has no dealings with humanity and does not direct the world is simply the god of Epicurus, who does nothing for himself or others. In truth God exercises providence over all things and gives counsel. That is why even some Gentiles recognised the Maker of the universe as the Father who orders the affairs of the world.
sources.quote: God does, however, exercise a providence over all things, and therefore He also gives counsel; and when giving counsel, He is present with those who attend to moral discipline.
sources.raw_question: Is the supreme God a being who has no contact with the human race and exercises no providence over the world?

question: Is it legitimate to read the bodily images of "hand" and "finger" as distinguishing members of a body, with the Father, Son and Spirit as parts of differing rank?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter V. The writer sums up the argument he had commenced, and confirms the statement that unity is signified by the terms finger and right hand, from the fact that the works of God are the same as are the works of hands; and that those of hands are the same as those of fingers; and lastly, that the term hand applies equally to the Son and the Spirit, and that of finger applies to the Spirit and the Son.
sources.answer: No. Ambrose calls that reading madness. It would fashion the Father, Son and Holy Spirit into one bodily form and picture distinctions among its members. The images point instead to the inseparability and oneness of divine power.
sources.quote: he indeed will fall into such madness as to appear to fashion the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as it were into one bodily form, and to picture to himself certain distinctions of its members.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to read the bodily images of "hand" and "finger" as distinguishing members of a body, with the Father, Son and Spirit as parts of differing rank?

question: When does the rational soul live in a degenerate way with respect to the trinity of the outer man?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > The Unity of the Three Takes Place in Thought, Viz. Of Memory, of Ternal Vision, and of Will Combining Both.
sources.answer: It does so when it cleaves to the things that form the bodily sense out of base desire. The right course is to refer those things by a praiseworthy will to some useful end. The fault therefore lies in how the will relates to sensible things, not in the senses themselves.
sources.quote: not a praiseworthy will, by which to refer them to some useful end, but a base desire, by which to cleave to them
sources.raw_question: When does the rational soul live in a degenerate way with respect to the trinity of the outer man?

question: How does Christ's entering the closed room after the resurrection bear on belief in the Son's birth from the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: It shows that a certain fact can lie beyond human explanation. Christ stood bodily among the disciples though the doors were shut, without breaching walls or dispersing his body; we cannot explain how, yet it happened. Likewise the Son was truly born of the Father, and incomprehensibility of the manner is no ground for denying the fact.
sources.quote: The Lord did stand in a closed house in the midst of the disciples; the Son was born of the Father. Deny not that He stood, because your puny wits cannot ascertain how He came there
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's entering the closed room after the resurrection bear on belief in the Son's birth from the Father?

question: Did Christ come to save only those who believed in Him during His earthly lifetime, or also the righteous who lived before His coming?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXII.—Christ did not come for the sake of the men of one age only, but for all who, living righteously and piously, had believed upon Him; and for those, too, who shall believe.
sources.answer: Christ came for all who from the beginning, according to their capacity, feared and loved God, practised justice and piety, and desired to see Christ. The Father's providence was not limited to those then alive. Hence at His second coming Christ will first rouse such persons from sleep and give them a place in His kingdom.
sources.quote: For it was not merely for those who believed on Him in the time of Tiberius Cæsar that Christ came, nor did the Father exercise His providence for the men only who are now alive, but for all men altogether
sources.raw_question: Did Christ come to save only those who believed in Him during His earthly lifetime, or also the righteous who lived before His coming?

question: Is the God who guided the Old Testament patriarchs the same God who justifies both Jews and Gentiles through faith in Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXII.—Christ did not come for the sake of the men of one age only, but for all who, living righteously and piously, had believed upon Him; and for those, too, who shall believe.
sources.answer: Yes. It is truly one God who directed the patriarchs toward His dispensations and who justifies the circumcision and the uncircumcision by faith. The patriarchs prefigured the Church, and they are in turn represented in the Church, where they receive the reward for what they accomplished.
sources.quote: For it is truly “one God who” directed the patriarchs towards His dispensations, and “has justified the circumcision by faith, and the uncircumcision through faith.”
sources.raw_question: Is the God who guided the Old Testament patriarchs the same God who justifies both Jews and Gentiles through faith in Christ?

question: How does Christ as the New Man reverse the bondage brought in through the first parents?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXII.—Christ did not come for the sake of the men of one age only, but for all who, living righteously and piously, had believed upon Him; and for those, too, who shall believe.
sources.answer: Through the first parents all were brought into bondage by being made subject to death. At the last, through the New Man, all His disciples from the beginning are cleansed and washed from what pertains to death and come to the life of God. Irenaeus sees this signified when the Word Himself washed the disciples' feet and so sanctified the whole body.
sources.quote: so at last, by means of the New Man, all who from the beginning [were His] disciples, having been cleansed and washed from things pertaining to death, should come to the life of God
sources.raw_question: How does Christ as the New Man reverse the bondage brought in through the first parents?

question: Does God's saying of Sodom 'I will go down and see... and if not, I will know' imply that God was ignorant?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. God knew their sins were grievous, yet speaks of coming to know; His not knowing what He knows is an economy in word and deed. When the time for action comes He knows, and this is not a change from ignorance but the coming of the fulness of time.
sources.quote: This knowledge is not, therefore, a change from ignorance, but the coming of the fulness of time.
sources.raw_question: Does God's saying of Sodom 'I will go down and see... and if not, I will know' imply that God was ignorant?

question: Do the physical claims in Proverbs 8 (inhabited extremes of the earth, strong clouds, a throne set on the winds) hold true when read literally of visible objects?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He then once more excellently, appropriately, and clearly examines and expounds the passage, “The Lord Created Me.“
sources.answer: No. The extremes of the earth are uninhabitable through excessive heat or cold, and clouds are slight vapour with no strength. Winds are by nature unstable and could not support a throne. Since the literal sense is at variance with the facts, the whole passage, including "The Lord created me," requires a deeper interpretation.
sources.quote: If any one should interpret the passage with reference to visible objects, he will find that the facts are at considerable variance with the words.
sources.raw_question: Do the physical claims in Proverbs 8 (inhabited extremes of the earth, strong clouds, a throne set on the winds) hold true when read literally of visible objects?

question: Was a single drop of Christ's blood sufficient to redeem the whole world?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Those who say so err, not knowing the desert of sin nor the severity of God's justice. If one drop less or one pang less would have sufficed, the others would not have been laid on, for God did not afflict his beloved Son for nought.
sources.quote: If one drop less than was shed, one pang less than was laid on, would have done it, those other drops had not been shed, nor those other pangs laid on.
sources.raw_question: Was a single drop of Christ's blood sufficient to redeem the whole world?

question: What does Christ's comparison of himself with Jonah (Matthew 12:40) show about the meaning of the word 'as' in Scripture?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: It shows that 'as' denotes a parallel between different things in a certain respect, not identity or equality. Jonah was not as the Saviour, did not descend into hades, and brought no one up with him; the likeness lies only in the three days.
sources.quote: Therefore there is no identity nor equality signified in the term ‘as,’ but one thing and another; and it shews a certain kind of parallel in the case of Jonah, on account of the three days.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's comparison of himself with Jonah (Matthew 12:40) show about the meaning of the word 'as' in Scripture?

question: How does the Incarnation of the Word bring about the perfecting and unity of believers?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: By the Word bearing our body and becoming man, men are redeemed from sin and no longer remain dead but are deified. Without His coming none would have been perfected and all would have stayed corruptible. Their perfecting in the Spirit shows the world that the Father sent the Word.
sources.quote: the work is perfected, because men, redeemed from sin, no longer remain dead; but being deified, have in each other, by looking at Me, the bond of charity
sources.raw_question: How does the Incarnation of the Word bring about the perfecting and unity of believers?

question: Were Jacob, or the pregnant animals' own souls, the creators of the colours in the offspring when Jacob set the peeled rods before the flocks?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > God Alone Creates Those Things Which are Changed by Magic Art.
sources.answer: No. Jacob only applied an external operation, and the mothers' souls, affected through their eyes, only influenced the colour of the offspring as far as nature permitted. That cattle are born of cattle, and that soul and body affect one another at all, arises from the unchangeable reasons existing in the wisdom of God, by which all things are created.
sources.quote: it was the unchangeable and invisible reason of the wisdom of God, by which all things are created, which caused not rods, but cattle, to be born from cattle
sources.raw_question: Were Jacob, or the pregnant animals' own souls, the creators of the colours in the offspring when Jacob set the peeled rods before the flocks?

question: Why did God prepare the economy of salvation in the Word before the creation of the world rather than devising it after the Fall?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: It was not fitting that God should take counsel about us only afterwards, lest he seem ignorant of what would happen to us. Creating us through his Word and foreseeing our transgression, he lovingly prepared beforehand in that same Word the redemption by which we would rise again and remain immortal.
sources.quote: It beseemed not that God should counsel concerning us afterwards, lest He should appear ignorant of our fate.
sources.raw_question: Why did God prepare the economy of salvation in the Word before the creation of the world rather than devising it after the Fall?

question: In whom was the kingdom 'prepared from the foundation of the world' (Matthew 25:34) prepared, given that we did not yet exist?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
