sources.answer: It was prepared in the Lord, who was 'founded before the world' for this very purpose. Built upon him like well-compacted stones, we might then share the life and grace that come from him.
sources.quote: How then, or in whom, was it prepared before we came to be, save in the Lord who ‘before the world’ was founded for this purpose; that we, as built upon Him, might partake, as well-compacted stones, the life and grace which is from Him?
sources.raw_question: In whom was the kingdom 'prepared from the foundation of the world' (Matthew 25:34) prepared, given that we did not yet exist?

question: Do the scriptural images of heaven as God's throne and earth as His footstool imply that God has bodily extension in space?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. The same heaven that is His throne and the same earth that is His footstool are also said to be held in His palm and hand, so the images cannot describe a body located in space. They teach instead that God both controls all things from without and dwells within them.
sources.quote: This was not written that from throne and footstool, metaphors drawn from the posture of one sitting, we should conclude that He has extension in space, as of a body
sources.raw_question: Do the scriptural images of heaven as God's throne and earth as His footstool imply that God has bodily extension in space?

question: Could the Gnostics have learned from Paul hidden and unspeakable mysteries that were unknown to Luke, Paul's constant companion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XIV.—If Paul had known any mysteries unrevealed to the other apostles, Luke, his constant companion and fellow-traveller, could not have been ignorant of them; neither could the truth have possibly lain hid from him, through whom alone we learn many and most important particulars of the Gospel history.
sources.answer: No. Luke was Paul's inseparable fellow-labourer: he records their journeys together in Acts, and Paul himself says "Only Luke is with me" and calls him "the beloved physician." Since Luke learned nothing different from Paul, men who were never attached to Paul cannot boast of having received secret mysteries from him.
sources.quote: learned nothing different from him (Paul), as has been pointed out from his words, how can these men, who were never attached to Paul, boast that they have learned hidden and unspeakable mysteries?
sources.raw_question: Could the Gnostics have learned from Paul hidden and unspeakable mysteries that were unknown to Luke, Paul's constant companion?

question: Does every voluntary human action come from a prior inner word?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > We Conceive and Beget the Word Within, from the Things We Have Beheld in the Eternal Truth. The Word, Whether of the Creature or of the Creator, is Conceived by Love.
sources.answer: Yes. Every bodily word or action for which people are approved or blamed is first anticipated by a word uttered within. No one willingly does anything he has not first said in his heart.
sources.quote: For no one willingly does anything, which he has not first said in his heart.
sources.raw_question: Does every voluntary human action come from a prior inner word?

question: In John 4:35-38, who are the 'others' who laboured and into whose labours the apostles entered?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXIII.—The patriarchs and prophets by pointing out the advent of Christ, fortified thereby, as it were, the way of posterity to the faith of Christ; and so the labours of the apostles were lessened inasmuch as they gathered in the fruits of the labours of others.
sources.answer: They are the patriarchs and prophets. They prefigured the Christian faith and spread abroad the news of the coming of the Son of God, who He would be and what He would be like. Because of this, later generations who feared God could readily accept Christ, and the apostles reaped what the prophets had sown.
sources.quote: It is clear that they are the patriarchs and prophets, who even prefigured our faith, and disseminated through the earth the advent of the Son of God, who and what He should be
sources.raw_question: In John 4:35-38, who are the 'others' who laboured and into whose labours the apostles entered?

question: Is the God who rewards the righteous with the kingdom the same God who prepares eternal fire for the wicked, or are these two different gods (as the Gnostics and Marcionites claim)?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XL.—One and the same God the Father inflicts punishment on the reprobate, and bestows rewards on the elect.
sources.answer: One and the same God the Father does both. The same Lord, speaking at the judgment, says both "Come, ye blessed of My Father" and "Depart... into everlasting fire, which My Father has prepared," so one Father prepares fit things for both. If there were two gods, their sons would also differ, one sending men into the kingdom and another into fire, but Christ is one Judge who sends both into their fit places.
sources.quote: If, however, it were truly one Father who confers rest, and another God who has prepared the fire, their sons would have been equally different [one from the other]; one, indeed, sending [men] into the Father’s kingdom, but the other into eternal fire.
sources.raised_by_detail: Marcionites/Gnostics who distinguish a good Father from a judging God
sources.raw_question: Is the God who rewards the righteous with the kingdom the same God who prepares eternal fire for the wicked, or are these two different gods (as the Gnostics and Marcionites claim)?

question: Does Isaiah's statement that God is "making peace, and creating evil things" mean God is the author of moral evil?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XL.—One and the same God the Father inflicts punishment on the reprobate, and bestows rewards on the elect.
sources.answer: No. The "evil things" are the punishments of eternal fire and outer darkness, which are evils to those who fall into them. God makes peace with those who repent and prepares these punishments for the impenitent who shun the light. The verse therefore shows that one God both rewards and judges, not that He causes sin.
sources.quote: preparing for the impenitent, those who shun the light, eternal fire and outer darkness, which are evils indeed to those persons who fall into them
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah's statement that God is "making peace, and creating evil things" mean God is the author of moral evil?

question: In the parable of the wheat and tares, who sows the tares, and does this make the devil a creator or God the cause of evil?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XL.—One and the same God the Father inflicts punishment on the reprobate, and bestows rewards on the elect.
sources.answer: The enemy who sows the tares is the apostate angel, the devil. Envious of God's workmanship, he tried to make it hostile to God. God banished him for the transgression he brought about but had compassion on man, and He turned His anger against the serpent. Christ, born of a woman, summed up this enmity in Himself and crushed the serpent's head.
sources.quote: Hence we learn that this was the apostate angel and the enemy, because he was envious of God’s workmanship, and took in hand to render this [workmanship] an enmity with God.
sources.raw_question: In the parable of the wheat and tares, who sows the tares, and does this make the devil a creator or God the cause of evil?

question: According to Titus 3:4-7, what part do God the Father, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit each play in saving and justifying believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Salvation starts in the kindness and love, that is the grace, of God our Saviour. It is applied not through our works but through the Holy Ghost, whom God pours out richly. Jesus Christ is the one through whom the Spirit is obtained for us. The result is that believers are justified by grace and made heirs of eternal life.
sources.quote: The way of communication, negatively, is not by works of righteousness that we have done; — positively, by the communication of the Holy Ghost, verse 5; the means of whose procurement is Jesus Christ, verse 6
sources.raw_question: According to Titus 3:4-7, what part do God the Father, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit each play in saving and justifying believers?

question: Does Caiaphas's saying that one man should die 'for the people' (John 11:50) use 'for' in the sense of substitution?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Yes. Caiaphas feared the Romans would destroy the nation if Christ were spared. He therefore devoted Christ to death in lieu of the people, so that one would perish in place of many. The same sense recurs in John 18:14, 'perish for the people.'
sources.quote: The way to free them, he thought, was by the destruction of Christ; him, therefore, he devoted to death, in lieu of the people.
sources.raw_question: Does Caiaphas's saying that one man should die 'for the people' (John 11:50) use 'for' in the sense of substitution?

question: Does the Greek preposition ἀντί, used when Christ gives his life 'a ransom for many', denote substitution?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that ἀντί always denotes equality, contrariety, or substitution, and that only substitution can fit here. He compares Archelaus reigning 'in the room of' Herod and 'an eye for an eye'. So when Christ gives his life a ransom ἀντί many, he dies in their stead. In 1 Tim 2:6 both markers of substitution, ἀντίλυτρον and ὑπέρ, are joined together.
sources.quote: And this answers unto ἀντὶ in the Greek; which is also used in this matter, and ever denotes either equality, contrariety, or substitution. The two former senses can here have no place; the latter alone has.
sources.raw_question: Does the Greek preposition ἀντί, used when Christ gives his life 'a ransom for many', denote substitution?

question: Is the incarnate Christ, God and Man, a proper object of adoration and worship?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: Yes. Because Christ is God the Word himself, one and the same before the ages and in the last times, adoration and worship belong to him who was, is, and ever shall be.
sources.quote: To Him be the adoration and the worship, who was before, and now is, and ever shall be, even to all ages.
sources.raw_question: Is the incarnate Christ, God and Man, a proper object of adoration and worship?

question: Is Hieracas's image of two flames burning from one lamp a valid model of the shared substance of Father and Son?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. The image makes the substance something separate from both Persons, like the oil or the wick that feeds and joins two flames, and it ignores the Son's birth. In God there is nothing bodily or lifeless. The bond between Father and Son is not anything outside themselves. Such an illustration comes from human folly trusting itself rather than God.
sources.quote: Their bond of union is not, like that of two flames, two wicks of one lamp, something outside Themselves.
sources.raw_question: Is Hieracas's image of two flames burning from one lamp a valid model of the shared substance of Father and Son?

question: Should the phrase 'Light from Light' be avoided because Hieracas used it in a heretical sense?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Its heretical use does not mean there is no true sense of it. Rightly understood, it means God born from God, as light pours itself forth without diminishing itself, giving what it has while still having what it gave. The Arians use the condemnation of Hieracas to draw faith away from this true doctrine.
sources.quote: Because the phrase has been used in an heretical sense, and condemned both now and in earlier days, they want to persuade us that there is no true sense in which it can be employed.
sources.raw_question: Should the phrase 'Light from Light' be avoided because Hieracas used it in a heretical sense?

question: Can spiritual substances cast a shadow, such that the material world could be the shadow of the Gnostic Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VIII.—Created things are not a shadow of the Pleroma.
sources.answer: No. Only bodies cast shadows; spiritual substances cannot darken anything. So if the lower world were a shadow of the higher realm, the beings of the Pleroma would have to be bodies, which contradicts the Gnostics' own claim that they are spiritual.
sources.quote: For those bodies which are above do cast a shadow, but spiritual substances do not, since they can in no degree darken others.
sources.raw_question: Can spiritual substances cast a shadow, such that the material world could be the shadow of the Gnostic Pleroma?

question: If the world were the shadow of eternal spiritual beings, would the world have to be eternal as well?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VIII.—Created things are not a shadow of the Pleroma.
sources.answer: Yes. A shadow lasts as long as what casts it. If the Aeons above are eternal, their shadow would endure for ever, so the world below would not pass away. If the world below does pass away, then what casts it would have to pass away too.
sources.quote: If, on the other hand, these things [below] are transitory, it is a necessary consequence that those [above] also, of which these are the shadow, pass away; while; if they endure, their shadow likewise endures.
sources.raw_question: If the world were the shadow of eternal spiritual beings, would the world have to be eternal as well?

question: Why was it fitting for God to let human beings come to know evil (disobedience) by experience as well as good (obedience)?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIX.—Man is endowed with the faculty of distinguishing good and evil; so that, without compulsion, he has the power, by his own will and choice, to perform God’s commandments, by doing which he avoids the evils prepared for the rebellious.
sources.answer: So that, having experienced both, the mind might judge rightly, choose the better, and hold fast to obedience to God more firmly. Knowledge gained by experience is surer than mere opinion. Just as the tongue learns sweet and bitter by tasting, the mind that has tasted disobedience through repentance learns how bitter it is and clings more firmly to the good.
sources.quote: For there is thus a surer and an undoubted comprehension of matters submitted to us than the mere surmise arising from an opinion regarding them.
sources.raw_question: Why was it fitting for God to let human beings come to know evil (disobedience) by experience as well as good (obedience)?

question: Does 'the love of God shed abroad in our hearts' in Romans 5:5 mean God's love to us or our love to God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: It means God's love to us, as the context makes plain. This love, whether of purpose or of acceptation, is shed abroad not in itself but in a spiritual sense and apprehension of it. The Comforter gives a plentiful evidence and persuasion that God in Christ loves the soul.
sources.quote: That it is the love of God to us, not our love to God, which is here intended, the context is so clear as nothing can be added thereunto.
sources.raw_question: Does 'the love of God shed abroad in our hearts' in Romans 5:5 mean God's love to us or our love to God?

question: On what ground can sinners have boldness to draw near to a holy God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Only in Christ, on account of his oblation and intercession. God's infinite holiness and terror would make the soul conclude it cannot serve him and that drawing near would only add to its destruction. But by the blood of Jesus and his high priesthood, believers may draw near in full assurance of faith.
sources.quote: It is in Christ alone, and on the account alone of his oblation and intercession, that we have any boldness to approach unto him.
sources.raw_question: On what ground can sinners have boldness to draw near to a holy God?

question: Is the Gnostic rite of 'redemption' a higher, spiritual perfection beyond Christian baptism, which they regard as merely for the remission of sins?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XXI.—The views of redemption entertained by these heretics.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus holds that these teachers, at Satan's instigation, deny the baptism that is regeneration to God, and so renounce the whole Christian faith. Their 'redemption' has no fixed nature: each teacher hands it down as he pleases, so there are as many schemes of redemption as there are teachers. A rite that varies and contradicts itself in this way cannot be the one redemption in Christ.
sources.quote: this class of men have been instigated by Satan to a denial of that baptism which is regeneration to God, and thus to a renunciation of the whole [Christian] faith.
sources.raw_question: Is the Gnostic rite of 'redemption' a higher, spiritual perfection beyond Christian baptism, which they regard as merely for the remission of sins?

question: Does Scripture present Jesus Christ as a true and proper human being, with genuine human development, suffering and emotion?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ was spoken of by himself, his disciples and his enemies as a proper human being: his intellectual powers grew like other children's, he knew labour, hunger, weariness and grief, and he suffered anguish of soul, crying out on the cross. Trinitarians hold to his humanity with conviction second to none, standing on the words "The Word was made flesh."
sources.quote: Believe me, we yield to none in the strength of conviction with which we hold to the humanity of Jesus Christ. “The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture present Jesus Christ as a true and proper human being, with genuine human development, suffering and emotion?

question: Does Christ's refusal to worship Satan in Matthew 4:10 show that worship is excluded only from evil spirits or from those claiming supremacy, or from every being but God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: From every being but God. Satan did not claim to be supreme and asked only for an outward act of adoration. Christ's reason for refusing was not that Satan was evil or unappointed by God. It was the general reason that none are to be worshipped but God only.
sources.quote: the reason given for refusing it is not that he was a bad spirit, an enemy to God; or that God had not commanded that he should be worshipped ; but the reason is general, that none are to be worshipped, but God only.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's refusal to worship Satan in Matthew 4:10 show that worship is excluded only from evil spirits or from those claiming supremacy, or from every being but God?

question: Can reasons of human wisdom justify worshipping creatures besides the Creator, as Celsus, Porphyry and the Romanists argued?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. Whatever reasons human wisdom invents are never to be set against a clear and plain divine law. God in his unerring wisdom best knows to whom worship should be paid. God may also have good reasons of his own, such as his glory and our good, for claiming all worship.
sources.quote: those are never to be set against a clear and plain law; or opposed to the unerring wisdom of God, who best knows to whom worship is proper to be paid, and to whom not.
sources.raw_question: Can reasons of human wisdom justify worshipping creatures besides the Creator, as Celsus, Porphyry and the Romanists argued?

question: Does God 'draw nigh' to the Son in the same way Scripture says He draws nigh to His people?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > The substantiality of the Word proved from Scripture. If the One Origin be substantial, Its Word is substantial. Unless the Word and Son be a second Origin, or a work, or an attribute (and so God be compounded), or at the same time Father, or involve a second nature in God, He is from the Father's Essence and distinct from Him. Illustration of John x. 30, drawn from Deut. iv. 4.
sources.answer: No. God draws nigh to things that have come into being because they are strange to Him (Deuteronomy 4:7; Jeremiah 23:23). He does not draw nigh to the Son, because the Son is His own and is in Him. The Son is not attached to the Father but co-exists with Him.
sources.quote: for to things originate He draws nigh, as being strange to Him, but to the Son, as being His own, He does not draw nigh, but He is in Him.
sources.raw_question: Does God 'draw nigh' to the Son in the same way Scripture says He draws nigh to His people?

question: Is the will of God the first cause even of changes in bodies that come about through proximate bodily causes and through human choices?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > Of the Same Argument.
sources.answer: Yes. Physicians identify only proximate corporeal causes, such as dryness of the body, and the wise man's self-imposed toil is a higher cause proceeding from his soul. Higher still is the unchangeable wisdom that he obeyed in love. So nothing but the will of God is found to be most truly the first cause of the illness.
sources.quote: and so nothing else but the will of God would be found most truly to be the first cause of that illness
sources.raw_question: Is the will of God the first cause even of changes in bodies that come about through proximate bodily causes and through human choices?

question: Can God's invisible and unchangeable will be the cause of visible changes that are carried out by bad men, irrational animals and senseless bodies?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > Of the Same Argument.
sources.answer: Yes. Through the upright soul of the wise man, which is the seat of His wisdom, God's will uses bad souls, irrational animals and inanimate bodies alike. It does so even though these instruments do not intend the good work, being moved by carnal desire or natural appetite. Every movement, decay or change in them therefore has no other cause than the invisible and unchangeable will of God.
sources.quote: could there be, I say, any other cause of all these visible and changeable facts, except the invisible and unchangeable will of God, using all these, both bad and irrational souls, and lastly bodies
sources.raw_question: Can God's invisible and unchangeable will be the cause of visible changes that are carried out by bad men, irrational animals and senseless bodies?

question: How does a human being fall from bearing the likeness of God to bearing the likeness of the beasts?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Image of the Beast in Man.
sources.answer: He falls gradually, through pride. Wanting to be like God, that is, under no one, and to test his own power, man first sinks to himself as a middle grade. As punishment he is then pushed down to the lowest level, the things beasts delight in. This happens when he neglects the love of unchanging wisdom and craves knowledge of temporal, changeable things by experiment, a knowledge that puffs up rather than builds up.
sources.quote: while he wishes to be as God is, that is, under no one, he is thrust on, even from his own middle grade, by way of punishment, to that which is lowest, that is, to those things in which beasts delight
sources.raw_question: How does a human being fall from bearing the likeness of God to bearing the likeness of the beasts?

question: What does the upright posture of the human body signify about how the human mind ought to be directed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Of What Kind are the Outer and the Inner Man.
sources.answer: It is an admonition from our Maker that we should not be like the beasts in our better part, the mind. As the body is naturally raised toward the highest bodily things, the heavens, so the mind, a spiritual substance, must be raised toward the highest spiritual things. This is not done through pride or by seeking rest in exalted bodily things, which would prostrate the mind, but through the dutifulness of righteousness.
sources.quote: so the mind, which is a spiritual substance, must be raised upright to those things which are most elevated in spiritual things, not by the elation of pride, but by the dutifulness of righteousness.
sources.raw_question: What does the upright posture of the human body signify about how the human mind ought to be directed?

question: Can the Unitarian view of Christ as a highly exalted but created being be reconciled with trusting in him for salvation?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Preface
sources.answer: No. If Christ is only a creature, then trusting wholly in him for eternal salvation is trusting in a creature, which Scripture condemns as idolatry. Yet refusing to trust in him rejects the only name under heaven by which we must be saved. The Unitarian hypothesis therefore faces a disastrous dilemma with no escape, which shows that Christ must be God.
sources.quote: if men trust in Him for eternal salvation, reposing their entire confidence in Him, they are trusting in a creature, which is idolatry. (Jer. 17:5–8.) Whereas if they do not so trust in Him, they are rejecting the only name under heaven
sources.raw_question: Can the Unitarian view of Christ as a highly exalted but created being be reconciled with trusting in him for salvation?

question: What does 2 Corinthians 5:19, "God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself," reveal about how God's attributes are harmonized?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It shows that God manifests himself in Christ as one whose justice has been fully satisfied. He now has nothing more to do, for the glorifying of all his attributes, but to forbear, reconcile and pardon sin in Christ.
sources.quote: manifesting himself in him as one that hath now no more to do for the manifestation of all his attributes, — that is, for the glorifying of himself, — but only to forbear, reconcile, and pardon sin in him.
sources.raw_question: What does 2 Corinthians 5:19, "God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself," reveal about how God's attributes are harmonized?

question: Why does Christ, who is above every name, bear many different names such as Light, Life, Way, Door, Rock and Vine?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > The tenth book discusses the unattainable and incomprehensible character of the enquiry into entities. And herein he strikingly sets forth the points concerning the nature and formation of the ant, and the passage in the Gospel, “I am the door” and “the way,” and also discusses the attribution and interpretation of the Divine names, and the episode of the children of Benjamin.
sources.answer: He receives these names according to the variety of his gracious dealings with us, not as definitions of his essence. He is called Light when he disperses ignorance, Life when he grants immortality, and Way when he leads us from error to truth. In the same way, the other titles describe how he gives himself to us under various aspects through his benefits.
sources.quote: He Who is above every name has for us many names, receiving them in accordance with the variety of His gracious dealings with us
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ, who is above every name, bear many different names such as Light, Life, Way, Door, Rock and Vine?

question: What is the 'body of humiliation' that Christ will transfigure into the likeness of his glorious body, according to Philippians 3:21?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIII.—In the dead who were raised by Christ we possess the highest proof of the resurrection; and our hearts are shown to be capable of life eternal, because they can now receive the Spirit of God.
sources.answer: It is plainly the body composed of flesh, which is humbled when it falls into the earth. This mortal and corruptible flesh will be transformed so that it becomes immortal and incorruptible, conformed to the body of Christ's glory.
sources.quote: Plainly it is this body composed of flesh, which is indeed humbled when it falls into the earth.
sources.raw_question: What is the 'body of humiliation' that Christ will transfigure into the likeness of his glorious body, according to Philippians 3:21?

question: How can Scripture call Christ a Curse, Sin, a Heifer, a lion's Whelp, a bereaved Bear, or a Leopard without blasphemy?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Only if these names are predicated of God through conception, as figures aimed at a particular idea. Taken in their literal and obvious sense they seem suspect and would carry the taint of blasphemy. Understood through the conceptive faculty, they can be reconciled with the reverence due to God.
sources.quote: each single one of them, unless we allow it to be predicated of God by some process of conception, will not escape the taint of a blasphemous suggestion.
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture call Christ a Curse, Sin, a Heifer, a lion's Whelp, a bereaved Bear, or a Leopard without blasphemy?

question: Since God is everywhere, what is meant by 'a place by me' in Exodus 33:21, where Moses would stand on a rock?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > How the Back Parts of God Were Seen. The Faith of the Resurrection of Christ. The Catholic Church Only is the Place from Whence the Back Parts of God are Seen. The Back Parts of God Were Seen by the Israelites. It is a Rash Opinion to Think that God the Father Only Was Never Seen by the Fathers.
sources.answer: It cannot be an earthly place, because God reaches from end to end and fills heaven and earth, so no place is not 'by' him. The 'place by him' is what touches him spiritually, namely the Catholic Church. Standing on that rock, one rightly sees the Lord's 'passing by' and his back parts by believing in his resurrection.
sources.quote: What earthly place is “by” the Lord, unless that is “by Him” which touches Him spiritually? For what place is not “by” the Lord, who “reacheth from one end to another mightily, and sweetly doth order all things,”
sources.raw_question: Since God is everywhere, what is meant by 'a place by me' in Exodus 33:21, where Moses would stand on a rock?

question: Did the prophets foretell that the divine Word who saves would become a real, visible man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XX.—God showed himself, by the fall of man, as patient, benign, merciful, mighty to save. Man is therefore most ungrateful, if, unmindful of his own lot, and of the benefits held out to him, he do not acknowledge divine grace.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah says 'thine eyes shall see our salvation,' showing that the Word giving salvation would himself become very man and be visible. Habakkuk's 'His feet shall advance in the plains' is likewise an indication proper to a man.
sources.quote: And that He should Himself become very man, visible, when He should be the Word giving salvation, Isaiah again says: “Behold, city of Zion: thine eyes shall see our salvation.”
sources.raw_question: Did the prophets foretell that the divine Word who saves would become a real, visible man?

question: What does the bunch of hyssop used to sprinkle sacrificial blood typify for Christians?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: It typifies the free promises of Christ. The cleansing virtue of Christ's blood lies in the promises, as the sacrificial blood lay in the hyssop, ready to pass to those who draw near. For this reason Paul argues from having the promises to cleansing ourselves from all filthiness.
sources.quote: The cleansing virtue of the blood of Christ lies in the promises, as the blood of sacrifices in the hyssop, ready to pass out unto them that draw nigh thereunto.
sources.raw_question: What does the bunch of hyssop used to sprinkle sacrificial blood typify for Christians?

question: Does David's prayer to be purged with hyssop in Psalm 51 refer specifically to cleansing from the defilement of sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: Yes. After the paschal lamb, the law prescribes sprinkling with hyssop only in rites of purification from uncleanness, such as leprosy and other defilements. David therefore prays for cleansing from sin's pollution, which these rites typified as the cleansing that comes by Christ's blood.
sources.quote: there is no mention made, in the institution of any sacrifice (after that of the lamb before mentioned), of sprinkling blood with hyssop, but only in those which respected purification of uncleanness
sources.raw_question: Does David's prayer to be purged with hyssop in Psalm 51 refer specifically to cleansing from the defilement of sin?

question: If we can only imagine what we remember, and only remember what we have sensuously perceived, how is it possible to imagine false things such as a black swan?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > The Imagination Also Adds Even to Things We Have Not Seen, Those Things Which We Have Seen Elsewhere.
sources.answer: The will, which unites and separates memory and inner vision, leads the mind's gaze through the stores of memory and takes one element from here and another from there, combining them into a single image. The result is called false because it does not exist among bodies or was never seen as a whole. Yet everything combined is still drawn from memory, so imagination works under the law of memory. Thus the will's role as combiner in this trinity of the outer man is confirmed.
sources.quote: leads the vision of the conceiver that is to be formed, after its own will and pleasure, through the hidden stores of the memory; and, in order to conceive [imagine] those things which we do not remember, impels it to take one thing from hence, and another from thence
sources.raw_question: If we can only imagine what we remember, and only remember what we have sensuously perceived, how is it possible to imagine false things such as a black swan?

question: In Song of Songs 5:13, what is meant by the Beloved's lips being 'like lilies, dropping sweet-smelling myrrh' when applied to Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: It signifies the word of Christ, its savour, excellency and usefulness. Owen grounds this in Scripture's saying that grace was poured into Christ's lips and that men wondered at the words of grace from his mouth. Lilies and myrrh are the most glorious and fragrant things in nature, and Christ's word surpasses them, being sweet and precious to believers in its precepts, promises, exhortations and even its threats.
sources.quote: So that by the lips of Christ, and their dropping sweet-smelling myrrh, the word of Christ, its savour, excellency, and usefulness, is intended.
sources.raw_question: In Song of Songs 5:13, what is meant by the Beloved's lips being 'like lilies, dropping sweet-smelling myrrh' when applied to Christ?

question: In what respects is Christ 'altogether lovely' according to Song of Songs 5:16?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: He is lovely in every respect. This includes his person, in the all-sufficiency of his Deity and the purity of his humanity, and his incarnation, his holy life and his death for sinners. It extends to his mediatorial work and his present exaltation at God's right hand. The bride's comparisons with the best of creatures fall short, so she concludes that he is wholly desirable.
sources.quote: Lovely in his person, — in the glorious all-sufficiency of his Deity, gracious purity and holiness of his humanity, authority and majesty, love and power.
sources.raw_question: In what respects is Christ 'altogether lovely' according to Song of Songs 5:16?

question: What does Isaiah mean by 'the pain of the stroke' that the Lord will heal?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXIV.—He fortifies his opinions with regard to the temporal and earthly kingdom of the saints after their resurrection, by the various testimonies of Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, and Daniel; also by the parable of the servants watching, to whom the Lord promised that He would minister.
sources.answer: It means death, the stroke inflicted at the beginning on disobedient man in Adam. The Lord heals this stroke when He raises us from the dead and restores the inheritance of the fathers. So the prophecy refers to the bodily resurrection and the renewal of creation in the kingdom of the righteous.
sources.quote: Now “the pain of the stroke” means that inflicted at the beginning upon disobedient man in Adam, that is, death; which [stroke] the Lord will heal when He raises us from the dead
sources.raw_question: What does Isaiah mean by 'the pain of the stroke' that the Lord will heal?

question: Is the Son's work of salvation (the economy) a compulsory ministration performed in a slave's subordinate status toward the Father?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: No. It is a voluntary solicitude working for his own creation out of goodness and pity, yet according to the will of God the Father. True religion requires both acknowledging the perfection of the Son's power in all he does and never separating his work from the Father's will.
sources.quote: We must not, however, regard the œconomy through the Son as a compulsory and subordinate ministration resulting from the low estate of a slave, but rather the voluntary solicitude working effectually for His own creation in goodness and in pity
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's work of salvation (the economy) a compulsory ministration performed in a slave's subordinate status toward the Father?

question: What does it mean that Christ is called the Way and that no one comes to the Father except through him?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what sense “with whom” is more suitable. Explanation of how the Son receives a commandment, and how He is sent.
sources.answer: It is meant in a higher sense than the ordinary one: an orderly, stage-by-stage advance to perfection through works of righteousness and the illumination of knowledge, leading to the knowledge of God. Christ is an essentially good Way, with no straying, to the essentially good Father. That is our way up to God "through the Son."
sources.quote: For our Lord is an essentially good Way, where erring and straying are unknown, to that which is essentially good, to the Father.
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that Christ is called the Way and that no one comes to the Father except through him?

question: Is it legitimate to read Paul's sentences with their words rearranged in order to recover his meaning?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VII.—Reply to an objection founded on the words of St. Paul (2 Cor. iv. 4). St. Paul occasionally uses words not in their grammatical sequence.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul frequently transposes the order of words because of the rapidity of his discourse and the impetus of the Spirit in him, as in Galatians 3:19 and 2 Thessalonians 2:8-9. If the reader does not observe the proper pauses, he falls into incongruities and even blasphemy, as if the Lord's coming were according to the working of Satan, so the hyperbaton must be shown in the reading.
sources.quote: the apostle frequently uses a transposed order in his sentences, due to the rapidity of his discourses, and the impetus of the Spirit which is in him.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to read Paul's sentences with their words rearranged in order to recover his meaning?

question: In Augustine's analysis of bodily perception and recollection, how many 'species' (forms) are generated in succession, and how does each arise from the previous one?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Species is Produced by Species in Succession.
sources.answer: Four species arise step by step, each born from the one before. From the form of the bodily object arises the form in the sense of the percipient; from that arises the form in the memory; and from that arises the form in the mind's eye of the one who thinks. This chain of parent and offspring is what allows a trace of a trinity to be found even in the outer man.
sources.quote: we find four species born, as it were, step by step one from the other, the second from the first, the third from the second, the fourth from the third
sources.raw_question: In Augustine's analysis of bodily perception and recollection, how many 'species' (forms) are generated in succession, and how does each arise from the previous one?

question: Why could the devil appear to fallen man as a mighty chief even though he led man into death?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > As Christ is the Mediator of Life, So the Devil is the Mediator of Death.
sources.answer: Because the devil never underwent the death of the flesh himself. He bore the death of the spirit through his ungodliness, but having no fleshly covering he did not die bodily. So he did not go where he had led man, and he seemed powerful. In this way he puffed up proud men through false philosophy, sacrilegious rites and magic, and he promised a false cleansing of the soul by disguising himself as an angel of light.
sources.quote: he bare indeed in his ungodliness the death of the spirit, but had not undergone the death of the flesh, because he had not assumed the covering of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Why could the devil appear to fallen man as a mighty chief even though he led man into death?

question: Does Ephesians 5:30, "we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones," refer to a spiritual, invisible man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter II.—When Christ visited us in His grace, He did not come to what did not belong to Him: also, by shedding His true blood for us, and exhibiting to us His true flesh in the Eucharist, He conferred upon our flesh the capacity of salvation.
sources.answer: No. A spirit has no flesh or bones, so Paul refers to the dispensation by which the Lord became an actual man of flesh, nerves and bones, whose members we are, nourished by the cup and bread that are his blood and body.
sources.quote: He does not speak these words of some spiritual and invisible man, for a spirit has not bones nor flesh;
sources.raw_question: Does Ephesians 5:30, "we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones," refer to a spiritual, invisible man?

question: Why does Psalm 36:8 call the Spirit the "river of God's pleasures"?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Because the Holy Spirit is God's own infinite delight and pleasure. That is why the river is called "the river of God's pleasures," not "God's river of pleasures." This river is the same one that proceeds from the throne of the Father and the Son in Revelation 22. It is also the same as the fatness of God's house, which the anointing oil typified.
sources.quote: the Holy Ghost being the infinite delight and pleasure of God, the river is called the river of God's pleasures (Ps. 36:8), not God's river of pleasures
sources.raw_question: Why does Psalm 36:8 call the Spirit the "river of God's pleasures"?

question: Why is faith necessary for reaching blessedness when every human being already wills to be blessed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What Has Been Treated of in This Book. How We Have Reached by Steps to a Certain Trinity, Which is Found in Practical Knowledge and True Faith.
sources.answer: Because willing blessedness is not enough to attain it. All men will to be blessed, but not all have faith, and faith is what cleanses the heart so that blessedness is reached. Many despair of immortality, and so they do not live in a way that could attain it. Faith is therefore needed to reach blessedness in all the goods of human nature, of both soul and body.
sources.quote: It belongs to all men to will to be blessed; yet all men have not faith, whereby the heart is cleansed, and so blessedness is reached.
sources.raw_question: Why is faith necessary for reaching blessedness when every human being already wills to be blessed?

question: Can anyone be freed from the dominion of the devil and have sins forgiven except through Christ?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What Has Been Treated of in This Book. How We Have Reached by Steps to a Certain Trinity, Which is Found in Practical Knowledge and True Faith.
sources.answer: No. True faith must be centred on Christ, who rose in the flesh never to die again. No one is freed from the devil's dominion through the forgiveness of sins except by Him. Those who remain in the devil's abode face a life both miserable and endless, which should rather be called death than life.
sources.quote: no one is freed from the dominion of the devil, through the forgiveness of sins, save by Him
sources.raw_question: Can anyone be freed from the dominion of the devil and have sins forgiven except through Christ?

question: Was it a different being from the creator, as the Valentinians held, who fashioned the human body, and was man made from some substance other than earth?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XV.—Proofs of the resurrection from Isaiah and Ezekiel; the same God who created us will also raise us up.
sources.answer: No. Christ formed the blind man's eyes from earth, which shows that man was fashioned from earth at the beginning. It would be incompatible for the eyes to come from one source and the rest of the body from another. Nor could one being fashion the body and another the eyes, so the one Creator-Word made both.
sources.quote: For it were incompatible that the eyes should indeed be formed from one source and the rest of the body from another; as neither would it be compatible that one [being] fashioned the body, and another the eyes.
sources.raw_question: Was it a different being from the creator, as the Valentinians held, who fashioned the human body, and was man made from some substance other than earth?

question: Why did the Fathers hold that the Person who declared himself God and Lord in the theophanies could not have been a mere angel?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 2: Whether the texts of the New Testament (in the second column) do
sources.answer: Because it would be blasphemous and absurd for a mere angel to declare in his own person that he is God and Lord. If he were only relaying the Father's words, any angel could truthfully say the Father is God, and the Fathers' argument would collapse. Their reasoning therefore shows they took the speaker to be God in his own person.
sources.quote: It is blasphemous and absurd for any mere angel to make such declaration. But, supposing it meant of the Person of the Father, why might not any angel declare, what is certainly true, that the Father is God
sources.raw_question: Why did the Fathers hold that the Person who declared himself God and Lord in the theophanies could not have been a mere angel?

question: Is the being and life of an understanding mind the same kind of being and life as that of a dead body or of cattle?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Every Mind Knows Certainly Three Things Concerning Itself—That It Understands, that It Is, and that It Lives.
sources.answer: No. Whatever understands must live, and whatever lives must be. So the mind both is and lives. But it does not exist as a dead body exists without life, nor live as a beast's soul lives without understanding. It is and lives in a proper and more excellent manner, as an understanding.
sources.quote: that which understands both is and lives; not as a dead body is which does not live, nor as a soul lives which does not understand, but in some proper and more excellent manner.
sources.raw_question: Is the being and life of an understanding mind the same kind of being and life as that of a dead body or of cattle?

question: What does the bride mean in Song of Songs 8:6 when she says that love is strong as death and jealousy is cruel as the grave?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: It expresses the believer's holy greediness of delight in Christ, a love that cannot be satisfied without constant fellowship with him. Like death and the grave, which are never satisfied unless they have all, the soul's love counts itself as having nothing unless it has Christ wholly. Its jealous fears that Christ has forsaken it give it no rest.
sources.quote: So is my love; if I have thee not wholly, I have nothing. Nor can all the world bribe it to a diversion; it will he no more turned aside than death in its time.
sources.raw_question: What does the bride mean in Song of Songs 8:6 when she says that love is strong as death and jealousy is cruel as the grave?

question: Why did God form Christ's humanity from Mary rather than taking fresh dust from the earth, as he did with Adam?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: So that no new, different formation would be called into being needing salvation. Instead, the very same human formation that existed in Adam would be summed up and saved in Christ, while the analogy with Adam was preserved.
sources.quote: It was that there might not be another formation called into being, nor any other which should [require to] be saved, but that the very same formation should be summed up [in Christ as had existed in Adam], the analogy having been preserved.
sources.raw_question: Why did God form Christ's humanity from Mary rather than taking fresh dust from the earth, as he did with Adam?

question: What did the Transfiguration reveal about Christ's coming in His Kingdom?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: It showed the Apostles the glory of Christ's reigning body as He comes into His Kingdom. This fulfilled His promise that some standing there would see the Son of Man coming in His Kingdom. In the Transfiguration the Lord appeared in the splendour of His reigning body.
sources.quote: Thus was shewn to the Apostles the glory of the body of Christ coming into His Kingdom: for in the fashion of His glorious Transfiguration, the Lord stood revealed in the splendour of His reigning body.
sources.raw_question: What did the Transfiguration reveal about Christ's coming in His Kingdom?

question: What does Christ's saying that the righteous shall shine as the sun in the Kingdom of their Father teach about the relation between Christ's reign and the Father's Kingdom?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Christ reigns in the splendour of His body until all things that cause stumbling are removed from His Kingdom. The righteous are then conformed to the glory of His body. They shine in the Kingdom of the Father with the same splendour He showed at the Transfiguration. The words 'He that hath ears to hear' signal that this is a mystery of faith, not a matter of bodily hearing.
sources.quote: And we see ourselves, in consequence, conformed to the glory of His body in the Kingdom of the Father, shining as with the splendour of the sun, the splendour in which He shewed the fashion of His Kingdom to the Apostles
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's saying that the righteous shall shine as the sun in the Kingdom of their Father teach about the relation between Christ's reign and the Father's Kingdom?

question: Is it reasonable to assent to a proposition whose terms appear to conflict but are not plainly repugnant?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: Yes. Such propositions, like God's certain foreknowledge of contingent events or an omnipresent substance that is not extended, may rightly be believed. The opposite side of the question may carry a greater appearance of repugnancy, or there may be no sufficient reason to suspend assent.
sources.quote: Propositions of this kind may be, and are assented to; because there may be a greater appearance of repugnaney on the opposite side: of the question; or, because there is not reason sufficient for suspending assent.
sources.raw_question: Is it reasonable to assent to a proposition whose terms appear to conflict but are not plainly repugnant?

question: When a distracted person seems not to have heard someone speaking or not to have read a page, has the sense failed to perceive, or has the will failed to apply memory to the sense?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Different Modes of Conceiving.
sources.answer: The sense did perceive; what failed was memory. Because the will's attention was fixed elsewhere, it did not apply the memory to the sense, so the impressions slipped away unretained. It is therefore more accurate to say "we do not remember" than "we did not hear." The case of a walker who reaches a place without remembering the way shows the same thing: he must have seen in order to walk easily, yet he recalls nothing of it.
sources.quote: Therefore, we should say more accurately in such a case, we do not remember, than, we did not hear
sources.raw_question: When a distracted person seems not to have heard someone speaking or not to have read a page, has the sense failed to perceive, or has the will failed to apply memory to the sense?

question: Do the early Fathers' similitudes of the sun and its rays, or the fountain and its streams, show that they regarded the Son as uncreated?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: Yes. These similitudes for the Son's procession include the sun and its rays, the fountain and its streams, the root and its branches, and one fire lighting another. They manifestly show that the Fathers never dreamed of the Son's being created.
sources.quote: the sun and its rays, the fountain and its streams, the root and its branches, one fire lighting another, and the like, manifestly shew that they never dreamed of the Son’s being created.
sources.raw_question: Do the early Fathers' similitudes of the sun and its rays, or the fountain and its streams, show that they regarded the Son as uncreated?

question: How can John 7:39 say 'the Holy Ghost was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified', when the prophets and others were filled with the Spirit beforehand?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: The Spirit had been given before, to the prophets, John the Baptist, Zacharias, Mary, Simeon and Anna. The giving after Christ's glorification was of a special kind never seen before. Visible signs such as speaking in unknown tongues showed that all nations would believe in Christ through the Spirit's gift.
sources.quote: unless because that giving, or granting, or mission of the Holy Spirit was to have a certain speciality of its own in its very advent, such as never was before?
sources.raw_question: How can John 7:39 say 'the Holy Ghost was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified', when the prophets and others were filled with the Spirit beforehand?

question: Could an angel have assumed the person of the incarnate Son, or only prefigured him?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: Angels could only prefigure him. In the fullness of time, man was united with the Word of God so as to be one Person, the Son of God made of a woman. Angelic nature could foreshadow and pre-announce this person, but could not appropriate it so as to be that person.
sources.quote: And this person angelic nature could prefigure beforehand, so as to pre-announce, but could not appropriate, so as to be that person itself.
sources.raw_question: Could an angel have assumed the person of the incarnate Son, or only prefigured him?

question: Does Paul's phrase 'the Jerusalem which is above' in Galatians refer to a Gnostic Aeon or a power that fell from the Pleroma, such as Prunicus?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXV.—He contends that these testimonies already alleged cannot be understood allegorically of celestial blessings, but that they shall have their fulfilment after the coming of Antichrist, and the resurrection, in the terrestrial Jerusalem. To the former prophecies he subjoins others drawn from Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the Apocalypse of John.
sources.answer: No. Paul does not mean an erratic Aeon, a power that departed from the Pleroma, or Prunicus. He means the Jerusalem that has been delineated on God's hands, as Isaiah says. John saw this same city descending upon the new earth.
sources.quote: He does not say this with any thought of an erratic Æon, or of any other power which departed from the Pleroma, or of Prunicus, but of the Jerusalem which has been delineated on [God’s] hands.
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's phrase 'the Jerusalem which is above' in Galatians refer to a Gnostic Aeon or a power that fell from the Pleroma, such as Prunicus?

question: Why does Matthew write "the birth of Christ was on this wise" rather than "the birth of Jesus"?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit, foreseeing corrupters of the truth, chose the wording to guard against them. By saying it was Christ who was born, Matthew excludes the claim that only Jesus was born of Mary while Christ descended from above. The wording itself teaches that the one born of Mary is the Christ.
sources.quote: Matthew might certainly have said, “Now the birth of Jesus was on this wise;” but the Holy Ghost, foreseeing the corrupters [of the truth], and guarding by anticipation against their deceit, says by Matthew, “But the birth of Christ was on this wise;”
sources.raw_question: Why does Matthew write "the birth of Christ was on this wise" rather than "the birth of Jesus"?

question: Does the fact that Christ's arresters fell back before Him show that His body was not subject to weakness?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes. His pursuers reeled and fell prone, unable to endure His majesty as He offered Himself to their chains. A body whose nature had such power could not be enthralled by weakness.
sources.quote: Weakness in His body, at Whose approach the pursuers reeled and broke their ranks and fell prone, unable to endure His Majesty as He offered Himself to their chains?
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that Christ's arresters fell back before Him show that His body was not subject to weakness?

question: How can God's substance be called both simple and manifold at the same time?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > How God is a Substance Both Simple and Manifold.
sources.answer: God is called by many names, such as great, good, wise, blessed and true, but in Him each of these is the same as all the others and the same as His very being. His greatness is His wisdom, because He is great by power, not by bulk. So the manifold names do not mark different parts or qualities in God. To see why, one first considers why creatures are manifold and in no way truly simple.
sources.quote: His goodness is the same as His wisdom and greatness, and His truth the same as all those things; and in Him it is not one thing to be blessed, and another to be great, or wise, or true, or good, or in a word to be Himself.
sources.raw_question: How can God's substance be called both simple and manifold at the same time?

question: Why is bodily nature manifold and in no respect simple?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > How God is a Substance Both Simple and Manifold.
sources.answer: Because every body is made of parts, some greater and some less, and the whole is greater than any part. Also, in each body size, color and shape are different things. One can change while the others stay the same. Since what is said of a body can be changed separately, its nature is shown to be manifold.
sources.quote: And in each several body, size is one thing, color another, shape another; for the same color and the same shape may remain with diminished size
sources.raw_question: Why is bodily nature manifold and in no respect simple?

question: Do the orthodox, as Eunomius charges, give names priority over realities and so make unequal things equal?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The charge is groundless, because no name has any substantial reality in itself. Every name is only a recognizing mark placed on some reality or idea. Names therefore cannot have a prerogative over the things they signify.
sources.quote: there is no single name that has in itself any substantial reality, but that every name is but a recognizing mark placed on some reality or some idea, having of itself no existence either as a fact or a thought.
sources.raw_question: Do the orthodox, as Eunomius charges, give names priority over realities and so make unequal things equal?

question: Can perishable, temporal created things serve to honour eternal, incorruptible realities, as the Valentinians claim the Saviour made the world as images to honour the Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VII.—Created things are not the images of those Æons who are within the Pleroma.
sources.answer: No. If created things were made to honour the higher realities, they would have to endure perpetually. Temporal, corruptible things cannot confer honour on what is eternal, and even among mortals only lasting honour is valued. Things that pass away as soon as they are made would rather dishonour the eternal, which is insulted when its image is corrupted and dissolved.
sources.quote: For what honour can those things which are temporal confer on such as are eternal and endure for ever? or those which pass away on such as remain? or those which are corruptible on such as are incorruptible?
sources.raw_question: Can perishable, temporal created things serve to honour eternal, incorruptible realities, as the Valentinians claim the Saviour made the world as images to honour the Pleroma?

question: If the ignorant Demiurge was made as an image of the Only-begotten (the Nous of the Father), does it follow that the Only-begotten himself is ignorant?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VII.—Created things are not the images of those Æons who are within the Pleroma.
sources.answer: Yes, on the Valentinians' own hypothesis, which shows the hypothesis is blasphemous and self-refuting. Both were produced spiritually, not fashioned or composed. So either the image is like its original, and the Only-begotten would be ignorant of himself, the Father and his works, or it is unlike, and the Saviour is a poor workman. Since the Only-begotten truly has knowledge, an image of him would also have to know, so the Valentinian scheme is overthrown.
sources.quote: If, on the other hand, it is similar, then the same ignorance will be found to exist in the Nous (mind) of their Propator, that is, in the Only-begotten.
sources.raw_question: If the ignorant Demiurge was made as an image of the Only-begotten (the Nous of the Father), does it follow that the Only-begotten himself is ignorant?

question: Was Christ created on account of the works, as a servant or instrument made to build the universe?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. That would make Christ a servant and builder rather than the Lord of Glory and eternally beloved Son. The very passage shows God the Father as Maker of the universe with Wisdom present beside Him even in His eternal preparation of the works, so Wisdom was not created for the sake of the works, having been present before them.
sources.quote: Whence Wisdom would have us understand that it was not created on account of God’s works, by the very fact that it had been present at the eternal preparation of works yet to be
sources.raw_question: Was Christ created on account of the works, as a servant or instrument made to build the universe?

question: Is the exodus of Israel from Egypt, carried out by the God of the Old Testament, connected to the work of Jesus the Son of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXX.—Refutation of another argument adduced by the Marcionites, that God directed the Hebrews to spoil the Egyptians.
sources.answer: Yes. The whole exodus, done under divine guidance, was a type of the Church's exodus from among the Gentiles. The tabernacle built from Egyptian goods foreshadowed believers serving God with others' goods. The inheritance which Moses did not give, Jesus the Son of God will give. So one God works through both covenants, and the end-time plagues on the nations mirror Egypt's plagues.
sources.quote: For the whole exodus of the people out of Egypt, which took place under divine guidance, was a type and image of the exodus of the Church which should take place from among the Gentiles
sources.raw_question: Is the exodus of Israel from Egypt, carried out by the God of the Old Testament, connected to the work of Jesus the Son of God?

question: Do the analogies of the sun and its radiance and the fountain and its stream show that an offspring can be coeval with its source?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether we may decide the question by the parallel of human sons, which are born later than their parents. No, for the force of the analogy lies in the idea of connaturality. Time is not involved in the idea of Son, but is adventitious to it, and does not attach to God, because He is without parts and passions. The titles Word and Wisdom guard our thoughts of Him and His Son from this misconception. God not a Father, as a Creator, in posse from eternity, because creation does not relate to the essence of God, as generation does.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Arians asked the sun about its radiance or the fountain about its issue, as they asked women about time, they would find that these offspring always exist with their sources. Since such things share nature and duration with what they come from, denying this to God would make Him inferior to created things.
sources.quote: so they inquire of the sun concerning its radiance, and of the fountain concerning its issue. They will find that these, though an offspring, always exist with those things from which they are.
sources.raw_question: Do the analogies of the sun and its radiance and the fountain and its stream show that an offspring can be coeval with its source?

question: How could the many different Old Testament prophets all prefigure the one Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: They did so as members of one body, Christ. Each prophet, in his place as a member, foreshadowed the particular work of Christ connected with that member. As a whole man is shown not by one limb but by all together, the many prophets together foretold the one Christ. This unity of prophecy shows that the same Word and Father stand behind both Testaments.
sources.quote: so also did all the prophets prefigure the one [Christ]; while every one of them, in his special place as a member, did, in accordance with this, fill up the [established] dispensation
sources.raw_question: How could the many different Old Testament prophets all prefigure the one Christ?

question: Who holds supreme authority over the gospel ordinances and the dispensing of the Spirit in the church, and for whose benefit is it exercised?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: The Lord Christ holds it, and he exercises it for the benefit of God's adopted children. God made Christ head over all things to the church and committed to him the institution of ordinances and the dispensation of the Spirit that makes them effective. He does all this for the many sons he is bringing to glory, and he is faithful over God's house.
sources.quote: The supreme administration of the house of God in the hand of the Lord Christ, as to the institution of ordinances and dispensation of the Spirit, to enliven and make effectual those ordinances for the end of their institution
sources.raw_question: Who holds supreme authority over the gospel ordinances and the dispensing of the Spirit in the church, and for whose benefit is it exercised?

question: If the gospel is preached to the whole world, does everyone have a right to the privileges of God's house, the church?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: No. The word is preached to all in order to gather God's scattered children and to leave the rest without excuse. Only God's adopted children have a right to the privileges of his house. The church is made up of living stones, saints and a holy people, so others who creep in have no right or title there.
