sources.quote: Now, who shall have any right in the house of God, but only his children? We will not allow a right to any but our own children in our houses: will God, think you, allow any right in his house but to his children?
sources.raw_question: If the gospel is preached to the whole world, does everyone have a right to the privileges of God's house, the church?

question: Does a believer who comes to faith quickly and trustfully possess salvation as truly as one who reaches it through long intellectual investigation?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: Yes. The author compares the Gospel to a key that opens a cabinet of jewels. Whether one first verifies the key exhaustively or simply tries it in trust, the lock yields and both alike possess the treasure. The careful investigator gains a more intelligent understanding of how the key works. The life-giving efficacy, however, is the same for both, because the question is one of obedience to the Gospel.
sources.quote: They may not have so intelligent a knowledge of the way in which that elaborate key turns back one secret spring after another; that knowledge, whenever acquired, belongs to the patient painstaking investigator. But both alike possess the jewels.
sources.raw_question: Does a believer who comes to faith quickly and trustfully possess salvation as truly as one who reaches it through long intellectual investigation?

question: Why do human beings need words and names at all?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Because our nature is encumbered with flesh, our thoughts cannot be directly revealed to one another. We therefore give things names as signs of their meaning so that thoughts are not left uncommunicated. If thought could be laid bare directly, we would converse more lucidly without words.
sources.quote: inasmuch as the thoughts which arise in us are incapable of being so revealed, because our nature is encumbered with its fleshly surrounding, we are obliged to express to each other what goes on in our minds by giving things their respective names
sources.raw_question: Why do human beings need words and names at all?

question: Does Scripture, in both the Old and New Testaments, direct our ultimate confidence away from human creatures and toward God the Creator alone?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 2. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, detaches our ultimate confidence from man the creature, and attaches it to God the Creator; – by contrasting the sinfulness and feebleness of mortal man with the goodness and omnipotence of the Eternal Jehovah: by direct prohibition and precept: by exhibiting the holy Jealousy of God.
sources.answer: Yes. Bickersteth calls this his first great proposition and holds that both Testaments alike enforce it. He traces three lines of Scripture teaching that support it: the contrast between sinful, feeble man and the good, omnipotent Jehovah; direct prohibition and precept; and God's holy jealousy when any creature usurps His place in our trust and regard.
sources.quote: That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, detaches our ultimate confidence from man, the creature, and attaches it to God, the Creator.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture, in both the Old and New Testaments, direct our ultimate confidence away from human creatures and toward God the Creator alone?

question: Does Christ's taking on our slavery in the Incarnation mean that he is himself a slave?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Christ took our disease, death, curse, sin and slavery, not so as to keep what He took, but to purge our nature of these evils. Our defects are swallowed up in His stainless nature. So in the life to come slavery will vanish along with sin and death, as His words "I call you no more servants, but friends" show.
sources.quote: so took our slavery also, not in such a way as Himself to have what He took, but so as to purge our nature of such evils, our defects being swallowed up and done away with in His stainless nature
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's taking on our slavery in the Incarnation mean that he is himself a slave?

question: Does Christ's promise at the Last Supper to drink the fruit of the vine new with his disciples in his Father's kingdom point to a bodily resurrection and a renewed earth?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXIII.—Further proofs of the same proposition, drawn from the promises made by Christ, when He declared that He would drink of the fruit of the vine with His disciples in His Father’s kingdom, while at the same time He promised to reward them an hundred-fold, and to make them partake of banquets. The blessing pronounced by Jacob had pointed out this already, as Papias and the elders have interpreted it.
sources.answer: Yes. By promising to drink of the fruit of the vine with his disciples, Christ indicated both the inheritance of the earth, where the new fruit of the vine is drunk, and the resurrection of his disciples in the flesh. He cannot be understood as drinking wine in some super-celestial place, and those who drink cannot be without flesh, because drinking what flows from the vine belongs to flesh and not to spirit.
sources.quote: nor, again, are they who drink it devoid of flesh, for to drink of that which flows from the vine pertains to flesh, and not spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's promise at the Last Supper to drink the fruit of the vine new with his disciples in his Father's kingdom point to a bodily resurrection and a renewed earth?

question: Is the flesh that rises in the resurrection the same flesh that received the cup of the new covenant?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXIII.—Further proofs of the same proposition, drawn from the promises made by Christ, when He declared that He would drink of the fruit of the vine with His disciples in His Father’s kingdom, while at the same time He promised to reward them an hundred-fold, and to make them partake of banquets. The blessing pronounced by Jacob had pointed out this already, as Papias and the elders have interpreted it.
sources.answer: Yes. The new flesh that rises again is the same flesh that also received the new cup. This is why Christ's promise to drink with his disciples again implies that they will rise in the flesh.
sources.quote: For the new flesh which rises again is the same which also received the new cup.
sources.raw_question: Is the flesh that rises in the resurrection the same flesh that received the cup of the new covenant?

question: When will Christ's promised hundred-fold rewards and the repayment for feeding the poor be given?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXIII.—Further proofs of the same proposition, drawn from the promises made by Christ, when He declared that He would drink of the fruit of the vine with His disciples in His Father’s kingdom, while at the same time He promised to reward them an hundred-fold, and to make them partake of banquets. The blessing pronounced by Jacob had pointed out this already, as Papias and the elders have interpreted it.
sources.answer: They will be given in the times of the kingdom after the resurrection of the just. This is the seventh day, sanctified as the true Sabbath of the righteous. In that age the righteous will do no earthly work, and God will prepare a table for them supplied with all kinds of food.
sources.quote: These are [to take place] in the times of the kingdom, that is, upon the seventh day, which has been sanctified, in which God rested from all the works which He created, which is the true Sabbath of the righteous
sources.raw_question: When will Christ's promised hundred-fold rewards and the repayment for feeding the poor be given?

question: Was Isaac's blessing of Jacob, promising plenty and lordship over the nations, fulfilled in Jacob's earthly life?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXIII.—Further proofs of the same proposition, drawn from the promises made by Christ, when He declared that He would drink of the fruit of the vine with His disciples in His Father’s kingdom, while at the same time He promised to reward them an hundred-fold, and to make them partake of banquets. The blessing pronounced by Jacob had pointed out this already, as Papias and the elders have interpreted it.
sources.answer: No. The blessing belongs to the coming kingdom, when the righteous rise and rule. In his own life Jacob served Laban for twenty years and bowed before Esau instead of ruling him. He also went down to Egypt because of famine and became subject to Pharaoh. Reading the blessing as fulfilled in this life therefore produces contradiction, as happens with the Jews.
sources.quote: The predicted blessing, therefore, belongs unquestionably to the times of the kingdom, when the righteous shall bear rule upon their rising from the dead
sources.raw_question: Was Isaac's blessing of Jacob, promising plenty and lordship over the nations, fulfilled in Jacob's earthly life?

question: How can the Lord bring about the enormous fruitfulness promised for the times of the kingdom?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXIII.—Further proofs of the same proposition, drawn from the promises made by Christ, when He declared that He would drink of the fruit of the vine with His disciples in His Father’s kingdom, while at the same time He promised to reward them an hundred-fold, and to make them partake of banquets. The blessing pronounced by Jacob had pointed out this already, as Papias and the elders have interpreted it.
sources.answer: Irenaeus answers with the Lord's reply to the traitor Judas, as Papias reports it: those who come to those times will see it. These things are credible to believers. In the renewed creation the earth will bear superabundant fruit, and the animals will live in peace with one another and in subjection to man.
sources.quote: the Lord declared, ‘They who shall come to these [times] shall see.’
sources.raw_question: How can the Lord bring about the enormous fruitfulness promised for the times of the kingdom?

question: Why could Pharaoh's magicians produce frogs and serpents but not lice (the minute flies)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Original Cause of All Things is from God.
sources.answer: Because the greater power of God, acting through the Holy Spirit, was present to prohibit them. The magicians themselves confessed this by saying, "This is the finger of God," the finger of God signifying the Holy Spirit. Angels can do some things only when permitted, and God may withhold permission even for what their nature can do.
sources.quote: the greater power of God was present prohibiting them, through the Holy Spirit; which even the magicians themselves confessed, saying, “This is the finger of God.”
sources.raw_question: Why could Pharaoh's magicians produce frogs and serpents but not lice (the minute flies)?

question: Can lordship and servitude coexist in one simple nature, given that they are opposed attributes?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: No. Like life and death, domination and servitude are contradictory and admit no middle term. No single definition applies to both, and where definitions differ, natures differ. What is simple in nature cannot be split into contradictory attributes.
sources.quote: For just as the contradictory opposition of life and death admits of no mean, so in its distinguishing characteristics is domination diametrically and irreconcilably opposed to servitude.
sources.raw_question: Can lordship and servitude coexist in one simple nature, given that they are opposed attributes?

question: What follows for Christian worship if the Only-begotten is a slave?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book X > After this he shows that the Son, who truly is, and is in the bosom of the Father, is simple and uncompounded, and that, He Who redeemed us from bondage is not under dominion of the Father, nor in a state of slavery: and that otherwise not He alone, but also the Father Who is in the Son and is One with Him, must be a slave; and that the word “being” is formed from the word to “be.” And having excellently and notably discussed all these matters, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: It leads to a double enormity. Calling the Son a slave makes him one's fellow-servant. Either the believer despises his fellow-slave and casts off Christ's lordship, denying the faith. Or he worships a slave and so in effect worships himself, seeing his own condition in the one he worships.
sources.quote: either he will despise his fellow-slave and deny the faith, having shaken off the yoke of the lordship of Christ, or he will bow before the slave, and, turning away from the self-determining nature that owns no Lord over it, will in a manner worship himself instead of God
sources.raw_question: What follows for Christian worship if the Only-begotten is a slave?

question: If God already knows what we need, why do we pray, and does prayer inform God of anything?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Still Further of the Difference Between the Knowledge and Word of Our Mind, and the Knowledge and Word of God.
sources.answer: Prayer does not inform God of our necessities. He knew beforehand, without any beginning, all things to come in time, including what we would ask, when, and whether he would grant it.
sources.quote: For we too pray to Him, yet do not inform Him what our necessities are. “For your Father knoweth,” says His Word, “what things ye have need of, before you ask Him.”
sources.raw_question: If God already knows what we need, why do we pray, and does prayer inform God of anything?

question: Does Isaiah's prophecy of the wolf feeding with the lamb and the lion eating straw refer only figuratively to converted savage peoples, or also literally to animals in the resurrection of the just?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXIII.—Further proofs of the same proposition, drawn from the promises made by Christ, when He declared that He would drink of the fruit of the vine with His disciples in His Father’s kingdom, while at the same time He promised to reward them an hundred-fold, and to make them partake of banquets. The blessing pronounced by Jacob had pointed out this already, as Papias and the elders have interpreted it.
sources.answer: It applies to both, and literally to the animals. Irenaeus grants that the words are now fulfilled in men of various nations coming to the harmony of the faith. But in the resurrection of the just they will also apply to the animals themselves, because God is rich in all things. When creation is restored, the animals will again be subject to man, as they were to Adam, and return to the food God first gave them, the produce of the earth.
sources.quote: But although this is [true] now with regard to some men coming from various nations to the harmony of the faith, nevertheless in the resurrection of the just [the words shall also apply] to those animals mentioned.
sources.raised_by_detail: some persons who refer the words to savage men who come to believe
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah's prophecy of the wolf feeding with the lamb and the lion eating straw refer only figuratively to converted savage peoples, or also literally to animals in the resurrection of the just?

question: What, according to the early Church, actually made a doctrine Tritheistic?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 22: Whether his (the Doctor’s) whole performance, whenever he differs Jrom us, be any thing more than a repetition of this assertion, that being and person are the
sources.answer: Only denying the unity of principle (one source, the Father) or making the divine Hypostases heterogeneous, separate, or alien from one another. Those who held this were condemned as Tritheists; merely confessing three coessential, inseparable Persons was not.
sources.quote: None were ever condemned by the Church as Jritheists, but such as either denied the unity of principiwm, or made the Hypostases heterogeneous, ἡ separate, or alien from each other.
sources.raw_question: What, according to the early Church, actually made a doctrine Tritheistic?

question: Is Jesus Christ the Judge of all the earth, an office the Old Testament attributes to God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Abraham calls God 'the Judge of all the earth.' The New Testament says we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, and that Christ will come rendering to every man according to his work, as the Psalmist says God does. The office of universal Judge therefore belongs to the Son as well as to the Father.
sources.quote: We must all appear before the judgement seat of Christ. – 2 Cor. 5:10.
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus Christ the Judge of all the earth, an office the Old Testament attributes to God?

question: If Jehovah declares that beside Him there is no Saviour, what follows from Scripture calling Jesus the Saviour?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: It follows that Jesus is Jehovah, for Jehovah says there is no Saviour beside Him. The New Testament nevertheless repeatedly names Jesus as the one who saves His people from their sins and as the Author of eternal salvation. It adds that there is salvation in no other name. Being the sole Saviour is a mark of Deity, and it belongs to Christ.
sources.quote: I, even I, am Jehovah, and beside Me there is no Saviour. – Isa. 43:11.
sources.raw_question: If Jehovah declares that beside Him there is no Saviour, what follows from Scripture calling Jesus the Saviour?

question: Does Titus 2:13–14 identify Jesus Christ with the Jehovah who redeems Israel from all iniquities in Psalm 130:8?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. In the Septuagint, Psalm 130:8 says Jehovah will redeem Israel from all his iniquities. Titus 2:13–14 uses almost identical Greek of 'our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ,' who gave Himself to redeem us from all iniquity. The redeeming work promised by Jehovah is thus fulfilled by Christ, who is called 'great God.'
sources.quote: Our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, Who gave Himself for us, That He might redeem us from all iniquity (ίνα λυτρώσηται ημας απο πάσης ανομίας) – Titus 2:13–14.
sources.raw_question: Does Titus 2:13–14 identify Jesus Christ with the Jehovah who redeems Israel from all iniquities in Psalm 130:8?

question: Is Christ, like Jehovah, the source of life and the conqueror of death?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The Psalmist says the fountain of life is with God, and Isaiah and Hosea promise that Jehovah will swallow up death and redeem from the grave. Of the Word it is said that in Him was life. Christ is also said to have abolished death and to have destroyed him that had the power of death. These divine works and attributes belong equally to the Son.
sources.quote: Our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death. – 2 Tim. 1:10.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ, like Jehovah, the source of life and the conqueror of death?

question: Does Scripture direct believers to depend on Christ for spiritual life, strength and hope in the way the Old Testament directs them to depend on God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Israel is told to cleave to the Lord, to find their fruit from Him, to seek strength from Him and to hope in Him. Believers in turn are told to abide in Christ, apart from whom they can do nothing. They are told they can do all things through Christ who strengthens them, and that Jesus Christ is their hope. The dependence and trust due to God alone are thus rightly placed in Christ.
sources.quote: Jesus Christ, which is our hope. – 1 Tim. 1:1.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture direct believers to depend on Christ for spiritual life, strength and hope in the way the Old Testament directs them to depend on God?

question: Can a mind that naturally loves itself be truly said to hate itself if it does not love God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Mind Loves God in Rightly Loving Itself; And If It Love Not God, It Must Be Said to Hate Itself. Even a Weak and Erring Mind is Always Strong in Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself. Let It Be Turned to God, that It May Be Blessed by Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Him.
sources.answer: Yes. Hating someone means wishing to injure him, and the mind that loves iniquity wills what is harmful to itself, even if through ignorance. So though self-love is implanted by nature, the one who does not love God acts against himself as his own enemy. Only he who loves God knows how to love himself rightly.
sources.quote: He, therefore, who knows how to love himself, loves God; but he who does not love God, even if he does love himself,—a thing implanted in him by nature,—yet is not unsuitably said to hate himself
sources.raw_question: Can a mind that naturally loves itself be truly said to hate itself if it does not love God?

question: Does the scriptural statement that 'all have gone aside, there is none that doeth good' include the Holy Spirit among creatures who have failed?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, since He sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor subject to change. He is always good, since He is given by the Father and the Son; neither is He to be numbered amongst such things as are said to fail. He must be acknowledged as the source of goodness. The Spirit of God's mouth, the amender of evils, and Himself good. Lastly, as He is said in Scripture to be good, and is joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, He cannot possibly be denied to be good. He is not, however, said to progress, but to be made perfect in goodness, which distinguishes Him from all creatures.
sources.answer: No. If the opponents exclude the Spirit from this 'all,' they admit He is not among creatures. If they include Him, they must say the Spirit has gone aside and become unprofitable, which is absurd. Either way, the Spirit is not one of the creatures who fail.
sources.quote: If they except the Holy Spirit, even they themselves confess that He is not amongst all; if they do not except Him, then they, too, acknowledge that He has gone aside amongst all.
sources.raw_question: Does the scriptural statement that 'all have gone aside, there is none that doeth good' include the Holy Spirit among creatures who have failed?

question: How do the Levitical laws on clean and unclean animals figuratively signify faith in the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VIII.—The gifts of the Holy Spirit which we receive prepare us for incorruption, render us spiritual, and separate us from carnal men. These two classes are signified by the clean and unclean animals in the legal dispensation.
sources.answer: The divided hoof stands for steady faith moving toward the Father and the Son, and chewing the cud stands for meditating on God's words. The Jews have God's words in their mouth but are not rooted in the Father and the Son, so they are like cud-chewers without the divided hoof. Heretics claim faith in the Father and the Son but do not meditate on God's words or do good works, so they are like animals with the divided hoof that do not ruminate.
sources.quote: Those who make their way by faith steadily towards the Father and the Son; for this is denoted by the steadiness of those which divide the hoof
sources.raw_question: How do the Levitical laws on clean and unclean animals figuratively signify faith in the Father and the Son?

question: Did Christ perform divine works such as raising the dead and healing the blind apart from his body, or through it?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: He did them through his own body. The works proper to the Word, such as raising the dead, giving sight to the blind and healing the woman with the issue of blood, were done through his flesh, because the Godhead was in it. Thus he stretched out his hand humanly but stopped the illness divinely.
sources.quote: while on the other hand the works proper to the Word Himself, such as to raise the dead, to restore sight to the blind, and to cure the woman with an issue of blood, He did through His own body
sources.raw_question: Did Christ perform divine works such as raising the dead and healing the blind apart from his body, or through it?

question: Why does the prophet say Christ 'carried' our infirmities rather than that he 'remedied' them?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Introductory to Texts from the Gospels on the Incarnation. Enumeration of texts still to be explained. Arians compared to the Jews. We must recur to the Regula Fidei. Our Lord did not come into, but became, man, and therefore had the acts and affections of the flesh. The same works divine and human. Thus the flesh was purified, and men were made immortal. Reference to I Pet. iv. 1.
sources.answer: If the Word had only healed men from outside the body, as he always had done, he would have left them still subject to death. By carrying our infirmities and bearing our sins in his own body, he showed that he had truly become man. In this way we were redeemed from our affections and filled with his righteousness, while he himself received no hurt.
sources.quote: lest, as being external to the body, and only healing it, as He has always done, He should leave men subject still to death; but He carries our infirmities, and He Himself bears our sins
sources.raw_question: Why does the prophet say Christ 'carried' our infirmities rather than that he 'remedied' them?

question: How does God's forbearance as revealed in Christ differ in nature from the forbearance God shows to people apart from Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Forbearance outside Christ is merely a delay of immediate punishment together with temporal mercies, which men abuse and may perish holding. Forbearance revealed in Christ is full of love, tenderness and grace: it is God waiting to be gracious, managing his dealings to recover the sinner and endear him to himself. It also makes way for complete forgiveness of sins, which the other does not.
sources.quote: That which lies hid in Christ, and is revealed from him, is full of love, sweetness, tenderness, kindness, grace. It is the Lord’s waiting to be gracious to sinners; waiting for an advantage to show love and kindness
sources.raw_question: How does God's forbearance as revealed in Christ differ in nature from the forbearance God shows to people apart from Christ?

question: Does Isaiah 35:4 ('He will come Himself, and will save us') show that the coming Saviour is God himself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XX.—God showed himself, by the fall of man, as patient, benign, merciful, mighty to save. Man is therefore most ungrateful, if, unmindful of his own lot, and of the benefits held out to him, he do not acknowledge divine grace.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah declares that our God will come himself and save us, showing that salvation comes not from ourselves but from God's own coming. Irenaeus applies this to Christ, Emmanuel. In the following section he adds that the Saviour is neither a mere man nor an angel but the Lord himself made flesh.
sources.quote: He will come Himself, and will save us.”[^3698] Here we see, that not by ourselves, but by the help of God, we must be saved.
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah 35:4 ('He will come Himself, and will save us') show that the coming Saviour is God himself?

question: Does Romans 11:32 ('God hath concluded all in unbelief, that He may have mercy upon all') refer to spiritual Aeons, as Gnostics might claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XX.—God showed himself, by the fall of man, as patient, benign, merciful, mighty to save. Man is therefore most ungrateful, if, unmindful of his own lot, and of the benefits held out to him, he do not acknowledge divine grace.
sources.answer: No. Paul speaks of man, who had been disobedient to God and cast off from immortality, and then obtained mercy. Man receives that mercy through the Son of God, in the adoption the Son accomplishes.
sources.quote: not saying this in reference to spiritual Æons, but to man, who had been disobedient to God, and being cast off from immortality, then obtained mercy
sources.raw_question: Does Romans 11:32 ('God hath concluded all in unbelief, that He may have mercy upon all') refer to spiritual Aeons, as Gnostics might claim?

question: Does Scripture distinguish between mediate and ultimate, or inferior and sovereign, religious worship?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. Under the Old Testament all religious worship belonged to God only, because he is Jehovah, eternal, Creator and Governor. Christ confirmed this law without alteration, the Apostles taught it after his ascension, and an angel restated it. All religious worship was taken to have one meaning and one object: the divine nature, whether subsisting in one Person or more.
sources.quote: No distinction of worship, mediate and ultimate, was ever intimated; nor of inferior and sovereign: but all religious worship supposed to have one meaning, one significancy, one object, viz. the divine nature
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture distinguish between mediate and ultimate, or inferior and sovereign, religious worship?

question: Is the God who chose Jerusalem and instituted the Jewish priesthood the supreme God, or a lesser being produced from a defect, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: He is the supreme God. The angel Gabriel, who stands in the presence of the Lord, confessed this God simply and absolutely as God and Lord, because he knew of no other above Him. Had Gabriel known of a more perfect God, he would never have given this full confession to a being he knew to be the fruit of a defect.
sources.quote: For he knew of none other above Him; since, if he had been in possession of the knowledge of any other more perfect God and Lord besides Him, he surely would never—as I have already shown —have confessed Him
sources.raw_question: Is the God who chose Jerusalem and instituted the Jewish priesthood the supreme God, or a lesser being produced from a defect, as the Gnostics claim?

question: In Luke 1:16-17, who is 'the Lord their God' for whom John the Baptist prepared a people?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: It is Christ, the same Lord who said that John was 'more than a prophet' and that none born of women is greater than John. John prepared the people for this Lord's coming by preaching repentance. They were to be converted to Him, from whom they had been alienated by sin, and to receive remission from Him when He was present. So the 'Lord their God' of Israel is identified with the coming Christ.
sources.quote: Truly of Him who said that John had something even “more than a prophet,” and that “among those born of women none is greater than John the Baptist;” who did also make the people ready for the Lord’s advent
sources.raw_question: In Luke 1:16-17, who is 'the Lord their God' for whom John the Baptist prepared a people?

question: If necessary agents are not true causes but are acted upon, does it follow that God, when he acts by necessity of nature, is acted upon, or that all of God's acts must be voluntary rather than natural and necessary?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: No. The maxim holds for finite necessary agents, whose natural acts come from God, the author of their natures. It does not hold for God. Clarke himself says God is infinitely wise, good and happy by an absolute necessity of nature. Knowing, loving, contemplating and enjoying himself are perpetual acts, so an infinitely active being has natural, necessary acts without being acted upon by anything outside him.
sources.quote: This is very true of all finite necessary agents; for all their necessary
sources.raw_question: If necessary agents are not true causes but are acted upon, does it follow that God, when he acts by necessity of nature, is acted upon, or that all of God's acts must be voluntary rather than natural and necessary?

question: Since Revelation is the only rule, are going beyond it and falling short of it in honouring the Son equally culpable?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 30: Whether, supposing the case doubtful, it be not a wise man’s part to take the safer side; rather to think too highly, than too meanly of our blessed Saviour ; r
sources.answer: No. The objection equivocates on 'equally': both are faults, but not equal faults. To exceed the rule is culpable as well as to fall short, yet not in the same degree, since one extreme can be more dangerous than the other.
sources.quote: Equally culpable, signifies, either that one is culpable as well as the other, or that one is culpable as much as the other; equally a fault, or an equal fault.
sources.raw_question: Since Revelation is the only rule, are going beyond it and falling short of it in honouring the Son equally culpable?

question: Which person of the Trinity is most fittingly called the will of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Against Eunomius, Saying that the Son of God is the Son, Not of His Nature, But of His Will. Epilogue to What Has Been Said Already.
sources.answer: The Holy Spirit. If any person in the Trinity is specially to be called the will of God, the name suits the Spirit, just as the name love does. Love is nothing other than will.
sources.quote: if any person in the Trinity is also to be specially called the will of God, this name, like love, is better suited to the Holy Spirit; for what else is love, except will?
sources.raw_question: Which person of the Trinity is most fittingly called the will of God?

question: Did the Holy Spirit acquire the divine attributes by seizure or force, so that the Father suffered some loss?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XIX. Having proved above that the Spirit abides and speaks in the prophets, St. Ambrose infers that He knows all things which are of God, and therefore is One with the Father and the Son. This same point he establishes again from the fact that He possesses all that God possesses, namely, Godhead, knowledge of the heart, truth, a Name above every name, and power to raise the dead, as is proved from Ezekiel, and in this He is equal to the Son.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit did not seize these things through need or take them by superior power, which would injure the one deprived. He possesses them by unity of power with the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: For neither did He seize it through need, nor through superiority of greater power did He take it by force, but He possesses it by unity of power.
sources.raw_question: Did the Holy Spirit acquire the divine attributes by seizure or force, so that the Father suffered some loss?

question: Why did God reveal the truth first through types and shadows in the law and the prophets?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Objection that some were baptized unto Moses and believed in him, and an answer to it; with remarks upon types.
sources.answer: Because God in his wisdom spares human weakness and educates us gradually. Like eyes brought up in the dark, we were first shown shadows and the sun reflected in water, lest we be blinded by pure light. The law and prophetic types thus train the eyes of the heart, making easy the transition to the wisdom hidden in mystery.
sources.quote: Just so the Law, having a shadow of things to come, and the typical teaching of the prophets, which is a dark utterance of the truth, have been devised means to train the eyes of the heart
sources.raw_question: Why did God reveal the truth first through types and shadows in the law and the prophets?

question: Why was the knowledge of Christ's divine nature largely concealed from most people before his passion and resurrection?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Preface
sources.answer: It suited God's dispensation for the work Christ had to accomplish as mediator. Though in the form of God and equal with God, he emptied himself by taking the form of a servant so he might be obedient unto death; his divine glory was veiled for a season until he was declared the Son of God with power by the resurrection and glorified with the glory he had with the Father before the world was.
sources.quote: It was, indeed, suited, in the dispensation of God, unto the work that the Lord Jesus had to fulfil in the world, that, before his passion and resurrection, the knowledge of his divine nature, as unto his individual person, should be concealed from the most of men.
sources.raw_question: Why was the knowledge of Christ's divine nature largely concealed from most people before his passion and resurrection?

question: When light comes forth from light, can one part of the light be called older or younger than another?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus holds that light from light is one light, so no part of it can be called more recent or more ancient. Even torches lit from one another are distinguished only by when they were kindled, not by their substance. When their lights are blended, they return to the one original light.
sources.quote: But we cannot speak, with respect to light itself, of some part being more recent in its origin, and another being more ancient (for the whole is but one light)
sources.raw_question: When light comes forth from light, can one part of the light be called older or younger than another?

question: Is it by faith or by knowledge that the soul draws near to God and is justified?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: By faith. Abraham's history teaches that one cannot draw near to God unless faith mediates and unites the seeking soul with God's incomprehensible nature. God counts faith, not knowledge, for righteousness. Knowledge deals only with what is known, whereas faith is the substance of things hoped for and makes the unseen our own.
sources.quote: it is impossible to draw near to God, unless faith mediate, and bring the seeking soul into union with the incomprehensible nature of God.
sources.raw_question: Is it by faith or by knowledge that the soul draws near to God and is justified?

question: What is the source and standard of true faith concerning God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: God Himself. The one true faith concerning God is that of which He is at once the Author and the Witness, received through His own self-revelation rather than through the conclusions of human philosophy.
sources.quote: sure that for us the one true faith concerning God is that of which He is at once the Author and the Witness.
sources.raw_question: What is the source and standard of true faith concerning God?

question: Does Scripture's presentation of Jesus as the Saviour of sinners prove that he is God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Jehovah declares that there is no Saviour beside him. When Scripture directs our hope of eternal salvation to Jesus as Saviour, this is conclusive evidence that he is God.
sources.quote: we had found that in the matter of eternal salvation, our hopes are there directed to Jesus as our Saviour, this would have been conclusive evidence, when we remember “I am God, and beside me there is no Saviour.”
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's presentation of Jesus as the Saviour of sinners prove that he is God?

question: Does the New Testament's claim that prophecies about Jehovah are fulfilled in Jesus Christ testify to his supreme Godhead?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. When the New Testament claims that prophecies concerning God Jehovah are fulfilled in Jesus Christ, this is inspired testimony to the supreme Godhead of the Messiah. The ascription to him of the names God, Saviour, Redeemer and Lord confirms the same point. Misdirected faith in this matter would be idolatry.
sources.quote: If, once more, we see how prophecies regarding God Jehovah are claimed by the New Testament as being fulfilled in Jesus Christ, here is inspired testimony to the supreme Godhead of the Messiah.
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament's claim that prophecies about Jehovah are fulfilled in Jesus Christ testify to his supreme Godhead?

question: Does the Antichrist's false prophet perform his wonders by divine power?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXVIII.—The distinction to be made between the righteous and the wicked. The future apostasy in the time of Antichrist, and the end of the world.
sources.answer: No. He works his wonders by magic, not by divine power. Demons and apostate spirits serve him, and through them he does wonders that lead the inhabitants of the earth astray.
sources.quote: Let no one imagine that he performs these wonders by divine power, but by the working of magic.
sources.raw_question: Does the Antichrist's false prophet perform his wonders by divine power?

question: Why is tribulation necessary for those who are saved?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXVIII.—The distinction to be made between the righteous and the wicked. The future apostasy in the time of Antichrist, and the end of the world.
sources.answer: Tribulation purifies the saved and fits them for the royal banquet. Like wheat, they are broken up, made fine, sprinkled by the patience of the Word of God, and set on fire for purification. Irenaeus cites the martyr who called himself the wheat of Christ, ground by beasts to become the pure bread of God.
sources.quote: And for this cause tribulation is necessary for those who are saved, that having been after a manner broken up, and rendered fine, and sprinkled over by the patience of the Word of God
sources.raw_question: Why is tribulation necessary for those who are saved?

question: Is there clear historical evidence that the early Catholic Church professed a Trinity of consubstantial and coeternal Persons?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 28: Whether it be at all probable, that the primitive Church should mistake in so material a point as this is; or that the whole stream of Christian writers should
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland argues that the Church's public forms prove it: baptismal professions, creeds, doxologies, hymns, and the public censures passed on heretics. These are supported by the declared views of leading Church writers, by their interpretations of the creeds, and by ecclesiastical history. Taken together, they show the Church always professed three consubstantial, coeternal Persons in one nature, substance and Godhead.
sources.quote: we have very clear and full proof that the Catholic Church did all along profess a Trinity of consubstantial, coeternal Persons, in unity of nature, substance, and Godhead.
sources.raw_question: Is there clear historical evidence that the early Catholic Church professed a Trinity of consubstantial and coeternal Persons?

question: Is it likely that the apostolic churches quickly departed from the Apostles' meaning on so important a doctrine as the Trinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 28: Whether it be at all probable, that the primitive Church should mistake in so material a point as this is; or that the whole stream of Christian writers should
sources.answer: No. It is highly improbable that the churches the Apostles founded did not know their mind, or soon came to contradict Scripture. Those churches had the best opportunity to know what Scripture meant. They were made up of wise and good men who would sooner die than err in such a matter wilfully.
sources.quote: We think it very unlikely that the apostolic churches should not know the mind of the Apostles; or should suddenly vary from it, in any matter of moment.
sources.raw_question: Is it likely that the apostolic churches quickly departed from the Apostles' meaning on so important a doctrine as the Trinity?

question: In what respect is Christ a foundation and a vine on which believers are built and grafted: according to His Godhead or His manhood?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, the Context of Proverbs viii. 22 Vz. 22-30. It is right to interpret this passage by the Regula Fidei. 'Founded' is used in contrast to superstructure; and it implies, as in the case of stones in building, previous existence. 'Before the world' signifies the divine intention and purpose. Recurrence to Prov. viii. 22, and application of it to created Wisdom as seen in the works. The Son reveals the Father, first by the works, then by the Incarnation.
sources.answer: According to His manhood. A foundation must be like what is built on it, and branches like the vine. As Word and Only-begotten, He has no one like Himself to be joined with Him. Having become man, He has the likeness of those whose flesh He took, so we are built on Him according to the flesh.
sources.quote: Being then the Word, He has not, as Word, any such as Himself, who may be compacted with Him; for He is Only-begotten; but having become man, He has the like of Him
sources.raw_question: In what respect is Christ a foundation and a vine on which believers are built and grafted: according to His Godhead or His manhood?

question: Why would God allow the good of salvation to be attained through human struggle rather than implanting it in people by nature?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVII.—Men are possessed of free will, and endowed with the faculty of making a choice. It is not true, therefore, that some are by nature good, and others bad.
sources.answer: Because a good that is won by striving is valued and loved, while one received without effort would be unappreciated and virtually irrational. Irenaeus argues that the harder we strive for the crown of immortality, the more valuable it is to us and the more we esteem it. For this reason the Lord and the apostle urge us to love God more, so that we reach the prize by our own striving.
sources.quote: And the harder we strive, so much is it the more valuable; while so much the more valuable it is, so much the more should we esteem it.
sources.raw_question: Why would God allow the good of salvation to be attained through human struggle rather than implanting it in people by nature?

question: What does Christ mean when he says that the kingdom of heaven belongs to 'the violent' who 'take it by force'?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVII.—Men are possessed of free will, and endowed with the faculty of making a choice. It is not true, therefore, that some are by nature good, and others bad.
sources.answer: He means those who strive with strength and earnest effort. They stay watchful so as to seize the kingdom at the right moment. Irenaeus reads the saying as evidence that the kingdom is gained through free and strenuous effort, not possessed by nature.
sources.quote: those who by strength and earnest striving are on the watch to snatch it away on the moment
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean when he says that the kingdom of heaven belongs to 'the violent' who 'take it by force'?

question: Why did God permit and patiently endure man's apostasy?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVII.—Men are possessed of free will, and endowed with the faculty of making a choice. It is not true, therefore, that some are by nature good, and others bad.
sources.answer: So that man might be instructed by it and learn rationally to love God. Just as sight, health, light and life are prized more by knowing their opposites, the heavenly kingdom is honoured more by those who have known the earthly one. God ordered all things beforehand for man's edification and perfection. He did this so that goodness might be revealed, righteousness perfected, and the Church conformed to the image of His Son.
sources.quote: for God has displayed long-suffering in the case of man’s apostasy; while man has been instructed by means of it, as also the prophet says, “Thine own apostasy shall heal thee;”
sources.raw_question: Why did God permit and patiently endure man's apostasy?

question: Is the teaching that Christ reigns in his glorified body and is later subjected so that God may be all in all supported only by Paul, or also by Christ's own words in the Gospels?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: It is also taught by Christ himself. In John 13:31-32 he first speaks of the glory of the Son of Man, the glory of the body drawn from its union with the divine nature. He then speaks of a further glorification by which God glorifies him in himself. This is the promotion into the Godhead that Paul later describes as the subjection.
sources.quote: So there is first signified the glory of the body, which it borrows from its association with the divine nature: and then follows the promotion to a fuller glory derived from an addition to the glory of the body.
sources.raw_question: Is the teaching that Christ reigns in his glorified body and is later subjected so that God may be all in all supported only by Paul, or also by Christ's own words in the Gospels?

question: Are mind, knowledge, and love in the human image of the Trinity united like the ingredients of a mixed drink, such as wine, water, and honey?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: No. Wine, water, and honey are not of one substance, although one substance results from mixing them. Mind, knowledge, and love, by contrast, are of one essence, because the mind itself knows and loves itself and is known and loved by nothing else. And if they were blended by commingling, they could not remain three.
sources.quote: But water, wine, and honey are not of one substance, although one substance results in the drink made from the commingling of them.
sources.raw_question: Are mind, knowledge, and love in the human image of the Trinity united like the ingredients of a mixed drink, such as wine, water, and honey?

question: What does the birth of Tamar's twins, Pharez and Zarah with the scarlet thread, signify?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXV.—Both covenants were prefigured in Abraham, and in the labour of Tamar; there was, however, but one and the same God to each covenant.
sources.answer: It typifies the two peoples and covenants. Zarah, who first put forth his hand bearing the scarlet token, signifies faith shown beforehand in the patriarchs and then withdrawn, while Pharez born first stands for the intervening law; the scarlet token also signifies the passion of the Just One, prefigured in Abel and perfected in the Son of God.
sources.quote: that is, the passion of the Just One, which was prefigured from the beginning in Abel, and described by the prophets, but perfected in the last times in the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: What does the birth of Tamar's twins, Pharez and Zarah with the scarlet thread, signify?

question: Why was a woman, Mary, made the first witness and messenger of Christ's resurrection?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > This twelfth book gives a notable interpretation of the words of the Lord to Mary, “Touch Me not, for I am not yet ascended to My Father.”
sources.answer: So that the woman, who was first in the transgression and brought the beginning of evil by passing on the serpent's counsel, might undo that overthrow through faith. By carrying to the disciples the words of him who slew the dragon, she becomes the guide to faith, and the first proclamation of death is annulled.
sources.quote: she is the first witness of the resurrection, that she might retrieve by her faith in the resurrection the overthrow caused by her disobedience
sources.raw_question: Why was a woman, Mary, made the first witness and messenger of Christ's resurrection?

question: Does the account in Luke of an angel strengthening Christ in Gethsemane prove that the Son was weak and needed a creature's help?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The Creator of the angels does not need the support of His creatures. His comforting must be explained in the same way as His sorrow: just as He was sorrowful on our account, so He was comforted on our account, the object of comfort being the same as the object of sadness.
sources.quote: let not the heretics encourage themselves that herein lies a confirmation of His weakness, that He needed the help and comfort of an angel. Let them remember the Creator of the angels needs not the support of His creatures.
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who assert the Son's weakness
sources.raw_question: Does the account in Luke of an angel strengthening Christ in Gethsemane prove that the Son was weak and needed a creature's help?

question: How can Christ pray for his persecutors and yet pray only for the elect, as mediator?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: He did some things merely as a man subject to God's law and some things as mediator. As a man he forgave and prayed for those who crucified him; as mediator he prayed for his elect only, and those prayers the Father always heard and answered.
sources.quote: he who is mediator did some things merely as a man, subject to the law of God in general; so he prayed for his persecutors, — those that put him to death, Luke xxiii. 34; — some things as mediator; so he prayed for his elect only, John xvii. 9.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ pray for his persecutors and yet pray only for the elect, as mediator?

question: Did the early Church reserve the title 'Maker of all' (poietes) for the Father alone, so that the Son was not properly Creator?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: No. The ancients used the titles technites, demiourgos and poietes almost interchangeably and applied them to Father or Son as occasion required. If they are applied more often to the Father, that is only because he is the first Person and so primarily or eminently Creator. The Son is still strictly, properly and fully Creator, the immediate and efficient cause of all things together with the Father.
sources.quote: not that the Son is not strictly, properly, and completely Creator also, according to the fullest sense and import of any, or of all those words.
sources.raw_question: Did the early Church reserve the title 'Maker of all' (poietes) for the Father alone, so that the Son was not properly Creator?

question: Is God subject to change, composition, or transitions between states such as silence and speech, rest and action?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. God is a simple Being with no variability and no parts, so His will does not follow inaction, nor His speech silence, nor His work rest. He is not subject to nature's laws, since nature received its law from Him, and His boundless power suffers no weakness or effort.
sources.quote: In God is no variability, no parts, as of a composite divinity, that in Him will should follow inaction, speech silence, or work rest
sources.raw_question: Is God subject to change, composition, or transitions between states such as silence and speech, rest and action?

question: Is goodness limited by anything other than its opposite?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in making the being of the Father alone proper and supreme, implying by his omission of the Son and the Spirit that theirs is improperly spoken of, and is inferior.
sources.answer: No. Every good is checked only by its opposite: strength by weakness, life by death, light by darkness. Therefore a good that is incapable of its opposite has no bounds to its goodness.
sources.quote: Good, as long as it is incapable of its opposite, has no bounds to its goodness: its opposite alone can circumscribe it, as we may see by particular examples.
sources.raw_question: Is goodness limited by anything other than its opposite?

question: Does being earlier in time make one being more truly a being than a later one of the same nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He does wrong in making the being of the Father alone proper and supreme, implying by his omission of the Son and the Spirit that theirs is improperly spoken of, and is inferior.
sources.answer: No. Abraham was not more a man than David, who lived fourteen generations later, because the definition of their being is the same and time does not change it. Nature remains self-contained and firm within its own limits, while time flows past it.
sources.quote: For it is not in the power of time to define for each one the measures of nature, but nature abides self-contained, preserving herself through succeeding generations
sources.raw_question: Does being earlier in time make one being more truly a being than a later one of the same nature?

question: Did the apostles heal and confer the Holy Spirit by the laying on of hands through a superior kind of magic, and could the power to bestow the Holy Spirit be bought?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XXIII.—Doctrines and practices of Simon Magus and Menander.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus says Simon wrongly supposed that the apostles worked cures by magic rather than by the power of God, and that their giving of the Holy Spirit came from greater magical knowledge. Peter's rebuke shows that the Spirit is the gift of God, which cannot be bought with money. It is given to those who believe in God through Christ Jesus.
sources.quote: supposing that the apostles themselves performed their cures by the art of magic, and not by the power of God; and with respect to their filling with the Holy Ghost, through the imposition of hands
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles heal and confer the Holy Spirit by the laying on of hands through a superior kind of magic, and could the power to bestow the Holy Spirit be bought?

question: Does the greater wonder of a sign, such as an angel's miracle compared with a human act, make it signify something greater about God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > In How Many Ways the Creature is to Be Taken by Way of Sign. The Eucharist.
sources.answer: No. A sign done by angels is more wonderful to us but may signify the same thing as a humble human sign, just as God's name written in gold or ink signifies the same. Indeed Jacob's stone signified something better than the magicians' serpents, though their deed was more wonderful.
sources.quote: That which is understood from both, is perhaps one and the same; but those things from which it is understood, are different. Just as if the name of God were written both in gold and in ink
sources.raw_question: Does the greater wonder of a sign, such as an angel's miracle compared with a human act, make it signify something greater about God?

question: What did Moses' rod turned into a serpent signify about Christ?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > In How Many Ways the Creature is to Be Taken by Way of Sign. The Eucharist.
sources.answer: It signified Christ made obedient unto death, the serpent standing for death wrought by the serpent in paradise. The rod passing into a serpent is Christ passing into death, and the serpent returning into a rod is the whole Christ with his body, the Church, rising in the resurrection at the end of time, signified by the tail Moses held.
sources.quote: Therefore the rod passed into the serpent, Christ into death; and the serpent again into the rod, whole Christ with His body into the resurrection; which body is the Church
sources.raw_question: What did Moses' rod turned into a serpent signify about Christ?

question: Can the Son's 'coming down from heaven' be explained as the man Jesus being taken up into heaven during his forty days in the wilderness to be taught the gospel?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. The claim has no scriptural warrant, and the Socinians cannot say who told them so. It is also refuted by Mark, who states that Jesus was those forty days in the wilderness with the wild beasts, and so was not bodily in heaven with God and the angels. The interpretation is forced and absurd, and it cannot be reached by any reasonable investigation.
sources.quote: one of the evangelists plainly affirms that he was “those forty days in the wilderness with the wild beasts,” Mark i. 13, and so, surely, not in heaven in the same nature, by his bodily presence
sources.raw_question: Can the Son's 'coming down from heaven' be explained as the man Jesus being taken up into heaven during his forty days in the wilderness to be taught the gospel?

question: In Christ's acts, such as weeping over Lazarus and raising him, which nature is responsible for which act?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > Thereafter he shows that there are not two Christs or two Lords, but one Christ and one Lord, and that the Divine nature, after mingling with the Human, preserved the properties of each nature without confusion, and declares that the operations are, by reason of the union, predicated of the two natures in common, in the sense that the Lord took upon Himself the sufferings of the servant, and the humanity is glorified with Him in the honour that is the Lord's, and that by the power of the Divine Nature that is made anew, conformably with that Divine Nature Itself.
sources.answer: The human acts belong to the Man and the divine acts to the Godhead. The tear comes from the Man, while the life that raises Lazarus comes from the true Life. Weariness and being pierced with nails belong to the servant's form, while creating the world and being the brightness of glory belong to the Word.
sources.quote: It is not the Human Nature that raises up Lazarus, nor is it the power that cannot suffer that weeps for him when he lies in the grave: the tear proceeds from the Man, the life from the true Life.
sources.raw_question: In Christ's acts, such as weeping over Lazarus and raising him, which nature is responsible for which act?

question: Did the Word (Logos) exist after and derive from Man (Anthropos), as some Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. These Gnostics, transferring human passions and experiences to the divine reason, invent the Word's origin in the fifth place and make man prior to the Word. They thereby lie against God with no plausibility, ascribing to Him what happens to men.
sources.quote: heaping together with a kind of plausibility all human feelings, and mental exercises, and formation of intentions, and utterances of words, they have lied with no plausibility at all against God
sources.raw_question: Did the Word (Logos) exist after and derive from Man (Anthropos), as some Gnostics claim?

question: Does Christ's saying "Seek, and ye shall find" refer to inquiring into the Gnostic sequence of emanations of Aeons?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus presents this as the heretics' misuse of the text to authorize speculation about how Nous and Aletheia came from Bythus and Sige, and so on. He treats these supposed sublime mysteries as human passions falsely transferred to God, not what the Lord meant.
sources.quote: It was, [they affirm,] concerning these that the Lord said, “Seek, and ye shall find,” that is, that they should inquire how Nous and Aletheia proceeded from Bythus and Sage
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "Seek, and ye shall find" refer to inquiring into the Gnostic sequence of emanations of Aeons?

question: Does Paul's phrase 'whether in heaven or in earth' in 1 Corinthians 8:5 refer to gods who formed the world, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: No. Paul is not speaking of world-formers. His meaning matches Moses' prohibition of images of things in heaven, on earth and in the waters. Moses explains that the things in heaven are the sun, moon and stars, which people wrongly adore and serve.
sources.quote: But in this [clause], “whether in heaven or in earth,” he does not speak of the formers of the world, as these [teachers] expound it; but his meaning is similar to that of Moses
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's phrase 'whether in heaven or in earth' in 1 Corinthians 8:5 refer to gods who formed the world, as the Gnostics claim?

question: Does 'The Lord thy God in the midst of thee' in Zephaniah 3:17 refer to Christ dwelling among us by taking our nature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen reads 'the Lord thy God in the midst of thee' as God dwelling among us by taking our nature, as in John 1:14. The verse therefore describes Christ, who is the Lord God incarnate, rejoicing over his people.
sources.quote: “The Lord thy God in the midst of thee” (that is, dwelling amongst us, taking our nature, John i. 14) “is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy;
sources.raw_question: Does 'The Lord thy God in the midst of thee' in Zephaniah 3:17 refer to Christ dwelling among us by taking our nature?

question: Can Arians who hold only a figurative or specific consubstantiality lay claim to the Nicene Creed?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: No. The confession was made in direct opposition to their principles, and even a specific consubstantiality would not help them, since God and creatures are not of the same rank, kind, or species; they must resort to a figurative sense, which has been refuted.
sources.quote: Would that give you any claim to the Nicene Confession? Are God and his creatures consubstantial, of the same rank, sort, kind, or species?
sources.raw_question: Can Arians who hold only a figurative or specific consubstantiality lay claim to the Nicene Creed?

question: Does an attack on the dignity of the Son also strike at the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > He further proceeds notably to interpret the language of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “Life” and “Light,” and “The Word was made flesh,” which had been misinterpreted by Eunomius; and overthrows his blasphemy, and shows that the dispensation of the Lord took place by loving-kindness, not by lack of power, and with the co-operation of the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says that he who honours the Son honours the Father. It follows that an assault on the Son strikes at the Father, and Eunomius's attack on the Only-begotten ends up directed against the majesty of the Father.
sources.quote: For if he that honoureth the Son honoureth the Father, according to the Divine declaration, it is plain on the other side that an assault upon the Son strikes at the Father.
sources.raw_question: Does an attack on the dignity of the Son also strike at the Father?

question: What part of the soul is most properly called the mind, as distinct from the part that forms images of bodies?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > Why the Soul is Enjoined to Know Itself. Whence Come the Errors of the Mind Concerning Its Own Substance.
sources.answer: It is the rational understanding, which keeps the power to judge freely about the images. The parts of the soul that are shaped by likenesses of bodily things are shared with the beasts. The judging reason is what is most properly the mind.
