sources.quote: yet preserves the while something by which it may judge freely of the species of those images; and this something is more properly the mind, that is, the rational understanding, which is preserved that it may judge
sources.raw_question: What part of the soul is most properly called the mind, as distinct from the part that forms images of bodies?

question: Can a human being, such as the Gnostic teacher Marcus, command the prophetic Spirit of God to speak through someone whenever he wishes?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XIII.—The deceitful arts and nefarious practices of Marcus.
sources.answer: No. The gift of prophecy is given only to those to whom God sends his grace from above, and they speak where and when God pleases, not when a man orders them. Whatever commands is greater and of higher authority than what is commanded. So if a man could command the prophetic spirit, a mere man would be greater than that spirit, which is impossible.
sources.quote: For that which commands is greater and of higher authority than that which is commanded, inasmuch as the former rules, while the latter is in a state of subjection.
sources.raw_question: Can a human being, such as the Gnostic teacher Marcus, command the prophetic Spirit of God to speak through someone whenever he wishes?

question: Are spirits that prophesy on human command, as in Marcus's rites, the Spirit of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XIII.—The deceitful arts and nefarious practices of Marcus.
sources.answer: No. Spirits that are commanded by men and speak whenever those men wish are earthly, weak, audacious and impudent spirits. Satan sends them to seduce and destroy those who do not hold fast the faith first received through the Church. The true prophetic Spirit is subject to God's pleasure alone, not to human command.
sources.quote: But such spirits as are commanded by these men, and speak when they desire it, are earthly and weak, audacious and impudent, sent forth by Satan for the seduction and perdition
sources.raw_question: Are spirits that prophesy on human command, as in Marcus's rites, the Spirit of God?

question: Why did God give the first (Old) Testament if he needs no service from men?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXII.—That one God was the author of both Testaments, is confirmed by the authority of a presbyter who had been taught by the apostles.
sources.answer: Not for God's need but for man's benefit. It subdued its recipients to God's service for their good, exhibited a type of heavenly things since man could not yet see them directly, foreshadowed realities now in the Church to strengthen faith, and contained prophecy so man would learn God foreknows all things.
sources.quote: it subdued those to whom it was given to the service of God, for their benefit (for God needs no service from men), and exhibited a type of heavenly things
sources.raw_question: Why did God give the first (Old) Testament if he needs no service from men?

question: Is Christ merely a servant and teacher of divine wisdom like Solomon, or is he of a higher rank?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVII—The sins of the men of old time, which incurred the displeasure of God, were, by His providence, committed to writing, that we might derive instruction thereby, and not be filled with pride. We must not, therefore, infer that there was another God than He whom Christ preached; we should rather fear, lest the one and the same God who inflicted punishment on the ancients, should bring down heavier upon us.
sources.answer: Christ is of a higher rank. Solomon was only a servant who announced the wisdom God had given him, while Christ is truly the Son of God and Solomon's Lord. The wisdom Christ speaks comes directly from the Son of God. That is why the queen of the south, who submitted to the wisdom of a servant, will condemn those who reject the wisdom of the Son himself.
sources.quote: For Solomon was a servant, but Christ is indeed the Son of God, and the Lord of Solomon.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ merely a servant and teacher of divine wisdom like Solomon, or is he of a higher rank?

question: Is the exclusive supremacy of the one God the foundational truth of biblical religion?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 2. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, detaches our ultimate confidence from man the creature, and attaches it to God the Creator; – by contrasting the sinfulness and feebleness of mortal man with the goodness and omnipotence of the Eternal Jehovah: by direct prohibition and precept: by exhibiting the holy Jealousy of God.
sources.answer: Yes. The truth "I am God, and there is none else" stands on the forefront of the temple of religion. The first commandment forbids having any other gods. The adoration of both earth and heaven ascribes creation and preservation of all things to the Lord alone.
sources.quote: For this truth stands on the forefront of the temple of Religion: “I am God, and there is none else.” (Isa. 46:9.)
sources.raw_question: Is the exclusive supremacy of the one God the foundational truth of biblical religion?

question: Does the ability of demons to work marvels show that they are superior to faithful souls, or that their wonders should be sought or admired?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Miracles Which are Done by Demons are to Be Spurned.
sources.answer: No. Demons work their marvels easily through their aerial bodies and through hidden inspirations that delude the senses, much as worthless men perform astonishing feats in theatres. A pious soul need not envy or prefer them. It belongs to the company of holy men and good angels, who through the power of God, to whom all things are subject, accomplish far greater wonders that are not deceptive.
sources.quote: accomplish, through the power of God, to whom all things are subject, wonders which are far greater and the very reverse of deceptive.
sources.raw_question: Does the ability of demons to work marvels show that they are superior to faithful souls, or that their wonders should be sought or admired?

question: Do the numbers and measurements of the Mosaic tabernacle (the ark, table, candlestick, curtains, anointing oil and incense) serve as types of the Gnostic Pleroma of Æons such as the Tetrad, Ogdoad and Decad?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIV.—Folly of the arguments derived by the heretics from numbers, letters, and syllables.
sources.answer: No. If the Gnostics' Mother or Saviour had meant to set forth types of the Pleroma through the Demiurge, those types should appear above all in the holiest objects, such as the Ark of the Covenant. Yet the measurements of the ark, mercy-seat and table of shew-bread do not match the Tetrad, Ogdoad or Decad. The candlestick has seven branches, not eight. The coverings of skin number eleven. The anointing oil and incense have five ingredients. The heretics count only the numbers that suit them and ignore the rest.
sources.quote: These stood before the holy of holies, and yet in them not a single number is of such an amount as contains an indication of the Tetrad, or the Ogdoad, or of the rest of their Pleroma.
sources.raw_question: Do the numbers and measurements of the Mosaic tabernacle (the ark, table, candlestick, curtains, anointing oil and incense) serve as types of the Gnostic Pleroma of Æons such as the Tetrad, Ogdoad and Decad?

question: Why is faith in God necessary above all things in this mortal life?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Faith is Necessary, that Man May at Some Time Be Blessed, Which He Will Only Attain in the Future Life. The Blessedness of Proud Philosophers Ridiculous and Pitiable.
sources.answer: Because every good thing, and especially those goods by which a man becomes good and by which he will become blessed, comes to man from no other source than God. Since this life is full of errors and hardships, faith by which men believe in God is the necessary path to the goods that only God gives.
sources.quote: For there are no good things whatever, and above all, not those by which any one is made good, or those by which he will become blessed, of which any other source can be found whence they come to man, and are added to man, unless it be from God.
sources.raw_question: Why is faith in God necessary above all things in this mortal life?

question: What will make up the blessed life of the future, and what role does God play in it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Faith is Necessary, that Man May at Some Time Be Blessed, Which He Will Only Attain in the Future Life. The Blessedness of Proud Philosophers Ridiculous and Pitiable.
sources.answer: In the future life a man will truly live as he wills, because he will not will anything evil, nothing he wills will be lacking, and whatever he loves will be present. The supreme God will be the supreme good, present to be enjoyed by those who love Him. Its greatest blessedness is the certainty that it will last forever.
sources.quote: Everything which will be there will be good, and the supreme God will be the supreme good and will be present for those to enjoy who love Him; and what altogether is most blessed, it will be certain that it will be so forever.
sources.raw_question: What will make up the blessed life of the future, and what role does God play in it?

question: Can the philosophers' ideal of blessedness, in which a man patiently wills only what he can because he cannot have what he wills, be true blessedness?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Faith is Necessary, that Man May at Some Time Be Blessed, Which He Will Only Attain in the Future Life. The Blessedness of Proud Philosophers Ridiculous and Pitiable.
sources.answer: No. Such a man does not live as he wills. He merely bears willingly what he would not have happen, and he would prevent it if he could. Terence's maxim, 'will that which thou canst,' is sound advice to keep a miserable man from being more miserable. But it does not describe the blessed man, who never wills what cannot be.
sources.quote: That this is aptly said, who denies? But it is advice given to the miserable man, that he may not be more miserable.
sources.raw_question: Can the philosophers' ideal of blessedness, in which a man patiently wills only what he can because he cannot have what he wills, be true blessedness?

question: Is a person who is blessed through hope already truly blessed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Faith is Necessary, that Man May at Some Time Be Blessed, Which He Will Only Attain in the Future Life. The Blessedness of Proud Philosophers Ridiculous and Pitiable.
sources.answer: No. He who is blessed through hope is not yet blessed. Through patience he awaits a blessedness he does not yet grasp. Someone who endures torment without such hope is not blessed at all, only bravely miserable.
sources.quote: But he who is blessed through hope is not yet blessed: for he expects, through patience, a blessedness which he does not yet grasp.
sources.raw_question: Is a person who is blessed through hope already truly blessed?

question: When Christ answered Satan with 'Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God,' was He quoting a foreign authority or His own Father's words?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXII.—The true Lord and the one God is declared by the law, and manifested by Christ His Son in the Gospel; whom alone we should adore, and from Him we must look for all good things, not from Satan.
sources.answer: He was quoting His own Father's words. Christ did not confound the adversary by the saying of any other but by that of His own Father, and He acknowledged the law's commandment as expressing His own sentiments, showing unity of will between the Son and the God of the law.
sources.quote: For He did not confound the adversary by the saying of any other, but by that belonging to His own Father, and thus overcame the strong man.
sources.raw_question: When Christ answered Satan with 'Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God,' was He quoting a foreign authority or His own Father's words?

question: Can immortality admit of degrees, so that angels and men, or God and creatures, are more or less immortal by comparison?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The immortal, as long as it is immortal, admits no degrees of more and less. If one member of a comparison suffers a diminution of immortality by contrast, it cannot be called immortal at all, since mortality is detected in it by the comparison.
sources.quote: The immortal, as long as it is immortal, admits of no degrees of more and less arising from comparison.
sources.raw_question: Can immortality admit of degrees, so that angels and men, or God and creatures, are more or less immortal by comparison?

question: Does privation apply only to separation from good things and not to the absence of bad things, so that God's immortality is not a privation of death?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Restricting privation in this way would take the truth from the Apostle's words that God "only hath immortality," which He gives to others. The privative sign does mark the absence of the bad.
sources.quote: If he is to get his way here, he will take the truth from the Apostle’s words, which say that He “only hath immortality,” which He gives to others.
sources.raw_question: Does privation apply only to separation from good things and not to the absence of bad things, so that God's immortality is not a privation of death?

question: Is there any real difference between saying God is Life and saying God is unreceptive of death?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. With opposites it makes no difference whether we say something is A or that it is not the opposite of A. Saying God is Life implicitly excludes death from Him, and saying He is unreceptive of death in the same breath shows Him to be Life.
sources.quote: we hold that in the case of opposites, it makes no difference at all whether we say that something is A, or that it is not the opposite of A
sources.raw_question: Is there any real difference between saying God is Life and saying God is unreceptive of death?

question: Why did the one who destroys sin and death have to become a man himself, rather than act from outside human nature?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: He had to become the very thing that was enslaved, namely man. Then sin would be destroyed by a man, and man would go forth from death. By the disobedience of one man, formed from virgin soil, many were made sinners. So by the obedience of one man, born of a virgin, many must be justified. The law could expose sin but not destroy it, because sin ruled over man, not over the spirit.
sources.quote: it behoved Him who was to destroy sin, and redeem man under the power of death, that He should Himself be made that very same thing which he was, that is, man
sources.raw_question: Why did the one who destroys sin and death have to become a man himself, rather than act from outside human nature?

question: When Paul says 'that rock was Christ,' does the rock signify Christ's Godhead or his flesh?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Preface.
sources.answer: It refers to his flesh, not his Godhead. Ambrose reads the rock from which fire burst forth in Gideon's sacrifice as a figure of Christ's Body. Like the rock that watered Israel, Christ's flesh watered the hearts of the thirsting people with the perpetual stream of his Blood.
sources.quote: Which certainly refers not to His Godhead, but to His Flesh, which watered the hearts of the thirsting people with the perpetual stream of His Blood.
sources.raw_question: When Paul says 'that rock was Christ,' does the rock signify Christ's Godhead or his flesh?

question: What does the fire coming out of the rock at the touch of the Angel's staff in Gideon's sacrifice signify about Christ's flesh and the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Preface.
sources.answer: It signifies that the Lord's flesh, filled with the Divine Spirit, would burn away all the sins of human frailty. The flesh of the kid stands for sins of deed and the broth for sins of desire, and Christ crucified does away with both. This is why the Lord says he came to send fire on the earth.
sources.quote: shows that the Flesh of the Lord, being filled with the Divine Spirit, would burn away all the sins of human frailty. Wherefore, also, the Lord says: “I am come to send fire upon the earth.”
sources.raw_question: What does the fire coming out of the rock at the touch of the Angel's staff in Gideon's sacrifice signify about Christ's flesh and the Holy Spirit?

question: Why is the seven-year-old bullock Gideon offered a type of Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Preface.
sources.answer: Because in Christ, as Isaiah said, dwelt the fulness of the seven gifts of the Spirit. The offering also showed that after the Lord's coming all Gentile sacrifices would be abolished. Only the sacrifice of the Lord's passion would remain, offered for the redemption of the people.
sources.quote: For that bullock was, in a type, Christ, in Whom, as Esaias said, dwelt the fulness of the seven gifts of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Why is the seven-year-old bullock Gideon offered a type of Christ?

question: Does the Jews' remark to Jesus, 'Thou art not yet fifty years old, and hast Thou seen Abraham?', show that Christ was well past thirty during his ministry?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXII.—The thirty Æons are not typified by the fact that Christ was baptized in His thirtieth year: He did not suffer in the twelfth month after His baptism, but was more than fifty years old when He died.
sources.answer: Yes. Such words fit someone past forty who is nearing fifty. To a man of only thirty they would have said 'not yet forty.' Men trying to convict him of falsehood would not have exaggerated his age by twenty years; they named a figure close to the age they actually saw.
sources.quote: Now, such language is fittingly applied to one who has already passed the age of forty, without having as yet reached his fiftieth year, yet is not far from this latter period.
sources.raw_question: Does the Jews' remark to Jesus, 'Thou art not yet fifty years old, and hast Thou seen Abraham?', show that Christ was well past thirty during his ministry?

question: Does the question "Who hath directed the Spirit of the Lord, or being his counsellor hath taught him?" in Isaiah 40:13 mean that no one at all knows the mind of the Lord?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That v: not found “of whom” in the case of the Son and of the Spirit.
sources.answer: No. Here "who" signifies rarity, not absolute impossibility, as in other scriptural questions such as "Who will rise up for me against the evil doers?" The Son knows the Father's mind, for "the Father loveth the Son and sheweth him all things."
sources.quote: Now the word “who” in this passage does not mean absolute impossibility, but rarity
sources.raw_question: Does the question "Who hath directed the Spirit of the Lord, or being his counsellor hath taught him?" in Isaiah 40:13 mean that no one at all knows the mind of the Lord?

question: According to the Rule of Faith, what is the first thing Christians must believe about God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Novatian, with the View of Treating of the Trinity, Sets Forth from the Rule of Faith that We Should First of All Believe in God the Father and Lord Omnipotent, the Absolute Founder of All Things. The Works of Creation are Beautifully Described. Man's Free-Will is Asserted; God's Mercy in Inflicting Penalty on Man is Shown; The Condition After Death of the Souls of the Righteous and Unrighteous is Determined.
sources.answer: That God the Father is the Lord Omnipotent, the absolutely perfect Founder of all things. The Rule of truth puts belief in the Father as almighty Creator first. The ordered works of heaven, earth and sea testify to the intelligence of this one Artificer.
sources.quote: The Rule of truth requires that we should first of all things believe on God the Father and Lord Omnipotent; that is, the absolutely perfect Founder of all things
sources.raw_question: According to the Rule of Faith, what is the first thing Christians must believe about God?

question: Was there evil in the fruit of the forbidden tree, and why did God give man a command concerning it?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Novatian, with the View of Treating of the Trinity, Sets Forth from the Rule of Faith that We Should First of All Believe in God the Father and Lord Omnipotent, the Absolute Founder of All Things. The Works of Creation are Beautifully Described. Man's Free-Will is Asserted; God's Mercy in Inflicting Penalty on Man is Shown; The Condition After Death of the Souls of the Righteous and Unrighteous is Determined.
sources.answer: No, there was no evil in the fruit itself. Evil would arise only if man used his free will in contempt of the law. The command was added so that unbounded liberty would not break out into contempt of the Giver.
sources.quote: He laid down a command, in which man was taught that there was no evil in the fruit of the tree; but he was forewarned that evil would arise if perchance he should exercise his free will, in the contempt of the law that was given
sources.raw_question: Was there evil in the fruit of the forbidden tree, and why did God give man a command concerning it?

question: Did God bar fallen man from the tree of life out of envy?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Novatian, with the View of Treating of the Trinity, Sets Forth from the Rule of Faith that We Should First of All Believe in God the Father and Lord Omnipotent, the Absolute Founder of All Things. The Works of Creation are Beautifully Described. Man's Free-Will is Asserted; God's Mercy in Inflicting Penalty on Man is Shown; The Condition After Death of the Souls of the Righteous and Unrighteous is Determined.
sources.answer: No. It was not the malignant poison of envy. God acted so that man would not live forever without Christ's pardon of his sins and so bear an immortality of guilt as his punishment. This was mercy, just as God tempered the punishment by cursing man's labours rather than man himself.
sources.quote: is not caused by the malignant poison of envy, but lest, living for ever without Christ’s previous pardon of his sins, he should always bear about with him for his punishment an immortality of guilt
sources.raw_question: Did God bar fallen man from the tree of life out of envy?

question: Could Christ be in Hades and in Paradise at the same time, as he was in heaven while preaching on earth?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Yes. When he descended to Hades he was never absent from Paradise, just as the Son of Man was always in heaven while preaching on earth. His divine nature is present in all things everywhere, and his indivisible nature cannot be split so that one part suffers in Hades while another reigns in Paradise.
sources.quote: When He descended to Hades, He was never absent from Paradise (just as He was always in Heaven when He was preaching on earth as the Son of Man)
sources.raw_question: Could Christ be in Hades and in Paradise at the same time, as he was in heaven while preaching on earth?

question: Can the text 'I change not' (Malachi 3:6), which seems to refer to the Father, also be applied to the Son?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. How the Word has free will, yet without being alterable. He is unalterable because the Image of the Father, proved from texts.
sources.answer: Yes. Though it may be said to signify the Father, it suits the Son also. This is especially so because, when made man, He shows His identity and unalterableness to those who think the flesh changed Him into something other than He was.
sources.quote: It may be said indeed that what is here signified relates to the Father; yet it suits the Son also to say this, specially because, when made man, He manifests His own identity and unalterableness
sources.raw_question: Can the text 'I change not' (Malachi 3:6), which seems to refer to the Father, also be applied to the Son?

question: Can an agent's activity be conceived apart from the agent, so that the activity merely 'follows' the one who acts?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Discussion as to the exact nature of the 'energies' which, this man declares, 'follow' the being of the Father and of the Son.
sources.answer: No. Gregory says the worker and the work are thought of together. Saying that someone works in iron or in wood conveys both the working and the craftsman at once, so if one is removed the other has no existence. Naming the energy brings to mind the one who acts, and naming the worker implies the energy.
sources.quote: This single expression conveys at once the idea of the working and of the artificer, so that if we withdraw the one, the other has no existence.
sources.raw_question: Can an agent's activity be conceived apart from the agent, so that the activity merely 'follows' the one who acts?

question: Even if past sins were forgiven, could fallen people fulfil the law perfectly from then on?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Owen holds that even if all former debts were blotted out, people would still be unable to meet the law's perfection in the future. Doing so is as impossible as moving the earth with a finger. Therefore by the works of the law no flesh is justified.
sources.quote: That if all former debts should be blotted out, yet they are no way able for the future to fulfil the law; they can as well move the earth with a finger, as answer the perfection thereof
sources.raw_question: Even if past sins were forgiven, could fallen people fulfil the law perfectly from then on?

question: Can a person know the will of another person in the same way he knows his own will?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Some Desires Being the Same in All, are Known to Each. The Poet Ennius.
sources.answer: No. A person directly sees his own will, but he can only conjecture another's will, however certainly, from himself or from others' signs and testimony. Augustine compares this to being certain of Constantinople's existence by others' testimony and of Rome's by sight. In both cases one may be certain, but only the first kind of knowledge is seeing.
sources.quote: But it is one thing to see one’s own will; another to conjecture, however certainly, what is another’s.
sources.raw_question: Can a person know the will of another person in the same way he knows his own will?

question: Is there any will that all human beings share and that each can know to be in all others?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Some Desires Being the Same in All, are Known to Each. The Poet Ennius.
sources.answer: Yes. That will is the will to be blessed and not to be wretched. Other supposedly universal desires are not truly universal. Some people sell cheap and buy dear out of vice or generosity, and some do not wish to be praised for faults they hate in themselves. But everyone recognizes the will to be blessed in his own will, and it is well known to be in all men.
sources.quote: But if he had said, You all will to be blessed, you do not will to be wretched; he would have said something which there is no one that would not recognize in his own will.
sources.raw_question: Is there any will that all human beings share and that each can know to be in all others?

question: Can a believer who is elected by the Father, redeemed by the Son, and justified attain settled peace through his own reasoning on the gospel promises, apart from the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. Even a person with full right to all the gospel promises cannot be brought to established peace by any reasonings of his own heart or consideration of the promises, the Father's love, or Christ's grace. Peace is produced only as a fruit and consequent of the Holy Spirit's work in him, for peace is called the fruit of the Spirit.
sources.quote: yet this person can by no reasonings nor arguings of his own heart, by no considerations of the promises themselves, nor of the love of God or grace of Christ in them, be brought to any establishment in peace
sources.raw_question: Can a believer who is elected by the Father, redeemed by the Son, and justified attain settled peace through his own reasoning on the gospel promises, apart from the Holy Spirit?

question: Can one being conceive the idea of the world while a different being actually produces it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter III.—The Bythus and Pleroma of the Valentinians, as well as the God of Marcion, shown to be absurd; the world was actually created by the same Being who had conceived the idea of it, and was not the fruit of defect or ignorance.
sources.answer: No. As soon as God forms a conception in his mind, what he has conceived is accomplished. It is not possible for one being to conceive the world mentally and another to produce what was conceived, so the world was not made by any other than God.
sources.quote: For it was not possible that one Being should mentally form the conception, and another actually produce the things which had been conceived by Him in His mind.
sources.raw_question: Can one being conceive the idea of the world while a different being actually produces it?

question: Is the resurrection of the dead bound up with Christ's own resurrection, so that denying one denies the other?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIII.—In the dead who were raised by Christ we possess the highest proof of the resurrection; and our hearts are shown to be capable of life eternal, because they can now receive the Spirit of God.
sources.answer: Yes. Following Paul, if the dead do not rise, then Christ has not risen, and preaching and faith are vain. But Christ has risen as the first-fruits of those who sleep. As death came by a man, so the resurrection of the dead comes by a man.
sources.quote: But now Christ has risen from the dead, the first-fruits of those that sleep; for as by man [came] death, by man also [came] the resurrection of the dead.
sources.raw_question: Is the resurrection of the dead bound up with Christ's own resurrection, so that denying one denies the other?

question: If a person cannot both have everything he wants and want only good things, is it better to have what he wants or to will rightly even without obtaining it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Why, When All Will to Be Blessed, that is Rather Chosen by Which One Withdraws from Being So.
sources.answer: It is better to will rightly even without obtaining what one seeks. Whoever obtains what he wickedly desired is further from the blessed life than one who merely fails to obtain what he desired. A good will is already a good, and not a small one. Someone who wills well and pursues attainable goods prudently, temperately and courageously comes near to blessedness. He is good even amid evils, and he will be blessed when all evils end and all goods are fulfilled.
sources.quote: since he certainly is further from it who obtains things which he wickedly desired, than he who only does not obtain the things which he desired); whereas the good will ought rather to be chosen, and to be preferred, even if it do not obtain the things which it seeks?
sources.raw_question: If a person cannot both have everything he wants and want only good things, is it better to have what he wants or to will rightly even without obtaining it?

question: Why do people, though they know blessedness requires both having what one wills and willing nothing evil, usually prefer having what they want to willing rightly?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Why, When All Will to Be Blessed, that is Rather Chosen by Which One Withdraws from Being So.
sources.answer: It is because of the depravity of the human race. Men know that neither the one who lacks what he wills nor the one who wills wrongly is blessed. Yet when they cannot have both, they choose the option that takes them further from blessedness, which is getting what they want.
sources.quote: Is it the depravity itself of the human race, in such wise that, while they are not unaware that neither is he blessed who has not what he wills, nor he who has what he wills wrongly
sources.raw_question: Why do people, though they know blessedness requires both having what one wills and willing nothing evil, usually prefer having what they want to willing rightly?

question: Do good things or bad things make a person blessed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Why, When All Will to Be Blessed, that is Rather Chosen by Which One Withdraws from Being So.
sources.answer: Only good things make men blessed, never bad ones. So a person who wills good things is already close to blessedness, because his good will is itself a real good. He longs to rejoice in goods suited to human nature and not in doing or gaining anything evil.
sources.quote: And certainly not bad things, but good, make men blessed, when they do so make them. And of good things he already has something, and that, too, a something not to be lightly esteemed,—namely, the very good will itself
sources.raw_question: Do good things or bad things make a person blessed?

question: Do the Son's titles and works (King, Judge, Creator, Life, Light, Wisdom) leave any honour to be paid exclusively to the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His elaborate account of degrees and differences in 'works' and 'energies' within the Trinity is absurd.
sources.answer: No. The Son is King. All judgment is committed to him, and all things were made by him. He is the True Life and the True Light, and he is God's power and Wisdom. Since every ground for honour is found in Christ, no excess of honour remains to be reserved for the Father alone.
sources.quote: what further excess of honour is left us to pay exclusively to the Father, as inappropriate to the Son?
sources.raw_question: Do the Son's titles and works (King, Judge, Creator, Life, Light, Wisdom) leave any honour to be paid exclusively to the Father?

question: What is meant by God's all-sufficiency, and how does his all-sufficiency in himself differ from his all-sufficiency for others?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: God's all-sufficiency in himself is his absolute and universal perfection, so that nothing is lacking in him and nothing can be added to or taken from his fulness. His all-sufficiency for others is his power to communicate his goodness and himself to creatures so as to satisfy and fill them to their utmost capacity with whatever is good and desirable.
sources.quote: God’s all-sufficiency in himself is his absolute and universal perfection, whereby nothing is wanting in him, nothing to him: No accession can be made to his fulness, no decrease or wasting can happen thereunto.
sources.raw_question: What is meant by God's all-sufficiency, and how does his all-sufficiency in himself differ from his all-sufficiency for others?

question: In this present life, how are believers to behold Christ, since they cannot yet see the form of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > How the Back Parts of God Were Seen. The Faith of the Resurrection of Christ. The Catholic Church Only is the Place from Whence the Back Parts of God are Seen. The Back Parts of God Were Seen by the Israelites. It is a Rash Opinion to Think that God the Father Only Was Never Seen by the Fathers.
sources.answer: By faith, not sight. Believers behold the 'back parts' of Christ, his flesh, while standing on the solid foundation of faith signified by the rock. They view it from the safe watch-tower of the Catholic Church. Recognizing in his flesh how much Christ first loved us makes us love more surely the face we long to see.
sources.quote: we ought to see the “back parts” of Christ, that is His flesh, by that very faith, that is, standing on the solid foundation of faith, which the rock signifies
sources.raw_question: In this present life, how are believers to behold Christ, since they cannot yet see the form of God?

question: Does a substitutionary expiatory death, such as Christ's, only avert evil from those it is offered for, or does it also procure good for them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: It does both. Those in the ancient world who devoted themselves to die for others intended, first, that the threatened evils would fall on themselves so the people might go free. Second, they intended that the good things they desired would be given to the people. Owen treats these examples as a notable shadow of Christ's great expiatory sacrifice.
sources.quote: First, That the evils which were impendent on the people, and feared, might fall on themselves, so that the people might go free. Secondly, That all good things which themselves desired, might be conferred on the people.
sources.raw_question: Does a substitutionary expiatory death, such as Christ's, only avert evil from those it is offered for, or does it also procure good for them?

question: How can Christ have wept, slept, hungered, feared, and professed ignorance if He is God, who is incapable of these things?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: These belong to His human nature and the weakness of His flesh, not to His Godhead. God is incapable of tears, fear or sleep, yet Christ experienced them as man without impairing the reality of His Only-begotten nature. His statement of not knowing the hour must likewise be referred to His humanity.
sources.quote: As man He wept, and slept, and sorrowed, but God is incapable of tears, or fear, or sleep.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ have wept, slept, hungered, feared, and professed ignorance if He is God, who is incapable of these things?

question: What do 'grace' and 'truth' in John 1:14 ('full of grace and truth') signify in relation to knowledge and wisdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What in the Incarnate Word Belongs to Knowledge, What to Wisdom.
sources.answer: Grace may be referred to knowledge and truth to wisdom. Among temporal things the highest grace is that man is joined with God in unity of person; among eternal things the highest truth is rightly attributed to the Word of God. The same Only-begotten is both, so that through faith in his temporal deeds we are cleansed to contemplate him in things eternal.
sources.quote: For in those things that have their origin in time, this is the highest grace, that man is joined with God in unity of person; but in things eternal the highest truth is rightly attributed to the Word of God.
sources.raw_question: What do 'grace' and 'truth' in John 1:14 ('full of grace and truth') signify in relation to knowledge and wisdom?

question: Why did pagan philosophers who knew the invisible things of God through creation still fall into error and idolatry?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > What in the Incarnate Word Belongs to Knowledge, What to Wisdom.
sources.answer: Because they philosophized without a Mediator, the man Christ, believing neither the prophets nor the apostles. Being in the lowest things, they had to seek some media to reach what they understood, and so fell upon deceitful spirits and changed God's glory into images of corruptible creatures.
sources.quote: because they philosophized without a Mediator, that is, without the man Christ, whom they neither believed to be about to come at the word of the prophets, nor to have come at that of the apostles.
sources.raw_question: Why did pagan philosophers who knew the invisible things of God through creation still fall into error and idolatry?

question: Does Christ's acceptance of the title 'Master' from the apostles show that He objected to the rich young man not because of the title but because of his unbelief?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Yes. To the faithful apostles He said 'Ye call Me Master and Lord, and ye say well, for so I am,' and elsewhere 'Christ is your Master.' He accepts the title from those who acknowledge Him as Lord and Christ but rejects it from one who sees in Him only body and flesh. So the rebuke targeted the unbelief, and He does not distinguish Himself from the one good God.
sources.quote: From the faithful, to whom He is master, He accepts the title with words of praise, but here He rejects the name “good master,” when He is not acknowledged to be the Lord and the Christ
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's acceptance of the title 'Master' from the apostles show that He objected to the rich young man not because of the title but because of his unbelief?

question: Is power in itself evil, so that Christians should shun it in favour of righteousness?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Man Was to Be Rescued from the Power of the Devil, Not by Power, But by Righteousness.
sources.answer: No. Power is not to be shunned as something evil, but the right order must be kept, in which righteousness comes first and power follows. Mortals should cleave to righteousness, and power will be given to them when they are immortal. Power joined to righteousness then makes up judicial authority.
sources.quote: Not that power is to be shunned as though it were something evil; but the order must be preserved, whereby righteousness is before it.
sources.raw_question: Is power in itself evil, so that Christians should shun it in favour of righteousness?

question: Can we know exactly how angels produced the clouds and fires through which God was signified in the Old Testament appearances?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > In How Many Ways the Creature is to Be Taken by Way of Sign. The Eucharist.
sources.answer: No, not with certainty. Augustine says he cannot penetrate by sight, reason, or intellect how God works these things through angels, good or bad, by permitting, commanding, or compelling; human thoughts are uncertain and the things of heaven are unsearched. Yet by the Spirit given from above we can affirm the unchangeability of God, and Scripture's authority teaches that these appearances were wrought through the creature by angels.
sources.quote: this I can neither penetrate by the sight of the eyes, nor make clear by assurance of reason, nor be carried on to comprehend it by reach of intellect
sources.raw_question: Can we know exactly how angels produced the clouds and fires through which God was signified in the Old Testament appearances?

question: Does a bodily sign through which God is manifested, like the sacrament on the altar, show that the Lord himself appeared in that very form?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > In How Many Ways the Creature is to Be Taken by Way of Sign. The Eucharist.
sources.answer: No. Just as infants who saw the eucharistic elements only during the rite and were told whose body and blood they are might wrongly believe the Lord appeared in that form, so one should not infer that the corporeal forms in the theophanies were God himself appearing. They are creaturely signs taken for signifying, not the divine substance.
sources.quote: they will believe nothing else, except that the Lord absolutely appeared in this form to the eyes of mortals
sources.raw_question: Does a bodily sign through which God is manifested, like the sacrament on the altar, show that the Lord himself appeared in that very form?

question: Even if creatures could hear prayers and help us, may religious worship be given to them?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. Even granting that creatures might know our needs, hear us, and relieve us, God has expressly forbidden religious worship of anything but himself. That is sufficient for us, whether or not we can see the harm in it. God may have good reasons, such as keeping our minds from being drawn away from the Creator and keeping us dependent on and united to him.
sources.quote: These, or a thousand better reasons, infinite Wisdom may have, for appropriating all acts of religious worship to God. It is sufficient for us to know that he has done it: and of this holy Scripture has given abundant proof
sources.raw_question: Even if creatures could hear prayers and help us, may religious worship be given to them?

question: Do Exodus 20:3 and Matthew 4:10 reserve only absolute, supreme honour to the Father, leaving room for relative, inferior worship of creatures?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. The distinction between supreme and inferior religious worship is the same one pagans and Romanists used to excuse idolatry, and it has neither truth nor probability. The question concerns acts of religious worship, not mere honour or esteem. Scripture appropriates all such acts to God alone.
sources.quote: This is the famed distinction, pleaded by the heathens of old, for Pagan, by the Romanists of late, for Popish, and by you, for Arian idolatry.
sources.raw_question: Do Exodus 20:3 and Matthew 4:10 reserve only absolute, supreme honour to the Father, leaving room for relative, inferior worship of creatures?

question: Why does Christ hold believers accountable for their words and thoughts, and not only for their deeds?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVI.—Perfect righteousness was conferred neither by circumcision nor by any other legal ceremonies. The Decalogue, however, was not cancelled by Christ, but is always in force: men were never released from its commandments.
sources.answer: Because believers have been adopted as sons and given true liberty. Sons owe more reverence and love to their father than slaves do. So God judges them not only for deeds, as slaves are judged, but also for words and thoughts. Their liberty is the means by which they are more severely tested, to show whether they will reverence, fear and love the Lord, and not a cloak for wickedness.
sources.quote: we shall give account to God not of deeds only, as slaves, but even of words and thoughts, as those who have truly received the power of liberty, in which [condition] a man is more severely tested
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ hold believers accountable for their words and thoughts, and not only for their deeds?

question: Who is the speaker in Isaiah 65:13-16, the one who will slay the unbelievers and give His servants a new name?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: The Lord, that is, Christ. The phrases "Thus saith the Lord" and "the Lord shall slay you" show that the same Lord speaks, judges, and gives His servants the new name. This new name is "Christian," which Christ bestows. So the true God whom these servants bless and swear by is Christ himself.
sources.quote: this new title of Christian, awarded to our faith, is that heavenly blessing which is our reward upon earth.
sources.raw_question: Who is the speaker in Isaiah 65:13-16, the one who will slay the unbelievers and give His servants a new name?

question: Do New Testament writers other than Paul, such as Peter, Jude, the author of Hebrews, and John in Revelation, share the same Trinitarian understanding of God?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. They too assume that God's redemptive activities rest on a threefold source in the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit. Examples include 1 Peter 1:2, Jude 20-21, and Revelation 1:4-5, where the Seven Spirits stand between the Father and Jesus Christ. This shows a fixed Trinitarian consciousness that was universal in apostolic circles.
sources.quote: Clearly these writers, too, write out of a fixed Trinitarian consciousness and bear their testimony to the universal understanding current in apostolical circles.
sources.raw_question: Do New Testament writers other than Paul, such as Peter, Jude, the author of Hebrews, and John in Revelation, share the same Trinitarian understanding of God?

question: In Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh, are 'the God which fed me' and 'the Angel who delivered me' two different beings or one person?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God Also Appeared to Jacob as an Angel; Namely, the Son of God.
sources.answer: They are one person who is both God and Angel. Jacob used the singular verb 'bless.' If he had meant God and an angel as two, he would have used the plural.
sources.quote: if he had meant the one to be understood as God, and the other as an angel, he would have comprised the two persons in the plural number; but now he defined the singular number of one person in the blessing
sources.raw_question: In Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh, are 'the God which fed me' and 'the Angel who delivered me' two different beings or one person?

question: Could the creative command "Let there be a firmament" have been obeyed by the not-yet-existing things themselves rather than executed by a divine Agent?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: No. Scripture teaches that all things were made out of nothing, not by transforming things that already existed. So there was nothing yet in existence that could obey and bring itself into being. The Evangelist identifies the one through whom all things were made as the Word, who was with God and was God.
sources.quote: For all things, as the Prophet says, were made out of nothing; it was no transformation of existing things, but the creation into a perfect form of the non-existent. Through whom? Hear the Evangelist: All things were made through Him.
sources.raw_question: Could the creative command "Let there be a firmament" have been obeyed by the not-yet-existing things themselves rather than executed by a divine Agent?

question: Whom did Isaiah see when he beheld the glory of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: He saw God the Only-begotten Son. The Evangelist says Isaiah spoke these things when he saw His glory and spoke of Him, meaning Christ. Isaiah also foretold this same God's taking flesh from the Virgin.
sources.quote: And if you, in your heresy, do not know that it was God the Only-begotten Whom the prophet saw in that glory, listen to the Evangelist:—These things said Esaias, when he saw His glory, and spake of Him
sources.raw_question: Whom did Isaiah see when he beheld the glory of God?

question: How does union increase bodies differently from spiritual beings, and what does this show about God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > In reply to the argument alleged against the equality of the Son from the apostle’s words, saying that Christ is the ‘power of God and the wisdom of God,’ he propounds the question whether the Father Himself is not wisdom. But deferring for a while the answer to this, he adduces further proof of the unity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that God ought to be said and believed to be a Trinity, not triple (triplicem). And he adds an explanation of the saying of Hilary—Eternity in the Father, Appearance in the Image, and Use in the Gift. > No Addition Can Be Made to the Nature of God.
sources.answer: Bodies grow larger by union, as husband and wife joined in one body make a greater body than either alone. In spiritual things, which are not great by bulk, to be greater is to be better. A creature joined to the Creator becomes better and so greater, but the Creator does not become greater by that union.
sources.quote: For in those things which are not great by bulk, to be greater is to be better. And the spirit of any creature becomes better, when it cleaves to the Creator, than if it did not so cleave; and therefore also greater because better.
sources.raw_question: How does union increase bodies differently from spiritual beings, and what does this show about God?

question: Do the 'riches' Christ had before becoming poor in 2 Corinthians 8:9 refer to the riches of his divine nature?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. The riches are those of the Deity, the eternal glory he had with the Father. This is evident from their opposition to the poverty he undertook as man, and the same person who was rich was also poor.
sources.quote: That the riches here meant can be none but those of the Deity, is evident, by its opposition to the poverty which as man he undertook.
sources.raw_question: Do the 'riches' Christ had before becoming poor in 2 Corinthians 8:9 refer to the riches of his divine nature?

question: Does the Greek phrase in Luke 1:3 refer to Luke's knowledge coming 'from above' or to his tracing things 'from the beginning'?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Owen holds it is better rendered "having obtained perfect knowledge of things from above." It points to the source of Luke's understanding, which enabled him to set things down infallibly as a rule of faith. It does not refer to the beginning of the events narrated, a sense he says the word will not easily allow.
sources.quote: is better rendered, “Having obtained perfect knowledge of things from above,” — noting the rise and spring of his so understanding things
sources.raw_question: Does the Greek phrase in Luke 1:3 refer to Luke's knowledge coming 'from above' or to his tracing things 'from the beginning'?

question: Does the New Testament's use of 'call upon' (epikaleomai) for invoking Jesus Christ show that he receives divine worship?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. In the Septuagint epikaleomai is the ordinary term for the sacred invocation of God, and in the New Testament it is used of prayer to the Father and is tied to salvation. Yet it is plainly applied to invoking the Lord Jesus, so Christ receives the same saving, divine invocation as the Father.
sources.quote: It describes such spiritual worship that, whether offered to the Father, or to the Son, salvation is indissolubly connected with it, – “Whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved.”
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament's use of 'call upon' (epikaleomai) for invoking Jesus Christ show that he receives divine worship?

question: What does the bush that burned without being consumed signify about Christ and the Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIV. Each Person of the Trinity is said in the sacred writings to be Light. The Spirit is designated Fire by Isaiah, a figure of which Fire was seen in the bush by Moses, in the tongues of fire, and in Gideon's pitchers. And the Godhead of the same Spirit cannot be denied, since His operation is the same as that of the Father and of the Son, and He is also called the light and fire of the Lord's countenance.
sources.answer: It signified that the Lord would come to illuminate the thorns of our body. He would not consume those in misery but relieve their misery. He would baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire, so as to give grace and destroy sin.
sources.quote: the Lord was showing that He would come to illuminate the thorns of our body, and not to consume those who were in misery, but to alleviate their misery
sources.raw_question: What does the bush that burned without being consumed signify about Christ and the Spirit?

question: Who is the 'light of Thy countenance sealed upon us' in Psalm 4:6?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XIV. Each Person of the Trinity is said in the sacred writings to be Light. The Spirit is designated Fire by Isaiah, a figure of which Fire was seen in the bush by Moses, in the tongues of fire, and in Gideon's pitchers. And the Godhead of the same Spirit cannot be denied, since His operation is the same as that of the Father and of the Son, and He is also called the light and fire of the Lord's countenance.
sources.answer: It is the Holy Spirit. The light that is sealed is the seal of the Spirit, as Paul says, 'ye were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise.' The Spirit is also the fire that burns before God's face, which refines good deeds like gold and consumes sins like stubble.
sources.quote: What is, then, the light that is sealed, but that of the seal of the Spirit, believing in Whom, “ye were sealed,” he says, “with the Holy Spirit of promise.”
sources.raw_question: Who is the 'light of Thy countenance sealed upon us' in Psalm 4:6?

question: Why did John fall as dead when he saw the glorified Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: So that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "No man sees God, and shall live." John's collapse before the glorified Word fulfils this saying. The Word then revived him and declared that He is the first and the last, who was dead and is alive for evermore.
sources.quote: But when John could not endure the sight (for he says, “I fell at his feet as dead;”[^4102] that what was written might come to pass: “No man sees God, and shall live”[^4103])
sources.raw_question: Why did John fall as dead when he saw the glorified Christ?

question: Who carries the burden of proof when someone claims the Nicene doctrine of Christ's divinity was a corruption of the original faith?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: Those who deny the received doctrine carry the burden, and it requires proof amounting nearly to demonstration. Their claim implies that the ancient heretics were the soundest Christians. It also implies that the first general council, with no bias, either did not know its churches' inherited faith or deliberately corrupted it on an article concerning the object of worship. Finally, it implies that nearly all churches in every age, including after the Reformation's re-examination, shared that error. Without very weighty proof, such dissenters are unreasonable to demand attention and inexcusable in unsettling simple believers.
sources.quote: If they have not something very weighty and momentous to urge; something that carries the force and evidence of demonstration with it, they are first very unreasonable in calling us to attend to what so little deserves it
sources.raw_question: Who carries the burden of proof when someone claims the Nicene doctrine of Christ's divinity was a corruption of the original faith?

question: Does "the end of the world" in Matthew 28:20 mean only the end of the Jewish age, so that the promise does not imply Christ's divine omnipresence?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: No. Even on that reading, a mere man could no more be continually present with apostles scattered in widespread labours for forty years than for eighteen centuries. Moreover, Matthew's other uses of the phrase plainly refer to the final judgment and the second advent.
sources.quote: for such unfailing presence of a mere man with his apostles in their widespread evangelistic labours was as impossible for forty years as for eighteen centuries
sources.raw_question: Does "the end of the world" in Matthew 28:20 mean only the end of the Jewish age, so that the promise does not imply Christ's divine omnipresence?

question: According to Romans 5, how are believers able to glory even in tribulations?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: They are able to glory in tribulations because the Holy Ghost sheds abroad the love of God in their hearts. Paul says that believers rejoice in hope of glory and also glory in tribulations, and verse 5 gives the source: the Spirit's work of pouring out God's love. Likewise, 1 Thessalonians 1:6 speaks of receiving the word in much affliction with joy of the Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: He tells us, verse 5, it is from the “shedding abroad of the love of God in our hearts by the Holy Ghost.”
sources.raw_question: According to Romans 5, how are believers able to glory even in tribulations?

question: Why do people reject Christ or refuse communion with him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Because they do not know him. Owen applies Paul's statement that those who crucified Christ would not have done so had they known him: anyone acquainted with Christ would not reject the Lord of glory. Those who despise him are people whose eyes the god of this world has blinded so that they cannot see his glory.
sources.quote: There are none who despise Christ, but only they that know him not; whose eyes the god of this world hath blinded, that they should not behold his glory.
sources.raw_question: Why do people reject Christ or refuse communion with him?

question: Can anything else the human soul seeks for rest and delight compare to Christ as an object of communion?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: No. The soul naturally seeks something to rest in and delight in, whether pleasure, profit, or acceptance with God. Compared with Christ's fitness, fulness and suitableness to save, all these pursuits are vanity and vexation of spirit. Only Christ is a fit object for our choicest affections: in him the soul finds rest, and in him there is nothing that will grieve it for eternity.
sources.quote: Behold here a fit object for your choicest affections, — one in whom you may find rest to your souls, — one in whom there is nothing will grieve and trouble you to eternity.
sources.raw_question: Can anything else the human soul seeks for rest and delight compare to Christ as an object of communion?

question: If being outside the Pleroma means being in ignorance, could the Gnostic Christ or Saviour who went outside it give knowledge to others?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter V.—This world was not formed by any other beings within the territory which is contained by the Father.
sources.answer: No. If 'outside' means ignorance, then the Saviour and Christ, by going outside the Pleroma to form the Mother, placed themselves in ignorance. One who is himself beyond the pale of knowledge cannot communicate knowledge. Christ would even become the author of ignorance by casting the Mother out.
sources.quote: How then could He communicate knowledge to her, when He Himself was beyond the pale of knowledge?
sources.raw_question: If being outside the Pleroma means being in ignorance, could the Gnostic Christ or Saviour who went outside it give knowledge to others?

question: Are the Son's works and gifts the Father's own works and gifts?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Yes. The Word is not separate from the Father, nor unlike or foreign to the Father's essence. Therefore what He works are the Father's works, His framing of all things is one with the Father's, and what He gives is the Father's gift. Whoever hears the Word knows that he hears the Father.
sources.quote: the Word, as being not separate from the Father, nor unlike and foreign to the Father’s Essence, what He works, those are the Father’s works, and His framing of all things is one with His; and what the Son gives, that is the Father’s gift
sources.raw_question: Are the Son's works and gifts the Father's own works and gifts?

question: Do the spies whom Rahab the harlot received and hid in Jericho serve as a type of the Trinity?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus reads the spies Rahab received as a type of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Rahab, a Gentile guilty of all sins, received them in faith and was preserved through the scarlet sign. She thus prefigures sinners from the Gentiles who receive the triune God and are saved, while those who reject Christ's coming are shut out.
sources.quote: nevertheless receive the three spies, who were spying out all the land, and hid them at her home; [which three were] doubtless [a type of] the Father and the Son, together with the Holy Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Do the spies whom Rahab the harlot received and hid in Jericho serve as a type of the Trinity?

question: What did the prophet Hosea's marriage to 'a wife of whoredoms' and the naming of his children signify?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: It signified that God would take a Church out of unfaithful humanity, sanctified by fellowship with his Son. This parallels how the woman was sanctified by union with the prophet. The children's names 'Not a people' and 'Not having obtained mercy' foretold, as Paul shows, that those who were not God's people would become children of the living God. What the prophet did typically, Christ did truly in the Church.
sources.quote: That which had been done typically through his actions by the prophet, the apostle proves to have been done truly by Christ in the Church.
sources.raw_question: What did the prophet Hosea's marriage to 'a wife of whoredoms' and the naming of his children signify?

question: What did Moses' marriage to an Ethiopian woman foreshadow?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: It foreshadowed the marriage of the Word with the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Moses made the Ethiopian an Israelite, showing in advance that the wild olive is grafted into the cultivated olive. Those who deride this Church, like Miriam, will be unclean and expelled.
sources.quote: by means of the marriage of Moses, was shown forth the marriage of the Word; and by means of the Ethiopian bride, the Church taken from among the Gentiles was made manifest
sources.raw_question: What did Moses' marriage to an Ethiopian woman foreshadow?

question: When we stop loving a man we wrongly believed to be good, does the eternal truth by which we judge him change?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > There is One Knowledge of the Thing in the Thing Itself, and Another in Eternal Truth Itself. That Corporeal Things, Too, are to Be Judged the Rules of Eternal Truth.
sources.answer: No. Neither the man nor the eternal truth changes; only our estimate of him changes. At the bidding of unchangeable righteousness, our love turns from the purpose of enjoying him to the purpose of taking counsel that he may become good. The same form of stable truth shines with the same light in immovable eternity. Our love was really directed to the form of goodness we believed was in him.
sources.quote: But the form itself of unshaken and stable truth, wherein I should have enjoyed the fruition of the man, believing him to be good, and wherein likewise I take counsel that he may be good, sheds in an immoveable eternity the same light
sources.raw_question: When we stop loving a man we wrongly believed to be good, does the eternal truth by which we judge him change?

question: Why does Paul speak of all things as already subjected under Christ's feet when their subjection is still in the future?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: Because what is to be accomplished at the completion of time already exists in Christ, in whom is all fulness. The past tense expresses Christ's immutable power, while the future refers only to the temporal order of the Dispensation, not to any new development in Christ, signifying the consummation at the end of the ages.
sources.quote: for that which is to be wrought by the completion of time already exists in Christ, in Whom is all fulness, and ‘future’ refers only to the temporal order of the Dispensation, not to a new development.
sources.raw_question: Why does Paul speak of all things as already subjected under Christ's feet when their subjection is still in the future?

question: Why would God permit heretics such as Cerinthus to deny the Deity of Christ while the apostle John was still alive?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Preface
sources.answer: It was an act of God's holy and wise providence. Because the doctrine was opposed before John's death, the apostle could, by infallible inspiration, further reveal and declare it. This settled the matter for the church in later ages, as if immediately from heaven.
sources.quote: it was of the holy, wise providence of God to suffer some impious persons to oppose this doctrine before the death of that apostle, that he might, by infallible inspiration, farther reveal, manifest, and declare it
sources.raw_question: Why would God permit heretics such as Cerinthus to deny the Deity of Christ while the apostle John was still alive?

question: Whose stripes or wounds are meant in Isaiah's prophecy that 'by his stripes we are healed', as quoted in 1 Peter 2:24?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IX. The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ, and the oil of gladness; and why Christ Himself is not the ointment, since He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It is not strange that the Spirit should be called Ointment, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. And there is no confusion between them, since Christ alone suffered death, Whose saving cross is then spoken of.
sources.answer: Christ the Lord. Isaiah prophesied that his stripes would be our healing. Paul likewise says that he who knew no sin was made sin for us. So the one who bore our sins in his body on the tree is Christ.
sources.quote: Who, then, is He by the wound of Whose stripes we are healed but Christ the Lord? of Whom the same Isaiah prophesied His stripes were our healing
sources.raw_question: Whose stripes or wounds are meant in Isaiah's prophecy that 'by his stripes we are healed', as quoted in 1 Peter 2:24?

question: Why is Christ's sinlessness remarkable, if the Godhead by nature cannot sin?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IX. The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ, and the oil of gladness; and why Christ Himself is not the ointment, since He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It is not strange that the Spirit should be called Ointment, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit.
