And there is no confusion between them, since Christ alone suffered death, Whose saving cross is then spoken of.
sources.answer: Because his created flesh also did no sin. It would be no wonder for the Godhead alone to be sinless, since it has no incentives to sin. What was divine in Christ is that the creature of his body did not take on sin.
sources.quote: This, indeed, was divine in Him, that His Flesh did no sin, nor did the creature of the body take in Him sin. For what wonder would it be if the Godhead alone sinned not, seeing It had no incentives to sin?
sources.raw_question: Why is Christ's sinlessness remarkable, if the Godhead by nature cannot sin?

question: Does conceiving God as extended (an ell or a mile of God) avoid the difficulties raised against the Trinity?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: No. If an ell of consciousness is a solecism, an ell or a mile of God is as great a one. Unextended attributes in an extended subject are as unintelligible as anything objected to the Trinity. Part and whole apply to the divine attributes as properly as to the divine subject, so both or neither.
sources.quote: many may think that an οἰ, or a mile of God (which is the Doctor’s notion) is as great a solecism as the other.
sources.raw_question: Does conceiving God as extended (an ell or a mile of God) avoid the difficulties raised against the Trinity?

question: Who is the one who will reign over the house of Jacob for ever as foretold to Mary, and why did the Son of God become the Son of man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: It is Jesus Christ our Lord, the Son of the Most High God, for no one else can reign uninterruptedly for ever. He promised through the law and prophets to make his salvation visible to all flesh, and he became the Son of man so that man might become the son of God.
sources.quote: so that He would become the Son of man for this purpose, that man also might become the son of God?
sources.raw_question: Who is the one who will reign over the house of Jacob for ever as foretold to Mary, and why did the Son of God become the Son of man?

question: Does the 'knowledge of salvation' proclaimed by John the Baptist consist in knowledge of a higher God or Father beyond the Creator, such as the Gnostic Bythus and Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: No. The knowledge of salvation was the knowledge of the Son of God, whom John pointed out as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world and who was prior to him. It did not consist in another God, another Father, Bythus, the Pleroma of thirty Aeons, or the Mother of the Ogdoad.
sources.quote: the knowledge of salvation was the knowledge of the Son of God, who is both called and actually is, salvation, and Saviour, and salutary.
sources.raw_question: Does the 'knowledge of salvation' proclaimed by John the Baptist consist in knowledge of a higher God or Father beyond the Creator, such as the Gnostic Bythus and Pleroma?

question: What is meant by the wicked servant being 'cut asunder' at the judgment?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: It means the complete and eternal separation of the soul from the Holy Spirit. It cannot mean dividing the body, since it would be unjust for only half of a sinner to be punished, nor dividing the soul, which sinned as a whole. Rather, the Spirit, who now seems in a manner present to the sealed awaiting their conversion, will then be wholly cut off from the soul that defiled His grace.
sources.quote: The cutting asunder, as I have observed, is the separation for aye of the soul from the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: What is meant by the wicked servant being 'cut asunder' at the judgment?

question: Do the gifts and worship of the Magi fulfil Isaiah's prophecy that the labour of Egypt and the merchandise of the Ethiopians and Sabeans shall come to the King raised up by God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: Yes. The Magi's toilsome pilgrimage represents the labours of Egypt. Their gold, frankincense and myrrh are the merchandise of the Ethiopians and Sabeans, as Psalm 72 also foretells. As representatives of the heathen world, they worship Christ as Lord, so the prophecy concerns the Son.
sources.quote: The Magi and their offerings stand for the labour of Egypt and for the merchandise of Ethiopians and Sabeans; the adoring Magi represent the heathen world, and offer the choicest gifts of the Gentiles to the Lord Whom they adore.
sources.raw_question: Do the gifts and worship of the Magi fulfil Isaiah's prophecy that the labour of Egypt and the merchandise of the Ethiopians and Sabeans shall come to the King raised up by God?

question: Among intelligible and unchangeable realities, can one thing be more truly than another?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > It is Shown by Reason that in God Three are Not Anything Greater Than One Person.
sources.answer: No. All such things are alike unchangeably eternal. What is called great there is great only by that through which it truly is. So nothing among them exceeds another in reality.
sources.quote: But in respect to whatsoever is intelligible and unchangeable, no one thing is more truly than another, since all alike are unchangeably eternal
sources.raw_question: Among intelligible and unchangeable realities, can one thing be more truly than another?

question: In Titus 3:4, does 'the kindness and love of God our Saviour' refer to the Father rather than to Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen holds that the apostle speaks of the Father, because verse 6 says this love is shed on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour, distinguishing the one who loves from the one through whom the love is conveyed.
sources.quote: It is of the Father of whom he speaks; for, verse 6, he tells us that “he makes out unto us,” or “sheds that love upon us abundantly, through Jesus Christ our Saviour.”
sources.raw_question: In Titus 3:4, does 'the kindness and love of God our Saviour' refer to the Father rather than to Christ?

question: How is Christ related to the Father's love, as illustrated by the image of the sun and its beams or a fountain and its streams?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Christ is to the Father's love as the beam is to the sun or the stream to the fountain. All our light and refreshment actually lie in Christ, but through him we are led up to the Father as the source, the sun of eternal love itself.
sources.quote: Jesus Christ, in respect of the love of the Father, is but the beam, the stream; wherein though actually all our light, our refreshment lies, yet by him we are led to the fountain, the sun of eternal love itself.
sources.raw_question: How is Christ related to the Father's love, as illustrated by the image of the sun and its beams or a fountain and its streams?

question: Do Trinitarians hold to the unity of God any less firmly than Unitarians do?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 1. Introduction. Preparation of heart. Our position before God.
sources.answer: No. The author says Trinitarians hold to the Unity of God just as tenaciously as Unitarians. That is why he uses the name 'Unitarian' only under protest. In his view the name misrepresents the real point at issue, which is not whether God is one.
sources.quote: under protest, that it does not fairly set forth the points at issue betwixt us, if for no other reason, for this that we cleave to the Unity of God as tenaciously as they.
sources.raw_question: Do Trinitarians hold to the unity of God any less firmly than Unitarians do?

question: Is prayer needed before inquiring into the doctrine of God and the Godhead of Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 1. Introduction. Preparation of heart. Our position before God.
sources.answer: Yes. Eternal life consists in knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent, and God rewards those who diligently seek him. The inquirer should therefore pray to be guided into all truth. Since God cannot be found out to perfection by human searching, the inquirer must ask the Father for the Holy Spirit's guidance, as Christ promised.
sources.quote: I would ask him to pause, and to pour out his heart in prayer that he may be guided into all truth.
sources.raw_question: Is prayer needed before inquiring into the doctrine of God and the Godhead of Christ?

question: Can a person attain holiness by his own strength, vows, and endeavours apart from Christ and the Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: No. Those who try to spin holiness out of their own bowels by vows and resolutions usually end in hypocrisy and apostasy. The saints know they lack the indwelling Spirit, an infused habit of holiness, and actual assistance, and that without these they cannot perform any act of holiness, since without Christ they can do nothing.
sources.quote: Convinced persons who know not Christ, nor the fellowship of his sufferings, would spin a holiness out of their own bowels; they would work it out in their own strength.
sources.raw_question: Can a person attain holiness by his own strength, vows, and endeavours apart from Christ and the Spirit?

question: According to the Ante-Nicene Fathers, may religious worship of any kind or degree be lawfully paid to a creature?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: No. Waterland gathers testimonies from Justin, Athenagoras, Theophilus, Tatian, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Irenaeus and Origen showing that God alone, the Creator as opposed to all creatures, is to be worshipped. He therefore fixes it as a maxim, grounded in Scripture, the consent of antiquity and reason, that no kind or degree of religious worship is due to any creature.
sources.quote: let it be a rule and maxim with us, fixed, as far as Scripture and the concurring judgment of antiquity can fix it, (besides what might be justly pleaded from the reason of the thing,) that no kind or degree of religious worship is due, or can be lawfully paid, to any creature.
sources.raw_question: According to the Ante-Nicene Fathers, may religious worship of any kind or degree be lawfully paid to a creature?

question: Can corruptible, compound and bounded created things be images of spiritual, incomprehensible beings?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter VII.—Created things are not the images of those Æons who are within the Pleroma.
sources.answer: No. Things contrary to one another cannot be each other's images, just as fire and water, or light and darkness, cannot. A true image requires its archetype to have a definite figure and limits. So either the higher beings are bounded and therefore not spiritual, or they are spiritual and incomprehensible and so cannot have shaped, limited images.
sources.quote: how can those things which are possessed of figure, and confined within certain limits, be the images of such as are destitute of figure and incomprehensible?
sources.raw_question: Can corruptible, compound and bounded created things be images of spiritual, incomprehensible beings?

question: Can one consistently accept the grace of regeneration while denying the divinity of the Holy Spirit who gives it?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is no less the author of spiritual creation or regeneration than the Father and the Son. The excellence of that creation, and wherein it consists. How we are to understand holy Scripture, when it attributes a body or members to God.
sources.answer: No. The benefit cannot remain when its Author is shut out, since the Author is not without the gift nor the gift without the Author. Whoever denies the Spirit denies the gift too; if the Author is of no account, His gifts cannot be precious.
sources.quote: But the benefit cannot remain when its Author is shut out; the Author is not without the gift, nor the gift without the Author. If you claim the grace, believe the power; if you reject the power, do not ask for the grace.
sources.raw_question: Can one consistently accept the grace of regeneration while denying the divinity of the Holy Spirit who gives it?

question: In Job's words 'the Spirit of God which is in my nostrils,' does 'Spirit' mean merely the bodily breath of life?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is no less the author of spiritual creation or regeneration than the Father and the Son. The excellence of that creation, and wherein it consists. How we are to understand holy Scripture, when it attributes a body or members to God.
sources.answer: No. Job did not mean the vital breath and bodily breathing passages but the nostrils of the inner man, by which he drew in the fragrance of eternal life and the grace of the heavenly ointment. Scripture speaks of spiritual members inferred from their actions, not to be imagined in a fleshly way.
sources.quote: He certainly did not here signify by His Spirit the vital breath and bodily breathing passages, but signifies the nostrils of the inner man within him, wherewith he gathered in the fragrance of eternal life
sources.raw_question: In Job's words 'the Spirit of God which is in my nostrils,' does 'Spirit' mean merely the bodily breath of life?

question: In worshipping Jesus, do Christians make a god out of a mortal man?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 6: Whether the same characteristics, especially such eminent ones, can reasonably be understood of two distinct Beings, and of one infinite and independent, the ot
sources.answer: No. Citing Origen against Celsus, the one believed to be God and Son of God from the beginning is the Word itself, Wisdom itself and Truth itself. His mortal body and human soul, by intimate union with the Word, received the greatest dignity and participated in his divinity, being taken into God, rather than a mere man being raised to deity.
sources.quote: whom we believe to “ have been God, and the Son of God from the beginning, is no * other than the Word itself, Truth itself, and Wisdom itself
sources.raw_question: In worshipping Jesus, do Christians make a god out of a mortal man?

question: How can Scripture say both that the Lord is one and that the Lord rained fire from the Lord or grants mercy from the Lord?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XV. Though the Spirit be called Lord, three Lords are not thereby implied; inasmuch as two Lords are not implied by the fact that the Son in the same manner as the Father is called Lord in many passages of Scripture; for Lordship exists in the Godhead, and the Godhead in Lordship, and these coincide without division in the Three Persons.
sources.answer: There is no contradiction. 'One Lord' means unchangeable and always abiding in unity of power. When the Lord rains fire from the Lord, or grants mercy from the Lord, the Lord is not divided or separated. In each case the oneness of the Lordship is expressed.
sources.quote: The Lord is neither divided when He rains from the Lord, nor is there a separation when He grants mercy from the Lord, but in each case the oneness of the Lordship is expressed.
sources.raw_question: How can Scripture say both that the Lord is one and that the Lord rained fire from the Lord or grants mercy from the Lord?

question: Why did the Word take on human weakness such as fear of death?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Twelfthly, Matthew xxvi. 39; John xii. 27, &c. Arian inferences are against the Regula Fidei, as before. He wept and the like, as man. Other texts prove Him God. God could not fear. He feared because His flesh feared.
sources.answer: To destroy these affections and free humanity from them. He combined His own will with human weakness so that, destroying the affection, He might make man undaunted before death; as He abolished death by death, so by His so-called terror He removed ours. The fearlessness of the apostles and martyrs shows that the Godhead was not in terror but the Saviour took away our terror.
sources.quote: For as He abolished death by death, and by human means all human evils, so by this so-called terror did He remove our terror, and brought about that never more should men fear death.
sources.raw_question: Why did the Word take on human weakness such as fear of death?

question: Why did Christ's corruptible flesh not see corruption, and what does this mean for believers?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Twelfthly, Matthew xxvi. 39; John xii. 27, &c. Arian inferences are against the Regula Fidei, as before. He wept and the like, as man. Other texts prove Him God. God could not fear. He feared because His flesh feared.
sources.answer: Because of the Word who had put it on, the flesh no longer remained mortal according to its own nature but abode incorruptible, as Psalm 16 foretold. As the Word was conformed to our condition by coming in our body, so we, receiving Him, partake of the immortality that comes from Him.
sources.quote: For as He, having come in our body, was conformed to our condition, so we, receiving Him, partake of the immortality that is from Him.
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ's corruptible flesh not see corruption, and what does this mean for believers?

question: What are the different senses in which something can be said to be "of" (ex) another, and how do they apply to the Son, the Spirit, and creatures?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, as well as the Father and the Son, is pointed out in holy Scripture as Creator, and the same truth was shadowed forth even by heathen writers, but it was shown most plainly in the Mystery of the Incarnation, after touching upon which, the writer maintains his argument from the fact that worship which is due to the Creator alone is paid to the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: What is "of" anyone is either of his substance or of his power. The Son, who "came forth of the Mouth of the Most High," is of the Father's substance. So is the Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and receives of the Son. All things are "of" the Father only by his power, as creatures.
sources.quote: For that which is “of” [ex] any one is either of his substance or of his power. Of his substance, as the Son, Who says: “I came forth of the Mouth of the Most High;” as the Spirit, “Who proceedeth from the Father;”
sources.raw_question: What are the different senses in which something can be said to be "of" (ex) another, and how do they apply to the Son, the Spirit, and creatures?

question: Does Philippians 3:3 really say Christians "serve the Spirit of God," given that some Latin manuscripts read differently?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, as well as the Father and the Son, is pointed out in holy Scripture as Creator, and the same truth was shadowed forth even by heathen writers, but it was shown most plainly in the Mystery of the Incarnation, after touching upon which, the writer maintains his argument from the fact that worship which is due to the Creator alone is paid to the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Some Latin codices vary, and heretics have falsified some of them. The Greek codices read "οἱ πνεύματι Θεοῦ λατρεύοντες," which means "who serve the Spirit of God."
sources.quote: let him look at the Greek codices, and observe that it is there written: “οἱ πνεύματι Θεοῦ λατρεύοντες,” which is, being translated, “who serve the Spirit of God.”
sources.raw_question: Does Philippians 3:3 really say Christians "serve the Spirit of God," given that some Latin manuscripts read differently?

question: Can the thought (Ennoea) or silence (Sige) of a being be sent forth outside him as a separate entity with its own figure?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XII.—The Triacontad of the heretics errs both by defect and excess: Sophia could never have produced anything apart from her consort; Logos and Sige could not have been contemporaries.
sources.answer: No. A person's thought or silence cannot be understood apart from the person himself. It cannot be sent forth beyond him and still have a distinct form of its own. If it remained one with the Father, it should not be counted among the other Aeons, which are separate from him and ignorant of his greatness.
sources.quote: For it is impossible that the thought (Ennœa) of any one, or his silence (Sige), should be understood apart from himself; and that, being sent forth beyond him, it should possess a special figure of its own.
sources.raw_question: Can the thought (Ennoea) or silence (Sige) of a being be sent forth outside him as a separate entity with its own figure?

question: If what is sent forth remains inseparably one with its source, must what proceeds from that union also be united with it and not unlike it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XII.—The Triacontad of the heretics errs both by defect and excess: Sophia could never have produced anything apart from her consort; Logos and Sige could not have been contemporaries.
sources.answer: Yes. A union that is inseparable and constitutes one being must produce something that is likewise unseparated and united, so that it is not dissimilar to the one who sent it forth. Such things are mutually bound together and cannot be conceived apart, as water cannot be conceived without moisture or fire without heat. So each pair produced from such a union must always co-exist as one.
sources.quote: should proceed an unseparated and united production, so that it should not be dissimilar to Him who sent it forth.
sources.raw_question: If what is sent forth remains inseparably one with its source, must what proceeds from that union also be united with it and not unlike it?

question: What is the purpose of God's anger and threats toward humans?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > If We Regard the Anger, and Indignation, and Hatred of God Described in the Sacred Pages, We Must Remember that They are Not to Be Understood as Bearing the Character of Human Vices.
sources.answer: God's anger arises not from vice but is exercised for our advantage, as a medicine. He is merciful even when He threatens, since threats recall men to rectitude, and fear moves those who have forsaken reason toward virtue. Thus these angers come from wisdom, not from frailty.
sources.quote: For that God is angry, arises from no vice in Him. But He is so for our advantage; for He is merciful even then when He threatens, because by these threats men are recalled to rectitude.
sources.raw_question: What is the purpose of God's anger and threats toward humans?

question: What is the source of the believer's power to obey God freely, according to Owen?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: It comes from a principle of life, Christ living in the believer by the Spirit of life. The law of the Spirit of life in Christ sets believers free from the law of sin and death and carries them out to obedience. Living acts come only from a living principle; the fruits of a dead root are dead.
sources.quote: There is, then, power for all living unto God, from Christ in them, the Spirit of life from Christ carrying them out thereto. The fruits of a dead root are but dead excrescences; living acts are from a principle of life.
sources.raw_question: What is the source of the believer's power to obey God freely, according to Owen?

question: How does Paul's statement in Galatians 2:20 that 'Christ liveth in me' bear on the Christian's obedience?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: It shows that the obedience a believer yields to God while in the flesh springs from a principle of life, namely Christ living in him. The 'life which I now live in the flesh' means the obedience rendered to God in this life. That obedience is lived by faith in the Son of God.
sources.quote: The life which I now live in the flesh (that is, the obedience which I yield unto God whilst I am in the flesh), it is from a principle of life, Christ living in me.
sources.raw_question: How does Paul's statement in Galatians 2:20 that 'Christ liveth in me' bear on the Christian's obedience?

question: Were the smoke, fire, cloud and darkness on Mount Sinai the very substance of God (whether of the Son or the Holy Spirit)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Of the Appearance on Sinai. Whether the Trinity Spake in that Appearance or Some One Person Specially.
sources.answer: No. No sane person could believe these things to be the substance of the Word and Wisdom of God or of the Holy Spirit; even the Arians never said they were the substance of the Father. They were wrought through the creature serving the Creator and presented in a fitting economy to human senses.
sources.quote: All these things, then, were wrought through the creature serving the Creator, and were presented in a suitable economy (dispensatio) to human senses
sources.raw_question: Were the smoke, fire, cloud and darkness on Mount Sinai the very substance of God (whether of the Son or the Holy Spirit)?

question: Does the statement that the elders of Israel 'saw the place where the God of Israel had stood' imply that the Word of God in His own substance occupied a local place?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Of the Appearance on Sinai. Whether the Trinity Spake in that Appearance or Some One Person Specially.
sources.answer: No. The Word 'reacheth firmly from end to end, and sweetly ordereth all things,' and by Him all things were made; to suppose He stood within an earthly space would make Him changeable, contracting and expanding, which is impious.
sources.quote: that the Word of God, by whom all things were made, is in such wise changeable, as now to contract, now to expand Himself; (may the Lord cleanse the hearts of His faithful ones from such thoughts!)
sources.raw_question: Does the statement that the elders of Israel 'saw the place where the God of Israel had stood' imply that the Word of God in His own substance occupied a local place?

question: Can it be determined whether the Trinity or a particular Person spoke on Mount Sinai, and if one Person, which?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Of the Appearance on Sinai. Whether the Trinity Spake in that Appearance or Some One Person Specially.
sources.answer: It is not clearly determinable; but as a hesitant conjecture, it may be understood of the Holy Spirit. The Law was written by the finger of God, which the Gospel shows signifies the Spirit; fifty days separate Passover from Sinai as Resurrection from Pentecost; and the fire on Sinai matches the tongues of fire at Pentecost. Yet since Father or Son could not appear there without the Spirit, Augustine does not see that a special Person appeared distinguished by a proper mark.
sources.quote: why do we not rather understand the Holy Spirit to be spoken of, since the Law itself also, which was given there, is said to have been written upon tables of stone with the finger of God
sources.raw_question: Can it be determined whether the Trinity or a particular Person spoke on Mount Sinai, and if one Person, which?

question: How does our ability to judge one good thing as better than another show that we have some knowledge of the supreme good, God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How God May Be Known to Be the Chief Good. The Mind Does Not Become Good Unless by Turning to God.
sources.answer: We could not truly judge one good to be better than another unless a notion of the good itself had been impressed on us. This standard lets us approve things as good and prefer one to another. That standard is the good itself, which is God, so God is known as the norm behind all our judgments of goodness.
sources.quote: we could not say that one was better than another, when we judge truly, unless a conception of the good itself had been impressed upon us, such that according to it we might both approve some things as good, and prefer one good to another.
sources.raw_question: How does our ability to judge one good thing as better than another show that we have some knowledge of the supreme good, God?

question: Is God the Father inactive when 'silent', so that He gains the power to create only by speaking or begetting the Word?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Marcellus and his disciples, like Arians, say that the Word was, not indeed created, but issued, to create us, as if the Divine silence were a state of inaction, and when God spake by the Word, He acted; or that there was a going forth and return of the Word; a doctrine which implies change and imperfection in Father and Son.
sources.answer: No. Even humans are active in thought when silent, so to call God inactive in silence gives Him less than us. If the Father could not make when silent, He must have gained power by begetting, which implies imperfection in Him. If He could make with the Word within Him, then begetting for the sake of creation would be needless.
sources.quote: For we oftentimes, even when silent, yet are active in thinking, so as to form the results of our thoughts into images; but God they would have inactive when silent
sources.raw_question: Is God the Father inactive when 'silent', so that He gains the power to create only by speaking or begetting the Word?

question: Why can the human soul hope to pass from wretchedness to blessedness, given that God is unchangeable?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Although the Soul Hopes for Blessedness, Yet It Does Not Remember Lost Blessedness, But Remembers God and the Rules of Righteousness. The Unchangeable Rules of Right Living are Known Even to the Ungodly.
sources.answer: Because the soul itself is changeable. If it were not changeable, just as it could not have become wretched after being blessed, so neither could it become blessed after being wretched. Its mutability, unlike God's immutability, is what makes both its fall and its restoration possible.
sources.quote: nor can it hope for the possibility of this on any other ground than its own changeableness for if it were not changeable, then, as it could not become wretched after being blessed, so neither could it become blessed after being wretched.
sources.raw_question: Why can the human soul hope to pass from wretchedness to blessedness, given that God is unchangeable?

question: Where do even ungodly people see the unchangeable rules of righteousness by which they rightly judge human conduct?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Although the Soul Hopes for Blessedness, Yet It Does Not Remember Lost Blessedness, But Remembers God and the Rules of Righteousness. The Unchangeable Rules of Right Living are Known Even to the Ungodly.
sources.answer: In the divine Light called Truth, not in their own minds. Their minds are changeable and unrighteous, while these rules are seen as unchangeable and righteous. The rules are impressed from that Light onto the heart, as a ring's seal passes into wax without leaving the ring.
sources.quote: Where, then, are they written, unless in the book of that Light which is called Truth? whence every righteous law is copied and transferred (not by migrating to it, but by being as it were impressed upon it) to the heart of the man that worketh righteousness
sources.raw_question: Where do even ungodly people see the unchangeable rules of righteousness by which they rightly judge human conduct?

question: Why did Peter baptize the Gentile household of Cornelius, and what does the Holy Spirit's coming upon them show?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Peter baptized them because the Holy Spirit had visibly rested upon them, as it had on the Jewish believers. He would not otherwise have admitted them so readily, since he still held to the old covenant. The Spirit's coming was the divine warrant that removed any objection to their baptism. Through it the apostles yielded the Gentiles up to the Spirit of God.
sources.quote: Neither, for a like reason, would he have given them baptism so readily, had he not heard them prophesying when the Holy Ghost rested upon them.
sources.raw_question: Why did Peter baptize the Gentile household of Cornelius, and what does the Holy Spirit's coming upon them show?

question: What do divine attributes such as "incorruptible" or "Giver of life" actually tell us about God?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: They either forbid us to conceive what we ought not to conceive of God or teach us what we ought to conceive of Him, but they do not explain what His nature is. "Incorruptible" declares what His nature does not suffer, not what it is that does not suffer decay; "Giver of life" shows what He gives, not what the Giver is. Each term has a distinct sense fitted to the divine nature without expressing its essence.
sources.quote: when we say that He is incorruptible, we declare what His nature does not suffer, but we do not express what that is which does not suffer corruption
sources.raw_question: What do divine attributes such as "incorruptible" or "Giver of life" actually tell us about God?

question: Can the Father be pictured as containing lower beings in concentric spheres or squares, the farthest of which is ignorant of Him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. That would shut God up within a definite form and space. It would also imply something outside Him that surrounds Him, and the chain of containers and contained would run on to infinity. All such beings would plainly be bodies enclosed by one another.
sources.quote: they must shut up their Bythus within a definite form and space, while He both surrounds others, and is surrounded by them; for they must of necessity acknowledge that there is something outside of Him which surrounds Him.
sources.raw_question: Can the Father be pictured as containing lower beings in concentric spheres or squares, the farthest of which is ignorant of Him?

question: Could God be a vacuity, an empty space containing other beings without filling them?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: No. Saying so is the greatest blasphemy because it denies God's spiritual nature. A being that cannot fill even the things within Him could not be a spiritual being.
sources.quote: If, on the other hand, they acknowledge that He is vacuity, then they fall into the greatest blasphemy; they deny His spiritual nature. For how can He be a spiritual being, who cannot fill even those things which are within Him?
sources.raw_question: Could God be a vacuity, an empty space containing other beings without filling them?

question: Does the parable of the rich man and Lazarus teach that human souls survive death without passing into other bodies, keeping their recognisable form and their memory of earthly life?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXIV.—Souls can be recognised in the separate state, and are immortal although they once had a beginning.
sources.answer: Yes. In the narrative the rich man recognises Lazarus and Abraham after death, remembers his former deeds, and each remains in his proper place. This plainly shows that souls continue to exist, do not transmigrate, keep the form of a man so they can be recognised, and receive a dwelling according to their deserts even before the judgment.
sources.quote: By these things, then, it is plainly declared that souls continue to exist, that they do not pass from body to body, that they possess the form of a man, so that they may be recognised, and retain the memory of things in this world
sources.raw_question: Does the parable of the rich man and Lazarus teach that human souls survive death without passing into other bodies, keeping their recognisable form and their memory of earthly life?

question: Was Cicero right that the blessed would need none of the virtues and would be happy solely by knowing and contemplating nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > Whether Justice and the Other Virtues Cease to Exist in the Future Life.
sources.answer: Only in part. Augustine accepts that blessedness lies in contemplation, but he holds that the nature to be contemplated is the nature that created and appointed all other natures, namely God. Because justice is subjection to the government of that nature, justice does not become unnecessary in blessedness. It reaches its greatest perfection there.
sources.quote: It is that nature which created and appointed all other natures. And if it belongs to justice to be subject to the government of this nature then justice is certainly immortal
sources.raw_question: Was Cicero right that the blessed would need none of the virtues and would be happy solely by knowing and contemplating nature?

question: In what sense is the exalted Christ above the angels, both good and bad?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: He is exalted far above all angelic principalities and powers, which are all under his feet. Seated at God's right hand in the highest possible exaltation, he possesses a kingdom over the whole creation and a name above every name, so that angels are at his command and absolute disposal.
sources.quote: They are all under his feet, — at his command and absolute disposal. He is at the right hand of God, in the highest exaltation possible, and in full possession of a kingdom over the whole creation
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the exalted Christ above the angels, both good and bad?

question: What does the bride's description of her Beloved's head as fine gold (Song of Solomon 5:11) signify about Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Taken politically, the golden head signifies the splendour and eternity of Christ's government. Taken naturally, it may point to the glory of his Deity or to the fulness of his wisdom, since the head is the seat of wisdom. The allegory need not be narrowed to one meaning, so long as the reading stays within the analogy of faith.
sources.quote: either the glory of his Deity is here attended to, or the fulness and excellency of his wisdom, which the head is the seat of. The allegory is not to be straitened, whilst we keep to the analogy of faith.
sources.raw_question: What does the bride's description of her Beloved's head as fine gold (Song of Solomon 5:11) signify about Christ?

question: Should exousia in John 10:18 be read as mere delegated 'authority' rather than 'power'?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. The same word is rendered 'power' when used of the Father in Luke 12:5 and Acts 1:7. The preceding clause, 'no one taketh it from me', declares that the gift of his life is spontaneous.
sources.quote: Unitarians object to εξουσία being here translated “power,” (they would prefer “authority,”) but it is so rendered of the Father’s power, Luke 12:5, Acts 1:7
sources.raw_question: Should exousia in John 10:18 be read as mere delegated 'authority' rather than 'power'?

question: Do the miracles done 'by the name of thy holy child Jesus' show that the Son is only an instrument and not the author of miraculous healing?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Acts 4:29-30 exalts the Father. Acts 9:34, 'Jesus Christ maketh thee whole', just as clearly exalts the Son as the immediate Author of miraculous healing.
sources.quote: If the first exalts the Father; the second, as distinctly, exalts the Son as the immediate Author of miraculous healing.
sources.raw_question: Do the miracles done 'by the name of thy holy child Jesus' show that the Son is only an instrument and not the author of miraculous healing?

question: Does the fact that conception can fabricate falsehoods, such as monsters and lying wonders, show that it is unable to reach real truth?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. The same art serves opposite ends: a physician can heal or poison, and a helmsman can steer for port or for the rocks. In the same way, conception was implanted for good, though it can be abused. Its ability to give plausible shape to what is unreal is itself evidence that it can investigate what truly subsists, and so arrive at higher knowledge.
sources.quote: it is none the less competent to investigate what actually and in very truth subsists, and its ability for the one must in fairness be regarded as an evidence of its ability for the other.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that conception can fabricate falsehoods, such as monsters and lying wonders, show that it is unable to reach real truth?

question: What must a scriptural type have in common with the reality it foreshadows?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIII.—The woman who suffered from an issue of blood was no type of the suffering Æon.
sources.answer: A type may differ from the truth it signifies in matter and substance. But it must keep a likeness to that truth in its general form and features. Only so can present things shadow forth things to come.
sources.quote: For a type and emblem is, no doubt, sometimes diverse from the truth [signified] as to matter and substance; but it ought, as to the general form and features, to maintain a likeness [to what is typified]
sources.raw_question: What must a scriptural type have in common with the reality it foreshadows?

question: How can the unchangeable God receive glory, since he cannot gain or lose anything?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: Nothing is added to God's glory, because it never decreased and cannot be replenished. The Father is glorified when he is made known to ignorant and fallen humanity. This happens through the Son, who uses the power over all flesh given him to bestow eternal life through the knowledge of God.
sources.quote: Nothing was added to God’s glory; it had not decreased, and so could not be replenished. But He is glorified through the Son in the sight of us, ignorant, exiled, defiled
sources.raw_question: How can the unchangeable God receive glory, since he cannot gain or lose anything?

question: When we count several things under one name, how do specific names and generic names relate to each other?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three Hypostases, the Latins of Three Persons. Scripture Nowhere Speaks of Three Persons in One God.
sources.answer: Whatever several things can be named in the plural by one specific name can also be named by one generic name, but not the reverse. Three horses are also three animals. A horse, an ox and a dog, however, can only be called three animals or three substances, because they differ in nature. Things share a name in the plural only when they have in common what that name signifies.
sources.quote: But whatsoever things are expressed in the plural number specifically by one name, can also be expressed generically by one name. But all things which are generically called by one name cannot also be called specifically by one name.
sources.raw_question: When we count several things under one name, how do specific names and generic names relate to each other?

question: What does Romans 8:16 mean when it says the Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: It alludes to a judicial trial over a title: the soul pleads before God's law that it is God's child, producing the evidences of its faith, while Satan, sin and the law contest them. In the midst of this contest the Holy Spirit comes in as a witness of approved integrity, and by a word of promise or otherwise overpowers the heart with a comfortable persuasion that its plea is good. He also enables filial obedience, called crying 'Abba, Father.'
sources.quote: In the midst of the plea and contest the Comforter comes, and, by a word of promise or otherwise, overpowers the heart with a comfortable persuasion (and bears down all objections) that his plea is good, and that he is a child of God.
sources.raw_question: What does Romans 8:16 mean when it says the Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God?

question: Why does the Holy Spirit's witness of adoption sometimes come only after a long delay?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Because the Spirit works effectually, voluntarily and freely, when and how he wills. The soul's own witness from its faith and experience may keep up the plea for years. But the matter is not settled until the Spirit freely adds his testimony.
sources.quote: the work is not done, the conquest is not fully obtained, until the Spirit, who worketh freely and effectually, when and how he will, comes in with his testimony also
sources.raw_question: Why does the Holy Spirit's witness of adoption sometimes come only after a long delay?

question: What does Paul mean in 2 Corinthians 5:21 when he says God "made" Christ, who knew no sin, "to be sin"?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > The sixth book shows that He Who came for man's salvation was not a mere man, as Eunomius, falsely slandering him, affirmed that the great Basil had said, but the Only-begotten Son of God, putting on human flesh, and becoming a mediator between God and man, on Whom we believe, as subject to suffering in the flesh, but impassible in His Godhead; and demonstrates the calumny of Eunomius.
sources.answer: Here Paul gives the name "sin" to the flesh. The verse therefore refers to the Son's taking on human flesh, not to his divine essence. By parity of reasoning, Eunomius cannot refer the word "made" in other texts to the Son's pre-temporal essence, or he would have to say the Son's essence was made sin.
sources.quote: He made Him to be sin for us, Who knew no sin,” giving once more the name of “sin” to the flesh.
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean in 2 Corinthians 5:21 when he says God "made" Christ, who knew no sin, "to be sin"?

question: Does divine counsel involve God deliberating over uncertain or doubtful matters?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter II. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are One in counsel.
sources.answer: No. The counsel shared by Father, Son, and Spirit does not concern doubtful matters. It concerns things already foreknown and determined.
sources.quote: Counsel, not concerning any doubtful matters, but concerning those foreknown and determined.
sources.raw_question: Does divine counsel involve God deliberating over uncertain or doubtful matters?

question: Is faith in the Son's oneness with the Father what distinguished Peter, who received the keys of the kingdom, from Judas, who perished?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVII. St. Ambrose shows by instances that the places in which those words were spoken help to the understanding of the words of the Lord; he shows that Christ uttered the passage quoted from St. John in Solomon's porch, by which is signified the mind of a wise man, for he says that Christ would not have uttered this saying in the heart of a foolish or contentious man. He goes on to say that Christ is stoned by those who believe not these words, and as the keys of heaven were given to Peter for his confession of them, so Iscariot, because he believed not the same, perished evilly. He takes this opportunity to inveigh against the Jews who bought the Son of God and sold Joseph. He explains the price paid for each mystically; and having in the same manner expounded the murmuring of the traitor concerning Magdalene's ointment, he adds that Christ is bought in one way by heretics in another way by Catholics, and that those in vain take to themselves the name of Christians who sever the Spirit from the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Peter believed that Christ is one with the Father, and for this he received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power to forgive sins. Judas did not believe it and strangled himself with the cord of his own wickedness. Confession of the Son's unity with the Father is thus the dividing line between salvation and ruin.
sources.quote: Thou hast Thyself said that Thou art one with the Father. Because Peter believed this, he received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and without anxiety for himself forgave sins. Judas, because he believed not this, strangled himself
sources.raw_question: Is faith in the Son's oneness with the Father what distinguished Peter, who received the keys of the kingdom, from Judas, who perished?

question: Why was Christ sold for thirty pieces of silver while Joseph, his type, was sold for twenty?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XVII. St. Ambrose shows by instances that the places in which those words were spoken help to the understanding of the words of the Lord; he shows that Christ uttered the passage quoted from St. John in Solomon's porch, by which is signified the mind of a wise man, for he says that Christ would not have uttered this saying in the heart of a foolish or contentious man. He goes on to say that Christ is stoned by those who believe not these words, and as the keys of heaven were given to Peter for his confession of them, so Iscariot, because he believed not the same, perished evilly. He takes this opportunity to inveigh against the Jews who bought the Son of God and sold Joseph. He explains the price paid for each mystically; and having in the same manner expounded the murmuring of the traitor concerning Magdalene's ointment, he adds that Christ is bought in one way by heretics in another way by Catholics, and that those in vain take to themselves the name of Christians who sever the Spirit from the Father.
sources.answer: Christ's true value cannot be limited, so any price set on him is an error. Still, the difference is meaningful. The truth is worth more than the type, grace is more generous than training, and Christ's presence is better than the Law. The Law promised his coming, and his coming fulfilled the Law.
sources.quote: The sale is for twenty pieces in the Old Testament, for thirty in the New; for the Truth is of more value than the type, Grace is more generous than training, the Presence is better than the Law
sources.raw_question: Why was Christ sold for thirty pieces of silver while Joseph, his type, was sold for twenty?

question: Since God ordained apostles, prophets and teachers in the Church, does that mean they were not ordained by Christ?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: No. Paul himself says that grace was given according to the measure of the gift of Christ, and that He who descended and ascended gave some to be apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers. Hence what God ordains is equally Christ's gift.
sources.quote: But perhaps thou maintainest that they have not been ordained by Christ, because it was God Who ordained them. But thou shalt hear what the Apostle says himself
sources.raw_question: Since God ordained apostles, prophets and teachers in the Church, does that mean they were not ordained by Christ?

question: Is it fitting that the righteous receive their reward in the same created world in which they suffered, rather than only in a heavenly realm?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXII.—In that flesh in which the saints have suffered so many afflictions, they shall receive the fruits of their labours; especially since all creation waits for this, and God promises it to Abraham and his seed.
sources.answer: Yes. It is just that the righteous be rewarded, revived and made to reign in the very creation where they toiled, were slain for love of God, and endured servitude. God is rich in all things and all things are His, so creation restored to its first condition should be under the dominion of the righteous. Paul confirms this when he says creation waits to be delivered from corruption into the liberty of the sons of God.
sources.quote: For it is just that in that very creation in which they toiled or were afflicted, being proved in every way by suffering, they should receive the reward of their suffering
sources.raised_by_detail: certain orthodox persons whose opinions derive from heretical discourses
sources.raw_question: Is it fitting that the righteous receive their reward in the same created world in which they suffered, rather than only in a heavenly realm?

question: Since Abraham never possessed the land God promised him, how is God's promise to Abraham fulfilled?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXII.—In that flesh in which the saints have suffered so many afflictions, they shall receive the fruits of their labours; especially since all creation waits for this, and God promises it to Abraham and his seed.
sources.answer: It will be fulfilled at the resurrection of the just. Abraham lived in the land as a stranger and pilgrim and even bought his burial place rather than accept it as a gift. Because God is true and faithful, Abraham and his seed, those who believe, must receive the inheritance when the just are raised. This is also why Christ said the meek shall inherit the earth.
sources.quote: If, then, God promised him the inheritance of the land, yet he did not receive it during all the time of his sojourn there, it must be, that together with his seed, that is, those who fear God and believe in Him, he shall receive it at the resurrection of the just.
sources.raw_question: Since Abraham never possessed the land God promised him, how is God's promise to Abraham fulfilled?

question: Could a wise man be blessed while remaining indifferent to whether death takes his blessed life away?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Blessedness Cannot Exist Without Immortality.
sources.answer: No. A life whose flourishing or perishing a man accepts with indifference is not loved by him. A life its possessor does not love is unworthy to be called blessed. Such indifference would also contradict the certain truth that all men will to be blessed. The Creator implanted that will in human nature.
sources.quote: For how is that a blessed life which the blessed man does not love? Or how is that loved, of which it is received indifferently, whether it is to flourish or to perish?
sources.raised_by_detail: philosophers who counsel an even heart toward death
sources.raw_question: Could a wise man be blessed while remaining indifferent to whether death takes his blessed life away?

question: When Christ, wearied by his journey, asks the Samaritan woman for a drink at the well, what does his thirst signify?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XVI. The Holy Spirit is that large river by which the mystical Jerusalem is watered. It is equal to its Fount, that is, the Father and the Son, as is signified in holy Scripture. St. Ambrose himself thirsts for that water, and warns us that in order to preserve it within us, we must avoid the devil, lust, and heresy, since our vessels are frail, and that broken cisterns must be forsaken, that after the example of the Samaritan woman and of the patriarchs we may find the water of the Lord.
sources.answer: His thirst is not for ordinary water but for our salvation. Ambrose says Christ is wearied by long seeking the unbeliever, and he asks to drink as the one who is about to give. What he drinks is our salvation, our good dispositions, and the cup of his Passion, which atoned for sin. The believer, drinking his blood, has the world's thirst quenched.
sources.quote: He asks to drink Who is about to give. But He drinks not the water of a stream flowing by, but thy salvation; He drinks thy good dispositions, He drinks the cup, that is, the Passion which atoned for thy sins
sources.raw_question: When Christ, wearied by his journey, asks the Samaritan woman for a drink at the well, what does his thirst signify?

question: Could Christ, who is the truth, have acknowledged as his Father and as supreme God a being (the Gnostic Demiurge) that he knew to be defective and imperfect?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter V.—Christ and His apostles, without any fraud, deception, or hypocrisy, preached that one God, the Father, was the founder of all things. They did not accommodate their doctrine to the prepossessions of their hearers.
sources.answer: No. Christ is the truth and no lie is in him, and a lie has no fellowship with truth as darkness has none with light. Therefore he would never have called an imperfect being, originating from a defect, the God of all and his own Father. The one he named as Father and God is truly the supreme God.
sources.quote: Our Lord, therefore, being the truth, did not speak lies; and whom He knew to have taken origin from a defect, He never would have acknowledged as God, even the God of all, the Supreme King, too, and His own Father
sources.raw_question: Could Christ, who is the truth, have acknowledged as his Father and as supreme God a being (the Gnostic Demiurge) that he knew to be defective and imperfect?

question: Did Christ and the apostles accommodate their teaching about God to their hearers' opinions, preaching the Demiurge to some and a hidden higher Father to others?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter V.—Christ and His apostles, without any fraud, deception, or hypocrisy, preached that one God, the Father, was the founder of all things. They did not accommodate their doctrine to the prepossessions of their hearers.
sources.answer: No. Teaching that adapts to error belongs to those who spread disease and ignorance, not to those who heal. Christ came as physician to the sick, and a physician prescribes what the cure requires, not what the patient wishes. So the Lord and the apostles taught according to revealed truth and saving doctrine, without hypocrisy or respect of persons.
sources.quote: He therefore did not address them in accordance with their pristine notions, nor did He reply to them in harmony with the opinion of His questioners, but according to the doctrine leading to salvation, without hypocrisy or respect of person.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ and the apostles accommodate their teaching about God to their hearers' opinions, preaching the Demiurge to some and a hidden higher Father to others?

question: Are the deliverances performed by angels the angels' own works?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: No. It is proper to an angel to minister at God's command, as in casting out the Amorite or guarding the people; these are not the angel's doings but God's, who commanded and sent him and to whom alone it belongs to deliver.
sources.quote: It is proper then to an Angel to minister at the command of God, and often does he go forth to cast out the Amorite, and is sent to guard the people in the way; but these are not his doings, but of God
sources.raw_question: Are the deliverances performed by angels the angels' own works?

question: Why is the Word of God truly Truth and incapable of anything false?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > The Word of God is in All Things Equal to the Father, from Whom It is.
sources.answer: Whatever is in the knowledge from which the Word is born is also in the Word, and whatever is not in that knowledge is not in the Word. The Word is also unchangeable, as the Father is, so it can contain nothing false.
sources.quote: this Word is truly truth, since whatever is in that knowledge from which it is born is also in itself and whatever is not in that knowledge is not in the Word
sources.raw_question: Why is the Word of God truly Truth and incapable of anything false?

question: What, strictly speaking, counts as 'passion', and are the natural processes of the body such as birth, growth and dissolution properly passions?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: Only what tends to sin and opposes the virtuous unimpassioned state is truly passion, namely a diseased condition of the will. The natural routine of a composite body, being combined from elements and later dissolved back into them, is rather a work of nature than a passion. It is called passion only by a customary abuse of terms.
sources.quote: nothing is truly “passion” which does not tend to sin, nor would one strictly call by the name of “passion” the necessary routine of nature, regarding the composite nature as it goes on its course in a kind of order and sequence.
sources.raw_question: What, strictly speaking, counts as 'passion', and are the natural processes of the body such as birth, growth and dissolution properly passions?

question: How can those who hear and learn from the Father come to the Son when no one has ever seen or heard the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: The Father teaches through the words of the Son. Though seen by none, he speaks to us in the manifestation of the Son. The Son by his perfect birth possesses all the properties of the Father's nature, so to hear the Son's teaching is to hear the teaching of the Father.
sources.quote: it is manifest, therefore, that the Father teaches through the words of the Son, and, though seen of none, speaks to us in the manifestation of the Son, because the Son, by virtue of His perfect birth, possesses all the properties of His Father’s nature
sources.raw_question: How can those who hear and learn from the Father come to the Son when no one has ever seen or heard the Father?

question: Do the angels worship and ascribe divine honour to Christ the Lamb, and on what account?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. In Revelation 5 the whole host of heaven ascribes power, riches, wisdom, strength, honour, glory and blessing to the Lamb together with him who sits on the throne. The reason given is that he was the Lamb that was slain, that is, because of his work of redemption in bringing sinners to God.
sources.quote: The reason given of this glorious and wonderful doxology, this attribution of honour and glory to Jesus Christ by the whole host of heaven, is, because he was the Lamb that was slain
sources.raw_question: Do the angels worship and ascribe divine honour to Christ the Lamb, and on what account?

question: Does a being's will correspond to its nature, so that beings unlike in nature must also be unlike in will?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Proof that the Anomœan teaching tends to Manichæism.
sources.answer: Yes. Will is intimately joined to nature, so things unlike in nature will also be unlike in will. If their powers are equal as well, this difference in will produces mutual discord and a contest for primacy. That is why a Son different in nature from the Father could not truly be one with Him.
sources.quote: we must perforce allow that will corresponds with, and is intimately joined to nature; and that if two things are unlike in nature, they will be so also in will.
sources.raw_question: Does a being's will correspond to its nature, so that beings unlike in nature must also be unlike in will?

question: Is there anything in the human mind that helps us understand the procession of the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are.
sources.answer: Yes, in a limited way. The love joined to the mind's word by the will offers an analogy for the procession of the Holy Spirit. Like the analogy for the Word's generation, it gives only conjecture and is hindered by the great disparity between the image and God.
sources.quote: and, again, respecting the procession of the Holy Spirit, from the love that is joined thereto by the will.
sources.raw_question: Is there anything in the human mind that helps us understand the procession of the Holy Spirit?

question: What does Christ's request in John 12, that the Father glorify his name, mean?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Christ asked the Father to make his name glorious in the work of redemption, and 'name' here means God's nature, properties, and will. The answer from heaven, 'I have both glorified it and will glorify it again,' shows that God gives his attributes their utmost glory in Christ.
sources.quote: to make in him his name (that is, his nature, his properties, his will) all glorious in that work of redemption he had in hand, — he was instantly answered from heaven, “I have both glorified it and will glorify it again.”
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's request in John 12, that the Father glorify his name, mean?

question: Does 2 Samuel 23:2-3 identify the Spirit of the LORD who spoke by David with the God and Rock of Israel?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. David says the Spirit of the Lord spoke by him and, in the next verse, that the God of Israel and the Rock of Israel spoke to him. Unless one posits two or three divine speakers inspiring David, the Spirit of Jehovah must be the God and Rock of Israel.
sources.quote: Therefore, unless you admit that there were three, or at least two, Divine speakers who inspired David, the Spirit of Jehovah is the God and the Rock of Israel.
sources.raw_question: Does 2 Samuel 23:2-3 identify the Spirit of the LORD who spoke by David with the God and Rock of Israel?

question: When the soul becomes 'one spirit' with the Lord by cleaving to Him, does God increase in His nature, truth or blessedness?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Mind Loves God in Rightly Loving Itself; And If It Love Not God, It Must Be Said to Hate Itself. Even a Weak and Erring Mind is Always Strong in Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself. Let It Be Turned to God, that It May Be Blessed by Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Him.
sources.answer: No. The soul becomes one spirit with the Lord by drawing near to share in His nature, truth and blessedness. God does not grow in His own nature, truth or blessedness. The change is entirely on the side of the creature, while God stays unchangeable.
sources.quote: And this by its drawing near to partake of His nature, truth, and blessedness, yet not by His increasing in His own nature, truth and blessedness.
sources.raw_question: When the soul becomes 'one spirit' with the Lord by cleaving to Him, does God increase in His nature, truth or blessedness?

question: What is the unchangeable good that will satisfy the desire of the soul made in God's image?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Mind Loves God in Rightly Loving Itself; And If It Love Not God, It Must Be Said to Hate Itself. Even a Weak and Erring Mind is Always Strong in Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Itself. Let It Be Turned to God, that It May Be Blessed by Remembering, Understanding, and Loving Him.
sources.answer: It is the very Trinity itself, the soul's own God, whose image it is. Cleaving to Him, the soul will live unchangeably and will be so filled with Him that sin will never again delight it.
sources.quote: “His desire will be satisfied with good things,” good things unchangeable,—the very Trinity itself, its own God, whose image it is.
sources.raw_question: What is the unchangeable good that will satisfy the desire of the soul made in God's image?
