question: Was Thomas's cry "My Lord and my God!" in John 20:28 an exclamation of surprise addressed to God the Father, or an address to Jesus Christ as God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: It was addressed to Christ as God. The text says Thomas "answered and said," showing the words were a response directed to the One standing before him, his proven risen Saviour. Anyone who knows the language of the heart cannot read it as a mere exclamation to the Father; it was the deep response of Thomas's heart to Christ.
sources.quote: not without reason is the word “answered” here inserted – the words were addressed as an answer to One who stood his proven Saviour before him: – it was the deep response of the heart of Thomas to Christ
sources.raw_question: Was Thomas's cry "My Lord and my God!" in John 20:28 an exclamation of surprise addressed to God the Father, or an address to Jesus Christ as God?

question: What is the source of heretical dissensions over the doctrine of God in the interpretation of Scripture?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: Such dissensions come from a distorted mind. It twists the words of Scripture to fit its own opinion instead of adjusting its opinion to Scripture. Right doctrine requires conforming one's views to the text.
sources.quote: these dissensions concerning the faith result from a distorted mind, which twists the words of Scripture into conformity with its opinion, instead of adjusting that opinion to the words of Scripture.
sources.raw_question: What is the source of heretical dissensions over the doctrine of God in the interpretation of Scripture?

question: Does Exodus 33:20, 'No man shall see God and live,' refer to a hidden supreme Father (the Gnostic Bythus) distinct from the Creator of the world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XIX.—Passages of Scripture by which they attempt to prove that the Supreme Father was unknown before the coming of Christ.
sources.answer: No. The words do refer to the invisible Father, but that Father is the Maker of the universe, not a supposed Bythus above him. The Gnostics wrongly hold that the Creator was seen by the prophets and so reserve invisibility for a higher deity. In fact the Creator himself is the invisible God, as Irenaeus promises to show more fully later.
sources.quote: but that they are not used concerning that Bythus whom they conjure into existence, but concerning the Creator (and He is the invisible God), shall be shown as we proceed.
sources.raw_question: Does Exodus 33:20, 'No man shall see God and live,' refer to a hidden supreme Father (the Gnostic Bythus) distinct from the Creator of the world?

question: Why is Christ, the only Son of God, the most fitting priest to offer a true sacrifice to God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Christ the Most Perfect Victim for Cleansing Our Faults. In Every Sacrifice Four Things are to Be Considered.
sources.answer: Because he alone is perfectly righteous and holy. A true sacrifice can only be rightly offered by a holy and righteous priest, and the Son of God had no need to purge any sins of his own by sacrifice, neither original sin nor sins added in the course of human life.
sources.quote: Who then is so righteous and holy a priest as the only Son of God, who had no need to purge His own sins by sacrifice,
sources.raw_question: Why is Christ, the only Son of God, the most fitting priest to offer a true sacrifice to God?

question: Why was Christ's human flesh, born of a virgin, the fitting offering for cleansing mortal men?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Christ the Most Perfect Victim for Cleansing Our Faults. In Every Sacrifice Four Things are to Be Considered.
sources.answer: Because a sacrifice must be taken from those for whom it is offered, and it must be without fault. Human flesh was taken from men, and mortal flesh could be immolated. Flesh born of a virgin without any infection of carnal concupiscence was clean, so it could cleanse the faulty.
sources.quote: And what so clean for cleansing the faults of mortal men as the flesh born in and from the womb of a virgin, without any infection of carnal concupiscence?
sources.raw_question: Why was Christ's human flesh, born of a virgin, the fitting offering for cleansing mortal men?

question: Does the fact that demons desire sacrifices show that true sacrifice is owed only to the one true God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > Christ the Most Perfect Victim for Cleansing Our Faults. In Every Sacrifice Four Things are to Be Considered.
sources.answer: Yes. Even the proudest spirits could not delight in the honour of sacrifices unless a true sacrifice were owed to the one true God. They covet that honour precisely because they want to be worshipped in God's place.
sources.quote: not even the proudest of spirits themselves could rejoice in the honor of sacrifices, unless a true sacrifice was due to the one true God, in whose stead they desire to be worshipped
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that demons desire sacrifices show that true sacrifice is owed only to the one true God?

question: Do Isaiah's vision of the seraphim and John 12:39-41 show that the glory of the LORD seen by Isaiah was the glory of Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen reads Isaiah 6 together with John 12:39-41: the angels who cover their faces in the vision do so in the presence of "our Beloved," Christ. They know they cannot bear the rays of his glory. Christ is therefore the LORD whose glory Isaiah saw.
sources.quote: do cover their faces at the presence of our Beloved, as conscious to themselves of their utter disability to bear the rays of his glory, Isa. vi. 2; John xii. 39–41
sources.raw_question: Do Isaiah's vision of the seraphim and John 12:39-41 show that the glory of the LORD seen by Isaiah was the glory of Christ?

question: What is the difference between the service Christians owe one another (douleuein) and the service owed to God alone (latreuein)?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Douleuein is the service of love that believers are commanded to give one another. Latreuein is the service due to God alone, which may not be given to any creature. The command "Him only shalt thou serve" uses latreuseis, and it is this kind of service that is paid to the Spirit.
sources.quote: not in the sense in which we are commanded to “serve” one another by love, which is in Greek δουλεύειν, but in that in which God alone is served, which is in Greek λατρεύειν.
sources.raw_question: What is the difference between the service Christians owe one another (douleuein) and the service owed to God alone (latreuein)?

question: Is the Gnostic scheme of emanations from a first principle (Bythus and the Pleroma) a true account of the divine origin of things, or is it borrowed from Pythagorean number-philosophy?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIV.—Valentinus and his followers derived the principles of their system from the heathen; the names only are changed.
sources.answer: It is borrowed. The Pythagoreans made the One the first principle and substance of all things and derived the Dyad, Tetrad and so on from it. The heretics repeat this word for word, applying it to their Pleroma and Bythus, and Marcus simply presents the Tetrad of Pythagoras as the mother of all things.
sources.quote: These things the heretics repeat, word for word, with a reference to their Pleroma and Bythus.
sources.raw_question: Is the Gnostic scheme of emanations from a first principle (Bythus and the Pleroma) a true account of the divine origin of things, or is it borrowed from Pythagorean number-philosophy?

question: Were the prophetic utterances about divine truth hidden mysteries unintelligible to the prophets themselves and to their hearers?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIV.—Valentinus and his followers derived the principles of their system from the heathen; the names only are changed.
sources.answer: No. The things predicted were not of such a nature as to be intelligible to no one. The prophets knew what they were saying, as did their disciples and those who succeeded them. Scripture's revelation is therefore not a secret code passed on by an unknowing Demiurge's instruments.
sources.quote: the things which were predicted were not of such a nature as to be intelligible to no one; for the men themselves knew what they were saying, as did also their disciples, and those again succeeded these.
sources.raw_question: Were the prophetic utterances about divine truth hidden mysteries unintelligible to the prophets themselves and to their hearers?

question: Can a person who claims not to know God come to know God by loving his brother?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > That He Who Loves His Brother, Loves God; Because He Loves Love Itself, Which is of God, and is God.
sources.answer: Yes. Whoever loves his brother knows the love with which he loves more than the brother he loves, and that love is God. So God can be known more than the brother: more present, more within, more certain.
sources.quote: For he knows the love with which he loves, more than the brother whom he loves. So now he can know God more than he knows his brother: clearly known more, because more present; known more, because more within him; known more, because more certain.
sources.raw_question: Can a person who claims not to know God come to know God by loving his brother?

question: Why does John in 1 John 2:10 seem to place the perfection of righteousness in brotherly love while saying nothing about the love of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > That He Who Loves His Brother, Loves God; Because He Loves Love Itself, Which is of God, and is God.
sources.answer: Because John means God to be understood within brotherly love itself. A little later in the same epistle he says plainly that love is of God and that God is love. Brotherly love is thus not only from God but is God.
sources.quote: And yet he seems to have passed by the love of God in silence; which he never would have done, unless because he intends God to be understood in brotherly love itself.
sources.raw_question: Why does John in 1 John 2:10 seem to place the perfection of righteousness in brotherly love while saying nothing about the love of God?

question: What does 1 John 4:20 mean in asking how one who does not love his visible brother can love the unseen God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > That He Who Loves His Brother, Loves God; Because He Loves Love Itself, Which is of God, and is God.
sources.answer: Augustine reads it to mean that a person does not see God precisely because he does not love his brother. Without brotherly love he does not abide in love, and so not in God, who is love and light, and he remains in darkness. If he loved with spiritual love the brother he sees with bodily sight, he would see God, who is love itself, with inner sight.
sources.quote: because the reason that he does not see God is, that he does not love his brother.
sources.raw_question: What does 1 John 4:20 mean in asking how one who does not love his visible brother can love the unseen God?

question: Did the devil create any beings, so that wicked angels and men are evil by nature as his creation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XLI.—Those persons who do not believe in God, but who are disobedient, are angels and sons of the devil, not indeed by nature, but by imitation. Close of this book, and scope of the succeeding one.
sources.answer: No. The devil created nothing whatsoever, since he is himself a creature of God like the other angels, and God made all things. Those called 'angels of the devil' or 'children of the wicked one' are so called not by nature but because they follow him in apostasy and do his works.
sources.quote: But He made neither angels nor men so by nature. For we do not find that the devil created anything whatsoever, since indeed he is himself a creature of God, like the other angels.
sources.raw_question: Did the devil create any beings, so that wicked angels and men are evil by nature as his creation?

question: In how many senses can someone be called a 'son', and how do being born a son and being made a son differ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XLI.—Those persons who do not believe in God, but who are disobedient, are angels and sons of the devil, not indeed by nature, but by imitation. Close of this book, and scope of the succeeding one.
sources.answer: The word 'son' has a twofold meaning. One is a son by nature, being born from the person referred to; the other is made a son by him, whether through creation or by being taught his doctrine, as a disciple is called the son of his teacher. There is a real difference between being born a son and being made one.
sources.quote: For [the word] “son,” as one before me has observed, has a twofold meaning: one [is a son] in the order of nature, because he was born a son; the other, in that he was made so, is reputed a son
sources.raw_question: In how many senses can someone be called a 'son', and how do being born a son and being made a son differ?

question: Why was faith necessary for human beings with respect to the eternal Word, according to John 1:5 ('the light shineth in darkness')?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Attempt is Made to Distinguish Out of the Scriptures the Offices of Wisdom and of Knowledge. That in the Beginning of John Some Things that are Said Belong to Wisdom, Some to Knowledge. Some Things There are Only Known by the Help of Faith. How We See the Faith that is in Us. In the Same Narrative of John, Some Things are Known by the Sense of the Body, Others Only by the Reason of the Mind.
sources.answer: Faith was necessary because the 'darkness' signifies mortal hearts turned away from the divine light and hardly able to behold it. Since they could not see the Word, they had to believe what was not seen. For this reason John the Baptist was sent as a witness, so that all might believe through him.
sources.quote: For by “darkness” he intended to signify the hearts of mortals turned away from light of this kind, and hardly able to behold it
sources.raw_question: Why was faith necessary for human beings with respect to the eternal Word, according to John 1:5 ('the light shineth in darkness')?

question: What does the image of the manslayer fleeing to the city of refuge in Hebrews 6:17-18 teach about Christ and the Spirit?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: It teaches that Christ is the sinner's great and only refuge from the guilt of sin. The passage alludes to the manslayer under the law who fled to the city of refuge for deliverance. As believers flee to Christ in the same way, the Holy Spirit gives them consolation.
sources.quote: Our great and only refuge from the guilt of sin is the Lord Jesus Christ; in our flying to him, doth the Spirit administer consolation to us.
sources.raw_question: What does the image of the manslayer fleeing to the city of refuge in Hebrews 6:17-18 teach about Christ and the Spirit?

question: Does the ability of an untaught person to answer geometry questions correctly prove, as Plato held, that the soul pre-existed the body and that learning is really recollection?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > In Opposition to the Reminiscence of Plato and Pythagoras. Pythagoras the Samian. Of the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge, and of Seeking the Trinity in the Knowledge of Temporal Things.
sources.answer: No. If learning were recollection of a former life, then only those who were geometricians before could answer, yet nearly everyone can, though geometricians are very few. Rather, the intellectual mind is made by the Creator to see intelligible things by a unique incorporeal light, just as the bodily eye is made to see things in bodily light without having known them before.
sources.quote: the intellectual mind is so formed in its nature as to see those things, which by the disposition of the Creator are subjoined to things intelligible in a natural order, by a sort of incorporeal light of an unique kind
sources.raw_question: Does the ability of an untaught person to answer geometry questions correctly prove, as Plato held, that the soul pre-existed the body and that learning is really recollection?

question: Do the reported memories of Pythagoras and others of lives lived in earlier bodies show that souls transmigrate?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > In Opposition to the Reminiscence of Plato and Pythagoras. Pythagoras the Samian. Of the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge, and of Seeking the Trinity in the Knowledge of Temporal Things.
sources.answer: No. Such memories are likely false, like the false recollections in dreams, perhaps suggested by deceitful spirits who wish to spread false beliefs about the transmigration of souls. If souls truly remembered former lives, almost everyone would have such memories, since the transmigrationists hold that the living continually come from the dead.
sources.quote: it may be conjectured that these were untrue recollections, such as we commonly experience in sleep, when we fancy we remember, as though we had done or seen it, what we never did or saw at all
sources.raw_question: Do the reported memories of Pythagoras and others of lives lived in earlier bodies show that souls transmigrate?

question: How can one know the true apostolic faith about God against competing claims of secret knowledge?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter III.—A refutation of the heretics, from the fact that, in the various Churches, a perpetual succession of bishops was kept up.
sources.answer: By the public tradition preserved through the succession of bishops from the apostles. Anyone in any Church can contemplate this tradition, and the continuous succession, especially in the Church of Rome founded by Peter and Paul, is abundant proof that one and the same vivifying faith has been preserved from the apostles until now.
sources.quote: And this is most abundant proof that there is one and the same vivifying faith, which has been preserved in the Church from the apostles until now, and handed down in truth.
sources.raw_question: How can one know the true apostolic faith about God against competing claims of secret knowledge?

question: Why could a mere man not be the first of the new creation and renew humanity?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: A man made of earth alone, as we have become through the transgression, could not do it. Through such men the first creation had been lost. Someone else was needed to renew the first creation and preserve the new one, and that could be none other than the Lord himself.
sources.quote: now a man, made of earth only, such as we are become from the transgression, he could not be. For in the first creation, men had become unfaithful, and through them that first creation had been lost
sources.raw_question: Why could a mere man not be the first of the new creation and renew humanity?

question: Are thought, reflection, sensation, counsel, judgment and reason (logos) distinct beings, or are they stages of one mind's activity?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIII.—The first order of production maintained by the heretics is altogether indefensible.
sources.answer: They are one and the same activity of the mind, named differently as it develops. Like a human body called young, mature or old without any change of substance, these mental exercises all come from Nous and get different names according to their growth. Nous governs them all, and the spoken word proceeds from the inner logos.
sources.quote: But all the [exercises of thought] which have been mentioned are [fundamentally] one and the same, receiving their origin from Nous, and obtaining [different] appellation according to their increase.
sources.raw_question: Are thought, reflection, sensation, counsel, judgment and reason (logos) distinct beings, or are they stages of one mind's activity?

question: How do the Father and the Word (Christ) each act in the salvation of humanity from Satan?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: The Father, moved by tender mercy, had compassion on his own handiwork and gave it salvation. He restored it by means of the Word, that is, Christ. The Man exposed Satan as a transgressor, and the Word then bound him as a fugitive from Himself and spoiled his goods. This shows that man receives incorruptibility as God's free gift, not from himself.
sources.quote: according to the tender mercy of God the Father, who had compassion on His own handiwork, and gave to it salvation, restoring it by means of the Word—that is, by Christ
sources.raw_question: How do the Father and the Word (Christ) each act in the salvation of humanity from Satan?

question: Do the Magi's gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh show that the child Jesus was God as well as man and king?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IX.—One and the same God, the Creator of heaven and earth, is He whom the prophets foretold, and who was declared by the Gospel. Proof of this, at the outset, from St. Matthew’s Gospel.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus reads the gifts as showing who was being worshipped. Myrrh signified that he would die and be buried for mortal humanity. Gold signified that he was a King whose kingdom has no end. Frankincense signified that he was God, the one 'known in Judea'.
sources.quote: myrrh, because it was He who should die and be buried for the mortal human race; gold, because He was a King, “of whose kingdom is no end;” and frankincense, because He was God
sources.raw_question: Do the Magi's gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh show that the child Jesus was God as well as man and king?

question: Since the Word of God became flesh, of which God was John the Baptist the messenger: the Creator or a higher unknown God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: John was sent by the Creator. He was sent by the God whose angel Gabriel announced his birth, and who promised through the prophets to send His messenger before His Son in the spirit of Elijah. Elijah served the Maker of heaven and earth. So the Word to whom John bore witness is the Word of the Creator, not of an unknown power above Him.
sources.quote: By what God, then, was John, the forerunner, who testifies of the Light, sent [into the world]? Truly it was by Him, of whom Gabriel is the angel, who also announced the glad tidings of his birth
sources.raw_question: Since the Word of God became flesh, of which God was John the Baptist the messenger: the Creator or a higher unknown God?

question: Did the apostles accommodate their preaching about God to prevailing Jewish opinions, so that later teachers could discover a purer doctrine of another god?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. The apostles and martyrs like Stephen died for the Gospel, which they would not have done had they merely spoken in accordance with established opinion; they suffered precisely because they preached things contrary to their hearers. They therefore boldly preached the truth: to the Jews that the crucified Jesus is the Son of God and Judge, and to the Greeks one God who made all things and Jesus Christ His Son.
sources.quote: Those, therefore, who delivered up their souls to death for Christ’s Gospel—how could they have spoken to men in accordance with old-established opinion? If this had been the course adopted by them, they should not have suffered
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles accommodate their preaching about God to prevailing Jewish opinions, so that later teachers could discover a purer doctrine of another god?

question: Was the one God present with humanity throughout all the dispensations of history?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. The perfected martyrs knew one and the same God, who from beginning to end was present with mankind in the various dispensations, as Hosea says that God multiplied visions and used similitudes through the prophets.
sources.quote: Thus were they perfected who knew one and the same God, who from beginning to end was present with mankind in the various dispensations
sources.raw_question: Was the one God present with humanity throughout all the dispensations of history?

question: Does Paul's use of Isaiah 45:23 to prove that all will stand before Christ's judgment seat identify Christ with the one God of Isaiah 45?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul proves that we shall stand at Christ's judgment seat by citing Jehovah's oath that every knee shall bow to him. So Christ is that Jehovah, who says there is no God besides him, a just God and a Saviour.
sources.quote: St. Paul incontrovertibly establishes his assertion, that we shall stand at the judgment seat of Christ, by this solemn oath of Jehovah, recorded by Isaiah. Therefore, Christ is Jehovah,
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's use of Isaiah 45:23 to prove that all will stand before Christ's judgment seat identify Christ with the one God of Isaiah 45?

question: Does Stephen's statement that Israel received the Law by the disposition of angels prove that the theophany at Sinai was mediated by angels?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: Yes. Stephen plainly says the Law, which all the faithful agree God gave to Moses, was received by the disposition of angels, and here not a single angel or 'men' but simply angels are named. This is the clearest proof that God spoke through angels in these appearances.
sources.quote: who have received the Law by the disposition of angels,[^428] and have not kept it.”[^429] What is more evident than this? What more strong than such an authority?
sources.raw_question: Does Stephen's statement that Israel received the Law by the disposition of angels prove that the theophany at Sinai was mediated by angels?

question: If the Law was given by angels, how was the Son of God involved in giving it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: The Word of God was in some wonderful and unspeakable manner in the angels through whom the Law was given. Through them the Son was preparing and announcing his own advent, which is why Christ says Moses wrote of him.
sources.quote: He Himself, as the Word of God, was in some wonderful and unspeakable manner in the angels, by whose disposition the Law itself was given
sources.raw_question: If the Law was given by angels, how was the Son of God involved in giving it?

question: Does a change in the name we give to a thing change that thing's essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > He says that all things that are in creation have been named by man, if, as is the case, they are called differently by every nation, as also the appellation of “Ungenerate” is conferred by us: but that the proper appellation of the Divine essence itself which expresses the Divine Nature, either does not exist at all, or is unknown to us.
sources.answer: No. Names do not make things but only signify our concepts of them; things remain as they naturally are, while the mind expresses its thought with whatever words are available. Just as Peter's essence did not change when Simon became Peter, so nothing we contemplate is changed by a change of names.
sources.quote: For the things remain in themselves as they naturally are, while the mind, touching on existing things, reveals its thought by such words as are available.
sources.raw_question: Does a change in the name we give to a thing change that thing's essence?

question: Could any created man or angel share the temple and light of the heavenly Jerusalem with God, as the Lamb does in Revelation 21:22-23?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. The coequal and cooperating glory of the Lamb with the omnipotent God could belong to no creature. Christ alone, in the unity of the Holy Ghost, is one with God and is God.
sources.quote: Could you substitute any created man or angel for His excellent Name? Never. For He alone, in the unity of the Holy Ghost, is One with God, and is God.
sources.raw_question: Could any created man or angel share the temple and light of the heavenly Jerusalem with God, as the Lamb does in Revelation 21:22-23?

question: Did Clement of Alexandria's remark on the article before Θεὸς teach that the Father has a superior dignity of nature above the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: No. Clement did not comment on John 1:1 or claim the article marks the Father's supereminent nature above the Son. He only argued against Tatian, citing Genesis 4:25, that the true God and not the Devil is author of procreation. By his own rule Christ, who is called ὁ Θεός, must be true God in the same sense.
sources.quote: By the very same rule, Christ must be true God, in the same sense, according to Clemens. He is ὁ Θεός.
sources.raised_by_detail: Dr. Clarke's school, appealing to Clement of Alexandria, Origen and Eusebius
sources.raw_question: Did Clement of Alexandria's remark on the article before Θεὸς teach that the Father has a superior dignity of nature above the Son?

question: Does Christ's saying "Ye cannot serve two masters" imply that mammon is a second Lord or God alongside the true God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VIII.—Answer to an objection, arising from the words of Christ (Matt. vi. 24). God alone is to be really called God and Lord, for He is without beginning and end.
sources.answer: No. Christ himself interprets the saying as "Ye cannot serve God and mammon," acknowledging God as God while merely mentioning mammon as an existing thing. Just as he calls those who serve sin "slaves of sin" without calling sin God, so he calls those who serve mammon its slaves without calling mammon God or Lord.
sources.quote: He does not call mammon Lord when He says, “Ye cannot serve two masters;” but He teaches His disciples who serve God, not to be subject to mammon, nor to be ruled by it.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying "Ye cannot serve two masters" imply that mammon is a second Lord or God alongside the true God?

question: If God could later remove ignorance by revealing Himself, could He not have prevented it from the beginning?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: Yes. If at a later time, when He willed, He could take away ignorance that had grown deep, much more could He have prevented it before it existed. So on the heretics' view the cause of ignorance becomes the Father's own will, which is absurd for a good and foreknowing God.
sources.quote: much more, had He so willed it might He formerly have prevented that ignorance, which as yet was not, from coming into existence.
sources.raw_question: If God could later remove ignorance by revealing Himself, could He not have prevented it from the beginning?

question: Does God's infinite greatness, which makes Him incomprehensible, conflict with His infinite love toward the beings He produces?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVII.—Inquiry into the production of the Æons: whatever its supposed nature, it is in every respect inconsistent; and on the hypothesis of the heretics, even Nous and the Father Himself would be stained with ignorance.
sources.answer: No. Even if God's infinite greatness leaves Him incomprehensible, His infinite love should have preserved His creatures from passion. Nothing prevented them from knowing from the beginning that the Father is altogether incomprehensible, since His greatness was the same from the start.
sources.quote: For if, on account of His infinite greatness, He remained unknown, He ought also on account of His infinite love to have preserved those impassible who were produced by Him
sources.raw_question: Does God's infinite greatness, which makes Him incomprehensible, conflict with His infinite love toward the beings He produces?

question: Can the will in sight, when it becomes intense love or desire, affect the body as well as the soul?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > A Certain Trinity in the Sight. That There are Three Things in Sight, Which Differ in Their Own Nature. In What Manner from a Visible Thing Vision is Produced, or the Image of that Thing Which is Seen. The Matter is Shown More Clearly by an Example. How These Three Combine in One.
sources.answer: Yes. When the will is vehement enough to be called love, desire or lust, it affects the rest of the body and, where matter does not resist, changes it to a similar shape and colour. This is seen in the chameleon and in offspring bearing marks of what mothers beheld, as with Jacob's rods placed before the flocks.
sources.quote: And if it is so vehement that it can be called love, or desire, or lust, it vehemently affects also the rest of the body of the living being; and where a duller and harder matter does not resist, changes it into like shape and color.
sources.raw_question: Can the will in sight, when it becomes intense love or desire, affect the body as well as the soul?

question: If a perfect reduplication of a mind's states did produce another subject, would it yield distinct Persons within one Being?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. If repeating mental states did duplicate the mind, the result would be a plurality of Beings, not a plurality of Persons in one Being. So Edwards's model, even granting its premise, would give tritheism rather than the Trinity.
sources.quote: The mind does not consist in its states, and the repetition of its states would not, therefore, duplicate or triplicate it. If it did, we should have a plurality of Beings, not of Persons in one Being.
sources.raw_question: If a perfect reduplication of a mind's states did produce another subject, would it yield distinct Persons within one Being?

question: What service does reason render to faith in the doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Reason performs two services. Negatively, it shows that the doctrine is self-consistent and consistent with other known truth. Positively, it finds in the Trinity the only adequate conception of God as self-conscious spirit and living love.
sources.quote: Reason thus not only performs the important negative service to faith in the Trinity, of showing the self-consistency of the doctrine and its consistency with other known truth, but brings this positive rational support to it
sources.raw_question: What service does reason render to faith in the doctrine of the Trinity?

question: Is Christian Trinitarian theism the only stable form of theism?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes, in the sense that theism needs the enriching conception of the Trinity to keep a permanent hold on the human mind. The mind finds it hard to rest in an abstract unity as its God. The heart longs for a living God whose Being has the fullness of life that only the Trinitarian conception provides.
sources.quote: theism requires the enriching conception of the Trinity to give it a permanent hold upon the human mind – the mind finds it difficult to rest in the idea of an abstract unity for its God
sources.raw_question: Is Christian Trinitarian theism the only stable form of theism?

question: Did Christ give a new and peculiar law of his own, by keeping which believers are justified, as the Socinians teach?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: No. The gospel requires no more than that we love the Lord our God with all our heart and soul, which the law also required. Christ has brought believers into a state of acceptance with God in which their obedience pleases him. Because we honour him as we honour the Father, we give him a special regard in all our obedience.
sources.quote: Not that I suppose there are peculiar precepts and a peculiar law of Jesus Christ, in the observance whereof we are justified, as the Socinians fancy
sources.raw_question: Did Christ give a new and peculiar law of his own, by keeping which believers are justified, as the Socinians teach?

question: How does Paul's saying that we no longer know Christ after the flesh bear on distinguishing Christ's eternal existence from his incarnate dispensation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > Then he again mentions S. Peter's word, “made,” and the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which says that Jesus was made by God “an Apostle and High Priest”: and, after giving a sufficient answer to the charges brought against him by Eunomius, shows that Eunomius himself supports Basil's arguments, and says that the Only-begotten Son, when He had put on the flesh, became Lord.
sources.answer: It teaches two kinds of knowledge of Christ: one shows His temporary dispensation, the other His eternal existence. So words about the dispensation must not be transferred to His eternal being.
sources.quote: in the sense that the one knowledge manifests to us His temporary dispensation, the other His eternal existence
sources.raw_question: How does Paul's saying that we no longer know Christ after the flesh bear on distinguishing Christ's eternal existence from his incarnate dispensation?

question: Is the doctrine Basil defends about the Holy Spirit a recent innovation, or has it been handed down from earlier generations of the Church?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Exposition of the present state of the Churches.
sources.answer: It is not an innovation. Basil says the doctrine he defends against the blasphemers of the Spirit has been kept by the tradition of the Fathers in an unbroken sequence of memory down to his own day. For that reason he will not shrink from defending it, even almost alone, trusting in the Spirit himself as his ally.
sources.quote: should shrink from the service of that doctrine, which by the tradition of the Fathers has been preserved by an unbroken sequence of memory to our own day
sources.raw_question: Is the doctrine Basil defends about the Holy Spirit a recent innovation, or has it been handed down from earlier generations of the Church?

question: What is the fault of those whom Psalm 94 rebukes for saying vain things about God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > How Any One Can Forget and Remember God.
sources.answer: Their fault is a failure to understand God. Augustine reads the rebuke, "He that planted the ear, shall He not hear?", as aimed at those who spoke vainly about God because they did not understand Him. He takes it as Scripture's testimony that understanding God, alongside remembering Him, belongs to the mind's right relation to Him.
sources.quote: For this is spoken to those, who said vain things concerning God through not understanding Him.
sources.raw_question: What is the fault of those whom Psalm 94 rebukes for saying vain things about God?

question: Did the Son of God perform His miracles out of a need for human praise or for self-display?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book III
sources.answer: No. The Son needs nothing from us. All that we have was created through Him, and countless angels and heavenly powers praise Him ceaselessly as the Image of the Invisible God who made all things. He worked these inexplicable signs because God foresaw that unbelief would presume to judge divine things, so He checked that presumption with tokens of His power.
sources.quote: There was nothing, then, that He might gain from us, that could induce Him to assume the splendour of these mysterious and inexplicable works, as though He needed our praise.
sources.raw_question: Did the Son of God perform His miracles out of a need for human praise or for self-display?

question: Who is the fourth figure seen walking in the fiery furnace with Ananias, Azarias, and Mishael, and how does he relate to the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter V.—The prolonged life of the ancients, the translation of Elijah and of Enoch in their own bodies, as well as the preservation of Jonah, of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, in the midst of extreme peril, are clear demonstrations that God can raise up our bodies to life eternal.
sources.answer: He is the Son of God, the 'hand of God,' present with the three youths. He worked marvels impossible to human nature in obedience to the will of God the Father. Irenaeus cites Nebuchadnezzar's words that the fourth was 'like the Son of God.'
sources.quote: working in obedience to the will of God, even the Father? Now this is the Son of God, as the Scripture represents Nebuchadnezzar the king as having said
sources.raw_question: Who is the fourth figure seen walking in the fiery furnace with Ananias, Azarias, and Mishael, and how does he relate to the Father?

question: Were Enoch and Elijah translated in their actual bodies, and by what agency?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter V.—The prolonged life of the ancients, the translation of Elijah and of Enoch in their own bodies, as well as the preservation of Jonah, of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, in the midst of extreme peril, are clear demonstrations that God can raise up our bodies to life eternal.
sources.answer: Yes. Enoch was translated in the same body in which he pleased God, and Elijah was caught up in the substance of his natural form. Nothing prevented their bodies from being translated. They were taken up by the very hands of God that molded man at the beginning and placed Adam in paradise. Irenaeus treats this as a prophetic anticipation of the assumption of the just.
sources.quote: For by means of the very same hands through which they were moulded at the beginning, did they receive this translation and assumption.
sources.raised_by_detail: those who say Elijah's flesh was consumed in the fiery chariot
sources.raw_question: Were Enoch and Elijah translated in their actual bodies, and by what agency?

question: Does Ephesians 1, with its rich account of believers' privileges in Christ, put the saints on a level with Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. Paul closes his account of believers' privileges not by claiming Christlike honour for himself and his brethren but by praying about Christ. He describes Christ as raised to the Father's right hand, far above every name and principality, with all things under his feet and head over all things to the church. The Son is on the everlasting throne, and believers are under his feet.
sources.quote: Behold, the Son is on the everlasting throne: and we are under his feet.
sources.raw_question: Does Ephesians 1, with its rich account of believers' privileges in Christ, put the saints on a level with Christ?

question: Is the Word who was manifested to men as Jesus Christ the same as the Creator of all things who sits upon the cherubim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus identifies the Word, the Artificer of all who sits upon the cherubim and contains all things, with the one who was manifested to men and gave the fourfold Gospel. David's prayer to the one enthroned between the cherubim to shine forth is read as a plea for this Word's manifestation, so the Creator and the incarnate revealer are one and the same divine Word.
sources.quote: it is evident that the Word, the Artificer of all, He that sitteth upon the cherubim, and contains all things, He who was manifested to men, has given us the Gospel under four aspects, but bound together by one Spirit
sources.raw_question: Is the Word who was manifested to men as Jesus Christ the same as the Creator of all things who sits upon the cherubim?

question: What do the four faces of the cherubim, or living creatures, signify about the Son of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: They are images of the Son's dispensation. The lion signifies his effectual working, leadership and royal power, and the calf his sacrificial and priestly order. The man signifies his advent as a human being, and the flying eagle the gift of the Spirit hovering over the Church. The four Gospels correspond to these aspects: John, Luke, Matthew and Mark respectively.
sources.quote: For the cherubim, too, were four-faced, and their faces were images of the dispensation of the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: What do the four faces of the cherubim, or living creatures, signify about the Son of God?

question: Did the Christ depart from Jesus before the crucifixion so that he did not suffer, as the Gnostics claim?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: No. Christ himself exhorted his disciples to take up the cross and follow him, which would be meaningless if he had flown away from Jesus and relinquished the suffering. His words about losing one's life and about the persecution of his disciples refer to the suffering he would himself undergo first, and his disciples afterwards.
sources.quote: If, however, He was Himself not to suffer, but should fly away from Jesus, why did He exhort His disciples to take up the cross and follow Him,—that cross which these men represent Him as not having taken up
sources.raw_question: Did the Christ depart from Jesus before the crucifixion so that he did not suffer, as the Gnostics claim?

question: Does Christ's command to take up the cross refer to acknowledging a heavenly 'Stauros' (Cross) in the upper world rather than to actual suffering?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: No. Christ meant the suffering he would himself undergo and that his disciples would endure. This is shown by his saying that whoever loses his life will find it, and by his predictions that his disciples would be scourged, slain and persecuted for his sake.
sources.quote: For that He did not say this with reference to the acknowledging of the Stauros (cross) above, as some among them venture to expound, but with respect to the suffering which He should Himself undergo, and that His disciples should endure
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's command to take up the cross refer to acknowledging a heavenly 'Stauros' (Cross) in the upper world rather than to actual suffering?

question: Was it the Word of God himself who suffered on the cross and prayed for his persecutors?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: Yes. The Word of God, who taught us to love our enemies, did this very thing on the cross by praying for those who were killing him. This shows the patience and goodness of Christ, who both suffered and excused those who mistreated him.
sources.quote: For the Word of God, who said to us, “Love your enemies, and pray for those that hate you,” Himself did this very thing upon the cross; loving the human race to such a degree, that He even prayed for those putting Him to death.
sources.raw_question: Was it the Word of God himself who suffered on the cross and prayed for his persecutors?

question: Is the Comforter whom Christ promised a divine person of the Trinity, so that despising his gifts is despising God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. One infinitely holy and blessed person of the Trinity has taken on the office of comforter, sent to make up for Christ's bodily absence so that believers lose nothing by it. Contemning his gifts and graces is therefore opposing and despising a divine person. It is not merely a slight against men.
sources.quote: when one infinitely holy and blessed person of the Trinity hath taken this office upon him to be our comforter, but they must oppose and despise him also?
sources.raw_question: Is the Comforter whom Christ promised a divine person of the Trinity, so that despising his gifts is despising God?

question: Does what is spiritual need to descend into flesh in order to be perfected, as the Valentinians claim about their spiritual seed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIX.—Absurdities of the heretics as to their own origin: their opinions respecting the Demiurge shown to be equally untenable and ridiculous.
sources.answer: No. It is the flesh that needs the spiritual, so that it may be sanctified, cleansed, and have its mortality swallowed up by immortality. The spiritual has no need of the things here below. We do not benefit it; it improves us. So the Gnostic claim that spiritual seed must be formed in earthly souls inverts the true order.
sources.quote: but that which is spiritual has no need whatever of those things which are here below. For it is not we who benefit it, but it that improves us.
sources.raw_question: Does what is spiritual need to descend into flesh in order to be perfected, as the Valentinians claim about their spiritual seed?

question: Are souls that supposedly received spiritual seed from the Mother superior to others and honoured by the Creator as princes, kings and priests?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIX.—Absurdities of the heretics as to their own origin: their opinions respecting the Demiurge shown to be equally untenable and ridiculous.
sources.answer: No. If this were true, Caiaphas, Annas, the chief priests, the rulers and Herod would have been the first to believe in the Lord. Instead the beggars, the deaf and the blind believed while the eminent rejected him. This accords with Paul's statement that God chose the despised things of the world, not the wise, noble or mighty.
sources.quote: Such souls, therefore, were not superior to others on account of the seed deposited in them, nor on this account were they honoured by the Demiurge.
sources.raw_question: Are souls that supposedly received spiritual seed from the Mother superior to others and honoured by the Creator as princes, kings and priests?

question: In Song of Songs 5:10, what does the Beloved being 'white and ruddy' signify about the two natures of Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Whiteness signifies the glory of Christ's Deity and ruddiness the preciousness of his humanity. Whiteness is the complexion of glory, as seen in the Ancient of days and in Christ's transfiguration, and even the Chaldee paraphrast ascribes the passage to God. Ruddiness recalls Adam, named from the red earth, so that Christ appears as the second Adam who shared flesh and blood with his brethren.
sources.quote: He is white in the glory of his Deity, and ruddy in the preciousness of his humanity.
sources.raw_question: In Song of Songs 5:10, what does the Beloved being 'white and ruddy' signify about the two natures of Christ?

question: What makes Christ a fit Saviour?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: His fitness comes from the grace of union, the joining of the divine and human natures in one person. Because he partakes of God's nature and of ours, he is an umpire between both. He fills up the distance that sin made between God and us, and he has the capacity to bear all the wrath prepared for sinners.
sources.quote: The uniting of the natures of God and man in one person made him fit to be a Saviour to the uttermost.
sources.raw_question: What makes Christ a fit Saviour?

question: Why did Christ pass through every stage of human life, from infancy to old age, before his death?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXII.—The thirty Æons are not typified by the fact that Christ was baptized in His thirtieth year: He did not suffer in the twelfth month after His baptism, but was more than fifty years old when He died.
sources.answer: He did so in order to sanctify every age of human life and to be an example to people at every stage. He came to save all who are born again to God through him: infants, children, youths and old men. So he became an infant for infants, a youth for youths and an old man for old men. Finally he went on to death itself, so that he might be the first-born from the dead and have pre-eminence in all things.
sources.quote: He therefore passed through every age, becoming an infant for infants, thus sanctifying infants; a child for children, thus sanctifying those who are of this age, being at the same time made to them an example of piety, righteousness, and submission
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ pass through every stage of human life, from infancy to old age, before his death?

question: Can there be a will to remember something that has been entirely forgotten?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > There is Another Trinity in the Memory of Him Who Thinks Over Again What He Has Seen.
sources.answer: No. The will to remember presupposes that we already retain the whole or some part of the thing in memory. For example, to wish to recall what one supped on yesterday, one must already remember yesterday, the usual time of supper, and what supping is.
sources.quote: the very will to remember cannot arise in the case of a thing which we have forgotten altogether and absolutely
sources.raw_question: Can there be a will to remember something that has been entirely forgotten?

question: Does Isaiah's prophecy that the Servant was 'stricken, smitten and afflicted' and 'wounded for our transgressions' show that Christ suffered for his own sake or out of natural weakness?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. He was wounded for our transgressions, not his own; he bore our sins by assuming our body of sin while himself sinless. As Paul says, he who knew no sin was made sin on our behalf, so that through the flesh he might condemn sin in the flesh. The suffering was not a suffering for himself.
sources.quote: The wound was not the wound of His own transgressions: the suffering not a suffering for Himself. He was not born man for His own sake, nor did He transgress in His own action.
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah's prophecy that the Servant was 'stricken, smitten and afflicted' and 'wounded for our transgressions' show that Christ suffered for his own sake or out of natural weakness?

question: Are reconciliation through the non-imputation of sin and justification through the imputation of righteousness the same thing?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: No. Scripture mentions them distinctly: reconciliation is by the non-imputation of sin, and justification is by the imputation of righteousness. They are never separated, and each is affirmed of the other. This shows not that they are identical but that they are eminently conjoined.
sources.quote: although these things are so far from being separated, that they are reciprocally affirmed of one another: which, as it doth not evince an identity, so it doth an eminent conjunction.
sources.raw_question: Are reconciliation through the non-imputation of sin and justification through the imputation of righteousness the same thing?

question: What does the removal of Joshua's filthy garments and the giving of a change of raiment in Zechariah 3:3-5 signify about justification?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: It pictures the two things needed for our acceptance before God. Taking away the filthy robes is the removal of the guilt of sin, which is the fruit of Christ's death. The change of raiment is the bestowal of righteousness and the right to eternal life, which becomes ours only through Christ's obedience. Isaiah 61:10 calls this clothing the garments of salvation and the robe of righteousness.
sources.quote: there is more also required, even a collation of righteousness, and thereby a right to life eternal. This is here called “Change of raiment;”
sources.raw_question: What does the removal of Joshua's filthy garments and the giving of a change of raiment in Zechariah 3:3-5 signify about justification?

question: Does the justification of the publican over the Pharisee show that the publican worshipped a different Father than the God of the Jews?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: No. The publican was justified not because he worshipped another Father but because he confessed with great humility, free of boasting and pride, to the same God. The parable therefore supports one and the same God across both covenants.
sources.quote: it was not because he worshipped another Father that he received testimony from the Lord that he was justified rather [than the other]; but because with great humility, apart from all boasting and pride, he made confession to the same God.
sources.raw_question: Does the justification of the publican over the Pharisee show that the publican worshipped a different Father than the God of the Jews?

question: Do the parable of the fig tree and Christ's lament over Jerusalem show that the Word of God visited Israel through the prophets before the Incarnation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ says "three years I come seeking fruit" and "how often would I have gathered thy children." These words would be false if he had come to Israel only once, at his incarnation. They must therefore refer to his earlier comings through the prophets. So the Word who came in the flesh is the same one who visited Israel by the prophetic Spirit.
sources.quote: shall be [found] a falsehood, if we do not understand His advent, which is [announced] by the prophets—if, in fact, He came to them but once, and then for the first time.
sources.raw_question: Do the parable of the fig tree and Christ's lament over Jerusalem show that the Word of God visited Israel through the prophets before the Incarnation?

question: Is the Word of God who chose the patriarchs and spoke through the prophets the same Word who came in Christ and called the Gentiles?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: Yes. The same Word of God chose the patriarchs and visited them through the prophetic Spirit, and has now called believers from every quarter by his advent. Christ's promise that people from east and west will recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob shows this. It presents one and the same God, who chose the patriarchs, visited Israel and called the Gentiles.
sources.quote: He who chose the patriarchs and those [who lived under the first covenant], is the same Word of God who did both visit them through the prophetic Spirit, and us also who have been called together from all quarters by His advent
sources.raw_question: Is the Word of God who chose the patriarchs and spoke through the prophets the same Word who came in Christ and called the Gentiles?

question: Is it legitimate to reject John's Gospel, with its promise that the Lord would send the Paraclete, and with it the continuing prophetic gift of the Spirit in the Church?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: No. In the latter times the gift of the Spirit has been poured out on the human race by the good pleasure of the Father, as the Lord promised in John's Gospel when he said he would send the Paraclete. Those who reject this Gospel set aside both the Gospel and the prophetic Spirit. Paul also expressly recognises men and women prophesying in the Church. By sinning against the Spirit of God in these ways, such people fall into the irremissible sin.
sources.quote: that they may set at nought the gift of the Spirit, which in the latter times has been, by the good pleasure of the Father, poured out upon the human race
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to reject John's Gospel, with its promise that the Lord would send the Paraclete, and with it the continuing prophetic gift of the Spirit in the Church?

question: Does the soul fall all at once from seeking higher things into the worst degradation of loving bodily things as its final good?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Lowest Degradation Reached by Degrees.
sources.answer: No. The soul does not leap straight into such shameless fornication but declines gradually. Augustine cites Scripture: he who despises small things falls little by little. The following chapter adds that the fall begins with a perverse desire to be like God and ends in the likeness of beasts.
sources.quote: Yet it would not leap on at once from the commencement to such shameless and miserable fornication, but, as it is written, “He that contemneth small things, shall fall by little and little.”
sources.raw_question: Does the soul fall all at once from seeking higher things into the worst degradation of loving bodily things as its final good?

question: Do men and women share the same rational mind, so that the bodily difference of the sexes only symbolizes a division of functions within one mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Turning Aside from the Image of God.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine holds that a common nature is recognized in the minds of men and women. The bodily distinction of sex only represents a division within the one mind: the higher part contemplates eternal reasons, and the lower part governs temporal things. The image of God, which lies in the higher part, therefore belongs to women as well as men.
sources.quote: A common nature, therefore, is recognized in their minds, but in their bodies a division of that one mind itself is figured.
sources.raw_question: Do men and women share the same rational mind, so that the bodily difference of the sexes only symbolizes a division of functions within one mind?

question: At what point, ascending through the parts of the human mind, does the 'inner man' begin?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > Turning Aside from the Image of God.
sources.answer: The inner man begins where reason begins. Reason is the first thing we meet, ascending within the mind, that we do not share with the beasts. The senses and whatever else is common with animals belong to the outer man.
sources.quote: there where something first meets us which is not common to ourselves with the beasts reason begins, so that here the inner man can now be recognized
sources.raw_question: At what point, ascending through the parts of the human mind, does the 'inner man' begin?

question: Does God's promise to raise up a king for David "from the fruit of his belly" point to a virgin birth?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: Yes. "Fruit of the belly" is the term proper to a virgin conceiving, unlike "fruit of the loins," which suits a man who begets. So the promise excludes any part played by a man. Elisabeth confirmed its fulfilment in Mary when she said, "blessed is the fruit of thy belly."
sources.quote: In this promise, therefore, the Scripture excluded all virile influence
sources.raw_question: Does God's promise to raise up a king for David "from the fruit of his belly" point to a virgin birth?

question: What do Isaiah's "depth below" and "height above" signify about Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXI.—A vindication of the prophecy in Isa. vii. 14 against the misinterpretations of Theodotion, Aquila, the Ebionites, and the Jews. Authority of the Septuagint version. Arguments in proof that Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.answer: They indicate that He who descended is the same who also ascended. This points to the one Christ who came down and went up again.
sources.quote: was meant to indicate, that “He who descended was the same also who ascended.”
sources.raw_question: What do Isaiah's "depth below" and "height above" signify about Christ?

question: Are the Socinians, who deny the deity of Christ while worshipping him, really defenders of monotheism?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. Although they appear to contend most for one God, they are in fact polytheists. They give religious respect, which is due to God alone, to someone they hold not to be God.
sources.quote: who, whilst of all others they seem to contend most for one God, are indeed direct polytheists, by owning others with religious respect, due to God alone, which are not so.
sources.raw_question: Are the Socinians, who deny the deity of Christ while worshipping him, really defenders of monotheism?

question: Is the devil outside the power and goodness of the omnipotent God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
