sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > All, on Account of the Sin of Adam, Were Delivered into the Power of the Devil.
sources.answer: No. Even the devil is not separated from the power of the Omnipotent, nor from His goodness. Evil angels subsist in whatever life they have only through Him who quickens all things. So man placed in the devil's power still remains under God's power.
sources.quote: since even the devil himself is not separated from the power of the Omnipotent, as neither from His goodness. For whence do even the evil angels subsist in whatever manner of life they have, except through Him who quickens all things?
sources.raw_question: Is the devil outside the power and goodness of the omnipotent God?

question: Why is the Arian heresy worse than heresies such as Docetism, which deny Christ's true flesh?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Contrast between the Father's operations immediately and naturally in the Son, instrumentally by the creatures; Scripture terms illustrative of this. Explanation of these illustrations; which should be interpreted by the doctrine of the Church; perverse sense put on them by the Arians, refuted. Mystery of Divine Generation. Contrast between God's Word and man's word drawn out at length. Asterius betrayed into holding two Unoriginates; his inconsistency. Baptism how by the Son as well as by the Father. On the Baptism of heretics. Why Arian worse than other heresies.
sources.answer: Other heresies lie against the truth in some particular respect, such as Christ's body. The Arians, however, are openly irreligious against the Father himself. Scripture shows the Father's Godhead represented in the Son as in an image, and the Arians call that Image a creature and say of it 'He was not'.
sources.quote: For hearing from the Scriptures that His Godhead is represented in the Son as in an image, they blaspheme, saying, that it is a creature
sources.raw_question: Why is the Arian heresy worse than heresies such as Docetism, which deny Christ's true flesh?

question: How can Christ be both 'not of this world' and yet in some manner of this world?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: Because Christ is both God and man. He is not of this world according to the divinity of the Word, and he is of this world according to the frailty of the body he assumed, for man is joined with God and God linked with man.
sources.quote: As reasonably in the way in which He is not of this world according to the divinity of the Word, so He is of this world according to the frailty of the body that He has taken upon Him.
sources.raw_question: How can Christ be both 'not of this world' and yet in some manner of this world?

question: Why does Christ in John 8:23 speak only of his divinity and say nothing of his humanity?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
sources.answer: Because the Jews saw only his flesh. He stressed his divinity alone and passed over his bodily frailty to draw them, in proportion as they thought him mere man, to consider him God and overcome their unbelief.
sources.quote: this Christ here laid more stress on the one aspect of His sole divinity, because the Jewish blindness contemplated in Christ the aspect alone of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ in John 8:23 speak only of his divinity and say nothing of his humanity?

question: Is knowledge of temporal things necessary, or is it harmful because it puffs up?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > What is the Difference Between Wisdom and Knowledge. The Worship of God is the Love of Him. How the Intellectual Cognizance of Eternal Things Comes to Pass Through Wisdom.
sources.answer: Knowledge is necessary and has its own good measure, provided that whatever in it puffs up is conquered by love of eternal things, which edifies. Without knowledge the virtues by which we live rightly cannot be possessed. Through those virtues this life is governed so that we may attain eternal life.
sources.quote: Certainly without knowledge the virtues themselves, by which one lives rightly, cannot be possessed
sources.raw_question: Is knowledge of temporal things necessary, or is it harmful because it puffs up?

question: Why did God need to show us both how much He loved us and what manner of men we were whom He loved?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > We are Made Perfect by Acknowledgement of Our Own Weakness. The Incarnate Word Dispels Our Darkness.
sources.answer: The first was shown so that we would not despair of daring to look up to God. The second was shown so that we would not become proud of our own merits and fall away. This is shown in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners and enemies. So in the weakness of humility, the virtue of charity is perfected by grace given freely.
sources.quote: Man, then, was to be persuaded how much God loved us, and what manner of men we were whom He loved; the former, lest we should despair; the latter, lest we should be proud.
sources.raw_question: Why did God need to show us both how much He loved us and what manner of men we were whom He loved?

question: Does the 'spontaneous rain' of Psalm 68:9 signify grace given according to merit?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > We are Made Perfect by Acknowledgement of Our Own Weakness. The Incarnate Word Dispels Our Darkness.
sources.answer: No. The 'spontaneous rain' means nothing other than grace, which is not rendered to merit but given freely. God gave it not because we were worthy but because He willed. Knowing this keeps us from trusting in ourselves, and that is what it means to be made 'weak' and then perfected.
sources.quote: For by “spontaneous rain” nothing else is meant than grace, not rendered to merit, but given freely, whence also it is called grace; for He gave it, not because we were worthy, but because He willed.
sources.raw_question: Does the 'spontaneous rain' of Psalm 68:9 signify grace given according to merit?

question: How does 1 Timothy 3:16 ('manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit... received up in glory') show the order and meaning of the Incarnation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XI
sources.answer: It sets out the whole system of the faith in its proper order. From godliness proceeds the mystery, and from the mystery the manifestation in the flesh. From the manifestation in the flesh comes the justification in the Spirit, and the consummation is the receiving up in glory. Every stage is one and the same mystery of great godliness. By faith in this Dispensation believers are prepared to be received up and conformed to the Lord's glory.
sources.quote: From godliness proceeds the mystery, from the mystery the manifestation in the flesh, from the manifestation in the flesh the justification in the Spirit
sources.raw_question: How does 1 Timothy 3:16 ('manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit... received up in glory') show the order and meaning of the Incarnation?

question: Are faith, love, hope and the other graces distinct habits in the soul, or one principle?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: They are one principle. Habitual grace is a single spiritual habit, one root with many branches. It puts itself forth in various operations according to the objects it goes out to. The graces are distinguished by their actual exercise toward objects, not by distinct inherent habits.
sources.quote: it is called and distinguished, as above, rather in respect of actual exercise, with relation to its objects, than habitual inherence; it being one root which hath these many branches
sources.raw_question: Are faith, love, hope and the other graces distinct habits in the soul, or one principle?

question: Are names like Shepherd, Vine, and Physician said of Christ only because of his relation to creatures?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Then he ends the book with an exposition of the Divine and Human names of the Only-Begotten, and a discussion of the terms “generate” and “ungenerate.”
sources.answer: Yes. Christ would not have been called a vine except for the planting of those rooted in him. He would not have been called a shepherd unless the sheep of Israel had been lost, nor a physician except for the sick. These titles depend on the actions of his providence toward those he benefits.
sources.quote: The Lord would not have been called a vine, save for the planting of those who are rooted in Him, nor a shepherd, had not the sheep of the house of Israel been lost, nor a physician, save for the sake of them that were sick
sources.raw_question: Are names like Shepherd, Vine, and Physician said of Christ only because of his relation to creatures?

question: Is it fitting to think that God, who is above every name and thought, settles human terminology like a schoolmaster?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. It is trifling and Jewish folly to think the Most High, who governs the world by his will alone, would fix the niceties of terminology. Instead God speaks through the Prophets in a way adapted to our capacity, as one signs to the deaf. He leads us to higher truths by descending to our limited comprehension, since the great cannot be contained by the little.
sources.quote: ordering their voices conformably to our capacity and the modes of expression with which we are familiar, and that by such means it leads us, as with a guiding hand, to the knowledge of higher truths
sources.raw_question: Is it fitting to think that God, who is above every name and thought, settles human terminology like a schoolmaster?

question: Does Paul's being caught up to the third heaven and into paradise show that the spiritual realities he saw belong to the Creator rather than to some higher realm above the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul, who was certainly not inferior to the Gnostics, describes his ascent only to the third heaven as something great and pre-eminent. Had he been learning mysteries above the Demiurge, his inner man could have risen further, since nothing could resist the Father's providence. So the spiritual mysteries he saw are the operations of the God who made heaven and earth, formed man and placed him in paradise.
sources.quote: it is therefore thus far permitted even without the body to behold spiritual mysteries which are the operations of God, who made the heavens and the earth, and formed man, and placed him in paradise
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's being caught up to the third heaven and into paradise show that the spiritual realities he saw belong to the Creator rather than to some higher realm above the Creator?

question: Why did Paul say 'whether in the body or out of the body, God knoweth' about his vision of the third heaven?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXX.—Absurdity of their styling themselves spiritual, while the Demiurge is declared to be animal.
sources.answer: He said it so that no one would think the body shared in the spiritual vision, and so that no one could claim he went no higher because of the body's weight. Spiritual mysteries can be seen even without the body. They are seen by those who, like the apostle, are perfected in the love of God.
sources.quote: that the body might neither be thought to be a partaker in that vision, as if it could have participated in those things which it had seen and heard; nor, again, that any one should say that he was not carried higher on account of the weight of the body
sources.raw_question: Why did Paul say 'whether in the body or out of the body, God knoweth' about his vision of the third heaven?

question: Why is the Father never said to be sent, even when He is known by someone?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be Sent by the Father. Of the Mission of the Holy Spirit. How and by Whom He Was Sent. The Father the Beginning of the Whole Godhead.
sources.answer: The Father is not said to be sent because He has no one of whom He is, or from whom He proceeds. The Son came out of the mouth of the Most High, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, but the Father is from no one. Being sent presupposes being from another.
sources.quote: But the Father is not said to be sent, when from time to time He is apprehended by any one, for He has no one of whom to be, or from whom to proceed
sources.raw_question: Why is the Father never said to be sent, even when He is known by someone?

question: Did Christ's return from the dead depend on someone else bringing him up from the abyss?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. He who was free to descend to earth is free to return to heaven. Paul's gloss on "Who hath descended into the abyss" excludes the idea that another must bring Christ back; God Almighty was the cause.
sources.quote: He is free to return into heaven, Who was free to descend to the earth. All hesitation and doubt is then removed.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ's return from the dead depend on someone else bringing him up from the abyss?

question: Did Peter and Paul preach the same God and the same Son of God, or was Paul alone the apostle of the true Father, as the Marcionites claimed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XIII—Refutation of the opinion, that Paul was the only apostle who had knowledge of the truth.
sources.answer: They preached the same God and the same Son. Paul himself says that one and the same God wrought in Peter for the apostolate of the circumcision and in him for the Gentiles. So the God and Son of God whom Peter preached among the Jews is the very one Paul declared among the Gentiles.
sources.quote: Peter, therefore, was an apostle of that very God whose was also Paul; and Him whom Peter preached as God among those of the circumcision, and likewise the Son of God, did Paul [declare] also among the Gentiles.
sources.raw_question: Did Peter and Paul preach the same God and the same Son of God, or was Paul alone the apostle of the true Father, as the Marcionites claimed?

question: Does human flesh that is nourished by the Eucharist go to corruption without sharing in life?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVIII.—Concerning sacrifices and oblations, and those who truly offer them.
sources.answer: No. The consecrated bread is no longer common bread: it is the Eucharist, made of two realities, one earthly and one heavenly. In the same way our bodies that receive it are no longer corruptible but have the hope of eternal resurrection. Those who deny the salvation of the flesh must therefore either change their view or stop offering the Eucharist.
sources.quote: so also our bodies, when they receive the Eucharist, are no longer corruptible, having the hope of the resurrection to eternity.
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics denying salvation of the flesh
sources.raw_question: Does human flesh that is nourished by the Eucharist go to corruption without sharing in life?

question: When Christ says to the workers of iniquity and the foolish virgins "I never knew you" / "I know you not," does this show a real lack of knowledge in Christ?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: No. Christ plainly knows them, since he identifies them as workers of iniquity and the virgins come before him; his profession of not knowing refers to his will, not his nature. They are unworthy to be known (acknowledged) by him, so by the mystery of his will he refuses to know them, though by the virtue of his nature he cannot be ignorant.
sources.quote: By the virtue of His nature He could not be ignorant, by the mystery of His will He refused to know.
sources.raw_question: When Christ says to the workers of iniquity and the foolish virgins "I never knew you" / "I know you not," does this show a real lack of knowledge in Christ?

question: Can action and passion be predicated of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > Whatever is Spoken of God According to Substance, is Spoken of Each Person Severally, and Together of the Trinity Itself. One Essence in God, and Three, in Greek, Hypostases, in Latin, Persons.
sources.answer: Action, or making, may perhaps be said most truly of God alone, since God alone makes and is not himself made. God is not subject to passions with respect to the substance by which he is God.
sources.quote: And as respects action (or making), perhaps it may be said most truly of God alone, for God alone makes and Himself is not made. Nor is He liable to passions as far as belongs to that substance whereby He is God.
sources.raw_question: Can action and passion be predicated of God?

question: In what sense can distinct worship of the Son be said to have begun with his title of Son or Redeemer?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 18: Whether worship and adoration, both from men and angels, was not due to him, long before the commencing of his mediatorial kingdom, as he was their Creator and
sources.answer: Only in the sense that he was then first worshipped, or commanded to be worshipped, under that distinct title or character. Before, he had no title peculiar to himself, only what was common to him and the Father. All three Persons share in creation, redemption and sanctification, yet each work is attributed to one Person: the Father Creator, the Son Redeemer, the Spirit Sanctifier. Distinct worship of each among men might begin as these titles began.
sources.quote: our blessed Lord was then first worshipped, or commanded to be worshipped by us, under that distinct dile or character ; having before had no other ¢itle or character peculiar and proper to himself, but only what was Scommon to the Father and him too.
sources.raw_question: In what sense can distinct worship of the Son be said to have begun with his title of Son or Redeemer?

question: What does Jacob's wrestling with the man, prevailing yet asking a blessing and then limping, prefigure?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God Also Appeared to Jacob as an Angel; Namely, the Son of God.
sources.answer: It prefigures the conflict between Christ and Jacob's descendants that the Gospel records. The people prevailed against Christ by the wicked victory of condemning Him. Because of that crime they began to halt in the walk of faith and salvation, and they still need His mercy and blessing.
sources.quote: this struggle was prefigured as that which should be between Christ and the sons of Jacob, which is said to be completed in the Gospel
sources.raw_question: What does Jacob's wrestling with the man, prevailing yet asking a blessing and then limping, prefigure?

question: What does Christ mean in John 6 by calling himself 'the living bread which came down from heaven' with respect to the origin of his body?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: It signifies that the Word himself is the origin of his own body, assumed from heaven and not sprung from ordinary human conception. By calling it 'his' bread he shows the Word did not abandon his own virtue and nature for the flesh. The added words about eating the flesh of the Son of Man show that the bread from heaven means the Word's assumption of flesh conceived by the Holy Ghost and born of the Virgin.
sources.quote: calling Himself the Bread since He is the origin of His own body. Further, that it may not be thought the Word left His own virtue and nature for the flesh, He says again that it is His bread
sources.raw_question: What does Christ mean in John 6 by calling himself 'the living bread which came down from heaven' with respect to the origin of his body?

question: If Christ did not truly suffer but withdrew from Jesus before the crucifixion, how could he consistently tell his disciples to take up their cross and follow him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVIII.—Continuation of the foregoing argument. Proofs from the writings of St. Paul, and from the words of Our Lord, that Christ and Jesus cannot be considered as distinct beings; neither can it be alleged that the Son of God became man merely in appearance, but that He did so truly and actually.
sources.answer: He could not. Christ's call to take up the cross refers to the suffering he himself would undergo first and his disciples afterwards, not to some heavenly Stauros. So the one who exhorted them must himself have suffered.
sources.quote: If, however, He was Himself not to suffer, but should fly away from Jesus, why did He exhort His disciples to take up the cross and follow Him
sources.raw_question: If Christ did not truly suffer but withdrew from Jesus before the crucifixion, how could he consistently tell his disciples to take up their cross and follow him?

question: Did the apostles, when preaching to the Jews, conceal a higher Father above the Creator and accommodate their teaching to the Jews' existing belief about God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. If the apostles and the Lord merely spoke according to each hearer's prior opinion, no one could learn the truth and no rule of truth would exist, and Christ's coming would be pointless. Moreover the apostles boldly told the Jews the harder truth that the crucified man was the Son of God and that they had slain the Lord, so they would far more readily have proclaimed a higher Father had they known one. As they told the Gentiles their gods were demons, they would likewise have corrected the Jews.
sources.quote: they, who told them to their face that they were the slayers of the Lord, would themselves also much more boldly preach that Father who is above the Demiurge, and not what each individual bid himself believe
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles, when preaching to the Jews, conceal a higher Father above the Creator and accommodate their teaching to the Jews' existing belief about God?

question: Would the coming of Christ have any purpose if he only confirmed each person's existing idea of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. The Lord's advent would be superfluous and useless if He came merely to tolerate and preserve each man's long-held idea of God. Christ came to reveal the truth about God, the true Father.
sources.quote: the advent of the Lord will appear superfluous and useless, if He did indeed come intending to tolerate and to preserve each man’s idea regarding God rooted in him from of old
sources.raw_question: Would the coming of Christ have any purpose if he only confirmed each person's existing idea of God?

question: Would it have been more fitting to God's majesty for the Son to take an angelic nature or a more glorious form of sacrifice, rather than human flesh and the cross?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 5. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, •presents to us the incarnation and the mission of the Saviour, as the extremity of condescension in Jehovah, that thereby He might exalt us to everlasting life. The Scriptural order to be observed in this enquiry. The moral and spiritual majesty of the incarnation of Christ. The examination of those passages which assert his humanity by the light of others which assert his Divinity. The derived glory to which He raises believers compared with his own essential glories.
sources.answer: No. God's ways are higher than ours, and his work is perfect. Whatever material and physical glory we add to Christ's mission beyond what is needed as evidence for it, we subtract from its moral and spiritual glory. Even assuming the nature of the highest archangel would have been an infinite descent for the uncreated Jehovah. So choosing this small world, human flesh, and the cross displays omniscient love.
sources.quote: For the increate Jehovah to have assumed the nature of the highest archangel would have been an infinite descent.
sources.raw_question: Would it have been more fitting to God's majesty for the Son to take an angelic nature or a more glorious form of sacrifice, rather than human flesh and the cross?

question: Could a Trinity that grew by addition also suffer loss or further increase?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Subject Continued. Third proof of the Son's eternity, viz. from other titles indicative of His coessentiality; as the Creator; One of the Blessed Trinity; as Wisdom; as Word; as Image. If the Son is a perfect Image of the Father, why is He not a Father also? because God, being perfect, is not the origin of a race. Only the Father a Father because the Only Father, only the Son a Son because the Only Son. Men are not really fathers and really sons, but shadows of the True. The Son does not become a Father, because He has received from the Father to be immutable and ever the same.
sources.answer: Yes, which shows the Arian view is untenable. Whatever took its consistence by accessions might receive further accessions without limit, and what is added can also be subtracted. The Christian faith confesses the Triad as unalterable and perfect, admitting neither addition nor loss.
sources.quote: For probably it will receive some fresh accession, and so on without limit, since at first and at starting it took its consistence by way of accessions. And so undoubtedly it may decrease on the contrary, for what is added plainly admits of being subtracted.
sources.raw_question: Could a Trinity that grew by addition also suffer loss or further increase?

question: Does Christ's condition 'if it is possible' imply uncertainty about what is possible for the Father?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. Nothing is impossible to the Father, as Christ himself says, 'Father, all things are possible to Thee.' The condition refers rather to men: it is impossible for man to withstand the fear of suffering, and faith can only be proved by trial, as shown by his prayer that Peter's faith might not fail.
sources.quote: though with God nothing is impossible, as Christ Himself says, Father, all things are possible to Thee, yet for man it is impossible to withstand the fear of suffering, and only by trial can faith be proved.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's condition 'if it is possible' imply uncertainty about what is possible for the Father?

question: Why was it necessary for created nature to be shown first, before mortality was swallowed up by immortality?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVIII.—Why man was not made perfect from the beginning.
sources.answer: Because God works through an ordered progression. Nature had first to be exhibited, and only afterwards could what is mortal be conquered by immortality and the corruptible by incorruptibility. In this way man is brought to the image and likeness of God. God foreknew human weakness but will overcome it through His love and power.
sources.quote: For it was necessary, at first, that nature should be exhibited; then, after that, that what was mortal should be conquered and swallowed up by immortality, and the corruptible by incorruptibility
sources.raw_question: Why was it necessary for created nature to be shown first, before mortality was swallowed up by immortality?

question: How does our knowledge of righteousness differ from our knowledge of a city we have seen, such as Carthage, or a city we have only heard of, such as Alexandria?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: Carthage is known through a memory image received by the senses. Alexandria is known through an image built from hearsay, which may not match the reality. Righteousness is not known in either way. The mind does not picture something absent or imagine it as best it can. It discerns something truly present within itself, and others who hear the definition recognise and approve it within themselves.
sources.quote: I do not think of anything absent, as Carthage, or imagine it as I am able, as Alexandria, whether it be so or not; but I discern something present, and I discern it within myself, though I myself am not that which I discern
sources.raw_question: How does our knowledge of righteousness differ from our knowledge of a city we have seen, such as Carthage, or a city we have only heard of, such as Alexandria?

question: Is loving God by faith necessary in order to come to see God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > God Must First Be Known by an Unerring Faith, that He May Be Loved.
sources.answer: Yes. Seeing God is granted to the pure in heart, and the heart cannot be cleansed and made fit to see Him unless He is first loved by faith. We shall never see Him face to face unless we already love Him now.
sources.quote: except He is loved by faith, it will not be possible for the heart to be cleansed, in order that it may be apt and meet to see Him.
sources.raw_question: Is loving God by faith necessary in order to come to see God?

question: What danger arises when the mind believes in and loves a God it does not see?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > God Must First Be Known by an Unerring Faith, that He May Be Loved.
sources.answer: The mind may feign to itself something that is not, and so hope for and love what is false. That would not be charity out of a pure heart, a good conscience and faith unfeigned. So faith in the unseen God must be unerring and not a fiction of the imagination.
sources.quote: we must take care, lest the mind believing that which it does not see, feign to itself something which is not, and hope for and love that which is false.
sources.raw_question: What danger arises when the mind believes in and loves a God it does not see?

question: What are the sources in Christ's mediatorial work from which purchased grace flows?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: There are three: the obedience of Christ's life, the suffering of his death, and his continued intercession. Every action of Christ as mediator that leads to grace being given to us either falls under one of these heads or serves or follows from them.
sources.quote: It hath a threefold rise, spring, or causality in Christ:— (1.) The obedience of his life. (2.) The suffering of his death. (3.) His continued intercession.
sources.raw_question: What are the sources in Christ's mediatorial work from which purchased grace flows?

question: How do the order in which Christ procured the benefits of his life and death compare with the order in which those benefits are applied to believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: In the order of procurement, Christ's life necessarily comes before his death. In the order of application, the benefits of his death are given to us first, before those of his life. This follows necessarily from the sinful state and condition in which we are found.
sources.quote: in the order of procurement, the life of Christ (as was necessary) precedeth his death; and therefore we shall handle it in the first place: but in the order of application, the benefits of his death are bestowed on us antecedently
sources.raw_question: How do the order in which Christ procured the benefits of his life and death compare with the order in which those benefits are applied to believers?

question: Is it legitimate to call the incarnation, 'God manifest in the flesh', a mystery, or is appealing to mystery an evasion?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: It is legitimate. Scripture itself calls it a great mystery, confessedly so, and we must speak as God directs. That it is a mystery does not make it any less a great and sacred truth that Christ is God manifest in the flesh.
sources.quote: Christ is God manifest in the flesh; which we acknowledge, own, and believe to be true, but a great mystery, — yet no less great and sacred a truth notwithstanding.
sources.raw_question: Is it legitimate to call the incarnation, 'God manifest in the flesh', a mystery, or is appealing to mystery an evasion?

question: How can 1 John 3:16 say that God laid down his life for us?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Person of Christ
sources.answer: He who was God laid down, for a season, the life that was his own in the human nature he had assumed. This taking of our nature is his coming in the flesh, and John says that whoever denies it is of the spirit of Antichrist.
sources.quote: He who was God laid down for a season and parted with that life which was his own, in that nature of ours which he had assumed.
sources.raw_question: How can 1 John 3:16 say that God laid down his life for us?

question: Does Christ's promise that the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church mean that the confession of his divine Sonship would face no serious opposition?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Preface
sources.answer: No. In denying that the gates of hell would prevail against the confession that Jesus is the Son of the living God, Christ also foretold a great and vigorous attempt to overthrow it. History bears this out: early heresies attacked the person of Christ and so the Trinity, and the same errors returned after the Reformation. Christ has nonetheless kept this confession secure.
sources.quote: For whereas the prevalency of the gates of hell in an enmity unto this confession is denied, a great and vigorous attempt to prevail therein is no less certainly foretold.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's promise that the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church mean that the confession of his divine Sonship would face no serious opposition?

question: Since God's love toward creatures is directed by divine wisdom, does the creation of the world serve the love that is in Christ?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. God's love as it flows outward is wholly directed by divine wisdom, which chooses its objects. Christ is that divine wisdom. So the world is made to satisfy divine love as Christ exercises it, the love in Christ's heart, by providing a spouse for Christ. That spouse is made up of the elect creatures that wisdom chooses and makes the end of the rest of creation.
sources.quote: But Christ is Divine wisdom so that the world is made to gratify Divine love as exercised by Christ or to gratify the love that is in Christ's heart, or to provide a spouse for Christ.
sources.raw_question: Since God's love toward creatures is directed by divine wisdom, does the creation of the world serve the love that is in Christ?

question: Should Christians condemn actions of the patriarchs that Scripture records without censure, or should they look for some other meaning in them?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXI.—We should not hastily impute as crimes to the men of old time those actions which the Scripture has not condemned, but should rather seek in them types of things to come: an example of this in the incest committed by Lot.
sources.answer: They should not condemn them but should look for a type in them. We are not more exact than God, nor superior to our Master. Nothing set down in Scripture without condemnation lacks significance.
sources.quote: we ought not to become the accusers [of those who committed them], for we are not more exact than God, nor can we be superior to our Master; but we should search for a type [in them].
sources.raw_question: Should Christians condemn actions of the patriarchs that Scripture records without censure, or should they look for some other meaning in them?

question: When and how did the Word of God pour out the life-giving Spirit of the remission of sins on the human race?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXI.—We should not hastily impute as crimes to the men of old time those actions which the Scripture has not condemned, but should rather seek in them types of things to come: an example of this in the incest committed by Lot.
sources.answer: He did so when he lived incarnate among men, eating and drinking wine on earth, and when he lay down and slept, that is, in his death. Irenaeus cites 'The Son of man came eating and drinking' and the Psalm 'I slept, and took repose' to show that the Spirit, through whom we are quickened, was given through the incarnate life and death of the Word.
sources.quote: At what time, then, did He pour out upon the human race the life-giving seed—that is, the Spirit of the remission of sins, through means of whom we are quickened? Was it not then, when He was eating with men, and drinking wine upon the earth?
sources.raw_question: When and how did the Word of God pour out the life-giving Spirit of the remission of sins on the human race?

question: What does the episode of Lot and his two daughters typify concerning the incarnation and the Church?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXI.—We should not hastily impute as crimes to the men of old time those actions which the Scripture has not condemned, but should rather seek in them types of things to come: an example of this in the incest committed by Lot.
sources.answer: It typifies the union of the seed of the Father of all, the Spirit of God by whom all things were made, with flesh, God's own workmanship. Through this commingling the two churches, Jewish and Gentile, bore living sons to the living God from one Father. Lot acted without lust or knowledge, so the type was carried out apart from the lust of the flesh.
sources.quote: the seed of the Father of all—that is, of the Spirit of God, by whom all things were made—was commingled and united with flesh— that is, with His own workmanship
sources.raw_question: What does the episode of Lot and his two daughters typify concerning the incarnation and the Church?

question: Does the incarnate Word hold power over all things and judge all, as both God's Word and true man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVIII.—God the Father and His Word have formed all created things (which They use) by Their own power and wisdom, not out of defect or ignorance. The Son of God, who received all power from the Father, would otherwise never have taken flesh upon Him.
sources.answer: Yes. He has power from the Father over all things because He is the Word of God and very man. He communicates with invisible beings intellectually and appoints a law for visible things. He reigns openly and brings just judgment on all, as David foretold that 'our God shall openly come.'
sources.quote: For it is He who has power from the Father over all things, since He is the Word of God, and very man
sources.raw_question: Does the incarnate Word hold power over all things and judge all, as both God's Word and true man?

question: Does the fact that God condescends to commune with human beings imply that from the beginning He Himself instituted words and names appropriate to things?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. God's willingness to commune with men comes from His love for mankind, and because finite nature cannot rise to the Most High, He brings His power down to the level of human weakness. Like a mother joining in her infant's babble, He adapts Himself to what we can receive and speaks in human language. This is an act of accommodation, not proof that He fixed particular words and syllables for things.
sources.quote: like a tender mother who joins in the inarticulate utterances of her babe, gives to our human nature what it is capable of receiving; and thus in the various manifestations of God to man He both adapts Himself to man and speaks in human language
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that God condescends to commune with human beings imply that from the beginning He Himself instituted words and names appropriate to things?

question: How should Scripture's statements that God repents, wakes from sleep, sits, stands or walks be understood?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: These things are not really true of God. They are accommodations, useful to those under instruction, each fitted to the spiritual state of the hearers. God's repenting accompanies the penitent and warns the prosperous, as in the case of Saul. His waking corresponds to those who rise from vanity, and His standing or sitting to those firm in righteousness. His walking in the garden signifies Adam's instability and fall.
sources.quote: it makes mention of His sitting, and standing, and moving, and the like, which are not as a fact connected with God, but are not without their use as an accommodation to those who are under teaching
sources.raw_question: How should Scripture's statements that God repents, wakes from sleep, sits, stands or walks be understood?

question: Is there any interval of time between God's willing something and its coming to be?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. In God there is no difference between will and performance; the accomplishment keeps pace with the purpose. As light is produced along with the kindling of fire, created things are an effect of the divine will but not posterior to it in time, which is what "and it was so" shows.
sources.quote: as light is produced along with the kindling of fire, at once coming out from it and shining forth along with it—in the same manner the existence of things created is an effect of the Divine will, but not posterior to it in time.
sources.raw_question: Is there any interval of time between God's willing something and its coming to be?

question: Do the Old Testament writers Moses and David share the same divine Teacher?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Both Moses and David have one and the same Teacher, the Holy Spirit. So the Psalm's teaching that creation declares without voice may be used to interpret Moses' account of the divine fiat.
sources.quote: since both Moses and David have one and the same Teacher, I mean the Holy Spirit, Who says that the fiat went before the creation
sources.raw_question: Do the Old Testament writers Moses and David share the same divine Teacher?

question: Has the inflexible righteousness of God shown in the Old Testament judgments (the flood, Sodom, the plagues on Egypt) been softened or modified by the 'milder genius of the Gospel'?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. The New Testament itself cites these very judgments as examples and warnings. The New Testament also gives abundant witness to God's unchanging justice, in the preaching of John the Baptist, the words of Jesus, and the epistles and Revelation. God is now withholding his judgments in a limited day of grace, but his justice is immutable.
sources.quote: though they who make the assertion forget, that these cases are adduced as examples in the New Testament
sources.raised_by_detail: those who speak of the 'milder genius of the Gospel'
sources.raw_question: Has the inflexible righteousness of God shown in the Old Testament judgments (the flood, Sodom, the plagues on Egypt) been softened or modified by the 'milder genius of the Gospel'?

question: Can the biblical teaching of God's wrath and judgment be dismissed as merely figurative language?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. If it rested on one isolated passage, it might be called figurative. But it is written across history, prophecy, sermon, epistle and vision. All of these together prove that God is a consuming fire and that the end of the enemies of the cross is destruction.
sources.quote: If it were only one isolated passage, you might urge it was figurative language: but here it is written in history, prophecy, sermon, epistle, vision, – all alike proving that our God is a consuming fire
sources.raw_question: Can the biblical teaching of God's wrath and judgment be dismissed as merely figurative language?

question: Is a God conceived as all compassion and benevolence, without righteous judgment, the true God revealed as Father, Son, and Holy Ghost?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. Such a God may be imagined and worshipped, but he is not the righteous Judge of all the earth. However much benevolence one ascribes to the Father, that is not the name of the one living and true God. That name is the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, whose love includes righteousness.
sources.quote: you may beautify the name of the Father whom you adore with every trait of benevolence, and tenderness, and grace, but it is not the name of the one living and true God, for that is the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: Is a God conceived as all compassion and benevolence, without righteous judgment, the true God revealed as Father, Son, and Holy Ghost?

question: Is the present time of God's patience and grace unlimited, so that pardon will always remain available?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. It is now the day of grace, and God's goodness leads to repentance, but this season is limited. When the master of the house has risen and shut the door, the last hour of pardoning mercy will have passed. Then God will not answer those who call on him.
sources.quote: the season is limited, and when once the master of the house has risen up (Luke 13:25) and has shut to the door, then the last hour of pardoning mercy will have passed away
sources.raw_question: Is the present time of God's patience and grace unlimited, so that pardon will always remain available?

question: Is it better to believe in God and remain in his love without knowing the reasons for created things than to pursue speculative knowledge?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVI.—“Knowledge puffeth up, but love edifieth.”
sources.answer: Yes. It is better to know no reason why anything in creation was made, and simply to believe in God and continue in his love. One should seek no knowledge beyond Jesus Christ the Son of God, crucified for us. Pursuing subtle questions and hair-splitting expressions leads to impiety and falling away from love, which is the life of man.
sources.quote: he should search after no other knowledge except [the knowledge of] Jesus Christ the Son of God, who was crucified for us, than that by subtle questions and hair-splitting expressions he should fall into impiety
sources.raw_question: Is it better to believe in God and remain in his love without knowing the reasons for created things than to pursue speculative knowledge?

question: If sin is forgiven through Christ, why do death and the evils of this world still remain for believers?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Remains of Death and the Evil Things of the World Turn to Good for the Elect. How Fitly the Death of Christ Was Chosen, that We Might Be Justified in His Blood. What the Anger of God is.
sources.answer: They remain fittingly, even after sin is forgiven, as a field of exercise for the faithful. Though death and the world's evils come from sin, especially original sin, they give man something to contend against for truth and a way to exercise and prove his goodness. So the new man is prepared for a new world by bearing this life's misery wisely while patiently awaiting future blessedness. The good use of death has even made glorious martyrs.
sources.quote: yet have fitly remained, even when sin is forgiven; that man might have wherewith to contend for truth, and whereby the goodness of the faithful might be exercised
sources.raw_question: If sin is forgiven through Christ, why do death and the evils of this world still remain for believers?

question: What purposes do the evils endured by the faithful serve in God's providence?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Remains of Death and the Evil Things of the World Turn to Good for the Elect. How Fitly the Death of Christ Was Chosen, that We Might Be Justified in His Blood. What the Anger of God is.
sources.answer: They serve the correction of sins, the exercising and proving of righteousness, or the showing of this life's misery. Showing that misery makes the true and lasting blessedness of the life to come desired more ardently. All things work together for good to those who love God and are predestinated to be conformed to the image of His Son.
sources.quote: are of profit either for the correction of sins, or for the exercising and proving of righteousness, or to manifest the misery of this life
sources.raw_question: What purposes do the evils endured by the faithful serve in God's providence?

question: Can names that a Gnostic teacher coins for the supreme first principle (such as Monotes, Henotes, Monad and Hen) give genuine knowledge of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XI.—The opinions of Valentinus, with those of his disciples and others.
sources.answer: No. By saying 'whom I call Monotes' and 'which I also call Henotes', the teacher admits that the names are his own invention and were never suggested by anyone before him. If anyone may assign names at pleasure, nothing prevents another from calling the same powers Gourd, Utter-Emptiness, Cucumber and Melon. Such names are arbitrary fabrications and teach nothing true about the divine.
sources.quote: it is most manifest that he confesses the things which have been said to be his own invention, and that he himself has given names to his scheme of things, which had never been previously suggested by any other
sources.raised_by_detail: a renowned Valentinian teacher (Marcus or Colorbasus)
sources.raw_question: Can names that a Gnostic teacher coins for the supreme first principle (such as Monotes, Henotes, Monad and Hen) give genuine knowledge of God?

question: Can one validly conclude that the work of redemption did not require a Redeemer of infinite power, so that Christ's eternity need not have been revealed?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: No. No one can fathom the full depth of the work of redemption and judging the universe, so it is presumptuous to pronounce that any power less than infinite could suffice for it. Arguing for Christ's divinity from what we know of the greatness of redemption may fall short of demonstration, but arguing the negative from what we do not know is impossible a priori.
sources.quote: it is much surer arguing for the affirmative, from what we know; than for the negative, from what we know not. It is possible our proof may not be sufficient: but it is, d priori, impossible that yours should.
sources.raw_question: Can one validly conclude that the work of redemption did not require a Redeemer of infinite power, so that Christ's eternity need not have been revealed?

question: Did Christ weep at the tomb of Lazarus because he grieved over Lazarus's death or his own absence?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The death was 'not unto death, but for the glory of God,' so it could not cause sorrow. Christ's absence was something he rejoiced in, for the apostles' sake. With divine omniscience he knew of the death from afar, so there was no necessity for tears, yet he truly wept; and the One who wept was also the Giver of life.
sources.quote: We can find, then, no necessity for tears, yet He wept.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ weep at the tomb of Lazarus because he grieved over Lazarus's death or his own absence?

question: How should Paul's statement that 'in Him we live, and move, and have our being' (Acts 17:28) be understood with respect to the human mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Trinity in the Mind is the Image of God, in that It Remembers, Understands, and Loves God, Which to Do is Wisdom.
sources.answer: It should be taken in a spiritual, not a bodily, sense. In respect of the body it could apply even to the physical world, in which we also live and move. So it must refer more excellently to the mind, which is made after God's image. All things are in God, since of him, through him, and in him are all things.
sources.quote: And therefore it ought to be taken in a more excellent way, and one that is spiritual, not visible, in respect to the mind, which is made after His image.
sources.raw_question: How should Paul's statement that 'in Him we live, and move, and have our being' (Acts 17:28) be understood with respect to the human mind?

question: What does 'the change of the right hand of the Most High' in Psalm 77 refer to, and does it imply a change in the Son's divine nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: The 'Right Hand' of the Father is the Son, the Power of God that made all things. He is from the Father yet subsists individually, not as a part of a whole. The 'change' is solely the dispensation of the flesh, His being veiled in flesh as to what is seen. In the idea of His nature the Right Hand does not differ from Him whose Right Hand it is.
sources.quote: neither does the Right Hand vary from Him Whose Right Hand It is, in regard to the idea of Its Nature, nor can any other change in It be spoken of besides the dispensation of the Flesh
sources.raw_question: What does 'the change of the right hand of the Most High' in Psalm 77 refer to, and does it imply a change in the Son's divine nature?

question: How is the everlasting glory of believers related to the grace Christ purchased for them in this life?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: Glory is simply the purchased grace of this life brought to perfection. The grace believers share with Christ now consists in acceptance with God, holiness, and the privileges of adoption. When these are carried to completeness, as perfect acceptance, perfect holiness, and perfect adoption or inheritance of sons, that is what is called everlasting glory.
sources.quote: Perfect acceptance, perfect holiness, perfect adoption, or inheritance of sons, — that is glory.
sources.raw_question: How is the everlasting glory of believers related to the grace Christ purchased for them in this life?

question: By condemning the claim that 'the Son was not before he was begotten,' does the Nicene anathema indirectly affirm that the Son existed before his generation, as Bishop Bull proposed?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Excursus B. On §22 (Note 3).
sources.answer: No. The Arian formula is best read as an enthymematic argument, a reductio drawn from the word 'Son.' It takes as granted the absurdity of 'he existed before he was begotten.' What it actually denies is that the Son existed from everlasting. The anathema therefore defends the Catholic doctrine of the Son's eternity rather than endorsing the position of certain early writers. The formula matches Arius's main argument: 'He is a son, therefore he had a beginning.'
sources.quote: it being, as they would say, a truism, that, ‘whereas He was begotten, He was not before He was begotten,’ and the denial of it a contradiction in terms.
sources.raw_question: By condemning the claim that 'the Son was not before he was begotten,' does the Nicene anathema indirectly affirm that the Son existed before his generation, as Bishop Bull proposed?

question: Can a thought (Enthymesis) or an affection go out from a spiritual being and become a separate, self-subsisting substance?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVIII.—Sophia was never really in ignorance or passion; her Enthymesis could not have been separated from herself, or exhibited special tendencies of its own.
sources.answer: No. A thought is always understood as belonging to some person and can never exist in isolation by itself. Likewise an affection is necessarily tied to an individual and cannot come into being apart. In Sophia's case the thought simply was the passion, so neither the thought apart from the Æon nor the passion apart from the thought could have its own substance, still less become the substance of matter.
sources.quote: Neither, therefore, can Enthymesis apart from the Æon, nor the affections apart from Enthymesis, separately possess substance; and thus once more their system breaks down and is destroyed.
sources.raw_question: Can a thought (Enthymesis) or an affection go out from a spiritual being and become a separate, self-subsisting substance?

question: Are the mind's love and knowledge in the mind as accidents in a subject, like color in a body?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself, and the Love, and the Knowledge of It. That the Same Three Exist Substantially, and are Predicated Relatively. That the Same Three are Inseparable. That the Same Three are Not Joined and Commingled Like Parts, But that They are of One Essence, and are Relatives.
sources.answer: No. They exist substantially, as the mind itself does. Color or shape cannot pass beyond its own subject, but the mind can love other things with the same love by which it loves itself, and can know many things besides itself. So love and knowledge are not contained in the mind as in a subject.
sources.quote: Wherefore love and knowledge are not contained in the mind as in a subject, but these also exist substantially, as the mind itself does
sources.raw_question: Are the mind's love and knowledge in the mind as accidents in a subject, like color in a body?

question: Did the Christian Church abolish the Old Testament practice of oblations, so that the God of the Old Testament differs from the God worshipped in the Church?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVIII.—Concerning sacrifices and oblations, and those who truly offer them.
sources.answer: No. The class of oblations remains in both covenants, and only the species has changed: offerings are now made by freemen rather than by slaves. The Lord is ever one and the same. The difference in the kind of oblation is designed to signify the liberty given to believers, since with God nothing is without purpose.
sources.quote: but the species alone has been changed, inasmuch as the offering is now made, not by slaves, but by freemen. For the Lord is [ever] one and the same
sources.raw_question: Did the Christian Church abolish the Old Testament practice of oblations, so that the God of the Old Testament differs from the God worshipped in the Church?

question: Were sins laid upon Christ in his death on the cross or only at his entrance into heaven?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: In his death on the cross. Peter says he bore our sins in his own body on the tree, and Isaiah says God made our iniquities meet upon him; this laying of sin on the victim is the formal reason of all propitiatory sacrifice, as Lev. 16 shows. 'Bearing sin' constantly means undergoing the punishment due to sin.
sources.quote: Therein were the sins of men laid upon him, and not in his entrance into heaven; for “he bare our sins in his own body on the tree,” 1 Pet. ii. 24.
sources.raw_question: Were sins laid upon Christ in his death on the cross or only at his entrance into heaven?

question: If God himself designed the way of reconciliation, can atonement and satisfaction still be said to be made to God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Though God in wisdom appointed this means of reconciliation, as he appointed Job's friends to offer sacrifices he would accept, atonement is still made with him as supreme Governor, attended with infinite justice and holiness. His appointing the remedy does not cancel the satisfaction rendered to his justice.
sources.quote: yet, as he was the supreme Governor, the Lord of all, attended with infinite justice and holiness, atonement was made with him, and satisfaction to him thereby.
sources.raw_question: If God himself designed the way of reconciliation, can atonement and satisfaction still be said to be made to God?

question: Did the ante-Nicene Church Fathers genuinely teach and defend the divinity of Christ, as Bishop Bull argued, despite later attempts such as Whitby's to discredit their testimony?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: Yes. Waterland holds that the main substance of Bishop Bull's case cannot be refuted, any more than truth can be extinguished. The Fathers, when examined, are found faithful. They defended the divinity of Christ against Jews, pagans, and heretics while they lived, and their surviving works still maintain it, so attempts to undermine their credit fail.
sources.quote: The Fathers have been tried, and are found faithful: what they defended while living, the divinity of our blessed Lord, against the insults of Jews, Pagans, and Heretics, they still maintain in their works
sources.raw_question: Did the ante-Nicene Church Fathers genuinely teach and defend the divinity of Christ, as Bishop Bull argued, despite later attempts such as Whitby's to discredit their testimony?

question: Is the unity of the God worshipped on the heavenly throne in Revelation a simple unity that excludes any plurality within it?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: No. Christ himself says he is set down with his Father in his throne, and the Lamb is seen in the midst of the throne, with heaven's worship addressed equally to him that sits on the throne and to the Lamb. The One on the throne is thus not alone in infinite solitariness but includes a plurality of Persons.
sources.quote: Is then the unity of the One there worshipped so simple an unity as to preclude any plurality subsisting therein? The throne was set in heaven, and One sat on the throne. But is this One alone in infinite solitariness?
sources.raw_question: Is the unity of the God worshipped on the heavenly throne in Revelation a simple unity that excludes any plurality within it?

question: Does comparing Genesis 6:3 with 1 Peter 3:20 show that the Spirit who strove with men before the flood is God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Genesis says 'My Spirit shall not always strive with man', while Peter attributes the same forbearance to the longsuffering of God in Noah's days. It was therefore the forbearance of God the Spirit with which the antediluvians contended.
sources.quote: It was then the forbearance of God the Spirit with which they before the flood contended.
sources.raw_question: Does comparing Genesis 6:3 with 1 Peter 3:20 show that the Spirit who strove with men before the flood is God?

question: Are the 'cheeks' of the beloved in Song of Songs 5:13 rightly taken, as the Chaldee paraphrase takes them, to be the two tables of stone of the law?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: No. That allusion is strained, as are most of that scholiast's conjectures. The cheeks are the seat of comeliness and manly courage. They signify Christ's fulness of grace for his people and his fulness of authority in his rule. These are set out in order in the gospel like a sweet-smelling bed of spices.
sources.quote: makes these cheeks of the church’s husband to be the two tables of stone, with the various lines drawn in them; but that allusion is strained
sources.raw_question: Are the 'cheeks' of the beloved in Song of Songs 5:13 rightly taken, as the Chaldee paraphrase takes them, to be the two tables of stone of the law?

question: Do the Old Testament episodes of Moses' outstretched hands defeating Amalek and the healing of the serpent's wound point to Christ, the Son of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXIV.—The conversion of the Gentiles was more difficult than that of the Jews; the labours of those apostles, therefore who engaged in the former task, were greater than those who undertook the latter.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus identifies Christ, the First-begotten of the dead, as the one who destroyed Amalek through the spreading forth of hands and gave life to man from the serpent's wound through faith directed toward Him. For this reason the Jews, who knew Moses and the prophets, could readily receive Him, because the Scriptures foretold Him and He came just as He had been announced.
sources.quote: Him who, by the spreading forth of hands, did destroy Amalek, and vivify man from the wound of the serpent, by means of faith which was [exercised] towards Him
sources.raw_question: Do the Old Testament episodes of Moses' outstretched hands defeating Amalek and the healing of the serpent's wound point to Christ, the Son of God?

question: What does the angels' phrase "in the city of David" show about which God sent Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: It shows that Christ's birth fulfils the promise God made to David, that an eternal King would come from the fruit of his body. That promise was made by the Creator of heaven and earth, whom David names as his help and Maker. So the God who sent Christ is the Creator, not some other god.
sources.quote: But why did [the angels] add, “in the city of David,” if they did not proclaim the glad tidings of the fulfilment of God’s promise made to David, that from the fruit of his body there should be an eternal King?
sources.raw_question: What does the angels' phrase "in the city of David" show about which God sent Christ?

question: Whom did the angels glorify when they sang "Glory to God in the highest" at Christ's birth?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter X.—Proofs of the foregoing, drawn from the Gospels of Mark and Luke.
sources.answer: They glorified the Creator of the highest, super-celestial things and the Founder of everything on earth. This is the God who sent the blessing of salvation to His own handiwork, men. The shepherds, who glorified this same God of the law and prophets, did likewise. If the angels had glorified some other god, they would have brought error and not truth.
sources.quote: they have glorified with these words Him who is the Creator of the highest, that is, of super-celestial things, and the Founder of everything on earth: who has sent to His own handiwork, that is, to men, the blessing of His salvation from heaven.
sources.raw_question: Whom did the angels glorify when they sang "Glory to God in the highest" at Christ's birth?

question: Can any believer whom Christ values be finally lost, whether through outward opposition, Satan, or indwelling sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: No. Christ will not lose any of them to eternity though all the world combine against them. No man can pluck them out of his or his Father's hand, the gates of hell shall not prevail, and he bears with their sins and by his power preserves them from such sins as the covenant of grace provides no remedy for.
sources.quote: he hides all, covers all, bears with all, rather than he will lose them; by his power preserving them from such sins as a remedy is not provided for in the covenant of grace.
sources.raw_question: Can any believer whom Christ values be finally lost, whether through outward opposition, Satan, or indwelling sin?

question: Does Christ as high priest truly suffer with and feel the temptations and infirmities of believers (Hebrews 4:15)?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. The double negation of Hebrews 4:15 vehemently affirms that we have a high priest who can be and is touched, and the Greek word means to 'suffer together.' Having been tempted as we are, he has a compassionate fellow-feeling with us in our temptations and spiritual weakness, which shows both in friendly grieving and in gracious supply of help.
