sources.quote: The two negations do vehemently affirm that we have such an high priest as can be, or is, touched. The word “touched” comes exceedingly short of expressing the original word; it is [^281]συμπαθῆσαι, — to “suffer together.”
sources.raw_question: Does Christ as high priest truly suffer with and feel the temptations and infirmities of believers (Hebrews 4:15)?

question: Is the Word of God, who healed the sick in the Gospels, the same one who made all things and formed man in the beginning?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XII.—Of the difference between life and death; of the breath of life and the vivifying Spirit: also how it is that the substance of flesh revives which once was dead.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus identifies the Word of God as the Maker of all things who formed man from the beginning, and says that this same Word, finding his handiwork damaged by wickedness, healed it. The Word's healing and restoring work is therefore the Creator caring for and renewing what he himself made.
sources.quote: For the Maker of all things, the Word of God, who did also from the beginning form man, when He found His handiwork impaired by wickedness, performed upon it all kinds of healing.
sources.raw_question: Is the Word of God, who healed the sick in the Gospels, the same one who made all things and formed man in the beginning?

question: Does Paul's account of his calling in Galatians show that the converted and renewed man is the same bodily person who was born from the womb?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XII.—Of the difference between life and death; of the breath of life and the vivifying Spirit: also how it is that the substance of flesh revives which once was dead.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says God set him apart from his mother's womb and revealed his Son in him. So the person born of flesh and the person who preached the Son of God were one and the same. Only his ignorance was driven out by knowledge, just as the healed blind men kept the substance of their eyes and only lost their blindness.
sources.quote: it was not, as I have already observed, one person who had been born from the womb, and another who preached the Gospel of the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's account of his calling in Galatians show that the converted and renewed man is the same bodily person who was born from the womb?

question: What is the chief good of the saints, and is it the sight of Christ as Son of man at the judgment?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: The chief good is the contemplation of the unchangeable substance of God, which is promised to the saints alone. It is the vision that Scripture calls "face to face" and "seeing him as he is." The sight of the Son of man at the judgment is not this chief good even for the righteous. After it they are still called onward into the kingdom and into eternal life.
sources.quote: that sight alone, I say, is our chief good, for the attaining of which we are directed to do whatever we do aright.
sources.raw_question: What is the chief good of the saints, and is it the sight of Christ as Son of man at the judgment?

question: Did second-century writers reserve titles such as 'Maker of all' and 'Framer of the universe' to the Father alone, so as to deny them to the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 26: Whether the Doctor did not equivocate or prevaricate strangely, in saying, 4 The generality of writers before the Council of Nice were, in the whole, clearly on
sources.answer: No. It is a notorious untruth that the Son was not given those or like titles, as Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria show. What is true is only that such titles were eminently and emphatically given to the Father, which holds equally of all later centuries and of the creeds, and so implies nothing against the Son's divinity.
sources.quote: if he means only, that those and the like titles were eminently and emphatically given to the Father, that indeed is very true of the second century; and as true of all the centuries following, down to this present, as appears by our creeds
sources.raw_question: Did second-century writers reserve titles such as 'Maker of all' and 'Framer of the universe' to the Father alone, so as to deny them to the Son?

question: Can philosophical contemplation and love of truth by reason alone bring mortals to blessedness and return to God without faith in the Mediator?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > John is Rather to Be Understood of Our Perfect Likeness with the Trinity in Life Eternal. Wisdom is Perfected in Happiness.
sources.answer: No. Contemplative wisdom is truly wisdom only by sharing in God, from whom alone a rational mind is made wise. Cicero rightly learned from the greatest philosophers that souls are eternal. Even so, the course of reason and inquiry is not enough for wretched mortals who lack faith in the Mediator.
sources.quote: But that course which consists in the love and investigation of truth does not suffice for the wretched, i.e. for all mortals who have only this kind of reason, and are without faith in the Mediator
sources.raw_question: Can philosophical contemplation and love of truth by reason alone bring mortals to blessedness and return to God without faith in the Mediator?

question: Did Moses foretell the passion of Christ, including its day, place and time?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter X.—The Old Testament Scriptures, and those written by Moses in particular, do everywhere make mention of the Son of God, and foretell His advent and passion. From this fact it follows that they were inspired by one and the same God.
sources.answer: Yes. Moses foretold Christ's passion figuratively by the name of the passover, and the Lord suffered at that very festival, fulfilling it. Moses also described the place and the time of day, prescribing that the passover be sacrificed in the chosen place at evening toward the setting of the sun.
sources.quote: at that very festival, which had been proclaimed such a long time previously by Moses, did our Lord suffer, thus fulfilling the passover.
sources.raw_question: Did Moses foretell the passion of Christ, including its day, place and time?

question: Does Jacob's prophecy that a ruler shall not fail from Judah until he comes who is the hope of the nations refer to Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter X.—The Old Testament Scriptures, and those written by Moses in particular, do everywhere make mention of the Son of God, and foretell His advent and passion. From this fact it follows that they were inspired by one and the same God.
sources.answer: Yes. If inquirers examine when a prince failed from Judah and who is the hope of the nations, along with the vine, the colt, the garment, the eyes, the teeth and the wine, they will find that no one is announced but our Lord Jesus Christ.
sources.quote: and thus let them investigate every one of the points mentioned; and they shall find that there was none other announced than our Lord, Christ Jesus.
sources.raw_question: Does Jacob's prophecy that a ruler shall not fail from Judah until he comes who is the hope of the nations refer to Jesus Christ?

question: What is the 'manifold wisdom of God' made known by the church to the principalities and powers in Ephesians 3:10?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: It is the mystery of adoption: that the Gentiles should be fellow-heirs and of the same body. Sinners are taken from slavery in the family of the world into sonship in God's family. This was first revealed by the Spirit to the prophets and apostles.
sources.quote: The mystery of adopting sinners of the Gentiles, taking them from their slavery in the family of the world, that they might have a right of heirship, becoming sons in the family of God, is this wisdom, thus made known.
sources.raw_question: What is the 'manifold wisdom of God' made known by the church to the principalities and powers in Ephesians 3:10?

question: Who testifies to the believer's conscience that he is freed from Satan's family and has become a son of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: The Spirit of Christ does. He testifies to the believer's heart and conscience that he is freed from all engagements to Satan's family and is now God's son. He also enables the believer to cry 'Abba, Father' and to behave as a child.
sources.quote: The Spirit of Christ testifies to the heart and conscience of a believer that he is freed from all engagements unto the family of Satan, and is become the son of God
sources.raw_question: Who testifies to the believer's conscience that he is freed from Satan's family and has become a son of God?

question: What do the 'new name' and the 'white stone' of Revelation 2:17 signify, and on what is adoption by the Spirit grounded?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: The new name is 'A child of God,' given in adoption. The white stone is a token of judicial acquittal. Adoption by the Spirit rests on absolution in the blood of Jesus: the white stone cancels the old family's claim, and the new name gives entrance into God's family.
sources.quote: Our adoption by the Spirit is bottomed on our absolution in the blood of Jesus; and therefore is the new name in the white stone privilege grounded on discharge.
sources.raw_question: What do the 'new name' and the 'white stone' of Revelation 2:17 signify, and on what is adoption by the Spirit grounded?

question: What does John mean in John 21:25 when he says the world could not contain the books if all Jesus' works were written?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: He does not mean unrecorded healing miracles, which the Gospel covers in general terms, but the works of the Son as Creator of heaven, earth and all the world. Since God made all things in infinite wisdom, the bounded world cannot contain a full account of that wisdom; so the majesty of the Son is to be learned from creation, not only from miracles done in the flesh.
sources.quote: that we are to learn the majesty of the Son of God not by the miracles alone which He did in the flesh. For these are little compared with the greatness of His other work.
sources.raw_question: What does John mean in John 21:25 when he says the world could not contain the books if all Jesus' works were written?

question: Are all created beings, including the heavenly powers, servants of God by virtue of being created?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Against those who maintain that the Spirit is in the rank neither of a servant nor of a master, but in that of the free.
sources.answer: Yes. As soon as creatures were created their bondage to God began; the heavenly powers do not rule one another but all bow to God as Master and Creator. Even the apostate powers are not different in nature but fling off their bondage through disobedience; all men too, whatever their social rank, are fellow slaves as chattels of the Creator.
sources.quote: For no sooner were they created than bondage was commenced. The heavenly bodies exercise no rule over one another, for they are unmoved by ambition, but all bow down to God
sources.raw_question: Are all created beings, including the heavenly powers, servants of God by virtue of being created?

question: What does the parable of the king who made a marriage feast for his son teach about the identity of God the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: It shows there is one King and Lord, the Father of all, who prepared the marriage for His Son from the beginning. The same King is called the great King in Christ's saying about Jerusalem. He kindly invited the people of the old dispensation through successive servants. When they refused and killed the messengers, He destroyed their city and gathered guests from all nations.
sources.quote: there is one King and Lord, the Father of all, of whom He had previously said, “Neither shalt thou swear by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King;”
sources.raw_question: What does the parable of the king who made a marriage feast for his son teach about the identity of God the Father?

question: What do the expressions of the Spirit being given, sent, and poured out teach about the covenant of grace?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: They show its three great properties. It is free, because the Spirit is given. It is orderly and sure, because he is sent from the Father's love by the Son's procurement. It is efficacious, because he is poured out abundantly.
sources.quote: First, That it is free; he is given. Secondly, That it is orderly, ordered in all things, and sure, from the love of the Father, by the procurement of the Son;
sources.raw_question: What do the expressions of the Spirit being given, sent, and poured out teach about the covenant of grace?

question: In what sense does Christ 'go away' from his disciples in John 16:7, given that he promised to be with them to the end of the world?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Christ's departure means only the withdrawal of his bodily presence from the earth after his resurrection, heaven receiving him until the restitution of all things. In respect of his Deity, and in the exercise of his love and care toward them, he remains with them always, as he promised in Matthew 28:20.
sources.quote: the withdrawing his bodily presence from the earth after his resurrection, the "heaven being to receive him, until the times of the restitution of all things," Acts iii. 21; for in respect of his Deity, and the exercise of love and care towards them
sources.raw_question: In what sense does Christ 'go away' from his disciples in John 16:7, given that he promised to be with them to the end of the world?

question: What does 2 John 9 imply for those who deny the eternal Sonship of Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: It implies that they do not have God. Owen reads the text to mean that whoever denies Christ as the eternal Son loses the Father as well. A God who always existed but was not always the Father is not the true God.
sources.quote: Whoever denies Christ the Son, as the Son, that is, the eternal Son of God, he loses the Father also, and the true God; he has not God.
sources.raw_question: What does 2 John 9 imply for those who deny the eternal Sonship of Christ?

question: Why, in the love of carnal and temporal things, is the conception of the mind's word distinct from its bringing forth?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > In the Love of Spiritual Things the Word Born is the Same as the Word Conceived. It is Otherwise in the Love of Carnal Things.
sources.answer: Because in such love what is conceived by desiring is born only by attaining. Knowing and loving gold, food, or honors does not satisfy unless they are actually possessed, and even when obtained they do not suffice, as Christ says that whoever drinks this water shall thirst again. Thus the mind conceives pain and labors with want until it brings forth the thing, as lust conceiving brings forth sin.
sources.quote: But in the love of carnal and temporal things, as in the offspring of animals, the conception of the word is one thing, the bringing forth another. For here what is conceived by desiring is born by attaining.
sources.raw_question: Why, in the love of carnal and temporal things, is the conception of the mind's word distinct from its bringing forth?

question: When Christ says 'by thy mouth thou shalt be justified, and by thy mouth thou shalt be condemned', what mouth is meant?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > In the Love of Spiritual Things the Word Born is the Same as the Word Conceived. It is Otherwise in the Love of Carnal Things.
sources.answer: Not the visible bodily mouth but the inner, invisible mouth of thought and heart. Christ thereby refers all right actions and sins to the bringing forth of the inner word.
sources.quote: intending thereby not the visible mouth, but that which is within and invisible, of the thought and of the heart.
sources.raw_question: When Christ says 'by thy mouth thou shalt be justified, and by thy mouth thou shalt be condemned', what mouth is meant?

question: Do the colours of the sunbeams and the rainbow in Scripture represent the Holy Spirit and his graces?

sources.author: Jonathan Edwards
sources.work: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.section: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture uses the rainbow, the coloured dove's feathers and the coloured precious stones to signify the love and grace of God and the varied graces of the Spirit. Edwards holds that the Creator designed the variety of the sun's rays for this very purpose.
sources.quote: These beautiful colors of the sunbeams we find made use of in Scripture for this purpose, viz., to represent the graces of the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Do the colours of the sunbeams and the rainbow in Scripture represent the Holy Spirit and his graces?

question: What does Christ's argument from 'I am the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob' to the Sadducees prove about God and the resurrection?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter V.—The author returns to his former argument, and shows that there was but one God announced by the law and prophets, whom Christ confesses as His Father, and who, through His word, one living God with Him, made Himself known to men in both covenants.
sources.answer: It proves both the resurrection and that the God who spoke to Moses from the bush is the one supreme living God. Since He is the God not of the dead but of the living, yet is called God of the sleeping fathers, they live to God as children of the resurrection. And the God of the living can only be He above whom there is no other God.
sources.quote: He who spake to Moses out of the bush, and declared Himself to be the God of the fathers, He is the God of the living. For who is the God of the living unless He who is God, and above whom there is no other God?
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's argument from 'I am the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob' to the Sadducees prove about God and the resurrection?

question: Is Christ, together with the Father, the God of the living who spoke to Moses and appeared to the patriarchs?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter V.—The author returns to his former argument, and shows that there was but one God announced by the law and prophets, whom Christ confesses as His Father, and who, through His word, one living God with Him, made Himself known to men in both covenants.
sources.answer: Yes. The Word is He who spoke to Moses, silenced the Sadducees, and bestows the resurrection. Christ calls Himself the resurrection and the life, and the fathers are His children, so Christ with the Father is the God of the living manifested to the fathers.
sources.quote: Christ Himself, therefore, together with the Father, is the God of the living, who spake to Moses, and who was also manifested to the fathers.
sources.raw_question: Is Christ, together with the Father, the God of the living who spoke to Moses and appeared to the patriarchs?

question: Does the Hebrew word kopher in Numbers 35 properly express the idea of satisfaction for sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: Yes. In Numbers 35:31-33 God refuses any compensation, sacred or civil, that would free a murderer from his due punishment. The word is therefore rightly rendered 'satisfaction', and it properly expresses what is meant by the doctrine: a compensation answering the punishment due for a crime.
sources.quote: where God denies that any compensation, sacred or civil, shall be received to free a murderer from the punishment due unto him; which properly expresses what we intend
sources.raw_question: Does the Hebrew word kopher in Numbers 35 properly express the idea of satisfaction for sin?

question: What are the things by which a person is saved, according to Paul in 1 Corinthians 6:11?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XI.—Treats upon the actions of carnal and of spiritual persons; also, that the spiritual cleansing is not to be referred to the substance of our bodies, but to the manner of our former life.
sources.answer: A person is saved by the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God. Paul contrasts the vices that lead to destruction with being washed, sanctified and justified 'in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Spirit of our God.' Whoever brings forth the fruit of the Spirit is saved altogether through communion with the Spirit. Whoever remains in the works of the flesh, not having received the Spirit of God, cannot inherit the kingdom.
sources.quote: Now he says that the things which save are the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Spirit of our God.
sources.raw_question: What are the things by which a person is saved, according to Paul in 1 Corinthians 6:11?

question: When believers are washed and come to bear the image of the heavenly one, is the substance of their body removed or replaced?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XI.—Treats upon the actions of carnal and of spiritual persons; also, that the spiritual cleansing is not to be referred to the substance of our bodies, but to the manner of our former life.
sources.answer: No. What is washed away is not the substance of the body or the image of our original formation, but our former vain manner of life. We bore the image of the earthly when we did the works of the flesh. We bear the image of the heavenly when we believe in the Lord's name and receive His Spirit. Thus the very members that once worked corruption are made alive by working the works of the Spirit.
sources.quote: Now we have washed away, not the substance of our body, nor the image of our [primary] formation, but the former vain conversation.
sources.raw_question: When believers are washed and come to bear the image of the heavenly one, is the substance of their body removed or replaced?

question: Is the second-century Logos-Christology, which treated the Son as a prolation of Deity reduced to dimensions suited to relations with a world of time and space, an adequate account of the Son?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. Warfield regards it as a deflection of Christian thought into subordinationist channels, caused by the dominant neo-Stoic and neo-Platonic philosophies of the day. In his account it also largely neglected the Spirit, and it eventually ran to seed in Arianism.
sources.quote: In the second century the dominant neo-Stoic and neo-Platonic ideas deflected Christian thought into subordinationist channels, and produced what is known as the Logos-Christology
sources.raw_question: Is the second-century Logos-Christology, which treated the Son as a prolation of Deity reduced to dimensions suited to relations with a world of time and space, an adequate account of the Son?

question: How can God's reward and punishment of human beings be just?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVII.—Men are possessed of free will, and endowed with the faculty of making a choice. It is not true, therefore, that some are by nature good, and others bad.
sources.answer: They are just because human beings have the power to choose. God freely gives what is good, but each person must keep it. Those who do good when they could have done otherwise receive glory and honour. Those who despise God's goodness when they could have done good receive his righteous judgment, as Paul teaches in Romans 2.
sources.quote: they who work it shall receive glory and honour, because they have done that which is good when they had it in their power not to do it
sources.raw_question: How can God's reward and punishment of human beings be just?

question: Do Christ's exhortations and warnings in the Gospels show that human beings have free will?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVII.—Men are possessed of free will, and endowed with the faculty of making a choice. It is not true, therefore, that some are by nature good, and others bad.
sources.answer: Yes. Commands such as 'let your light shine', 'take heed to yourselves' and 'why call ye me Lord, Lord', together with the parables of watchful and unfaithful servants, all assume that people can choose to obey. They show God giving counsel and urging people to submit to him, without forcing them.
sources.quote: by which He exhorts us to submit ourselves to Him, and seeks to turn us away from [the sin of] unbelief against Him, without, however, in any way coercing us.
sources.raw_question: Do Christ's exhortations and warnings in the Gospels show that human beings have free will?

question: Is the distinction between good and evil, righteous and unrighteous, merely a matter of human opinion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXII.—Further exposure of the wicked and blasphemous doctrines of the heretics.
sources.answer: No. If good and evil existed only in human opinion, Christ would never have taught that the righteous shall shine as the sun in their Father's kingdom while the unrighteous are sent into everlasting fire. His teaching therefore presupposes a real, objective difference between righteousness and unrighteousness.
sources.quote: if there were really no such thing as good and evil, but certain things were deemed righteous, and certain others unrighteous, in human opinion only, He never would have expressed Himself thus in His teaching
sources.raw_question: Is the distinction between good and evil, righteous and unrighteous, merely a matter of human opinion?

question: Is it consistent to claim Jesus as one's Master while teaching that one must experience every kind of deed, including abominable ones?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXII.—Further exposure of the wicked and blasphemous doctrines of the heretics.
sources.answer: No. Christ forbade not only evil acts but even the thoughts and words that lead to them, condemning lust as well as adultery and anger as well as murder. Those who call him a superior Master yet teach the opposite are put to confusion and condemned by his own teaching.
sources.quote: how then can they escape being put to confusion, when they affirm that such a Master was more highly toned [in spirit] and better than others, and yet manifestly give instruction of a kind utterly opposed to His teaching?
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent to claim Jesus as one's Master while teaching that one must experience every kind of deed, including abominable ones?

question: Can mere men possess souls equal or superior to that of Jesus?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXII.—Further exposure of the wicked and blasphemous doctrines of the heretics.
sources.answer: No. The Lord rose from the dead on the third day, showed himself to his disciples and was taken up into heaven before their eyes. Those who claim souls like his die and do not rise again or appear to anyone. This proves their souls are in no respect similar to his, and their works bring no real benefit compared with his.
sources.quote: inasmuch as these men die, and do not rise again, nor manifest themselves to any, they are proved as possessing souls in no respect similar to that of Jesus.
sources.raw_question: Can mere men possess souls equal or superior to that of Jesus?

question: What makes Christ a common or public person who acts in the place of the elect?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Chiefly the covenant he made with his Father for this purpose. The terms of this covenant are set out at length in Isaiah 53 and summed up in Psalm 40:7-8 and Hebrews 10:8-10. Under it the Father designated the Son to the work of redemption, and the Son undertook it.
sources.quote: In general, from the covenant entered into by himself with his Father to this purpose.
sources.raw_question: What makes Christ a common or public person who acts in the place of the elect?

question: Between whom is the 'counsel of peace' of Zechariah 6:13 made?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Between the Father and the Son. It is the eternal compact concerning redemption. In that undertaking the Son rejoiced from eternity, as Proverbs 8:22-30 shows.
sources.quote: Thus the “counsel of peace” became to be “between them both,” Zech. vi. 13; that is, the Father and Son.
sources.raw_question: Between whom is the 'counsel of peace' of Zechariah 6:13 made?

question: How can Titus 1:2 say eternal life was promised 'before the world began', when no human beings then existed to receive the promise?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: The promise was made to the Son of God on our behalf. He had undertaken to act for the elect, and as their head and representative he received all the promises of mercy and grace for them. Likewise, grace given 'before the world began' (2 Tim 1:9) was given in Christ as our appointed head and mediator.
sources.quote: eternal life is said to be promised of God “before the world began,” Tit. i. 2; that is, to the Son of God for us, on his undertaking on our behalf.
sources.raw_question: How can Titus 1:2 say eternal life was promised 'before the world began', when no human beings then existed to receive the promise?

question: Were the saints of the Old Testament saved by Christ's blood, even though they lived before his death?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. As to the efficacy and merit of his work, Christ was absolved immediately upon his faithful engagement in the covenant. All the Old Testament saints were therefore saved by his blood no less than those who came after him.
sources.quote: and thereby all the saints of the Old Testament were saved by his blood no less than we.
sources.raw_question: Were the saints of the Old Testament saved by Christ's blood, even though they lived before his death?

question: How can Christ call the elect his 'sheep' before they are called or believe?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Because the Father gave them to Christ in the covenant to be redeemed. They belonged to the Father by eternal election and were committed into the Son's hands. So Christ laid down his life for them as his sheep even before their calling.
sources.quote: They were God’s by eternal designation and election, and he gave them to Christ to be redeemed. Hence, before their calling or believing, he calls them his “sheep,”
sources.raw_question: How can Christ call the elect his 'sheep' before they are called or believe?

question: May the term 'Homoousios' (of one substance) be dropped from the written Creed for the sake of peace and unity with the emperor?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His charge of cowardice is baseless: for Basil displayed the highest courage before the Emperor and his Lord-Lieutenants.
sources.answer: No. Basil holds that nothing may be taken away from or added to the Faith, and he would not change even the order of the Creed's words. He wanted the emperor in the Church for the sake of his soul, but not at the price of altering the confession of faith.
sources.quote: but a diminution of or addition to the Faith was so far from his (Basil’s) thoughts, that he would not change even the order of the written words.
sources.raised_by_detail: Modestus, the lord-lieutenant of the Emperor Valens
sources.raw_question: May the term 'Homoousios' (of one substance) be dropped from the written Creed for the sake of peace and unity with the emperor?

question: In the first bestowal of saving grace, when the Spirit raises a soul from spiritual death to life, does the believer actively hold communion with Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IX.
sources.answer: No. In that first communication of the Spirit the saints only passively receive Christ's life-giving, quickening Spirit and power. They are like the dry bones in Ezekiel, which live when the wind blows on them, or like Lazarus, who came forth when Christ called. Active communion with Christ belongs to the further work of the Spirit and the increase of grace, by which believers grow in holiness and obedience.
sources.quote: the saints have no kind of communion with Christ therein but only what consists in a passive reception of that life-giving, quickening Spirit and power
sources.raw_question: In the first bestowal of saving grace, when the Spirit raises a soul from spiritual death to life, does the believer actively hold communion with Christ?

question: Why does speculative inquiry into the divine essence lead to heresy?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Because trying to trace hidden things by human reasoning admits false notions as readily as true ones. A person seeking to know the unknown may take falsehood for truth. Where such speculation is at rest, error is precluded. The many heresies about God, including the Eunomians' error, arose from intruding recklessly into matters above comprehension.
sources.quote: For in speculative enquiry fallacies readily find place. But where speculation is entirely at rest, the necessity of error is precluded.
sources.raw_question: Why does speculative inquiry into the divine essence lead to heresy?

question: In what sense is Christ compared to 'the apple-tree among the trees of the wood' in Song of Songs 2:3, and how does he differ from angels and the best of men?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Christ alone bears the two excellent things of a tree: fruit for food and shade for refreshment. All other 'sons', whether angels (sons of God by creation) or the best of Adam's offspring, are like fruitless, leafless forest trees to a hungry, weary soul. Christ's fruit is his flesh and blood, his everlasting righteousness and his graces. His shade gives shelter and rest.
sources.quote: because he hath the two eminent things of trees, which the residue of them have not:— 1. Fruit for food; 2. Shade for refreshment.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is Christ compared to 'the apple-tree among the trees of the wood' in Song of Songs 2:3, and how does he differ from angels and the best of men?

question: What is meant by the 'banqueting-house' or 'house of wine' into which Christ brings his spouse in Song of Songs 2:4?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: It means the preparations of grace and mercy: the love, kindness and supplies that are revealed in the gospel, declared in the assemblies of the saints, and given by the Spirit. Whether it refers to the Scriptures, the gospel, the ordinances, or special manifestations of love makes no difference. In all of these Christ gives grace that refreshes, strengthens and comforts the saints.
sources.quote: These are the preparations of grace and mercy, — love, kindness, supplies revealed in the gospel, declared in the assemblies of the saints, exhibited by the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: What is meant by the 'banqueting-house' or 'house of wine' into which Christ brings his spouse in Song of Songs 2:4?

question: Can eternal life be both God's free gift through Jesus Christ and a reward for the believer's obedience?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes, in different respects. In itself and originally, eternal life is God's gift by Jesus Christ. But God has constituted obedience as the means of attaining it. With regard to that constitution, eternal life is a reward and God is a rewarder in bestowing it.
sources.quote: which, as in itself and originally [it] is his gift by Jesus Christ, so, with regard to his constitution of our obedience, as the means of attaining it, [it] is a reward, and God in bestowing of it a rewarder.
sources.raw_question: Can eternal life be both God's free gift through Jesus Christ and a reward for the believer's obedience?

question: Who is the one of whom the Father says in Isaiah 45:13, "I have raised him up in righteousness, and all his ways are straight"?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: The Son. The Father bears this witness of the Son in the flesh, and Paul confirms that the Father raised up Christ Jesus from the dead. So the prophecy distinguishes the Father, who raises, from the Son, who is raised.
sources.quote: It is of the Son that the Father says, “I have raised Him up in righteousness.”
sources.raw_question: Who is the one of whom the Father says in Isaiah 45:13, "I have raised him up in righteousness, and all his ways are straight"?

question: Can one hold that the Holy Spirit renews the earth but did not create it, without dividing the work of the Trinity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, as well as the Father and the Son, is pointed out in holy Scripture as Creator, and the same truth was shadowed forth even by heathen writers, but it was shown most plainly in the Mystery of the Incarnation, after touching upon which, the writer maintains his argument from the fact that worship which is due to the Creator alone is paid to the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: No. If the Spirit renews but did not create, then His operation would be superior to that of the Father and the Son, since the restored earth is better than the earth as first made, which is false. Alternatively, if the Spirit's work were added later, the work would have needed His help and the Creator would undergo change, which is the Manichean error. So the Spirit must be held to share in creation itself.
sources.quote: they who desire to sever the Persons must maintain that the operation of the Holy Spirit is superior to that of the Father and the Son, which is far from the truth
sources.raised_by_detail: those who desire to sever the Persons
sources.raw_question: Can one hold that the Holy Spirit renews the earth but did not create it, without dividing the work of the Trinity?

question: Do the pagan poets' statements that a spirit sustains heaven and earth support the claim that the Spirit of God is Creator?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter V. The Holy Spirit, as well as the Father and the Son, is pointed out in holy Scripture as Creator, and the same truth was shadowed forth even by heathen writers, but it was shown most plainly in the Mystery of the Incarnation, after touching upon which, the writer maintains his argument from the fact that worship which is due to the Creator alone is paid to the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes, as a shadow of the truth. Gentile writers, following Scripture as it were through shadows, said that a spirit within nourishes heaven, earth and the stars. Even if they meant a spirit of the air, if they made such a spirit the author of all things, Christians should all the more not doubt that the Spirit of God is Creator of all things.
sources.quote: If they declared a Spirit of the air to be the Author of all things, do we doubt that the Spirit of God is the Creator of all things?
sources.raw_question: Do the pagan poets' statements that a spirit sustains heaven and earth support the claim that the Spirit of God is Creator?

question: Can the question 'Is the Unoriginate one or two?' be answered without first defining what 'unoriginate' means?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Objections Continued. Whether is the Unoriginate one or two? Inconsistent in Arians to use an unscriptural word; necessary to define its meaning. Different senses of the word. If it means 'without Father,' there is but One Unoriginate; if 'without beginning or creation,' there are two. Inconsistency of Asterius. 'Unoriginate' a title of God, not in contrast with the Son, but with creatures, as is 'Almighty,' or 'Lord of powers.' 'Father' is the truer title, as not only Scriptural, but implying a Son, and our adoption as sons.
sources.answer: No. 'Unoriginate' is an unscriptural word borrowed from the Greeks with several meanings: what has not yet come to be but can, what never can come to be, what exists without coming from any or having a father, and (per Asterius) what is not made but always is. Those asking must specify the sense, and the answer differs by sense.
sources.quote: They ought then, when they ask the question, to add in what sense they take the word ‘unoriginate,’ and then the parties questioned would be able to answer to the point.
sources.raw_question: Can the question 'Is the Unoriginate one or two?' be answered without first defining what 'unoriginate' means?

question: Can the numerical value of the letters in the Lord's names, such as Jesus totaling 888, prove the Valentinian system of Aeons in the Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIV.—Folly of the arguments derived by the heretics from numbers, letters, and syllables.
sources.answer: No. If the Lord's names encoded the Pleroma, his Greek name Soter would have to fit as well, but it has five letters and a value of 1408, which match nothing in their system. In Hebrew, the original language of the name, Jesus has only two and a half letters, so the reckoning of 888 collapses. The names Christ, Father, and the supreme divine name Baruch also fail to fit, which shows that their calculations are forced and arbitrary.
sources.quote: But these things do not in any way correspond with their Pleroma; the account, therefore, which they give of transactions in the Pleroma cannot be true.
sources.raw_question: Can the numerical value of the letters in the Lord's names, such as Jesus totaling 888, prove the Valentinian system of Aeons in the Pleroma?

question: Did the apostle Peter, in his preaching after healing the lame man, proclaim a God different from the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. Peter preached that the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God of the fathers, glorified His Son Jesus and fulfilled the promise made to the fathers. He did not proclaim another god but the Son of God who was made man and suffered.
sources.quote: not certainly proclaiming another god, but the Son of God, who also was made man, and suffered; thus leading Israel into knowledge
sources.raw_question: Did the apostle Peter, in his preaching after healing the lame man, proclaim a God different from the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob?

question: Why would persecutors of Christ's disciples think they were doing God service by killing them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Because they know neither the Father nor the Son. Their blind and desperate ignorance is the cause of both their fury and their confidence. The disciples therefore should not be troubled in conscience by the persecutors' confidence.
sources.quote: know that their blind and desperate ignorance is the cause of their fury and persuasion
sources.raw_question: Why would persecutors of Christ's disciples think they were doing God service by killing them?

question: What does the statement that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob "live unto God" show about whether death could destroy the divinity in Christ?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > And that It Does Not Follow Thence, that Because Christ Died It Must Also Be Received that God Died; For Scripture Sets Forth that Not Only Was Christ God, But Man Also.
sources.answer: It shows that death dissolves only what is mortal. The patriarchs, mere men, still live because death could not touch their souls. Much more could death in Christ act only on his body and not on the divinity of the Word, since the power of death is broken when immortality intervenes.
sources.quote: much rather death in Christ could have power against the material of His body alone, while against the divinity of the Word it could not bring itself to bear.
sources.raw_question: What does the statement that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob "live unto God" show about whether death could destroy the divinity in Christ?

question: If the three Persons are coequal and coeternal, why is each manifested under a distinct title or work, such as the Son being Judge?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 19: Whether the Doctor hath not given a very partial account of John v. 23. founding the honour due to the Son on this only, that the Father hath committed all judg
sources.answer: Each Person is manifested under a distinct title so that each receives the honour due to him. If the Catholic doctrine is true, the fittest way to secure each Person's honour is for each to be shown to us under some peculiar character and to back his claim to homage by some remarkable dispensation. This is why the Son, whose dignity is more liable to be questioned than the Father's, is made Judge.
sources.quote: what more proper method can we imagine, to secure to each Person the honour due unto him, than this; that every Person should be manifested to us under some peculiar title or character
sources.raw_question: If the three Persons are coequal and coeternal, why is each manifested under a distinct title or work, such as the Son being Judge?

question: Can someone consistently accept some parts of Luke's Gospel as true while rejecting other parts on the ground that Luke did not know the truth, as Marcion and Valentinus did?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XIV.—If Paul had known any mysteries unrevealed to the other apostles, Luke, his constant companion and fellow-traveller, could not have been ignorant of them; neither could the truth have possibly lain hid from him, through whom alone we learn many and most important particulars of the Gospel history.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus argues that the heretics must either receive the whole of Luke's narrative or reject all of it, since no one of common sense can treat Luke as reliable in some places and ignorant in others. Through Luke alone we know many important parts of the Gospel that the heretics themselves use. If Marcion's followers reject Luke, they have no Gospel at all, and Valentinus's followers lose the texts they build their speculations on. If they accept the whole, they will be led by the full Gospel and the apostles' teaching to repent.
sources.quote: For no persons of common sense can permit them to receive some things recounted by Luke as being true, and to set others aside, as if he had not known the truth.
sources.raw_question: Can someone consistently accept some parts of Luke's Gospel as true while rejecting other parts on the ground that Luke did not know the truth, as Marcion and Valentinus did?

question: In the great commission, was Jesus giving a new Name to Jehovah, or introducing a new God in place of Jehovah?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: He was giving a new Name to Jehovah. His disciples could only have understood Him as substituting the threefold Name of Father, Son and Holy Ghost for the Name of Jehovah, meaning that Jehovah was now to be known by this Name. The only alternative, that Jesus was supplanting Jehovah with a new God for His community, is monstrous.
sources.quote: this could not possibly have meant to His disciples anything else than that Jehovah was now to be known to them by the new Name, of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost.
sources.raw_question: In the great commission, was Jesus giving a new Name to Jehovah, or introducing a new God in place of Jehovah?

question: How can Psalm 2's command to trust in the Son be reconciled with the curse on the man who trusts in man?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: They can be reconciled only in the Gospel of the Son of God, which teaches that the Son is God. Psalm 2 pronounces a blessing on all who put their trust in the Son. Jeremiah curses the one who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm. The Son in whom we are told to trust must therefore be more than a mere man.
sources.quote: Is there not food here for the most thoughtful enquiry? How can you reconcile these texts? I venture to assert only in the Gospel of the Son of God.
sources.raw_question: How can Psalm 2's command to trust in the Son be reconciled with the curse on the man who trusts in man?

question: Is there in God, as in a human craftsman, a distinction between possessing a capability and actually exercising it?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. A shipbuilder is always a shipbuilder by ability but operates only when he works, so capability and execution can be viewed apart. In God everything we can conceive is wholly work and action, and His will passes immediately to its object, so there is no gap between His power and its exercise.
sources.quote: It is otherwise with God; for all that we can conceive as in Him is entirely work and action, His will passing over immediately to its object.
sources.raw_question: Is there in God, as in a human craftsman, a distinction between possessing a capability and actually exercising it?

question: Are the author of the Old Testament law and the author of the Gospel one and the same God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XII.—It clearly appears that there was but one author of both the old and the new law, from the fact that Christ condemned traditions and customs repugnant to the former, while He confirmed its most important precepts, and taught that He was Himself the end of the Mosaic law.
sources.answer: Yes. In both the law and the Gospel the first and greatest commandment is to love God with the whole heart, and the second is to love one's neighbour as oneself. Since the precepts of a perfect life, without which salvation cannot be attained, are the same in both Testaments, they point to the same God. That God also gave particular laws suited to each.
sources.quote: the first and greatest commandment is, to love the Lord God with the whole heart, and then there follows a commandment like to it, to love one’s neighbour as one’s self; the author of the law and the Gospel is shown to be one and the same
sources.raw_question: Are the author of the Old Testament law and the author of the Gospel one and the same God?

question: When Christ rebuked the scribes and Pharisees, was he condemning the law of Moses as coming from another God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XII.—It clearly appears that there was but one author of both the old and the new law, from the fact that Christ condemned traditions and customs repugnant to the former, while He confirmed its most important precepts, and taught that He was Himself the end of the Mosaic law.
sources.answer: No. Christ told his hearers to observe what those sitting in Moses' seat bade them. He blamed the persons, who repeated the words of the law yet lacked love. Likewise, the 'commandments of men' rebuked through Isaiah are the elders' invented traditions, not the law given by Moses.
sources.quote: He therefore did not throw blame upon that law which was given by Moses, when He exhorted it to be observed, Jerusalem being as yet in safety; but He did throw blame upon those persons, because they repeated indeed the words of the law, yet were without love.
sources.raw_question: When Christ rebuked the scribes and Pharisees, was he condemning the law of Moses as coming from another God?

question: Does Paul's statement that Christ is the end of the law imply that Christ was also the author and beginning of the law?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XII.—It clearly appears that there was but one author of both the old and the new law, from the fact that Christ condemned traditions and customs repugnant to the former, while He confirmed its most important precepts, and taught that He was Himself the end of the Mosaic law.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ could not be the end of the law unless he were also its final cause. He who brings in the end also wrought the beginning.
sources.quote: And how is Christ the end of the law, if He be not also the final cause of it? For He who has brought in the end has Himself also wrought the beginning
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's statement that Christ is the end of the law imply that Christ was also the author and beginning of the law?

question: Will love of God cease in the world to come, or will it continue to grow?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XII.—It clearly appears that there was but one author of both the old and the new law, from the fact that Christ condemned traditions and customs repugnant to the former, while He confirmed its most important precepts, and taught that He was Himself the end of the Mosaic law.
sources.answer: It will continue. When other things pass away, faith, hope and love remain, and love is the greatest. We never cease loving God; the more we contemplate him, the more we love him.
sources.quote: For we do never cease from loving God; but in proportion as we continue to contemplate Him, so much the more do we love Him.
sources.raw_question: Will love of God cease in the world to come, or will it continue to grow?

question: If likeness follows the manner of generation, would all things generated in the same way resemble one another?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His dictum that 'the manner of the likeness must follow the manner of the generation' is unintelligible.
sources.answer: Yes, that absurd consequence would follow, which refutes the rule. Since most animals share the same manner of generation and things like the same thing are like one another, Eunomius's sweeping assertion would establish a mutual resemblance between men, dogs, camels, mice and elephants.
sources.quote: this sweeping and unqualified assertion of his establishes, by virtue of this similarity of birth, a mutual resemblance between men, dogs, camels, mice, elephants, leopards, and every other animal
sources.raw_question: If likeness follows the manner of generation, would all things generated in the same way resemble one another?

question: What was the condition of Adam's knowledge at his creation, before the fall?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Adam was fully furnished with all the knowledge needed for man's ultimate end, apart from things not yet existing such as languages and history. His understanding had no narrowness or darkness. His naming of the creatures, which Scripture approves, shows he clearly knew their natures. He was made perfect for ruling the creatures and living to God, which required knowing both the creatures' nature and God's will.
sources.quote: Adam was made perfect, for the whole end of ruling the creatures and living to God, for which he was made; which, without the knowledge of the nature of the one and the will of the other, he could not be.
sources.raw_question: What was the condition of Adam's knowledge at his creation, before the fall?

question: Was Adam's natural knowledge in innocence merely natural, or was it spiritual?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: It was spiritual. Knowledge was given to man so that he could walk with God toward his supernatural end. After Adam received his endowments, the law of life and death was given so he would know why he had them. So even his natural knowledge was spiritualized and sanctified in its principle and its end.
sources.quote: Therefore, knowledge in him was spiritualized and sanctified: even that knowledge which he had by nature, in respect of its principle and end, was spiritual.
sources.raw_question: Was Adam's natural knowledge in innocence merely natural, or was it spiritual?

question: Was the 'new covenant' foretold by the prophets fulfilled in the rebuilding of the temple under Zerubbabel after the return from Babylon?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIV.—Proof against the Marcionites, that the prophets referred in all their predictions to our Christ.
sources.answer: No. The stone temple was rebuilt then, but no new covenant was given; the Jews continued to use the Mosaic law until the coming of the Lord. Only from the Lord's advent did the new covenant and the life-giving law go forth over the whole earth, as the prophets foretold.
sources.quote: yet no new covenant was given, but they used the Mosaic law until the coming of the Lord; but from the Lord’s advent, the new covenant which brings back peace, and the law which gives life, has gone forth over the whole earth
sources.raised_by_detail: one advocating the cause of the Jews
sources.raw_question: Was the 'new covenant' foretold by the prophets fulfilled in the rebuilding of the temple under Zerubbabel after the return from Babylon?

question: Does the prophecy that the law will go out from Zion and nations will beat swords into ploughshares refer to Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIV.—Proof against the Marcionites, that the prophets referred in all their predictions to our Christ.
sources.answer: Yes. The word of God preached by the apostles, who went out from Jerusalem, changed the nations so that they turned weapons into tools of peace and, when struck, offer the other cheek. Since the prophecy was effected by Christ's word, the prophets spoke of no other person but of Him who accomplished it.
sources.quote: then the prophets have not spoken these things of any other person, but of Him who effected them. This person is our Lord, and in Him is that declaration borne out
sources.raw_question: Does the prophecy that the law will go out from Zion and nations will beat swords into ploughshares refer to Christ?

question: Does Isaiah's prophecy that the Messiah would not judge by appearance or by hearsay show that Christ is God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IX.—One and the same God, the Creator of heaven and earth, is He whom the prophets foretold, and who was declared by the Gospel. Proof of this, at the outset, from St. Matthew’s Gospel.
sources.answer: Yes. Not judging according to glory nor reproving after the manner of speech belongs to him inasmuch as he was God. As John says, he needed no one to testify to him of man, for he himself knew what was in man. That knowledge of the heart is divine.
sources.quote: But inasmuch as He was God, He did not judge according to glory, nor reprove after the manner of speech.
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah's prophecy that the Messiah would not judge by appearance or by hearsay show that Christ is God?

question: Does the phrase "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" in Acts 15:28 show that the Holy Spirit acts with sovereign authority?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter XIII. Prophecy was not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Spirit; the authority and operation of the latter on the apostles is signified to be the same as Theirs; and so we are to understand that there is unity in the three points of authority, rule, and bounty; yet need no disadvantage be feared from that participation, since such does not arise in human friendship. Lastly, it is established that this is the inheritance of the apostolic faith from the fact that the apostles are described as having obeyed the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. "It seemed good" marks the Spirit not only as the worker of grace but as the author who commands what is to be done. Scripture says in the same way that "it pleased God," so the phrase portrays one who is master of his own power.
sources.quote: For as we read of God: “It pleased God;” so, too, when it is said that, “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit,” one who is master of his own power is portrayed.
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" in Acts 15:28 show that the Holy Spirit acts with sovereign authority?

question: Why can believers hope to be raised and taken up to eternity?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Son of God Became Incarnate in Order that We Being Cleansed by Faith May Be Raised to the Unchangeable Truth.
sources.answer: Because what had a beginning in Christ has passed over into eternity. Christ was born, died, rose again and was taken up. We know birth and death in ourselves, and we rightly hope for resurrection and ascension because we believe them accomplished in him. Through union of the eternal to ourselves, by way of our own beginning, we are transferred to his eternity.
sources.quote: Since, therefore, in Him that, too, which had a beginning has passed over to eternity, in ourselves also it will so pass over, when faith shall have arrived at truth.
sources.raw_question: Why can believers hope to be raised and taken up to eternity?

question: In John 8:31-32, what does the truth make believers free from?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Son of God Became Incarnate in Order that We Being Cleansed by Faith May Be Raised to the Unchangeable Truth.
sources.answer: From death, corruption and changeableness. Christ promises that those who continue in his word will know the truth, and the truth will make them free. Since truth itself remains immortal, incorrupt and unchangeable, knowing it frees mortals from mortality and brings them into eternity.
sources.quote: From what, except from death, from corruptions, from changeableness? Since truth remains immortal, incorrupt, unchangeable.
sources.raw_question: In John 8:31-32, what does the truth make believers free from?

question: Does Christ's citation of Psalm 8, "Out of the mouths of babes and sucklings," show that he is the Son of God foretold by David?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XI.—The old prophets and righteous men knew beforehand of the advent of Christ, and earnestly desired to see and hear Him, He revealing himself in the Scriptures by the Holy Ghost, and without any change in Himself, enriching men day by day with benefits, but conferring them in greater abundance on later than on former generations.
sources.answer: Yes. By quoting it in reply to the leaders, the Lord showed that what David declared about the Son of God was fulfilled in his own person. He is the Christ announced by the prophets, whose name is praised in all the earth and who perfects praise to his Father from the mouths of babes.
sources.quote: thus pointing out that what had been declared by David concerning the Son of God, was accomplished in His own person
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's citation of Psalm 8, "Out of the mouths of babes and sucklings," show that he is the Son of God foretold by David?

question: Does the New Testament teach that the Persons of the Trinity are ordered by subordination in their modes of operation, that is, in their works toward the world and in redemption?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Yes. Warfield holds it is beyond question that in modes of operation the Father is first, the Son second, and the Spirit third. Whatever the Father does He does through the Son by the Spirit; the Son is sent by the Father and does His will, and the Spirit is sent by the Son and takes of Christ's things to show them to His people.
sources.quote: The Father is first, the Son is second, and the Spirit is third, in the operations of God as revealed to us in general, and very especially in those operations by which redemption is accomplished.
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament teach that the Persons of the Trinity are ordered by subordination in their modes of operation, that is, in their works toward the world and in redemption?

question: Was the soul, and not only the body, lost in Adam's fall, so that it needed to be assumed and saved?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: Yes. The soul was lost even sooner than the body. Disobedience is a sin of the will, and the will belongs to the soul. The whole disaster of our nature therefore began in the soul, so salvation must reach the soul.
sources.quote: For disobedience is a sin, not of the body, but of the will: and the will properly belongs to the soul, from which the whole disaster of our nature had its beginning
sources.raw_question: Was the soul, and not only the body, lost in Adam's fall, so that it needed to be assumed and saved?

question: In John 7:23, what does Christ mean by making a man 'every whit whole'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He expounds the passage of the Gospel, “The Father judgeth no man,” and further speaks of the assumption of man with body and soul wrought by the Lord, of the transgression of Adam, and of death and the resurrection of the dead.
sources.answer: It means healing both soul and body. The other Gospels show this when Christ forgives the paralytic's sins (healing the soul) and bids him walk (healing the body). In John 5 He likewise heals the body and then frees the soul, saying 'sin no more.' This shows that the Lord's saving work concerns the whole man.
sources.quote: “Thy sins be forgiven thee,” which is a healing of the soul, and, “Arise and walk[^440],” which has regard to the body
sources.raw_question: In John 7:23, what does Christ mean by making a man 'every whit whole'?

question: Was the Old Testament's emphasis on God's unity a preparation that had to come before the plurality within God was revealed?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: Partly, but this is not the main reason. Warfield grants the customary remark, going back to Gregory of Nazianzus, that it would have been dangerous to speak of plurality before unity was firmly fixed. However, this 'may carry us a little way' only. The real reason lies in the historical unfolding of God's redemptive purpose.
sources.quote: it was the task of the Old Testament revelation to fix firmly in the minds and hearts of the people of God the great fundamental truth of the unity of the Godhead
sources.raw_question: Was the Old Testament's emphasis on God's unity a preparation that had to come before the plurality within God was revealed?

question: What do the Son's titles "Angel," "Word," "Seal," and "Image" have in common?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XI > He then exposes the ignorance of Eunomius, and the incoherence and absurdity of his arguments, in speaking of the Son as “the Angel of the Existent,” and as being as much below the Divine Nature as the Son is superior to the things created by Himself. And in this connection there is a noble and forcible counter-statement and an indignant refutation, showing that He Who gave the oracles to Moses is Himself the Existent, the Only-begotten Son, Who to the petition of Moses, “If Thou Thyself goest not with us, carry me not up hence,” said, “I will do this also that thou hast said”; Who is also called “Angel” both by Moses and Isaiah: wherein is cited the text, “Unto us a Child is born.”
sources.answer: They are equivalent in meaning: each expresses that the Son reveals the Father through Himself. As a messenger gives information from someone, a word reveals the thought within, a seal shows the original mould, and an image interprets the beauty of its archetype.
sources.quote: the Seal shows by Its own stamp the original mould, and the Image by Itself interprets the beauty of that whereof It is the image, so that in their signification all these terms are equivalent to one another
sources.raw_question: What do the Son's titles "Angel," "Word," "Seal," and "Image" have in common?

question: Must Christ be expected only as the Creator promised him in the Old Testament, against heretics who reject the Old Testament's authority?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > Further, that the Same Rule of Truth Teaches Us to Believe, After the Father, Also in the Son of God, Jesus Christ Our Lord God, Being the Same that Was Promised in the Old Testament, and Manifested in the New.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ is not to be expected in the Gospel in any other way than as the Creator promised him beforehand in the Old Testament Scriptures. The things predicted of him were fulfilled, and the things fulfilled had been predicted. A Christ cut off from the Old Testament is a fiction with no claim on the Creator's world or the Creator's man.
sources.quote: Christ was not to be expected in the Gospel in any other wise than as He was promised before by the Creator, in the Scriptures of the Old Testament; especially as the things that were predicted of Him were fulfilled
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who reject the authority of the Old Testament
sources.raw_question: Must Christ be expected only as the Creator promised him in the Old Testament, against heretics who reject the Old Testament's authority?

question: Is an exact understanding and precise expression of doctrines like the manner of eternal generation, the procession of the Spirit, and the mutual in-being of the divine persons necessary for saving faith and worship?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
sources.answer: No. These matters are true and defensible, but their distinct apprehension and accurate expression is not necessary unto faith as our guide to worship and obedience. The explications are not ranked equally with the original revelations themselves but are offered as proper expressions of what is revealed, to increase light and edification.
sources.quote: because the distinct apprehension of them, and their accurate expression, is not necessary unto faith, as it is our guide and principle in and unto religious worship and obedience, they need not here be insisted on
sources.raw_question: Is an exact understanding and precise expression of doctrines like the manner of eternal generation, the procession of the Spirit, and the mutual in-being of the divine persons necessary for saving faith and worship?

question: When a dispute arises about an important doctrine concerning God and Christ, where should Christians look to find the true teaching?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter IV.—The truth is to be found nowhere else but in the Catholic Church, the sole depository of apostolical doctrine. Heresies are of recent formation, and cannot trace their origin up to the apostles.
sources.answer: They should turn to the most ancient Churches founded by the apostles and learn from them what is certain and clear. The apostles placed all things pertaining to the truth in the Church, as a rich man deposits money in a bank. So the truth does not need to be sought among others, since it is easily obtained from the Church's tradition.
sources.quote: should we not have recourse to the most ancient Churches with which the apostles held constant intercourse, and learn from them what is certain and clear in regard to the present question?
sources.raw_question: When a dispute arises about an important doctrine concerning God and Christ, where should Christians look to find the true teaching?

question: Why was Christ baptized by John if he had no need of baptism?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: He had no need of it for himself. He submitted 'to fulfil all righteousness' on behalf of his people, who have no righteousness of their own and are bound to fulfil all of it. His baptism, like all his obedience, was done for them.
sources.quote: Suffer it to be so, now; for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness;” — “I do it for them who have none at all, and stand obliged unto all.
sources.raw_question: Why was Christ baptized by John if he had no need of baptism?

question: Do the Hebrew Scriptures of Moses and the prophets teach that God is to be worshipped as a solitary God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: No. Hilary says the sacred volumes of Moses and the prophets taught him that God must not be worshipped as a lonely God. Their pages reveal a God who is not different from the Father in nature but one with Him in a mysterious unity of substance.
