sources.quote: From them I learnt Thy revelation, that we must not worship Thee as a lonely God. For their pages taught me of God, not different from Thee in nature but One with Thee in mysterious unity of substance.
sources.raw_question: Do the Hebrew Scriptures of Moses and the prophets teach that God is to be worshipped as a solitary God?

question: Can a nature that possesses goodness, wisdom or power by nature rather than as an external gift suffer diminution in them?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > His acknowledgment that the Divine Being is 'single' is only verbal.
sources.answer: No. Nothing which possesses wisdom, power or any good rooted in its nature can be diminished in it. Good is diminished only by the presence of evil, and where a nature cannot deteriorate there is no limit to its goodness.
sources.quote: Nothing which possesses wisdom or power or any other good, not as an external gift, but rooted in its nature, can suffer diminution in it
sources.raw_question: Can a nature that possesses goodness, wisdom or power by nature rather than as an external gift suffer diminution in them?

question: Are the writings of Moses and the prophets the words of Christ himself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter II.—Proofs from the plain testimony of Moses, and of the other prophets, whose words are the words of Christ, that there is but one God, the founder of the world, whom Our Lord preached, and whom He called His Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ tells the Jews that if they had believed Moses they would have believed Him, because Moses wrote of Him, and that disbelieving Moses' writings means disbelieving His words. This shows plainly that Moses' writings are Christ's words, and the same holds for the other prophets. Hence the God of the law and the prophets is the Father whom Christ preaches.
sources.quote: He thus indicates in the clearest manner that the writings of Moses are His words. If, then, [this be the case with regard] to Moses, so also, beyond a doubt, the words of the other prophets are His [words]
sources.raw_question: Are the writings of Moses and the prophets the words of Christ himself?

question: Can a being who has a superior over him properly be called 'God' or 'the great King'?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter II.—Proofs from the plain testimony of Moses, and of the other prophets, whose words are the words of Christ, that there is but one God, the founder of the world, whom Our Lord preached, and whom He called His Father.
sources.answer: No. A being properly described as God or the great King admits no other being compared with him or set above him. Christ calls the Creator 'the great King' and refers to heaven as God's throne, echoing Isaiah's words about the Creator. Therefore there is no other God beside the Creator.
sources.quote: For he who has any superior over him, and is under the power of another, this being never can be called either “God” or “the great King.”
sources.raw_question: Can a being who has a superior over him properly be called 'God' or 'the great King'?

question: Is the Holy Spirit poured out in the last times the same Spirit who was active from the creation of the world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: Yes. It is at all times the same Spirit of God, though he has been poured out on us in a new way in these last times. He comes upon the human race from the creation of the world to its end, and through him believers receive salvation.
sources.quote: acknowledging also at all times the same Spirit of God, although He has been poured out upon us after a new fashion in these last times
sources.raw_question: Is the Holy Spirit poured out in the last times the same Spirit who was active from the creation of the world?

question: Do Old Testament psalms such as 'Lift up your heads, O ye gates' and 'I laid me down and slept' foretell Christ's resurrection and ascension?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: Yes. These texts proclaim beforehand his resurrection from the dead through the Father's power and his reception into heaven. The words 'his going forth is from the height of heaven' announce that he was taken up again to the place from which he came down.
sources.quote: proclaimed beforehand His resurrection from the dead through the Father’s power, and His reception into heaven.
sources.raw_question: Do Old Testament psalms such as 'Lift up your heads, O ye gates' and 'I laid me down and slept' foretell Christ's resurrection and ascension?

question: Why does Christ count the souls of his saints beautiful?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Because he himself has made them so. Their beauty is not their own but comes from his comeliness, which he puts upon them. On that basis he calls them fair, and even perfect.
sources.quote: Christ redoubles it, that the souls of his saints are very beautiful, even perfect, through his comeliness, which he puts upon them, Ezek. xvi. 14
sources.raw_question: Why does Christ count the souls of his saints beautiful?

question: How do the errors of confounding the divine Persons and of dividing the divine nature relate to Judaism and paganism, and to the true doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Exposition of the present state of the Churches.
sources.answer: They are opposite deviations from the right rule of true religion, one by excess and one by defect. Those who confound the Persons, as the modalists do, slide into Judaism, keeping a bare unity of God without real distinction. Those who set the natures of Father, Son and Spirit in opposition, as the Arian parties do, pass into heathenism, effectively positing several unlike gods. The orthodox faith holds the distinction of Persons together with the unity of nature.
sources.quote: On the one hand are they who confound the Persons and are carried away into Judaism; on the other hand are they that, through the opposition of the natures, pass into heathenism.
sources.raw_question: How do the errors of confounding the divine Persons and of dividing the divine nature relate to Judaism and paganism, and to the true doctrine of the Trinity?

question: If Christians admit they do not know the essence of God, does Christ's saying 'Ye worship ye know not what' condemn their worship?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He discusses the incomprehensibility of the Divine essence, and the saying to the woman of Samaria, “Ye worship ye know not what.“
sources.answer: No. We know the loftiness of the glory of Him whom we worship by the very fact that reason cannot comprehend His incomparable greatness. So we truly worship what we know. Christ's rebuke fits those who confine God within limited conceptions, not those who confess His infinity.
sources.quote: we know the loftiness of the glory of Him Whom we worship, by the very fact that we are not able by reasoning to comprehend in our thoughts the incomparable character of His greatness
sources.raw_question: If Christians admit they do not know the essence of God, does Christ's saying 'Ye worship ye know not what' condemn their worship?

question: What did Christ mean when he told the Samaritan woman 'Ye worship ye know not what' (John 4:22)?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He discusses the incomprehensibility of the Divine essence, and the saying to the woman of Samaria, “Ye worship ye know not what.“
sources.answer: He was rebuking the Samaritans for corporeal ideas of God. They supposed the Deity was settled in a place, so they worshipped Him in name only and in fact worshipped something other than God. A God thought to be confined to a place is no God.
sources.quote: the Samaritans, thinking that they worship God, and at the same time supposing the Deity to be corporeally settled in place, adore Him in name only, worshipping something else, and not God
sources.raw_question: What did Christ mean when he told the Samaritan woman 'Ye worship ye know not what' (John 4:22)?

question: How does Paul's teaching that God's judgments are unsearchable and His ways past finding out bear on knowledge of God's essence?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > He discusses the incomprehensibility of the Divine essence, and the saying to the woman of Samaria, “Ye worship ye know not what.“
sources.answer: It shows a fortiori that the divine essence is unknowable. If God's judgments cannot be searched, His ways cannot be traced, and His promised goods surpass all imagining, then the Godhead itself is far higher and more unapproachable than these attributes that accompany it. The 'ways past finding out' are the ways leading to knowledge of Him, and these remain untrodden by human reasoning.
sources.quote: by how much more is His actual Godhead higher and loftier, in respect of being unspeakable and unapproachable, than those attributes which are conceived as accompanying it
sources.raw_question: How does Paul's teaching that God's judgments are unsearchable and His ways past finding out bear on knowledge of God's essence?

question: Does prefixing a negative particle to a predicate change the category (predicament) under which it is said?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Addition of a Negative Does Not Change the Predicament.
sources.answer: No. Adding a negative only denies what was affirmed without it, within the same predicament. Denying 'man' denies according to substance, denying 'white' according to quality, denying 'near' according to relation, and likewise for quantity, position, condition, time, place, action and passion. So whatever is affirmed relatively is denied relatively.
sources.quote: there is no kind of predicament according to which we may please to affirm anything, without being proved to deny according to the same predicament, if we prefix the negative particle
sources.raw_question: Does prefixing a negative particle to a predicate change the category (predicament) under which it is said?

question: Would the grace of Baptism cease if the name of Son ceased once its need had been supplied, as the modalist view implies?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Marcellian illustration from 1 Cor. xii. 4, refuted.
sources.answer: Yes, it would. That is one of the absurdities Athanasius draws from the modalist view. Baptism was given in the Son, so if the Son were only a temporary name that lapses when the need is met, the grace of Baptism would end along with it.
sources.quote: And the Name of Son ceasing, as they hold, then the grace of Baptism will cease too; for it was given in the Son.
sources.raw_question: Would the grace of Baptism cease if the name of Son ceased once its need had been supplied, as the modalist view implies?

question: Why does seeing God give life and immortality?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XX.—That one God formed all things in the world, by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit: and that although He is to us in this life invisible and incomprehensible, nevertheless He is not unknown; inasmuch as His works do declare Him, and His Word has shown that in many modes He may be seen and known.
sources.answer: Seeing God means being within God and sharing His splendour, and that splendour gives life. It is like those who see light: they are inside the light and share its brightness. Since no one can live apart from life, and fellowship with God, which is knowing Him and enjoying His goodness, is the means of life, those who see God are made immortal.
sources.quote: For as those who see the light are within the light, and partake of its brilliancy; even so, those who see God are in God, and receive of His splendour. But [His] splendour vivifies them
sources.raw_question: Why does seeing God give life and immortality?

question: What does Gabriel's greeting to Mary, "Hail, full of grace," signify about the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is not a creature, seeing that He is infinite, and was shed upon the apostles dispersed through all countries, and moreover sanctifies the Angels also, to whom He makes us equal. Mary was full of the same likewise, so too, Christ the Lord, and so far all things high and low. And all benediction has its origin from His operation, as was signified in the moving of the water at Bethesda.
sources.answer: It declares the grace of the Holy Spirit in her, because the Spirit had come upon her and she was about to conceive the heavenly Word. The Angel is thus a herald announcing the Spirit's operation, not its source.
sources.quote: plainly declaring the grace of the Spirit which was in her, because the Holy Spirit had come upon her
sources.raw_question: What does Gabriel's greeting to Mary, "Hail, full of grace," signify about the Holy Spirit?

question: What does the Angel stirring the pool of Bethesda signify about the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter VII. The Holy Spirit is not a creature, seeing that He is infinite, and was shed upon the apostles dispersed through all countries, and moreover sanctifies the Angels also, to whom He makes us equal. Mary was full of the same likewise, so too, Christ the Lord, and so far all things high and low. And all benediction has its origin from His operation, as was signified in the moving of the water at Bethesda.
sources.answer: It was a type of the Spirit's descent, which now consecrates the waters of baptism when invoked by the priest's prayers. The Angel was the Spirit's herald, showing that the Spirit has the same ministers as the Father and Christ. The Spirit works all in all in the same manner as the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: The Spirit, then, has the same ministers as God the Father and Christ. He fills all things, possesses all things, works all and in all in the same manner as God the Father and the Son work.
sources.raw_question: What does the Angel stirring the pool of Bethesda signify about the Holy Spirit?

question: How are particular acts of will (such as willing to see a scar or a window) related to the final end of the human will?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Of What Kind We are to Reckon the Rest (Requies), and End (Finis), of the Will in Vision.
sources.answer: Each act of will has its own proximate end, but all are referred to the final end, by which we will to live blessedly. That final life is not referred to anything else and suffices of itself to the one who loves it. A will that depends on another, such as wishing to see passers-by through a window, is a distinct will with its own end.
sources.quote: all these and other such acts of will have their own proper [proximate] ends, which are referred to that [final] end of the will by which we will to live blessedly
sources.raw_question: How are particular acts of will (such as willing to see a scar or a window) related to the final end of the human will?

question: What makes a connected series of wills right or wrong?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Of What Kind We are to Reckon the Rest (Requies), and End (Finis), of the Will in Vision.
sources.answer: The whole series is right if the one end to which all the wills are referred is good, and all are bad if that end is bad. Right wills form a road of steps by which one ascends to blessedness. Depraved and distorted wills form a bond that binds a person so that he is cast into outer darkness.
sources.quote: But all the several wills that are bound to each other, are at once right, if that one is good, to which all are referred; and if that is bad, then all are bad.
sources.raw_question: What makes a connected series of wills right or wrong?

question: Is a thing in which the will rests with delight necessarily the ultimate end of a person?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > Of What Kind We are to Reckon the Rest (Requies), and End (Finis), of the Will in Vision.
sources.answer: No. Even something that satisfies the will with delight may still be referred to something further. Such rest is like the foot resting in walking, or like a place of refreshment for a traveller, not like a citizen's native country.
sources.quote: so as to be regarded not as the native country of a citizen, but as a place of refreshment, or even of stopping, for a traveller.
sources.raw_question: Is a thing in which the will rests with delight necessarily the ultimate end of a person?

question: Why does the Apostle mention Christ's Godhead right after speaking of His humanity and high priesthood in Hebrews?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts explained; Fourthly, Hebrews iii. 2. Introduction; the Regula Fidei counter to an Arian sense of the text; which is not supported by the word 'servant,' nor by 'made' which occurs in it; (how can the Judge be among the 'works' which 'God will bring into judgment?') nor by 'faithful;' and is confuted by the immediate context, which is about Priesthood; and by the foregoing passage, which explains the word 'faithful' as meaning trustworthy, as do 1 Pet. iv. fin. and other texts. On the whole made may safely be understood either of the divine generation or the human creation.
sources.answer: He mentions it at once to safeguard us on every side. When speaking of Christ's humility, he wants us to know immediately His loftiness and His majesty, which is the Father's. He therefore contrasts Moses as servant with Christ as Son over the house.
sources.quote: most of all when he speaks of His humility, that we may forthwith know His loftiness and His majesty which is the Father’s
sources.raw_question: Why does the Apostle mention Christ's Godhead right after speaking of His humanity and high priesthood in Hebrews?

question: How does Paul's use of 'dilated' in 2 Corinthians 6:11-13 show that dilatation does not produce distinct persons?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > Such a doctrine precludes all real distinctions of personality in the Divine Nature. Illustration of the Scripture doctrine from 2 Cor. vi. 11, &c.
sources.answer: When Paul urges the Corinthians to be dilated, he advises the same persons to change from straitness to dilatation; once dilated they are not others but still Corinthians. Likewise 'Our heart is dilated' and Noah's 'May God dilate for Japheth' keep the same heart and the same Japheth. So if the Father were dilated into a Triad, the Triad would again be the Father alone.
sources.quote: as, supposing the Corinthians being straitened were in turn dilated, they had not been others, but still Corinthians, so if the Father was dilated into a Triad, the Triad again is the Father alone
sources.raw_question: How does Paul's use of 'dilated' in 2 Corinthians 6:11-13 show that dilatation does not produce distinct persons?

question: Can anyone in this present life, such as the Gnostic teachers Valentinus, Ptolemaeus or Basilides, attain a complete knowledge of the deep things of God and of realities supposedly above the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: No. As the apostle affirms, we know only in part. Those who claim perfect knowledge cannot even explain ordinary things before their eyes, such as the number of hairs on their heads or the sparrows caught each day. So their confident claims about spiritual, super-celestial things, and about what they say lies above God, deserve no belief. Such questions must be left to God.
sources.quote: But if those who are perfect do not yet understand the very things in their hands, and at their feet, and before their eyes, and on the earth, and especially the rule followed with respect to the hairs of their head, how can we believe them regarding things spiritual
sources.raw_question: Can anyone in this present life, such as the Gnostic teachers Valentinus, Ptolemaeus or Basilides, attain a complete knowledge of the deep things of God and of realities supposedly above the Creator?

question: Can the Holy Spirit rebuke the world concerning judgment, as John 16 says, or is the Spirit incapable of judging?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VI. The Spirit rebukes just as do the Father and the Son; and indeed judges could not judge without Him, as is shown by the judgments of Solomon and Daniel, which are explained in a few words, by the way; and no other than the Holy Spirit inspired Daniel.
sources.answer: The Spirit can and does judge. Human judges cannot judge except through the Spirit, as Solomon's judgment shows. The Spirit gives the word of wisdom, removes doubt from judgment and grants the successful issue, so it is absurd to deny that He rebukes the world concerning judgment.
sources.quote: how, then, do men deny that the Spirit can rebuke the world concerning judgment, Who removes doubt from judgment, and grants the successful issue?
sources.raw_question: Can the Holy Spirit rebuke the world concerning judgment, as John 16 says, or is the Spirit incapable of judging?

question: Does the Holy Spirit's ability to penetrate hidden thoughts, as in Solomon's judgment, show that He has a divine power of oversight?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VI. The Spirit rebukes just as do the Father and the Son; and indeed judges could not judge without Him, as is shown by the judgments of Solomon and Daniel, which are explained in a few words, by the way; and no other than the Holy Spirit inspired Daniel.
sources.answer: Yes. Solomon discovered deceit and maternal affection in hidden thoughts only by the gift of the Holy Spirit, for the inmost mind cannot be penetrated by steel but only by the Spirit. Wisdom 7 says the Spirit of understanding is one only and oversees all things, which is a divine attribute.
sources.quote: For the inmost mind cannot be penetrated by steel, but by the Spirit: “For the Spirit of understanding is holy, one only, manifold, subtle, lively,” and, farther on, “overseeing all things.”
sources.raw_question: Does the Holy Spirit's ability to penetrate hidden thoughts, as in Solomon's judgment, show that He has a divine power of oversight?

question: Does the testimony that Israel tempted God, tempted Christ, and tempted the Holy Spirit in the wilderness prove the unity of the Trinity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VIII. The aforesaid unity is proved hereby, that as the Father is said to be grieved and tempted, so too the Son. The Son was also tempted in the wilderness, where a figure of the cross was set up in the brazen serpent: but the Apostle says that the Spirit also was there tempted. St. Ambrose infers from this that the Israelites were guided into the promised land by the same Spirit, and that His will and power are one with those of the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture says that God was tempted, that Christ was tempted (1 Corinthians 10:9), and that the Spirit was tempted (Hebrews 3). There was a single temptation, by the same unbelievers. So it was one temptation of the one Godhead of the Trinity. The punishment by serpents was therefore an offence against the whole Trinity.
sources.quote: for the temptation is one wherewith the one Godhead of the Trinity was tempted by the unbelieving.
sources.raw_question: Does the testimony that Israel tempted God, tempted Christ, and tempted the Holy Spirit in the wilderness prove the unity of the Trinity?

question: Why was the brazen serpent, rather than a real serpent, a fitting type of Christ on the cross?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter VIII. The aforesaid unity is proved hereby, that as the Father is said to be grieved and tempted, so too the Son. The Son was also tempted in the wilderness, where a figure of the cross was set up in the brazen serpent: but the Apostle says that the Spirit also was there tempted. St. Ambrose infers from this that the Israelites were guided into the promised land by the same Spirit, and that His will and power are one with those of the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: The serpent was only a likeness because Christ took the likeness of a sinner. He had the truth of a real body but not the truth of sin. Under the appearance of human weakness He could destroy the cunning of the true serpent, the devil. The brazen serpent also signifies the world crucified in its allurements.
sources.quote: because the Lord took on Him the likeness of a sinner, in the truth, indeed, of His Body, but without the truth of sin
sources.raw_question: Why was the brazen serpent, rather than a real serpent, a fitting type of Christ on the cross?

question: How does Psalm 39:6, "Although man walks in an image, yet he disquieteth himself in vain," bear on whether sin destroys the image of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Image of God is to Be Sought in the Immortality of the Rational Soul. How a Trinity is Demonstrated in the Mind.
sources.answer: The verse shows that the image is defaced but not destroyed. Scripture would not attribute vanity to the image of God unless the image had been defaced. Yet by saying man still "walks in an image," it shows the defacing does not take away its being an image. So the sentence can equally be read: "Although man disquieteth himself in vain, yet he walketh in an image."
sources.quote: Yet it sufficiently shows that such defacing does not extend to the taking away its being an image, by saying, “Although man walks in an image.”
sources.raw_question: How does Psalm 39:6, "Although man walks in an image, yet he disquieteth himself in vain," bear on whether sin destroys the image of God?

question: Why can the soul be corrupted, and yet still be a great nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > The Image of God is to Be Sought in the Immortality of the Rational Soul. How a Trinity is Demonstrated in the Mind.
sources.answer: The soul can be corrupted because it is not the highest nature. Yet it is a great nature because it is capable of the highest nature and can partake of it.
sources.quote: although it can be corrupted, because it is not the highest; and although it can be corrupted, because it is not the highest, yet because it is capable and can be partaker of the highest nature, it is a great nature
sources.raw_question: Why can the soul be corrupted, and yet still be a great nature?

question: Can we come to love the Trinity by a general or special notion drawn from known instances, as we love the Apostle Paul through knowing what a man is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Trinity May Be Loved Though Unknown.
sources.answer: No. We know Paul's kind because we are men ourselves, so we can believe things of him by likeness. But there are not many trinities that we have learned by experience. So no notion of a class can tell us what the divine Trinity is like.
sources.quote: What then do we know, whether specially or generally, of that most excellent Trinity, as if there were many such trinities, some of which we had learned by experience
sources.raw_question: Can we come to love the Trinity by a general or special notion drawn from known instances, as we love the Apostle Paul through knowing what a man is?

question: Does believing that Christ was born of a virgin depend on knowing particulars such as what Mary looked like?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Trinity May Be Loved Though Unknown.
sources.answer: No. We certainly know what a virgin is, what being born is, and what a proper name is. Our faith is framed by these general notions, which keeps it from being feigned. One may doubt what Mary's face was like without harming the faith, but no one may say 'perhaps Christ was born of a virgin' without violating it.
sources.quote: It is allowable, then, in this case to say without violation of the faith, perhaps she had such or such a countenance, perhaps she had not: but no one could say without violation of the Christian faith, that perhaps Christ was born of a virgin.
sources.raw_question: Does believing that Christ was born of a virgin depend on knowing particulars such as what Mary looked like?

question: Did Jesus Christ perform his miracles only in appearance, as the Carpocratian magicians claimed of their own wonders, or did they truly happen?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXII.—Further exposure of the wicked and blasphemous doctrines of the heretics.
sources.answer: They truly happened. Irenaeus says he will answer this claim from the prophetic writings. Those writings show that all these things were foretold about Christ and really took place, and that he is the only Son of God. Christ's true disciples still work real miracles in his name, which confirms that his own works were real.
sources.quote: If, however, they maintain that the Lord, too, performed such works simply in appearance, we shall refer them to the prophetical writings, and prove from these both that all things were thus
sources.raw_question: Did Jesus Christ perform his miracles only in appearance, as the Carpocratian magicians claimed of their own wonders, or did they truly happen?

question: Do sinners in their sins still seek a likeness of God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > The Trinity of the Outer Man, or of External Vision, is Not an Image of God. The Likeness of God is Desired Even in Sins. In External Vision the Form of the Corporeal Thing is as It Were the Parent, Vision the Offspring; But the Will that Unites These Suggests the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Yes. Souls in their very sins strive after nothing but some kind of likeness of God, though in a proud, preposterous and slavish liberty. Thus our first parents could only be persuaded to sin by the promise "Ye shall be as gods."
sources.quote: For even souls in their very sins strive after nothing else but some kind of likeness of God, in a proud and preposterous, and, so to say, slavish liberty.
sources.raw_question: Do sinners in their sins still seek a likeness of God?

question: In the analogy of external vision, which element suggests the Holy Spirit, and why?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That even in the outer man some traces of a trinity may be detected, as e.g., in the bodily sight, and in the recollection of objects seen with the bodily sight. > The Trinity of the Outer Man, or of External Vision, is Not an Image of God. The Likeness of God is Desired Even in Sins. In External Vision the Form of the Corporeal Thing is as It Were the Parent, Vision the Offspring; But the Will that Unites These Suggests the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: The will that unites the seen object (quasi-parent) and the vision (quasi-offspring) suggests the person of the Spirit. It is more spiritual than either, since the bodily object is not spiritual at all and the vision is only partly spiritual, being a sense of the body.
sources.quote: Therefore the will which unites both is confessedly more spiritual, as I have said; and so it begins to suggest (insinuare), as it were, the person of the Spirit in the Trinity.
sources.raw_question: In the analogy of external vision, which element suggests the Holy Spirit, and why?

question: In the work of satisfaction, is God to be considered as a private offended person or as an offended ruler?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: As an offended ruler, not as a private offended person. God acts as the supreme, absolute rector and Lord of the law and of sinners. As such he has the right to exact punishment for transgressions, and the righteousness of his rule requires that he do so.
sources.quote: not as an offended person, but as an offended ruler, who has right to exact punishment upon transgressions, and whose righteousness of rule requires that he should so do
sources.raw_question: In the work of satisfaction, is God to be considered as a private offended person or as an offended ruler?

question: Can the numerical value of a Greek word, computed from its letters, show whether the thing it names is material and corruptible or spiritual and saved?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIV.—Folly of the arguments derived by the heretics from numbers, letters, and syllables.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus answers by reductio. If every name whose letters total less than one hundred belongs to the corruptible 'left hand,' then Agape (love), worth ninety-three, and Aletheia (truth), worth sixty-four, would be material and perishable, which is absurd. Inquiries about God should not be pursued through numbers, syllables and letters. Numbers must be fitted to the true system, not the system drawn out of numbers.
sources.quote: they will be compelled to acknowledge that all those sacred names which do not reach a numerical value of one hundred, but only contain the numbers summed by the left hand, are corruptible and material.
sources.raw_question: Can the numerical value of a Greek word, computed from its letters, show whether the thing it names is material and corruptible or spiritual and saved?

question: Does the parable of the ninety-nine safe sheep and the one lost sheep support the Valentinian reading that the ninety-nine belong to the corruptible 'left hand' and the Saviour moves the lost one to the 'right hand'?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIV.—Folly of the arguments derived by the heretics from numbers, letters, and syllables.
sources.answer: No. On the Valentinian reading, the ninety-nine sheep that stayed safely in the fold would belong to the left hand, which they say must perish. It would follow that enjoying rest and safety does not mean salvation. That self-defeating result shows their number-based exegesis of the parable is false.
sources.quote: yet were of the left hand, it follows that they must acknowledge that the enjoyment of rest did not imply salvation.
sources.raw_question: Does the parable of the ninety-nine safe sheep and the one lost sheep support the Valentinian reading that the ninety-nine belong to the corruptible 'left hand' and the Saviour moves the lost one to the 'right hand'?

question: Why must God's will and the possession of what he wills be simultaneous, unlike in human beings?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > He then discusses the “willing” of the Father concerning the generation of the Son, and shows that the object of that good will is from eternity, which is the Son, existing in the Father, and being closely related to the process of willing, as the ray to the flame, or the act of seeing to the eye.
sources.answer: Because God's nature is simple and all-powerful. Our heavy and inert nature often wishes for what it lacks, or obtains what it does not wish. In God, by contrast, all things are conceived together. His eternal good will dwells in his eternal nature, does not arise from any separate principle, and is never apart from its object.
sources.quote: in the case of the simple and all-powerful Nature, all things are conceived together and at once, the willing of good as well as the possession of what He wills
sources.raw_question: Why must God's will and the possession of what he wills be simultaneous, unlike in human beings?

question: Do natural explanations of physical events given by philosophers exclude God's will as their cause?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Will of God is the Higher Cause of All Corporeal Change. This is Shown by an Example.
sources.answer: No. Such explanations at best identify proximate causes, and sometimes merely false ones drawn from guesswork. The true first cause remains God's will, which stands above all corporeal causes. In the illustration that follows, the physicians name bodily causes, but the higher cause lies in the soul and finally in the unchangeable wisdom.
sources.quote: but both would pronounce concerning proximate causes only, that is, corporeal ones
sources.raw_question: Do natural explanations of physical events given by philosophers exclude God's will as their cause?

question: Can souls be cleansed and reconciled to God through magical arts, incantations, or rites mediated by demons?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Devil the Mediator of Death, Christ of Life.
sources.answer: No. The devil is a false mediator who does not lift souls to higher things but blocks the way by inspiring proud and malignant affections. These weigh the soul down with vices rather than nourishing virtues, so that the soul falls more heavily the more it imagines itself raised up.
sources.quote: In no wise therefore are souls cleansed and reconciled to God by sacrilegious imitations, or curious arts that are impious, or magical incantations; since the false mediator does not translate them to higher things
sources.raw_question: Can souls be cleansed and reconciled to God through magical arts, incantations, or rites mediated by demons?

question: If God made not death, how can death come upon humanity as part of God's order?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Devil the Mediator of Death, Christ of Life.
sources.answer: God is not the cause of death, yet death is inflicted on the sinner by His just retribution. A judge inflicts punishment, but the cause of the punishment is the desert of the crime, not the judge's justice. In the same way, sin is the cause of death.
sources.quote: Just as the judge inflicts punishment on the guilty; yet it is not the justice of the judge, but the desert of the crime, which is the cause of the punishment.
sources.raw_question: If God made not death, how can death come upon humanity as part of God's order?

question: Is the matter of visible things subject to the command of wicked angels, so that they have independent power over nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > God Alone Creates Those Things Which are Changed by Magic Art.
sources.answer: No. Matter is subservient to God, who gives power to wicked angels only so far as He, the unchangeable one, determines. Like convicts in the mines who use earth and fire only as permitted, the evil ones act wrongfully in will but receive their power rightly from God, for their own punishment, the punishment of the wicked, or the praise of the good.
sources.quote: neither do the good angels do these things, except as far as God commands, nor do the evil ones do them wrongfully, except as far as He righteously permits.
sources.raw_question: Is the matter of visible things subject to the command of wicked angels, so that they have independent power over nature?

question: Who is the creator of the hidden 'seeds' from which living things arise, and how do creaturely agents relate to God's creative work?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > God Alone Creates Those Things Which are Changed by Magic Art.
sources.answer: God, the Creator of all things, is the creator of the invisible seeds concealed in the elements. Whatever is born receives its beginnings from these hidden seeds as from original rules, and the outward actions of parents, farmers, or angels merely provide occasions while God's power operates within to create.
sources.quote: For the Creator of these invisible seeds is the Creator of all things Himself; since whatever comes forth to our sight by being born, receives the first beginnings of its course from hidden seeds
sources.raw_question: Who is the creator of the hidden 'seeds' from which living things arise, and how do creaturely agents relate to God's creative work?

question: What does Paul mean in 1 Corinthians 3:6 by 'I planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase'?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > God Alone Creates Those Things Which are Changed by Magic Art.
sources.answer: Paul distinguishes God's creating and forming within from the operations of creatures applied from without. As only God works righteousness in minds while men preach outwardly, so in visible creation God works from within, while external operations of angels, men, or animals are applied to nature as agriculture is to soil.
sources.quote: the Apostle Paul, distinguishing God’s creating and forming within, from the operations of the creature which are applied from without, and drawing a similitude from agriculture, says, “I planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.”
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean in 1 Corinthians 3:6 by 'I planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase'?

question: Does Isaiah 54:5 ("Thy Maker is thine husband... thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel") describe Christ's marriage to his church?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. The text gives the reason why the church shall not be ashamed or confounded in her troubles: she is married to her Maker, and her Redeemer is her husband. Isaiah 61:10 and 62:5 carry the same theme, comparing God's joy over his people to a bridegroom's joy over his bride.
sources.quote: This is yielded as the reason why the church shall not be ashamed nor confounded, in the midst of her troubles and trials, — she is married unto her Maker, and her Redeemer is her husband.
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah 54:5 ("Thy Maker is thine husband... thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel") describe Christ's marriage to his church?

question: What is the main design of the ministry of the gospel with respect to Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: To persuade people to give themselves up to the Lord Christ as he reveals his kindness in his promise to betroth them. Paul says he had espoused the Corinthians to one husband so that he might present them as a chaste virgin to Christ. He had won this from them through the preaching of the gospel.
sources.quote: it is the main design of the ministry of the gospel, to prevail with men to give up themselves unto the Lord Christ, as he reveals his kindness in this engagement.
sources.raw_question: What is the main design of the ministry of the gospel with respect to Christ?

question: Do the passages of Scripture that speak of God's thoughts show that there is discursive or changing thought in God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Our Word is Never to Be Equalled to the Divine Word, Not Even When We Shall Be Like God.
sources.answer: No. Scripture speaks of God's thoughts in the same accommodated way that it speaks of God's forgetfulness. In strict propriety of language there is certainly no forgetfulness in God, and likewise no revolving thought.
sources.quote: There are, indeed, passages of Holy Scripture that speak of God’s thoughts; but this is after the same mode of speech by which the forgetfulness of God is also there spoken of
sources.raw_question: Do the passages of Scripture that speak of God's thoughts show that there is discursive or changing thought in God?

question: When the saints are made like God and see Him as He is, will they or their inner word become equal to God or to the divine Word in nature?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Our Word is Never to Be Equalled to the Divine Word, Not Even When We Shall Be Like God.
sources.answer: No. A nature that is made is always less than the nature that makes it. In glory our word will no longer be false, and perhaps we will see all our knowledge at a single glance. Yet even then the formable creature, though fully formed, cannot equal the simplicity that is only form: eternal and unchangeable substance, neither formless nor formed.
sources.quote: not even then shall we be equal to Him in nature. For that nature which is made is ever less than that which makes.
sources.raw_question: When the saints are made like God and see Him as He is, will they or their inner word become equal to God or to the divine Word in nature?

question: Can one determine from the pillar of cloud and fire, or the glory in the cloud, whether it was the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, or the whole Trinity that appeared?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Of the Appearance in the Pillar of Cloud and of Fire.
sources.answer: No, it is not clear. Augustine judges that the text does not distinguish whether the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, or the Trinity itself, the one God, appeared. The same holds where the glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud and the Lord spoke to Moses. He therefore declines to assign these appearances to one Person specifically.
sources.quote: But it is not similarly apparent whether the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, or the Trinity itself, the one God.
sources.raw_question: Can one determine from the pillar of cloud and fire, or the glory in the cloud, whether it was the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, or the whole Trinity that appeared?

question: Is there any cause in the creature for which God the Father fixes his special love on a particular person?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. The Father has as much cause to love one person as any other, which is none at all outside himself; his love is free and grounded in himself alone. Therefore whoever believes and receives the Father as love will infallibly find him so.
sources.quote: And for cause of love, he hath as much to fix it on thee as on any of the children of men; that is, none at all without himself.
sources.raw_question: Is there any cause in the creature for which God the Father fixes his special love on a particular person?

question: What is the right way to love oneself and one's neighbor, and does loving oneself unto wickedness count as self-love?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: One should love men, and oneself, either because they are righteous or so that they may become righteous. In this way one loves one's neighbor as oneself without risk. Whoever loves himself to the end that he may be unrighteous does not truly love himself at all. As Scripture says, he who loves iniquity hates his own soul.
sources.quote: He therefore who loves men, ought to love them either because they are righteous, or that they may become righteous. For so also he ought to love himself, either because he is righteous, or that he may become righteous
sources.raw_question: What is the right way to love oneself and one's neighbor, and does loving oneself unto wickedness count as self-love?

question: Does the anointing 'for My burial' (Matthew 26:12) mean that the divine Word Himself was buried?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The ointment was poured on His body for His burial, and 'His body was buried' is not the same as 'He was buried.' God was neither dead nor buried. Yet we must not deny that Christ was buried, nor divide Him.
sources.quote: God then was neither dead nor buried: and yet He said, In that she has poured this ointment upon My body she did it for My burial
sources.raw_question: Does the anointing 'for My burial' (Matthew 26:12) mean that the divine Word Himself was buried?

question: Are the cry of forsakenness and the promise of Paradise to the thief spoken by two different subjects in Christ, a dying man and a reigning God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The same Christ speaks both. He complains that He is left to die because He is Man, and He declares that He reigns in Paradise because He is God. The words and the voice are equally His, so He is one who dying reigns and reigning dies.
sources.quote: the mystery of the Son of God and Son of Man means that He is One, Who dying reigns, and reigning dies.
sources.raw_question: Are the cry of forsakenness and the promise of Paradise to the thief spoken by two different subjects in Christ, a dying man and a reigning God?

question: When Christ commended His Spirit to the Father and then gave it up, was it the body that commended the soul?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The one who commended His Spirit is the same one who gave it up and died. To say the body commended the soul would mean the perishable commended the living and the corruptible commended the eternal. As Son of God, Christ commends His Spirit to the Father; as Son of Man, He gives it up to death.
sources.quote: as Son of God commends His Spirit to His Father, as Son of Man gives up to death the Spirit He commended to the Father.
sources.raw_question: When Christ commended His Spirit to the Father and then gave it up, was it the body that commended the soul?

question: What is the difference between a definition and a description (title) when applying the name 'God'?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: A definition gives knowledge of the object defined and expresses its nature and kind, while a description depends on the arbitrary will of the speaker. A conferred title originates only in the speaker's words, not in the thing itself, so 'I have said, Ye are gods' is a description, not a definition.
sources.quote: A definition gives us knowledge of the object defined; a description depends on the arbitrary will of the speaker.
sources.raw_question: What is the difference between a definition and a description (title) when applying the name 'God'?

question: Is it consistent for a Christ who hates the body to take on the form or likeness of a body?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That Jesus Christ is the Son of God and Truly Man, as Opposed to the Fancies of Heretics, Who Deny that He Took Upon Him True Flesh.
sources.answer: No. If he hated the reality of a body he ought also to have hated its imitation. Taking even the form of a body would make him called the Son of the Creator. If he hated being born of the Creator's marriage-union, he should have refused even the likeness of a man born of it.
sources.quote: For thou oughtest to have hated the imitation of a body, if thou hatedst the reality; because, if thou art something else, thou oughtest to have come as something else
sources.raw_question: Is it consistent for a Christ who hates the body to take on the form or likeness of a body?

question: Did Christ, in answering the rich young man, direct people to the precepts of the Mosaic law as the way to eternal life and to following him?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XII.—It clearly appears that there was but one author of both the old and the new law, from the fact that Christ condemned traditions and customs repugnant to the former, while He confirmed its most important precepts, and taught that He was Himself the end of the Mosaic law.
sources.answer: Yes. When asked what to do to inherit eternal life, Christ told the man to keep the commandments and listed the precepts of the Decalogue. He set them out as a series of steps leading those who wished to follow him into life. What he said to one he said to all, showing that the law beforehand taught mankind the necessity of following Christ.
sources.quote: setting as an ascending series (velut gradus) before those who wished to follow Him, the precepts of the law, as the entrance into life; and what He then said to one He said to all.
sources.raw_question: Did Christ, in answering the rich young man, direct people to the precepts of the Mosaic law as the way to eternal life and to following him?

question: Does Christ's teaching show that giving possessions to the poor does away with former covetousness?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XII.—It clearly appears that there was but one author of both the old and the new law, from the fact that Christ condemned traditions and customs repugnant to the former, while He confirmed its most important precepts, and taught that He was Himself the end of the Mosaic law.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ exposed the rich man's covetousness by telling him to sell all and give to the poor, so that good works would undo his former greed. Zacchaeus made this evident when he gave half his goods to the poor and restored fourfold to anyone he had defrauded.
sources.quote: But that possessions distributed to the poor do annul former covetousness, Zaccheus made evident
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's teaching show that giving possessions to the poor does away with former covetousness?

question: Why does the human body feel pain, according to Hilary's account of the soul-body relation?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Because the body lives by admixture with a weak soul. Pain is felt by the soul pervading the body; where the soul is absent, as in nails, withered limbs, or drugged sleep, no pain is felt. Hence the body's susceptibility to pain derives from the weakness of the soul animating it.
sources.quote: It is, therefore, because the body lives by admixture with a weak soul, that it is subject to the weakness of pain.
sources.raw_question: Why does the human body feel pain, according to Hilary's account of the soul-body relation?

question: What does Paul mean by calling Christ 'the second man from heaven' in 1 Corinthians 15:47?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: 'Man' expresses his birth from the Virgin, who performed a mother's role, while 'from heaven' testifies to his origin from the Holy Ghost who came upon her. Thus this Man was born of the Virgin and conceived of the Holy Ghost.
sources.quote: Calling Him ‘Man’ he expresses His birth from the Virgin, who in the exercise of her office as mother, performed the duties of her sex in the conception and birth of man.
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean by calling Christ 'the second man from heaven' in 1 Corinthians 15:47?

question: Does a person who becomes a "child of wrath" or a "child of God" by moral choice change their human nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book III > Thereafter he expounds the appellation of “Son,” and of “product of generation,” and very many varieties of “sons,” of God, of men, of rams, of perdition, of light, and of day.
sources.answer: No. Because human nature is equally inclined to vice and virtue, we can become sons of night or of day while our nature remains within its proper limits. The sinner is not alienated from his human generation, nor does the virtuous person reject his human origin; only the differences of purpose take on names of relationship.
sources.quote: while their nature in each case remains the same, the differences of their purpose assume the names of their relationship, according as they become either children of God by virtue, or of the opposite by vice
sources.raw_question: Does a person who becomes a "child of wrath" or a "child of God" by moral choice change their human nature?

question: Why do the angels worship Christ under the name 'First-begotten' at His return?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > He then again admirably discusses the term πρωτότοκος as it is four times employed by the Apostle.
sources.answer: They worship Him because they rejoice over the restoration of humanity, which He accomplished by becoming the first-born among us. The angels count humanity's perdition as their own loss and rejoice over sinners rescued. So when the lost sheep, humanity, is brought back to the hundred, they offer intense thanksgiving and worship to God, who by being first-begotten restored the wanderer.
sources.quote: the company of all the angels worships Him Who comes in the name of the First-begotten, in their rejoicing over the restoration of men, wherewith, by becoming the first-born among us, He restored us again to the grace which we had at the beginning
sources.raw_question: Why do the angels worship Christ under the name 'First-begotten' at His return?

question: Did God expel Adam from Paradise and keep him from the tree of life because He begrudged man immortality?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIII.—Arguments in opposition to Tatian, showing that it was consonant to divine justice and mercy that the first Adam should first partake in that salvation offered to all by Christ.
sources.answer: No. God removed Adam from the tree of life out of pity, not envy. He did not want man to remain a sinner for ever, with sin immortal and evil endless and beyond remedy. So He set a limit to sin by bringing in death, which ends sin through the dissolution of the flesh, so that man, dying to sin, might begin to live to God.
sources.quote: not because He envied him the tree of life, as some venture to assert, but because He pitied him, [and did not desire] that he should continue a sinner for ever, nor that the sin which surrounded him should be immortal
sources.raised_by_detail: some who venture to assert God envied man
sources.raw_question: Did God expel Adam from Paradise and keep him from the tree of life because He begrudged man immortality?

question: Why did God curse the serpent directly but not curse Adam, and why did He question Adam and Eve but not the serpent?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIII.—Arguments in opposition to Tatian, showing that it was consonant to divine justice and mercy that the first Adam should first partake in that salvation offered to all by Christ.
sources.answer: The curse fell first and fully on the serpent so that man would receive only a milder rebuke. God did not question the serpent because He knew it was the prime mover of the sin. God detested the one who led man astray but gradually showed compassion to the one who was beguiled. Unlike Cain, Adam showed fear of God and repentance, and God shows compassion to the penitent.
sources.quote: For God detested him who had led man astray, but by degrees, and little by little, He showed compassion to him who had been beguiled.
sources.raw_question: Why did God curse the serpent directly but not curse Adam, and why did He question Adam and Eve but not the serpent?

question: In Ephesians 2:8–10, does Paul exclude even the works of believers as the ground of salvation?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul goes straight on to say 'For we are his workmanship', and the 'we' means believers with their obedience and works. So the works he excludes are believers' works. He adds that we cannot be saved by them because we do not do them by our own strength; they are produced in us by effectual, undeserved grace.
sources.quote: all our works are wrought in us, by full and effectual undeserved grace.
sources.raw_question: In Ephesians 2:8–10, does Paul exclude even the works of believers as the ground of salvation?

question: Can one subject be described by several distinct terms, each with a different meaning, without being divided, so that some terms hold of it only in some respects and not in others?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. Man is called both rational and capable of speculation and knowledge, each phrase attached to him with a different idea. It would be absurd to argue that insofar as he is capable of knowledge he cannot be rational. In the same way, distinct names applied to God's one life each apply to the whole of it.
sources.quote: It is just as if, when one had said that man was rational, as well as capable of speculation and knowledge, attaching each phrase to the subject of them according to a different application and idea, some one was to jeer
sources.raw_question: Can one subject be described by several distinct terms, each with a different meaning, without being divided, so that some terms hold of it only in some respects and not in others?

question: What is the means by which sinful and proud human beings are cleansed so as to be able to contemplate God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > How We are Rendered Apt for the Perception of Truth Through the Incarnate Word.
sources.answer: The one cleansing is the blood of the Righteous One and the humbling of God Himself. The Son was made what we are by nature, man, but not what we are by sin. This was so that through Him we might contemplate God, which by nature we are not.
sources.quote: the one cleansing of the unrighteous and of the proud is the blood of the Righteous One, and the humbling of God Himself;[^448] that we might be cleansed through Him, made as He was what we are by nature, and what we are not by sin
sources.raw_question: What is the means by which sinful and proud human beings are cleansed so as to be able to contemplate God?

question: What does it take, in the Scripture notion, for a being to be truly and properly God?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 3: Whether the word (God) in Scripture can reasonably be supposed to carry an ambiguous meaning, or to be used in a different sense, when applied to the Father and
sources.answer: It takes the full set of essential divine perfections: infinite wisdom, invincible power, all-sufficiency, eternity, immutability, omniscience and omnipresence. Supreme dominion follows from these. A being must be a sovereign Ruler and an almighty, eternal Creator and Preserver. Whatever falls short of this is called God only by figure.
sources.quote: Whatever falls short of this is not properly, in the Seripture notion, God; but is only called so by way of figure ;
sources.raw_question: What does it take, in the Scripture notion, for a being to be truly and properly God?

question: Why does the soul's pride, in seeking more than its share under God's governance, end up making the soul less rather than more?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Same Argument is Continued.
sources.answer: Because nothing is greater than the whole, which God governs by his laws. A proud soul that loves its own power and tries to rule by a law of its own is pushed out of its part in the common whole into caring for a private part, so by lusting after more it is made less. It then becomes bound to bodily things and their images, and falls into either arrogance or carnal pleasure. This is why pride is called the beginning of sin and covetousness the root of all evil.
sources.quote: by seeking something more than the whole, and struggling to govern this by a law of its own, is thrust on, since nothing is more than the whole, into caring for a part; and thus by lusting after something more, is made less
sources.raw_question: Why does the soul's pride, in seeking more than its share under God's governance, end up making the soul less rather than more?

question: Are the divine triads of pagan religions, such as the Egyptian Osiris-Isis-Horus or the Hindu Trimurti, analogues or sources of the Christian doctrine of the Trinity?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. These triads arise from the analogy of the human family, syncretism, pantheistic cycles, or a mere tendency to think in threes. None has the slightest resemblance to the Christian Trinity, which embodies much more than "threeness"; beyond their threeness these triads have nothing in common with it.
sources.quote: The Christian doctrine of the Trinity embodies much more than the notion of “threeness,” and beyond their “threeness” these triads have nothing in common with it.
sources.raised_by_detail: Gladstone, Hegel, Soderblom, Knapp, Jules Martin, H. Zimmern
sources.raw_question: Are the divine triads of pagan religions, such as the Egyptian Osiris-Isis-Horus or the Hindu Trimurti, analogues or sources of the Christian doctrine of the Trinity?

question: Can God be found by seeking him outwardly through the powers that rule the world or by aspiring to do the wonders angels do?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Of True Love, by Which We Arrive at the Knowledge of the Trinity. God is to Be Sought, Not Outwardly, by Seeking to Do Wonderful Things with the Angels, But Inwardly, by Imitating the Piety of Good Angels.
sources.answer: No. Those who seek God through such powers are removed from him not by space but by difference of affection, since they seek outwardly and forsake the inward things within which God is. They covet the angels' marvellous deeds out of pride rather than imitating the piety by which one is united to the Omnipotent.
sources.quote: are removed and cast away far from Him; not by intervals of space, but by difference of affections: for they endeavor to find a path outwardly, and forsake their own inward things, within which is God.
sources.raw_question: Can God be found by seeking him outwardly through the powers that rule the world or by aspiring to do the wonders angels do?

question: Does 1 Timothy 4:10, which calls God 'the Saviour of all men, specially of them that believe,' exclude the Son and the Spirit from the work of salvation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: No. No one argues from this phrase that the Son does not save believers or that salvation comes without the Spirit. God over all is the Saviour, while the Son works salvation by the grace of the Spirit. Yet Scripture does not call them three Saviours.
sources.quote: no one from this phrase argues either that the Son does not save them who believe, or that salvation is given to those who receive it without the intervention of the Spirit
sources.raw_question: Does 1 Timothy 4:10, which calls God 'the Saviour of all men, specially of them that believe,' exclude the Son and the Spirit from the work of salvation?

question: Can the spirit die or be decomposed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VII.—Inasmuch as Christ did rise in our flesh, it follows that we shall be also raised in the same; since the resurrection promised to us should not be referred to spirits naturally immortal, but to bodies in themselves mortal.
sources.answer: No. To die is to lose vital power and break down into one's component parts. The spirit is simple and not composite, so it cannot be decomposed, and it is itself the life of those who receive it. The soul likewise does not die, since it is the breath of life.
sources.quote: nor to the spirit, for the spirit is simple and not composite, so that it cannot be decomposed, and is itself the life of those who receive it
sources.raw_question: Can the spirit die or be decomposed?

question: Why does Augustine regard the number six as perfect, and how does he connect it to the ratio of Christ's single death to our double death?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Ratio of the Single to the Double Comes from the Perfection of the Senary Number. The Perfection of The Senary Number is Commended in the Scriptures. The Year Abounds in The Senary Number.
sources.answer: Six is perfect because it is completed by its own aliquot parts. Its sixth (one), third (two) and half (three) add up to six. The ratio of single to double that marks Christ's one death healing our double death arises from three, since one plus two makes three. One, two and three together make six. So the saving correspondence between Christ's work and our need is grounded in this perfect number.
sources.quote: And this number is on that account called perfect, because it is completed in its own parts: for it has these three, sixth, third, and half; nor is there any other part found in it, which we can call an aliquot part.
sources.raw_question: Why does Augustine regard the number six as perfect, and how does he connect it to the ratio of Christ's single death to our double death?

question: What does the woman healed by Christ after eighteen years of infirmity signify?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Ratio of the Single to the Double Comes from the Perfection of the Senary Number. The Perfection of The Senary Number is Commended in the Scriptures. The Year Abounds in The Senary Number.
sources.answer: She is a type of the church. The church is made whole and upright by the Lord after being bowed down by Satan's binding. Her eighteen years are thrice six, and the months of those years make the cube of six. This shows that the renewal received under grace leads to the full healing of both soul and body at the resurrection.
sources.quote: And thence that woman is understood to be a type of the church, who was made whole and upright by the Lord, after she had been bowed by infirmity through the binding of Satan.
sources.raw_question: What does the woman healed by Christ after eighteen years of infirmity signify?

question: Did the apostles preach a God or divine Fullness (Pleroma) other than the God of the prophets?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: No. Peter's preaching at Pentecost shows that the apostles proclaimed one and the same God the Father, the God who spoke through David and the prophets. They did not preach another God or another Fullness, as the Gnostics claim.
sources.quote: Thus the apostles did not preach another God, or another Fulness
sources.raw_question: Did the apostles preach a God or divine Fullness (Pleroma) other than the God of the prophets?
