question: When God is considered as the first Truth on whose authority all divine faith rests, is he considered as a particular person or as the whole Godhead?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: As the whole Godhead. God as prima Veritas is considered essentially, comprehending the whole Deity, which undividedly is the prime object of faith, not as expressive of any one person. Yet faith may also be distinctly fixed on the Father's own testimony and authority as Father; otherwise the Son could not add "Believe also in me."
sources.quote: is not to be considered ὑποστατικῶς, as peculiarly expressive of any person, but οὐδιωδῶς, comprehending the whole Deity; which undividedly is the prime object thereof.
sources.raw_question: When God is considered as the first Truth on whose authority all divine faith rests, is he considered as a particular person or as the whole Godhead?

question: In Song of Songs 3:2, what do the city and its streets through which the spouse seeks her beloved signify?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: The city is the church, the city of God, and going through its broad and narrow streets is the diligent inquiry the believer makes in all the paths and ordinances given to the church. When a soul does not find Christ in private duties, it turns earnestly to public worship, seeking Christ in prayer, preaching and the sacraments.
sources.quote: the city here intended is the city of God, the church; and the passing through the broad and narrow streets, is the diligent inquiry that the spouse makes in all the paths and ordinances given unto it.
sources.raw_question: In Song of Songs 3:2, what do the city and its streets through which the spouse seeks her beloved signify?

question: Was Christ simply a man who possessed the Word of God more fully than other holy and wise men?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Creature is Not So Taken by the Holy Spirit as Flesh is by the Word.
sources.answer: No. Christ is "above his fellows" not because he had more of the word or more surpassing wisdom than they did, but because he was the very Word himself. Augustine distinguishes the word in the flesh, as in prophets and saints, from the Word made flesh. The first is the word in a man; the second is the Word that is man.
sources.quote: For the word in the flesh is one thing, and the Word made flesh is another; i.e. the word in man is one thing, the Word that is man is another.
sources.raw_question: Was Christ simply a man who possessed the Word of God more fully than other holy and wise men?

question: Why were some of the Church's doctrines ("dogma") handed down in silence rather than publicly written and proclaimed ("kerugma")?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Of the origin of the word “with,” and what force it has. Also concerning the unwritten laws of the church.
sources.answer: They were kept in silence to guard the awful dignity of the mysteries. What is spread about carelessly becomes despised through familiarity. Basil compares this to Moses, who restricted access to the inner parts of the tabernacle. He holds that the obscurity of Scripture is itself a form of this silence, benefiting the reader by making dogmas harder to grasp.
sources.quote: “Dogma” and “Kerugma” are two distinct things; the former is observed in silence; the latter is proclaimed to all the world. One form of this silence is the obscurity employed in Scripture
sources.raw_question: Why were some of the Church's doctrines ("dogma") handed down in silence rather than publicly written and proclaimed ("kerugma")?

question: Is the Jesus who suffered under Pontius Pilate the same person as the Lord of all, King, God and Judge?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. Irenaeus says the mystery revealed to Paul is that the very one who suffered under Pilate is Lord of all, King, God and Judge. This is why Paul, after his conversion, preached in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God, the Christ. Christ received this power from the God of all because he became obedient unto death on the cross.
sources.quote: that He who suffered under Pontius Pilate, the same is Lord of all, and King, and God, and Judge, receiving power from Him who is the God of all, because He became “obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”
sources.raw_question: Is the Jesus who suffered under Pontius Pilate the same person as the Lord of all, King, God and Judge?

question: Is the people who believe in God under the rule of angels or under the Lord himself?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Under the Lord himself. Moses says the Most High set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels. But the people who believe in God is no longer under the power of angels. It is under the Lord's rule, for Jacob was made the Lord's portion.
sources.quote: but that people which believes in God is not now under the power of angels, but under the Lord’s [rule]. “For His people Jacob was made the portion of the Lord, Israel the cord of His inheritance.”
sources.raw_question: Is the people who believe in God under the rule of angels or under the Lord himself?

question: Does Malachi 3:1's 'the Lord whom ye seek … the messenger of the covenant whom ye delight in' describe Jesus Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes. Owen reads the verse as a description of Christ in which the saints' delight in him serves as his title. Christ is the one the saints seek and delight in, the person they long for. In the same way Haggai 2:7 calls him 'The Desire of all nations.'
sources.quote: “He whom ye seek, whom ye delight in,” is the description of Christ. He is their delight and desirable one, the person of their desire.
sources.raw_question: Does Malachi 3:1's 'the Lord whom ye seek … the messenger of the covenant whom ye delight in' describe Jesus Christ?

question: Will Christ, the Son, return in the Father's glory to raise the dead and judge all?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter X.—Unity of the faith of the Church throughout the whole world.
sources.answer: Yes. Christ will be manifested from heaven in the glory of the Father to gather all things in one and to raise all flesh. He will execute just judgment, sending the wicked angels and ungodly men into everlasting fire. By his grace he will confer immortality and glory on the righteous.
sources.quote: His [future] manifestation from heaven in the glory of the Father “to gather all things in one,”[^2787] and to raise up anew all flesh of the whole human race
sources.raw_question: Will Christ, the Son, return in the Father's glory to raise the dead and judge all?

question: What does 'the world' mean in Christ's sayings that the world does not know the Father and cannot receive the Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Establishment of the natural communion of the Spirit from His being, equally with the Father and the Son, unapproachable in thought.
sources.answer: It means mortal life enslaved to the flesh, not the physical heaven and earth. The carnal man, who keeps his mind buried in fleshly lusts and sees only with material sight, cannot look up to spiritual light, just as a weak eye cannot bear a sunbeam.
sources.quote: meaning here by the world not the complex whole compounded of heaven and earth, but this life of ours subject to death,
sources.raw_question: What does 'the world' mean in Christ's sayings that the world does not know the Father and cannot receive the Spirit?

question: Since the Holy Spirit is beyond the world's reach and seen only by the pure in heart, what honour is due to Him?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Establishment of the natural communion of the Spirit from His being, equally with the Father and the Son, unapproachable in thought.
sources.answer: The highest honour, beyond any that can be counted adequate. Basil's rhetorical question implies that the Spirit, whom the world cannot receive and only saints can contemplate, deserves honour beyond measure, equal to that given to the Father and the Son.
sources.quote: What then ought to be thought of Him whom the world cannot receive, and Whom saints alone can contemplate through pureness of heart? What kind of honours can be deemed adequate to Him?
sources.raw_question: Since the Holy Spirit is beyond the world's reach and seen only by the pure in heart, what honour is due to Him?

question: Did all mankind sin in Adam when he, having been created upright, sinned against God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. Owen sets it as the first head of the scriptural doctrine of satisfaction. Adam was made upright in God's image and sinned against God, and all his posterity sinned in him. Scripture says sin and death entered by one man, condemnation came upon all, and many were made sinners by one man's disobedience.
sources.quote: That Adam, being made upright, sinned against God; and all mankind, all his posterity, in him
sources.raw_question: Did all mankind sin in Adam when he, having been created upright, sinned against God?

question: Did the sin of our first parents bring all humans into a state of sin, apostasy and enmity against God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. By the first sin all people are brought into an estate of sin and apostasy from God, and of enmity toward him. Scripture testifies to this: men are shapen in iniquity, all have sinned, the carnal mind is enmity against God, and men are alienated from the life of God.
sources.quote: That, by this sin of our first parents, all men are brought into an estate of sin and apostasy from God, and of enmity unto him
sources.raw_question: Did the sin of our first parents bring all humans into a state of sin, apostasy and enmity against God?

question: In which nature did Christ die on the cross?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter IX. The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ, and the oil of gladness; and why Christ Himself is not the ointment, since He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It is not strange that the Spirit should be called Ointment, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. And there is no confusion between them, since Christ alone suffered death, Whose saving cross is then spoken of.
sources.answer: Christ died in the nature He took from the Virgin, not in the Godhead He had from the Father, for the eternal Godhead is incapable of dying. He was crucified in that nature in which He had flesh and bones, which the Holy Spirit did not have.
sources.quote: For of a truth He died in that which He took of the Virgin, not in that which He had of the Father, for Christ died in that nature in which He was crucified.
sources.raw_question: In which nature did Christ die on the cross?

question: Is a person's intellect or mind a substance distinct from the soul, which could enter a higher realm separately from it?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIX.—Refutation of the views of the heretics as to the future destiny of the soul and body.
sources.answer: No. A person's intellect, mind, thought and mental intention are nothing other than the soul. The soul's emotions and operations have no substance apart from the soul. So if the soul stays in the intermediate place and the body is consumed, no part of the person is left to enter the Gnostic Pleroma.
sources.quote: For the intellect of man—his mind, thought, mental intention, and such like—is nothing else than his soul; but the emotions and operations of the soul itself have no substance apart from the soul.
sources.raw_question: Is a person's intellect or mind a substance distinct from the soul, which could enter a higher realm separately from it?

question: How does God relate to the ongoing order and continued existence of the world?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > God is Above All Things, Himself Containing All Things, Immense, Eternal, Transcending the Mind of Man; Inexplicable in Discourse, Loftier Than All Sublimity.
sources.answer: God is a Mind generating and filling all things, always intent on His work, pervading, moving, quickening and beholding all things. He binds discordant elements into one world so firmly that it can be dissolved only when He commands it, and He governs the linked causes of things by perfect reason for the benefit of all.
sources.quote: For He is a certain Mind generating and filling all things, which, without any beginning or end of time, controls, by the highest and most perfect reason, the naturally linked causes of things, so as to result in benefit to all.
sources.raw_question: How does God relate to the ongoing order and continued existence of the world?

question: Does the desertion and destruction of Jerusalem show that it was not truly 'the city of the great King', and so that the God of the Old Testament is not the supreme God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IV.—Answer to another objection, showing that the destruction of Jerusalem, which was the city of the great King, diminished nothing from the supreme majesty and power of God, for that this destruction was put in execution by the most wise counsel of the same God.
sources.answer: No. Jerusalem was like vine twigs, which are made for the sake of the fruit and are left behind or cut off once the fruit has been gathered. Once Christ and the apostles had come forth from Israel according to the flesh, and the fruit had been sown throughout the world, the city had served its purpose and was rightly forsaken. What has a beginning in time must also have an end in time, so its end takes nothing away from the majesty of the God who made it.
sources.quote: they venture to assert that, if it had been “the city of the great King,” it would not have been deserted. This is just as if any one should say, that if straw were a creation of God, it would never part company with the wheat
sources.raised_by_detail: heretics who separate the Creator from the Father of Christ
sources.raw_question: Does the desertion and destruction of Jerusalem show that it was not truly 'the city of the great King', and so that the God of the Old Testament is not the supreme God?

question: In what sense is the Son the 'measure' of the unmeasurable Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IV.—Answer to another objection, showing that the destruction of Jerusalem, which was the city of the great King, diminished nothing from the supreme majesty and power of God, for that this destruction was put in execution by the most wise counsel of the same God.
sources.answer: Irenaeus approves the saying that the unmeasurable Father is subjected to measure in the Son. His reason is that the Son comprehends the Father. In the Son, therefore, the Father who is beyond measure is grasped and made known in an ordered way.
sources.quote: Well spake he, who said that the unmeasurable Father was Himself subjected to measure in the Son; for the Son is the measure of the Father, since He also comprehends Him.
sources.raw_question: In what sense is the Son the 'measure' of the unmeasurable Father?

question: Is the Lord whose 'day' burns up sinners like stubble in Malachi the same as Christ?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IV.—Answer to another objection, showing that the destruction of Jerusalem, which was the city of the great King, diminished nothing from the supreme majesty and power of God, for that this destruction was put in execution by the most wise counsel of the same God.
sources.answer: Yes. John the Baptist shows who this Lord is when he says of Christ that He will gather His fruit into the garner and burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire. The Lord of the prophetic day of judgment is therefore Christ.
sources.quote: Now, who this Lord is that brings such a day about, John the Baptist points out, when he says of Christ, “He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire, having His fan in His hand to cleanse His floor
sources.raw_question: Is the Lord whose 'day' burns up sinners like stubble in Malachi the same as Christ?

question: Is the Son immaterial and bodiless in the same way as the Father?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes. The Son is immaterial and without body in the same manner as the Father, not merely in a similar way. For that reason, communication between them cannot happen by voice reaching the Son's ears.
sources.quote: in communicating His counsels with the Only-Begotten Son, Who is similarly, or rather in the same manner, immaterial and without body
sources.raw_question: Is the Son immaterial and bodiless in the same way as the Father?

question: What is the 'circumcision of Christ' in Colossians 2:11-12?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: It is not a fleshly circumcision but rebirth into a new man through baptism. Buried with Christ in baptism, we die entirely to the old man and live henceforth entirely to him, since baptismal regeneration has the force of resurrection. We rise in him through faith in God, by whose working Christ was raised from the dead.
sources.quote: The circumcision of Christ does not mean the putting off of foreskins, but to die entirely with Him, and by that death to live henceforth entirely to Him.
sources.raw_question: What is the 'circumcision of Christ' in Colossians 2:11-12?

question: If miracles show God's power, how can magicians such as Pharaoh's wise men also perform miracles?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > Great Miracles Wrought by Magic Arts.
sources.answer: Magicians work wonders only through fallen angels, and those angels can do nothing except by power given from above by God. The proof is that Pharaoh's magicians, who could make serpents, failed entirely at producing tiny lice and confessed, "This is the finger of God."
sources.quote: can do anything except by power given from above
sources.raw_question: If miracles show God's power, how can magicians such as Pharaoh's wise men also perform miracles?

question: For what purposes does God permit evil spirits to work wonders through magic arts?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > Great Miracles Wrought by Magic Arts.
sources.answer: For three purposes. The first is to deceive the deceitful, as with the Egyptians and their magicians, who are then condemned by God's truth. The second is to warn the faithful not to desire such things as though they were great. The third is to exercise, prove and display the patience of the righteous, as with Job.
sources.quote: or lastly, for the exercising, proving, and manifesting of the patience of the righteous
sources.raw_question: For what purposes does God permit evil spirits to work wonders through magic arts?

question: Was the worship paid by Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Manoah and Ezekiel to divine appearances in the Old Testament worship directed to Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The Angel of Jehovah at the bush, the man before whom Joshua fell, the one to whom Gideon built the altar Jehovah-shalom, the angel named Wonderful in Manoah's sacrifice, and the likeness of a man on the throne in Ezekiel were all God the Son. Since these saints fell down and worshipped, these are instances of direct worship paid to Christ.
sources.quote: It was God the Son, for “upon the likeness of the throne was the likeness of the appearance of a man above upon it,” before whom Ezekiel fell upon his face. (Ezek. 1:26) In all these instances, we have direct worship paid to Christ.
sources.raw_question: Was the worship paid by Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Manoah and Ezekiel to divine appearances in the Old Testament worship directed to Christ?

question: What is the true wisdom of man according to Scripture?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > What the Wisdom is of Which We are Here to Treat. Whence the Name of Philosopher Arose. What Has Been Already Said Concerning the Distinction of Knowledge and Wisdom.
sources.answer: The true wisdom of man is the worship of God (theosebeia), or piety. Scripture shows this in Job, where the Wisdom of God says to man, "Behold piety, that is wisdom." God himself is the chiefest wisdom, while the worship of God is the wisdom of man.
sources.quote: Therefore God Himself is the chiefest wisdom; but the worship of God is the wisdom of man, of which we now speak.
sources.raw_question: What is the true wisdom of man according to Scripture?

question: Does being called wise require that a person be without sin?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > What the Wisdom is of Which We are Here to Treat. Whence the Name of Philosopher Arose. What Has Been Already Said Concerning the Distinction of Knowledge and Wisdom.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says, "Rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee." Whoever thinks a man ought to be rebuked judges him to have sin, so a wise man in Scripture's sense is not sinless.
sources.quote: But our Scriptures do not say this, which say, “Rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.” For doubtless he who thinks a man ought to be rebuked, judges him to have sin.
sources.raw_question: Does being called wise require that a person be without sin?

question: Can faith, which exists in time, help us attain eternal things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He speaks of the true wisdom of man, viz. that by which he remembers, understands, and loves God; and shows that it is in this very thing that the mind of man is the image of God, although his mind, which is here renewed in the knowledge of God, will only then be made the perfect likeness of God in that image when there shall be a perfect sight of God. > What the Wisdom is of Which We are Here to Treat. Whence the Name of Philosopher Arose. What Has Been Already Said Concerning the Distinction of Knowledge and Wisdom.
sources.answer: Yes. Faith concerning eternal things is itself temporal and dwells in time in believers' hearts, yet it is necessary for reaching the eternal things themselves. Faith in what the eternal One did and suffered as man in time is likewise profitable for obtaining things eternal.
sources.quote: faith respecting things eternal is itself a thing temporal, and dwells in time in the hearts of believers, and yet is necessary in order to attain the things eternal themselves
sources.raw_question: Can faith, which exists in time, help us attain eternal things?

question: If the Word received glory and power for his own sake according to his Godhead, what would follow for human salvation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: Men would have no hope. If the Word as Word received, was hallowed and rose for His own sake, men would remain naked, wretched and dead, with no share in what was given to the Son. The Word became flesh to redeem, hallow and deify mankind, so what He received was received for the flesh, and through it for us.
sources.quote: if He according to His Godhead is He who is hallowed and has risen again, what hope is there for men? for they remain as they were, naked, and wretched, and dead, having no interest in the things given to the Son.
sources.raw_question: If the Word received glory and power for his own sake according to his Godhead, what would follow for human salvation?

question: How do we know what a mind is, given that no mind can be seen with the eyes?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How the Man Not Yet Righteous Can Know the Righteous Man Whom He Loves.
sources.answer: We know what a mind is from ourselves, because we have a mind. Nothing is known so intimately as the mind, by which all other things are perceived. We infer other minds from bodily movements like our own, and we learn what a mind is by reflecting on our own.
sources.quote: For not only do we perceive that there is a mind, but we can also know what a mind is, by reflecting upon our own: for we have a mind.
sources.raw_question: How do we know what a mind is, given that no mind can be seen with the eyes?

question: When the prophets record God rejecting Israel's sacrifices, did God reject them out of anger like an angry man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVII.—Proof that God did not appoint the Levitical dispensation for His own sake, or as requiring such service; for He does, in fact, need nothing from men.
sources.answer: No. God rejected their sacrifices out of compassion for their blindness. His aim was to point them to the true sacrifice by which they could appease Him and receive life. If He had rejected them in anger as people unworthy of mercy, He would not have gone on to urge on them the very things by which they might be saved. Because God is merciful, He did not withhold good counsel from them.
sources.quote: For it was not because He was angry, like a man, as many venture to say, that He rejected their sacrifices; but out of compassion to their blindness, and with the view of suggesting to them the true sacrifice
sources.raised_by_detail: many who say God was angry like a man
sources.raw_question: When the prophets record God rejecting Israel's sacrifices, did God reject them out of anger like an angry man?

question: What do the Psalms and prophets that disparage burnt-offerings teach about the sacrifice God actually desires?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVII.—Proof that God did not appoint the Levitical dispensation for His own sake, or as requiring such service; for He does, in fact, need nothing from men.
sources.answer: They teach that God desires obedience, a broken and contrite heart, and the sacrifice of praise, rather than holocausts. Holocausts do nothing to make a person righteous, whereas obedience makes people secure and draws them near to God. In saying this, David was also prophesying the new covenant.
sources.quote: He thus teaches them that God desires obedience, which renders them secure, rather than sacrifices and holocausts, which avail them nothing towards righteousness; and [by this declaration] he prophesies the new covenant at the same time.
sources.raw_question: What do the Psalms and prophets that disparage burnt-offerings teach about the sacrifice God actually desires?

question: Does Christ's role as Mediator imply that he is God only in name, honoured with a bare title of Godhead?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > He thus proceeds to a magnificent discourse of the interpretation of “Mediator,” “Like,” “Ungenerate,” and “generate,” and of “The likeness and seal of the energy of the Almighty and of His Works.”
sources.answer: No. The idea of a mediator itself teaches the doctrine of the Creed. The Mediator truly became man and was not merely deemed one. In the same way, being very God, he is not merely honoured with the title of Godhead, as Eunomius would have it.
sources.quote: not by being merely deemed a man, but having truly become so: in like manner also, being very God, He has not, as Eunomius will have us consider, been honoured by the bare title of Godhead
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's role as Mediator imply that he is God only in name, honoured with a bare title of Godhead?

question: Is the worship and devotion of the saints, such as faith, love, prayer, and praise, directed respectively to each person of the Trinity?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture distinctly assigns faith, love, trust, joy, prayer, and praise to the Father, Son, and Spirit. In both moral and instituted worship the saints respect each person respectively. For example, faith is acted immediately on the Father when we receive his testimony to the Son, and Christ commands belief in himself alongside belief in God.
sources.quote: That the Scripture doth distinctly assign all these unto the Father, Son, and Spirit, — manifesting that the saints do, in all of them, both as they are purely and nakedly moral, and as farther clothed with instituted worship, respect each person respectively
sources.raw_question: Is the worship and devotion of the saints, such as faith, love, prayer, and praise, directed respectively to each person of the Trinity?

question: Is it coherent to hold that the same divine seed gave spiritual knowledge and perfection to certain men while leaving the God who made them in ignorance?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIX.—Absurdities of the heretics as to their own origin: their opinions respecting the Demiurge shown to be equally untenable and ridiculous.
sources.answer: No. The Gnostics say they share the same soul-substance as the Demiurge, and that he received the whole of the seed while they received only a particle. Yet they claim it made them knowing and 'spiritual' while it left him ignorant and merely animal. That the same cause should produce knowledge in creatures and ignorance in their Maker is utterly irrational.
sources.quote: For to imagine that the very same seed conveyed knowledge and perfection to the souls of these men, while it only gave rise to ignorance in the God who made them, is an opinion that can be held only by those utterly frantic, and totally destitute of common sense.
sources.raw_question: Is it coherent to hold that the same divine seed gave spiritual knowledge and perfection to certain men while leaving the God who made them in ignorance?

question: Does Paul's teaching in Romans 13 about the 'higher powers' ordained by God refer to angelic or invisible rulers, or to human authorities?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXIV.—Of the constant falsehood of the devil, and of the powers and governments of the world, which we ought to obey, inasmuch as they are appointed of God, not of the devil.
sources.answer: It refers to actual human authorities, not to angelic or invisible powers as some interpret it. Paul shows this by commanding that tribute be paid to them as God's ministers. The Lord confirmed it by directing that tribute be paid for Himself and Peter.
sources.quote: not in regard to angelical powers, nor of invisible rulers— as some venture to expound the passage—but of those of actual human authorities, [he shows when] he says, “For this cause pay ye tribute also
sources.raised_by_detail: some who expound the passage as referring to angelic powers
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's teaching in Romans 13 about the 'higher powers' ordained by God refer to angelic or invisible rulers, or to human authorities?

question: Why did God institute human government and its power of the sword?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXIV.—Of the constant falsehood of the devil, and of the powers and governments of the world, which we ought to obey, inasmuch as they are appointed of God, not of the devil.
sources.answer: God set up human rule because man, having departed from God, fell into fury, murder and avarice and no longer acknowledged the fear of God. God therefore imposed the fear of man, so that people restrained by laws and by the sword might attain some degree of justice. Earthly rule is thus appointed by God for the benefit of nations, so that men may not devour one another.
sources.quote: God imposed upon mankind the fear of man, as they did not acknowledge the fear of God, in order that, being subjected to the authority of men, and kept under restraint by their laws, they might attain to some degree of justice
sources.raw_question: Why did God institute human government and its power of the sword?

question: If God appoints all rulers, does God appoint bad and tyrannical rulers as well as good ones?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXIV.—Of the constant falsehood of the devil, and of the powers and governments of the world, which we ought to obey, inasmuch as they are appointed of God, not of the devil.
sources.answer: Yes, in a sense. By the law of the same Being who calls men into existence, kings are appointed to suit their subjects. Some are given for correction and justice, and others, as the subjects deserve, for fear, punishment, or deception. Rulers who act unjustly will themselves perish, because God's just judgment falls equally on all.
sources.quote: For by the law of the same Being as calls men into existence are kings also appointed, adapted for those men who are at the time placed under their government.
sources.raw_question: If God appoints all rulers, does God appoint bad and tyrannical rulers as well as good ones?

question: What is the limit of the devil's power over human beings?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXIV.—Of the constant falsehood of the devil, and of the powers and governments of the world, which we ought to obey, inasmuch as they are appointed of God, not of the devil.
sources.answer: The devil, as an apostate angel, can only deceive and mislead the human mind into disobeying God's commandments. He gradually darkens people's hearts so that they forget the true God and worship him as God. He does not possess genuine authority to rule.
sources.quote: can only go to this length, as he did at the beginning, [namely] to deceive and lead astray the mind of man into disobeying the commandments of God
sources.raw_question: What is the limit of the devil's power over human beings?

question: Why did the devil become an apostate from God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXIV.—Of the constant falsehood of the devil, and of the powers and governments of the world, which we ought to obey, inasmuch as they are appointed of God, not of the devil.
sources.answer: The devil was one of the angels set over the spirit of the air. He became envious of man and so turned apostate from the divine law, since envy is foreign to God. Once man exposed his apostasy, he set himself against man with growing determination.
sources.quote: being one among those angels who are placed over the spirit of the air, as the Apostle Paul has declared in his Epistle to the Ephesians, becoming envious of man, was rendered an apostate from the divine law: for envy is a thing foreign to God.
sources.raw_question: Why did the devil become an apostate from God?

question: How did the Word of God, the Maker of all things, defeat the devil?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXIV.—Of the constant falsehood of the devil, and of the powers and governments of the world, which we ought to obey, inasmuch as they are appointed of God, not of the devil.
sources.answer: The Word conquered the devil by means of human nature, exposed him as an apostate, and put him under the power of man. The devil gained dominion over man through apostasy. Fittingly, that apostasy is stripped of power through man turning back to God, as Christ's gift of power to tread on serpents and scorpions shows.
sources.quote: The Word of God, however, the Maker of all things, conquering him by means of human nature, and showing him to be an apostate, has, on the contrary, put him under the power of man.
sources.raw_question: How did the Word of God, the Maker of all things, defeat the devil?

question: Does the fact that the Son, not the Father, destroyed death and judges mankind show that the Father is unable to save or judge?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: No. The Father commits judgment and works salvation through the Son not because He is unable, but because the Son is His own Power, by which He works all things. Thus those saved by the Son are saved by the Power of the Father, and those judged by Him are judged by the Righteousness of God.
sources.quote: not doing all things by the Son for the reason that He is unable either to save the lost or judge the sinner, but because He does these things too by His own Power, by which He works all things.
sources.raw_question: Does the fact that the Son, not the Father, destroyed death and judges mankind show that the Father is unable to save or judge?

question: Should the Father be excluded from thanksgiving for the salvation accomplished through Christ's Passion?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > He then gives a notable explanation of the saying of the Lord to Philip, “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father;” and herein he excellently discusses the suffering of the Lord in His love to man, and the impassibility, creative power, and providence of the Father, and the composite nature of men, and their resolution into the elements of which they were composed.
sources.answer: No. If the work were evil, both Father and Son would have to be separated from it. But since saving the lost is good and an act of love for men, the Father deserves thanks too. He wrought freedom from death through His own Power, which is Christ.
sources.quote: why do you alienate from our thanksgiving for our salvation the Father, Who by His own Power, which is Christ, wrought for men their freedom from death?
sources.raw_question: Should the Father be excluded from thanksgiving for the salvation accomplished through Christ's Passion?

question: How does the Old Testament ritual of the scape-goat represent both satisfaction and pardon?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: An Appendix
sources.answer: The sins of the people were laid on the goat, so that their punishment was transferred to it in type, and the goat was then sent away. This pictured forgiveness following the transfer of punishment. The sent-away goat does not suffer, and that lack is supplied by the other goat, which was slain as a sin-offering. No single type could fully represent the grace it pointed to.
sources.quote: denoting the oblation or forgiveness of sin, after a translation made of its punishment, Lev. xvi. 21, 22.
sources.raw_question: How does the Old Testament ritual of the scape-goat represent both satisfaction and pardon?

question: If the outward works of the Trinity (opera ad extra) are common and undivided, how can particular works like creation and redemption be attributed to particular Persons?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Some outward works, such as common providence, are common in every respect. Others are common as to the act itself but are distinguished by their principle, the immediate source in the manner of operation. In this sense creation is appropriated to the Father and redemption to the Son.
sources.quote: being common in respect of their acts, they are distinguished in respect of that principle, or next and immediate rise in the manner of operation: so creation is appropriated to the Father, redemption to the Son
sources.raw_question: If the outward works of the Trinity (opera ad extra) are common and undivided, how can particular works like creation and redemption be attributed to particular Persons?

question: How can it be coherent that the immortal God died and the eternal was buried in Christ?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: It is not a matter of the rational order but a unique work of divine power. Just as God becoming man and the Immortal dying are acts of omnipotence, so too it is an effect of omnipotence, not intellect, that He who is man is also God, He who died is immortal, and He who was buried is eternal.
sources.quote: it is an effect not of intellect but of omnipotence that He Who is man is also God, that He Who died is immortal, that He Who was buried is eternal
sources.raw_question: How can it be coherent that the immortal God died and the eternal was buried in Christ?

question: What does Romans 10:9 require for salvation regarding Christ, and does it call for speculative investigation into his nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: Salvation requires confessing with the mouth that Jesus is Lord and believing in the heart that God raised him from the dead. God does not call us through arduous investigations or rhetoric; we should not debate God's powers or limit his might, but confess in simplicity. Hence depreciating Christ's nature is folly, since salvation lies in knowing that he is the Lord.
sources.quote: What folly is it to depreciate the nature and character of Christ, when this alone is salvation, to know that He is the Lord.
sources.raw_question: What does Romans 10:9 require for salvation regarding Christ, and does it call for speculative investigation into his nature?

question: Does the Shema, "Hear O Israel, Jehovah our Elohim is one Jehovah" (Deuteronomy 6:4), teach an absolutely solitary unity in God that excludes all plurality?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 7. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, assures us that in the trustful knowledge of one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, is the spiritual life of man now and forever. On the mysteries of faith. On the revealed evidences of faith. On creeds or definitions of faith. On the obedience of faith. On the full satisfaction of faith.
sources.answer: No. Had an absolutely solitary unity been meant, the text would naturally have said "one Eloah," using the singular. Instead it uses the plural Elohim alongside the affirmation that Jehovah is one. It thus conveys that Jehovah remains one notwithstanding a real plurality.
sources.quote: they appear to be in the most definite and expressive manner designed to convey the idea, that, notwithstanding a real plurality intimated in the form Elohim, Jehovah is still ONE.
sources.raw_question: Does the Shema, "Hear O Israel, Jehovah our Elohim is one Jehovah" (Deuteronomy 6:4), teach an absolutely solitary unity in God that excludes all plurality?

question: Is loving to know unknown things the same as loving unknown things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > The Love of the Studious Mind, that Is, of One Desirous to Know, is Not the Love of a Thing Which It Does Not Know.
sources.answer: No. A man can love to know things unknown, but he cannot love things unknown. The word 'to know' is not idle: one who loves to know unknown things loves the knowing of them, not the unknown things themselves. This also answers the objection that one can no more hate what is unknown than love it.
sources.quote: it is not the same thing to say he loves to know things unknown, as to say he loves things unknown. For it is possible that a man may love to know things unknown; but it is not possible that he should love things unknown.
sources.raw_question: Is loving to know unknown things the same as loving unknown things?

question: Does Scripture forbid giving supreme trust, worship and love to Jesus Christ on the ground that such emotions are due only to God the Father?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 3. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, requires us to repose our ultimate confidence in the Lord Jesus Christ: as One who is distinct from the Father: as One to whom all the attributes of essential Deity are ascribed: as One whose infinite perfections claim supreme trust, adoration, and love.
sources.answer: No. Prophecy foretold and blessed such confidence, and when Christ was on earth sinners worshipped him and he did not refuse it. He declared their whole trust in him not merely suitable but essential, since eternal life hangs upon believing in him.
sources.quote: But does Scripture forbid them? nay, verily. Prophecy, as we have seen, foretold that thus it should be, and blessed the confidence. And when the Saviour walked our fallen world, suppliant sinners worship him, and He refuses it not.
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture forbid giving supreme trust, worship and love to Jesus Christ on the ground that such emotions are due only to God the Father?

question: Does Christ's saying that what comes out of the mouth defiles a man teach that the heart has its own mouth from which thoughts proceed?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > Concerning the Word of the Mind, in Which We See the Word of God, as in a Glass and an Enigma.
sources.answer: Yes. In one sentence Christ includes two mouths, one of the body and one of the heart. Food enters the bodily mouth. What defiles proceeds from the mouth of the heart, as Christ himself explains: 'out of the heart proceed evil thoughts'.
sources.quote: In one sentence He has comprised two diverse mouths of the man, one of the body, one of the heart.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's saying that what comes out of the mouth defiles a man teach that the heart has its own mouth from which thoughts proceed?

question: Do the healing signs that Isaiah 35 links to God's coming prove that Christ, who performed them, is God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That Christ is God, is Proved by the Authority of the Old Testament Scriptures.
sources.answer: Yes. Isaiah says that at the coming of God the blind will see, the deaf hear, the lame leap and the dumb speak. These signs appeared at Christ's coming and were done by him, so those who deny his divinity are bound by the prophets' words and cannot deny that Christ is God. They must either confess him as God the Son or fall into the opposite heresy of calling him the Father.
sources.quote: Since the prophet says that at God’s advent these should be the signs which come to pass; let men acknowledge either that Christ is the Son of God, at whose advent and by whom these wonders of healings were performed
sources.raw_question: Do the healing signs that Isaiah 35 links to God's coming prove that Christ, who performed them, is God?

question: If man, once fallen, were never restored to life, would God's will have been defeated by the serpent?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIII.—Arguments in opposition to Tatian, showing that it was consonant to divine justice and mercy that the first Adam should first partake in that salvation offered to all by Christ.
sources.answer: Yes. If man, created by God to live, were abandoned to death forever, God would have been conquered and the serpent's wickedness would have prevailed over God's will. But God is invincible and long-suffering, and through the second man (Christ) He bound the strong man, abolished death, and vivified the man who had been dead.
sources.quote: God would [in that case] have been conquered, and the wickedness of the serpent would have prevailed over the will of God. But inasmuch as God is invincible and long-suffering
sources.raw_question: If man, once fallen, were never restored to life, would God's will have been defeated by the serpent?

question: Did God curse Adam personally after his transgression?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIII.—Arguments in opposition to Tatian, showing that it was consonant to divine justice and mercy that the first Adam should first partake in that salvation offered to all by Christ.
sources.answer: No. God pronounced no curse against Adam himself but transferred the curse to the ground; Adam received toil and death as punishment, so that man would neither perish altogether nor despise God. The full curse fell upon the serpent who beguiled them.
sources.quote: He pronounced no curse against Adam personally, but against the ground, in reference to his works
sources.raw_question: Did God curse Adam personally after his transgression?

question: Was eternal fire originally prepared for man?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXIII.—Arguments in opposition to Tatian, showing that it was consonant to divine justice and mercy that the first Adam should first partake in that salvation offered to all by Christ.
sources.answer: No. Christ's words show that eternal fire was prepared for the devil and his apostate angels, the one who beguiled man; men will justly suffer it only if, like him, they persevere in wickedness without repentance.
sources.quote: indicating that eternal fire was not originally prepared for man, but for him who beguiled man, and caused him to offend
sources.raw_question: Was eternal fire originally prepared for man?

question: Are the doctrines of perichoresis and interior generation illegitimate because they are unscriptural terms?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. They are appendages to the scriptural doctrine of one God in three Persons, introduced only as answers to objections that are themselves unscriptural, drawn from the supposed nature of the thing. If opponents laid aside their unscriptural objections, there would be no need for unscriptural answers; and such answers suffice to confute mere conjectures about matters above human reach.
sources.quote: Lay you aside your unscriptural objections, and we shall have no occasion for unscriptural answers.
sources.raw_question: Are the doctrines of perichoresis and interior generation illegitimate because they are unscriptural terms?

question: Did the pride of reason that kept pagans from Christianity consist in a love of philosophical mysteries rather than in refusing to submit to mysteries?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 21: Whether he be not forced to supply his want of Scripture-proof by very strained and remote inferences, and very uncertain reasonings from the nature of a thing
sources.answer: No. History shows that pagans, Jews and early heretics took offence precisely at mysteries such as the resurrection, God incarnate, and the Trinity itself. So the pride of reason worked then as now, as an aversion to receiving mysteries, contrary to Mr. Emlyn's claim.
sources.quote: the very mystery of the Trinity, which is the “ rock of offence” to some even at this time, gave very early offence to the Pagan wits; and was much disrelished by them::+so averse were they to the receiving of mysteries
sources.raw_question: Did the pride of reason that kept pagans from Christianity consist in a love of philosophical mysteries rather than in refusing to submit to mysteries?

question: Do the Holy Spirit's different offices in different ages imply that there are different Spirits?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Next Teaches Us that the Authority of the Faith Enjoins, After the Father and the Son, to Believe Also on the Holy Spirit, Whose Operations He Enumerates from Scripture.
sources.answer: No. The Spirit's offices differ because the times call for a different order of occasions. The one who discharges these offices is not different. He is one and the same Spirit, distributing his offices according to the times and the needs of things.
sources.quote: He who discharges these offices is not different, nor is He another in so acting, but He is one and the same, distributing His offices according to the times
sources.raw_question: Do the Holy Spirit's different offices in different ages imply that there are different Spirits?

question: Did a mere man accomplish the salvation of the world, according to the orthodox teaching defended against Eunomius?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VI > The sixth book shows that He Who came for man's salvation was not a mere man, as Eunomius, falsely slandering him, affirmed that the great Basil had said, but the Only-begotten Son of God, putting on human flesh, and becoming a mediator between God and man, on Whom we believe, as subject to suffering in the flesh, but impassible in His Godhead; and demonstrates the calumny of Eunomius.
sources.answer: No. Gregory says the saving grace cannot be referred to any ordinary man, or even to Peter, Paul, or an angel; anyone who did so should be anathema. Paul was not crucified for us, nor were we baptized into a human name. The saving power of Christ is more potent than human nature, since it is the Only-begotten Son who took flesh.
sources.quote: So far are we from referring to an ordinary man the cause of this great and unspeakable grace, that even if any should refer so great a boon to Peter and Paul, or to an angel from heaven, we should say with Paul, “let him be anathema.”
sources.raw_question: Did a mere man accomplish the salvation of the world, according to the orthodox teaching defended against Eunomius?

question: Can the Son be understood as one creature among many that, like the sun, moon and stars, cooperates with other creatures in a shared ministry of creation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: No. Created things like the sun, moon, stars, earth and firmament each have a limited office and are insufficient alone, being like members of one body, the world. To conceive of the Word this way makes Him a part of the universe insufficient without the rest, which is irreligious. Rather the Word is not among things originate but is the sole and proper Word of the Father and their Framer.
sources.quote: let them acknowledge that the Word is not in the number of things originate, but the sole and proper Word of the Father, and their Framer.
sources.raw_question: Can the Son be understood as one creature among many that, like the sun, moon and stars, cooperates with other creatures in a shared ministry of creation?

question: Does what is possessed by learning rather than by nature remain secure, and what does this imply about the Son's creative power?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Introduction to Proverbs viii. 22 continued. Absurdity of supposing a Son or Word created in order to the creation of other creatures; as to the creation being unable to bear God's immediate hand, God condescends to the lowest. Moreover, if the Son a creature, He too could not bear God's hand, and an infinite series of media will be necessary. Objected, that, as Moses who led out the Israelites was a man, so our Lord; but Moses was not the Agent in creation:--again, that unity is found in created ministrations, but all such ministrations are defective and dependent:--again, that He learned to create, yet could God's Wisdom need teaching? and why should He learn, if the Father worketh hitherto? If the Son was created to create us, He is for our sake, not we for His.
sources.answer: What accrues by learning and not by nature can at some time be unlearned. So if the Son's creative power were learned, He would be Wisdom only so long as He kept what He learned. Hence the Son must be essential Wisdom, creating by nature.
sources.quote: For what has accrued not by any nature, but from learning, admits of being one time unlearned.
sources.raw_question: Does what is possessed by learning rather than by nature remain secure, and what does this imply about the Son's creative power?

question: Which Person of the Trinity spoke with Adam and walked in the garden in Genesis: the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, or the Trinity without distinction?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: Augustine holds that this cannot be determined from this text of Scripture. The context shows no change of speaker, so it seems to be the same God who said 'Let there be light,' usually taken to be the Father. Yet Scripture might have passed silently from the Father to the Son, intimating this only to those able to understand. Since it is not even clear whether Adam saw God with bodily eyes, he judges the question not discoverable from this testimony.
sources.quote: but the thing itself, so far as concerns this testimony of Scripture, where God spake with man, is, in my judgment, not discoverable, because it does not evidently appear even whether Adam usually saw God with the eyes of his body
sources.raw_question: Which Person of the Trinity spoke with Adam and walked in the garden in Genesis: the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, or the Trinity without distinction?

question: Was the Law on the tables of stone written by a bodily finger of God, or by the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter III. The same Unity may also be recognized from the fact that the Spirit is called Finger, and the Son Right Hand; for the understanding of divine things is assisted by the usage of human language. The tables of the law were written by this Finger, and they were afterwards broken, and the reason. Lastly, Christ wrote with the same Finger; yet we must not admit any inferiority in the Spirit from this bodily comparison.
sources.answer: It was written by the Holy Spirit. God did not write those letters with a finger of flesh; he gave the law by his Spirit. As the Apostle's letter is written 'with the Spirit of the living God', so the Law was written by the Spirit, who enlightens the heart.
sources.quote: For God did not with a finger of flesh write the forms and portions of those letters which we read, but gave the law by His Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Was the Law on the tables of stone written by a bodily finger of God, or by the Holy Spirit?

question: Can the example of the three youths be dismissed on the ground that they felt no pain only because the fire lost its power to burn?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. It is natural for bodies to fear and be burnt by fire, yet through the spirit of faith their bodies could be neither burnt nor made afraid. The fire kept its nature in all other respects, for it consumed the bystanders. What faith produced in men against the order of nature should in God's case be seen as an activity of the Spirit present from his earthly origin.
sources.quote: What, therefore, in the case of men was a violation of the order of nature, produced by faith in God, cannot be judged in God’s case natural, but as an activity of the Spirit commencing with His earthly origin.
sources.raw_question: Can the example of the three youths be dismissed on the ground that they felt no pain only because the fire lost its power to burn?

question: Are the higher reason, which contemplates eternal truth, and the lower reason, which handles temporal and corporeal things, two separate minds or one mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Higher Reason Which Belongs to Contemplation, and the Lower Which Belongs to Action, are in One Mind.
sources.answer: They are one mind. The part of reason that deals with temporal things is not separated so as to sever the mind's unity. It is diverted, as it were, to serve as a help for its proper work. Just as Eve was taken from Adam and the two are one flesh, so intellect and action, or counsel and performance, are embraced by one nature: they two are in one mind.
sources.quote: And so a certain part of our reason, not separated so as to sever unity, but, as it were, diverted so as to be a help to fellowship, is parted off for the performing of its proper work.
sources.raw_question: Are the higher reason, which contemplates eternal truth, and the lower reason, which handles temporal and corporeal things, two separate minds or one mind?

question: Who is the God whom Baruch (Jeremiah) says was seen upon earth and dwelt among men, given that no one has seen God at any time except the Only-begotten?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: It is the Son. Since the Father confessedly cannot be seen except by the Son, the God seen on earth and dwelling among men must be the Only-begotten, God visible in human form whom men can handle. He is therefore 'our God.'
sources.quote: The Father confessedly cannot be seen except by the Son; Who then is This who was seen and dwelt among men? He must be our God, for He is God visible in human form, Whom men can handle.
sources.raw_question: Who is the God whom Baruch (Jeremiah) says was seen upon earth and dwelt among men, given that no one has seen God at any time except the Only-begotten?

question: What works of the Only-begotten show that none can be likened unto Him?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IV
sources.answer: All things in heaven and earth, and all times and worlds, were made through Him. He instructed Abraham, spoke with Moses, abode in the prophets, and was born of the Virgin from the Holy Ghost. He conquered hostile powers and death and destroys the corruption of flesh by His glorified Body. These are the peculiar powers of God the Only-begotten, who alone was born from God.
sources.quote: Therefore none shall be likened unto Him. For these are the peculiar powers of God the Only-begotten; He alone was born from God, the blissful Possessor of such great prerogatives.
sources.raw_question: What works of the Only-begotten show that none can be likened unto Him?

question: How can a Christian tell when heretics such as the Valentinian Gnostics are misusing the words and parables of Scripture to support their own system?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter IX.—Refutation of the impious interpretations of these heretics.
sources.answer: By holding unchanged in his heart the rule of truth received at baptism. He will recognise the scriptural names, expressions and parables, but not the blasphemous use made of them. Irenaeus compares this to Homeric verses stitched into a new story: once each passage is restored to its proper place and fitted to the body of the truth, the heretical construction is exposed as baseless.
sources.quote: he also who retains unchangeable in his heart the rule of the truth which he received by means of baptism, will doubtless recognise the names, the expressions, and the parables taken from the Scriptures, but will by no means acknowledge the blasphemous use which these men make of them
sources.raw_question: How can a Christian tell when heretics such as the Valentinian Gnostics are misusing the words and parables of Scripture to support their own system?

question: Does Christ's teaching 'I will have mercy and not sacrifice' show agreement between Christ and the God who spoke through the Old Testament prophets?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVII.—Proof that God did not appoint the Levitical dispensation for His own sake, or as requiring such service; for He does, in fact, need nothing from men.
sources.answer: Yes. When the Lord quoted Hosea's 'I will have mercy, and not sacrifice', he bore witness that the prophets preached the truth. The fault lay with his hearers, who were foolish through their own fault, not with the prophetic teaching. The same divine will is therefore taught by the prophets and by Christ.
sources.quote: Thus does He bear witness to the prophets, that they preached the truth; but accuses these men (His hearers) of being foolish through their own fault.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's teaching 'I will have mercy and not sacrifice' show agreement between Christ and the God who spoke through the Old Testament prophets?

question: Does Malachi's prophecy of a pure sacrifice offered in every place among the Gentiles refer to the Church's eucharistic offering?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVII.—Proof that God did not appoint the Levitical dispensation for His own sake, or as requiring such service; for He does, in fact, need nothing from men.
sources.answer: Yes. Malachi foretold that the former people would cease to make acceptable offerings to God. Instead, a pure sacrifice would be offered to him in every place and his name glorified among the Gentiles. This is fulfilled in the new oblation which the Church received from the apostles and offers throughout the world.
sources.quote: indicating in the plainest manner, by these words, that the former people [the Jews] shall indeed cease to make offerings to God, but that in every place sacrifice shall be offered to Him, and that a pure one
sources.raw_question: Does Malachi's prophecy of a pure sacrifice offered in every place among the Gentiles refer to the Church's eucharistic offering?

question: Was Philip's request "Lord, shew us the Father" (John 14:8) an act of unbelief or a demand to see the Father bodily?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. It was a mistake made in ignorance, not a tampering with the faith. Philip did not deny that the Father had been seen. His words "and it sufficeth us" show that he wanted a mental enlightenment, so that he could understand how, by seeing the Son as Man, he had seen the Father.
sources.quote: His adding, And it sufficeth us, to the prayer, Lord, shew us the Father, reveals clearly that it was a mental, not a bodily vision of the Father which he desired.
sources.raw_question: Was Philip's request "Lord, shew us the Father" (John 14:8) an act of unbelief or a demand to see the Father bodily?

question: Did Christ the Word redeem humanity from the apostasy by force or by persuasion, and why?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter I.—Christ alone is able to teach divine things, and to redeem us: He, the same, took flesh of the Virgin Mary, not merely in appearance, but actually, by the operation of the Holy Spirit, in order to renovate us. Strictures on the conceits of Valentinus and Ebion.
sources.answer: By persuasion, not violence. Though the apostasy unjustly seized us, who belonged by nature to God, the Word, being just and a God of counsel, reclaimed his own property righteously and without violence. In this way justice was not infringed and God's ancient handiwork was not destroyed.
sources.quote: not by violent means, as the [apostasy] had obtained dominion over us at the beginning, when it insatiably snatched away what was not its own, but by means of persuasion, as became a God of counsel
sources.raw_question: Did Christ the Word redeem humanity from the apostasy by force or by persuasion, and why?

question: Is the Athanasian Creed's way of speaking ('this eternal, and that eternal, yet not two eternals but one eternal') coherent?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 9: Whether the divine attributes, Omniscience, Ubiquity, &c. thosé individual attributes, can be communicated without the divine essence, from which they are insep
sources.answer: Yes. Dr. Clarke's own hypothesis, on which God's substance has distinct substrata (parts) united and not existing separately, forces the same manner of speaking: this substance and that substance, yet one substance. The Trinitarians have better reason for such language, since the Persons have no separate existence and are more closely united by common essential attributes, being equally present everywhere.
sources.quote: this is being, and that being; and yet not two beings, but one being: this eternal, and that eternal; and yet not two eternals, but one eternal. I might go on almost the length of an Athanasian Creed.
sources.raw_question: Is the Athanasian Creed's way of speaking ('this eternal, and that eternal, yet not two eternals but one eternal') coherent?

question: How is all being ultimately divided, and where does uncreated being fall in that division?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He has no right to assert a greater and less in the Divine being. A systematic statement of the teaching of the Church.
sources.answer: All being divides first into the Intelligible and the Sensible. The Apostle calls these 'that which is seen' and 'that which is not seen.' Reason further divides the unseen, intelligible world into the uncreate and the created. The uncreate is what effects creation, and the created owes its origin and its force to the uncreate.
sources.quote: Reason again divides this “which is not seen” into the uncreate and the created, inferentially comprehending it: the uncreate being that which effects the Creation, the created that which owes its origin and its force to the uncreate.
sources.raw_question: How is all being ultimately divided, and where does uncreated being fall in that division?

question: Can one and the same prophet speak both from a Spirit of truth and light and from a spirit of ignorance and error?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXV.—A refutation of those who allege that the prophets uttered some predictions under the inspiration of the highest, others from the Demiurge. Disagreements of the Valentinians among themselves with regard to these same predictions.
sources.answer: No. It is impossible for perfection and defect, knowledge and ignorance, truth and error, light and darkness to exist in one and the same being. The prophets preached the word of the Lord from one God and proclaimed the advent of his Son.
sources.quote: how can it be, that in one and the same being there exists perfection and defect, knowledge and ignorance, error and truth, light and darkness?
sources.raw_question: Can one and the same prophet speak both from a Spirit of truth and light and from a spirit of ignorance and error?

question: Does the Lord's saying about new wine and old wineskins refute the claim that the Demiurge's prophets spoke truths of the Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXV.—A refutation of those who allege that the prophets uttered some predictions under the inspiration of the highest, others from the Demiurge. Disagreements of the Valentinians among themselves with regard to these same predictions.
sources.answer: Yes. If the prophets were sent by an inferior Demiurge, they could not have uttered the new things of the Pleroma, because the Lord declares that new wine cannot be put into old bottles. The Gnostics must therefore either reject the prophets altogether or accept that the prophets came from the one God.
sources.quote: let them be convinced by our Lord, when He declares that new wine cannot be put into old bottles
sources.raw_question: Does the Lord's saying about new wine and old wineskins refute the claim that the Demiurge's prophets spoke truths of the Pleroma?

question: What is meant by 'the spirit of Elias' in which John came, and by Moses' spirit being put upon the elders?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Father and the Son the Only Beginning (Principium) of the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: Both refer to the Holy Spirit. 'The spirit of Elias' is the Holy Spirit whom Elijah received. The Lord's words to Moses, 'I will take of thy spirit', mean that God would give the elders of the same Holy Spirit he had already given Moses.
sources.quote: by the spirit of Elias is meant the Holy Spirit, whom Elias received
sources.raw_question: What is meant by 'the spirit of Elias' in which John came, and by Moses' spirit being put upon the elders?

question: Does Psalm 103:8 ('The Lord is full of compassion and mercy') show that names of God can be derived from His works and arise in time?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: Yes.
