These names indicate His operations, not His nature; and since pity requires an object and sin entered after man, the exercise of pity and the name derived from it came after man. Thus David rightly applied to God names drawn from knowledge of His works, and Eunomius cannot convict him of error.
sources.quote: The exercise, therefore, of pity, and the name itself, came after man.
sources.raw_question: Does Psalm 103:8 ('The Lord is full of compassion and mercy') show that names of God can be derived from His works and arise in time?

question: Does Paul's claim that he was made an apostle and received the Gospel from Jesus Christ, not from man, support Christ's divinity?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Truth is Proved from the Sacred Writings of the New Covenant.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul sets Jesus Christ apart from men as the source of his apostleship and of his Gospel. This shows that Christ is more than man, and so Christ is reasonably held to be God.
sources.quote: the same apostle declares that he was ordained “an apostle not by men, nor of man, but by Jesus Christ;”
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's claim that he was made an apostle and received the Gospel from Jesus Christ, not from man, support Christ's divinity?

question: What does the "baptism with the Holy Ghost and with fire" in John the Baptist's words mean?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Reply to the suggested objection that we are baptized “into water.” Also concerning baptism.
sources.answer: The baptism of fire means the trial at the judgment. Christ's baptism is with the Holy Ghost, set in contrast to John's baptism with water. The fire is the testing of every man's work at the last day, as Paul teaches.
sources.quote: Here He calls the trial at the judgment the baptism of fire, as the apostle says, “The fire shall try every man’s work, of what sort it is.”
sources.raw_question: What does the "baptism with the Holy Ghost and with fire" in John the Baptist's words mean?

question: Why do human beings, even saints who know God's goodness, feel dread and terror at God's presence?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Because of sin. Adam had no thought of hiding himself from God until he had sinned. Guilt on the conscience, together with the common notion that God is a righteous avenger of sin, fills people with horror at his presence. They fear he has come to call their sins to remembrance.
sources.quote: The dread and terror of God entered by sin; Adam had not the least thought of hiding himself until he had sinned.
sources.raw_question: Why do human beings, even saints who know God's goodness, feel dread and terror at God's presence?

question: Can anyone share God's own end, the advancement of his glory, apart from Jesus Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. Two cannot walk together unless they aim at the same end. God's end is the advancement of his own glory, and no one can aim at this except in the Lord Jesus. So the whole wisdom of walking with God is hidden in Christ and can be obtained from him alone.
sources.quote: The end of God is the advancement of his own glory; none can aim at this end, but only in the Lord Jesus.
sources.raw_question: Can anyone share God's own end, the advancement of his glory, apart from Jesus Christ?

question: Is the Trinity itself the one Lord God of whom it is said "Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and Him only shalt thou serve"?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the Fathers, or Any One Person of the Trinity. The Appearing of God to Adam. Of the Same Appearance. The Vision to Abraham.
sources.answer: Yes. Augustine treats the Trinity as the one God to whom this command refers, so "Lord" can denote the whole Trinity and not only a single person.
sources.quote: or God Himself the Trinity, of which one God it is said, “Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and Him only shall thou serve.”
sources.raw_question: Is the Trinity itself the one Lord God of whom it is said "Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and Him only shalt thou serve"?

question: Does Lot's bowing to the ground before the two visitors prove he knew them to be angels of God rather than men?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Appearance to Lot is Examined.
sources.answer: Not necessarily. Lot offers them hospitality and food as though they needed human help, which suggests he may have taken them for men; they were honorably called lords perhaps because they were thought to be men. Augustine leaves the matter partly open and moves on to his main point.
sources.quote: Why, then, is both hospitality and food offered to them, as though they wanted such human succor?
sources.raw_question: Does Lot's bowing to the ground before the two visitors prove he knew them to be angels of God rather than men?

question: If the two visitors to Lot represent two persons of the Trinity addressed as one Lord, which two persons are most fittingly understood?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The equality of the Trinity maintained against objections drawn from those texts which speak of the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. > The Appearance to Lot is Examined.
sources.answer: Most suitably the Son and the Holy Spirit. The visitors said of themselves that they were sent, and Scripture speaks of the Son and the Holy Spirit as sent, but nowhere says that the Father was sent.
sources.quote: The last, perhaps, is the more suitable; for they said of themselves that they were sent, which is that which we say of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For we find nowhere in the Scriptures that the Father was sent.
sources.raw_question: If the two visitors to Lot represent two persons of the Trinity addressed as one Lord, which two persons are most fittingly understood?

question: Why could Christ alone rise from the dead in integrity when all other descendants of Adam remained dead?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: Because, being God, he became man. Others merely born of Adam died and death reigned over them, but he is the Second Man from heaven, since the Word descended and was made flesh; therefore he was not held under death and quickens all by his own power.
sources.quote: To man it was not possible to succeed in this; for death belongs to man; wherefore, the Word, being God, became flesh, that, being put to death in the flesh, He might quicken all men by His own power.
sources.raw_question: Why could Christ alone rise from the dead in integrity when all other descendants of Adam remained dead?

question: Can the nature or being of an agent be defined from the works or energies it produces?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > He falsely imagines that we can have an unalterable series of harmonious natures existing side by side.
sources.answer: No. Showing that something acts does not tell us what the acting principle itself is. Learning that a mason builds a house does not teach that man is risible. Pointing to sand or chaff blown about does not explain the nature of the wind. Defining an entity by its products is foreign to the question.
sources.quote: What ground, then, has he for attempting to explain beings by their energies, and making the definition of an entity out of the resultants of that entity.
sources.raw_question: Can the nature or being of an agent be defined from the works or energies it produces?

question: Was the temple at Jerusalem built at the direction of the true God, the Father of our Lord, rather than an inferior creator-being?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXV.—The fraud, pride, and tyrannical kingdom of Antichrist, as described by Daniel and Paul.
sources.answer: Yes. Speaking in his own person, Paul calls it 'the temple of God.' The apostles, when speaking for themselves, call no one God except Him who truly is God, the Father of our Lord. So the temple was built by the true God's direction, and it is in this temple that Antichrist will sit.
sources.quote: no one is termed God by the apostles when speaking for themselves, except Him who truly is God, the Father of our Lord, by whose directions the temple which is at Jerusalem was constructed
sources.raw_question: Was the temple at Jerusalem built at the direction of the true God, the Father of our Lord, rather than an inferior creator-being?

question: In how many senses can the term 'word' be used of what is in the mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > Whether Only Knowledge that is Loved is the Word of the Mind.
sources.answer: In three senses. First, words that occupy time by their syllables, whether spoken aloud or only thought. Second, anything known that is imprinted on the mind and can be brought forth from memory and defined, even if disliked. Third, and most properly, what the mind conceives and likes.
sources.quote: For those are called words in one way, which occupy spaces of time by their syllables, whether they are pronounced or only thought; and in another way, all that is known is called a word imprinted on the mind
sources.raw_question: In how many senses can the term 'word' be used of what is in the mind?

question: Can knowledge of things we hate, such as vices, still be a word of the mind joined with love?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > Whether Only Knowledge that is Loved is the Word of the Mind.
sources.answer: Yes. When we rightly dislike and censure evil things, we approve and like the censure itself, and so it becomes a word. What displeases us is the vice itself, not the knowledge of it. Defining intemperance belongs to the art of morals and is approved, just as knowing what a solecism is belongs to the art of speaking.
sources.quote: Nor is it the knowledge of vices that displeases us, but the vices themselves. For I like to know and define what intemperance is; and this is its word.
sources.raw_question: Can knowledge of things we hate, such as vices, still be a word of the mind joined with love?

question: Can God be conceived as any changeable spiritual thing, such as angels or all angelic spirits united into one?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Every Corporeal Conception Must Be Rejected, in Order that It May Be Understood How God is Truth.
sources.answer: No. Nothing changeable, even in spiritual things, may be thought of God. Angels animating celestial bodies, or thousands of them gathered into one, are still not God. Neither are such spirits conceived without bodies.
sources.quote: But also in spiritual things let nothing changeable that may have occurred to the mind be thought of God.
sources.raw_question: Can God be conceived as any changeable spiritual thing, such as angels or all angelic spirits united into one?

question: Is it useful to know what God is not before we know what God is?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Every Corporeal Conception Must Be Rejected, in Order that It May Be Understood How God is Truth.
sources.answer: Yes. When rising toward God it is no small step in knowledge to know what He is not before we can know what He is. He is neither earth nor heaven, nor anything seen or unseen in the heavens. He is not even the sun's light magnified without limit in the imagination.
sources.quote: it is a step towards no small knowledge, if, before we can know what God is, we can already know what He is not.
sources.raw_question: Is it useful to know what God is not before we know what God is?

question: In what sense is God called light and truth, and how can the mind grasp this?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > Every Corporeal Conception Must Be Rejected, in Order that It May Be Understood How God is Truth.
sources.answer: God is light not as bodily eyes see light but as the heart sees, when He is called truth. The mind glimpses this in the first flash on hearing 'Truth', before corporeal images and phantasms intrude. We cannot remain there, because the stains of appetite and the errors of our wandering drag us back to earthly things.
sources.quote: For it is written that “God is light;” not in such way as these eyes see, but in such way as the heart sees, when it is said, He is truth [reality].
sources.raw_question: In what sense is God called light and truth, and how can the mind grasp this?

question: Can faith save without love, given that even the devils believe?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > No Gift of God is More Excellent Than Love.
sources.answer: No. Faith can exist without love, but it cannot profit without it. Paul commends only the faith that works by love, which distinguishes it from the faith by which the devils believe and tremble.
sources.quote: faith itself is only rendered profitable by love, since faith without love can indeed exist, but cannot profit.
sources.raw_question: Can faith save without love, given that even the devils believe?

question: Does 'the Spirit' in 1 Thessalonians 5:19 ('Quench not the Spirit') refer to the Holy Ghost himself, or to spiritual gifts in others or the natural light in our hearts?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter VII.
sources.answer: It refers to the Holy Ghost himself, though considered in his operations rather than his person. Taking it as others' spiritual gifts would make it merely repeat verse 20, 'Despise not prophesying.' Taking it as an inner light fails because that light is nowhere absolutely called 'The Spirit.'
sources.quote: It is the Holy Ghost himself that is here intended, not immediately, in respect of his person (in which regard he is said to be grieved, which is a personal affection); but in respect of his motions, actings, and operations.
sources.raw_question: Does 'the Spirit' in 1 Thessalonians 5:19 ('Quench not the Spirit') refer to the Holy Ghost himself, or to spiritual gifts in others or the natural light in our hearts?

question: Did Eusebius apply the highest title 'Maker of all things' (ποιητὴς τῶν ὅλων) to the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 11: Whether if the Doctor means by divine powers, powers given by God (wn the same sense as angelical powers are divine powers) only in ὦ higher degree than are giv
sources.answer: Yes. Eusebius, whom the opponent cites in his favour, applies the title ποιητὴς τῶν ὅλων to the Son no less than three times, as Irenaeus did before him; and all the Fathers, by interpreting Gen. 1:26 of Father and Son jointly, implicitly said the same.
sources.quote: he applies the title of ποιητὴς τῶν ὅλων, (the highest which you think the Father himself can have,) to the Son, no less than thrice
sources.raw_question: Did Eusebius apply the highest title 'Maker of all things' (ποιητὴς τῶν ὅλων) to the Son?

question: Was God bound to take the human nature of the Mediator from Adam's race, or could he have assumed manhood from some other source?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Why the Son of God Took Man Upon Himself from the Race of Adam, and from a Virgin.
sources.answer: God could have done otherwise, but judged it better to take it from Adam's race. Just as he created Adam without deriving him from anyone else's race, he could have created another man to conquer the devil. Yet it was more fitting that the enemy of the human race be conquered by a man from the very race he had conquered.
sources.quote: But God judged it better both to take upon Him man through whom to conquer the enemy of the human race, from the race itself that had been conquered
sources.raw_question: Was God bound to take the human nature of the Mediator from Adam's race, or could he have assumed manhood from some other source?

question: Why was Christ conceived of a virgin, without carnal concupiscence?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Why the Son of God Took Man Upon Himself from the Race of Adam, and from a Virgin.
sources.answer: So that he would inherit from the first man only the origin of the race and not its guilt. Original sin is passed on through the concupiscence by which other men are conceived. The Virgin conceived by faith, with no lust involved. So Christ was born without sin, as the remedy for corruption, and the devil found in him nothing deserving death.
sources.quote: so that that which was born from the root of the first man might derive only the origin of race, not also of guilt
sources.raw_question: Why was Christ conceived of a virgin, without carnal concupiscence?

question: Could the gifts of redemption through the Mediator exist unless the Word had been made flesh?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Why the Son of God Took Man Upon Himself from the Race of Adam, and from a Virgin.
sources.answer: No. These great gifts could not exist unless the Word had been made flesh. They include the example of obedience, the conquest of death, and freedom from guilt. Only one who was both God and man could be the sinless Mediator who conquers the devil from within the conquered race.
sources.quote: These so great gifts of God, and whatever else there are, which it is too long for us now upon this subject both to inquire and to discuss, could not exist unless the Word had been made flesh.
sources.raw_question: Could the gifts of redemption through the Mediator exist unless the Word had been made flesh?

question: Why is God the chief good, incapable of increase or diminution?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How God May Be Known to Be the Chief Good. The Mind Does Not Become Good Unless by Turning to God.
sources.answer: Because God is simple good, nothing other than the good itself, not good by participation in something else. Only that which is good from some other good can be diminished or increased; hence the good itself is the supreme and unchangeable good.
sources.quote: This is truth, and simple good: for it is nothing else than the good itself, and for this reason also the chief good. For no good can be diminished or increased, except that which is good from some other good.
sources.raw_question: Why is God the chief good, incapable of increase or diminution?

question: Is God, the supreme good, far from us, given that we depend on him for our being?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He advances reasons to show not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but that neither are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor any two together in the same Trinity anything greater than one, nor all three together anything greater than each singly. He also intimates that the nature of God may be understood from our understanding of truth, from our knowledge of the supreme good, and from our implanted love of righteousness; but above all, that our knowledge of God is to be sought through love, in which he notices a trio of things which contains a trace of the Trinity. > How God May Be Known to Be the Chief Good. The Mind Does Not Become Good Unless by Turning to God.
sources.answer: No. The good by which we exist is not far from any of us, for in it we live, move and have our being; it is that by which we are and in whose absence we could not be at all.
sources.quote: This good then is not far from every one of us: for in it we live, and move, and have our being.
sources.raw_question: Is God, the supreme good, far from us, given that we depend on him for our being?

question: Does Christ ever manifest himself to believers immediately, apart from the ordinary means of grace (ordinances), and if so to whom?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: Yes, but only to those who wait for him in his ordinances. Christ sometimes honours his immediate, absolute actings, so that his appearing may plainly be of grace, though ordinarily he crowns his ordinances. Owen knows of no promise that he will do this for those who despise the ordinances: he may meet men unexpectedly in his way, but never outside it.
sources.quote: Christ often manifests himself immediately, and out of ordinances, to them that wait for him in them; — that he will do so to them that despise them, I know not.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ ever manifest himself to believers immediately, apart from the ordinary means of grace (ordinances), and if so to whom?

question: What does the bride's holding Christ and not letting him go in Song of Solomon 3:4 signify about the believer's communion with Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: It signifies faith laying fast hold on Christ and love refusing to part with him. After communion is restored, the soul grasps Christ by faith, since 'to hold fast' (κρατεῖν) is an act of faith. In the vehemence of its love it refuses to let him go and seeks to keep him in the ordinances of the church, its 'mother's house'. All of this shows the greatest delight the soul is capable of.
sources.quote: the soul lays fast hold on him by faith (κρατεῖν, “to hold fast,” is an act of faith), refuses to part with him any more, in vehemency of love, — tries to keep him in ordinances in the house of its mother, the church of God
sources.raw_question: What does the bride's holding Christ and not letting him go in Song of Solomon 3:4 signify about the believer's communion with Christ?

question: Does the phrase 'the lower parts of the earth' in Ephesians 4:9 refer to this present world?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXI.—The preservation of our bodies is confirmed by the resurrection and ascension of Christ: the souls of the saints during the intermediate period are in a state of expectation of that time when they shall receive their perfect and consummated glory.
sources.answer: No. It refers to the realm of the dead, where Christ tarried until the third day. Christ observed the law of the dead so that he might become the first-begotten from the dead. Those who read 'the lower parts' as this world, so that their inner man rises straight to a super-celestial place, are confounded by Christ's actual descent and bodily resurrection.
sources.quote: how must these men not be put to confusion, who allege that “the lower parts” refer to this world of ours, but that their inner man, leaving the body here, ascends into the super-celestial place?
sources.raw_question: Does the phrase 'the lower parts of the earth' in Ephesians 4:9 refer to this present world?

question: Do the souls of believers go directly to heaven at death, or do they await the bodily resurrection?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXXI.—The preservation of our bodies is confirmed by the resurrection and ascension of Christ: the souls of the saints during the intermediate period are in a state of expectation of that time when they shall receive their perfect and consummated glory.
sources.answer: They await the resurrection. Disciples follow their Master, who did not fly at once to heaven but went where the souls of the dead were, rose bodily, and then was taken up. So the souls of the disciples go to an invisible place allotted by God until the resurrection. Then they receive their bodies and come, bodily, into God's presence.
sources.quote: the souls of His disciples also, upon whose account the Lord underwent these things, shall go away into the invisible place allotted to them by God, and there remain until the resurrection, awaiting that event
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics, and some orthodox influenced by them
sources.raw_question: Do the souls of believers go directly to heaven at death, or do they await the bodily resurrection?

question: Is it adequate to describe the Holy Spirit's role toward Christian combatants as merely 'cheering on those who are contending'?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book II > Lastly he displays at length the folly of Eunomius, who at times speaks of the Holy Spirit as created, and as the fairest work of the Son, and at other times confesses, by the operations attributed to Him, that He is God, and thus ends the book.
sources.answer: No. Such language degrades the Spirit to the rank of a spectator or attendant who neither determines the contest, awards the victory, nor contends, but merely wishes the athlete well. In truth the Spirit of power strengthens the combatants and distributes His gifts, dividing to every man severally as He will, as Paul's struggle against principalities and powers requires.
sources.quote: while the Spirit of power does not strengthen the combatants nor distribute to them His gifts, “dividing to every man severally as He will,” but His influence is limited to cheering on those who are engaged.
sources.raw_question: Is it adequate to describe the Holy Spirit's role toward Christian combatants as merely 'cheering on those who are contending'?

question: Does God exercise providence over the world, so that creatures can come to know Him as their ruler and Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXV.—This world is ruled by the providence of one God, who is both endowed with infinite justice to punish the wicked, and with infinite goodness to bless the pious, and impart to them salvation.
sources.answer: Yes. God exercises providence over all things, gives counsel, and is present with those who attend to discipline. Because the things governed have understanding derived from His providence, they should know their ruler; hence even some Gentiles, moved by His providence, called the Maker of the universe the Father who arranges the affairs of the world.
sources.quote: God does, however, exercise a providence over all things, and therefore He also gives counsel; and when giving counsel, He is present with those who attend to moral discipline.
sources.raw_question: Does God exercise providence over the world, so that creatures can come to know Him as their ruler and Father?

question: Does 'who only doeth wondrous things' (Psalm 72:18) mean the Father alone works wonders, excluding the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the Father. Not Only the Father, But the Trinity, is Affirmed to Be Immortal. All Things are Not from the Father Alone, But Also from the Son. That the Holy Spirit is Very God, Equal with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. The Son says that whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. He also says that the Son, like the Father, raises and quickens the dead, the greatest of wonders. So 'only' here means the one only true God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: How, then, does the Father alone “do wondrous things,” when these words allow us to understand neither the Father only, nor the Son only, but assuredly the one only true God, that is, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit?
sources.raw_question: Does 'who only doeth wondrous things' (Psalm 72:18) mean the Father alone works wonders, excluding the Son?

question: Is the alternation of day and night produced by some impersonal Nature rather than by God?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That God is the Founder of All Things, Their Lord and Parent, is Proved from the Holy Scriptures.
sources.answer: No. In saying "I am the Lord, who made the light and created the darkness," God teaches that no vague Nature is the artificer of the vicissitudes of nights and days. Rather we must recognise God as their Creator.
sources.quote: that we might deem not that some Nature,—what I know not,—was the artificer of those vicissitudes whereby nights and days are controlled, but might rather, as is more true, recognise God as their Creator.
sources.raw_question: Is the alternation of day and night produced by some impersonal Nature rather than by God?

question: Why is baptism performed with three immersions and three invocations?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Reply to the suggested objection that we are baptized “into water.” Also concerning baptism.
sources.answer: So that the type of death, the burial with Christ, may be fully figured, and so that through the tradition of divine knowledge, the invocation of Father, Son and Spirit, the souls of the baptized may be enlightened.
sources.quote: In three immersions, then, and with three invocations, the great mystery of baptism is performed, to the end that the type of death may be fully figured
sources.raw_question: Why is baptism performed with three immersions and three invocations?

question: How does the prophecy that he 'shall wash His garment in wine, and His clothing in the blood of the grape' show both Christ's humanity and his divinity?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > That the Same Divine Majesty is Again Confirmed in Christ by Other Scriptures.
sources.answer: The garment and clothing are the flesh and body of the Word, washed in blood through his passion. Because what is washed is flesh, he is shown to be man. Because the one who washes is the Word, who took up the garment in order to wash it, he is shown to be God.
sources.quote: Whence, if indeed He is washed, He is man, because the garment which is washed is the flesh; but He who washes is the Word of God, who, in order that He might wash the garment, was made the taker-up of the garment.
sources.raw_question: How does the prophecy that he 'shall wash His garment in wine, and His clothing in the blood of the grape' show both Christ's humanity and his divinity?

question: Is it valid to infer that terms which share a meaning in one respect must share it in every respect?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book I > Several ways of controverting his quibbling syllogisms.
sources.answer: No. Gregory calls this a 'frigid and feeble paralogism.' One thing can carry two ideas at once, as a loaf is both made of flour and food, or as a man is both human and someone's father. Granting one meaning does not exclude the other.
sources.quote: that “that which has a common meaning, in one single point, with something else retains that community of meaning in every possible point;” and with this he takes their shallow intelligences by storm.
sources.raw_question: Is it valid to infer that terms which share a meaning in one respect must share it in every respect?

question: Is the God who sent John the Baptist to testify to the Light (Christ) the same God who made heaven and earth?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: Yes. John was sent by the God whose angel Gabriel announced his birth, the God who promised through the prophets to send His messenger before the face of His Son in the spirit and power of Elijah. Elijah himself confessed that he served the Maker of heaven and earth. So John was sent by the Creator of this world. This refutes the heretics, who claim the Demiurge was ignorant of the higher Power to whom John bore witness.
sources.quote: John, therefore, having been sent by the founder and maker of this world, how could he testify of that Light, which came down from things unspeakable and invisible? For all the heretics have decided that the Demiurge was ignorant of that Power above him
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who distinguish the Demiurge from the higher God
sources.raw_question: Is the God who sent John the Baptist to testify to the Light (Christ) the same God who made heaven and earth?

question: Why did Christ call John the Baptist 'more than a prophet', and does this show that prophets and apostles come from one God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: John was more than a prophet because he both foretold Christ's coming, as the other prophets did, and actually saw Him, pointed Him out, and persuaded many to believe in Him. He therefore held the place of both prophet and apostle. Both offices come from one and the same God.
sources.quote: so that he did himself hold the place of both prophet and apostle. For this is to be more than a prophet, because, “first apostles, secondarily prophets;” but all things from one and the same God Himself.
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ call John the Baptist 'more than a prophet', and does this show that prophets and apostles come from one God?

question: What do Christ's miracles of turning water into wine and multiplying loaves show about the relation between the Creator and the Father of Jesus?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St. John’s Gospel. The Gospels are four in number, neither more nor less. Mystic reasons for this.
sources.answer: They show that the God who made the earth and the waters is the same God who, through His Son, gave food and drink to mankind. Christ could have supplied food and wine without any created substance. He chose instead to work through created things such as bread and water. In this way the Incomprehensible acted through the comprehensible and the Invisible through the visible.
sources.quote: showing that the God who made the earth, and commanded it to bring forth fruit, who established the waters, and brought forth the fountains, was He who in these last times bestowed upon mankind, by His Son, the blessing of food and the favour of drink
sources.raw_question: What do Christ's miracles of turning water into wine and multiplying loaves show about the relation between the Creator and the Father of Jesus?

question: Does the diversity and apparent opposition among created things imply that they come from several different creators or gods?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXV.—God is not to be sought after by means of letters, syllables, and numbers; necessity of humility in such investigations.
sources.answer: No. Like the many opposite notes of a lyre that together make one melody, the varied parts of creation are harmonized into one whole, which proves a single artist. The lover of truth should not suppose one author made one part and another another, but should hold that one and the same God formed all things, displaying His judgment, goodness and wisdom.
sources.quote: nor should he imagine that one was due to one artist and author, and another to another, nor that one person fitted the treble, another the bass, and yet another the tenor strings; but he should hold that one and the same person [formed the whole]
sources.raw_question: Does the diversity and apparent opposition among created things imply that they come from several different creators or gods?

question: When one thing is given several names (such as heaven and firmament, or earth and dry land), are those names empty words, or do they signify real distinct properties of a single nature?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They signify real properties. Most things are not simple, so one word cannot take in everything they involve. Speech therefore gives a separate name to each power or quality observed in the thing. Calling fire bright or consuming is not merely naming it, because these words denote qualities physically inherent in it. In the same way, 'heaven' and 'firmament' each pick out a different characteristic of one nature.
sources.quote: And one cannot say that only a name has been given to fire when it is spoken of as bright, or consuming, or anything else that we observe it to be. For such words denote qualities physically inherent in it.
sources.raw_question: When one thing is given several names (such as heaven and firmament, or earth and dry land), are those names empty words, or do they signify real distinct properties of a single nature?

question: What does the rescue of Jeremiah from the pit by the Ethiopian Abdemelech signify about the Jews and the Gentiles?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter X. Being about to prove that the will, the calling, and the commandment of the Trinity is one, St. Ambrose shows that the Spirit called the Church exactly as the Father and the Son did, and proves this by the selection of SS. Paul and Barnabas, and especially by the mission of St. Peter to Cornelius. And by the way he points out how in the Apostle's vision the calling of the Gentiles was shadowed forth, who having been before like wild beasts, now by the operation of the Spirit lay aside that wildness. Then having quoted other passages in support of this view, he shows that in the case of Jeremiah cast into a pit by Jews, and rescued by Abdemelech, is a type of the slighting of the Holy Spirit by the Jews, and of His being honoured by the Gentiles.
sources.answer: It is a figure of how the Gentiles honour the word of prophecy, and with it the Spirit who spoke it, while the Jews had slighted it. The Jews cast the prophet into the pit, and no Jew drew him out. The Ethiopian represents the Gentiles, black through sin but made comely through grace, who raise from the mire the word of prophecy that the Jews had thrust down. The rags used in the rescue signify the bad and good alike who were called to the marriage feast.
sources.quote: we, sinners of the Gentiles, black beforehand through our transgressions, and aforetime fruitless, raised from the depth the word of prophecy which the Jews had thrust down
sources.raw_question: What does the rescue of Jeremiah from the pit by the Ethiopian Abdemelech signify about the Jews and the Gentiles?

question: Does the biblical practice of calling heaven, earth, stones or angels as witnesses mean these things share divine rank?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > Statement of the reason why in the writings of Paul the angels are associated with the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: No. Those entrusted with souls provide witnesses of whatever kind, to produce at a future judgment. Moses, Isaiah and Jeremiah called on heaven and earth, and Joshua even set up a stone. Such summoning meets the need of the moment and says nothing about the nature of the witness.
sources.quote: In this manner they who have been entrusted with the stewardship of souls provide witnesses, whatever they may be, so as to produce them at some future day.
sources.raw_question: Does the biblical practice of calling heaven, earth, stones or angels as witnesses mean these things share divine rank?

question: Does God's providence extend even to the smallest individual things, or only to the world as a whole?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > It is This God, Therefore, that the Church Has Known and Adores; And to Him the Testimony of Things as Well Visible as Invisible is Given Both at All Times and in All Forms, by the Nature Which His Providence Rules and Governs.
sources.answer: It extends to every individual thing. God embraces and contains all things, and the whole is made up of individuals, so a providence that reaches the whole must reach each part. Christ teaches that not one sparrow falls without the Father's will and that the hairs of our head are numbered. God also kept the Israelites' clothes and shoes from wearing out and kept the garments of the young men in the furnace from burning.
sources.quote: for if He embraces all things, and contains all things,—and all things, and the whole, consist of individuals,—His care will consequently extend even to every individual thing, since His providence reaches to the whole, whatever it is.
sources.raw_question: Does God's providence extend even to the smallest individual things, or only to the world as a whole?

question: What does Scripture's image of God enthroned above the Cherubim on a chariot, with crystal, wheels and eyes, signify?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > It is This God, Therefore, that the Church Has Known and Adores; And to Him the Testimony of Things as Well Visible as Invisible is Given Both at All Times and in All Forms, by the Nature Which His Providence Rules and Governs.
sources.answer: It is a figure of God presiding over the variety of His works in the created world. The living creatures that govern other things are subjected to His throne. The crystal covering is the firmament, made solid out of the waters. The wheels are the seasons that roll the world onward, and the eyes show that God's works must be watchfully contemplated. The fire in the midst points either to the coming fiery judgment or to the living, vital character of His works. David's 'chariot of God multiplied ten thousand times' means that the world, which is His chariot, is innumerable and immense.
sources.quote: Hence it is that He also sitteth above the Cherubim; that is, He presides over the variety of His works, the living creatures which hold the control over the rest being subjected to His throne
sources.raw_question: What does Scripture's image of God enthroned above the Cherubim on a chariot, with crystal, wheels and eyes, signify?

question: Do all creatures and the human mind bear witness to the one God whom the Church worships?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > It is This God, Therefore, that the Church Has Known and Adores; And to Him the Testimony of Things as Well Visible as Invisible is Given Both at All Times and in All Forms, by the Nature Which His Providence Rules and Governs.
sources.answer: Yes. The whole of nature, visible and invisible, testifies to Him. Angels adore Him, the stars, seas and lands honour Him, and all natural motions happen at His command. The whole mind of man is conscious of Him even when it does not say so.
sources.quote: to whom the universal and entire nature of things as well visible as invisible gives witness; whom angels adore, stars wonder at, seas bless, lands revere, and all things under the earth look up to; whom the whole mind of man is conscious of
sources.raw_question: Do all creatures and the human mind bear witness to the one God whom the Church worships?

question: Why did the Word, who knew all things, take on human ignorance and ask questions as a man?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Tenthly, Matthew xi. 27; John iii. 35, &c. These texts intended to preclude the Sabellian notion of the Son; they fall in with the Catholic doctrine concerning the Son; they are explained by 'so' in John v. 26. (Anticipation of the next chapter.) Again they are used with reference to our Lord's human nature; for our sake, that we might receive and not lose, as receiving in Him. And consistently with other parts of Scripture, which shew that He had the power, &c., before He received it. He was God and man, and His actions are often at once divine and human.
sources.answer: He did it for our salvation. By carrying our ignorance he might grant us knowledge of his only and true Father and of himself, who was sent for the salvation of all. No grace could be greater than this.
sources.quote: that so carrying our ignorance, He might vouchsafe to us the knowledge of His own only and true Father, and of Himself, sent because of us for the salvation of all
sources.raw_question: Why did the Word, who knew all things, take on human ignorance and ask questions as a man?

question: Can the truth of God be identified with or composed of the letters of the Greek alphabet, as Marcus taught?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XV.—Sige relates to Marcus the generation of the twenty-four elements and of Jesus. Exposure of these absurdities.
sources.answer: No. The Greek letters were received from Cadmus only recently and later supplemented by others such as Palamedes. If truth were constituted by these letters, truth would be posterior to Cadmus and to those who added letters, even posterior to Marcus himself, which is absurd, since truth did not come into existence with the alphabet.
sources.quote: Was it so, then, that until these things took place among the Greeks, truth had no existence? For, according to thee, Marcus, the body of truth is posterior to Cadmus and those who preceded him
sources.raw_question: Can the truth of God be identified with or composed of the letters of the Greek alphabet, as Marcus taught?

question: Can the Father, who contains all things and is himself uncontained, be divided into parts such as a Tetrad, Ogdoad, Decad and Duodecad?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XV.—Sige relates to Marcus the generation of the twenty-four elements and of Jesus. Exposure of these absurdities.
sources.answer: No. The Father cannot be contained but contains all things, and his nature is unspeakable and indivisible. Subdividing him into numerical groupings, or building a substance for the incorporeal out of letters, contradicts his nature, and Irenaeus calls it the highest blasphemy and grossest impiety.
sources.quote: subdividing the Father, who cannot be contained, but contains all things, into a Tetrad, and an Ogdoad, and a Decad, and a Duodecad
sources.raw_question: Can the Father, who contains all things and is himself uncontained, be divided into parts such as a Tetrad, Ogdoad, Decad and Duodecad?

question: Is it coherent to call the supreme divine power indivisible and immaterial while composing it of letters such as consonants, vowels and semi-vowels?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XV.—Sige relates to Marcus the generation of the twenty-four elements and of Jesus. Exposure of these absurdities.
sources.answer: No. Marcus calls the power incorporeal, immaterial and indivisible, yet he builds a nature and substance for it from a multitude of letters and divides it into kinds of letters. This contradicts his own description of God's simplicity.
sources.quote: And that power whom thou affirmest to be indivisible, thou dost nevertheless divide into consonants, and vowels, and semi-vowels
sources.raw_question: Is it coherent to call the supreme divine power indivisible and immaterial while composing it of letters such as consonants, vowels and semi-vowels?

question: To whom must sinners look for salvation: to a creature, or to God alone?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 1. Introduction. Preparation of heart. Our position before God.
sources.answer: To God alone. The author answers the sinner's cry "Lord, to whom shall we go?" from Isaiah. There God declares that besides him there is no just God and Saviour, and commands all the ends of the earth to look to him and be saved. Saving trust is therefore reserved for God, and this prepares the author's coming claim that Scripture moves our ultimate confidence away from every creature and onto God the Creator.
sources.quote: There is no God else beside me, a just God and a Saviour, there is none beside me. Look unto me and be ye saved all the ends of the earth, for I am God and there is none else.
sources.raw_question: To whom must sinners look for salvation: to a creature, or to God alone?

question: Does the parable of the workers in the vineyard show that one God called people both under the old dispensation and in the last times?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: Yes. The parable declares one householder calling workmen at different times, from the world's creation to the end of time. There is one vineyard, one righteousness, one dispensator, and one Spirit of God who arranges all things, and one hire, the knowledge of the Son of God, which is immortality.
sources.quote: so that there are many workmen in their generations, but only one householder who calls them together. For there is but one vineyard, since there is also but one righteousness, and one dispensator, for there is one Spirit of God who arranges all things
sources.raw_question: Does the parable of the workers in the vineyard show that one God called people both under the old dispensation and in the last times?

question: What is the 'wedding garment' required of those called to God's supper?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: It is being adorned with works of righteousness after one's calling, so that the Spirit of God may rest upon us. Those called who have not received the Holy Spirit because of wicked conduct are cast into outer darkness, as Paul speaks of being 'clothed upon' that mortality be swallowed up by immortality.
sources.quote: we ought, after our calling, to be also adorned with works of righteousness, so that the Spirit of God may rest upon us; for this is the wedding garment
sources.raw_question: What is the 'wedding garment' required of those called to God's supper?

question: Does the Israelites' taking of Egyptian goods in the Exodus serve as a type of the Christian's salvation and of the Christian's use of property gained among the Gentiles?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXX.—Refutation of another argument adduced by the Marcionites, that God directed the Hebrews to spoil the Egyptians.
sources.answer: Yes. Following the presbyter, Irenaeus treats the historical Exodus as a type of the Christian's true exodus from among the Gentiles by faith. Christians bring with them houses, clothing and goods acquired from the 'mammon of unrighteousness', and they continue to profit from pagans through trade and service. If God had not allowed this in the type, no one could be saved in its fulfilment.
sources.quote: For if God had not accorded this in the typical exodus, no one could now be saved in our true exodus; that is, in the faith in which we have been established
sources.raw_question: Does the Israelites' taking of Egyptian goods in the Exodus serve as a type of the Christian's salvation and of the Christian's use of property gained among the Gentiles?

question: Why did Christ suffer death on the sixth day, the day before the Sabbath?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXIII.—The devil is well practised in falsehood, by which Adam having been led astray, sinned on the sixth day of the creation, in which day also he has been renewed by Christ.
sources.answer: Christ died on that day in order to recapitulate in Himself the day on which Adam sinned and died. In summing up the whole human race from beginning to end, He also summed up its death. He suffered in obedience to the Father on the very day Adam died in disobedience, which was also the day on which man was created. By His passion He thus granted man a second creation, a creation out of death.
sources.quote: For by summing up in Himself the whole human race from the beginning to the end, He has also summed up its death. From this it is clear that the Lord suffered death, in obedience to His Father, upon that day on which Adam died while he disobeyed God.
sources.raw_question: Why did Christ suffer death on the sixth day, the day before the Sabbath?

question: What did the serpent's speaking in the garden reveal about the devil's knowledge of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXIII.—The devil is well practised in falsehood, by which Adam having been led astray, sinned on the sixth day of the creation, in which day also he has been renewed by Christ.
sources.answer: It revealed his ignorance of God's greatness. In the garden of God he disputed about God as though God were not present. This shows he did not grasp God's greatness or His omnipresence.
sources.quote: in the garden of God he disputed about God, as if God was not there, for he was ignorant of the greatness of God
sources.raw_question: What did the serpent's speaking in the garden reveal about the devil's knowledge of God?

question: Is the Lord who brought the flood in Noah's day and destroyed Sodom the same Lord who will judge the world at Christ's coming, or a different god from the God of the New Testament?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: He is one and the same Lord. Christ himself, warning of his coming, compares it to the days of Noah and Lot. In doing so he identifies the judge of the flood and of Sodom with the Lord who will bring the final judgment. This refutes the Gnostic separation of the Old Testament God from the Father revealed by Christ.
sources.quote: He declares one and the same Lord, who in the times of Noah brought the deluge because of man’s disobedience, and who also in the days of Lot rained fire from heaven because of the multitude of sinners among the Sodomites
sources.raw_question: Is the Lord who brought the flood in Noah's day and destroyed Sodom the same Lord who will judge the world at Christ's coming, or a different god from the God of the New Testament?

question: Are the God who judges and punishes and the God who saves and gives grace two different gods?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVI.—The prophets were sent from one and the same Father from whom the Son was sent.
sources.answer: No. The one Son of God both gives eternal life to believers and justly punishes the unfruitful. Judgment and grace flow from the same Lord, who extends equal justice to all. He gives more to some and so exacts more from them.
sources.quote: thus extending equal justice to all, and being to exact more from those to whom He gives the more
sources.raw_question: Are the God who judges and punishes and the God who saves and gives grace two different gods?

question: Does the Seraph's cleansing of Isaiah's lips (Isaiah 6:7) show that an angel can forgive sins, so that forgiving sin does not prove the Spirit's divinity?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter X. That the Spirit forgives sin is common to Him with the Father and the Son, but not with the Angels.
sources.answer: No. The Seraph does not say "I will take away" but that the coal "shall take away" sin. The fire from God's altar stands for the grace of the Spirit, and in its mystical sense for Christ, who like a coal in the flesh burned up our sins. Even if the Seraph had removed sin, he would have done so only as a minister sent by God, not by his own authority.
sources.quote: Shall take away, he says, and shall purge, not I will take away, but that fire from the altar of God, that is, the grace of the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does the Seraph's cleansing of Isaiah's lips (Isaiah 6:7) show that an angel can forgive sins, so that forgiving sin does not prove the Spirit's divinity?

question: How should the coal from the altar in Isaiah 6 and the brand plucked from the fire in Zechariah 3 be understood in relation to Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter X. That the Spirit forgives sin is common to Him with the Father and the Son, but not with the Angels.
sources.answer: They point to Christ's passion. Christ, like a coal according to the flesh, burned up our sins. The words "it hath taken away thy sins" do not mean that Christ, who did no sin, put away sins of his own. They mean that in Christ's flesh the whole human race is loosed from sin, a mystery of common redemption that the prophets revealed.
sources.quote: all men should be cleansed by the passion of Christ, Who as a coal according to the flesh burnt up our sins
sources.raw_question: How should the coal from the altar in Isaiah 6 and the brand plucked from the fire in Zechariah 3 be understood in relation to Christ?

question: Did Origen hold that the Son has the same right to religious worship as the Father?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 17: Whether, notwithstanding, worship and adoration be not equally due to Christ; and consequently, whether it must not follow, that he is the one God, and not (as
sources.answer: Yes. Origen said only the Creator of the universe is to be worshipped. He called the Son that Creator, distinguished him from creatures, and called him uncreated and immutable. He used the same word, εὐσέβεια, for worship of the Son as for worship of the Father, and spoke of worshipping Father and Son jointly as one God.
sources.quote: Origen thought the Son to have the fullest right and title to religious worship, the same that the Father himself had, as being eternal, immutable, Creator and Governor of all things.
sources.raw_question: Did Origen hold that the Son has the same right to religious worship as the Father?

question: Is our general definition of the human mind gathered by abstracting from many observed minds, or by gazing on eternal truth?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > There is One Knowledge of the Thing in the Thing Itself, and Another in Eternal Truth Itself. That Corporeal Things, Too, are to Be Judged the Rules of Eternal Truth.
sources.answer: It comes from gazing on eternal truth. We do not form generic knowledge of the mind by seeing many minds with bodily eyes and noting their resemblances. Instead, we look upon indestructible truth, and from it we define, as far as we can, what the mind ought to be according to the eternal plan.
sources.quote: we gaze upon indestructible truth, from which to define perfectly, as far as we can, not of what sort is the mind of any one particular man, but of what sort it ought to be upon the eternal plan
sources.raw_question: Is our general definition of the human mind gathered by abstracting from many observed minds, or by gazing on eternal truth?

question: Does human love for God require a cause or reason in God, unlike God's love for us?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. Our love is consequent: God must first set his heart on us, and he must be revealed to us as lovely and desirable before we can love him. The saints do not love God for nothing but for the excellency and loveliness that is in him.
sources.quote: The saints (in this sense) do not love God for nothing, but for that excellency, loveliness, and desirableness that is in him.
sources.raw_question: Does human love for God require a cause or reason in God, unlike God's love for us?

question: Why does the New Testament demand greater perfection and threaten heavier punishment than the Old if it is from the same God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVIII.—Those persons prove themselves senseless who exaggerate the mercy of Christ, but are silent as to the judgment, and look only at the more abundant grace of the New Testament; but, forgetful of the greater degree of perfection which it demands from us, they endeavour to show that there is another God beyond Him who created the world.
sources.answer: Because in the New Testament faith in God has been increased by receiving the Son of God, so that man might partake of God. Correspondingly, conduct is required to be stricter (abstaining even from evil thoughts and idle words), and the punishment of those who despise the Word's advent is increased from temporal to eternal.
sources.quote: in the New Testament, that faith of men [to be placed] in God has been increased, receiving in addition [to what was already revealed] the Son of God, that man too might be a partaker of God
sources.raw_question: Why does the New Testament demand greater perfection and threaten heavier punishment than the Old if it is from the same God?

question: Who was the God who 'came down' to see the tower of Babel in Genesis 11?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > It Is, Moreover, Proved by Moses in the Beginning of the Holy Scriptures.
sources.answer: It was the Son of God, the Word. It cannot be the Father, who is infinite, contains every place and cannot be enclosed in a place, and so can neither descend nor ascend. Nor was it an angel, since Deuteronomy says it was God who did these things. So it was the one Paul says descended and ascended above all heavens, the Son, who is Christ, and therefore Christ is God.
sources.quote: Neither, therefore, did the Father descend, as the subject itself indicates; nor did an angel command these things, as the fact shows. Then it remains that He must have descended
sources.raw_question: Who was the God who 'came down' to see the tower of Babel in Genesis 11?

question: Can sacrifices for sin, even those appointed by God in the Old Testament, make atonement with God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. In the cross of Christ God has shown that no sacrifices, even of his own appointment, could perfect those who offered them or take away sin. He therefore rejected all sacrifices for that purpose and set Christ in their place, by whom believers are justified from what the law could not justify them from.
sources.quote: God hath there discovered that no sacrifices for sin, though of his own appointment, could ever make them perfect that offered them, Heb. x. 11.
sources.raw_question: Can sacrifices for sin, even those appointed by God in the Old Testament, make atonement with God?

question: Does atonement for sin consist only in human repentance and new obedience, or can people make atonement by their own efforts?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: No. By setting forth his only Son to be a propitiation, God made plain that people can make no atonement themselves. If righteousness came by the law, Christ died in vain. He died to make atonement precisely because we were without strength.
sources.quote: by setting forth his only Son “to be a propitiation,” he leaves no doubt upon the spirits of men that in themselves they could make no atonement
sources.raw_question: Does atonement for sin consist only in human repentance and new obedience, or can people make atonement by their own efforts?

question: How do Christ and his Spirit supply the obedience to God that sinners cannot perform themselves?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: In two ways. Christ's perfect obedience is imputed to believers, and the sincere obedience they actually render is worked in them by his Spirit. Sin is condemned as to its guilt, and the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in believers through Christ's obedience. Our need of both shows that we are impotent and dead in sin.
sources.quote: So that that perfection of obedience which we have in him is imputed to us; and the sincerity that we have in obedience is from his Spirit bestowed on us.
sources.raw_question: How do Christ and his Spirit supply the obedience to God that sinners cannot perform themselves?

question: Do the hours of the parable of the labourers in the vineyard (first, third, sixth, ninth, eleventh, adding to thirty) and Christ's thirty years without public ministry reveal a divine Pleroma of thirty Æons, as the Valentinians claimed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter I.—Absurd ideas of the disciples of Valentinus as to the origin, name, order, and conjugal productions of their fancied Æons, with the passages of Scripture which they adapt to their opinions.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus treats the thirty Æons as an erroneous system. He regards this reading as the Valentinians picking out whatever they can find among the many things in Scripture and bending it to fit their own groundless speculations. Adding up the hours or counting Christ's years does not disclose hidden mysteries about the divine nature.
sources.quote: and so they proceed when they find anything in the multitude[^2669] of things contained in the Scriptures which they can adopt and accommodate to their baseless speculations.
sources.raw_question: Do the hours of the parable of the labourers in the vineyard (first, third, sixth, ninth, eleventh, adding to thirty) and Christ's thirty years without public ministry reveal a divine Pleroma of thirty Æons, as the Valentinians claimed?

question: Why does the Song of the Three Children, in calling all the works of the Lord to bless him, not include the Word or Wisdom among them?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: Because the Word is not a work nor among those who praise. The three martyrs enumerate everything in heaven and earth as works that praise, but do not say 'Bless, O Word'. The Word is praised and worshipped with the Father and confessed as God, being the Framer of the works.
sources.quote: the Word is not a work nor of those that praise, but is praised with the Father and worshipped and confessed as God, being His Word and Wisdom, and of the works the Framer.
sources.raw_question: Why does the Song of the Three Children, in calling all the works of the Lord to bless him, not include the Word or Wisdom among them?

question: When Irenaeus says the Word conversed with the patriarchs 'in a divine and glorious' way, did the Son act merely as the Father's representative or in his own proper divine character?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: He acted in his own proper divine character, as God and Son of God. Irenaeus explains that character as the Word, Framer of all things, who sits upon the cherubim and contains all things, referring to John 1:1. The Son was God before any supposed acting in the form of God as representative, and it is that antecedent character Irenaeus means.
sources.quote: is God, then acted in his own proper character, and not in the Person of the Father only, which the Doctor would infer from this passage.
sources.raw_question: When Irenaeus says the Word conversed with the patriarchs 'in a divine and glorious' way, did the Son act merely as the Father's representative or in his own proper divine character?

question: Can the theophanies to Moses prove a plurality of divine Persons if the one who appeared is taken to be only an angel or representative speaking in God's person?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 27: Whether the learned Doctor may not reasonably be supposed to say, the Fathers are on his side, with the same meaning and reserve as he pretends owr Church forms
sources.answer: No. On Clarke's principles the Jew could reply that an angel spoke in the Person of God, so the Father alone remained God. Justin's argument works only because he insists there was another Person besides the Father who was really the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
sources.quote: the Jew might reply, that it was an angel speaking in the Person of God; and that therefore the Father only was God notwithstanding. But Justin insists upon it, that there was another Person, besides the Father, who was really “God of Abraham,” &c.
sources.raw_question: Can the theophanies to Moses prove a plurality of divine Persons if the one who appeared is taken to be only an angel or representative speaking in God's person?

question: In what way is the Son God, Lord, and Angel of God's Great Counsel?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father from Everlasting, Who Was Always in the Father, is the Second Person to the Father, Who Does Nothing Without His Father's Decree; And that He is Lord, and the Angel of God's Great Counsel, to Whom the Father's Godhead is Given by Community of Substance.
sources.answer: The Son is truly God and Lord, but as begotten and born of the Father for that very purpose. He is also called an Angel, or messenger, because the Father destined him to announce the Great Counsel of God. His divinity is declared in such a way that no dissonance or inequality of divinity could make two Gods.
sources.quote: He therefore is God, but begotten for this special result, that He should be God. He is also the Lord, but born for this very purpose of the Father, that He might be Lord. He is also an Angel
sources.raw_question: In what way is the Son God, Lord, and Angel of God's Great Counsel?

question: Does God in his providence deliberately frustrate the counsels of the worldly wise for his own glory?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. God has made it a constant way of advancing his glory to mix the counsels of the wisest men with folly. They end up advising things that bring about their own disappointment and ruin. Scripture says he destroys the wisdom of the wise, gives them a spirit of giddiness, and holds their plots in derision.
sources.quote: That God hath made this a constant path towards the advancement of his own glory, even to leaven the wisdom and the counsels of the wisest of the sons of men with folly and madness
sources.raw_question: Does God in his providence deliberately frustrate the counsels of the worldly wise for his own glory?

question: If many saints, martyrs and apostles imitate God and are like the Father, why is the Son alone called the Image of the Father?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Ninthly, John x. 30; xvii. 11, &c. Arian explanation, that the Son is one with the Father in will and judgment; but so are all good men, nay things inanimate; contrast of the Son. Oneness between Them is in nature, because oneness in operation. Angels not objects of prayer, because they do not work together with God, but the Son; texts quoted. Seeing an Angel, is not seeing God. Arians in fact hold two Gods, and tend to Gentile polytheism. Arian explanation that the Father and Son are one as we are one with Christ, is put aside by the Regula Fidei, and shewn invalid by the usage of Scripture in illustrations; the true force of the comparison; force of the terms used. Force of 'in us;' force of 'as;' confirmed by S. John. In what sense we are 'in God' and His 'sons.'
sources.answer: Because the Son alone is the true and natural Image of the Father, while saints are like God only by imitation. None of them is Word, Wisdom or Only-begotten, and none dared to say 'I and the Father are One' or 'I in the Father and the Father in Me.' Of all creatures Scripture says, 'Who is like unto Thee among the gods, O Lord?'
