sources.quote: And yet no one of these is Word or Wisdom or Only-begotten Son or Image; nor did any one of them make bold to say, ‘I and the Father are One,’ or, ‘I in the Father, and the Father in Me;’
sources.raw_question: If many saints, martyrs and apostles imitate God and are like the Father, why is the Son alone called the Image of the Father?

question: What is the difference between using something and enjoying it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > That there is yet another and a more manifest trinity to be found in the mind of man, viz. in his memory, understanding, and will. > In Memory, Understanding [or Intelligence], and Will, We Have to Note Ability, Learning, and Use. Memory, Understanding, and Will are One Essentially, and Three Relatively.
sources.answer: To use is to take something up into the power of the will. To enjoy is to use with joy, not of hope but of the actual thing, resting in it as an end. So everyone who enjoys also uses. But not everyone who uses enjoys, since one may take something up for the sake of something else.
sources.quote: For to use, is to take up something into the power of the will; and to enjoy, is to use with joy, not any longer of hope, but of the actual thing.
sources.raw_question: What is the difference between using something and enjoying it?

question: Why was it necessary that the one anointed to unite man to the Holy Spirit be God rather than a creature?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: Because no originate nature could warrant this, since angels transgressed and men disobeyed. Only the Word, the Image of the Father in which we were made and whose own the Spirit is, could unite man to the Holy Ghost and free those under the curse. If He were from nothing, He would be one among others and could not be the Christ.
sources.quote: If then He was of nothing, He would not have been the Christ or Anointed, being one among others and having fellowship as the rest
sources.raw_question: Why was it necessary that the one anointed to unite man to the Holy Spirit be God rather than a creature?

question: Can a person truly prophesy without understanding what he is saying, as Caiaphas did?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In How Many Ways Things Future are Foreknown. Neither Philosophers, Nor Those Who Were Distinguished Among the Ancients, are to Be Consulted Concerning the Resurrection of the Dead.
sources.answer: Yes. Many things are foretold by a kind of instinct or inward impulse in people who do not understand them. Caiaphas did not know what he said, but because he was high priest he prophesied. God uses such unknowing speakers so that the truth sounds abroad from all sides, helping the faithful and witnessing against the ungodly.
sources.quote: Many things, too, are foretold by a kind of instinct and inward impulse of such as know them not: as Caiaphas did not know what he said, but being the high priest, he prophesied.
sources.raw_question: Can a person truly prophesy without understanding what he is saying, as Caiaphas did?

question: Why do demons sometimes speak truths about the saints and the true Mediator, and does this lend credibility to their oracles?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > In How Many Ways Things Future are Foreknown. Neither Philosophers, Nor Those Who Were Distinguished Among the Ancients, are to Be Consulted Concerning the Resurrection of the Dead.
sources.answer: It does not. The proud and deceitful powers of the air repeat truths they heard from the holy prophets or the angels. Their aim is to seduce the faithful, by means of these borrowed truths, into their own falsehoods.
sources.quote: did so with the purpose of seducing even the faithful ones of God, if they could, by these alien truths, to revolt to their own proper falsehoods
sources.raw_question: Why do demons sometimes speak truths about the saints and the true Mediator, and does this lend credibility to their oracles?

question: When Christ, the Son of God, said "Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God," how could he speak of God as "his" Lord God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXI.—Christ is the head of all things already mentioned. It was fitting that He should be sent by the Father, the Creator of all things, to assume human nature, and should be tempted by Satan, that He might fulfil the promises, and carry off a glorious and perfect victory.
sources.answer: He spoke as man. By the word of the law He pointed out the duty of man not to tempt God. Since He appeared in human form, He also declared that He Himself would not tempt the Lord His God. He made no remark on the words "If thou be the Son of God," but acknowledged His human nature, and so the humility of the man Christ overthrew the serpent's pride.
sources.quote: in regard to Himself, since He appeared in human form, [declaring] that He would not tempt the Lord his God
sources.raw_question: When Christ, the Son of God, said "Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God," how could he speak of God as "his" Lord God?

question: Does the devil's malice escape the providence of God's wisdom?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life Subdued the Mediator of Death. How the Devil Leads His Own to Despise the Death of Christ.
sources.answer: No. The most excellent wisdom of God uses both the devil's snares and his fury to bring about the salvation of the faithful. This wisdom orders all things from one end to the other and passes through all things by its purity, so nothing defiled can touch it.
sources.quote: the devil does not know how the most excellent wisdom of God makes use of both his snares and his fury to bring about the salvation of His own faithful ones
sources.raw_question: Does the devil's malice escape the providence of God's wisdom?

question: Does the angel's announcement to Mary show that the Son of the Highest and the Son of David are the same Person?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: Yes. The angel says that the one who will be called Son of the Highest will receive the throne of his father David. This acknowledges that the Son of the Highest is himself also the Son of David.
sources.quote: acknowledging that He who is the Son of the Highest, the same is Himself also the Son of David.
sources.raw_question: Does the angel's announcement to Mary show that the Son of the Highest and the Son of David are the same Person?

question: Does the worship given to the infant Jesus show that he was Lord and eternal King from birth?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XVI.—Proofs from the apostolic writings, that Jesus Christ was one and the same, the only begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man.
sources.answer: Yes. John the Baptist, still in the womb, recognized him as Lord and leapt for joy. The Magi worshipped him and bowed down to the eternal King. This shows that the child born of Mary was himself the Christ and Lord.
sources.quote: whom the Magi, when they had seen, adored, and offered their gifts [to Him], as I have already stated, and prostrated themselves to the eternal King
sources.raw_question: Does the worship given to the infant Jesus show that he was Lord and eternal King from birth?

question: According to Acts 28:25-26, was it the Holy Spirit who sent the prophet Isaiah?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXI. Isaiah was sent by the Spirit, and accordingly the same Spirit was seen by him. What is meant by the revolving wheels, and the divers wings, and how since the Spirit is proclaimed Lord of Sabaoth by the Seraphim, certainly none but impious men can deny Him this title.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul, as recorded and approved by Luke in Acts, says "Well spake the Holy Spirit through Isaiah the prophet," quoting the very commission "Go to this people" from Isaiah 6. Since the Spirit shares the kingdom with the Father and Son, nothing hinders us from understanding that the Spirit was the one by whom Isaiah was sent.
sources.quote: Since, then, He has a share in the kingdom, what hinders us from understanding that it was the Holy Spirit by Whom Isaiah was sent?
sources.raw_question: According to Acts 28:25-26, was it the Holy Spirit who sent the prophet Isaiah?

question: Is the Lord of Sabaoth whom Isaiah saw enthroned in Isaiah 6 the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXI. Isaiah was sent by the Spirit, and accordingly the same Spirit was seen by him. What is meant by the revolving wheels, and the divers wings, and how since the Spirit is proclaimed Lord of Sabaoth by the Seraphim, certainly none but impious men can deny Him this title.
sources.answer: Yes. If the Spirit sent Isaiah, as Paul states, then the Lord whom Isaiah saw on the throne and who commissioned him after Uzziah's death is the Spirit. Hence the Seraphim's cry "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Sabaoth" is addressed to the Spirit.
sources.quote: If the Spirit sent him, it is certainly the Spirit Whom, after Uzziah’s death, Isaiah saw
sources.raw_question: Is the Lord of Sabaoth whom Isaiah saw enthroned in Isaiah 6 the Holy Spirit?

question: What does Ezekiel's vision of a wheel within a wheel signify?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter XXI. Isaiah was sent by the Spirit, and accordingly the same Spirit was seen by him. What is meant by the revolving wheels, and the divers wings, and how since the Spirit is proclaimed Lord of Sabaoth by the Seraphim, certainly none but impious men can deny Him this title.
sources.answer: It signifies the grace of the two Testaments, not a bodily appearance. Life under the Law runs within life under grace, as the Law is included in grace and the true Jew (circumcised in heart) is within the Church. This also explains how the Seraphim's wings could be both still and flying.
sources.quote: The wheel, then, within a wheel is life under the Law, life under grace; inasmuch as Jews are within the Church, the Law is included in grace.
sources.raw_question: What does Ezekiel's vision of a wheel within a wheel signify?

question: If the appearances were wrought by angels, why does Scripture say "The Lord said to Moses" rather than "The angel said to Moses"?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: Because the speech is attributed to the one whose words are delivered, not to the messenger. When a crier proclaims the judge's words, the record says the judge spoke. Likewise when a prophet speaks we mean the Lord spoke, without putting the prophet aside, so "the Lord said" only indicates who spoke through the angel.
sources.quote: when the crier proclaims the words of the judge, it is not usually written in the record, so and so the crier said, but so and so the judge.
sources.raw_question: If the appearances were wrought by angels, why does Scripture say "The Lord said to Moses" rather than "The angel said to Moses"?

question: Does 'holding the Head' (Colossians 2:19) require confessing both the divinity and the true humanity of the Son of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIV.—Unless the flesh were to be saved, the Word would not have taken upon Him flesh of the same substance as ours: from this it would follow that neither should we have been reconciled by Him.
sources.answer: Yes. Holding the Head means acknowledging that the Son of God came in the flesh and that He is God, while steadfastly confessing His human nature. With this confession, backed by proofs from Scripture, the believer can easily overthrow the later-invented notions of the heretics.
sources.quote: that is, acknowledging the advent in the flesh of the Son of God, and [His] divinity (deum), and looking forward with constancy to His human nature
sources.raw_question: Does 'holding the Head' (Colossians 2:19) require confessing both the divinity and the true humanity of the Son of God?

question: What moved Christ, as mediator, to leave his glory, suffer, and carry out his saving work?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: His love for believers and the value he places on them. Owen says that everything Christ parted with, did, suffered and still does as mediator, he does because he loves his spouse and values believers. Having undertaken from eternity to bring them to God, he rejoices in this design. He pursues it through suffering and power until it is complete.
sources.quote: He parted with the greatest glory, he underwent the greatest misery, he doth the greatest works that ever were, because he loves his spouse, — because he values believers.
sources.raw_question: What moved Christ, as mediator, to leave his glory, suffer, and carry out his saving work?

question: How should God's goodness, greatness, presence, and eternity be conceived if He is neither corporeal nor changeable?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What the Author Entreats from God, What from the Reader. In God Nothing is to Be Thought Corporeal or Changeable.
sources.answer: God is to be understood without the categories of created things. He is good without quality, great without quantity, and everywhere whole yet without place. He is eternal without time, and He makes changeable things without change or passion in Himself. Whoever thinks of God this way may not find out all that He is, but takes care to think nothing of Him that He is not.
sources.quote: as good without quality, great without quantity, a creator though He lack nothing, ruling but from no position, sustaining all things without “having” them, in His wholeness everywhere, yet without place, eternal without time
sources.raw_question: How should God's goodness, greatness, presence, and eternity be conceived if He is neither corporeal nor changeable?

question: Why did Jesus tell the Scribe who confessed one God and the two great commandments that he was only 'not far from' the kingdom of God rather than already in it?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book IX
sources.answer: Because the Scribe did not know the mystery that had been accomplished. His confession of one God and his love of God and neighbour were praiseworthy and close to the Gospel, since he set them above burnt offerings. But he did not know that Christ, the Son of God, is included by His birth in the confession of the one God. So he was praised but not given possession of the kingdom.
sources.quote: But the Scribe was debarred from perfection, because he did not know the mystery which had been accomplished.
sources.raw_question: Why did Jesus tell the Scribe who confessed one God and the two great commandments that he was only 'not far from' the kingdom of God rather than already in it?

question: What does it mean that Christ 'appears in the presence of God for us' (Hebrews 9:24)?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: It means Christ, like the high priest carrying sacrificial blood into the most holy place, presents himself before God after offering himself as a sacrifice. He appears as it were to remind the Father of the engagement made to him for redeeming sinners by his blood. In this way he lays claim on our behalf to the good things his death procured, and this is a continuation of his oblation.
sources.quote: appears in the presence of God, as it were to mind him of the engagement made to him, for the redemption of sinners by his blood, and the making out the good things to them which were procured thereby
sources.raw_question: What does it mean that Christ 'appears in the presence of God for us' (Hebrews 9:24)?

question: How is each Person of the Trinity distinctly glorified in the justification and acceptance of believers?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: Each Person is glorified in his own proper work. The Father is glorified in his free love, the Son in his full purchase, and the Holy Spirit in his effectual working. This order of salvation, through Christ by one Spirit to the Father, was fixed so that the whole Trinity would be glorified.
sources.quote: And thus are both Father and Son and the Holy Spirit glorified in our justification and acceptation with God; the Father in his free love, the Son in his full purchase, and the Holy Spirit in his effectual working.
sources.raw_question: How is each Person of the Trinity distinctly glorified in the justification and acceptance of believers?

question: Do the Father's testimonies at Christ's baptism, transfiguration and passion show that Amos 4:13 ("declaring unto men His Christ") refers to the coming of Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter VI. To those who object that according to the words of Amos the Spirit is created, the answer is made that the word is there understood of the wind, which is often created, which cannot be said of the Holy Spirit, since He is eternal, and cannot be dissolved in death, or by an heretical absorption into the Father. But if they pertinaciously contend that this passage was written of the Holy Spirit, St. Ambrose points out that recourse must be had to a spiritual Interpretation, for Christ by His coming established the thunder, that is, the force of the divine utterances, and by Spirit is signified the human soul as also the flesh assumed by Christ. And since this was created by each Person of the Trinity, it is thence argued that the Spirit, Who has before been affirmed to be the Creator of all things, was the Author of the Incarnation of the Lord.
sources.answer: Yes. The prophet adds "declaring unto men His Christ" to show he spoke of Jesus' coming. The Father declared the Son at the baptism ("Thou art My beloved Son") and on the mount ("This is My beloved Son"). He declared Him again at the Passion through the darkened sun and through the centurion's confession.
sources.quote: And that you might know that he spoke of the coming down of Jesus, he added that He declared His Christ to men, for in His baptism He declared Him
sources.raw_question: Do the Father's testimonies at Christ's baptism, transfiguration and passion show that Amos 4:13 ("declaring unto men His Christ") refers to the coming of Christ?

question: How can Psalm 24's 'Lift up your gates… and the King of Glory shall come in' be said of Christ, who is Lord and Maker of heaven?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; And First, Phil. II. 9, 10. Various texts which are alleged against the Catholic doctrine: e.g. Phil. ii. 9, 10. Whether the words 'Wherefore God hath highly exalted' prove moral probation and advancement. Argued against, first, from the force of the word 'Son;' which is inconsistent with such an interpretation. Next, the passage examined. Ecclesiastical sense of 'highly exalted,' and 'gave,' and 'wherefore;' viz. as being spoken with reference to our Lord's manhood. Secondary sense; viz. as implying the Word's 'exaltation' through the resurrection in the same sense in which Scripture speaks of His descent in the Incarnation; how the phrase does not derogate from the nature of the Word.
sources.answer: The gates were never shut on him. They were shut on us, to whom paradise was closed. In a human relation, because of the flesh he bore, he is spoken of as entering like a man. In a divine relation, since the Word was God, he is called the Lord and King of Glory.
sources.quote: in a human relation, because of the flesh which He bore, it is said of Him, ‘Lift up your gates,’ and ‘shall come in,’ as if a man were entering; but in a divine relation on the other hand it is said of Him
sources.raw_question: How can Psalm 24's 'Lift up your gates… and the King of Glory shall come in' be said of Christ, who is Lord and Maker of heaven?

question: Do recurring numbers in Scripture and nature, such as the frequent appearance of five, prove the existence of corresponding divine beings like the Gnostic Aeons?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIV.—Folly of the arguments derived by the heretics from numbers, letters, and syllables.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus shows that the number five, which the Valentinians do not use, occurs just as often in Scripture and nature as their favoured numbers: five loaves, five wise virgins, five books of Moses, five senses. Anyone could gather thousands of such cases for any number. Frequency alone therefore proves nothing about divine realities, and it would be absurd to posit five Aeons or to treat the Pentad as divine. To turn God's well-ordered creation into types of things that do not exist is vain and impious.
sources.quote: nor do we consecrate the Pentad, as if it were some divine thing; nor do we strive to establish things that are untenable
sources.raw_question: Do recurring numbers in Scripture and nature, such as the frequent appearance of five, prove the existence of corresponding divine beings like the Gnostic Aeons?

question: Is the division of the year into twelve months of thirty days, and of the day into twelve hours, a type of the Valentinian Pleroma of thirty Aeons?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXIV.—Folly of the arguments derived by the heretics from numbers, letters, and syllables.
sources.answer: No. The supposed type does not match what it is said to represent. Each Aeon is a thirtieth part of the Pleroma, yet a month is a twelfth of the year. The Pleroma has three parts, but the year has four seasons. Months are not exactly thirty days, and daylight ranges from nine to fifteen hours. If these divisions had been made to signify the Aeons, they would correspond exactly.
sources.quote: It cannot therefore be held that months of thirty days each were so formed for the sake of [typifying] the Æons; for, in that case, they would have consisted precisely of thirty days
sources.raw_question: Is the division of the year into twelve months of thirty days, and of the day into twelve hours, a type of the Valentinian Pleroma of thirty Aeons?

question: Are the names God gives the stars different names, unknown to human language?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Scripture itself uses the names in common use among the Greeks, such as the Pleiads, Hesperus, Arcturus and Orion, which shows it employs ordinary human words for our instruction. It says God 'maketh' these stars, not that He names them, so the things come from God, not their names.
sources.quote: teaching us that all things whatsoever that are named among men have their origin from God—the things, not their names. For it does not say Who nameth, but “Who maketh Pleiad, and Hesperus, and Arcturus.”
sources.raw_question: Are the names God gives the stars different names, unknown to human language?

question: Does Scripture's use of names drawn from pagan mythology, such as Amalthea's horn or the Sirens, mean those names are divinely given or endorsed?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: No. Scripture freely borrows words in common human use, even from mythological fables, for the benefit of its hearers. Job names plenty after the Greek conceit of Amalthea's horn, and Isaiah represents the pleasure of hearing through the figure of the Sirens, without thereby making God the source of such names.
sources.quote: the inspired word has made use of names drawn from mythological fables, with a view to the advantage of the hearers, so here it freely makes use of the appellations given to the stars by human fancy
sources.raw_question: Does Scripture's use of names drawn from pagan mythology, such as Amalthea's horn or the Sirens, mean those names are divinely given or endorsed?

question: Did Christ's teaching in the Sermon on the Mount ("But I say unto you") overturn and oppose the Mosaic law, as Marcion's followers claimed?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIII.—Christ did not abrogate the natural precepts of the law, but rather fulfilled and extended them. He removed the yoke and bondage of the old law, so that mankind, being now set free, might serve God with that trustful piety which becometh sons.
sources.answer: No. Christ's sayings do not overturn the precepts of the past but fulfil and extend them. Forbidding lust as well as adultery, and anger as well as murder, would only be contrary to the law if he commanded something the law prohibited. Commanding abstinence even from longing after forbidden things widens the law's scope rather than destroying it.
sources.quote: For all these do not contain or imply an opposition to and an overturning of the [precepts] of the past, as Marcion’s followers do strenuously maintain; but [they exhibit] a fulfilling and an extension of them
sources.raw_question: Did Christ's teaching in the Sermon on the Mount ("But I say unto you") overturn and oppose the Mosaic law, as Marcion's followers claimed?

question: What does the righteousness that must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees consist in, and does it include faith in the Son as well as the Father?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XIII.—Christ did not abrogate the natural precepts of the law, but rather fulfilled and extended them. He removed the yoke and bondage of the old law, so that mankind, being now set free, might serve God with that trustful piety which becometh sons.
sources.answer: It includes, first, believing not only in the Father but also in His Son now revealed, because the Son leads man into fellowship and unity with God. It also means doing and not merely saying, and abstaining even from evil desires. Faith in the Son is therefore the first part of the greater righteousness of the new covenant.
sources.quote: In the first place, [we must] believe not only in the Father, but also in His Son now revealed; for He it is who leads man into fellowship and unity with God.
sources.raw_question: What does the righteousness that must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees consist in, and does it include faith in the Son as well as the Father?

question: Was the commandment given to Adam in Eden delivered by the Word, the Son of God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVII.—There is but one Lord and one God, the Father and Creator of all things, who has loved us in Christ, given us commandments, and remitted our sins; whose Son and Word Christ proved Himself to be, when He forgave our sins.
sources.answer: Yes. Adam is said to have heard the voice of the Lord God, and this voice was the Word. Therefore the same Word who gave the commandment rightly says to man in the end, "Thy sins are forgiven thee."
sources.quote: Now the commandment was given to man by the Word. For Adam, it is said, “heard the voice of the Lord God.”
sources.raw_question: Was the commandment given to Adam in Eden delivered by the Word, the Son of God?

question: Could sins against one God be truly forgiven by a different, foreign being?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVII.—There is but one Lord and one God, the Father and Creator of all things, who has loved us in Christ, given us commandments, and remitted our sins; whose Son and Word Christ proved Himself to be, when He forgave our sins.
sources.answer: No. Such a being would be neither good, nor true, nor just, because he would be giving what is not his own and snatching away the goods of another. Sins can be truly remitted only when the one against whom we sinned grants the remission himself, which he did through his Son.
sources.quote: For how can he be good, who does not give from what belongs to himself? Or how can he be just, who snatches away the goods of another?
sources.raw_question: Could sins against one God be truly forgiven by a different, foreign being?

question: Which God did the crowds glorify when Jesus healed the paralytic?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XVII.—There is but one Lord and one God, the Father and Creator of all things, who has loved us in Christ, given us commandments, and remitted our sins; whose Son and Word Christ proved Himself to be, when He forgave our sins.
sources.answer: They glorified the God proclaimed by the law and the prophets, who is the Father of our Lord. They could not have glorified an unknown Father invented by the heretics. Had Christ come from another Father, he would have made them ungrateful to the Father who sent the healing.
sources.quote: It is evident, therefore, that the Israelites glorified Him who has been proclaimed as God by the law and the prophets, who is also the Father of our Lord
sources.raw_question: Which God did the crowds glorify when Jesus healed the paralytic?

question: What is the foundation of faith from which every objection against the Son's divinity can be answered?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: Peter's confession, 'Thou art the Son of the living God.' This is the one immovable rock of faith. On it an answer can be built to every objection that perverted ingenuity or treachery may raise against the truth.
sources.quote: Thus our one immovable foundation, our one blissful rock of faith, is the confession from Peter’s mouth, Thou art the Son of the living God.
sources.raw_question: What is the foundation of faith from which every objection against the Son's divinity can be answered?

question: Is the incarnation, with its birth, wailing and cradle, unworthy of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book II
sources.answer: No. The less such condescension seems to befit God's majesty, the greater our debt for the benefit. God had nothing to gain by becoming man; the gain was ours. We were raised because he was lowered, and his shame was our glory.
sources.quote: If any man deem all this unworthy of God, the greater must he own his debt for the benefit conferred the less such condescension befits the majesty of God.
sources.raw_question: Is the incarnation, with its birth, wailing and cradle, unworthy of God?

question: Is despising all things for Christ essential to being a true disciple of Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Yes. Despising all things for Christ is the very first lesson of the gospel. Christ tested his disciples by calling them to give away all, take up the cross and follow him. Anyone who lacks this same mind and heart is none of his.
sources.quote: A despising of all things for Christ is the very first lesson of the gospel.
sources.raw_question: Is despising all things for Christ essential to being a true disciple of Christ?

question: Is the Mediator who gave the Law at Sinai true God or God only in name?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book V
sources.answer: He is true God. The Mediator was the Giver of the Law, God came down on the mountain, and the terrifying signs and Israel's fear of dying at his voice, as well as the glory transfiguring Moses' face, show a God whose nature, not merely name, is divine.
sources.quote: Enquire whether He, Who gave the Law, were not true God; for the Mediator was the Giver.
sources.raw_question: Is the Mediator who gave the Law at Sinai true God or God only in name?

question: What does Paul mean by feeding the Corinthians with milk and not meat in 1 Corinthians 3:2?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXVIII.—Why man was not made perfect from the beginning.
sources.answer: The milk is their learning of the Lord's advent as a man. The meat is the Spirit of the Father, the food of eternal life, which had not yet rested on them because of their carnality and imperfection. Paul had power to give the Spirit, since those on whom the apostles laid hands received Him, but they were not capable of receiving it.
sources.quote: ye have indeed learned the advent of our Lord as a man; nevertheless, because of your infirmity, the Spirit of the Father has not as yet rested upon you.
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean by feeding the Corinthians with milk and not meat in 1 Corinthians 3:2?

question: Does the perfection of a representation require that it possess objective reality?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. A perfect representation must have all the reality proper to a representation, but objective reality is not proper to a representation at all. A representation that acquired objective reality would cease to be a representation. This is the logical flaw in the self-consciousness argument for the Trinity.
sources.quote: A perfect representation must, of course, have all the reality proper to a representation; but objective reality is so little proper to a representation that a representation acquiring it would cease to be a representation.
sources.raw_question: Does the perfection of a representation require that it possess objective reality?

question: Does divine self-consciousness require a real hypostatic distinction between God as thinking subject and God as thought object?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. There is no reason to deny God the power of self-contemplation that every finite spirit has without its contemplating and contemplated self becoming distinct persons. The argument also tends to yield two substances, that is two Gods, rather than two persons. It also cannot account naturally for a third hypostasis, the Holy Spirit.
sources.quote: Why, however, we should deny to God the power of self-contemplation enjoyed by every finite spirit, save at the cost of the distinct hypostatizing of the contemplant and the contemplated self, it is hard to understand.
sources.raw_question: Does divine self-consciousness require a real hypostatic distinction between God as thinking subject and God as thought object?

question: Does the nature of love, as Richard of St. Victor argued, necessarily prove that God is a Trinity of lover, beloved and co-beloved?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: No. The argument's artificiality appears once its details are worked out. It is not clear that God's own all-perfect Being could not supply a satisfying object for His all-perfect love. Saying that love is by nature self-communicative and so needs an object other than self is an abuse of figurative language. Augustine's lover, loved and love remains a sympathetic analogue, not a proof.
sources.quote: And after all is said, it does not appear clear that God’s own all-perfect Being could not supply a satisfying object of His all-perfect love. To say that in its very nature love is self-communicative, and therefore implies an object other than self, seems an abuse of figurative language.
sources.raised_by_detail: Richard of St. Victor; Augustine; Valentinus
sources.raw_question: Does the nature of love, as Richard of St. Victor argued, necessarily prove that God is a Trinity of lover, beloved and co-beloved?

question: Is the Son's existence limited to His human birth from Mary, as Photinus holds?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. The Gospels show Christ to be more than the Son of Mary; He was born as God before the worlds and was the Creator of the universe. Photinus, in maintaining Christ's manhood, forgets that Christ was born as God before the ages.
sources.quote: Photinus maintains His manhood, though in maintaining it he forgets that Christ was born as God before the worlds.
sources.raw_question: Is the Son's existence limited to His human birth from Mary, as Photinus holds?

question: In allegorical readings of Genesis where the man signifies the mind, is it right to take the woman as signifying the bodily sense?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Opinion of Those Who Have Thought that the Mind Was Signified by the Man, the Bodily Sense by the Woman.
sources.answer: No. Scripture says no helpmate like to man was found among all the beasts and flying things, and only then was the woman made from his side. So the woman must signify something the beasts lack. The bodily sense is common to us and the beasts, so it is better understood as the serpent, which was more subtle than all beasts of the field.
sources.quote: I have rather thought the bodily sense should be understood to be the serpent, whom we read to have been more subtle than all beasts of the field.
sources.raised_by_detail: earlier Catholic expounders who held that the man was the mind and the woman the bodily sense
sources.raw_question: In allegorical readings of Genesis where the man signifies the mind, is it right to take the woman as signifying the bodily sense?

question: Given that the apostle calls the man the image and glory of God, how should the one human mind be ordered toward eternal things and toward temporal things?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > The Opinion of Those Who Have Thought that the Mind Was Signified by the Man, the Bodily Sense by the Woman.
sources.answer: The mind, intent on God's invisible things, should be formed by His eternity, truth and charity. Part of the same rational mind must still be directed to using changeable and corporeal things, without which this life does not go on. It must not place its end or its desire for blessedness in them. Rather, it should use temporal things with a view to attaining eternal things, passing through the former and cleaving to the latter.
sources.quote: whatever we do rationally in the using of temporal things, we may do it with the contemplation of attaining eternal things, passing through the former, but cleaving to the latter
sources.raw_question: Given that the apostle calls the man the image and glory of God, how should the one human mind be ordered toward eternal things and toward temporal things?

question: Does being 'under the law' in Galatians 4:4-5 mean only liability to the law's penalty, or also obligation to its duties?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: It includes obligation to its duties. Christ was made under the law as those were whom he redeemed, and we were under it both as liable to its penalties and as bound to all its duties. Galatians 4:21 shows that those who desired to be under the law desired to be under it in respect of obedience, not penalty.
sources.quote: Now, we were under the law, not only as obnoxious to its penalties, but as bound to all the duties of it.
sources.raw_question: Does being 'under the law' in Galatians 4:4-5 mean only liability to the law's penalty, or also obligation to its duties?

question: Is 'passive obedience' properly speaking a coherent notion?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: Not properly. Obeying is doing, and passion or suffering cannot belong to doing. It is commonly called so when men obey until they suffer, but that is not obedience in proper speech.
sources.quote: obeying is doing, to which passion or suffering cannot belong: I know it is commonly called so, when men obey until they suffer; but properly it is not so.
sources.raw_question: Is 'passive obedience' properly speaking a coherent notion?

question: What is the righteousness 'which is of God by faith' in Philippians 3:9?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VI.
sources.answer: It is Christ's obedience to the law, imputed to the believer. It is set against our own legal obedience not as something of another kind but as the same kind, excluding ours from obtaining the end that it obtains. Thus Christ is 'made to us righteousness' (1 Corinthians 1:30).
sources.quote: opposed to it, not as something in another kind, but as something in the same kind excluding that from such an end which the other obtains.
sources.raw_question: What is the righteousness 'which is of God by faith' in Philippians 3:9?

question: What does Paul mean when he says that Christ sums up (recapitulates) in himself all things in heaven and on earth, and how does this relate Christ, the Holy Spirit and humanity?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XX.—Those pastors are to be heard to whom the apostles committed the Churches, possessing one and the same doctrine of salvation; the heretics, on the other hand, are to be avoided. We must think soberly with regard to the mysteries of the faith.
sources.answer: Christ recapitulates both spiritual realities and the human order in himself. The things in heaven are spiritual, and the things on earth are the dispensation in human nature. He joins them by uniting man to the Spirit and making the Spirit dwell in man. In this way Christ becomes the head of the Spirit and gives the Spirit to be the head of man, since it is through the Spirit that we see, hear and speak.
sources.quote: by uniting man to the Spirit, and causing the Spirit to dwell in man, He is Himself made the head of the Spirit, and gives the Spirit to be the head of man
sources.raw_question: What does Paul mean when he says that Christ sums up (recapitulates) in himself all things in heaven and on earth, and how does this relate Christ, the Holy Spirit and humanity?

question: Do the images of brightness and fragrance fall short because a ray is not the same in essence as the sun, nor a scent as the ointment?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VIII > Then, after showing that the Person of the Only-begotten and Maker of things has no beginning, as have the things that were made by Him, as Eunomius says, but that the Only-begotten is without beginning and eternal, and has no community, either of essence or of names, with the creation, but is co-existent with the Father from everlasting, being, as the all-excellent Wisdom says, “the beginning and end and midst of the times,” and after making many observations on the Godhead and eternity of the Only-begotten, and also concerning souls and angels, and life and death, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: These images are not the whole teaching, and any worry about them is answered by John. John declares that the Word was in the beginning, was with God, and was God. The Son is therefore all that the Beginning is and exists before all things. This makes up for any shortcoming in the material analogies.
sources.quote: let the true Word correct his fear, Who was in the Beginning and is all that the Beginning is, and existent before all
sources.raw_question: Do the images of brightness and fragrance fall short because a ray is not the same in essence as the sun, nor a scent as the ointment?

question: Is it self-contradictory to deny that the flesh can partake of life while being alive in the body?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter III.—The power and glory of God shine forth in the weakness of human flesh, as He will render our body a participator of the resurrection and of immortality, although He has formed it from the dust of the earth; He will also bestow upon it the enjoyment of immortality, just as He grants it this short life in common with the soul.
sources.answer: Yes. Those who deny the flesh's capacity for life either confess themselves dead, which their moving and speaking refute, or confess that their whole body now partakes of life. It is like holding a sponge full of water or a burning torch and declaring the sponge cannot partake of water or the torch of fire.
sources.quote: In this very manner do those men, by alleging that they are alive and bear life about in their members, contradict themselves afterwards, when they represent these members as not being capable of [receiving] life.
sources.raw_question: Is it self-contradictory to deny that the flesh can partake of life while being alive in the body?

question: Does God's wisdom in redeeming sinners through Christ surpass his wisdom in creating the world?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: Yes. Making a fine building takes wisdom, but rebuilding a defaced one to greater beauty than before is excellence of wisdom indeed. By the design in Christ, God pardons sin, satisfies justice and fulfils the law. He also repairs his own honour and brings believers into a better condition than before the fall. So saving sinners through believing will be found a far more admirable work than creating the world from nothing.
sources.quote: To save sinners through believing, shall be found to be a far more admirable work than to create the world of nothing.
sources.raw_question: Does God's wisdom in redeeming sinners through Christ surpass his wisdom in creating the world?

question: Does condemning marriage, as the Encratites did, amount to rejecting the work of God the Creator?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XXVIII.—Doctrines of Tatian, the Encratites, and others.
sources.answer: Yes. By preaching against marriage the Encratites set aside God's original creation. They thereby indirectly blame the God who made male and female for the propagation of the human race, so the one God is both Creator and the author of marriage.
sources.quote: preached against marriage, thus setting aside the original creation of God, and indirectly blaming Him who made the male and female for the propagation of the human race
sources.raw_question: Does condemning marriage, as the Encratites did, amount to rejecting the work of God the Creator?

question: Is abstaining from animal food on principle consistent with honouring God as the maker of all things?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XXVIII.—Doctrines of Tatian, the Encratites, and others.
sources.answer: No. Those Encratites who introduced abstinence from animal food showed themselves ungrateful to God. God formed all things, so rejecting his creatures as evil dishonours their Creator.
sources.quote: Some of those reckoned among them have also introduced abstinence from animal food, thus proving themselves ungrateful to God, who formed all things.
sources.raw_question: Is abstaining from animal food on principle consistent with honouring God as the maker of all things?

question: Why is Adam called by Paul 'the figure of him that was to come'?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XXII.—Christ assumed actual flesh, conceived and born of the Virgin.
sources.answer: Adam is called a figure of Christ because the Word, the Maker of all things, planned beforehand the dispensation of the human race in connection with the Son of God. God predestined the first, animal man to be saved by the spiritual One. Since the Saviour pre-existed, what was to be saved had to be brought into existence, so that the Saviour would not exist in vain.
sources.quote: For inasmuch as He had a pre-existence as a saving Being, it was necessary that what might be saved should also be called into existence, in order that the Being who saves should not exist in vain.
sources.raw_question: Why is Adam called by Paul 'the figure of him that was to come'?

question: Does the ordered sequence of the six days of creation in Moses imply intervals or disconnected thoughts in God's working?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: No. Though each act of creation has its proper order, the creation of heaven, earth and the elements is not separated by any interval in God's working, since their preparation was completed in the eternity of God's counsel.
sources.quote: yet the creation of the heaven and earth and other elements is not separated by the slightest interval in God’s working, since their preparation had been completed in like infinity of eternity in the counsel of God.
sources.raw_question: Does the ordered sequence of the six days of creation in Moses imply intervals or disconnected thoughts in God's working?

question: Does the supreme majesty Jehovah claims in Isaiah 45:21-25, including that every knee shall bow to him, belong also to Jesus Christ?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The glory that Isaiah ascribes to the one God, besides whom there is no other, is ascribed in the New Testament to the only-begotten Son. Paul quotes this very oath of Jehovah about every knee bowing and applies it to the judgment seat of Christ. Philippians says that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow. Scripture also calls the Branch 'the Lord our righteousness,' which matches Isaiah's 'In the Lord have I righteousness.'
sources.quote: We shall all stand at the judgment seat of Christ; for it is written, as I live saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.
sources.raw_question: Does the supreme majesty Jehovah claims in Isaiah 45:21-25, including that every knee shall bow to him, belong also to Jesus Christ?

question: Does Jesus Christ exercise the divine prerogative of forgiving and blotting out sins, which the Old Testament reserves to Jehovah?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Jehovah says that he, even he, blots out transgressions for his own sake. The New Testament says the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses from all sin and that Christ by himself purged our sins. Christ also directly declares, 'Son, thy sins be forgiven thee.' So the divine work of forgiveness is ascribed to the Son as to the Father.
sources.quote: The blood of Jesus Christ his Son, cleanseth us from all sin. – 1 John 1:7. When He had by himself purged our sins. – Heb. 1:3. Son, thy sins be forgiven thee. – Mark 2:5.
sources.raw_question: Does Jesus Christ exercise the divine prerogative of forgiving and blotting out sins, which the Old Testament reserves to Jehovah?

question: Is Jesus Christ the divine Shepherd whom the Old Testament identifies as Jehovah, the Shepherd of Israel?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Jehovah is the Shepherd of Israel who feeds his flock and seeks that which was lost. Christ calls himself the good Shepherd of the one flock and says he is come to seek and save that which was lost, using the same Greek phrase as the Septuagint of Ezekiel. Scripture also names him the chief Shepherd and the Shepherd of souls. Christ calls the sheep 'my sheep,' though Scripture calls them 'the flock of God.'
sources.quote: The Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost (το απολωλός). – Luke 19:10.
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus Christ the divine Shepherd whom the Old Testament identifies as Jehovah, the Shepherd of Israel?

question: Does Christ's stilling of the storm show him performing a work Scripture attributes to God alone?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. The Psalm says it is the Lord who makes the storm a calm so that the waves are still. The Gospel records that Jesus arose, rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. The author sets these side by side to show that this mark of divine majesty appertains to the Son.
sources.quote: He arose and rebuked the winds and sea, and there was a great calm. – Matt. 8:26.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's stilling of the storm show him performing a work Scripture attributes to God alone?

question: In what sense did Jesus truly advance, if the divine Word could not advance?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse III > Texts Explained; Eleventhly, Mark xiii. 32 and Luke ii. 52. Arian explanation of the former text is against the Regula Fidei; and against the context. Our Lord said He was ignorant of the Day, by reason of His human nature. If the Holy Spirit knows the Day, therefore the Son knows; if the Son knows the Father, therefore He knows the Day; if He has all that is the Father's, therefore knowledge of the Day; if in the Father, He knows the Day in the Father; if He created and upholds all things, He knows when they will cease to be. He knows not as Man, argued from Matt. xxiv. 42. As He asked about Lazarus's grave, &c., yet knew, so He knows; as S. Paul says, 'whether in the body I know not,' &c., yet knew, so He knows. He said He knew not for our profit, that we be not curious (as in Acts i. 7, where on the contrary He did not say He knew not). As the Almighty asks of Adam and of Cain, yet knew, so the Son knows[as God]. Again, He advanced in wisdom also as man, else He made Angels perfect before Himself. He advanced, in that the Godhead was manifested in Him more fully as time went on.
sources.answer: The body advanced in stature, and as it grew the manifestation of the Godhead in it advanced to those who saw it. As the Godhead was progressively revealed, his grace as man increased before men, until he was confessed by Peter and others as Son of God. The Evangelist's mention of stature shows the advance belongs to the body, since the Word is not measured by stature.
sources.quote: Of the body then is the advance; for, it advancing, in it advanced also the manifestation of the Godhead to those who saw it.
sources.raw_question: In what sense did Jesus truly advance, if the divine Word could not advance?

question: Is the "God of gods" who "shall come openly" in Psalm 50 the Son?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God.
sources.answer: Yes. It is the Son, who came and was manifested to men, as he says: "I have openly appeared to those who seek Me not."
sources.quote: that is, the Son, who came manifested to men who said, “I have openly appeared to those who seek Me not.”
sources.raw_question: Is the "God of gods" who "shall come openly" in Psalm 50 the Son?

question: Should a divine, spiritual birth be judged by the properties of fleshly birth, as Nicodemus judged the new birth by bodily birth?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IV > The fourth book discusses the account of the nature of the “product of generation,” and of the passionless generation of the Only-Begotten, and the text, “In the beginning was the Word,” and the birth of the Virgin.
sources.answer: No. The Lord corrected Nicodemus by teaching that the properties of the flesh and of the spirit are distinct. Anyone who ponders the truth must contemplate a subject according to its own properties. One must not slander the immaterial by a charge that belongs only to things material.
sources.quote: For he who ponders on the truth ought, I imagine, to contemplate his subject according to its own properties, not to slander the immaterial by a charge against things material.
sources.raw_question: Should a divine, spiritual birth be judged by the properties of fleshly birth, as Nicodemus judged the new birth by bodily birth?

question: What distinguishes desire (cupiditas) from love (charitas) in the love of creatures, according to Augustine?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > In What Desire and Love Differ.
sources.answer: Love of a creature is charity when it is referred to the Creator, and desire when the creature is loved for itself. Loving creatures is not wrong in itself, but loving them for their own sake corrupts a person in the enjoying rather than helping him in the using. Inferior creatures are to be used for God's sake, and equals are to be enjoyed in God.
sources.quote: if that love [of the creature] is referred to the Creator, then it will not be desire (cupiditas), but love (charitas). For it is desire when the creature is loved for itself.
sources.raw_question: What distinguishes desire (cupiditas) from love (charitas) in the love of creatures, according to Augustine?

question: Should a person enjoy himself and his neighbour in himself, or in God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He instructs us that there is a kind of trinity discernible in man, who is the image of God, viz. the mind, and the knowledge by which the mind knows itself, and the love wherewith it loves both itself and its own knowledge; these three being mutually equal and of one essence. > In What Desire and Love Differ.
sources.answer: In God. Augustine says one ought to enjoy oneself not in oneself but in Him who made us, and likewise the neighbour whom one loves as oneself. So we should enjoy ourselves and our brethren in the Lord, and not relax ourselves downward toward ourselves.
sources.quote: For as thou oughtest to enjoy thyself, not in thyself, but in Him who made thee, so also him whom thou lovest as thyself.
sources.raw_question: Should a person enjoy himself and his neighbour in himself, or in God?

question: Is the work of giving life (quickening) a work proper to God's eternal majesty rather than to a creature?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book II. > Chapter IV. The Holy Spirit gives life, not in a different way from the Father and the Son, nor by a different working.
sources.answer: Yes. Quickening is the work of the Eternal Majesty. Scripture shows that the one who is quickened is a servant, that is, man, who did not have life of himself but received it as a privilege. So the one who gives life stands on the side of God, not of the servant.
sources.quote: And who can deny that quickening is the work of the Eternal Majesty? For it is written: “Quicken Thy servant.”
sources.raw_question: Is the work of giving life (quickening) a work proper to God's eternal majesty rather than to a creature?

question: Do people have any strength of their own, or from other creatures, to walk with God, or does all such strength come from Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression II.
sources.answer: All such strength comes from Christ. Of ourselves we are without strength, and without Christ we can do nothing acceptable to God; no creature in heaven or earth can help us. In Christ, however, we can do all things, because from his fulness we receive grace for grace and from him we have the Spirit of life and power.
sources.quote: All strength to walk with God is from him. “I can do all things through Christ, which strengtheneth me,” saith St Paul, Phil. iv. 13, who denies that of ourselves we have any sufficiency
sources.raw_question: Do people have any strength of their own, or from other creatures, to walk with God, or does all such strength come from Christ?

question: Should we disbelieve truths about God, such as the Word being with God in the beginning, simply because we cannot comprehend them?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Human reason can only conceive what it perceives within itself or can produce from itself, so God's works must be measured by boundless faith rather than by our powers of perception. Hilary refused to disbelieve what he could not understand, trusting that the will to believe would bring the power to understand.
sources.quote: refused to disbelieve, because it could not understand, that God was in the beginning with God, and that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us
sources.raw_question: Should we disbelieve truths about God, such as the Word being with God in the beginning, simply because we cannot comprehend them?

question: Are God's thought and will separate powers or consorts that must combine, one after the other, for God to produce something, as the Ptolemaeans claimed of Bythus with Ennoea and Thelesis?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter XII.—The doctrines of the followers of Ptolemy and Colorbasus.
sources.answer: No. The true God of the universe does not deliberate in stages like Homer's anxious Jove. As soon as he thinks, he performs what he has willed, and as soon as he wills, he thinks what he has willed. This is because he is wholly thought, will, mind, light, eye and ear, the one entire fountain of all good things, not a compound of separate faculties.
sources.quote: He, as soon as He thinks, also performs what He has willed; and as soon as He wills, also thinks that which He has willed; then thinking when He wills, and then willing when He thinks
sources.raw_question: Are God's thought and will separate powers or consorts that must combine, one after the other, for God to produce something, as the Ptolemaeans claimed of Bythus with Ennoea and Thelesis?

question: Does the church have authority to institute rites or ceremonies in the worship of God beyond what Christ himself has appointed?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: No. Christ alone holds the privilege and power of making laws for his church. The church may only order the circumstances that necessarily attend the ordinances Christ instituted. Owen holds that the contrary principle lies at the root of superstition, idolatry and persecution in Christian history, and that much of the Revelation is designed to expose it.
sources.quote: that the church hath power to institute and appoint any thing or ceremony belonging to the worship of God, either as to matter or to manner, beyond the orderly observance of such circumstances as necessarily attend such ordinances as Christ himself hath instituted
sources.raw_question: Does the church have authority to institute rites or ceremonies in the worship of God beyond what Christ himself has appointed?

question: What does the second commandment chiefly forbid in the worship of God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: It forbids human invention of worship, not merely images as such. Owen endorses the reading 'not image, not likeness is forbidden, but thou shalt not make to thyself.' What is severely forbidden is our making, inventing or finding out ways of worship or means of honouring God that he has not appointed. God has never allowed the creature's will to be the measure of his honour.
sources.quote: it is a making to ourselves, an inventing, a finding out, ways of worship, or means of honouring God, not by him appointed, that is so severely forbidden
sources.raw_question: What does the second commandment chiefly forbid in the worship of God?

question: Why does Scripture call false worship 'adultery' or 'fornication' in relation to Christ and his church?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Because Christ has married the church to himself. The church's chaste affection to him chiefly consists in keeping his institutions and worship as he appointed them. Departing into false worship is therefore a breach of the marriage bond, and Christ calls it whoredom. He is a 'jealous God' with respect to his institutions.
sources.quote: Christ marrying his church to himself, taking it to that relation, still expresseth the main of their chaste and choice affections to him to lie in their keeping his institutions and his worship according to his appointment.
sources.raw_question: Why does Scripture call false worship 'adultery' or 'fornication' in relation to Christ and his church?

question: Is there any proof, testimony or probability supporting the Valentinian doctrine that the Deity unfolds through successive emanations, such as ten Aeons from Logos and Zoe and twelve from Anthropos and Ecclesia?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIV.—Valentinus and his followers derived the principles of their system from the heathen; the names only are changed.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus says the Valentinians lure people in with familiar language about the production of the Word and the emanations of the Deity. They then advance inconsistent claims about further emissions. For these they have neither proof, nor testimony, nor probability, so their scheme is simply lies from beginning to end.
sources.quote: although they have neither proof, nor testimony, nor probability, nor anything whatever of such a nature [to support these assertions]
sources.raw_question: Is there any proof, testimony or probability supporting the Valentinian doctrine that the Deity unfolds through successive emanations, such as ten Aeons from Logos and Zoe and twelve from Anthropos and Ecclesia?

question: Do the many names the Valentinians give their Aeons, modelled on the twelve gods of the heathen, suitably express divinity?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XIV.—Valentinus and his followers derived the principles of their system from the heathen; the names only are changed.
sources.answer: No. Irenaeus argues that the Valentinians detract from the dignity of their own Aeons by multiplying names of this kind, and that the nomenclature is confused and absurd. Even the heathen gods, which the Valentinians call mere images of the Aeons, have names that are more seemly and better suited by their etymology to indicate divinity than the supposed prototypes.
sources.quote: For they themselves detract from [the dignity of] their Æons by a multitude of names of this sort.
sources.raw_question: Do the many names the Valentinians give their Aeons, modelled on the twelve gods of the heathen, suitably express divinity?

question: Do so-called inseparable accidents, like the blackness of a raven's feather, show that some accidents cannot be lost and so might belong to God?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > The Accidental Always Implies Some Change in the Thing.
sources.answer: No. Even an inseparable accident is lost when its subject is changed or ceases to be. The feather keeps its blackness only as long as it remains a feather, and it does not exist forever. Such accidents still rest on changeable matter, so they give no model for anything in God.
sources.quote: yet the feather loses that color, not indeed so long as it is a feather, but because the feather is not always. Wherefore the matter itself is changeable
sources.raw_question: Do so-called inseparable accidents, like the blackness of a raven's feather, show that some accidents cannot be lost and so might belong to God?

question: In Song of Songs 5:11, what do the Beloved's bushy locks, black as a raven, signify about Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: They signify Christ's thoughts, counsels and ways in governing his kingdom. They are called black because they are deep and unsearchable, as God is said to dwell in thick darkness. They are called curled because his infinite wisdom interweaves them exactly. To a carnal eye they seem dark and tangled, but to his saints they are ordered and comely.
sources.quote: They are black or dark, because of their depth and unsearchableness, — as God is said to dwell in thick darkness; and curled or bushy, because of their exact interweavings, from his infinite wisdom.
sources.raw_question: In Song of Songs 5:11, what do the Beloved's bushy locks, black as a raven, signify about Christ?

question: What does the image of the Beloved's eyes as doves' eyes in Song of Songs 5:12 teach about Christ's knowledge and his disposition toward the church?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: The eyes stand for Christ's knowledge, understanding and discerning Spirit. Four things are ascribed to them: tenderness, purity, discerning and glory. As doves are gentle birds rather than birds of prey, Christ looks on his church with tender compassion and without anger or revenge. He uses his wisdom and knowledge for its care and guidance, as Deuteronomy 11:12 shows of the Lord's eyes resting on the land he cares for.
sources.quote: He looks on it with the eyes of galless doves; with tenderness and careful compassion; without anger, fury, or thoughts of revenge.
sources.raw_question: What does the image of the Beloved's eyes as doves' eyes in Song of Songs 5:12 teach about Christ's knowledge and his disposition toward the church?

question: Since Christ is of purer eyes than to behold iniquity, how can he take delight in a church that is defiled by sin?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Christ himself removes the church's filth so that he may delight in it. Because no other means could cleanse it, he does this by his own blood. He partly takes away its stains by the renewing of the Holy Ghost, and he wholly adorns it with his own righteousness. In this way he presents the church to himself holy and without blemish (Ephesians 5:25-27).
sources.quote: Partly, he takes away our spots and stains, by the “renewing of the Holy Ghost;”[^137] and wholly adorns us with his own righteousness: and that because of the purity of his own eyes, which “cannot behold iniquity,”
sources.raw_question: Since Christ is of purer eyes than to behold iniquity, how can he take delight in a church that is defiled by sin?

question: What does the early heretical objection that the Catholic doctrine implied a division of the Father's substance show about what the Church taught concerning the Son?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 25: Whether it be not clear from all the genuine remains of antiquity, that the Catholic Church before the Council of Nice, and even Srom the beginning, did believe
sources.answer: It shows the Church taught a proper communication of the same substance from Father to Son. No one would object that creating angels or creatures divides God's substance, so the objection, standing from Justin to Arius, only makes sense if a proper consubstantiality was taught.
sources.quote: Now, what colour or pretence could there have been for the objection, had not the Catholics professed a proper communication of the same substance?
sources.raw_question: What does the early heretical objection that the Catholic doctrine implied a division of the Father's substance show about what the Church taught concerning the Son?

question: Can anyone be perfectly justified in this present life?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > Augustin explains for what the Son of God was sent; but, however, that the Son of God, although made less by being sent, is not therefore less because the Father sent Him; nor yet the Holy Spirit less because both the Father sent Him and the Son. > The One Death and Resurrection of The Body of Christ Harmonizes with Our Double Death and Resurrection of Body and Soul, to the Effect of Salvation. In What Way the Single Death of Christ is Bestowed Upon Our Double Death.
