sources.answer: No, not in comparison with the righteousness to come. While the corruptible body weighs down the soul and earthly life is all temptation, no one living is justified in God's sight. That is measured against the righteousness that will make us equal with the angels. Our justification will be perfected only at the end, when we shall see Him as He is.
sources.quote: in His sight shall no man living be justified,[^455] in comparison of the righteousness in which we shall be made equal with the angels
sources.raw_question: Can anyone be perfectly justified in this present life?

question: Is the fundamental rule of worship 'worship God only', or 'worship God and whomever else God appoints to be worshipped'?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: The rule is that God only is to be worshipped. Neither the Law, the Prophets, Christ nor the apostles ever hinted that worship might go to anyone God might nominate besides himself. Christ, the angel in Revelation and St. Paul all speak of God or the Creator alone, and the supposed exception is constantly omitted where it would naturally have been mentioned.
sources.quote: Nothing therefore can be plainer, than that the fundamental rule for worship is, that God only is to be worshipped.
sources.raw_question: Is the fundamental rule of worship 'worship God only', or 'worship God and whomever else God appoints to be worshipped'?

question: What was the main reason the early Church Fathers opposed Arianism in relation to worship?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 16: Whether by these (of the first column) and the lke teats, adoration and worship be not so appropriated to the one God, as to belong to him only ?
sources.answer: They saw that it turned Christianity into creature-worship. Waterland endorses Cudworth's observation that Arianism paganized and idolatrized Christianity, which God intended as the means of rooting out pagan idolatry. It did so by giving religious worship to the Son while holding him to be a creature. Fathers such as Athanasius, Basil and Augustine therefore charged the Arians with the same idolatry as the pagans.
sources.quote: Christianity, which “ was intended by God Almighty for a means to extirpate “ Pagan idolatry, was thereby itself paganized and idolatrized
sources.raw_question: What was the main reason the early Church Fathers opposed Arianism in relation to worship?

question: If Christ promised that the Comforter would abide with believers forever, how can a believer lose all sense of comfort?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part III. Of Communion with God the Holy Ghost. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: The Comforter may always abide without always comforting. He remains with believers for other purposes, such as sanctification, as with David, who still had the Holy Spirit yet prayed for the restoration of the joy of salvation. His actual comforting depends on his sovereign will. Often he also offers consolation that believers refuse to receive.
sources.quote: The Comforter may always abide with us, though not always comfort us; he who is the Comforter may abide, though he do not always that work.
sources.raw_question: If Christ promised that the Comforter would abide with believers forever, how can a believer lose all sense of comfort?

question: Is the efficacy of the sacraments (such as baptism) due to the human minister or to God?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Preface.
sources.answer: To God. The ministers (Damasus, Peter, Ambrose, Gregory) do not themselves cleanse; theirs is only the ministry, while the sacraments belong to Christ. It is not in man's power to confer what is divine; it is the gift of the Son and the Father, given through the outpouring of the Spirit.
sources.quote: Damasus cleansed not, Peter cleansed not, Ambrose cleansed not, Gregory cleansed not; for ours is the ministry, but the sacraments are Thine. For it is not in man’s power to confer what is divine
sources.raw_question: Is the efficacy of the sacraments (such as baptism) due to the human minister or to God?

question: Does a theological system become scriptural simply because it uses the words, parables and sayings of Scripture?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book I > Chapter VIII.—How the Valentinians pervert the Scriptures to support their own pious opinions.
sources.answer: No. Words of Scripture can be torn from their proper order and connection and rearranged to support a false doctrine. Irenaeus compares this to taking apart a jeweled image of a king and making the gems into a fox, then claiming it is the king's image. The materials are genuine, but the arrangement destroys the truth. So the true meaning of Scripture depends on keeping the order and connection of its passages, not on merely citing its words.
sources.quote: In doing so, however, they disregard the order and the connection of the Scriptures, and so far as in them lies, dismember and destroy the truth.
sources.raw_question: Does a theological system become scriptural simply because it uses the words, parables and sayings of Scripture?

question: Does Paul treat 'Grace be with you' and 'The Lord Jesus be with you' as equivalent expressions?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter II.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul says the grace-salutation is the token in every epistle, yet sometimes he uses one formula, sometimes the other, and sometimes both together, showing he takes them as equivalent. This confirms that grace is what we peculiarly receive from Christ.
sources.quote: he makes these two, “Grace be with you,” and, “The Lord Jesus be with you,” to be equivalent expressions; for whereas he affirmed the one to be the token in all his epistles
sources.raw_question: Does Paul treat 'Grace be with you' and 'The Lord Jesus be with you' as equivalent expressions?

question: Did Novatian use 'semper' (always) of the Son in a loose sense rather than a strict sense of unlimited duration?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 8: Whether eternity does not imply necessary existence of the Son; which is inconsistent with the Doctor’s Scheme? And whether the * Doctor hath not made an elusiv
sources.answer: No. Novatian meant 'semper' strictly, a parte ante. He explains 'semper' by 'ante omne tempus', which for him means having no beginning. His saying that no time can be assigned to the Son, since the Son is before time, confirms the strict sense.
sources.quote: Some indeed have thought, that Novatian understands not the word semper there in the strict sense of unlimited duration; wherein I humbly conceive they are mistaken.
sources.raised_by_detail: Some who thought Novatian's semper is not strict
sources.raw_question: Did Novatian use 'semper' (always) of the Son in a loose sense rather than a strict sense of unlimited duration?

question: Are both the love of good pleasure (benevolence) and the love of friendship (approbation) ascribed peculiarly to the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter III.
sources.answer: Yes. John 3:16 ascribes to the Father the love of purpose and good pleasure, as the cause of sending the Son. John 14:23 ascribes to him the love of friendship and approbation: Father and Son come and dwell with the believer by the Spirit, but "My Father will love him" gives the Father a peculiar prerogative in love.
sources.quote: whereas there is a twofold divine love, beneplaciti and amicitiæ, a love of good pleasure and destination, and a love of friendship and approbation, they are both peculiarly assigned to the Father in an eminent manner
sources.raw_question: Are both the love of good pleasure (benevolence) and the love of friendship (approbation) ascribed peculiarly to the Father?

question: Is spiritual progress achieved by discovering a higher Father beyond the Creator God preached from the beginning?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter IX.—There is but one author, and one end to both covenants.
sources.answer: No. If progress meant finding another Father besides the one first preached, there would be no end: one would proceed from a second to a third, a fourth, and so on, never resting in one God. Such a person is driven from the true God and swims in a limitless abyss unless he repents and confesses one God, the Father, the Creator.
sources.quote: he who thinks that he is always making progress of such a kind, will never rest in one God. For, being driven away from Him who truly is [God], and being turned backwards, he shall be for ever seeking, yet shall never find out God
sources.raw_question: Is spiritual progress achieved by discovering a higher Father beyond the Creator God preached from the beginning?

question: Where should Christians learn the true interpretation of Scripture about the one God and his Son, according to Irenaeus?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVI.—The treasure hid in the Scriptures is Christ; the true exposition of the Scriptures is to be found in the Church alone.
sources.answer: From the presbyters who hold the succession of the Church from the apostles and who are sound in life and incorrupt in speech. God has placed his gifts in the Church, apostles, prophets and teachers, so the truth is to be learned where those gifts are. These teachers keep the faith in one God who created all things and increase love for the Son of God. They expound the Scriptures safely, without blaspheming God or dishonouring the patriarchs and prophets, as the heretics do.
sources.quote: For these also preserve this faith of ours in one God who created all things; and they increase that love [which we have] for the Son of God, who accomplished such marvellous dispensations for our sake
sources.raw_question: Where should Christians learn the true interpretation of Scripture about the one God and his Son, according to Irenaeus?

question: Did God give circumcision and the Sabbath as means of making people righteous?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVI.—Perfect righteousness was conferred neither by circumcision nor by any other legal ceremonies. The Decalogue, however, was not cancelled by Christ, but is always in force: men were never released from its commandments.
sources.answer: No. Circumcision and the Sabbaths were given as signs, so that Abraham's race might stay recognisable and know the Lord who sanctifies them. They were not meaningless, since a wise Artist gave them: fleshly circumcision typified spiritual circumcision, and the Sabbath signified continual service of God and the coming rest of the kingdom.
sources.quote: God gave circumcision, not as the completer of righteousness, but as a sign, that the race of Abraham might continue recognisable.
sources.raw_question: Did God give circumcision and the Sabbath as means of making people righteous?

question: Can people be justified before God without circumcision and without the law of Moses?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVI.—Perfect righteousness was conferred neither by circumcision nor by any other legal ceremonies. The Decalogue, however, was not cancelled by Christ, but is always in force: men were never released from its commandments.
sources.answer: Yes. Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness before he was circumcised or kept Sabbaths. Lot, Noah, Enoch and the other righteous men before Moses were saved and pleased God without circumcision. This shows that such ceremonies were signs and not the cause of justification.
sources.quote: Abraham himself, without circumcision and without observance of Sabbaths, “believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness; and he was called the friend of God.”
sources.raw_question: Can people be justified before God without circumcision and without the law of Moses?

question: Why did God not give the covenant of the written law to the patriarchs?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVI.—Perfect righteousness was conferred neither by circumcision nor by any other legal ceremonies. The Decalogue, however, was not cancelled by Christ, but is always in force: men were never released from its commandments.
sources.answer: Because the law is not laid down for the righteous. The fathers had the meaning of the Decalogue written in their hearts: they loved their Maker and did no harm to their neighbour. Only when this love was forgotten in Egypt did God, out of goodwill to men, reveal himself by a voice and give the written commandments.
sources.quote: the righteous fathers had the meaning of the Decalogue written in their hearts and souls, that is, they loved the God who made them, and did no injury to their neighbour.
sources.raw_question: Why did God not give the covenant of the written law to the patriarchs?

question: Was the Decalogue, spoken by the Lord himself, abolished by Christ's coming in the flesh?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVI.—Perfect righteousness was conferred neither by circumcision nor by any other legal ceremonies. The Decalogue, however, was not cancelled by Christ, but is always in force: men were never released from its commandments.
sources.answer: No. The Lord spoke the words of the Decalogue in his own person to all alike, so they remain permanently in force. Through his advent in the flesh they receive extension and increase, not abrogation. This identifies the incarnate Lord with the God who gave the law. The ceremonial laws of bondage, by contrast, were cancelled by the new covenant of liberty.
sources.quote: the Lord Himself did speak in His own person to all alike the words of the Decalogue; and therefore, in like manner, do they remain permanently with us, receiving by means of His advent in the flesh, extension and increase, but not abrogation.
sources.raw_question: Was the Decalogue, spoken by the Lord himself, abolished by Christ's coming in the flesh?

question: Could a merely holy and innocent creature have borne the sins of all the elect and made atonement?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: No. If all the sins of the elect had been laid on a mere holy, innocent creature, they would have overwhelmed him and buried him forever out of the presence of God's love. Only one who is God could bear that burden.
sources.quote: laid them on a mere holy, innocent, creature; — O how would they have overwhelmed him, and buried him for ever out of the presence of God’s love!
sources.raw_question: Could a merely holy and innocent creature have borne the sins of all the elect and made atonement?

question: Does Zechariah 13:7, which speaks of the sword awaking against the Lord's 'fellow', show that the shepherd who suffered is equal with God?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter III. > Digression I.
sources.answer: Yes. The sword awoke against him who was the fellow, or equal, of the Lord of hosts, that is, the divine Son. By the wounds of that great shepherd the sheep are healed (1 Peter 2:24-25).
sources.quote: The sword awaked against him that was the fellow of the Lord of hosts, Zech. xiii. 7; and by the wounds of that great shepherd are the sheep healed, 1 Pet. ii. 24, 25.
sources.raw_question: Does Zechariah 13:7, which speaks of the sword awaking against the Lord's 'fellow', show that the shepherd who suffered is equal with God?

question: Has God bound his truthfulness and faithfulness, in the sanction of the law, not to leave sin unpunished?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: Of the Satisfaction of Christ
sources.answer: Yes. God engaged his veracity in the threatening attached to the law, as in the warning to Adam that he would surely die and the curse on all who do not keep the law. Hence mankind, left without divine help, must have perished eternally.
sources.quote: That God, has also engaged his veracity and faithfulness in the sanction of the law, not to leave sin unpunished
sources.raw_question: Has God bound his truthfulness and faithfulness, in the sanction of the law, not to leave sin unpunished?

question: Does Christ's command to pray to the Lord of the harvest give warrant for praying to the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 6. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Godhead of the Holy Spirit with that of the Father and of the Son: as One who is to be distinguished from the Father and the Son: as One to whom such personal properties and actions are assigned as prove independent and intelligent personality: as One to whom Divine attributes are ascribed and by whom Divine offices are exercised: as One worshipped in parity with the Father and the Son: as One declared to be Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. In Matthew 9:38 Christ commands prayer to the One who sends forth labourers. Acts 13 shows that sending forth ministers is an especial office of the Holy Ghost, who says "Separate me Barnabas and Saul" and sends them out. Therefore we have Christ's own warrant for praying to the Spirit.
sources.quote: Here Christ himself enjoins prayer to him who sends forth ministers. That this is one especial office of the Holy Ghost, we learn from the Acts; and we have, therefore, Christ’s warrant for praying to the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's command to pray to the Lord of the harvest give warrant for praying to the Holy Spirit?

question: What does the 'banner' of love in Song of Songs 2:4 signify about Christ's relation to his saints?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: It signifies safety, protection and victory that come from Christ's love. A banner marks the presence of an army under which its members camp securely. Christ's banner over his saints is love, so all their protection comes from his love. That love guards them from hell, death and every enemy. Whatever presses on them must first pass through the banner of his love.
sources.quote: Christ hath a banner for his saints; and that is love. All their protection is from his love; and they shall have all the protection his love can give them.
sources.raw_question: What does the 'banner' of love in Song of Songs 2:4 signify about Christ's relation to his saints?

question: Is Jesus Christ our Saviour because he satisfied God's justice for our sins, or only because he declared and confirmed the way of eternal salvation by his life and resurrection, as Socinus taught?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: A Brief Declaration and Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: To the Reader
sources.answer: Christ is our Saviour because he fully satisfied God's justice for our sins, and that satisfaction is imputed to believers through faith. Owen calls Socinus's position, that Christ only revealed and exemplified the way of salvation and that no satisfaction was needed, the true state of the question. He holds that Covetus overturned it by grounding the case in God's justice, which necessarily requires the punishment of sin. He adds that Crellius uses words close to the orthodox ones while still meaning what Socinus meant.
sources.quote: Jesus Christ is therefore our Saviour, because he has satisfied the justice of God, by which we, being sinners, deserved to be condemned for all our sins
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus Christ our Saviour because he satisfied God's justice for our sins, or only because he declared and confirmed the way of eternal salvation by his life and resurrection, as Socinus taught?

question: Why is whatever is done to Christ's people counted as done to Christ himself?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter V.
sources.answer: Because Christ is present in his people and dwells in them by his Spirit. His name is in the Spirit and with him. What is done to those in whom Christ dwells by his Spirit is therefore done to Christ.
sources.quote: it is upon this account that whatever is done to any of Christ’s is done to him, because it is done to them in whom he is and dwells by his Spirit
sources.raw_question: Why is whatever is done to Christ's people counted as done to Christ himself?

question: Why would God allow His apostles, such as Paul, to suffer infirmity and buffeting rather than removing it when asked?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter III.—The power and glory of God shine forth in the weakness of human flesh, as He will render our body a participator of the resurrection and of immortality, although He has formed it from the dust of the earth; He will also bestow upon it the enjoyment of immortality, just as He grants it this short life in common with the soul.
sources.answer: Because strength is made perfect in weakness. By experiencing his own infirmity a man learns that he is weak and mortal by nature while God is immortal and powerful. This keeps him from becoming lifted up against God and claiming God's glory for himself, and it increases his love toward God.
sources.quote: For strength is made perfect in weakness, rendering him a better man who by means of his infirmity becomes acquainted with the power of God.
sources.raw_question: Why would God allow His apostles, such as Paul, to suffer infirmity and buffeting rather than removing it when asked?

question: Does the Father's testimony to John the Baptist confirm that the Spirit rests on Christ?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book III. > Chapter I. Not only were the prophets and apostles sent by the Spirit, but also the Son of God. This is proved from Isaiah and the evangelists, and it is explained why St. Luke wrote that the same Spirit descended like a dove upon Christ and abode upon Him. Next, after establishing this mission of Christ, the writer infers that the Son is sent by the Father and the Spirit, as the Spirit is by the Father and the Son.
sources.answer: Yes. The Father told John that the one on whom he saw the Spirit descend and remain would baptize with the Holy Spirit. John heard this from God, saw it fulfilled in the Lord, and believed it was the Spirit coming down from heaven.
sources.quote: God the Father said this to John, and John heard and saw and believed. He heard from God, he saw in the Lord, he believed that it was the Spirit Who was coming down from heaven.
sources.raw_question: Does the Father's testimony to John the Baptist confirm that the Spirit rests on Christ?

question: Does Isaiah's prophecy of the lamb led to the slaughter refer to Jesus, the Son of the one God whom the prophets preached?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book III > Chapter XII.—Doctrine of the rest of the apostles.
sources.answer: Yes. Philip told the eunuch that this Scripture was fulfilled in Jesus. The eunuch believed and confessed Jesus Christ to be the Son of God. He then preached that there is one God proclaimed by the prophets, whose Son had appeared in human nature and been led as a sheep to the slaughter.
sources.quote: that there was one God preached by the prophets, but that the Son of this [God] had already made [His] appearance in human nature (secundum hominem), and had been led as a sheep to the slaughter
sources.raw_question: Does Isaiah's prophecy of the lamb led to the slaughter refer to Jesus, the Son of the one God whom the prophets preached?

question: Why could only the Son, and not an angel or other creature, accomplish the 'better' ministry that abolished death and brought salvation?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Thirdly, Hebrews i. 4. Additional texts brought as objections; e.g. Heb. i. 4; vii. 22. Whether the word 'better' implies likeness to the Angels; and 'made' or 'become' implies creation. Necessary to consider the circumstances under which Scripture speaks. Difference between 'better' and 'greater;' texts in proof. 'Made' or 'become' a general word. Contrast in Heb. i. 4, between the Son and the Works in point of nature. The difference of the punishments under the two Covenants shews the difference of the natures of the Son and the Angels. 'Become' relates not to the nature of the Word, but to His manhood and office and relation towards us. Parallel passages in which the term is applied to the Eternal Father.
sources.answer: Because the Law spoken through angels perfected no one and needed the visitation of the Word. The Son, by taking flesh, condemned sin in the flesh, made the flesh capable of the Word, took the judgment on Himself and gave salvation to all. This shows He is other than originated things and the very Son in the Father. The following context concludes that this 'better' could be brought about by none but the Son seated at the Father's right, which shows that the Father's Godhead is the Son's.
sources.quote: Formerly the world, as guilty, was under judgment from the Law; but now the Word has taken on Himself the judgment, and having suffered in the body for all, has bestowed salvation to all
sources.raw_question: Why could only the Son, and not an angel or other creature, accomplish the 'better' ministry that abolished death and brought salvation?

question: Does the New Testament show the same God exercising wrath and vengeance as in the Old Testament, so that God's justice is continuous across both covenants?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXVII—The sins of the men of old time, which incurred the displeasure of God, were, by His providence, committed to writing, that we might derive instruction thereby, and not be filled with pride. We must not, therefore, infer that there was another God than He whom Christ preached; we should rather fear, lest the one and the same God who inflicted punishment on the ancients, should bring down heavier upon us.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as the idolaters and fornicators perished then, the apostle declares that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom; just as God avenged Israel on the Egyptians, Christ promises God will avenge His elect; and the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against unrighteousness, with Christ coming in flaming fire to take vengeance. The same righteousness of God appears in both Testaments, though in the New it is real, enduring, and heavier.
sources.quote: And as the wrath of God did then descend upon the unrighteous, here also does the apostle likewise say: “For the wrath of God shall be revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness
sources.raw_question: Does the New Testament show the same God exercising wrath and vengeance as in the Old Testament, so that God's justice is continuous across both covenants?

question: Does Basilides' theory that each heaven was produced by efflux from the one before it lead to an absurd conclusion?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXV.—Refutation of Basilides, and of the opinion that the prophets uttered their predictions under the inspiration of different gods.
sources.answer: Yes. If each heaven arises from the efflux of the preceding one, then our heaven, which Basilides calls the last, must also produce another like it, and that one another. So the process could never stop at three hundred and sixty-five but would go on without end, producing an indefinite number of heavens.
sources.quote: then it follows, as a matter of necessity, that from the efflux of our heaven, which he indeed terms the last, another be formed like to it, and from that again a third
sources.raw_question: Does Basilides' theory that each heaven was produced by efflux from the one before it lead to an absurd conclusion?

question: Do the various Hebrew names for God in Scripture, such as Sabaoth, Eloe and Adonai, show that there are different gods or powers?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXV.—Refutation of Basilides, and of the opinion that the prophets uttered their predictions under the inspiration of different gods.
sources.answer: No. All such expressions are announcements and titles of one and the same Being. Each name describes some aspect of that one God, for example as "that which contains all" or as "one who bounds and separates the land from the water." The same holds for titles like Lord of Powers, Father of all, Almighty, Most High and Creator. Through all these names the one God and Father is revealed.
sources.quote: These are not the names and titles of a succession of different beings, but of one and the same, by means of which the one God and Father is revealed, He who contains all things, and grants to all the boon of existence.
sources.raw_question: Do the various Hebrew names for God in Scripture, such as Sabaoth, Eloe and Adonai, show that there are different gods or powers?

question: Was Christ baptized in his thirtieth year in order to signify thirty divine Aeons in the Pleroma?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXII.—The thirty Æons are not typified by the fact that Christ was baptized in His thirtieth year: He did not suffer in the twelfth month after His baptism, but was more than fifty years old when He died.
sources.answer: No. The Gnostics' own system cannot keep the count of Aeons at thirty: sometimes it has too few and sometimes too many. Making Christ's age a sign of thirty Aeons would also force them to separate the Saviour himself from the Pleroma. So his age at baptism is no proof of their scheme of divine emanations.
sources.quote: There are not, therefore, thirty Æons, nor did the Saviour come to be baptized when He was thirty years old, for this reason, that He might show forth the thirty silent[^3121] Æons of their system
sources.raw_question: Was Christ baptized in his thirtieth year in order to signify thirty divine Aeons in the Pleroma?

question: Did Old Testament saints such as Abraham, Enoch and David have real communion with God, and if so, how did it differ from that of believers under the gospel?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: Yes, they enjoyed communion with God in its substance, but not with the boldness and liberty given in the gospel. The way into the holiest was not yet manifest while the first tabernacle stood, and a veil lay on them, so they lacked freedom and confidence in access. That boldness follows the entrance of Christ our High Priest into the most holy place and is administered by the Spirit in the gospel.
sources.quote: Though they had communion with God, yet they had not παῤῥησίαν, — a boldness and confidence in that communion.
sources.raw_question: Did Old Testament saints such as Abraham, Enoch and David have real communion with God, and if so, how did it differ from that of believers under the gospel?

question: By whom is the distance between sinful man and God removed so that sinners can have communion with the Father?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: By Jesus Christ alone. Grace and pardoning mercy, the only door into communion, is committed to him alone, who purchased it, dispenses it and reveals it from the bosom of the Father. He consecrated a new and living way through his flesh, and through him we have access by one Spirit unto the Father.
sources.quote: By Jesus Christ alone, then, on all considerations as to being and full manifestation, is this distance taken away.
sources.raw_question: By whom is the distance between sinful man and God removed so that sinners can have communion with the Father?

question: Does the infinite disparity between God and man rule out any friendship or communion between them, as Aristotle concluded?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: No. Aristotle concluded this, and others saw only the general intercourse of providence, because nature alone, being sinful and corrupt, leads only to terror at God's presence. But this knowledge is hid in Christ, who gives a new foundation and discovery of this privilege of fellowship with the holy God.
sources.quote: This knowledge is hid in Christ; as will afterward be made to appear. It is too wonderful for nature, as sinful and corrupted.
sources.raw_question: Does the infinite disparity between God and man rule out any friendship or communion between them, as Aristotle concluded?

question: In what sense was God the God and Father of humanity, and how was that relation lost?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > This twelfth book gives a notable interpretation of the words of the Lord to Mary, “Touch Me not, for I am not yet ascended to My Father.”
sources.answer: God is Father of all existing things as their author, and the name 'Godhead' implies oversight or foresight toward what He made. Humanity lost the impress of the Father's image through sin, was engrafted by similarity of will into the family of the devil, and so honoured false gods and a false father instead of the true God and Father.
sources.quote: And the name of Godhead itself, whether it indicates the authority of oversight or of foresight, imports a certain relation to humanity. For He Who bestowed on all things that are, the power of being, is the God and overseer of what He has Himself produced.
sources.raw_question: In what sense was God the God and Father of humanity, and how was that relation lost?

question: Can the many gods or principles posited by Valentinus, Marcion and Cerinthus avoid the conclusion that one God is the cause of all things?

sources.author: Hippolytus of Rome
sources.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
sources.section: Against the Heresy of One Noetus.
sources.answer: No. Even these heretics are forced, unwillingly, to admit that the All runs up into one, and so that the One is the cause of all things. Thus they too fall in with the truth that one God made all things according to His good pleasure.
sources.quote: If, then, all things run up into one, even according to Valentinus, and Marcion, and Cerinthus, and all their fooleries, they are also reduced, however unwillingly, to this position, that they must acknowledge that the One is the cause of all things.
sources.raw_question: Can the many gods or principles posited by Valentinus, Marcion and Cerinthus avoid the conclusion that one God is the cause of all things?

question: Did the Jewish high priest's question 'Art Thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?' show that the Jews held the true Messiah must be the Son of God?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VI
sources.answer: Yes. The Jews erred about the Person, not about the Sonship: they doubted whether Jesus was the Christ, but did not doubt that the Christ must be the Son of God. So even in their blindness they confessed what the heretics deny. The perfect knowledge is that Christ, the Son of God existing before the worlds, was also born of the Virgin.
sources.quote: They did not ask whether Christ be the Son of God; they asked whether He were Christ, the Son of God. They were wrong as to the Person, not as to the Sonship, of Christ.
sources.raw_question: Did the Jewish high priest's question 'Art Thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?' show that the Jews held the true Messiah must be the Son of God?

question: Why does John 14:23 use the plural "we will come and make our abode" of the Father and the Son?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He resolves the question he had deferred, and teaches us that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one power and one wisdom, no otherwise than one God and one essence. And he then inquires how it is that, in speaking of God, the Latins say, One essence, three persons; but the Greeks, One essence, three substances or hypostases. > Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and Three Essences. What He Ought to Believe Concerning the Trinity Who Does Not Receive What is Said Above. Man is Both After the Image, and is the Image of God.
sources.answer: The plural refers to the relatives, the Father and the Son, which are terms used relatively to one another. The unity of essence is simply left unexpressed here.
sources.quote: Sometimes also the unity of the essence is left unexpressed, and the relatives alone are mentioned in the plural number
sources.raw_question: Why does John 14:23 use the plural "we will come and make our abode" of the Father and the Son?

question: If God can be found when sought (as Isaiah says), why does Scripture command us to seek His face evermore?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He embraces in a brief compendium the contents of the previous books; and finally shows that the Trinity, in the perfect sight of which consists the blessed life that is promised us, is here seen by us as in a glass and in an enigma, so long as it is seen through that image of God which we ourselves are. > God, Although Incomprehensible, is Ever to Be Sought. The Traces of the Trinity are Not Vainly Sought in the Creature.
sources.answer: Because God is incomprehensible, He is both sought in order to be found and found in order to be sought. Finding Him includes finding how incomprehensible He is, so the seeker never gives over seeking but makes progress and becomes ever better. He is sought that He may be found more sweetly, and found that He may be sought more eagerly.
sources.quote: For things incomprehensible must so be investigated, as that no one may think he has found nothing, when he has been able to find how incomprehensible that is which he was seeking.
sources.raw_question: If God can be found when sought (as Isaiah says), why does Scripture command us to seek His face evermore?

question: Is Jesus' teaching about the Father and the Spirit Trinitarian only in the Gospel of John, or also in the Synoptic Gospels?

sources.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
sources.work: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.section: The Biblical Doctrine of the Trinity
sources.answer: It is Trinitarian in the Synoptics as well. There Jesus claims a unique Sonship to God and accepts the title Son of God. He also speaks of casting out demons by the Spirit of God, as though God's own activities were at his disposal. So the Trinitarian conditioning of his teaching is not confined to John.
sources.quote: It is not merely in the Gospel of John that such representations occur in the teaching of Jesus. In the Synoptics, too, Jesus claims a Sonship to God which is unique
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus' teaching about the Father and the Spirit Trinitarian only in the Gospel of John, or also in the Synoptic Gospels?

question: Do the words of Psalm 45:7, 'Thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity,' show that the nature of the Word is alterable?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse I > Texts Explained; Secondly, Psalm xlv. 7, 8. Whether the words 'therefore,' 'anointed,' &c., imply that the Word has been rewarded. Argued against first from the word 'fellows' or 'partakers.' He is anointed with the Spirit in His manhood to sanctify human nature. Therefore the Spirit descended on Him in Jordan, when in the flesh. And He is said to sanctify Himself for us, and give us the glory He has received. The word 'wherefore' implies His divinity. 'Thou hast loved righteousness,' &c., do not imply trial or choice.
sources.answer: No. Rather, by their very force they signify His unalterableness. Created natures are alterable and uncertain in their conduct, so there was need of one unalterable whose immutable righteousness could serve men as an image and type of virtue. The Lord, ever unalterable in nature, loving righteousness, was anointed and sent so that, remaining the same, He might take alterable flesh and condemn sin in it.
sources.quote: Nor do the words, ‘Thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity,’ which are added in the Psalm, show, as again you suppose, that the Nature of the Word is alterable, but rather by their very force signify His unalterableness.
sources.raw_question: Do the words of Psalm 45:7, 'Thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity,' show that the nature of the Word is alterable?

question: In what way is the Holy Spirit related to the souls of rational beings as form is related to matter?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: As form perfects matter, the Spirit perfects rational beings and completes their excellence. One who no longer lives after the flesh but is led by the Spirit of God is made a son of God, conformed to the image of the Son, and is called spiritual.
sources.quote: inasmuch as the Holy Spirit perfects rational beings, completing their excellence, He is analogous to Form.
sources.raw_question: In what way is the Holy Spirit related to the souls of rational beings as form is related to matter?

question: If the Holy Spirit is present in the worthy, why does He not continually work miracles and prophecies through them?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is understood of the Spirit.
sources.answer: Because the Spirit is in them as an art is in the artist: always present potentially, but active only when needed. He is ever present with the worthy but works as need requires in prophecies, healings, or other actualizations of His potential action.
sources.quote: so also the Spirit is ever present with those that are worthy, but works, as need requires, in prophecies, or in healings, or in some other actual carrying into effect of His potential action.
sources.raw_question: If the Holy Spirit is present in the worthy, why does He not continually work miracles and prophecies through them?

question: Is non-existence before coming to be essentially the same condition as non-existence after ceasing to be?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book IX > Then, having shown that Eunomius' calumny against the great Basil, that he called the Only-begotten “Ungenerate,” is false, and having again with much ingenuity discussed the eternity, being, and endlessness of the Only-begotten, and the creation of light and of darkness, he concludes the book.
sources.answer: Yes. Just as night before dawn and night after nightfall are both night under different names, the state antecedent to formation and that following dissolution are one condition of non-existence. Hence positing non-existence of the Son before his generation is as impious as positing his future death.
sources.quote: For the state of “not being” of that which has not been generated, and of that which has died, save for the difference of the names, are the same
sources.raw_question: Is non-existence before coming to be essentially the same condition as non-existence after ceasing to be?

question: Is affliction a privilege of God's adopted children rather than a sign of his displeasure?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter X.
sources.answer: Yes. Affliction is a privilege of children because it comes from the Father's love and leads to spiritual advantages. It also conforms believers to Christ and is sweetened by his presence.
sources.quote: Affliction, also, as proceeding from love, as leading to spiritual advantages, as conforming unto Christ, as sweetened with his presence, is the privilege of children
sources.raw_question: Is affliction a privilege of God's adopted children rather than a sign of his displeasure?

question: Does Christ's promise that the pure in heart shall see God prove that the visible Christ was not the Father?

sources.author: Novatian
sources.section: A Treatise of Novatian Concerning the Trinity. > He Proves Also that the Words Spoken to Philip Make Nothing for the Sabellians.
sources.answer: Yes. If Christ had been the Father, the vision of the Father would already have been given, since Christ was seen and touched. Promising it as something still future would then have been superfluous. So the Son, who was seen as the image of God, promised a vision of the invisible Father that was yet to come.
sources.quote: But if Christ Himself had been the Father, why did He promise as future, a reward which He had already granted and given?
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's promise that the pure in heart shall see God prove that the visible Christ was not the Father?

question: Is Jesus a mere man in whom the Word dwelt as an extended divine power, as the Spirit dwelt in the prophets, so that Jesus and Christ are two distinct subjects?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book X
sources.answer: No. The Church refuses to separate Jesus Christ so that Jesus is one and Christ another, or to distinguish the Son of Man from the Son of God. It holds that Christ is none other than Jesus and Jesus none other than Christ; there is a dispensation but no division.
sources.quote: It knows of the dispensation, but of no division: it refuses to make a separation in Jesus Christ; whereby Jesus is one and Christ another; nor does it distinguish the Son of Man from the Son of God
sources.raw_question: Is Jesus a mere man in whom the Word dwelt as an extended divine power, as the Spirit dwelt in the prophets, so that Jesus and Christ are two distinct subjects?

question: What does Christ's promise in Revelation 3:20 to 'sup with' believers signify about communion with him?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter I.
sources.answer: It signifies a mutual fellowship. Christ sups with believers by delighting in and refreshing himself with his own graces, the fruits of the Spirit he has bestowed on them, as the Song of Songs pictures him eating the fruits of his garden. In turn, believers sup with him as he provides spiritual dainties for them, a feast and wedding, which completes the fellowship.
sources.quote: Christ will sup with believers: he refreshes himself with his own graces in them, by his Spirit bestowed on them. The Lord Christ is exceedingly delighted in tasting of the sweet fruits of the Spirit in the saints.
sources.raw_question: What does Christ's promise in Revelation 3:20 to 'sup with' believers signify about communion with him?

question: Did Christ choose the twelve apostles as a type or figure of the twelve Æons that the Valentinians say were produced by Anthropos and Ecclesia?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXI.—The twelve apostles were not a type of the Æons.
sources.answer: No. If the apostles were chosen to typify Æons, the Saviour would have typified all of them, especially the superior and earlier Ogdoad and Decad, not only the junior and inferior ones. Moreover, Christ also sent out seventy disciples. On the Valentinians' own reasoning these would have to typify seventy more Æons, making eighty-two rather than thirty. So the theory is inconsistent and the apostles are no type of the Æons.
sources.quote: if the twelve apostles were chosen with this object, that the number of the twelve Æons might be indicated by means of them, then the seventy also ought to have been chosen to be the type of seventy Æons
sources.raw_question: Did Christ choose the twelve apostles as a type or figure of the twelve Æons that the Valentinians say were produced by Anthropos and Ecclesia?

question: What is the "living water" that flows from the Fount of Life?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter XV. The Holy Spirit is Life equally with the Father and the Son, in truth whether the Father be mentioned, with Whom is the Fount of Life, or the Son, that Fount can be none other than the Holy Spirit.
sources.answer: It is the Holy Spirit. Whether the Fount is the Father or the Son, it is not a fount of created water but of divine grace, which is the Holy Spirit. Christ calls this "living water" when speaking to the Samaritan woman. This water purifies the mind and washes away sin.
sources.quote: we certainly do not understand a fount of that water which is created, but the Fount of that divine grace, that is, of the Holy Spirit, for He is the living water.
sources.raw_question: What is the "living water" that flows from the Fount of Life?

question: Is it a sin to take pleasure in thinking about unlawful things, even without deciding to carry them out in action?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > There is a Kind of Hidden Wedlock in the Inner Man. Unlawful Pleasures of the Thoughts.
sources.answer: Yes. When the mind gladly holds and ponders unlawful things that it should have rejected at once, this cannot be denied to be a sin. It is far less grave than determining to commit the act outwardly. Pardon must still be sought for such thoughts through the prayer "Forgive us our debts," joined with forgiving others.
sources.quote: it cannot be denied to be a sin, but far less than if it were also determined to accomplished it in outward act. And therefore pardon must be sought for such thoughts too
sources.raw_question: Is it a sin to take pleasure in thinking about unlawful things, even without deciding to carry them out in action?

question: In a single human being, can sins of thought alone (the 'woman' eating without the 'man') be condemned apart from the whole person?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > There is a Kind of Hidden Wedlock in the Inner Man. Unlawful Pleasures of the Thoughts.
sources.answer: No. With Adam and Eve, each bore a separate person, so Eve alone could have been punished if she alone had eaten. Within one human being, the lower and higher functions belong to one person. That person as a whole will be condemned for sins of thought unless they are pardoned through the grace of the Mediator.
sources.quote: For here is one person, one human being, and he as a whole will be condemned, unless those things which, as lacking the will to do, and yet having the will to please the mind with them, are perceived to be sins of thought alone
sources.raw_question: In a single human being, can sins of thought alone (the 'woman' eating without the 'man') be condemned apart from the whole person?

question: How does the Genesis account of the serpent, the woman, and the man figure the process of temptation and sin within one human mind?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > After premising the difference between wisdom and knowledge, he points out a kind of trinity in that which is properly called knowledge; but one which, although we have reached in it the inner man, is not yet to be called the image of God. > There is a Kind of Hidden Wedlock in the Inner Man. Unlawful Pleasures of the Thoughts.
sources.answer: It figures a hidden 'wedlock' within one mind. The serpent is the sensuous movement of the soul that invites the reason concerned with temporal things to enjoy them as a private good. To consent to this is to eat of the forbidden tree. If the consent stays in the pleasure of thought, the woman alone has eaten. If the mind determines to commit the sin in act, the woman has given the food to her husband, because the higher intention that commands the bodily members has yielded.
sources.quote: then, as it were, the serpent discourses with the woman. And to consent to this allurement, is to eat of the forbidden tree.
sources.raw_question: How does the Genesis account of the serpent, the woman, and the man figure the process of temptation and sin within one human mind?

question: Should believers think of God the Father as austere, angry, and implacable toward them?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part I. Of Communion with God the Father. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: No. Such hard thoughts of God are a slander that grieves the Spirit of God and serves Satan's design. From the beginning Satan overthrew mankind by putting hard thoughts of God into our first parents. God himself protests against such thoughts in Zion, and he commends his love to us. These thoughts bear the bitter fruit of estrangement, unbelief, and drawing back from God.
sources.quote: Now, there is not any thing more grievous to the Lord, nor more subservient to the design of Satan upon the soul, than such thoughts as these.
sources.raw_question: Should believers think of God the Father as austere, angry, and implacable toward them?

question: Does Paul's prayer in 1 Thessalonians 5:23 show that body, soul and spirit together share in one salvation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter VI.—God will bestow salvation upon the whole nature of man, consisting of body and soul in close union, since the Word took it upon Him, and adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, of whom our bodies are, and are termed, the temples.
sources.answer: Yes. Paul would have no reason to pray that spirit, soul, and body be preserved until the coming of the Lord unless he knew they would be reunited and share one and the same salvation. He calls 'perfect' those who present all three to the Lord without offence.
sources.quote: Now what was his object in praying that these three—that is, soul, body, and spirit—might be preserved to the coming of the Lord, unless he was aware of the [future] reintegration and union of the three
sources.raw_question: Does Paul's prayer in 1 Thessalonians 5:23 show that body, soul and spirit together share in one salvation?

question: How could David know the heavenly converse in which the Lord speaks to the Lord, and what does this show about the Holy Spirit's role in Scripture?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book VII > The seventh book shows from various statements made to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and from the words of the Lord, that the word “Lord” is not expressive of essence, according to Eunomius' exposition, but of dignity. and after many notable remarks concerning “the Spirit” and the Lord, he shows that Eunomius, from his own words, is found to argue in favour of orthodoxy, though without intending it, and to be struck by his own shafts.
sources.answer: David spoke "in the Spirit," not from his human nature. The holy men are inspired by the power of the Spirit, which is why all Scripture is called "given by inspiration of God" as the teaching of the Divine afflatus. Christ's question about how David's son can be David's Lord confirms that David spoke by the Spirit.
sources.quote: Thus it is by the power of the Spirit that the holy men who are under Divine influence are inspired, and every Scripture is for this reason said to be “given by inspiration of God,” because it is the teaching of the Divine afflatus.
sources.raw_question: How could David know the heavenly converse in which the Lord speaks to the Lord, and what does this show about the Holy Spirit's role in Scripture?

question: Why are the Scriptures perfect, and why do humans lack full knowledge of the mysteries they contain?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXVIII.—Perfect knowledge cannot be attained in the present life: many questions must be submissively left in the hands of God.
sources.answer: The Scriptures are perfect because they were spoken by the Word of God and His Spirit. Humans are inferior to, and later in existence than, the Word and the Spirit. For that reason we lack complete knowledge of God's mysteries.
sources.quote: the Scriptures are indeed perfect, since they were spoken by the Word of God and His Spirit; but we, inasmuch as we are inferior to, and later in existence than, the Word of God and His Spirit
sources.raw_question: Why are the Scriptures perfect, and why do humans lack full knowledge of the mysteries they contain?

question: What is the name that, according to Malachi's prophecy, is glorified among the Gentiles?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVII.—Proof that God did not appoint the Levitical dispensation for His own sake, or as requiring such service; for He does, in fact, need nothing from men.
sources.answer: It is the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. No other name is glorified among the Gentiles than that of our Lord, through whom both the Father and man are glorified. So Malachi's "My name is glorified among the Gentiles" refers to Christ's name, which is glorified throughout the world in the Church.
sources.quote: But what other name is there which is glorified among the Gentiles than that of our Lord, by whom the Father is glorified, and man also?
sources.raw_question: What is the name that, according to Malachi's prophecy, is glorified among the Gentiles?

question: Is the Church's offering through Jesus Christ an offering made to the Father's name?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XVII.—Proof that God did not appoint the Levitical dispensation for His own sake, or as requiring such service; for He does, in fact, need nothing from men.
sources.answer: Yes. The Church makes offerings to the omnipotent God through Jesus Christ, and the Son's name belongs to the Father. So the Father rightly says that incense and a pure sacrifice are offered to "My name." Following the Apocalypse, the incense is the prayers of the saints.
sources.quote: Since, therefore, the name of the Son belongs to the Father, and since in the omnipotent God the Church makes offerings through Jesus Christ, He says well on both these grounds,
sources.raw_question: Is the Church's offering through Jesus Christ an offering made to the Father's name?

question: Why was it fitting that the Son of God should die in the flesh, given that demons claim superiority over humans because they lack bodies?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > Other Advantages of the Incarnation.
sources.answer: Because by uniting human flesh to God and dying in that flesh, the Son showed that lacking flesh gives demons no claim to be above man. His death also showed that seeming immortality gives them no claim to be worshipped as gods. In this way the proud spirits, who pose as mediators in order to deceive, are exposed.
sources.quote: chiefly because the Son of God deigned to die also in the same flesh, lest they, because they seem to be immortal, should therefore succeed in getting themselves worshipped as gods
sources.raw_question: Why was it fitting that the Son of God should die in the flesh, given that demons claim superiority over humans because they lack bodies?

question: If Christ were a creature, would he share the creature's subjection to vanity, bondage, corruption and anxious waiting described in Romans 8?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book XII
sources.answer: Yes, and that shows the premise is impious. Paul teaches that the creature waits in long expectation, is subjected to vanity against its will, and is enslaved to corruption. If Christ were a creature, he would have to hope, serve as a bondservant, dwell in a corruptible nature and await freedom into a glory that is ours. It is absurd to say this of the one by whose gift we ourselves progress.
sources.quote: If, therefore, Christ is a creature, it must needs be that He is in uncertainty, hoping always with a tedious expectation, and that His long expectation, rather than ours, is waiting
sources.raw_question: If Christ were a creature, would he share the creature's subjection to vanity, bondage, corruption and anxious waiting described in Romans 8?

question: Were God's dispensations for mankind, both in the Old Testament and in Christ, accomplished through the Holy Spirit?

sources.author: Basil of Caesarea
sources.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
sources.section: De Spiritu Sancto. > That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable from the Father and the Son, alike in the creation of perceptible objects, in the dispensation of human affairs, and in the judgment to come.
sources.answer: Yes. Whether one looks at the patriarchal blessings, the law, types, prophecies, and the signs of just men, or at the coming of the Lord in the flesh, all is through the Spirit. No one can gainsay that the dispensations of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ were accomplished through the grace of the Spirit.
sources.quote: or on the other hand the things done in the dispensation of the coming of our Lord in the flesh;—all is through the Spirit.
sources.raw_question: Were God's dispensations for mankind, both in the Old Testament and in Christ, accomplished through the Holy Spirit?

question: Should Christ's flesh, body and passion make us doubt his Godhead?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VII
sources.answer: No. Christ asked to be believed on his word so that his condescension in becoming human would not shake our faith. If his flesh and sufferings seem to make his Godhead doubtful, we should still believe from the evidence of his works that God is in God, God is from God, and they are One.
sources.quote: If His flesh, His body, His passion seem to make His Godhead doubtful, let us at least believe, on the evidence of the works, that God is in God and God is from God, and that They are One.
sources.raw_question: Should Christ's flesh, body and passion make us doubt his Godhead?

question: Was the baptism of the disciples at Ephesus, who had received John's baptism and then were baptized in the Name of Jesus, a repetition of baptism?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Chapter III. The statement of the Apostle, that all things are of the Father by the Son, does not separate the Spirit from Their company, since what is referred to one Person is also attributed to each. So those baptized in the Name of Christ are held to be baptized in the Name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, if, that is, there is belief in the Three Persons, otherwise the baptism will be null. This also applies to baptism in the Name of the Holy Spirit. If because of one passage the Holy Spirit is separated from the Father and the Son, it will necessarily follow from other passages that the Father will be subordinated to the Son. The Son is worshipped by angels, not by the Spirit, for the latter is His witness, not His servant. Where the Son is spoken of as being before all, it is to be understood of creatures. The great dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the absence of forgiveness for the sin against Him. How it is that such sin cannot be forgiven, and how the Spirit is one.
sources.answer: No. Baptism was not repeated but administered differently, for there is only one baptism. John baptized unto repentance in the Name of the coming Jesus, not in Christ's Name or with faith in the Spirit. Where the complete sacrament is lacking, there is no baptism at all.
sources.quote: So they were baptized in the Name of Jesus Christ, and baptism was not repeated in their case, but administered differently, for there is but one baptism.
sources.raw_question: Was the baptism of the disciples at Ephesus, who had received John's baptism and then were baptized in the Name of Jesus, a repetition of baptism?

question: What does the high priest's breastplate bearing the names of Israel on his heart and shoulders signify in relation to Christ?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: It represents the priesthood of Christ, who bears the names of all his people before his Father in the heavenly holy of holies. The high priest wore the names engraven like seals on his heart and on his shoulders as a memorial before the Lord, and this foreshadows Christ's continual intercession and remembrance of his own before the Father.
sources.quote: both representing the priesthood of Christ, who bears the names of all his before his Father in the “holy of holies,”
sources.raw_question: What does the high priest's breastplate bearing the names of Israel on his heart and shoulders signify in relation to Christ?

question: What is meant by the spouse's request in the Song of Songs to be set as a seal upon Christ's heart and upon his arm?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter IV.
sources.answer: The seal on the heart signifies near, inward, tender love that leaves a lasting impression of the beloved, while the seal on the arm signifies the manifestation and power of that love. The heart is the hidden fountain and the arm is its visible expression, so the request is both for Christ's continual mindfulness of the soul with his power exerted to preserve it, and for the hidden love of his heart to be made evident by its fruits.
sources.quote: The heart is the fountain, but close and hidden; the arm is manifestation and power.
sources.raw_question: What is meant by the spouse's request in the Song of Songs to be set as a seal upon Christ's heart and upon his arm?

question: How do Scripture's sayings that the Son judges by the Spirit and casts out devils by the Spirit of God bear on the unity of divine action?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: On 'Not Three Gods.'
sources.answer: They show that the Son perfects every power through the Holy Spirit. Christ's statement that he casts out devils by the Spirit of God is a partial description that stands for every form of doing good, because the action of the Persons is one. The name drawn from an operation cannot be divided among many when the result of their joint operation is one.
sources.quote: the name derived from operation cannot be divided among many where the result of their mutual operation is one.
sources.raw_question: How do Scripture's sayings that the Son judges by the Spirit and casts out devils by the Spirit of God bear on the unity of divine action?

question: Is the contemplation of God the final end of all human action and the fullness of joy?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > The Texts of Scripture Explained Respecting the Subjection of the Son to the Father, Which Have Been Misunderstood. Christ Will Not So Give Up the Kingdom to the Father, as to Take It Away from Himself. The Beholding Him is the Promised End of All Actions. The Holy Spirit is Sufficient to Our Blessedness Equally with the Father.
sources.answer: Yes. Contemplating God is held out as the end of all actions and the everlasting fullness of joy. When we see him as he is, nothing further will be sought, because nothing more will remain to be sought. Faith now purifies the heart for this vision, which is the reward of faith.
sources.quote: For this contemplation is held forth to us as the end of all actions, and the everlasting fullness of joy.
sources.raw_question: Is the contemplation of God the final end of all human action and the fullness of joy?

question: In what does eternal life, the chief good of the righteous, consist according to John 17:3?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The unity and equality of the Trinity are demonstrated out of the Scriptures; and the true interpretation is given of those texts which are wrongly alleged against the equality of the Son. > Diverse Things are Spoken Concerning the Same Christ, on Account of the Diverse Natures of the One Hypostasis [Theanthropic Person]. Why It is Said that the Father Will Not Judge, But Has Given Judgment to the Son.
sources.answer: Eternal life is to know the one true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. But Christ is to be known in the glory he had with the Father before the world was, not merely in the form of the Son of man seen at the judgment. This sight comes when Christ delivers up the kingdom to God the Father and the good servant enters into the joy of his Lord.
sources.quote: But what is life eternal, except “that they may know Thee,” He says, “the One true God, and Jesus Christ, whom Thou hast sent?” but know Him now in that glory of which He says to the Father, “Which I had with Thee before the world was.”
sources.raw_question: In what does eternal life, the chief good of the righteous, consist according to John 17:3?

question: Does Israel's disobedience prove that the God who gave the law was limited in power?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XV.—At first God deemed it sufficient to inscribe the natural law, or the Decalogue, upon the hearts of men; but afterwards He found it necessary to bridle, with the yoke of the Mosaic law, the desires of the Jews, who were abusing their liberty; and even to add some special commands, because of the hardness of their hearts.
sources.answer: No. The same failure appears under the Christian dispensation, where many are called but few are chosen and some are wolves in sheep's clothing. God has always preserved human freedom and self-government while urging obedience. This is so that the disobedient may be justly condemned and the obedient honoured with immortality.
sources.quote: God has always preserved freedom, and the power of self-government in man, while at the same time He issued His own exhortations, in order that those who do not obey Him should be righteously judged (condemned)
sources.raised_by_detail: those who say the lawgiver was limited in power
sources.raw_question: Does Israel's disobedience prove that the God who gave the law was limited in power?

question: How does Christ's obedience on the cross undo the disobedience of the fall?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIX.—A comparison is instituted between the disobedient and sinning Eve and the Virgin Mary, her patroness. Various and discordant heresies are mentioned.
sources.answer: Christ recapitulates the fall by reversing it. The disobedience that happened in connection with a tree is undone by the obedience he showed when he hung on a tree. In the same way the sin of the first-formed man is corrected by the First-begotten, and the bonds that tied humanity to death are loosed.
sources.quote: was making a recapitulation of that disobedience which had occurred in connection with a tree, through the obedience which was [exhibited by Himself when He hung] upon a tree
sources.raw_question: How does Christ's obedience on the cross undo the disobedience of the fall?

question: Was the one whom the Virgin Mary conceived and bore truly God?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XIX.—A comparison is instituted between the disobedient and sinning Eve and the Virgin Mary, her patroness. Various and discordant heresies are mentioned.
sources.answer: Yes. At the angel's announcement Mary received the glad tidings that she would bear God, and she obeyed his word. Her obedience reversed Eve's disobedience: the race that fell into bondage to death through a virgin is rescued through a virgin.
sources.quote: so did the latter, by an angelic communication, receive the glad tidings that she should sustain (portaret) God, being obedient to His word
sources.raw_question: Was the one whom the Virgin Mary conceived and bore truly God?

question: When a righteous man becomes God's friend, does God begin to love him with a new love that He did not have before?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > What is Said of God in Time, is Said Relatively, Not Accidentally.
sources.answer: No. The righteous man is the one who is changed. God, for whom past things have not passed away and future things are already done, loved all His saints before the foundation of the world, as He predestinated them. They are said to begin to be loved when they are converted only because that is how human affections can grasp it.
sources.quote: far be it from us to say, that God loves any one in time with as it were a new love, which was not in Him before, with whom things gone by have not passed away and things future have been already done.
sources.raw_question: When a righteous man becomes God's friend, does God begin to love him with a new love that He did not have before?

question: Is it reasonable to hold, as some Arians did, that the Word emptied itself in the incarnation so as to become like a human soul, dormant in infancy and growing in wisdom?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 7: Whether the Father’s omniscience and eternity are not one, and the same with the Son’s, being alike described, and in the same phrases ?
sources.answer: No. On the Arian scheme itself this makes the Logos, the greatest being next to God who once framed and governed the whole universe, become a child in understanding. It turns the mystery of 'God manifest in flesh' into God confined and locked up in flesh.
sources.quote: This is making the Adyos, that greatest and best of beings, (upon the Arian scheme,) next to God himself, become achild in understanding; though once wise enough to frame and govern the whole universe.
sources.raised_by_detail: a late writer, in the name of Dr. Clarke and the Arians
sources.raw_question: Is it reasonable to hold, as some Arians did, that the Word emptied itself in the incarnation so as to become like a human soul, dormant in infancy and growing in wisdom?

question: Does the Council of Antioch's condemnation of homoousios (against Paul of Samosata) count against the Nicene doctrine of consubstantiality?

sources.author: Daniel Waterland
sources.section: Query 29: Whether private reasoning, in a matter above our comprehension, be a safer rule to go by, than the general sense and judgment of the primitive Church, in the fi
sources.answer: No. Antioch condemned the word only as Paul of Samosata had misunderstood and misapplied it, in a Sabellian sense of individual consubstantiality. It established the very same doctrine as the Nicene Fathers. As Hilary remarked, the word was ill understood then but rightly received later.
sources.quote: They condemned the word, as it had been misunderstood and misapplied by Paul of Samosata; but established the very same doctrine with the Nicene Fathers.
sources.raw_question: Does the Council of Antioch's condemnation of homoousios (against Paul of Samosata) count against the Nicene doctrine of consubstantiality?

question: Is it certain that all human beings will to be blessed and not to be wretched?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Will to Possess Blessedness is One in All, But the Variety of Wills is Very Great Concerning that Blessedness Itself.
sources.answer: Yes. Even Cicero the Academic, who doubted everything, chose this as the one certain starting point no one doubts: we all will to be blessed. Augustine refuses to call it false, though it raises a further puzzle, since not all will to live in the way in which alone one can live blessedly.
sources.quote: who, when he wanted in the dialogue Hortensius to find some certain thing, of which no one doubted, from which to start his argument, says, We certainly all will to be blessed? Far be it from me to say this is false.
sources.raw_question: Is it certain that all human beings will to be blessed and not to be wretched?

question: Is to live blessedly simply to live as one pleases?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Will to Possess Blessedness is One in All, But the Variety of Wills is Very Great Concerning that Blessedness Itself.
