sources.answer: No. Augustine endorses Cicero's refutation of this view. To will what is not fitting is itself most miserable, and it is less miserable not to obtain what one wills than to will what one ought not. So living according to one's own pleasure cannot be what blessedness is.
sources.quote: But this is indeed false. For to will what is not fitting, is itself most miserable; neither is it so miserable not to obtain what one wills, as to will to obtain what one ought not.
sources.raised_by_detail: people prompt to dispute, cited by Cicero
sources.raw_question: Is to live blessedly simply to live as one pleases?

question: Is the supreme Father a God who exercises judgment, or is he (as the Gnostics claim) a Father who neither judges nor cares about human affairs?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book V > Chapter XXVII.—The future judgment by Christ. Communion with and separation from the divine being. The eternal punishment of unbelievers.
sources.answer: The Father exercises judgment. If he did not judge, he would either lack judicial power or consent to all deeds, and all persons would be in the same condition. The coming of Christ, who separates believers from unbelievers and sends the goats into the fire prepared by his Father, would then be pointless and even absurd.
sources.quote: If the Father, then, does not exercise judgment, [it follows] that judgment does not belong to Him, or that He consents to all those actions which take place; and if He does not judge, all persons will be equal, and accounted in the same condition.
sources.raised_by_detail: Gnostics who imagine another Father who neither cares nor exercises providence
sources.raw_question: Is the supreme Father a God who exercises judgment, or is he (as the Gnostics claim) a Father who neither judges nor cares about human affairs?

question: If God could simply have spoken a word to undo the curse, does it follow that the Saviour could be a creature and the incarnation of the true Word unnecessary?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse II > Texts Explained; Sixthly, Proverbs viii. 22, Continued. Our Lord not said in Scripture to be 'created,' or the works to be 'begotten.' 'In the beginning' means in the case of the works 'from the beginning.' Scripture passages explained. We are made by God first, begotten next; creatures by nature, sons by grace. Christ begotten first, made or created afterwards. Sense of 'First-born of the dead;' of 'First-born among many brethren;' of 'First-born of all creation,' contrasted with 'Only-begotten.' Further interpretation of 'beginning of ways,' and 'for the works.' Why a creature could not redeem; why redemption was necessary at all. Texts which contrast the Word and the works.
sources.answer: No. One must consider what was expedient for mankind, not merely what is possible with God, as God acted through Noah's ark, Moses and the judges though he could have done otherwise. A mere word of pardon would have left man as Adam was, holding grace from without and not united to the body, so he would keep falling and need endless pardon. The Word taking flesh unites grace to the body and truly frees man.
sources.quote: we must consider what was expedient for mankind, and not what simply is possible with God
sources.raw_question: If God could simply have spoken a word to undo the curse, does it follow that the Saviour could be a creature and the incarnation of the true Word unnecessary?

question: Why was the death of Christ chosen as the means of human redemption, when an omnipotent God could have freed humanity in innumerable other ways?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > The Remains of Death and the Evil Things of the World Turn to Good for the Elect. How Fitly the Death of Christ Was Chosen, that We Might Be Justified in His Blood. What the Anger of God is.
sources.answer: Christ's death was fittingly chosen above all other ways. In it nothing of His divinity was diminished or changed, while through the humanity He assumed He, the eternal Son of God who was also Son of man, rendered an undue temporal death to free men from the eternal death that was due. Because He had no sin of His own and was led to death undeservedly, the devil can justly detain no one who has put on Christ.
sources.quote: that death, I say, wherein neither was anything diminished or changed from His divinity, and so great benefit was conferred upon men, from the humanity which He took upon Him
sources.raw_question: Why was the death of Christ chosen as the means of human redemption, when an omnipotent God could have freed humanity in innumerable other ways?

question: Could the prophecies fulfilled in Jesus have been spoken about some other person and matched Jesus only by chance?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIV.—Proof against the Marcionites, that the prophets referred in all their predictions to our Christ.
sources.answer: No. All the prophets foretold these same things, yet none of them happened to any of the ancients, or later prophets would not have placed them in the last times. At no one else's death did the sun set at midday, the veil tear, the earth quake and the dead rise. No one else rose on the third day, was taken into heaven, or had the nations believe in his name. Since all these signs come together only in the Lord, the prophets spoke of him alone.
sources.quote: Therefore the prophets spake not of any one else but of the Lord, in whom all these aforesaid tokens concurred.
sources.raw_question: Could the prophecies fulfilled in Jesus have been spoken about some other person and matched Jesus only by chance?

question: In the sacrifice of Isaac, was the God who commanded the sacrifice a different speaker from the angel who stopped it?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > The appearances of God to the Old Testament saints are discussed. > The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine Appearances to the Fathers Wrought by the Ministry of Angels. An Objection Drawn from the Mode of Speech Removed. That the Appearing of God to Abraham Himself, Just as that to Moses, Was Wrought by Angels. The Same Thing is Proved by the Law Being Given to Moses by Angels. What Has Been Said in This Book, and What Remains to Be Said in the Next.
sources.answer: No. It is absurd to think God commanded Isaac's death and an angel overruled him. The angel says "thou hast not withheld thy son... on account of me," which can only mean the one who gave the command. So it was God speaking by an angel.
sources.quote: Was then the God of Abraham the same as the angel, or was it not rather God by an angel?
sources.raw_question: In the sacrifice of Isaac, was the God who commanded the sacrifice a different speaker from the angel who stopped it?

question: Does a relative term always need a corresponding reciprocal name, so that the absence of one shows the term is not relative?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics put forward, not out of the Scriptures, but from their own conceptions. And first he refutes the objection, that to beget and to be begotten, or that to be begotten and not-begotten, being different, are therefore different substances, and shows that these things are spoken of God relatively, and not according to substance. > In Relative Things that are Reciprocal, Names are Sometimes Wanting.
sources.answer: No. In many relatives no name exists by which the two terms correspond in word, though the relation is real. 'Earnest' is plainly relative, since an earnest is always an earnest of something, yet we cannot say 'the Father of the earnest.' With 'gift' a reciprocal word can be found ('the giver of the gift'), with 'earnest' it cannot. This is a matter of usage, not of the relation itself.
sources.quote: For it is the case in many relatives, that no designation is to be found by which those things which bear relation to each other may [in name] mutually correspond to each other.
sources.raw_question: Does a relative term always need a corresponding reciprocal name, so that the absence of one shows the term is not relative?

question: If the Gnostic Pleroma had been shaped by the Father's foresight for the sake of the created world, would it still be superior to creation?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XV.—No account can be given of these productions.
sources.answer: No. If the Pleroma was arranged for the sake of creation, it was not formed for its own sake. It would then be like a clay model made only for the sake of the bronze or gold statue. In that case creation would have greater honour than the Pleroma, which overturns the Gnostics' own ranking of spiritual Aeons above the material world.
sources.quote: then creation will have greater honour than the Pleroma, if, for its sake, those things [above] were produced
sources.raw_question: If the Gnostic Pleroma had been shaped by the Father's foresight for the sake of the created world, would it still be superior to creation?

question: In Romans 5:6-10, how do Paul's terms 'weak,' 'ungodly,' 'sinners,' and 'enemies of God' relate to one another?

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.section: On the Holy Trinity. > He expounds this trinity that he has found in knowledge by commending Christian faith. > There Was No Other More Suitable Way of Freeing Man from the Misery of Mortality Than The Incarnation of the Word. The Merits Which are Called Ours are the Gifts of God.
sources.answer: Paul describes the same people with paired terms, one mild and one harsh. 'Sinners' corresponds to 'weak,' and 'enemies of God' corresponds to 'ungodly.' Our weakness before grace was severe enough to be called impiety, yet it remained weakness, which is why it needed a physician, the Saviour.
sources.quote: Those whom he called weak, the same he called ungodly. Weakness seems something slight; but sometimes it is such as to be called impiety. Yet except it were weakness, it would not need a physician
sources.raw_question: In Romans 5:6-10, how do Paul's terms 'weak,' 'ungodly,' 'sinners,' and 'enemies of God' relate to one another?

question: Does explaining creation as an image of higher realms lead to an infinite regress of images?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XVI.—The Creator of the world either produced of Himself the images of things to be made, or the Pleroma was formed after the image of some previous system; and so on ad infinitum.
sources.answer: Yes. If creation is an image of things above, those must in turn be images of others above them, and so on without end, yielding innumerable images of images. Basilides tried to escape this with 365 heavens formed by succession, but he still must say either that the Unnameable formed the model of himself or that some further power lies above him.
sources.quote: why should we not affirm that those are, in turn, images of others above them, and those above these again, of others, and thus go on supposing innumerable images of images?
sources.raw_question: Does explaining creation as an image of higher realms lead to an infinite regress of images?

question: If heaven is God's throne and earth his footstool, and heaven and earth will pass away, does it follow that the God who sits upon them must also pass away?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter III.—Answer to the cavils of the Gnostics. We are not to suppose that the true God can be changed, or come to an end because the heavens, which are His throne and the earth, His footstool, shall pass away.
sources.answer: No. The objection assumes God sits like a man and is contained within bounds, whereas God contains all things and is not contained. Scripture plainly distinguishes what passes away (the heavens and earth, which wax old like a garment) from the Lord who remains the same and whose years do not fail. Isaiah likewise says God's salvation and righteousness endure forever.
sources.quote: For they do not know what God is, but they imagine that He sits after the fashion of a man, and is contained within bounds, but does not contain.
sources.raw_question: If heaven is God's throne and earth his footstool, and heaven and earth will pass away, does it follow that the God who sits upon them must also pass away?

question: Is it compatible with the divine nature to have sex and lines of begetters and begotten among gods, as pagan mythology teaches?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Deities endowed with sex and lineages of begetters and begotten are incompatible with the pure and mighty nature of the Godhead. What is divine and eternal must be one, without distinction of sex. What is self-existent cannot have left outside itself anything superior to itself.
sources.quote: it was sure that that which is Divine and eternal must be one without distinction of sex, for that which is self-existent cannot have left outside itself anything superior to itself.
sources.raised_by_detail: pagan teachers narrating births and lineages of gods
sources.raw_question: Is it compatible with the divine nature to have sex and lines of begetters and begotten among gods, as pagan mythology teaches?

question: Can God be heedless and indifferent to the affairs of the world He has created?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Neglect of a world created by Himself cannot worthily be attributed to God. Hilary rejects the opinion of those who admit God's existence but deny His care for human affairs.
sources.quote: It could not hold that neglect of a world created by Himself was worthily to be attributed to God
sources.raised_by_detail: those who proclaimed God heedless of men (Epicureans)
sources.raw_question: Can God be heedless and indifferent to the affairs of the world He has created?

question: Does the rain coming down 'like rain upon a fleece' in Psalm 72 refer to the gift of the Holy Spirit at Christ's coming?

sources.author: Ambrose of Milan
sources.section: On the Holy Spirit. > Book I. > Preface.
sources.answer: Yes. Scripture promised a health-giving shower of grace on the whole earth, to water the world with the dew of the Divine Spirit at the Saviour's coming. The Lord has come bringing the heavenly drops with him, so those who were thirsty now drink in the Divine Spirit inwardly.
sources.quote: The divine Scriptures promised us this rain upon the whole earth, to water the world with the dew of the Divine Spirit at the coming of the Saviour.
sources.raw_question: Does the rain coming down 'like rain upon a fleece' in Psalm 72 refer to the gift of the Holy Spirit at Christ's coming?

question: What do Christ's anointing by the Spirit and the voice from heaven at His baptism show about the Son's nature?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book VIII
sources.answer: They show that the incarnate Son shares the Father's nature. The Father, designated as the Spirit of the Lord, anoints and sends the Son. The Son cannot rest upon Himself, come to Himself from heaven, or give Himself the title of Son. All this was shown for our faith, so that we might recognise that the unity of the divine nature dwells in the Son even after He became man.
sources.quote: in order that under the mystery of a complete and true birth we should recognise that the unity of the nature dwells in the Son Who had begun to be also man
sources.raw_question: What do Christ's anointing by the Spirit and the voice from heaven at His baptism show about the Son's nature?

question: Would it be consistent with God's character to create rational human beings only for them to perish entirely at death?

sources.author: Hilary of Poitiers
sources.section: De Trinitate or On the Trinity. > Book I
sources.answer: No. Even unaided reason judges it unworthy of God to give man a share in His thought and wisdom only to sentence him to eternal death. It would be equally unworthy to create him out of nothing merely so that he may perish. The rational purpose of creation is that non-existent things should come to be, not that existing things should cease to be. Moreover, true faith in God would otherwise go unrewarded.
sources.quote: For, on the only rational theory of creation, its purpose was that things non-existent should come into being, not that things existing should cease to be.
sources.raw_question: Would it be consistent with God's character to create rational human beings only for them to perish entirely at death?

question: Is asking Jesus for help in the Gospels different in kind from asking the apostles for help?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. Jesus worked his mighty works in his own right as the Messiah of God. The apostles refused all self-dependence and worked everything in the name and by the power of Jesus Christ. So petitions to Jesus are not parallel to requests made to the apostles.
sources.quote: Jesus in his own right, as the Messiah of God, wrought his mighty works; and they, utterly repudiating self-dependence, (Acts 3:12) wrought all in the name and by the power of Jesus Christ
sources.raw_question: Is asking Jesus for help in the Gospels different in kind from asking the apostles for help?

question: Did Jesus teach people to pray to him and to trust in him as they trust in God?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. He urged the Samaritan woman to ask him for living water. He invited the weary to come to him and rebuked the Jews for not coming to him, and coming to him can only mean prayer. He also asked for the same trust given to God: 'ye believe in God, believe also in Me.' Reliance on a love, power and wisdom beyond any human's is the essence of worship, and Christ claimed it for himself.
sources.quote: confidence in a love, reliance on a power, dependence on a wisdom beyond that of our fellowmen and beyond our own – this, is the soul of prayer, this is the essence of worship. But this trust He solicits for himself.
sources.raw_question: Did Jesus teach people to pray to him and to trust in him as they trust in God?

question: Did Jesus accept praise of the kind given to God when the crowds cried 'Hosanna'?

sources.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
sources.work: The Rock of Ages; or, Scripture Testimony to the One Eternal Godhead (later: The Trinity)
sources.section: Chapter 4. That Scripture, in the Old and the New Testament alike, proves the coequal Deity of Jesus Christ with that of the eternal Father; – by a comparison of the attributes, the majesty, and the claims of the Father and the Son: by the appearances of God to the Old Testament saints: by the direct and Divine worship paid to Christ: by the conjunction of the Father and the Son in Divine offices: by explicit assertions that Christ is Jehovah and God.
sources.answer: Yes. When the chief priests objected, Jesus did not rebuke this thanksgiving. Instead he defended it, saying the stones would cry out, and he applied to it the psalm about praise perfected from the mouths of babes. This shows the praise was a rightful tribute, comparable to the angels' 'Glory to God in the highest.'
sources.quote: instead of rebuking this giving of thanks, He says, “I tell you if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out.
sources.raw_question: Did Jesus accept praise of the kind given to God when the crowds cried 'Hosanna'?

question: Was the Spirit of God present and active with mankind in all God's dispensations from the beginning, including the prophetic age?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book IV > Chapter XXXIII.—Whosoever confesses that one God is the author of both Testaments, and diligently reads the Scriptures in company with the presbyters of the Church, is a true spiritual disciple; and he will rightly understand and interpret all that the prophets have declared respecting Christ and the liberty of the New Testament.
sources.answer: Yes. The Spirit of God was present with mankind from the beginning in all of God's dispensations. He announced things future, revealed things present and narrated things past. The spiritual disciple who receives this same Spirit can therefore judge all things.
sources.quote: truly receiving the Spirit of God, who was from the beginning, in all the dispensations of God, present with mankind, and announced things future, revealed things present, and narrated things past
sources.raw_question: Was the Spirit of God present and active with mankind in all God's dispensations from the beginning, including the prophetic age?

question: Does the human soul exist in previous bodies before its present one, as the doctrine of transmigration of souls teaches?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXIII.—Absurdity of the doctrine of the transmigration of souls.
sources.answer: No. Since the soul remembers nothing of a former existence but perceives the things of this life, it never existed in other bodies, never did things it has no knowledge of, and never knew things it cannot now contemplate. Rather, just as each person receives his body through God's skilful working, so he receives his own soul from God.
sources.quote: If, therefore, the soul remembers nothing of what took place in a former state of existence, but has a perception of those things which are here, it follows that she never existed in other bodies
sources.raw_question: Does the human soul exist in previous bodies before its present one, as the doctrine of transmigration of souls teaches?

question: In the resurrection, will people rise with their own bodies and souls, and when will this happen?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XXXIII.—Absurdity of the doctrine of the transmigration of souls.
sources.answer: Yes, they will rise with their own bodies and souls. When the number of mankind that God predetermined in His counsel is complete, those enrolled for eternal life will rise with their own bodies, souls and spirits in which they pleased God. Those worthy of punishment will go into it with their own souls and bodies. Begetting and marriage will then cease, so that the Father's plan is fully carried out.
sources.quote: all those who have been enrolled for life [eternal] shall rise again, having their own bodies, and having also their own souls, and their own spirits, in which they had pleased God.
sources.raw_question: In the resurrection, will people rise with their own bodies and souls, and when will this happen?

question: Why did the Word take human nature and become one with it?

sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.section: Against the Arians. (Orationes contra Arianos IV.) > Discourse IV > That the Son is the Co-existing Word, argued from the New Testament. Texts from the Old Testament continued; especially Ps. cx. 3. Besides, the Word in Old Testament may be Son in New, as Spirit in Old Testament is Paraclete in New. Objection from Acts x. 36; answered by parallels, such as 1 Cor. i. 5. Lev. ix. 7. &c. Necessity of the Word's taking flesh, viz. to sanctify, yet without destroying, the flesh.
sources.answer: To renew fallen man unto lasting permanence and raise him to a diviner lot. Since man is the formation of God the Word, the Word took enfeebled man into himself, putting on our first-fruits, and was made one with him so that the titles of the man became the Word's own.
sources.quote: If then after taking him, when enfeebled, into Himself, He renews him again through that sure renewal unto endless permanence, and therefore is made one with him in order to raise him to a diviner lot
sources.raw_question: Why did the Word take human nature and become one with it?

question: If Christ is glorified by taking away our sins, does it follow that the more we sin the more he is glorified, so that obedience is unnecessary?

sources.author: John Owen
sources.work: Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost
sources.section: Part II. Of Communion with the Son Jesus Christ. > Chapter VIII.
sources.answer: No. Owen says the Holy Spirit himself anticipated this objection. In Romans 6:1-3 the apostle raises it against the same doctrine of imputed righteousness taught in Romans 5:18-20, and he answers and rejects it there. Owen also refers back to his earlier argument for the necessity of obedience notwithstanding the imputation of Christ's righteousness.
sources.quote: A man could not suppose that this objection would be made, but that the Holy Ghost, who knows what is in man and his heart, hath made it for them, and in their name, Rom. vi. 1–3.
sources.raw_question: If Christ is glorified by taking away our sins, does it follow that the more we sin the more he is glorified, so that obedience is unnecessary?

question: Does Christ's calling the disciples His 'brethren' mean that the Son, in His Godhead, shares brotherhood and the same rank as men?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book XII > This twelfth book gives a notable interpretation of the words of the Lord to Mary, “Touch Me not, for I am not yet ascended to My Father.”
sources.answer: No. As God, the Only-begotten has no brethren. If He had any, the property of being Only-begotten could not be preserved. Brotherhood with men belongs to the human nature He assumed, which is akin to that of His disciples.
sources.quote: if the Only-begotten has no brethren, (for how, if He had brethren, could the property of being Only-begotten be preserved?)
sources.raw_question: Does Christ's calling the disciples His 'brethren' mean that the Son, in His Godhead, shares brotherhood and the same rank as men?

question: If the faculty of reason is given by God, are the particular names for realities also given by God, or are they invented by humans?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book.
sources.answer: They are invented by humans. Sight is common to all, yet the skilled use of sight comes by training. In the same way, reason is a God-given property of our nature, while the invention of significant terms is the work of men. They use that reason to devise words that make plain what they perceive.
sources.quote: the invention of terms significative of realities is the work of men who, possessing from above the power of reason, are continually finding out, according as they wish for them towards the elucidation of that which they plainly see, certain words expressive of these things.
sources.raw_question: If the faculty of reason is given by God, are the particular names for realities also given by God, or are they invented by humans?

question: How does the Only-begotten restore fallen human nature to life through the Incarnation?

sources.author: Gregory of Nyssa
sources.section: Against Eunomius. > Book V > He shows the falsehood of Eunomius' calumnious charge that the great Basil had said that “man was emptied to become man,” and demonstrates that the “emptying” of the Only-begotten took place with a view to the restoration to life of the Man Who had suffered.
sources.answer: The Only-begotten made all things, human nature among them, and He has full power over them. When that nature fell into evil and death, He drew it back to immortal life by means of the Man in whom He tabernacled, taking humanity in completeness. He mingled His life-giving power with our mortal nature and so changed our deadness into living grace. As "a consuming fire," He destroys the evil in Himself.
sources.quote: He mingled His life-giving power with our mortal and perishable nature, and changed, by the combination with Himself, our deadness to living grace and power.
sources.raw_question: How does the Only-begotten restore fallen human nature to life through the Incarnation?

question: Can the Valentinian aeons Logos (Word) and Sige (Silence) both exist together in the same Pleroma as members of the first Ogdoad?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XII.—The Triacontad of the heretics errs both by defect and excess: Sophia could never have produced anything apart from her consort; Logos and Sige could not have been contemporaries.
sources.answer: No. Speech and silence destroy each other, as light and darkness cannot exist in the same place: where Sige is, Logos cannot be, and where Logos is, Sige cannot be. Saying that the Logos exists only inwardly, unexpressed, does not help, because an inward Logos would still destroy an inward Sige. So the Valentinians must drop one of the two, and with it their first Ogdoad collapses.
sources.quote: But it is impossible that Sige (silence) can exist in the presence of Logos (speech), or again, that Logos can manifest himself in the presence of Sige. For these are mutually destructive of each other, even as light and darkness can by no possibility exist in the same place
sources.raw_question: Can the Valentinian aeons Logos (Word) and Sige (Silence) both exist together in the same Pleroma as members of the first Ogdoad?

question: Can the Valentinians consistently leave Christ, the Holy Spirit, Horos and the Saviour out of the thirty aeons of the Pleroma, even though these were produced in the same way as the others?

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
sources.section: Against Heresies: Book II > Chapter XII.—The Triacontad of the heretics errs both by defect and excess: Sophia could never have produced anything apart from her consort; Logos and Sige could not have been contemporaries.
sources.answer: No. These beings were produced in the same manner as the other aeons, so they should be counted, which gives more than thirty. They cannot be weaker than the other aeons, since they were produced to establish and correct them. Nor can they be superior to the Tetrad that produced them, since the Tetrad is itself counted among the thirty. So the Triacontad fails by excess.
sources.quote: For what just reason can they assign for not reckoning along with the other Æons, either Christ, whom they describe as having, according to the Father’s will, been produced by Monogenes, or the Holy Spirit
